**COMPLETE COURSE OF PATROLOGY, OR UNIVERSAL LIBRARY: COMPLETE, UNIFORM, CONVENIENT, ECONOMICAL, OF ALL THE HOLY FATHERS, DOCTORS, AND ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS WHO FLOURISHED FROM THE APOSTOLIC AGE TO THE TIME OF INNOCENT III; A CHRONOLOGICAL REPRINTING OF ALL THE MONUMENTS OF CATHOLIC TRADITION WHICH HAVE SURVIVED THROUGH THE FIRST TWELVE CENTURIES OF THE CHURCH, ACCORDING TO THE MOST ACCURATE EDITIONS, COMPARED WITH ONE ANOTHER AND WITH CERTAIN MANUSCRIPT CODICES, AND CORRECTED WITH THE UTMOST CARE; CONTINUALLY ILLUSTRATED WITH DISSERTATIONS, COMMENTARIES, AND VARIANT READINGS; ENLARGED WITH ALL WORKS DISCOVERED AFTER THE MOST EXTENSIVE EDITIONS COMPLETED DURING THE LAST THREE CENTURIES; FURNISHED WITH SPECIAL ANALYTICAL INDEXES FOLLOWING INDIVIDUAL VOLUMES OR AUTHORS OF SOME IMPORTANCE; PROVIDED WITH CHAPTERS PROPERLY ARRANGED WITHIN THE TEXT ITSELF, AND WITH HEADINGS DISTINGUISHING THE UPPER MARGIN OF EACH PAGE AND INDICATING THE SUBJECT MATTER TREATED; EXPANDED WITH WORKS BOTH DUBIOUS AND APOCRYPHAL, PROVIDED THEY POSSESS SOME AUTHORITY IN RELATION TO ECCLESIASTICAL TRADITION; ENRICHED WITH TWO GENERAL INDEXES: ONE, NAMELY, OF SUBJECTS, BY CONSULTING WHICH WHATEVER EACH of the Fathers has written upon any topic may be seen at a glance; THE OTHER, OF HOLY SCRIPTURE, FROM WHICH THE READER MAY READILY DISCOVER WHICH FATHERS HAVE COMMENTED UPON INDIVIDUAL TEXTS OF THE INDIVIDUAL BOOKS OF SCRIPTURE, AND IN WHAT PLACES IN THEIR WORKS. A MOST ACCURATE EDITION, EASILY TO BE PREFERRED TO ALL OTHERS IF THE FOLLOWING ARE WEIGHED: THE CLARITY OF THE TYPE, THE QUALITY OF THE PAPER, THE INTEGRITY OF THE TEXT, THE THOROUGHNESS OF THE CORRECTION, BOTH THE VARIETY AND THE NUMBER OF THE REPRINTED WORKS, THE VERY CONVENIENT FORMAT OF THE VOLUMES, CONSTANTLY UNIFORM THROUGHOUT THE COURSE OF THE WHOLE WORK, THE LOW PRICE, AND, ABOVE ALL, THIS SINGLE METHODICAL AND CHRONOLOGICAL COLLECTION OF SIX HUNDRED FRAGMENTS AND LITTLE WORKS HITHERTO SCATTERED HERE AND THERE, BUT NOW FOR THE FIRST TIME ASSEMBLED IN OUR LIBRARY FROM WORKS BELONGING TO EVERY AGE, PLACE, LANGUAGE, AND FORM.**

## In the Year of the Lord 1203: Absalon, Abbot of Springiersbach

[Col. 0009]

### Notice

(Oudin, *Commentaries on Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. II, p. 1173)

Absalon, abbot of Springiersbach, of the Order of the Regular Canons of St Augustine, in the archbishopric of Trier, was first a regular canon in the abbey of St Victor at Paris. Thence he was summoned to govern the aforesaid abbey, and flourished about the year 1210, according to Caesarius of Heisterbach, who in his work *On the Miracles of His Times* cites him as either his contemporary or a man close to him in age. He wrote learned and elegant sermons, which Daniel Schilling, abbot of the same church of Springiersbach, caused to be printed in folio at Cologne in 1534 under this title: *Fifty Festival Sermons of Absalon, Abbot of Springiersbach*. Some of them Peter de Alva y Astorga subsequently caused to be reprinted in his *Mariale*, where he discusses this printing.

[Note: [Col. 0009] Reprinted later, in 1605, at Milan, in quarto, under this title: *Sermons on the Principal Solemnities of Christian Worship, by Lord Absalon, Abbot of Springiersbach, Regular Canon, published almost five hundred years ago and now newly corrected, enlarged with scholia and indexes for the benefit of the Reverend Father and Lord Celsus Dugnani, General Abbot of the Canons Regular of the Saviour of the Lateran, through the work of Lord Basil Serenius, canon of the same congregation, Milanese priest, preacher of the word of God.*]

There was, however, at the same time another Absalon, abbot of St Victor at Paris—

[Note: [Col. 0009]

Dom Brial judges that the two Absalons—namely, the Victorine and the Springiersbach Absalon—must be regarded as one and the same person, because of the identity of name, the agreement of the periods in which they are said to have flourished, the profession of both among the Victorines, and, finally, the writings attributed to each alike; see *Histoire littéraire de la France*, vol. XVI, p. 452. He relies upon the testimony of Caesarius of Heisterbach, a contemporary author, whose words are these:

> “Master Absalon, an honourable and learned man, a canon in the church of St Victor at Paris, was elected abbot some years ago at Springiersbach. This monastery lies in the diocese of Trier. Before this same Absalon came to the place of his election, one of the brothers saw in a vision of the night a burning candle entering the aforesaid monastery; by its light it rekindled all the extinguished candles which the brethren held in their hands. The interpretation of the vision was that there would come one who would restore relaxed discipline. Having become abbot, he introduced the honourable customs which he had learned in his own monastery, commanding among other things that all the brothers of his congregation, the subject sisters, and their provosts should abstain from meat.”

Therefore, after reforming the monastery of Springiersbach, Absalon was recalled to Paris and, in 1198, received the mitre of abbot of St Victor, after Abbot Bernard died on 28 May of that year. He died in that monastery of St Victor five years later, that is, on 17 September 1203. If, then, he acted as abbot of Springiersbach—which is granted—he certainly did so before 1198; for in a manuscript codex of the library of St Victor his epitaph is read in these words:

> Here Absalon received a pleasant end,  
> Snatched to the serene throne by everlasting light;  
> An illustrious elder, to whom the world’s glory was cheap,  
> He was the seventh shepherd of this fold from the first.

This is the judgment of a most learned man, though based somewhat on conjecture. — Editor.]

—who died in 1203, on 17 September. Under his name, according to the old catalogue of the library of St Victor, compiled in 1513, there survive thirty-four sermons *On Various Subjects* in the library of St Victor, shelf-mark JJ. 10. The first, on the Ascension of the Lord, begins with these words: “You set the cloud as your ascent, O Lord, you who walk upon the wings of the winds. The words which you have heard, most beloved brethren, provide us with abundant matter for joy,” etc.

But I have very great doubts—indeed, I now know—that these sermons are among the fifty printed under the name of Absalon, Abbot of Springiersbach, since he had been a canon of this abbey of St Victor at Paris. Secondly, this ancient codex is anonymous: Absalon’s name was added only in 1513, when the first catalogue of the library of St Victor was compiled. Finally, all the same sermons occur word for word among the manuscripts of the sermons of John, abbot of St Victor, who succeeded Absalon in the prelacy, in the library of St Victor, shelf-mark JJ. 13, fol. 29 through fol. 261. There the ancient title bears John’s name and is contemporary with the manuscript writing of the codex.

Yet these thirty-four sermons in no way appear to belong either to Absalon, abbot of St Victor at Paris, or to John the Victorine, likewise abbot, although the manuscript codex of which we shall speak presently supports that attribution. They certainly belong to Absalon, abbot of Springiersbach. For I also saw in the Victorine library a third manuscript codex in which these sermons bear the following heading: “Sermons of the venerable Absalon, regular canon at St Victor outside the walls of Paris, and afterwards abbot in Germany.” These remarks are made as a precaution against the varying headings of the Victorine manuscripts.

On him Aubertus Miraeus writes in his *Supplement to On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 337, p. 242, where he wrongly places him in the year 1120, when he had not yet been born; Antonio Possevino speaks of him very briefly in vol. I of the *Apparatus sacer*, p. 3. John of Toulouse, in the manuscript *Antiquities of the Abbey of St Victor*, book V, chapter 20, is mistaken in attributing the sermons of Absalon, abbot of Springiersbach, to Absalon, abbot of St Victor at Paris, who lived at the same time. Charles du Fresne, Sieur du Cange, makes the same mistake concerning the date of Absalon as Aubertus Miraeus in the *Index of Writers* prefixed to his *Glossary of Medieval and Late Latin*, col. 79.

[Col. 0011]

## Festival Sermons of Lord Absalon, Abbot of Springiersbach, Especially Useful and Learned

Now newly published through the care of Lord Daniel Schillinck, abbot of the same monastery.

(Cologne, Johann Gymnich, July 1534, with an imperial privilege for four years, small folio. — We publish from the copy preserved in the public library at Douai, from the holdings of Anchin Abbey, which Mr Duthilloeul, keeper of that library, very kindly shared with us.)

### Johann Gymnich, Printer, Sends Greetings to the Reverend Father in Christ, Lord Daniel Schillinck, Most Worthy Abbot of the Illustrious Monastery of Springiersbach

If ancient paganism was so grateful and generous, Reverend Father, that it bestowed divine honours in part upon those who first revealed to mortals the use and potency of gems, crops, or certain herbs, and in part secured for them an undying glory by consecrating their memory to posterity, what ought Christians to do for you, since you have communicated to the world through printing this writer, incomparable though known to very few, from the darkness of your library, where he lay buried in neglect and decay?

Certainly, I should judge that you have laid those who are truly devoted to sacred theology under a proportionately greater obligation, as the goods of the mind excel bodily advantages, and as things perishable and destined shortly to destruction, however splendid they may be, yield to immortal things which are never exposed to the injury of devouring antiquity.

Nor, in your great and singular zeal to benefit your neighbour, were you content simply to hand this author over to me for printing out of the densest darkness. You also promised to make money available to me, so that I might more readily undertake the work both of correcting and printing him, lest I might perhaps be deterred from printing him both by the obscurity of the author and by the difficulty of the exemplar, arising from the minuteness of the characters and the manner of the writing: it consisted, as it were, of an intricate Gordian knot made up of countless abbreviations and tangled letters.

Roused by this trumpet-call of yours, although I was by no means reluctant to undertake this assignment—for after reading one or two pages of the book more attentively, recognizing the lion, as the saying goes, from his claws, I could see that my labour here would be worthwhile—I was nevertheless so encouraged in spirit that, undeterred by any consideration of the expense or labour to be borne, I determined to undertake this task, both to oblige you and to serve students of ancient authors.

I thought it should be done chiefly for two reasons. The first was that the world might have proof that even in our own age there are abbots in whom we see, to their eminent credit, the very thing occurring which Marcus Antoninus, the emperor surnamed “the Philosopher,” recorded of himself in writing. He wrote of himself as follows:

> “Some love horses, others birds, others wild beasts; but from childhood a strong desire for the acquisition of books has been implanted in me.”

If I proceeded here to proclaim with great pomp of words what a devourer of books, and especially of sacred books, you are, I greatly fear that I should incur the appearance of flattery. But I cannot pass over in silence this one point: if nearly all abbots followed your example and, instead of warhorses, hunting, fowling, gambling, feasting, and things of that kind, applied their minds to the day-and-night study of orthodox writers of the Church, it would soon come about that they would free themselves, if not from every part, at least from a good part, of the ill will under which they suffer not merely among the common people:

> “But these things lie on the knees of the gods.”

The second reason that led me to print this writer was that it is not only our duty diligently to rescue authors of better reputation from the injury of oblivion [Col. 0013] [lacuna]

[Note: [Col. 0013] Here the leaf is mutilated in the exemplar.]

whoever even briefly turns over our book, I do not doubt, will enroll Absalon with us in their number: so abundantly does he display learned piety and pious learning alike. For besides explaining the divine mysteries devoutly and clearly, treating allegories and comparisons with great success, frequently and aptly citing testimonies of Scripture, excellently exhorting us to make our life correspond to our profession, and sharply assailing—with great severity—the wicked and those who abuse God’s benefits, he also employs such a manner of expression as might appear capable of satisfying even this most learned age.

Unless there are some who will be so captious and fastidious that, because of one or two little words which they do not judge to have been polished in Cicero’s workshop, they will not hesitate to disparage a book which is sound throughout. I hope easily to blunt such persons with this couplet of Martial:

> There are thirty bad epigrams in the whole book;  
> If there are as many good ones, Lausus, the book is good.

Indeed, I would have them reflect, with Cicero himself as witness, that in every matter the selection of bad things in preference to better things gone by is blameworthy and to be condemned.

Now, if antiquity commends writers just as it does wines, I am confident that Absalon will not lack the favour of such commendation; for he flourished four hundred years ago, at a time when genuine theology had not yet wholly deserted the purity of Roman speech for the camp of barbarism and sophistical disputations—a fact to which the very rich style of our author bears ample witness.

Since this was so, Reverend Father, I did not at all decline the labours of correcting and printing this your Absalon. And although I trust that his piety and learning will sufficiently commend him and defend him against the petulance of Momuses, nevertheless, because it is known that even the greatest authors, sacred as well as secular, do not go safely enough into public without some protecting patron, I thought that Absalon too ought to be fortified by a like defence.

Nor was it necessary to seek far for one to whom this responsibility might be entrusted, since I know that your paternity, in view of your goodwill toward this writer, will readily undertake it, and, in view of your authority, will have no difficulty carrying it out. Therefore, honoured Father, receive as dedicated to you both our labours, such as they are, and Absalon himself; undertake to defend him from slanders and malicious accusations by the authority of your name.

But let this not escape you: there are still a few passages in these sermons which do not seem free from corruption and which require the aid of a better exemplar in order to restore the work to its integrity. We considered it a matter of conscience rashly to alter anything. Farewell; and allow your Absalon to be a happy beginning of friendship between us. Cologne, from our workshop, on the Ides of July, in the year 1534.

## Sermons of Absalon, Abbot

[Col. 0013]

### Sermon One: On the Advent of the Lord

[Col. 0013A]

Today, most beloved brethren, an elegant discourse, full of devotion, ought sweetly to murmur in your hearts, extolling the Advent of the Saviour with worthy praise. But the person of the speaker restrains you from this expectation, for neither abundance of understanding nor any appearance of holiness commends him.

Nevertheless, because the solemnity of the season affords us a common subject of joy, though uncircumcised in speech and understanding, I shall yet meet the Lord who comes with such proclamation as I can offer, and shall intrude myself, though unwelcome, upon your rejoicing, to whom in a special manner the presence of the Saviour has been granted. And who could restrain the bridegroom’s children from joyful affection while the bridegroom remains with them? (Matt. 9.)

Behold, [Col. 0013B] Christ invites you to joy. Solomon advances adorned with the diadem with which his mother crowned him; Joseph has been clothed in a long robe; and David celebrates a feast-day for you upon the harp. David, I say—Christ made man—plays upon the harp of the humanity which he assumed, concerning which it is written: “Awake, my glory; awake, psaltery and harp” (Ps. 56). By this harp he pours into our hearts a threefold sound: humble, sweet, and joyful.

The cries of infancy, a mother’s embraces, the touching of breasts, the rattles of a new-born child, and other such things which the majesty of the Word deigned to take upon himself, seem to belong to the humble sound. [Col. 0014A] Yet this harp gave forth an even humbler sound, so humble that not even the disciples could comprehend it, when Jewish faithlessness struck it, opening his hands and feet with nails and his side with a lance. Finally, hanging upon the cross, it rendered that mournful sound: “Into your hands, O Lord, I commend my spirit” (Ps. 30; Luke 23).

Of this sound the prophet says in the person of the Saviour: “I am weary with crying; my throat has become hoarse; my eyes have failed while I hope in my God” (Ps. 68). “My throat has become hoarse,” he says: that is, my words have been regarded as useless [Col. 0014B]—so much so that even my eyes, that is, my disciples, have failed while I hope in my God.

The sweet sound was the novelty of miracles and the working of healings, when he healed the sick and freed all who were oppressed by the devil. But still sweeter was the voice of his preaching, by which he inscribed the law of life upon the hearts of the children of men, teaching them how to live—those, I mean, who, entangled in the monstrosity of their crimes, did not know how to live, but rather how to confound life.

The joyful [Col. 0015A] sound truly began in the resurrection, but will be consummated in the future, when the children of adoption hear the voice of the Son of God saying: “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matt. 25).

All the righteous who awaited the redemption of Israel wished to hear the sound of this harp. Hence the prophet Daniel counts the years and months until the time when transgression is brought to an end, iniquity is wiped out, everlasting righteousness comes, and the Holy of Holies is anointed (Dan. 9). Balaam too consoles himself in the hope of Christ’s birth, saying: “I shall see him, but not now; I shall behold him, but not near: a star shall arise out of Jacob, and a rod shall rise from Israel” (Num. 24). And Isaiah, beside himself with excessive longing, speaks to the Son: “Would that you would rend the heavens and come down” (Isa. [Col. 0015B] 64). David likewise, broken by long expectation, raises the voice of his cry to heaven: “Send forth your hand from on high” (Ps. 143), that is, your Son from the bosom of your fatherhood.

And behold, the desires of the prophets have been fulfilled; the highest joy has been given to us, to whom Christ has come—or rather, to speak more truly, he came for our sake: for our sake, I say, that he might heal our wounds and take away sin, himself made the price of redemption and a sacrifice for sin.

But consider, O man, in what condition he found you, enslaved to so harsh a servitude, so ungrateful for benefits received; and you will scarcely be able to marvel enough that a thing so worthless and abject deserved such and so great a redeemer. For who, considering your faithlessness, would judge you even worthy of pardon? [Col. 0015C] You cast off your Lord, subjected yourself to another’s slavery, threw yourself down into voluntary misery, and rejected the benefits conferred upon you.

For your redeemer, wishing you to live in happiness, had set before you three goods:

First, the innocence of your created state. Second, a place of delight. Third, the blessedness of eternity.

He had granted the first two in actual possession, lest you should depart from your God through want of anything. But he had granted the third in hope, so that by the greatness of the promised thing you might adhere to him more steadfastly.

But behold: “Adam, where are you?” “Lord,” he says, “I heard your voice and hid myself, because I was naked” (Gen. 2). Truly naked: that is, stripped of that garment of innocence, you plunged yourself into such dregs of iniquity that you can scarcely remember how generous [Col. 0015D] the liberality of your Creator had been toward you.

The place of delight likewise was changed into exile. The daily calamities bear witness to this: namely, distresses of mind, infirmities of body, dangers outside, pestilences falling upon us from above, the loss of immortality, and finally the expectation of death. After all these things, the very blessedness promised was about to be changed into punishment, had not mercy and truth met together, and righteousness and peace kissed one another, as the time of propitiation drew near (Ps. 84).

For at Christ’s birth, when truth appeared according to God’s promise, mercy followed in the liberation of the sinner; and thus righteousness and peace kissed one another, when man, justified by God’s grace, [Col. 0016A] was reconciled to God after the wall of enmity between himself and God had been removed (Eph. 2).

Therefore, when our redeemer came to heal our infirmities, he brought with him three remedies: an ointment, a cautery, and an antidote. For the one Word was like an ointment laid upon the wound of our mortality.

Consider the maker of this ointment, consider its workshop, consider its material. Its maker was the Holy Spirit; its workshop, the blessed Mother of God; its material, the flower of assumed nature and the richness of divinity. Does it not seem to you that this maker descended into this workshop when the angel said to Mary: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (Luke 1)?

[Col. 0016B] There this maker compounded this ointment, when the Son of God assumed everything that belonged to man and the fullness of divinity bodily poured itself into the assumed nature. I wonder whether you too do not marvel at these three things in this ointment: its fragrance, sweetness, and fluidity.

Men of the natural law were refreshed by the fragrance of this ointment, because, though still far off from Christ who was to be born, they awaited him in the devotion of faith alone, as it were by a fragrance arriving from afar. Men of the written law were delighted by the sweetness of this ointment: standing, as it were, on the threshold of Christ’s birth, they had received the sweetness of promise in the Law and the Prophets, and in sacrifices prefiguring Christ they understood the spiritual sweetness of the thing signified. Men of grace were healed by the fluidity [Col. 0016C] of this ointment, since Christ was not only presented to them bodily, but they were also beneficially drenched by the sacraments which flowed from his side—by baptism for sanctification and by the others for strengthening.

This is the ointment which the sinful woman, having kept it in an alabaster vessel, poured upon the head of Jesus as he reclined, and the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment (Matt. 26). The ointment stored in the alabaster vessel was the Word united to flesh. But when the alabaster was broken—that is, when Christ’s humanity was consummated through the Passion—the sinful woman poured the ointment upon Jesus’ head, when the Church, formerly defiled by the filth of sins but cleansed in Christ’s blood, offered to God the Father faith in the incarnate Word. For the head of Christ is God, as [Col. 0016D] the Apostle says (1 Cor. 2). The house of the Church was filled with the fragrance of the ointment when Christ, who is God, distributed the gifts of grace among the children of the Church.

This ointment was necessary above all things; without it neither could our wounds be healed nor the offence of the first transgression be expiated. For the nature of the disease that came upon us through the first man (Gen. 2) appears unable to have admitted any other way of healing than through the Incarnation of the Word. For if a comparison is made between the fault and the satisfaction due for it, someone will judge it fitting that, just as man was exalted in pride even to God—for he wished to be like God—so, in a satisfaction proportionate to the crime, God should be humbled even to man.

[Col. 0017A] He who perhaps could not redeem otherwise, nevertheless could have delivered otherwise, so that by his command alone, or in whatever way he wished, he might remove captivity and drive back the invader. For another mode was possible to God, as it is written (Matt. 19); but that possibility looks rather to the power of the deliverer than to the equity of redemption. Thus in redemption understand both the just satisfaction for sin and the price of captivity. For to redeem is to give, in an equivalent valuation, a price for a thing alienated.

There are two further remedies which our redeemer has provided for us: namely, a cautery and an antidote. The cautery, by which harmful things are cut away, is the bitterness of tribulations. The antidote given against poisons is that singular remedy for vices, the virtue of humility. [Col. 0017B] He set these two before us as a pattern of life, because it was not enough to restore freedom unless it were preserved through holiness of life; nor is there any other return to the fatherland except in humble conduct and patient endurance of tribulations.

But we see many who embrace the incarnate Word in faith, yet refuse to imitate the pattern of his life. If you show them the places of the nails, if they put their hands into his side, they say with Thomas, “My Lord and my God” (John 20); but if you invite them to sufferings and humility, they say to the Lord God, “Depart from us; we do not desire knowledge of your ways” (Wisdom 3). Very many prove this who pursue riches and honours, or rather learning than conscience—not in order to be regarded as lowly and humble, but rather lest they be so regarded [Col. 0017C]: so that they may seem honoured in the world and make for themselves a name alongside the name of the great who are on the earth.

Proofs of this are countless labours, journeys across lands, attendance upon princes, studies prolonged at length, and other such things in which people consume their days. But suppose that everything answers to your wish: you are rich in wealth, distinguished in learning, endowed with honours. I ask, in all these things, what do you finally wish to attain—salvation, or eminence? Yet salvation is sought better through poverty than through riches, through subjection than through prominence; and Augustine’s saying is true, that the unlearned frequently seize heaven, while those weighing the words of the law together with their letters descend into hell [Col. 0017D].

Perhaps you wish to appear lofty and great; but in all your labour under the sun you cannot attain this, because you will always see persons better and loftier than yourself. By comparison with them you will be accounted as a dwarf among giants, and will seem to have spent your days in vain—though no loss is heavier than that of time. Why, unhappy soul, do you pursue empty air, steaming smoke? If you grasp it, your garment will be stained, your palate bitter, your eye dim-sighted. For by what is the garment of holy conduct more stained than by useless labour, when a person expends his whole endeavour upon riches and honours but nothing upon virtue? Or by what is the palate of reason more embittered than by the pleasures of life, when nothing tastes good to reason except what the love of the world seasons [Col. 0018A]? The eye of charity likewise becomes dim when the affection of love, which ought to contemplate God, is covered over by a certain thick cloud of avarice and covetousness.

Such a class of people is rightly compared to those mockers of Elisha, who, while he was ascending to the house of the Lord, mocked his baldness, and were therefore handed over to bears to be devoured (4 Kings 2). Elisha’s baldness, indeed, is the bitterness of tribulations, the poverty and humility of the Saviour; this the boys—that is, the foolish lovers of this world—mock, either when they do so in fact or when they refuse to imitate it. Therefore they too are handed over to bears, that is, demons, to be devoured, so that amid punishments they may acknowledge as powerful the one whom they despised on earth as humble. They are truly mockers, not imitators.

For, unless I am mistaken, they would mock Peter’s nets, Paul’s tent-making, John the Baptist’s leather belt, Elijah’s ash-baked bread, Martin’s nakedness; indeed, they would count even the Saviour’s little donkey madness [Col. 0018B]. Oh, if a familiar example did not fail us, and if we, who have become poor in possessions, were also poor in spirit, and if the performance of the work bore witness to what our profession has undertaken. Yet often the potter’s vessels, upon which he applies greater diligence, turn out for dishonour, while those upon which less care is expended become vessels for honour and for better uses.

Thus, if shrubs planted in desert places have moisture at their roots, and if their small branches attain freedom of air and warmth, they will at length produce from themselves a beautiful tree, branches, poles, dense leaves, budding flowers, and useful fruit [Col. 0018C]. Conversely, if you plant a young tree in pleasant and green places, drench it with bitterness, prick it with thorns when you ought to apply a basket of manure, hold its emerging shoots bent down into the earth, and confine them on every side with stakes so that they cannot rise into the freedom of the air, I judge that, when this plant has grown strong, it will produce a shapeless trunk, twisted branches, sparse leaves, imperfect flowers, and tasteless fruit, less pleasant to eat.

Have you not read that the Lord chose not a people because of a place, but a place because of a people? (2 Maccabees 5.) Certainly, woman was made in Paradise and man outside Paradise; yet woman sinned sooner and more grievously than man. Likewise the proud Pharisee sinned more in the Temple than Matthew the tax collector in the customs-house [Col. 0018D]; and Judas more at the Lord’s supper than the dancing girl at Herod’s banquet. Why is this? For occasions of danger are customarily attached to necessary things, and, through intervening causes, events contrary to what is good in itself arise from those good things.

Thus, when the sea is calm and favourable winds blow, sailors raise the mast and yards, spread the sails, and make ready everything else by which they may more easily reach harbour. But when contrary winds rush upon them, the sails themselves and the other equipment of the ship, which ought to have led them to harbour, become the cause of shipwreck unless the foresight of the helmsman carefully guards against it. In the same way those who enter the ship of the monastery take with them the equipment of their own guidance [Col. 0019A]: namely, a mean garment, scanty food, contempt for the world, a form of poverty, and the other observances of discipline, by which they may more easily reach the harbour of salvation. But when memory of their former way of life returns, they sometimes begin to love the world, desire pleasures, seek honours, and despise poverty. And, fearing to be seen poor and despised with Christ, they likewise reject with Christ—the leader of the way—the way of humility.

Thus Porphyry, that most hostile persecutor of Christians, having heard of Christ’s virtues, asked his familiar demon whether Christ was good and worthy of imitation. The demon replied: “Christ indeed is good, but all who follow him are miserable.” That impious man, unwilling to endure miseries, then began from that hour [Col. 0019B] to detest him and to swear that he did not know the man. The judgment of that liar is undoubtedly true, because, as the Apostle testifies, all who wish to live devoutly in Christ suffer persecutions (2 Tim. 3). What then: do you wish to be a Porphyrian and abound in every good thing, or a Christian and be subject to miseries? It is better to endure miseries and afflictions with Christ for a time, because this sorrow shall be turned into joy—and into such joy as no one shall take from you (John 16). I say this provided that you are a willing participant in tribulations.

Who, when hungry and with fish set before him, has eaten a scorpion? Who, possessing harbour, has sought shipwreck? I would certainly call it sought shipwreck if someone who, by the habit of holy conduct [Col. 0019C], has put on Christ’s image and has, as it were, entered with one foot into the joy of his Lord, looks back and wishes to become entangled in the pleasures of life and worldly cares. In religious persons, however, such things seem deliberately sought, because they can easily avoid them; for their state, habit, and profession oppose them, and a sufficient administration of temporal goods excludes every necessity of seeking such things.

Therefore consider the other kinds of evils: those committed through weakness, and, conversely, those committed through deliberation. You will see that deliberate evils—that is, those committed by deliberation—reach the height of evils. For evils committed by surprise are lighter for this reason: under the sudden pressure of an emotional impulse, they forestall the judgment of reason—for example, if in a movement of anger I call my brother *racha* or “fool.” Therefore the devil himself, the instigator of evil, is compared to a bird because of the swiftness of this suggestion in such temptation, as in: “They gave the corpses of your servants as food to the birds of heaven” (Ps. 88 [89]) [Col. 0019D].

Those things also which are done through lack of discernment are in some measure excused because they deceive the judgment of reason: they seem good but are not—for instance, if someone wishes to fast while others eat, or chant psalms while others sleep, and the like. Therefore, because of the deceitfulness of the suggestion, in such cases the devil is compared to a fox, as in: “Catch for us the little foxes which destroy my vineyard” (Song 2). Likewise, in those things done through weakness there is some mitigation of blame [Col. 0020A], because the temptation is so violent that strength to resist is lacking—for example, in Esau’s dish of lentils (Gen. 25), and in the temptation of that foolish woman who, seizing Joseph’s cloak, said, “Sleep with me” (Gen. 39). For the greater the violence of temptation, the less the will to sin; and conversely, the less the violence of temptation, the greater the will to sin. Because of the violence of temptation, the instigator of evil is compared to a boar, as in: “The boar from the forest has laid it waste, and the wild beast has fed upon it” (Ps. 79 [80]).

Therefore, one who has assumed poverty and humility and put on the image of Christ—what will he say if he stamps the king’s coin with the image of Herod? This judgment belongs not to a servant but to an emperor. One counsel alone remains: to reform in ourselves Christ’s image and restore the king’s coin, so that, when he comes to settle accounts with his servants, he may demand it with interest [Col. 0020B]. Let tears of repentance, works of mercy, and purity of life go before the terrible Judge, so that they may blunt the edge of that turning sword while the striking hand is held back. For who would not fear that incurable blow, where the material is fragile, the sword penetrating, and the striker powerful?

Let prayers and tears therefore obtain that the sword of eternal damnation may be changed into a rod of correction, which may so correct the brethren in the present that in the future it makes them heirs of that inheritance which Jesus Christ our Lord has kept incorruptible and undefiled in heaven for his saints [Col. 0020C], whose kingdom and dominion remain for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON II. ON THE ADVENT OF THE LORD

“The sun stood still in the midst of heaven, and did not hasten to set for the space of one day” (Joshua 10). And if we recall to memory the ancient wonders—namely, the mighty deeds God performed in Egypt, the marvels he wrought in the land of Ham, the terrible things he displayed in the Red Sea (Ps. 105 [106])—yet we see greater marvels in the present time. For behold, according to Jeremiah’s prophecy, “The Lord has made a new thing upon the earth” (Jer. 3). What new thing? A wondrous and unheard-of thing: a solstice took place in the Virgin.

I do not now speak [Col. 0020D] of the natural solstice, when this visible sun, in its returning course, turns away from us or turns toward us; nor of that miraculous solstice which occurred at Gibeon, where, while the children of Israel fought and the sun stood fixed in the midst of heaven, the day was doubled so that they might gain victory over their enemies. Rather, I speak of that ineffable solstice when the Son of God, the boundless and incomprehensible sun of righteousness, in some manner made himself comprehensible; and, with the majesty of his divinity as though gathered into a single globe, poured himself bodily into the Virgin’s womb.

The first, then, is a natural solstice; the second, a miraculous one. But that which took place in the Virgin is a solstice of salvation. Perhaps I may fittingly call the incarnation of the Word a solstice. For just as this visible sun is said [Col. 0021A] to make a solstice when, being placed near us, it cannot come any closer to us, so the Son of God, the sun of righteousness, made a solstice when, by assuming our nature, he joined it to himself so completely that, once God and man had been united, he could not draw nearer to it. For how could he draw nearer, he who made God man and man God?

This union of God and man, therefore, is signified for us by the saying of Joshua which I set forth: “The sun stood still in the midst of heaven,” etc. Since the name “heaven” is understood in many ways in Sacred Scripture, in this place it is understood as the present Church, by this comparison: just as the ethereal heaven shines and is adorned by the diverse ordering of planets and stars, so the present Church is adorned and shines through the diverse virtues and merits of the saints [Col. 0021B]. Hence in the Apocalypse the present Church is designated by the name “heaven,” and holy men by the name “stars,” when it is said of that ancient serpent, namely the devil, that “with his tail he drew a third part of the stars of heaven down to earth” (Rev. 12). And elsewhere: “There was silence in heaven for about half an hour” (Rev. 8)—in heaven, that is, in the present Church. For because the silence of contemplation cannot be maintained in it for a full hour—that is, continuously—on account of the various temptations which impede the soul’s repose, it is said: “There was silence in heaven for about half an hour”; because, even if not always, nevertheless holy Church is sometimes raised upward through heavenly longing.

The middle of this heaven was the Blessed Virgin Mary [Col. 0021C], who, established as a kind of middle boundary between law and grace, conceived within herself the sun of righteousness, namely the Son of God, so that he might send forth the rays of his knowledge to each people, that is, Jews and Gentiles. Thus the sun is Christ; heaven, the present Church; the middle of heaven, the Blessed Virgin Mary; the solstice, the incarnate Word.

We can identify two solstitial signs of this sun of righteousness. The first is Eve; the second, the Blessed Virgin Mary. Eve the sinner, through whom death entered the world and who was the gate of destruction, was the sign of the winter solstice, because through her, as the night of sin was prolonged, the sun of righteousness withdrew farther from us. The Blessed Virgin Mary was the sign of the summer solstice, because in her, through a kind of renewed warmth [Col. 0021D] of grace, the sun of righteousness drew near to us.

Between these two signs, namely Eve and the Blessed Virgin Mary, the sun of righteousness of whom we have spoken gradually poured forth the rays of his knowledge throughout this world’s course: to some through inspiration, to others through visions, to others through created things placed before them, and to still others by other means, he willed to make himself known, until one born of a Virgin “was seen upon the earth and conversed with men” (Baruch 3).

“The sun therefore stood still in the midst of heaven.” But what is meant by what follows: “And it did not hasten to set for the space of one day”? Though this refers literally to the history just mentioned, in which at Gibeon, while the sun stood fixed in heaven, the space of one day was increased for the children of Israel as they defeated their enemies, yet mystically it concerns the human race, which was attacked by spiritual enemies now violently, now deceitfully, now secretly, now openly [Col. 0022A].

Its first enemy was the inclination of a corrupt conscience. The second was the vanity of worldly glory. The third, fear of death. The fourth, despair of salvation. The fifth, spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places. The sixth, hell gaping beneath. The first enemy acted to remove purity of heart. The second, to prevent our aspiring toward the homeland. The third threatened the punishment of torment. The fourth denied hope of mercy. The fifth acted to separate us from God. The sixth, to imprison us as captives. Who could defeat such strong adversaries in one day? Therefore the span of one day was increased, so that through a prolongation of time victory might come more readily [Col. 0022B].

The span of the first day was the time of the Law; the span of the second day was the time of grace, or of the new Law. For the Law was a day which, driving away the darkness of ignorance, taught the worship of the one God, showing what we owed to God and to neighbour, what punishment was laid up for sins, and what reward for virtues. But this day was not sufficient for defeating spiritual enemies, because the Law had a commanding voice but not assisting grace. Hence the Apostle says: “The law brought no one to perfection” (Heb. 7). And elsewhere: “If righteousness is through the law, then Christ died in vain” (Gal. 2).

Concerning the Jews, moreover, it is said in the psalm: “The sons of Ephraim, bending and shooting the bow, turned back in the day of battle” (Ps. 77 [78]) [Col. 0022C]. As if to say: the sons of Ephraim—that is, the Jews themselves, a part being taken for the whole—bending and shooting the bow, that is, making a certain preparation for spiritual battle against vices, saying, “All that the Lord commands us, we shall do”: these same persons turned back in the day of battle, that is, turned away in the time of temptation.

Thus long ago Elisha’s staff could not raise the woman’s dead son, until, at Elisha’s arrival, the boy’s flesh was warmed and received the vital spirit (4 Kings 4). Elisha’s staff—that is, the Law established by God for the correction of transgressors—could not give life to the human race dead in sins, until, at the coming of Elisha, that is, Jesus Christ the mediator of God and men, it was kindled by assisting grace and returned to the way of salvation [Col. 0022D].

Therefore, since the first day was insufficient for victory over enemies, the length of the day was doubled when grace was added to the Law, so that through Jesus Christ, mediator of God and men, we might conquer the enemies of the human race—that is, sins together with their author, the devil. Behold, beloved brethren: now Elisha has come; now Christ made human stands with us in the battle-line. “If God is for us, who is against us?” Therefore, faithful and devoted soul, fight the battles of your God bravely. There is now nothing for you to fear or dread. For he has not come to this battle alone; rather, he stands accompanied by a great host.

For around his bed—that is, the mystery of the Incarnation—stand sixty mighty men, from among the strongest of Israel [Col. 0023A], all holding swords and most skilled in war (Song 3): namely, the prophets, who foretold that he would come; the apostles and martyrs, who bore testimony to him by the constancy of their suffering; others brilliant through miracles, others renowned through preaching—all holding “the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. 8 [probably 6:17]).

Consider, soul worthy of God, with what arms your king is clothed, so that you too may be clothed in like manner. Do you wish to see with which? Behold, he stands clothed in the sackcloth of our flesh: humble, patient, despised, gentle, full of sorrows, poor, a stranger. Therefore put on the king’s armour if you wish to be enrolled under the name of soldier. Be patient in injuries, humble in obedience, secure in adversity, moderate in prosperity; joyful in poverty, gentle in conduct [Col. 0023B], strict in abstinence, fervent in charity. For such is your beloved, and he is your friend.

Let not these weaknesses of your God be an occasion of stumbling for you; they ought to be a cause of salvation. Thus it happened long ago with those impious persons who, despising his mortal condition, spat in his face, pierced him with spears, and cried out: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19). Rather, adore him made human; embrace him in weakness; have compassion for him in his patience and despised state; devote works of kindness to him in his poverty and need. For he assumed all these things for you, not for himself. For you he came to this battle; indeed, for you he fell in this battle. Why did he fall? Because it had been so ordained by the divine oracle: that the army whose leader fell in the first battle should conquer.

Nevertheless, as Scripture says, “He did not hasten to set for the space of one day” [Col. 0023C]: he did not undergo the punishment of death until he had completed the sacraments of our restoration. Hence, placed upon the cross, he said: “It is finished” (John 19). But, to pursue this spiritual battle more fully, we see that many are called to it who, when the violence of war is at hand, are separated from the Lord’s army as sluggish and cowardly.

For in the Law of Moses it is commanded that, when battle is imminent, fearful Israelites, men taking wives, and men building houses should return to their own homes. The fearful are those who, when they come to fight against vices through vigils, fasts, and prayers, begin [Col. 0023D] to fear the burden of labour, bodily discomfort, and occasions of illness. Thus it happens that, desiring to avoid bodily troubles, they abandon their purpose and dare to attempt nothing virtuous.

Yet they may not administer in this way the beast which they hired for their master’s work and valued at a daily denarius, so as to receive the pay for a divine work and not complete the day’s work. For what labourer would hire out an ox or an ass to a householder and expect the stipulated pay before the animal has sweated? Behold, we wretches have put our hand to the plough. We feed our beast—that is, our body—from the alms of the poor and from the sins of the dead, so that we may repay their material things with our spiritual ones; and yet we are lukewarm in prayer, sluggish [Col. 0024A] in work, lazy in vigils, and disorderly in discipline.

I fear greatly lest Ezekiel’s saying which follows be said of us: “I saw,” he says, “and behold, at the entrance of the temple, between the vestibule and the altar, twenty-five men with their backs toward the temple and their faces toward the east; and they worshipped toward the rising of the sun” (Ezek. 8). By these twenty-five men are rightly represented the faint-hearted and sluggish, who offer neither the incense of holy devotion in the temple of the heart nor the sacrifice of good work upon the altar of the body, and thus, placed as it were between temple and altar, show themselves idle. Accordingly it is suitably said of them that they have their backs toward the temple and their faces toward the east: because they refuse to accept discipline with a humbled mind, yet wish to share in consolation, signified by the east [Col. 0024B].

This is why they worship toward the rising of the sun: to worship is to give thanks to God for benefits and consolations. Hence it is said: “He will praise you when you do him good” (Ps. 48 [49]). And this is concerning the fearful.

Those who are separated from the Lord’s battle because they take wives signify persons devoted to lust, which makes even the wise foolish, throws down the strong, bends the upright, and casts down the exalted. Who, then, would not beware the snares of so great a plague? Who would not fear being deceived by its wiles? “Behold,” says blessed Job, “those who serve him”—that is, holy men—“are unstable, and in his angels he found perversity; how much more [will this be true of] us, who dwell in houses of clay and bear an earthly foundation?” (Job 4). This enemy is near at hand [Col. 0024C]; even if he does not always prevail when he suggests temptation, he sometimes seduces through an opportune place and time.

Thus Shechem son of Hamor was overcome by Dinah (Gen. 34), David by Bathsheba (2 Kings 11), the elders of Babylon by Susanna (Dan. 13), and Holofernes, captured by Judith, fell (Judith 13). None of these would have burned with desire unless an opportunity for desire, placed close at hand, had presented itself. Consider, therefore, how wretched is the daughter of Babylon—that is, the condition of the flesh: necessarily destined to die, to live only briefly, the keeper of a grave, to be joined to worms, subject to judgment, and, unless mercifully delivered, to perish eternally.

Therefore, so that we may be delivered from this wretched servitude, let us be governed by the instruction of Sacred Scripture, which raises its lover upward from earthly contaminations [Col. 0024D]. It first instructs him through discipline in bodily dress and gesture; second, through knowledge in matters to be done; third, through prudence in morals; fourth, through wisdom in heavenly things, or the contemplation of heavenly things.

For when a person first turns away his eyes lest they see vanity, does not raise his voice in laughter, does not speak foolish talk irrelevant to the matter, and does not carry his foot where it is not permitted, he has already attained through the discipline of a good life its beginning: namely, the outward form of religious life. Afterwards, when he is found diligent, tireless, watchful, cautious, and provident in works or matters to be done, then, with knowledge as his teacher, through the very exercise of good work he cuts off the occasion of sinning. Thirdly, when the things I have mentioned have become pleasing, conscience gradually begins [Col. 0025A] to be purified of vices, and, as prudence enters, to be adorned with virtues and good morals. Fourthly, when he has acquired virtues, it is too little for him merely to abstain from vices; through the sweetness of divine wisdom he begins to relish the things of God, so that it is delightful to him to converse with God and investigate heavenly things, saying with the prophet: “But for me, it is good to cling to God and to place my hope in the Lord God” (Ps. 72 [73]).

These are the four wheels by which Sacred Scripture forms its lover and carries him upward, teaching him to offer his body “a holy, living sacrifice, pleasing to God” (Rom. 12), and to keep himself unstained from this world (Jas. 1). Of these it is said in the prophet that “when the living creatures were lifted up, the wheels also were lifted up with them” (Ezek. 1). Indeed, holy men look toward God through heavenly longings in no other way than when this four-horse chariot of virtues has followed them [Col. 0025B].

By the third kind of people who are separated from the battle to remain at home because they build houses are signified the curious, those more occupied than they should be with external concerns. Such are the people of this world, who make a way on the sea, travel around lands, make riches unjustly, join boundary to boundary as if they alone were to inhabit the earth (Isa. 5). But what business have we to judge those outside, when we find this evil of curiosity in ourselves, and all the more dangerously because we examine other people’s deeds or words more closely than our own? For who among us is so solicitous concerning himself that he does not concern himself with outward administrations and judge offices to be disordered [Col. 0025C]?

Here he says there is more strictness than is proper; there, more dispensational latitude. Indeed—to say more fully what I mean—while we wish more fully to investigate what others do, inventing things which have not occurred, we rush headlong into the vice of detraction. One says to another: “Have you learned what he says in silence? What he does in secret? What he is like in his walk? What he is like in dress? Yet keep it secret until the matter becomes better known.” Why do you, sinful root, wish it to be secret, when you have already shed your brother’s blood? “Behold, his blood cries to the Lord from the earth” (Gen. 2 [probably 4:10]). His case has already become known to all in the palace of the eternal King; Cherubim and Seraphim lament him—the innocent man whom you slandered, the sound man whom you wounded [Col. 0025D], whose blood you unjustly shed.

What soundness of mind can remain to you, wise as you think yourself, when your brother meditates upon this in prayer, in reading, in work—indeed, everywhere he groans, bleeding from the wound which you unjustly inflicted upon him? O perfected religion, which places the summit of its perfection in disparaging another’s virtue! Perhaps you say that you are a spiritual man, who judges all things and is judged by no one. And I will answer you, without judging you, with the verse of that pagan: “Every vice of the soul bears within itself a crime so much the more evident as the person who sins is thought greater.”

Finally, if you are spiritual, you are contemplative. If contemplative, you see God. Do not therefore be angry if I ask you, though I am dust and ashes: when you see God, what do you see in him? Unless your sight deceives you [Col. 0026A], you will say: humility, gentleness, charity, and patience toward all. Turn your eye toward yourself: what do you see in yourself? Unless you are ashamed to accuse yourself, you will say: pride, impatience, harshness, and distrust toward all. Therefore, using sound counsel, you rebuke yourself first. Indeed, if you are righteous, “at the beginning you are your own accuser” (Prov. 18), like that righteous Job of old, who, when he looked upon God with the eye of contemplation, saw and accused his own weaknesses and cried out: “I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye has seen you; therefore I rebuke myself” (Job 42).

As if he said: “At first I heard you through knowledge of your will; now my eye sees you through contemplation of the mind; and because I see you, I rebuke myself.” “Myself,” he says, “not you.” Thus every spiritual man, the more he approaches God, the more he sets before his eyes what he is in himself, insofar as he recognizes himself to be more illuminated by grace [Col. 0026B].

Yet in all that I have said I do not condemn religious zeal, which is to be loved and maintained by all good persons; rather, I accuse and rebuke the envy of detraction. Therefore, beloved brethren, because “he is not crowned unless he has contended lawfully” (2 Tim. 2), let the fearful assume courage, the carnal chastity, and the curious tranquillity of mind. And, having good conduct in the charity of God and the patience of Christ, let us meet our spiritual enemies, against whom we must fight not with the clash of weapons but with virtues and good works [Col. 0026C].

The battle is indeed strong, but great rewards of victory are laid up where mourning is changed into joy, labour into rest, poverty into abundance, misery into gladness, mortality into eternity; where the saints reign with God, and the Lamb of God is with them. Therefore, with equal longing and unanimous desire, let us strive to serve as soldiers of our King. Although at his humble advent he makes us participants in tribulation, at his second advent, when he comes in his majesty with his angels, he will make us heirs of the everlasting kingdom. May our King, Jesus Christ our Lord, deign to bring us to it: his kingdom and dominion remain for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON III. AT THE ADVENT OF THE LORD
[Col. 0026D] “On that day the Branch of the Lord shall be in magnificence and glory, and the fruit of the earth exalted” (Isa. 4). The prophet points out with burning desire the long and greatly desired day of Christ’s coming—a day which he could not point out with his finger—when he says, “On that day,” and so forth. It is as though he said: I do not speak of that day of distress and tribulation, when there will be signs in sun and moon and stars, while people wither away from fear and expectation of what is coming upon the whole world (Luke 21). Nor indeed do I speak of that day of desolation, when the fountains of the great deep were broken open and the floodgates of heaven opened, so that, when the flood came, they might destroy every living creature. Rather, I speak of that day when, as the heavens rained down from above, flashes of grace shone upon the world, and the Son of God, appearing in the robe of flesh, removed the covenant of death and brought peace to the world: not peace of just any sort, I say, but such peace that—wonderful to tell—the wolf should dwell with the lamb, the child should take delight over the hole of the asp, and the weaned child should put his hand into the den of the basilisk (Isa. 11). On that day, so solemn and so long awaited, the Branch of the Lord shall be in magnificence, and so forth.

What Branch? Surely that Branch whose seed the Holy Spirit cast forth, whose flower the angel brought forth, whose fruit Mary produced, and whose savor Mother Church received. And I rightly say that this Branch flowered in the angel: when he announced to the Virgin the mystery hidden from the ages, he revealed it in the very word of his greeting; and what had lain hidden in the secret counsel of God, he promised would be born as Christ in the Virgin’s greeting, as fruit is promised in a flower. “Hail,” he says, [Col. 0027A] “Mary, full of grace” (Luke 1). Who could despair that a Branch would spring forth in the flower of so sweet a conversation—a Branch which goodness dispensed, truth promised, and power proclaimed as good news? Yet this may seem worthy of wonder, because he says that not grass, not a plant, not even a branch or a tree, but a *germen*—a shoot—will be in magnificence. A shoot is not normally large; indeed, a small shoot barely breaking out from dead seed is merely an indication of future fruit.

Nevertheless, we may judge the magnificence of this shoot by the greatness of its seed. For just as in the shoot of the incarnate Word we may rightly understand the conception, so in the seed we may understand the working of the Holy Spirit. What could be more magnificent than that shoot which was filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit? Hence Christ is said to have been conceived of the Holy Spirit. For as that which is born of flesh is flesh, so that which is born of the Holy Spirit is wholly—I say wholly—spiritual (John 3): wholly, I say, not only according to the spiritual nature, but even according to the nature of the flesh. To state what I believe to be true: Christ, in the affections of the flesh, was as spiritual as Paul, by that loftiness of virtue through which he could not be separated from the love of Christ. Therefore this shoot is elsewhere compared not only to a mountain but to one “curdled” and rich: curdled because of the union of humanity and the Word, rich because of the fullness of gifts. For into this shoot the sevenfold grace descended bodily, not as a small drop [Col. 0027B] but as a mighty river; from it, like a streamlet, it flowed to spiritual men, and from them, like dripping water, it issued forth to the lowest members of the Church.

What else, finally, does that throne of Solomon signify, to which none other in all kingdoms could be compared by nature or craftsmanship, except the magnificence of that shoot? For the nature of the assumed manhood, in which supreme Majesty sat as upon a throne, surpassed all others because of the purity of its humanity and the fullness of its graces; as though it had been distinguished above the rest of the children of men by a certain workmanship of the Holy Spirit. That same fullness of gifts was also prefigured by the flask of oil which, while filling all the widow’s vessels, was itself not diminished; indeed, from its own abundance it sustained her sons after they had been freed from their creditors. For Holy Church, long ago made a widow because God had been extinguished in her through unbelief, received—when Elisha, that is, God the Father, bestowed blessing—the flask full of oil (4 Kings 4), namely Christ, filled with sevenfold grace. As he poured grace into the children of the Church, he not only freed them from the exacter, the devil, but also poured out from his fullness an abundant gift of grace, so that those adopted as children of God might live devoutly.

O blessed soul that has tasted, if only a little, of so great a fullness, and on the day of Christ’s coming has received the pledge of its own visitation, lest it deserve to hear with that faithless people: “The swallow knew its nest, and the stork the time of its coming; but Israel did not know me” (Jer. 8). O pure [Col. 0027C] conscience, so cleansed and adorned for the presence of its King that it may behold him securely in that height of glory, when the angels shall tremble in his sight and the powers of heaven shall be shaken (Luke 21). For that same shoot which now appears in magnificence will appear in glory in the age to come.

The prophet continues concerning this height of glory when he says: “And the fruit of the earth shall be exalted.” Although this exaltation may be referred to the mighty deeds which he performed on earth—such as healing infirmities, raising the dead, walking upon the sea, and the like—it more fittingly looks to the glory of the resurrection, by which he was raised above all things, blessed for ever. Elsewhere the prophet speaks of this exaltation, saying: “There shall be a root of Jesse, standing as a sign for the peoples; the nations themselves shall entreat him” (Isa. 11). For how can he be a sign to all peoples unless he is exalted? Therefore the exaltation of this sign is the glory of the resurrection, which first went before in the Head; and he is the sign of the peoples so that they too may live in hope of resurrection, awaiting that same glory which they see has gone before in their author. The Prophet asks for this sign for himself when he says: “Make with me a sign for good” (Ps. 85).

But why does he call that root so exalted, when the root is lower than all the branches of a tree? “There shall be,” he says, “a root of Jesse,” and the rest. Christ is compared to a root because, as the root supports the tree, so Christ supported others and was not supported by them. Or rather, Christ’s humility is prefigured in the root: for Christ was first humble and afterward exalted. The plain indications of this humility are evident if we recall what the prophets, the Gospels, and the other Scriptures say of him. But behold, he is a sign to us in exaltation; would that he might also be a sign in his humility. For every action of Christ, as Scripture says, is our instruction. “You,” Christ says, [Col. 0027D] “call me Master and Lord, and you speak rightly; for so I am” (John 13). Certainly, if he is the Master and we are disciples, we ought in our study to imitate his discipline.

Let anyone, therefore, who calls himself truly his disciple consider whether, if he should be invited to Christ’s humility, patience, gentleness, poverty, and the endurance of injuries for his name, he would in this respect be a disciple of this man. I greatly fear that he would answer in Peter’s words: “Man, I do not know what you are saying” (Luke 20). Or rather, that he would curse the one who invited him, saying: “You be that man’s disciple; but I am a disciple of Moses” (John 9). For how am I his disciple when he commands humility and I follow pride; he commands patience and I embrace impatience; he warns us to endure injuries, while I not only do not endure injuries but even inflict them without cause upon others? Hear, if you please, what kind of disciple of Christ the Psalmist says one ought to be: “Myrrh, and stacte, and cassia are from your garments” (Ps. 44), that is, from your saints. In myrrh, which is bitter, is figured patience in tribulations; in stacte, which soothes pains [Col. 0028A] and reduces swellings, the virtue of humility; in cassia, which grows in watery places and rises high, the desires of holy devotion. These ought to flow from ivory houses—that is, from consciences made white by virtues and chastity—by which the daughters of kings, that is, the souls of those who conduct themselves well in your fear, are delighted.

Certainly, the scholars say—and it is very true—that four things are necessary in every study: a humble mind, a quiet life, practiced meditation, and love of moderation. A humble mind is required, lest pride cause one to act against the master’s commands. Such was the mind of him who said: “O Lord, my heart has not been exalted, nor have my eyes been lifted up; neither have I walked in great things, nor in wonders above me” (Ps. 130). A quiet life is also required, lest, distracted in different directions by varied commotions, one pursue less attentively the end of the study one has well begun. Thus it is said of certain restless persons: “They were troubled and moved like a drunken man, and all their wisdom was swallowed up” (Ps. 106). Third is practiced meditation, so that the mind may always meditate on what it has taken up in its studies, lest, lying idle, it flow away into unlawful desires. The Prophet possessed this meditation when he said: “I meditated by night”—that is, amid the failing of this life—“with my heart; and I shall be exercised,” thus meditating upon those things which are right, “and I searched” (Ps. 76): that is, I purified my spirit from unlawful desires. Fourth among the requirements of good studies is love of moderation, lest the mind, dissolved in pleasures, abandon its purpose through ambition for temporal things. He was content with this moderation who said: “Give me neither riches nor poverty, but grant me only what is necessary for my livelihood” (Prov. 30). We know that all these things were in Christ our Master: we read that he was humble and quiet (Matt. 11), ever intent upon heaven in meditation, and not merely content with moderation but not even possessing a place where he might lay his head (Luke 9).

The Apostle cries out to us: “He who says that he abides in Christ ought himself also to walk as he walked” (1 John 2). How do we imitate him? “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” [Col. 0028B] (Exod. 32). And indeed, whether we truly keep in deed the discipline of Christ which we profess with the outermost lips may be inferred from the very end toward which we ought to tend. Runners and boxers certainly have their end, namely the crown of victory; the mechanical arts have their end, having been devised ultimately to support life. So the orator’s study ultimately strives to persuade what appears just, useful, or honorable. But the end of our study ought to be Christ, who is “the end unto righteousness for everyone who believes” (Rom. 10). Or at least, let us not possess less than a philosopher of the world, seeking finally with the orator what seems just, useful, or honorable. But how does a person attain the end of usefulness who benefits no one? How the end of honorableness, one who continually damages not only his own reputation but that of another? Nor can one be said to possess the end of justice who despises the commands of justice. For the end of the useful consists in benefit; the end of the honorable in the esteem of good reputation; the end of the just in the root of charity, so that what belongs to man may be rendered to man, and what belongs to God to God.

Indeed, to speak more plainly, I should say that you pursue the end of the unjust; and see how the Lord himself cries: “Woe to the man through whom scandal comes” (Matt. 18). The trumpet of the Gospel thunders: “Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble, it is expedient for him that a millstone be hung around his neck,” and so forth (ibid.). The Apostle cries aloud: “Rendering evil to no one for evil, be patient toward all” (Rom. 12). How then does one attain the end of the just who does not rebuke himself as a transgressor of God’s commandments, yet rises with all the agitation of his mind against one who did not attend the procession? “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel” (Matt. 25). For God’s sake I ask you: when you hear the word *scandalum*—stumbling or scandal—what does it sound like in your ears? Certainly, though *scandalizare* may sometimes be understood as “to grieve,” as the Lord says to Peter, “Get behind me, Satan; you are a scandal to me” (Matt. 16), that is, “you grieve me,” nevertheless, as the term is prohibited in the Gospel, *scandalum* implies a brother’s death. To cause scandal is to furnish one’s brother, by word or deed, an occasion of mortal sin. O pure conscience that rejoices in a brother’s blood through its speech or action!

Perhaps someone who willingly causes scandals hears this and seeks excuses in the testimony of Scripture which says: “If scandal arises because of truth, scandal is better admitted than truth abandoned.” Do you wish, then, to hear where scandals are to be admitted and where they are to be avoided? If my brother is scandalized by my evil action, I ought to cease, for my own sake and his. But if he is scandalized by my good action, there are cases in which I ought to admit the scandal, and cases in which I ought not. If I am bound to the good which I do by God’s command or by the profession of my order, and my brother is scandalized by it, I should not therefore cease; for here scandal is more safely admitted than truth abandoned. But if I am not bound to the good which I do by command or vow, but that good is voluntary and depends upon free choice, and my brother is scandalized by it, then—even if it is a very great good, such as fasting for two or three days, secret vigils, or private prayers—I ought to refrain from it because of the scandal. I say this as one placed in a community, who ought to dwell united in one house and, so far as lies in me, guard against scandal to a brother’s soul. I said, however, “one placed in a community,” because a person living a private life is not bound to omit even voluntary good works because of another’s scandal.

Thus Anselm of Canterbury, perfect in learning and religion, says, for the prevention of scandals: “If one of the cenobites perhaps undertakes the religious purpose, it is fitting that, whatever monastery he has entered, he should there be rooted in the roots of charity; unless perhaps it is such a monastery that he is compelled unwillingly to do evil. Nor should he judge the customs of others, even if they seem useless, provided they do not appear contrary to the divine commandments.” This is the pattern of Jesus’ discipline which he himself observed and commanded us to keep: to which he invited us by his deeds and instructed us by his commands, lest we be able to cloak our guilt under any mist of ignorance. If, therefore, we are his disciples, let us revere him as Master; if sons, love him as Father; if servants, fear him as Lord—lest we make his presence not merely useless but even harmful to ourselves. Who, I ask, saw a fish and received a scorpion? Who wandered in a trackless place and recognized the way? Who walked in darkness and perceived light? Behold, [Col. 0028C] the light of the world is set before us, and none is deprived of its ray except one who, with closed eyes, wishes to turn away from it. Let us therefore, dearest brothers, walk in this light while we have time, following the footsteps of his humility and the lessons of his patience, so that, trained in this present life according to the pattern of his humility, we may be transferred in the future to the kingdom of his brightness, through the granting of our Lord Jesus Christ himself, whose kingdom and dominion endure for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON IV. ON THE ADVENT OF THE LORD

“He shall descend like rain upon the fleece, and like drops dripping upon the earth” (Ps. 71). Seeing in the Spirit that comfort was impending for our low estate—comfort for those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death—the prophet wished to promise it, lest captivity prolonged too long should cast them into despair if the hope of future deliverance did not temper the accumulation of misery. Therefore, opening up the manner of our visitation, he bursts into a voice of exultation and joy, saying:

“He shall descend like rain upon the fleece.” Let us first consider, then, the different kinds of fleece. There is a fleece of birth, a fleece of oldness, and also a fleece of newness. We have the fleece of birth from nature, the fleece of oldness from sin, and the fleece of newness from grace. Where it is said, “And I shall again be clothed with my skin” (Job 19), understand the fleece of nature; and in Jeremiah, “He has made my skin and my flesh old” [Col. 0028D] (Lam. 3), understand the fleece of sin. In the Song of Songs, too, the Holy Spirit, signifying the fleece of newness, says: “I am black but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar” (Song 1), “like the skin of Solomon.” She compares herself with the tents of Kedar because of the blackness of vices; with Solomon’s skins because of the adornment of virtues.

“He shall descend,” he says, “like rain upon the fleece, and like drops dripping upon the earth.” Rain upon fleece first moistens the wool, second cleanses it, and third, beyond nature’s own benefit, makes it white. Therefore the Son of God descends like rain upon the fleece when, visiting our nature through grace, he cleanses us from the stain of oldness and, through the progress of virtues, clothes us in garments of newness. “He shall descend,” he says, “like rain upon the fleece,” and so forth. Rain cleanses by the force of its waters; morning dew tempers; but a drip moistens the earth as though in separated drops. Thus the Son of God descends like drops dripping upon the earth when, according to the variety of the time and the manner of temptation, he pours the grace of consolation into our minds. Hence the prophet David, setting out the consolations of beginners, says: “In its drops, that which springs forth shall rejoice” (Ps. 64). “He shall descend,” he says, “like rain upon the fleece.”

By the testimony of Sacred Scripture we may establish four principal descents of God to humankind. The first is for liberation, the second for instruction, the third for consolation, and the fourth for examination. First we are freed from Egypt; second, we are instructed in the desert; third, we are strengthened in battle; fourth, each person’s merits are judged. If, dearest brothers, there is among us anyone who has a living heart and strives to imitate the Spirit of God rather than that of man, a prudent mind will certainly find in these matters material from which to draw fear, and will also recognize, raised by the comfort of hope, the time for mercy and the day of its visitation. For who, seeing God descend to earth for the salvation of humanity, could despair? Or who, awaiting so terrible a Judge, could ever be secure? O how cautiously and carefully we must walk, where one and the same Lord is both a mighty defender for our salvation and so strict a judge, examining what sort each person’s work may be! Therefore, when I recall in myself your mercies, O Lord, which are from eternity (Ps. 24), I say: “It is good for me to cling to God; to place my hope in the Lord God” (Ps. 72). But when I look toward judgment, I desire already to hide in hell until your wrath passes over (Job 4). Yet if you appoint me a time in which you will remember me, since mercy nevertheless triumphs over judgment, let us flee to the Lord as servants, to the Redeemer as captives, to the Comforter as wretched persons, saying with the prophet: “Remember, O Lord, what has befallen us; behold and look upon our reproach” (Lam. 5). You freed us from Egypt, and we murmured, saying: “Would that we had died in Egypt when we sat over the flesh-pots” (Exod. 16). You gave us the Law, and we said: “Depart from us; we do not desire knowledge of your ways” [Col. 0029A] (Wis. 3). You come to us through grace to release us from sins, but, ungrateful for your benefits, we say: “Who is this, who even forgives sins?” (Luke 5). Without you we can do nothing, yet we refuse to follow you and to be with you.

Let us pursue, then, if you please, those four descents of God to humanity which we noted above, and let us lay more deeply in the bosom of memory both God’s benefits and our iniquities. “Seeing, I have seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt; I have descended to free them” (Exod. 3). If we wish to have recourse to a moral understanding, this Egypt is the life of carnal people who make provision for the flesh in its desires. For since the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many thoughts (Wis. 9), anyone who, so long as he is in this mortal body, is overcome by vices and desires is compelled to serve the Egyptians in mud, brick, and straw.

For a certain warrior-woman comes from Egypt, called the desire of the flesh, and says: “It is good to enjoy pleasures and to use good things. For who was ever an enemy of nature? Who ever hated his own flesh?” And the wretched soul answers: “Behold, I am here; you have judged rightly.” “Come now,” says avarice, “gather silver coins, enlarge your purses, live frugally, possess much; for you are worth as much as you possess.” And the unhappy soul answers: “All these things I have kept from my youth” (Luke 18). And pride says: “Go up upon this very high mountain; take hold of weapons and shield, and arise to help me” (Ps. 34). “Let us strive to despise our inferiors, oppress our equals, and disparage our superiors. The simple will not notice, the patient will not rise up, the wise will overlook it, the rebellious will not prevail.” And you answer: “Behold, I hasten, I hurry; I will follow you wherever you go” (Matt. 8). Behold what miserable slavery!

The Egyptians come and say to our soul: “Bend down, that we may pass over”; and we render obedience without delay, unwilling or unable to resist. Perhaps these are the three cities which the children of Israel built for Pharaoh. One was called Rameses, the second Pithom, and the third Heliopolis (Exod. 1).
