Rameses means “the stirring of the moth”; Pithom, “the mouth or depth of the abyss”; and Heliopolis is interpreted “city of the sun.” By Rameses, therefore, understand avarice, prohibited where it is said: “Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth, where moth and rust destroy, and thieves break through and steal” (Matt. 6). By Pithom, which is called “mouth” or “depth,” understand carnal desires and the other passions, concerning which Scripture says: “When the wicked man comes into the depth of vices, he despises” (Prov. 18). By Heliopolis, the city of the sun, understand pride, which, attended by vainglory, wishes to shine far and wide, and to burn others incessantly by detraction and agitation. Who will free us from this slavery? “If the Son,” he says, “shall free us, then we shall truly be free” (John 8). But Pharaoh’s heart has been hardened (Exod. 7), [Col. 0029B] and he will not let us go except through the smiting angel, except by a mighty hand.

Wishing, therefore, to snatch us from the hand of the wicked, he sends his angel to strike the firstborn of Egypt: that is, fear, which, with conscience accusing, threatens the punishment of eternal suffering. “And which of you,” fear says, “will be able to dwell with devouring flame? Who shall remain with everlasting burnings?” (Isa. 30; 33). Therefore, while fear of eternal punishment recalls to the sinful soul its evil ways, it truly kills the firstborn—that is, the wicked deeds committed in the former time—with the sword of contrition. Perhaps this is the angel who, striking Peter in the side, awakened him, saying: “Rise quickly” (Acts 12). For the angel enters to Peter, whose name is interpreted “recognizing,” when anyone recognizes his sins and is shaken by fear of punishment; he strikes him in the side when he compels him to leave behind the former pleasures in which he seemed to find rest. “Rise,” he says, man—as if to say, “It is now time for you to rise from sleep. Rise, you who sleep, lest perhaps you be condemned with the wicked at the Judge’s coming.”

Every faithful soul, then, freed from Egypt by the angel’s blow, needs the second descent of God, by which he may write in its heart the flawless law of the Lord which converts souls, and teach it to run in the way of the Lord’s commandments, lest it return again by the varied circuits of error to Egypt—that is, to the sea and waves of vices. Hence the Law of the Lord is said to have been given to Moses, whose name is interpreted “drawn” or “saved from the waters.” God’s commandments and discipline are certainly useful to the person who, converted from his most wicked way, detests vices and, scorning to serve Pharaoh, tries to extinguish carnal desires within himself. But in order that this Law may be free from disturbance, it is given not in Egypt but in the wilderness—that is, in the cloister, in the place of holy religion—where those rescued from this world sing with the spirit and sing with the mind, and, searching his testimonies (1 Cor. 14), meditate day and night on God’s Law (Ps. 118).

This descent of God to humanity, when one receives the Law, occurs in darkness, thunder, lightning, and fire. In darkness is the remembrance of sins; in thunder, affliction for sins; in lightning, fear of discord and sedition; and in fire, the affection of brotherly love. Therefore in darkness he teaches us to be humbled by the remembrance of sins; in thunder, to afflict ourselves for them by hunger and thirst, vigils and fasts; in lightning, to undertake the way and discipline of religion in fear and gentleness; and in fire, to fulfill the same by works through zeal for charity. In these four, indeed, the whole way of religion is contained: in inward contrition, outward affliction, gentleness of conduct, and the bond of brotherly charity.

Thus Abraham, about to sacrifice his son, is reported to have taken fire and a sword with him (Gen. 22). By the sword, which cuts on both sides, we may understand inward penitence and outward penitence. Inward penitence cuts through contrition of heart; outward penitence through chastisement of the body. Likewise, two things are found in fire: brightness and heat. In brightness may be understood gentleness of conduct, concerning which it is said: “Let your light shine before men” (Matt. 5); in heat, the ardor of heavenly love. Therefore let the person who wishes to offer himself to God bring with him the sacrifice—namely, fire and sword—so that by the sword he may correct himself, and by fire preserve and nourish peace with his neighbor.

These are the guards appointed over Jerusalem, who do not cease, day and night, to praise the Lord’s name. For these four guards are assigned to this our city: sorrow in the heart, labor in the body, gentleness in conduct, and love in the love of heavenly things. Sorrow guards faithfully, labor manfully, gentleness sweetly, charity confidently.

In this our Jerusalem are two very strongly fortified towers, constructed from the foundations upward with four-sided stones. One is called the tower of strength, the other the house of peace. The first is active, the second peaceful. Martha holds the first, Mary the second. Hence the Lord says: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things” (Luke 10). You are anxious through labor, troubled through sorrow. Therefore, if Martha keeps guard over this tower, without doubt it is guarded by sorrow and labor: sorrow through contrition of heart, labor through the performance of good work. But Mary is unconcerned that she leaves her sister to serve alone. Hear what Scripture says: “Mary,” it says, “sat at home”: [Col. 0029C] she sat in quietness, she sat in security—quiet through the virtue of gentleness, secure through the virtue of charity. Secure indeed, because perfect charity casts fear out (1 John 4).

These are the four little doors of which the history of Kings speaks, set at the entrance of the Temple and arranged in this way (3 Kings 6): two and two were joined to each other to form one double door, so that, if it should please one to open them, those which in a manner concealed themselves might be folded back, one after another. Sorrow and labor therefore make one double door, so joined together that they rarely, if ever, leave one another. The remaining double door is made of charity and gentleness, likewise so joined together that gentleness is generated from charity. The double door consisting of labor and sorrow is joined by the bond of strength, because unless strength of mind is present, labor is sometimes separated from inward contrition. The other, consisting of gentleness and charity, is joined by the bond of patience, because unless patience is present, gentleness sometimes departs from charity. These doors turn upon the hinge of humility and are shut by the bar of discretion, so that through humility they may avoid boasting, and through discretion may admit neither excess nor folly. Thus this door is movable through humility, enduring through strength, measurable through discretion, praiseworthy through patience, watchful through sorrow, firm through labor, radiant through charity, [Col. 0029D] and polished through gentleness. “And he made,” it says, “two doors of fir wood; and each was double, and they opened while holding one another” (ibid.).

Fir, it is said, is a tree beautiful in appearance, tall in height, with branches spreading broadly in every direction. These doors, therefore, ought to be of fir wood: beautiful in the cheerfulness of the spirit, lofty in long-suffering, broad in mercy or compassion for one’s neighbor. But now that the Law of the Lord has been received in holy profession, the third descent of God to humanity, which we called consolation, is necessary. We need its help all the more as the battle with the adversary is fiercer. For when the new soldier of Christ believes himself secure and now advances manfully along the path of his purpose, behold, from the opposite side the assaults of the mighty rise around him; on every side they block the way of escape and shoot very sharp missiles that wound not only the body but the soul as well. That excessively attractive hope or abundance of riches presses in; frequent and greatly importunate remembrance of letters comes upon him; worldly and pleasant recreations appear; and carnal temptations also assail him.

In this danger of storm, God’s wisdom comes to us, strengthening us by the grace of consolation and enlightening us by knowledge of the truth. At this critical moment of the storm, he strengthens the faint-hearted, consoles the despairing, refreshes the exhausted, and supplies the aid of faith to the one making progress, as it is written of him: “He shall not break the bruised reed, and he shall not extinguish the smoking flax” (Isa. 42). Hear then, you who have now been separated from the world, who know the vow made to the God of Jacob, who are drawn in different directions by temptations; you whom, as you suppose, the happiness of your former life delights, and whom the austerity of holy religion terrifies. Hear, I say, what the Lord God speaks within you: for, as I judge, “he will speak peace to his people” (Ps. 84).

First, I wish to place before you silver, gold, fine clothing, and the other things in which human curiosity delights, and to examine them carefully with the eye of the mind, not the flesh. If you do so, you will find not consolations but rather the greatest desolations. What happiness can there be in something acquired with labor, possessed with fear, and lost with grief? Hence a certain man, mocking such happiness, ironically exclaimed: “O splendid riches of wealth, which, once you have acquired them, cause you to cease being secure!” Remember that rich man in the Gospel who was preparing to enlarge his barns, to whom it was said: “Fool, this night they will take your soul from you; and whose shall those things be which you have gathered?” (Luke 12). And so it came to pass. David the prophet says of those who loved the glory of this world: “The just shall rule over them in the morning, and their help shall grow old in hell, away from their glory” (Ps. 48). For in proportion to the glory in which they indulged in this world, by God’s just judgment they shall be numbered among the dead and receive in hell the distress of torment.

Hence, when two most learned philosophers wished typologically to represent the glory of this world and the holy life which is in Christ Jesus, one described a tree at the entrance of hell bearing a golden branch; the other dreamed of a golden chain hanging down from heaven to earth. What else, I ask, is signified by that golden branch except the beauty and glory of this world? It is said to stand at the entrance of hell because, through love of this world, its lovers are sent to hell. Let every seed of Israel fear to touch this tree, because easy is the descent to Avernus; but to retrace one’s step and escape to the upper air—this is labor, this is grief. The other, by the golden chain, wished to signify the life of the saints: though established on earth, it is joined to heavenly things only by holy meditation and devout devotion, as the Apostle says: “But our commonwealth [Col. 0030A] is in heaven” (Phil. 3). And although religious men are placed on earth, they are nevertheless connected, as if by a chain, through the steps of virtues and good works.

If love of letters should tempt you, remember first this: the unlearned often seize heaven, while learned men, though acquainted with letters, often descend into the depths of hell. But he who speaks within you desires to know from you whether, in this desire of yours, you set vanity as your end or the knowledge of truth. For if you set vanity before yourself as your end, you err and deceive yourself, and are to be numbered with those who, although they knew God, did not glorify him as God; therefore they became foolish and failed away in their vanities (Rom. 1). But if through learning you endeavour to investigate truth, [Col. 0037C] even in this you err and deceive yourself: while with Pilate you ask, “What is truth?” (John 18), you have nevertheless found Truth himself. “I,” he says, “am the way, the truth, and the life”: the way in rule, truth in knowledge, life in fruition; the way in merit, truth in promise, life in reward. “I am,” he says, “the way, the truth, and the life.” And the Prophet: “Blessed is the man whom you instruct, O Lord, and teach him out of your law” (John 14). For he indeed is the one who teaches man knowledge (Ps. 43), writing the divine law in the book of the heart, not through empty philosophy or in the learned words of human wisdom, but in the Spirit of God (1 Cor. 1). And if you seek true wisdom—that is, holy wisdom—the practice of prayer will reveal it to you better than the study of reading.

[Col. 0037D] But perhaps the eloquence of Tully, the wisdom of Plato, and the genius of Aristotle will delight you—things which make the wise ignorant and the foolish learned. But what concord is there between Christ and Belial? “Take these things hence, and do not make the house of your Father a house of trade” (John 2); for the Spirit of Christ does not reign where the spirit of Aristotle is condemned. Strengthened by these and similar consolations, Christ, who delivered us from the world, will not suffer us to be tempted beyond what we are able, lest, once we have put our hand to the plough, we look back and become unworthy of the kingdom of God (Luke 9).

Therefore, beloved brethren, armed by works of righteousness on the right hand and on the left, let us prepare the way of the Lord; let us make straight in this wilderness the paths of our God [Col. 0038A]. Running in the way of his commandments, let us ever stretch forward, in the gentleness of discipline and the service of obedience; entering from virtue into virtue, may we deserve to see the God of gods in Zion (Ps. 83). Let us not be ungrateful to him who delivered us from Egypt—that is, from the present age. Let us hold fast the law which he taught us in the wilderness, that is, in this earthly paradise, namely the monastery. Let us reverence the coming of our visitation, in which he takes our weaknesses into himself—that is, consoles us in every tribulation and distress—so that we may safely await that final coming of examination, when the Son of Man shall come in great power and majesty (Matt. 19). May our same judge, creator, and [Col. 0038B] redeemer, Jesus Christ, deign to grant this to us, he whose kingdom and dominion endure for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON V. ON THE ADVENT OF THE LORD

“I will cause the morning and latter rain to come down upon you, and I will restore to you the years which the locust, the grub, the rust, and the caterpillar have consumed” (Joel 2).

The word which you have heard, beloved brethren, holds the promise of our deliverance and the affection of paternal consolation, as having been sent to us from God, the Father of orphans and judge of widows.

For the Father of mercies, proclaiming a year of favour, a day of remission, a time of compassion, promises the morning and latter rain in abundance, so that, made fruitful by its drops, the earth may open [Col. 0038C] and bring forth the Saviour. “I will cause,” he says, “the morning and latter rain to come down upon you.” Understand rain not bodily but spiritual, of which the Prophet says: “He shall come down like rain upon the fleece” (Ps. 64). And Isaiah: “As rain comes down from heaven and waters the earth and pours itself upon it, so shall the word be that goes forth from my mouth” (Isa. 55).

By the rain he intended to signify the Word of God, the Son of the Virgin, who, like rain, washes sinners, nourishes new plantations in the house of God, and gives drink to those thirsting for righteousness—I mean perfected persons. Thus he washes in compunction, nourishes in advancement, and gives drink in consummation. Would you see this rain washing? Consider the tears of Mary the sinner; the penitence of Paul the persecutor [Col. 0038D]; the confession of Peter who denied; the entreaty of the thief who pleaded. “If,” says the prophet, “he shall have washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion, and washed the blood of Jerusalem from her midst in a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning” (Isa. 4)—as though to say: then everyone left in Jerusalem shall be called holy.

Consider next, if you please, the rain as nourishing: “And the Lord shall help them, and deliver them, and rescue them from sinners, and save them, because they hoped in him” (Mark 14). Whom shall he help? Surely those whom he separated from the world and called by his grace; those who, fervent in spirit, stand in the battle line with him, saying with Peter, “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you”: strong indeed in their resolve for holiness, yet weak in steadfastness of virtue. These, I say, the Lord helps [Col. 0039A] in battle against enemies; he frees from the slavery of vices; he rescues from sinners, that is, from the scandal caused by neighbours; and at last he saves them because they hoped in him. O how sweet is this upbringing, which leads from the flower of an initial manner of life to the fruit of final reward!

Would you see this rain giving drink? Recall, in the historical sense, the spring for Hagar fleeing from her mistress’s presence (Gen. 21), the vessel of water refreshing Elijah (3 Kings 17), the waters for the murmuring people in the wilderness (Exod. 15), or finally the wedding-feast of the chief steward (John 2). Thus, spiritually, he gives some drink through the greatness of revelations, others through the depth of the Scriptures, some through the practice of holy meditation, others through the sweetness of devotion. Such indeed is the rain; but where is its descent? [Col. 0039B] For it was said, “I will cause it to come down.”

Do you think it a small descent for the Son of God to be wrapped in swaddling clothes, to hang at his mother’s breast, to be incarnate, and finally to be crucified? Hear of his descent: “I have become like a pelican of the wilderness; I have become like a night-raven in a dwelling-place” (Ps. 101). The pelican is a lean bird, slender in body; the night-raven is a nocturnal bird, ugly in colour. He became like the pelican when he assumed the leanness of our nature; he became like the night-raven when he hung upon the cross, having neither form nor beauty. And elsewhere: “I was delivered up and did not go forth; my eyes languished because of want” (Ps. 87). “I was delivered up,” that is, exposed to suffering according to the weakness of the body; “I did not go forth,” by displaying the power of divinity.

[Col. 0039C] Great is this descent, great the humiliation, great indeed the condescension of the physician entering the infirmary of the sick person. Many sick people lay in it: Peter’s mother-in-law (Luke 4), the royal official’s son (John 4), the centurion’s servant (Matt. 8), and a great multitude of sick persons, blind, lame, and withered (John 4), longing for the coming of the healing physician. Is not he truly blind who says, “My heart is troubled; my strength has forsaken me, and even the light of my eyes is not with me” (Ps. 37)? Likewise, he is withered who said, “My days declined like a shadow, and I withered like grass” (Ps. 101). And elsewhere it is said of the lame: “Alien sons lied to me; alien sons have grown old [Col. 0039D] and limped from their paths” (Ps. 17). The blind are those who do not know God; the lame, those deficient in good works; the withered, those without the moisture of virtues.

Therefore the Son of God entered this infirmary—that is, the misery of our mortality—when he himself took our infirmities and united to himself, in the Blessed Virgin, a share in our nature. Accordingly, I rightly call the Blessed Virgin Mary the door of this infirmary. For she is the gate of which the prophet says: “This gate shall be shut and shall not be opened, and no man shall pass through it, because the Lord of hosts has entered through it” (Ezek. 44). But when, or where, did he enter through this gate? Let us ask the archangel Gabriel, who both carefully observed the entry and faithfully announced it: [Col. 0040A] “Hail,” he says, “Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with you” (Luke 2). The Lord is with you by protection; the Lord is in you by indwelling; the Lord is from you by the Incarnation. Behold, a little earlier he was with the Father in heaven; now he is incarnate in the Virgin’s womb. “Hail, Mary,” he says, “full of grace, the Lord is with you.”

What is *ave*, “hail”? Perhaps it means *sine vae*, “without woe.” Eve, the mother of transgression, received manifold woe as the punishment for disobedience. The first woe: “I will multiply your afflictions”; the second: “in pain you shall bear children”; the third: “you shall be under the power of your husband” (Gen. 2). And which of these do you find in the Blessed Virgin? Neither affliction in conception nor pain in childbirth; nor was she subject to a husband, by reason of her perpetual virginity.

[Col. 0040B] This, then, is what the angel says: “Hail, Mary”—that is, “without woe”—who was full of grace, that is, fruitful through the Holy Spirit. For it was fitting that she should be full of grace, through whom, as through a certain bodily channel, the fountain of divine grace overflowed to the whole human race. She is the earth from which that fountain sprang, of which it is written in Genesis: “The Lord had not yet rained upon the earth, nor was there a man to cultivate the earth; but a fountain rose from the earth and watered the surface of the earth” (Gen. 2). The fountain indeed rose from the earth when the Son of God, the splendour of glory and fountain of life, willed to be born from the Blessed Virgin. He watered the surface of the earth when he converted to the grace of faith sinners themselves and those abounding in the world, both Jews and Gentiles; and not [Col. 0040C] only converted them, but also redeemed them from the snare of death, as it is written of him: “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save what was lost, and to give his life as a redemption for many” (Luke 19).

Perhaps I should say more expressly, “for all,” because all had sinned and needed the glory of God (Rom. 3); and therefore they cried to the Lord in their tribulation, and he delivered them from their necessities (Ps. 106). What else, I ask, do those four verses sung at nocturnal praises in the first responsory signify except the common desire of all for common deliverance? The first verse, “All earthborn people and sons of men” (Ps. 18), concerns earthly men who lived before the Law. The second, “Give ear, O shepherd of Israel” [Col. 0040D] (Ps. 79), concerns Israelites who had received knowledge of the Law. The third, “Stir up your power” (ibid.), concerns men under grace who, at the second advent, seek release from mortality. The fourth, namely “Glory be to the Father,” concerns the joyful common happiness of all in eternity. You have now heard, dear friends, of the rain and its descent; but in what sense is it morning and latter rain?

To apply these matters to our edification: our day is the brightness of a devout way of life, of which it is said, “Let your light shine before men” (Matt. 5). The morning of this day is the beginning of a good life; its evening is the completion of that same life. What else, then, should I call the morning rain except that by which God pours himself into [Col. 0041A] the sinner through compunction? Or what the latter rain except that by which he brings one who has begun well to a perfect man through the consummation of virtue? For just as seasonable rain makes seed spring from the earth, so God, through the spirit of compunction, melts the earthly and animal heart into tears. He pours out the latter rain when the whole person, already transformed into spirit, grieves to dwell with the inhabitants of Kedar, desiring to be dissolved and to be with Christ.

Would you see the morning rain? “Streams of waters flowed down from my eyes, because they did not keep your law.” And Jeremiah: “My eye pours forth water, because the comforter who would restore my soul has been removed far from me” (Rom. 8). Hear also the latter rain: “Who shall deliver me from this body of death?” [Col. 0041B] For, now suffused with longing for eternal life, he calls it not a mortal body but a body of death, since he judges to be death whatever delays or separates him from eternal life, which is Christ. I think that this latter rain distilled into the soul of blessed Job when he said: “My soul chose hanging, and my bones chose death” (Job 7): by “hanging” wishing to signify the height of contemplation; by “the death of the bones,” the mortification of the flesh.

And certainly it is sweet, through prayer, to strike at heaven; through holy meditation, to penetrate it; to marvel at the blessedness of angels; to reverence the happiness of the just; to seek God in devotion; and to grasp him in love. Would that the Spirit might take me with the prophet between heaven and earth, so that I, who cannot rise [Col. 0041C] to the height of contemplation, might at least be lifted for a little while from the earth and not draw near to the gates of death. Awake, my soul; and you who cannot rise to the heights of God, embrace his weaknesses—I mean the Incarnation and Passion—with what strength you have. You who cannot rise to God’s sublimities with perfected men, direct the gaze of your mind to the piercings of the nails and the scars of the wounds; take down from the cross him whom you cannot behold reigning above the choirs of angels.

You too, sinner, whom the testimony of conscience accuses, prepare your heart for the morning rain, so that he may restore to you the years which the locust, grub, rust, and caterpillar consumed. These are the four vices which scatter Jerusalem and Judah [Col. 0041D] to every wind, which leave neither you nor anyone else untried, and which hinder, as much as they can, all who walk in the way of God. The locust, which leaps and quickly falls, signifies pride; the grub, which is wholly in its throat, signifies *gastrimargia*, that is, gluttony; rust signifies impatience; the caterpillar, a foul worm, signifies lust.

Pride first arises and says within itself: “When you were in the world, you girded yourself and walked where you wished. You ran freely to the ends of the streets, to gatherings of dancers, and finally, wherever the impulse of the spirit was, there you went; nor did you turn back when you walked. It is hard to be reduced to the state of a child, to endure rebukes, to expose your back to lashes, always to bear the form of a servant, and in all things to obey another’s will.” Thus the flesh plots against chastity [Col. 0042A] through unlawful desires; gluttony against sobriety, through excessive craving for foods and drinks; impatience against meekness, through slanders and insults.

But you, good man, who have vowed a vow to the God of Jacob (Ps. 131), do not consent to them. Consider the misery of this prison, the brevity of time, how sudden death is, and how enduring the punishment of sin. Do you not know that the evangelical thief daily breaks through your house? The body is frequently seized by fever, the head tormented by pain, the eyes grow dim, often incurable weakness comes upon one, death hastens, and the tomb is plainly before us. Why, then, do you not keep watch? What householder, seeing crumbling walls, rotten timber, fallen ceilings, a weak foundation, and a roof pierced on every side, would not fear thieves and flee [Col. 0042B] from enemies?

Therefore let us flee, beloved brethren, from the enemies of the soul, who thirst for human blood, set snares in ambush, and capture many. Let us flee, I say, praying in accordance with the Lord’s counsel that our flight may not be in winter or on the Sabbath (Matt. 24). In winter flight is arduous because of the severity of the cold; on the Sabbath it is unlawful because of transgression of the Law. Winter is obstinacy of mind; flight is repentance; Sabbath is the rest of eternity.

Repentance must not be deferred until winter, because then the dominion of sin hinders it; nor until the Sabbath, because in the future repentance has no place. How then must one flee?

> Resist beginnings; medicine is prepared too late,  
> When evils have grown strong through long delay.

[Col. 0042C] The firstborn of Egypt must be slain; unlawful suggestion must be resisted at its outset. “You struck the head from the house of the wicked; you laid bare its foundation up to the neck; you cursed its sceptres” (Hab. 3). The head of the wicked—that is, the origin of wickedness—is remembrance of our corrupt manner of life; the foundation is the hidden place of unlawful thought; the sceptre, the insignia of royal power, is the dominion of sin. Therefore the head must be struck from the house of the wicked, lest remembrance of corrupt living affect us; the foundation must be laid bare, so that we confess the hidden things of thought; the sceptres must be cursed, by detestation of corrupt action.

Therefore, if you please, let us set before ourselves the flight of Elijah. Let us see [Col. 0042D] how he fled, so that we too may do likewise. It is written of Elijah that he fled from the face of Jezebel into the wilderness; there he cast himself beneath the shade of a juniper tree and fell asleep; afterwards, refreshed with ash-baked bread and a draught of water, he walked in the strength of that food as far as Horeb, the mountain of God (3 Kings 19). Jezebel, whose name means “dunghill,” persecutes Elijah whenever any lover of chastity is attacked by the concupiscence of the flesh. We must therefore flee into the wilderness—that is, to the dwelling of a solitary life, or to the manner of life within the cloister—where neither may the eye see what it desires, and solitude itself may cut off an occasion for vain glory.

Yet you will not be safe even there unless you cast yourself beneath the shade of the juniper—that is, unless you conform yourself to the humility and Passion of Jesus Christ. The juniper [Col. 0043A] is a lowly, contemptible, rough, and fruitless tree, and it signifies Christ. For he was contemptible when incarnate; whence the prophet says: “We saw him and did not esteem him” (Isa. 53). He was rough—that is, crowned with thorns; fruitless, according to many people’s estimation, when hanging on the cross. Hence they said: “But we hoped that he was the one who would redeem Israel” (Luke 24). Beneath the shade of this juniper we ought to cast ourselves, conforming ourselves to his manner of life in labours and hardships, vigils and prayer. But what does the poet say about the juniper?

> Let us rise: the shade  
> Of the juniper is commonly oppressive to those sitting [singing].”

[Col. 0043B] The shade of the juniper is oppressive and enfeebling to the body; thus, indeed, it is laborious and burdensome to imitate Christ immediately—to mortify the body, to persevere in prayers and vigils, to bear calmly the silence of the cloister, the hardness of the bed, the length of vigils, the divisions and losses of the hours. Therefore most of us, with Jonah, flee from the face of the Lord to Tarshish, a name meaning “the exploration of joy.” We turn aside from the shade of the juniper lest we endure the heavy labour of the body. Therefore we seek earthly and transitory consolations, saying that it is good to use delights and enjoy good things.

Yet this is the way, this is that narrow path which leads to life (Matt. 7), because one enters the kingdom of heaven only through many tribulations. What great thing, after all, is acquired without labour? Thus a ship is guided to port amid dangers; bronze is turned into brass through many hammerings [Col. 0043C]; linen is transformed to whiteness through much rubbing; the furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the trial of tribulation tests the just man (Ecclus. 27).

Let us therefore cast ourselves beneath the shade of the juniper and be refreshed with a draught of water and ash-baked bread. Ash-baked bread is remembrance of death; the vessel of water is the tears of devout confession. In fear of this food we shall walk to Horeb, the mountain of God—that is, to the heavenly Jerusalem—by reason of the unfailing love of the saints. For remembrance of death guards us from sinning on the way, as the wise man says: “My son, remember your last things, and you shall never sin” (Ecclus. 7). Tears of confession bring us back to the way after sins.

[Col. 0043D] Therefore, beloved brethren, while we have time, let us walk in this way, for the way is short and life transitory. Let us beseech our mediator Jesus Christ that he himself may be the guide of the way and giver of grace, until we arrive at Horeb, the mountain of God—that is, the heavenly Jerusalem—with Jesus Christ our Lord going before and leading us, he whose kingdom and dominion endure for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON VI. ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

“While all things kept a deep silence, and night in its course had reached the middle of its way, your almighty Word, O Lord, came from the royal thrones” (Wis. 18).

From the beginning God spoke to humanity in many parts and in many ways [Col. 0044A], so that through the familiarity of conversation the creature might acknowledge the Creator and, with every occasion for silence removed, might never cease from the praise of its God. God therefore spoke three principal words, by which humanity might be instructed unto life. The first was the word of the creation of the world; the second, the word of prophetic foreannouncement; the third, the word of human reconciliation.

The first word, that is, the immensity of created things, proclaimed the invisible power of God (Rom. 1), so that humanity might fear to offend by sin one so powerful. The second word, that is, the prophetic oracle, proclaimed the goodness of the coming Saviour, so that the sinner might hope for pardon. The third word, which was made flesh and dwelt among us, promised blessedness to humanity, so that by living justly and devoutly it might hasten [Col. 0044B] to glory.

Three silences followed these three words. The first silence was the failure of human reason; the middle silence was the longing for fulfilment of the promise; the third silence was the secrecy of inward contemplation. After the first word humanity fell silent because, as human reason gave way, it could not know the invisible things of God through created things; and therefore it was cast far from God, neither praising nor invoking his name. After the second word humanity likewise fell silent because, having received the promise, it desired him alone in whom its hope was laid up: that in him sin might receive its end, transgression be removed, and everlasting righteousness come, when Christ appeared in the flesh.

The third silence then entered: [Col. 0044C] that is, the peace and tranquillity of heart in which holy men rest from the noise of this world—those who have turned to God from their vain manner of life and dead works, and serve him in the joy of the spirit and the affection of good will. Therefore, while all things kept a deep silence. What “all things”? Surely the elements of this world desired Christ’s advent, in order to render service to their Creator. Humanity desired Christ’s advent, that the captive might receive freedom. The angel desired Christ’s advent, for the restoration of the angelic fall. And, if it may be said, God himself desired Christ’s advent, for the truth of the promise’s fulfilment.

Therefore, while all things kept a deep silence, and night [Col. 0044D] in its course had reached the middle of its way: the night of sin had its first stage in heaven, when the transgressing angel was cast down by reason of his pride. It had its middle stage in the world, when before Christ’s advent all things were shut up under sin, and none could glory in their own merits. Its third stage was in hell, where Adam’s children were subjected to penal punishment on account of sin. You see how great was the course of this night, which ran from the height of heaven to the depth of hell. Therefore, while this night had reached the middle of its way, “your almighty Word, O Lord, came from the royal thrones.”

The throne of Christ is the divine nature, in which he sits by the stability of eternity. Hence it is said: “Your throne, O God, is for age upon age” (Ps. 44). The thrones of God are also angelic spirits, in whom he sits [Col. 0045A] by the repose of contemplation. Hence it is said: “You who sit upon the cherubim, reveal yourself” (Ps. 79). The thrones of God are the souls of the just, in whom he sits by the grace of justification. Hence it is said: “The soul of the just is the throne of God” (Wis. 7). Christ therefore came to us from the royal thrones when he showed to humanity, by the condescension of assumed human nature, that presence which he displayed to blessed spirits through divinity.

Therefore, while all things kept a deep silence through longing for fulfilment of the promise, and night had reached the middle of its way—that is, while sin had subjected all things to its dominion—your almighty Word came from the royal thrones. While Christ, known to angelic spirits according to the divine nature, made himself manifest [Col. 0045B] to humanity according to human nature. This Word is almighty because he is the Word of God. The Word of God is God—that is, Christ.

Now then listen carefully to this Word and write him in your heart as in a book. For he teaches you the way of salvation not in the vanity of much speaking nor in loftiness of words, but in the way of humility, awareness of weakness, and the example of poverty. This Word sets before you Christ’s humility, so that, when you see him humble and despised, you too may despise whatever seems proud and lofty in this world. It sets before you Christ’s weaknesses, so that, when you see him surrounded by so many weaknesses and miseries, you may despise all the strong things of this world which promise some stability in themselves. This Word sets before you the poverty [Col. 0045C] of Christ, so that, when you see him wrapped in cheap cloths and having nowhere to lay his head, you may judge unworthy of esteem whatever lovable and pleasant thing is possessed in this life.

Yet nature itself taught you this way of living from the beginning, when it introduced you naked, surrounded by many pains, into this light. But led astray by certain erroneous paths, you departed from it for a time. For an inward presumption of spirit came upon you, so that, thinking highly of yourself, you did not recognize your weakness. The appearance of visible things came upon you from without, and you were again enticed by them, so that, forgetting your native poverty, you judged happiness to consist in them. Therefore the Word of God was directed to you, to bring you back to the way which you lost, so that, while he teaches you in the way [Col. 0045D] of this mortality that nothing is to be desired, you may hear more willingly and commit the words of salvation more firmly to memory.

Would you hear what words? The words of this Word are few, since it is brief and concise—so much so that it is completed in the number of six words. The first word of this Word is the washing away of guilt; the second, the restoration of grace; the third, escape from exile; the fourth, attainment of the kingdom; the fifth, fellowship in divinity; the sixth, acquisition of eternity. O that you who learn much might retain even one of these words, and might learn to glory not in the learned words of human wisdom but in the words which justify the ungodly and make the righteous blessed. Search now the corners of your heart, and speak with your conscience, to see whether perhaps one of these words murmurs within it.

If you have mourned your crimes, and washed them away by true confession and worthy satisfaction, the first word, the washing away of guilt, sounds in your heart. If, now justified, you walk in the Lord’s commandments and do works of righteousness, the second word, the restoration of grace, reaches the ears of your heart [Col. 0046A]. The remaining words speak to you in this life only for consolation, lest perhaps you fail amid the tribulations of this age; for in the life to come you will know them better, when, hearing them, you live in them. By these words the Word of God speaks to you at the prompting of divine wisdom; yet by certain deceitful words you repel them from your heart, and thereby incur a graver judgment, since, hearing the words of God, you have refused to fulfil them in deed.

[Col. 0046B] There are three kinds of human wisdom which utterly oppose this Word. The first is worldly wisdom, of which it is said: “The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1 Cor. 1). The second is carnal wisdom, of which it is said: “The wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God” (Rom. 8). The third is animal wisdom, concerning which it is said: “The natural man does not receive the things which are of God” (1 Cor. 1). Worldly wisdom belongs to pride; it makes a person clever at seeking honours, pursuing gain, enlarging possessions, and the like, so that the mind, occupied with transitory things, through excessive desire for temporal goods, forgets eternal ones.

Carnal wisdom belongs to concupiscence. It teaches a person to make [Col. 0046C] provision for the flesh in its desires—in revelries and drunkenness, in sexual indulgence and shamelessness, and the like—which belong to the pleasures of the flesh. Of these it is written: “Those who do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God” (Gal. 5). Animal wisdom appears to belong to pride. It is the teacher of those who disdain to rely upon the sayings and examples of the holy Fathers, and therefore teach perverse doctrines contrary to faith. As they proceed through the mysteries of God with the singular presumption of their own spirit, they cannot penetrate them—mysteries better understood by living devoutly than by subtle reasoning.

O how many gladly listen to the words of this wisdom and, despising the wisdom of God which speaks from heaven, strive to bend all the thought and effort of their heart [Col. 0046D] toward appearing wise in satisfying pleasures, outwitting neighbours, and worldly cares. Such persons are truly comparable to one who fishes with a golden hook. Once he has cast it into muddy water, some cheap and fruitless thing holds it fast in the depths; nor can any previous catch of fish make up for its loss. What else is it to direct the sharpness of one’s intellect toward wicked pursuits than to cast a golden hook into muddy water? But when the image of the incorruptible God—that is, the human mind, rightly signified by gold—has been held fast in the depth of vices, this loss cannot be measured by any temporal advantage. “For what does it profit a man if he gain the whole [Col. 0047A] world and yet suffer loss to his soul?” (Luke 9). Absolutely nothing.

Perhaps those cast this golden hook into muddy water who gladly learn and teach poetic fictions and other writings of the pagans, while they pass by with a deaf ear the undefiled law of the Lord which converts souls (Ps. 18). They speak often of the marriage of Mercury and Philology, but seldom or never of the union of Christ and the faithful soul. They carefully investigate whence comes the spot upon the moon, but refuse to consider whether there is a stain on their conscience. Surely they must fear lest they burn in punishments with those whose studies they wished to imitate with such reverence and diligence.

Behold, the wisdom of God cries, saying: “Weep, [Col. 0047B] weep; come to your senses, come to your senses!” And all say: “This saying is hard; who can hear it?” (John 6). Human wisdom cries aloud: “Enjoy pleasures; follow the desires of your heart.” And all say, “That is good indeed. Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (Isa. 22). What is it to you, O wretched soul, amid the waves of this life? Does not even affliction itself give you understanding (Isa. 28), where there is no peace, no security, no certainty of life? Who, ever situated upon the sea, tossed on every side by winds and storms, with the rudder broken, has been secure of life?

Certainly you are placed amid the waves of this sea, and until now you have not known it—or perhaps rather have pretended not to know it. For what else is human life but a kind of ship which, loaded with good works as with merchandise, ought to make its way [Col. 0047C] toward the day of future judgment?

Its rudder is the Word of God, which amid the prosperity and adversity and diverse temptations of this sea of life ought to guide it to the harbour of salvation. But when the sinful soul has driven the Word of God from its heart, then, as winds and storms rush upon it from every side, it is endangered in the tempest of vices, as though its rudder were broken.

From the east the wind of its own will shakes it through disobedience. From the south the wind of worldly manner of life shakes it through vain glory. From the west the wind of another’s harassment shakes it through impatience. From the north the wind of diabolical suggestion shakes it through malice. [Col. 0047D] You see, unless I am mistaken, how dangerous it is for you to be tossed by these waves. But one way of salvation remains, because the mainland is before your eyes. Therefore, girded with your tunic, cast yourself into the sea, and seize that land if you can.

In it are lofty mountains, which it is advantageous to climb because of the violence of the storms. In it are low valleys, in which you may hide because of the force of the winds. In it are caves, in which you may conceal yourself because of fear of enemies. This land is Christ the man, who, earth from earth, was born a man from the Virgin. He is the solid land, because he remained firm and steadfast against every flood of vices. The mountains of this land are the heights of his virtues and miracles; its valleys, the lowly [Col. 0048A] and weak circumstances of his birth; its caves are the places of the nails and the openings of his wounds, from which flowed the blood of our redemption. Climb, therefore, the mountains of his virtues, if you are great. Hide in the valleys of his humility and weakness, if you are small. Conceal yourself in the caves—that is, look to the remedy of his wounds—if you are fearful. For in Christ salvation and protection are found everywhere. And behold, this land is before your eyes. For Christ was born for us on this day; today he came to us from the royal dwelling-places. Let us therefore look upon him with the eyes of our heart, that we may fear him as judge and love him as redeemer. Let us receive him with our hands, so that we may serve him by works of justice and by deeds of mercy. Let us receive him, I say, and not let him go [Col. 0048B] until he brings us into the house of our mother and into the chamber of her who bore us (Song of Songs 3), namely the heavenly Jerusalem, where are peace, security, and everlasting joy; where he lives as God with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON VII. ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

“He shall eat butter and honey, that he may know how to reject evil and choose good” (Esdras 7).

The longed-for day of the Savior’s birth ought to be spoken of with devotion rather than with speech, since the depth of its great matters presses down not only the service of the tongue but also that of [Col. 0048C] our understanding. As it is written in the book of Job: “It is higher than heaven—what can I do? Deeper than hell—how can I know it?” (Job 11). “Its measure is longer than the earth and broader than the sea.” Hence Moses does not speak with him except in darkness (Exod. 16). Elijah nevertheless saw the back parts of the one passing by (Isa. 53); Isaiah does not know how to unfold his generation; nor can John untie the strap of his sandal (John 1)—that is, explain the mystery of his Incarnation. Yet, since today, clothed in the hair-shirt of flesh, he deigned to recline and feast with us, I too will approach, with those invited, the banquet of the newborn King. Reclining even in the lowest place, I may receive something from his table with the little dogs, something which I may set before your charity and supply to my own devotion.

Therefore I desire to attempt that prophecy of Isaiah in which the mysteries of the Incarnate Word are contained, where he says: “He shall eat butter and honey,” and so forth. But who is this son so tender and delicate that he is not fed on bread, rejects wine, and yet, among all the other things nourished by land and sea, eats butter and honey—of which one fattens and the other delights? He is, unless I am mistaken, the Son of the great King, whom God the Father appointed heir of all things, through whom he also made the ages (Heb. 1). Yet, “as long as the heir is a little child, he differs in no respect from a slave, though he is lord of all” (Gal. 4), and therefore he is fed with richer dishes, lest his tender infancy, offended by solid foods, turn them into loathing rather than nourishment. Meanwhile, then, he shall eat butter and honey, that he may know how to reject [Col. 0049A] evil and choose good.

But how does it appear to follow that, if he eats butter and honey, he therefore knows how to reject evil and choose good? Understand that this was said because, according to the philosopher’s dictum, the same sense discerns contraries: that is, by the sense through which one contrary is distinguished, the other is also distinguished. Thus, by touch what is soft and what is rough; by taste what is sweet and what is bitter, are discerned. Butter is soft, and roughness is opposed to it; honey is sweet, and bitterness is its contrary. Therefore our Emmanuel shall eat butter and honey, so that by desiring in these things what is soft and sweet he may know how to choose good, and by the judgment of the same senses condemn what is rough and bitter—which is to reject evil.

Yet because the food of our Emmanuel is spiritual, let us see what these dishes signify, [Col. 0049B] one of which—butter—is drawn from udders, while the other—honey—is drawn from flowers. Thus, as Christ’s divinity is signified in honey, so his humanity is signified in butter. And perhaps human nature in Christ is fittingly figured by butter. For butter is rich, pleasant, meltable, and nourishing. The richness of butter refers to the mystery of the conception; its pleasantness, to the humility of the birth; its melting, to the bitterness of the Passion; its refreshment, to the sacraments of our redemption.

Does it not seem to you that, in the conception, Christ as man received a certain richness of butter, when he was anointed with the anointing of graces above his fellows; when that fatted calf was prepared in the womb of the Virgin [Col. 0049C] to renew a rich feast for the prodigal son returning from the land of unlikeness—and so rich that he might fatten with his richness all the elect invited to that feast? You may also observe the pleasantness of this butter if you recall the humility of the birth: the lodging of the manger, the cheapness of the swaddling-clothes, the food of a humble woman, and finally that he who is God blessed above all things was subject to her. O necessary pleasantness, which at once brought us both a remedy and an example! Therefore, whoever you are, if you are distressed by pains and pierced by the thorns of sins, set before yourself the pleasantness of this butter if you desire relief from pain. If nobility exalts you, nothing is more powerful than Christ. If knowledge puffs you up, nothing is wiser than he. If riches swell you, nothing is richer than he. And [Col. 0049D] yet he appeared in the world so pleasant and humbled that his own not only did not receive him when he came among them, but even despised him.

At last, this butter, melted by the fire of the Passion, poured certain drops of graces into the Church: it made some rich in charity, others pleasant in humility; it made some strong through constancy in suffering, and sanctified others by the refreshment of the sacrament. Mary Magdalene received from this butter an anointing through the richness of devotion; David, pleasantness through the virtue of humility; Peter felt its melting when he was hung on the cross through the bitterness of suffering; and all who have been reborn in Christ are refreshed through participation in his sacraments.

This butter was pressed from two udders, namely Judaism and the Gentiles, because Christ according to his human nature descended from both [Col. 0050A] peoples, becoming the cornerstone who made both one, breaking down in his flesh the middle wall of hostility (Eph. 2). For he not only descended from David’s seed according to the promise, but was also sent from the rock of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion. From the rock of the desert—that is, from the hardness and unbelief of the Gentiles. Of these udders the bridegroom speaks to the bride in the Song of Songs, saying: “Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a gazelle, feeding among lilies until the day breathes and the shadows incline” (Song of Songs 2). Of the breast of the Synagogue too it is written in the Law of Moses: “When a beast has been born, it shall be under its mother’s udder for seven days; but from the eighth day onward it may be offered to the Lord” (Lev. 22).

Here [Col. 0050B] the seven days signify the carnal life, and the eighth day the spiritual life. For as long as the children of the Synagogue served carnal ceremonies, they were like little children under the Synagogue’s breast, until Christ, appearing in the flesh, made an offering to the Lord through the newness of spiritual life. Hence Paul also says: “When it pleased him who separated me from the womb and called me through his grace to reveal his Son in me, I did not immediately yield to flesh and blood” (Gal. 1).

From these udders not only butter but also blood was pressed. For, as Solomon says: “He who presses breasts hard to draw out milk produces butter, and he who milks too violently draws out blood” (Prov. 30). This blood was drawn by Christ’s bloody persecutors, who said: “Let us lie in wait for his blood; let us hide snares against the innocent; though innocent, let us swallow him alive like hell” (Prov. 1). At last they cried out: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27). Therefore the prophet Ezekiel says concerning the blood of adulterous Jerusalem: “Her blood is in her midst; she poured it out upon a very clear rock” (Ezek. 24). “It was not poured out upon the earth so that it might be covered with dust.” For her blood was poured upon the very clear rock when men of blood exercised the wickedness of their cruelty against Christ, who is the very clear rock. “It was not,” he says, “poured out upon the earth”—that is, upon some earthly and sinful person—“so that it might be covered with dust,” that is, so that it might have any appearance of excuse on account of guilt. [Col. 0050D] You see in butter a pleasantness to be chosen as good, and in blood a harshness deservedly to be rejected as evil. Therefore our Emmanuel ate butter, that he might know how to reject evil and choose good.

Nor did our Emmanuel eat butter only, but honey also. Honey is compared with the divine nature for three reasons. For honey is cleansing, preserving, and sweet. It has sweetness in taste, cleanses corruptions, and keeps from corruption unharmed those things it receives into itself. Therefore the divine nature is cleansing honey when, by forgiving sins, it justifies the ungodly; preserving honey when, by increasing grace, it directs the righteous; and sweet honey when, in the joy of that everlasting life, it grants [Col. 0051A] a reward. You may understand from this itself that our Emmanuel, by eating honey, rejected evil and chose good: for by the nature of his divinity he both destroyed our death by dying and restored life by rising again.

The flowers from which this honey was drawn were the works of God which he performed from the beginning in order to make his power known. For the everlasting power and divinity of God—which are eternal in themselves—sprang up, as it were, in the world under the law of nature, when, as though a kind of dawn were rising, only slight traces of the Godhead appeared in creatures. This honey flowered in the time of the written Law, when, after the Law had been given, the knowledge of God became more widely known through the multitude of commandments. But the fruit of this honey appeared when, with the fullness of time at hand, our land gave its fruit, [Col. 0051B] and Christ became Emmanuel—that is, God with us—showing himself to be both God and man: God, in that he ate butter by assuming human nature; man, in that he ate honey by receiving into himself the sweetness of divinity.

Nor should it escape you that there is honey which is sweetness itself, and honey of sweetness. There is sweet honey, and there is honey that may be called sweetened. Honey as sweetness is the divinity of the Word. Honey of sweetness is the pleasantness of evangelical preaching. This honey is called “of sweetness” because evangelical preaching was uttered—or alternatively inspired—by Christ’s sweetness. Sweet honey is the spiritual understanding of the Scriptures. Sweetened honey is the subtlety of philosophical investigation.

Of the first honey [Col. 0051C] it is said: “I ate my honeycomb with my honey” (Song of Songs 5). The honeycomb with honey is humanity with divinity. Of the second honey the Lord says to Ezekiel: “Take this book and devour it, and it shall become sweet as honey in your mouth” (Ezek. 3). John too ate wild honey in the desert (Mark 1), when he offered the sweetness of evangelical preaching to unbelievers. Yet, as the historian says, the substance John used was not actually honey. He maintains that in the desert of Judaea there grows a certain low tree with whitish leaves which, when rubbed and tasted, have the flavor of honey; and he says that this was the wild honey which John ate in the desert. Yet it makes no difference, provided that evangelical [Col. 0051D] preaching is figured through such honey.

Of the third honey, which is the spiritual understanding of the Scriptures, Solomon says: “My son, have you found honey? Eat what is sufficient, lest perhaps, filled with it, you vomit it up” (Prov. 25). “Eat what is sufficient,” he says; that is, investigate the secrets of the Scriptures for edification, not for curiosity. For elsewhere Solomon says: “He who searches into majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory” (Prov. 25). The fourth honey, which I called sweetened, is mentioned in the Law when the first-fruits of honey are forbidden to be placed upon the altar of the Lord. Therefore our Emmanuel ate sweetened honey when he united divine and human nature in one person. He ate honey of sweetness when, by preaching, he made known to the world the ways of life. He ate sweet honey when he opened the mysteries of the Scriptures to his disciples. But he partly ate and partly rejected sweetened honey.

If you wish to see him eating this honey, recall that riddle of Samson: “From the eater came forth food, and from the strong came forth sweetness.” For Samson, wishing to take a wife from the land of the Philistines, killed a lion that met him on the road; and a short time afterward, returning to its corpse, he found in its mouth a swarm of bees and a honeycomb, which he removed and ate as he went on his way (Judg. 14). This Samson, taking a wife from the land of the Philistines, is Christ joining to himself the Church from the unbelief of the Gentiles. While he was on the road of this our pilgrimage, he killed the lion: when the Word [Col. 0052B] became flesh, he cast down the enemy of the human race, namely the devil. When the devil sought the food of flesh in him, he was pierced by the sting of divinity, as blessed Gregory says. The swarm of bees is the multitude of Gentile philosophers, who are said to have been in the lion’s mouth because, although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God, and therefore became reprobate and vain in their reasonings (Rom. 1). The honeycomb is the pleasantness of philosophical inquiry. Our Emmanuel ate it when it had been taken from the lion’s mouth, because he converted to the benefit of the Church, which is Christ’s body, those things well argued in the doctrines of philosophers which pertained to uprightness or to the formation of character.

Thus it is also said in the Law of the Lord that a Jew could take as wife a virgin [Col. 0052C] captured in battle after her nails and hair had been cut (Deut. 21), because a Christian who truly confesses God can take secular learning, which is signified by such a virgin, for his own instruction—provided, however, that her nails and hair have been cut off, that is, that the fictions and superfluities have been removed which were rejected by our Emmanuel in sweetened honey, since they contribute more to the subversion of hearers than to their benefit. For what profit is there in disputing about Plato’s Ideas, turning over the Dream of Scipio, or engaging in that vulgar tangle of sophisms and subtle knowledge of things, in which many, setting their end in what was not due, have perished and been destroyed? Although all these things are bitter, they seem sweet to an unhealthy palate, so much so that people are willing to acquire them at the price of revenues, a spacious estate, and finally even their lives.

O Greeks! Greeks, you are always children, and there is no mature wisdom in you. Do you not know that God has made foolish the wisdom of this world (1 Cor. 1), in which only the roots of learning are set before children, not a rule for mature persons to live well? Sweetened honey is permitted to little children; honey of sweetness is given to the weak; sweet honey is set before boys; honey as sweetness is reserved for the blessed, who in the future shall see him with bodily eyes unto glory and with spiritual eyes unto joy. May Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns, deign to grant this to us, and so forth.

## SERMON VIII. ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

[Col. 0053A]

“The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1).

For the matter of our joys it is enough that the only Son of the heavenly King, on this day, came forth from the bosom of the Father and, having become man, came into this world to seek and save what had perished; and that what the human race could not find with God through its own merits, he mercifully found in the inexhaustible treasury of his mercy. Truly, Christ Jesus was a fitting mediator for restoring peace between God and man. Joining divine and human nature in one person, he set himself between them as a middle term between two opposed extremes. In this middle [Col. 0053B] term, when the extremes themselves—God and man—met in harmonious agreement through union, God the Father offered the human race, as it were, a kiss of reconciliation.

For, to speak by analogies of things, the Word of God is the Father’s mouth, by which he spoke to the world; the assumed manhood is the mouth of the human race, which, according to human nature, is humanity’s advocate and intercedes for us. Thus mouth is joined to mouth and a kiss is made, because human nature is personally united to the Word and the mystery of the Incarnation is completed. Because of this mediation the Son of God is also rightly called the Word: for, just as a human word intervenes as a middle term in conducting affairs and deciding cases, so in the case between God and man the Son of God was mediator, because, having removed hostilities, [Col. 0053C] he brought God the Father and humanity back into agreement.

Or the Son of God is called the Word for another reason. A word by its nature is perceived not by sight but by hearing. Let us see, then, how this Word sounded in many ways and came through hearing even to the human heart. At one time it sounded in a secret whisper in the minds of the Fathers through spiritual revelation; to them the mystery of Christ’s Incarnation was revealed, which the other carnal persons could not hear. At another time this Word sounded in jubilation, namely among those angelic spirits who, from the beginning, rejoiced with inexpressible joy in the Word of God. For jubilation is a sound of spiritual joy which, because of its greatness, cannot be explained in words. Hence the Lord says in Job: “Where were you, when all the sons of God praised me and the morning stars shouted for joy?” (Job 38).

Today it sounds in song, when holy Church rejoices and sings a spiritual song concerning the generation of the Word of God, not only eternal but temporal as well. For concerning his eternal generation we heard the Church’s song in the night offices, when it sang: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son” (Ps. 2). And elsewhere: “With you is dominion on the day of your power, in the splendors of the saints” (Ps. 109). Likewise concerning his human generation we heard the Church’s song saying: “A child is born to us, and a son is given to us” (Isa. 9). And there: “The kindness and humanity of God our Savior appeared” (Titus [Col. 0054A] 3). Finally, all the sons of God who spiritually rejoice in Christ’s birth sing this song today. But those who rejoice in the foolish joy of this world—namely in pleasures of the flesh, in revelries, and in the pomp and pride of this life—sing the old song, not the new; in it they render service not to the Son of God who has been born, but to the enemy of the human race.

This Word of which we have spoken, therefore, became flesh. By the name “flesh” is signified not merely man but weak man, by reason of likeness. For flesh is a frail thing, readily subject to corruption: now it is cut, now burned, now crushed, or else fails through some other suffering. Thus the Word of God became flesh—that is, a weak man for us, like ourselves in weakness—because he assumed the form of our frailty. Nor was any other form fitting for him to assume, because he had come into this world to visit the sick. Just as a skilled physician, entering to visit a sick person, assumes the bearing of one who suffers with him so that the sick person may be relieved. For if he enters the sickroom laughing, clapping his hands, and displaying foolish merriment, he does not cure the patient but makes him worse.

For another reason also, he came to weak humanity more in the form of one who suffers with us than in the form of majesty. The form of majesty is terrible and a sign of vengeance to be exacted. The form of humility, however, is a sign of compassionate pity. Compassion naturally proceeds from the fountain of God’s mercy; vengeance comes from God’s justice as though from a distance. Therefore the Son, who appeared in the flesh not to carry out vengeance but to show compassion, chose to display to us a humble rather than a terrible form. Recognize a very similar instance of what we have said: a mother at one time nurses, feeds, and cherishes her child, and at another beats and rebukes that same child; yet feeding and nourishing proceed more from the tenderness of a mother’s breast than beating and rebuking. The former she does by natural affection; the latter when provoked by the child. So too the Son of God naturally displays mercy to us; when provoked by our crimes, he brings vengeance. Hence in Isaiah he says with lament that he will bring vengeance upon guilty men: “Alas! I will console myself upon my enemies; I will take vengeance upon [Col. 0054D] my foes” (Isa. 1).

The Word is also said to have become flesh because Christ’s humanity nourishes and feeds after the likeness of flesh. The bites, as it were, of this flesh are his conception, birth, Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension, by which the soul is spiritually fed while it holds in mind faith in the birth, Passion, and the other things that we have mentioned. This flesh—that is, Christ’s humanity—when spiritually eaten, presents us with the taste and food of diverse kinds of flesh. If you live among people innocently and gently in likeness to Christ, you have eaten the flesh of the Lamb. If, set in authority, you take diligent care of your flock in likeness to Christ, carefully providing them spiritual and temporal things, you have eaten the flesh of the ram. If you suffer injuries and tribulations for Christ, if you crucify your flesh with its vices and desires as Christ too was crucified, you have eaten the flesh of the calf. If, in holy devotion, you bear the people’s sins up to heaven, interceding for them, you have eaten the flesh of the scapegoat. If by contemplation you penetrate heavenly things, dwell among angels, and cling to God, becoming as it were one spirit with him, you have eaten the flesh of the dove. If you sigh from weariness of the present life and from love of the future life which you long for, as did the one who said: “Alas for me, because my sojourn has been prolonged” (Ps. 119), you have eaten the flesh of the turtle-dove. Thus in Christ’s flesh—that is, in his humanity—we find both compassion and refreshment.

We may also understand in another way the statement, “The Word became [Col. 0055B] flesh.” For the Word of God morally has bones and likewise flesh. The bones of the Word are virtues and spiritual gifts, by which the soul is strengthened for righteousness. The flesh of the Word is bodily goods, by which the body is refreshed for comfort. Thus, in spiritual persons the Word is spirit: they love the Son of God for his own sake and, despising temporal goods, cling to him in righteousness and holiness. In lovers of this world the Word becomes flesh: they do not love the Son of God for his own sake but for the temporal goods received from him; abandoning all spiritual sweetness, they cling to temporal goods with their whole purpose.

Does it not seem to you that the Word has become flesh in those who, merely participants in the Christian name, devote every effort to the pleasures of this life, revelries and drunkenness, fleshly enticements, and the gathering of wealth? Does it not seem to you that the Word has become flesh in those who, living from the estate of the Crucified, feed from it not the poor but dogs, hawks, and entertainers, and spend it on wicked and sacrilegious uses which it would be shameful to describe and might perhaps scandalize their hearers?

O wretched soul, you who have settled so stubbornly upon these temporal goods through love, learn what you ought to do from the man who carries a hawk on his left hand in order to cast it to the right and thus take the prey for which he has laid snares. For if he lets it fly to the left, he gains nothing but loses his labor and expense. So you also, worldly person, whose heart rests in affection upon the left [Col. 0055D] hand—that is, temporal goods—make your hawk, that is, your mind, fly to the right—that is, to gain eternal life—so that it may pass from left to right as you spend temporal goods on pious causes; and thus attain that highest blessedness signified by the right hand. For in this manner too the Word became flesh and dwells in us, when we so love temporal goods that by spending them we strive to attain heavenly things.

For through virtue the Word dwells in us, as Paul says: “That Christ may dwell through faith in our hearts” (Eph. 7). But you, whoever desire to have Christ dwelling in you and have prepared for him the house of your conscience through faith, examine carefully whether faith lives in you through charity; for thus Christ dwells in you. If your faith is without charity, your faith is dead, and thus Christ is dead in you. Therefore let no one flatter himself on the ground of a good hope, displaying outwardly a form of piety in good works, if his conscience is guilty, if he burns inwardly with fleshly desires, if he is inwardly possessed by hatred, envy, and the other spiritual vices. For Christ is not fed by outward good works that are not formed by the richness of charity. And just as a dead man, if delicate foods are offered him, does not receive them for nourishment, so the Son of God rejects good works done by evil people which do not tend toward a good end.

There are three things that drive a man from his material house: smoke, dripping water, and a quarrelsome woman. These same three, understood spiritually, drive Christ from our hearts. Smoke, then, is the vanity of temporal things, which vanish like smoke through changeability, mortality, or every sort of failure: riches, honors, nobility, beauty, and the power of this age, and other such things, which lovers of the world love beyond all measure as though they were everlasting. As these pass away like smoke, filling the human heart with bitterness, they drive Christ the indweller out of the conscience.

Certainly, whatever appears useful, beautiful, or pleasant in this world may be compared to an actor, who takes upon himself now the gestures of a happy man and now those of a grieving man, so that he seems at one time overcome by great joy and at another by great sorrow. Yet anyone who knows him thoroughly will judge him foolish and almost mad in either gesture. In the same way these temporal goods show us the appearance of an actor: by their beauty and usefulness they draw us into foolish joy, and by their failure they induce our minds to sadness. Therefore whoever has a sound eye of the mind ought so to direct his gaze toward temporal things as to prefer despising them to loving them. For “if anyone loves this world, the love of God is not in him” (1 John 2).

By the dripping water that drives a man from his house are understood words of discord and detraction. For just as drops of water, when they penetrate the roof, do not allow those on whom they fall to be at rest, so words of this kind [Col. 0056D] drive a man from peace of mind when malicious people hurl them against others. From them discords are nourished, the simple are stirred up, the discerning are troubled, the impatient quarrel, and malicious persons derive fuel for their malice. Thus, by such dripping water, that peace of mind which is God is driven out of a person, because God dwells only in peace, as it is written: “His place came to be in peace” (Ps. 74). Therefore whoever wishes to have the Word of God dwelling in him must protect his house with the roof of patience, so that this dripping may run down from the roof onto the ground; thus the repose protected by the virtue of patience is not disturbed by malicious words.

The quarrelsome woman who drives a man from his house is our flesh, always warring against the soul through fleshly desires. For “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5). This quarrelsome woman—that is, our flesh—drives Christ from our hearts when fleshly thoughts, delight in temporal things, and love of this world’s pleasures rule in us. If, therefore, you wish to test whether Christ dwells in you, consider whether corrupt affections prevail in you and whether you make provision for the flesh in its desires. For if you are subject to passions of this sort, you have driven from your house, to your own confusion, Christ whom you received as a guest.

Conversely, Christ dwelling in your house—that is, in your heart—has companions: peace, patience, charity, long-suffering, kindness, goodness, self-control, [Col. 0057B] chastity, and the other virtues which, according to Paul’s testimony, belong to the fruit of the Spirit. If you possess them, Christ has a dwelling in you and remains with you through these companions until the end of life, so that he for whom you prepared a dwelling in this present life may grant you eternal blessedness in the life to come. May Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns, deign to grant this to us, and so forth.

## SERMON IX. ON THE EPIPHANY OF THE LORD

The greatness of today’s solemnity commands us to meet our King, still little and delicate, with festive joys and also to prepare magnificent gifts befitting both his tender age and the divine majesty remaining in [Col. 0057C] him. Indeed, we are bound to render him such service. For “he has gone before us in blessings of sweetness” (Ps. 20), himself first offering and bestowing gifts upon us, so that by such generosity he might commend his love to devout minds. This is clearly shown if we wish to consider the benefits of this day, called Epiphany, and of the other solemnities which we have now commemorated as past—namely, the Nativity and the Circumcision.

On the day of his birth Christ bestowed on us the gift of poverty, because, born poor and lowly into this world, he had nowhere to lay his head. On the day of his Circumcision he bestowed on us the gift of his weakness, when he, fulfilling the commandment of the Law by the sign of Circumcision (Luke 9), endured in the flesh through experience the pains and distresses of human weakness. On this day he offered us the gift of humility, when he, King of heaven and Lord, humbled himself so far before his servant John as to deign to receive from him the sacrament of baptism (John 3).

Let us now consider the three gifts by which Christ, coming to us, wished to enrich those enrolled in his service: poverty, weakness, and humility. Behold, the wages are ready. But let a good imitator of Christ and lover of poverty now come forward—one who does not wish to possess estates or slaves, offices or dignities; who rejects riches already held and despises those offered. Let him, I say, come forward and receive this glorious gift of poverty offered him by the Lord. But there is no one who wishes to serve his King under the banner [Col. 0058A] of poverty, because everyone judges it disgraceful to be wrapped in rags with Christ and, pressed by want, to lie in the manger of the Lord his God.

At least now let some lover of weakness be found—the weakness which Christ wished to assume for us—who willingly endures pains and distresses for his name, hunger and thirst, labors and dangers; who, when insulted, does not answer with a curse, and who opposes the thorn of patience to every injury. For in all these things is displayed the zeal of the servant faithfully imitating his Lord, who did all these things. And certainly everyone shakes his hands free of this gift, because it seems to bring more burden than honor.

But perhaps some devout person will receive that chief gift of humility, which we named third in number; and through it a person will become dear to God and to human beings, humbling himself under the mighty hand of God (1 Pet. 2), subject to every human creature for Christ’s sake, desiring to minister to all (1 Pet. 5) and to receive ministry from no one, choosing to be cast down in the house of my God rather than reign in the tents of sinners (Ps. 83). Yet no one appears eager even for this gift, because he has in himself the misery of human dregs, a love of exaltation rather than subjection; nor is there anyone who wishes to minister with Christ provided that he may be judged greater than others.

It is clear, I think, that there are many servants of this King if they are invited to riches, honors, and the delights of this world, but very few if they are invited to endure miseries, pains, [Col. 0058C] and every kind of abasement for his name—at least if anyone is willing to observe human failings with keen attention.
