For just as an entire building collapses when its foundation is weak, so, when the conscience is sick, the works of outward conduct are very corrupt or altogether fruitless.

Let us now look to the root of a tree. When it is green and sound, its trunk is strong, its branches spread wide, and its foliage is dense; flowers and suitable fruits also come from it in their proper season. But if the tree’s root is dry, its trunk stands useless, its branches are leafless and withered, without hope of flowers and fruit to come.

As, then, we apply to ourselves the comparison we have introduced: [Col. 0058D] a good root is a good conscience; a weak root, a weak conscience. The former loves God above all things; the latter loves the world above all things. Offer poverty to a weak conscience, and it does not accept it, because love of the world and poverty do not agree; nor does it embrace pains and miseries, because lovers of the world do not desire such things. Again, a weak conscience rejects humility, because it wishes to appear exalted in the world; whereas a good conscience seeks poverty, because its desire lies not in riches but in God. It loves to bear labours and troubles for God, because it seeks not the rest of men but that which is in God. It also loves humility, because this is the way that leads to God and comes from God. Therefore, if we are to love those gifts which our Redeemer has set before us, it is necessary that we have a pure [Col. 0059A] conscience. For such as the root is, such also is the fruit; and such as the conscience is, such is its work. A clean conscience never performs a wicked work; a weak conscience never performs a great work. For even if it seems to do great things, they are nevertheless not great, because they are done neither with a good disposition nor a good intention. But God weighs the affection rather than the amount, as it is written.

Hence it is that in the Lord’s vineyard—which is the Church—many labour much, give many alms, make pilgrimages, pray, and fast, and yet make little progress. Others labour little and do few outward things, and yet, because they are pure in heart, accomplish much; and, to state more plainly what I think, many who glory in their works have been sunk more deeply into the abyss of hell, because [Col. 0059B] they followed the appearance of works rather than purity of conscience. For purity of conscience itself is the storehouse of virtues and good works, from which everyone who wishes to please God must bring forth gifts for His service.

Of this, too, the three magi or kings who came from the East and, at the Lord’s birth, received the first fruits of the Spirit, offered gold, frankincense, and myrrh; and they taught us that we too must offer these to God. For this is no ignoble example, since it is commended to us by royal authority. They offered, I say, the gold of precious goodwill, the frankincense of devout prayer, and the myrrh of laborious action. These three are understood through the three gifts just mentioned, for the following reason: gold shines, frankincense gives fragrance, and myrrh is bitter. [Col. 0059C] Therefore, by gold is signified right intention, because of the fire of charity shining within it; by frankincense, prayer, because of the fragrance or affection of devotion; by myrrh, a good work, because of the bitterness of labour.

Three kings offer these gifts. The first is the vigour of reason; the second, the command of sacred instruction; the third, the ray of divine inspiration. It is expedient for us in this mortal life to be ruled and governed by these kings. If you ask reason what we must offer God, it answers you: a pure will, holy prayer, and good action. The commandment of God and inspiring grace will proclaim the same. These kings come from the East, because in reason the sun rises for us through the judgment of discernment; in God’s command, the sun rises for us through the illumination of truth; in inspiring grace [Col. 0059D] the sun rises for us through the infusion of virtue. If anyone wishes to call these kings magi because of the greatness of their knowledge, this does not conflict with what has been said, since whatever comes to our knowledge becomes known chiefly through the assistance of reason, the command of God, and the grace of inspiration.

We therefore offer the aforesaid gifts—namely gold, frankincense, and myrrh—to Christ in such a way that God may be glorified by us in heart, mouth, and work. And according to the saying of blessed Augustine: when we pray to God with psalms and hymns, let us hold in will and heart what we utter with our mouths, lest discord in the affection of the heart take away the power of prayer. Yet the thought of the heart is sometimes in what is said by the mouth, sometimes directed toward [Col. 0060A] what is said, sometimes beneath what is said, and sometimes contrary to what is said.

Thought is in what is said when the intention of the person praying is fixed upon the force of the psalm or other prayer and directly regards nothing else. Such prayer is living and acceptable to God, possessing merit according to the measure of devotion. Sometimes thought is carried not toward what the mouth utters, but toward something else of equal or greater worth—for example, feeding the poor, clothing the naked, or ministering to the sick. Such thought is directed toward what is said by the mouth, because it strives to obtain that very thing; and because it is moved by the Spirit of God, it does not diminish but often increases the merit of prayer.

Thought is beneath what is said by the mouth when, while a servant of God is praying, his thought falls back upon some [Col. 0060B] bodily need: for example, when after much fasting he thinks while praying of refreshment; after many vigils, of sleep; or in sickness, of his own pain. Because this thought is prompted by a certain necessity without sin, it does not altogether take away the power of prayer. Yet because it regards natural things and does not merit above nature, it partly diminishes the merit of the person praying. This thought is beneath what is said by the mouth, because it proceeds from the human spirit, whereas the spoken utterance proceeds from the Spirit of God.

But thought of the heart is contrary to what is said when, while the lips pray to God, the heart is cast down to unlawful and shameful thoughts—such as hatreds, perjuries, carnal enticements, lies, and pretences. Then the voice uttered by the mouth ought not to be called good prayer but pretence, [Col. 0060C] because feigned righteousness is double iniquity. Let us therefore see through a comparison how the affection of the heart ought to agree with the voice. Thought and prayer stand in relation to one another as a watchman keeping the night watches stands to those within a fortress. If, when an enemy force attacks, that watchman cries anxiously to those in the fortress, shouting that they should rise, wake, arm themselves, and defend themselves, but those inside do none of these things and are consequently captured by the enemy, does not the whole labour of the watchman perish? Entirely.

In the same way, the outward voice is like the watchman and guardian of the inward person. For when we utter psalms or other prayers with our mouths, we do so in order to stir the inward person to devotion, [Col. 0060D] charity, and the service of God, as though saying to him: “Awake, you who sleep; attend to yourself, and Christ will enlighten you.” If, at this voice, the heart sleeps in vices, the sound of prayer has profited nothing at all.

Nor should we perhaps judge otherwise concerning things apparently said from zeal for righteousness—for example, reproving the perverse, attacking vices, resisting evil, and the like. For in these things too purity of conscience is required, so that one intends to benefit rather than harm those to whom one speaks, and to supply fuel for concord rather than dissension. Thus this manner of speaking too is acceptable to God, so much so that He wishes both little and great ones to be zealous for righteousness and to resist malice by the word of defence, especially when falsehood prevails after truth has been oppressed, and injustice crushes equity. Hence it is written of [Col. 0061A] the simple, though holy, that as much as they profit by the example of their good conduct, so much they harm by their silence. To resist evil and correct the wicked is a singular almsgiving that extinguishes sin as water extinguishes fire; indeed, *eleemosyna* (“almsgiving”) is interpreted as “the water of God.”

There are three principal kinds of almsgiving: the distribution of temporal goods, the instruction of the ignorant, and the correction of offenders. The last, of which we have spoken, is judged superior to the others. Yet it frequently happens that the human heart deceives itself and regards as good thoughts, words, or deeds that are not in fact good. I have been pleased to demonstrate this presently by a simple example.

We heard in our childhood that a very mighty king assembled a council of men and beasts, [Col. 0061B] to determine which animal had brought forth offspring more beautiful than the rest. When this was done, a monkey came forward, dragging into the midst its young, uglier than all the others, and said that it ought to be judged beautiful above the children of men. What is more rightly understood by the monkey than a perverse heart? Though its offspring are evil thoughts, foolish speech, and perverse works, it nevertheless sometimes judges itself to feel rightly when true judgment proves it foolish.

Therefore the spirits must be tested whether they are from God (1 John 4), in this way: that we look sometimes to the beginning and sometimes to the end of the matter we propose. For the beginning of our thought is sometimes so honourable that what we intend can immediately be approved from it—for instance, when we think of saying or doing something [Col. 0061C] to which we are compelled by a divine commandment, such as believing in God or honouring father and mother. Sometimes the beginning of our thought is so vicious that it ought deservedly to be rejected at the very outset together with its end—for example, when we think of saying or doing what the law of the Lord forbids, such as murders, adulteries, and the like. But sometimes the beginnings of our thoughts are doubtful, so that good things appear evil or evil things good; in these cases judgment must be taken from the end. For, as the Wise Man says, “Prudence measures the outcomes of things.”

If the end of the deliberation you have begun is honourable to you, useful to your neighbour, and acceptable to God, judge it expedient to proceed. But if the very end of the matter prepares dishonour for you, scandal for your neighbour, [Col. 0061D] and offence to God, it is more necessary to stop at the beginning. And, to continue the matters which seem to be said from zeal for correction: even if they taste bitter outwardly, they ought nevertheless finally to tend toward concord and unity, so that, once the tumults of vice and discord have been overcome, all may preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.

For unity is the guardian of hearts; it makes friends of God even those who cannot attain perfect conduct. It is the first inhabitant of the human heart in reconciliation, and the last to carry it away justified. Moreover, the heavenly unity is signified by that one of whom it is written: “From a city from which a thousand went out, a hundred shall go out; and from which a hundred went out, ten shall go out; and from which ten went out, [Col. 0062A] one shall go out” (Amos 5). There, by the thousand is signified perfection of example; by the hundred, perfection of counsel; by the ten, perfection of commandment; and by the one, heavenly unity.

Therefore, whoever cannot possess the perfection of example possessed by the apostles and martyrs, who added something for the example of others to commandments and counsels, let him hold fast to unity, and in it he will possess God. If he cannot possess the perfection of counsel held by those who added counsels to commandments, let him hold unity. If he cannot attain perfection of commandment, so as to keep every commandment of God to the letter, let him hold unity. If he does not hold it, he loses even those other things that seemed to conduce to that life. For when the one departs from the city, barrenness and desolation remain.

[Col. 0062B] From what has now been said, unless I am mistaken, it is clear that in divine service harmony of heart and mouth is required, and likewise harmony of heart and work; and that every merit rests upon the guarding of conscience, because life proceeds from it. Therefore all ought to devote effort to this guardianship.

The old, whose course in the world is nearly finished and who have, as it were, already placed one foot outside the gate of this age, ought to do this, so that with purified mind they may enter into the joy of their Lord (Matthew 7). Those advancing in middle age, who have now drawn near to this gate, ought to do it, lest they be led along that broad way which leads to destruction. The younger too, who have completed, as it were, the middle stretch of their journeying, ought to do this, lest, overthrown by enemies, they seem to spend the remaining time of their life [Col. 0062C] in vain.

Let each examine his own life. If he has the testimony of a good conscience, let him burst forth in a confession of praise. If he is pricked by the worm of an evil conscience, let him mourn the crime he has committed; let him approach the physician and show his wounds while He is near—the One who came to heal our pains and forgive sins. Let no one trust in his youth or strength, promising himself days of repentance and the grace of reconciliation after a long time; for he who exists today may perhaps not exist tomorrow, and many who undertook long journeys came to a halt midway. What is more contrary to human nature than not to seek health in sickness, or not to desire joy in pain, especially when health is offered and joy promised?

And that joy is indeed a joy that is not turned into sorrow (Isaiah 54): singular, surpassing, the sum of all joys, which neither eye has seen nor ear heard (1 Corinthians 2), and so forth. [Col. 0062D] Let no one say in his heart that the immensity of this joy does not concern him, that the misery of his defect does not deserve it, and that he is separated from it by such a great distance through the mortality of this life. For this joy comes only to the one who has closed its entrance to himself by the stain of a wicked will.

There are those who seize this joy by force; there are those who buy it; there are those who steal it; and there are those who are compelled to it. Spiritual men seize this joy by force: despising the delights of this world, they strive to please and serve God alone. Those who buy it are rich in possessions and poor in virtues; the heavenly joy which they cannot attain by loftiness of life, they acquire for themselves through liberality in almsgiving. Those who steal this joy are those who, after sins committed, wish to approach the Lord by the hidden fruit of repentance, avoiding in all the good things they do both glory [Col. 0063A] and the gaze of men. They are rightly signified by that Gospel woman who, standing behind Him, touched the hem of the Lord’s garment and was healed (Matthew 9). Those compelled to this joy are the despised of this world, who, pressed by miseries and deprived of every human consolation, turn to God, who rejects no one, under the compulsion of necessity.

Let us therefore all approach this king, who came to us in humility in order to give us this joy and make us exalted in it. Nor ought we to reckon it a great matter if, in this present life, He makes us sharers in His poverty, weakness, and humility. For in exchange for poverty He will grant inestimable riches; in exchange for weakness, health; and in exchange for humility, glory—Jesus Christ our Lord Himself, the brightness of glory and figure of substance (Hebrews 1), whose kingdom and dominion, etc.

## SERMON X. ON THE EPIPHANY OF THE LORD

“The Lord has made known His salvation; in the sight of the nations He has revealed His righteousness” (Psalm 97).

[Col. 0063C] The mother Church, dearest brethren, calls the solemnity of this day the feast of the manifestation: first, because today, with a star as guide, God the Father wished to make His salvation—that is, His Son—more fully known; secondly, because the Son Himself showed Himself to them, humble and wrapped in swaddling-clothes, as one more worthy of adoration; or again, because in the Jordan the dove descending upon Him made known that He was the Son of God.

Thus, in the first manifestation He drew them by the example of novelty; in the second He instructed them by the example of humility; in the third—that is, in baptism—He sanctified them by the sacrament of necessity. Do you wish to see how the first manifestation drew them? A new star aroused wonder; wonder, devotion; devotion, service; service prepared them for worship. The second manifestation, which occurred in [Col. 0063D] the house, gave into our bosom “a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over” (Luke 6), because He who had first given life there taught them to live rightly. For what a model of humility He displayed to you when the King and Son of a King, taking the form of a servant, emptied Himself! What charity, do you think, when He wished to show Himself so lowly and so despised for the ungodly and sinners?

Consider each point. As at the rising of a new star the power and brightness of divinity were displayed, so, when He showed Himself as a little child to the eyes of the magi, the humility and charity of His humanity were shown. The order of our salvation undoubtedly required this work: that by humility He should conquer the proud, by charity free captive humanity, by power despoil the greedy enemy, and by brightness glorify the wretched. By humility, therefore, He taught you; by charity, He healed you; by power, He protected you; and by brightness He will glorify you hereafter.

The third manifestation was in the Jordan, when the King came to be baptized by the soldier, the Word by the herald, the Lord by the servant, the Bridegroom by the bridegroom’s friend. [Col. 0064A] And why was this? That, conferring regenerative power on the waters, He might restore innocence to fallen humanity by the forgiveness of sins, confer righteousness through the infusion of grace, and sanctify through the indwelling of the Holy Spirit. If He granted us all these things by the benefit of the sacrament, what did He grant us by the triumph of His Passion? There He prepared the way to heaven; there He opened the gate of the kingdom.

Someone may perhaps ask: since this does not perhaps come from the power of the sacrament, but from the power of the Passion alone, why did He wish to place this power in the waters of this sacrament? For the present, if you please, setting aside other reasons, we may assign this one: water is found to be moist, cold, and fluid. In being moist it signifies the sin of carnality; in being fluid, the sin of vanity; in being cold, the sin of malice or iniquity. If one wishes to consider it, every kind of actual sin is included within this threefold kind of sin. You see, therefore, how reasonably this was done: water, which by its properties signified every kind of sin, having been sanctified by contact with the Lord’s body through the Holy Spirit, cleansed every kind of sin.

[Col. 0064C] You have, then, how the Lord made known His salvation: first by the sign of the star; secondly when He was adored by the magi in the house; thirdly when He was baptized in the Jordan by His servant. Thus the Lord made known His salvation. Yet God the Father first made Himself known, and afterward made His salvation known. At first God the Father wished to make Himself known as exceedingly severe and through terrors; afterward, in making His Son known, He tempered threats and terrors with the sweetness of grace.

For God the Father was made known to the first parents in a grave rebuke, saying to one: “Cursed is the earth in your work” (Genesis 3); and to the other: “In pain you shall bear children” (ibid.). He was also made known to the children of Israel by signs and wonders, when at the giving of the Law lightning was seen and thunder heard (Exodus 19). [Col. 0064D] He was made known also to the prophets through visions and dreams: everywhere terror, everywhere threat. First, in Adam and Eve, the pronouncement of a severe sentence; second, among the children of Israel, command without the assistance of grace. For the Law brought no one to perfection (Hebrews 7), because the commandment lacked assisting grace. Third, in the prophets, the obscure promise of the Saviour.

Hence it is said of the obscurity of the prophets: “His shadow covered the mountains, and His shrubs the cedars of God” (Psalm 79). The mountains are the prophets, because of the greatness of revelation; the shadow is the veil of the letter, because of obscurity. Thus the shadow covered the mountains of God when the covering of obscurity veiled the meaning of prophecy. It follows: “And His shrubs [covered] the cedars of God.” The shrubs are legal observances because of their uselessness; [Col. 0065A] the cedars, the heights of the promises made to the fathers. Thus the shrubs covered the cedars of God when the shadows of legal observance concealed the truth of God’s promise. You see, therefore, how great are the threats, terrors, and obscurities everywhere. Thus God the Father appeared to the Egyptians in blood, to Jacob in wrestling (Genesis 32), to Moses in fire (Exodus 3), and to Elijah in the whirlwind (4 Kings 2).

At last, at the end of the ages, the Lord made known His salvation, not with the rod of wrath but in the spirit of gentleness. How? In order that He might heal the broken-hearted and proclaim pardon and remission of sins to captives. Hence it is said: “In the sight of the nations He revealed His righteousness” (Isaiah 61). Whose righteousness? His own—that of the Father—or that of His salvation, that is, the Son.

[Col. 0065B] For He Himself revealed His righteousness in the sight of the nations, having innocence with respect to Himself, peace toward His neighbour, and devotion or love toward God. Do you wish to see Him innocent? “Behold, I have walked in my innocence” (Psalm 25). Do you wish to see Him peaceable toward His neighbour? “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you” (John 14). Do you wish to see Him devout? “And being in agony, He prayed more earnestly” (Luke 22). Jesus began first to do and afterward to teach all these things, when He wished to reveal His righteousness in the sight of the nations.

But what innocence can man possess, since he is dust and ashes? I speak of myself to myself. How shall I keep innocence and behold equity—I who have so often been wounded by the darts of desire, torn apart by envy, and ruined by vain [Col. 0065C] glory? How often have I scandalized my brother by a sign, slandered him in word, grieved him in deed? Yet to me, as to the rest, it has been said: “Keep innocence and behold equity” (Psalm 36).

Therefore, dearest brethren, our innocence ought not indeed to consist in being without sin, but in not serving sin. For whoever desires sin is a slave of sin; and every mortal sin is service rendered to our adversary. Therefore, good man, you who have put your hand to the plough and received the Lord’s sweet yoke and light burden, you, I say, need battle if you wish to rejoice in innocence. If perhaps carnal desire has invaded your soul, remember the Scripture which says: “Death is set beside the entrance of pleasure.” For when the ancient enemy has opened the gate of the heart to unlawful pleasure, he is already secure concerning the fruit of the whole tree whose root he has wounded with the poison of wicked pleasure.

For as it is said by the prophetic voice, “Blood has touched blood” (Hosea 4), so one sin draws and introduces another. When first, as though from outside, an evil thought strikes the mind, delight follows; and delight, set in the light, sometimes relaxes even a manly mind. Thirdly, consent weakens; fourthly, action stains; fifthly, habit binds; sixthly, contempt casts down. These are the steps by which, in an easy descent, one reaches the gates of death. Indeed, “easy is the descent to Avernus.” Therefore, halt your step at the perception of pleasure if you wish to escape danger.

[Col. 0066A] Attend carefully to how Abraham fought and how Paul proved strong in temptation. This assault reaches not only the imperfect but even the perfect. What, then, do you suppose is meant by what is written: that while Abraham enjoys conversation with angels, Sarah laughs in the tent (Genesis 18), though when rebuked by the angel she merits the promise of a son?

Abraham therefore enjoys conversation with angels whenever a devout soul attends to prayer and gives itself to holy desire. But meanwhile Sarah laughs behind the tent-door when the flesh, resisting the spirit, suggests unlawful delights. Later, when rebuked, she received the promise concerning a son, because, when the flesh has been restrained by the spirit, the body too will receive its reward in the future. As the prophet also says: “My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God” (Psalm 83).

Likewise, when Paul is delivered from the danger of the sea, he is attacked by a serpent on land; but quickly repelling the danger, he shook the beast from his hand, and thereby escaped the poison. [Col. 0066B] Who, do you think, is Paul delivered from the sea (Acts 28), if not the good cloistered man who is rescued from the malice of the world, and who, when he wishes to put wood on the fire, sees a serpent come forth from that very wood? While he wishes to consume former evils by the flame of charity, the source of temptation is generated from the very recollection of evils. What, then, must be done? He must quickly shake his hand—that is, deny the consent of action to the evil suggestion.

What more need be said? If, cleaving to Christ’s footsteps, you wish to maintain continual innocence, you must have discord not only with the flesh but also with the other vices. But what shall I say concerning peace and concord? “Great peace have those who love Your law, and there is no stumbling-block for them” (Psalm 118). Two things especially ought to invite us to peace and concord: the greatness of the reward and consideration of a lower creature.

Of the greatness of the reward it is said: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the children of God” (Matthew 5). What could be greater than this promise? For if children, then heirs also (Romans 8). Consideration of a lower creature should also draw us, so that, if we wish to be peaceable after the example of our Redeemer, we may at least take a pattern of life from irrational beasts.

[Col. 0066D] For while all other things preserve harmony by a certain law of nature, man alone, through pride, contrary to peace, brings insult upon his Creator. O pride, greatest sin, deadly plague, singular evil! From you comes the beginning of every sin (Ecclesiasticus 10); in you also those redeemed by Christ’s blood suffer every punishment anew. Every other iniquity is exercised in evil works so that they may be done; but you lie in wait for good works so that they too may perish. As a shoot grafted upon a trunk draws to itself all the moisture of the earth and all the vitality of the tree, and turns the fruit of the whole tree to its own nature, so whatever good works you do, if the plant of pride is present, it corrupts the whole mass.

[Col. 0067A] The ant first left us a living example of peace and concord: when it finds its companion perhaps laden beyond measure, it lightens her burden with a certain natural charity, lest her small body, weighed down by too great a load beyond its strength, fail. Thus cranes, arranged in the air in an ordered formation, restore with a kind of social kindness the one flying ahead and, as it were, bearing the onrush of the wind: when she is already weary, they place her in the rear position and protect her from the violence of the winds as though beneath their wings. When a multitude of deer wishes to change its place, each places its head upon the back of another, so that the one going before bears all, while the last seems supported by all; and in this manner, succeeding one another and bearing each other’s burdens, they fulfil in their own way the law of Christ.

Let us conform ourselves in this respect to the beasts of the earth, so that what our impenitent heart refuses to receive from the benefit of its Creator, it may at least discover in a lower creature to its own shame. Yet do you wish to be instructed by the example of your Saviour? Hear Him saying: “I will seek that which was lost; I will bring back that which had been cast away; I will bind up that which was broken; I will heal that which was weak” (Ezekiel 34). [Col. 0067B] And Isaiah says of Him: “Behold, your Saviour comes, and His reward is with Him” (Isaiah 62).

Therefore, dearest brethren, admonished by so many examples and invited by so great a reward, let not consideration of one’s own strength flatter; let not awareness of another’s weakness exalt; let not the pursuit of hostile slander divide. For consideration of one’s own strength does not wish to have a companion; awareness of another’s weakness produces contempt; the poison of slander grows into hatred. Let us learn to humble ourselves for God’s benefits, to have compassion on the weaknesses of others, and to console those who despair in the Lord, so that we may thus dwell in one house with one disposition. Behold, we have said something concerning the preservation of innocence, and likewise concerning peace and concord.

The third topic was love of God, in which lies the perfection of every virtue. Hence, to the person wishing to possess eternal life, the Lord first set forth the commandment of love, when He said: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, all your soul, all your strength, and all your mind” (Deuteronomy 6). “Do this,” says the Lord, “and you shall live” (Luke 10). See how in these words life, heart, soul, strength, and mind are four things. By the heart, indeed, we are contrite over sins; by the soul, we are made alive; by strength, we are exercised; by the mind, we are raised upward.

[Col. 0067D] The person who loves God with his whole heart mourns and laments his sins with every affection of the heart, leaving nothing unshaken, according to the prophet’s counsel: “Pour out your heart like water before the Lord” (Lamentations 3). For as, when water is poured out, nothing remains in the vessel, so where there is true contrition nothing ought to remain hidden in the secret place of conscience.

Likewise, the person loves God with all his strength who applies himself with all his powers to good works: not rash in beginning, not lukewarm in acting, not negligent in omitting, lest perhaps, having begun in the Spirit, he be completed in the flesh. Of such persons it is said: “They rise up to the heavens and descend to the depths.” He loves God with all his mind [Col. 0068A] who, as though made higher than the world, has trampled underfoot all earthly things and turns himself, with the whole desire of his mind, only to the things of God. But not all receive this word.

He loves God with all his soul who perseveres in holy conduct as long as he lives. For by the soul we live, as I have already said. These four are, as it were, steps by which one ascends into heaven: contrition of heart frees from sin; the exercise of virtue appeases the offence against God; elevation of mind, or contemplation, strengthens by the taste of sweetness; perseverance in good confirms, so that neither angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor hunger, nor sword, nor things present, nor depth, nor any creature may separate us from the charity of God (Romans 9), until we comprehend with all the saints where He reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XI. ON THE EPIPHANY OF THE LORD

“We have from the holy Scriptures” (1 Corinthians 2) that adults are to be fed with solid food, but little children with milk; and from this it is signified to us that simple hearts are to be instructed by simple speech, whereas those of subtle intellect and great learning are to be instructed by a higher power of the Word of God. Since many of you have greatly surpassed the understanding of little children through extensive knowledge of the Scriptures, I am pleased at present to break the bread of God’s word for little ones in a humble manner of speaking. For just as it is superfluous to give to those who do not need, so it is miserly to withhold from those who do need.

[Col. 0068C] Let the rusticity of the style cause no one contempt, or an ear itching with indignation; for contemptible chests sometimes contain precious treasure, earthen vessels delicious foods, and unadorned speech is sometimes filled with much sweetness of edification and spiritual delight. Nor can defects of expression diminish the gifts of the supreme Rewarder, provided there is no defect in the affection of sincere will. He crowned the equal devotion of the three magi with an equal reward, although the gifts they offered—gold, frankincense, and myrrh—were unequal in value. If we take the beginning of our speech from these gifts, they provide us with ample material for casting out nets for a catch, because they are full of divine mysteries.

For by gold a king, by frankincense God, and by myrrh a mortal man are mystically signified: Christ Jesus Himself, who was born of the Virgin. Look now, O soul, upon your Saviour: how exalted He is, how humble—He who in Himself is the almighty King and eternal God, yet for you deigned to become mortal man. Certainly, if you wish to look upon Him with the eye of a purified mind, you will see that inasmuch as He is King, He threatens and strikes; inasmuch as He is God, He justifies and crowns; and inasmuch as He is mortal, He admonishes and instructs. You also, then, render to man what belongs to man, to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and to God what belongs to God: that is, to the King, fear and spiritual soldiery; to God, love and veneration; and to the mortal man who wished to undergo death for you, thanks and requital.

[Col. 0069A] He has gone very far from God and forgotten himself who does not fear this King so mighty—indeed, who does not tremble at His remembrance—because He terrifies with unbearable threats and inflicts incurable blows without mercy, sparing neither age nor condition, always holding the sword extended and punishing transgressors according to their crimes. Therefore let lovers of this world look upon this King coming to them in great wrath, and fear the indignation of One who threatens so cruelly and strikes so harshly. Let all who are choked by pleasures and carnal desires look upon this King and fear the sight of One who threatens so cruelly. Let all those who have entered the broad way of destruction through every kind of iniquity look upon this King and fear [Col. 0069B] One who threatens so cruelly and strikes so harshly.

For He not only threatens, but subjects them to punishments without mercy and without mitigation, as the Prophet testifies when he says: “There is no regard”—that is, mercy—“for their death; and firmness”—that is, strength and stability—“is in their affliction” (Psalm 72). And rightly so, because in their life they refused to subject themselves, with holy men, to labours and hardships for God. Therefore they are not punished with them in time, but are instead reserved for the torment of demons in the future. And this is what follows: “They are not in the labour of men”—that is, of the just—in this life; “and therefore they shall not be scourged with men”—that is, with the just—in the present life.

We wish to set before you an example, if perhaps the remembrance of a likeness may persuade where the weak power of our speech cannot [Col. 0069C]. There was a man who planted a tree beside the course of a river flowing with great force and speed. It grew, became lofty, and was adorned with many little branches; its fruit also was beautiful and pleasant to eat. A traveller came by, passing that way. Drawn by the sweetness of its fruit, he climbed into it; and while, resting upon the branches of the same tree, he greedily delighted in its fruit, troublesome birds came and persistently gnawed at the branch on which he leaned. While the wretched man was wholly intent upon plucking fruit, the branch supporting him, gnawed through by the birds, was torn away; and the man fell into the river and, [Col. 0069D] swept along by that river’s current, was swallowed in its depths.

The man who planted the tree is God; the tree is the world. Its little branches signify the lifespans of all creatures, each in its kind; its fruit, every care and pleasure of this age in which lovers of this world gladly occupy themselves. The traveller is the human being, who passes swiftly away like smoke. The river is to be understood as the rush of death; the birds are the years and days by which human life is continually gnawed away and tends toward its end. Therefore, while a person rests upon one of these branches, promising himself a longer span of life, and plucks and gathers the delights of this world, he is led into forgetfulness of his salvation; suddenly he is cut off from this life, falls into the river of death, and, carried along swiftly, is at last plunged into hell.

For just as, in the days [Col. 0070A] of Noah, people were eating and drinking and taking wives, and were swallowed up by the sudden waters of the flood; and just as in the days of Lot, while people were building and planting (Matt. 24) and intent upon the pleasures of this life, sulphur and fire suddenly came upon them from heaven, and all who were in the cities of Sodom perished: so those who, despising the fear of God, entangle themselves in the cares and delights of this age are, as if unawares, torn from their very pleasures by the peril of death. Descending to the lower world, they carry nothing with them except their sins. Oh, how many, too intent upon the fruit of this tree, have forgotten God who saved them, descending like a stone into the deep! And the examples lie openly before us.

For when a man has become rich and abounding [Col. 0070B] in the goods of this life, he often accounts this alone as his portion: that he may use the days which God has granted him for repentance by making provision for the flesh in its desires. If he is noble and powerful, bearing a name alongside the names of the great who are on earth, then his chief concern is to sport with the birds of heaven, to follow the carefree ways of courtiers, and with dogs to range freely among wild beasts. If, perhaps, he has a more subtle intellect for investigating the Scriptures, then, often setting aside the law of the Lord, spotless and converting souls (Ps. 18), he strives with every study to know how to square the circle and to prove that it is impossible to traverse the stadium. Or indeed, by many studies and vigils, he devises a soul which the Most High God did not create, fashioning it out of divisible and indivisible substance, out of [Col. 0070C] a nature at once the same and different; yet he neither governs nor keeps unstained his own soul, made in the image of God and capable of that highest and blessed divinity, because of such cares and useless inquiries, which can bring no one to eternal life. Truly, the fear of the heavenly King is not in such persons; these are not the arms by which spiritual warfare is discharged to the supreme Emperor. Rather, these and things like them are weapons of iniquity, by which one serves demons better than God.

Let us recall, if you please, with what arms David, carrying on warfare for the heavenly King, fought against Goliath—that is, the devil (1 Sam. 17). We read [Col. 0070D] that, when David was about to fight Goliath, he put on Saul’s armour, which suited the warfare of this world; but he laid it aside because it was burdensome, and, taking a sling with a stone, overcame and killed the Philistine.

Certainly, Saul signifies any worldly person who seems to possess some importance in the judgement of those who savour earthly things—for example, if he is rich, powerful, noble, or has attained the wisdom of this world beyond others. Saul’s arms are the cares and occupations of this life and the appetite for pleasures, all of which the nations seek. But David—that is, any spiritual man—when about to fight against Goliath, that is, the devil, lays aside Saul’s heavy arms: that is, casting away all by which one serves this world in fear of the eternal King, and taking up [Col. 0071A] a sling with a stone, he strikes down the Philistine.

The stone is God’s commandment; the sling is holy meditation, which always holds God’s command in mindful recollection; and the hand which swings the sling signifies good action. For one who intends rightly to serve the heavenly King must meditate upon God’s law day and night (Ps. 1), and must carry out by living devoutly, through good works, what he has conceived in holy meditation. Therefore, with these arms—namely, divine commandments, holy meditation, and good action—we must serve the heavenly King.

As Scripture says elsewhere: “The sun and moon stood in their habitation; they shall go in the light of thy arrows, in the brightness of thy flashing spear” (Hab. 3): that is, in the brightness of good action shining from afar. The sun and moon—that is, Christ [Col. 0071B] and the Church—stood in their habitation. The elect in the Church shall go forward—that is, make progress—in the light of thy arrows, that is, in the righteousness of thy commandments; in the brightness of thy flashing spear, that is, in the brightness of good action shining from afar.

And let not the labour of this warfare terrify you who fear the heavenly King, for this King’s gifts are generous and his rewards generous. If you ask what they are, the answer is readily given: he gives each of his soldiers a denarius. Or if you judge this a small gift, he sets before you all the riches of his glory; indeed, he gives according to the desires of your heart, so that you may possess them in your delights—provided only that his fear always remains with you and that you do not cease to serve him by living justly and devoutly. Yet the fear of this King is not to be set as [Col. 0071C] the limit of our hope, because the King himself is God, to whom we owe love: namely, that we should love him above all things and, for his sake, embrace all else with the affection of charity.

This love of charity is spiritual fire, as the Lord himself says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12). And the Prophet says: “My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation fire blazes forth” (Ps. 38). Material fire, as you know, has three properties: burning, heat, and brightness. It burns what is in it, warms what is near it, and illuminates what is far away. This spiritual fire does likewise. The fire of charity burns up the vices that are in a person through penitence [Col. 0071D] and true contrition; it warms those who are near through the word of life and spiritual consolation; it illumines those far from the way of righteousness through good action.

Therefore, the soul that loves God must first consume, with the fire of charity, the vices it finds in itself contrary to the divine will. Following the Apostle’s saying, we say that these are three: wood, hay, and stubble (1 Cor. 3). Wood is perverse action; hay, wicked speech; stubble, disordered thought. Perverse deeds must therefore be consumed with the fire of charity, because they build hell for the soul that is perishing. For a perverse act is either unjust—that is, contrary to equity, and it takes away from a person his neighbour—or unchaste, and it takes away from a person himself; or else hypocritical, and [Col. 0072A] it takes away God from a person.

Likewise, wicked speech must be burned with this fire. For it is either superfluous, lacking usefulness and reason; or slanderous, in gnawing away at neighbours; or flattering, in the pouring out of that false oil of which it is written: “Let not the oil of the sinner make fat my head” (Ps. 140). Similarly, whoever loves God with pure love must destroy disordered thoughts, because they separate a person from God, and the Holy Spirit cannot have a dwelling in a conscience wounded by attachment to disordered thought.

There are three kinds of thoughts that chiefly wage war against our souls. Either the thoughts of our heart are foul and shameful, and [Col. 0072B] have their origin in lust; or transitory things are excessively desired or retained, having their origin in avarice; or human hearts are swollen against their neighbours or raised above them, having their origin in pride. Altogether blessed is the person who has stumbled in none of these thoughts, because they are what make all—or nearly all—the inhabitants of this pilgrimage depart from the way of righteousness.

Since these thoughts are more hostile to the human heart than others, the Prophet, commanded by the Lord to search the conscience of a person, makes especial mention of them, since they more frequently intrude upon the human heart and leave a person with greater difficulty. For when the Lord had said to Ezekiel, “Dig through the wall,” the same prophet shortly afterwards adds: “I saw, and behold, [Col. 0072C] every likeness of animals and creeping things, and the idols of the house of Israel, were depicted on the wall” (Ezek. 8).

This wall, which the Lord commanded to be dug through, is the darkness of conscience. A person’s dulled perception is sometimes unable to penetrate it, because, driven far from the light of truth by the weight of sins, he does not know how to recognize his evils, understand his sins, or mourn the infirmities by which he is oppressed, so that he may return to the Lord and the Lord may forgive him. This indeed is the wall by which very many, who think themselves religious and just, have been shut out from the way of salvation, because they do not know themselves; having become blind, “they wandered in a trackless place and not in a way” (Ps. 106).

When this wall is therefore pierced through, the likenesses of animals and creeping things, and idols, are found depicted [Col. 0072D] upon it. For when a person strives more subtly to examine the hidden recesses of his heart, he finds there the abominations of thoughts that separate from God, depicted there in manifold attachment: thoughts of lust, signified by likenesses of animals; thoughts of avarice, signified by likenesses of creeping things, since they bend altogether toward the earth; and thoughts of pride, rightly understood through idols. For just as humility is especially Christ’s virtue, so pride is the devil’s vice.

In cleansing the vices of thought, therefore, the soul must be watchful, because the life and fruit of outward work consist in purity of conscience. As the vigour of the whole tree proceeds from the root, so the vigour of good action proceeds from thought. We frequently see that when [Col. 0073A] a tree’s root is bad, its fruit also turns out bad; if the root is good, the fruit is good; if the root is parched and dry, its fruit is either absent or entirely fruitless. In the same way, outward action conforms to thought: evil action is built upon evil thought, good action upon good thought, and fruitless action upon parched thought.

By parched thoughts I mean vain thoughts, which arise often and in great number, not from purpose or study, but from the frivolity and instability of the human heart. Though they are not in themselves condemnable, they nevertheless either take away or diminish the fruit of good action. For as the Psalmist says: “The thought of man shall confess to thee, and the remnant of thought shall keep festival to thee” (Ps. 75). Why does thought rather confess to God than speech or action? Not because we do not also confess to God in deed and speech, [Col. 0073B] but because the power of both lies in thought. The remnant of thought is good action, which keeps festival to God, because it pleases him and he rejoices in our progress.

Once, therefore, our disordered thoughts have been consumed by the burning of charity, the one who truly loves God must send out to those about him the warmth of this fire, which is charity, so that through teaching and spiritual consolation he may call them back from love of this world and inflame them with the sweetness of the Holy Spirit.

For as the earth bears fruit according to the nature of the seed cast into it, and as a ship is directed according to the favourability of the wind that drives it, so a person is surely formed in character according to the manner of instruction by which he is [Col. 0073C] outwardly trained. For example, let us look at a ship. If it is carried by a favourable wind, it advances on its begun voyage and swiftly reaches the harbour at which the helmsman intended to arrive. But if the wind is contrary, it soon drives the ship back to the land from which the helmsman had set sail; or, what is worse, it is battered in the midst of storms until it is swallowed in the depths of the sea without hope of salvation.

In the same way, the soul guided by good teaching and rejoicing in spiritual consolation makes progress day by day and, as though borne by a favourable wind, comes to the harbour of salvation. But if it is stained with perverse conversations, which corrupt even good morals (1 Cor. 15) and separate a person from God, then, as though [Col. 0073D] the wind were contrary, it either returns to land—that is, to earthly and carnal actions—or, if an opportunity for a wicked act is lacking, it is battered inwardly by storms of temptations until it is plunged into the abyss of despair, so that at last it is swallowed in the depth of damnation.

If, therefore, you have charity within yourself, kindle it, if you can, in your neighbour. Teach him how he ought to be a guardian of conscience, a lover of discipline, diligent in the service of others, patient under injuries, ready to obey, humble in carrying out what his superiors command him. Do not let your speech with the spiritually sick be a shared conversation about their sickness: for example, with the avaricious about riches, with the ambitious about rank and honours, with the proud about eminence, with one who loves quarrels [Col. 0074A] about discord, with the carnal about lust; nor converse with the glutton about the delights of the table. For this is not to foster the warmth of charity in him, but rather to extinguish it.

Of this heavenly and spiritual edification it is written in the law of Moses: “If one of two brothers dies without offspring, the other shall take his wife and raise up the seed of his brother. If he refuses to do this, the woman shall spit in his face and remove his sandal, and his house shall be called in Israel the house of the unsandaled man” (Deut. 25). The man who died childless is Jesus Christ, because while he suffered in the flesh, his disciples did not yet believe in him. Hence that saying: “But we had hoped that he was the one who was to redeem Israel” (Luke 24).

Any one of us is his brother, because we have in common with him the identity [Col. 0074B] of the nature which he assumed from the Blessed Virgin. We must therefore beget children for our deceased brother, that is, Christ, by sowing the word of life in the hearts of our neighbours and arousing in them the affection of charity by spiritual exhortation. Whoever refuses to do this, the woman—that is, the Church—will spit in his face, because he will bear reproach in the Church. The woman will also remove his sandal.

Sandals, which are the product of a dead animal, can signify the fruit of that blessed life which Christ acquired for us with his blood, concerning which it is said: “He will revive us after two days; on the third day he will raise us up” (Hos. 6). Therefore, whoever neglects to raise up his brother’s seed by sowing the word of truth and exhorting spiritually will be unsandaled: that is, deprived of the fruit [Col. 0074C] of eternal life, he will appear before the Church and the holy angels, because he separated from the way of salvation, by perverse teaching, his brother whom he could have gained by spiritual teaching.

But while the fire of charity burns within through the fervour of devotion and gives warmth outwardly in spiritual teaching and exhortation, it must consequently also give brightness through honourable conduct and the example of good works: so that it may nourish perseverance by good example in those who do good, and those who act wickedly, illumined by the light of good works, may abandon their evils. Now this light of good works sometimes shines above the lampstand; sometimes it comes forth through glass with a dimmed light; and sometimes [Col. 0074D] it shines under a bushel, where it fails within itself, granting no benefit or advantage to anyone.

Here by lampstand we do not mean the obscurity of the Law, signified by that lampstand of Moses in which globes and lilies are described (Exod. 25); nor the subtlety of the prophets, signified by the lampstand mentioned in Zechariah, on whose top two olive trees are described (Zech. 4); nor yet evangelical truth, signified by the lampstand of which the Lord says in the Gospel: “No one lights a lamp and puts it in a hidden place, nor under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, that all who are in the house may see the light” (Luke 8). Rather, here we call the holy Church the lampstand, as John says in [Col. 0075A] the Apocalypse: “The seven stars are the seven angels, and the seven lampstands are the seven churches” (Rev. 1).

Therefore, the light of good works shines above the lampstand when those set, as it were, above the heads of others—whether through pre-eminence or through some charge of administration—preside over others with anxious care, labour for them, and provide for them with greater zeal and alacrity than they would expend upon their own affairs. Likewise, the works of those shine above the lampstand who devote themselves to works of mercy and care for others who cannot help themselves in their needs. And, in general, all shine above the lampstand who bear their neighbours’ burdens whenever an opportunity arises, because this is that true charity of which it is written that it [Col. 0075B] “does not seek its own things” (1 Cor. 15): it prefers common interests to private ones, not private interests to common ones.

The light of good works also shines through glass, though not with a light so radiant as that which gleams above the lampstand. There are spiritual kinds of glass: for example, the virtue of charity, through which the light of remission of sins pours itself; likewise, the purity of humility is called glass, through which the light of confidence pours itself and removes the darkness of distrust. Likewise, the subtlety of understanding is called glass, through which the light of divine knowledge pours itself and drives away the darkness of ignorance.

There are also bodily kinds of glass, of which we now wish to speak: namely, human bodies weakened by age or infirmities. Just as glass, struck hard against something, is immediately broken, so these bodies fail and are worn away by labours, fasts, [Col. 0075C] vigils, and the other works belonging to the mortification of the flesh. Through these kinds of glass, therefore, the works of those who are not physically strong enough to labour vigorously for others nevertheless shine: in their infirmity they humbly do the little that they can.

Such are those aged men of virtue who gladly attend long vigils, who, supported by a staff, rejoice to take part in the divine mysteries; and those sick persons who, because of bodily ill-health, cannot leave the edge of their bed, yet there, as they can, praise and confess God. They count blessed those who can bear the Lord’s cross through many labours, and judge themselves as though they had committed some crime because they cannot bear the burden and heat of the day in the Lord’s vineyard (Matt. 20). These [Col. 0075D] are truly numbered among the children of God: by venerating and loving the good works of others which they themselves cannot do, they make them their own. Speaking in their person, the prophet David utters that consoling saying: “I am a companion of all who fear thee and keep thy commandments” (Ps. 118).

We have now, then, how we ought to render fear to our King and love to God. But since he became a mortal human being, we too owe him a return. And [Col. 0076B] I see none more fitting than that I should die for him, just as he deigned to die for us. And if perhaps we do not wish to end our lives by torments, at least let us die to vices and desires, that we may live to righteousness. For in this very way we shall render fear to the King, love to God, and recompense [Col. 0076A] to the mortal human being, Jesus Christ our Lord, whose kingdom and dominion endure unto ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XII. ON THE EPIPHANY OF THE LORD

“Scatter the nations that desire wars; envoys shall come from Egypt; Ethiopia shall hasten her hands to God” (Ps. 67).

You have heard, most beloved brethren, Paul teaching us that Christ is our peace (Eph. 2), making peace between the things in heaven and those on earth. In heaven he gave peace when he expelled from there that proud and restless one; on earth, when he rejoiced like a giant to run his course and, clothed in the breastplate of our flesh, standing with us in battle against our enemies, restored peace to the world and triumphed.

For if we believe the histories of the ancients [Col. 0076B], before Christ’s Incarnation wars and rumours of wars occupied the whole world. Changes of kingdoms, dispersions of the Jews, devastations of lands, and deaths of peoples prove this, as you have learned by examples in the course of the Scriptures. But I pass all these over in silence, since I intend to speak of the wars of vices, which had so troubled the peace of hearts in which God dwells that, as they rushed in from every side, no one could boast of tranquillity of mind or purity of conscience.

In these wars that most mighty Samson fell (Judg. 16). Here wise Solomon, at Pharaoh’s daughter’s prompting, was led into idolatry (3 Kings 2). Here David, holiest of the prophets, was struck down when he committed both adultery and homicide (2 Kings [Col. 0076C] 2). Indeed, the enemies of vice inflicted wounds upon every just man before Christ’s Incarnation.

But because peace was promised to the world in Christ, the prophet David invokes his help with longing, saying: “Scatter the nations that desire wars.” The prophet Isaiah had announced peace at his coming when he said: “His dominion shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of peace” (Isa. 9). And elsewhere: “Thou, O Lord, wilt give us peace, because we have hoped in thee” (Isa. 26). And David says: “Removing wars unto the ends of the earth, he shall break the bow and shatter the weapons, and burn the shield with fire” (Ps. 45).

Christ removed wars to the ends of the earth, he who made the human being peaceful inwardly and outwardly. He broke the weapons and bow by destroying all [Col. 0076D] the enemy’s stratagems. He burned the shields with fire when he kindled, with the flame of the Holy Spirit, hearts that were hard and nearly impenetrable. If you wish to know how Christ scattered the nation of vices, consider how he was born, how he lived, and finally how he suffered. In being born in an inn and wrapped in poor cloths, he gave the pattern of poverty through which the covetousness of this world is destroyed. Later, when advancing in age, he was subject to Joseph; when he paid tribute to Caesar; when he was baptized by John, his servant: he gave the example of humility through which the vain glory of this world was scattered. By enduring pains and miseries, he defeated the pleasure of this age.

The Prophet therefore says: “Scatter the nations that desire wars” (Ps. 67). Do you suppose that covetousness brought with it only a small nation [Col. 0077A] to fight alongside it? Violence and robbery followed it; usuries and simonies; lies and perjuries; deceits and unjust judgements. Nor did vain glory rush upon all with a lesser following: elation, pride, arrogance, insolence, contention, contempt, stubbornness, impudence, indignation, irreverence, and disobedience toward superiors followed it. Pleasure also drew along with itself a wicked and perverse nation: unchastity, dishonourableness, shamelessness, immodesty, intemperance, prodigality, gluttony, drunkenness, buffooneries, and idle talk. Christ destroyed all these in his elect by the pattern of poverty, the example of humility, and patience under tribulations.

But let us now look to the condition of our own age, whether any may be found who will go forth with Christ [Col. 0077B] to fight covetousness through love of poverty; for he too invites you to poverty when he says: “Woe to you who have your consolation in the present” (Luke 6). And Paul, writing to Timothy, says: “Command the rich of this age not to think proudly, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches” (1 Tim. 6).

Let a good imitator of Christ therefore come forth into the midst: one who despises honours and does not seek dignities; who abandons riches and does not strive to obtain them, accounting all things as dung that he may gain Christ (Phil. 3). Yet no one wishes here to imitate him: to be clothed in poor garments and laid in the manger of his Lord. If, however, we seek a humble person who chooses to be abject in the house of the Lord his God (Ps. 83), to become the refuse of all [Col. 0077C], to minister and not be ministered to, and, content with the lowest abasement, to glory that all despise him, each answers: “May my latter end be like theirs.” For I cannot imitate their beginning or their progress, though the Lord himself says: “If anyone among you wishes to become first, let him be your servant” (Mark 9).

And Isaiah says: “Enter into the rock; hide in the pit from the face of the wrath of the Lord” (Isa. 2), wishing by “pit” to signify the virtue of humility. If Christ invites us to patience under tribulations, where now is anyone found who wishes to endure pains and miseries, hunger and thirst, injuries and persecutions? Certainly nowhere—although many are the tribulations of the just, and the Son of God declares blessed [Col. 0077D] those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake (Matt. 5).

It is also said in the Book of Kings (3 Kings 6) that the stones of the Temple were hewn and hammered before they were placed in the building, so that neither craftsman nor axe was heard when they were laid in the Temple’s structure. By this the Holy Spirit signifies that whoever wishes to be fitted into the peace of that spiritual Temple which is in the heavenly kingdoms must first be polished here by blows and pressures.

For the delicately bred persons of our age say: “Christ became poor in order to make us rich; he became humble in order to exalt us; he suffered tribulations in order to free us from them. And the patrimony of the Church, which he acquired by his blood, he distributed through dignities and other benefices, so that he might grant us stipends, who serve him in divine [Col. 0078A] offices.”

Granted that Christ has bestowed on you who say these things many dignities, four prebends, perhaps seven churches, which nevertheless you hold, against the decrees of the canons and against the law of charity, to your own destruction. Did he grant you painted saddles, gilded spurs, bridles hung with silken straps, and chambers painted in varied colours? Did he wish to clothe you with a fuller’s pole of changing garments while leaving the naked poor person uncovered in the harshness of cold? Did he grant you the sport of hunting birds in the sky, the keeping of mimes and jesters, the support of sons or daughters and concubines beyond number? By no means. Therefore you must acknowledge yourself guilty of a double sacrilege: first, because you receive God’s benefices wrongly; [Col. 0078B] secondly, because you expend them on evil uses.

What share, then, do you think you have in Christ’s victory, which he won for his elect by the power of poverty, humility, and patience? It is plainly ridiculous if you presume to claim anything in it—just as it is ridiculous if a woman who coos to a dove at home wishes to divide spoils with the soldier who bravely defeated his adversary in war.

Oh, if only the examples of these righteous persons would draw you to the imitation of Christ! The prophet promised that, as a model for lovers of this world, they would imitate the new star’s path in the firmament, saying: “Envoys shall come from Egypt.” By these envoys we understand the firstfruits of the Gentiles, namely, the three kings who came on this day with women to adore the Lord. They were envoys, [Col. 0078C] sent by the Holy Spirit and inspired by him: sent, I say, not only for Christ’s sake but also for ours, so that they might proclaim Christ born to us, invite us to service, and urge worship upon us. And this they did. When they say, “Where is he who has been born King of the Jews?” (Matt. 2), they announce Christ’s birth; when they offer gifts to him, they urge service; when they fall down and adore, they invite worship.

Leaving Egypt, where there are pots of meat, melons, and cucumbers, they reject pleasure. Offering gold, frankincense, and myrrh—the things mortals chiefly desire—they condemn covetousness. Falling down in humility, they extinguish the spirit of elation and vain glory, embracing Christ’s humility.

“Envoys shall come from Egypt”: that is, from the darkness of unbelief to the light of divine knowledge. Concerning darkness [Col. 0078D] he says: Some came from darkness to Christ; others came from light to Christ; some came from light illumined, others from darkness darkened; and children of darkness came illumined. Those who came from light illumined were just persons under the Law, who had known through the light of the Law and the prophets that he was promised to them, and received him when he came with faithful devotion: such as righteous Simeon, Anna, and many others. Those who came from light to Christ darkened were people who knew the mysteries of the Scriptures and knew him to be the Messiah foretold by the prophets, yet, blinded by their own wickedness, delivered him up through envy: certain scribes and Pharisees, for example.

Those who came from darkness darkened [Col. 0079A] were Gentiles who, illumined by no light of knowledge and remaining in their darkness, crucified Christ: namely, Herod and Pilate. Those who came illumined from darkness were the three Magi, inwardly taught by the instruction of the Holy Spirit, who believed faithfully in Christ upon the sign of the star. For this reason it is said: “Envoys shall come from Egypt.”

Let the lovers of this age, who still love the darkness of their sins and delight to be defiled by their crimes, hear this—let them hear, I say, and marvel at Christ’s mercy. Since they refuse to leave Egypt with these envoys and to receive Christ by living soberly and devoutly, he sends to them in Egypt three envoys, whom we may fittingly [Col. 0079B] understand as the fear of hell, shame for guilt, and confidence in forgiveness.

For when a sinner placed in the depth of vices reflects upon the punishments—namely, that dark prison, weeping and gnashing of teeth, iron chains, indissoluble bonds with which the impious are to be bound in every limb, the worm that does not die, the fire that is not extinguished, that land of forgetfulness in which the damned, because of the anguish of punishments, cannot remember God, since, as the Prophet says, “there is none in death who remembers thee” (Ps. 6)—when, I say, the sinner set in the Egypt of vices places all these things before his eyes, he is pierced by fear and begins to abhor the very crimes for which he is held liable to such kinds of punishment.

Another messenger immediately follows this messenger, whom we have called fear: namely, [Col. 0079C] shame for guilt. For when any impious person recalls God’s benefits toward him—that God brought him into this life, redeemed him from death by his blood, was his defender in dangers and giver in poverty, consoles him with so many temporal benefits, and promises eternal rewards—when, I say, he recalls these things, he is ashamed of the fault by which he offended the Lord his God, whom he remembers to have been toward him so favourably disposed, so beneficent, and so full of the bowels of mercy.

Then, from this very remembrance of divine mercy, after shame, a third messenger is sent to the sinner: confidence in forgiveness. For what sinner would not hope for pardon when he remembers [Col. 0079D] that thief confessing, Mary weeping, the publican beating his breast, the Canaanite woman mourning her sins, finally Peter denying and Paul persecuting? All of these, after such great crimes, obtained not only pardon but glory in the fullness of divine mercy. Admonished by these envoys while in Egypt, the sinner passes from Egypt into Judea, so that, in imitation of the Magi, he may there adore the Lord with gifts.

Through Judaea, indeed, there is passage for those who press on toward him, because he is born there and found there. Judaea is interpreted “confession,” in which Christ is found: for through the truth of confession a person comes out from the darkness of vices and reaches Christ, who is the true light for all who hope in him. [Col. 0080A] In this Judaea—that is, in true confession—a person finds three gifts to offer to the Lord at his birth: humble confession, simple confession, and faithful confession. For whoever wishes through confession to draw near to the newborn Lord must first ensure that his confession is humble, stained by no blemish of pride or boasting, such as are sometimes heard: when a scholar confesses that he cleverly brought his companion to the point of refutation; an advocate, that he skilfully prevailed in an unjust case; or a monk, when he laments that he was tempted by vainglory because he prays, keeps vigil, or sings psalms more than others. In all these cases, because some pride is mixed in, it can be called not true confession but an imitation of confession.

Likewise, true [Col. 0080B] confession must be simple—that is, without excuse or minimization of sin. For I would not call that person truly confessing who inclines his heart to words of wickedness, to make excuses for excuses in sins: as when someone laments that he was deceived, that he fell into the sin of lust; that he sinned through gluttony because of the companionship and favor of his associates; or that he uses excessive clothing because the times demand it. For in none of these is there true confession, where the offender’s excuse excludes the simplicity of confession. Confession must also be faithful, so that the sinner does not despair of obtaining the pardon sought by weeping and tears, following the example of that prodigal son who, coming to his father from the place of horror with feet worn down, while lamenting his sins [Col. 0080C] receives the best robe, a ring on his hand, and the fatted calf at the feast (Luke 15). Thus, as we have said, the sinner, visited in Egypt by three messengers, passes into Judaea, offering there to Christ three gifts: namely, the humility, simplicity, and faithfulness of true confession.

What follows accords sufficiently with what has been said: “Ethiopia shall hasten her hands unto God.” His hands are the hands of God: one, the severity of divine vengeance, concerning which Job says, “Put thy hand far from me” (Job 13); the other, the goodness of divine recompense, concerning which it is written: “Thou openest thy hand, and fillest every living thing with blessing” (Psalm 144 [145]). Yet in the word “shall hasten” something very necessary is added: [Col. 0080D] namely, that one must leave Ethiopia hastily and swiftly anticipate those hands. For since Ethiopia signifies the same thing as Egypt, namely the blackness and darkness of wicked conduct, who would not hurry to depart from it? This Ethiopia is a very sandy land, lacking every moisture of charity, and therefore it produces no fruit of good works. Its inhabitants, scorched by heat, are hideous in face, dreadful in appearance, dissolute in conduct, and altogether disfigured by the blackness of sins; and therefore one must leave it, not with a moderate step or slow pace, but with swift running.

For many who wished to leave Ethiopia by small steps failed and died in it: such were those who, filled with every iniquity, scarcely ever remembered God even in thought, [Col. 0081A] and meanwhile were swallowed up by their vices. Those contrived to leave it at a slow pace who, after a good thought, put on the form of religious life, but, distracted by comforts of the flesh and unlawful desires, became slothful; and the more they advanced in years, the more they fell away in religious observance. It remains, therefore, that by swift running—that is, by fervent desire and great zeal in good works—we leave Ethiopia, and so anticipate the avenging hands of God, namely the punishments of torments. For time is short, the hour uncertain, and the road by which we must walk dangerous. Time is short, because life daily abandons us; the hour uncertain, because we do not know when the Lord will come to stretch out his hand in recompense (Psalm [Col. 0081B] 54 [55]); the road dangerous, because of the enemy’s manifold temptations and deceptions.

We must, I say, depart swiftly, so that, once we have left, with the star—that is, purity of conscience—going before us, we may come by the narrow way of God’s commandments to that house not made with hands in heaven. There is the Child—that is, there he remains, impassible and unchangeable, glorious in his humanity and perfect in divinity. May Jesus Christ, our God and Lord, bring us there: his kingdom and dominion endure for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XIII. ON THE EPIPHANY OF THE LORD

“We have seen his star in the east, and have come to worship him” (Matthew 2). I do not now take these words as spoken [Col. 0081C] by the mouths of the Magi; rather, they are the voice of the rejoicing Church, which joyfully goes forth to meet the newborn Savior and sees the star of a new light, announcing the end of the preceding night and the approaching light of the coming day. Let all who have attained the hope of salvation in Christ, seeing this star, rejoice with exceedingly great joy. I speak of the spiritual star—that is, Christ—which invisibly shone upon the minds of the Magi through faith.

Nor is it strange if I call Christ by the name of a star, since any one of the saints is also called by this name in Holy Scripture. Of them it is written in Daniel: “Those who are learned shall shine as the brightness of the firmament; and those who instruct many unto righteousness, as stars unto everlasting [Col. 0081D] eternities” (Daniel 12).

And in Genesis the patriarch Joseph calls his brothers stars when he says: “I saw, as it were, the sun and moon and eleven stars worshipping me” (Genesis 37). In the Gospel too the Lord says: “The sun shall be darkened, and the moon shall not give her light, and the stars shall be falling, and the powers of heaven shall be moved” (Matthew 24). Thus the Lord himself is called the morning star in the Apocalypse (Revelation 2); and in Job he is called Lucifer, the light-bringer, where it is said of him: “Canst thou bring forth the morning star, or cause the evening star to rise over the children of the earth?” (Job 38). And elsewhere it is said of him: “A star shall arise out of Jacob, and a rod shall rise out of Israel” (Numbers 24).

Christ, therefore, is a star—a unique star indeed, because he flashes, shines, and [Col. 0082A] sparkles. The flashing of this star is the splendor of divinity, the inaccessible light which enlightens every person coming into this world (John 1). Of this splendor the prophet Habakkuk says: “His brightness shall be as light; horns are in his hands” (Habakkuk 3); and Isaiah: “For Zion’s sake I shall not be silent, until her righteous one goes forth as splendor” (Isaiah 62). And Paul says: “Who, being the brightness of glory and the image of substance, sits at the right hand of Majesty on high” (Hebrews 1).

This star flashed with this splendor when Christ poured the whole light of his divinity bodily—that is, wholly—into the humanity he had assumed. Would you see this star shining? First consider that a ray is not the immensity of light but a part of it. For we are not said to see a ray of the sun or moon [Col. 0082B] when they shine upon us in their power, but when they direct toward us a part of their light through a window or crevice. This star, therefore, shone in the assumed reality of human nature, where divinity, veiled by the weakness of our flesh, outwardly displayed to us through virtues and deeds, as it were, certain rays of its majesty. Or it shone in being born of the blessed Virgin: for as a ray does not diminish the integrity of the heavenly body, so Christ in being born did not diminish the integrity of his virgin Mother. Or it shone for this reason: as materially a ray is not the substance of a heavenly body, so the Word of God, born of the Virgin, was not, insofar as he was the Word, from the substance of the Virgin.

This star also sparkled when Christ taught us the commandments of righteousness and the words of eternal life. These are called [Col. 0082C] sparks because, as sparks are fiery and burn up nearby material, so the words of God kindle the hearts of hearers with the fire of divine love. Hence the Prophet says: “Thy word is exceedingly fiery, and thy servant has loved it” (Psalm 118 [119]). And the disciples going to Emmaus say: “Was not our heart burning within us because of Jesus, while he spoke to us on the way?” (Luke 24). Their hearts burned while he spoke because his words inflamed them with love. Because of these sparks the prophet Ezekiel says of him: “His appearance was like sparks of glowing bronze” (Ezekiel 1). And elsewhere it is written of the saints: “The righteous shall shine and shall run about like sparks among reeds” (Wisdom 3). [Col. 0082D] For as sparks, if they catch reeds that rise on high, reduce them to ashes, so the words of the saints, through the earnestness of preaching, reduced to nothing whatever was lofty in this world.

This star sparkles, says, unless I am mistaken, the philosopher of the world, because a star that sparkles is not a planet. For a star’s sparkling is a sign that it is farther from the earth, higher than other stars, and nearer heaven.
