Truly, the star of which we speak was not a planet, because it did not wander through the broad roads of this world, since “he committed no sin, nor was guile found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2); but rather, “his going forth is from the summit of heaven.” “He who comes from heaven is above all,” as Paul attests when he says: “He who is above all, God blessed for ages” (Romans 9). [Col. 0083A] Therefore the children of the Church proclaim in a voice of exultation concerning this star: “We have seen his star.” Let us understand this as we say “his person,” “his divinity,” “his light”; thus “his star” means the star which he himself is.

What follows, “in the east,” may be understood in two ways: either that the star was placed in the east, or that its beholders were placed in the east. This star, which is Christ, was at one time placed in the east, at another in the west, at another in the north, and at another in the south. It was placed in the east in being born; in the west in dying; in the north in descending to hell; and in the south in rising again.

Those see the star placed in the east who imitate the humility of his birth; who, with him, are wrapped in poor cloths [Col. 0083B] and laid in a manger; who humbly do all that is despised and lowly for the sake of him who humbled himself so greatly as to empty himself and take the form of a servant (Philippians 2). In their person David says: “I have become like a vessel cast away, because I have heard the reproach of many dwelling round about” (Psalm 30 [31]). For as a rejected vessel is adapted to whatever lowly uses, so the truly humble servant of Christ, while despised by others and judged useless, is found useful to all by the example of humility and patience.

Those see this star placed in the west who imitate the Lord’s passion, who mortify their members upon earth along with vices and concupiscences, so that they do not serve sin (Colossians 3). They receive Christ as hanging upon the cross, as it were, between their arms, when by keeping hard paths in this life they do not depart from the trace of his passion. Of their number was Paul, who said: “In many labors, [Col. 0083C] more abundantly in prisons, exceedingly in stripes, frequently in deaths” (2 Corinthians 11). And in the Psalm: “For thy sake we are put to death all day long; we are accounted as sheep for slaughter” (Psalm 42 [44]).

Those see the star placed in the north who are strong against the devil’s temptation; who are not overcome by the flesh, not enticed by the vanity of the world, and not deceived by spiritual wickedness, but stand manfully in the battle of the Lord, strong to crush the power of the enemy. Those see this star placed in the south who despise this world and, through strength of soul, have risen with Christ from earthly affections; being higher than the world by contemplation, they see Christ where he sits at the right hand of God the Father.

We may also say that some of those who see this star are placed in the east, others in the west, others in the north, others in the south. Those in the east are newly converted; those in the west, backsliders; those in the north, obstinate persons; those in the south, the perfect. The newly converted are placed in the east because, leaving the darkness of sins behind, they have received the light of grace as though it were the rising of a sun; and, while they strive to be reconciled to God by good works, they look toward the star as it were through desire for righteousness.

Backsliders are placed in the west: having left the Sun of righteousness, [Col. 0084A] they have immersed themselves in the darkness of vices. Rebuked by conscience for ingratitude toward God’s benefits, they are required by God, along with that wicked servant, to pay the entire debt of their former offences. The obstinate are placed in the north: numbed by the cold of malice and wickedness, they feel no warmth of divine grace; shaken by fear of divine vengeance, they expect in the future not God’s mercy but the power of his wrath. For as the name of God’s mercy is sweet and pleasant to the righteous, so the name of power is not merely holy but terrible to those who have made themselves distant from God by sinning.

The perfect are placed in the south: inwardly burning with love and outwardly shining in good works, they enlighten others by the example of a good life (John 12). Hence they are called children of light, where it says: [Col. 0084B] “Walk as children of light.” And the Lord says in the Gospel: “The children of this world are more prudent in their generations than the children of light” (Luke 16).

Here it is pleasant to consider by what sight this star is to be contemplated. This sight is not bodily but spiritual. The sight by which we see Christ is, therefore, an invisible illumination of the mind through grace, by which, through loving or knowing him, we contemplate him. This sight is exercised in a threefold way: by consideration of spiritual nature, by consideration of bodily creation, and by consideration of Holy Scripture.

It is exercised by consideration of spiritual nature, because in that nature the trace of divinity shines, since it is capable of knowledge and love. Through knowledge it was made in the image; through love, in his likeness. Likewise, this sight is exercised by consideration of bodily creation, because therein are found the immeasurable majesty of God, the beauty of God’s wisdom, and the usefulness of God’s goodness. These are the invisible things of God which, as Paul says, are understood and perceived from the creation of the world through the things that have been made (Romans 1). This sight is exercised by consideration of Holy Scripture, in which not only his divinity but also his humanity is understood: we see it as promised through the prophets and as presented to us through the law of the Gospel. Christ, God and man, is therefore the star toward which the sight of our mind ought to be directed; indeed, it terminates in him as in a kind of horizon, [Col. 0084D] since in his humanity we behold the work of our salvation.

Spiritual sight, therefore, has its horizon, just as bodily sight does. The horizon of bodily sight is that circular meeting-point where, because sight fails, heaven and earth seem in some way to be joined. The horizon of spiritual sight is where the height of divinity bends down to assume human nature. If you ask how sight fails there: likewise here the human mind cannot grasp how divinity and humanity are united in one person. Christ, therefore, is the end of our desire, because once we possess him nothing further is to be sought. Nor should the sight of our mind rest below this end, lest worldly affections or any unlawful desires drive it away from contemplation of its Creator.

There are many impediments to this sight. At times it is impeded from above, at times from below, at times from within, and at times from without: from above by pride, from below by avarice, from within by concupiscence, and from without by deadly sorrow. [Col. 0085A] To speak first of pride: there are chiefly four things that make a person proud—the height of authority, nobility of birth, greatness of learning, and beauty of appearance. When, therefore, the wretched soul sees itself surpassing others in these things, as in so many flowers of this world, it immediately swells inwardly through the exaltation of its mind, considering them as though they came by its own power, and outwardly despises its neighbor through boasting. Thus, when pride is placed like a cloud between it and God, the mind’s sight is prevented from seeing him.

We compared pride to a cloud because, as clouds arise from mountains, so pride arises from swollen hearts. But the proud should heed this: lightning strikes mountains, and the proud suffer torments mightily (Ecclesiasticus 10). By avarice this sight is impeded from below, since the avaricious person—than whom nothing is more wicked—is compared to a brute animal. As such an animal always fixes its eyes on the ground through desire for food, so the avaricious person always turns the eyes of the mind toward earthly things, for earthly gain and the transitory goods of this life. Such a person has forgotten not only God but even himself. For a human being is defined not as a brute animal but as a rational mortal. [Col. 0085C] He is called an animal, that he may know he has a soul; rational, that, remembering the dignity of his heavenly origin, he may look upward to God; mortal, that, knowing he will soon die, he may not desire the goods of this world.

The mind’s sight is impeded from within by concupiscence, because it dwells and is born in the human being, as Paul says: “I see another law in my members, opposing the law of God and making me captive to the law of sin” (Romans 7). Therefore, while the soul is inwardly heated by wicked thoughts and unlawful desires, the mind’s sight is caught, as it were, by the glue of perverse pleasure, lest it be directed to God by holy desire. Hence the prophet David complains: “For our soul has been humbled into the dust; our belly has been glued to the earth” (Psalm 43 [44]). First the soul is humbled by the dust of evil thoughts; afterward sensuality is glued to the earth—that is, to carnal desires—so that it cannot rise to spiritual devotion.

The mind’s sight is impeded from without by deadly sorrow when the wretched soul is so swallowed up in grief over this world’s adversity that, forgetful of the joys of the future life, it cannot breathe again toward God. But when the eye of the mind has been cleansed, the children of mother Church, as though no obstacle hindered them, freely direct spiritual sight toward Christ.

“We have seen his star in the east, and have come to worship him.” As sight belongs to the exercise of the mind, so coming belongs to the body’s action. And [Col. 0086A] because not all come by acting well, let us say that some come and look upon the star, while others do not come and yet look upon the star. The first are those who have ordered their lives so holy that, walking blamelessly in all the Lord’s commandments, they do not turn aside from the way of righteousness; and, becoming daily better than themselves, they draw near to God by good works. Hence they are said to be coming, not to have come: forgetting what lies behind, they stretch themselves toward what lies ahead.

The second, namely those who do not come and look upon the star, are those who see many things and do not keep them, who speak and do not act, who see Christ in books but find nothing of him in their consciences. Of them the Prophet says: “Let their table”—that is, Scripture—“become before them a snare and a stumbling block” (Psalm [Col. 0086B] 68 [69]). These are that barren fig tree in which, when the Lord sought fruit, he found only leaves. They have leaves of words alone, without the fruit of good works. But I fear that they may then wish too late to bear fruit, when the sentence has been pronounced by the Lord: “Let fruit no longer grow from thee” (Mark 11).

Tell me, wretched soul: you know God and do not glorify him as God; where is that fountain of gardens and well of waters flowing with force from Lebanon? (Song of Songs 4). The waters of Holy Scripture, called a fountain where it is level and a well where it is deep, ought to flow from Lebanon—that is, from the whiteness of a good conscience, not from uncleanness of life. John confirms this in the Apocalypse, saying: “The voice which I heard was like that of harpists playing on their harps” (Revelation [Col. 0086C] 14). Whoever’s voice is heard in teaching or preaching must play the harp upon the harp of his own body, so that the witness of good work follows the sound of his voice. Thus he will come in the company of the faithful to worship him.

We should not err if we say that to worship is spiritually to serve God for his own sake. Yet, because we wish to set before simpler brethren the conclusion of this discourse, we shall say simply what worship is and how God ought to be worshipped. To worship, therefore, is devoutly to ask God in prayer for salvation and for those things which belong to salvation. You, then, good man, when you wish to worship God, must consider three things: who asks, whom he asks, and what he asks. With regard to the one who asks, two things must be considered: guilt and misery. [Col. 0086D] Guilt: so that the petitioner, on account of his sins, always sets himself before the eyes of divine majesty as guilty, as it is written: “The righteous man is the first accuser of himself” (Proverbs 18); and in the Psalm: “I considered my ways and turned my feet unto thy testimonies” (Psalm 118 [119]). The petitioner must also set his misery before his eyes, so that consideration of the failure of his own powers presumes nothing from himself. And when these two—guilt and misery—are set before his eyes, he will worship humbly.

Likewise, with regard to the one whom he asks, the worshipper must attend to two things: goodness and power. Goodness, because he is always ready to hear just prayers; power, because he is able to grant what is asked. These two—God’s goodness and power—make us pray confidently. [Col. 0087A] With regard to what is asked, two things likewise must be considered: what is good and what is necessary. These two make us pray perseveringly.

Accordingly, dearest brethren, let us who rejoice in Christ appearing in the flesh, with minds enlightened see his star, and in the east reverence his birth. Let us come by good works; let us worship humbly, confidently, and perseveringly, asking salvation from him, so that he who wrought salvation in the midst of the earth may work our salvation in his eternity—Jesus Christ our Lord, whose kingdom and dominion endure for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XIV. ON THE PURIFICATION OF BLESSED MARY

[Col. 0087B] Rejoice and be glad, O Zion, going forth to meet your God. Those who have received from the Lord the gift of greater grace today carry the child Jesus in their hands with holy Simeon, or, coming with him to his holy temple, offer a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons. But I, still far from God and scorched by the ancient rust of sins, do not presume to approach him closely: I do not say that I may receive him in my arms, but not even that I may touch the fringe of his garment.

I have found one counsel for myself: with the rest of the faithful, I shall go to meet the coming Lord—even if I am troublesome—and thus, in celebrating the Lord’s *hypapante* (“meeting”), I shall offer the present, however inadequate, affection of my devotion. I shall go to meet him, I say, secure in hope, because he excludes from his mercy no one who comes to meet him with a devout mind. Rather, he presses as an enemy those who turn their backs, or those who resist him and contradict his commandments to his face. [Col. 0087C] Now, to translate the Greek term *hypapante* by the Latin word *obviatio* (“going to meet”): one kind of meeting is reconciliation, another contradiction, another examination.

The meeting of reconciliation took place on this day, when holy mother Church devoutly received the long-desired child Jesus and, with the covenant which it had made with death abolished in Christ, found the peace of reconciliation. The meeting of contradiction occurred when that people, grievous in iniquity, the sons of strangers, lied to him; spat in his face, struck him with blows, and, weaving a crown of thorns upon his head, mocked him with bent knee. This had also been prophesied by righteous Simeon when he said: “Behold, this child is set for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel, and for a sign that shall be contradicted” (Luke 2). [Col. 0087D] The meeting of examination will occur on the great day of judgment, when silver shall be separated from dross, grain from chaff, lambs from goats, and reprobate from elect. Of this meeting the Gospel says: “At midnight a cry was made: behold, the bridegroom comes; go out to meet him” (Matthew 25).

Holy Church, therefore, is invited to rejoice because the peace of reconciliation has been found, when it is said: “Rejoice and be glad, O Zion”; and the word of exultation will be multiplied because the manifold peace of reconciliation has been found. For through Christ reconciliation has been effected between flesh and spirit, between human being and angel, between Gentile and Jew, and between human being and God. Flesh and spirit were at discord because the flesh approved carnal things and the spirit heavenly things. Human being and angel were at discord because the human being who ought to have repaired the ruin of the first apostasy, which occurred among the angels, himself also fell, drawn down to earth with the third part of the stars of heaven. Gentile and Jew were at discord because the one served idols and the other God. Human being and God were at discord because the human being, withdrawing from the service of his Lord, had subjected himself to an alien power. But all these discords are to be pacified in Christ, when all rational creatures, united through charity, become participants in one Spirit [Col. 0088B] and co-heirs of one kingdom. Therefore, rejoice and be glad, O Zion, going forth to meet your God.

It is now pleasing to consider by what way, in what manner, and with what devotion one must go to meet him. Of the ways on which one meets the Lord, one is watered, another waterless, another royal, another bright. The watered way is penitence; the waterless way is holiness; the royal way is mercy; the bright way is Holy Scripture.

Those walk by the watered way who, after many falls into crimes and wanderings in error, return to themselves, consider into how deep an abyss of misery they have fallen, wash their sins with tears, and return to God with the prodigal son, saying: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before thee, and am no longer worthy [Col. 0088C] to be called thy son; make me as one of thy hired servants” (Luke 15).

Those walk by the waterless way who, not yielding to flesh and blood, have kept their garments white lest they appear naked; who, keeping themselves unstained from this world, offer chastity to the child Jesus, fulfilling the Apostle’s command: “Maintain holiness, without which no one shall see God” (Hebrews 12).

Those walk by the royal way who abound in good works and almsgiving, fear God in the commandments of the Lord their God, are feet to the lame, eyes to the blind, hands to the weak, and fathers to orphans, while awaiting that promise: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matthew 5).

Those who investigate Holy Scripture walk by the bright way, reading the book of God’s law within and without: within by knowledge of truth, without by the practice of good works. Within, this book contains those manifold words of Law and Prophets, Gospel commandments, and sayings of the holy Fathers—all ways by which one goes to the Lord. Without, this book contains in the lives of the saints good works: namely, the struggles of martyrs, the constancy of confessors, and the devout conduct of all the righteous, by which one comes to the heaven of God Most High.

Whoever wishes to walk rightly by the bright way should read the book of God’s law within through knowledge and without through experience, so as to learn by experience what bodily mortification, the pallor of vigils, patience in tribulations, [Col. 0089A] the dryness of fasts, the sighs of penitents and of tears, and the harshness of discipline are directed toward. Let them learn with holy David to dance in lowly dress before the ark of the covenant (2 Kings 6), and with Paul the Apostle not only to abound but also to endure want (Philippians 4). For those who read the book of God’s law within but not without—that is, who speak and do not act—should be called brooding sitters upon Holy Scripture rather than its investigators.

Those walking on this way ought to be illumined by a threefold light: first, the testimony of a good conscience; second, brightness of understanding; third, uprightness of discipline. They should be inwardly illumined by the testimony of a good conscience through virtue, by brightness of understanding through truth, and outwardly shine by the uprightness of discipline through good conduct. Thus those who walk by these ways go straight to meet the Lord; yet not all meet him in one manner. Some are drawn, some carried, some walk, and others run to meet him.

There are many criminals in this world who seek earthly things and savor carnal things, so buried in vices that they cannot even lift their eyes to heaven; worn out by the filth of sins, they forget the heavenly homeland toward which they ought to advance. You could see them living amid pleasures, indulging in the luxury of this world, giving themselves to beds and acts of impurity, now committing scandals, now shameful deeds; and, blaspheming the Holy One of Israel, they set up an idol of Venus where the most holy passion of the Savior ought to be adored. [Col. 0089C] The Prophet recalls both their disgrace and punishment, saying: “They defiled his covenant; they were divided by the wrath of his countenance, and his heart drew near” (Psalm 54 [55]). “They defiled his covenant,” he says—that is, as far as lies in them, they have polluted the promise of eternal life by living wickedly. Therefore, because they have been separated from the righteous and elect by the wrath of his countenance, “his heart drew near”—that is, his will concerning them is made manifest, so that those now hidden and secret may be revealed here, and so that it may become manifest what sentence of eternal damnation they are to receive in the future by God’s just judgment.

Yet God’s mercy does not abandon these persons, because what they do not wish to do of free choice they are sometimes compelled to do by the harshness of the lash. Now by poverty, now by sickness, [Col. 0089D] now by some other outward tribulation, now by the shame they endure for their crimes, they are forcibly drawn back to God (Psalm 82 [83]). Thus it is written: “Fill their faces with disgrace, and they shall seek thy name, O Lord.” Yet the Lord draws these same criminals in other ways as well: by presenting a commandment, showing an example, and heavenly inspiration. He draws them by presenting a commandment when the teaching of God’s word calls them back from their evils; they are drawn by showing an example when the good works of the righteous provoke them to better things; they are drawn by heavenly inspiration when, inwardly illumined by invisible grace, they are freely justified. Therefore, although the Lord draws sinners in the four ways mentioned, in the first way—that is, forcibly by the harshness of the lash—he draws them; in the other three, more gently.

There are others who are carried to meet God: those who have renounced dead works and, in a certain fervor of spirit, have left the world and clung to the Lord, but, held back on the way by the storm of carnal desires and secular life, are not allowed to advance along the path on which they walk. These, therefore, must be carried by exhortation from God’s word and spiritual consolation, so that renewed again, they may learn through the disposition of their mind to despise earthly things and love heavenly ones. [Col. 0090A] For what does a flower that quickly falls, or a joy that passes in a moment, profit? Behold, whatever is beautiful in this world grows vile, and nothing delightful remains in it: youth passes away, beauty falls, strength weakens, power declines, rank is emptied, health fails, riches cannot last; joy turns into grief, and all pleasant things end in bitterness.

Let us look back at those who were before us: what did their pride and boastful wealth profit them? Absolutely nothing; indeed, they passed away like smoke. O how wretched are those who refuse to serve for a little while in order to be free forever; who evade a brief labor in order to be at rest forever; who refuse to weep in this life in order to be joyful eternally. Nor should the sufferings of this present time be reckoned against the future glory that shall be revealed in us (2 Corinthians 3), since merchants of this world also acquire temporal merchandise at great expense and toil, in the hope that in future they will obtain an abundance of profit from it. [Col. 0090C] Let us therefore press on toward the weight of glory, which is cheap when purchased and precious when possessed, in which the members, with Christ their head, enjoy perpetual blessedness.

There are many others in the world who advance to meet the Lord at a measured pace. Since they still love the comforts of this life, they cannot rise to the heights of the virtues; yet, as far as they are able, they avoid grave sins and the abyss of vices. Thus they walk pleasantly through the level ground of a flowering field set between two waters, where the companionship of flesh and spirit may sustain each other with mutual consolation. For example, when the spirit is willing and proceeds too hastily into God’s service, it should be restrained by the affliction of the flesh; and when the weak flesh desires comforts too eagerly, it should be urged onward by the vigor of the spirit [Col. 0090D]. Therefore, loving riches, possessing gold and silver, clothing themselves in many colors, and not rejecting the other delights of this life, they walk through the flowering field of this world; and so they go between the two waters of virtues and vices to meet him. Yet they cannot reach him unless they cross the river (Job 28), for he is not found in the land of those who live pleasantly, as Scripture says.

Therefore the rod of Moses must be held: after the river has been struck and divided by it (Exod. 4), they may cross on dry ground. For lovers of this life ought so to hold the virtue of discernment, which is the rod of Moses, that they divide down the middle the waves of this world and the carnal desires mingled with vices and lusts [Col. 0091A], allowing what is vicious in them to flow downward into the sea, so that it does not remain with them; while, on the other side, they retain as a safeguard those things necessary to nature and useful to the body. Thus, once the river has been divided, even those who have not despised these temporal goods may pass over to the Lord with dry feet.

There remain others still, who are borne at a swift run to meet the Lord: namely, those who have entered the way of perfection, renouncing the world with all its pomps, and who, made higher than the world by the fervor of the spirit, desire to possess nothing except what conduces to the blessed life. You would see them at one time rejoicing in the Lord [Col. 0091B], because he has separated them from the world; at another lamenting the time which, by lingering in worldly life, they have rendered useless to themselves; at another opening the gates of paradise by the devout urgency of their prayers; at another learning God’s will by searching the Scriptures. They devote themselves to this alone: that they may pass through the course of this life without offending God.

Of those who run, some run quickly, some more quickly, and some most quickly. They run quickly who observe with all diligence the commandments of Gospel teaching; they run more quickly who have added to these the observance of regular discipline; they run most quickly who are led by a private spirit and, reckoning almost nothing sufficient for themselves, have added the burden of a singular manner of life.

It must now not be passed over with what devotion the Lord ought to be met [Col. 0091C]. We ought not to appear empty before the Lord, but by the service of an offering to declare the affection of our devotion. For him who dwells in inaccessible light, the carrying of candles seems particularly fitting—the candles which holy Church bears in her hands today—both because the candle signifies our Savior, and because the condition of the human state is recalled to our memory in the candle.

How the candle bears the figure of our Savior I pass over briefly as something known: for the wax is understood to pertain to his humanity, the wick to his mortality, the flame to his divinity, and the light spread all around to the illumination of virtues that comes from him. It is more important to consider how the course of our life is signified in the candle. Virgin and pure wax [Col. 0091D] represents to us the first state of the human condition, in which man was made like God through innocence. The wick, which is fragile, signifies our mortality, by which man was punished because of transgression. The light proceeding from the flame figures our restoration, accomplished through Jesus Christ. The flame, which naturally tends upward, signifies the future glory prepared for the saints.

Therefore, O human being, when you see virgin wax, recall the dignity in which you were created. When you see the wick reduced to ashes, lament your sins, on account of which you have been cast into the condemnation of death. When you are illumined by the light, praise and give thanks to God, through whom you have been mercifully restored. When you look upon the flame, hasten to that glory [Col. 0092A] prepared for you in heaven, through the generosity of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honor and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XV. ON THE PURIFICATION OF BLESSED MARY

“After Hannah had weaned the child, she brought him to the house of the Lord in Shiloh” (1 Sam. 1).

The words I have set before you, taken from the book of Samuel, relate the history of Hannah, who, long barren and sterile, sought a son from the Lord with great longing and urgent prayers. Having received him and weaned him, she brought him to the house of the Lord in Shiloh, that he might remain there continually.

Understood spiritually, however, they may be adapted to today’s feast, because Samuel’s being brought to the house of the Lord fittingly signifies the offering of Jesus Christ in the Temple [Col. 0092B]; and Hannah, whose name is interpreted “grace,” signifies holy Church. Samuel, moreover, whose name means “God’s petition,” signifies Christ, as is evident from the careful exposition of the Fathers.

For just as Hannah sought a son, so also the Church, which began with righteous Abel, before Christ’s Incarnation sought from the Lord, with most fervent desire, that the Holy of Holies might be given to her: a man of unique blessedness and singular holiness, in whom transgression might be removed, sin taken away, and everlasting righteousness come. For now all the voices of the prophets had fallen silent: made hoarse by their long cries, they could no longer present him whom they had promised. Therefore the vows of all and the desires of the whole world yearned for Christ [Col. 0092C], who was held in reserve and who himself was the expectation of the nations (Isa. 63).

Yet they did not then desire to see him in that form in which he is fairer than the children of men; not beautiful in his robe, ascending into heaven in the multitude of his strength; not advancing into those beautiful places of the wilderness, to the flowers of roses and lilies of the valleys. Rather, with Isaiah, they desired to receive him as despised and the last of men (Isa. 53), acquainted with infirmities; with Zechariah, clothed in filthy garments (Zech. 3); such as the prophet David foretells him (Ps. 68), where he says in his person: “I am poor and sorrowful; your salvation, O God, has sustained me.” Finally, this is the one whom the righteous man, speaking in the person of the Church in the Book of Wisdom, asks to be given him when he says: “Send her from the throne of your greatness, that she may be [Col. 0092D] with me and labor with me” (Wis. 9). “May she be with me,” he says, “through likeness of humanity; and labor with me, through experience of suffering.”

Behold: moved by such great prayers, the Son of God bowed the heavens and came down. Appearing to us in mortal flesh, he was given to the world—indeed, to all—provided that, having long been desired, he is received with desire. Would I not rightly call him given to us, he who was born for us, offered in the Temple for us today, and finally died for us? Do you wish to see how all these things were for us? Certainly our birth was impure, our life perverse, and our death perilous. Therefore he was born for us, that by his birth he might cleanse the impurity of our birth; he was offered in the Temple for us, that, subject to the Law, he might shape our life through obedience; [Col. 0093A] he died for us, that by his death he might destroy our death.

O wretched soul, who receives so great a grace of God in vain and, by evil living, drives away from yourself your Savior offered to you: blush and be ashamed within yourself. Even if the desires of the saints cannot bend the hardness of your heart, at least the very condescension of the Son of God should have admonished you, as also should that inestimable love of the Father by which, to redeem a slave, he exposed his only-begotten Son to suffering. Repent, therefore, repent; and become little with the little one, subject with the one offered, and die with the one who died, so that you may crucify your flesh with its vices and lusts and may say with Paul: “We died with Christ, and our life is hidden with him in God” (Col. 3).

And, that we may pursue the surface meaning of the passage proposed at the beginning [Col. 0093B], Christ was also weaned for us—that is, separated from milk. From what milk? By the testimony of Scripture, we can distinguish a threefold milk.

There is the milk of human nature, concerning which the Bridegroom says to the bride in the Song of Songs: “Honey and milk are under your tongue” (Song 4)—that is, divinity and humanity are under your flesh. There is the milk of simple teaching, of which Paul says: “As to little children, I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Cor. 3). There is the milk of worldly pleasure, concerning which a promise is made by the Lord to the carnal people of the Jews when he says: “I will give you a land flowing with milk and honey” (Deut. 6).

But to speak first of the milk of human nature: before Christ’s coming, holy mother Church had two breasts, namely the Law and the Prophets, in which the milk of Christ’s humanity was contained by promise [Col. 0093C]. For the Law signified Christ the man by figures and sacrifices, while the prophets foretold in manifest oracles that he himself would come in the flesh. From these breasts the Word of God drew milk when that very Word made flesh united human nature to himself. Hence, once this milk had been drawn out, the same breasts dried up: because, when Christ appeared in the flesh, that sweetness of spirit and that affection of devotion which the holy Fathers had toward Christ from the promise of the Law and the Prophets entirely failed.

But the Church weaned Christ when it believed him, though born contrary to the laws of the flesh, to be God above human nature. Hence the Evangelist: “For what shall be born from you, holy, shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1). And Isaiah says of him: “Truly you are a hidden God, and apart from you there is no God” (Isa. 45). And elsewhere: “We saw his star in the east, and we have come to worship him” (Matt. 2).

Christ was also weaned from the milk of simple teaching when he taught that the literal surface of the Law must be understood spiritually [Col. 0093D]. Yet we may take “simple teaching” more broadly, so that every teaching not fruitful in spiritual understanding is called simple teaching. In this sense philosophical teaching, and whatever else is reckoned under the name of secular learning, should be called milk. Therefore those who suck this milk are also called children by a certain wise man, who says: “Greeks, you are always children, and there is no aged knowledge in you,” etc.

From this milk, therefore, all adults must be weaned with Christ, so that, leaving secular teachings, they may be nourished by spiritual precepts as by solid food [Col. 0094A]. For what sweetness of spirit can there be in such milk if you understand Plato or Cicero, when this learning is sprinkled with much bitterness and often deprives its devotees of time for repentance, the fruit of a good life, and the crown of eternal life? Or what useful and honorable end is there if you investigate Aristotle’s deceptions with subtlety—unless perhaps you set yourself the end of refuting another by false surprise and entrapping your neighbor by other foolish trifles, and thus suppose that you have reached the goal of study, the finish-line of falsehood? This is not an end that brings to completion, but one that consumes; not one that perfects, but one that makes deficient—that is, that draws one toward the failure of virtues.

Therefore we must seek rather that end of which David says: “I have seen the end of every completion; your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Ps. 118). And Paul: “Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10). This end is not far removed from us, because Christ, infinite in himself, became finite for us and was set near. For the inaccessible one is now approached; the incomprehensible one is received in the hands of righteous Simeon; and he whom the heaven of heavens cannot contain is today presented as a little child in the Temple.

Let us rejoice with the little child, who has brought us with himself the joys of eternal salvation. Let us show him a cheerful face, render the service owed, and return thanksgivings for his benefits. First, a joyful face must be displayed in this spiritual joy [Col. 0094C]; yet understand that this means the face of the heart or conscience, not of the body. This face—that is, your conscience—must be cheerful and beautiful, cleansed from vices and lusts and adorned with virtues; for the service of a slave is not pleasing unless the face of the heart appears beautified with spiritual joy.

There is indeed a twofold adornment of the soul which a person ought to offer to God: innocence from vices, and the virtue of humility. The soul received its first adornment from God, but lost it through sin, when all sinned in Adam in such a way that no one ever has been, or can be, able to glory in the purity of innocence. Therefore a person must have recourse to the soul’s second adornment, humility, so that the beauty of conscience blackened by sins may be restored through the mother of virtues—that is, humility [Col. 0094D].

For this, a threefold humility is necessary: humility of confession, of submission, and of self-abasement. The first washes away guilt, the second nourishes virtues, and the third preserves them. These three kinds of humility seem to be signified by the birds offered before the Lord, namely the turtledove and the dove. They have groaning instead of song, in which the humility and sorrow of confession are expressed. They yield if attacked by another animal, and in this is figured the humility of submission. The turtledove, moreover, which, after losing its mate, never perches on green branches but on dry ones, signifies the humility of self-abasement.

This last and chief kind of humility is especially necessary for all, so that without it not even holy men retain any hope of salvation [Col. 0095A]. Paul possessed the adornment of this virtue when he said (1 Tim. 1): “Christ came into this world to save sinners, of whom I am the first.” Likewise Peter, when he said: “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man” (Luke 5). And that woman of the Gospel: “If I touch,” she said, “the fringe of his garment, I shall be saved” (Mark 6).

Therefore, whoever wishes to appear beautiful in God’s sight must consider himself vile and despised, so that, considering his own weaknesses, he always judges another better than himself. You ought to place before your eyes your own sins, which are great and many; and whatever virtues seem to be in you, because they are mingled with so many sins, you ought to judge them unfruitful [Col. 0095B]. But the good qualities of others which are manifest to you, you ought to honor and regard as great; and their faults, hidden from you, you ought not to judge—or, if they are known to you, excuse them through the affection of charity. Thus, from consideration of your own weakness, which you clearly understand, judge yourself despised and vile; but judge your neighbor always better than yourself because of the manifest goods that you see in him. This is that joyful and cheerful face which we ought to show Christ.

Let us now proceed to the service owed, by which we are bound to serve him. But concerning the service to be rendered, the commandments of the Law must be observed. They sufficiently distinguish what sort of service is above all to be rendered to God in the Temple, and what should today be rendered to him who is offered in the Temple.

[Col. 0095C] The Law commands animals to be slaughtered upon the altar, incense to be burned, and the purest oil to burn in honor of God. Therefore those who wish worthily to receive Christ as he comes to the Temple must first kill upon the altar of their heart the animals—that is, carnal impulses, lustful desires, and perverse pleasures. They must slaughter them with the knife of compunction and burn them with the fire of repentance, so that they may thus present their bodies to God as a living, holy, living sacrifice pleasing to God (Rom. 12).

For carnal pleasure and spiritual joy, which must be offered to God, cannot coexist; just as sweet and bitter water cannot flow from the same fountain, nor can the same person be at once sad and joyful, laughing and weeping [Col. 0095D], or subject to contrary passions at one moment. Therefore, as we have said, the animals must be slain in God’s Temple. Those who wish to behold beasts in their wildness should withdraw far from God’s Temple into the wilderness of this world, where bears, lions, and eagles that live by plunder are found.

The bears, I say, are foul people who have defiled themselves by lust and impurity. The lions are the greedy and avaricious, who by robbery, theft, ambition, simony, and every other kind of avarice have wronged both God and their neighbor. The eagles, which fly high and live by plunder, are the proud, who exalt themselves above themselves and glory in oppressing and casting down others.

Incense also is commanded to be burned in God’s service, and by a fitting likeness it signifies the prayers of the saints [Col. 0096A]. When incense is kindled, three things occur together: smoke, fragrance, and fire. These three can also be found morally in prayer. Whoever intends to offer fruitful prayer to God must first set before his eyes his miseries and iniquities, from which the smoke of compunction arises. Second, he must consider God’s great mercy: how ready he is to forgive, inclined to spare, and gracious in rewarding. When these are considered, the fervor of charity is kindled, so that a person may love him ardently, without whom he can neither escape his miseries nor attain those goods which God has prepared for those who love him.

Thus one who prays devoutly to God emits the smoke of compunction from the consideration of his own weakness. From considering God’s mercy, he gives forth the fragrance of holy devotion [Col. 0096B]. From considering both, the fervor of love, or fire, is kindled, as has already been said.

For all this it is necessary that the purest oil be kindled in lamps. If I call the lamps our hearts, I shall not unfittingly call the oil of the lamps the sweetness of the heart, or the affection of compassion. For just as olive oil extends to a threefold use—because it relieves pains, nourishes bodies, and burns in God’s Temple—so spiritually the virtue of compassion has three functions. It relieves pains, because it assists the miserable, consoles the faint-hearted, strengthens the sorrowful, instructs the ignorant, and corrects offenders. It also feeds the soul with the refreshment of spiritual joy, because it rejoices with others’ progress [Col. 0096C], applauds the virtue of neighbors, and desires them to be raised in dignities, enlarged in honors, and to grow in religion; and whatever grace comes to others, it rejoices as though it had increased something belonging to itself.

From these two, as from the purest oil, the fire of charity is nourished. This fire is often kindled more by those affections of compassion that concern one’s neighbor than by spiritual exercises that look immediately to God, because reading without understanding and prayer without affection lack the seasoning of the virtue of compassion.

Lastly, now that Christ has been presented to us, thanksgiving remains to be given. There are two things for which we should especially give him thanks: the manner of our visitation and the greatness of the reward [Col. 0096D]. For who with a devout heart would not burst forth into praise and thanksgiving, when he considers that the Lord of lords became a servant for him; that he whose are the earth and its fullness became poor; that the incomprehensible became little; and that the immortal was subjected to the necessity of death?

Likewise, the greatness of the reward invites us to thanksgiving. What greater thing could he have given us than his power, his joy, and his kingdom? Those will have his power who, by his gift, shall judge this world. Those will have joy who, with that faithful servant of the Gospel, shall enter into the joy of their Lord. Those will have the kingdom who shall hear that voice: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. [Col. 0097A] 25).

Far banished from that kingdom are pain and groaning, weakness and misery, sin and every spiritual malice. It is never shaken by an enemy or disturbed by discord; there are tranquil eternity and joyful tranquility. May Jesus Christ our Lord deign to bring us to it, whose kingdom and dominion endure for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XVI. ON THE PURIFICATION OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY

“If a woman, having received seed, bears a male child, she shall be purified for seven and thirty-three days” (Lev. 12).

What is it, brothers and my dearest lords? What, I say, can uncircumcised speech offer to minds trained in perfect wisdom? What profit can a sinful man—and a great sinner—bring to your holiness? Plainly, none. For you do not need my goods, since from him who gives generously and does not reproach you receive abundantly, at the proper time, both through reading and through prayer [Col. 0097B].

For you are those true worshipers who worship the Father in spirit and truth (John 4); buried with Christ and dead to sin, you continually bear the suffering of Jesus Christ in your body. You hate your souls in this world, and with burning desire you have cried aloud in the words of that most blessed Thomas Didymus: “Let us also go, that we may die with him” (John 8). To die to the world and live to God.

You are therefore dead to the world, because you have despised the kingdom of this world and every worldly adornment for the love of God. You live to God, whom you carry in your mind, seek in deed, and preach in word [Col. 0097C]. But for me, born in sins, the matter has been reversed: every day I come alive again to sin, so that every day I may die to God. I live to the world through pride and vain glory; I live to the flesh through gluttony and lust; I live to sin through frequent sinning and neglect of repentance. What, then, will become of me? Lord Jesus, answer for me.

O that that beautiful young maiden of David might be sought for me too—I mean God’s wisdom—that she might warm my limbs, stiffened by the cold of sin, with the inspiration of divine love; and that she might, by the illumination of truth, teach what is fitting for so great a solemnity and appropriate to your exhortation. For she alone gives confidence to one speaking, because she alone gives the speaker skill [Col. 0097D]. Since, therefore, I am not sufficient of myself, may she speak in me and perfect what is imperfect in me: she who opened the mouth of the sinful Caiaphas to words of prophecy (John 18), and was eloquent through the mouth of a brute animal (Num. 22).

“A woman,” he says, “if, having conceived seed, she bears a male child.” You hear, dearest brothers, by what precept of the old Law a woman bearing a male child is enjoined a time of purification of forty days, so that at last, on the fortieth day, coming to the Temple with propitiatory sacrifices, she may be fully and perfectly purified by the legal rite.

Yet this law was given for one needing purification, not one already purified; for a sinner, not one sanctified from the womb; for a woman, not a virgin; for corruption, not integrity [Col. 0098A]. For what need of purification had she whom the Father sanctified, whom the Holy Spirit overshadowed, who conceived the Son of God by a word alone and gave birth without pain? Certainly no purification is needed where no stain of guilt preceded. Yet, although she did not need to be purified, she ought to observe the days of purification, because she too was born under the Law and was to bear a male child, who came not to dissolve the Law but to fulfill it (Matt. 5).

She is indeed the woman who, having conceived seed, bore a male child: a woman by condition, not by frailty; by nature, not by softness. “Woman” (*mulier*) is said as though “softer” (*mollior*) from softness (*mollities*); therefore she was not soft but strong—strong, I say, that woman whom Solomon sought when he said: “Who shall find a strong woman?” (Prov. 30). For she had to be strong who was to bear the male child [Col. 0098B] who cast out the prince of this world, and who, rescuing the needy from the hand of those stronger than he, humbled the mighty of the earth by his own power.

This woman, therefore, bore a male child, conceived indeed by seed. And by what seed? Certainly by that of which it was said to Abraham: “In your seed all the kindreds of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 23). Isaiah likewise signified this seed to us when he said: “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we should have been like Sodom and made like Gomorrah” (Isa. 1). It was, finally, not carnal but spiritual seed; not the seed of guilt but of grace; not of a man but of the Word of God; not of corruption but of faith.

It is the very seed by which “the Lord gave goodness and our land shall give its fruit” (Ps. 84), the seed that [Col. 0098C] fell into good ground—I mean the Virgin Mary—and brought forth fruit in some thirtyfold, in others sixtyfold, and in others a hundredfold (Matt. 15); but in her, by a singular privilege, it brought forth thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold at once.

This seed brought forth thirtyfold fruit when Christ consecrated the marriage feast by his presence (John 2); it brought forth sixtyfold fruit when, during the time of his preaching, he preached and taught continence; and a hundredfold when on the cross he commended his virgin mother to John the virgin (John 19). But because that virgin of Israel was to become for us the Mother of God, the bridegroom’s chamber, the beloved of the Beloved, the unique one of the Unique One, the Son of God therefore willed to work in her singularly—indeed, wonderfully—so that she who was to bear the price of the whole world might have something in common with every state of human life [Col. 0098D].

With married persons she had the birth of offspring; with continent persons, a vow of chastity; and with virgins, perseverance in virginity. Thus, while by giving birth she redeemed continent persons, married persons, and virgins, the thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and hundredfold fruit accrued to her together. But, O religious man, you who think rightly of the blessed Virgin, understand that the thirtyfold fruit in her was no less than the sixtyfold or hundredfold. You may safely maintain that she merited no more by giving birth than by preserving virginity. Therefore, according to the various comparison in her, God’s fruit due to her receives a varied designation in respect of its name. Yet it is not so in others, because they neither live continent lives without difficulty nor give birth without corruption [Col. 0099A].

The meaning of the number we have set out seems, to some, to agree with this exposition: it contains seven days and thirty-three. Thirty refers to married persons; three, which admits no equal division of itself, to continent persons; while seven, a sacred number because of sevenfold grace, refers to virgins. Therefore the blessed Virgin observed the days of purification not so much from any necessity of purification as for the sacrament, as we have said, of mystical signification. But the words previously set forth can be adapted by a moral exposition not only to Mary but also to every faithful soul.

For every soul devoted to God is that woman [Col. 0099B] who, having conceived the seed of spiritual grace, bears the male child of good action. She is the woman of whom we read in the Apocalypse that the dragon stood before the woman who was about to bear a male child, so that, when she had given birth, he might devour her son (Rev. 12). She is the Canaanite woman who came out from the regions of Tyre and Sidon—that is, from the depths of worldly life—and who cries to God for her daughter, that is, for her sinful conscience, saying: “Son of David, have mercy on me” (Matt. 15). She is the woman who suffered from a flow of blood—that is, who was poured out like water through unlawful desires of the flesh—and who at last touched the fringe of his garment and was healed (Mark 5).

Christ’s garment is the habit of virtue; the fringe of the garment is the fruit of good action. For just as the fringe adorns [Col. 0099C] the garment, so good action adorns virtue. Therefore that woman touched the fringe of the garment when the sinful soul, stirred by the example of good works, leaves behind former errors by doing good.

This woman must observe a time of purification of seven days and thirty-three days, which together make forty. In forty, moreover, there is ten multiplied by four: for four times ten makes forty. By ten, therefore, because of the commandments of the Law, we understand the Law; and by four, the fourfold observance of the Law: namely history, tropology, anagogy, and allegory.

For the commandments of the Law brought no one to perfection without spiritual understanding (Heb. 7) [Col. 0099D], since “the letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3). Hence Moses, who bears the figure of the Law, is shown the land of promise (Deut. 24), but is not brought into it; because the Law showed by what way those under the Law ought to proceed toward the true and heavenly land of promise, but nevertheless could not bring them into it.

Elsewhere, too, Moses’ hands are said to have been heavy, but they are supported and raised by Aaron’s help (Exod. 17), because the carnal works of the Law, signified by Moses’ hands, were heavy and unbearable unless our Aaron, the priest according to the order of Melchizedek, tempered and raised them by spiritual understanding. Therefore the observance of these four—history, tropology, anagogy, and allegory [Col. 0100A]—by which the soul must be purified and reconciled to God, is necessary.

History externally instructs people through commandment; tropology inwardly rules the soul through moral formation; allegory, which lies in contemplation of heavenly things, brings one to perfection. History shows the way of acting well; tropology forms the will; allegory cleanses the heart through faith; anagogy purifies the inner person by contemplating only those things that are God’s. In history obedience is found because of the commandment; in tropology, discipline; in allegory, sincerity of faith; in anagogy, charity.

History teaches you how to live humbly toward a superior through obedience; tropology, how to live sociably toward an equal or inferior [Col. 0100B]; allegory teaches you to believe faithfully; anagogy teaches you to love perseveringly. The first two show the way of righteousness toward one’s neighbor; the latter two, the worship of devotion toward God.

These are the four wings of the cherubim, with two of which they fly and with two cover their bodies (Ezek. 1). For holy men, who are cherubim—that is, illumined by the fullness of divine knowledge—cover their bodies with two wings when they shape their present conduct through history and tropology; and they fly with two wings when, by allegory and anagogy, they are raised upward through faith and charity to contemplation.

These are the four wheels by which the ark of God is brought back from the land of the Philistines to the tabernacle of the covenant. And these are the four [Col. 0100C] by which the soul is recalled from the region of dissimilarity to the bosom of mother Church.

This is also shown by the time of purification, where seven and thirty-three days are named. First, indeed, after seven days she is admitted to association with human beings; afterward, when thirty-three days have been completed, she is brought to the Temple. By the seven days, therefore, through which the whole of time revolves, understand the whole duration of time, during which we ought to be admitted to communion with human beings—that is, we ought to devote ourselves to fraternal charity.

See how, if you do not have something to give, you may at least graciously offer to all, as far as you can, the affection of compassion. Be merciful to the wretched, compassionate toward the weak, and a comforter of the despairing. Do not oppress anyone by an unjust act; do not inflict slander on anyone by detraction; do not return evil for evil to anyone. Patiently endure with joy the injury done to you in tribulation [Col. 0100D]. Bless those who curse; pray for those who persecute and slander you, that you may be a child of your Father who is in heaven. Always keep in your heart that saying of truth: “In your patience you shall possess your souls” (Luke 21).

In these and similar ways you will be purified in this present time, if you devote yourself to fraternal charity through the affection of mercy and compassion. By the thirty-three days I think we should understand that time of blessed purification when we shall all, as though thirty-three years old, come to a perfect man, according to the measure of the age of Christ’s fullness; when we shall enter the Holy of Holies—that is, the temple not made by hands in heaven; when, as it is written, we shall be cleansed from every defilement of flesh and spirit (2 Cor. 7).

There, brothers, fully knowing and fully known, your light will not shine in darkness; rather, by the manifest light of deeds and hearts you will carry burning lamps in your hands [Col. 0101A]. I mean lamps not only of the glorified body, but also of a conscience radiant with the light of divine love. Perhaps this is prefigured by the lights which you offer today at the Lord’s table—that is, at the altar—not without light, but burning.

Observe, if you please, how the little worker-bee makes wax, how it works and goes about its business. It flies over the plains of the fields, through the paths of gardens and the thickets of groves, seeking flowers that contain the seed of sweetness [Col. 0101B]. Then, having found the flowers, it extracts with its biting mouth the power of their flavour by drawing it from the blossom; and returning to the hive, by marvellous skill it produces a honeycomb—that is, wax with honey. But later, through another’s operation, when the honey has been separated from the wax, the wax is made into a candle, which, lit with fire, is presented at Christ’s altar. All these things, faithful soul, you will find in yourself; all may be applied to you. For by the bee understand within yourself holy meditation, which flies hither and thither while, by diligent thought, it recalls and turns over the mercies of the Lord in this present age, the rewards of the righteous and the punishments of the wicked in the future.

This bee, then—that is, holy meditation—has two wings: inquiry and [Col. 0101C] wonder. For there are certain knowable things of God which can be investigated and known by us who dwell in this valley of misery, through reading and meditation. Other things are deep and unsearchable, such as those which eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor have entered into the human heart (1 Cor. 2); all these we may indeed admire, but not scrutinize.

This is what it means that in the Song of Songs the bridegroom is seen by the bride through windows and lattices, as though ensnared by love (Song 2): for through windows or lattices one looks upon another, neither wholly reveals himself nor wholly conceals himself. So too Christ, in this life, partly conceals himself from his bride—that is, from the faithful soul—that she may have something toward which to stretch herself in longing; and partly reveals himself, that through a taste of divine sweetness [Col. 0101D] she may burn still more ardently in love for him. For if he offered himself wholly to the bride’s embraces, perhaps his very presence would cause satiety. Likewise, in Isaiah the seraphim are said to veil God’s feet and face with their wings, while only the middle parts are open (Isa. 6): because certain lofty things concerning God are unknown and veiled to us, while others come within our knowledge.

Our bee, therefore, proceeds into the field upon her two wings, inquiry and wonder. Into what field? Into the field of the Scriptures, concerning which the Lord says to Ezekiel: “Go out into the field, and there I will speak with you” (Ezek. 3). For God speaks to us in the Scriptures when through them he shows us what we ought to do. This field is that field [Col. 0102A] in which the precious pearl is found; whoever found it sold all that he had and bought it (Matt. 13). It is the field in which grows the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys. The flower and the lily are Christ himself: he is found in the field because every page of Holy Scripture bears witness to him; he is a flower on account of beauty, and a lily on account of fragrance. Beauty is recognized outwardly by sight; fragrance is perceived inwardly, not by a sense but by affection. Christ, therefore, is a flower through the manifest works of righteousness; he is a lily through the hidden longing for the heavenly homeland. Or perhaps he is a flower in the active life, but a lily in the contemplative life. In this field our bee seeks the flowers of diverse sayings, from which she draws sweet juice: for, drawing out their spiritual meaning through the mouth of memory, [Col. 0102B] she carries it back and deposits it in the hive of the heart.

Afterward, through her own industry, she makes the honeycomb, in which, as we have said, honey is found mixed with wax. By wax we understand the frailty of human nature: for, just as wax readily receives any image impressed upon it, so we bear within ourselves now the image of the old human being, now that of the new, according to the variation of the time. Hence the Apostle says: “As you have borne the image of the earthly human being, so bear the image of the heavenly” (1 Cor. 15). We therefore make a honeycomb, that is, honey in wax, when, by the flavour of virtues and a certain taste of divine sweetness which we find in the divine Scriptures, we give form to our frailty through God’s cooperating grace.

Why say more? At last, when the mother-bee has been suffocated, the honey is separated from the wax; and when the end of our life is at hand [Col. 0102C] and every office of meditation ceases, the soul, in which is the seat of virtues, is separated from the body. Through another’s operation the wax is made into a candle, and on the day of glorification our nature will be refashioned into a true body. The candle is lit with fire, and the body will again be given life through the infusion of the soul. Wick and wax are consumed by the fire, because mortality, which is signified by the wax, will be utterly burnt away by power. For now our body is natural; then it will be spiritual. At last the burning candle is offered at the Lord’s table, where we are refreshed by the bread of blessing; and we shall be admitted to that final supper of heavenly life, which is as without end as it is beyond comprehension. May Jesus Christ our God, our judge and saviour, whom on this day we venerate together with his blessed [Col. 0102D] Mother and Virgin Mary, deign to bring us to it; his kingdom and dominion endure for ages of ages. Amen.

## Sermon XVII. In Lent

“Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown” (Jonah 3).

Beloved brothers, God speaks to us in many ways and by many means, now instructing us by writings, now by sermons and examples, so that, denying ungodliness and worldly desires, we may live soberly, righteously, and devoutly in this age (Titus 2).

For behold: by the saving voice of the Lord we have all now heard the way of salvation—how one must walk in it, and what rewards are laid up for those who proceed [Col. 0103A] by it. Yet we are always found less affected by these things than we ought to be, childish in understanding, rightly compared with those who hear without understanding, or who, being half-blind, become more darkened when light comes upon them. For although we sometimes gladly hear saving admonitions, examples of virtues, and the way of perfection, we do so not from love of virtue or zeal for imitation, but merely on the surface, like children who gladly look at pictures of the Trojan War on walls. If, in such a picture, they see a painted man overpowering enemies with strength and weapons, acquiring a name for himself by the deaths and wounds of men, they praise and magnify him, saying that he has done a brave deed bravely. Yet if they are invited to something similar, when they stand in battle-line and see blood being shed, they collapse from fear alone and turn to flight without engaging [Col. 0103B] in battle.

The same is true of us, if we are willing to look searchingly at our own failings. For, to pass over the strong contests of Christ’s soldiers and come to smaller matters: we praise a meal of bread and water, provided it is not at our own table but at another’s; the harshness of haircloth pleases us, and the rod of correction, provided it is not upon our own back. We say that fasts and vigils are good, so long as we do not become fellow-heirs of this good. The delight of that eternal promise does not please us; we do not endure the tribulations of this present life through which we must enter into life. Failing in both respects, we receive the reproach of the children playing in the marketplace, who say: “We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we lamented, [Col. 0103C] and you did not weep” (Luke 7).

Nevertheless, the prophet, seeing in the Spirit that the way of salvation would be restored to sinners through days of repentance, confidently proclaimed a promise of consolation for the ages to come, saying: “Yet forty,” and so forth. As though he said: Let Nineveh now spend its days in pleasures, abound in delights, and pursue enjoyments; nevertheless, forty days will yet come in which Nineveh shall be overthrown. Nineveh, I say—that broad and spacious city, a journey of three days in extent, likewise built up with gates and walls, renowned among kingdoms, head of an empire, mistress of peoples—such and so great a city is to be overthrown within the number of forty days. Let us first see, if you please, how this city is built; afterward, by what means it is to be overthrown.

Since, then, by Nineveh—which is interpreted “beautiful”—this world is understood [Col. 0103D], there are four gates through which all enter into love of this world. The first is worldly exaltation; the second, bodily pleasure; the third, the desire of possessing; the fourth, transitory prosperity. Do you not see how all these four draw people to themselves, how everyone runs and hastens to enter through these gates?

To speak, then, of the first gate, worldly exaltation: reverence is now not given to holiness, nor honour bestowed upon knowledge or virtue. Rather, through pursuits and services each person wishes to seize honour for himself, lest he appear lowly and despised. It is little concern to become contemptible before God, provided one appears exalted in worldly glory. Many indeed [Col. 0104A] enter through this gate; but more enter through the gate we have called bodily pleasure, because the entrance leading to it is broader, the way smoother and more pleasant. This is shown by those who spend their days in revelries and drunkenness, in beds and indecencies; who clothe themselves in purple and fine linen and feast splendidly every day, spreading their couches and dining rooms with Egyptian tapestries; who offer varied delights to their outward senses and are inwardly distracted by unlawful desires.

We see others burning with thirst and desire for possession, who reckon gain to be godliness and do not turn aside from any injustice in acquiring, provided they can attain what they seek (1 Tim. 6). They steal the idols of Laban—that is, the idols of Satan—which are covetousness and avarice, not that, like Rachel, they may sit upon them and cover them by humble confession (Gen. 31) [Col. 0104B], but that they may worship and venerate them, making gods for themselves from them. These are they who enter through the third gate, which we have called the desire of possessing. By the success of earthly prosperity some also strike their roots more deeply in this world, while everything prosperous and healthful happens to them. They are thereby cast off by the Lord, because they are not visited with the scourges of sickness nor struck by any outward vexations. The world smiles upon them, provides consolations, multiplies joys, so that, buried in transitory prosperity, they forget to wipe away their stains, cleanse their conscience, reform their habits, order their deeds, govern their life, and preserve discipline.

Behold the four gates of Nineveh; but a wall still stands [Col. 0104C] all around it, lest any man powerful in strength and greatness of virtue should be able to storm it. The first side of the wall is raised by corrupted sensuality, which seeks only vain and transitory things perceived by the outward senses. The second side is built by blinded reason, which, pressed down by the darkness of ignorance and the weight of sins, cannot discern its own misery. The third is destructive security, which, having come into the abyss of vices, promises itself impunity. The fourth is hardened perversity, which, beset by so many dangers, admits no correction.

This city is spacious, a journey of three days. The journey of the first day is the world’s wantonness, which draws people to itself through pleasure. The journey of the second day [Col. 0104D] is made by treacherous deceit, which deceives those drawn in with false happiness. The journey of the third day is made by final malice, which sends those consummated in evils without mercy to torments. We now have that city of refuge—I mean Nineveh—to which all the guilty and criminal flee, not that they may be saved in it, but rather that they may lose their souls. And behold, those forty days are at hand in which it must be overthrown—yet by a good overthrowing—so that the kingdom of sin may be destroyed in it and it may be converted to the Lord its God.

Let strong men therefore come forward and wage the wars of their God. Let them break down the gates, destroy the walls, and lead the inhabitants into captivity, so that it may no longer glory in its sorceries and impieties. In the first [Col. 0105A] battle-line religious men ought to stand, as those mighty in the first contest, correcting vices by the example of innocence and holiness. Those who are set as watchmen of this world should walk before God in righteousness and holiness all their days, so that even sinners and those abounding in worldly goods, built up by their good manner of life, may glorify the Father who is in heaven, saying: “Truly, God dwells in them.” Their religious habit, the seclusion of their solitary life, and the very place consecrated to God exhort them to this—a place in which, as though invited to spiritual marriage, he has chosen a dwelling for himself. Do you wish to see how he dwells with them? In the oratory, through the devotion of prayer; in the cloister, through the study of reading; in the chapter-house, through humble confession; in the refectory [Col. 0105B], through the frugality of abstinence; in the guesthouse, through hospitality; in the infirmary, through brotherly compassion; in almsgiving, through mercy; within and without, through regular discipline.

Take heed, then, good man, and be watchful whether you are doing that for which you came. Following the counsel of that holy man, set your works to account, and see whether you pass your life—indeed, even one day—without envy, without pride, without murmuring or detraction; whether you are lax in food or drink, sleep or idleness; whether you read, pray, or lament less than you should; whether by some example of yours you have destroyed one who was beginning; whether you have been disobedient to your superior; whether you have been overcome by anger, gluttony, or any other vice. For this is not to overthrow Nineveh, but to build it up.

[Col. 0105C] On the other side stand strong auxiliaries, namely penitents, execrating vices through the laments of repentance and confession; recalling their years in the bitterness of their soul; confessing their injustice against themselves to the Lord; washing away their sins by mourning and tears; subjecting to servitude the members that they presented as weapons of iniquity unto iniquity. While these fight, the vices of the Ninevites are overthrown: the one who stole steals no longer (Eph. 4); the proud becomes humble, the lustful embraces chastity, the impatient becomes gentle, the angry becomes mild, the envious and avaricious—and all other workers of iniquity—set a limit to their iniquities.

But in this battle-line of penitents some fight deceitfully, some uselessly, and some manfully; for one repentance is hypocritical, another fruitless, another fruitful. The repentance of those is hypocritical who confess their sins in part and in part refuse to confess them, preferring to bear the stain of conscience before the Lord rather than blush before people on account of their sins.

There are, however, four things that chiefly produce this imperfect repentance: shame, fear, hope, and despair. Shame produces imperfect repentance when people see their sins to be disgraceful and monstrous beyond the common measure of sinning, and therefore blush to confess them. Of them it is said: “They were confounded, because God rejected them” (Ps. 32). Fear also hinders repentance [Col. 0106A] when people refuse to confess because they fear that they will not be able to bear the severity of satisfaction. The earthly Adam represented them when he said: “I heard your voice in paradise and I was afraid, because I was naked, and I hid myself” (Gen. 2). Hope also produces imperfect repentance when people hope to obtain some advantage in the world which they fear they will lose if people come to know what they are inwardly. To them it is said: “If riches abound, do not set your heart upon them”—that is, do not hope in them (Ps. 61). Despair likewise makes repentance imperfect when people, bound by the habit of sinning, despair that they can abstain from vices. Of them the Apostle says: “The wrath of God comes upon the children of distrust” (Eph. 5).

[Col. 0106B] Fruitless is the repentance of those who, prompted by a habit of long time, speak at the appointed hour but do not weep for their sins. For they immediately lay down the burden of satisfaction, return to their vices, drink the cup of shame even to the dregs, and the last condition of such people becomes worse than the first. You would see people of this kind, forgetful of God’s commandments, turning even the days of fasting into a mockery for themselves rather than into fruit; for even if they sometimes fast, they fast neither wholly, nor devoutly, nor soberly.

They do not fast wholly, because, fasting once or twice in the week, they give the other days over to revelry and drinking cups dry; although all from their fifteenth year and above are bound to the entire fast [Col. 0106C], unless excused by sickness or another certain and reasonable cause. They do not fast devoutly, because although they abstain from foods, they never abstain from vices; yet abstinence from food is fruitless unless abstinence from vices accompanies it. They also do not fast devoutly because what they deprive the body of by fasting they put away in a chest, to offer it again to the belly. According to the testimony of blessed Gregory, this fast ought to be called a fast not of God but of the belly, because what we can deny ourselves by abstaining from food ought to be bestowed upon another’s poverty.

They do not fast soberly, because they break the fast either more greedily, more splendidly, more quickly, or with food and drink more abundant than is fitting. Greedy eating is rebuked in Esau, who lost the dignity of his birthright for greedy eating of lentils [Col. 0106D] (Gen. 25). So too excessively splendid eating is rebuked in the rich man of the Gospel, of whom it is said that “he feasted splendidly every day” (Luke 16). To break the fast sooner than one ought is likewise shown to be faulty by the Church’s ordinance, which established that one must fast until the ninth hour. Hence blessed Jerome says: “There is no one who does not know the third, sixth, and ninth hours, and also evening and dawn; nor should food be taken before these prayers are offered to God.” This may rightly be understood of the time of fasts. Likewise, to break the fast with food or drink more abundant than is proper is shown by reason itself to be faulty, since this is not abstinence but service to pleasure.

Fruitful, however, is the repentance of those who [Col. 0107A] lament and confess their offences both from hatred of vices and from love of virtue; who bear with them the fruit of repentance in fasts, almsgiving, and other good works, exchanging the delight of their former life for mourning and sorrow. This is shown by the deep sighs of sinners, abundance of tears, beatings of breasts, and tearful voices with which, during these days, God’s house resounds, while choirs and theatrical entertainments cease; dice, the great snare of the devil, are cast away; those jesting gestures, detested by God and people alike, by which even manly spirits are weakened, are banished afar; songs of Venus fall silent, as do obscene songs which represent a kind of idolatry.

Yet for this repentance to be perfect, it must have five companions: contrition of heart, confession of the mouth, mortification [Col. 0107B] of the flesh, amendment in deed, and perseverance in virtue.

The treatment of spiritual sickness has something in common with the remedies employed by physicians, who first apply purgatives, secondly soothing agents, thirdly healing remedies, and fourthly preservatives.
