Contrition of heart and confession are purgatives, because contrition washes sin away lest it adhere to the soul through perverse affection; confession subsequently cleanses and expels it, lest it remain within to create an obligation to punishment. This is like what we see happen in a vessel stained with filth: water is poured into it, so that the dirt may be washed away and not cling to the vessel through stickiness; yet the dirt must afterward be poured out, lest it remain inside to defile the vessel.

Mortification of the flesh soothes pain, lest vices revive in us through concern for the flesh. For such is the familiar habit [Col. 0107C] of that enemy whom we always carry with us, namely our body: the greater the benefits we bestow upon it, the more sharply we find it urging vices upon us. Amendment in deed, however, brings healing, while a person does only those things which he knows to be healthful for himself, useful to his neighbour, and acceptable to God. Perseverance in virtue preserves this healing; without it every repentance must be judged imperfect.

This is the true repentance by which the vices of the Ninevites are overthrown, whose report reaches even the king, and for whose sake the entire city is spared. For behold, the king of Nineveh—indeed, the King of Heaven and Lord—descending from the throne of paternal majesty, clothes himself [Col. 0107D] in the haircloth of flesh and fasts in the desert for forty days and forty nights, that by his own example he might show forth the pattern of repentance. For who, hearing that the Son of God is clothed in haircloth, would not fear to wear soft and variegated garments? Who, hearing that he fasted unto hunger, would not blush at luxuries and the pleasures of the table during these days? He fasts in the desert also, not in the city or before the eyes of people, in order to teach us in good works to avoid empty glory and the praise of people.

Temptations are not absent from us because the tempter himself does not appear to us in a visible form, or because he does not afflict us with blows and insults as he was accustomed to assail Christ’s ancient champions. Indeed, the very fact that he does not show himself visibly to us reflects upon our shame [Col. 0108A]: he judges us, as rejected and worthless persons, unworthy of violent temptation, since he sees us thrown down from the height of virtues by pride and vain glory, or even by any other slight vices. Therefore, that we may overthrow Nineveh by mourning and groaning, let us keep the pattern of repentance set before us by the Lord, abstaining not only from foods but also from sins; so that, crucifying our flesh with its vices through the austerity of repentance, we may reach the delights of the heavenly homeland, through the aid of our Lord Jesus Christ, whose kingdom and dominion endure for ages of ages. Amen.

## Sermon XVIII. In Lent, “Laetare”

[Col. 0108B] “The beginning of a human being’s life is water, bread, clothing, and a house protecting his shame” (Ecclus. 25).

What is this, my most beloved brothers and lords? What, I say, is it that you have wished to do? Why have you appointed as your steward of God’s word a man uncircumcised in heart and ears, to your injury? I am not a physician of souls, and the bread of God’s word is not in my house (Isa. 3), especially not to be set before you, who are accustomed to be refreshed with sweet, spiritual bread. Besides, the observance of this sacred season, in which remembrance is made not only of our misery but also of deliverance and joy, required a living and effective sermon, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit (Heb. 7). For insofar as the face of the Church is changed—both in worship, [Col. 0108C] in the variety of divine service, and in the universal frequency of mourning and fasting—we remember our misery, into which we fell through the first parent, sighing as though in captivity. But insofar as today’s voice breaks forth into a voice of exultation and joy, as though liberated from exile, saying, “Rejoice, Jerusalem, and assemble, all you who love her,” it is a remembrance of that joy which we expect after the labours of this pilgrimage, when we shall be transferred into the liberty of the glory of the children of God.

Although I am not fit for this, I shall nevertheless say something suited to the occasion, excused by obedience and aided by your prayers. And, to begin speaking from the beginning of our calamity: Why, O Adam, lost man, did you bring great sin upon yourself [Col. 0108D] and upon your children? Why did you come from the delights of paradise into these places of exile? Truly, when you were in honour, you did not understand. For when all things desired came to you in the garden of delight, behold, labour now torments you, hunger wastes you, servitude oppresses you, pain burns you, danger constrains you, and death at last destroys you.

Hear, then, O child of man, the counsel for returning to life—you who received in Adam the sentence of death. “The beginning of a human being’s life is water, bread, and clothing.” Water and bread are food altogether fitting for fasting and repentance. But there are certain nocturnal waters very hostile to those who wish to begin a good life. The bridegroom complains of these in the Song of Songs, saying: “My head is full of dew, and my locks with the drops [Col. 0109A] of the nights” (Song 5). This dew or these drops of the nights signify the affections of carnal desires. There is another water, salty and undrinkable sea-water, which does not give life, of which the prophet says: “Your way is in the sea, and your paths in many waters” (Ps. 67). This is the bitterness of wicked action.

But we see other waters that are healthful: some spring upward from the veins of the earth, from below; others descend from above, that is, from the clouds of heaven to the earth; and thirdly, waters that are established in their places above the heavens and do not reach us. In the first waters, which bubble up from the earth, are signified tears of repentance. For when any sinner remembers his evils—how he has always been intent upon earthly works, has lived for nothing of God and wholly for the world—he is at some point touched by prevenient grace; and thus it happens that, while he washes away past sins with tears, he brings forth, as it were, a fountain of water from the depths of the earth. These waters are the beginning of a human being’s life.

By the second waters, which drip down from the clouds to the earth, we understand examples of holy conduct that come down to us from righteous men. For while sinners strive to conform themselves to their lives by doing good, water descends, as it were, from the height of clouds to the earth. By the third waters, which are above the heavens, we understand the abundance of future glory, of which the Psalmist says: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. 16). These are unknown to the earth, for they are things “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the human heart, which God has prepared for those who love him” [Col. 0109C] (1 Cor. 2). Yet someone may perhaps think historically that the firmament containing those waters is porous, and that drops of dew reach the earth through its pores; and in this dew the devotion of the mind—which is a foretaste of the future life—is not inappropriately signified. For just as dew sometimes signifies sin, as we said above, so it is also understood in a good sense, as there: “May God give you of the dew of heaven and abundance of the fatness of the earth” (Gen. 27).

Of this threefold water, the first moistens, the second washes, and the third intoxicates. But we see many who are moistened only a little by the waters of repentance through contrition of heart, and who are not washed by the second waters through zeal for good work. Thus they are not intoxicated by the third waters [Col. 0109D] that are above the heavens through the attainment of glorification. For behold, lovers of the world are in some degree moved to compunction for a short time by the season of observance in this sacred time; but when they ought to redeem their sins by fasts, prayers, and almsgiving, overcome by their evil habit, they return to their former sins.

Throughout the whole fast their mind is on their dishes; and if they fast once a day, they compensate by eating for the meals they have missed—sometimes by anticipating the hour of supper, sometimes by taking food immoderately, sometimes by the artifice of more luxurious food, sometimes by desiring beyond measure. These are the four attendants of *gastrimargia*, or gluttony, by whom the merit of fasting is diminished or indeed made altogether useless. Bodily fasting must observe these four things: namely, the hour of fasting, sober abstinence, moderation of preparation, and measure of appetite [Col. 0110A]. The person who fasts should therefore consider whether any of these is lacking; if it is, this is not the fast which the Lord has chosen. Rather, the left hand is mingled with the right; one fasts for the belly rather than for sobriety.

We have now said something about water, which is the beginning of a human being’s life; but where is bread? “The beginning,” he says, “of a human being’s life is water and bread,” and so forth (Ecclus. 29). In Holy Scripture we find four recognized kinds of bread. First, the ash-cake, which Elijah is read to have eaten in the desert (3 Kings 19). Then the other three distinguished by Moses in Leviticus: bread baked in an oven, bread roasted on a griddle, and a third fried in oil in a pan (Lev. [Col. 0110B] 2).

The ash-cake, because of its ashes, signifies remembrance of death. Bread baked in an oven signifies endurance of tribulation, for fire is a sign of tribulation. Bread on a griddle—where the griddle is placed between the fire and the bread—denotes the affection of compassion; for when we extend the inward tenderness of compassion to others’ calamities, we temper, as it were by an intervening griddle, the fire of their tribulation. The fourth bread, fried in oil, denotes the sweetness of divine consolation.

For the penitent, then, ash-cake is altogether necessary: that is, remembrance of death, so that in every work he may remember his last things—how swift and uncertain destruction is, how changeable life is, how uncertain the hour is—so that remembrance of death may always cut off the pleasures offered by the world. The second bread, likewise, which is baked in the oven, and the third, roasted on the griddle, concern living well: that is, endurance of tribulation and the affection of compassion. For everyone wishing to live well ought to strive not to change the settled state of his mind through impatience when injuries are inflicted, and also to yield to the injuries of neighbours in an affection of compassion.

Therefore, if a word of rebuke, the lash of correction, or the dart of detraction or reproach comes upon you, endure it patiently, because “the present momentary and light affliction of our tribulation works in us beyond measure an eternal weight in the sublimity of glory” (2 Cor. 4). Scripture says: “Woe [Col. 0110D] to those who have lost endurance” (Ecclus. 2). For whoever could not bear evil persons patiently is by his very impatience a witness against himself that he is not good. Do you wish to hear the affection of compassion? “Who is weak,” says the Apostle, “and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 3). Learn, human being, from the members of your body, which assist one another, how you ought to aid your neighbour’s need with the inward tenderness of compassion. If one of your members suffered sickness, would eye deny sight, ear hearing, foot walking, or hand service to its aid? (1 Cor. 12). By no means. Go, therefore, and do likewise toward your neighbour. For, as the Apostle says, we are members one of another (Rom. 12).

The fourth [Col. 0111A] bread, fried in oil, is the sweetness of divine consolation, necessary not only for the beginning of a good life but also for its completion. You and the other holy men know this well, you who taste how sweet the Lord is. O delicate bread, O sweetest bread, who will grant that my soul may be refreshed by your food, that the hunger of the inward human being may be satisfied as you feed it? For you are that bread which strengthens the human heart (Ps. 103). Let us now consider wherein this spiritual bread consists, namely, the sweetness of divine consolation.

It consists plainly in the devotion of holy prayer, the meditation of divine reading, and the promise of eternal blessedness. For what can be sweeter to a human being than to knock upon heaven through the affection of prayer, penetrate heavenly secrets through holy meditation [Col. 0111B], and exult in the promise of blessedness? The first, the ash-cake, is without oil because it is wholly occupied with mourning. The second, baked in the oven, and the third, placed upon the griddle, have oil in part because, as the lawgiver says, they ought to be anointed with oil. For endurance of tribulation has a portion of joy and a portion of sorrow, as is written of the apostles: “They went rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they were judged worthy to suffer reproach for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5). Likewise, compassion for one’s neighbour has the oil of consolation; for one does not truly have compassion if, when able, one does not console. But the last bread is soaked with oil both within and without, because everything which the sweetness of divine consolation pours in is pleasant to the palate.

The Church, still militant upon earth, meanwhile consoles herself by prayer, meditation, and hope in the promise which she has not yet attained. But the heavenly Jerusalem—that is, the saints who reign with God—already eats this bread, having attained the joy of eternity. In memory of this, on this day the Church’s voice exults, singing a song of joy when it says: “Rejoice, Jerusalem, and assemble, all you who love her.” As though she said to her children: “Be comforted, my people, for a little while yet, and you shall feast with your brothers and be satisfied from the breasts of your consolation.” We now have water and bread.

The third thing is clothing, because the beginning of human life is water, bread, and clothing. This clothing [Col. 0111D], if I am not mistaken, is the safeguard of humility. Clothing is necessary in every respect: it covers nakedness, keeps off the harshness of cold, and preserves warmth.

Would you see how it covers our nakedness? Certainly, among every kind of evil nothing exposes our weakness more than the wind of unrestrained self-exaltation. But the safeguard of humility covers this nakedness when it produces in a person contempt for self: so that one does not think highly of oneself (Rom. 12), judges oneself inferior to everyone, and is always one’s own accuser not only in speech but in bearing, countenance, and gesture, saying in word and deed: “I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people” (Ps. 21).

This clothing also wards off the harshness of cold—that is, the seedbed of rivalry and discord—because [Col. 0112A] precisely insofar as a person despises oneself, one has reverence for one’s neighbour. Thus one is ready to serve everyone, whom one judges to surpass oneself in worthiness of merits; and so the harshness of cold is removed from the midst, while, through reverence for one’s neighbour, one submits oneself by eager service to the will of all. For, as someone has said, “Service produces friends; truth produces hatred.”

This clothing also preserves warmth through the fear of God. For, as Scripture says, “It belongs to good minds to recognize faults there,” that is, “to fear where there are none.” A person should always be fearful in God’s sight, lest through some intervening fault one offend him with whom one hastens to be united in the whole desire of one’s mind. Thus, while one fears offending him whom one loves, one’s mind is ever more firmly established and grows in the fervour of his love [Col. 0112B].

This clothing, then—the safeguard of humility—has these three elements: contempt for self, reverence for one’s neighbour, and fear of God. It may perhaps seem hard to someone to present oneself humble and despised before all; but herein lies consolation, because, as the Apostle says, “Discipline at the present time is not joyous but sorrowful; yet in the future it will receive a most peaceful fruit” (Heb. 12).

Certainly, when Rachel was giving birth, as her soul was departing because of pain, she called her son, as Scripture says, *Ben-oni*, that is, “son of my sorrow”; but his father called him Benjamin, that is, “son of the right hand” (Gen. 35). For Rachel—that is, every soul seeing God through holy desire—does not bring forth the fruit of good works without pain [Col. 0112C]. These works are called by God the Father “the son of the right hand,” because on their account they shall receive in eternity that consolation signified by the right hand.

Therefore, for the beginning of a good life, not only water and bread but also clothing are highly beneficial; and besides these there is a fourth thing, namely, a house protecting human shamefulness. This shamefulness seems great: water cannot altogether wash it away, nor can clothing wholly cover it; rather, a house of sufficient size is needed to cover it.

This shamefulness is not in one part of the human body, which one garment would be enough to conceal. On the contrary, it is so widespread that from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head it has left no soundness: it is the corruption of sin. Blessed Job laments this shamefulness, saying: “My flesh is clothed with rottenness and the filth of dust” (Job 7) [Col. 0112D]. How clothed? Entirely surrounded.

For the foot offends in walking, the ear in hearing, the hand in action, the tongue in speech, the eye in looking upon vanities—so much so that we may say with that pagan: “No place remains in us for a new wound.” This indeed is a heavy yoke upon the children of Adam from the day of their birth until the day of their burial. Under its burden that holy man groans, saying: “Why was I received upon the knees? And why nursed at the breasts? For now, sleeping, I should be silent, and in my sleep I should rest with the kings and counsellors of the earth; or, like a hidden untimely birth, I should not endure; or like those conceived who did not see the light” (Job 3).

But what shall I say? We have the disease; it is necessary [Col. 0113A] to seek a remedy. Let us therefore see what that house is, so necessary that it can protect this shamefulness. It is, if I am not mistaken, the discipline of cloistered life, which governs and regulates not only the conscience of the heart but also every outward action of a person.

For example: silence governs the tongue; the cloister, the foot; obedience, the hand; solitude, the sight; divine discourse forms the hearing—so that in holy persons all outward things may be done with discipline and all inward things peacefully. For what brightness is in fire, serenity in air, tranquillity in the sea, and pleasantness in the earth, discipline is in a community and peace in the heart.

The beginners are the foundation of this house; those who labour are its walls; those who contemplate are its roof. Do not those truly lay a foundation who, converted from an evil manner of life, take upon themselves the form of religion? Likewise, the labourers are walls: after courageously beginning to act, they vigorously assist their Church not only in spiritual matters but also in bodily administration, provision, and execution of work [Col. 0113B].

Those who contemplate complete the roof: they have washed their feet with the bride and do not wish to rise lest they defile them (Song 5). Free from earthly occupations, they stand before God and serve him in spirit and mind, meditating upon his law day and night (Ps. 1).

Behold, most beloved brethren: “the sparrow”—that is, any weak person—“has found a house for itself, and the turtledove a nest for itself, where it may lay its young” (Ps. 83): that is, a spiritual nest. In this house the weak person heals [*sanat*, perhaps “heals”] sickness, and the healthy person preserves the health [Col. 0113C] which is granted to mortals in the present life as a remedy, until we enter the house not made by hands, which is in heaven, for joy in the life to come. There he will hide us in the secrecy of his face from the disturbance of men; he will protect us in his tabernacle from the contradiction of tongues (Ps. 30). May Jesus Christ lead us there: our king, humble man and exalted God, whose kingdom and dominion endure for ages of ages. Amen.

## Sermon XIX. In Lent

“The beginning of the life of a human being is water and bread and clothing and a house that protects his shamefulness” (Ecclus. 25).

Just as there are stages of descent into death, so there are stages of ascent into life [Col. 0113D]. There are three stages by which one descends into death. The first is to neglect God’s commandments; the second, to devote oneself to the pleasures of the flesh; the third, to make oneself prone to every spiritual vice. Likewise, there are three stages of ascent into life. The first is devout conversion; the second, good conduct; the third, holy consummation.

Therefore, although conversion to God is the beginning of human life, bread and water are called the beginning of human life because water—namely, that of penitence—and the bread of Holy Scripture are necessary for one converted to God.

First, the water of tears is necessary: just as water cleanses the eye, so tears cleanse the affection of the mind—provided that they spring up like a fountain from the depths of the earth, that is, provided they arise from remembrance of one’s earthly [Col. 0114A] or sinful conduct.

This water is especially necessary, provided it has companions which ought fruitfully to accompany the penitent: namely, sighing, weeping, and clapping. Sighing proceeds from the heart, weeping from the mouth, and striking from the hands: sighing for the sin of thought, weeping for the sin of speech, and striking for the sin of action. All these must be wiped away in the remembrance of sins.

Yet you, good man, who have been converted to God, ought to know that frequent recollection of sins is harmful to some and good for others. It is useful for those who are fervent in spirit and strong in action, because through detesting their sins they are kindled more strongly toward love of God. But there are others whose conscience is weak and who are feeble in resisting vices; it is not beneficial for these frequently to recall their sins. For just as a body is sometimes corrupted by the stench of a corpse, so a sick conscience is defiled by frequent remembrance of sins [Col. 0114B].

Physicians commonly say that remnants of illnesses remaining in bodies cause relapses; the same thing occurs with remnants of spiritual illnesses. For just as someone beginning to recover from a grave illness sometimes relapses and falls back into sickness if he uses food contrary to him, so too a weak soul, affected by recollection of sin, is strongly drawn toward consent to sin.

[Col. 0114C] The bread of the Scriptures is likewise necessary for life. Of it it is said: “The little children asked for bread, and there was none to break it for them” (Lam. 4). Elsewhere it is said of the same bread: “They knew the Lord in the breaking of bread” (Luke 24). And in the Gospel the Lord is reported to have satisfied many thousands of people with this bread.

For Holy Scripture forms the human will both through knowledge of truth and through love of virtue. This bread, however, is not to be set before everyone uniformly, but must be varied according to readers’ condition and their capacity of understanding. Some know much and love little; others love much and know little; others know much and love much; others both know little and love little.

Those who know much [Col. 0114D] and love little ought to read moral Scriptures, which cleanse the affection and kindle charity: such as the writings of blessed Gregory, the Proverbs of Solomon, the Book of Wisdom, and other works of this kind which pertain to the formation of character.

Those who love much and know little ought to read Scriptures suited to the capacity of their understanding, which illuminate the intellect toward knowledge of truth: Genesis, Exodus, the Books of Kings, Chronicles, and other such works which pertain to the knowledge of truth.

Those who know much and love much ought to read Scriptures at once aphoristic and affective, by which both intellect and affection are nourished.

Those who know little and love little, although they may lawfully read simple Scriptures, would do better [Col. 0115A] to hear a word of exhortation from one who knows how to exhort in doctrine. For the living voice teaches and is more effective for instruction than the reception of written letters.

This exhortation ought to be given by those who are illumined not only through knowledge but also kindled by charity, because the preacher must first conceive children in the womb of charity, and afterwards give birth through the word of preaching. Hence Paul says: “My little children, whom I labour to bring forth again until Christ be formed in you” (Gal. 4).

But a criminal person, even if he has much knowledge, is nevertheless enjoined to keep silence. As it is written: “Their throat is an open tomb; with their tongues they acted deceitfully” (Ps. 5). For though through knowledge of truth they know how to speak rightly, they nevertheless frequently speak crookedly and harmfully, being driven by the affection of a perverse will [Col. 0115B].

And observe, you member of the cloister, that reading is to be used at one time, prayer at another, and meditation at another. In a time of tribulation, when a good man is placed in distress, persecution, or any tribulation whatever, he ought to use prayer, so that the Lord may deliver him from these things. Thus Daniel prayed in captivity, Judith prayed when about to fight against Holofernes, and Jacob, fearing his brother Esau, fought against danger through prayer.

But in the temptation of sin—that is, when someone has fallen into a grievous sin—he ought then to use reading. It shows a person the way of righteousness, instructs character, reveals the temptations of the devil and how he must be resisted. By all these means the sinful person is made more humble for receiving God’s grace [Col. 0115C].

But in a time of tranquillity one ought to use meditation, which should claim the whole human mind for itself, so that one is not delayed from one’s inward thought either by outward tribulation or by inward temptation.

Likewise, clothing is necessary for one advancing toward life, lest one walk naked and one’s shamefulness appear. According to the authorities of Scripture, we can distinguish a threefold clothing: the garment of haircloth, of which we read that the king of Nineveh put on sackcloth (Jonah 3); the wedding garment, as the Gospel says of a certain man, “How did you enter here without a wedding garment?” (Matt. 22); and the garment of gladness, as we read of Judith, that “she took off the garments of her widowhood and put on the garments of her gladness” (Judith 10).

Therefore, the garment of haircloth is the sorrow of contrition; the wedding garment is the virtue of charity; the garment of gladness is the gravity of outward conduct [Col. 0115D]. This threefold clothing is most fitting for every member of the cloister: that one may weep for one’s sins through sorrow of contrition; love with affection the things that are good through charity; and through the gravity of one’s conduct advance by good living as an example to others.

The three things we have mentioned—water, bread, and clothing—remove three vices from cloistered persons, by which they are most greatly delayed upon the way of perfection: complacent security concerning past sins, lukewarmness in doing good, and frivolity in a person’s outward manner.

We see many who, when they enter a monastery and ought to undertake the office of mourning, become so secure, having already forgotten their former fault, that they seem to display in their manner of life not the fruit of penitence but a certain leisure of security [Col. 0116A].

Learn, O member of the cloister, if you are such a person—learn, I say, what you ought to do in secular warfare. For when the soldiers of an earthly emperor stand in battle line, if they see farmers, vine-dressers, or anyone whatever rejoicing in foolish merriment, none of these things moves them. They are concerned only to press their enemies courageously and obtain victory.

How much more, then, ought you, member of the cloister, to be watchful and not secure, since your struggle is not against flesh and blood, but rather against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world [Col. 0116B], against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places.

Jacob teaches you, whose pattern you ought to follow in overthrowing vices, that in your manner of life you ought not to be secure. Jacob wrestled with Esau in the womb; he wrestled with Laban in Mesopotamia; he wrestled with the Lord at Bethel.

Jacob wrestles with Esau in the womb when a cloistered person fights against carnal affection, as though against something born with him in the womb of a perverse will. He fights with Laban in Mesopotamia when, in this world, he fights the devil against the incitement of malice and secular vanity. He fights with the Lord at Bethel when a religious man, in the house of God—that is, in the cloister—strives in vigils and prayers, hunger [Col. 0116C] and thirst, and many other labours, as if by violence to obtain from the Lord the kingdom of heaven. For as it is written: “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. 11).

The second vice of which we spoke, namely lukewarmness of spirit in doing good, is most contrary to the advancement of cloistered persons, because it extinguishes the fervour of the spirit, removes the fruit of good work, and corrupts every diligence of spiritual endeavour and every devotedness to divine service with a certain slothful torpor and negligence.

The Lord himself abhors this torpor of spirit, reproaching such persons when he says: “Would that you were hot or cold! But because you are lukewarm, I shall begin to vomit you out of my mouth” (Rev. 3). Look at lukewarm water: it provokes nausea in one who tastes it and gives off denser smoke than water boiling with heat does [Col. 0116D].

So too those who are lukewarm in their conduct, being lax in works, faint-hearted in mind, and disorderly in manner, emit from themselves a most foul smoke, as it were, by which they cloud the eyes of observers as with a kind of darkness. For they offer others an example of idleness, by which others are delayed from spiritual conduct. Oh, how miserable is the life of that member of the cloister who pours not light but darkness upon the brethren living with him!

The third vice, frivolity of outward manner, must especially be avoided by the cloistered person, not only because of sin but also because of scandal. Since one’s manner and bearing ought to be like a mirror for those outside, if one is quick to laugh, jocular in speech, immature in countenance, and uncomposed in gesture, all these things testify against him: there is less virtue in one whose outward appearance displays so many signs of dissipation [Col. 0117A].

For one who has professed the religious life ought to bear upon one’s forehead the *tau*, that is, the form of the Crucified One; because “whoever says that he remains in him ought also himself to walk as he walked” (1 John 2). But whoever outwardly presents himself with immature bearing carries not the *tau* but leprosy upon his forehead. Therefore, just as a leper is excluded from human fellowship because of his face, so also the cloistered person who is such must be expelled from the fellowship of the righteous, lest he corrupt others by his bad example.

Therefore, the three things we mentioned at the beginning—water of penitence, bread of Holy Scripture, and clothing of mature conduct—have been given to cloistered persons as three remedies against the three vices of which we spoke, namely security, lukewarmness, and frivolity of outward bearing: sorrow of penitence against security; reading of Holy Scripture, which illuminates and kindles the mind, against lukewarmness; and the garment of maturity against frivolity of outward bearing [Col. 0117B].

Nor is it without reason that a house protecting one’s shamefulness is said to be necessary for one tending toward life. For if we wish to interpret this house as the Church, or the congregation of the faithful—of which it is said, “Wisdom has built herself a house” (Prov. 9), and elsewhere, “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John 24 [probably 14])—it is highly necessary and highly fruitful to remain in such a house.

For in it the master of the household, that is, Christ, has a dining room in which he is fed; he has his bridal chamber in which he rests; he has his private chamber in which he arranges his counsels; and he has a judicial seat in which he discerns judgments.

The dining room of this house is merciful persons, who diligently devote themselves to alms and other works of mercy, upon which Christ gladly feeds. The bridal chamber of the same house is contemplative persons, in whom Christ rests through tranquillity and love of heavenly things, since they have been withdrawn from the cares and pleasures of this world [Col. 0117C].

The private chamber of this house is perfect persons who, illumined by divine wisdom, give others warnings and counsels concerning how they ought to advance toward life. The judicial seat in this house is the prelates of the Churches, in whom Christ sits to discern just judgments, whether for the correction of offenders or for the peace of the righteous.

Therefore, whoever you are who see in yourself the stain of shamefulness—that is, sin—you can protect it in this house. If you are unmerciful and are not touched by compassion for your neighbour, go to the dining room of this house, that you may learn to act mercifully. If you are distracted by the cares of this world, go to the bridal chamber of this house, that you may learn to devote yourself to contemplation. If you lack counsel or knowledge, so that you do not know how to govern your life, go to the private chamber of this house, that you may receive counsels of life from perfect persons. If you have fallen into some more grievous sin, go to the judicial seat of this house [Col. 0118A], that you may receive the rod of discipline from ecclesiastical prelates.

And, to say something about the prelates of the Churches: they ought to be such that, when they judge others, they do not appear to be liable to judgment because of the enormity of their own lives. For, as blessed Gregory says, “No one harms the Church of God more than one who lives perversely while bearing only the name of holiness.”

There are, therefore, four things which a prelate of the Church ought to possess: a clean life, sound doctrine, zeal for justice, and love of discipline.

A clean life is necessary for a prelate, that he may live holily, because when one’s life is despised, one’s doctrine must also be despised. Sound doctrine is also necessary, as it is said of prelates: “Be instructed, you who judge the earth” (Ps. 2) [Col. 0118B]. Thus, whether he speaks to his subjects in exhortation or teaches for instruction, he may do everything according to the rule of the catholic faith, lest one who ought to be a herald of justice and truth seem in any respect to oppose truth.

A prelate must also have zeal for justice, that he may steadfastly oppose with a free voice those who walk disorderly, defending the righteous with the sword of God’s word and correcting the restless. If a prelate lacks this zeal for justice, he is altogether unworthy of the honour of prelacy.

The fourth of the things belonging to a prelate is love of discipline: having become a pattern for his flock, he should willingly possess discipline and show himself readier than the rest for everything required by the order of regular life, so that what he teaches in speech he may also fulfil by the practice of deeds. Otherwise perhaps he will hear that Gospel saying directed against himself: “Do what they say, but do not do their works” (Matt. 23).

When all these things are duly observed, a cloistered person, both subject and prelate, finds what one ought to do and how one should pass from holy conversion to good conduct, and thence to the consummation of the perfect life, until one arrives at the place of the wonderful tabernacle, unto the house of God [Col. 0118C]. There joy in their Lord is given to good and faithful servants; and to those who lawfully contend in this life our Lord Jesus Christ grants the crown of righteousness—he who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## Sermon XX. On the Annunciation of Blessed Mary

[Col. 0118D] “The Lord shall send forth from Zion the rod of your power: rule in the midst of your enemies” (Ps. 109).

I wish, dearest brethren, if gracious Jesus had inspired grace, to address you by deeds rather than by words. For deeds advance edification more than words: words contain an exhortation to virtue through a certain sweetness of eloquence, whereas deeds draw people to imitation through the example of good conduct.

I, indeed, entirely devoid of virtue, am compelled to render to your charity some measure of the ministry of exhortation. I shall excuse myself with the saying of that wise man: “I perform the office of a whetstone, which can make iron sharp, though itself incapable of cutting” (Horace, *Ars Poetica*, v. 304). But because I am a sinner, should I alone therefore not approach my Lord? Should I alone not know where they have laid him [Col. 0119A]?

At least you, good man, religious man, who converse with your God day and night in spiritual whispering, who have looked toward the table of his consolation—you, I say, tell me where he feeds, where he lies down at noon; and when you have found him, report to me, that I too may come and worship him (Matt. 11).

Or rather, following my Saviour’s counsel, lest I undertake unarmed the stewardship of God’s word, I shall sell my tunic and buy a sword (Luke 22): the tunic of sin, the tunic of oldness. I shall exchange it for a better one—that is, for newness of life—in which I shall receive the weapons of righteousness and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God (Gal. 6).

And from the word which I have proposed in accordance with the feast, I seem to have taken an appropriate beginning. [Col. 0119B] Of the prophetic utterance of the Word it is said: “The Lord shall send forth from Zion the rod of your power,” and so forth. What other rod, do you suppose, is this except the blessed Mother of God, from whom proceeded that flower of the field, a flower singular in fruit, fragrance, and beauty?

Filled with the fruit of this flower, the bridegroom’s beloved exclaims joyfully in the Song of Love: “Under the shadow of him whom I desired I sat, and his fruit was sweet to my throat” (Song 2), calling the gifts of charisms “fruit.” O sweet fruit, O pleasant fruit, which hunger desires without torment, eats without weariness, by which it is satisfied without excess and healed without relapse! O good fruit, most savoury fruit, possessing every delight and every flavour of sweetness—for those, however, who have tasted how sweet the Lord is!

For in some respects it is manna because of sweetness [Col. 0119C]; in others, the tree of life because of eternity; in others, bread because of strength; in others, wine because of compunction; and in very many, oil because of the consolation of the Spirit.

Of the fragrance of this flower it is written in the Songs, where the faithful soul speaks to God, saying: “Draw me after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments” (Song 1). And elsewhere: “Behold, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a full field which God has blessed” (Gen. 27).

A fragrance necessary above all things: cleansing for the sick, strengthening for those who are advancing, and healing for the perfect. “Behold,” he says, “the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a full field.” Do you not see the field of this world filled with this fragrance, when you see some strong in justice and fervent in charity; others ready for obedience and the service of humility; these abundant in tears and lavish in almsgiving; and very many bursting forth into praise, not only because they have received pardon, but also because they have received grace for grace?

Of the beauty of that flower, holy Church rejoices for herself in the Songs, saying: “My beloved is white and ruddy” (Song 5): truly beautiful, truly lovely, who, though ruddy in his passion, nevertheless remained white in the essence of divinity [Col. 0119D]. Recalling his beauty, the prophet Daniel also says: “His garments were white as snow, his hair white as clean wool, his body like chrysolite, and his throne like a flame of fire” (Dan. 7).

[Col. 0120A] Therefore the blessed Mother of God was the rod of this flower, so illustrious in fruit, fragrance, and beauty. On this day the angel Gabriel sowed her seed when he announced that Christ, the power of God, would be born from her through the working of the Holy Spirit.

Hence the Prophet calls her the rod of his power (Ps. 109), because the Son himself, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God, proceeded according to the flesh from the nature of the blessed Virgin as a flower from a rod. Or she is called the rod of power because in the humanity which he assumed from her he mightily overthrew that ancient enemy, as the prophet Habakkuk testifies, saying: “Horns are in his hands”—understand, the horns of the cross—“there his strength was hidden” (Hab. 3).

The prophet therefore says: O Christ, the Lord shall send forth from Zion, that is, from the Jewish people, the rod of his power: namely, the blessed Virgin Mary [Col. 0120B]. This is that rod of Moses which devoured the dragons of Egypt. For the blessed Mother of God, foretold by Moses and the prophets, through the sun of righteousness proceeding from her illuminated the poisons of sins and the darkness of this world. Hence also it is said in her praise: “You alone have destroyed all heresies throughout the whole world.”

She is the rod of Aaron, which, placed in the tabernacle among the other rods of the tribes of Israel, flowered and put forth almonds. It flowered, certainly, by giving birth to Christ; it put forth almonds when by her example she converted many thousands of the righteous to newness of life.

If we examine carefully why Mary is called a rod, we see the likeness of a rod fitting her in this: a rod is flexible, slender, straight, tall, and uniform in shape—uniform, I say, not spread around with branches or leaves.

Certainly, as it is written, “Iniquity sits upon a talent of lead”: for it is weighty, not slender, not subtle. Therefore, because the blessed Mother of God was delivered from this heaviness of sin by the power of the Holy Spirit, the purity of her innocence is rightly understood through the rod’s slenderness. Her flesh, so purified, is called a light cloud by the prophet when he says: “Behold, the Lord ascends upon a light cloud” (Isa. 9) [Col. 0120C].

In the flexibility of the rod is understood the virtue of obedience, which you find in Mary when she says: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (Luke 1).

Learn, O sinful root, ash of eternal fire—learn, I say, from Mary’s example to humble yourself before God and to be subject to every human creature for God’s sake. Do you not know what Isaiah cries concerning the proud who walk in marvels beyond themselves? “Because,” he says, “the daughters of Zion have been exalted and have walked with neck outstretched, the Lord shall trample their crown and lay bare their hair” (Isa. 3).

Pride is deservedly punished thus, because, as Bernard, the master of that famous valley, says, “Not even Mary’s virginity would have pleased God without humility.” In the rod’s straightness are signified works of justice; in its length, perseverance in virtue; and in its uniformity, harmony of character.

Behold the rod proposed for imitation to everyone seeking the homeland. Let each see whether he wishes to imitate it, because the Lord will scourge with a rod of fury [Col. 0121A] those who have despised it. For there are also other rods of the Lord: some for the justification of the good, some for the punishment of the wicked. There is a rod of power, a rod of inheritance, a rod of direction, and a rod of fury.

The rod of inheritance is the generation of the upright, who are heirs of the kingdom and participants in future blessedness, of which the Psalmist says: “You redeemed the rod of your inheritance” (Ps. 73). This rod was signified in Jacob’s action when he took rods of poplar, almond, and plane tree, partly stripped their bark, and left some of one colour, so that the sheep, looking upon them, might conceive offspring sometimes variegated and sometimes uniform (Gen. 30).

By those partly stripped he represented the saints who gave skin for skin by enduring passions, torments, and injuries. By those of one colour he portrayed those who, without torments, gave light to God’s Church through orthodox faith, doctrine, and piety of character. The sheep—that is, the simple—ought to look upon these rods so that they may conceive in looking upon them. For from their examples they ought to learn sometimes to endure willingly and patiently injuries, insults, and the vexations of wicked people; or, in others, humility, obedience, gentleness, and the other virtues necessary for salvation [Col. 0121B].

The rod of direction is understood as the rigour of discipline: that in voice, countenance, gesture, bearing, speech, and action we may live holily, justly, and piously. Of this rod the Prophet says: “Your throne, O God, is for ages of ages; the rod of direction is the rod of your kingdom” (Ps. 44).

[Col. 0121C] The rod of fury is the devil and his angels, through whom God punishes those who are plunged into the lowest pit and the shadow of death. Of this rod it was said: “Assyria is the rod of my fury,” with Assyria signifying the angels of Satan.

Therefore, the rod of power defends the weak in temptation (Isa. 10); the rod of inheritance directs the righteous; the rod of direction corrects the crooked; and the rod of fury scourges the ungodly. Choose for yourself, then, which of these rods you will hold: whether you wish to be counted among God’s friends or among his enemies. Of these it is said, “Rule,” that is, “You shall rule in the midst of your enemies.” For he will rule over them either by converting them to righteousness or by punishing them in vengeance.

But some in God’s house wish to appear not as a rod but as an immovable pillar. If you admonish them, they disregard it; if you rebuke them, they despise it; if you entreat them, they do not listen. Rather, they murmur against the master of the household, saying: “These last have worked one hour, and you have made them equal to us, who have borne the burden and heat of the day” (Matt. 20) [Col. 0121D].

“We,” they say, “in nightly vigils; we in the daytime hours; we in the silence of the cloister; we in hymns and songs, cry to heaven that our God may have mercy upon us.” Oh, that we might chant, dearest brethren, not only with the voice, but also with spirit and mind! For, as someone has said: “When the voice does not reproach the life, the harmony is sweet.”

Plainly, this vocal music is quite fitting for praise, [Col. 0122A] but there is another kind, taught by that heavenly musician, and it is more necessary for our salvation. But what is that music which God teaches? It is indeed distinguished into three kinds: one is animate, another spiritual, another heavenly.

Animate music exists when the outward senses seek nothing superfluous and do not in any way depart from the guidance of reason: when the eye does not look upon vain things, the ear does not hear slanders or judgments of blood, the sense of smell does not seek pleasant odors, the taste does not seek excess, and the hand is not stretched out toward unlawful things. These are the five notes of animate music, making the harmony called *diapente*, which means “of five.” For it is composed of the five bodily senses, rightly ordered, as has already been said.

Spiritual music consists in [Col. 0122B] the advancement of virtues, in spiritual joy and sweetness of conduct, in the fear of God and the love of brotherhood. Through it there is produced the harmony called *diatessaron*, that is, “of four.” Four principal virtues therefore produce it: namely courage, justice, temperance, and prudence—so that in every good action there may be courage for assistance, justice for direction or judgment, temperance for consolation, and prudence for counsel.

Heavenly music, however, consists in the contemplation of God, the attainment of eternity, the gladness of the mind, and the immortality of the body. This music produces the harmony called *diapason*, which means “of eight.” For the eight beatitudes produce it: when the kingdom of heaven is given to poverty, the land of the living to meekness, consolation to those who mourn, [Col. 0122C] satisfaction to those who hunger, and so with the rest, as is described in the Gospel.

Practice yourself, therefore, my dearest brother, in these kinds of music taught by that heavenly musician; choose rather to sing in harmony of conduct than of voices, and prefer strength of mind to strength of body, as that holy man says: “He will not delight in the strength of a horse, nor will the Lord take pleasure in the legs of a man.” What then is pleasing to the Lord? “Those who fear him, and those who hope in his mercy” (Ps. 146).

Finally, you who serve in the camp of Israel and are strong in the battle of the Lord, I ask you: on which side do you guard the tabernacle of the Lord—toward the east, [Col. 0122D] the south, the north, or the west? Certainly, as Moses writes, Issachar, Judah, and Zebulun keep watch on the eastern side of the tabernacle; Reuben, Gad, and Simeon on the southern; Dan, Naphtali, and Asher on the northern; Ephraim, Manasseh, and Benjamin on the western (Num. 2). All these things were written for our instruction.

By the eastern side of the tabernacle is signified the rising, or beginning, of religious life. There keep watch Issachar, whose name means “memory of the Lord”; Judah, “confessing”; and Zebulun, “dwelling-place of strength.” Therefore everyone who undertakes a new life ought to possess remembrance of the Lord, through contrition of heart for sins committed; likewise [Col. 0123A] confession of the mouth in self-accusation; and he should be a dwelling-place of strength, bravely enduring the harshness of satisfaction.

By the southern side is understood the progress or increase of virtue. There keep watch these three: Reuben, meaning “a son who sees”; Gad, “girded”; and Simeon, “the hearing of the Lord.” Whoever wishes to advance in virtues in the house of the Lord must be a seeing son—that is, watchful—so that he may carefully discern what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of the Lord. He must be girded with the belt of chastity through purity of the flesh. He must also be the hearing of the Lord, obeying his superior according to God’s command.

By the northern side is signified the struggle of temptation, [Col. 0123B] where keep watch Dan, “judgment”; Asher, “blessedness”; and Naphtali, “breadth.” Whoever wishes to be strong in temptations must set before his eyes that judgment without mercy in which the sheep will be separated from the goats; also the future blessedness owed to the righteous; and likewise the road which leads to it—namely, the breadth of charity—so that fear of judgment may keep him from unlawful things, and the promised blessedness may lead him into the breadth of charity.

By the western side—so called morally not from “setting” but from “slaying”—is understood tranquility of mind, when, after vices have been slain by mortification of the flesh, flesh and spirit are subjected to the divine will. On this side keep watch Ephraim, “fruitful”; Manasseh, “forgetful”; and Benjamin, “son of the right hand.” [Col. 0123C] Whoever wishes to serve God with a tranquil mind after vices have been killed must be fruitful in works of righteousness, forgetful through the erasure of his former life, and also a son of the right hand through desire for eternal happiness. For this is what is signified to us in the holy Scriptures by the right hand.

Thus, O man who considers yourself among the warriors of Israel, be Issachar—that is, mindful of the Lord through contrition of heart; Judah through confession of the mouth; Zebulun through the labor of satisfaction. Be Reuben through watchfulness; Gad through chastity; Simeon through obedience; Dan through fear of the divine judgment; Naphtali through the breadth of charity; Asher through hope of the promised [Col. 0123D] blessedness; Ephraim through zeal for good works; Manasseh through forgetfulness of former conduct; Benjamin through desire for future joy. Such ought those to be who serve the tabernacle of God.

What then shall become of those who destroy God’s tabernacle through schisms and scandals, through insults and slanders? I fear that with Dathan and Abiram they may descend alive into hell—that is, while understanding and recognizing their own iniquity. For how can they fail to know what they hear and understand through the divine Scriptures, through nocturnal readings, through psalms and hymns? Therefore the men of Nineveh will rise in judgment against such a generation, since they repented at Jonah’s preaching (Matt. 12).

[Col. 0124A] Jonah preached the overthrow of the city, and all turned from their evil ways to the Lord. Christ threatens condemnation to eternal death, and there is no one who heeds him. Therefore, dearest brothers, lest Christ the Lord speak harshly to us in that dreadful judgment, let us take of the finest fruits of the land and bring him gifts: a little resin, honey, *stirax*, *stacte*, and terebinth—that is, the virtues and works of virtues signified by these things—because perhaps he will forgive and leave behind a blessing. May my God make him merciful and grant release, both to this your brother who speaks and to him whom he holds in bonds—that is, to those who have bound themselves in the bonds of discipline in order to obey God. May he grant release, I say, to their Father: to the vision of that supreme and [Col. 0124B] eternal Father, where life is without end and joy without cloud. May Jesus himself, our king and savior, deign to lead us there, whose kingdom and dominion endure for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXI. ON THE ANNUNCIATION OF BLESSED MARY

“The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1).

The solemnity of today, dearest brothers, is honored by the title of the Lord’s Annunciation, because the beginnings of our salvation are believed to have been announced today to the blessed Virgin. For Wisdom, which from eternity had played before the Father in the hiddenness of the Godhead, wished also, by assuming the diadem of flesh, to make itself a spectacle to the world—thus reaching [Col. 0124C] mightily from end to end: from the end, I say, of supreme majesty to the end of utmost humility. For it was not enough, for the restoration of the created condition, to have reached that end of majesty and glory at which angelic nature rejoiced; it was also necessary to reach the end of humility, by which it might become a remedy for sinners.

At the novelty of this spectacle, namely the incarnation of the Word, that whole multitude of patriarchs and prophets through whom the Holy Spirit thundered to the world invited the generation to come, that it might recognize in the flesh the Holy of Holies whom the multitude of saints had foretold.

For what did Abraham signify by that action when he said: “Put your hand under [Col. 0124D] my thigh, that I may make you swear by the God of heaven and earth that you will not take a wife for my son from the daughters of Canaan” (Gen. 24)? To put the hand, which is accustomed to be extended as the support of faith, beneath the thigh is to hold in faith the humanity of Christ that would descend from Abraham. To swear by the God of heaven and earth is to declare with the mouth that he is the same God—as though he said: “Touch my thigh, and swear by my God.”

That same humanity of Christ was signified by Jeremiah’s loincloth, which, hidden in a hole in the rock at the river Euphrates, rotted until it seemed fit for no use (Jer. 13). The loincloth, namely the flesh assumed by the Word, rotted at the river Euphrates—that is, in the flow of our mortality—when that man, filled with reproaches and pierced with wounds, [Col. 0125A] became the outcast of the people. Hence blessed Job speaks in the person of the Son of God: “My flesh is clothed with rottenness and the filth of dust” (Job 7).

Nor do I think it should be passed over that this loincloth is said to have rotted in a hole in a rock. A hole is usually a defense for things placed in it, lest they be scattered by the force of a breeze or any violence of winds. In the rock, therefore, Christ is understood; in the hole of Christ, obedience, which preserved him from every outward disturbance and temptation. Yet in that hole the loincloth rotted, because he became obedient to God the Father unto death.

The Lord also promises that highest patriarch, saying: “In your seed all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 23), thereby foretelling that the mystery of the Incarnation would come [Col. 0125B] from Abraham’s seed. Yet when Christ is said to have been born from the seed of Abraham or David, a devout Catholic mind must understand this not according to the transmission of seed—for Christ was not so born from male seed—but should say rather that he was born from Abraham’s seed according to succession of lineage.

For the angel himself foretells to Mary that he will be born not from a man but from the Holy Spirit, when he says: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you,” and the rest. Receive then, Virgin Mary, the word sent to you from the Lord through the angel. He does not address you in order to terrify one who is fearful, ensnare one who is unsuspecting, or shake one who is weak. You who know [Col. 0125C] how to converse with the Lord in the secrecy of your chamber, to penetrate heaven by prayer, and to see visions of angels—why should you fear their speech or doubt their promises?

Certainly the Holy Spirit will come upon you, so that the fulfillment of the promise may prove the trustworthiness of the messenger. “He will come upon you,” he says. The Spirit certainly came to the Virgin through election, hastened through sanctification, drew near through address, and finally came upon her—that is, came upon her through that ineffable operation of the Incarnation.

Let us ask all the daughters of Eve which among them was free from that threefold woe of all flesh which Adam passed down to his descendants. The first was in corruption of the flesh; the second in transgression of the mind; the third in the punishment of condemnation. Absolutely no one was free, until [Col. 0125D] the Holy Spirit came upon—came, I say, over—the woe of the blessed Virgin and removed that whole woe, so completely that neither corruption of flesh made her impure, nor transgression of mind guilty, nor condemnation miserable.

O how effective is the medicine of the Holy Spirit, which made her so healthy, so innocent! I think it could not be found in the land of those living pleasantly, nor did it take its origin in the dwelling-place of our valley; and therefore it “came upon”—that is, it came down from above, from the heights to the lowly—so that our nature, which could not be preserved by lower causes (for all flesh had corrupted its way), might at least receive from above a medicine for the remedy of its sickness. It further pleases me to consider the effect of this medicine and compare the manner of the illness with it, in case it may be useful [Col. 0126A] to oppose such a disease with such a remedy.

There were indeed two infirmities in our nature to be healed. One proceeded from an excess of moisture; the other from the violence of cold. The excess of moisture is the flood of carnal desires; coldness is despair of heavenly promises. Against these two, the medicine of the Holy Spirit possessed two contraries in itself: namely heat and dryness, so that contraries might be cured by contraries. Its heat was the ardor or desire of heavenly things; its dryness was the power of chastity, or the resolve of virginity.

The Holy Spirit therefore placed heat in the blessed Virgin against cold, so that by ardor for heavenly things she might despise earthly things. [Col. 0126B] He also placed dryness against moisture, so that by her resolution of virginity and continence he might utterly extinguish carnal desires in her. Hence it is also added: “And the power of the Most High will overshadow you.” That is, it will grant refreshment from the heat of carnal desires.

But if we call the power of the Most High Christ—who, according to the Apostle, is the power of God and the wisdom of God—then, since the Son of God himself is called inaccessible light, the sun of righteousness, Lucifer or the morning star, it seems that he ought rather to have said, “The power of the Most High will shine upon you,” than “will overshadow you,” since luminous things usually provide brightness rather than shade. This might perhaps be true if we could assess even God’s miracles according to the form of natural things.

For every shadow-casting body in the natural order [Col. 0126C] throws its shadow upon that which is opposite to the source from which brightness proceeds. By this likeness observe how the power of the Most High overshadowed the blessed Virgin. The thing from which brightness proceeded was the divinity of the Word; what stood opposite that brightness was the frailty of our mortality. But Christ’s humanity, united to the Word in conception, received in itself the splendor of divinity; and thus, placed between divinity and our frailty, it cast its shadow not only over Mary but also over the whole world. Thus understand the overshadowing as the mediating role of assumed flesh.

And just as a ray of the solar orb casts the shadows of bodies opposite it into different places, as daily experience proves, [Col. 0126D] so Christ, the sun of righteousness, extends the shadow of his humanity to the various parts of the Church at different times. He made a shadow toward the east when, at the rising or beginning of his conception, he took the form of a servant and gave an example of humility. He made a shadow toward the west when, in the Passion, he supplied the remedy for sin. He made a shadow toward the north when, descending into hell, he bit hell. He cast a shadow toward the south when, ascending, he bore the witnesses of his glory into heaven.

O that Christ might also show us, dearest brothers, where he feeds, where he lies down at noon, so that his shadow might cover us—not, I say, as mountains, but like shrubs. For who has rested in it and been scorched? Who has sat beneath it and not been protected? [Col. 0127A] Here the heat of desire finds refreshment, the wind of pride an obstacle, gluttony moderation; whatever other infirmity there may be finds a remedy. Yet there is one kind of overshadowing which, because of excessive cold, makes a person numb; another, against the violence of heat, provides refreshment.

For whoever seeks shade in winter, when the sun is far from us, is plainly gripped all the more strongly by cold. But if anyone enters into shade in the days of summer, when the sun shines nearer to us in its power, he receives the comfort of shade. Is it not similar in that overshadowing which the power of the Most High makes, so that it is for some an occasion of danger and for others a cause of salvation?

Indeed Christ is remote from some through the fervor of charity [the wording is uncertain], though he overshadows them through the sacraments [Col. 0127B] of faith, warming them beneath the wings of the Church. They belong to the Church in letter, not in spirit; in name, not in commitment. This overshadowing of the sacraments, because the fervor of love is absent, makes them numb rather than refreshed. “For it is better not to know the way of truth than, after knowing the truth, to oppose it by corrupt pursuits and works” (2 Pet. 2).

Whom else do these signify but Joseph’s brothers, who, after receiving grain from him, carried back in their sacks the money which they ought to have paid, and in addition the silver cup in which the lord of the land was accustomed to divine? (Gen. 44). By the name of grain is understood the power of the Eucharist and the other sacraments, as in the passage: “He fed them with the fat of wheat, and satisfied them with honey from the rock” (Ps. 80). [Col. 0127C] The money, however, is God’s gifts themselves, by which they ought to repay his benefits, received in the unity of the Church. The silver cup in which Joseph customarily divines is the brightness of the divine word, in which he foretells the future rewards of the righteous and punishments of the wicked.

But they hide not only the money but also the silver cup in their sacks when they do not display outwardly through the performance of good works either the gifts of God they have received or the testimonies of Holy Scripture which they understand. Hence the Prophet too, sighing, laments: “Upon the willows in its midst”—speaking of Babylon—“we hung our instruments” (Ps. 136). By the willows, which are unfruitful trees, we understand sinful and unfruitful people, upon whom the instruments of sacred speech [Col. 0127D] hang as though useless: they receive laws and prophets through hearing, yet do not resound with the melody of holy devotion and the harmony of good works.

Can those resound in God’s praise whom tongue, conscience, and deeds alike condemn? “Whoever does not offend in speech,” says Scripture, “is a perfect man” (Jas. 3). Indeed—to say what I think—among all the things forbidden by God’s law, there is none that more frequently separates a person from God than the sin of speech.

Do you wish to see how frequently? Among those called whisperers in a people are some who conceive evil things from themselves and afterward bring them to birth by reporting them to others. Others receive evil things from others and repeat the same to yet others. There are a third sort [Col. 0128A] who do not themselves repeat others’ offenses, but gladly listen to those who do report them. The Prophet marks this kind of slander when he says: “He has not accepted reproach against his neighbors” (Ps. 14). One punishment of condemnation awaits all these, whom one kind of mortal sin envelops, especially since those who commit and those who consent are to be punished with equal penalty.

“But,” you will say, “I do not consent because I listen to speakers whom I cannot stop. I do not wish to quarrel, nor to turn away my ear, lest by doing so I grieve my brother.” On the contrary, you give full consent and wholly complete the sin of detraction, because if there were no listener, there would be no slanderer. Do you wish to understand consent? Certainly, in this kind of sinning as in others, consent is admitted in four ways: [Col. 0128B] by instigating, when someone suggests to another that he should cast reproach upon his brother; by cooperating, when he defends him so that he may remain unpunished for speaking thus; by keeping silent, when he does not warn him to cease, thereby lending authority—when a prelate who ought to correct those who err does not chastise a slanderer. Such a man himself sins all the more gravely inasmuch as he could more easily correct him, if he wished to devote his effort to his brother’s advancement.

Yet you are free from the mark of detraction when you can recount your brother’s offense. For an offense is sometimes recounted for the sake of correction, sometimes for the sake of the common good, and sometimes for the sake of disparagement.

[Col. 0128C] If, then, your brother has sinned to your knowledge—even where the offense is secret—and has perhaps not accepted your correction, you may report this in secret either to one who holds the office of prelate, or to some good and holy man whose religious standing is established, or indeed to someone possessing the authority of learning. But you must firmly judge that such persons will both keep the secret and, with the inward compassion of charity, wish to labor for the correction of the brother. For everyone whom you admit to awareness of a secret offense must be such that he can either restrain it by authority of power, correct it by authority, or instruct by authority of knowledge in what should be done or avoided.

An offense may also be recounted without blame for the common good: for instance, if some wish to appoint to the Church of God a man who is a murderer, or admit into the fellowship of brethren someone marked by a public crime. Those wishing to object may then bring forward, in support of their objection, the crime which is publicly known concerning him. [Col. 0128D] But if someone recounts another’s crime, public or private, in order to harm him—so that he may be regarded as more contemptible and abject—the person who does this has thereby become a child of Gehenna, because he has acted against fraternal charity. And this is concerning speech.

But to pass to the witness of conscience: who, finally, is so secure that he is not pierced by the sword of conscience when he hears that proclamation of humility in the Gospel: “Whoever wishes to be greater among you shall be your minister; and whoever wishes to be first shall be your servant” (Matt. 20). “Just as the Son of Man [Col. 0129A] came not to be served, but to serve.”

O those blessed times of the saints, in which the doctrine of humility flourished in practice, so that whatever love of one’s own superiority or display of vain glory offered, the purity of conscience cast all away as evil! No one should doubt that the virtue of patience is necessary for salvation, since the Lord commanded us to preserve it not only through himself but also through his servants the prophets.

Thus David says: “By day the Lord commanded his mercy, and by night his song” (Ps. 41). By day—that is, in prosperity—the Lord commanded us to bear his mercy: that is, patiently to endure injuries, vexations, and hardships, which are also called mercy in blessed Job, as in this passage: “Did I not dissemble? Did I not keep silence and become quiet? Yet your mercy came upon me, O Lord” (Job 3). But in the night of adversity he commanded his song: that is, the consolation of eternal blessedness, lest we fail in tribulations.

Let each person therefore examine the secrets of his own heart, and he will be able to find something to weep over. For if taking revenge for one’s own injuries, breaking out in harsh words, and opposing the commands of one’s elders are to be counted under the name of impatience, do you suppose that you will find patience on earth? For it is a rare bird on earth, most like a black swan.

Which of us, finally, fears that Gospel warning: “Whoever is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment; whoever says, ‘Raca,’ shall be liable to the council; whoever says, ‘You fool,’ shall be liable to the Gehenna of fire” (Matt. 5)? Everywhere understand the qualification: “without cause.” But this always occurs without cause when no reason of correction or common good intervenes.

And because we do not fulfill in deed the law of the Lord which we have received, John’s saying in the Apocalypse seems already to be fulfilled in us, where it is said: “And the sun became black as a sackcloth of hair” (Rev. 6). For Holy Scripture, which shines upon us like the sun by showing what leads to salvation, is regarded as rejected and worthless because there is no one who fulfills it in deed. Behold, the law of nature which God wrote in the human heart cries aloud: “What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another,” and we pay no attention. We cast aside the law of Moses and do not keep the commands of the Gospel. Upon what, then, will he strike, when we add transgression to transgression? [Col. 0129D] There is now no place in us for a new wound.

O that those golden ages might return, and that, as in the primitive Church, the Lord might send into the earth that fire of the Spirit which would consume this rust of vices and soften the iron of our hardened mind, so that it might at least be polished for the use of the Lord’s work by the hammerings and pressures which we experience daily.

In material things we see that those which are harder are tempered by two things, namely water and fire. So certainly, when those same two are understood spiritually, the hardness of the mind is softened into a certain sweetness of spiritual delight by the fire of charity and the water of compunction.

Observe and see: when a blacksmith wishes to soften [Col. 0130A] the material of iron, he puts it into fire and sprinkles water upon the burning coals, not in order to extinguish the fire but to make it revive more fully, until at last, having taken in the heat of the fire, the iron is shaped by hammerings according to the craftsman’s will. I believe that no differently should one who desires to be the diligent smith of his own mind labor with fire and water, softening the hard obstinacy of the mind, so that the water of contrition and tears of penitence may wash away past sins, and the ardor of charity kindle the soul to love virtue.

What else do the groans of a contrite heart, the tears of those confessing, the beatings of the breast, the rod of discipline, the harshness of haircloth, and, finally, the frequent prostration of the sinner signify in the Church? For all these draw after them the tears of those mourning their sins, so that a sinful person, [Col. 0130B] polished by such beatings, may at last begin to become a lover of virtue—until that small fire which, by coming beforehand, stirred the languishing affection of the mind to compunction, grows daily in its advances into a furnace of zeal for righteousness and love of virtue.

And since this does not belong to one who runs or wills, but to the merciful God, who works willing and accomplishing in all, let us strive to obtain this from him by such prayer as we can: so that, with the coldness of sin banished and the fire of charity kindled in our hearts, we may feel the refreshment of his overshadowing, until at last he hides us in the secret of his face from the disturbance of men, where life is without end and joy without cloud. May he grant this, our Lord [Col. 0130C] Jesus Christ, whose kingdom and dominion endure for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXII. ON THE ANNUNCIATION OF BLESSED MARY

“Hail, Mary, full of grace; the Lord is with you. The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1).

The passage you have heard, dearest brothers, contains the history of the Lord’s Annunciation, in which the Word that was in the beginning with God is announced as about to come in the flesh, as John says: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1). This is that shortened Word which the Lord made upon the earth—indeed, truly most brief. For although in the nature of his divinity [Col. 0130D] he is incomprehensible and infinite, in our nature he was made so small that he was covered by the veil of a little body, wrapped in swaddling clothes, and contained by a virgin’s womb—he whom the whole world could not contain from eternal days.

Nor without reason is the Word, who is Christ, announced with a word of greeting, since Christ himself is the author of our salvation. You may understand this by considering his birth, life, death, and resurrection. His birth purified our nature; his life instructed our life; his death destroyed our death; his resurrection bestowed salvation upon us.

Therefore the angel addresses the Virgin with the word of greeting, saying, “Hail, Mary.” We find three [Col. 0131A] celebrated greetings in the Gospel narrative. Christ greets his disciples when he says, “Peace be with you” (Luke 24). The angel greets Mary when he says, “Hail, Mary, full of grace” (Luke 1). Mary greets Elizabeth, as we read: for Mary went up with haste into the hill country to the house of Zachariah and greeted Elizabeth.

By this threefold greeting a threefold concord is signified to us: that of God with humankind, of angel with humankind, and of human with human. For God was at variance with humankind because of the sin of the first transgression. Angel was at variance with humankind because, although they ought to have been fellow-servants in the service of God, humankind had subjected itself to the dominion of the devil. Human was at variance with human, Jew with Gentile, because the former worshiped God while the latter worshiped idols.

Therefore in the first [Col. 0131B] greeting is signified the reconciliation of God with humankind, because God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself. In the second is signified the reconciliation of angel with humankind, since through Christ they became co-heirs of eternal life. In the third is signified the reconciliation of human with human, because Jew and Gentile, through the corner-stone which is Christ, were joined together in one faith.

And because this threefold reconciliation was accomplished through the blessed Virgin, let God speak, let the angel speak, let humankind speak: “Hail, Mary.” This reconciliation, I think, is also signified in the change of the first mother’s name, Eve, into the word of greeting. For the name Eve contains two sounds that display the double misery of human nature, namely, “etc.” For humankind is born into [Col. 0131C] this world with a double misery: guilt and punishment. Therefore, when Mary is addressed by reversing that name—“Ave”—this indicates that through the blessed Virgin both guilt was changed into pardon and punishment into glory.

And observe, if you please, that *ave* is sometimes the voice of one wishing, sometimes of one praying, and sometimes of one congratulating. It is the voice of one wishing when I say to my neighbor, “Hail,” because I wish him health. It is the voice of one praying when I say, “Hail, precious cross.” For I do not wish salvation to the wood, which it cannot possess, but pray that the power of the cross may work salvation for me. It is the voice of one congratulating when the Church now says, “Hail, Mary,” or when it says, “Hail, holy parent”—as though it said, “I congratulate” or “I rejoice with you in your salvation.”
