[Col. 0131D] Therefore let the Church say it in congratulation, and the angel in wishing: “Hail, Mary,” which means “star of the sea.” O that I might be granted an abundance of him who called her the star of the sea; O that I might be allowed to argue closely with him! For whichever god among the gods he was who called her so, I would show myself to him not merely verbose but contentious. Why did he not call her rather the star of heaven? Why not rather the star of the world? Surely the name “sea” signifies bitterness. Do sweet and bitter water draw from the same fountain? Is she who is the mother of mercy and compassion also the mother of bitterness? Far be it!

Therefore I shall rightly call her the star of heaven, the star of the world, and finally the star of the sea. The star of heaven, because of the reward of her exalted glory; [Col. 0132A] the star of the world, because of the consolation of the righteous; the star of the sea, because of the refuge of the wretched. She is the star of heaven, illuminating the other saints by her brightness; the star of the world—that is, of the righteous, who are rightly called *mundus*, “world,” because of purity of heart—because they look to her in devotion and receive the benefits of consolation against the pressures of this world. She is the star of the sea because all wretched people, all who toss in the bitterness of sins, seek from her the help of refuge.

Therefore let all souls devoted to the Virgin Mother say joyfully: “Hail, star of heaven; hail, star of the world; hail, star of the sea; hail, Mary.” Or rather, as I now see, she is rightly called the star of the sea. For at the time of this greeting there were no blessed persons in heaven, no righteous persons in the world—or [Col. 0132B] very few—but all were in the sea, that is, involved in the bitterness of sins. Therefore she was rightly named star of the sea, that is, star of the wretched.

For as this star is a sign of the right path for those sailing at sea, so Mary shows in this world to those living crookedly: to some the straight way of good action, to others the straight way of humility, to others the straight way of chastity. To remove this misery Gabriel was sent to the Virgin; his name means “strength of God.” For strength was needed to free the human race from so great a misery.

Observe that the announcer is strength, the messenger is strength, and the one announced is strength; but God the announcer may be called strength, the messenger strength of God, and the one announced [Col. 0132C] deified strength. By “the one announced” we mean the man assumed by the Word, who was deified—that is, made God. For as that great Hugh of Saint Victor said: “Whoever denies that the assumed man is God denies that he was assumed into God.” Nor does that authority of Jerome stand in the way which says, “We read that God was made man, not that a man was made God.” It must be understood thus: he was not first man and afterward made God, but from the moment he existed he was at once both man and God.

The messenger, therefore, was strong, so that he might strongly fulfill God’s command; the one announced was strong, so that in assumed flesh he might strongly conquer the devil; the announcer was strong, so that he might strongly bind the devil once conquered.

To return to our star: those who are at sea see her from afar; those who are in the world see her from near at hand; those who are in heaven see her most closely. Whoever sees something from afar sees the thing itself, certainly, but discerns neither its kind nor its individual identity. Whoever sees something nearby discerns the thing and its kind, but not its individual identity. Whoever sees something most closely knows the thing, its kind, and its individual identity. Therefore those who are at sea look upon our star from afar: for people tossed about, as it were, upon the sea of great crimes, although through fear of punishment or a slight affection may sometimes look toward God or to the things of God, are nevertheless enveloped in the darkness of sins and driven back from contemplation of heavenly things. Thus, experiencing no spiritual grace within themselves, they see heavenly things, in a manner of speaking, from afar, but cannot perceive their condition or presence. But the righteous, who are in the world—that is, established in purity of heart—see this star from nearby; for, while living holy lives and having their citizenship in heaven, they taste beforehand the future life through the drops of grace and, according to the measure of this life, conceive even the condition of the saints. But those who are in heaven see this star most closely, because, immediately enjoying God and with the eye of contemplation made clear, they delight perceptively alike in the presence and vision of the saints.

And this is with reference to what was said: “Hail, Mary.” But what great or surpassing thing is attributed to the Virgin Mother when she is called “full of grace”? For Christ too is full of grace and truth; Stephen was full of grace (Acts 6); and the apostles are read to have been full of the grace of the Holy Spirit (Acts 2). Accordingly, this distinction must be made: there is equal fullness, fitting fullness, and overflowing or poured-out fullness. Equal fullness exists when nothing empty remains in the thing filled, as in a measure of wine or oil. Fitting fullness, however, fills according to what is appropriate to the thing; as when a city or church is said to be full of people—not because no vacant place remains there, but because those present suffice for the place according to its proper capacity. Overflowing fullness exists when that which fills exceeds the capacity of the measure.

In the Blessed Virgin Mary there was equal fullness, because she was so filled with spiritual grace that nothing empty remained in her—that is, no place for sinning. Hence Jerome says: “When sins are in question, I wish no mention at all to be made of the Blessed Mary.” For from the time she conceived Christ, she was so strengthened that she could not sin. In the other saints there was fitting fullness—not that they could not sin, for even the apostles were commanded to shake the dust from their feet (Matthew 10)—but because they received fullness of grace sufficient for salvation. In Christ there was overflowing fullness, because he received grace without measure, so that from his fullness we might all receive. Therefore Mary was pre-eminently called “full of grace.”

There is grace of natural goods, grace of spiritual charisms, and grace of heavenly gifts. She was full of the grace of natural goods because, when the Holy Spirit came upon her, she alone among the daughters of Eve received, according to the dignity of the first creation, the integrity of natural endowments. She was full of the grace of spiritual charisms because, once Christ had been incarnate, she could sin no more. She was full of the grace of heavenly gifts because she was in some manner granted the homeland of heaven by the power of contemplation. For as great as the difference between the scent and the taste of an aromatic substance is the difference between Mary’s contemplation and that of the other saints. For just as she received from Christ a singular active office—namely, to carry his human nature, nurse it, wrap it in swaddling clothes, and render him the other services of humanity—so too, if I may say what the devotion of my heart supplies, he granted his mother a singular experience of the sweetness of his divinity.

Hence he added: “The Lord is with you.” The Lord Father is with you, because you are his bride; the Lord Son is with you, because you are his mother; the Lord Holy Spirit is with you, because you are his friend. For he who is love would not show you the affection of love unless you returned to him the love he gave. Therefore the Father is with you, whose Son you are to conceive; the Son is with you, whom you are to conceive; the Holy Spirit is with you, by whom you are to conceive. For “the Holy Spirit will come upon you.” He will first come through the sanctification of the Virgin, afterward come upon her through the sanctification of the virginal conception. He will come upon you because you will conceive by the Holy Spirit.

You who hear this, understand faithfully in this way how Mary conceived by the Holy Spirit. As the Word of God is the image of the Father, so the soul of Christ is the image of the Holy Spirit. I am not now speaking of that image according to which man is said to have been made in God’s image. In bodily things, that is called the image of something which explicitly possesses the form of that of which it is the image. But just as bodily things have their forms, so also do spiritual things. The form of the Holy Spirit is sevenfold grace—not a form that is in the Spirit, but one that is from the Holy Spirit; just as brightness on a wall is called the brightness of the sun, not because it is in the sun but because it is from the sun. Therefore the man Christ was conceived by the Holy Spirit because he received pre-eminently the form of the Holy Spirit, that is, sevenfold grace. Thus “from” is to be understood not materially but formally: Christ was conceived from the Holy Spirit not because the Holy Spirit supplied him with the material of seed, but because he more elegantly impressed upon him than upon all other creatures the form of holiness.

It follows: “And the power of the Most High will overshadow you.” Understand here by “power” that of which the Psalmist says: “You have made known your power among the peoples; with your arm you redeemed your people, the children of Jacob and Joseph” (Psalm 76); and of which the Apostle says: “Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1). This power of the Most High, which is Christ, once overshadowed those wicked sons—the Jewish people, I mean—it overshadowed the Blessed Virgin, and it also overshadowed us.

The shadow that overshadowed the Jewish people was the veil of the literal sense, by which spiritual understanding concerning Christ and his sacraments was veiled in the Law, lest they understand it. Hence when Moses spoke to the children of Israel, he placed a veil over his face, because they could not look upon him because of the glory of his countenance, which is abolished. This shadow was signified by the shade of the ivy beneath which Jonah sat near Nineveh to see what would happen to the city.

The shadow by which he overshadowed the Blessed Virgin was the weakness of the assumed flesh, by which the splendor of divinity was at once moderated and shaded, so that in this obscurity the Virgin’s womb could contain him whom the immensity of all things could not contain in his brightness. Of this shadow it is written in the person of the Blessed Virgin in the Song of Love: “I sat beneath the shadow of him whom I desired” (Song of Songs 2).

But the shadow by which he overshadowed us is the ignominy of the Passion: when he who was beautiful in form beyond the children of men became disfigured and shadowed, so that he was bruised by wounds, pale in death, and filled with every reproach.

This change in him was our overshadowing; and although there were many changes in him, this alone overshadowed us. For his exaltation was changed into humility when he took the form of a servant; his weakness was changed into majesty when he took Peter, James, and John and led them up a high mountain and was transfigured before them; his mutability was changed into eternity when he rose from the dead; his beauty was changed into ugliness when, in the Passion, he was suspended upon the cross for us. And this is the shadow by which he overshadowed us, by which he delivered us from Egyptian bondage and the power of the devil.

Elijah sat beneath this shadow in the wilderness, for it is also written of him: “He sat beneath the shade of a juniper tree and asked for himself that he might die” (3 Kings 19). For the juniper is a low and bristly tree, and signifies Christ humbled and despised in the Passion. To this shadow we are all invited in this sacred season of the Lord’s Passion, that we may sit beneath it as imitators of him; for whoever says that he abides in him ought also to walk after him (John 2). By this shadow the holy Church is now overshadowed, while songs of joy cease from her mouth, the adornment of ministers and the furnishing of altars cease, and souls are contrite over their sins—as the tears and sighs of penitents confess.

Now therefore, O Christian soul, marked with the character of Christ, sit beneath this shadow. Turn your joy into mourning, and weep for your Lord; or, if you do not wish to weep for him, weep at least for your own dead man. Your dead man is your spirit, slain as though by many wounds through the multitude of crimes. Dead, I say, not because it has suddenly met with calamity, but because you inflicted upon it the cause of death. Nor is this a dead man four days in the tomb, already fallen from your memory; nor a dead man at the gate, already vanishing from your eyes. He is in your own house, before your eyes, so that you may always see him, be shaken with horror, and endlessly weep for the dead man whom, while he lived, you would not spare.

I ask a just judgment from you: do not detract from the truth. A nobleman and his disobedient servant were entrusted to your custody on this condition: that you should maintain the servant with bread and water in the manner of a servant, but provide splendidly for the nobleman according to the dignity of his birth. You, however, acted contrary to this: you reduced the nobleman through hunger, thirst, and many other injuries; but you made the servant insolent and proud through every kind of luxury, so that, rising against his lord, he killed him, pierced with many wounds. What will you answer him who entrusted both to you? You did this cruelly; you, I say, killed the nobleman, since you did not refresh your spirit with any virtues, any richness of devotion, or good works. You nourished the disobedient servant delicately when you indulged your flesh in feasting, drunkenness, and the other pleasures of this life. Therefore, when you should have extended a helping hand, the flesh rose up against the spirit, compelling it to serve the vices of the flesh—that is, luxury and impurity.

And oh, if only it had sufficed for you merely to kill so great a man, and you did not mock the dead, rage against what was extinguished, or inflict wound upon wound—as all do who add sin to sin. Recall the notorious sinners of this age, who afflict the spirit by monstrous vices, outrages against nature, and shameful passions: the simoniacs, robbers of the Holy Spirit, who possess the patrimony of the Crucified by a double sacrilege, that is, by acquiring it wrongly and living wrongly. All such people rage against the extinguished soul, to the injury of their Creator.

Therefore come to your senses, O wretched soul. Sit beneath Christ’s shadow; conform yourself to his disfigurement; mortify your flesh by fasts and abstinence from pleasures. For through these things even the extinguished spirit comes back to life. For if Peter’s shadow could raise the dead (Acts 5), could not the shadow of Christ do the same? Certainly, if you were suffering some bodily illness, and Hippocrates or Galen commanded you through his attendant to abstain from wine and rich foods and to take modest portions, you would gladly obey in order to regain bodily health. God the Father commands you to do the same through his Christ, that you may be healed in your soul—and you do not obey. Yet one ought rather to obey God than men, as Peter says (Acts 5).

Do not say: “I wish to sit beneath Christ’s shadow, but the disfigurement or ignominy of his Passion is not apparent.” Look upon all who are afflicted, sick, imprisoned, poor, and grim with hunger and thirst: in all these you see Christ shadowed and filled with contempt. Therefore sit beneath Christ’s shadow through compassion for your neighbor, so that you clothe the naked and break your bread for the hungry. Give alms to one suffering need—give, I say, to the suffering person; indeed, rather store it up for yourself, because in the future you will receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life.

If some powerful person had bestowed much wealth upon you, and enemies rose against you who wanted to take away not only your money but even your life, and the one who had made you rich said to you: “Entrust your money to me; I shall free you from your enemies, preserve your life for you, and restore the money whole,” would you not gratefully consent? Behold, you have received temporal goods from Christ. Let luxury rise against you: it wishes to claim a share of them for itself and take away your life. Gluttony does the same by seeking feasting and drunkenness; pride does so by desiring luxurious clothing and worldly pomp. Therefore give temporal goods to the poor; indeed, entrust them to Christ in the poor. Having done so, you have preserved your life, and you will receive them back on the day of need.

And lest it perhaps seem burdensome to remain long beneath Christ’s shadow and be conformed to his sufferings, know that he offers himself to be seen not only in shadow, but also in a mirror and sometimes face to face. The mirror is Holy Scripture, in which he shows us his exceedingly beautiful image for consolation. In this mirror the soul sees how pure Christ’s divinity is, how sweet his goodness, how enduring his eternity, and how inestimable the joy which he promises to those who suffer for him. His appearance is not yet seen in this mirror as it is; for “we know in part and prophesy in part,” as the Apostle says. For the thing whose image we see in a mirror is behind us (1 Corinthians 14). So too Christ, whose appearance we see in Holy Scripture, is yet to come in great glory, when we shall see him face to face. Therefore let us go for a short time beneath the shadow of his Passion by imitation; let us behold his form in the mirror for consolation, so that at last we may see him in his beauty, receiving that joy which can neither be expressed in speech nor conceived in the heart, which will neither be shadowed by grief nor ended by failure—through the gift of our Lord Jesus Christ, whose kingdom and dominion remain for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXIII. ON THE LORD’S PASSION

“Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his footsteps” (1 Peter 2).

Behold, most beloved brothers, Christ Jesus, standard-bearer of the Christian religion, advances to fight for the salvation of humankind: truly a mighty champion in saving, who, himself stronger, comes upon that strong armed man guarding his court and casts him out from the company of the saints, so that no place may any longer be found in him. He chose to establish the sign of this victory upon the wood of the cross because, according to the prophet’s saying, “his strength was hidden there” (Habakkuk 3). There, when the ancient enemy sought the bait of flesh, he was pierced by the sting of divinity. And if you wish to know by what weapons of divine power Christ conquered the devil, they were the fullness of his wisdom, the breadth of his charity, the strength of his humility, and the greatness of his mercy.

The fullness of wisdom overcame the deceiver, who by a deceitful suggestion had seduced man, created innocent, as is clear from the history of the book of Genesis. The breadth of charity conquered the envious one, who had cast down through envy the man fraudulently deceived from the happiness of eternity. The strength of humility conquered the proud one, who obstinately held, to the injury of his Creator, a man who owed him nothing. The greatness of mercy conquered the cruel one, who mercilessly tormented the man he had unjustly possessed.

But now let us turn the eye of consideration, attending more carefully to the rationale of the dispensation by which Christ wished to undergo the cross and endure so shameful a death, which was indeed judged a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Greeks. Meanwhile, three reasonable causes may be assigned as to why Christ wished to undergo the cross. The first is the common misery of all; the second, the filial obedience that he owed to God the Father; the third, his singular victory over the enemy.

The prophet David recalls the first cause, that is, the common misery of all, saying: “Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, now I shall arise and be made manifest, says the Lord” (Psalm 11). “I shall place the cause of the human race in salvation,” that is, in Christ; “and I shall act in him not sluggishly, but confidently”—as happened at the hour of the Passion. This misery was threefold: weighty, universal, and everlasting. It was weighty because it oppressed humanity with such a burden of sins that it could look neither to heaven nor to the heavenly powers. Hence the Psalmist: “Children of men, how long will you be heavy of heart?” (Psalm 4). And blessed Job says of this heaviness: “Would that my sins, by which I have deserved wrath, and the calamity I suffer were weighed in a balance: this would appear heavier than the sand of the sea!” (Job 6). And elsewhere: “A heavy yoke is upon all the children of Adam from the day of their birth to the day of burial” (Ecclesiasticus 40).

That misery was also universal, because death, which had entered the world through one human being, had spread so widely that it enveloped alike all the righteous and the unrighteous, good and evil, so that one punishment afflicted all whom the one fault of paternal transgression embraced. That misery was likewise everlasting, because humankind would have endured it without end and without remedy, unless Christ Jesus, mediator of God and humanity, had intervened by his death and set an end to that misery.

The second reason why he wished to undergo the cross was the filial obedience he owed God the Father, concerning which the Apostle says: “Christ became obedient to God the Father unto death, even death on a cross” (Philippians 2). And the Son himself says to the Father: “I have made you manifest upon earth; I have completed the work which you gave me to do” (John 17). For the sake of this obedience he wished to undergo the cross, so that through it the expiation of the first disobedience might be accomplished, and Christ, humbled even to the cross, might make satisfaction for the human being who, through disobedience, had proudly raised himself even to equality with his Creator.

The third reason why he wished to undergo the cross was his singular victory over the enemy: that by dying he might overcome the author of death; and, having obtained victory, might not only himself be victor but also make his imitators victorious. Concerning this victory John says in the Apocalypse: “The lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has conquered” (Revelation 5). And Isaiah says: “How you have fallen, Lucifer, who rose in the morning! You have fallen to earth, you who wounded the nations” (Isaiah 14).

Now, therefore, O Christian soul, you who bear the banner of this victory, carry the Lord’s cross in such a way that you also imitate the Crucified One; for true bearing of the cross is imitation of the Crucified. The four arms of the cross—length, breadth, height, and depth—show us four kinds of suffering by which we ought to imitate Christ. The first is the suffering of bodily distress; the second, the continual mortification of fleshly desire; the third, patience under insult inflicted; the fourth, renunciation of one’s own will.

By the first kind of suffering the mighty conquerors of this life imitated the Crucified One: those whom neither death nor life, nor danger nor sword nor any other creature could separate from Christ’s charity, offering their bodies to punishments for God’s sake. Of them it is said: “These are they who have come from great tribulation and have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (Revelation 7).

By the second kind of suffering, those imitate him who by voluntary discipline mortify their members upon earth, and, lest sin rule in their mortal body, crucify their flesh with its vices and desires. By the third kind of suffering, those imitate him who for the cause of justice endure injuries, reproaches, and the assaults of another’s malice, imitating by the virtue of patience him who “was led as a sheep to slaughter, and was silent before the one shearing him and did not open his mouth.” By the fourth kind of suffering, those imitate Christ who renounce, along with the world and those things which are in the world, even their own will, and reserve nothing of themselves for themselves. Subjecting themselves to another’s rule for God’s sake, they follow in the footsteps of him who came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many. Hence the Savior himself says elsewhere: “I came not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 5).

Those who imitate Christ through these kinds of suffering venerate his blood as though at the site of the wound. Yet there are others who venerate Christ’s blood as it drips in his members. There are also some who venerate Christ’s very blood as it falls dusty and scattered upon the ground. But Christ’s blood at the site of the wound is triumphant; as it drips in his members, it is medicinal; fallen upon the ground, it consoles and assists.

Therefore those who are too weak to ascend the cross with Christ venerate his blood dripping in his members. This occurs when they seek forgiveness of sins and the ground of salvation in the sacraments of the Church which flowed from his side. For the Evangelist himself testifies that the Church’s sacraments flowed from his side when he says: “One of the soldiers opened his side with a lance, and immediately blood and water came out” (John 19). Explaining this word, the commentator says: he does not say “struck”; he does not say “wounded”; but “opened,” so that in his side the door might be opened through which the sacraments of the Church flowed forth, without which one does not enter into life.

His members, moreover, are all the faithful who are enlivened by the same Spirit as their head; rooted firmly through charity in Christ’s body, they carry out the diverse offices of that body—that is, the Church—according to the distributions of graces. Christ’s eye is the person who rightly administers the office of governance. Christ’s tongue is that which, abounding in divine utterances, teaches and instructs others. His ear is the one who readily inclines his hearing to divine precepts and commands of obedience. His shoulder is the one who bears the burden and heat of the day in the Lord’s vineyard. Christ’s foot is the one who is diligent in frequent service to relieve others’ needs; and so with the rest.

Through these members, then, Christ’s blood flows, when the children of the Church are made participants in the redemption which the Lord worked in the midst of the earth through his Passion: now through the water of sanctification, now through his body and blood, now through receiving the other sacraments of the Church.

But there comes before us a word full of grief and anguish: just as some build up Christ’s body by living justly and devoutly, so others destroy it by the monstrosity of their lives, thus surpassing Jewish unbelief. For they suspended Jesus on the gibbet, but these people tear him limb from limb and, having thrown him to the ground, trample him beneath their feet. Thieves, robbers, criminals, the defiled, fornicators, murderers, and the shameful cut off the hand in Christ’s body: by withdrawing themselves from good works, they cut off, as it were, the hand from Christ’s body. Others are liars, perjurers, blasphemers, slanderers, who utter foul and buffoonish words. Since they do not build up their neighbor with holy exhortations and words of edification, they undoubtedly cut the tongue off from Christ’s body. He stops up Christ’s ear who does not incline his hearing to the commands of obedience; and so likewise with the rest.

What are you doing, wretched soul? Pilate himself fears to crucify Christ, saying, “Shall I crucify your king?” (John 19), and do you not fear to tear him limb from limb? Certainly, if you saw a person standing near you deprived of eyes, with lips cut off, ears mutilated, tongue cut out, or drenched everywhere in his own blood, I think you would recoil from the sight and detest the author of the crime who had dared to do these things. Why, then, do you likewise not recoil from laying your hand upon Christ the Lord and conspiring with Judas the betrayer in his death?

Surely this alone ought to have terrified you: the very weapons with which you tear Christ’s body are turned against yourself. You are pierced by your own missiles, wounded by your own arrows, and your very crimes, by which you cut yourself off from Christ’s body, tear your wretched soul limb from limb and make it bloody with wounds inflicted. Do you not think that the soul has certain spiritual members: sense, memory, will, reason, and understanding? By these members the soul is mutilated when neither sense seeks God, nor memory recalls him, nor will desires him, nor reason chooses him, nor understanding comprehends him. Thus the wretched soul, which God gave you as your companion, wherever you may be—whether you sleep, wake, walk, or sit—cries out against you, rolling in the blood that you have shed.

Return, miserable human being, to the Lord your God. When all the children of Israel were delivered from Egypt by the blood of the lamb, will you alone serve Pharaoh? When the rock pours out water most abundantly so that the people and their beasts may drink, will you alone wither with thirst? When the master of the house kills the fattened calf, will you alone perish from hunger, excluded from this banquet?

Behold, the widow of Zarephath gathers two sticks in order to make from the little flour she has stored away a hearth-baked loaf (3 Kings 17). Ask her for a morsel of this bread, lest perhaps you be consumed by hunger. This hearth-baked loaf is Christ as mortal—or rather, given over to death for us. The two sticks upon which this bread is baked are the Lord’s cross; upon it he is scorched by the fire of the Passion. The widow of Zarephath makes this loaf from fine flour when, from the spiritual understanding of the Law and Prophets, she comprehends that Christ is to be born and to die. The morsels of this bread are Christ’s incarnation, birth, Passion, resurrection, and ascension. Therefore ask for even one of these morsels, namely Christ’s Passion; chew it in your mouth and carefully store it in the stomach of memory, in case even Christ’s blood may soften the hardness of your heart.

Moses himself also raises up for you in the wilderness the bronze serpent (Numbers 21). If you wish to look upon it, you will receive healing, cleansing from your crimes, medicine for your wounds, and growth in virtues; and you will be restored to perfect health if you are willing to gaze upon it with the faithful eye of the mind. In it you will find the support of faith, the consolation of hope, the throne of charity, the title of grace, growth in devotion, the vehicle of mercy, and the banner of peace. Therefore look upon this bronze serpent raised upon the pole: that is, acknowledge Christ crucified with the devotion of faith. Look upon him with the eye of knowledge, so that you may know him as the true God sent for the salvation of humankind. Look upon him with the eye of love, so that you may embrace in charity him who suffered for you. And so his blood will flow over you also, if through charity you are united to his members.

There are others who venerate Christ’s blood not at the site of the wound, nor dripping in his members, but rather as fallen upon the earth. I would say that Christ’s blood then fell upon the earth when, by his blood, he acquired these earthly and transitory things which we call Christ’s patrimony: namely extensive possessions, fixed tithes, revenues from offerings, and the other stipends of the Church. He wished these to be given for the consolation of those who would share his tribulations and imitate his sufferings. For he wishes these benefices to be granted to those who use them in such a way as not to neglect spiritual things, and who so eat the sins of the people that, by rendering the services due for the dead—the public celebrations of Masses and prayers fixed for souls—they are found to be intercessors of faith.

“If we have sown spiritual things among you,” says Paul, “is it a great thing if we reap your material things?” (1 Corinthians 9). And the prophet David says: “Take up the psalm and give the tambourine, the pleasant psaltery with the harp” (Psalm 80). And the Lord himself says: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life” (John 6). To eat Christ’s flesh is to receive the Church’s material benefices for one’s consolation; to drink his blood is to share in his tribulations and Passion.

Oh, how many in the Church of God, called through the clerical character to the Lord’s portion, gladly eat, while utterly detesting his blood! Clerics in the pursuit of wealth, soldiers in dress, neither in manner of life; while they receive material benefices for pleasure, they continually fail to do good for the salvation of souls. You see them more often in the marketplace than in choir, and more often chanting songs than bewailing their sins, reserving the care of souls for the Samaritan alone but the sum of pleasures for themselves. To this is added that ecclesiastical benefices, which they have received not as private property but as loans to be distributed to the poor, orphans, and widows, are received not by the needy but rather by dogs, hawks, parasites, and entertainers; and into Christ’s patrimony are admitted not only daughters and sons, but even bedfellows. You might see them purchasing with the alms of the poor gilded bridles, shining spurs, painted saddles upon which pictured maidens frolic wantonly, and garments dyed in various colors—not sympathizing with Christ, who is suspended on the cross for their sake.

O friends of God, who ended your lives through diverse tortures, why did you not also approach the Lord’s cross by this delightful path? But this manner of worshipping the cross had not yet been revealed, the Holy Spirit reserving it for these times. Why do you, ruined man, not consider that the Crucified One sees you? He certainly sees you now, and in the future he will rebuke you and set your deeds before your face, so that even amid torments you may recognize that you were not Christ’s heir but a violent invader of his patrimony.

Where is the example? Where are the footsteps which he left for us to imitate—“leaving you an example, that you should follow his footsteps” (1 Peter 2)? Perhaps we may yet find some footsteps, if we are willing to imitate them. To speak more plainly, for we who cannot see subtle things: a footprint is the place upon which a traveler’s foot is set, in some way indicating the passer-by. And who else was this traveler but Christ, of whom it is written: “He rejoiced as a giant to run his course” (Psalm 18); and elsewhere: “He drank from the torrent on the way; therefore he lifted up his head” (Psalm 109).

The foot of this traveler is the holy desire of the mind by which righteous persons are drawn to work well. Of this foot it is written: “My foot stood in the straight way; in the churches I shall bless you, O Lord” (Psalm 25). Therefore Christ’s footprints are holy persons, who through holy desire are led to serve the living God. Peter was Christ’s footprint through the love of voluntary poverty when he said: “Behold, we have left all things and followed you” (Matthew 9). Paul was Christ’s footprint through the strength of bodily discipline, for lest he burden anyone, he sought his livelihood with his own hands. John the Baptist was Christ’s footprint through rejection of costly attire, for he wore a garment of camel hair and a leather belt about his loins. Elijah was Christ’s footprint through the austerity of abstinence; David through contempt for worldly life; Job through the virtue of patience. The holy martyrs too were Christ’s footprints, in whom he impressed his foot even to the endurance of suffering.

By such footprints, therefore, Christ calls us back to the way, so that if perhaps through love of the world or any other unlawful pleasures we have wandered away, we may return by their example to the way which is Christ. In him we shall receive both the end of our labor and the reward of everlasting life—through the same our Lord Jesus Christ, whose kingdom and dominion remain for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXIV. ON PALM SUNDAY

“But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians 6).

You, dearest brethren, whom the anointing itself teaches concerning all things, and indeed all of you who retain the Scriptures by heart, also remember well that there is a time for weeping and a time for laughing, and that these very times are ordinarily distinguished from one another by intervening intervals. Yet today, by a certain rational discord, the time for weeping and the time for laughing meet together, while the face of the Church is now expanded by joy, now contracted by sorrow; for the very author of times, through the things done concerning himself, presents to us the cause of this variation. For on this day, as the Lord entered the holy city, the children of the Hebrews went out to meet him, crying, “Hosanna to the Son of [Col. 0143C] David,” while some cut branches from the trees and others spread their garments in the way (Matt. XXI): hence the joy of the festal procession. But from the remembrance of the Lord’s Passion—in which we are reminded how he who “did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth” was filled with reproaches, and how the very author of life, who owed nothing to death, tasted death for us—comes the cause of sorrow. Although Christ did not historically suffer on this present day, nevertheless his Passion is rightly commemorated today, because on this day he voluntarily came into the hands of sinners, his Father himself delivering him up to the Passion—he who “spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all.” Yet we may not unfittingly [Col. 0143D] say that one thing, namely the Lord’s Passion, is simultaneously a matter of sorrow and of joy for different reasons: of sorrow, because we were the cause of his death; of joy, because his Passion was the cause of our salvation. Does not that typical and legal history also invite us to rejoice in the Lord’s Passion—the history which relates that, when the Paschal lamb was sacrificed, the people of Israel were delivered from Egypt? Pharaoh, indeed, is the devil himself. Though struck with ten plagues—that is, with the ten commandments of the divine Law—he was not utterly overcome, but still held God’s people in captivity, until, the Paschal lamb being sacrificed—that is, Christ’s blood being poured out—God’s people joyfully departed from the house of bondage into the land of promise, as David the prophet says: “And he brought forth [Col. 0144A] his people in exultation, and his chosen ones in joy” (Ps. CIV).

Likewise, the Shunammite woman does not rejoice over her son restored to life until Elisha, that great prophet, contracts himself to the measure of the dead boy; when he lay upon the boy, the latter received the spirit of life (IV Kings IV). For Elisha, that great prophet—that is, Christ—immeasurable and infinite in the nature of his divinity, contracted himself to the measure of the dead boy when, for our sake, he willed to become mortal—indeed, for our sake to die in human nature. And as he lay upon the boy—that is, as he shared in the sufferings of the human race—the boy himself, namely the human race, received the spirit of life; and he sneezed seven times when he burst forth into manifold praises of God. Hence [Col. 0144B] the Shunammite woman, that is, Mother Church, also rejoiced. Nor are symphony and dancing heard in the house of the householder until, upon the prodigal son’s return, the fattened calf has been killed (Luke XVII), because God the Father is reconciled to the Gentile people only in the death of his only-begotten Son. Therefore, invited by these examples to rejoice in the cross of God, let every soul say:

“But far be it from me to glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.” For there is the anchor of our hope, the price of redemption, the poultice for the wound, the medicine of health. What sick person, after all, does not rejoice in the presence of a physician, or what wounded person in the healing medicine? Truly, the Lord’s Passion was a medicine not only healing, but also penetrating and cleansing. It was penetrating [Col. 0144C] because at his death the veil of the Temple was torn, the earth was shaken, the rocks split, and the tombs were opened. It was penetrating because through it the gates of death were broken down, and the iron chains and those exceedingly hard bonds by which captives were held in hell were broken. And the dark prison was opened when it was said to those who were in bonds, “Come out,” and to those who were in darkness, “Be revealed.”

I wonder whether you too have not at some time experienced the penetrating power of this medicine—you, I say, sinful human being, who lay buried in the tomb of a biting conscience; who were bound by the cords of sins; whose face was veiled with that most evil cloth of forgetfulness of God; who, like Lazarus, already stank in the tomb (John XI). This penetrating medicine dug you out from the sepulchre of foul conscience through contrition of heart; it broke, through forgiveness of sin, the bonds of sins by which you were bound. It also removed the cloth when it mercifully took away the veil of iniquity which had been placed like a great chaos between God and you, so that with unveiled face you might look upon God, whom you had once forgotten—your Lord and Creator. Therefore let every soul devoted to God, holding the Lord’s Passion in faith and venerating it with pious affection, say:

“But far be it from me to glory, save,” etc. And although we all ought to glory in the Lord’s cross, there are some who glory especially in the Lord, and others who glory especially in the Lord’s cross. Those [Col. 0145A] who glory especially in the Lord are holy and perfect men, to whom contempt for temporal things has given the intimate boldness to approach God, and the breathing-in of divine grace has sweetened their affections. They contemplate the nature of divinity; they are touched by spiritual sweetness; in prayer they speak with God; in devotion they knock at heaven; they participate in heavenly secrets; and with Paul they can say, “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III). There are others whose conscience is still darkened by the rust of sins and who, drawn by unlawful desires, are driven back from contemplation of God; the Lord judges them unworthy of such delights as to be able to taste beforehand, through the sweetness of contemplation, the joys of the life to come.

These, therefore, as sick persons, devoutly look upon Christ’s [Col. 0145B] humanity, in which they recognize the cause of their salvation. They stand by the Lord’s cross and, with Thomas, put their hand into the places of the nails; and they most devoutly receive the blood which was poured out for the washing away of sins. Let everyone, then, whose conscience makes him fearful as he stands guilty before God, approach the Lord’s cross. For to what can he flee more securely than to the refuge of the cross? Where, finally, can Christ’s soldier be safer than under the standard of his commander? Here the strength of the heavenly army was restored; here those wounded in the front line and cast down by sins received their former vigor. Here, indeed, is the righteousness of the patriarchs, the constancy of the martyrs, the innocence of all the righteous, “who washed their robes and [Col. 0145C] made them white in the blood of the Lamb.” Here too are those great sinners who killed the prophets, pierced Christ, and persecuted the Church of God; and, having all obtained pardon for their crimes, they also give you confidence that pardon may be obtained. Why, then, do you delay? Why do you tremble to come? There is no enormity of sin which Christ’s blood cannot expiate. If the greatness of punishment terrifies you, grasp the depth of the cross; if the height of the reward delights you, grasp the loftiness of the cross; if your soul is dry and you need the benefit of virtues, grasp the breadth of the cross; if you are assailed by temptations, grasp the length of the cross. For in the depth of the cross is the destruction of punishment; in its loftiness, the height of reward; in its breadth, the abundance [Col. 0145D] of benefit; and in its length, the strength of help.

Although, then, all are invited to the Lord’s cross, some distance themselves from it and others draw near to it. Of those who distance themselves, some are far away, others farther away, and others farthest away; and of those who draw near, some are near, others nearer, and others nearest. Far from the Lord’s cross are those who, devoted to the vanities of this age, look upon the Crucified, as it were, from behind: they feed their eyes upon his Passion rather than imitate it. For while they extend themselves toward the delights of this life through worldly living, they withdraw, as it were, from the Lord’s cross. But when they wish to be marked with the character of the Crucified in obtaining church benefices, they look upon the Lord’s cross, as it were, from behind. Such are [Col. 0146A] the dandies of our day: in gaining benefices, they wish to be clerics; in dress, princes; in tonsure, soldiers; in life, they wish to appear neither one nor the other. For they neither fight as soldiers nor govern their subjects as good princes; and, if inquiry is made regarding their life, they are more often found in the dances of dancers than in the choir singing psalms to God. Let Christ now ask such men, as once he asked the sons of Zebedee: “Can you drink the cup which I am about to drink?” (Matt. XX). What will they answer him? Will they say, “We can”? Let us see. Christ drank the cup of patience and labor; he drank the cup of distress and pain; he drank the cup of joy and consolation. He first drank it when, before his Passion, he patiently endured in our [Col. 0146B] nature curses, injuries, reproaches, and very many labors. If those of whom we have just spoken are invited to drink this cup, they utterly disdain it, because they regard it as their lot to indulge in pleasures and enjoy good things. Christ drank the cup of pain and distress when he endured spittle and bonds, a crown of thorns, and death on the cross. But they can in no way drink this cup, because in it lies the destruction of every temporal joy which they have decreed to pursue with the utmost zeal. But can they drink the cup of joy and consolation which Christ drank in the resurrection? All say, “We can.” But this would not be to drink the Lord’s cup, but rather to confuse it, because, according to the saying of a holy man, the times of reigning [Col. 0146C] cannot precede the times of suffering.

Others are farther from the Lord’s cross: namely, those who devoutly undertake the discipline of the religious life but do not pursue it obediently. Religious discipline is rightly compared to the cross, because, just as the cross restored the world to life, so religious life restores a human being to innocence; and, just as Christ on the cross obeyed unto death, so too a person under religious discipline ought to obey unto the mortification of the flesh. But we see some becoming farther away from this obedience. When tasks are imposed upon them in which are the traces of the Lord’s Passion—having a taste of bitterness and labor, nakedness and poverty—they refuse to obey; murmuring, they flee from the face of the Lord with Jonah, saying: “This is not [Col. 0146D] a man of God who decrees such commands.” But if an obedience is imposed upon them in which there is worldly pleasure and a certain position of authority, they accept it not only humbly but willingly and quickly. I mean that obedience in which barns abound in harvests and winepresses in wine; where the court is crowded with servants and storytellers; where the table is full of cups and dishes; where they celebrate Passover with leaven and eat the Paschal lamb without wild lettuces. These men, therefore, because they are not corrected toward perfection of character by religious discipline, are rightly said to cast away the Lord’s cross which they have undertaken. “Your discipline,” says David, “has corrected me unto the end, and your discipline itself will teach me” (Ps. XVII). It surely has its good end, the perfection [Col. 0147A] of virtues. Therefore religious discipline ought to correct unto the end, because it ought to lead a human being from the depth of vices to the perfection of virtues.

Farthest from the Lord’s cross are those who are swallowed up as though in the depths of vices and who, through the atrocity of crimes, foulness, impurity, and the flames of desires, have withdrawn farther from Christ than others. And just as they are more sinful than others in their monstrous manner of life, so they are also farther from the Crucified. But may that great Babylon, which intoxicated the earth with its sorceries and fornications, someday come into remembrance before God, so that it may drink from the cup of God’s wrath and become a dwelling-place of demons and of every impurity; and may it at last lament in punishments that here it refused to imitate the traces of the Lord’s Passion.

[Col. 0147B] Others are near the Crucified: namely, those who stand beside the Lord’s cross; others are nearer, like those who anoint the members undergoing punishment with myrrh and aloes. Nearest, however, are those who carry his cross. They stand beside the cross, therefore, who come to Christ with the affection of devotion and the desire to suffer, wishing to endure for his name’s sake injuries and tribulations; but, considering their own weakness—that they are frail, weak, and unable to bear labor—they do not presume actually to undertake what they had desired in affection. Thus they are not altogether strangers to the effect of the Lord’s Passion, because, although they do not imitate it through the actual experience of tribulations, nevertheless, coming to him with certain good affections, they are seen by their desire [Col. 0147C] to stand beside the cross. But those who cannot suffer hard things for Christ ought to draw near to the cross through four affections: by remembrance of sins, recollection of punishments, consideration of this pilgrimage—namely, that they have here no abiding city—and hope of future recompense. Remembrance of sins in God’s sight makes them humble; recollection of punishments makes them earnest in doing good and obedient to God’s commandments. Consideration of this pilgrimage, that they have here no abiding city, calls them back from excessive desire for temporal things. By hope of recompense they are at times lifted up in love of heavenly goods. And these stand beside the Lord’s cross.

Others, as nearer persons, anoint the buried one’s [Col. 0147D] members with myrrh and aloes, as Joseph of Arimathea is read to have done (Matt. XXVII). The members of the buried one are rightly called the wretched and despised of this age, who, oppressed by their calamities, are reckoned as though among the dead. And just as they are united to Christ’s members by the union of charity, so through the distresses of tribulations they are buried with him. Myrrh and aloes are the affections of compassion and the care to give aid. Those, therefore, who have compassion on and aid the needs of the poor, the anxieties of the oppressed, the troubles of the sorrowful, the pains of the sick, and the other miseries of the wretched are rightly said to anoint with myrrh and aloes the members of the crucified Christ.

Those who are nearest carry his cross. I have said *his cross* because not every [Col. 0148A] cross ought to be called Christ’s cross. There is the cross of the thief who hung on the left; there is the cross of the thief who hung on the right; and there is the cross of the Savior, who hung between them. The cross of the thief who was on the left is the punishment of those who sin finally; the cross of the thief who was on the right is the punishment of those who repent after a fall; the Savior’s cross is the punishment of those who live innocently. Therefore they carry the Lord’s cross who, although they maintain innocence of life and walk before God in righteousness and holiness, nevertheless, as though guilty of every crime, voluntarily subject themselves to many tribulations and miseries for God’s sake; or are afflicted by another’s malice, now through slanders of tongues, now through unjust oppressions; or even, at the hands of persecutors, are put to death by the shedding of blood [Col. 0148B] with Christ, glorying in the Lord’s cross, through whom the world has been crucified to them and they to the world. The crucifixion of the world is contempt for temporal things, just as the crucifixion of the saints is endurance of tribulations. Thus to holy men who bear the Lord’s cross the world has been crucified, because for his sake they despise all earthly glory, counting all things as dung in order that they may gain Christ (Phil. III). But they too have been crucified to the world: that is, to lovers of the world, from whom they endure the bitterness of sufferings. And because there is henceforth laid up for them the crown of righteousness, they rejoice at once to be made conformed to the Lord’s Passion, knowing that through patient endurance of tribulations they come to the glory [Col. 0148C] of the Lord’s resurrection, through the grant of our Lord Jesus Christ, whose kingdom and dominion remain for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXV. ON THE LORD’S PASSION

“He spread out the book before me, which was written within and without; and in it were written lamentations and a song and woe” (Ezek. II). You, most beloved brethren, who have received the spirit of adoption as sons and, by holy conduct, have put on our Lord Jesus Christ, retain alike in memory and in conduct that every action of Christ is a lesson for us. Therefore he is rightly reckoned under the name of a book, because in him we ought to read the pattern of our life.

But some holy man, poor in spirit, whose heart burned for Jesus, would expound better the sequence of this book, which contains the whole history of [Col. 0148D] our restoration; for he understands it better who lives more holily. And worthy of reading this book are not those who pronounce the pious name of the Lord Jesus with merely the tips of their lips, but those who attain his piety in life and conduct. Yet, since I may not be silent and do not know how to speak, let the Lord God speak in me; and let the key of David open the mysteries—he who can open the book and loose its seals. The book mentioned, then, is Christ, of whom the Apocalypse says: “I saw in the right hand of him who sat upon the throne a book written within and without, sealed with seven seals” (Apoc. V). Daniel also says of him: “At that time your people shall be saved, [Col. 0149A] everyone found written in the book; and many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake” (Dan. XII). He is the book of which Ezekiel says: “He spread out the book before me,” and the rest (Ezek. II). It is a book sufficient for all: it offers to those who delight in such things a reading for delight, and to the diligent a reading for exercise. How great a thing in this book is that ineffable union of God and man, in which, as if through seven musical tones, one ascends from the lowest to the highest, so that human lowliness is raised up to God and, conversely, in descending, God’s loftiness is bent down to human lowliness. Do you wish to hear the seven tones of this song? Recall how humble, how despised Christ appeared at his birth, and this song gives you a low [Col. 0149B] tone. Recall how gentle and pious he showed himself in word and deed, and it gives you a sweet tone. Call to mind with how many signs and powers he shone forth, and you hear a subtle tone. Call to mind that he joined human and angelic nature in one charity, that he reconciled humanity to God, and you hear a harmonious tone. If you recall how he was subjected to insults, pierced with wounds, crowned with thorns, and at last fixed to the cross, this song gives you a grave tone. But when, by the power of divinity, he rose from the dead after conquering death, this song gives a high tone. And when he ascended victoriously into heaven, it gives a very high tone. This song, indeed, is offered not to the [Col. 0149C] worldly refined, but to God’s refined ones, who delight in meditating on such things as though amid every kind of wealth. The reading of this book is no less necessary. For it does not teach how to reconcile Gratian’s decrees, weigh Justinian’s laws, or deride the subtleties of sophisms; nor does it teach one always to learn and never to make progress. Rather, it teaches one to recognize faults, sigh for pardon, reform one’s conduct, order one’s life, seek salvation, and find God.

This reading is now plain to see, but it was not always so. For this book was at one time sealed, at one time closed, but it is now opened. Before Christ’s incarnation this book was sealed with seven seals, because its promise was so shrouded in certain obscurities that either no one, or [Col. 0149D] very few indeed, knew the mystery of the Incarnation. For what else were those personal manifestations of the patriarchs, angelic apparitions, offerings of sacrifices, images of revelations—all of which prefigured Christ either in deed or by likeness—than certain seals? If you add to these the obscurities of Scripture, the delay of the promise, and the despair that the truth would be fulfilled, you will in sum find seven seals with which this book was sealed before the Incarnation. Once Christ was incarnate, the book appeared, but was kept closed, because the power of his divinity did not come outwardly forth, being overshadowed by the weakness of human nature. For even if he was called a prophet mighty in deed and word, this was thought to be attributable not to divine power but to the merits of a holy [Col. 0150A] man’s virtues. “For if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (I Cor. II). At last, in the Passion, this book was opened, and the eternal power and divinity hidden in the man began to burst forth, when created things felt their Creator’s rule: the rocks split, the earth quaked, and the veil of the Temple was torn from top to bottom. For when the sackcloth in which the sun of true light was enclosed was cast off, that same sun began to shine in its power, so that it poured forth its rays on every side and illumined not only those who sat in darkness and the shadow of death, but also infused the light of faith into the hearts of many unbelievers. Hence the Gospel centurion, seeing the wonders that occurred, cried out: “Truly this was the Son [Col. 0150B] of God.”

Thus, when this book was opened in the Passion, its writing began to be read; and it was written within and without. The inward writing was the Word of God written in Christ’s flesh by the working of the Holy Spirit. The outward writing was that which impious persecutors inscribed upon his body with injuries and blows, the shedding of blood, and the disgrace of the cross—not in golden, but in dark letters. This writing has since been read, though not understood by all. For this writing, like other writings, has three things: letter, sense, and meaning. And to speak first of the outward writing: its letter is the historical Passion of the Lord; the sense conceived from that letter [Col. 0150C] is imitation of the Lord’s Passion; and the meaning discerned according to that sense is the fruit of our redemption. One who holds the Lord’s Passion by faith alone and not in practice is a child and does not understand what he reads. But one who imitates the Lord’s Passion through patience and labors for Jesus’ name, observing hard paths, reads this writing and makes progress by understanding. He, however, who perseveres to the end, carrying the Lord’s cross, is the one who knows this writing perfectly. Likewise, the inward writing has these three things: its letter is the purity of faith concerning the Word of God; its sense is the affection of pious devotion; its meaning is the joy of divine contemplation. The reading of this writing is especially suited to the perfect, [Col. 0150D] whose citizenship is in heaven and who, despising earthly consolation, are kindled by love of heavenly goods. And we see something remarkable happen concerning this writing: here a child teaches an old man, an unwise person a prudent one, a stammerer an eloquent speaker, a disciple a master, an unlearned person one who is lettered. Behold, a lowly little man or poor little woman subdues the flesh with haircloth; they mortify themselves all day by vigils and fasts; they distribute to the poor the bread they earn by hand and skill; and they never depart from the trace of the Lord’s Passion. By contrast, the noble and prudent people of this age consume their days in luxurious wealth, in an abundance of pleasures, and in human desires—so far removed from the Lord’s cross that they consider miserable only [Col. 0151A] those who faithfully imitate the misery of the Lord’s Passion.

Which of these, do you suppose, understands better the Scripture of which we have spoken? I judge that those who are more deeply affected understand it better, because they comprehend better by affection than by intellect. But it will now be more useful to consider whether any of the books we read has been written according to the pattern of the book of life, since what is committed to writing and inspected more frequently is also committed to memory more effectively. Nor would I unfittingly call all the consciences of the righteous, well formed by Christ’s virtues, books, because in them a certain image of the virtues of the Lord Jesus is represented. Of these books Daniel says: “The judgment sat, and the books were opened” (Dan. VII). And [Col. 0151B] elsewhere: “Hear, Israel, the commandments of your God, and write them in your heart as in a book.” And the prophet says: “The law of his God is in his heart” (Ps. XXXVI). These books are written according to the pattern of the book of life, because “of his fullness we have all received,” and whatever good, whatever grace we see in ourselves has all been derived into us from him, as a little stream from a spring. Let each person therefore see whether the book of his conscience is rightly written and well distinguished by virtues, lest that forger, who was a liar from the beginning, have brought some stain of sin upon the writing of truth. For if you are tormented by hatred or envy, your book is faulty; if you burn with ambition or avarice, your book is faulty; if you are defiled by any bodily uncleanness, your [Col. 0151C] book is faulty. Indeed, whatever you find in yourself contrary to Christ, count that as defective in your book. Therefore, Christian, carefully inspect the book of your conscience and inscribe it with the virtues of your Savior, so that you may always keep present in your heart him whose likeness in innocence you strive to preserve through a clean conscience. For what good is it to adorn with such care, and correct with such labor, books that we put away in a chest, while leaving uncorrected the book of conscience, from which life proceeds? We see many paint the psalmist David in precious colors in the Psalms, venerable old men grey with age in the Prophets, and make codices precious here and there with golden letters; yet they leave the book of conscience so neglected, so foul, that the Holy Spirit does not deign to dwell in it with the light [Col. 0151D] of his grace.

There are others who, having cast aside Christ’s life-giving knowledge, have devoted all their zeal to secular philosophy; and, lest any requisite service be lacking, they have placed it to be carried upon the shoulders of human beings, following it in a certain hasty procession. Recall that vehicle of philosophy which they entrusted to two boys—Labor and Love—and two little girls—Vigilance and Care—to carry, thereby signifying that one can attain knowledge of philosophy only through labor and love, vigilance and care. O fruitless labor! O erring love! O foolish vigilance! O superfluous care! Truly, fruitless is the labor relieved by no rest; erring the love kindled by no [Col. 0152A] spiritual fire; foolish the vigilance followed by no benefit; superfluous the care accompanied by no security. Tell me, wretched soul: in all these things, what comfort is there for the spirit? What aid toward good? What cause of salvation? None at all. Therefore restore your conscience; look upon the book of life, so that from it you may learn what you find lacking in your own. There you will find certain words of consolation, words of eternal life, which may lead you back to the way of salvation from which you have strayed while walking along the broad paths of this age.

And because lamentations, a song, and woe are written in that book, each of these has its own words by which it speaks to you, whether for terror, correction, or consolation. Lamentations, then, concern imitation of the Lord’s Passion; [Col. 0152B] the song concerns the glory of the resurrection; woe concerns the judgment of final retribution. In the lamentations you will find harsh words concerning the labors of penitence, such as: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” (Gen. I); “Pour out your heart like water before the Lord”; afflict yourself with weeping and groaning; and reduce your body to servitude through bodily mortification; and other such things, by which a human being imitates the Lord’s cross in this mortal body. But in *woe* there are found certain terrible words: weeping and gnashing of teeth, the bitterness of flames, the density of darkness, the cruelty of torturers, and the other kinds of torments prepared for the devil and his angels. The song, however, speaks words of consolation, [Col. 0152C] joyful words: complete absolution from guilt, restoration of grace, escape from exile, bestowal of a kingdom, fellowship with divinity, attainment of eternity. Therefore, if you are still a sinner and still lie, foul-smelling with Lazarus, in the tomb of a biting conscience, read those terrible words which belong to *woe*, so that, shaken at least by the terror of punishments, you may come to your senses from your crimes. But if you have been pierced with fruitful contrition for your sins, look upon the harsh words found in the lamentations, so that by works of penitence you may make satisfaction to God, whom you have offended. And if you have already been justified by good works, attend to the consoling words which belong to the song—set forth in this present life for consolation and, in the future, for full joy. Therefore let every imitator of Christ, for whom it is good to cleave to God, be exercised in the book of life in such a manner that, having escaped [Col. 0152D] the punishments of Gehenna, he may through many tribulations and the narrow way press on to life. There all the saints, when that which is partial has been done away, will perfectly understand the book of life and know Christ as they have been known by him. May Jesus Christ himself bring us to that knowledge, whose kingdom and dominion remain for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXVI. ON THE LORD’S RESURRECTION

“He drank from the torrent in the way; therefore he lifted up his head” (Ps. CIX). Amid so many heralds of Christ triumphant, unequal in praise, I fear that I shall appear unlike them, as though with a discordant voice; and, while I cannot worthily sing “Hosanna to the Son of David,” I fear that I shall be rebuked by those who go before [Col. 0153A] and told to be silent rather than invited to confess praise. Nevertheless, instructed by the example of that blind man, whether bashful or importunate, I too will sit beside the way and cry out; and, as the heavenly throng receives Jesus rising again, I shall follow with joy in affection and desire, saying: “Son of David, have mercy on me.” For I cannot otherwise follow him so long as this torrent, from which Christ too drank, separates me from him: so precipitous and so deep is it that those who wish to cross from here to Jesus cannot, nor can they pass from there to here.

This torrent is the course of this mortal life, which runs from the origin of conception into the prison of mortality, and thence into the misery of birth, from which it proceeds again into the straits of death. At [Col. 0153B] last it ends, unless mercy intervenes, in the punishment of eternal damnation. This torrent is plainly dangerous, and it is all the more dangerous because certain additional waters swell it into a great river. Thus blessed Job calls this torrent by the name of a river when he speaks of that ancient serpent, saying: “He will swallow up the river and will not marvel; and he hopes that Jordan may flow into his mouth” (Job XL). It is as though he said: the enemy of humankind does not regard it as great or marvelous if he swallows up with himself into the share of his damnation the river—that is, human nature entangled in sins and crimes; but he even hopes that the Jordan, that is, the people reborn in Christ, may flow into his mouth.

[Col. 0153C] Certain tasteless waters, as I said, rise up into this torrent and cause its waves to swell. From one side come marsh waters, which make it muddy and turbulent; from another, sea waters, which make it bitter; from yet another, snow waters, which by excessive cold render it undrinkable. The marsh waters are fleshly desires, which make this torrent—that is, the course of this life—somehow muddy and turbulent. For as often as the soul, filled by pleasure of the flesh, is turned away from contemplation of its Creator, so often it is flooded, as it were, by the muddy waters of a bodily marsh. The sea waters are the cares and occupations of this age. When the soul gives itself to these, distracted by a certain restlessness, it grows bitter within itself like wormwood: love drives it to desire; labor, to acquire; fear makes it anxious lest it lose; grief arises if it either fails to obtain what it has sought or must abandon what it has acquired. But the snow waters are the deliberate malices of the human heart: envy, factions, heresies, hatreds, and discord against fraternal unity. These are called colder than the others because they withdraw farther from the warmth of charity. You see that snow waters descend from above to earth and occupy it for a longer time, unless they are melted by the benefit of warmth. For spiritual vices were first born above, that is, in angelic nature; through the prompting of their author, the devil, they descend to earth—that is, to earthly and sinful human beings—and hold them fast for a longer time, unless, with a more merciful spirit blowing, they are loosened by contrition [Col. 0154A] of heart. See how muddy, bitter, and cold this torrent is. And who has ever drunk from it? Christ certainly—but from the torrent, not from the river. For the torrent denotes the course of nature, whereas the river denotes the transgression of sin. Christ, I say, drank from this torrent when he assumed the weaknesses of human nature and tasted the bitterness of the Passion. He drank, I say, and crossed over; and he invites you to follow him.

If, then, you wish to cross unencumbered, lest perhaps the storm of this water submerge you or the deep swallow you up, make yourself a bridge of planed timbers: you shall raise columns upon it, set beams upon them on either side, lay planking above, and secure it with nails; and thus you shall complete it. These columns, however, are holy men, [Col. 0154B] perfect men, whom we must raise up above the torrent of this life—that is, set before the eye of our mind—so that whatever hardship or temptation may befall us in this life, we may bear it with equanimity and, following the example of their virtue, may not fail in good works. Such men are rightly compared with columns. For just as columns cannot be moved from their stability by the violence of winds, the flooding of rains, or the force of storms, so neither tribulation nor distress nor danger nor sword, nor indeed any calamity, could separate these men from the love of Christ. These, unless I am mistaken, are the columns which God’s Wisdom hewed out in the house—that is, in the mass of the human race—to the number of seven; because throughout the [Col. 0154C] seven ages of the world there have never been lacking holy men who, by the example of their good manner of life, stirred up the weaker sort to desire heavenly things. Of these columns it is written in the Apocalypse: “Whoever conquers, I shall make him a column in the temple of my God” (Rev. III).

Beams must be placed upon these columns, so that they may be supported by them and may in turn support the planking above. These are the two branches of that golden lampstand: that is, the two Testaments founded in Christ, from each of which proceed three reeds—that is, the threefold understanding of history, tropology, and allegory. These are the two sides of Jacob’s ladder, which are said to touch the earth below and heaven above (Gen. XXVIII). For the utterances of God touch the earth, as it were, below when, through the threat of punishment, they stir earthly people to fear; but they seem to touch [Col. 0154D] heaven when, through God’s promises, they kindle the hearts of the righteous with love for heavenly things. The aforesaid columns support these beams, as it were, on the left side, when holy men show by the testimony of Scripture to the wicked what is the wrath of the coming Judge, the darkness of the prison, the cruelty of the tormentor, the dreadfulness of punishment, and the duration of that eternal condemnation. Yet, as it were, on the right side these columns support the beams when, according to God’s promises, they declare to the elect what that endless life is, the fellowship of the blessed, the immensity of the reward, and the joy of the kingdom prepared for the saints from the foundation of the world.

When these columns and beams have thus been arranged, planking must be placed above them; for good works, which are understood by the planks, ought to rest upon the divine commandments, [Col. 0155A] so that the soldier’s zeal may strive to do those things which he knows have been commanded to him by the herald’s voice at the emperor’s command. For the commandments of God are certain decrees of the highest King, which the heralds of God’s word have thundered forth to this world, so that those who do them may live by them, while their despisers may be punished. For however much works may bear the appearance of rectitude, if they do not retain the form of evangelical teaching, they are judged reprobate by the supreme Judge.

Certainly, there are some people of exceptional life who seem to themselves to do many good things by fasts, vigils, and extraordinary prayers; yet these things are not good, because they are found to conflict with the divine commandments by giving occasion for scandal. One man, having an immoderate zeal for justice, judges another’s servant against the Apostle’s will (Rom. XIV); another, under the appearance of gentleness, overthrows the zeal of justice and equity. All these things are evil, although they appear good, because they conflict with the divine commandments. This is what is meant by the bronze sea said to have been placed in Solomon’s temple, in which the priests who were to offer sacrifices washed their hands. Here the bronze sea is to be understood as the divine law, and the hands as actions. Whoever, therefore, wishes to offer God a sacrifice worthy of him must wash his hands in this bronze sea—that is, direct his actions according to the divine commandments. Elsewhere this sea is compared to crystal, as in the Apocalypse: “Before the throne,” it says, “was something like a glassy sea, like crystal.” For just as crystal, a most clear stone, sends forth sparks of fire when exposed to the sun, so the divine law, [Col. 0155C] fulfilled in deed, kindles the fire of charity in the hearts of believers through the example of good works.

Nails too are necessary, so that the structure of the whole work may hold firmly together. They are the four principal virtues: justice, fortitude, prudence, and temperance. In these the life of good works consists: so that in matters that must be well done, justice may furnish right judgment; fortitude, assistance; prudence, counsel; and temperance, support. Therefore, once this bridge has been completed in this way, the crossing of this torrent lies open. No longer is there any reason why the faint-hearted should despair, the weak give up, the ignorant go astray, the fearful be afraid, the little one fail to begin, or the grown person fail to arrive. For Christ has become the leader of the way: strong, that [Col. 0155D] he may guard; wise, that he may direct; mighty, that he may bring through.

If, then, you wish to cross this torrent, if you desire to imitate Christ, direct your journey along the middle of this bridge; and if you wish to avoid the precipice, do not turn aside to the right or to the left. For there are some who walk crosswise over this bridge and thus fall; others walk along it obliquely and fail; others walk straight on and cross over. Those who walk crosswise over this bridge are those who, abandoning the evils of their ways through the tears of confession and repentance, take up the path of the good life that leads to Christ; but, returning to the vices they had left behind even at the outset, now dissolved in luxury, now puffed up with pride, now distracted by ambitions and other [Col. 0156A] tumults of vices, they walk as it were crosswise and plunge into the precipice. Of them it is written in the Psalm: “Surely because of their deceits thou hast set them there; thou hast cast them down when they were lifted up” (Ps. LXXII). “Because of their deceits,” he says—that is, because they are deceitful and do not persist in truth—“thou hast set these temporal delights before them,” so that they may be deceived by them; “thou hast cast them down in their very delights when they were lifted up,” that is, when they seemed to themselves to have been raised.

But those who walk obliquely along this bridge are those who begin good works with much devotion and serve God through persistence in good conduct, not departing from his temple day or night.
