Yet when the time of temptation draws near, when their faces begin to grow pale from vigils and their bodies to waste away from fasts, when on this side the she-ass groans [Col. 0156B] beneath its burden and on that side the vexation of another’s malice sometimes pricks them, they begin to lag behind; and in temptation, where they ought to have been strong, there they abandon their good work. Of them it is written: “The sons of Ephraim, bending and shooting the bow, turned back on the day of battle” (Ps. LXXVII). The sons of Ephraim—that is, of fruitfulness—who ought to have borne fruit, “bending and shooting the bow,” that is, boldly entering upon the fight, “turned back on the day of battle,” that is, at the time of temptation.

But those who walk straight along it are those who, still set in the land of this mortal life, look across the intervening torrent toward the land of the living in hope and desire. Inflamed by the examples of the saints and instructed by the divine commandments, they strive by living well to accomplish the virtues and works which they have conceived in their minds, [Col. 0156C] drinking with Christ from the torrent of suffering, so that with him they may be made drunk with the joy of the future resurrection. For this is why Christ drank from the torrent on the way, and for this he lifted up his head: so that those who are humbled in this present life through the struggles of this age and through the bitterness of sufferings may be lifted up with their head in the joy of future glory.

This head is Christ, of whom the Apostle says that God made him head of the Church, which is his body (Eph. V): head of the Church by the authority of creation; head of the Church by the fullness of grace and truth; head of the Church as the beginning of the Christian religion. This head is exalted by us in four ways: first, by the immensity of his majesty; second, by the veil of our weakness; third, by the cross of his voluntary passion; fourth, through the glory of this day’s resurrection. He is exalted by us through the immensity of his majesty, because in his own nature he is immeasurable and infinite, surpassing every creature. Hence Job says: “It is higher than heaven—what can I do? deeper than hell—how can I know it? Its measure is longer than the earth and broader than the sea” (Job XI). He is exalted by us through the veil of our weakness, because the human soul, obscured for us by the cloud of bodily weakness, can behold him only through a mirror and in an enigma. Hence David says: “Man shall approach unto the deep heart, and God shall be exalted” (Ps. LIII). This is what is meant when the bride, in the Song of Songs, sees the bridegroom through windows and lattices, as though he stood behind a wall [Col. 0157A] (Cant. II). For through windows and lattices—that is, partially—she beholds him whom she cannot fully comprehend because the partition or wall of her weakness stands between.

This, too, is why Elijah covered his face with his cloak when the Lord passed by. This passing is to be understood as a certain breathing of divine grace by which the soul is visited for a time. In this passing Elijah—that is, any contemplative man—covers his face with his cloak (III Kings XIX), when, because the veil of human weakness stands between, he does not extend to God in fullness that knowledge which is understood through the face.

Of the exaltation of voluntary suffering it is written in the Gospel: “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, shall draw all things to myself” (John XII). And concerning this exaltation the bridegroom says in the Song of Songs: “I shall climb the palm tree and take hold of its fruits” (Cant. VII). But the present solemnity offers many testimonies concerning the exaltation of this day’s resurrection; these are not merely known but firmly held by those who, drawn away from their vain manner of life, have put on Christ in righteousness and holiness, and, though still placed in their mortal bodies, are exalted with their own head in a certain spiritual resurrection through progress in virtues and good works. For if the head alone is exalted, where are the feet and hands? Where are the other members of the Church, which desire to be joined to their head?

Therefore the elect also are exalted in four ways: first, when they are drawn away from earthly affections through contempt for the world; second, when [Col. 0157C] they are raised to the invisible things of God through faith and knowledge; third, when they are lifted up toward God, whom they love above all things, by the affection of devotion; fourth, they will be exalted when they enjoy with their head the joy of both robes, namely of body and soul. These are the exaltations which that holy man signified to us in the Psalm, saying: “Blessed is the man whose help is from thee: he has set ascents in his heart, in the valley of tears, in the place which he has appointed” (Ps. LXXXIII). For these exaltations are certain steps by which one ascends from this mortal life to God: passing from contempt of the world to the knowledge of God, from knowledge to love, and from love to enjoyment. The first three exaltations are possessed in this valley [Col. 0157D] of tears, namely in the place of our pilgrimage. The fourth is reserved in that place which he has appointed—that is, the place which he has prepared for his saints to enjoy God—in which Christ now reigns with the angels and will reign in the future with all the saints. May Jesus Christ himself make us co-heirs of that kingdom, whose kingdom and dominion endure for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXVII. AT THE GENERAL CHAPTER

“The tongue of thy dogs [is] from the enemies, from him” (Ps. LXVII).

When we wish to speak of Christ through resemblances drawn from things, it is more fitting to do so through weak creatures than through those of higher dignity, because among these more lowly [Col. 0158A] creatures a closer comparison is sometimes found. Therefore, although I call Christ the sun—because, as the sun illumines the world, so he enlightens every person coming into this world—I shall more fittingly, in one respect, call him with the Prophet a worm, who speaks in Christ’s person: “I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. XXI). For as a worm is born from earth without a father, so Christ was begotten of the blessed Virgin without male agency.

In the same manner and for a similar reason, the rulers of churches are very often more fittingly represented by less worthy creatures. Although we may rightly call them oxen, because through preaching, working, and fulfilling their ministry they vigorously cultivate the Lord’s land—that is, the hearts of believers—I shall describe them more expressly as dogs, because a greater likeness to dogs is found in them. Thus the Lord himself calls them dogs in the Gospel, where he says of Lazarus: “But the dogs came and licked his sores” (Luke XVI). And the Prophet says: “The tongue of thy dogs [is] from the enemies, from him.” That is to say: Let thy enemies become thy dogs, and let this be from thee yourself and not from another. A dog also follows Tobias as he goes to Rages, a city of the Medes (Tob. VI), because a multitude of teachers accompanies Christ as he comes into this world.

Consider the resemblance of the animal. A dog is domestic in its caresses, hostile in its barking, pursues the wolf with its bite, heals with its tongue, and keeps the night watches with diligent care. To assign all these features to prelates and subjects: by dogs are understood the rulers of churches; by those of the household, observers of a good rule; by strangers, transgressors of a defective order; by wolves, stubborn invaders of the rule. The tongue of the dog is penitential medicine; its watchful care is pastoral solicitude. We customarily call someone a member of the household who is joined to us by heartfelt affection, common dwelling, and social life. Thus in the Church we rightly call that person a member of the household who is devoted to all by charity, assiduous in the congregation, and acceptable to all through good works, as if by a shared life. Such a member of the household ought therefore to be cherished by the caresses of the dogs—that is, of the prelates—namely by the sweet affection of the mind, by the bestowal of bodily benefit, and by the offering of spiritual consolation. For [Col. 0158D] prelates ought not to oppress holy men by the terror of authority, but rather show themselves to them as friends and companions. For just as the law is not laid down for the righteous person (1 Tim. I), so neither is authority, which is ordained more for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good.

Hence blessed Gregory says that all human beings are equal by the condition of nature, but because they are unequal in the state of their merits, it is necessary that some should be governed by others in order to repress vices. Even our ancient fathers were called not kings of peoples but shepherds of sheep. To Noah and his sons, too, the Lord says: “Let your terror and fear be upon all living creatures and beasts of the earth” (Gen. IX). He does not say, “upon human beings,” so that it may thereby be understood that not holy and righteous men, but rather bestial and criminal people, are to be restrained by the terror of authority.

Among holy men themselves, however, some are little ones, some adults, and some advanced. The little ones are called those simple people who have much holiness but little discretion; adults are those who possess holiness and discretion alike; while the advanced are those who, together with these, have long practice in good works. Those who have much holiness and little discretion are indeed to be cherished with love and benefits, but in matters which they say or do with insufficient discretion they must be checked with a certain severity, so that through such rebuff or correction they may become wiser and more discerning. Thus a schoolmaster does not listen to an innocent little boy who asks not to be beaten, but rather flogs and corrects him, so that he may afterwards be trained toward better things by the harshness of words and blows [Col. 0159B].

Those who possess holiness together with much discretion, I think, are those who came to the cloistered life from the deep engagement of worldly life; in that secular way of life, they learned worldly prudence and the shrewdness required for conducting affairs. But after being called and justified by the Lord, and abandoning the vanity of the world, they retained worldly prudence. Of them the Lord said: “The children of this world are wiser in their generation than the children of light” (Luke XVI). These people ought not only to be loved, but also to be treated as more intimate than the rest, because they are more useful to the Church.

Those advanced through long practice in good works are certain mirrors of the holy Church, in which, as the light of divine grace shines more brilliantly, others ought to marvel and look upon themselves, so that by looking into such mirrors they may correct in themselves what is faulty and preserve what is virtuous. These are more worthy of honor and reverence.

Strangers, however, are those whom neither the union of charity, nor unity of communion, nor uniformity of action joins to us. Hatreds, envies, angers, quarrels, dissensions, and divisions of minds—where God does not dwell—make one a stranger to the union of charity. More sumptuous foods, softer bedding, disorderly clothing, irregular tonsures—whose opposites pertain to communion—make one a stranger to unity of communion. Singular fasts, untimely vigils, unusual prayers, and [Col. 0159D] other things of this kind, which seem capable of being rightly done in the liberty of the Spirit, make one a stranger to uniformity of action. Such persons are therefore to be reproved by the barking of dogs—that is, by the harsh rebukes of prelates. The first group, because of sin, since they tear apart the kingdom of charity; the second, because of danger, lest the rest be drawn by their example; the third, because of scandal, since “woe to the man through whom scandal comes” (Matt. XVIII).

Yet scandal sometimes arises from evils, sometimes from necessary things, and sometimes from indifferent things. If scandal arises from evil, the evil must at once be cut off. If scandal arises from necessary things—that is, things necessary to eternal life—then scandal is better allowed than truth abandoned. But if scandal arises from indifferent things—that is, things which can lawfully be done or omitted—a distinction must be made. If scandal concerning such matters arises in the whole community, or in a large part of the community, then even such good things must be discontinued. But if scandal arises for one person over indifferent things which I do for some individual, I shall not on that account cease to satisfy my own devotion.

Such strangers must therefore be reproved, though in different ways according to the differing kinds of offenders. There are some who sin and, setting aside the fear of God, do not fear sin; others who, enticed by desires, love to sin with excessive ardor; and others who sin in such a way that they do not understand their sins. You who alone know the sin of one who does not fear to sin because he has set aside the fear of God, reprove him—but not personally; rather, through another. Thus, if you are a private person, report it to the prelate of the Church, so that he may be corrected by him and restrained by the fear of authority [Col. 0160B]. You who alone know the sin of one who loves sinning too ardently may report it to some holy man, so that, corrected by him, he may be drawn by the example of holiness into hatred of sin. You may also reprove through some wise and learned man one who does not understand his own sin, even if you alone know that person’s sin, so that, corrected and instructed by him, the offender may come to recognize his fault.

But wolves must be pursued by the bite of dogs. Wolves are the obstinate, the invaders of justice, who transgress God’s commandments not because they are drawn by weakness, but rather seize them like enemies through rebellion and obstinacy. They think little of falling from justice themselves unless they see the condition of justice collapse together with them. They are comparable to wolves for two reasons. For a wolf not only rends by tearing, but also makes a person whom it has first looked upon hoarse by its poisonous gaze, so that he can speak only with a dim and imperfect voice. Similarly, obstinate invaders of justice not only tear the body of the Church apart by their manner of life, but also by evil conversations, seeds of discord, and darts of detraction make others so tongue-tied that they cannot speak in God’s cause for the freedom of justice. Such wolves, therefore, are to be attacked by the bite of dogs—that is, by the severity of ecclesiastical discipline—so that, now by excommunication, now by suspension, sometimes by bodily discipline, sometimes [Col. 0160D] by the weariness of silence, broken and crushed as if by certain teeth, they may be corrected and brought back into the body of the Church.

For just as harder wax, melted by fire, is easily shaped into any image; just as rust is struck from iron; just as the vessels of the Lord are forged between hammer and anvil; just as linen, through much rubbing, turns white; and just as a vineyard which, gripped by prolonged frost, could not put forth buds later bears most abundant fruit when warmth arrives: so a sinner hardened for a long time by the frost of sins, when the heat of tribulation comes near, together with that warmth of grace, afterward becomes more reformed.

The tongue of the dog is penitential medicine, by which those are healed who rise stronger after grave falls into sins and crimes. For when they are visited by the fruitful counsels of the prelates of churches, they are restored, as it were by the licking of a dog, to their former health. To attain this health, two things are especially necessary: the true humiliation of the offender, and the merciful compassion of the pastor. Thus, when the one who has offended shows himself corrected by mourning and groaning, confession and tears, the good prelate should graciously receive him, humbled and contrite as he is, with merciful compassion, and soothe with fatherly consolation the one whom he had first lost as a criminal and now has justified. Thus that good shepherd joyfully carried the lost sheep upon his shoulders; thus the father killed the fatted calf for his prodigal son returning to him (Luke XV); thus the Lord mercifully looked upon Peter as he wept; and many sins were forgiven Mary Magdalene because she loved much [Col. 0161B] (Luke VII).

And, if we speak through the resemblance of things, a good farmer loves land which, after thorns have been uprooted, bears abundant fruit more than land which never had thorns and never produced a rich harvest. It is also commonly said that ravens, when they see their young becoming black and like themselves, provide for and feed them with diligent care; but as long as they see them turning white and departing from the likeness of their parents’ color, they are not diligent in providing them food. In the same way, when a prelate of the Church sees his subject becoming black through contrition and works of repentance, and being ashamed of his sins, he ought to feed him with spiritual consolation and wholesome counsel and nurture him toward better things. But if the prelate sees a criminal subject turning white—that is, justifying himself, preferring himself to others, and judging the rest as though he had done well—it is right that such a person be beaten not with caresses but rather with whips and scorpions. For when the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul and the wicked person is blessed, the sinner provokes the Lord.

Over and above all these things, pastoral solicitude is necessary. To gather some observations concerning this solicitude of pastors through a comparison with similar things is worthwhile. A good plowman who wishes to cultivate his land well diligently follows his plow and urges his oxen on in order to complete the day’s work, lest, numbed by sleep or idleness, he fail to receive the fruit of his labor. With provident care he sometimes refreshes the oxen with song, [Col. 0161D] sometimes pricks them with a goad, and sometimes restores them with fodder, so that aided by all these things they may cultivate well the land which will yield its fruit in due season.

In the same way, a good shepherd or prelate must attend his flock with pastoral care, so that he may be made the model of his flock through the example of good conduct. Thus he should be with the brethren in the cloister for reading, in the oratory for prayer, in the refectory for common meals, in the dormitory for the hardness of the bed, and in chapter for the correction of faults; and he should be the first to fulfill in deed those things which he commands others to do. Let him have a song in his mouth—that is, the promise of future blessedness and angelic fellowship—so that by such a promise those who live justly and holily may be refreshed in their labors. Let him also hold the goad—that is, the threat of eternal punishment [Col. 0162A] and unquenchable fire—so that those who live badly may be restrained from their crimes by fear of punishment.

They must also refresh the faint-hearted with fodder—that is, strengthen them with sound teaching and spiritual exhortation—when they are found less fervent in divine services. Thus in a prelate of the Church deeds and words, life and teaching, must agree, lest, if he says but does not do, he hear that word of the Lord directed against him: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat upon the chair of Moses: do what they say, but do not do their works” (Matt. XXI). Tell me, I ask you, what good will it do me if you drink pure water but offer it to me turbid and stirred up by your feet? This is not to refresh me, but rather to offer me a drink of death. “When you yourselves drank the clearest water,” says the prophet, “you muddied the rest with your feet; and my sheep fed on what had been trampled, and drank what your feet had muddied” (Ezek. XXXIV).

For shepherds to drink the clearest water is for rulers of churches to retain in their minds the commandments of God, the way of truth. But to muddy that same water with their feet is for those rulers of the Church to confuse by evil works the things which they rightly say or think. The sheep drink water muddied by feet when subjects take their pattern of life not from the things their prelates rightly think, but from the things they wrongly do. Therefore pomegranates are set in Aaron’s garment together with bells: that is, the union of virtues and good works with the sound of preaching, lest someone who wishes to instruct others appear to condemn himself.

[Col. 0162C] Do you wish, then, to know what sort of teaching a prelate ought to have? It must have something in common with ordinary coinage. Ordinary coinage must have three things: material, weight, and form—its material must be tested, its weight equal, and its form authentic. In the same way, a pastor’s teaching must have these three things: it must be tested—that is, just, so that he teaches only what is just and good; it must also be weighty—that is, he himself must set forth teaching with weight, meaning that he must strive to do the things he wishes to teach by words. Likewise, a prelate’s teaching must be authentic—that is, in no respect contrary to the authority of the holy Fathers, but teaching the things which the authority of the saints has handed down or which Christ’s truthful utterance has proclaimed. For this reason, on the breastpiece worn upon the breast by the legal high priest were inscribed the twelve names of the sons of Israel, together with the two names “teaching” and “truth,” signifying thereby that a prelate’s teaching ought to rest upon the footsteps of the holy Fathers.

Therefore the rulers of churches ought to draw their subjects by the example of good works and form them by sound instruction, so that by living well and teaching rightly they may gain a reward for themselves and advancement for their subjects, and, for the good administration of their temporal office, may deserve on the day of recompense to enter with their subjects into the joy of their Lord, through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, whose kingdom and dominion endure for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXVIII. AT THE GENERAL CHAPTER

[Col. 0163A]

“You shall make bars of setim wood, and overlay them with the purest gold; and you shall pass them through the golden rings which are on the sides of the ark, so that it may be carried by them” (Exod. XXV).

What was written and commanded historically in the law of Moses, we who are children of grace ought to fulfill spiritually in deed, so that in doing God’s commandments we may walk not according to the letter which kills, but according to the Spirit which gives life. For what benefit does it bring us to have historical knowledge of the ark of the covenant, the bars by which it is carried, the golden rings into which the bars are inserted, and the sides of the ark to which the golden rings adhere, unless these things are also understood spiritually? Therefore, by the bars we ought to understand prelates; by the four [Col. 0163B] golden rings, the four exercises of prelates; by the ark, the Church; and by the four corners of the ark, the four principal virtues—prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice—through which the Church is more firmly strengthened.

“You shall make bars,” he says, and so forth. Three things are necessary to make a bar: wood, iron, and human workmanship. In the Scriptures, wood frequently signifies a righteous man, as in the book of Job: “If a tree is cut down, it grows green again, and its branches put forth shoots” (Job XIV). And Christ says in the Gospel: “If they do these things in the green”—with *wood* understood—“what will be done in the dry?” (Luke XXIII). And in the Psalm: “He shall be like a tree planted beside streams of water” (Ps. I). Wood, therefore, is necessary for making a bar, because a just and good man must be chosen as prelate.

This bar is not made from just any wood, but from setim wood. Setim wood is incorruptible and light, and is said to resemble the white thorn. Thus a prelate ought to be incorruptible through purity of mind—that is, free from the corruption of vices. He ought also to be light, so that, freed from the weight of sins, he may be borne upward by desire for heavenly blessedness. A prelate is also compared to the white thorn: for just as a thorn pricks, so he ought to prick vices by the severity of discipline, with zeal for justice and not with the rancor of malice. This is indicated by his being compared not to any thorn whatever, but to a white thorn.

Iron, too, is necessary for making a bar, so that superfluous branches may be cut away [Col. 0163D]. This iron is to be understood as the judgment of discretion, by which a prelate ought to cut off from himself the delights and pleasures of this world: for instance, luxury, excess in food, and the words and deeds of worldly people that savor of their way of life. Otherwise his subjects may stumble over these things as though over branches growing from his own conduct. For if someone were to place crosswise in a road much frequented by people a tree with branches, passers-by would stumble over it with their feet and often fall. So too, if the life of a prelate, who ought to go before others on God’s way, sprouts forth with worldly inclination like certain branches, he creates an occasion of stumbling for those who ought to imitate him.

Let us suppose an army arrayed in battle with its commander and about to engage the enemy: if the commander in battle should go astray, the soldiers turn to flight. So too when prelates and subjects stand in the Lord’s battle to fight against spiritual wickedness. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble, it would be better for him that a millstone be hung about his neck and that he be drowned in the depth of the sea” (Matt. XVIII). As blessed Gregory testifies, the millstone signifies the round of secular life, and the depth of the sea final damnation. The sense is this: for a prelate who scandalizes one of the little ones—that is, one of his subjects—by a depraved manner of life, it would be better to perish alone in the world than to draw his subjects with him into destruction.

Human workmanship is also required for making a bar, by which the examples of the earlier Fathers ought to be understood [Col. 0164B]. For modern prelates, who succeeded them, ought to imitate their life and teaching, so that they may glory in being their imitators rather than their successors in rank. For those Fathers are lamps placed not under a bushel but upon a lampstand, so that all who enter may see the light. Moses also commands that the man who takes his deceased brother’s wife should raise up offspring for his deceased brother, so that the children may be born in the dead man’s name. By this it is signified that modern prelates ought to nurture such children as imitate the life and character of the ancient Fathers. “You shall make bars,” he says, “of setim wood, and overlay them with the purest gold.”

By “purest gold” is signified divine wisdom, through which in the present life we are instructed unto holiness and kindled with love for the life to come. [Col. 0164C] This wisdom is contained in the Law, the Prophets, the Gospels, and the other Holy Scriptures, of which it is written: “The wisdom that is from above is first indeed chaste, then peaceable” (James 3). A prelate ought in some manner to be covered with this knowledge, so that, knowing God’s commandments, he may do them; for “understanding is good to those who do it.” This is what the priest under the Law bore upon his breast: the rational, upon which were written doctrine and truth. Upon the ephod, which he also bore upon his shoulders, were written the twelve names of the sons of Israel; because the prelate ought to bear doctrine and truth in his breast, and the names of the sons of Israel upon his shoulders—that is, to live by doing good through their example.

There is also another wisdom, called practical skill [industria] [Col. 0164D] in the management of affairs, concerning which Paul says that “a bishop must be prudent, and one who governs his own household well” (1 Tim. 3). This wisdom is necessary to a prelate, so that he may provide the necessities for those in the cloister who devote themselves to contemplation. Wisdom is also called knowledge of the causes of created things, which Solomon is read to have possessed, where it is written of him: “For he discoursed on all things, from the hyssop even unto the cedar” (3 Kings 4), that is, concerning the least and the greatest things. Aristotle too possessed this wisdom. When he had wisely investigated the causes of all things and, through inquiry, had arrived at the highest cause, which was the cause of all causes, and could not discover the cause of that supreme cause, [Col. 0165A] he said: “O cause of causes, make me acceptable to thee.”

Therefore, although an ecclesiastical pastor may possess practical skill in secular affairs or knowledge of the causes of creatures, he ought not to place the highest point of his religious life in these things. Rather, he ought to be covered with purest gold, that is, divine wisdom, so that in everything he does, whether within or without, the form of holiness may always shine forth in him.

In order, then, that we may compare the prelate of the Church to purest gold by reason of likeness, observe that gold placed in the sun shines, flames, and sparkles. So an ecclesiastical pastor, placed in the sun—that is, set conspicuously over the Church of God—ought to shine by the example of good conduct, as it is written: “Let your light shine before men,” etc. (Matt. [Col. 0165B] 5). He ought to flame inwardly with the fire of charity, so that he may be a lamp not only shining but also burning, as the Prophet says: “Who maketh his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire” (Ps. 103).

Likewise, the prelate ought to sparkle, so that, just as tinder emits sparks from itself when touched, he too, when visited by God through grace, may emit from the fire of charity sparks of holy devotion and meditation. “Thou shalt cover them,” he says, “with purest gold”; he does not say with silver, but with gold.

For just as wisdom is signified by gold, so eloquence is signified by silver. Rulers of churches ought not to devote themselves to eloquence, study legal pleadings, conduct the turmoil of lawsuits, attend litigation from morning until evening, and expend their whole selves upon others [Col. 0165C] while giving nothing to themselves. All these things better become an imitator of Justinian than of Augustine. The bars, moreover, are commanded to be inserted through four golden rings.

The four golden rings are the four occupations of prelates in the Church of God. For we read in Leviticus that priests had four offices: to sacrifice the flesh of animals, to burn aromatics, to pray for the people, and once a year to enter the Holy of Holies with blood. Therefore, he who presides must first sacrifice flesh by mortifying the flesh, so that he may offer his body as a holy, living sacrifice, pleasing to God; that he may chastise his body and bring it into subjection, lest, after preaching to others, he himself should become reprobate.

For this purpose it is useful to experience the fare of the refectory, [Col. 0165D] the hardness of the bed in the dormitory, the long length of the morning offices, continual residence in the cloister, the roughness of garments, and other such things by which the body is tamed and subjected to the rule of the soul. The prelate must also burn aromatics; that is, he must kindle the virtues of the soul with the fire of charity, so that, when all the virtues of the soul are inwardly moved by charity, they may yield a most sweet fragrance in which God delights.

Observe that aromatics sometimes yield fragrance when kindled upon the altar, sometimes when carried in the hand, and sometimes when crushed to powder with a pestle. When kindled by fire upon the altar, they yield fragrance when, through charity cooperating, the virtues within the mind are moved by the affection of devotion. When carried in the hand, they yield fragrance when outwardly they are moved toward the fruit of good action. But when [Col. 0166A] crushed to powder with a pestle, they yield fragrance when a man, having received virtues, considers himself little and humble and reduces himself to dust in his own estimation, as Paul says: “Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners, of whom I am the chief” (1 Tim. 1). And the Prophet says: “I am a worm and no man” (Ps. 21).

The third office of prelates is to pray for the people, so that he may be a mediator between God and men and, by praying, turn away God’s indignation from them. Therefore, he who presides ought to present himself in such a way that God delights in his prayers and willingly grants the petitions of one praying, whether for himself or for the people, as though to a beloved son. For it is written: “If one who is displeasing is sent to intercede, the mind of the angry person is provoked to worse things.”

The fourth occupation of a prelate is [Col. 0166B] to enter the Holy of Holies with blood: that is, by shedding blood for Christ, to obtain the kingdom of heaven. For, as it is written, “The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep” (John 10), so that when the time of trial threatens, he would rather himself die in the body than permit any one of those subject to him to perish in soul. Hence Blessed Gregory, expounding that saying of the Apostle, “He who desires the episcopate desires a good work” (1 Tim. 3), says that martyrdom is signified there by “good work.” For in the primitive Church prelates were of such perfection that in ecclesiastical dignities they desired the crown of martyrdom more than the summit of honour.

Therefore the bars are commanded to be inserted into the aforesaid golden rings, so that they may never be withdrawn from them; because an interrupted life [vita interrasilis]—that is, a life cut up into intervals, so that a man is now good and now evil—is not sufficient for a prelate. Rather, he ought always to possess the form of holiness and good works, [Col. 0166C] in which his subjects may imitate him.

By the four corners of the ark we ought to understand the perfect men who are in the body of the Church, through whom it stands more firmly; and they too devote themselves to the four spiritual occupations which we assigned above to prelates. Or by the four corners we should understand the four principal virtues: prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice. For these strengthen the Church against the four vices that attack her: ignorance of the good, immoderate delight in the world, fear of adversity, and the affection of disordered [Col. 0166D] love.

Some are blinded by the darkness of ignorance: they do not know the way of life and therefore neither love it nor follow it. For these, prudence is necessary, since, having driven ignorance away, it shows them the way of salvation and knowledge of the truth. Others, abusing with immoderate delight the things of this world granted them for use, are cast down into harmful pleasures. For these, temperance is necessary, through which, by using lawful things, they are recalled to sobriety. There are also many who, broken by the adversities of this world—bodily illness, loss of temporal goods, or whatever other tribulation there may be in the world—fail inwardly in the virtues of the soul. For these, fortitude is necessary, producing in them constancy of mind for enduring adversities. Others are drawn away by disordered love for those joined to them by nature, kinship, or whatever bond of familiarity, and therefore depart from the way of rectitude. For these, justice is necessary: declining to neither side, it gives to each what is his own and preserves it unimpaired. [Col. 0167A]

Nor should we pass over the fact that not only the bars but the ark itself was made of setim wood. This means that not only prelates but indeed the whole Church of subjects ought to be free from vices and incorruptible through virtues. We read, moreover, in Hebrews 9 that these three things were placed in the ark of the covenant: the tablets of the testament, Aaron’s rod which blossomed, and manna which descended from heaven.

Since, in relation to our edification, we may understand by the ark the Church, which we are, we may fittingly understand by the tablets of the testament the twofold ordinance of the order. One, as though the first tablet, contains commands that concern consolation; the other, as though the second tablet, contains the commands of the order for the edification of the mind. Those who are carnal read in the first tablet of food, clothing, and other things belonging to bodily consolation. They seek abundance in speaking and taking walks, often devoting themselves more to tales than to chants, and to dishes rather than fasts. But what is spiritual in the second tablet they regard little or not at all. [Col. 0167B] Spiritual men read that tablet most diligently; setting aside care for the body, they serve God day and night in fasts, vigils, and prayers. Yet those in the cloister need instruction from both tablets, so that they may have temporal things in the present life for support, and practice spiritual works in order to obtain life.

By the rod placed in the ark we should understand the discipline of regular severity, by a very fitting likeness. A rod is straight, slender, and flexible. Thus discipline—whether of beating, rebuke, reproof, or whatever else may be brought forward for the correction of a brother—ought to be straight, that is, just, so that it may not proceed from malice of heart but rather from the root of charity. Discipline ought likewise to be slender, that is, humble on the part of the one who undergoes it, so that he may humbly bear the punishment which washes away his fault, [Col. 0167C] lest perhaps, if he is rebellious and impatient, he should by resisting discipline provoke God’s anger more than his mercy.

And just as a rod is flexible, so that it can be bent and curved this way and that at the will of the one holding it, so cloister discipline ought to be flexible—that is, not too rigid—lest excessive severity make the person rebuked worse and a wound result from the medicine.

The manna placed in the ark, which was sweet as honey in the mouth of the eater, is the consolation of divine grace in the Church. Through it righteous men are spiritually refreshed amid the labours of this present life, so that they may patiently endure the tribulations of this world until, the course of this life ended, they arrive at eternal and invisible goods. By this food—which we have called manna—all that constancy of the saints was nourished: inwardly consoled through God’s grace, they gave their bodies over to tortures for God’s sake. This is the food of religious men who, by their own will, have buried themselves in the cloistered prison in order to endure hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness, vigils, and many other labours. [Col. 0168A] For what human strength would suffice to endure these things unless the grace of divine consolation strengthened the inner man? Therefore, in the present Church God strengthens his elect through grace, to whom he will give in the future eternal life, troubled by no pain and ended by no boundary; through the gift of our Lord Jesus Christ, whose kingdom and dominion endure unto ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXIX. AT THE GENERAL CHAPTER

[Col. 0168B]

“There is one boy here who has five barley loaves and two fishes” (John 6). Most beloved brethren, we do not invite you to the table of that rich man who feasted splendidly every day, nor to pots of flesh or the fatted calf, for these are the foods of the luxurious; rather, we invite you to simple food suitable for spiritual men—not food procured by a multitude of servants, but that which one boy brought with him, having five barley loaves and two fishes.

By this boy we mean a religious man, whether a member of the cloister or a prelate, who ought to be an imitator of a boy through innocence of life. For three things are necessary for a boy: nourishment of nature, purity of innocence, and the keeping of discipline. First, then, one in the cloister ought to possess nourishment of nature, so that, having food and clothing, he may be content with these; in order that he who has set his foot in the track of the Crucified One may, by voluntary poverty, retain the form of the Crucified. [Col. 0168C]

But he must also possess purity of innocence, for a boy [puer] is so named from purity; thus he should keep himself pure in mind and body, undefiled by this world, and by living innocently offer himself as a holy, living sacrifice pleasing to God. He must also have the keeping of discipline, so that, diligently observing the precepts of the rule, he may abstain from these excesses and by holy conduct give others an example for their advancement.

This cloistered boyhood has three goods supporting it: the spirit of liberty, the joy of security, and the strength of love. The spirit of liberty: so that, free from inward vices, the spirit may not in the mind serve the law of sin. The joy of security: so that, secure through outward good works, it may not fear the malice of another’s wickedness. The strength of love: so that it may strongly cleave to God through the affection of charity. For as it is written, “Love is strong as death” (Song 8), because just as death separates the soul from fellowship with the flesh, so the love of God separates the soul from fleshly desires. [Col. 0168D]

But three vices oppose the three above-mentioned goods of penitence: avarice opposes the need of nature; concupiscence opposes purity of innocence; negligence opposes the keeping of discipline. Avarice corrupts the need of nature when those in the cloister desire superfluities and, having despised the form of poverty, wish to possess honours, prelacies, and riches; when prelates receive gifts from usury and robbery; when they seek revenues for receiving novices; when, from the common property, from God’s treasury, they make for themselves unfailing purses. Such men ought rather to be called hirelings than shepherds, because they seek what is their own, not what belongs to Jesus Christ. Of such it is written: “Nothing is more wicked than to love money; and these men have their soul for sale, since in their lifetime they have cast away their innermost parts” (Ecclus. 10).

They are also rightly compared to the idol Dagon, which, placed beside the ark of the covenant, was found mutilated, with its hands and feet cast upon the ground [Col. 0169A] (1 Kings 5). For what is understood by the ark of the covenant except the fellowship of saints? And what is signified by the idol Dagon except any avaricious person? Hence avarice too is called “the service of idols” (Col. 3). Therefore the idol Dagon is placed beside the ark of the covenant when any avaricious person is joined to the fellowship of saints. Its hands and feet are cut off and cast to the earth, because temporal goods, which the avaricious man desires through avarice, are cut away from him, and at the end he is hurled into the land of the dead, where inward destruction is found.

Concupiscence, however, opposes the purity of innocence when a cloistered man, drawn away and enticed by his own concupiscence, follows fleshly desires and, by a miserable exchange, changes the purity of innocence into the stain of lust. Such a man is aptly signified by Moses himself, who, born of a Hebrew mother and placed in a little ark upon the river against Pharaoh’s persecution, was found by Pharaoh’s daughter; adopted by her as a son, he was again given to his Hebrew mother to be nursed (Exod. 2). [Col. 0169B]

The boy born of a Hebrew mother is the cloistered man, instituted by the Church in newness of life. By the name of the river we should understand the abundance of regular discipline; the river’s little ark is the imprisoning custody of the cloister. Therefore, when Pharaoh persecutes, this boy is placed in the river’s little ark, when, against the devil’s temptations, he is committed to the imprisoning custody of the cloister. Having escaped Pharaoh’s persecution, he is there found by Pharaoh’s daughter, who is concupiscence of the flesh. For it frequently happens that one who is not overcome by the temptations [Col. 0169C] of the devil falls grievously under the temptations of the flesh. He is therefore adopted as a son by Pharaoh’s daughter and yet given to the Hebrew mother to be nursed, because such a cloistered man is nourished outwardly by temporal goods from the Church, while inwardly concupiscence of the flesh nevertheless rules him.

Negligence opposes the keeping of discipline when cloistered men, living disorderly lives, do not keep the precepts of the rule; when prelates are negligent in watching over their subjects and do not correct them for their transgressions; and when those who ought to have given everyone a pattern of life instead display an example of laxity rather than an example of religious observance. They ought indeed to attend to their flock with threefold diligence: correction, consolation, and prayer. By correction, correcting the unruly; by consolation, comforting the fainthearted; by prayer, continually beseeching the Lord for their subjects, lest they be led astray by the temptations of the enemy. [Col. 0169D]

This too is rightly shown to us by the prophet where he says: “I will raise up over her seven shepherds and eight principal men, and with the sword they shall feed upon the land of Assyria” (Mic. 5). By the seven shepherds and eight principal men are understood all prelates of the Church, who ought to possess the sword of the word, cutting on both sides: on one side through rebuke, on the other through consolation. Thus they feed upon the land of Assyria—that is, earthly men serving the devil—by converting them to the way of truth through the word of preaching. Therefore, when the aforesaid vices—avarice, concupiscence, and negligence—have been removed from a cloistered man, it may rightly be said of him: “There is one boy here,” etc. [Col. 0170A]

Observe that a cloistered man ought to be one in unity, one in uniformity, and one in unanimity. He ought to be one in unity, so that mind and life, conscience and work, may agree; lest through hypocrisy or pretence he be one thing within and another outwardly, showing men the appearance of religion in order to be seen by them, desiring to please men more than God. For the Lord says in the Gospel of those who do their works before men through hypocrisy: “They have received their reward” (Matt. 6). Against hypocrites the prophet David says of the righteous: “O Lord, they shall walk in the light of thy countenance; in thy name they shall rejoice all the day, and in thy righteousness they shall be exalted” (Ps. 88).

Just as fools walk in the light of their own countenance when, deceived by error or ignorance, they choose evil as good according to their own judgment, [Col. 0170B] so hypocrites walk in the light of men’s countenances when they exchange the good which they do outwardly for human praise. But the righteous walk in the light of God’s countenance when, by the good works they do, they desire to please God alone, saying with Paul: “If we pleased men, we should not be servants of Christ” (Gal. 1).

A cloistered man ought also to be one in uniformity, so that through gravity of character he may always maintain an even manner of life, lest, following the fickleness of his own mind, he appear rooted in no fixed dwelling-place of conduct. For we see many such men: modest in the cloister, dissolute in the streets; appearing clerical among clergy, secular among secular soldiers, childish among boys, foolish among fools. By this manner of conduct they imitate actors more than cloistered men. [Col. 0170C]

A cloistered man ought also to be one in unanimity, so that, being in concord with the rest, he may be careful to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. Father Augustine invites us to this unity when he says: “The first reason for which you have been gathered into one is that you may dwell in the house with one mind, and that you may have one heart and one soul in God.” And in the Acts of the Apostles: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts 1), where it is also written: “They all persevered unanimously in prayer with the women, and the little children, and Mary the mother of Jesus.” This unanimity of good men is the foundation [Col. 0170D] of religious life, the nourishment of virtues, and the consummation of good works; in it all religious who live peacefully are called sons of God.

There is another unanimity, that of evil men, by which the wicked are confederated in the persecution of the righteous. It is the foundation of dissolution, the nurse of crimes, the hammer of the righteous. By this unanimity many righteous men have been harassed unto death; through it cloistered religious observance has frequently been destroyed; and, what cannot be said without groaning, through it many monasteries have become heaps of stones. Therefore, just as concord among good men is to be desired, so discord among evil men is to be desired: the discord of the wicked ought to be the peace of the good.

Knowing this, the eminent preacher Paul, when he was attacked unanimously by Pharisees and Sadducees, endeavoured to make discord among them, saying: “I am a Pharisee, the son of Pharisees; concerning hope and resurrection I am judged this day” (Acts 15). When the Pharisees, who believed in the resurrection, heard this, they became divided from the Sadducees, who did not believe it, and the council was dissolved. Thus Paul, who in their unanimity was being attacked unto death, escaped unharmed through their discord. Therefore that cloistered man is truly one who maintains unity, conformity, and the unanimity of good men, of whom it is said: “There is one boy here,” etc. [Col. 0171A]

The reference is made demonstratively to the place of discipline, which is the chapter-house. In it cloistered boyhood is reformed and guarded in three ways: by confession, correction, and beating. By confession, when the cloistered man there confesses his sins to the Lord purely, wholly, and orderly: purely, that is, without admixture of falsehood, pretence, or excuse; wholly, that is, without cutting away the truth, lest the confession be half-made and he seek a corner of conscience there where he ought to make his entire offence manifest to God.

For, as the Lord says in the Gospel, “No man puts a patch of unfulled cloth onto an old garment; otherwise the old garment is torn and the rent becomes worse” (Matt. 9). The old garment is the sinful conscience; the new cloth is the lamentation of outward penitence. Therefore, if a man mourns his sins by outward penitence—which is compared to the new garment—namely, confession of the mouth, abundance of tears, [Col. 0171B] groaning, and beating of the breast, but inwardly, by concealing his guilty conscience, retains his sins, he joins, as it were, a new patch to an old garment, and the old garment is torn. The rent becomes worse when the stain of conscience is made worse by concealment of the old fault.

Of such a conscience the prophet says: “There the hedgehog has its den” (Isa. 34). The hedgehog, full of prickly spines, is compared to the sinner who craftily conceals his sins. For when a hedgehog is seized, it draws its head, feet, and other limbs together as though into one ball; and, although all were formerly distinctly visible, when it is seized all vanish from sight. Thus the hedgehog is rightly like the sinner who hides his sins in his heart because he fears that they may be made known. For it often happens that someone’s sins are made apparent by the signs or indications of others; but when, in confession, he is confronted about them by his prelate, he draws himself entirely into one corner of conscience by excusing himself—indeed, by concealing himself. Thus, though he was previously manifest through certain indications of crime, by crafty evasion he wholly vanishes from view. [Col. 0171C]

Confession must also be orderly, so that a cloistered man makes his faults known to his own prelate and not to another; because it chiefly belongs to him to apply the remedy who has undertaken the care of the sick person. If a temporal prince appointed in each of his cities an individual judge to decide the cases arising there and punish sins, would not one who passed by the judge of his own city and went to another make himself guilty before both the prince and his own judge? Certainly, then, that supreme Emperor and Lord, when he appoints prelates in individual churches and commits the care of souls to them, is resisted in his ordering by those who, seeking other judges for their conscience, conceal their sins from their own pastors.

But there is some cloistered man who, having become a brother in different monasteries, thinks it lawful to confess to any prelate who has admitted him into the fellowship of his brotherhood. Evident reason shows this to be altogether unlawful and contrary to truth. For the cloistered man is bound to the duty of confession in that Church in which he holds the title of profession, because in other churches in which he possesses a canonry [Col. 0171D] he has only the fellowship of brotherhood, and is not bound there by any duty of subjection or confession.

Cloistered penitence is also reformed in chapter by correction, which is carried out in three ways: by private rebuke, denunciation, and proclamation. By private rebuke, when one corrects his brother between himself and him alone. By denunciation, when someone secretly reports his brother’s fault to the prelate, whom he understands cannot be corrected by him personally. This is not the ruining of a brother’s reputation but correction, provided that it is done with a good intention. Correction by proclamation occurs when someone is publicly accused in chapter before everyone for his transgression, because he did not choose voluntarily to confess it himself. But such proclamation ought to be made only concerning venial sins, [Col. 0172A] since no mention should be made in chapter concerning crimes unless a brother has first confessed, or has been convicted by two or three witnesses.

There are others in cloisters who, caring more for their own peace than for the benefit of others, evade making accusations, saying that he ought not accuse another who sees himself bound by a similar or greater fault. In defence of their error they bring forward Scriptures that appear to establish this. First, the Gospel authority which says: “First cast the beam out of thine own eye, and then thou shalt see to cast the mote out of thy brother’s eye” (Matt. 7). And elsewhere: “He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her” (John 8). And Paul: “Wherein thou judgest another, thou condemnest thyself” (Rom. 2).

But these authorities are directed against those who correct others not from zeal for justice but rather with the intention that, though they are wicked, they may appear righteous through blaming others. Therefore, it is permissible even for a cloistered man who is secretly guilty to accuse his brother openly, provided that he does not seek to establish his own righteousness, but principally seeks his brother’s correction. But the public accusation of one who is openly guilty is forbidden, because [when] it does not effect the correction of a brother but scandalizes the whole community. [Col. 0172B]

Cloistered penitence is also reformed in chapter by beating, when one is punished with a bodily penalty for his offence. Yet all should carefully observe that “beating” here is to be understood not passively but actively: thus purity of innocence is said to be reformed by beating, not because the penalty is inflicted on the cloistered man, but because he patiently endures that bodily punishment. For one punished for his transgression who nevertheless does not endure patiently not only gains no merit but, by murmuring and defending himself, incurs the punishment of murmurers and becomes even worse.

Therefore, with the foregoing order observed, let us say:

“There is one boy here who has five barley loaves and two fishes.” By the five barley loaves we understand the five principal vows which those in the cloister make at the beginning of their conversion: renunciation of the world, renunciation of property, the vow of chastity, the vow of obedience, and the vow of common life. These are fittingly compared to barley loaves because, just as barley, said to be cold in nature, is made into drink and food for feverish persons to cool their heat, so the aforesaid vows are observed against the incentives of vices. Or this may be so because, just as barley has tough husk outside and useful grain within, so the aforesaid vows contain outward austerity but, when observed, have inwardly a most sweet fruit, as Paul says: “All discipline at present seems to be sorrowful, but in the future it has a most peaceable fruit” (Heb. 12). [Col. 0172C]

The first barley loaf is renunciation of the world. Many who make this vow do not understand themselves, because they do not know what they ought to understand by the name “world.” For if by “world” is understood the fabric of the universe, we do not renounce the world, which we enjoy along with other human beings. Or if by the name “world” are understood secular sins, not only we but all good people have already renounced them. Therefore we say that “world” here is called worldliness [secularitas], that is, a secular manner of living. We renounce the world, then, when for God’s sake we cast off the secular manner of life.

Now the secular manner of life is that a man lives according to his own choice: he arranges clothing, food, bedding, sleep, vigils, travel, actions, serious affairs and leisure, and all things that concern him, according to his own choice. The cloistered man renounces this manner of secular life by vow when, having cast these things aside, he adopts a fixed form of living for God’s sake, observing in all things that concern him a fixed and determined rule, and doing so not according to his own choice but another’s. [Col. 0172D]

The second loaf is renunciation of property. For a cloistered man, property is whatever he has contrary to the command of the rule or the institution of the order, unless he is excused by the indulgence of a prelate. Some cloistered men are officials, while others are ordinary members of the cloister. Officials receive and keep the goods of the Church; they possess them not as their own but as deposits. For just as to defraud a deposit in any respect is a most evident crime, so if an official spends anything from the Church’s property beyond what the necessity of his office or the rule given him by the Church requires, it is akin to sacrilege.

Yet there are officials upon whose office the receipt or custody of temporal goods does not depend; beyond the form prescribed by the order, they have no right to possess anything. Ordinary cloistered men, therefore, ought to have nothing beyond what ordered necessity requires, unless perhaps some spiritual work is imposed on them, such as writing, binding books, or something of that kind. In that case, even without obtaining permission, they may possess for use the things without which the imposed task cannot be completed: a knife, parchment, ink, and so forth, which belong to such an office. [Col. 0173A]

Just as possession of money is forbidden to all, so too is possession of clothing. The stain of property is contracted through clothing in many ways: sometimes from the material of the thing, sometimes from its colour, sometimes from its fineness, and sometimes from its form. Property is contracted from the material of the thing, as when someone wears fox or hare fur under lambskin. Property is contracted from the colour of clothing if a cloistered man has a garment dyed differently from what the order or the custom of the Church has prescribed. The stain of property is contracted from fineness if a cloistered man wishes to use finer garments than the others. For example, if his shirt, tunic, or rain-cloak is made of finer or better material than custom requires. The stain of property is contracted from the form of clothing when a cloistered man has his garments made in a form different from the others, as when he wishes to use shoes, stockings, or even sleeves tighter than those of the others, in a singular fashion.

In some of these matters no dispensation ought to be allowed, namely, in material or colour, since no usefulness or necessity requires this and since there is also matter for scandal. But in fineness or an honourable form, when a just cause is present, a dispensation may be granted. [Col. 0173B]

There are also other kinds of property: that of one’s own will and that of private familiarity. Cloistered men are found who, wishing to retain their own will in everything, do not fear to become disobedient to prelates and opponents of their brothers. From this kind of property anger, quarrels, dissensions, and insults frequently arise, while those wishing to possess it seek to establish their own righteousness and therefore are not subject to God’s righteousness. Of them Paul says that “their foolish heart was darkened, and they became vain in their thoughts; and, professing themselves to be wise, they became fools” (Rom. 1).

Cloistered men retain the property of private familiarity when, having withdrawn from the world, they desire to keep the familiar associations of relatives, companions whom they had in this world, or secular princes. This property is exceedingly harmful, because from it proceed the sins of excessive talking, neglect of divine service, distaste for the cloister, dissension among the brethren, and sometimes the affection of disordered charity. Therefore a cloistered man ought to renounce not only property in things but also the property of his own will and the property of private familiarity. [Col. 0173C]

The third bread is the vow of chastity, that is, continence. A cloistered religious, however, vows continence of bodily act, not of bodily or mental inclination. Hence, if through thoughts or any desires of the flesh he is brought as far as consenting to a carnal act, though without performing it, he indeed sins mortally, but does not violate his vow [Col. 0175B]. Thus a virgin who has vowed virginity is not guilty of violating her vow if she consents in her mind to marry or to fornicate, provided that in act she preserves bodily integrity. And just as a religious man vows continence explicitly, so too, in the fifth vow, which is that of the common life, he vows abstinence—not explicitly, but implicitly. By these two vows, namely continence and abstinence, the dignity of the body is restored, just as bodily dignity is corrupted by the two contrary vices, namely the appetite of gluttony and the outflow of lust. Continence restrains the outflow of lust; abstinence, the appetite of gluttony.

Obedience, which pertains to the fourth vow, concerns only good things. For if a superior commands a subject [Col. 0175C] something that pertains to sin, then, by the very fact that he expresses his own error in the command, his order has no force, and therefore no obedience ought to accompany it. Thus, if a superior excommunicates his subject because he performs works of piety or believes in God, then, by the very fact that he expresses his own folly, his excommunication does not bind. Yet neither is a subject bound to obey his superior in every good thing. For if he commands him to put himself in prison in place of someone held captive there, to adopt a stricter life, or to go to Spain to preach the word of God, then—even if all these things are good—the subject is nevertheless not bound to obey. For he promises obedience only in accordance with the institutions of the order and the customs of the Church.

Therefore, when he vows obedience and the common [Col. 0175D] life, at the end of these vows there is added, “according to the institutions of the Church,” whether those already established or those which shall in the future be established with the Church’s consent. This qualification must be referred not only to the common life, but also to obedience. The fifth vow is that of the common life; and it is called “life” here, not the life by which we live, but the manner of living according to which we live. Thus “common life” means that manner of life according to which all of us live, or can live, without just reproach. I add this because the sick in the infirmary have a different manner of life in food and bedding from that of the healthy in the community. Yet the sick maintain the common life, because the healthy can live in the same way for a like reason, without reproach.

But if, in [Col. 0176A] the community, certain persons are treated more delicately than others in food or clothing, this is not a departure from the common life but a dispensation of the common life. The common life is chiefly observed in these three matters: food, clothing, and bedding. In these they ought to maintain what is common, unless excused by the allowance of a dispensation. According to what has been said, one who drinks water while the others drink wine, one who eats herbs while the others eat fish, or one who wears haircloth while the others wear shirts, will appear to be a violator of his vow, because the others do not observe this manner of living. But what improves a vow cannot be called a transgression of it. Therefore, one who does such things is not guilty of violating his vow, since a person may lawfully advance to what is better, unless he is compelled to desist because of scandal to his neighbour.

If, indeed, someone causes scandal to the brethren by an excessively austere life, he must necessarily return to the common life—not because he has violated his vow, but to avoid scandal [Col. 0176B]. But if, without illness or another just cause, someone lives more delicately than the others—for example, while others drink ordinary wine, he drinks superior wine; while others eat beans, he eats chicken; and while others eat gudgeon, he eats salmon—that person is a violator of his vow, because without just cause he departs from the rigor of the common life. Truly, the aforesaid vows belong to the substance of the order; they cannot, without mortal sin, be set aside by persons remaining in their religious state, except insofar as, in the last vow, that of the common life, an allowance is made by dispensation when necessity arises.

Indeed, with respect to the first four vows—renunciation of the world, renunciation of property, the vow of chastity, and the vow of obedience—no dispensation is allowed to cloistered persons remaining in their state, because in these matters no just cause for dispensation arises. In the fifth, which concerns the common life, the Rule of blessed Augustine itself grants dispensation, so that the superior is not the dispenser but the executor of the dispensation. The Rule itself dispenses concerning the common life when it says:

> If something in the way of food or clothing is given to those who came from more delicate habits, which is not given to others who are stronger and therefore happier, those to whom it is not given ought to consider how far the former have descended from their secular [Col. 0176D] life to this one, even though they have not been able to attain the frugality of others who are stronger in body.

And elsewhere:

> If those who are infirm because of former habit are treated differently in food, this ought not to be burdensome to the others, because all are not to be given equally, since all are not equally strong.

As Augustine says, observe that in all these matters the Rule grants dispensation, but in such a way that the superior is, according to the condition of persons, the executor of the dispensation.

All the remaining written or unwritten traditions of conventual observance are neither vows nor precepts of life, but indications: for they show cloistered religious the form of honorable conduct. Although their omission is not a transgression [Col. 0177A] such as that of a precept or vow, nevertheless those who have undertaken to live according to such traditions sin in omitting them. In omitting other traditions, however, cloistered religious sin not mortally but venially, unless they omit them out of contempt. Contempt occurs when a cloistered religious deliberately refuses to observe them. Thus, if he says in his heart, “I will not keep silence; I will not attend the procession; I will not sit, stand, or walk as the others do,” then in such omissions the contempt of a perverse will constitutes mortal sin.

With the five barley loaves there are also two fishes. Fishes, as is known, are nourished in waters; but according to the Law it is not lawful to eat all of them, only those which leap upon the waters. By the waters [Col. 0177B] we understand Sacred Scripture, as in the passage, “Fill the jars with water” (John 2); and elsewhere, “A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters which flow in Lebanon.”

In these waters of the Scriptures two fishes are nourished: the allegorical and the moral sense. In accordance with the commandment of the Law, these two fishes leap upon the waters, because they summon the reader of the Scriptures beyond the literal sense to higher things. The allegorical sense of Scripture nourishes the cloistered religious devoted to the divine page through the mysteries of Christ and the Church, strengthening faith, because “the righteous lives by faith.” The moral sense, which pertains to the formation of conduct, nourishes him toward good action. Thus the religious man ought to possess, together with the five barley loaves, two fishes, so that, tending toward God in faith and action [Col. 0177C], he may at last, when his course has been completed, lay hold at the end upon Him to whom he has proved himself faithful—our Lord Jesus Christ, whose kingdom and dominion endure for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXX. AT THE GENERAL CHAPTER

“You shall make a lampstand of beaten work from the purest gold, with its branches and cups and bowls and lilies proceeding from it” (Exod. 25).

Most beloved brethren, to whom it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, who have learned to draw honey from the rock, spirit from the letter, and the light of evangelical truth from the shadow of the Law—to you, I say, we think it known that nearly all the precepts of the Mosaic Law were shadows of things to come and mystically signified the Church [Col. 0177D], or those things which are carried out in the Church.

Among these is the command, given by the Lord, that a golden lampstand be made as a figure of the Church; the Church is also designated by the name of lampstand in many places in Scripture. Thus John, writing in the Apocalypse to the angel of Ephesus, says: “I will come soon and remove your lampstand from its place” (Apoc. 2). There, by the lampstand, he intends the Church to be understood spiritually. And the Lord says in the Gospel: “No one lights a lamp and puts it in a hidden place, nor under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, so that all who enter may see the light” (Matt. 5). Here the lamp signifies the light of evangelical preaching, and the lampstand signifies the Church. For [Col. 0178A] a lamp is lit upon a lampstand when the present Church, situated below, is kindled toward heavenly desires by the light of evangelical preaching.

The Church is suitably called a lampstand by this likeness: just as the lampstand does not shine by itself, but bears the lamp placed upon it, so too the Church, in itself somewhat dark through the nature of human frailty, is made radiant and illumined with the light of virtues when the ray of divine grace shines upon it from heaven. Therefore, as the Church is signified by the lampstand, so Christ as man is signified by the shaft of the lampstand; prelates by its branches; learned men capable of the word of God by its cups; the simpler members in the Church by its bowls; and the reward of eternal life by its lilies. All these are said to be of the purest gold.

First we must see why the prelates of the Church are compared to gold, so that we may apply the same rationale of likeness to the rest [Col. 0178B]. They are called gold because of the splendor of holiness, as it is written in Jeremiah: “How the gold has grown dim, how the finest color has changed!” (Lam. 4). Elsewhere, of the heavenly Jerusalem it is said: “Its streets shall be paved with pure gold” (Apoc. 21). The prophet David too, denoting holy men from pagan Arabia by the name of gold, said: “Gold from Arabia shall be given to him” (Ps. 71). Therefore understand the comparison of gold to the prelates of Churches in three respects: because it is pure, because it is shining, and because it is precious.

Gold is pure, because when it is buried in the earth it contracts neither rust nor stain from the soil, but wholly preserves its purity. Likewise, a prelate of the Church, living upon earth—that is, among earthly and sinful people—ought not to contract any stain of sin from them, but, guarding his heart with all diligence, ought to retain cleanness of mind and purity of conscience [Col. 0178C]. For if the hand which must wipe dirt from an object is not clean but defiled, it increases rather than removes the dirt from that object. So too, one set over others is not fit to remove uncleanness from subjects if he bears an unclean conscience.

Gold is so shining that, when it reflects the sun’s ray, it makes nearby objects shine. So also a prelate ought to shine outwardly through good works; yet his works must shine by the ray of divine grace, and, enlightened by such light, must illuminate and kindle others to good action. The light of divine grace itself makes human works truly radiant. We add this because of a certain false light of hypocrisy and pretence, which, under a painted and counterfeit appearance, makes some people’s works seem good when they are evil—far removed in truth from the works which they feign in their pretence. The gift of divine grace makes the works of the righteous appear as they are; hypocrisy makes the works of the wicked appear as they are not. For if you ask a hypocrite what he himself, or his works, are like, his own conscience will compel him to say that he is evil and that his works are evil. Therefore the works of pretenders are not radiant [Col. 0179A], but only seem so, painted with a certain counterfeit color of religion. Let no prelate, then, be a hypocrite; let him beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and of hypocrisy, conducting himself outwardly in body as he is inwardly in mind.

Gold is also more precious than other metals; by this preciousness divine wisdom, which ought to be in prelates, is rightly understood—not that wisdom which consists in a multitude of letters, but that which lies in the savor of virtues, concerning which it is said, “He is wise who loves more.” And elsewhere: “The wisdom from above is first indeed chaste, then peaceable” (Jas. 3). This is the wisdom which teaches a man not to speak learnedly, not to speak grammatically, not to solve Aristotle’s problems, but rather to detest vices [Col. 0179B], cleanse the conscience, govern conduct, order life, and preserve discipline. Truly this wisdom is precious; indeed, as the Wise Man says, it is more precious than all riches, and all things desired on earth cannot be compared with it (Prov. 3).

Perhaps someone desirous of worldly honor will say that much learning is more precious than the wisdom of virtues. For if a learned man and a holy man come among us, we show more honor and reverence to the person who knows much than to the one who lives holily. But a distinction must be made in the word “precious.” Knowledge of letters is more precious in the present Church—that is, more honorable—but wisdom of virtues is more precious—that is, simply better. Thus a valiant soldier who daily kills and destroys is more honored among worldly people than a holy man, although the latter is incomparably better than the former. Therefore, as we have said, prelates are bound to be pure in mind, shining in deed, and wise through the savor of spiritual affection.

Observe that the branches, which we have said signify prelates, proceed from the shaft of the lampstand itself and cling to it [Col. 0179C]. Thus those who preside, and all the righteous, ought to be grafted into Christ through the Catholic faith, without which it is impossible to please God, because “the righteous lives by faith” (Rom. 1). For as a severed foot is indeed a foot but useless, and a hand cut off from the body is indeed a hand but has no use for work, so also one who does not have the Spirit and faith of Christ is dead in Him and wholly unfruitful.

The branches, then, clinging to the shaft, are raised upward and bear lamps; that is, they are kindled by the gifts of the Holy Spirit. In these lamps, oil—the nourishment of flames—is supplied when the fire of charity is nourished in prelates through works of mercy, signified by the oil. Nor do I think it should be passed over that a reed is a musical instrument; and therefore it bears the figure of prelates, because it ought to resound with the voice of preaching, as is said of them: “Go up upon a high mountain, you who evangelize Zion” (Isa. 40). And elsewhere: “Cry aloud, do not cease; raise your voice like a trumpet” (Isa. 58).

Thus the useful pastor of the Church, proclaiming the word of life [Col. 0180A], ought at one time to produce a grave sound, at another a sweet one, at another a subtle one, and at another a sharp one: grave, reproving the impious with the harsh voice of rebuke; sweet, consoling the righteous with gentle exhortation; subtle, searching out the corners of consciences by careful inquiry; sharp, promising the joys of heavenly rewards.

Notice that shepherds discovered the use of reeds not in cities or amid crowds of people, but in desert places, so that, lacking the consolation of worldly people, they might give themselves consolation by musical melody and more lightly endure the loneliness of the desert. In the same way, the voice of pastors of the Church ought not, insofar as possible, to be heard in the disputes of lawsuits, at the courts of princes, or in cities and streets; rather, they ought to utter their voice in deserts—that is [Col. 0180B], in cloisters—where it may be both consolation to themselves and advancement to their subjects.

Next let us see that by the golden cups on the lampstand are to be understood learned men capable of the word of God, who are bound, by expounding the Scriptures to others, to offer them the drink of life.
