They do this when through God’s commands they kindle others to charity; through precepts instruct them toward righteousness; through counsels advance them toward perfection; and through testimonies concerning the future life raise them to contemplation of heavenly things. Thus, by intoxicating others with the wine of spiritual teaching, they bring about in them forgetfulness of this world.

Therefore, whoever you are who wish to be a golden cup and contain the word of life, sow [Col. 0180C] the word of God; offer drink to your thirsty brother; and without envy share what you have received freely. For learning is a noble possession, as someone has said, which, scorning an avaricious possessor, slips away unless it is made public. Nor is it fitting that a golden cup should contain water or must mixed with dregs, but the purest wine. For it does not belong to a religious man to devote himself to letters of secular learning, which are understood by water. Thus some are reproached: “Your wine is mixed with water.” Let the cloistered religious person, therefore, not be anxious about how Tully pleads in legal cases, what Plato investigates among the stars, what Euclid measures in lines, what Boethius harmonizes in music, or how Donatus distinguishes the parts of speech. Rather, having entered the wine-cellar of Sacred Scripture [Col. 0180D], let him draw from it what will enable him to compare spiritual things with spiritual.

Nor is wine mixed with dregs fit to be held in a golden cup, because a religious man ought, when he preaches and teaches the word of God, to blow away all ambition, vain glory, and human praise, lest he become like those who saw the Son of God—for the Word of God is the Son of God—and hear this reproach from the Lord: “You have received your reward” (Matt. 5). Those of whom the Apostle says, “Although they knew God, they did not glorify Him as God; and therefore they became foolish and vanished in their thoughts” (Rom. 1), were infected with these dregs. These golden cups should instead contain pure wine, so that learned men in cloisters may teach and preach [Col. 0181A] the words of life with a single eye and a pure intention, awaiting only that fruit which God has promised to those who love Him.

Moreover, on the lampstand of which we have spoken, the cups are described as shaped like nuts; as though it were said that they ought to have a cover which may sometimes be placed upon, sometimes removed from, the cup. This signifies that learned men should sometimes keep their knowledge closed within themselves for consolation, and sometimes reveal it to others for edification. The bowls on the lampstand are movable and round in form, and signify simple cloistered religious who are governed by the command of their prelates, considering whatever the virtue of obedience commands to be wholesome for them and to be done. Truly these bowls are mobile, not turned to the right or to the left, but rolling straight before [Col. 0181B] themselves, because good cloistered religious, walking confidently in their simplicity, forget what lies behind and always stretch themselves toward what is before.

But when a bowl rolls, it may have a threefold impediment preventing it from running well: a slack hand that pushes it negligently; a rough road that delays and obstructs it; and an obstacle which wholly prevents its advance. These are the three things which delay the progress of a cloistered religious and sometimes extinguish it altogether. The slack hand is negligent authority, by which the cloistered religious ought to be governed. For authority is signified by the name “hand,” as in: “In whose hand is the soul of every living thing” (Job 12); and elsewhere: “In your hand are all the ends of the earth” (Ps. 94). Therefore a slack hand hinders the course of the bowl when a prelate uses the power of governance over his subjects less carefully and less providently; for this reason subjects either wholly abandon their holy purpose or are delayed in it.

The roughness of the road which hinders them is singularity of life: when they themselves, exceeding the measure of common life, choose for themselves certain more austere observances in a singular fashion. Since they cannot bear these, they collapse under the burden and fail upon the road by which they should have journeyed toward their country—that is, heaven [Col. 0181C]. The obstacles by which the bowls, that is, the spheres, are prevented from running—*Teutonice* “kloitzer”—are the scandals of false brethren. By these the simplicity of the good often suffers such damage that, as though rebounded from a hard material, they cease to do good; and, forgetting the goal toward which they should have tended, they become like malicious people and grow worse than before. Poisonous detractions, indecency, foolish talk, and buffoonery irrelevant to the matter, together with looseness of conduct—all these provide an impediment to the simple person living uprightly [Col. 0181D].

By the lilies on the lampstand is signified the reward of the future life, promised alike to prelates who govern their subjects well, to learned men who rightly expound the word of God, and to simpler persons who live holily: a reward which eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and which has not entered into the human heart. To these things already said must be added that this golden lampstand is described as “beaten work,” that is, formed by hammering and frequent blows. By this we are rightly shown that, just as Christ attained the blessedness of eternal life through the straits of passion and death, so all who imitate Christ must walk by the narrow way of tribulations. The time of reigning cannot precede the time of suffering; rather, in this life the righteous must endure distresses and miseries, to whom the crown of righteousness is due. May our Lord Jesus Christ render it to us, whose kingdom and dominion endure for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXXI. ON THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD

[Col. 0182B] “You make the cloud your ascent, you who walk upon the wings of the winds” (Ps. 103).

The words you have heard, most beloved brethren, afford us abundant matter for spiritual joys. By them the voice of prophetic utterance impresses upon our minds the victory of Christ ascending, when the humanity united to the Word of God, clothed in the robe of joy, took its seat above David’s throne in the heavenly Jerusalem. For His glorification is signified to us by that cloud of which the prophet speaks, saying: “You make the cloud your ascent.”

If we wish to interpret that cloud mystically, we ought to understand by it nothing more fitting than the nature of the assumed humanity [Col. 0182C]. In accordance with a suitable likeness of things, it could be called both water before the Passion and cloud in the Passion. Before the Passion it is called water because Christ, still mortal and passible, could melt and be dissolved, hunger and thirst, be afraid and sorrowful, be handed over to condemnation of death, and be fastened to the cross. At the Ascension, however, Christ’s humanity is compared to a cloud because, just as water drawn vaporously up from the low earth is afterwards condensed into a cloud and, lifted by winds, suspended in the air, so Christ’s humanity was separated by the Holy Spirit, who is the vapor of the Father’s majesty, from the low earth—that is, from the dregs of our corruption. Afterwards, by rising again and overcoming the descent of death, strengthened as it were and made denser through immortality and impassibility [Col. 0182D], it ascended above heaven—indeed, above the heavens—lifted by spiritual winds, that is, by the agility and subtlety of its nature.

There are three heavens which, with faithful devotion, we must hold that Christ ascended according to His human nature. The first heaven is the dignity of ecclesiastical purity; the second heaven is the subtlety of angelic condition; the third heaven is the incomprehensible majesty of divinity. Of the heaven of ecclesiastical purity it is written in the Apocalypse: “There was silence in heaven for about half an hour,” and “that great dragon with his tail drew after him a third part of heaven to earth” (Apoc. 8). Of the heaven of angelic subtlety it is written in the book of Job: “Take up the heaven and behold, and contemplate the air, how much higher it is than you” [Col. 0183A] (Job 35). There, as blessed Gregory says, heaven signifies the angelic nature. Of the heaven of incomprehensible divinity, the apostate angel says in Isaiah: “I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I will exalt my throne; I will ascend above the heights of the clouds and will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14).

Therefore Christ was assumed above the first heaven when He became, as man, the head of the Church. Thus the Apostle says: “For He is the head of His body, which is the Church” (Col. 1). And the Psalmist, in the person of the assumed man, says: “I have been established as king by Him over Zion, His holy mountain, proclaiming His command” (Ps. 2). Isaiah saw Him ascend above the heaven of the angelic condition when he said: “I saw the Lord seated upon a throne high and lifted up” (Isa. 6). Since the high throne signifies angelic nature and the lifted-up throne human nature, He is rightly said to preside over each, because by ascending into heaven He has been exalted above both angelic and human nature. Hence Paul says in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “He sits at the right hand of Majesty on high, having been made so much better than the angels as He has inherited a more excellent name than they” (Heb. 1).

Christ’s humanity was raised to the heaven of divine majesty when it was united to the Word of God in such a way that the assumed nature became the assuming, and the assuming nature the assumed; so ineffable was their union that they admitted no division in majesty or power [Col. 0183C]. For evangelical truth testifies that human nature possesses the same power as the Word, saying: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28). The venerable Bede, explaining this, says that it was not spoken of the divinity coeternal with the Father, but of the assumed humanity. Pope Leo also very clearly maintains that the assumed humanity has the same power as the Word when, speaking of the gifts of the three Magi, he says: “They offer frankincense to God, myrrh to man, gold to the king, knowing that the divine and human natures are to be venerated in unity, because what was proper to the substances was not different in power.” Our Hugh also, who among modern writers possesses singular authority in Sacred Scripture [Col. 0183D], cries out and proclaims, saying: “We believe that the humanity of the Word, in its rational soul, from the first moment of its conception, possessed through the ineffable union with divinity full and perfect power, goodness, and virtue.” For, as he says elsewhere, the Son of God assumed man so that He who assumed and that which He assumed might be one person in the Trinity. Therefore those who deny that the human nature assumed into the person possesses the fullness of power thereby deny that the assuming person possesses the truth of divinity.

These three heavens which we have distinguished are those to the third of which Paul recalls that he was caught up (2 Cor. 12). For he was placed above the heaven of the Church by the authority of prelateship; raised above the heaven of angelic nature by the eminence of knowledge; and caught up to the heaven of divinity by a certain singular kind of revelation. He was placed above the first heaven when he undertook the governance of God’s Church; he was raised above the second heaven when he was instructed concerning the orders of angels, their names, and their ministries, as may be seen in the text of his Epistles [Col. 0184A]. He was caught up to the third heaven when he heard secret words which it is not lawful for a human being to speak.

You see, unless I am mistaken, how our beautiful Christ, walking in His own school in the greatness of His strength, ascended the heavens. But exceedingly difficult is the ascent that is directed from earth even to heaven; and what will you do, who are still held by the body of this death? If you wish to ascend, sloth of spirit, bodily mass, and love of this life delay you; and finally the enforcement of the divine sentence: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3). Most mournful is the sentence upon the children of Adam by which all are bound to earth. Yet would that, if they render to earth what is earth’s, they might also render to heaven the spirit which has a heavenly origin and which they received from heaven.

For the rational spirit is a deposit entrusted to us from heaven, to be guarded with all diligence and restored inviolate in faith to Him who entrusted it. To commit fraud in this deposit is surely to deny faith. What, then, will those wretched souls say when He who deposited it calls them to account—souls which have subjected so noble a deposit, marked with the seal of the heavenly King [Col. 0184B], to so many crimes and enormities? Certainly He threatens, He threatens, and is already near, to reclaim what He entrusted: to restore to heaven what was entrusted to us from heaven. And behold, almost everything that ought to ascend above is being hurled headlong downward.

For three rivers of Babylon run between heaven and earth, dragging downward those who desire to ascend. The first is the flood of carnal desires; the second, the course of spiritual temptations; the third, the distress of impending troubles. The first river carries away carnal people who, having destroyed every purity and cleanness of life, have subjected themselves to vices and desires; choked by pleasures and the uncleanness of life, they prepare for Gehenna the soul which they ought to have restored to heaven [Col. 0184C].

The second river, the course of spiritual temptations, is no less perilous. These are hatred, envy, anger, quarrels, dissensions, ambition, pride, and the like. By them are dragged downward those unhappy souls to whom another’s prosperity is burdensome, who always devise evil and envy another’s virtue, who are suspicious, deceitful, treacherous, inventors of crimes, without affection, without covenant, unruly with the good and moderate, and allied with perverse people. The third river draws downward the faint-hearted and unstable in heart, who because of their smallness of spirit cannot endure injuries inflicted upon them outwardly, and therefore are driven from the path of upright conduct by every wind of detraction and affliction.

Therefore, that a passage may be opened here and these rivers crossed dry-footed, three aids are necessary: the rod of Moses, the ark of the covenant, and Elijah’s cloak [Col. 0185A]. For by these three divisions of waters are recorded to have occurred. First, the Red Sea was divided by Moses’ rod; second, with the ark of the covenant going before, the Jordan turned back and gave passage to the children of Israel; third, Elisha touched the river with Elijah’s cloak and, the waters having been divided, likewise crossed over with dry feet.

By Moses’ rod we ought to understand discernment of reason; by the ark of the covenant, observance of the divine law; by Elijah’s cloak, the power of the Lord’s Passion. Thus the first river must be divided by Moses’ rod, because carnal desires must be restrained by discernment of reason. For the spirit presides over the flesh so that unlawful movements of sensuality may be restrained through it, and thus it may make a path through the midst: so that movements of sensuality may stand on one side with regard to the appetite of necessity, and on the other flow toward the testing of virtue.

The second river must be divided with the ark of the covenant going before, because spiritual vices must be fought by the instruction of Sacred Scripture: so that, by meditation upon the divine law, holy exhortations, precepts of righteousness, and examples of the righteous, a mind infected by such a pestilence may be summoned to better things. And because this river runs through wickedness into condemnation, a path must be made through the midst, so that on one side the traveler may avoid wickedness and on the other [Col. 0185C] escape condemnation.

The third river must be divided by Elijah’s cloak because, in all injuries and afflictions which we suffer in mortal life, we ought always to set before ourselves the example of the Lord’s Passion. For when we keep in mind how unjust and how unworthy were the things our Savior suffered for us, we bear with equanimity injuries and vexations inflicted upon us. Notice, however, that the river was not divided when struck the first time, but the second time, because the spirit of Elijah was invoked. “Where,” Elisha says, “is the spirit of Elijah now?” (4 Kgs. 2). For many endure troubles inflicted upon them, labors, and many hardships; but because they do not possess the spirit of Elijah and are not governed by the Spirit of Christ, they gain nothing by their labors. With the waters remaining undivided [Col. 0185D], hardened in their sins, they are borne into ruin. “Bodily exercise is useful for a little, but godliness is useful for all things,” as Paul says (1 Tim. 4).

Thus, having escaped certain dangers, the ascent is easier; but there are different ways of ascending. Some ascend by the zeal of inquiry, others by the guidance of wonder, others by the desire of love, others by the savor of contemplation. By the zeal of inquiry ascend those wakeful searchers into heavenly mysteries, to whom Christ makes known in the Holy Scriptures whatever He heard from His Father: namely, the mystery of the Trinity, the incarnation of the Word, the condition of the future homeland, and the distinctions among the blessed dwelling-places. This ascent is indeed delightful; but, if it is to be fruitful, it must be completed by a heavenly manner of life. Hence that great investigator of things above the heavens, Paul, when he boasts that he is not unskilled in knowledge, adds this also: “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III). For one who is the salt of the earth through knowledge and teaching ought to be the light of the world through a good life, as the Prophet says: “From thy commandments I have understanding; therefore I have hated every way of iniquity” (Ps. CXVIII [119]). For of those who retain God’s commandments in their heart but do not observe them in deed, it is written in Ezekiel: “When you yourselves drank the clearest water, you troubled the rest with your feet; and my sheep fed upon what had been trampled by your feet, and drank what your feet had troubled” (Ezek. XXXIV). What else is it to drink the clearest water [Col. 0186B] than to retain God’s commandments in one’s heart? Or what else is it to trouble that same water with one’s feet than to corrupt God’s commandments by wicked deeds? Hence this troubled water is offered for the sheep to drink when the simpler people take their example of life not from the good things they hear, but from the wicked deeds they see. Knowledge of heavenly things, therefore, is good; but a heavenly life is more necessary.

By the guidance of wonder ascend those who cannot comprehend the joys of the future life or the greatness of the promises; yet, when they hear these things promised to holy persons, they rise toward what they cannot grasp by understanding through the astonishment of wonder. Paul was ascending in this manner [Col. 0186C] when he said: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. II). And the Prophet says: “How great is the multitude of thy sweetness, O Lord, which thou hast hidden for those who fear thee!” (Ps. XXX [31]). By the desire of love ascend upward those who set before their eyes the misery of this life and all things beneath the sun as transitory; and, seeing in them nothing stable or abiding, nothing but toil and pain, they ascend all the more fervently to God, in whom is the peace and rest of spirits, through the desire of love. The prophet ascended in this manner when he says: “My soul desired thee in the night” (Isa. XXVI). And another says: “As the deer longs for fountains of water, so my soul [Col. 0186D] longs for thee, O God” (Ps. XLI [42]).

By the savor of contemplation ascend upward perfect men, who, withdrawn from the cares and desires of this life and having subdued earthly affections within themselves, are touched by the sweetness of heavenly grace and feel no outward bitterness from the course of temporal affairs; inwardly they attend upon the delights of the eternal King through the savor of contemplation. Nor do I think that the prophet meant by the winds mentioned above in the text I proposed anyone other than people comparable to winds because of subtlety of intellect and heavenly meditation or affection, since from the four quarters of heaven—that is, of the present Church—they emit certain spiritual breaths.

The winds blowing from the east are those who devote themselves to the Holy Scriptures and meditate upon God’s law [Col. 0187A] day and night. For while they pour the light of divine knowledge upon those who are in the darkness of ignorance through orthodox instruction, they emit, as it were, a spiritual breath from the east. The winds blowing from the west are those who marvel at heavenly mysteries, who cannot comprehend the weight of eternal glory; and therefore, with understanding—as though with a certain intelligible sun—setting within them, they turn to wonder and send forth a breath as from the west. The winds blowing from the north are those who, sighing amid the tribulations and evils of this present life, look toward God in longing for the future homeland. The winds blowing from the south are those who, with every disturbance and cloud removed, send forth with a tranquil mind—as though from a clear sky—the breath of holy devotion as from the south.

[Col. 0187B] These winds have their wings: namely, the investigations of the Scriptures, wonder at heavenly things, the desire of love, and the savor of contemplation, by which they ascend to heaven in a certain spiritual flight. Yet higher than these wings is He “who makes the cloud his ascent, who walks upon the wings of the winds.” Someone may perhaps think that our Savior does not ascend over these wings in one manner only, since at times He sits, at times walks, and at times flies upon the wings of the winds. Christ’s sitting is understood in the nature of His humanity; His walking, in the sacraments; His flying, in the nature of His divinity. For when our understanding, or any affection of our heart, is occupied with Christ’s human nature or with what He did in the body—things by which, stooping down to our capacity for knowledge, [Col. 0187C] He willed to make Himself known to us—then He sits upon the wings of the winds. But when our heart is occupied with His sacraments, in which our understanding is weak, where “we know in part and prophesy in part,” then He walks upon the wings of the winds. But by the height of His divinity, whereby He surpasses all the capacity of humankind and does not come within our knowledge, He flies upon the wings of the winds. Therefore, if you cannot follow Him as He flies, hold fast to Him as He sits; follow Him as He walks. For though He is above you in divinity, He is certainly beside you in humanity. He is beside you, I say, so that, if you show yourself miserable and weep for your sins, He may show mercy to you. He is above you so that He may judge you without mercy if [Col. 0187D] He finds you obstinate and estranged from the way of righteousness. Therefore let us all flee to the merciful One who is near us, so that, comforted and strengthened in Him, we may not fear the Judge in the future, but may await the blessedness which He promised us through Jesus Christ our Lord, our fellow-heir, whose kingdom and dominion endure for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXXII. ON THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD

“Blessed are those who are called to the wedding supper of the Lamb” (Rev. XIX).

These weddings seem to surpass all others in certain unheard-of delights. In them there is promised not choice wine, not dishes of this creation, not bodily satiety, not temporal gladness, but blessedness—and such blessedness as is eternal peace, an unfailing treasure, the height of joys, the consummation of every consummation.

Therefore they are not to be understood as those weddings of the human king which he made for his son, for to those the blind, the lame, and all who are weak are compelled to enter (Matt. XXII); nor as those held at Cana of Galilee (John II), to which Jesus was called with His disciples, since there, when the wine failed, something deficient was found. Rather, the weddings of the Lamb are the delights of the eternal King, to which Christ was assumed this day with the victorious company of blessed spirits. These weddings are greatly different from those already mentioned: to the first the wretched are called, to the second the righteous, and to the third the blessed. If we wish to distinguish the weddings by both name and number, we shall say that there are three kinds [Col. 0188B] of weddings: the first, of betrothal; the second, of propagation; the third, of consummation. We may call the weddings of betrothal the first grace of reconciliation, by which the sinful soul returns to God, so that it may no longer serve the law of sin; the weddings of propagation, the innocence of life, when, now justified, it strives to bring forth the fruit of good works; and the weddings of consummation, the joys of the future life, when it has entered into the presence of its Lord.

But to speak first of the first weddings, those of betrothal: now, O wretched soul, you alone who have been called to these weddings, now, I say, enter the secret chamber of your heart and consider what you were before you had been called to these weddings—when you were moved about on the wheel of this world without stability, labored [Col. 0188C] without rest, ran without arriving, and lived without order—so worn out by the foulness of your crimes that not even any image of your God shone forth in you. You were then indeed base and foul, cast far away from the face of your God—and deservedly so. For, to set you before your own eyes: you are the one who placed a crown of thorns upon the head of your Bridegroom; who, after putting a reed in His hand, mocked Him with bent knee. You will understand this better if you take the crown of thorns as the pricks of your sins and the winding paths of your error, while you take Christ’s head as the beginning of a good life. For just as the head is the beginning of the body in a material body, so in the spiritual body, which is a good life, the beginning of a good life is fittingly called Christ’s head. Thus you placed a thorny crown upon His head when, by returning to your vomit through evil living, you destroyed the beginning of the good life which God had worked in you through the sacrament of regeneration or through the tears of repentance. Likewise, you changed that iron rod of God’s inflexible justice into a reed, which is hollow within, when you supposed in presumptuous confidence of pardon that God’s just judgment, reserved for the wicked on account of their crimes, could be made void. Finally, what else is bending the knee than the humiliation of the body, or mockery than the obstinacy of the mind? Thus to mock God by bending the knee was, after humbling the body by the labors of repentance, to prove ungrateful to God through a mind obstinate in renewed vices. And behold, you have been made so honorable in [Col. 0189A] God’s sight that He has wished not only to redeem you, though so base, but even to unite you to Himself as a bride—unless perhaps you are of such stubborn impurity that you refuse to delight in His weddings and in the dishes prepared for you.

Therefore, on the very day of your betrothal, your Bridegroom sets before you three dishes. The first is the washing away of crimes; the second, the emulation of virtues; the third, the restoration of natural goods. You must feed upon these courses if you are to please your Bridegroom, to whom you have pledged yourself: first, that through the washing away of crimes you may appear clean and spotless in His sight. For He did not redeem one so deformed in order that you might remain so, but in order that, washed in the waters of repentance and without every blemish of foulness, He might possess you as His bride. Nor must you be clean from vices only; you must also be adorned by the emulation of virtues [Col. 0189B], for He who is wholly beautiful desires one wholly beautiful. And He Himself, “beautiful in form above the children of men,” desired you in order that you too might be beautiful; and lest you perhaps excuse yourself by poverty, the Bridegroom commands ornaments to be brought to you from His treasures, saying: “Bring forth quickly the first robe and put it on her; give a ring for her hand and shoes for her feet” (Luke XV). Here we should understand by the ring the seal of faith; by the shoes, the mortification of the flesh; and by the first robe, the consolation of the future promise. Therefore your Bridegroom gives you a ring for your hand when faith, which had been put to death in you through the failure of good works, is restored by the practice of good action. He gives shoes [Col. 0189C] for your feet when, through mortification of the flesh, you chastise your body and reduce it to servitude, so that the members which you presented as weapons of iniquity for iniquity may serve righteousness unto sanctification. You are clothed in the first robe when you are consoled amid the pressures and labors of this world by the promise of the future life. And, that you may better know yourself, He wishes you to arrange and contemplate your countenance, bearing, and attire in the mirror of sacred speech; for as beauty and ugliness are recognized in a material mirror, so virtues and vices are recognized in the mirror of God’s word. Therefore you must seek your adornment there: so that in God’s commandments you may learn how you ought to live and walk in God’s way, what you owe to yourself, to God, and to your neighbor, and in general those things which pertain to choice [Col. 0189D] and avoidance—that is, to the love of virtues and the hatred of vices. Afterwards the third dish is set before you: the restoration of natural goods, namely memory, will, reason, and understanding, so that memory may remember God, will may desire Him, reason may seek Him, and understanding may comprehend Him.

Now the transition is made to the second weddings, those of propagation, in which nothing bitter, nothing joyless, nothing dishonorable is found. For the bride, admitted to the inner chamber of her Bridegroom, thinks of Him, loves Him, and clings to His chaste embraces, saying: “My beloved is mine, and I am his” (Cant. II). Now let the old delight of sins be far away; love of the world ceases; the affection of blood, or whatever can be desired upon earth, does not draw her, because [Col. 0190A] she judges that she possesses all things in Him whom she has chosen before all things and above all things. At these weddings likewise three exceedingly delicate dishes are set before the bride. The first is instruction in sacred discipline; the second, the supplication of prayers; the third, a foretaste of the heavenly life. The soul, firmly cleaving to God in love, is fed on these dishes so as to produce the fruit of good works; for instruction in sacred discipline teaches it to recognize good things, the supplication of prayers to preserve good things, and the foretaste of heavenly life teaches it to love good things. Thus, perfected in every way on the path of God’s commandments, it is now called not barren but fruitful in Israel. Here you would see a manifold offspring propagated: namely, awareness of one’s own weakness, humility of submission, comparison with one better, and reverence for the Creator. For one who truly loves God first sets his own weaknesses before his eyes, so that he may think nothing lofty or exalted of himself; rather, he fears all his works, always carrying with him the consciousness of his weakness, and, when he has done all things well, will say that he is an unprofitable servant and a sluggish worker in the service of his God. After this is born humility of submission: the one who is small in his own eyes humbles himself, subject for God’s sake to a higher authority, entrusts his whole self to another’s rule, and reserves nothing for his own will. Third is born comparison with one better: in all good actions he always judges another better than himself, sets others’ goods and his own evils before his eyes, [Col. 0190C] so that, having perceived others’ goods, he may love and revere his neighbor, while, considering his own evils, he may accuse himself before the sight of the divine Judge. For in this these people truly differ from those who pursue false righteousness: the former, small in their own eyes, humble themselves; the latter, magnifying themselves though they are nothing, judge all others inferior to themselves. Reverence for the Creator is this: that a person ascribes every good thing he has done to God and not to his own strength, sets Him as the guide and helper of his way, and, if anything doubtful or suspicious, laborious or dangerous should arise, judges that He ought to be consulted first.

Indeed, the righteous are invited to these weddings; but blessed are those who are called to the Lamb’s supper. Perhaps they are blessed because they shall hunger no more nor thirst any more, since the Lamb who is in their midst will rule them; He Himself will gird Himself, make them recline, and, passing among them, minister to them. Therefore at these weddings too three dishes are set before the bride. The first is incorruption of nature; the second, glorification of the body; the third, the perpetual vision of God. What can be more blessed than this blessedness, in which incorruption takes away vice, glorification takes away affliction, and the vision of God takes away grief and pain? Blessed, therefore, are those who are called to the wedding supper of the Lamb, in which full satiety, consummate delight, and blessed joy are found, so that the guests at that supper can desire nothing outside it, since they know that there they possess perfectly God, who is all in all (I Cor. XXVIII). Blessed, then, [Col. 0191A] in hope are those who are called—that is, predestined—to the wedding supper of the Lamb; or blessed in reality are those who are called to that supper—that is, admitted to it. The glory of the future life is compared to a supper because, as no further meal follows supper, so nothing succeeds the future life. Behold, most beloved brethren, these weddings are prepared, to which Christ withdraws this day with the blessed spirits of human beings and angels, inviting us likewise to them, provided that we are willing at once to keep to the way by which He ascended to them.

The way by which He was exalted was the way of the east, as it is written of Him: “He who ascends above the heaven of heaven toward the east” (Ps. LVII [68]). Therefore all who wish to recline at those weddings with Him must imitate Him by the way of the east. Let each person then consider the path on which he walks, lest perhaps he walk in a trackless place and not on the way; for as kinds of people differ, so different ways of living are found. Some follow the way of the east, others the way of the south, others the way of the west, others that of the north. The way of the east is good, because it is safer, straighter, and shorter than the others. The way of the south is dangerous, because it burns its traveler with excessive heat and causes him, weakened, to fail on the road. The way of the west is more dangerous, because the darkness rising from the west takes away the brightness of day, so that one who walks along it stumbles with his feet. The way of the north is most dangerous, because the excessive cold coming from that quarter of heaven makes the traveler so hardened and sluggish that [Col. 0191C] he does not even wish to aspire toward that straight way which looks toward the east. The way of the east is the way of the Savior, for it is written of Him: “Behold, the man—East is his name” (Zech. VI). The way of the south is delight of the flesh, as is said in the Song of Songs: “Tell me where thou feedest at noon” (Cant. I). The way of the west is the blindness of ignorance, as Solomon says: “The sun rises and sets, and returns to its place” (Eccl. I). The way of the north is the cold of wickedness, as Ezekiel says: “I saw, and behold, a whirlwind came from the north” (Ezek. I).

Those who walk by the way of the south are those who love the desires of their flesh and the pleasures of this life, devoting themselves to revelries and drunkenness, offering up their whole selves to all this world’s delights that pertain to the pleasure [Col. 0191D] of the body. From this pleasure an immoderate heat is kindled: namely evil affections, carnal pleasures, luxury, and impurities, which so burn the wretched soul that it cannot be refreshed by any spiritual consolation or delight. For as spirit and flesh are contrary to one another, so are carnal and spiritual delight; so much so that, as spiritual delight increases in the soul, carnal delight decreases in it, and as carnal delight increases in it, spiritual delight decreases. Hence the followers of this way love carnal rather than spiritual people, jokes rather than serious matters, and indecent rather than honorable speech; for each person loves most what he recognizes as most suited to his own habits.

But those who walk by the way of the west are those who do not see their evils and therefore do not repent, nor do they recognize good things and therefore do not love them. They stray more dangerously than others because they do not know to seek the way of salvation. We see something similar occur in the sick: those who do not feel their illness and thus do not seek a remedy for health suffer more dangerously than those who are gravely ill indeed, but, recognizing their disease, endeavor to help themselves through medical counsel. Of this kind are those who, wandering in darkness, strive to justify the ungodly and oppress the godly, killing souls that do not die and giving life to souls that do not live. Among other forms [Col. 0192B] of ignorance, that is worse in which a person wishes to be ignorant of what he can and ought to know: for example, if someone turns his ear away from God’s commandments so that, once he understands them, he may not be obliged to fulfill them; or when he wishes to remain ignorant of his neighbor’s offense because he does not wish to correct him; or neglects that person’s merit because he does not wish to commend him.

Those who go north are those so hardened by the wickedness of their heart—that is, by hatred, envy, and bitterness of spirit—that they cannot love their neighbor as God commands, always striving with their whole purpose to harm and undermine others. And if perhaps they cannot do so in deed, yet they do it through the zeal of a perverse will. Of them blessed Augustine says: “In some people we see vices cease, but not be absent.” They cease in them while they do not fulfill them in deed, because they lack the power; yet they are not absent, because by the zeal of a perverse will such people love and desire them. Such persons rightly come from the north, since from that quarter of heaven one may at times observe both a bright spring and a cold wind. So too lovers of this way often display outwardly the appearance of a good manner of life; but inwardly, bound fast by the cold of iniquity, they are so cast down that nothing they have is acceptable among the things which appear good in their outward conduct. For just as a powerful man despises the outward and zealous service of a servant whom he knows to have an affection of hatred toward him, so God judges those who pretend outwardly to offer Him service [Col. 0192D] while through the wickedness of their heart they are far separated from Him. Behold, we have distinguished three paths which lead a human being to perdition. Nor do I wish anyone to accuse me of severity because, in distinguishing them, I may perhaps have spoken more harshly than I should. For just as one who wishes to straighten a crooked rod sometimes bends it more than is right in the other direction because he fears its springing back, so those who pursue vices sometimes inveigh against them more than is right, because they fear a relapse.

It remains for us to keep to the way of the east, that is, to imitate the life of our Savior. His life was to cast Himself down and exalt others. You will recognize how He cast Himself down if you consider in what poverty He was born, what persecutions and contradictions [Col. 0193A] He endured, and then the reproach of the cross. Likewise, how He exalted others is clear if you consider both the life of the righteous in this world and their glory in the world to come. Therefore, if we are to imitate the life of our Savior, we must be lowly and despised, because He Himself set before us such a manner of life. “You are dead,” says the Apostle, “and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. III). If we are dead, we must also bear the image of the dead person, who is not exasperated when treated with insults, is not provoked by injuries, and, though assailed by every vexation, shows himself unmoved; rather, he bears all things. In this He sets before us a manner of life, that we too may reckon ourselves lowly and despised amid insults and pressures, and patient amid every adversity—more ready to serve than to be served, and to bear injuries than to inflict them. For this is that eastern way which leads to the weddings of the heavenly kingdom. You read of a certain philosopher that, as he was going along a road surrounded on both sides by companions, he encountered a foolish woman holding bread in her hand. When he urgently asked her for bread, he was refused; and when he still persisted in his request, she reproached him with many insulting words. When his companions asked why he did this, he replied: “I am learning to bear rejection, considering the way of the virtue of patience to be that of perfection.”

Nor ought we merely to cast ourselves down; we must also exalt others—correcting our neighbors’ evils, rejoicing with them in their good, teaching those who do not know, [Col. 0193C] and supporting in the Lord those who are less able—so that we always desire to do for others what we ask them to do for us. Look at the foundation of a building, laid in the lower place—that is, in the earth—and yet supporting and raising the whole structure of the walls and the roof itself. When a violent wind rushes in, it often happens that the roof and walls collapse while the foundation remains unmoved. So it is with those who, considering themselves lowly, exalt and support others for God’s sake: when the wind of temptation rushes in and others fall, they remain steadfast, strengthened by the Lord. Firm and unshaken stands that saying of the Lord: “He who humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke XIV). For that way of exaltation truly exalts the humble, the way which by the east leads the guests of the heavenly kingdom to the wedding supper of the Lamb through Jesus Christ our Lord, whose kingdom and dominion endure for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXIII. ON THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD

“Eat, my friends, and drink, and be intoxicated, my beloved” (Cant. V).

Today, most beloved brethren, our Redeemer, exalted above the heavens and entered into the place of that eternal banquet, invites His elect also to the riches of His glory, that they too may eat and drink at His table in the kingdom of God.

For this place of horror and vast desolation could not contain a banquet of such blessedness. Its lovers desire it daily and daily grow weary of it, since it has been prepared for want, not for satiety. For all things that seem sweet in the kingdom of this world are closed by a most bitter end, so that they neither please the one tasting them nor refresh the hungry. Bearing with them the testimony of their own bitterness, at one time they are harmful, at another joyless; and if anything is found in them that delights, because it is momentary and quickly passes, it must be counted among things to be fled. Hence the Apostle Paul, calling us back from love of such things and inviting us to the delights of eternity, says: “If you have risen with Christ, savor the things that are above, not the things upon the earth” (Col. III). For as Christ died for our sins and rose for our justification, so [Col. 0194B] He also ascended, in order to make us ascend from these darknesses into His wonderful light, to those delights of blessedness which He prepared for His elect from the foundation of the world.

Yet because it is very hard and difficult for a person still weighed down by bodily mass to imitate with equal steps God, “who makes the cloud his ascent and walks upon the wings of the winds” (Ps. CIII [104]), God has prepared two other banquets for him as well, lest he fail on the way, so that he might at last be perfected by a threefold nourishment. The first banquet was in the paradise of delight; the second is in this valley of pilgrimage; the third will be in the blessedness of future happiness. The first was for assistance; the second is for remedy; the third will be for joy. To the first banquet our first parents were invited. Among them the ancient serpent sat in the middle, as though master of the feast; by wickedly serving them a fetid tree, he deceived them through forgetfulness of God. Thus they were made transgressors and lost the tunic of immortality and the wedding garment. Its fruit indeed, O Adam, was sweet to your throat, but I fear that it made your belly bitter. For from that same first tree there followed another fruit, very bitter—indeed, most bitter. Do you wish to see what it was? Weakness of nature, affliction of spirit, the appetite for evil, and the calamity of punishment: weakness without remedy, affliction of spirit without consolation, an appetite for evil without measure, and penal suffering without end. Already the torment itself ought to have given you understanding, so that by experience [Col. 0194D] you might perceive the evil figs, exceedingly evil, which your fellow guest, the enemy of the human race, set before you. By tasting them you experienced the evil of perversity in guilt, and afterward the evil of adversity in punishment. Behold, death was offered to you in the pot, and you did not recognize it. For you ate and died. How much more wisely the sons of the prophets once feasted! When they had cut bitter wild herbs into the pot, by Elisha’s counsel they sweetened the death they found in the pot with an admixture of flour, so thoroughly that no bitterness remained after the flour was added (IV Kings IV). Was not death also set before you in the pot when the serpent’s poisonous suggestion, premeditated as though cooked in a pot, caused you to transgress the commandment of your God (Gen. II)? But by Elisha’s counsel—that is, by God’s prohibition that you should not eat of the fruit of the tree—you ought to have tempered this death with the admixture of flour, that is, with the subtle examination of reason, so that it might in some way have become sweet to you, while your victorious conscience rejoiced over the defeated enemy by not consenting to temptation.

But counsel is now too late after you have fallen. Yet even now God does not forget to show mercy to you, because in your present misery He has prepared a second banquet for you. And in place of the tree of life by which you ought to have preserved temporal life in the paradise of delight, He offers you another tree of life, whose fruit is far better and exceptionally more effective, since by eating it you attain eternal blessedness. Of this tree John writes in the Apocalypse: “To him who conquers I will give to eat of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God” (Rev. II). This tree of life, unless I am mistaken, is the cross of Christ, or the imitation of His passion. This tree is planted in God’s paradise—that is, in the Church—so that all who labor and are burdened may be refreshed by its fruit, and those who died in Adam may stretch out their hand to this tree and live forever. Of this tree blessed Job says (Job XIV): “For if it be cut down, it grows green again, and its branches sprout anew.” For whoever bears the Lord’s cross in his body and imitates His passion, when worn down by bodily afflictions, grows green again, made stronger by hope of future reward; and thus its branches sprout more abundantly, when the soul is strengthened by patience to endure greater and more weighty things for the sake of Him to whom it has proved itself faithful.

The fruit of this tree, by which the human being’s second banquet is restored, is to bear reproaches, love poverty, afflict the body by labors and miseries, and lay down one’s life for one’s brothers in need (Luke XIX). Zacchaeus ate of the fruit of this tree when, becoming a lover of poverty, he gave half his possessions to the poor and restored fourfold to anyone whom he had defrauded. Likewise, those ate of this fruit by enduring reproaches of whom the Apostle writes: “You endure it if someone reduces you to slavery, if someone devours you, if someone takes from you, if someone strikes you in the face” (II Cor. XI). John the Baptist too, clothed in camel’s hair and fed on wild honey, sat down at this banquet through mortification of the flesh. Thus also the Author of life was refreshed at the same banquet when He laid down His life for His brothers. There are many examples of such people; but now I speak to you, O human being, who have vowed a vow to the God of Jacob. When you are treated with insults, when you see yourself clothed in poor rags, when your face grows pale through vigils, when your body is worn down by fasts—does this banquet to which Christ has invited you please you? O that it may please you, and that you may not grow weary of feasting thus in the present, so as to receive in the future a most peaceful fruit. For although the taste of this refreshment is bitter, its fruit is sweet. So certainly a bitter potion stings while it is taken, a cautery when it cuts, and battle in the contest is dangerous while it is joined; yet from the first comes the recovery of health, from the second relief of pain, and from the third the joyful end of victory.

But not all accept this saying. Different people eat the fruit of the tree which we have mentioned in different ways. Some eat and desire more; some eat and grow weary of it; while others do not eat but disdain it. Those who eat and desire more are the true imitators of Christ, who delight in the silence of the cloister, bodily labor, sparing food, long vigils, the rigor of discipline, and the freedom of poverty, not judging the sufferings of this present time worthy to be compared with the glory that shall be revealed in them. Those who eat and grow weary are those who bear the burden and heat of the day, yet murmur under their load like a cartwheel; they are disobedient to their superiors, discordant with their equals, obstinate toward their inferiors, impatient of discipline, and lovers of discord. To speak of their distaste for food: if you set beans before them, they do not like them because they nourish melancholy; if leeks, they reject them because of bile; cheese harms the chest, fruits of trees cause indigestion. In short, to include all else in a brief statement, they love only what accords with the judgment of their own will.

The third sort—those who do not eat of this banquet but despise it—are kings of the nations, rulers of provinces, shepherds of churches, indeed deserters, and all other lovers of this world: those clothed in soft garments and feasting splendidly every day. For them it is not enough not to imitate the footsteps of Christ’s Passion unless, by life and conduct, they persecute Christ’s cross so far as lies within them. [Col. 0196C] Their banquet is plainly and rightly prefigured in that action of Herod of which we read in the Evangelist: “When his birthday came, he gave a banquet for his princes, tribunes, and the leading men of Galilee. While they were feasting, Herodias danced before the king and pleased those reclining with him; and when the king offered her a gift according to her desire, she asked for the head of John the Baptist” (Matt. 14).

Herod means “of skin,” Herodias “glorious,” and John “the grace of God.” Herod’s birthday is the success of earthly prosperity; the princes, tribunes, and leading men of Galilee are the pre-eminent virtues of the soul, through which one ought to pass over from vices to virtues. For Galilee is called “passing over” or “migration.” [Col. 0196D] Thus Herod is every person entangled in the pleasures of life and desires of the flesh, and is therefore suitably called “of skin.” “Skin for skin,” says Job, “and a man will give all that he possesses for his life”: by “skin” he means riches and pleasures, in which all who live voluptuously are cherished in this life.

This Herod makes a banquet for his nobles on his birthday when, in the success of earthly prosperity, the carnal mind leads the soul’s powers—namely reason, memory, and will—into delight in temporal things. Herodias, whose name means “glorious,” is pride itself. She dances before those reclining at table when the minds of the wicked, precisely because they pour themselves out in pleasures and unlawful desires, seek the wind of empty glory and the favour of human praise. Thus it happens that, at her request, John is beheaded. John means “the grace of God.” The head of John, therefore, is the right intention of virtue. John is beheaded at Herodias’ request when, pride knocking at the minds of worldly people, the intention of their action is established in no body of virtue.

Therefore holy men eat of Jesus’ banquet and desire it; false brethren eat and are disgusted; worldly people do not eat but despise it. For this reason they do not attain that third banquet of the eternal King which we mentioned at the beginning, to which our Head and Beginning has today gone before us, and in which Jesus will gird himself, make them recline, and, passing by, minister to them. Solomon recalls this blessed banquet, saying: “We shall rejoice and delight in you, remembering your breasts more than wine” (Song 1). And David the prophet: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. 16).

But lest anyone should be excused from this banquet, the master of the household sent his servants, the prophets, to announce it among the peoples and make it known. At last the steward came at supper-time to tell those invited to come, because “the bulls and fattened cattle have been killed, and everything is ready” (Matt. 22). Truly everything is ready, unless those invited are themselves unready. For what can be lacking from that banquet in which charity satisfies, joy intoxicates, prudence dispenses, justice ministers, immortality clothes, impassibility guards, health longs for us, eternity bestows itself, truth enlightens, and concord makes peace? [Col. 0197C] Behold, dearest brothers, the Son of God has called us to this banquet, and we delay in coming; he compels us to enter, and we resist; he has gone before by ascending into heaven, and we do not imitate him.

Certainly, if an edict had gone out from Caesar Augustus to princes and tyrants, to all earth-dwellers and sons of men, commanding them to present themselves before him, all would press on, hurry, and run together in obedience to the royal decree—even though perhaps they were to risk hardships, die in war, or suffer loss of property or honour on a charge of violating majesty. Likewise, if a decree of a council had proceeded from the Roman see, you would see rulers of churches no longer saddling she-asses, as in ancient days, but filling their purses from the treasures of the Church for horses and mules “which have no understanding,” so that they might appear with honour before their judge, perhaps to hear a grievous sentence.

And you, Christian soul, invited to the delights of the eternal King, why do you not hasten to enter that rest where there shall be no death, nor mourning, nor crying, nor any pain, because the former things have passed away? Do you not know that the grace of your Redeemer calls you where your heavenly nature also leads you? For you have a heavenly origin, since you bear the image of the highest King—namely reason and understanding. Thus Paul says: “We know [Col. 0198A] that we are children of God, but it has not yet appeared what we shall be.” The philosopher of the world also, declaring to you your origin, says of you and your like:

> Their force is fiery, and their origin heavenly,  
> So far as harmful bodies do not delay the seeds  
> (that is, the souls),  
> And wearying limbs and dying members weigh them down.

[Note: Col. 0197D]

> Their vigour is fiery and their origin heavenly,  
> So far as harmful bodies do not delay the seeds,  
> And earthly limbs dull them, and dying members.  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* 6.731–33.)

Attend therefore, wretched soul, and see whether any sorrow is like yours. All creatures obey the law of nature: the sun rises and sets, and naturally returns to its place; rivers enter the sea and return to their source in order to flow again. All things rejoice in their like; you alone, having become ignoble, have cast yourself down from the dignity of your condition, because, weighed down in an earthly dwelling, you are compelled to serve the passions of the flesh. The Mantuan poet also shows this when he says:

> Hence they fear and desire, rejoice and grieve, nor do they behold the air,  
> Shut up in darkness and a blind prison.

[Note: Col. 0198D]

> Hence they fear and desire, grieve and rejoice, nor do they discern the air,  
> Shut up in darkness and a blind prison.  
> (*Ibid.* 6.734–35.)

Would that, even while placed in this prison, you might have wisdom and understanding: precisely because you cannot remain in the midst of miseries, because toil and pain exhaust you, you are thereby warned not to establish for yourself here an abiding city, but to seek the city to come. And, to make a comparison from visible things to invisible, as someone says:

> Though it fare well late for Pandion’s daughter shut in a cage—  
> that is, Philomela—  
> she strives to return to her own woods.  
> [Col. 0198C] (Ovid, *Epistulae ex Ponto* 3.39–40.)

Take any little bird and shut it in a cage; give it drink and provide abundant food: it is not tamed by all this, but, if it has a means of escape, it returns to its beloved solitudes. Why is this? Because it sees deserts as more fitting to its nature than cities. And you, Christian soul, do not merely dwell in a cage, but are held captive in the dreadful prison-house of the body: do you not hasten to return to your beginning, from which you came forth? But why did I say, “Do you hasten”? Indeed, you do not even look upward, worn out by the filth of your prison and by the rottenness of the dust which you have put on.

I wish that, from the example of your murderer—that is, the flesh in which you dwell—you would learn how you ought to live. For Aristotle says of it in the *Metaphysics* that, when the body is weary, it is relieved by an opposite position. This means that bodily weariness is refreshed by a contrary posture: if the body has been wearied by sitting, it is refreshed by standing; if by lying down, by rising; if by walking, by resting. Similarly, wretched soul, you ought to observe this: when weary, you should be refreshed by the contrary state, seeking rest in labour, security in fear, abundance in poverty, happiness in misery, remedy in weakness, and joy in pain.

[Col. 0199A] Go then, lazy person, not merely to the ant—which nevertheless is set before humanity as an example for life—but to the phoenix, the bird of Arabia, a marvellous nature, that is, a unique being. It will tell you what you ought to do. For when it has lived five hundred years or more and sees itself failing through old age, it gathers fragrant wood and builds a pyre. Turning toward the sun’s ray, it beats its wings and kindles for itself a voluntary fire; throwing itself into the fire, it is wholly burned. Reduced to ashes, it is afterwards restored to life from that very ash. Thus it earns renewal of life through much danger and peril.

Therefore, dearest brothers, since through the decay of this corruptible life we daily tend, like the phoenix, toward destruction, let us also gather fragrant wood—that is, the fragrance of virtues and good works—and, having become fellow-workers with God, kindle within ourselves the fire of God’s Spirit, so that our evils which wage war against the soul may be burned up. Thus, when the old man has been turned to ashes, we may rise into that newness of life where Christ sits at the right hand of God the Father. May Jesus Christ, our Lord, who invited us, deign to bring us there; his kingdom and dominion remain for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXXIV. ON THE DAY OF PENTECOST

“I saw a mighty angel coming down from heaven, clothed with a cloud, with a rainbow upon his head; his face was like the sun and his feet like a pillar of fire” (Rev. 10).

Today, dearest brothers, the ancient curse upon the earth has been changed. For, as the time of propitiation draws near, the voluntary rain which God set apart for his inheritance has come down upon the earth; and that good cultivator of hearts, the Holy Spirit, has by the dew of spiritual grace made earthly soil fruitful in its condition, lest the farmer be unable to cultivate it for fruit as though it were thirsty and dry.

The apostle John knew this saving rain to be contained in that cloud of which he said: “I saw a mighty angel coming down from heaven, clothed with a cloud”—the Angel of Great Counsel coming down from the Father’s bosom and clothed in flesh. This cloud, drawn up by the sun as vapour and long buffeted by the collisions of winds, was at last dissolved into rain by the benefit of heat. Do you wish to see how? The invisible sun certainly drew this cloud up when, hidden beneath the cloud of flesh, he displayed himself as visible, as the ray of the Holy Spirit poured itself into the Virgin’s womb, lest the light should become hateful to diseased eyes when they beheld the Son of God under flesh, the sun beneath a cloud, the ray in shadow, the light in a lantern.

How this cloud was shaken by the storm of winds is evident if we recall the wind of Herod’s persecution, under whose pressure the Lord fled into Egypt (Matt. 2); the wind of diabolical persuasion, by which he was tempted in the desert when he heard: “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become bread” (Matt. 4). Were not the scandal of the cross, the soldier’s spear, and the traitor’s tongue also most violent winds? But now, when the storm has been stilled, this cloud is dissolved into rain by the benefit of heat, because, on account of the exceeding charity with which he loved us, he made the minds of the faithful rich with gifts of grace, that they might no longer produce thorns and thistles of sins as in former days.

[Col. 0200A] Truly the exacter has ceased and tribute has rested, when humanity, restored to liberty and reconciled with God, received the sign of the covenant, the pledge of inheritance, and the earnest of propitiation. This is signified precisely by the statement that the rainbow was upon the angel’s head. The rainbow is the arch of heaven which appears on a rainy day, concerning which the Lord says: “I will set my bow in the clouds, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and the earth” (Gen. 9).

Certainly, when the sun’s ray reaches the elements of this world, the same ray, reflected into a cloud, imparts to the cloud such a colour as it finds in the obstacle from which it is reflected: from earth, an earthy colour; from water, blue; from air, hyacinth-blue; and from fire, fiery. These four varieties are found in that bow of glory. Since that bow is the sign of propitiation, does it not seem to you that the propitiation of the divine counsel assumed the colour of earth when it put on the earth of our flesh and the weakness of our mortality, in order to heal our misery through sharing our misery?

Did it not also draw, as it were, the colour of water when it caused that flood of our sanctification—the water of baptism—to dwell upon the earth from its side, in order to remove our guilt and restore innocence? Likewise it took on the colour of air, which is itself the colour of heaven, when, earthly affections having been softened, it raised the minds of believers through [Col. 0200C] faith, hope, and charity to desire heavenly things, saying with the Apostle: “But our commonwealth is in heaven” (Phil. 3). Nor was the colour of fire lacking to divine propitiation when, on this day, it set its body—that is, the Church—ablaze with the fire of the Holy Spirit, so that those who had received the first fruits of the Spirit, strengthened and fearing nothing, bore his name before nations and kings and before the children of Israel.

Why, indeed, are the apostles called “feet,” unless because they carried him? Through their ministry his face—that is, knowledge—became like the sun. For whereas God was formerly known only in Judaea, through the apostles’ preaching the light of faith and the truth of the Gospel shone not only upon Jews but also upon the nations. Observe, if you please, that the rainbow is said to be upon the angel’s head, not in the cloud. Since the head of Christ is God (1 Cor. 11), the rainbow is rightly said to be upon the angel’s head, because God effected our propitiation according to the nature of divinity through the nature of humanity as an instrument. Hence the Apostle says: “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5).

“His feet,” he says, “were like a flame of fire.” Three kinds of fire occur to us, representing three gifts of the Holy Spirit. There is burning fire, warming fire, and shining fire. Burning fire consumes the material set under it, as we see in ordinary conflagrations. Warming fire is an inborn heat which cherishes and nourishes bodies placed under it. Shining fire is the splendour of luminous bodies, which drives away darkness and brings brightness. Are not three gifts of the Holy Spirit rightly represented by this threefold fire? By the fire called burning is understood the spirit of love; by that called warming, the spirit of consolation; by the third, called shining, the spirit of truth.

Those who said, “Was not our heart burning within us concerning Jesus while he spoke to us on the way?” (Luke 24), burned with the heat of the first Spirit. The prophet David possessed the Spirit of consolation when he said: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul” (Ps. 93). Concerning the Spirit of truth, the Lord says: “When that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all [Col. 0201B] truth and will declare to you things to come” (John 16).

The first Spirit works in the desire for heavenly things; the second, in patience amid tribulations; the third, in the instruction or illumination of preachers. These three were represented by the Holy Spirit’s descent upon the apostles in fiery tongues (Acts 2). The tongue signifies the teaching of preaching; fire, insofar as it burns, the fervour of holy desire; and insofar as it shines, the sweetness of divine consolation. O how sweet the Paraclete, how good the Comforter, who warms and strengthens what is afraid, and enlightens what is darkened! Whence comes such a messenger to you? By whom is he sent? Into whom is he poured? Certainly Christ the Lord sends him from heaven and pours him into the servant, so that through that same Spirit the humility of the servant may reach the place where the majesty of the Commander sits.

Therefore be watchful, faithful soul, and so run that you may grasp it, establishing your end in him from whom your Paraclete, the guide and governor of your way, has proceeded.

The end of your pilgrimage ought to be Christ; but you—or any other righteous person—are brought to that end, and the one who brings you there is the Holy Spirit. Do you think this finisher is of little necessity? Not at all. He guides the mind’s sight so that it may end in him to whom a person has committed himself: beneath whom there is nothing better, above whom nothing is to be desired, and to whom the Prophet, desiring to attain, says: “Make known to me, Lord, my end” (Ps. 38). But there are some who do not tend toward their due end because they have no finisher, the Holy Spirit, to guide them. Without him they do not know where they are going; without him they cannot know the way.

Just as the spiritual person sets Christ before himself as his end, so the carnal person sets pleasure as his end, and the worldly person vanity. This is an evil end: it is not consummated but rather consumes; concerning it it is said, “Their end is destruction, and their glory is in shame” (Phil. 3). O senseless person, root of bitterness, vessel of dishonour, enemy of uprightness: why is it in your heart to forsake the end of all consummation, namely Christ, and to be tortured by ambition, puffed up by honours, neglect discipline, and destroy chastity? For their last things are bitter as wormwood and sharp as a two-edged sword: the last things, I say, of those [Col. 0202A] who consume their days in beds and indecencies, devoting themselves to dishes, flavours, and drained cups, and making provision for the flesh in its desires.

Do you wish to hear how iniquity lies to itself? “Come,” it says, “let one come to another; let us satisfy ourselves with breasts, let us enjoy the embraces we have desired until day dawns” (Prov. 7). “Who knows whether the spirit of Adam’s children goes upward and the spirit of beasts goes downward?” (Eccl. 3). “All that we live is ours,” they say. What then? Set out undiluted wine and dice; let him perish who cares for tomorrow.

I wish that the wine you command to be set before you were not from the vineyard of Egypt, but from the vineyard of Sorek, or at least from the vineyard of Engaddi. For Egypt’s vineyard produces the wine of confusion, which brings about forgetfulness of God in people; Engaddi’s vineyard, the wine of compunction; Sorek’s vineyard, the wine of exultation. Do you seek proof of how the wine of Egypt produces forgetfulness of God? “God gave them over,” says the Apostle, “to a reprobate mind, to do what is unfitting: filled with all iniquity, malice, fornication, avarice, wickedness, envy, murders, strife, deceit, malignity; whisperers, slanderers, hateful to God, insulting, proud, haughty, inventors of evils, disobedient to parents, senseless, disorderly, without affection, without mercy” (Rom. 1).

How long, wretched soul, will you be drunk with this wine of Egypt? Rather transfer yourself to the wine poured out by the vineyard of Engaddi: namely, the wine of tears and compunction. Peter drank of this fruit of the vine [Col. 0202C] when he remembered the word Jesus had spoken and, going out, wept bitterly (Matt. 26). That publican also drank of it, who struck his breast, saying: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke 18). Strike your breast likewise, and pour out tears by day and by night, because you have provoked God’s anger and done evil in his sight. Do you pour them out in vain? Not at all. They rise from the cheek to heaven, and no sacrifice is more acceptable in God’s sight. “Your sorrow,” says the Lord, “shall be turned into joy, and no one shall take your joy from you” (John 16).

O necessary pain, fruitful sorrow, which is turned into joy, and into such joy that those reclining are served, [Col. 0202D] from the vineyard of Sorek, the wine of gladness and exultation. For Sorek means “chosen” or “best.” It is the vineyard that produces that good wine concerning which the steward says to the bridegroom: “But you have kept the good wine until now” (John 2). Behold, in the future this wine of gladness awaits you; that bread of angels and the fatted calf await you, in whose fatness your soul may delight—provided, however, that in the present it has been cleansed by the blood of that same calf. For, as citizens of the heavenly homeland are fed by this calf’s fat, so in the present they are cleansed by its blood. Some are nourished by its flesh; others are winnowed by its horns.

Those are cleansed by its blood who bear the marks of his Passion in their bodies through vigils, abstinence, and other good works, prepared to endure every injury for Jesus’ name. Those are nourished by his flesh who strengthen the way of their pilgrimage through faithful reception of his sacraments, for remission of sins and growth in virtues. Those are winnowed by his horns who, regarding Christ’s Passion as scandal or folly, suffer persecution for his cross and are cast into the outer darkness, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth.

You understand, dearest brothers, that God has prepared that joyful dwelling for you. He sent you the Holy Spirit to guide you to it, yet scarcely anyone follows him. Another messenger has come, from the power of darkness—namely the spirit of flesh—which draws people to punishment, and all follow it. Go across, O human being, to the islands of Kedar, to the kingdoms of Kittim, [Col. 0203B] and to barbarous nations: will you find anyone so hostile to nature, so contemptuous of happiness, so desirous of pain and loving of poverty, that, if joys come, he refuses them; if riches come, he despises them; if happiness comes, he does not receive it? Yet you find in no one else what you find in yourself, O Christian: adopted as a child of God, you do not seek from God the inheritance of the kingdom prepared and promised to you by him. Rather, becoming your own adversary, you cherish and feed your enemy; you love him, follow him, and have no intimate friend greater than he.

What enemy? Your flesh: that most wicked murderess, upon which you bestow care beyond all things, offering it not only necessities but even superfluities. Whence come God’s wrath upon the children of perdition, the worm that does not die, and the fire that is not extinguished, except because of works of the flesh? When the flesh has been clothed in soft things, when you have spread its bed with tapestries from Egypt and nourished it with every kind of delicacy, it immediately rises against the spirit, urges idleness, introduces pleasures, fulfils the flesh’s desires, and makes the overthrow of the one who has benefited it the end of its victory. Would that this enemy were felt only by a citizen of Babylon, and did not at times prevail over David or any religious person!

We read that David had three enemies: Goliath the Philistine, King Saul, and his own son. Goliath was an external enemy, Saul a civic enemy, and the son a domestic enemy. By Goliath are understood the manifest snares of those outside; by Saul, the familiar vexations of false brethren; by the son, the inborn inclinations of carnal desires. Which of these enemies did more harm? David killed Goliath, patiently endured Saul, but was for a time driven from his royal throne by his son. For it sometimes happens that, after a religious man has conquered external snares and patiently borne the unjust vexations of brethren, he is expelled from the royal seat by his son, because through unlawful desires inborn within him he is cast down from the summit of virtues.

Since, therefore, dearest brothers, the spirit of flesh always resists the Holy Spirit, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit and prepare the secret places of our hearts for him who today fills the whole world. Thus, guided and taught by him, we may wish to seek and love that end which we desire to attain: [Col. 0204A] our Lord Jesus Christ, whose kingdom and dominion remain for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXXV. ON THE DAY OF PENTECOST

“He will send forth his word and melt them; his spirit will blow, and the waters shall flow” (Ps. 147).

I know, dearest brothers, that the sublimity of today’s solemnity and the reverence of your holiness would demand a vigorous dispenser of God’s word, one who might bear witness with great power to the resurrection of Jesus Christ and the coming of the Holy Spirit.

For this ought to be done, with the Spirit himself teaching, by a spiritual man who has tasted how sweet the Lord is, such as the Apostle indicates when he says: “The Spirit himself [Col. 0204B] bears witness to our conscience that we abide in him” (Rom. 8). Would that I had remained silent and had not opened my mouth, especially since praise of God is not fitting in the mouth of a sinner, the Holy Spirit himself saying to the sinner: “Why do you recount my righteousness and take my covenant in your mouth?” (Ps. 49).

Yet because it is now the Jubilee year, that is, the year of remission, I too hope, according to God’s command, to return free to my Lord, relying upon his promise which says: “You were sold for nothing, and you shall be redeemed without money” (Isa. 52). Truly this is a year of remission and a time of grace, when the field of this world, long unfruitful, receives the Holy Spirit as its cultivator; and when the violent possessor has been driven out, the hearts of the faithful return in freedom of spirit to their Lord.

For God the Father sent forth—that is, sent from heaven to earth—his Word and his Son, and “melted them,” that is, made them liquid, when through the Word of his Only-Begotten and the operation of the Holy Spirit he softened hearts formerly hard and stony, making them obedient to God. Therefore it continues: “Your Spirit will blow, and the waters shall flow.” Understand that Spirit of whom the Apostle says: “For charity has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us” (Rom. 5). And elsewhere: “I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh.”

This Spirit blew with a manifold breath. The first breath was in the creation of the world; the second in the Incarnation of the Word; the third in the renewal of humanity. Of the first breath it was said [Col. 0204D] that “the Spirit of the Lord was borne upon the waters” (Gen. 1). At his breathing, they flowed—that is, flowed together, that is, flowed into one place—because the waters beneath heaven were gathered into one place so that dry land might appear. For the elements of this world were opposed to one another by a certain natural confusion: cold things fought with hot, moist with dry, until at last, under the Holy Spirit’s instruction, they settled in a firm covenant of peace, taking care in their own way to preserve the unity of the spirit in the bond of peace. Thus the earth received into its bosom water, unstable and wandering of itself; water irrigates the earth, thirsty and dry of itself; fire, by the benefit of heat, brings forth the earth’s fruits; and air preserves them by its unviolated temperateness.
