The second breath of the Holy Spirit was when the Word, the Son of God the Father, assumed humanity and, through the Holy Spirit’s operation, poured the fullness of grace into the nature assumed. Nor did this Spirit merely blow then: he also fused. For by his breathing he reduced two natures, so different—God’s and humanity’s—to one person. The craftsman of this structure was the person of the Father; the workshop, the Virgin’s womb; the bellows, the announcing angel; the blast, the Holy Spirit at work; the mass, human nature; the flame cleansing rust, the nature of divinity.

At this Spirit’s blowing, the waters flowed: that is, the testimonies of Scripture issued forth. Before the Incarnation of the Word, the garden was enclosed and the fountain sealed. The garden was enclosed because the sacraments of the Church had not yet been made manifest; the fountain was sealed because the spiritual meanings [Col. 0205B] of the Scriptures had not yet flowed forth.

The third breath of the Holy Spirit is a certain sweetness of divine inspiration, which pours itself into the hearts of spiritual people and, according to the distributions of graces, leads one person in this way and another in that along the way of God’s commandments. While this Spirit blows, waters flow as though through seven streams, because the gift of grace is bestowed upon each according to the measure of Christ’s giving.

The poor in spirit drink from the first stream: those who choose to be despised in God’s house rather than dwell in the tents of sinners (Ps. 83); ready to obey, eager to minister, outdoing others in honour, and themselves contemptuous of honour and glory. From the second stream the meek draw, of whom it is said: “But the meek shall inherit the earth and dwell upon it for ever and ever” (Matt. 5). They are moderate in speech, modest in appearance, composed in bearing, and tranquil in action.

Those who mourn drink from the third, of whom Job says: “Before I eat I sigh, and my groaning is like rushing waters” (Job 3). Such people are fearful from consciousness of sin, distressed with sighs, overflowing with tears, and worn down by scourges and blows. The merciful drink from the fourth, of whom it is said: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5). They are ready to forgive, cheerful in helping, compassionate toward the miserable, and rejoicing with those who prosper in the way of virtue.

[Col. 0205D] Those hungering for righteousness draw from the fifth stream; in their person the prophet says: “Lord, I will remember your righteousness alone.” They are fervent in spirit and strong in action, zealous for righteousness, guardians—indeed cultivators—of discipline. From the sixth stream, namely purity of heart, the pure in heart drink; in their person blessed Job says: “My heart does not reproach me in all my life” (Job 24). They are pure in clean thoughts, uplifted in meditation, discerning in action, and devoted in prayer. The peacemakers are intoxicated from the seventh, of whom the Prophet says: “Great peace belongs to those who love your law” (Ps. 118). They are calm in prosperity, secure in adversity, and, with flesh not resisting spirit, withdrawn from every temptation of vice.

These are the spiritual waters of which spiritual men drink, [Col. 0206A] which the apostles drank today when they received the power of the Spirit coming upon them. He set them aflame through the inspiration of divine love, enlightened them by knowledge of truth, and strengthened them by certainty of reward. These three things seem to have been signified by the facts that the Holy Spirit appeared in fire, in tongues, and on such a number of days—namely the fiftieth. Fire is the sign of divine love; tongue, of knowledge; and the number fifty, at which remission was made according to the Law, is the sign of freedom or reward.

These three keep the sight of the inward eye always directed toward God and do not permit it to wander from him through any intervening darkness. We see that three things are necessary for outward sight: an inward light, which is emitted through the windows of the eyes; an outward light, namely the brightness joined to the inward light of which we have spoken; and some bodily object toward which sight itself is directed. Inward light does not suffice for seeing without outward light, as darkness proves; nor does outward light suffice without inward light, as is evident in the blind. Nor would these two joined together avail anything unless something to be seen met our gaze.

Likewise, for the illumination of the inner person, three things must come together: inward light, which is the ray of divine love; outward light, that is, the knowledge of truth which ought to direct us beyond ourselves; and the object toward which spiritual sight must be directed, namely certainty of reward. Remove inward light—that is, the flame of charity—and your lamp is quickly extinguished; and with the foolish virgins you will deserve to hear: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you.” Suppose outward light is present, namely knowledge of truth: without charity, what does it profit? Nothing. “Where,” says Isaiah, “is he who weighs the words of the law?” (Isa. 33). And the Apostle: “If I have all knowledge and all faith, so as to remove mountains, but have not charity, I am nothing” (1 Cor. 14). If certainty of reward is absent, I judge that the light of charity soon fails. Therefore let every child of the apostles consider whether he burns inwardly with the fire of divine love. This fire ought to be perpetual upon the altar of our hearts and never be extinguished while we serve in this life.

You have heard that the sons of Aaron, offering strange fire [Col. 0206D] before the Lord, died (Lev. 10). What is this strange fire? Strange fire is lust, which consists in chambers and shameless acts; strange fire is anger, which consists in dissensions and insults; strange fire is envy, which consists in disparaging another’s virtue. Of this fire it is said through the Prophet: “They, burned by fire and dug down, shall perish at the rebuke of your countenance” (Ps. 79). Let each of you examine his heart: are his works directed, by knowledge of the truth, toward their due end—that is, toward the prize of eternal reward—so that no wrinkle of duplicity and no deceit of pretence intervenes? That Balaam, who “falling, had his eyes opened” and saw the revelations of the Lord, said: “There is no idol in Jacob, nor an image in Israel” (Num. 23).

[Col. 0207A] By Jacob, whose name means “supplanter,” he wished to signify those who overthrow vices; by Israel, interpreted as “a man seeing God,” the contemplative. Now an idol is properly a statue which, owing to its diversity of forms, bears the likeness of no creature—as if a painter should wish to join a horse’s neck to a human head. (Horace, *Art of Poetry*, vv. 1–2.) Hence the Apostle also says that “an idol is nothing” (1 Cor. 8): that is, it bears the likeness of no creature. An image (*simulacrum*), however—so called from imitation—is a statue made in the likeness of some creature. By an idol, therefore, are understood wicked works, which bear no likeness to any good works; by an image, evil works which retain the appearance of good works but not their truth. Thus there is no idol in Jacob [Col. 0207B], because true overthrowers of vices admit no criminal acts; nor image in Israel, because true contemplatives receive no pretences in their works. For “the Holy Spirit of discipline flees deceit and does not dwell in a body subject to sin.” This I have said concerning the spirit of freedom.

For there are other spirits of error, always resisting the Holy Spirit; as enemies of freedom, they subject a human being to wretched slavery. The first is the spirit of this world, which enslaves to vanity; the second, the spirit of the flesh, which draws into slavery to pleasure; the third is the spirit of the adversary, which makes one a slave of iniquity. How many there are in the world who follow the spirit of the world with a mind inclined downward, considering themselves free if they spend their days in the vanities of this life, not [Col. 0207C] recalling that sorrow overtakes the end of joy and that the final end of such persons goes to destruction. They dress in silks, build palaces, furnish banquets, distribute gifts. And why do they do these things? “That they may make for themselves a name, according to the name of the great men who are on the earth” (Prov. 14). I mean an empty name: a vapour appearing for a little while, failing smoke, passing mist. Where now are those famous men of old, mighty in strength, who followed this spirit of vanity? Their memory has perished; and if any trace perhaps still remains, it has been left not in blessing but in curse.

Of such persons it is rightly said through the Prophet: “They wandered in the wilderness, in a waterless place; they found not the way of a city for habitation” [Col. 0207D] (Ps. 106). They wandered in the wilderness because they were alone—that is, abandoned by God; in a waterless place, that is, in dryness, in a heart not watered by the dew of the Holy Spirit. Hence they did not find the way of a city for habitation. They did indeed find the way of the city of a tent—that is, the way of this world, which is unstable and transitory, just as in former times the tent was moved from place to place—but they did not find the way of the city for habitation: the way of everlasting dwelling, of which the Apostle says, “Here we have no abiding city” (Heb. 13). Would that they had been content with this spirit of vanity and had not followed the spirit of the flesh, which distracts them through unlawful desires of the flesh, through pleasure. For of them it is said through Ezekiel: “Where the impulse of the spirit was, there they went” [Col. 0208A] (Ezek. 1). Certainly the impulse of the beast is the spirit of the flesh, which leads wretched man away, in the desires of his soul, to every unlawful and shameful thing.

But from where, senseless man, root of sin, comes this foolish wisdom of yours: that, putting aside the guidance proper to a rational being, you imitate a beast? Who would not be astonished? Who would not be afraid? Imagine a man exiled from his homeland and ignorant of the road: would he not seem to you misguided if, abandoning the path indicated to him by a wise man, he followed the trackless ways of cattle and wild beasts? Trackless indeed, because, abandoning the way of truth, they lead to the trackless regions of eternal damnation. Hence it is written in the book of Maccabees concerning the beast which, pierced by Eleazar son of Mattathias, fell dead: that by its fall it hurled down with itself the tower and the armed men whom it carried [Col. 0208B] (1 Macc. 6). So too, when the spirit of the flesh is overtaken by death, it plunges into the depths of hell those lying in wait for it—that is, all fleshly persons who follow the impulse of their own flesh.

Moreover, these two spirits take with them a third, namely the devil’s spirit, more wicked than themselves; and, entering, they dwell there. Then the last state of that person becomes worse than the first. Worse in what respect? The adversary lies in wait in order, at the end, to seize a sinner rendered either hardened by despair or secure through presumption. Understanding their condemnation, the prophet said in the Spirit: “Because of iniquity I saw the tents of Ethiopia; the skins of the land of Midian shall be troubled.” “I saw,” he says—that is, I understood in the Spirit—“the tents of Ethiopia” (Hab. 3), that is, the hearts of the wicked, which are receptacles of demons. [Col. 0208C] For Ethiopians signify demons. “And what more did you see, most holy of prophets? Because of iniquity the skins of the land of Midian shall be troubled.” What are these skins, and what is the land of Midian? Midian means “judgment.” Therefore the land of Midian is every earthly person assigned, in judgment, to eternal damnation; the skins, stripped from dead animals, are dead works without the power of charity. Thus, because of iniquity, the skins of the land of Midian—that is, the works of the wicked, who have already received through judgment the sentence of eternal damnation—shall be troubled, that is, punished.

For this—presuming upon mercy or despairing of pardon—is a sin written with an iron stylus and an adamantine nail [Col. 0208D], which is forgiven neither here nor hereafter, save in the sound of a vehement spirit—that is, of the *woe* which takes away—who alone enlightens the sinner’s heart unto repentance. For he breathes where he wills, and calls back from the midst of Babylon one serving sins to the freedom of grace. Let us therefore return to our heart, most beloved brothers; let us seek this Spirit while he may be found, let us call upon him while he is near. Let us seek him through the humility of repentance and confession; let us call upon him through the persistence of devout prayer. For behold, he is near. Already the Spirit of the Lord fills the whole world; today he fills the hearts of the faithful. Let us beseech this Spirit of truth, that he who fills the world by his presence may visit our hearts through indwelling grace, until we know by sight in the future him whom we now see by faith [Col. 0209A], our Lord Jesus Christ, whose kingdom and dominion remain for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXXVI. ON THE FEAST OF PENTECOST

“Arise, north wind, and come, south wind; blow through my garden, and its spices shall flow” (Song 4). Among the other songs of love, this seems especially suited to today’s feast, in which the bride, wearied by longing for her beloved, no longer seeks, as at the beginning, that he may kiss her with the kiss of his mouth, but asks that his absence not produce a separation. She asks for the spirit of his mouth as a pledge of love. Do you think the spirit of his mouth a small pledge? Give gold, give silver, give whatever satisfies human desire: it is little. One thing suffices for the lover while the bridegroom comes: the spirit of his mouth [Col. 0209B].

But what does it mean that she rises against the north wind with so harsh a rebuke, saying, “Arise, north wind!”—as though she said: “Depart; I flee your company, detest your presence, fear your harshness; I have laboured in enduring you”? I think it troubled her in some way, since she strives so forcefully to repel it from herself. And why should it not have troubled her? For just as the Holy Spirit is understood under the name of the south wind, so, if we attend to its properties, the evil spirit is understood under the name of the north wind. For the north wind is cold, violent, and dry. In its coldness is understood the frost of unbelief; in its violence, the heat of persecution; in its dryness, the lack of spiritual grace.

For what other wind was that of which we read in blessed Job: “A wind rushed in from the desert region and shook [Col. 0209C] the four corners of the house, and crushed Job’s children, and they died” (Job 1)? Certainly the four corners of the house—that is, of the Church—by which the Church is strengthened against spiritual wickedness, are the Incarnation of the Word, the Passion, the Resurrection, and the Ascension. These corners fell through the impiety of unbelief, when the north wind blew—that is, when the devil suggested error—when Job’s children, that is, those whom God had adopted as sons, did not receive faith in the incarnate Word. Therefore they were suffocated beneath the ruin: dying in their unbelief, they carried with them nothing except their sins.

Do you wish to see the violence of the whirlwind? “And I saw,” Ezekiel says, “and behold, a whirlwind came from the north” (Ezek. 1). When? When some endured mockeries and scourgings; others were stretched on the rack [Col. 0209D]; others given to fires; others died by the slaughter of the sword. Concerning the dryness of the north wind Solomon says: “The north wind scatters the clouds” (Prov. 21). And what are these clouds if not the spiritual understanding of the Law and the Prophets? These clouds were certainly scattered by the north wind when, as Scripture says, “those who held the Law did not know” (Jer. 2); entirely emptying the things foretold according to the Spirit concerning Christ, they remained dry and empty of all the spiritual richness contained in the Law.

Your charity has understood how the north wind stood opposed to the Church while it was still unbelieving. But afterwards, instructed by the apostles’ preaching, stirred by miracles, raised up by promise, it cries to the Lord in the face of tribulation; and [Col. 0210A] now, judging itself to know nothing except “the Lord Jesus, and him crucified” (1 Cor. 2), whom it cannot have present bodily, it wishes to have present spiritually, when it says: “Come, south wind.” Under the name of the south wind, if its properties are considered, the Holy Spirit is rightly understood. For it is a moist, gentle, and warm wind. These three things nourish every fruit of the earth: all things are brought forth by warmth and moisture, and preserved by gentleness or temperateness. For moisture gives nourishment, warmth gives growth, and temperateness gives stability.

By these three properties the threefold gift of the Holy Spirit is received. The first, cleansing, is signified by warmth; the second, inflaming, is signified by moisture; the third, peace-making, is signified by gentleness [Col. 0210B] or temperateness. The first washes away sins; the second draws the soul upward by holy desires; the third arranges the human heart in peace through tranquillity of mind. To speak of the first gift of grace, called cleansing: it was given to some in the shedding of their own blood, to others in the font of baptism, and to others in contrition of heart alone.

In the primitive Church it was given to apostles and martyrs through the shedding of their own blood; and whatever stain the frailty of human nature had introduced, the outpouring of their holy blood entirely wiped away and cleansed. This gift was bestowed in the font of baptism upon the children of apostles and martyrs, who, reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, obtained remission of sins and kept the garment of innocence unstained through holy conduct. But to us, who after baptismal regeneration have suffered relapse, this gift of grace is given in contrition of heart. For the palm of martyrdom does not belong to our time, nor is the remedy of the sacrament repeated. One remedy therefore remains for us: repentance and compunction [Col. 0210C].

The second gift of the Holy Spirit, which we have called inflaming, is likewise divided into three kinds. In some, the Holy Spirit is flame; in others, light; in others, a spark. Therefore Ezekiel says: “In the midst of the four living creatures there was fire, and lightning issuing from the fire, and sparks like the appearance of glowing bronze” (Ezek. 1). By fire is understood flame, naturally tending upward; by lightning [Col. 0210D], light spreading abroad; by sparks, certain fiery embers which are carried upward by a slight impulse but, quickly failing in themselves, fall back again to the depths.

To those, therefore, who received the first-fruits of the Spirit, he was given as a flame, because, raised upward by desire for heavenly rewards, they tended wholly toward the crown. Later, to the teachers of the Church, the Spirit was as light, while by the word of teaching and seed of faith they spread abroad, so greatly that through the four regions of the world they begot new children for God. But in our time the Spirit is compared to a little spark, because, although there are those who at times look toward God with good disposition of heart, yet, not maintaining an unbroken fervour throughout the year, they quickly grow lukewarm in their purpose.

Likewise, the third gift of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0211A], called peace-making, is given to some for the peace of reconciliation, to others for the peace of mutual love, and to others for the peace of eternal blessedness. It was given to the apostles for the peace of reconciliation, of whom it is sung: “For they were bearing peace.” For God was in them, reconciling the world to himself. It is given to all for the peace of mutual love, to whom it is granted to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. Hence it is said: “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give you” (John 14). But only to the elect will it be given in the future for the peace of eternal blessedness.

We now possess those gifts which the Church received from her Bridegroom as a dowry. What remains? That the person who calls himself a child of the Church should test himself, whether he has received by hereditary right those very gifts with which the Church was endowed on the day of her betrothal [Col. 0211B]: namely, whether through the cleansing gift he weeps for what he has committed; whether through the inflaming gift he desires what he has lost; whether through the peace-making gift he brings into peace and harmony what is at discord within himself.

But how shall we prove that we possess these gifts? We must look to the works themselves. For works themselves are, as it were, windows of the Holy Spirit, through which he breaks forth outside and is known to be present in a person. And, as it seems to me, this visible light has some likeness to spiritual light—that is, to the grace of the Holy Spirit. When this light which we see strikes this house of prayer, or any other, with its rays, you clearly see that it makes a way for itself not only outside but within: it enters through doors, penetrates windows, passes through openings, and [Col. 0211C] wherever it finds an entrance pours in the brightness of its light.

In the same way, most beloved brothers, there are in us certain windows of the Holy Spirit through which his light goes forth: namely, good works—hands, feet, eyes, and tongue—which we ought always to keep consecrated to God’s service, so that the tongue may speak for exhortation, the hand work for edification, the eyes see with circumspection, and the feet walk for usefulness. What else, finally, are these outward signs in religious persons but certain windows of the Holy Spirit? Such as the spreading of hands, bending of knees, beating of the breast, and bowing of the head. The spreading of hands signifies desire for heavenly grace; bending of knees is a sign of reverence; beating of the breast, of repentance; bowing of the head [Col. 0211D], of obedience.

Yet we see many receive gifts of the Holy Spirit which, because they do not refer them to their due end, make them worse through the very occasion of grace by which they ought to have become good. The Prophet also indicates this to us when he says: “Your way was in the sea, and your paths in many waters, and your footprints shall not be known” (Ps. 76). By the sea, which is salt and bitter, are signified those sins which bring bitterness with them: anger, quarrels, dissensions, envies, strife, rivalries. By the other waters, which are sweet, are signified the other passions of the soul that seem to bring delight with them: fornication, uncleanness, lust, revelry, drunkenness, and other such things. In this sea [Col. 0212A] and in these waters there is sometimes a way or path of God through the bestowal of gifts; but his footprints are not known, because through those very gifts God is not glorified as he ought to be.

Who doubts that skill in the Scriptures, eloquence of speech, distinct reading, and accurate singing are gifts of the Holy Spirit? And yet many with these gifts are indecent in speech, wanton in look, lax in conduct, and disorderly in dress and manner of life. What good then do these things do? Indeed, they do more harm. This may also be inferred from Ezekiel’s words, who says that he saw a book in which were written lamentations, song, and woe: “He spread out the book before me,” he says, “which was written inside and outside; and in it were written lamentations, song, and woe.” Certainly lamentations pertain to pardon, song to glory, woe to Gehenna.

Thus the Scriptures are lamentations to those who, in them—whether reading, singing, or praying—find their sins as matter for grieving. They are song to those who, with the testimony of good works, conceive hope of future glory through the promises of Scripture. But to those who, while receiving the grace of reading or singing, pursue vanity and thereby become futile in their thoughts, they are woe [Col. 0212B]. Do you therefore wish to sing psalms well? You must join the psalter to the psalm. What the psalm sounds in the mouth, the psalter resounds in the heart.

I do not now mean the ten-stringed psalter on which psalms were formerly sung in the Old Testament, but another seven-stringed psalter: the [Col. 0212C] spiritual psalter on which psalms are sung in the New Testament, namely the Spirit of sevenfold grace. The Holy Spirit himself, therefore, is the psalter; his seven strings are the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit: the spirit of fear of the Lord, the spirit of piety, the spirit of knowledge, the spirit of fortitude, the spirit of counsel, the spirit of understanding, and the spirit of wisdom. The first gift pertains to humility; the second, to meekness; the third, to contrition of heart; the fourth, to desire for righteousness; the fifth, to an affection of mercy; the sixth, to purity of heart; the seventh, to the repose of contemplation.

Thus the first string gives a low note, the second a sweet one, the third a mournful one, the fourth a resonant one, the fifth a harmonious one, the sixth a high one, and the seventh an exceedingly high one. Touch [Col. 0212D], then, the first string of the psalter, and you will sing humbly; the second, and you will sing sweetly; the third, and you will sing prudently; the fourth, and you will sing courageously; the fifth, and you will sing harmoniously; the sixth, and you will sing sincerely; touch the seventh, and thus you will sing wisely.

Psalm and psalter, words and mind, must therefore agree. For if we honour only with words—for we honour also by virtues and deeds—I fear perhaps it may be said to us: “The voice indeed is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau” (Gen. 27); as though he said: “The words which you utter are indeed God’s words, but the works are works of the flesh.” For the hand pertains to action. Of the hand it is said: “Esau’s hands are hairy.” The hairs are evil thoughts [Col. 0213A] and unlawful desires. Esau’s hands are not reproved because hairs grew upon them, but because they were not cut off. For they were hairy—that is, full of hairs. We can prevent evil thoughts from prevailing in us, but we cannot prevent them from arising. Hence the Levites are commanded (Num. 8) to shave, not pluck out, the hairs of their flesh.

How then must one fight against unlawful desires? Certainly a good fighter in the field, while his adversary aims darts at him, puts out his hand to turn aside the wound from his heart. In the same way, every person led by God’s Spirit, lest he receive the enemy’s darts into his heart, must put out his hand—that is, undertake the exercise of good work. Let him go around the altars not only with his feet but with devotion; let him strike God’s ears with prayers; let him call upon the aid of the saints; let him show kind service to his brothers [Col. 0213B], ready service to his superiors, and pious service to God. With such work let him confidently call upon the Holy Spirit, the cultivator of his garden, saying: “Come, south wind, blow through my garden.”

What is this garden? The Church’s garden is the congregation of the faithful; individual gardens are the hidden places of hearts. Therefore let the Church say, let every faithful soul say: “Blow through my garden.” First breathe in through inspiration; breathe out through holy conduct; blow through completely by the perfection of virtues. Blow through, I say, “and the spices of the garden shall flow.”

And what are the garden’s spices, which the Holy Spirit cultivates? Let us ask the Apostle Paul: “But the fruit of the Spirit,” he says, “is joy, charity, peace, patience, long-suffering, kindness, goodness, faith, modesty, continence, chastity” (Gal. 5) [Col. 0213C]. How do the spices flow in those in whom is the fruit of the Spirit? Joy in the Holy Spirit makes one cheerful; charity, fervent; peace, tranquil; patience, proved; long-suffering, persevering; kindness, gracious; goodness, holy; faith, secure; modesty, disciplined; continence, pure; chastity, modest.

This, most beloved brothers, is a certain foretaste of the Spirit, given in the present life for consolation; in the future, when Christ our life appears, it shall be given for satisfaction. For as Solomon says in Proverbs: “The man is not in his house, but has gone on a very long journey; he took with him a bag of money; he will return on the day of the full moon” (Prov. 7). The man is Christ [Col. 0213D]; he is not in his house—that is, in the Church—by bodily presence, but went on a very long journey when he ascended into heaven. He took with him a bag of money, because in him are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, which he will bring back with him on the day of the full moon—that is, on the day of judgment, that is, at the consummation of the Church—when he will return, so that he who in the present bestowed grace upon his bride may in the future lavish glory upon her. May Jesus Christ, God and Son of God, deign to grant this to us, whose kingdom and dominion remain for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXXVII. ON THE FEAST OF PENTECOST

“The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world, and that which contains all things has knowledge of speech” (Wis. 1) [Col. 0214A]. As John the Evangelist teaches us: “By this we know that we abide in Christ, because we have received of his Spirit.” And would that I might have a share in this saying: that, abiding in Christ, I may have received of the Spirit—especially as I am about to speak of the Holy Spirit, since no one speaking except in the Spirit of God can be found a worthy praiser of him. May that same Spirit therefore touch my heart with the sweetness of his presence; indeed, may my soul be filled as with fatness and richness, and may spiritual anointing teach all things suitable both to so great a feast and to the benefit of our devotion.

This anointing of the Spirit has indeed been promised in many ways: by an individual, a special, and a general promise. The individual promise was made to Christ, who uniquely received the Holy Spirit, where it is said: “The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. 11). The special promise was made to the apostles, who received the first-fruits of the Spirit, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles, where it was said of them: “You shall receive the power of the Holy Spirit coming upon you, and you shall be my witnesses in Judaea and Jerusalem and unto the uttermost part of the earth” (Acts 1) [Col. 0214B]. The general promise was made to all who would believe in Christ, where it is said: “I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and daughters shall prophesy” (Joel 2). In these degrees of promise the order of bestowal was foreshadowed, because the Holy Spirit was to descend from Christ upon the apostles and through them upon all the children of the Church.

The chapter which we have set before you contains a general promise of the Spirit—and not only a general but an utterly universal promise—so that by “the whole world” may be understood either the whole body of churches or the whole created order. According to the general promise, therefore, “the whole world” must be understood as the whole body of churches, and its filling as the abundance of spiritual charisms bestowed in the time of grace upon the children of the Church. This filling is wrought in the Church by a threefold spirit, though it is one in itself: the spirit of compunction, the spirit of compassion, and the spirit of adoption.

The soil of sinners, untilled and producing thorns and briars, is filled with the spirit of compunction; the soil of the miserable, dry and thin, is filled with the spirit of compassion; the soil of the perfect, rich and fruitful, is filled with the spirit of adoption [Col. 0214D]. To the spirit of compunction belong sighs and groans, bodily affliction, abundance of tears, labours of repentance, and those mournings for which blessedness and consolation are promised, where it is said: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5). To the spirit of compassion belongs assisting the anxieties of the sick, the calamities of the oppressed, and the needs of the poor, as well as all works of mercy which the merciful render to the wretched, through which they themselves will obtain mercy.

But the spirit of adoption belongs to the perfect, and especially makes them children of God, as the Apostle says: “You have not received again the spirit of slavery in fear, but the spirit of adoption as sons”—that is, through which you were adopted as sons and received the pledge of eternal inheritance. This Spirit has its own works: rejoicing in spiritual joy, being fervent in spirit, praying devoutly, applying oneself watchfully to reading, searching out heavenly things through holy meditation, and other acts of this sort. By these the soul is so sweetened that the world, with its pleasures, becomes worthless to it.

If we wish to compare spiritual things with bodily things, we shall say that the spirit of compunction is a surgical instrument; the spirit of compassion, an ointment; the spirit of adoption, an electuary. The spirit of compunction is compared to an instrument because, as medicinal iron pricks and cuts away bodily disease, so the spirit of compunction pricks the soul’s disease through sorrow and in some way expels it through humble confession [Col. 0215B]. The spirit of compassion is compared to ointment because, as ointment is applied outwardly to lessen bodily pains, so works of mercy are outwardly applied to relieve the needs of the wretched. The spirit of adoption is rightly called an electuary, compounded of aromatic spices, sweet to the palate, and preserving health, because it has an abundance beyond the other spiritual graces by which the soul is sweetened and receives the vigour of inward health, as Paul says: “But the fruit of the Spirit is charity, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, goodness, meekness, faith, modesty, continence, chastity” (Gal. 5) [Col. 0215C].

And because one Spirit works this manifold fullness in the churches of God, it was said: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world.” That is, the whole body of churches. Understand the word “has filled” as a past tense used for the future, because of the certainty of the promise’s fulfilment, as elsewhere we read: “All things whatsoever I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 5); and a similar usage is found in many other places.

Observe that from the beginning the Spirit filled not the whole world but certain corners of it. By the corners of the world I mean righteous men: the patriarchs and others who lived in ancient ages, few in number and obscure in comparison with the multitude of evildoers among whom they lived. Since the Spirit of God dwelt in them but did not show himself outwardly either by prophetic speech or miraculous signs, content with the boundaries of inward conscience, he filled them as though they were certain corners. Therefore in ancient times the Holy Spirit was in some sense sparing—not to say miserly—because then he stored up and gathered riches for us, so that in the time of grace he might distribute them and the fountain of divine goodness might flow forth more abundantly through grace, and the anointing of spiritual charisms might descend in all fullness upon the children of the Church.

For how could it fail to descend? It was placed on the summit of a mountain, and around its base were plains and valleys. Fire approached, and the ointment melted [Col. 0216A] and thus ran down [Latin: *decucurrit*; variant reading: *decurrit*] to all the borders of the mind. The mountain, indeed, was Christ: that mountain “curdled and fat,” in which mercy and truth met one another, righteousness and peace kissed one another; in which the anointing of spiritual charisms was placed in all fullness. When the fire of the Holy Spirit approached, this ointment descended from the mountain’s summit to the plains, because through the working of the Holy Spirit the grace of the Holy Spirit was poured out from Christ upon all the children of the Church.

This, finally, is the ointment of anointing by which the tabernacle and all its vessels were anointed (Exod. 30); this is the ointment which descended from Aaron’s head to his beard, and from there to the hem of his garment (Ps. 132). It rightly descended from the beard to the hem of the garment, because the ointment belonged not to the beard but to the head. The head, moreover, was head not only of the beard but of all the members; therefore the ointment rightly had to flow from the head to the beard and from the beard to the other members.

You see, I think, how the Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world with the abundance of spiritual gifts. Whether he is called the Spirit of the Lord—that is, of God the Father—or of the Lord—that is, of Christ—the truth is one. If the foregoing words contain a most general promise, then by “the whole world” the totality of creatures is to be understood; and this totality must be distinguished, so that we say that there is the earth of the worldly creation, the earth of the present Church, and the earth of the heavenly homeland. Of the first it is said: “In the beginning [Col. 0216C] God created heaven and earth,” etc. (Gen. I). Of the second it is said: “You visited the earth and made it drunk; you multiplied to enrich it” (Ps. LXIV). And in Job: “He stretches out the north over the void and hangs the earth upon nothing” (Job XXVI). For to hang the earth upon nothing is to extend the Church over the nations, which are called nothing in Isaiah, where it is said: “All nations are as though they were not before God, and are reckoned as nothing and emptiness” (Isa. XL). Of the earth of the heavenly homeland it is written in the Psalm: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. XXVI). If you wish to know how this totality of lands has been filled, consider the works of God: for there are works of creation, works of restoration, and works of reparation. The works [Col. 0216D] of creation are heaven and earth and whatever is contained in them; the works of restoration are those by which a human being is re-formed unto holiness of life, and these include Christ’s incarnation, passion, resurrection, and all the inward works which the elect perform from the time of Christ’s incarnation until the end of the age; the works of reparation are those which renew the whole human being in the life to come, and these include the glorification of the body, the delight of the mind, and the blessedness of joys which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the human heart. The difference between works of restoration and works of reparation is this: the former make what had been lost no longer lost; the latter make what has been restored blessed. Therefore the Spirit of the Lord filled the earth of the worldly [Col. 0217A] creation through works of creation, the earth of the present Church through works of restoration, and the earth of the heavenly homeland through works of reparation. Do not wonder that we attribute the works of creation to the Holy Spirit, since they seem rather to be ascribed to the Father, according to Augustine, who says: “If you ask through whom? through the Word; if you ask why? because he is good”—as though he meant, on account of the Holy Spirit; and thus that same Spirit seems not to be the author but the cause of creatures. Yet without doubt it is true that, just as Father and Son and Holy Spirit are one in substance, so they have nothing divided in operation. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “My Father works until now, and I work” (John V). And in the Church it is sung: “May all your creatures praise you, may they glorify you, O blessed Trinity.” Rightly, therefore, is it said that the Spirit of the Lord filled the whole world, and that which contains all things has knowledge of speech. By this a general, not a personal, reference is made—that is, to many, not to one—as in Ecclesiastes, where it is said: “Fear God and keep his commandments: this is every human being” (Eccl. XII). There the reference is made to every person, not to one alone, as if Solomon said: “Do not ask to whom I speak when I say, ‘Fear God and keep his commandments.’ For I do not speak to one, but to all.” This must be understood in the same way: namely, the universal Church, which contains all things—that is, every fullness of the Spirit—has knowledge of speech. Of what speech? There are three things here: sound, voice, and word. Sound is [Col. 0217C] that noise which is made without the instrument of the tongue and the aid of the mouth, as the collision of stones or something of that sort. Voice, however, is sound formed by the instrument of tongue and mouth. A word, indeed, is the meaning of a voice, conceived in the rational mind in its utterance. From the beginning of the world to Moses there was sound; from Moses to Christ, voice sounded; from Christ’s incarnation until the end of the age, the word sounds. Do you wish to know how, under the law of nature, there was sound without the aid of tongue and mouth? The tongue of God is the Holy Spirit, of whom it is said: “My tongue is the pen of a scribe writing swiftly” (Ps. XLIV). The mouth is the wisdom of God, that is, Christ, of whom it is said: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song I). And in the prophets one often reads that the mouth of the Lord has spoken. [Col. 0217D] Therefore, because the speech used by people before the law contained no wisdom of God and nothing of spiritual grace, they made only sound without the aid of tongue and mouth, as it were amid the tumult of the age. Under the written law, voice sounded; and this was the law and the prophets, which were issued as if with the aid of mouth and tongue—that is, with the wisdom of God dictating and the Holy Spirit teaching. But to those who received the law, voice alone sounded, because they did not receive the mysteries of the law and its spiritual understanding. This is what was signified when Uriah the Hittite carried with him the sealed letter of his own death: the Jewish people received sacred Scripture, closed to them in its spiritual understanding, to the increase of their condemnation (II Kings II). This was signified by the veil [Col. 0218A] over Moses’ face while he spoke to the children of Israel (Exod. XXXIV); indeed, even today a veil is placed over their hearts, while that elder son, standing outside, hears the symphony and the chorus—that is, the spiritual joy of the Church promised in the Scriptures—and, not understanding it, refuses to enter.

In the time of grace the word sounds, because the mysteries of the law and the prophets have been opened to the children of the Church, so that they understand them now not carnally but spiritually. This, then, is what is said: “That which contains all things has knowledge of speech.” This is the word of the voice—that is, the spiritual understanding of the law and prophets, and of the sacraments of Christ and the Church, revealed in the Scriptures through the Holy Spirit. Or, when it is said, “That which contains all things,” the reference [Col. 0218B] is to the human heart, which contains all things in this respect. First, it contains the Holy Spirit, who enters it invisibly; it contains the angelic nature through likeness of creation, because in its creation it received reason and understanding, knowledge and love of God. It also contains every bodily creature through knowledge of causes, because it investigates and understands the causes of all things. Accordingly, we may call the human heart, which contains the Holy Spirit, a container. The human heart is therefore like a vessel of God’s grace; and a vessel that is to contain so great a treasure must necessarily be pure and polished.

Let each person therefore look to his own vessel, whether it is sincere, and whether it has been made for honor or for dishonor. Of vessels of this kind, one is pure and polished; another pure but not polished; another polished but not pure; another neither polished nor pure. The one who is inwardly clean in mind and outwardly honorable in religious conduct has a vessel pure and polished, so that divine grace in some way shines in him, and on seeing him you can say that God dwells in him. The one who is well formed in virtues of mind, but outwardly conducts himself among people in a somewhat worldly manner in food, dress, and worldly business, has a vessel pure but not polished. The false religious person has a vessel polished but not pure: empty of virtue of mind, he bears in his body a feigned appearance of religion—humility in gesture, kindness in speech, [Col. 0218D] simplicity in countenance—and, while lying, appears religious only so long as he cannot, upon finding an opportunity, be truly wicked. For pour out his vessel and you will find envies, detractions, deceitful schemes, refined malices, besides what lies hidden within; and you will find him so alien from spiritual love that he cannot even love those who love him. The person deformed inwardly by vices and outwardly by scandals has a vessel neither polished nor pure, and he is manifestly wicked.

Therefore the human heart which contains all things has knowledge of speech. Observe that from the beginning God taught creatures two voices: one vocal, the other real. The vocal voice was that which all human beings used from [Col. 0219A] the beginning until the division of languages. The real voice was the dignity of creatures’ created condition, through which God was shown to be praiseworthy. Every creature had in its created condition something by which God could truly be praised. Hence it is written: “Heaven and earth and sea praise him, and all creeping things in them.” Knowledge of this real voice was given to humankind alone as a pattern for living: so that, understanding how the other creatures spoke God by preserving the dignity of their created condition, humans too, persevering in their own dignity, might proclaim God with a real voice. But behold what a remarkable thing—indeed, a pitiable thing—has happened: while the other creatures speak God by preserving their natural condition, in humankind alone the speech of the whole creation has been confused, so that there is no gift of nature in a person able to say to God, “You made me thus.” Look at criminal people, in whom iniquity confuses everything in a monstrous tumult. Do they not seem to have fallen into a kind of confusion of languages when, as spiritual vices rage against carnal ones and carnal vices against spiritual ones, they cannot recognize the image of God utterly deformed, nor even the purpose for which they were made? O how great a stupefaction—indeed, how great a shame, how great a crime—it is to deform the image of God, that is, a Christian soul, so that its appearance would not become even an actor’s, though it ought to display the form of the supreme King. Who, finally, prostituted the supreme King’s daughter, worthy of royal marriage, and went unpunished? The Christian soul is the daughter of the supreme [Col. 0219C] King, because she too calls him Father when she says: “Our Father who are in heaven” (Matt. VI). A wicked person, sold under sin, truly prostitutes her to every unclean spirit: one is defiled by lust, another by pride, another by avarice; and at last she is plunged into such an abyss of vices that even respectable vices disdain to rule her, while she is subject to horrid and shameful crimes whose very naming would insult the hearers. Therefore you, human being, who have been so deformed through fault and have been silenced from that voice by which every creature praises God, break silence, learn to speak, and recover the use of the voice whose knowledge you retained. Let insensible creatures and brute animals teach you to speak; abiding in the state of their created condition, they praise God. And if this teaching is too little, let the Holy Spirit teach you, who through the infusion of grace is the author of our regeneration. Prepare your heart for newness of life, so that, having received the grace of the Holy Spirit and with the natural goods restored in you, you may praise God with the other creatures in the present life; so that, when the course of this present life has been run, through the working of the same Spirit you may glorify God with all the saints in the life to come, through our Lord Jesus Christ, whose kingdom and dominion remain for ages of ages. Amen.

SERMON XXXVIII. ON THE DEDICATION OF A CHURCH.

“My house shall be called a house of prayer” (Matt. XXI). Beloved brothers, I have decided to set before you a brief word, because hasty obedience and [Col. 0220A] the shortness of time did not allow me to prepare more carefully what I should say, since the exhortation for today has been entrusted to a torrent-like tongue and a fruitful breast. From whose fullness we all hope to receive.

Yet lest it seem an injury to so great a solemnity—or rather to your charity—if, according to the custom of the day, the word of God does not proceed, I shall say something and, in the tabernacle of God, offer not what I wish but what I can, taking confidence in speaking from this: that God does not despise even the smallest gift offered with the affection of good will.

And, to take the beginning of my discourse from the solemnities of the present day, the feast of the Dedication seems to have something more eminent than the others. In them it is enough to celebrate a feast day when the sanctuary is adorned by the worship of the altar, the array of ministers, and divine praises resounding to heaven. But in this feast the whole surface of the temple, illuminated with light, is presented to us as more joyful, and therefore today the joys of the universal Church seem to be represented to us. For in it the sinful soul has cause for joy, since a city of refuge is established for it against the savagery of pursuing enemies. The soul advancing and justified has cause for joy, since a tower of strength is built for it as a defensive help against various temptations. The perfect soul has cause for joy, since a house of prayer is dedicated to it for the inner chamber of contemplation. Whether you call the Church a city, a tower, or a house of prayer, you will not be wrong, provided that the reason for these terms is inferred [Col. 0220C] from the likeness of things. The Church is called a city on the testimony of the prophet, where he says: “Mount Zion is founded in the exultation of the whole earth, the sides of the north, and the city of the great King” (Ps. XLVII). And elsewhere: “They shall return at evening and suffer hunger; like dogs they shall go round the city” (Ps. LVIII). Therefore in the old law the Church was fittingly signified by three cities of refuge. I say three, in the plural, because the Church is both one and many: hence it is said in the Song: “You are one, my dove, my beautiful one” (Song II); and elsewhere: “In the churches bless God the Lord, from the fountains of Israel” (Ps. LXVII). It is one through the union of charity, and many because of the different congregations of the faithful.

[Col. 0220D] We may also say that the Church is signified by the three cities of refuge because of the three remedies conferred in it upon sinners: namely, regeneration, confession, and conversion of life. These three remedies were instituted against a threefold woe: original woe, actual woe, and penal woe. The remedy of regeneration was instituted against original woe, so that the fault of birth, through which all by nature become children of wrath, may not harm those who have put on Christ through the sacrament of baptism. The remedy of confession was instituted against actual woe; in it actual sins are forgiven and former merits restored, lest the stain of crime remain after the humility of tearful confession has washed it away. The remedy of conversion of life was instituted against penal woe—namely, the woe of hellfire or purgatorial fire—so that those who, having abandoned worldly life, punish their sins in themselves by the labors of penance and exercises of good works, and leave nothing in themselves to be punished after departing this life, may direct their spirit without impediment to God who made it.

The Church is also called a tower in the Song, where it is compared with a tower built with battlements (Song IV). And elsewhere: “You who are in the towers, open the gates, for God is with us” (Judith XIII). It is compared with a tower for three reasons: because it is fortified, lofty, and strong. The Church is fortified not only because it is built upon a mountain, but because it is encircled by a river and a wall. It is built upon a mountain—upon a mountain made solid and fat, solid [Col. 0221B] by passion, fat by charity—of which Isaiah says: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob, and he will teach us his ways, and we shall walk in his paths” (Isa. I). This mountain is Christ, upon whom the Church is founded as upon a foundation; hence it is written: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (I Cor. III). The river surrounding the Church is the abundance of spiritual gifts, by which the faithful are watered according to the measure of Christ’s gift; of this river the Prophet says: “The rush of the river makes glad the city of God” (Ps. XLV). The wall surrounding this city is the strength of continence, by which holy men in the Church of God are fortified against [Col. 0221C] the desires of the flesh. The loftiness of the tower which we have called the Church is the height of ecclesiastical dignity; its strength is the rigor of ecclesiastical severity. Therefore you, advancing soul, who wish to be defended in this tower, preserve yourself in the Church of God in this way: humble yourself in obedience to those placed above you in dignity; submit yourself in patience to discipline for correcting your transgressions; and, fortified besides with virtues, maintain the innocence of life.

The Church is also a house of prayer for those who, leaving worldly tumult, desire to be occupied with God alone and, after cleansing their conscience from every defilement of flesh and spirit, sing psalms to God in their hearts not only with their voice but with holy devotion and the pious affection of their minds. For the Church is spiritually a house [Col. 0221D] of prayer for those who devote their tongue, affection, and effort to prayer; in the Gospel (John III) the Lord himself calls them true worshippers, who worship the Father in spirit and truth. The prophet David certainly sought such a manner of prayer when he said: “Let my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness, and my mouth shall praise with lips of exultation” (Ps. LXII). And elsewhere: “Let my prayer be directed as incense before you” (Ps. CXL). Why as incense? When incense is kindled, it gives forth smoke, flame, and scent; so also prayer pleasing to God gives forth now the smoke of contrition through remembrance of sins, now the flame of charity through love of heavenly things, now the odor of devotion through the good affection of the mind toward God. For what value has letter without spirit, [Col. 0222A] voice without sense, food without appetite, prayer without affection? If a comparison is made of spiritual things with bodily things, then, just as bodily food is the refreshment of the body, prayer too is the food of the soul. Certainly, if you take bodily food without appetite, you acquire for yourself more harm than nourishment, because what is excessively poured in will become either harmful or unpleasant. In the same way, prayer without affection, which ought to be food for the soul, does not refresh it, because prayer is fruitless when it is defiled by unclean thoughts and wounded by the spiritual wounds of hatred, envy, pride, and other such things, and lacks devotion. Therefore I now speak to you, O my wretched soul, who in the house of prayer—indeed, while praying—have thought so many shameful, so many curious, so many vain things: what will you answer your God when [Col. 0222B] he calls you to account because you performed his work deceitfully? What will you answer the pious souls whose sins you ought to have borne, whose good things you received in your life, so that you might turn away God’s indignation from them? What, finally, will you be able to answer the angelic spirits, whose presence you did not revere, whose assistance you despised, whose offices you neglected? For angelic spirits are accustomed to stand beside those who pray, not only to defend them from the assaults of the enemy, but also to present their prayers before God’s throne, as the Prophet says: “The princes went before, joined with those singing psalms amid maidens beating timbrels” (Ps. LXVII). These princes, who are angelic spirits, go before those singing psalms, now by helping, now by suggesting what they should ask; and this amid maidens beating timbrels—that is, amid Churches that mortify their flesh through the virtue of abstinence and many labors. And elsewhere the Prophet agrees to the same effect, saying: “The princes of Judah, their leaders; the princes of Zebulun, the princes of Naphtali” (Ps. LXVII). Angelic spirits, who are princes to others living justly and piously by ruling them and giving assistance, are also called leaders of those praying, because they are especially favorable in this to true petitioners [those truly praying]: they direct and convey together before God both their devotion and their prayers. Hence it is said that the princes of Judah are their leaders—that is, leaders of those confessing; the princes of Zebulun, that is, of those practicing continence; the princes of Naphtali, that is, of contemplatives, [Col. 0222D] are their leaders—that is, of those singing psalms. For Judah, interpreted “confessing,” signifies those confessing; Zebulun, interpreted “dwelling of strength,” signifies those practicing continence; Naphtali, interpreted “a released hind,” signifies contemplatives. Their princes, then, are leaders of devout people praying, directing them in things pleasing to God. I greatly fear that you will find the pious souls for whom you have not faithfully interceded to be your accusers before God, the angels witnesses, and God himself your judge, when you are convicted of having been so negligent and so undevout in divine services.

Come to your senses at last, therefore, O my soul, and whatever sinful soul you are that resembles me, so that in the divine offices you may diligently sing psalms with spirit and with mind; and, leaving [Col. 0223A] those things which fight against you, be subject to the Lord, and pray to him: pray, worship, obtain by prayer. Pray sincerely, worship faithfully, obtain by prayer perseveringly. If you are in the house of prayer, pray; if, through the demands of your merits, you are outside, knock at the doors of this house, and they will be opened to you. But as there are different dwellings in the house of prayer, so there are different kinds of doors. For the house of God, which is the Church, is distinguished by three dwellings. The first is of those entering, the second of those fighting, the third of those reigning. The doors of the first dwelling are the sacraments of the Church, through which all criminals are received into the bosom of the Church; of these doors it is said: “The Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the tabernacles of Jacob” (Ps. LXXXVI). The doors of the second dwelling are the teachings of truth, namely, the Gospel, [Col. 0223B] law, and prophets, through which the just are instructed in works of righteousness and in living piously in this age; of them it is said: “Open to me the gates of righteousness; having entered them, I shall confess to the Lord” (Ps. CXVII). The doors of the third dwelling are the virtues, namely charity, peace, goodness, and the others which endure here and in the future. These are the eternal gates of which it was said: “Lift up your gates, O princes; and be lifted up, O eternal gates, and the king of glory shall enter” (Ps. XXV). Those who have entered these gates into all the dwellings worship, but not in one manner. For in the first dwelling those praying lie prostrate at the Lord’s feet; in the second, worshipping as though raised up, they long for his hands; in the third, obtaining by prayer, they stand erect and look always upon his face.

[Col. 0223C] Those who worship prostrate in the first dwelling are newly converted persons, who, still conscious of their evils, subject to carnal desires, and surrounded by temptations, pour forth tearful prayers to the Lord for their sins. For those who still look upon the fresh scars of their crimes ought not presumptuously to ask God for angelic purity or for that blessed life which eye has not seen nor ear heard; rather, they ought to seek with tears forgiveness of sins, time for penance, and a shower of tears with which to wash their sins. The prophet David taught us this form of prayer when he said: “Wash me still more, Lord, from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin” (Ps. L). Likewise did that blessed sinful woman [Col. 0223D] who, falling prostrate upon her face, washed the Lord’s feet with tears and wiped them with her hair. In the second dwelling, however, the justified worshippers long for the Lord’s hands, asking him for the hand of defense and assistance. For while righteous people still fight in the present life and ask God for the strength of continence against desires of the flesh, and the virtue of patience against injuries inflicted on them, they direct themselves, as it were, toward God’s hands, through which they desire a benefit to be bestowed upon them; hence it is written: “You open your hand, and fill every living thing with blessing” (Ps. CXLIV). Those worshipping in the third dwelling, which is the triumphant Church, look always upon his face, ever cleaving to God in the affection of praise and exultation. They also plead for us by vow and desire, so that those whom they once had as companions in tribulations may sometime also have as co-heirs of the kingdom, through the bounty of our Lord Jesus Christ, whose kingdom and dominion remain for ages of ages. Amen.

SERMON XXXIX. ON THE DEDICATION OF A CHURCH.

“Zacchaeus, come down quickly, because today I must stay in your house” (Luke XIX). The solemnity of this day should be received with festive joy and, so to speak, joy of joys, because on other days, although the glory of any saint is worthily recalled according to his merit, yet in this feast the joys of the whole Church are represented to us.

For the very adornment of the material temple, which is outwardly set before our eyes, figures for us the sanctification of the spiritual temple, which is the Church—a Church consecrated to his name through the blood of redemption and placed in the midst of the earth as a certain refuge of salvation for the soul whom God has blessed. This is why the Church itself is called in the Scriptures now a house of refuge, now a tower, now a house of prayer. Is it not itself the house of refuge to which the guilty flee and are freed from the power of the tyrant, the prison of death, and the bonds of sins? This is the Church which in the old law (Deut. IV) was signified by those three cities of refuge, in which fleeing criminals remained until, at the death of the high priest or in the year of jubilee, they returned to their former possessions. These three cities of refuge indeed figured the Church because of the three remedies, namely regeneration, [Col. 0224C] confession, and conversion, conferred upon sinners in the Church against the threefold woe by which the world has fallen. The first of these, regeneration, was instituted against original woe; the second, confession, against actual woe; the third, conversion, against penal woe. In these cities, which are in the Church of God, the guilty who remain return at last to their former possessions, which are the innocence of the present life and the joys of the future, because here they will be restored to innocence through the death of the high priest, that is, Christ, and in the year of jubilee, which prefigures the glory of resurrection, to the happiness of blessedness. The Church is also called a tower for three reasons: height, strength, and beauty. The height of the Church pertains to the loftiness of dignity; its strength to the severity of authority; its beauty to the loveliness of virtue. Hence Solomon compares it to a tower built with battlements: “A thousand shields,” he says, “hang from it, all the armor of the strong” (Song IV). The battlements of this tower are perfect men and doctors of the Church, who, established on high as an example of good life, rule and defend the rest. The hanging shields are all the lower members, who guard themselves from the enemy’s attack with the shield of humility and patience. The Church is also called a house of prayer because of those who, whether from consciousness of sin or desire for reward, devote themselves to entreaties and prayers and do not depart from God’s temple by day or night. Of [Col. 0225A] this house it is written: “For the sparrow has found herself a house, and the turtledove a nest where she may place her young” (Ps. LXXXIII). Here the flight of the contemplative person is denoted by the sparrow, and the groans of the sinner by the turtledove.

This is the house in which Christ wishes to stay with Zacchaeus, saying: “Zacchaeus, come down quickly,” etc. But what is the tree from which Zacchaeus is commanded to descend before he receives Christ into his house? It is the sycamore, namely a foolish fig tree, luxuriant and bearing useless fruit in bark and leaves. It signifies the delight of this life, bearing very evil figs—figs, I say, of pleasure, bark of vanity, and leaves of frivolity. Those who have entangled themselves in the pleasures of this life, spending their days in good things and appointing for themselves this portion, to use delights and enjoy goods, know more fully the fruit of this tree. But, O Zacchaeus, who taught you to come down from this tree? Who taught you to flee from the wrath to come? Certainly he who justified you. For Zacchaeus is interpreted “just” or “justified.” Truly justified—and by a threefold justice: the justice of command, the justice of example, and the justice of counsel. The justice of command is to direct one’s ways according to God’s commandments; Zacchaeus did this, as he says of himself: “If I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore fourfold.” The justice of example is, beyond God’s commandments, to leave the testimony of a good work as an example of virtue to be imitated, as in: “Behold, I give half of my goods to the poor.” The justice [Col. 0225C] of counsel is, scorning transient things, to cling firmly to God through contemplation, as is written of Zacchaeus: “And he came down quickly and received him joyfully.” Certainly, in the foregoing words Christ speaks to us, who are signified through Zacchaeus, in Zacchaeus, commanding us to come down from the sycamore tree by the aforesaid steps of justice, lest any traces of pleasure, vanity, or frivolity remain in us, by which our house—that is, the Church—being defiled might offend the reverence due to the majesty that comes.

Therefore this house in which Christ wishes to remain must be prepared with a threefold furnishing: it must have a beautiful house, a rich table, and suitable servants. For the beauty of this house it is enough to state that every precious stone is placed in its construction: jasper, sapphire, chalcedony, emerald, sardonyx, sard, chrysolite, beryl, topaz, chrysoprase, hyacinth, and amethyst. Jasper, moderately green in color and placed first in the foundation of this house, signifies the imperfect members in the Church who, not yet attaining the highest path of virtues, flourish only with the simplicity of faith; of them it is written: “But my righteous one lives by faith” (Hab. II). Upon it is placed sapphire, which has an airy color marked by certain spots, signifying those who are often carried away by desire for heavenly things but are stained, as it were, by certain spots through earthly care and the business of this age. Chalcedony occupies the third place; it has a red but dark color, and if it is hollowed out, it displays with greatest brightness the color that it formerly had dark. It signifies those who are prepared to endure everything for Jesus’ name: obscure in a time of peace, but if the heat of persecution has pricked them, then patience and struggle make manifest what sort of persons lay hidden within. The fourth stone completes the foundation: the emerald, whose green is so intense that it affects the surrounding grasses and leaves with its greenness. It signifies the holy doctors of the Church, who, flourishing perfectly through the vigor of faith, affect others by the word of preaching and exhortation and turn them to the way of truth. The fifth, sardonyx, begins to raise the walls of this house. White in color and in some measure tending toward red, it figures holy men in the Church who, although white in innocence and purity of life, have nevertheless imposed on themselves for God’s sake a voluntary martyrdom—expressed by the red color—through vigils, fasts, and other tribulations. Upon it is placed sard, wholly red, signifying holy martyrs who, through many persecutions and injuries, finally offered themselves to God as a living sacrifice, drenched in their own blood. The seventh, chrysolite, is wholly golden; in gold the heavenly gift of wisdom is expressed. This stone signifies those who have divinely received this gift: John in the Apocalypse, Paul through revelation, and the prophets through inspiration, who set forth the mysteries of Christ and the Church. The eighth is beryl, of exceptional brightness with an admixture of blue color; it signifies cloistered and religious men [Col. 0226C] who, though pure in holy conduct, have withdrawn themselves from earthly occupations in order that they not be defiled by any contagion of the world, being occupied with God alone. Once the walls have been completed, the roof of the house begins. Topaz, mingled with airy and golden color, denotes those who are perfect in both lives and have passed from the active to the contemplative life. For the airy color, which is also heavenly, denotes contemplation. The golden color, because it approaches red, denotes the tribulations of the active life, as in this passage, and at times the splendor of miracles, as will be said below. The tenth, chrysoprase, is distinguished by green and golden color and has, according to the natural philosophers, a medicinal power. It signifies those who, in addition to the virtue of faith, have also received the working of miracles, such as those who merited to heal infirmities, raise the dead, and cast out demons. The eleventh is hyacinth, wholly of heavenly or airy color; it signifies men devoted to the highest contemplation, meditating only upon God and the things of God, wholly absorbed in the spirit, bodily on earth but in their way of life in heaven. The twelfth, amethyst, completes the roof and has a purple color. Purple is customarily the ornament of kings; therefore the apostles are fittingly denoted by amethyst, because by word and martyrdom, carrying Christ throughout the whole world, they made him known to the world in a singular manner above the rest. And this concerning the beauty of the house.

[Col. 0227A] The table of this house is Sacred Scripture, of which Solomon says: “When you sit at the table of a rich man, carefully consider what is set before you, so that you too may prepare similar things” (Ecclus. XXXI). This is the table of the ancient tabernacle, upon which twelve loaves of presentation were placed, by which the priests and their sons were refreshed (Lev. XXIV). Those twelve loaves were the apostles and the other apostolic men, who meditated day and night at the table of divine Scripture and ministered the word of life to the other children of the Church, feeding them with the bread of life and understanding and giving them to drink from the water of saving wisdom. Of this water and food the Prophet says elsewhere: “The river of God is filled with waters; you have prepared their food, for such is its preparation” (Ps. LXIV).

We may distinguish four dishes of this table [Col. 0227B]: namely, the historical sense, which instructs toward truth; the moral sense, which forms the will; the allegorical sense, which strengthens faith; and the anagogical sense, which draws upward through contemplation. Or, following the Apostle, we may distinguish the dishes of this table differently. “There are,” he says, “divisions of gifts. To one is given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, to another the interpretation of utterances, to another the revelation of mysteries, to another prophecy”—all of which dishes the one and same Spirit sets forth, distributing to each as he wills (I Cor. XIV).

We may also understand this table otherwise: namely, as the sacrament of the altar, of which it is written: “You set a table before me against those who afflict me” (Ps. XXII). And of which the Apostle says: “You cannot partake of [Col. 0227C] the table of Christ and the table of demons” (I Cor. X).

For one who attends carefully, four kinds of bread are set upon this table. The first is sacramental, of which the Apostle says: “The bread which we break, is it not a sharing in the body of the Lord?” (I Cor. X). The second is bodily bread, of which the Prophet says: “Let us put wood into his bread” (Jer. II). The third is spiritual: it is the Word of God itself, of which it is said: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John VI). The fourth is intellectual: it is the bond of ecclesiastical unity, of which it is said: “Believe, and you have eaten.” The first bread outwardly nourishes faith through its appearance; the second presents the truth of human nature; [Col. 0227D] the third works justification inwardly; the fourth sustains the union of ecclesiastical charity. Thus a careful investigator may also discover different kinds of wine.

Therefore, once the house and table have been prepared, it remains to arrange that the ministers of this table be fit to render service while Christ reclines at it. Truly, those who stand before the Lord of the earth, who bear the child Jesus, who are placed as mediators between God and men so that he may be merciful to their iniquity, must be wholly fit. The ceremonial dress of the ancient priesthood mystically represents the beauty of virtues with which a minister of the altar ought to be adorned. For the legal priest used eight kinds of ornaments as figures of virtues: breeches, a linen tunic, a girdle, a hyacinth-blue tunic, an ephod, a breastpiece, a turban, and a golden plate (Exod. XXVIII). Thus bodily purity was signified by the breeches; purity of mind by the linen tunic; the guarding of both by the girdle that binds the garments; the virtue of contemplation by the hyacinth-blue tunic; strength in good work by the ephod; the discernment of knowledge by the breastpiece, which was an ornament of the chest; the governance of the five senses, which chiefly have their seat in the head, by the turban which covered the head; and memory, or the cross of the Lord’s Passion, by the golden plate that hung over the forehead—so that the priest may do nothing through rivalry or vainglory, but that all his works may be done in the Lord’s name.

[Col. 0228A] With these kinds of ornaments each person ought to approach Christ’s table; with these signs and arms he ought to serve as a soldier of his king, so that even from the heavenly attire of warfare itself it may be plain toward what end the victory tends.

Certainly those who serve an earthly emperor bear certain insignia of their distinctive military service: some eagles, others lions, some roses or lilies, some crescents, and other things of this kind, so that, when they have accomplished something bravely, it may be known by these signs to whose name it should be attributed. You likewise, who serve the heavenly King, ought to bear your own signs with you: instead of an eagle, the loftiness of charity; instead of a lion, strength in action; instead of a rose, patience in tribulation; instead of a lily, the brightness of chastity; instead of a crescent, perseverance unto perfection.

But one who is not adorned with virtues of this kind cannot be a fit minister of Christ; for he has a blemish and must therefore be excluded from the Lord’s ministry. Hence in the law of the Lord such a man is prohibited from the priesthood, as it is written: “A priest of the seed of Aaron who has a blemish shall not minister in the tabernacle, nor offer bread to the Lord his God: if he is blind, if lame, if he has a large, small, or crooked nose, if his foot or hand is broken, if he is hunchbacked, if bleary-eyed, if he has a white spot in his eye, continual scab, skin disease, or swollen testicles” (Lev. XXI).

[Col. 0228B] For a priest ought not to minister at the Lord’s table if he is blind through ignorance of the divine law; lame through inconsistency of conduct, so that his deeds contradict what he says in words; small-nosed through failure to discern good and evil; large- or crooked-nosed through excessive worldly prudence; broken-footed, that is, without affections of mercy and truth; broken-handed, that is, without the practice of good works; hunchbacked, that is, burdened by the vice of curiosity; bleary-eyed, that is, with a mind disturbed by carnal desires; having a white spot in the eye of reason; afflicted by continual scab through the scandals of lust; by skin disease through the fever of avarice; or swollen, weighed down by the burden of hidden thoughts. Hence it is that in the law a man polluted by nocturnal emission—that is, stained by a hidden thought—is commanded to remain unclean until evening (Lev. I). For if anyone conscious in himself of such faults presumes to frequent the Lord’s table, his blessings [Col. 0229A] are turned into curses for him, because he does not discern the body of the Lord.

Whoever, therefore, offers praise to God—whether the solemnities of Mass, the daytime hours, or the night hours—fulfil your ministry with an unblemished body and a pure heart, lest, if either is lacking, that threat against the Pharisees resound against you: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, who cleanse what is outside the cup, while within it is full of uncleanness” (Matt.
