XXIII). Sing psalms, then, with your voice; sing psalms with your works; sing psalms also with your mind. For just as you owe the Lord vocal hours, so you owe him real and spiritual hours.

The vocal hours are seven, which are sung every day in the churches of God, of which it is said: “Seven times a day I have given praise to you” (Ps. CXVIII). The real hours are those sung through good works rather than words: giving alms, receiving pilgrims, clothing the naked, visiting the sick, burying the dead, and the like. [Col. 0229B] The spiritual hours are the virtues of the soul which move it to act well: humility, charity, peace, patience, long-suffering, goodness, kindness, modesty, self-control, chastity, and others of this kind. May our Creator, Jesus Christ our Lord, grant that we be constantly exercised in these virtues in the present life and happily attain their fruit in the life to come—he whose kingdom and dominion remain for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XL. FOR THE DEDICATION OF A CHURCH

“Wisdom has built herself a house; she has hewn out [Col. 0229C] seven pillars” (Prov. IX).

This house, most beloved brothers, is not material but spiritual, in which the Bridegroom joins the bride to himself in a spiritual marriage: the Beloved his beloved, the Beautiful One his beautiful bride, betrothing her to present her as a chaste virgin to one husband, Christ.

Therefore, lest he should seek through streets and squares her whom his soul loves, he commanded a house to be made for himself in which the wedding solemnities might be held; where the daughters of Jerusalem might behold King Solomon in his splendor; where, finally, they might praise him in the choir and sing to him with tambourine and psaltery. Nor did he appoint some wise man to complete this work, but Wisdom itself, which is the Word of the Father, power and strength, so that the Word might act swiftly, strength might act powerfully, and Wisdom elegantly.

[Col. 0229D] Wisdom, then, built herself a house. Wisdom built this house for herself, because whatever accrues to the Bridegroom’s proper possession does not in any way depart from the possession of his Wisdom; for, begotten with him, of the same essence, she always stands by him with equal will and power.

This house is divided into a threefold dwelling. The first is that of those who labor; the second, of those who desire; and the third, of those who enjoy. To speak first of the first dwelling: among those who labor, some are lower and some higher (Exod. III). The first are those who, like Moses, were adopted by Pharaoh’s daughter and placed in the river of Egypt, but afterward reject that adoption and, leaving the Egyptians, return to the children of Israel. For, nourished through carnal desire in the river of vices, when they have grown up they begin to walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit; abandoning their evil ways, they desire to return to the children of Israel—that is, to those who see God. Considering the ends to which the ages of the world, that is, worldliness itself, come, they bring an accusation, as it were, against themselves and cry out in the prophetic voice: “Wretched daughter of Babylon, blessed is he who shall repay you with the recompense which you rendered to us” (Ps. CXXXVI). They complain against the daughter of Babylon—that is, against carnal pleasure—saying to her: “Blessed is he who gives you a fitting recompense: that just as you have slain the spirit in the flesh, so you too may be slain through the Spirit in the flesh.”

[Col. 0230A] They therefore cast aside the herd of swine which they had fed in the region of dissimilarity and return to the house of their Father, where there are many dwelling places. Having made an agreement for the daily denarius—that is, for the reward of eternal life—they are established as workmen of the foundation in God’s house. First, therefore, they dig the earth; afterward they arrange the foundation of stones in a threefold order. They dig the earth when they make manifest through oral confession whatever earthliness lies hidden in the heart. They adorn the foundation with a threefold distinction of stones when, first through compunction of heart, second through detestation of evil, and third through caution against future evil, they strengthen themselves in the purpose of goodness. They make cement from tears and the fervor of devotion, so that when temptation and stormy winds arise, the craftsmanship of so great a work may not be pulled apart.

Observe, however, that even this foundation, driven deep into the earth, is assailed on every side by earth: for one who strives to escape from evil custom into newness of life is very frequently struck outwardly by the world’s enticements and inwardly by unlawful desires. These are the outer and inner waters that often beat against our house; yet they fear and recede from God’s spiritual entry into the human heart. “The waters saw you, O God; the waters saw you and feared, and the depths were troubled” (Ps. LXXVI). There is an inner deep and an outer deep. The inner deep is the deep of the heart; the outer deep is the deep of the world. The waters of the inner deep are vain thoughts and perverse pleasures; the waters of the outer deep are vainglory, the concupiscence [Col. 0230B] of the eyes, and pride. These waters first see God when they fear judgment; and this is what is meant by: “The waters saw you, O God; the waters saw you and feared.” The deeps are troubled when the peace of vanity is interrupted and the heart begins to be drawn back from love of the world.

There are others of the class of laborers who, although they do not walk in the way of all flesh (Gen. VI), that is, of all carnality—for all flesh corrupts its way—nevertheless draw pleasures through the outward senses. Set between outer and inner sense, these pleasures do not permit the soul to rise to the invisible things of God. Hear Jeremiah lamenting this delight of the senses: “My eye,” he says, “has plundered my soul among all the daughters of my city” (Lam. III). Nor is sight alone delighted by such things; every other sense is also delighted in them. Sight is refreshed by running streams, laughing fields, dense woods, and other things of this kind that contribute solace to our mortality. Hearing is refreshed by hymns and songs, at times by idle words, by lyres and tambourines and other musical instruments. Taste is refreshed in the pot of meat with the Egyptians, in the number of birds with the Hebrews; with Esau in a dish of lentils; with Lot in the flavor of rare wine; with Elijah it craves a meal of bread baked under ashes; never with the sons of the prophets, the pot of Elisha. Likewise the other senses: smell by fragrant things, touch by things pleasant and soft.

[Col. 0231A] The result of one’s actions follows the vanities of the senses. For sight wishes to perform what refreshes it; hearing, what delights it; taste, what is savory; smell, what affects it; touch, what caresses it. Such delight of the senses sometimes wholly casts down the soul, when it withdraws it in part from the degree of perfection. We have an example of the first in that Delilah [sic] from the land of the Philistines, who cut off from mighty Samson the hair of his strength; when enemies came upon him, he was captured and deprived of his eyes (Judg. XVI). Delilah is interpreted “little poor woman,” that is, brief and passing pleasure. She cuts off the hair of strength from Samson—that is, from any strong man—when she does not permit the manly motions of the soul to rise to the accomplishment of perfect work. Hence, when enemies come upon him, he is deprived of his eyes: first of the eye of reason, so that he cannot know the truth; afterward of the eye of contemplation, so that he cannot love God.

We have an example of the second in the history of Genesis concerning Judah (Gen. XXXVIII): when he wished to go up to Timnah to shear his sheep, Tamar met him on the road and, having put off the garments of widowhood and arrayed herself in fine clothing, drew him into her love. Judah means “confessing”; Tamar, “bitterness”; Timnah is interpreted “sign” or “covered.” Therefore, when anyone who confesses in heart and deed wishes to ascend to Timnah—that is, through progress in virtues to cover former excesses, to offer others a sign and example by good conduct, and to separate the softness of temporal things from works of innocence—Tamar, meeting him at the crossroads, draws him into her love. For the pleasure of temporal things, which is truly the bitterness of the soul, intervening between outer and inner sense, [Col. 0231B] draws him back from the degree of perfection. Yet although these people delight in the vanity of temporal things, through works of piety and mercy they are reconciled to God for what they have done short of perfection.

The second dwelling is arranged by a certain wonderful artifice. According to Ezekiel’s description, the higher the first dwelling is, the lower that same dwelling is. For the more contemplative men excel others in charity, the humbler than all others they are in poverty of spirit. They devote themselves to exalted charity; they give themselves to holy meditation; indeed, they desire him who saved them from faintness of spirit and tempest. These are those who always offer before God’s presence bowls full of perfumes and kindle the incense of devotion upon the altar of their heart with the fire of charity. They also subject themselves to every creature for God’s sake and, walking in humility of spirit, always devoted to another’s rule, leave nothing to their own will. Thus, setting their minds on things above, they guard their court like strong men armed, and, mounting their horses, prevail over their enemies with bow and arrow, sling and stone.

[Col. 0232A] John described their victory and strength in the Apocalypse when he said: “And behold, a white horse, and he who sat upon it had a bow; and a crown was given to him, and he went forth conquering in order to conquer” (Rev. V). Understand sensuality in the horse and reason in the rider. Reason is said to sit upon the horse whenever neither flesh desires against spirit nor spirit against flesh, but whatever is animal in a human being is entirely subjected to the command of reason. “And he who sat upon it had a bow.” In a bow two things are found: wood and string. In the wood, which does not bend by itself, understand one’s own will; in the string, the necessity of obedience. The wood is bent by the string when, by the command of obedience, freedom of will is curved back from its own limits. This bow requires three arrows: the first, to obey humbly; the second, to obey swiftly; the third, to obey wisely. Humble obedience wounds pride, swift obedience sloth, wise obedience malice. Not every obedient person uses this bow, but only one who imitates Simon Peter in this obedience.

[Col. 0232B] For three kinds of obedient persons are indicated to us in the Gospel by the name Simon, which is interpreted “obedient.” We read of Simon of Cyrene, of whom it is said that “they compelled him to carry his cross” (Matt. XXVII). We also read of Simon the leper, in whose house Jesus reclined, to whom it was said: “You did not anoint my head with oil; you did not give water for my feet” (Matt. XXVI). We also read of Simon surnamed Peter, who imitated Christ’s Passion in his own passion.

Of the first kind of obedient persons are those who indeed carry the Lord’s cross through fasts, vigils, and the other observances of discipline, yet voluntarily do nothing at all of what ought to be done. Rather, like those serving only before the eye, they are moved not by freedom of spirit but solely by the strictness of rule. Hence it is said: “They compelled him,” that is, forced him, to carry his cross.

Of the second kind of obedient persons are those in whose house Jesus reclined through the inspiration of conversion, but who still appear leprous by the example of their wicked conduct. They have too little devotion to God, little—indeed, none—love for their neighbor; and, what is detestable before God and men, they strive to turn light into darkness, good into evil, even by lying in wait against good works. Of them the Psalmist speaks: “For sinners, bending the bow, have prepared their arrows in the quiver, to shoot the upright in heart in darkness” (Ps. X). For they send from the quiver of a wicked heart the arrows of biting detraction. Hear how: “To shoot,” he says, “the upright in darkness.” He rightly says “in darkness,” because, when they find no opening for true reproof, they nevertheless fashion false murmurs, as though by feeling their way.

[Col. 0232C] Let each person beware, then, lest he become like the wicked men of Sodom, who desire to overthrow Lot dwelling in the house but, struck with blindness, cannot find the doors of the dwelling. For when wicked men strive to overcome Lot—that is, one who turns away from evil (Gen. XIX)—they do not find the doors of the dwelling, that is, an opening for reproof, because, blinded by the good conduct of any upright person, they cannot enter upon it. Let each of us fear and beware that saying of Isaiah: “For hell has enlarged its soul and opened its mouth without any limit; and detractors shall descend into it, and the eyes of the exalted shall be cast down” (Isa. V).

Of such people it is said: “You did not anoint my head with oil,” that is, you did not ascend through the desire of devotion to the sweetness of my divinity. “You did not anoint my head with oil”: there is an oil by which Christ anoints us, and an oil by which we anoint Christ (Matt. XXVI). The oil by which Christ anoints us is the sweetness of divine inspiration, by which the soul, dry and arid in itself, is made rich, while grace, which it formerly lacked, is poured into it solely through God’s goodness. “Let my soul be filled, as it were, with marrow and fatness.” There is a twofold oil by which we anoint Christ. The first is the oil of exultation, when any soul, now having received grace, exults and rejoices in hope of future glory. [Col. 0232D] The second is the oil of devotion, when, with the whole desire of the mind, our prayer is directed like incense in God’s sight. It is especially of this that it is said: “You did not anoint my head with oil”—as though to say, “You did not ascend through the devotion of prayer to the height of my divinity”—and it continues: “You did not give water for my feet” (ibid.).

As anointing the head belongs to the desire of the contemplative, so washing the feet belongs to the reconciliation of the sinner. For God comes to sinners with two feet: the foot of mercy and the foot of justice. He comes with the foot of mercy when he freely justifies the undeserving ungodly person; he comes with the foot of justice when he condemns or crowns each person according to the merit of justice. Those do not pour water over these feet who neither implore God’s mercy for their sins nor dread the judgment of the future examination.

The third kind of obedient persons are those who hear the word of obedience in a good and excellent heart, and who fulfil and accomplish, solely out of love for justice, whatever has been commanded concerning things according to God. Of such an obedient person it is rightly added: “And a crown was given to him, and he went forth conquering in order to conquer” (Rev. VI). There are three crowns given to the truly obedient: the first is the crown of victory; the second, of dignity and power; the third, the crown of glory. The first is obtained from a conquered enemy; the second for acquiring dominion; the third for attaining blessedness. The first belongs to those who have fought against the enemy and conquered. [Col. 0233A] The second belongs to those who govern themselves, judge themselves, and command themselves, so that the enemy may be unable, by any cause or occasion, to take peace from their hearts. “And he went forth,” it says, “conquering in order to conquer.” First, indeed, they go forth by conquering their enemies; afterward they go forth also by conquering themselves.

The third dwelling, which we have called that of those who enjoy, belongs to those who are filled with the good things of his house and, numbered with that good and faithful servant, have now entered into the joy of their Lord. In order that their joy may be full, the Lamb who is in their midst clothes them with a twofold garment. The first is the splendor of eternal brightness; the second, the delight of divine contemplation. If they were illuminated without delight, the good would be incomplete; if they delighted without illumination, that good also would be less than full. Therefore both are given: one for the glory of the body, the other for the delight of the mind.

The Psalmist speaks of their refreshment, saying: “They shall be inebriated with the abundance of your house, and you shall give them to drink from the torrent of your delight” (Ps. XXXV). In the present life saints are refreshed, but not inebriated; in the future they are both refreshed and inebriated. Here refreshment is partial; there it is universal, when “he will gird himself, make them recline, and, passing by, minister to them” (Luke XII).

[Col. 0233B] There is one refreshment of the soul in the sacraments; a second in the Scriptures; a third in the power of prayer; a fourth in the blessedness of glorification. In the first refreshment the fattened calf is slain; in the second the book sealed with seven seals is opened; in the third Jacob’s ladder is raised; in the fourth the Lamb’s wedding supper is renewed. In the first refreshment, through the sacraments of the Passion, the soul lays aside its old nature; in the second, through the consolation of the Scriptures, hope receives strength; in the third, as though by a ladder, it ascends from virtue to virtue; in the fourth, it obtains the blessedness of that eternal banquet.

I mean blessedness in body and blessedness in mind; for each substance, bodily and incorporeal, possesses its own goods there. There are two chief goods of the mind: knowledge of truth and perfection of charity. Likewise, there are two goods of the body: one is the beauty of splendor; the other is soundness of wholeness. The first consists in the glorification of the body; the second in the casting off of corruption. Although these virtues are there distinct from one another, perhaps in their exercise there is no difference, because each virtue will have the use of all and all the use of each, so that the prophetic saying may be fulfilled: “All my bones,” that is, all our virtues, “shall say: Lord, who is like you?” (Ps. XXXIV).

[Col. 0233C] Perhaps these are signified by that woman clothed with the sun, having the moon beneath her feet and a crown of twelve stars (Rev. XII). Clothed about with the sun of justice, they dwell in inaccessible light and leave no part of themselves outside it. They tread the moon beneath their feet—that is, the mortality of this life or the vanity of worldly things—and hence they are said to possess a crown of twelve stars. In the crown there is neither beginning nor end, by which the joy of unending eternity can be understood. In the stars are the life and teaching of apostolic preaching. They are therefore rightly said to have a crown of twelve stars, because, having imitated in this life the life and teaching of those apostles, they have been crowned in heaven in their likeness.

These things concerning that threefold dwelling we have spoken according to the course of our subject. Much more could still be said concerning the seven pillars, the adornment of bride and bridegroom, and the preparation of the banquet, if there were one who could bring gold from the earth and if the urgency of the solemnity, on account of the reverence due to the office, did not press upon us. Meanwhile, setting these matters aside, let us direct the whole intention of our mind toward that heavenly dwelling, toward the tabernacle not made by hands, so that [Col. 0233D] at last we may be transferred from this slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God. Let us advance, most beloved brothers, on the journey of our pilgrimage in the fear of God and love of neighbor, so that in that heavenly homeland we may deserve to become heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ, through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, whose kingdom and dominion remain for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XLI. FOR THE DEDICATION OF A CHURCH

“Now the dedication feast took place at Jerusalem” (John X).

I have long recognized, most beloved brothers, that many of you have received the key of knowledge, and that the spotless law of the Lord which converts souls has been written by the finger of God in your hearts. For that key of David [Col. 0234A] which shuts and no one opens, opens and no one shuts, has been pleased to open to you the depths of God and the mysteries of the Scriptures—to you, I say, to whom it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, while to others it is given in parables.

Fear, therefore, dismays me when I follow you as a little one—wise as a little one, still to be nourished with milk and not with solid food; ignorance reproves me; and finally shame confounds me. For among the perfect one ought to speak wisdom and compare spiritual things with spiritual, among those who, forgetting the things behind, direct their whole mind toward contemplating God and meditate upon his law day and night. Since, therefore, it is the greatest wrong to offend the presence of such great men even by speech, I would rather break forth into a voice of lamentation than of discourse, ready, insofar as I can, to make satisfaction with a fountain of tears to those whom, by the necessity of obedience, I am compelled, though unwillingly, to offend.

Yet because you are men of mercy, a holy nation, a people for possession (Hos. VI), knowing what it means, “I desire mercy and not sacrifice,” I look rather to your mercy than to judgment, being more secure of pardon than fearful of offence. For you gladly bear with the foolish, being wise yourselves, because it belongs to your virtue to spare rather than punish, to excuse rather than judge—especially in matters whose occurrence is pressed by necessity and whose completion is prevented by the difficulty of an undertaking not yet prepared. But lest the discourse, whether through negligence of style or the fault of prolixity, run on to weariness, let us strive to attain an end by brevity, so that those who desire subtlety of intellect, profundity of meaning, and beauty of expression may, through the swift conclusion of the discourse, begin to be less wearied.

[Col. 0234B] “Now the dedication feast took place,” says the Evangelist, “at Jerusalem.” *Encaenia*, according to the etymology of the name, are so called as though from *en-caenia*; the word means renewal or dedication. This solemnity was instituted by Judas Maccabaeus, according to the truth of the history (II Macc. VIII), when, having expelled idols and their worship from the temple of the Lord, he once more devoted it to divine worship.

You know, dearest brothers, that “whatever things were written were written for our instruction” (Rom. XV), so that through patience and the consolation of the Scriptures we may have hope. Especially you who know how to crush the calf of Lebanon and to satisfy many thousands of men with five barley loaves: in the construction of this visible temple, there is proposed to us, unless I am mistaken, an inquiry into some invisible temple. We are taught that it must be built and, after its overthrow, cleansed, so that every building being constructed may grow into a holy temple in the Lord. Not unfittingly, then, we call the soul of the just person the temple of God: it is the image and likeness of God and the sanctuary of the Holy Spirit.

Let us first see, therefore, how this temple is built in three ways. It rises and is completed in height through knowledge, love, and good action: knowledge is laid as the foundation; love is raised in the walls; good action, like a roof, embraces the walls at their summit. For, as Augustine says: “As much as you know, so much you love; so much you act.” For no one can love what he does not know or act upon what he does not love.

[Col. 0234C] We arrive at perfect knowledge in three ways: through meditation, practice, and instruction. Meditation is the frequent consideration of the mind, amid doubts, for the investigation of truth. Practice is the frequent use of inquiry, either by oneself or in relation to another. Instruction is the diligent forming of the mind, either to do what ought to be done or to know what it does not know.

There is one kind of knowledge below the human being, another concerning the human being, and another above the human being. That which is below the human being concerns created things made for the human being, by which the human being knows the dignity of his condition. Through that which concerns the human being, he knows the fault of his own weakness. Through that which is above the human being, he knows the grace of goodness. By the first, you know what you have received; by the second, what you have lost; by the third, what you are going to receive.

After knowledge, love, like a wise architect, raises the foundation, placing discernment at the entrance, devotion at the top, compassion on the left side, and gentleness on the right. Discernment is placed first, so that we may know how to distinguish clean from unclean, holy from profane, evil from good, lest through the union of virtue and vice the sanctuary of God be profaned upon earth. For evils are neighbors to goods through error itself:

> For evils are close to goods through error itself; virtue has often borne the charges of crimes in place of vice.  
> —Ovid

[Col. 0234D] “In every sacrifice of yours you shall offer salt,” that is, you shall have discernment, as the Lord commands you (Lev. II), lest, if you bind up unbearable burdens, you soon succumb beneath the burden; or if you gather useless mastic shrubs, you become slothful, as is read in the Apocalypse: “Would that you were hot or cold; but because you are neither hot nor cold, I will begin to vomit you from my mouth” (Rev. III).

After discernment follows devotion in prayer, compassion for the weakness of one’s neighbor: devotion in relation to God, compassion in relation to one’s neighbor, gentleness in relation to oneself. With these four walls every building that is constructed grows into a holy temple in the Lord, because discernment builds wisely, devotion diligently, compassion mercifully, and gentleness fittingly. The Prophet reveals to us the fruit of gentleness, saying: “He will guide the gentle in judgment; he will teach the meek his ways” (Ps. XXXIV). And in the Gospel: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. V). And elsewhere: “Upon whom shall my Spirit rest, except upon one who is meek and humble,” and so forth (Isa. LXVI).

[Col. 0235A] These are the four golden rings which were at the corners of the ark of the covenant, by which it was lifted when the camp was to move and set down when the tents were to be pitched. For the holy soul is called the ark of the covenant because it keeps the law of God in its heart and fulfils it in good action. By these four aforesaid virtues it is raised above earthly affections and, after overcoming the movements of temptations, is kept at rest in tranquility of mind.

The Bridegroom exhorts us to devotion in the Song of Love, saying: “Eat and drink, my friends, and be inebriated, beloved ones” (Song V). Eat from the fruit of good action; drink from the wine of compunction; be inebriated in the joy of holy devotion. That merciful Samaritan gave us an example of compassion: when the priest and Levite had passed by, he showed mercy to the man, tended his wounds, and poured in oil and wine (Luke X). And what else did the Hebrew midwives provide us but an example of compassion? They did not fear to oppose Pharaoh’s command, so that they might rescue the children of the Hebrews from death (Exod. I).

There follows the final part of the spiritual building, that is, good works. [Col. 0237D] In the ancient history (Lev. I) we read that three kinds of animals were to be offered in sacrifice to the Lord: animals from the herd, from the flock, and birds. In these three kinds of animals three kinds of works are indicated. For some things we do for the mortification of the flesh, some for the safeguarding of virtue, and some for the service of charity. The first and last we do for ourselves, but the middle for our neighbours. Those works which serve the mortification of vices ought to be laborious and harsh, in strength of spirit and humility of body, in hunger and thirst, in cold and nakedness, in many fasts, in unfeigned charity. Those which serve the office of charity ought to be devout, gentle, full of mercy, performed cheerfully, zealously, and without delay. [Col. 0238A] Those which serve the safeguarding of virtue ought to be simple and chaste, with self-abasement and contempt for the world: simple and chaste with respect to guarding the inner person; with self-abasement and contempt for the world, with respect to protecting the outer person. The works which we named first are referred to the sacrifice of animals from the herd, which are laborious and strong; those named second, to the sacrifice of animals from the flock, which are gentle and innocent; those named third, to the sacrifice of birds, namely the turtle-dove and the dove, because they are simple and chaste.

The house of the Lord has been built as far as we were able; let us now briefly consider its dedication. In the material temple we read of three dedications: one under Solomon, a second after the return from the Babylonian captivity, and a third through Judas Maccabaeus in the temple’s desolation. In this manner our spiritual temple has three dedications: one in baptism, a second in renunciation of the world, and a third in laying aside the flesh. In baptism, indeed, the rational soul is dedicated to God: it is cleansed by putting off its old state, sanctified by the indwelling grace of the Holy Spirit, armed by the confession of faith, and strengthened by the anointing with oil.

Paul glories in the second dedication of the temple when he says: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. VI). We see some who despise the world, though the world does not despise them; some who are despised by the world, though they do not despise the world; some who both despise the world and are despised by the world; and some who neither despise the world nor are despised by it. Those who despise the world and are not despised by it are those who, although in body they are in the world, yet in their manner of life are in heaven. The world admires their life because it is difficult and reveres it because it is holy. [Col. 0238C] But those who are despised by the world and do not despise the world are those whom the world rejects because of poverty of possessions, the cheapness of their clothes, the lowliness of their person, and the disorderliness of their life. Although necessity makes them leave the world, in their will they possess all things. There are also others who despise the world and are despised by it: such were the saints, who “experienced mockings and scourges, moreover also chains and prisons; they were stoned, sawn asunder, tempted, and put to death by the sword” for Christ, through whom the world was crucified to them. For they despised the world for his sake, and they were crucified to the world because, for Christ’s sake, the world rejected them. [Col. 0238D] No examples need be given of those who neither despise the world nor are despised by it: their multitude is great even in mercy, and their way of life is manifest.

This second renewal of the spirit must be acquired in three ways: by rejection of one’s own will, by endurance of tribulation, and by desire for the heavenly homeland. The Saviour himself prescribed these three things when he said: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up [Col. 0239A] his cross, and follow me” (Luke IX). Let him deny himself by laying aside his own will; let him take up his cross by patiently enduring tribulation; and let him follow me by longing for the homeland and by imitating my works. “For whoever says that he abides in Christ ought himself also to walk as he walked” (I John II).

The final renewal of the spirit is in the laying aside of the flesh, when they “shall be filled with the abundance of thy house, and thou shalt give them drink from the torrent of thy delight,” when they shall enter into thy light to behold the God of gods in Zion. The more excellent this renewal of spirits is than the others, the more wonderful it is beyond them. Then that which is perfect shall come, and that which is partial shall be done away with. For either the senses [Col. 0239B] will be destroyed, or the intellect will be purified, or gratuitous gifts will be completed and confirmed.

When the body of this death has been laid aside, some senses will be destroyed both as to use and as to faculty—for example, touch, which is not suited to a spiritual creature, since it must be exercised only upon bodily things. Others will be destroyed as to their present use, not as to faculty—for example, taste and smell. Taste then will consist in being satisfied by that eternal blessedness; smell will have the function of delighting in it. Sight and hearing, however, will be destroyed as to their instrument, not as to use or faculty. For the souls of the blessed, once the body of death has been laid aside, both see the deeds of human beings and hear the voices of those who praise God. In order that we may see [Col. 0239C] how the intellect is purified, it is necessary to take timber from Lebanon for the building of the temple.

They assert that it is written in Plato’s *Timaeus* that intellect belongs to God alone and to very few human beings. But if intellect belongs to few human beings, while human beings are many, it follows that some are without intellect. Yet one kind of understanding comes from created things, another from the Scriptures, and another from the infusion of heavenly truth. The first belongs to the common crowd, the second to the philosopher, the third to the religious person. The first belongs to all, the second to many, the third to very few people. Therefore our intellect will then be purified, when we understand not through created things, but from the infusion alone of that highest truth, in which and through which we shall understand all things, as it is written [Col. 0239D] in the prophets: “And they shall all be taught by God” (John VI). Charity too will then be perfected, because then neither anything else nor anything otherwise than it ought will be loved.

There is a twofold perfection of charity: one in constancy of loving, the other in the intensity of love. The first perfection consists in being strong against adversities that must be endured, in being ready to go to prison and death for Christ and to lay down one’s life for one’s neighbour. The second consists in being so inflamed that it cannot be kindled further. The first perfection belongs to the way; the second, to the homeland. We have distinguished three renewals of the spirit: we have already received the first; in the second we walk by grace; the third we still await. [Col. 0240A] May Jesus Christ, our God and Lord, creator and redeemer, deign to grant it to us, whose kingdom and dominion endure for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XLII. ON THE FEAST OF SAINT VICTOR

“These are they who have come out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (Rev. VII). From the beginning of the Church as it was being born, founded and planted in the blood of the righteous, holy martyrs were made a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to human beings. They were made a spectacle to the world when tyrants and persecutors of Christ took delight in the shedding of their blood; to human beings when the righteous and faithful were edified by their endurance; [Col. 0240B] and to angels when angelic spirits rejoiced alike in their victory and glory. To this spectacle, dearly beloved brethren, the angel who speaks to John—and in John to all his fellow-servants and brethren who have the testimony of Jesus—invites us. He invites us, I say, when he says:

“These are they who have come.” Therefore, you who have been invited to this spectacle, behold the struggles of the martyrs, their virtues, and their glory. Behold their struggles and marvel that, in fragile flesh, in an earthen vessel, in this body of death, they were able to endure such great tortures. Behold their virtues, the signs, wonders, and miracles which God worked through them; and in the holy martyrs praise God’s benefits. Behold their glory, which they enjoy [Col. 0240C] in heaven, and implore their aid.

Nor are you invited from afar to this spectacle, which is shown close at hand when it is said, “These are they.” Those whom you see with the spiritual eye, address in frequent prayers, touch in some fashion with your hands through imitation of good works, and firmly retain by the devotion of your heart, are truly said to be near you. Rightly are they shown near you because you are spiritual: spiritual persons see spiritual things near at hand, since they love them, seek them, and desire to possess them. Temporal things, however, they see from afar, because they do not desire them and do not wish to enjoy them in this world, counting them as dung that they may gain Christ.

This is why, when God or an angel speaks [Col. 0240D] to spiritual persons, he separates them and leads them apart from the tumult and pleasure of the world. Just as the Lord Jesus Christ took Peter, James, and John alone up a high mountain when he was transfigured before them (Matt. XVII), so, when the Lord gave the law to Moses, he separated him from the crowd and spoke with him in the darkness of the mountain (Exod. XIX). In the same way God spoke with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and the angel with Elijah in the wilderness. By all these examples we are taught that those who behold spiritual things near at hand ought to be far removed from temporal things.

Conversely, carnal persons, who pursue and desire to possess carnal things, behold them with the eye of the heart close at hand. But they see spiritual things from afar, because if [Col. 0241A] you speak with a carnal person about holiness, religion, or the life of the world to come, you will seem to him to be speaking in a dream; they do not direct the eye of their heart to such matters because they are not stirred by love for them. We read of Eli the priest, whose eyes had grown dim so that he could not see the lamp of God before it was extinguished (I Kings II). This should be understood literally as follows: the nature of dim eyes is such that they cannot look upon the flame of a lamp because of its excessive brightness, but once the lamp’s flame is extinguished, they see its ember more clearly.

Now spiritual persons are understood by the flame: they burn inwardly with charity and shine outwardly in good works. By the ember, which does not shine, carnal persons must be understood. Thus Eli, by whom carnal persons are signified, can see not the lamp but its ember: because carnal people have a keener vision of the heart for seeing carnal things than spiritual things. Therefore, for the reason we have stated, holy martyrs are shown near to spiritual persons when it is said: “These are they who have come.”

But observe that the spiritual vision of the heart requires two illuminations if it is to behold God’s saints spiritually. One is external, in which the saints are with Christ in their homeland; the other internal, because righteous persons are inwardly illumined in the soul through virtues. Only those who are illumined inwardly by grace behold in contemplation that brightness in which holy martyrs and other righteous persons live, glorious and illumined together with angelic spirits in Christ. Whoever is therefore in the darkness of sins [Col. 0241C] does not see the holy martyrs set in brightness. No one can see brightness through darkness; indeed, through darkness one cannot even see darkness itself, because it is only through brightness that both brightness and darkness are seen. Therefore the person admitted to this spectacle must have an illumined eye—the spectacle to which those were invited of whom it was said: “These are they who have come out of great tribulation,” and so forth.

Here the word “are” is fittingly added, for they have attained true being: being neither broken by labours, corrupted by weakness, passing away through changeability, nor failing through any end, but enduring ever the same in immutability and without end in eternity. These, then, are they who have come out of great tribulation. Yet they first came to tribulation and afterwards came out of tribulation. They came to tribulation when they suffered torments. “They came” is aptly said because they came to the sufferings of martyrdom not drawn or compelled, but of their own free will. For the holy martyrs freely strove to suffer for Christ in this life, so that they might quickly be delivered from this world. Carnal people, on the contrary, strive by fleeing the tribulations of this life to take root in this world for a long time.

Thus holy persons came to the tribulation of this life; carnal people flee the tribulations of this life, yet do not escape them. Even if they evade the great tribulations of this world, they are nevertheless drawn—indeed, not merely come—to those greatest tribulations of eternal punishment, dragged even unwillingly by the cords of their sins. [Col. 0242A] First see that what I say is true in the lustful, and consider in them the heat of desire, the gluttony of the belly, the extravagance of clothing, and the dissipation of idleness. These are, as it were, bonds by which they are dragged to the torments of eternal death. You will find the same in the greedy if you consider their rapacity, inhumanity, contempt for God, and forgetfulness of death: by these, as by certain bonds, they are dragged to the punishments of Gehenna. The same is true in other sinners, “for when they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them” (I Thess. V).

But that I may teach you by an example that martyrs came willingly to torments, consider the wondrous victory of our unconquered martyr Victor. He was beaten with scourges, stretched on the rack, dragged through the middle of the city by the fury of horses, his whole body broken in a millstone for grinding grain, and at last put to death by the sword. [Col. 0242B] Yet he endured all these things willingly. The evident proof is that, having been led by an angelic hand out of the horror of prison, he willingly returned to the place of his suffering. Thus Lawrence taunts his executioners; Vincent invites his torturers. Dionysius and other martyrs did this: through the savagery of their torments they came to the company of angels.

They also came out of tribulation when, having overcome both their torturers and their torments, they passed as victorious and glorious ones into the heavenly kingdom. Clearly they were victors and made superior to their torturers when, after they themselves had been brought into glory, their persecutors were plunged into eternal punishments. And where are Maximian, Datianus, Fecenninus, and the other persecutors of martyrs? Certainly they were conquered and utterly destroyed, so completely that not even their memory remained among the dead.

Therefore holy martyrs came to tribulation and came out of tribulation; both points must be retained in memory, because the Church celebrates for each. In the vigils of holy martyrs, the Church recalls that the holy martyrs came to tribulation, when by vigils, fasts, and other mortifications of the flesh she in some way imitates the sufferings of the saints. But on their feast-days the Church joyfully recalls in the Spirit that they came out of great tribulation, solemnly chanting matters that concern [Col. 0242D] their glory. So we do today in praise of blessed Victor the martyr, when we say: “In thy strength, O Lord, the righteous man shall rejoice; thou hast set upon his head a crown of precious stone,” and other such words which are sung today in his praise and veneration. Thirdly, in their octaves the Church celebrates the future glorification of the bodies in which they endured their torments. Thus the Church celebrates holy martyrs in three ways: in their vigil, on their feast-day, and in their octaves, for the reasons stated. “They have come out of great tribulation.”

The tribulation of martyrs is called great in comparison with the other tribulations of this world, which are rightly called small in comparison with martyrdom. [Col. 0243A] The punishment of martyrdom is called great tribulation not because of its duration, since many other punishments last longer, but because of its severity, since no punishment in this life is harsher than martyrdom, and because of its effect, since no other punishment of this world is so effective for purging sins. However criminal a person may have been, if, contrite in heart and in faith in Jesus Christ, he endures martyrdom, then as soon as the sword of martyrdom has cut away whatever in him required purging, he passes to the glory of eternal blessedness. This is not found to occur in any other kind of suffering.

But what reason can there be why, in the punishment of purgatorial fire, which is incomparably greater than any martyrdom, even those who have sinned less are not purged as quickly as those who have sinned more are immediately liberated through the punishment of martyrdom, which is much less severe than purgatory? We must observe that the punishment of martyrdom is both purgative and meritorious; the punishment of purgatorial fire is purgative but not meritorious; and the punishment of Gehenna is neither purgative nor meritorious. The punishment of martyrdom is purgative because of the suffering which the martyr endures; it is meritorious because of the act by which he endures martyrdom. To endure is an act. Nor is any action so effective for earning merit as this, by which a person immediately in martyrdom deserves to be purged and, once martyrdom is completed, to be transferred to glory.

But purgatorial fire is indeed purgative, because one is purged by suffering it; yet it is not meritorious, [Col. 0243C] because the one who endures it does not earn anything by undergoing it, since after this life there is no place for earning merit. Therefore a person’s liberation from the punishment of purgatory arises not from human merit but only from the ordinance of the divine will. That the punishment of Gehenna is neither purgative nor meritorious is clear, because no one consigned to that punishment can thereafter be delivered from it.

Therefore, as we said: “They have come out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes.” A robe is a kind of garment, and we may distinguish three kinds of robe: the penitential robe, the nuptial robe, and the triumphal robe. The penitential robe is satisfaction for sin, of which it is said: “Quickly bring forth the first robe and put it on him” (Luke XV). The nuptial robe is love of God and neighbour, concerning which robe it is written of Judah: “He shall wash his robe in wine, and his cloak in the blood of grapes” (Gen. XLIX). [Col. 0243D] The triumphal robe, in which holy martyrs have triumphed, is the garment of the body; and of it it is said here: “They have washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb.”

The penitential robe is washed with water when the sinner laments his sins and, with an abundance of tears, forestalls the future weeping and gnashing of teeth. The nuptial robe is washed in wine when a holy person who loves God and neighbour becomes more devout and more fervent through the fervour of the spirit. For this fervour of the spirit is that wine of which the steward says in the Gospel: “But thou hast kept the good wine until now” (John II). Charity is said to be washed in wine not because the stain of charity is removed, [Col. 0244A] but because, through fervour of spirit, it becomes more sincere and pure. The holy martyrs washed the triumphal robe in blood when, becoming imitators of Christ’s passion, they shed their own blood for him.

And observe that, just as it is said that Judah washed his robe in wine, so it can be said that Judah washed his robe in water; likewise, that Judah washed his robe in blood. For since “Judah” is interpreted “confessor,” we can distinguish a threefold confession: confession of sin, confession of praise, and confession of faith. Judah, then, as confessor of sin, washed his robe in water. Judah, as confessor of praise, who praises God and gives thanks for the virtues he has received, washes his robe in wine. But Judah as confessor of faith—such as blessed Victor and the other martyrs, who confessed Christ’s faith before kings and governors—washed their robes in blood.

Both matters must be noted, because it is said: “They washed their robes and made them white.” Washing concerns the remission of sins. They received remission of sins when, in their sufferings, they washed their bodies in their own blood. Whitening, however, concerns the glorification of their bodies, which holy martyrs await in the future. They earned that glorification by shedding their blood, and therefore they made their robes white in the blood of the Lamb.

Perhaps someone may be troubled by the statement, “They washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb,” when they rather washed and [Col. 0244C] made them white in their own blood. Yet not without reason is the blood of holy martyrs called the blood of the Lamb, or of Christ, for they are members of Christ. Just as blood flowing from your hand, side, or any other limb is truly called your blood, so too that blood which flowed from Christ’s members—namely, blessed Victor and the other martyrs—is truly declared to be the blood of the Lamb. Or the blood of holy martyrs is called the blood of the Lamb because in martyrdom they offered it to Christ. The blood of the Lamb may also be understood as the power of Christ’s passion, when it is said: “They washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb.” Holy martyrs were rightly washed by the merit of Christ’s passion—that is, cleansed from their sins. By merit of that same passion they were also made white, because through it they will receive the glorification of their bodies in the life to come. This is the meaning of the statement that they “washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb”: that is, by the power of Christ’s passion, through whose merit they received both remission of sins in the present [Col. 0244D] and glorification of their bodies in the future.

For no one, however righteous, can earn future glory; and therefore all the good which the saints await in the other life comes wholly from grace and from the merit of Christ’s passion. No one, whatever good he may do or whatever suffering he may endure, can earn future glory in such a way that it is owed him as a matter of right, or that God would wrong him if he did not give it. This may be shown by the following reasoning: all the good things we do are gifts of God, and therefore God is not obligated to us by them; rather, we are obligated to God. For when someone gives gifts to another, it is clear that not the giver but the recipient is obligated. Rightly, therefore, holy martyrs expect washing and whitening from the merit of Christ’s passion, which, as we have said, they cannot have from their own merits.

But what is attributed specially to martyrs when it is said, “They washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb,” since not only they, but also virgins, confessors, and all other righteous persons are washed from sins and glorified by the merit of Christ’s passion? It is one thing to say, “Christ washed their robes in his blood,” and another to say, “They washed their robes in Christ’s blood.” Christ washed and made white all the righteous through the power of his passion; [Col. 0245B] but martyrs alone washed and made themselves white in the blood of the Lamb, because they in some way mingled their own blood with Christ’s blood and, in faith in his passion, drenched their bodies with blood in likeness to him.

Washing is mentioned first and whitening afterwards because, as it is written, “the times of reigning cannot precede the times of suffering.” Therefore holy martyrs walked by the narrow way of martyrdom, so that by this very fact they might show us that through many tribulations lies our way to heaven. If, walking by that path, we imitate them in this life, we shall share their glory in the life to come, through the aid of our Lord Jesus Christ, whose kingdom and dominion endure for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XLIII. ON THE ASSUMPTION OF THE GLORIOUS VIRGIN MARY

[Col. 0245C]

“Who is this who comes forth like the rising dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun?” (Song VI.) To one who carefully considers the order of our restoration, certain beginnings of our salvation seem to have dawned when the blessed Mother of God, like the heralding dawn of the day now imminent, shone upon the world by her birth. Becoming the limit of the preceding night, she uniquely received certain first fruits of the Spirit and gifts of graces. For she arose at a kind of boundary between night and day. While the grim darkness of death and sin enveloped the world before the sunrise—that is, before Christ’s advent—she appeared to the world, so that, as the light gradually increased, night might bring forth dawn and dawn the sun, [Col. 0245D] which, when risen, would illuminate with the light of its brightness not only what is in heaven but also what is on earth.

Certainly a very long night ran from Eve to Mary. Though dark with the shadows of sins, it was nevertheless marked by its watches, as though by certain flashes of lightning. The first of these was the illumination of hidden inspiration; the second, the sanction of legal instruction; the third, the certainty of prophetic foretelling; the fourth, the intense desire for the promise now about to be fulfilled. From the beginning, the saints kept these watches of the night—not, I say, over their flock, but to see this dawn, should she appear anywhere, should she give any sign of herself anywhere—for they understood that she had been prefigured in mystical things and promised by the prophets.

Noah and the others of his time kept the first watch of this night, for they were illumined by hidden inspiration. Moses and the other holy fathers kept the second, for they were spiritually instructed through the law. The prophets kept the third, for they foretold the birth of the blessed Virgin. Those saints kept the fourth who, standing as it were at the very moment when dawn was about to break forth, most ardently desired to see not only her but also Christ about to be born from her: Anna, Elizabeth, the righteous Simeon, and the others who awaited Israel’s redemption.

And, to show by examples that she was prefigured in types, what else was that dove which went out from Noah’s ark at the time of the flood and brought into it a branch of green olive? (Gen. VIII.) The dove coming from Noah’s ark is Mary, sprung from the Church; she brought back to it a branch of olive at the time of the flood because, while the waters of vices enveloped the world, she poured forth into the Church Christ incarnate from herself. This branch was rightly one of green olive, said to be a sign of peace and concord, because Christ made peace between what is in heaven and what is on earth, breaking down in his flesh the dividing wall of enmity.

Job also fashioned an oracle concerning her when he said: “Silver has the beginnings of its veins, and gold has a place where it is melted” (Job XXVIII). [Col. 0246B] Silver, indeed, was Christ’s humanity, which according to the flesh descended successively from the holy fathers as from certain veins. Gold was the divinity of the Word; and the place of its melting was the blessed Mother of God, in whom the Holy Spirit, by an ineffable operation, fused divine and human nature into one person.

Moses’ rod, too, by which he performed signs in Egypt (Exod. IV), is Mary, through whom God performed wonders in the world. Among the greatest of these was that, when the rod was changed into a serpent, it devoured the dragons of Egypt. For when she bore Christ from herself in the likeness of sinful flesh, she destroyed all crimes and all heresies of the impious which mocked in the Egypt of this world—both by the power of her offspring and by the example of her holiness.

Nor do I think that any other is signified by the almond tree of which Solomon speaks, saying: “The almond tree shall blossom, the locust shall grow fat, and the caper shall be scattered” (Eccl. XII). The almond tree, which flowers before other trees, signifies Mary, [Col. 0246D] who surpassed all other saints in the flowers of virtues; indeed, before all others she brought forth from herself that flower outstanding in beauty and fragrance, namely Christ, who says: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song II). At her rising the locust grew fat, because unstable Gentile life became fruitful through grace; and the caper was scattered, because Judaea, thorny with the prickles of sins, remained empty of spiritual richness.

Thus in the ark of the covenant, which was covered with purest gold, Mary and her virginity were signified, if I may so speak; in the burning bush which was not consumed, Mary and her fruitfulness; in Solomon’s throne, with which no other in all kingdoms could be compared, the royal sublimity of Mary was signified. Seeing her so designated by many mystical things and prophecies, Solomon cries out in a voice of wonder, saying: “Who is this who comes forth,” and so forth.

These three—the dawn, moon, and sun—may be applied to Mary in this manner: the dawn to her birth, the moon to the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit which was in her, and the sun to her glorious assumption. Dawn fittingly corresponds to her birth because, when it rises, night seems in a sense bright and day seems dark. The frailty of mortal life is often signified by night, as it is written: “My soul desired thee in the night” (Ps. XLI). Divine grace’s illumination is signified by day, as Paul testifies when he says: “The night has passed; the day has drawn near” (Rom. XIII). Therefore, when Mary was born, a kind of dawn arose, because in her the night of human frailty was bright through grace, while the day of divine grace was in some sense darkened through frail nature.

[Col. 0247B] She is also called beautiful as the moon because, just as the moon, naturally dark in itself, receives the sun’s ray and is kindled by borrowed light, so Mary, still established in a mortal body, received the Holy Spirit within herself as though the ray of that highest majesty, and was made fruitful by the true light, the Son of God. The moon shines at night and diminishes its darkness; Mary, made fruitful by the Holy Spirit, wipes away the darkness of sins. But as the moon shines at night, so the sun shines by day. Day sometimes signifies the brightness of the life to come, as in the words: “For one day in thy courts is better than thousands” (Ps. LXXXIII). Blessed Virgin Mary is therefore rightly said to be chosen as the sun, because as the sun surpasses the other stars in brightness of light and greatness, so in the joy of heavenly life she is set above all the saints in delight and glory. Thus she was like a rising dawn in her birth, beautiful as the moon in that overshadowing of the Holy Spirit, and chosen as the sun in her assumption.

But let us look a little longer at this dawn. We find in it three things that profit our edification: the end of sleep, the beginning of work, and the sign of fair weather. Strong labourers commonly rise from sleep at dawn and, as fair weather seems to brighten, go out to their work, lest the householder come and find them standing idle in the marketplace. [Col. 0247D] Hence King Solomon puts an end to sleep at this dawn, goes out to his work, beholds the beautiful one, marvels at the immaculate one, and praises Mary, saying: “Who is this who comes forth,” and so forth.

To understand these three points morally, the end of sleep may be referred to penitence, the beginning of work to the active life, and the sign of fair weather to the contemplative life. If you wish to find in Mary a pattern of the penitent, read of her standing beside the cross. If you wish to find a pattern of the active person, read of her visiting Elizabeth. If you wish to find a pattern of the contemplative person, read of her praying with the apostles in the upper room and conversing with Gabriel in the chamber.

Therefore, whoever you are who lie prostrate in the sleep of sins, follow the example of the king of Israel: you too must put an end to sleep; awaken, and let it suffice that you have slept until now. Stand beside the cross with Mary the mother, and through the labours of penitence imitate Christ’s passion as far as you can, exacting from yourself by torments what, through evil living, you denied to the Crucified One. [Col. 0248A] Look upon your sins and remember from where you have fallen; nevertheless, look upon them in such a way that you are not swallowed up by sorrow or distrust. Bear the cross of the thief in such a way that you expect paradise from the Saviour’s promise. For there are some who look upon their sins in too great a light, and through the magnitude of their crimes despair of pardon.

Others look upon them in too slight a light and, judging them evil only to a small degree or not evil at all, remain always in guilt. But those who are truly penitent ought to behold their sins in a measured light, so that they may mourn them with lamentation while, conceiving hope, they trust that they shall attain the reward of penitence.

Jacob the patriarch prefigured for us this pattern of repentance. Desiring to inherit his father’s blessing, he took from the flock two choice kids, wrapped their skins about his hands, covered his bare neck, and, clothed in Esau’s very good garments, went in to his father. Having been felt by him, he was at last confirmed with the blessing (Gen. 27). The kids are the works of repentance, on which God the Father gladly feeds; they ought to be cooked in the water of tears and the fire of tribulation. The skins of the kids are the mortification of the flesh and the rejection of one’s own will, which Jacob must wrap about his hands: for the true supplanter of vices ought to have nothing in works of repentance that pleases the flesh or delights his own will [Col. 0248C]. The covering of the neck is caution regarding the future. The garments of Esau—that is, of the sinner, rough and hairy with the vices of crimes—in which Jacob ought to be clothed, are integrity of life and maturity of discipline. For one who truly wishes to supplant vices must, by integrity of life, put to death within himself what is carnal, and by mature conduct not offend the eyes of his neighbours outwardly. Having done these things, he enters to the Father with the affection of devotion; he is felt by the Father through the prompting of secret inspiration; and at last he is blessed by him with the reward of eternal recompense.

You now have, in our dawn, the end of sleep; see now the beginning of work. The beginning of work in the dawn is the example of the active life in Mary—an example most fitting for this purpose [Col. 0248D]. In her are found to have shone three kinds of active life, of which the first may be called joyful, the second diligent, and the third tearful. To the first belong those services which the blessed Virgin rendered during the Saviour’s infancy: carrying him in her arms, nursing and feeding him, wrapping him in swaddling clothes—all of which were pleasant, sweet, and full of joy. To the second kind of activity belong the purification in the Temple, the offering of victims, the visitation of Elizabeth, the journey into Egypt, and such things, which no one can doubt were full of care and labour. To the third belong those works of Mary that were full of sorrow and misery: for example, standing by him when crucified, mourning him when dead, fleeing persecutions, and other things like these [Col. 0249A].

Therefore, you who wish to be active but cannot attain the first kind of active life because it is above you, nor the third because it is bitter, should at least attempt the middle kind, which we have called diligent. And with blessed Job be an eye to the blind, a foot to the lame, a father of the poor, and a comforter of orphans (Job 23). See whether you have compelled the pilgrim Christ to enter; whether you have mercifully regarded the blind beggar beside the road; whether you have not, like the priest and Levite, passed by the wounded man who fell among robbers; whether you have spent your coins upon his care. For these are Christ’s weak members, through whom God wishes to work salvation for you, and to bestow consolation upon them through you.

Certainly, it commonly happens that we apply softer fomentations and greater medical care to a limb touched by wound, fracture, burning, or bruise [Col. 0249B]. So it is with Christ and the Church: he wishes his weaker members to be cherished with greater service. Thus in vain does a person boast of cloistered silence, of the burden and heat of the day, of prayers and supplications, if he does not know how to bend with compassionate affection toward the needs of others. Nor does it disdain to be Anna with Peninnah, Rachel with Leah, John with Cephas, Mary with Martha, the right hand with the left, or the contemplative with the active life—both of which were present in outstanding measure in the blessed Virgin Mary, our dawn.

For contemplation is that serenity which appeared with our dawn. It is compared to clear weather because it is tranquil and peaceful, dwelling in silence and far removed from the disturbances of the world. Hence it was said that Mary chose the best part, which shall not be taken from her [Col. 0249C]. He called it “best,” perhaps not happier, but sweeter; for good is sometimes called sweet, and accordingly the comparative expression must be understood as preferential, not comparative. Thus contemplation is sweet, whereas activity is rather laborious and burdensome.

What may instead trouble us is the addition, “which shall not be taken from her.” For as the mind’s affection when desiring a thing differs from its affection when possessing the thing itself, so the experience of a fruit differs while it is smelled from when it is tasted. As the imaginary vision of one asleep differs from the immediate vision of one awake, so the contemplation of this life, which is in a riddle, differs from that of the future life, which will be in direct vision. Therefore, as faith will be done away with, so hope will not exist in the future [Col. 0249D]; and as knowledge will be destroyed, so too the contemplation of this life will be taken away. Accordingly, the statement that it “shall not be taken from her” concerns the state of the present life, not the future.

For contemplation pertains to God, while activity pertains to one’s neighbour. In this life the active life may be taken away, because the capacity and opportunity for doing good to one’s neighbour may fail; but in this life contemplation cannot be taken away, because in whatever condition of this life a person may be, that person has the ability to contemplate God.

Or, if we wish to refer the statement, “it shall not be taken from her,” to the state of the future life, let us posit three kinds of contemplation. The first two are taken away in this life; the third remains both in this life and in the future [Col. 0250A]. The first is in created things, the second in the Scriptures, the third in divine secrets. The first is of inquiry, the second of illumination, the third of wonder.

The first occurs when the Creator is sought through creatures and the invisible things of God are perceived by understanding through the things that have been made. Even the philosophers of the nations possessed this mode of contemplation, as Aristotle did, who in his theology, investigating the causes of things—indeed, the causes of causes—found one highest cause, of which there was no other cause, but which itself was the cause of all causes. Of it he said: “O Cause of causes, make me acceptable to you.”

The second, which is in the Scriptures, occurs when the mind is illumined either by reading unto knowledge or by praying unto devotion. The third occurs when the human mind, unable to comprehend by reason the ineffable mysteries of God, beholds and reflects upon things above itself in devout wonder: for example, that the Virgin who remained a virgin bore a son; that the Word of God assumed flesh; that the Immortal died; that the Eternal became temporal; and similar things, which are more wonderful to reason than plain [Col. 0250B].

The blessed Mary is recorded as having possessed this mode of contemplation when she said to the angel: “How shall this be, angel, since I do not know a man?” (Luke 1). She did not say this in doubt, but in wonder at the greatness of the matter. Perhaps Job too had this mode of contemplation when he said: “My soul has chosen hanging, and my bones death” (Job 7). For to choose hanging is to cling through wonder to heavenly secrets.

This is Mary’s best part, which shall not be taken from her even in the future life, where, the more familiarly she is admitted to the divine secrets, the more fervently she wonders at them. The first kind, which is in creatures, will be taken away because it belongs to imperfection—that is, it is partial. The third belongs to perfection: it is begun in this life and completed in the future, where there will be joyous wonder and wonderful joy, prepared for the co-heirs of Christ, who are enrolled in the kingdom of the saints. May Jesus Christ himself grant this to us, he whose kingdom and dominion endure for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XLIV. ON THE ASSUMPTION OF THE GLORIOUS VIRGIN MARY

“Return, return, Shulammite; return, return, that we may behold you” (Song 6). Today, most beloved brothers, she who is found in heaven and on earth is assumed to sit with God the Father, the blessed Mother of God having completed the contest of the world; and the festive choir of angels comes to meet her, while Mother Church follows her with praises [Col. 0250D].

Great indeed is the cause for joy, when the Son of God, the Word of the Father, has brought that beautiful queen among the choirs of virgins, chosen above all the tribes of Israel, into his wine-cellar, sharing with her the riches of the heavenly Jerusalem, in which reigns the King of kings and Lord of lords.

Yet I would not say that he is to be extolled with unequal praise, since he is abundant in riches, generous in goodness, eloquent in wisdom, terrible in power to all living beings, illustrious in lineage, desirable in beauty [Col. 0251A], incomprehensible in immensity, and unfailing in eternity; his dominion reaches from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth. Such a one therefore addresses such a one: he urges her to come, asks her not to delay entering his chamber, to return from earth to the court of heaven, from exile to her homeland, from death to life, from misery to glory.

But who is this singular Virgin, so pleasing to supreme Majesty that today she is assumed to sit with the eternal King and receives the diadem of a kingdom—indeed, the diadems of kingdoms—so that she may deservedly be called not only queen of the world but queen of heaven also?

She is Mary, most necessary to both kingdoms. This queen is wholly to be desired by the earth [Col. 0251B], who on the way of this world—indeed, amid the loss of this life—turns penitents to God by a threefold path: namely, by the intervention of reconciliation, by the example of imitation, and by the aid of protection. Thus, by interceding for the sinner, she obtains pardon; by her example, she shows the ignorant the discipline of living well; and by granting help to act bravely, she provides confidence.

O Mary, O star of the sea, you direct those who travel rightly, bring back those who wander, and restore those in peril to the harbour of salvation. You have rightly been called the star of the sea, since by a certain analogy, as that star was to benefit the sea, so you were to benefit the world. Indeed, that star of the sea of which we have spoken is found to surpass the other stars in three ways: in height, immovability, and the sharing of light.

In height, because it is set at the summit of the world and, as the head above the limbs, is raised above the other stars [Col. 0251C]. Hence the poet says: “This summit is always lofty to us; but black Styx and the deep shades see its opposite beneath their feet.” In immovability, because, being set as it were at the centre of the firmament, while the other stars by their varied motion sometimes tend toward setting, it remains unmoved. In the sharing of light, because while the others provide their light in turns, this one, without alternation and always with an equal ray, so far as lies in it, pours out brightness upon all living beings. This is said of the star; but the diligent investigator will find the same things in Mary.

For among all creatures that are in heaven and on earth she is higher, because the other saints, when they depart, are received into the choirs of angels according to the measure of their merit, whereas Mary is exalted by a certain surpassing majesty of glory above the choirs of angels [Col. 0251D]. Do you wish to see that Mary is higher than the other saints? Isaiah says: “I saw the Lord seated upon a high and exalted throne; the house was full of his majesty, and what was beneath him filled the Temple” (Isa. 2). Certainly I should rightly interpret this high and exalted throne as the Virgin’s womb, and the sitting of him who sits as the mystery of the Incarnation: “I saw,” he says, “the Lord seated upon a high throne.”

Consider, if you please, the Lord’s three sittings and three thrones corresponding to their number. His first sitting is the perfection of creation, of which it is said: “God rested on the seventh day from the work which he had accomplished” (Gen. 1) [Col. 0252A]. The second sitting is God’s dwelling in the rational mind, of which the Song says: “While the king was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance” (Song 2). The king is at his table when he settles upon the mind in the repose of contemplation; the nard gives fragrance when, through the sweetness of a good work, one’s neighbour is stirred to emulation of virtue. The third sitting is the Incarnation of the Word, of which it is said: “You have known my sitting down and my rising up” (Ps. 138).

The throne of the first sitting is the structure of this world; the throne of the second sitting is the soul of the righteous; the throne of the third sitting is the Virgin’s womb. The first throne is high because of the dignity of its creation; the second is exalted because of the prerogative of virtue; the third, that is, the chamber of the blessed Virgin, is super-exalted because of the union of the Word and humanity [Col. 0252B]. Beholding in the Spirit the height of this third throne, the prophet said: “I saw the Lord seated upon a high and exalted throne” (Isa. 2). Understand also “super-exalted,” and assign these three things to the blessed Virgin.

For she did not lack the dignity of creation, by which her throne was high; nor the prerogative of virtue, by which it was exalted through grace; nor the reception within herself of the Son of God, by which it was super-exalted. And the house—that is, the Church—was full of his majesty, because from his fullness we all receive; and the things beneath him who sat, or beneath the throne—that is, angelic and human nature—filled the Temple: that is, they completed that Temple, I mean, which had suffered ruin and was first made from the nine orders of angels [Col. 0252C].

Do you also wish to see the immovable star of the sea—I mean the blessed Virgin Mary? Turn your gaze, then, toward the other children of men, who fell through their own mutability, and you will be able to see how she remained unchanged and immovable. For by a fourfold motion man was moved from his stability: through pride, inconstancy, impenitence, and impatience. He was moved through pride when, as a transgressor, he despised God’s command; through inconstancy when he succumbed to the serpent’s temptation; through impenitence when he stubbornly excused his sin; through impatience when he rebelliously murmured amid the scourges of divine vengeance.

Will Mary not appear to you free from all these things? If you consider her purpose, her action, or her soul [Col. 0252D], she is indeed that immovable castle into which Jesus entered when a certain woman named Martha received him into her house (Luke 10). This castle stands immovable by a fourfold strength: ditch, river, wall, and hill. These are what render every fortification unconquered and immovable—much more that castle which Jesus entered, intending to defeat the prince of this world and the armed strong man.

In the ditch, where the excavated earth slopes together, the virtue of humility is signified, as Isaiah says: “Enter into the rock; hide in the ditch from the face of the Lord’s wrath and from the glory of his majesty” (Isa. 2). In the river, which spreads itself broadly, is understood the breadth of zealous good work, as Job says: “He searches out the depths of rivers and brings hidden things to light” (Job 28) [Col. 0253A]. The firmness of the wall is the integrity of virginity, as Ezekiel says: “I saw, and behold, a wall round about the house on every side” (Ezek. 40)—whose house, if not that which above we called a castle? For the power of God entered the virginal hall without breaking down the wall of her chastity. In the height of the hill is the sublimity of heavenly desire and devotion, as Isaiah says: “Go up upon a high mountain, you who bring good tidings to Zion” (Isa. 40).

O strong castle, immovable castle, where humility conquers pride, work sloth, integrity corruption, and the devotion of holy desire vanity. Yet it will appear still more wonderful to you if you consider the inhabitants of this castle: namely, Martha and Mary. Martha, then, a citizen of this castle, is solicitude for good work; Mary is the sweetness of divine inspiration. Martha’s house is a pure conscience, so that no discord may intrude into work; Mary’s house is tranquillity of mind, so that it is not embittered by any outward disturbance [Col. 0253B]. Jesus entered this castle when he assumed flesh in the Virgin; he is received by Martha into her house when the Virgin’s conscience is formed by zeal for good work.

Let us now see the third privilege of the star of the sea: how it surpasses the other stars in the sharing of light.
