This seems first to pertain to the fact that the other saints grant aid to mortals in differing ways [Col. 0253C]. For they can benefit those more whom they have specially received, by a certain right of patronage: thus Peter at Rome, the martyr Thomas at Canterbury, Victor at Marseilles, Martin at Tours, and similarly in other cases. For any saint can do more in the court of the Most High for his own king than for a stranger.

Mary, however, as she is queen of all, is also patroness of all; and, so far as lies in her, she shows herself equally ready to be entreated by all, she who received above all others the fullness of dignity. Therefore she illumines those far away by the ray of mercy; those who are near—that is, religious persons—by the sweetness of consolation; and those who are with her in the homeland by the excellence of glory. For whether righteous persons or sinners entreat Mary, whether angels or archangels look toward Mary [Col. 0253D].

Such, then, is that beloved of the Beloved whom the Son of the highest King calls into his embrace, saying: “Return, return, Shulammite,” and so forth. But why does he call her by the word “return” repeated so often, or from where does he call her? The force of the word seems to indicate one banished far away in exile, who, as though returning to her homeland, receives both consolation in captivity and its end. Hence in the same passage she is called *Sunamitis* [Shulammite], which is interpreted “captive.”

Nor would it be inappropriate to say that she is called back from exile, since human nature, so long as it journeys away from the Lord, is condemned to a fourfold exile. I see, first, the exile of suffering; second, of pleasure; third, of vanity; fourth, of curiosity [Col. 0254A]. A sound mind will rightly declare that in the exile of suffering a beast has something more than a human being. For when a beast first begins its life, it in some way governs itself, treads the earth and walks upon it, is clothed in its natural covering, and receives the sufficiency of its nature without another’s aid. By contrast, a man born of woman is cast upon the earth powerless over himself, naked in body, needing another’s assistance, burdened with sins, empty of virtue, and full of every misery.

Would that its own evil were enough for this exile, so that it might not be cast still more miserably into the exile of pleasure. For, surrounded by so many miseries of the first exile, it seeks through pleasure to compensate for what it suffers, so that, while the body is soothed by pleasure, the burden of suffering that it bears may become more tolerable [Col. 0254B]. Therefore it wishes to be clothed in costly garments, to rest upon a soft bed, to have exquisite dishes, to overflow in unlawful desires, to speak buffooneries, and to do shameful things—as if it said with the pagan: “Jupiter decreed that whatever was useful was pious.”

But, O most wicked person, you who meditate day and night upon Jupiter’s law: what do you say about the commands of Jesus, which forbid every saying, act, or desire contrary to God’s law? To a perverse heart this is a lesser concern.

But behold, the third exile follows, which casts a person still farther from God: namely, the exile of vanity, when one begins to seek outside oneself, among this world’s vanities, things with which to satisfy one’s pleasure. Then come the forerunners of death [Col. 0254C]: possessing superfluities, loving transitory things, being driven by popular favour, seeking honours, despising poverty, and praising the fortunes of kings. Yet Solomon says: “A poor and wise child is better than a foolish king” (Eccl. 4), because the former sometimes proceeds from prison and chains to a kingdom, while he who was born in a kingdom is sometimes consumed by want.

Attend, therefore, ambitious and proud person, how fittingly Solomon’s judgment condemns you: namely, that a poor and wise child—that is, any innocent, poor-in-spirit, and peaceable person—may emerge from the prison of subjection and the chains of obedience to the kingdom of prelacy, or rather to the kingdom of perfected virtue; while you, born through regeneration into the kingdom of virtues, voluntarily cast down, are consumed by the poverty of vices [Col. 0254D]. For if one is poor in spirit, is one not thereby worthy of the kingdom? Surely, as the same Solomon says: “The lizard supports itself with its hands and dwells in kings’ houses” (Prov. 30).

Now the *stellio* is a creature that cannot be raised on high by the aid of wings, but nevertheless crawls upward on its feet to make its dwelling in the towers of kings. So every humble person, small in his own eyes, is not raised aloft by the wings of pride, ambition, or even secular learning; yet by crawling with his hands—that is, by working humbly—he is in kings’ houses, that is, in the fellowship of the saints.

The fourth and last exile of the soul is the evil of curiosity. For when the mind has become attached to many vanities, superfluous care follows, and it investigates what Solomon finds most difficult: now the way of the eagle flying in heaven, now the way of the serpent upon the earth, now the way of a ship in the sea, now the way of a man in his youth (ibid.) [Col. 0255A]. The vice of curiosity seems especially occupied with these four things. By the eagle flying in heaven is meant the contemplative person; by the serpent upon earth, anyone slippery and criminal; by the ship on the sea, the merchants of the world; by the youth of a man, the beginning of a good manner of life.

Those who pursue superfluous concerns therefore seek quarrels among religious persons, that they may accuse them; excuses among the criminal, that they may justify them; advantages in secular business affairs, that they may do like things; and instability among the newly converted, that they may overthrow them [Col. 0255B]. Thus, while they expend themselves wholly on superfluous concerns, they bestow no care upon themselves or upon Providence concerning what is outward.

On account of these four exiles of the soul, therefore, the blessed Mother of God is commanded by a fourfold summons to return, when it is said: “Return, return, Shulammite,” and so forth. But should she be believed to have been exiled in the ways described above, especially by pleasure, vanity, and curiosity? Far be it. For she is called from these exiles not because of defilement, but because her dwelling with God, made as it were one spirit through heavenly desire, counted it captivity to dwell with the inhabitants of Kedar and to be delayed from that crown of glory which she knew was laid up for her [Col. 0255C].

Or the word of recall is repeated four times because, if we attend carefully, four kinds of assumption befit the blessed Virgin. First, she was assumed by election; second, by purification; third, by confirmation; fourth, by exaltation. She was assumed by election when Gabriel found the strong woman, long sought by Solomon, and chose her above all others, saying: “Blessed are you among women” (Luke 1). She was assumed by purification when, set apart from the other children of men, she was cleansed from original and actual sin by the purifying work of the Holy Spirit. She was assumed by confirmation when she received in her journeying state that same confirmation in virtues which the good angel possesses in the homeland [Col. 0255D]. She was assumed by exaltation today, when she was raised above every creature in the kingdom of heaven.

Shall I say that she was exalted with her body, or without it? Truly, I shall say: with her body. Even if I err in this point, the error itself is most pleasing to me, since it leans toward the fount of pity, the Mother of mercy, and is to be excused. Shall I say that the Son of God withheld honour from his mother which he would not refuse to grant to a servant? Elijah is lifted to heaven in a fiery chariot, and the Mother of God decayed in the tomb? Moreover, if, after her holy spirit departed, the earth held her most sacred body, why did her Son refuse on earth that veneration for his mother’s remains which he wished to be shown to any martyr or confessor?

Indeed, he wished the head of John or the relics of any other saint to be held in the greatest veneration upon earth; but did he judge the body of the blessed Virgin worthy neither of veneration on earth nor honour in heaven [Col. 0256A]? Did not the Son of God give this command: “Honour your father and mother”? And this applies more to father and mother than to others, because greater honour ought to be shown them than to others. Yet according to those who think that she did not depart with her body, he himself seems especially to have acted contrary to his own command: he wished the relics of a martyr to receive greater honour on earth than the most sacred body of his Mother.

Quite otherwise sounds that prayer of the universal Church in which it is said of her: “Yet she could not be held down by the bonds of death, she who gave birth from herself to our Lord Jesus Christ incarnate” [Col. 0256B]. If this is true, it follows that, death having been conquered, she ascended glorified with her body. And, to bring this discourse briefly to an end: since the debt of death has been discharged, let those who maintain that she was entrusted to the earth with her body either produce her as buried, or else, indeed, join us in venerating her as risen and exalted with her body, praying that through her intercession we may deserve to be transferred to the same blessedness of glory which she entered on this present day. May our Lord Jesus Christ grant this, he whose kingdom and dominion endure for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XLV. ON THE ASSUMPTION OF THE GLORIOUS VIRGIN MARY

“The Lord God had planted a paradise of delight from the beginning, in which he placed the man whom he had formed” [Col. 0256C]. Concerning the praise of today’s solemnity, most beloved brothers, you have long since learned many things carefully discussed, which flourish outwardly with the flower of words and are inwardly full of spiritual sweetness.

Therefore, to add something less worthy to such great praises may perhaps seem to some rather a detraction than an increase of praise—just as, if someone added the sound of a broken little bell to cymbals sounding harmoniously together, the sweetness of the melody would be impaired rather than helped. Yet, because we know that the riches of others cannot be defiled by our poverty—especially since in the tabernacle of the Lord some are recorded to have offered gold and silver, others hyacinth, purple, and fine linen, while some offered even goat-hair, things lowly and cheap—we offer to the Lord, from our meagre portion, what we can. Content with the sacrifice of the poor, we judge that the gift has sufficiently befallen us if we are found occupied, with however small a devotion, in praising the Virgin Mother.

But, to return to the word we set forth, the diligence of Sacred Scripture mentions three paradises of delight made for humankind. The first is the earthly paradise, of which it is written: “Lord, I heard your voice in paradise, and I hid myself” (Gen. 3). The second is the paradise of the present Church, of which the Song says: “Your shoots are a paradise of pomegranates” (Song 4). The third paradise is that of future glory, which Paul mentions when he says that he was caught up into God’s paradise and there heard secret words which it is not permitted for a human being to speak (2 Cor. 12) [Col. 0257A].

In the first paradise created humanity was placed; in the second, restored humanity was placed; in the third, glorified humanity is to be placed. These are three paradises, as it were three gardens of delights, in which the fruits of divine planting grow, ripen, and are gathered. For if we recall the beginnings of the human race—its first parents, that is—they were certain shoots of divine planting in the earthly paradise, placed there so that they might grow and, by doing good, bear fruit in service to their Creator.

But after these shoots withered through the merit of the first transgression and bore harmful fruit, they were transplanted into the paradise of the Church [Col. 0257B], so that, as the fire of charity shone down upon them like a certain summer sun, they might grow and bring their fruit to maturity, and then at last, through the hand of the highest gardener, who is Christ, be transplanted with their fruits into the third paradise, which is glory. For in this paradise God placed man from the beginning—that is, he ordained that he should be placed there, in the manner of speech by which things yet to come are said to have been made, and the Lamb is said to have been slain from the beginning of the world.

But because these shoots could not grow without moisture, the four rivers of paradise came to them, by whose irrigation they might grow stronger, so that, firmly rooted, they could thereafter be moved by no wind of temptation. Understand the first river of paradise as the cleansing of the sacraments; the second as the sequence of the divine Scriptures; the third as the dripping of spiritual gifts—tears; the fourth as the gifts of graces, which confirm in good works [Col. 0257C].

Human nature, infected with vices, first needed to be cleansed from sins through the Church’s sacraments. Second, because it did not know the way of righteousness, it needed to be enlightened through God’s commands. Third, after receiving knowledge of truth, it needed to exercise itself in good works by mourning and tears. Fourth, it needed to be confirmed in good by gifts of grace.

Among the shoots of that paradise there sprang up a certain noble branch, namely the Virgin Mary. To her the river of spiritual charisms flowed more abundantly than to the rest, since she was to bring forth a fruit better and loftier than all others, by which human beings on earth and angelic spirits in heaven would be fed [Col. 0257D]. For what else were the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit, fullness of grace, fervour of faith, and virginal chastity than certain droplets of graces descending upon her, so that she might grow and bear fruit? She grew, therefore, and bore fruit; and grew so greatly that she is now called not a lowly branch but a lofty and fruit-bearing tree: lofty because she ascended above the heavens; fruit-bearing because she produced manifold fruit—bitter fruit, sweet fruit, and delightful fruit.

If you wish to know where this tree brought forth bitter fruit, recall those most bitter afflictions which she endured: when she stood by the Crucified One, when she saw him dead [Col. 0258A], when she followed him fleeing into Egypt, and when she endured persecutions with the others who imitated his ways. In all these she produced bitter fruit, when through these and many other tribulations she followed the presence of her Creator.

All the saints who now reign with Christ tasted this bitter fruit. Their life was to despise the world, endure adversities, crucify their flesh with its vices and desires, and be filled with reproaches. Although all these things were full of bitterness, they expected in them the most peaceful fruit: the vision of their God.

But this laborious path of seeing God through the bitterness of this life has now been reduced to solitude, because people now flee from the face of the Lord so that they may escape bitter things, lest they encounter tribulations, and may obtain pleasures and the sweet things of this life [Col. 0258B]. They make little account of seeing the good things of the Lord in the land of the living, while they enjoy this life’s consolations. Is it not truly to flee from the face of the Lord to reject God’s commands, follow desires, loosen the reins of chastity, and restrain the mind from no pleasure? In all these things the taste is sweet at the beginning, but their end is bitter as wormwood, because many miseries follow many pleasures, and the final outcome of joys is changed into mourning and pain.

For when a person has first set out good wine and has been made drunk with it, then at last follows what is worse. The good wine that a person—that is, any carnal person—sets out is the beginning of that person’s joy: the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, the pride of life, and the other pleasures of this life. But when that person has been made drunk by these—that is, when he has drunk the cup of confusion and disgrace to its dregs—then follows the worse wine [Col. 0258C]. What wine is that? The sting of an evil conscience, fear of hell, dread of the strict Judge, hardening of the mind, and despair of salvation. Behold the sweet things of this life; behold the bitter things. Fear, therefore, to touch the sweet if you wish to avoid the bitter.

For in this way fish, birds, and beasts are caught: a small morsel that delights is placed upon a hook or snare, so that, once they seize it, they may afterwards be held by the bitterness of the iron or binding. Take care, then, lest, baited by the deceptive food of this life, you be held captive. And if this is so, loosen the bonds from your neck, lament your misery, and run to the remedy.

Who, indeed, falls into such foolishness of degenerate nature as not to judge the better thing to be chosen when offered a choice of two? Let these two things now be proposed: the bitterness of this life and its pleasure. The philosopher of the world teaches you which of them should be considered better. For according to Aristotle’s teaching, if there is doubt as to which is better, one must look to the consequence of each; and that whose consequence is better must also be judged better. See, then, what follows from this life’s pleasure. It is certain that everlasting mourning follows; hence it is written: “Mourning occupies the end of joy” (Prov. 14). But eternal joy follows the bitterness of this life [Col. 0259A], as it is said: “Your sorrow shall be turned into joy” (John 16). Joy is better than everlasting mourning; therefore the bitterness of this life is to be chosen rather than its pleasure.

Therefore the sweet things of this life must in every way be fled, since their end is so bitter. Or, if sweet things delight, let those who desire such things put their hand to that fruit which is sweet to eat and necessary for refreshment.

Behold, our fruitful tree, namely the Virgin Mary, stretches out her branches, upon which they may find sweet fruit in greatest abundance—unless perhaps, with appetite weakened like sick people, they reject what is pleasant and sweet. For it commonly happens that bread is a punishment to an unhealthy palate, and light, beloved by clear eyes, is hateful to diseased ones. [Col. 0259B] The blessed Mother of God has bestowed three benefits upon us, to which, as to certain branches, all works of righteousness look, and from which depend the fruits of every spiritual exercise. The first benefit is that she removed from us the yoke of ancient captivity; the second, that she remitted for us the wrath of divine displeasure; the third, that she erased the stain of human iniquity. Behold: you were held captive, O man, and through Mary you were set free; you incurred the offense of your God, and through Mary you were reconciled; you were unrighteous and a sinner, and through her you were justified. What is sweeter than freedom after captivity, and reconciliation after ungodliness? Therefore all the life of the righteous, holy desires, meditations, good works, acts of thanksgiving [Col. 0259C] look to this end: that in all these things the blessed Mother of God may especially be honored, she who, beyond the other saints, has wrought for us the cause of salvation. Now then, you who breathe amid such great benefits of the blessed Virgin, turn your vows and desires toward her; and let it be sweet for you to rest beneath the shade of that tree, since until now you have labored on the long road of a crooked manner of life.

There are three things that compel travelers to flee to the shelter of a tree: heat, whirlwind, and rain. Likewise, there are three things which take away peace of mind from those walking in the way of God: desire, pride, and discord. Heat corresponds to the burning of desire; the whirlwind to the swelling of pride; [Col. 0259D] rain to the quarrels of discord. Therefore the blessed Mother of God protects from the heat of desire by the example of chastity; she protects from the swelling of pride by the example of humility; she protects from the rain of discord by the example of gentleness. Certainly, the evils we have done can teach us how pleasant it is to rest beneath the branches of this tree, how shameful it is to be oppressed by the servitude of the devil, and how sweet it is to render obedience to God.

For as a sailor, tossed by many waves, becomes wiser in steering his vessel, and a soldier, after receiving many wounds, becomes more cautious in the clash of battle: so calm weather is more welcome after rain, rest after labor, and through experience of evils love of the virtues grows. Let us look to those who have put their hand to the sweet fruit of the spiritual life, and we shall see that what we say is true. [Col. 0260A] Some of them, after perhaps committing many crimes in the world, were converted to God; others, in the very innocence of life which they maintained, offered themselves to God as a sacrifice. And we see that those who were sinners in the world, and great sinners, are often more ready in vigils, more sparing in abstinence, more devout in prayer, more diligent in good work, and more watchful in every fruit of spiritual life, than those who, glorying in the purity of their conscience, have never fallen from the path of righteousness. Therefore let no one fear to put his hand to the sweet fruit of spiritual life, since a good attained later is sometimes held more fervently when it has been acquired.

[Col. 0260B] There is also a third fruit of this tree, which above we called delightful; and it is perhaps delightful because it is rare, because it is precious. Since this fruit is gathered at the tops of the branches, the one who feeds upon it must ascend on high, so that what is mortal in him may be swallowed up by life, what is lowly may be changed into glory, and what is sad into joy. For the other fruits—that is, the bitter and the sweet, which we distinguished above—are close to the earth, since those who still wear the body of this death feed upon them. But the delightful fruit, which the blessed alone enjoy, is above, in the attainment of heavenly happiness: that which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart. And indeed, to those who still wander from the Lord in this mortal life, [Col. 0260C] this fruit of future blessedness has been promised in hope. But to those who, when the course of this life is completed, have overcome the world, it is now set before them in reality, so that, according to the promise made by the Lord, they may be heirs indeed of God and fellow-heirs of Christ in the heavenly paradise—of Christ, I say, who is the blessed fruit, the uniquely delightful fruit, in whom are all the delights of the saints who with the blessed Virgin Mary have been assumed into the paradise of heaven. May Jesus Christ our Lord himself make us sharers in it, whose kingdom and dominion endure unto ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XLVI. ON SAINT AUGUSTINE

[Col. 0260D] “The oxen were ploughing, and the she-asses were feeding beside them” (Job 1).

In prudently managing his household affairs, the master of the house diligently procures what agriculture requires, so that, when the soil has been cultivated by care and labor for fruitfulness, he may avert the want of the coming season by yearly fertility.

Oxen and ploughs are especially necessary for this work. When he has tilled the land with them, “the sower goes out to sow his seed,” so that in due season one portion may yield thirtyfold, another sixtyfold, another a hundredfold (Matt. 13). But if, according to evangelical truth, the seed is the word of God and the sower is Christ, then we may fittingly understand the land as human hearts and the stewards of God’s word as Augustine and the other teachers of the Church. [Col. 0261A] For there are four features of an ox by which it is rightly compared to the teachers of the Church. It feeds with its flesh, protects with its hide, fights with its horn, and enriches sterile soil with its dung. The flesh is the rendering of due humanity; the hide, the safeguard of disciplined conduct; the horn, the rigor of ecclesiastical severity; the dung, the word of just rebuke. These four things are necessary to a teacher of the Church.

First, yielding to those beneath him through an affection of humanity, he should strive to feed them rather than oppress them, to govern rather than plunder them; and, by a certain carnal affection, be little with the little, weak with the weak, all things to all, that he may gain all for Christ. The safeguard of disciplined conduct is also necessary, by which he may both govern himself and shape the conduct of others by a good example: [Col. 0261B] so that there may be seriousness in his countenance, moderation in his dress, gravity in his walk; truth may shine forth in his word and usefulness in his work; and nothing may be done in all that concerns him which offends anyone’s sight, but only what befits his holiness. For blessed Gregory also says of teachers themselves: “They ought to know, from the office which they have undertaken, that they have acquired not license to sin but the necessity of living well.”

There are, moreover, two horns with which a teacher of the Church ought to fight. The first is the authority of divine law; the second, the severity of penal punishment. With the first horn—that is, the authority of divine law—heretics outside the Church must be struck down: “They went out from us, but they were not of us.” With the second horn—that is, penal severity—the obstinate and rebellious who are with us [Col. 0261C] must be punished within the Church.

The word of just rebuke is also necessary, by which the vices and excesses of those who walk disorderly are corrected, so that the sinful earth, fertilized by the word of rebuke as by a kind of dung, may become more fit to bear the fruit of good work. For it is written: “The sluggard shall be stoned with the dung of oxen” (Ecclus. 22). To stone the sluggard with ox-dung means nothing other than, through the teachers of the Church, to assail the sinful soul with reproaches, bring its vices to remembrance, oppose its habits, and rebuke its life, so that, filled with shame, it may from such harassment receive both understanding and the form of holy conduct. These teachers, then, must be bound to the plough of evangelical doctrine by the bonds of wisdom; being so bound and made the pattern of their flock, [Col. 0261D] they cannot turn aside either to the right or to the left.

There are four bonds of wisdom by which teachers of the Church ought to be bound: love of holiness, zeal for righteousness, humility in prosperity, and constancy in adversity. Of these bonds it is written in the book of Jesus son of Sirach: “My son, put your feet into the fetters of the Lord, and do not be vexed by his bonds”; and afterward, concerning the bonds of wisdom, it adds: “For there is beauty of life in her, and in her bonds a binding of salvation” (Ecclus. 6). The first bond, love of holiness, makes teachers of the Church peaceable with the good, and this bond binds sweetly. The second, zeal for righteousness, makes them severe with the perverse, [Col. 0262A] and this bond binds strongly. The third, humility in prosperity, makes them gracious in tranquility, and this bond binds gently. The fourth, constancy in adversity, makes them tested in temptation, and this bond binds firmly.

When they are thus joined to the Lord’s plough, the master of the house follows—that is, Christ, who directs them—with a song in his mouth and holding a goad in his right hand, so that by the sweetness of the song, promising eternal goods, immortal life, and unending glory, he may lighten their labor. This is the sweetness of that song. And by the prick of the goad—that is, by the threat of eternal punishment and unquenchable Gehenna—he may make the sluggish more laborious. You would see these oxen, thus harnessed to the Lord’s plough, strongly cultivating uncultivated and unfruitful ground. No character of the land delays them: neither flower, nor greenery, nor any other pleasant feature prevents them from cutting through and overturning everything, that they may produce fruit; indeed, the more pleasant such things appear, the more vigorously they endeavor to uproot them.

[Col. 0262B] Therefore you, unfruitful and barren ground—you, I mean, sinner—prepare yourself, even late, to bear fruit; willingly receive these ploughing oxen and hear the voice of your watchmen saying to you: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass” (Isa. 40). Let not the flower of earthly prosperity now delight you; nor the greenery of deceptive youth; nor the pleasantness of rank in this world. All these things often contribute more to the accumulation of damnation [Col. 0262C] than to the fruit of salvation. For if in such things any appearance of happiness is seen, it is deceptive, painted over, artificial, and quickly passes away—or rather, it does not pass away until first it has infected its lover with the enormity of crimes and deadly poison.

Consider, I beg you, and call back to mind what you have often heard and seen: places that are flowery and pleasant are often less suitable for fruit. Indeed, beneath the appearance of flowers there sometimes lie hidden scorpions, lizards, and serpents; and while you wish to pick a flower, you will tread upon a serpent. Therefore, if the delight of a flower refreshes you, let the suspicion of poison terrify you, because a pleasure comparable to the danger of poison must especially be shunned. And if beneath this flower you have sometimes experienced poison, beware, and be vigilant lest something worse happen; [Col. 0262D] for even little fish more cautiously avoid baits in which they have at some time discovered the burning point of a deceitful hook. But if you still live innocently amid the pleasures of this world, let the examples of many who have perished through such things instruct you—let examples instruct you, I say—for when a pestilent person is scourged, the wise person is always corrected, and blows are felt less on another’s back.

Do you believe that it is as I say? Or do you still wish to be taught by an example how shadowy the happiness of this world is, and how miserable its end? Look upon a merchant ship crossing the sea in great pride. You see it rich in merchandise and luxuries, carefully equipped with sail and oars, wisely steered by the diligence of sailors, and fearing no danger threatening it. And behold: as the wind breaks forth, the sea is troubled; rising storms dash against that ship, and the sea swallows it in the deep, so completely that no sign of the ship appears to those looking upon the surface of the sea. [Col. 0263A] Do not those seem rightly compared to this ship who are consumed in the pleasures of this life, who have reckoned their portion to be the use of luxuries and the enjoyment of good things, without considering the judgment of death and the coming of the glory of the great God? Therefore they descended into the depths of hell without remembrance of their own name. And if any memory of them remains, it remains not in blessing but in curse.

Therefore, because the beautiful things of this world do not advance the fruit of life, cut them down and root them out utterly, so that your soil may bear fruit, yield many crops, and manifest in you the strength of the laboring ox; for, as Solomon says, “Where there are very abundant crops, there the strength of the ox is evident” (Prov. 14).

Yet even when you wish to make your land fruitful, consider what fruit you should produce in it. For not every soil suits one and the same fruit: this soil produces one fruit better, that another. There is rough and uncultivated soil, suited to barley, on which servants feed; there is delicate soil, suited to wheat, on which masters feed; and there is middling soil, suited to mixed grain, on which those feed who have neither risen to the luxuries of masters nor been cast down to the condition of servants. [Col. 0263B] Rough and uncultivated ground means sinners called late to repentance; delicate ground means contemplative men; middling ground means active men. Again, understand barley as the labors of repentance; wheat as the fruit of the contemplative life; mixed grain as works of mercy.

Rough ground, therefore, ought to yield barley, because sinners must be burdened with the labors of repentance—namely, vigils, fasts, and other disciplines; for “a load and straw are due to an ass, a rod and work to a servant.” Delicate ground ought to yield wheat, because contemplative men ought to produce the fruits of the contemplative life: to pray, read, meditate, and the like. Middling ground ought to bear mixed grain, because active men ought to perform works of mercy: feeding [Col. 0263C] the needy, clothing the naked, and so forth, as are described in the Gospel (Matt. 25).

It is clear, unless I am mistaken, how the things said concerning the properties of an ox apply to the venerable Father Augustine. There is still another characteristic of the ox which may be assigned more particularly to Augustine. An ox brings back into its mouth food that has been swallowed and, by chewing the cud, grinds it more finely in order to make it more nourishing. This repeated chewing of the cud is the manifold and subtle investigation of the Scriptures. In this Augustine surpassed the other teachers of the Church. For by a fourfold series of writings, as by the four rivers of Paradise, he watered the face of the earth. If you wish to distinguish them by names, one may be called natural, another juridical, [Col. 0264A] another speculative, and another disciplinary.

The natural pertains to the liberal arts, all of which, except grammar and rhetoric, are natural, because they adhere together through a certain natural connection of things. The juridical is rhetoric, which pertains to the law of the court and disputes in legal cases; concerning Augustine it was said in this regard that he taught his pupils deceits without deceit. The speculative is that by which he taught scholars the truth of divine law. The disciplinary is that by which he taught those in monasteries the virtue of religious life. The first two are handmaids, whereas the following two are mistresses, because the former teach a person to know, but the latter to live.

From these very diverse studies Augustine left diverse pursuits to his imitators. For [Col. 0264B] some learn to live well and not to know; others always learn to know and never to live well; others learn both to know and to live. Those who learn to live and not to know are holy and simple men, more desirous of holiness than of knowledge, because “in much knowledge there is much indignation.” Thus they learn humility from one person, patience from another, gentleness from another. One teaches them silence, another seriousness, another frequent service; and so, trained in the school of virtues, they write the law of the Lord—undefiled and converting souls—on their hearts by virtues, not by letters.

These, unless I am mistaken, are the she-asses of whom it was said: “The oxen were ploughing, and the she-asses were feeding beside them.” Such persons are she-asses because, entering the Lord’s vineyard at the first hour of morning, they bear the burden and heat of the day without [Col. 0264C] murmuring and pretense. They are she-asses because, patient under injuries, they endure all things for him to whom they have proved themselves. They are asses because, content with the lowest abasement, they rejoice to be cast down in the house of God; indeed, they receive in this the answer of conscience if they seem inferior to all.

But those who always learn to know and to live well are those who, puffed up with empty philosophy, delight that they have subtly investigated many things: kinds of problems, angles of syllogisms, the arrangement of the earthly globe, the summit of the elements, the beginning and ending of times, changes of alternation, the course of the year, configurations of the stars, the natures of animals, the rages of beasts, the force of winds, differences among shrubs, the power of roots, and [Col. 0264D] things of this kind. They establish the end of their studies in appearing to have grasped the causes of things with the penetrating eye of the mind. But that Cause of causes, which is the beginning and end of all things, they behold with a bleary—indeed, rather with a blind—eye; for it must be sought not by philosophizing but by living well. This kind of study, laid up for the righteous alone, they have not yet attained—unless perhaps we call “living well” that manner in which lost people speak in the world, saying that he lives well who feeds himself well; or that manner of speaking by which those are said to have a good age who omit nothing, so far as they can, of the pleasures of this life.

O that you who learn many things would at last teach yourself, and would begin to philosophize not from the summit [Col. 0265A] of heaven but rather from yourself, so that you may see what you are, what you ought to have been, and what you will be. For it is no small knowledge to know oneself, since from heaven came down the saying γνῶθι σεαυτόν, that is: “Know yourself.” Perhaps, if you are asked what you are, you will answer philosophically: “a rational mortal animal,” for this is the true definition of a human being. And behold: *animal* gives you the antiquity of sin; *mortal*, the necessity of punishment; *rational*, heavenly dignity. Therefore, when you hear “animal,” mourn your misery, because you are an animal and a sinner. When you hear “mortal,” fear eternal fire, because you will die shortly. When you hear “rational,” recall your dignity, because you were made in the image of God.

Hear and understand, O man, that you are called rational and mortal: rational pertains to life, mortal to death. Therefore, if you understand your own definition, death and life contend around you as to which of them you will rather belong to. [Col. 0265B] Therefore now philosophize wisely and be watchful whether you choose rather to be and be called a son of death or a son of life. And if you choose life rather than death, beware lest by living badly you depart from him who is the true life, he himself saying: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 10). Therefore, because it was necessary to do this also and not omit that, learn in such a way that you also live well; love wisdom in such a way that you do not lose righteousness. For although learning is good, living well is certainly more necessary.

So that we may hear together the conclusion of the matter: “Fear God and keep his commandments: this is the whole human being.” Therefore let us strive to bring the purpose of our study [Col. 0265C] and the progress of our life to this fulfillment: that knowledge may govern our life and life may preserve knowledge, so that, advancing in both, we may walk by the straight way to that eternal blessedness in which is fullness of knowledge and inestimable delight of life, which neither eye has seen nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of humankind, which God has prepared for those who love him. May our Lord Jesus Christ himself deign to grant this to us, whose kingdom and dominion endure unto ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XLVII. ON THE NATIVITY OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY

“I am like a beautiful olive tree in the fields, and like a plane tree exalted beside water in the streets” (Ecclus. 27).

[Col. 0265D] The feast of this day admonishes us to devote ourselves to divine praises and observances, on which God, the author of wonders, wished through the blessed Virgin to disclose to the world the mystery of eternal predestination and the truth of his promise. Therefore we must embrace with every desire of our heart the joys which make Mary’s birth a feast, so that we may not merely carry them in our bodies, but pursue them inwardly by the affection of the mind and outwardly by the testimony of good works. Otherwise we may be found like those who gladly watch theatrical games and performances, yet, judging them reprehensible by the judgment of reason because they rightly incur rebuke, have no desire to imitate them.

And what greater matter for spiritual joys can there be than that we have received the pledge of our redemption, which might wash away the offense of paternal transgression, restore innocence, appease the wrath of the strict Judge, open the gate of heaven, and grant freedom to captives? For in her is every grace of way and truth, and in her every hope of life and virtue. She is not like that mother who brought upon the face of the whole earth the fourfold decree of curse and woe, by which all Adam’s children are oppressed from the day of their birth until the day of their burial.

[Col. 0266A] If you do not recall the first woe by which human posterity was condemned through Eve, the weakness of bodily corruption brings it to your mind. The second is the distress of temporal afflictions. The third is the snares of the hidden enemy. The fourth is the anguish of final retribution. O impious mother Eve, who kill your daughters before you give them birth: why have you done this? Why have you brought great sin upon [Col. 0266B] yourself and upon them? But to you, blessed Virgin Mary, look the remedies for this ruin; you who were long ago promised in the Law and the Prophets and foreshown by many signs, so that at your birth sinners might place their hope of pardon, and, on the basis of the promise already made concerning you, might bear more patiently the weight of their misery.

Do you wish, then, O sinner, to hear Mary promised to you? Recall the rod of Jesse of which Isaiah speaks (Isa. 2), and behold: in it Mary’s birth is promised to you. Recall the ark of the covenant, covered with purest gold (Exod. 37), and in it Mary’s virginity is prefigured for you. Recall the flowering almond tree, of which Solomon speaks, and there Mary’s fruitfulness is signified for you. Recall Solomon’s litter, whose pillars were silver, its couch gold, and its ascent purple (Song 3); there Mary’s royal dignity is shown to you. Hence she is also compared to the olive tree because of the fullness of graces, in the chapter which we prefaced with these words: “Like a beautiful olive tree in the fields,” and so forth.

For if we examine the nature of the olive tree, it first fits the blessed Mary very elegantly in this respect: it is green in winter and summer, and loses none of the appearance of its greenness through any harshness of cold or storm, or even of summer heat. Summer, however, must be understood as the brightness of the life to come, just as the Lord says in the Gospel of trees: “When they put forth fruit of themselves, you know that summer is near.” It is compared to summer because when it comes, the clouds of our sorrow pass away and the days of life shine with the brightness of the eternal sun. [Col. 0266D] Winter, however, signifies the present life, which is bound by the cold of mortality and driven by the varied winds of temptations. Of it it is written in the Song of Songs: “For now the winter has passed; the rain has gone and departed.”

Therefore our olive tree retains its greenness both in summer and winter, because the blessed Virgin Mary, drenched in the moisture of spiritual graces, did not wither in the chill of the present life and received gloriously, above all the daughters of Eve, the loveliness of eternal life. In this olive tree consider together its branches, leaves, fruit, and oil. Its branches are righteous men, whom the Lord in the Gospel calls branches, when he says of the mustard seed, “It became a great tree, and the birds of heaven rested in its branches” (Matt. 13). [Col. 0267A] The branches, I say, are holy men, who by the imitation of virtue and the resolve of holiness have in some manner been grafted into the blessed Virgin, spread out on every side by the length of hope and the breadth of charity.

The leaves are words of evangelical truth, by which she herself taught the apostles and the other children of the nascent Church. These are the leaves of the tree of life of which the Apocalypse says that they are for the healing of the sick (Apoc. 22), because in the words of evangelical preaching there is medicine and salvation for sick souls. The fruits of this olive tree are works of the active and contemplative life: namely, bending the ears of God by prayers, taking part in divine secrets, feeding the child Jesus with milk, and similar things.

From this olive tree oil of diverse kinds flowed forth: oil of outpouring, oil of purity, oil of gladness, [Col. 0267B] and oil of anointing. The oil of outpouring, of which it is written, “Your name is oil poured out” (Song 1), is the innocence of outward conduct by which others are invited to the good life. The oil of purity, of which Exodus commands that the purest oil from olive trees should burn in the tabernacle of the Lord (Exod. 27), is purity of good works. The oil of gladness, of which it is written, “God anointed him with the oil of gladness above his companions” (Ps. 44), is the fervor of charity. The oil of anointing, with which that bronze basin in which the priests washed themselves before entering the tabernacle is commanded to be anointed, is the affection of mercy and compassion (Exod. 40). For the bronze basin with water signifies repentance watered by tears. Therefore our olive tree—that is, the blessed Mother of God—distilled oil poured out for those living simply; purest oil for those working courageously; oil of gladness for those loving ardently; oil of anointing, that is, mercy, for sinners returning after their fall.

[Col. 0267C] You see, therefore, that this olive tree is beautiful in its branches, beautiful in its leaves, beautiful in its shoot, beautiful in its liquid. But why is it beautiful in the fields rather than in the forests? Because forests nourish thorns and briars; by their density of foliage they make shade which excludes the ray of the sun; and forest trees are in every way found less suited to human usefulness.

What, then, should we understand by forests except the wild minds of sinners, darkened by the gloom of vices, which shut out from themselves the sun of righteousness and, wholly barren of the fruit of good works, nourish briars and thorns? Their perverse consciences fear within themselves the enormity of crimes, above themselves the power of the Judge, and beneath themselves the cruelty of the torturer. In forests of this kind are found robbers, murderers, serpents, and scorpions—that is, an exceedingly great multitude of vices—so that no place for righteousness or approach to holiness can exist there. Therefore, lest you be found in this place of horror and vast desolation, level this forest into a field. Cut down those tall trees of vices which have grown up: the arrogance of worldly pride, the evil of ambition, the flame of lust, the wasting sickness of envy, and the other kinds of vice. Then, when the vices have been cut down, the even surface of the field—that is, a pure conscience—will appear; and so you may freely look upon this olive tree [Col. 0268A] and behold Mary without cloud.

Fields, indeed, signify humble minds, leveled from the swelling of worldly conduct through fear of divine judgment, as in the words: “The mountains rise and the plains descend to the place which you founded for them” (Ps. 103). But perhaps you have not yet appeared in this field, because you remain still in the darkness of sins and the light of righteousness has not shone upon you. Yet even in your darkness look upon the blessed Mary with whatever gaze you can; think of her upon your bed and hold her in the memory of your heart. For even an object toward which the ray of the sun is not directly directed is sometimes illuminated by reflected light; and a weak conscience, untouched by the ray of inspiring grace, is sometimes changed for the better by the lives of the righteous and by the example of good works. For what else are the righteous who associate with the ungodly but lightning shining in darkness?

[Col. 0268B] “The righteous,” Scripture says, “will shine, and will run to and fro like sparks among reeds” (Wis. 3). This brightness—that is, the splendor of holiness—when directed toward the unrighteous, sometimes stirs up smoke in them, sometimes fire, sometimes darkness. It stirs up smoke when, by the example, they are ashamed within themselves, begin to blush for their crimes, and thus dissolve into tearful compunction (Song 3). For smoke signifies the compunction of holy minds, as in the words: “Who is this who comes up through the wilderness like a slender column of smoke from the fragrances of myrrh and incense?” At times, however, this brightness stirs up fire in sinners, when, upon hearing of that blessed life, they are set aflame as by a kind of fire with love for invisible goods. Concerning this fire Moses is commanded (Lev. 6) that it should be continual and perpetual upon the altar of the Lord.

[Col. 0268C] At other times this brightness also stirs up darkness in the reprobate, when, having seen the lofty conduct of the righteous, they despair of being able to ascend to it and are thus blinded by the darkness of despair. Of this darkness it is said in the Psalm: “He bowed the heavens and came down, and darkness was under his feet” (Ps. 17). For from fear of final retribution—which is rightly understood by the Lord’s feet—there arises in the minds of the reprobate the blindness of despair.

Therefore, as we have said, the righteous will shine and will run to and fro like sparks among reeds. Sparks signify holy men, who shine outwardly in good work and burn inwardly with charity. Reeds signify sinners, who, dried up from all moisture of the virtues, are rightly prepared by reason of their iniquity for eternal fires. But holy men run among the reeds like sparks, because, just as sparks of fire consume reeds and reduce them to ashes, so holy men by the example of a good life destroy what is animal and old in sinners and, applying the flame of charity, burn up the straw of vices.

[Col. 0268D] Thus the wicked placed among the good are like reeds beside sparks, and like dry streets beside waters. For ungodly people are those streets of which it is written in the lament of Jeremiah: “How the gold has become dim, the finest color changed; the stones of the sanctuary are scattered at the head of every street” (Jer. 4). Some of these streets are situated beside water. For there are many criminals who keep to the broad ways of this world but are at times pierced in heart, whether by words of holy exhortation, by gifts of virtue which they see in others, or by the tears and groans of true penitents.

Therefore, one who devoutly receives the exhortatory words of sacred Scripture, even though he does not abandon his former life, is placed beside the water of sacred speech, of which it is said: “He fed him with the bread of life and understanding, and gave him the water of saving wisdom to drink” (Ecclus. 15). One who reveres and loves in others gifts of grace which he does not possess in himself is placed beside the water of spiritual grace, of which it is said: “I will pour clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all [Col. 0269B] your defilements” (Ezek. 36). One who is ashamed and confounded in himself at the tears of penitents is placed beside the water of repentance, of which it is written: “Before I eat I sigh, and my groaning is like overflowing water” (Job 3). Thus they are streets, yet in a certain manner they are placed beside waters, because, although they keep to the broad ways of this life, since they revere and love God’s gifts in others, they become more capable and ready to receive grace.

You can now see how the Virgin Mother, who was previously compared to a beautiful olive tree in the fields, is like a plane tree raised up beside the water in the streets—that is, among those established there. The plane tree is a broad tree, with spreading branches and a very ample shade, a fitting shelter for those exhausted by the excessive heat of the sun. The shade of this plane tree is most certainly understood as nothing other than the incarnation of the Word, of which it is said: “The power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1). For, if we examine more closely the nature of a shadow, it is produced from light and a body. Therefore this plane tree cast its most abundant shade when the light of incorporeal divinity assumed, in the blessed Virgin, the body of our humanity. And the shade of this plane tree has been spread abroad in the streets, because she extends the help of her protection to all sinners and to all who groan beneath the burden of sin—to all, I say, who return after their fall and desire the way of salvation.

Consider now all the plants that have sprung from the root of mother Eve, and see whether any is so exalted as Mary, who, though equal to the rest by the condition of nature, has nevertheless been exalted above all by gifts and merits. We plainly see her exalted above all the daughters of Eve in three ways: by sanctification, through which she is raised above every inclination to earthly corruption; by fullness of knowledge, through which she is raised above every cloud of error; and by highest contemplation, through which she is raised above every tumult of worldly activity. Therefore, dearest brothers, since we cannot rise to this eminence of virtues, we must rest beneath her shadow, where we may obtain refreshment in the heat of vices, shelter amid the pressures of the world, and rest in all labours that make this life burdensome. Let him who is far away hasten to the shadow of her protection; let him who has already taken hold of it hold fast and not let go. For she is the guide of safety for pilgrims and leads those who arrive to the way of the harbour of salvation—may Jesus Christ our Lord grant this to us through her intercession, he whose kingdom and dominion endure for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XLVIII. ON THE FEAST OF ALL SAINTS

“Let lights be made in the firmament of heaven, and let them divide day and night; and let them shine in the firmament of heaven and illuminate the earth” (Genesis 1).

As we have learned from the holy Scriptures, all the works of the Lord bless him, since no creature is so lowly that it does not appear to contain the praise of God through some particular benefit. Yet God is blessed more excellently in the firmament of heaven, not only because it surpasses the other creatures, but also because, adorned with the multitude of stars and other lights, it wonderfully displays the wondrous power of God. These lights were placed in it not merely that they might shine there, but also that they might distinguish day from night and illuminate the earth.

Although in this visible firmament and its adornment we find much material for praise, I wish to turn the words set before us to the spiritual firmament and to the spiritual lights, in which the power and wisdom of God shine forth more brightly, so that they may be more fitting to today’s feast and may promote devotion. The firmament of which we wish to speak is the man Christ Jesus. As the firmament surpasses the other works of creation in beauty, magnitude, and loftiness, so he surpasses all other saints: in beauty, because “he is beautiful in form above the sons of men”; in magnitude, because he himself is the bound of his own greatness; and in loftiness, because he is “God above all, blessed for ever.”

Christ is also called the firmament because, as the blessed Gregory says, the firmament has the nature of water, which is constricted by frost into ice and afterwards solidified into crystal. So Christ as man, before the resurrection, was like water: through hunger, thirst, and many other infirmities—namely being born, suffering, and dying—he flowed away like water. Hence the Psalmist speaks in his person: “I am poured out like water, and all my bones are scattered” (Psalm 21 [22]). But after the resurrection he was made firm and solid like crystal, because he was impassible and immortal, as the prophet David says: “Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand, and upon the son of man whom you have strengthened for yourself” (Psalm 79 [80]). Hence the prophet Ezekiel calls him the firmament and says that it has the appearance of crystal, where he speaks thus: “Above the heads of the four living creatures was the likeness of a firmament, like the terrible appearance of crystal, stretched out above the heads of those four” (Ezekiel 1).

The lights of this firmament are all the saints, who are founded in him: first, in this life, by faith, hope, charity, and the other virtues which they have received from him; and, in that heavenly glory, they are rooted in him by the blessed enjoyment of the vision of him. Hence the Lord himself says: “He who remains in me, and I in him, bears much fruit” (John 15). And John says: “By this we know that we remain in him, because we have received of his Spirit” (1 John 4). And the Apostle: “Through him and with him and in him are all things” (Romans 11).

Therefore all saints are called lights or stars, as Paul says of them: “Among whom you shine as lights in this world, holding forth the word of life” (Philippians 2). And elsewhere: “Star differs from star in glory” (1 Corinthians 15). And in Job the Lord says: “Where were you when all the sons of God rejoiced with me, and the morning stars praised me?” (Job 38). They are called stars because, just as one star surpasses another now in beauty, now in brightness, now in redness, now in purity, so it is among God’s elect. Beauty commends virgins; brightness, confessors; redness, or the flame of charity, apostles and martyrs; while purity of spiritual nature makes angels more excellent.

Virgins are commended for beauty because in this life they preserved bodily modesty and chastity, keeping their garments white and staining them with no corruption of fleshly desire. Hence they are without blemish before the throne of God and follow the Lamb wherever he goes (Revelation 14). For he himself is beautiful and gladly looks upon, speaks to, touches, kisses, and binds in embraces those who are beautiful; and they, out of desire for the Beautiful One, follow him wherever he goes. In this life he sees them with the eye of election; he speaks to them by the promise of future blessedness; he touches them with the touch of divine inspiration; he kisses them with the kiss of inward love; he embraces them by the gift of heavenly contemplation.

Confessors, however, are stars brighter than the rest: through sound doctrine and the brightness of the word of God they enlightened those who were in the darkness of unbelief and led them to the light of ecclesiastical faith. They enlightened upwards, by teaching what rewards are laid up in heaven for the just; downwards, by showing what punishments await the ungodly in hell; on the right, by displaying the virtues and good works through which one advances toward life; on the left, when they taught people to avoid the crimes through which one descends to punishment. They enlightened behind, by teaching people to beware the wiles and deceits of the devil; ahead, when they taught us to despise the world with its pleasures.

These are those mountains of which the Prophet says: “You shine wondrously from the everlasting mountains; all the foolish of heart were troubled” (Psalm 75 [76]). For just as mountains first receive the brightness of the sun, and from the mountains it descends into the valley, so these everlasting mountains—that is, those who proclaim eternal life—shone wondrously, that is, with miracles accompanying them. They themselves, being loftier than the rest in life and merit, received the light of faith and then communicated that same light through their ministry to the weak and ignorant. Sprinkled with this light, the foolish of heart were troubled, marveling that eternal life, of which they had not heard, should be proclaimed. Nor did this light shine only in the valleys; indeed, it radiated everywhere, because their teaching is compared with lightning, which illuminates all around, as is said of the holy living creatures: “They went and returned in the likeness of flashing lightning” (Ezekiel 1).

The stars that burn more brightly and are more inflamed with the fire of charity are the apostles and martyrs. They were kindled with such fervour of the love of God that, just as a material flame consumes and reduces its fuel to ashes, so the flame of charity consumed them. This certainly happened when they gave their bodies over to punishments for God’s sake. Afterwards they were reduced to ashes by that same flame when, through a glorious death, they attained the end of this corruptible life, desiring to live with Christ. The fervour of charity that was eminent in the holy martyrs is compared to a flame because of this likeness.

For a flame sometimes burns by its heat; sometimes it blinds those who look at it by excessive brightness; sometimes it both illuminates and warms those nearby, by its light and heat. In like manner, because the apostles and martyrs burned with the flame of charity, persecutors and tyrants who inflicted penalties and tortures upon them were burned. For, while they tried to deprive them of life, they were first scorched in their souls by the fire of wickedness, and afterwards, by the just judgment of God, were wondrously and without remedy tormented in the fires of Gehenna. Others were made blind at the sight of that flame: though they saw the saints of God opening prisons, loosing chains, healing the sick, and raising the dead, they attributed this not to divine power but to magical arts. Thus, through the very occasion of light by which they ought to have been enlightened, they lost the light. But the rest, who devoutly revered their deeds and words, were enlightened by them to faith and kindled by their example to love.

I would rightly call the holy angels purer stars, since by virtue of their spiritual nature they surpass the other saints in subtlety. Thus the apostate angel, because in his original purity and subtlety he was more like God, was lifted up into pride and desired to have another likeness that was hostile to God, saying: “I will ascend into heaven; I will set my throne toward the north; and I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14). He wished to be like God in this: just as God had no dominion of any power above himself, so he too, freed from every dominion, refused to maintain toward God any regard of obedience.

Because of the likeness which his angels have with God, those who have attained greater purity always stand before divine contemplation. Others, who received less subtlety in their created condition, are sometimes sent to earth to carry out God’s works, as we read of the angel who rolled the stone from the entrance of the tomb (Matthew 28); of the angel who descended into the pool when the water was stirred (John 5); of the angels who wrought the burning of Sodom (Genesis 19); and in many other places. Others are sent to us to care for our salvation, suggest to us the good things we ought to do, and present our prayers before God. These are the princes who stand by those praying and lifting pure hands to God, of whom the Psalmist says: “The princes went before, joined with those singing psalms, in the midst of young maidens playing tambourines” (Psalm 67 [68]). Thus, because of their various offices, we may call some contemplative, some active, and some ministering spirits.

To these spiritual stars, which we have said are placed in the firmament that is Christ, I wish to add two others of wondrous beauty, one called the star of the sea, the other the morning star. The star of the sea is the blessed Virgin Mary, who guides and protects us upon the sea of this world and, by her merits together with her prayers, leads us to the harbour of salvation. Christ is the morning star, because just as the morning star rises at dawn and is a sign of the coming day, so Christ rose in the morning when he was the first to rise from the dead, and by rising he foreshadowed the coming day—that is, our resurrection.

Nor would I think that the moon and sun are lacking from the same firmament of which I have spoken, those great lights made to rule the day and night. The moon is the Church itself, of which it is said: “The sun and moon stood in their dwelling-place” (Habakkuk 3). And elsewhere: “He made the moon for its appointed times; the sun knows its setting” (Psalm 103 [104]). This moon is placed in the firmament because it is built and founded in Christ. The holy Church is rightly called the moon because, just as the moon receives light only from the sun, so the Church can have the light of virtue only from Christ. Nor do we doubt that the sun—that is, the power of divinity—is placed in the firmament already mentioned, since in Christ the man, according to the Apostle’s word, “the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Colossians 2).

But although I have called stars the saints reigning with Christ, on considering them more closely I can truly say that they are brighter than all stars. For, just as the light illuminating them, which is God, is brighter than every other light, so they, illuminated by that light, are brighter than other luminaries.

Indeed, in that heavenly kingdom has been fulfilled what he who sat on the throne said: “Behold, I make all things new” (Isaiah 43). For there the saints of God are renewed in reason, because they know God perfectly and therefore are without all error. They are renewed in will, because they have attained the full peace that comes from God and therefore love God without any disturbance. They are renewed in memory, so that they may always direct their affection toward God and therefore think of God without interruption.

Reason, I say, is renewed: it retains there only that knowledge by which the intellect is enlightened to know and the affection is kindled to love. In this life we see that, just as there is one sort of brightness without heat, which illuminates but does not warm, and another with heat, which both illuminates and warms, so it is with branches of knowledge. There are certain kinds of knowledge that enlighten the intellect but do not kindle the affection, such as the liberal arts, the doctrines of philosophers, and the like; these make one learned, not wise. There is another knowledge that enlightens the intellect and kindles the affection to love, such as knowledge possessed concerning God and the state of heavenly life. This alone is possessed and understood by the intellect of the saints, so far as its use is concerned. Every other knowledge, according to the Apostle’s saying, will there be destroyed, because secular forms of knowledge, even if perhaps they are to be possessed there in cognition, will nevertheless have no effect in those who know them.

The will too will be pacified in God from every alien disturbance, because neither worldly prosperity will trouble it through unsuitable joy, nor adversity through pressing distress, nor desire through seeking what it lacks, nor fear through dreading the loss of what it possesses. Of these four passions the philosopher says: “Drive out pleasures; drive out fear; banish hope; let there be no grief. The mind is clouded and bound by reins wherever these rule.” And the poet:

> Hence they fear and desire, grieve and rejoice, nor do they behold the air,
>
> shut within darkness and a blind prison.

And memory there will always be continuously occupied in remembering God. In this life it is exiled far from God and distracted by innumerable thoughts through the countless creatures of this world; but then, when all things of this world have been consigned to oblivion, it will love God alone and therefore meditate upon Jesus alone. Then, therefore, will be fulfilled what was said: “God will be all in all” (Colossians 3). For God will be brightness in reason, charity in will, and eternity in memory.

From this it is quite clearly gathered that the saints of God are not merely like stars but brighter than all stars. We therefore have the lights which God placed in the firmament of heaven to divide day and night, just as in the order of nature we see that the sun illuminates the day and the moon and stars the night. The night is understood as the present life, while the day is the future life. Thus the sun illuminates the day because God, who is the true sun, makes that blessed life brighter than present things; and, just as he himself is wholly light, so that life is wholly day, without any cloud of darkness.

The moon and stars illuminate this night when, in the present life, the holy Church and the saints of God—whether serving as soldiers or triumphant within it—illuminate it by miracles, instruction, and conduct, yet in a manner far different from the illumination of the day. For when night is illuminated, brightness appears in some manner dark and darkness bright; because in the present life neither goods can exist wholly without evils nor vices wholly without virtues, so that even the just appear in some manner bright and in some manner dark. For just as there is always a blemish in the moon, so there is in the Church. Hence it is that, because of the cloud of sin, we cannot clearly behold heaven and the lights of heaven; indeed, what is more grievous, sometimes we cannot even lift our eyes to heaven, where our hope ought to have been laid up, hindered by the cloudiness of sins.

Behold, many people who wish to look upon heaven and the bodily stars with bodily eyes cannot do so: either because they are bent over, or because an obstacle hinders them, or because they are deprived of light. I would call those bent over who, bowed by earthly desire, seek only transitory things and therefore, always fixing the eyes of their hearts upon the earth, cannot raise them to heavenly things. Certainly, just as love directs the eye toward the face, fear toward the hand, so desire always directs the eye toward the earth. For example, a son always looks toward the face of the father whom he loves; a servant looks toward the hand of his master, lest he be whipped for offences he has committed; but the greedy person always fixes his heart upon riches, since “where your treasure is, there also is your heart” (Matthew 6). The Lord himself in the Gospel, where he speaks of the seed that fell among thorns, signifying the greedy, says: “These are those who hear the word and, going on their way, are choked by the cares and pleasures of life and bring forth no fruit” (Matthew 13).

Those hindered by an obstacle from seeing heaven are the proud and high-spirited, who have placed the covering of pride of mind between themselves and God, as the prophet David says: “They are not in the labour of men, neither shall they be scourged with men” (Psalm 82 [73]). “Therefore pride has taken hold of them; they are covered with their iniquity and impiety”: that is, with a double pride. Impiety is called the pride by which a person does not humble himself before God; iniquity, the pride by which a person desires to be preferred to his neighbour. Pride, therefore, is the covering by which a person is hindered from seeing God, while he seems in it to possess the benefits which ought to have been obtained from God through humility.

For when the proud-hearted person thinks of virtues, at the prompting of pride he presumes that he possesses them; when he thinks of knowledge, he arrogantly ascribes it to himself above others; when he thinks of honours, he considers himself worthier than everyone else. And, not looking at the deficiencies of his own weakness, while he reckons even goods which he does not possess as though they were in him, he is always either a despiser or an envier of another’s virtue. Why is this? Because, hindered by pride, he cannot look to Christ and see in him how humble, how patient, how gentle, how good the Lord is; so that, looking upon his own weaknesses, he might humbly lament what he understands to be lacking in himself, as blessed Job is recorded to have done when he said: “By the hearing of the ear I have heard you, but now my eye sees you; therefore I condemn myself and do penance” (Job 42).

Because pride does not look to God in order to recognize its own darkness in his light, it is therefore more difficult than all other sins to bend toward repentance. For it is the first sin among those who depart from God and the last among those who return to virtues previously undertaken, as Scripture says. Hence also the devil is said principally to rule over the proud, Scripture bearing witness: “He sees every high thing, and he himself is king over all the children of pride.”

There are others who, through the failure of the light of their eyes, being in darkness cannot see heaven. Such are the simple and unlearned: all indeed are capable by reason of knowing and loving God and walking in his commandments, but, through the lack of outward light—that is, teaching and preaching, which ought to be supplied to them by the ministry of pastors—they remain in the darkness of sins, because there is no one to work for the salvation of souls and teach the pattern of holy conduct.

For the clerics of our time, who undertake the care of souls together with ecclesiastical benefices, show themselves clerics only in profit, soldiers in dress, but neither in life nor in preaching, as their works declare. They do not blush to buy with the alms of the poor royal horses, secular garments, gilded shoes and bridles, and embroidered stars. Their table is delighted with courses of food; their bedchamber with shameless games; in the palace everywhere resounds the song of the deeds of Hector, while in the holy Church the words of the Saviour are condemned to silence. Thus it happens that the weak members of the Church, who ought to have been led to God by the preceding light of pastors, persist in darkness because the preaching of truth has been withdrawn from them.

Therefore the bentness of avarice, the covering of pride, and the blindness of ignorance must be removed from our midst, so that we may behold God and the saints of God with the eyes of the mind and strive for that heavenly glory which we know has been promised to us. Yet, if we are to be able fruitfully to direct our gaze toward heaven, we must lift our eyes to heaven not backwards or sideways, but straight ahead before us. For those who look at heaven behind them or from the side either stumble with their feet or lose their way.

Those look at heaven behind them who place too much confidence in their past life and the good works they have performed, when they ought rather to forget the things behind and stretch themselves forward to those before them. For, setting before their eyes how they have left vices, fought against temptations, associated with their betters, kept discipline, and borne the burden and heat of the day, they thereby judge themselves worthy; they begin to grow lukewarm in charity, become lax in discipline, and near the end of life—when they ought to be more fervent in spirit—are found almost cold and without virtue.

Certainly not so does an exile make for his homeland: he journeys ever more vigorously until he arrives. Not so does the day labourer, who works continually until he completes the day’s task. Not so does one thirsting for a fountain of water, until he reaches it. Neither should the soul thirsting for God cease from the course of good work until it reaches him whom it has desired to enjoy.

Those look at heaven from the side who, on account of temporal goods and the pleasures of this life, in which they seem to have rest for themselves, worship God, give alms, and frequent churches—being more devout to God because of what they have received than for the hope of eternal life, which they love less. Thinking Job to belong to their number, Satan said: “Does Job fear God for nothing? You have blessed the works of his hands, and his possession has increased upon the earth” (Job 1); as if to say: It is no wonder that one who has received so many goods from the Lord on earth behaves innocently for their sake. Therefore those who look to God in this way from the side do not at all direct the sight of their minds along the road that leads to God. For the straight road is that by which we endure labours, hardships, persecutions, and injuries; because to proceed from pleasures to pleasures is a wholly crooked journey and never leads the traveller to the goal of salvation.

We must therefore look at heaven straight before our face, so that we may turn face, eyes, ears, mouth, hands, and feet toward God: the face itself by knowing him; the eyes by directing the intention of the mind toward him; the ears by obeying; the mouth by speaking what is right and good; the hands by doing what is just; the feet by thinking good thoughts. Let no member of our body be absent from service to its Creator. For why should we not walk the straight way? Both the reward of labour and aid against dangers have been set before us in the saints of God. For it is said of them that “they shine in the firmament of heaven and illuminate the earth”: *to shine* is said with reference to light, *to illuminate* with reference to that which is illuminated.

Therefore the saints of God shine because they have already attained the brightness of the vision of God. They illuminate the earth while, by miracles, instruction, and conduct, they form those who are pilgrims on earth, so that by their example we may both hope for the heavenly reward and receive from them instruction in holy life. Who, then, is so lacking in sound counsel as not to hasten from poverty to sufficiency, from sadness to joy, from straits to delights? For these three things are laid up as a reward for the saints: eternal fellowship, of which it is said, “I shall be united with you when your glory appears” (Psalm 16 [17]); inward joy, of which it is written, “Let the just rejoice in the presence of God” (Psalm 67 [68]); and joyful delight, of which it is said, “Delights are at the right hand of God unto the end” (Psalm 15 [16]). Thus those who were miserable for Christ in this life receive in that life sufficiency of every good; those who mourned for him attain perfect joy; and those who suffered calamities for him possess everlasting delights there, through the gift of our Lord Jesus Christ, whose kingdom and dominion endure for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XLIX. ON THE FEAST OF ALL SAINTS

“Two wings of each were joined together, and two covered their bodies” (Ezekiel 1).

The word you have heard, brothers, contains matter both for joy and for sorrow. For the fact that the bodies of those living creatures are said to be covered with wings is a sign of weakness; but the fact that the remaining wings were joined together is a sign of future glorification.
