Therefore, because in the present life the mind conscious of sin needs protection, we are all admonished by this word to cover our weaknesses, lest we appear naked, so that, set free in the glory of that future life, we may take up wings prepared not for weakness but for perfect health.

The soul, then, still weak, needs wings—not whichever wings it wishes, but wings with which it may cover and defend itself—being still frail in body, unstable in mind, divided in character, entangled in error, sluggish in earnest pursuits, prone to pleasures, slow toward wisdom, swift toward impiety; naked with regard to the past, meagre with regard to the present, uncertain with regard to the future; guilty from birth, and in life subject to labour and sorrow.

Accordingly, in this present life two wings are given to it, with which it can cover its nakedness: the understanding of the Scriptures, by which it may defend itself through knowledge of truth; and contemplation of creatures, by which it may defend itself through the bond of charity. Beneath these wings it ought to have hands, so that it may always demonstrate both knowledge of Scripture and love of the creature by the testimony of good work: it must first walk by practice and labour, and afterwards fly, because one must first labour and afterwards receive the prize.

Thus Martha meets the Lord before Mary; thus the law of servitude is given before the law of liberty; thus Zion is inhabited before Jerusalem; thus Leah is married before Rachel; thus Peter is called by the Lord before John; and thus, finally, one passes from the left to the right. By all these things it is shown that one must pass through the discipline of the present life into the rest of future glory. The divine law is therefore set before a person so that he may shape his life according to it and walk in it; and it is compared to a wing for a twofold reason. For in a wing two things are considered: beauty, because it adorns; and usefulness, because it protects. In the same way the commandments of God have beauty in the light of knowledge, usefulness in the fulfilment of the commandments.

Therefore the diligent searcher of God’s commandments must first enlighten his intellect in the law of the Lord, so that he may know what he is, what he lacks, how great his own weakness is, what his deficiency of virtues is, how long his misery, how brief his consolation, how much he owes his Lord, and how little he can repay. These are the riches of the children of Adam from the day of their birth until the day of their burial. O how worthless is this treasure, how rejected the coinage, for one who, indebted by ten thousand talents, has stored up for himself nothing but wrath and indignation all his days! What will you do, miserable soul, when you render an account of your trading? Look again to the treasure of your knowledge, to see whether perhaps you may find there something with which you can redeem this debt.

Perhaps there is something there very useful to you, since it is written: “He who increases knowledge increases sorrow” (Ecclesiastes 1). With this penny of approved coinage, the prodigal son who had wasted his goods in luxurious living restored to his father the money of which he had deprived him, saying: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you, and am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me as one of your hired servants” (Luke 15). Put this penny of sorrow in the purse of your conscience; display it outwardly by earnest endeavour, inwardly by affection; and exact from yourself by torments and sufferings what you have defrauded from your Lord’s entrusted money. Certainly, if you ask, he forgives; if you grieve, he has mercy; if you weep, he too spares; if you open [to him], he will dwell with you, because his delights are to be with the children of men. And in this especially is the usefulness of the divine law commended to you: that you may have dwelling with you the very one who teaches it.

But if you wish to observe carefully, the usefulness of the divine law is commended to you in a threefold way: through zeal, earnest endeavour, and affection. Understand zeal as compunction, earnest endeavour as action, and affection as devotion: so that through the zeal of compunction, as by a sword, you may kill the old man within you; through earnest endeavour, make satisfaction by good works; and through affection always cling to him whom you await as your reward. Thus no ambition for temporal things may hinder you from hastening, from obtaining, or finally from running so as to lay hold.

But some possess this wing of the divine law only for beauty, whereas others possess it for usefulness. I would say that those possess it for beauty for whom the mysteries of Scripture are accessible, to whom the precepts of virtue and the prohibitions of vices are not hidden. Yet in all these things they desire rather to enlighten their intellect than to cleanse their affection: not submitting themselves to the law but rather subjecting the law to themselves; retaining not their heart in the law but the law in their heart; making from the Lord’s commandments not medicine but money.

Why, miserable soul, has the table of the divine law become before you a snare? Why do you look at the fountain bubbling up and not drink the water? Why, holding honeycomb in your mouth, do you crush the wax and cast away the sweetness of the honey? It would have been profitable for you, according to the Lord’s commandment, to take this book and devour it, so that it might make your stomach bitter while becoming sweet as honey in your mouth (Revelation 10). You ought surely to have taken the book of the divine law and devoured it in holy meditation, so that it might become sweet in the mouth of memory while it stirred the belly of weak conscience to the bitterness of compunction.

For just as looking into a mirror and not arranging oneself, looking at a fire and not being warmed, or certainly preparing food and not being refreshed, has nothing useful in it, so also there is no benefit in the law of the Lord except for those who remember his commandments in order to do them (Psalm 110 [111]). “Good understanding is for those who put it into practice.” But oh, if only such people would recall the mercy of that Samaritan, the diligence of the innkeeper, and the use of the two denarii (Luke 10)! Consider that they too would not store away the two denarii of the Old and New Law as money, but would rather apply medicine to the sick person. Would you not judge it exceedingly profane if you saw someone afflicted by poison carrying an antidote with him and not using it?

The Apostle, learned in the whole law of the Lord, cries out that he knows nothing except the Lord Jesus, and him crucified (1 Corinthians 2). And Ezekiel, speaking spiritually of the spiritual temple, says: “The higher they were, the lower they were.” By this the Spirit signifies that the greater the gifts of grace a person has received, the humbler he ought to be in conduct, lest wounds arise from the very source from which medicine ought to have come.

For just as one who lives well and teaches well instructs another how he ought to live, so one who teaches well but lives badly instructs God how he ought to condemn him. Thus long ago Uriah the Hittite, sent into battle by David and carrying with him the letters of his own death, fell where the assault of battle was strongest. For whoever in the Church of God has received the light of divine knowledge—for Uriah is interpreted “God is my light”—carries with him the sentence of his own condemnation when he refuses outwardly to fulfil by deeds the law of God which he keeps enclosed in his heart as though in an ark.

There are others who prefer to consider the commandments of God in terms of their usefulness. They are rightly compared to the dove sitting beside very full streams: for as that bird, by looking upon the river, guards against the snares of the hawk, so these men use the commandments of God to guard against the snares of the devil, the delights of the world, and the enticements of the flesh. They are always eager to pursue what they see commanded them by the law of the Lord; and, lest the domestic enemy be able to hinder them in anything, they subject their body to servitude, crucifying their flesh with its vices and desires. Do you wish, then, to see examples? They are at hand. Beside these streams sat those of whom it is said that they were “walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord without blame” [Col. 0280B]. Beside these streams also sat the prophet Daniel, against whom the Babylonians could find no accusation except only in the law of his God. So too did he who said: “I have hidden your sayings in my heart, that I may not sin against you” (Ps. 118).

John compares these persons to a tree bearing fruit, whose leaves are for the healing of the nations: “He showed me,” he says, “a river of living water, shining like crystal, proceeding from the throne of God and of the Lamb; and on either side of the river, a tree bearing fruit, and its leaves for the healing of the nations” (Apoc. 22). The trees placed on either side of the river signify holy men meditating upon both pages of the Old and New Testaments. For the river signifies the commandments of the divine law; the fruit of the tree [Col. 0280C] is understood as examples of good works, and the leaves as words of exhortation. These are for the healing of the nations when we confirm in ourselves by examples of good works what we set before others through words of exhortation.

But by the contemplation of creatures, which we called the second wing, necessary for covering our weakness—provided, however, that by “creature” man is understood—we protect our nakedness, as it were by the spreading of a wing, in two ways: namely, by the bond of charity and by the rendering of reverence and fear. The first serves the relief of need; the other, the preservation of humility. I said that the bond of charity serves the relief of need because no one is so self-sufficient, [Col. 0280D] so entirely in need of no one, that here he does not need to be joined to others by the bonds of charity. For although God ought to be loved first in the affection of love, one’s neighbour must nevertheless often be loved more in the rendering of service. Indeed, charity toward one’s neighbour must be maintained in acts of service to such an extent that, when a neighbour’s need is urgent, we ought to desist even from prayer, holy meditation, hymns, and spiritual songs. Behold: before the table of the Lord, set yourself with eyes and hands raised toward heaven; if you see Christ dying of hunger in a poor man, will you not give him bread? If you see your brother lying in bed, placed in agony, will you not visit him, or, if he falls into a pit, support him? Certainly you will do so, because he is bound to you by the bond of charity; [Col. 0281A] and, while you are present, he cannot fall unless you fall with him—especially if you are able to sustain him. There are many examples of this among the holy martyrs, who left us a living example of charity. For although they could safely have devoted themselves alone to divine converse and prayer, they nevertheless chose to benefit others, to exhort, to teach, and to shed their blood, so that, bound by the bond of charity, they might share with others through the torments of their passion that blessed life which they could have sought for themselves alone in peace.

From this root of charity there ought to flow the rendering of reverence and fear, so that we may fear to offend by a failure of reverence and fear those whom we are bound to embrace with so great an affection of charity. We are taught to do this also in that hierarchy of blessed spirits, [Col. 0281B] after whose pattern the present Church is ordered. There they honour one another in accordance with the arrangement of that supreme power, each lower being obedient to his superiors, regarding as commanded by that highest emperor whatever has been commanded him by the presiding angelic power. For if angels should say to archangels, thrones to dominions, or cherubim to seraphim, “We will not obey you; we do not wish you to preside over us,” do you suppose that this would please that supreme Majesty? By no means. For that king of pride was cast down because he wished to be like the Most High (Isa. 14), not by participation in divinity, but “like,” that is, free from dominion as He is, so that he might render to no superior the reverence of due submission.

Have you never read that David, when Saul turned aside [Col. 0281C] into the cave, cut off the edge of his cloak? For when in Saul a superior rank, in David an inferior rank, and in the cloak authority are understood, to cut off the edge of the cloak is to diminish something of the reverence due to one’s superior (2 Kings 24). David grieved that he had taken this from Saul when he repented that he had presumed anything against one to whom he owed the honour of reverence. Likewise, once when the ark of the Lord was being carried from Gibeah to Jerusalem, and the ark tilted, Uzzah the Levite put forth his hand and therefore, struck by the Lord, perished. Here the ark signifies prelates, and Uzzah subjects. Uzzah applies his hand to the tilting ark when a subject presumes to oppose prelates who are accommodating themselves to the age or weakness [Col. 0281D] of others. Therefore he is struck by the Lord, either for correction in the present life or for condemnation in the future. It is preferable, then, that with the wing of charity we cover our own weaknesses and bear those of others, lest we appear naked when that which is mortal in us has been swallowed up by life; and those wings must be assumed by which it will be necessary not to be covered, but to be raised up.

These wings seem to have lifted our very Head to heaven. If you wish to know them, they are the renewal of nature and the session at the right hand. Our Redeemer himself first assumed these wings, intending to bestow them upon us in the future, when we shall be like him. Thus in the Apocalypse they are called the wings of the great eagle, where it is written: “Two wings of the great [Col. 0282A] eagle were given to the woman, that she might fly into the desert place.” By the eagle he means Christ, by the woman the faithful soul, and by the desert the heaven to which she flies.

This renewal of nature, which will occur in the body, ought to be understood, if we consider the nature of bodies, according to the elements of this world. For we see that earth, by its present heaviness, weighs down the body; water, by the inequality of its humours, weakens it; air, by the necessity of breathing, troubles it; and fire, by the excess of its heat, consumes it. These things must therefore be renewed, not removed altogether, so that not the weakness which weighs us down, but the whole truth of nature may be restored; as the Lord says: “Not a hair from your head shall perish” (Luke 21). The bodies of this death—indeed, bodies truly dead through the elements of this world—will then possess the truth of nature, [Col. 0282B] not corruption: that is, they will be tangible from earth, mobile from water, light from air, and radiant from fire. Yet they will receive more from air and fire than from the other elements, because their lightness will be compared with the lightness of thoughts, and their splendour with the splendour of the stars; as the Apostle says: “Star differs from star in brightness; so also is the resurrection of the dead” (1 Cor. 15).

On the contrary, the reprobate, who loved earthly things above all and subjected themselves to the passions of desire, receive more from these lower elements, namely earth and water, so that in those bodily conditions more suited to passions they may undergo suffering. O how unhappy is that soul which will be tortured by a threefold prison: namely, of conscience, of body, and of Gehenna [Col. 0282C]; so that it will be neither without anguish within nor without punishment without. Its immortality in essence and its capacity for suffering will endure forever in punishment; nor will it receive any part of that gift which the grace of the heavenly Giver will bestow upon the saints in impassibility. But the impassibility and immortality of the saints will be wonderfully above nature: life and being—indeed, the entire course of nature—will be natural, so that nature itself may rejoice in its wholeness, and, in what it has received beyond this, may burn yet more ardently in love for its Giver.

But to this renewal of our nature will be added the session at the right hand, consisting in the fullness of knowledge, love, and joy: so that neither erroneous knowledge, unlawful love, nor joy can admit sorrowful things [Col. 0282D]. There righteousness will shape knowledge, lest it become proud; there knowledge will direct charity, that it may be ordered; there unfailing eternity will produce joy, lest it can ever be darkened by any cloud of pain. Thus all the soul’s goods, now distinct within it, will then be united in God, so that knowledge may love and charity may know, and in one affection all things may reach their end in God which have established for themselves the one end, Christ. This is what the philosopher of the world said when he declared that the soul consists of divisible and indivisible substance, of the same and differing nature: because even now it has divided affections, applying itself to diverse things; but it will be of indivisible, or of the same, nature when, wholly directed toward God in knowledge and love, it is united in him by the single affection of the virtues.

[Col. 0283A] Therefore the Lord also, on account of the identity of affection, comprehends under the single name of knowledge all the soul’s powers by which God is enjoyed, saying: “This,” he says, “is eternal life: that they may know you, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17). O that the abundance of that knowledge may someday come, the use of which concerns not inquiry but rather blessedness! For that knowledge does not entangle questions, does not set forth rules, does not reveal causes of natural things or make hidden things manifest, because knowledge holds there only what pertains to the enjoyment of that joyful blessedness. There is a threefold perfection of knowledge there: of the Creator, so that through the dignity of the creature we may praise the wisdom of God; of restoration, so that through the works of assumed humanity we may praise the goodness of God; [Col. 0283B] and there will also be perfect knowledge of divinity, so that in it we may venerate the majesty of God.

Behold, dearest brethren, you have heard what that session at the right hand is like, which is promised to all saints; which Christ received, which the blessed Virgin Mary also received, and which the universal Church of the saints will receive, though in a different manner. For Christ sits at the right hand of the Father; but the blessed Virgin alone also sits at the right hand of the Son. All the other saints indeed will be at his right hand, but they will not sit at his right hand. To sit at the right hand of the Father is to be equal to him, or to be among his greater goods; this the Son alone received. To sit at the right hand of the Son is to abound before others in gifts of grace; this the blessed [Col. 0283C] Mother of God received in a unique way. But to be at the right hand of God is to share in that glory, as it is written: “Then the king will say to those who are at his right hand” (Matt. 25). This, however, will be common to all who are called to the supper of the eternal King.

Thus all the blessed will be at the Son’s right hand—indeed, all will sit on his right, not at his right hand—in accordance with the saying: “It is not mine to give you to sit at my right hand or at my left, but it belongs to those for whom it has been prepared by my Father” (Matt. 10). For to sit *on the right* pertains to glory; to sit *at the right hand* pertains to preeminence of glory, which Christ bestowed upon his Mother today when he raised her above the angelic powers. There sits that queen of the blessed spirits and mediator of sinners, always interceding for us, that we too may receive [Col. 0283D] the same session at the right hand which she received on this day when she departed from the body. May our Lord Jesus Christ deign to grant this to us. Amen.

## COMMON SERMON L. ON THE DAY OF ALL SAINTS

“God will render the reward of the labours of his saints, and will lead them in a wondrous way” (Wis. 10).

Let all who willingly endure the afflictions of this world hear this word—those who share in the penitence and tribulation of Jesus. Let them, I say, hear this word and be comforted, because an end to their labours and a reward are alike promised them—not any sort of reward, but that which God has prepared for those who love him. What more precious, more desirable, or greater reward could have been promised, for which the holy martyrs and other righteous persons strove [Col. 0284A] even unto death, and with which all the saints who reign with him have also been rewarded? You therefore who inwardly practise some good within yourselves, and who, because of his words, keep the hard ways, do not repent of this labour. For life is brief; the end of labour comes; that supreme Judge is at hand to render the reward of the labours of his saints.

“The reward,” he says, “of their labours.” Those for whom this life is sweet labour in the world; and those for whom this life is bitter labour as well. Those for whom this life is sweet labour by acting: through lawful work they provide what they shall eat, what they shall drink, and what their body shall wear, doing all this in order to enjoy this world for a long time. But the Lord reproves their labour when he says: “Do not be anxious about what you shall eat or drink, or [Col. 0284B] what you shall wear” (Matt. 15). For your Father knows that you need all these things. But those for whom this life is bitter labour by suffering, as those holy persons laboured who were stretched on the rack, chilled by cold, filthy in prisons, drenched in blood, bruised with blows, worn away by hunger, and finally consumed by death; and they endured all this in order that they might more quickly be taken from this world.

God, therefore, will render the reward of the labours of his saints to those who, in voluntary self-affliction or in the violent persecution of the impious, have imitated the patience of the Lord Jesus. Let criminal persons, then, not flatter themselves as if they too would not receive their reward; for as God will render a reward to the righteous, so also to the unrighteous. Indeed, according to four kinds [Col. 0284C] of persons, four kinds of reward are found. There is the reward of those who love the good things of this world without restraint; the reward of those who commit the evils of this world outrageously; the reward of those who live justly and devoutly in this world; and the reward of those who reign with God. The first reward is a temporal benefit, of which it is said: “They have received their reward.” The second is eternal punishment, of which it is said: “Give them according to the works of their hands; render to them their recompense.” The third is spiritual grace, of which the Lord himself says: “Whoever has left house, or lands, children, or parents for my sake will receive many times more in this present world, and eternal life in the future” (Matt. 19). By “many times more” he intends the gifts of grace bestowed upon saints in this life. [Col. 0284D] The fourth reward is that of eternal glory, of which it is said: “Behold, your reward is great in heaven” (Matt. 5).

How many people in this world keep many vigils, offer prayers and alms, and perform other works of piety, yet, when they consider the beauty of this world’s creatures and their delights, are immediately captured by the desire of their eyes. Making a homeland out of exile, as it were, they desire and love temporal goods above all, though these were bestowed upon them solely for necessity in divine service. Why is this? Because they do not see in themselves the image of God, who is supremely beautiful, and cannot behold with their blinded eye the beauty of the One who loves them. If they saw him, they would certainly despise all [Col. 0285A] these outward things, which swiftly pass away even through their own defect, or become cheap by comparison when new things arrive. God therefore gives these persons the reward of the temporal goods which they seek with the greatest eagerness, so that in those goods they may be rewarded for the good they do. But woe to that unhappy soul which, at the end of the world, when all the saints receive the kingdom, will hear for its consolation: “You have received your reward.”

And the number is infinite of those who commit this world’s evils outrageously: thieves, robbers, fornicators, unclean persons, simoniacs, the ambitious, and many such monsters among humankind. With their whole spirit extinguished, they hasten to destruction, so that, buried in their vices, they may not be added again to rise. For how could those rise [Col. 0285B] who do not abhor their crimes and, having in some manner become insensible, do not even perceive themselves? Therefore they are neither pierced by compunction, washed by confession, nor softened by piety; they are not moved by prayers, nor do they yield to threats. Indeed, if you sometimes rebuke them, they become worse. What creature would not marvel at this? Behold, a human being made in the image of God does not acknowledge his Father in heaven; unworthy of the name of son, he despises to seek and possess the heavenly homeland, which is due to him by hereditary right. He plunges himself with all his effort into hell in order to have a share with those of whom it is written: “The righteous shall have dominion over them in the morning, and their help shall grow old in hell, away from their glory” (Ps. 48). Therefore weep, all angels of God, and you souls of the righteous, for your lost fellow-citizens [Col. 0285C] who ought to have been your household in the kingdom of God and co-heirs of Christ. For, abandoning the land of promise, they have chosen to serve Pharaoh in mud, brick, and straw; and, as though numbered among the dead, they have been erased from the book of the living and shall not be written with the righteous.

Come to your senses, miserable soul, and turn at least late to the Lord your God. For just as a mother’s affection does not abhor the filth of her little child, so Christ’s mercy does not abhor your crimes, provided that you are willing to be cleansed from them. Let the seal of your nature draw you upward, because you were made in the image of God; let the trust of faith draw you upward, since it promises you invisible good things under a visible form. And if you are a religious, let the title of your profession draw you [Col. 0285D] upward, by whose bonds you have been devoted to the service of God. If all these things do not move you, look upon your fragile body, a vessel of clay: it will tell you what you ought to do.

Behold, your body, preserving the dignity of its condition, stands upright, raises its eyes to heaven, and stretches both hands toward the Lord, in order by all these things to admonish you to aspire to heaven in desire. Be astonished, O heavens and all who dwell in them, because weak flesh in some manner disdains partnership with its own spirit, which it sees has degenerated from its dignity into such great baseness. Let us now pass to those who live devoutly in this world, who themselves are endowed with a double reward, one in the present and the other in the future. For righteous men receive in this life gifts [Col. 0286A] of grace as a consoling reward, lest they fail in tribulations. This happens when they are inflamed with charity, touched by the sweetness of devotion, lifted upward to the heights of contemplation, and strengthened in many other ways so that they may endure the afflictions of this world. For how, unless strengthened by the grace of God, could the holy martyrs and other righteous persons have been so steadfast in God’s cause as to bend their necks when the sword threatened, refuse to escape when prison lay open, seek death of their own accord, and provoke their persecutors? It will be more useful to consider inwardly how those who have been anticipated by the grace of God on this [way] ought to govern their lives, so that they may attain the reward of eternal glory.

[Col. 0286B] Every good man rightly serving God, then, ought to exercise four forms of watchfulness concerning his life. First, he should be intent in expectation of his end; second, fearful for satisfaction for his sins; third, devoted in the work of God; fourth, diligent in multiplying his talent. He should, I say, be intent in expectation of his end; and because nothing is more uncertain than the hour of death, he should say in his heart: “Behold, my days pass away; today or tomorrow I shall die; that supreme Judge is now coming. Therefore I shall keep watch, I shall keep watch; I shall prepare myself to meet him, lest, when he comes, he find me unprepared. I shall keep watch in the first watch of the night, that I may wash away past sins by sorrow and repentance; I shall keep watch in the second watch of the night, that by good works I may make satisfaction to my God; [Col. 0286C] I shall keep watch in the third watch of the night, that I may cautiously avoid committing similar sins in the future.” If he comes in the first watch, or if he comes in the second or third and finds him thus, blessed is that servant.

The righteous man must also be fearful concerning satisfaction for his offences, saying within himself: “O how often have I offended God; how many crimes have I committed! I believe I have not yet fully confessed, I have not yet wept enough. I shall still cast myself at the Lord’s feet and, with the publican, beat my breast; with Peter in his denial I shall weep bitterly, so that by abundance of tears I may wash away the stain of my sin.” Let the good man also be devoted in the work of God, so that in every action which he ought to do for God, he may look to him with the affection of devotion, lest perverse desires stain the work of God [Col. 0286D] and curiosity and vain glory confuse it; but rather let the intention of the work be directed to him from whom he expects the recompense of the work.

Now the affection of devotion is the eye of the soul, by which it ought to look toward God; concerning it it is said: “It is better for you to enter into life with one eye than, having two eyes, to be cast into the Gehenna of fire” (Matt. 5). Or rather, there are two eyes of the soul: intellect and affection. With the one, that is intellect, it ought to see God through knowledge; with the other, that is affection, through devotion. Thus the first eye of the soul causes scandal to those who, although they know much about God, depart from him by their wicked manner of life. Of such persons it is written: “Although they knew [Col. 0287A] God, they did not glorify him as God, and therefore they became foolish and were made vain in their thoughts” (Rom. 1). For them it would surely be better to enter life with one eye—that is, with the simple affection of devotion—than, having two eyes, to be cast into the Gehenna of fire.

The multiplication of the talent is also necessary for those who wish to enter into life. A talent is every gift of God, bodily or spiritual, by which a person can work out salvation. The Lord entrusts it to us as his money, so that from it he may receive from us interest in good works, as is read in the Gospel concerning the faithful servants (Matt. 25), since one gained five talents and another two. But as the money is from the Lord, so the interest in good works must be from us. Therefore, he [Col. 0287B] who has received the riches of this world should be diligent in aiding the needy; he who has received power, in aiding the oppressed; he who has received justice, in rendering right judgment in God’s cause; he who has received prudence, in giving good counsel; he who has received charity, in showing it by the performance of good work. Otherwise, if he is insufficiently diligent in multiplying any gift of God, he may hear from the Lord the reproach of that wicked servant: “Why did you not give my money to the bankers, so that I might certainly have demanded it with interest?” (ibid.).

Since the continuance of good works is necessary, then, let no one trust in his past life, saying: “I have worked bravely; now I shall rest.” For mighty David, who had slain the bear and lion with his own hand, fell through the enticements of a woman. Samson, who struck down a thousand men with the jawbone [Col. 0287C] of an ass, was blinded, deprived of strength, and led to the mill. The son of the widow woman, whom Elijah raised, was nurtured in great holiness but died in a woman’s bosom. By all these things it is signified that many who begin well end miserably; and therefore the multiplication of the talent is required unto the end, as Solomon says: “Whatever your hand is able to do, do unceasingly” (Eccl. 9), and especially as the Lord commands: “Conduct business until I come” (Matt. 25). Whoever fortifies his life by these watchfulnesses will no more be excluded from the labours of the saints than he will be deprived of sharing their reward. But what is that glory which the righteous in this life so greatly desire in the reward of the saints, and by which in the life to come they are made blessed with so great an abundance of happiness?

[Col. 0287D] The elect certainly await three supreme goods in that reward: supreme delight, inward satisfaction, and eternal joy. I call them three supreme goods because of the threefold experience of enjoyment, not because of the essence of the thing, according to which there is but one supreme good; in the same way that seven beatitudes are spoken of, although there is only one blessedness. For the saints possess supreme delight in the heavenly homeland, so that, enjoying the delights of God, they are no longer embittered by any bitterness. As it is written: “Delights are at the right hand of God unto the end” (Ps. 15). At God’s left hand—that is, in the present life—there are certain delights, but [Col. 0288A] not unto the end, because every delight of this life ends in bitterness. But at God’s right hand delights are unto the end: an ending that completes bitterness, not one that fails, because they end with no subsequent bitterness. For there is an end under an end and an end beyond an end, as scholars are accustomed to say.

The saints also possess inward satisfaction, because they are filled with God’s good gifts and, having every desire within themselves, are not distressed by want of anything. Of this satisfaction the Prophet says: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. 16). And in the Song of Songs: “Eat, friends, and be intoxicated, beloved ones” (Song 5). They also rejoice in eternal joy, which can neither be diminished nor taken away by any pain or sorrow. Of this the Lord says in the Gospel [Col. 0288B]: “Your sorrow shall be turned into joy, and no one shall take your joy from you” (John 16). Delight will be in the sweetness of the mind, satisfaction in the vision of God, and joy in the fullness of divine love. Yet Christ will be the one reward of all: he will be delight in the sweetness of the mind, satisfaction in the vision of God, and joy in the fullness of divine love, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “God shall be all in all” (Eph. 4). And because God is wonderful in his saints, he will then lead them in a wondrous way.

This way is Christ, of whom it is said: “They have not known the way of peace” (Rom. 3). And elsewhere: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14). For if we consider the works of our restoration, Christ appeared wonderful in all things [Col. 0288C]. That God was incarnate was wonderful; that the impassible one suffered was wonderful; that the dead one rose was wonderful. Therefore he will lead them in a wondrous way, because from faith in the incarnation he will lead them to imitation of his passion, and from imitation of the passion he will lead them to the reward of resurrection.

Yet by this way we may understand the passage of the saints from this life into rest. For if entrance into this life is rightly called a miserable way, because we are born into the labours and miseries of this world, and progress in this life is rightly called a difficult way, in which we are reconciled to God—for “narrow is the way that leads to life” (Matt. 7)—then departure from [Col. 0288D] this life is not inappropriately called a wondrous way. It is wondrous because it is unusual and new, incomparable with anything for a mortal person in this life; because finally that departure occurs by wondrous and invisible means. Therefore he will lead them in a wondrous way, by which he will lead them from the cleanness of ecclesiastical purity to the fellowship of angelic subtlety, and thence to the vision of unbounded divinity, in which all the saints will rest from their labours, reign with God, and the Lamb of God reign with them—he himself granting it, whose kingdom and dominion endure unto ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON LI. FOR NO FEAST DAY

“The partridge has brooded what she did not bring forth; it has made riches, and not with judgment” (Jer. 17).

Just as “the invisible things of God are beheld, being understood through the things that are [Col. 0289A] made, from the creation of the world” (Rom. 1), so the son of perdition is known to possess in creatures his own figures and likenesses. In and through these, by God’s so-ordering judgment, an example of his malice is set forth to some for imitation and to others for caution. This is sufficiently indicated in the single name of the partridge, for anyone who wishes to interpret its nature and actions as moral instruction. For, as those who pursue such inquiries say, the partridge steals another’s eggs, broods over them, diligently rears the chicks, and brings them up as its own; it does not fear consciousness of its crime, but rather glories when it has done evil and exults in most wicked things. But when it has brought them forth into living creatures, and, through the benefit of growing age, the little ones have attained strength, by nature’s counsel they discover the deceit of that [Col. 0289B] thieving mother. Leaving her, they seek, find, and recognize their natural parents; embracing them with inborn love, they thereafter detest and despise being called sons under the name of adoption.

Thus in the partridge is signified to us that son of perdition, the author of death, inventor of deceit, and head of all malice. He steals, broods over, nourishes, and possesses another’s eggs when, by temptation, he deceitfully seduces a human being made by God and owing him nothing; broods over him by pleasure, nourishes him by evil work, and freely possesses him through despair.

“The partridge,” he says, “has brooded what she did not bring forth.” It has two wings by which it strives to gather to itself not only the impious but even the elect: the first is delight in sin; the second, despair of repentance. The first is on the [Col. 0289C] right hand; the second on the left. It uses the first for brooding, when through the delight of pleasure the soul is in some manner delighted within itself. It uses the second when any soul, overcome as if by despair through the difficulty of labour and the harshness of repentance, is frightened, so that, according to the Apostle’s saying, “the wrath of God may come upon the children of distrust” (Rom. 1). Elsewhere Scripture says: “Cursed is the man who sins in hope.”

First, through pleasure the affection is inwardly corrupted by unlawful desire; afterward sensuality is stirred to seek unlawful things; finally reason, conquered by concupiscence, is subjected to the will of the flesh. Hence Jeremiah complains: “He has made old, I say, my skin and my flesh; he has crushed all [Col. 0289D] my bones” (Lam. 3). To make the skin old is to corrupt the soul’s affection by the desire of the old man or by perverse delight; to make the flesh old is to direct the sensuality inherent from the flesh according to the will of the flesh; but to crush the bones is to reduce to nothing, through wicked desires, the powers of the mind or the manly motions of reason.

The son of perdition stretches out the wing that is on the left when he places before the eyes, first, the harshness of repentance; second, fear for the flesh; third, weakness of strength; fourth, despair of completion. First he awakens negligence; second he instils care for the flesh; third, sloth; fourth, perseverance in wicked work. Therefore the person who is beset by temptations of this kind ought to set before the gaze of his mind [Col. 0290A] Paul’s saying: “Although our old man is corrupted, nevertheless the new is renewed day by day” (2 Cor. 4). For the more the flesh is outwardly worn down by labours and hardships, hunger and thirst, the more the soul, nourished by the consolation of the Spirit and the increase of virtues, is strengthened in God’s love. Hence the Prophet promises his soul not old age but rather renewed youth, saying: “Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s” (Ps. 102). Old age is whatever we contract from the flesh; youth is whatever we receive from God through the infusion of grace. By this he plainly intended to signify to us that it is advantageous for us to walk not according to the flesh, which is from the earth and will return to earth, but rather according to the Spirit, who is from above.

Therefore, O human being, that you may be delivered from these temptations, have recourse to him who does not permit you to be tempted beyond what you are able to bear, and say: “Protect me beneath the shadow of your wings” (Ps. 16): first conceal me, that I may lie hidden from the enemy; afterward protect me, that I may not endure his violence. Conceal me with respect to my iniquity; protect me with respect to your mercy. For unless you come to aid me, the partridge broods what it did not bring forth.

First he cherishes, secondly he brings forth, thirdly he nourishes. While he cherishes, the offspring is still hidden; while he brings forth, it already appears; while he nourishes those brought forth, the foetus is manifest. If there is anyone attentive to these things, three kinds of temptations are signified to us. The first is hidden, the second apparent, the third manifest. The first occurs when we offend and do not know it; the second, when we partly recognize the fault [Col. 0290C] and partly do not know it; the third, when, recognizing the fault, we sin freely and yet cannot resist.

By the first temptation, therefore, those are ensnared who have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge. While, through excessive zeal, they believe that they are rendering service to God, they turn the vineyard into a wild vine and their silver into dross. For while, according to Paul, they want all men to be like themselves, they rebuke the weak, drive on the feeble, and through impatience cast in their brothers’ teeth things that ought to be endured in charity. Hear what is commanded you (Exodus 23): “If you see your brother’s ox or ass fallen on the road, you shall not despise it, but shall lift it up with him.” In the fall of the ass, bodily weakness may be understood; in the collapse of the ox, failure in good action [Col. 0290D]. Therefore do not despise him, but lift him up with him, because you ought to assist your brother’s bodily infirmity with service and consolation, and to heal the infirmity of his soul, insofar as you can, by exhorting and strengthening him in word and deed.

Nor can you otherwise offer God a sacrifice freely given, since elsewhere also you are commanded (Deuteronomy 17): “You shall not offer to the Lord your God an ox or sheep that has a blemish or any other defect, for it is an abomination to the Lord.” In the ox, therefore, diligent action is understood; in the sheep, the innocence of a pure heart. If, then, while you seem innocent in your own eyes, you presume to judge another’s servant in your heart, you now offer the Lord a sheep having a blemish—that is, your innocence—as a sacrifice [Col. 0291A]; making yourself guilty of transgression, you render yourself liable to punishment in the very act of your offering.

Likewise, if, while you think yourself vigorous in action, you wish to provoke others—or rather, to scandalize them—your gold is already darkened and its finest colour changed; because, now that your sacrifice has a blemish, “This is not the sacrifice that I have chosen,” says the Lord. Thus perhaps one among you has borne the Lord’s yoke from his youth, strong in vigour and able to bear the burden and heat of the day; yet he gives advice in the parlour, quarrels in the cloister, shouts in chapter. He complains that this man chants too little, that man is absent from the cloister more than he ought, another did not attend the hour; and, as though someone had committed a crime, he calls him a subverter of the order if he happened not to attend the procession [Col. 0291B]. Thus, while he desires to appear the master of the order, he becomes a whirlwind and the author of murmuring.

Such a man, therefore, ought to remember that householder who, setting out on a journey, divided his goods among his servants, giving to each according to his own ability: to one five talents, to another two, and to another one. There are, then, five talents which the householder distributes to his servants (Matthew 25): first, that you are able; second, that you are willing; third, that you love; fourth, that you act; lastly, that you persevere. He gives all these to one person when, granted both willingness and ability to act well, someone acts well out of love and, persevering in goodness, is brought to completion as a perfect man without interruption of good work.

But he gives two when someone, possessing a good will, does indeed perform good works, but, being deprived of strength and ability, by no means reaches the perfection of completion [Col. 0291C]. But he who can and does not will is the one who, having received one talent, hides his lord’s money; because he did not put it out at interest, he deserved to be cast, bound hand and foot, into the outer darkness (Matthew 25).

Therefore let each strive to multiply the money received, and let him not wish to be burdensome to one who has received less, lest, if he presumptuously undertakes too curious a judgment of another’s servant, forgetful of himself, he be unable to render an account of the talents received at his lord’s return. This too may happen: he may be stronger in body, while the man whom he accuses is sounder in mind [Col. 0291D]; this one may be louder in choir, while that one is more devout in the inner chamber of his heart; this one is torn asunder in different directions through impatience, while that one, possessing patience, glories in his infirmities; this one sets himself above all through pride, while that one subjects himself to all through humility.

Let us therefore test the spirits, brothers, whether they are from God or not. If we see that we possess zeal for God, let us observe whether it is according to knowledge. If an impulse to slander arises in the mind, let us consider the source from which it arises and attend to the end toward which it tends. Let us investigate in ourselves whether, if we were placed in the condition of the person whom we accuse, we could justly bring similar accusations; and thus, by our own judgment of mind, we can say how deceitful is this temptation of the enemy by which he attacks us so secretly.

[Col. 0292A] There is another mode of temptation, which comes, as it were, from the side. What is at our side we partly see and partly do not see; similar are certain temptations of the devil, which we recognize indeed, because it is a fault to do such things, but which we neglect to correct because we judge them not to be mortal sins. We look rather to God’s mercy, which forgives, than to his justice, which justly punishes offences.

For example, if grace to understand Scripture has been given to a man who has renounced the world in the fervour of his mind; if he has received keenness of intellect in distinguishing gifts, he often desires more to turn over a multitude of questions than a book of confessions; more to investigate the subtleties of sophisms than to examine the ruins of his mind; to dispute more often than to pray; to read more [Col. 0292B] than to sing. In short, he wishes to have the law in his heart, not his heart in the law; chewing over its words in the manner of a beast, yet not inwardly tasting the savour of the Spirit. To him it is rightly said: “This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Matthew 15). And elsewhere: “Their heart was not right with him, nor were they found faithful in his covenant” (Psalm 77). Therefore do not be deceived, brothers: God is not mocked, as it is written: “God searches hearts and reins” (Jeremiah 17).

To speak one thing in the heart and utter another with the mouth belongs to falsity; to speak only to God belongs to devotion; but to speak the same thing in heart as with the mouth belongs to truth. I shall add an example of the same matter. There is another kind of people who, while seeking the favour of kindness, fall into the vice [Col. 0292C] of laxity. They love rejoicing more than mourning, laughing more than grieving, speaking more than silence, wandering about more than contemplation. They complain of the harshness of clothing, the hardness of the bed, the weariness of the cloister, the duration of silence, and the length of vigils. They say that Lot, rescued from Sodom, was saved in Zoar, which is interpreted “little”; and likewise that they, delivered from the great sea of this world, can be saved by a moderate manner of life.

Therefore, most beloved brothers, when such thoughts come to our minds, we ought to set before the eyes of our mind Paul’s saying: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us” (Romans 8). Let us hear the Prophet saying [Col. 0292D]: “For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are counted as sheep for slaughter” (Psalm 43). If, therefore, our enemy strikes us on one cheek, let us offer him the other also; if he strikes the left, let us present the right. Certainly he strikes us on the left cheek when he brings on the troubles of temptations, whether by recollection of past pleasures or by suggestion of present hardships. We ought to offer him the right—that is, against adverse temptations, namely transient pleasures, we ought with steadfast mind to set the glory of the saints and those eternal gifts which God promised to those who contend lawfully (2 Timothy 2)—so that the greatness of the rewards may overcome the straits of present pains.

Let us recall what is commanded in the old law [Col. 0293A] (Numbers 8) concerning Levites consecrated for service in the house. They are commanded to be purified with water of purification, to shave all the hair of their flesh, to wash their garments, and afterwards to offer two oxen, one for sin and the other as a burnt offering. Those who wish to offer themselves to God as a sacrifice of sweet savour ought first, by intense contrition of heart and by a flood of tears, to correct their former transgressions; and thus, through waters of purification, they will rinse and wash away the stains which they contracted in their minds by sinning. Then they ought to shave the hair of the flesh—that is, insofar as they are able, to remove from the face of the mind all superfluous and unlawful thoughts.

Thirdly, we ought to wash our garments: that is, by honourable conduct inwardly and outwardly, to acquire the testimony of a good reputation, so that [Col. 0293B] our good works may shine before men and they may glorify our Father who is in heaven (Matthew 6). By the two oxen, one of which is offered for sin and the other as a burnt offering, two kinds of actions are signified to us: the first pertains to mortification of the flesh, the other to devotion of the mind. For when we chastise our body and reduce it to servitude, offering God fruits worthy of repentance, we slaughter the ox for sin. But when, inflamed with the fire of charity, we are raised upward through the affection of contemplation, then we sacrifice to the Lord the ox as a burnt offering.

If, therefore, these things are commanded to Levites who did not yet know the way of the saints and from whom truth was still hidden beneath the shadow of figures, how much more are ministers of the New Testament [Col. 0293C] bound to observe them, since they are permitted to see with their eyes, handle with their hands, and touch with their mouths that mystery dreadful to angels and archangels? Therefore let us chastise the vice of security with the scourge of fear, because in this life a human being does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred (Ecclesiastes 9).

The third temptation, which we have called manifest, is so named because we manifestly know whence it arises and toward what end, as toward its completion, it tends. Such are pleasures of the flesh, or of any other impiety, when the wretched soul is affected by recollection of sin which it has committed, or even by an unlawful desire for something apprehended by the outward sense, so much so that it finds it pleasant to think of such things and, as though they were delights of pleasure, to imprint these and similar things more deeply upon the memory [Col. 0293D]. If such pleasure is without consent and quickly passes, it is venial; but if we linger over it longer, it undoubtedly becomes mortal. Therefore, beloved brothers, if the enemy rises up through corrupt pleasure, as though before our face, let us beware lest through consent [lacuna] in our head. “See, O Lord,” says the Prophet, “and consider, for my enemy has risen up” (Lamentations 1). Behold, he complains that his enemy rises up—that is, through corrupt pleasure toward consent; therefore he asks the Lord’s help, lest he be led to consent.

[Col. 0294A] Against this temptation the following are especially necessary: the exercise of work and solitude of life. Through exercise the mind is guarded from returning to past things by recollection; through a solitary way of life, the outward sense is guarded from drawing in vanity. For if David had fought in war against the enemies with the rest, he would not have burned with the fire of lust into love for Bathsheba (2 Kings 11). And if the elders of Babylon had restrained their sight from vanity, desire would not have overthrown their hearts, deceived by Susanna’s appearance (Daniel 13).

Since, therefore, that enemy of the human race subjects many souls to his dominion by wicked suggestion or temptation, the Prophet rightly says of him: “He has made riches, and not by judgment.” By riches I mean not money, but souls [Col. 0294B]; not possessions, but possessors; and not for himself. At times, indeed, you make riches for yourself, O man [lacuna], at times for him. You make riches for yourself when, under the rule of desire or avarice, he drags you through every unlawful thing, so that, if by his prompting the splendour of your household can be increased, he may wholly possess your soul, as though incarnated in the vanity of riches—a soul which, perhaps without riches, he supposes might sometime breathe again toward its Creator. You gather these riches for yourself in order to satisfy in every respect your own pleasure through them. For minds generally luxuriate in prosperity, and it is not easy to endure favourable circumstances with an even mind.

And all these things tend to this end: that when you perish, you may not take all things with you, nor may your glory descend with you; but rather, stripped of every fruit of virtues, he may assign you a portion with those descending into the pit, where, without hope of deliverance, he may possess you and afflict you with punishments without remedy. Thus it comes about that he no longer makes riches for you as a consolation, but for himself, for whatever execution of his malice may be possible. Yet this happens to him as a greater accumulation of condemnation, because he makes these riches for himself through wickedness and deceit, not by judgment. “He has made riches,” he says, “and not by judgment.”

Judgment certainly involves choosing what is just and rejecting its opposite, that is, what is unjust. How, then, can one who is the author of wickedness and injustice claim anything by just judgment? He makes riches, therefore, and not by judgment, when first he craftily suggests evils, then corrupts the soul through pleasure and consent, thereafter [Col. 0294D] binds and constrains it by the habit of wicked action, and finally, possessing it freely, though unjustly, drags it with himself into the place of horror and vast solitude.

Let us, most beloved brothers, strive to escape the yoke of this most cruel master; and, ever watchful in mind, let us commend ourselves, in fear of God and love of neighbour, to him who chose us as his inheritance, so that, escaping the sentence on the wicked on the day of vengeance, we may be admitted with the blessed of God the Father into eternal life. Amen.

**IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1203: STEPHEN, ABBOT OF SAINT GENEVIEVE OF PARIS, AFTERWARDS BISHOP OF TOURNAI**

[Col. 0295]

## Historical Notice

*(Edition of the Works of Stephen of Tournai, edited by the Reverend Father Claude du Molinet, regular canon of the Congregation of France.—Paris: published at the expense of Louis Billaine, bookseller of Paris, 1679, with royal privilege, quarto.)*

[Col. 0295A] Stephen was born at Orléans in Gaul [Note: [Col. 0295] See Letter 191, to the abbot of Saint-Euverte at Orléans: “The unity of the city, which gives us and you a community of birth,” etc.], in the year of the Lord 1135. It is not easy to say how greatly he was inclined from his earliest age toward exercises of piety, and with how great a zeal he at the same time burned to embrace the ecclesiastical life. His parents fostered this most devout purpose, taking diligent care that he should be instructed both in knowledge of the finest arts and in the precepts of every virtue. At first he learned the elements of grammar from a man equally wise and learned. This man entered the monastery of Charity on the Loire in order to follow there the strictly observed Rule of Saint Benedict; he compelled Stephen to complete the course of studies already begun, first in the schools of the cathedral church of Orléans and afterwards at Chartres.

So great was his diligence in reading books, and so early and subtly did he cultivate his natural talent in the knowledge derived from them, that before long he learned to speak and write with polish and elegance both in concise and extended discourse. I shall offer no other proof of this fact [Col. 0295B] than the works of our Stephen, concerning which he himself also speaks in Letter 277, written to an abbot among his friends, who had entrusted to him the task of composing an office in honour of Saint Gerard.

Equipped with so great a knowledge of humane letters, he advanced to higher studies and devoted himself wholly to philosophy and theology. In these, as a learned master and celebrated doctor alike, he attained no lesser renown. To all this he added so perfect a knowledge of councils and sacred canons that, having composed a *Summa of Canons* and published Commentaries on Gratian, he taught this discipline publicly with great glory and applause from men. It is even credible that he studied civil law at the Academy of Bologna, since his letters show how he won for himself, there and elsewhere, the friendship and favour of very many eminent men. Among them Urban IV, supreme pontiff, Cardinal Gratian, and Peter of San Crisogono deserve particular mention.

[Col. 0296A] Nor should it here be passed over in silence how dear he was to William of Champagne, son of Theobald, count alike of Troyes and Blois, whose sister had married King Louis the Younger. When William had been raised to the archbishoprics of Sens and Reims, and had discerned Stephen’s equal virtue and tested his rare learning, he chose him as his almoner and confidential secretary.

He might certainly not have found it difficult to be brought to hope that, partly by his merits and partly through the favour of his most powerful lord, he would be raised to the highest ecclesiastical honours, had not his mind, wholly remote from all ambition and free from avarice, resolved to cling to and serve God alone wherever he might lead. Therefore, when he learned that Gruis, abbot of Saint Victor, had sent some of his men to Orléans in the year of the Lord 1158, to restore the ecclesiastical discipline wholly fallen into ruin in the monastery of Saint-Euverte; and that, relying on the auspices of the celebrated Roger, first abbot of that house, they followed the devout way of life already established in the towns of Beaugency and Blois [Col. 0296B], then, by a certain divine impulse, he withdrew from the court and assumed the habit of Regular Canons, either at the abbey of Saint-Euverte or at Saint Victor. This occurred about the year 1165.

It can scarcely—indeed, not even scarcely—be said how wonderfully his virtue shone forth. Saint Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, also perceived its rays, while he was then living in exile among the French, forced there by the hostility of his enemies. Stephen was bound to him by such close bonds of friendship that in a letter written to John, bishop of Poitiers, who had been a disciple of that same glorious martyr, he did not hesitate to call him his master, patron, and intimate friend.

After Robert, abbot of Saint-Euverte, had died, Stephen was appointed in his place. This most distinguished dignity, as though adding a new crown to Stephen [Col. 0297A], commended him to everyone. All eminent men who came to Orléans frequently visited him. Among them especially, the bishop of Le Puy, charmed by Stephen’s pleasant conversation, offered him the monastery of Doyen in his diocese, so that he might establish there henceforth the order which the bishop had seen observed by Stephen’s own brethren. Having happily accomplished this matter and carried through to the end the devout plans of Robert, whom he had succeeded, Stephen directed his mind toward wholly repairing the church of Saint-Euverte, long since overthrown and fallen into decay.

This work was worthy of so great a man, though he did not seem equal to accomplishing it. Nevertheless, trusting in God almighty and immortal, he undertook the arduous and difficult task. I cannot adequately express to you how ingenious his piety was on this occasion, how many heavy penalties he endured, how many bitter labours he undertook. At one time, preaching in churches, at another through the streets of the city of Orléans, he sought the assistance—or rather the wealth—of the people. At another, he sent some of his brethren with relics to the city of Tours and other neighbouring towns [Col. 0297B], to collect from the faithful alms intended for completion of this building.

Meanwhile Peter, bishop of Clermont, consulted him together with Maurice, the very learned bishop of Paris, whether the sacrament of baptism should be regarded as valid or invalid when conferred in his diocese by rustic and untrained people in the following manner. They poured water over the child’s head, using these words: “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit”; for they did not add, “I baptize you.” Maurice held that the sacrament of baptism was invalid. Stephen opposed him, but with such modesty that he declared himself not so much to define the matter as to state what he thought; and he willingly submitted this opinion to the judgment of the bishop of Paris, a man most learned and wise alike.

At that time the bloody death of John the dean inflicted a sad and grievous wound upon the church of Orléans [Col. 0297C]. He had exerted every effort to restore to his chapter goods usurped by a nobleman, to whom they belonged; and he felt the rage of his enemy. For that cruel man, unmindful that the dean had previously preserved his life, attacked him with a sword and killed him, piercing his head with many wounds.

The church of Orléans resolved to avenge so grave an injury done to itself. Accordingly, when all the clergy of the province had been called together in the city of Sens concerning this matter, the abbot of Saint-Euverte was entrusted with the task both of pleading the cause and of stirring that most distinguished assembly to avenge the crime committed.

The incredible force of his eloquence shone out powerfully in this affair. Moved both by his words and by the atrocity of the deed vividly laid before them, the Fathers, inflamed with a certain righteous indignation to exact vengeance, resolved unanimously and by common consent to seek the king’s aid and bring the case before the tribunal of his justice. Stephen was chosen to write the letters to be presented to the king in everyone’s name. But the affair turned out far otherwise [Col. 0297D] than had been intended. The guilty party, having secured the court’s favour and blocked the way of justice, not only went unpunished for his crime, but the defenders and avengers of innocence also incurred the king’s displeasure. The king especially showed himself offended with Stephen on account of the letters he had composed, although the entire assembly gathered in Sens had read and approved them by its judgment.

This unjust anger of the king strengthened the rage and audacity of the enemies of the Church. Accordingly, they threatened Stephen with plundering his goods, destroying his house, sword, firebrands, and a most dreadful death unless he abandoned his undertaking. To whom could he have fled more suitably, reduced as he was to such misery and calamity, than to William of Champagne, bishop-elect of Chartres? Protected by William’s authority and power, he fortified himself against the unjust designs and wicked attacks of his adversaries, and through William’s efforts at last restored himself to the king’s friendship, diminished—or rather wholly lost—in the manner described.

[Col. 0298A] Meanwhile Stephen was no less celebrated and revered among his own brethren. On account of his outstanding virtue and singular prudence in conducting affairs, they raised him to the highest honours of his order. When Aubert, abbot of Saint Genevieve of Paris, died in the year of the Lord 1177, Stephen, abbot of Saint-Euverte, was elected to hold his place in the administration of this ancient and royal abbey. It is not easy to say how painfully he was separated from his first spouse—I mean the church of Orléans—and with how much grief and sadness he was torn from the most dear and pleasant embrace of his sons. Yet they, not unmindful of benefits received from their most loving father, granted him, by documents executed in their own hands, half the revenues of the estate of Gondreville as an annual pension.

Hardly had he entered the house of Saint Genevieve when he filled all hearts with singular joy and, like some new and unfamiliar star, illumined those lofty and steep heights [Col. 0298B]. He did so partly by a greater increase of the regular observance already established, partly by necessary repair of collapsing buildings, and partly by stirring among the religious the study of the liberal arts. Accordingly, he established private schools, although public teaching took place in the vestibule of the abbey. In these schools the minds of noble young men, who under his guidance consecrated themselves to God, might be formed more effectively and appropriately in the best precepts both of learning and, much more, of every virtue. He did not wish his own men to mix with outside students, lest faith and piety, offended by insufficiently decent conduct and examples, and so rendered for a time less secure, should suffer some loss.

This is clear from Letter 80, written to Absalon, archbishop of Lund in Denmark. He had earnestly begged Stephen to allow his nephew, a regular canon of the church of Saint Genevieve of Paris, who later became bishop and chancellor of Denmark, to study at the University of Paris [Col. 0298C]. Stephen replied that this was foreign to his institute and in no way suited to preserving good morals. “As for what you have intimated to us in your letter concerning sending him either to the Mount, or to the schools of secular Parisians, and to vendors of words, with your leave we do not permit it, because it conflicts with our institution and custom, lest through him a new spectacle be presented to the brethren now present which may be drawn into a harmful example for those to come. Wisdom has its own rules in the cloisters, establishing for itself schools—here of truth, there of virtue.”

Stephen devoted himself wholly not only to cultivating the minds of his brethren but also to adorning his church and house. The latter had been so shaken and weakened by frequent Norman incursions that scarcely any glorious traces survived of the celebrated church built in mosaic work. He therefore caused the walls to be repaired; the vault and roof, as they now stand, to be strengthened; the cloisters, chapter-house, and dormitory [Col. 0298D] to be erected; and the chapel called that of the Blessed Virgin of Mercy to be built. He also laid and brought to completion the foundations of the refectory and adjacent places. He completed these works thereafter, as he did many others, with such applause from his own community and such benefit that he may deservedly be called, after King Clovis, not the restorer but the founder of the abbey of Saint Genevieve.

Thus, under the direction of this most distinguished and wise abbot, the house of Saint Genevieve was restored, enriched with abundance of every good thing, and adorned with a corresponding cultivation of virtues and learning. It flourished wonderfully, as may be seen in Letter 148, which he wrote to William, abbot in Denmark, in these words: “By God’s grace all things concerning us and the brethren prosper, and there is neither adverse encounter nor Satan. In the highest tranquillity and peace they dwell unanimously in the house of the Lord, competing only in serving the Lord and, with all humility, in outstripping one another. Temporal things answer to spiritual ones: the spacious and handsome regular workshops are almost completed, and in the estates rustic buildings rival urban ones in extent and beauty [Col. 0299A]. We turn our care and solicitude to renewing and shoring up the old walls of the Church, decayed by age and fire and threatening collapse and ruin. We have acquired new timber for repairing the roofs, to be laid upon the walls and underlaid with sheets of lead.”

Nor could the immense virtue of so great a man be confined within the narrow bounds of his monastery, nor could that extraordinary zeal with which he pursued his order be restrained from breaking out against the canons of the cathedral church of Reims, who had resolved to abandon the regular discipline formerly observed. On this matter he admonished the dean and exhorted him in sharp words to oppose so novel and destructive a scheme vigorously and steadfastly. With exactly the same greatness of spirit he repressed the wicked attacks of adversaries who either plundered the possessions of his brethren or disturbed their peace, as we learn happened to the canons of the church of Bourg-Moyen in the city of Blois, of Saint Samson at Orléans, and others [Col. 0299B].

As Stephen’s fame increased daily, matters of the greatest importance then being conducted were entrusted to his care and zeal. For he was assigned to Cardinal Alberic, the legate appointed to expel the Albigensians and Coterels, who were infecting all Provence and the region of Toulouse with the poison of their heresy. This task certainly appeared full of dangerous risk. Robbers lay in wait on the roads, ambushes were prepared, and manifest enemies of God and humankind were devastating everything with sword and fire. Stephen himself is a most truthful witness of this in Letter 73, sent to Raymond, prior of Saint Genevieve of Paris.

At about the same time, the long-standing dispute between the archbishop of Tours and the bishop of Dol in Brittany was renewed. The latter, assuming the title of archbishop, was striving to remove and withdraw himself and the bishops of Brittany from the jurisdiction of the metropolitan of Tours. The matter was sharply debated before the supreme pontiff. On the one side, the duke of Brittany supported the bishop of Dol; on the other, Philip Augustus, king of France, by envoys and letters strove with all his power to ensure that the archbishop of Tours retained the ancient honour of his dignity [Col. 0299C]. Nevertheless, since the arbitrators favoured the duke of Brittany to some extent, the king of France was so inflamed with anger that he wrote fresh letters to the pope through Stephen. In them he complained of the injury done to him, reproached the Apostolic See with benefits bestowed upon it by his ancestors, and moreover threatened most serious consequences unless the pope ordered the judgment rescinded as swiftly as possible.

Nor should it be passed over in silence that Stephen, together with the bishop of Paris and the abbots of Saint-Germain, Saint Victor, Saint-Denis, Cîteaux, and Clairvaux, was chosen to settle disputes which had arisen in the Order of Grandmont. The lay brothers, exceeding the number of clerics in that religious community and becoming over-proud because the management of temporal affairs had been entrusted to them, did not obey the commands of their superiors. Indeed, having violently driven both priests and clerics from the house, they unjustly claimed all authority for themselves. Stephen, intending with the others delegated by the supreme pontiff to provide for the threatening evil, omitted nothing relevant to granting peace to the Order of Grandmont: partly through prayers, partly through exhortations, partly through the force of authority which he exercised [Col. 0299D].

Accordingly, those judges determined that the rebellious lay brothers must be struck with anathema unless they came to their senses as quickly as possible. Having restored all clerics to their former rank, they threatened excommunication if the lay brothers should thereafter perpetrate anything of this sort. Some, terrified and utterly crushed by these thunderbolts, submitted; but the spirit of others was hardened in such obstinacy and stubbornness [Col. 0300A] that royal authority also had to be used to bring them back to due obedience.

In the year of the Lord 1190, King Philip Augustus, having undertaken a journey to the Holy Land, entrusted the administration of the kingdom during his absence to William of Champagne, archbishop of Reims. Since William needed the work and counsel of men most wise and faithful for the exceedingly difficult administration of all France, he summoned the abbot of Saint Genevieve of Paris to share and participate in the immense labour. For Stephen’s extraordinary and singular prudence and sagacity in conducting both private and public affairs had long been known and tested. Nor was he less acceptable to the king himself than to the king’s uncle, since Philip frequently entrusted matters of the greatest importance to his fidelity, especially when he once sent him as ambassador to Rome to the supreme pontiff. In a letter, the king recorded the merits of our abbot in these words [Col. 0300B]: “And because the affair is great and deeply fixed in our heart, we send to you our beloved and familiar servant Stephen, abbot of Saint Genevieve, discreet and faithful to the kingdom. Receive him kindly in our place, and in matters which he tells you on our behalf, have undoubting faith in him as in us.”

The same Philip Augustus honoured Stephen’s virtue with greater and more extensive monuments of glory. Among all the prelates of France, he especially chose him to perform the office of sponsor—or, as they say, godfather—at the baptism of his firstborn son. He gave him the name Louis; he was later called Louis VIII and held the sovereignty of the kingdom. A letter from our abbot to him still survives, in which he called him his godson and especially commended three things: piety toward God, the honour and reverence owed to one’s father, and devotion to learning.

[Col. 0300C] But in the year 1192 Stephen was elected to the bishopric of Tournai, in nearly the same manner as Saint Ambrose had formerly been raised to the archbishopric of Milan. For after the death of Erard, bishop of Tournai, when the people together with all the clergy had been summoned to choose a successor, the greater part of the assembly fixed its attention upon Peter, cantor of the Church of Paris, a man then distinguished alike by rare learning and by innocence of life.

This plan, however, did not please the archbishop of Reims, who at that time was both metropolitan and administrator of all Gaul. He vigorously opposed Peter’s election, judging it to be as unlawful as it was invalid. In Peter’s favor our Stephen wrote to him, adding moreover that the factors valid and requisite for a canonical election were especially present in this case. But William, judging that he should by no means yield to the arguments put forward, proposed our abbot as equal to bearing so great a burden. This was immediately accepted with the immense applause and joy of all—even of those who had contended for the other candidate—if Stephen alone be excepted. He recounts this in Letter 177, written to the archbishop of Tours in these words:

> Called by the hidden judgment of the Lord to the Church of Tournai, I commend myself to your prayers, that through others’ intercessions I may attain what I do not merit by my own merits. And because, Father, I do not know whether from so great a calling I ought, as one worthy of love or of hatred, to expect punishment or reward, at the first sound of this report:
>
> I was stunned; my hair stood on end, and my voice stuck in my throat.

At last, as though awakening from a heavy sleep, I entrusted the whole matter to God, who, by His grace, if it be pleasing in His sight, will accomplish and establish the whole thing.

The archbishop of Tours replied courteously, congratulating him on the dignity he had obtained, and at the same time sent him as a gift a mitre, gloves, and sandals.

Meanwhile Pope Celestine, having learned what had happened and suspecting that Stephen had been elevated to the bishopric of Tournai by human favor rather than by God’s providence, took this election badly. Perceiving this, Stephen not only soothed the wounded mind of the supreme pontiff by words bearing a notable mark of obedience and reverence, but also won for himself his singular affection and goodwill:

> Called to the Church of Tournai while far away in place and mind, ignorant, and expecting nothing less than a bishop’s chair—why did I transgress if I approached?
