What sin did I commit if I did not entreat? Did I offend because I did not abandon it? Certainly I could not divine whether this would please or displease the supreme pontiff, whose decisions are laws, and in whose right hand is a fiery law. But since it belongs to good minds to acknowledge faults where there is no fault, and since it is very dangerous for a son to remain separated too long from his father’s sight, I omit defenses, ask pardon, seek favor, implore mercy, etc.

It is remarkable how much grief the loss of so great a man brought upon the religious of Sainte-Geneviève at Paris [Col. 0301B], whose house he had governed with such moderation and prudence for fifteen years. Nevertheless, this misfortune had to be endured, and provision had at once to be made for the election of a new abbot. The lot fell upon John, who appeared advanced not so much in age as in character. Stephen took him to the bishop of Meaux to be initiated by the ceremonies of blessing on Palm Sunday; then, when he had returned to Paris, placed him over the monastery of Sainte-Geneviève. Having at last taken leave of his religious brethren, and taking with him two men, namely Gerard and Marcellus, he set out in order to celebrate the solemnities of Easter at Tournai.

He received consecration from the archbishop of Reims, his lord and friend. Then, applying himself to his task, he devoted himself wholly and immediately to reforming both regular and secular clergy. For these reasons he called a synod and established many measures highly useful for promoting ecclesiastical discipline [Col. 0301C]. In particular, canons were forbidden to possess two prebends or to keep women in their houses, and monks were forbidden to administer parishes.

When the abbey of Saint-Martin at Tournai had departed from the right way of living, when love of regular discipline had been extinguished there, and when moreover its abbot lived a disgraceful life and set the worst example, the most vigilant shepherd, intending promptly to address this evil as it grew daily, tried by gentle words and exhortations to lead the religious back to the path of virtue. When he found these entirely useless and vain, he struck the abbot, who was becoming ever more hardened, with the thunderbolt of excommunication.

If this most vigilant shepherd exercised such severity against bad shepherds, who fed themselves rather than the flock, how great was the strength of mind which he displayed in defending and protecting the good. An abbot of Saint-Amand, of the Order of Saint Benedict, was accused before the archbishop of Reims by his own religious [Col. 0301D], as appearing insufficiently versed in ecclesiastical discipline and inadequately instructed in the ceremonies of his order. Stephen was chosen arbiter of this dispute. Entering the monastery of Saint-Amand and hearing the arguments of both sides, he judged the abbot to be a man most worthy of every praise, distinguished by temperance, charity, thrift, patience, and finally by the glory of every virtue. The sole ground on which he was hated by his own men was the zeal with which he restrained and repressed vices; they brought against him as a grave charge that he did not know how to indicate with his fingers beans, cheese, eggs, and other such things, which it was customary to request and designate by certain signs during the time of silence.

Although the outstanding piety and singular love with which our Stephen burned toward God and the Church were fortified, as it were, by the two strongest bulwarks of learning and prudence, some nevertheless condemned him as a young man in ferment and unequal to episcopal care. But Stephen, learning that the archdeacon of Cambrai, otherwise his friend, was opposing and resisting him more vehemently, defended himself in a letter in which he set before his eyes a certain splendid and excellent mirror of episcopal life. The substance of this Letter 208 is as follows:

> I rarely leave the city; as far as possible, I observe the canonical hours with the others. According to the grace bestowed upon me, I proclaim God’s word to my parishioners. Speaking out against the new heresy and the other monsters of that kind as far as I am able, I fight, as it were, against wild beasts. The sacraments which I received freely, I impart freely. I always shake my hands free, if not from every gift, at least from an unlawful one. To those who come to me I give, in confession, counsel; in penitence, a remedy; in tribulation, consolation, as far as the Lord permits. In hours free from business and from the court, in a place suitable for this purpose, I apply myself to Holy Scripture, reading and ruminating upon what, after reading, I digest and convey to the chamber of memory. At table I do not wish to be either alone or obscure, where nature may more easily accuse excess than curiosity hunger. I do not squander Christ’s patrimony upon actors and jesters. These are the outward matters; but God, who searches hearts and reins, knows the hidden things.

Since he had always applied his mind to adorning the temples of God and to embellishing his brides—that is, as I understand it, the churches of Saint-Euverte and Sainte-Geneviève—it should not seem surprising that he carried out so many remarkable works in the Church of Tournai. He caused a vault to be made, the high altar to be built, an altar-front of silver to be ornamented, and the church to be richly supplied with sacred vessels and precious ornaments [Col. 0302B]. He also consecrated a chapel in the episcopal palace at Tournai in the name of Saint Euverte and Saint Geneviève, adorning it with painted glass and images of them and endowing it with revenues, so that their feast might be celebrated in his church. He further bequeathed one hundred pounds for his anniversary, together with seventeen acres of land and a fourth part of his right over the River Scheldt. Thus this most upright bishop expended his goods [Col. 0302C] upon all things pertaining to God’s honor, the worship of his church, and the increase of the solemnity of the divine office.

Although Stephen was endowed with a very calm and gentle spirit, he may nevertheless be seen tossed by three dreadful storms and assailed by most dangerous tempests. The first disturbance was raised by the agents of the supreme pontiff, to whom he had not yet paid the sum of money imposed upon him. The prudent man did not pour out upon the authors of the wrongs unjustly done to him the grief he had conceived; rather, he secretly disclosed it to his friends, especially to the bishop of Soissons, who was entangled in the same difficulties. He withdrew into that bishop’s diocese, namely to the estate of Marizy, which belonged to the abbey of Sainte-Geneviève, in order to surrender two annual revenues of his bishopric for payment of this debt.

When this storm had been quieted and suppressed, he returned to Tournai; but behold, suddenly a new tempest arose. Baldwin, a citizen of Tournai, had founded in the cathedral church a fifth prebend [Col. 0302D], intended for priests celebrating the high mass. The bishop, while the chapter was still reigning, conferred it upon one of the canons of Sainte-Geneviève whom he had brought with him. After a year of peaceful possession of the benefice, he somehow incurred the chapter’s hatred, so that it not only deprived him of the benefice but also prohibited him from entering the church. The bishop, thinking this utterly intolerable, implored the aid of the archbishop of Reims, who by forceful letters moved the canons so strongly that they restored the excluded man to his former dignity.

Count Baldwin of Flanders added the final burden to these troubles. For, having broken the peace which he had earlier concluded with Philip Augustus, in the year of the Lord 1198 he invaded the territory of Cambrai with a great army, intending to lay it waste with sword and fire. The archbishop of Reims, legate of the Apostolic See, sent commands from the supreme pontiff and also from the king of France to the bishop of Tournai that he should strike him with anathema [Col. 0303A] and lay his lands under interdict. The matter appeared exceedingly dangerous; accordingly, the bishop consulted the clergy assembled for this purpose. Present at the council was Bernard of Robais, the great bailiff of Flanders, who appealed to the supreme pontiff from the sentence which was on the point of being pronounced.

Meanwhile Stephen informed the archbishop of Reims of what was being done and judged that the pronouncement of the interdict should be deferred for a time. But when he perceived the prince’s audacity growing day by day, he vigorously and steadfastly hurled the thunderbolts of excommunication and interdict against the count and his supporters. Offended by this exceptionally noble action of the bishop, the prince omitted nothing by which he might exact punishment from him through the plundering of his goods. To avoid this promptly, Stephen determined to go into France; but since fear of ambush prevented this, he shut himself within his city and thus fortified himself invincibly against the many plots laid against his life, with divine aid and the unshaken loyalty of the people.

The more gloriously the life of so great a bishop, nourished by virtue [Col. 0303B] amid harsh labors, was strengthened, the more readily his bodily powers, exhausted by the weakness of old age and the number of years—for he had already reached his seventieth year—failed. He testified to this to the archbishop of Reims when he excused himself by letter for being unable to attend the consecration of the bishop of Châlons in the year 1203, according to Alberic’s Chronicle.

[Col. 0304A] Therefore, as he felt frequent illnesses to be heralds of approaching death, he wished to imitate Augustine in death as in life, breathing out his soul amid hostile assaults and tears drawn forth by a proper movement of repentance. For just as that most famous teacher died rather than see the ruin of his people while the Vandals surrounded Hippo with siege, so the bishop of Tournai, after the sorrowful wounds inflicted upon his city by the count of Flanders, could not survive long. And just as Augustine wished to offer to God a soul wholly washed by tears of repentance, so our bishop, toward the end of his life, frequently withdrew to his country estate in order to devote himself to prayer and continual supplications. This appears especially in the letter written to the bishop of Reims.

When he foresaw that the last period of his life was at hand, he wished to perform a father’s office toward his own people, inserting counsels of salvation in two letters, one written to the canons of Sainte-Geneviève, the other to the canons of Saint-Euverte at Orléans. At last [Col. 0304B], Stephen, having completed the course of so illustrious a life and endured many labors, both for the honor and adornment of his order and for the benefit of the Church, in the sixty-eighth year of his age, in the year of restored salvation 1203, on the ninth day of September, departed to heaven to obtain God; his body, however, was buried with great ceremony in the cathedral church.

[Col. 0303]

R. P. DU MOLINET. PREFACE TO HIS EDITION OF THE WORKS OF STEPHEN OF TOURNai.

[Col. 0303C] Learned Reader, to renew the monuments of one’s ancestors is an act no less full of gratitude than of distinguished and praiseworthy devotion. And if there was ever an occasion for gratitude or devotion on our part, surely none has seemed to me more ample and honorable than the renewal and restoration of the works of Stephen of Tournai.

For the exceedingly great services of so great a man to our house of Sainte-Geneviève—which, as abbot, he more generously than almost all others, not merely adorned but restored anew—have long been known to me; and they have strongly stirred me to consecrate to eternity the memory of so dear a father.

Accordingly, after most diligently examining his works for several years, I found three kinds: namely, a *Decretum*, sermons, and letters. The library of Saint-Victor at Paris supplied the *Decretum*, comprising a larger folio volume, as it is called [Col. 0303D]. When carefully read and more closely examined by most discerning men, it was found to be a mere commentary on Gratian’s *Decretals*. But since it is by no means very rare to find commentators of this sort at present, and since I also feared that the learned reader might be overwhelmed, beyond all reason, by so bulky a volume of unprofitable notes, I judged with my friends that it would be better to say nothing of this work in the present edition. I have therefore selected only its preface, which may serve as a sure specimen, as it were, for those who wish to know the work.

I turn now to Stephen’s sermons. Thirty of them in summary are listed in four manuscripts: those of the cathedral of Tournai, the abbeys of Sainte-Geneviève [Col. 0304C] and Saint-Victor, and the Royal Abbey of Navarre. The high reputation they once enjoyed is plainly evident from their careful collection and preservation. Nevertheless, since the elegance of our age differs from that of the preceding age, they themselves appear to their readers so tasteless and simple—indeed, at times childish—that they did not seem at all worthy of publication. For they breathe neither the learned homilies of the holy Fathers, nor their brilliance and felicity in expounding Holy Scripture, nor that grave moral doctrine polished with the purest colors of eloquence. Rather, they draw their whole force and ornament from elaborate divisions; from insipid fictions devised with more cleverness than solidity; from passages of Scripture summoned up in whatever fashion; or, finally, from certain petty allusions and pointed expressions. Hence it is no wonder that, through their humble and obsolete diction and their meager and arid moral teaching [Col. 0304D], they produce disgust and weariness, since they have scarcely any vigor or weight either to please or to persuade.

This will be sufficiently proved by two sermons, from which it will not be difficult to judge the rest. One was delivered to the canons on Pentecost upon this passage of Wisdom (1:4–5): “The spirit of discipline will flee deceit and will not dwell in a body subject to sins.” In it he imagines a marriage of the Devil with Malice and Hypocrisy; clothes and adorns the brides in garments appropriate to their rank; places various dishes upon the wedding table; and assigns diverse functions to their children. What could be said more coldly in these refined times? Another, delivered on Christ’s Nativity, is enlivened by the theme [Col. 0305A], “The Word abbreviated,” with such charms now unfamiliar; speaking grammatically, he does not hesitate to assign conjugations, tenses, and moods to the divine Word, more frivolously than vigorously. Yet although some weightier matters may be found in them, it has been rightly understood that none sufficiently instruct or delight the reader. This is plainly to be attributed to the inelegance of the age rather than to the author’s incompetence.

Therefore, having deliberately suppressed these sermons, it seems preferable to set apart the one delivered in a synod, in order that notice may be given of the rest, which I list here at the end of the work.

In Stephen’s third work, namely his letters, I have invested the greatest part of my labor. They had formerly been published in quarto, together with the writings of Gerbert and John of Salisbury, by Jean-Baptiste Masson, archdeacon of Bayeux, brother of the very famous Papire Masson. Shortly afterward they were also inserted into the *Library of the Fathers*, but so disfigured and obscured [Col. 0305B] that scarcely any light was thrown upon the author’s genuine meaning. Moreover, since they became ever rarer, I, wishing to uphold the merits of so great a man and to hand down to posterity the renowned name of the restorer of the house of Sainte-Geneviève at Paris, devoted my industry, care, and thought to elucidating, to the best of my ability, a more recent edition of his letters by scholia.

But because each person’s due honor must plainly be rendered, I confess that I undertook this task the more willingly because Monsieur Baluze, very mindful of the public good, most kindly yielded to me the part which he had already proposed to undertake himself. For although that man, outstanding in every kind of learning and praise, had promised at the very beginning of his edition of the letters of Lupus of Ferrières that he would publish the works of Stephen of Tournai together with notes, once he learned of my identical undertaking and was informed that I had in hand a great many materials drawn from both the abbeys of Sainte-Geneviève and Saint-Euverte at Orléans which would contribute greatly to illustrating the letters of Abbot Stephen [Col. 0305C], that most obliging man immediately abandoned what he had begun and most generously assigned the credit of the work to me, though I was far his inferior in that regard.

Made bolder by his permission and encouragement, while I was working upon the scholia for the first edition of the letters, I spared no effort in ensuring that I had identified any letters still unpublished. While I pursued this one object, friends informed me that the Reverend Father Joseph Ignatius of Saint Anthony, a Carmelite of the Strict Observance, had found several in two Belgian manuscripts. At once, delighted, I wrote to Tournai to this religious man letters concerning my purpose as earnest and diligent as I could make them. Without delay, he came to my assistance at the proper moment; and, to speak plainly, I think no one could be found more obliging in goodwill or more ready to bestow a favor. For he most willingly promised me his assistance in this matter, and promptly sent sixty letters which he had unearthed from two Belgian monasteries, copied out in his own hand and so closely akin and consonant with Stephen’s style that they remove every doubt that Stephen himself was their author.

One of these Flemish manuscripts does not differ at all from the one which the most illustrious archbishop and duke of Reims possessed from the library of the abbey of Saint-Amand. Armed, as it were, with a new engine by the considerable aid both of this and another manuscript, and of the Thuan Library—used, that is, by Jean-Baptiste Masson—and perhaps also of the very manuscript which Monsieur du Sausay testifies was found in his own day at Chartres in the monastery of Saint Peter [Col. 0306B], I corrected more easily the errors which had slipped into the first edition.

I would have it observed that I have scarcely departed at all from the first sequence of the letters. Since they appeared quite properly divided into three parts—those which he wrote as abbot of Saint-Euverte, those as abbot of Sainte-Geneviève, and finally those as bishop of Tournai—I thought it worthwhile still to preserve the same order. Nevertheless, because I was compelled, in consideration of chronology, to mingle the newly discovered letters among the old, I marked only the former with an asterisk as a distinction. But since you will find that the numbering of the old letters has been altered by the addition and insertion of the new, an index has been provided so that citations formerly made from them may be available to you and you may more conveniently dispel every obscurity.

[Col. 0306C] Finally, I judged it best to ensure that a Life of the author should faithfully be placed before his works, so that the virtues and dignities of so great a bishop might become better known. Its entire authority rests upon his letters and upon the records of the abbeys of Sainte-Geneviève and Saint-Euverte, which he administered for many years with the highest distinction and equal prudence.

[Col. 0305]

NOTICE OF LATIN MANUSCRIPTS OF THE KING’S LIBRARY, NOS. 8630 A, 8566 A, 2923, CONTAINING THE LETTERS OF STEPHEN, SUCCESSIVELY ABBOT OF SAINT-EUVERTE AT ORLÉANS AND OF SAINTE-GENEVIÈVE AT PARIS, THEN BISHOP OF TOURNAI. BY M. J. J. BRIAL.  
[Note: [Col. 0305] *Notices of the Manuscripts of the Royal Library*, vol. X, part II, p. 66.]

I

1. Manuscript 8630 A, Colbert 4367, Regius 4353, is a small quarto of one hundred folios, written on vellum in a fourteenth-century hand, from which folios have been torn out in several places. This is the manuscript used for the first edition of Stephen of Tournai’s letters, published at Paris in 1611 in quarto by Jean Masson, archdeacon of Bayeux, after the epistles of Gerbert—who was pope under the name Sylvester II—and of John of Salisbury. This may be judged from the lacunae which occur in that edition at the same places as in the manuscript. This edition contains only 240 letters.

[Col. 0307] 2. Number 8566 A, originally belonging to the library of the abbey of Saint-Martin at Tournai, had passed into that of Charles-Maurice Le Tellier, archbishop of Reims, and from there into the old collection of the Royal Library, no. 4083, 2. It is a vellum quarto, in a fine thirteenth-century hand, composed of 125 folios or 250 pages. It contains only 216 letters, arranged in an order wholly different from that which they occupy in the preceding manuscript. Properly speaking, it is only a selection of letters: their superscriptions or addresses have been removed and replaced by explanatory summaries of the matters contained in each. Yet it contains several letters absent from the manuscript already cited.

With the aid of this manuscript and Jean Masson’s edition, corrected in Étienne Baluze’s hand, Charles du Molinet, a regular canon of the Congregation of France, undertook a new edition of Stephen of Tournai’s letters with notes. He published it in octavo at Paris, Billaine, 1679; it contains 286 letters.

At the end of this manuscript is found a treatise by Guibert, called of Tournai, a Friar Minor, entitled *On the Restoration of Peace*; but this is not what we intend to discuss.

3. Manuscript 2923, after having belonged to Francesco Petrarch, is catalogued under different numbers in the Library’s collections: 1702, 4353. It is a quarto volume of 169 vellum folios, in a fourteenth-century hand. It contains: (1) the letters of Peter Abelard; (2) his apology by Berengar of Poitiers; (3) the letters of Cassiodorus; (4) the letters of Stephen of Tournai, from folio 94 through 169. Our notice will concern only these last.

This manuscript is wholly conformable to no. 8630 A, but it is sound and complete and may serve to fill the lacunae in the former. It contains 300 letters, all having the superscriptions or addresses that are missing in no. 8566 A.

It was from this manuscript that Étienne Baluze, dissatisfied with Father du Molinet’s edition, conceived the plan of producing a new edition of Stephen of Tournai’s letters, whose importance for the civil and ecclesiastical history of the late twelfth century he recognized. It is regrettable that a scholar so versed in medieval literature did not give the public the benefit of his work, which is preserved among his manuscripts in the King’s Library. A new edition was all the more necessary because Father du Molinet’s edition swarms with errors, especially in the pieces which he published for the first time, the greater number of which lack titles and leave one to guess to whom they are addressed.

That edition is still incomplete, both because considerable lacunae and a great number of essential words and phrases entirely omitted are found in its old letters as well as in its new ones, and because, with the assistance of Petrarch’s manuscript, the number of letters could be greatly increased. Father du Molinet published only 286; we have seen that this manuscript contains 300, and Baluze had collected more than 320.

Father du Molinet had adopted a plan which, if carried out, would have shed much light upon these letters. He intended to distribute them in three parts: in the first, letters Stephen wrote as abbot of Saint-Euverte at Orléans, from 1167 to 1177; in the second, those he wrote on a broader stage while abbot of Sainte-Geneviève at Paris, from 1177 to 1192; and in the third, those he composed after he received the bishopric of Tournai, until his death in 1203. To follow this plan, the editor rightly moved some of these letters which manifestly were not in their proper place. But since in most of the others, deprived of their superscription formula, the author gives no title for himself, he left in their first positions a greater number which ought to have been moved.

It was not enough to determine to which of the three parts each letter belonged: it was also necessary to establish a chronological order among them, and this the editor did not do. It may be said that the further he departed from the order established in the manuscripts, the more confusion he introduced into the arrangement of these letters chronologically. This is particularly noticeable in the third part, where the editor placed almost all the new letters he published. One is truly struck by seeing that they are almost always placed in reverse chronological order, though these are the very letters to which it was easy to assign a date, since nearly all concern events known from public history.

In light of all these considerations, Étienne Baluze formed the plan of producing a new edition of Stephen of Tournai’s letters, restoring them to the same order that they have in the manuscripts. It would be difficult to assign precise dates to most of them, and absurd to move them without certainty of restoring them to a better order. His work exists, and it would be possible, by putting the finishing touches to his notes, which are only sketches, to make it available to the public, if the taste of the age favored enterprises of this kind. Unable to bring this new work as a whole out of obscurity, we believe we shall do something useful and agreeable to scholars by publishing, as a supplement to existing editions, twenty letters not yet printed.

We would also have many corrections to make in the text of both Masson’s edition and Father du Molinet’s, but this minute detail would lead us too far. We shall content ourselves with reprinting some of the letters most badly treated by Father du Molinet, especially those in which he omitted passages, and sometimes whole pages, and with restoring the formulas or addresses missing from his edition.  
[Note: [Col. 0307] “The passages which M. Brial restored from manuscript codices we have placed in brackets in our edition.” —Editors of the Fathers.]

II.

Étienne Baluze, having had access to a manuscript belonging to Chancellor Séguier which contained the letters, or part of the letters, of Stephen of Tournai, extracted from it twelve that had not yet seen the light. We shall not depart from the purpose proposed in this notice by publishing them after those not yet made public which we have just collected. Since most of these letters lack an address, we have tried to discover, by conjecture, the names of the persons to whom the author wrote. If they are found not to be arranged in chronological order, this is because we did not wish to alter the order they occupied in the manuscript. We should have wished to recover this manuscript, which, from Chancellor Séguier’s library, may have passed into that of Saint-Germain-des-Prés and thence into the King’s Library; but our investigations in this respect were fruitless.

[Col. 0309]

[LETTERS.]

FIRST PART OF THE LETTERS OF STEPHEN, BISHOP OF TOURNAI. Containing those which he wrote when he was abbot of Saint-Euverte at Orléans [Note: [Col. 0309B] The abbey was founded in honor of Saint Euverte, sixth bishop of Orléans, on the same site where there had formerly been a chapel consecrated under the invocation of the Blessed Mary and called “of the Mountains,” in which the sacred relics of this bishop had been deposited. Stephen had first been a secular canon of that church; afterward, having become a regular canon, he was elected abbot. He delivered this address at the Council of Sens.] from approximately 1163 to 1177.

1. FIRST LETTER. The lament of the Church of Orléans over the murder of John [Note: [Col. 0309C] This is John of La Chaîne, dean of Sainte-Croix at Orléans, who fell by the sacrilegious swords of assassins in 1163, while he was defending the possessions and rights of his church against the unjust depredations of certain nobles and courtiers.] the dean, which he set forth at Sens in a council of the bishops and clergy of the province.

[Col. 0309A]

Your sister, the holy daughter of this see—the Church of Orléans—pours forth, through the ministry of our voice, tears dripping with blood and prayers sprinkled with bitterness. She raises the lament for her only-begotten; with motherly wailings she seeks the son of her womb, whom she bore—and behold, he does not appear. And where shall she herself go? She has been set up like a target for the arrow; she has become a reproach to her neighbours, and those who see her shake their heads over her. But she, groaning and turning backward, cries into the ears of the Lord of Hosts: “Avenge, O Lord, the blood of thy Levite that has been shed.”

> [Note: He calls the Church of Orléans his daughter of the Church of Sens, and sister of the other churches of the province—whose prelates and more eminent clergy were then present at Sens—because the Church of Orléans was always subject to the archbishop of Sens until 1622. For in that year the bishopric of Paris was raised to an archbishopric by Gregory XV, and the prelates of the Churches of Orléans, Chartres, and Meaux were separated from the metropolitan of Sens and enrolled among the suffragans of the archbishop of Paris.]

> [Note: That John, though dean, was only a deacon. Yet it had been forbidden at the Council of Clermont under Urban II in 1095, and at the Council of London under Honorius II in 1127, that anyone should be made dean in a church unless he were a priest, or archdeacon unless he were a Levite.]

And who, unless he is mad, would forbid her to weep at her child’s funeral? Who would see her tears upon her cheeks and despise them? Who would behold her bloody obsequies and follow that lamentable bier with dry eyes? My fathers, a thing has happened in our days at which the ears of everyone who hears it will ring. Men of blood and deceit went forth in treachery; men of a thicket-like mind sprang together from the hiding-places of the bushes against a minister of the altar, servant alike and son of the Cross.

> [Note: Because he was dean of Holy Cross at Orléans, which he cherished and defended as a mother. This church had been built in honour of the Holy Cross by blessed Evurtius, bishop of the same city, from the munificence of Constantine—or, as Saussaye prefers, *Annals of the Church of Orléans*, book II, no. 22, of the emperor Constantius. After it had later been consumed by fire, it was restored in a more elegant work about the year 1000 by Arnulf, bishop of this see. It burned again through the sacrilegious torches of the Calvinists in the preceding century; but now, through the generosity of our kings, it is rising again in its former form—indeed, in a more beautiful one.]

In their hands were instruments of death, although he expected anything rather than death from them. By his intervention he had redeemed from the jaws of death and the sentence of exile the very leader of that wicked faction—a man who had stained himself with another murder. That crooked and perverse generation, the seed of Canaan and not of Judah, the brood of vipers, did not fear to plough deep wounds into a sacred Levite of God, beneath the sign of the Lord’s Passion which each of us bears upon his shaven crown, nor to disfigure with shameful marks the face fashioned in the likeness of heavenly beauty. Executioners and assassins removed from the flock of men an outstanding man: a man who, gathering together what had been scattered in his church, raising what had fallen, restoring what was worn out, had so recovered the lost possessions of the Church that he did not lose them once recovered.

Our John was made a martyr at once by cause and by punishment: the cause was the rigour of ecclesiastical justice; the punishment, the suffering of the Passion inflicted upon him. Because John had said—or rather the lord pope had said through John—“It is not lawful for thee to possess the portion of thy clerical brother,” Herod raged; becoming himself an executioner, he displayed to the world a cruel spectacle in John’s head. Yet if any stains of earthly contagion clung to him, we believe that the sacrament of the Lord’s Body and Blood, which he received with such reverence as he could amid deep groans and the great sighs of a contrite heart and humbled spirit, wholly erased them, together with the pains of death that surrounded him. After receiving the Eucharist, in our presence, he fulfilled the due of fate; and he who saw it bore witness, and his testimony is true.

It concerns you, watchmen of the house of Israel, guardians of the walls of Jerusalem, shepherds of Christ’s sheep; it concerns you both to apply a remedy to what has passed and to provide for what is to come. And though that saying is offered to you late—“It is better to meet danger in time than to exact vengeance after ruin”—nevertheless the God of vindications, the Lord (Ps. 93 [Vulgate]), shall be invoked by you with unutterable groanings (Rom. 8). With you the voice of your brother Abel’s blood shall cry from the earth (Gen. 4); it shall cry and shall shake not only the earth but also heaven (Hag. 2). For truly, what place can be safe, or what cause can be excused, if the venerable ministers of the altar are reckoned as sheep for slaughter? What wall for integrity or rampart for faith can we provide if the accursed frenzy of the sword bloodies sacred inner sanctuaries? Finally, what can be guarded or secure if a sacrilegious hand breaks with impunity the pillars of the Church?

We have also a Caesar who can and will sympathize with our infirmities; those who have offended not only against the Cornelian law concerning assassins, but also against the Julian law of majesty, shall not escape his long hands.

> [Note: The Cornelian law was enacted by Lucius Cornelius Sulla, dictator, against murderers who kill with the sword. For “assassins” (*sicarii*), Josephus testifies in *Jewish Antiquities*, book XX, were robbers using knives comparable in size to the curved Persian daggers called *acinaces*, and like those which the Romans call *sicae*; hence those who practise robbery received their name. Seneca mentions this law in book I of *On Providence*.]

> [Note: The Julian law was enacted by Julius Caesar, dictator, against those who plotted anything against the emperor or the commonwealth; it embraced several different heads. Tacitus discusses it in book I of the *Annals*. By these two laws the author seeks to prove that those privy to this murder were guilty on a double count: both by reason of the person killed, who exercised the office of dean in the Church, and by the manner of death, which had been treacherously inflicted upon him by assassins.]

He has drawn the sword divinely entrusted to him; he shall pursue and seize them, and there shall be none to rescue them. For the pardon of the highest Deity is most readily hoped for in a matter by which the safety and security of many are procured. Let the ecclesiastical laws rise together; let the heavenly laws be armed, so that, with the two swords joining in action—which, we read, were enough for those who were to suffer in Christ’s defence—they may be crushed in a twofold confusion. Let the tearful sighs of the widowed Cross move you: the common danger of all, the private cause of each. And so bring relief to our grief, that you may at once provide for your own honour and safety.

## Letter II. To William, Elect of Chartres

> [Note: This letter was written about 1164, when William of Champagne, provost of Troyes, was elected bishop of Chartres after the death of Robert. Alexander III writes of him to Louis the Younger in these words: “We received with paternal kindness our beloved son William, bishop-elect of Chartres, when he came into our presence—both at the request of your magnificence, out of regard for his whole family, and in consideration of his honour and probity.”]

He asks him to reconcile him with the favour of the king, who had taken amiss the letter written concerning the death of John, dean of Orléans.

To keep one’s ears occupied with sacred and weightier business is not far removed either from sacrilege or from the crime of treason. Fearing even the appearance of this fault, I compress the multitude of my petitions to my lord into brevity of speech. As you know, my lord, I was charged by the lord archbishop to write to the lord king concerning the lamentable prayers of the Church of Orléans and the common complaint of the bishops over the death of John, so that he might be moved to mercy and kindled to vengeance.

> [Note: Namely Hugh, surnamed de Toucy, then archbishop of Sens.]

> [Note: See Letter I and what we have said to elucidate it concerning the killing of John of the Chain, dean of Holy Cross at Orléans, of whom this passage speaks.]

> [Note: Namely Louis VII, called the Pious and the Younger.]

I wrote briefly, and before all your ears I read through the letter which was sent to the king. We sought good, and behold disturbance. He took it ill, and was moved against me—a dead dog and a living flea. Neither the violent outpourings of his indignation and anger through angels or evil interpreters, nor the faint-heartedness of my soul, nor the poverty of our church, will be able to endure it. Therefore I pray you, my lord, by Christ, the Anointed of my lord: since I had a single eye in that letter, excuse me through your intervention before my lord, and obtain for me the favour which I grieve to have lost through no fault of my own.

## Letter III. Pontius, Bishop of Clermont, to Maurice, Bishop of Paris, and Stephen, Abbot of Saint Evurtius

He asks them whether the baptism of one of his diocesan flock was valid.

To his reverend lords and fathers in Christ, MAURICE, bishop of Paris, and STEPHEN, abbot of Saint Evurtius, PONTIUS, by the same grace bishop of Clermont, greeting and the service of entire affection.

We judged that our question should be referred especially to you two, whom both the spiritual affection of love which we bear toward you commends, and a special understanding of the Scriptures makes famous and worthy of commendation among all. The bearer of this letter once loved a certain woman, to whom, as he says, he had been betrothed; but before taking her as wife he made her pregnant. When the child was born and a priest could not suitably be found to baptize him, his father immersed him in water, saying, “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28). It is a very bad custom in our land that, in such an emergency, they say, “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,” but do not utter the entire verbal formula which ought to be uttered in baptism, which they call *undeiare* [to administer emergency baptism].

We therefore ask whether this is baptism, or whether the child should subsequently be baptized; and also whether this man can take that woman as his wife, since he is reported to be of sufficiently good repute. We ask your graciousness to inform us by your letters concerning all these matters. Farewell.

## Letter IV. Maurice, Bishop of Paris, to Pontius of Clermont

He answers the questions and sets forth his judgment on the validity of this baptism.

To the most reverend father and lord PONTIUS, bishop of Clermont, MAURICE, humble servant of the Church of Paris, greeting and fullness of service.

Concerning the matter on which your highness has consulted our lowliness, we answer briefly. We have received from the authority of the divine Scriptures and the testimony of the holy Fathers that the form in which baptism ought to be conferred or received is as follows: “I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” Such is the force of these words that nothing should be altered and nothing introduced anew. Unless indeed all these words are uttered together, by whomever and in whatever language, we do not believe that there is baptism. Therefore, since, as we learned from the testimony of your letter, the bearer of this letter was silent, at the immersion of his son, as to “I baptize you,” and uttered only “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,” there was no baptism. Therefore that child must be baptized, because he did not receive baptism at all. Thus no question remains concerning the rest. Farewell.

## Letter V. Stephen to Pontius, Bishop of Clermont

He states his opinion concerning the same baptism.

To the most holy father and lord PONTIUS, bishop of Clermont, brother STEPHEN of Saint Evurtius, greeting and reverence with every devotion.

> [Note: The old heading of this letter must be corrected: it should read “Pontius,” not “Peter.” For this Pontius, formerly abbot of Clairvaux, was elected bishop of Clermont in Auvergne in 1170. Henriquez, in the *Fascicle of Saints of the Cistercian Order*, enters him in the roll of the blessed. By a messenger he had consulted Maurice, bishop of Paris, and Stephen, then abbot of Saint Evurtius at Orléans, whether a minister of baptism who pours water while uttering only the words, “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,” while suppressing “I baptize you,” validly confers baptism, as is learned from Letter III. In Letter IV Maurice sets forth his view on this question, and in the present Letter V Stephen explains what he thinks.]

I confess that both the authority of him who asks and the novelty of the question press heavily upon my ignorance. There is added, Father, the burden of my shame, because in so grave a consultation you join me with the lord of Paris—comparing a camel with a gnat, a thistle with a cedar, Hylas with Hercules.

> [Note: He was Maurice, the sixty-eighth bishop of Paris, successor of Peter Lombard, most distinguished in virtue and learning. He wrote sermons to the people and a treatise *On the Care of Souls* for priests. He built almost the whole basilica of Blessed Mary at Paris, and toward the end of his life withdrew to Saint Victor, where he was buried. Rigordus, under the year 1196, says of him: “In the same year, on the third Ides of September, Maurice, bishop of Paris, of venerable memory, father of the poor and orphans, happily departed to the Lord. Among the innumerable good works which he did, he founded four abbeys and most devoutly endowed them at his own expense: namely Hérivaux, Hermeray, Hédée, and Gif; and what else he possessed he distributed to the poor.” In Letter 262 you have his epitaph, composed in his praise by our Stephen.]

> [Note: Our author often uses this comparison to signify the immense disparity between a weak and strong man, a small and great one, an ignorant and learned one—such as that between Hylas and Hercules. Hylas was a boy whom Hercules had as a companion in his wanderings.]

A scribe learned in the kingdom of heaven, bringing forth from his treasury things new and old, answered your questions from the depth of his understanding and height of his learning; with a straightforward letter his blessed tongue resolved for you its heavenly oracle. His divine response I follow as the *Thebaid* follows the *Aeneid*:

> “[lacuna] Yet do not attempt the divine *Aeneid*,  
> but follow at a distance, and ever revere its footprints.”

> [Note: The poet Statius Papinius wrote, as everyone knows, a twelve-book epic poem which he called the *Thebaid*, following Virgil in his *Aeneid*, though, in our author’s judgment, not attaining him. Statius himself truly acknowledged this in these verses.]

“… I follow at a distance, and ever revere its footprints.”

I should be moved to the contrary view if the question were put to me without his sacred written pronouncements.

> [Note: In this letter Stephen gives his opinion concerning baptism, saying that the words “I baptize you” are not necessary to the sacrament. Yet he does not intend to defend or assert this opinion, but only to set it out: “I plunge opinions deep,” he says, “not assertions.” He appears to support it by this argument: for the validity of the sacrament, only what Christ commanded to be done is required; but Christ commanded only that the child be baptized, or immersed in water, “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” Therefore one who immerses the child in water with these words, “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,” does what Christ commanded and truly baptizes; there is no need to express verbally “I baptize you,” when he expresses it in deeds. Saint Thomas, part III, question 66, article 5, replies to this argument in replies 1 and 2. This author should be excused if he seems in some degree to incline toward this opinion; for it had not yet been clearly and distinctly declared which words were necessary for baptism. This was decreed around these times by Alexander III in the *Decretals*, book III, title 42, *On Baptism*, chapter 1: “If anyone immerses a child three times in water in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, amen, but does not say, ‘I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, amen,’ the child is not baptized.”]

He who instituted the sacrament of baptism gave the form of baptizing: “Go,” he says, “teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28). He who retained for himself the power of baptizing granted to others the ministry in this form. No one will say that the words “Go, teach all nations” either possess the substance of the sacrament or express its form. Let us hold to what follows: “Baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” I do not there yet read: “Baptizing them, and saying, ‘I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.’” If to baptize is to immerse, and baptism is immersion, what are those baptizing except those immersing? Therefore, one who immerses with the intention of baptizing, if he utters what Truth commands—that is, “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit”—seems to have baptized and to have completed the form handed down by Christ.

Even heretics, if they have uttered these dread names, we shall say have retained the catholic form. Innocent says: “The Novatians baptize in the dread names of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Nor has any question ever arisen among them concerning the unity of the divine power—that is, of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” And Father Augustine, in *On Ecclesiastical Rules*: “If any have been baptized among those heretics who baptize in confession of the Holy Trinity and come to the catholic faith, let them indeed be received as baptized, lest the invocation or confession of the Holy Trinity be annulled.” If those baptized by heretics in confession of the Trinity are received by the Church lest the invocation or confession of the Trinity be annulled, why shall he not be called baptized who has been immersed three times by a catholic layman saying, “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit”?

> [Note: Triple immersion was formerly observed in baptism; for Apostolic Canons 49 and 50 read: “If any priest or bishop does not celebrate the threefold immersion of the one mystery, but immerses only once in baptism—something which some say was delivered in the Lord’s death—let him be deposed.” Later, however, usage in the Church was indifferent, so that baptism was conferred sometimes with triple and sometimes with single immersion. Saint Gregory says this in his letter to Leander, book I, letter 4: “It cannot in any way be blameworthy to immerse an infant either three times or once in baptism.” Finally, at the Council of Toledo held under Honorius I in 635, canon 6, triple immersion was abolished and reduced to one: “Because in Spain”—these are the council’s words—“some priests performed triple immersion, others, as is said, a single immersion, a schism was perceived by some to exist and the unity of the faith seemed to be divided”; it was decreed that henceforth only one immersion should be performed in baptism. This decree, however, was not immediately received in all churches; indeed, this letter shows that in these times the rite of baptism with triple immersion still prevailed in Gaul.]

For if this is not accepted, the confession or invocation of the Trinity made there is annulled as having achieved nothing. Augustine likewise, *To Orosius*: “The baptism of heretics—namely, those who baptize in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit—and that of the Catholic Church is the same; and therefore the Church does not rebaptize them, because they were baptized in the name of the Trinity, and this indeed is the form of the sacrament.” Behold: he says that the form of the sacrament is immersion in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit; “I baptize you” or “I immerse you” is not added. The same author, *On the One Baptism*: “I should by no means doubt that those possess baptism who, wherever and by whomever they received it, received it consecrated without pretence and with some faith by the words of the Gospel.” You see, Father, that baptism is consecrated by the words of the Gospel alone. Yet nowhere in the entire Gospel do I read, “I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,” but only “BAPTIZING in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”

Likewise Pope Zachary to Bishop Boniface: “At the synod of the English it is known to have been decreed, most firmly commanded, and carefully shown that whoever had been immersed without invocation of the Trinity did not possess the sacrament of regeneration.” This is wholly true: for if anyone is immersed in the font of baptism without invocation of the Trinity, he is not a complete Christian, unless he has been immersed in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. He does not say: unless the baptizer has said, “I baptize you in the name of the Father.” I could gather more, Father, which move me on this side and advance the solution of the question raised. But because I fear both being accused of prolixity and charged with impudence, I spare the little sheet and spare my reputation.

I plunge opinions deep, not assertions; as I have said, I am ready to follow the footsteps of the supreme and catholic man, the lord of Paris, though not bound to swear by anyone’s words. Yet I kiss with the highest reverence and embrace with the greatest zeal the concluding clause which baptizers customarily do and ought to say, namely, “I baptize you.” Mother Church introduced it so that it might belong to the solemnity of the ministry, not to the substance of the sacrament. For if we say otherwise, we shall confess without qualification that those whom we know to have been baptized by laypersons in an emergency are damned. For this alone is what those who do not know letters customarily say when they *undaizant* [administer emergency baptism] infants: “En nome Patres, et Files, et Esperites santes” [“In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit”].

> [Note: This is the same as what we say in French, *ondoyer*, when baptism is privately conferred without the ceremonies and anointings prescribed by the Church.]

We both believe and confess that these words have the same force as Latin syllables conveying the same meaning. Nevertheless, I would say that priests who, through negligence or ignorance, omit anything from the dignity of the solemn words are to be sharply rebuked and subjected to penance. Whoever accepts the foregoing reasons will not baptize again one baptized in this manner, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Therefore he who thus baptized him became both the spiritual father of the child and the *compater* [co-parent/godfather] of his mother. Hence, even if she was not previously his wife, in my judgment he will not contract marriage with her, because spiritual co-parenthood prevents it; and, even if he had already contracted it, he could in no way retain her in marriage, as Pope Deusdedit declares.

> [Note: Namely, in his letter to Gordian, bishop of Seville, where he says: “No Christian ought to take his own godmother as wife; and whoever presumes to do so shall be bound by the bond of anathema forever, unless he performs worthy penance. Women separated from their own husbands on account of this unlawful act shall receive the whole dowry which they received on their wedding day, and after a year has been completed may take another husband; likewise the man may take another wife.”]

Nor does what Pope John writes to Bishop Anselm, in the chapter *At the Thresholds of Blessed Peter*, contradict this. There he deals with persons already joined; here the question concerns the manner of joining them. Certainly many things hinder a marriage from being contracted which do not dissolve one already contracted. For the same pope, in the same chapter, gives the reason why persons joined together should not be separated for such a cause: “This,” he says, “must by no means be done, since Scripture says that a wife has been joined to her husband by the Lord, and ‘what God has joined, let no man separate’” (Matt. 19). There he plainly speaks of persons already joined; perhaps he would say otherwise concerning those to be joined. May your holiness flourish.

## Letter VI. To Aldebert, Bishop of Mende

He clears himself of certain statements falsely reported to the bishop.

To ALDEBERT, bishop of Mende, constancy in adversity and fairness in prosperity.

> [Note: He was a regular canon under the Rule of Saint Augustine and provost of the Church of Mende, commonly called Mande, and was then raised to this episcopal see in 1151.]

A common disease of princes and nobles is to believe quickly and condemn quickly. The first is trivial; the second cruel. May he who at his coming made both one keep both far from you. Your letter attributed what you believed about me not to rashness but to your innocence, which believes every word. Therefore the man who reported me to you has the greater sin. I kiss the judgments of your will with full lips; I embrace them with all my heart. Mindful of the benefits which you have shown me, I lay aside remembrance of complaints. I offer myself to my lord, and shall go wholly into his service. And because you did not wish for the firstfruits of my labour and study, I reserve the tithes for you. Let my lord not hesitate either to command what he wishes or to obtain what he commands. I thank you for the favour restored to me, intending, if occasion and time arise, to return favour for favour.

## Letter VII. To Godfrey, Abbot of Saint Satyrius

He asks him to retain one of his canons with him.

To his dearest friend GODFREY, abbot of Saint Satyrius, brother STEPHEN, minister of Saint Evurtius, fullness of salvation in the service of health.

> [Note: Having been a canon of Saint Evurtius at Orléans, he was elected abbot of Saint Satyrius near the town called Sacrum Caesaris, commonly Sancerre, in the diocese of Bourges. This abbey was founded in 1113 by Matilda, lady of that place, in honour of Saint Peter and Saint Satyrius and his many fellow martyrs, for the service of clerics living there canonically, as is read in the charter of foundation. This monastery was later united to the Victorine congregation, of which Godfrey was a canon; to him this letter and several others were written.]

Help is sought from the powerful, counsel from the knowledgeable. If goodwill is present, these two promise a remedy for hope. We believe that you can know and are willing to do what our prayers contain, our affection desires, and our desire expects. We send to you our most beloved son and brother, Gislebert, that in his need—which is ours as well—he may find in you a father and protector. He suffers from a hidden illness, unknown to us; unless it is met at the beginning, there is reason to fear for the end. Let your affection be stirred and your help become effective; let charity and compassion work, so that his former health may be restored through your ministry. And because we know his faint-heartedness, even if he should wish to return quickly, we ask you to keep him with you until you see either us or our messenger.

## Letter VIII. To the Dean of Saint Martin of Tours

He seeks alms for the rebuilding of the church of Saint Evurtius.

We are compelled to trouble our friends, and necessity compels us to rise in petition. We are rebuilding the burned church of Father Evurtius, and because our own resources are insufficient, we beg for the assistance of others. We go out in public; not without shame have we cast aside shame, stirring up, as best we can, the devotion of the people through streets and squares. Therefore we have sent these brothers of ours with the pledges of the saints. I beseech you that, through your authority and assistance, they may be given opportunity in the church of Saint Martin to collect the alms of the devout people.

> [Note: Since the abbey of Saint Evurtius at Orléans lay outside the city walls, it was exposed to the incursions of war and consequently suffered the greatest devastation, especially from the Normans, who utterly destroyed it by sword and fire. When Stephen held the office of abbot there about 1174, aflame with zeal to rebuild God’s house, he sent some of his canons to neighbouring cities in order to obtain the funds necessary for so great a work. As was then customary, they carried with them relics of this blessed bishop and patron of the Church, so that, at the sight of them, the faithful might bestow alms to be spent on restoring his church. This is the matter at issue concerning the carrying of such relics. Canon 12 of the Council of Poitiers states: “Those who carry about relics of saints for the sake of money and gain are not to be admitted to preach.”]

The pious and merciful confessor will not take offense either at rendering service to his priest or at preparing lodging for him. For the one whom he has as a fellow-citizen and companion in heaven, he will gladly receive as a guest on earth and cherish in a most welcome embrace. We have sent them with the pledges of the saints, so that an offering of the people’s devotions may be made in certain churches—an offering which may grow into merit for those who give and consolation for those who receive. What we ask is great; but on the one hand our necessity compels us, and on the other your kindness invites us.

## Letter IX

He writes to a friend about the restoration of the same church.

Among the smoking ashes of our church and the charred timbers of its rising walls, weeping and astounded, we are compelled to appear in public and, with a brow worn thin, to beg the aid of others’ alms. A new building is being raised for Confessor Evurtius, so begun with our own expenditure that it desires to be completed by that of others. We have sent these brothers of ours with the pledges of the saints, so that through the people’s devotion an offering, however modest, may be made in some churches, which may grow both into merit for those who give and consolation for those who receive. What we ask is great; but on the one hand our necessity compels us, and on the other your kindness invites us.

## Letter X. To the Abbot of Cluny

> [Note: Cluny, the monastery most celebrated throughout the world, lies in the diocese of Mâcon and has always been the head of a very extensive congregation. It was founded under the Rule of Saint Benedict by Abbot Berno, with the support of William I, count of Auvergne and duke of Aquitaine, in 910. Glaber, *History of the Franks*, book III, chapter 5, says: “The monastery called Cluny, which took this name from the steep and low situation of the place itself—or, what suits it better, from *cluere*, because we call ‘to grow’ *cluere*—obtained from its beginning a remarkable increase of diverse gifts. Thus Berno, father of the monks of the monastery of Baume, first built the aforesaid abbey at the command of William, most devout duke of Aquitaine, in the district of Mâcon, upon the little river Grosne.”]

He urges him to remove the prior of the monastery of Pont-aux-Moines, who was dissipating the possessions of his church.

> [Note: Pont-aux-Moines is a Cluniac priory about twelve miles from the city of Orléans.]

Things before our eyes become known more easily; but things far away, because they occur less frequently, move the mind more tepidly. Hence, Father, because your houses are remote, if anything happens there less suitably, it affords you excuse as long as you remain unaware of it. But once the truth of the matter is known, there is no room for an excuse which knowledge excludes. In our territory there is a certain monastery of yours, whose prior, it is said, does not walk according to what is fitting. We have heard frequent complaints from neighbours, and from persons whose testimony should be trusted, that he gives attention neither to the restoration of the house nor to the benefit or peace of the brethren; and his very conduct bears witness to the truth of these reports. Within a short time the debts have increased immeasurably, though the revenues have not been enlarged, the number of brothers has not increased, and buildings worn down by age have not been restored. I am weary of recounting what the neighbours, from whose patrimony the monastery is supported, lamentably and repeatedly tell us. Let your fatherhood see to it that you provide for the place, now tending toward desolation, such a prior as loves both the honour of God and that of the Order, and reforms the place itself to a better condition.

## Letter XI. To William, Archbishop of Sens

> [Note: He was the son of Theobald, count of Champagne; first provost of the Church of Troyes, then elected bishop of Chartres, as we said, in 1164; thence raised to the metropolitan see of Sens in 1169 and consecrated by Maurice, bishop of Paris; finally called to the archbishopric of Reims in 1175, and ultimately granted the purple of a cardinal. Several letters here are addressed to him.]

He commends the Church of Saint Samson at Orléans.

> [Note: This church in the city of Orléans was originally dedicated to Saint Symphorian, martyr, and honoured with abbatial rank. But when the canons of Dol, fearing the Normans, brought the body of blessed Samson from Lesser Brittany to Orléans about 930, Hugh, count of Paris and margrave of Orléans, gave this abbey, together with other churches, to the aforesaid canons of Dol, with the consent of Anselm, bishop of Orléans. Later Philip I, king of the Franks, assigned this abbey—then called Saint Symphorian and Saint Samson—together with half the market which he established on the site of the monastery, to the canons of Saint Martin-des-Champs near Paris, on the day of dedication of the same church, 1 November 1067, drawing up an instrument concerning these matters.]

In you, Father, the eyes of all Israel look, that you may rescue the poor from the powerful and break the horns of sinners. In its steadfastness the daughter of Zion—the church of Saint Samson—cries aloud in the ears of the Lord of Hosts.

[Note: Col. 0319D]

He calls the church of Saint Samson the daughter of Zion because Louis VII, returning to France from the Jerusalem expedition in 1152, brought with him certain regular canons who were occupied with divine worship in the patriarchal church of Mount Zion, as James of Vitry notes in his *Oriental History*, chapter 18. Louis introduced them into the church of Saint Samson at Orléans, replacing the canons who had lived there secularly and separately, and caused an authenticated charter of this gift to be drawn up. Saussaye reports it in book X of his *Ecclesiastical History of Orléans*, no. 4.

Hence, in the charter granting to the church of Saint Samson a certain place called Frameer, with all its lordship, the brethren of this church are called the Jerusalemites of Saint Mary of Mount Zion. I have therefore thought it worth while to reproduce it here. It reads as follows:

“A and Ω, beginning and end. Things bestowed upon the holy churches of God through pious generosity ought to be strengthened by due security, lest the peace and repose of those churches and persons upon whom they are conferred should in any way be disturbed by anyone’s annoyances or vexations. Therefore I, Hervé of Virsion, wish it to be known to those present and to those to come that I have judged the place of Fraamer, situated on the boundary of the churches of Clinum and Briennum, together with its appurtenances, to be granted, for the salvation of my ancestors and myself, to the Jerusalemites of Saint Mary of Mount Zion and to the brethren of the church of Saint Samson at Orléans, under the following condition: that neither the aforesaid place nor its possessions may be alienated, disposed of, sold, or in any manner encumbered without the consent of myself or of my heirs who shall be invested with my inheritance. Moreover, I grant to the same brethren that they may freely use whatever they are able to acquire from my fief for the increase of that place. I have commanded this present document to be confirmed by the authority of my seal, in the presence of the witnesses Acio Ciconius, Bricius the provost, Rembaud Combustus and Venand his brother, Maubert, canon of Holy Cross, and Haimeric, priest of Pierre-Fitte. Publicly enacted, in the reign of King Louis, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1175.”

This place of Fraamer enjoys the status of a priory. It is now held by one of the regular canons of our French congregation, who supplied me with this charter.]

Against an unprincipled woman, as against another Jezebel, it seeks rest and consolation beneath the shadow of your wings. Unjustly she not only disturbs but also takes away the civil and lawful possession of the church, while the testimony of almost the entire city marvels at her wickedness and abhors her shamelessness. We believe that the sentence pronounced against her by the Church of Holy Cross is canonical and just; and, as seems fitting to your fatherhood, with their common desire we humbly ask and entreat you to confirm it.

## 21. LETTER XII. TO POPE ALEXANDER III

He asks him to show favour to John, a cleric of Orléans.

[Note: Col. 0321D]

In this letter he commends to the supreme pontiff Alexander a young man named John, asking that he may be pleased to grant him a prebend in the Church of Orléans. We learn from the letter written below [Col. 0322D] that this was done, and that papal documents to that effect were obtained, whose execution was entrusted to our Stephen.

To the most holy lord and Father ALEXANDER, supreme pontiff, STEPHEN, called abbot.

Your throne, Father, is prepared so that all may receive from its fullness. It promises advancement to the young and stability to the more mature. Trusting in your mercy, a young man of good disposition, as it seems to us—John, brought up and educated in the Church of Orléans—devoutly seeks counsel from you and awaits [Col. 0321B] your assistance. We know that he was born of lawful marriage and honourable parents, who, although not rich in possessions, are distinguished in character. We believe him worthy to earn canonical stipends either in the Church of Orléans or in another church.

## LETTER XIII. TO WILLIAM, ARCHBISHOP OF SENS

He asks on behalf of a scholarly cleric that his property may be preserved for him.

To his dearest lord and Father WILLIAM, archbishop of Sens, brother STEPHEN, abbot, greeting and reverence with every veneration.

Compassionating both the calling and the condition of the bearer of this letter, I reverence him as a cleric and embrace him as a poor man. [Col. 0321C] He fights with beasts in a lay court, litigating against a layman concerning his paternal inheritance, with judges who neither know letters nor love those who are learned. Your judgment, Father, no less equitable than just, referred the cleric’s case, when he was appearing before you, to the court of the person by whose annual service the estate acknowledges its rent. Subject to that reservation, you pronounced your decision: that his absence for the sake of studies should not have prejudiced him.

A malicious—indeed, not to say accursed—crowd that cannot read strives to judge otherwise. For the fourth time the litigants met before the judge, and for the fourth time “the sons of men who judge the earth,” as the common phrase has it, postponed judgment. We have certainly learned that they intend, no [Col. 0321D] less shamelessly than unwisely, to decide at the first agreement that the pursuit of studies is not a just cause of absence; and that consequently he whose inheritance was disposed of while he was absent and studying either was not injured by operation of law or does not deserve restoration. Should they pronounce the parties thus liable, their judgment will oppose both the common law and the sentence you gave, as something hostile and unjust.

But, Father, this may be drawn into precedent in similar cases, so that no one will any longer leave his native home for the sake of study, lest, while seeking [Col. 0322A] the liberal arts, he lose his temporal means. Be pleased, Father, in this matter to give counsel and assistance, not only to this cleric but to all others as well, since the cause is common to all and personal to each. May your holiness fare well.

## 23. LETTER XIV. TO ALBERIC, JURIST OF BOLOGNA

He entreats him to be at hand for Hugh, a cleric of Orléans.

To Lord ALBERIC, jurist of Bologna.

Your frequent remembrance supplies for me the lack of your presence, and the sweet recollection of your character awakens a pleasant applause in my soul, [Col. 0322B] celebrating a delightful dramatic performance. Hence I frequently make known, praise, and extol your name among my friends and household. For this reason I have sent to you with confidence my dearest friend, the bearer of this letter, asking that for my sake you receive him with both kindness and beneficence. For we believe him worthy of both honour and favour from you.

## LETTER XV. TO WILLIAM OF BOLOGNA

He commends the same cleric of Orléans.

To Lord WILLIAM of Bologna.

The favourable report of you, conveyed by travellers and daily surpassing itself, [Col. 0322C] gives me an agreeable spectacle and provides welcome refreshment. May it grow, I pray, and, like the fragrance of a full field which the Lord has blessed, spread far and wide, awakening distant peoples to your aid. This is both my continual wish for you, my unceasing prayer, and my tireless desire. Meanwhile I commend to your affection this my dearest friend Hugh, that for my sake you may receive him kindly and willingly give him your counsel and aid.

## 24. LETTER XVI. TO A CERTAIN PRIOR OF NAPLES

He commends one of his canons who is residing at Naples.

To his dearest friend, the Prior of Naples, whom he embraces with his whole heart, brother STEPHEN, greeting and the service of mutual charity.

With such pleasure and joy, most beloved brother, do I recall your name as brings to a soul tasting true friendship no less the benefit of affection than the seasoning of delight. Therefore, whenever I see persons who have seen you or those who are with you, I repeatedly ask: What is the state of your dwelling? What manner of life do you have? What concern does the lord cardinal [Col. 0323A] show for you? And finally, what is the disposition of our brethren: to remain there longer or to return sooner?

[Note: Col. 0323C]

He means John Pinzutus, cardinal-priest of Saint Anastasia, Neapolitan by birth but a regular canon by profession at Saint-Victor. Having restored the church of Saint Peter ad Aram at Naples, he obtained from Gruisius, then abbot of Saint-Victor, two of his fellow canons, namely Peter of Périgueux and Hugh of Saint-Germain, in order to introduce them into his new church. But after one of them had died and the other, crushed by grave illness, could scarcely breathe, Guarinus, abbot of Saint-Victor and successor of Gruisius, moved by these misfortunes, wrote to Cardinal John a letter which Quercetanus inserted in volume IV of the *Writers of French History*, p. 749, having taken it from the manuscripts of the Library of Saint-Victor. It contains the following:

“At last, if I may speak humanly and disclose the secret of their infirmities, the brethren greatly fear death because of the unfamiliar harshness of the land and the corrupt quality of the air. For if our laymen, when they go there, though they have complete liberty to travel, to depart and return, can scarcely live even a little while, how could these men, shut within a cloister, live there? The brethren put forward these causes and occasions; hence I consider it most grievous to impose this. If it is done, it is accepted against their will; if it is not done, it is very dangerously refused. Therefore, lord, let the greatness of your clemency now spare our infirmities, and attend to the pressing needs of the Church. For my part, I am prepared to obey your commands in whatever I can.”

Although the abbot of Saint-Victor resisted for some time, he was nevertheless overcome by the prayers of this cardinal [Col. 0324C] and the commands of the supreme pontiff Alexander—to whom he wrote in reply a letter which may be seen in the same place in Quercetanus—and sent new canons to Naples. Among them was R., a canon of Saint Geneviève, of whom this letter speaks. He did not, however, remain long in Italy, for death carried him off. Hence in Letter 29 Stephen commends him to the prayers of the abbot of Saint Bartholomew at Noyon.

I inquire into these matters more carefully, not in order—far be it!—to rejoice in adversity, but to share in prosperity with delight. Above all things, dearest friend, I commend to you our brother R., giving thanks for the benefits you have shown him in the past and offering prayers for those to come. Remember, Father and brother, that common son of ours; form his youth by wholesome admonitions, foster him with counsel, strengthen him with instruction. Whatever good you do for him, I shall proclaim as bestowed upon me, in streets and in corners.

## 25. LETTER XVII. TO ROGER, ABBOT OF SAINT-EUVERTIUS

He writes that he will return to the monastery, as the abbot had ordered.

[Col. 0323B]

To Lord ROGER, [Note: Col. 0324C]

Roger is to be read, not Robert as in the earlier edition; this was plainly an error of the copyist, who wrongly interpreted the letter R. as Robert instead of Roger.

[Col. 0324D]

Roger was a regular canon of Saint-Victor. Gunther, abbot of that monastery, sent him with companions to the monastery of Saint-Euvertius at Orléans in order to restore the regular discipline that had collapsed there; he was the first to be invested with the dignity of abbot there. Under him our Stephen changed his clothing and assumed the spirit and habit of a regular canon.

abbot of Saint-Euvertius at Orléans.

By three commands, Father, and more besides, I am urged to return, lest I pay the penalties of contumacy. Since at last a peremptory summons has been sent, that one would suffice for all, even if none had preceded it. Therefore, lest I have no right of identity [*identitatem*, probably an uncertain legal reading] by law itself, or fail to deserve the aid of restoration, or receive no help through the benefit of delay, I cast myself at your feet and ask that you do not impute to contumacy the delays required by necessity which I have hitherto alleged; lest default be entered against me,

[Note: Col. 0324D]

This is the same as what we call in French *défaut*: that is, lest judgment therefore proceed against an absent party, so that he may be judged and condemned as contumacious.

lest judgment proceed against one who is absent because he is labouring for the advantage of our commonwealth. Setting aside dilatory exceptions, [Col. 0323C] lord Father, I promise that at Easter, God willing, I shall come over to you among the flock of the Lord; and, if not as a lamb, at least as a kid, I shall humbly enter his pastures.

I have sent ahead this boy, who will return to me soon. If necessary, I beg you to assist him, lest his brothers seize for themselves by force or wrongful judgment the share of paternal property which has fallen to him. [Col. 0324A] I would already have hastened my return, but I had no conveyance. May God provide for me, so that I may return to you with my books on a double mount. It would be presumption, Father, to ask you for anything in this matter; but it would be kindness to offer it to one who is restrained by modesty from asking.

## 27. LETTER XVIII. TO WILLIAM, ARCHBISHOP OF SENS

He gives an account of a matter entrusted to him.

We found the bishops of the province of Tours difficult men, seeking, I believe, either their own glory or that of the king of England. On the first day, our meeting was drawn out until evening rather than conducted. They thought it sufficient satisfaction if the canons said that they had offended them and, asking pardon, promised not to do anything of the kind thereafter. But since in these few words a great source of evil lay concealed, and since it seemed capable of injuring the dignity of the realm in the future, neither did we offer counsel nor did they grant assent. On the following day, when they were making no progress, they spared either their own labours or expenses, or showed deference to the person, as they themselves said. They promised both impositions of hands—the ordaining and the consecrating—while preserving their own right.

## LETTER XIX. TO THE BISHOP OF LE PUY

He asks him to keep and fulfill his promise.

[Note: Col. 0324D]

Peter, bishop of Le Puy—commonly Le Puy-en-Velay—while staying at Orléans, gave Stephen, abbot of Saint-Euvertius, the monastery of Doa, or Doe, situated in his diocese, so that Stephen might reform it through his regular canons into a better state. By their agency it was eventually united to the congregation of Saint-Victor at Paris. It is now subject to the rule of the Premonstratensian canons.

[Col. 0324C]

Blessed be God, who after the storm makes calm weather, and after tears and weeping pours out consolation. And now, since tranquillity and peace have been restored to you, and since we believe you solicitous and devoted in matters concerning the honour and increase of the Church of God, [Col. 0325A] we ask and entreat you to complete without delay, if you are willing and able, the gift which you made to our church and to us in our chapter, in the presence of certain of our clerics. For this reason I have sent our canon to you, and I myself shall come if you command, always ready to offer my service to you and your church, near and far. Let my lord inform me if there are any objections capable either of taking your gift from us or delaying it. For it is not expedient for us, nor fitting for you, that we should undertake so much labour in vain. Farewell.
