## LETTER XX. TO B., CANON OF LE PUY

He asks him to show himself kindly toward his people.

[Col. 0325B]

Mindful of your former generosity and friendship, I long to see the day and place when and where I may enjoy your welcome presence and conversation. There is a matter ready at hand, if you are willing to advance and support it. I believe you have heard from someone that the lord bishop, with the consent of certain of your canons, granted the house of Doe to our church, so that regular observance may be kept there more fervently for the honour of God and the advancement of the place, and so that I, who am yours, may associate with you more frequently. Therefore I beg your illustrious kindness, in which I place full confidence, to see that the affair is brought to completion without delay, and, if any objections have arisen, to strive through yourselves and your friends to extinguish them.

## LETTER XXI. TO HUGH, ABBOT OF SAINT BARTHOLOMEW AT NOYON

He asks him to receive a fugitive canon.

[Col. 0325C]

Since a sheep outside the flock lies open to the bites of wolves unless it is swiftly brought back to the sheepfold, both the beast and the shepherd are in danger. Bearing this in mind, we have received and approved the good intention of I., the bearer of this letter, formerly your canon and brother, to return to the cloister. We beg your mercy that the entrance may be opened to the suppliant; that the wanderer and exile upon the earth may be gathered in; that the Father may restore the first robe and the ring, lest he be compelled any longer either to feed swine or [Col. 0326A] to hunger after their husks. The entreaty of the man for whom we pray has moved us; in order to escape punishments, he makes up by desire what he did too little in deed.

## LETTER XXII. TO JOTHON, ARCHBISHOP OF TOURS

He entreats his favour on behalf of the bishop-elect of Comminges.

To the venerable Father and lord JOTHON, [Note: Col. 0325C]

He is elsewhere called Gotho, or Jolcius in the *Chronicle of Tours*, [Col. 0325D] or also Gocius in Matthew Paris, under the year 1166.

archbishop of Tours, brother STEPHEN, humble servant of Saint-Euvertius, fullness of health and joy.

Nothing is more honourable than charity, which binds strangers and reconciles the separated. It has joined North to East, Cadiz to Ocean, [Note: Col. 0325D]

Cadiz, Pliny says, book IV, chapter 22, consists of two islands beyond the boundaries of the province of Baetica and at the western extremity of our world, beyond the narrow straits by which Africa is divided from Europe. The larger is called Erythia by Pomponius, because Tyrians originating from the Erythraean Sea founded a city on that island; hence Lucan calls them Tyrian Cadiz. Beside it lies a second, smaller island called Gades, separated from the other by a channel only one stadium wide, and possessing very rich pastures. There stood a most famous temple consecrated to Hercules, where he is said to have set up his columns; thence he was called Hercules of Cadiz, as may be seen on a gold coin of the Emperor Hadrian.

and barbarians to Latins by the commerce of salvation. Through charity’s service the bishop-elect of Comminges [Note: Col. 0325D]

Augustine, bishop-elect of Comminges, is mentioned in Letter 18 in these words: “They promised both impositions of hands—the ordaining and the consecrating”—that is, the bishops of the province of Tours did so [Col. 0326C] when they ordained him priest and [Col. 0326D] consecrated him bishop.

has come to us: a son of concord, heir of gentleness, and, as [Col. 0326B] I believe, not a lodger but a citizen of virtues; not their evaluator but their judge. In him speech measures prudence, laughter temperance, bearing fortitude, and movement justice, according to the square measure of virtue. He stayed with us no less devoutly than diligently: in one respect a bishop, in another a philosopher; mature in both, dissolute in neither. It accords with charity and is required by honour that you offer prayers for so great a man. If your Stephen has any favour in your sight, let it abound toward the man before you; let him feel that the prayers of his common friend, offered on his behalf, have benefited him. Nor do we offer prayers only for his future; for the past also we render full thanksgiving.

## 31. LETTER XXIII. TO WILLIAM, ARCHBISHOP OF SENS

He asks that he protect the cantor and archdeacon, lest their enemy prevail against them.

[Col. 0326C]

Craft is accustomed to trip up innocence, and deceit, plotting against truth, attacks simple consciences so that they may pay what they have not taken. You, Father, as minister of truth and justice, observe and redress this whenever you condemn the deceitful or acquit the innocent. These considerations compel me to pour out prayers to you for the cantor and archdeacon, whose fidelity, truthfulness, and integrity their conduct proclaims, public report declares, and the sincere testimony of religious men commends; and, what is not a small matter, the authority of a great patriarch supports them, [Note: Col. 0326D]

From the following letter it appears clearly enough that this patriarch is none other than Peter de la Chastre, archbishop and patriarch of Bourges, who died in 1171. The cantor and archdeacon of Bourges, to whose service they had been attached, are the persons for whose benefit this letter to the archbishop of Sens and the following letter to the supreme pontiff were written. We read that the archbishop of Bourges was decorated with the title of patriarch from ancient times: Saint Desiderius, bishop of Cahors, writing to Severus Sulpicius, already addressed him by the name of patriarch. But in these times all metropolitans were commonly designated patriarchs, as is clear concerning Priscus and Nicetius, archbishops of Lyons, in Gregory of Tours. Pope Nicholas also, writing around 860 to Rudolph, archbishop of Bourges, acknowledges him as primate of Aquitaine and addresses him with the title of patriarch.

whose counsels and service they faithfully attended [Col. 0327A] until the end of his life. With all the affection of my heart I ask that you too write kindly to the lord pope for them, lest man prevail against them; lest falsehood be preferred to truth, vice to virtue, deceit to fidelity.

## 32. LETTER XXIV. TO THE LORD POPE

He pours out prayers before the supreme pontiff on behalf of the same cantor and archdeacon.

We believe it akin to sacrilege, Father, deliberately to deceive your holiness. Nor should anyone who thinks himself able to stain with his own falsehood the wall of your faith or the rampart of your integrity suppose that license to lie will go unpunished for him. Whoever he may be, let him bear the penalties of his craft, and let the innocent be acquitted. We have learned, not merely from common report but by careful inquiry and personal presence, that the cantor and archdeacon are men of faith and good testimony among us. [Col. 0327B] For in their city we received so many testimonies on their behalf, so many proofs of virtue, so many harmonious voices affirming their innocence, that it is almost wickedness to doubt their fidelity, especially concerning the money of their patriarch Peter of blessed memory, whether deposited with them or left to them.

That prudent maker of his testament did everything openly and said nothing in secret. Through the hands of religious abbots and clerics of good repute—none of whom could be anything but faithful and prudent concerning their lord’s money—all was disbursed and distributed to churches, monasteries, [Col. 0327C] and the poor, as that great priest had entrusted to their fidelity. If anything was done deceitfully, this guilt stains them all, and there is no one who can hide himself from that deceit. But, Father, just as religion forbids that they should be involved in so great a crime, so public reputation forbids their being believed guilty of it. Therefore we pour out prayers to your holiness that your fatherhood may spare their labours and their honour, and that those who are strangers to fraud may be strangers to punishment. In this examination, Father, let truth not feel severity, nor honourable conduct succumb to its burden, nor disgraceful suspicion swallow up a good name.

## LETTER XXV. TO JOHN, LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE

He congratulates him on his fortunate return.

[Col. 0328A]

To the most holy Father JOHN, [Note: Col. 0327C]

John called de Bellemains, a man of great learning and eloquence, as Robert of Torigni calls him in his *Chronicle*, was appointed bishop of Poitiers in 1162. He governed that church most holily [Col. 0327D] for nearly twenty years, for in 1181 he was elevated to be archbishop of Narbonne.

bishop of Poitiers and legate of the Apostolic See, greeting and that peace which the world cannot give.

Your pilgrimage had been made burdensome to me by the absence of so great a Father, but welcome by devotion to so great a martyr. [Note: Col. 0327D]

That is, Saint Thomas of Canterbury, to whose tomb this John, bishop of Poitiers, had undertaken a pilgrimage. He had formerly been Saint Thomas’s friend, as had our Stephen. He was English by nationality, and before being called to the bishopric of Poitiers had been a canon and treasurer of York.

I meet your return with joyful and abundant thanksgiving, although I had sorrowfully attended your departure with urgent and abundant prayers. I desired your return for the common welfare; I was less concerned for the prince’s peace because I was less accustomed to pray for it. The duty of greeting and the sign of peace, given to you by the prince in a kiss of his mouth, [Note: Col. 0327D]

The prince seems to have been Henry II, king of England, formerly hostile to John because he defended the cause of Saint Thomas, but now reconciled to him, as this letter shows.

have come to my wishes in fuller measure: a light little letter announced it to me, but a weighty tongue confirmed it. [Col. 0328B] May favour increase day by day; yet may it not displease the giver of all graces, nor dare to test your reputation with that *dulia* [Note: Col. 0327D]

Since *dulia* is the honour shown to kings and princes of the earth, while *latria* is the worship rendered to God, the King of kings, he rebukes the slothfulness of certain priests who preferred service to earthly rulers to the worship of God. He especially notes clerics and prelates of England who had abandoned Saint Thomas’s cause [Col. 0328C] in order to support the wishes, even unjust wishes, of the king.

which in certain priests of our time has excluded *latria*.

## 34. LETTER XXVI. TO THE PRIOR AND BRETHREN OF THE CONVENT OF CHARITY

He entreats them on behalf of a fugitive monk who had been his teacher.

To his dearest lords and Fathers, the prior of [Note: Col. 0328C]

La Charité was a famous monastery of the Cluniac congregation, under the Rule of Benedict and situated on the Loire. It was begun in 1056 according to the *Chronicle of Vézelay*, or in 1069 according to the *Chronicle of Maillezais*, and was founded by a certain noble and devout man, Giraud, who embraced the religious life there.

La Charité and the holy congregation of that church, brother STEPHEN, servant of Saint-Euvertius.

Even in our own times Satan’s sieve is set in motion, while he waits and demands to sift repeatedly [Col. 0328C] the sons of those who have been sifted. But Peter’s faith will not fail: measuring our weakness in his own fall, he at length returns and strengthens the brethren; he heals Aeneas, raises Tabitha, [Note: Col. 0328D]

He speaks of miracles performed by blessed Peter, as found in Acts, chapters III and IX. Letter 96 repeats these matters.

and strengthens the ankles and feet of the man begging alms. Imitate him if you preside; embrace him if you are subject, so that you may recall the scattered and settle those recalled.

One who was of us has departed from you—our former and dearest A.—and, separated from so great a fellowship, was released by a departure less to be approved. Yet he did not follow the way of Balaam and Bosor, [Note: Col. 0328D]

He alludes to what is said in II Peter, chapter II: “following the way of Balaam from Bosor.” That is, he did not turn from the straight and just way in order to follow the crooked and perverse one.

but, joining himself to the flock of white [Note: Col. 0328D]

He means the Cistercian monks, to whom the man under discussion had fled in pursuit of perfection. But after experiencing the very laborious and harsh manner of their life, in which they cultivated fields with their own hands, he attempted to return to his first house of Charity and again employed the prayers of Stephen, once his pupil, that he might be kindly admitted there.

wool, [Col. 0329A] he encountered ways hard and unlike those which he had formerly known. The man’s devotion is praiseworthy in this: having gone out from Jerusalem, he did not go down to Jericho, but preferred to remain in Bethlehem. Yet there he heard a language he did not know, nor did they turn his back away from burdens. Unfamiliar novelty confronted him, and from the leisure of his former contemplation they cast him down to axe and sickle; he who had been nourished amid the saffron-coloured words of sacred discourse had his hands serve at the basket.

His biting conscience moves and admonishes him to return to Charity’s bosom and be satisfied from her breasts—he who burns with those who are scandalized and becomes weak with those who are weak. He confesses his error, pursues and renounces his fault, and, wishing to cleanse his transgression, desires to be led to the victim of discipline. [Col. 0329B] Let the father run to meet the returning son, kiss the wretch, restore the first robe and the ring, lest, if man hardens himself against man, he find the Lord hardened against himself. Nor let the cruelty of the elder brother, returning from the field, grumble among the brethren and prevent their going before with blessings of sweetness to welcome him who was lost and has been found.

The long acquaintance of the man from my first rudiments of letters, the common civic community [Note: Col. 0329]

They were born in the same city, namely Orléans, and shared a common native land.

which bore and reared us both, and—what is greater—his teaching, which I received at the very beginnings of grammatical study, compel me to rise to such earnest prayers. His gentle character, abundance of learning, and the penitence he displays commend him to the urgency of our prayers. If I have any standing in [Col. 0329C] your eyes, receive my prayers, so that for the benefit bestowed upon my brother I may rise wholly to offer you full thanksgiving. Whatever you do for him will be done for me, since I share in his adversities and rejoice with him in prosperity.

## 36. LETTER XXVII. TO THE SUBPRIOR OF LA CHARITÉ

He asks on behalf of the same fugitive that he may be admitted again.

To his dearest lord and friend A., subprior of La Charité, brother STEPHEN of Saint-Euvertius, the exchange of mutual prayer.

[Col. 0330A]

Gravity is commended in prelates, humility in subjects. Mercy moderates the former; obedience makes the latter great. I see that you embrace both, since by the welcome art of religious life you know both how to preside and how to be subject. Therefore I offer prayers to you with all the greater confidence because I understand that you are especially fitted both to correct errors and to bear weakness.

This friend of mine, once also my teacher, after his departure from you experienced harsh things and was deprived of gentle ones; now in a spirit of humility and a contrite heart he returns to his mother Charity, which is accustomed to close its bosom to no returning person. He grieves that he left the sacred fellowship; both the confusion of the suppliant and the confession of the petitioner show tears, the marks and witnesses of repentance. [Col. 0330B] I ask with all the feeling I can: pour out your hearts over him, and lead him from inward darkness into the brightness of eternal light. Let him feel that, if I have not deserved something from you, I have nevertheless obtained it; receive me in him, for whatever is bestowed upon him I shall count as bestowed upon me.

## LETTER XXVIII

He entreats a friend’s favour for the same monk.

Necessity compels, and charity persuades, us to intercede for friends. Indeed, I would call charity itself a necessity, for though it is patient and kind, [Col. 0330C] it is nevertheless strong as death and is accustomed to reduce difficult things to ease. Therefore I am compelled to entreat and write on behalf of the bearer of this letter, a certain friend and former teacher of mine, that he who has fallen and asks pardon for his error may, if he is insufficient in his own cause, deserve to be heard for ours. I rise wholly to prayers; I shall rise wholly to thanksgiving. Stand, I beg, for me in this conflict of prayers, and ask with me that he may be restored to his mother’s bosom. Whatever benefit and mercy you confer upon him for my sake, I count as mine.

# SECOND PART OF THE LETTERS OF STEPHEN, BISHOP OF TOURNAI

Containing those written while he was abbot of Saint Geneviève at Paris, from the year 1177 to the year 1192.

[Col. 0331]

## 38. LETTER XXIX. TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT BARTHOLOMEW

He relates what is happening among the canons at Naples.

[Col. 0331A]

To the abbot of Saint Bartholomew, greeting, prosperity, and peace.

So that what is said may be fulfilled, “Let him who hears say, ‘Come’” (Revelation XXII): you say that we have heard, and you ask me to come. I have made no vow of pilgrimage, though I would not delay it if an opportunity presented itself. Occupations take away the opportunity—occupations whose evil is sufficient for the day, whose troublesome noise hinders not only my Mary but confounds even Martha. Meanwhile I seize hours and consider moments, in case I may steal leisure from business, rest from labour, and the face of a friend from the conversation of rivals. [Col. 0331B]

I have learned nothing further about our Neapolitan establishment, except that between abbot and prior it displays some monstrous form of prelation unknown to me: thus it signifies both while presenting neither; thus it declines into neither office that it may be adorned by neither. From the cardinal’s household supplies are distributed to them by number, weight, and measure; hence they are accounted hired servants rather than sons, stipendiaries rather than soldiers, prebend-holders rather than canons.

Brother R., whom we sent with them, ended his last day among them, and made us sadder inasmuch as, singing the Lord’s song in a foreign land, he did not obtain burial among his brethren. The cord of this lot—indeed, of this death—fell upon us and upon our son. Let him see what he has done, who by such importunities drove us to allow him violently to snatch from our bosom such a young man, only to bury him alone, apart from the others, in a foreign land. [Col. 0331C] [Note: Col. 0331C]

He seems to speak of Guarinus, abbot of Saint-Victor, who, by the authority he exercised over all houses enrolled in the Victorine congregation, sent R., a regular canon of Saint Geneviève mentioned in Letter 16, to Naples and compelled Stephen, the abbot, although wishing to retain him, to let him go against his will.

We ask, Father, that you commend his soul before the Lord Jesus by your prayers and assist it by offerings.

## 40. LETTER XXX. TO MASTER ROBERT

He offers prayers to him for a certain friend who needed his help.

[Col. 0332A]

To his dearest friend Master Robert, fullness of health and perfection of joy.

I take pleasure in the delightful sight whenever I hear the sound of your name or enter into the thought of remembering you. This comes both from the long-standing fellowship of our studies and from a disposition of character suited to the shared grace of your manners. Therefore, in the affair of this friend of mine, I appeal to you with confident security, that for love of me you may give him counsel and assistance, so that he may perceive that my prayers have benefited him and may know that I have someone who is my friend at my lord’s court. [Col. 0332B] He has a case before my lord; and since, through absence, I cannot make myself available to him, I ask that my absence be supplied by your presence. Some think of me more highly than I deserve, and others’ estimation so exceeds my own conscience that at times I find others’ confidence odious. The bearer of this letter, my friend, is one of these; and at my lord’s court [Note: [Col. 0332C] This was William, archbishop first of Sens and afterwards of Reims, to whose service Stephen had at one time attached himself and whose clerk he professes himself to have been. “Court” here means the forum in which cases were argued and judgments delivered.], where he has his business, he acknowledges and trusts that I can do something, and urgently presses me to solicit you and my other friends on his behalf. I pour forth prayers to your charity that, for love of me, you may both devise counsel for him in conducting his case and furnish him patronage in making his petition.

## 41. LETTER XXXI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS, ON BEHALF OF THE ABBOT OF SAINT BARTHOLOMEW OF NOYON

He asks him to show himself kindly toward this abbot.

[Col. 0332C]

I had presented humble prayers to you, Father, on behalf of the abbot of Saint Bartholomew, a simple and upright man who fears the Lord; and you received them kindly with the paternal spirit that is your custom. [Col. 0333A] An old, sick, and frail man, beset by many hardships, if he sets out upon the road of an adverse pilgrimage, will easily enter upon the road of all flesh. Spare, I beseech you, his grey hairs; and lest a man of God be unjustly harassed, set your authority against the aggressor, restrain him who troubles him, and curb the vexations. Trusting in the kindness of your reply, I have kept the man back, deferred the journey, and promised him security. Act, Father, I beseech you, so that so great a minister of the altar may peacefully possess the altar over which there is dispute [Note: [Col. 0333C] Here “altar” does not mean the table upon which the holy and bloodless sacrifice of the Mass is offered, but, as ancient writers use the term, the priesthood or parish. A controversy concerning it was before the metropolitan archbishop of Reims between a certain bishop and Hugh, abbot of Saint Bartholomew of Noyon.]; that he may find the bishop who contests it peaceable; and that he may give thanks to the author of peace and founder of his tranquillity. For I know that he will be neither ungrateful for so great a favour nor undevout in return for such great benefits. Farewell.

## 42. LETTER XXXII. TO THE KING’S ALMONER

[Note: [Col. 0333D] The king’s almoners are those clerics whom the king employs in divine worship, the ministry of sacred rites, and the distribution of alms. Mention of a royal almoner occurs in the capitularies of Charles the Bald, issued at Quierzy in 877, where the king says: “If death overtakes us in the service of God and His saints, our almoners shall contend concerning our alms according to what we have entrusted.” Those called almoners include some prelates—such as Archbishop Hincmar, Bishop Franco, and Abbot Goslin—and some secular counts, such as Arnulf and Bernard. It is also found that under the kings of the second dynasty, the cleric who ministered most prominently to them was honoured with the title of archchaplain. Nor is the dignity of chief almoner found introduced into the royal palace before Louis the Younger; Roger, bishop of Sées, is called his almoner by Sigebert in the year 1160. The person to whom Stephen sends this letter, however, I judge to have been some prelate, since he addresses him as “Father,” a form by which he was accustomed to address only bishops and abbots, as may be observed in his other letters.]

He asks that a Jew converted to the faith be enabled to benefit from the king’s almsgiving.

[Col. 0333B]

It rarely happens that anyone is faithfully converted from the hardness of the uncircumcised people to the new infancy of the Church’s rebirth. If such a case should occur beyond the examples we have seen, it should be embraced the more dearly because it is rarer. This poor man, born of Jewish parents, did not blush at the stumbling-block to the Jews—the cross of Christ. Baptized by the bishop of León [Note: [Col. 0334D] León is a very celebrated city of Spain, commonly called Léon, and the capital of the whole kingdom of León.], he was transferred from the mass of perdition among Catholics and the canons of his church. [Col. 0333C] Having been extensively instructed in ecclesiastical disciplines and ministries, in both reading and singing, he devoted himself to scholastic labours. There he is supported both by your alms—for, God willing, you once opened your hand to him—and by those of others. We ask, Father, if it please you, that you cause him to be counted among those poor persons who are supported for your lord, the son of our lord the king. For from his modesty and his voluntary endurance of poverty [Col. 0334A] and hardships, we anticipate in him the fruit of faith, salvation, and labour. The *capicerius* of Holy Cross [Note: [Col. 0334D] The office of *capicerius*, called *chevecier* in French, in cathedrals and monasteries is to care for and guard sacred objects; we call him by another name the sacristan. He is called *capicerius* as though “one who takes wax,” because his office is to receive the candles offered in pious devotion by the faithful to the altar and the relics of the saints, and to prepare them for the Church’s use. Some suppose that *capicerius* and *primicerius* were the same, because of the nearly similar meaning of their names; but I do not agree, because their offices differ.], when he was going to Saint James, heard in the chapter of León a good testimony to his conversion, by which he himself might benefit him and might invite us to be more earnestly devoted to benefiting him.

## 43. LETTER XXXIII. TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT BARTHOLOMEW

He speaks devoutly of contempt for temporal things.

The occasion that gave me material for writing in correction of you is welcome. Your diligence marked the form of my greeting, attending to the surface of the letter [Col. 0334B] rather than its marrow. I confess that I am poor in spiritual things and abundant in temporal ones; yet in neither do we possess anything as from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God. Now at last, freed from the yoke of anxiety and care that burns and troubles the heart, I delight in prayer and reading, knowing and pondering that the time will come when all men of riches will find nothing in their hands. But seeing my own poverty, I say with Paul that we have become rich in Him (1 Cor. V), who gives abundantly to all and does not reproach them (James I). Neither our age nor our purpose is such that we should love those riches which rust and moth destroy, and which thieves dig up and steal. I judge the same of you, considering your prudence and your age.

## 44. LETTER XXXIV. TO THE KING OF HUNGARY

[Note: [Col. 0334D] In the printed letters the title is “To R., illustrious king of Hungary,” but R. has wrongly been printed for B., by which Béla, king of Hungary, is indicated. According to Ranzanus, in his *Epitome of Hungarian Affairs*, he ruled that kingdom from 1172 to 1190.]

He testifies that a certain Hungarian youth who died lived piously at Paris.

[Col. 0334C]

To the most noble B., king of Hungary, STEPHEN, called abbot of Saint Geneviève, and the whole humble convent of the same church.

[Col. 0335A] From the clear indications of those who come to us, we have learned by experience that you love justice and cultivate truth. This is the sublimity of your kingdom; this is the glory of your rule. Therefore we wish Your Excellency to know that the youth Bethlehem, of blessed memory [Note: [Col. 0335C] The proper name of the noble Hungarian youth who was taken from the living at Paris and buried in the church of Saint Geneviève. His death is recorded in that church’s necrology on the Kalends of December in these words: “Bethlehem, a cleric from Hungary, died; for him his father and mother gave precious ornaments to our church.”], who rests among us in the Lord, was buried in our church in holy confession and the Catholic faith, before all men, without objection or complaint from creditors or sureties. And when recently, for this same reason, messengers from his parents came to us, we caused careful inquiry to be made whether he was held at Paris by any debt, whether to a Christian or to a Jew. 45 This inquiry having been conducted for about ten days, no one was found who claimed that the aforesaid youth was bound to him, either principally [Col. 0335B] or secondarily. The aforesaid messengers were ready to pay if anyone acknowledged that anything was owed him on the young man’s account. Yet, just as no creditor appeared, so no surety was found. The clerics James, Michael, and Adrian, from your kingdom, were present at these proceedings. May Your Holiness prosper, and may your kingdom be strengthened before the Lord.

## LETTER XXXV. TO L. AND HIS WIFE

He consoles parents afflicted by their son’s death.

To L. and to Christina, his wife: salvation and frequent remembrance in prayer.

[Col. 0336A] You ought not to grieve over your son Bethlehem, of blessed memory, as do others who have no hope; for in holy confession, in the Catholic faith, in the common hope, and in unfeigned charity, he commended his spirit into the Lord’s hand. In our church, before a faithful multitude of clergy and laity, after the Masses had been performed and the life-giving sacrifice offered for him, he was buried. There was no mention of credit or debt, no recollection of complaints. On account of certain rumours, which we later learned were false, your messengers came to us; and, as we have said, they found nothing of what had been reported. An inquiry was carefully conducted by us for about ten days, and neither Christian nor Jew appeared who claimed that your aforesaid son was bound to him by any [Col. 0336B] debt. These things we saw; these things we testify.

Furthermore, every day we render you ample thanks for your benefactions, since you have added a second set of gifts to the first. They brought us tokens of your devotion: two silk chasubles [Note: [Col. 0335C] Although *xenia* properly means gifts which friends customarily send one another at the beginning of the year, here it is taken for any gift. In the *Capitularies* of Louis the Pious, chapter 5, one reads: “Let them see whether bishops, in visiting their parishes, exact undue *xenia* from priests.” These *xenia*, or gifts, are mentioned in the necrology of Saint Geneviève, as I reported above.], [Note: [Col. 0335C] A chasuble is the outer garment worn by a priest while he performs the sacred sacrifice of the Mass. It is also called a *planeta*, as may be read in the Council of Toledo under Honorius I, canon 27: “If a priest, deposed from his rank, is restored in the holy synod, let him receive from the bishop’s hand the stole and the *planeta*.” It is recorded that the *planeta* of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, brought from Antioch to Paris, was once preserved in the church of Saint Geneviève, where it healed a paralytic in the presence of Hugh of Cluny, as is related in his *Life* in Surius. It is also mentioned under the name “Chasuble of Saint Peter” in Suger’s letter to Pope Eugenius, in du Chesne, vol. IV.], one banner [Note: [Col. 0335D] Among the Romans a *vexillum* was a military standard. Vegetius, book II, says: “When a hundred soldiers followed not only their standard but also the centurion, who bore a device on his helmet.” Pliny, book X, lists among these the eagle, wolf, horse, and boar, mounted on spears and carried before the individual military units. In the second year of his consulship Gaius Marius, having removed the other standards, assigned the eagle alone to the Roman legions; its bearer was called an eagle-bearer. Later, under the emperors, their names were inscribed on standards and their images placed upon them. Suetonius, *Vespasian*, ch. 6, says: “Without delay they inscribed his name upon all the standards.” Tacitus says: “They would choose as emperors those whose images they had followed in place of standards.” Hence, when Constantine became a Christian, he inscribed Christ’s name upon his standards, as Eusebius notes; and his coins and those of his sons attest this, as may be seen in a coin of Constantine taken from our museum. From this arose the form of sacred banners, embroidered with images of Christ and the saints, carried by Christians when they proceed anywhere to pray, as Prudentius notes in book II *Against Symmachus*, where he calls the standard by its ancient name, *labarum*:

[Col. 0336D]

> Christ, woven in purple upon jewelled gold,  
> marked the *labarum*.

], a mark of silver, with a gold coin and five solidi [Note: [Col. 0336D] The ancient Romans had gold coins of this kind, which we still preserve in our numismatic collections. In size and weight they differ little from the Spanish doubloon, and they do not exceed a value of thirteen or fourteen Tours pounds. The gold solidi of the kind discussed here—for silver ones were not yet in use in Gaul—weighed somewhat more than our gold coins and approached a value of about six Tours pounds. Gold solidi of the same sort are assessed in the Salic Law at forty denarii. A standard weight of an ancient gold solidus is preserved in the same Saint-Geneviève collection.], for making a chalice; and they generously offered a white horse for carrying stones for our building-work.

May God repay you in eternal life and, for your great benefactions, do good to you for ever. Farewell.

## 47. LETTER XXXVI. TO THE BISHOP OF PORTO

[Note: [Col. 0337C] The bishop of Porto is one of the six cardinal-bishops who are suffragans of the Roman see. Porto [Col. 0337D] is a city not far from Ostia, eighteen miles from Rome. Emperor Claudius built it long ago for the convenience of mariners. Pope Calixtus II, in 1120, united to the see of this city the bishopric of Silva Candida. The bishop of Porto to whom this letter is addressed seems to have been Theodinus, who, according to Ughelli, held this see in the time of Alexander III.]

He asks him to receive the petitions of the dean and precentor of Chartres and see them fulfilled.

[Col. 0337A]

The Church of Chartres [Note: [Col. 0337D] This church is most celebrated and foremost in antiquity among all sacred buildings, not only in Gaul but throughout the Christian world. For it is said to have been dedicated by the Druids, priests of this people, in honour of the Virgin who was to bear a child, two hundred years before the Blessed Virgin Mother of God was born. Later, when the faith had been brought into Gaul, it was consecrated according to Christian rites. About 1020 Bishop Fulbert restored it to the elegance in which we now see it, especially through the benefactions of Cnut, king of England, as William of Malmesbury testifies in book II of *The Deeds of the English Kings*: “King Cnut, sending money to churches overseas, enriched Chartres above all, where Bishop Fulbert, most renowned then for holiness and philosophy, flourished.”] is as pre-eminent in authority among neighbouring and distant churches as it will be illustrious in reputation. For we are bound to love her more deeply the more lavishly we have received both caresses and nourishment from the breasts of her consolation. Her inward parts are wounded, and among some of her children she finds perversity. Moved by zeal for this compassion, the dean and precentor of the Church of Chartres both await and expect the mercy of the lord pope. They are our friends through long association, and our former fellowship bears witness to their honourable conduct. [Col. 0337B] We pour forth prayers to your holy fatherhood for both of them. We do not wish either to be defrauded of his just desire, and we trust that each will be aided through the other. Receive their petitions as our own, and let your favour make them commendable in the eyes of the lord pope—men who, trusting in us, do not know how to beg help from strangers.

## 49. LETTER XXXVII. TO THE BISHOP OF PRAENESTE

He entrusts to his care the cause of the dean and precentor of Chartres.

[Col. 0337C]

To the bishop of Praeneste [Note: [Col. 0338D] The bishop of Praeneste is one of the pope’s six suffragans. Praeneste is a most ancient city of Latium, twenty-five miles from Rome. The bishop to whom this letter is addressed was, as may be inferred from the same Ughelli, Bernaredus, formerly abbot of Saint Crispin at Soissons; Peter of Celle writes to him in letter 21 of book VIII.], STEPHEN of Saint Geneviève.

Both common report and ancient dignity proclaim the Church of Chartres worthy of commendation in the kingdom of the Franks. We ought to love its rest and peace all the more closely because we have felt, and still feel, its benefits more deeply. In it, sons of contention and quarrelling are stirring; they strive to stretch the slightest occasions into the gravest scandals. The dean and precentor, more compassionate toward their mother than the rest, approach the lord pope as suppliants, so that those presumptuous offenders may be punished for injuries from the source from which laws are drawn. [Col. 0338A] We love them especially, and are loved by them; we retain the remnants of our ancient fellowship and long association in the memory of honourable recollection. We offer prayers to your holiness, that you may receive their desires, petitions, and vows kindly, and fulfil them beneficently.

## 50. LETTER XXXVIII. TO CARDINAL GRATIAN

He asks not to be compelled to receive a certain canon who had been expelled five times.

To the venerable lord, worthy by God’s grace, GRATIAN, cardinal [Note: [Col. 0338D] Master Gratian of Pisa was made cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church by Alexander III, having previously been an apostolic subdeacon and scribe. Stephen became his friend while both were pursuing letters under the same master.] of the holy Roman Church, STEPHEN of Saint Geneviève: greetings.

[Col. 0338B] The remnants of my thoughts keep festival for me whenever I recall that I was your fellow-student in the lecture hall of Bulgarus [Note: [Col. 0338D] Bulgarus was a celebrated doctor of law at the academy of Bologna; he will be treated more fully elsewhere.], whom I now gladly revere as my lord in the ministry of Peter. And because your favour surpasses the merits and wishes of many, though they have plainly deserved something from you, I ask that I may find beneficent the man whom I have deserved to find well-disposed. A certain son of dissension and scandal, formerly our canon, who has been expelled five times from our church because of his intolerable and monstrous offences, is attempting to deceive the lord pope with his falsehood. By command of the lord king, who knew that man’s perverse conduct, he abjured the boundaries of the kingdom. He beat several of our brethren; and finally, with repeated blows, he impiously struck our prior, a religious [Col. 0338C] and honourable man, with his fist. After returning from the curia, he also inflicted many bitter insults upon me. By a letter of our chapter we have made known to the lord pope the character of the man, whom he does not know, so that, once he has recognized the truth, he may command what he wills and we may do what he commands. For, if it please the lord pope, we would rather receive that plague at our own peril than appear disobedient. I ask your kindness that, for the love of God and for the preservation of concord in our Church, you may free us from so great an inconvenience.

## LETTER XXXIX. TO WILLIAM, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS

[Note: [Col. 0339B] In the king’s name he asks the archbishop of Reims, who had gone to Rome for the general Lateran council in 1179, to excuse before Pope Alexander III Bartholomew, archbishop of Tours, because illness had prevented him from travelling to Rome. He also treats the controversy of that archbishop with the bishop of Dol.]

He deals with the celebrated controversy between the archbishop of Tours and the bishop of Dol, because the latter presumed to enjoy the title and right of archbishop and metropolitan.

[Col. 0339A]

To WILLIAM, archbishop of Reims, STEPHEN of Saint Geneviève: prosperity with health, etc.

Your absence, Father, is for us meanwhile more deadly than joyful, burdensome rather than welcome, fearful rather than fair. For what remains, we daily offer sacrifices of prayer for you and our companions, so that we who were rightly saddened by your departure may rejoice, perhaps suddenly, at your return. We saw at Paris your lord and familiar friend, who, as we believe, loves you with deepest affection—the archbishop of Tours—on his way to [Col. 0339B] the sacred council. [Note: [Col. 0339C] He uses *Parisius* for *Parisiis* (“at Paris”), a usage especially common among the ancients. Innumerable examples might be produced: first, an ancient coin minted in the time of Charles the Bald, “Citizen at Paris,” whose likeness is given here; second, concerning Hulbold of Liège, who lived in the time of King Robert: “When as a young man he fled from scholastic discipline to Paris”; third, in a diploma of Pope Eugenius III: “To Odo, first abbot of Saint Geneviève, which is beside Paris.” I found on an ancient sepulchral inscription, more than a thousand years old, *annus* for *annis*, and *Januarins et Julius dies* for *Januarii et Julii die*, with this inscription: “Leudelinus rests here in peace; he lived 50 years; he died when the fifteenth day of January was completed.” On the opposite side the cenotaph of his wife reads: “Valdolina rests here in peace; she lived 30 years; she died when the thirty-third day of July was completed.” These two inscriptions occur upon a stone tablet found in a grave excavated at Amiens near the monastery of Saint-Acheul and sent to me; in the judgment of experts its characters indicate the age of the kings of the first dynasty.] He was afflicted by chronic illness beyond what could be believed, and, like a man passing away as an image, he was a man without strength wishing to proceed yet unable. A helpless man struggled against his own nature; he struggled against the counsel and wish of his people, so that he might depart without making progress, die without delay, obey at peril, and obey unto death. The lord king saw, and did not disregard, his manifest infirmity; and, compassionate toward the sickness of his metropolitan, he judged rightly and did not falsely judge. [Col. 0340A] Having kept him back, he informed the lord pope, as he ought and as befitted him, that the reason for his absence was most just. Our most Christian king also commanded me, his humble faithful servant, to write to the lord pope on behalf of the aforesaid archbishop what I had perceived by eyewitness evidence; and this I did.

I also write to your fatherhood as your faithful and devoted servant, earnestly asking and beseeching that at the sacred council you hold excused that friend of yours whom illness, not will, detains. Concerning the cause of the people of Dol [Note: [Col. 0339D] Alberic’s *Chronicle* speaks of it as follows: “At this time the case of the Church and John, bishop of Tours—or, more correctly, Joscius, predecessor of Bartholomew—was argued before the pope against the bishops of Brittany, who had the archbishop of Dol; the archbishop of Tours maintained that they belonged to him by right. When matters had proceeded to final judgment, Geoffrey the archdeacon, advocate for Tours, offered the archbishop of Dol before the pope, for the sake of peace, that if he wished, before sentence was rendered, he should always be archbishop through a peace settlement and should always have one bishopric. He refused; the case came to judgment; and after many disputes the pope gave judgment for Tours and the archbishopric of Dol was abolished.” Matthew Paris says that this controversy was concluded in 1199, when Bartholomew governed the bishopric of Tours. Therefore, since Alberic’s Chronicle speaks of this case under John or Joscius, bishop of Tours, it must be supposed that he only initiated it, not concluded it. Matthew Paris, under the year 1199, says: “This year the very ancient case between the churches of Tours and Dol was decided at Rome by Pope Innocent in a final judgment, the archbishop of Tours demanding subjection from the bishop of Dol and the bishop of Dol resisting.” He then relates the entire history and sets out the origin and cause of the controversy, adding: “The continual suit and contention between the bishops of Tours and Dol endured until the present year, as has been said, when it was determined by the aforesaid pope’s sentence that both the bishop of Dol and the other bishops of Brittany should be subject to the archbishop of Tours and should for ever obey his canonical commands.” Therefore the pope mentioned, when pronouncing final judgment, being learned, bold, and skilled in law, began thus: “Let Dol grieve, and Tours rejoice.” See the following letters.], the lord king greatly marvels that a matter put to rest by the authority of the holy Roman Church should be stirred up; and he is so moved by its revival that he will not endure its advancement. Let your fatherhood work earnestly, I beseech you, so that the Church of Tours, which until the old age of our most holy [Col. 0340B] king [Note: [Col. 0340D] Namely Louis VII, who was then sixty-nine years old. This letter was written in 1179, when the Lateran council was held; in the following year, 1180, he died at the age of seventy, according to William the Breton, although Rigord extends his life to the year 1181. Our author calls him “most holy,” since he acquired above our other kings the surname “the Pious.” William of Newburgh, book III of his *English History*, ch. 5, expresses his piety toward God and subjects in these few words: “A man of fearless devotion toward God and exceptional gentleness toward his subjects, and a chief reverencer also of holy orders.”] possessed tranquillity and peace in this dispute, may not lose in his final days the dignity which she has possessed. I know his will and mind: whoever opposes the Church of Tours in this cause he will judge to be his own adversary; whoever stands for her, he will maintain has stood for him. At last I shall speak to my lord, though I am dust and ashes. Therefore, I ask, let your holy discretion so conduct itself in matters concerning the lord king that he may praise you in the Laon affair and not grieve over you in the Dol affair. [Note: [Col. 0340D] When William, archbishop of Reims, was going to the Lateran council, the king had especially entrusted two matters to him: first, that he should defend the archbishop of Tours in the Roman curia against the bishop of Dol; second, that he should uphold the king’s side at the council against Roger of Rozoy, bishop of Laon. Roger, being personally present there, complained that the king had compelled him by unjust force to abandon his bishopric. The cause of the king’s anger against him was this, recorded in the Chronicle of Laon under 1177: “The men of the district of Laon, to the prejudice of the bishop and Church of Laon, having offered King Louis a valuation of money, arranged to establish a commune; and so, thinking perversely, they supposed they would shake from their necks the yoke of servitude, for themselves and their heirs. But Roger, the distinguished bishop of Laon, came in person and through friends before the king and earnestly entreated him in every way, lamenting the commune of his serfs, to have pity on his church. Yet the king, it is said, adhering to the promised money, did not heed the bishop and his men. The bishop, being high-minded, saw that his often-repeated pleas before the king made no progress; he summoned his own kindred, that through them he might take vengeance upon his ungrateful and rebellious serfs. Princes of his family assembled to him from every side, together with other necessary friends, namely the lord of Avesnes and the count of Rozoy. The opposing party, not ignorant of their arrival, awaited them with their own helpers; many others came armed to assist them, including other communes, through the agency of Geoffrey of Senlis, then provost of Laon. Six men of Saint-Médard of Soissons gathered to their aid by the king’s command; the commune of Crépy and the commune of Vailly came to help them. Thus, when forces of armed men had been arrayed on both sides, the whole rustic multitude, frightened merely by the name of the knights who had assembled, chose flight. A considerable number were slain there, but the number of those who perished in the waters is uncertain. In the following summer King Louis prepared to go … [lacuna] the destruction of those of the district of Laon … [lacuna] against Rainald, the bishop’s brother and lord of Rozoy. He came to the castle of the count of Rozoy, called Nizy, where reconciliation was effected when the friends of the aforesaid lord of Rozoy made satisfaction to the king on his behalf—on the condition, however, that thereafter he would acknowledge that he held his castle from the king. The venerable bishop, avoiding the king’s anger, lay hidden in Burgundy with Walter, then bishop of Langres.”]

## 53–55. LETTER XL. TO THE SUPREME PONTIFF

He asks that Bartholomew, archbishop of Tours, be excused because he was unable to travel to Rome.

[Col. 0341A]

To the supreme pontiff [Note: [Col. 0342D] This letter appears to be the one mentioned in the preceding letter to William, archbishop of Reims, which Stephen wrote to the supreme pontiff in the king’s name.], STEPHEN of Saint Geneviève: greetings and devoted obedience.

It is a domestic joy to us and to your other sons, Father, that the bosom of your blessed fatherhood extends itself to individuals in such a manner as to receive all. From the breasts of its consolation the faint-hearted are helped and the sorrowful refreshed. Strengthened by this hope, your devoted son B., archbishop of Tours, although afflicted with a long illness and worn away beyond human appearance, had undertaken the journey to [Col. 0341B] your sacred council, striving in spirit to fulfil what he could not do in body. When he had arrived at Paris, intending on his passage to speak with the lord king, he was seized by a recurrence of illness. Thus he could not, though it was necessary, complete the journey he had begun without danger of death, as we believe. 56 I, sick myself, bear witness for the sick man, speaking from my own awareness: if he went away, he would die; if he set out, he would not make progress; if he did not remain, he would perish.

Furthermore, holy Father, concerning the affair of the Churches of Tours and Dol, I wish you to know the will of the lord king, whose merits live effectively before you and leave their memory perpetually to your successors. Whoever harms the Church of Tours [Col. 0341C] harms the apple of his eye, and even a slight diminution of it would inflict the greatest injury upon his crown. He is deeply distressed at the deceits of the people of Dol, who strive to revive a settled lawsuit and attempt to circumvent your holy religious devotion. Spare, Father, I beseech you, your holy son the king; spare his peace [Col. 0342A] and tranquillity; spare the kingdom of the Franks, which has always remained faithful and devoted to the most holy Roman Church in every persecution.

## LETTER XLI. TO BARTHOLOMEW, ARCHBISHOP OF TOURS

He excuses himself from delivering sermons because of illness.

After spare diets and sleepless nights, which chronic illness conceived and brought forth amid my pains, the less pressing daily care of my church promises and permits me a little rest and relief. I consult the disciples of Hippocrates and Galen in order that they may advise me, always bringing back uncertain oracles from them. They discern faults of colour and substance in a glass vessel [Note: [Col. 0342D] He means physicians, who ascertain the nature and symptoms of diseases by inspecting urine contained in a glass vessel; he calls them disciples of Hippocrates and Galen. He repeats this elsewhere.]. While I seek and await their aid and care; while I attend to their constricted art; while I endeavour to have them cut the knots of my illness, they cut knotty questions instead, while, as though my health were in danger, they forbid me study and work. [Col. 0342B] These are what prevent me from adding willingness beyond ability, lest, if I wish what I cannot do, I make so little progress in either that I fail in both. These are what bring sloth both to the writing of sermons and to desire [Note: [Col. 0342D] Stephen was reckoned among the most distinguished and celebrated preachers of his age. Accordingly, his sermons were carefully gathered from all quarters so that they might be preserved from the injury of time. It should therefore not seem surprising if many prelates sought him for the office of preaching, as the archbishop of Tours does here.] and take away my voice from my wish. Let your fatherhood spare me, I beseech you, and grant me a respite concerning what you request until full health and complete recovery. Farewell.

## 58. LETTER XLII. TO THE SUPREME PONTIFF

He asks him to support the cause of the abbot of Saint Victor and to receive him kindly.

[Col. 0342C]

To the supreme pontiff, STEPHEN of Saint Geneviève: greetings and devoted obedience.

We believe, Father, that ignorance of the fact is excusable—not the kind that commonly befalls men of sluggish and gross minds, but that which the hostility of times or places imposes even upon accomplished and truly philosophical men. The abbot of Saint-Victor, a son of innocence and guardian of obedience, having suffered the snares of this ignorance, is not to be believed to have evaded, nor to be said to have eluded, the sacred command of your apostolic authority.

[Note: This is Guarinus, fifth abbot of Saint-Victor at Paris, a man distinguished for piety and learning. He was made abbot in 1172; Pope Alexander III was pleased to write him a congratulatory letter upon his election. He composed sermons in an elegant and polished style, which are still preserved in the Victorine library. He died in 1180.]

For although the messenger received those divine letters of yours on the Kalends of January, as is clear from their subscription, he delivered and handed them to the aforesaid innocent and straightforward man on the Monday after the octave of Pentecost. Whether this happened through anyone’s diligence or negligence, we do not know; but that it happened we do not doubt in the least. And since that religious and God-fearing man is ready, at the sound of even one command of yours, to go both to prison and to death, may his own innocence render him excusable before you, though another’s rashness perhaps makes him blameworthy.

Meanwhile the man’s infirmity cries out; it cries out and pleads bodily weakness, asking that in this summons of yours you may, if it please you, spare him, lest he be unable to make progress if he begins his journey. Yet, because he does not doubt that idolatry and disobedience walk with equal step—an image at once so foul and monstrous that one recoils from it—his spirit indeed being willing though his flesh is weak, he will not fear to undertake the journey, so that we may deserve to obey your commands.

## LETTER XLIII. TO PETER, BISHOP OF TUSCULUM

He asks him to receive under his patronage the abbot of Saint-Bartholomew of Noyon.

To the most holy lord Master Peter, bishop of Tusculum, Stephen of Saint-Geneviève sends greeting.

[Note: Peter, cardinal bishop of Tusculum, was created by Alexander III in 1178. Peter of Blois wrote to him Letter 6 of Book IX. Roger of Howden, however, calls him Peter of Pavia.]

Father, I have fulfilled as far as I could the small service enjoined upon me by you—like carrying wood into a forest, like striving to assist the sun with torches. I ask you to receive my childish offerings, though they deserve laughter, with a kindly look. Your sons in the church of Blessed Geneviève continually offer sacrifices of prayer for you, sacrificing, as it were, calves of their lips and hearts for your welfare.

[Note: I do not see why he calls the canons of Saint-Geneviève at Paris his sons, unless perhaps because, as Ughelli notes, under Lucius III he acted in the Roman Church as the pope’s deputy in its administration. Therefore the canons of this abbey, who belonged by a special title to the Apostolic See, called him Father and could be called his sons. His death is recorded in the necrology of Saint-Geneviève in these words: “Peter, bishop of Tusculum, of pious memory, died; he gave us thirty pounds for buying land.”]

I too, mindful of your benefits, which your kindness has bestowed on me above every mortal, keep the remembrance of you fixed in my inmost heart, conversing and playing with it, tasting and savoring with it the firstfruits and tithes of my delight. For the abbot of Saint-Bartholomew, an honorable and just man, I beseech your fatherhood to provide him, in the needs of his Church, with kindly counsel and beneficent help. May your holy fatherhood prosper and, advancing from good to better, be increased.

## LETTER XLIV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF TOLEDO

Concerning a man ordained simoniacally.

It is fitting that such concern rest upon prelates that they correct the errors of their subjects by teaching and rebuke them by discipline. Nor should serenity be absent from severity where the priest pronounces sentence and the father a punishment. Let dispensation temper rigor in the vicar of Christ, equity strict law, and the father’s bosom the power of a judge. A sacrifice of fat, fine flour mingled with oil—mercy triumphing over judgment—is commended. These, Father, are the things that move us concerning your present son, poor in spirit; and they invite you, not unwillingly, to compassion.

He has disclosed his offence to us and confessed that, in receiving holy orders, he drank something of the stain and cloud of Simon, though in simplicity. A payment for service, no less than a payment from the hand, is condemned in this sacred transaction. To a certain man who caused hands to be laid upon him, he both promised and supplied an annual service by agreement, as though he were not ungrateful for a favor—which nevertheless, if it is not freely given, is not grace. In fulfilling a promise contrary to faith, he erred through ignorance—ignorance that perhaps would not have befallen a philosopher; yet simplicity excuses one whom ignorance of the law accuses.

We pour forth prayers to your mercy that, since you have received authority to bind and to loose over him, you may receive the weak man and grant him pardon through mercy, though perhaps you can condemn him by justice. Farewell.

## LETTER XLV. TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT-SATYR

[Note: That is, to Godfrey, mentioned above.]

He asks him to send back one of his canons, who is lying ill.

He who asks is importunate; he who gives is beneficent. Necessity excuses the former; generosity commends the latter. May your friendship, I pray, bear with this importunity of mine, and with wholesome counsel, work, and assistance comfort the father now present, whom you too begot in Christ. We do not know the cause of his illness, nor its cure. He has long lain ill with an acute fever—

[Note: He means a continuous and rather severe fever.]

—and has not recovered after the crisis, because the illness prevailed. He still burns with lingering fevers, his pulse rapid and feverish; he often rises and relapses, and seems readier to fall ill than to recover. If you can do anything, help him, out of pity for us. Whatever good is done to him I shall count as done to myself. Write us your advice, and send him himself to us. We wish neither to remain nor to die anywhere but among ourselves. He will oblige us if he does not delay with you.

## LETTER XLVI. TO PETER, PRIEST-CARDINAL OF SAINT-CHRYSOGONUS

[Note: He was made cardinal by Alexander III; previously he had been bishop-elect of Meaux, having been an abbot and an archdeacon. But it is not known of what order and monastery he was abbot, or of what church he was archdeacon. Concerning his legation to King Henry of England, Roger of Howden writes under the year 1179: “Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint-Chrysogonus, legate of the Apostolic See, formerly bishop-elect of the Church of Meaux, came into France and received commands from Pope Alexander that all Normandy and all the king’s lands on this side and beyond the sea should be placed under interdict unless he allowed Richard his son, count of Poitou, to marry Alys, daughter of Louis king of France, whom the king of England had kept in his custody for so long and beyond the term agreed between them.”]

He congratulates him upon his promotion to the cardinalate.

I confess that the remembrance of you affords me a delightful spectacle, while I behold you ascending, as it were, by a song of degrees: while virtues draw our Peter upward from lesser to greater things on one side, and honors on the other. Grace calls forth grace, glory glory, just as curtain draws curtain; and now you shine fully before all who are in the house of the Lord, because from His fullness God has given you grace and glory. These are the things that gladden the faces of your friends with oil, and rejoice and strengthen their hearts.

I rejoice to be a participant in this feast; I glory to be its companion. For though I hold a small place among your own, I claim for myself no small fruit of such great affection and delight. I embrace the scholar, follow the archdeacon, kiss the abbot, rise before the bishop, and revere the cardinal. As these ranks ascend by stages and are added to him rather than succeeding one another, honors smile upon character, and character rejoices together with honors.

Let that common proverb hold true of others: “Honors change manners.” In your case I pray only that, if they change or move them, they may not exclude that kind of movement called increase. Meanwhile, Father, I offer for you such sacrifices of prayer as I can: doves of groaning, calves of the lips. I trust that one whom you loved in private life you will not cease to love when promoted. If it please you, receive me myself as a burnt offering of service to you: may love, strong as death, slay me at your pleasure, and may the flame of charity kindle me.

## LETTER XLVII. TO ARALD, ABBOT OF SAINT-BENEDICT

[Note: This letter is addressed to Arald, abbot of Fleury, or Saint-Benedict-on-the-Loire, in the diocese of Orléans. That most celebrated monastery is known to have been founded about the year 623 by Leobold, abbot of Saint-Aignan. In 660 the relics of Saint Benedict were brought there from the monastery of Cassino by the monk Aigulphus; hence it afterwards acquired the name of Saint-Benedict, though it was originally called Fleury. The abbot of this place possesses complete temporal jurisdiction both in the town of Fleury and in various surrounding estates and lordships. He has many men bound to his lordly patronage and jurisdiction, among whom the man for whose benefit this letter was written should be reckoned.]

He commends to him a certain widow and her son.

With my customary insistence and importunity, I commend to your affection our widow and orphan, whose slender means and small property depend on your favor and are sustained by your protection. The greed of creditors gapes over them, so as to take the little ward from the widow’s bosom and swallow up her spark, whose life is in bitterness, her livelihood in want, and her clothing in cold and nakedness.

I ask, Father, that your judgment may proceed from equity rather than strict law, and that her brother, who stood surety and made payment for his sister’s orphaned son, may by your authority be preferred to the other creditors as having the stronger claim upon the pledge. For through your hand he has the natural possession of the fief, and he is ready to render the oath of fealty, as is proper.

[Note: A fief, which according to Cujacius, On Fiefs, Book I, title 1, part X, was anciently called a beneficium, is “a right in another’s estate, to use and enjoy it perpetually, which the lord gives as a benefice under the law on condition that the recipient render him faith and military service or some other service.” A fief, therefore, is properly not an estate but a right in an estate. The necessity of military affairs gave rise to the fief. For when the earliest ages were troubled by most grievous wars, emperors, kings, and princes distributed whole regions, especially those bordering the enemy, among dukes and, as they call them, captains—not that they might possess them alone, but that they might distribute them in suitable portions among individual soldiers, according to the status of persons, under the name of fief, that is, pay; their pledge of faith having been received, so that they might defend their country and, when summoned, hasten to the aid of the prince under whom they served.]

## LETTER XLVIII. TO POPE ALEXANDER III

He informs him that he has carried out his command concerning the pension of a certain cleric.

To the most holy lord and Father Alexander, supreme pontiff, Stephen of Saint-Geneviève sends greeting and, with every devotion and reverence, due obedience.

Father, in obedience to the voice of a single command of yours, I took care, though absent, to provide for the son of Laxius of Archeri, as I had promised in your presence, although you have been informed otherwise by his intimate neighbors. I established him with grain and wine, so that by the one the heart of man might be strengthened and by the other he might feel gladness.

[Note: He alludes to what is written in Psalm 103: “Bread strengthens the heart of man, and wine gladdens the heart of man.”]

When a messenger arrived, the command was changed and made more burdensome by an order that I should convert his daily provisions into a monthly sum of money and pay the young man ten Parisian shillings every month. It has been done as you commanded; and we, both I and our brethren, are ready and willing both to receive and generously to perform this and whatever else you command. Yet let your fatherhood know that we bear similar burdens in maintaining certain clerics through some of my lord cardinals.

[Note: Supreme pontiffs and cardinals were accustomed to confer certain prebends, called profit-bearing prebends, upon poor clerics and others whom they pleased in cathedral churches, and to assign annual pensions in more celebrated monasteries.]

## LETTER XLIX. TO THE CHANCELLOR OF THE ROMAN CHURCH

He asks him to ensure that his business is committed to equitable judges, with the clause “appeal being excluded” inserted.

To the most holy lord and Father A., chancellor of the Roman Church, Brother Stephen of Saint-Geneviève sends greeting and, with every devotion, sincere obedience.

He is importunate and does not depart from the character of a troublesome man who by empty words either offends his lord when tranquil or hinders him when occupied. Lest this happen to me, I pray; and, forgiveness having been obtained, I shall speak, since I am unable either to discover the suitable moments for speech or, being far away, to keep watch in order to discover them.

In this matter your cleric, and likewise our friend, Alvard, will be solicitous on our behalf. We have found him honorable in companionship, serious in character, and not burdensome in expense. We believe him worthy either to be joined to so great a Father by blood or bound to him by friendship. If we have bestowed anything upon him for your sake, both the humility of the recipient and the authority of the one commanding made it pleasant.

I beseech you to admit our petitions in a fatherly manner and, if it please you, with the article “appeal being excluded” added, to cause them to be entrusted to God-fearing judges. May your holiness prosper.

## LETTER L. TO ALBERT, CHANCELLOR OF THE LORD POPE

[Note: He was a native of Benevento, called de Mora, a Cistercian by religious profession, and cardinal-deacon of Saint Adrian, created by Adrian IV. He was sent as legate into England to grant absolution to King Henry II after he had cleared himself of the murder of Saint Thomas. He was made chancellor of the Holy Roman Church by Alexander III. Peter of Celle wrote several letters to him.]

He assures him that, for his sake, he has paid a pension to a certain cleric.

In carrying out your requests on behalf of Aernaud, your cleric, whenever they were presented to me, neither indifference made me negligent nor pretence deceitful. During that chronic illness of mine, which for about a year and a half almost wore me down to the point of death, I saw him once; and although I told him in gentle, not stammering, speech to return, he neither wished to appear before me nor to obey me until Pentecost. From that time onward, at the beginning of each month, for your sake I have five Parisian shillings given to him without delay.

I have said this not so that I may appear an importunate commender of myself, but lest I be thought an ungrateful recipient of benefits. Therefore let your holy fatherhood know that, in our petitions—neither many nor great—which are offered to the lord pope, I have found difficulty both from those who present petitionary requests and from those who ought to have admitted those common letters called letters “of justice,” in which Greek and Latin, barbarian and Scythian rejoice that they may obtain the addition “appeal being excluded”; while we, who are called special sons of the Roman Church, could not obtain it.

[Note: The Church of Saint-Geneviève at Paris was called apostolic, as is read in the Life of Saint William in Surius under 6 April; and it was directly subject to the Apostolic See even before regular canons were reintroduced there in 1148. This is clear from a diploma of Pope Paschal, issued at Meaux in 1108, in these words: “May the clerics of the same Church rejoice in the protection of the king and likewise in the guardianship of the Apostolic See; and may their cloister be preserved in the liberty which it has possessed until now.” In a bull of Eugenius III, issued in 1150, these words occur: “We also decree that your Church shall be subject to no archbishop or bishop, but only to the Roman pontiff.”]

O small addition—“appeal being excluded”—how splendid you have become: so difficult for sons, so easy for strangers!

## LETTER LI. TO BROTHER JOHN OF SAINT-SATYR

He demands back money lent to him.

If you remembered our shared journey and the favor we enjoyed while travelling and remaining together, you ought surely to have rendered grace for grace. But since, with your leave, I may say that you have shown yourself ungrateful, either indifference has made you negligent or pretence deceitful. You know that when I departed from Rome, I paid you, at your urgent request and, as you said, because you were in need, forty Parisian shillings, which I had myself borrowed—no less willingly than generously.

A year has passed since I satisfied the creditors on your behalf. If you reckon interest—not to mention usury at one percent a month—even five-twelfths will readily overtake the principal. I have not yet approached your abbot about this; I have not yet stated the case; I have not yet made a complaint, sparing your modesty and sparing your reputation. Pay what you owe, so that, because I have been patient with you, I may not suffer punishment or loss from my patience. Farewell. Brother Guy demands from you five shillings in a similar dispute and with equal indignation.

## LETTER LII. TO GODFREY, ABBOT OF SAINT-SATYR

He excuses himself because he cannot visit him.

To the most holy lord and Father Godfrey, abbot of Saint-Satyr, Brother Stephen sends greeting and shared prayers in the Lord.

It is a feast to me whenever the festive remembrance of you is renewed for me, whether by messenger or by letter. Whoever wishes to disturb or take away this feast is, I confess, hostile to me. Certainly, because you have kindly invited me to the feast of your martyrs, I do not refuse the shared joy, but I excuse my particular absence. On that day I must appear at Reims before the lord archbishop concerning the affairs of our Church, and contend against certain plunderers and adversaries of ours.

Moreover, our common Father and abbot R. earnestly asked both me and the beloved old man, the good abbot of Saint-Bartholomew, with fatherly affection, to present ourselves to him on the octave of the Purification.

[Note: I believe this to be Roger, first abbot of Saint-Euverte at Orléans. Under his rule Stephen learned and lived the regular life with Hugh, abbot of Saint-Bartholomew of Noyon, and Godfrey of Saint-Satyr, as will appear from Letter 285 to the abbot of Saint-Euverte, in which he says: “From your bosom fathers and pastors have been taken: Ambrose of Bourges, Satyr of Sancerre, Bartholomew of Noyon, and, to speak as one less wise, [the abbot] of Saint-Geneviève at Paris.”]

I believe that you too have not omitted his own great son in this summons. And because it is wrong not to obey so great a Father when present in his need, I ask, advise, and urge you to meet us, your brethren, on that same day, so that by the threefold cord of sons, which is not easily broken, the weakness of the aged Father may be strengthened and any distress relieved. Farewell.

## LETTER LIII. TO THE SAME

He gives thanks for benefits bestowed upon one of his canons.

To Godfrey, abbot of Saint-Satyr.

Besides the other benefits which you have often shown me, Father, you have granted me a yearly and most welcome comfort in our brother of our Church.

[Note: This is Gilbert, canon of Saint-Geneviève at Paris, whom he had sent to the monastery of Saint-Satyr.]

We offer you fitting thanks for this, so that, if perhaps we were importunate in asking, we may not be found ungrateful in serving. And because the time has come to have mercy upon him, we present prayers to your affection that you may have him conducted to the common dwelling of our father of Saint-Euverte, so that from the shrine of the martyrs he may pass to the mountain of the Virgin through the chamber of the confessor. Farewell.

[Note: By “the shrine of the martyrs” he means the church of Saint-Satyr and his companions; by “the mountain of the Virgin,” the abbey of Saint-Geneviève; and by “the chamber of the confessor,” the monastery of Saint-Euverte at Orléans, through which he had to pass in returning from Saint-Satyr to Paris and the house of Saint-Geneviève.]

## LETTER LIV. TO THE LORD POPE

He implores his protection for the Church of Corbie.

[Note: Corbie, situated on the bank of the Somme, four leagues from Amiens, possesses a notable monastery of the order of Saint Benedict, founded in honor of Saints Peter and Paul in 662 by Blessed Bathildis, queen of the Franks, and her son Clotaire.]

We believe that you have zeal for the house of the Lord and wish discipline to be so maintained in the Church of God that your tempered discernment humbles the proud and embraces the humble. Therefore may it please your holiness that, against certain rebellious and disobedient sons of contention and discord, who have gone out from Corbie, your fervor may be kindled, your indignation stirred, and the sword of vengeance drawn.

As we have heard from religious and trustworthy men who were present and informed us of the affair as it happened: notwithstanding the oath sworn concerning themselves and on behalf of the whole convent of Corbie, before the count of Flanders, who was there on the lord king’s behalf with eight abbots, upon the holy Gospels, the aforesaid notorious monks—unworthy of a hearing—are striving to raise in the monastery of Corbie the incitement of schism and the seedbed of litigation, openly enough, through men who break pledged faith and roam unlawfully to the loss of their mother and the dishonor of their father. The most holy Roman Church ought neither to receive them into its protection nor support them in their undertaking.

## LETTER LV. TO THE BISHOP OF SENLIS

He presents testimonial and dimissory letters for the ordination of one of his canons as priest.

At your return, Father, your sons, our brethren, exult in dancing and rejoice in jubilation, taking a crown instead of ashes, joy instead of mourning, and a garment of praise instead of a spirit of sorrow.

[Note: Meier, *Annals of Flanders*, Book VI, says that King Philip Augustus dismissed his wife with the consent of all the bishops except Henry of Senlis, with whom the queen took refuge. Perhaps for this reason, because the king was hostile to him, he was driven into exile and afterwards recalled.]

Our consolation has been doubled: the comforter Paraclete at His feast, and the general joy of the Holy Spirit’s coming, have been more abundantly fulfilled by the particular joy of your arrival among your own. Meanwhile, we send to your holy fatherhood our brother Richard, a deacon commendable among us for integrity of life and blameless reputation, that for the love of God and of Blessed Geneviève, her servant, you may ordain him priest. Farewell.

## LETTER LVI. TO WILLIAM, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS

He complains of the monks of Longpont, who were troublesome and hostile to him.

It is a feast to me whenever I am so harassed that I am compelled to be summoned before your judgment; for it is safer to appeal to you yourself than to appeal from you. One of the fathers of Longpont—

[Note: This abbey is situated in the diocese of Soissons. It was founded in 1131 by Joscelin, bishop of that city, who brought there a colony from the household of Saint Bernard. It is also made noble by many tombs of the counts of Vermandois. The following charter, taken from the cartulary of the abbey of Saint-Geneviève, will shed light upon this letter:

“Henry, by the grace of God bishop of Senlis, to all whom these letters shall reach, greeting in the Lord. Since, by command of the lord pope, we were hearing a certain case pending between the church of Blessed Geneviève and Droco, brother of the priest Ascelin, and Odo, the latter’s nephew, concerning the holding of Milo and the land which the said Ascelin had cultivated with his plough-team, they at last reached a settlement in the following form of peace and concord, etc.

“This must also be added: the aforesaid Ascelin had left to the aforementioned Droco and Odo, as they said, another piece of land, as much as can be sown with one measure of seed, on condition that every year forty shillings should be distributed, at the discretion of the abbot of Longpont, to poor persons receiving the customary allowance. But Stephen, abbot of Saint-Geneviève, asserting that Ascelin had not been permitted to do this and saying that the land of the Church could not be burdened with such an obligation, claimed that land and maintained that it ought to be restored to the Church as its own.

“Since the aforesaid plaintiffs, Droco and Odo, named the abbot and monks of Longpont as their warrantors and promised that they would appear as their defenders on the day assigned, we appointed a day.
