When the aforesaid abbot and the canons of Blessed Geneviève came on that day, the said Droco and Odo came as well; but neither the abbot of Longpont nor the monks who were to defend them were present. Therefore, by authority of the lord pope’s mandate, and with Odo and Droco themselves consenting, we invested the abbot of the church of Saint-Geneviève with the aforementioned land, namely as much as can be sown with one measure of seed, and restored the land to him as his own, etc.”

Nor should it seem surprising if that Droco, treated of in this charter and called a Cistercian monk, possessed certain estates by hereditary right in the present letter: among the ancient monks it was lawful and common to enjoy a paternal inheritance and to add it to the resources of the monastery.]

—I do not accuse that holy community on this account—under the appearance of piety does not impiously attack me with his fist; and, thinking to drag me to a judge as with a halter, ignorant of the common proverb, he makes me secure, because I shall see my Father. The man’s name and his action make me uncertain whether I should more properly call him Droco or Draco. He is proclaimed to be endowed with such charity that it does not suffice him to give his own goods to the poor unless he adds those of others. He contends to make an alms from what is ours. Since we do not grant him the fruit of it, whether for himself or for us, we shall not yield.

I believe, Father, that Cistercians are among those who seize heaven by violence; but whether they may violently seize land for themselves, I have not yet read. On the day appointed at Reims, I placed myself at the plaintiff’s disposal to answer before your officials; but because I did not see your fatherly face, I feared being judged under another’s examination. I give thanks to your holy fatherhood because those who sat in your place, at the invocation of your name, granted me a postponement until the octave of the Nativity of Blessed Mary the Virgin.

I ask, Father, that you appoint for me, your little son, such a day as you will undoubtedly be present and sitting at Reims. If it should happen that I must litigate before another, I shall lament that I am at last deprived of your favor, which I have continually experienced. Farewell. I ask that our John of Orléans may be commended to you both by his person, fit for service, and by our devoted supplication, fit for obedience.

## LETTER LVII. TO HUGH, ABBOT OF SAINT-BARTHOLOMEW OF NOYON

He excuses himself, on account of various duties in administering justice, for being unable to come to him.

I would come to you with the utmost speed if necessity did not stand in the way of desire. An apostolic command detains me; not to comply with it is to perish, not to obey is to die. On the approaching Sunday, by its command, I have a threefold necessity to sit in judgment and discharge a judge’s office in the hearing of three cases. The cases do not admit delay: they have both been begun by joinder of issue and assigned for the next day at the parties’ request. When the affairs have been completed, I shall come to you as willingly as you please, and as freely.

## LETTER LVIII. TO THE LORD POPE, IN THE PERSON OF THE ABBOT OF SAINT-BARTHOLOMEW OF NOYON

He testifies that the Church of Saint-Euverte at Orléans is free from the bishop’s right of procuration.

The Church of Saint-Euverte at Orléans is made commendable in the sight of angels and men both by the merit of its confessor and by the testimony of its city. To these is added the holy way of life of the brethren who regularly serve God there; they so excel their own in life that by their reputation they stir up outsiders. In the time of the secular canons, now forty years ago, I was both canon and cantor of that Church; and, when its condition was changed to the regular form, I too later became a disciple of Augustine and received in it the habit of penitence.

Father, I know and truthfully testify that, so far as the memory of men still living extends, that Church and the three other abbeys of clerics in the same city—namely Saint-Peter of the men, Saint-Peter of the women, and Saint-Avitus—have enjoyed until this day this liberty and immunity: that no archbishop of Sens, whoever he may have been, has received procuration in any of them. The whole city knows this, and clergy and people alike attest it.

Since the archbishop of Sens intends, contrary to custom and the Church’s liberty, to burden the aforesaid Church by demanding procuration, we pour out prayers to your holy fatherhood that you may entrust the hearing of this case to some religious and discerning person. For it is not easy for that poor Church to bring its witnesses before your presence and establish its liberty by proof from documents and witnesses. For if there are any burdens which the archbishop of Sens wishes to impose upon the aforesaid four abbeys in demanding his procurations, the bishop of Orléans, by a custom approved over many ages, ought to assume and discharge them, because they are said to belong to his table. Farewell.

## LETTER LIX. TO THE SAME

He provides the same testimony for the same Church of Saint-Euverte.

To the lord pope, Stephen of Saint-Geneviève.

Nurtured from childhood in the church of Holy Cross at Orléans, and afterwards professing the religious life under regular discipline in the church of Blessed Euverte the confessor, I so remember the customs worthy of remembrance of each Church that I judge neither that I myself am mistaken in them nor that I intend to mislead others. Hence, with a conscience now secure, I testify truthfully that, so far as memory extends, etc.

## LETTER LX. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS

He commends the case of a certain Simon, which was being litigated in his court.

In your eyes, Father, neither integrity begs for renown nor truth for intervention. There virtue is its own reward; and he who is sufficient to himself by his own merit does not need another’s support. Therefore Master Simon, a man outstanding among the professors’ chairs, has no need either to beg wordy prayers or to solicit before you proclamations of praise put up for sale. His authority of character on the one hand and his learning on the other make him welcome and commendable. Your illustrious clemency is accustomed to summon, love, and promote such men.

The whole world cries this out, as it were, from east to west, when Italy sees her Etruscans and Ligurians, greater Britain her Englishmen, and both Gauls their Belgians and Celts in your court, either loaded with riches or honored with dignities. The saying is fulfilled to the full measure of your glory: “They come from East and West and recline in your bosom.” Those see it and envy it to whom generosity is displeasing, to whom virtue is at once hateful and wearisome, and whom honorable men provoke to laughter and learned men to nausea.

But lest I seem to anoint your head with the oil of a sinner, prostrate at your feet—though I am dust and ashes—I speak to my lord, offering prayers and supplications for Master Simon: that in the business which he has with his bishop and his canons, you may receive him as kindly as you support him beneficently. If it please you, so advance the case that he has brought forward that, if anyone has been promoted in violation of the canons, he may likewise be removed canonically and lawfully. As for what should be done concerning the aforesaid man, your own judgment will provide better and more fully than we can. Farewell.

## LETTER LXI. TO THE LORD POPE

He complains of the rebellion of the canons of Saint John of Soissons residing in parish churches, who refused to obey Abbot Hugh.

[Note: A celebrated monastery of the order of regular canons, founded in 1076 by Hugh, lord of Château-Thierry, was originally called the church of St. John on the Hill. But when the same Hugh assigned many surrounding vineyards for the support of the canons, it took from them the name St. John among the Vineyards in 1181. A serious quarrel arose between Nivelon, bishop of Soissons, and Hugh, abbot of St. John, because the latter at his discretion recalled his canons from rural parishes to the cloister, while the canons, who took this badly, sought the bishop’s protection in order to remain in them even against the abbot’s will. The dispute went so far that it was referred to the supreme pontiff Lucius III. Both parties therefore went to Rome; after the case had long been argued in the Roman curia, they finally chose arbitrators by whose judgment they would abide. When these had weighed all the circumstances of the affair, they rendered a sentence by which the canons were removed from their parishes. Later, however, a settlement was reached, especially through the intervention of our Stephen, between Bishop Nivelon and Abbot Hugh. By it the former restored to the abbot the entire liberty of his parish churches, in these words:

“NIVELON, by the grace of God bishop of Soissons, to all persons forever. Let all of you know that, in the presence of Master Stephen, abbot of St. Geneviève, Master Peter the Cantor, and Master Robert Paujent, canon of Amiens, we have restored his parish churches in the state in which the canons had formerly held them, saving our dignity and authority and saving the liberty of the churches, by our assent, as it had formerly existed in the time of our predecessor bishops and of the predecessors of Hugh, the late abbot. Done in the year of the Incarnate Word 1186.” See Letter 95.]

[Col. 0354A]

Father, the solemn discipline formerly observed by regulars presents to you a dreadful and pitiable spectacle of itself, at once assailed and afflicted by sons of contradiction and disobedience. That glorious and golden Rule, which Augustine had, as it were, borrowed from the apostles and, as a faithful steward, had lent to others at interest as his lord’s money, is now being stolen by the accomplices of Achan son of Carmi.

[Note: See Joshua, book 7, concerning Achan son of Carmi, who, contrary to Joshua’s command, stole some of the spoils of the city of Jericho.]

They do not fear Jericho’s anathema, but heap up private gold in order to gather popular favor. This is proclaimed in the canons of St. John of Soissons as an example at once sad and shameful. Contrary to the common life which they professed, contrary to the teaching of so great a master, contrary to the decree of the holy Lateran Council—

[Note: This council was held in 1179 and is called the Third Lateran Council. In Part XXVII, chapter 5, one reads: “Let no one possess private property; whatever he acquires, let him assign to his superior.”]

—they secretly amass private funds in little personal bags and chests, intending by this to please and appease their bishop, so that they are found both disobedient to God and rebellious against their abbot. They are armed and encouraged in disobedience both by money acquired through unlawful practices, which they lavish abundantly, and by the influence of those who eagerly accept it from them.

May your severity, Father, oppose this disgraceful plague and cut off the opportunities for ambition from which ambitious persons presume to draw their material. The disease has grown so strong that it deserves the punishment of wickedness unless it finds a heavenly remedy. Your devoted son, the abbot of this aforesaid Church, a man of good repute and sound reputation among us, has exposed himself to such great dangers; and, while he intends to rebuke what he cannot correct, he loses both labor and expense. He finds as his greatest adversaries those by whose assistance and effort he ought to restrain the insolent and proud. Farewell.

## LETTER LXII. TO THE LORD VIVIAN, CARDINAL OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH

[Note: Vivian—or, as Ciaconius prefers, Vibian Tomasius—priest-cardinal of the title of St. Stephen on the Caelian Hill, was created by Alexander III in 1173. Roger of Howden calls him Vivian and says that in 1176 he was sent as legate a latere into Ireland.]

He devotes his service to him.

Your letter, [Col. 0355A] gave me a delightful spectacle: it both refreshed my idleness by its display and stirred it by its example. I ought to have sought out so great a lord and friend with letters and visited him with small gifts. Diligence will excuse delay, memory will erase forgetfulness, so that I may appear neither ungrateful nor undevoted toward my lord.

At almost the very hour when the messenger delivered your letter, he departed and withdrew as though he had already delayed. I was scarcely allowed either to write back briefly or to reply to what your fatherhood had requested of us. The narrowness of time begrudged me the chance to delay the departing messenger’s haste by any preparatory token of service. Soon, God willing, through someone passing to you, I shall entreat your goodwill with no empty greeting and shall seek to please your favor. May my lord Vivian be well and live long.

## LETTER LXIII. TO HERACLIUS, BISHOP OF CAESAREA

He commends his kinsman, who was travelling to Palestine.

To the most holy lord and Father Heraclius, bishop of Caesarea—

[Note: Heraclius appears to have been a Gaul by birth, formerly Stephen’s companion and intimate friend. Having set out for the lands beyond the sea, he became archbishop of Caesarea. I find five cities called Caesarea: those of Phoenicia, Cilicia, Cappadocia, Armenia, and Palestine; it is the last of these that is meant here. It lies not far from Mount Carmel, on the seashore. It was first called Straton’s Tower; but when Herod restored it more splendidly, he dedicated it in honor of Augustus, called it Caesarea, and built there a magnificent house gleaming everywhere with marble. It was eventually honored with an archiepiscopal see.]

—Brother Stephen, called abbot of St. Geneviève of Paris, wishes that he may dwell in the heavenly Jerusalem.

I pray that our once playful conversations may often be expiated by fruitful prayers. We used to call the pleadings of the gown-clad advocates “merchandise”; the clashes of litigants, “a battle of the blind”; the lecture halls of Bologna, “workshops of craftsmen.” Amid these diverse pursuits we followed different paths: I pursued the *carpentaria* of Bulgarus, which I had mocked; you, the Calvary of the Crucified One.

[Note: By these words he means to establish what he said: namely, that they had pursued different studies and unlike occupations. Heraclius, moved by piety, had undertaken a journey to Jerusalem and a pilgrimage to Mount Calvary; Stephen, however, devoted himself to jurisprudence, which he had once despised and mocked. He said that the pleadings of the gown-clad advocates were a forum or market, called in an old word *Coua*, now *Cohue*; that the conflicts of litigants were a battle of the blind; and that the schools and lecture halls of the Bolognese academics were like a workshop of craftsmen, noisy and clamorous. Mockingly, he called these the *carpentaria* of Bulgarus.

Concerning Bulgarus, Otto Morena says in the Chronicle of Lodi that, when Guarnerius, that celebrated founder of the Bolognese academy, was near death, his pupils came to him and said: “Lord, whom do you wish to appoint as our teacher after your death?” He answered them in the two verses written below:

> Bulgarus is the golden mouth; Martin, the abundance of laws;  
> Hugh, the mind of laws; Jacob is what I am.

The same writer adds concerning Bulgarus that, when Emperor Frederick was riding with Bulgarus and Martin on either side of him, he asked them whether by law he was lord of the world. Bulgarus replied that he was not lord with respect to ownership; Martin, however, replied that he was lord. Then the emperor dismounted from the palfrey on which he sat and ordered it to be presented to Martin. Hearing this, Bulgarus said, playing upon the word: “I lost my horse because I said what was fair” (*aequum*).

It is likely that Stephen pursued the study of both civil and canon law at this celebrated Italian academy together with Heraclius, and that he also taught this learning there.]

Blessed is your pilgrimage, [Col. 0355C] which both expiates sins and raises you to things sublime. Meanwhile, Father, I beseech you, remember your Stephen, who retains remembrance of you in such a way that he embraces your presence as though by an unbroken vision. For the bearer of this letter I offer you my prayers: he is connected to me both by blood and by much service, in which he has not been undevoted. Farewell.

## LETTER LXIV. TO THE BISHOP OF LYDDA

He likewise commends to him his kinsman, who was hastening to the Holy Sepulchre.

[Col. 0356A]

To the most holy lord and Father, the bishop of St. George—

[Note: In the published letters he is called bishop of Lydda, whereas here he is called bishop of St. George. Lydda, or Lyda according to Ptolemy, book V, chapter 16, is a city of Judaean Palestine, also called Diospolis and Rama, in which there was an episcopal see.]

—Stephen of St. Geneviève, temporal and eternal well-being.

Father, I would write more confidently to you on behalf of the bearer of this letter if I had deserved anything from you. But this alone remains as consolation for one absent: if he suffers a fruitless rebuff, he is not ashamed when he is not heard. A letter incurs no embarrassment. Being importunate—whether like the woman who appealed to the judge, or like the friend who asked for three loaves—I may perhaps obtain some small thing.

The bearer of this letter, joined to me by both blood and service, has departed to visit the glorious Sepulchre of the Lord. I ask that, if need arises, you may kindly and generously bestow upon him your counsel and assistance.

## LETTER LXV. TO JOHN, NOTARY OF THE POPE

He asks him to bring his petitions to effect.

To his beloved John of Orléans—

[Note: Many men of Orléans then performed the office of scribe for the supreme pontiffs. Besides this John, we find in Letter 85 that Robert and William, natives of the city of Orléans, were papal scribes.]

—scribe of the lord pope, STEPHEN of St. Geneviève.

For men born beneath the air of Orléans and washed by the waters of the Loire, to remain in Rome during the summer season is nothing other than to die. It is better to enjoy golden poverty with health than to scrape together dangerous money, which both troubles the mind with anxiety and exhausts the body with labor. I would therefore urge you to return, if I thought you content with your lot, if I did not suppose that former successes were enticing you toward greater things than you possess.

Meanwhile, I ask your affection to see, if you can, that our petitions are brought to effect—above all, concerning confirmation of the excommunication of the commune of Meaux. For we have found their bishop negligent regarding the sentence of excommunication pronounced against the aforesaid commune by John, bishop of Chartres, of good memory—

[Note: This was John of Salisbury, celebrated for his writings, who died in 1182; this letter was written after his death.]

—and contemptuous of the apostolic mandate. If you can, obtain letters from the lord pope to him, so that, just as the aforesaid bishop of Chartres excommunicated the authors of the commune—

[Note: In this century the cities of France began to establish mayors, provosts, and aldermen, who were to administer public affairs. This began to the prejudice of bishops, to whom even the temporal lordship of their cities belonged. A fuller account may be seen concerning the commune of Laon in Letter 39.

We read in Rigord that, when Philip Augustus set out for Palestine in 1190, he established aldermen at Paris: “The city of Paris, which he loved greatly, he ordered to be enclosed around its circuit by walls and stone towers. Seven men, to whom he had entrusted the government of the town and who were called aldermen, most diligently completed this work from the resources of the citizens within a short time.”

The people of Reims obtained letters from Louis the Younger to establish a commune during a vacancy of the archiepiscopal see, in 1137. Samson opposed them when he attained that see; his successor William of Champagne promised the chapter that he would not permit such a commune to be established, in these words: “To God and to the present chapter we vow, in the word of the Lord, confirming it by the witness of this present writing, that for as long as we live we shall permit neither a commune nor a bond of any fraternity nor any oath to be made among the aforesaid citizens.”

The people of Beauvais obtained royal diplomas to establish a commune among themselves in 1144. According to Buzelin, the people of Lille first elected aldermen in 1195, and the people of Tournai established their commune at almost the same time. The citizens of Meaux attempted something similar, for which reason they were bound by the chain of excommunication.]

—so may he likewise declare them excommunicated in his own church and cause all persons to avoid them. For the bearer of this letter, my household member and our friend, I beg you to assist him in his affairs as much as you can. Farewell.

## LETTER LXVI. TO POPE ALEXANDER III

He begs him to protect the canons of St. Mary at Blois.

To the most holy lord and Father ALEXANDER, supreme pontiff, Brother STEPHEN of St. Geneviève: greeting and perfect obedience in all things.

He renders the duty owed to charity who burns with those who are scandalized and is weak with those who are weak. The matter, Father, moves and admonishes our insignificance to display toward our brothers, the canons of St. Mary of Blois, the affection of compassion in their adversities, to open wide the bosom of pity, and to extend the arm of aid and service.

[Note: The abbey of Blessed Mary at Blois, situated on the Loire and popularly called of Bourg-Moyen, was always subject to the canonical rule. In this period it was restored to a stricter observance, which, according to James of Vitry, chapter 21 of the *Western History*, flourished there especially.]

Since we are less than sufficient in this matter, we have recourse to your fullness, that you may graciously and generously satisfy from the breasts of your consolation these sons lately bereft of their father. That community bears such good testimony of itself to those who know it that a friend may rejoice in it and an envious person be confounded.

Near them—would that it were not against them—there springs up a certain new planting of individual, or secular, canons.

[Note: In the church of St. Saviour in the castle of Blois, Count Theobald founded a college of secular canons to perform divine worship there. The regular canons of Blessed Mary had a controversy with these canons regarding the church of St. Carileph, which depended upon them. It was a conventual priory of regular canons established within the walls of the same castle; hence he said, “A new planting springs up near them.” See the following letter.]

Whether the heavenly Father planted them, we do not yet know. May it please the eyes of your benevolence, Father, that seculars do not diminish the rights of regulars and that strangers do not eat the bread of sons.

## LETTER LXVII. TO THE SAME

He again asks him to protect the rights of the regular canons of Blois, which the secular canons were usurping.

[Col. 0358A]

Whenever I dare to write to you, Father, whether on our own affairs or those of others, my heart fears and my hand trembles. Fear and trembling come upon me; and the darkness of ignorance—or, I do not know, God knows, perhaps of uncertainty—covers me, lest I either offend one at rest or hinder one occupied. I put forward charity as my excuse: it does not seek its own interests in such a way as to value its own advantage any less than another’s.

Our most beloved brother in the Lord, Nicholas, abbot of St. Mary of Blois, who has professed with us the common order under the Rule of Father Augustine, is compelled, amid the daily distresses of reforming the order in his church and amid the ruins of a house almost devastated beyond hope, now being restored through his industry, to drain a cup of new sorrow and a draught of unforeseen sadness. Together with the whole Church committed to him, he hastens toward death unless the holy apostolic see opposes to so great an evil the life-giving remedies of heavenly antidote.

In the time of Count Theobald of holy memory, through Pope Innocent of everlasting remembrance, the right hand of the Most High changed the slippery steps of secular canons in the town of Blois into the discipline of regulars, and restrained that individualistic manner of life, so that, as disciples of the apostles, they might live from the common stock in common. But the bishops and princes of our own age, seeing more sharply and understanding more cunningly, introduce a planting which I do not know whether the heavenly Father approves. They assemble clerics of this modern way, men who contribute their houses and little vineyards to the shapeless form of prebends, who set up, as it were, altar against altar, who place before the saints walking in God’s way both a stumbling-block in word and a snare in example.

These things might perhaps have been overlooked and tolerated somehow, had they not stretched out their hands to greater matters and entered, with violence at once rapacious and voracious, into the labors of others. They demand that a new cemetery, new masters of schools, and new opportunities for hunting after parishioners not their own be granted to them, so that they may rejoice that what they have taken from others has been added to their own wickedness. Let your holy solicitude provide, Father, lest those new seculars who have come in should by some usurpation wrest away for themselves what the blessed Fathers and your predecessors granted the regulars in pious religion.

## LETTER LXVIII. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF POITIERS

He exhorts him to constancy in adversity.

To the most holy lord and Father JOHN, bishop of Poitiers: the spirit of counsel and fortitude.

Father, in your affliction—

[Note: John, bishop of Poitiers, suffered persecution on account of the rights of his Church, which he was striving vigorously to defend against certain invaders. See Letter 182 of John of Salisbury, where these matters are discussed; another letter asserts that he was poisoned, though not killed.]

—heaven and earth alike ought to be shaken, crying in the ears of the Lord of Hosts: “Render vengeance to your enemies, and repay those who hate you” (Deuteronomy 32). Yet we too, the smallest portion of God’s Church, drink with you the cup of compassion and sorrow, grieving that these things are done to the green wood and fearing worse things to be fulfilled in the dry.

I do not know, Father, whether those thousand years have been completed at whose end Satan was to be loosed. We see his satellites so loosed that they have begun to bind the servants of God. But Peter’s faith shall not fail: you sit in his church—

[Note: The cathedral church of Poitiers is dedicated to St. Peter.]

—and have held, both by office and benefice, his charge of feeding the Lord’s flock. Far be it that one who ought to strengthen his brothers should grow weak at the threats of a young tyrant, as though he were to deny again at a servant-girl’s voice. Far be it that one who maintained justice in prosperity should lose constancy in adversity.

By such afflictions the Church is accustomed to grow; and the more fiercely the ministers of death rage against the children of life, the more Mother Zion has learned to subdue and drive away the wretched daughter of Babylon. May your fortune increase day by day, I beseech you; and from the breasts of divine consolation may you daily receive an increase not only of the milk needed by little children, but also of solid food—the bread that strengthens the human heart—of long-suffering and perseverance.

## LETTER LXIX. FROM PETER, LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE, TO R., DEAN OF ROUEN

He orders that a priest be removed from the nuns of St. Cyr because he behaved insufficiently chastely.

PETER, by divine favor bishop of Tusculum and legate of the apostolic see, to his beloved son R., dean of Rouen: greeting and sincere affection.

It has been reported to us that a certain Manerius, living at Villocelles among consecrated virgins, intends by his shameful and dishonorable conduct to corrupt and defile the Lord’s flock. Since we believe his life displeases both God and men, we have ordered the abbess of St. Cyr—

[Note: The abbey of nuns of St. Cyr, in French *Saint-Cyr*, is in the diocese of Chartres, fifteen miles from the city of Paris. Its founder was Robert, bishop of Chartres, about the year 1160. It possessed a priory called Villocelles in the diocese of Rouen, where several nuns lived.]

—to remove this aforesaid monster from the said house and all her other houses, and henceforth not to permit him to return to any of her houses, lest the foul-smelling goat infect the simple sheep and the son of iniquity profane God’s sanctuary by his sacrilegious conduct.

Therefore, as to a most beloved son and friend, we command and enjoin you, by our authority, through the lord archbishop and through your own diligence, that this abominable persecutor and enemy of virginity be separated from the aforesaid community of brides of Christ and, if necessary, be compelled to withdraw by excommunication.

## LETTER LXX. TO WILLIAM, ARCHBISHOP OF SENS

He rebukes the same priest’s most unchaste life.

[Col. 0360B]

To the most reverend lord and Father WILLIAM, archbishop of Sens, STEPHEN of St. Geneviève: greeting.

It belongs to you, Father, to defend what pertains to God’s honor and the increase of religion and, by your authority, to remove as far as possible from God’s house the scandals of shame and disgrace. Therefore, for the virgins of Christ enclosed in the service of God at St. Cyr, I offer such prayers as I can to your holiness, according to the charity which is in Christ: do not admit Manerius, the enemy of their honor and chastity, and believe him in nothing. Through the lord bishop of Tusculum—

[Note: This was Peter of Pavia, mentioned above in connection with Letter 43, and to whom another letter is addressed. He is mentioned in the necrology of St. Geneviève.]

—legate of the apostolic see, he was removed and cast out from the fellowship of nuns because of the enormous and intolerable excesses of his shamefulness.

Let your holiness believe us; believe the abbot of St. Victor; believe Brother B. of Vicenza and other neighboring religious men, who neither wish nor ought to deceive your discernment or assert falsehood to you. Believe our testimony: because of the proximity of the place, we can be better informed concerning the dishonorable conduct of that priest of Baal. Let your religious discernment, if it please you, abandon the question whether he should be received by Christ’s virgins; for if he is received, he will, like a foul-smelling goat, mortally pollute the undefiled flock of the Lord.

But if you are altogether unwilling to refrain, and if it is necessary by your command that the abbess and her enclosed sisters enter into litigation with the aforesaid monster of Venus, may it please you, I beseech you, to entrust this inquiry to the bishop of Paris, who will be able through neighboring clerics and laypeople more fully to investigate and discover the truth of the matter.

## LETTER LXXI. TO ROBERT, MONK OF PONTIGNY

He raises and resolves the question whether novices of the Grandmontine order may lawfully receive the Cistercian habit.

[Col. 0361A]

To ROBERT, monk of Pontigny—

[Note: Pontigny, in French *Pontigny*, is a distinguished abbey of the Cistercian order, founded in the diocese of Auxerre in 1114 by Theobald the Great, count of Champagne, who was buried there after his death. It was famous for sheltering the exile St. Thomas of Canterbury and for the relics of St. Edmund.]

—distinguished alike by birth and manner of life, beloved by God and men, STEPHEN of St. Geneviève: may you comfort the faint-hearted and exhort those of one mind in the house of the Lord.

Commendable, Robert, is the concern you bear; and with brotherly affection for your novices you raise a new question. I wish you had asked someone else, both more skilled in examining it and readier in resolving it. I confess that my lack of learning commands me to be silent and draws my hand back from a bold undertaking before the great name of the Grandmontines. [Col. 0361B]

[Note: [Col. 0361D] The Order of Grandmont was founded in the diocese of Limoges by Stephen called of Muret. Here the author eloquently extols the holiness of their life; it is also described more fully by James of Vitry, chapter 19 of the *Western History*: “There is another religious order or regular institution called that of Grandmont, whose head and original monastery is in the regions of Aquitaine,” etc.]

If I answer your question according to my conscience, they will be offended; and if I offend them, I shall sin against public opinion. They please men, and they are servants of Christ; they are called the Good Men. For the proof of their goodness is both their excluded avarice and their enclosed poverty. Moreover, ambition, which attacks almost all and conquers many, is as far removed from them as it is from men who are certain that they will never acquire Cîteaux. Although God gave the earth to the children of men, they stretch their measuring-line and their inheritance into heavenly things; they embody evangelical men, and are not anxious about what they shall eat or drink or wear, because they are fed with the birds and clothed with the lilies by their Father who is in heaven. [Col. 0361C]

Neither bleating flocks hinder their prayers, nor lowing herds disturb them, nor all the noises of the household interrupt them. Blessed are they if they have fled the world and the world does not follow them. Since avarice, the root of all evils, has withered among them, ambition has withdrawn; the material for litigation has been removed; solitude encloses them, poverty weighs upon them, humility binds them. Having embraced discipline, which consists in the ordered correction of morals, they assuredly will neither provoke the Lord’s anger nor perish from the right way.

Let them themselves see what they do within their domestic walls, and what testimony their hidden works—accusing or defending one another—publish before Him to whom every heart lies open and from whom no secret is concealed. [Col. 0361D] We ought to remain ignorant, since we are not permitted to enter. Yet we believe that their labour will not be without reward, their contest not without victory, nor their exercise without fruit, since among the other children of consolation they too will receive a crown instead of ashes, joy instead of mourning, and a mantle of praise instead of a spirit of heaviness.

You asked concerning brothers who left them and passed to the Cistercians: whether they ought, by the obligation of the vow they had formerly made, to return to them, or whether they should more beneficially remain at Pontigny. [Col. 0362A] If they had not preferred their latter purpose to the former, neither should I advise that they prefer it. Had they remained within the bounds of their earlier vow, perhaps I too would have remained there and would not have urged them toward another course. But now, because they have sought better things and things nearer to salvation, and, ascending from Shiloh to Jerusalem, have transferred their tent, who would dare to obstruct in them the freedom of the Spirit of the Lord? For truly, where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom: “Do not quench the Spirit.” Those who oppose His works quench Him, so far as lies in them.

Certainly the Holy Spirit is a dove, because He was seen descending upon the Lord in the form of a dove while He was baptized. Among the dove’s other qualities, which the Church admits and mystically represents, the dove chooses the better grains. [Col. 0362B] She does not despise good grains; for if better ones did not occur, she would surely feed upon good ones. Yet she prefers better things to good and the best to better things. Those who belong to her imitate her. “Be zealous for the better gifts.” Blessed, indeed, is not merely one who distinguishes between day and night, but one who distinguishes among every kind of day.

Who in the Church of God would not say that the Cistercian order, like a lamp set upon a mountain, has attained the highest and foremost summit? Fulfilling the Gospel, they so observe the monastic rule, which Father Benedict added beyond requirement, as the innkeeper of the faithful Samaritan, that they appear not to let even one iota of it pass away. Blessed is their poverty: although it presses them with hunger and cold, it compels them neither to beg nor to flatter the rich. By their own hands, or those of their brethren, they seek food and clothing, not fearing to follow Paul, who, though he could lawfully live by the Gospel and reap material things while sowing spiritual things, nevertheless preferred to work with his own hands lest he place an obstacle before the Gospel of Christ. [Col. 0362C]

They honour the Lord from their own resources, not those of others; and from the first-fruits of their crops—not another’s, but their own—they give to the poor. More accurately, however, I should call these possessions not their own but everyone’s, since, ordered according to the degrees of charity, they serve all alike as though held in common. They do not eat their morsel alone, nor does the orphan fail to eat from it with them. They do not despise the passer-by or the poor person without covering; rather, they bless the sides of the poor and warm them with the fleeces of their sheep. Around those sides they place cloths which are as contemptible in price as they are unsuitable for display. [Col. 0362D]

Nature itself, ordinarily content with little, complains that their coverings do not suffice for it in winter and burden it in summer. Their door stands open to the traveller; no stranger remains outside. In the sweat of their faces they eat their bread; idleness and food supplied by another do not lead them into wantonness or quarrelling. Such is their frugality in food [Col. 0363A] that they use only two dishes, which either field offers from legumes or garden from vegetables. They eat fish so much more rarely as it is more commonly heard of among them than seen.

They break up the earth voluntarily, and the violent seize heaven. If you count how many benefits flow from them to the people, they confer more upon the whole community than the community confers upon them. These are small matters, such as might either entice or occupy earthly desires. Among them Leah does not envy Rachel’s fruitfulness, nor does Leah diminish Rachel’s beauty; rather, she strengthens it. Martha does not murmur at Mary’s silence; and—strange to say—Mary, sitting at the Lord’s feet, does not leave Martha to serve alone. Among them there is continual joy and common exultation, where there is nothing outside discipline and nothing contrary to it. [Col. 0363B]

Men marvel; angels delight in them; hostile powers flee, because that holy congregation is terrible as an army arrayed in ranks. There the plough is not preferred to the oxen; the master does not hang head downward; the unlearned man does not teach the cleric; nor does a layman command a priest. There elders govern juniors, and the more prudent govern the unlearned: men who excel both in holiness of life and in understanding of the Scriptures. In that ark there is no rod without the tablets of Moses’ covenant, because whoever has authority to rebuke also has knowledge to correct.

They celebrate the divine offices with such solemnity and devotion that, in their harmony, you would think the voices of angels resounded. By psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs they invite men to God’s praises and imitate angels. They do not delight in participating in the tales of laymen, [Col. 0363C] and they are farther removed from such things in proportion as they serve Christ more devotedly. Outside the oratory, they either apply themselves to manual labour, so that the devil may always find them occupied; or they conceive by reading; or by holy meditations they penetrate the heavens, so that in paradise they may hear those secret words which it is not lawful for a human being to utter.

Having returned from heavenly things, they set such a guard upon their mouths, such a door upon their lips, that they do not interrupt silence—the practice of righteousness—even with articulated words. They do not, two or three at a time, occupy themselves separately with talk in the corners of the cloister; indeed, they are not permitted even to sow serious conversation among themselves. They hold in memory that “in much speaking sin will not be escaped”; and, as though declaring war upon nature, they restrain by no slight discipline that small member which boasts great things. [Col. 0363D]

Attend, whoever you are, young man of good disposition, who desire with Isaac to be offered to the Lord in sacrifice upon one of the mountains: you will not find a mountain greater than this mountain, so holy and so near to heaven. Truly this mountain is a curdled mountain, a rich mountain: curdled through unity of spirit in the bond of peace; rich through the infusion of heavenly grace. What great mountain is greater than this mountain? It pierces the clouds, reaches the heavens, leaves all other mountains and hills far beneath it, and receives the full blessing of the dew of heaven above and of the fatness of the earth.

Here, bound by regular disciplines, with the wood of the Lord’s cross laid upon you and the fire of holy zeal and burning charity kindled, [Col. 0364A] wait patiently and silently to see what the Lord will do with His sacrifice. What have you to do with rumours concerning princes’ affairs, clerics’ promotions, or the empty opinions of the crowd? What have you to do with idle words, for which people will render account on the day of judgment? If these things are common in certain cloisters, that is for you to see. Those evangelical and angelic men are not sons of night or of darkness, because their light shines before men in such a way that, seeing their works, men glorify their Father who is in heaven. They are a spectacle to angels and men, so that angels may receive the joy of congratulation and men an example for imitation from their manifest way of life.

In that holy fellowship, neither pretence nor concealment from the leaven of the Pharisees is mixed in at all. [Col. 0364B] They are unwilling either to pretend to what is not or to conceal what is, knowing that pretenders and the crafty provoke God’s wrath. Anyone may enter any of their workshops and may handle with his hands each person’s duties, distinctly bounded by fixed limits; inspect them with inquisitive eyes; judge them in his mind; and pronounce upon them with his tongue. For those who fear divine judgment alone do not shun human judgment. Truth has no corners, but corners have filth.

Remember, whoever you are who have purposed to bear the Lord’s yoke from your youth, what you and your companion once wrote and said about certain men whom you knew: “If anyone intends to destroy what he has built, he makes himself a transgressor.” Be like the merchant seeking good pearls. You have found a good pearl, to which neither kings’ diadems nor queens’ necklaces have anything comparable. [Col. 0364C] You sold all you possessed and bought it: for first you left parents, homeland, ecclesiastical revenues, riches and pleasures, the slippery impulses of youth, and alike sensual pleasure and the carnal will. Secondly, passing from what you had purposed to better things, being made perfect in a short time, you will fulfil many years.

See that you do not expose the pearl which you bought at such a price to be trampled by swine. “No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.” You may say: “Is it looking back if I return to the good which I had purposed, and for whose sake I had perhaps meanwhile set aside another and greater good?” Do not believe me, but believe holy Father Gregory. That eminent teacher will not deceive you: since he did not wish to deceive, he could not be deceived.

“Whoever,” he says, “has purposed to undertake a greater good makes the lesser good unlawful for himself. For no one who puts his hand to the plough, etc. A person who directs himself toward a more strenuous pursuit is rightly proved to look back if, abandoning greater goods, he turns back to lesser ones.” Thus speaks that successor of Peter, pillar of the Church, instrument of the Holy Spirit. And do you doubt where so great a watchman warns, counsels, and teaches?

Hear also what the same holy Father says on Ezekiel: “There are some who practise the good things they know; while practising them, they deliberate upon better things; but afterwards, reconsidering, they change the better things upon which they had deliberated. They indeed do the good things which they began, but they fall away from the better things which they had resolved upon. Such people seem to stand in their works before human judgments, but before the eyes of almighty God they have fallen in their deliberation.” [Col. 0365A]

If you still doubt, if you still fear, rebuke yourself and set yourself before your own face. These things are plain and need an executor less than an expositor. You began to fly more loftily with the winged creatures and to walk before your face; do not turn back, do not look behind. For those holy creatures did not turn back as they went, but each walked before its own face. Certainly they had eyes before and behind: behind, that they might despise what they had passed; before, that they might attain what they had not yet reached. Like those winged creatures was Paul, who, equally with them, had flown up to the third heaven. Thus he says: “Forgetting what lies behind and stretching forth to what stands before, I pursue the prize of the high calling” (Phil. 3). [Col. 0365B]

Behold, you have Paul with eyes before and behind: before, that he may advance; behind, that he may not fall short. The poet, instructing the pagan traveller, says:

> Seek not how many thousands you have passed through, but how many remain for you.

Therefore, stretched forth toward what lies before, pursue the prize of the high calling. “The Lord will instruct you in this way in which you shall walk” (Ps. 31); and He will surely fix His eyes upon you (ibid.).

“But,” you say, “I made a vow; I vowed a vow to the God of Jacob. Am I not compelled to render [Col. 0365C] the vows which my lips uttered? This above all terrifies me: I vowed to the Terrible One, who takes away the spirit of princes; if I do not render what I vowed, I fear lest He who takes away the spirit of princes take away my spirit also.”

But what did you vow? You vowed either your soul or something else. If something else, your vow admits of commutation. If you vowed silver, gold, clothing, or anything similar, you may certainly commute it if you render what is better or greater than what you vowed. The soul alone, if you have vowed it, admits no commutation: “What exchange shall a man give for his soul?” (Matt. 16). Answer, if you can; and when you can, say: “None.”

“You say: ‘I vowed my soul, but in a definite place, under a definite master, under a manner of life ordered by definite observances; I vowed stability of place, obedience to a superior, and community of life for the salvation of my soul. It is not lawful to commute this.’” Attend, fearful boy, and do not fear where there is no fear. The vow which does not admit commutation is, as it were, the substantial and principal one: to vow one’s soul to God. The rest—place, superior, habit, manner of life—are accessories, added by human beings making vows, not because the soul which is vowed cannot be saved without them, but because through them the way to salvation becomes more expedient.

What if the place is destroyed, wholly abandoned by its inhabitants, or transferred elsewhere? Can you not be saved in another place? If the superior dies, departs, or refuses to preside, what will you do? Will you perish because there is no one to govern whom you ought to obey? [Col. 0366A] If the habit is changed and the institutions assume another form, then, if you do not observe the former ones, will you be guilty of the vow you made? You see that all these things are accessories and can be commuted; the substance of the vow alone, namely the soul, admits no commutation. Here dispensation has no place, because no equivalent recompense can be found.

Almsgiving, fasting, vigils, and pilgrimage are great goods among human beings. If anyone vows any of these, he makes a commendable but commutable vow. In place of fasting you may render almsgiving; in place of pilgrimage, conversion; in place of vigils, fasting or reading. Observe only this: if you vowed something greater, do not render something lesser; if you commute something lesser for something greater, it will be accepted by Him who receives it. [Col. 0366B]

The prophet says: “Cursed is he who has a male in his flock and, making a vow, sacrifices a weak animal to the Lord” (Mal. 1). What if he vowed a weak one and offers a stronger? I say boldly that one who so sacrifices after the vow is neither a transgressor nor deceitful, and therefore is not accursed. You formerly vowed a victim not weak, I do not say, but less strong than a stronger one. Behold, now, in place of the moderate victim you had vowed, you have sacrificed one greatest and strongest. You vowed a sheep and rendered an ox. Be secure: you have been released.

Blessed by the Lord be your youth, which has put its hand to strenuous things, which has thus girded your loins with strength and strengthened your arm. Rejoice, young man, in your youth; blessed are you because from it you began to bear the Lord’s yoke, henceforth sitting alone, [Col. 0366C] silent, and raising yourself above yourself. This commutation of a vow is a commutation wrought by the right hand of the Most High.

Certainly, those who have learned the penitential canon allow frequent commutations of vows to be made for their penitents. I know a priest who, when he was consulted by a certain noblewoman living in the world, because she had made a vow which she could not fulfil, as to what she ought to do and whether she could somehow commute it, allowed a suitable commutation. That woman had vowed—I do not know whether because of toothache or for some other reason—that henceforth she would not spit in church. “I cannot,” she said, “keep what I vowed.” He said: “Go and spit in church when you need to, but henceforth do not speak in it. For spitting is not sin; but ‘in much speaking sin is not lacking’” (Prov. 10). [Col. 0366D]

A sound commutation of a vow: it freed the person who made the vow and rendered God propitious. “But,” you ask, “what am I to do about the obedience I promised to my superior?” If the foregoing does not suffice, receive this as well. Parish priests owe the obedience they promise to their bishops, and are sacramentally bound to the churches which they govern as to their own wives. By the common law of the canons, they ought neither themselves to withdraw without their bishops’ permission, to whom they should be obedient, nor should others receive them. Yet by the private law written in the heart through the prompting of the Holy Spirit, if they pass to a monastery or a house of regular canons, such men may be received even against their bishops’ opposition. [Col. 0367A]

For Pope Urban says: “If anyone retains a people in his church under a bishop, and, inspired by the Holy Spirit, wishes to save himself in some monastery or house of regular canons, let him go free by our authority, even if his bishop objects. For the law is not laid down for the righteous.” But where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom; and “if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law” (2 Cor. 3). Behold: neither obedience promised to a bishop nor a church entrusted to a priest can hinder one who wishes to pass to the fruit of a better life.

Perhaps you will object, saying that these things are spoken of clerics and priests living in the world, whereas the case is different with religious persons living in community. Certainly consecrated virgins dwelling in a monastery are religious; nevertheless, concerning them it was established at the Council of Tribur: [Col. 0367B]

[Note: [Col. 0367D] This council was held at Tribur in Germany, near Mainz, in the year 895 under Pope Formosus, and dealt with reforming ecclesiastical discipline. Canon 26 states: “If a monk, for the gain of his soul or of souls, proposes to leave his monastery and enter another, with the consent of the bishop, abbot, and brethren, we consent and agree, because we read that many saints did this. But if, escaping regular discipline in flight, he tramples upon the purpose of holiness, he must by every means be restrained.” Note here that the text of the council names monks, whereas this letter names nuns.]

“Consecrated virgins, if for the gain of their souls and for the sake of a stricter life they decide to proceed to another monastery and decree to remain there, the synod permits it. But if they seek another place in flight from discipline, they shall be compelled to return to their former place.” Behold, at the end of the chapter the reason is stated: one who passes from monastery to monastery must be compelled to return, namely when it is a flight from discipline. You must see whether you made this passage for the gain of your soul and for a stricter life, or in flight from discipline. Yet, with your conscience as witness, you fled discipline in order to seize discipline. And because you have made a leap close to heaven for the gain of your soul and for a stricter life, [Col. 0367C] do what you are doing; work at what you are working.

That what is said of consecrated virgins should consequently be understood also of monks is affirmed by that great interpreter of the canons, Gratian. But you will say that a different rule is observed concerning regular canons. For the Council of Autun and Pope Urban—already mentioned above—appear to affirm this. Thus the Council of Autun reads:

[Note: [Col. 0367D] We read that two councils were once held in the Burgundian city of Autun, or Augustodunum: the first under Pope Adeodatus in 670, when St Leodegar was bishop of that city; the second convened in 1055, when Aganon occupied that city’s episcopal see. Of the latter Hugh the monk writes in the *Life of St Hugh of Cluny*: “Robert, Duke of Burgundy, violently harassed Aganon, bishop of Autun; therefore Geoffrey of Lyon, Hugh of Besançon, Aycard of Chalon, and Drogo of Mâcon assembled at Autun,” etc. I believe this canon derives rather from the second than the first council, since in the earlier period there was as yet no mention of regular canonries. Yet the acts and canons of that second Council of Autun have perished through the injury of time; it is mentioned only by the aforesaid Hugh.]

“No abbot or monk shall dare to recall regular canons from the purpose of their canonical profession and receive them into the monastic habit, to make them monks, so long as they can find a church of their own order in which, living as canons, they may serve God and save their souls. If they attempt this by rash presumption, let them be bound by the bond of anathema.”

The same Pope Urban says: [Col. 0368A] “We command and universally forbid that any canon professed under a rule should become a monk, unless—God forbid—he has publicly fallen.” If anyone, presuming to act contrary to our decree, attempts it, we command that he return to the canonical order, wear the monastic cowl thereafter, and sit last in choir.

Likewise: “We decree that no one of canonical profession, after he has placed a man over his head in God’s stead, shall dare, prompted by any fickleness or under the pretext of a stricter religious life, to withdraw from that same cloister without permission from the father of the entire congregation. No abbot, bishop, or monk shall receive those who depart without the common security of letters.”

To this, having obtained leave, and preserving due reverence and gratitude toward our elders, we reply: [Col. 0368B] What have regular canons to do with the hermits of Grandmont? They are certainly neither called canons nor wish to be called canons; how, then, can they share in the reality with those with whom they disdain to share even the name? Nor should I believe that those are canons whose more numerous members, and those greater in authority, are not clerics but laymen—not educated men but illiterate—unless perhaps someone says that their clerics are canons and their laymen hermits. If this is so, we have found an order either two-headed like Janus or two-formed like a Centaur.

If you ask them what order they belong to, they answer: “We are sinners”; if you ask others, they call them Good Men. In that province from which they derive their origin, where their head and seat are situated, [Col. 0368C] their cells are called *bonhominae*—“houses of the Good Men.” We know, moreover, that the regular canons of our time serve Christ under the Rule of blessed Augustine and dwell in the house of the Lord with one manner of life under that Rule. But these men profess as their master not Augustine, but a certain good man, as they call him, Stephen of Muret. The little book containing their constitutions is not called by them a Rule but a Life. Therefore, just as our canons are called “regular” from the Rule which they observe, these men must similarly be called, from the Life which they profess, “vital” clerics or laymen.

Pope Urban speaks concerning those regularly professed—that is, those who serve God under the Rule of blessed Augustine—when he says: “For he grants this privilege also to the abbot of St Rufus, [Col. 0368D]

[Note: The monastery of St Rufus was first founded near Avignon about the year 1000 by four regular canons of that city’s cathedral church. When the rest wished to abandon common and regular life, these four, dissenting, asked that a chapel near Avignon, consecrated to St Rufus, be granted them, so that there they might observe their ancestral laws and regular institutions. By the renown of their virtue they attracted very many, and in a short time grew so greatly that they sent colonies into neighbouring provinces to restore and spread the canonical order. Thus that abbey became the origin and head of a most illustrious congregation. But later, when it had been utterly destroyed by the fury and impiety of the Albigensian heretics, the canons of St Rufus migrated elsewhere and took refuge at Valence, where they built a new monastery under the former name of St Rufus.]

who undoubtedly follow the Rule of blessed Augustine, [Col. 0369A] and to regular canons and similar persons.” We believe that the Rule of these men had not yet been handed down by Lord Stephen of Muret; or, if it had been handed down, it was unknown to the holy Roman Church. How could the supreme pontiff grant a privilege to those who did not yet exist, or who had not yet come to his knowledge?

Although, if those regular canons themselves today wished to ascend to the height of the Cistercian order, perhaps they could not be recalled by those decrees of Pope Urban. Certainly I, unworthy as I am, preside over regular canons; and when, not long ago, I sought from the lord pope a privilege that no one should dare retain our canons against our will, he added to the privilege the clause: “where they have passed to a stricter order for the sake of a stricter life.” Thus, so that examples need not be sought far away, Pope Urban’s privilege appears to be restricted by Pope Alexander’s privilege.

Truly, if one of our own wished to pass to the Cistercians, before his passage I would dissuade him; after his passage I would not call him back. I would not resist the Holy Spirit; I would not quench the Spirit; I would not hinder the Spirit’s freedom. What sin have you committed, strong warrior? If you ascended a hill, not in order to fight upon level ground, but so that you might strike the enemy more effectively, you are not to be called a deserter, soldier of Christ, because you did not flee to the enemy; nor a deserter from military service, because you did not withdraw from the standards. These considerations may suffice you; there is no reason why you should doubt or fear on account of your vow.

But your thought still murmurs: [Col. 0369C] “I shall return to my house from which I came out” (Matt. 12); for I proposed and said: “This is my resting-place for ever and ever; here will I dwell, because I have chosen it” (Ps. 131). I fear, brother, lest, as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning, so your thoughts may be corrupted and fall away from the simplicity which is in Christ Jesus. Satan sometimes transforms himself into an angel of light, and sells a bladder as a lantern to the simpler sort.

[Note: [Col. 0370D] A worn and popular proverb which has not yet become obsolete.]

The memory of a corrupt repose flatters you: permission to talk, granted at certain places and hours; longer sleep; softer clothing; more delicate food. More dishes there, more cups—sometimes taken short of hunger and thirst, and beyond them—strive to call your youth back. There coverings of skins drive away the stiffness of cold; [Col. 0369D] the hidden softness of linen or hemp tempers the wool laid over it. There are the greetings of princes, visits of kings, encounters with crowds, and gifts from all. There it is said to the north, “Give,” and to the south, “Do not withhold”; all bring, convey, offer, and carry in gifts: all earthborn persons and children of men together, rich and poor. [Col. 0370A]

Perhaps this customary theatre is raised before you by your thought; and whenever you recall these things, the residue of your thought keeps a festival for you. Your youthful hands are delicate and tender and recoil from labour. The longer vigils and the night office prolonged until daylight do not permit morning sleep. Rustic food seasoned only with salt offends a noble young man’s palate and produces nausea at every serving. Regular silence stimulates your itching tongue, and the desire to hear disturbs your open ears at every sound.

I beg you, son, by Jesus Christ hanging on the cross as the medicine for our wounds: let these things neither move nor trouble you. They are vain; at their first onset they impede one who is running, but at the bare sign of the cross and invocation of the Lord Jesus they quickly vanish. And because, as I have heard, your greater conflict is against the memory of your vow, as though you had made your first faith void, answer firmly: “I came not to discharge the vow, but to fulfil it” (cf. Matt. 5).

Dearest Robert, the broad commandment of the Lord compelled me to compose a long and broad letter. When I had begun to write to you, carried away by love for your novices and fear of their returning, I changed the direction of my pen, judging that if I directly rebuked or warned them, I would more easily obtain in them my faithful purpose. [Col. 0370B] For the farmer reaps more gladly what he sows with his own hand than what another’s hand has sown.

Meanwhile, dearest one, be solicitous for your novices. Through yourself and other teachers exhort them; admonish, rebuke, reprove, entreat them, because plants moved from place to place most easily wither unless they are watered frequently. May my God fulfil every desire of mine and yours according to the riches of His glory in Christ Jesus our Lord. Amen. [Col. 0370C]

107. EPISTLE LXXII. TO PETER, LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE. Concerning the same Grandmontine novices.

To his benevolent and beneficent lord and father, PETER, bishop of Tusculum, legate of the Apostolic See: greeting, together with complete obedience offered in all devotion.

It provokes laughter in onlookers if a sheep approaches a goat [Col. 0370D]

[Note: [Col. 0370D] This was a worn and popular adage among writers of that age, used to signify that a rich and wealthy person was borrowing something from one in need. Thus St Bernard, in a letter—number 87—to Oger, says: “The sheep seeks wool from the goat.”]

to obtain wool from it. So it has happened, Father. You were pleased to ask something from me in which you abound more fully. I did what I could, lest, if I did nothing, I should prove undevoted and ungrateful. I sent you the letter above written to the novices of Pontigny. Brother Robert of Galardon had asked you, in my presence, [Col. 0371A]

[Note: [Col. 0371B] He was of the noble family of the lords of Galardon in the district of Chartres, whose castle’s ruins may still be seen from afar.]

what those novices ought to do who, through fear of their former vow, were tempted to return. You then imposed on me the burden of answering. Mindful of your benefits, we daily offer God sacrifices of prayers for you. May the good angel of the Lord accompany your journey.

EPISTLE LXXIII. TO RAYMOND, PRIOR OF ST GENEVIEVE. He recounts the various dangers he underwent.

To his dearest Raymond, prior of St Genevieve:

[Note: [Col. 0371B] Raymond served as prior in the monastery of St Genevieve while Stephen was its abbot. Afterwards he was transferred to the monastery of St John at Soissons, as will be said below, and there attained the rank of abbot. Epistles 104 and 113 are also addressed to him.]

STEPHEN, abbot: greeting.

The fear of a graver danger makes the task I have undertaken seem lighter and less formidable; yet for that very reason I ought to be afraid, since the journey is long, and beset by the dangers of rivers, the dangers of robbers, the dangers of the Coterelli, the Basculi, and the Aragonese; the road is suspect, more deadly than pleasant.

[Note: [Col. 0371B] Saint Antoninus, vol. II, title 17, fol. 17, says of these people: “In the year 1183, in the province of Bourges, seven thousand Coterelli and more were killed by the inhabitants of that land, who had united against the enemies of God. For these men, ravaging the king’s land, carried off plunder; they dragged along with them most cruelly the people whom they had captured. When they took priests and religious men captive, they mocked them even amidst their torments, saying, ‘Singers, sing, sing!’ Then at once they struck them with blows and beat them with thick rods. Some, so scourged, rendered up their blessed souls to God; others, half-dead after a long imprisonment, returned home after money had been given for their ransom. Finally, as human sins deserved, these same Coterelli plundered churches; taking the Body of the Lord out of gold and silver vessels in which it was reserved for the needs of the sick, and—alas!—casting it contemptuously upon the ground, they trampled it underfoot. They carried off the chalices irreverently, broke them with hammers and stones, and sold them; from the corporals their concubines made veils for their heads.

“William the Breton, *On the Deeds of Philip Augustus*, under the year 1183, says: ‘In the same year, in the district of Bourges, seven thousand Coterelli—commonly called Ruptarii—were killed in a single day. They had invaded the borders of the realm, sparing no one on account of age, sex, religious profession, or sacred place, but either killing all or compelling them by diverse tortures to pay money for their ransom. When this was heard, the king sent an army to aid the lord of that province, and all, from the greatest to the least, were slaughtered.’

“The errors of the heretical Coterelli were that they said, first, that the Blessed Virgin Mary had been an angel; second, that Christ’s body is not glorious in heaven; third, that the souls of the saints will not be in glory before the Day of Judgment.]

[Note: [Col. 0371D] The Basculi and Waldensians, heretics, derived both their error and their name from a certain Waldo, a wealthy citizen of Lyons, who flourished about the year 1170. Having distributed his possessions among the poor, he concealed his errors under the cloak of poverty. Peter, the monk of Vaux-de-Cernay, says in his *History of the Albigensians* [Col. 0372B] that, since they wore sandals after the manner of the Apostles, they used to say that any one of them, if necessity required and he had sandals, could make the body of Christ without having received orders from a bishop. Walter recounts many such inventions of theirs in his *Chronology*.

“They were condemned at the Third Lateran Council, chapter 27, in these words: ‘Because in Gascony, the Albigensian country, the regions of Toulouse, and elsewhere, the condemned perversity of heretics—whom some call Cathars, others Paterines, others Publicans, and still others by other names—has prevailed so greatly that they now practise their wickedness not in secret, as some do, but publicly display their error and draw the simple and weak to agree with them: we decree that they, their defenders, and those who receive them are subject to anathema.’ A little later it adds: ‘Concerning the Brabançons, Aragonese, Navarrese, Basques, Coterelli, and Triaverdins, who exercise such savagery against Christians that they spare neither churches nor monasteries,’ etc.

“Such heretics were called Aragonese, Navarrese, Basculi, and Albigensians because they came from Aragon, Navarre, Gascony, and the Albigensian territory.]

I follow the bishop of Albano through mountains and valleys, through vast solitudes, through the frenzy of robbers and the image of death, through villages in flames and ruined houses—where nothing is safe, nothing quiet, nothing that does not threaten welfare and lie in wait for life.

[Note: [Col. 0372C] That bishop of Albano was Cardinal Walter, predecessor of Henry, abbot of Clairvaux. When he had come, together with Stephen, abbot of St Genevieve, and others, to crush the heresies rife in the region of Toulouse, he was captured by Roger, count of Béziers and Saint-Gilles, their supporter, and cast into prison. Peter, cardinal-priest of St Chrysogonus and legate, wrote of this in a letter found in Roger of Howden under the year 1188: “When the aforesaid Raymond and Bernard and others [Col. 0372D] had met our venerable brother Reginald, bishop of Bath, and the noblemen the viscount of Turenne and Raymond of Châteauneuf, who, on our advice, had come into Roger of Béziers’s land for the liberation of our venerable brother, the bishop of Albano,” etc.]

Amid these things, I earnestly entreat God and the Blessed Virgin together with our beloved brethren that, if I am to be useful to His Church, He may bring me back unharmed. Beyond Toulouse, near the Spaniards, I shall find that man, as they say.

[Note: [Col. 0372D] Roger, count of Saint-Gilles, whom Walter, with his followers, was seeking, as he himself recounts in these words: “When we entered with the said bishop of Bath that utterly ruined country, which, like the cesspool of all wickedness, had received into itself the entire flood of heresy flowing there, the aforesaid Roger, wickedly desperate, had withdrawn to the furthest and inaccessible borders of his territory. For the author of evil scented the light of truth, and could not endure our approach for conversation, since he had wholly retreated into works of darkness.”]

If any dispute should arise among you concerning external affairs, refer the matter to B., formerly provost, upon whom Lord Robert has imposed, on the king’s behalf, the duty that whatever you request in your affairs shall be done for you through his assistance and exertion.

[Note: [Col. 0372D] I suppose this is Robert Clement, a minister of the realm, whom he mentions elsewhere.]

You do not know why I am going to the lord legate; the reason is other than that which I had communicated to you. But be wholly silent about it, lest someone interpret it adversely.

## 110–111. LETTER LXXIV. TO THE BISHOP AND DEAN OF BAYEUX

Concerning a certain affair of the archbishop of Tours with the bishop of Dol, mentioned above.

[Note: [Col. 0373D] The matter which the pope had entrusted to the bishop and deans of Bayeux, as well as to Stephen, abbot of St Genevieve, for examination, concerned the elevation of the bishopric of Dol to an archbishopric; the archbishop of Tours opposed it with all his strength.]

[Col. 0373A]

To the reverend father and lord, the bishop and dean of Bayeux, Brother Stephen of St Genevieve sends greetings and affection.

It provokes laughter in onlookers if a sheep approaches a goat in order to take wool from her. Under this common proverb you have consulted a man of little skill and no great authority. Yet since the lord pope has joined me to you as a companion in the matter of Tours and Dol—like Hylas to Hercules, not walking with equal strides—I shall say what I think and agree with whatever you say, lest perhaps either party may justly complain of us.

We ought, in my judgment, to meet at the appointed place and time and deliberate together whether we should proceed with the matter or withdraw from it. Farewell.

## 112. LETTER LXXV. TO JOHN, LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE

He congratulates him upon his transfer to the church of Narbonne.

To the reverend lord and father John, bishop of Poitiers, legate of the Apostolic See, Brother Stephen of St Genevieve sends greetings and, with sincere devotion, faithful service.

The remembrance of you sets before me a delightful spectacle: I am refreshed by the sight of it and moved by its charm. The pontifical mitres of different provinces contend for the same head; and while Narbonne tries to take its priest from the see of Poitiers, the first see of Gaul, Lyons, with a holy leap forestalling the rest, claims for itself the bishop-elect of Narbonne.

[Note: [Col. 0373D] John, bishop of Poitiers, was elected archbishop of Narbonne. Then, while travelling to Rome to be confirmed by the supreme pontiff Lucius, he was made by that same pope archbishop and primate of Lyons; because of his outstanding learning, Lucius also created him legate of the Apostolic See in the kingdom of France. [Col. 0374D]]

[Note: [Col. 0374D] The church of Lyons bears the same title on a coin of Louis the Pious and Charles the Bald, a specimen of which survives in the treasury of St Genevieve.]

This is an admirable and lovable sport of churches, in which the superior despoils the inferior; and, by a holy rivalry, those unequal in rank seem equal in will. Far be it from your gentleness, Father, to decline toward the barbarism of the Goths, the frivolity of the Gascons, and the cruel, savage customs of Septimania, where faithlessness is valued above faith, hunger above reputation, and deceit and suffering beyond measure.

Recently, when the lord king sent me to Toulouse, I saw in passing, in that land, a widespread and fierce terrible image of death: half-ruined walls of churches, burnt sites of sacred buildings, foundations dug up, and, where human dwellings had stood, neglected dens of beasts.

[Note: [Col. 0374D] See Letter 73.]

I confess that I trembled and was afraid when I heard that you were being invited to those places, in which, even if it should happen that you presided, it would be easy not to be of use. But when at last I heard that the Rhodanusia of Sidonius was calling you, I rejoiced greatly and desire to see our primate in glory—one whom I had previously experienced as a father in affection, generous alike in goodwill and benefaction.

[Note: [Col. 0374D] That is, the city of Lyons, which Sidonius Apollinaris, in Letter 5, calls *Rhodanusia*, because it is situated on the Rhône. “When I had gone out from the walls of our Rhodanusia,” he says, “I made use of the public post, having been summoned by sacred letters.” Irenaeus, however, called both the religion itself and the district around the Rhône *rhodanoisian* (ῥοδανοισίαν).]

As you commanded me, I am ready to provide your nephew, the archdeacon—a young man of good character—with counsel and assistance.

## 114. LETTER LXXVI. TO GODFREY, ABBOT OF ST SATYRUS

He asks him to assist his friend.

To the venerable father and lord Godfrey, abbot of St Satyrus.

[Col. 0374B]

A testimony drawn from a good conscience and unfeigned faith ought to be welcome. This is the treasure from which everyone who would be a scribe learned in the kingdom of heaven brings forth things new and old. On account of this good report of you, we commend to you your young son Th. Although he withdrew from his Father for a time, he neither fed swine nor satisfied his belly with their husks under one of the citizens. Having gone out from Jerusalem, he did not go down to Jericho; rather, pitching his tent in Shiloh, he either devoted himself to the work of his hands or occupied his mind with honourable studies by which sons of adoption ought to be instructed.

While staying with us, he preserved his conscience and reputation no less honourably than uprightly: in the former he was provident for himself; in the latter, not troublesome to his neighbour. We pour out devout prayers to you and your brethren on his behalf, that, as befits a father and benefits a son, you may receive him on his return with kindness and beneficence, offering him not so much a father’s blows as a mother’s breasts.

## 115. LETTER LXXVII. TO THE BRETHREN OF ST EVURTIUS AT ORLÉANS

He demands again the annual pension granted to him.

To his dearest friends and brethren B., prior, and the holy community of St Evurtius at Orléans, Brother Stephen of St Genevieve, their equal in works and words.

It is hateful to me to hate those whom I had loved. Lest I should worship even for an hour the semblance of this fault, I beg the Son of God—who taught the children of men by word and example to love one another. But behold, unwillingly I am compelled to declare war upon my own entrails and, as it were, to set out gougers against the very sockets of my eyes. For if, when struck, I remain silent; if, injured, I do not groan; if I compensate the greatest wrongs with the slightest gain, I have displayed patience, but not peace.

Brothers, receive this in a fair spirit. If I ask what is just, I entreat you by the breasts of your church, our common mother, which nursed us; by the glorious memory of the confessor Evurtius; and by the fidelity which ought to be found in you both in word and deed: faithfully preserve and happily fulfil your grant, made to me by you in your chapter, confirmed by word, writing, and the bond of excommunication. Consider, in the light of both conscience and reputation, what you ought to do concerning the promise made to me so solemnly and dreadfully, so that you may provide both for conscience and reputation.

For the present I would rather settle the matter more privately between us and receive without scandal what is owed me than demand it publicly before the tribunals of legates and prelates. And lest someone perhaps say either that I have not yet made demand or that you have not denied the debt, send me through the bearer of this letter the share of the revenues of the land of Godreville which falls to me under your promise, or inform me by the same messenger in a definite reply what you intend to do concerning it.
