[Note: [Col. 0375D] Godreville is a parish in the diocese of Orléans, commonly called Gondreville, where the abbey of St Evurtius possesses lands and estates. From their revenue the chapter of this monastery had established an annual pension for Stephen, as a memorial of its gratitude, when he was called to govern the church of St Genevieve in Paris.]

I send you the rescript of your ordinance, confirmed by you in your chapter through grant, drafting, sealing, and excommunication, so that, if any one of us—God forbid!—is unwilling to keep his faith, the mute charter may accuse him and stand against his face. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXVIII. TO THE ABBOT OF CHARLY

He asks him for rams for his flock.

[Col. 0375C]

To the venerable father and lord, the abbot of Charly, Stephen, abbot of St Genevieve, sends greetings and affection.

[Note: [Col. 0375D] Carolilocus, or Carlilocus, commonly Charly, is a notable Cistercian abbey in the diocese of Senlis. Near it lie the village and land of Borreto, commonly Borrest, subject in temporal lordship to St Genevieve. Stephen, then abbot, cultivated this land at his own expense and maintained there a very numerous flock of sheep; for them he was seeking rams from the aforesaid abbot of Charly.]

It provokes laughter in onlookers if a sheep comes to a goat to take wool from her. If the she-goat asks it, it will be a glory to the wool-bearing flock if you hear the beggar. In this humble form, therefore, I address a lowly request to you: I ask that three or four rams from the fruitful folds of your sheep may be lent or given to us. The season of mounting approaches, and the bleating voices of the sheep hasten to arrange their rough marriage shortly. I preferred to write in absence what I feared to ask in person. For I know that a letter does not blush if it suffers a refusal in vain, nor incur shame if it is not heard. If you think of recompense, we offer ourselves and what is ours to you; and though we may not be able to answer adequately in a similar case, by God’s grace we shall be able to make compensation in other matters. The benefit will be increased if the giver is cheerful, the wool soft, and the climbers strong.

## LETTER LXXIX. TO A., ARCHBISHOP OF LUND

He informs him that Peter, his nephew, has made canonical profession at St Genevieve.

To the venerable lord and father A., archbishop of Lund.

[Note: [Col. 0375D] Lund, commonly Lunden, is a most distinguished city of Denmark, renowned for its archiepiscopal see and its primatial dignity over the whole realm. Its prelate is called by Saxo Grammaticus, that most elegant historian of this people, the supreme pontiff. The man to whom this letter is directed was Absalon, an outstanding person, greatly praised by writers. [Col. 0376D]]

Both the sacrifice and what is offered from a good conscience and unfeigned faith are pleasing and propitiatory. God does not reject this at any age, estate, or sex: He approves the morning sacrifice in the young and the evening sacrifice in the old. Concerned and diligent about this rite of offering, your Peter—and henceforth ours—has bound himself by the bonds of obedience upon the mountain of the virgin Genevieve, patiently awaiting what the Lord will make of him as an acceptable offering.

He had undertaken a stricter and, we believe, higher vocation.

[Note: [Col. 0376D] By these words he indicates that this Peter had entered the Order of St Benedict or the Cistercian Order; he could not endure its rigour and therefore moved to the canons of St Genevieve.]

But lest unfamiliar toil and austere severity strike down and crush his tender age, it is better for him to be saved in Zoar than to be endangered on the height, to the dishonour of himself and his family. Lawfully and freely he has turned his back from burdens; and, lest his hands should serve among gardens and fields with a basket, he has become a cleric with us, intending to devote himself more frequently to reading, that he may conform to clerics. Let your holy fatherhood rejoice over him, and let his parents be consoled in the Lord, since from such a flower we expect abundant fruit in the Church of God. For my part, I and our brethren are ready to bestow upon him whatever instruction, affection, and teaching we can, offering more often a mother’s breasts than a father’s blows.

## LETTER LXXX. TO THE SAME

He judges that his sick nephew Peter should be sent back to his native land, that he may fare better.

[Note: [Col. 0376D] He was Absalon’s nephew. Sent into France, he became a regular canon at St Genevieve, where he devoted himself to study; afterwards he returned to Denmark and was appointed bishop of Roskilde and chancellor of the whole kingdom, as we learn from the Necrology of St Genevieve for 27 November: “The anniversary of the pious memory of Peter, bishop of Roskilde, chancellor of the king of Denmark, our professed canon.”]

A young man gives promise of good things when, at the beginning of life, signs of virtue grow together. This applies alike to our and your Peter, who, professing the rule with us, has obediently undertaken both learning in study and discipline in conduct. Since in him the spirit indeed is willing but the flesh weak, according to your command we commend and entrust him to you, judging it better and more welcome that he should stay with you than die with us. He often suffers the troublesome attacks of quartan fever, and the lingering effects of that affliction make every day mournful for him. We believe that his tender years can be helped by the benefit of his native soil and natural air, and that the humours imbibed from a mother’s breast can be warmed by the consolation of both father and mother.

There is one thing which, as for a most beloved son, we advise, command, and enjoin upon him: so long as he remains in that land, he must not begin roaming after the flocks of his secular companions; rather, he should either apply himself in the cloister to regular discipline with his brethren serving the Lord under our venerable brother William, or, whenever and as often as you wish, live devoutly with you in your court, as is fitting and expedient.

As for what you notified us in your letter—that he should be sent either to the schools on the Mount or to the schools of secular Parisians and sellers of words—we do not admit this, saving your favour, because it conflicts with our institution and custom, lest through him a new spectacle be proposed to the present brethren which may be drawn into a ruinous precedent for those to come.

[Note: [Col. 0377D] The schools of St Genevieve on the Mount were among the most ancient and famous, and many men distinguished for learning either taught or pursued studies there. Among others was Hulbodes, a cleric of Liège, in the time of King Robert. It is written of him that, when as a young man he fled scholastic discipline and went to Paris, he attached himself to the canons of St Genevieve and soon became master of many schools. Though Lord Notger, bishop of Liège, did not know where he was for some time, Hulbodes was finally compelled to return by the execution of a canonical episcopal sentence, leaving there many marks of scholarship and moral character. Abelard also, as is read in the *Life of Goswin, Abbot of Anchin*, conducted a public school in the cloister of St Genevieve, having gathered many secular students to himself. These were the external schools assigned to secular persons, mentioned here. But besides these, internal schools were established in the same monastery, in which the regular canons of that house cultivated letters, as is clear from this letter. [Col. 0378D]]

[Note: [Col. 0378D] He means the external schools of St Genevieve, as we have said, or the schools of Blessed Mary, or those which secular persons, even married men, conducted in private houses. See James of Vitry, chapter 7 of the *Western History*, who says: “In one and the same house schools were above and brothels below; in the upper part masters lectured, while in the lower prostitutes performed the offices of shame; from another side clerics disputing and arguing contentiously cried out,” etc.]

Wisdom has its own rules in cloisters, setting up schools there: on the one hand of truth, on the other of virtue. But if your counsel should perhaps turn toward seeking to make a secular man out of one bound by rule, choose for him a city other than Paris in which to study, lest, before our eyes, instead of the morning and evening sacrifice which he ought to have offered to the Lord with us, he offer the din of words and the windings of disputations, and what we hoped would be fruit should turn to reproach and contempt for us.

## LETTER LXXIX. TO A CERTAIN ARCHBISHOP

He asks on behalf of a priest unjustly oppressed.

[Note: [Col. 0378D] This letter appears to have been written to William, archbishop of Rheims, since Stephen calls him his lord, as he does frequently elsewhere.]

For the bearer of this letter, a priest unknown to me but known to my acquaintances, I ask my lord that those who have asked me for him may rejoice that they asked me on his behalf. He complains of his bishop, who, he asserts, unjustly takes away his church without judicial process, so that, against his will, he is compelled outside the Church to beg for another’s bread, though he ought to eat the bread of presentation in the Church. I beg that the eye of your compassion may be opened over him and the bosom of your mercy enlarged, so that he who has found his bishop not merely a hireling but a wolf may find his metropolitan a father and protector.

## 120–121. LETTER LXXXII. TO POPE LUCIUS III

He commends the chancellor of France against the resistance of canons who object to him the defect of his birth.

[Col. 0378B]

To the most holy lord and father Lucius, supreme pontiff, Stephen of St Genevieve sends greetings and devoted obedience with every service and submission.

The Roman Church, common mother of all, possessing from the Lord fullness of power and grace, extends herself to individuals in such a way as to receive all. Holding vessels of discernment by weight, number, and measure, according to individual merits she pours wine and oil into some, and gives to others one separate from the other. Yet, more frequently and gladly pouring herself wholly into affection for her children, she both expresses and offers the breasts of maternal compassion rather than the paternal rods of severity—often to the idle, always to those who desire them.

Running in the remnant and fragrance of this hope, we fall at the knees of your sacred apostolate, commending to your grace a young man of great promise, soon, as we believe, to become a man of still greater virtue: the chancellor of the lord king of the French.

[Note: [Col. 0378D] I suppose this chancellor was Hugh of Puiset, who held this office in France at this time and died in the year 1186.]

Placed in a position and rank in which some are accustomed to do more harm than good, he is so diligent and vigorous in the affairs of churches that he supports them in the palace and consoles them outside it. Since in the kingdom of the Franks some churches, out of a certain punctilious nobility, have adopted for themselves the glorious custom, as they deem it, that only persons born of lawful union may be promoted, they subordinate excellence of merit and virtue to birth and throw the title of his birth in the aforesaid chancellor’s face—proudly rather than from on high—lest he approach or rise among them.

The Roman Church, Father, is not subject to their laws, and has power, if it wishes, either partly to derogate from them or wholly to abolish them. And since, as we believe, great men offer you prayers on his behalf, I too, the least portion of your flock, ask that your divine consolation may endeavour to grant what human enactment strives to take away, so that in him severity may not prevail over abundance, nor grace be less than nature.

[Note: [Col. 0379D] This word was used by the ancients, as can be seen on a silver coin of Decius, taken from our numismatic collection and described below.]

May the apostolic hand, if it please you, loose in him the bond which, excluding virtue, encloses birth, so that in the few churches which observe this custom he may deserve to receive a privilege through whom many churches obtain privileges in the royal court.

## 123. LETTER LXXXIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS

He asks on behalf of a priest from whom the bishop of Soissons had taken part of a benefice.

[Col. 0379B]

To the most holy father and lord, the archbishop of Rheims, Stephen of St Genevieve sends greetings.

Compassion is difficult to overcome when grace promotes it on the one side and nature on the other. In you it is assisted by both benefits, so that it neither fails individual suppliants nor ceases to benefit all. I presume always to solicit its favour from you on behalf of G., a poor cleric and bearer of this letter, without fearing that you will reject me as an unscrupulous man or cast me off as one who drives others out.

He fears that your serenity has turned to severity toward him. Because, hindered by illness, he did not dare to follow his lord and serve him on the journey, fearing and trembling he begs at your feet that the fault of necessity, not of will, may not be counted against him for punishment. Let your holy fatherhood forgive him this offence, so that you, who are accustomed to avenge your own injuries sparingly, may punish another’s injuries even more sparingly from the accumulated treasury of your clemency.

The benefice which this same G. obtained from the lord bishop of Soissons through Melior, archdeacon of Laon—who, as we hear, will soon enjoy better fortune—the same bishop has greatly curtailed, taking away this year’s harvest, so that he who ought to eat from the altar is compelled to beg beside the altar.

[Note: [Col. 0379D] Perhaps I shall not be mistaken if I say that this Archdeacon Melior is the man who was afterwards made cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, to whom Letter 113 is addressed—especially since Stephen adds that he would shortly enjoy better fortune, implicitly referring to the cardinal’s dignity to which, very probably, he was being called.]

I ask, if it please you, as the least portion of your clerics, that he who deserved to obtain the title of a benefice through your court may, through your care, deserve to receive the good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing measure of harvest which he requests, no less kindly than beneficently.

## 124. LETTER LXXXIV. TO HENRY, KING OF THE ENGLISH

He asks him to confirm and have executed the will of the supreme pontiff’s nephew, who was the king’s cleric.

[Note: [Col. 0379D] Henry II, under whom Blessed Thomas of Canterbury was slain in 1171; Henry himself died in 1185, as the *Chronicle of Normandy* notes: “King Henry died on the Nones of July at Chinon and was buried at Fontevraud, in the abbey of nuns; his son Richard succeeded him.” [Col. 0380D]]

[Col. 0380A]

To Henry, by the grace of God king of the English, Brother Stephen, abbot of St Genevieve, sends greetings and eternal glory with every prosperity.

After the mournful funeral rites and lamentable bier, illustrious prince, we pour out before you the remainder of our tears, expecting from your abundant clemency consolation for our sorrow. Gentilis, nephew of Pope Alexander of holy memory and likewise your cleric, closed his last day—though the order of mortality was disturbed as regards his surviving parents. A young man of good promise, he concluded his praiseworthy life with a faithful end; amid his last words of holy Catholic confession, being of sound mind and sound counsel, he lawfully disposed of his possessions, made a solemn will, and distributed and bequeathed them to pious causes.

[Note: [Col. 0380D] These words appear to indicate that a nephew of Alexander III, named Gentilis, a cleric—or, as we call him, almoner—of the king of England, of whom this letter speaks, was buried in this church of St Genevieve. His death is recorded in the necrology of the same abbey on 22 November: “Gentilis, acolyte of the Holy Roman Church, nephew of Pope Alexander III of blessed memory, died.”]

Since nothing is more due to human beings than that the pen of a last will be free and its irrevocable choice lawful, we address prayers to your highness that by your authority you may confirm the will of your aforesaid cleric, and cause his goods remaining in your realm from the revenues granted to him by you to be assigned without difficulty or delay to his faithful administrator and master, Albert, through whose hand the alms are to be distributed. Thus your name may shine more brightly through your generosity, the deceased’s will may take effect, and the reward of eternal recompense may increase for both you and him. Renew in the nephew the memory of so great an uncle; and do not withhold favour from one dead to whom, while living, you generously and beneficently bestowed royal support and expenditure.

## 126. LETTER LXXXV. TO WILLIAM AND ROBERT, PAPAL NOTARIES

He deals with the advancement of his affairs in the Roman curia.

To his dearest William and Robert, scribes of the lord pope, Brother Stephen of St Genevieve.

I offer you this common reminder, rejoicing that you have gone abroad, if your departure may produce for you alike profit and advancement. Two virgins of the divine palace, humility and honourableness, will easily obtain both for you. If either or both of you excludes either one of them, whoever he may be will himself be excluded. Many men of Orléans are accustomed to be golden among strangers who were not even silver among their own people. I mean the metals of character, though I should not be lying if I mentioned money.

May God increase His grace toward you, so that those at court may hold us in favour and, through you, make us rejoice. We have entrusted certain petitions of ours, containing the affairs of our church, to Hervé de Roches. I ask you to exert, through yourselves and your friends, all the help and effort you can, so that these petitions of ours may be graciously heard by the lord pope and the lord chancellor, and beneficially fulfilled. If you think of recompense, I am ready, at a place and time appointed by you, to repay the favour shown me.

## 127. LETTER LXXXVI. TO POPE LUCIUS III

He asks him to preserve the ancient rights of the chaplain of St Benedict at Paris.

[Col. 0381B]

To the most holy lord and father Lucius, supreme pontiff, Brother Stephen sends greetings and vigilant, sincere obedience with every devotion.

The holy Roman Church has customarily either approved, or at least not judged fit to disapprove, ancient usages of churches that conflict neither with reason nor with law. Encouraged by this confidence, your devoted son Simon, chaplain of Saint Benedict’s, has recourse to the bosom of your mercy. He is being troubled by certain canons of that church, who demand that, contrary to an ancient custom observed both in his own time and in that of his predecessors, he withdraw from the altar at which the parish offices of divine worship have hitherto been celebrated for the people, and be compelled to set up a new altar in some corner of the church.

The unusual layout of that church—unlike other churches, it faces west at the sanctuary end and east at the entrance—does not allow parish offices to be suitably celebrated anywhere other than at the place in which those before us celebrated them from ancient times down to our own day. May it please Your Holiness, if it seems fitting to you, that the custom hitherto prevailing, of offering sacrifices for the people, be retained—especially since it does not interfere with the offices of the clerics: they celebrate their divine offices at other hours, while at other times the chaplain performs the parish sacraments.

[Note: [Col. 0381D] Since among Christians the upper part of churches, where the altar is placed, faces east, the church consecrated to Saint Benedict, formerly in a suburb of Paris but now on the Rue Saint-Jacques, was, unlike other churches, turned westward. This was, I think, for the following reasons: that the door of the church might be placed beside the public road, so that passers-by might have easier entry; and that the divine offices might not be disturbed by noise. But in the time of Francis I, when this building was collapsing through its location and age, the parishioners restored it more suitably, placing the principal entrance on the opposite side, so that henceforth this church, like the others, might face east.

It has always been Christians’ custom to pray facing east. For Justin Martyr says, Question 118: “At the time of prayer we all turn our faces toward the east.” And Origen, Homilies on Numbers, Book 5: “Of all the regions of heaven, we turn toward the east alone in offering prayer.” Saint Athanasius gives three reasons for this rite, Book IX, Question 14. First, because it is written: “We shall worship in the place where his feet stood” (Psalm 131); and through Zechariah: “On that day his feet shall stand upon the Mount of Olives to the east” (Zechariah 14). Second: “Because God is light” (1 John 1). Therefore, when praying, we look toward that quarter from which light comes. Third, because Paradise, from which humanity was expelled, lies in the east, and the mind desirous of returning there directs its eyes thither.]

## LETTER LXXXVII. TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT BARTHOLOMEW OF NOYON

He asks him kindly to receive a certain fugitive canon and show mercy toward him.

[Col. 0382A]

To the lord and father, the venerable abbot of Saint Bartholomew of Noyon: from one already growing old, wishes for good days and a happy end.

One of those whose number is infinite—Robert, formerly yours—came to us in a misshapen guise and presented to our brethren a pitiable spectacle, by which they might both be moved at the sight and instructed by the example. Covered with a cheap and short cloak, which gave neither the appearance of a garment to one looking at it nor the benefit or service of a covering to the wearer, he struck us with horror by his error, inspired fear by his fortune, and invited mercy by his misery.

[Note: [Col. 0382D] He alludes to what is said in Ecclesiastes 10: “The number of fools is infinite.” He is speaking of a certain canon of Saint Bartholomew of Noyon who, led by instability of mind, had deserted the cloister.]

A merely natural man, not perceiving the things that are of God—one to whom neither affliction gives understanding nor labour is fashioned by a command—believes this one plea sufficient for himself: either that he may find persons freely merciful, or that he may not conceal his calamity from those who look upon it.

For his sake, excellent Father, we offer you earnest prayers of compassion: kindly receive and generously restore this wretched man—an autumnal tree, salt that has lost its savour, a dead dog, a living gnat—who has experienced the deceits of his own fickleness and has not been spared its pains. Thus let not, through you, a bruised reed be broken in him or smoking flax extinguished. I should think myself troublesome to you if I had ever perceived you to be troubled. I trust that neither the folly of this man for whom I plead diminishes your clemency, nor my importunity causes you offence.

## LETTER LXXXVIII. TO THE PRIOR AND BRETHREN OF CHARITÉ

He offers prayers for a certain fugitive monk.

To the prior and holy community of Charité, Stephen of Sainte-Geneviève: greetings, and spiritual increase accompanied by joy.

As I recall the delightful memory of you, I receive a fruitful assurance in my conscience, knowing that I am counted among your own and have deserved to be enriched by you. The most ample bosom of your charity adds confidence to my petitions, so that I dare ask of you what piety ought to grant and charity ought not to refuse.

[Col. 0383A] The bearer of this letter, once one of our canons, led by a slippery counsel, went out from us though he was of us. Having begun, like a fool, to wander after the flocks of his companions, he shortly returned to himself and came weeping, imploring pardon, after the slight chill had subsided.

[Note: [Col. 0383D] *Frigusculum*, in Ulpian, denotes a slight estrangement sometimes arising between spouses or friends, what we call in French *froideur* (“coolness”). Here it is understood as a certain sullenness of mind, as though he said: after the movement of an obstinate mind had been calmed.]

Having found some of ours not devoid of compassion, he sought through the prayers of many to reopen the way of return that had been closed to him; yet he cannot return to the house from which he went out. Sent by us to the depths of your mercy, he both seeks and expects to be filled from the breasts of so great a consolation.

I ask for him, as you may remember, being some small portion of your friends: receive kindly and generously, for the love of God and of us, this man who strives to ascend to your stricter and higher order, lest we have poured out our prayers in vain—we who hope for greater things from your grace. Moreover, lest you judge his manner of life burdensome and useless, we testify that he is trained in the divine offices of singing and reading, and instructed in regular discipline.

## LETTER LXXXIX. TO THE LORD POPE

He pleads for an acolyte ordained by a schismatic bishop.

Ignorance is excusable when either the weakness of age or the simplicity of innocence commonly produces it. It departs so far from malice that it approaches gentleness; it so approaches pardon that it does not kindle severity. This ignorance, Father—whether it proceeds from weakness of age or arises from innocent simplicity—the common mother, the Roman Church, has always endeavoured to relieve and assist in such a way that dispensation tempers rigour and justice does not abandon dispensation.

These considerations move and instruct me, your least servant, to offer prayers to your holy fatherhood for Odo, the cleric who bears this letter, together with the others who ask you on his behalf—prayers which proceed from charity and will benefit charity. In his boyhood he somehow received the rank of acolyte from Herbert, the schismatic of Besançon, after he had previously been made a cleric by a Catholic. Poor man, he did not know how much danger that leprous hand brought upon him, both then and for the future. I beg that the fatherly eye of apostolic mercy be opened over him, and that the motherly bosom of the Roman Church be spread wide, so that he who erred in receiving the minor orders may be enabled humbly to advance to the greater ones. Farewell.

[Note: [Col. 0383D] Herbert was intruded into the see of Besançon by Emperor Frederick, who had departed from the party of Alexander III, the legitimate pope, and he occupied it for about eight years. In a certain charter of William II, archbishop of the same see, it is read that privileges granted by Humbert to the monastery of Saint Vincent had long remained unknown because of the prohibition of Herbert the schismatic, who, as an apostate, acted as archbishop of Besançon in fact but not in law.

The author of the Life of Saint Peter of Tarentaise describes his ill-fated death as follows: “When at that time that most holy bishop arrived at Besançon, a multitude gathered to him from every side. Among other things, speaking about the aforesaid heretic Herbert, fearing neither his malice nor the presence of the emperor by whom he was supported, he ordered prayer by all, that the hand of the Lord might hasten either to free the Church from that man’s tyranny by changing him or by punishing him—so that he might be converted to repentance or removed from the midst. Prayer was offered, and within four or five days that same schismatic breathed out his wretched soul.”]

## LETTER XC. TO LUCIUS, POPE

He asks that Hervaeus, a cleric, be enabled to enjoy a benefice.

Youth is praiseworthy when both uprightness of character and learning bear witness to it. By God’s grace these qualities, as far as we understand, so belong to and meet in Hervaeus the subdeacon, the bearer of this letter, that they suffice for his merit and serve as an example for others. Hence we offer prayers for him with greater confidence: since he has no benefice in the Church, may you open to him a bosom at once kindly and generous, that he may be satisfied at the breasts of your consolation with the desired comfort of his hope.

The practice he has imbibed from childhood makes him fit for the divine offices; and he ought to live fully from the sanctuary who fully knows how to serve the sanctuary. Pope Alexander of happy memory wrote on his behalf to the dean and canons of Saint Anianus of Orléans. You too wrote once and twice. Yet they were unwilling to heed either your prayers or your command, although three prebends were vacant. God forbid, Father, that your prayers should be empty, your authority contemptible, or your command a subject of mockery. Rather, may your majesty now at last thunder over them with such force, if it please you, that those whom kindness could not help may learn to be overcome by command. Receive, if it please you, the requests that we present to you through him, to be fulfilled; and send them back fulfilled.

## LETTER XCI. TO HENRY, BISHOP OF SENLIS

He declares himself ready for the bishop’s commands.

Welcome is the occasion that either grants me your presence or recalls it to mind. I always kiss it when it is offered and embrace it when it is yet to come. But because the chapter of Senlis and the abbot of Saint Vincent, without mentioning you, directed me through Peter de Valle to come to them, setting aside every excuse and delay, at the chapter hour in the octave of Epiphany, concerning a certain agreement which, as they say, must be made between you and them that day under a compromise, I was both surprised and delayed. For I ought not to have hastened without your command, lest I appear either wanting in duty or idle.

[Note: [Col. 0384D] This abbey was established at Senlis in honour of Saint Vincent by Queen Anne, wife of Henry I, king of the Franks, in 1059: “That there, men of religion, quiet and peaceful, serving the Lord and renouncing the world, may be able canonically to embrace and live the regular life—that is, the written rule of the holy apostles and of blessed Augustine.”]

Whenever it pleases your fatherhood, I am ready to appear before you and obey you, both in these affairs and in others. If you invite me, you will not find me unwilling. Far be it that my most beloved Father should find me unwilling whenever he invites me to come. Yet I shall more freely and gladly present myself to you, if it please you, on Wednesday or Friday of the following week.

## LETTER XCII. TO WILLIAM OF ORLÉANS, SCRIBE OF THE LORD POPE

He explains what he did at Meung concerning a benefice granted to William by the pope.

[Col. 0385B]

Happy are the successes of youth when necessity imposes labour upon it and usefulness draws fruit from that labour. In these things I take delight and rejoice with you: following courageous and fortunate spirits, you do not devote the playful years of youth to spectacles but expose them to dangers. As though not accepted in your own country with the prophets, you seek and await from the holy apostolic see a benefice earned by the sweat of your brow. May the Lord advance and fulfil your desire, so that your friends may rejoice in the increase of your favour and your rivals be confounded.

In accordance with the lord pope’s command, I followed the bishop of Orléans as far as Meung on your business. There, in the presence of the canons of that church, after the papal letters had been read, I first gave thanks to the bishop for the benefice promised to you at the pope’s request. Then, firmly and subsequently, by the authority of the mandate laid upon me, I forbade him to grant the benefice in the church of Meung to anyone else before you; and I forbade the canons to receive or permit anyone but you to be invested as a fellow canon. I declared, by the authority of the lord pope, that any promise, grant, or investiture which the bishop had made or would make concerning the prebend not yet vacant was and would be void.

That man replied obediently, as usual, and promised that he would carry out the pope’s command. The canons murmured and objected on behalf of a wealthy archpriest to whom, as they said, they had assigned thirty solidi in the name of a prebend until the prebend became vacant. In our requests, through yourself and your friends, help us if you can.

[Note: [Col. 0385C] Meung is a town on the Loire in the diocese of Orléans, famous as the birthplace of the celebrated poet Jean Clopinel, from which he was called Jean de Meung. In the History of the Bishops of Auxerre it is written: “Manasses, bishop of Orléans, built at the episcopal castle of Meung—where the bishop had no suitable dwelling of his own—a palace of great nobility, with towers and fortifications: an impregnable defence of the town and a noble residence of the bishop. When he transferred his residence to that castle, he also built stone bridges there and at Jargeau on the Loire.”

[Note: [Col. 0385C] Namely, the collegiate church of Saint Liphard of Meung.

[Col. 0385D] In the Life of this saint in Surius it is said: “In the district of Orléans there was a hill called Meung by the inhabitants of the region. In ancient times a castle had been built there, but the Vandals had entirely destroyed it, so that, as woods grew over the ruins on every side, the place had become a wilderness. There Liphard wove himself a cell out of twigs. Meanwhile Marcus, bishop of Orléans, having heard of the virtues of the man of God, ordained him priest and built there a small church, which survives even to the present day.”

Speaking of Saint Liphard’s death and burial, it says: “When Bishop Marcus heard of the man’s death, he hastened with the greatest speed to his funeral and, together with the brethren, committed his body to religious burial. By his blessing he confirmed Veritius as the future successor in the monastery of Meung; Veritius afterwards raised its structure higher.” This church, therefore, was in ancient times a monastery, as is also recorded in the Constitutions of Theodulf, bishop of Orléans. But when the monks of this community threw off the yoke of regular discipline, they were transformed into secular canons, in precisely the same way as at Orléans the monasteries of Saints Anianus, Avitus, Peter of the men, and Peter of the women.

When this church of Saint Liphard had been destroyed and levelled with the ground by incursions of war, it was restored anew and solemnly dedicated in 1104, in the presence of Ralph, archbishop of Tours; Galon, bishop of Paris; John, bishop of Orléans; Christian, abbot of Saint-Maximin; and others. It has twenty canons and four dignities: dean, cantor, subcantor, and keeper of the cope.]

## LETTER XCIII. TO THE LORD POPE

He asks him kindly to receive the messenger of the canons of Sausseuse.

The seamless tunic of Christ, woven from above throughout, so covers all Christ’s members that it neither rejects the lesser nor fails sufficiently to admit the greater. Covered by this garment of joy and salvation, all who profess the common life under Augustine, father of regulars, are bound to love one another with special charity and to bear one another’s burdens in fraternal necessities.

[Note: [Col. 0386C–D] The monastery of Sausseuse is a priory of the canonical order in the diocese of Rouen, not far from the town of Vernon. This community of canons was founded in 1155 by a certain Richard, parish priest of Tillières, who, having bestowed all his possessions there, embraced the canonical rule with certain devout men of the same purpose.]

[Note: [Col. 0386D] Saint Augustine is called the father and patriarch of regulars, or of canons living in common, for two reasons: either because, following the apostles’ example, he established and conducted that common life among the clerics of the church of Hippo and wrote for their use a treatise and Rule concerning the clerics’ common life; or because those canons called regular adopted the Rule composed by him as the norm of their life. Whether it was first written for men or women, and whether it was received among them in the earlier or later thousand years, is not a matter to be discussed here.]

Therefore, for the brethren of Sausseuse, who serve God according to the Rule, we pour out to your holy fatherhood such prayers as we can: may you receive their messenger kindly and send him back generously provided for. The cheerful report of their holy way of life bears witness to them, and the reputation of their unimpaired fruit so invites others that a friend rejoices and an envious person is tormented.

## LETTER XCIV. TO HENRY, BISHOP OF SENLIS

He pleads for Hubert, the bishop’s chaplain, that he may deign to forgive his offence.

The bosom of charity is not narrow, since it stretches itself out to each individual so as to receive all. It extends itself more carefully to members of the household, burning with those who are scandalized and becoming weak with those who are weak. This, Father, moves and urges me to present a petition for just excuse on behalf of our brother Hubert, your chaplain.

[Note: [Col. 0387D] It is not unprecedented for bishops to take regular canons into their service for ecclesiastical ministries. Henry of Senlis did this all the more willingly because he had chosen Hugh, a regular canon of Sainte-Geneviève, as his chaplain or cleric; Henry himself had professed the canonical life at Saint-Quentin of Beauvais.]

Because of illness he came to us, so that, while caring for himself, he might consult those who deceive the sick with venal aphorisms and discern faults of colour and substance in a glass vessel. Fickleness is excusable when wickedness has not caused it. I beg that the gaze of your gentleness receive him whom the impulse of his own instability and the pressure of a just necessity compelled to come to us. Far be it that he should find your favour diminished, which for so long he deserved to enjoy as generous and kind. If there has been any fault, whether in a slip of the tongue or the scandal of negligence, forgive it for our sake, that we who fear because of the offence may rejoice because of the pardon.

## LETTER XCV. TO THE LORD POPE

He asks him to restrain the disobedience of the canons of Saint John of Soissons who reside in parishes.

[Col. 0387C]

Besides the common afflictions of God’s Church, through which new monsters in our days crucify Christ anew and lavish upon pleasures the revenues of souls belonging to his patrimony, Augustine, father of regulars, cries out that the golden Rule which he had received in turn from the apostles is being plundered, broken, and trampled underfoot. Among the sons of this corruption and madness, like leaders of a deadly cohort, the canons of Saint John of Soissons raise their heads and miserably arrogate to themselves liberty for wrongdoing. They make the Rule a mere thing, display the habit upon themselves, and introduce a secular death.

Armed against their father, they pierce their mother with a mortal wound. Setting him up as a target for the arrow, while neglecting their own reputation they prove even more cruel toward other companions of the same profession. They live disobediently through their obediences; they will neither answer their abbot when he recalls them, nor submit to him when he corrects them, nor believe him when he reproves them. As a covering for this wickedness and as the ground of their excuse they put forward the authority of their bishop, who, contrary to the sacred discipline which they professed, arms and encourages them not to show reverence to their abbot—the reverence which, at the first auspices of their conversion, before God and all his saints, they promised him as sworn soldiers of the heavenly commonwealth.

This disease can receive and obtain a remedy only from your healing hand, since among the cedars of Lebanon the wretched abbot can find not even one which is willing or able to withstand opposite the violent assaults of the oaks of Bashan. By the lord bishop of Paris and the dean of Saint-Germain he had obtained restoration through your authority; yet the bishop would neither observe their sentence—indeed, yours—nor would the canons, children of contradiction, obey the judicial mandates. Let your severity arise, Father—or rather, let truth exert itself—against the stubborn beasts of such insolence. Rescue the poor man from the powerful, for apart from the apostolic see he has no helper, so that by these men’s example others may learn alike to accept discipline and instruction under the obedience of their prelates.

[Note: [Col. 0387D–0388D] The canons of Saint-Germain of Paris, formerly called “the Round” and now “of Auxerre,” at the royal Louvre, were governed by abbots, since this church enjoyed abbatial status, as is recorded in a bull of Alexander III cited by Chopin in *De sacra politica*. But when those canons were granted secular dress, their abbots became deans, as I have elsewhere shown to have happened in many other regular churches of Gaul.]

## LETTER XCVI. TO THE LORD POPE

He commends the abbot of Saint-Satyrus, extolling his life and virtues.

Even to our own time Satan’s sieve is being shaken, as he waits and seeks frequently to sift through sons of contention the children of those who have been sifted. Yet Peter’s faith shall not fail: he strengthens brethren who have turned back, raises Tabitha, heals Aeneas, and strengthens the feet and ankles of the man who asks alms. In this spirit and power we trust that Your Holiness, Father, knows, wills, and is able both to correct the unruly and to console the faint-hearted.

Two wicked sons have departed from the venerable community of Saint-Satyrus—going out from them because they were not of them—and, secretly carrying away certain church property and defiling their impious hands by sacrilege, they have dared, as we hear, to appear before your holy presence. Seeking to deceive your religious judgment with wicked lips and a deceitful tongue, they are neither afraid to report falsehood to you nor ashamed to keep silence about the truth.

They employ a certain Raymond, excommunicated and expelled by the brethren because of grave excesses and seditious acts, the daughters of disobedience. As we have fully learned, he has always been impatient of peace and accustomed to disturb that holy church, glorious among the daughters of Zion before God and humanity. As the common saying has it, he is a serpent among eels, a kite among doves; more truly, by the leaven of his malice and wickedness, he contaminates and attempts, so far as he can, to contaminate the unleavened bread of brotherly sincerity and truth.

We testify truthfully to you, Father, that the abbot’s person is and has been religious, honourable, and prudent; and that for thirty-five years and more he has faithfully served God in that church and in the churches of Saint Ambrose and Saint Evurtius—first as subprior in one and afterwards as abbot in the other—in the sight of human beings and, as we believe, of angels.

[Note: [Col. 0389D] The abbey of Saint Ambrose of Bourges, of ancient foundation and of the canonical order, was restored by Geoffrey, Viscount of Bourges, in 1012. Regular canons of Saint-Victor of Paris were later introduced into it.]

May the severity of your holy fatherhood drive out and terrify from its presence the aforesaid sons of wickedness, so that they may not continue to harm an innocent man or prevail, under any covering of their lies, against that church, terrible as an army arrayed for battle. Down to this day it has shone among its sister churches, as a mirror and exemplar, by its pre-eminent title of religious life, divine services, and regular discipline.

## LETTER XCVII. TO THE LORD POPE

He commends the monks of Compiègne and asks that they be protected against their attackers.

[Note: [Col. 0389D–0390D] The celebrated monastery of Saint Mary and Saints Cornelius and Cyprian in Compiègne was restored by Emperor Charles the Bald, as noted in his Capitularies, title 43, no. 2: “Let the monastery which we have built at Compiègne in honour of Saint Mary be honoured by our son and our faithful men according to the tenor in which we began it.” But the canons dwelling there had so departed from the straight path of religious life that Suger, writing to Pope Eugenius, says that this church would be among the noblest in Gaul if the notorious enormity of the canons did not stand in the way.

Moved by this, the same supreme pontiff ordered the aforesaid Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, to reform the churches of Sainte-Geneviève of Paris and Saint-Cornelius of Compiègne into a better state. In obedience to the apostolic letters, as Suger had introduced Victorine canons into the former in 1148, so he brought his monks of Saint-Denis into the latter in 1150. Yet this restored monastic observance did not long flourish among them; after about thirty years it still had to be restored by the bishop of Senlis and the abbots of Saint-Germain-des-Prés and Ourscamp, as we learn from this letter.]

[Col. 0389B]

To the most holy lord and father, the supreme pontiff, Stephen of Sainte-Geneviève: greetings and renewed obedience in all things.

We have recourse to the bosom of your fatherly concern whenever either our own need presses us or fraternal charity persuades us. Therefore, at the request of the abbot and monks of Compiègne, I have perhaps rashly and presumptuously dared to write to your fatherhood, so that, if my merits are insufficient, at least those of others may avail. We have heard that through the care and industry, enjoined upon them by you, of the lord bishop of Senlis, the abbot of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, and the abbot of Ourscamp, the aforesaid monastery has begun to be reformed into a better state and, as we have more fully understood from the bishop’s letters, to produce for itself both progress and advancement before God and humanity.

Therefore I, the least portion of your flock, rejoicing fraternally in the merits of which I hear, pour out prayers to your mercy: may you kindly hear the messengers of the aforesaid brethren and send them back generously provided for. If anyone should try to stir or advise Your Holiness against them, may your serenity, if it please you—as you have always been accustomed—not admit the matters advanced from the opposing side against the liberty of the Church and monastic discipline.

## LETTER XCVIII. TO GEOFFREY, ABBOT OF SAINT-SATYRUS

He asks him kindly to receive a certain canon of Sainte-Geneviève who desired to live at Saint-Satyrus.

Desires are to be helped when devotion gives them their beginning and discernment their advance; one should neither obstruct their beginnings, disparage their middle stages, nor begrudge their fulfilment. Observing these things in our most dear brother and fellow canon John, a young man of good natural disposition and, we believe, fruitful future promise, we have received with grateful assent his commendable wish to live among you and, through your example, to be more fully formed in regular discipline. We send and entrust him to your holiness for a time.

We offer prayers for him, that while he dwells among your brethren you may preserve him with fatherly care, at once kindly and generously. If meanwhile an opportunity occurs for him to be ordained deacon in the church of Saint Geneviève the Virgin, you may present him to your archbishop or to another Catholic bishop. In due course, when his age requires it, he may, God willing, be advanced through your church to a higher rank.

## LETTER XCIX. TO THE MASTER, ARCHDEACON OF CAMBRAI

He announces that he has set out on a journey to meet his lord.

[Col. 0390C]

Obedient to my lord at the hearing of his word, I came to Paris very early this Saturday morning. Since daylight still sufficed for travelling, because our malice was not quite sufficient for the day, I stopped with my body weary, admitting and restoring sleep through the night watches, lest I fail on the road, making little progress while setting out for a great distance. Yet I shall proceed, lest I fail to render service to my lord. Taking a little sleep at Épinay, tomorrow, God willing, about the third hour, I shall appear before my lord. Send word to me through the bearer of this letter where I shall find you when I arrive, intending to purge my excusable delay under my lord’s rod.

[Note: [Col. 0390D] Spinogilum or Spinolium, commonly Épinay, is a village in the diocese of Paris, not far from Corbeil, subject in both spiritual and temporal lordship to the church of Sainte-Geneviève.]

## LETTER C. TO MANASSES, BISHOP OF ORLÉANS

He urges him not to delay payment of a certain debt.

[Col. 0391A]

To Manasses, by the grace of God bishop of Orléans, Stephen of Sainte-Geneviève: greetings and faithful service.

[Note: [Col. 0391C–D] Manasses of Garlande, nephew of Stephen of Garlande, formerly dean of Orléans, concerning whom Saint Bernard often writes in his letters, was descended from the noble Garlande family of Gournay-sur-Marne. He was appointed bishop of Orléans in 1146 and was kindly and generously disposed toward the regular canons of Saint Evurtius, so that he finally wished to be buried among them in the middle of the chapter.]

At your request, which you conveyed to me through your cleric Lord Odo and then expressed in your own words when I was with you, I granted you a delay in the case of Master Benedict, acolyte of the holy Roman Church, hoping better things from you and a nearer approach to peace. In confidence of this hope, the aforesaid Benedict came to you. If you satisfy him concerning what is owed to him, you will both protect your reputation and spare your honour. For, trusting in an episcopal word, he considers your statement as binding as an oath, and likewise judges an outcome contrary to that statement to be sacrilege.

Satisfy him, Father, either in full or at least in part of the debt, lest I be compelled, by command of the lord pope, to proceed to a sentence troublesome to you. For unwillingness to comply with apostolic commands is the sin of divination, and unwillingness to obey is the crime of idolatry. Unwillingly I shall offend your old age, but I fear that the pope will punish my disobedience. For if it comes to the pope’s ears either that you have not paid or that I have failed in my duty, offended and indignant he will apply the final hand, and thus, I fear, strike us both, so that your punishment will not excuse my negligence.

## LETTER CI. PHILIP, KING OF THE FRANKS, TO THE SUPREME PONTIFF

He asks him to place complete trust in Stephen, whom he sends to Rome on business that he has entrusted to him.

To the most reverend father and lord, by the grace of God supreme pontiff: Philip, by the same grace king of the Franks, due reverence with the highest devotion.

The constant devotion of our kingdom to the Roman Church has deserved both easy access to petition before you and a fortunate return from you. Let the present times, Father, vie with and answer to the days of old, so that the kingdom may not fail the priesthood, nor the priesthood the kingdom. Powerful men assail our youth and strive to disturb the auspices of our reign; and those who, for many reasons, ought to have kept faith with us have become faithless adversaries. Their wickedness compels us both to seek new counsels and to summon aid.

[Note: That is, Philip, count of Flanders, with whom he waged wars in order to recover the county of Vermandois, which the Belgian had usurped. Of this war Rigord writes: “Accordingly, in the fifth year of Philip Augustus’s reign, the twentieth year of his life, he marched out with an army through all that land, and they covered the face of the earth like locusts. When the count of Flanders saw the king’s great and strong army, his spirit was greatly crushed, and the heart of his people melted away as they sought the refuge of flight,” etc.]

Above all our friends and faithful men stands by us our dearest uncle William, archbishop of Rheims: a watchful eye in our counsels, a right hand in our affairs. For him to withdraw from us, even temporarily, is for him to join our enemies, who, as they desire and expect us to be without arms, so also, in their faithless wishes, they irreverently desire and expect us to be without friends.

[Note: That is, William of Champagne, archbishop of Rheims and cardinal legate, son of Theobald the Elder, count of Champagne. The latter had given his daughter Adela in marriage to King Louis VII; by her he had Philip Augustus. William was therefore Philip’s uncle. We have discussed him above.]

You have summoned him, Father, as we have heard, and by your sacred letters invited him to present himself before you. He was ready to obey and to appear before you, comparing disobedience with the image of the sin of divination, and detesting the will not to comply with you as the crime of idolatry. Yet, at this moment of our utmost necessity, trusting in your especial affection, we have retained him: a nail in the eyes of our enemies and a spear in their sides. Without him we judge that nothing can be done, whether peace or war with our enemies must be considered.

Receive, Father, our prayers—the prayers of your son, whom you have always loved from his cradle. Since before our birth you kindly desired our coming forth, by your beneficent authority restrain those who desire our downfall.

[Note: When Louis VII had had two wives who bore no male offspring, and had taken a third, Adela, who had already remained four years without children and appeared barren, “the king,” says Rigord, “with his wife Adela, and all the clergy and all the people of the whole kingdom, turned to prayers and almsgiving and asked God for a son, not boasting of his own merits, but trusting solely in God’s mercy. Their prayers were heard in the sight of the Lord, and a son named Philip was given him by God; for this reason he was called Adeodatus [God-given].”]

Let it be acceptable to you, Father, that amid so great a peril to the kingdom we retain so great a friend, whose presence is most necessary to us and whose absence most ruinous. And because this matter is great and deeply planted in our heart, we send to you our most beloved and intimate associate Stephen, abbot of St Geneviève, prudent and faithful to the kingdom. Receive him kindly in our place, and place unhesitating faith in him as in ourselves in those things which he shall tell you on our behalf.

[Note: From this letter one may infer how highly our Stephen, then abbot of St Geneviève, was valued by kings, princes, and magnates.]

## 147. LETTER CII. STEPHEN TO CARDINAL OCTAVIAN

[Note: This heading is supplied by Royal Library manuscript no. 2923.]

He relates how certain Apulians cleared themselves before Roman scholars.

[Col. 0393A]

A third tongue disturbs brothers and entangles the friendly harmony of simplicity in the scandal of dissension. We believe that this happened between certain Roman scholars and citizens—N., nephew of the lord pope, and G., nephew of Lord Hyacinth—with certain others, and certain Apulians: namely B., nephew of Lord Pope G. of good memory; another B.; and a certain John of Naples. The occasion was certain letters which, it was said, the aforesaid Apulians had presumed to send to the curia for the disparagement and defamation of the aforesaid noble Romans.

By their mutual consent, the aforesaid Apulians, who were reported to have written defamatory letters, came before us and into our presence. Frequently and earnestly excusing themselves, and having touched the most holy Gospels, they swore that they had never written either those letters or any others against the persons named above; that they had neither given consent or counsel for such letters to be written, nor had any knowledge of the matter. At the wish of both parties we have written to you, so that the innocence of the former may be cleared before you and the indignation of the latter remitted toward them.

## 148. LETTER CIII. TO ALBERT THE CARDINAL, CHANCELLOR OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH

[Note: From the same manuscript.]

He reports how he made peace between certain persons quarrelling among themselves.

[Col. 0393C]

In carrying out your command, Father, we proceeded with such diligence as we could. Having summoned before us your nephews B. and E., we found that the matter of their quarrels had been stirred more by high spirits than malice, less by hatred than by youthful frivolity. Once the complaints of each side had been heard, within the space of a brief hour the entire cause of dissension was settled, with a remedy at once gentle and slight, and through our labor. At the first words of our reproof and correction, the tractable youth of both complied. Before us they exchanged the brotherly kiss, which we understood as the surest sign of peace.

As for your instruction in your letters that we should inform you more fully concerning their habits and conduct, may your holy fatherhood pardon us. We devote what little attention we can to the churches entrusted to us; we neither wish nor ought to be censors of others, examining their habits and actions. They, separated from us, devote themselves in the city to scholastic learning; we, outside the city, to cloistered disciplines. All the brethren greet you with a common longing, hoping for prosperity for you and fearing adversity. Farewell, as we desire.

## 149. LETTER CIV. TO PRIOR RAYMOND

He informs him of the state of his health.

Stephen, abbot of St Geneviève, to Prior Raymond: the health which he desires.

Having set out on my journey, I suffered a feverish attack throughout the night on Friday; early in the morning I arrived at Troyes.

[Note: He was setting out for Rome, whither he had been delegated by the king, as appears from the preceding Letter 101.]

Having greeted the lord archbishop, I rested that Sunday in the house of our John. Meanwhile, by God’s grace, the attack did not recur.

[Note: That is, an attack of fever; in French, accès de fièvre.]

Only the remnants of heat and thirst trouble me; but I hope shortly for better things, nearer to recovery. On Monday morning the lord archbishop went to Dijon, while I went to the abbey of Ripatorium.

[Note: The monastery of Ripatorium, commonly La Rivour, a Cistercian daughter-house of Clairvaux in the diocese of Troyes. At the request of St Bernard it was founded in 1140 by Haton, bishop of that city. Its first superior was Alan, later elected bishop of Auxerre.]

I am going to Clairvaux.

[Note: The abbey of Clairvaux is celebrated throughout the world for the life, death, and ashes of St Bernard.]

I shall remain there for a little while, and through God’s mercy and the prayers of the saints shall recover my health completely. Greet all our brethren—each one among all, and all among each one.

## 150. LETTER CV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS

He asks on behalf of Master Hugh that he may obtain a benefice.

How much I owe you, Father, both my memory witnesses and my conscience judges. You freely admitted me into the secret places of your counsels, and showed me paternal concern both when I was well and when I was ill. Some believe that I enjoy favor in your eyes and that my prayers avail for them with you; they measure this by their own wishes, not by my measure.

One of them is Master Hugh of Novara, an old friend and a clerk of yours. On behalf of his clerk you offered your prayers, both orally and in writing, to Lord G., archdeacon. Since I remember nothing which your hand has begun and left incomplete, I—the least portion of your clerks—ask that, because your prayers have not yet obtained their effect, you add weight to them, so that through you your faithful and honorable friend may attain his desire, and the clerk may obtain the church which he expects to receive through your generosity.

## LETTER CVI. TO LORD ALBINUS, CARDINAL PRIEST

[Note: Albinus, a Milanese regular canon of the monastery of St Mary of Crescenzago, was first cardinal deacon of St Mary the New; then, created cardinal priest by Lucius III; and finally made bishop of Albano by Clement III. He published a book entitled *Collection of Canons*. Geoffrey, monk of Clairvaux, wrote to him the acts of the Council of Rheims. He died about 1198.]

He sends him a new, full-length surplice.

[Col. 0394D]

I have exchanged few words with you, Father, but have gained much fruit: I learned humility and drank in gentleness. If I do not remember your gravity, I shall incur frivolity. Yet greed excluded and frugality enclosed showed me that you are a disciple of Augustine. By God’s grace you so wear the religious habit outwardly that you preserve it inwardly. I send you a principal token of this habit: a new, white, full-length surplice, representing for you newness of life, the whiteness of purity, and perseverance unto the end.

[Note: A *superpelliceum* is the linen garment worn over other clothing by canons. It acquired this name because ancient canons wore it over a robe made from lambskins, by which they kept off winter cold while occupied with divine worship in church. This surplice reached to the ankles and resembled the alb used by priests when celebrating the sacred sacrifice of the Mass. Hence it was forbidden by a synod at Soissons, convened under Riculf in 889, “that priests should use in the sacred mysteries that alb which is for daily and outward use.” And at the Council of Constance: “clerics are to wear a surplice extending below the middle of the calves.” We have seen such garments with our own eyes among the ancient regular canons of St Denis at Rheims.]

Receive, Father, this small token from your son, valuing less the price of the cloth than either the sender’s intention or the sacramental meaning of the gift. And since, on the feast of the blessed virgin Geneviève, I gave our brethren a moral exposition of the mystical making of the surplice, with the material surplice I send you also the moral one, so that the gift may be accepted through the sermon, and the sermon through the gift.

[Note: This sermon is the last among the sermons of our Stephen. Its theme is the following words from Wisdom 31: “She sought wool and flax, and wrought with the work of her hands.” It portrays St Geneviève seeking from the Blessed Virgin Mary the flax of purity with which to weave a surplice for her new regular canons, and from blessed Mary Magdalene the wool of penitence with which to make them cloaks.]

## 152. LETTER CVII. PHILIP, KING OF THE FRANKS, TO POPE LUCIUS III

He asks him to protect the cause of the archbishop of Tours against the bishop of Dol, who claimed for himself the title of archbishop.

To the most holy lord and Father Lucius, supreme pontiff: Philip, by God’s grace king of the Franks, greeting and due reverence with all devotion.

If a mother can forget the children of her womb, and the Roman Church forget the kingdom of the Franks—although each is legally impossible, naturally difficult, and in fact monstrous. What more ought we to have done for our mother that we have not done? Down to the present day, in our lands, we have rejoiced with her when she rejoiced and wept with her when she wept; without the idol of rivalry or discord, we have drunk together both cups, of suffering and of joy.

[Note: Whenever supreme pontiffs were oppressed or expelled, they sought refuge with the kings of France. Stephen II, harassed by Aistulf, king of the Lombards, was received by Pippin and restored to his see and all his dominions. Charlemagne did the same for Leo III, when he was attacked by certain seditious Romans, and thereby earned the title Defender of the Church. Louis the Pious received and protected Stephen IV when he fled into Gaul because of persecution. Charles the Bald kindly supported John VIII when he sought protection with him. Louis the Fat assisted Gelasius, oppressed by Emperor Henry V, in every way, and protected Innocent II against Anacletus, invader of the papal see. Finally Louis the Younger received Alexander III when he came as an exile into these regions, and vigorously defended his cause against Octavian, the antipope, and Emperor Frederick. King Philip sets this service before Pope Lucius in this letter when he says: “And because you know all these things better, Father, and shared in the consolation afforded to our father Alexander, of holy memory, both in another’s persecution and in your own.”]

The kings of the Franks, our fathers, bore her persecutions—which occurred more frequently—upon strong shoulders and defended her with outstretched arms. To set forth examples is to recall benefits; those upon whom they were bestowed ought to remember them, not those who conferred them. And because you know all these things better, Father, and shared both in the comfort afforded during another’s persecution and in your own, in our father Alexander of holy memory, we lay before you with more secure confidence those matters which concern the glory of our crown or its shame and loss, so that we may obtain consolation from the fullness of your counsel and aid.

That the Church of Tours has always been ours and our fathers’ is affirmed both by the memory of those now living and the annals of the ancients. He who presided over the Church of Tours has hitherto been metropolitan of all Lesser Brittany; in him the furthest regions of our kingdom, as far as the Ocean, find their resting place. Behold, Father: in the days of our youth we are attacked not only by those who practice armed warfare, but also by those called to the Lord’s inheritance. The clerics of Dol seek, perhaps not without deceit, to inflict pain upon us, attempting to break the ancient crown upon our tender head.

[Note: That is, Philip, count of Flanders, mentioned above.]

[Note: On the controversy between the archbishop of Tours and the bishop of Dol, who aspired to archiepiscopal dignity, see what we have said on Letter 39.]

At the suggestion and, it is said, with the favor of some person, you have summoned within the straits of a very brief period our most dear and faithful archbishop of Tours, to answer concerning a cause which is more ours than his; and thus to put the condition of our crown into an uncertain balance—surely dangerous and shameful to us and to our successors. Therefore from our whole heart we pour forth prayers to your holiness: for the sake of God and of the peace of the kingdom of the Franks, which, if this matter proceeds, will perish at this point, abandon this cause entirely.

Rather, as in the times of our predecessors the Church of Tours held its metropolitan authority throughout Lesser Brittany, so let it hold and preserve it in our days, which you neither ought nor wish to disturb. But if, contrary to our belief, we find you inexorable, let your kindness grant delays to our archbishop of Tours until a suitable time, when the Lord may be pleased to give peace and quiet to our kingdom. For we have retained him for causes necessary to our kingdom: first, because of the most difficult war we are waging with the count of Flanders; second, because of disturbances more than civil that have arisen in the province of Brittany among the princes of that province and the sons of the king of England; third, because of the approaching date for the conference which, God willing, we are to hold with the emperor after Easter. In all these matters we need the archbishop’s skill, presence, counsel, and aid.

[Note: Rigord speaks of this assembly under the year 1184: “Philip, most Christian king of the Franks, summoned all the archbishops, abbots, counts, and all the barons, who unanimously assembled to tame the savagery of that count of Flanders and break his pride.”]

Know, moreover, holy Father, that in our general assembly, which at the beginning of Lent we summoned at Paris on account of this matter and other necessities of the kingdom, we retained the aforesaid archbishop from the journey he had begun, since he was necessary to us and useful to the undertakings begun and, by God’s grace, to be completed for the honor of our kingdom. We have sent to you as bearers of this letter our faithful men, the abbot of Sarcocellum and Master P., your and our intimate associate and Parisian clerk, so that you may believe them in what they say to you on our behalf, and may, if you please, send us back your will through them.

[Note: Sarcocellum, or Sacra Cella, in French Cercanceau, is a Cistercian abbey in the diocese of Sens, founded by Philip Augustus himself in 1181.]

## 155. LETTER CVIII. TO THE SAME, IN THE PERSON OF KING PHILIP

He commends the same cause of the archbishop of Tours.

Finding your paternal bowels closed to us and to the kingdom of the Franks, hitherto the Roman Church’s most faithful kingdom, even with respect to the delay which we requested for the Church of Tours; and now experiencing your inexorable mind, not without our disgrace, we call heaven and earth to witness. Thus, if ever we close our royal ears to you or to your brethren, we may appear excusable before God and men.

We looked for your peace, and behold disturbance. In the injury to the Church of Tours—which in the time of our fathers held unimpaired metropolitan jurisdiction throughout Lesser Brittany—the Roman Church strives shamefully to diminish and mutilate our kingdom, to cast the crown from our head, break it, and trample it underfoot. For what else is it to wish to establish an archbishop in the same province against its metropolitan and against the integrity of our kingdom, than to expel and drive us from the inheritance of our fathers as weak men unable to resist?

May the Lord see and judge that, if this deed proceeds, henceforth we shall esteem you less as a father than as a stepfather, and you shall find us less a son than a stepson. This sword will pierce even to our soul, so that, disinherited, we shall cry out; stripped bare, we shall lament; despised and rejected by you, we shall await at some time God’s and men’s vengeance. For this blow will wound not us alone, but will also inflame all the barons of the whole kingdom to compassion, so that the Lord may one day demand from your hand the blood which can therefore be shed; and may impute to those who deserve it the occasion of secession and perpetual war which may arise between the kingdom and the chief princes of the kingdom.

From examples of the past, indeed, we infer the material of the future. And as in ancient times much blood was shed on the occasion of this dissension, so in our own days, unless your prudence swiftly meets the coming disease, common disaster and a general slaughter between Franks and Bretons may be stirred up. It is better to meet it in time than to exact vengeance after the event.

## 157. LETTER CIX. TO LORD OCTAVIAN, IN THE PERSON OF KING PHILIP

He complains that the Roman curia is insufficiently well disposed toward him.

Unwillingly we are compelled today to invoke heaven and earth and stir them up as witnesses on our behalf, because our youth is irreverently attacked. Here ecclesiastical fathers, there secular princes assail us; and, contrary to all expectation, we find the Roman Church hostile to us. This sword descends even to our soul when those who at least ought to have defended our royal crown by Peter’s sword stretch out their hands to break it.

Against the Church of Tours, which is ours, the apostolic see strives to set up in Lesser Brittany an archbishop of Dol, and to injure, diminish, and cut away the integrity of our kingdom, which remained unharmed in the times of our fathers. Such are the rewards for the services of our kingdom. Such are the recompenses and thanksgivings for the devotion and faith which our fathers always displayed toward the Roman Church: in every persecution of yours, ready faithfully to command their own men for God’s Church and bravely to resist others.

You seek to stir up the occasion for perpetual dissension and war between us and the western princes of our kingdom, so that, casting aside the reverence which we have hitherto shown the Roman Church, we may answer you with an adverse face. You kindle fires of hatred which, if they grow into flame, will pass unquenchably into embers. Disinherited, despoiled, stripped bare by the Roman Church, so far as you are concerned, we are compelled either to fight dangerously or to go shamefully into exile.

Let your authority oppose such great evils; do not permit recurring examples to be reborn, by which much innocent blood was shed and may again be shed, if, through the favor of some person—as is said—who was not elected bishop of Dol without deceit, you take from us the western parts of our kingdom.

## LETTER CX. TO MASTER MELIOR, CARDINAL, IN THE PERSON OF THE LORD OF RHEIMS

[Note: Melior was a learned man of Gallic nationality, and perhaps archdeacon of Laon, as may be seen above. He was created cardinal of SS. John and Paul by Lucius III in 1185. Rigord thus speaks of his legation to France: “Pope Celestine, at the complaint of the Danes, sent his legates into France—namely Melior, cardinal priest, and Cencius, subdeacon. On arriving at Paris, they convened a council of all the archbishops, bishops, and also abbots of the entire kingdom, in which they treated the reform of the marriage between King Philip and his wife Ingeborg.”]

He commends the same business of the archbishop of Tours.

[Col. 0399A]

We are bound to attend with watchful eye to those things which concern the welfare and peace of the holy Roman Church, and to suppress and destroy, dashing them against the rock like little children, the first stirrings of discord. Because of the controversy between Tours and Dol, so great a bitterness of resentment has entered the mind of the lord king and his princes that, before the archbishops, bishops, and barons of the kingdom, he complains that the Roman Church disinherits him and that the dignity of the Church of Tours, which is his, is diminished and shamefully mutilated otherwise than it was in the time of his fathers.

He declares that the Roman Church is ungrateful to him and his fathers, and forgetful of the benefits it has received up to this time from the kings of the Franks in times of persecution and peace; he says that, in place of a mother, he has received a stepmother. Therefore we warn, ask, and advise your belovedness—upon whom we specially and not without reason rely—that by whatever means you can, you prevent this deed. Do not allow the peace and concord which has hitherto remained inviolate between the Roman Church and the kingdom of the Franks to be disturbed because of favor toward that person who is joined to you by nationality.

For we believe that if the lord pope proceeds in this affair against the Church of Tours, the lord king and all his barons, stirred and armed with indignation, anger, and hatred beyond belief, will be compelled, temporarily laying aside the reverence they owe the Roman Church, to deliberate upon new and dangerous courses. What could rashly be kindled cannot easily be extinguished. It is better to meet it in time than to exact vengeance after the event.

## 161. LETTER CXI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF LONDON

He sends him a flask of theriac.

[Col. 0400A]

Your letter, Father, touched my sense of shame and covered my face with a chastened blush. It recalled that I had been diligent with the lord pope concerning your affairs, and, in the counsels of your envoy Master Tobias, less idle than devoted. It is no small fruit of services when those to whom they have been rendered, especially the powerful and noble, remember them even in a small matter. I am pleased that my service pleased you; by your expression of thanks I am wholly equipped and inflamed for greater things, if occasion does not fail opportunity, or opportunity meets with occasion.

Your Peter—and ours as well—is outstanding among young men for the commendable nobility of his character. As you instructed, so far as the Lord permits us, we admonish him with the words of the Fathers and advance him by the examples of the brethren.

[Note: That learning, easily the chief of all—the discipline now called theology—was once also designated by other names; its teachers were called sometimes masters in divinity, sometimes masters in sacred page. Nor was the name “theology” foreign among them. Abelard says in Letter I: “It happened that I composed for our scholars a certain theological treatise on the divine unity and trinity.” Rigord mentions both names: “They taught sacred page and theological questions.”]

Studying sacred page, he attends the schools of truth in the lecture hall and the schools of virtue in the cloister, so that neither here may he drink in virtue without truth nor there truth without virtue. Suckling at two breasts, he may swiftly be made fat, so that, like a fattened calf or a strong ram, or a son of rams from the Lord’s flock, he too may be offered upon His altar and, whenever it pleases you, may offer sacrifice for others.

[Note: That is, celebrate the sacred sacrifice of the Mass.]

As I considered what I might send you, my lord, nothing occurred to me in which you did not yourself abound. Therefore, amid western riches and delights, I send you an eastern little gift: a flask full of the finest theriac, given me by the archbishop of Messina, a suffragan of the patriarch of Antioch, our fellow canon and friend. It is a quite humble but useful gift, welcome to great and powerful men, whose state of life is fruitful in this world and whose departure from the world is mournful.

[Note: *Tyriaca* or *theriaca* is a most excellent medicinal preparation, a singular remedy against poisons, made from viper flesh and other ingredients. Hence Jerome, *Against Jovinianus*, II, says: “Physicians know how useful are the flesh of vipers, from which theriac is made.” It is thus named ἀπὸ τῶν θηρίων, “from wild beasts,” such as venomous creatures: either because this preparation admits their flesh, or because it counteracts their poisons, as Pliny thinks. Pliny also calls *theriace* a kind of vine growing in Thessaly, because it repels poisons.]

[Note: Messana, commonly Messina, is a very famous city of Sicily. Its citizens were called Mamertines from certain Mamertine barbarians who invaded it in the time of King Agathocles, just as Roman citizens were called Quirites.]

[Note: Rudolph II was at that time patriarch of Antioch, as may be seen in Genebrard’s *Chronology*.]

[Note: There are two kinds of suffragan bishop: one is placed under an archbishop, as the bishop of Meaux is called a suffragan of the archbishop of Paris; the other performs the functions of some pontiff. Thus prince-bishops of the Empire who are not in holy orders appoint suffragan bishops to exercise their offices. We suppose that the bishop of Messina mentioned here was a suffragan of this latter kind in relation to the patriarch of Antioch.]

If anything else should please you which can be found in France, a land free from monsters, we are ready to seek it without concealment and convey it without delay.

[Note: He alludes to what St Jerome wrote in praise of the kingdom of France in his letter against Vigilantius: “Gaul alone has had no monsters, but has always abounded in men most brave and most eloquent.”]
