## 162. LETTER CXII. TO PRIOR RAYMOND OF ST GENEVIÈVE

He asks him to excuse him before his fellow abbots because he cannot be present at the chapter.

Fortuitous occurrences which cannot be foreseen by human judgment, since they depend upon the snares of fortune, the Lord has reserved knowledge of them to Himself alone. I am lying ill at Marisy with a fever [Note: [Col. 0401C] Marisiacum, commonly Marisy, is a village in the diocese of Soissons, belonging to the lordship of St Geneviève and given to that church by the most noble Hermogald, whose anniversary is entered in its obituary on the sixth day before the Kalends of December in these words: “Hermogald, a great man, died; to secure his everlasting remembrance, he enriched this church with the village of Marisy.” The shrine of St Geneviève was deposited there when it was avoiding the imminent slaughter of the Normans. This altar, or parish, was given to the canons of St Geneviève in 1085 by Hilgot, bishop of Soissons, formerly dean of that same church of St Geneviève, as appears from his charter transcribed here: “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Hilgot, by God’s grace bishop of the Church of Soissons, wish it to be known to all faithful of holy mother Church, future as well as present, that Servinus, dean of St Geneviève, together with the other brethren, came before us, humbly praying and requesting [Col. 0401D] that we should grant to the brethren of the aforesaid church, to possess in perpetuity under the present instrument, two altars in our bishopric: one situated in the village of Marisy and dedicated in honour of St Geneviève the virgin; the other consecrated to blessed Vedastus, near La Ferté upon the river Ourcq. Willing fully to comply with their requests, and providing solely from the impulses of charity for the welfare of the church of blessed Geneviève, of which I had been a pupil and dean, I granted those altars to the canons of blessed Gervasius, over whom I presided in pastoral dignity, and personally to the dean of that same church, whoever he may be, with the consent of Hugh, archdeacon of the aforesaid altars, and Gotbert, their archpriest, on this condition: that the canons of the aforesaid virgin St Geneviève should hold those two altars from them in perpetuity, etc. Done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1085, the seventh indiction, epact 22, concurrent II, in the thirty-first year of King Philip’s reign, in the first year of Lord Renaud [Col. 0402B] as archbishop of Reims, and likewise in the year … of Lord Hilgot as bishop of Soissons.”], fearing that, if I undertake a more arduous journey, the additional motion of the vehicle may inflame the danger of illness more violently. I disdain the food offered to me; I neither seek nor desire its presentation. Yet I have a persistent, though not yet excessive, fever and thirst; restless sleep; concentrated urine; pain in the head and limbs; and certain other febrile symptoms, called by their proper names by those who discern faults of colour and substance in a glass vessel. I nevertheless hope that, if I allow myself bodily rest for a few days, better things, nearer to health, will follow through God’s mercy.

Meanwhile, dearest brother, at the approaching general chapter [Note: [Col. 0402B] Every year a general chapter was held of all the superiors and abbots enrolled in the Victorine congregation, as may be seen from the instrument transcribed [Col. 0402C] here: “To all who inspect these present letters: Brother John, humble abbot of St Geneviève of Paris; the abbot of St Evurtius of Orléans; and the abbots of St Mary of Eu, St Mary of Hérivaux, St Mary of Juilly, St Martin of Ruricourt, St Mary of Cagia of Meaux, St John of Jard, and St Mary of Cantiprat—to all who inspect these present letters, greeting in the Lord. We wish it to be known that if it should happen, as commonly happens, that a canon leaves an abbey of our order for any reason without the leave or command of his abbot, or is even cast out of our society for his sin, as the venerable Father Augustine says in our Rule, lest he destroy very many by a pestilential contagion, and if such a brother is afterwards mercifully received, he cannot lawfully claim a stall or anything else—especially since this is the approved custom in our mother church, namely St Victor of Paris, from which we have all received [Col. 0402D] our order and habit: that a canon who, as stated, has departed and slept outside the monastery for even one night shall thereafter never recover his former status, as a perpetual memorial of his transgression. Done in the provincial chapter, in the year of grace 1224, in May, on the Sunday upon which is sung: ‘Sing unto the Lord.’”], supply my place in the assembly, so that you may hear and understand what is being said. For the Lord has given you understanding in all these matters [Col. 0402A]. And because my absence proceeds not from choice but from necessity, I ask you to excuse me before our lords and fellow abbots. Greet in our name all our dearest and most beloved brethren, who alone are my crown and my joy in the Lord. Farewell, and pray that I may recover.

### 163–164. LETTER CXIII. TO L., CARDINAL OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH

[Note: [Col. 0402D] The letter L. unquestionably denotes Laborans, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, priest of St Mary in Portico, created in 1179. He compiled a most elaborate collection of canons in 1182; therefore this priest was sent to him as to a most learned jurist.]

He asks that a dispensation for receiving holy orders be granted to a certain judge of the count of Flanders.

Whenever I recall the pleasant memory of you, Father, I derive a fruitful consolation of conscience from the fact that, within a brief period of time, you both gladdened me by word and built me up by example. I shall run and make progress in the fragrance of your virtues [Col. 0402B]; but if I do not attain perfection, this must be attributed more to my negligence than to your instruction. Meanwhile I entreat you for the bearer of this letter. Having consulted me, he has been sent by me to seek your counsel, and awaits from the sacred oracle of your wisdom an answer alike salutary and wise.

For a long time, in the service of the count of Flanders, he exercised civil jurisdiction up to its full severity [Note: [Col. 0402D] That is, up to a punishment inflicted on the body, which some call *imperium mixtum*, comprising civil and capital jurisdiction together.], in a representative capacity [Note: [Col. 0402D] That is, he performed the office of examiner and prosecutor for the public treasury and the prince; in French, *procureur fiscal*.]. By virtue of the office he had undertaken, he was obliged [Col. 0403A] both to acquit the innocent and to condemn the guilty. Yet, as he himself confesses, he condemned no one by his own utterance to the shedding of blood. Rather, those who confessed to or were convicted of a crime he handed over to the commune of Amiens, to which jurisdiction in cases of blood belongs, so that, according to the offender’s desert, they might be judged and punished. There followed the capital punishment of many: some were hanged, others, as the custom required for persons so condemned, were put to death in another manner. Yet he handed over no one to that commune for judgment or condemnation through hatred, money, or any other motive contrary to justice.

Having returned to himself, he renounced all these things; and, conceiving in his heart fruits worthy of repentance, he desires and earnestly seeks to serve God in the priestly order. Receive his desire [Col. 0403B] and give him salutary counsel. Temper the severity of the rule by a dispensation, lest he be swallowed up by sorrow if the way to the divine mystery is closed to one who so laments what he has done that he admits nothing further to lament.

### LETTER CXIV. TO THE DEAN AND CHAPTER OF HOLY CROSS, ORLÉANS

He urges them to show goodwill to a certain cleric, on whose behalf the pope had written to them.

You ought to receive the fatherly prayers, admonitions, and commands of the lord pope with such gladness and diligence that your obedience may procure for you both divine and human favour. And since the supreme pontiff has written to you—admonishing, [Col. 0403C] requesting, and commanding—on behalf of John, the bearer of this letter, your cleric, nurtured and educated in your church, I too, as your cleric and friend, admonish and advise you to open to him, in the matter of this cleric’s petition, a hand both willing and beneficent. For not to comply with so great a Father is to perish; not to obey is to die.

Let the not dishonourable poverty of this same cleric, his not obscure birth, and his not unlettered youth move and admonish you alike. To add weight and urgency to this petition, the lord [Col. 0404A] pope has entrusted the matter to the lord archbishop of Reims, joining my insignificance to so great a power as Hylas to Hercules and a nettle to a lily. If you prove remiss, he will execute the apostolic command no less swiftly than powerfully. Let your prudence know, moreover, that a spontaneous benefit is more welcome than an involuntary one, and a free gift than one extorted.

### LETTER CXV. TO FULCO, MASTER OF THE SCHOOLS OF HOLY CROSS, ORLÉANS

[Note: [Col. 0403C] Since councils decreed that younger persons should be taught both sacred and secular disciplines, as is read in canon 10 of the Council of Tull, held in 859 under Charles the Bald: “Public schools are to be established everywhere, so that in God’s Church the fruit of both kinds of learning, divine and human, may increase.” We also read in the Capitularies [Col. 0403D] of Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, chapter 19: “If any priest wishes to send his nephew or some kinsman to school in the church of Holy Cross, or in the monastery of St Aignan or St Lifard, or in the other monasteries entrusted to our governance, we grant him permission to do so.” Since, therefore, public schools existed from ancient times in the church of Holy Cross at Orléans, there also had to be there, as in other cathedral churches, a master and certain overseer to govern them, in whose hands lay the administration of all literary affairs. In different churches he bore different titles: now *scholaris* and master of the schools; now chancellor and theologian. These officials are discussed in canon 18 of the Third Lateran Council in these words: “Lest poor persons who cannot be aided by their parents’ resources be deprived of the opportunity to read and advance, let a suitable benefice be assigned in every cathedral church [Col. 0404C] to a master, who shall teach without charge the clerics of that church and the scholars, so that the teacher’s need may be relieved and the way of learning may be open to pupils.” It also belonged to them to grant other masters the licence and authority to teach, a function still performed by chancellors of academies and universities. In a decretal Alexander III reproved [Col. 0404D] certain persons among them who, for very sordid gain, demanded money from masters for granting such licences: “We judge those worthy,” he says, “of a still more severe punishment who assume the title and dignity of master of the schools and do not grant ecclesiastical persons leave to teach others without payment.”]

He asks that he permit a certain cleric to lecture publicly in the school at Orléans.

It grieves me whenever I am compelled to trouble anyone, especially my lords, to whom I am bound to rise and serve, whether through gratitude for their merits [Col. 0404B] or through reverence for their dignity. I count you among them; I am more ready to defend than to offend your honour, even in legal matters. But because apostolic commands are like the walls of a city, which one may not leap over, struck by the fear that I may, at least in civil terms, incur together the lot of Romulus’ brother [Note: [Col. 0404D] He alludes to the story of Remus, who perished because he transgressed and despised the edict of his brother Romulus, the founder of the city.] and the death of losing my head, I advise you, as I first admonished you, so now by a second admonition, to permit Master G. lawfully to lecture in accordance with the lord pope’s command. But if perhaps you refuse, I announce to you, by a peremptory edict whether I wish it or not, that on the first Monday of the coming Advent of the Lord you are to appear at Paris and demonstrate that the same G. is unfit for such [Col. 0404C] governance of the schools.

### 168. LETTER CXVI. TO WILLIAM, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS

[Note: [Col. 0404D] It is clear that this letter was written in August, near the feast of St Augustine. When he speaks of the demands of August and of domestic management at that time, he means the imminent harvest, which gave our abbot, provident in household matters, no small concern, since he cultivated his fields and villages at his own expense and by the labour of canons and lay brethren.]

He implores his aid for a certain peasant unjustly oppressed by the king’s officials.

The demands of the month of August on one side, and the feast of Father Augustine on the other, constrain me from writing to you in an Augustan style. In the former, household and domestic concerns admit no writer; in the latter, pastoral and canonical care dismisses no arranger [Col. 0405A]. Amid these things I preferred to be uncultivated yet unharmed, rather than invoke the Muses in order to seem learned.

I send you a rustic man, taken after his breeding sows, who stands tongue-tied and mute in the palaces of kings and the courts of governors. Without your counsel his cause will perish; without your powerful aid he will have no strength. The king’s lofty officials seize him and condemn him though innocent, wishing to plunder his small substance, which is insufficient to support his wife and children, while there is no one to ransom or save him.

### 169. LETTER CXVII. TO THE SAME

He writes on behalf of a certain dependant of St Geneviève, that he may be freed from the exaction of the provost of Poissy.

[Col. 0405B]

The provost of Poissy [Note: [Col. 0405C] Pinciacum or Pisciacum, commonly Poissy, lies fifteen miles from the city of Paris, though it is situated in the diocese of Chartres. It ranks first among the seven provostships dependent upon the Châtelet of Paris. The town is famous for the baptism of St Louis. There is there a notable monastery dedicated to blessed Mary, founded by Constance, wife of Robert, later more fittingly restored by Philip the Fair and entrusted to nuns of St Dominic.]—contrary to the undertaking he had made to you, and setting aside in this matter all remembrance of you—leaves your sheep half unshorn, while striving not merely to shear the rest but to flay it. He demands a hundred shillings from our poor man, which he will borrow at usury if the provost’s purpose is not changed. Since I remember that your hand has never begun anything which it left unfinished, I ask that by your counsel and help you secure the complete acquittal of this innocent man, free until the present time from royal exaction, a dependant and servant of blessed Geneviève the virgin [Note: [Col. 0405C] The church of St Geneviève possessed many servants and handmaids of this sort, both at Paris in the borough of Mont and St Medard and in its villages of Auteuil, Vanves, Épinay, Rueil, and elsewhere; they were called men and women “of the body.” There were fourfold rights of lords over such servants, as is explained in a charter from the archive of that abbey: “They may not make their sons clerics except with permission of the Church; they may not marry their sons or daughters to persons of another bailiwick or lordship; they owe the *caducum*, that is, the dead hand; in the needs of the Church they shall give suitable assistance from their own goods according to the custom of the realm.” The servants of St Geneviève bought their manumission for a price about 1245, during the reign of St Louis, on these conditions: “First, that they should remain dependants or vassals of the same church; second, that if they married a wife of servile condition, their children should nevertheless remain free; third, that they should be bound to come in person for the defence of the persons and rights of the church, or in the prosecution of injuries. The first day shall be at their own cost, but for the remaining days we shall give each of the said men six Parisian denarii, until they are dismissed [Col. 0406C] on behalf of our church.”], so that he may not be condemned for a hundred shillings.

[Col. 0405C] The benefit will be complete if fullness follows the acquittal. If it please you, have the cantor of Senlis—who obstinately and arrogantly inflicted grievous injuries upon our canons, forgetful of his manumission [Col. 0406A] which he ungratefully received gratis from our church [Note: [Col. 0406C] That cantor of Senlis had formerly been a servant of St Geneviève; the abbot granted him freedom so that he might become a cleric. For councils had ordained—namely Orléans III, canon 26; Tribur, canon 29; Bourges, canon 9; Poitiers I, canon 9—“that servants should not be promoted to orders or admitted to ecclesiastical honours unless they had first received freedom from their lords.” By a diploma of Clement III in 1289, the abbot of St Geneviève obtained authority to confer the first tonsure upon his servants, whom he emancipated for that purpose.]—summoned to a specified day and place, that he may answer us for so great an offence. For we do not believe that you will be present at Noyon on the Wednesday which you assigned us.

His purse is stretched out, and, like that animal, it is full of wind [Note: [Col. 0406C] He means the cantor of Senlis, whom he denotes by this perhaps unsuitable term. Yet the author must be pardoned: he writes to his friend the archbishop of Reims, with whom he was on more familiar terms, concerning his former servant. One should also recall what Cicero says: “How many things are jocular in letters which, if spoken aloud, would seem foolish.”]; so too his money-bag is full of silver. A man who deserved to be accused criminally may be punished financially.

### 170–171. LETTER CXVIII. TO R., ELECT OF CHARTRES

[Note: [Col. 0406D] This letter is recognized as having been written in 1187, when Renaud de Bar was elected bishop of Chartres after the death of Peter of Celle, as is recorded in the Chronicle of Robert of Torigni. Peter of Blois mentions him in Letters 15 and 20; he died in 1217, as noted in the necrology of Chartres.]

He commends to him his church and canons at Choisy, that they may not be unjustly burdened by officials.

May the discipline of the Holy Spirit receive the beginnings of your sacred promotion and the merits of your future priesthood, God [Col. 0406B] willing; may He give a sound direction to your counsels and a happy end to your affairs. Both the reverence common to all prelates of churches which we owe, and the particular obedience and fidelity which we have long been bound to show to the lord archbishop of Reims, your magnificent and beneficent uncle [Note: [Col. 0406D] For Renaud was the son of Agnes of Champagne, daughter of Count Theobald and sister of William, archbishop of Reims.], invite us to offer this vow and sacrifice of desire. Since we are prepared to return these bonds of favour to you at fitting times, and utterly abhor the vice of ingratitude both toward you and toward our other lords, we ask your eminent and illustrious nobility to show us favour freely, with equal steps—and, if possible, with greater—as did your predecessors, bishops of Chartres, especially our lord [Col. 0406C] your uncle, and after him J. and P., bishops of Chartres of blessed memory [Note: [Col. 0406D] After William, the bishopric of Chartres had been administered by John of Salisbury and Peter of Celle, very well known from their letters.].

There is in your diocese a church of ours in our little village called Sosiacum [Note: [Col. 0407B] Sosiacum, commonly Choisy, in the diocese of Chartres, is wholly subject to the lordship of the church of St Geneviève. This parish was formerly called St Peter at [Col. 0407C] the Oxen, and the village itself is called in French *Choisy aux boeufs*, because a very celebrated market was held there, where oxen brought from every direction were sold on specified days of the week; this was later done in the village of Poissy. When this church had fallen into other hands, it was finally restored to the canons of St Geneviève by William, then archbishop of Sens, who also administered the bishopric of Chartres. Robert of Torigni testifies in his continuation of Sigebert in these words: “When the archbishop of Sens departed this life, William, elect of Chartres, succeeded him, though Pope Alexander granted him the bishopric of Chartres for two years, that is, until 1171.” At that time he confirmed by the charter appended here the parish of Sosiacum to the canons of St Geneviève: “William, by God’s grace archbishop of Sens and legate of the apostolic see, to all sons of holy mother Church, future and present, to whom these present letters shall come, greeting in the Lord. When jurisdiction over the church of Chartres had been entrusted to us, Hugh, abbot, and the canons of St Geneviève of Paris frequently and earnestly presented a complaint about the church of Sosiacum, which they saw being alienated from their church, though it was known to be of its jurisdiction. Having therefore investigated the truth of the matter through the account of our beloved son Odo, sometime abbot of the aforesaid church, and of other lawful persons, we found with certainty that the matter stood thus. Therefore, both in consideration of justice and at the intervention of the lord pope and our friends, we grant that church to the aforesaid brethren, so that the abbot of St Geneviève may place his canons there, the episcopal right in all things being preserved. That these provisions may remain ratified in the future, we confirm them by the testimony of this writing and the impression of our seal.” Alexander III confirmed this grant by his diploma issued at Tusculum on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May.], obscure both in name and scant in resources. Two regular canons [Note: [Col. 0408B] In the reform of the order made about the twelfth century, two or three canons—and sometimes more—lived in each parish. That this was always observed in those dependent upon the monastery of St Geneviève is learned from its ancient Rules and constitutions. In the chapter “Concerning those assigned to obediences,” it is commanded “that brethren dwelling in obediences, that is, parishes, should be three in each place if possible, or at least two.” This is also decreed in diplomas of the supreme pontiffs Celestine, Alexander III, and Clement III: “We decree that you may establish in your churches four, or at least three, of the brethren, provided that one of them be presented by you, son abbot, to the diocesan bishop, from whose hand he shall receive care of souls. When circumstances require and it is expedient, you shall be free to recall them to the cloister and to substitute others in their place, as we have said, provided that he who is to preside receives the care of spiritual matters from the diocesan bishop.”], conducting the parish’s pastoral care, serve God there [Note: [Col. 0408D] Since regular canons are truly and properly clerics, it belongs to them to devote themselves to the salvation of their neighbours’ souls and to administer parishes. But in the twelfth century certain bishops, observing that externally they led in cloisters a life not very unlike that of monks, wished to exclude them from parish government. This happened especially in the diocese of Limoges concerning the canons of Sterp, and in that of Orléans concerning those of Beaugency. But Ivo of Chartres, a most vigorous defender of his order and a most diligent investigator of the canons, wrote two letters—Letter 69 to Walter, provost of Sterp, and Letter 213 to John, bishop of Orléans—in which he clearly proves that regular canons are eminently suited to the care of souls.]. Your officials, claiming that you have imposed a certain levy, place upon them a burden of forty shillings, which neither we nor our fathers have been accustomed either to undertake or to bear. 172 Remit this forced service to us, Father: it is a burden to us and will bring you no honour. In other dioceses, namely Paris and Soissons [Note: [Col. 0408D] The abbey of St Geneviève has, in the diocese of Paris, the parishes of Vanves, Nanterre, Rueil, Roissy, and Épinay; and in that of Soissons, La Ferté-Milon and Marisy.], our brethren are free from these burdens. Nor, God willing, will they begin to be burdened by you, by whom, as we trust, they ought especially to be defended [Col. 0407B].

### 173–174. LETTER CXIX. TO WILLIAM, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS

He requests the transfer of a certain monk to another monastery.

The bosom of your favour, Father, is capacious and so open to all that it does not fail individuals and benefits everyone. Let the ungrateful blush and stand in awe—those whom your benefits forestall more often than their service follows. We believe that your monk Th., who hopes for your goodwill in his affliction and trusts in your favour, is not among that undevoted number [Col. 0408A].

As we understand, he is a brother of dragons, a companion of ostriches, and dwells among scorpions. He feels the hostilities and hatreds of monks all the more deeply because he sees them at closer hand. No one consoles him unless you quickly provide for him. He is a man who, though he has no need to be commended to you by borrowed intercessions, thinks more highly of me than I deserve and believes himself helped by another’s prayers. If it please you, lead him out of Ur of the Chaldeans—which is interpreted “the fire of captives”—so that, delivered from lying lips and a deceitful tongue, he may offer to God on your behalf a sacrifice of praise and pay his vows to the Most High.

### 175. LETTER CXX. TO HUGH, ABBOT OF ST VINCENT, SENLIS

He asks that he grant pardon to a certain canon returning to his monastery.

[Col. 0408B]

To his dearest brother and friend HUGH, abbot of St Vincent of Senlis, brother STEPHEN of St Geneviève sends greeting and sincere affection.

The old age and supplication of J., our brother and fellow canon, have moved us. He asks you for pardon in such a way that he does not deny his fault. He is ready to submit to satisfaction and, lest he perish, to forestall your mercy by confessing his offence. We also make prayers for him: in consideration of his advanced [Col. 0409A] age, his long-standing religious life, and divine compassion, open your fatherly bosom to the returning man and receive him as penitent whom you excluded as a sinner [Note: [Col. 0409C] The Rule of St Augustine commands that the obstinate be expelled and excluded from the fellowship of the rest, in these words: “If he refuses to endure this, even if he does not himself depart, let him be cast out from your society; for this is done not cruelly but mercifully, lest he destroy very many by contagion.” The Rule of St Benedict, chapter 28, says of stubborn religious: “If he has not been cured even in this way, then at last let the abbot employ the sword of excision, as the Apostle says: ‘Put away evil from among yourselves’ [1 Cor. 5]; and again: ‘If the unbeliever departs, let him depart’ [1 Cor. 7], lest one diseased sheep infect the whole flock.”].

### 176. LETTER CXXI. TO URBAN, SUPREME PONTIFF

He asks him graciously to receive and fulfil the petitions which he presents for his church of St Geneviève.

We receive the beginnings of your sacred apostolate, Father, with such devotion that from it we conceive firm confidence both that grace is given to the humble and that the proud receive confusion. By this balance of justice [Note: [Col. 0409D] Although this passage shows us that the downward inclination of the scale or balance hanging from the right hand of Justice is not recent, this was not the ancient Romans’ representation of that virtue. Their coins of Hadrian, Antoninus Pius, and Alexander Severus portray her seated, bearing a staff in her left hand and a patera in her right. Antonius Augustinus explains this symbol of Justice in Dialogue II: “She sits because maturity befits the wise man; accordingly judges sat when they were to pronounce sentence. The sceptre denotes sovereignty over the world and the administration of the commonwealth; the patera signifies divinity.” Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights*, book XIV, chapter 4, gives another image of Justice, from Chrysippus: “She is maidenly in form, stern and awe-inspiring in appearance, with sharp brightness in her eyes; neither lowly nor cruel, but possessing the dignity of a certain venerable sadness.” Thus we see the varied image of Justice conceived by Greeks, Romans, and Frenchmen.], so great a vicar of Peter will weigh the merits of each person, since the Lord has abundantly given him knowledge and, with knowledge, power. Nor can there be lacking to these two their most welcome third companion [Col. 0409B]: a good, acceptable, and perfect will. By this threefold cord holy desires, upright counsels, and just works are more perfectly bound together.

Meanwhile I, the least portion of your sons, glory within myself that I once saw my present lord and father in the schools, where, like Hylas, I marvelled at Hercules advancing with great strides of virtue and prudence. From that time I conceived reverence for your name and absorbed remembrance of your authority, setting before myself a fruitful example: instruction from your words and discipline from your conduct. Behold, I and the church entrusted to me, though unworthy, are yours, ready with all gladness to receive every command of yours without disguise and fulfil it without delay. We pour out prayers to your holiness that you may [Col. 0409C] receive with goodwill, and beneficently fulfil, our petitions which we lay before you through your acolyte, Lord B., insofar as you judge them advantageous for your church.

### 177. LETTER CXXII. TO MASTER REGINALD, ARCHPRIEST OF THE CHURCH OF ORLÉANS

He requests that he ensure that an injury done to his brother is repaired by fitting satisfaction.

[Col. 0410A]

Friendship is drowsy when it is slow to awaken in the needs of a friend. Lest you incur this fault, I ask you to show yourself eager in the affair of Stephen my brother, whose injury, because it is mine, you ought to have considered yours. And because the apostolic command pronounced through the lord bishop of Paris has not yet been fully satisfied, you, in whom no small share of ecclesiastical jurisdiction resides—and I rejoice in this [Note: [Col. 0410C] Archpriests are found of two kinds, urban and rural, as stated in the notes on the Third Council of Toledo. An urban archpriest, established in a city, performs the bishop’s duties in his absence, begins the divine office in church, gives blessings, and performs other acts contained in the title “On the Office of the Archpriest” from the constitutions of Pope Leo. A rural archpriest presides only over the people. They are discussed in canon 13 of the Synod of Rieg, convened under Lothair in 850 [Col. 0410D], where the following occurs: “Because of the continual care owed to the people of God, we will that archpriests preside over individual communities, so that they may care not only for the uninstructed populace but also, with unceasing watchfulness, guard the lives of those priests who reside at lesser churches, reporting to their bishop the diligence with which each performs the divine office. Nor may a bishop allege that the people have no need of an archpriest because he himself can govern them alone. For although he may be very capable, it is fitting that he bear his burdens; and, just as he presides over the mother church, so archpriests should preside over parish communities, lest ecclesiastical care falter in any respect. Yet they must refer everything to the bishop and presume to ordain nothing contrary to his decree.”]—supply vigilantly and courageously what is lacking to the excuse, so that I may then give you thanks and, through your exertion, receive redress for the wrong I have suffered.

[Col. 0410B] I beg that this be done without delay, 178 which will altogether draw danger to itself if the wrongdoer passes through Easter unpunished—Easter which in Latin is called *transitus*, “passage.”

### LETTER CXXIII. TO MASTER BERTER, ARCHDEACON OF CAMBRAI

He asks that he intercede with his lord in a certain matter.

What I say is modest, yet no less true: I fear offending my lord and yours [Note: [Col. 0410D] He means William, archbishop of Reims, whom that archdeacon of Cambrai served in ecclesiastical affairs.] by improper complaints or importunate requests. His favour suffices me; I prefer it alone to every consolation and set it before every remedy. But since all receive from his fullness, I ask you to convey to him the prayers which I offered him [Col. 0410C] at Paris, so that, through your diligence, he may be induced, and through your counsel moved, to grant what I ask.

A favourable time has presented itself, in which he can speak more privately with the elect [Col. 0411A] of Orléans [Note: [Col. 0411D] This letter, together with the following one, is said to have been written about 1186, when Henry, elected to the bishopric of Orléans, hastened to William, archbishop of Reims, perhaps to receive from him the office of consecration. This seems to be suggested by the following words: “He is to keep a feast-day at Reims, where, with the opportunity of time and place concurring, he will deny nothing to our lord.”], and more easily obtain from him what he wishes. As we have heard, he is to keep a feast-day at Reims; there, with the opportunity of time and place coinciding, he will deny nothing to our lord, whom he has lately found not merely well disposed but exceedingly beneficent in his own affair.

### LETTER CXXIV. TO HENRY, BISHOP OF ORLÉANS, IN THE PERSON OF THE ABBOT OF ST EVURTIUS, ORLÉANS

He complains of a royal tax collector by whom he was oppressed.

The present day is a day of tribulation and distress. We delivered to the royal minister and tax-collector the letters of the lord king which we had obtained through our solicitude; and in offering them we looked for peace, but it did not come; we sought good things, and behold, trouble. He answered proudly, and [Col. 0411B] his anger has not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out. He said that he would obey neither letters nor commands unless he received special tokens, known and recognized by himself and the lord king. He has not only failed to restore our plunder, but has taken away and carried off what remained. May our grief move your fatherly heart; and in our deliverance consecrate the first-fruits of your advancement, lest, if the palace officials find you lukewarm in comparable matters, the danger become common to you and yours alike. I neither dare nor presume to return home, while our Church fails amid daily lamentations and her tears are still upon her cheeks. I have remained in Paris with the abbot of Sainte-Geneviève, waiting to be refreshed from the breasts of your consolation and to be delivered in this present distress by your counsel and aid together.

## LETTER CXXV. TO G., ABBOT OF SAINT AMBROSE OF BOURGES

He commends a certain canon residing with him at Paris.

Brother STEPHEN, abbot of Sainte-Geneviève, to his dearest brother and friend G., abbot of Saint Ambrose of Bourges: greetings and affection.

Regarding the recall, or transfer, of Brother Al., your canon, we answer you with the Gospel’s words: “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matt. xiv). He wished to sever brotherly charity who, with wicked and deceitful speech, said that we did not wish to receive so suitable and useful a brother—although we endeavour to honour, cherish, and love your sons as much as our own. His companionship is welcome to us; his recall unwelcome; and still more unwelcome is the doubt by which a third party’s tongue wished to separate him from us. May it please you that he remain with us, lest, if he is transferred to others by your command, he should pay us no heed under another’s command.

## LETTER CXXVI. TO ROLAND OF DINAN

He exhorts him to complete the work he has begun.

[Col. 0412A]

To the nobleman ROLAND of Dinan—[Note: [Col. 0411D] Dinannum or Dinantum, commonly Dinan, is a town in Lesser Brittany in the diocese of Saint-Malo; Roland, to whom this letter is addressed, was its lord]—STEPHEN, called abbot of Sainte-Geneviève, and the entire humble convent of that Church: greeting and eternal life.

Abundant is the bosom of divine grace: it fails none individually and suffices for all; it gathers the scattered, recalls the wandering, embraces those who return, draws the unwilling, and compels the reluctant to enter. We rejoice that your devotion has been kindled by desire for this grace: despising the unfruitful labours of earthly soldiery, it has, as we hear, wholly stretched itself toward the prize of the heavenly calling, whether gladly expending its possessions on works of mercy [Col. 0412B] or humbly pursuing the good deeds of others as an example of justice. May this good, pleasing, and perfect will grow day by day, so that the church which you are building may, through your diligence, be instructed in regular discipline, supplied through your abundance, and governed through your providence.

[Note: [Col. 0412D] He founded an abbey in the parish of Megrat, or Megrest, near his castle of Belloloco, from which it later took its name; he established there eight regular canons and endowed them with ample revenues. This abbey was formerly called that of Blessed Mary of Pont-Pillari, because it stood beside the bridge of that name. There lie Roland the founder and Alan of Vitré, among the principal benefactors of this monastery.]

And since, by the secret judgment of God, you leave no heirs of your flesh, appoint that new plantation of yours heir to a portion of your goods, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings; lest, if you perhaps leave them needy and orphaned, they be forced to beg, while someone else obtains glory and honour from your labours. Moreover, lest your benefits appear transitory or illusory after your death, for your salvation [Col. 0412C] we admonish, advise, and beseech you to confer them upon the Church you are establishing with such security that they can neither be taken away by anyone’s malice, diminished by greed, nor disturbed by power. Then indeed the brethren whom you gather there for God’s service will give into your bosom “good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing,” if their poverty is sufficiently supplied from your abundance and your alms continually nourish God’s servants.

Meanwhile, we commend to you Brother W., our canon and yours, of holy conduct and outstanding disposition in Christ. His manner of life among us, pleasing to God and men and beyond all complaint, has won universal favour and earned singular esteem. Receive in him a portion of our very heart. We have granted him our Church on such terms that, as one of us, he receives both temporal and spiritual things in brotherly fellowship and renders what is due in the common fraternity. We pursue your liberality with full thanksgiving: without any merit of ours, you sent us [Col. 0412D] your palfrey, and in so fitting a gift familiarly displayed the affection of the giver.

[Note: [Col. 0413C] *Palefridus*, French *palefroi*, denoted a riding-horse. William of Tyre, book XIII of *The Sacred War*, chapter 27, says: “He had sent to the aforesaid nobleman, through one of his retainers, a very white palfrey shod with silver.”]

## LETTER CXXVII. TO WILLIAM, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS

[Note: [Col. 0413C] From this letter and others it may be gathered how great was our abbot’s influence with the king, who entrusted to his care and prudence frequent embassies most useful to the commonwealth.]

He reports that the king has excused him from the journey to Rome.

As I had informed you, Father, I approached the lord king on the day appointed for my departure: prepared for a journey whose beginnings are fearful, whose middle course perilous, and whose end full of pride. After some deliberations, God, in whose hand are the hearts of kings, changed the lord king’s counsel; and the benevolent prince released me from the labour of the forthcoming journey, commending my good will in his affairs and, if great things may be compared with small, returning grace for [Col. 0413B] grace. Meanwhile, Father, from your servant come thanksgiving and a voice of praise, since through your letters you did not deny me—beyond what I deserved—useful encouragement to undertake the labour, abundant consolation, and humble compassion.

## LETTER CXXVIII. TO NIVELON, BISHOP OF SOISSONS

[Note: [Col. 0413D] Nivelo of Chérisy was promoted to the bishopric of Soissons in 1175. His mother was Agnes, lady of Longpont; she became a converted sister in the abbey of Longpont itself, founded in 1131 by Joslen, bishop of Soissons. In Nivelo’s time arose that serious dispute between the abbot and the canons of Saint John in the Vines, who did not wish to be removed from their benefices, of which we have spoken above.]

He exhorts him to complete what he had begun in the church of Saint John.

Fruitful are works which charity begins and perseverance completes. The branch follows the root; the stream has the flavour of its spring; the work commends the intention. What was sincerely begun by you and us [Col. 0413C], under the authority of the lord pope, concerning the ordering of the church of Saint John in the Vines, awaits completion. The need of the languishing Church strikes the ears of the Lord of Hosts with daily cries, so that those who dwell in the land of the south may meet the thirsty man with bread. These things will be imputed to you and to us if what was begun with a good purpose is not brought to a good conclusion. Give swift and distinguished help and effort, so that during the octave of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin you may send representatives to Paris to conduct, escort, and install the canons honourably on your behalf.

[Note: [Col. 0413D] Nivelo called regular canons of Sainte-Geneviève at Paris to the monastery of Saint John, in order that they might restore the regular discipline that had to some extent declined there, as the supreme pontiff had commanded him. Raymond, prior of the same abbey of Sainte-Geneviève, to whom various letters here are addressed, accordingly became the eighth abbot of Saint John of Soissons.]

But because, owing to the postponement of the royal conference, we do not believe that the lord archbishop of Reims will be present, inquire carefully when and where we may most suitably meet him with you, and deliberate and treat concerning what remains. Inform us of your will in all these matters, lest we run uncertainly or, fighting, beat the air as it were.

## LETTER CXXIX. TO WILLIAM, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS

He complains of the bishop of Senlis, who had struck his mayor of Borret with an anathema.

[Note: [Col. 0414C] We have said that Borret was a village four miles from Senlis, assigned to the lordship of Sainte-Geneviève, where there were formerly a mayor and aldermen. Its road-toll was granted to this abbey by Geoffrey, count of Anjou, as appears from the following charter of donation: “In the name of God Almighty, Creator of visible and invisible things, Geoffrey, count of the Angevins. I wish it to be known to my faithful men and to all whose knowledge this matter ought to concern that the canons of the congregation of the Parisian monastery of the most blessed virgin of Christ, Geneviève, came into my presence and humbly begged that, for love of the divine name and reverence for that virgin, their patroness, we might confer upon them and their holy place some special alms and necessary relief. Receiving their petition humbly and willingly, for the souls of my parents, the illustrious Count Fulk and the religious Countess Hildegard, and also for remission of my own sins, I granted to the most holy monastery of Geneviève the entire road-toll, in full, from their village situated in the county of the people of Senlis and called Borret,” etc.]

The order of judicial proceedings, Father, devised by many careful and wakeful deliberations, is today disturbed by certain governors of the Roman Church. Having either not read or disregarded the sacred canons, they are no less rash in passing sentence than cruel in carrying it out. They bind without summons, excommunicate without discrimination, condemn without investigation. The bishop of Senlis claims to be among their number. Disregarding every judicial procedure, he did not so much excommunicate our servant, the mayor of Borret, as vomit forth at first sight an unlawful and irregular sentence of whatever sort of excommunication, presenting itself to him as though it were law; and, on the slightest cause or none, he shut up our village under interdict. Since, lord, you have become a refuge for us, we pour out prayers to your fatherhood, whose goodwill and beneficence we have experienced, [Col. 0414C] that, if it please you, you may absolve our servant after he has sworn to stand by your command; and that, concerning both his case and the interdict upon the village, you may appoint a day and place for us and the bishop, whenever and wherever it pleases you.

## LETTER CXXX. TO NICHOLAS, PRIOR OF SAINT BARTHOLOMEW OF NOYON

He commends to him his nephew Peter.

May no occasion extinguish our friendship, which charity kindled. I speak to a wise man, to one whom I see but seldom, yet think of frequently. I was ill even unto death and worn out by prolonged pain, yet I received no consolation from your presence, your letter, or your messenger. Your negligence will be forgiven if diligence makes amends. Honour, I beseech you, our common Father [Col. 0415A]—I mean your aged abbot—and one, as I fear, near his end, so that you may be long-lived upon the earth.

[Note: [Col. 0415C–D] That is, Hugh, abbot of Saint Bartholomew of Noyon, under whose discipline they had both been trained in religious observance.]

Correct my Peter if he goes astray; defend him if he has need. I do not encourage his faults, but favour nature, by which he is bound to me.

## LETTER CXXXI. TO W. …

He gives thanks for an elegant horse sent to him from Denmark.

[Col. 0415B]

To the reverend father and friend, Elder W.—[Note: [Col. 0415D–0416C] William, initially a secular canon of Sainte-Geneviève, embraced the regular rule when regular canons of Saint-Victor were introduced into that church by Pope Eugenius and Louis the Younger in 1148. Subsequently, sought and summoned to Denmark by Absalon, bishop of Roskilde, he was brought there by the celebrated Saxo Grammaticus, the most elegant historiographer of his people, then provost of Roskilde. He devoted himself, not without severe hardships, entirely to reforming a monastery of his order on the island of Eskil and to building another. Thus full of merits, nearly a centenarian, he departed to Christ in 1202 or 1203. He was later numbered among the saints. His Life, written by a contemporary and companion, is found in Surius and Bollandus under 6 April. Pontanus, book VI of *Danish Affairs*, under the year 1207, writes concerning his death: “This year also proved fatal to William, abbot of the monastery of Æbelholt, which the Latins called Saint Paraclete. Absalon had caused him to be summoned into Denmark, together with other companions from the community of Saint Geneviève at Paris. Among the Danes these men first instituted monastic life according to the Rule of Saint Augustine, which they had practised at Paris under the institution of Saint-Victor. William, moreover, both because of the holiness of his life and because certain miraculous deeds are said to have been observed after his death, was thereafter numbered among the saints and called Saint William of Paris.” The following epitaph is circulated:

> Born at Paris, blessed in word and deed,  
> Taken from the world, William lies buried here.]—

May you grow old, live, and see good days.

It is a worthy saying that one who receives a benefit ought to acknowledge himself obliged to make a return-gift (*antidora*) to every benefactor. Otherwise, whoever acts differently either worships the statue of the undevout or adores the image of the ungrateful. These are the ill-starred offspring of monstrosity: the first shapeless, the second infamous; each without praise and neither without filth. The darkness of lack of devotion and the obscenity of ingratitude bury past benefits, corrupt present ones, and repel future ones. We flee their contagion and detest their company. We receive your gift in such a way as to reverence in the present the effect of your affection, and in the giver of the present the affection of the giver. It is fitting that for [Col. 0415C] so splendid a horse we should return solemn thanks—a horse which would befit the seat of great bishops or palace princes. Riders upon other horses see it and envy it; and it is not easy among us to purchase an equal by price or earn one by service.

If there was any delay in giving it, that delay has been suitably excused; nor did it bring any danger upon itself, since it displayed so full an increase of the gift. Its guide spared no expense in fodder and did not appropriate the horse as a vehicle for himself. This is shown by the delightful softness of its coat, the straight arrangement of its mane, its well-fleshed neck, fat and even haunches, loins not sunken, flat flanks, golden colour: it is altogether beautiful, and there is no blemish in it. As to what you asked concerning the state of our brethren, [Col. 0416A] let your solicitous affection know that, through God’s mercy, they advance day by day in spiritual things and abound in temporal things; nor is there among them “an encounter or Satan,” since each meets in brotherly concord and all rejoice together.

## LETTER CXXXII. TO ALBERT, CHANCELLOR OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH

He commends to him the affairs being conducted in the Roman curia by a certain noble cleric.

We are compelled, Father, to ask for others, since we are not sufficient to obtain things for ourselves. The impulse of charity commands the first; the failure of necessity reproaches the second. In these circumstances, following no less that charity which casts fear outside than trusting in your goodwill, I commend to your fatherhood the bearer of this letter, Subdeacon A. [Col. 0416B] If we count his years, he is young; if we reckon the merits of his character, he is old. He has devoted his youth to sacred learning beyond his contemporaries, conceiving and drinking in the prophets in the Gospel and the Gospel in the prophets. To this is added what does not often occur: nobility of lineage, which, though it is not sufficient by itself, advances toward virtue when joined with other things. He is worthy for whom prayers should be poured into holy ears and received by pious minds. I, your devoted servant, ask that through you in the holy curia there may be opened to him not merely access for petitioning, but also a happy and easy outcome in obtaining what he seeks in his affairs.

## LETTER CXXXIII. TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT-DENIS

[Note: [Col. 0416D] The abbey of Saint-Denis in France, two miles from the city of Paris, of the Benedictine order, most illustrious for the tombs of our kings, was founded by Dagobert, the first Frankish king of that name.]

He grants permission to a canon of Sainte-Geneviève to receive the habit of Saint Benedict.

[Col. 0416C]

God alone, to whom every secret lies open and who will judge the ends of the earth, judges the ends of works and the bounds of wills. Therefore we neither wish to commend nor dare to condemn the desire of Brother H., our canon, who wishes to transfer to your monastery, reserving all things to Him who, at the time of recompense, will weigh the merits of each person in balance and scales. But, in order to satisfy your request and the most ardent wish of the brother, we grant him freely and absolutely to you—saving to us the alms of the house which he and his mother [Col. 0417A] bestowed upon our Church—so that he may serve God with us in the monastic habit, and Blessed Benedict may reap from him fruit, to whom Saint Augustine offered the first-fruits of holy religion. We bear witness concerning him that during the almost two years and four months in which he remained with us, he conducted himself religiously, soberly, and honourably; and, applying himself to regular disciplines, he gained the favour of all the brethren in such a way as to incur offence from none.

## LETTER CXXXIV. TO THE ABBOTS OF CÎTEAUX AND CLAIRVAUX

He deals with the lay brothers of Grandmont rising up against the clerics.

To the venerable fathers, the abbot of Cîteaux and the abbot of Clairvaux: may you be animated by the spirit of counsel and armed by the spirit of strength.

I beseech your prudence to remain watchful, lest what you have begun well end weakly: lest crafty barbarism, plotting, secretly undermining, and poisoning, beset, steal away, or corrupt the sentence which you pronounced with the utmost deliberation. They are wiser in their generation than the children of light; and in their error they will easily find counsellors and supporters—either men corrupted by money or men softened by flattery. The sentence has not yet been carried into execution; it has not yet become a decided case. Through wicked delays, informers grow proud, judges are mocked, clerics beg, Christ’s poor are exiled; and still, in the houses you assigned to them, foxes have holes and birds of heaven [Col. 0417C] nests. May the judicial vigour of your order burn strongly within you, fearing neither the threats of princes nor admitting the feigned hiding-places of hypocrisy, nor yielding to long and polished appeals under the appearance of religion; so that the Judge of all may reward your conscience and human favour commend your reputation.

## LETTER CXXXV. TO A., CHANCELLOR OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH

He asks him to show favour to the clerics of Grandmont against the lay brothers.

They carry on a mournful spectacle in the Church of God, worthy of faithful and tearful compassion. The lay brothers of Grandmont, shaking their long beards like horned goats [Col. 0417D]—

[Note: [Col. 0417D] By “horned goats” he means goats which have horns and beards, to which he compares and likens the lay brothers of the Order of Grandmont. Concerning their controversy with the clerics, Jacques de Vitry, *Western History*, chapter 15, says: “The enemy of the human race and crafty assailant of all religion, envying institutions so holy and salutary, on this occasion stirred up a very pernicious murmur, sedition, and scandal among the clerics and laymen, monks and lay brothers of the aforesaid monastery of Grandmont,” etc.]—

are wiser in their generation than the children of light; and the serpent’s craft does not so much deceitfully circumvent the dove’s simplicity as violently swallow it up. From that once venerable college the ministers of the altar have been set up like a target for arrows; and those who see them shake their heads over [Col. 0418A] them. They beg; they wander in exile, fugitives and refugees upon the earth; they are filled with reproaches. And behold, dogs eat the children’s bread, while foxes have holes and birds of heaven nests in the dwellings of the just. Laymen grow proud against them and, placing hope in corrupt money, promise them—under an accursed clinking sound—the gold in which men trust, whose eyes are blinded by gifts.

The judges delegated by the lord pope—[Note: [Col. 0418D] Namely, the bishop of Chartres and the abbot of Saint-Victor at Paris]—proceeded as far as they were able; but, when a new mandate of the holy apostolic see required two fellow-judges to be joined to them, so that the matter might not be treated except under the number seven—

[Note: [Col. 0418D] Besides these two judges, the following were named with them in the cause of the Grandmontines: the abbots of Cîteaux, Clairvaux, Saint-Denis, Saint-Germain-des-Prés, and Sainte-Geneviève. Consult the other letters concerning this dispute.]—

they chose humbly to desist rather than labour uselessly. Earlier they had subjected to excommunication a certain Stephen, whom the lay brothers had irreverently and contrary to the sacred canons intruded [Col. 0418B] into the place of the prior, who had neither resigned nor died; and they enclosed under the same sentence all who obeyed him as prior. They also assigned twenty cells to the clerics, where they might peacefully serve God without harassment from the lay brothers, in accordance with the lord pope’s letters, judging it better that they should live in their own houses than beg in those of others. Likewise, they subjected to excommunication all of the Order of Grandmont who hindered this command. The lay brothers and their adherents, fearing neither God nor respecting man, incurred both articles of excommunication.

Therefore, holy Father, I, the least portion of your clerics, who was present at all these things, pour out prayers to your holiness: by the zeal for justice with which you burn, meet the proud laymen; by the spirit of mercy with which you love, come to the aid of the oppressed and humble clerics.

## LETTER CXXXVI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF LUND

He commends his nephew Peter, canon of Sainte-Geneviève, asking that he ensure Peter enjoys a benefice.

The pleasant companionship of Peter, ours and yours alike, is so much the more grievous for us to lose, even for a time, as it would be more agreeable never to lack it. If we count the years, he is young; if we reckon the merits of his character, he is old. Among scholars he is subtle; among cloistered men humble; there modest, here [Col. 0418D] truly pure; everywhere eagerly praiseworthy, because he was never eager for praise. In our Church, which is also his, he contracted with the Blessed Virgin a natural obligation by word, a civil one by writing, and a canonical one, combining both, by deed and consent—

[Note: [Col. 0418D] That is, Saint Geneviève.]—

whom we serve.

[Note: [Col. 0418D–0420D] He means the canonical profession which Peter had made orally and in writing in the church of Sainte-Geneviève. It was not then ancient practice among either canons or monks to make religious profession and publicly pronounce vows in certain settled and prescribed words, recorded in writing. It is written of Blessed Stephen of Muret, founder of the Order of Grandmont and earlier a regular canon, that, after writing his profession on a charter, he placed it on his head and said: “Almighty and merciful God, I, Brother Stephen, promise you that from now on I shall serve you in this wilderness in the Catholic faith; and for this reason I place this charter upon my head and this ring upon my finger, so that on the day of my death this promise and this charter may be a shield and defence to me against the snares of my enemies.”]

Neither prelate ought to grant, nor subject request, release from that obligation. [Col. 0419A] We have cared for him with such diligence, advanced him at such expense, and cherished him with such favour that to send him away freed from our obedience we consider nothing other than to lose him. Far be it that he should leave us headless and, like a cleric exposed to the winds—without title, a soldier without pay, a man in a gown without comfort—wander about, a marvel to his own people and a spectacle to strangers. Yet, lest we offend your goodwill or incur your displeasure, we do not restore him to you as a deposit held among us, but for the present commend him to you as one entrusted to us.

But if, by God’s providence and through your aid and effort, it should happen that you call him from a humbler to a higher rank, from footstool to chair, from the dust of subjection to the watchtower of governance—

[Note: [Col. 0420D] He asks the archbishop of Lund to honour his nephew Peter, canon of Sainte-Geneviève, on his return to his homeland with some prelacy. This was in fact accomplished when Peter succeeded his uncle in the bishopric of Roskilde, which, after resigning Eskil, he had held together with the primacy of Lund by dispensation of the supreme pontiff.]—

then in this praiseworthy advancement and success we grant him [Col. 0419B] full release and full freedom.

## LETTER CXXXVII. TO G., ABBOT OF SAINT SATYRUS

He asks pardon for a certain fugitive.

To his dearest lord and father G., abbot of Saint Satyrus, STEPHEN, called abbot of Sainte-Geneviève: common prayers in the Lord.

Many accuse us of harshness and severity whenever we correct those in error somewhat more sharply or rebuke the unruly. But if we neglect to lift up one who has fallen, receive one who is perishing, or hear a beggar at the doors, [Col. 0419C] they denounce us as cruel and akin to murderers. In the first case, if we have exceeded the proper measure, it will not be required of us that we seek pardon from those subject to us.

[Note: [Col. 0420D] He took this passage from the Rule of Saint Augustine, chapter 10: “But if you perceive that you have exceeded the measure, it is not required of you that you seek pardon from those subject to you.”]

In the second, one must consider with how much discernment those who govern ought to act, so that mercy may watch over subjects who are perishing, compassion be aroused, and fatherly affection overcome both the impulse and the measure of punishment. Therefore I offer prayers for the bearer of this letter, formerly our brother and canon: may access be opened to him as he pleads; may he, wandering and fugitive upon the earth, be gathered in, lest he lose salvation in the forest, perish in his transgression, or incur death through delay. Quickly returned to himself, he strives manfully by much penance to redeem the few days which he childishly spent outside with his carnal mother, within the bosom of his spiritual mother.

## LETTER CXXXVIII. TO THE ABBOT OF CÎTEAUX, IN THE PERSON OF THE CLERICS OF GRANDMONT

They give thanks for the benefits bestowed upon them.

[Col. 0419D]

Although not with thanksgiving equal to your deserts, still with pious [Col. 0420A] and humble solicitude we acknowledge your benefits, adoring on bended knees in you Him from whose fullness you have received: that your charity may not fail any individual and may suffice for all. Some were breaking the bruised reed; others extinguishing the smoking flax. But behold: as the Spirit of God breathes upon us from the four winds, our dry bones live again through your benefits and prayers. Having endured perils among false brethren, deceits in counsel, prejudice in judgment, violence in flight—cast out, struck, afflicted with insults, filled with reproaches—while priest and Levite passed by, we were received half-dead by the true disciple of the Samaritan, the holy Cistercian Order; and we were led not merely to the inn but even to his mother’s chamber. We shared abundantly in the children’s bread with those for whom crumbs falling from our masters’ table ought to have sufficed.

You gathered exiles, received the expelled, helped the faint-hearted, refreshed the grieving; you bestowed upon beggars alms sufficient for them, upon the weak help effective for them, upon the simple counsel, and upon suppliants aid. In all these things, what can we render to our lords for all that they have rendered to us? May God render you the reward of the righteous, since you received us, although unrighteous, in the name of the Righteous One. But because our case, as though weighed in a balance, is still moving and wavering and awaits the judgment of the supreme pontiff, we, hoping in God’s mercy alone, prostrate at the knees of your holy fatherhood [Col. 0420C] beseech, ask, and entreat you in the Lord to complete happily and beneficently what you have begun in us faithfully and kindly. We commend our cause to your prayers and counsel, fearing, from what has gone before, indignation and wrath, assaults by evil angels, and the cunning, power, pride, arrogance, expense, ambition, and other traits of our lay brothers which are terror to the poor and error to the rich. Farewell in the Lord, most holy and blessed Fathers.

## LETTER CXXXIX. TO PETER OF DENMARK

He exhorts him ever more and more to embrace higher things.

[Col. 0420D]

To his most beloved brother PETER of Denmark, canon of Sainte-Geneviève, STEPHEN, called abbot of Sainte-Geneviève: may you, having laid aside the cold of the North, burn with the flame of charity.

We preserve for you in faithful remembrance our customary, not dissolved, friendship of brotherhood and grace; [Col. 0421A] neither compensating for your absence nor crossing the long spaces of lands by an easy leap of longing. By these steps of affection, cultivators and disciples of charity encounter one another: they comfort their concern, disregard negligence, banish sadness, and converse with one another though absent by a certain artful intercourse of nature. Let these religious exchanges pass between us; and let communion of wills supply what the rarity of travellers begrudges. We rejoice with you that, having laid aside the ancestral barbarism of your old birth, you have wholly softened into a Christian shaping of character; and that what Ethiopians cannot achieve by changing their dark skin, the white offspring of icy Denmark rejoice has been granted in you and from you.

[Note: [Col. 0421D] The kingdom of Denmark—also called Dacia or Dania—is situated upon the peninsula of the northern ocean formerly inhabited by the Cimbri. Saxo Grammaticus, its inhabitant, describes it elegantly, as was his custom: “Denmark, divided in the midst by waves of the sea, possesses only a few portions of firm and continuous land, which so great an interruption of waters distinguishes according to the varying direction of the strait.” It is called icy because its northern region is stiffened by more severe cold.]

To these are added [Col. 0421B] the discipline of regular observance in which you were trained in the cloister and the doctrine of Holy Scripture which you learned in the schools. From both comes your good, pleasing, and perfect will to offer God morning and evening sacrifice. We wish you to hold fast to these things in your tender age. It delights us that your youth advances in this advancement. If it be granted that your last days grow old in years, let it not happen that they fail to know themselves in spirit. Meanwhile, solicitous for your state, we desire to be assured by messenger or letter what you are doing, what your people around you are doing, and what we too ought to hope concerning either your return to us or your establishment among your own people.

[Note: [Col. 0421D] Here it is useful to recall what Stephen had written to the archbishop of Lund, Peter’s uncle, in letter 137, asking him to procure for Peter some prelacy among his own people in the kingdom of Denmark.]

All our brethren greet you with one common longing, hoping good things concerning you and fearing [Col. 0421C] adverse ones. Farewell as we wish; wish that we may fare well.

## LETTER CXL. TO THE LORD POPE, IN THE PERSON OF THE QUEEN OF THE FRANKS

[Note: [Col. 0421D–0422D] That is, Adela, wife of Louis the Younger and mother of Philip Augustus. When Philip set out for overseas lands in 1190, he entrusted the administration of the kingdom to her; this letter seems to have been written in that year. Rigord mentions these matters in the testament which Philip made before his departure: “We will and command that our most dear mother, Queen A., together with our most dear uncle and faithful William, archbishop of Reims, appoint at Paris one day in every four months, on which they shall hear the complaints of the men of our kingdom and resolve them there for the honour of God and the benefit of the kingdom.” The king’s expedition is discussed at the beginning of this letter, etc.]

She asks him to postpone judgment in the matter of the archbishop of Tours and the bishop of Dol until the king’s return.

Compelled by maternal affection, as the successive passing of each hour brings it, in my son the king of the Franks’ absence I endure certain new and freshly inflicted wounds, and at every moment I feel a sword piercing my own soul. I seem to see [Col. 0422A] [200] a part of my entrails offered in sacrifice to the Lord, and my only son, like Isaac when bound, laid upon the altar; yet I cannot either imitate or attain Abraham’s patience and obedience, because both a mother’s heart excludes it and my female sex does not allow it. Amid these pains of renewed childbirth and the revived distresses of my former confinement, nothing suffices for my consolation except the remembrance of the Lord’s cross and Passion, for whose exaltation and honour my son—so glorious upon earth—has undertaken in this pilgrimage to suffer, and, if necessary, to be crucified with the Lord.

He sins against the Son of God; he sins against the Holy Spirit, who, during this so devout and religious absence, disturbs his kingdom in any respect and strives, or permits others to strive, to cast it into a condition other than that in which the king’s peaceful departure, with some measure of consolation, left his subject people less sorrowful. Therefore, Father, I write these things to you because the special charge of the kingdom laid upon me moves and admonishes my motherly heart to see with provident concern that no changes occur, whether concerning churches, greater or lesser princes, cities, towns, or the people, at which my son the king’s devout pilgrimage ought to take offence or be troubled.

Accordingly, I ask and beseech you, and, as a devoted daughter of the Roman Church, faithfully advise, that the business of the Church of Tours and that of Dol be deferred until the king’s return, which we desire and hope for in the Lord; and that the Church of Tours, which, as one of the chief members of [Col. 0422C] the royal crown, holds the greatest place among the others, may rejoice in royal patronage and not suffer hurt from the violence or incursion of the men of Dol. For our pilgrim—still, by God’s grace, strong and powerful—will not be able to endure this patiently; nor will the princes of the realm look with equanimity upon the rights of their churches being subjected to a different rule from that under which they have hitherto proceeded in the time of his father, King Louis of blessed memory, or in his own time. Nor will they in any way permit the metropolitan of Lesser Brittany to vaunt himself under some monstrous guise, two-headed with Janus,

> [Note: Col. 0422D] The ancients portrayed Janus as double-faced, and the Romans placed his image upon their earliest coins, which they called asses. Janus was a most ancient king of Latium and exceptionally shrewd in foreseeing future events; therefore they fashioned for him a double countenance. [Col. 0423B] Others, however, said that he was Noah himself, or at least his son Japheth, who bore two faces because he had seen two worlds: namely, the one which perished in the waters of the Flood, and the other later renewed. Whoever Janus was, he had a temple at Rome which was closed in time of peace and opened in time of war. In our cabinet of coins we possess one of Nero, on the reverse of which this temple may be seen with the inscription:
>
> *Having secured peace on land and sea, he closed Janus.*
>
> Some also imagined Janus as four-faced [Col. 0423C] and supposed him to be identical with the sun, assigning him four faces so that he might behold the four quarters of the world from the four winds.

or two-faced with a Centaur.

> [Note: Col. 0422D] Elsewhere he calls it “two-formed,” and more correctly, since its upper part was human and its lower part equine. The poets took occasion to invent such a monster because the Centaurs, a people of Thessaly, were the first to tame horses, fight from them, and seemed so attached to them and to move them at will that they appeared to be horses themselves. Hence those same people were called Hippocentaurs. Virgil, *Aeneid* VI, calls the Centaurs two-formed:
>
> *A mixed race and two-formed progeny*,
>
> which is also found in another letter of our Stephen.

## 202. LETTER CXLI. TO R., DEAN OF REIMS

He exhorts him not to allow the rule of common life, which had hitherto endured in the Church of Reims, to be banished from it.

[Col. 0423A]

To the venerable and discreet Master R., Dean of Reims,

> [Note: Col. 0423C] The chapter of the Church of Blessed Mary at Reims was formerly governed by provosts, in whose hands lay all authority, both spiritual and temporal. Yet they had under them certain deans who watched over regular observance and the preservation of discipline. This is evident in those rules which Ebbo, Archbishop of Reims, delivered to the administrators of his church’s offices; they were appended to the end of Flodoard’s works.

Stephen of Saint Geneviève, greeting and the reverence owed to the ancient Fathers.

Bear a little with my folly, Father and great priest, and do not despise the reminder of a little man.

> [Note: Col. 0423D] From this passage and others it is inferred that our Stephen was small in stature; for in another letter he calls himself “a little fellow,” “a small and insignificant man.”

A report has spread among many that some of you are striving to alter the ancient traces of the Fathers,

> [Note: Col. 0423D] Namely, the common life and regular observances which had long flourished in this cathedral church.

instituted by sacred councils,

> [Note: Col. 0423D] Namely, the Councils of Mainz, Tours, Chalon, Arles, Meaux, and Aachen.

and hitherto observed for so long by the glorious Church of Reims; and that they are labouring, by a certain singularity, to erase, cast down, and trample underfoot the golden plate

> [Note: Col. 0423D] He alludes to the golden plate worn upon the brow by the high priest of the Mosaic Law, as is recorded in Exodus 28.

of religious [Col. 0423B] custom, which is set upon the brow of the metropolitan church and shines before all who are in the kingdom.

> [Note: Col. 0423D] That they may introduce into it the secular life, which Letter 85 calls “singularity.”

By a certain unique privilege the see of Reims stood pre-eminent among the other churches of Gaul, continuing [Col. 0424A] with the apostles in the fellowship of bread

> [Note: Col. 0423D] He means the common table, which they still frequented in the refectory.

and prayer, and, in its social fellowship, displaying the sacramental communion: a spectacle to its superiors, an example to its inferiors. Of the remnants of regular institutions,

> [Note: Col. 0423D] Therefore the canons of the cathedral Church of Reims [Col. 0424B] had observed all regular institutions, the greater part of which they had already abandoned, retaining only two: common life in the refectory and nightly sleep in the dormitory.

they retained for themselves two places: the upper room of refreshment and the house of sleep; in the one following chaste abstinence, in the other observing stainless continence. Going together from Mass to table, from spiritual refreshment to bodily refreshment, after the Lord had first been invoked,

> [Note: Col. 0424B] It has always been the custom among Christians to invoke God before a meal. Tertullian says: “They do not recline before prayer to God has been tasted beforehand.” Jerome, from Philo, says of the Essenes, or the earliest Christians of the Church of Alexandria: “At their tables they begin the feast with praises of God.”

and after the sign of blessing had been extended over the food,

> [Note: Col. 0424B] That is, the sign of the cross, which Christians have always customarily made before taking food, as Origen testifies in Book II on Job: “It is indeed true that, when we eat or drink, we shall be mindful of faith if we invoke His dread name, if we sign ourselves, or our food or drink, with the sign of Christ’s venerable cross.” Gregory of Nazianzus also says against Julian: “They report that some of those who, through error and ignorance, had fallen into that crime of idolatry, after committing it returned home and had companions and fellow-guests share their table. Then, when the banquet proceeded to the customary drinking of cold water, as though nothing more serious had happened to them, they raised their eyes over the cup of water and invoked Christ with the sign of the cross.”

the Lord’s guests refreshed themselves—less their bellies than their minds—while through the service of a reader the divine word sounded to them,

> [Note: Col. 0424C] The Rule of St Augustine directs that reading be done at table in these words: “Listen without disturbance or contention to what is customarily read to you; let not your throats alone receive food, but [Col. 0424D] let your ears also hunger for the word of God.” The Council of Aachen under Louis the Pious, in its final canon, says of canons: “While they eat in the refectory and reverently maintain silence, a reading is to be read continuously.” In the *Life of Alcuin* it is written of his master Egbert that “as evening drew near, especially excepting Lent, at every season, summer as well as winter, he took with his household a modest yet suitably prepared meal, not sparing the reader’s tongue, that they might be refreshed with both breads.”

now admonishing them with commandments, now restraining them with prohibitions, sometimes urging them by [Col. 0424B] threats and terrors, at other times soothing them with consolations and promises. O happy feasts, which provoke not drunken excess but serve sobriety, and which, when they have been taken, are closed with thanksgiving,

> [Note: Col. 0424D] The earliest Christians also customarily ended their banquets with a devout prayer to God. Tertullian says in these words: “Prayer likewise breaks up the banquet; then they depart.” And Philo, speaking of the president of the Essenes’ feast, says: “Then he rises and is the first to sing a hymn in praise of God.” We learn from the Gospel that Christ also observed this at the Supper: “When they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives” (Matthew 26).

leaving bodily sustenance to the poor [Col. 0425A] and preserving spiritual fruit for their fellow-guests! In these and other regular observances the Church of Reims proceeded, terrible as an army arrayed in battle, beloved by her own people and admirable to outsiders. If these things begin to be changed,

> [Note: Col. 0425B] Stephen wrote this letter to urge the Dean of Reims to oppose certain canons of his church who were attempting to cast off the yoke of regular observance which they had hitherto maintained, and who wished to dissolve the common table in order to live privately in their own houses. Besides this letter, three others on the same subject are found in the archives of the same Church of Reims, entitled “Concerning the Refectory.” One is by Pope Alexander III, another by the Abbot of Saint-Victor, and the third by Pope Innocent III, from which I here transcribe part:
>
