> “We have received word that the following custom was observed in that church: all the canons had one refectory and a common table, at which, although not every individual ate every day, nevertheless some of the canons ate every day, etc. Although these practices are still maintained fairly honourably in the same church, you show no small negligence in attending the common table, since neither all of you nor on every day, but only certain persons, are served in the common refectory; and by your negligence what was customarily continuous in the days of your predecessors has become intermittent.”
>
> From this letter it appears by what stages common life gradually disappeared from the Church of Reims. First, while regular discipline flourished there, all took their food in the refectory every day. Secondly, as charity grew cold, although some were present each day, many were absent. Thirdly, neither all nor any attended every day, but only on more solemn occasions; and thus what had been continuous became intermittent. At last they abandoned the common life observed among them for so many centuries. Peter Cocquault, canon and official of Reims, notes that this happened in 1201 in his chronological table, where he says that they abandoned “the apostolic and angelic common life, in order to lead a life of men, subject to secular cares.”

what will her sister Germany say, her sister both by place and order,

> [Note: Col. 0425D] The Church of Reims is called the sister of the churches of Germany by place because they were near each other and all lay within Belgic Gaul. It is also called their sister by order because most of them still practised the common life.

which, among its other ecclesiastical institutions, still so observes the fraternal fellowship of meals and rest that it does not admit the modern dissolution?

> [Note: Col. 0425D] By these words he states clearly enough that the secularization, as it is called, of cathedral churches had recently been introduced throughout Gaul. We read in Camusat that the canons of Troyes were given secular dress in or about 1080.

Whether sympathetically or mockingly, it will cry: “How the gold has grown dim, how the finest colour has changed!” (*Lamentations* 4). The Gallican churches also will cry, more willingly accepting the easing of dispensation than the rigour of austerity: “Behold, the Church of Reims has become like one of us, covering our shame by her association and defending our negligence by her authority.” This twofold song ought rather to be called an epitaph than an epithalamium.

Until now, and not without reason, the city of Paris claimed learning for itself,

> [Note: Col. 0426B] For letters greatly flourished in the Parisian academy in this age, to which students gathered from every region of the earth. Rigord writes in his *Life of Philip Augustus*: “In those days the study of letters flourished at Paris; nor do we read that such a multitude of schools existed at Athens, Egypt, or any part of the world, as inhabited the aforesaid place for the sake of study, etc. Since in that most noble city complete and perfect instruction was found not only in the trivium and quadrivium, but also in questions of canon and civil law, and in the discipline written for healing bodies and preserving health, they taught sacred Scripture and theological questions.”

and the Church of Reims discipline.

> [Note: Col. 0426C] The canons of Reims had always observed regular discipline so devoutly that they proceeded with greater severity against offenders. The author previously praised recalls two examples in his chronological Table of Reims: certain canons who, having sinned against the Rule and the customs of their elders, were publicly reproved and beaten in chapter. One was Radbolbus, or Rotardus, born of royal lineage and elected to the bishopric of Châlons. Having attended, in his Church of Reims, the funeral rites of Blessed Albert, Bishop of Liège, he appeared with a crowd of nobles and not in proper dress with his fellow canons. After the funeral, the dean, as Cantipratensis relates, Book II, chapter 39, “called the chapter together and rebuked Radboldus, saying: ‘Rise and make satisfaction to the Church, and prepare your back for discipline before the brethren, because you entered the choir with the canons, contrary to the Rule, without a wedding garment.’ Without delay the elect rose and prostrated himself, removed his clothes, and received a very severe discipline from the dean’s hand. When he had received it, the elect put on his clothes again, rose, and before all said to the dean with the greatest graciousness of expression: ‘I give thanks to God and to the patroness of the Church of Reims, His most merciful mother, that I leave you here as such a man in authority. Henceforth I shall love this place all the more, and in this see I shall honour a worthy memorial of severity.’”

Paris retains both things it began; Reims, if it begins to decline, is close to danger and not far from a fall. Father, meet this destructive novelty with outstretched arms and an open heart;

> [Note: Col. 0426D] By this name he characterizes the secular life recently admitted among cathedral canons.

resist it, and raise for the struggle the manly spirit which common opinion proclaimed you to possess.

> [Note: Col. 0426D] Cantipratensis writes of this dean in the passage cited above: “We have heard from those who knew the man that there was in the Church of Reims a certain most diligent dean, English by birth, who corrected his canons manfully for their offences.”

Do not let an ageing dean obey the young men who particularly desire to live separately—indeed, not to say secularly—lest, heaven forbid, through the favour or attachment of some petty glory, someone [204] trample your reputation into the earth and bring your glory down to dust. I know that the gentleness of my lord the Archbishop of Reims is so great that, with that charity which bears all things and endures all things, he readily yields to the will of his sons—especially since the general custom of the Gallican Church permits and approves the distribution of separate portions to its canons, [Col. 0426B] and the authority of the supreme pontiff does not object. Yet again I know that his integrity and prudence are so great [Col. 0427A] that he will preserve in all things the ancient dignity of the Church of Reims and will abandon the plan conceived and, as they say, already begun, if you should wish to persuade him of this together with some members of your sacred college, and either firmly admonish him or humbly beseech him not to introduce this ugly form of novelty.

## 205–208. LETTER CXLII. TO GODFREY, ABBOT OF SAINT-SATYR

He commends one of his canons.

I would have sent a reminder, if I did not fear receiving a contemptuous response. Yet brotherly affection urges me not to be silent concerning good things, and, although I invite one not unwilling, to invite him to consider the ministry he has undertaken a burden rather than an honour. In authority, brother, both you and I must endure many things, overlook many things, and punish most things—but with love for persons and hatred of vices. “Who is wise and will observe this?” Amid these burdens, anxieties, and dangers, we must remember the past, take charge of the present, and make provision for the future. Engaged in this contest with you, I have less confidence in my own sufficiency than in yours, but I distrust my own perseverance more than yours. Meanwhile let us pray to the Most High that He who, by His hidden but just judgment, has set us at the summit of prelacy, whether for a crown or, heaven forbid, for punishment, may grant us His preventing and following grace, by which we may both be of use to the brethren entrusted to us, [Col. 0427C] over whom it has fallen to our lot to preside, and, as they advance, may advance with them to eternal life.

Meanwhile I earnestly offer prayers to you and to all our brethren, my lords, that you may treat Brother Gilbert, our canon, who greatly commends himself to your goodwill, more kindly for love of me and love him more fully. As I offer my whole self for service to you and your Church, so I present myself as devoted.

## 209. LETTER CXLIII. OF THE ABBOTS OF SAINT-DENIS, SAINT-GERMAIN, SAINT-VICTOR, AND SAINT-GENEVIÈVE TO THE POPE

They give an account of what they did and decreed in the affair of the Grandmontines.

[Col. 0427D] To the most holy lord and Father, by God’s grace supreme pontiff: H., Abbot of Saint-Denis; F., Abbot of Saint-Germain; G., Abbot of Saint-Victor; and S., called Abbot of Saint-Geneviève: greeting, and, with [Col. 0428A] all submission and devotion, full obedience in all things.

The old wound of the Grandmontine schism, concealed under an ulcerous scar by a kind of pretended peace, their *conversi*—having turned back from the truth which they had promised—are striving to revive by the recurrent plague of litigation. They put no trust in justice, but, as they themselves boast, place their hope in the corruption of money and the lavish distribution of gifts. After long labours; after many journeys to the Roman Church and returns from it; after the lamentable spectacle made public by their order while they ran about cities and towns litigating; after the exposing to all of their supposed keeping of secrets: the lord king of the Franks, who today offered himself to God as a sacrifice,

> [Note: Col. 0427D] This letter is said to have been written in 1190, on the feast of Saint John the Baptist, when, as Rigord says: “King Philip came with a very great retinue to the church of the most blessed martyr Denis to receive permission to depart. For the kings of the Franks had anciently been accustomed, whenever they took up arms against enemies, to carry with them for protection the banner from above the altar of Saint Denis and place it in the first battle-line of the combatants; when their adversaries saw and recognized it, they were often terrified and fled. Therefore the most Christian king, humbly prostrate in prayer upon the marble pavement before the bodies of the holy martyrs Denis, Rusticus, and Eleutherius, commended himself to God, the Blessed Virgin Mary, the holy martyrs, and all [Col. 0428D] the saints. At last, rising from prayer in tears, he there most devoutly received the pilgrim’s scrip and staff from the hand of William, Archbishop of Reims, his uncle and legate of the Apostolic See. Then, over the bodies of the saints, he received with his own hands two suitably decorated banners, called *étendards* in French, in memory of the holy martyrs and for protection while he was to fight against the enemies of Christ’s cross. Finally, commending himself to the prayers of the brethren, and having received the blessing of the nail, the crown of thorns, and the arm of Saint Simeon, he departed.”

having summoned [Col. 0428B] his barons and prudent, religious ecclesiastical persons, moved and exhorted the parties toward concord and peace. Each side gave an undertaking, under an attestation to the truth—which among religious persons has the force of an oath—that those present would observe the form of peace which had been granted and drawn up before the royal highness, and would urgently and steadfastly cause its observance by those absent. It was granted and written down, sealed with the royal seal; and the most clement king himself made himself surety that, if any persons thereafter wished to oppose so solemnly celebrated a peace, he would be their adversary and would not receive them in his realm, whereas those who observed the peace he would gather under his protection [Col. 0428C] and safeguard in his land by royal patronage.

These terms were read in the chapter of Grandmont and confirmed by the prior—who, in whatever manner, presides over that place today—

> [Note: Col. 0428D] The prior of Grandmont at that time was called William Itherius, appointed in place of William of Treignac by the votes of the general chapter in 1188.

into the hand of the Archbishop of Bourges, upon his word of truth and at peril of his soul; and all, both laymen and clerics, gave this promise, attesting their agreement. And behold, suddenly a north wind came and shook the corners of that house, so that the said prior and the *conversi*, with a very few clerics whom they retain with themselves by flattery or fear, have, no less imprudently than shamelessly, drawn back from the pledged faith. Not fearing to corrupt truth, they sacrilegiously contradict what they had sworn.

Brother Bernard, a simple man, fearing God and departing from evil, followed the integrity of his faith in the matter conceived by the lay brothers; with nearly five hundred brethren, he does not follow the lay brothers’ deceit, keeps the promise, shuns cunning, and detests perfidy. Against him, faithful in his promise, and against the clerical brethren—who are held two by two or one by one in the cells like captives—certain *conversi*, puffed up with arrogance, clever in craft, glorying in words and trusting in gifts, have approached the Roman Church in order, if they can, to deceive your holy religious devotion and strike down and bend the cedars of Lebanon to their will.

The clerics, for themselves and Brother Bernard, duly fled to the common refuge of appeal, wherein the dignity of the Roman Church resides and all who are oppressed find refuge, before any sentence was pronounced. As they appealed canonically, so they proceed canonically, [Col. 0429B] awaiting from you or delegated judges a canonical sentence according to the sacred canons.

Holy Father, do not let the confused clamour of the lay brothers against enclosed clerics move you: let not the ass bray against its rider; let not the saw boast against him who holds it; let not an unlearned man teach letters to a cleric; and let not a layman command priestly matters to a priest. For the clerics and Brother B., who fights unceasingly for justice, cry out in the ears of the Lord of Hosts; and your most Christian kinsman, the king of the Franks, cries out also in your sacred ears. He daily sheds his blood for Christ, and, as it were, lives in exile from his kingdom for the cross of Christ, that you may cause the form of peace which he granted, drew up, and confirmed—and which was afterward violated by the sacrilege of the faithless—to be observed; that you may receive the appeal made by the clerics as canonical; that you may not admit the seditious laymen and sons of contradiction, Philip of Beaumont and his accomplices; that you may annul the sentence prematurely and improperly delivered against the clerics by the prior, whose wicked accession and most evil conduct are reported; and that you may commit the cells of Grandmont situated in his land to the administration of Brother B., the Bishop of Paris,

> [Note: Col. 0429D] At that time Maurice most worthily occupied the see of Paris, a man most distinguished in piety, learning, and all other gifts, as we have already noted above.

and other prudent and religious men.

If these things are accomplished by your authority, the soul of the lord king, who fights daily for Christ and lives, as it were, in exile from his kingdom for Christ’s cross, will rejoice; he will rejoice and give you thanks, exalting the Roman Church with praises and, following in his fathers’ footsteps, receiving and honouring it in its necessities. But if otherwise should happen—God forbid!—there is reason to fear that his indignation may be aroused, that he may show less deference to the faith for which he fights, offer less devotion to the Roman Church, and prove less obedient. Since the whole Gallican Church [Col. 0430A] will profess itself injured and disgraced in the humiliation of the Grandmontine clerics, and glad and joyful in their protection and victory, we beseech your holy fatherhood and, insofar as sons may, advise our father: since you have always loved the kingdom of the Franks and the churches established within it, graciously hear him in this petition and beneficially fulfil what is requested.

## 213. LETTER CXLIV. TO THE LORD POPE, IN THE PERSON OF THE CLERICS OF GRANDMONT

They complain of the insults of their *conversi*.

May a father attend to his son’s grief: before his venerable countenance religion begs for glory, and truth for intervention. Your holy love freely offers what is due to each person, so that from the same throne of justice the humble may receive consolation and the proud confusion. We have experienced this in ourselves, Father, being deprived of the aid and counsel of many; our *conversi*

> [Note: Col. 0429D] He speaks of the *conversi* of the Order of Grandmont, of whom he treated above.

seek rather to hunt their favour with money than to win it through innocence, trusting in man and making flesh their arm. They do not fear the truth of the prophetic curse. They arm and encourage the princes of this world, stir up the people, and even approach some bishops, so that those whom they have violently driven out of our cells may not be received by monasteries or protected by churches. Me, though unworthy, their pastor,

> [Note: Col. 0429D] These words show that this letter was written in the name of Bernard, prior of the monastery of Grandmont, driven out by his rebellious *conversi*, together with his other clerics likewise oppressed by their violence.

they expelled, together with a multitude of clerical brethren numbering more than [Col. 0430C] two hundred, not so much deceitfully as violently, amid confused clamour and popular error. They installed another,

> [Note: Col. 0429D] Namely Brother Stephen, of whom Letter 136 speaks.

who succeeded neither one who had died nor one who had resigned.

In all these things their wrath has not been turned away, but their hand is stretched out so far that, through the power of secular people whom they never cease to win to their side by unlawful arts and pecuniary profit, they mercilessly labour by fair means and foul to break the reed in us and extinguish the smoking flax. Our sole hope after God, Father, rests in your elevation [214] to office:

> [Note: Col. 0429D] This letter appears to have been written at the beginning of Urban’s elevation to the supreme pontificate. While he was still a cardinal, this very affair of the Grandmontines had been handled by him, and he had supported the prior’s side against the wrongs of the *conversi*.

may the authority entrusted to you find means, so far as is permitted and expedient, to accomplish and bring to completion that whose good, pleasing, and perfect will had previously stood beside us in this matter. Let the yoke [Col. 0430D] of the lay brothers rot away before your oil, if it please you,

> [Note: Col. 0430D] This is a manner of speaking customary in Holy Scripture, namely in Isaiah 10. It signifies the ease with which one is enabled to free oneself from a weighty matter. The metaphor is drawn from the yoke of oxen, which, repeatedly drenched with oil, eventually rots and is easily broken and dissolved.

so that neither Eliezer may rule Abraham,

> [Note: Col. 0430D] That is, let a servant not command his master; he alludes to what is read in Genesis 15 concerning Abraham and his household servant Eliezer.

nor Hagar despise Sarah, nor an unlearned man despise a cleric, nor a layman command a priest. Restore the fallen; help the fainthearted; comfort those who weep and the stricken shepherd; healing the despised sheep of the flock, bring them back [Col. 0431A] to the folds in such peace that those who ought to be subject may understand that they are to be led and taught.

## 215. LETTER CXLV. TO PETER OF DENMARK

> [Note: Col. 0431D] See Letters 139 and 150.

He informs him of the brethren’s goodwill.

To the most dear and beloved brother and friend Peter: Stephen, called Abbot of Saint-Geneviève, greeting and sincere affection, whether the envious will it or no.

I grieve for you, my brother, beloved exceedingly beyond the love of Jonathan, because at the sound of one false little rumour you were troubled and spoke, although from your past way of life we believe your mind to be prudent in discernment, steadfast in courage, firm in justice, and moderate in temperance. Established upon this fourfold foundation like an immovable pillar, not like a reed shaken by the wind, you should not have received either the breath of flatterers, the hissing of detractors, or the fabricated and deceitful words of informers. Often, singing psalms and praying in the chamber of your heart, you said to the Lord that He should deliver your soul from wicked lips and a deceitful tongue. Behold, a third tongue, which troubles brethren, almost moved the lampstand of your brotherly concord from its place; and the mouth which lied, not fearing to kill its own soul, charged innocent and simple brethren with the most wicked crime of detraction—brethren who love you without deceit, remember you without hostility, and cherish you without envy.

With all the diligence I could, in chapter and outside chapter, under an attestation of obedience, I investigated, brother, that malicious, blasphemous, wicked, and deceitful report; but I found neither its author nor anyone who knew or reported it. All alike denied it in astonishment and, while denying it, wondered at it. [216] By the authority entrusted to me over them, I also prohibited them from exposing tongues that are loose in this way to such matters, lest by much speaking they harm your gentleness, by vain speaking provoke your indignation, or by foolish speaking destroy or extinguish in the flower the fruit alike of our hope and yours. Confident of their integrity and of the love which they maintain toward you without pretence, I assure you that they have neither said the things maliciously reported to you nor will ever say or do anything that ought to offend you.

I, whatever manner of prelate I may be, beseech you by the breasts of your mother the Church, in which you made your profession by word and writing; by the merits of the virgin Geneviève, whom you have loved and love intimately; by the social and sacramental communion of the brethren; and by me, who sincerely love you: if any memory of it remains with you, let this scruple be removed from your mind, your tongue, and your hand, so that you retain no remnant of it within you [Col. 0432A] and admit no signs of a recurrence of similar disturbance through false persuasions.

For the gifts sent by you I thank you; each of the brethren thanks you; all thank you. By God’s grace all things prosper with us and our brethren, since we abound in necessities and, from the brethren’s religious and holy manner of life, spiritual things correspond to and provide for temporal things. The number of brethren increases, buildings are renewed, possessions multiply, and—what is greater—peace and tranquillity among the brethren, the observance of regular discipline, and devout zeal in the church offices, which commends their hidden conscience before God and their secure reputation before men. Hoping in God’s mercy, who causes us to abound beyond what [Col. 0432B] we ask or understand, we have begun to restore the leaky, wind-permeable, age-worn roofs of our church,

> [Note: Col. 0431D] Namely, the basilica of Saint Geneviève at Paris, partly destroyed by the Normans and partly collapsing through age, since it had already stood for almost seven hundred years.

procuring new timber to be laid upon the walls and beneath the lead roof. We are also renewing the walls, supporting them on the outside with cut and polished stones. God, who gave my brethren and me the purpose of undertaking this work, is able to provide the expenses necessary for it.

### Letter 146. To the Archbishop of Lund

He congratulates him on the promotion of his canon Peter to the episcopate.

To the reverend father and friend A., Archbishop of Lund, primate of Sweden [Note: That is, Absalon, of whom we have reported more above. Since he was distinguished by a double bishopric—namely, the sees of Roskilde and Lund—he resigned one of them to his nephew Peter, a canon of St. Geneviève.], Stephen of St. Geneviève.

We recall our lords and friends whom we cannot see with frequent thought; we embrace them with constant affection, pursue them with longing, and venerate them with service. Among others—and above them—the authority of your name raises for us a special theatre: beneath its shade we receive refreshment, and at its spectacle applause. Reputation proclaims your person, and your person lends strength to your reputation: the former, by a truthful judgment that does not lie concerning your deeds; the latter, by a just moderation that measures your character.

We do not say this because we wish to anoint with the oil of the sinner a head already anointed with sacred chrism. For, because of your purpose, we ought to emulate virtues, not flatter virtue. We once presented to you prayers on behalf of our dearest brother, your cleric and son Peter; now we turn those prayers into thanksgiving, because, as we have heard, you have so honoured and burdened him that honour may not fail because of the burden, and the burden may prove beneficial because of the honour. May God also increase His grace, and increase your favour, so that, having received grace for grace, he may both serve God in His ministers and please you in your ministries.

What follows I shall say in jest, and it should provoke not indignation [Col. 0433A], but invite you to mercy. Your fathers according to the flesh [Note: Namely, the Normans, northern peoples who, from Denmark, Sweden, and the other neighbouring regions, frequently attacked Gaul in the middle and toward the end of the ninth century, devastating all churches and holy places with sword and fire; among these especially the monastery of St. Geneviève at Paris.]—still held by pagan rite and superstition—invaded Gaul by the strength of their arms and, in the might of their power, captured cities, castles, and other strongholds; they devastated hamlets, villages, and fields; they carried some people away as plunder and captives, and struck others with the sword; they reduced holy places to the ground by fire and ruin.

Among other places, what we cannot—and ought not—recount without sighing and sobbing, they burned in a wretched conflagration the church of the apostles Peter and Paul, where the blessed virgin Geneviève rests bodily [Note: This church was founded near Paris by Clovis, king of the Gauls, about the year 608, in fulfilment of a vow which, at the urging of the most devout Queen Clotilde, he had made, saying—as the author of the Deeds of the Kings of France testifies—“Let a church of the blessed apostles be made, when, with God’s help, we return,” namely from the war against the Goths who were devastating Aquitaine. The body of the blessed virgin Geneviève was buried in it, as Gregory of Tours notes; and her tomb, which to this day shines there on every side with miracles, proves this most clearly.]. This church, built by royal aid and labour, adorned and painted within and without with mosaic work [Note: Mosaic works are those which Suetonius, in *Julius*, ch. 46, calls tessellated and inlaid: “On his campaigns he carried about tessellated and earthen pavements.” And Seneca, Letter 86: “A man thinks himself poor and shabby unless his walls gleam with great and beautiful circles, unless Alexandrian marbles are distinguished by Numidian veneers, unless an elaborate coating, varied in the manner of a painting, is applied to them on every side.” Likewise St Augustine, *City of God*, XVI.8: “The other kinds of men, or quasi-men, which are pictured in mosaic in the maritime square at Carthage.” Vitruvius, ch. 1, recalls having seen remains of pavements of this kind “in which tessellated marbles, with figures of fish and other things no larger than very small beans, imitate them artistically in diverse colours.” Such pavements may still be seen in the basilicas of St Denis in France [Col. 0434C], St Remigius at Reims, and elsewhere.], as its remains still testify, they burned in a pitiable fire [Col. 0433B], sparing neither the holy place nor showing reverence to the blessed virgin or the other saints resting there.

At length, through God’s grace, that ancient barbarism was softened and transformed by Christian gentleness. The northern cold, melted by the heat of faith, cast away idols and acknowledged its Creator. The Norsemen and Danes, reborn in Christ, retain, inhabit, and cultivate for themselves and their descendants that part of Gaul called Normandy from the name of the North [Note: After the many burnings and massacres perpetrated by the Normans throughout Gaul, Charles called the Simple, seeing himself unequal to resisting the ferocity of that people, made peace with them, chiefly on the condition that they should worship Christ. Therefore their leader, named Rollo, was immersed in the bath of regeneration, changed his name to Robert, married Gissa, the king’s daughter, and received with her as dowry the province of Neustria, which thereby acquired the name Normandy.].

In that persecution the walls of our church were burned; excessively consumed by age and decay, they threaten ruin, cry out to be strengthened by support, and await to be covered by a roof. Timber has been procured [Col. 0433C] to be placed upon the repaired walls and beneath sheets of lead. We hope in the Lord that He who began the work will complete and establish it [Col. 0434A], and will provide the necessary expenses—He who never abandons His servants who hope in Him.

Since, in so great a work—or burden—we are compelled to beg alms from others, we appeal to your generosity. You have been accustomed at times to purchase Roman lead [Note: He alludes to the lead of papal bulls, which, he says, strips the churches of his time—that is, is purchased at so great a price that the prelates of churches are reduced to poverty. He intended to cover the church of St Geneviève with lead, but his resources proved unequal to it.]; now, in purchasing English lead, open a willing heart and extend a beneficent hand. Churches are stripped by that lead; by this they are covered. The transactions differ: in the former the recipient often grieves, while in the latter the giver always earns merit. That is always redeemed with contentious gold; this is procured at the devout price of prayers. We have sent our brother G., bearer of this letter, that he may prudently carry out our commission and faithfully bring us back another’s benefit [Col. 0434B].

### Letter 147. To Valdemar, Bishop of Schleswig

He asks for lead for the repair and adornment of the church of St Geneviève.

To the venerable and illustrious man Valdemar, bishop of Schleswig [Note: Valdemar was of royal Danish blood and was raised to the bishopric of Schleswig. But when he sought to have a share of the kingdom assigned to him, he incurred the king’s hostility. He was compelled to leave his bishopric and, having sworn—so as to escape imprisonment—that he would never remain in a place where he was suspect to the king, he withdrew to Bologna, where he devoted himself to study. But when Hartwig, Archbishop of Bremen, died in 1207, Valdemar himself was chosen by the people of Bremen in his place, notwithstanding the objections of the people of Hamburg, who were accustomed to cast votes in the election of the Archbishop of Bremen. A grave controversy consequently arose between them, on which see Letters 158 and 159 in Book I of Innocent III’s letters. Meursius also narrates these matters more fully in *Danish History*, II, toward the end of the year 1207.], brother Stephen of St Geneviève, an unworthy minister, greeting and faithful service with all affection.

Your absence has left us the pleasant memory of you; if we delight in its traces, so we are refreshed by its charms. We admired mature old age in a young man, episcopal dignity in a future bishop, profound humility in noble stock, liberal munificence in a scholar, sociable affability in royal blood, and Gallic refinement in a northern man. We do not believe that honours have changed in you the character which, by God’s grace, nature rather than fortune bestowed upon you [Col. 0435A].

From these things we have drawn confidence to write to you and, with a brow worn smooth, as they say, to ask some favour without merit on our part. This one consolation remains in the request: if it meets refusal, a letter does not blush when it is not heard; it incurs no shame.

Your ancient forefathers, while still held in pagan error beneath idolatry, invaded Gaul by God’s just judgment; they captured cities and towns, destroyed municipalities, and overthrew churches. Among others, they burned in a miserable fire the church of the blessed virgin Geneviève, built by royal assistance and labour. The witnesses of this are the walls, burned then and eaten away, displaying their decay in lime rotted into ashes [Col. 0435B], and threatening collapse.

We have begun to repair them, timber already having been procured to be laid upon the renewed walls and beneath a lead roof. Begging with some shame, we ask and request that you send us something from your kindly and beneficent generosity, with which we may buy lead—not Roman, but English—because churches are covered with English lead and stripped by Roman. In our church, the happy memory of your name will live continually, under the testimony of the benefit you have generously conferred upon the blessed virgin Geneviève. We have sent our brother G., bearer of this letter, that he may prudently carry out our commission and faithfully bring us back another’s benefit [Col. 0435C].

### Letter 148. To William, Abbot of the Paraclete

He also asks him for lead.

To the venerable brother and friend William, abbot of the Paraclete [Note: See the letter written above to him, and what we have set down to elucidate it.], Stephen of St Geneviève, growing old with his elder, fullness of joys in the fullness of days.

“We praise the ancients, yet we make use of our own years.”

What we have said is poetic, not prophetic, but it is nevertheless true. Our fathers preceded us in the way of the Lord, as much in time as in authority and religion. For, like Hylas after Hercules, we do not follow them with equal steps. Moses gave a rule of life to the Hebrews, Numa Pompilius to the Romans, Phoroneus [Col. 0435D] to the Greeks, Trismegistus to the Egyptians, and the Son of God to Christians. Augustine, serving Him, like the innkeeper of the Samaritan, faithfully and prudently expended for our care the two denarii he had received from Him—namely, the word of teaching and the example of life—and will receive his reward when the Samaritan returns.

In this contest, though in different churches, we have laboured and do labour with you [Col. 0436A], fighting not as one who beats the air, and running not as though toward an uncertain goal [Note: Stephen was head of the monasteries of St Geneviève and St Evurtius of Orléans. William, however, was subprior of St Geneviève and afterward became an abbot in Denmark.]. Uncertain of your condition, we inform you of ours, knowing that you are ready both to rejoice with those who rejoice and to weep with those who weep.

Through God’s grace, all things prosper among us and the brethren. There is no opposing force, nor Satan, since they dwell united in the house of the Lord in the utmost tranquillity and peace, striving only in their contest to serve the Lord to outdo one another in humility. Temporal things answer to spiritual needs: the spacious and handsome regular buildings are almost completed [Note: Namely the dormitory, chapter house, refectory, chapel of the Blessed Mary, and cloister, which he had built with elegant construction and which we use to this day.], as are rustic buildings in the villages, matching urban ones both in spaciousness and beauty.

We have turned our concern and care to renewing and supporting [Col. 0436B] the old walls of the church, rotted by age and fire and threatening dissolution and collapse. We have also purchased fresh timber for repairing the dilapidated roofs, to be laid upon them. With this material, if God permits, we hope to cover the church, attending not to the symbolic meaning of the prophetic lead, which is said to sit upon iniquity, but to the usefulness and beauty of our basilica. We seek the substance of this metal, not its figure.

Since we are unequal to meeting the cost of so great a burden—or work—we are compelled to beg alms from our friends, by whose assistance and labour we may supply what we lack. Perhaps importunate and shameless, I redeem the length of the letter by a short speech [Col. 0436C]. But help us insofar as you can.

### Letter 149. To Omer, Bishop of Ribe

He commends his canon G., whom he sends to Denmark.

[Note: Ribe is a Danish city on the River Nipsia, by which it is divided into three parts. Saxo Grammaticus treats of Omer at the end of Book XIV of his history, and says that Absalon, bishop of Roskilde and Lund, consecrated Omer, bishop-elect of Ribe, to the religious ministry of a bishop.]

Four things either create new friendships or preserve old ones: reciprocal conversation, mutual services, the frequent coming and going of letters, and a reputation for virtue corresponding to truth. By the benefit of this last, we embrace in imagination your face, which we have not deserved to see with our eyes, applauding the reputation that both proclaims your generosity and commends your religious devotion. In the schools you learned truth; in the priesthood, virtue. Yet neither in the former did you learn truth without virtue, nor in the latter virtue without truth.

Trusting in your goodwill rather than our merits, we commend to your goodwill our dearest brother and canon G., the bearer of this letter, whom we have sent on the affairs of our church. In whatever he may need, for the love of God and of us, strengthen him with counsel and sustain him with protection [Col. 0436D]. God will reward you: He who rewards those receiving a righteous man in the name of a righteous man with a righteous man’s reward, and who will give into your bosom a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing, for the holy works of mercy [Col. 0437A].

### Letter 150. To the Archbishop of Lund

Under the name Solomon, he commends Peter, the archbishop’s nephew.

To the Archbishop of Lund: temporal and eternal salvation.

Happy the work and expenditure whose intention a fruitful bosom receives, whose outcome fulfils desire, and whose confidence of hope is neither disappointed nor deceptive. These things in your Solomon, truly peaceful in word and deed, should invite you—not unwillingly—to bring kindly to completion what you have benevolently [Col. 0437B] begun in him, continuing to foster the young man’s good disposition. He applies himself so to literary studies that he does not depart from the paths of virtue.

He is a plant which, through God’s grace and your watering, will grow into a fruitful tree, whose leaf will not soon fall and which will yield its fruit in its season. We bear testimony to him while he dwells with us on the mountain: diligent in the schools, honourable in his lodging, neither extravagant in superfluities nor miserly in necessities. He so merits the goodwill of his companions that he loses the favour of none. Let your holy fatherhood rejoice over him, and so exalt in him the illustrious eminence of your blood that his honour may correspond to so great a lineage, and that the lineage [Col. 0437C] may be proportionate to such honour. Thus may the uncle glory in the nephew, and the nephew be raised by the uncle.

### Letter 151. To a Certain Canon

He grants one of his canons permission to enter and remain in another order.

Wills should be aided when devotion gives them their beginning and discretion confirms their progress. Having considered this in our beloved fellow canon II., bearer of this letter, we neither dare longer oppose his petitions nor judge it right wholly to detract from them. We therefore grant him free permission to seek and enter a religious house, so that, with God’s help, among others rather than among us, he may live more strictly and conduct himself more rigorously.

We therefore offer prayers for him: that wherever he may be pleased to reside, he may be received kindly and treated generously because of his commendable knowledge of reading and chanting [Col. 0437D].

### Letter 152. To Canute, King of Denmark

He writes concerning a noble Danish youth who died and was buried at St Geneviève.

To the noble man Canute, descended from grandfathers and great-grandfathers who were kings [Col. 0438A], Brother Stephen, called abbot of St Geneviève, and the entire humble community of the church: greeting in the Author of salvation.

It is especially fitting for illustrious men and those who derive their origin from royal blood that, as they are magnificent in lineage, so they should be munificent in generosity. If generosity extends as far as churches, and if, for their own salvation and for the repose of the dead—especially parents and relatives—those who abound in wealth visit religious places, feed the poor, and distribute alms, they win grace before God and favour before men.

Your brother by blood, the well-disposed young man Waldemar [Note: He is entered in the necrology of St Geneviève in these words: “Waldemar, nephew of the king of Denmark, our canon for assistance, died.” This letter explains what a “canon for assistance” means when it adds: “He shares, like one of us, in prayers and spiritual benefits.”], whose memory is blessed, answered the royal lineage of your family with virtue worthy of it. With us he rendered his spirit to God [Col. 0438B] and entrusted his body among us to burial. Like one of us, he shares—and forever will share—in prayers and spiritual benefits. On the day of judgment he will rise with the blessed virgin Geneviève and, with those at the right hand and with her alike, receive the sentence of final blessing.

Since we have begun to renew the walls of the church in which he rests—burned by your forefathers when still pagans and since consumed by excessive age—and since we have determined to cover its dilapidated roofs with fresh timber and sheets of lead, we offer prayers to your nobility that, through G., our canon and bearer of this letter, you may send us some gift for purchasing lead [Col. 0438C]. Thus your generosity may be rewarded by God; the fame of your lineage may be commended by men; and among us the everlasting memory of your brother may be kept more solemnly and more frequently.

### Letter 153. To the Same

He also asks him for lead to cover the roof of the church of St Geneviève.

To Canute, most illustrious and most Christian king of the Danes [Note: Meursius writes of him in *Danish History* [Col. 0438D], under the year 1182: “When Waldemar I died, his son Canute VI received the kingdom, already, through his father’s care, initiated at Ringsted in the year 1170, when his grandfather Canute V was enrolled among the saints.”], Brother Stephen, called abbot of St Geneviève, and the entire humble community of that church: greeting, life, and victory.

The annals of history record, common report recounts, and the half-ruined walls of cities and towns attest the glorious and fortunate power and strength of the Danish kingdom [Col. 0438D], by which your ancient forefathers, still held in pagan error, invaded Gaul in the strength of their arm and the might of their power. Mother Church rejoices that you have descended from their noble stock and changed that pagan tyranny into Christian gentleness [Note: The first of the princes of Denmark to embrace the Christian religion was Harald, through the action of Emperor Louis the Pious, in the year 826. Saxo Grammaticus relates in *Danish History*, IX [Col. 0439C]:

> “Harald came to Louis at Mainz to seek assistance. Louis, consumed with the greatest zeal for spreading religion, offered terms to the barbarian, promising aid if he agreed to practise the worship of Christ. By this decision he gained salvation for his guest and a proclamation of piety for himself. Harald, having undergone the solemn washing, was then strengthened by Saxon forces. Relying on them, he devoted earnest expenditure to building a church for dedication to God in Schleswig territory. Thus, taking an example of this most holy order from Roman rites, he destroyed temples defiled by the error of unbelievers, proscribed sacrificers, abolished pagan priesthoods, and first introduced Christian rites into his uncivilized country. Rejecting the worship of demons and emulating the divine worship, he observed with most scrupulous care everything belonging to the safeguarding of religion; but he began the undertaking more piously than effectively. For Hoguerus came, violated the rites introduced through him, banished true religion, restored an adulterous religion in its former place, and honoured its ceremonies as his own. Harald, an exile, transferred his fortune into sacrilege: as he had been the chief example of religion begun, so he became the first spectacle of its abandonment, and from a splendid author of holiness became its infamous deserter. Eric, his brother, baptized with him at Mainz, also fell away from the faith and raged against Christians. But about the year 860, at the persuasion of Ansgar, bishop of Bremen, he turned his mind back to the piety he had cast off, again abolished the worship of idols, and, casting aside the error of his sacrilegious mind, expiated all that he had committed through insolence. He showed himself as active in cultivating religion as he had been in despising it. Eric’s son, following his father’s footsteps, propagated religion in the year 900; he too had long before presented himself in England to be moistened with the solemn waters of Christianity. Moreover, wishing his private salvation to overflow into the public good, he asked Agapetus, who then presided over the sacred affairs of the Roman city, that Denmark might be divinely consecrated. Then, in 981, when the most devout King Harald died, his successor Sweyn again became hostile to Christians. Rejoicing that an advantageous opportunity to rage against God had come to him, he tore up the whole stock of religion by the roots; and under his leadership the Danes exchanged the worship of God which they had adopted for renewed superstition. But when that Sweyn was stripped of his kingdom by God’s avenging hand, he at last came to his senses. Compelled by this harsh fortune to embrace the charity of religion, he flooded eyes drawn away by darkness with the contemplation of saving light.”

This is Saxo’s account. He adds [Col. 0440D] that the same prince established four bishoprics in his kingdom—Aarhus, Schleswig, Ribe, and Roskilde—upon which, as on four hinges, the Christian religion in Denmark was established and strengthened in the year 993.].

You render Mother Church constant worship, offer devoted service, and bestow beneficent increase [Col. 0439A]. By God’s grace, you do not oppress the priesthood with royal arrogance or deny it due reverence. While in certain other kingdoms the Church has been subjected to servitude through the tyranny of princes, in yours it is free and at peace through your royal clemency.

The church of the blessed virgin Geneviève, where—though unworthy—we serve God, drank the cup of the persecution then inflicted by powerful pagan men; made drunk with the wormwood of grief, it was broken, destroyed, and burned. The walls, consumed by that fire and rotted, their lime turned into ashes, bear witness to this; eaten away, they tremble [Col. 0439B] and threaten ruin. We have begun to renew them, placing fresh timber above and beneath a lead roof.

We do not say this, most victorious prince, [Col. 0439B] in order importunately or improperly to request anything from your clemency with plaintive or begging voices. Rather, we ask that you mercifully admonish your noble kinsman, the nobleman Canute [Note: Of Canute’s zeal in propagating religion, Meursius writes in *Danish History* under the year 1093: “Meanwhile the Danes brought arms into Livonia and subdued the unbelievers of that region, who rebelled when the word of God had begun to be preached to them by Bishop Meinard and his successor Berthold; they compelled them universally to embrace the Christian faith.”], not to be wholly forgetful of his brother Waldemar. At his blessed end Waldemar became our canon [Note: That is, a canon for assistance, as we have noted from the necrology of St Geneviève.], was buried in a distinguished place of our cloister, and shares as brother and companion in all the benefits and prayers performed in our church. Yet neither in life did he possess any share—as it is said—or cord of his inheritance, nor after death did he himself, or the church on his behalf, receive anything from it.

The voice of justice itself cries to his brother from the earth: “Brother, give me the portion of the paternal substance which falls to me” (Luke 15). We ask, entreat, and beseech that you, who so often overcome idolaters by arms and subject them to the Christian yoke [Col. 0440A], may conquer with prayers the heart, though iron, of that noble man, so that he may not refuse favour to his dead brother. In the great necessity of the church in which his brother both closed his final day and awaits the last day, let him send something in lieu of the whole inheritance that he possesses. Thus his conscience may be safer before God, his reputation more cheerful before men, his due generosity toward the dead may be evident, and his brotherly goodwill may be made manifest.

We commend to your clemency our dearest brother and canon G., bearer of this letter, that you may assist him with royal patronage and, if necessary, protect him with aid. May your magnificence ever prosper and increase from day to day.

### Letter 154. To Nivelon, Bishop of Soissons

He asks him to relieve his canons at La Ferté-Milon from a certain burden.

[Col. 0440B]

Among the other afflictions under which the Church now groans, it is compelled to pay new and unjust exactions. Although sons ought to be free, they pay taxes and tithes as though they were utter strangers. Yet what all endure is more easily borne by each individual, although the groaning of all does not lessen the pain of individuals.

This common scourge touches us, father, and not only invites but drags even the unwilling, so that you both pay tithes and exact tithes [Note: Tithes were instituted in 1188 by Philip Augustus when he undertook the journey to Jerusalem. Rigord gives this account: “A council was held by King Philip, all the archbishops, bishops, abbots, and barons of the whole kingdom having been summoned. In it an innumerable multitude of knights and foot soldiers were marked with the most holy cross; and because of the pressing necessity—for the king ardently desired to undertake the journey to Jerusalem—with the consent of clergy and people he decreed that certain tithes should be taken from everyone for that year only, and these were called Saladin’s tithes.”].

The successors of Melchizedek do not exempt the sons of Aaron, nor is the immunity of the Levites permitted to enjoy the allotted portion [Col. 0440C], when the treasury absorbs all; yet Christ is not thereby freed from that by which the Christian is afflicted [Col. 0441A].

Yet amid these groans and daily sighs, we offer prayers to your holy fatherhood that, insofar as may please you, you spare our brethren dwelling at St Vedast [Note: The church of St Vedast at La Ferté-Milon was given to the church of St Geneviève at Paris by Hilgot, bishop of Soissons, as we have already said.], and grant this favour to us, to whom you have always been accustomed to show a cheerful and kindly face. Their chapel is small, and they do not live from an extended purse. For almost two years, with the parish services suspended [Note: Here he takes the part for the whole: “organs,” namely, for all singing and celebration of the divine office. Organs began to be used in the churches of Gaul under Pippin, in 757, as Einhard relates: “Emperor Constantine sent Pippin many gifts, among them organs, which reached him at the royal estate of Compiègne, where he was then holding a general assembly of his people.”], they have been subject to your interdict because of the count’s fault [Note: This interdict imposed upon the diocese of Soissons appears to be the same as that mentioned by Cantipratensis, II.v: “I saw the city of Soissons in Gaul subjected for a long time to excommunication, and the clergy administering the divine mysteries only in silence.”].

### Letter 155. To the Pope

He asks him, on behalf of the church of St Victor, to preserve for it the annual revenues of the Church of Paris granted to them.

To the most holy lord and father, by God’s grace supreme pontiff [Col. 0441B], Brother Stephen, called abbot of St Geneviève, the fullness of every devotion, obedience, and service.

Prudent and powerful men of their generation, who at that time held titled offices in the Church of Paris, pursued the church of Saint Victor with such affection and devotion that, touched and at the same time drawn by the fragrance of sacred religion within it, most of them not only bestowed their possessions but offered themselves as well. [Note: [Col. 0441D] Several bishops of Paris, and most of the canons of Blessed Mary [Col. 0442C], were enrolled among the canons of Saint Victor: namely Stephen and, according to some, Odo, bishops; Berner, dean; Adam, precentor; and Theobald, Bernard, and Maurice, archdeacons and canons of Paris.]

In this glorious contest of giving their goods to the blessed community of regulars, all so stimulated each individual, and each individual all, that from the resources of individual persons there accrued lands and money for the aforesaid needy brethren; and from the kindly and beneficent devotion of all together [Col. 0441C] came the annual revenues of their prebends. [Note: [Col. 0442C] The regular canons of Saint Victor enjoy the annual income of a vacant prebend in the Church of Blessed Mary of Paris [Col. 0442D], a right enjoyed by other abbeys of the same order in various cathedral churches of the kingdom, at Orléans, Chartres, Amiens, and elsewhere. These annual revenues were principally granted to them so that they would be bound to offer prayers for the deceased canon. Stephen, bishop of Paris, assigned them to the Victorine canons, as is read in their necrology on 29 July: “The anniversary of Stephen, bishop of Paris, of pious memory: during his life he embraced this our church with a wonderful affection of sincere love, bestowed upon it many great benefits, and left to posterity a worthy and lasting memorial of his name and love. For he gave us one prebend in every church in which there are prebends: one prebend in the senior church of Blessed Mary; one in the church of Saint Marcellus; one in Saint Germanus of Auxerre; and one in Saint Martin in the Fields. He also gave us, in all the aforesaid churches, the annual revenues of prebends,” etc.]

The sons who have been born in the Church of Paris in place of their fathers, though they ought to imitate their pious freedom, strive to alter it. In this matter they follow customs which their fathers did not cultivate, so that what those men bestowed, these men may take away; and what those men brought forth or established, these men may dig up and scatter abroad. Hard is the condition of sons who will not even follow, in a contrary work, those who built the tombs of their fathers lest the memory of those who had slain the prophets should be destroyed. But these men, who wish to oppose the good works of their fathers, so far as lies in them attempt to diminish and strive to obliterate the everlasting remembrance in which the righteous endure.

Nor, Father, should these young men be heard in this new will of theirs, since they do not honour their fathers and their mother, the eminent Church of Paris; nor do they fear what truth says: “Honour thy father and thy mother, that thou mayest be long-lived upon the earth” (Exod. 20). Certainly, the annual revenues of the Parisian prebends are owed in their entirety to the church of Saint Victor: the authenticated written declaration of the Church of Paris itself, both of its bishop and of its chapter, bears witness; the privileges of the holy Roman pontiffs confirm it [Col. 0442B]; and prescription extending beyond the longest possible time cries it aloud under both civil and canon law.

Your holy fatherhood too, by the discernment and knowledge given by God to you and to the holy Roman Church, has set down an interpretation of the phrase contained in the privilege, namely, “in their entirety”; and to the prudent men, the bishops of Arras and Amiens and the abbot of Prully, you sent not an inquiry but an order for execution. Just as they may not omit even one iota of your command, so neither is it fitting for you—if this may be said—to alter anything in matters which you have established canonically. For, to use the words of a prince, who is far inferior to your sacred apostolic office, the interpretation lying between law and equity [Col. 0442C] belongs to you alone both by necessity and by right.

And because your interpretation is general and necessary, we beseech you, holy Father—I, the least portion of your children, and all of us who, to the extent of our ability, observe the institutions of the Order of Saint Victor—that you cause the interpretation lawfully and canonically pronounced by us to be firmly observed, and preserve intact the rights of the most religiously and orderly established church of Saint Victor; lest perhaps, which God forbid, malicious persons may say [Col. 0443A] that “he did not deliver the poor from the mighty, and the poor man who had no helper.”

## LETTER CLVI. TO THE LORD OF ARRAS

[Note: [Col. 0443D] Atrebatum, commonly called Arras, capital of Artois between France and Flanders, is called *Rigiacum* by Ptolemy. For many successive years this city was subject to the bishop of Cambrai in spiritual matters; but at last it received its own bishop by a diploma of Urban II in 1096, which reads as follows: “The Church of Arras, one of the nobler churches of the province of the metropolitan see of Reims, supported by the solemn records of the canons, was formerly the principal seat of a bishopric, had its own bishop and its own diocese. We therefore desire that, having cast off from the Church of Arras the yoke of subjection to Cambrai and recovered the dignity reasonably and firmly possessed in former times, you shall endeavour to elect a cardinal-bishop useful to yourselves and to your church; to have the elected man consecrated by the hand of your metropolitan; and to establish him in your church.” The Church of Arras was then governed by Peter, who had been abbot of Cîteaux.]

He commends and praises the abbot of Les Vaux-de-Sernay, rashly accused. [Note: [Col. 0443D] The abbey of Vaux-de-Sernay was of the Cistercian order [Col. 0444D], in the diocese of Chartres near Caprois, French *Les Vaux de Sernay*. It was founded in 1128 by Simon of Neauphle, constable of France, and his wife Eve, who lie buried in that church. Its abbot was Guy, who went with Simon de Montfort against the Albigensians and was eventually made bishop of Carcassonne.]

Envy, the mother and fuel of detraction, accustomed to murmur with veiled head, comes forth publicly in our days. It no longer shoots the upright in heart in darkness, nor, sitting in ambush, kills the innocent; rather, before all, it brandishes a sword at the head of the righteous and inflicts the deadly wound of a false accusation. Mingling even with venerable communities, it not only tramples the thistles of the field, but, as far as it can, infects the cedars of Lebanon with poison, burns them with fire, and destroys them by ruin.

It professes itself the mistress of severity and the minister of severity; it conceals iniquity, pretends innocence, and, that it may more readily be believed, adds perjury to falsehood and sacrilege to perjury. It suborns false witnesses, deceives the simplicity of judges, until the innocent is condemned and swallowed up alive—the man whom it strives to put to death. Holy and religious ears neither admit nor receive the hissing, deadly plague of this monster, but reject it as it presses on. I trust, Father, that you are armed and resolute against so great a prodigy, so that according to your discernment it may neither circle about in plotting, creep in by hiding, nor corrupt by infecting.

I have said so much because I have learned in secret that certain lay brothers—perverse rather than converted—of the Limousin mountain [Col. 0443C] are forging and contriving plots against a righteous man: a man simple and upright before men and, as we believe, before God; namely, the abbot of Sarnay. The elevation of his conscience makes him illustrious from a humble station, and the brightness of his reputation makes him commendable and welcome on both accounts. [Note: [Col. 0444D] He means the lay brothers of the Order of Grandmont, dwelling in the Limousin district near Muret, as noted above.]

They have contracted the tinder of resentment and envy because, in a dispute which they had against their clerics, this man, fired by zeal for God, stood by the oppressed clerics as far as he could. He did not cease to help the faint-hearted, counsel the afflicted, and comfort wanderers and fugitives. That wicked and perverse generation, more shrewd than the children of light in the affairs of this world which lies in evil, seeks, through certain abbots [Col. 0444A] of the Cistercian Order—perhaps too credulous, and either eager to be believed themselves or inclined to complain—to besmear the purity of this man’s reputation. It seeks to inflame against a righteous man your most holy assembly of abbots, worthy of reverence even from angels, with the foul corruption of false calumny, so that iniquity may crush justice [Col. 0444A] and falsehood swallow truth. [Note: [Col. 0444D] He means the general chapter of the abbots of the Cistercian Order, of whose monastery that bishop of Arras, to whom this letter is addressed, had been abbot.]

Let the firmness and strength of your authority stand in this conflict, should it be necessary, for the holy and just man—or rather, to prevent scandal to the whole order—lest those who said, “We shall magnify our tongue” (Ps. 11), gain the victory desired by their impious will, and he who committed no offence suffer no injury.

## LETTER CLVII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF LUND

He excuses himself for not having handed over money entrusted to him.

[Col. 0444B]

To the reverend Father and lord, the archbishop of Lund, primate of Sweden, Stephen, called abbot of Saint Geneviève, greeting and due reverence to so great a Father.

We received with proper caution your deposit entrusted to us through Absalon, your cleric; we put it away carefully and preserve it faithfully. Returning from Saint James, he asked us, at your request, that the silver be carried as far as Clairvaux, at our expense and under his escort. I confess that we feared offending your prudence: if we restored without letters that which we received under the authority of your letters [Col. 0444C], someone might scrutinize our simplicity, accuse our fidelity, wound our constancy, or charge us with rashness. Whenever you wish the deposit to be taken out or conveyed, send open letters, bearing your seal, that indicate your will; by their testimony we may prove both that your money has been paid over to you and that our custody has been discharged by you.

## LETTER CLVIII. TO THE CHAPTER OF LAON

He asks the canons willingly to release their dean Michael, elected dean of Paris. [Note: [Col. 0444D] Michael of Corbeil was first a canon and chancellor of Paris, then dean of Meaux, afterwards dean of Laon, and was finally elected to Paris in 1191, after the death of Matthew of Montmorency. Alberic has this in his Chronicle: “Michael, dean of Paris, a theological and religious man, was elected patriarch of Jerusalem; but before setting out thither, he was made archbishop of Sens.” William the Breton says this happened in 1194 and calls him a theological and holy man. Rigord, however, notes in the same year the exact day, 24 April, and adds: “What and how great he had been in governing the schools at Paris, distributing alms, and many other good works before his archbishopric, it is not within our capacity to unfold.” [Col. 0445C]]

The play of the Churches is admirable and lovable whenever one supplies another’s lack through brotherly charity—not by a reckoning of money, but by an exchange of persons. The dove of the Lord is one, her tunic is seamless, and the parts of one body agree in serving one another so that they regard as the property of each what belongs to all. By the same art of religious life, the same spirit of charity, and the same provident zeal by which the Church of Laon had taken the dean of Meaux for itself, the Church of Paris, in a leap at once festive and swift, has carried him off for itself. It did not judge itself to commit robbery if it subsequently appointed as its dean the man whom it had earlier made its canon.

Let not your holy rivalry be disturbed in any respect, as though the Church of Paris had done you an injury by consulting its own interest in this matter, or as though the person had been led by fickleness or ambition, since in this election he followed not his own will but another’s compulsion. He was snatched away from his fellow canons—a man especially to be desired because least of all ambitious. Rejoice with the man; rejoice also with the Church. For here and there he will be yours: serving you, obeying you, and in all things ready and compliant for your service.

## LETTER CLIX. TO W. OF BIÈRE

[Note: [Col. 0445C] William, formerly a regular canon, led an ascetic life in a certain cell in the forest of Bières, commonly *la forêt de Biere*, not far from the town of Fontainebleau, in the diocese of Sens.]

He neither recommends nor discourages the eremitical life which he had embraced, but gives certain counsels for living it rightly.

To Brother W. of Bières, Stephen, called abbot of Saint Geneviève [Col. 0445C], greeting in both respects from Him who at his coming makes the two one.

Brother, you have entered a hard road, following as far as you can Pauls, Antonies, Macarii, and Hilarions in emulation; amid French comforts, you set before others and impose upon yourself the austerity of the Thebaid and the rigour of Nitria. This burden requires sturdy, strong shoulders; this arena demands the unencumbered arms of athletes in the contest of the spirit. Yet though I would not have advised you to begin, I do not advise you to desist.

Your frequent infirmities made me doubt your victory: a weak brain, a dry and parched chest, a cold stomach inadequate for the warfare of fasts—in short, your whole little body, exposed indeed to labours but not fitted for labours. Moreover, the horror of an unfamiliar solitude was equally a terror and a fear to me: uncultivated dwelling-places of wild beasts rather than of men; dry ground [Col. 0446B], bearing neither abundant herbs nor plentiful moisture. Indeed, even the water which flows drop by drop outside your cell can offer or furnish those who drink or behold it neither a taste fit for drinking nor a colour pleasant to the sight, being wholly contrary to the nature of waters.

Within your cell itself, the harshness of your clothing; the dryness of your food; the hardness of a little bed barely admitting snatches of sleep; your resolve not to go out without a grave cause; and fear of the robbers who killed your two predecessors [Note: [Col. 0445C] One of them was called William, as is inferred from a certain charter of Philip Augustus.], lest they should add you as their third successor—all urged and moved me to dissuade you from beginning so great a perfection.

But when I reflected that you had been trained in regular discipline, had served the Lord for nearly forty years [Col. 0446C] under obedience to prelates in the holy community of brethren, had borne many things, overlooked some, passed with equanimity through pleasant and harsh things within the priory and beyond it, and had lived humbly and profitably [Col. 0447A] with those dwelling with one mind in the house of the Lord, I conceived no slight confidence that you would be able to endure even higher things in the wilderness.

[Note: [Col. 0445D] That is, in the monastery of Saint Evurtius at Orléans, where that William, a man of the highest piety and religious devotion, had served as prior for fifteen years. To understand this letter, one should know that the priory called Saint Mary of Franchard, situated in the forest of Bières, was formerly an ascetic retreat in which a recluse lived an eremitical life. This continued until 1197, when Philip Augustus gave this cell to the regular canons of Saint Evurtius at Orléans. The following instrument of donation, drawn from the archive of that monastery, establishes this:

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Philip, by the grace of God king of the Franks. Let all men, present, past, and future, know that, for the sake of God and at the petition of Brother William, hermit of Bières, we have given and granted to the church of Blessed Evurtius of Orléans, to possess in perpetuity after the death of the same William, that place of Bières which we gave to him to hold during his lifetime. This is so that at all times there may be there, appointed by the abbot of Saint Evurtius from among his brethren or from elsewhere, two priests who may continually serve God for us and ours, both living and dead. Living there an eremitical life, they shall maintain in food the manner of life which the preceding William kept there, unless they choose to live there under a stricter rule.

“We grant this, however, on the condition that the brothers dwelling there may not enlarge that place without our permission; within our forest they shall have neither oxen nor cows, nor flocks of sheep, nor goats, nor pigs. The brothers dwelling there, whether placed there by Brother William while he lived or afterwards by the church of Saint Evurtius, shall render obedience and act at the command of the abbot of Saint Evurtius. Yet the abbot shall not be permitted to remove or transfer elsewhere the brothers established in the aforesaid place while they conduct themselves well and honourably, unless they themselves wish it. But if, which God forbid, they are found guilty of some grave offence, it shall be at the abbot’s discretion whether they humbly amend their faults there or elsewhere according to the requirements of the order. Those brothers shall be like hermits in food and inward dress; in outward dress they shall strive to conform themselves, so far as the resources of their house permit, to their brethren of Saint Evurtius and Saint Victor, among whom they will sometimes have to live.

“Done at Moret in 1197, the nineteenth year of our reign, while the chancellorship was vacant.”

This was confirmed by a diploma of Pope Innocent III in the second year of his pontificate, falling in 1200. Regular canons from the community of Saint Evurtius were afterwards established in this retreat or priory, as appears from a charter of Walter, archbishop of Sens, issued in 1224 and addressed to the canons dwelling in the church of Franchard.]

You have experienced in the convent the rigour of fasts, the burdens of vigils, the bridle of silence, stability of place, sometimes also hardness of bed and dryness of food, and the long daily and nightly round of divine worship. In all these things we have known you as experienced in regular observance and unacquainted with secular life. In that novice-training of the cloister you had learned how you ought to fight in the wilderness against the common adversary. These are the things which make your purpose commendable to me, so that we gladly accept what you have done and joyfully embrace what you are doing.

Afterwards I acquiesce: what displeased me pleases me; what I hated I approve, overcome by your counsel, overcome by your resolve. [Col. 0447B] By God’s grace you have broken, burst, and despised the aforesaid impediments, preparing to leap from the wilderness into heaven, from solitude into the city of habitation, from the desert and trackless place into the land of the living flowing with milk and honey.

You have declared war upon your enemies—the devil, the flesh, and the world—who, fiercer than every beast, sought the blood of your soul and, conspiring for your death, were ready “to seize the poor man when they drew him in.” You set before the devil the humility which he especially fears; before your body, crosses and torments; before the world, which lies in evil, contempt and flight. When you entered the wilderness, those monsters of malice and wickedness—the snare and the partridge of men wishing to serve God—were together pierced by one blow for me. The mighty captains in Pharaoh’s army turned their backs [Col. 0447C] to you and not their faces; they have become like the dung of the earth and lie beneath your feet. Tread, press down, crush; watch lest they rise again.

The enemy will set his snares and will not refrain from injuries, knowing that your patience has so despised prosperity that it does not fear adversity. Answer the plotter: “Get behind me, Satan” (Mark 8). “Even if you transform yourself into an angel of light” (2 Cor. 11), and call evil good and good evil (Isa. 5), you will not deceive the servant of Christ. “For we are not ignorant of your devices”; “from the beginning he is a liar, and its father” (John 8).

Answer the murmuring flesh: “You have spoken like one of the foolish women. Return, Hagar, to your mistress, and be subject to her”—to the mind, to reason, to a pure and religious will. And if it should still impudently grow proud [Col. 0447D] and snarl, raise the sign of the cross, secure in victory: “The Lord is my helper” (Ps. 118); “I shall not fear what flesh may do to me” (Ps. 56).

If the world seeks to move you by flatteries and offer pleasures, meet it saying: “I have accounted all things that are in the world as dung” (Phil. 3), “for the world passes away and its desire” (1 John 2). I am the disciple of him who said, “I am not of this world” (John 8). By God’s grace I shall not return “as a dog to its vomit” (Prov. 26), nor, after putting my hand to the plough, shall I look back (Luke 9).” If you conquer these three, whom we believe you have conquered, you have subjected all monsters beneath your feet. Yet this threefold kind of demons can be cast out only through prayer and fasting.

But one must act with discernment rather than severity [Col. 0448A], lest you offer your sacrifice without salt; lest, hastening incautiously, you dash your foot against a stone; or lest, if you begin to fail on the road, it be said of you: “This man began to build and was not able to finish” (Luke 14). Let prayers be short and interrupted, lest, if they are perhaps extended into excessive length, they turn to weariness, are overtaken—as often happens—by sleep, or the mind of the praying person is far from the words, as fantastic clouds of thoughts meet him through recollection of things once done or that might have been done.

In prayer, spontaneous tears should neither be spontaneously rejected nor forced against their will. Closed and tightened eyelids, a brow drawn into a wrinkle, harsh and gasping words in prayer, convulsive sighs, and groans brought forth into a shower of tears produce something as unwelcome as they offer something undevout. Tears are ordinarily poured in gently and wish to flow out silently and cautiously, without the torment of the weeper or the scrutiny of the examiner. If the tears of one praying become a spectacle for human beings, they will become a stumbling-block or a laughing-stock for angels.

If that grace should sometimes fill you, imitate the sinful Magdalene, who for three causes, or on behalf of three persons, poured out a threefold sacrifice of tears. She wept for herself; she wept for her brother; she wept for the Lord and Saviour. For herself, when she washed the feet of the Lord Jesus with her tears and dried them with her hair; for her brother, when, after Lazarus’s death, sitting in her house and weeping, she went at Martha’s word to meet the Lord as he came, while the Jews said that she was going to the tomb to weep (John 11); for the Lord, as the Gospel says: “Mary stood outside the tomb [Col. 0448C] weeping” (John 20).

So you also, between the upper and lower watering-place, whenever it pleases the Lord to give drink by measure in tears, weep for yourself, weep for your neighbour, and weep also for the Lord. Weep for yourself by recalling your years in the bitterness of your soul; for your neighbour, for living and dead worshippers of the Christian faith; and for the Lord, by wearying of the present life and desiring the eternal one. In the first weeping, pray that God may not remember the sins of your youth and your ignorances. In the second, pray that the living may turn away from evils and persevere in good works, and that the dead may rest in peace and attain eternal life. In the third, desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ, saying: “Alas for me, because my sojourning has been prolonged” (Ps. 120).

The first tears, brother, are of compunction and repentance; the second, of compassion and mercy; the third, of rejoicing and confidence. From prayer make a leap to reading, and from reading to meditation, so that you may healthfully digest and chew over what you have read, and place in the treasuries of memory what you have chewed over.

But do not, through excessive reading, dull your eyes with dimness or weigh down your head with dizziness. After a short reading, walk about your cell; or, going out into the little garden, refresh your failing sight with the green herbs, though they are few and sparse. Or look at the beehives, which may provide both comfort and an example. Amid these varieties you will count the harshness of the wilderness among the delights of paradise.

Moderate also the rigour [Col. 0449A] of fasting, so that on summer days you take a little food after the third hour [Note: [Col. 0449D] These hours must be reckoned according to ecclesiastical usage, not as they are reckoned in our natural day. The third hour of the ecclesiastical office corresponds to the ninth hour of the day after midnight.], and take the regular meal after the ninth. If you wish to compare summer days with winter ones, so as to abstain as much during the heat of the dog-days as in midwinter, you will begin either to tempt God or to become your own murderer. You cannot equal or overtake the ancient monks of Nitria by fasting [Note: [Col. 0449D] This is equivalent to saying the Egyptian monks, taking the part for the whole; for Nitria is a province of Egypt.], nor set yourself beside Germanus of Auxerre. [Note: [Col. 0449D] It is read in his Life in Surius, chapter 8: “He never took wheaten bread, wine, vinegar, oil, pulse, or even salt for seasoning food. On the day of the Resurrection or of the Lord’s Nativity he took single drinks, in which the flavour of wine was so diluted by an excess of water as the harshness of vinegar is commonly softened by abundant mixture.
