At meals he first tasted ashes, then took barley bread, which he himself had shaken out and ground. And since this food was judged too burdensome for fasts, it was never set out except in the evening, though sometimes in midweek and most often on the seventh day.”]

Let the moderation of Augustine suffice you [Note: [Col. 0450D] The Rule of Saint Augustine teaches a common and easy way, not a narrow path such as the other rules—those of Pachomius, Basil, Benedict, and the remaining monks. Peter Comestor says in his Sermon on Saint Augustine: “Augustine established the Rule for clerics living canonically, extending the line of canonical moderation.” Augustine himself, according to Possidius, followed this moderation in food, clothing, and everything else.]; if you wish to exceed it, abstain from flesh, whether solid or, as they say, liquefied.

I have exceeded the proper measure; may your charity pardon me, since I came to comfort you but have assumed the office of teacher. Make me a participant in your prayers, dearest brother. For, set in the field of governance [Col. 0449B], even though I sometimes offer counsel to those who labour in the mill of marriage when they consult me, I need the support of those who rest upon the bed of contemplation: to be helped by their intercessions and instructed by their examples. I do not say this as one repaying in kind: I remember you where both son is offered to Father and sinner petitions Saviour in the saving sacrifice.

## LETTER CLX. TO THE LORD POPE

He pleads for a cleric unjustly accused.

In the eminence of that dignity the Saviour established the holy Roman Church, committing to its hands the balance of mercy and judgment, so that, after considering persons and times [Col. 0449C], will and act, intention and deed, it may neither override equity with severity nor moderate severity excessively with equity. These are the breasts of its consolation, flowing with wine and milk. These are the healing applications of the supreme pontiff, the Samaritan; by their distinct application it is brought about that neither the faint-hearted is swallowed up nor the proud becomes insolent.

Drawing breath through these things and hoping in your mercy, your devoted son, the bearer of this letter, falls at the feet of your holiness, that punishment may not follow an intention which arose from zeal for justice. He fears lest, with paternal severity kindled against him, the bruised reed be broken in him or the smoking flax extinguished. He is the man about whose affair our littleness consulted your holiness, and in response to our consultation you deigned [Col. 0449D] to reply from the highest sanctuary of your prudence. We embrace your answer; but, seeking mercy, we ask and desire that the bowels of dispensation be opened to us.

The holy doctors have written that the Lord regards the will, not the deed, saying that sin is voluntary to such a degree that, if it is not voluntary, it is not sin. They also expound the chapter, “The Lord judges the ends of the earth,” that is, the intentions of each person. Therefore the aforesaid man, who had neither an intention to injure nor to harm, but rather to correct and reprove, ought to be excused from a punishment which no fault preceded—especially since the woman, by her insults and abusive speech, provoked her opponent and ought to have been removed and punished.

Nor should the woman be believed, since poverty incited her greed, and greed her impudence. For the sake of extorting money from the aforesaid man [Col. 0450B], as indeed happened, she is thought to have said these things, though it was not established that she had been pregnant or had caused an abortion. For what was seen, after earth had been removed, as though buried, by another priest and a certain woman, was found to be wholly without form, like a clot of flesh and blood. But this could have been deceitfully done for the sake of greed: it could have been thrown there from elsewhere, whether from some animal or from a woman’s ordinary discharge, and covered with earth.

In doubtful matters, holy Father, the laws proclaim that one ought to follow the more kindly and humane judgment, for they are always more inclined to acquit than to condemn. The Church, moreover, customarily judges evident matters, not hidden doubts. And we read that, even in cases of manifest homicide, supreme pontiffs have by dispensation granted clerics and priests permission to minister in their orders [Col. 0450C].

## LETTER CLXI. TO A CERTAIN PRELATE

He gives thanks for gold and gems contributed to adorn the tomb or shrine of Blessed Geneviève.

He worships the idol of ingratitude who, wickedly, either extinguishes the memory of a benefit bestowed upon him or neglects it irreverently. We reject the image of this fault, blow away its covering, detest its haughty brows, and condemn forever its face and the whole idol itself together with its worshippers.

Meanwhile, we receive with the fullest thanksgiving the little gifts which you have offered to our blessed virgin Geneviève [Note: [Col. 0450D] He thanks some prelate—for he calls him Father—for the gold and gems which he sent to adorn the tomb or sacred shrine in which Saint Geneviève’s relics are preserved.]; we kiss them with our utmost lips and handle them with the greatest desire. Your affection is more desirable in our hills [Col. 0451A] than much gold and precious stone, since you have sent these latter two things to our virgin and have not omitted the former. For from the first the latter two take their form and attain their end, since affection is valued more from the giver of the gift than from the gift of the giver.

The virgins of this world commonly glory in gold and pearls, displaying their bodies’ corruptible beauty by such adornment either as marketable or offering it for sale when displayed. But while our virgin still lived, she despised carnal allurements [Note: [Col. 0451C] He alludes to what is sung in her ancient office: “The virgin Geneviève, while she despises carnal allurements, deserved to become the most welcome handmaid of the eternal King.”]; and she preferred before every delight and placed above every wealth a bronze coin stamped with the sign of the cross, in place of gems and gold. The lord Germanus of Auxerre had hung it around her neck as a pledge of her betrothal to Christ. [Note: [Col. 0451D] The most ancient manuscript Life of Saint Geneviève says: “Saint Germanus, by God’s prompting, picked up from the ground a bronze coin bearing the sign of the cross and gave it to her as a great gift, saying: ‘Always wear this pierced coin suspended from your neck in memory of me; and I shall not allow your neck and fingers to be adorned with ornament of any metal—neither gold nor silver—nor with any kind of pearl.’”]

Now, among the choirs of virgins, if perhaps not first, yet preeminent among the foremost in attending upon the highest Virgin, she rewards, protects, and preserves with prayers and merits those who honour her body and tomb. [Note: [Col. 0451D] By Saint Geneviève’s “tomb” he here means that precious shrine in which her venerable relics are kept. It had been made by Saint Eligius, bishop of Noyon, as is read in his Life written by Saint Audoenus; but when it was falling apart through age, it was renewed in 1242, and the bones of this blessed virgin were then transferred and deposited in it with solemn rite, as may now be seen.] She permits ornaments which, while alive, she did not wish to have placed upon herself to be placed by the devotion of the faithful upon her tomb—not that she may draw any little glory from them, but that the liberality of those offering them may thereby be advanced and increased, and that those who admire the spectacle of offerings may deserve to imitate the examples.

Therefore, Father, we firmly believe and hope that your devotion will be rewarded by our blessed virgin: that God may repay you in eternal life for the gold and gem which you sent to be set upon her tomb, and that you too may attain the Lamb whom she follows wherever he goes [Col. 0451C]. Meanwhile, for the grace already bestowed upon you and to be bestowed hereafter, may God make you a participant in all who fear him; and, as we have promised you, we make and desire you to be a participant in our prayers, whatever they may be.

## LETTER CLXII. TO THE POPE

[Note: That is, Urban III, to whom he had already written a letter on behalf of Hugh, abbot of Saint John of Soissons; this letter should be referred to that one and to the observations appended for its elucidation.] He deals with the canons of Saint John of Soissons living in parishes, who refused obedience to their abbot.

The canonical order, regularly established by the holy Fathers, rejoices under your governance, Father, praying and beseeching God that in your days salvation may be directed in your hand, the condition of the Church may flourish, and the horns of the proud may be broken. And because, in an impulse of compassion, you have received our brother and fellow priest, the abbot of Saint John of Soissons, the whole order of regulars among us rises in full thanksgiving to you.

He labours and sets himself up as a wall against the sons of disobedience, who wish to remain—and die—outside the cloister under the pretext of parochial duties. They strive to ensure that, when they transgress, they cannot be rebuked and corrected by their abbot; rather, turning for protection to the bishop, they buy themselves free from canonical discipline by a monetary penalty. If this plague gains strength, the canonical order perishes; the regular institutions of the holy Fathers perish as well; the bounds and cords of obedience are loosened; and in our communities there will be as many abbots as parish priests.

[Note: That is, those assigned to the government and administration of parishes, whom we now call *priores curati*, “pastoral priors.” By the force of their titles they now suppose themselves permanently bound to their churches, whereas formerly they could be removed and recalled at their superior’s pleasure, as is clear from this letter: either for the needs of the monasteries, which required their assistance and labour, or for the correction of their faults when they did not duly perform their office.]

Yet we bear witness that from the beginning of our order we have customarily removed our parish canons, in the bishoprics where they are established, freely and without any objection, and returned them to the cloister, whether for the necessity or benefit of our churches or for the correction of their own faults; and whenever circumstances demanded it, we have excommunicated them. May your holy fatherhood provide a remedy for these great evils, which proceed from greed, the root of all evils—evils through which the purse is drained but life is not corrected, etc.

## LETTER CLXIII. TO THE ABBOT OF OURSCAMP

[Note: The abbey of Ourscamp, commonly Orcamp, in the diocese of Noyon, was founded in 1129 by Simon of Vermandois, bishop of Noyon. His charter begins thus: “Simon, by God’s grace bishop of Noyon and Tournai, etc. Having diligently sought to establish among us brothers from the monasteries and holy congregations of Cîteaux and Clairvaux, and, with God’s help, to found an abbey of the same order, we have so decreed.”] He asks him to confirm in this purpose the treasurer of Noyon, who had embraced monastic life.

Not a few testimonies of Scripture teach us how meritorious it is to look after the sick, support the weak, and console the faint-hearted. Although this concerns all who possess grace for such things, it is especially the duty of those set over any children of humankind.

Father, I say this not as one busy in leisure, darkness to light, night to day, or an ignorant man to a wise one, presumptuously undertaking to impart knowledge; rather, I recall to your memory matters which, if you have heard them, you may perhaps have forgotten amid the many occupations that present themselves; or, if you have not heard them, may at least now come to your notice, though late.

I have been informed that that young man of Noyon, formerly treasurer, troubled by some circumstance whose nature I do not know, burns less fervently than usual with zeal for his order, acts otherwise than he began, has his conscience wounded, has been overthrown from his purpose, and has his will changed. This change, unless I am mistaken, has not been wrought by the right hand of the Most High. His acquaintances know it—people who cannot remain unmoved when he is moved; and, as I judge, they sympathize more with one who suffers than they rejoice with one who prospers. Nor would they embrace his prosperity with as much joy as they would bear his adversity with grief.

Learn, I beg you, the cause, and quickly apply care, lest, if the enemy’s temptation gains strength in his heart, it extend to something worse and he return to the fleshpots of Egypt which he had formerly vomited up.

## LETTER CLXIV. TO THE ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX

[Note: This abbot appears to be Garnier of Rochefort, who governed the monastery of Clairvaux in 1190. The subject of this letter is that certain persons had falsely reported that Stephen had said that the archdeacon of Meaux, who had withdrawn into Clairvaux, had entered into a civil contract smelling of simony for their profit. Here he endeavours to clear himself and denies that he ever uttered this.] He clears himself from the stain of simony, a charge recklessly brought against him before the abbot by detractors.

At the first sight of your letter, Father, I was astonished, since I know neither the substance nor the form of that detestable statement which, you say, was mentioned to you by certain persons who lied. Therefore, the person who reported that statement to you did not yield to truth and bears the greater sin.

As for that venerable evangelical man, formerly archdeacon of Meaux, who, mindful of his last things, made his passage to your angelic order lest he should perish eternally, I could hardly believe that he either incurred the leprosy of Gehazi or entered into Simon’s bargain. For how could I have believed what I had not heard? Whoever it was who told you that I had either heard or believed this, lied fittingly to his own ruin, unafraid to plaster over truth with wicked lips and a deceitful tongue.

Moreover, their insertion of the claim that I had heard—from you or from your brothers—that some unlawful contract had either a beginning of agreement or a completion of consummation is as far from truth as it is from your severity.

Meanwhile I beseech you, great Father, I a very small man, that you may teach in a fatherly fashion the aforesaid man—who, leaving all things, followed the Saviour and began to labour in the Lord’s vineyard about the ninth hour—so far as you can, and cherish him in a motherly fashion; providing both the lamp of counsel for his feet and the staff of assistance for his old age.

## LETTER CLXV. TO THE ABBOT OF CÎTEAUX

[Note: This letter agrees with another already discussed, concerning Guy, abbot of Vaux-de-Cernay, who had departed for Palestine with the count of Montfort and the king in 1190.] He commends the abbot of Cernay and asks that he not be compelled to return.

We speak with the greater confidence of obtaining pardon because we believe and hope that you will keep more secret the counsel of our insignificance. It seems to us prodigious and nearly monstrous that you compel your son, the abbot of Cernay—rescued from the jaws of death and afflicted both by perils at sea and by false brothers—to make a fruitless return under the bond of obedience.

[Note: This is also read in Letter 146, under the attestation of obedience.]

Thus, as one running uncertainly and fighting as though beating the air, he would bring back with him nothing but labour and ingratitude. He has experienced an expedition devoid of success, and shoulders of a small body and a slight spirit unequal to the burden undertaken—especially since he has often attempted the purpose for which he undertook the pilgrimage, and has often been repulsed, so that he has advanced in nothing and sufficed not even in one thing.

Spare the man’s honour; spare the dignity of your order. Lest, when you have no Isaiah volunteering to be sent, even Jeremiah fail you by excusing himself. This work belongs to prophets or apostles, to whom, through the grace of miracles granted them, it was permitted to put enemies to flight, conquer and overthrow them, and convert unbelievers to the faith, the Lord confirming the word by the signs that followed.

If you judge that someone should be sent, send one most tested in your order: one pleasing in the eyes of our princes, terrible in conflict with enemies, serviceable and prudent in the framing of counsels; one who, whenever he raises his hands, causes Israel to triumph over its enemies and Amalek to turn in flight.

I fear—and believe it true—that, if the man who has returned is sent back, his return will become a subject of ridicule, and his name will be held dishonourable by everyone. Perhaps there will be men in the army who, like Eliab, David’s elder brother, will mockingly say: “Why have you come? Why have you left the few poor sheep in the wilderness? Have you come down to see the camp and the battle?” (1 Samuel 17.)

Indeed, if he withdraws, the house entrusted to him will incur spiritual danger and temporal loss. For he will serve not at his own expense but at another’s, and his poor house, burdened with debt, cannot meet those expenses. But when the shepherd is absent, the sheep of the flock will either be scattered or begin to stray.

This is the particular counsel of the lord abbot of Saint Victor and of the cantor of Paris, not my own—the counsel of an insignificant man.

## LETTER CLXVI. TO WILLIAM, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS

He asks him graciously to receive and protect the abbot of Saint Vincent of Senlis.

Your name and remembrance, Father, hold so great a place among the desires of my soul that, if someone speaks of you in my presence, my inmost parts rejoice from affection and leap for joy at hearing of you. Your goodwill causes this, for it has embraced me freely, placed me in fellowship, and not excluded me from counsel. May God preserve this favour for me, so that—far be it from me!—I may not grieve, much less deserve, to lose what I do not grieve to have gained.

Meanwhile, I ask your fatherly affection graciously to receive, for the love of God and of myself, and generously to support, the bearer of this letter, lord R., canon of Saint Victor, unanimously elected to the administration of the abbey of Saint Vincent of Senlis.

[Note: Understand Roger or Robert, who was abbot of Saint Vincent of Senlis.]

He has long been my intimate and friend, bound to me by mutual services and joined to me by our common birth. He is a man whom gravity of character, skill in letters, and integrity render commendable, so that we believe his ministry pleasing to God and acceptable to men.

The bishop of Senlis opposes him and his Church, demanding, as he says, an undue subjection from that Church—far too hastily and perversely—and has pronounced a sentence of excommunication after an appeal, contrary to the privileges of Roman pontiffs and French kings.

[Note: Namely Geoffrey, who in 1213 resigned his bishopric in order to become a monk at Chaalis.]

[Note: Philip I, in the diploma by which he confirms the foundation of this monastery made by his mother, says: “My mother Anne, divinely inspired by mercy, came into my presence, earnestly entreating me with maternal affection that I should make free the church in the suburb of Senlis, in the district called Vicellus, in honour of Saint Vincent—long previously desolate, but piously and generously restored by her at her own expense for the soul of my father and her own—according to the custom and practice of other churches belonging to kings, namely Saint Frambald, Saint Martin of Paris, and Saint Geneviève the Virgin. Most humanely yielding to the prayers of her humility, I assented for the soul of my father and in memory of my parents. And that this might remain inviolate and unshaken, I impressed the sign of the cross with my finger, ordered the character of my name to be impressed, and confirmed it with my seal. Done in the year 1069.”]

Receive him, Father, I beseech you; and, so far as justice permits, assist him through your protection and that of my lords, your brothers; cherish him with consolation and sustain him with counsel.

## LETTER CLXVII. TO CARDINAL SOFREDUS

[Note: Sofredus of the Caetani family of Pisa was created cardinal-deacon of Blessed Mary in Via Lata by Lucius III in 1182. Innocent III calls him “a man held in honour, distinguished in learning and integrity, mighty in deed and word.” Others call him Gualfredus.] He asks him to show goodwill to the archbishop of Reims and informs him of that archbishop’s friendship.

The tearful crises of the present time would have supplied us with matter for writing more sorrowful than fruitful, when we see the Church of God violently oppressed by manifest enemies of the faith—

[Note: That is, in the East by unbelievers, against whom Philip Augustus had led an army.]

—and deceitfully seduced by false brothers—

[Note: That is, in the West by Waldensians, Albigensians, and other heretics.]

—in the East dying, in the West being killed, while the faithful everywhere on earth fail and wither through grief and the persecution that has come upon the whole world.

Amid these distresses, this alone ought to remain to us as consolation: that we flee to our common mother, holy Church, awaiting from her breasts of consolation both counsel in the present danger and aid in a seasonable time. The ointment of compassion and prudence descends from the head of Aaron, the supreme pontiff, not merely upon his beard but to the uttermost members of the whole body, so that from the apostolic treasury new things and old may be brought forth; through their collation, those who sigh may breathe again, those who fail may advance, those who doubt may be strengthened, and those who err may be instructed.

Meanwhile, I, the least portion of your clergy, hold, cherish, and ponder your remembrance as my highest consolation, always prepared to comply with your faithful wishes, though I am unable to follow you in good works.

Being certain of the goodwill of the lord of Reims towards you, I ask and, as your faithful servant, advise that you love him in return and meet his friends with open affections; for they undoubtedly proceed from a good conscience and sincere faith. That secret which your nephew, lord T., communicated to me on your behalf, I have pursued as far as I could, and I found an open door, provided someone is not lacking who wishes to enter, as R., your clerk and canon of Champeaux, will explain to you more fully.

[Note: At Campellis-in-villa, commonly Champeaux, there is a college of secular canons in the collegiate church dedicated to Saint Martin.]

## LETTER CLXVIII. TO WILLIAM, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS

He asks him to protect the abbot of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, unjustly oppressed.

Amid the cares of the court—

[Note: The king Philip had entrusted to him the administration of the whole kingdom when he departed for Palestine in 1190, as we noted above; hence the following words: “They lay upon you the burden of the twofold honour and burden of priesthood and kingdom.”]

—and the mysteries of the sanctuary, we earnestly desire that the happy course of your days may suffice for your daily concern and advance the common good. The burden of the twofold honour and burden of priesthood and kingdom lies upon you, drawing your person in divergent rather than opposing directions, more exposed to labours than disposed for them. Those who are unjustly oppressed, and those who fear that they will be oppressed, flock to your aid and counsel.

Among others, F., abbot of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, has recourse to the bosom of your protection, asking you to preserve uninjured and defend, once preserved, the rights of the Church entrusted to him, as he and his predecessors have hitherto held them.

[Note: Fulco then presided over the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés; he died in 1192. Other letters are addressed to him.]

Each year he has had and has in his territory a moderate levy, which by customary right he has received and receives as revenue due to him. And now, by some disturbance, officers of the palace prohibit the men and tenants of the said Church from paying what they themselves and their fathers paid. Consequently they grow insolent and begin, as it were, to yelp like servants against their masters, so that Hagar despises Sarah and the children of the slave woman become like the children of the free woman.

The aforesaid abbot, together with his whole Church, petitions you; and I, the least portion of your clergy, petition for them and with them, that, as they have hitherto been accustomed to receive it from their men and tenants, they may receive it peaceably; and that you may powerfully correct the prohibition against payment, if it was made without you, or mercifully revoke it if you ordered it to be made.

You compel an old man, burdened by frequent illnesses, to undertake a journey, so that I may fight, as it were, with beasts, snatch prey from the hands of the Grandmontines as from the jaws of bears or lions, though they are warriors from their youth and I am but a little one, tending a few sheep in the wilderness. But because at your command I am ready to go both to prison and to death, I shall begin the journey; but whether I shall succeed, God knows.

## LETTER CLXIX. TO THE SAME

He complains of the count of Dammartin, hostile to him.

In great affairs lesser persons are sometimes admitted, so that at least the unlearned may fill a place. Bees make honey and redeem their own labour, in small bodies, by common usefulness. The ant, a creature intermediate between a fly and a creeping thing, invites the slothful by its example to store in summer what will be dispensed in winter. So too I, the least among your servants, have never deserved through your favour either to hear your counsels or to be heard in your counsels.

At this critical point in the present days, in which each day has enough of its own evil, ministers of the altar, struck by the novelty of a terrible wound, are disturbed and stirred, and demand from you great vengeance for a great sacrilege. You are girded with both swords, of kingdom and priesthood alike, which, as the Lord himself testifies, are read to be sufficient for the defence of Christ, suffering even to this day.

The young count of Dammartin stretched out impious hands to plunder ecclesiastical property and, a greedy robber, fastened the sharp claws of impiety even upon the sacred vessels of the altar. He violently seized, shamelessly carried off, and irreverently scattered horses, baggage, necessary supplies, and—an outrage in word and deed—vessels consecrated to sacred use, belonging to the great man, the bishop of Ely, chancellor of the king of England.

[Note: Dammartin in French, in the diocese of Meaux. That count was Reginald, son of Albert, who waged war against Philip together with the count of Flanders and the king of England.]

[Note: His name was Eustace, who, as is written, was elected bishop of the city of Ely, commonly so called, on 11 August 1196. Ely lies beside the River Grant in Cambridgeshire. The office of chancellor was established in England by William the Conqueror, according to Polydore Vergil, in these words: “He established a college of scribes to write diplomas, and called the master of that college chancellor; he gradually became the highest magistrate and is so regarded to this day.”]

In the realm of the lord king of France, the fraternal alliance of the two kings on pilgrimage, the dignity of episcopal office, and finally your protection—which ought to be shared alike by the lowly and the great—had made him secure, so that he might resist the wicked and cherish the humble.

[Note: Namely Philip Augustus, king of France, and Richard, king of England, who took the cross for the Jerusalem expedition in 1190.]

What, Father, can be safe or secure if Churches are oppressed in your very hands, the poor are stripped naked, priests are exposed to injuries and robberies, everyone is allowed whatever he wishes, and “as the people, so the priest”? Let the zeal of Mattathias arise in you; with Phinehas against Zimri let the laws of heaven be armed, and let the earthly laws be stirred by the power that has conceived the spirit of divine and human vengeance. Meet the robber; snatch the prey from his hand, for in such great wickedness he neither fears God nor respects men.

Your commands seem mockery to him: he has sent back even your messengers empty-handed, and the bishop’s chapel, which he had promised to restore, he not only retains in disobedience but profanes in irreverence. Let your providence, Father, see and provide what must be done concerning this crime, so that the gentleness which clothes you with beauty may put on strength and gird itself; then those who grieve for what has been plundered may rejoice over what has been restored, and those who heard of the robbery may subsequently hear also of vengeance for the robbery.

## LETTER CLXX. TO CERTAIN JUDGES

[Note: A controversy arose between the archbishop of Sens and the religious of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, and was settled by the following instrument:

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Guy, by God’s grace archbishop of Sens, greeting in the Lord all to whom the present letter shall come. We wish it to be known to all alike, present and future, that the dispute which existed between us and Fulco, abbot of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, and that church, concerning the procurations which we demanded from them at Emant, at Bagneaux, and at Saint-Germain near Montereau, was settled in the presence of lord Philip, king of the Franks, as follows.

“We released in perpetuity to the abbot and Church of Saint-Germain the procurations which we claimed from them in the aforesaid places, on this condition: the abbot and his successors shall render each year to us, our successors, or our appointed messengers, for those procurations, eight Parisian pounds at Emant on the octave of Easter. If we or our successors come once in a year to Emant, Bagneaux, or the village called Saint-Germain near Montereau, the abbot, his successors, or the person holding the house shall receive us and our successors; and we and our successors shall live there for one night at our own expense, so that the person holding the house shall not be obliged to give us or our successors anything beyond lodging, unless he wishes to do so freely. If we or our successors have once been received in one of the aforesaid places, the monks shall not be bound to receive us or our successors in any of those three places in the same year.

“We have also caused the said Church and abbot to be released from one half of the tithe on wool paid by priests in the churches of Saint-Germain situated throughout the archbishopric of Sens, namely at Emant, Bagneaux, the village called Saint-Germain near Montereau, and Matrioles; and the priests of those churches shall have the other half of the same tithe. The messengers of the abbot of Saint-Germain shall render fealty to the priests who shall be in the said churches; and the priests, through their messengers, shall jointly and faithfully seek and divide the said tithe with the messengers of the abbot.

“Lest this matter be erased by anyone’s forgetfulness or maliciously perverted, we have caused it to be confirmed by our seal. Present were the persons of our church: Salone, dean; Manasses, archdeacon; William, treasurer; and Geoffrey, precentor. Witnesses to this matter are Stephen, abbot of Saint Geneviève, and his canons Hugh and Amalric; Milo, abbot of Saint-Remi of Sens; Master Anselm of the Chancery; and Ogerius of Avonne. Done at Fontainebleau in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1191.”]

He deals with the case pending between the archbishop of Sens and the Church of Saint-Germain-des-Prés.

It is judged absurd and close to arrogance if someone wishes to advise one whom he ought to consult, whether at a moment of necessity or in danger to truth. Avoiding the appearance of this fault, having obtained leave, I shall speak to my lords—not in order to increase from my small chapel the treasures of your great wisdom, but rather to anticipate those who are prepared with a slight reminder than to precede them.

I have heard that the lord pope has entrusted to your prudence the examination of the case pending between the lord of Sens and the Church of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, a case which seems to involve no small difficulty and no less danger both to the authority of the judges and to the will of the parties.

The matter concerns provisions for bodies, not salvation for souls; the number of beasts of burden and men, not the merit of virtues or the victory over vices. Yet, in this conflict, the supreme pontiffs Alexander, Lucius, Urban, Clement, and Celestine, who now sits, are believed to have imposed an end upon the dispute when it arose concerning procuration, by their privileges fixing the number of mounts.

I have seen and read these privileges, obtained neither through suppressed truth nor false representation, but supported by every formality and strengthened by the subscriptions of cardinals. What can be secure or safe if anyone wishes to doubt, debate, or dispute about such matters, when apostolic safeguards preserve and protect for you and us—indeed, for all churches—their possessions and rights?

Spare, Fathers, your authority; spare your dignity and prudence; reserve this examination for the supreme pontiff, who alone has the power both to make new canons, expound old ones, interpret his own privileges, and correct those of others.

## LETTER CLXXI. TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT BARTHOLOMEW

He advises him to relinquish his administration.

To the reverend father and lord, the abbot of Saint Bartholomew, Stephen of Saint Geneviève wishes a righteous life and a blessed end.

We cannot recall past years or command future events. At some time one must withdraw and pay nature’s debt, so that we may depart under the condition in which we entered. I say this, Father, lest either the inconvenience of sickness or the weariness of old age be intolerable to you.

The care of prelacy, which you have hitherto borne usefully and manfully, requires both bodily strength and watchfulness of mind. If any prelate is deprived of either, he excites among his subjects’ self-indulgent minds either hatred or contempt. When these things intervene, care for the household perishes, discipline is relaxed, order is confused, and those who ought to be subject begin to become equals.

Lest this happen to you, Father, provide during your final days for your Church, so that what you expect to be wages of life may not turn to your loss in death. Desiring no less to advise you than to console you, I ask, warn, and exhort you humbly to lay down through the hand of the lord of Reims the burden of honour for which you are now less able to suffice through the decline of age. Let him, by your counsel and ours, appoint a suitable person in your place and assign you a consolation appropriate to your life. He has power and knowledge in both these matters: both to reach mightily from end to end and to order all things sweetly.

## LETTER CLXXII. TO THE LORD ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS

He requests the same thing.

There are many whom nature rather than care, necessity rather than will, often compels to difficult things. They make a virtue of necessity, so that at last what had previously been merely delaying may become meritorious. Perhaps I would count among them our venerable old man, the abbot of Saint Bartholomew: a religious and honourable man, yet one who has now begun to fail in bodily strength, to be consumed by sickness, and to be brought to an end by old age and senility.

Behold, into your hand he resigns the administration entrusted to him, in which we have seen him, down to his final days, not so much preside humbly as benefit usefully. He asks two things from you, and I too, the least portion of your clergy, ask them with him and on his behalf, as consolation and support for the very brief remainder of his life: that you provide him with sufficient sustenance from the goods of the Church over which he presided, and that you consider his successor in such a way that his brothers may not be permitted in the election to follow their own will rather than the common good.

## LETTER CLXXIII. TO THE CONVENT OF SAINT BARTHOLOMEW OF NOYON

He admonishes them to render honour to their abbot even if he resigns the abbey.

The first commandment of the second table is: “Honour thy father and thy mother” (Matthew 15). I beg you, keep the first fruits of this table in memory, taste them sweetly, and fulfil them faithfully.

Honour, as is fitting, your aged father G., a man of outstanding authority in our order; bear him as is appropriate; cherish him as is expedient. Until now he has been our debtor through outward care, inward compassion, brotherly equality, fatherly correction, and motherly tenderness. But behold: humbly released from honour and usefully from burden, he has become as one of you, now knowing through experience both the good of subjection and the evil of prelacy.

In turn you are his debtors: render to him the example of your life, reverence for his dignity, obedience to his gravity, comfort for his old age, and relief for his sickness. Through God’s grace, we trust that you will hear more attentively what we say and add to it more liberally. It remains that the things done for you by him should not be undone by you; indeed, it is in your interest that they be preserved.

You granted on a precarial tenure a certain vineyard near Auxerre to his nephew H.; he is prevented, as he reports, from cultivating and caring for it, so that he whom you established as usufructuary during his life cannot, through another’s hindrance, use the benefit which you granted him.

Far be from the sacred community both “is” and “is not”; remove the occasion for maligning; let no wicked and deceitful word be found among you. Otherwise, among those whom religious severity customarily enclosed, banished severity will complain that it is excluded. For just as the freely bestowed gift is the glory of the generous giver, so the revocation of a grant once made is disgrace to the donor.

In this matter consult the honour and order of your community. Spare the reputation of your father and pastor, and spare your own name. If possession of your gift is hindered by yourselves, desist; if by another, resist, asserting such authority as you can and giving the protection you ought. It will be shameful if what has been confirmed by your seal is disturbed by another’s whistle.

## LETTER CLXXIV. TO WILLIAM, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS

He deals with the resignation of the abbot of Saint Bartholomew of Noyon.

Stephen of Saint Geneviève sends to William, archbishop of Reims, greeting and due and devoted loyalty.

Your son, the abbot of Saint Bartholomew, seeks and awaits the completion of his long-conceived wish to renounce the burden and labour laid upon him as abbot. In his first request he found his sons and brothers favourable: by kind and unanimous consent, they granted him suitable and sufficient support.

Therefore I offer prayers to your holiness, that what his brothers have willingly granted and conferred upon him, you may, through your favour, confirm with beneficent authority. For the rest, holy Father, he asks counsel and help from you concerning the appointment of his successor, so that the Church which, by his assistance and labour, he has to the extent of his ability raised up and exalted may simultaneously have temporal revenue and spiritual progress.

I beseech your holy fatherhood to command the bishop of Senlis to go to that Church and, exhorting the brothers to concord, to induce them by your authority to elect for themselves as father and shepherd a suitable and religious person. For the more experienced he is in the institution of our order, the less ignorant he is of other matters; he will be able both to calm dissension and summon them to agreement. Farewell.

## LETTER CLXXV. TO THE SAME

He writes on behalf of Peter, cantor of Paris, elected bishop of Tournai, asking that he favour his election as lawful and canonical.

The gentleness of Your Fatherhood, an open common refuge for all, so extends itself to individuals that it gathers everyone together. They come from East and West and recline in your bosom; and one once admitted is not readily sent away, unless he should commit something which does not deserve forgiveness. This gives confidence to me and to many others, that for your devoted son, Master P., Cantor of Paris [Note: Concerning his praises James of Vitry writes: “Master Peter, the venerable Cantor of Paris, a man mighty in deed and word, melting down alike his gold and silver and making a balance of his words, giving weight and gravity to his teaching through the honesty of his morals; for he began both to do and to teach, like a burning and shining lamp, a city set upon a mountain, and a golden lampstand in the house of the Lord.” After the death of Everard of Avesnes, bishop of Tournai, he was chosen in his place in 1191. But, since this election was judged by some to be insufficiently canonical and invalid because of certain defects, William, archbishop of Reims and then viceroy of France, opposed it. Stephen therefore asks him to allow his friend to obtain the bishopric of Tournai, unaware of what he himself was soon to undergo. Nevertheless, his death is recorded in the necrology of the same church in these words: “On the tenth day before the Kalends of October died the distinguished teacher Peter, Cantor of Paris, who, having at one time been elected bishop of this church, humbly declined the call. And after he had for no short time been to his hearers both a source of learning and a standard of conduct, he assumed the Cistercian habit in the monastery of Longpont and brought the holiness of his life to its blessed end.” He wrote much, among it the Summa called *Verbum abbreviatum* (“The Abbreviated Word”), which is found among the manuscripts of Sainte-Geneviève in Paris. Nor can I agree with the author of the *History of Tournai*, nor with Buzelin, who follows him, when they write that Peter the Cantor was appointed bishop of Tournai after Stephen’s death. They support this with no arguments; and, since it is certain from the necrology of Longpont Abbey that he died in 1197, they even fall into the error of freely asserting that this letter is spurious and forged, not composed by our author. I could demonstrate with strong reasons that this is false, were it not that the author of this calumny, Cousin himself, advances it hesitantly, as though doubtful of his own opinion, and were not the very style of the letter evidence that it is a genuine offspring of our author. As for the office of cantor, it is found to be most ancient in the Church and to have been received among the first Christians, as Philo relates concerning the Essenes: “When all have risen, two choirs are formed in the middle of the dining room, one of men and the other of women; over each is set its own leader, outstanding in dignity and skill in singing. Then they sing hymns composed in praise of God in various kinds of meters and songs, now with one voice, now in alternation, not without graceful and reverent gestures and tones.” It was decreed at the Council of Aachen, canon 137, concerning those devoted to church singing, “that senior brethren of more approved life should be appointed among them, who in their turn should be with the school of singers at the appointed time.” From ancient times, moreover, certain persons in cathedral churches and more distinguished monasteries were assigned to this ministry, to direct the chant and carry the staff, the emblem of their rank. Thus one reads in the necrology of the same monastery concerning a certain Theobald, precentor of Sainte-Geneviève, who lived in the twelfth century: “Died Theobald, priest and precentor, who raised the tower as far as the first story and adorned the precentor’s staff with gold, silver, and precious stones.”], an opportunity to make supplication may be opened before you: lest he who does not lay claim to dignity provoke your indignation; lest another’s deed harm one for whom his own merit is sufficient.

[Col. 0463A] He is a man whose good repute is sweetly spread throughout all the churches; brilliantly endowed with a double learning, he adorns doctrine by admonitions and discipline by conduct. In some respect we believe him equal to Origen: he teaches as he lives, and lives as he teaches. Such lamps ought to shine upon your lampstand, such stones to be set in the diadem upon Aaron’s head, such suffragan bishops to be in the holy Church of Reims, so that neighboring provinces may be stirred by holy emulation to promote men like them, and so that the charge entrusted to you may more easily and more often be helped by their religious devotion and prudence.

If anything was done less than properly in his election by the clergy of Tournai, it ought neither to affect the ignorance of one absent nor to injure the innocence of a just man; for, if it please you, whatever has been wrongly done can very easily be corrected by the authority granted you by God to rebuke errors and by your knowledge to amend them. For, speaking with due respect and without prejudice to your grace, the four things mentioned by Leo I concur in that election [Note: Namely, Letter 89 to the bishops of the province of Vienne against Hilary, bishop of Arles, after his departure from Rome, no. 3: “Let there be maintained the subscription of the clergy, the testimony of the leading men, the consent of the order, and of the people.”]: the wishes of the citizens, the testimony of the people, the decision of the leading men, and the election of the clergy. To these are added the integrity of the person, the cheerfulness of his reputation, and both the need and the advantage of the widowed church.

Moreover, this is frequently and solemnly said: the lord king—may God preserve him and restore him to us—has expressly named this person, expressly petitioned for him, and expressly has wished and intends that he should preside over the Church of Tournai. If matters proceed otherwise, it is to be feared—and perhaps it is true—that he may conceive indignation, wrath, and visitations through evil angels, and kindle royal and youthful anger against those who have obstructed the promotion of so great a man. In all these matters, holy Father, provide for your honor; consult the witness of your sound reputation; defer to the royal command; and, after first correcting as is fitting the error of those electing, confirm the election and receive your chosen and beloved son into your paternal bosom.

## Part Three of the Letters of Stephen, Bishop of Tournai

Containing the letters which he wrote from the year 1192 to the year 1203.

[Col. 0463]

### 272–273. Letter CLXXVI. To the Abbot of Hautvillers

[Note: The abbey of Altovillare, commonly Hautvillers, in the diocese of Reims, of the Order of St. Benedict, was founded by St. Nivard, bishop of Reims, about the year 650. The most ancient record of its foundation is read in the diptychs of the same monastery as follows: “I, Nivo or Nivard, although a sinner, bishop—while all my brother bishops, and likewise Christian men and good men, did not cease to build monasteries according to the rule of the holy Fathers—was asked by Abbot Bercharius with his brethren that we should seek out for them on our property such a little place in which they might live according to the Rule of St. Benedict and St. Columbanus. There was found for us together with them a little place called Altivillaris, in the territory of Reims, upon the river Marne,” etc. The abbot of Hautvillers was named Odo, according to a document of the year 1192.]

He informs him that his nephew John has been elected abbot of Sainte-Geneviève.

[Col. 0463C]

Called by the hidden permission of God to the governance of the Church of Tournai [Note: This occurred in 1191 or 1192, after Everard’s death], although less adequate, less suitable, and less worthy, I poured out my whole spirit upon arranging the affairs of the church previously entrusted to me, lest the labors in which I had toiled there should be lost and the tranquility granted me by heavenly permission disturbed on the occasion of a successor.

[Col. 0464C] At last, after many agitations of thought and varied, carefully considered feelings, not without the divine will, as we believe, we cast the lot and line of our election upon our dearest brother John, your nephew [Note: He took care that this man, old in character rather than years, should be elected abbot of Sainte-Geneviève], a young man whom, so far as we can know from long association with him, we find honorable and trained in letters and regular discipline. With the common consent of all the brethren we named him abbot and successor in the charge entrusted to us.

These things were done on the day of the angelic salutation, the virginal conception, and the divine Incarnation. On the following Sunday, when the Church commemorates the Lord’s entry into Jerusalem and the applause of the children singing “Hosanna,” he received, in my presence and at my presentation, the blessing from Lord Ans., bishop of Meaux [Note: That is, Anselm, to whom he led the new elect so that he might receive from him the gift of blessing]. Returning with me to the church entrusted to him, he humbly undertook, according to the grace bestowed upon him by God, to guard and rule the flock entrusted to him, hoping that God, who has begun, will complete and establish the work.

And because his youth is troubled and burdened by the novelty of the honor and burden imposed upon him, he has recourse with us to your prudence, that you may commend him and the church entrusted to him, as your very own, to Lord Jordan, the legate [Note: Jordan, cardinal-priest of St. Pudentiana, created by Clement III in 1188, was sent as legate to France], who is, we hear, your very dear and intimate friend; so that he may receive him kindly in your place, foster and defend him, and commend him to Lord Octavian, bishop of Ostia [Note: Octavian, cardinal-bishop of Ostia, was sent by Celestine III as legate to Normandy together with the aforesaid Jordan, so that they might settle the dispute between the archbishop of Rouen and the bishop of Lisieux], as his own son. For a great journey remains before him; inexhaustible greed gapes after other people’s resources; his spirit is small and afraid; and his inadequate purse despairs.

### 275. Letter CLXXVII. To the Archbishop of Tours

[Note: This letter is said to have been written when Stephen had been called to govern the Church of Tournai. On that occasion Bartholomew of Vendôme, then archbishop of Tours, sent him certain pontifical ornaments as a gift: namely, a mitre, sandals, and gloves.]

He announces that he has been promoted to the bishopric of Tournai.

Called to the Church of Tournai by the hidden judgment of the Lord, I commend myself to your prayers, that by others’ intercessions I may succeed in that for which my own merits do not suffice. And because I do not know, Father, whether, being worthy of love or hatred, I ought from so great a calling to expect punishment or reward, I still run as though toward an uncertain goal. May the Almighty grant that I do not begin to fight as one beating the air. At the first sound of this report:

> I was stunned; my hair stood on end, and my voice stuck in my throat.

Finally, as if awakening from a heavy sleep, I entrusted the whole matter to God, whose grace, if it be pleasing in His sight, will complete and establish everything. Meanwhile I wished to inform your holy Fatherhood what has happened, lest I appear either ungrateful for your benefits or undevoted in my service.

About the coming Easter, God willing and if life attends me, I shall pass to the church which calls me, to celebrate the Passover with the true Hebrews; and, as the lord of Reims has arranged, in the octave of the holy Resurrection I shall, by God’s grace, receive the gift of consecration. Untrained in such matters, I desire to be strengthened and formed by your counsel, so that you who are experienced may instruct one inexperienced yet faithful: a lord, a great priest, obedient to great priests.

### Letter CLXXVIII. To the Same

He gives thanks for the gifts sent to him.

[Col. 0466B]

You have sent me gifts, Father, with which I can fittingly adorn not only my feet, but also my hands and head. They are great in cost, greatest in sacramental significance. In the first respect they can satisfy the lust of the eyes; in the second they can advance the mystery of ministers. If I wished to return fitting thanks, neither my feeling nor my action would suffice. Your letter accompanied the gifts, pouring into me a twofold joy and displaying manifold kindness.

### Letter CLXXIX. To Celestine, Supreme Pontiff

[Note: Celestine III, proclaimed supreme pontiff in 1191, when more than seventy years old, did not welcome Stephen’s appointment to the see of Tournai—perhaps because he believed Peter the Cantor’s election to have been canonical, that Peter ought to be regarded as the lawful pastor of that church, and that Stephen was an intruder.]

He treats of his promotion to the Church of Tournai, which the supreme pontiff had not received favorably.

[Col. 0466C]

Standing between hope and fear, I approach, a son to his father, a servant to his lord, the least of Christ’s disciples to Peter’s successor. Perhaps the father will soften his anger, the lord will remit his indignation, and Peter’s successor will look upon a humble priest. Who knows whether he will turn, forgive, and leave a blessing upon me?

Called to the Church of Tournai while far away in place and mind, ignorant of all, and breathing of nothing less than a bishop’s chair: why did I transgress if I approached? What sin did I commit if I did not guard against it? Did I offend because I did not abandon it? Certainly I could not divine whether it would please or displease the supreme pontiff, whose decisions are laws; in whose right hand is the fiery law, which weighs the merits of each person in the balance of the canons, seizes subtleties by the plumb-line of laws, and measures them by the compass of decrees.

But since it belongs to good minds to acknowledge faults where there is no fault, and since it is exceedingly dangerous for a son to remain long separated from his father’s presence, I omit defenses, ask pardon, seek favor, and implore mercy. I beg that the bosom of the holy Roman Church, which is accustomed to be closed to no one, may be opened to me; that access for supplication may be granted and maternal breasts extended; that with the mother the Father may show himself gracious, both providing for the simple man and consoling him.

### 278. Letter CLXXX. To the Archbishop of Reims

He inveighs against certain preachers who adulterate the word of God and lead lives infected with vices.

Certain sellers of God’s word bring dangerous and repeated assaults upon us and our deans [Note: Two kinds of deans are found among the ministers of the Church: some preside over colleges of canons; others supervise rural priests and are called rural deans, of whom mention is made here. Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, in the statutes which he made for his archdeacons so that they might properly perform their office, says in chapter 13: “If a dean in your ministry is negligent, useless, or incorrigible, or if one of them dies, do not elect a dean without consideration; and if I am nearby, refer this election to me.” From this it is clear that those rural deans were always established under the jurisdiction of archdeacons]. They declaim boldly in churches, live disgracefully in houses, quarrel in streets, rage in taverns; they are blasphemous in fabricating miracles, greedy and crafty in remitting money, sacrilegious everywhere and modest nowhere.

At the instigation of one of them named Constantius—who at one time also heaped verbal insults upon us—you have firmly resolved to summon the dean of Ghent, a man truly honorable, grave in character, and burdened with illness, since he suffers incurably both from stone and from an iliac disorder. If it please you, let the aforesaid infirmities of the old man excuse him, rather than the hired work of an informer in preaching, practiced in lies. The complaint for which he is summoned is neither admissible nor accepted; and, if we may dare say so, our supplication has been offered on his behalf.

Deliver us, Father, from these plagues, from wicked and deceitful men who, unfaithfully begging alms from the faithful, frighten our timid deans under the pretext of your sacred name and ensnare fainthearted priests, threatening to drag them before the court of Reims.

### 279. Letter CLXXXI. To Lambin of Bruges

He asks him to prepare lodging for him at Amiens on the day of the queen’s coronation.

[Note: This letter appears to have been sent to Amiens in 1193, where Engelberga, wife of Philip Augustus, received the rite of coronation, with many prelates present and Stephen of Tournai foremost among them, as may be seen in the *History of Tournai*, chapter 58.]

To his most desired friend LAMBIN of Bruges: every expression of affection and greeting.

[Col. 0468A] Your pleasant speech leaves delightful remnants of itself behind when you are absent. Whenever I embrace your gracious company and cherish your fruitful friendship, I make a feast-day for myself. God willing, a day and place will present themselves in which, with renewed rejoicing, we shall discover new modes of conversation and renew the old ones. And because

> To have pleased distinguished men is no small praise,

I ask meanwhile that, when and where the lord of Reims is to speak with the count of Flanders [Note: William, archbishop of Reims, met Baldwin, count of Flanders, at Arras on the king’s behalf, in order to divide Flanders, over which they had made war. Buzelin wrote concerning this in the *Annals of Gaul and Flanders*, book VI, under the year 1198: “The Frankish king allowed Baldwin to choose certain arbitrators with the fullest power to divide Flanders and assign an equal share to each party, whose decision was to stand; in particular, William, archbishop of Reims, Peter, bishop of Arras, Simon, bishop of Aquicinctum, and Daniel, abbot of Cambron, were named.”], you notify me not merely orally through the bearer of this letter, but designate it in writing.

I cast upon you the care of providing me a little lodging on the day of the coronation, lest I run as toward an uncertain goal and, when I arrive, begin to wander after the flocks of unstable women and foolish virgins. In this matter also give me a favorable sign, so that I may come confidently to the feast, which will be common to all in such a way as to belong to each individually. Assure your Stephen, so that your Stephen may, as far as he can, honor his Lambin.

### Letter CLXXXII. To the Pope

He writes on behalf of Hugh Clement [Note: Hugh Clement was elected dean of Paris after Michael of Corbeil, who had been elevated to the bishopric of Sens in 1194, the year in which this letter was written] elected dean of Paris.

To the most holy lord and Father, the supreme pontiff.

Both your mercy and another’s friendship move and urge me, Father, to approach your exaltedness with prayers. It is unfitting that the Church of Paris, a noble member of the kingdom of France, should not yet have agreed upon a dean, when those concerned with electing him have often already assembled in one place but not in one will, before the lord of Chartres [Note: That is, Reginald, to whom he wrote another letter] and the abbot of Châtre-Nantouais [Note: That is, Stephen, the fourth abbot after this monastery’s reform. The supreme pontiff appointed him together with the bishop of Chartres to attend the election of the dean of Paris and settle the disputes which had arisen among the canons].

By your command the individual members of the opposing parties gave and wrote down their names; and at one time, in my presence, these were publicly presented and reread before the same judges. A great part of the canons, especially of the resident canons [Note: Not all canons in those early centuries lived at the churches to which they were attached in order to perform their office. Hence there once arose a serious controversy among the secular canons of Sainte-Geneviève: some, living elsewhere, opposed the others, who were continually present in the church, determining anything in chapter without their counsel and consent. This was settled by a charter of Louis the Fat in 1118, in these words: “In the name of the one and indivisible Trinity, I, Louis, by the grace of God king of the Franks, wish it made known to present and future persons that Lord Stephen, dean of Sainte-Geneviève, and the canons have reverently obtained from our serenity that at all times the dean, and only those canons who reside permanently and continually in the town of the aforesaid church for its daily service, shall have authority and permission, confirmed by our authority, to arrange, transact, and determine irrevocably all affairs of the church, without consulting those canons who live elsewhere and even against their will. For it is fitting that those diligent in God’s service should possess the strength of a higher dignity than those who, without service, possess a share of an ecclesiastical benefice. The provident discretion of royal serenity established this in order that disagreement producing unrest might not perhaps arise among them. To prevent its violation, we ordered it confirmed by the seal of our majesty, by the character of our name, and by the names and marks of the nobles. Whoever rashly usurps this decree shall pay a pound of gold to our treasury, and his usurpation shall be void. Enacted publicly at Paris in the king’s palace in the tenth year of his reign. Mark of the king; mark of Hugh the constable; mark of William the steward; mark of Gilbert the cupbearer. I, Stephen the chancellor, have subscribed.” I find, moreover, that about this same period Cardinal Gregory, Peter bishop of Senlis, and the archdeacon of Auxerre were canons of Sainte-Geneviève], desires Hugh, son of Robert Clement—a young man of good repute, renowned alike for honorable conduct and skill in letters—to preside over them in such a way as to consider how he may benefit them. This part is believed to be inferior to the other neither in merit nor in number.

His intimate familiarity with the lord king, and the continual attentive service of his brothers and kinsmen [Note: Hugh Clement had as brothers Alberic and Henry, marshals of France. The first fell at the siege of Acre in Syria in 1191; the other, lord of Argentan, conducted himself so vigorously in every matter that the king, in consideration of him, ennobled all his descendants with the title of marshal], who have great influence at court, promise that he will be useful to the church. And he who judges that, in these days, more useful benefits will accrue to the Parisian clergy and people from this man than from another surely does not lie.

In conclusion, though I am dust and ashes, I speak to my lord: receive with paternal affection the envoy of so great a man—one whom neither his own will puts forward nor another’s can thrust in—and return him as graciously as you receive him.

### 282. Letter CLXXXIII. To the Bishops of Arras and Amiens

[Note: The bishop of Amiens at that time was Theobald, a kinsman of William, archbishop of Reims. He held this see for thirty-four years and died in 1204. The bishop of Arras was Peter, formerly abbot of Cîteaux, who governed that church from 1180 to 1203.]

He asks them to act as patrons in the case between himself and the abbot of Saint-Bertin [Note: The abbey of Saint-Bertin, of the Benedictine Order, situated in the diocese of Saint-Omer, was founded in 630 by Adroald, a noble Frank, in a place called Sithieu; hence the monastery took the name Sithieu. The charter of its foundation enumerates the villages granted to this church, among which is read Lonsantana, which I suspect to be Listrevele, of which there is discussion here].

[Col. 0469B]

As sons of peace and concord, to whom disputes and lawsuits are hateful, they seek peace and pursue it, so far as lies in them—“pursue” in that sense in which, by the preposition attached to the verb, it either expresses completion or indicates perseverance. Attending to this, and trusting in your holy discretion and prudence, in the case pending between us and the abbot of Saint-Bertin concerning the church of Listrevele, we have chosen you as arbitrators, prepared to accept whatever you pronounce in that case, whether by settlement or judgment.

Therefore we ask your holinesses to undertake this labor of restoring peace between the churches, appointing us a suitable place and day, when and where we may happily see your desired presence and usefully obtain the justice due to our cause.

### Letter CLXXXIV. To Lambin, Bishop of Thérouanne

He complains about the monks of Saint-Bertin.

To Lord Lambin, bishop of Thérouanne [Note: Lambin, or Lambert, formerly chancellor of Reims, was elected bishop of Thérouanne in 1191. The bishop of the Morini formerly resided in the city of Thérouanne. When it was destroyed by Emperor Charles V in 1553, the episcopal see was transferred to Boulogne for that part of the diocese under French rule; and there the abbey of the regular canons of Blessed Mary, having been granted secular clerical status, was erected into a cathedral church by a bull of Pius V in 1566. From the territories belonging to the county of Artois, however, the bishopric of Saint-Omer was created, and the abbey of Saint-Omer was made a cathedral church.]

Days and months have passed since we received neither a word, because of your absence, nor perhaps a letter, because of your neglect. We have known your pleasant conversations; meanwhile we are deprived of your consolation, though once accustomed to it, now released from it. We grieve and complain that either your secretary has gout in his hands or your post-horse is lame—both slow, neither prompt. This delay will be excused if, accommodating yourself to us, you both write and come.

Meanwhile we wish your affection to know that your monks of Saint-Bertin [Note: The bishop of Tournai complains of the Bertinian monks to the bishop of Thérouanne because they belonged to his diocese] are hastening in hostility toward us into quarrels, raising lawsuits, and, through one of their number who limps in his paths, wish—and are attempting—to overturn and entangle the straight course of our justice by a tortuous appeal. They have a church at Coclers, where through annual, hired, and mercenary priests, and often even by themselves, they perform parochial duties, which is forbidden by the sacred canons [Note: The Council of Poitiers in 1109, canon 11, reads: “Let no monk presume to perform the parochial ministry of priests—to baptize or preach”], although in our synod, in the presence of their abbot, we have forbidden this to them and to all other monks, and continue daily to forbid it.

The prior of that place absolved, without our knowledge, one of our parishioners whom we had excommunicated; and, giving her in marriage to a certain knight as though parochially, unlawfully joined them. When we also were passing through those parts, he refused us his lodging, although we wished to spare them expense and provide for ourselves in every way. This hostile man shut his doors against us, neither admitting us as guests [the text perhaps reads *non*, “not”], with muttering enclosed and charity shut out. Rebuke them in these matters, if you cannot correct them.

### 285. Letter CLXXXV. To Octavian, Bishop of Ostia

He excuses the abbot of Saint-Germain-des-Prés from responsibility for the killing of a certain student.

To Lord Octavian, bishop of Ostia [Note: We have already treated of him in the observations on Letter 109. He presided over the Council of Soissons in 1198 concerning the divorce between King Philip and his wife Engelberga. This legate was then staying at Sainte-Geneviève while he was in Paris, as appears from his charter copied from the archives of the monastery of Blessed Geneviève: “Octavian, by the grace of God bishop of Ostia and Velletri, to all who inspect these present letters, greeting in the true Savior. Lest any prejudice at any time be generated against the Church of Sainte-Geneviève in Paris because our venerable brother Odo, bishop of Paris, ate with us there once during our legation, we make known and acknowledge by these present letters that, when the same bishop, as our familiar friend, said that he wished to dine with us there for reasons of friendship and refreshment, we granted his request, telling him beforehand that he could not thereby claim any right in that church. But when this came to the knowledge of our venerable brother J., the abbot, and the canons, and they showed themselves troubled by it, we told them, in the bishop’s presence, that we wished no prejudice to be generated against that church. The abbot himself then sat at table with us; and on that day we had our provision not from the Church of Sainte-Geneviève but from the diocese of Paris. For full knowledge of the foregoing, we have caused these present letters, with our seal appended, to be issued as testimony.”]

In fear and trembling I reflect upon and reconsider you and my other lords. I have been transferred from a low seat to a chair, from the care of a little flock to the governance of a populous church, from a humble condition to heights beyond what I believed, deserved, or hoped. Though I am not sufficient to pray for myself, I offer you recommending prayers for the abbot of Saint-Germain [Note: Namely Fulk, of whom we spoke above], a humble man useful to his church, whose works among his brethren are profitable for present use and exemplary for posterity.

If anyone should raise a case against him in the court of the lord pope, especially concerning the memory of the quarrel which this year arose between the men of Saint-Germain and the students [Note: Such quarrels frequently occurred between the students of the Parisian schools, who sought the meadow called “of the clerics” for walking, and the inhabitants of the suburb of Saint-Germain near Paris, as we read happened in 1531 and 1557], in which one student died through the infamy of the peasants, regard the aforesaid man as excusable. As he is free from guilt, so he ought to be exempt from disgrace or punishment. He sufficiently cleared his innocence before the lord of Reims and a multitude of clerics; and when those who had committed the homicide fled, he was roused to vengeance and demolished and laid waste their houses.

Come to the aid and assistance, if need be, of an innocent man, lest falsehood swallow truth, a lie obtain credit for itself, and the envy of spite corrupt religious devotion.

### 286–287. Letter CLXXXVI. To Fulk, Abbot of Saint-Germain-des-Prés

He gives thanks for a benefice conferred upon his brother.

I rejoice that I have found what many seek, few find, and all desire: I mean a friend faithful in necessity, present in absence, devoted in will, effective in deed. Witnesses to this are the goodwill which you willingly show to my brother, the benefice which you have conferred upon him with such liberality, and the labor and concern which you continually sustain for his business [Note: He speaks of his brother in other letters and indicates that he was a monk of the Benedictine Order. For he speaks of the benefice received from the abbot of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, and in another letter of the annual pension granted him by the abbot of Saint-Denis; he could not have enjoyed it unless he himself had been a religious of that order]. These are the things which carry my whole self into the ardor of affection for you and wholly stir me to test [the remaining sentence is not supplied], etc.

### Letter CLXXXVII. To the Same

He asks him to allow his brother peacefully to enjoy the benefice conferred upon him.

[Col. 0472B]

Old friendships revive through new letters. And we, lest our affection fall asleep or grow sluggish, spare neither pen nor parchment. Let the reader’s weariness be removed, and the writer’s service shall not cease. I shall awaken my friend, prick him with the spur of love, and call him away from regular business, so that he may remember our former companionship, mutual delight, and reciprocal conversation. Let exchanges of affection run and flourish between us, containing enclosed sincerity and excluding suspicion.

In my brother’s affairs, I give thanks for what is past and offer prayers for what is to come. One thing is sufficient: that he may enjoy the advantage of possession, he who through your gift has obtained ownership. But if it please you and does not displease the lord legate, without loss to your church—as is usually done in other cases and was once done in this one—I ask that, in the presence of your brethren, he be presented to the bishop through the archdeacon. Meanwhile, leaving aside mention of our drink, we have fresh cheeses, the seasoning of which seems suspicious to us and pleasing neither to the eyes nor to the palate of Parisians.

### Letter CLXXXVIII. To the Bishop of Soissons

He requests permission to administer the sacrament of confirmation at Marisiac.

To the Bishop of Soissons, unjustly condemned to pay debts; [I am] unjustly condemned to work the mines. [Note: [Col. 0473D] So far as can be conjectured, the subject of this letter is that officials of the Roman chancery exacted a large sum of money from Stephen, bishop of Tournai, for payment of the Roman lead bulls, by which, as he said in Letter 147, the churches were stripped bare. As he was unable to pay, he was compelled to leave his bishopric and withdraw for two years to Marisiac, an estate of Saint Geneviève in the diocese of Soissons, so that he might reserve the revenues of his benefice with which to satisfy his debts to the Roman curia. This may be inferred both from this letter and from the following letter of the bishop of Soissons.], greetings, and a shared endurance of pent-up complaint.

It is a most wretched kind of consolation to wish to have companions in punishment, whether equal or unequal in guilt, so that the wounded person may feel his penalty lighter, as though through association with another. I do not worship but abhor the semblance of such a fault; I lament my own misfortune in such a way that, without any diminution of it, I grieve also for your sorrow and sympathize with your suffering. I had thought that, in a place of dreadful judgments, I might make a bridge [Col. 0473B] by which other bishops are accustomed to find passage. But behold: the storm has grown strong, the waters have swollen, and the torrent has risen which cannot be forded—so that there may meet me something by which I can say: “Perhaps my insufficiency would have passed through intolerable water” (Psalm 123). For the time being I have withdrawn, and in your diocese I have chosen a place of rest and silence at Marisiac, intending to remain there for some time, sitting alone and silent, if perhaps I may catch my breath from faintness of spirit and the storm. And since many of your parishioners come to me that I may lay the confirming hand upon them, with your permission, if it pleases you, I shall do this, being in this office your obedient servant and minister. Living in the country, I often reconsider that couplet of Sollius Sidonius. [Note: [Col. 0474D] Sollius Apollinaris Sidonius, bishop of the Arverni, flourished in the year 475 and wrote various eloquent letters. The couplet is read in Letter 17, addressed to his brother Volusianus:]

[Col. 0473C]

This little corner pleases me, this modest retreat,  
And the cottage whose roof-ridges are pressed with thatch.

290. LETTER CLXXXIX. N., BISHOP OF SOISSONS, TO THE BISHOP OF TOURNAl. [Note: [Col. 0474D] This letter of Nivelon, bishop of Soissons, answers the preceding letter sent to him by Stephen, bishop of Tournai. It appears that he too was suffering oppression at the hands of officials of the Roman curia.] He most willingly grants the permission requested.

We gladly received the letter of your kindness, in which we observed a sweet mixture of good things: graceful elegance in its words and pleasing gravity in its thoughts. Here were words suited to the laws; there, expressions familiar from sacred discourse; elsewhere, phrases at home among the poets—sent by your grace, out of the abundance of your heart, for our consolation. Truly, our private affliction does not disturb us so much as the general scandal of the whole Church. For who can see, without bitterness of heart, a fountain of tears, and repeated sighs, the teacher of the Church of Peter—or rather, Christ’s vicar—depart from the path of truth, so that “truth is in his mouth and is not found”? [Col. 0474A] “If the enchanter is struck, who will heal him?” Now that judge to whom it is often said, “Let your eyes behold equity” (Psalm 16), enters the land by two ways, limps in two directions, and does not hesitate to annul what has once proceeded from his lips. Who, then, will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes, that I may weep—not for the slain of my people, but for the shepherds of my people, for the chief of shepherds? Yet we judge it preferable to bear the burden of suspension—as most people call it an honour—than to provoke an occasion of scandal and a seedbed of perpetual confusion for the Gallican Church. But lest we seem to lament only ourselves, we sincerely sympathize with you; we share your sorrow, and we rejoice with you, [Col. 0474B] because, necessarily sailing between Scylla and Charybdis, you rejoice to have reached port somehow or other. Know that it will be most pleasing to us if your fatherhood, should you wish, performs the duties of a bishop not only in that more secluded place but also in the cathedral church. Finally, we wish you to keep before your eyes this thought: our prelates do not put gold beneath their feet, but place it upon their heads.

LETTER CXC. TO MASTER BERTER, ARCHDEACON OF CAMBRAI. He complains of the hardship which he was wrongly suffering because of debts.

Considering the abyss of the debt incurred, and shuddering at the ravenous bites of wicked usury, after gathering two annual revenues insufficient for payment, [Col. 0474C] I am shaken by fear and terror lest—far be it!—I follow a headlong end, forgetful of myself, and, leaving my garment behind, flee naked. Yet when I consider the gratuitous kindness of my lord and behold the abundant heaps of his benefits toward me, I regard as lighter the burden which had seemed unbearable; and for this reason I am prepared, if need be, to travel abroad, flee, or beg.
