By God’s grace, the wood cast into the water will moderate all these things, and Elisha’s meal will make the gourds in the pot milder, because I entrust my affair into the hand of my lord of Reims, so that he who delivered me from the iron furnace may provide for me, condemned to work the mines. Now at last I have begun to understand [Col. 0474D] that the abyss of business [Note: [Col. 0474D] He alludes to what is said in Psalm 41: “Deep calls to deep.”] calls upon the abyss of expenses; the abyss of expenses calls upon the abyss of robberies; and the abyss of robberies calls upon the abyss of infernal punishments. If the diligent calculator of the Roman well [Col. 0475A] had either joined the fourth to the fifth, or placed the fifth before the fourth. [Note: [Col. 0475D] That is, if, considering the abyss of infernal punishments, he had been deterred from falling into the fourth abyss, namely that of robberies.]

LETTER CXCI. TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT EVURTIUS OF ORLÉANS. He commends William, his kinsman, asking that the abbot show him kindness.

A pitiable person has come to us: V., your kinsman, made a stranger’s son, limping in his paths. By his misery he invites us to mercy; by his poverty he stirs us to compassion; by his troubles he draws us to sympathy. Let both the bond of blood, by which he is joined to you, and the unity of the city, which grants both us and you a common birthplace, move you; and let the title of your prelacy move you, since it is bound to extend mercy to all who are afflicted. Therefore, lest he be compelled any longer [Col. 0475B] to remain outside the flock, exposed to the bites of wolves and, hungry, to eat the husks of swine, we ask, advise, and urge that he who deserved by nature to have you as an uncle may deserve through your diligence and care to have you as a father and patron.

293. LETTER CXCII. TO THE SAME. He writes again on behalf of the same William.

If a mother can forget the children of her womb, then your man of Tournai will forget his dearest mother. [Note: [Col. 0475D] That is, the church of Saint Evurtius at Orléans, which long cherished and nourished him.] Yet this seems difficult by nature and monstrous in fact. The ardour of the charity which we have hitherto had for you, now have, and shall have as long as we live utterly drives out and uproots this monstrosity from your heart; by God’s grace neither delays of any sort will disturb it nor many waters extinguish it. [Col. 0475C] We have had, and have long had, the eager intention of visiting you, as those whom we always carry in our hearts; but waves of occupations and the encounter of countless affairs begrudge us the fulfilment of this intention. As soon as we can, God willing, we shall visit you; and we shall rejoice with one another and console one another in brotherly charity and devotion.

Your brother and son William has come to us. Having set forth and explained his distress, he moved our hearts to a remarkable compassion, since it seems to us that you have not treated him [Col. 0475D] according to the Rule of our order and law. We ask you as our lords, in whom we have complete confidence, that you recall him—who, as you know, [Col. 0476A] is our kinsman according to the flesh, and for whom we feel compassion as for our own flesh—for love of God and of us; and, rescuing his soul from bitterness, assign him a stall in the choir, [Note: [Col. 0475D] A *stallum*, or stall, is the seat in which canons sit while performing the divine office, and into which they are placed when they are inducted into possession of their prebend—when, to use the derived word, they are installed. Thus we read in Hoveden, under Richard I, p. 659: “When the same Henry came to York with the king’s letters to receive the deanery, he found no one to place him in the dean’s stall; for the clergy of the church of York said that no one except the archbishop ought to place him in the dean’s stall.” Lower down it is said: “They caused the canons to be introduced into their stalls, from which the archbishop had dispossessed them.”] as he is accustomed to have one, a seat in chapter, and a place in the refectory; and when we come to you, we shall have his offence and fault duly corrected according to the Rule.

LETTER CXCIII. TO THE SAME. He asks for the third time that his kinsman William be kindly received.

Solomon says that he is wholly ignorant of the way of a man in his youth. It is changeable, now turning here, now there, and is led astray and wanders at the Pythagorean crossroads. Yet the error of the young is pardonable when through rebuke they return to amendment; and, though they previously walked in paths that were not good, they direct their steps into the paths of righteousness, manfully accomplishing through repentance what they childishly committed through fault. Taking this into account in the case of William, a young man of good will, as we now believe, [Col. 0476B] [Note: [Col. 0476D] This letter was also written by Stephen, bishop of Tournai, to Berter, abbot of Saint Evurtius at Orléans, his relative, on behalf of William, the nephew of that abbot and consequently related to Stephen by kinship. He asks that William be kindly received upon his return, after youthful frivolity had carried him away and he had abandoned the cloister.] who carelessly departed from you and earnestly desires to return, we entreat and ask that, for love of God and of us, if you see him contrite and humble, you receive him kindly, without prejudice to the discipline of the order, and treat him with goodwill and generosity—lest perhaps, God forbid, if he finds you cruel and hard, you break in him the bruised reed and extinguish the smoking flax.

LETTER CXCIV. TO THE POPE. He asks that the apostolic command concerning all persons ordained be restricted to particular orders.

[Col. 0476C]

Just as we have learned that by civil law the walls of the blessed City are holy and inviolable, so that those who cross them are to be punished by capital penalty, with Romulean severity, [Note: [Col. 0476D] He means the penalty imposed upon Remus, who transgressed Romulus’s command, concerning which Livy, Book I, says: “The more widespread report is that Remus, in mockery of his brother, crossed the newly built walls and was then killed by the enraged Romulus.”] so we confess that the commands of the holy Roman Church ought to be inviolable by canon law, and that contempt for them ought to be punished with apostolic severity. Yet we trust in the benevolence of your fatherhood, that you do not intend to impose upon us, as obedient sons, commands that are impossible and intolerable, but commands which ought to be acceptable and useful to those now living and beneficial to posterity.

Very frequently and everywhere, many in number but few in merit come to us with your divine letters, without any examination of origin, condition, offence, or crime, arousing our obedience by a terrible admonitory or threatening command [Col. 0476D] [Col. 0477A]: namely, that we are meanwhile to provide necessities for all persons upon whom we have conferred ordaining imposition of hands, from the first clerical tonsure up to and including sacred orders, or whom we know our predecessors to have ordained, until we confer benefices upon them. Some, although they have private means by which they can live, nevertheless seek ordination so that, as a title under the dispensation of the sacred canons, they may use their own property. Others, in order to evade the jurisdiction of secular authorities, deceitfully pretend to be enrolled among the clergy merely by tonsure or minor orders. With all due reverence to your holiness, this seems new and unusual to us, since in the sacred and ancient canons this observance is restricted to priests and [Col. 0477B] deacons alone; and at the holy Lateran Council, [Note: [Col. 0477D] Convened under Alexander III in 1179, where chapter 5 reads: “If a bishop ordains anyone as deacon or priest without a certain title from which he may receive the necessities of life, he shall furnish him with necessities until he assigns him, in some church, suitable stipends for clerical service—unless the person being ordained is such that he can have support from his own or his paternal inheritance.”] under Pope Alexander of most blessed memory, at which several of us were present and all who attended gave their assent, it was enacted and decreed concerning priests and deacons alone. We gladly embrace this, faithfully approve it, and, God willing, shall obediently observe it—and do observe it. But it is impossible for us to remember the names or number of those whom we have ordained below the diaconate; nor is it less impossible to confer benefices upon all of them or provide them with necessities. It would be preferable for us henceforth not to celebrate ordinations than to undertake these unbearable burdens. If, perhaps, this should happen because we cease, no one doubts or is ignorant how great a danger would threaten future times or [Col. 0477C] persons.

In the Gallican regions also, most people, whether children or adults, learn letters for this very purpose: that, advancing step by step through orders in God’s Church, they may serve and minister to God. If those who ordain fail, those to be ordained will fail; and the mysteries will cease if the ministries happen to cease. Let the devout and just Father consider that a new law must be possible in its observance at its establishment; it should not prescribe a form for matters past, but for those to come. For all these reasons we entreat your fatherhood and pour out prayers that you may, if it please you, moderate this difficult, intolerable, and burdensome command, which both difficulty prevents and impossibility does not permit us to obey.

LETTER CXCV. TO THE LORD OF REIMS. He asks that, by his authority, a canon of Saint Geneviève be received by the chapter of Tournai to administer a benefice.

[Col. 0478A]

I am ashamed, Father, so often to trouble your tranquillity and to overwhelm your sacred occupations, as it were, with so many bundles of letters. At one time my own need, at another the charity owed to another, makes me excusable. But, that I may redeem for myself a little of this weariness which I cause you, I append for you, in Solomon’s proverbial style, the delightful trifles of our Garnaud of Orléans:

There are three things murmuring upon the earth, and a fourth that does not readily become quiet: the commons of peasants ruling, a gathering of women [Col. 0478B] disputing, a herd of pigs grunting at the cry of one, and a chapter pursuing divergent wishes.

We fight with the first, mock the second, despise the third, and endure the fourth. From the first and fourth, deliver us, O Lord. Compelled by the last, I both seek and await the final intervention of your correction. There is a certain companion of mine [Note: [Col. 0477D] When Stephen was called from the monastery of Saint Geneviève to govern the church of Tournai, he brought with him two of his regular canons, namely Marcellus and Gerard, that they might assist him in counsels and ecclesiastical ministries, as may be gathered from Letter 207.] at my table, simple and innocent before God and men, beyond reproach. Our chapter had conferred on him one vicarage at the high altar, assigning him a benefice from a certain burgess [Note: [Col. 0477D] That burgess, according to the records of the church of Tournai, was called Baldwin, son of Hanuid. In 1193, before a synod assembled there by the bishop, he established a certain prebend, endowed it, and added it to the other four which he had previously founded. It was conferred upon one of the two regular canons of Saint Geneviève. We read, moreover, that there were formerly also in the church of Blessed Mary of Paris five similar priestly prebends for five priests who served the altar; but by a charter of Alexander III each was divided into two, and ten canons were established, called *semipraebendati*, “half-prebendaries,” from their halved prebends.] from which he could live in adequate modesty as a priest. The canons presented him to me for ordination to the title of the high altar, and granted him a common share with the others in the refectory. [Col. 0478C] But after he had been ordained by us, had served at the altar for nearly two years, and had received the benefice of the refectory [Note: [Col. 0478D] The canons of Tournai therefore still maintained a common life, since the use of the refectory flourished among them. Since this letter appears to have been written two years after the conferral of such priesthood, it follows that it was issued in the year 1195.] with the others, they deprived him—without citation, without his having been convicted of anything, and with legal procedure disregarded—both of service at the altar and of the refectory’s benefit. The burgess, though unwilling, took back into his own hand the benefice which he had conferred. All who hear of it are astonished; but our canons either disregard or despise their astonishment. We entreat your fatherhood that, for love of God and through the intercession of our humble prayers, you write to our dean and chapter, asking them, if you please, to restore for your sake our companion, a priest of good reputation and honourable life, unjustly despoiled; and, if he has committed anything for which he deserves condemnation, that they deal with him by judicial procedure, lest perhaps they may be accused either of ignorance of the law [Col. 0479A] or marked for cruelty.

299. LETTER CXCVI. TO WILLIAM, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS. He gives thanks for the letters written to the chapter of Tournai.

Thank you, Father: among your other benefits toward me, your cleric, by letters sent to our chapter you have both rebuked the incorrigible and taught the unteachable. That fourth kind of thing murmuring [Note: [Col. 0479D] That class would not readily have been identified unless he himself had indicated it to us in Letter 195 with these words: “There are three things murmuring upon the earth, and a fourth that does not readily become quiet: the commons of peasants ruling, a gathering of women disputing, a herd of pigs grunting at the cry of one, and a chapter pursuing divergent wishes.”] upon the earth, from which I often pray to be freed and defended, at the first sight of your letters took it impatiently and badly that I should either lay my complaint before you or not endure their insult. They began with murmuring and ended in quarrelling. Those who ought to have been corrected did not fear to rise up; those deserving the rod offered a straw. But [Col. 0479B] because I wish to be peaceable with those who hate peace, I forgave the injury and left the injurers alone. The time will come, God willing, when in your presence they will either blush for their irreverence or be punished for their insult.

300. LETTER CXCVII. TO THE POPE. Concerning a fugitive monk of Saint Martin of Tournai.

Father, in sacred communities there are customarily found certain sons of contradiction and disobedience, who love lawsuits and disputes, sow quarrels among the brethren, deliberately stir up scandals, and prepare and produce schisms and civil wars—danger for their own people and mockery for others. Among their number was a certain Nicholas, formerly a monk [Col. 0479C] of Saint Martin of Tournai. Driven by levity and instability, and not without the corruption of malice, he secretly departed from them, because he was not of them, readier to leap and go out from the cloister than to sit solitary within it. When his clandestine departure was reported to us, we came to the church; and, having summoned the community and entered the chapter, I asked each one whether that fugitive had departed by anyone’s counsel or consent, or had taken with him any letters, either sealed or unsealed, as some people outside the monastery were murmuring. They all answered unanimously that he had departed neither with their knowledge, counsel, nor consent; and if he had taken any letters with him, they declared them stolen. Therefore, holy Father, because we know the truth of the matter, we pour out prayers to you that, if perhaps that seditious man and deserter comes to you, as some suspect, and attempts to deceive your religious community by a lie, you may not believe him; nor let him pollute your sacred ears with falsehood and attempt to corrupt them by feigned deceits. Let your holy fatherhood know concerning the state of that church that, if anything in it required correction, whether in head or members, by God’s grace we have taken, and shall take, pains that all may be corrected. We hope in the Lord that that church proceeds under regular discipline, terrible as an army drawn up in battle array. We have inspected [Col. 0480B] and read, through the clerk John, those letters which the abbot and chapter sent to you, and we bear them witness to their truth.

301. LETTER CXCVIII. TO THE POPE. He writes concerning the same fugitive monk, asking that the pope not allow himself to be deceived by him.

The more excellent way which the Apostle shows does not rejoice in iniquity but rejoices together with truth (1 Corinthians 13). That truth with which it rejoices is self-sufficient in your sight, holy Father: it neither begs for purchasable glory nor rejects pardonable intercession. Trusting in it, we truly assure you that that wandering monk and deserter of Saint Martin of Tournai [Note: [Col. 0479D] This monastery, destroyed by the Normans, was granted in 1191 by Rabo, bishop of Noyon and Tournai, to a certain Odo of Orléans, a learned and devout man, who withdrew there with four of his pupils, clerics devoted to religion. After they repaired the church and monastery, they embraced there the institution of regular canons, which they afterward abandoned in order to follow the monastic rule. Aimeric, abbot of Anchin, had persuaded them to this purpose with arguments and words such as these: “Since you live near the city, your younger brethren are deceived by their secular-cleric companions and brought back to the world, because one habit is yours and theirs. But if you were monks, afterward they would attempt to bring none of yours back, because the habit of monks is black while that of clerics is white; clerics have so great a horror of monks’ dress that, once they have seen someone a monk, they never thereafter deign to have him as a companion.” This passage shows that clerics and canons in this age were accustomed to wear white garments.] dared to come to your see [Col. 0480C] and attempted to deceive your holy religious community with his lie; he departed from his brethren neither with their knowledge nor by their counsel. The seal which he carried away he either secretly stole or, guilty under the Cornelian law concerning forgery, [Note: [Col. 0480D] Lucius Cornelius Sulla, dictator and consul with Quintus Caecilius Metellus in the 673rd year from the founding of the City, promulgated this law: “Whoever, in the name of a praetor, delivers forged letters or posts a forged edict, let inquiry be made concerning his life. Whoever partly clips, partly dyes or counterfeits gold coins; whoever introduces any defect into gold; whoever mints counterfeit silver coins; whoever, when able, fails to prevent this; whoever fraudulently buys or sells tin or lead coins—let inquiry be made concerning his life, and, if convicted, let him be forbidden fire and water.”] sacrilegiously transformed into a false seal. We carefully investigated these matters in chapter, questioning each individual, and received from all the common answer: they neither knew of his departure nor approved his transgression. Since no one ought to be aided by his own fraud, we pray your fatherhood, lest falsehood overwhelm truth, to condemn, if you please, that harmful document by which, through forged letters and a forged seal, a false monk sought to bind the Church, so that it may not be compelled [Col. 0481A] to render what it did not receive, pay what it did not take, or approve what it did not know.

We rejoice that that church, close to us both in place and affection, is sound in manner of life and reputation, neither “running as though uncertainly” nor “fighting as though beating the air.” If anything is lacking in it for perfection, by God’s grace we hope daily for better things and for things nearer to salvation.

303. LETTER CXCIX. TO THE ABBOT AND COMMUNITY OF SAINT GENEVIÈVE, PARIS. He explains what should be done in the matter pending between them and the archdeacon of Paris concerning the chaplain of Saint Geneviève’s parish chapel in the city.

My spirit is distressed whenever either your peace [Col. 0481B] is shaken or your unanimity hindered. For I have always been accustomed—and, God willing, shall not cease from this custom—both to rejoice with you when you rejoice and to weep with you when you weep. For who shall separate me from your charity, which is in Christ Jesus? Tribulation? Or distress? Or persecution? Or famine? Or nakedness? Or danger? Or the sword? For if I am prepared to die for each one of you, I am prepared, if necessary, to die also for all of you. In the trouble which surrounded you concerning the chapel of the blessed virgin Geneviève, [Note: [Col. 0481D] It is situated in the city of Paris beside the church of Blessed Mary, and is now a parish church, commonly called Sainte-Geneviève-des-Ardents. From its original foundation it was a chapel called Saint Mary the Little. It was dedicated by the clergy and people of Paris under the patronage of this virgin in perpetual memory of the remarkable miracle by which those suffering from the sacred fire were healed through the merits of Blessed Geneviève in 1130. It was granted to the canons of her church, who governed it until 1202, when they yielded it to the bishop and chapter of Paris in exchange for the church of Saint Eligius of Roissy, which the canons of Saint Geneviève received as compensation from the Parisians. In the charters of Alexander III, Lucius, Clement, and Celestine it is called a chapel in these words: “May your chapels—namely the chapel on Mount Saint Medard, Saint Geneviève in the City, and their chaplains—remain in the same liberty which they had in the time of the clerics and are known to have now.”] concerning which you also consulted us through our and your dearest brother R., I do not dare give you definite counsel, because I understand that our brethren’s wishes are always diverse, and I neither foresee as a prophet nor dream as a poet the outcome of a matter which may perhaps depend upon fortune’s snares.

If, while the wrongdoing was still inflamed, when the young archdeacon violently entered your chapel and, with a bold hand almost amounting to sacrilege, attacked your brother the priest—after an appeal had been made to the lord pope—seized and carried off the sacred ornaments and violently expelled that same brother from the chapel, someone had laid this lamentable complaint at the feet of the supreme pontiff, I should have thought this rightly done. Nor, merely because the matter has grown numb through lapse of time, [Col. 0481C] and because the archdeacon boasts that he is in some sort of possession, should you refuse arbitration if, as we have heard, he is willing to submit the matter to arbitrators whom you consider lovers of law and equity. Accept the arbitration, however, only on condition that the case [Col. 0481D] is not heard in the city of Paris or nearby, lest our and your smallness be crushed by the weight of its multitude—both advocates and prudent and powerful men, of whom the city has no small abundance. If they refuse to choose another place, I think it better that the entire matter be referred to the supreme pontiff. But if, [Col. 0482A] God willing, it happens that you can peacefully retain your chapel, it seems better that you govern it through honourable brethren from your own community rather than appoint a secular person there.

305. LETTER CC. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS. He asks that he arrange for the church of Bredenai [Note: [Col. 0482D] Bredenay, otherwise Brandenay, is a conventual priory of the Benedictine order situated in the diocese of Tournai.] to be restored anew to monks, so that they may perform the divine office there.

We came to the church of Bredenai to hold our synod, and at first sight a great miracle met us: a sad spectacle to us, ridiculous to others. We learned from the neighbours that in that church monastic order had customarily been observed communally under the conventional number of twelve brethren; the divine office [Col. 0482B] had been regularly celebrated; the poor received food, pilgrims lodging, and the sick comfort. But behold, everything has been turned to the opposite: the buildings are ruined, the divine offices are silent, since there is not even one monk there to celebrate them. The place has been reduced to solitude, made like a shelter in a vineyard and a hut in a cucumber field. The extensive possessions and rich tithes by which the monks were supported have partly been sold off; they are burdened under a mortgage by another’s lordship. Nevertheless, this wretched and enslaved church has been entrusted to a priest, whereas there ought to be a prior there to preside over and benefit the other monks. The parishioners mourn and grieve, for the church was endowed and enriched from their gifts and their predecessors’ offerings. They mourn and cry in the ears of the Lord of Hosts, and amid sighs and sobs both seek and await vengeance from God and correction from you. [Col. 0482C] Considering these things and inwardly touched by grief of heart, at the counsel of prudent men present with us, and consumed by zeal for the house of God, we gird ourselves for rebuke and correction. We place that desolate and tearful church under interdict, and forbid the celebration of divine offices there and the payment by parishioners of tithes, offerings, or any other parochial revenues, until the customary number of monks is brought to the place and a prior is appointed there to preside over and benefit the others. Nevertheless, at the request of V., the priest, and of the men who were with us, we suspended the sentence pronounced and postponed its observance until the octave of Epiphany. [Col. 0482D]

LETTER CCI. TO THE SAME. He writes that, at the archbishop’s command, he will confer a prebend in the church of Tournai upon a certain cleric.

Far be it from my soul, Father, that I should appear in any respect [Col. 0483A] either ungrateful for your benefits or undevoted to your goodwill. These are two images which I abhor, two idols which I detest. If anyone perhaps—far be it!—has whispered anything else to you, he is either a hostile interpreter of my intention or a slanderous detractor. As to my seeming hesitation about conferring or transferring the grant of a prebend from the lord Boniface of Tournai to L., your cleric, I was compelled by the authority of your first command, the novelty of the second, and reverence for not breaking a promise. But now, understanding your will more fully, I am ready to do what you commanded: freely, without pretence; willingly, without concealment. Let the said L. come whenever he wishes; whenever he comes, he will find us willing.

307. LETTER CCII. TO A CERTAIN ABBOT. He answers a question concerning the marriage of a novice who, after abandoning the habit, had contracted it; he considers it valid.

[Col. 0483B]

You have asked us what ought to have been asked of you. We do not know the custom of your order, but we both read and observe the words of blessed Benedict: “If anyone wishes to leave within the year of probation, let him depart free with his possessions.” He who called the entrant free did not forbid marriage to the one departing. And because B., the bearer of the present letter, withdrew his foot from the probationary training, he did not deserve to be separated from Christian society by a prohibitory cautery. So far as concerns the solace of human weakness, what he contracted [Col. 0483C] is a marriage; so far as concerns the summit of your community, he has departed from perfection. We believe and declare that this marital union is a marriage. Consider yourselves whether, because of such an absence, you ought with a secure conscience to retain his possessions.

LETTER CCIII. TO POPE CELESTINE. He commends G., elected abbot of Corbie, [Note: [Col. 0483] Gerard, abbot of Saint Cornelius of Compiègne, was elected abbot of Corbie in 1194.] and extols his prudence and piety.

Although, Father, amid the abundance of royal and pontifical banquets in your sight, our prayers occupy but a small place, like a drop from a bucket, [Col. 0483D] nevertheless both necessity urges and charity persuades us to intercede for others. The church of Corbie, worn down and afflicted by many great labours, has now at last, we believe, begun to breathe again, if your holy fatherhood displays its favour and bestows its goodwill upon it. They have as abbot Lord G., who can recover in it possessions that have been lost and not lose those recovered. He is prudent and diligent, and equal, as we believe, to so great a burden and honour. We ask your holy fatherhood, if it please you, to bestow your favour more fully on the aforesaid man, of good standing among his own people, useful and faithful to his Church.

LETTER CCIV. TO BERTER, ABBOT OF SAINT EVURTIUS OF ORLÉANS. He consoles him, weighed down by illness.

[Col. 0484A]

Having heard of your chronic illness, we both grieve with the grieving and sympathize with the sufferer. May the Author of salvation heal you—he who heals the broken in heart, saves those who hope in him, and has wrought salvation in the midst of the earth. We would have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you and, at your house, to temper and season the wild lettuces of our sorrow with the flesh of the Paschal Lamb. But the necessity of the times forbids it: the cause of necessity, the unbearable yoke laid upon our shoulders. We hope in the Lord that we shall soon be delivered from this affliction, although the scars of so many wounds [Col. 0484B] will not be effaced at once. Once prosperity has been restored to us by God’s grace, we shall visit you and our brothers as soon as we can, so that together we may enjoy shared conversation, rejoice in one another’s company, and delight in consolation. Greet our brothers, each individually in all, and all in each individually.

## LETTER CCV. TO JOHN, ABBOT, AND THE CHAPTER OF ST. GENEVIEVE, PARIS.

He exhorts the canons of St. Genevieve to show themselves perfect in all things.

Though placed at the furthest bounds of the earth and at the furthest bounds of life, I remember with pleasure your honorable [Col. 0484C] way of life, your undivided fellowship, and your devout humility. Some among you I begot in Christ; others I found already grown. I cultivated and loved both alike, and offended neither except under necessity’s compulsion. In the sweat of my face and the distress of my spirit, I labored faithfully for fifteen years and more in our Church and yours together; and, if I may say so, by God’s grace I did not labor unsuccessfully—neither beating the air nor running uncertainly. Judge for yourselves, lest perhaps someone, grumbling in a corner, say to me: “Your testimony is not true” (John 8). Meanwhile, brothers and sons, I, an old man, admonish and exhort old men to prepare themselves for life’s end; young men, for the observance of regular discipline; adolescents, for the preservation of submission [Col. 0484D] and modesty; and all, for unity in brotherly love and for rendering full obedience in all things to our most dear son, your abbot.

By God’s mercy we abound in every temporal success, while awaiting, through your prayers, the yield and fruit of spiritual things. Your brothers greet you, my most dear sons: Marcellus and Gerard, young men distinguished by uprightness, 310 eminent in humility, diligent and vigorous in my service and yours, constantly present in our counsels, affairs, and confidences. My mind is ready, if my hand is ready, to meet, assist, and serve the business of your Church at a suitable time and place.

## LETTER CCVI. TO THE ABBOT OF ST. BERTIN.

He asks him for a horse suitable to his use.

[Col. 0485A]

The bonds of friendship arise from conversation, are strengthened by counsel, and grow strong through benefits. Let these venerable exchanges pass between us and be nourished reciprocally by mutual services. In the remnants of this hope, we ask your affection to send us one palfrey: one which does not shy at a sight, stumble in its gait, or jolt an old man in its movement; which pleases a friend to look upon and befits a priest to mount. If you think of recompense, places and times will arise, God willing, in which we may suitably repay this kindness.

## LETTER CCVII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS.

He discusses the disputes between the monks of St. Amand [Note: [Col. 0485C] The distinguished and very wealthy monastery of St. Amand, under the Rule of St. Benedict, is situated in the diocese of Tournai and was founded by King Dagobert in recognition of the merits of St. Amand, who, as is read in the foundation charter, had baptized his son Sigebert.] and their abbot, whom he commends.

[Col. 0485B]

At your command, Father, we went to St. Amand, where we found monks who were not lovable. They were seditious; they persist in sedition and perhaps will die in sedition. They could allege nothing against 311 their abbot except that, although learned, sober, chaste, peaceable, and thrifty, he is nearer to frugality than prodigality; that he is, as they say, insufficiently experienced in the observance of monastic order, as one who does not know how, in the language of the fingers, [Note: [Col. 0485C] The monks observed silence so strict that they were not permitted even to utter necessary things with the mouth, but had to express their thoughts by gestures and signs of the fingers [Col. 0485D]; this was also adopted among the ancient canons of the congregation of St. Victor, as may be gathered from the book of their constitutions called the *Liber ordinis*, in which there is a chapter entitled “On the Signs of the Order,” by which they expressed what they wished to make known to another.] to signify beans, cheese, or eggs; or that he either neglects or disdains to rebuke or correct those who err in such matters.

We wished to separate temporarily from that community certain men who were the heads [Col. 0485C] of the whole conspiracy, forbidding them, under the cautery of excommunication, either rashly to leap away or to depart, without our permission and that of their abbot, from the monasteries to which we assigned them. They proved disobedient to us; but the intervention of the abbot of Anchin [Note: [Col. 0485D] The abbey of Aquicinctum, commonly Anchin, of the Benedictine order in the diocese of Arras, was founded in 1079 by two knights, as is read in the charter of Gerard, bishop of Cambrai, in these words: “Two knights of our diocese, distinguished in birth and wealth, namely Walter and Suher, laying aside the belt of worldly knighthood and despising every such possession, promised to follow the contemplative life; giving themselves and their possessions to God, they promised to serve him alone forever,” etc. It is called Aquicinctum because it is situated on an island of the river Scarpe, surrounded on every side by water.] and of your lord vice-lord, Philip [Note: [Col. 0485D] In those cities in which bishops formerly possessed temporal lordship and jurisdiction, which they could not exercise in person, they appointed certain noble laymen to whom they entrusted the care of matters belonging to their secular right and lordship, so that they might supply the bishops’ place. These were therefore commonly called *vicedomini*, “vice-lords,” or *vidames*, as may be seen at Rheims, Châlons, Amiens, Chartres, and elsewhere. Gregory of Tours (book IX, letter 66) says: “We wish that our aforesaid brother Paschasius appoint both a vice-lord and a major-domo for himself, so that he may be fit and prepared both for arriving guests and for matters which arise.” And the Council of Mainz (canon 50): “We command all bishops, abbots, and the whole clergy absolutely to have good vice-lords and provosts.”] cleansed the stain of their disobedience, so that those who deserved excommunication by their own fault might be absolved through another’s merit. [Col. 0486A]

In all these matters, let your holy fatherhood consider what ought to benefit the holy monastery and what ought to hinder the unholy monks. We found the abbot honorable and learned and, apart from the disadvantage of old age and infirmity, as we believe, blameless—no less free of malice of his own than experienced in the malice of others.

## LETTER CCVIII. TO MASTER BERTER, ARCHDEACON OF CAMBRAI.

He reproves him for rashly diminishing his reputation and sets forth the course of his own life.

If what is said is true, you speak ill of one absent, accuse the innocent, and without cause tear to pieces, censure, and condemn a bishop who is both a new bishop and [Col. 0486B] an old friend. You say, to pass over the rest, that I do not know how to conform myself to the episcopal chair. Teach me, I beg you, what that episcopal pattern is which you depict, so that, if it is not shapeless, I may conform myself to it.

I rarely leave the city; as far as I can, I attend the canonical hours with the others. According to the grace granted me, I proclaim God’s word to my parishioners. Declaring against the new heresy [Note: [Col. 0486D] He perhaps means the heresy of the Waldensians, Cotarelli, and Albigensians, concerning whom we have spoken above; or the one concerning which Genebrard, following William of Nangis and Vincent of Beauvais, writes under the year 1183: “Many heretics were burned in Flanders by order of Philip, count of Flanders, and William, archbishop of Rheims, legate of the Apostolic See. They said that all eternal things were from God, but that the human body and temporal things had been created by Luciabel; they rejected infant baptism and the Eucharist.”] and other monsters of that kind, to the extent of my ability I fight as though against wild beasts. The sacraments which I received freely I impart freely. I abhor, detest, and anathematize in every way Simon’s wickedness and Gehazi’s leprosy. Even if not from every gift, I always keep my hands clear of unlawful gifts.

To those who come to me, I give, as the Lord permits, counsel in confession, remedy in penance, and consolation in tribulation. [Col. 0486C] In free hours and in hours released from public business, in a place suited to this purpose, I devote myself to Holy Scripture, reading and ruminating upon what I digest after reading and transfer to the little chamber of memory. I gladly welcome honorable guests and generously hasten to meet them. At table I do not wish to be either alone or obscure; there nature can more easily accuse superfluity [Col. 0487A] than curiosity accuse hunger. I do not squander Christ’s patrimony on actors and buffoons. These are outward matters. But God, the knower of hidden things, who searches hearts and reins, will show himself a true judge and a severe avenger of our deeds.

I ask that, if these things belong to the episcopal pattern, you do not mock them. In other matters which are lacking, God is able to increase his grace in me; and he who gave the beginning will, according to his good pleasure, give increase. Had you loved more sincerely, you ought to have admonished more privately, advised more gently, and rebuked more safely. But now, casting aside the modesty of love, you have set your friend up like a target for arrows, defaming him everywhere, in every ear, at oven and mill, as they say—a spectacle to his own people and a laughingstock to strangers. [Col. 0487B] Spare, I beg you, my good name; spare your own honor; spare both our reputations, so that, if it should happen that we someday see and are seen by one another, each may more favorably either condemn what is notable in the other or commend what is excusable.

## LETTER CCIX. TO HUGH, DEAN, AND PETER, CHANTER OF PARIS.

[Note: [Col. 0487D] Namely Hugh, surnamed Clement, concerning whose election as dean of Paris we have spoken, and Peter the Chanter.] He asks them to support his friend’s case.

God knows, and men do not fail to know, that you are defenders of right and lovers of equity in God’s Church. Whoever judges otherwise of you sins against the common opinion, becoming a companion of those who sin willingly, for whom no sacrifice remains. In confidence of this hope, we rejoice that, in our brother’s business concerning the Church of Nes, we have obtained such and so great judges—judges whom neither cunning may deceive, malice pervert, nor greed defile. The facts are known to all; the right is clear; the apostolic document contains a full and plain account. Yet, in order that those who sit may sit and carry out the supreme pontiff’s command, we beseech you, for the sake of our affections, on behalf of our said brother: having found you, in faith and truth, generous but indirect benefactors, may we now at last find you stable and upright executors in justice and equity. The aforesaid S., 315 secure and confident both in his justice and in your goodwill, comes to you. May my God make you [Col. 0487D] gracious to him and send him back to us with a fruitful return, not with mournful groaning. Receive your old—not aged—friend in his just petitions; and, having loved him when present, do not cast him off when absent.

## LETTER CCX. TO THE LORD OF RHEIMS.

He seeks his favor for the dean of Tournai.

[Col. 0488A]

Living in the countryside among fig-eating Fauns [Note: [Col. 0487D] Pan and the Fauns are rural and woodland gods. They were called “fig-eating Fauns” because they were thought to eat figs or to linger around fig trees. In Jeremiah 50 one reads: “Dragons shall dwell with fig-eating fauns, and ostriches shall dwell there.” Isaiah likewise repeats this, though in other words: “Their houses shall be filled with dragons; ostriches shall dwell there, and shaggy creatures shall dance there” (Isa. 13). Those shaggy creatures [Col. 0488D] are Fauns and Satyrs, who had the upper part of a human being and the lower part of a beast. Blessed Jerome testifies that St. Anthony saw and addressed such a monster. Isidore, *Etymologies*, book VIII, says of them: “The being whom the common people call an incubus, the Romans call a fig-eating faun.”] and woodland Pans, having for a little while buried my sacramental duties, I sometimes fall at the feet of the Lord Jesus and weep bitterly for my sins; sometimes I fly back up to his head and faithfully recall and reconsider God’s benefits. Between these there is no place for remedy: for if I attend to domestic cares, they leave me confused; if I neglect them, they leave me desolate.

Meanwhile, fearing that I may be crushed beneath the stones of your rebuke if, by importunate prayers bestially poured out for another, I touch the mountain [Note: [Col. 0488D] He alludes to the passage where, while Moses remained on Mount Sinai to receive the law, it was commanded: “Whatever beast touches the mountain shall be overwhelmed with stones” (Exod. 21).] of your highness, nevertheless, with the modest boldness of presumption, I beg for the dean of our Church, [Col. 0488B] an innocent and simple man, whom you have summoned to the priestly rank by admonishing, as they say, and threatening. If it please you, let your kindness grant him some delay, in which the man may prove himself, so that he may thus eat healthfully of that bread and drink of that cup; and, forewarned by you to good purpose, may humbly obey you, now fortified by warning.

You know the man’s simplicity; and, to speak truthfully, one must fear that a merely elementary priest, at first making a barbarism, may utter there a mute consonant in place of a vowel—where, for someone who has lived in barbarism and wishes to celebrate, it is more fitting to be mute than vocal. Father, let your mercy admit our prayers into the sanctuary of hearing, so that he for whom they are offered may rejoice that he has received from you [Col. 0488C] oil instead of ashes, joy instead of mourning, and a garment of praise instead of a spirit of sorrow.

## LETTER CCXI. TO JOHN, ABBOT OF ST. GENEVIEVE.

He invites him to attend the dedication of a chapel which he had built.

Among the other benefits of divine grace granted us by God, we glory greatly in the Lord because, dearest brother, we were fellow-workers and ministers in your promotion, and at our departure deserved to leave behind us such a successor. We frequently hear joyful reports of you and of our brothers, conveyed by those who pass through to us: that your person is useful to the Church, [Col. 0488D] and the Church suited to your person. We gladly embrace this peace, joyfully seek this shared concord, commend your integrity, praise your sobriety, approve your thrift and prudence in outward matters, and discipline in [Col. 0489A] inward matters.

And because we wish you to rejoice with us, just as we rejoice with you and our brothers in prosperity, we ask and exhort you in the Lord to make yourself available to us at Tournai on the vigil of holy 317 Pentecost; for, God willing, on the Tuesday after the feast we propose to dedicate our new chapel, [Note: [Col. 0489D] He had a new chapel built in the episcopal palace in honor of St. Vincent in 1198, and established there a chaplain who was to celebrate Mass every day for the deceased bishops of Tournai, with a collect for the prelate then seated in that same cathedral.] no less glorious in material than gracious in design. St. Evurtius and Genevieve [Note: [Col. 0489D] His two patrons and protectors, toward whom he was disposed with singular devotion because he had attained the dignity of abbot in their monasteries. Hence, to show his gratitude more and more, he arranged for their feasts to be celebrated forever in Tournai cathedral under the double rite of nine lessons, with specified revenues assigned for this purpose.] will run delightfully, before you and the others looking on with you, contending in holy rivalry and equal splendor in the individual stained-glass windows.

It is fitting that we double our *paraclysis*—that is, our consolation—with you, [Note: [Col. 0489D] Here he uses *paraclysis* in the sense of consolation, just as *Paraclete* means “comforter.”] both through the solemnity and savor of the Holy Spirit and through the pleasure and benefit of our little building. We desire to have you at this spectacle of the theatre [Col. 0489B] both as a participant in the labor and as a companion in the joys. Farewell; come and see.

## LETTER CCXII. TO THE BISHOP OF THÉROUANNE.

He also invites him graciously to attend the dedication of his chapel.

For God’s honor and the confusion of the murmuring community, we have a free and secure entrance into our house: free from crowds and storms, secure from night terrors. We have raised a triumphal 318 arch [Note: [Col. 0489D] Our Stephen of Tournai raised and built a chapel in the episcopal palace over a high vault, in the likeness of a triumphal arch; it still exists. By this letter he invited the bishop of Thérouanne to its consecration. As we have said, that bishopric, after its city was destroyed, was transferred to Boulogne.], victory having been granted us from heaven; and, extending open passageways for those passing through, we have built a new chapel in the air, as glorious in material as it is gracious in design. [Col. 0489C]

Your friend asks us—whether I should call him old or rather a little old, I do not know; yet I shall not call him worn-out—that, if possible, you would grant us your welcome presence on the Tuesday of Pentecost for the dedication of our chapel by your hand, so that we may rejoice together with a twofold joy of paradise: in the festive coming of the Holy Spirit and in the pleasant entrance into the new oratory. It will be a happy day, because you, a great guest, will fill our little huts.

On the aforesaid arch, which adjoins the sacred walls, one of our people had painted some little verses [Note: [Col. 0490D] We have judged these fit to omit here, as somewhat less serious and proper, although they occur at the end of Letter 219 in the first edition.] lest passers-by pollute an honorable place with filth. We send you some of them, so that the letter may not end without laughter or playful jest.

## LETTER CCXIII. TO JOHN, ABBOT OF ST. GENEVIEVE.

He excuses himself for being unable, because of business, to attend this dedication ceremony.

[Col. 0490A]

Although, in response to the urgency of your prayers, we had intended to present ourselves on the appointed day for the consecration of your chapel, no pleasure is unalloyed: some troubling matter intervened, changing our plan and indicating that danger threatened our house. Since delay was drawing danger toward us and the event itself commanded haste, relying on God’s help and trusting in the support of the brothers, trembling, insofar as the slenderness of our courage allowed, I opposed myself with all my strength; and thus, while Phinehas struck, the shaking ceased. Therefore [Col. 0490B] we implore your fatherhood not to take it hard, but patiently to bear the fact that we could not come on the appointed day. For so great an occasion of necessity deserves pardon without asking for it.

You should know of us that we stand ready for whatever we have learned to be necessary to your advantage and fitting to your honor; whenever it is useful to you, the performance of the deed will prove this. Farewell in peace.

## LETTER CCXIV. TO WILLIAM, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS.

He explains certain forgers who were counterfeiting bulls.

To your counsel, Father, we have recourse in doubts; to your help, in adversity. In the first case we ask for the third, in the second for the fourth, Spirit of the sacred sevenfold gift. [Note: [Col. 0490D] He means the seven gifts of the Spirit, concerning which Isaiah, chapter 2, says: “The spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, the spirit of the fear of the Lord.” Thus in doubts he asks for the third gift, counsel; in adversities, the fourth, fortitude.] [Col. 0490C]

At your command, we induced certain forgers, by caution and skill rather than power, to confess. We promised impunity, so far as it lies within our power, to one of them, who restored to us in chapter the upper and lower die [Note: [Col. 0490D] This is the same as what he later calls counterfeit anvils; they are implements for making coins or seals.] of a forged bull. Under a fearful adjuration and oath, he confessed that he had never used it, but that he had been the associate of a certain priest who sold false letters and that he sometimes received a share of the ill-fated price. He also returned to us a notebook containing several letters issued in the apostolic name. That priest holds a benefice from the chapter attached to the service of the high altar. Who and what sort of man he is, and how he may seek to excuse himself, the bearer of this letter can tell you. We keep for you the counterfeit dies, whose frauds [Col. 0491A] may be condemned by your authority’s judgment and restrained by the hammer.

## LETTER CCXV. TO THE ABBOT OF LAUDE.

[Note: [Col. 0491D] The Abbey of Laude of Blessed Mary is situated one mile from the city of Lille, in the diocese of Tournai, and belongs to the Cistercian order. It was founded in 1146 by Count Thierry of Flanders and his wife Sibyl of Anjou. The abbot to whom he writes was named Simon, the third abbot of this monastery. He journeyed to Palestine with Count Philip of Flanders and died about 1200. Here is the inscription on his tomb:

> I am Abbot Simon, who, eagerly desiring to behold Zion,  
> Served Count Philip the Black at Jerusalem,  
> And presided for twenty-one years as shepherd.

] He asks him to show kindness toward a certain brother William who had sinned.

Paternal severity deserves commendation when it is tempered by maternal affection and, after blows, offers breasts; when angry, it remembers mercy. A play is no less useful than honorable for the soul, when in the theatre of virtues, before the spectatorship of angels, reason, standing between the soul’s two powers—desire and anger—guides them in such a straight course that anger neither boils beyond measure nor desire wanders too far from compassion.

Considering this, we ask your holy religiousness to open the bosom of paternal gentleness [Col. 0491B] to Brother William, whom we believe useful to you and your Church. And if you strike with the rod, do not extinguish the spirit of gentleness. He is ready to cease from superfluous things, avoid what is forbidden, pursue what has been promised, and obey you as a father—provided only that he may be permitted to remain with you and die with you in your sacred community. Receive our prayers, that we may not suffer refusal in this small request, we who are always ready both to offer you service and to show you reverence.

## LETTER CCXVI. TO THE BISHOP OF LISIEUX.

[Note: [Col. 0491D] Jordan du Hommel was installed as bishop of Lisieux in 1197, as the Norman Chronicle records. He completed the building of his cathedral church and enriched it with wealth and estates. Then, proceeding on the Jerusalem expedition, he was made bishop of Heliopolis in Syria and died there in 1214. The anniversary of his death is celebrated yearly at St. Victor’s, Paris, on 19 Kalends of February; in the necrology of that house he is called “our brother,” from which it may be inferred that he was a regular canon.] He exhorts his friend to care for his own salvation and that of his subjects.

In your transfer from Lisieux to the city of Heliopolis, [Col. 0491C] I do not know whether I should rejoice or grieve. If you attend to the beginnings of the names, you have been transferred from the Cyprian planet [Note: [Col. 0492D] That is, Venus, so called by the ancients because she was especially worshipped on that island.] to the sun, from darkness to light, from slippery movements to the solidity of splendor. This change would please me if our separation from one another did not cause harm.

I ask only this: in your passage, take care not to begin, as you once jokingly told me of certain inhabitants of those regions, to make mistakes in calculation and wish to celebrate Pentecost around Easter. I believe that if you should ever fall into that error, you have become a companion of those to whom the Apostle says, “But you have been washed; but you have been sanctified” (1 Cor. 6). For what else should be expected of an archdeacon except that he should be concerned first for his own salvation, [Col. 0491D] and secondly for that of his subjects?

Amid the cares of court and the companions’ playful conversations after work, [Col. 0492A] I want you to stand so much in the middle that neither the former oppress you with their heavy burden nor the latter dissolve you in soft leisure. You who were lovable to scholars, be admirable to courtiers. Let us not derive *curiales* (“courtiers”) from *cruor* (“blood”), but from *curia* (“court”), where trifles are sometimes treated as serious matters and serious matters as trifles, where scarcely anyone wishes to have an equal and no one ever a superior.

[Remember the distich which, in a spirit more poetic than prophetic, yet truthful, was spoken to you by someone at your departure from Bologna:

> You deal with the causes of bishops and the affairs of kings,  
> Which win for you wealth and delights.]

Greet for me your bishop, legate, and chancellor; and frequently remind him that, amid this threefold promotion, he should recognize himself as a servant of the Trinity and learn so to preside [Col. 0492B] over men that he confesses himself subject to his Creator. Love him, because he loves you, although both the cheerfulness of his reputation proclaims and the loftiness of his life commends him as one to be loved for his own sake.

## LETTER CCXVII. TO THE ABBOT AND CHAPTER OF CÎTEAUX.

He discusses a certain cleric, whom he clears of the usurious loan.

In matters that are honestly requested and shamefully withheld, the petitioner’s purpose ought to be helped. Having therefore examined and learned the origin of the contract concluded between the Church of Clairmarais [Note: [Col. 0492D] Clairmarais, commonly Clermarez, is a Cistercian abbey in Artois, founded in honor of Blessed Mary by Count Thierry of Flanders, at St. Bernard’s urging, in 1140. He writes to the abbot and chapter of Cîteaux, who refused to ratify a certain contract which they considered usurious; and he maintains that no agreement of illicit interest was involved.] and G., our cleric of Lille, it does not appear to us to incur the crime of usury, since even between churches and honorable [Col. 0492C] persons, as we have often seen, it was not usurious. It resembles purchase and sale more closely, as when one buys the casting of a net, than the contagion of moneylending profit, which we detest together with you. Therefore we ask your holy fatherhood to provide in this matter for our cleric’s indemnity and to spare the good name of men of so sacred a community, lest in this act they may be accused more of greed than praised for charity.

## LETTER CCXVIII. TO ODO, BISHOP OF PARIS.

For Th., archdeacon of Tournai.

The nobility of your lineage, the uprightness of your life, and the authority of your dignity give us confidence to appeal to your goodwill. These three win for you human favor [Col. 0492D] and God’s grace. [Col. 0493A] Moved by these three, we both ask from you what befits you and seek what benefits us.

Th., archdeacon of Tournai, our familiar and friend—a man of good natural disposition at present and of great hope for the future, who by his honorable conduct gives us signs of his promise—became, through generous sociability both kindly and beneficent, surety for a certain companion of his to one of your parishioners, Renaud the money-changer, for ten Parisian pounds and additional civil increments, which those equally ignorant of law and expert in usury call interest. He paid the principal and its additions, up to fifteen pounds. The aforesaid creditor accepted payment and released the archdeacon from his suretyship, promising to return immediately his books, which had been pledged for the said debt. He delayed returning them; and, speaking in his heart and heart, he strives to turn “delay” into “take away.”

We ask your fatherhood to restrain and correct by your authority such outrageous dishonesty in an exacter. Cause the archdeacon’s books to be restored to him, as befits you, lest he be compelled to pay what he did not seize; for he has suitable and sufficient witnesses both to the creditor’s acknowledgment of payment and to the release pronounced by the same creditor. Once the books have been restored, the archdeacon is ready, in your presence, either personally or through a sufficient procurator, to submit to the law and answer the unscrupulous creditor as the law may direct.

## LETTER CCXIX. TO EVRARD, ABBOT, AND THE CONVENT OF ST. BAVO.

[Note: [Col. 0493D] The Church of St. Bavo is located at Ghent, then in the diocese of Tournai. Formerly it was a distinguished Benedictine abbey, founded about 640 and restored by Lothair in 950; finally it was made a cathedral in 1537, through the efforts of Emperor Charles V with Pope Paul III.] He commends a certain craftsman whose son was seeking the monastic habit.

A petition is favorably received when the petitioner’s merit and the justice of the petition concur to advance it. Considering these matters in the bearer of this letter, our friend and familiar G.—whose merits, on account of the integrity and gentleness in which he excels, flourish not only with us but also in public places and churches through magnificent works and notable craftsmanship, leaving an enduring remembrance of himself—we have warmly received the support of the desire which he himself has laid before us, so that we may earnestly wish together with him that it be brought to effect.

Following the patriarch’s example, he wishes to offer his son upon one of the mountains which the Lord showed him—namely, your Church, [Col. 0493D] holy, harmonious in wills and spirits, and rich in an abundance of holy graces; truly a compacted and fat mountain—as a sacrifice, that his merit may be increased through this change from so great an exemplar and that your whole community may gather the fruit of a holocaust in the daily service both of himself and of the aforesaid son. We have heard and found him quite suited both by the knowledge of letters appropriate to his age and by his aptitude for reading and singing, and disposed toward divine offices and monastic disciplines. [Col. 0494A]

We earnestly ask your holiness, for the love of God, in consideration of us, and for the affection and devotion which the aforesaid Master G. bears toward you, to receive his aforesaid son into your fellowship, so that both we and he, with our prayers granted and his vow fulfilled, may rise together in thanksgiving.

## LETTER CCXX. TO PETER, BISHOP OF ORLÉANS.

He complains of the monks of St. Bertin, who had chosen him as arbitrator.

The dishonesty of certain monks troubles us. Though what is theirs ought continually to suffice them, they irreverently wish to invade what belongs to others. These are the abbot and monks of St. Bertin, who claim that they redeemed for themselves, notwithstanding our opposition and that of our Church, one church belonging to our table, [Col. 0494B] held and oppressed for a long time in the captivity of lay servitude, without our or our Church’s consent; and they chatter that it is theirs by their own authority.

When we raised a dispute against them on these matters, we submitted the case to arbitrators, imposing a penalty of one hundred marks if either party should withdraw from what was accepted. They got ahead of us by quickly choosing your person as arbitrator; we too had wished first to name you, trusting in your prudence. On the appointed day and at the appointed place we met at Douai, bringing with us the dean of Cambrai in place of our arbitrator. We regretted your absence, hoping in the Lord that, had you been present, we would either have obtained our right [Col. 0494C] or reached a settlement and peace with our adversaries.

And because the case has been postponed until the Friday after Ash Wednesday, we ask you as father, lord, and friend, with all the affection and effort we can, that for the love of God and the restoration of peace between the churches, you grant us your welcome presence at Douai on that day. For if you are present, we trust in the Lord that our case will be settled by your authority.

## LETTER CCXXI. TO ARNULF, DEAN OF BRUGES.

He asks him to arrange for herrings to be prepared.

We are importunate in asking, but we do not wish to be unbearable in demanding. We are sending you a conveyance, [Col. 0494D] which perhaps we call a *quarrum*, with the *d* changed to an *r*, because of the number of its four wheels.

[Note: [Col. 0494D] Or rather *currum*, a carriage which in French we call *char* or *chariot*, borne on four wheels.]

We did not wish to send a two-horse carriage or two-wheeled cart, because perhaps it would either not suffice for the load or, turning aside on one side in muddy slopes, would overturn itself together with its burden. For as to what we said to you jokingly about a *triga*, know that, just as we abominate a *triga* in a vehicle, so too we detest it in deed and word.

[Note: [Col. 0494D] He plays on the equivocal sense of this word, which in old French means “cheat” (*tricheur*) and also a carriage drawn by three horses.]

We wish, moreover, that through the bearers of this letter you send us our cheeses, or the larger part of them in number and quality, [Col. 0495A] and what Abbot Emmanuel of Etot owes us in provisions.

[Note: [Col. 0495D] Or perhaps better, Eton, a monastery situated in the Black Forest, not far from the Rhine; founded around the year 700 by the monk Wiger, later bishop of Strasbourg, and renewed by Count Etho of Habsburg, from whom it took its name.]

Meanwhile, see that herrings, whether given freely or bought, are carefully prepared and dried for us, so that during the time of fasting they do not take away from the hungry their desire to eat, or give the thirsty an incentive to drink.

328. LETTER CCXXII. TO THE SAME PERSON. He asks him to send fish and certain ecclesiastical services.

As we recently instructed you: if we are importunate in asking, we shall not be unbearable in demanding. We shall settle accounts with you fairly, so that you incur neither loss nor the forfeiture of our favour. The lean days are near: the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, the Friday of the Protomartyr, and the Saturday of John [Col. 0495B] the fisherman. Since on these days the earth will deny us the beasts of the field and the air the birds of heaven, we are compelled to eat fish of the sea. Therefore we ask your customary goodwill: buy fish for us from your own resources, and hire a packhorse for me on the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord,

[Note: [Col. 0495D] A packhorse, or sumpter horse, is so called because it carries a *sagma*. According to Casaubon, a *sagma* is that which is put upon a beast of burden so that it may carry more softly and without injury to itself. Others understand *sagma* as any burden whatsoever; hence they hold that horses are called *sagmarii* because they carry burdens—French, *cheval de somme*.]

so that we may make supper serve as dinner; and on the feast of blessed Stephen and blessed John, from the remains—let us not say twelve baskets—we may at least fill twelve dishes. Make haste; do not delay, so that our messenger may return quickly and Christmas may make for us a festive, not a hostile, supper.

329. LETTER CCXXIII. TO HUGH, ABBOT OF SAINT-DENIS. He asks him not to delay payment of his brother’s pension.

[Col. 0495C]

He who promises is kindly disposed; he who gives is beneficent. But if the giver’s cheerfulness accompanies both, the recipient ought to pour out his whole self in the fullest thanksgiving. We ask that you pay without delay to our brother the annual pension which you promised him, lest, should he be put to trouble in going and returning, he be compelled either, as it were, to run into uncertainty or to beat the air.

330. LETTER CCXXIV. How Lord Stephen, bishop of Tournai, having taken with him the abbots of Saint-Amand and Saint-Calixtus, in the presence of Lord Peter, bishop of Arras, came to the church of Saint Martin of Tournai in order to reform for the better the peace and condition of that monastery, and to rebuke and correct its abbot concerning his transgressions. Also, how the same abbot swore that he would observe the matters proposed to him by the bishop.

[Col. 0495D]

STEPHEN, by God’s permission humble minister of the Church of Tournai, [Col. 0496A] to all who profess the monastic life: greeting in the Lord.

Since, by the office imposed upon us, we are bound to give paternal care to the churches entrusted to us, to raise up what has fallen and restore what is exhausted, we must give especial provision to those in which the monastic order, or that of clerics called regular,

[Note: [Col. 0495D] Regular canons have borne various names. [Col. 0496D] At one time they were called canons living canonically, at another clerics living according to rule, and also regular clerics, as in this passage and in canon 10 of the Council of Poitiers in 1109.]

instituted by the holy Fathers, ought to be observed without the stain of filth or the wrinkle of pretence. And because it is written, “to neglect, when you can correct, the perverse is nothing other than to encourage them”; nor is one free of the scruple of another’s complicity who ceases to oppose a manifest crime.

Having heard again and again that certain things, remarkable and shameful if true, were said to be done in the monastery of Saint Martin, we took pains to break through another’s wall and see, and more fully understand, whatever abominations might be within, lest the blood of those who perish be required at our hand—we who [Col. 0496B] have been appointed watchmen in the house of Israel. When, therefore, concerning the disgraceful things said to be done by the clerics, contrary to decency, we wished to correct our brother John, abbot of the aforesaid monastery, and to restore both him and the church entrusted to him to a better condition, we endeavoured according to the evangelical precept first to rebuke him alone, privately between ourselves and him; then with two brothers present, the prior and another. Finally, rather than, after not merely a third, fourth, or fifth admonition, waste in vain the effort of counsel offered and assistance promised, while the scandal increased and was publicly spread among the people—as though we were about to tell it to the Church, and lest, God forbid, [Col. 0496C] that church become, in head and members alike, as a heathen and a publican—we came to the place, taking with us the venerable abbots of Saint-Amand and Cisoing.

[Note: [Col. 0496D] Cisoing is an abbey in the diocese of Tournai, about two leagues from the city of Lille, under the order of canons living according to rule. It was founded about the year 838 by Count Everard, lord of that domain and duke of Friuli, who had married Gisela, sister of Louis the Pious. He caused that church to be consecrated under the title of Saint Calixtus, because the relics of that holy pontiff had been deposited there, where they are still preserved.]

When we carefully investigated the condition of that church, we found at first sight that the monastery was burdened with debt and that the debt had grown beyond measure. Nor was there any evident reason why so great a sum should have been incurred, since its possessions are extensive and its revenues abundant; and during the time of this abbot, who had presided for three years, nothing had been bought, built, or renewed, nor had the number of brethren increased, or anything else occurred that might at least excuse the debt. As for the ill repute under which the abbot’s [Col. 0496D] person laboured, and certain of the younger brethren, whom, like the sons of Eli, he did not know how or did not wish to correct in their insolence—or, most miserable to say, did not dare to correct—we understood that it could neither be diminished nor erased [Col. 0497A] except by the burning of a cautery and the cutting of iron.

Therefore, by the counsel of the venerable men who were present with us, we suspended the aforesaid abbot from the administration of his abbacy, by the authority of the archbishop of Reims and our own—not out of hatred for his person, nor placing hope in corrupt money, as God knows, but under the compelling zeal of God’s house. A few days later, when he came to us with his prior and certain of his monks, humbly seeking mercy and promising amendment, at the earnest prayers of the lord bishop of Arras, who was present, and of our whole chapter, we absolved him and restored him to his former rank. But we first received from him an oath to abide by our command, which, by the counsel of the aforesaid lord of Arras and [Col. 0497B] our chapter, we framed as follows:

> “I, John, abbot of Saint Martin of Tournai, promise that I shall observe in all things the matters which the lord of Arras has here proposed to me. So help me God and the holy Gospels of God.”

The abbot therefore promised, under the oath he had taken, that he would preserve bodily chastity perpetually, according to the grace granted him by God; attend the canonical hours; sit in the cloister with the others, whenever he could, more frequently than was customary; take food in common in the refectory; and be bound by the same promise to lie in the dormitory. Outside the refectory—that is, in chambers or infirmaries—without a most evident reason, he himself shall neither eat nor give others permission to eat, unless [Col. 0497C] perhaps on account of certain persons deserving reverence, to whom he may offer the offices of humanity and hospitality. Likewise, if he returns so late from the Church’s business that he cannot suitably eat in the refectory, whether because of winter’s severity or an inundation of rain, he may take refreshment in his chamber devoutly and quietly, especially after Compline. Neither there nor elsewhere, at that hour or any other, shall he permit gatherings to take place which furnish matter for murmuring to those who serve in the divine offices and to others who bear the burden and heat of the day in the observances of monastic discipline.

If the Church’s external affairs draw him away, and he cannot be absent from them without loss to its household resources, he shall take with him monks of the more mature and discreet sort, and shall keep with him companions and servants whose association does not bring him into disrepute. He shall not allow any monk whatsoever to leave the gate without a horse, except only those who are customarily and properly sent into the city on the Church’s business, whether to us, our chapter, or secular justice. He must keep with him four or six monks, whom the bishop shall name to him from among the more mature and honourable, by whose counsel he may order and administer both the Church’s outward and inward affairs. He shall not permit younger monks to go out, without the testimony and company of more mature men, either to secular spectacles, fairs, or any festivals which they customarily leave for on grounds of necessity. [Col. 0498A] If he does not observe all these things which he has confirmed by his oath, let him know that he is both guilty of disobedience and a transgressor of the oath he has made.

333. LETTER CCXXV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS.

[Note: [Col. 0497D] This letter, it seems to me, was written to William, archbishop of Reims. I infer this from his saying that he had sent him certain forged letters fabricated at Tournai, of which there is discussion above [Col. 0498D].]

He complains of the improper administration of the same abbot.

For a long time languishing in a state midway, if there is anything between, the dying and the dead, the Church of Saint Martin of Tournai has recourse to your bosom as the one refuge of the poor, that in its desolation you may open to it your fatherly heart and offer it motherly breasts. Long weeping, it has wept in death, and still its tears are upon its cheeks [Col. 0498B] (Lamentations 1). Its head is sick and its heart sorrowful; from the sole of the foot to the crown there is no soundness in it (Isaiah 2). That monastery outwardly overflows with disgrace and inwardly is empty of discipline. He who presides fears his subjects more than he is feared by them. He both indulges them in idle leisure and corrupts them by a pernicious example. In him there is nothing firm in virtue, nothing conspicuous in honour, nothing of him safe below the groin. I have rebuked him repeatedly and have not corrected him, for his wound is incurable. He swore in my hand to obey the command of the lord of Arras and our own. The lord of Arras set out the command; he neither obeyed nor kept faith, and the last state of that man has become worse than the first (Matthew 12). By forged letters fabricated at Tournai, copies of which we sent you, through the agency of the abbot of Anchin, [Col. 0498C] he procured his absolution, although an elementary schoolboy could have understood the falsity of those letters. Fearing for himself because of a certain young monk of disgraceful reputation whom he had made provost of the monastery, he appealed; and under cover of this appeal he wastes and overturns everything. Let the tearful sighs of a monastery so grievously enslaved move you, Father; and free the flock of poor monks from that aforesaid monster.

LETTER CCXXVI. He complains again concerning the same abbot.

We speak seriously—we who are accustomed sometimes to speak with you playfully. The Church of Saint Martin of Tournai outwardly overflows with disgrace and inwardly lacks [Col. 0498D] discipline. It is oppressed by debts and crushed by offences. The abbot lives more secularly than can be believed: he lays waste everything, dissipates everything, fears his subjects, and is not feared by them. I have often rebuked him and have not corrected him, for his wound is incurable. Fearing removal, he stirs up disturbance with certain younger brethren. The older and sounder brethren oppose his deeds. Appeals have been made on both sides, and he has involved me in his appeal, as though intending to drag me before the court. I ask you as one most dear: for the love of God and zeal for [Col. 0499A] justice, write together with us on behalf of the monks against a monster redeemed by no virtue, in whom there is nothing firm, nothing ordered, and, as is said, nothing of him safe below the groin.

LETTER CCXXVII. TO LOUIS, SON OF KING PHILIP AUGUSTUS. He urges him above all to apply himself earnestly to study, and promises to send the horse he requested.

To his illustrious and most dear lord, and, if we dare say it, his godson,

[Note: [Col. 0499D] He writes this letter to Louis, son of King Philip Augustus, who succeeded him in the kingdom as Louis VIII, father of Saint Louis. According to William the Breton, he was born in 1187; at that year William writes: “On the Nones of September, Monday, in the eleventh hour of the day, Louis, son of Philip the Magnanimous and his most chaste wife Elizabeth, was born.” Stephen, then abbot of Saint-Geneviève, received him from the sacred font, as this letter shows.]

LOUIS, firstborn of the lord king, STEPHEN, his own, by divine permission humble minister of the Church of Tournai: greeting, and increase of wisdom, age, and grace before God and men.

We received your letter gladly and joyfully, by which you informed us of your wish that a suitable and handsome palfrey be sent to you. What you requested pleases [Col. 0499B] us; and, God willing, we shall soon send you through your own messenger one which ought to please you and which, in present circumstances, may be judged worthy of so great a rider. The Lord has crushed Satan under your feet,

[Note: [Col. 0499D] That is, King John of England, or Philip, count of Flanders. For Rigord writes: “In the year 1200, in May, at Ascension, peace was renewed between Philip, king of the Franks, and John, king of England, between Vernon and the island of Andely. On the following Monday Louis married Blanche, daughter of Alfonso, king of Castile, and niece of John, king of England.” [Col. 0500D]]

by which name we understand the enemies of our lord king and of yourself. My most dear lord, we ask, exhort, and counsel you, in the fidelity which we owe you, that above all things, after love of God and of the lord king your father, you devote yourself to learning letters, because they will be useful and necessary to you and to your kingdom in the counsels of the palace, the affairs of the realm, the concord of peace, and victory in war.

LETTER CCXXVIII. TO LAMBINUS, APPARENTLY BISHOP OF THÉROUANNE. Concerning a certain Hugh who was reported to have risen from the dead.
