[Note: [Col. 0500D] Rigord appears to speak of him under the year 1198 in these words: “In Vermandois a certain knight who had died came back to life.” And William the Breton says under the year 1197: “In those days a certain knight died and came back to life in the territory of Vermandois; and enjoying life for many days, neither eating nor drinking, he foretold many things, though incredible ones.” John of Saint-Victor also mentions him in the *Memorial of Histories*.]

[Col. 0499C]

A sheep came to a she-goat and asked to borrow wool. The goat was alarmed, replying that the mother of the wool-bearing flock abounded in shaggy fleeces. The fable is plain to the bleary-eyed and to barbers; under its cover we may either suspend or defer our inadequacy in responding to your consultations. Since, God willing, we hope soon to see your desired face at the conference to which our lord of Reims has invited both you and us at Saint-Quentin, let us, if it please you, meanwhile defer questions and reciprocal answers. The matter about which you asked is intricate and needs fuller exposition. [Col. 0499D]

But, to close in a serious vein: neither questions are to be raised, [Col. 0500A] nor any business transacted, nor buildings constructed, nor churches divided, until the month of August, when all things shall be completed and consumed, according to the prophecy reportedly uttered among you by a certain Hugh, said to have risen from the dead, as the bearer of your letter announced to us in a marvellous and terrifying manner.

337. LETTER CCXXIX. TO A CERTAIN PRELATE OF THE ROMAN CHURCH. He petitions for the renewal of a privilege.

A friend is a precious thing, since among a thousand scarcely one—and scarcely half of one—is found. I confidently confess that I am such to you, if we use “friend” in the sense in which one is called such because he loves. Nor do I either doubt or distrust your reciprocal friendship: I embrace it with all [Col. 0500B] my arms, kiss it with all my lips, grasp it with all my inmost being. Meanwhile, devoted to your service, I shall always be ready to obey your commands and willingly to will them. Meanwhile, I urgently beg that you have our privilege renewed for us, if it please you, through yourself or through the same Subdeacon B., who has its transcript sealed with the seal of the lord of Reims.

[Note: [Col. 0500D] The Church of Saint-Geneviève of Paris, of which Stephen had been abbot, enjoyed very extensive privileges, both regarding immunity of temporal goods and spiritual matters. Whenever a new supreme pontiff was elected, its abbots took care to have these privileges renewed and confirmed by him, as is shown here.]

338. LETTER CCXXX. TO A CERTAIN FRIEND. He sends small gifts which he explains morally.

Small gifts exchanged among friends do not create friendship; they foster and preserve friendship once created. As friendship is conceived in a well-disposed mind, so it is strengthened by a beneficent hand. [Col. 0500C] We send small gifts

[Note: [Col. 0500D] He sent his friend a bridle and breastplate to adorn a horse, as well as stirrups for riding, which he explains no less elegantly than morally. [Col. 0501D]]

which are fitting to behold, useful to employ, and instructive to understand. By the bridle we wish your holiness to be restrained, whether in ordering your affairs among others or in receiving deposits from others. By the breastplate we remind you to be steadfast in adversity and prudent in prosperity; for both courage and prudence are customarily assigned to the breast. The stirrups on which the feet rest remind you to stand firm in what you owe a subordinate and in what you owe a superior. If you fail in either respect, you will quickly fall; if in neither, you will stand firm. This is the form of justice: to render to each what is his own. If you carefully consider this greeting, the four principal virtues meet you: courage and prudence are signified in the breastplate, temperance in the bridle, [Col. 0500D] justice in the stirrups. Read and [Col. 0501A] understand: for to read and not understand is to neglect.

339. LETTER CCXXXI. TO THE LORD OF REIMS.

[Note: [Col. 0501D] In the first part of this letter he complains about the commune of the citizens of Tournai, with whom the bishop and canons of Tournai were in dispute, because they had refused to submit to the judgment of the king and the archbishop of Reims or to accept the arbitrators upon whom they had agreed.]

He deals with the interdict imposed in the land of the count of Flanders.

Clerics living among laymen are brothers of dragons and companions of ostriches. And if those who ought to serve are permitted by some secular jurisdiction to rage against churches, then under the name of a commune scale is joined to scale among them, so that no breath passes between them. Whirling in this madness against us, our citizens, having first despised the command of the lord king in our disputes and theirs before the lord of Arras and the castellan of Lille,

[Note: [Col. 0501D] This man was called John; when Count Baldwin of Flanders departed for Palestine, he appointed him the most faithful adviser of his wife Mary. He was a highly judicious man, for through his efforts peace was concluded between the count and the king in 1200, according to Buzelin.]

and having later returned to you and accepted common arbitrators under the form laid down by you, were unwilling [Col. 0501B] either to acquiesce in your counsel or to bind themselves to arbitration. Therefore our canons, your clerics, have recourse to you as to the counsel of the whole Church; and we, with them and for them, cast ourselves at your feet, that in so perilous a matter you may, as you have always been accustomed, provide both kindly counsel and beneficial assistance.

Furthermore, concerning what we can and ought not to say without groaning and sighing—the new command of the lord cardinal and legate Master Melior

[Note: [Col. 0501D] Rigord writes concerning his legation: [Col. 0502D] “Pope Celestine sent his legates into France concerning the complaint of the Danes: namely Melior, cardinal priest, and Censius, subdeacon. Coming to Paris, they summoned a council of all the archbishops, bishops, and also abbots of the whole kingdom, in which they discussed the restoration of the marriage between King Philip and his wife Ingeborg.”]

to place the land of the count of Flanders under interdict

[Note: [Col. 0502D] The cause of this interdict was the violation of faith owed to the king of France by Baldwin, count of Flanders, who had deserted the king’s party in order to assist Richard, king of England. Hence he entered by force of arms into the territories of Tournai, Arras, and Cambrai and devastated everything. From the continuation of the Anchin chronicle.]

—we seek your counsel. And the whole Church of Flanders, with unutterable groans, casts all its thought upon you, that you may not permit those whom you have hitherto [Col. 0501C] nourished to be exposed to such dangers. The wounds of the earlier interdict still breathe fresh, and the wounded do not recover. If a second blow is added, death will be at the gates, and under sad silence the heresies which had begun to sprout will gain strength. Churches will be closed; divine chants will fall silent; those accustomed to eat the bread of offering at the Lord’s table will be compelled to beg. We know that the wicked heart of that man is so hardened that he despises excommunication, does not fear interdict, and prefers temporal things to spiritual. It seems to us, and to many prudent men, that he would be wounded more deeply and put to more open shame if he and all who communicate with him were excommunicated every Sunday, and if the places to which he came [Col. 0501D] ceased from divine worship as long as he remained there.

While these matters were being discussed in our chapter, in the presence of envoys [Col. 0502A] of the lord of Oxford, who had come to us for this reason, Bernard of Robais, bailiff of all Flanders, in order that an interdict might not be imposed upon the count’s land, prohibited it by appeal to the lord pope, setting the octave of Saint John the Baptist as the date for pursuing the appeal. Concerning all these things, Father, provide counsel through your counsellors, for your clerics and your churches.

341. LETTER CCXXXII. It treats of the same interdict.

We wish to be disciples of that charity which burns with those who are scandalized and is weak with those who are weak. In its fire we burn with you; we are weakened by compassion; we run at its spur; we pant with concern. Our conscience is witness, and God, the searcher of reins and hearts, is witness, that in your adversity [Col. 0502B] we are ready both to gird ourselves with you for vengeance and to be strengthened for perseverance. At the arrival of F., canon of Reims, after inspecting the letters which he brought with him, we held and still hold the count of Hainaut and his son Baldwin excommunicated. Desiring heavenly aid and fraternal counsel concerning the pronouncement of an interdict upon his land, we wrote through the aforesaid Canon F. to the lord of Thérouanne, asking that he either reply or confer with us shortly in a manner worthy of your profession and advantageous to your interest.

While this expectation of ours was pending, we saw your messenger, without letters from the lord of Thérouanne transmitted to you containing any sentence, whether of excommunication or interdict, urging and advising us to pronounce a sentence of interdict in the count’s [Col. 0502C] land. Since on the following day we were ready to go to the lord archbishop of Reims, in whose arrival we ought to rejoice and be strengthened, we deferred what remained of the sentence until his divine response, [342] considering that no great harm lay in a delay of a short time. May your most gracious affection pardon us this delay, since we are prepared to clear ourselves of it by the severity of the sentence, the integrity of compassion, and perseverance in truth.

LETTER CCXXXIII. TO WILLIAM, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS. He writes concerning the same interdict and implores his assistance.

Lord, who gave me bread to eat [Col. 0502D] and clothing with which I am covered, rescue me from the hand of our prince,

[Note: [Col. 0502D] Namely, the count of Flanders.]

for I greatly fear him. He oppresses by power, terrifies by threats, devises assaults through evil angels, and commands the goods of our altars to be seized. For I have always obeyed the lord pope and you: I pronounced against him a sentence of excommunication and upon his land one of interdict. But our abbots, deans, and priests refuse to observe the sentence, saying that they have appealed, although we have informed them that the appeal is invalid. I was ready to leave the city and go into exile, but the prince’s wrath has closed my ways, so that no safe route of departure is open even to anyone acting on my behalf. Counsel me, Father, your creature, for in these days I do not do what I wish, but do what I do not wish.

343. LETTER CCXXXIV. It concerns the fortification of the city of Tournai and the truce or armistice granted.

[Col. 0503B]

To use the words of Vegetius Renatus

[Note: [Col. 0503D] Vegetius Renatus composed an elegant treatise on military matters, divided into four books, which he dedicated to the Emperor Valentinian.]

on military affairs: nothing in all things is so miserable as to be shut in by siege. Considering this, our citizens, caught between the sword hanging over their necks and the inescapable slavery of surrender, were surrounded by hostile forces, while the entire army of Flanders, Hainaut, Holland, Louvain, Hurpia, and other barbarian nations stood over them from every side. The spirit of counsel for escape and the spirit of courage for resistance had failed them. We were like a ship without a helmsman, a people without a leader, a cohort without a soldier: devoid of arms and inexperienced in war. Those outside thirsted for our blood and, like a lion ready for prey, [Col. 0503C] divided among themselves our persons and little possessions; in their camp they exulted as victors rejoicing over captured spoil when they divide the plunder.

We looked for human help, and there was none. It seemed good to our citizens, soon to perish or be taken captive, and to us, who had resolved to live or die with them, that they should obtain a truce or armistice in whatever way they could. At length this was done, not without great labour, not without a great sum of money, and not without our own shame—though we should have wished otherwise. A truce was granted

[Note: [Col. 0503D] Concerning this truce or armistice, the author of the history of Tournai, drawing from the archives of his church, records: “The registers of the chapter of Tournai recount that the count of Flanders and Hainaut, on account of the war between him and King Philip of France, besieged Tournai; but at last the jurors and aldermen, after great difficulty, made an agreement with the count, furnishing him with four thousand marks of Flanders. In the year [Col. 0504D] 1198 he promised to keep a firm truce with them until a peace should follow.”]

upon these terms, for as long as war should last between the count and the king:

[Note: [Col. 0504D] This war between Philip Augustus, king of France, and Baldwin, count of Flanders, was extremely famous among writers of that age; in it the conflict at Bouvines was undertaken. Since at that time the city of Tournai was under the king’s dominion, it was attacked by the count.]

> “Meanwhile our citizens shall not fortify the city beyond its present fortification; they shall not receive [Col. 0503D] any persons who might harm the count; they shall send him, if they can travel safely, the three hundred servants whom they owe to the lord king whenever the king commands.”

Concerning all these matters, give them such counsel as you see fit. In accordance with your command, [344] we have promulgated before the clerics and laypeople of Tournai a sentence of excommunication against the count and his helpers, and against all their land; and we have enjoined its execution and strict observance upon him, by your authority, after summoning our deans into our presence.

LETTER CCXXXV. He laments the miserable effects of the same interdict.

We lay before your sacred ears, not without our sobbing and sighing, the lamentable complaint of our whole diocese, and especially of the churches of Flanders. We throw ourselves at your feet, asking that at this moment of so great a necessity you open to us your kindly heart and extend a beneficent hand. Instruments are hung upon the rocks; the mouths of those who sing to you, [Col. 0504B] our God, are closed. Those who were accustomed to administer the divine sacraments at sacred altars mourn in the streets; and it comes to be, as the people, so the priest. The insolence of the laity insults us. Taking occasion from our silence, armed with wicked threats, they plot in public and private conversations the expulsion of priests, the plundering of goods, and insults to persons. They say that they are paying for what they did not seize, being unjustly punished for another’s sin, and deprived of sacraments which, as Catholics, they are prepared to obey.

Our affliction is close at hand unless your merciful fatherhood swiftly provides a remedy. From the customs and severity of that people, we know for certain that Flemish threats will be followed by blows. [Col. 0504C] They intend, after expelling our priests, to introduce alien, lame sons and priests of Baal wandering from orthodox paths, transferring them into our gentleness with indecent barbarity—changing the place, not their morals. Come to meet this calamity, Father; expose yourself to these dangers; and extinguish with the oil of your mercy the cautery of their sentence, which not only burns but consumes, lest the enemy rejoice over us, lest the uncircumcised and unclean pass through our churches.

LETTER CCXXXVI. Letter of John, bishop of Cambrai, addressed to the lord of Tournai concerning the preceding letters sent by the same bishop of Tournai to the lord of Reims.

[Col. 0504D] “Wonderful has your knowledge become to me, reverend master” [Note: [Col. 0504D] Stephen is distinguished by this title because he was a teacher of canon law and had publicly professed that discipline; indeed, in a diploma of Innocent III he is called a jurist.]; it has been strengthened, and I cannot attain to it. For who has known the mind of the lord of Tournai? That is, with what intention he dissuaded, by his letters, the lord [of Reims] from judging for the needy and [Col. 0505A] the orphan, from justifying the lowly and the poor? Hence, although the wording of the letters sent, in the sense which they convey, displeases those who hear them, yet because of the intention from which they are produced [p. 346], those who know you reverently adore them with me. For since it would be wicked to suspect that a man possessing so great a zeal for God—and according to knowledge—has written anything against justice, I readily persuade myself that the reader’s perception has erred rather than the writer’s judgment.

Since, then, master and lord, your judgments are a great deep, explain this parable to us. Tell us plainly what, in our cause and so far as we are concerned, displeases your fatherhood. For I would find it more bearable for my action to be examined in the fire of your judgment, worthy as it is, and, if my wrongdoing were discovered, to be refuted by a just judgment, than [Col. 0505B] not to obtain justice after judgment has been rendered. Or perhaps, in accordance with the tenor of your letters, you fear that strangers may rise against you, presuming to put a sickle into your harvest.

There are those who say—saving your peace—that you tremble with fear where there was no fear. For it is incredible that fearful men, solicitous for the salvation of their souls, for which they did not hesitate to come as far as us, should bend their knees before Baal. Yet even if matters were otherwise, this fear ought not to fall upon a steadfast man, who has sworn and resolved to keep the judgments of his righteousness. For, to send a syllogism to a master, since those who said, “Let us do evil that good may come,” were deservedly reproved, and since it is more commendable to do [Col. 0505C] good than merely to turn away from evil, let them see how thoroughly entangled they are who turn away from the good and equitable, believing the evil hanging over them to be unavoidable.

But since it is not safe for a disciple to dispute before his master, lest, if he searches into the master’s riches, he be overwhelmed by the glory of the respondent, I have chosen to entreat an elder as a father and, prostrate at his feet, with tears and inexpressible groanings to request that you not allow the fire of your judgment to be extinguished by the oil of sins upon the prince’s head. For the lord of Reims, as you know very well, has added oil to its [p. 347] furnace by his act of confirmation. By his command he comes to cast it into your land; he wishes it to burn, he wishes it to be kindled fiercely, because he hopes in the Lord that the aforesaid fire, if it finds the hearts of the disciples [Col. 0505D] clean receptacles, will not burn but illuminate, not consume but shine.

## LETTER CCXXXVII. Reply of the lord bishop of Tournai to the preceding letter sent to him above by the lord John, bishop of Cambrai.

I received the letter of your prudence—partly sprinkled with salt, partly steeped in suspicious honey—with devout reverence; I read it with exact diligence; in bewildered shame I closed it, put it away, and sealed it. In it and from it, although I have not deserved this, I find that I deserve to experience the third and fourth degrees of retribution.

I wept with those who wept for you; I burned with those who were scandalized; and behold, a scorching wind blowing violently from the desert region burst through your letter into my face, to swallow up the tears of one weeping and dry up the feeling of one who sympathizes. For labor I receive punishment; for the service of diligence, contention; to one thirsting for justice, ingratitude is returned; to one seeking bread, a stone is offered. What more ought I to have done for your affair and for your Church that I did not do? I caused the prince of the land and his son [Note: [Col. 0505D] Namely Baldwin, count of Flanders.]—both I and our Church—to be denounced as excommunicated under a general interdict; [Col. 0506B] I shut their land under a dreadful interdict; I forbade the celebration of divine [p. 348] offices everywhere. In our synod, in the presence of [Master A., your archdeacon], we proclaimed the prohibition of benefices, burials, marriage solemnities, childbirth rites, purification, and every other sacrament, except the baptism of infants, and penance and viaticum for the dying; and we strictly commanded abbots, deans, and priests to observe it and to command others to observe it. If anyone in our parish presumes to act against these things, he will not have me as the author of his contempt and disobedience.

When the count himself—the head and prince of the entire sacrilege committed against you and your Church—came to Tournai on the holy day of the [Lord’s] Supper, [Col. 0506C] I personally declared him excommunicated before all. I subjected to excommunication the burgess who had received him in his house, and forbade all divine offices to be performed for as long as he remained in the city. Thus, on that most holy night, neither was the solemn mandatum celebrated in the evening, nor was the morning synaxis [Note: [Col. 0505D] This term was used among the ancients to signify the divine office, as is frequently read in various lives of saints. For *synaxis* is an ecclesiastical assembly for hearing the word of God, praying, and receiving the sacraments. Epiphanius says that the apostles instituted synaxes, “to perform assemblies” (*synaxeis epiteleisthai*, συνάξεις ἐπιτελεῖσθαι).] celebrated at night, so that the saying, “Zeal for your house,” which was customarily sung aloud, might rightly be fulfilled by our action and fervor.

For all this I receive worthy wages of quarrels: rebukes among the people, indignation and wrath, and assaults by evil messengers. Would that my sins, by which I have deserved the anger of the lord of Cambrai, and his indignation, were weighed in a balance! These would appear heavier than the sand of the sea. Good God! [Col. 0506D] What has subtle ingenuity, lofty intelligence, or faithful interpretation found blameworthy in those simple letters of mine? Is it because I asked the common Father [Note: [Col. 0506D] Namely the archbishop of Reims, whose suffragans were the bishops of Cambrai and Tournai.] on behalf of my sons, that he might heal their sicknesses and stretch out a saving hand to those lying prostrate? I neither dissuaded, nor do I wish, nor have I wished, nor do I wish to have wished, that—as your letter says—the lord of Reims should not judge for the needy and orphan, or should not justify the lowly and poor. Nor do I remember writing anything [Col. 0507A] against justice; rather, while preserving your case, I devoutly and humbly invited the vessel of overflowing mercy to that mercy [p. 349] which exalts itself above judgment.

This is the parable which, under a jocular encomium, you commanded me to explain to you. This is what I speak to you openly and say no proverb. But if you wish to press me more severely, so that, by squeezing too hard, you draw blood, then, without offense to the other, let us descend into the field of the Scriptures and play in the arena of the canons, preserving that knowledge which edifies, not that which puffs up. Although neither am I Jerome nor is the lord of Cambrai Augustine [Note: [Col. 0507C] He alludes to that well-known dispute [Col. 0507D] which once occurred between Saints Augustine and Jerome.], let the younger teach the elder; let the great priest instruct the least of priests. Let one armed with syllogisms not attack an unarmed man with [Col. 0507B] conclusions. For you write that you sent me a syllogism, or rhetorical argument, whose major proposition I do not accept because I do not admit its premise.

Is it doing evil to temper severity, once the case is known, and to allow a dispensation? Rather, is it not evil, for temporal gains, to close churches to the peril of the faithful, to cause the sacraments to cease, divine songs to fall silent, and souls to perish and be destroyed, in order that lost animals may be restored? This is the entanglement of your syllogism: those do evil that good may come who prefer the profit of animals to the loss of souls. Setting aside for a little while custom, which it is not safe to resist, let us meanwhile speak of law and confer about equity.

To be separated from the sacraments of the Church is a spiritual punishment; but no one is to be struck with a spiritual punishment for others; therefore no one is to be separated from the sacraments of the Church because of another’s offense. This is a theological syllogism in logical form, Catholic in right faith, manifest in evident truth. And lest anyone either deceive or be deceived through an equivocation over “spiritual punishment,” by spiritual punishment we do not mean matters of orders or honors, in which one person is sometimes punished for another, but sentences of excommunication, whether major or simple, by which a person is spiritually struck and separated from the fellowship of the faithful.

I have exceeded the manner proper to a letter—but I was [p. 350] provoked, unjustly injured, and compelled to answer. Meanwhile I pray the lord of Cambrai [Col. 0508A] henceforth to spare my modesty and spare his own authority. Even if he does not wish to commend the faithfulness of my service, at least let him not condemn it, lest he break the bruised reed of my littleness and extinguish the smoking flax.

## LETTER CCXXXVIII. TO THE DEAN AND CANONS OF BRUGES

[Note: [Col. 0507D] He explains an edict of the count of Hainaut, by which all his subjects were ordered to pay a double rent this year. Accordingly, his collectors maintained that the double rent was to be paid together with the first and customary rent. Stephen says that this is not the intended meaning, but rather that only a single relief-payment was to be made together with the original rent, which, when added to it, thereby made and was called a double rent.]

He deals with the doubled rent and explains in what sense it should be understood.

We are astonished at your discretion, if some persons wish or are able to ensnare you by their cunning, so as by a perverse interpretation to explain what is contained in the lord count’s letters—namely, the double rent in the payment of reliefs—as though the rent itself [Col. 0508B] which is due were excluded, and twice its amount were paid together with it. That would be to treble, not double, and both the good [p. 351] faith of honorable men and the established custom of the kingdom of France reject this. There, when rent is said to be doubled, the relief-payment is understood to be doubled together with the rent itself. Far be it from your discretion that, because a “double rent” is mentioned, anyone should be able to entangle your straightforward understanding. You may confidently declare that, in a doubled rent, a single relief-payment added to the rent must be understood.

## LETTER CCXXXIX. TO THE LORD ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS. He complains that the king summons him to arms.

That I trouble my lord too frequently [Note: [Col. 0507D] This was William, archbishop of Reims, the king’s uncle, to whom he directs this letter. Stephen had formerly been his clerk and member of his household, as we have often said, and through his influence had been raised to the bishopric of Tournai. It is therefore not surprising that he so often acknowledges himself to be his creature.], [Col. 0508C] on the one hand his kindness draws me, and on the other my necessity compels me. I, untrained in war, am called to wars; unarmed, to arms; so that I who ought to minister in sacred things must serve as a soldier in the camps. The lord king has commanded me: first, to be ready on the vigil of the Ascension; second, on the vigil of Pentecost, with soldiers and arms [Note: [Col. 0507D] Formerly, when the king waged war, not only nobles but also most bishops and abbots were obliged to be present with soldiers. Bishops therefore had *vicedomini*, who took their place in the camps and led their subjects, armed for war. Our Stephen nevertheless asserts that he is exempt from this burden and asks to be released from it through the authority of the archbishop of Reims.], at Mantes [Note: [Col. 0508D] A city in the diocese of Chartres, on the Seine in the Vexin, commonly called Mantes.], though I am without military experience and have never had soldiers.

From the time of King Chilperic, who was the grandfather of the elder Dagobert [Note: [Col. 0508D] This is Chilperic I, who began to reign in Gaul in the year 567. He had a son, Clotaire, father of Dagobert, and was therefore Dagobert’s grandfather. He is called “the elder” in distinction from another Dagobert, who assumed the reins of the kingdom in 715 and was called the younger.], down to these days, the bishops of Tournai held the city of Tournai from the kings of France as though it were their own [Note: [Col. 0508D] The city of Tournai was famous not only among the ancient Gauls, as is evident from the Itinerary of Antoninus, but also at the beginning of the Frankish monarchy. Its fourth king, Childeric, was buried there, and his tomb, with various golden ornaments, was found in 1653, as the book written by Chifflet on this matter, entitled *Anastasis Childerici*, indicates. A reproduction of his ring from the royal Cabinet of Medals, where it is preserved along with the other objects discovered there, may be seen at the end of the work.]. The kings claimed nothing in it for themselves except the bishop’s fidelity and service.

[Col. 0509A] But now the lord king [Note: [Col. 0509B] The city of Tournai was originally under the temporal lordship of the bishop, as we have said. But in 1187 the citizens placed themselves under the dominion of the king of France, as is read in the ancient *Annals of Flanders*, vol. III, ch. 36: “The king of France Philip, on the third day of the Christmas feast in the year 1187, came from the city of Valenciennes, where Count Baldwin of Hainaut received him most honorably in his lodging; on the fourth day he went to the city of Tournai. Never before had it been heard that any of his predecessors [Col. 0509C] had been there; and then the citizens, who had previously served their bishop, submitted themselves to the first king of France and served him at his will in his expeditions.” Mejer says: “The king came to Tournai and, the first of all kings of the Franks, received the people of Tournai into his protection and patronage.”]—may he, by God’s will, live long, happily and [p. 352] victoriously—holds the city in his own hand, taking from it three hundred men-at-arms on every expedition [Note: [Col. 0509C] From these words it is inferred that, once the citizens of Tournai came under the king’s rule, they were required to send three hundred equipped soldiers to his army whenever he waged war.], so that not even the bishop’s name is invoked over it.

Advise me, Father, your creature, for it is difficult to contend against the lord king and impossible to go on campaign. Help one faint-hearted, placed between the upper and lower millstones: one urging him to render an undue military service; the other moving him to offend the prince. I cannot sufficiently render you thanks for what you commanded through your chaplain to the bishop of Arras and to us.

[p. 353]

## LETTER CCXL. He answers an obscure and intricate question proposed to him, explaining several matters relating to law.

[Col. 0509B]

Saving your favor, Father, we say that a clear answer can hardly be given to an obscure question. Had the text of the commission made to you by the lord [Col. 0510A] pope been produced, we should have girded ourselves to answer more confidently, as more fully informed.

By the common civil law [Note: [Col. 0509C] Civil law is called common because it was observed by all nations that had been subject to Roman rule. Canon law too was sometimes called common law and written law.], which we do not believe canon law opposes in this respect: if one who possesses before the joinder of issue [Note: [Col. 0509C] The joinder of issue is completed by three elements: the plaintiff’s claim, the defendant’s contradiction, and the judge’s pronouncement; that is, claim, defense, and the setting down of the issue in law.] becomes contumacious [Note: [Col. 0509C] One contumacious before joinder of issue was guilty of failing to appear on a recognizance; one contumacious after joinder of issue was guilty of abandoning the action or failing to defend. This is called: default for failure to appear; and default for failure to defend.], the plaintiff must be put into possession for the purpose of preserving the thing [Note: [Col. 0509D] A person put into possession by the first decree holds custody of the possession; he does not himself possess it. Under the first decree, the plaintiff was put into possession in order to preserve the thing, so that he might ensure that the true possessor did nothing to its detriment. Cicero says in his first speech for Quintius: “Possess it in such a way that Quintius possesses together with you; possess it in such a way that no violence is done to Quintius.”]. Nevertheless, if the defendant does not appear within a year, then by the second decree [Note: [Col. 0509D] Under the first decree one was merely put into possession; one did not become possessor, as Cujas says in his *Paratitla* on the title *On Things Adjudged*: for not everyone who is in possession is a possessor.] the person who had been put into possession becomes possessor.

But since, in the present affair, we believe that the brother of the lord of Noyon possesses—or, to speak more properly, quasi-possesses [p. 354], since rights are not possessed [Note: [Col. 0509D] Possession is acquired by body and mind; therefore only corporeal things are properly said to be possessed. “For nothing can touch or be touched except body,” as Lucretius says. Rights are incorporeal and are said to be quasi-possessed. See Cujas, *Paratitla*, on the title *On Acquiring and Retaining Possession*.]—there is no person to whom possession can be transferred [Note: [Col. 0510B] In the case of this letter, it must be assumed that the plaintiff was in possession or quasi-possession, because the case concerned some right; he could therefore not be put into the possession in which he already was. Yet it seems somewhat novel that the plaintiff himself should be in possession, since he might have been repelled by the exception, “What you seek, you have within.” It must be assumed, I say, that after the action was brought he obtained possession on his own authority. For there are quite a few cases in law in which an action may be brought by the possessor himself.].

Therefore, since fraud or contumacy ought to benefit no one [Note: [Col. 0510C] In the proposed case, one who neglected to present himself for judgment could not be punished by the penalty usually imposed on contumacious persons—namely, that the plaintiff should be put into possession—because the plaintiff was already in possession.], we think the contumacious party ought to be punished by another penalty, suspension [Note: [Col. 0510C] This was indeed introduced by canon law, but is contrary to our customs. For among us it is scarcely tolerated that a sentence of suspension or excommunication should be pronounced for money, a thing, or a temporal right.] or [Col. 0510B] excommunication—unless perhaps because the lord pope appointed you not as judges but as executors [Note: [Col. 0510C]

For one thing is a judge, appointed to examine and decide a dispute; another is a mere executor, to whom only the execution of a mandate or judgment has been committed.

[Col. 0510D] To me, who was little versed in imperial law and asked what was the sense of this letter, the most illustrious William de Lamoignon, president of the Parliament of Paris, a man richly endowed with every learning and virtue, dictated this immediately, word for word, in his supreme kindness. We rightly mourn him, recently deceased.

From the Fourth Lateran Council under Innocent III, 1215, canon 45: “It sometimes happens that, when possession of a thing is awarded to the plaintiff for its preservation because of the contumacy of the opposing party, the plaintiff cannot obtain the thing to be preserved within a year, or loses it after obtaining it, owing to the power of the thing or to the fraud of the defendant. Thus, according to the assertion of many, the plaintiff does not become true possessor after the year has elapsed, and the defendant profits from his own malice. Therefore, lest the contumacious be in a better condition than the obedient, we decree in canonical equity that, in the aforesaid case, the plaintiff be constituted true possessor after a year has elapsed.”]

The pope’s authority compels you to proceed. For we have not yet read that, before joinder of issue concerning ownership, a definitive judgment ought [Col. 0511A] to be pronounced for contumacy alone. These things we bring forth from our small and narrow purse to those who bring forth new and old things from their treasury—not begrudging, nor prejudging, their answers.

[pp. 355–356]

## LETTER CCXLI. TO MASTER BERTER, ARCHDEACON OF CAMBRAI. He praises a young man whom he commends to him.

You did not hide, keep silent about, or conceal, either timidly or negligently, your genuine intention in our absence. And because no one knows what is in a man except the Spirit that is in him, we were neither able nor inclined to prophesy or divine concerning your intention. Why did you doubt, man of little faith? If you were thinking of bringing him back to us, you ought not to have concealed that or pretended something else.

[Col. 0511B] You had forgotten the rule which says that friends have the same likes and dislikes. I love the young man because he loves letters, and because you love him. Let us too love one another through the moods and tenses of the first conjugation; let us run, diligently serving one another. He is a young man of good reputation and honorable conduct; and, to end serious matters with laughter, he is free from a mark well known to you.

## LETTER CCXLII. TO THE POPE. He asks him not to protect his adversary, who is attacking legal rights.

Since your holy kindness remitted the indignation conceived against me, your servant, and received me into the bosom of your favor, all the darkness of doubt immediately fled away, as though [Col. 0511C] the light of security had been poured in [Note: [Col. 0511D] He took these words from the office recited on the feast of Saint Augustine, which was excerpted from Augustine’s *Confessions*.]. More abundantly than my rivals would have wished has come to me from the sacred oracle of your divine rescript: with fatherly [p. 357] consolation you helped my faint-heartedness and revived me in my tears.

For you wrote to me that in my petitions you would open an easy way for petitioning, and would hear favorably and beneficently one who asks. And because a certain enemy of mine has solicited your holy religious concern, asking you to write to me on his behalf that I should assign him a prebend in our church, I lie suppliant at the feet of your holiness, begging that, if it please you, you do not lead my soul into this snare, nor permit my gray hairs to be brought down to hell in sorrow.

From the beginning of the days [Col. 0511D] of my necessity [Note: [Col. 0511D] Namely, when at the beginning of his episcopal office he withdrew to Maroilles, so that for two years he might leave his revenues to be collected by officials of the Roman curia; see Letter 188.], this man has harmed me as much as he could. By wicked suggestions he hindered, repelled, and turned away my friends who wished freely to help me by lending money in my great distress. His kinsmen, [Col. 0512A] with whom and by whom he was reared in the same house, have inflicted serious losses upon me by plundering my goods; they do not cease to inflict them, and their hand is still stretched out, if they can, toward worse deeds. If I receive him into my Church, I shall have burning coals shut within my bosom, a nail in my eyes, a spear in my side, and a scorpion in my chamber. Deliver me, I beseech you, Father, from his harassment. Spare my old age; spare one who is infirm; spare me from the danger which I fear to be imminent, lest my enemy rejoice over me and, taunting, say: “I have prevailed against him,” and bring my gray hairs in derision to the grave.

[p. 358]

## LETTER CCXLIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS. He implores his help against the citizens of Tournai who are hostile to him.

[Col. 0512B]

This is a day of tribulation and distress. The children have come to the birth, and she who is giving birth has no strength. Long have we been tormented as though unto death; we have fought as though beating the air. Yet when after shipwreck a harbor, after sickness health, and after labor rest were hoped for by us, the children of dissension and pride—our citizens—seek to invalidate what has been established by the authority of the lord king and of yourself concerning the questions at issue between us and them, placing their confidence in the corruption of money rather than in the judgment of justice.

We have written customs, both of the chapter and of the commune of Senlis, sealed with the seal of the bishop and the commune; and the envoys of the aforesaid [Col. 0512C] burgesses similarly brought them with us. Father, we ask that these be confirmed both by the lord king and by you [Note: [Col. 0511D] From these words it is inferred that this letter was written to William, archbishop of Reims, the queen’s uncle and administrator of the realm. It concerns a burden which the citizens of Tournai wished to impose upon both the bishop and the clergy of Tournai.], lest—God forbid—renewed litigation arise in the future, lest a wound so often inflicted rot into a scar, and the scar into pus. Provide, Father, for the liberty of our Church and the peace of your clergy, laboring under the Egyptian yoke; lest Hagar become insolent against her mistress; lest Babylonians lead the ministers of the Church captive; lest laymen oppress priests. We put our trust in your protection alone. You alone, after God, have hitherto set yourself as a wall for our Church; you have aided your sons and resisted our adversaries with a mighty hand and outstretched arm, for there is none to redeem us [Col. 0512D] or save us.

[p. 359]

## LETTER CCXLIV. He deals with the same controversy involving the citizens of Tournai.

[Note: [Col. 0512D] From this letter and those following it, it is inferred that Stephen had a serious controversy, both in his own name and in that of the chapter, with the citizens of Tournai. The king committed its hearing and judgment to the archbishop of Reims and commanded that, after they had taken an oath into the hands of Stephen and the abbot of Cisoing, they should appear before him. They repeatedly refused this, until they had received a surety that they would pay no money for their offense. When the bishop refused to agree to this, they approached the king in order to forestall matters by their tricks and quibbles. But when the bishop perceived that his citizens were not obeying the archbishop of Reims’s command, he punished them as disobedient by ecclesiastical censures [Col. 0513D] and an interdict. At last, coming to their senses, they promised that on the following Wednesday [Col. 0514D] they would take the oath as the king had ordered.]

The hearts of Pharaoh’s citizens have been hardened against us, and in their public and private gatherings they vomit out the words of the salutary admonitions of our Moses, infected with venomous bites. They charge and accuse the king’s letters, which they received concerning the oath to be made to us, of being false, saying that they were neither composed by royal command nor sealed with the royal seal. When asked by me and the abbot of Cisoing to take the oath to abide by your command, they replied that they would never answer without qualification unless this clause were added: that they were not bound to pay any money for their offense. They further added that we should give them such security that, if money were demanded from them, we would pay for their offense—which we did not commit. Meanwhile they sent their messengers to the king, in the hope that they might circumvent the royal dignity [Col. 0513B] either through the corruption of money or through lying falsehood.

Therefore, holy Father, prostrate at your knees, we and the whole Church of Tournai beseech you to seize them in their own cunning, both by your authority and by royal power, restraining their pride and holding back their malice.

[p. 360]

## LETTER CCXLV. He writes about the same matter and dispute.

With the utmost devotion we embrace your commendable solicitude for the Church of Tournai, giving thanks for the past and conceiving the firmest hope for the future. Our burgesses, sons of contradiction and disobedience, rebels against holy Church and contumacious against royal dignity, [Col. 0513C] charge and accuse the lord king’s letters as false, saying that they were neither composed by royal command nor sealed with the royal seal. The oath which they ought to have taken by the king’s will—namely, that they would abide by the command of the lord of Reims—they refuse, reject, and abjure.

Because we love you with fervent affection, we report to you their insolence, pride, and wickedness: in both private and public gatherings they tear apart and condemn your person with shameless barking, in order that they may circumvent royal dignity either through the corruption of money or through lying falsehood. And because it is better to meet a danger in time than to seek redress after the event, we beseech, request, and implore you in the Lord that what you have usefully [Col. 0513D] begun for us you may courageously complete, and that what has been begun with a good beginning may be brought through to a good end.

[p. 361]

## LETTER CCXLVI. He describes the hostile disposition of the citizens of Tournai toward him.

Among the pressures and distresses which the Church of God suffers in her members, the Church of Tournai labors and groans, afflicted, oppressed, bereft of every consolation, a stumbling block to her own and a spectacle to outsiders. From the day of the Lord’s Circumcision she has hung her instruments upon the willows, her songs among unfruitful citizens, and her laments among those inveterately limping in their own paths. Altars are polluted, cemeteries profaned, [Col. 0514A] and the sacraments of the Lord prostituted for tribute.

Amid these sufferings, after our report had been made to the lord of Reims and the king, both their ears rang; and, as the counsels and commands of both concurred, the citizens under interdict were ordered to appear before them in obedience to the command of the lord of Reims, and thus the interdict might be lifted. We labored over this on the preceding Saturday, the following Sunday, and Monday; and, fighting with beasts and beating the air, we accomplished little and achieved nothing. In all these things their anger has not turned away, but their hand is still stretched out. At last, with much difficulty and labor, they promised that they would swear on this coming Wednesday.

These are the circumstances which excuse us before you and our dearest brothers and sons, the canons of Lille, [Col. 0514B] for being unable to attend on the day appointed for us. But, God willing, on whichever day you desire within the octave of Pentecost, we shall be ready to set out, so that we may be able to proceed. If it please you, we ask that you supply for our absence by your presence, and we shall ratify whatever has been decided by you.

[p. 362]

## LETTER CCXLVII. He gives thanks concerning the dean of Tournai, for whom a service had been rendered.

May the necessary cause of our absence excuse us before you, since, God willing, this delay will in time be cleared away. Meanwhile we wish your charity to know that the lord of Reims, in response first to your petitions presented in writing and afterwards made orally, [Col. 0514C] revoked the command by which he seemed to press our dean to receive the rank of priesthood.

We give you full thanks for the gratuitous benefit of your loan; we shall act with still fuller gratitude, since, by God’s grace, should you have need, we are ready—with a cheerful desire to repay—to spare neither our resources nor our efforts for your wish and advantage.

## LETTER CCXLVIII. TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT-AMAND. He reproves him because he had caused monks to be advanced to sacred orders through another bishop.

Your brothers set before us jocular and splendid letters [Col. 0514D] on Sunday, and we received them with them in gladness and exultation. When the meal had been taken and thanks had been rendered, first to God and second to you and your brothers, they reserved for us at our departure scraps, dripping with tears and sprinkled with bitterness. From them we learned that certain of our [p. 363] monks and yours had received sacred orders in another bishopric and not from their own bishop, and that two of them, while we were still dwelling in your house, had celebrated new masses in your monastery—masses bordering upon sacrilege.

We departed grieving and weeping that we had fallen into such a dangerous snare that it is necessary either to lose a friend or our honor. For if [Col. 0515A] we conceal the matter, we are stripped of our honor; if we wish to proceed against, or prosecute, the deed, we shall offend a friend. Yet we are compelled, unwilling though we be, to do one or the other, since we cannot retain both at once. And lest this seem harsh and severe to you, we wish you to know that it is terribly laid down in the sacred canons that an ordination not received from one’s own bishop must be held invalid, and that he who has had a minister of his ordination other than his own bishop must not perform the priestly ministry. Let your discretion consider how this wound of ours may be healed without an unsightly scar.

## LETTER CCXLIX. TO THE BISHOP OF ARRAS. He complains that he conferred sacred orders upon the monks of Saint-Amand without his permission.

[Col. 0515B]

We are astonished that your holy discernment could have been induced recently to promote our monks of Saint-Amand to holy orders without our being asked, informed, or consulted. For we do not believe that you acted through ignorance either of law or of fact, since the mysteries of the sacred canons lie open to you, and you do not in the least doubt that the monastery of Saint-Amand belongs to us. Nor have we previously heard it to be your custom to put your sickle into another’s harvest or to usurp, even in the slightest degree, another’s fraternal rights. You also know how terribly the sacred canons condemn this transgression, declaring [Col. 0515C] that an ordination performed by bishops other than one’s own must be held invalid, and that one who has had another than his own bishop as the minister of his ordination ought not perform the priestly ministry. My lord, what have we done to you, or in what have we troubled you, that we should suffer from you the evils of so great an injury? Let your holy prudence consider how this wound of ours may be healed without an ugly scar. The wrong which we suffered from your abbots has not yet cooled: in our diocese, in the monastery, as we notified you in writing and by word of mouth, they caused a sentence of excommunication to be pronounced arrogantly and unlawfully against the supreme pontiff, against the lord of Reims, and against our own lowliness. Therefore, if it pleased you, they ought to have been sharply corrected and reprimanded by you; and behold, before the first wound is healed, we are struck, pierced through, and wounded by a second dagger.

## LETTER CCL. TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT GENEVIEVE AT PARIS

He instructs him concerning what he ought to do in order to maintain peace.

[Col. 0516A]

Having heard what is being done maliciously and sorrowfully among our brethren, my spirit is distressed within me, and my heart is troubled within me. I grieve that in my last days my grey hairs should be brought down with sorrow to the grave, and that, now near my burial, a spectacle should be enacted not so much funereal as mournful. For what place will there be for joy and gladness where my very heart is wounded by cruel cuts, and my brethren and sons arm themselves with disputes and quarrels; where brotherly unity is torn apart, and ancient peace is dissolved and driven away? Behold, the ashes of fires raging under Abbots O. and [Col. 0516B] A. revive, and grow miserably into devouring flames, in order to root out among us every shoot of virtue.

[Note: [Col. 0515D] That is, Odo and Albert. Odo, once prior of Saint-Victor, became the first abbot of the regular canons of Saint-Genevieve. When, broken by old age, he had resigned the governance of that monastery, Albert was appointed in his place. What dispute arose among the canons of Saint-Genevieve in Odo’s time does not appear; but the cause of the dissension which arose under Albert is read in the *Life of Saint William* in Surius, 6 April—namely, concerning the election of the prior of the same monastery.]

Must my labours then perish—labours illustrious for three five-year periods, useful to the Church, acceptable to men, and, would that they were, pleasing to God?

[Note: [Col. 0515D] From these words it is inferred that our Stephen presided over the abbey of Saint-Genevieve at Paris for about fifteen years, namely from 1176 to 1192 or 1193.]

O blind ambition, where are you rushing? I say this not in insult, but in compassion. O pride, how powerful you are! O envy, why are you mad? You can lay it to the charge of one very dear to you, because you wished to graft the fertile roots of other trees onto the bitter olive-tree that is ours. Can a wild olive, grafted contrary to nature onto an olive-tree, bear good fruit? What have you to do with deserters to the Charterhouse?

[Note: [Col. 0515D] It is recorded in the necrology of Saint-Genevieve that certain regular canons of this house, in pursuit of a more perfect life, entered the Carthusian order; thus, on 13 March: “Peter died, a professed canon of this Church, later a Carthusian monk.” And on 2 August: “Brother Bernard died, a priest, our professed canon, later a Carthusian monk.” Some, moved by the same purpose, withdrew to the monastery of Arrouaise, in the diocese of Arras, of the canonical order, where the strictest discipline was observed; for, on Saint Bernard’s counsel, they abstained from meat and linen. Perhaps the departure of these men from the monastery of Saint-Genevieve provided the occasion for the murmuring and quarrelling.]

What have you to do with the inhabitants of Arrouaise? Amid these things, gird up like a man not only your loins, but all your thoughts, affections, and actions. Arm yourself with courage, patience, and virtue, [Col. 0516C] for by God’s grace more will be with us than with them. And I, God willing, shall shortly come to you, setting aside all my own business, to preserve your peace and authority and, to the extent of my power, to restore concord among your brethren and sons.

## LETTER CCLI. TO THE POPE

He reproves the excessive multitude of decretals and the professors who abused them.

Having obtained leave, let us speak to our lord, whose gentleness awakens our boldness, whose prudence supports our ignorance, and whose patience promises impunity. On one side the authority of our elders compels us; on the other, a disease gradually creeping onward, whose harm, if it is not met at the beginning, is incurable at the end. We do not say this, Father, as though we wished to be [Col. 0516D] censors of morals, judges of teachers, or examiners of doctrines; this burden requires stronger shoulders, and this contest awaits the stout spiritual arms of athletes. We only wish to indicate to your holy fatherhood what grieves us, you to whom God has granted both the power to rebuke errors and the knowledge to correct them.

Among us the studies of sacred literature have fallen into a workshop of confusion. Pupils applaud novelties alone, while masters attend more to glory than to teaching; everywhere they write new and recent little summaries and commentaries purporting to establish theological matters, with which to flatter, retain, [Col. 0517A] and deceive their hearers—as though the works of the holy Fathers did not already suffice. We read that these Fathers expounded sacred Scripture by the same Spirit by which we believe the apostles and prophets composed it. They set unknown and foreign dishes before the guests, although at the wedding-feast of the king’s son his oxen and fattened cattle have been slaughtered and all is ready; nothing remains for those coming to the wedding but to take and eat what has been set before them.

Publicly, in defiance of sacred ordinances, the incomprehensible Godhead is disputed over; flesh and blood argue irreverently and wordily about the Incarnation of the Word. The undivided Trinity is cut and torn to pieces in the crossroads, so that there are now as many errors as teachers, as many scandals as lecture rooms, and as many blasphemies as streets. Again, when matters come to judgments which ought to be dealt with by canon law, whether entrusted by you or cognizable by ordinary judges, the sellers bring forward an inextricable forest of decretals, [Col. 0517C] letters allegedly issued in the name of Pope Alexander of holy memory; and the more ancient sacred canons are cast aside, rejected, and spat out. Once this covering has been produced in public, the measures wholesomely established in the councils of the holy Fathers impose neither form upon councils nor end upon cases, since letters prevail which perhaps advocates and hired writers fabricate and compose in their shops or chambers under the names of Roman pontiffs.

A new volume compiled from them is solemnly read in schools and put up for sale in the market, to the applause of a band of notaries, who rejoice both that their labour in writing suspicious little works is reduced and that their payment is increased. Two woes have been foretold, and behold, the third woe remains. The disciplines called liberal arts, having lost their former liberty, are reduced to such servitude [Col. 0517D] that long-haired youths shamelessly usurp their masterships and, still beardless, sit in the chairs of elders; those who do not yet know how to be disciples labour to be called masters. They abandon the rules of the arts and cast away authoritative books; they trap, as in little spider-web snares, the flies of the word-artificers—their empty words and sophisms. Philosophy cries out that her garments are being torn and rent; she is neither consulted according to the old ways nor consoled in her antiquity.

All these things, Father, require the hand of apostolic correction, so that the deformity of teaching, learning, and disputing may by your authority [Col. 0518A] be reduced to a definite form; lest divine discourse become cheap through common handling; lest it be said in corners, “Behold, here is Christ,” or “Behold, there”; lest what is holy be given to dogs and pearls be handed over to be trampled by swine.

## LETTER CCLII. TO A CERTAIN PRELATE

He asks him to obtain from the king a dispensation so that he may not be compelled to attend court.

An advocate is necessary in a lawsuit, a comforter in tears, a harbour in shipwreck, medicine in illness. In these and similar things I have found one refuge: your favour, Father—that neither threats may frighten, nor frauds deceive, nor rivals disturb, nor informers convict me. What I set forth is a petition, [Col. 0518B] not a parable or a riddle. A certain friend of mine from the palace of the lord king has told me that I shall shortly hear a harsh word and receive a bitter command to go to court. The perils of that journey are certain, its remedies uncertain: it threatens death; in men’s minds there is no hope of return; its end is ambiguous. In that palace there is combat without victory, labour without favour, and profit as punishment.

I, the child of your holiness, have completed my sixtieth year and more—a number which by the custom of the realm forbids monks to fight, which, after the enticements of the flesh, admonishes widowed continence from the Gospel, and which by civil law suffices for the honourable discharge of veteran soldiers. Broken in body, incapable of labour, near to death, feeling and tasting the discomforts of old age, I pour out prayers to your holy [Col. 0518C] fatherhood: if it please you, oppose your authority to this danger, and through your intervention—which alone can suffice—deliver my soul from death, my eyes from tears, and my feet from stumbling.

## LETTER CCLIII. TO A CERTAIN DEAN

He asks him to grant pardon to his nephew Peter.

The rod of your correction recently laid upon my wretched Peter moves me strongly and admonishes me to pour out prayers for him to your affection, although he himself has begun to limp no less in the paths of conduct than in the tracks of his feet. Spare, I beg you, this small portion of my blood; spare my few remaining possessions [Col. 0518D] and a weak man, lest amid your blows he be swallowed up by faintness of spirit and the storm of poverty. Do not, if you please, break in him the bruised reed or quench the smoking flax. In consideration of my prayers, let him deserve to receive the benefit of absolution, he who grieves under the bond of suspension. Far be it from your gracious liberality that I, who have always trusted in you, should be found put to shame in this matter. But if perhaps you should wish to punish him in some respect, spare, I beg you, the purse of a poor man.

[Note: [Col. 0517D] In this letter he deals with a kinsman who had obtained a benefice in the Order of Saint Benedict, and asks that, as punishment for his fault, he not be deprived of its revenues, by which he sustained his life.]

There is neither money in it nor anything but immense want.

## LETTER CCLIV

He pours forth prayers for the same nephew.

[Col. 0519A]

One who loves a person present often remembers one absent. Believing you to be a disciple of this rule, I trust that you both recall more frequently and observe more frequently the ancient friendship between us. By the indissoluble pledge of this covenant, I beg you in the Lord to pour out ardent and effective prayers to the dean for my wretched kinsman, although he suffers from no less a lack of good conduct than a lack of money. I am certain that for you an easy way of petitioning is open; if you choose to press the matter, the outcome of your request will be happy. Through you may I experience this favour, for I have often found you kindly disposed toward me. I pray that through your aid and effort he may be absolved from the bond of suspension by which he is bound [Col. 0519B], from the disadvantage of infirmity, and from the bond of poverty. In the fullness of thanks I shall be indebted to the lord dean, and to you for what remains of them.

## LETTER CCLV

He judges that subjects who make improper appeals should not be heard, since they thereby undermine the correction exercised by regular prelates.

The form of regular institutions, devised through many watchful labours, is discipline to the humble, but is hostile to rebels. The sons of contradiction and disobedience now fly about its integrity, enclosed within fixed boundaries, laying snares; now secretly undermine it; now corrupt it by infection. They put forward an appearance of religion while lacking its virtue; and, in order to evade the authority of judges, they are not ashamed to overthrow the truth. That cup is suspect, Father, whose exterior is smeared with honey but whose interior tastes not of wine, but poison. We have heard that you have heard the agents of this artifice and, at their suggestion, have written certain things to the abbot of Saint-Satyrus, a religious and honourable man. Under a certain form of prohibition and command, these bring him a rod for rebuking, not a rule for correcting.

To your command you have added the harsh word, the terrible cautery of excommunication: that no one in the church of Saint-Satyrus, after making profession or after an appeal to a higher hearing, may be forcibly expelled or unjustly harassed until his case receives a canonical hearing in your presence. In this are contained the hunger of total dissolution and the fire of dissension. [Col. 0519D] For whenever someone in that hitherto venerable church commits an offence for which he ought to be subject to regular discipline, he will immediately avoid reproof and correction by rushing to the refuge of appeal, saying that he is being expelled unjustly and forcibly. Certainly, if his offence is such that he must be expelled [Col. 0520A] lest he destroy the rest by pestilential contagion, he will meanwhile demand an ordinary judge, forge excuses, seek advocates, and matters which ought to have been corrected more privately in chapter will be aired publicly in the consistory.

[Note: [Col. 0519D] In canonical order it was always lawful to expel from the monastery those who either refused to undergo correction or, after correction, did not reform, but were a scandal and a perverse example to others. This is also commanded in the Rule of Saint Augustine in these words: “But if perhaps he refuses, even if he does not depart of his own accord, let him be cast out from your fellowship; for this too is done not cruelly but mercifully, lest by his pestilential contagion he destroy many.” These words are employed here.]

Others will be stirred to similar noisy proceedings; and impunity for wrongdoing will produce an incentive to wrongdoing. These things are contrary to the sacred canons, contrary to the chapter of the Lateran Council which begins, “Blameworthy,” and contrary to the privileges granted to our order.

[Note: [Col. 0520D] This is canon 6, which begins, “Irreproachable”; but this canon contains these words: “Let not monks or any religious persons, when they are to be corrected for some transgression, presume to appeal against the regular discipline of their prelate and chapter; but let them humbly submit to what shall be imposed upon them,” etc. The Lateran Council of which this passage speaks was convened by Alexander III in 1179.]

If these are not observed, religion will be dissolved and the order disturbed; and, once everything is thrown into confusion, those who ought to be subject will begin to rule, the tail will turn into the head, and the head into the tail. We pray and beseech you in the Lord [Col. 0520B] to revoke commands so dangerous and to restore his mandate and authority to the aforesaid abbot, a religious and honourable man, so that—as was customarily done in our order in the time of Abbot R. of blessed memory, and is still observed in churches—the prelate may be permitted to correct faults according to rule and, whenever he judges it necessary, to appoint, transfer, institute, or remove his officials.

## LETTER CCLVI. TO THE BISHOP OF CAMBRAI

He consoles him while he suffers from illness.

We look upon your affliction, Father, with the feeling proper both to a friend and to a neighbour. We are not strangers to Him who does not seek what is his own, who burns with those who are scandalized and is weak with those who are weak, because we ought to weep with those who weep. We compassionately share the suffering of one who is humbled, because strength is made perfect in weakness; and we usefully console a bishop. [Col. 0520C] The scourges of God are benefits; his blows are remedies; his cautery is medicine. Let patience be tested in pain; let long-suffering not fail under torment; let chaste love remain watchful in thanksgiving. By these things he may be appeased who strikes and heals, kills and makes alive, loves and chastises.

Sharing your suffering, we drink with you part of this cup; nor shall we be strangers to the tribulation of one ill, since we have experienced the love of one healthy. Meanwhile we do what we can, praying the Lord Jesus that he who freed Peter’s mother-in-law from fevers may stretch forth his saving hand to his servant lying ill and [Col. 0520D] restore the bishop, tried like gold in the furnace, to his ministry, to his people, and to his clergy.

Besides this, bear with a little of my complaint: your priest of Saint-Brixius has grievously injured me though I am innocent, shot at me unaware, and struck me unexpectedly. He whispered in the ears of your priests [Col. 0521A] that he had heard that hostilities and hatreds either openly run or secretly lie between you and us. If there is a sufficient cause for hatred, satisfaction will follow, prompt and ready alike. But if not, let the third tongue be punished, which wished both to divide brethren and to sow quarrels between friends.

## LETTER CCLVII. TO A CERTAIN PRELATE OF THE ROMAN CHURCH

He asks him to prevent a certain cleric from obtaining a prebend in his church.

At the beginning of my promotion, after suffering indignation and wrath and assaults by evil angels, I was so overwhelmed by the force of so great a storm, Father, that I was wearisome to myself, mixed a cup of sorrow for my friends, and gave my enemies material for mockery. At last, when the lord pope had been pacified and appeased [Col. 0521B] by God’s mercy, after my many labours I had scarcely begun to breathe again, when behold, a certain enemy of mine, seeking my life, obtained letters from the supreme pontiff ordering that I receive him into our church and assign him a prebend when one becomes vacant.

Deliver me, Father, I beg you, from this plague; and intercede with the lord pope for me, your servant, your cleric, and, if I dare say it, your friend, that he may not again add affliction to one already afflicted or rouse to my ruin the remnants of his indignation which I believed he had extinguished. Hear, if you please, at this moment of storm, if not my prayers, at least those of your nephew, to whom, in accordance with your will, I have willingly promised and granted a prebend in our church. [Col. 0521C] One who promises is well-disposed; one who gives is beneficent. And if the giver’s cheerfulness accompanies the gift, the recipient ought wholly to devote himself to the fullest thanksgiving for both.

## LETTER CCLVIII. TO THE DEAN OF COURTRAI

He complains of someone who had disregarded his command.

We are weary of writing so often when our little letters bring you neither benefit nor honour. I waited and waited for the priest of Lincelles, and he pays no attention to me: either he is negligent or he is contemptuous. If negligent, he must be rebuked; if contemptuous, punished. He must be rebuked through reprimand and punished through suspension. We command both of these to you, unless you too wish to be reproved with him for negligence or condemned for disobedience [Col. 0521D].

## LETTER CCLIX. TO THE BISHOP OF ARRAS

He treats of his own condition and that of the city.

[Col. 0522A]

Since you have been pleased to inquire about our condition, we can answer nothing but this: the state of our city awaits unforeseen events, struggles with uncertainty, hangs upon the snares of fortune, stumbles on a pathless way, and trembles in darkness. We gird ourselves upon the wall and are enclosed by a rampart, like the children of Israel who, after the Exile, rebuilt the walls of the ruined city, holding a sword in one hand and a mason’s trowel in the other. In the sweat of our face we labour, throwing out earth with a spade and carrying it away in a basket. This is our anxiety while we await [Col. 0522B] one who may save and deliver us from the enemies hemming us in on every side, so that we have neither free entrance nor free exit.

## LETTER CCLX. TO ROBERT, ABBOT OF SAINT-VICTOR AT PARIS

He sends the epitaph of Maurice, bishop of Paris, which he had composed at their request.

We have been told that you wish to stir up our bashfulness and, sparing not our embarrassment, entrap me in an old game. You lay upon us an unbearable burden, for which neither Virgilian gravity nor Ovidian lightness would suffice: namely, that we should inscribe something upon the tomb of the great priest—our father M., bishop of Paris [Col. 0522C]—which may bring his memory before those who look upon it.

[Note: [Col. 0521D] That is, Maurice, bishop of Paris. Bishops are called greater priests because they preside over others and confer upon them the office of consecration, and are greater than other presbyters in dignity and power. Maurice died in 1196, on 11 September; this letter appears to have been written in that year. He is buried in the middle of the choir of Saint-Victor’s church, where this epitaph is read, though in a later form: “The reverend Father Maurice, bishop of Paris, who first began the basilica of Blessed Mary.”]

If we do it, we shall be a laughing-stock to readers and ridiculous to hearers. They will cry, “A doting old man!” They will accuse the bishop of imprudence, because one who ought to attend to sacraments occupies himself childishly with little verses. Again, it is difficult to confine Maurice’s virtues in a short epigram or to comprehend them in a brief epitaph. Yet, lest we seem ungrateful to you, suppressing our shame for the moment, we write a few elegiac verses [Note: [Col. 0521D] Elegiac verses to be inscribed on the tomb; but only four of them were placed there, as the ancient monuments of Saint-Victor testify, in this form:

> A teacher and bishop, worthy of each chair,  
> From the first he deserved to hold both without break.  
> Sound faith, abundant teaching, unceasing almsgiving—  
> Paris proclaims that it had no equal to him.  
> The day before the third Ides of the virgin month  
> Buried brightness, itself buried beneath a cloud.], 

so that you may select two or four of them, whichever please you most. We ask and beseech you in the Lord that they be recited with the author’s name unspoken:

> Cut off in the wretched world’s vale of tears,  
> The living stone is set in the eternal city.

[Col. 0522D]

[Note: [Col. 0522D] He confers this title upon Bishop Maurice, since bishops, after Christ’s example, are living and corner-stones, making both one. He also alludes to what occurs in the hymn for the dedication of a church, *Blessed City Jerusalem*, which is built in heaven out of living stones.]

> A teacher and bishop, worthy of each chair,  
> He deserved from the first to hold both without break.

[Note: [Col. 0522D] Namely, the episcopal chair of Paris and the scholastic chair, in which, as an outstanding doctor, he publicly taught theology. The chronicle of the monk of Auxerre says of him: “Maurice the bishop flourished; because of his industry, his outstanding learning, and the exceptional eloquence of his speech, he was raised from the lowest poverty to the summit of pontifical dignity.”]

[Col. 0523A]

[Note: [Col. 0523C] By these words he indicates that Maurice was the first publicly to profess theology at Paris, an office which, after being made bishop, he did not disdain to discharge as well.]

> Sound faith, abundant teaching, unceasing almsgiving—

[Note: [Col. 0523C] Rigordus relates a notable example of his faith, writing: “Because he most firmly believed in the resurrection of bodies—a doctrine concerning which he had heard many learned persons in his time hesitate—and because he wished, even in dying, to recall them from their unbelief, he ordered a roll to be written containing this text: ‘I believe that my Redeemer lives, and that on the last day I shall rise from the earth; and in my flesh I shall see God my Saviour, whom I myself, and not another, shall see, and my eyes shall behold. This hope has been laid up in my bosom’ (Job 19). When he was at the end, he ordered his faithful friends and household attendants to lay this roll spread out upon his breast, so that all learned men assembling at his burial on the day of his death and reading this sacred Scripture might most firmly believe the common resurrection of all bodies and thereafter in no way doubt it.”]

> Paris proclaims that it had no equal to him.

[Note: [Col. 0523D] Rigordus says this of him: “Whatever property he possessed, he distributed to the poor.”]

> The magnificent structure of his house and the building of the church  
> Declare him generous—to stranger, poor man, and needy alike.  
> Granaries and chests stood always open to the poor;  
> His hand was always open and extended to the wretched.  
> Guard your Maurice, Virgin Mary,  
> A bishop of such great merit and a faithful servant.

[Note: [Col. 0523D] For, after Solomon’s example, he built the house of God and his own house—the episcopal palace, which still survives, at least its chapel and its very large and spacious hall.]

[Note: [Col. 0523D] He also built the elegant and renowned basilica of Blessed Mary, though perhaps he neither began nor completed it. The same monk of Auxerre left this testimony: “Among his notable works, he built from the foundations the church over which he presided, and two stone bridges, one over the Seine and the other over the Marne.”]

## LETTER CCLXI. TO HUGH, CANON OF SAINT-GENEVIEVE AT PARIS

He tries to lighten the grief caused by the death of his nephew.

An old man advises, counsels, and urges an old man; an infirm man an invalid; one far away one absent: as you had counsel in prosperity, so have consolation in adversity. Do not mourn the death of your little nephew, who was taken away lest malice should change his understanding. We believe him as unstained in mind as in body; he has not so much departed from you as gone before you to the Lord. Tears poured out over the dead are empty; they harm the mourner and do not benefit the one for whom he mourns. I wish that you were with me, and I with you, so that prosperity and adversity alike might be common to us, and our like old age might be a consolation to each, pleasing to each other, and burdensome to neither. Would that we might one day see one another, so that we might envy no one and no one might envy us.

## LETTER CCLXII. TO WILLIAM, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS

He writes on behalf of Queen Ingeborg, seeking his assistance and aid for her.

[Col. 0523C]

Assuming boldness for a little while, I shall speak to my lord: neither presumptuous through lowliness nor despairing through faintness of heart. My maker will not reject his clay, the potter his little vessel, the craftsman the work of his hands. He will not reject, I say, me, whom he has raised and preferred, as one who complains (*queror*), mourns (*moereor*), asks (*quaero*), or merits (*mereor*). What I set before you is a petition, not a parable, worthy both of compassion from a kindly mind and consolation from a beneficent hand.
