There is among us a precious pearl, trodden underfoot by men, honoured by angels, worthy of a royal treasure, worthy of a palace, worthy of heaven. I mean the queen [Note: [Col. 0524C]

Namely Isemburg, or Ingelburg, of Denmark, whom King Philip had repudiated—whether through fickleness of mind, some degree of kinship, or, as some think, bewitched by spells—in order to take Mary, daughter of the duke of Thuringia. On this divorce the *Memorial of Histories* by John of Saint-Victor, under the year 1198, has the following: “In the same year, because King Philip was unwilling to accept as his wife the sister of the king of the Danes, after being admonished by the pope through cardinals, Peter of Capua excommunicated him, having first convened a council at Dijon; and because he kept another woman whom he had taken in, and did not yield to the king’s appeal, the kingdom of France was placed under interdict, on the feast of Saint Nicholas. But the sentence was not promulgated until after Christmas. Then Philip sent envoys to the pope and withdrew. When the king had sent to the pope, he again sent into France Octavian, bishop of Ostia, and John of Velletri; through them King Philip put away Mary, whom he had introduced in addition, and received back his first wife only outwardly, not rendering marital duty, but later put her away again.” Innocent III’s diploma concerning the interdict of the realm, of which this passage speaks, is found among his *Registers*: “Given at the Lateran, in the third year of the pontificate.” It begins: “Since the most beloved …” [(a) See the works of Innocent III in our edition, vol. I. Editors.]

That unhappy queen, thus dismissed, fled to our Stephen, who prepared lodging for her at the monastery of Cisoing, of regular canons in his diocese of Tournai. There, removed from worldly cares and the pomp of court, she devoted herself to God and prayer. Here our author sets out plainly before William, archbishop of Reims and uncle of the king, her pious life, though one afflicted by poverty and hardships; he asks for the archbishop’s aid and, if it is lawful to say so, begs alms for a queen in want and reduced to the utmost straits.]

—who is shut up at Cisoing as though in a prison, burdened by poverty, and banished in exile. We lament the fortune of her person; we leave the cause of her misfortune and the outcome of that cause to God. For who could be of such iron heart and stony breast as not to be moved in so great an adversity by a maiden illustrious in royal birth, distinguished in character, modest in speech? With the Ambrosian virgin, she is fair of face but fairer in faith; young indeed in years, but grey in mind; I might almost say more mature than Sarah, wiser than Rebecca, more gracious than Rachel, more devout than Hannah, more chaste than Susanna. Those accustomed to dispute about women’s beauty judge her neither less beautiful than Helen nor more contemptible than Polyxena.

Her daily occupation is prayer, reading, or work with her hands. She knows no gaming-table and is ignorant of dice. From morning until the sixth hour she pours out prayers extended in tears and groans, not so much for herself as for the lord king. In the oratory she never sits: either she always stands upright or, with bent knees, is always raised and bowed down. We believe that, if our Ahasuerus knew such a woman, he would cherish his Esther and, extending the sceptre of favour, the sceptre of love, the sceptre of his kingdom, [Col. 0524C] would call her back into royal embraces—exchanging divorce for union, softening resentment with gentleness, and banishing hatred by truth. For we believe that in word or will he would say to her: “In your splendour and your beauty, press on, prosper, and reign” (Psalm 45); and that loving saying of Solomon: “Return, return, O Shulammite; return, that we may gaze upon you” (Song of Songs 6), on account of the honourable elegance of her conduct.

Such and so great a blessed offspring of kings and martyrs [Note: [Col. 0525D] For she was the daughter of Valdemar, king of Denmark, son of Canute, grandson of Saint Canute, king and martyr, whose feast is commemorated in the Church on 19 January, as appears [Col. 0526D] from the genealogical succession of the kings of Denmark.], a noble shoot, holy seed, is compelled through lack of sustenance to expose, sell off, and auction her little belongings—that is, her modest clothes and few vessels. She asks for food, petitions for alms, stretches out her hand to receive, and entreats the one who stretches out his hand. I have often seen her weeping; and I too, weeping with and for her, felt my heart tremble and grow afraid. I urged her as much as I could to cast her care upon the Lord, which she herself did not cease to do. To every point she answered: “My friends and my neighbours have departed from me; my sole refuge is my lord the archbishop of Reims, who from the beginning of my adversity [Col. 0525B] has generously cherished, fed, and supported me.”

May the tearful sighs and mournful groans of so noble and outstanding a maiden, born of kings and forefathers who were kings, move you, Father; and may you, who distribute alms to so many and such great numbers of poor people, not close the inward compassion of your mercy against a queen begging after such glory. The letter has exceeded its proper length, but the subject reproached brevity and compassion set the pen aflame. Farewell.

## LETTER CCLXIII. TO THE SAME PERSON, IN THE PERSON OF THE SAME QUEEN

[Note: [Col. 0526D] It seems to have been written for the purpose that the same queen might render thanks to the archbishop of Reims for the assistance he had given her when she was in the utmost distress, as he had been asked through the letter written above. That letter shows that she lacked even the necessities of food required to sustain life.]

She asks him not to permit the dissolution of her marriage or compel her to enter another marriage and pass into other hands.

In reckoning and assessing your benefactions, Father, my soul is unequal to rendering fitting thanks [Col. 0525C]: it does not suffice in feeling and fails in understanding. Truly the Lord has looked upon the lowliness of His handmaid, who by His grace inspired you to help one faint-hearted, to comfort one who weeps, to provide for an exile, and to be her sole consolation, lest the onset of so great a calamity crush in me, your servant, the bruised reed and utterly extinguish the smouldering flax. Your benefits abound beyond measure and exceed both the merits and the prayers of your suppliant, since you expect no one but God to repay you; nor do you readily give ear to anyone who would dissuade you. May my lord not permit, I beseech him, in this course of his mercy, that I should fall into alien hands [Note: [Col. 0526D] She seems to request of him that he not allow her marriage, contracted with the king, to be declared void, lest she be compelled to enter a second and alien marriage—something she, distrusting that it could be done with a safe conscience, feared as a grave evil.]; for if, God forbid, this should happen, it would be ruin for me, [Col. 0525D] not a fall; a precipice, not a descent. Meanwhile [Col. 0526A] I send you small gifts from my small treasury, not as deserving of your favour, but as reminders of my fortune [Note: [Col. 0526D] Those insignificant gifts which she sent, unsuited to royal munificence, showed the meagreness and humility of her circumstances.].

## 386. LETTER CCLXIV. TO LORD SOFREDUS, CARDINAL OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH

Since I desire to be aided by the support of just repentance, I fall at your feet, ready to serve, submit to, and obey both you and your nephew. Forgive me, I beg you; help one faint-hearted, and extend the hand of help and counsel, because it is the time to have mercy on her, because the time has come. May your clemency swallow up indignation, your generosity restrain resentment, and grace—not merit—renew friendship.

## LETTER CCLXIV (again). TO JOHN, SON OF THE CHANCELLOR OF THE NOBLE CITY

[Col. 0526B]

Old friendships must neither be cast aside in contempt, nor crushed by disdain, nor erased by forgetfulness; they desire to increase, not diminish; to grow strong, not perish. Through their interchange we were once so joined that each wished both to share the other's suffering in adversity and rejoice with the other in prosperity. Warned and moved by this confidence, I beg you, by that ancient bond of mutual fellowship and affection, to offer urgent prayers on my behalf to your lord father, chancellor of the holy city, a man whom we love in Christ, so that he may both receive kindly and handle beneficently the matter which I have communicated to him by letter. By his counsel may he free me from the wicked and deceitful man who, pursuing and harassing me together with my friends [Col. 0526C], thirsts for my blood and does not cease to disturb the peace.

## LETTER CCLXV. TO A CERTAIN REGULAR PRELATE

He urges him carefully to examine and correct faults discovered in the course of his visitation.

It belongs to a good shepherd to undertake the care of the flock entrusted to him by God with such earnestness of mind that he may not only preserve those who live religiously in their condition, but may even advance them to the highest summit of religious life by the example of his conduct and reputation. Hence I wonder—and cannot wonder enough—what necessity, what haste, compelled you to pass through our parts at such a rapid pace, without [Col. 0526D] turning aside to the hospitality of our house; so that, cheered by [Col. 0527A] your presence, strengthened by your counsel, and supported by your help, we might correct whatever had been done with insufficient order and bring whatever had been adorned with insufficient propriety to the degree of perfection. We therefore implore your fatherhood to bring to a better conclusion the burden which you have undertaken through zeal for justice and the prompting of divine love: that, in visiting the communities of brothers of our order, you may examine faults with diligent scrutiny, correct those examined, and transform those corrected, so that you may find all who have been entrusted to your discernment transformed before the tribunal of the Judge.

## 388. LETTER CCLXVI. TO HIS FRIEND

He warns him to beware lest he suffer some loss from his nephews.

[Col. 0527B] Let the discernment of your affection know that I have laboured by every means in my power for the peace of my country and the stability of our Church, yet have not been able firmly to restore it to the good of peace. For my nephews, placing confidence in the support of Lord H., and therefore proceeding with haughty eye and pursuing me with implacable hatred, have sworn in a treacherous conspiracy to lay waste my land. And because, through the reports of envious men and the whispering of slanderers, they suppose that I have deposited with you an immense sum of money, I fear that you may feel the first encounter of war—may the Lord avert it! Therefore I beseech your affection to place in a more secret location all your household goods which you do not presently need, lest, should an enemy attack occur, you may find consolation in the loss of only a few things [Col. 0527C].

## LETTER CCLXVII. TO THE ELECT OF ORLÉANS

[Note: [Col. 0527D] Hugh was appointed bishop in the year 1190; in that year Stephen of Tournai sent him this congratulatory letter.] He congratulates him on his election.

A delightful report, worthy of all acceptance, has sounded in our ears; a brief phrase has poured great joy into us: “The dean has been elected bishop.” It has twelve syllables and ends in an apostolic number; it signifies that our priest is to be counted among the apostolic priests. Let the Church of Orléans rejoice: a lack of suitable persons did not compel it to borrow, as a beggar, a bishop sought from other Churches. The man whom it had nourished from childhood, whom it had brought [Col. 0528A] into the perfect way, whom it had instructed in ecclesiastical disciplines, it took for itself, sufficient from its own bosom; setting him over its head, it made a father from a son—one not unknown in character, not foreign to the province, not low-born [Note: [Col. 0527D] For he was a nephew of Manasses de Garlande, descended from the illustrious Garlande family.], experienced in just responsibilities and free from unjust dissipation. Truly, he did not serve for another's pay; he is worthy to preside in that Church in which he had been accustomed also to be of service.

Let the elect himself rejoice also; we too rejoice with him, and let no one take our joy from us—whether envy murmurs, malice persecutes, or detraction bites. A burden is joined to honour: as it is heavy with labours, so too it is laden with mysteries. Let our lord and friend understand what we say: “For the Lord will give him understanding in all things” (2 [Col. 0528B] Tim. 2). We declare him a commendable bishop for our times, one who has kept himself free from unlawful contact. May God increase His grace toward you, and raise in virtues him whom He has raised in rank.

Meanwhile, excellent Father, happy successor, honour, love, and cherish your blessed predecessor Saint Evurtius and his Church; often reflect that from the place whence you were taken to the chair [Note: [Col. 0527D] The bishops-elect of Orléans, before entering the city to take possession of their Church, visited the church of Saint Evurtius, once situated outside the walls; from there they were led in solemn procession to the basilica of Holy Cross, an observance still maintained.], there you shall be taken to the tomb [Note: [Col. 0527D] He had, as is gathered from this, chosen burial in the chapter of Saint Evurtius beside the tomb of his uncle Manasses, who lies in its midst.]. We send you a small gift dispatched to us from distant regions: a cypress pastoral staff [Note: [Col. 0527D] Perhaps the very one which the abbot of La Sauve-Majeure had sent him.], suited to your office and to the nature of its mystery, and proportionate in size to its ministry.

## 390. LETTER CCLXVIII. TO A CERTAIN ABBOT

He reproves him because he sent a horse that was insufficiently elegant.

[Col. 0528C]

The lord of Reims asked you for a horse, and you sent him a little ass; hence we are compelled to marvel not so much at the gift as at the author of the gift. You ought to have considered not what sort of animal you were sending, but what sort it befitted the lord of Reims to receive. We therefore send it back to you, valuing you and your horse at an equal price.

## LETTER CCLXIX. TO LAMBINUS, BISHOP OF THÉROUANNE

Concerning the transfer of the abbot of Sunebecca [Note: [Col. 0527D]

This abbey is situated near Ypres and now belongs to that diocese. This Lambinus, bishop of Thérouanne, was a native of the city of Bruges; indeed, elsewhere he calls him “Lambinus of Bruges.” Nor will it be irrelevant here to relate the letter of the abbot of Sunebecca to a certain prior of the Hospitallers in Poland, in these words:

> “To Lord B., by God's providence procurator of the Hospital of Jerusalem in Poland and Pomerania: Jo., called abbot of Sunebecca, and his little flock, greeting and prayers in Christ.
>
> “We have received your letter, from which we learn of the vigour of your Hospital and the advancement of its honour, and we have been filled with the warmest affection of congratulation. Therefore, although we are paying the cost of many expenses in repairing the ruin of our church, which by a lamentable accident has suffered a grave loss of its integrity, we nevertheless do not hesitate to grant your request through Brother Almaricus, specially appointed by you, and we inform your diligence concerning the Arm of Saint Caesarius. Know, therefore, that the arm itself is carefully fitted into a silver arm and is decently kept and adorned among us. Meanwhile [Col. 0529C], because the event of this life is changeable, that brother might indeed, God forbid, be taken from the midst on the road. If your generosity should decide to send us anything, we wish it to be made known to us in letters sealed within, what, how much, and for what purpose you assign it, so that your generosity toward us, your brothers and friends, may shine forth more clearly to us. Farewell.”]

—into the abbey of Saint Bartholomew of Ekout.

At Compiègne you answered us briefly [Col. 0529A] concerning the transfer of the abbot of Sunebecca: that he should return to the house from which he came. Yet, to the detriment of our effort, as we have heard, you say that you have no recollection of this promise. Far be it that the passage of a few days should have overwhelmed your memory, so capacious and retentive—a memory for which envious old age has not yet produced forgetfulness, nor dull ignorance negligence. We ask the lord, we entreat the friend, we advise our equal, that in the present matter he provide for us; that, when asked, he grant help and supply the lack of one who asks, receiving from us a return not only in a like case but also, if possible, in matters depending upon the snares of fortune. Kindly receive our prayers.

Consider the need of the poor Church of Saint Bartholomew [Note: [Col. 0529D] It belonged to regular canons in the city of Bruges, where that abbot of Sunebecca had taken the religious habit. The city of Bruges, however, lay in the diocese of Tournai.], beside which [Col. 0529B] you sucked maternal breasts, received paternal nurture, and found fraternal consolation. Without delay command the aforesaid man to accept the election made of him and, as though entering again into his mother's womb, to be compelled to be born anew from her and perform for her a father's office—she who has rendered him a mother's benefit and nurture. Farewell.

## 392. LETTER CCLXX. TO INNOCENT, SUPREME PONTIFF

He asks him to protect the privileges of the Church of Saint Geneviève.

The Church of Blessed Geneviève of Paris, your special daughter [Note: [Col. 0529D] It is called a special daughter of the apostolic see because it is immediately subject to it. It is called the full sister of the churches of Saint-Germain and Saint-Denis because they enjoyed the same privilege and acknowledged the same father and shepherd, namely the supreme pontiff.], full sister of Saints Denis and Germanus, offers you the sacrifice of a contrite heart and humbled spirit, and her tears are upon her cheeks. Against its liberty and dignity, which it obtained in ancient times from the holy Roman [Col. 0529C] Church, its mother, the new bishop of Paris [Note: [Col. 0529D] That is, Odo de Sully, son of Archambald, lord of Sully, and Matilda of Baugency. He was raised to the bishopric of Paris after the death of Maurice in 1196. Seeing that the lands of Saint Geneviève and Saint-Germain, recently built within the city walls, were enclosed there, he could not tolerate two abbots exercising episcopal jurisdiction in his own city while he himself was deprived there of spiritual right. He therefore continually devised new measures in their parishes [Col. 0530C], and finally placed the parish of the Mount under interdict. A grave controversy subsequently arose before Pope Innocent III; John, abbot of Saint Geneviève, went to Rome to defend his right before the pope himself, formerly his fellow student, and brought him this letter from the bishop of Tournai. The bishop of Paris, however, sent him Master Peter of Corbeil, canon of Paris and former teacher of Innocent [Col. 0530D], to defend his cause. At length came the judgment contained among the decretals, chapter *Olim*, “On the Restitution of Those Despoiled.” For when the bishop complained that he had been despoiled by the abbot of his right in the parish of the Mount and asked that it be restored, the judgment declared: “Because it was not in any way proved that, at the time when the bishop himself pronounced the sentence of interdict, he possessed or had previously possessed any right of parish jurisdiction over them, we could not adjudge restitution to him in law, since it was not established that he had been despoiled in any respect.” Nevertheless, so that they might enter into a covenant of peace, Odo, bishop of Paris, and John, abbot of Saint Geneviève, made a settlement in 1202 concerning the rights of the parish of the Mount; later the abbot and monks of Saint-Germain of Paris did likewise.] is attempting to forge new arguments and weave subtle questions, usurping, in head and members under the pretext of prelacy, a jurisdiction which neither ought nor may be usurped.

Because of these and many other grievances, which it can neither endure nor ought to endure, your devoted son, the abbot of that Church, approaches and falls at your feet, that you may cause the privileges of the holy apostolic see, granted and conceded to the Blessed Virgin by your predecessors and fortified and secured by so many authorities, to be firmly observed [Col. 0530A], lest man prevail against the divine and apostolic see, and lest the enemy rejoice through insolence against your children. Our adversaries see with sorrow and envy your three special daughters in and around the city of Paris, 393 joined in the sacred number of the Trinity—namely, the churches of Saint-Denis, Saint-Germain, and Saint Geneviève. Knowing that the threefold cord of our fraternal charity cannot easily be broken, they attempt to diminish, injure, trample upon, and encrust it.

Receive, Father, your son and hear his prayers; receive and cherish our very heart in him, who especially places confidence in you [Col. 0530B] because of former fellowship at school and personal acquaintance, lest, if he should suffer some rebuff from you—God forbid!—the envious should say with laughter and mockery: “See how he loved him” (John 11). What he asks is just, as one who fights for his country and contends for liberty.

## 394. LETTER CCLXXI. TO A CERTAIN PRINCE

He asks him not readily to credit those who report unfavourably about him.

The affection with which I have loved your nobility from the beginning has in no way grown cold within me; rather, through your subsequent and preceding benefits toward me, it burns more and more ardently. Therefore I urge your excellence by asking, and ask by urging, that if any unfavourable accusation should be laid before you that I have done or said anything against you [Col. 0530C] or yours, you should not believe it at all. Nor should you immediately decide anything that your servants may demand when anger dictates. But when, God willing, you come to us, you will learn all matters more fully, because, on the basis of what you have heard, you will adopt the sounder counsel. May your highness prosper and not abandon its good purpose. May your strength and glory prosper and live through long times.

## 395. LETTER CCLXXII. TO THE SUPREME PONTIFF

Concerning a controversy that arose between the regular canons of the churches of Seclin and Phalempin.

[Col. 0531A]

Most high Father and Lord, in whose governance God's providence has deigned to place Peter's little ship, lest it be tossed amid various dangers, we humbly implore the dignity of your apostolic office with knees of heart and body bent: that what has been done by us in the service of dutiful devotion may not be recalled as void. For you committed to our obedience for determination the case pending between the canons of Seclin [Note: [Col. 0531C]

Seclin has a college of secular canons in the diocese of Tournai. It recognizes as its founder Saint Eligius, bishop of Noyon and Tournai, who established clerics there for the worship of Blessed Plato the martyr, buried in that place, so that they might perform the divine office. Receive a letter written by Innocent III to our Stephen, in which this college is mentioned:

> “INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Stephen, bishop and cantor of Tournai.
>
> “But since certain charges were made by R., a canon of Seclin, against John [Col. 0531D] of Béthune—namely, the multiplicity of both dignities and prebends, the vice of ambition and avarice, to which he has not yet set an end; his attempt and intrusion, contrary to the terms of our decree and the statutes of the Lateran Council, to obtain the provostship of Seclin; and his presumption to minister on the day of his intrusion before confirmation, as well as after the annulment of his confirmation—we command that, if you find that the aforesaid J. holds several other dignities and prebends, or find any other of the foregoing matters to be true that suffices for his annulment, you impose silence upon him concerning the aforesaid provostship and free the Church of Seclin from the conferral of it upon him. For many things are tolerated through patience which, if brought before a court, ought not to be tolerated when justice requires.”]

and the canons of Phalempin [Note: [Col. 0532C] Phalempin is an abbey of the order of regular canons, founded by Susuvalon, castellan of Lille, in the diocese of Tournai, in honour of Blessed Christopher the martyr, “that he might establish there a clergy of Christ's poor,” as is read in the instrument of its foundation in the year 1039, in the reign of the most glorious King [Col. 0532D] Henry.], concerning a certain tithe. In pursuing the honour of obedience, we duly summoned the various parties into our presence [Col. 0531B], carefully heard the pleadings, thoroughly examined the testimony, and proceeded according to canonical order. Finally, once the truth was known, after manifold deliberation, with the approval of authoritative men, and in the hearing of experts in law, we adjudged the tithe to the canons of Phalempin, to be possessed as they had possessed it from ancient times. In this matter we implore your fatherhood to cause that which we have adjudged in good conscience to be maintained for ever inviolably, lest the sincerity of our judgment incur shame and stain.

## 396. LETTER CCLXXIII. TO THE SAME

He writes concerning a dispute between two canons of Seclin.

[Col. 0531C]

By your letters you informed us that we should investigate by diligent inquiry the dispute which has long been debated among the canons of the same Church, between R. and I., canons of Seclin [Col. 0532A]. Accordingly, pursuing the tenor of your command more fully, we summoned the canons of Seclin; and, after summoning them, we admonished them on your behalf to inform us concerning the aforesaid dispute and to instruct us, once informed, what we should report to you. But the said canons, being insufficiently informed on this point, declared in their reply that a dispute had long ago arisen between R. and I.; but what the dispute was, they wholly did not know. And because we are insufficiently informed about it, we are able to inform you less fully.

## LETTER CCLXXIV. TO WILLIAM, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS

He excuses himself from the consecration of the elect of Châlons.

[Col. 0532B]

Many troubles surround an old man. I ask my lord not to cast me off in the time of my old age, when my strength fails. You raised the lowly from the dust, lifted me from the footstool to the chair [Note: [Col. 0532D] These words make it clear that the letter was written to William, archbishop of Reims; through his action our Stephen was elevated to the chair and bishopric of Tournai.], took me from the little flock [Note: [Col. 0532D] That is, from the governance of the abbey of regular canons of Saint Geneviève of Paris, of which he had been abbot for fifteen years or more.] as from behind the ewes with young, and set me over thousands upon thousands. These are the secret walks of my thoughts, the daily courses of my affections; in the night my dreams return to them, applauding the wakeful, delighting the sleeping, soothing the sad, and consoling the faint-hearted.

Amid these things fear and trembling came upon me, an old man already nearly trembling, through your two summonses and a third issued as though peremptory [Col. 0532C] by the lord king: the first, to the joyful and festive consecration at Reims of my lord and dearest friend, the elect of Châlons [Note: [Col. 0532D] This was Gerard of Douai [ [Col. 0531D] (a) M. Brial (*Histoire littéraire de la France*, XV, 425) considers that this is to be understood not of Gerard of Douai, of whom the letter says nothing, but of Rotrou of Perche, who, although elected as early as 1190, had not yet received consecration in 1195 (*Gallia Christiana*, IX, 883). For the see of Reims is known to have been vacant after William's death; it was still vacant when Gerard of Douai was consecrated. It must therefore be admitted that William, already dead, did not attend Gerard's consecration. Hence it may be inferred that the letter was written in this very year 1095 to William; accordingly Father du Molinet's reckoning, eight years too late, must be corrected, and Stephen's birth assigned to 19 February 1128. EDITORS OF THE PATRISTIC EDITION.], who succeeded Rotrou in the year 1203, as may be seen in Alberic's Chronicle; from that year, 1203, it is inferred that our Stephen had died.], on the Sunday called *Oculi*; the second, to the solemn conference of the lord king, on the Sunday called *Laetare*, [Col. 0533A] near the valley of Rodolio [Note: [Col. 0533D] Perhaps Rueil in Brie, where there is a notable priory of the Cluniac order.]; the third, at Paris, on the Sunday called *Isti sunt dies*, concerning the case pending between the bishop of Paris [Note: [Col. 0533D] At that time Odo de Sully governed the Church of Paris.] and the church of Kala [Note: [Col. 0533D] Commonly Chelles: an abbey of Benedictine nuns in the Paris region, founded by Saint Bathild, queen and wife of King Clovis II.], to which the lord king summoned me, Father, with many attestations and adjurations.

In Septuagesima, if I remember rightly, I completed my seventieth year less two [Note: [Col. 0533D] From this text it is inferred that Stephen first saw the light in 1135; for if he was sixty-eight years old in 1203, the year in which he died, it follows that he was born in 1135.], the number of years which the Psalmist assigns to old age. I do not blush to set before you my infirmities and lowly condition: the signs foretelling my approaching dissolution; the failure of my senses and limbs, and also of my joints and marrow. The longer and more frequently these have endured labours until now, the more rarely they now seek them and the more reluctantly admit them. Spare me, Father, I beseech you, your servant; for [Col. 0533B] the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak. I am certain that without grave injury to my body and detriment to my health, I cannot now undertake or bear this labour. If I begin to run, I shall not arrive; if I set out on a journey, I shall fail on the road. Let your kindly and beneficent grace, if it please you, make known to me your will in these matters. Once I know it fully, I am ready, at your command, to go both to prison and to death.

## 399. LETTER CCLXXV

He asks that he be excused from the same consecration because of his frail age.

[Col. 0533C] Among the many troubles that surround an old man, two especially vex me: weakness of the limbs and continual illnesses. A third is added, followed by a fourth: on the one side scarcity of resources, on the other slender means for expenses. Under this frail fourfold constraint, I shall be insufficient for the consecration of the lord of Châlons, which I hear is to take place on the octave of Pentecost, if I set out to travel there. Therefore I beseech your affection, in which I have always placed confidence, carefully to ascertain my lord's will: whether I may remain free from so great a labour without offending him. And if necessary, humbly entreat him to grant me leave to rest, since I have so often experienced the frequency of labour. Write back to me [Col. 0533D] a brief note concerning my lord's will in this matter.

## LETTER CCLXXVI. TO WILLIAM, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS

Complying with his wishes, he writes that he will shortly be present at the aforesaid consecration.

[Col. 0534A]

Conscience chastens my fear, strengthens my doubt, changes my plan, and recalls the excuses which had beset me in sickness, so that, God willing, I may hasten to gird myself for the feast: those who are present may rejoice, and those who departed may blush. I shall be guilty of ingratitude, and may no less be charged with folly, if I forget my lord, the elect of Châlons; if I exclude myself from so great a joy, having once experienced both the favour of so great a man and the glory of so great a sacrament. Confidence will arm me against ill health; hope will animate me against old age; my native land [Col. 0534B] will shake off my labours; endurance will break fear. In running I shall be young; in mounting I shall be old; in both anxious, in neither undevout.

The obligation of becoming obedience and the worthiness of the person to be consecrated [Note: [Col. 0533D] Namely, Gerard of Douai, elect of Châlons.], together with the desire to see the consecrator [Note: [Col. 0533D] William, archbishop of Reims, his patron and friend.], move and urge me toward this, so that these three may work together for good and advance as one toward increase. Moreover, holy Father, if I acted outside the Church's rules in appointing outsiders within our Church, because I gave consent without your assent, I humbly seek pardon, like Aaron prostrate before Moses. For, as he was compelled by the cries of the people to make a golden calf, so I too, compelled by the exhortations of the chapter, did not withhold my consent. Let your fatherhood know [Col. 0534C] concerning the oath made by your clerk Laurence that I neither advised him to make it nor was present when he swore. Whatever you decide, I am prepared both to follow the decision and to obey its maker.

## 401. LETTER CCLXXVII. TO THE ABBOT AND CHAPTER OF LA SAUVE-MAJEURE

[Note: [Col. 0533D] The monastery of La Sauve-Majeure, of the Benedictine order, commonly called *Selve Majeure*, is situated in the diocese of Bordeaux. It was founded in 1077, as is read in the Chronicle of Maillezais, by Blessed Gerald or Gerard, a disciple of Saint Arnulf, bishop of Soissons. When, because of the sanctity of his life, he had been enrolled among the saints, the abbot of La Sauve-Majeure wrote to Stephen, bishop of Tournai, asking him to compose the office to be sung on the feast-day of this blessed man. In this letter Stephen excuses himself from the task; and he writes the following Letter 278 to the archdeacon of Bordeaux, entrusting the work to him as a man more distinguished and practised in this kind of writing. Nevertheless, overcome by the abbot's prayers, Stephen finally composed the office of Blessed Gerald, as is gathered from Letter 279, in which the abbot gives him thanks. The fragments that have reached us will be given at the end of this work.] In compliance with their prayers, he writes that he will compose a proper office to be recited on the feast of Saint Gerald.

To the abbot and chapter of La Sauve-Majeure: common prayers in the Lord.

A certain young man, eloquent in speech and learned in knowledge, Master A., came to us on your behalf, urgently requesting through a reminder of prayers that we offer to Blessed [Col. 0534D] Gerald, your confessor and patron, who has recently been canonized by the Roman Church among the number of saints [Col. 0535A], some calves of our lips, by which we may both proclaim the glory of so great a man and merit his favour. You impose upon us a new and unfamiliar task. If perhaps we undertake it, it will weary the reader and make the listener laugh. They will charge that an old man is raving, call the bishop foolish, since, setting aside for the present the sacraments of the Church and the care owed to his parishioners, he seems to be mad while fitting unpolished words to new melodies. Once we played with verse, perhaps also prose; we are not ashamed to have played, but to begin the game now.

Yet since charity conquers all things, setting aside for the time being other pressing occupations, we shall take care to revive a similar pursuit and, God willing, aided by your prayers and those of the aforesaid confessor, shall attempt with a stammering pen [Col. 0535B] to fulfil what you ask. Let whoever wishes laugh; a good conscience and unfeigned faith will excuse us.

## 402. LETTER CCLXXVIII. TO THE ARCHDEACON OF BORDEAUX

He invites him to compose hymns for the aforesaid office.

The venerable abbot of La Sauve-Majeure, having heard that I was established at Paris in the schools when you judged me worthy of your affability and acquaintance, obtained this supplicatory letter to your majesty. Though it may seem presumptuous—indeed ridiculous—for a servant to dare speak to his lord, a Davus to an Oedipus [Note: [Col. 0535D] A proverb well worn among the ancients: “I am Davus, not Oedipus,” that is, ignorant, not learned. Davus is introduced in the *Andria* to signify a rude and ignorant man, unequal to solving riddles.], a beginner to a wise man, yet, begging—would that I might obtain—pardon on bended knee [Note: [Col. 0535D] This word is used adverbially here to mean “with knees bent.”], in shame and trembling, made like one mute and [Col. 0535C] not opening his mouth, I stammer in this letter and little sheet to your majesty.

Indeed, Blessed Gerald, drawing his origin from the regions of Gaul [Note: [Col. 0536D] The Chronicle of Maillezais says under the year 1077: “Girandus began to build the monastery of Saint Mary of La Sauve-Majeure.” And under the year 119: “Girandus, abbot of good memory, died; on the same night on which he died, stars were seen falling from heaven like a torch.”], whose life flourished honourably and beautifully before men, and whose death, precious in the Lord's sight, shines forth as attested by signs and gleams with miracles—he who came to the Bordeaux region, founded the monastery of La Sauve-Majeure from its first stone, and reformed it with regular discipline—has this year been formally enrolled among the saints by the lord pope at Rome, with the due solemnity of Masses. How, by God's grace, the order flourishes and burns with zeal in that monastery beyond the ordinary rules of monks, your greatness can learn more reliably and effectively from the renown of report than [Col. 0535D] from the service of my pen.

But because your name is oil poured out, and the talent of your learning cannot be hidden but is spread throughout the whole body of the Church like a greater light, and old men together with young run after the fragrance of your lips and words: the abbot of the aforesaid monastery and the whole convent request it; the entire diocese of Bordeaux, poured at your feet, cries out [Col. 0536A] that, according to the grace given you, you should provide an office in antiphons for the psalms, responsories for the readings, and a prose and collect for the Mass. Thus, besides the intercessions of the Church which will be owed you forever, your memory may flourish and live forever in blessing.

Although those who strive to draw away your hands, entangled in so many affairs, and your ears, so due and bound to business, may seem to sin against the public good, nevertheless, merciful Father, bend down: take ink and pen for praises and songs of Blessed Gerald, and grant a little time to his service, so that if by playful composition you once contracted any stain in secular poems, you may now, when the opportunity is offered, more devoutly amend it by offering your labours to the Lord and to Blessed Gerald [Col. 0536B]. May your reverend fatherhood always and everywhere fare well.

## 404. LETTER CCLXXIX. TO THE BISHOP OF TOURNAI

They give him thanks for the office of Saint Gerald which, at their request, he had composed.

To the lord bishop of Tournai, the abbot and convent of La Sauve-Majeure.

To recount your grace and mercy toward us—how great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have revealed to your little ones and perfected for those who hope in you—and to say what thanks we owe for it: language and reason fail, and our profound reflection stands astonished before such generosity on your part [Col. 0536C]. Yet these things may not be left unspoken, even if they cannot be fully expressed.

Giving thanks, therefore, to your graciousness, through which we have deserved to receive whatever our soul requested and desired from you in praise and proclamation of Saint Gerard—composed in powerful words, most fittingly arranged for devout prayer to God, and readily available for clothing these meanings—we rightly exult with inexpressible joy amid so great a subject of rejoicing. We are refreshed and delighted in the Lord by the sweet cadences of your tongue and the jubilant praises, where, in so brief a space of time, the word of wisdom was so swift, God himself so prompt a teacher, and tongue, hand, and grace, fulfilling their promises, became the pen [Col. 0536D] of a scribe writing swiftly.

This deed, this generosity, this greatness of condescension has made us your servants and established us as your most devoted people in every respect for ever. We shall pray all the more for you to the boundless mercy of the Almighty, that he may repay you for all this with the reward of the righteous. We have granted you, as far as lies in our power—for we can offer nothing more worthy—the full fraternity of our monastery [Col. 0537A], making you a participant in all the benefits of our church, both in life and in death. May almighty God grant you a good and long life for the salvation and honour of his Church, in which he has established you as a very great pillar.

We send your most dear fatherhood, as a sign of our devotion and pledge of perpetual service, a small gift unworthy of your rank but suited to our duty: namely, a staff of cypress wood. We consider not how much it is, but from how great a heart it is offered, presuming upon the example of him who regarded Abel more than his gifts. You may receive this offering without any scrupulous hesitation, following the example of that holy man whose fame for sanctity is celebrated in the Lives of the Fathers: he did not refuse to receive from a beast the hide of an unknown [Col. 0537B] animal which it offered him as a gift, as you know better, from its hunting, for the illumination of its young.

As for your name—which indeed you forbade us to mention—we have resolved to exalt and proclaim it everywhere, according to that Gospel saying: “The more he charged them, the more they proclaimed it, saying: He has done all things well” (Mark 7). For we consider it unworthy that such a cultivation of words should lack its author’s authority, and that writings which, because we read that they are particularly yours, deserve greater favour should be recited as though apocryphal. Your name will nevertheless be kept secret as regards your conscience inwardly before God; outwardly, however, it shall be public for the sake of your reputation with [Col. 0537C] others. May your holy and most dear fatherhood always prosper in all things, unto length of days.

## LETTER 280. TO HUGH, BISHOP, AND THE CHAPTER OF ORLÉANS

He asks that certain abuses which had sprung up in the church of Saint Evurtius be corrected.

The church of Saint Evurtius, a special daughter of the Holy See, has hitherto deserved, by ancient and approved custom, to be fostered through you and your predecessors with temporal benefits and refreshed with spiritual sacraments.

> [Note: [Col. 0537D] The church of Saint Evurtius at Orléans was, by papal diplomas, under the protection and patronage of the Holy Apostolic See; for this reason he calls it a special daughter of the Holy See.]

It is itself bound to you, as it were in a spiritual relation of giving and receiving, both to furnish solace to the sick and to provide burial for the dead. Repay the offices of paternal consolation to one that is sick, for its weakness is most severe and its disease has gained strength unto despair and death unless it is raised up by your swift counsel and assistance [Col. 0537D].

It is your church: for you it will die or live. It concerns you to take part in its counsels. Its head is sick, its heart mournful, its limbs numb and weak, accustomed more to decline than to advancement. They rashly cast aside regular discipline and shamelessly despise it. Among them the old are [Col. 0538A] excluded and exiled, the young rule and command, and the unlearned usurp the office of teaching. Those to whom the administration of the Church’s small resources has been entrusted squander them uselessly; striving to please people rather than God, they purchase the favour of great men through ambitious expenditure.

This would be tolerable if they preserved the regular observance of their profession and order; if, as befits saints, they consecrated and offered in God’s sacrifice seriousness of character, maturity of conduct, and honourableness of person. But now, prodigal even of their reputation and insecure in conscience, inwardly and outwardly they seem neither to fear the Lord nor to respect men. I do not speak of all: the Lord knows those whom he has chosen; each person’s deeds prove his merits.

Come to meet such evils, [Col. 0538B] Father, and with all your strength rebuke the restless, restrain the proud, and curb the undisciplined. To you, Father Hugh, upon whom this care and labour rests by reason of the pastoral office entrusted to you, I pour out earnest prayers with sighing and sobbing: assume the zeal of Mattathias and Phinehas, and, casting aside human favour, compel the children of contradiction and disobedience, willing or unwilling, to observe their order.

For it will be required of you that you uproot and destroy, build and plant; rebuke and reprove with all authority. Let not those things which blind the eyes of the wise move you, lest the corrupters of the order and lovers of themselves—who make provision for the flesh in its desires—put their trust in the corruption of money. Visit the tomb of your uncle,

> [Note: [Col. 0537D] Namely Manasses of Garlande, whom we have said was buried in the midst of the chapter-house of Saint Evurtius.]

and in that community entrusted to you cut away [Col. 0538C] the putrid flesh and burn with the cautery of correction what you cannot heal with the fomentation of exhortation.

I ask you to ensure that the letter which I send on this matter

> [Note: [Col. 0538D] This letter is the very same as that found under the following number, 281.]

to the abbot and his chapter is delivered by two of your canons, lest some should perhaps bury or suppress it so that it cannot be seen by the others.

## LETTER 281. TO BERTER, ABBOT, AND THE CHAPTER OF SAINT EVURTIUS

He rebukes the same abbot because he neglects the duties of his office.

I believed that two consolations remained to me: the memory of the virgin Geneviève and of Blessed Evurtius the confessor, whose alternating sight delighted me and whose example invited me. With joyful steps of thought I walked [Col. 0538D] both upon the virgin’s hill and upon the confessor’s plain, when in each place I encountered a holy community, a delightful shoot, a chaste generation joined in charity, terrible as an army arrayed in order.

But now, driven by grievous reports, like one with a broken foot, limping and half-blind with one eye put out, I am drawn back from the vineyards of Engaddi

> [Note: [Col. 0538D] Formerly the abbey of Saint Evurtius lay outside the walls of the city of Orléans and was surrounded by vineyards. The abbey of Saint Geneviève at Paris stands on the summit of a hill.]

to the rich and fertile mountain, where tranquil rest and restful tranquillity are found. Woe to me in the last days [Col. 0539A] of my life, when I hear that my inward parts are troubled in you: that you envy one another, quarrel, rise to appeals, and flee from unity of spirit and the bond of peace!

Who would not grieve to see old men exiled among you, youths reigning, beginners usurping instruction, and the soft usurping discipline? I might almost say what is spoken through the prophet: “Children shall be their princes, and effeminate persons shall rule over them” (Isaiah 3). Yours is the fault, Abbot: you are like the priest Eli, who either dare not rebuke undisciplined sons, do not know how to correct them, or neglect to reform them.

Your name, which means “son of thunder,” does not thunder over them; instead it weakens through flattery, softens through caressing, or corrupts through consent. Remember Solomon’s saying: “Have you daughters? Do not show [Col. 0539B] your face cheerful toward them” (Ecclesiasticus 7). Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty one (Psalm 44), so that those whom you ought to have led and instructed by your example may fear you rather than despise you.

O glorious and religious church of Blessed Evurtius, how far you have fallen from so great a height! You had nurtured cedars, and now you have been reduced even to thistles. From your bosom the holy Fathers and pastors took for themselves Ambrose of Bourges, Satyrus of Sancerre, Bartholomew of Noyon, and—if I may speak foolishly—Geneviève of Paris.

> [Note: [Col. 0539D] Four abbots were taken from the community of Saint Evurtius at Orléans: namely Geoffrey of Saint Satyre at Sancerre, Hugh of Saint Bartholomew at Noyon, N. of Saint Ambrose at Bourges, and Stephen of Saint Geneviève at Paris.]

Truly they can say, brother Abbot, concerning the house entrusted to you: “I passed by the field of the sluggard, and behold, thorns and nettles had filled it all” (Proverbs 24). Use the counsel of better and older men. Do not follow the footsteps of Rehoboam; remove from your intimacy [Col. 0539C] those whose company wounds both the reputation of your name and the dignity of the Church.

I too, who am still a novice canon and a brother of your church, and who ought not to be excluded from your counsels, admonish, advise, and exhort you to order your house differently. Do not take masters of the order from the footstool—men whom it does not become to sit with the elders and masters. This also is disgraceful to you: your debts have grown beyond measure into immensity, though no evident cause excuses you; rather, the abundant fertility of your crops accuses you.

## LETTER 282. TO HUGH, BISHOP OF ORLÉANS

He testifies that the church of Saint Evurtius is under no obligation to provide procuration for the bishop of Orléans.

[Col. 0539D]

To the venerable lord and Father HUGH, by God’s grace bishop of Orléans; to his most dear friends and lords, the dean and chapter of Holy Cross; and to all to whom these present letters shall come: STEPHEN, by God’s permission humble minister of the Church of Tournai, greeting in the Lord.

[Col. 0540A] What we have seen and heard and know, we wish and ought to testify by faithful assertion. Nearly forty-five years have passed since, by God’s will, we received the religious habit in the church of Blessed Evurtius under the regular order. From that time our lords and Fathers, the bishops of Orléans, afforded such tranquillity, quiet, and peace to the church of the aforesaid confessor that they received no procuration at all, either in its head or its members, nor, to use common speech, lodging or *gistum*.

> [Note: [Col. 0539D] Elsewhere we have discussed the right of procuration or lodging which bishops possessed in certain monasteries or in their parishes and houses. [Col. 0540D]]

We also once saw the lord Manasses, bishop of good memory, when it pleased him to come to dine in the church, bringing through his servants the food and whatever was necessary for him at table. Therefore, Fathers and bishops, we beseech your fatherhood [Col. 0540B] to foster the aforesaid church—which is yours—with counsel and to defend it with assistance; and henceforth to demand from it or its members no procurations, oppressions, or exactions against the salvation of your soul.

## LETTER 283. TO POPE CLEMENT III

He gives the supreme pontiff an account of what he did against the bishop of Troyes, by virtue of an apostolic mandate entrusted to him, Dean Berner, and Peter the cantor of Paris.

Let your fatherhood know that we received your mandate in this form:

> “CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the abbot of Saint Geneviève, the dean, and the cantor of Paris: greeting and [Col. 0540C] apostolic blessing.
>
> “We wish it to come to your knowledge that our venerable brother, the bishop of Troyes, was once and again commanded by the Apostolic See, and ordered, in the parish church of Marigny,
>
> > [Note: [Col. 0540D] A village in the diocese of Troyes, commonly called Marigny, to which regular canons from the community of Saint Lupus had been assigned to administer the parish church; Manasses, bishop of Troyes, refused to admit them.]
>
> “while preserving all his rights, to admit regular canons, who should establish there, in accordance with the pious desire of the founders, the order of religious life and serve almighty God under regular discipline. Yet the aforesaid bishop could neither be moved by love of religion nor softened by apostolic commands [Col. 0540D] to turn from the hardness which he is accustomed to show in fulfilling apostolic mandates to the kindness of charity, and to grant the favour of consent to the pious petition and praiseworthy vow of the petitioner.
>
> “We have therefore commanded your discretion by apostolic letters diligently to admonish and induce him to receive, as he has so often been commanded, regular canons from the church of Saint Lupus at Troyes, and establish them in the aforesaid church, all the rights of diocesan jurisdiction being preserved. Through them the order of religion may be extended and increased, and he may satisfy both apostolic commands and the founder’s [Col. 0541A] desire. If, within thirty days after your admonition, he does not freely choose to do this, you shall compel him, by our authority and without impediment of appeal, through ecclesiastical censure, to carry this out before you. If all of you cannot be present for its execution, nevertheless let two of you carry it out. Given at the Lateran, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July, in the first year of our pontificate.”

Desiring, therefore, to carry your mandate into effect, we laboured to induce the aforesaid bishop by admonitions, prayers, and even a stricter command, that, for the increase of divine religion, in reverence for the Apostolic See, and in regard for our prayers and admonitions, he should bring your mandate to effect.

[Col. 0541B] But although he was repeatedly admonished and requested, he refused to obey either prayers, admonitions, or finally our command—though in this matter we acted in your place. Having taken counsel with wise and discerning men, we suspended him from every episcopal office as contumacious and as a despiser of the mandate sent from the Apostolic See. We informed our metropolitan, his archbishop of Sens, and the dean and chapter of the church of Troyes, and by your authority commanded them to regard him as suspended.

By authority of the Roman See we commanded the abbot of the aforesaid place to introduce his canons into the aforesaid church, relying on your authority and ours, notwithstanding any pretext [Col. 0541C] or opposition of the bishop; and we invested those canons with that church, all episcopal rights nevertheless being preserved. We judged it right to report the course of this affair to the ears of your holiness, humbly asking and entreating you to approve and confirm our investiture, made by your authority, as valid. For by being “compelled through ecclesiastical censure” we understand nothing other than a sentence of excommunication or suspension.

## LETTER 284

He pleads for a certain cleric who had committed a grave offence.

> [Note: [Col. 0541D] This letter is incomplete; its beginning is lacking.]

An ecclesiastical judge ought to follow—and although we could adduce much for the restoration of one who has fallen in this manner, we write not to dispute but to entreat: since in the general chapter you promised him exercise of the order he had received, do not alter the first sentence, lest one faint-hearted be swallowed up by sorrow; lest, despairing, he perish; lest, disobedient and grieving, he deserve to die.

We believe that this dispensation can be made without loss, so that neither the laws are thrown into confusion nor the canons offended. Let the tearful sighs of an afflicted brother, certain dangers, and uncertain remedies move the bosom of your fatherhood [Col. 0542A]. If, in strictness, you remove from him the exercise of his office, at least permit him to serve God among monks as a cleric wearing a monk’s habit—which you may safely do—until the time comes to show him mercy.

## LETTER 285. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS

He complains of the disputes and quarrels that arose among the regular canons of Saint Evurtius at Orléans.

To the most holy Father, the lord archbishop of Reims.

When I came, I found my mother, the church of Blessed Evurtius, disturbed by the hostility of certain persons. Moved by their disturbances, I grieved no less at the deceits of one party than at the sufferings of both. I beseech you, Father, my sole consolation and support [Col. 0542B], to write to the abbot and community that they may not cast down the form of their customary religious life into the disgrace of lax deformity; and that those who ought to be encouraged and armed only with prayers and tears may not, impatient of peace, rush to the weapons of quarrels.

## LETTER 236. 

He declares that the abbey of Saint Bartholomew at Noyon is bound by no right toward the bishop of Tournai.

We make known to all of you that the church of Saint Bartholomew at Noyon received us as a brother and canon before we were promoted to the abbey of Saint Geneviève at Paris, or even, by God’s grace, transferred to the episcopal see of the Church of Tournai. For this reason, by virtue of the aforesaid fraternity and in view of [Col. 0542C] our common order—not by right of any custom—that same church at times regarded us with every devotion and kindness, and showed us grace and honour.

Therefore, wishing to provide for the future security of that church, and unwilling that what it bestowed upon us from grace and devotion should in any way be turned into a right of custom, we make known to present and future alike, and affirm under the testimony of this present writing, that by reason of pontifical jurisdiction we neither have demanded nor ought to demand from the aforesaid church any procuration or anything else, just as our predecessors did not demand it. This is without prejudice to the fact that its abbot is bound to attend our synod as long as he holds the altar of [Col. 0542D] Bouinchora, or anything else within our bishopric which owes attendance at the synod; he shall also be bound to pay us *sumniatae*, as the neighbouring churches are bound to do.

> [Note: [Col. 0541D] This word has the same meaning as *sonnia*, *sunnia*, or *saunia* among the ancients, denoting certain assemblies and pleas; commonly, *saunes*. [Col. 0542D]]

Lest the oft-mentioned church of Saint Bartholomew should in future suffer any injury or burden on these grounds, we caused this present charter to be drawn up and confirmed with our seal.

Done in the year of the Lord 1194, the third year of our consecration.

# SUPPLEMENT TO THE LETTERS OF STEPHEN OF TOURNAI

(*Notices of the manuscripts of the Royal Library*, p. 66.—See above, col. 306, what M. Brial prefaced concerning these unpublished letters.)

[Col. 0543]

## I. To a Lord and Friend, That He Should Not Heed the Slander of the Envious

[Col. 0543A]

Some are accustomed to be angered by the successes of others, in which they perceive themselves to have failed, and they envy the advancement of others. Amid these things the steadfastness of the elect remains unmoved; long-suffering rises into glory; perseverance does not succumb; and, as the envy of detractors gradually fails, the merits of the perfected increase.

If you have ever experienced these things either in others or in yourself, make yourself a stranger to the agreement and company of such people, for it is no novelty: “Evil conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Corinthians 15). Amid these things, I, your devoted clerk, bow down and reverence the footsteps of your goodwill, fleeing the image of all ingratitude [Col. 0543B] and avoiding every failure of devotion toward your benefits.

## II. To Gregory VIII, Supreme Pontiff—On Behalf of the Clerics of Grandmont

(Year 1187.)

At your elevation, Father, we believe heaven and earth rejoice, confidently presuming that by God’s grace salvation is directed in your hand, poverty of spirit rises again, and the horns of sinners are broken. At the first sound of this report, ambition seated upon the corruption of money trembled; the harshness of denunciation subsided; avarice was afraid; envy was suffused with pallor; excess sought excuse, dissipation flight, and impurity a hiding-place [Col. 0543C].

In short, every contract and every unlawful bargain fears utter destruction, since so great a successor of Peter will confront them as a true judge and severe avenger. Rejoicing in the delights of this hope, we, a certain small portion of your faithful, earnestly entreat you on behalf of the prior

> [Note: [Col. 0543C] William of Trahiniac.]

and clerics of Grandmont. Through the cunning, power, and pride of the *conversi*—not to say the perverse—they have been made a spectacle to angels and men. Beggars and exiles, with outside support now failing, they are continually worn down by hunger in a few cells from which they daily await expulsion, in hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness.

Their sole and supreme hope rests upon [Col. 0544A] your good pleasure: that you, who until now have benevolently covered them with the bowels of compassion and counsel, may now generously extend to them breasts of consolation and aid. If it please you, grant full restoration, with the prior’s consent—a simple and modest man, cast down because of discipline, rejected because of humility, and fraudulently as well as violently coerced and expelled because of the fatherly care he showed toward the clerics. Let apostolic authority compel the *conversi* to obey their pastor. By this remedy we believe that certain authors of that greater conspiracy will go elsewhere, choosing to perish rather than submit, and to depart rather than obey.

Once these have departed, the rest will easily become quiet, for they are neither swollen with such great pride nor insolent through such great wealth. And because the error of pretence has grown so powerful in that irregular order that it may be called a sect rather than a religious order, let your holy fatherhood see to it that no shameful reform is made among them, under a semblance of peace and concord, by secular persons or powerful laymen—which the *conversi* urgently seek—lest, if that should happen, the last error become worse than the former [Col. 0544B].

Rather, undertake yourself, if possible, this care and concern for correcting and reforming that order; or entrust it to religious men trained in regular discipline. Among them, if it please you, let [Geranimus], abbot of Saint Victor, a religious man who fears God, together with those whom he has taken with him, be either the foremost or one among the foremost, by whose help and work a fixed rule of order may be imposed upon those disorderly men.

And since sons ought to be free, let the freedom of clerics not obey; let the servile element be subject, obedient, and silent; let Uzziah not usurp priestly offices. This, Father, must be observed and guarded: lest, if perhaps according to their usual practice three or four clerics are joined in the cells to twelve or fifteen laymen, the few be oppressed by the multitude and simplicity be overthrown by cunning [Col. 0544C]. Fare well, Father.

## III. To Pope Clement III—On the Same Matter

(Year 1188.)

Amid the pressures and distresses which the Church suffers in these days, Father, she grieves most deeply for her clerics [Col. 0545A], whose glorious name and order the apostles established, the doctors formed, and princes exalted. Today the sons of Levi are tithed; Aaron pays unjust dues; nor is Melchizedek free from tribute.

This common affliction might somehow be endured if Egyptians were oppressed by the means through which Hebrews are despoiled. But since the Most High does not receive a sacrifice from robbery, he permits the tributes of needy souls, extorted with brutality, to expire fruitlessly.

Added to the spur and accumulation of our groaning and sighing—we who are clerics called into the Lord’s portion—is the fact that we see one of Israel’s tribes perish in the community of Grandmont. There the *conversi*, in an inverted—indeed, I might say perverted—order, rule the ministers of the altar, so that the house [Col. 0545B] hangs upside down, oxen are put before the plough, an unlearned person teaches a cleric, and a layman commands a priest.

Today the Scripture is fulfilled which says: “Their clerics shall not profit them.” Driven from their cells, begging for others’ support, exiles, half-naked, despised, and satiated with reproaches, they are displayed as a spectacle to us and as a laughing-stock to strangers. Let the tearful sighs, certain dangers, and uncertain counsels of so many and such great exiles move your clemency, merciful Father. Spread out your fatherly bosom to sons who languish and are near to perishing, lest those who ought to be free by the dignity of their order and by the order of their dignity return to their former servitude.

These are the common prayers of all the clerics of the Gallican Church: that in that irregular order [Col. 0545C] the few may not be swallowed up by the multitude, poverty by power, and simplicity overthrown by cunning. May your holiness prosper for long, Father.

## IV. To Lord Soffred, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church

Much has accrued to me, and indeed much has succeeded for me, since you made me a participant in your favour. Although I do not deserve its fullness, I shall not grieve in fullness [perhaps: “repent in fullness”]. I confess that there is no one whose memory I recall more often or cultivate more devotedly. When its remnants keep a feast-day for me, I always gather what is fruitful and drive away what is sorrowful.

[Col. 0545D] My lord was with me late in conversation, cheerful at table, severe in neither, and companionable in both; neither tending toward wantonness nor withdrawing from joy. He viewed my jokes without mocking them; he heard my serious remarks with attention. He thought more highly of me than I, who knew myself better, either dared to trust or presumed to confess.

These things continually move and admonish my littleness to erect, in the ark of my heart, a pleasant theatre of your memory, through which I may walk with you and delight in the sole consolation of remembrance. I ask, if it please you, that you present to the lord pope whatever petitions of ours seek justice, and obtain judges for us concerning justice.

## V. To the Brothers of the Charterhouse, for the Reception of a Certain Cleric: Greeting and the Best Part Chosen by Mary

[Col. 0546A]

We ought to admire the Carthusian order, sublime and neighbour to the stars, though we cannot imitate it; worshipping him in his saints, who fed Elijah in the wilderness and Daniel in prison, preserving and instructing individuals in their cells and all together in their communities. Happy are those who aspire to men of so high a summit; happier those who breathe with them; happiest those who breathe their last among them.

The last of the last strengthen the first and the middle, when by a blessed end they complete their perseverance, provoke by their example, and console by their memory their brothers still journeying in the body. [Col. 0546B] Among those aspiring and desiring union with your holy fellowship, we commend to you John, bearer of this letter, who burns with zeal for religion. If we count his years, he appears a youth; if we reckon his merits, an old man.

We believe that he has dashed his first impulses against the rock, regarded the things of the world as dung, and, according to the grace granted him by God, has either fled or driven away the threefold concupiscence. He has laid upon himself the Lord’s light yoke and sweet burden, living in the wilderness with another, not under another. Formed by his example and strengthened by his testimony, he has offered us no small grounds for hope in the resolve he has conceived: to begin at once and persevere steadfastly.

With respect to religious habit or observance, he has bound himself to no one; he has made profession to no one, promised stability of place to no one, and promised obedience to no one. Free, that he may be bound by you, he comes, so that, like Isaac, bound by the bonds of your obedience and discipline, he may be offered on your holy mountain, which the Lord sees, as a true sacrifice pleasing to God and perfect [Col. 0546C].

He has received the grade of deacon from the lord archbishop of Sens, the seventh order, which singularly surpasses those preceding it. If it please God and he himself deserves by God’s grace to enter your sacred community, he seeks and awaits reception among you. We pour out prayers to your holiness that you may meet the thirsty man with loaves and open to him when he knocks, lest, perhaps—far be it!—if he finds you hard in this petition, the bruised reed [Col. 0546D] be broken in him and the smoking flax extinguished.

## VI. To the Abbot of Cîteaux, on Behalf of a Certain Monk

Ignorance is excusable when it is usually caused either by chance dependent on fortune’s snares or by the weakness of age. It departs so far from malice that it approaches gentleness; it approaches pardon in such a manner that it does not kindle severity. A sacrifice from fat, fine flour mixed with oil, and mercy exalting itself over judgment commend it.

These considerations concerning your present son, poor in spirit, move us and invite us, not unwillingly, to urge you toward mercy. Under age, not yet having reached his seventh year—an age at which offences ought not to be punished—he fell into misfortune, grieving and against his will. We examined the account of it in letters of his lord bishop of Chartres, which he had sent to the lord bishop of Albano, legate of the Apostolic See; and we caused them to be sealed with our seal together with this present charter.

[Col. 0547A] Since in both legal affairs and offences discerning judges consider age, intention, cause, place, manner, necessity, and the other circumstances which either mitigate strictness or admit dispensation, let your mercy set before itself a boy not yet seven years old, not yet capable of deceit, not yet fit even for making contracts or culpable in offences. In childish levity he shot an arrow into the air; and, flying and driven by the noonday demon, it wounded a sleeping boy whom the innocent archer did not know.

To this is added that the person so wounded was cut for an acute condition by a surgeon who, perhaps through inexperience—as often happens—cut him wrongly. Either of these, if it caused his death, exonerates the innocent archer [Col. 0547B].

An ecclesiastical judge ought to follow the more merciful course in doubtful matters. Although we could adduce much for the restoration of one who has fallen in this manner, we write not to dispute but to entreat: since in the general chapter you permitted him the exercise of the order he had received, do not alter the first sentence, lest one faint-hearted be swallowed up by sorrow; lest, despairing, he perish; lest, disobedient and grieving, he deserve to die.

We believe that this dispensation can be made without loss, so that neither the laws are thrown into confusion nor the canons offended. Let the tearful sighs of an afflicted brother, certain dangers, and uncertain remedies move the bosom of your fatherhood [Col. 0547C]. If, in strictness, you remove from him the exercise of his office, at least permit him to serve God among monks as a cleric in a monk’s habit—which you can safely do—until the time comes to show him mercy.

## VII. To John, Son of the Chancellor of the Noble City

Ancient friendships ought neither to be cast aside with contempt, weighed down with disdain, nor erased by forgetfulness. They wish to be increased, not diminished; strengthened, not destroyed. By their intercourse we were once so united that each wished both to sympathize with the other in adversity and rejoice with the other in prosperity.

[Col. 0547D] Warned and moved by this confidence, I beseech you, through that ancient bond of mutual fellowship and affection, to offer frequent prayers for me to your lord Father, chancellor of the holy City, a man whom we love in Christ, that he may receive kindly and handle generously the affair which I have communicated to him by my letters. By his counsel and assistance may he free me from an unjust and deceitful man who, pursuing and harassing me with his friends, thirsts for my blood and does not cease to disturb my peace.

## VIII. To Lord Peter, Bishop of Arras

When recently we were in the northern regions, whence every evil is opened out (Jeremiah 1), and had entered the torrent [Col. 0548A] that cannot be forded, a contrary wind suddenly blew in my ears. At its sound my spirit was distressed and my heart troubled within me. Triflers, cobblers of tales, spread among the people that you were burdened with such grave illness that you had reached the extremity of sickness’s danger.

I was alarmed and grieved, and was not without fever when that fever possessed you. When the report turned to its contrary and I received certain news of your recovery, I gave thanks to the Saviour, who healed two in one and made one in two. Now at last a clearer day has shone forth, and the brightness of congratulation swallows up the cloud of sorrow; thus I have begun, as it were, to breathe again concerning you and in you.

I send you my chaplain, that he may bring you the service of greeting and bring back to me the consolation [Col. 0548B] of your health. Through him I advise you to take counsel for me, your friend, and concerning the affair which he will explain to you on my behalf, to assist me as is useful and generously instruct me as to what is expedient for me, what is fitting, and what may help or harm.

## IX. To Peter, Bishop of Arras
Recently, your Holiness was pleased to inquire of us concerning the condition of our city, while we were in the whirl of tempest, in the smoke of darkness, between the critical days of illness and recovery. We replied as the circumstances then allowed. Subsequently, by a monetary outlay we beneficially met the danger of surrender and destruction; shut in on every side by enemies and wholly deprived of human aid, we have neither, as we wrote back to you, free permission to leave [Col. 0548C] nor to enter. Wounded with us by the same charity with which we too are wounded for you, in that distress of ours you drank deeply with us from the cup of brotherly suffering. We ask you to inform us, by a secret bearer of your letters, of your own condition, of the lord king, of your city, of the lord of Reims, of the count’s attack and advance, and of Fortune’s play concerning you and yours—would that it be peaceful!—answering sheet for sheet.

### X. To William, Archbishop of Reims, concerning the Church of Saint Martin of Tournai

Our lowliness cries into the ears of the Lord of Hosts against the shameless insolence of certain monks; and our groans—which ought to move not only earth but heaven—seek to have your zeal roused and armed against the sons of contradiction and disobedience. By your authority and command, Father, we went to the monastery of Saint Martin, taking with us the abbots [Walter] of Saint-Amand and [Roger] of Cysoing, equipped to correct the foul notoriety under which Abbot [John] and some of the younger monks grievously laboured. We proceeded as far as we could, but made no progress: as though washing a brick, sowing on sand, or casting an anchor into the abyss.

A few days later, before us and the lord [Peter], Bishop of Arras, in the presence of the greater part of our chapter, the abbot swore that he would abide by our direction. The Bishop of Arras composed, explained, and prescribed the form of the oath [Col. 0549A]. The command was honourable, but burdensome to a dishonourable man: a command which not only the abbot, but every person professing the religious life, is bound to observe even without an oath, especially that henceforth he should live continently, according to the grace bestowed on him by God.

A few days after this, without our knowledge, the said abbot brought with him three abbots from the diocese of Arras: namely, [Simon] of Anchin, [Stephen] of Marchiennes, and [Arnulf] of Vicogne. In our diocese and in our monastery, by their counsel and authority, they caused a sacrilegious excommunication to be pronounced against the supreme pontiff, against your person, and against our lowliness; and they themselves pronounced it with the abbot. Namely, they decreed that none of the monks [Col. 0549B] of Saint Martin should reveal or report to you or to us anything concerning the condition of the monastery or matters pertaining to its correction.

The convent also confessed this in chapter, with the abbot present among us, except that they said neither you nor we had been named specifically in that excommunication, but that the sentence had generally forbidden the revelation to anyone of what justice required concerning the condition of the monastery. Let your Holiness consider how gravely those abbots have offended and in what manner they should be punished by you, since they have presumed thus to diminish your authority and to injure our lowliness.

At length the abbot of Anchin, on the pretext of certain letters—utterly false letters, emanating from the workshop of the craftsmen who were named to you—without our knowledge and without our having seen the letters themselves, absolved the aforesaid abbot of Saint Martin from his holy and religious oath [Col. 0549C], so that he who had sworn to preserve chastity, as though now released from his oath, with his belt already loosened and a pit made, might safely frequent brothels.

The remaining matters not contained in this writing will be supplied orally by your familiar and cleric, the abbot of Cysoing. Meanwhile, Father, we ask your Holiness that, should the aforesaid abbot, or anyone with him or on his behalf, come to you, their persuasions and promises may not easily circumvent or deceive your religious integrity, as you once promised us; lest perhaps—God forbid!—we have run as though toward no goal and fought [Col. 0549D] as though beating the air.

### XI. To John, Abbot of Saint Geneviève at Paris

Unwillingly we cry out; deceived, we complain; injured, we groan and grieve. We have become a mockery to all your people, their song all day long. The smoke of an intolerable disgrace, both ours and yours, like a stench rising from our corpses, provokes men to indignation and angels to vengeance.
