“Is this,” they ask, “your religion of the hill, the purity of your regulars, the chastity and honour of the virgin Geneviève: to gather crowds of boys not yet of age, entice them with little gifts, shut them in a chamber by day, and place them in a bed by night?” What shall we answer to this, when it is true? With what paint of words [Col. 0550A] shall we excuse excuses amid these evils? With what covering shall we conceal the face of our unchastity?

If these things were done in secret, the wound would be bearable, since they might either be overlooked, suppressed, or hidden. But now, even if men were silent, the timbers would speak and the stones cry out. We are pointed at with the finger, mocked with curled nostrils, driven off with laughter and guffaws. Laymen condemn us in the streets; clerics insult us in churches; boys are beaten in schools; little women chatter in their workshops. The injuries inflicted upon us by that detestable man Servandus, though monstrous, we somehow endure; the disgrace we cannot endure.

We beg and entreat you, dearest brother, by the virtue of obedience to command Brother Marcellus—whom we are certain is a son of honour and modesty, and who only at last learned all these things with us, as the poet says, “He will be the last to know the disgrace of his household”—[Col. 0550B] to set each matter before you, conceal nothing, and excuse nothing; for you ought neither to favour anyone who conceals nor to believe anyone who excuses. Receive and restore our very heart, and without delay send back Brother M., who serves us faithfully and honourably and whose absence we cannot long endure.

### XII. To John, Abbot of Saint Geneviève at Paris

Struck inwardly by grief of heart, I say: “What I have written, I have written” (John 19). I shall not alter it or retract it, unless perhaps continuous pain compels me to do so by that mode which is called amplification [Col. 0550C].

O incorrupt holiness! O chaste generation! O sacred dwelling of the modest hill, the hill in which God has been pleased to dwell! Who has endeavoured to bewitch you, to make you foolish, to solicit you, so that you receive into your college an idol of manifest foulness and public crime, whose infamy drags us down to hell, so that both I and my whole household at Tournai may be called princes of Sodom and a people of Gomorrah?

This mournful song is cast back upon our entire Church: not an epithalamium, but an epitaph, as though for our chastity already foul and buried. Let no one deceive you. For if he returns to the house from which he was cast out, which at his departure was swept and adorned as with brooms, and enters it, the last error will be worse than the former [Col. 0550D].

### XIII. To a Certain Canon of Tournai

Clouds suddenly change: those driven by the dreadful north wind are afterwards dissolved and poured forth by the wet south wind. Times change, and affairs change; truth, however, does not change.

A certain clerk of Lord Aldebrandinus, nephew of the lord pope, came to us, bringing letters of the lord pope himself and of [Anselm], bishop-elect of Meaux, addressed to us and to our chapter, and attempting to invalidate and revoke the grant of the prebend which we conferred upon you with all solemnity. Let your discretion consider what is expedient for us and for you in this matter [Col. 0551A], since we neither ought nor wish to act against our own deed, yet do not dare to kick against the goad against the lord pope.

### XIV. To the Lord of Reims

The bosom of your benevolence, Father, by the grace of God poured into you, lies so open to the small together with the great that it neither admits rebels nor sends away the obedient. There, those who ask receive, those who seek find, and to those who knock it is opened (Matt. 7).

In the strength of this hope I would have hastened to you, fallen at your feet, and lifted my eyes to the mountain of your exalted rank, had not the many inconveniences that surround an old man hindered me in these last days. I implore, writing with a trembling hand what I would scarcely dare to utter with a timid tongue [Col. 0551B], and offer fervent prayers to your Holiness for my most dear son and chaplain M. [Marcellus], whom for sixteen years I have nourished and instructed in every honourable quality and in regular discipline: that you may kindly receive and favourably confirm him upon the presentation of the canons of Cysoing, since they have canonically elected him, by the common assent of all and the individual assent of each.

If we consider his years, he is young; if the merits of his virtue, he is mature and old. With a sound conscience, God being witness, I say to you that he is commendable for purity of body, gravity of character, and skill in letters.

### XV. Privilege concerning the Prebend of the Chaplaincy of the Bishop of Tournai

[Col. 0551C]

We are taught by the sacred authorities of the Fathers, and in right faith believe and hold, that the souls of faithful departed persons who died confessing the Holy Trinity, and are commended to God by the prayers of the Church and the offering of the Lord’s Body, obtain eternal rest.

But we, who by divine power and not by our own merits have been placed in a higher rank, must prove by example what we preach to others in word. Therefore we wish it to be known to future as well as present persons that, mindful of our condition and hoping in the mercy of the Lord, with the assent of our chapter we establish a perpetual chaplain in the oratory of Saint Vincent the martyr [Col. 0551D]—which is the episcopal chapel, which we graciously built at great expense, and in which we obtained, by the authority of the lord king and not without much opposition from laymen, a free entrance into the greater church that the Bishop of Tournai had previously been unable to have.

This chaplain, as our personal chaplain, shall celebrate Mass there each day for the souls of the bishops of Tournai and of other faithful departed persons, and shall include in that Mass a proper collect for the living bishop. Since the labourer is worthy of his wage, we have assigned the episcopal table to the aforesaid chaplain, so that he may receive from it suitable and honourable daily sustenance, whether the bishop is present or absent.

We have also assigned and granted him seven pounds in Flemish money [Col. 0552A], to be paid every year by the monastery of Saint-Bertin out of the rent which it owes yearly to the bishop, within twenty days after the Sunday of the Nativity, for the church of Lestrem, which with much labour and expense we recovered from lay control, the abbot of Saint-Bertin assisting and labouring with us.

And because we do not wish our mother church of Blessed Mary, or its brother canons, to have any ground for complaint against us on the occasion of this chaplaincy, we forbid the aforesaid chaplain, when the bishop is absent from the city, to receive parishioners of the churches of Tournai or their offerings. Upon the death of Gilo, to whom we first granted the chaplaincy, the bishop then in office shall appoint in his place another whom he chooses.

[Col. 0552B] Done in the chapter of Tournai, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1198.

### XVI. To the Abbot and Convent of Saint Geneviève the Virgin

To the praise and glory of God and the honour of our Blessed Virgin, our brother and yours, M. [Marcellus], has been elected abbot of the Church of Cysoing, by the common assent of all and the individual assent of each. Rejoice with us over this event, dearest brothers, and pray with us that what, by God’s will, has been well begun may be brought to a happy conclusion.

The canons of the aforesaid church come to you, asking that you restore and release to them as their abbot and appointed shepherd the man so unanimously elected. Together with them we ask that he whom we nurtured in his youth [Col. 0552C] may comfort us and be joined to us in our old age. We add this also to our prayers: because the times are dangerous and the outcomes of affairs are subject to uncertain fortune, preserve intact and grant to him, both spiritually and temporally, the brotherly and canonical fellowship which he has hitherto possessed alike in our church and yours.

### XVII. To the Same

Receive our very heart, most dear in Christ, and our common son and yours, M. [Marcellus], our chaplain, elected to the Church of Cysoing. Whatever he tells you on our behalf [Col. 0552D] concerning the recall and restoration to the bosom of your mother church of the brethren who, on our advice, had been temporarily removed on account of a certain boyish disturbance, carry it out both kindly and generously. For we are not sons of dissension or schism, but of love and peace.

And we ask you, dearest and most beloved brother, to come to us with our elect, that you may rejoice and exult with us at his blessing. For we desire to see you and to enjoy your presence in the Lord.

### XVIII. To the Lord of Tournai, from the Abbot of La Sauve-Majeure

To you, dearest lord father, as to a man venerable in every respect, a lord of great authority and an eminent teacher, our humility has thought fit to make known [Col. 0553A] that, to the honour of God and at his prompting—by whose inspiration right things are conceived and done—the blessed Gerald, special patron and founder of our monastery, was recently glorified by elevation under a decree of the Apostolic See. In accordance with the excellence of his merits and the miracles which the Lord has worked through him in our midst, the minds of all—clergy, people, and the eminent persons of our land—have been stirred. In addition to the day consecrated at his passing, they have established by common vows and earnest efforts that a solemn day be observed for him perpetually, at the time when, God willing, his sacred body will be elevated, around the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist.

Together with them, having experienced the greatness of his miracles, we hope that we may deserve to be raised up, both temporally and spiritually [Col. 0553B], by the frequent consolation of divine favour through his elevation. Therefore, since Scripture testifies that honey proceeds from the mouth of the wise, sweetness of honey is upon his tongue, and his lips are a dripping honeycomb (Prov. 16), we humbly ask you, in memory of the glorious confessor, to compose hymns of divine praise for us: namely antiphons and responsories. Thus, on his feast days, we may proclaim God our Lord as wondrous in his saint, magnify the merits of that saint with more solemn praises, and fittingly and devoutly take delight in his praises, together with those who particularly enjoy his protection [Col. 0553C].

We ask indulgence for our lowliness, that this request, so piously and humbly made, may not be imputed to us as presumption. We beg pardon for presuming to disturb your holy leisure and to trouble a mind occupied with many thoughts.

### XIX. To the Lord of Tournai, from the Abbot of La Sauve-Majeure and the Whole Convent

Your fiery utterance, lord, is intensely loved by your servants whose hearts it has set aflame; for it gave joy and gladness to our hearing. When your servants recently brought us the letters of sacred writing, after a greeting had first been offered, we were as though comforted; and, as though we had already obtained the fulfilment promised by your kindness, our soul, wounded by love, was filled as with marrow and fatness [Col. 0553D]. My mouth, now grateful for the benefits received, gave praise with exulting lips, so that the receipt of present gifts may make our expectation of future ones firm.

We give thanks to your condescension, which deigns to honour our humility with such honour and favour that you care for us and have looked upon the prayer of the humble and have not despised their petition. Indeed, the beautiful expressions in those same letters, in which you gave us hope, delight us greatly and rightly: in them we behold, as in a model, with what precious splendour the beauty and luminous body of the whole desired work ought alike to shine and to have force.

Therefore [Col. 0554A], since a good and just man, an imitator of God, whose faithful promise does not know how to render void the things that proceed from his lips, speaks once and does not repeat the same thing a second time (Job 33)—which we say subject to the more sacred mystery, revealed more perfectly to us by him who reveals mysteries concerning the sole and eternal generation of the Word—may our lord, we ask, show this mercy to his servants: that, by God’s will and his own gracious favour, what we desire may soon come to us, all the more ardently because the words of his mouth sound to us more fruitfully and eloquently.

Let therefore the word of your spiritual harmony sound like an organ of the Holy Spirit, so that your spirit, which dwells in the gardens, may make us hear its voice, for giving splendour to our celebrations and enlarging the name of holiness; so that, on the great day of the feast [Col. 0554B], holy praises of the most blessed man may give voice from among the rocks. Through you, whom the Lord has anticipated with blessings of sweetness, may we draw sweet melodies of speech from the sweetness of your grace and the inexhaustible treasures of wisdom, tasting in them how sweet the Lord is and how sweet to our palate are your words, above honey to our mouth.

For words that surpass others in authority and eloquence, and shine forth as the words of so great a man and lord of such majesty, will provide us with abundant edification and awaken devotion. Nor should your prudence in this matter humbly allege old age as an excuse, for among you and from you the memory of wisdom is immortal; and old age itself, as you know better, gains you trust [Col. 0554C] and favour. For Scripture says that wisdom is in the aged, and that the saints seek out the wisdom of the ancients (Ecclus. 39).

Hope firmly strengthens us to obtain these things, especially because you fully understand and can express what you understand, since the spirit of wisdom and understanding is itself with you as guide of speech. What could make noble magnanimity reluctant to undertake, or weary of what it has begun? Would that we may soon deserve to obtain what we so devoutly desire! Would that some among us—since perhaps it is not granted to all—may deserve to see your face, rejoice in your presence and in the words of your wisdom, and rightly take delight in contemplating so great a lord, whose special servants and devotees in all things within our power we profess ourselves to be [Col. 0554D]! May the Lord preserve your health, holy Father and dearest lord, for the welfare and honour of his whole holy Church, unto length of days!

### XX. To the Abbot and Sacred College of La Sauve-Majeure: Though Not Rustic nor Worldly, in the Service of the Lord, the Tail of a Sacrificial Victim and an Ankle-Length Tunic

May God forgive you, dearest brothers, for driving a weak man to mighty things, an old man to youthful rites, and one bound by episcopal duties to *κολακεύματα* (“flatteries”) and rhetorical periods. It ought to suffice as our excuse that I was unknown to you, distant in place, foreign in nation, language, and customs—especially since you have men more learned in France, more eloquent in Aquitaine, and readier in song and applause in Gascony [Col. 0555A].

Sharp are the wounds of charity. Its master is the Word of God, living and active and sharper than every two-edged sword: it rouses the sluggish, kindles the idle, converts rebels, and even subjects the unwilling and reluctant to its command. Your love has violently fixed its arrows in our heart, and, as though heaping coals upon our head, has inflamed us for those things which we were accustomed to stammer in childhood with saliva-dripping syllables.

Compelled by your charity, we have set down, with such diligence as we could and not such as we ought, the praises of your patron—and henceforth ours—the blessed Gerald, in antiphons, responsories, and hymns: perhaps a laughing-stock to our own people, a spectacle to you, a marvel to strangers [Col. 0555B]. If what is written pleases you, receive it without naming its author; if it displeases, either cut it apart with the knife or burn it in the flames.

Whatever your judgment may be concerning the approval or rejection of this most humble composition, remember Stephen the sinner, your friend; and make him a participant in your prayers, whom you wished to be a companion in the joys of the revelation and elevation of Saint Gerald. The bearer of this letter is our servant and belongs to our household. Passing through your region, he will, God willing, fulfil the vow he made to journey to Saint James. Through him we send you this business more faithfully and securely; and through him you may more safely and amicably communicate your will to us by your letters [Col. 0555C].

### XXI. To the Most Holy Lord and Father A. [Alexander], Supreme Pontiff, Brother Stephen, Humble Minister of Saint Geneviève at Paris, Greeting and Obedience with Every Devotion

My lord, the Archbishop of Sens, legate of the Apostolic See, committed last year to [Hugh], the venerable and religious abbot of La Cour-Dieu, and to us jointly, the investigation of a certain case between R., archdeacon, and R., an aged priest, concerning the church of Combres. The priest alleged that the aforesaid church had been given to him by the archdeacon; the archdeacon denied it. We asked the priest [Note: [Col. 0555D] Stephen is not speaking of himself, but in the person of Hugh of Noyon, abbot of Saint Bartholomew; he is to be considered the author of this letter.] [Col. 0555D] whether he possessed any proofs of the gift which he alleged. The priest asserted that he would prove it; he came on the appointed day, had no proofs, appealed, withdrew, and died.

After his death, his nephew—who said that the church had neither been given nor promised to him—approached your clemency and brought to the Archbishop of Sens certain letters fraudulently obtained from you, after another man had been instituted and ordained in the aforesaid church. These things [Col. 0556A] we saw and heard, Father, and our testimony is true. May your Holiness prosper, Father.

### XXII. To the Lord of Reims  
*(Year 1179)*

You know, Father, my infirmity; you know also my old age. These are what call me back even from the affairs of our Church. These are what impede and delay me. Therefore, with the utmost affection, I earnestly entreat your fatherhood, already known to me through many and great benefits, to excuse me in the ears of the lord pope, because I cannot undertake the labour of going to the council, when I can scarcely breathe.

Moreover, concerning our affair with Archdeacon Boniface [Note: [Col. 0555D] We believe him to be the Boniface, archdeacon of Noyon, of whom John of Salisbury speaks in Letter 234: the marquis of Cortemilia in the region of Montferrat [Col. 0556D], born of Agnes, sister of Simon, Bishop of Noyon, as is read in the genealogical fragment published in vol. XIV of *Rerum Francicarum*, p. 3.], I offer such prayers as I can to your kindness [Col. 0556B], that, as we place special confidence in you, we may experience your special favour at this juncture. For there is no one who can rescue us from the hand of so powerful an adversary unless, by your help and efforts, we may be freed from his assault.

### XXIII. To Peter, Bishop of Tusculum  
[Note: [Col. 0556D] Peter, priest-cardinal of Saint Chrysogonus and legate of the Apostolic See in France, was made Bishop of Tusculum in 1178.]  
*(Year 1180)*

You have gone before me, Father, with your blessings, and long ago extended to me a beneficent hand from a benevolent heart. Why has this happened to me: that my lord should open his eyes upon a dead dog and a single flea, and should choose to turn a mind intent upon divine occupations toward remembrance of me?

I confess that [Col. 0556C], when I received your letter from the hand of its bearer, my soul immediately melted, and the heat of burning desire stirred tears, signs of the joy conceived. For tears, contrary to the common rules of opinion, are accustomed either to be poured out for joy or held back for grief.

And every day, in a certain solemn theatre of recollection, I set before myself the spectacle of you, and said: “Behold, my lord, my beloved, my desired one will come; for I shall rejoice with joy in my soul and be comforted at the breasts of his consolation. I shall meet him; leaving the borders of the kingdom, I shall follow, overtake, and embrace him even to a people of another speech and an unknown tongue. Do you suppose that he will reject one who greets him, drive away one who falls at his feet [Col. 0556D], despise a visitor, refuse a kiss, or close his bosom? But if I know well his soul fruitful in virtues, then amid episcopal mitres and amid the sickles of the Roman summit he retains humility so deeply implanted that he is neither oppressed by glory nor oppresses the obscure; he so favours the humble that he resists the contentious.”

These are the remnants of my thoughts keeping festival concerning you—or rather, their first fruits and tithes—which I frequently offer in sacrifice, which I keep before my eyes, and which I neither delay to bring nor to offer before you [Col. 0557A].

As for your gracious inquiry concerning my condition and that of our Church, we humbly honour and reverently receive so great a token of concern and humility. Through God’s grace and your favour, all things prosper with us, and there is no hindrance and no Satan, except the illness of the lord king [Note: [Col. 0557D] King Louis VII, struck by paralysis in 1179, lay ill for a full year.], upon which hangs both the common danger of all and the individual danger of each.

Our fathers dwell with us in one mind in the house of God; while each submits to regular discipline, all advance. I desire only their perseverance in what they do, because uprightness answers to charity in their deeds, and charity to uprightness. I pray that the hour may come when I shall come to you, or you shall come into France [Col. 0557B]. May your Holiness prosper for ever!

### XXIV

I drink a joyful cup whenever I recall as my lord, raised to pontifical mitres in the Roman Church, sitting with princes and holding the throne of glory, the man whom I had honoured as a friend [Note: [Col. 0557D] This letter appears to have been written to Bernered, abbot of Saint-Crépin at Soissons, who became cardinal-bishop of Palestrina in 1179 and died in 1181.].

In this solemn theatre of my thoughts I walk not so much proudly as securely. Father, my confidence in you is armed and encouraged by your former intimacy, which though unworthy I had enjoyed: your sweet and gentle conversation, and the moral cultivation alike of your words and deeds. The remnants of all these things keep festival for me.

Father, I ask that amid the many and great affairs of the whole world resounding about you [Col. 0557C], amid the fervent and frequent tumults of cares, amid the cries of rich and poor, you may sometimes remember even your Stephen. For if I see you even on a lofty throne, I shall perhaps answer my thought—which reproaches me and, as it were, chastises the presumption of speaking to you—with that saying of Anianus, slightly altered in wording, perhaps more imprudently than shamelessly:

> Yet to me you will always be the friend you once were.

If John of Orléans [Note: [Col. 0557D] John, to whom Stephen wrote Letter 65 among those published by Molinet.] the secretary of the lord chancellor should solicit you concerning certain petitions of ours, whether to be presented or obtained, I beg you to take care that what we ask may be done.

### XXV. To the Revered Fathers and Lords N. [Nivelo], by the Grace of God Bishop of Soissons, and William, Dean of the Same Church, Brother Stephen of Saint Geneviève: Greeting and Faithful Service with Every Affection

[Col. 0557D]

The venerable old man and H. [Hugh], Abbot of Saint Bartholomew of Noyon, worthy of every honour, is anxious concerning the case between himself and the abbot of Saint-Crépin [Col. 0558A], which the lord pope entrusted to you. As he believes, he has been frustrated by delaying tactics from the opposing party. Judge him with the fairness fitting in this matter; and, lest he be further wearied by litigation and expense over so slight a matter, spare his infirmity and age.

On the day when we departed from you, an agreement was made in a defined form of peace by both parties, confirmed by priestly words as by an oath. If either party wishes to withdraw from it, this will be close to sacrilege and alien to the priesthood. The text of the settlement, written by us on that day, is as follows:

> With the consent of H. [Hugh], Abbot of Saint Bartholomew, and Abbot [Bernered] of Saint-Crépin, it was granted that Peter and Crispin, monks, and Nicholas, provost, should swear that, in good faith and without fraud, they will state the truth according to the investigation they have conducted and their own conscience, concerning both possession and the duration of possession, and also the right and ownership of the contested tithe, for both the church of Saint Bartholomew and the monastery of Saint-Crépin. According to what they swear, the Bishop of Soissons and the dean shall assign to each party its right.

This was done before you and the Dean of Reims, with William, Abbot of Saint-Léger, ourselves, the abbot of Saint-Crépin of La Cave, and many others present [Col. 0558B]. Therefore we pour out prayers to your holy fatherhood that, by the judicial authority entrusted to you by the lord pope in this affair, you may compel the parties not to depart from their promise and may ensure that it is completed without delay, in obedience to your command.

### XXVI

[Col. 0558C]

The sin of divination and the crime of idolatry, if what is written is true, we have learned to walk step for step with disobedience (1 Sam. 15); and a man guilty of treason in the city may be a schismatic in the monastery. Wherever it may occur, the Roman Church has customarily pursued this kind of thing more strictly, because she has more often experienced division and more intimately embraces unity.

We have heard that B. of Alenac is mortally infected with that plague: rebellious against his prior, he erects altar against altar; establishing his seat from the north, he endeavours improperly and monstrously to make the Church of the Benevento convent appear two-headed. An alien son persecutes his father; a diseased sheep persecutes its shepherd [Col. 0558D], infecting the rest with its contagion and making them worse.

Let your zeal rise against such persons; let justice be armed and severity blaze forth, so that those who despise the judgments of their superiors, compelled at last, may learn that permission to resist will not go unpunished.

[Note: [Col. 0558D] We infer that this letter was addressed to the bishop and canons of the Church of Limoges, because the Benevento priory of the Order of Saint Augustine was under their jurisdiction.]

I offer you these prayers on behalf of Prior Simon [Note: [Col. 0558D] Simon and his predecessors are unknown to the authors of *Gallia Christiana*, who compiled the catalogue of priors of the Benevento monastery, vol. II, col. 619.]; this sacrifice I offer, this encomium I chant.

### XXVII

[Col. 0559A]

On this coming Friday, Father, you set a day for us and certain knights [Note: [Col. 0559D] The author addresses William, Archbishop of Sens, together with the Bishop of Chartres, as seems clear to us and will seem so to anyone who carefully considers the author’s words. William held both bishoprics from 1168 to 1176.]. I was packing my little bundles and preparing household goods for the readiness of the journey and the progress of business, when I suddenly received your letters—always of happy omen to me—which compelled me, without violating your command, to come down to Blois.

Yet, lest my adversary rejoice and suppose that he has won because I am absent, and lest he consider me slothful and contemptuous of our right, I have sent this our brother, whom we have appointed our procurator in this matter, to act in our place, carrying letters of ratification from our chapter. With lips faltering in joy and fear, I recall to your memory the final word which you spoke to me concerning the purchase of a revenue for the perpetual commemoration of G. in our church [Col. 0559B], so that, if it pleases you, your word in which you gave me hope may soon be fulfilled.

We have reached an agreement with the seller, who consents to the contract. I beg you to inform us of whatever may seem good to you in this matter. We appoint this bearer of the present letter, our brother and fellow canon, as procurator; whatever is done by him before you, whether by settlement or judgment, we shall and do ratify.

### XXVIII  
*(Year 1168)*

We have heard of the investigation of the question entrusted to you by the lord pope [Col. 0559C], which appears to concern our lord [Manasses], Bishop of Orléans. Since we ought not fail the same lord bishop in his just cause, so far as the course of the matter in which we took part is known to us, we simply state and attest it to you. We remember that we wrote the same to the lord pope.

Just as we must not establish falsehood, so neither, when we are called upon, ought we to conceal the truth. What was done before our eyes, while we were present, we set forth and attest to you with straightforward intent; for we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard. After John, dean of Orléans, had been removed from the flock of men by an unworthy death [Note: [Col. 0560D] Toward the end of the year 1167 John, dean of Orléans, was put to death. Stephen of Tournai delivered an address concerning his funeral at the synod of Sens; it is published among his letters, p. 1.], the canons assembled on the day jointly appointed by the chapter for the election of another [Col. 0559D]. We too were summoned. As is usual in such matters, various and conflicting reports were circulated according to the diversity of men’s minds. At last it pleased all that we, taking with us the good and religious man Roger—who recently, in humility and of his own accord, resigned the burden of prelacy which he had long borne in the Church of Saint Evurtius—should hear each man’s wishes separately, under the seal of confession. We withdrew, heard them, and committed them to writing. One spoke thus, another otherwise. We returned [Col. 0560A] to the assembly, observing the limits of our commission, beyond which we were not permitted to go. Again there arose in their midst a conflict of words and a disagreement of wills; and because there seemed to be two parties especially at variance with one another, it pleased both that the subdean should name three brethren, and likewise the cantor three, to undertake and complete the task of election. It was agreed that whatever the six together, or five of them, should decide concerning the future dean would be held valid by all. We and the six were instructed to speak together again in greater secrecy, and to shape their election according to what they heard from the confessions previously made to us, insofar as we could disclose this by permission of the whole chapter. For in that election we undertook and did nothing else [Col. 0560B].

Five assembled, while the sixth waited and kept silence. Those who had elected returned to the chapter; and when they were again asked before all to confirm the commission by ratification, no one objected. One of the aforesaid six, H., the archdeacon, said: “We have elected and nominate Hugh, the subdean, as dean.” Many acclaimed it; no one contradicted it. They went with applause to the bishop. The dean-elect was presented and, as the solemnity of their custom requires, was placed by the bishop’s hand in the dean’s seat, both in chapter and in choir. The Gospels were brought forth; the new dean took the oath concerning the preservation of the Church’s property and the fidelity owed by him to bishop and chapter; and thus all was completed. These things were done in our presence [Col. 0560C]; hence we attest what we saw and heard, and our testimony is true.

XXIX. To the most reverend lord and Father W. [WILLIAM], by God’s grace Archbishop of Sens, brother STEPHEN of Saint Evurtius, greeting.

This woman, the daughter of one of our servants, is, it is said, shamefully and dishonourably treated by her husband, who neither shares nor grants her companionship at table, intercourse in bed, or cohabitation in the house. In this her affliction she petitions you, and we petition with her, that by fatherly counsel and assistance you may support the widow of a living husband. For she now seeks not mercy but judgment [Col. 0560D], entrusting the merit of her cause to justice and commending it to equity.

XXX. To the most reverend lord and Father H. [Note: [Col. 0560D] Hugh, who held the abbacy of Saint Bartholomew at Noyon from 1158 to 1187.] Abbot of Saint Bartholomew of Noyon, brother STEPHEN, strength to be girded with the spirit of fortitude.

“Cast out the scoffer, and his quarrel will go out with him” (Prov. 22); for this is done not cruelly but mercifully, lest through its pestilential contagion he destroy very many [Col. 0561A]. If those who trouble us are to be cut off (Gal. 5), how much more ought they not to be admitted? We have learned that the evil of disobedience and the crime of idolatry, or the sin of divination, go forward with equal steps (1 Sam. 15). Where guilt is alike, the penalty ought not to be unlike. And what portion has the faithful with the unfaithful? The earth swallowed some schismatics, and fire consumed others. Jerome says of them: “Who would doubt that the act committed was the more criminal because it was punished more severely?” The same author says (24, question 3, canon 16, *Resec.*): “Putrid flesh must be cut away, and the scabby sheep driven from the fold, lest the body decay and the flock perish. Arius was one spark in Alexandria; and because he was not immediately suppressed, his fame devastated the whole world.”

You too, Father, follow the counsel of so great a man [Col. 0561B]. The Fourth Council of Carthage teaches that associations of schismatics are to be avoided, and that one must neither pray nor sing psalms with them. And lest you doubt that the man about whom you ask and complain is a schismatic, hear Pope Pelagius (24, question 1, canon 34, *Schism.*): “Schism denotes a division, and division cannot exist in unity.” Therefore whoever does not communicate with unity, whoever makes a party for himself, is a schismatic. Nor should you spare the conspirator, being ready to punish all disobedience. For we too have heard, and you have experienced, that this same man conspired against his spiritual father. Consult the Council of Chalcedon concerning what must be done with conspiracies.

What then? Because he fled for aid to the wickedness of secular soldiery [Col. 0561C] and power, he has incurred sacrilege by the testimony of both divine and human law. Let the constitution concerning bishops and clerics be read, which begins thus (17, question 4, canon 29, *Si quis suad.*): “If anyone [falls] into this kind of sacrilege.” Pope Pius likewise judges as sacrilegious both him who ravages the Church of God and him who persecutes priests. And because he has added to such excesses the cursing of his Father and the slandering of mother Church or his brethren, let him fear the severity of the Council of Orléans (3, question 1, canon 2, *Eos qui*), where it is said that “those who have brought false accusations against brethren are not to communicate until their end.” Let him observe the judgment of Pope Adrian (5, question 6, canon 5, *Delatori*): “For an informer,” he says, “let either his tongue be cut out, or, if convicted, let his head be cut off.” [Col. 0561D]

But how deserving of punishment is that act by which, rushing upon his Father, he sought to lay hands upon him! Let him who excuses it conceal it; let him who reproves it pronounce judgment. By the authority of Pope Stephen (3, question 5, canon 13, *Omnes*), “all who take arms against fathers are marked with infamy throughout the world” [Col. 0562A]. With the same severity they rightly wished the intention of this crime to be punished as its accomplishment. For the crime of lèse-majesté bears the guilt of parricide. And lest anyone murmur and claim that I have spoken contrary to the mercy whose disciples we are, let him hold to the judgment of Father Ambrose, who says in the book *On Duties* (23, question 4, canon 33): “As there is an unjust mercy, and it is written of a certain man in the law: ‘You shall not spare him’ (Deut. 19), so the rule of justice must be observed most strictly, lest anyone separated from the fellowship of communion, by a brief tear easily summoned for the moment, or even by more abundant weeping, extort from a priest’s indulgence that communion for which he ought to ask over a very long time. For easiness in pardon provides an incentive to sin.” [Col. 0562B] Therefore, if he appears incorrigible, he must not be received at all; but if there is hope of his correction, after much contrition and manifest humility he must be restored under a very severe and prolonged penance.

XXXI. [Note: [Col. 0561D] This letter appears to have been written to Godfrey, Abbot of Saint-Satyr; for several letters on the same subject, addressed to him, survive among Molinet’s published editions: 7, 45, 53, 76, 98, 137, 142.]

The bearer of this letter had a great desire to see you and to stay with you. At last his desire has been fulfilled. For when an opportunity arose, we advised him to accomplish what he had wished. He himself will disclose to you orally the nature of that opportunity. If he is useful to you, you may retain him. He promised us that he would be no burden to you but an honour; his conduct would be not harmful but useful.

XXXII. (A.D. 1177.) To the venerable Father and dearest friend W. [Note: [Col. 0561D] William of Pavia, cardinal priest of Saint Peter in Chains, became Bishop of Porto in 1178 and died in the following year.] by God’s grace Bishop of Porto, W. [WILLIAM], humble minister of the Church of Rheims, greeting and the affection of sincere love.

[Col. 0562C]

Especially trusting in you, we commend to your affection Master Stephen, Abbot of Sainte-Geneviève, a special friend and most devoted son of the holy Roman Church, to be loved both for his own merits and through our favour. We ask, therefore, that you support his messenger and the cause of his Church against a certain, as we hear, false brother named Ludoycus [Note: [Col. 0562D] On the same matter see letter 38 among Molinet’s published letters, addressed to Gratian, cardinal of the Roman Church.], who, because of the enormity of his offences, at last forswore the borders of the realm before the lord king [Col. 0562D]; but later, having deceived the ears of the lord pope by a false representation, obtained letters ordering that he be received back. Hold fast to this matter, and do not permit the flock of the Lord to be scandalized by so destructive a person.

[Col. 0563]

SOME SYNODAL STATUTES OF STEPHEN OF TOURNai.

(Edition of the Works, prepared by R. P. Du Molinet.)

[Col. 0563A] I. By the sacred authorities of the Fathers we are taught, and by right faith believe and maintain, that the souls of departed faithful persons who died confessing the holy Trinity, and who are commended to God by the prayers of the Church, obtain eternal rest through the offering of the Lord’s body. But we, who by divine forbearance and not by our merits have been placed in a higher rank, ought to prove by example what we preach to others in word.

II. With the Apostle Paul bearing witness, we have learned that, when the natural order of succession is observed, fathers lay up treasure for sons, not sons for fathers; having regard to this, etc.

III. The form of ecclesiastical institution, devised through many watchful labours, is ordered and governed, arranged and preserved by diverse customs according to the diversity of places and times and the variety of persons and causes [Col. 0563B]. Yet the Church is one, God’s dove is one, the catholic faith is one, and the Christian religion, though surrounded by diversity, is one. In this all the apostolic and evangelical Fathers have given unanimous consent: those who serve the altar should live from the altar; those who feed the flock should eat of the flock’s milk; those who plant the vineyard and labour in it should gather its fruit. For just as the mouth of the threshing ox must not be muzzled, and the labourer is worthy of his wage, so it is commanded that whoever does not work shall not eat.

Yet in our days the times are wholly infirm, and men, loving themselves and seeking what is their own, wish to be enrolled and titled in many churches and to receive stipends in each, although they serve, if at all, only scantily [Col. 0563C] in one. Sparing the multitude and sympathizing with the weaknesses of the brethren, we do not wish wholly to deprive of benefice those of our college who shall henceforth be instituted canons in our church if they are not resident therein continually; nor do we wish them to receive full stipends along with those who bear the burden and heat of the day in the Lord’s vineyard [Col. 0564A]. We therefore decree, etc.

IV. Just as prescriptions have been introduced against the idle and despisers of their own obligation, so imminent perils or losses must be met by prudent foresight and caution. Since in our times the days are evil, in which an abyss of business calls upon an abyss of expenses, we desire in fatherly solicitude that the daily stipends of our brethren and canons should be increased rather than diminished, should grow rather than perish. Therefore, by the common counsel and assent of our chapter, etc.

V. Since it is known to be not only disgraceful but also dangerous for ecclesiastical stipends, which are [Col. 0564B] the tribute of needy souls, to be spent and consumed on shameful and detestable uses, we have decreed, by the common counsel of our chapter, that the house be cleansed from the pollution of filth and brothel-impurity. For his concubine, a snare and trap for his soul, lavishly and excessively displaying, spending, pouring out, and squandering ecclesiastical revenues—both in the adornment of clothing and in the embellishment of her shameless body and, it is said, in the embraces of others—casts, devours, and swallows up in the service of shamefulness those revenues which have been assigned to the divine service of those who serve God. Therefore we ask your fraternity, and prohibit you not only fraternally but also paternally, from paying out any portion of the revenue of his prebend to anyone on his behalf or on behalf of the aforesaid mercenary woman without our knowledge; for [Col. 0564C] we wish all that belongs to him to be managed and arranged through the hands of honourable and venerable persons, and to be expended soundly and reasonably for the needs of a man infirm in body and soul.

[Col. 0563]

FRAGMENT from the Office of Saint Gerald, composed by Stephen of Tournai.

LESSONS.

[Col. 0563D]

I. The birthday feast of the most blessed Gerald, both an eminent Father and an outstanding confessor, commends the death of the saints, ever precious in the sight of the Lord. For rightly should I call the day of his sacred departure from the world his birthday, on which, emerging from the squalor of the worldly prison [Col. 0564D], he deserved to ascend to the palaces of the heavenly kingdom; transferred from the left hand to the right, he exchanged the dreadful claims of death for everlasting immortality; and from the perishing and passing world he was raised to heaven. Truly blessed, truly most worthy of every kind of praise, he purposed so to serve as a soldier in [Col. 0565A] the world that he might reign with Christ for ever.

II. Following the victorious arms of the eternal Emperor, enrolled among strong athletes, and bound by military oaths, he did not grow slack in the divine warfare, nor allow the mark of a deserter to be branded upon him. Rather, engaging manfully with the enemy, by the disciplined method of combat, he not only eluded opposing blows, protected by the shield of faith, but as a renowned combatant crushed the hostile assaults of the enemy by the mighty weight of virtue.

III. Thus emerging victorious over all things, carried in an ethereal chariot, he led a noble triumph to the heavenly Capitol; and, endowed alike with the palm and laurel of immortality, he augmented the starry companies by the privilege of his merits. There, happily everlasting and ever happy [Col. 0565B], reigning with Christ himself, he dwells with angels, walks with archangels, and finally rejoices with the countless multitudes of all the saints. From this source have flowed the celebrations of today’s feast; from this source have come to the Christian people the joys of so great and splendid a solemnity. Hence the clergy sing together; thence the people applaud; the poor rejoice; the rich exult.

IV. Young men and virgins, old men with the young, praise the name of the Lord, by whose gift this man shone forth so great, celebrated, and illustrious: great in the summit of holiness and greatest in the abundance of miracles, deserving by merit and reward to be proclaimed comparable to any of the saints. Whose continence did not equal the zeal of his singular self-denial? Who was his equal in the virtue of patience? Who proved inferior to him in faith or lesser in hope? Whom, finally, did he not surpass in the advances of highest charity [Col. 0565C]? He denied both what was his and himself for Christ, that in love of God and neighbour, taking up his cross daily, he might follow Christ with the steps of both feet and deeds; leaving parents and homeland, fleeing the height of honour and human favour, and abiding in solitude in order to serve God with chaste observances; giving himself to the conversion of sinners, that he might rescue their souls from death, win them, and restore them to the Redeemer.

V. How greatly he shone with the splendour of spiritual signs, I judge superfluous to explain, since they are so great that by their very magnitude they have readily claimed the knowledge of many, indeed of all. If, then, while dying he was able to do such things, we believe—nor is the faith vain—that, immortal, he will be able to obtain far [Col. 0565D] greater things; if while fighting he bestowed such gifts, reigning with the Lord he will bestow incomparably better ones. Therefore the deeds wrought during his earthly life and the signs after his departure testify that he is rightly to be numbered among the just: wondrous works while he lived; more wondrous after he departed.

VI. Especially since he reached one summit of holiness by diverse ascents, [for] there is not merely one way that leads to the kingdom of your glory, O Christ. For what is harder: to bear the cross through time, or immediately to undergo death by wounds? What is lower: to conquer the world, or not to fear the sword? One mortified for your sake is not different from one who is dead, since in each it is glorious both not to wish to misuse what pleases and not to wish to use what is permitted.

[Col. 0566A] VII. For, as we believe, refusing enticements through rigor is equal to not yielding to torments through pain. Where there is an equal spirit in love, faith lacks a persecutor, not a confessor. He who serves as a soldier wishes to triumph and does not cease to serve until he completes his course. But amid these things human frailty must claim nothing for itself without your help. For he who conquered ought to ascribe it to your gifts, Lord, since it was surely by your strength that he bore what he endured. O highest God, set him before yourself as an intercessor for our sins, whom by the gift of your grace you made illustrious in life and distinguished by the ending of death.

VIII. Therefore let us honour such and so great a man with the services of due devotion; nor let the spirit grow numb in its duties if it does not wish to be frustrated in its vows. For Saint Gerald, when asked, will be present; when appealed to, will grant favour; removing every evil, he will provide every good. He will bend the Judge by prayers; he will intercede with the Creator for the guilty and frail; he will obtain from God pardon for sins; and, having obtained the gift of immortality, will grant fellowship in rewards. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom are praise, everlasting glory, unfailing victory, now and through all ages. Amen.

A reading from the holy Gospel according to John. At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “I came as light into the world, so that everyone who believes in me may not remain in darkness,” etc. Homily of Saint Augustine, bishop, from Tractate 54 on John, before the middle, on the same passage.

[Col. 0566C] Rhythmic responsories are inserted between the lessons. In honour of the author’s dignity, we add one of them here.

Take delight, Great Forest, in the name of Gerald:

He, by the splendour of the true sun and by heavenly light,

Has freed your shade from the gloom of death,

And cleansed your woods from blood that was shed.

This is the first responsory. The rest, drawn from different parts of his life and praises, are almost like this one and do not contribute to historical knowledge. The antiphons for the individual psalms, of both the Matins and Vespers offices, vary with an equal grace of metre and rhythm; but for brevity’s sake we omit them. Here we give the hymns to be sung in the same office.

HYMN AT VESPERS AND MATINS.

[Col. 0566D]

Let Aquitaine exalt the praises of our Father,

At whose presence it rejoices and whose benefits it experiences.

In this solemn joy, let our devotion increase,

That we may enjoy the gracious protection of Gerald.

From tender age, amid works of virtue,

He neither feared hardships nor sought prosperity.

A distinguished man, a renowned man, he was a vessel of the Holy Spirit,

Both prelate and subject, exposed to labours.

Simple and upright in mind, pleasing to God and neighbour,

May he from inmost affection offer our prayers to the Most High.

AT LAUDS.

Joyfully let us sing today a hymn of praise and glory,

That the voice of joy conceived may be a sign of grace.

Gerald, pure from enticements and celebrated by the world,

[Col. 0567A] Goes forth from the hiding places of flesh, neither doomed nor funereal.

Under the monastic rule, free from wrinkle and stain,

Through signs and miracles he broke the bonds of death.

Running, but not in vain, he paid nature’s debt:

The merit of his completed course commends his departure.

O confessor equal to martyrs, be present to those who trust in you:

[Col. 0568A] By your prayers join us as fellow citizens to the citizens of heaven.

Let there be praise to the Father with the Son, and to the Third among the two:

Whose union is simple unity, not mere conjunction.

Amen.

PRAYER.

Grant us, almighty God, to be sustained by the merits of Saint Gerald, your confessor and abbot, so that, by the intercessions of him whom you willed to make known on earth by many miracles, we may be commended in heaven.

[Col. 0567]

SERMONS OF STEPHEN OF TOURNai.

(Edition of the Works of Stephen of Tournai, prepared by R. P. Du Molinet.)

FIRST SERMON. At a synod.

[Col. 0567B]

“He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom, because he hears his voice” (John 3). Sacred and solemn assemblies in the Church are embraced by the friend and abhorred by the enemy. For the battle-line of the heavenly host, armed together, is so lovable to its own that it is terrible to outsiders. In it neither theatrical spectacle, nor contest of the circus, nor criminal displays of beasts claims anything for itself; rather, all is turned to the praises of him whose praise is in the Church of the saints. In this sacramental theatre one is enclosed, not mocked.

O priest, you are the spectacle of this day; it concerns you to be present. Lift up your eyes all around and see: all these gathered with you have come to you! I speak to you in such a way as to address all in each individual: you have business with a certain virgin, and in that business lies the sacrament of all priests. A wonderful matter! You who had promised celibacy have contracted marriage. John was pleasing in celibacy, Abraham in marriage; in both you gather fruit. A singular and pre-eminent virgin has been betrothed to you and led even into your house. If you ask her name, she is the dignity of the priesthood of priests, with whom you have entered into an indivisible manner of life. For the Lord has established for you . . . . . . . . . . the dignity of priesthood. A covenant of peace, as is T. S. D., for ever. For ever this virgin has been given and joined to you by the supreme householder [Col. 0567D]; flee grounds for divorce and do not seek dissolution.

Let temporal covenants run their course and endure between the priest and the dignity of priesthood. This virgin is no commoner: she has not only touched persons most illustrious and conspicuous, but has even attained the rank of women of highest distinction. She is illustrious in birth, distinguished in deeds, fruitful in conduct, fruitful in speech. If you turn to the glory of her lineage, she took origin from the king of Salem, who tithed all the sons of Abraham in his loins, except one; from Aaron, whose rod, though dry, blossomed, put forth leaves, and bore fruit; from Eleazar, who with Joshua divided by lot among the children of Israel the land of promise. In short, from that great priest who in his days pleased God and was found righteous, who, as high priest of the good things to come, entered once into the holy places, having found eternal redemption. Truly she sprang from noble parents, truly she was born from ancestors who were kings.

If you review her splendid works: through the hand of Phinehas she pierced with a dagger the Israelite committing shameful acts with the Midianite woman. For by her ministry it came about that Phinehas stood, was approved, and the plague ceased. Likewise, through the hand of Azariah the priest, she steadfastly rebuked King Uzziah of Judah when he irreverently usurped priestly functions and expelled him, covered with leprosy, from the temple [Col. 0568C]. Through the hand of Mattathias, in the city of Modein, she slew upon the altar the man performing sacrilegious rites against God together with the envoy of King Antiochus. These are the things she wrought by the counsel of her hands; her great works are sought out in all her desires. And, to make the best inquiry concerning her character, she is Sarah more mature, Rebekah wiser, Leah more fruitful, Rachel more pleasing, Hannah more devout, Susanna more chaste. O holy and glorious virgin, because the Lord of all loved her! Truly many daughters have gathered riches; you have surpassed them all.

Let us consider also the grace of her speech. She greets gladly, answers kindly, speaks wisely, and is modestly silent [Col. 0568D]. Certainly she greets gladly whenever she sees two or three gathered in the Lord’s name; preceding them with a gentle greeting, she says: “The Lord be with you.” O saving greeting, which wishes that the Lord of salvation be with us! Truly grace has been poured out upon your lips. She answers kindly whenever, to a sinner confessing his wrongdoing and beating his breast with the publican, saying with David, “I have sinned against the Lord,” she adds in her sweet and gentle utterance, helping the faint-hearted and comforting the tearful: “May the Lord grant you absolution [Col. 0569A] and remission of all sins.” For what answer is kinder than that which soothes the sorrowful, consoles the grieving, raises the oppressed, and frees the bound? The law of mercy is on her tongue. By this answer of yours, blessed virgin, your lips are a dripping honeycomb; honey and milk are under your tongue.

She speaks wisely because, in every one of her utterances, having first invoked divine aid and shared counsel with the brethren, she begins: “Let us pray.” She invokes divine aid, that when she speaks to God he may put right and well-sounding speech in her mouth. She shares counsel with the brethren when, standing and trusting in the assembly of the righteous, she thus avoids arrogance and strives to possess humility. For she keeps well in mind that what individuals cannot accomplish, all together often can. This is she who opened her mouth to wisdom, and whose lips scatter knowledge.

She is modestly silent because, in that threefold silence in which life-giving and wonder-working mysteries are celebrated, in which heavenly things are joined to earthly, in which the Son is offered to the Father, bearing the gravity of highest devotion and reverence, she does not stir restlessly, run about negligently, or yawn; she does not rove with her eyes or look about at those standing by, but, observing the worship of justice and silence, distinguishes the time to be silent from the time to speak. Such is your soul, and such is your beloved: she is wholly beautiful, and there is no blemish in her.

Observe also that she is not unadorned or covered with a cheap veil when the sacred maiden comes into your embrace [Col. 0569C]. Fine linen and purple are her clothing, from that treasury of the householder from which things new and old are brought forth. She has brought with her eight ornaments of great price and great sacramental significance: namely, a linen tunic, a hyacinth-blue tunic, a girdle, the rational breastpiece, an ephod, a mitre or tiara, a golden plate on the forehead; and, beyond the custom of her sex, for greater protection of modesty, she is covered with linen breeches. In the linen breeches is purity of flesh; in the linen tunic, purity of mind; in the hyacinth-blue tunic, the secret of contemplation; in the girdle, the rigour of discipline; in the rational breastpiece, the virtue of discernment; in the ephod, the burden of compassion; in the mitre or tiara, the sign of perfection; in the golden plate, the eminence of charity. This is her glory, which the king’s daughter brought forth from within, clothed about in fringes of gold and varied adornment [Col. 0569D]. Behold what kind of queen stands at your right hand, surrounded by beauty.

But there is a chief reason why you ought to cleave to her in chaste embraces. For if we consider not what is done, but who ought to be made, she chose you; you did not choose her.

For that is a general rule, holding good for every priest, highest, middle, or lowest: he must be sought out under compulsion, withdraw when asked, flee when invited, and have only the necessity of not being able to excuse himself to support him. If marriage has been contracted otherwise in any case, the rule has been corrupted and lost its office. For she herself anticipated you with services, invited you with gifts, reminded you by greeting, caressed you by an admonition, and sent you her household and familiar messengers [Col. 0570A], who might win favour by gifts and incite you more ardently to love so great a virgin.

First she sent a vigorous and learned young man, experienced in deed and instructed in speech: I mean the order of clerics. He did not appear before you empty-handed, but bearing fitting gifts. “Receive,” he said, “from my lady as a pledge and earnest of love, scissors and a cloth, that with the one you may cut away every superfluity and with the other wipe off stains and dirt. And henceforth you will be able to sing songs of love, little rhythms, and sounds suited to her love; for today she has made you both singer and psalmist. Yet see to it that what you sing with your mouth you believe in your heart, and what you believe in your heart you prove by deeds.” Having spoken and given these things, the messenger withdrew. Consider what reverence you showed to the gifts and what obedience to the words.

If you have drunk in the fires of her love alone, and have not begun thereafter to wander among the flocks of your companions, you have deserved greater things than the former. Therefore she in turn sent another, her secretary, to guard her treasures and chrism: namely, the order of doorkeeper. He gave you the keys as a sign of secrecy and, as it were, of the closed womb and the opening love of his lady. “Act thus,” he said, “live thus, as one who must render account for those things opened by the keys.” While he was still speaking, behold another, privy to the same secret, very eloquent and of circumcised lips, came to teach you to speak without fault with his lady: namely, the order of reader [Col. 0570C]. He also gave you a book suited to his ministry: “Receive,” he said, “and be a zealous guardian of the divine word. You shall have a share with those who have ministered the word of God, if you faithfully fulfil your office.”

He had not yet completed his words when behold another follower of the aforesaid virgin, who would recite and teach you her songs, which have power to drive away every power of the enemy: namely, the order of exorcist. He also gave you a little book containing the efficacious chants, saying: “Receive, commit it to memory, and have power to lay hands upon one possessed, whether catechumen or baptized.” He was speaking, and behold the virgin’s chamberlain, who ministers to her chamber by its lights: namely, the order of acolytes. In his hand was a candlestick and a candle, which he sent to you [Col. 0570D], so that all your things might be done in light. For she is the daughter of light, not of night or darkness. And he added: “Receive this bearer of light, that through it you may be able to flee the darkness of adversaries and faithfully find the true light which enlightens every human being coming into this world.”

See how highly she esteemed you, she who arranged your union by such gifts and messengers. If you have lived honourably and chastely in the aforesaid orders, worthily without violation of so great a virgin, rejoice and be glad, worthy to receive what follows. If you have loosened the reins of continence and followed alien lovers, you have offended the jealousy of the holy virgin. Let a torrent of tears flow day and night, and let not the pupil of your eye be silent. Yet in all these things her love was not turned away, and her affection was still extended [Col. 0571A]. At last she sent to you one whom, excepting another, she holds dearer and more familiar than any other among her sacred ministers, one who attends her more secret and sacred counsels and works: namely, the order of subdeacon.

Introducing you to converse with his lady, among other things he brought you—a chalice and water-jug, a cloth and hand-towel, that you might come cleaner into the presence and embrace of so great a virgin—he gave you a maniple. “Receive,” he said, “the maniple in your hands, to wipe away the stains of your heart and body.”

You bound yourself to this messenger so firmly that thereafter you did not possess authority over your body: I do not mean merely authority to take your limbs and make them the limbs of a prostitute [Col. 0571B], but not even authority to seek marital union. For if marriage is contracted in the earlier orders—although people of our time have rarely seen this—it is not dissolved; but this order so prevents contracting it that it dissolves a marriage already contracted.

At last, impatient in love and, as it were, exposing her whole self to you, she sent that most sacred and most secret counsellor of hers, admitted to her innermost familiarity, who hears from her own mouth words which it is scarcely lawful for a man to speak: he is the order of deacon. She also gave what was most precious and dear in her lady’s caskets, namely the book containing the holy Gospels. “Receive,” he said, “this volume of the holy Gospel; read and understand it, hand it on to others, and fulfil it in deed.” By these services she anticipated you; by these gifts she invited you. What more ought she to have done for you that she did not do?

At last, rushing wholly into love for you and offering her entire self to your desires, she herself who had spoken to you through her messengers came. Behold, she is present. The day of your betrothal is appointed. The virgin is introduced through priests and archdeacons as through matchmakers and bridal attendants, and the parties contract marriage in this form: “Holy mother Church requests that this present deacon be promoted to the rank of priesthood” [Col. 0571C]. But we receive no matchmaker’s payment in this contract, because it bears the wickedness of Simon, whose heresy we detest. For if grace is not given freely, it is not grace. Then, while her lips first distilled myrrh, you received the kiss transmitted by the virgin herself. And did you not hear, at her coming, from the kiss received from the ordaining minister: “Peace be with you”?

Thus she has been betrothed to you and led even into your house: betrothed in consecration, led into the house in the granting of a title. For we call that a betrothal which, through present consent, makes marriage. They also made a welcome meeting with one another: on her side a dowry, on yours a marriage-gift. The sacred virgin established for you a rich dowry: namely, the altar and its appurtenances. By “appurtenances” we do not mean civil or natural additions but sacramental ones: such as offering sacrifice, baptizing, giving penance, binding, and loosing.

If you complain that these fields are barren because they yield no temporal produce, consider the income of weddings, first-fruit tithes, vows of the faithful, offerings of the poor, and payments of penitents. [Col. 0572A] For it is fitting that those who serve at the altar should live by the altar. This is the altar from which those who serve the world have no authority to eat; and compared with it, both the golden altar of incense and the bronze altar of burnt offering are less worthy and lower. This estate given as dowry cannot truly be alienated, being exempt from every human transaction.

She brought with her into your service two slaves, not mercenary ones but endowed with every propriety, because they too are great virgins: authority, namely, and execution—authority at the betrothal, execution in her conveyance. She brought with her and gave you this *profectitious* dowry, that is, one proceeding from the goods of the highest householder. You, in return, bestowed a gift on account of the marriage, not indeed equal to the dowry, [Col. 0572B] yet suitable to your means. For you dedicated to the service of so great a virgin not only the use, but the usufruct, indeed even the ownership, of your limbs, senses, and actions, so that henceforth you may present yourself to her as a living sacrifice, pleasing to God—your rational service.

You also gave her two virgins in whose service she delights: holiness and propriety. For the Apostle commands that the care and guarding of the whole household be entrusted to them, so that, he says, each may know how to possess his own vessel in holiness and honor (1 Thess. 4). Holiness perfects and completes the inward person; propriety arranges and orders the outward person. Holiness preserves the conscience; propriety, one’s reputation. Holiness provides what is good before God; propriety also [Col. 0572C] before all people. Holiness makes one hold fast to what is good; propriety, abstain from every appearance of evil. Holiness is to gird the loins; propriety, to hold burning lamps in the hands.

The chaste virgin thus requires these virgins as the marriage-gift: without them the marriage is not lawful. You also rightly offered a ring—faith, namely, by which you would henceforth cling to so great a wife, so as not to pass over to another’s vows—and also a necklace, by which the breast is enclosed: namely, the continual recollection or remembrance of chastity, and, in the ears, perfect obedience.

Amid these dowry agreements and these marital solemnities, entrance is made into the wedding feast. Gatekeepers stand at the doors, [Col. 0572D] rejecting the unworthy and admitting the worthy: namely, the severity of the Law and the rigor of the canons. The severity of the Law holds a staff; the rigor of the canons, a rod. For the former threatens the punishment of death; the latter, the sentence of deposition.

The severity of the Law forbids and cries out that no blind man, lame man, man with a small, large, or crooked nose, man with a broken foot, maimed man, hunchback, bleary-eyed man, man having a white spot in his eye, persistent scab, bodily eruption, or an excessively heavy or herniated man may enter. The blind man does not see the light of truth; the lame man does not walk straight along the way of justice; the man with a small, large, or crooked nose does not exercise discernment; the man with a broken foot does not even set his foot upon the path of faith; the maimed man performs no good works; the hunchback bears the burden of sins; the bleary-eyed man is dim-sighted in sound understanding; [Col. 0573A] the man with a white spot in his eye mixes arrogance with good intention; the man with persistent scab itches with the heat of lust; the man with an eruption upon his body pursues the gains of avarice; the excessively heavy man is bent down toward the earth by shameful thought.

On the other side stands the rigor of the canons, barring those who seek to enter and crying: no recent convert; no man married twice; no husband of a widow; no unlettered man; no man physically defective; no son born of a priest; no man bound by the ties of servile, civic, or registered-colon status; no one who has ever stolen; no one not trained in ecclesiastical disciplines; no one stained by the marks of infamy.

Amid this is heard the voice of exultation and salvation, the voice of harpists playing upon their harps: rejoice [Col. 0573B] and pour forth from a full heart good words—Davidic words upon psaltery and harp, those of Amos upon the shepherd’s pipe, those of Paul upon the evangelical trumpet. Before one approaches the table, confession asks for water for the hands; contrition pours it forth in tears; satisfaction dries the hands with the cloth of cleanness. The banquet is completed by the service of these three virgins, while the herald cries through the halls: “Wash yourselves; be clean” (Isa. 6); likewise: “Be cleansed, you who bear the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. 52).

Then one goes up to the table—not the table of presentation, on which every Sabbath warm loaves were set out after the old ones had been removed, but the table which Wisdom has set—the one of which it is said, “You have prepared [it] before me against those who trouble me.” Unleavened loaves are placed upon it, made by the sincerity and truth, the bakers of the highest [Col. 0573C] King. This is the bread of angels, which man ate, lest he fail on the way, refreshed by such provision for the journey.

The flesh of the spotless Lamb is also brought in: not that lamb which Moses sacrifices, but the one whom John points out with his finger, [Col. 0574A] the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world, who was silent before the shearer, and in whose blood all the elect washed their robes and made them white. Wine, making virgins flourish, is also mixed for those reclining at table: wine that gladdens the human heart, pressed out in the winepress of the Cross, from the true vine whose branches you are. The Lord himself, who sets forth this food, explains it thus: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (John 6). These are the feasts which those who truly and worthily receive them shall neither hunger nor thirst any more.

You have celebrated these weddings, O priest; you have joined yourself to this marriage. For this reason you left father and mother, that you might cling to your wife. Nor will offspring be lacking in this union. For unless—God forbid!—they should not be begotten through the poison of sterility, your [Col. 0574B] seed will be multiplied like the stars of heaven and like the sand on the shore of the sea. Whatever you have washed in the water of sacred baptism, however many souls you have converted to repentance by your preaching, and every good work you have done—these are your children and sons of blessing.

Your seed can also be multiplied otherwise, but damnably: namely, in works and likewise in words of different kinds. For example, evil deeds or words not done or spoken out of malice are venial sins. But there are other false deeds and words, of which the Psalmist speaks: “Wicked and deceitful words against their neighbors” (Ps. 14); and elsewhere: “You will destroy all who speak falsehood” (Ps. 5). There are also words of the heart, such as evil judgments against one’s neighbor, concerning which [Col. 0574C] the apostle says: “You see the speck in your neighbor’s eye and not the beam in your own” (Luke 6). Hence, because you judge another, you condemn yourself. Beware of those who are children of death, so that you may be able to escape the sentence of the strict Judge. Amen.

[Col. 0575]

# Prologue to Stephen of Tournai’s *Summa on the Decrees*

[Col. 0575C] If you invite two guests to dinner, you will not set contrary dishes before them when they ask for the same thing; when one asks for what the other dislikes, you will not alter the courses, lest you confuse the seating or offend those at table. The Latin embraces unleavened bread; the Greek, leavened bread. If they approach the altar together, neither should despise the other’s sacrifice.

I have invited two persons to a feast: a theologian and a jurist, whose wills are scattered among diverse desires, since the one delights in sour things and the other craves sweet things. What shall we give, and what shall we not give? You refuse what the other asks for. If I propose, in this little work, to expound the laws currently in force, the legal expert will take it ill, wrinkle his nose, shake his head, purse his lip, and judge what he considers known to himself to be unnecessary for others. Moreover, if [Col. 0575D] I begin to recount the mystical deeds of the Old or New Testament, the theologian will regard them as useless and accuse our little work both of prolixity and of unprofitableness.

Let them yield to one another, join in sound agreement, balance losses against usefulness. Let not the theologian reject divine laws under the pretext of histories; nor let the jurist, through disdain for laws, lose what he embraces in the histories. I ask pardon for prolixity: I could not cross the sea in an instant, nor traverse long expanses of land in a few steps. Having briefly poured out these things as a washing of hands, let us set the promised dishes before those reclining at table.

In the same city, under the same king, there are two peoples; corresponding to the two peoples are two lives; corresponding to the two lives are two sovereignties. Thus a twofold order of jurisdiction proceeds. The city is the Church, and Christ is the king of the city. The two peoples are the two orders in the Church, clerics and laypeople; the two lives are spiritual and carnal; the two sovereignties are priesthood and kingship; the twofold jurisdiction is divine law and human law. [Col. 0576C] Render each thing to its proper recipient, and all will agree.

Much is read concerning human law, variously and at length, in the enactments of princes and in the opinions of jurists. But divine law must be discussed, and first its earliest development. Some say that the origin of divine law began with the beginning of the world. For when Adam was reproved by the Lord for disobedience, he objected, as though raising an exception to an action, and shifted the charge of guilt to his wife—indeed, to the maker of his wife—saying: “The woman whom you gave me as a companion deceived me, and [Col. 0576D] I ate” (Gen. 3). Thus the form of litigation—or, to use common speech, pleading—seems to have arisen in Paradise.

Others hold that judicial procedure had its beginning in the Old Law. Moses says in the Law: “At the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand” (Deut. 17). In the New Testament too, the apostle Paul says: “Therefore, if you have secular lawsuits, appoint for judgment those who are despised in the Church” (1 Cor. 6). Others, treating the origin of divine law more briefly, derive it from the primitive Church. For when the persecution of the martyrs had ceased and the Church began to breathe again under Emperor Constantine, the holy Fathers began to assemble, to hold councils, and in them, according to the diversity of ecclesiastical affairs, to issue and write various canons.

Of councils, some are general and some particular. General councils are those held in the presence of the lord pope, or of his legate representing him, when bishops and the other prelates of the Church are universally summoned. Provincial councils are those held in a province by a primate or archbishop, after summoning his own suffragans for this purpose. Canons issued in general councils extend their force universally to all churches, and those who do not observe them are held to be transgressors. But canons issued in provincial councils do not go outside the province and bind no persons except those subject to the jurisdiction of the bishops of that province. Hence some canons are called general, that is, promulgated in a general [Col. 0577A] council; others provincial, that is, promulgated in a provincial synod.

Among general councils there are four principal ones, almost comparable to the Gospels: Nicaea, Ephesus, Chalcedon, and Constantinople. Moreover, “canons” are those enactments promulgated in councils by the authority of many bishops. “Decrees” are enactments which the Apostolic Lord establishes, on some ecclesiastical matter, in the presence of cardinals who give their authority, and commits to writing. A decretal letter is one which the Apostolic Lord writes and sends to a bishop or another ecclesiastical judge who is uncertain about some case and consults the Roman Church. Nevertheless, canons are indiscriminately called decrees, and decrees canons. [Col. 0577B] These are the authorities by which ecclesiastical matters ought to be handled and decided.

Yet in deciding ecclesiastical cases this order of care must be observed: first place belongs to Gospel precepts; when these are silent, then to the sayings of the apostles; then to the four councils mentioned above; afterward to the remaining councils; finally to decrees and decretal letters. In the last place come the words of the holy Fathers—Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome, and others. All these are the common material of everyone who treats divine law. Since they sometimes seem to oppose one another, they require a fourfold examination.

The aforementioned ecclesiastical enactments [Col. 0577C] are some according to counsel, some according to command, some according to permission or indulgence, and some according to prohibition. These four concern four kinds of persons: some are perfect, some are to be perfected, some are weak, and some are lukewarm.
