Those containing counsel are given to the perfect; those containing command, to those being perfected; those containing promise, to the weak; those containing prohibition, to the lukewarm. Counsel is to sell everything and give it to the poor; command, to love the Lord; permission, to marry; prohibition, not to kill or commit adultery. Counsel is at the higher level; permission at the lower; command and prohibition in the middle. Command, as it were, hangs from counsel; prohibition, as it were, restrains permission.

Counsel [Col. 0578A] does not threaten punishment but promises reward; permission does not promise reward but supplies a remedy. The two outer categories are matters of will; the two middle categories, matters of necessity. For if you wish, you will neither assent to counsel nor accept permission; but you cannot resist command and prohibition with impunity. Understand, however, that what we have called voluntary applies before acceptance or a vow. After a vow of continence, which belongs to counsel, you are compelled to observe it; and after marriage, which belongs to permission, you cannot dismiss your wife.

Of commands and prohibitions, some are mutable and some immutable. Immutable commands are those whose observance bestows salvation and whose nonobservance takes it away; they have force at every time, as: “You shall love the Lord your God” (Deut. 6), [Col. 0578B] etc. Mutable commands are those which were once observed but are not observed now, such as those concerning circumcision or the Sabbath; or those which the Law never enacted but later diligence devised for reasons of usefulness, as: “After a second and third correction avoid a heretical person” (Titus 3).

Likewise, immutable prohibitions are those against which it never was, nor ever will be, lawful to act: thus, “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery” (Exod. 20). Mutable prohibitions are those that vary according to the status of persons and the necessity of times or cases—for example, that a cleric who has previously fallen should not be restored, or that the son of a priest should not be ordained.

Certain permissions have likewise been mutable. At one time it was permitted to take one’s paternal uncle’s daughter as wife, and to join relatives in the fourth and fifth degrees, which is not permitted today. Matters belonging to counsel have also sometimes stood otherwise. For whereas today virginity belongs to the counsel of perfection, in the Old Testament it seemed forbidden, where one reads: “Cursed is the barren woman who does not bear” (Job 24), and again: “Cursed is he who has not left seed upon the earth.”

Therefore, in this work and in others, the chapters of the Fathers must be considered in such a way that their character as counsel, command, prohibition, and promise is kept in view. Likewise, one must observe which chapters impose a sentence already incurred and which impose a sentence to be pronounced. Sentences already incurred are those which indicate that their transgressor has already been excommunicated; sentences to be pronounced are those which declare that he is to be excommunicated. This is analogous to persons of ill repute: some are infamous by the law itself, others by a judicial sentence. Likewise, certain chapters are given according to strictness, others according to dispensation or equity.

Again, some are given for a time, some for a place, some for a person, some for necessity—that is, some are temporal, some local, some personal, and some local [the final classification is apparently corrupt or repetitive in the source]. Whoever does not carefully attend to all these matters will run into knots of complication.

What has been said applies to everyone who treats divine law. But concerning the book now in our hands, the following must be considered: what the compiler’s subject matter is, what his intention is, what the end of his intention is, what the cause of the work is, what its method of treatment is, and what its division is.

I would rightly call Gratian the compiler of this work, not its author. For he compiled and arranged in this volume chapters issued by the holy [Col. 0579A] Fathers; he was not their author or creator—unless perhaps someone wishes to call him author because, in his own paragraphs, he sets down much material of his own by distinguishing and explaining the statements of the saints. Such materials are canons, decrees, and decretal letters, whose distinction you read above; and the authorities of the holy Fathers, who, although they did not possess the right and power of making canons, nevertheless hold no small place in the Church.

His intention is to gather into one the diverse rules of diverse Fathers, which are called canons, and to bring into harmony the apparent contradictions found in them. The end and usefulness are to know ecclesiastical affairs, to deal with them according to canon law, and to decide cases so considered canonically. The cause of the work is this: divine law had begun to fall into disuse through ignorance, and individual churches were governed by customs rather than canons. Gratian considered this dangerous; he collected various codices containing chapters of councils and Fathers and, including in this volume those that seemed more necessary for the adjudication of cases, produced the work.

His method is as follows. First he sets down the distinctions and differences of law; then the reason for the establishment of laws and canons; afterward he proceeds to the order and number of councils and to their decrees, showing which are to be preferred to which. [Col. 0579B] Subsequently he comes to ecclesiastical dignities and orders, teaching to whom they are to be conferred and how one ought to live in them; concerning orders, [Col. 0580A] and at what intervals of time they are to be bestowed; and how those who have fallen are to be restored.

Finally he proceeds to the *causae*, where he first shows what persons and what procedure ought to be employed in accusations, witnesses, and judicial order in various ecclesiastical matters. Then, coming to marital affairs and treating them sufficiently, he appends at the end material on the consecration of churches, the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, baptism, and confirmation.

This book is divided in one way according to the care of readers and in another according to the custom of scribes. Readers divide it into three parts, as Gratian himself also seems to have intended. The first part extends to the *causa* concerning simoniacs, which Gratian divided into fifty *distinctions*. The second proceeds from the first *causa* to the treatise *On Consecration*, and is divided into thirty-six *causae*, determined by their questions. The third extends from the treatise on consecration to the end, divided into five *distinctions*. They assign the first of these to ministries, the second to affairs, and the third to ecclesiastical sacraments.

The custom of scribes divides the book into four parts, each of which they call a quire (*quaternum*). The first is from the beginning to the first *causa*, namely, “On Simoniacs”; the second from the first *causa* to the thirteenth, which begins, “Diocesans”; the third [Col. 0580B] from there to the twenty-seventh, which is “On Marriage”; and the fourth from the twenty-seventh to the end of the book. With these preliminaries stated, let us come to the text.

[Col. 0579] (The commentary on the same Decree of Gratian follows; we have thought fit to omit it here, both because it is rather lengthy and because what it contains has seemed, in the judgment of experts, excessively worn and commonplace.)

## In the Year of the Lord 1203: Adam, Abbot of Perseigne

[Col. 0579]

## Notice

(Oudin, *Commentary on Ecclesiastical Writers and Writings*, II, 1682)

[Col. 0579D] Adam, abbot of Perseigne, of the Cistercian Order in the bishopric of Le Mans, flourished in 1190 and the years following. He was first a monk of this monastery and afterward, in the course of time, became its abbot. The abbey of Perseigne, commonly called Perseigne, is a daughter house of Cîteaux and takes its name from a forest in the district of Le Mans. It was founded there in 1145 by William of Talvas, count of Ponthieu and Alençon. The dating of the year is made clearer by Angelus Manriquez, confirmed by volume IV of the Sammarthani brothers’ *Gallia Christiana*, under “Persenia.”

An anonymous manuscript author in the library of Saint-Victor of Paris speaks thus of Adam under the year 1190:

> “At this time there was a certain abbot (Joachim), not far from the city of Rome, of the Cistercian Order but by no means subject to the Cistercians. He published a certain Exposition on the seven visions of the Apocalypse, through wisdom divinely received, as they say, although he was almost unlettered, etc. He says that in the year 1199 the sixth vision and the opening of the sixth seal will begin; under this vision he proves by the authority of the Apocalypse that every persecution of Antichrist, together with his death and destruction, will be completed. But before his persecution, he says, the Gospel of Christ must be preached everywhere and the Church of the faithful extended among all nations.

> “When he was questioned at Rome by the venerable Adam, abbot of Perseigne, a man most eloquent in the word of God and equally religious, as to what boldness led him to preach such things—whether prophecy, conjecture, or revelation—he replied that he had no revelation concerning these matters. ‘But God,’ he said, ‘who formerly gave the spirit of prophecy to the prophets, has given me the spirit of understanding, so that in God’s Spirit I may understand with complete clarity all the mysteries of sacred Scripture, just as the holy prophets formerly understood it when they published it in God’s Spirit.’ Asked by the same abbot what he thought about Antichrist, he replied that Antichrist was already a young man. Adam refuted this reply.”

Thus, in 1190 Adam was already abbot of Perseigne and renowned for learning. Spondanus, in the *Epitome of Baronius’s Annals*, and Angelus Manriquez, *Annals of the Cistercians*, vol. III, under 1190, chap. 2, nos. 5–6, date this episode concerning Joachim to 1190. Hence the same Manriquez, under the year of Christ 1191, chap. 7, writes:

> “At the same time Adam flourished at Perseigne (a house in the diocese of Le Mans, a daughter of Cîteaux, as we mentioned above), an abbot equally learned and devout, whom in the preceding year we reported as disputing with Abbot Joachim. Thomas of Cantimpré, a nearly contemporary author, remembers him with exceptional praise in *On Bees*, II, chap. 22, while describing the death of Maria, countess of Champagne and daughter of Louis, king of the Franks. This is that distinguished abbot of Perseigne whose sermons survive, and whom we mentioned from Claude Robert in our account of the foundation of Perseigne.

> “Conrad Gesner, Philip Seguin, and John Trithemius also list him among the doctors, calling him a man learned in divine Scripture through long practice, exceedingly rich in reading the holy Fathers, adequately instructed in secular learning, and of most celebrated reputation in delivering homilies to the people. Trithemius, as usual, suppresses Cîteaux but identifies the monastery of Perseigne; he does not deny it, and all other authors attest it. Chrysostom Henriquez could have enrolled the man in his *Menologium*, as one deserving reverence above the others he lists for antiquity, learning, and religious devotion.”

This is Manriquez’s account. How eminent Adam, abbot of Perseigne, was at this time in preaching the divine word is attested by Jacques de Vitry, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, in his *Western History*, book II, chap. 9:

> “When the aforesaid athlete of Christ—namely, Fulk, priest of Paris—had died, he who by holy barking had, as it were, awakened the world and partially illuminated clouded regions with the light of truth, many, inflamed by the zeal of charity and stirred by his example, began to preach and teach, instructing many unto righteousness and drawing the souls of sinners from the jaws of Leviathan by holy exhortations. Among the foremost and most renowned of these were the abbot of Perseigne, of the Cistercian Order, along with many others whose names are written in the book of life. Laboring faithfully and wisely in the Lord’s field, they hunted beasts from caves of rock and mountains, drawing fish with nets and seines from the lake of misery and the mire of filth.” [Col. 0581D]

John Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, writes of him in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*:

> “Adam, abbot of Perseigne, of the Order of Saint Benedict, a man learned in divine Scripture through continual practice and adequately educated in secular learning, of most celebrated reputation in delivering homilies, passed his name on to posterity with praise by composing various treatises. There survive one book of devout and useful Sermons to the Brothers; one book on Saints and Various Subjects. He is also said to have expounded certain treatises of sacred Scripture in which he displayed the abundant gift of his talent, but these have not come to my knowledge.” [Col. 0582A]

Trithemius is mistaken in making him a Benedictine monk, since he is known to have been abbot of the Cistercian Order.

> [Note: D. Brial, in *Histoire littéraire de la France* (XVI, 442), argues that Adam was first a regular canon, then a Benedictine monk, and finally a Cistercian, from this passage at the beginning of Letter 10: “Since at some time I darkened from the whiteness of canonical purity into a monk through an unhappy exchange, and now have returned from that complete blackness to the brightness of the lily-white Virgin,” etc.] [Col. 0581D; 0582D]

Moreover, Trithemius places him after the monk Theodoric, who flourished in 1040, and before Saint Anselm, bishop of Lucca, who is known to have flourished in 1080. From this one may infer what he thought about Adam’s date: he evidently thought Adam flourished around 1040, before the Cistercian Order was born. Thus he makes this Adam a hundred years older than he truly was, since Adam died after 1200, as is said immediately below.

This learned man therefore wrote a work of Sermons for his brothers assembled in chapter, most worthy of publication. It was formerly in manuscript at Rome in the hands of the most distinguished Hilarion Rancati, abbot of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme, having been taken from the library of the monastery of Casamari, renowned in the diocese of Veroli in the Roman province. Casamari was formerly Benedictine but, as Gaspar Jongelinus says in his *Notice of Cistercian Abbeys*, had been occupied by the Cistercians from the year of the Lord 1140. From this codex of sermons by Adam, abbot of Perseigne, containing many sermons on the liturgical seasons, the chief festivals of the year, and other subjects, sermons on the Blessed Virgin Mary were extracted, annotated by Hippolytus Maracci, priest of Lucca, and printed at Rome in 1652, in sextodecimo, by Ignatius de Lazzaris. Maracci entitled them: *Mariale of Adam, Abbot of Perseigne, a Frenchman, a most learned and eloquent man, alumnus of the Sacred Cistercian Order.*

Fragments of such sermons also occur in the *Work of Allegories of the Old and New Testament*, printed in Paris in folio in 1550 by Gotfrid Titmann, alumnus of the Parisian Carthusian house, as the same Hilarion Rancati testifies in a note prefixed to these manuscript sermons of Adam. Hence I do not doubt that Gotfrid possessed a manuscript codex of them when he wrote his *Allegories*. I also hear that a manuscript codex of these sermons is preserved in Perseigne Abbey, although I confess that I have not seen it.

He also wrote certain letters to Osmund, monk of Mortemer Abbey in Normandy, published from manuscript codices by Étienne Baluze in volume I of his *Miscellanea*, p. 423. Abbot Adam was present, or arrived intending to be present, at the death of Maria, countess of Champagne, daughter of Louis VII, king of the Franks, and Eleanor of Aquitaine, who paid nature’s debt in 1197, according to William Marlot, vol. II of the *Metropolis of the Church of Reims*, book I, chap. 23, p. 75. This may be established from Thomas of Cantimpré, book I of *On Bees*, chap. 9:

> “Near our own time there was a most noble woman, Maria, countess of Champagne. Married to the most noble Henry, count of Champagne, she was the daughter of Louis VII, king of the Franks, sister of Philip, likewise king of the Franks. She had four brothers who were kings in England, and a son who was king overseas. After her husband had been dead for many years, she went about in most pompous ambition and came to such an end.
>
> “When she was laboring at the point of death and about to depart, she summoned Adam, abbot of Perseigne, a most holy and eloquent man, to come. When he arrived, he was not admitted but waited before the doors. For the countess had already died, and women, servants, and all her people were carrying off utensils, gold and silver vessels, precious garments, purple coverlets, and at last even the linen cloths together with the veils.
>
> “Finally one of her more favored attendants, delayed unknowingly, seized the bed by its posts and, from a distance, cast the dead body, which had rolled onto its back, down upon the straw. While the abbot endured the delay with weariness, a nobleman among the bystanders, indignant, [Col. 0583A] violently broke open the door and admitted the venerable man. On entering and finding that noble body naked upon the straw, he would not permit one of the household, who wished to cover it with straw. Mindful of the lesson, the abbot cried aloud freely: ‘Come, all of you, and see the pomp of Maria, most noble countess. Look upon that most delicate body and see with what disgraceful shame it has been cast down. See what the world finally pays her in return for her manifold honor and glory.’”

Adam died after 1200, though we cannot assign the year. He must, however, be carefully distinguished from another Adam, abbot of Chaalis, of the Cistercian Order, and afterward bishop of Senlis, who likewise composed learned sermons and of whom we shall speak below under the year 1230. For more about him, besides the authors cited, see Angelus Manriquez, *Annals of the Cistercians*, vol. II, under 1145, chap. 10, no. 6; vol. III, under 1190, chap. 2, nos. 5–6, and under 1191, chap. 7; Charles Visch, *Library of Writers of the Cistercian Order*, p. 5; and others. Charles du Fresne du Cange, in the index of authors prefixed to his *Glossary of Medieval and Late Latin*, col. 79, wrongly assigns him to 1100—unless 1200 should be read, the error being probably typographical. [Col. 0584A]

[Col. 0583]

# Letters of Adam, Abbot of Perseigne

(The first five, to the monk Osmund, were published by Baluze, *Miscellanea*, Mansi edition, vol. II, p. 236; those following are taken from D. Martène, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. I, col. 669 ff., from Clairvaux manuscripts, and from the *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. I, cols. 1013 and 1025.)

## First Letter. To Osmund, Monk of the Monastery of Mortemer in Normandy: On the Formation of Novices

[Col. 0583B]

Brother Adam, such as he is, abbot of Perseigne, to his beloved brother in Christ, OSMUND, monk of Mortemer: may you live well and prosper in the Lord.

A prudent mind carefully considers, so that it does not presume to request what may offend the person asked or exceed his powers. Importunity, indeed, is the mother of weariness; and it persists all the more burdensomely in its petition the more opportune it believes everything it desires to be. Whence, I ask, whence comes this in you—that you think me greater than I am, and thus have become importunate to one who loves you? You are loved [Col. 0583C], certainly, but perhaps not in the measure you suppose; for although you may perhaps be worthy to be loved, I cannot bestow upon a human being that measure of love which I cannot even bestow upon my Creator. Yet I love, in whatever degree I can thus far recognize as lovable. But the effect produced does not always sufficiently declare love’s affection. He can readily perform what is asked in whom affection corresponds equally to achievement; but I do not deserve to be so divinely renewed that both these goods may be found in me. My love is slight, my knowledge scanty, my occupations manifold, my sorrow of mind very great, and the toil of mind and body beyond my strength. What then has Martha’s anxiety to do with Mary’s leisure? Or how do you seek in Leah, who is laborious and bleary-eyed, Rachel’s [Col. 0583D] beauty? Your opinion deceives you, my son, and your love presumes too much of me; nor meanwhile can the assumed person of Leah grant you what you desire to obtain from Rachel’s gaze.

The old things have not yet departed from [Col. 0584B] my mouth; oldness has not yet been shaved away from my mind; and you compel me to philosophize about newness of life—namely, how those newly converted from the world may be re-formed into the new man. Truly, those turning from the world must with great diligence be shaped by the splendors of the new life, so that, in accordance with the meaning of their name, having put off the old man, they may rightly be called novices. But how could this be taught by me, who was never a novice in the Order, and did not deserve, through the teaching of experience, either to learn this or to impart instruction about it to others? I do not deny that I was once master of novices. Yet I could not sufficiently instruct novices in the rules of this art, since I undertook this ministry without experience. Nevertheless, I think that six things are necessary [Col. 0584C] for this work; when these are possessed and observed, the Ethiopian may change his skin and grow white into blessed newness.

First is fervour of faith; second, fear of God; third, love of wisdom; fourth, the master’s religious manner of life; fifth, his pious care for the novice; sixth, friendly and frequent conversation about spiritual matters or regular observances.

Faith expels ignorance and provides understanding. Hence Isaiah: “Unless you believe, you shall not understand” (Isa. VII). For one who does not believe does not receive the light of divine knowledge; and therefore is not moved by fear or love of him whose understanding he has not merited.

The effect of divine fear is twofold: it both brings wickedness to an end and begins wisdom. Of the first effect it is written: “The fear of the Lord [Col. 0584D] expels sin” (Ecclus. I). And again: “The fear of the Lord does not work evil” (Prov. VIII). Of the holy effect of fear the Psalmist says: “Holy and terrible is his name. The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. [Col. 0585A] XI). Rightly, where wisdom begins, wickedness ends, because wisdom conquers wickedness. How happy is the beginning of wisdom, which drives out all negligence and folly! For, as it is written, “He who fears the Lord neglects nothing” (Eccles. VII); and therefore he does not sluggishly fail to oppose wickedness.

Love of wisdom, placed third, devotes diligent care from affection to those things which should be known or done; it eagerly brings justice to completion and perfection. Love preserves the innocence of mind which fear restores; and, by adding the justice of works to it, advances it also to contemplation of eternal things. Thereafter the lover of this wisdom may rightly and ought to be called a philosopher, because, while the splendour of truth illumines him, the love of virtue also delights him.

Fourth [Col. 0585B] is placed the master’s religious conduct, which should be offered to the novice as though in a mirror; for when an example of integrity is set before him at close range, he is more effectively stirred to the zeal of imitation. For on the mountain an exemplar was shown to Moses, according to whose likeness he was to construct the tabernacle; because the life of those who preside ought to be so exalted that the conduct of those subject to them may be shaped after its example.

Fifth is placed the master’s pious care for the novice, by which he may test and discover whether the novice is found ready and willing for God’s work, for bearing reproach, and for the good of obedience. Certainly, if the master finds him ready for these three things—if he knows him to be fervent in God’s work, displaying with good and cheerful heart the good of obedience toward superiors, equals, and inferiors [Col. 0585C], and patient in bearing reproaches—he may understand that he truly seeks God, provided that he does not fail to bring a happy beginning to its close through happy perseverance.

Let the master teach him to apply himself fervently to the divine work, so that he may guard himself from that sentence of curse which the Holy Spirit pronounces upon all who perform God’s works deceitfully and negligently. Is not he deceitful in God’s work whose mind dissents from the sound of his tongue, and who, though seeming to honour God with his lips, does not fear to withdraw from him through idle, pleasurable, or even malicious thoughts? The Holy Spirit complains through the prophet of such wicked praisers, saying: “This people honours me with their lips, but their heart [Col. 0585D] is far from me. Thus they worship me in vain” (Matt. XV).

The lips of one praising God ought to be well-sounding cymbals. But cymbals do not sound well when the intention and affection of the heart do not agree with the lips that praise. The praiser is negligent who conducts himself carelessly in God’s praises. Nor is it surprising that the numbness of sloth is present in one who, dead in heart, pursues God’s praises only with the sound of his tongue. Whoever thus behaves in the praises of God incurs the curse promulgated by the Holy Spirit. Therefore novices must be admonished more earnestly, lest those who came to receive God’s blessing fall back into this pit of curse.

The master’s pious care ought also to instruct novices concerning the good of obedience, which must be rendered to superiors as to God by the right of the Rule; to equals from [Col. 0586A] brotherly charity; and to inferiors from the virtue of humility. Now he who loves the brethren through charity and denies himself through humility does not greatly care to be affected by reproaches brought against him; indeed, rather, crucifying himself with Christ, he rejoices to be joined to the disgrace of his cross. Thus, in fervour for the divine work, he shows that he loves the worship of God; in rendering obedience, that he loves his neighbour; in patiently bearing reproaches, that he has denied himself.

Sixth is placed friendly and frequent conversation about spiritual matters or regular observances. Those newly converted from the world, however great their devotion, often suffer from the vice of acedia; and therefore the master’s friendly and frequent conversation should be set against the weariness which is accustomed to arise from acedia. [Col. 0586B] At times the conversation should concern spiritual matters: the mysteries of Scripture, the examples of the saints, heavenly rewards and how they are gained by good works, or indeed the torments of Gehenna, which the greatly to-be-feared severity of divine justice threatens to inflict on those who serve impurity and injustice. Frequent discussion of these matters and unceasing meditation upon them greatly move and kindle the mind, so that it may desist from vices and sins and apply itself eagerly to works of virtue.

From friendly, frequent, and honourable conversation there also arises a certain commendable familiarity, through which the master becomes bolder in rebuking, the rebuked person more patient under discipline, both more learned in understanding the Scriptures, and the novice more practised in [Col. 0586C] regular observance. Thereafter the master, according to the Rule, should not indeed impose upon him, but preach to him, the hard and harsh things by which one goes to God. To preach this to him is nothing other than to show, from the Scriptures or from one’s own examples, that narrow and steep is the way which leads to life—a way which beyond doubt he does not walk who does not strive to enter through the narrow gate according to the Lord’s command. “Strive,” says the Lord, “to enter through the narrow gate” (Luke XIII). And elsewhere: “Steep and narrow is the way which leads to life” (Matt. VII). And holy David: “Because of the words of your lips, I have kept hard ways” (Ps. XVI).

What, I ask, can be harder in the Lord’s way than to deny oneself, take up one’s cross, and subject one’s entire [Col. 0586D] will to another’s will? What, I say, can be harsher in the way by which one goes to God than to afflict one’s flesh with its vices and desires, than to show oneself crucified to the world and the world crucified to oneself? Without doubt all do this who truly wish to belong to Christ. “Those who belong to Christ,” says the Apostle, “have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Gal. V).

Therefore the master preaches to the novice the hard and harsh things by which one goes to God, when he shows him, by the example of his deeds and the word of his preaching, that the way of salvation is narrow and steep. This way of salvation, so narrow and so steep, is the Lord Christ: narrow because of the humility of the flesh he assumed; steep because of his freedom from sin. For he [Col. 0587A] “did no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth.” He does not walk this way at all who does not become little in imitation of Christ’s humility; nor can he ascend to this way’s steep height if he chooses to burden himself with the loads of sins or loves of visible things.

For this reason the Holy Spirit cries through the Prophet to people weighed down by the burdens of this Babylon: “Children of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood? Know that the Lord has made his Holy One wonderful” (Ps. IV). Rightly is he holy and made wonderful by the Lord who is not crushed beneath the burdens of worldly misery; so that, finding pleasure in nothing vain or transitory, he may leap over all things in his mind and receive the spirit of freedom. “For where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom”—freedom, I say, from sin, necessity, and misery. [Col. 0587B] This Spirit is sent by God; characters are renewed, and the face of the earth is renewed. Then you will be able to rejoice in your novices, when power from on high makes them participants in this wondrous newness.

Then they will rightly be called novices, when from this newness a wedding garment is fitted to them; nor thereafter will they be cast out from the wedding of the Lamb, when they shine in a wedding garment to the honour of bridegroom and bride. This wedding garment is the inward splendour and glory of newness. It is made from three things: chastity of body, love of heart, and the elegance of discipline.

In this garment chastity is like cloth, which is made from wool, signifying chastity because it does not know bodily passion. [Col. 0587C] Love is compared to skins, which are sewn onto the cloth to make the garment warmer. The passibility and immortality of the spotless Lamb bestowed these skins upon us: for the love which he bore toward us, he gave skin for skin, and everything that he could possess for his soul—that is, to free his Church, which he loved as his own soul, indeed more than his own soul.

The border placed on a garment for adornment is the splendour and elegance of discipline; when this is observed outwardly beyond reproach, it seems thereby to signify the affections both of chastity and of love. The bride had fitted this garment to herself, to whom the bridegroom cries in the Book of Wisdom: “O how beautiful is a chaste generation with charity!” (Wis. I). Thus in the Psalm she asks to be taught concerning discipline, desiring that she might be increased in the goodness [Col. 0587D] of continence and charity: “Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge, for I have believed your commandments” (Ps. CXVIII). And having at length obtained the discipline she had requested, she says: “I rose early and cried out” (ibid.). For discipline makes a person mature: it is the ordered movement of all the limbs and their seemly arrangement in every bearing and action.

That we may briefly recapitulate what has been said: the novice must begin with faith, which truly draws the mind out of the darkness of ignorance and incorporates it into Christ. Incorporated into Christ, he becomes believing and faithful: believing in reliance upon the promises, faithful in keeping the commandments. Fear both enjoins fitting repentance for past evils and forbids tempting evils [Col. 0588A] entry into the heart. Love of wisdom most diligently guards the innocence restored through the office of fear, and does not cease zealously to add to that innocence the equity of most dutiful generosity. The master’s religious conduct provokes the novice, through the example of its integrity, to the desire of emulating virtue. His pious care for the disciple diligently considers, as far as it can, the state of the inward and outward person, so that, according to what it sees in him, it may know how to encourage or accommodate itself to him. Thus it is written: “Carefully consider the countenance of your cattle” (Prov. XXVII).

Friendly and spiritual conversation is wisely set, as said above, against the sickness of acedia; for the more the soul becomes accustomed to holy discourse, the more powerfully fiery speech melts it. [Col. 0588B] Hence the bride, accustomed to divine sayings, declares: “My soul melted when he spoke” (Song V). In this sixfold scheme almost the whole instruction of a devout mind consists: during the time of probation it is to exercise itself in these six things which have been named, and, once its probation is completed, bind itself to the three things expressed in the form of profession.

For stability, conversion of manners, and obedience according to the Rule are solemnly promised in the formula of vowed profession; and in these three, arising from the aforesaid sixfold scheme, a certain perfection is contained. By the tether of promised stability, like pious beasts of burden, we are bound to the heavenly manger. By conversion of manners, we are made like angelic devotion. By rendering obedience, we imitate the ministries of the angels.

Thus faith and fear have regard to establishing stability. Love of virtues and imitation of the master have regard to conversion of manners. The master’s attentive care and the friendly intercourse of spiritual conversation have regard to the formation of obedience [Col. 0588C] to be rendered. For when the numbness of acedia is put to flight through spiritual conversation, the mind revives to the fervour of obedience.

Moreover, to the final question which you yourself proposed, you have, I think, answered quite sufficiently. For God, and those who preside over others according to God, often act dispensationally, so that, in the presence of a pestilent person, the patience of the meek may be scourged. Sometimes, when this is done with good intention, a double fruit results: merit is increased in the patient person through the rebuke, and the one who formerly seemed incorrigible is healed by such an example. Thus the Apostle is permitted by the Lord to be buffeted, not merely so that such buffeting might preserve humility in him, but so that Christ’s whole Church, by a like example, might patiently bear God’s scourges in acquiring humility for itself.

And did not Christ himself, the head of the Church, endure before the eyes of all scourges, reproaches, the cross, and death, which he had not deserved, and thus, through the example of his passion and the price of his blood, call back from everlasting death those who were lost? Consider also the patience of innocent Job: by how many afflictions, under God’s dispensation, he is subjected—not merely so that the invincible patience of the righteous man [Col. 0589A] might be proved, but so that the unhappy world might be instructed by his most righteous examples to patience in its adversities.

Moreover, if scourges sometimes occur for the glory of God, as the Lord Christ declares in the Gospel concerning the man blind from birth, is not an innocent person profitably afflicted with punishments by God or by man, when God’s glory is revealed through the light of his patience? “Let your light shine,” says the Lord, “before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V). It often happens that a teacher, in the presence of perverse people, more harshly rebukes by dispensation the one in whose patience he trusts; because, when wicked people behold God as wondrous in his saints through the patience they display and the innocence they bear, they are transformed, through the tenderness of mercy, from their former perversity into another kind of person.

Behold, brother, compelled by your insistence, I have said some things; but perhaps I have by no means satisfied your expectation. For fuller streams cannot flow from a slight vein. Yet if, as your assertion maintains, you truly love me in Christ, intercede, I beg, before God for my iniquities, and commend me more earnestly to those whom Christian devotion holds and moves according to conscience. Greet your novices in my name, and exhort them on my behalf to apply themselves so to holy newness that in heart and mind they renounce worldly oldness.

## LETTER II. TO THE SAME PERSON. On the Seven Festivals and the Seven Meltings

To his beloved brother in Christ, OSMUND, monk of Mortuimaris [Col. 0589C], brother ADAM, servant of the servants of God who serve Christ at Persenia, greeting and perseverance in true religion.

When something honourable is asked of a friend, and the person asked is a friend, such a petition ought not to be refused, provided that the ability to fulfil it is not lacking. Trusting in the honourableness of your petition and our friendly familiarity, you earnestly ask that you may deserve to be stirred to the pursuit of virtue by some letters. If your disposition is good and you are willing toward what is right, a friendly admonition will not hinder your endeavour to accomplish it. If perhaps your mind is slower toward what is right than it ought to be, exhortation may nevertheless apply a remedy to the sickness. In every way the word of salvation is useful to its hearer, especially when the speaker loves, and there is no doubt that the person addressed loves in return.

And what subject ought there to be in friends’ conversations except love—love, I mean, upon which no suspicion falls when it is called affection or charity? The name *amor* is common to diverse things; but the term *caritas* is confined only to those things which have the force of truth and virtue. Since, then, God is properly and especially called love, charity, or affection, what subject could be more fitting, what discourse sweeter between us, than one concerning such love?

Indeed, since the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, and to love God is wisdom itself, it is clear that the holy savour [Col. 0590A] of love takes its beginning from the affection of divine fear. For when fear of God empties the mind’s dwelling-place of vices, it restores to the heart, once the bitterness of vices has been excluded, an appetite for wisdom. From then on the mind begins to hunger and thirst for righteousness; and undoubtedly it would never hunger so greatly unless the savour already tasted had provoked hunger. “Those who eat me,” says Wisdom, “will still hunger; and those who drink me will still thirst” (Ecclus. XXIV).

For what is love of righteousness except a certain delight in wisdom, since to be just is nothing other than to be seasoned with divine savours and imbued with divine fragrances? Are not the conduct and works of the just certain fragrances of virtues, which are known to have acquired this because they delight in the inward dishes of wisdom? For *sapientia* takes its name from *sapor*, because it makes one relish the things above and is a delightful seasoning of conduct.

What, then, is happier in life than to fear God and, through the diligent office of divine fear, prepare the mind’s dwelling-place for divine love? The vigilance of fear guards the mind with every guard, so that the pleasant festival of love may celebrate its solemn holidays there. The mind must be at leisure if you are to be free to see how great God’s sweetness is and to experience the solemnity of devout love.

There are, therefore, seven solemn festivals in which one is free for God, and in which the soul, that it may be more freely occupied with God, rests from every servile work. The first festival is the spirit of fear of the Lord; by putting an end to sins and vices, it sets spiritual rest before servile work. For the fear of God neglects nothing; and, detesting Pharaoh’s mud and bricks and Egypt’s straw, [Col. 0590C] it is already prepared to keep festival and be free for the Lord.

The second festival is the spirit of piety, in which God is worshipped with greater sincerity and affection the farther the tumult of laborious perversity is excluded from the mind. Piety is the worship of God and compassion for one’s neighbour. In this festival begins that rest and silence which the prophet calls the worship of righteousness (Isa. XXXII).

> Note that in this silence, called the worship of righteousness, which is kept in heaven—that is, in the soul of the righteous—Michael battles with the dragon. For the quieter the heart is from attention to servile work, the more sharply spiritual wickedness assails it. Hence one rightly asks how silence came to pass in heaven when battle, and so great a battle, is waged there. “Battle came to pass in heaven,” it says: “Michael and his angels fought with the dragon” (Apoc. XII). Observe that heaven is the soul of the righteous; in this heaven silence is kept when the soul, quiet from the world’s clamour and free from sinful action, delights wholly in the worship and love of righteousness. Yet because of this rest, in which it renews itself after God’s likeness, it is not thereby excused from having to contend against the powers of the air. For Michael is interpreted “Who is like God?” By this name is signified the likeness of God which justice alone retains. Certainly Paul dwelt in this silence of mind and celebrated these festivals of love when he said of himself and those like him: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood [Col. 0591A], but against the rulers of this darkness, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. VI).

The third festival is the spirit of knowledge, which illumines the devout mind with knowledge of truth and equips it to impart teaching to its neighbour. He ought to speak and teach outwardly the good things which he has deserved to learn inwardly. Whoever has been granted knowledge of God and of himself ought not, in teaching, to neglect the advancement of his neighbours. This spirit of knowledge is not incongruously called a festival, because whoever has attained it rests from all errors and perverse doctrines. This must not be understood of that knowledge which, according to the Apostle, “puffs up” (I Cor. VIII), because this knowledge always builds up in fellowship with the piety joined to it.

The fourth festival is the spirit of fortitude, in which love now begins to be strong as death; when it falls into diverse temptations, it is accustomed to count even all this as joy. Those celebrated this festival to whom the apostle James said: “Count it all joy, dearest brethren, when you fall into diverse temptations” (Jas. I). Whoever acts in the spirit of fortitude either does not feel whatever adverse thing happens to him, or most easily overcomes it with tireless strength.

The fifth festival is the spirit of counsel. It is not enough for this spirit to fulfil God’s commandments; with great eagerness of mind it strives and aspires to follow God’s counsels. For after you have fulfilled God’s commandments, if, according to the Apostle’s exhortation, you seek the better gifts, you stretch yourself upward to fulfil the counsels which the Saviour has proposed to those zealous for perfection. Therefore to the man [Col. 0591C] who asserted that from his youth he had kept all God’s commandments, the Lord says in the Gospel: “One thing is lacking to you. If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give it to the poor; and come, follow me” (Matt. XIX). Therefore whoever acts in this festival—that is, in the spirit of counsel—does nothing without counsel and seeks to give good counsel to everyone in need; for he both possesses within himself the spirit of counsel and is taught by Christ, the angel of great counsel.

The sixth festival is the spirit of understanding, in which the mind, now sufficiently instructed by observance of the preceding festivals, is at leisure to fix its thought upon invisible things. Purified and cleansed, as has been said, by observance of the preceding festivals, it is fit through meditation to attend upon heavenly [Col. 0591D] substances and, with images of visible things removed from the mind, to direct understanding toward invisible essences. For understanding is the naked and manifest knowledge of each invisible thing.

The seventh festival, that is, the Sabbath, is the spirit of wisdom, where the soul, now illuminated by divine splendours, begins meanwhile also to taste a certain seasoning of savour. Here the soul is divinely taught to relish the things above and seek the things above, as it experiences how great and how wondrous is the sweetness of inward savour.

> Note that the festival called the spirit of understanding is wholly in splendour, so that whoever has reached it becomes nothing less than a cherub—that is, fullness of knowledge. But that festival which is called the spirit of wisdom [Col. 0592A] is wholly in savour, so that whoever deserves to reach it becomes nothing less than a seraph, that is, one burning or setting aflame. For one whom the ardour of divine love has set aflame sets others aflame, being melted by that same ardour. That soul which had kept festival had reached this ardour when it said: “My soul melted when he spoke” (Song V). Surely, the mind melted by the fire of this love kindles others, when it makes known, by its meltings, how greatly it loves them.

There are, moreover, many meltings of the soul which burns with heavenly desire and kindles others to desire this ardour. First, through the work and persistence of initial fear, it is dissolved into tears of compunction. For love of righteousness is mingled with this fear, since it is the beginning of wisdom. Second, [Col. 0592B] the soul is dissolved into tears of devotion, which are accustomed to arise from remembrance of a spiritual benefit. When it recalls God’s benefits which it has received though unworthy, it is moved to tears while giving thanks. Third, when melted, it is dissolved into tears of love, which proceed from hope and an ardent desire one day to see the Creator’s face. Fourth, when melted, it is dissolved into tears of piety, which the affection of compassion produces toward a brother’s misery. The fifth melting occurs when, in ardent charity, it spends and gives its whole self in the devout exercises of the active life. The sixth melting occurs when the whole soul melts and is refined into the delights of heavenly contemplation. Hence it is written of such a soul: “Who is this who comes up from the desert, abounding in delights?” (Song VIII). The seventh melting [Col. 0592C] occurs when such a soul wholly flows out and is dissolved into the fragrance of a good name, and for the consolation of many diffuses itself into the aromatic sweetness of a fragrant reputation, so that it may be said of it: “Your name is ointment poured out” (Song I).

Therefore such a soul is called in the Song of Songs “a column of smoke from the aromatics of myrrh and frankincense and every powder of the perfumer.” Such a soul attracts others by the fragrance of its odour and makes them run rejoicing after it toward God’s love, saying: “We shall run after you in the fragrance of your ointments” (ibid.). Such meltings are those outpourings for which the bride is praised when the bridegroom’s voice says to her in the Song: “Your outpourings are a paradise [Col. 0592D] of pomegranates with fruits of apples” (Song IV).

But, my beloved, those who do not conceive innocence from the fear of God never attain these goods. Certainly, neither can those rejoice in the birth of righteousness in whom fear of God does not beget the conception of innocence. Nor does fear bring forth such conception in those whom the splendour of right faith does not illumine. Believe me: hear God’s words with affection; hear so that you may fear; fear so that you may love; love so that you may fulfil the commandments. For from the fulfilment of the commandments follows the happy attainment of rewards. Therefore fear God and keep his commandments. This is the whole duty of man. Farewell always in the Lord, and live so that your conscience may bear inward witness to you, and you may outwardly be an example to the brethren.

## LETTER III. TO THE SAME PERSON. He Consoles One in Affliction. Let Him Flee to Jesus Christ, the True Physician. Let Him Refrain from Writing to Him.

[Col. 0593A]

To his beloved brother in Christ, OSMUND, monk of Mortuimaris, brother ADAM, servant of the servants of God who serve at Persenia, greeting in the Holy Spirit.

Importunity is the mother of weariness where it is not excused by a more ardent sincerity of love. Yet nothing is more trusting than true affection, nor does it judge anything more fitting than to press importunately upon one in whom it trusts. This confidence gives those who love God constancy in prayer; nor do they cease from persistence in prayer because they know that they place their confidence in him whom they love. You seem to have this confidence of love toward me. [Col. 0593B] Therefore you do not fear to be marked as troublesome, because the inward consciousness of charity grants you confidence. But, I ask you, why do you complain so much to me about yourself, and set before me and disclose the various ailments of your mind as though for a remedy? Or what advantage can there be in showing one’s illness to someone suffering from the same weakness? Does not he, in some fashion, aggravate the pain of a sick man who presents him with his own lamentations and tears, when he ought rather to console him? You should instead have revealed your infirmities to one to whom the strength that is the soul’s health has been granted, and to whom, together with health of mind, skill in healing has also been given. For one who possesses health of mind—that is, virtue—does not thereby at once possess skill in healing. But he who receives both from God is happily at hand for those who are ill [Col. 0593C] and heals them.

For it is ridiculous for anyone to undertake the office of the healing art and yet show himself weak to those for whom he provides care. And one whom the signs of manifest sickness make contemptible can scarcely be effective in administering remedies. Since, then, virtue is the health of the mind, whose sickness is vice, I do not offer a remedy for your sickness, for I lie everywhere wounded by this disease in the infirmary of worldly misery. Yes, yes: because the guarding of the heart has been neglected, life abounds and overabounds in vices; and from the ailments of overflowing vices, once consent has been given, a viperish brood of sins is born. For the inward adhesion of vices brings it about that the remembrance of sin is almost continual within us. [Col. 0593D] Yet, if this remembrance has neither delight nor consent with it, it produces nothing in those who fear God except warfare. From warfare, however, if the mind persists in the strength of constancy, victory results; and victory advances to the crown, which no one deserves unless he has contended lawfully.

Therefore the soul devoted to virtue strives, since it cannot oppose the first movements, at least not to slip into the danger of delight or consent, lest it be drawn even from nearby into the perversity of an act. But my unhappy soul is continually shaken, as is its custom, by its first movements; it is dangerously enticed by the thoughts arising from them; and delight and consent grow so strong from such a disease that they very often draw me into the act of unlawful consent. Oh, if, as [Col. 0594A] wisdom commands, the heart were guarded with every vigilance, then the mind would not conceive iniquity from the delight of sin, nor would the offspring of wickedness proceed from such conception! Certainly, if the fear of God kept vigilant watch, it would utterly deny every wickedness entrance at the gateway of the heart; and, just as through vigilance sin would wither at the soul’s entrance, so what had been allowed through negligence to enter wrongly would be driven from its inward parts through repentance.

For the fear of God loves innocence and is no less a champion of justice, accustomed to restore the losses of innocence through the uprightness of justice. When the soul that has lost innocence to the injury of its Creator renders justice to God from itself through repentance, does it not seem to you to restore innocence through repentance? Yet it would surely have been far better for it not to have gone down from Jerusalem to Jericho, [Col. 0594B] not to have fallen among robbers, than, after being wounded by robbers, to have sought remedies of salvation. Nevertheless, blessed is the person who, by repenting, rises from innocence once lost to justice. But happier is the person so fortified by the guard of divine fear that he disdains to do anything against innocence.

Nothing, therefore, is more blessed than divine fear. When the mind is fixed by its weight, it is not tossed about by various vain thoughts. For when it continually touches and pricks the heart with the spur of its office, it scarcely permits anything other than that very pricking or the cause of the pricking to come to mind. While it keeps watch at the door of the heart as a vigilant guardian, usefully and happily, it gives love a place to celebrate inwardly. Holy fear, indeed, while it attends to God, very readily blows idle thoughts away from before the heart; it pursues pleasurable thoughts through desire for the proposed good; and it drives out malicious thoughts by the resistance of simplicity and compassion. Therefore, when the assaults of vices have been restrained by the devout vigilance of holy fear and the tumults of thoughts have been calmed, the conscience now keeping Sabbath, love celebrates inwardly; and it keeps holidays all the more joyfully because it knows the mind to be free for aspiring to heavenly things.

Therefore, dearest one, whenever a festival of this kind, through the benefit of love poured into you, makes your mind glad, receive me as a companion in that inward celebration. Do not make the good bestowed on you a private possession, but remember, amid your delights, a friend who is still outwardly a beggar. [Col. 0594D] Break, I say, your bread for your begging and hungry friend; for in this you will prove yourself truly a friend: if you refresh your friend’s hunger with your bread. Your bread is Christ; your bread is your charity; your bread is your prayer; your bread is the compunction of tears, by which you wash away not only your own sins but also those of your friends. The holy Prophet declares that he refreshes himself day and night with these breads: “My tears,” he says, “have been my bread day and night” (Ps. 41). Certainly, the more eagerly he was refreshed with these breads, the stronger he became for bearing the burdens of others. For the refreshment of heavenly bread so strengthens a person’s heart that he can both endure labors himself and willingly and effectively show himself strong in carrying his brothers’ burdens.

Certainly, [Col. 0595A] one who feeds on breads of this kind becomes so strong, is made so firm by such weight, that vain and useless thoughts cannot, I do not say overthrow him, but can scarcely even move him. For while the soul laboring in the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts is sweetly and eagerly refreshed by the bread either of the Scriptures or of tears, it is neither driven nor disturbed by the various winds of thoughts. Those thoughts, precisely because they are vain, do not bend from its upright stability a mind made firm by the strength of its customary food. When you have been filled with such breads, keep at least something for me from the remnants, so that, refreshed by them, I too may endure in my labors, which, as you know, have increased beyond measure and beyond my strength.

Moreover, concerning the ailments of your soul, of which you complain to me in your letter, [Col. 0595B] hasten to flee for help and care to him who, according to his own word, came not for the healthy but to offer a remedy to those who are ill. He is called Christ, because he applies saving anointing to the wounds of the stricken. He is called Jesus, because he restores those anointed by him to complete health. I want you commended to the efficacy of his medicine. Devoutly and humbly beseech him that the effective medicine of his grace may also assist my weakness. Henceforth, my son, do not trouble me, nor ask anything further of me; for, although I do not intend henceforth to reply to your requests, I shall nevertheless not cease to love you in truth, as long as you stand in the truth. Farewell always in the Lord.

## LETTER IV. TO THE SAME PERSON

He reproves him for having tried to obtain a reply from Adam through an intermediary.

[Col. 0595C]

Brother ADAM to Brother OSMUND.

You are clever, and act shrewdly: what you despair of obtaining through yourself, you seek from me through an intermediary. And indeed you introduced such a person that on this occasion I could not refuse what you requested through her. But perhaps another time I would do otherwise, if I had to endure such insistence from her on your behalf. Now, therefore, you have the letter you sought. You also have my heart in the bowels of Jesus Christ. And although I am glad to rest from the necessity of writing, I shall nevertheless never cease to love you in the Holy Spirit.

Would that you kept the little letters of my humility stored away with you and did not make known to others the poverty of my slightness! For if Scripture forbids you to praise a person during his lifetime, how do you labor to exalt with praises the little works of my rusticity—especially since the secret conversations of our hidden love ought to be concealed from all worldly people? Holy affection has always been accustomed to delight in private converse. This flame is more easily extinguished when it is imprudently exposed to the winds. Therefore, whatever I say or write to you more privately out of great love, see that through you it does not become public. For, as I have said, the force of love often grows lukewarm or is extinguished by the blasts of windy praise. Farewell always in the Lord.

## LETTER V. TO THE SAME PERSON

On the love of God.

[Col. 0596A]

Brother ADAM, humble servant of the brethren of Perseigne, to his beloved brother in Christ OSMUND, monk of Mortemer: may you die to vices and live to virtues at Mortemer.

Would, my son, that the Dead Sea might be for you what the Red Sea was for Israel, so that, while by the leadership of grace a free passage through it is granted to you, the Egyptians pursuing you may be drowned in it with their Pharaoh! For, triumphing gloriously over them under the hand of Moses, you hasten through it into the wilderness. Indeed, you have learned by experience that solitude is most friendly to divine love. One who gives himself to love of heavenly things flees the crowd, avoids noise, and, like Mary, disdains Martha’s busy and frequent service, so that he may more safely hear and see Christ the more privately. [Col. 0596B]

Certainly, nothing so furthers the business of love as being solitary—that is, being a monk. For the religious and tranquil manner of life of a monk is itself the solitude that holy love desires. Yet the devotion of this love is not situated in the leisure of so great a solitude in such a way as to be free from the fear of devout concern. Rather, the loving soul is always fearful and apprehensive, lest, through negligence, it be idle from a good work to the peril of its love. Such, indeed, is divine love. Yet brotherly love too is full of devout concern; and one who sincerely loves another scarcely turns away the eye of his regard from the beloved.

Behold, my son, I have received your letter; it has been read to me, and from reading it I learned more clearly that love is truly never idle. For where it fixes its affection, there it directs its eye; nor does it allow its insatiable eye not to see what it delights to love with tenacious and eager affection. This appears to be the meaning of the poet’s saying, although he speaks of a contrary kind of love, when in a certain line he says:

> Love is a thing full of anxious fear.  
> (Ovid, *Heroides* I.)

For just as the nature of fire does not rest from drawing into its fuel the material placed beneath it, so the mind, kindled with the desire of a lover’s love, draws the whole thing it loves into the increase of its joy: it thinks anxiously about it, speaks gladly [Col. 0596D] about it, and wherever it has laid up the treasure of its love, there it delightfully places both the affection and the gaze of its mind. For where love is, there is the eye; and, according to the evangelical saying, “Where your treasure is, there also is your heart” (Matt. 6).

Everyone has his own joy in what he loves; and concerning the thing toward which he is more strongly inclined, he rejoices more fully and meditates more delightfully. And what wonder, my son? Certainly, among the powers of the soul none is freer than love, none more liberating, none sweeter, none equally strong. When that flame finds material suited to it, it burns fiercely, glows sweetly, and blazes pleasantly; and when it has been strongly kindled, scarcely anything can interrupt it. But you must consider what fuel you apply to your fire. You can most easily be deceived when you strongly love something that you have by no means established with certainty to be worthy of your love. Love must be bestowed upon virtue. In human beings, virtue of the soul alone is to be loved. But virtue of the soul alone, since it is to be sought, must especially and eagerly be imitated; and wherever it may be found, it must be loved in a singular way.

I have said this, dearest one, because you are captured far too quickly and seem to love me as though you knew my holiness. Yet although I rejoice, unworthy as I am, to be loved by you, I would not have you suffer deception in loving anyone. Love God: the fountain of wisdom, author of virtue, giver of grace, promiser of glory, bestower of blessedness. To serve him is to reign; to love him is virtue; to cling to him is holiness; to attain him is salvation; to possess him is honor and glory; [Col. 0597B] to be with him is everlasting blessedness and happiness.

Moreover, as you state in your letter that you ask nothing of me, you seem to be observing my prohibition well. But what, I ask, is writing to me except asking for a written reply of some sort, so that, while I am seemingly compelled to answer letters, you may appear indirectly to be seeking letters? Nevertheless, I shall not be angry with you on this account, if you wish and are able to write back to me more frequently; for frequent letters are truly a certain proof of enduring love. I ask nothing else of you except that your prayer to God for my sins may persevere, and that by his grace you may so live as to be worthy to obtain what you ask. For I have no confidence in my own merits unless another’s prayer helps and supports me. Farewell always in the Lord.

## LETTER VI. TO ODO, BISHOP OF PARIS

> [Note: [Col. 0597D] Odo of Sully, who, when Bishop Maurice of Paris died in 1196, succeeded him.]

He reproves him because he imposed tallages upon the priests of his diocese.

[Col. 0597C]

Brother A., least of all monks, to the dearest father in Christ, O., by God’s grace bishop of Paris: greeting in the spirit of knowledge and piety.

Whenever my friend writes, the claims of friendship and the custom of former love return to mind. Yet I confess, venerable Father, that my affection does not find you so suited to itself as it was formerly accustomed sometimes to experience you. But I would attribute this not to the fault of a friend, but rather to a defect in affection—although something occurs to me from which love may seem not without reason to have been altered. [Col. 0597D] For according to the varying condition of things, the nature of love varies itself; and toward unlike causes and unlike objects it is accustomed to burn differently.

Since, therefore, in one and the same man I regard both a friend and a bishop, and while one delights in familiar affection, the other, because of his rank, claims reverence for himself, love—ignorant of reverence and impatient of lordship—does not consent to so great a discord. Where, in the affair of love, the necessity of reverence intervenes, love suffers loss through inequality and charity complains that it is robbed of its right, when it is exiled from the fellowship of unity. Therefore, while the honor due to rank is paid in reverence, affection, ignorant of necessity, is forced beyond the limits of reciprocal attachment and is undoubtedly diminished in feeling. Hence it becomes slower to visit, more hesitant in conversation, more fearful in greeting, more timid in asking, and more retentive in giving. Since I, then, am the least among the small, and you great among the greatest, what union, I ask, can there be between things so discordant that friendly love might delight in equality with itself amid things so unequal?

I have not said this, venerable Father, because I shall ever cease to revere and love you, provided that virtue and truth do not cease to dwell with you. For, with Jesus’ help, it is wholly my purpose to love these wherever they may betake themselves; nor can I fail in affection toward him whom grace has chosen to illuminate with such splendors. And certainly, although gratuitous love regards nearly every necessity of reverence with suspicion, one who loves virtue cannot but love these things affectionately even in bishops, though he strives to restrain his feeling lest he betray it outwardly in action. For the demonstrations of the lowly toward the distinguished are easily condemned as improper familiarity; therefore the purity of love more prudently keeps itself within the affection than reveals itself outwardly by certain signs.

Accordingly, I, a dweller in the cloister, have chosen more sweetly and safely to frequent the humble dwelling of Cistercian philosophy than to follow and visit through cities a friend whom I grieve to have almost lost in the bishop. Nevertheless, I receive adequate compensation for this loss if, through your reverence, mercy and truth among others, and especially among your subjects, accomplish what they have enjoined you to do through the ministry of priesthood. [Col. 0598C] You are a pillar of salt: offer yourself to animals alike for food and benefit, so that, having been raised from the bushel-measure to the height of the lampstand, you may shine as a lamp for all.

The time has come for some greater splendor of your glory to shine forth, now that that Lucifer has set from the firmament of the Church—the man who so often illuminated the hemisphere by the rays of his life and the splendors of his teaching. I think you understand me, for I speak to a wise man: I mean the Parisian cantor of pious memory.

> [Note: [Col. 0597D] He seems to mean Peter the Chanter of Paris, celebrated for his writings, who became a Cistercian monk at the monastery of Longpont and died with a reputation for holiness. [Col. 0598D]]

Would that you mourned the death of so great a man, though, according to the opinion of some, you did not in the least grieve over [Col. 0598D] his absence—a report to which, however, I could not give credence! For the present, other matters must be omitted which common popular opinion charges against your reputation—indeed, matters most deserving of harsher rebuke, if there were anyone who truly loved you and, finding them true, found you truly open to the corrections of friends.

But perhaps you accuse me of speaking too irreverently, and say that it does not at all savor of humility that I attack a bishop so boldly. But this is truly what I had said: love does not know reverence; indeed, as the mind speaks to itself, so it speaks freely with a friend. I confess that I have forgotten episcopal reverence, still retaining something of the old love; nor, even when absent, shall I ever spare you. However great the reverence owed to rank, zeal is owed against vices and love to virtues. Would that our zeal did not find in a friend something from which it might receive or inflict a wound, but rather something that might gladden him and delight itself!

Moreover, when I have deserved to see your fatherhood in person, I shall express to you orally what I have now judged better to leave unsaid. Yet I do not think it ought to be passed over in silence that it is almost universally reported: namely, that you have levied tallages upon the priests of your diocese. This seems wholly foreign not only to perfection but even to piety and justice. In this, venerable Father, you have caused grave scandal to those who love you. Those who expected from you, as from a lamp set upon a lampstand, flame rather than smoke, marvel and grieve that in this matter you emit smoke rather than flame. [Col. 0599B] For smoke is accustomed to trouble eyes and nostrils; and those who hoped to see examples of light from you and to conceive the fragrance of good hope suffer distress from contraries in both respects.

Oh, what is more faithful than true love? What is more sincere than charity that is steadfast? Since it does not doubt that a whole mass is corrupted by a little leaven, it does not permit the conscience to be cauterized by some evil that can be avoided. Would that you neither make this evil customary nor, by your example, draw the wretched world into imitation; but rather, by remedies of manifest repentance, teach that one must not do what you have taught by the example of your deed to be less blameworthy! For so great a bishop, so greatly desired by all, sought from the Lord by the prayers of so many saints, watered by the tears of so many faithful people in order to produce the shoots of perfection, ought not to have in his conscience—and still less ought to do openly—anything by which his reputation may be harmed or the devoted expectation of all may be disappointed.

But if, as some say, necessity compelled you, being burdened by many debts, to do something—where no tyrannical extortion or authoritative exaction intervened, but merely a humble and supplicatory statement of necessity requested something kindly—then I would call this not so much a tallage as a collection. Although even this does not savor of perfection, it was nevertheless better to do it once in a lifetime than, when the moment of uncertain death obstructed you, to leave many debts unpaid, to the grave peril of the debtor and irreparable loss of the creditor. [Col. 0599D] For this very often—indeed almost always—happens to bishops: when they die, their goods are so plundered by temporal power that what they have owed or ordered cannot be allowed to be paid.

Charity is accustomed to interpret ambiguities in the better sense. What intention you had in this deed, you must see to; lest perhaps—God forbid!—avarice, the service of idols, should make a bishop of Christians into a worshiper of idols. Yet even if your heart does not rebuke you, the deed has become an evil appearance and a scandal to all: the wicked are given an opportunity for mockery, and the good grieve that they have lost in you what they had hoped for. [Col. 0600A] Besides, Father, I have certain matters in my heart which it would be lengthy, and perhaps unworthy, to write. When our messenger—or messengers, through the ministry of the living voice—has expressed them to your reverence, if you judge them worthy of hearing, I humbly and earnestly ask you to carry them out.

## LETTER VII. TO ODO, BISHOP OF PARIS

It is wholly about love and humility. At the end, he gives thanks for charity bestowed upon two women during a famine.

ODO, venerable bishop of Paris, whom he loves in the Holy Spirit: Brother ADAM, a sinner, greeting.

It often comes into my mind, dearest one, to write you something by which both the affection I have toward you may be made known to you in some measure [Col. 0600B] and the affection of your love toward me may grow warmer. Would that my speech might serve you in place of oil, so that, when it is cast into the flame of your love, that flame might thereby be nourished and increased—nourished and increased toward me, I mean. For although I am not worthy of your love, I do not doubt that you love whatever things are worthy.

But the poverty of my soul has no need of any other good, nor does it desire any other profit from the business of friendship than that it may happily deserve to love and be loved. This is the whole concern that I have with friends. This alone is my material in writing; nor can I praise or love in my letters anything other than that which is sufficient to unite us so firmly. O happy union, from whose bond holy love cuts off and separates everything that does not separate itself from worldly vanity! [Col. 0600C] O happy love, which, as it takes its origin from the virtue of the soul, so has no incentive from anywhere but deeds of truth! Happy love, I say, to which hope of the world is hostile, whose entire ambition lies in desire for eternal things. Holy love, indeed, the more impatient it is of corruption, the more it mistrusts everything it knows to be subject to vanity.

Finally, just as it is not without the vehement zeal of rivals, so it is not without knowledge of the things to be sought, lest it be deceived. It is therefore instructed by the splendor of truth, lest manifold vanity of shadowy variety darken it. And while virtue is at work, it is kindled and stretched out toward the desire of incorruption, lest the lust of the flesh soften and weaken it. Oh, if perseverance does not fail its advances, what reward will holy love obtain in perfection? What glory will be its lot when truth shines in full splendor? What pleasure and sweetness will be its lot when it burns toward the noon of full love with the desire of persevering virtue?

O blessed expectation! O recompense worthy of every desire! O happy soul which, when it has found this pearl, does not hesitate to sell everything else in comparison with it! Therefore possessions of body and soul must unhesitatingly be sold, so that you may more happily seek, more vigorously dig up, more certainly find, more firmly retain, and more joyfully possess the treasure hidden in the field. The burdens of the world must be cast off, honors reckoned as nothing, and every wickedness driven from the mind, so that it may in some measure taste beforehand the first fruits of holy love. For just as it graciously flows into pure minds, so it desires to find minds free, which are not disturbed or occupied by the noise of earthly activity.

[Col. 0601A] Where the Holy Spirit’s customary Sabbath is kept, a mind at leisure is needed, one that does not in any degree cloud the joy of spiritual holidays with the ugliness of servile work. In the holiday of fear, love takes its beginning from the beginning of wisdom, putting an end to the tumults of sins. In the holiday of piety, this is done: that attention be sincerely directed to divine worship and that the miseries of the oppressed be helped by compassionate concern. In the holiday called the spirit of knowledge, the soul, withdrawing itself inwardly, weighs carefully the judgment of its own reason, lest, when its little fire grows dim or cold, it be left in darkness regarding what must be done. In the holiday of the spirit of fortitude, provision is made that, when the time of temptation comes, the soul, armed with necessary defenses, may resist manfully. In the spirit of counsel a happy holiday is celebrated when, in everything it undertakes, the mind places no confidence in itself, seeks the counsel of the Holy Spirit, and in the same Spirit offers itself to others as a counselor wholly faithful.

In the holiday of the spirit of understanding, a festival of such purity is kept that not only do earthly affections weigh down the soul, but even images of bodies do not enter it, so that heavenly things may be contemplated all the more clearly as earthly things are meanwhile more happily absent from memory. What shall I say of that final and highest holiday, called the spirit of wisdom? It has not been given to me to experience how great is the abundance of sweetness in this Sabbath. For I have not yet deserved to celebrate the preceding holidays, but have not yet, in the spirit of the fear of the Lord, bade farewell to the slavery of crimes and the tumults of vices. How, then, should I dare to speculate about the other holidays of wisdom, or about wisdom’s Sabbath itself? [Col. 0601C] From this very presumption it is easy to understand that I have not yet received the spirit of understanding or wisdom, since, without experience, I have dared to discuss matters so hidden.

Nevertheless, I trust that love will excuse the excess in the mind of one who loves. For holy love has this as its office: just as it does not at all conceal a fault in the beloved, so neither does it refuse, with kindly readiness, to grant pardon to one who confesses. Truly, if the spirit of the fear of the Lord were in me, I would have feared appearing boastful, and I would rather hide myself under the bushel of humility than walk in things great and wonderful beyond me. Nearly every presumption is hateful to holy humility; and however greatly it has risen to eminence, it judges nothing safer for itself than to remain wisely hidden. It strives for heaven while, according to the meaning of its name, it does not separate itself from the ground; and the lower it bows itself in its own estimation, the more it inclines toward the height of heavenly things.

I do not know how, but the voluntary abasement of humility is even able to bend the heavens and, with marvelous ease, attains heavenly exaltation while sitting joyfully on the ground, desiring nothing from the ground, and glorying in the testimony of conscience alone. Not so, not so, that pride heavenly by origin: when, in accordance with the meaning of its name, it strives to go above itself and surpass itself, it is cast down by its own weight and shattered below with incurable ruin. [Col. 0602A] Therefore every height is suspect to humility, for it knows that height is a friend to pride.
