Whatever the flesh considers glory, humility hates and abhors, though in its simplicity it so restrains itself that it neither wishes nor dares to judge about anything. Loving silence and desiring secrecy, it confines itself within the limits of its own moderation, so that it seeks nothing other than to know itself. It believes it superfluous to know other things; it judges it vanity to be known by others. It is as free from superfluity as from boastfulness, practicing temperance in the former and burning with a desire for justice in the latter.

Here you can observe great prudence in humility, which fortifies the commonwealth of the mind with these defenses and provides it with invincible strength for every conflict. O happy and truly necessary virtue, humility, which, while it seeks to know nothing but itself, does not find the treasure of heavenly wisdom hidden from its knowledge! For the humble mind covers the fire of hidden love beneath reflection on its own worthlessness, as beneath a kind of ash; from this fire the workshop of the devout heart kindles itself for illumination and fervor. O how gladly humble Christ withdraws to such a lodging, where the vigilance of humility keeps the fire of his love always ready for his coming! For, as the Psalmist says, “Fire shall go before him” (Ps. 96); and the soul is fit to receive him when it need not beg for fire or oil. These come from within and from heaven; and whoever wishes the fire once kindled within to endure must carefully secure every entrance through which the lightness of windy vanity may blow in to extinguish [Col. 0602C] the fire.

Yet even though a fire that burns intensely is not extinguished but rather kindled more strongly when the wind blows, humility is so cautious that it never judges it safe to go forth from the humble lodging of conscience. There it freely contemplates Mary, star of the sea; there it happily stands by the Virgin’s childbirth; there it delightfully plays with that blessed infancy; there it wholly adapts itself to the Word’s cradle; it joyfully plays with that infancy through innocence of character; and in the joy of its heart it babbles along with the cries of the child. It counts it more precious than silks to be adorned with those little cloths in which the infant Word is wrapped. Thereafter it carries itself with complete eagerness to that divine sanctuary of the most holy breast, and, as much as opportunity allows, sucks the breasts, full from heaven.

Meanwhile, tender infancy delights in such nourishment, so that when, in more advanced age, it has grown into a perfect man, it may be able to bear and accomplish the work of the cross. This is indeed the work of grace: grace which, through the advance of virtue, has given it a beard in the studies of wisdom, its senses having been exercised by habit. It would go very well with me if my Jesus counted me among his fellow nurslings, if he sometimes admitted me to his mother’s breasts and shared with me small draughts of his tenderness. For this purpose the Word of the Father, the bread of life, willed to be broken into pieces in the milk of flesh: he who, in the form of God, was the solid food of angels, emptied himself through the abbreviation of flesh into a little draught for children.

I beseech you, dearest one, when the banquet of stronger food pleases you, when the food of the mature delights you, do not, amid your delights, forget [Col. 0603A] my littleness. If at times, advanced by the Holy Spirit, you attain the celebration of wisdom’s Sabbath, obtain at least this for me: that I may not be cast out from the lodging of the infant Word. Here, meanwhile, lies the whole rationale of my philosophy; nowhere else could I be more sweetly situated; from here hangs the whole expectation of my hope. I am a little child, who needs milky food, not solid food—although I do not doubt that whatever the blessed hunger of my friends consumes of stronger food passes into my own growth.

Moreover, dearest one, I shall see your face when you are free, for you are not yet free. The barrenness of the present year and the common ruin of the whole world keep me at home and compel me to attend, as it were, a funeral. Yet, God willing, I shall sometime come out of such a tomb [Col. 0603B] and be raised again in visits and conversations with friends. Meanwhile greet in my name those whom you have found me to love with unfeigned charity. For those two poor women, fearing God, I believe, I give thanks to your generosity, because at Balneolum, during this time of famine, you mercifully provided for them in very large measure.

> [Note: [Col. 0603D] The brief Chronicle of Saint-Amand seems to speak of this famine under the year 1197: “As the supply of provisions failed, an exceedingly severe famine and a dreadful calamity occurred.” [Col. 0604D]]

I beg you: let not compassion withdraw its hand from those from whom the necessity of famine has not yet withdrawn. Farewell.

## LETTER VIII. TO STEPHEN, A CARTHUSIAN MONK AND PRIOR OF PORTES

On meditating upon Christ’s infancy and passion.

To Brother STEPHEN, his truest friend in Christ’s love, Carthusian monk and prior of Portes, [Col. 0603C] from the abbots of Carolilocus and Sarnay, and from the last of all, the abbot of Perseigne: may he happily love in the Holy Spirit and be faithfully loved in return.

From your letters, dearest friend, I have taken the occasion of replying to you. In them you ask that, through one of us, the union of our threefold affection, uniting itself to you alone, may write back to you some consolation concerning that one Good. This indeed we do willingly, assenting to your request and rejoicing in your affection—except that you ought to have been more sparing in praising those whom you have not seen inwardly. Oh, how unsafe it is to dwell upon the praises of persons whose conscience is still cauterized by sin, lest, as easily happens, pride tempt the one so praised, just as flattery commonly stains the praiser! Yet this takes place among impure minds, which the sincerity of holy love does not refine—whereas by blessed experience we find that yours is refined and melted toward us.

Therefore, since by the workmanship of the Holy Spirit you have twisted us three into a threefold cord of chaste love, to which your affection might bind itself: just as that cord, because it is threefold, cannot easily be broken, so, because it is tenacious, it can with the greatest difficulty be untied by you. The skilful condescension of the Holy Spirit has woven this cord; and it is the more tenacious in itself through the glue of indivisible charity, the sweeter its construction is to those bound together by it. How much happier it is to be constrained by these knots, bound by these ties, held by these bonds against the theatrical wantonness of the world, than to be entangled in secular affairs, hemmed in by the perplexities of vices, or detained by the enticements of the flesh! O yoke of holy love—how sweetly you seize, how gloriously you ensnare, how gently you press, how delightfully you honour with rewards, how happily you burn, how strongly you bind, how wisely you instruct! O happy love, from which come strength of character, purity of affections, subtlety of understanding, holiness of desires, brightness of works, fruitfulness of virtues, worthiness of merits, and sublimity of rewards! O happy love, whose ambition is contempt for the world, whose zeal is directed against vices, whose hatred is against sins, whose conflict is against the flesh, whose moderation is in prosperity, whose patience is in adversity, and whose desire is for the eternal promises!

This love unites us; this love joins you to our union; and he who makes us of one disposition in the house of God will at some time, through God’s grace and through perseverance in holy unanimity, advance us to the one denarius of the one vineyard. Yet meanwhile love must be nourished, fed with the foods of wisdom, and warmed with the sweetest caresses of Mother Grace. We are little children and need draughts of milk; but let it be drawn from our Virgin’s . . . Therefore we wisely flee to her childbirth, choosing not to depart from the lodging of the woman in labour, so that we may drink our fill from the sacred treasury of the Virgin’s breast. She is our mother, and a most sweet mother; the tender weakness of those who suck cannot endure to be absent from so great a sweetness. Nowhere else could we be safer, more sweetly nourished, more gently warmed, more firmly guarded, more rightly instructed, or more holily renewed.

How delightful it is to adapt oneself to the cradle of the infant Word, to stand beside the manger, and to have no place elsewhere than in the lodging where there is no place for the woman in labour! “There was no room for him in the lodging” (Luke 2); therefore she laid him in a manger. May it never happen that we turn aside from that lodging or be turned away from that manger, where the grain of angels was made into barley for animals. For when the grain of heavenly wheat fell into the earth, it offered, as it were, to pious beasts the flavour and hope of barley within itself: both because it clothed the marrow of his divinity in the husk of a mortal body, and because he made himself rough to me with the awns of my necessities. Even now the marrow of truth is wrapped in the husks, as it were, of certain figures.

[Col. 0604D] O when mortal man attains the angelic state, no roughness will then remain in his food: naked Truth will satisfy him most fully with the fatness of wheat. But why do we, frail beings, speak of enjoying either the burdens of beasts or the honours of angels, when, because of the tenderness of our infancy, we still need maternal soothing? It is enough for us if we may lean upon the mother’s breast, if we are allowed to remain between her breasts. From there come streams of grace; from there nourishment for the humble; from there the rushing flood that makes glad the city of God; from there flow milk and honey of supreme sweetness. From there our little one has grown into a perfect man—the one who, shortening himself from heavenly greatness into a child, adopted us as his fellow-nurslings.

Do you suppose that the most loving child begrudges his fellow-nurslings the mother’s womb or her breasts? He chose her as his mother precisely so that she might also be a nurse to the humble. Therefore, since the tenderness of infants is not accustomed to feed on the roughness of barley and is less fit for eating wheat, let them meanwhile be nourished at the breasts and warmed in the softer lap of their mother. Let them learn to adapt themselves to the cradle of the Word, to play with pious simplicity, to babble in response to his infant cries, and to share the games of the smiling little child.

This is the whole philosophy of the simple, until a more advanced age of virtue is present—an age fit to use the customary food and suited to endure suffering.

[Col. 0605B] If you wish to admit your Odo to games of this kind, we not only do not refuse, but gladly receive one who plays with this innocence. For he is a lover of the simple and a most genuine friend of ours, although you have deserved to obtain a special privilege in his affection. Bring the man with you, and establish him with us within the lodging of the Word, so that they may rejoice with equal joy in the birth of our Virgin. If shepherds arrive bearing among them angelic signs, let them not wonder at the mystery of so great a matter without us. If a star brings the Magi, let them share the joy of those who arrive; and while those men bring mystical gifts, let us offer what has been signified to them.

Nor is there any doubt that gold abounds with you to offer, since for the gold of Jerusalem you despised the dung-heap of Babylon. You should take care to supply, from the abundance of your gold, the poverty of your singer, who, though he still seems outwardly to serve this world, also appears in his heart to trample the mud of the age. It will be happier to display the desire of the heart through the garment of the body, and to bear before the face of one’s actions the marks of the Lord’s Passion. Yet he places great confidence in your gold, and cannot conceal from us the joy of his good will because he has deserved to find you as a treasure hidden in a field. For where the splendour of heavenly wisdom shines, where the fervour or brilliance of burning charity glows, there are golden ages; there abounds that by which the dignity of the royal child may be honoured.

[Col. 0605D] O if we offer the incense of divine prayer to the cradle of the Word, and so incense that divine altar that we fill the whole lodging of the Virgin in labour with good fragrance! There indeed it is fitting not only to set incense alight with the flame of fervent prayer, but also to burn up spices with the fire of love and virtue, so that the sweet fragrance of a good reputation may not be lacking to the testimony of a conscience that gives forth fragrance. Happy is the one who has offered gold and incense to our child; happy the one who joins myrrh to such a sacrifice! You see that our child does not at present offer myrrh but receives it. How, then, shall we, who are his fellow-nurslings, offer the bitterness of sufferings? Yet we shall offer it when his grace has advanced us so far that a stronger age of virtue can endure hard and harsh things.

Meanwhile the harshness of suffering, the bitterness of myrrh, does not suit tender age—except insofar as myrrh is accustomed to keep worms away from preserved bodies. Therefore, in faith in the Passion and in mortification of the flesh, we receive myrrh rather than offer it; for though we cannot put our hands to mighty deeds, we nevertheless in some measure keep ourselves, within Christ’s lodging, from the worms of vice and the rot of sin. It is delightful for us to meditate on such matters, and rightly the festival of our hearts celebrates in these things, from which it receives the incentive of solemn joy.

Rightly you have joined your pair to our threefold union, since in bringing your singer—who is ours as well—you have greatly increased our festival. For in joining two to three in the bond of charity, you have, as it were, made us five virgins among those who are not foolish. “Five of them,” he says, “were foolish, and five prudent” (Matthew 25). O if that foolishness may be excluded from our number of five which, it is said, excluded the five foolish women from the Bridegroom’s wedding! It is altogether foolish to pride oneself upon the title of virginity while lacking, in the virtue of the mind, the reality denoted by that name. O if we may be five prudent virgins and preserve, with uncorrupted faith, the fivefold continence of the senses! Uncorrupted faith and an unwavering purpose of continence make the mind virgin; love of justice makes it wise. O prudent virginity! O virginal prudence, which, while it acts according to its zeal for charity, rightly remains a virgin—that is, whole in the faith of the mind!

[Col. 0606C] Blessed is the person granted to join to the glory of this virginity the lily of bodily virginity. The virgin blossoms within and without, in flesh and spirit, displaying the rose of love and the lily of chastity in the flesh. Prudent virginity is a friend of anointing; it does not lack the oil of gladness; it does not go forth without lamp and oil. Its lamp is glass-like through the clearness of purity, narrow below and closed through voluntary poverty, wide above and open through desire for eternal things. But whence will it have oil, unless it keeps itself within the lodging of our woman in labour, unless it gathers itself to the Virgin’s childbirth? For she is the fruitful olive, the beautiful olive in the fields, so that her grace and mercy may be common to all. Set in the fields, she brought forth the flower of the field; through the beauty of that flower the nakedness of human disgrace procured for itself most beautiful garments of the field. These garments of the field are girdles, coverings of shame, which all who, through faith and love of the virginal birth, cast off the shame of sins procure for themselves by that flower [the reading is uncertain].

[Col. 0606D] We must take care not to be without oil, lest we be reckoned among the foolish virgins. We possess our woman in labour as a fruitful olive: since she is the mother of mercy, she pours oil into our lamps; and since she is queen of justice, she kindles the fire of love. Having now received and lit our lamps, let us hasten to meet the nuptial joy of Simeon. The honourableness of holy conduct surely performs in us the office of a lamp, since it is narrow below by poverty and closed by chastity, clear within through purity, expanded above through charity, and opened through the contemplation of heavenly things.

Having therefore received, as has been said, our lamps; having received oil from the womb of the Virgin Mother; and having borrowed a ray of light from the star of the sea, let us in the joy of our hearts join ourselves to Simeon’s joy. Will our little one be presented in the Temple without us, or will Simeon rejoice in our consolation without us? It is not fitting for us to abandon the little child as he departs there, nor to fail to hear Simeon’s praises there. For all that is done is dedicated to the joy of our feast. But shall we, who along with the Magi offered gold, incense, and myrrh to our child, offer a dove and a turtledove in order to reclaim him? Nor will dove-like simplicity and chastity arising from the lengthening of our sojourn be lacking to us here; if the equality of twofold charity is present in these, our devotion will retain Jesus for itself. Children everywhere follow the child, if we join him in purity of body and innocence of heart.

[Col. 0607B] As he increases in age and wisdom before God and men, let us also take growth from like nourishment. Once we have clung to him, he will not abandon his fellow-nurslings in any tribulation, but will strengthen them amid the troubles of temptations. Those whom he has made to grow in himself he will not permit to fail in himself; rather, with his accustomed generosity, he will make them perfect and bring them to a perfect man. If we live with diligent attention to those things which we have seen in him, or heard of him as done by him and heard from him, how greatly, do you think, shall we grow in faith and love for him?

Such nourishment is certainly necessary for those hastening to the cross, because unless they have used more solid and more abundant food, there is reason to fear that they will be unable to bear the weight of suffering. Here it is now pleasant to behold our young man displaying supreme patience on the cross, whom we saw as a child displaying supreme innocence in the manger. How fitting it would be that those whom he wished to have as fellow-nurslings in infancy should have as fellow-soldiers in punishment! Therefore, we who stood by him crying in the cradle, why should we not stand by him suffering upon the nails? Why do we not rush to kiss and embrace him as he hangs, when he invites us to this with arms outstretched? Because of the excessive love by which he loves us, though undeserving, he stretches out hands and feet to the fastening of nails. He yielded without resistance the head to be crowned with thorns which the trembling Baptist scarcely dared to touch. He did not turn away that blessed face from spitting and blows, upon which the loftiness of angelic purity gazes without satiety.

[Col. 0607D] I say “without satiety,” because although they are fully refreshed by the vision of Jesus, no weariness is produced by their fullness. In their complete satisfaction is full desire, and in the fullness of their desire is the satisfaction of every good. Perhaps you would more willingly hear us speaking of such matters, but we fear to walk amid great and wonderful things above us. Let us rather return to what fits the present occasion; let us return to the consolation afforded by the saving victim.

Consider that the innocent mouth of the incarnate Word, from which streams of heavenly wisdom flow, is given in its thirst the bitterness of gall and vinegar to drink. In a wonderful manner the King of justice exposes his whole self to injury, and the side of the innocent one is pierced by the spear of a sinful soldier. Do you not observe five fountains opened in the virginal body of the Lamb for five virgins? How happily we are five, if, as was said above, we are prudent virgins and not foolish! For prudent virgins have two fountains in the Lamb’s feet, in which the affections of their hearts are washed through hope in mercy. They have also two in the piercing of the two hands, from which the gifts of graces flow richly and magnificently. The fifth fountain flows from the side of the Lamb; rising from the deeper abyss in the region of the heart, it sends forth a river of overflowing grace. There indeed it flows and overflows, where Christ’s fullness keeps hidden within itself all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.

[Col. 0608B] The rush of this river makes the whole city of God glad; it waters the whole earth so that it may bring forth fruit; and no good seed can exist in it except through the watering of this fountain. Would that, dearest brother, our union might earnestly strive to admire these things, meditate on them continually, venerate them devoutly, love them ardently, contemplate them subtly, and desire them faithfully! If we persevere in this philosophy in the cells of our hearts, if by an indivisible union of minds we cling to this one Good, we shall truly be monks, joining the fivefold number of our union to the one holy and indivisible Trinity. For the blessed Trinity and threefold Unity is the one expectation of the saints and the happy recompense of the saints’ labours. May he, who made us one through the bond of love, make us live with one mind in desire for it.

But because we are sinners and miserable, exposed to the storms of the great sea, lift the eyes of your heart to the star of the sea, so that she who bore for us the Sun of justice may never fail to seek pardon for our injustice. We more earnestly commend to your prayers and those of your community our friends whom we love in the Holy Spirit—not only those whom you have deserved to know, but also those whom you are known to possess through our acquaintances. Let this letter end here, but let love have no end; and let the effect of the work prove how earnest is love’s affection. Amen, amen.

## LETTER IX. TO THE COUNTESS OF PERCHE

[Note: [Col. 0607D] Apparently Mahaut (Matilda) of Blois, daughter of Theobald the Great, Count of Champagne, who had married Rotrou III; or Matilda of Saxony, daughter of Henry the Lion and wife of Geoffrey III, son of Rotrou. The words occurring below, “in accordance with the demands of your lofty blood,” seem to indicate one or the other.]

He sets before her an excellent rule of life.

[Col. 0608D]

To his beloved in Christ, the illustrious Countess of Perche: Brother A., a sinner, greeting in the Holy Spirit.

The insistence of your devotion asks me to admonish you by some letter concerning strength of soul and to stir you to desire eternal things. A happy and praiseworthy request indeed—and would that I possessed the means by which it might obtain a happy result! Yet great is the rashness of that soul into which the anointing of the Holy Spirit has not been poured; nor can it have any other source from which it might supply material for spiritual advancement either to itself or to another.

[Col. 0609A] Let us therefore turn in heart and mind to the Holy Spirit: you, by clinging to him in hearing; I, by drawing from him, so that you may be wholesomely taught. O how much a clean and humble mind is needed by one who dedicates herself as a workshop of the Holy Spirit! Serviceable humility, indeed, removes every swelling of pride; conversely, fear of the Lord becomes the beginning of wisdom. Prudent humility carefully provides that this remedy may be set against that evil. Thus, while humble fear opposes the impulses of proud fear, it does not allow the soul to be defiled by sins. Moreover, one who is without fear will not be justified; for when the entrance to the heart is neglected, pride is not barred from the inner chambers of the soul.

The virtue of humility extinguishes the pride of the heart through the spirit of fear and likewise crushes the pride of the flesh by the holy remedy of restraint. Humility is certainly a friend of the Holy Spirit and always prepares a clean dwelling-place for him, since no one doubts that an unclean heart displeases him. “Upon whom,” says the Lord, “shall my spirit rest, except upon the humble and quiet person who trembles at my words?” (Isaiah 66). Where humility is, there are rest, fear, and reverence for the commandments.

Humility shows you, human being, what you are, what you were, and what you will afterward be. A short while ago you were nothing; when you began to be, you were worthless seed; now you live as a worthless vessel of dung; shortly you will be food for worms. Why are you proud, earth and ashes? Why do you forget your own condition? Why do you not remember that you will die soon? Why do you set your attention upon a falling world, which in the crashes of its own overthrow threatens ruin to its lovers?

[Col. 0609C] Deceptive indeed is favour and vain is beauty: they not only fail to produce lasting joy, but quickly vanish into the torment of eternal lamentation. Things which pass away are not to be loved; things which flee are not to be embraced. We must rather pursue those things which happily endure forever. The way must be blocked to vices; a boundary must be set before sins; we must breathe again toward the light of grace, so that the day of glory and honour may shine upon us. The vanity of the fleeting world must be cast aside; the pleasure of the slippery body must be mortified; every superfluity must be cut away, so that holy frugality may adopt you as a daughter of God.

The spirit of life is sober and has nothing of intemperance. It does not enter a mind from which it sees frugality banished. It takes no part in games of dice; the idle diligence of chess is not dear to it; the buffoonery of actors does not suit its purity. Divine purity does not seek long trains of garments, useful for nothing except stirring dust and delaying the steps of those who hurry. O superfluous vanity! O useless display—that it should not be enough to adorn the dung-heap of the body with costly dress unless, by an even longer train, stirred-up dust is also drawn after it! This effeminacy of hearts has brought injury upon eyes and nostrils, because from dust stirred up by such contrivance we are accustomed to close our eyes, stop our nostrils, and turn away our faces. O unhappy invention, wholly unknown to former times, which blocks the road and offends the sight!

[Col. 0610A] It blocks the road, I say, because the display of superfluous vanity turns the heart away from pursuing truth; it confuses sight because, while it introduces to observers the temptation of effeminate custom through what they see, it draws away the eyes of reason from contemplating heavenly beauty. O merciless custom: that the material which ought to cover the nakedness of the poor should instead cover and draw up the dust of streets! The shameful women of our time are not ashamed to resemble little foxes, so that, as those small beasts have longer tails, so these women glory in the long trains of flowing garments. O how often, worse still, are garments of this sort procured from the plunder of the poor, the despoiling of widows, and the exactions imposed upon orphans! From these sources come changes of clothing hung upon poles; from these are drawn expenditures for costly benefactions; from these bellies are fattened at elaborate banquets; and from them the nobility of the age obtains more sumptuous foods and every precious thing, while those people live almost continually in the utmost poverty.

[Col. 0610B] Would that you, daughter, might reflect frequently upon these matters, and might not, in accordance with the demands of lofty birth, seek so eagerly to conform yourself to this age as to please him who, though Son of the Most High Father, chose humbly to become human. Consider what you owe to him who made you from nothing, marked you with his image, distinguished you with his likeness, visited you by his incarnation, taught you by his manner of life, redeemed you by his Passion, glorified you by his resurrection, raised you by his ascension, and strengthened you through the grace of the Holy Spirit. You owe your whole self to him who gave his whole self to you. Although you must please your husband according to the flesh, he nevertheless does not cease to claim his own right in you.

Certainly, though he created soul and body, though both belong by right to him, he yields for the time being the right over your body to your husband under the law of marriage; but claiming your soul for himself, he does not permit it to pass into another’s jurisdiction. Your carnal husband is the bridegroom of your flesh; your God is the bridegroom of your soul. Yet no jealousy disturbs either of them, provided you remain faithful and chaste in every respect. You owe chastity of soul to your heavenly bridegroom, just as you must present a chaste body to your earthly husband. He endowed the chastity of your soul with the splendours of angels, an endowment which you received in the mystery of faith and the certainty of hope.

[Col. 0610D] O if you love this endowment; if you do not reject this bridegroom as though he had given you too little! You were born of noble parents and, according to the flesh, issued from royal blood or stock; yet you are incomparably nobler through this endowment with which that noble bridegroom has invested you. Attend to him, love him, sigh for him, for he is unique sweetness, supreme beauty, singular joy. Do not deny him his right for another’s sake; and while that carnal husband is embraced in the life of the flesh, delight in embracing spiritually the heavenly one.

For he is just—indeed, justice itself. He established the law of marriage; and when you render to each what belongs to each, you too are not excluded from heavenly justice. Thus render to your husband his right in your flesh without robbing God of his right; for it will not turn out well for you if you usurpingly transfer another’s right to another’s use. You are bound to your husband and necessarily obliged to obey him insofar as he commands nothing contrary to the law of marriage. For he must be preferred in all things who both ordained transitory marriage in mortal flesh and gave himself as the immortal bridegroom to the immortal soul.

[Col. 0611A] Therefore adorn that part of yourself according to which you are betrothed to Christ with the precious adornment of virtues, so that you may conceive offspring of good works from the Holy Spirit. Whatever good you think, whatever good you say, whatever good work you do, you conceive wholly from the Holy Spirit; nor can the desire of the soul be made fruitful from any other source than the conception of the grace of the Holy Spirit. The greatest vigilance is therefore necessary, so that you may guard your heart with every safeguard, if indeed you have dedicated it as a dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit. If you do not, what are you doing? How—or in what condition—will you endure the day of death when it comes near?

It will come, it will come, and quickly will come the most uncertain hour of most certain death; and blessed are you if, when it comes, it finds you prepared. Let your mind therefore be humble, your body chaste, your marriage-bed undefiled, your clothing moderate, your diet sober, your expression modest, your speech chaste, and your hand generous, distributing necessities to the needy according to your means. Otherwise marriage cannot be excused, especially since it is granted not by command but by concession. Observe that concession, when it does not choose better things, provides a remedy indeed but gains no reward. Therefore marriage, granted by concession, is instituted as a remedy—and is itself ineffective unless it is defended by observance of three goods.

[Col. 0611C] The first is fidelity; the second, hope of offspring; the third is called sacrament. Fidelity means that spouses so keep faith with one another that neither deprives the other of the marital debt, nor, while both live, seeks union with another. Hope of offspring means that they come together with such purpose and intention that what they beget may be educated in the sacraments of faith and formed in the knowledge of God. Sacrament means that two persons living as one flesh so express, by their unanimity, the likeness of Christ and his Church that for no reason do they seek divorce from their indivisible union.

If, to these three goods that defend marriage from sin, you add works of mercy and piety; if in the lawful work of the flesh itself you maintain moderation and measure; if you do not appropriate for this use of the flesh the solemn days and fast-days assigned to the advancement of the soul, you will by no means be far from salvation. The Mother instituted those days and assigned the seasons of fasting to observances so that whatever sin is committed in bodily intercourse may be washed away in those times by confession, prayer, and almsgiving. At such times the soul should be free to attend and see how sweet the Lord is—the soul which sufficiently experiences at other times how foul the flesh is and how worthless the world.

[Col. 0611D] Behold, my most beloved one, you have compelled me to draw this pattern for you. If you correct your way and life according to it, you will increase glory for yourself and joy for me. May he grant you strength; may he guard you, your husband, and your offspring in every peace and safety—he who always regards the prayers of those who love him and gives himself as the reward of happy perseverance. Farewell.

## LETTER X. TO WILLIAM, A NOBLE YOUNG MAN

He commends to him, above all, fear of God and devotion to the Virgin Mary.

To his William, a young man of good disposition: Brother A., a sinner, may you soar above the empty eminence of lofty blood by the nobler grace and glory of character.

You ask, son, and urgently request in your letter, that I outline for you some pattern of virtues upon which you may impress the beginnings of your youth. O truly praiseworthy request, worthy of every answer, which is an evident sign of future integrity! Would that I possessed sufficient reason, talent, shining knowledge, and abundant eloquence, by which I might truly form you in prophetic studies! A boy distinguished in character and conspicuous through the elevation of his birth ought not to degenerate into a base pursuit or be made mad by the deceits of empty learning. Truth is needed, not falsehood; certainty, not deception; one must cling to what is stable, not movable; apply oneself to what is full, not empty; rely on what is solid, not vain. Whoever acts otherwise will fall and deservedly make a laughingstock of himself for the observer.

[Col. 0612B] “Children of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” (Psalm 4), when neither vanity nor falsehood will endure. Each is evil, each vain, and neither is in any respect worthy of your love, since both are condemnable and harmful. There is a solid truth and a true solidity, which may be loved more securely, sought more rightly, and held more profitably. This is strength of soul: namely, love for the incarnate Word, whom to know is life, whom to serve is to reign, and whom to love is salvation alone. This is the philosophy of the humble, the wisdom of the simple, the joy of those making progress, the fullness of those who arrive.

Learn, son, to give yourself to this philosophy and to honour it with your beginnings, so that you too may attain its beginning. Its beginning is fear, which is wisdom; while it nourishes and instructs little children toward knowledge of the liberal arts, it sets the rod of its correction against every vice. Under the instruction of fear, the tender beginnings of children ought to be trained, so that later they may advance more freely to the disciplines called liberal. Fear chastises the mind with a friendly rod, lest it grow proud either of noble birth or learning, become wanton through bodily health, or insolent through successes or pleasures. Fear is a good teacher everywhere; it keeps the mind alert by continual reading, lest, after serious studies are interrupted, it turn aside to the idle pursuits of vanity.

[Col. 0612D] It reads about moderation at banquets; about chastity in beds; about frugality in conversation; about justice in actions; about innocence in conduct; about modesty in service; and about discipline in all things. Son, if you do not withdraw your hand from the rod of this teacher during your youth, it will make you teachable by God and therefore not ignorant of mortal wisdom. For the knowledge of God is immortal wisdom; and if love accompanies knowledge, they will make you good and blessed: good first, blessed afterward. For goodness is a step toward blessedness, just as in natural things a flower precedes fruit. Where the good has not opened itself into flower, expectation of fruit is vain; nor should blessedness be hoped for by the one in whom goodness does not bloom.

O if your youth may spring into bloom with the beauty of this flower, and if the sweetness of fragrance may be joined to its blooming beauty! This flower never lacks loveliness of appearance or sweetness of scent, because the gravity of discipline and the esteem of a good reputation serve goodness. Yet the species of this flower is cultivated by manifold diligence, and one is carried to the mystery of this philosophy by seven steps, as though by the same number of liberal arts.

[Col. 0613B] The first of these arts is humility, by which a person is brought back to self-knowledge and taught that the vanity of the world is to be despised. The second is chastity of the flesh, which resists carnal enticements, so that the antidote of continence may be set against the incentives of lust. The third is sobriety, mother of continence and chastity; by cutting away every superfluity, it does not permit the body, soon to die, to become insolent. The fourth is truth, which trains the tongue by the rules of justice and forbids vanity and falsehood to the lips. The fifth is kindness, which acts toward every person with such careful consideration that it does to none what it would not itself wish justly to suffer. The sixth is piety, which gives itself to the needs of brethren with as generous a liberality as it asks to be helped in its own need. The seventh is charity, which embraces God with such love that it in no way resists his commands.

[Col. 0613C] From these seven liberal disciplines comes goodness, to which the supremely good One promises blessedness. These disciplines are rightly called liberal because they make those whom they train in heavenly philosophy unencumbered, free, and full of the spirit of freedom. But they are called arts belonging to the instruction of fear, the school of this teacher, because without doubt whoever refuses to be a disciple of fear can neither be good nor blessed. For it is written: “He who is without fear shall not be justified” (Ecclesiasticus 1). Therefore, since fear is the beginning of wisdom, if you desire to be wise, fear God.

I say nothing of his love, because for the present it is enough that, through the beginning of fear, you resist the vices of slippery youth, until in the course of time you advance to virtues—which comes through the practice of love. For since health, to which it is joined, is the beginning of good habits for the soul, it is enough for the moment to cut away the causes of illness, so that nourishment may not be supplied to vices.

[Col. 0613D] But, son, at the end of this letter I wisely urge upon you one thing: as delightful and easy as it is, so it is honourable, useful, and full of glory and honour. Cultivate and love Mary; venerate and praise her; strive to please her with pure and wholehearted services. Do not doubt that she possesses a fullness of every sweetness and fragrance surpassing all else. Receive her as your mother; dedicate her as your nurse; choose her as your bride; establish her as your friend. Once you have invested her with the gift of your charity and experienced the exceedingly sweet delights of her sweetest love, you will permit absolutely no other to touch you.

[Col. 0614A] O blessed violence by which the kingdom of heaven is seized! For indeed very great violence is needed to preserve a purpose of enduring chastity in fragile and corrupt flesh. Yet this is easy for those drawn by love for our Virgin. Although she is everywhere commanding and mighty, she is also freely merciful; if you love her and dedicate your body to her, my love too will not be lacking to you. Otherwise, how could I even look upon one whom I saw to find no pleasure in the delights of such sweetness? Farewell; live, and love her whom to love is to live and to flourish.

## LETTER XI. TO G., A MONK OF PONTIGNY

He sets before him a rule for the instruction of novices.

To his dearest brother and friend in Christ, G., monk of Pontigny: Brother A., a sinner, greeting in the Holy Spirit.

You pressed me too insistently, dearest brother, to write you something on the building up of the soul, especially concerning the formation and instruction of novices. Certainly you asked a difficult thing: that I should teach how novices ought to be formed, though I was not a novice at my own conversion, nor have I yet, in this present conversion of mine, remained renewed. For whereas once, by an unhappy exchange, I darkened into a monk from the whiteness of canonical purity, and now, God willing, have returned from that complete and alien blackness to the brightness of the lily-white virgin, although that merciful one received me as a penitent, she did not receive me as a novice. And indeed, since the formation of newness, which I have not yet undertaken, has not erased from me the ugliness of inveterate blackness, how do you compel me to philosophize about the splendors of holy newness? For a novice, if he possesses the reality of his name, is stripped of the deformity of the old man precisely insofar as he is refashioned into the beauty of the new man through zeal for a more corrected life. I—I, not yet stripped of the old man—must necessarily fashion for you the form of the new. Nevertheless, I am bound by the debt of my promise to say something, because your insistence forced me to promise. Therefore, since novices derive their name from newness, let us inquire what this newness itself is, and what oldness is opposed to it. And because “that which is spiritual” is not first, but “that which is natural,” we must first consider the old man. [Col. 0614C]

There are four matters in which this oldness is especially seen: love of the world, superfluous care for one’s own body, the practice of sinning, and the defense of sin. Love of the world corrupts the mind with a threefold oldness: it kindles it with desire for rank, puffs it up with appetite for empty praise, and burdens and weighs it down with wealth acquired for gain. All these either come from the pride of the heart or furnish and feed that same pride. One infected with the poison of pride must necessarily grow old and decay through the loss attendant upon natural corruption, and so draw near to destruction. For the ancient serpent, when it most venomously instilled pride—the beginning of every sin—into human nature while it was still in its original condition, made it subject to his own lethargic antiquity and stripped it of the glory of blessed newness that had been granted to it. [Col. 0615A]

Therefore, the man whom ambition inflates and exalts through pride in earthly dignity, whom panting after windy praise blows up and overthrows, whom avarice scatters into dust and destroys through the gain of riches—such a man grows old through the great age of many vices. This is what love of the age commonly does in its followers. Since the world lies in evil, and seeking it is most wicked; since it is vanity and a fleeting shadow, and running after it is madness, loving it belongs not to a sound mind but to one that has lost its senses. For what is love of the world except a kind of frenzy of mind which, because it does not know how to seek or relish the things above, but only things upon the earth, makes the mind—as it were—estranged from the sense of good health? Therefore whoever desires to become a novice must turn his heart away from the madness of this utterly vain oldness; otherwise he cannot share in the new pursuits of wisdom until, having removed the madness of insane love, he becomes restored to his senses. [Col. 0615B]

But he first begins to return to his mind when he resolves with firm purpose to forsake the world, taking pains that worldly affection may not accompany him beyond the threshold of his own house; rather, at the very threshold where he begins to depart from his possessions, there he must begin to die to the world. I say that love of the world must not follow him to the monastery gate, because there he takes the second step, where he will also leave his body. Hence God spoke thus to Abraham: “Go forth from your country and from your kindred, and come into the land that I shall show you” (Gen. 12). For he would not be fit to see, much less enter, the good and excellent land, the land flowing with milk and honey, unless he first departed from the land that brings forth thorns and thistles and from the carnal attachment of kinship that enfeebles the strength of the mind. [Col. 0615C]

Hence the Holy Spirit speaks through the Psalmist to the soul he instructs: “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear” (Ps. 44). Hear, that you may believe, for faith comes by hearing; see, that you may love, for love greatly advances through affection; incline your ear, that you may obey and carry out commands, for love is proved by action. But in what will you obey? “Forget your people and your father’s house”; otherwise the king will not desire your beauty. I say that there will be no beauty in you that the king might desire unless you have gone out from your country and kindred, unless you have forgotten your father’s house and your people, unless through forgetfulness you die to the vices and desires of the flesh. Hence the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “Whoever has not left house, or brothers, or sisters, or fields, for my name’s sake, is not worthy of me” (Matt. 19). And certainly, if lawful and necessary things must be left for God’s sake, how much more must unlawful and superfluous things be avoided for his sake? But since we have brought the fugitive from the world as far as the monastery gates, that he may take the second step of his renewal, having taken the first in leaving Egypt, let us also pause here in the course of our discourse, so that, having recovered our breath a little, we may climb more vigorously according to this second step and its consideration. [Col. 0615D–0616A]

Perhaps, dearest brother, as you read these things you are angry, and perhaps you mock me for writing matters less necessary when you had asked that useful things be sent to you. Certainly, since you would receive neither excuse nor delay, I have become foolish—you compelled me. Yet I shall not cease to pursue what I once began; and if I cannot satisfy your request, at least I shall somehow satisfy my promise. For I promised you, if you recall, to comply not according to your will but according to my ability. Therefore he who, through zeal for conversion, has taken the first step of his renewal in contempt of the world, is to take the second on entering the monastery: namely, in setting aside care for his own flesh—care which, nevertheless, according to the Apostle, is not denied in necessary things. “Make not provision for the flesh,” he says, “in its desires” (Rom. 13). Nature must be cared for, not guilt; necessity must be provided for, not pleasure indulged. For pleasure has punishment, while necessity produces a crown. And again, that saying of the Rule, chapter 7: “Death is placed beside the entrance of delight.” [Col. 0616B]

When, therefore, you come to the monastery gate, there strip off the flesh, the garment of the soul; and return it to the world, though it still protests, the garment that you brought from the world. For you took this garment from what was accursed; you received it from corruption; you nourished it with vices and desires. Therefore outside the sanctuary you must leave behind whatever worldly impurity may claim in it. God created nature; he was not the author of guilt. Nor ought we to hate or persecute what is not returned to its Creator. Nature must be cherished and made subject to the service of its Author; but corruption and vices, which do not come from God, must be pursued. “No one,” says the Apostle, “has ever hated his own flesh; but he loves and cherishes it, as Christ also does the Church” (Eph. 5). Yet you leave the flesh to the extent that you die to its affections, and bid farewell to its vices and desires. [Col. 0616C]

Into the schoolroom of the Holy Spirit nothing at all of the flesh is to be brought; the spirit alone, without flesh, must enter where attention is to be given only to spiritual things. Flesh and blood ought not to participate in spiritual business, nor are they worthy to share in things pertaining to the kingdom of God and his righteousness, since they will not possess the kingdom of God. “Flesh and blood,” says the Apostle, “will not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 15). Thus to leave the flesh outside is to seek for it nothing beyond necessities, and to judge necessary only those things which, according to the discernment of the Fathers, the form of the Order can permit and the place you have sought can provide. Do not remain below, nor seek anything beyond; but proceed by the royal road through the middle. For it is excessive to advance beyond the Fathers’ limits, and faulty to linger below their boundaries. If you wish, as a mediator, to join friendships; if you wish worthily to attend the ministry of the mediatrix, take care not to depart from the middle. Take care to do nothing too much, nothing without measure. [Col. 0616D]

In the eyes of godly people, conform yourself to the habits of those with whom you live; but inwardly, in knowledge before God, if you can, surpass others in love. This alone is the matter in which the Governor of the ages delights in our lack of moderation: when the affection of our love for him is stretched without measure or limit. He, the author of all things, created all things, and requires what he is known to have bestowed upon his creatures. Have weight, keep number, preserve measure, and you cannot be separated from the Author. Falsehood has no weight; hence it is carried away and flies into destruction. Lightness knows no weight and does not allow the heart to be stable or firm. Singularity does not preserve number, since number is a collection of units. Where diversity reigns, there is no collection but a division of unities. Superfluity knows no measure, and nothing measured is admitted by it. [Col. 0617A]

Let holy newness avoid falsehood, lest anything be deceptively covered over in it under the appearance of holiness. Let it regard singularity with suspicion, lest, divided from others, it not be counted with others. Let it flee the superfluity of intemperance, lest through immoderation it resist the Governor. Let it stand firm in the weight of seriousness for discipline, in the weight of truth for justice, in the weight of stability for perseverance, lest it fall from its resolve or depart from the place it has chosen. Blessed indeed is the one whom the gravity of weight makes stable, the principle of number makes sociable, and the moderation of measure makes frugal: stable in faith, sociable in charity, frugal in manner of life. What remains here of flesh to prevent the spirit from giving itself wholly to the Holy Spirit? [Col. 0617B–C]

Now let it enter, for the reading of so great a teacher, into the inner chamber of the mind, concerning the various offices of the soul. Diverse offices assemble there; and, enjoying the abundant and overflowing wisdom that flows in, they disdain to think of bodily matters. For although within the monastery bodily observances concerning the formation of obedience abound, they nevertheless have a spiritual translation, so that the intention of the doer may be heavenly. For just as heavenly things performed with an earthly intention often become carnal for those who do them, so bodily things performed with a spiritual intention become spiritual for those who perform them. Henceforth, let those who strive to be spiritual beware lest Satan transform himself for them into an angel of light, lest under the pretext of salvation he conceal a business of destruction. [Col. 0617C–D]

Let them take care, I say, lest, just as in the time of their oldness they had the practice of sinning, so in the time of newness they lack the watchful fear of sin. Against the practice of sinning let them diligently possess the suitable remedy of fear. For as the habit of sinning is born from insolent security, so it is driven away by habitual fear; because, just as security is the beginning and progress of wickedness, so the fear of the Lord is the beginning and advancement of wisdom. Here, since we are beginning to speak of the third step of those who are converting, it is fitting that, having recovered our breath a little, we prepare ourselves for carrying out what follows.

However much, dearest friend, you may disagree with this work of my smallness, because perhaps I have said different things and said them differently than you expected, still, as I hope, you will never turn your eyes away so completely as not to read the whole thing through. But I ask you, when you have read it, not to condemn me too hastily; first examine everything carefully, and then you will judge more fittingly about what is blameworthy. Certainly, since you are a friend, you will not uncover a friend’s shame; rather, you will take pains that what you see should be concealed because of his fault may remain concealed with you. But lest I seem to cease from what I began through fear of blame, I shall nevertheless continue what I began. He to whom it has been given from heaven, for love of poverty, to despise love of the world and to prefer the labor of continence to the pleasure of the flesh, must strive in every way to eliminate the practice of sinning through the fear of God. [Col. 0618A]

“But,” someone will say, “how can one who has already left the world and the flesh have a habit of sinning?” Certainly, he who through contempt of the world and disregard for the flesh has avoided fleshly allurements still has left to him unceasing combat against spiritual wickedness. What if he perhaps retains in affection what he abandons in deed and action? How many today live under the habit of religion who, though outwardly they serve neither world nor flesh, have nevertheless returned in heart to Egypt and inwardly fallen back into sin! They display an appearance of holiness in action and clothing; they are committed to holiness by vow and profession. But although they have the name of being alive, inwardly they are dead, because, though outwardly they appear poor and continent, in mind they aspire to the glory of passing praise or to the rank of some dignity. [Col. 0618B–C]

For when through those two things previously named—contempt of the world and disregard of the flesh—the unclean spirit has gone out of a person, and, passing through dry and waterless places, that is, the spiritual hearts of saints, finds no rest for himself, he always intends to return to the dwelling-place of his former house and says, “I will return to my house from which I came out” (Luke 11). When he sees that house cleansed indeed of its former filth, adorned with religious observances, but vacant of spiritual desires and occupied with idle thoughts, then he returns to it in greater force and thereafter guards it more carefully for himself. For, as the Lord testifies, he takes with him seven other spirits more wicked than himself, and they enter and dwell there. Then the last state of that person becomes worse than the first, because one who before religious habit and vow openly appeared what he was—evil—afterwards aims at what he does not endeavor to be: namely, to be called holy. [Col. 0618C–D]

O what an unhappy exchange: one who had expelled the world together with its unclean prince by the Holy Spirit, and had subjected his own spirit, by the binding necessity of his vow, to the teaching of the Holy Spirit, again expels and drives away from himself the grace of the Holy Spirit, and hands his own spirit back to an unclean possessor! From this point the hypocrite persecutes and drives away the Holy Spirit, just as the Holy Spirit of discipline flees the false person. Clearly, the Holy Spirit would not flee unless someone pursued and drove him away. The person who pursues and drives him away is one who, by the intention of a perverse will, rejects him through whom piety is bestowed, yet presumptuously retains the appearance of virtue in order to deceive and mock grace. The false person indeed persecutes the Spirit of truth with a double injury: he both violently casts him out of himself and, more violently still, as a cruel robber usurps his appearance for contrary uses. [Col. 0619A]

O detestable evil! O almost inexpiable crime: under a pretext of meekness, to exasperate the supreme meekness of goodness! O supreme misery: under the form of the new man to conform oneself wholly to the old, and under the name and habit of a novice to retain in one’s affection the old age of vicious antiquity! O if, after renouncing the world and casting off the body, the door of the heart had been shut and entrusted to the vigilance of fear, the spirit of falsehood would not have entered the heart! For this gatekeeper is most vigilant, and serves love so humbly and ministers so faithfully that he admits absolutely nothing by which love’s festivity may be disturbed. But now, because the door has been wrongly opened to the traveler, the unclean spirit, having taken with him seven other spirits more wicked than himself, returns to his house. Understand in the number seven the measure of the accompanying vices: because all temporality is conducted in seven days, seven signifies universality. [Col. 0619A–B]

Therefore let novices be warned that at the third step they must entrust themselves to fear. For they have become continent in vain if they have in any degree left the doors of the heart without the guard of fear. Blessed indeed is the person who is always fearful; for just as the fear of the Lord does not work evil, so one devoid of fear may also be devoid of salvation. Whoever is without fear shall not be justified; he cannot be wise as long as he lacks the beginning of wisdom. For fear is the beginning of wisdom and permits nothing tasteless to enter where love delights in the splendors of wisdom. The splendors of wisdom are the virtues of the soul, through which feasts of love are continually kept in the inner chamber of the devout heart. O happy newness! O new festival, celebrated not amid the filth of the world but in the heaven of the pure mind! Novices are invited to such feasts, and they are celebrated inwardly all the more festively as holy fear more vigilantly guards the entrance of the heart. O how courageously souls act when secure in so great a gatekeeper! Nor can our heart be better guarded by every kind of vigilance than by having this watchful gatekeeper. [Col. 0619B–D]

Moreover, humility, the inseparable companion of fear, arranges the offices of the heart all the more securely as it does so more secretly; and whatever it sees ordered in the light of wisdom, it orders and arranges according to the judgment of love. Humility never proceeds without the companionship of discernment; but it conducts itself everywhere and in all things all the more cautiously because, from its familiarity and fellowship with fear, it is always apprehensive and always suspicious of itself. Humility, remarkably, overflows with abundance of graces precisely insofar as it thinks less of itself, because the fountain of wisdom, which goes forth from the midst of the paradise of delight, gladly flows down from above into it as into a lower place. [Col. 0619D–0620A]

Hence welcome and grace-filled humility establishes in the mind its dwelling-places for each several virtue, arranges each one’s offices, and permits nothing in bodily senses or in the affections of the soul that is not governed by the instruction of humble fear. Thus it assigns rectitude and simplicity to intention; it assigns wisdom to reason; and, so that discernment may hold the chief dwelling-place there, emulation gathers itself to the irascible faculty, and zeal for God is to be exercised according to knowledge. Charity distributes itself to the concupiscible faculty and kindles it with a twofold affection for God and neighbor. Truth illuminates the understanding, and, when by its splendor it has driven away every error, leads it also to the grace of contemplation. The merciful devotion of compassion dwells with purity of affection, and from there offers itself, without respect of persons, to the miseries of those in need. [Col. 0620A–B]

In the palace of the will justice establishes its tribunal, and from there with authoritative severity sets forth the decrees of equity for manners and deeds, senses and affections. Peace establishes for itself a quiet bedchamber in the man’s testimony of conscience; and justice offers it a kiss all the more sweetly as its resolve for truth removes every scar of sin. “Justice and peace have kissed” (Ps. 84). Justice clearly kisses peace when, as justice labors, the will is corrected wholly and exactly, so that conscience is not bitten by any scar of it. But peace itself also kisses justice when the reception of eternal peace rewards the laborious work of justice. [Col. 0620B]

See what things, and how great, come to those who do not allow fear to be absent from the new joys of their conversion. Truly there is no place there for the habit of sinning, where, according to the Psalmist, the Lord is served in fear (Ps. 2). On the other hand, those frequently lose their senses who neglect the fear of God, the beginning of wisdom; and they not only fall more often into sins, but, what is graver, defend their sins. For just as one who renews justice always accuses himself at the beginning of his speech, so conversely one who desires not to be righteous but to seem righteous, when accused by another defends himself. The more subtly the false person veils himself by the laborious art of simulation, the more grievously the unveiling of his disguise distresses him. For one who is false can scarcely prevail so far in concealing himself by his simulation that he cannot be detected by some signs. But since we now intend to begin speaking of the fourth step of those converting, let us end here what concerns the third. [Col. 0620C–D]

Although at the beginning of this little work I promised that I would speak first of oldness and afterwards of newness, I have now spoken too much of both and in a mingled manner. Thus I do not deserve the favor of a reader, since I either did not know or neglected to follow my own promise. Indeed, the matter is done. But you, dearest brother, would not let me rest until you compelled me to expose my foolishness. Therefore it must be charged to you—to you—whatever you find in these writings less than correct. Yet I, having begun to expose my foolishness, shall not cease to speak concerning the promised fourth step. How harmful it is, how subject to oldness, to defend sins, is sufficiently understood from this: among all remedies for salvation, nothing is proclaimed more health-giving than confession. [Col. 0620D–0621A]

And what is confession except the accusation of one’s own guilt, when a person humbly, openly, wholly, and faithfully confesses his sins to him who has received authority over him in this matter, saying: “I am bound to disclose my sins through confession to him to whom the keys of my soul have been entrusted by the Lord.” The ordinance of divine humility supplied a remedy; the pride of diabolical self-defense discovered the hiding-place of excuse. For by the same malice with which the enemy of virtue wills and brings about sins, he also wills by the same malice that they be hidden. O if the first parent of the human race had not sought an excuse for his sins! Certainly, if he had humbly accused [printed: “excused”] his own fault, he would not have received so cruel a sentence of death. [Col. 0621A–B]

But now he wished to sin and to hide, he who “inclined his heart to words of wickedness.” “The woman,” he says, “whom you gave me as a companion, gave me from the tree, and I ate” (Gen. 3). What are you doing, wretch? Why do you cast your guilt back upon your Creator? Did he sin because he granted you a woman as companion? Rather charge it to yourself; accuse yourself the more, since it lay within your power to know and to be able to avoid sin. Therefore, just as among remedies nothing is more health-giving than humble confession, so among crimes nothing is found more harmful than the defense of sin. One who defends sins both denies truth and persecutes godliness. One who confesses and accuses himself merits justice and becomes a friend of truth. [Col. 0621B]

This is what humble fear does, thereby obtaining justification from sins. The whole and continual office of fear is to devote itself to virtues and to persist in the confession of sins. The diligence of fear wonderfully aids the holy work of renewal, since it both defends the entrance of the heart outwardly against every crime and strives to wipe away by the bath of confession the dust that falls within. There is no need to show you what crimes are, since you see the world full of them. But perhaps I have said “falling dust,” especially since, because of its subtlety, it is perhaps seen only by eyes more thoroughly cleansed. What, then, is this falling dust but the countless thoughts flying before the eyes of the soul during prayer? Do not a thousand encounters of images produce, as it were, most troublesome dust, by which those praying or meditating are most importunately troubled when we stand before the most present divine majesty and think or say one thing after another, matters fitting neither our purpose nor the place nor the time? What else do we do but stir up dust by which we hide from ourselves the clear light of truth? [Col. 0621C–D]

Certainly, though this dust does not pluck out our eyes, it confuses our sight and turns us from the vision of true light: at the time of prayer, while bodily present before God in choir with others, we wander animal-like through worldly spaces or fleshly vices, as though neglecting or despising God’s presence. The Holy Spirit indeed withdraws himself from thoughts that are without understanding. Those without understanding are plainly irrational and therefore bestial. If, then, your work is without understanding—that is, irrational—will not your service be bestial? “If a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned” (Exod. 14), because one who serves in divine offices with a bestial mind—that is, without understanding—is tormented more by the stony hardness of his heart than he is delighted by the sweetness of the divine presence. Therefore confession must be made continually and assiduously of these matters; it always finds in abundance around the innermost parts of the heart what it ought to accuse and lament before the priest. [Col. 0622A]

Let it come into the soul’s lamentation that it has not yet worthily repented of past evils; that it falls very far short of watchfulness against evils pressing upon it; that it shows itself unworthy to receive God’s benefits; that it is ungrateful for benefits received so many times and so often. Let it not neglect to lament and articulate the stirrings and impulses of the unclean flesh against purity and the grace of honorableness. Let it not neglect to accuse the bodily senses, wandering according to their several kinds toward the destruction of seriousness and discipline. “Who understands transgressions?” Who fully comprehends the matter? How often do we lend the ears of the mind to the enemy’s suggestions! How often do we return in affection to the delights of the world! How often do we become transgressors of our vow! How often do we neglect God’s commands! How often are we sleepy or lukewarm in the divine offices! How often sluggish and slow in obedience! How often do we neglect care for our neighbor! How often do we do to him what we would not wish him to do to us! [Col. 0622B–C]

How often do we exact strictly from him what we would by no means do if he exacted it from us! Often we are cast down by adversity and lifted up by prosperity. Often, regarding good things that we either possess or do through God’s grace, we seek not God’s glory but our own. Often we conceal what we greatly desire; often we pretend to be something other than what we are. Often we are less ashamed than we should be of evils recognized within ourselves; often, with undiscerning zeal, we inveigh against others. Often we murmur against God’s righteous judgments. Often, when we ought to build up our brothers, we show them examples of corruption instead.

All these things are indeed sufficiently common to all people like me, apart from spiritual matters that happen to individuals according to the variety of their circumstances. Those who, under the habit of religion, feel and consent to such things in themselves are undoubtedly strangers to holy newness. But those who feel them and dissent from them, who grieve and lament because they feel them, who continually accuse themselves through confession and correct them insofar as they can: just as they do not lose on this account the name and virtue of a novice, so they shall not lack the joy of festive newness. Let them strive for perseverance; let them persist in the desire for purity; and, that they may more easily obtain what they desire, let fear not leave the door of the heart. Where such a doorkeeper remains, there can be no fear of perishing. [Col. 0622D]

Fear is the nourisher of humility, the seedbed of confession, the guardian of innocence, the foundation of patience. Fear is zeal for discipline, the bridesman of chastity, the rod of justice, the counselor of mercy, the beginning of wisdom, the forerunner of love, the chamberlain of conscience, the adornment of life. O happy soul, whose paths to vice fear blocks, so that it may celebrate with free devotion amid these splendors of wisdom! Here blessed poverty, arising from contempt of the world, still thirsts with the ambition of new life for the riches of a better life. Here the virtue of continence, rejoicing in the forbidden superfluity of the flesh, joins the spirit stripped of its oldness to the new joys of spiritual life. Here fear of God, driving out the practice of sinning, does not permit the inward solemnities of newness to be disturbed by vices. [Col. 0623A]

Here humble confession, moving through the heart’s interior by the diligence and operation of fear, cautiously rebukes and accuses each instance of sin, lest the solemnity grow insolent through security; and, in a wonderful manner, comparing what has been done, it sets before the eyes as an example for what must be done the Lord’s Passion. And when it recalls to the heart’s memory Jesus Christ—and him crucified—it does not account its own action important in the estimation of so great a thing. And indeed, what estimate of virtue can there be in us when the patience of the most merciful Redeemer is considered? He did not shrink from exposing to spittle and blows that glorious face upon which angels desire to gaze. He did not fear to submit his back to scourges, his head to thorns, and his limbs to nails—things which deserved absolutely nothing. I mean, they deserved nothing of punishment. For while they endured these things without guilt, they freed us from the debt of punishment and guilt by undeserved grace. [Col. 0623A–B]

Therefore, clinging to him, let us imitate him; and what we promised him of our own will for our necessity, let us pay, for our glory, by his grace and according to the measure of our ability. If the undertaken purpose of the journey seems hard, let us flee to the help of our Virgin; for she to whom that most merciful helper offers herself as aid will be strong in every tribulation and distress. Let us draw into ourselves the whiteness of her lily-like innocence through purity of conscience; and let there not be lacking to us, together with chastity of body, the exertion of fruitful work, by which virginal fruitfulness may be adorned. For we must direct our whole regard toward the childbirth of our Virgin; and if we are truly to be novices, and if we truly desire to be renewed, let us direct new and full desires toward the grace of that new birth. For if through her we can obtain the grace of justification, so with her as our guide we shall be able to reach glory, through him who was born from her, Jesus Christ our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## LETTER XII. TO MARGARET, A VIRGIN

He commends himself to her prayers.

To MARGARET, virgin: Brother A., a sinner, wishes to please the Bridegroom of virgins through the unfading lily of chastity.

Since we are bound to love Christ, we ought equally to venerate and honor his temples. For sincere chastity is his dwelling-place, especially that chastity which true love of Christ has consecrated. Truly, in gardens and lilies is found Christ the Lord, the flower of the field and lily of the valleys. O that the rose may not be lacking to the lily, so that the whiteness of chastity may be suffused with the rosy color of charity! How beautiful are the cheeks to which love of honorable conduct joins itself for their full adornment—charity to chastity! The elegance of this appearance binds to itself him who is “fair in form above the children of men,” because simplicity of manners commends beauty of countenance. Simplicity of manners, purity of affections, justice in deeds, and praiseworthy discipline in observances make the soul worthy of the kisses and embraces of its Creator. [Col. 0624A]

O venerable union! O honorable marriage, from which every foulness is excluded and in which no corruption has a place! O happy offspring proceeding from such a union, which, just as it is conceived by the Holy Spirit, is also nourished at the breasts of the holy mother Church! These breasts are full from heaven, distilling the milk of spiritual teaching, by which simplicity and innocence of the senses are advanced to manly strength of character, to the understanding of divine love and perfection. I judge that by God’s grace you have reached an age in which you no longer play in Christ’s cradle like an infant fostered with Christ, but, fit to be crucified with Christ, can eat harder food. For because of the words of his lips you both desire and are able to keep hard paths, glorying after the example of the Crucified One in the inscriptions of the cross. But if you have not shrunk from being united to your bridegroom upon such a bed, you will one day reach the joy of the bridal chamber, which is entirely free from cross, sorrow, and labor. [Col. 0624B–C]

I beg you, most beloved, when you are well situated in your Jesus, to pray to him for my transgressions. When that eager splendor smiles upon you more abundantly than usual, commend your lover more earnestly to your Beloved, so that through your effort and prayer I may be able to attain with you him whom I adore and love in mind. Amen. Farewell.

## LETTER XIII. TO WILLIAM, BISHOP OF ELY

[Note: [Col. 0623] William Longchamp, chancellor of England, bishop of Ely from 1189 to 1197, and administrator of the realm.]

He silently dissuades him from the king’s service.

To WILLIAM, bishop of Ely and chancellor of the lord king of England: Brother A. sends greetings in the spirit of truth.

[Col. 0624D] That we are troublesome to your exalted rank by such frequent letters or messengers arises partly from your friendliness, which we enjoy though unworthy, and partly from our necessity, under which we are burdened. Yet neither matter is taken ill by generous minds: for the truth of a rejoicing friendship ensures that familiarity does not fall into contempt, and compassion of mercy is not denied to necessity. Taking courage, therefore, from both, I do not fear to press upon your eyes a letter even longer than usual, although they are held fast by so varied and manifold an occupation with affairs that it does not allow your mind to be at leisure even for an hour.

In so great and so general a [Col. 0625A] ruin of collapsing affairs, to have one’s mind is to have lost it; for where danger threatens virtue on every side, scarcely can any virtue endure—the one thing alone which we love in friends. When indeed that has perished, we cease to have friends; and what, preserved, could produce joy from a friend, when lost brings sorrow and grief. Happy love, whose sole ground is virtue! Praiseworthy too is the friendship which, as it has no foundation except the virtue of the soul, so seeks no incentive for itself from elsewhere. In that virtue and for its sake we love the person of your venerable self; and would that the flood of worldly vanity, in whose dangerous whirlpools you are swimming, might not begrudge us this good in a friend.

I shall certainly call you a friend so long as virtue of soul remains in you: so that [Col. 0625B] either you may preserve with anxious purpose the virtue still possessed, or, if it has slipped away, hasten as quickly as possible to restore it whole. How difficult it is not often to stumble, or slip, when walking on slippery ground! How difficult it is for one walking in darkness not often to strike his feet, fall more grievously, and be dashed down more harshly! It is beyond ordinary experience to walk with wavering step along a mountain ledge, while winds blow and swell, and not to be driven violently from the heights down to the depths.

Such things readily happen to those whom love of virtue does not make firm and knowledge of truth does not enlighten. Where these two are lacking, the matter is in danger; and the life of such persons is nothing but an abyss. An abyss, I say, is a land whose face is wholly wrapped in darkness, where knowledge of truth gives no help at all to the pursuit of virtue. How happy is the soul that does not neglect to possess treasures such as these, which ambition for such things draws upward and does not allow to be entangled in the foulness of lower things and vices! For it belongs to the dignity of the soul to seek what is higher, provided it is not deceived in its own judgment.
