For this purpose the radiance of truth is useful: when it has driven every cloud of error from the sky of reason, it enables the soul also to weigh and assess truth itself clearly and without deception. Thereafter that radiance, shining so happily upon a soul that assesses itself, will not become cheap in its estimation; rather, it becomes as though noon after morning, when, from the sight and enjoyment of that radiance, the soul is inflamed into longing for love. From this, love of virtue is joined to the radiance of truth, [Col. 0625D] and in the mind rejoices one day, known to the Lord: a day of gladness, a festal day.

This is the day which the Lord has made: a day of exultation, a feast day and day of gladness, whose rays the unhappy children of darkness are not worthy to experience. By children of darkness we mean those who do not emerge from the subterranean realm of wretched flesh; who, serving the works of darkness in the prisons of their bodies, never dwell anywhere except in the tombs of desire. O wretched servitude, submission to be mourned with every fountain of tears: to think that delight consists in being subject to the senses; to believe the advance and impunity of wickedness to be glory; to prefer the license of crimes to the freedom of virtues!

How far these things are from the children of light, citizens of heaven, despisers of the world, lovers of justice, followers of the Crucified One! The Israelites certainly do not remain in [Col. 0626A] Egypt, nor do they desire the slavish sins of mud and brick; much less do they strive to become apostates among the Egyptians. Passage through the Red Sea does not deter them, nor the unfamiliar harshness of the wilderness, from aspiring to the delights of the promised sweetness. What shall we say of Moses, leader of Israel, who not only abominates the service of Pharaoh but also, with devoted persuasion, urges the people to long for the homeland flowing with milk and honey?

It does not become a leader of the people, a president of the Church, to serve in the retinue of an earthly king. Rather, his task is to depart from Egypt and enter upon the road which returning Israel may imitate. It is fitting for the bearer of Christ’s cross, as a guide upon the way, to proceed at the head of the procession, and by his examples to encourage his followers to endure whatever crosses are necessary for the adoption of salvation.

O unhappy times of ours! O lamentable conduct of men! O those to be mourned—especially those whom we ought to have had as defenders! The leaders of the people have forgotten the land of promise; enticed by the sweetness of pleasurable servitude, they have subjected themselves and their people to Pharaoh’s dominion almost beyond escape. Would that at last this Egyptian slavery might displease you because of your desire for true liberty, and that you might love with a brave heart what the knowledge bestowed upon you does not permit you to ignore. For it takes a brave heart, and the substance of manly virtue, not to live as a woman in Egypt, where Pharaoh has decreed that the males of the Hebrews be slain. It is happier to live in virtues than to be effeminized into the softness of vices, since the dreadful [Col. 0626C] end of false sweetness is changed into the wormwood of eternal bitterness.

Your discernment knows this very well; and if the world, which rules you, allowed you to philosophize upon these matters, you would possess fuller knowledge and more effective eloquence. Then you too would someday do what you know ought to be done, and what you seem to approve and praise in those who do it. If those whom the pattern of a venerable life makes praiseworthy are praiseworthy in your eyes, it is worthy of praise that you should join yourself, in fellowship of a praiseworthy life, to those whom you judge praiseworthy. If the court of a dying king, full of cares, hinders you, think rather of the care of your own office, in which you believe that your sheep have need of so much concern from you.

Moreover, Father, just as we truly wish you what is good, so [Col. 0626D] we are constantly praying for you. Would that nothing might oppose our prayers and render their effectiveness vain! We especially commend to your generosity the bearer of this letter, whom at your command we agreed should cross the sea into England, so that your care may provide for him, lest—God forbid!—the labor of such a journey, especially since it was undertaken at your arrangement, should remain without its expected fruit, to the detriment of your glory and to the injury of our filial friendship. Farewell.

## LETTER XIV. TO A FRIEND

He excuses himself for being unable to satisfy his friend’s request.

To his father and dearest friend in Christ, Brother A., his humble [Col. 0627A] son: may he be restrained from the desires of the flesh in Christ’s prison.

Father, I owe everything to your humility; and would that my willingness to comply were as great as my desire to comply! But now the impossibility which brings shame upon my will also causes a friend to suffer refusal in his request. The unusual barrenness of the present time has compelled me to wean my little ones and, most recently, with great grief of heart, to send them to the breasts of other houses. Therefore, for the present, while the community is absent, no one may be received—especially since without the counsel of our brothers we never promise or presume anything of this kind.

Your discernment will readily accept the excuse; and among true friends true love does not complain of a failure caused by impossibility. Yet filial love prompts us to inquire after the condition of your holiness; and would that I could learn more often what is taking place around you! I should indeed call that person happy to whom Christ’s solitude is so sweet that it makes whatever is savory in Egypt distasteful. Blessed indeed is the one to whom the world’s delight has become wearisome, who has scorned Pharaoh’s mud and bricks, and for the gold of Jerusalem has trampled underfoot Babylon’s dung-heap.

How happy is the expectation of one who has given himself to the pursuit of virtues; for whom Christ alone is the object of desire; upon whose soul the radiance of blessed immortality has shone! I do not doubt that either a tenacious love of Christ holds you fast or that, however many ruins you may see falling around you, a steadfast resolve of mind in the love of enduring things will make you firm. The way of virtue is indeed narrow and steep, but for despisers of the world the sweet anointing that flows into gentle hearts from the sweetness of the Holy Spirit makes it smooth. I beg you, make me a sharer in that experience of yours. Though, because of the difficulty, I do not grant effect to your request, I shall nevertheless not cease sincerely to love you as one bound to Christ. Farewell.

## LETTER XV. TO NICHOLAS

He exhorts him always to cling to Christ in mind, and especially to contemplate His infancy.

To his Nicholas, Brother A., a sinner: faithfully to love, and happily to be loved, in the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0627D] I made myself debtor to your urgency when I promised to satisfy your request. Yet, although I may have satisfied your request to some extent, I do not think I have satisfied devotion; for the hunger of holy devotion is eager, and while it suffers hunger and thirst, it will receive the food of righteousness, which is in no way inadequate because of want. Therefore let your gaze be upon Jesus, from whom full satiety will flow to you. For He is rich toward all who call upon Him, and one who becomes one spirit with Him will lack no good thing.

He is indeed the fountain of goodness, the sea of mercy, from which flow and overflow the gifts of charisms, rivers of graces. From there a great abundance of love flows into devout hearts, love which He Himself—who alone is to be feared and loved—has hidden for those who fear Him. His fear is [Col. 0628A] the beginning of wisdom; and love, once made perfect, is the fullness of wisdom. Happy the soul which fear initiates into wisdom, which love perfects in wisdom and advances to everlasting radiance.

The first fear, while turning away from evil, sets the foolish person against darkness. In it, indeed, as in the dawn of true light, the night of crimes receives its end and the light of salvation its beginning. In that morning of wisdom a boundary is prescribed to the night of wickedness; and wisdom, even from its beginnings, conquers and expels wickedness. O day of wisdom! O radiance of grace, which by its morning dispels the darkness of ignorance and wickedness! O lovable and wonderful light, now to be drunk in by pure eyes, until the light of full love shines forth and grows warm!

Certainly, when love comes, when noon burns hot, [Col. 0628B] when it commands the north wind to depart, the south wind will leave nothing thereafter dark or cold in the sky of our reason. For the noonday ardor of love will take nothing away from the spirit of understanding which the morning radiance pours in through the beginning of wisdom. Rather, the more ardently that invisible beauty is loved, the more manifest purification will make itself to the mind. Thus the solemn Sabbath of that secret contemplation will at last be celebrated, to which observance of the preceding weekdays leads and directs.

The first weekday is the spirit of the fear of the Lord, which, dissolving the darkness of vices, suffuses the mind with a certain delight of new light. The second weekday is the spirit of piety, which lays and orders the foundation of devout faith and softens the mind toward love of divine worship. The third weekday is the spirit of knowledge. While it confines under the judgment of reason the unstable impulses and wave-like courses of slippery sensuality, and shows the firmness of a right intention to be alien and separate from those slippery impulses, it gathers, as it were, the lower waters into one place and makes the dry land of right intention appear. Because of the weight proper to it, or because of the fertility of spiritual grasses, it calls this dry land earth. Of this dry land David speaks, saying: “Our soul is like a land without water to you” (Ps. 142 [Vulgate numbering]).

The fourth weekday is the spirit of fortitude, which kindles us with the zeal of discernment against rebellious impulses and hostile attacks, and makes us strong and patient in carrying out good works. It adorns and paints the firmament of our faith with, as it were, certain stars. “For faith without works is dead” (Jas. 2), just as the firmament, unless it had luminaries also, would be dark.

The fifth weekday is the spirit of counsel, which, while it strips bare and reveals to the mind the crafty counsels of the evil enemy, displays before the face of our earthliness, for the watchfulness of our caution, certain beasts and creeping things as it were. On this weekday too—that is, in the spirit of counsel—we dwell when, concerning matters in which God has given us counsel, we take counsel with our neighbors.

The sixth weekday is the spirit of understanding, which, while it makes the sight of our region certain and noble through knowledge of invisible things, introduces into the paradise of delight a human being as though then first fully formed. [Col. 0629A] The seventh of these weekdays—that is, the Sabbath—is the spirit of rest, the spirit of wisdom. Through it the mind is so affected not only by the radiance of knowledge of heavenly things but also by the savor of love that whatever is not heavenly is changed into weariness and bitterness.

Then the soul that experiences this will be able to say from the judgment of its heart that prophetic word: “My secret is mine; my secret is mine” (Isa. 24). Then the bride, seeking nothing else and desiring not to fall back to lower things, cries out joyfully and in praise: “My beloved is mine, and I am his” (Song of Songs 2). What joy, do you suppose, will then belong to the soul when, from among the children among whom that Lamb feeds, there sounds in its ears a song more pleasant than every sweetness, sweeter than every delight: “Now winter has passed; the rain has gone and departed; the flowers have appeared; the flowering vines have given forth their fragrance” (Song of Songs 2)?

And truly, there will no longer be in the mind a winter of wickedness to sharpen against it the moderation of love in bloom. There will be no place in the flesh for misery, which the rain of tears, flooding from the force of sorrow, may bewail. Nothing will be present or remain to prevent either full clarity in the enlightened mind from the love of the Creator, or delight in the glorified flesh from corruption. Then heart and flesh shall truly rejoice in the living God and, blooming anew in wondrous and unfading freshness, shall sing that Davidic saying: “We rejoiced for the days in which you humbled us, for the years in which we saw evils” (Ps. 89 [Vulgate numbering]). It would indeed be good for us to be here; but we must first observe the preceding weekdays which we have named, before we deserve [Col. 0629C] to experience what this Sabbath is—or rather, what it tastes like.

Leaving aside, then, the things above us, to which we have flown without experience, let us return to the weekday of fear, whose observance sometimes better suits our perversity. On this weekday of the fear of the Lord, as at the beginning of wisdom, as at the dawn of the day of grace, as at the entrance of eternal light, little ones must strive to learn the first elements of heavenly prophecy. Accordingly, our infancy must be placed under the instruction of the infant Word, if perhaps God may deign to perfect His praise from the mouths of infants and nursing children.

For His anointing is the teacher that teaches a human being knowledge, and teaches little ones concerning all things, thereby making them grow strong into men. Thus the anointing will be present—whose instruction humble persons submit themselves to—the instruction of the Holy Spirit … “who flees deceit and withdraws himself from thoughts” [cf. Wis. 1:5]; to such persons that anointing does not grant understanding. Yet fear, because it humbles the mind, enlightens it; and therefore God gives grace to the humble and gives understanding to little ones through the anointing that is their teacher. Fear humbles for this reason: either by pricking like a goad or by crushing like a hammer, it causes the swelling of the mind’s pride to subside.

The swelling of the mind subsides when vain and windy worldly love, badly gathered within the bladder of the heart, is expelled, and in its place love of voluntary poverty takes possession. Thereafter, reverent humility orders the affections, corrects speech, makes gesture restrained, [Col. 0630A] and disciplines action. In short, it removes pride far from the affections, boasting from speech, arrogance from gesture, and ostentation from action. Then, enlightened by this light, it understands more clearly that the devil must be guarded against, because he is the enemy of salvation; that the world must be despised, because it is vanity; that the body must be scorned, because it is corruption; that the spirit must be mourned, because it has consented to sin; and that God alone must be served—for to serve Him is to reign, to know Him is truth, to love Him is virtue, and to attain Him is the highest good.

Little ones should learn the first elements of this prophecy, as has been said, around the cradle of the Word. They correspond to the mystery of the abbreviated—that is, incarnate—Word by the simple innocence of their infant minds, devoutly conforming themselves to the cries of the heavenly infant through the pursuit of humility. Let us therefore go over to Bethlehem and, turning aside from the affairs of the world, let us in no way disdain to enter Christ’s humble lodging. There a child is born to us; there a son is given to us. His emptying was our filling; His abbreviation is the instruction of little ones.

O happy hut! O lodging to be preferred to the palaces of kings! It has become a schoolroom of heavenly instruction, where the Word teaches little ones from the manger all the more intelligibly because, by the silence of His infancy, He sets before them new decrees of wondrous humility.

Therefore, son, if you truly desire to prophesy, do not depart from Christ’s lodging. There the infant Word indeed cries in the cradle, but that cry is eloquent beyond the eloquence of Tully—indeed, beyond the utterances of angels: He has made the tongues [Col. 0630C] of infants eloquent. There the nourishment of angels is fed with a little milk; but by that food the simplicity nourished in the humble is advanced into mature age. There inaccessible radiance is wrapped in worthless rags, rags by which the filth of sin is wiped away. In that manger the grain of angels is changed into barley, but by its fodder beasts are strengthened for bearing burdens.

And certainly Christ’s lodging is the cloister within the monastery—I mean the monastery to which, turning aside from evil in order to do good, you have turned. The manger within the lodging is the cloister within the monastery, to which you have bound yourself, like a gentle animal, by the bond of profession and in the place of discipline. What then should I call the barley in the manger, except the rule kept in the cloister; or the understanding of sacred utterance, which is extracted only with difficulty from the covering of the letter; or certainly the most holy body of Christ, received sacramentally from the altar?

For the ears and chaff of barley signify both the hardships and difficulties that must be endured amid the observances of the established rule, and likewise the figures and coverings of sacred utterance; they also signify those sacramental species under which Christ’s true Flesh is received. What, I ask, are those species—color and taste, form and weight—by which so great a mystery is veiled, except those swaddling-clothes in which the infant Word is wrapped in the narrowness of the manger? By faith in and love of these things, by frequent participation in and imitation of them, the tender infancy of simplicity is nourished as by a certain milk, until in time it can receive stronger food.

Stronger food indeed is to love enemies, to rejoice in self-contempt, to follow Christ even to the disgrace of the cross, to be crucified with Him, patiently to embrace punishment without fault, and through desire and contemplation to forget whatever is earthly. This food belongs to the mature, and to those who, according to the Apostle, “by practice have their senses trained.” Would that you may be one of those judged fit to use such solid food! It goes very well with me if the infant who dwells in the manger, the lover of the lodging, gives something from His little draughts to my tenderness. Would that I might be granted to stand by His Mother’s breasts, to attend the infant’s cries, and from these to learn what it is safe to understand and delightful to retain.

Moreover, dearest brother, because the letter has exceeded its limit, [Col. 0631B] here I shall make an end of speaking, not of loving. I beg you to persist in prayer and work. Subjecting the years of your youth to truth and virtue, greet your venerable Father in my name; greet also, faithfully on my behalf, the prior and the cellarer, whom I sincerely love. Greet for me, when they suitably come to hand, all whom you know to be joined to me by the bond of charity.

If you are altogether willing to keep this little sheet with you, copy the letter and send it on my behalf to Brother Evrard of Sarnay, placing his name in the salutation; for I am bound to his request by the same promise by which I was obligated to your urgency. But if, as often happens, what has been written should not sit well with your mind, do not delay, when convenient, to send this very sheet on my behalf to the aforesaid man, after placing his name, as stated, in the salutation. Here ends.

## LETTER XVI. TO THE ABBOT OF TURPINIAC

[Note: [Col. 0631] Turpiniac, a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, in the diocese of Tours, not far from the island of Burchard and Chinon.]

It deals especially with love, with devotion toward the Mother of God, and toward her Son.

To the venerable abbot of Turpiniac, father and dearest friend in Christ, Brother A., a sinner: greeting in the Holy Spirit.

Holy love, which has bound us more closely in a mutual bond of minds, no longer delays to render what it did not neglect to promise. You remember well, most loving friend, and I do not think it has slipped from your mind, what was promised to you at your urging. Certainly your love, which rejoiced so greatly in the promise, has not allowed the joy of its expectation to be suspended or forgotten. But what do you expect from me in order that you may rejoice, except to be loved faithfully and to experience this faithfully [perhaps “happily”]?

The form of a sweeter letter will indeed be a measure of that experience, if only it proceeds from a sweet affection. Experience in my letters the sweetness of my affection, although affection is customarily judged more certainly from affection itself and from the testimony of deeds. Yet the force of love is directed in affection, and you seek no other expression of my love than that I might wholly pass into you through affection.

For the holiness of chaste love gathers itself into the inner parts of the heart. Since it suspects everything outside, it judges nothing safer than to conceal itself, with conscience as witness. [Col. 0632A] O happy love, to which worldly hope is hostile, which takes no heed of the cares of the passing world and draws no nourishment from fleshly pleasure! It has its incentive elsewhere: anxious for the attainment of heavenly things, not negligent of contempt for earthly things, impatient with all that is unfitting, and not ungrateful for benefits received.

Holy love, therefore, has its seedbed in virtue of soul, whose foundation and course lie in desire for incorruptible truth. My whole subject with you is love—but that love whose ground is virtue, whose pursuit is truth, whose desire is purity, whose work is piety, whose manner of life is the discipline of a rule. Nothing is sweeter than love; and, since it is its own price, it is also a price to itself. Certainly the name “love” is shared by contrary things, but from what has been said every ambiguity is removed.

If we wish to assign it its proper term, it is called *dilectio* (“cherishing love”) or *caritas* (“charity”) in Scripture. The distinction is that the word *amor* more strongly suggests a natural power, whereas the efficacy of grace is expressed by the name *caritas*. Among the powers of the soul none is worthier than love, none sweeter, none equally strong. It is wholly unworthy that what is best in us should incline toward desire for a more worthless thing; or that love should rejoice in itself; or, if it does not suffice for itself, that it should seek happier joy in the things above.

In the things above is the joy received from worship and love of the highest good, when it is cultivated with singular devotion and zeal. This good, which alone is highest, is sought by love alone, attained by love alone, and, once attained, held by love alone. [Col. 0632C] Love seeks, love finds, love holds and retains, and does not let go: “I held him,” it says, “and I shall not let him go” (Song of Songs 3). Love seeks devoutly, finds happily, enjoys blessedly, and is fulfilled. It does not seek without light, does not find without sweetness, does not enjoy without satiety, and does not come to an end.

This good, believed to be the highest, has nothing above itself and nothing beneath itself that suffices. The highest good is God the Trinity: highest because existing from Himself, sufficient through Himself, mighty in full power [*ingens*, perhaps *vigens*, “vigorous”], possessing full wisdom, and unfailing in complete goodness. His power is unconquerable: it bestowed existence upon all things. His wisdom is incapable of deception: it gave order and form to created things. His goodness is incorruptible: according to the decision of His will, it allotted to individual creatures their measure of usefulness.

Knowledge of this good makes you good; delight—or love—in it makes you happy; perseverance in it will make you blessed through enjoyment. Yet toward the radiance of so great a grace and the delights of so great a glory, the advancing soul flies upward through certain steps.

The first step is wholly to abstain from all unlawful things. The second is to despise unlawful things so completely that they do not even enter the affections. The third is, insofar as necessity permits, to reject even lawful things. The fourth is constant and fervent observance of the commandments. The fifth is diligent and continual watchfulness of soul for the preservation of purity. The sixth is ambition for virtues and a hunger for spiritual progress. The seventh is, amid virtues themselves, to strive eagerly after the better charisms. [Col. 0633A] The eighth is humble and devout thanksgiving and a voice of praise for charisms received. The ninth is that, because of desire for the highest good, nothing visible should enter the affections. The tenth is to discipline memory and drive away bodily images.

Let not the importunity of Bilhah deceive the mind of Rachel’s desired sweetness. For it often happens to one contemplating that, while he desires Rachel’s beauty—that is, purity of contemplation—Bilhah, Rachel’s maidservant, that is, bodily imagination, intrudes herself importunately upon Jacob’s desires. But at last Jacob embraces Rachel, and Ahasuerus, fainting with love, is joined to beautiful Esther.

When the soul has ascended these steps and attained, insofar as pure mortality can bear it, the perfection of purified purity, it melts in the experience of wonderful sweetness. Melted, it cries and says: “My soul has failed for your salvation, and I have greatly hoped in your word” (Ps. 118 [Vulgate numbering]). Having experienced the remembrance of abundant sweetness, it pours forth praise, marvels, and cries: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you!” (Ps. 30 [Vulgate numbering]).

I beg you, dearest friend: if, with the Holy Spirit advancing you, you should someday arrive at that place, do not set aside the memory of your friend amid such delights. Remember me, I say, when it goes well with you; and though you may not dare introduce, lest you be ashamed, one lacking a wedding garment, seek for your friend at least forgiveness of sins. [Col. 0633C] For I am the most unhappy of men: though I rashly dare to write reflections upon such matters, I do not deserve even to have touched the first step. I am wholly a lodger among unlawful things; since I have so often committed unlawful things, I have deserved that even lawful things should not be permitted me.

How do I dare to set my mouth in heaven and discourse on the nature or glory of the highest good, when the oppressive heap of my evils makes me almost devoid of goodness? What has a wretch to do with blessed things? What has a vicious man to do with discourse on virtues? What belongs to one falling downward in showing things above? Alas! Wretched and dying, poor and lowly, lying on the dung-heap of crimes—with what face does he speak and plead? By a new kind of presumption, a fool philosophizes about philosophical studies; and the inexperienced man is not ashamed to teach what he has not learned.

I have indeed become foolish, but your love compelled me, as did the promise by which I was bound. If I have exceeded the bounds, forgive me, for the slenderness of my littleness has ventured into things marvelous and great beyond itself. Henceforth I must use a humbler voice and speak rather of matters that concern the care of wounds. Therefore, since the splendor of heavenly things is difficult for weak eyes, let us turn our bleary eyes toward the pillar of cloud and darkness.

The pillar of cloud and darkness is the firm sublimity of our Virgin, from whom the brightness of divinity drew a covering of darkness about itself. For when the radiance of the almighty Word is wrapped, through the Virgin’s conception, in a cloud of flesh, what else was the likeness of sinful flesh in that flesh but darkness in the cloud? “Cloud and darkness are round about him” (Ps. 96 [Vulgate numbering]), because the radiance of the Word is wrapped in the cloud of most pure flesh, and in that same flesh is surrounded by weakness. But let us fix our attention upon the pillar we have set before us.

Consider how firm, how strong, how upright, how light, how extended it is; how lofty; how firm, it is, upon which heaven and earth rest; how upright, because it knows no stain of sin; how light, because it admits no turning aside of duplicity; how erect, because by the height of merits it transcends every creature; how sublime, because from eternity the Son of the Most High foresaw her as the worthiest mother for Himself; how happy, because she is both God’s mother and bride, gate of heaven, beauty of paradise, [Col. 0634B] lady of angels, queen of the world, joy of the saints, advocate of believers, strength of those who fight, recalling of those who wander, medicine of penitents.

O sure salvation! O short way of life! O sole hope of pardon! O incomparable sweetness! Rightly are you Lady. With you is stored the fullness of all good things. With you are hidden the inexhaustible treasures of truth and grace, peace and mercy, salvation and wisdom, glory and honor. You are my anchor in tossing, harbor in shipwreck, support in tribulation, consolation in sorrow. You are help in oppression, assistance in need, moderation in prosperity, joy in expectation, refreshment in labor. Whatever I can chatter about your praises falls short of your praise, O you most worthy of every praise. Though I should speak with the tongues of human beings and angels, even if I poured out my whole self, it would be little.

Rather, I turn myself to that praise of you which is sung thus in the song of love: “Who is she that comes forth like the rising dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army arrayed in battle order?” (Song of Songs 6). In these words the praise of her glory in its fourfold form is expressed briefly and subtly, truly and sublimely.

For when you are born, you rise like a glowing dawn. Your birth indeed fulfilled the role of dawn: in it the day of grace began, while the night of unbelief and ignorance came to an end. When you conceive the Sun of righteousness, you too are illuminated, like the shining moon, by the Sun’s beneficence. For the moon borrows light from the sun, because its nature as a denser body denies it the source from which it might possess light itself; thus whatever beauty it has, it has by the benefit of borrowed radiance.

When you bring forth the Sun of righteousness, you are fittingly compared to the sun. For just as the body of the sun is neither corrupted nor diminished when it sends forth a ray, so the bringing forth of your sacred child neither violated you nor diminished you as you gave birth. And what, O chosen as the sun, is your childbearing except the eternal radiance of a certain sun? This radiance shines everywhere, even in darkness, although the darkness is not worthy to comprehend it. Finally, this radiance enlightens every person coming into this world; but human beings loved darkness rather than light. Yet to you, Mother of mercy, belongs the election of the sun, since you display to all the rays of eternal radiance.

Moreover, when you were taken from the wicked world to [Col. 0635A] heaven, you became terrible to every spiritual wickedness, like an army arrayed in battle order. Thus you were a rising dawn at your birth; you had indeed the beauty of the moon when you were made full of grace; as conceiver of the incarnate Word, you were rightly compared to the sun, remaining inviolate in childbirth; and you were terrible as an army arrayed in battle order in your passing, when—while heaven rejoiced, angels attended, saints exulted, and the banners of virtues flashed—you appeared terrible to demons.

Therefore, dearest friend, all our confidence is in the childbearing of our Virgin; and although I consider myself unworthy, I shall not cease to dwell upon her praises. If you need mercy, it is found more abundantly in the Virgin’s womb; if you are a worshipper of truth, give thanks to the Virgin, because Truth sprang from the virginal flesh [Col. 0635B] out of the earth—the Truth whom you worship. If you are a follower of peace, likewise give thanks, because from her there is born for you the peace that surpasses all understanding. If you are a doer of justice, see that you are not ungrateful to the Virgin, through whose womb justice looked forth from heaven. If your faith is shaken by some assault from the opposing side, look to the Virgin, and what was wavering will be firmly and solidly established. If the desire of the flesh delights you, look to the Virgin, and the danger to chastity is removed. If pride assails your mind, turn your gaze upon the Virgin, and through the merit of virginal humility the swelling of the heart subsides. If you are inflamed by the torches of anger, raise your eyes to the Virgin, and by her tranquillity you will grow gentle. If ignorance or error has led you away from the way of life, look to Mary, the star of the sea [Col. 0635C], and by her light you will be led back to the path of truth. If the vice of avarice has imposed idolatry upon you, recall the Virgin’s generosity, and, together with love of poverty, devotion to liberality will come to you. In every danger the Virgin’s compassion comes to aid, and she is able to aid powerfully. Give thanks for her childbirth, from whose fullness of gifts the whole is derived. The virgin bore for us; the child is ours; for us a boy was born, and a son was given to us. How delightful and innocent it is to play with the little child, to fit oneself to the cradle, to answer his cries with cries! O how blessed the infancy that babbles along with such a little child and wraps itself in his little swaddling-clothes. By the cloths in which the infant Word is wrapped, indeed, the filth of sins is wiped away; by the cries of the little child the eternal weeping is repaid, which the mockers of innocence deserved. The band with which he is bound in the cradle is the strict discipline of holy religion, by whose rule we are bound in cloisters. The hay on which he lay, which he had beneath him, signifies flesh subjected to the spirit. What does it mean that God was placed in a manger, except that he was set upon the altar as food for souls? For that manger represents the altar, because in the most holy body of Christ it feeds devout animals. These are the things by which God’s love for us is shown. These are the things by which our love is kindled and nourished. Consideration of them inspires fear, moves to devotion, instructs toward knowledge, strengthens toward courage, sharpens toward counsel, illumines toward understanding, inflames toward wisdom, and prepares for the crown. [Col. 0636A] For this reason, surely, the almighty Word made himself small as a little child, that as an infant he might be suited to infants, and, humble, might fit himself to the humble.

Meanwhile, let our whole philosophy concern the infancy of the incarnate Word, and let us strive, according to our strength and faithfully, in some measure to return toward him the love of God for us that is reaped from it. I do not dare to call it the same measure, because, just as there is no number to his goodness and wisdom, so his love is immense and eternal. He loves himself wholly, for he is wholly, essentially, love; for him, to love is nothing other than to be. How differently do love and the lover, affection and the one who affects, love—he who is love and he who participates in love! The whole Godhead poured itself out into humanity; the whole soul offered itself to obedience; the whole body gave itself over to death—[Col. 0636B] even death on a cross. Thus the Almighty loved us with his whole self; and it is little if we expend all that we are, all our small possession. We are willing to die for him, and he preferred to die rather than fail our love. But it is too early to speak now of the death of the little child, whose cradle we were embracing a short while ago, playing with his blessed infancy. I beg you, let us return still to the cradle; let us still become infants with the little child, taking nourishment for our infancy from his little draughts. Let us join ourselves to the one suckling at the breasts, in case some drop of that most sweet milk may be instilled into us. Since he does not bare his mother’s breast to me among his foster-brothers, he makes room for them also to dwell between the breasts. Those breasts are full from heaven and restore with unfailing sweetness; they are not emptied by the multitude of those who suck [Col. 0636C]. Nor does that merciful mother customarily deny herself to those who suck, although she keeps her whole self for her only Son. O unfailing abundance! O great multitude of sweetness, which the hunger of little children sucks from the breasts of the tender-hearted Virgin! If you wish, it is good for us to be here; it is good for us to remain here longer; meanwhile, nowhere can we be better than here. Here is the wondrous novelty, known only to little children: Wisdom, the nurse of angels, needs to be nourished by a Virgin’s milk. What wonder if the infancy of our poverty desires the food of this milk, when the Power and Wisdom of God glories in being refreshed by that milk? Indeed, with this milk of the mother our hunger is fed, if the flames of hell are extinguished by the tears of the crying child.

Therefore, as we celebrate the great festivals of our hearts, let us listen to what the shepherds themselves tell us about the splendours of the East. Our East lacks neither the testimony of shepherds nor the proclamations of angels: “Your testimonies, O Lord, have become exceedingly trustworthy” (Ps. 92). “Your testimonies are wonderful, O Lord; therefore my soul has searched them out” (Ps. 118). What could be holier? What sweeter to experience? What more health-giving can be believed? What more useful can be heard? What more sublime can be thought? What truer can be preached? And fittingly, amid so great a festival of the heart, we keep joyful holy days. Yet the approaching severity of the day causes dread; and not without reason the splendour of such sublimity is clouded when the harshness of circumcision wounds the tenderness of undefiled flesh. Who [Col. 0637A] could hear without compassion that tender flesh is harshly cut—flesh which, having known no fault at all, came to put an end to sins? With good reason we protest against the law which thinks that the Lamb of unique innocence needs its remedies. Far too harsh is a circumcision celebrated in letter rather than spirit, which cuts flesh rather than vice. Let us pass instead to the circumcision of the heart. Yet allow, I beg you, allow the child to be circumcised; allow the lawgiver to be subjected to the dispensation of the law; let him receive what he himself gave, and let the law there end where it began. The law of Christ is the truth of love, which cuts away every vice. Love is a law: it binds and obliges; and though it cuts away all that is evil, it itself can scarcely ever be cut away. For charity never fails. This love unites us; this love celebrates the feast [Col. 0637B] in hearts that do not leave Christ’s cradle. This love visits the child in the Magi and reveres him in the mysteries of the three gifts. Behold, meanwhile our festival has shone forth, and the star of faith, more radiant than the world’s east, has brought us to the true East. Or rather, I should not say “has brought,” unless perhaps it has carried us away from him. It is better to remain with him; nowhere else is salvation, nowhere is there security without him. Let us always hold fast to what is ours; let our festival be extended as far as Simeon’s joy. Let not his mother offer him in the temple without us. May his solemn presentation find us present. Would that the purity of chaste love might make us one pair of turtledoves in that offering! Would that the holy simplicity of charity might present us as two young pigeons! By these virtues, figured in these birds, we shall be able to redeem our Redeemer for ourselves. Certainly this offering of his is not yet for death; the Passion does not yet suit either the time or his age. With love of chastity and desire for simplicity, if the double number of twofold charity is lacking in neither, we can retain Jesus for ourselves. Let Jesus be nourished in us; let him increase among us in age and wisdom, so that in due time he may be fit for his Passion. Meanwhile he is a little child and does not think of the Passion; rather, we must concern ourselves with the breasts in his presence. If, escaping Herod’s swords, he flees, let Egypt not receive him without us. It is more blessed to shelter in hiding with him than presumptuously to avoid great things in the eyes of men by relying on our own strength. But if he himself should wish it, or [Col. 0637D] if his mother should counsel it, it is devout for us to remain for the swords and be slaughtered for innocence. When he returns from Egypt, let us live with him at Nazareth, so that we may be able sweetly to give off the fragrance of the flowers of a life in bloom. Nazareth is called “flower”; and it befits one to bloom in virtues who is accustomed to offer familiar companionship to the Virgin’s Son. If, when he has become twelve years old, he should wish to remain in Jerusalem without his parents’ knowledge, blessed are we if he should wish us to be companions in this deed. O blessed three days! O feast of all joy! To be free throughout those three days, to attend to him, to be refreshed by the words of grace that proceed from his mouth. It is not fitting to seek him elsewhere: he always wishes to be in the things of his Father; may we never be separated from him! If he comes to the streams of the Jordan [Col. 0638A] to be immersed in John’s baptism, we must follow the fountain there, since we need to be washed by him in so many and such great ways. Washed by him, we shall make manifold progress in him, so that, by the opening of the heavens, the testimony of the Father’s voice, the descent of the Holy Spirit in a dove, and John’s proclamation, we may love him more, having known him more perfectly. We have followed Jesus this far: how thereafter shall we abandon him when he is led by the Spirit into the wilderness or tempted by the devil? Otherwise, with what face shall we dare to attend the wedding, or experience with delight the tasteless water transformed into wine, or how shall we be able to share in joys if we are unwilling to share in afflictions? “You,” says the Lord, “are those who have remained with me in my temptations, and I appoint for you, as [Col. 0638B] my Father appointed for me, a kingdom” (Luke 22). How blessed is the voluntary endurance of temptations for which the disposition of the heavenly kingdom is prepared!

Moreover, for the strengthening of faith, the increase of hope, and the incentive of love—we who have gained strength from the innocence of the infant—there is now a need to say something about the virtue of the young man, now perfect. The child has now grown into a young man, speaking wonderful things and doing wonders. He now heals paralytics, cleanses lepers, gives sight to the blind; he restores hearing to the deaf, walking to the lame, and the use of speech to the mute. He raises the dead, walks over the sea with dry feet, puts demons to flight, commands winds and sea, heals every sickness by command alone, receives sinners out of mercy; understands the thoughts of minds [Col. 0638C]; feeds five thousand men with five loaves; and, at every word, confounds the pride of the Pharisees and the learning of the scribes with a wondrous answer. More wonderful than all these things is that he strives to show complete patience toward every injury; and though he is in the highest innocence, his highest power nevertheless preserves the utmost obedience. In all these things he is ours, and he does not exclude from the fruits of his obedience those whom he undoubtedly wished to have as foster-brothers at his mother’s breasts. I beg you, when he begins to tremble, to be weary, and to be sorrowful at the approach of death, and when he himself, innocent, consents to be struck by the hands of evildoers, let us not flee after abandoning him. Rather, let us follow him with hearts most closely joined: sold, betrayed, and dragged away to insults. For by his redemption he redeems us; [Col. 0638D] by his betrayal he keeps us safe; by his nakedness he clothes us. And because he does not refuse to be undeservedly beaten, spat upon, and mocked, he removes from us the everlasting disgrace that we deserve. Because his face is veiled and beaten; because, with bent knee, he is mockingly greeted; because a crown of thorns is plaited for him, everlasting reproach is cut off from us. Because his cross is laid upon him to carry; because he is cast outside the city; because his whole body is stretched upon the wood of the cross; because his whole body is pierced by spear and nails—the sentence of eternal curse is thereby revoked. Now consider the five most necessary fountains issuing from the body of the Lamb. We have two corresponding ones in the two feet, as many in the two hands; and when the fifth flows forth from the opening of the side [Col. 0639A], come, sweetest friend, let us draw waters with joy from the fountains of the Saviour.

But perhaps you say: “From the wounds of my Lord I see blood and water flowing.” To this I reply: blood and water are believed to have flowed from Christ’s side. Yet Christ’s blood, which by its price heals, redeems, and crowns, is water in that it washes, refreshes, and cools. It washes from sin, refreshes with hope, and cools the heat of fleshly desire. But waters are drawn from the Saviour’s fountains when streams of grace are drawn by the lips of faith from Christ’s wounds. Thus the wounds of the feet are fountains—but fountains of oil; the wounds of the hands, fountains of balsam; the wound of the side, a fountain of wine. “How,” you ask, “when nothing but blood seems to flow from places such as these?” [Col. 0639B] Hear how. Oil heals, balsam gives fragrance, wine intoxicates. Oil is mercy, which the guilty person receives at Jesus’ feet when he humbly asks pardon. Behold, you see oil flowing from the feet. Balsam, because it flows forth from the fountains of the hands, has its effect. It is the precious reputation for virtues which the righteous person receives from Christ’s generosity. It is enough for the guilty person if he obtains pardon; it does not suffice for the righteous person unless he deserves the glory of virtues. Mercy grants the former to one humbly prostrate at the feet; magnificence grants the latter, raising in virtue of spirit one who approaches the generosity of the hands. But from the wine-cellar of the pierced side wine overflows: wondrous, or life-giving, charity. And certainly, if Christ is the true vine, if flesh is the grape of the vine [Col. 0639C], how can the blood that runs from the flesh not be wine? Or how could the bride, the Church, please the bridegroom at her wedding if she did not have from him this wine in the most holy mysteries? This is the wine that gladdens the human heart, when Christ’s blood generates in the soul the sobriety of love.

But behold, most beloved, what are we doing? Why were we not at the embrace of him hanging, when he himself invites us to it with outstretched arms? Why do we not come to kiss him, when we see that most peaceful face exposed and made ready for us? Why do we not continually suck at the breasts of his wounds, especially those of the feet, before which we lie prostrate? Behold, our comforter has returned to the Father and, as a true obedient son, with bowed head receives permission to return. For he receives permission to return, as it were, when, bowing his head, he gives up the spirit. The good shepherd departs, the wise teacher, the gentle Lord, the sweet friend, the loving father; and what shall we orphans do? You see that bodily nature cannot bear his departure from the body, but is wholly turned into mourning. The sun was darkened, showing the grief proper to the setting of the true light; an earthquake takes place, rocks are split, and the veil of the temple is torn, when heaven’s impatience at the death of its maker is displayed. Alas! How inconsolable would our desolation be, unless we trusted in the nearness of the resurrection! He will soon rise from the dead. We ought not to abandon the good tomb; rather, with the blessed women let us buy spices to anoint the body of the dead man. Would that [Col. 0640A] Jesus, returning from the underworld, might find us preparing spices, so that we may season his body—that is, the members of the Church, especially the chosen and poor—with the spices of devotion and mercy! O that when that reviving love gives himself back to his loving Magdalene, he may not refuse to make us participants in her joy! O blessed are we if the splendour of the resurrection shines upon our hearts; if, having cleansed out the leaven of malice and wickedness, we devour the unleavened bread of sincerity, the flesh of Christ, with devout eagerness! Yet care must be taken that wild lettuce is not lacking at this feast of ours, because neither bitterness of death nor fear of sin troubles that joy … There is reason to fear the danger of presumption. Therefore, if in this festival of ours we rejoice with trembling, and if no leaven of pride is mixed into our conduct, then, even after the joy of the Ascension has been accomplished, we shall be granted to experience the coming of the Holy Spirit.

Behold, the Holy Spirit is love; and, most loving friend, it is fitting that my prayer should end where it began. I began from love; from great love I wished to write; and I have said what I could about love. Sweet is the subject of love, sweet and most sweet its affection; and for one whose office is so sweet, the reward too will be sweet. Holy love expects nothing else as its reward and aspires to no other glory than to deserve to attain its own fullness. It will be fulfilled when Jesus, the fountain of love, bursts forth from the paradise of delight, so as to produce in his spices a kind of flood of glory. [Col. 0640C] Let us love him, and in him let us love one another, because nothing in life is happier than to love faithfully and to be loved. Let no love of the world ever draw us away from this love, for love of the world is not love but friendship. The love of the world disorders or carries off the mind, empties the heart of sweetness, and, while resisting Christ’s wisdom, does nothing but rage madly. Christ is our head. The mind of this head is love of heavenly things; to will or do foreign things is madness, not love. Therefore I shall leave you in the love of heavenly things; nowhere else can I leave you better, though in this love I shall not cease to love you. I shall love, I say, insofar as the love of the world allows me; for I confess that I am not free from that oft-mentioned friendship. Wretched that I am, I cling to worldly cares under the pretext of religion; [Col. 0640D] and I who had vowed contempt for the world often slip back into Egypt. Remaining in body within the Church, I roam about in mind as a worldly man; and when, because I see, I ought to think of heavenly things, I am wholly carried away into the pursuit of temporal things. Help your friend, I beg; help me, and by the persistence of your prayer cause the prayers of the sons to be joined. This is the proof of true love: that we offer our souls to Christ for those whom we love in Christ. But remember me especially there, and cause me to be remembered, where the spotless Lamb is sacrificed; for this is more acceptable than every burnt offering.

Moreover, greet in my name the venerable prior, whom both affection for me has touched and Christ’s charity has wounded. Greet your brother, most beloved by me, but nearer to you in faith and affection [Col. 0641A] than in flesh. Greet that monk whose name has slipped my mind; yet, God willing, the soul which he seemed to place in my bosom has not slipped from me. Greet that young man who sucks so much honey from the rock—which is Christ—that he has drawn both his name and firmness of soul from the rock. Greet him in whom there is grace, who accords with the grace of God both in the name he bears and in the devotion of his soul. Greet G., the porter, who, standing in the gates of justice, will bring me some news of heavenly things. Greet the brother in charge of hospitality, who not only devoutly serves earthly guests but has made a lodging for Christ within himself. Greet the whole fellowship of the holy community, because, binding me to itself in holy charity, it has also gathered itself into my inmost heart. Above all and before all, greet for me [Col. 0641B] that soul which you know to be united and bound to me with the closest heart; named, indeed, from the name of the Lamb, and kindled by the flames of the Holy Spirit. You will convey my whole self to her, bring my whole self before her; and although in holy love she possesses me wholly, nevertheless through fresh remembrance you will renew her affection. Remind her of perfect love of God and contempt for the world; of fleeing human praises and avoiding familiarity with secular persons, so that, with a heart more silently and closely bound, she may cling to the bridegroom, in proportion as the world claims nothing of him for itself. Let her stand and persist before God for my failings, because the loveliness of her charity has wholly captivated me in her Lord. Let her too greet in my name all those souls whom she knows we love, since we need the love of every good person [Col. 0641C]. That sweetest soul could not be stirred more fruitfully on my behalf than if you allow this letter to be shown to her. May her holiness flourish, endure, and be perfected in the Lord; and may all of you prosper in the Lord.

## LETTER XVII. TO B., A CANON OF TOURS

He explains how Mary magnified the Lord.

To his lord and friend, Master B., canon of Tours: Brother ADAM, a sinner, sends charity from a pure heart.

I was indeed preparing to obey the command of your affection; but while I find myself wholly unequal to what you command, I almost reject the burden I have undertaken. For the slenderness of my talent does not answer to the sublimity of the subject you impose, nor does a conscience wounded by the cautery of sin dare confidently to speak of the magnificent praises of God’s magnificent mother. For a certain majestic magnificence terrifies my mind, which declines to low things under the weight of earthly concern—magnificence which, though with bleary eyes, I nevertheless in some manner perceive in the most excellent Mother of God. Already greeted by the angel, already made pregnant by the Holy Spirit, already raised into the mountains of every virtue, honoured by the movements of John not yet born, commended by Elizabeth’s prophetic words, she cries out from the excessive exultation of her heart and says: “My soul magnifies the Lord” (Luke 1). I greatly fear lest the Mother of God, most worthy of every praise, may regard as a diminishing of her praise whatever I can chatter with uncircumcised lips [Col. 0642A], especially since praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner. Yet because I am bound by my promise and rely upon the support of your charity, I betake myself to the chamber of spices, the storehouse of wisdom, Mary the mother of mercy, so that she whose soul magnifies the Lord may not refuse to be magnified—that is, praised—through my mouth.

Mary says, “My soul magnifies the Lord.” Observe first where she magnifies the Lord: certainly, in the hill country, in the city of Judah, in the house of Zechariah. The Lord is magnified in the mountains, whom he is blasphemed in the plains. They pray in the plains who, according to the prophet, blasphemed the Holy One of Israel and were estranged backwardly (Isa. 1). In the plains, I say, of curse and confusion are Adam and Eve, who, having lost the integrity of the flesh and been estranged from the height of truth, made plains for themselves; for they had lost the mountains of truth and virtue. Therefore Mary, rising from the valley of worldly vanity, from the depth of human corruption, from the plains of common iniquity, went with haste into the mountains. The mountains are the heights of perfection; these heights themselves are the truth of a mind most fully illumined, the virginity of a body most wholly intact, and the power of the Most High overshadowing the mountain for conception. These are the mountains which Mary ascended; here too are the house of Zechariah and the city of Judah. A city is a numerous gathering of persons living under one law. Let this people be Mary’s rational thoughts, holy virtues, and most orderly actions, which the law of charity orders in the confession [Col. 0642C] of divine praise. For Judah means “confession”; Zechariah, “the Lord remembers”; the house of Zechariah is the virginal breast, retentive of the memory of God’s commandments. Established in these mountains, the Mother of God hears Elizabeth prophesying what she will be; she recalls what she heard from the Lord through the angel’s announcement; she considers the purity of her conscience; she reflects that her flesh is free from every foreign corruption; she sees herself wholly divinely raised on high. Now higher than the world, now surpassing every creature by merit, by right, by the prerogative of singular grace, and by the immensity of joy, she sings a new song to the Lord, saying: “My soul magnifies the Lord.”

Mary’s soul magnifies the Lord, and she herself is magnified by the Lord. Unless Mary’s soul were first magnified by the Lord, it could not magnify the Lord. Therefore it magnifies him by whom it is magnified; it magnifies him not only by praise of the mouth, not only by soundness of body, but by singularity of love. Many magnify with their tongues but blaspheme in their deeds and persecute with pride of heart; of them it is written: “They profess in words that they know God, but deny him in deeds” (Titus 1). Such persons do not magnify but, as far as lies in them, diminish the Lord’s name. These are those to whom the apostle says: “Through you the good name is blasphemed among the Gentiles” (James 2). But in Mary the tongue magnifies, life magnifies: “My soul magnifies the Lord” with the tongue, speaking in divine praises of the magnificence of your glory and holiness [Col. 0643A]; with life, deserving that same glory by works; with the soul, loving uniquely; by the flights of contemplation, attaining it; with mind and womb, comprehending the incomprehensible magnificence. “My soul,” she says, “magnifies the Lord.” How do you magnify him? Do you make greater one whose greatness has no end? “Great is the Lord,” says the Psalmist, “and exceedingly praiseworthy” (Ps. 95). He is great, and so great that his greatness admits neither comparison nor measure. How then does she magnify him whom she makes neither great from small nor greater from great? She magnifies him because she praises him; she magnifies him because, amid the darkness of the world, more brilliant than the sun, fairer than the moon, more fragrant than the rose, whiter than snow, she spreads abroad the splendour of divine knowledge. Thus she magnifies him not by adding increase to his original greatness, but by bringing the light of the true Godhead, unknown amid worldly darkness. For the Lord whom you magnify, just as he knows no diminution because he is eternal, so receives no increase because he is perfect. He is eternal because he has neither beginning nor end. He is perfect, because nothing is lacking to him for fullness. Yet you magnify him by raising yourself so high through surpassing merits that you receive fullness of grace, deserve the superabundant anointing of the Holy Spirit, and, made Mother of God, remaining a virgin and untouched, bear the Saviour for a perishing world. And this happens when the Lord is with you, who has made his gifts your merits. Hence you are said to magnify him all the more as you are more abundantly magnified by him in Christ.

What, then, does it mean that your soul magnifies the Lord, except that you yourself are magnified through him, so that you both gloriously attain fullness of grace and are stretched forth toward the magnificence of singular glory by glorious and supremely exalted virtues? Stretched forth, I say, because you are wholly drenched with the dew of the Holy Spirit, wholly suffused with heavenly anointing, so that, in the manner of an anointed skin, your soul may be stretched so greatly by love’s desire that it reaches the very Word of God. For you are Moses’ little basket; you are the vessel of the Word; you are the cellar of new wine, by which the intoxication of believers is intoxicated. You are the Mother of God, the boundary of sin, through whom one rises out of the depth of vices and reaches the delights of angels. How greatly magnified are your works, our Lady—but through him whom your soul magnifies! Here indeed [Col. 0643D] my smallness fails as I strive to speak of your magnificence. For while you climb the mountains of the magnificence of virtues, so that your soul may magnify the Lord there, I, unhappy man, plunge into the depths of misery and vices, and my wretched soul keeps no measure amid worldly desires. But you, Mother of Mercy, because I am like a stone in Mercury’s heap and like lead in rushing waters, and I am heavy because I cannot move myself: draw me after you, that I may be able to run after you in the fragrance of your ointments, breathe in the examples of your virtues, and be helped by the wings of prayers; so that, through your intercession, my soul may first learn, by fearing God, to depart from evil, and afterwards, loving with you and doing justice, to magnify the Lord, to whom belong honour and glory, dominion [Col. 0644A] and power unto all ages of ages. Amen.

## LETTER XVIII. TO HIS BROTHERS

He commends humility and gentleness to them and exhorts them to bear the Lord’s yoke.

To his brothers and most beloved friends in Christ, whom Christ’s love has made of one mind and God’s grace has made sharers in one name: Brother ADAM, a sinner, wishes them to remain true to the reality signified by their name.

The devout insistence of one of you moves me to remind you of something concerning the virtue of the soul; and certainly, since I love each of you sincerely, and you love one another with great sincerity, while I experience more fully in myself the good of your sincerity returning to me, what else can I say to you except what savours of love and virtue? Yet whatever your thirst has deserved to have offered to it through me must be drawn from the well of living waters. Christ is the well of living waters: the abyss of inaccessible light, the fullness of grace that cannot be attained. The well is deep, and my lowliness has nothing with which to draw from it, unless continual prayer performs the office of a rope and desire, plunging me down, serves as a bucket. O happy is he who has been able to draw from here streams of saving wisdom! The soul is dry which the streams of this well do not water. It is not fit for the fruitfulness of virtues. This spring flows into valleys and is accustomed to bestow its honey-sweet outpourings upon the humble. The humble soul experiences how sweet that infusion is, [Col. 0644C] with what abundance hearts sprinkled by such dew grow rich. How familiar humility is to heavenly Wisdom; how fruitful in virtues, how rich in merits, how capable of heavenly secrets! For all its action inclines downward; with all eagerness it bends over the living waters, and in no way allows itself to look back at anything that does not kindle in it a desire for life.

The living waters of the well, indeed, are the gifts of Christ’s manifold grace. They are waters because they wash, refresh, and restore; they are living because they abolish the business of death; they are in a well because they do not reveal to all the mystery of divine exaltation and the reasons for so secret an ordering. For these things, hidden from the wise and prudent, are revealed to little ones; truly, only to the humble are given their true knowledge and apprehension—knowledge which pride, presuming upon itself, does not deserve. Happy, therefore, is humility, which deserves to have a washing in these waters, lest any defilement appear or remain in it. It deserves restoration, that it may prove strong in every contest. For a truly humble person cannot be without the contests of temptations, especially since pride always envies humility, its opposite, and, if not its appearance, at least its glory. Nothing indeed is more glorious than humility. Although pride covetously seeks the sublimity of its glory, it scarcely assumes humility’s appearance, because that appearance is more lowly. Yet it sometimes assumes it, when without it pride is unable vainly to glory; and the more cunningly it conceals itself under the pretext of humility, [Col. 0645A] the more secretly its intention bursts forth toward the fulfillment of self-exaltation.

Learn, children, to be humble, and learn it from him who is the effective master of this discipline, Christ. For he is the master of this discipline, which he taught not merely in word and speech but showed must be kept in deed and truth. “Take,” says the good Master, “take my yoke upon you, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. XI), etc. If you understand and retain what he commanded, he has set before you four things to learn: what you ought to learn, from whom you ought to learn, how you ought to learn, and with what fruit. You ought to learn to be meek and humble of heart, and to learn from him who is meek and humble of heart. The manner of learning is to take his yoke upon yourself; the fruit of learning is to find rest for your soul: “and you shall find,” he says, “rest for your souls” (ibid.).

Therefore the art which a Christian and disciple of Christ ought to learn—indeed, that which makes a person Christ’s disciple—is called meek and humble gentleness. Mastery of this art is not acquired through a multitude of words, elegance of speech, tangled questions, or disputational conflicts, but through experience of conduct and the testimony of a purer conscience. For gentleness calms conduct and composes the mind. It harms no one, shakes no one, permits no one to inflict slander; it counts the world’s contempt as delights; disdaining the tumult of earthly activity, it forestalls occasions of sin, blocks the entrances of vices, and entrusts the gates of the bodily senses to the vigilance of discipline. Within, it keeps the Sabbath of innocence, celebrating it in the feast-days of eternal peace. For while gentleness regards everything outside as suspect, it gathers itself upward, in its customary manner, to the hand of its giver, so that it may await refreshment from within and from there. Gentleness is called *manus suetudo*, “the taming of the hand,” because it has so become accustomed to Christ’s hand that it aspires to nothing but his grace.

Humility, the inseparable companion of gentleness, likewise imitates the holy repose of its peacefulness. Hence, amid the troubles of injuries which one must often suffer, it strives not to grow angry. I have said too little: it strives not to grow angry; rather, true humility glories in tribulations. Paul’s humility gladly glories in weaknesses and counts as glory nothing except what breathes of Christ’s cross: “Far be it from me,” he says, “to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. VI). As gentleness delights in innocence, so humility trusts in patience, by which it counts it all joy when it happens to fall into various temptations. Thus humility itself, pressed down by the weight of its name, sits gladly upon the ground; almost every height is suspect to it. It is not ashamed to sit upon the ground; it does not blush to confess itself earth and ashes, so that when it has chosen the lowlier place, it may someday be raised with glory to a worthier one. For it is written: “He who humbles himself shall be exalted” (Matt. XXIII).

Sitting on the ground, it does not fear the thorns of scandals or the thistles of temptations, which are often brought forth from the earth to prick it. For, clinging to the earth, it is worn and crushed; and the usefulness of its crushing gladdens it under trampling, so that it bursts into a voice of exultation and says: “A contrite and humbled heart, O God, thou wilt not despise” (Ps. L). [Col. 0646A]

O wretched me! O unhappy me! Impurity of heart and wickedness of deeds make me unskilled in this art and ignorant of this happy prophecy. I still feel myself wholly among those to whom God’s Spirit cries out terribly in the Prophet: “Children of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” (Ps. IV). The heaviness of a leaden heart and love of manifold vanity delight in the falsehood of counterfeit pleasure within me. I serve truth only in outward appearance, and I fear that in reality I do not possess the virtue of godliness. Pray more earnestly; watch more earnestly and carefully, [Col. 0646B] lest our love suffer loss to its esteem in a friend.

But now let us return, both in speech and in mind, to the Master from whom we are to learn. This Master is God’s own Wisdom, the maker of all things, who gave being and form to all. He is the almighty Word, who teaches human beings knowledge. He is the Father’s only-begotten, the firstborn of our Virgin, who prefers mercy to sacrifice; for he is full of grace and truth, from whom every living creature receives blessing, as it is written: “And thou fillest every living creature with blessing” (Ps. CXLIV). Concerning this Master one must consider whence he came, what he suffered, whither he went, what he promised, and what he threatened.

He came from the Father’s heart, as the Father himself speaks, saying: “My heart has uttered a good word” (Ps. [Col. 0646C] XXXIV). He came into the Virgin’s heart, as it is said to that Virgin: “The Lord is with thee” (Luke I). He opened his heart to us when he emptied himself, in order to teach us the example of humility. He sought our heart for himself when he showed himself to be the lover and indweller of hearts, saying: “My delights are to be with the children of men” (Prov. VIII). It is evident, then, that he who is born from the heart dwells in the heart of his Virgin Mother, speaks from the heart, and declares that he loves the dwelling-place of hearts. As he is seen only with a pure heart, so too he is perceived only with a pure heart.

If therefore you are persons of heart, if you delight in sensing within yourselves Jesus, the indweller of hearts, you must keep your hearts with all vigilance, as it is written: “Keep [Col. 0646D] thy heart with all vigilance” (Prov. IV). He had this guardianship of the heart, and had drawn into his heart the lover of hearts, who said: “God is the God of my heart, and God is my portion for ever” (Ps. LXXII). Behold whence came, whence proceeded, the life of hearts: the Master of the heart, namely, from the heart.

Therefore all impurity must be cast out from our heart, so that its sweetness—the one singular joy—may be perceived. Let the truth of chastity remove the lust of the flesh; let the gravity of discipline and the desire for inward purity drive far away the lust of the eyes. Let love of poverty and contempt for honour dash down the pride of life. For this reason the Word came through flesh; for this reason he chose this manner of coming: so that in the flesh which he received within the Virgin, flesh might unlearn the love of carnal life. Nor ought the divinity of the Word to offer itself to fleshly persons without flesh; nor could love of carnal things die more effectively in human beings than if the presence of the incarnate Word instructed them concerning heavenly things.

What shall we now say of the teaching of so great a work? Its unquestionable truth and the heavenly sublimity of Wisdom commend his teaching. The works of consummate righteousness and the supreme tenderness of mercy proclaim the life to which his teaching bears witness. The purity of supreme innocence and the humility of singular patience honour the obedience of his Passion. [Col. 0647A]

Thereafter he returned to the place from which he came, and by the triumph over death raised your nature—which he had willed to be made a little lower than the angels—above all angelic heights, to the assembly at the Father’s right hand. Behold, there we are; there we live; there we reign. We reign, plainly, where we rejoice that our substance reigns. We cannot possibly be absent from there, where the better part of us already holds the place of a human being. O happy are we, who are members of this head, if we cling to this head in the unity of faith and the bond of love! In this we have already received the pledge of promise, because we do not doubt that he himself said in the Gospel: “Father, I will that where I am, there also my minister may be” (John XII).

Since he promised his own grace and glory, and meanwhile grants grace, be confident: to those who use grace well, he prepares glory. Yet even in the time of grace the saints do not live without glory, but glory with Paul in the testimony of conscience and say: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (II Cor. I). But lest anyone be overconfident concerning the promise of glory [Col. 0647C] or grow insolent at the successes of grace, let him always remember the divine threat. “Woe,” he says, “to those who have lost their support” (Ecclus. II). And in the Gospel: “Woe to you who are rich, for you have your consolation. Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep” (Luke VI). Therefore he threatens weeping of eyes and gnashing of teeth to those who fall away from virtue and trust in the comforts of the present life, while he consoles the meek and humble meanwhile by the testimony of conscience and, according to their measure, by enjoyment of glory.

These, children, are the things that must be learned and known concerning the Master, from whom must be learned whatever is usefully to be known. But one does not learn from him who disdains to keep the manner of learning. The Master himself describes the manner of learning, saying: “Take my yoke upon you” [Col. 0647D] (Matt. XI). For to take his yoke upon oneself is to keep the manner of learning. And what is his yoke but his love? His yoke, I say, is enduring, faithful, holy, and sweet love—upright and delightful. “My yoke,” he says, “is sweet, and my burden light” (ibid.). O yoke of love, how delightfully you burden, how sweetly you capture, how gently you bind, how mildly you press! This love, this yoke, is called a yoke because, joining the Word and the soul in a sweet marriage, it allows no divorce to separate them.

Do you not perceive your soul—young by the newness of faith, washed by confession, white with innocence, modest with the shame of chaste fear, mature through humility, composed by the guardianship of discipline, rosy through patience, joyful through charity, lovely through godliness, adorned in the garment of righteousness—betrothed to the Word of God by a certain covenant of faith? O when the soul has reached this place, when it has been led into this wine-cellar, what can it thereafter fail to know concerning the bridegroom, or in what can he conceal himself from his beloved? Here the happy soul now finds rest for itself and perceives the fruits of its discipline, when no labour of learning remains. This place is beautiful to behold, spacious for dwelling, and quiet for repose. When the soul reaches it and finds this blessed rest for itself, then rejoicing and praising it will cry: “This is my rest for ever and ever” (Ps. CXXXI), etc.

Then, leaning upon its beloved and wholly clinging to him, as it will be unable to love anything but him, [Col. 0648B] so it will neither be able nor ought to rejoice from any other source. Then, beautiful and sweet and wholly overflowing with delights, it will sing with wondrous joy that sweet bridal song: “My beloved is mine, and I am his” (Cant. I). He himself will be its full joy; he himself its complete glory.

When you arrive at the happiness of this rest—whether for the present, or swiftly and in passing through desire, or more happily through ecstasy of mind, or more blessedly through life’s end—pray, I ask, that I may become a participant in your glory, since here you have me as a companion in love. Meanwhile be solicitous to preserve virtue of soul, because through the unfailing exercise of virtue one arrives at the eternal reward. Therefore, since I am yours and count as mine whatever good is in you, now be concerned for me in Christ; for I cannot be in him [Col. 0648C] and forgetful of you. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XIX. TO A CERTAIN FRIEND

He exhorts him to contempt for the world.

You have often asked me, dearest brother, to write something for you by which both fervour of faith might increase in you and the edification of conduct might arise. The devotion of your request pleased me; and because, by assenting, I made myself your debtor, I am at last bound to pay what I promised. The subject, therefore, will be virtue of soul, which contempt for the world advances not a little. Certainly, as much as virtue of soul is to be sought, so much must love of the world be avoided; for love of the world makes one God’s enemy, whereas virtue produces desire for eternal things. Unless eternal things are desired, they are in no way sought from the heart. But they cannot be desired unless virtue enlightens one to see and inflames one to love.

The mind which the earthliness of worldly desire defiles and darkens is capable of neither light nor love. For this earthliness contains in itself a muddy foulness, contact with which stains the mind, and a dull heaviness, the obstacle of which prevents the light of supreme majesty and brightness from penetrating. Therefore earthly desire must be cast out from the appetite of the soul, so that the soul, raised from earth, may serve as a heaven for the inhabitant of heaven. Certainly, although God is the creator of all and Lord of heaven and earth, he is said to have his dwelling only in the heavens, because beyond doubt heavenly hearts are denoted by the name “heavens.” [Col. 0649A]

Heavenly hearts are those whose citizenship is in heaven, whose adornment and ornamentation are made of the stars of virtues, who separate themselves in mind from earthly dregs as far as heaven differs from earth in situation and order of things. O sublimity to be desired!
