O marvellous splendour of virtues, where love of passing things has no place, but the soul is happily fixed upon what endures: while vanity is rejected, wickedness avoided, the body subjected to the spirit, and temporal things sought only for the necessity of frail life! Thus love of the world finds no entrance to the heart, while love of truth and zeal for virtue generate in the sober heart a hunger for eternal things. O happy hunger, more delightful than every refreshment, which the fullness of infinite blessedness satisfies at the end!

For this fullness omnipotent love created humankind; but when humanity refused to understand in order to act well, it came to the want of most wretched poverty. Thus humanity became miserable: empty from fullness, needy from riches, a fugitive from stability, an exile from citizenship, ignoble from glory, dishonoured from honour. For by an unhappy exchange, from the likeness of the Creator and equality in angelic dignity, humanity was compared to senseless beasts and made like them. O that, human being, only human mortality had come upon you, so that, after losing the likeness of your most gracious Creator, you might be compared with unreasoning cattle, and not, by a greater unhappiness, be found inferior to cattle in almost every respect! For while you are more corrupt in flesh, more shameful in sinful life, more foolish by abuse of implanted reason, weaker also in bodily senses, and more unhappy by liability to eternal death—while in all these things a beast surpasses you—on what ground does nature, held captive in you, pride itself? Yet you surpass beasts by the benefit of implanted reason, according to which the most noble image of the Creator was impressed upon you. To use reason as is fitting is to preserve the impressed image; to love him whose image it is, is to retain his likeness. O how great a happiness and glory it is for the creature to become like its Creator! Sincerity of love grants you this glory, by which, as we are made conformed to God, we detest in every way the stains of sins. For holy love is so intolerant of corruption [Col. 0649D] because it always kindles the soul toward desire for incorruption.

This stretching-out of desire does not permit the wrinkle of duplicity in the heart, and at the same time removes the swelling of self-exaltation. The kindness of this love banishes the rancour of envy and opposes the motions of anger with the sweetness of gentleness. The cheerfulness of love excludes the anxiety of sadness and supplies against the rapacity of avarice the antidote of generosity. Holy love is so sober that, because it always suspects the softness of the flesh, it wishes moderation to rule appetite and belly. So greatly does it please love to pursue honourableness, and so great is its circumspection in preserving honourableness, that it not only abominates the foulness of lust, but cannot even look upon anything that can be an incentive to such shamefulness. [Col. 0650A] For it regards as suspect lewd words and gestures; it avoids places and opportunities, and strives to cut off every occasion from which the splendour of honourableness might incur either a wound to conscience or the peril of infamy. For the holy must have testimony from those outside and provide good things not only before God but also before human beings.

Moreover, you desire virtue, but you are still ashamed before people of the appearance of virtue. I do not think that one possesses virtue unto merit whose display he fears may displease the eyes of the worst people. There are many whom virtue delights, but who blush to be seen in it because they desire, do, or often pretend to do the contrary—valuing conformity to worldly people more highly than being guided, according to the testimony of conscience, by the judgment of their inward breast. He is surely cruel who neglects his reputation; and for one whose cruelty wounds his own reputation, there is no mercy that makes conscience sound.

In all things, dearest son, let your regard be toward Jesus: to know him is life; to love him, salvation; to follow him, glory; to attain him, the highest good. But if it does not suffice to behold the Word himself in the Father’s bosom, where solid food is joy, then behold with me the same Word made small in the Virgin’s childbirth, broken into the milk of virgin flesh, so that the infancy of little ones may have small draughts. For the almighty Word, just as by his power he created us, so by his compassion he restored us; and as the innocence of his humiliation instructs us, so the Passion of his innocence redeemed us. Therefore, made by him and restored through him, let us feast upon him and live in him; for to perceive and taste him gladdens the conscience; to praise and honour him commends one’s reputation; to enjoy and fully enjoy him grants everlasting glory. Amen. [Col. 0650C]

## EPISTLE XX. TO A. OF VITRÉ

He instructs him with devout words.

To his lord and friend Master A. of Vitré, brother Adam, called abbot of Persigne, wishes that he may savour the things above, not those upon the earth.

You accuse me of falsehood, most loving brother, because the zeal of sacred charity has not at last fulfilled what your devotion asked and the rashness of my inexperience promised [Col. 0650D], and because I have by no means discharged what was promised. Forgetfulness which defrauds a promise of faith of its performance deserves rebuke. Therefore, if there is place with you for repentance, grant pardon to my negligence, because I do not dare, without the torment of shame, to confess that I have at some time lied to you.

You devoutly ask and earnestly knock at the door, asking that something be written for you from which you may receive in yourself a rule, as though I were learned or capable of handing down the ordinances of a more corrected life to masters. My speech is not so powerful, my life not so venerable, my conduct not so conspicuous, that I can or ought to serve as an example to the wise. But Christ is the line of all direction, against which the unevenness of conduct and crookedness of soul are detected. To be under his mastership is the highest wisdom; to withdraw one’s hand from his rod is approved virtue.

For he is the sea of innocence, the fountain of mercy, the teaching of patience, the river of wisdom, the splendour of glory, the almighty Word. Although this Word was made small on earth within the Virgin and upon the cross, it retains and keeps hidden in itself the treasures of all wisdom and knowledge. This almighty Word is inscribed upon our heart; the parchment of conscience does not retain it unless purity of innocence, drawn in its own lines, gives it form. O happy inscription, more desirable than gold and topaz, where the Word of heavenly wisdom is written above the lines of the soul, which upright innocence, the purpose of equity, simplicity of intention, and the gentleness of spiritual childhood make and engrave! [Col. 0651A]

Toward this childhood the Word bends and opens itself; and although it is obscure by its own littleness—that is, by its self-emptying—it nevertheless reasons more clearly about itself through humility. While its splendour is hidden from the wise and prudent, it is revealed more intimately to the innocence of little ones. “Out of the mouths of infants and nursing children thou hast perfected praise”: he who was begotten by the Father before the ages and now begotten by a mother causes newborn infants, rational and without guile, to desire the milk of his incarnation, so that, nourished by it, they may be able fully to form the one Word. Otherwise, how would perfect praise arise from the mouths of infants unless childhood fully formed that Word in which perfection of merits is founded, from which the fullness of grace and truth flows?

Finally, that this Word makes and nourishes infants—that is, those who do not speak—is shown, according to the Prophet, by that midnight silence in whose time the almighty Word came from royal thrones (Wis. XVIII). While worldly wisdom makes him obscure, he grants a fuller understanding of himself to little ones. Certainly, just as this Word sounds only from the mouths of infants and hastens only to the silent, so the *glotta*—that is, tongue—of the Word himself, namely the Holy Spirit, expounds the sacrament of the Word only in the waters of Siloam which flow silently. [Col. 0651C]

The waters of Siloam which flow silently are the people of Zion, the people of the saints, in whose holy rest the silence of the worship of righteousness is preserved. The waters of Siloam which flow silently are streams of graces, heavenly teachings proceeding from the fruit of wisdom and the refreshment of life. “Upon whom,” says the Word of life, “shall my Spirit rest, except upon one who is humble and quiet and trembles at my words?” (Isa. LXVI). Finally, the Holy Spirit is not inappropriately called the *glotta*, that is, the tongue, of the Word; hence, coming upon the apostles in fiery tongues, he expounded to them concerning the sacrament of the Word all that was necessary for the fullness of teaching.

Whatever obscurity the incarnate Word had contracted through his abbreviation, the teaching anointing of the Holy Spirit wholly made clear, both teaching the causes of so great a self-emptying and instructing the tongues of infants to expound the ineffable teaching. Therefore the Word itself, obscure through the likeness of sinful flesh and contracted from the immensity of its majesty through the smallness of a body, speaks of its interpreter: “He shall glorify me, because he shall receive of mine and shall declare it to you” (John XVI). [Col. 0652A]

If, therefore, you wish to understand the Word of God, if you desire to read and understand its *glotta*, the Holy Spirit, you need humility and quietness together with obedience to the commandments. The spirit of wisdom seeks rest in all things; through humility it obtains quietness, and it preserves the quietness of conscience through fulfilment of the commandments. For one who trembles at God’s words carries them out reverently. In such fulfilment trembling is mingled with exultation; hence David says: “Serve the Lord with fear, and rejoice in him with trembling” (Ps. II).

Moreover, the devout labour of obedience is not completed by persevering diligence unless the love of changeable things, vain and slippery, meanwhile disturbs the stability of uprightness. A quiet mind is necessary where dutiful fear kindles the light of wisdom. A lamp is not easily lit in the wind, nor does the agitation of such disturbed air deserve to be clothed in the light of serenity. Therefore humility is necessary to exclude windy pride and to calm the air of the heart by a more serene purity. This tranquillity is fit to receive the radiance of divine illumination, and the Spirit of truth does not avoid that seat for which truthful humility has provided rest.

Here desire, sprouting into every evil, does not put down roots; here ambition does not rage; here contention, the enemy of peace, has no place; here the beam of pride does not darken the eye of the heart; here simulation does not conceal itself in shadow under a covering of virtue; here the softness of an effeminate heart does not parade shamelessness; here the proud ostentation of wealth does not glory in money-changing tables extended on poles; [Col. 0652C] here gluttony is not bred by stimulants of the appetite, nor does the intemperance of food itself excite the frenzy of lust.

The disciple of the Word, the cultivator of virtue and lover of poverty, renounces riches as well as vices. He is not defiled by vices, not dissolved by jokes, not enervated by idleness, not inflamed by fleshly desires, not overflowing in luxuries, not bent upon gifts, not greedy for estates, not intent on enlarging landed properties. For he considers how narrow and arduous is the way that advances to life, and how strait the gate by which it enters. With ready mind he embraces tribulations and hardships, wholly clinging to the cross; he counts as loss whatever does not present to him the image of the cross.

In short, the disciple of the Word is wholly in discipline, that from the breast of discipline he may be humbled to fear, instructed to knowledge, exercised to patience, and refined for glory. For when he recalls that divine saying, “Those whom I love I chastise and rebuke” (Rev. III), he judges himself to be God’s son in proportion as he feels himself subject to the blows of heavenly discipline. Discipline is not absent from the mastership of the Word; nor is discipline without a stroke, since the Word of the Father derives its name from a stroke (*verber*). For with the rod of his power he strikes the powers of the air, and by the rod from the root of Jesse—from which a prepared heart comes—he corrects our errors. [Col. 0653A] For when the incarnate Word endured in his flesh the blows owed to us, when he exposed his back to scourges, he instructed his followers in the endurance of discipline. “The chastisement of our peace was upon him, and by his bruise we were healed.” Truly he bore our infirmities and carried our pains; for, if sinners built upon his back the back of innocence, penitents ought to submit the harmful body corrupted by vices to scourges.

Let us consider, if you please, how many disciplines of innocence the Word received in his Passion, of which, beyond doubt, the faithful disciple of the Word is both imitator and preacher. There are seven, as I consider: the first he endured in scourges, the second in spittle, the third in blows, the fourth in thorns, the fifth in nails, the sixth in food of gall, the seventh in the piercing of his side. In these seven truly liberal disciplines consists the whole teaching of Christian patience.

Behold, I have set before you a mirror in which you may look upon yourself often, know yourself more truly, and receive more fully both the gift and form of grace and virtue. Let your knowing, your understanding, be wholly in Jesus; beyond him nothing is to be desired, and short of him the mind is not to rest. For in him shines the splendour of the Father’s glory; in him overflows the sweet anointing of the Holy Spirit. Thus, by the name Christ, with which he is marked, he has power to mark out his participants. Christ is the anointing of the weak, health for the sick, seasoning of life, illumination of conscience, anointing of mercy, the rich sweetness of goodness. He is provision on pilgrimage, strength in contest, victory in triumph, reward in the crown, fullness of glory in the return to the homeland.

O return to the homeland, sweet above all and before all, in which an end is set to misery, a day knowing no night breathes forth, and laughter rejoices which is not turned into sorrow! O delightful climate, in which renewed glory drives away the winter of mortality, ends the showers of tears, and, amid heavens flowering anew through the transformation of eternal renewal, that sweet song resounds upon well-sounding cymbals: “Winter has passed; the rain is gone and departed; flowers have appeared; flowering vineyards have given their fragrance,” etc. (Cant. II). [Col. 0653C] Then, within the abyss of light, disciples of truth will obtain both eternal security in escape from death and complete joy in the vision of God. “It is good for us to be here”: we neither wish nor ought to learn or seek anything further.

For my part, I shall end the discourse. You persevere in prayer and work, so that I may obtain with you what you have heard. Amen, amen.

## EPISTLE XXI. TO A FRIEND

He excuses himself for not writing against the Jews.

To his beloved one, Adam, called abbot of Persigne, sends earnest and importunate greetings.

You asked, dearest brother, that I write something for you by which the faith of believers might be strengthened and the obstinacy of unbelievers, especially Jews, might be refuted. But although many things with me hinder the accomplishment of this request, there are three which seem especially to oppose my efforts in this matter.

First, I seem to see that you pursue this contest with a contentious spirit rather than zeal for truth. Second, as truth does not shine forth for contentious people, so neither is it fitting for us to arm anyone for contention with any words. For as we do not wish to be contentious, so neither do we love contentious people; much less ought we to lead anyone into contention or lend aid to one who contends. As Paul says to Timothy: “The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but must be gentle toward all, teachable, patient, correcting with modesty those who resist the truth” (II Tim. II). Third, even if you sought this from zeal for piety, it is altogether useless labour to dispute with Jews about faith, since it is evident that by God’s judgment they have incurred the darkness of inward blindness.

“For the heart of this people has grown fat,” and until the fullness of the Gentiles enters, carnal Israel, blinded by its unbelief, will grope in the noonday as in the night. [Col. 0654B] For it has hardened into flint, though it is fleshly; indeed, in heart it has become hard with the hardness of diamond. Therefore it is said through the prophet: “The sin of Judah is written with an iron stylus, with a diamond point” (Jer. XVII). For just as a diamond is scarcely broken by any cleavage, so the hardness of Jewish unbelief is softened by no reasoning or authority. Therefore it is not an unequal blindness to engage them in conflict about truth, where conflict can prevail to obtain no fruit.

Yet there are many who devote themselves not so much to examination of matters as to contests of words, and who glory more in the vain applause of people than in the living judgment of truth. It is utterly condemnable madness to misuse the business of truth for the vice of vanity. Woe to those who hold truth in unrighteousness, who make light darkness, who argue vainly about justice, who support the empty things of vanity with the solidity of truth. Vanity is plainly hostile to truth, nor can a vanity rightly refuted overcome the enemies of truth. Therefore one who devotes himself to vanity ought not to handle the affairs of incorrupt truth. For truth is incorruption and the splendour and rule of all equity, against which every deformity and crookedness strikes. Far be it that incorrupt truth should need corrupt persons for its defence! Rather, it attacks the followers of vanity themselves.

Truth is certainly the friend of simplicity and glories in the innocence of humility. It does not seek its own interests, does not desire vain things, and has no place among lovers of the world. For truth is the splendour of heavenly wisdom, attained only by the poor in spirit.

What then have you to do with him? You have been carried across the sea of vanity and submerged in the flood of many waters—and you dare to dream of the splendors of truth? This wisdom has taken root only among a people held in honor. It is far from the concerns of the court, where rather a nearly incurable heedlessness holds sway. Under that rule faith perishes, justice is exiled, and the illumination of truth has yielded to the darkness of vices; that government strips Christ of his own cross, so that the Christian now serves the cross not in reality but in name alone.

Rather, it is with those who, having the Son of God as an object of display and having become partners of the Jews, crucify Christ anew, that one should discuss faith. Set yourself against these, if you profess yourself a friend of faith. For if you are a friend of faith, willing and able to fight for it, then surely love of the world—which makes you God’s enemy—is far from you. For it is written: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world is made an enemy of God” (James 4). O unhappy minds, which prefer the love of earthly things to heavenly friendships! The Lord of heaven and earth is to be preferred above all things, loved not merely in word and tongue, but in deed and truth. O minds fallen away from true nobility! Divine likeness has nothing in common with earthly dregs, nor does it accompany the madness of carnal love. Raising the heart on high, it joins it to the splendors of the stars [Col. 0655B], and does not permit the beauty of the divine image within to be defiled by ugliness.

There the idolatry of avarice finds no place, nor the swelling of pride, nor the foul frenzy of lust, nor the dreadful blindness of malice; there the dignity intended by divine likeness is preserved for you. That honor is not fed by jesting, dissipated in idleness, clothed in soft garments, stuffed with food, seeking human applause, or delighted by spectacles. There the idle subtlety of chess does not disturb the happy leisure of a gentle heart; there the game of miserable chance does not squander time badly—time which flows away with disgust as often as it is spent without crimes.

> O the cares of humankind! O how much emptiness there is in things!  
> (Persius, *Satires* I)

[Col. 0655C] Would that vanity alone existed among human concerns, and that iniquity did not make itself vanity’s inseparable companion! Indeed, vanity is the mother of iniquity, and by a viper’s birth vanity gives birth to iniquity. These are a brood of vipers; but the mind that uses reason alone for its proper purposes is free from them. For insofar as the proper use of reason brings about the understanding of heavenly things, so far does the mind withdraw from mortal concerns. In reason is situated the condition of the divine image and the honor of likeness; hence, in turning aside anywhere beyond the lines of reason, a person savors of a beast, not of a human being. For action led and directed by the lines of reason either preserves faith from dying or restores it, once dead, to life: “Faith without works is dead” (James 2).

Accordingly, reason cannot be said to exist where no right intention is found. For if intention is right through the benefit of reason, the works will undoubtedly be rational; and these, as has been said, can either raise dead faith or guard it against death. Thus, by God’s grace, reason’s moderation gives order to our affections: it becomes the material of virtues, equity in conduct, discipline in works, and the seedbed of all uprightness. For the affections of the soul, ordered around reason, receive the effects and names of virtues.

But life is irrational where reason neither trains intention to be right nor disposes the will to be devout. For from the same light—namely, incorporeal reason—intention is illumined toward rectitude [Col. 0656A], and the will is made glad toward piety. Yet these things occur in the hearts of believers. The unbeliever is wholly without this grace: “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11 [printed: II]). And the Apostle says: “Whatever is not from faith is sin” (Rom. 14).

But should I call one faithful in whom faith is dead, and who contradicts faith by his works? Does not one contradict it in deeds who confesses in word that he knows God but denies him in acts? He does not appear to savor of faith whose mind is disordered, face troubled, speech tasteless, behavior dishonorable, eye shameless, touch seductive, and appetite greedily set upon vice. In faith covetousness does not rule, ambition does not rage, self-exaltation does not swell, anger does not roar, luxury does not grow foul, nor does gluttony of the belly savor of the pig. Whoever is such is not faithful, nor is it fitting that he handle the concerns of faith.

If your conscience bears witness to you that you are subject to evils of this kind, I advise you to make conflict with them your familiar concern. Once freed from them, join the number of the faithful, able also to call others back to the rule of faith. The anointing of works fights better for faith than speech. The example of a good work is more effective in persuading concerning faith than a lengthy verbal dispute for faith. Yet blessed is the teaching of the mouth when action speaks beforehand from knowledge! Blessed is the person in whom faith bears witness to both! Therefore strive to live honorably, so that your faith may be reckoned to you as righteousness. For you owe your whole self to the testimony of faith: by the right and office of priesthood, you have become a minister of faith and a herald of the Gospel.

[Col. 0656C] Take care that strength of soul not be lacking to your office, lest you be judged wholly unfit for the defense or proclamation of faith. For then faith makes you a participant in virtue, if faith is accompanied by both the truth of works and the honor of chastity. Emulate the glory of angelic incorruption, with whose name you have been joined through participation in the sublimity of office. For it is written in Malachi: “The lips of the priest preserve knowledge, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. 2). Therefore guard your lips from evil speech—lips to which it has been granted, by their office, to utter words of wholly gracious and effective power.

Certainly, this has not been granted to angels, nor does angelic nature merit the office and glory of handling most holy mysteries and consecrating fearful sacraments. This belongs not to spirits but to human beings, whom divine calling deigns to exalt by the glory of so great a rank. Angels indeed cooperate with priests, and they cannot altogether be absent from the mystery where the King of angels works incomprehensible things in the hands of a human being. How great, then, do you think is the sacrilege of polluting with vanity and falsehood a mouth once consecrated to incorruptible truth? How can sweet and bitter waters flow from the same fountain? How can the same lips of truth be deformed by the speech of falsehood? Grace has been poured out upon your lips; and milk and honey will be beneath your tongue as often as you pronounce those words for the efficacy of the mysteries. Honey and milk, I say, are beneath your tongue whenever, at your utterance, those words make God-man present under visible species. You know the words. Fearful [Col. 0657A] is their most holy utterance, and effective is the incomprehensible power of the mystery granted by God to the ministry of priests.

How, then, can there be beneath your lips “toil and sorrow and the venom of asps,” when such power of words may reside in your lips? Therefore restrain your mouth from much speaking and idle speech, foolish speech and obscene speech, false speech and evil speech, because it is known to be consecrated to heavenly mysteries. With how pure a heart, how clean hands, how simple eyes must that action be performed in which there is dealing with the Virgin’s childbirth, the Passion of the Lamb, the redemption of humankind, the forgiveness of sins, the fullness of virtues, and the joy of angels!

Who and what are you when, between your hands, the Virgin conceives by the Holy Spirit, while, as you utter the undefiled words of the mystery, the substance of the visible offering passes into the substance of the divine flesh? How can you deliberately turn those eyes toward the excesses of vanity, materials for wantonness, and fuel for lusts—eyes by which you behold enacted in your hands the purity of virginal childbirth and the innocence of the Lord’s Passion? With what face do you dare to touch shameful things with the fingers by which you handle the author of honor, the lover of innocence, the giver of grace? Your hands are full of blood, and yet you do not fear to place them upon the spotless linen of the Lord’s flesh.

Take care, son, lest perhaps the rapacity of avarice has made you a wolf, and the Lamb flee rather than wait for you. Truly, the gentleness of a lamb cannot endure the presence of a wolf [Col. 0657C]; just as a chick cannot endure the gluttony of a kite, nor a dove the rapacity of a hawk. This flight, indeed, does not occur because the Lamb is afraid, nor does he deny even the worst persons the presence of his true flesh; rather, he flees them when he allows himself to be received by such persons unto their destruction and judgment. Rather, the Lamb is slain by the wolf’s presence when one who receives unworthily or consecrates dishonorably is found guilty of the Lord’s body and blood.

How, then, does such a person rebuke the unbelief of the Jews and convict them of guilt for the Lord’s death, when, by receiving the sacraments unworthily, he entangles himself in the guilt of the same crime? They, indeed, “if they had known, would never have crucified the Lord of glory.” You know him and kill him whenever you become guilty of his body and blood by receiving unworthily. It is far more execrable to crucify anew by evil living one who lives and reigns forever than it was when a Jew, not knowing, wished to rage against one still mortal and human, subject to needs. A false Christian who knows and persecutes is a worse enemy of faith than a Jew who persecutes in ignorance. Yet within the bosom of faith none is more cruelly evil than the priest who persecutes Christ not through evil ignorance but through avarice—Christ whom he ought to serve more intimately, cling to more firmly, and minister to more faithfully, in proportion as he believes himself more worthily and wonderfully regarded by Christ.

But—what cannot be said without groaning—the priests of our time have so armed themselves with vices against Christ that they seem to have conspired against him rather than for him [Col. 0658A]. They bear arms against him for whom they ought to have fought; and, violating his virgin—that is, the Church—they have corrupted her even to the crown of her head, as the Prophet says (Jer. 2).

Finally, their life has become for everyone an example of malice, a sewer of crimes, a spectacle of disgrace, material for ambition, and a deformed pattern of every turning-away: theirs is avarice insatiable and indescribable, lust unappeasable, ambition without limit. Imitating Simon and Gehazi, they have transformed the house of God into a temple of an idol by miserable commerce. For “avarice,” as the Apostle says, “is the service of idols” (Col. 3); and, thinking gain to be godliness, they shrink from admitting no sacrilege.

[Col. 0658B] They care more for money than for souls, more for walls than for the mute, more for dogs than for the poor; finally, more for the children of their own flesh whom they receive through fornication than for the children of Mother Church, whom they are bound to govern and benefit. O these unhappy men, who wish to be honored through their ministry and yet dishonor ministry itself in every way! Their ministry is now reproached because through it they minister not to Christ but to themselves, striving to satisfy their own pleasure from the fruit of office. They profess themselves servants of Christ’s cross, provided that they receive carnal profit from it; but they blush to follow the blessed disgrace of the cross.

Thus they serve the cross so that they do not feel the cross. Under the pretext of the cross, they pursue through its benefit the luxury of the flesh and soft pleasures. O abuse detestable in every age! They honor the cross in order to have the means to give themselves over to allurements, to make liberty a covering for malice. In the cross of Christ and service of the cross there is supreme and sole freedom—but only for those whose heart is set upon anointing and whose affection holds truth. Those who love the world and despise heavenly things, however, often shelter themselves under the title of the cross while doing everything that is called devout. For the office of a priest is blind unless it serves the cross; but you must consider whether you truly bear the savor of a priest.

A good priest is one in whom the ordered zeal of action commends the dignity of his rank. A good priest is one who not only offers the Son to the Father but always strives to offer himself as well. Otherwise, how does one eat or offer the lamb who neither leaves Egypt [Col. 0658D] nor girds his loins? Only Hebrews departing from Egypt may offer the Paschal lamb. This is not an Egyptian sacrifice; indeed, Egyptians disdain to eat lamb or sheep. The worldly person is Egyptian: he delights in the darkness of sins, finds Pharaoh’s destruction pleasing, and takes pleasure in labor with mud and brick. “Egypt” signifies darkness, “Pharaoh” dissipation, and mud the softness of pleasures, which habit turns into the hardness of brick. It is not to those doing such things that the offering of the lamb is commanded, but to the Israelite hastening toward the wilderness. Continence girds the loins; truth and sincerity lead out from darkness; and wild lettuce produces the bitterness of repentance.

[Col. 0659A] Therefore see, you who offer the Lamb, whether you are leaving Egypt. If you truly are departing, offer reverently. Those who offer sacrifice must not lack the girdle of chastity upon their loins, the staff of faith in their hands, or the footwear of the saints’ examples upon their feet. The feet are affections; the hands are works. Both must be fortified: the affections by examples from imitation of the saints, the works by faith for the correction of many evils. If these are lacking in you and yet you do not refrain from offering the Lamb, you are not an Israelite but an Egyptian; not faithful but an apostate; not a priest but a sacrilegious person; not a defender of faith but an offender.

Moreover, what am I to say to you about the blasphemies so often heard to sound from your lips? Because you regard it as swearing, and have turned it into a habit from popular recklessness [Col. 0659B], we teach, say, and believe it to be blasphemy. Certainly, since a priest’s words are either true or sacrilegious, to take the name of his God in vain so often is not to swear but to blaspheme. What is this—that the blessed limbs of Jesus are brought, by a sacrilegious mouth, a heart so impure, lips so uncircumcised, even amid diabolical acts, into the habit of swearing—or rather, of blaspheming? It is not human but wholly diabolical for people of ruined mind, under the pretext of an oath, to babble in impious voices about that which ought to be loved with trembling hearts and one’s whole inward being.

The devil himself neither dares nor can sin against Christ’s majesty, nor could Jewish ignorance itself exceed so greatly in sinning against Christ as most wretched Christians sin against him. Had the devil known, had the Jew known, they would have spared the Lord of glory. The Christian believes and despises, recognizes and rejects, worships and blasphemes, prays and attacks. Therefore act for the sake of your faith and your office: putting aside for the present superfluous disputation with the Jews, since it does not concern you, instruct by word and life those Christians of your own household of faith who are worse than they are.

## Letter XXII. To Agnes, a Virgin

He commits to writing what he had publicly discussed in an assembly of virgins.

(From the manuscript of Blessed Mary of the Mercy of God and from Clairvaux.)

[Col. 0659D] To Agnes, virgin of Christ: Brother Adam, called abbot of Perseigne, wishes that she may be numbered among the prudent virgins.

Daughter, your love in the love of Christ means so much to me that, just as I cannot refuse what you ask, so I have in no way wished to delay what you requested. Holy love is so headlong toward everything virtuous that, while it always sighs for the growth of spiritual advancement, it unceasingly provides itself some stimulus. Yet, in a wonderful manner, for holy love to advance in this way is to languish; and the more the heart’s ardor stretches toward the desire of virtue, the more the mind, failing from itself, advances into God, melted by love’s desire.

Would that this love has made you languid, and that your soul has melted at the burning utterance of your Bridegroom, so that you may say with inward conviction that saying of the lover: “My soul melted when my beloved spoke” (Song 5). Desiring to be kindled by my words, you therefore asked more earnestly that I should not refuse to send you briefly, in writing and from memory, what I had once discussed in an assembly of virgins, with you present, for their edification. But since the tenor of that discourse has slipped away either wholly or in very great part, while the subject is the same and the occasion the same, the same Spirit will be present at your request, who from the same chapter will grant us to think, if perhaps not the same things, yet not different things.

The passage is, as you recall: “Lord, it is good for us to be here” (Matt. 17). Who says this? Peter, the friend of the Bridegroom and guardian of the bride: firm in Christ insofar as, loving Christ more especially, he was wholly inflamed with love’s flame. And truly, what is better than for a lover of love to remain in the love of incorruption—not only to behold unchangeable beauty with the eye of faith, but also to clasp it in the embrace of most certain hope, to mingle tender kisses of purest affection, and through conversations of a sincere heart either address the Bridegroom when present or invite him when absent?

For the Bridegroom of virgins is the fountain of love, a sea of sweetness, an abyss of glory, and the sole consolation of those who love. Although he is always most present to the faithful bride in majesty and near in love, the effect of unquenchable desire, which torments and melts the soul, nevertheless indicates a kind of absence from him [Col. 0660C]. While the mind, melted by the desire of pure love, is wholly suspended in longing for the joy of complete consolation, it bears with utmost pain the loss caused by delay. Yet, when it attributes to its own defects that it does not grasp what it loves, it advances all the more subtly in the desire of love, because, humbling itself from awareness of its own weakness, it attends from that defect to the sublimity of its love.

Therefore the bride of the Word, constrained by such pangs, sends word to her beloved by a messenger that she languishes with love, is distressed by longing for the absent one, and cannot endure the lovable wound of charity unless the Bridegroom, beautiful in form above the children of humankind, makes himself present. Then, following the Lamb wherever he goes, feeding and resting with him at noon, she no longer sends messengers to him as though absent. But seeing eye to eye and speaking face to face, she cries out and says: “Lord, it is good for us to be here.” It is as if she said: “I no longer languish from love because of your absence; the force of deferred desire no longer torments me. In your presence I have wholly recovered through love, because to possess your presence is not to languish but to be healed.”

Blessed, indeed most blessed, are those who fail away from themselves through such languishing, because there is no medicine for the soul that has not been melted by the desires of this languor. O how healthful is this languishing! How it satisfies and refreshes the longing for the Bridegroom! How far from health is the person who has not been wounded by this charity! Yet the bride experiences this better than the servant [Col. 0661A]. For the more tenderly she is loved, the more securely and secretly she glories in familiar dwelling with him. The bride is admitted to the hidden chambers, and amid the secrets of the marriage bed is united to the Bridegroom in a pure and ineffable union. Then, conceiving by the Holy Spirit, she blossoms and brings forth the virgin offspring of virtues, bears children of good works, and has this remedy for love’s languor: she seeks to be supported by these flowers and delights in being surrounded by such apples.

But love’s languor ensures, through the spirit and desire for the health that God’s presence brings and offers, that there are both unfading flowers and imperishable fruits. For the flowers in the Bridegroom’s garden are virtues in the soul’s desire, made unfading by charity that never fails [Col. 0661B] and by the desired eternity that knows no end.

Moreover, apples signify, both by the color of their skin and the multitude of their seeds, the many sufferings of the flesh in the saints and the multiplicity of good works in the union and ardor of charity. The bride experiences and understands these better in herself, since, as has been said, she is admitted within; and the purer she comes to the secret of divine counsel, the more closely, stripped of carnal coverings and bodily images, she enters the bridal chamber of incorruptible truth.

O how ineffable is the delight of this spiritual union! When everything carnal is removed from the midst, the more closely the soul embraces its beloved unto every joy, the less the nakedness of incorruptible truth hides itself from the nakedness of his innocence. But if at times the absence of this good causes the bride to languish—while she continually desires to possess what she can never possess enough, while that which she immovably longs for is inconsolably delayed—then meanwhile she seeks support in flowers. For she consoles and feeds herself for a time either with understandings of the Scriptures, examples of the saints, innocence of spiritual deeds, or indeed the progress of others: “Support me with flowers, surround me with apples, for I languish with love” (Song 2). It is as if she said: “Since I am tormented by the absence of my beloved and do not yet deserve to enjoy his lovable presence, perhaps, if I am supported by flowers, if our bed is flowering, my beloved will be restored to me through the fragrance of the flowers.”

Such is the bride. But what of the servant? He is scarcely permitted to stand in the vestibule; he is never admitted, is more often cast out, and more frequently beaten. For fear assigns him to carry burdens outside, and the guilt of his own conscience scourges him. Scripture says: “Cast out the slave woman and her son” (Gen. 21); a servant because he is the son of a slave woman; cast out because he is a servant, because “the servant does not remain in the house forever.”

I, I am that unhappy one from whom you—no slave woman, but the bride of my Lord and therefore my lady—ask concerning the Bridegroom’s love. Yet, if you do not violate the laws of the divine covenant, you experience it better through yourself, grasp it more tenderly, and enjoy it more delightfully. How, then, do you so lightly leave the Bridegroom’s chamber and consult, from your inner rooms, your Bridegroom’s servant outside—especially when the servant does not know what his master does? Within, within, good Jesus, you are sought more fittingly, found more swiftly, held more tightly, kissed more sweetly.

When Agnes, bride of the Lamb, has kissed you, because grace has been poured out upon your lips, she will be able to rejoice and sing that wedding-song of the holy virgin Agnes: “I have received honey and milk from his mouth” (Song 4), and: “His blood adorned my cheeks.” “Return, return, Shulamite; return, return, that we may behold you” (Song 6). Run through the enclosed garden, and know that your beloved delights in the resting places and gardens of spices. How beautiful and sweet you have become in your delights, if you keep undefiled the covenant of heavenly marriage!—if the scent of the virginal lily keeps its whiteness unfadingly [Col. 0662B], if the rose of chastity, mingled with virginal whiteness, gives a purple blush to the cheeks of your soul!

He who searches hearts and reins seeks such beauty in the cheeks of the soul. He seeks that his beloved may be wholly beautiful, because he himself is beautiful in form not only above the children of humankind but even above the countenances of angels. How graceful is the bride’s face! Virginal innocence gives it milky whiteness, and the blush of tender modesty suffuses it. Otherwise whiteness without any blush imitates pallor, and the lily of chastity has no grace if it is not kindled by the torches of love.

Such is your beloved: white and ruddy. The purity of virginal childbirth brings him forth as the lily of the valleys, while the rose-red blood poured out from inestimable charity has dyed him with the purple adornment of martyrs.

When, therefore, you contemplate, love, and experience these things after being brought within, whether the power of love makes you languid or intoxicates and absorbs you, I think you cry out and say: “Lord, it is good for us to be here.” For, brought into the wine-cellar, you are raised up to behold the Bridegroom’s Transfiguration; there you advance—yet, while you advance, you do not know it. Why is this? Because to notice one’s own advances and measure one’s virtues is as close to ruin as it is to pride. For pride, as a certain holy man says, is heavenly by origin, and impure exaltation often takes its beginning from the purity of virtues.

Therefore it is useful, amid great and wonderful things, to be as though ignorant of oneself, so that the more the piety of love raises the mind upward [Col. 0662D], the more, through that same love, it fails away from every swelling and melts down to the lowest places of humility. Thus it was that Peter, seeing marvelous things at the Transfiguration, was raised by marvelous dispensation to such a height that he did not know what he was saying. What, then, is the melting of the heart from the greatness of love except humility, which healthfully teaches a person to fail away from self when charity either advances that person in virtues or keeps them exalted upon the summit of perfection? Tears of devotion outwardly testify to this melting of humility at the fire of holy love.

Moreover, even in pure flesh there is made a watered garden, where the loveliness of virginity blossoms all the more unfadingly as the inward sprinkling of divine dew waters it more fittingly. [Col. 0663A] O necessary virtue of humility, which, by holding the middle in this way, moderates everything: modesty chastens virginal whiteness lest it grow unattractively pale; and it carefully provides for charity lest, forgetting reverence through security, it become insolent through pride! With these flowers the bed of conscience must be adorned; with these flowers the soul must be supported when it is prepared to ascend the mountain where the beloved is transfigured.

For the soul itself must be transfigured and put off the alien form of earthly desire, if it is to be fit to behold the hidden brightness of the transfigured Bridegroom. Thus Christ, ascending the mountain where he was to be transfigured, took with him only three disciples: Peter, James, and John. In Peter note the steadfastness of perfect love, for Peter loved more than the others and drew his name from the firm rock because of the constancy of his unfeigned faith. James, whose name is interpreted “wrestler” or “supplanter,” signifies humility, which both supplants vices through innocence and wrestles against adversities through patience. John expresses integrity of the flesh, which merits this privilege: to be led up to the secret of incorruptible truth.

If you have plucked these flowers from the garden of delight, delighted the Bridegroom’s grace with their marvelous fragrances, called back the absent one, held the present one firmly, and said: “I held him and will not let him go” (Song 3), and, “My beloved is mine and I am his” (Song 1), then, transfigured and conformed to him in his likeness, you must take every care that your countenance is no longer changed into different forms [Col. 0663C]. For your Bridegroom loves unity and wholeness; ever remaining one and the same, he regards every variation with suspicion, because nearly every variation is a friend to changeability, changeability to vanity, and vanity to falsehood—which the truth of your Bridegroom detests. Thus you will be fit to see how his face shines like the sun, to behold his garments like snow, and to be overshadowed by a bright cloud.

Further, if you are not ignorant of yourself—unlike Peter, who did not know what he was saying—you know and have the means to make three tabernacles: one for your Bridegroom, one for Moses, and one for Elijah. For what is your Bridegroom but eternal love? Let him feed and rest and have his tabernacle at noon—that is, in the fervor of your charity. Moses, bearer and zealous guardian of the divine Law, signifies knowledge or zeal for regular discipline; his tabernacle is in a basket of rushes, that is, in the tractable conscience of a humble heart without the knot of iniquity. Elijah, who is believed to have been chaste in body and whose name, according to some, derives from *Helios*, “sun,” signifies truth or the manifestness of works of light, which have, as it were, their tabernacle in the candlestick of the excellence of virginity.

The vision of splendor in the Bridegroom’s face is the reward and recompense of charity meanwhile languishing in suspense from deferred desire. The splendor and brightness of the snow-white garment is the glory of humility, meanwhile rejoicing in lowliness and extremity. The overshadowing of the bright cloud is both protection here and, hereafter, the complete liberation of virginity. [Col. 0664A] Those received within this cloud “neither marry nor are given in marriage.” Then Agnes, leaning upon her beloved, will follow the Lamb wherever he goes; and, led along his paths of eternity, she will say securely, out of love’s eternity: “Lord, it is good for us to be here.”

When you arrive there and it is well with you, take care not to forget my unhappiness. When you have clasped the Bridegroom in a more tender embrace, plead with him the cause of his servant, that he may be brought from the vestibule of fear into the bridal chamber of love. Do not begrudge the servant his possible adoption at least as a son, since the bride’s privilege is sufficient for you—to the praise and glory of the Bridegroom of the Church, to whom be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

## Letter XXIII. To N., His Friend

He treats of hatred of vices, love of virtue, and contempt for vanity.

[Col. 0664B]

To his beloved N.: Brother Adam, however unworthy, abbot of Perseigne, wishes that he may be distinguished by the pursuits of true philosophy.

Love commands that I join conversation with a friend concerning hatred of vices, love of virtue, and contempt for worldly vanity. I call you friend, dearest son, not because I deserve to be loved by you, but because I gather you into that bosom of charity whose breadth passes over no one. Indeed, the breadth of the world does not surpass the expanse of charity. The gathering of friends does not exclude from charity’s bosom even the love of enemies. Nothing, then, is happier than charity: it has hatred toward vices, love toward human beings, passage toward angels, and desire for eternal things.

This charity unites those at variance, binds together those divided, corrects what is perverse, loves good things, and preserves whatever is best. It has bound you to me in spirit, though you are little known to me by face, separated by places, different in manner of life, and distinct in profession. For you live in the world and serve in the world; I, bidding farewell to worldly affairs, have resolved to serve Christ in the enclosure of the cloister. I speak from my knowledge of your mind. For I think that you love the world, since I see you entangled in secular business and pursuing the things of the world with excessive zeal. For where a person’s treasure is, there also is the heart.

What wonder, then, if you slip, when by clinging to slipping things you are drawn downward with the same force of desire by which the vain appearance of things hurls down its lovers? To love the things that are of the world is certainly to despise heavenly things; it is to become an enemy of eternal things. The seeker of present things is exiled from inward goods, and one who does not know how to prefer the Creator himself to his work is unworthy of the Creator’s love. I say “prefer” not merely by the judgment of reason but by love’s choice. This love makes the mind blessed when it loves that of which it cannot be deprived unwillingly; for, since nothing is freer than the human will, it alone cannot admit loss so long as it wishes to possess that by enjoying which it is made blessed.

It is therefore necessary to desire and seek that good with which, once the mind has been endowed, it cannot be deprived except by its own will. And if the blessed mind steadfastly retains this endowment of good, then, when the corruption of its flesh has been conquered and [Col. 0665A] every resistance lulled to rest, it will pass into eternal freedom. O happy passage, from which it is neither pleasing nor permitted to turn back! O good possession of eternity, purchased only at the price of transitory tribulation! O noble pursuit of blessed philosophy, in which the mind, yearning for the things above, disdains the whole body, and from the slavery of the flesh which it subdues obtains true freedom for flesh and soul alike! For what is more servile than mortal flesh? Yet, in an inverted order, we compel the noble spirit of the freer nature to serve in common subjection. Thus among the children of this world the nobility of human reason is held captive, so that, in a strange manner, reason renders irrational service to the flesh and is cunning in appropriating its own ministry to the flesh’s service. For the children [Col. 0665B] of this world are more prudent in their generation than the children of light, because reason, in worldly persons, being subjected to sensuality against reason, is certainly more shrewd for evil than it is for good in spiritual persons, in whom it is rightly set above their flesh. Why, then, do you misuse reason and efface and erase the image of the Creator—which is reason alone—by an irrational love of fleshly things? Like surely seeks like, and this rule scarcely fails in any class of things, since all things turn toward participation in and likeness to their own kind. How, then, has the Creator alone lost in man His own likeness, when the deformity of injustice makes man so unlike Him? Indeed, I should call that man unjust who, created for eternal things, lingers by desire [Col. 0665C] among temporal things, fixes his heart upon things that slip away, and does not instead regard it as a burden that he is held back from the true light, as if by a wall, through the intervening burden of the flesh. But if you consider the obstructing burden of this wall, wisdom would counsel not to thicken the mud but to tear it down; not to increase it but to lessen it. Certainly the lover of eternal things refuses to prop up the troublesome wall of the flesh if he cannot demolish it. He heaps no honours upon it, seeks no revenues for it, crams it with no food; rather, he takes care to grant it more temperately what necessity requires. How far this manner of philosophizing is from the lovers of the world, whose god is their belly, who suppose gain to be godliness, and who count it a loss not to sin. These are they for whom virtue is a burden and vice an honour; who, abhorring the poverty [Col. 0665D] of Jesus and the disgrace of the cross, desire to flourish in the world through the ministry of holiness. Would that you, dearest son, were willing to stand far from these people and to hold to the paths of the saints, which you do not hesitate to begin from the cross! For upon the chair of the cross our Master instructed us in our philosophy; and whoever refuses to follow His teaching can by no means attain what was promised. My soul, my love, invites you to this philosophy. Read, then, read through, and reread often this letter of love. Although its words do not savour of the rhetorician, yet may they present to the palate of your heart the taste of sincere affection. Farewell, dearest one; and though you do not perform all that you read, I nevertheless wish you to live more rightly than you have lived. Farewell.

## LETTER XXIV. TO MASTER PHIDEBALON

Against the judges and lawyers of the world.

[Col. 0666A]

To his beloved master in Christ, PHIDEBALON: brother ADAM, unworthy servant of the poor of Persenia, wishes that he may prefer in deed and truth the spotless law of the Lord to the laws of Justinian.

Although it is plainly possible to recognize from your letters, dearest son, your good will toward us, yet the soundness of that will is proved more clearly and effectively by the testimony of deeds. I confess that the seedbed of my friendship—of which, through affection and by God’s granting of remembrance, an abundant harvest now springs up—did not take its beginning from me, but rather from you. By the free anticipation of your generosity, while you were [Col. 0666B] first unknown to me and afterwards ever more frequently known through your deserts, you cheerfully offered yourself for diligent service. Benefits which outstrip the merits of their recipients are deservedly judged more welcome because they are not gained by merit; and certainly those that proceed from unmerited affection ought to be repaid with a more fruitful effect.

I mean those benefits by which you have shown yourself ready and cheerful toward me in greetings, affable in conversation, friendly in business, helpful in giving advice, devout in showing reverence, and humane in service whenever I have been received in your lodging. As I do not doubt that all these things flowed from the abundance of your heart, so I ought not to nullify them by the vice of ingratitude. From them [Col. 0666C] your concern may plainly understand that I cannot but love you, because you are mine; and would that no distance of places or diversity of pursuits might in any way snatch you from me! For it commonly proves difficult for the bond of love to remain unbroken for long among people whom manner of life separates, intention divides, place sunders, activity makes unlike, a dissimilar purpose alters, and disagreement in study does not permit to cleave together.

For you, for the friendship of the world, do not reckon heavenly enmities; holding mud, longing for mire, devoted to fleshly, changing, and transient things, you have clung to them with an immovable mind and steadfast desire. My purpose is plainly otherwise, and my intention far different: by God’s inspiration, despising all visible things, I rejoice in the blessed and sole expectation of things to come. There shines the brightness [Col. 0666D] of true knowledge, which no darkness of doubt or ignorance confuses. There is the sweetness of full wisdom, which no falsehood or bitterness causes to lose its savour. There the pleasant temperateness of everlasting spring pours into us an unfailing fullness of more secure joy. To this divine law’s knowledge leads; this it bestows—a law which converts souls, rather than overturning them. The Cistercian colony taught me the knowledge of this law, where Christ, teacher and giver of righteousness, instructs His followers in the knowledge of heavenly law.

But you, because you are of the earth, think otherwise; and your pursuit of worldly wisdom shows that you do not yet taste this great wisdom. Yet perhaps you count this boastfulness and accuse me of presumption because I seem, contrary to custom, to praise myself and do not hesitate to rebuke you. Love, I admit, commands me to speak thus; and if you wish to obtain the pardon you request, you too will grant pardon to one speaking thus. True love is as free from flattery as from fear: just as it does not know how to stroke and cajole, so neither does it know how to spare; rather, it assails a friend all the more vehemently, the more confidently it does so.

Therefore, whoever you are and however you stand, for my part I shall not cease to love you, striving as far as I can that Christ may be the cause of my love. O if you would pour oil upon my flame, and the increase of my affection would depend upon your progress! O if you would apply yourself to strength of soul and, bidding farewell to worldly vanity, put behind you things that deserve contempt! O if you possessed reason, illumined by the rays of faith, which by the rectitude of judgment would reject everything that does injury to law! For it is distorted, and swerves from the rule of law and equity, that men should become judges of men and that almost all should seem to have conspired against justice. They despoil their Author, the Judge of the ages, of His right; and, with rash presumption, they strive to drive out the justice of Him whose judgment they cannot escape. Thus they subject body to uncleanness and mind to pride, and wretchedly serve under the tyranny of vices—though under the king of virtues they might happily reign.

You see now that chastity is in exile, humility has gone abroad, justice has withdrawn, faith has fled, charity has grown cold; and, while the flood of iniquity everywhere overflows, truth has withdrawn within the household walls of heaven. Our times are indeed to be lamented, and the people of this generation ought to be blotted out: although [Col. 0667C] almost all either seek or possess knowledge of law, they make light of obedience to law. The Judge of the ages suffers injustice everywhere, and among the lawyers you will find no one who now offers himself as His advocate in heaven. If everyone pays, even unjust causes find many advocates; Christ alone, though He is the giver of all things and His cause is most just, is not thought worthy to have anyone. Everywhere His bride is oppressed; He Himself is blasphemed by all; the poor, orphans, and widows have become the prey of the rich. Neither knowledge of our law nor the discipline of statutes comes to their aid: knowledge that puffs up serves gain alone, and windy loquacity seeks only the advantage of money or honour.

We see ecclesiastical dignities and goods pass to lawyers, and, strangely enough, while they are ashamed to follow the Crucified One, they do not fear to usurp the Crucified One’s patrimony. It is altogether detestable abuse that the more learned they prove in law, the more ready they are found to violate law. They are powerful in verbal quibbles and skilled at overturning judgment: either to justify the impious for bribes or to convict an innocent person of injustice. Would that you, dearest one, might seek knowledge of law for the sake of observing law, so that, having lived rightly with respect to the deprivation of law, you might be ashamed to offend against the rules of heavenly law. This will be oil for [Col. 0668A] my stream: to bring to my love news of progress toward a more upright life, and to make joy for me, whose purpose is to rejoice only in the salvation of souls.

Would that you might be eager to pursue virtue of soul, which readily produces contempt for the world. For virtue so trains the mind of its possessor that it counts honours burdens, is indignant at dignities, and recommends moderation, which is akin to holy poverty. The restraint of virtue is especially vigorous in this: that it compels the flesh to renounce pleasures and humbly to serve the spirit. Would that my condition and that of the poor who serve with me may be occupied with life-giving pursuits, so that you too may rejoice when you hear of it, since you asked after this matter. We rejoice daily, son, though wearied by great pressures; and, as worldly changeableness has it, we are subject to much peril. We long indeed to cross the sea, but upon this sea of uncertainty a daily storm arises; and unless merciful Jesus stretches forth the hand of gracious rescue, we shall scarcely be able to swim to harbour. Behold, this is the greatest knowledge; and I have already said above that these visible things are contemptible to us, because they entail danger and toil. Yet we trust that He who gave us our calling will not deny perseverance in the purpose of our warfare.

You requested the support of our prayers, and you also devoutly and humbly asked for our reply. Your request has obtained its effect in both respects—except that perhaps my letter will not be welcome to you. For I am prolix and harsh, both of which commonly offend a reader, unless zeal of charity excuses me with a friend. Farewell.

## LETTER XXV. TO THE VENERATORS OF SAINT MARTIN

He proves that Saint Martin may fittingly be called equal to the apostles.

To all who devoutly venerate the memory of blessed Martin [Note: [Col. 0667D] This letter occurs in the Cluniac Library published under the name of Saint Odo, where Quercetanus observes that the manuscript codices bear the name of Adam, not Odo.], ADAM, least among his venerators, wishes to follow in the footsteps of the same Father.

I hear that many are scandalized because the Church sings and glories that our Martin is equal to the apostles—the praise of Martin resounding almost everywhere throughout the world, especially in those places where his sanctity is honoured more solemnly and devoutly. My purpose, therefore, is to refute Martin’s enemies and pursue his detractors, imploring, of course, the grace of aid from Him from whom Martin deserved to receive that he should be, and be called, equal to the apostles.

For the glory granted to a man by spiritual grace could make him equal to the apostles; and without doubt He made him equal who alone, being incomparable, is supremely exalted without comparison, whose peace exceeds every understanding. As for those things beneath Him, however much the dignity of their nature or the goodness of their Creator may have exalted them, they do not refuse fellowship in equality; and what the authority of the Creator has ordained, the communion of charity does not begrudge.

What, then, could prevent Martin’s being made equal to the apostles? Could it not be done? If it could not, then God’s omnipotence is confined by certain limits. Where, then, is the Scriptural statement that God is called omnipotent? Or perhaps God is omnipotent, but He was unwilling to grant to the perfect followers of the apostles the privilege of grace that He gave to the apostles? But if—since it is true—[Col. 0669A] the Omnipotent One could bring it about that those who had maintained evangelical perfection by living well should obtain equality of glory as well, what prevents Martin from being endowed with the exalted rank of the apostles? Was it because he did not receive sufficient grace to merit it? Or did he receive it, but the apostles’ envy—an impious thing to say—denied him fellowship in their glory? Who would dare even think this?

Perhaps someone says that Martin is not equal to the apostles in glory because he was inferior to them in holiness. From what do you prove this, whoever you are who say it? Do you draw your argument from the fact that the apostles were chosen earlier, called by the Lord while He was present in the flesh, and called apostles by Him in the emphatic sense? If Martin is inferior to them for this reason, because he had none of these things, then Paul too is inferior: he came to faith later, did not see the Lord in mortal flesh, and did not deserve to be honoured by Him with the conferral of the apostolic name, as the others were, of whom it is written that “he named them apostles” (Luke 6).

But if you prefer the apostles because they deserved to see the Lord present in the flesh before He suffered, and after the resurrection appearing and speaking to them—a privilege granted also to many others, since, as the apostle Paul testifies, He was seen by more than five hundred brethren—then Martin certainly attained the like privilege as well. For of no one else do we read that, before he had been reborn, he deserved to see Christ the Lord. O glorious cloak of our catechumen, in which Christ did not judge it inglorious to be clothed [edition: “judged it glory”]; yet more glorious by far was the faith of the reborn man, who denied Christ nothing that He asked!

If anyone contends about miracles and wishes to prefer the apostles in powers, the whole world cries out in testimony to Martin that he performed more signs—or rather, that Christ performed more signs in him—than any authentic writing ever attests concerning anyone else. Finally, if someone objects that the sick were laid in Peter’s shadow and were healed, we likewise read that miracles were frequently performed through the straw upon which Martin had lain. Certainly it is greater for lowly straw, in Martin’s absence, to work a miracle than for Peter’s shadow, since without Peter’s presence the shadow could not give relief to the sick. Yet without Christ neither Peter present nor Martin absent could do anything mighty.

These miracles are indeed wonderful and worthy of every admiration: Peter’s shadow, with Peter present, or the straw on which Martin had lain, in Martin’s absence, working marvels. But we find miracles far more wonderful, and pre-eminent in Martin alone. It sometimes happened that, when he was hastening to visit a sick person, before he had completed half the journey, the sick person sensed the power of his approach and came out [Col. 0670A] to meet the one who was coming, restored to health. For the sufferer’s recovery it would have been enough not merely that Martin should arrive, but that he should, as it were, begin the journey—begin to come. Severus Sulpicius attests this concerning his uncle Evantius.

Perhaps someone places before this, in the apostles, the prerogative of martyrdom. But Martin was not a martyr through the shedding of blood—except that his whole life was martyrdom. Certainly will and the necessity of the times made the apostles martyrs; but why, properly speaking [edition: “because of this”], should Martin lose the glory, when, although the necessity of the time did not offer him the persecutor’s sword, the will to suffer was not absent from his heart? He does not lack the glory of martyrdom who is known to have been a martyr by desire. Otherwise, the glory of martyrdom is denied to the apostle John because suffering did not wrench his life away, though Truth testifies that he was to drink His cup. Martin undoubtedly drank this cup of suffering: voluntarily mortifying himself through countless crosses of incredible abstinence, he breathed out his spirit in ashes and haircloth, a most unconquered witness of Jesus.

If, then, Martin was a martyr, so far as lay in him, in the sight of Him who judges intentions, shall the most holy efficacy of his will not have the weight of the deed—especially since all human merit consists in good will? For a person’s works are not that person’s merits but signs of merits; although, even if we gather perfection from works, no one is preferred to Martin. If perhaps anyone judges Martin inferior [Col. 0670C] to the apostles because they were princes of peoples, teachers of the world, foundations and founders of the Church, and the first instructors of the faithful—as those who hold the dignity of a master’s chair in Christ’s school—then reason does not allow pupils to be equated with masters, especially when the Master and Lord of all says: “The disciple is not above the master, nor the servant above his lord” (Luke 6).

What then? Because the authority of the highest Master forbids a disciple to be preferred to a master, does it therefore deny that he can be made equal? Consider what follows: “It is enough for the disciple,” He says, “that he be like his master” (ibid.). Behold, equality with the master is not denied to disciples, if the disciple emulates the master’s perfection through zeal for imitation. Therefore, since Martin was the perfect disciple of the disciples, the apostles; apostolic in sacerdotal rank; distinguished by apostolic acts; and in the working of signs almost more than an apostle—what prevents him from obtaining equality of glory, when likeness in every aspect of life commends him?

What then? In affirming these things concerning Martin, do we detract from apostolic exaltation? Far from it! Rather, so far as we can, we exalt the apostles when we do not deny that Martin’s perfection was formed in imitation of them. Nevertheless, even if Martin’s glory is not unlike theirs because his life was not unlike theirs, apostolic exaltation still surpasses in one respect: it precedes as cause precedes effect, matter that which is made from matter, and a principle those things that begin to have their being from it. Thus apostolic [Col. 0671A] doctrine is the cause, material, and principle of the discipline of faith and religion in the Fathers; in this respect it ought and can be preferred to all others, yet it does not therefore surpass all in merits or glory.

For how are those not equal to the apostles who lead a life like the apostles’, perform equal miracles, will judge alike, reign alike, and alike receive one denarius for one labour in the one vineyard? This alone is the difference: in the distribution of the denarius, the householder shows no partiality; the last become first and the first last; and among those receiving it there is neither envy nor boasting of merits. How then do you begrudge Martin’s being equal to the apostles, when the dispenser’s justice is so great and the recipients’ charity so great that he who was last in labour is found first in receiving the denarius? “The last shall be first, and the first last. Is your eye evil?” (Matthew 19), because the dispenser of the reward is good, because it is the good pleasure of the rewarder that, though all are made equal by receiving the same denarius, the last should nevertheless be rewarded before the first.

What inequality can there be among those to whom the same and equal denarius is distributed? Certainly, although there is unequal brightness among the elect, because star differs from star in brightness, yet in this unequal brightness there is equal joy, when God is all in all. And if all the elect, however much they differ in merit, have this equality—that for all there is one and the same joy in the consummation of charity, in the vision of the Creator, and in the eternity of immortality—what glory, do you suppose, did Martin obtain beyond the others, he whom apostolic perfection, prerogative of virtues, and power of signs, as he followed the apostles’ footsteps, distinguished above the rest?

If the matters I have pursued do not suffice as an assertion concerning his character, let something further be set forth to show plainly that Martin was not unequal to apostolic perfection. Certainly the Holy Spirit was given to the apostles and to imitators of the apostles; but He has never, or only rarely, descended upon any saint in the manner in which He came upon the apostles. Yet He who visibly appeared over the apostles in fire also showed Himself, in visible form and power, in a globe of fire above Martin’s head while Martin was offering the sacraments. And although He did not grant Martin to speak in diverse tongues, because there was no need, He nevertheless so kindled him with the singular flame of divine love that, while living in the body, he was wholly fiery through the charity of his heart; and after he departed from the body he visibly appeared wholly fiery on several occasions.

Thus He appeared in fire to Trojanus, bishop of Sacton; and at the funeral rites of Pelagia, mother of Abbot Aredius, a fiery globe came from heaven and illuminated the whole church, while demoniacs cried out that Martin had arrived for the dead woman’s funeral. He appeared in like manner to Gregory of Tours as he was carrying Martin’s relics into the New Basilica. A certain man named Brachio also, upon entering the oratory, was accustomed repeatedly to see a fiery globe moving through the upper part [Col. 0672A] of the church. Therefore it is not heretical to confess that an apostolic man is in every respect raised to fellowship in apostolic equality.

Let him, then, who through ignorance detracts from Martin’s merits look, read, and learn that the Lord said not only of apostles but also of imitators of the apostles: “Father, I will that where I am, there also may be my minister” (John 12). What is “where I am” except “such as I am”? As if He said: “I will that my ministers may attain by grace to likeness [edition: “equality”] of the glory which I possess by nature.” Hence it is written: “When he shall appear, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3). What then? Are the apostles alone ministers of Christ? Is not Martin also Christ’s minister, and indeed the most perfect among the perfect? If, then, Christ’s ministers are like Christ in glory, and thereby equal to Him, how can equality among Christ’s ministers be impossible?

And if anyone, through envy of Martin, takes away his titles, let that person be corrected. Otherwise Martin’s God, who works wonders in Martin, has power to avenge His saint and impose an end upon rash assertion—especially since for you a pious doubt about hidden matters is better than contentious dispute about uncertain ones. Therefore henceforth venerate Martin, whom until now you have disparaged either through ignorance or envy; and do not deny that he is equal to the apostles when you do not doubt that he is like Christ in glory, provided that you think true the saying: “We shall be like him, because [Col. 0672C] we shall see him as he is” (ibid.).

Here there is need of Martin’s intercession: that he, who by living apostolically, imitating Christ, and Christ’s gift, deserved to be like Christ and thereby not unequal to the apostles, may obtain pardon for us who still live in the region of unlikeness, restore us to grace, and present us to the glory which he possesses with Christ—Christ who lives and reigns unto ages of ages. Amen.

## LETTER XXVI. TO R., ABBOT OF VERNUSIA

[Note: [Col. 0671] Vernusia: a monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine in the diocese of Bourges.]

He instructs him concerning repentance, or confession.

To his lord and venerable friend R., abbot of Vernusia, brother ADAM, least of all monks, wishes that he may flourish at Vernusia in flowers which no flame of vice may wither.

[Col. 0672D] You have often asked me, most loving one, to write something to you concerning repentance, and I confess that I promised to do so. But when I weighed my strength and measured my ability, I began to repent of my obligation and of the burden I had undertaken, which I could not carry. For I preferred to suffer shame in my inadequacy rather than, endangered beneath an imposed burden, rashly incur the peril of presumption. Yet see: you oppose my purpose with impunity, resist my quiet, and compel me to exceed my measure. When nature has no wealth, you hope for a flood from a slender vein. The matter you request is indeed very useful and necessary, greater than suits my efforts, and too difficult and exceedingly arduous for my smallness. Nevertheless, with Christ’s help sought in prayer and generously given, I shall venture to speak what I do not know and begin to teach what I have not learned, trusting that obedience’s humility, your charity, and God’s abundant goodness will supply the strength that ignorance denies.

As the Creator of the universe is one Lord of all, so He willed that there should be one service for all. Therefore, when the eye of human reason had been dimmed by the blearedness of sin, and visible creation no longer sufficed, He willed through the substance of flesh to join the homeland of spirits to the homeland of bodies.
