That He might order both into one commonwealth—being Governor and Lord of this commonwealth—He so harmonized the heavenly with the lowly that He made the riches of the higher homeland common to earthly beings and relieved the poverty of the lower homeland from the abundance of the higher.

Therefore the imperial Majesty, descending from the heights of the heavenly court to the lower parts of His own house, sitting in assumed flesh and taking the place of human habitation as His tribunal, proposes and causes three edicts to be proposed.

The first edict is wisdom; the second is repentance; the third is glory. He proposed the first by assuming humanity; the second by preaching among human beings; the third by justifying human beings. The edict of wisdom sounded from the cloud of flesh; the edict of repentance thundered from the bowels of mercy; the breadth of divine charity promulgates the edict of glory. Let us now go out into the streets of Scripture, if perhaps we may hear heralds there [Col. 0673C] proclaiming these edicts. The edict of wisdom is proposed when Christ, the power of God and wisdom of God, is announced to Mary by an angel. The edict of repentance is promulgated when Truth, reproving the malice of the lying world, exhorts humankind to repentance: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matthew 3). Once enlightened through wisdom and amended through repentance, the edict of manifold glory is repeatedly impressed when, through the working of miracles, the resurrection of the body, and the glorious ascension, the glory of God is most plainly declared.

Wisdom had first to come, both to make the wisdom of the world foolish and to reveal its own darkness to the human mind. Repentance follows it immediately. For when the type of puffed-up wisdom is cast out and the mind beholds itself in the light of divine wisdom, it is then surely ashamed of the practice of its own ugliness: having measured itself wrongly before, it had falsely claimed beauty for itself. From this point it dislikes itself, though at first it perversely pleased itself, and considers eradicating the ugliness which offends the noble eyes of the enlightened heart. This displeasure is repentance; to repent is to be corrected; to be corrected is to be justified; to be justified is to be restored to glory. Wisdom therefore shows a person his sickness; repentance heals the sickness once shown; glory preserves in salvation the person healed and saved.

The light of wisdom illuminating the heart is imitation of Christ: when, in Christ’s imitation as in a mirror, we see the wound of our life, we discover what in us is blameworthy [Col. 0674A] and what deserves correction. Now, therefore, because we have heard the first edict of our King, have run in faith to the wisdom of God thundering in Christ, and have learned from His own teaching how many evils our life suffers, what remains except to take up repentance’s remedy, that our sickness may be healed? Since we are speaking to those who have suffered shipwreck, let us discuss, insofar as God grants, what the harbour of repentance is, where it is, and how it may be found.

Repentance is grief of soul in one who knows himself, who, with a purpose of amendment, mourns and pursues whatever he knows in himself to displease God. No one can grieve, surely, unless through true self-knowledge that person has first become contemptible to himself. One cannot become contemptible to oneself unless one knows oneself; one cannot know oneself unless one has come to the light; one will not come to the light unless one has followed, both in faith and imitation, the wisdom of God—that is, Christ, the mirror of human life. Nor can one follow Him unless the Redeemer’s grace has first gone before free will.

Thus the regard of grace generates humility in the heart, and humility grief. Humility is the virtue by which a person, through the truest knowledge of himself, becomes contemptible to himself. Pride produces its contrary: through it a person, raised above himself and loving his own excellence in a disordered way, falsely represents himself as greater than he is. The grief of heart by which one repents of having sinned punishes in a person whatever it finds distorted from the line of truth. Carrying in its hand an illuminating ray, kindled by the regard of merciful grace, it runs through every corner of the heart as a diligent pursuer of evil. It bears with it not only the ray of knowledge but also the goad of compunction and the hammer of contrition.

Indeed, repentance’s grief, acting like a physician around the soul’s wounds, first pricks the heart, then crushes it, and thirdly anoints it. In pricking it sharpens; in crushing it strikes with a hammer; in anointing it applies a plaster. It first produces compunction, secondly contrition, thirdly devotion. Let us see by what goads the piercing, or compunction, of the heart is now effected. Repentance surely pricks the heart with a threefold sting, so that it may be called not simply “pierced” but “pierced on every side” (*compunctum*). The first is shame arising from the considered ugliness of the deed; the second is anxiety produced by the manifold offence against [Col. 0674D] the Creator; the third is dread of infernal punishment. Thus one is ashamed because one acted shamefully; one grieves anxiously because by living wickedly one has embittered God’s kindness; and, because God is the avenger of evils, one is intensely afraid. Do you think blood will be drawn unless so many goads are driven deeply into the heart? Understand the blood of the pierced heart as tears appearing in the eyes. These tears are winged: having in themselves nothing of fleshly weight, by the marvelous workmanship of divine wisdom they immediately rise from the heart to the eyes, and from the eyes fly to heaven.

Would you see that they fly to heaven? Consider what the King of the ages says: “There is joy,” he says, “among the angels of God over one sinner doing penance” (Luke 15). How impetuous is the water bursting forth from the abyss of the heart [Col. 0675A]! In one and the same moment it washes the soul, moistens the eyes, strikes heaven, gladdens the angels, and despoils hell; for, just as the flame of divine love is kindled through tears of compunction, so the flames of hell are extinguished. Thus the rush of this stream gladdens the city of God, while the blessed citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem delight in the tears of penitents. So impetuous, I say, is the torrent of compunction that it moves God, removes the soul’s filth, and moves the tongue to the heart’s self-accusation, the reproach of sin, and oral confession in the presence of the priest. Certainly these tears are both bitter and sweet, and thereby effective: bitter insofar as the violence of intense pain wrings them out; sweet insofar as pardon is hoped for from them. Thus, indeed, the poison deriving from pleasure must be healed by the antidote of bitterness [Col. 0675B].

You have seen what the act of compunction is; now see the hammer of contrition. Both are fear, but from different perspectives. Initial fear is a needle, but perfect fear is a hammer. The needle of initial fear, by pricking, opens the heart to health and releases the pus of its mad swelling; but the hammer of contrition, by making the heart wholly dead to the world through its resolve not to sin, also kills the world’s love within the heart. Initial fear therefore produces in the heart hatred of evil and, in part, love of good. Perfect fear causes one entirely to despise the world and to follow Christ with all one’s desire.

There are four things in which perfect love consists: hatred of sin, contempt for the world, contempt for oneself, and love of God alone [Col. 0675C]. For initial fear it is enough to hate sin and love good; but to despise the world and deny oneself belongs only to that heart whose every grossness has been ground down by the hammer of perfect fear, so that it can truly say: “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. 1). And again: “A contrite and humbled heart, O God, thou wilt not despise” (Ps. 50); for it is crushed, broken into pieces, and reduced to dust.

Then the heart is reduced to dust by the hammer of contrition when, having utterly laid aside its swelling pride, a person truly judges and confesses himself to be mud. It is dust, yet not dust which the wind casts away from the face of the earth. It is dust into which Jesus spits, and which the saliva of saving wisdom moistens. This dust is drenched from heaven with the rain of devotion [Col. 0675D], lest it be stirred at all by the wind of the devilish whirlwind. For the tears of devotion are from heaven, because they are not drawn from the well of swelling pride but descend from the cloud of love. Compunction is the well of fear; devotion is the cloud of love. Devotion is a cloud because it rains and gives shade: it rains the upper watering; it makes shade so that heat may not burn. The upper watering consists in tears which the devout mind pours forth from the greatness of love. Heat is the concupiscence of the flesh.

Therefore, after the mind has been pierced by the needle of initial fear, and afterwards crushed by the hammer of perfect fear, and thirdly watered by the showers of the upper watering, then, drinking the rain that comes upon it, it produces suitable vegetation. What is this? Immediately truth springs up from the soil of the heart, made fruitful because it has been rained upon by devotion [Col. 0676A]. Behold the finest fruit from good soil. This fruit of truth is a truthful confession of sin. Confession is a voluntary and truthful accusation of the soul and an orderly manifestation of sins before a priest: voluntary, not wrung out by tortures; orderly, so that it is made to the person to whom it ought to be made, and concerning the things concerning which it ought to be made.

You must confess only to one who has received authority over you in such matters, or to one whom he himself has permitted. You must confess your own sins, not another’s, and with the same simplicity with which you remember having committed them: adding nothing through false humility and withholding nothing through deceptive self-justification or disordered shame. Confession must be made fearfully, not irreverently; humbly, not proudly; simply, not boastfully; modestly, not shamelessly; privately, not publicly; only to your priest [Col. 0676B], not to anyone whatsoever; before God, not before human beings. Therefore it is written of certain persons: “They proclaimed their sin as Sodom did; they did not hide it” (Isa. 3).

It should be noted that there are three kinds of confessors. Some confess while having no resolve to cease from sins. Others confess with a purpose of amendment, but when the time of temptation arrives do not persist at all. The third confessors are those who propose to refrain from sins and, through the aid of grace, bring their purpose to its end.

Among those without a purpose of amendment, some love their own iniquity so much that they do not wish to cease from sin even if they could. Others indeed would wish to abandon iniquity, but through the habit of sin [Col. 0676C] are held, as if against their will, in the pleasure of sin. The former are wretched; the latter pitiable. The former are dead Lazaruses, marked by death and burial; the latter are living persons buried alive: although unwillingly they bear the stone of evil habit, nevertheless they live under the stone through their desire for liberation. The former are most difficult to free, because they rage in their tombs. To rage in tombs is to be held in the depths of mortal sin and nevertheless to scorn resurrection.

The latter are more easily and more often recalled: although the binding chain of accustomed pleasure powerfully drags them to destruction, and the frailty of nature, more prone to evil, drives them toward death, they nevertheless often return to their hearts. They often look behind them, in the hope that they may somehow deserve the regard of the grace of him who brings forth the bound in his strength [Col. 0676D]. Hence, even while given over to their sins, they often do many good things: they devote themselves to works of mercy, feed the hungry, clothe the naked, receive guests, and perform offices of humanity for the needy. By both prayers and deeds they implore God that, through the divine inspiration and change wrought by the right hand of the Most High, they may at last, converted through true penance, abandon those sins which they love too much, to which they have adhered against their conscience in carnal pleasure, by which they draw themselves toward death, and which they cannot abandon by themselves.

To these it must be said that “the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. 11), and that the overcoming of evil habit requires the utmost violence [Col. 0677A]. For those who are willing, with God’s help, to use force against seductions that wickedly flatter them may someday, through God’s grace, rise from the depths of iniquity to the remedy of penance and return to the grace of the Father of mercies, who does not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should be converted and live. Otherwise, if—God forbid!—the hour of death finds them rotting in their own dung, both for them and on their account grief is certainly called for; for, leaving this place wickedly, they will find evils, and those whom God’s mercy waited longer to bring to penance will, if unconverted, be condemned more harshly by divine severity.

They must place no confidence whatever in the good works which they perform while living amid their very sins. For though no good goes unrewarded, not every good deed [Col. 0677B] merits salvation. Thus, for the good things they did, they either received temporal recompense from God during their life, or, if those works are reserved after death, they will not indeed be rewards leading to salvation, but to some slight mitigation of eternal punishment. Woe to those who, in their lifetime, received their reward for the good work they did! Many received it either in bodily health, in the gift of literary learning, in riches, or in any other successes of earthly and transitory happiness. Though these are temporal and common to good and evil alike, they are nevertheless granted by the eternal and just God to miserable mortals.

We have said something concerning those whose will is so captive that they endure the tyranny of evil habit, yet ask that their will [Col. 0677C] be changed for the better: that is, they will in a certain sense, since they would wish not to will what they carnally will, yet are unwilling to use force against their carnal will. But what is to be said about those who know themselves to possess an evil will, yet do not wish to will its correction? They love their own darkness so greatly that they not only do not wish to be corrected, but do not even wish to possess the will to wish this. Such a will is diabolical; for the devil not only has no good will, but would not even wish to have one. Yet, although this cannot be corrected in the devil, a human being can be corrected as long as he lives. Let him change his will and he will find grace; indeed, his will itself must be changed through grace.

But although without grace we cannot be good, God is nevertheless not to be blamed if he does not choose to bestow grace. If we are evil, we are blameworthy; if good, not deserving of praise, because we are not good by ourselves [Col. 0677D]. God is to be praised for our good, not blamed for evil; conversely, we are to be blamed for evil, but not praised for good, because the evil that we are is from ourselves, whereas whatever good we can have or do have in us is from God.

Let us now turn our attention to that class of confessors who approach the judgment of the priest with a purpose of amendment but do not persist in that purpose. These are to be praised because they make a good beginning, take up arms against the devil, declare battle against their vices, enter into conflict with the devil, receive within themselves through penance Jesus, formerly a stranger and guest [Col. 0678A], and offer themselves to be healed by heavenly medicine. But they must be strongly rebuked because they so quickly abandon the battle and cast aside their arms. They drive out from themselves with such irreverence the Jesus whom they had received; with the point of renewed iniquity they pierce wounds healed by penance, and can rightly say with the Prophet: “My scars have rotted and become corrupt because of my foolishness” (Ps. 37).

Thus their preceding lamentations have profited them nothing where sins are repeated. Let them return to the fountain of mercy and renew their lamentations of penance, groaning all the more bitterly as they recognize that they have provoked God’s grace more proudly. Henceforth let them regard every place as suspect; let them fear occasions of events and opportune times [Col. 0678B]; let them trust no age; let them by every effort avoid the company, sights, and conversations of persons whom they have been accustomed to have as accomplices in their sin. In food and drink let them keep moderation, devoting themselves more to works of charity than to enlarging earthly resources. In this way their wounds can be healed—wounds inflicted upon them all the more dangerously because they have more often been renewed, to the physician’s provocation, by the poisoned point of pleasure.

We must come to those whose compunction is effective, whose confession is truthful, and whose purpose is persevering. Taking occasion from these, we must speak more fully about confession. A priest holding Christ’s place, when he sees a wounded man by the roadside, ought not to pass by the wretch without mercy [Col. 0678C]; rather, by gesture, voice, service, and feeling, he ought to display and show the merciful compassion of the Samaritan—that is, Jesus—adapt himself, living, to one half-dead, and pour oil into the wounds. Since both are necessary, wounds must first be soothed with oil, so that, when the wounded person has shown himself manageable through experiencing the gentleness of the oil, the astringency of wine may afterwards be poured in more safely.

Therefore the priest, that is, one established as guardian of souls, must receive the penitent kindly, instruct him carefully about the manner of confession, and encourage him with hope of pardon. Behold the oil, through whose gentleness the sinner is drawn, lest he flee terrified by fear or, confused by shame, blush to confess what he has done. He must be carefully taught what confession is, how much it avails, and in what order it must be made [Col. 0678D]; for there must be groaning in the heart, sobbing in the mouth, and weeping in the eyes. In contrition of heart there must be remembrance of every evil; on the lips, accusation; in the purpose of amendment, satisfaction.

The truly penitent person must humbly and truthfully confess to Christ’s vicar—that is, the priest—what he has done, the manner in which he did it, how often he did it, where and when he did it. If the matter concerns lust, he must state with which sex he sinned; what profession, rank, or law the person was of; and through or with what woman he sinned. All these things must be considered by the discerning in true confession. Since there are many kinds of sinning, the kind of sin must be specified, as must whether it was committed through ignorance, weakness, or deliberate intent. The manner of sinning must be stated because even [Col. 0679A] in natural lust, which alone is lawful between spouses, the manner can be abominable.

It should be noted here that one kind of lust is unnatural and therefore wholly unlawful; another is natural yet unlawful; and another natural and lawful. It is shameful indeed to speak of such things, but more shameful to do them. If people did not do things that are shameful and altogether reprehensible, neither would it be necessary for us to rebuke them or, in speaking of shameful matters, to use shameful language. But now it is shameful to leave utterly shameful human acts unreproved, because they are hateful to God; and, because it is pleasing to God, it is therefore a noble human work to correct the ugliness of such acts by whatever rebukes we can.

Unnatural lust, and therefore unlawful, consists in abuse of persons of the same sex or of different sex—even between spouses—using members not granted for this purpose [Col. 0679B]. Natural and unlawful lust consists in fornication. Natural and lawful lust consists in spouses, provided that they observe the customary measure, preserve moderation even in this matter, and render the debt of mutual weakness in the proper place and time. For because something is lawful in some fashion, it does not immediately follow that it is lawful in every fashion, in every place, and at every time. Place must be observed, lest it be consecrated; also the time of pregnancy, the prescribed time of separation, and the times when one must attend to divine observances. If all these are neglected between spouses, the acts are very reprehensible and offend God. What offense, do you suppose, will there be if they are practiced in the abominable lust of fornicators? Thus the deed must be judged according to manner, place, and time. And when these things have been added to acts always unlawful [Col. 0679C], to increase their iniquity, the merciful severity of the spiritual judge ought to be moved more sharply against their perpetrators.

Nevertheless, in every judgment mercy must be put first. Whoever is conscious of his own iniquity ought, in judging his own case, to weigh and measure another’s weakness, lest, while rust is scraped from a fragile vessel by the hand of an insufficiently discerning severity, the fragile vessel be entirely broken. Thus oil must be mixed with wine, and wine in turn with oil, moderately: so that neither the gentleness of oil alone, through the softness of remission, may eliminate fear, nor the harshness of wine, through excessive aggravation of terror, drive away the gentleness of pardon.

The number of offenses must also be investigated, and evil must be punished more strictly in proportion as it has been more frequently repeated [Col. 0679D]. In sexual matters too this discernment is necessary. It must be asked whether the person was a cleric or a layperson; if a layperson, whether free from a wife or not. For if the persons are free under the law of marriage, the sin remains simple fornication; among blood-relatives and relatives by marriage, incest. Rape, however, occurs when robbers of chastity use force; it is worse than adultery among those professing any religious state. If the matter concerns a cleric, it must be asked what order he belongs to, whether deacon or priest; for one sins more or less grievously according as the dignity of sacred ministry binds him more or less to holiness.

Likewise it must be asked concerning the woman whether she was married or not, whether virgin or widow, whether she had made a vow of continence, whether she wore religious dress [Col. 0680A], and finally whether she consented to sin from desire for payment or from love of pleasure alone. To investigate all these belongs to the priest’s discernment. To confess humbly, distinguish carefully, and amend wholesomely belongs to the penitent’s contrition. For it does not suffice to make known to the physician where you hurt or how you are sick, unless you disclose the cause of the disease and the force of the sickness.

Once the wounds have been exposed, it is the wise physician’s task to pour in oil and wine, bind up the remedy, place the patient upon a beast of burden, and lead him to the inn. Oil is God’s mercy, which mitigates the pain of penance through hope of pardon. Wine is the severity of divine justice, which leaves no sins whatever unpunished. We pour in oil when we declare God to be of such mercy that, by his justice, the evils committed must be punished [Col. 0680B]. In this lies the oil: that the truly penitent person is not eternally condemned. Understand in this the wine: that the iniquity committed must necessarily be punished, either here temporally or heavily after death. For it is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God. It is better that you yourself punish your evils while you live than reserve them after death for divine vengeance. If you are willing to punish them, he himself will spare you in mercy; for he will not judge twice for the same thing. If you wish to spare your evils, he himself will punish more strictly in justice, because God is not a lover of evils but their avenger.

After the pouring in of oil and wine, the wounds are bound: medicines are then bound around them when a purpose of better life is undertaken. The beast of burden upon which the patient is raised is the assistance of grace [Col. 0680C], by which he is protected through the various stages of progress. The inn into which he is placed is the useful remembrance of one’s own humility, which does not allow the mind to forget its former felicity.

Henceforth the priest must use the keys of his ministry, so that, when he sees someone divinely brought out of the pit of filth, he may hasten to open for him the treasures of salvation. These keys are two: the knowledge of judging and the power of binding and loosing. These are the keys of the kingdom of heaven, bestowed on Peter and on every priest. The spiritual judge must therefore listen carefully, examine prudently, and act subtly, so that, insofar as possible, he may know the mind and purpose of the confessor. Groaning is certainly an interpreter of contrition [Col. 0680D]; the shame of a subdued and afflicted expression, the witness of a spontaneous promise, and humble submission to every satisfaction are certain signs of one truly penitent.

Therefore, since there is contrition toward God in the heart, signs of contrition should appear outwardly before human beings. But contrition cannot exist at all without charity. It is now manifest that the sinner has been inwardly raised through grace and has received pardon, because “charity covers a multitude of sins.” Finally, it is written that at whatever hour a sinner groans over his sin, he shall be saved from it. When the judge’s knowledge has weighed these things, let him suspend judgment; meanwhile let him fear to pronounce sentence where he can marvel at such great mercy of God, because the bond of imposed satisfaction must not be tightened as much as [Col. 0681A] the merciful goodness of divine pity absolves. In many cases one must presume upon God’s mercy, especially when a person is known to have turned with his whole heart to him who justifies the ungodly. For where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom; and where there is freedom, there is no necessity. Hence Truth says in the Gospel: “If the Son shall make you free, you shall be truly free” (John 8).

What then? Do priests not have in such penitents the power of binding and loosing? You say that those whom God has absolved both from the bond of sin and from the debt of eternal punishment through true contrition of heart are not to be bound by the necessity of imposed satisfaction. But again, what does priestly authority loose if, as you assert, whatever charity belongs to a truly contrite heart has broken every bond of iniquity? If, therefore, the priest binds or looses nothing there [Col. 0681B], where are the keys he received? Oral confession too seems to be made superfluously if it is certain that sins are remitted before confession by contrition of heart alone.

That sins are remitted in compunction, the Psalmist testifies when he says: “I said: I will confess against myself my injustices to the Lord,” and so forth (Ps. 31). He did not say, “I made confession,” but: in a contrite heart he resolved to make confession, and you, merciful one, forgave the wickedness of my sin. And likewise, as we stated above: “At whatever hour a sinner groans over his sin, he shall be saved” (Ezek. 33). Therefore the priest is sought in vain, the sinner confesses in vain, and the power of binding and loosing is given in vain to Christ’s priests.

But behold: if contrition of heart alone is believed to cleanse sins [Col. 0681C], why is confession of the mouth commanded, to be made both in body and heart? For the time being, oral confession is said to be necessary for penitents, so that one who has the opportunity to confess but neglects it cannot at all obtain forgiveness of sins. Behold how he who has knowledge of all things unties the knots of this question not merely in one way but in many ways.

It must therefore be said that contrition of heart cleanses sins, and nevertheless oral confession must be made. If you ask why confession must be made when contrition is sufficient to wipe away sins, I answer you: because it has been commanded. If it has been commanded, you are bound to obey; if you are bound and, though able, do not obey, you despise; if you despise, you are proud; if you are proud, God resists you, because, knowing lofty things from afar [Col. 0681D], he looks only upon the humble. And if you further ask the reason for the command, it ought to have been enough for your humility to know God’s will, not to seek its rationale. He therefore commanded it because he so willed; he willed it because he knew it to be advantageous for us. Thus he not only commanded it but also established in this command a spiritual remedy for our salvation.

Why God wished this, and chose to place the sum of our salvation in this command, is as dangerous to inquire into presumptuously as it is ruinous not to believe it. For God willed that what he himself does—by infusing the grace of compunction in the heart—should be made manifest through oral confession to those who act in his stead in the Church. Why this? So that the stewards of heavenly mysteries, the rulers of souls, the priests, may loose by the power of their ministry those whom they know to have been inwardly loosed through the grace of God [Col. 0682A]; may know that those whom they loose are loosed; may regard them as loosed and pronounce them loosed. Let them free from fear of punishment those whom charity has absolved from the bond of guilt.

For this is what it means for a priest to show as loosed those whom the graciousness of divine mercy has itself loosed. Thus the Lord himself restores Lazarus to life and himself brings him raised out from the tomb; but he commands the apostles to loose the one raised and brought out, saying: “Loose him, and let him go” (John 11). He had indeed come forth alive, but was still bound with wrappings. There are three wrappings by which the dead are bound even after they have been invisibly raised by God: namely, the ill repute which they cruelly incurred by sinning publicly; the horror of Gehenna, which, because they do not doubt that they deserved it, they despair of having been remitted to them through contrition because of excessive fear [Col. 0682B]; and participation in the sacraments, of which they made themselves unworthy by committing injustice.

The first wrapping is loosed when the conversion of one formerly held in ill repute among the people is healed by the priest’s testimony. The second is loosed when, through the priest’s teaching on how great the efficacy of true contrition is, bitterness is changed into spiritual joy by the consolation of promised hope alone. The third is loosed when the priest confidently urges one truly contrite and truly amended to approach the sacraments. He also binds when he carefully instructs him in religious teaching, lest, once loosed, he flow away again through vain desires. In this manner the ecclesiastical judge looses and binds penitents.

But confessors who are entangled in many crimes and are found to be less compunctive [Col. 0682C] he ought to bind more strongly, tightening them more firmly with the bonds of fitting satisfaction, so that what the sorrow of the heart accomplishes less fully may at least be supplied by the labor of the flesh. The sorrow of a contrite heart can indeed suffice for every amendment even without bodily labor; but the labor of outward penance can never suffice if sorrow of heart is wholly absent. Since penance is a sacrament, moreover, and a sacrament is the visible form of invisible grace, a person is truly said to do penance here when he both possesses inwardly the reality of the sacrament in the compunction of his heart and outwardly represents the visible form of the sacrament in the labor of satisfaction.

Concerning satisfaction it must be said [Col. 0682D] that its measure ought to be imposed according to the kinds of sins and the differing conditions of sinners. This is left to the discernment of priests, who also have the power of binding and loosing in this matter of discernment: they bind penitents by the satisfaction due, and then, in loosing them from penance, mercifully relax something of it. There are also other modes of binding and loosing, which do not concern the present matter—for example, when someone is bound by the bond of anathema and again freed from that bond through priestly absolution. But enough of these matters.

Furthermore, much remained to be said about penance, which we omit either for brevity’s sake or perhaps because we lack sufficient ability to pursue every detail. Yet I would have you know this [Col. 0683A]: those who receive a penitent entangled in several crimes cannot repent of one while persisting in the others, because God does not approve the satisfaction of one who abandons one sin while persevering in others. Therefore, in order to make worthy satisfaction to God, let him confess and abandon each one.

To soldiers established in occupations which cannot be carried on without sin, and through whose occasion many crimes have been committed, it must be said that they cannot produce fruits worthy of penance unless, abandoning the occupations of sin, they change their lives. Sins once disclosed in humble confession and punished by fitting satisfaction according to the priest’s judgment are not to be repeated further in confession, unless those confessing wish to do so for humility’s sake. Yet those renouncing the world and taking on the religious habit commonly, upon entering a monastery [Col. 0683B], humbly lay out their whole life in order before their spiritual father. Satisfaction is not to be imposed on penitents at the point of death, but made known to them. Arsonists and murderers are to be reserved for the judgment of the diocesan bishop.

There are many other matters, perhaps necessary ones, which could profitably be written about penance; but let these things suffice for you meanwhile, venerable Father, until he who sends forth springs in the valleys and gives those thirsting for justice the water of saving wisdom opens for you the veins of a more abundant fountain. Receive, therefore, this little gift, and excuse its rustic speech when set against the grandiloquent, knowing surely that I have cared little for elegance of words or subtlety of thoughts, provided only that I might seem in some measure to have fulfilled my promise [Col. 0683C].

## LETTER XXVII. TO THE COUNTESS OF CHARTRES

[Note: [Col. 0683D] Either Alice, daughter of Louis VII, king of the Franks, widow of Theobald, who died in 1191 during the siege of Acre; or Catherine, daughter of Ralph, count of Clermont near Beauvais.]

He urges her toward contempt for worldly things and love of God.

To the noble Countess of Chartres, his most beloved in Christ, Brother ADAM, unworthy servant of the poor of Perseigne, greeting in the Lord.

After I departed from you, dearest lady, in body—though I could not depart in heart—I often recalled your generous goodwill, which received me, though little known to you, with such joy. Firmly fixed in my mind was that eager devotion of yours which, by a certain pious compulsion, forced me to remain with you even for two days. There come to mind [Col. 0683D] the sweet words of our new friendship, the conversations which we held together concerning hatred of sin, contempt for the world, the pursuit of virtues, the sayings of Scripture, the examples of the saints, and the joys of heavenly life to be desired. These are the matters about which we conversed during almost the whole of those two days, and from them I began to conceive and entertain hope concerning you—may my desires not, I pray, be disappointed.

Inflamed by this zeal, I resolved to write something to your affection, by which I might remind you to seek that thing which alone effects salvation. Certainly in Jesus alone is salvation, whole and supreme; and true contempt for human vanity readily attains it [Col. 0684A]. For favor is deceptive and the beauty of the age is vain: it is a light and fleeting shadow, a form of transitory vanity like a dream of the night, able only to deceive one who sleeps. But a wakeful mind does not endure such phantasms, for it is formed by reason, illumined by faith, stirred by fear, moved by charity, stretched forth by hope, struck by ambition for heavenly glory, and crucified by pious compassion for the poor. Thus the gaze of the mind is directed to Jesus, and the sharpness of understanding, intent upon the true light, shakes off from itself the sleep of deception and admits no madness.

Sleep, dreams of vanities, and false madness abound more copiously with you: namely, the luxury of riches, the pomp of precious garments, pride of rank, excess of dress and expenditure, the meticulous [Col. 0684B] refinement of foods, the swallowing of so many delicacies, the great frequency of banquets, such nobility of lofty blood, such a multitude of attendants, such prosperity in worldly affairs, and the utterly vain vanity of human praise, acquired at so great a cost to moral character and possessions. Almost all these things serve the seductions of the pleasure-loving flesh.

I beg you not to be angry with a friend speaking truth; for although truth gives rise to hatred, it does not do so among those bound by the ties of holy charity. Holy love is always inflamed into hatred of vices: it speaks and inveighs more against those whom it is proved to love more. To spare a friend’s vices is flattery, not affection; and not to rebuke those whom we love has the taste not so much of friendship as of enmity.

I would indeed call you blessed, and most worthy of the longed-for vision of the lovable Jesus [Col. 0684C], if for love of him you drove from the eyes of your heart the dusts named above, so that you might see more clearly what you might more dearly love. For he is beautiful and desirable to behold, “fair in form above the children of men”; and, being “the splendor of glory, and more elegant than every form” (Ps. 44), he lacks no less in the fullness of goodness than in perfection of splendor: as good as he is beautiful, as fair as he is precious, as patient as he is wise, as humble as he is sublime.

Look upon him; attend to him; stretch yourself out toward him; strive toward him; and do not hesitate to abandon in heart and mind whatever does not belong to him. Put away luxury, cut off superfluities, enter the bounds of frugality, and immerse your sober spirit in the torrents of divine truth [Col. 0684D]. Yet none drink in this intoxication except those whom love of holy moderation makes sober amid drunkenness; nor does one deserve the glory of the Mediator whom the moderation of mediocrity does not heal.

By the pursuit of medicinal frugality, the loss of the life already spent is restored, and provision is made lest what remains of life perish. Moderation does not depart from the middle; it does not abandon measure. While it longs for the Governor of the ages and clings to Christ, Mediator between God and human beings, it detests everything superfluous on either side. Here no long trailing garments hinder the feet of matrons or offend the sight of the eyes with the whirlwinds of stirred-up dust [Col. 0685A].

Where moderation reigns, I say, estates are not enlarged from the lands of orphans, nor are wardrobes burdened with costly changes of clothing by which bodies—vessels of dung—may be adorned. Moderation does not allow a more ambitious display to deck out the trappings of horses from exactions imposed upon widows. It does not allow the gullet’s gluttony to gorge itself upon the spoils of the poor, nor to seek out more sumptuous food as stimulants to appetite. No, I say, that holy moderation does not allow to be given to actors that by which the need of the wretched ought to have been fed or clothed.

Certainly, if moderation had pleased the rich man clothed in purple, hunger would neither have tormented Lazarus at his gate, nor would the torments of hell have received the rich man himself. He feasted splendidly every day and was clothed in purple and fine linen; [Col. 0685B] and although Sacred Scripture does not say that he acquired these things through robbery or usury, it nevertheless shows that he incurred the danger of eternal damnation. Observe that the truth of Scripture accuses that rich man of absolutely no crime except that, living in luxury, he did not extend mercy to the poor man. What if he lived in luxury and had acquired those same luxuries unlawfully? Certainly the Apostle considers living in luxury a great sin, when, concerning the instruction of widows, he says to Timothy: “The widow who lives in luxury is dead while living” (1 Tim. 5). It would not have been remarkable to say this if he were accusing a widow of luxuries acquired unlawfully. It would not have been remarkable to say this if a widow living in luxury gave nothing to the poor. But now he said simply [Col. 0685C] that one living in luxury is dead, although he does not accuse her either of rapine against her dependents or of stinginess toward the poor. You should therefore regard luxuries with suspicion, and carefully attend to where they come from and where they go. They commonly come, indeed, from unjust exactions from dependents, from the burdens of the poor, from the tears of orphans, from the despoiling of widows; and where those who plunder rejoice, there those who lose mourn inconsolably. It is sufficiently clear, however, where things thus plundered go: no other use is sought from them than that, with the utmost care, the dung-heap of flesh soon to die may be defiled by them.

Therefore [Col. 0685D] one must keep watch with every zeal over the adornment and care of the soul, to which the author of life bestowed life and immortality in its creation, impressed his own image by gratuitous goodness, and promised, out of excessive love, the unfailing delights of heavenly glory. Moreover, lest there should be any doubt about another manner of life, he came in person, himself set forth the precepts of life, offered in himself examples of conduct; and what was difficult for our incapacity, he made easy by the example of his own action. We must therefore receive and fulfill the precepts, admire and imitate the examples, love and desire the promises. The precepts forbid every vain thing to every soul. The examples proclaim and set forth the glory of the cross; the promises raise you up through the consolation of blessed hope, lest you fail in crucifixion. But all our hope and consolation is in the childbearing of our Virgin, in [Col. 0686A] the flower of singular fragrance.

O fruitful flower of everlasting spring, precious with every grace, full of every glory, beautiful in every elegance! How inestimable is its sweetness of scent! How incomparable its loveliness in beauty! How great an abundance of sweetness is in its taste! Would that, my soul, this fragrance might always be in your nostrils! Would that this taste might never depart from the throat of your heart! Through you, certainly, by the inestimable fragrance of so great a sweetness, whatever the world exhales is accounted foul. In comparison with the sweetness of this taste, whatever is accustomed to become sweet to the flesh is judged most bitter. Whoever is delighted by the pleasure of such wondrous loveliness cannot so much as look upon vanity.

O rod from the root of Jesse! O Virgin most worthy of all praise, who, [Col. 0686B] without the loss of your own flower, brought forth this flower of angels and satisfied the hearts both of angels and of human beings with wondrous sweetness! She is for us, amid the waves of the world and the shipwrecks of the stormy sea, a singular protection. She is the harbor for the shipwrecked, comfort for the desolate, consolation for the sorrowful, restoration for the lost, medicine for the sick. She is the rod by which the anointing of truth, our teacher, works, bestowing the discipline of correction upon its followers: namely, the Holy Spirit, most fully inhabiting the workshop of discipline, made her pliant through mercy and extended through the rectitude of justice. For this rod is pliant, extended, slender, straight, light, fruitful, fertile, fragrant, and sweet: pliant through mercy, extended through excellence, slender through humility, straight through fairness, [Col. 0686C] light through freedom from sin, fruitful through fecundity, fertile through fullness of virtues, fragrant through reputation, sweet through love.

Look upon her, embrace her, praise and love her, because the one for whom Mary has been willing to act as advocate will prevail against every enmity. Praise the Virgin with your voice, and see that your life does not in any respect contradict your voice. Since she is wholly praiseworthy, let nothing in you cease from her praises, because I think nothing more praiseworthy than to devote oneself wholly to her praises—she who is the honor and glory of the Creator, the praise and joy of angels. But let this letter now attain its conclusion in Mary’s praises, though perhaps its very length makes it burdensome to you. If anything hard or difficult for your understanding [Col. 0686D] occurs in it, you have near you the venerable chaplain G., who can and knows how to explain each difficulty to you.

I ought to have written to you in the vernacular, had I not learned that you had acquired some understanding of Latin. May it not weary you to greet in my name that woman whom, at the secret counsel between us, you called the third person—after I had first urged you to do so. She has clung so steadfastly to my heart through her devotion and integrity that no forgetfulness can begrudge me her sweet memory. When you greet her on my behalf, remind her also in my name that she should cleave with such undivided love to Christ, the bridegroom of virgins, that the lily of her virginity, which is still believed to be [Col. 0687A] in bloom, may not be allowed to wither through any corruption of the world. Farewell.

## LETTER XXVIII. TO AGNES, A VIRGIN.

On the pious union of their two souls.

To Agnes, a virgin, whom Brother Adam the sinner embraces with all the affection of his soul: greeting in the Lamb, the bridegroom of virgins.

I hold with undoubting faith that the Holy Spirit has established his dwelling in you. By the working of his grace, having scorned the shamefulness of carnal desire, you have loved the beauty of angels. For this reason I too cling wholly to you, because with you are kept the treasures of my desire: namely, love and desire for the Creator. O happy love, by which true things are preferred to vain, certain things to doubtful, [Col. 0687B] useful things to harmful, honorable things to slippery, eternal things to transitory! O delightful desire, by which he alone is sought whose search sweetly torments, whose finding is fullness of joy! When he has bestowed the gift of himself upon you, will he allow you to forget me—he who does not allow me even for an hour to forget your affection? O how greatly the remembrance of the sincerity of your love gladdens me, although the desire for your progress and the long-awaited consolation of seeing you piously trouble me. Mutual conversation between those who piously love one another contributes greatly, certainly, to holy affection; and, in a wonderful way, even from bodily sight spiritual affection is kindled. How great, do you think, is the delight of seeing him who alone is salvation and supreme sweetness, if it is so health-giving and sweet to behold the dwelling-places of so great a sweetness? [Col. 0687C] I shall see you, when there is leisure, even with the eyes of flesh; for there is always leisure to see you in spirit.

Since we are greatly lacking in mounts, and the queen, in your hearing, promised us a palfrey, do not hesitate to approach her and remind her to make good her promises. For it has long been my desire to visit this holy convent; and if I had the means by which I could suitably travel to you, the fulfillment of my desire would not be delayed. Farewell.

## LETTER XXIX. TO J., ARCHDEACON OF BELISME.

On silence.

To his beloved in Christ, J., archdeacon of Belisme, [Col. 0687D] Brother Adam the sinner: greeting.

The urgency of your request, dearest brother, imposes upon me something which I confess I undertake with fear, since I possess neither inward strength based on experience nor sufficient knowledge to supply understanding. Certainly, one lacking these two things cannot possess praiseworthy eloquence, especially when the mind has nothing from which the pen of the tongue may be dipped, nor the morals anything which may be expressed in words. You would better advise me to be silent than ask me to write something on the judgment and usefulness of silence. Indeed, the reason of the matter you ask about is found only by lovers of silence, followers of quiet, to whom it is given to emulate silence as the cultivation of justice. Nevertheless, though I have not deserved this grace, [Col. 0688A] perhaps your devotion will deserve to find, even in barrenness, the fruit you desire. Therefore the Trinity, friend of silence, will be present as I discuss silence—the Trinity that is accustomed to perfect its praises even from the mouths of infants and nursing children.

Whoever, in the role of a disciple of the incarnate Word, frequents the schoolroom ought to love and keep silence for this reason: that he chooses God’s Word as his teacher. For Christ, teacher of the humble, is called not only the Word of the Father because he is his omnipotent will, but is also called the Word because he always demands a hearing. One who hears listens; one who listens is silent; one who is silent and hears offers another a hearing. Therefore the Father always requires silence from the rational creature to whom he always speaks such a Word. For the ineffable [Col. 0688B] generation of this Word is itself the instruction of the rational creature; spiritual infancy alone gives it the reverence of due hearing insofar as it keeps inviolate innocence in silence and quiet. The Father always speaks to us, while he eternally begets the ineffable Word; and the creature owes continuous silence to his eternal utterance.

But one does not know, understand, or love the omnipotent Word if one does not fear to turn the hearing of one’s heart away from him. Hence it is written: “A man of many words shall not be directed upon the earth” (Ps. 139); for he is not directed upon earth who does not deserve to receive or understand the meaning of the divine utterance. The talkative man does not deserve this, because, while he speaks trivial things with tongue upon tongue, he does not experience what the Spirit of the Word brings in tongues of fire. You see how greatly the whole [Col. 0688C] Trinity approves the discipline of silence.

The Father loves silence because, when he ineffably begets and sets forth from his own substance the Word coeternal with himself, he undoubtedly requires an attentive ear of the heart for understanding this mystery. Thus he says in the Psalm: “My heart has poured forth a good word” (Ps. 44). The Word himself likewise justly demands that silence be made for him, because, while he keeps within himself all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, in order to impress them, as it were, upon our ears, he assumed our human nature as a language not unknown to us. Hence Moses: “The Word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart” (Deut. 30). And John the Evangelist: “The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1). The Spirit also wished that the highest obedience be rendered to the Word when, explaining the abbreviated—and therefore more obscure—Word as though by certain glosses, he revealed himself in tongues of fire; for *glossae* means “tongues.” For the Holy Spirit made, as it were, an exposition of the obscurity of the abbreviated Word—that is, of the Word emptied even unto the form of a servant—when he impressed the causes of so great a mystery upon the disciples of the Word through that most manifest dispersal of tongues.

Concerning this Spirit, his interpreter and expositor, the Word of the Father speaks thus: “He will glorify me, for he will receive of mine” (John 16). And again: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you from the Father, he will bear witness concerning me” (John 15). [Col. 0689A] The Lord testifies through the prophet that the Holy Spirit loves silence: “Upon whom,” he says, “shall my Spirit rest, except upon the humble and quiet person who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66). Where humility and quiet are, there the movement of spiritual silence, peace, and tranquility keep festival. Silence is friendly to peace and friendly to tranquility. The sabbath of the heart cannot be kept where the labor of the lips blunts the discipline of silence. Thus the Holy Spirit is said to be sevenfold, because through seven working days he orders and arranges the sabbath of the heart for leisure in the school of the Word. Hence those working days are the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit which Isaiah enumerates, and they are like seven silences because they compel the whole mass of vices to be silent and cease in the soul; for the number seven also stands for universality, and “to be silent” is said to mean “to cease.” [Col. 0689B] Thus they are like seven silences, which by their authority impose silence upon all vices. They are silences which, while putting to sleep the guilt of sins and the tumult of vices, make the ears of the heart fit to choose and love the mysteries of the incarnate Word.

Therefore, amid all these silences, the omnipotent Word chooses for himself the middle place, because he comes more intimately from the royal seats to him who, in the Spirit of strength, overcomes and casts down whatever is contrary to purity. “While all things kept the middle of silence, the omnipotent Word came from the royal seats” (Wis. 18): because the mediator judges him worthy of a royal seat who, standing in the middle, bravely resists sins. Silence is imposed upon vices only in the Spirit of strength, and this nowhere but in the middle of the field, because virtue is called by the wise the mean reduced from either extreme of vices. Strength of mind is indeed needed if you are to do violence to the kingdom of heaven, seize it by violent eagerness, turn your ears away from evil hearing, and apply them only to the hearing of the Word and to obedience to the commandments.

This silence is the middle by which the omnipotent Word, the mediator, is brought into the midst; and, setting himself as a little child in the midst of the disciples, he presents himself to little ones, as to newly born infants, to be imitated as their teacher. Such infants, therefore, are *non-fantes*, that is, non-speaking or silent: they await the salvation of God in silence. The prophet says, “It is good to await the salvation of God in silence” (Lam. 3). The salvation of God is the mystery and grace of the incarnate Word. Those who do not make their ear ready to hear it and do not offer it a hearing do not dry up the tongue of the Egyptian sea—that is, they do not restrain the overflow of superfluous talkativeness or discipline the tongue against much speech: “He who lets water go,” Scripture says, “is the beginning of strife” (Prov. 17). To let waters go is not to restrain the tongue of the Egyptian sea—that is, not to curb the flow of a bitter tongue. What is as swollen and unstable as the sea? What is as bitter as strife? And what is the Egyptian sea but the bitter and dark heart? For Egypt is interpreted as “darkness.” He lets out the waters of the Egyptian sea who, through the service of the tongue and the passage of the mouth, pours out the bitterness and swollen vanity of his heart. [Col. 0690A]

Does it not seem to you to be a strife against the mystery of the incarnate Word, against the precept of the rule, against the testimony of conscience, to exceed the limits of speaking and break the vows of silence? Certainly God’s Word prescribed a law of silence for every human being when he threatened and foretold that an account must be rendered on the day of judgment for every idle word. For silence is not simply never to speak at all, but to set a guard upon one’s mouth and have a door of circumspection upon one’s lips: that is, to speak what is fitting and from what source, how and when, where and how much one ought. For there is “a time to keep silence and a time to speak.” Therefore let the voice of the Lord be upon the waters, so that they may become the waters of Siloam and flow in silence; so that God the Word may preside over your words and the rash volatility of the tongue may be restrained by the law of silence.

[Col. 0690B] Faith, reason, and authority strongly commend the discipline of silence to professors of heavenly philosophy: first, because the Wisdom of God, “reaching from end to end mightily, disposes all things sweetly and silently.” Second, because that Wisdom assumes for itself the name of Word; hence: “In the beginning was the Word,” etc. (John 1). Third, because that same Word appeared in our flesh as an infant—that is, as silent; hence: “The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1). Fourth, because he chose the time of middle silence for assuming our infancy. Fifth, because, although the treasures of wisdom and knowledge were hidden in him, when he was already twelve years old in the flesh he taught in the synagogue, yet humbly listened to human teachers of the Law. Sixth, because in his Passion [Col. 0690C] he was silent like a lamb before its shearer. Seventh, because the voice of that same Word, namely John the Baptist, imposed silence upon the Law and the prophets: “For the Law and the prophets were until John” (Luke 16). Eighth, because when the Spirit of the Word came in fiery tongues, he found the disciples of the Word silent and praying, and stirred the hearts of the hearers by a sudden sound. Ninth, because the bride of the Word herself—that is, the Church—does not abandon the silence of eternal rest, and lends her ear all the more affectionately because she hears God say to her: “Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear” (Ps. 44). Hear, so that you may believe, because faith comes by hearing; see, so that you may love, because love advances and is perfected through sight; and incline your ear, so that you may obey from an affection of humility and persevere [Col. 0690D] in the practice of obedience.

Hear the fame of your bridegroom, because his name is poured-out oil; see the beauty of the beloved, because he is beautiful in form beyond the children of men; and incline your ear to the performance of the commandments and imitation of the examples. Hear first, and see afterward, because faith leads to understanding, and through faith one arrives at sight. Thus it befits the bride of the Word not to speak and chatter, but to hear and see, because she cannot see unless she has first heard. Hence she abandons silence and loses the grace of the Word and the dignity of her name. *Ecclesia* means “a calling together” or “one called together”: for she would not have come unless she had been called together; she would not have heard herself called unless, in silence, she had offered a hearing to the voice of the Word.

The calling of the Word so desires silence in his disciples [Col. 0691A] that, when he sends the disciples out to preach, he permits them to greet no one on the way: “Greet no one on the road” (Luke 10). Certainly, when the divine law is set before God’s people, Israel is admonished at its very beginning to give God a hearing and to keep silence: “Hear, Israel, and be silent: the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. 4). Therefore a disciple of the Word either falsely professes himself to be a disciple of the Word, or truly keeps and loves the sacrament. What shall certain professed members, both of monastic and canonical orders, say here? Though they have dedicated tongue and lips to God’s Word and bound themselves by the obligation of their profession to the discipline of silence, they nevertheless continually pour themselves out in much speaking and labor in every way not to keep what they have vowed. [Col. 0691B] There is no truth in their mouth, because their heart is vain. Nor can pure truth sit upon lips that speak from an abundance of vanity. For, as the Lord Christ, the omnipotent Word, says: “Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” (Luke 6).

What shall I say of those who, having the poison of asps, often imprudently utter shameful things beneath their lips, devote themselves to poisonous detractions, and are in no way ashamed to lie, swear falsely, quarrel, and perversely interpret whatever good they see in others? Their throat indeed is a tomb; and from the tomb of their throat they carry out as many things as dead as the examples of death which they set forth for the ruin of others, both by speaking perversely and by doing the same things. Let these things for the present suffice, brother, concerning the usefulness of silence. Even if they do not satisfy [Col. 0691C] your devotion, they nevertheless exceed the measure of my smallness. It remains for us to emulate silence and ourselves keep what we have commended—yet not to be silent from the praises of him toward whom our hearing ought to be directed: the omnipotent Word, Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## LETTER XXX. TO BLANCHE, COUNTESS OF CHAMPAGNE.

He sends her the sermons she requested and explains that four things are necessary for obtaining grace.

To the beloved and most beloved B., illustrious Countess of Champagne, always to be loved in Christ, Brother A., [Col. 0691D] servant of the servants of God who serve Christ at Perseigne: greeting, and the will always to maintain a devotion to the things of God.

The devotion of your affection urgently requested, daughter, that I should send you copies of my little sermons; and indeed you seemed to ask this out of great desire. It would plainly be a worthy and praiseworthy request if you could understand what has been said in Latin, or if those things had been said in such a manner that a benefit of edification could come to you from them.

> **Note:** [Col. 0691D] This shows that the Cistercians of old delivered their sermons before the brethren in chapter not in French but in Latin. On this matter see, if you wish, Mabillon’s observations on the sermons of St Bernard.

For, as I suppose, you ask for the sermons themselves so that, built up by reading them, you may advance, provided that, when you have leisure, [Col. 0692A] someone may perhaps explain them to you. Know, daughter, that if the sense of any saying is translated from one language into another, its own flavor or composition will scarcely remain in the foreign idiom. For when liquid is poured from one vessel into another, it is altered somewhat in color, taste, or scent. Yet I would devote myself wholeheartedly to your edification in whatever ways I could; and would that you would attend so diligently to Catholic exhortations and to the things that have been said that you might find favor before God and humankind.

Certainly, it is clear that four things are necessary for attaining this grace; you ought quickly to apply yourself with all the capacity of your heart to possessing them. The first is the rectitude of undoubting faith. Once it has made you orthodox, it will enlighten you by true knowledge to recognize and avoid [Col. 0692B] every sort of error and fabrication. The rectitude of faith consists in believing both that God is truthful and, in one’s mind, that he is the highest good: that is, that one should be united to him, that one should truly become a member of Christ, truly be adopted as a child of God. Those alone who believe in God receive the spirit of adoption; and therefore, being incorporated into Christ, they are not improperly called children of adoption. “Everyone,” says the Apostle, “who believes in him shall not be put to shame” (Rom. 10). And undoubtedly to believe in him is to show oneself wholly estranged from works of shame. If you hold this rectitude of faith, you will be reckoned among the children of God, and thus will become heir of God and co-heir of Christ; and you will in no way die eternally, as he himself said: “Whoever believes in me shall not die [Col. 0692C] forever” (John 11).

For the passing of God’s children from this life is not truly death but is rather called a birth, because in their passing, stripped of mortal bodies, they are born anew to the refreshment of true life. The second is innocence of conduct. When faith’s ministry has been restored through confession and repentance, this innocence is thereafter most safely entrusted to the guardianship of divine fear. Blessed indeed is the anxious care of fear which diligently strives to obey faith, does not omit to punish through repentance what has been lost, and attends to the restoration of innocence while, with every vigilance, it guards [lacuna] of them. Therefore fear is born from faith: for, unless one believed, what would one fear? Repentance is born from fear: for, unless fear of punishment affected [Col. 0692D] the mind, who would correct himself for his transgressions? “It is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God” (Heb. 10). While faithful fear constantly impresses and instills this terror in the mind, it chooses rather to correct itself for its guilt through repentance than to reserve the guilt itself for punishment by the hands of the living God. Thus, while repentance is performed, while the mind, pricked and contrite through the office of fear, confesses what it had wrongly swallowed; while guilt is covered, innocence is restored. Thus good conduct comes to be when, all harmful things having been excluded, people begin to be innocent.

You see, daughter, that from faith by which one believes in God all wickedness is excluded from the [Col. 0693A] soul, and war is declared upon vices and depraved desires. Even though these are felt within us against our will, we must nevertheless resist them, lest they at least be able to rule. “Let not sin reign,” as the Apostle says, “in our mortal body” (Rom. 6). He did not forbid sin’s being present, but commanded that it should not have kingship or dominion in us. Therefore, if we still feel vices and desires to be present within us but do not consent to them, we have no condemnation from these things in Christ Jesus. For as long as we feel them and deny consent, so long do we triumph over them with God’s help. To consent is to succumb and lose innocence, which we preserve through God’s grace as long as, denying them consent, we endure their assaults.

From innocence [Col. 0693B] of conduct follows justice in works, which we place third as necessary for producing God’s grace. For we said above that there are four things by which God’s grace is necessarily acquired and preserved. The final two are justice of works and perseverance in virtues. Justice consists not merely in rendering justice to God for injuries done to him by oneself, from fear of hell; it is also the virtue of justice faithfully and filially obeying everything God commands. To this justice belongs bearing the fruit of works—one thirtyfold, another sixtyfold, another hundredfold—according to the place where the holy seed has fallen upon good ground. Is not the holy seed faith by which one believes in God? Is not [Col. 0693C] innocence of conduct the good ground, diligently raised up by the office of holy fear? From it proceeds that threefold fruit: the thirtyfold, understood as faithfulness in marital chastity; the sixtyfold, which is the fruit of widowly continence; and the hundredfold, which the excellence of virginity brings forth. The thirtyfold and sixtyfold fruit are required of you, because you have both been faithful in marriage and now attained the freedom of widowly continence. Of the hundredfold fruit which virginity produces I say nothing to you at present, although I know that before the bond of marriage you had a most fervent desire for so great a thing. May he who judges intentions make that purpose most fruitful for you, although unwillingly you were led away from it by the counsels of friends. Act, therefore: make amends in carrying out the thirtyfold and sixtyfold fruit for what, for the present, you have achieved less fully of the hundredfold. Apply yourself to works of justice, whether by rendering justice to God concerning yourself through repentance, or by applying yourself filially to fulfilling his commandments and ordinances. [Col. 0694A]

Observe that the practice of this justice is fourfold. First is the examination of sacred reading; second is application to sacred meditation; third is persistence in devout prayer; fourth is religious diligence in active conduct. Sacred reading, like a mirror, directs you to what must be done; in the practice of meditation you seek and find the manner you should observe in doing it. Persistence in prayer obtains from heaven help in doing it. Active conduct, trusting in God’s help, undertakes the good work. These four, brought into practice and habit, lead the purified soul to the contemplation of heavenly things.

But alas! What have you to do with [Col. 0694B] contemplation of heavenly things, when the ocean of worldly vanity has almost wholly submerged you on account of the opportunity afforded by earthly and transitory rule? Hence arise in a widow the blameworthy curiosity of clothing, extravagance of expenses, the multitude of dishes, the multiplication of collections, the pomp of riders, the despoiling of the poor, the manifold debasement of attendants, the unpunished perfidy of Jews prompted by greed, the criminal license of moneylenders, and the constant tumult in the courts of litigants. Yet however contrary all these things may be to divine justice and the salvation of the soul, if, while placed in this position, you endeavor to remove them from yourself, you will endure human mockery and reproach. What, then, is more miserable than to remain against one’s conscience where it is necessary [Col. 0694C] to be in danger, and knowingly to hold things that are transitory, which daily flee away and, in fleeing, either diminish or extinguish in the soul the love of eternity?

Think, then, my dearest, think often on the justice of works and perseverance in virtues, because that person alone reaches the harbor of salvation who perseveres in justice of works and patience in virtues. For good ground thus bears fruit in patience: it receives the seed of faith with innocence of conduct, brings forth good fruits as works of justice, and through patience carries and advances those same fruits by perseverance to the crown of eternal recompense. Moreover, most loving one, I send you in this book my sermons, whatever they may be, which you have asked for so eagerly, so that, if you use them and they bring you any improvement, you may also remember your lover through their occasion. Farewell.

[Col. 0695]

# THE MARIALE OF ADAM, ABBOT OF PERSEIGNE, MEMBER OF THE HOLY CISTERCIAN ORDER, A FRENCHMAN, A MAN MOST LEARNED AND ELOQUENT;

in which Adam’s golden sermons and precious fragments on the praises of Mary, Virgin Mother of God, are transmitted to the knowledge of posterity.

## A WORK HITHERTO UNPUBLISHED,

drawn from a very ancient manuscript codex on parchment, formerly brought forth from the library of the monastery of Casamari and elucidated with notes by Father Hippolytus Marracci of Lucca, of the Congregation of Clerics Regular of the Mother of God.

(Rome, printed by Ignatius de Lazzari, 1652, duodecimo.—We publish according to the copy preserved in the library of the Catholic University of Louvain, which Mr Nève, librarian of that institution, most kindly shared with us.)

> **Note:** [Col. 0695] The notes of Hippolytus Marracci on this document were printed by Migne as a separate document in columns 753–772. Each number in the text of the *Mariale* refers to the number of the note in that separate document.

> And again after darkness  
> I hope for light.  
> —Job 17.

# TO ADAM, ABBOT OF PERSEIGNE, A MAN MOST LEARNED, MOST HOLY, AND WHOLLY DEVOTED TO MARY.

[Col. 0695]

[Col. 0695A]

To him for whom

Mary, Mother of the God-man,  
was an anchor amid tossing waves,  
a harbor in shipwreck,  
aid in tribulation,  
consolation in sorrow,  
assistance in oppression,  
help in need,  
moderation in prosperity,  
joy in expectation,  
and ever refreshment in labor;

whose judgment—and indeed an excellent one—was that:

to seek Mary, Queen of Heaven, is virtue;  
to find her, salvation;  
to grasp her, joy;  
to love her, praise and honor;  
to hold her and not let her go, the highest good;

who

judged that to depart from Mary, Lady of the world, [Col. 0695B] even for a point or a moment was not merely unsafe but altogether dangerous;

who clung to her always inseparably, with the tenderest affection of heart and the purest integrity of conduct; and who recognized her, through the illumination of heavenly light, most clearly, and revered her most humbly, as the sure salvation of his soul after God, [Col. 0696A] the compendium of life, the path to the heavenly homeland, the sole hope of pardon, the enlightener of the heart, and the singular sweetness of the spirit:

these writings, which he himself long ago composed—among other monuments of great talent and outstanding religious devotion—with a pen not merely golden but with a mouth and heart full of piety, in praise and encomium of the great Mother of God; Hippolytus Marracci, least of mortals, gives, dedicates, and consecrates these writings, together with his own heart and whole self, to the virginal bridal chamber as a sacred votive offering [Col. 0696B] to be hung there by her most welcome hands, so that they may be more acceptable.

# TO THE MOST EMINENT PRINCE MARCO ANTONIO FRANCIOTTO, MOST ILLUSTRIOUS CARDINAL OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH, PROTECTOR OF THE SACRED CISTERCIAN ORDER.

[Col. 0697]

After the Marian founders consecrated to your most eminent name (being unconcerned about my own lowliness because secure in your kindness), I come again to you, most eminent Prince, intending to place in the most brilliant light of your protection the Marian Works of Adam, Abbot of Perseigne, of the Cistercian Order—hitherto untouched by the press and buried in neglect and darkness for more than four hundred years. I come to you a second time, moreover, not merely, as on the first occasion, gladly and willingly to declare the due respect owed by myself and my entire congregation to you and yours; but because, if I came to another, I could rightly be reproved by everyone as seeking protection without a protector.

For since you alone, by decree of the Apostolic See, are Protector of the Cistercian Order, to whom could I offer, more fittingly and more justly for protection, a work composed by a son of the Cistercian Order than to Your Eminence? Who properly protects except the protector by office? Nor is this work due to you by a special right only because it comes from the Cistercian Order, but also because it treats of the praises of the Virgin Mother of God. From your very birth you have been wholly devoted to that same Virgin Mother of God; with a remarkable sense of piety, whether through daily exercises of devotion or through continual imitation of Marian virtues, you never cease from her praises.

On the feast of the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin you were born into this light of the world to most devout parents, Curtius Franciotto and Clara Balbania, Lucchese patricians, illustrious no less for ancestral nobility than for their most brilliant virtue. Thus it was signified that from your very birth to the final term of life you would live in most steadfast piety and unchanging devotion toward the most august Queen of Heaven; and that, with most diligent zeal, you would promote her worship, honour, and veneration—first in yourself and afterwards also in others—up to that final boundary of all things.

Indeed, the connexion of your most noble blood with the mighty family of Sixtus IV and Julius II, Roman Pontiffs (for Luchina, niece of Sixtus and sister of Julius, was joined in marriage to Giovanni Francesco Franciotto), is nothing—though otherwise it is much—when compared with the most splendid ornaments of your virtues, and especially with your most ardent devotion to the great Mother of God.

And certainly I would in no way omit, in this place at least, briefly to touch upon, for the everlasting remembrance of posterity, the clear examples in you of the kindness and benevolence of the most sweet Mother of God, and, in return, the most manifest testimonies of your most devout mind and most obedient will toward that same most sweet Mother of God, unless this letter of mine, submitting itself to the modesty of your spirit, considered for the present not what is owed to your virtues, but rather what your ears can endure.

My Adam rejoices, moreover, and gives God deserved and immortal thanks that, through the most provident and wise kindness of the Virgin Mother of God, such a patron has been provided for his Marian Work—a patron than whom, in devotion to the Mother of God and in every other adornment of Christian virtues, he himself could scarcely have wished for one greater or better. His work hopes that, having first seen the light under the most fortunate auspices of Your Eminence, it will live its whole life under those same auspices and will in no way fear adverse fortune. Nor does it doubt that it may rightly and deservedly be called *porphyrogenitus*, “born in the purple,” since it was first born in your purple. It delayed so long before coming into the light that it might see your times and present itself to you as its protector. Perhaps it emerged from darkness later than was fitting; but it did not emerge so late without divine providence, lest it be deprived of the glory of your protection. It waited long, but not badly—indeed, most excellently—since it compensated for the delay in appearing by the happiness of your protection.

It credits you with this: though it lay so long buried in darkness, restored to life beneath your light it now lives again in its work. Grateful for the benefit, although it itself is able to repay, it nevertheless entrusts its recompense also to the Mother of God, that she may reward Your Eminence with worthy increase.
