It is worthy of your protection not only because it belongs to the Cistercian Order (whose protection, by the most prudent judgment of our Most Holy Lord Innocent X, has been entrusted to your care), but because it also comes from that Order which, as Pope Gregory XI bears witness, is distinguished among other religious orders by the singularity of its devotion to the Virgin Mother of God; and which serves her everywhere most devoutly, unanimously and “with one shoulder,” as James of Vitry, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, says in his *Western History*. Even if you were not its protector, it could not be deprived of your protection on account of your exceptional devotion toward the most august Queen of Heaven.

Receive therefore, most eminent Prince, with your innate kindness, this Marian Work of Adam, Abbot of Perseigne. Rescued from destruction and restored to life, I commit it to your patronage as wholly due to you by right of protection; embrace it with paternal affection, and, by the duty of your office and also by your most ardent love for the Mother of God, cherish and protect it.

Whatever here is mine—and I see how slight it is and how unworthy of your greatness and merits—I most humbly offer wholly to Your Eminence, since nothing greater is presently available to me. I offer it, I say, both as a testimony to my most devoted service and due reverence toward you, and as some, however small, acknowledgment of those benefits by which you and your most illustrious brothers, Nicolaus and Bartholomaeus Franciotto—men of most choice piety and most tested virtue—have bound our whole congregation to you in the closest obligation.

Although we can never, even if we wished, repay the favours with which your kindness deems us worthy, everlasting remembrance and a grateful heart will preserve them always most deeply impressed, more deeply than this page can. Yet, lest we be wholly ungrateful, we shall meanwhile beseech God, best and greatest, with constant and fervent prayers, that he may daily increase your brothers and your entire family in grace and every good thing. May he preserve you safe upon earth beyond Nestor’s years, through the intercession of the Mother of God and your holy patroness, so that, established in a higher rank, you may fill with a still brighter light, for the happiness of the whole Christian world, the citadel of the Roman Empire—which you have hitherto filled and daily fill with the radiance of your virtues.

From Rome, from the house of St Mary in Campitello, 15 March, in the year 1652 from the Virgin Birth.

The humblest servant of Your Most Eminent Lordship,  
**HIPPOLYTUS MARRACCIUS**

## TO THE READER

[Col. 0699]

In the library of the monastery of Casamari—Casamari is a celebrated abbey in the diocese of Veroli in the Roman province, formerly Benedictine but possessed by the Cistercians from the year of the Lord 1140, as Gaspar Jongelinus says in his account of the Cistercian abbeys—in the library, I say, of this monastery there was an exceedingly ancient parchment manuscript in Latin, written in a beautiful, though in many places corrupt, hand. In it, together with literary monuments of other ancient Fathers, were preserved, enclosed like gems, the sermons of Adam, Abbot of Perseigne.

When this codex had been given as a gift by the Fathers of that monastery to the Most Reverend Father Dom Hilarion Rancato, of the Cistercian Order, General Superior in the Holy City—a man who valued not silver or gold but virtue and good letters alone—and when, by his kindness (for he is most learned in virtue and so generous toward his friends), it had also been communicated to me, I observed that among the said sermons of Adam there were several concerning the great Mother of God and ever-Virgin which had hitherto been buried in the darkness of oblivion. If made public, they could greatly benefit devotion and bring immense profit and usefulness to those who proclaim Marian praises.

I therefore resolved to publish them in print for the common good, together with Marian fragments gathered from other sermons of the same author, under the title *Mariale*, with notes added, as a most illustrious monument of antiquity. For I judged it altogether contrary to reason that these Marian studies, most worthy of the continual remembrance of humankind and of eternity itself, should be wrapped any longer in prolonged darkness.

I hope, moreover, that there will not be lacking persons who, tasting this Marian Work, will be effectively stirred to publish all Adam’s works. Those who do so will recall to life, as if rescued from the underworld, a most learned and eloquent writer who has been dead not for four days but for more than four hundred years. They will be judged to have served excellently the splendour of the illustrious Cistercian Order and the ornament of the Catholic Church itself; and they will render themselves most fruitfully deserving of the republic of letters, both for the present and for posterity.

Meanwhile, friendly reader, enjoy this labour in good health, and receive kindly and favourably this my humble effort in editing the Marian Work. Farewell.

# THE *MARIALE* OF ADAM, ABBOT OF PERSEIGNE

[Col. 0699]

## 1–11. FIRST SERMON: ON THE ANNUNCIATION OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN

[Col. 0699A]

“A rod shall go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root; and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him” (Isa. 11).

Now that the age was growing old, the Author of the age deigned to appear in order to restore humankind. The wretched world was becoming ancient and growing old, and was drawing near to destruction. Against the world as it perished, the Ancient of Days set himself in marvellous newness, according to Jeremiah’s prophecy: “Making a new thing upon the earth, so that a woman should encompass a man” (Jer. 31), in the womb of her body.

Therefore, while through this new thing he did away with the old age of our antiquity, he restored us in the new light of his immortality. He restored mercifully what he had created powerfully.

For so great a work there was need of a rod from the root of Jesse, from which might be born a fruit that, when tasted, would not bring death but would restore to life. Therefore, as an antidote to the former tree, whose fruit brought death, from the shoot of David’s stock there proceeded this Rod, fruitful with life: this Rod is the Virgin Mary; the fruit of the Rod is the Virgin’s offspring.

This Rod grew into so great a tree that, bringing forth the fruit of common salvation, while she became the Mother of the Almighty, she is proclaimed also Queen of angels and Lady of the ages. Without limit this tree spread itself: “Its shadow covered the mountains, and its branches the cedars of God” (Ps. 79).

Understand by the mountains the saints exalted in merits; by the shadow of our tree, the privilege of singular grace which the power of the Most High bestowed upon our Virgin when it overshadowed her, filled her mind with the fullness of grace, and made her womb pregnant with a divine birth.

[Col. 0699B]

This shadow has in itself nothing shadowy, nothing imaginary or empty. There is the highest and sole solidity of truth, and solid truth: for the true Only-Begotten assumed true humanity—that is, body and soul—in a true Virgin: nature, not guilt. The truth of innocence was not absent from the new nature assumed. “For he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2).

Therefore, when the incorporeal light of true divinity truly united to itself a human body, it made a shadow on the other side from the body united and set before it. That shadow is true faith: the true faith which, through the mystery of the Incarnation, justifies the ungodly, glorifies the righteous (Prov. 17), and makes high mountains out of valleys.

Of this shadow the bride says in the Song of Love: “Under his shadow, whom I had desired, I sat” (Song 1). O shadow necessary for moderating unlawful ardours! If you flee to the shadow of that tree—that is, if you believe in and love the Virgin’s offspring—“the sun shall not burn you by day, nor the moon by night” (Ps. 120).

[Col. 0701A]

Its branches are her merits, which surpass the height of the cedars—that is, the sublimity of the angels. (2)

O fruitful tree, planted in the midst of paradise, spreading in branches, firm in root! For she is the one who says: “In Zion I was established, and likewise I rested in the holy city” (Ecclus. 24); and again: “I took root among an honoured people, and in the portion of my God is his inheritance” (ibid.).

That tree of the knowledge of good and evil (Gen. 2), by its taste, conveyed experience of evil, partly took away knowledge of good, and made humankind wretched from a state of good. This tree, bringing forth the fruit of wisdom, both restores the palate of the soul to the taste of good and unteaches the experience of evils, restoring humankind to lost blessedness.

Thus the rod grew into a tree; the virgin advanced into Mother of the Most High. In the garden of the heavenly Husbandman (John 15) there are evil, barren, and fruitful trees. Evil trees are those which bear harmful fruit. Barren trees are those which bring forth no good fruit. Fruitful trees are those which are rich in the abundance of good fruits (Ps. 64).

The axe is laid at the root of evil and barren trees, to cut them down unless they change. Among good trees, incomparably the best is the rod from the root of Jesse, from which the fruit of life proceeded. For this fruit is the highest good; and a tree which does not share in its goodness cannot be good (Matt. 7).

[Col. 0701B]

The goodness of this fruit, when shared, gives much even to evil trees, that they may become good; it makes barren trees fruitful, that they may bear fruits; and it prunes fruitful trees, that they may bear more fruit. Those which it does not change in this way, it cuts down and casts into the fire (ibid.), that they may burn. For this fruit is also the axe by which unfruitful trees are cut down.

The axe, I say, is the incarnate Only-Begotten, whose handle, as it were, is humanity, because the cutting iron is the subtle sharpness of divinity. Where the trees of the woods clap their hands, emulate rather the rod that goes forth from the root of Jesse. From it you can have an example and power for bearing fruit, rather than from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil (Gen. 2), from which comes your barrenness, making you liable to the axe.

Love the fruit; fear the axe. In the Virgin’s Son love mercy; fear truth. For he either cuts by truth and is an axe, or [shows] mercy and is the lofty fruit of the earth. Love is due to mercy; fear is due to justice cutting down through judgment. Let either love move our barrenness or fear terrify it.

Certainly I would not call fear itself unfruitful, since, by cutting off evils, it thereby empties out barrenness, as through it the hands become accustomed to good works, or at least are disaccustomed from evils through dread of punishment. It is a great benefit when necessary fear, the extermination of sin and seedbed of virtue, is instilled into unfruitful trees; but this is so only if it is laid at the root of the tree (Matt. 3), that is, at the intention of the heart. For from intention, which a human being has as a root, one is either useless or fruitful.

[Col. 0701C]

Therefore the axe is placed not at the branches but at the root, because it is futile to cut away outwardly the branches of evil action if inwardly evil remains in the root of intention. Thus, as has been said, the axe laid to the root inspires fear. Why should unfruitful trees not fear when they see an axe preparing their cutting and threatening burning? For he who cuts with that very axe says: “Every tree which does not bear good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire” (ibid.).

This is the word of John the Baptist, who, while preceding the Saviour’s coming and pointing out the one who comes, places the axe, as it were, at the root of the trees. Therefore, when the birth of the Son of God from the Virgin is proclaimed, the axe that will proceed from the rod is, as it were, promised.

Note the mystery. The Virgin of God and Mother of humankind is the rod; God-man, the Virgin’s Son, is the axe.

[Col. 0702B]

The rod yields, in order to rebuke; the axe cuts down, in order to destroy. The rod rebukes in order to correct; the axe destroys in order to cast into the fire. We use a rod in correcting little children; an axe in destroying thorns.

The rod’s correction is in mercy, as it is written: “The righteous shall correct me in mercy” (Ps. 14 [reading uncertain; cf. Ps. 140:5]); the axe’s cutting is in fury and wrath. The correcting rod reforms toward virtue; the exterminating axe strikes toward destruction. Whoever is not corrected by the rod in the spirit of gentleness must await the axe in the spirit of judgment and the spirit of burning.

Whoever does not correct himself after the example of his mother’s mercy feels her terrible Son in judgment. This is the Rod by which the world is first rebuked and corrected, of which the Creator of the world himself says through the Prophet: “I shall visit their iniquities with a rod” (Ps. 88).

For the world is rebuked by the rod when, through the example and the offspring of the Virgin, it is shown what in it is blameworthy and condemnable. But how merciful was this correction! It is not the judge’s fury but the dove’s wrath that makes this vengeance upon crimes. Such punishment belongs not to hatred but to peace: by it a father chastises his son lest he perish; for severity is applied not to the guilty person but to guilt, and the Lord shows himself not as judge but as friend.

[Col. 0702C]

The zeal of the Lord of hosts does this, when in the rod he visits the iniquities of the world and crushes human sins with as many blows as he illuminates the Virgin’s offspring with virtues (Ps. 88). This is the rod which struck the backs of the foolish with as many blows as, through virtues displayed in itself, it defeated the vices of the foolish world.

And because it was the boundary of vices and origin of virtues, it is rightly called the rod of power, when it says: “The Lord shall send forth the rod of your power from Zion” (Ps. 109). Not undeservedly is the Virgin Mary called the rod of divine power, since through her faith, life, and offspring, the age, breathing out its vices, breathed again toward virtue.

The Lord sent this rod from Zion, because, as Isaiah says, “A rod went forth from the root of Jesse”: the Virgin arose from the line of David, who, as he himself testifies of himself in the Psalm, “was established over Zion, his holy mountain, proclaiming his commandment” (Ps. 2).

This rod is flexible, straight, outstretched, fruitful: flexible through mercy, straight through judgment, outstretched through the excellence of virginity, fruitful through the conception of the Only-Begotten. This rod brings forth a rod from a rod; for through this rod of power it was brought about that the Lord did not leave the rod of sinners—that is, the rod of the divine inheritance, of which it is said through the Psalmist: “You redeemed the rod of your inheritance” (Ps. 73), etc. (3)

[Col. 0703A]

This is Moses’ rod, which is read to have swallowed the rods of the Egyptian magicians, because the Truth of the virginal birth exposed and destroyed the heresies of the whole world. (4) This is Aaron’s rod, which blossomed, put forth leaves, and bore nuts without sap (Num. 17), because the blessed Mother of God conceived and bore the Saviour without a man.

O how flexible, how strong, and how fertile a rod of guidance: Mother of mercy, Queen of virtues, Mother of the Saviour! Boundless compassion makes you flexible; incorrupt power makes you strong; the fruitfulness of the divine birth makes you fertile. Your compassion is as great as your power. You are as merciful in sparing the wretched as you are powerful in obtaining what you ask.

For when do you not suffer with your wretched children, Mother of mercy? Or when can you not bring them help, since you are the mother of omnipotence itself? You undoubtedly obtain from the Almighty whatever you will with the same ease with which our misery becomes known to the bowels of your compassion.

[Col. 0703B]

O how great a confidence can we have in God through you! As you cannot fail to feel our sufferings through compassion, since, most merciful Mother, you cannot hate your children, so you cannot fail to obtain their remedy, if you ask, since for this—and only for this—the Son of the almighty Father of mercies willed to be born from you.

For you are mother of the exile; you are mother of the King. You are mother of the accused; you are mother of the Judge. You are mother of God; you are mother of man. Therefore through you the accused became brother of the Judge; through you the King and the exile came to share one inheritance. For since you are mother of both, you have both as sons, and through you the Only-Begotten becomes brother of the adopted.

What then is the accused to fear, when in his case the same one is both brother and judge, and such a judge as is always merciful and sparing by his very nature (*Prayer in the Mass for the Dead*), and who exalts mercy above judgment? (Jas. 2.) Should he fear lest he perish, when the most merciful Mother shows herself the most loving mother and most powerful advocate of her most clement brother and judge?

[Col. 0703C]

Will you, Mother of mercy, not ask the Son for your son, the Only-Begotten for the adopted, the Lord for the servant, the Judge for the accused, the Creator for the creature, the Redeemer for the redeemed? Indeed you will ask, because he who placed your Son as Mediator between God and humankind placed you also as mediatrix between the accused and the judge.

For this you were chosen and taken to be Mother of the Almighty: that in your childbearing the sinner’s iniquity might find a place of pardon. For this the physician raised you into his chamber of spices (5): that through you and with you the sick person might receive health.

Therefore, if you consider the cause of so great an exaltation of yours, you owe yourself wholly to the wretched, that you may bring them the antidote of reconciliation; nor can you ever find the judge’s face harsh, just as the accused never finds you inexorable.

[Col. 0704A]

For you abound and superabound in bowels of compassion, because the Holy Spirit not only filled you but came upon you unto the fullness of more abundant grace (Luke 1). Therefore let not the abundance of our daily crimes, nor iniquity added upon iniquity against our purpose, turn your face from us (Ps. 50).

We appeal to you, our medicine, on the word of your Son, who says: “Those who are well do not need a physician, but those who are ill” (Luke 5). Surely, if the physician is necessary not for the healthy but for the sick, by the same reasoning greater care of the physician must be bestowed on those whose wounds are more abundant and severe.

Therefore, Lady, since you know that all of us suffer from the wounds of our sins, intercede for all with the physician whom you bore for all. But, merciful one, bestow greater care upon those in whom you see graver weakness.

[Col. 0704B]

For why should you deny to all the aid of your magnificence, you who, just as you suffer no narrowness of compassion, suffer no narrowness of power? Your compassion is infinite; your power is infinite. The outpouring of your munificent generosity can neither exhaust nor even diminish the treasures of your glory. Give what you will: you have nothing less. You can enrich the need of each individual, yet your unfailing abundance remains.

For he is your fullness, who, being immense, receives no increase; being simple, suffers no loss; and, being eternal, has no end. Therefore now bring the exiles home, because the Mother of mercy wills and is able to dispense the sentence of judgment—she through whom God willed to adopt us, children of judgment, as sons.

Only hate the things that belong to the world and cast away the work of injustice. For although our mother is Mother of mercy, she is nevertheless also parent of justice. The rod of our correction is flexible through mercy and straight through the truth of judgment. In correction the rod is a means of return; in direction (6), the staff is a support. By the rod the accused is amended lest he perish; by the staff the righteous person is supported lest he fall.

[Col. 0704C]

Both the accused and the righteous need the Mother of the Lord. For she corrects the erring with the rod of mercy and sustains the corrected with the staff of her justice. She is flexible in the rod and strong in the staff. The rod’s stroke reforms a servant into a son; the staff’s support brings a son to the kingdom.

Therefore one who is such cries out and says, giving thanks to God: “Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me” (Ps. 22). For the Mother of the Lord has both from God: through mercy she is a rod, correcting the accused and bringing him back to grace; through uprightness she is a staff, leading the righteous and bringing him to the homeland.

The Good Shepherd used this rod and this staff when he sought the sheep which had strayed, placed it when found upon his shoulders, and brought it back to the flock (Luke 15). So great is the strength in the Mother of the Lord that in her and through her the strength of the Almighty truly humbled itself to the weakness of human flesh.

[Col. 0704D]

For the Virgin Mary is made strong precisely because in her womb the Lord, strong and mighty in battle (Ps. 23), was made frail through assuming flesh. Indeed, the Virgin’s love is strong and mighty as death (Song 8): it was able to invite, and deserved, the strength of the Almighty to endure frailty.

O Queen of angels, Lady of heaven, singularly strong in faith, privileged in merits, incomparable in power, unique in glory! For she is the iron rod by which the world is governed, the prince of the world is cast down, and hell is opened by being broken. With this strong rod the King of virtues, coming upon the strong man armed who held his court in peace, struck and crushed him (Luke 11).

Finally, this strong man’s bonds, by which he was bound, the Holy One himself fashioned and wrought in the sanctuary of the virginal womb. Do you wish to know what these bonds were? The bodily members assumed by the Word without guilt. While the unfailing strength of the Word endured our defects in these members, by thus becoming weak it overcame the strength of the enemy who had vain confidence.

[Col. 0705A]

O if the Word was so powerful in weaknesses, what if he exercised and displayed the powers of divinity?

Finally, what strength did not the rod of our power possess, to which the strength of God himself—that is, the angel Gabriel—announced the King of virtues? Gabriel, indeed, is called “strength of God”; he is said to have greeted the Virgin and brought the announcement of our salvation.

“Hail,” he says, “full of grace; the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women” (Luke 1). In these words of the angel, God the Word is made human, virginal integrity is made fruitful, and the solemnity of this day is consecrated. In his saying “full of grace,” observe the Virgin’s singular merit. In his saying “the Lord is with you,” note the virginal conception. When she is called “blessed among women,” he signifies the eternal honour of the sovereign Virgin.

How strong is the messenger’s speech! How almighty the Word whom he announces! How strong is Mary’s faith, who in a moment, believingly receiving the angel’s word, blessedly conceives God the Word and becomes Mother of God—she who scarcely dares to call herself his handmaid!

[Col. 0705B]

O Mary’s wondrous humility, to be proclaimed through all ages! Predestined from eternity to be Mother of the highest King, when from the angelic greeting she perceives the effect of a word of such great exaltation, she does not raise herself up in glory but lowers herself in heart and voice as a handmaid.

The angel speaks and greets the Virgin on behalf of him who commands salvation for Jacob (Ps. 63). The Virgin hears, is silent, and believes. She is silent reverently, hears wisely, and believes faithfully.

While all things rested and were silent in the Virgin—her most pure flesh being free from every contrary stirring of concupiscence and her most cleansed mind from every disturbance of malice—while such silence prevailed within the Virgin, the almighty Word was not silent. Coming from the royal thrones (Wis. 18), he found in the Virgin a dwelling prepared for himself.

For a dwelling fit for the Word of God is prepared where silence is kept. Otherwise, “a talkative man shall not be directed upon earth” (Ps. 138). For where concupiscence clamours in the flesh, malice cries aloud in the mind, and pride makes noise and chatters in the spirit, God the Word does not speak amid these tumults and cries, since his speech is felt through inspiration.

[Col. 0706A]

Three silences, indeed, were excellently kept in the Virgin; but of the three the almighty Word approves the middle one more. The first was brought about by virginity, restraining from the flesh every tumult of concupiscence. The last was brought about by incomparable charity, calming the mind from every disturbance. But humility maintained the middle one in a gentle spirit, safeguarding the excellence of virginity and providing for the privilege of charity, lest some danger of pride arise from the greatness of the virtues.

Therefore, while this middle silence of humility guarded all the inward and outward parts of the undefiled Virgin, and the singular humility of her gentle spirit both fostered outwardly the unfading flower of chastity and inwardly nourished the unquenchable fire of charity, the almighty Word came, as has been said, and “gave to the Virgin’s voice a voice of power” (Ps. 67), so that she might answer the angel announcing lofty things with humble words: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (Luke 1).

[Col. 0706B]

Although almighty God loves chastity in his Mother and greatly prefers charity to chastity, nevertheless in some way he prefers humility to all things, and the Lord of majesty inclines himself more familiarly toward it. For humility is capable of fullness of grace in proportion as, scorning every rigid and swollen height, it always seeks the humble plain of lower things.

Water always runs down to lower places; and moisture flowing from mountain heights is accustomed to abound more fully in the plains. For it is written: “God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. 4; 1 Pet. 5). If grace is not denied to the humble, what grace could she have possessed before all others, she who, though surpassing all highest things in incomparable dignity, surpassed all lowest things in incomparable humility?

Behold how the whole flood of divinity poured itself into the valley of virginal humility. That same valley was fruitful in wheat, for it is written: “The valleys shall abound with wheat” (Ps. 64).

[Col. 0706C]

In this valley, so watered, sprang up that grain of wheat which says of itself in the Gospel: “Unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone” (John 12). For while the heavens dropped dew from above and the clouds rained down the Righteous One, this valley opened itself to the abundance of this dew and brought forth the Saviour (Isa. 45).

From this full infusion of heavenly rain descending into the hollow depth of humility, there came to be in our Virgin a fountain of water springing up into eternal life (John 4). Woe to the tree which does not send its roots toward this moisture! It will be condemned to barrenness and will undoubtedly wither when the heat comes.

From this fountain are watered the gardens of spices—that is, the hearts of the saints fragrant with the spices of virtues. Beside the streams of these waters the God of my righteousness planted the vineyard of the righteous (Ps. 4). For the abundant vine, the vine that bears the fruit of fragrant sweetness (Ecclus. 24), is Mary’s fruitful virginity. From it proceeded that great cluster of Cyprus from the vineyards of Engaddi (Song 1), which, pressed and squeezed in the winepress of the cross, most abundantly gave the wine of all grace to drink.

[Col. 0707A]

But now “our vineyard has blossomed” (Song 2), because the rod from the root of Jesse conceived the Saviour. It put forth leaves when the power of the Most High overshadowed her and hid the mystery from angels and human beings. It bore fruit when she brought forth without pain the one whom she had conceived without contagion.

Therefore we call the conception of the Virgin Rod a flower, the veils of the mystery leaves, and the birth a nut brought forth from the rod. A nut is most fitting for the sacrament. For it signifies the one person, in three substances, of the one being born. Refer the nut’s skin to the flesh, its shell to the soul, and its kernel to the inner sweetness of inward divinity.

The skin has bitterness: the Saviour’s flesh endured passion. The stronger shell signifies the power of the soul that saves the world. The oil drawn from the kernel, because it refreshes, shines, and heals, corresponds to divinity, since it satisfies those thirsting for righteousness, enlightens the blind, and heals the wounds of sins.

[Col. 0707B]

For this purpose the Rod went forth from the root of Jesse: that it might so flower and bring forth such fruits for us. Do you wish to see the Virgin blooming with flowers? If with the eye of chaste contemplation you survey the enclosed garden, you will perceive and sense in it the unfading lily of virginity growing white, the inviolable violet of humility exhaling fragrance, and the rose of unquenchable charity growing red.

Where the Blessed Virgin flowered in virtues, she put forth leaves in the merits of works; in giving birth she produced the fruit, the Holy of holies.

But another says to me: Why do you speak of the fruit of the rod when the prophet spoke only of the flower? Certainly because the flower itself is also fruit: “My flowers,” she says, “are fruits of honour and integrity” (Ecclus. 24). These are words of Wisdom, but they are also fittingly applied to the person of the Mother of the Lord.

Do you then approve that the Virgin’s Son, God and man, should be called flower according to his humanity and fruit according to his divinity? For *fructus*, “fruit,” derives from *frui*, “to enjoy.” Therefore eternal divinity is fruit, in which the holy angels and the souls of the saints delight with perpetual joy.

[Col. 0707C]

Nor is divinity inappropriately called fruit, because it makes happy those who enjoy it. For we are not properly said to enjoy except things which make us happy. To enjoy is to cleave in love to some thing solely for its own sake.

[Col. 0707D]

But since man is God and God is man, we can without any distinction call our Redeemer both flower and fruit. Yet the tenderness of a flower more suitably signifies the frailty of the flesh assumed. For a flower has the sweetness of scent, while fruit has the solidity of taste. And although the flesh has been assumed into God, and thus the flower into the fruit, nevertheless, in view of the condition of the body still mortal and of tender age, the substance of flesh is called by the name of flower.

True flesh of Christ is also fruit in such a state; but this could be said more truly and perfectly when, through his Passion, he passed from the necessity of suffering and dying to impassibility and immortality; when, through his temporal death, he freed humankind from perpetual death. But since we are not yet fit [Col. 0708A] to taste the savour of the fruit, let us meanwhile—what is less, yet sufficient for the present, insofar as grace helps—apply the sense of faith to the fragrance of this flower. Let us consider the fruit of the rod, insofar as the prophet calls it a flower rather than fruit, although we undoubtedly hope for the fruit of our redemption in that very flower. For, according to the ordinance of the Father’s will, as he deigned to become man for human beings, so too he willed, for human beings, to die as man. Otherwise his being born would have profited us nothing unless our redemption had profited us (Office for Holy Saturday). This flower has beauty in appearance, sweetness in scent, softness in touch, tenderness in substance, and fruit in the form of flesh. How beautiful is this flower at its rising, how bright in whiteness!

[Col. 0708B] The Prophet indicates its beauty to you when he calls him fairer than the children of men (Ps. 44). Understand this beauty not as bodily brightness, but as innocence of life and the splendour of virtue. This flower is so beautiful that no ugliness of sin’s stain defiles him in any respect. So great is the fragrance breathed forth from this flower that the East itself breathes it in, and the first fruits of the Gentiles hasten to it in the three Magi (Matt. 2). They did indeed bring spices with them, but the fragrance of the new flower surpassed their scents. This fragrance drives away the stench of crimes and everywhere diffuses the fragrance of faith and virtue. What does it mean that this flower is soft to the touch, except that Christ, renewing the world by his birth, is everywhere meek and humble? Yet this flower [Col. 0708C] has tenderness in its substance, because Christ as man, before he suffered, being subject to our infirmities, was found frail in human flesh. And in all these respects the flower promised the fruit which he gave in his season (Ps. 1), namely when he died for our offences, freeing us from death, and rose again for our justification (Rom. 4), showing what we ought to hope for.

But because the frailty of passible nature made this Flower tender, it could therefore be crushed and bruised by the hands of the unbelieving Jews. For because his nature was capable of suffering, he could be killed by the Jews. Yet this crushing of the flower did not restrain its fragrance but increased it; did not diminish it but augmented it. [Col. 0708D] So greatly does this flower breathe forth fragrance while it is crushed and expires that, by its scent, the dead breathe again unto life. So greatly, I say, does it breathe forth fragrance that, expiring among the hands of the Jews, it inspires confession in the thief (Luke 23), faith in the centurion, and makes many bodies of saints who had slept breathe again unto life (Matt. 27). Does it not seem to you that the thief’s mind perceived this fragrance, when, rebuking his companion and reproving the stench of his own crimes, he said: “We indeed receive the due reward of our deeds; but this man has done nothing evil” (Luke 23)? Already, with the nostrils of a wholly converted mind, drawing in the fragrance of the trampled flower, he says: “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom” (ibid.). It is as though he said: “Wonderful indeed, Lord, is the fragrance which [Col. 0709A] I perceive in your Passion; but I delight more in the fullness of the eternal savour which you can bestow in your kingdom.” O fragrant flower, whose scent raises the dead, whose loveliness nourishes the angels! Fragrant everywhere, beautiful everywhere: beautiful in the rod from which it is born; beautiful in the enclosed garden from which it is brought forth; beautiful in the garden where it is betrayed; beautiful in the garden where it is laid away; beautiful on the tree of the cross where it is crushed; beautiful in the garden of paradise, where it is tasted by the holy angels in eternal fragrance and perpetual refreshment. Do you see how rightly he is called a flower, who is found almost nowhere except in a garden? By the fragrance of this flower, the guilty breathe again toward pardon, the sinner toward forgiveness, the martyr is strengthened toward victory, and the pilgrim is directed toward his homeland.

When [Col. 0709B] our Rod brings forth this Flower, our spring begins; winter passes, rain departs, while the renewed season of mercy washes away the extravagance of crimes and the old age of former life. Therefore, in this solemnity, while flowers appear in our land, the year of kindness and mercy begins; its beginning is prepared by the springtime season—that is, the season of flowers. Understand it as the day of salvation, when the Virgin of virgins brings forth from the root of Jesse the flower of virtues. Hence, as the earth opens and brings forth the Saviour, we may call the first month of the year, renewing the world unto grace, a kind of April. For April—because it is called April from the opening, at such a time, of mother earth’s bosom for producing the shoots of things—suits this mystery: this solemnity is celebrated [Col. 0709C] in springtime, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April [25 March]. For on this day and at this season, the virgin bosom of humility opened itself to the rain of the angelic salutation; and the Virgin, conceiving by the Holy Spirit, flowered like a rod, when, through the aid and operation of the Holy Spirit, she supplied her own most pure flesh for childbirth, creating flesh from it. This flower rose from the rod when the Son of God came from conception to birth. This flower rose when the Saviour increased in wisdom, age, and grace before God and men, and made known to men more and more that he was God.

Yet he did not increase in wisdom or grace in himself, since he was perfect; rather, he is said to have increased in human beings, who could advance by means of his perfection. What of the fact that the cruel Jew crushed this flower on the same day on which the rod of loving-kindness brought it forth? For Christ is believed to have been killed by the Jews on the same day on which he was conceived by the Virgin Mother—namely, the eighth day before the Kalends of April [25 March]. Hence the Law of Moses, prophesying, forbids the Jew, saying: “You shall not boil a kid in its mother’s milk” (Exod. 23). From the hour of conception a woman is said to have milk [Col. 0709D] in her breasts. The kid offered for sin signifies Christ, who is sacrificed for the crime of the world. But the Jew boiled the kid in its mother’s milk when, on the day of his conception, he applied the fire of the Passion to Christ.

Nor should it be passed over that this day is observed in March, the time at which kings customarily go forth to war. For the month of March takes its name from Mars—that is, from war. Rightly, then, this day marks the month of March, that is, the time of war, on which the Lord of hosts came through the Virgin, like a mighty warrior, to defeat the prince of the world. Hence, coming to overthrow our evils, he uses rod and axe: the rod as teacher, the axe as cultivator. What then remains for us except to live more uprightly, for whose sake God is known to have done all things? For the rod is the teaching of virginal virtue, by which he corrects us; the axe is the terrible judgment of God, by which he cuts down the uncorrected. Therefore let us attend to the rod and change, so that we may imitate it. Let us attend to the axe and be afraid, so that we may change. Let us consider that mercy [Col. 0710B] makes the rod flexible, truth straight. For in it mercy and truth have met one another. Let us learn from this example to be merciful in disposition and truthful in speech. Justice—that is, humility—makes the rod level, namely without any crookedness of fault. For humility is called justice, as the Lord, coming to John’s baptism, when John was preventing him, testified by saying: “Allow it now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfil all justice” (Matt. 3), that is, all humility.

But of what kind of tree is this rod? It is surely an olive tree; for the olive is a sign of peace. True peace is not ordinarily present without a kiss. But in this Rod, “justice and peace have kissed” (Ps. 84). For justice alone receives the kiss of true peace, which the swelling of pride does not admit at all. Therefore let us also, by this example, be humble in spirit, that we may have peace both with God and with our brothers. True humility, while gladly subjecting itself to each person, cannot lack that good of peace by which it strives to put itself before no one. For even suffering persecution for righteousness does not deprive humility of peace; rather, humility itself always rejoices in tribulation. If we have plucked these flowers from the rod of virtue, [Col. 0710C] let us fear losing them; if we have not yet plucked them, let us fear perishing. Nevertheless, through fear of the axe we can breathe again somewhat toward the scent of the flower, that is, toward hope of recovering virtue. The scent of the flower leads to the fruit, because hope invites us to the kingdom. Rod and axe work fear in us; the scent of the flower and the taste of its savour kindle love. Fear and love correct our life. Fear cuts away the thorns of vices; love plants the growths of virtues. Fear constricts you, whether because you have sinned or lest you sin; love expands you, so that you may hope and rejoice. Those whom the rod of heavenly teaching corrects and the fear of divine judgment stirs up, the flower refreshes meanwhile by its fragrance and afterward leads to the taste of eternal fruit. For in the present life our Saviour displays himself as a fragrant flower to the elect, to whom he promises the eternal goods to be hoped for. But when they attain the promises, he will be fruit that satisfies for ever.

But since without the grace of the Holy Spirit we can neither [Col. 0711A] withdraw from evils nor make progress in goods at all, let us raise both the sense of the heart and its sight toward the flower which rose from the Rod. For the scent of this flower both drives away the stench of carnal desire and restores the reputation of one’s good name. The flower’s beauty and loveliness, moreover, drives out the age-old ugliness of a deformed conscience. The scent of the flower is the Spirit of the Lord, who rests most fully in Christ. For how could the goodness of the Holy Spirit fail to find rest in him in whom there is absolutely no contradiction of sin? This scent is that power of which it is written: “Power went forth from him and healed all” (Luke 6). This same flower of the field and lily of the valleys breathed out this scent and offered it to the nostrils of the Jews when, taking up the scroll in their synagogue, he read in their hearing that passage of Isaiah the prophet: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me” (Isa. 61; Luke 4). And, to show that this Spirit made him fragrant, he added: “Because he has anointed me” (ibid.). And, because the dead were to breathe again at this scent, he added: “He has sent me to preach the gospel to the poor,” and the words following (ibid.). Hence, when the reading was finished, he said to them that “today this prophecy has been fulfilled in your hearing” (ibid.).

This Spirit indeed came upon the Virgin and overshadowed her for the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation (Luke 4). But the flower rising from the Rod had that Spirit in a far different manner, because the Holy Spirit rested most fully upon the Virgin’s Son. In the other saints the Spirit of the Lord dwells—for without him they cannot be holy—but not so excellently, not so truly, since they are neither one with him in unity of substance nor altogether without the stain of fault. For who shall boast that he has a pure heart, when the apostle John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1)? But the only-begotten Son of God, both insofar as he is God, is of the same nature as the Father and the Holy Spirit, although a different person, and insofar as he is man, received the same Spirit without measure (John 3). Whoever, following the example of the Virgin Mother, corrects himself everywhere, fears the axe of God’s strict judgment. By the laborious concern of fear he tends toward the rest of love. But [Col. 0711D] he does not yet attain the rest he desires unless he flowers anew through the scent of the flower which rose from the Rod, and in whom the Spirit of the Lord rests in all fullness. For faith, hope, and love of the Lord’s incarnation now bring about our sabbath in the repose of conscience and lead us from this sabbath of the heart to the sabbath of eternal rest. May the Son of the Virgin, bridegroom of the Church, Christ our Lord, bring us to it.

## SERMON II. ON THE CHILDBIRTH OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN

“Behold, the King comes” (Matt. 21); let us run to meet our Saviour. The bride exults all the more abundantly at the coming of the Bridegroom, the more certain she is concerning him. For she would not point out from afar one who was coming unless [Col. 0712A] she saw him present. Unless she rejoiced with sure consolation in the presence of the one approaching, she would by no means invite others to share in her joy. Therefore, rejoicing and praising, she sounds forth the proclamation of a laudatory invitation, saying: “Behold, the King comes,” and so forth. It is as though the Church, bride of the eternal King, said: “Not ignorant of the divine counsel, not deprived of the desire of my expectation: behold, ‘the Desired of all nations comes’ (Hag. 2); behold, the salvation of all comes. There will no longer be fear within our borders, because within the bounds of our allotted inheritance I behold the presence of the common Saviour. Behold, he comes—the one prefigured in the patriarchs, promised by the prophets, now presented by angels: ‘The Holy One to be born from you,’ the angel says to Mary, ‘shall be called the Son of God’” (Luke 1).

“Behold” is the voice both of one who points out and of one who marvels and rejoices. The one whom she points out as marvellous, she marvels at as visible; and thereby she perceives that the cause of this manifestation is the more lovable, proving and experiencing that it belongs to love alone. “Behold,” she says, “he comes whom I have always desired, whom I have sought with every prayer, whose promises and salutations I have so often received through messengers. Behold, he comes in person, that he may kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” Whence does he come, and where does he go? In what manner does he come, and whither does he pass? How does he come, and when? How far does he descend, and why does he come?

To come is to pass from place to place. To come is to leave the place in which one stood and approach another in which one begins to be. How, then, is he said to come who does not change? “I am God,” he says, “and I do not change” (Mal. 3). How is he said to pass from place to place who is believed with undoubting faith to be wholly present everywhere, and who is affirmed to fill heaven and earth with the uncircumscribed essence of his ever-present majesty? Yet he comes when he makes himself known to human minds through the grace of inward inspiration. He comes when he shows that he is not lacking through his help. He comes when he presents himself as visible in the substance of flesh. But whence he comes, he himself declares, saying: “I came forth from God and came” (John 8). Therefore God comes from God: the rising from on high, the good Word from the Father’s heart, the almighty Speech from the royal seats, the Lord from heaven, brightness from the Sun, power from omnipotence, the only Son from the Father’s bosom—as the Father himself says to the Son in the Psalm: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. 109).

Therefore he comes—he comes when he is born and proceeds from the Father. He comes when, graciously making this same ineffable generation known thus far, he draws human hearts to experience his sweetness. He comes when, by his display of kindness and assumption of humanity, preceding us in every charity, he teaches how greatly he loves and how greatly he wishes to be loved. Yet he comes from afar, not because he is not most present to every creature, but because he is highest in majesty, most hidden in invisibility, most simple in subtlety, most incorruptible in truth, most just in equity, and most alien to all iniquity. Thus he comes from afar not because he who is most present is far away, but because corruption—which creates distance between Creator and creature—is far from him.

[Col. 0713A] But he who thus comes, and comes from there—where does he go? Scripture says that “his face was set toward Jerusalem” (Luke 9), and therefore he was not received by the Samaritans. Yet he himself says: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15). Behold, the shepherd goes to the sheep, namely to seek and bring back those that had perished. He willingly turns aside to Jerusalem, because true peace eagerly gathers itself to him whom it recognizes as directing himself and aspiring toward the vision of peace. For Jerusalem is interpreted “vision of peace.” The vision of peace is knowledge, approbation, and contemplation of the Trinity. In knowledge there is faith; in approbation, choice; in contemplation, experience. The Trinity is not unsuitably called peace, because this name *pax* (“peace”) consists of three letters, just as the Godhead is in three persons.

The first letter of this name denotes the Father; the letter following denotes the Son, who says in the Apocalypse: “I am Alpha and Omega, [Col. 0713B] the beginning and the end” (Rev. 1); and in the Gospel: “I am the beginning, even I who speak to you” (John 8). For *alpha* is interpreted “beginning.” The double consonant *x* signifies the Holy Spirit, who is the bond and harmony of the two. Or it is called a double consonant because in the hearts of the elect it works a twofold love, through which concord toward God and neighbour is maintained. Or indeed it is called a double consonant because, when by the inward sprinkling of its dew it touches and anoints the soul and by necessary mortification extinguishes the pleasures of the flesh, it produces the harmony of sweet concord from psaltery and lyre; for “the psaltery is pleasant with the lyre” (Ps. 80). Through this also the Holy Spirit makes each of the elect a Jerusalem—that is, a vision of peace—when, having calmed the contradictions and conflicts of flesh and spirit, he shows each person to be a lover and pursuer of everlasting and eternal peace. For all these things are wrought by the one and same Spirit of peace and love.

But if Jerusalem is called the vision of peace—that is, of God—what else should the house of Israel be called but the Church of the elect, from which and in which God is seen? For Israel is interpreted “seeing God.” What, then, are the lost sheep of the house of Israel except certain persons predestined unto life, yet, by the exacting justice of God, wrapped in the darkness of sins? But why are they called sheep when through injustice they have abandoned innocence and are therefore said to have perished from the house of Israel? Nevertheless they are sheep by reason of election and by the merit of predestination, although for the present they seem lost by the ugliness of guilty action. For such people are those who, although they have abandoned the simplicity of innocence, do not flee the humility of repentance; remembering the good things which they had within, they groan outwardly and say: “Come, Lord, and do not delay; forgive the crimes of your people Israel” (Ecclesiastical Office).

Behold, then, whence he comes and to whom he comes. But in what manner does he come? Who could suffice to explain this? Certainly he comes weak and almighty, small and immeasurable, temporal and eternal, localized and uncircumscribed, capable of suffering and unchangeable, man and God, infant and Word; poor and rich, wise and choosing what is foolish in the world, innocent and appearing in the likeness of sinful flesh. Finally, he comes white and ruddy, as his bride describes him: white because he is “the brightness of eternal light” (Wis. 7); ruddy because he is bloodied by his Passion; white in freedom from sin; ruddy, burning with love; white, shining in the beauty of virtues; ruddy, burning with zeal. According to the “likeness of sinful flesh,” he comes “having neither form nor comeliness” (Isa. 53); according to freedom from sin, he comes “fair in form beyond the children of men” [Col. 0714B] (Ps. 44), as the Father says to him through the Psalmist: “In your splendour and your beauty, give heed; go forth prosperously and reign” (ibid.).

Let us now see by what way he came (7). The Virgin Mary was his way. Through the Virgin’s mind and womb he completed the journeys of his eternity. There “mercy and truth met one another” (Ps. 84), which are “all the ways of the Lord” (Ps. 24). For indeed all the ways of the Lord are “mercy and truth” (ibid.). With the Virgin too, “justice and peace have kissed” (Ps. 84), bringing the King of justice and Author of peace to the work of human salvation. These are called the journeys of eternity because our salvation came to us through them and eternity is found in each of them. Of the Lord’s mercy it is said: “The mercy of the Lord is from eternity” (Ps. 102); of truth: “And the truth of the Lord endures for ever” [Col. 0714C] (Ps. 116); “his justice endures for ever and ever” (Ps. 111); his peace “surpasses every understanding” (Phil. 4), and “of his peace there shall be no end” (Luke 1). These are the straight ways of the Lord, making hearts glad (Ps. 18); and by these straight ways the Lord led the Righteous One and brought him as far as the Virgin’s womb, where he might begin the work of our deliverance. There, as has been said, the Virgin Mary is in a sense both the way of life through which the King of virtues came to us and, no less, our way returning us to him (8). She is the Mother of mercy; she is she from whom truth springs (9); she is the Queen of justice; she is the completion of our peace.

And mercy, establishing in the Virgin’s affections and womb a dwelling most fitting for itself, as though in a mother’s bosom, both compassionated effectively the miseries of humankind and sweetly remembered the Lord’s mercies, saying: “Where are your ancient mercies, Lord, as you swore to David in your truth?” (Ps. 88). And again: “Have mercy, God, upon your people over whom your name has been invoked” (Ecclus. 36), and so forth. Truth, however, standing in the firm splendour of the incorruption of her virginal purpose and of her unviolated womb in childbirth, both disclosed the shadows of legal figures and exposed the darkness of sins, saying (10): “The Law and the prophets were until Mary” (Luke 16). And again: “Children of men, how long will you be heavy-hearted? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” [Col. 0715A] (Ps. 90, as printed). Namely, because within the Virgin’s womb the Lord made his Holy One wonderful (Ps. 4). Justice also, claiming the Virgin’s works as its own by singular perfection and eagerly longing with all desire for the kiss of peace, boasted even in the long-suffering of endurance and spoke thus: “When I called, the God of my justice heard me; in tribulation you made room for me” (ibid.). And: “We will run after the fragrance of your ointments” (Song 1).

Moreover peace, withdrawing itself into the innermost secret of most hidden purity, calmed the Virgin’s conscience under the testimony of fuller grace, gladdening her with the oil of joy and exultation and saying: “My beloved is mine, and I am his” (Song 2); and: “What have I in heaven, and what have I desired from you upon earth? My flesh and my heart have failed; God is the God of my heart” (Ps. 72). Thus, as has been said, the Virgin had mercy in affection, truth in childbirth, justice in action, and peace in spiritual repose, in which flesh and Spirit, all opposition ceasing, kept the joyful feast-days of inward solemnity. The Virgin’s holiness may fittingly be called the way of virtue through which Christ, the power and wisdom of God, came to the weak and foolish. He drank so deeply from the torrent of our mortality and passibility on this way (Ps. 109), and the Lord of majesty found this way so narrow (Matt. 7), that the necessity of suffering and dying—which he voluntarily received from the Virgin—both compressed the almighty Word into a child and emptied the Lord of glory even unto the form of a servant [Col. 0715C] (Phil. 2).

Nevertheless, equity makes straight this way by which he came; truth makes it sure; virginity, pure; fruitfulness, fruitful; piety, accessible; charity, common; humility, easy; singularity, wondrous; peace, lovable; eternity, secure. All these things are found in our Virgin, singularly marvellous and marvellously singular. Happy the way: whoever holds to it will not go astray (2 Pet. 2). Happy Mary: whoever perseveringly loves her will not perish! (John 3.) Blessed is he who comes through her; blessed is she through whom blessing comes; blessed is he who, with her as guide, meets the one who comes. But because we now hold the way through which he comes, it pleases us to examine how he comes.

[Col. 0715D] “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (John 12); blessed is he who comes in the clouds of heaven (Matt. 24); blessed is he who comes “leaping upon the mountains and skipping over the hills” (Song 2). The bride teaches us what his name is when she says: “Your name is oil poured out” (Song 1). How blessed is he who comes wholly in oil! He comes in the oil of grace, to pour it in for healing. He comes in oil, to enlighten unto knowledge. He comes in oil, to season morals unto wisdom. For he is the name of the Father, oil for the infirm, the Son as the brightness of oil, the seasoning of heavenly Wisdom. He comes in the clouds of heaven because, as the heavens drop dew from above and the clouds pour down voluntary rain (Isa. 45), Christ communicated to the children of the Church both the name of royal anointing and the anointing of the royal name. Christ indeed was anointed with this oil above his companions (Ps. 64, as printed), but he nevertheless granted participation in his anointing and his name to all Christians. Woe to one who shares the name of anointing but, through evil living, refuses to possess the reality of that name. For it befits a Christian, through the pouring forth of sacred anointing, to be receptive, and through the title of the royal [Col. 0716A] name to possess royal dignity. A Christian is called an anointed one, undoubtedly as priest and king, since anointing belongs only to priests and kings. Hence Peter speaks to all Christians: “But you are an elect race, a royal priesthood” (1 Pet. 2).

But Christ is the flask of this oil: although each believer is anointed from it, nevertheless the flask of oil is not diminished (3 Kgs. 17). For Christ did not receive the Spirit by measure, while grace has been given to each of the faithful according to the measure of the gift (Eph. 4). This anointing of grace comes to us in clouds and from the clouds of heaven. Rightly the prophet prays that the clouds may rain down the Just One (Isa. 45), because the rain of this anointing justifies the ungodly. For the yoke of sin rots away before the oil when sin is loosed in confession and love of Christ’s name. But what are the clouds of heaven except the hidden inspirations of the Holy Spirit, which drench the mind with the dew of the Holy Spirit, or the very members of Christ’s body, which cloud over the divinity hidden in him? For clouds both water the earth and cover heaven. The clouds of heaven are also the preachers of the kingdom, [Col. 0716C] who fly like clouds and flash as they move through the air of divine contemplation. If heaven is called Sacred Scripture, the clouds of heaven may be called the figures and enigmas of sacred speech; or if heaven is called the holy Church, what will the clouds of heaven be except the sacraments of the Church? In these clouds is contained the water of our washing—that is, knowledge and love of our Redeemer. Hence it is written: “He binds the waters in the clouds” (Job 26).

He also comes “leaping upon the mountains and skipping over the hills” (Song 2), because he transcends the heights of angels and human beings. He leaps on the mountains as the fountain of God leaping unto eternal life (John 4). For he is the mountain of olives, the rich mountain (Ps. 67), the mountain on the summit of the mountains. He skips over the hills because he surpasses by incomparable sublimity the merits of all the saints—which indeed he himself bestowed from his fullness. Behold how he comes. But when does he come, who comes in this manner? The Apostle speaks of the time of his coming, saying: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son upon earth” (Gal. 4). The Son of God never comes except in the fullness of time. The fullness of time is the time predetermined in his providence, when, according to his ordinance, he wills and ought to come. But what time accords with his ordering, and when it arrives as it has been preordained, he alone knows, and he has left us without knowledge of this.

“We do not know,” as he himself says in the Gospel, [Col. 0717A] “when our Lord will come: in the evening, or at midnight, or at cockcrow, or in the morning” (Mark 13). He comes in the evening when he corrects and pierces with compunction, by the unexpected prevenience of his grace, one who is approaching his end and does not deserve it, turning him away from his perversity. At this time he came to the thief, to whom, as he was at the point of death, he so suddenly both granted the merit of faith and opened paradise (Luke 23). He comes at midnight when he leads one placed in the darkness of ignorance or amid tribulations, by unmerited grace, to the haven of light or refreshment. He comes at cockcrow when, through the words of preaching or sacred reading, he turns the hearts of hearers. He comes in the morning when, after the night of crimes has passed and the will to sin has been laid aside, the radiance of mercy pours in the morning light of repentance.

Did he not [Col. 0717B] come to Adam in the evening, when, in the breeze after midday, as the day was declining toward evening and innocence declining into guilt, Adam hid himself from the face of the sun, the warmth of charity grew cold, and the brightness of immortality set? Did he not come at midnight into Egypt, when, intending to rescue his people set amid the greatest affliction, he struck down Egypt’s firstborn? (Exod. 12.) So too he came at cockcrow, when, in accordance with the promises of the legal sacraments and the utterances of the prophets, he came through a Virgin to liberate humankind. For the cock’s crow, herald of the coming light, signifies the prophetic utterance by which the advent of the true Light was foretold. And behold, he will come again in the morning, when, after the night of this age, the day of the final judgment shall dawn. Yet we do not know whether that day [Col. 0717C] will be for us the dawn of eternal light or—God avert it!—the twilight of eternal night. Therefore we must always remain in fear and watchfulness; for although by faith we are certain of the Judge’s coming, we have no certainty when he will come, or in what manner he will come to us. “For no one knows,” as it is written, “whether he shall then be worthy of love or hatred” (Eccles. 9).

But this first advent of our Savior is properly and spiritually called the fullness of time, since, that is, when the times ordained by divine providence had been fulfilled, the Scriptures were fulfilled, and to the fullness of human misery was opposed the fullness of God’s mercy. “For grace abounded all the more where iniquity abounded” [Col. 0717D] (1 Tim. 1). Where the consummation of righteousness brought about the consummation of iniquity, there the prophet David saw the end of every consummation. The time of this fullness was the fullness of this time: it is that mid-silence, or middle of the night, in which the almighty Word came from the royal thrones and, breaking the silence of unbelief or distrust, “made the tongues of infants eloquent” (Wis. 10). Rightly and fittingly the mediating Word hastens to the middle and to silence. For mid-silence—that is, a full and perfect cessation from good—had arisen in the deep night of ignorance from a long forgetfulness of God. Meanwhile the Son of our Mediatrix, the almighty Mediator, came into the midst in order to remove such silence from the midst; and he, the Word as an infant, poured himself into infants, in order to perfect praise from the mouths of infants [Col. 0718A] (Ps. 8). The Utterance came to silence; the Word came into infancy; and, wonderfully, through the silence of his infancy, he “made the tongues of infants eloquent” and, according to the prophet, “laid waste the tongue of the Egyptian sea” (Isa. 11). For through the mystery of the incarnate Word, while Wisdom appeared as infancy, “the mouth of those speaking iniquity was stopped” (Ps. 62). And according to the same prophet: “All iniquity shall stop its own mouth” (Ps. 106).

Therefore the swiftly running Word (Ps. 147), who so gently and silently ordered the mysteries of our salvation, while he “reaches mightily from end to end” (Wis. 8), also deigned to descend even into the depths of our misery. The depths of our misery are: to be conceived in frail flesh, to be born for labor, [Col. 0718B] to be subjected to the deficiencies of human necessity, to be confined in the prison of this exile, not to be without the likeness of sinful flesh, and to be bound by the laws of death. The almighty Word, God’s Son, assumed all these necessities without sin, not from necessity but by his will; and while he alone, “free among the dead” (Ps. 87), voluntarily submits himself to such necessities, he restores us to true freedom. Hence the Apostle says: “He delivered us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his charity” (Col. 1). Surely you have seen, O son of man, how far the Son of God descended, how greatly the Father of mercies bent down toward the wretched.

For everything that the merciful and compassionate Lord did for the wretched was wholly mercy and compassion. Yet, turning [Col. 0718C] to this, you will see still greater acts of compassion. Consider the kind of his passion and death; consider the depth of the lowest hell. Surely, ending his temporal life by the punishment of the cross, he triumphed over death’s dominion; and, in order to despoil hell, he did not shrink from descending there. There he bit hell, and, dying, inflicted a bite upon death, by which the bite of forbidden food—from which death arose—received its recompense. O marvelous humility of divine sublimity! O astounding condescension of heavenly mercy! What is harsher among torments than the punishment of the cross? What is more disgraceful among reproaches than the form of the cross? Yet he who emptied himself into the form of a servant did not shrink from humbly casting himself down even unto death, the death of the cross (Phil. 2). And he who, as King of Glory, [Col. 0718D] abides continually in heaven, also powerfully despoiled hell through the presence of his condescension.

For though our King appeared in weakness, he did not lose the fullness of power. Indeed, he did not lack royal power even in weakness; and as great as was his power in the creation of all things, so great was his patience in enduring evils. Just as the world, created from nothing—to which he willed and was able to give existence and form—proclaims the omnipotence of our King, so in him the invincible strength of patience displays the distinction of royal virtue, by which the world is reformed unto life. Therefore the King came in power and anointing: for without anointing he does not possess royal dignity, nor without royal power does he possess royal anointing. The King came, by royal power, strong and [Col. 0719A] upright; by anointing, gentle and peaceful. He came anointed with ointments, as the anointing of the sick; he came in the strength of a king, as the effective governance of souls. Therefore, since the King of kings has neither the name nor the dignity of king apart from anointing, our King is rightly called Christ, a name signifying both royal and priestly anointing. Christ is anointed as king and priest with invisible oil, whom, according to Peter’s statement, “God the Father anointed with the Holy Spirit and power” (Acts 10). Filled with this oil—that is, receiving the Holy Spirit without measure—he both grants the kingdom of grace to those who share in him and, offering himself for them, shows himself to be the true priest.

Therefore let us go out to meet our King; and because he comes anointed with the ointments from which he derives the name of anointing, [Col. 0719B] let us run to him, and let us run in the fragrance of his ointments (Song 1). His ointments are the charisms of the Holy Spirit, with which, as with the oil of gladness, he is anointed above his companions (Ps. 44). The fragrance of the ointments is faith and love of the virtues, which, just as they are possessed most fully in him, so are bestowed from his fullness, according to the purpose of his dispensation, upon whomever he wills. We meet him well if, attending to why he came and approving in unfeigned faith the cause of his advent, we gratefully and faithfully embrace the price of our redemption offered to us. For this purpose he came: to redeem us, not with corruptible gold or silver, but with the incorruptible price of his own blood (1 Pet. 1). The entire reason for his advent is our salvation. Therefore [Col. 0719C] we ought to meet our King with all the more devotion and festivity because we recognize that he, having no need, serves the interests of the undeserving by such gratuitous goodness. Let us therefore meet our Savior, who comes to us and for us, not with bodily movements but with the progress of faith, the steps of our affections, and works of virtue, so that, as he came to us by assuming humanity, he may likewise come into us and establish his dwelling in us. He who with the Father, etc.

## Sermon III. On the Birth of the Blessed Virgin

“Sing to the Lord a new song, for he has done marvelous things” (Ps. 149). Today’s celebration of newness must be extolled with new praises [Col. 0719D]. For what is not new where the Lord of heaven and earth makes a new heaven and a new earth? The Virgin’s childbirth is indeed a new heaven; the Virgin’s womb is a new earth. Through these two all things become new, while by the new birth of God’s Word in flesh the sorrowful oldness is cast off (12). O what marvelous newness, in which the Ancient of Days becomes a child of one night! In which the Word is flesh, Wisdom an infant, God a human being, a Virgin a mother, and the Lord and Creator of all the son of his own handmaid!

Therefore a renewed heart is needed to receive the joy of so great a newness. Let the voice of a horn trumpet sound (Ps. 97) on the solemnity of the new moon. Let the voice of exultation (Ps. 117) and salvation be heard in the tents of the righteous (Ps. 111), because the Sun of righteousness rises in the tents of sinners: for light has arisen [Col. 0720A] in the darkness for those upright in heart. And although the darkness did not comprehend the light shining in darkness (John 1), the children of light nevertheless discern his light amid the darkness. Therefore they sing a new song and say: “A child is born” (Isa. 9). To sing this, to believe it, love it, and hope for it, is urged not only upon the righteous but also upon sinners. “Sing,” he says, “to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth.” All the earth means every human being, lest perhaps the righteous should wish to exclude the sinner from this praise or joy. Indeed, almost everything here concerns the sinner; because Jesus came not to call the righteous (Matt. 9), but to seek and save what had been lost (Luke 19). It therefore belongs to all to sing a new song, and he who came, as Lord of all, to be born for all excludes no one from salvation, so far as depends on him.

For the righteous, the new song is the new life by which they feast in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (1 Cor. 5), rejoice before God, and delight in gladness (Ps. 67). For sinners, the new song is fear and repentance, by which, being reborn in the Son of God, they cast aside old things as new things come upon them, and rise again to feed upon the oldest of old things. New are the things which the new Adam instituted through the mystery of a new birth; old are guilt and punishment, in which the propagated generation of corruptible old Adam placed us; the oldest of old things is that ineffable and eternal birth by which God the Father, before Lucifer, generated from his own substance his Word, equal and like to himself in all things (Ps. 109). To love Christ’s temporal birth and, because of love for it, to despise everything else, is to prefer new things that come upon us to old things. But to believe and understand his eternal birth and, in contemplation of it, to drive away, as far as possible, everything that enters the mind, is to restore the oldest of old things as the mind’s food and delight.

The righteous person feeds upon these delights and cannot fail to sing a new song, when such sweet refreshment has made him new. By the same mercy of God, the sinner is reborn through repentance to these same delights; nor can he fail to sing a new song when, for his renewal, he sees the delights of angels set before him beyond his merits. Hence we hear “the sound of one feasting amid the voice of exultation and confession” [Col. 0720D] (Ps. 41). The humble sinner indeed feasts when he feeds upon his tears, saying: “My tears were my bread day and night” (ibid.). But amid the feast a sound is heard when groaning resounds among the tears, or indeed when praise of the Redeemer’s mercy is joined to accusation of one’s own iniquity. That praise has the voice of exultation, and the accusation has the voice of confession; thus the sound of one feasting is amid the voice of exultation and confession. “Why then are you sad, O my soul, and why do you trouble me?” (ibid.) Although you are earth through the mass of crimes, although weighty action drags you downward, nonetheless sing to the Lord a new song, which all the earth is commanded to sing. “Hope in God [Col. 0721A]” (ibid.), and the very longing of hope will be a new song for you. Suspended and stretched out by such desire, you will cast off downward the old human being with its deeds, and freely flying upward you will seek the new human being, created according to God (Eph. 4). Then you will follow the Apostle’s voice as he exhorts: “Set your minds on the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God” (Col. 3).

Therefore sing, my soul; sing to the Lord a new song, and now cease singing the old song. The old song is that discordant harmony by which, perversely associating yourself with the ancient enemy, you have shamefully conformed yourself to this age—against what the Apostle forbids when he says: “Do not be conformed to this age” (Rom. 12). The old song is exultation in earthly things, happiness in transitory things, joy in evil deeds, and impunity in sins. Finally, the old song is pride, the beginning of every sin, which took its beginning from the ancient enemy and made the first human being old through imitation of wickedness. Finally, this oldness, passing to all the children of old Adam as though by a certain hereditary right, made them so subject to the laws of the lethargic serpent that, unless the new birth in flesh of the Only-begotten came to their aid, that condemnable oldness would necessarily drag them to destruction. Hence the Apostle: “What is becoming old and aged is near to destruction” (Heb. 8).

Thus the sound of this old song had gone out over all the earth and had occupied everyone’s ears so completely that scarcely anywhere was the harmony of heavenly music heard [Col. 0721C], never was obedience rendered to the Word of God, and the sweetest commandments of life were not received by human hearing. For the old song is where there are shouting and indignation, contention and blasphemy, quarrels and hatred, tumult and unrest; where spiritual wickednesses join themselves to carnal vices; where, finally, from the pride of the heart the impurity of the mouth bursts forth into the iniquity of action. For with such badly harmonizing sounds the deceptive melody of the old song is played out—namely through breath, voice, and striking. Instrumental music too is performed in these three modes.

But, as concerns the present matter, breath pertains to the swelling of pride, which makes the heart’s understanding puffed up. Voice pertains to the use of speech, by which an impure word proceeds from the swollen heart. Touch pertains to the movement [Col. 0721D] of the body, by which an unjust work is performed. Therefore, while one serves the old human being with a swollen heart, impure mouth, and shameless bodily movement, a displeasing melody of the old song is struck up; by its deceitful sweetness the lusts of the flesh are nourished, the alluring world is drawn in, and the applauding impurity of the devil is delighted. While Herod bends and gives himself wholly to these deceptive measures, while shameless Herodias, dancing, makes herself alluring and provides for her incestuous union, she readily obtains the beheading of John the Baptist. John, indeed, means “the grace of God”; and this grace is, as it were, beheaded when its source is cut off by those who, captivated by the pleasurable sweetness of the old life, are found strangers to divine newness.

Now therefore, since we have said something about the old song, accusing ourselves because we have sung it almost constantly, let us pass, in tongue and mind, to the melody of the new song and the sweetness of new life [Col. 0722A]. Yet this must be added concerning the old song: it begins with excessively high notes and sends into its singer the dreadful hoarseness of misery. For pride raises itself in windy lightness above everything called or worshiped as God (2 Thess. 2). Hence it is written: “The pride of those who hate you rises continually” (Ps. 73). But the living and effective Word of God (Heb. 4), namely the omnipotent Word of the Father, from the firmness of his own being dashes against and crushes the pride that offends against him, and plunges it into the depths of hell, as it is written: “Whoever exalts himself shall be humbled” (Luke 14); and again, “God resists the proud” [Col. 0722B] (1 Pet. 5).—“But when the sinner comes into the depth of evils,” like one whose voice has been taken away by hoarseness, he neither praises God’s judgment nor humbly accuses his own sin, but “despises” (Prov. 18).

Hence that king, who above all the children of pride (Job 41) sounded out that song of utter discord as high as he could, said: “I will place my throne in the north; above the stars of heaven I will exalt my seat; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14). But this antiphon of his had no vocal harmony, because, striking against the harmony of heavenly music, it fell into a lapse of discordant consonance. But the melody of the new song begins with a low and humble voice and, with sweet modulation, rises to the ears of the Almighty, even soothing the angels, [Col. 0722C] as it is written: “Whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 14).
