For “the prayer of the humble and meek has always pleased God” (Judith 9). We are invited to the measures of this new song when it is said: “Sing to the Lord a new song, for he has done marvelous things” (Ps. 97).

How well, how fittingly, Mighty-Hand invites us to sing! For David is called Mighty-Hand. The joy of divine praise rightly belongs to the one who, by the assistance of the divine hand, has bravely overcome the desires of this world. Thus the same Mighty-Hand is also called desirable in appearance, because whoever receives strength of spirit against the ugliness of vices also receives from the desire for virtue a beautiful appearance. Thus holy Daniel, restraining himself from vices and burning with heavenly desires, is called “a man of desires” [Col. 0722D] (Dan. 10). Therefore one is desirable in appearance to God and the angels when, resisting vice with a strong hand, one desires the beauty of virtue and has in one’s mouth the song of beautiful praise. Such a person is fit to sing a new song and invite others to sing, because, as it is written, “praise befits the upright” (Ps. 32); and elsewhere it is said: “Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. 15).

Accordingly, this Mighty-Hand exults in one place, praises, and gives thanks, saying: “Blessed be the Lord my God, who teaches my hands for battle and my fingers for war” (Ps. 143). And that he is not without the new song he shows in what follows in this psalm, saying: “O God, I will sing [Col. 0723A] a new song to you; upon a ten-stringed psaltery I will play to you.” But since singing belongs to one who exults, exulting to one who loves, and loving to children, the commanded new song seems to be set forth for children alone. Why then is it not said, “Sing, children, to your Father God,” but rather, “Sing to the Lord”? Service in fear is certainly due to the Lord (Ps. 2). “If I am Lord,” he says, “where is my fear?” (Mal. 1). Therefore the servant who does not remain in the house forever (John 8) does not exult in songs, but fearfully awaits the scourge in grief and lamentation.

But we must know that there is “the faithful and prudent servant whom the Lord has appointed over his household” (Luke 12); there is the evil and slothful servant who hides his master’s money in a cloth (Luke 19); and there is the hired servant, who follows recompense in all things (Ps. 118). There is the conditional servant who serves only for appearance’s sake [Col. 0723B] (Col. 3), who does not love his lord but fears punishment.

Of all these, the faithful servant sings the new song, just as does the blessed child. The child sings and exults in charity; the faithful servant sings and exults in humility. Certainly each sings because each praises. The righteous praise because they give thanks for benefits received; humble offenders praise because, approving God’s judgments and marveling at his mercy, they condemn their own deeds. This alone is the difference between the child and the faithful servant, between the righteous person and the humble sinner: the child’s charity sings upon the psaltery, while the servant’s humility plays upon the cithara. The psaltery gives its sound from the upper side; the cithara, from the lower. The psaltery is [Col. 0723C] the righteous person’s exultation through contemplation and desire for things above; the cithara is the humble offender’s lament from consideration and horror of his evils. When he accords with divine purity and brotherly charity through harmony of character and deeds, then he inwardly sings upon the psaltery. When he subdues the passions of the flesh, when he “puts to death” his members which are upon the earth (Col. 3), then the humble servant plays the cithara. “The psaltery is pleasant with the cithara” (Ps. 80), because the innocence of the righteous is grateful and pleasing to God; nevertheless, the mortification of penitents is likewise acceptable to him.

Moreover, the same person is both psaltery for the righteous and cithara for the penitent—the one to whom God the Father speaks in the Psalm, saying: “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and cithara” (Ps. 56). And he himself, acknowledging that he is both, says: “I shall arise at dawn.” For Jesus, rising early on the first day of the Sabbath, appeared to his disciples for forty days by many proofs (Acts 1). From then, after the waiting of ten days, as though the stretching of ten strings, the Holy Spirit came with a sudden sound (Acts 2); and, by making the languages of all nations harmonious in the understanding of the almighty Word, as it were in the melody of the psaltery, he summoned the whole human race. The ten-stringed psaltery, I say, is the Father’s Only-begotten, because, by setting forth the ten commandments of the law for humankind’s justification, he stretched out, as it were, ten strings to his own praise in himself. But he made himself like a cithara for penitents when, through flesh “and the likeness [Col. 0724A] of sinful flesh” (Rom. 8), he stretched the limbs of his innocent body upon the wood of the cross for the guilty.

Thus our David calmed Saul’s madness when, playing the cithara in his body through the sufferings of the cross, he restrained by his death the devil’s assault. Therefore Christ is the psaltery according to his divinity, by whose sweet contemplation he delights those who love him; he is the cithara according to the passion of the body he assumed, when, dying for the guilty, he calls them to pardon. The sound of the psaltery is where he says: “I and the Father are one” (John 10), and again: “Father, I desire that where I am, there also may my servant be” (John 12). The melody of the cithara is where he says: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11). And playing the cithara yet more sweetly, he says: “Father, forgive them, for [Col. 0724B] they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23).

The cithara has two pieces of wood: one upper and solid, the other lower and hollow. The upper solid wood is almighty divinity; the lower hollow wood is humanity united to divinity. This wood is called hollow because human nature in Christ is found capable of so great a grace. Hence the Apostle: “In him all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. 2). The strings, stretched between the two pieces of wood and made resonant by the hollow of the lower wood, are the works of mercy by which the wretched human being is redeemed, and which are set before us as the effective means of our salvation through the mystery of the Incarnation. The cithara has no fixed number of strings, because there is no end to God’s mercies, as it is written: “There is no number to his mercies” [Col. 0724C] (*Ecclesiastical Prayer*).

But if you consider the nine orders of angels and, as it were, the surpassing excellence of glorified humanity as a tenth string, then, while you marvel at, praise, and love Wisdom’s goodness in this consideration, you touch, as it were, the ten strings of a certain psaltery. But who is sufficient for this? No one strikes or perceives the measures of such marvelous sweetness unless the purified intelligence of the mind has raised that person to the heights of virtue. These things belong to those who have become enemies of wickedness, lovers of righteousness, and emulators of angelic purity. The more such persons pant after the denarius of eternal recompense, the more sweetly and subtly they touch the ten-stringed psaltery. This number ten resounds with such inexpressible sweetness that its sweetness exceeds every understanding of human and angelic reason.

The first string is the birth of the eternal Word, consubstantial and coeternal with his Father; the second is the secret counsel of his preordination; the third is the power by which he gave the universe its beginning through essence; the fourth, the wisdom that granted form; the fifth, the goodness by which he exercised his governing providence; the sixth, the justice by which he exacted due punishment from rational creation in its transgression; the seventh, grace, by which he chose the fathers; the eighth, knowledge of truth, by which he gave the law; the ninth, mercy, by which he redeemed us; the tenth, the revelation of the children of God, for which expectation holds creation in suspense.

The cithara is either one for all—namely the manner [Col. 0725A] of our deliverance—or the individual cithara of each who plays the cithara upon his own cithara: that is, of those who rejoice in their own bodies, stripped of sin’s sting and the garment of mortality. For whoever here, in the mortification of his body, plays the cithara of the song of humble confession will there, in the glorification of that same body, play the cithara of the song of eternal jubilation. Therefore, because we hold the psaltery, let us sing upon it a new song, after the example and in imitation of the child born for us (Isa. 9), who is full of grace and truth (John 1). Let us be reborn into a new infancy, that through the innocence of a more upright life we may become capable of holy newness. Upon the psaltery of a pure heart and the cithara of a chaste body, let us sing around the cradle of the infant Word, mingling with his cries the necessary groans of tearful repentance.

Let the measures of the virtues sound in newness of life, since they perfect a new song in the ears of the Word. For there are nine things which rightly bring this newness to completion in us. And because, by the authority of Scripture, we call the new life a new song, we call those nine things, as it were, nine notes by which the new song is arranged. The first note of our song, therefore, is unfeigned faith; the second, true humility; the third, continence of the flesh; the fourth, the seriousness of discipline; the fifth, truthfulness of speech; the sixth, the piety of brotherly compassion; the seventh, patience amid adversities; the eighth, desire for eternity; the ninth, steadfast constancy of mind in all these things. The harmony and consonance of these virtues order the character [Col. 0725C] of those progressing rightly and yearning toward the nine orders of angels.

Why a new song should be sung to the Lord, the reason is added when it is said: “For he has done marvelous things.” God is marvelous in his majesty, marvelous in his saints (Ps. 67), marvelous in all his works; everywhere and in all things he is marvelous, who performed great deeds in Egypt, marvels in the land of Ham, and terrible deeds in the Red Sea (Ps. 105). The creation of the world with its elements is a marvelous work, but the Incarnation of the Word with its sacraments is far more marvelous. The works of nature are indeed marvelous, but because they have become cheap through familiarity, they are as though old, and meanwhile do not merit the exultation of a new song. But the new marvels by which God’s marvelous mercy renews us are new songs to be extolled in praise.

Among all the marvels which Wisdom the artificer has made, three are singularly marvelous and marvelously singular, which we have already touched upon in part: namely, that the mother is a virgin, the Word an infant, and God a human being. These are new because unheard of; and marvelous because they exceed nature. Our renewal depends upon faith and love for these marvels. Therefore the name of the child who is born and given to us is called “Wonderful” (Isa. 9), because in himself he prepares miracles of such astounding newness for minds to be renewed by his grace. Surely, when the same Father [Col. 0726A] “of the age to come” and “Prince of Peace” added a fourth marvel to the three aforementioned marvels (ibid.), so that just as the blessed and mighty God mercifully became human, so the wretched human being may marvelously be exalted into God, then the sound of the new song will be full; then there will be the sweet jubilation of complete joy, because “God will be all in all” (1 Cor. 15).

Then he who is now born to us as a child will appear as a perfect man (Eph. 4); and he who is now given to us as a son, to share our tribulation, will then present himself to us as giver and prince of eternal peace. Then we shall see and flow together, marvel, and our heart shall be enlarged (Isa. 60), when “as we have heard, so shall we see in the city of our God” (Ps. 47). Then by full experience we shall perceive how great is the multitude of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you (Ps. 30). May the child who [Col. 0726B] was born to us as a son for this purpose, who was given to us for this purpose, deign to prepare it for us—he who lives and reigns with you and the Holy Spirit, etc.

## Sermon IV. On the Purification of Blessed Mary

“They offered for him to the Lord a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons” (Luke 2). The Father of lights invites the children of light to celebrate the feast of Light with illumined minds. “Come therefore to him and be enlightened” (Ps. 33). For he “who dwells in inaccessible light” (1 Tim. 6) graciously made himself accessible, making the cloud of flesh his descent, so that the weak and lowly might have access. O descent of mercy! “He bowed the heavens”—that is, the heights of divinity—“and descended” [Col. 0726C] through the presence of flesh; “and darkness was beneath his feet” (Ps. 17). The feet by which he came to us are mercy and truth. That he took our flesh was the foot of mercy; that he took it without the falsehood of sin was truth. Yet darkness was beneath his feet, because in the body which he assumed through mercy and truth, that is, without guilt, there appeared the likeness of sinful flesh. Hence elsewhere it is written: “Cloud and darkness are round about him” (Ps. 96).

Cloud and darkness: because in the cloud—that is, in the flesh—there is darkness, namely the likeness of sin. O darkness necessary for restoring the light! Certainly, when the true Light joined to himself the cloud of flesh darkened by the likeness of sin, then through the interposition of this darkness the wisdom of the world, the malice of human beings, and the cunning of demons were darkened. Hence blindness happened to Israel (Rom. 11), and, failing to recognize the Lord of glory (1 Cor. 2), while judging the true Light to be darkness, it unknowingly accomplished the work of our redemption. Thus from the very source from which the true Light made flesh his hiding place, the children of darkness increased their own darkness.

Let flesh therefore come to flesh, in which it may unlearn the things belonging to flesh, and so we may be taught gradually to pass from flesh into spirit. Let it come, I say, especially now, because the new Sun already displays his radiance somewhat more than usual, and he who until now was confined at Bethlehem, known to few amid the narrow manger, is today presented in Jerusalem, in the Lord’s temple, before more people [Col. 0727A]. Until now, Bethlehem, you alone rejoiced in the common light; and, proud in the privilege of an unprecedented newness, you could rival even the east itself in equal splendor. Indeed—wonderful to say!—in your narrow manger there was more light than the rising of the world’s sun is accustomed to bring forth. Why then did you begrudge the common rays to the whole multitude of beings? You scarcely showed that light to a few shepherds. You scarcely admitted three men from the East to the manger of the new Light. But now the Sun comes forth from your hidden places to illumine the whole world; whether you have left anything of darkness behind with you, you must see.

Thus today the Lord of the Temple is offered in the Temple, and the birds named above are offered for him. For in this presentation a double offering is celebrated: one is made of him, the other for him. And when birds are offered for him, an offering is redeemed by an offering. By the price of birds our price is redeemed, and our Redeemer is redeemed before we are redeemed by him. A worthy indeed and singular offering: redeemed through the intervening price of cheap birds, but at the fitting time destined to redeem the human race by the inestimable price of its own blood! Here too we have the third offering, by which the Lamb of God offered himself to God the Father upon the altar of the Cross for the salvation of the world. He will also make a fourth offering at the end of the world, when, as it is written, he will offer and hand over the kingdom to God the Father (I Cor. XV).

We have, therefore, four distinct offerings [Col. 0727C]. The first was made of him by his parents; the second, for him, from birds; the third he made of himself; the fourth he will make for himself from his own. In all these we are instructed what we ought to believe, what to imitate, and what to hope for. The first offering teaches us humility, when the Lawgiver and Judge is humbly subjected to the Law. The second invites us to voluntary poverty, when the Author and Lord of the universe chose that the offering of the poor should be offered for him. The third softens us to compassion, when the merciful Lord did not shrink from dying for the ungodly at the hands of evildoers and by the punishment of the Cross. Now in the fourth offering lies our reward, if we present a fifth offering of ourselves for merit.

We make a fifth offering of ourselves if we make ourselves both humble in observing the Law, voluntarily poor in despising the world [Col. 0727D], and merciful in compassion for our neighbour. If in these three respects we offer ourselves, imitating the Lord, we shall belong to the fourth offering which he will make in glory from his own, through himself. But since the first and second especially mark this day, let us return both tongue and mind to considering them.

“They offered,” he says, “for him to the Lord a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons.” It is good and fitting that birds are offered for the Lamb. Let the lamb, I pray, be reserved for Passover; meanwhile let birds be sacrificed. This is not the place or time to sacrifice a lamb: that will be done better at Passover, when Christ, our Passover, is sacrificed (I Cor. V). For Christ is the Lamb, and because of his singular innocence the passage from vices to virtues is made—the passage denoted by the name Passover. The turtledove and the dove preserve this innocence for us. The turtledove signifies chastity; the dove, simplicity. Chastity excludes lust, and simplicity malice. Chastity is the friend of virginity, and simplicity of truth. Now the Son of our Virgin is both virginity and truth, our Lamb, all innocence.

Therefore, by the offering of the turtledove and dove we preserve the Lamb for ourselves, if through bodily purity and simplicity of heart we guard true innocence of soul. In this offering two pairs of birds are mentioned: namely, two turtledoves and two doves. The two pairs signify the twofold love of God and neighbour. The first pair signifies chastity through the kind of bird, and charity through the number. For the turtledove is a chaste bird: when it has lost its mate, it accepts no other; it flies alone, and has a groan instead of a song [Col. 0728B]. Such is holy widowhood after marriage; such is chastity restored through continence after a fall. While they fear for their beloved chastity, they seek seclusion, flee crowds, groan at the prolonging of their sojourn, and say: “Alas for me, because my sojourning has been prolonged! I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Cedar” (Ps. CXIX).

Surely chastity is white and the friend of angelic brightness. Since it fears to live with the inhabitants of Cedar—that is, with those who love the darkness of pleasures—it rightly mourns and groans at the prolongation of exile. The number two pertains to charity, because charity is properly said to exist only in relation to another. Thus in the pair of turtledoves is figured love of God, which only those living chastely can preserve; in the pair of doves, love of neighbour, which only those living with dove-like simplicity can guard.

Observe the mystery of this sacred offering, and offer the Lord comparable things in acquiring virtues. You have certainly offered a pair of turtledoves and two young pigeons if, with a chaste body, a simple heart, and fervent charity, you have put on newness of life. For the recent age of the young doves spiritually signifies the infancy of newness. And if we also consider that this offering is poor, what else are we taught but that poverty is to be sought and loved? “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. V). See how much the offering of the infant Word speaks to us in mysteries!

O miracle worthy of all wonder! The almighty Word, coming from royal thrones (Wis. XVIII), cries as an infant in a bodily cradle, he who reigns immeasurable in heaven; and what, because of the age of the flesh, he cannot yet utter [Col. 0728D], he teaches and cries out in the mysteries and sacraments of the prophets. Behold: through the devotion of faithful understanding, we both have and retain mute birds as interpreters of divine philosophy. Let us mingle with the cries of the immeasurable little child both the mourning of the turtledove and the groans of the dove. For each bird has groaning instead of song.

Let us offer in our flesh the turtledove of chastity; let us offer in our mind the dove of simplicity. Let there be no turtledove without groaning, no chastity without mourning for sin, so that we may be able to say: “The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land” (Song 2). What is the voice of the turtledove “in our land” [Col. 0729A], except the grief of those who live chastely in miserable, earthly flesh, still separated through misery from the goods of their homeland? For our flesh is a foreign land, in which we ought to give not jubilation but groaning, not song but lamentation, according to the voice of one groaning and saying: “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?” (Ps. CXXXVI). Truly foreign, for in it “we are pilgrims away from the Lord” (II Cor. V).

Yet the turtledove is not accustomed either to appear or to groan except in the season of flowers and the renewal of the vineyards. Hence, after the words, “The voice of the turtledove has been heard,” Scripture continues: “Flowers have appeared; blossoming vines have given forth fragrance” (Song II). For while the groaning of the heart, arising from love of rest, sounds in a chaste body, meanwhile the flowers of good works spring forth, in which the fruits of rewards ought to be hoped for. As the farmer hopes for fruit in the flower, so conscience, in merits emerging from the hidden sources of divine grace, smells by hope the fruit of eternity.

Blossoming vineyards are laborious acts of virtue made bright by beauty, colour, and fragrance. How happy and pure is the soul which has offered itself to God as such a turtledove in the nest of the flesh, and as a dove in the solitude of a peaceful mind. How great is the purity where no lust of the flesh defiles, and no bitterness of malice exasperates the mind. Whoever is such is fit to celebrate the solemnities of the Purification. For that is the name of the present day’s solemnity.

What then? (13) Must we believe that the most pure mother of the Lord was purified on this day [Col. 0729C]—she whose purity, both in childbirth and after childbirth, was so singular that she brought forth for us the Author of all purity? What impurity or defilement could she have contracted, from whom all purity flowed? Let this day be called the Purging of Mary, or the Purification, not because the blessed Mother of God was purified on it—she who, from the very conception of the Word, as she in no way consented to sin, so felt no resistance whatsoever of the flesh—but because through her childbirth, or the offering of her child, humankind, polluted by sin, was cleansed.

Or perhaps the custom of the Law, and the opinion of common people who did not know the miracle of the divine birth and the design of its hidden mystery, caused this day to be called the Purging of Mary. But (14) it was not Mary’s purification but ours through Mary that was accomplished: by conceiving and bearing the Son of God without any sin, she washed away our impurities. Therefore, if we embrace her childbirth with unfeigned faith, if we enact the mystery of today’s offering with the virtue of our soul in the temple of a devout mind, we ourselves are more especially purified in this celebration.

For if through a true confession of faith we are true Jews, we have in this offering of the Lord six stone jars set there for our purification. Do you not see in the poor offering an example of voluntary poverty; in the turtledove, continence of the flesh signified; in the dove, simplicity of heart; in the doubled pair, the figure of twofold charity; and in the young birds, the newness which follows from these? [Col. 0730A] These things have already often been mentioned. They may be called six jars because they are full to the brim with the water of saving wisdom. In Greek, water is called *hydōr*, whence they are called *hydriae* [water-jars]; they are of stone, not because of hardness, but because of the firmness of perseverance.

Go now and wash in them, and you will be cleansed, so that you may purely celebrate the solemnities of inward purification. Or if perhaps you seek other jars to purify the heart, hew from Christ the stone for yourself those six works of mercy which Christ himself, the cornerstone (Eph. II), sets before us in the Gospel. The first is to feed the hungry; the second, to give drink to the thirsty; the third, to clothe the naked; the fourth, to receive the stranger; the fifth, to visit the sick; the sixth, to ransom the prisoner. By these alms the soul is purified, and in the temple of the peaceable heart the feast of true purification is celebrated.

For *eleemosyna* [almsgiving], which washes the mind, also derives its name from water. *El* means God, and *moys* water. Almsgiving is rightly called the water of God, because sin is the fire of the devil. Water extinguishes fire, and almsgiving excludes sin (Ecclus. III). “Give alms,” says the Lord, “and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke XI). Apply to yourself the washing of this water, and “though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be whitened as snow” (Isa. V).

And what, I ask, is the inhabitant of the cloister to do, who cannot have these jars at hand? For those six works of mercy are set before persons possessing the goods of the world. What then shall the poor in spirit do, one who, together with worldly possessions, has abandoned even the desire to possess? Such a person should have the former jars in intention and act, and these latter ones in intention as well. For the inward Judge, who judges intentions, will not deny the reward even if the means to fulfil a good intention are lacking. For the angels promise peace not to those who do many works, but to those possessing a good will, when at the Saviour’s birth they sing and say: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke II).

But if the monk prefers to have the jars of his purification in the waters of Siloam, which “flow in silence” (Isa. VIII), that is, in cloistered observances, let him have the narrow and arduous way of obedience, whose perfection is contained in six observances (Rule of St Benedict, ch. 5) [Col. 0730D], as in so many jars. The first jar is that obedience be already complete: that is, that he perform without distinction every good thing commanded by his superior. The second is that he know no delay in doing it. The third is that, when carrying out the command, he prefer neither the answer of one unwilling nor the countenance of one angered. The fourth is that he do it willingly, lest, while feigning good or concealing evil in his heart, his face should lie about cheerfulness of mind. The fifth is discretion in commands: that he know also concerning what, how much, and how long he ought to obey, lest he be deceived. The sixth is the long-suffering of perseverance, which, fully purifying the mind, is endowed with the salvation of eternal glorification, as it is written: “Whoever perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matt. X).

Of the six jars which are hewn from the firm rock of perfect obedience, the first is called complete, the second swift, the third cheerful, the fourth willing, the fifth discerning, the sixth persevering. In jars of this kind those are washed and purified who need only to wash their feet, but are otherwise wholly clean (John XIII): those who, despising the world and despising themselves, hasten with such unencumbered steps toward eternal things that they place nothing before the love of Christ. Though they trample and crush beneath the feet of spiritual affections the earthly soil of flesh which they still bear, nevertheless they still contract upon their feet affections from the dust of the flesh. This dust is always contracted while life is lived here; yet it is continually wiped away once contracted, while the former life is tirelessly practised through true obedience [Col. 0731B].

How pure is that life, and how worthily does it celebrate today’s feast of purification, which casts away the defiling mire of the world; retains nothing of itself for itself; but, subjecting itself wholly to God, transcends in a purified mind everything that is flesh, and, avoiding the losses of self-will, entrusts itself to another’s judgment so as to gain freedom of spirit. The virtue of obedience, faithfully and perseveringly kept, will purify and cleanse the sons of Levi (Mal. III), so that they may be fit to meet the Saviour as he comes to the Temple, and to celebrate the Lord’s Hypapante. For this celebration is called *Hypapante*, that is, “the meeting.”

For today, when the parents of the child Jesus were bringing him to the Temple to offer him, the holy elders Simeon and Anna, forewarned by the Holy Spirit, are read to have met him [Col. 0731C], and to have proclaimed to all who awaited the redemption of Jerusalem that he was the one whom the Law and Prophets had foretold as Saviour (Luke II). This is one reason why the solemnity of this day is called Hypapante.

But one worthily meets God who cleanses himself from the contagion of vices, and by fitting order in the solemnity of the heart lets the pursuit of purification precede the joy of meeting. For vices do not meet the Lord of virtues; nor can impurity agree with purity. Purification clothes and renews the soul in the wedding garment, as both Anna’s religious devotion and the piety of righteous Simeon commend. Certainly, since Christ is peace and truth, if through his grace we live devoutly and justly, there is fulfilled in us the feast of that meeting of which the Psalmist says: “Mercy and truth have met one another; righteousness and peace have kissed” (Ps. LXXXIV).

Mercy meets truth when it faithfully fulfils the command; and righteousness meets peace when, after the labour of the command, it receives the promise of eternal peace. Hence the holy elder Simeon, in whom mercy and righteousness are found, deserves to find, hold, and kiss truth and peace in Christ. Therefore he cries out and says: “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace” (Luke II). First, as has been said, mercy finds truth; and when they have found one another in the human heart—for “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. XXIV)—then they introduce righteousness [Col. 0732A].

But what is this mercy? It is that by which a person has mercy on himself. Of it it is written: “Have mercy on your own soul by pleasing God” (Ecclus. XXX). Great mercy is to have mercy on one’s own soul in order to please God. For who is more cruel than one who kills himself by living badly? Or to whom will one be good who is wicked to himself? (Ecclus. XIV). Through this mercy one turns aside from evil, and the lie of sin is cleansed from the heart, so that truth may rise from the earth of the cleansed heart and teach it to do good. From these two is perfected the wholeness of righteousness, which, just as it does no evil, so does not omit to do good. Righteousness finds peace, because eternal peace is righteousness’ recompense.

Observe that when mercy and truth meet one another, nothing is said about a kiss [Col. 0732B] (Ps. LXXXIV), except when righteousness finds peace. Why is this? Because turning from evil and doing good (Ps. XXXVI), which is the work of mercy and truth, involves labour and struggle; but receiving the rest of eternal peace, signified by the kiss and belonging to the reward of righteousness, excludes every labour. Then, as it is written, “Light rises for the righteous, and joy for the upright in heart” (Ps. XCVI). Then God wipes every tear from the eyes of the saints, and death shall be no more (Apoc. VII). Then, if purification from vices and the meeting of virtues have gone before in us, there shall be for us the revelation of everlasting light and the glory of unending rest.

Here there now comes to mind the third name of this feast, which the common people also call the Feast of Candles [Col. 0732C]. The burning candle signifies that exultation which purification of heart deserves and toward which the aforesaid meeting of virtues tends. For although it represents the true light hidden in the wax of virginal flesh, which Simeon deserved to bear in his hands today (Luke II), it nevertheless also foreshadows the purity of heavenly life and the delight of the future light that will at last be manifested in the elect.

Three things appear in a lighted candle, and they indicate the three substances in Christ: wax signifies the spotless flesh; the wick surrounded by wax, the soul hidden in the flesh; the fire, the nature of the Word united to both flesh and soul. Simeon indeed deserved to be the bearer of this true light [Col. 0732D], but the spiritual offering of turtledove and dove had purified him, and the celebrated meeting of virtues in the temple of his devout mind made solemn festival. He himself was a turtledove in the flesh and a dove in the spirit. And because, for gaining the Lamb, he had offered these birds of virtue—he being himself the Lamb in mind, though aged in years—he had received the answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not see the darkness of death before seeing the light of life (ibid.).

Would that my soul might burn with Simeon’s longing, so that I might deserve to be the bearer of so great a light. But certainly, as has often been said, unless the mind has first been purified from vices, so that afterwards, flying out from the enclosures of the flesh on the wings of virtues, it may go forth “to meet Christ in the air” (I Thess. IV) in true freedom, it can neither rejoice with Simeon in the true light nor be dismissed in peace. It is therefore necessary that, with a purified mind and works of virtue, we meet the Lord, meanwhile celebrating the Lord’s Hypapante in this manner.

But we shall celebrate this solemnity more happily and festively when, at the Bridegroom’s coming, after a cry has arisen at midnight, we go out with lighted lamps among the prudent virgins to meet the bridegroom and bride (Matt. XXV). For this present procession of ours fittingly signifies the ineffable joy of that profession. Let us therefore love and imitate in Simeon and Anna what we have said is signified in the turtledove and dove. For then the song will no longer savour of the groaning of dove or turtledove, but will be changed into the jubilation of eternal praise. Then, as today—indeed, better than today—we shall sing in common joy the canticle of righteous Simeon, saying: “Now you dismiss” (Luke II), etc.

Observe that this canticle has four verses, because there are four stages of heavenly joy [Col. 0733B]. The first is in the expectation and desire of a devout heart; hence in the first verse he proclaims that he is dismissed in peace. The second is in the fruit and fulfilment of devout expectation; hence in the second verse he rejoices that even with bodily eyes he sees the salvation of God, that is, the Saviour. The third is in charity concerning the progress of others; hence in the third verse he announces that this salvation of God is communicated to all peoples, saying: “Which you have prepared before the face of all peoples” (ibid.). The fourth and final stage is the revelation of everlasting light and the manifestation of glory, which is mentioned in the fourth verse when it says: “A light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to your people Israel” (ibid.)—that is, the people of the saints who see God face to face, to whom be honour and glory for everlasting ages. Amen.

102. SERMON V. ON THE ASSUMPTION OF THE BLESSED MARY

“Who shall find a strong woman? Her price is far off, and from the furthest boundaries” (Prov. XXXI). This is said not because it is impossible, but because it is difficult, to find a strong woman. For today it is almost more difficult to find anyone who wishes to seek, or desires to find, than to find the strong woman herself. To seek this strong woman is virtue; to find her is salvation; to grasp her is joy; to love her is praise and honour; to hold her and not let her go is the highest good.

But let us now see what this strong woman should be understood to mean, where, when, and how she ought to be sought. For how can she be found unless she is sought? Or how can she be sought unless it is known where she may be found? How can anyone know this unless he has learned it? And whence can he learn unless he has subjected himself to the instruction of a teacher? Surely it is difficult for one to take on the form of a disciple and become patient under discipline if he lacks the humility that does not disdain subjection—one whom either the weakness of sloth makes negligent, or the swelling of pride contemptuous.

For pride, blinded by the coarse thickness of its own swelling, is driven by that very swelling not to be tractable; and the obstacle of that same swelling prevents it from receiving the light of truth [Col. 0734A]. Humility, however, is always delicate and fine; and it is open and passable to the true light precisely inasmuch as, conducting itself more narrowly and simply, it is always in harmony with holy poverty (15).

Thus by the strong woman we may rightly understand the wisdom of God; or Mary, the mother of Wisdom itself; or the Church, mother of the wise—that is, of the saints; or indeed the soul, the seat of wisdom. The wisdom of God is called a woman because of the fruitfulness of all the goods flowing from it. For it is she who says: “I am the mother of fair love, and of fear, and of knowledge, and of holy hope” (Ecclus. XXIV). The Psalmist shows her to be the parent of all things, speaking thus to the Lord: “You have made all things in wisdom” (Ps. CIII), etc.

Finally, she is called a woman by the Evangelist when Wisdom itself, through a parable, says: “What woman having ten drachmas, if she loses one of them …” (Luke XV), etc. In this place the mother is called woman, not because she was broken down into the softness of pleasure, but because of the nature of the weaker sex; therefore the Lord says to her: “What is that to me and to you, Woman?” (John II). And the angel Gabriel declares her blessed among women. The Apostle likewise recalls that the Son of God was made of a woman (Gal. IV), that is, that he assumed flesh from such a sex (16).

Elsewhere, however, Truth seems to exclude the name “woman” from the Virgin when, praising John the Baptist, it says: “Among those born of women none has arisen greater than John the Baptist” (Matt. XI) [Col. 0734C]. But there it calls women those who are not without experience of the contact of a man in the softness of pleasure; virginal integrity is wholly ignorant of this. The Church, mother of the wise—that is, of the saints—is called a woman because she is wearied by the distress of continual childbirth and groaning. In her are the pains of one in labour (Ps. XLVII); and while she bears, nourishes, and ardently loves the offspring of saints whom she receives by the grace of the Holy Spirit, she continually suffers and groans with maternal affection over their temptations and perils. Hence her Bridegroom speaks of her in the Gospel, saying: “A woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow, because her hour has come” (John XVI).

The soul also, which is the seat of Wisdom, is called a woman because, by an affective softness of tender devotion, it leans upon its beloved [Col. 0734D]. Soft through an affection of mercy and fruitful in the fertility of works, while it loves its Bridegroom Jesus above all things and in all things, it joins itself to him in undivided purity and says: “My beloved is mine, and I am his” (Song I). For it gives no heed to the deceptive favour of people or the vain beauty of things; but, applying to itself the safeguard of chaste fear, it carefully keeps and hears this: “Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain; a woman fearing the Lord shall be praised” (Prov. XXXI).

But because we said above that the wisdom of God can be understood as the strong woman, let us explain more fully how this should be understood.

She is called woman because of fruitfulness, strong because of power [Col. 0735A]. She is called powerful because of omnipotence; fruitful because of fullness. She is called strong because “she reaches mightily from end to end” (Wis. VIII); she is called fruitful because “she orders all things sweetly” (ibid.). Finally, her strength is especially considered in two ways: in complete power and complete patience. In complete power, because, having no need, she created all things from nothing; in complete patience, because, possessing all innocence, she bore every injury from the unjust with equanimity.

Likewise, her fruitfulness may especially be considered in two ways: in complete wisdom and complete mercy. In complete wisdom, by which she gave form and order to the whole universe; in complete mercy, by which she released the old human being from the debt of death through the grace of an undeserved death and the price of her own blood. O how powerful a fruitfulness, and how fruitful a power! How strong in weakness, how fertile in poverty, was this woman! In weakness, by which the Lord of all emptied himself even to the form of a servant (Phil. II); in poverty, by which the Creator of the world himself had nowhere to lay his head in the world (Matt. VIII).

But that emptying was the fulfilment of human salvation; and that poverty was the enrichment of the poor. For while omnipotent strength so graciously emptied itself, the emptiness of our vanity received solidity and strength. While the rich Lord of all submitted himself to the deficiencies of our need [Col. 0735C], the insufficiency of our poverty grew into the sufficiency of divinity, or Godhead. Finally, that emptying was so fruitful that it increased glory for angels, gave joy to shepherds, increased faith, and secured peace also for people of good will (Luke II).

This weakness was so powerful that it healed paralytics, cleansed lepers, enlightened the blind, restored hearing to the deaf, walking to the lame, and the function of speech to the mute; raised the dead (Matt. XI); walked over the waters with dry feet (Matt. XIV); calmed storms and seas by command alone (Matt. VIII); drove demons from possessed bodies; healed every infirmity by a word (Matt. IX); and by wondrous words refuted the learning of the scribes and the pride of the Pharisees (Matt. XXIII).

This weakness, I say, was so strong that when Christ died according to his passible nature, there came darkening of the sun, shaking of the earth, rending of the veil, splitting of rocks [Col. 0735D], opening of tombs, resurrection of the bodies of saints (Matt. XXVII), and despoiling of hell. And, wonderfully, the solidity of the elements is then shaken more powerfully when the weakness of our woman is reckoned more abject.

But I ask: where, or by whom, is this strong woman found? Surely, as Scripture says: “Wisdom is not found in the land of those who live pleasantly” (Job XXVIII). Those live pleasantly who serve the desires of voluptuous flesh; and the more they grow dark from works of righteousness, the less they grasp the light of wisdom. Therefore they do not seek who love darkness, persist in vices, do not keep the commandments of life, possess the appearance of godliness but deny and despise its power (II Tim. III).

Therefore the one who seeks and finds wisdom is the one who seeks well; and one seeks well who, as was said, seeks where, when, and how one ought. Let Wisdom herself say where she can be found. “I,” she says, “have dwelt in the highest places, and my throne is in a pillar of cloud” (Ecclus. XXIV). This is what Scripture says: “Her price is far off, and from the furthest boundaries” (Prov. XXXI). Elsewhere Scripture says that “wisdom is drawn forth from hidden places” (Job XXVIII). What are hidden things but the highest things? And what are the highest things but heavenly things?

Heaven can also be called hidden, because *occultare* means “to conceal.” Wisdom is drawn from hidden places—that is, from heaven—when “the kingdom of heaven suffers violence” (Matt. XI): when fear, which is the beginning of wisdom (Ecclus. I), sets itself against folly, and the sorrow of repentance, condemning the works of injustice, grasps the kingdom of heaven, which is due to righteousness alone.

Finally, we fittingly call the hearts of saints heavens: lofty in the height of virtue, exalted by heavenly contemplation, serene in the purity of innocence, clarified by subtle understanding, starry in their ordering of virtues, fiery in their ardour of charity, firm in the virtue of patience, uplifted in the long-suffering of hope [Col. 0736C]. While they flee the favour of human praise, hide themselves as much as lies within them from human eyes, and conceal God’s dwelling within the testimony of conscience, they represent in themselves the image of a particular heaven.

Wisdom is drawn from these hidden places, which conceal the treasure hidden in the field, because the examples of heavenly people instruct even the untrained in wisdom, though with difficulty. Finally, Wisdom dwells in counsel and is present among learned thoughts (Prov. VIII), and therefore “all the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Ps. XLIV), because Wisdom does not share the secret of her counsel with everyone. Hence Wisdom herself says in the Gospel: “I confess to you, Lord, Father of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. XI).

There the little ones—that is, the humble—are the confidants of Wisdom [Col. 0736D]; and however much she dwells in the highest places, humility reaches her more easily. The lower humility casts itself down, the more familiarly Wisdom’s loftiness bends itself toward it. “For God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble” (I Pet. V); and while waters pass through the midst of mountains, fountains flow forth in valleys (Ps. CIII).

Therefore in counsel, and in the counsel of the saints, the humble person finds wisdom, which “will not enter a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins” (Wis. I). Wisdom herself teaches when it ought to be sought, saying: “Those who watch for me in the morning shall find me” (Prov. VIII). Morning is the time of faith, because through faith we must meanwhile seek what will profit us in the future. For faith is the morning light by which we are meanwhile enlightened in hope, until the day breathes forth, the shadows decline, and full noon consoles us through direct sight [Col. 0737A].

For as morning light precedes the brilliance of noonday heat, so the mystery of faith comes before the direct vision of God. Hence the Prophet says: “In the morning I shall stand before you” (Ps. V), that is, I shall minister in faith and faithfully. And when direct vision comes—that is, when the heat of noon has brought clearer brightness—then I shall see “that you are not a God who wills iniquity” (ibid.).

Now that we have said where, by whom, and when Wisdom ought to be sought, it remains for us to see also how it ought to be sought.

She herself explains the manner of seeking, saying: “Come over to me, all you who desire me” (Ecclus. [Col. 0737B] 24); that is, she must be sought by desiring and by passing over: by desiring eternal things, by passing over from temporal things. To pass over is to make a passage; to make a passage is to celebrate Passover. For Passover is called a passage. To celebrate Passover is to offer the spotless Lamb. The paschal feast, moreover, properly belongs to the Hebrews, that is, to those who pass over; for “Hebrews” is interpreted “those passing over.” Therefore whoever abandons the wicked age in mind; whoever withdraws himself from the vices and desires of the flesh to spiritual desire; whoever passes in spirit from transitory things to eternal and abiding things—such a one seeks and finds Wisdom. For he offers the Lamb who presents himself to God pure in body, gentle in heart, harmless in conduct, serene in countenance, temperate in diet, truthful in speech, blameless in appearance, praiseworthy in reputation, merciful in brotherly compassion. In this manner Wisdom is sought, whose “price is far off, and from the uttermost bounds” (Prov. 30), as is said.

How far off is the bosom of the Father, from which she herself proceeds! How far off is that ineffable and eternal generation by which she is begotten from the Father before the ages! How far off is the virginal integrity of the incorrupt mother, from whom the Word is made flesh (John 1)! How far off is the loftiness of human nature before sin, from which immunity from sin is preserved in the flesh of the Word! How far off is that singular innocence, in which he is known to have lived as a human being and performed miracles! How far off is that patience without example, in which, through the punishment of an undeserved [Col. 0737D] death, the devil, author of death, is overcome; the human being liable to death is acquitted; and the freedom of eternal life is restored! Therefore her price—either that by which she is precious, or that which is paid for our redemption—comes from the uttermost bounds.

There seem to be four uttermost bounds: two highest bounds, beyond which there is nothing higher; and two lowest bounds, below which there is nothing further. The two highest bounds are the eternal generation, by which the Word is born of the Father without a mother; and the incorrupt birth, by which the same Word is generated of a mother without a father. The two lowest bounds are that he patiently endured the penalty of the cross without guilt, and that, having died, he descended to hell without punishment (17). Nothing is more sublime than the first and eternal generation; nothing more wonderful than the second and incorrupt [Col. 0738A] birth. Among torments, nothing is more ignominious than the punishment of the cross; among triumphs, nothing more terrible than the despoiling of hell. From these uttermost bounds came the price of our deliverance; and this should be so much the more precious to those redeemed as, coming from so far away, it could possess so great an efficacy.

Now let us see, by the grace which she, the Mother of grace, may have obtained for us, how these words, which we have understood in some fashion concerning Wisdom, also suit Mary, the mother of Wisdom.

She is therefore called a woman, not because she is broken by the softness of pleasure, but because the nature of the weaker sex is in her; or because, as Mother of mercy, she is softened by affection into the tenderness of compassion (18). How strong was this woman, who without example overcame both her sex [Col. 0738B] and the age by the strength of an unconquered spirit! How strong she was, who, placed in a frail body and still a pilgrim in this wicked world, rivalled angelic purity and transcended by the sublimity of her mind everything created! In short, to the strong woman the strength of God, Gabriel, is sent; he finds her full of grace and strength, and declares that she will bear the omnipotent Word.

Was not Mary strong, whose “love is strong as death” (Song 8), and was so strengthened by the overshadowing power of the Most High that the King of powers, the Lord strong and mighty in battle (Ps. 23), became weak in her; that the strong armed man abandoned the court which he possessed in peace (Luke 11); and that human weakness attained through her to complete salvation? But where, I ask, is this woman of such great strength found? Surely far off: for as she excels every creature by the fullness of grace, so she transcends them incomparably by the sublimity of glory. 115

Far off, I say, she is; for although she is mediatrix and propitious through her singular compassionate mercy, nevertheless by the privilege of incomparable excellence she is exalted above every height of the angels. Her price is far off, because “fairer in form than the children of men” (Ps. 44) is born from her precious flesh—the price by which humankind is redeemed—and she herself is preferred above all the saints, angels, and human beings in merits and glory.

The uttermost bounds are Mary’s incomparable virtues, in which the Prophet testifies that he sees the limit of every perfection, saying thus to the Lord: “I have seen the end of every perfection; your commandment is exceeding broad” (Ps. 118). For what commandment is broader than that by which he commands the salvations of Jacob (Ps. 43), who, in the greeting of Mary which Gabriel brought her from God, prepared salvation for all, as far as lay in him? The uttermost bounds, therefore, are Mary’s incomparable humility, singular virginity, spiritual charity, and privileged fruitfulness. Since no example whatsoever precedes all these things, so no merit whatsoever either equals or surpasses them—excepting altogether the Only-begotten of the Father, the firstborn of this Virgin. Although he did not receive the Spirit by measure (John 3), nevertheless from these uttermost bounds—that is, from Mary’s highest virtues—the price of our redemption came, according to [Col. 0739A] the nature which he drew from the flesh of the Virgin.

These, as has been said, are the uttermost bounds: the perfected virtues of the Virgin, from which we received a birth of inestimable price, as fruit from flowers. Yet the flowers remain unfading; and just as, in natural things, fruit is the end of the flower, so in the Mother of the Lord childbirth is not the termination of virginal chastity. For she is “a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed” (Song 4). The fertility of unheard-of fruitfulness makes her a garden; the integrity of inviolate modesty makes it enclosed. She is a fountain because from the fullness of grace she pours forth streams of mercy; sealed, because she admits no one foreign to the sign of faith.

“A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, flowing with force from Lebanon” (ibid.). Mary is a fountain, open and accessible through the abundance and readiness [Col. 0739B] of mercy; she is a deep and capacious well through the depth of an admirable mystery. For in her was fulfilled “the great mystery of godliness: which was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, appeared to 117 angels, was preached to the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory” (1 Tim. 3). The living waters are heavenly graces, “which flow with force from Lebanon”: they were bestowed upon the Virgin when the Holy Spirit came upon her from the height of the Father’s fullness.

The force may indeed be understood as the sudden fullness of the grace of the Holy Spirit; when the brightness of eternal light is poured into Mary, then, as it were from Lebanon, which is said to mean “whiteness,” a torrent of living waters bursts forth. Mary is therefore the fountain of gardens: namely, the washing, satisfaction, and refreshment [Col. 0739C] of holy congregations. For as many assemblies as the Church has, living in faith, as offspring of the Virgin, so many gardens there are. And certainly the childbirth of the most merciful Mother supplies all these with the washing of repentance, by which iniquity is wiped away; with the desire for righteousness, by which devotion is refreshed; and with the shelter of protection, by which the heat of carnal desire is cooled.

See how great is the fruitfulness of our woman, how great the abundance of the sealed fountain, whose ever-opportune watering grants such fertility to the gardens of the Church. To this well-watered fountain, to this most merciful Virgin, I would assign in a special way (19) the monasteries of the Cistercians, since all of them are dedicated in due devotion both to her memory and to the merits of that Mother. O how great ought to be the brightness of hearts among my own, and the purity of their morals (20), who imitate the whiteness of the virginal lily both by the brightness of their habit and by the title of their name! For they are called white monks not only because they shine with the whiteness of their garments, but because they are spiritual ministers of virginal brightness.

Why then do we wretched, miserable, and excessively black men beneath a white habit endure thorns and thistles growing in such dense profusion around the lily of our Virgin? Why do we unhappily plant, or still more unhappily cherish, there the thorns of hatreds and the stings of detraction, where the perfumes of virtues ought to breathe and flow forth? (21) Rather, we ought to imitate our Virgin and be conformed in filial affection to our most blessed Mother. For she was given not only as a remedy, but [Col. 0740A] set forth as an example of virtue.

It is therefore unfitting for a white monk, a cultivator of virginal sincerity and a special son of Mary, to swell with the breath of pride; to be excessive through the vice of curiosity; to surrender his mind to unclean desires; to be darkened by hatred of brotherly peace; to be tormented by the jaundice of envy; or, in the service of the Virgin, to neglect his purpose of holiness. For how can pride minister to such humility; impurity to such chastity; dishonour to such purity; hatred to such charity; detraction to such good will; murmuring to such peace; gluttony to such sobriety; falsehood to such truth; cruelty to such mercy—especially in those who have come to honour so great a mystery from the dungheap of sin, from utter poverty, and from lowliness of birth?

How often do we see such people in cloisters seeking for the care of the flesh things which they could not have possessed even in the world? [Col. 0740B] For this reason, under the shadow of religion, they serve vanity not shadowily but truly: they are proud among the humble; among penitents they wish to live more voluptuously; they seek honours although they had sworn contempt for the world. Bearing only the image of holiness before them, the wolf is concealed beneath the fleece of a sheep and is not recognized until his howling betrays him. That howling is detraction, excessively greedy for the blood of brothers, which its mother Envy has produced in the blackening of monastic sincerity.

Therefore it is left to your goodness, O propitious Mother of mercy, to cleanse the gardens which you water, so that, as you make your lovers drunk from the streams of grace unto the irrigation of devotion, so you may moisten the hard-hearted [Col. 0740C] and dry unto the fruit of repentance. Remove from the gardens of the Church the thorns of hatreds, the thistles of murmuring, and the stinging itch of lust, all of which are accustomed to arise from the hostile intemperance of the north wind against the flowers. At your command let the north wind arise; at your call let the south wind come, so that, when it blows, the gardens may flower anew, the perfumes of virtues may breathe forth, and the burning sweetness of your renown may come to the knowledge of all.

Otherwise, unless you stand beside the Church in labour and perform the office of a midwife for the bride of your Son, she who labours will have no strength. For “this woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow, because her hour has not yet come” (John 16). The people of the saints has not yet been completed; this woman has not yet brought her whole child into the light of glory. [Col. 0740D] But both Herod and Pharaoh still rage against the Church’s childbirth. Nevertheless the Church is a strong woman: a woman by reason of fruitfulness, because through the sacrament of faith she does not cease to bear children to God; strong by reason of the rock upon which she is founded, because she does not yield to temptation. For this woman, as is read in the Apocalypse, is “clothed with the sun, and the moon beneath her feet” (Rev. 12).

The moon signifies the changeableness and failing of temporal things, all of which the Church of the elect is said to have beneath her feet, because love of temporal things in no way rules her affections. Clothed with the sun, she is so illuminated by its brightness and inflamed by its heat that she contemplates nothing other than the very Sun of righteousness. O how difficult it is to find this woman, who is concealed in a few, like an elect [Col. 0741A] treasure hidden in a field! Hence her Bridegroom speaks thus in the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field” (Matt. 13).

For the kingdom of heaven is the glorious unanimity of those who hide themselves. The saints are hidden, who, as far as lies in them, hide and conceal themselves. They are always within; always they cover themselves behind closed doors; and while they bear the testimony of their own glory within their conscience, while they seek neither praise nor testimony from the mouth of human beings, they cause the inhabitant of heaven to enter into them. To him they say: “But you are in us, O Lord, and your name is invoked over us” (Jer. 14); and, “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1).

[Col. 0741B] Therefore, whether you call this Church of the saints an enclosed garden, a sealed fountain, a treasure hidden in a field, the kingdom of heaven, a cloister of modesty, or a strong woman, her “price is far off, and from the uttermost bounds,” because the inward love of her eternal Bridegroom makes her precious. For what is farther than the eternity of the heavenly Bridegroom, higher than his divinity, more inward than his charity, or more powerful than his virtue? Therefore his bride separates herself from the sight and desire of outward things; therefore she gathers herself into inward things—indeed, she shuts herself up within the cloister of conscience—because the more diligently she has hidden herself from human eyes, the more secretly she prepares heaven within herself for the inhabitant of heaven.

The constructed visible cloister bears the figure of this spiritual cloister, in which heavenly souls shut and [Col. 0741C] conceal themselves. Hence, according to the form of the material cloister, that invisible one also is built with four sides: the first is contempt of the world; the second, horror of hell; the third, the necessity of the vow; the fourth, desire for the heavenly kingdom. Between these four sides, by the obedience of regular discipline, those shut and hide themselves who abandon the vain liberty of the age, who tear themselves away from the sides of the north wind.

These words which were said above can also apply to any holy soul; except that it is difficult to find a holy one: “Who shall find a strong woman?”—“The holy man has failed; truths have been diminished among the children of men” (Ps. 11). Virtue has vanished, vice has prevailed, and, as the age has now grown cold, iniquity has abounded beyond measure. Who, then, shall find a strong woman? A holy soul is not inappropriately called a strong woman. For she is called holy (*sancta*) because she has been sanctioned (*sancita*), that is, confirmed in strength of mind. Therefore, because strength of mind sanctifies; because fear and love of the divine name confirm; because she is fruitful in good works; and because, through the constancy of virtue, she retains in herself a certain stability of the firmament. For while she is sanctified by grace in the purpose of holiness, she is lifted by sublimity of mind from low and weak works and is made firm as a stable firmament. 124

We call such a firmament heaven because, as Scripture says, “God called the firmament heaven” (Gen. 1). Therefore we say that God dwells in the saints—that is, in the heavens—because the saints, confirmed in the purpose of holiness, have themselves been made a firmament. And if a firmament, then a heaven, which is removed from every dreg of human earthliness. Hence the Greek *hagios* is called *sanctus* in Latin. *Hagios*, moreover, is interpreted “without earth.”

Thus, holy is what is sanctioned; sanctioned is what is confirmed; confirmed is what has been made into a firmament. A firmament is stable and firm, far divided from the earth, adorned with the wondrous variety of stars. Such is a holy heart: firm in the purpose of inviolate holiness, removed from earthly desires, adorned with diverse virtues as though with stars. Who, I ask, or where shall one find such a heart? “Surely her price is far off, and from the uttermost [Col. 0742B] bounds.” Would that you might find such a one in yourself, or that you might become such a one; do not be reluctant to seek and bring it from afar and from the uttermost bounds!

O how far off is that honour which it received at creation! How far off is the dignity of the divine likeness, by which, though endowed with it, it became foolish! For “when man was in honour, he did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48). Certainly, that the rational soul is of so great a price that, for its redemption, the inestimable price of the Word made flesh (John 1) is paid, was brought about by its wonderful creation. For when the Creator made it in his own likeness, he impressed upon it four notable marks of his own image: from the Creator’s eternity he drew [Col. 0742C] immortality; from the sublimity of wisdom, excellence of reason; from the invisibility of essence, simplicity of nature; from the liberality of generosity, freedom of choice.

How far off are those four from which the human soul drew these four? They are far off because they surpass every sense and exceed every reason and understanding of human beings and angels. They are uttermost bounds because, when the saints have arrived at comprehending them, they seek nothing further. “That you may be able,” says the Apostle, “to comprehend with all the saints what is the length, breadth, height, and depth” (Eph. 3). Length is the eternity of the Creator; breadth is his charity; 126 height is the loftiness of wisdom; depth is the incomprehensible subtlety of the invisible essence.

[Col. 0742D] O if the rational soul had preserved, together with the length of immortality, the long-suffering of perseverance; together with the breadth of free will, the freedom of righteousness; together with the height of reason, the loftiness of divine contemplation; together with the depth of simple essence, the simplicity of innocence—it would never have lost its price, which had come to it from so far away! But now, although it has lost the price of divine likeness because it abandoned the power of love, it was nevertheless not altogether without price, because it did not depart from the precious image of its Author. Precious indeed is the image which it retained ineradicably in the knowledge of truth; but far more precious is the likeness which, received in the love of virtue, an excessively hasty love of sin [Col. 0743A] effaced. But now let us return with heart and mind, truth and deed, to our Virgin.

She is our harbour; she is the anchor of our hope; she is the strong, fruitful, and powerful woman to whom we, poor and weak, must flee. Her fruitfulness is sufficient to drive away the poverty 127 of her children; her strength sufficient to deliver those who presume nothing upon their own powers. Mary, the star of the sea, is necessary to one sailing on this sea of uncertainty. She is the harbour of all mercy for a world suffering shipwreck. Let not the guilty person despair: she, our mother, who bore our Judge for us, has also made our Judge our advocate. If you desire pardon because of guilt, look confidently to Mary, and you will obtain mercy. If, placed in tribulation, you are cast down by faintheartedness, flee to Mary from your heart, and you will obtain the strength of patience.

[Col. 0743B] If a lover of the world whom you have renounced pursues you, return to Mary, Lady of the world, and you will trample all worldly things as dung. If the alluring softness of the flesh tempts you, invoke the Virgin, invoke Mary; and in the overshadowing which the power of the Most High wrought for her (Luke 1), you will find cooling for unlawful heat. Finally, in every assault of demons flee to Mary, Queen of angels, and at the nod of the Empress the craftiness of the tempter will cease. For she is the rising dawn, which reproves darkness, sets a limit to evils, puts an end to errors, and dispenses the rays of the true 128 light.

For Mary is Mother of grace, Mother of mercy, way of life, model of righteousness, medicine of repentance, instruction in patience, example of discipline, joy of the Church, end of misery, gate of paradise, and harbour. May Jesus Christ bring us to that harbour.

[Col. 0743]

## MARIAN FRAGMENTS OF ADAM, ABBOT OF PERSENIA

> **[Note: [Col. 0743] Hippolytus Maracius’s notes on this document were printed by Migne as a separate document, columns 771–780. Each number in the text of the *Fragmenta Mariana* refers to the note bearing that number in the separate document.]**

129

## FRAGMENT I

[Col. 0743B]

Christ descended as a virgin and in humility; and he descended through the virginal womb of a most humble mother, so that he who had undertaken to cure both natures corrupted by both maladies might possess in himself an abundance of both remedies. See how he descended and by what way he descended. He indeed descended through a virginal body; he descended as rain upon fleece and as drops falling upon the earth (Ps. 71): rivers of graces descended into Mary.

O necessary, impassible fleece of Mary’s virginity, which so silently and sweetly received the rain of saving grace! O voluntary rain, by which, when the fleece of most pure virginity was moistened (22), immeasurable brightness increased even upon the clean fleece itself, and our uncleanness received a washing in which it might be cleansed. Sprinkle me, my Lady, with this hyssop and I shall be cleansed; [Col. 0743D] wash me with this dew poured into you from the Father’s heart, and I shall be made whiter than snow (Ps. 50). You are wholly clean, wholly bright, wholly drenched with the sprinkling of divine dew; from an inviolate womb you bear the Lamb of singular innocence, and from inaccessible fleece you warm holy souls.

Through your womb Christ descended: innocence of supreme purity, a river of mercy full of an abundance of mercies; overflowing in the flood of all grace, he wiped away all the filth of the whole world. Through your words, dripping milk and honey of supreme sweetness, our little one grew into a perfect man; in the strength of his patience he bore the burdens of our insufficiency. “Truly he bore our infirmities and carried our sorrows” (Isa. 13); and he had from you the shoulders with which to bear them, when he received a passible body [Col. 0744B] from your flesh.

Through you he descended; through you he came as a little one to the humble. He appointed you advocate in our cause; he gave you yourself to the world as an immeasurable [Col. 0744C] gift. He chose you as the way of coming to us; he appointed you for us as the path of returning to our homeland. O way devoid of roughness and hardness, devoid of ignorance and error! Indeed, “mercy and truth have met each other in you” (Ps. 84). Mercy in you would not permit anything harsh or hard; nor would truth permit anything obscure to be in you.

O way of common salvation, devoid of iniquity and malice, devoid of trouble and toil! In you “peace and righteousness have kissed” (ibid.). The equity of righteousness would not allow anything distorted to be in you, nor would the tranquillity of peace endure anything burdensome to be in you. You are wholly sweet and bright, wholly pleasant and straight, gentle and peaceful; you bring us illumination of our hearts from the heart of the Father, and, speaking to our heart (Hos. 2), you draw believing hearts to yourself.

As has been said, you speak to our heart, because you bring forth for us the Lord of your heart, namely the incarnate Word. Let us therefore see how far down he descended through you. He descended certainly as far as the assumption of our body, as far as the likeness of sinful flesh. He descended as far as enduring hardships, as far as tolerating injuries. He descended 132 as far as the outrage of the Passion; he descended as far as the ignominy of cross and death; he descended as far as the service of a three-day burial; he descended as far as despoiling hell.

## FRAGMENT II

But since the splendour of heavenly things is difficult for weak eyes, let us turn our bleary eyes to the pillar of cloud and darkness. The pillar of cloud and darkness is indeed the firm sublimity of our Virgin, from which the brightness of the Godhead drew about itself a certain darkness. For while the splendour of the omnipotent Word is wrapped, through the Virgin’s conception, in the cloud of flesh, what else was the likeness of sinful flesh in that flesh but a certain darkness in a cloud? “Cloud and darkness are round about him” (Ps. 96), because the splendour of the Word is wrapped in the cloud of most pure flesh and, in that same flesh, surrounded by weakness (23).

But let us direct our attention to the pillar which we have set before us. Let us observe how firm, how straight, how upright it is! Let us observe, I say, how firm, how strong, how straight, 133 how smooth, how extended, how sublime it is! [Col. 0745B] (24) How firm, upon which both heaven and earth rest! How strong, which fights invincibly against all heresies and spiritual wickednesses! How straight (25), which knew no stain of sin! How smooth, which admits no wrinkle of duplicity! How upright, which surpasses every creature by the height of merits! How sublime, whom the Son of the Most High provided from eternity as a mother most worthy of himself! How blessed, who is God’s mother and bride, gate of heaven, delight of paradise, lady of angels, queen of the world, joy of saints, advocate of believers, strength of those who fight, recall of those who wander, and medicine of penitents!

O sure salvation, O compendium of life, O unique hope of pardon, O singular sweetness! You are my whole possession, Lady; with you is stored up for me the fullness of all good things. With you are hidden inexhaustible treasures of truth and grace, peace and mercy, salvation and wisdom, glory and honour. You are my anchor amid tossing waves, my harbour in shipwreck, my help in tribulation, my consolation in pain. 134 You are aid to your own in oppression, help at the fitting time, moderation in prosperity, joy in expectation, refreshment in labour. Whatever I can babble of your praises falls short of your praise, O one most worthy of every praise; yet I am bound to praise you. Though I speak of you with tongues of men and angels (1 Cor. 13), when I have poured out my whole self, it will be little.

Rather, I turn myself to that praise of you which is sung in the song of love: “Who is she that comes forth like the rising dawn, fair as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army arrayed in battle order?” (Song 6). In these words the praise of your fourfold glory is expressed briefly and subtly, truly and sublimely. For when you are born, you rise like a glowing dawn. Your birth, indeed, took the place of dawn: in it the day of grace began, while the night of unbelief and ignorance came to its end.

When you conceive the Sun of righteousness, you are illuminated, after the manner of the moon, by the benefaction of the shining sun. For the moon borrows from the sun the light which the nature of its denser body denies it; hence whatever beauty it has, it has through the favour of borrowed brightness. When you bear the Sun of righteousness, you are compared to the sun in an apt likeness: [Col. 0746A] just as the body of the sun is neither corrupted nor diminished by the ray it sends forth, so the bringing forth of the sacred birth does not violate you in bearing it.

And now, O chosen as the sun, what is your childbearing except the eternal splendour of a certain sun? This splendour shines everywhere, even in darkness, although the darkness does not deserve to comprehend it (John 1). In short, this splendour enlightens every human being coming into this world (ibid.); but human beings loved darkness more than light. To you, however, Mother of mercy, belongs the choice of the Sun, since you display rays of brightness to all.

Moreover, when you were taken from the wicked world to heavenly things, you became terrible to every spiritual wickedness as an army arrayed in battle order (Song 6). [Col. 0746B] Thus you were like the rising dawn in your birth; you possessed the beauty of the full moon when you were made full of grace in the conception of the incarnate Word; you were deservedly compared to the sun, remaining inviolate in childbirth; and you were terrible as an army arrayed in battle order in your passage, when, amid the rejoicing of heaven, the service of angels, the exultation of saints, and the flashing banners of virtues (26), you appeared terrible to demons.

Yet all our confidence is in the childbirth 136 of our Virgin, and although I am unworthy, I shall not cease to persist in her praises. If you need mercy, it is found more abundantly in the Virgin’s womb. If you are a worshipper of truth, give thanks to the Virgin, because truth, which you worship, has sprung up for you from the earth of virginal flesh (Ps. 84). If you are a follower of peace, likewise [Col. 0746C] give thanks to the Virgin, because from her is born for you “the peace which surpasses all understanding” (Phil. 4). If you are a practitioner of righteousness, take care not to be ungrateful to the Virgin, because through her womb “righteousness has looked down from heaven” (Ps. 84).

If your faith is shaken by some movement of a crooked conscience, look to the Virgin, and that which was wavering will be firmly established. If desire of the flesh delights you, look to the Virgin, and the danger to chastity is removed. If pride strikes your mind, turn your gaze upon the Virgin, and the swelling of the soul will subside through the merit of virginal humility. If you are inflamed by the torches of anger, raise your eyes to the Virgin, and through her tranquillity you will become gentle. If ignorance or error has led you away from the way of life, look to Mary, the star of the sea, and in her light you will be led back to the path of truth. If the idolatry of the vice of avarice has gained mastery over you, remember the Virgin’s generosity, and along with the 137 love of poverty there will come to you the piety of liberality.
