The Virgin’s compassion aids in every danger, and is powerful to aid. Give thanks for her childbirth, from whose fullness the entirety of charisms has flowed forth. The Virgin bore for us; the child is ours; for us a child is born, and a son is given to us.

## FRAGMENT III

“Mary says, ‘My soul magnifies the Lord’” (Luke 1). Observe first where she magnifies the Lord. Certainly, in the hill country, in the city of Judah, in the house of Zachariah. The Lord is magnified in the hills, whereas in the plains he is blasphemed. In the plains were those who, according to the prophet, “blasphemed the Holy One of Israel and were turned away backward” (Isa. 1). In the plains, I say, of the curse and confusion of Adam and Eve, who, having lost the integrity of the flesh and been estranged from the height of truth, made plains for themselves; for they had lost the mountains of truth and virtue.

Therefore Mary, rising from the valley of worldly vanity, from the depth of human corruption, from the plains of common iniquity, “went with haste into the hill country” (Luke 1). The hills are the heights of perfection. The heights themselves are the truth of a mind most illumined, the virginity of flesh most undefiled, and the power of the Most High overshadowing (ibid.) for the conception of the womb. These are the hills [Col. 0747B] which Mary climbed; this is the city of Judah; this is the house of Zachariah.

A city is a numerous collection of people living under one law. Mary’s rational thoughts, holy virtues, and most orderly actions constitute this people; the law of charity orders them in the confession of divine praise. For Judah is called “confession”; Zachariah, “remembrance of the Lord”; and the house of Zachariah is the virginal breast, retentive of the remembrance of God’s commandments.

Placed in these hills, the Mother of God hears, through Elizabeth’s prophecy, what she is to become; recalls what she had heard concerning the Lord through the angel’s announcement; considers the purity of her conscience; reflects that her flesh is entirely free from every foreign corruption; sees herself wholly divinely borne aloft. Now higher than the age, now surpassing every creature by merit of life, prerogative of singular grace, and immensity of joy, she sings a new 139 song to the Lord, saying: “My soul magnifies the Lord.”

Mary’s soul magnifies the Lord because she herself is magnified by the Lord; for unless Mary’s soul were first magnified by the Lord, it could not magnify the Lord. Therefore she magnifies him by whom she is magnified. She magnifies him not only with praise of the mouth, not only with holiness of body, but with singularity of love. Many magnify with their tongue, but blaspheme in their deeds and persecute in pride of heart; of them it is written: “They profess that they know God, but in their works they deny him” (Titus 1). These do not magnify but, as far as lies in them, diminish the name of the Lord. These are those to whom the Apostle says: “Through you the good name is blasphemed among the nations” (Rom. 2).

But in Mary tongue, life, and soul magnify the Lord. Her tongue magnifies by speaking the praises of the glory of divine holiness with magnificence; her life by meriting that same glory through works; her soul by loving singularly, attaining it in flights of contemplation, and comprehending with mind and womb the incomprehensible magnificence. As the Lord magnified Mary and Mary’s soul magnified the Lord, Mary’s voice sounded. But the Virgin’s voice is in power, the Virgin’s voice is in magnificence (Ps. 28): “My soul magnifies the Lord.”

It is very wonderful that she says that she magnifies the Lord, when in [Col. 0748A] her, through her, and for her the Lord was made a little lower than the angels (Ps. 8). “For a man was born in her” (Ps. 86): he was made man from her, and through what he assumed from her the Son of God was found lesser than the Father, lesser than angels, and subject to human beings. “What he assumed from her was the form of a servant; in taking this, though he was in the form of God, he emptied himself” (Phil. 2); and he who was incomprehensible in himself was made comprehensible in Mary.

How great an abasement it is, from being incomprehensible to become comprehensible! This abasement was accomplished in Mary. How, then, does Mary’s soul magnify the Lord whom the assumption of her flesh so greatly diminishes? For the Lord made the Word abridged [Col. 0748B] upon the earth within Mary. Tell us, then, Mary: how does your soul magnify God? Or perhaps the soul magnificently praises him whom the flesh assumed from you diminishes by the dispensation? It is indeed so. For in you is found both great and small he who is 141 immeasurable: great in the soul, small in the flesh; great in the height of a mind enlarged through the fullness of grace, small within the narrow confines of a maiden’s womb. Therefore your soul magnifies the Lord, because by his own shortening he so magnifies your womb. Thus Mary is wholly enlarged into the magnificence of the King: her spirit is enlarged, her womb is enlarged—her spirit by ineffable joy, her womb by ineffable conception. Therefore she magnifies the Lord by the exultation of a devout mind, which is magnified [Col. 0748C] by the Lord in the pure burden of her chaste womb. In both respects Mary bears joy: the joy by which the sorrow of sin is abolished, the world’s mourning driven away, penal lamentation released, and heavenly gladness restored. What, then, is Mary’s mind but a school of virtues, a ladder for angels, instruction for human beings, a pool of mercy, an object of justice’s regard? What is the Virgin’s womb but, as it were, the throne of the supreme King, from which he sets forth the decrees of heavenly Wisdom, displays examples of virtues, and renders the wisdom of the world foolish?

Mary therefore possesses within herself the joy of angels and human beings: “My soul magnifies the Lord,” she says, “and my spirit has exulted in God my Savior” (Luke 1). 142 Observe what she says. Her soul magnifies the Lord; her spirit exults in God. [Col. 0748D] Mary’s praise magnifies the Lord; the exultation of her spirit magnifies Mary. God’s Spirit gladdens Mary’s spirit; the Spirit of God is the Holy Spirit, and the Holy Spirit is invisible oil. Therefore Mary exults all the more truly and gloriously because, beyond all other women, she has been anointed in a more distinctive manner with invisible oil. Otherwise, how would Christ be born of the Virgin unless the Virgin had been singularly anointed with heavenly oil? For the wisest Virgin had oil in her lamp (Matthew 25), when she received the fullness of grace in purity of spirit.

What, I ask, does it mean that Mary’s spirit exulted in God, unless that the oil of gladness—cheering the countenance of her inward person—abounded in the Virgin’s lamp? A lamp, indeed, is a glass vessel for light: broad above [Col. 0749A] by reason of its material, narrow below by reason of its shape, fragile by nature. Such is Mary’s life: irradiated by heavenly splendor, full of the oil of mercy, transparent in purity, enlarged above by charity, restrained below by poverty of spirit, strong in the female sex, which is fragile by nature. Behold, 143 you have the lamp of the wisest Virgin, and you have oil in the lamp. Do you also wish to see iron in the oil, a rush in the iron, and fire kindled in the rush? The iron is the enduring and persevering humility of the mind; the rush is gentle virginity without the knot of sin. Therefore do not seek a knot in the rush. Otherwise, if the salvation of human beings had found in Mary a knot of guilt, how would it have untied in her and through her the knotted entanglement of worldly guilt? The fire in the rush is the Godhead in the Virgin’s [Col. 0749B] womb.

Visible rushes are indeed consumed by fire; yet virginity is not violated by the Author of integrity. Mary’s lamp, therefore, is unbreakable; its oil unfailing; its rush unconsumable; its fire unquenchable. Moses marvels in the wilderness that the bush burns and is not consumed (Exodus 3); marvel yourself that, in the oil of the virginal lamp, the rush is in no way consumed by fire. When fire is applied, the rush remains whole, because, while Mary conceives God and man, her virginal body remains inviolate. Therefore Mary’s spirit exults, because, through the oil of gladness abounding in her and the Holy Spirit coming upon her, her rush is kindled without consumption, 144 and her virginity made fruitful without corruption. Therefore she exults. Where does she exult? In God [Col. 0749C] her Savior, not in wicked things.

Note that the exultation of the world is one thing, that of God another. The world’s exultation consists in three things: bodily health, prosperity in possessions, and impunity in wrongdoing. This exultation is not from within, but outwardly, in wicked things; it belongs to the body, not the spirit. Therefore it is external and concerns outward things, not inward and spiritual ones. The spirit is not in God the Savior, but in worldly desire. But “all the glory of the King’s daughter is within” (Psalm 44). “My spirit,” she says, “exults in God my Savior.” Mary’s exultation is chiefly to be considered in three respects: from a handmaid she becomes queen of the world; from a poor girl, God’s mother and daughter; from a married woman, a virgin mother. [Col. 0749D] Measure, if you can, how much exultation consideration of these three things bestows upon Mary. Yet though she surpasses the angels in honor, though she possesses within herself him who is immense and “reaches mightily from end to end” (Wisdom 7), she cannot measure the greatness of her spirit’s exultation. Therefore she exults, although she does not express the measure of her exultation.

“Because he has regarded,” she says, “the humility of his handmaid” (Luke 1). Behold how great Mary’s humility is! She does not say: he has regarded the virginity of his bride, nor the holiness of his mother; but, “he has regarded,” she says, “the humility of his handmaid.” 145 O gracious regard, which none but the humble deserve! O Mary’s welcome humility, at which even the exaltedness of angels marvels! O most precious virginity, made fruitful by divine childbirth through [Col. 0750A] the merit of humility! Virginity would have been sterile if humility had been lacking. But now humility grants fruitfulness to virginity; fruitful virginity exalts and raises humility, because “whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 14). “He has regarded,” she says, “the humility of his handmaid”; and rightly so. For Truth, springing from the earth of virginal flesh, deserved the regard of justice looking down from heaven: “Truth has sprung up from the earth, and justice has looked down from heaven” (Psalm 84). Truth springing from the earth is true and flourishing virginity, which neither inward consent of mind has falsified nor outward lust of flesh corrupted.

Therefore the Lord regarded her and descended into his garden, from which breathed the hyssop of humility, blossomed [Col. 0750B] the lily of chastity, and in whose midst the rose of love was fragrant. That very regard was a descent. From this 146 regard, from this descent, the Mother of God was so heaped with grace that all generations truly call her blessed and most blessed above all others (Luke 1). Everywhere Mary’s glory is proclaimed; everywhere Mary’s excellence is extolled. Nothing is found sweeter than her remembrance, more health-giving than her grace, more effective than her mercy, or safer than her patronage. She is the gate of heaven, a harbor for the shipwrecked, the garden of paradise, the staff by which the weak world is supported, the rod by which the world’s iniquity is corrected (28), the dove in whom the Holy Spirit dwells for the cleansing of impiety. She is a dove, I say, by whose antidote of simplicity the many-formed cunning of the venomous serpent is exposed.

He who, disdaining worldly tumult, thirsted for the spiritual rest of a certain hidden solitude, asked that the wings of this dove [Col. 0750C] be given him, saying: “Who will give me wings like a dove’s, that I may fly and rest?” (Psalm 54). What is “that I may rest” except “that I may sleep”? Where shall I sleep except “between the two lots”? (Psalm 67). For between the two lots is felt the refreshment which “the dove’s wings” provide; and the wings of this dove are “silvered, and her back parts are in the pallor of gold” (ibid.). What different teachers have said concerning this passage you have read, I think; or, if you have 147 not read it, search the Scriptures and read. But also hear, as you have asked, not what I may say from myself, but what the Lord God speaks in me (Psalm [Col. 0750D] 84), without whom we can do nothing (John 14).

The wings of this dove are two: humility and virginity. They are silvered, marked by the divine utterance. For silver is God’s utterance; God’s utterance is God’s Word; God’s Word is the Son of God. What, then, is the silver on the dove’s wings except the Son of God in Mary through the presence of his flesh? By these wings the light and unencumbered fly to heaven; by them a canopy of refreshment is prepared for those who painfully burn below. “Her back parts are in the pallor of gold.” Behold, Mary has gone before us to glory. As we follow her who has gone before, what do we see of the one preceding us except her back? Her back parts are we ourselves: all who, left behind her back, strive in some measure to imitate her. Understand her face as her merits, her back as her examples. The former [Col. 0751A] she sent before; the latter she left to us, that we may be formed in the virtue of humility and the purity of chastity. These back parts are in the pallor of gold. By gold, than which no metal is more precious, Mary’s virginity is signified, than which nothing 148 after God is more excellent.

This gold has splendor and also pallor: splendor in the truth of its nature, pallor in the changeable surface of the mass—splendor naturally, pallor accidentally. The splendor of gold is uncorrupted chastity; its pallor is chastity restored after a fall through continence. Both splendor and pallor are in Mary’s gold, because by cleaving to her some remain in bodily integrity, while others, following her from afar, although they have lost the flower of virginity, nevertheless by love of chastity overcome within themselves the lust [Col. 0751B] of the flesh. What then? If we have lost virginity, do we therefore in no way belong to the Virgin or to the Virgin’s Son? Do not despair. For “her back parts” are “in the pallor of gold.”

Emulate, by continence and through the pallor of chastity, the splendor of golden virginity; and thus you will belong to the back parts that are in the pallor of gold. How beautiful and how rich is this dove! Her wings are silvered; her back parts gilded. In her wings silver resounds and shines; on her back gold gleams and is pale. The light of silver refers to grace, its sound to doctrine; the splendor of gold to wisdom, its pallor to patience. 149 Pallor, which is the sign of an afflicted countenance, denotes patience shown in adversities out of love for God. Thus both fullness of grace and soundness of teaching [Col. 0751C] are in the dove’s wings—that is, in Mary’s virtues; the radiance of heavenly wisdom and the pallor of patience are on the dove’s back—that is, in the outward conduct of the Virgin. But why is gold on the back? So that gold may be displayed on the back to those who follow and look only upon the back. What is more desirable than gold? What is more visible on the back of one who goes before? Whoever therefore bears gold on his back desires to have followers and imitators. Emulate, then, the better gifts (1 Corinthians 12). Silver is good, but gold is much better. Teaching is good, but wisdom is far better. For teaching without wisdom is knowledge that puffs up; wisdom is charity that builds up (1 Corinthians 8).

But who is fit for these things? To whom, I ask, has it been given to behold these wings [Col. 0751D] and emulate this gold? To whom has it been granted to sleep between the two lots? This is a usage of Greek expression. They say “between the two lots” where a Latin speaker would say “in the midst of the lots.” *Clēros* means a lot, and a lot is called an inheritance. 150 There are two lots, two inheritances, of the children of men: one which they have because they are children of God, the other which they have because they are children of men. The former is heavenly, the latter earthly; the former belongs to the soul, the latter to the body; the former is future, the latter present; the former ought to be an object of desire, the latter a necessary matter of use. Therefore whoever rests between the two, fleeing the tumult of the lower and seeking the quiet of the higher, in thus sleeping sees the beautiful one like a dove ascending above streams of water. Hence David also, seeing that rest [Col. 0752A] was good, says: “In peace, in the selfsame place, I will sleep and rest” (Psalm 4). And, wishing to have followers and companions in his sleep, he says: “If you sleep between the two lots, the wings of the dove are silvered, and her back parts are in the pallor of gold.”

The middle of the lots, where one must sleep, may be called charity, by which the tumultuous desire for the world is lulled in the mind and the peaceful desire for the eternal inheritance is awakened. Do you wish to see the middle of the lots? Look upon Mary the mediatrix. She is between heaven and earth, both middle and mediatrix between God and humankind. Let us understand her as 151 middle through the mercy of her condescension, she who has been raised so far above the heavens in glory. Therefore we must rest in her, because upon her rests the nourishing Spirit, without whom [Col. 0752B] every spirit is restless.

## FRAGMENT IV

And what does the Spirit of the Mediator say in the Prophet? “He who practices pride,” he says, “shall not dwell in the midst of my house” (Psalm 100). The house of the Mediator is the Church. The middle of this house is either Mary, the Mother of the Mediator and mediatrix; or truth, which knows no corner; or the virtue of charity as the middle. Therefore he “who practices pride” does not belong to the mediatrix, does not walk in truth, does not dwell in charity—pride which the communion of saints does not admit, as hostile to common goods and desirous of private glory. Since, therefore, the King of virtues rightly bears the name of Mediator, and Mary herself, the queen of virtues, presents herself as mediatrix [Col. 0752C] of humankind, the ecclesiastical judge ought rightly to devote himself to virtues and diligently strive, by the moderation of discretion, that no one do or say too 152 much. For it is not without reason that the infancy of the incarnate Word is recognized in the midst of two animals.

## FRAGMENT V

Humility is so awe-inspiring that one thinks it never safe to go forth from the lodging of a humble conscience. There one freely contemplates Mary, the star of the sea; there one happily stands by the Virgin’s childbirth; there one delightfully plays alongside that blessed infancy; there one wholly fits oneself to the Word’s cradle; with the innocence of one’s conduct one happily plays with the infancy, and in the joy of one’s heart lisps together with its tender cries. One considers it most precious to be adorned with those silken little cloths [Col. 0752D] in which the infant Word is wrapped. Then with all eagerness one carries oneself to that divine sanctuary of the most holy breast and, insofar as opportunity allows, drinks the breasts full of heaven. Meanwhile that tender infancy is nourished by such sustenance that, when it comes to perfect manhood and advances to a more mature age, it may be able to bear and accomplish the work of the cross. This is indeed the work of great persons: those whom a more advanced age of virtue, having senses trained through habit, 153 has made them bearded through the pursuits of wisdom. It goes very well with me (29), if my Jesus counts me among his companions; if, while he is sometimes received at his mother’s breast, he shares with me little draughts of his delight. For this purpose the Word of the Father, the bread of life, willed to be broken down in the milk of flesh, so that he who, in the form of God, was the solid food of angels might, [Col. 0753A] through the shortening of flesh, empty himself into a little draught for children.

## FRAGMENT VI

If the purpose of the path we have undertaken appears hard, let us flee to the help of our Virgin; for whoever that most merciful woman offers herself to as a helper will be strong in every tribulation and distress. Let us draw into ourselves the whiteness of her lily-like innocence through purity of conscience; and let the diligence of fruitful work not be lacking to us together with chastity of body, so that virginal fruitfulness may be honored. For we ought to direct all our attention to the childbirth of our Virgin. And if we wish to be true novices 154 and truly renewed, let us apply ourselves with desires full of grace to the new birth. For as through her we can obtain the grace of justification, so, with her as guide, we shall be able to arrive at glory, through the help of him who was born of her, Jesus Christ our Lord.

## FRAGMENT VII

“Like a beautiful olive tree in the plains” (Ecclesiasticus 24). If we call our Virgin an olive tree, her childbirth will be its oil (30). Our Virgin indeed is “a beautiful olive tree in the plains,” because her grace and mercy are common to all. Set in the plains, she brought forth the flower of the field; through that flower’s loveliness the nakedness of human ugliness obtained for itself most beautiful garments of the plain. Garments of the plain are the girdles or coverings of shame which all sew for themselves from this flower who, through faith and love of virginal childbirth, put aside the shameful things [Col. 0753C] of their sins. She is also “beautiful in the plains,” because she is the special beauty of the churches. For she has become beautiful and sweet, she from whom is born the holy sweetness of anointing—he who is “beautiful in form beyond the children of men” (Psalm 44). The fields may fittingly be called Christ’s churches, cultivated by the plow of heavenly discipline, sown with Gospel teaching, and made fruitful by the practice of justice. In these fields is the fruitful olive tree, the Virgin Mary, Mother of Mercy. From the olive flows the richness of oil; the Mother of Christ pours forth the fullness of grace and brings forth the anointing of mercy.

How pleasant and sweet it is to cling to her; how health-giving to remain within the lodging of the woman who has given birth! If you are weak, oil for the weak flows abundantly from that lodging. If you are healthy, and the soundness of justice smiles upon you through the testimony of your conscience, you receive the oil of gladness from Mary. Beauty of conduct, adornment of works, glory of merits—all is received from Mary’s grace when she is loved. For since she is full of grace and wholly abounding in the delights of mercy, we receive no grace whatever [Col. 0754A] which her childbirth does not bestow upon us. The Virgin is ours; the Virgin’s womb is ours; the Virgin’s childbirth is ours; ours are the heavenly things that are performed in her presence (31). It is therefore dangerous to depart from her even for a moment, since with her are stored the delights of our sweetness, 156 the riches of salvation, wisdom and knowledge, reserved by the Virgin for our use. In the Virgin’s childbirth the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden for the enrichment of the poor (Colossians 2).

“Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor” (Psalm 11), Christ came from the Father’s heart into the Virgin’s heart and placed in the Virgin’s womb the treasury of the poor. From it the poor in spirit were enriched—those whom the world’s pride, vanity, and falsehood had not made rich. “Children of men, [Col. 0754B] how long will you be heavy of heart?” (Psalm 4), having withdrawn from the Virgin’s heart? “Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” (ibid.), when “the Lord has made his holy one wonderful” within our Virgin’s womb (ibid.). Why do you not hasten to the oil? What is being done here is yours; for the God who is rich in all things would for no reason become poor except to adapt himself to the poor. For no reason would he place a fruitful olive tree in the plains except to show the Virgin’s mercy as common to all.

This is why the meaning of this mystery was first made known not to kings in palaces or rich persons in cities, but to shepherds in the fields, keeping watch over their flocks (Luke 2). O kindness of the Savior! O compassion of him who is born! O purity [Col. 0754C] and mercy of her who gives birth! O that I might be among the little ones to whom these things were revealed and done, so that I might not meanwhile care to philosophize about other matters! What is sweeter than to dwell at the Word’s cradle, than to be at leisure and free in Christ’s lodging, and to play with such blessed infancy? Forgive me, I beg, forgive the child if he does not leave the breasts full of heaven, if he does not abandon the most holy sanctuary of the virginal breast. At the undefiled footsteps of the Virgin is placed a pool of mercy, where children are bathed. You know that those of such an age need more frequent washing: they contract dirt very easily and must be cleansed by more frequent bathing through maternal solicitude. Therefore I do not consider it safe to go far from the companionship of the holy Virgin. For who would provide for me in such matters if [Col. 0754D] I withdrew from the mercy of the most indulgent Mother? I will hold her; I will not depart from her, because if the care of her mercy failed, I should easily become a miscarriage.

[Col. 0753]

158 NOTES TO THE *MARIALE*

[Col. 0753D] ON SERMON I

I also listed this sermon in Part I of the Marian Library, when discussing Adam, abbot of Perseigne, and his Marian writings. Since it contributes not a little to the advancement of the praise and devotion of the most blessed and immaculate Virgin Mother of God, [Col. 0754D] it will now, appearing for the first time, be read with benefit and great profit to souls.

(1) “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse.” The following 159 affirm that this passage of Isaiah concerns Mary, Virgin Mother of God: Tertullian, in *On the Flesh of Christ* and Book IV *Against Marcion*; St Gregory Thaumaturgus, [Col. 0755A] Oration I, on the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin; St Ambrose, in *On the Blessing of the Patriarchs*, ch. 4, and *On the Institution of Virgins*, ch. 9; St Augustine, Sermon 3 *On the Season*, and Book III *On the Creed for Catechumens*, ch. 4; St John Chrysostom, Homily 116 on Psalm 22; Pope St Leo, Sermon 4 on the Nativity of the Lord; St Ephrem the Syrian, in the oration *On the Praise of the Virgin*; St Jerome, on Isaiah 11 and in the letter to Eustochium *On the Guardianship of Virginity*; St Gregory the Great, on Book I of Kings, ch. 1; Germanus of Constantinople, Oration on the Nativity of the Mother of God; Cosmas of Jerusalem, Hymn 1 on the *Theogoria*; Damascene, Orations 1 and 2 on the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin; Chrysippus, in the oration on the Mother of God; Eusebius of Edessa, homily on the feast of the Visitation of the Blessed Virgin; Paul the Deacon, Sermon 2 on the Blessed Virgin; Ambrose Ansbert, homily on the feast of the Purification; George of Nicomedia, oration on the Presentation of the Mother of God; the Idiot, in *Contemplation of the Blessed Virgin*; Isidore of Seville, in the Commentary on Numbers, ch. 15, and in the *Allegories of the New Testament* [Col. 0755B]; St Ildefonsus, Sermon 6 on the Assumption and Book VII *On the Virginity of St Mary*, ch. 3; John Geometres, sermon on the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin; Vigilius of Trent, Book III *Against Eutyches*; Hesychius, Sermon 2 *On the Praise of the Blessed Virgin*; Venantius Fortunatus, elegy *In Praise of St Mary*; Eleutherius of Tournai, sermon on the feast of the Annunciation; St Anselm, treatise *On the Conception of the Blessed Virgin*; St Bruno 160 the Carthusian, Sermon 1 *On the Praises of the Virgin*; Rupert, abbot, Book II on Isaiah, ch. 6, Book I on the Song of Songs, Book II on Matthew, and Book XI *On the Victory of the Word of God*, ch. 8; Blessed Peter Damian, sermon on the Annunciation and sermon on the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin; Amadeus of Lausanne, Homily 8 *On the Praise of the Blessed Virgin*; St Bernard, Homily 2 on Advent, Homily 2 *On the Praise of the Virgin* on *Missus est*, and Sermon 2 on the Great Sign on the day of Pentecost; Peter of Blois, Sermon 1 on the Lord’s Advent; Philip, abbot, Book I on the Song of Songs, chs. 1–6; Honorius of Autun, in *The Seal of Blessed Mary*; Caesarius of Heisterbach, [Col. 0755C] in the homily on the Visitation of Blessed Mary and in the prologue to *On the Miracles of the Blessed Virgin*; Fulbert of Chartres, in verses on the Blessed Virgin; Radulfus Ardens, Homily 1 on the Annunciation and Homily 1 on the Nativity of Blessed Mary; Pope Innocent III, in the encomium on the most blessed Virgin Mary; Albert the Great, in *The Bible of Mary* on the prophet Isaiah and in the postils on Luke 10; St Thomas Aquinas, Sermon 1 on the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin; St Bonaventure, in *The Mirror of the Blessed Virgin*, ch. 3, and in the exposition of *Hail, Queen*; Hugh of St Victor, Book IV of *Theological Instruction*, Miscellany 2, title 27; Hugh of St-Cher, on Isaiah 11; St Antoninus, Archbishop of Florence, in the *Summa Theologica*, Part III, title 31, ch. 3, and Part IV, title 15, ch. 3; Abbot Trithemius, Book I *On the Miracles of the Blessed Virgin at Dittelbach*, ch. 10; John Picus Carthusianus, Book I on the Song of Songs, ch. 13; Blessed Thomas of Villanova, Discourse 2 on the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin; St Bridget, 161 in the sermon *On the Excellence of the Blessed Virgin*, ch. 11; Richard of St Lawrence, Book V *On the Praise of the Virgin*, col. 281; Maurice of Villa Probata, in *The Crown of the Blessed Virgin*, Sermon 3; and, to omit others, Richard of St Victor, who composed a notable treatise comparing Mary to the rod and Christ to the flower.

[Col. 0755D] Hence the Greek Church, in the *Menaea*, on 24 March calls Mary “the mystical rod, which brought forth the divine flower, manifestly sprung from the root of Jesse.” And there, on 25 July: “The rod blooming beforehand, greater than every proclamation, which brought forth from itself the flower that never withers.”

(2) “O fruitful tree.” Under the metaphor of a tree, the following also praise the Virgin Mother of God: St Cyprian, or the author of the sermon attributed to him on Christ’s Nativity; Eusebius of Emesa, homily on the feast of the Visitation of the Blessed Virgin; Rupert, abbot, Book II of the Commentaries on Leviticus; and St Ephrem the Syrian, in the treatise *On the Precious Pearl*, where he calls Mary “the tree of the eternal Father, made for the reception of a better nature.” Richard of St Victor also, in his exposition of the Song of Songs, ch. 39, calls the Mother of God “a lofty and noble tree [Col. 0756A] that brought forth a lofty fruit, namely the Son of God”; Amadeus of Lausanne, Homilies 1 and 8 *On the Praise of the Virgin*, calls her “the saving tree planted in the midst of paradise, whose unfailing fruit and immortal childbirth afford the heavenly and earthly inhabitants continual feasting, continuous exultation, happy and everlasting 162 praise”; Hugh of St Victor, Sermon 47, on the Assumption of Blessed Mary, calls her “the tree of Lebanon,” because she took her origin from the world of present flesh and, raising herself aloft, surpassed Lebanon itself—that is, the world’s height—by immeasurably transcending all worldly glory through the loftiness of her virtues; St Bruno the Carthusian, or rather Bishop Siguinus, in the sermon on the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin, calls her “a most beautiful tree, whose fruit—that is, Christ—we ought to receive in our infirmities; we ought never to forget it, but always look to her and seek from her the fruit of life and salvation”; St Bonaventure, in *The Mirror of the Blessed Virgin*, chs. 5 and 14, calls her “a great tree [Col. 0756B] that extends its branches broadly to human beings, far to angels, and high to God”; “a tree beautiful in the leaves of its mouth, more beautiful in the flowers of its heart, most beautiful in the most beautiful fruit of its womb”; and “a tree most high and yet most low: most high in dignity, most low in humility; most high in the Lord’s eyes, most low in her own eyes”; Absalon, abbot, in Sermon 3 on the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin, calls her “our fruitful tree, in whose branches all may find most abundantly sweet fruit, unless perhaps, with appetite weakened like sick people, they disdain what is pleasant and sweet. For it often happens that bread is a punishment to an unhealthy palate, and light, lovely to pure eyes, is hateful to diseased eyes”; Albert the Great, in the postils on Luke 11, calls her “a tree 163 flourishing in virtue, planted beside the courses of waters—that is, the most abundant streams of the gifts, consolations, and graces of the Holy Spirit—which bore fruit hanging from her holy womb and supplied to him, as he hung from the womb, her own most holy blood [Col. 0756C] as nourishment for formation and growth”; St Anthony of Padua, in the sermon for Palm Sunday, calls her “a most beautiful tree, whose fruits were humility and poverty; these fruits we must preserve for ourselves, according to Leviticus 23: ‘You shall take for yourselves the fruits of the most beautiful tree’”; lastly, St Mechthild, Book I of *Spiritual Grace*, ch. 45, calls her “a tree extended above every height and breadth of earth; transparent like a clear mirror, bearing golden leaves that give forth a most sweet sound, upon whose summit was a most delightful flower, which covered the whole world and sprinkled it with a wondrous fragrance.”

In the interest of brevity I pass over St Bernardino of Siena, Sermon 1 *On the Glorious Name of Mary*; Isidore of Thessalonica, in the *Mariale* published by us, Oration 4 on the Assumption; St Bridget, in the Angelic Sermon, ch. 8; Maurice of Villa Probata, in *The Crown of the Blessed Virgin*, Sermons 1 and 3; Richard of St Lawrence, Book XII *On the Praise of the Blessed Virgin*, from p. 1001 onward; the anonymous author in the Greek hymn in Buteo, [Col. 0756D] p. 125; and many others who celebrate Mary, Virgin Mother of God, under the symbol of a tree.

(3) This is the rod of Moses. On the Mother of God. Leo the Emperor admirably treats the Mother of God as mystically prefigured in Moses’ rod in the *Mariale* published by us, Oration 3; likewise Rupert, Abbot, Book I of the *Commentaries on the Song of Songs*; Absalom, Abbot, Sermon 1 on the Annunciation and Sermon I on the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin; Albert the Great, in the *Bible of Mary* on Exodus; St Thomas Aquinas, Sermon 1 on the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin; St Bernardino of Siena, Sermon 1 *On the Glorious Name of Mary*; St Antoninus, *Summa Theologica*, Part III, title 31, chapter 3, and Part IV, title 15, chapter 24; Mauritius de Villa Probata, *Crown of Blessed Mary*, Sermon 7; and Richard of St Lawrence, Book XII *On the Praises of the Virgin*, cols. 1025, 1026, 1027, and 1028. I shall set before the reader only his words, wholly worthy of insertion here in praise of the Virgin.

This [Mary] is the rod of Moses, by which he performed signs in Egypt, and to which he had recourse in every necessity [Col. 0757A] (Exod. IV), because Christ, through Mary, performed wonders in the world. This is the pastoral rod by which Moses drove his flock into the depths of the wilderness (Exod. III); for as sheep are driven by a guiding rod, so the morals of the faithful are corrected and, as it were, ordered by the example of Mary. Therefore Micah prays to the Lord at the end [of his book] (chap. V): “Lord our God, feed your people with your rod.”

Likewise (Exod. IV), the Lord said to Moses: “What is that which you hold in your hand?” Moses answered: “A rod.” This indicates that this rod must be held in the hand through the likeness of works, not merely in the mouth through invocation and praise, or in the heart through faith, which without works is dead (Jas. II).

Moses’ rod, changed into a serpent, devoured the dragons of Egypt (Exod. VII), because, when Mary clothed Christ in flesh resembling sinful flesh, she destroyed, by the power of her offspring and by the example of her holiness, the heresies with which the ungodly mocked in Egypt, that is, in the world. This was fulfilled when, as she entered Egypt with her son, all the idols [Col. 0757B] fell, as Isaiah had foretold (chap. XIX).

Or otherwise: the Blessed Virgin, opening her mouth to entreat her Son, devours and annihilates serpents—that is, the wiles of demons and the temptations that poison souls—as it was said to the serpent (Gen. III): “She shall crush your head.” Or she devours serpents—that is, the wiles of tempting demons—when she makes with temptation a way of escape, according to the words (Ps. CVI): “All their wisdom was swallowed up.”

Likewise, with this rod Moses struck the water of the river before Pharaoh and his servants; the water was turned into blood, and the fish in the river died (Exod. VII). Similarly Mary, through her prayers, merits, and examples, converts worldly and carnal pleasures—which pass quickly like water—into abhorrence and bitterness, as it were into blood which no one can drink, in those sinners who are converted, especially those devoted to her. Thus the river-fish die, that is, vain curiosities.

Likewise, when Moses stretched out this rod toward heaven [Col. 0757C] (Exod. IX), “the Lord gave thunder and hail, and lightning flashing over the land of Egypt.” This suggests that this rod strikes fear into certain proud persons who do not fear God unless there is thunder and lightning; it terrifies them, granting them grace to reflect upon their evils. This occurs especially when they consider how grievously she herself was punished in her Son, although she never sinned. Thus Simeon foretold to her: “A sword shall pierce your own soul also” (Luke II); for “if these things are done in the green wood, what shall be done in the dry?” (Luke XVIII).

Likewise, when this rod was stretched over the land of Egypt (Exod. X), “a scorching wind brought up locusts, which devoured every herb of the earth and all the fruit of the trees, leaving nothing green.” By such greenery are signified bodily endowments and beauty, which quickly pass away; for beauty is a fragile good and is often devoured by the locusts of pride or lust. But the Blessed Virgin, by granting grace to consider that favour is deceitful and beauty vain [Col. 0757D] (Prov. XXXI), that all outward freshness quickly withers, and that the fruit of good works is easily devoured by vainglory, helps many to hold all these things cheap.

Likewise, when the children of Israel withdrew from Egypt (Exod. XIV), hemmed in by the sea on one side, mountains on another, and Pharaoh on another: before them was the sea, which could not be crossed; at the side were lofty mountains, which could not be passed; behind them was Pharaoh, armed with his chosen men and all his armed princes, who could not be avoided. While they were perplexed and despaired of escape, the rod was stretched out over the sea. At its raising, that sea was divided, and at once a way through it was made as through dry land.

Morally understood: the Red Sea is the world bloodied by vices and sins; the difficult mountains are the hardships and miseries of this world, which prevent many from undertaking repentance; Pharaoh, prince of Egypt, is the devil, together with aerial powers and wicked people. Yet from all these things we who hope in her can easily be delivered by the aid of our Rod [Col. 0758A]. Therefore, after Moses’ example, in every necessity we must have recourse and flee to her.

Likewise, in a moral sense: by the Red Sea is signified true contrition, bitter from the recollection of preceding sins, which are there called “bloods”: “Deliver me from bloods, O God,” etc. (Ps. X). This sea ought to be divided, so that we may be made bitter over sins committed and omitted, carnal and spiritual sins, and the substance and circumstances of sins. Or the division of the sea is, through the grace of our Rod, a lessening of temptation; this happens when, by her help, the flame of fire is cut off.

This is the rod of Moses with which he struck the rock (Exod. XVII; Num. XX), and waters flowed so that the people and their beasts drank. The rock is Christ (1 Cor. I): “And the rock was Christ.” The hardness of this rock is the rigor or severity of divine justice. Yet he is never so severe or hard toward sinners that he does not pour out waters of grace or pardon, if this Rod touches him with devout prayer. Therefore it is said (Num. XX) [Col. 0758B] that when Moses raised his hand and struck the rock twice with the rod, most abundant waters came forth—that is, copious streams of mercy—so that the people drank, that is, rational creatures, and the beasts, that is, beastly and brutish persons.

But this rock, Christ, is, as it were, touched twice by this rod when first virginal purity and secondly maternal dignity are presented to him by his mother in prayers. Therefore the Son says (Song IV): “You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride; you have wounded my heart.” This twofold wounding is the double striking of this rock. Or the prayer to the Father and the command addressed to the Son are, as it were, the double blow; whence we say to the mother: “Pray to the Father; command the Son.”

Otherwise, as Peter Comestor says, this rock signifies the hardness of the human heart, which is, as it were, inflexible, especially toward obedience, because of a certain freedom seemingly innate in the human mind: it wishes to rule, not to be subject. But this rod struck that hardness by her example, when she so readily [Col. 0758C] obeyed the divine will, answering: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord” (Luke I), whose proper office is obedience.

Otherwise: then the hardness of the human heart is struck by this rod when a hardened sinner is mercifully touched by her in respect to grace, so that streams of tears flow from him.

Otherwise: through this rod the Lord broke the rock—that is, the hardness of the human heart—in the wilderness, that is, in the unfruitful sinner, full of wild beasts, that is, monsters of sins. When that hardness is broken, he waters sinners—that is, refreshes them with waters of tears, which call forth the waters of graces. Thus far Richard of St Lawrence, in the place cited.

(4) She is the rod of Aaron. Nor is the Mother of God only, as we have shown, the rod of Jesse and the rod of Moses, but also the rod of Aaron, which without sap flowered, put forth leaves, and bore nuts (Num. XVII). For she is celebrated as such by St Athanasius of Alexandria, Oration on the Meeting of the Lord, or on the Purification of the Blessed Virgin; St Ephrem the Syrian, Oration *On the Praise of the Virgin*; St Augustine, Sermon 3 *On Time*, and Sermon 19 *To the Brothers in the Desert*; [Col. 0758D] St Eleutherius of Tournai, Sermon for the Feast of the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin; St Ildephonsus of Toledo, Sermon 6, *On the Assumption*; Sergius of Hierapolis, Oration on the Nativity of the Virgin; St Isidore of Seville, Commentary on the Book of Numbers, chapter 15; St Germanus, in the *Mariale* published by us, Oration on the Nativity of the Virgin; St John Damascene, in the Greek *Menaea*, 17 January; Ambrose Autpert, Homily for the Feast of the Purification of the Blessed Virgin; George of Nicomedia, Oration on the Presentation of the Blessed Virgin; Fulbert of Chartres, Sermon 1 on the Nativity of the Virgin; Peter Damian, Sermon on the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin; Bernard of Clairvaux, Sermon on the Nativity of the Virgin, *On the Aqueduct*; Vigilius of Trent, Book III against Eutyches, volume V of the *Library of the Fathers*, Part III; Abbot Philip, Book I on the Song of Songs, chapter 16, and volume VI of the *Moral Exposition of the Song of Songs*; Peter of Celle, *On the Loaves*, chapter 21; Hugh of St Victor, Book IV *On the Properties and Epithets of Things*, chapter 2, in the *Explanatory Notes on the Gospel of St John*, and Book IV of *Theological Instruction*, miscellany 2, [Col. 0759A] title 27; St Bruno the Carthusian, Book *On the Praise of the Church*, chapter 3; St Thomas Aquinas, Sermon 1 on the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin; St Anthony of Padua, Sermon for the Twelfth Sunday after Trinity; Albert the Great, in the Postils on Luke chapters X and XI, and in the *Bible of Mary* on Numbers; Rupert, Abbot, Book I of the Commentary on the Song of Songs and Book II of the Commentary on Numbers; Absalom, Abbot, Sermon 1 on the Annunciation; St Bonaventure, *Mirror of the Blessed Virgin*, chapter 8; St Bernardino of Siena, volume I, Sermon 59; Blessed Lawrence Giustiniani, Sermon on the Annunciation of Blessed Mary; St Antoninus, *Summa Theologica*, Part III, title 31, chapter 3, and Part IV, title 15, chapters 5 and 24; Richard of St Lawrence, Book XII *On the Praises of the Virgin*, col. 1032; Hugh of Saint-Cher, on chapter XVII of the Book of Numbers; and very many others.

Since their words are readily found in the authors themselves, I refrain from bringing them forward here, especially since nearly all place the comparison in this: just as Aaron’s rod flowered and bore fruit without the cultivation of human assistance, so the Blessed Virgin [Col. 0759B] conceived and bore the Son of God by the Holy Spirit without the touch of a man.

(5) That through you, and by you, the sick person may receive health. Recognizing this healing and thoroughly curative power of the Virgin Mother of God over every illness, the Greek Church likewise addresses the Mother of God in its ritual, in the Office of Holy Oil, in this manner:

> O you who alone are pure, endowed with the sea of peace, by your unceasing prayers before God rescue your servant from diseases and calamities, that he may magnify you without ceasing.
>
> Look mercifully from on high, Mother of the Maker of all, and through your intercessions relieve the bitter infirmity of this sick person.
>
> Mother of God, most holy perpetual Virgin, mighty protectress, harbour and wall, ladder and defence: have mercy and compassion; for the sick person has recourse to you alone.
>
> O pure one worthy of praise, Lady most gracious above all, have mercy on those anointed with divine oil, and save your servant.
>
> In the house of your God you appeared as a fruitful olive tree, O Mother of God, [Col. 0759C] through whom the world has been filled with mercy; therefore preserve this sick person by the aid of your prayers.
>
> You who enclosed in your womb, by divine counsel, him who contains all things in his fist, and ineffably gave him a body: Mother of God, we pray, now intercede for the infirm.
>
> Virgin, having received the praises and prayers of your servants, by your prayer free from grievous infirmities and sicknesses him who through us has recourse to your divine protection, O undefiled one.

In the same ritual, in the funeral Office for a deceased priest, it addresses the Mother of God thus:

> Your protection, Virgin Mother of God, is a remedy and a spiritual dispensary; by fleeing to it, we are delivered from the diseases of the soul.

And in the canon for deceased children:

> You who bore Wisdom and the Word of the Father, heal the grievous wound of my soul and soothe the pain of my heart.

And in the canon in danger of a pestilential illness:

> Christ the Lord, the abyss proceeding from you, has made you a fountain of suitable remedies; therefore deliver your servants, tossed by the tempest [Col. 0759D] of infirmity.
>
> Struck by violent and continuous pains, all of us fall before you, O Virgin. Save all by your mighty protection, O pure one; have mercy, Bride of God. Preserve us from this destruction and severe disease, and heal our infirmities, O Lady.
>
> In the night of this life the darkness of infirmity has enveloped us, and the shadows of diseases have covered us everywhere; but shine upon me, O pure one, splendour of restoration, and lead me to the light of health.
>
> Mary, pure vessel of virginity, cleanse us from diseases and calamities, and rescue us from approaching infirmity, that we may celebrate you in faith.

You, O immaculate one, are the safest refuge and secure asylum, the hope of the despairing. Therefore visit your servants who are grievously ill; lighten the burden of bitter infirmity, avert the disease of pestilential calamity, and preserve your servants, Virgin Mother of God.

Finally, in the Office of Common Supplication, it addresses her in these words:

> O Virgin, you heal the deep infirmities of the soul and the pains of the flesh of those who faithfully praise you and highly exalt your ineffable offspring. [Col. 0760A]

See what we have said in the *Mariale* of St Isidore, Archbishop of Thessalonica, in the notes to Oration 1 on the Nativity of the Virgin, no. 11 throughout. See also Justin Miechow, volume II, on the Litany of Loreto, under that title of the Blessed Virgin, *Health of the Sick*, discourses 355, 356, 357, and 358; and Laurentius Chrysogonus, *The Marian World*, Part II, discourse 17, where he treats most fully of the Mother of God as physician of human infirmities and healer of every disease.

(6) Staff of support. The Mother of God is also honoured by the designation “staff” by St Sabbas, Abbot, in the Greek *Menaea*, 28 January, where he calls her the Staff of the Blind; by St Germanus, Patriarch of Constantinople, in his *Mariale* published by us, Oration I on the Presentation; and by Eutychianus in the *Life of St Theophilus*, printed in Surius, volume I, 4 February, where they call her the Staff of Old Age; [Col. 0760B] by St Bonaventure in the *Psalter of the Blessed Virgin*, where he calls her the Staff of the Poor and Wretched; by James, Archbishop of Genoa, Sermon 3 on the Annunciation and Sermon 6 on the Assumption, where he calls her the Staff sustaining and guiding the weak, and the Staff of the old age and weakness of the prophets; and by others.

That the Blessed Virgin, like a staff, supports her righteous servants, lest they fall and slip into sins, I have shown in the notes to the *Mariale* of Leo the Emperor, in the notes to Oration 2 on the Presentation, no. 6, to which I refer the eager reader.

Notes on Sermon 2 concerning the childbirth of the Blessed Virgin.

I omitted from my Marian library the present sermon concerning the childbirth of the most blessed Virgin, together with the one immediately following it, also prefaced as concerning the Advent and Nativity of the Lord. I did so because the codex of Casamari, in which the works of our Adam are contained, had not yet come into my sight and I relied only on others’ reports. Yet I shall include both in the second edition of that library, if God deigns to grant my wishes, since both are most worthy of everyone’s knowledge and reading. [Col. 0760C]

(7) Her way was the Virgin Mary. Adam proves here that Mary the Mother of God is the way of God coming to us, and likewise our way by which we make for God himself; and many of the ancient Fathers confirm this: Augustine, in the Oration *On the Five Heresies*, chapter 5, calls Mary the way which the Lord prepared for his journey; Anastasius, Archbishop of Antioch, Oration 1 on the Annunciation, calls her the Way of Our Salvation; Venantius Honorius Clementianus Fortunatus, Bishop of Poitiers, in the elegy *In Praise of St Mary*, calls her the Way to heaven for humankind fallen beneath Tartarus; John Geometres, Sermon on the Annunciation of the Most Holy Mother of God, declares her the Way by which the erring return again; the Seraphic Doctor Bonaventure, in the *Psalter of the Blessed Virgin*, celebrates her as the Way of Our Reconciliation and the Way to the Homeland of Holiness; St Bernardino of Siena, [Col. 0760D] Sermon 1 *On the Glorious Name of Mary*, proclaims her the “way by which light is spread and heat is distributed over the earth” (Job XXXVIII): for eternal light was spread, that is, made manifest, over the dark world through her; and heat, that is, the warmth of the Holy Spirit’s charity, was distributed over the earth, so that there is now none who hides himself from its heat (Ps. XVIII). Alan of Lille, in the *Anticlaudianus*, Book V, sings of her as the Way of Life. Finally, Mauritius de Villa Probata, in the *New Crown of Blessed Mary*, Sermons 2, 6, and 12, declares her our way, the royal way of entering into glory, the way of the refreshment of the Son of God Most High, and the way by which God is reached.

See our Adam in Marian Fragment 1, where he speaks again of Mary as a way free from roughness and hardness, free from ignorance and error.

(8) She is the mother of mercy. After that supreme designation of the Mother of God, unheard of in all previous ages, nothing can be said of Mary or for Mary more excellent in praise, more illustrious in commendation, or more divine in glory, than that she is truly and peculiarly mother of mercy.

She is called mother of mercy either because, by bearing for us as man God—whose proper attribute is always to have mercy and to spare—she made him merciful in a singular way: not merely in effect, as before, but in affection and through experience of our misery, according to the golden words of the Apostle in Hebrews II: “He took hold not of angels, but of the seed of Abraham; whence he ought in all things to be made like his brethren, that he might become merciful.” Or she is called mother of mercy because she is believed to open the abyss of divine mercy and clemency to whom she wishes, in whatever manner she wishes, and whenever she wishes, so that, although an enormous sinner, he may not perish, since the Holy of Holies does not permit the aid of her patronage to be lacking to him. Or finally, she is called mother of mercy because the most kindly disposition and character of that Virgin, entirely [Col. 0761B] compacted and formed from the native sap of mercy, may be called a kind of vapour of the power of God and an emanation of his mercy.

The Mother of God is called by this title, Mother of Mercy, not only by the Church, as is clear from the divine Office: “Mary, mother of grace, mother of mercy,” and “Hail, Queen, mother of mercy”; not only by angelic spirits, as Peter Dorland left on record in the *Carthusian Chronicle*, Book V, chapter 5; not only by innumerable holy Fathers, whose bare names alone would be too laborious to set forth; but the most blessed Virgin herself also applies this title to herself more than once, as is clear from the *Life of St Odo, Abbot of Cluny*, from Theodoric of Apolda, *Life of St Dominic*, Book II, chapter 13, and from St Bridget, Book VI of the *Revelations*, chapter 10.

And truly she is mother of mercy. As Andrew of Crete says, Oration 2 *On the Dormition*, on account of the kinship which wholly intercedes for her with her Son and guardian, it is altogether innate to her to have mercy on all. Truly she is mother of mercy, whose breasts, as Richard of St Victor writes in Part II on the Song of Songs, chapter 23, are so filled with compassion that, touched by knowledge of anyone’s misery, they pour forth milk of mercy; she cannot know miseries without aiding them. Truly she is mother of mercy, since, as St Bridget testifies, Book VI of the *Revelations*, chapter 10, there is no one so cursed by God that, while living, he lacks her mercy: through her he is tempted more lightly by demons than he otherwise would be, and there is no punishment in the fire of purgatory which, through her, is not milder and easier to bear than it otherwise would be.

Among others, Jean Gerson, Chancellor of Paris, speaks excellently of the Mother of God as Mother of Mercy, writing in these words in Treatise 2 *On the Canticles*: “What more could he refuse you, Mother of Mercy, if he consented that his own Son should be offered for you to such misery? What will she grant when beatified in heaven, she who gave such things while afflicted on earth? She has lost misery; has she then also lost mercy? She has indeed lost afflictive compassion, but retains elective [Col. 0761D] and succouring compassion.” Thus he.

And in Treatise 4 on the *Magnificat*, considering what King Ahasuerus said to Esther in joyful delight—“What do you desire, Queen Esther? What is your petition? Even if you ask for half of my kingdom, it shall be given you” (Esther V)—he affirms that what was promised to Esther in type was fulfilled in the Virgin. For God himself bestowed on her half of his kingdom. He says that God’s kingdom consists of two parts, namely power and mercy, according to Psalm LXI: “These two things have I heard: that power belongs to God; and to you, Lord, mercy.” God, retaining power, assigned mercy to the Virgin as his reigning bride.

(9) She is the queen of justice. That is, queen of all virtues. For justice, as Aristotle, prince of the Peripatetics, says in Book VI of the *Ethics*, is the most excellent of virtues and is itself every virtue. Gregory of Nyssa testifies to this in Book IV of the Orations *On the Beatitudes*, explaining Matthew V, “Blessed are they who hunger and thirst for justice”: “Every virtue is signified by the name justice.”

That the Mother of God possessed the kingdom of all virtues is asserted by the Idiota in his *Contemplation*, chapter 2, when addressing the Virgin he says: “You lacked no kind of virtues, O more than blessed Virgin. Whatever gift was ever given to any of the saints was not denied to you; rather, you have all the privileges of all the saints gathered together in yourself.” Rupert, Abbot, confirms this in Book IV on the Song of Songs, writing: “Whatever graces, O Virgin, whatever virtues, whatever heavenly operations the world has received, are your outpourings.” Blessed Peter Damian, in the Sermon *On the Assumption*, considers the words of Song III, “Like a little rod of smoke from spices of myrrh and frankincense and every fragrant powder,” and adds: “Therefore every fragrant powder was cast into the Virgin, because the assembly of virtues consecrated for itself in her a chamber worthy of reverence.” St Bonaventure, Book IV *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, near the end, says: “In her, the Mother of God, kinds of every virtue are implanted without measure and number.” Finally, to omit others, Jerome says in a Sermon on the Assumption: “If you consider carefully, there is no brightness, no splendour, no virtue which does not shine forth in the glorious Virgin.”

But the Virgin Mother of God is queen of justice not only insofar as justice is made up of the assemblage of all virtues, but also insofar as justice is the particular virtue that gives to each what belongs to him. She possessed this so eminently and royally that by right and merit she both is and may be called queen. Therefore Richard of St Lawrence, Book IV *On the Praises of the Virgin*, col. 277, speaking of the Virgin’s justice, says:

> Justice gives to each what is his; and Mary gave the angel who greeted her a discerning reply, namely: “How shall this be?” (Luke I); to God praise and thanksgiving, saying: “My soul magnifies,” etc. (ibid.); and to human beings sufficient instruction, saying (John II): “Whatever he tells you, do.”
>
> Likewise, she rendered “to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. XXII). For she gave God back to the world, whom the world had lost through Eve; and, insofar as lies in her, she never ceases through prayers, merits, and examples to return the world—that is, lovers of the world—to the Lord. For through her especially God became the God of the world, and the world became God’s.

Thus he. On the justice of the Blessed Virgin, Dionysius the Carthusian, among others, writes most fully and devoutly in Book III *On the Praises of the Virgin*, article 12, and Book III *On the Glory of Mary*, article 4; one will not regret having read him.

(10) The Law and the Prophets [were] until Mary. For in Mary the things spoken by the Law and the Prophets received their end, and to Mary came the end of all things, since she displayed the fulfilment of all figures, as George, Archbishop of Nicomedia, proves in his Oration on the Presentation of the Blessed Virgin. Looking to this, Andrew of Crete, in the Oration on the Dormition of the Mother of God, called Mary “the End of the Testaments which God made for us”; and St Ildephonsus, Sermon 1 on the Assumption, said that “all the utterances of the prophets and all the enigmas of Scripture” converged upon Mary.

Nor should Rupert, Abbot, be omitted: in Book I on Isaiah, chapter 34, he asserted that in Mary’s womb the prophecy of all the holy prophets was fulfilled. Hence St Bonaventure, in *Praise of the Blessed Virgin*, after showing that Mary the Mother of God was prefigured in Holy Scripture and the prophets in many ways—namely, by the spring rising from the earth (Gen. II); by the tree of life planted in the midst of paradise (ibid.); by the paradise watered by the river of delight (ibid.); by Noah’s ark, through which the human race was preserved in the time of the flood (Gen. VI and VII); by the heavenly bow which the Lord placed as a sign (Gen. IX); by the ladder Jacob saw in a dream (Gen. XXVIII); by the bush which burned and was not consumed (Exod. III); by the vessel in which manna was kept (Exod. XVI); by Aaron’s rod, which bore fruit beyond the operation of nature (Num. XVII); by the star and rod concerning which Balaam prophesied [Col. 0763A] (Num. XXIV); by Gideon’s fleece, of which Judges VI speaks; by the house of the Lord which Solomon built and which the glory of God filled (3 Kings VI); by Abigail, who made peace between Nabal and David (1 Kings XXV); by Judith, who killed Holofernes and delivered the people (Judith XIII); by Esther, who caused Haman to be hanged and Mordecai with the people to be delivered (Esther VII); by the dove which brought an olive branch to Noah and his sons in the ark (Gen. VIII); by the pole which bore the bronze serpent in the wilderness (Num. XXI); by the closed gate through which no man passed (Ezek. XLIV); and by the woman whom John saw (Rev. XII)—he finally concludes, addressing the Mother of God:

> In you is fulfilled in its entirety  
> Whatever, O Virgin, is foretold of you  
> In prophetic words  
> And in the enigmas of the Law.
>
> Or whatever is expressed to you  
> In angelic words:  
> The figurative utterances being ended,  
> The reality is plainly seen.
>
> You are the corner-stone  
> That gives figures their end.

See, if you wish, our notes to the *Mariale* of St Germanus, Patriarch of Constantinople, the notes to the Oration on the Nativity of the Mother of God, no. 14, on the phrase: “the most brilliant fulfilment of all prophecy.” [Col. 0763B]

(11) Whoever has loved her perseveringly shall not perish. Alphonsus Tostatus, Bishop of Ávila, Question 1 on chapter V of the First Book of Kings, asking why the Philistines did not perish when they touched the ark of God, whereas Israelites perished not only for touching it but even for looking upon it (1 Kings VI), gives this reason among others: “Because,” he says, “they were exceedingly devoted in venerating the ark, as is clear because they bestowed upon it the greatest honour they could bestow: they placed it in the holiest place in all their land, namely, in the temple of their great god Dagon.” Thus he.

If, therefore, the Philistines could not perish by a temporal death because of devotion to the ark, who would think that anyone devoted to the Blessed Virgin could perish by eternal death?

The priest Abiathar was worthy of death, as King Solomon said to him (3 Kings II): “Indeed, you are a man of death.” But because he had carried the ark of the Lord, his life was spared: “I will not put you to death, because you carried the ark of the Lord.” If, therefore, one carrying the ark did not perish, how can one who honours the Blessed Virgin from the heart perish?

There are those who think that sacrilegious Uzzah was delivered from eternal damnation and granted eternal salvation because he is said to have died beside the ark (2 Kings II). If one who died beside the ark does not perish but lives eternally, will anyone perish if he lives and dies beside the Mother of God?

A woman, even if guilty, cannot perish by a violent death while a child is in her womb, because of the child’s innocence. Neither can a faithful soul pregnant with devotion to the Virgin perish by eternal death [Col. 0763D] because of the merits of so great a Virgin.

That worshippers of the Virgin cannot perish by eternal death was asserted, besides our Adam, by St Anselm in the *Book of the Miracles of the Blessed Virgin*, when he said: “O happy Mary, just as every sinner turned away from you and despised by you must perish, so every sinner turned toward you and regarded by you cannot perish.” Blessed Hermann—or Joseph of Steinfeld—asserted it in his hymn to the Blessed Virgin, singing:

> Rejoice, fountain that is not dried up;  
> O how sweet you are when tasted!  
> Whoever drinks you shall not perish;  
> Whoever seeks you never perishes.

Blessed Peter Damian, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, asserted it when he wrote in Book II, Letter 14: “He who has secured for himself the aid of the Mother of the eternal Judge cannot perish before that Judge’s presence.” Albert the Great asserted it in the *Bible of Mary* on the prophet Isaiah [Col. 0764A], where he says: “The nation and kingdom that will not serve you, O my Mother, shall perish” (Gloss: “on the day of judgment”). As though to say: therefore those who serve her shall not perish.

St Bonaventure asserted it in the *Psalter of the Blessed Virgin*, addressing the Mother of God thus: “Great peace [belongs] to those who love you, Lady; their soul shall not see death for ever.” Richard of St Lawrence asserted it in Book II *On the Praises of the Virgin*, writing: “You ought to serve the Mother of God while you live, if after death you wish to live.” Louis Blosius asserted it when he used these words in the *Canon of the Spiritual Life*, chapter 18: “It cannot happen that one who has been a diligent and humble worshipper of Mary should perish.” Finally, a devout anonymous author, in the same Blosius among the *Sayings of the Fathers*, chapter 5, asserted it when he uttered this prayer there: “Indeed, whoever devoutly and perseveringly honours and invokes her [Mary] cannot perish eternally.”

Most fitting here is what Caesarius of Heisterbach relates in Homily 1 for Septuagesima Sunday: when two young men at Toledo were studying necromancy together, and one of them, weighed down by a worsening illness, was about to die, the other adjured him to appear to him within three days and tell him in what state he was. When he had promised this, after his death he visibly appeared to his companion, who was sitting in a church and reading psalms for his soul. He declared that he was in the greatest punishments and eternally damned for the study of demonic art, adding: “Truly necromancy, according to its name, is the death of the soul; and if you die in it, you will be subject to eternal torments with me.”

When his companion asked, “What manner of life do you advise for me?” he answered: “The Cistercian Order.” And he added: “There is no order in the Church from which so few descend into hell; for they have a special Advocate”—indicating the Mother of God—“who does not allow them to perish.” Thus far Caesarius. Consider carefully those final words: “who does not allow them to perish.”

186. NOTES ON SERMON III.

[Col. 0764C] (12) O wondrous newness, Virgin Mother! Although this wondrous newness of one who is at once virgin and mother—the stupendous union of virginity with fruitfulness—wholly surpasses our understanding and stands far above all our speech, many holy Fathers nevertheless celebrate it in their works: namely, St. Joseph the Confessor, in the Greek Menology, 4 January, Ode 8, in these words: “O miracle raised above all limits of miracles! How can you possess virginity together with childbirth, O Bride wholly pure in every respect of the Godhead?” St. John Chrysostom, Homily 49 on Genesis, says: “When you hear that a virgin gave birth, marvel and be astonished, but do not disbelieve the miracle.” Titus of Bostra, on Luke, chapter 1, at the words, “For he that is mighty hath done to me great things,” speaks thus in the person of the Virgin: “He has wrought wonders through me: for, though I was a virgin, by his almighty will I conceived, surpassing the bounds of nature; and, having had no intercourse with any man, I was made worthy to become the mother—not indiscriminately of anyone—but of the only-begotten Son of God.”

Origen, Homily 1 on various passages, writes: “O grace worthy of great wonder! She herself is both virgin and Mother of the Lord. Who ever heard such things? Who saw anything like it? Who could imagine that a mother should be a virgin, and that she should give birth untouched—remaining a virgin and yet bringing forth? For just as formerly the bush seemed to burn and the fire did not touch it; and just as the three boys were enclosed in the furnace of fire, yet the blaze did not harm them and there was no smell of smoke upon them; or as food was brought by Habakkuk to Daniel, shut within the lions’ den while its barriers remained unopened: so too this holy Virgin gave birth to God, yet remained untouched; she became a mother, yet did not lose her virginity.”

St. Cyril of Alexandria, Homily 6 against Nestorius, uses this language: “And who is so powerful in speech as adequately to celebrate Mary, so greatly praised? She is mother and virgin: O wondrous thing! This miracle renders me speechless.” Paul, bishop of Emesa, in his Homily on the Incarnation of Christ, delivered at Alexandria and found in Part III of the Council of Ephesus, exclaims: “O wondrous thing! A virgin gives birth; she becomes a mother, yet does not undergo in every respect all that belongs to mothers. The prophet Isaiah, foreseeing this miracle long ago, cried out, saying: ‘Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son’ [Isa. 7].” St. Gregory of Nyssa, in his Oration on the Nativity of Christ, bursts into these words: “O great miracle! A virgin becomes a mother and remains a virgin. Do you see nature’s new work? Among other women, so long as one is a virgin, she is not a mother; once she has become a mother, she no longer possesses virginity. But here these two names concur: she is both mother and virgin.”

And Alan of Lille, in the *Anticlaudianus*, Book V, sings:

> Here a Virgin excels the citizens of heaven in a distinction proper to herself,  
> Who, without losing by the law of childbirth her own modesty,  
> Has deserved the name of mother together with virgin.  
>
> In her two names agree, their conflict buried—  
> Names accustomed to fight with one another and stir up strife.  
> Mother and virgin are no longer at variance;  
> Their quarrels excluded, they turn toward kisses of peace.  
> Here nature is silent; all the force of logic is banished.  
> The judgment of rhetoric fails, and reason totters.  
> She it is who, by the worthy exercise of a divine gift,  
> Though born, conceived the Father and, as mother, the Begotten,  
> Retaining virginly honor and not losing a mother’s rights.

I pass over St. Proclus of Constantinople, Homily on the Nativity of Christ, where he declares this union of virgin and mother utterly astounding and unheard of; St. Ambrose, *On the Instruction of Virgins*, chapter 5, where he affirms that for a virgin to give birth is a greater miracle than for a dead man to rise again; and Arnold of Chartres, *On the Praises of the Virgin*, where he declares that the Virgin in childbirth is an object of wonder in heaven and hell. I refer the reader who thirsts for more on this matter to St. Ildefonsus, *On the Virginity of St. Mary*, chapter 2; St. Bernard, Homily 1 on *Missus est* and Sermon 3 on the Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord; Richard of St. Victor, *On Emmanuel*, Book I, chapter 12, and Book II, chapter 25; Richard of St. Lawrence, *On the Praises of the Virgin*, Book IV, cols. 253–254; and others. For he beautifully and truly says:

> What nature refuses,  
> What custom itself does not know,  
> What no mind comprehends,  
> At which the stars stand astonished,  
> At which the earth trembles,  
> Which all things revere—  
> Would you have me tell it, Christian?  
> A Virgin, and Mother of God.  
>
> (JACOB PONTANUS, *Florids*, Book V.)

## NOTES TO SERMON IV

That this sermon is a genuine offspring of our Adam is evident from Geoffrey Tilmann, in his allegories on Luke, chapter 2, where, under the name of Adam of Perseigne, he adduces two noteworthy fragments drawn from this sermon.

(13) *The most pure Mother of the Lord must be believed to have been purified in this manner*, etc. If the first snows can be wiped clean, if ivory’s whiteness can be stained, if an unstained spring can be cleansed, if a clear ray of sunlight needs to be immersed in water so that it may wash away the stains of its harmless light, then Mary too needed purification. But since only what is impure can be purified, only what is defiled can be cleansed of stain, only what is infected can be wiped clean, and only what is dirty can be washed—what was there in Mary that was impure and required purification, defiled and required cleansing, infected and required wiping, dirty and required washing? Certainly nothing.

Was not Mary, according to the testimony of St. Ephrem the Syrian in his Oration on the Praises of the Virgin, “purer than the sun’s ray and its brightness”? Did she not, according to Psellus on Canticles, chapter 6, surpass the cherubim and seraphim in purity? Does she not, according to Anselm, *On Virginal Conception*, chapter 18, “shine with such purity that no greater purity under God can be conceived”? What therefore could be purified in her, asks Guerric, abbot of Igny, Sermon 1 on the Purification, she who “conceived a virgin, gave birth a virgin, remained a virgin—indeed, who by the conception itself was altogether purified? What, I ask, had that conception to cleanse, which alone can make clean one conceived from unclean seed; which produced the fountain by which the unclean are purified, the fountain of the house of David, which today stands open and pours forth unceasingly for the washing of sinner and menstruous woman?” Thus Guerric.

Accordingly, the Blessed Virgin was aptly likened by the Holy Spirit to the moon: “fair as the moon” [Cant. 6]. For just as the moon, although to those looking at it it seems to have certain spots, in truth has no spot in itself, as philosophers teach, so the Blessed Virgin, although by coming for purification she appeared to people to possess some stain needing cleansing, was nevertheless always most beautiful and entirely immaculate. “Thou art all fair, my beloved, and there is no spot in thee” [Cant. 4]. Why, however, the Blessed Virgin, though she needed no purification and was not subject to the law of purification, nevertheless wished to be purified and to subject herself to the law of purification, is excellently explained, among others, by John Baptist Novatus, *On the Eminence of the Mother of God*, vol. I, chapter 14, question 2, where he gives nine reasons for this.

(14) *Purification was effected not for Mary, but for us through Mary.* Joseph de la Zerda, in his *Image of the Trinity*, Academy 23, section 1, learnedly and ingeniously proves that Mary’s purification removed our impurity; consult him.

## NOTES TO SERMON V

This sermon is altogether most beautiful and wholly worthy of its author; I have mentioned it in the *Marian Library*, Part I, under Adam, abbot of Perseigne.

(15) *Therefore by the strong woman we may indeed understand Mary, Mother of Wisdom.* By the strong woman of whom Solomon speaks in the final chapter of Proverbs, St. Bernard, with our Adam, understands the Mother of God: Sermon 9 among the shorter sermons and Sermon 2 on *Missus est*; Absalon, abbot, Sermon 3 on the Purification of the Blessed Virgin; Albert the Great, in the *Bible of Mary* on Proverbs; Richard of St. Lawrence, *On the Praises of the Virgin*, Book IV, cols. 221 and 225, Book VI, cols. 417–418, and Book XII, col. 989; St. Antoninus, archbishop of Florence, Part IV of the *Summa Theologica*, title 15, chapter 44; St. Bernardino of Siena, vol. I, Sermon 52, on the angelic salutation; Peter of Blois, Sermon 1 for Advent; and many others.

The Virgin Mother of God is most rightly and wisely called by the name *woman*—for the moment I pass over the surname “strong”—either because, as Mother of Mercy, she softens in affection unto the tenderness of compassion, as our Adam says here; or because by her merits and prayers she softens the Lord, so that he forgets punishment and vengeance toward humankind for sins, as Richard of St. Lawrence proves in *On the Praises of the Virgin*, Book VI, cols. 415–416; or lest, on account of her preeminence in divine motherhood and supreme holiness, exempted from the lowliness of creaturehood, she should be placed on the summit of divinity and worshipped by humans as a goddess, as may be inferred from Epiphanius, Heresy 79; or lest some should think her not truly a mother—for, according to Gotfrey, Book VII, question 6, there would be persons who would teach that the Virgin had not properly given birth, and who, with the Manichees, would believe Christ to be a phantom, as St. Augustine records in *On Heresies*, chapter 51, and Book I against Julian; indeed, with the Valentinians, that he had assumed no bodily substance from her, as Bernard of Luxembourg relates in his *Catalogue of Heretics*, but had descended from heaven and passed through her as liquid through a pipe.

Or, finally, the name derives from virginal fruitfulness: although she is a virgin, she is also a woman, that is, a mother. Albert the Great expressed this in the *Mariale*, chapter 35: “The prophecies speaking of the person of the most blessed Virgin call her now virgin, now woman. Isaiah [7]: ‘Behold, a virgin shall conceive’; Jeremiah [31]: ‘A woman shall encompass a man’; clearly indicating that she would possess both the integrity of a virgin and the fruitfulness of a woman.” Thus he.

Nor should the heretics be heard who falsely maintain that *woman* is used only for one who has been defiled and has known a man. For from the usage of Sacred Scripture and the common judgment of learned teachers, the word *woman* is a common designation of sex and is found to apply no less to a virgin than to a married woman. St. Augustine proves this, *On Faith against the Manichees*, chapter 22, both from Moses’ testimony and from the character of the Hebrew language.
