Origen also proves it from common speech, Homily 8 on Leviticus, and argues thus: “If a male is rightly called a man merely from the maturity of his age, though he has known no union with a woman, why should not a virgin who has remained undefiled likewise be called a woman merely from maturity of age?” Tertullian too, *On the Veiling of Virgins*, clearly teaches the same: namely, that Scripture uses the name *woman* such that it applies even to females who have not known men, and that it belongs to sex itself, not to a rank or condition within the sex. See Cyril of Jerusalem, Catechesis 10; Gaudentius, Sermon 9 on John; Primasius on the Epistle to the Galatians; and especially St. Ambrose, *On the Instruction of Virgins*, chapter 5, where he says: “Why are we troubled by the word *woman*? It refers to sex; it is not a term of corruption but of sex. Popular usage does not prejudice truth.” Thus he.

(16) *For elsewhere truth seems to remove the name woman from a virgin.* Although, as I have said, the name *woman* is a common designation of sex and applies no less to a virgin than to a married woman, nevertheless, because the word *woman*, at least sometimes in the judgment of foolish popular usage, signifies sexual defilement—as in Quintilian, Book VIII, chapter 4: when people reproached Cicero because at sixty he had married the virgin Popilia, he said, “Tomorrow she will be a woman”—some Fathers, speaking of Mary the Virgin Mother of God and wishing to signify that not even the slightest trace of corruption was in her, abstained from the name *woman* and distinguished virgin from woman, as may be clear to anyone from their words appended here.

Ambrose, on Luke 7: “Among those born of women there hath not arisen one greater than John the Baptist”: “Is he then greater even than the Savior? Far be it! For John was born of a woman, but Christ was born of a virgin: the one was poured forth from the recesses of a corruptible womb; the other sprang forth as the flower of an undefiled womb.” And the same author, on Luke, chapter 1, at the words, “And she considered what manner of salutation this might be”: “Mary therefore blushed, and Elizabeth also blushed. Let us therefore see the difference between the modesty of a woman and that of a virgin. The former blushed because of a cause; the latter through modesty. In a woman the measure of modesty is observed; in a virgin the grace of modesty is increased.”

Cyril of Jerusalem, Catechesis 12: “And let us receive the Word incarnate truly, not from the will of man and woman, as heretics say, but from a virgin and the Holy Spirit.” Epiphanius, Book I against Heresies, Heresy 30: “‘Behold, a Virgin shall conceive in the womb.’ But she is not called a virgin who is joined to a man and united in marriage as a woman.” Peter Chrysologus, Sermon 117: “Where are those who consider the Virgin’s conception and the Virgin’s birth equal to the births of women, when the latter are from earth and the former from heaven?” Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogus*, Book I, chapter 6: “Pregnant women, once they have become mothers, give milk; but the Lord Christ is the fruit of a virgin.” Pope Siricius, Letter 2 against Jovinian, in vol. I of the Councils: “Through a woman death came; through a Virgin salvation came.” Peter Damian, Homily on the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin: “Pain did not follow childbirth because lust did not precede conception. For it had been said to Eve: ‘In pain thou shalt bear a son’ [Gen. 3]. This sentence retained force in other mothers, but in Mary it lost the measure of its jurisdiction. It remained fixed among women; over a virgin it could not prevail.”

Origen, Homily 8 on Leviticus: “To this may also be added that this law, written concerning uncleanness, concerns a woman; but of Mary it is said that a virgin conceived and gave birth. Let laws therefore be applied to women; let virgins, however, be held exempt from them.” Finally, St. Ephrem the Syrian, *On the Precious Pearl*: “Holy Mary became, no longer a woman, but a virgin full of grace.”

If some have called her a woman, they immediately called her a virgin also, lest any suspicion of defilement creep in and a half-stated designation furnish occasion for error. Hear Dionysius the Areopagite in the Greek Menologies: “He indeed assumed our flesh, but beyond the measure of human substance; for though from a woman, yet not from just any woman, but from a virgin.” Hear Nazianzen, Oration 35: “He was born, yet he was also begotten: from a woman indeed, but nevertheless from a virgin.” Finally hear Chrysostom, on Isaiah, chapter 1, at the words “He shall eat butter and honey”: “For not every particular in him was different, nor were all things in him shared with us. That he was born from a woman is common to all; but that he was born from a virgin is loftier than the condition of us all.”

[Col. 0768B] (17) *Nothing is more sublime than the first and eternal generation; nothing more wonderful than the second and incorrupt birth.* St. Maximus speaks most beautifully of both generations of Christ, the divine and the human: Homily 6 on the Nativity of the Lord and Homily 5 on the Epiphany; as do St. John Damascene, Oration 1 on the Nativity of the Virgin; Albert the Great, in his Postils on Luke, chapters 2 and 11, and Matthew, chapter 1; Geoffrey of Vendôme, Sermon on the Purification of the Blessed Virgin; Hugh of St. Victor, vol. III, Third Conference on the Incarnate Word; Origen, Homily 3 on various passages; Blessed Thomas of Villanova, Conference 2 on the Nativity of the Virgin; and, to omit others, St. Augustine, vol. X, Sermon 18 on the Nativity of the Lord, which is Sermon 22 *On the Season*. Its words alone, most worthy of reading, I do not hesitate to give here:

“This day he was born of a Virgin Mother who before the ages was eternally begotten of God the Father. In that nativity he is born from an impassible Begetter; in this, he is born from an incorrupt Virgin. The Father alone who begot him knew that birth; this birth the undefiled Virgin and Mother alone knew in herself, she who endured no man in conceiving. In the Father is impassibility; in the Mother, incorruptibility. In the Father, perpetual divinity; in the Mother, eternal virginity. From the Father, invisibly; from the Mother, visibly—but incomparably from the Father, and incomparably from the Mother: because in that nativity he has God the Father incorruptibly, without a human mother; in this he has the Virgin as mother, but no human father. In that, he is coeternal with the Father and coeternal with his Creator; in this, he is the son of a Virgin and the creator of his Mother. For he formed the womb into which he descended; he came forth from the womb and did not corrupt the womb, so that he who has God the Father in heaven might have a Virgin Mother on earth. In that, begotten without time; in this, born at the end of times. In that, born without end; in this, conceived without seed. In that, without beginning of generation; in this, under the condition of law and flesh. In that, invisible God; in this, visible man in a body, because ‘the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us’ [John 1]. In that, impassible; in this, mortal. In that, most high; in this, subject—subject, namely, to the wrongs of suffering and death, even death upon the cross.” Thus he.

(18) *How strong was this woman!* Albert the Great treats excellently of the supreme strength of the Blessed Virgin in the *Mariale*, chapter 101, where he reasons in this manner: “Whatever is stronger than the stronger is stronger than the weaker. The most blessed Virgin was stronger than three beings stronger than every wayfarer; therefore she was stronger than every wayfarer. The three stronger than every wayfarer are God, death, and the devil. The humility of the Blessed Virgin in some manner overcame God when, drawing him by humility from heaven to earth, she imprisoned him in her virginity, bound at once by charity, humbled, and wounded. Hence, ‘While the King was at his repose,’ etc. [Cant. 1], and Proverbs 31: ‘Who shall find a strong woman? Her price is from afar and from the uttermost ends.’ The uttermost ends are divinity and humanity, most remote from one another. Therefore she was the strongest woman, who joined these together. Thus the strength of the most blessed Virgin overcame the rigor of strength and divine severity, concerning which it is said, ‘Whose strength is like that of the rhinoceros’ [Num. 23]. That strength grows gentle in the Virgin’s bosom, and thus it is plain in what manner the most blessed Virgin overcame God’s strength.

“Likewise, the second strong being is death, which no mortal can resist: ‘For we all die and glide away upon the earth like water that does not return’ [2 Sam. 14]. Stronger than this was the most blessed Virgin, who destroyed death. For just as death entered through a woman and destroyed life, so the most blessed Virgin was death’s destruction, and therefore was stronger than death. The third strong being is the devil, of whom it is said: ‘There is no power upon earth that may be compared to him’ [Job 41]. The most blessed Virgin was stronger than him, according to Genesis 3: ‘She shall crush thy head.’

“Again, an essential act of strength is to cleave firmly. The most blessed Virgin cleaved inseparably to God. Therefore she was incomparably stronger than others. Again, an act of strength is not only to restrain earthly desires, but to forget them utterly. Yet this does not happen to any wayfarer on the way, so long as the tinder of sin is in any manner active; but it could occur only in the Virgin, in whom the tinder was extinguished. Therefore she possessed the act of strength in the manner of the homeland, and beyond every wayfarer without comparison.” These are Albert’s words in the cited place, which he nearly repeats in the *Bible of Mary* on Proverbs, chapter 31.

Those thirsting for more on the Blessed Virgin’s strength from the Fathers and other authors may consult Novatus, *On the Eminence of the Mother of God*, vol. II, chapter 5, question 23; Miechovius, *On the Litany of Loreto*, vol. II, discourse 389; Raynaud, *Marian Diptychs*, Part II, point 6, no. 18; Posarel, *Crown of the Blessed Virgin*, Book III, chapter 5; and others.

[Col. 0769C] (19) *The Cistercian monasteries, all of which are duly dedicated in devotion to the memory and merits of that Mother herself.* Caesarius of Heisterbach gives the reason why all the monasteries of the Cistercian Order were dedicated by those first Fathers to the Blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of God, in Book I of his *Illustrious Miracles*, chapter 1, in these words: “Because the monastery from which they came forth, namely in the year 1098, had been constructed in honor of Blessed Mary, Mother of God, both they and their successors, propagated from that same new monastery—namely Cîteaux—held that all their churches should be dedicated in honor of that same glorious Virgin.” Thus he.

The words of those holy Fathers by which they consecrated all their churches to the Queen of Angels, taken from the Book of Ancient Definitions, distinction 3, chapter 1, as Chrysostom Henriquez reports in the *Cistercian Menology*, 26 January, are these: “Since the illustrious life, wondrous dignity, and eminent holiness of the glorious Virgin Mary, Mother of God, illumine, rule, and shape all churches, all our conventual churches shall be founded and deservedly dedicated in her honor.” Thus they.

Although the churches and monasteries of the Cistercian Order have been consecrated to the Mother of God by the inviolable law of the Cistercian Fathers, Chrysostom Henriquez observes in the above-mentioned *Menology*, 15 August, that experience establishes that almost all, or perhaps all, are dedicated in memory of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin. For everywhere the glorious Virgin is depicted above the high altar ascending to heaven amid the angelic companies; and he found that every monastery of his order which he had seen in Spain and Belgium was built in memory of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin. The same has been attested to me concerning monasteries and churches of the same order throughout France and Italy by the Most Reverend Father—whose friendship I greatly value because of his outstanding learning and scholarship—Fr. John Bona, of the Reformed Congregation of St. Bernard of the Cistercian Order, now Abbot General.

(20) *And by the whiteness of their habit.* Although the Cistercian Fathers wore black clothing from the beginning of their institution, in the year of salvation 1101, on 5 August, the most blessed Virgin Mother of God descended from heaven to Cîteaux and changed their habit from black to white, under St. Alberic as abbot. The story runs thus: While Blessed Father Alberic and his monks were devoutly singing Lauds and Matins, the Virgin Mother of God appeared, surrounded by a company of heavenly spirits and carrying in her hands a white and most shining cowl. She placed it upon Alberic’s astonished head. But behold, miracle follows miracle: as soon as that garment was placed upon Alberic, the cowls of the monks singing in choir changed color; those which had previously been black suddenly became dyed a most brilliant snowy white. Immediately the most blessed Virgin vanished from the sight of her servants. Thus far the story.

For its truth and confirmation, Chrysostom Henriquez, general historiographer of the Cistercian Order, cites many authors, both in the *Fascicle of Saints of the Cistercian Order*, Book I, distinction 2, chapter 2, and in the *Cistercian Menology*, 5 August; consult him. See also Colvenerius, *Marian Calendar*, 5 August, §2; Benedict Gonon, *Chronicle of the Mother of God*, under A.D. 1109; and our Marian Founders, chapter 9.

(21) *We ought rather to have imitated our Virgin.* Since true and solid devotion toward the Virgin Mother of God especially consists in imitation of her virtues, it is no wonder that the Fathers, ardently desiring every faithful Christian to be truly and solidly devoted to this Virgin Mother of God, took pains in their works not merely to exhort us but in some sense to compel us to imitate her.

St. Jerome, vol. IX, Sermon on the Assumption: “Love her whom you honor, and honor her whom you love; for then you truly honor and love her if you wish with all your heart to imitate her whom you praise.” St. Ambrose, Book II, *On Virginity*: “Let the virginity and life of Blessed Mary be set before you as though portrayed in an image; in her, as in a mirror, shines the beauty of chastity and the form of virtue. From her you may take examples for living, where, as in a pattern-book, are displayed the instructions of uprightness, showing what you ought to correct and what you ought to preserve.” St. Ildefonsus, Sermon 1 on the Assumption: “Imitate the Virgin Mother and all the saints whom you praise, because our praise profits them not nearly so much as their imitation profits us. Therefore the Bridegroom is more pleased by a devout imitator than by an idle praiser; yet true praise of the heart is imitation in deed.” Blessed Peter Damian, Sermon on the Epiphany of the Lord: “Mary left us an example, that we might follow in her footsteps and become such as she was. Thus, brethren, we shall be able to reach the true Sun if we imitate the steps of the Virgin and our Star.” St. Bernard, Homily 1 on *Missus est*: “If in Mary you can only admire virginity, strive to imitate humility, and that is sufficient for you.” Hugh of St. Victor, Sermon for any feast of Blessed Mary: “Let us strive, according to our powers, to imitate Blessed Mary, that by her merits and prayers we may be glorified with her. Let us imitate Blessed Mary during the briefness of time, that we may deserve to rejoice with her through the duration of eternity.” Paschasius Radbertus, Exposition of Psalm 44: “Then you truly love her, Mary, if you strive to imitate her; then you truly love her if you follow her wholly in conduct and life, she who loved nothing but God.” Amadeus of Lausanne, Homily 5 on the Praises of the Virgin: “Made like the Mother of God by likeness of conduct, we shall be led after her into the temple of the King and her Son.” Absalon, abbot, Sermon 1 on the Annunciation: “Learn, O sinful root, ash of eternal fire—learn, I say, from Mary’s example to humble yourself before God and to be subject ‘to every human creature for God’s sake’ [1 Pet. 2]. Behold the rod proposed for imitation to everyone seeking the homeland. Let each one see whether he wishes to imitate it, since the Lord will scourge with the rod of wrath those who have despised it.” An ancient anonymous author in a certain *Crown of the Blessed Virgin*, preserved in the Vatican Palatine Library, no. 3005: “Those who desire worthily to serve the Blessed Virgin ought, insofar as they can, to imitate her in virtues and at least run from afar after the fragrance of her ointments [Cant. 1], because, as an authority says: ‘To venerate saints and not imitate them is nothing other than to flatter falsely.’” St. Bonaventure, Letter 25 of the *Memorials*: “That your devotion may be acceptable and your reverence pleasing to the Blessed Virgin, strive with all effort to keep her purity and cleanliness undefiled in yourself, in mind and body, by every virtue, and to imitate the traces of her humility and gentleness.” St. Antoninus, *Summa Theologica*, Part IV, title 14, chapter 24, §4: “By imitating the Blessed Virgin we are made righteous; and just as we write correctly and do other things by following a wooden ruler, so we do upright works by imitating her steps.” Maurice of Villa Probata, *New Crown of Blessed Mary*, Sermon 9: “Bees have one king whose guidance they follow; so let us follow the Virgin Mary and imitate her.” Finally, not to be too lengthy, William Parvus, on Canticles, chapter 8, speaking with the Church in the person of God: “You rightly admire and venerate my loving Mother. But because the whole fruit of veneration consists in imitation, imitate her whom you venerate.” Thus he.

For more on imitation of the Virgin Mother of God, see Francis Arias in his special work on the subject, where he proposes that same Virgin Mother of God for imitation by all the faithful in humility, faith, hope, charity, devotion, obedience, chastity, modesty, and poverty.

[Col. 0771]

## NOTES TO THE MARIAN FRAGMENTS

[Col. 0771B] TO FRAGMENT I

This fragment, which may be prefaced concerning the praises of the Blessed Virgin arising from the Savior’s birth, is taken from our Adam’s Sermon 1 on the Ascension of the Lord, and is precious like pure gold.

(22) *To the clean fleece itself, immeasurable brightness was added.* St. Peter Chrysologus, St. Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, St. Ildefonsus of Toledo, and all who teach in the common manner that the brightness of Marian virginity was increased by the divine birth, or that the virginity of the Mother of God gained an increase through childbirth, agree with our Adam. St. Peter Chrysologus, Sermon 142: “In your childbirth modesty increased, chastity was heightened, integrity was strengthened, virginity was made firm, all virtues persevered. He through whom all things were increased for you diminished nothing.” And Sermon 175: “She gives birth happily who, by giving birth, acquired ever more fully the crown and glory of virginity.” Fulgentius, Oration on the Praises of Blessed Mary from the Savior’s birth: “The integrity of her body increased through childbirth rather than diminished, and virginity was enlarged rather than put to flight.” St. Ildefonsus, *On the Holy Virgin*, chapter 11: “Never a mother except when also a virgin, and after becoming a mother, a nobler virgin. When the appointed time is complete, she feels him who had come to her about to go forth; and joyfully, in the gentle course of his emergence, she beholds him proceeding otherwise than she knew him to have entered. She sees him clothed in the reality of her flesh, and does not perceive that the integrity of her brightness and modesty has diminished within her, but knows that it has rather increased.” Aurelius Prudentius, Hymn 11:

> Do you feel, noble Virgin,  
> Through mature pangs,  
> The untouched glory of modesty  
> Growing through the honor of childbirth?

Geoffrey of Vendôme, Sermon 1 on the Nativity of the Lord: “The holy Virgin was a virgin before childbirth; in childbirth, a holier virgin.” St. Epiphanius, Oration on the Praises of the Virgin: “I am still a virgin after childbirth, purer, if it may be said, than before.” Finally, St. Augustine, Sermon 10 *On the Season*: “The Virgin was joined in marriage to her childbirth; in giving birth she doubled her virginity.”

How the virginity of the Mother of God was made more perfect and more increased by the divine birth, when virginity, both materially and formally, is not capable of intensive increase, is fully explained, among others, by Joseph de la Zerda, *Mary, Image of the Trinity*, Academy 22, sections 3 and 5; and Theophilus Raynaud, both in the *Marian Nomenclator*, in the Glossary under the Virgin’s title “The woman made virgin by conceiving,” and in the *Marian Diptychs*, Part I, point 7, no. 24.

[Col. 0772B] TO FRAGMENT II

It is taken from the sermon our Adam left composed on the Most Holy Trinity, and is full of most elegant and beautiful praises of the Mother of God.

(23) *But let us attend to the column which we have set before us.* Mary is also celebrated by the title of “column” by Andrew of Crete, Oration 3 on the Dormition of the Blessed Virgin; Theophanes, in the Greek Menologies, 23 February; John Geometres, Oration on the Annunciation; St. Bonaventure, *Mirror of the Blessed Virgin*, chapter 3; Albert the Great, Sermon 2 on the Annunciation, Sermon 3 on the Assumption, and *Mariale*, chapter 220; a Greek hymn in Buteo, p. 131; St. Anthony of Padua, Sermon 5 for the Sunday after Trinity; Bartholomew of Pisa, *On the Praises of the Virgin*, Book I, fruit 2; and others whom I mention in the dedicatory epistle near the end of the *Marian Caesars*.

(24) *How firm is she upon whom both heaven and earth lean!* For, as St. Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe—by others called bishop of Carthage, but more correctly Fulgentius Placiadas, though many confuse these men, as the most learned and highly erudite Fr. Simon Wagnerech observes in *Greek Marian Piety*, Part I, no. 223—says in Book III of the *Mythologies*: “Heaven and earth would long ago have fallen had Mary not sustained them by her prayers.” Hence Galatinus, Book VII of *On the Secrets*, chapter 2, after reporting from Rabbi Anchelos that God sustains the whole world for love of the Blessed Virgin, Mother of the Messiah, added: “For the world itself could in no way endure because of our evil actions unless that glorious Virgin sustained it, praying for us by her mercy and clemency.” Thus he. Paul of Heredia subscribes to this in almost precisely the same words in his Treatise on the Conception of the Blessed Virgin.

St. Antoninus, archbishop of Florence, concurs when he says in the *Summa Theologica*, Part I, title 14, chapter 4, §4: “As these lower things change according to the motion of the moon, so Mary by her merits and prayers sustains and, as it were, governs the world; whence she is called Queen of the World.” Thus he. See Novarinus, *The Virginal Shadow*, Excursus 16 throughout, where, proving that the Blessed Virgin is the shelter and defense of the whole world, he writes among other things that she is the pillar of heaven, supporting heaven by her prayers; and likewise our Atlas, who truly and without any fictitious mythology supports the universe upon the shoulders of her prayers, lest it fall.

(25) *She who knew no stain of sin.* Indeed, the Blessed Virgin was also ignorant of the stain of original sin; lest she be infected by it in the first instant of her conception, she was preserved from it through God’s power and mercy. Hence in the hymns of a certain ancient missal, quoted by Fr. Anthony de Balinghen in the *Marian Parnassus*, from p. 23 onward, the following was once sung in praise of the same Blessed Virgin:

> She was conceived in a wondrous manner,  
> Like a rose in brightness  
> And like a shining lily.  
> As fruit proceeds from a flower,  
> She was brought forth with modesty,  
> Preserved beforehand by her Son.  
>
> As dew is not corrupted  
> When it is produced upon the earth  
> By the rust of the elements,  
> So the Virgin is not infected  
> When she is conceived in her mother  
> By original sin.  
>
> Meanwhile:  
>
> Hail, O sweet Mary,  
> Mother and daughter of Christ,  
> Without any stain.  
> Fashioned by God,  
> Preserved in conception,  
> You contract no crimes.  
>
> Finally, again:  
>
> Hail, Queen of heaven,  
> Most worthy of all praise,  
> Who were conceived  
> Without the stain of vices.
most pure.

Hail, incomparable Virgin,

211  
Truly sacred pearl,

Hail, for you are the star of the sea,

You were conceived without stain.

But more elsewhere on this matter. Meanwhile see what I wrote in the notes to the *Mariale* of Isidore of Thessalonica, in the notes to Oration 2, no. 5.

(26) You appeared terrible to demons. How terrible and fearsome the Mother of God is to demons is clear [Col. 0773C] from St. Ephrem the Syrian, in his prayer to the Virgin; St. Cyril of Alexandria, Homily 6 against Nestorius; St. John Damascene, Oration 1 on the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin; Chrysippus of Jerusalem, in his sermon on the Praises of the Virgin; St. Peter Damian, in his sermon on the Assumption; St. Anselm of Canterbury, Hymn 2 on the Blessed Virgin; Honorius of Autun, in his sermon on the Nativity of Mary; St. Bernard of Clairvaux, sermon *In signum magnum*; St. Amadeus of Lausanne, Homilies 2 and 8, *On the Praises of the Virgin*; Richard of St. Victor, chapter 26 on the *Song of Songs*; Albert the Great, in the *Mariale*, chapters 75 and 140; St. Bonaventure, in the *Mirror of the Blessed Virgin*, chapters 3, 6, 9, 10, and 12; St. Antoninus of Florence, Part IV of the *Summa theologiae*, title 15, chapters 14 and 45; St. Bernardino of Siena, vol. I, sermon 51, article 3, chapter 2, and sermon 3 on the glorious Name of Mary; St. Bridget, Book I of the *Revelations*, chapters 9, 16, and 46, and Book IV, chapters 108 and 203, and in the Angelic Sermon, chapter 20; Maurice of Villa Probata, in the *Crown of the Blessed Virgin*, sermon 21 and the last sermon; [Col. 0773D] Abbot Trithemius, Book I, *On the Miracles of the Blessed Virgin at Urticeto*; John Gerson, treatise 4 on the *Magnificat*; Dionysius the Carthusian, Book III, *On the Praises of the Virgin*, articles 11 and 20, and on the *Song of Songs*, articles 20 and 21; finally, John Hailgrin, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, on chapter III of the *Song*, on the words, “Your stature is like a palm tree.” I will not deprive the reader here of his words; they are as follows:

> Just as the palm tree—that is, the triumphant tree of the Lord’s Cross—is terrible to evil spirits, so the blessed Virgin, by the merit of her uprightness, terrifies and drives out evil spirits.

## ON FRAGMENT III

On the praises of the Blessed Virgin, and on her own canticle, the *Magnificat*, this fragment may be prefaced. I am readily persuaded that it is a substantial portion of those treatises which our Adam, as Trithemius and Possevin testify, composed laboriously on certain passages of Holy Scripture. Yet those [Col. 0774A] treatises, at least in their complete form, are wholly absent from the Casamari manuscript, the only one I have used—perhaps consigned to oblivion in some corner of a library, still struggling with moths and bookworms, or entirely consumed by the devouring power of time, which consumes all things. This fragment—or rather, this little work—accords with the piety of our Adam toward the Mother of God; and I think no one can read it without a great increase of Marian devotion.

(27) Above other women she was anointed with invisible oil. On this heavenly anointing of the Blessed Virgin—by which the blessed Virgin herself may be said to have been anointed, not outwardly but inwardly, consecrated not as a legal but as a spiritual priest—Hugh of St. Victor speaks most admirably. In volume II of his Works, in the sermon on the Assumption, addressing the Virgin, he said:

> You, tender daughter and full of every grace, most dearly beloved in your delights, have been anointed for the glory of your beauty and as a sign of love. Since you were to bear the Anointed One, you too were anointed, [Col. 0774B] so that the ointment itself might first be poured out with surpassing excellence in you, which he would afterwards receive singularly in your womb.

So he writes. Albert the Great likewise writes admirably, in the *Mariale*, chapters 100 and 211:

> The most blessed Virgin possessed incomparably more anointing than all others, and before all her companions she was anointed with the oil of gladness.

Amadeus of Lausanne also writes admirably, in Homily 3 on the Praises of the Virgin:

> The Word of God descended into the Virgin’s womb: a womb undefiled, immaculate, consecrated by the hand of divine anointing.

John Gerson likewise writes admirably. In volume III of his Works, treatise 9 on the *Magnificat*, he advances this proposition:

> On the evening of Holy Thursday, although Mary was not marked with the character of priestly office, nevertheless then, before then, and afterwards, she was anointed into a royal priesthood before her companions—not indeed in order to consecrate, but 214 to offer this pure, full, and perfect victim upon the altar of her heart.

Finally, Alanus Varenius [Col. 0774C] of Montauban speaks admirably in sermon 5, in praise of the most holy Mother of God Mary:

> Let us read the Scriptures: priests, prophets, and kings were anointed; the Virgin Mary was anointed, as queen and prophetess, and in a far higher degree, since she shone with priesthood. For she was the Mother of the Lord, and in this rank, illustrious above all, she surpassed the dignities and eminence both of ancient and recent Fathers. For hers was that maternal right which by its power contained and surpassed every inferior rank. It was unthinkable that she should be surpassed by any of the heroes, she who had contained the Lord in her womb; she who was Mother of God and man, Mother of the only-begotten Son of God, indeed of the living and true God himself—incomparable, ineffable, altogether wonderful. Rightly, before all others, she was to be exalted in dignity, rank, and order, since she had enclosed so great and such a Lord in her most holy womb. We read that David was anointed many times; the same must be understood of the most holy and undefiled Virgin, so that, after the likeness of the great David, Jesus Christ her Son, she was sprinkled with the oil of gladness—[Col. 0774D] the oil of the Holy Spirit, the oil of the holy mystery hidden from the ages—before her companions: anointed in her conception, anointed when she conceived her only-begotten Son, and then with the oil of more overflowing grace, of all consummate 215 perfection, and of deification.

Thus far Varenius.

(28) A dove in whom the Holy Spirit dwells. So many holy Fathers and sacred doctors apply to the Mother of God, together with our Adam, the designation and qualities of a dove that, were brevity not an obstacle, a very long catalogue could be compiled from them for the eager reader sincerely devoted to the worship of the Mother of God.

One should read St. Epiphanius, in his sermon on the Praises of the Virgin, where he calls the Mother of God a “pure dove”; St. Sabbas the abbot, in the Greek *Menaea* for 24 March, where he calls her “the unique dove of incorrupt beauty”; St. Proclus of Constantinople, Oration 6, where he calls her a “simple dove”; St. Augustine, volume X, sermon 35 on the Saints, where he calls her the dove [Col. 0775A] of her Son; St. Ildephonsus, sermon 6 on the Assumption, where he calls her the dove of the Holy Spirit; Hesychius of Jerusalem, sermon 2 on the Praises of the Virgin, where he calls her an undefiled dove; John of Euboea, in his Oration on the Conception of the Mother of God, where he calls her a most pure dove; St. John Damascene, in his Oration on the Assumption, where he calls her a most sacred dove; and in the Greek *Menaea* for 22 January, where he calls her the chosen dove, whose mind was splendid with golden wings.

St. Germanus of Constantinople, in the *Mariale* published by us, pages 102 and 103, calls her a rational and most pure dove, because of the divine whiteness of her soul, whiter than snow; uniquely beloved by the heavenly Bridegroom; wholly fashioned for the concerns of the spirit and, as it were, transformed into spirit; she showed humankind that the winter of error had now ceased.

St. Aldhelm, bishop of Sherborne, in the book *On the Praise of Virginity*, chapter 22, calls her the dove among sixty queens and twice forty concubines, who, by reason of her enduring privilege of purity, deserved happily to receive the Monarch of the world—with the archangel announcing, the Paraclete overshadowing, and her inmost heart rejoicing.

George of Nicomedia, Oration 1 on the Presentation of the Blessed Virgin, calls her an irreproachable dove which escaped the fowler of malice and was made loftier than his snares. Michael Psellus, on chapter VI of the *Song of Songs*, calls her the chosen dove among the souls of all persons who are saved. Franco, abbot of Afflighem, Book VI, *On the Grace of God*, calls her a dove without gall. Amadeus of Lausanne, Homily 6 on the Praises of the Virgin, calls her Christ’s dove by union. Hugh of St. Victor, sermon 34, calls her a dove by simplicity. Philip, abbot of Bonne-Espérance, Book III on the *Song*, chapter 7, calls her the dove of the heavenly Bridegroom, who groaned and sighed incomparably because eternal things were absent. William the Little, on chapter II of the *Song*, calls her a fruitful dove, beautiful in virginity, whose unique offspring was Christ. Rupert the abbot, Book III on the *Song of Songs*, [Col. 0775C] calls her a dove without gall, nourishing the young of others, gathering whiter grains, nesting among rocks, making groaning her song, and dwelling beside the streams of Scripture.

Honorius of Autun, in the *Seal of Blessed Mary*, calls her Christ’s dove, full of the Holy Spirit, into whom God poured the charisms of the Holy Spirit. Absalon the abbot, sermon 1 on the Assumption, calls her the dove which came forth from Noah’s ark—that is, which arose from the Church—and which brought back to it the olive branch at the time of the flood, because, while the waters of vices engulfed the world, she brought forth in the Church Christ incarnate from herself. James the monk, in his Oration on the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin, calls her the most undefiled dove. John Hailgrin, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, on chapter II of the *Song*, calls her a dove illumined by God the Holy Spirit. Albert the Great, sermon 1 on the Purification of the Blessed Virgin, calls her a prudent, simple, most fruitful, noble dove. St. Bonaventure, in the *Mirror of the Blessed Virgin*, chapter 8, calls her [Col. 0775D] the most faithful dove, who stood as the most faithful mediatrix between the supreme Noah and a world drowned in a spiritual flood.

James of Voragine, in the *Mariale*, sermon 2, letters O and V, calls her a most innocent dove, possessing no gall of bitterness but wholly full of the sweetness of compassion. Emperor Matthew Cantacuzenus, on chapters I and V of the *Song of Songs*, calls her the dove of the only-begotten Son of God, having nothing of iniquity in her eyes, but all things pure and all things ordered in beauty. 218 Blessed Lawrence Justinian, in *On Chaste Marriage*, chapter 9, and *On Christ’s Triumphant Struggle*, chapter 18, calls her the immaculate, beautiful, sweet, beloved, and lovable dove of the Bridegroom. St. Antoninus, archbishop of Florence, in Part IV of the *Summa theologiae*, title 15, chapter 24, calls her a dove without the gall of sin, made white, whiter than snow, made fruitful by the Holy Spirit through the splendors of her merits, chosen and pre-chosen above all by gifts.

St. Bernardino of Siena, volume I, sermon 61, calls her the dove [Col. 0776A] in the clefts of the rock and in the hollow of the wall, because, so long as she lived, with enlarged vision and spacious flight, through the openings of the sufferings of Jesus Christ’s body and through the hollow of his side-wound, she always groaned in his sorrows and continually hid herself there. Richard of St. Lawrence, Book XII, *On the Praises of the Virgin*, column 952, calls her the dove which, when the flood had ceased, carried an olive branch in her mouth to Noah in the ark, showing that God had been reconciled with humankind. Dionysius the Carthusian, on chapter I of the *Song of Songs*, article 8, calls her God’s dove, in whom there was never a root of bitterness or the harshness of gall, but inviolable wisdom-filled simplicity. Paul of Heredia, in his treatise on the Conception of the Blessed Virgin, calls her a dove devoid of the gall of original sin and clean from original sin. Abbot Trithemius, in *On the Miracles of the Blessed Virgin at Urticeto*, chapter 6, calls her a dove of most prudent 219 simplicity. Blessed Thomas of Villanova, in his discourse on the Visitation of the Blessed Virgin, calls her a swift dove, flying over mountain summits in the Visitation. Maurice of Villa Probata, in the *Crown of the Blessed Virgin*, sermon 17, calls her a divine, most white dove, sent by the supreme King, which came to us and bore to us the privilege of our restoration and salvation.

Finally, not to be too lengthy, John Picus, Book I on the *Song*, chapter 13, and Book III, chapter 3, calls her a dove in no way leavened by original gall, and God’s dove, which was able fittingly to express dovelike simplicity, gentleness, and humility, together with the fullness of the gifts of the Holy Spirit and the abundance of all his charisms. For divinity received so great an abundance of all these things that she seems almost to have obtained them without measure.

## ON FRAGMENT IV

This fragment on Mary as mediatrix is taken from a golden sermon of our Adam, which he formerly delivered in the Cistercian chapter. On the title “mediatrix,” given to the Mother of God, besides what I said in the notes [Col. 0776C] to the *Mariale* of St. Germanus, Patriarch of Constantinople, in the notes to the Oration on the Annunciation, no. 5, see, if you wish, Richard of St. Lawrence, 220 Book II, *On the Praises of the Virgin*, p. 86; Albert the Great on *Missus est*, chapters 9 and 10; St. Bonaventure, in the *Mirror of the Blessed Virgin*, chapter 8; and St. Antoninus, Part IV, title 15, chapters 5 and 13.

## ON FRAGMENT V

It is taken from a sermon which Adam wrote on the Sabbath of Wisdom, and it overflows with most devout feelings toward the childbirth of the most holy Virgin Mother of God.

(29) If my Jesus counted me among his fellow-nurslings. The principal fellow-nurslings of the child Jesus—that is, those placed at the most sacred breasts of the Virgin Mother of God and refreshed with her most pure milk—were St. John Chrysostom, St. Fulbert of Chartres, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, St. Dominic Guzmán, St. Catherine of Siena, and Blessed Alanus de Rupe.

For concerning St. [Col. 0776D] Chrysostom, as is found in the *Life of Henry Suso*, chapter 20, the Mother of God, once making herself visibly present to a certain holy man, is reported to have spoken thus:

> Go to the servant of my Son, Henry Suso, and say to him in my words: As it has been handed down in writing about that illustrious doctor John Chrysostom, when he was a schoolboy and bent his knees before the altar where I myself, in a wooden image, was nursing my Son in my lap, through that same 221 image I told my Son to pause for a little while.

Concerning St. Fulbert, Gononus records the following, on the basis of many weighty authorities, in the *Chronicle of the Mother of God*, under the year 1020:

> The venerable Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, was in danger of death from a disease called holy fire, which burned his tongue. One night, when he was afflicted by pain more severely than usual, he saw the most illustrious Lady, with a great retinue and splendor, warning him to open his mouth. When he had done so, that most beautiful maiden—the Mother of God—squeezed her most sacred milk from her breast, [Col. 0777A] and immediately cooled and healed his tongue completely. Fulbert’s cheeks were drenched by that most sacred milk; wiping away its drops on precious cloths as a sign of the miracle, they may still today be seen and venerated in the aforesaid church.

Concerning St. Bernard, Chrysostom Henriquez of Hortus, in his Cistercian *Menology* for 13 May, adduces this most weighty testimony, preserved hitherto at Châtillon and authenticated by the most reverend Lord Edmund de la Croix, General of the Cistercians:

> In the church of St. Berolus in the fortress of Châtillon-sur-Seine, in the diocese of Langres, there was formerly erected an image for the veneration and honor of the Blessed Virgin Mary. This image miraculously offered her Son to St. Bernard in the church, saying: “Bernard, receive my child, the Redeemer of the whole world.” Then, moreover, beyond every power of human nature, as though he were Christ’s natural brother, immediately, after he had taken the breast of the said image in his hand, three drops of milk flowing from that image’s breasts miraculously trickled into the open mouth of Blessed Bernard, devoted to her. [Col. 0777B] Having received the drops from the breast of that image, the preacher of that Mother of God, teacher of Christ her Son, and faithful confessor of the heavenly host composed very many praises of the Queen of Heaven, the holy Spirit breathing and the grace of that same Mary assisting.

Concerning St. Dominic, Blessed Alanus relates in Part II, chapter 3, of his *Marian Psalter*, from a revelation of the Virgin Mother of God herself:

> When Dominic was fighting most fiercely against the Albigensian heresy, he once withdrew into a forest near Toulouse. There, with burning sighs, abundant floods of tears, a three-day fast, and severe bodily mortifications—his flesh almost torn and variously mangled by thorns—he earnestly implored the aid and protection of the most august Queen of Heaven, whose special office it is to crush the head of the accursed serpent and to destroy and extinguish every heresy. [Col. 0777C] At last the gracious Mother appeared visibly; she raised him as he lay half-dead, received him into her virgin embrace, kissed him with a fixed kiss, and pressed him to her most chaste breasts.

Concerning St. Catherine, Hyacinth Choquetius recorded the following from the literary memorials of John Gavaston’s work *On the Holy Tertiaries of the Order of Preachers*, in the book *On the Maternal Entrails of the Blessed Virgin toward the Order of Preachers*, chapter 5:

> Among the splendid gifts of heaven by which Catherine, that most excellent virgin of Siena, famous throughout the whole world for the outstanding glory of every virtue, shone forth—and especially among her very many proofs of Marian love—there holds no small place the fact that the Queen of Angels descended from heaven to her and, after most sweet conversations, kisses, and truly maternal embraces, sometimes placed her at her most sacred breasts. She permitted her not merely to wash her lips with virgin milk; rather, intoxicated with the delights of heavenly nectar, she granted her the great gift of drinking, as it were, from the very bosom of mercy itself.

Finally, [Col. 0777D] Jodocus Beysselius writes the following concerning Alanus in his little work *On the Rosary of the Blessed Virgin*:

> About the year of the Lord 1470, the most devout Doctor Alanus de Rupe, imitating the father Dominic both in profession and in devotion toward the Mother of Christ, restored to light the almost obsolete brotherhood of the Rosary, which had languished for several centuries—certainly at the instruction of that same holy Lady who had once urged Dominic to this very undertaking.

And after much else:

> What they add, however, surpasses all belief: that the holy Virgin, from her exposed breast, once poured an abundance of milk into the mouth of Alanus as he prayed and contemplated. Where does Mary’s compassion not reach? Anyone might reasonably think these things unlike the truth, unless the highest nature’s especial work were to love the just and devout, though mortal persons. 

Thus Beysselius.

Nor shall I separate from the fellow-nurslings of the child Jesus that cleric wonderfully devoted to the Virgin Mother of God, to whom the same Virgin Mother of God granted the same benefit of nursing. Vincent of Beauvais recounts this in Book VII of the *Historical Mirror*, [Col. 0778A] chapter 84:

> A certain cleric, abundantly supplied with worldly goods and devoted to the world, had nevertheless so impressed upon his heart love for the Mother of God and reverent remembrance of her that, whenever he entered any church or happened to pass through one, no worldly care and no forgetfulness could steal from him the habit of kneeling with every devotion and humility and saying: “Blessed is the womb that bore you, Christ, and blessed the breasts which nursed you, our Lord and Savior.”
>
> Once, struck by a bodily affliction, he was overcome by such pain that he chewed his tongue and lips with his teeth, and would have done the same to his other limbs if he had been allowed. When his tongue and lips had already been completely consumed, and his attendants held him tightly to prevent injury to his other limbs, he lay horrible to behold and deprived of bodily senses. Beside the head of his bed he saw a figure standing, beautiful of face and venerable in appearance. This was, so far as can be understood, his angel, lamenting the sufferings of his sick charge. He seemed to lament in this manner: [Col. 0778B] “What is this, O Lady of mercy, fountain of compassion? Is this the glory and grace of his salutation? Is this the tongue so accustomed, by long practice and burning affection, to the blessing of your womb, breasts, and childbirth that it uttered almost nothing else but ‘Lady, Lady’? If you are wanting to your own, who will be there for his own? Not thus, Lady, not thus will the human form perish into nothingness, if people do not begin to find refuge in you.”
>
> As the angel said these things, the Mother of God appeared. As though answering the charge of negligence toward her little servant which had been brought against her, she came nearer to the sick man’s bed. Drawing out her breast, she was seen to send into his mouth the most sweet stream of milk, whereby she immediately restored the wholeness of his tongue, the former beauty of his lips, and his body’s prior health throughout. His senses being restored, he immediately rose healthy and unharmed; and, even if his tongue had been silent, by the sudden change of his life and conduct he began to proclaim the mercy shown to him. For dedicating himself and his possessions to God’s service, [Col. 0778C] he thereafter lived a religious life.

Thus far Vincent.

## ON FRAGMENT VI

This fragment on the protection and imitation of the Virgin Mother of God, copied from a sermon which our Adam wrote on confession, is more precious than extensive. But so that no one might miss even a portion of a good gift, I have appended it.

226

## ON FRAGMENT VII

This fragment on praise of the Virgin Mother, by which our Adam abundantly made his devotion to the Mother of God evident, is entirely absent from the Casamari manuscript I used. It appears, however, under the name of Adam, Abbot of Perseigne, in Geoffrey Tilmann, monk of the Parisian Charterhouse, in the *Allegories on Passages of Both Testaments*, on the book of Ecclesiasticus; from that work I borrowed it and appended it above.

(30) Our Virgin indeed is an olive tree. The comparison of the Virgin Mother of God with the olive tree—which our Adam develops at length [Col. 0778D] here—is also extensively developed by Absalon the abbot, sermon on the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin; Philip, abbot of Bonne-Espérance, Book IV on the *Song*, chapter 30; Honorius of Autun, in the *Seal of Blessed Mary*; James of Voragine, in the *Mariale*, letter O, sermon 2; St. Antoninus, Part III of the *Summa theologiae*, title 31, chapter IV; Bernardino Busti, in the *Mariale*, sermon 2, on the Assimilation of Blessed Mary; Maurice of Villa Probata, in the *Crown of the Blessed Virgin*, sermon 22; and, most extensively of all, Richard of St. Lawrence, Book XII, *On the Praises of the Virgin*, from p. 951 onward.

(31) It is therefore dangerous to depart from her even for a moment. St. Ildephonsus, well recognizing this, says in Book II, *On the Virginity of St. Mary*, chapter 4:

> Come with me to this Virgin; do not hasten without her toward Gehenna. Come, let us hide beneath the covering of her power, lest you be clothed with shame as with a double garment.

So he writes. And why did Lucifer become a demon, and the angels fall from heaven into hell, unless because—as Galatinus notes in [Col. 0779A] Book VII of the *Secrets*, chapter 4, and Paul of Heredia in his treatise on the Conception of the Blessed Virgin, not far from the end—they departed from the Blessed Virgin, refusing to honor her as the future Mother of God, as God had commanded them? Why likewise do the Jews, rejected by God, suffer so many evils and calamities, as we see, unless because—as the same Galatinus argues in Book IX, chapter 10—they withdrew from the Blessed Virgin, refusing to serve her as the Mother of the Messiah?

Hence St. Anselm, speaking with Mary: “Everyone,” he says, “who turns away from you must perish.” For just as devotion to and turning toward the Virgin is a sign of eternal predestination, so turning away from the Virgin and the failure of devotion toward her is a sign of eternal reprobation. To this end Solomon, speaking in the person of the Virgin, said in Proverbs VIII: “Whoever sins against me injures his own soul; all who hate me love death.” Hence St. Bonaventure says in the *Psalter of the Blessed Virgin*: “Whoever worthily honors her—Mary—shall be justified; but whoever neglects her shall die in his sins.” John of Cartagena likewise seems to signify this in Homily 2, *On Worship and 228 Devotion toward the Blessed Virgin*:

> Ecclesiasticus compares the Blessed Virgin to a rose, saying: “Like a planting of roses in Jericho.” For just as bees frequently gather around a rose and enjoy its virtue, while black beetles, unable to bear the fragrance of its odor, depart far from it, so the predestined, like industrious bees, come to the mystical rose Mary in order to enjoy her wondrous power; but the reprobate, like the foulest beetles, unable to endure the fragrance of her outstanding holiness, remove themselves far from her.

But who could recount how many evils, miseries, and calamities this turning away from Mary the Mother of God, and from her worship and devotion, brings with it? Blessed Peter Damian, in Book VI, Letter 32, explaining why monks who had departed from the Mother of God by omitting her customary praises suffered utterly countless evils, with no remedy aiding them, says among other things:

> Because they cast the Mother [Col. 0779C] of true peace out of their monastery, it is fitting that they be driven by restless storms and whirlwinds of calamities and tribulations.

So he writes. And what are we without Mary but fish without water, sailors without a star, a body without neck or head? Hence Maurice [Col. 0780A] of Villa Probata, in the *Crown of the Blessed Virgin*, sermon 27, citing Ecclesiasticus XXIX, “Water and bread are the beginning of human life,” and understanding the Blessed Virgin by “water,” says:

> Just as fish cannot live without water, so we would fare badly without the grace of the most blessed Virgin.

St. Bernard, Homily 2 on *Missus est*, speaking of Mary under the name of a star, rightly exclaims:

> O you, whoever you are, who understand yourself to be tossed in the flood of this age among storms and tempests rather than walking upon the land, do not turn your eyes away from the brightness of this star, if you do not wish to be overwhelmed by the storms.

And Philip, abbot of Bonne-Espérance, Book II on the *Song*, chapter 7, on the words, “Your neck is like necklaces,” speaks thus:

> She herself, Mary, is found to stand beneath Christ the head in such a way that there is no doubt that she also stands above the rest of the body. She seems to occupy the middle place between head and body. Nor can the bridegroom’s children attain to the Bridegroom except through the Mother acting as mediator. While the Bridegroom himself is present to us, it is good to cleave to him; but when he is absent, the members cannot adhere to the head. [Col. 0780B]

And indeed, what good can there be for wretched human beings without Mary?

> O pleasant spring of life  
> (most sweetly sang Blessed Hermann—or Joseph—of Steinfeld in his hymn to the Blessed Virgin),  
>
> My needy mind grows faint;  
> Nothing has strength without you;  
> It perishes as it goes, languishing miserably.  
> Rejoice, branch that never withers;  
> Yet whoever lacks you withers.

230 Thus the anonymous author, in the *Crown of the Blessed Virgin*, which survives in manuscript in the Vatican Library, chapter 3, wrote most truly:

> This woman, Mary, is she without whom, wherever she is absent, there is nothing but groaning and want, according to Ecclesiasticus XXXVI: “Where there is no woman, the needy man groans.” For wherever Mary is absent through grace, there can be nothing but misery and want.

So he writes. May God therefore grant that we never depart from the Blessed Virgin, through forgetfulness of her worship or neglect of devotion, [Col. 0780C] even for a moment or an instant, lest we fall into those evils and misfortunes into which those who depart from her and neglect her worship fall.

PRAISE TO GOD AND TO THE VIRGIN MOTHER OF GOD.

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1205, PETER OF POITIERS, CHANCELLOR OF THE UNIVERSITY OF PARIS

[Col. 0779]

# NOTICE

(OUDIN, *Commentary on Ecclesiastical Writers*, II, 1499)

Peter of Poitiers, faithful disciple of Peter Lombard, Master of the *Sentences*, later a most celebrated teacher of theology in the University of Paris and chancellor of that University, flourished in virtue of life and learning from the year 1160 onward. He set these forth for posterity in various volumes. He is to be distinguished from another man of the same period who was a disciple of St. Peter, abbot of Cluny.

This Peter wrote five learned books of *Sentences*, selected from the works of the holy Fathers. Walter, prior of St. Victor at Paris, later dared to attack these with a sufficiently malicious tooth in the work entitled *Against the Four Labyrinths of France: Peter Abelard, Gilbert of Poitiers, Peter Lombard, and Peter of Poitiers himself*. This work, written in ancient characters contemporary with the author himself, was sent by Nicolas Camusat, canon of Troyes, a man most worthy of the reputation shared by all learned men and of his own fame, not long before his death, to Dom Luc d’Achery as a token of mutual affection. From it, Hugh Mathoud, a Benedictine monk of the Congregation of St. Maur in France, arranged for an edition to be published at Paris in folio in 1655, by Simeon Piget, on the Rue Saint-Jacques, under the sign of Prudence, with the title: *The Distinctions, or Five Books of Sentences, of Peter of Poitiers, Professor and Chancellor in the University of Paris*.

His letter to Lord William, Archbishop of Sens, begins:

> Gathering manna in the desert, one collected a whole gomor, another more, another less, each according to his eagerness, etc.

Distinction I, chapter 1, on the existence and unity of God, begins:

> The invisible things of God are intelligibly perceived through those things which have been made. Man is called the creature of the world because of the excellence he possesses over creatures and the affinity he possesses with them, etc.

To withdraw himself from the taunts of jealous scholastic rivals, Peter dedicated this *Summa of Theology* to William, Archbishop of Sens and later of Reims, just as Peter Comestor had dedicated his *Ecclesiastical History* to the same man; this occurred in or about the year 1170. At that time he was chancellor of the University of Paris, in which he subsequently served as public professor of theology for thirty-eight years, as is clear from the praises written of him by Claude Héméré, doctor and fellow of the Sorbonne, in his book *On the University of Paris*, p. 40, and from the manuscript chronicle of Alberic for the year 1169:

> At Paris, after Master Peter Comestor, Master Peter of Poitiers held the chair of theology.

He composed these *Sentences*, dedicated to William, Archbishop of Sens, before 1175, at the end of which year William was transferred from the see of Sens to that of Reims. The cited Héméré, p. 115, states:

> Master Peter of Poitiers taught theology at Paris for thirty-eight years, as we reported above from the *Chronicle*. To him, together with the Dean of Paris and John, Abbot of Sainte-Geneviève, successor of Stephen of Tournai, was sent the letter of Innocent III concerning the complaint of the Countess of Blois and the chapter of Chartres, cited in the chapter *Ex parte*, *On the Signification of Words*. He is mentioned in a letter of Maurice, bishop, delivered to the Victorine canons regarding the terms for receiving annual payments from the prebends of the Church of Paris, dated 1196. Pope Celestine appointed Peter, together with Hugh Clement, Dean of Paris, to settle the dispute between the monks of St. Eligius on the island of Paris and the canons of St. Victor concerning the tithes of wine and grain at Vitry. From the instrument drawn up on that matter there still hangs intact the seal of Peter of Poitiers, bearing this inscription: “The seal of Peter of Poitiers, Chancellor of Paris.” In the library of the Sorbonne are preserved his Sermons and Ordinary Allegories on the three books of the Mosaic Law—Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers—etc., concerning which see above.

Thus far Héméré.

The same manuscript chronicle of Alberic says of him under the year 1205:

> Master Peter of Poitiers, Chancellor of Paris, died; he had taught theology at Paris for thirty-eight years, etc. The aforesaid Peter of Poitiers made a book *On Theological Sentences* for that same Archbishop William. His sermons, distinctions, and postils are also extant. And, providing for poor clerics, he devised trees of the histories of the Old Testament to be painted on skins, and likewise arranged materials concerning vices and virtues.

A further work of his also exists in the library of Saint-Victor, under the shelfmark D. I, containing, in a manuscript of excellent authority, namely, *Distinctions on the Psalter according to Master Peter of Poitiers*, whose prologue begins: “You shall make for me a tent at the entrance of the tabernacle, woven of precious skins. The tabernacle in which God dwells within us,” etc. There likewise is a distinguished Commentary by Peter of Poitiers, perhaps the first ever composed on the Master of the Sentences: a work other than Peter of Poitiers’s own *Sentences*. Its prologue begins: “The sum of sacred Scripture gives counsel in matters to be considered and undertaken, that is, in the affirmation of faith and the shaping of morals,” etc. “Desiring,” etc., as in the Master of the Sentences. “Following the custom of writers, the Master prefixes a preface; and this is the content of the preface,” etc.

Although Hugh Mathoud, a Benedictine monk, asserted that this work was one and the same as the *Sentences* of the same Peter which he published, saying: “That Victorine manuscript codex differs only in a few particulars from the cited printed Troyes manuscript, except that the Victorine manuscript is sometimes mutilated, and lacks the preliminary letter to William, Archbishop of Sens—or at least that letter escaped the eyes of those reading rather hurriedly.”

The work of the *Sentences* of Master Peter of Poitiers, beginning “Gathering manna in the desert,” etc., is also preserved anonymously in manuscript in the library of Saint-Évroult, of the Order of Saint Benedict, shelfmark T. 9. Finally, almost all, or at least the greater part, of Peter of Poitiers’s works survive in manuscript in the library of Clairvaux: namely, the *Sentences* of Master Peter of Poitiers, Peter of Poitiers’s *Distinctions on the Psalter*, and *Allegories on the Old and New Testament*, as I learned from its careful catalogue compiled in 1664, which I possess. Peter of Poitiers’s *Allegories on the Tabernacle of Moses* are in manuscript at Cambridge, in the Pembroke College Library, codex 75. His *Allegories on the Bible* are privately held in the library of Baron Lumley, codex 231.

Moreover, in the same library of Saint-Victor at Paris, shelfmark SS. 18, fols. 85–180, is the *Summa of Peter of Poitiers on the Mysteries of Christ’s Incarnation*, etc., beginning: “He who sows sparingly shall reap sparingly; and he who sows in blessings shall reap eternal life from blessings. Therefore, that we may reap in the future, we set forth the seed-bed of God’s word,” etc. But this treatise, being four hundred years old, is uncertain because anonymous; the author’s name was added in a later hand.

In the same library of Saint-Victor, the *Sermons of Master Peter of Poitiers* survive in manuscript under shelfmark QQ. 20, in a codex of excellent authority. Near the beginning of the codex, in an old script, stands: “Sermons through the cycle of the year, with exceptions, by Master Peter of Poitiers.” Then about the middle of the codex is a table or index of sixty-eight such sermons, after which follows: “In this half of the book are contained certain sermons through the cycle of the year, and notes excerpted from the sermons of Master Peter of Poitiers, Chancellor of Paris, and Master Stephen, bishop of Canterbury, and from other treatises, all of which are necessary for the care of souls, as will appear below.” Then follows: “Here begin certain sermons through the cycle of the year, and certain notes excerpted from the sermons of Master Peter of Poitiers, Chancellor.” “The bodies of the saints were buried in peace. If one cannot sufficiently set forth the preeminence and praises of a single saint, with practiced talent and an educated tongue,” etc.

Another work by the same author appears near the end of the same codex, in red-lettered script and of good authority: “Here begin the Sermons of Master Peter of Poitiers. The first is for the feast of All Saints. The saints through faith conquered kingdoms,” etc. “It is more certain than certain that the saints conquered all the kingdoms of the world, and especially those twelve leaders,” etc.

Since Peter taught theology for thirty-eight years, no one should doubt that he lived to old age. He subscribed to an instrument or charter of Maurice, bishop of Paris, in 1184, in this manner: “In the presence of Maurice, bishop of Paris, the archdeacon, etc., Peter of Poitiers.” In 1196, as Chancellor, he wrote an instrument concerning the construction of a house adjoining the Petit-Pont, at a time when Hugh Clement was dean of that same Church of Paris. Yet worn out by old age, he died in 1205. Alberic speaks of him in the manuscript chronicle cited above, as does the writer of the *History of the University of Paris* in the twelfth century.

[Col. 0783]

Moreover, lest the reader be misled by the mistakes of others, I have thought it necessary to note that there were two other men named Peter of Poitiers, or Peter Pictaviensis, besides this Chancellor of the University of Paris, not greatly removed from his time.

The first of these was a disciple of Peter the Venerable, Abbot of Cluny, and one of his little works may be found in the library of Cluny. [Note: [Col. 0783] See *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXIX.] The other was a regular canon of Saint Augustine at Saint-Victor outside the walls of Paris, whose work *On Penance, or Confession*, is preserved there. This *Penitential*, there with the author’s name explicitly given, is entitled in a manuscript of excellent authority, shelfmark II. 13: “The Penitential of Brother Peter of Poitiers, Canon of Saint-Victor.”

Likewise, under shelfmark QQ. 12, whose title I copied there in red letters four hundred years old: “The present compilation has confession as its subject matter; it professes no author for its subject matter, but has as many authors as it has authorities.” It begins: “Certain confessors observe this method and practice,” etc.; nor is it very lengthy. But in an entirely recent hand, scarcely twenty years old, at the beginning of the codex it is attributed, on the authority of another old manuscript codex, to Peter of Poitiers, canon of Saint-Victor. That codex once belonged to Alexander Petavius, councillor of the Paris Parlement. Jacques Petit speaks of it thus in volume I of his work on Theodore of Canterbury, p. 341: “In the manuscript codex of the late and illustrious Alexander Petavius, he is called Peter of Saint-Victor; for this is found at the end of the codex: ‘Here ends the *Penitential* of Master Peter of Saint-Victor, corrected by Master James, canon of that same Saint-Victor.’”

This man was later in date than our Peter of Poitiers, who died in 1205; for he wrote after Prévostin and John Beleth, whom he cites, indeed after Peter the Chanter, whom he imitates in his *Penitential* in many things—both words, opinions, and comparisons. It is enough to have noted this.

Philippe Labbe treats learnedly of these two Peters who are called Pictavienses, in the *New Library of Manuscript Latin, Greek, and French Books; or, A Specimen of Ancient Greek, Latin, and French Readings*, which he caused to be published at Paris in quarto in 1653, chiefly from manuscript codices of the Royal Library of France, by Jean Henault, part II, p. 25 of that library, in these words:

> “The Glosses of Master Peter of Poitiers, Chancellor of the University of Paris, on the *Sentences* of his teacher Master Peter Lombard, from the Victorine codex D. 1, in which are also his *Distinctions on the Psalter*. Almost contemporary with him was Brother Peter of Poitiers, canon of the Abbey of Saint-Victor, whose manuscript book called the *Penitential* is found in that same richly furnished library, together with another *Penitential* by Master Peter of Flamesburgo, canon of the same monastery.”

So writes Labbe in the cited place. Charles du Fresne du Cange also discusses these three Peters of Poitiers—briefly indeed, but learnedly and distinctly—in the index of authors prefixed to his *Glossary of Medieval and Late Latin*, col. 138.

# THE FIVE BOOKS OF SENTENCES OF PETER OF POITIERS, FORMER CHANCELLOR OF THE UNIVERSITY OF PARIS

First brought to light and furnished with notes through the work and study of Dom Hugh Mathoud, Benedictine monk of the Congregation of Saint-Maur.

(Paris: at the expense of Simeon Piget, Rue Saint-Jacques, at the sign of Prudence, 1655, folio; together with the eight books of *Sentences* of Robert Pullen, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and Chancellor, the most ancient, as they call them, of the scholastic theologians.)

[Col. 0783]

# PREFACE TO THE READER, NECESSARILY TO BE PREFIXED TO THE READING OF THIS WORK

[Col. 0783A]

Disappointed in the great hope I had conceived of finding other works of Pullen, so that the volume of his *Sentences*, soon to be submitted to the press, might not lack its proper bulk, I was compelled to direct my mind and eyes toward other authors of the same kind, intending to choose one of them as Pullen’s companion, lest he go forth alone.

Two authors of thoroughly approved authority presented themselves, not unlike Robert both in date and in manner of writing: the first, Robert of Melun, religiously preserved in the library of Saint-Victor; the other, Peter of Poitiers, the faithful disciple of the Master of the Sentences, Chancellor of the University of Paris and there a most celebrated teacher. Nicholas Camuzat, canon of Troyes, most worthy alike of the esteem of all scholars and of his own reputation, not long before his death sent the latter, copied in an ancient script contemporary with the author himself, to my colleague Luc d’Achery—a distinguished gift and pledge of mutual affection.

The Victorine codex of Robert of Melun pleased me because it came first in my reading, and I had already prepared my pen to adorn its birth, when I was informed that the initiates of that monastery, to whom the book belongs, wished more usefully to discharge this office of care for their own offspring. I did not resist them—although they have long carried the child in the womb—but did not delay to press forward the birth of the other, namely Peter of Poitiers, with an effort neither superficial nor, I think, useless.

I have marked in the margin, with asterisks, the passages of Sacred Scripture and sayings of the holy Fathers, which occur more frequently in it. I have repeatedly noted the agreement between teacher and pupil, which is certainly continuous—an agreeable labour for the reader, but one especially useful to the author. Since I wished to provide for the reputation which in many respects he has precariously maintained, I judged that nothing was better than to show him following his own guide in doctrine, that guide whom the school has hitherto revered as the standard-bearer of all theologians. For by what anathema should one be condemned who adhered closely, as the Master of the Sentences dictated and wrote, and did so without obstinacy? Or, if he may be condemned when he appears in some points to have strayed from the path of truth, who would not more fairly be angry with the short-sighted Lombard, from whom it was, for a most devoted disciple, a religious obligation not to depart even a finger’s breadth? This is why throughout this work I cite the Master as his surety: he had illuminated Peter by public lectures and private discussions.

After so many marginal notes, I judged that I ought to abstain from further observations, especially since almost everyone agrees with this view. They will have noticed that hardly anything is found in this author worthy of close attention, and demanding the reader’s fuller consideration, which has not already appeared in the Master’s *Sentences* and in commentaries upon them—corrected, explained, or at least marked by the learned. Of this last kind you have selected articles at the end of the last book of the *Sentences* of that same Peter Lombard, in which he met with the singular fate, and deservedly, of being rejected by the schools everywhere. Since the author likewise stumbled upon them, I would vainly have attempted to cure a disease with more immediate remedies when you may easily obtain them from each and every writer who has devoted the longest labour to elucidating the Master’s aforesaid *Sentences*.

Yet, lest the unwary be caught by our silence and suppose that, out of favour to the author, I intentionally ignored or concealed his errors, I shall not hesitate to enumerate here at least those points which inflict a wound or depart from the common course of theologians.

## IN THE FIRST BOOK

I.—At chapter 22. He has certain remarks on the image in the Godhead which we shall set forth below when satisfaction is given to Walter, who attacks the author with his customary jibes; and it is for Walter’s sake alone that we mention them here.

II.—At chapter 31 and elsewhere. He consistently maintains that the Holy Spirit, or God, is itself the charity dwelling in the soul, and that apart from it no other created and habitual charity is found. He follows the erring Master, *Sentences*, book I, distinction 17, § B, etc.; and the Parisian school deservedly condemned and set that teaching aside.

III.—At chapter 33. With the Master, I, distinction 24, he teaches that numerical names in God posit nothing but merely exclude. Yet he hesitates regarding the name *Trinity*, or *Threefold*, and does not dare determine whether it is merely exclusive, as the name *One* is; although no one should doubt that the same principle applies to both. Besides Ambrose, whom he himself cites, he might have consulted a passage of Hilary’s *On the Synods*, where, explaining the formula of faith issued at the Council of Sardica, Hilary intimates that the divine substance rejects number. Yet in both writers let this be their sense: that there are not several gods in the Trinity; for those holy Fathers have reference to the nature, not to the persons.

## IN THE SECOND BOOK

IV.—At chapter 4. Concerning the merit of angels and the attainment of their essential reward, he stumbles with the Master, II, distinction 11, whose opinion is struck by the Parisian anathema.

V.—At chapter 9. Thus he speaks gratuitously of Adam: “At that time he is said to have been present at the court of the angels, and to have prophesied about the flood and many other things; but not afterwards.”

## IN THE THIRD BOOK

VI.—At chapter 13. He judges confession to be a sacrament of the Old Testament and not to effect what it signifies—just as marriage does not. The Master, IV, distinction 2, § 1, shone before him with this spurious brilliance. Concerning marriage, he writes: “Some provide a remedy against sin and confer assisting grace, as baptism does; others serve only as a remedy, as marriage does.” And in distinction 22, at the final section of the same book, he says of both: “The sacrament of penance, like marriage, existed before the age of grace, even from the beginning of the human race; for both were instituted in our first parents.” For the remedy or condemnation of this opinion, consult the writers on the *Sentences*.

VII.—At chapter 16. Thus the author: “A priest does not loose sin either with respect to punishment or with respect to guilt; but he looses and forgives—that is, he shows that it has been loosed and forgiven by God with respect to guilt.” This is an error shared with the Master, IV, distinctions 17 and 18. See further the *Observations* on chapter 13 of part five of Robert Pullen. [Note: [Col. 0785D] *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXVI, col. 1064.]

VIII.—At chapter 24. Consistently indeed, but wrongly, he argues thus concerning the increase of charity: “For charity in itself is neither intensified nor diminished, but only in its effect.” The Master had gone before him in this, I, distinction 17, § H: “Charity is altogether unchangeable, and neither increases nor diminishes in itself, nor receives in itself more or less; but it increases and diminishes in a human being, or rather for a human being, and is given or possessed more or less,” etc.

## IN THE FOURTH BOOK

IX.—At chapter 2. “By circumcision only original sin was remitted; but neither assisting grace for good works was conferred, nor were virtues increased. All this occurs through baptism, besides the remission of original sin.” This blemish is likewise evident in the Master, IV, distinction 1, § K: “For there, in circumcision, sins alone were forgiven; but neither assisting grace for acting well, nor possession or increase of virtues, was granted there, as it is in baptism,” etc. This is numbered among the selected errors.

X.—At chapter 3. “Ceremonial observances were instituted for signifying, not for justifying, even if performed in charity.” By this obstacle the Master’s doctrine also becomes inconsistent, IV, distinction 1, § B, and was accordingly set aside by the Parisian censure. Yet the author corrects himself toward the end of the same chapter.

XI.—At chapter 10. In this chapter and those following, Peter dwells extensively on the existence of the assumed humanity. Because of this he had many bitter enemies, especially Walter of Saint-Victor, who, in a special book, *Against the Four Labyrinths of France*, so savagely attacked Peter Abelard, Gilbert of Poitiers, Peter Lombard, and Peter of Poitiers himself—assailing him with so many whispers and taunts—that he seems to have indulged anger no less than truth.

Peter holds that Christ as man was not *something* but *of something*, that is, of human nature; nor did he consist of soul and body as parts of himself, though he assumed them in order to appear visible in them. “So long as Christ lived,” he says, “he was not something composed of soul and flesh.” But he himself reveals why he held this opinion: “If therefore unity of person is denoted there, it is true that Christ, insofar as he is man, is something—that is, that he himself, this man, is something. But if it denotes a cause or condition, it is false. For humanity does not make him a *what*, unless, as it were by force, we assign to the word *something* a meaning other than substance; so that ‘insofar as he is man, he is something’ means ‘he is of some mode, of some nature.’”

You have the foundation and example of this opinion in the Master, III, distinction 6, § F, which the disciple adopted to a grievous degree. Thus there are those who readily think him among those on whose account Alexander III wrote to the Archbishop of Reims, *Decretals*, book V, title *On Heretics*, chapter 7, *Cum Christus*. From this opinion the author draws not a few conclusions that might injure Christian truth unless interpreted more generously, as is fitting. On this matter, theologians who wrote on the said distinction of the Master and the following one should be consulted, especially the older writers, who had more abundant material for discussion because the subject was controversial in their own time. The marginal references indicate only the passages which Walter polished with his pumice-stone and those which might cause some difficulty to less learned readers.

XII.—At chapter 21. He has certain matters concerning the power by which Christ could lay down his soul; against these Walter, the Victorine monk mentioned above, sharpened his pen and zeal. See the Master, III, distinction 21, § C.

XIII.—At chapter 22. Adhering excessively to his teacher’s footsteps, he teaches that Christ was a man during the three days of death, because in his case a substantial union between soul and body was not particularly necessary for the reality of human nature. Besides others, the same Master, III, distinction 22, and Hugh of Saint-Victor, *On the Sacraments*, book II, part I, chapter 11, and in his *Questions on Romans* I, taught this teaching—erroneous in faith, though familiar in that century. Saint Thomas, III, question 50, article [unspecified], teaches what censure they deserve. That bitter Walter did not possess the sincere disposition of the Christian and Angelic Doctor: he had discernment indeed, but not unto sobriety.

## IN THE FIFTH BOOK

XIV.—At chapter 5. He thinks baptism would be valid if the baptizer, free of every error concerning the faith, named only one person of the Holy Trinity, or the name of Christ alone. Peter teaches this only because he had sworn allegiance to the Master’s words, IV, distinction 3, § E. He is troubled by certain further scruples in that chapter, but these are readily excusable in the age in which he wrote.
