XV.—At the end of chapter 7. Again he appears to depart from truth when he writes that Christ’s baptism was not necessary for those who had been baptized by John, provided that they possessed faith in the Trinity. But, following the erring Master, IV, distinction 2, § F, he erred less seriously.

XVI.—At chapter 8. At the beginning of this chapter he has a singular assertion concerning the efficacy of baptism repeated without blame.

XVII.—In the same place. “God could have conferred on someone a created power by which that person might forgive sins, though not by his own authority but rather by Christ’s.” The Sacred Faculty of Theology of Paris condemned almost the same opinion in the Master, IV, distinction 5, final section; it is numbered among the selected errors.

XVIII.—At chapter 11. Again there is this singular assertion concerning the words of consecration in the Mass: “To this it must be said that Christ uttered those words twice. For when he blessed, he uttered them, and thus transubstantiation took place upon their utterance. Afterwards he broke and gave to them, and again said: ‘This is my body,’ etc. But then he did not utter them for the purpose of blessing, and therefore the sacrament was not repeated. Yet some say that at the other consecration he uttered other words,” etc.

XIX.—At chapter 13. “Although the other sacraments may be celebrated outside the unity of the Church, those who are excommunicated cannot confect this sacrament”—the Eucharist. So says Peter; so say the Master, Hugh, and others, as in the notes on Pullen, because it was a common disease of the age.

XX.—At chapter 18. With the Master and many other theologians of no mean reputation in that age, he holds that nothing external, and no food, passes into true human flesh—namely, into that flesh which shall rise on the final day of the world—but that what was cut off from Adam through propagation is miraculously increased and multiplied, etc. Since this opinion is dangerous to faith, it was rejected by the Parisians and punished with the same fate as the foregoing opinions.

These, then, are the obstacles found in our Peter of Poitiers. Though they stand out more than sufficiently, they had to be enumerated here: for the reader’s caution and for my own defence. But, as I have already warned, the author, wholly devoted to his teacher, must be excused; in those days everyone wished to follow him even when he erred. Much must also be attributed to the age, when theology—I mean scholastic theology—had scarcely left its cradle and had not yet matured into those truths which, through the long practice and study of disputants, certainly emerged at last from the dust.

But the chief reason why our author should either be excused or condemned lies in the character of the theologians then writing: they indulged unstable reasoning in everything; by its borrowed light they searched deeply into the dogmas of faith, although its illumination is only nocturnal. And—this is the most perilous rock of all—they so mingled everything with problems and the double hazard of debate that, unless one were wiser, one often could not know toward which side one ought to incline. No one’s method of writing was more marked by this than Peter of Poitiers’s. Since he possessed an intellect extraordinarily fertile and subtle almost to the point of miracle, whenever occasion presented itself he lavished arguments for either side of a problem so abundantly that their very mass nearly overwhelms the reader, who does not know where truth lies—though it clings to an atom—while anxiously considering how plausibly it may be urged on both sides.

This sophistical manner of writing disfigured theology when the use of dialectic was admitted into its holy inner sanctuary and Aristotle began to be heard there. Walter complains of this in the book mentioned above, *Against the Four Labyrinths of France*—so named from the various twists and windings of sophisms:

> “Those,” he says, “whom one Aristotelian spirit has breathed upon, while treating the ineffable mysteries of the Holy Trinity and the Incarnation with scholastic frivolity, formerly vomited forth many heresies, and even now errors continue to spring up.”

Yet although Peter indulged this sport too freely, he never wished to let his dialectic play at the cost of faith; when it sometimes grew excessive, he restrained it with the bridle of Christian modesty. Where he remained uncertain, he wished to define nothing rashly; where he was alone, he wished to say nothing. The diligent reader will observe this in many places.

Let what he says at chapter 14 of book IV stand for all: though the matter is not so difficult, he nevertheless expresses a truly Christian judgment:

> “It would not be burdensome for me to write a solution to these matters, since I know this to be necessary for myself and others; except that I know the disposition of seeking truths to be safer than taking uncertain things for certain. Let us seek as those who will find; let us find as those who will seek. In matters to be believed let us doubt with no unbelief; in matters to be understood let us affirm with no rashness.”

And in the final chapter, concerning whether Christ is truly composite:

> “But who,” he says, “will make me certain of these matters? I am not equal to explaining arguments of this kind. Remove arguments from sacred Scripture where faith is sought. Faith is not to think more highly than one ought. Believe that it is so, and do not ask why,” etc.

See also chapters 21 and 33 of book I; chapters 14, 19, and 23 of book II; and so forth. The aforesaid Galter, or Walter, refused to perceive this mark of Christian modesty and this devotion of a spirit wholly ready to obey faith. Everything unknown to him was hateful to him; he raged against those eminent leaders of rational theology, puffed up with zeal for truth, but not according to knowledge. I would have the reader observe, by one example alone, how frequently unjust was his attitude toward our Peter of Poitiers, whom he wished to proscribe by Archilochean edicts.

In book I, chapter 22, Peter has these words:

> “For the Son is called the image of the Father, if the relation of proportion is observed, because every image is derived from its exemplar. Nor is the exemplar compared with the image, as Achilles with his statue; rather the image is compared with the exemplar, as a statue with Achilles. Thus the Son is said to be equal to the Father, coeternal with him, and consubstantial with him. The converse is not said, although it may truly be said.”

Walter took these words badly, not knowing that the expression is Augustinian, from book VI, chapter 10 of *On the Trinity*. For Augustine, considering this statement of Hilary concerning the three persons of the Trinity, in book II of *On the Trinity*, near the beginning—“Eternity in the Father, form in the image, use in the gift”—and judging it difficult to understand why Hilary attributes eternity to the Father rather than the Son, writes:

> “I do not think that in the term ‘eternity’ he followed anything but this: that the Father does not have a Father from whom he is; whereas the Son is from the Father, both that he may be and that he may be coeternal with him. For if an image perfectly fulfils that whose image it is, the image is made equal to it, not it to its own image,” etc.

So writes Augustine, whom we have cited lest the author, so devoted to him, be blamed rashly. Walter contrives and writes many other things of this sort, no less unsuccessfully, against pupil and teacher, as though to please Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, whom he greatly admired. Again, with what remarkable elegance he mocks Lombard for having written that Christ was conceived from the bloods of the Blessed Virgin! But whether Lombard wrote foolishly, let others judge; and let them see how unjustly so many distinguished leaders of theology in that century are sometimes beaten, an age in which those who knew more and those who knew less had an equal desire to write.

[Col. 0789]

# THE FIVE BOOKS OF SENTENCES OF PETER OF POITIERS

## 1. PROLOGUE TO LORD WILLIAM, ARCHBISHOP OF SENS

While gathering manna in the desert, one man gathered a whole *gomor*, another more, another less, according to the eagerness of each (Exod. 16:17). We fare well if, after great labour, we are permitted to gather half a *gomor* from that which remains over for others. For we place our confidence in our labour in this: that he who had gathered more had no excess, and he who had prepared less found no deficiency. Thus, even if we cannot complete a *gomor* in penetrating the loftier mysteries of God’s word, awaiting from God the completion of what is lacking, we nevertheless do not cease from gathering at least according to what we can eat (ibid., v. 18). Gathering scattered fragments, which because of their smallness evade the hands of gatherers, according to the capacity of our understanding—as one gathers a few ears after harvest, or two or three olives left after the shaking—we carry them to the heap as though they were half a *gomor*.

Therefore, to assist beginners approaching Sacred Scripture, we arrange into sequence matters fit for disputation; we bring disordered things into order; we renew worn-out matters through modest inquiry; we supply solutions where they have flowed down from between the mountains. But where Scripture has been silent, taking a full handful of fine flour, we leave what remains of the sacrifice to Aaron’s sons. And if they too have not expounded it before the manna melts in the heat of the sun (ibid., v. 21), what we cannot eat of the lamb we leave to be burned with fire.

For the polishing of this work we have reserved it to you, illustrious Father William, bishop of Sens, who possess learning for discernment, eloquence for instruction, and an abundance of virtues for example. It will therefore belong to your goodness—as it is your custom to favour the humble—to receive with a fatherly hand this work humbly prepared and produced through many vigils for the common good; to illuminate it, once received, with the splendour of correction; and to confer authority upon it once corrected.

We have also distinguished an order of five divisions. In the first we treat of faith in the Trinity; in the second, of rational creation.

2. In the third, of the restoration accomplished through the restoration of virtues; in the fourth, of that restoration once accomplished through the Incarnation; in the fifth, of that which is daily accomplished through participation in the sacraments.

# [BOOK I]

[Col. 0791]

## HERE BEGIN THE DISTINCTIONS OF THE FIRST BOOK

That God exists and is one. That God must exist. A distinction of names said of God and of the nine categories. Whether the name *person* follows the rule of things predicated only essentially. Whether the verbs said of God fall under the aforesaid rule of terms predicated only essentially. Whether names such as *someone*, *one*, and *unbegotten*, taken in the masculine, fall under the same rule. On complex terms consisting of one word signifying substance and another signifying a quality, such as “one able to beget.” The question why God is called omnipotent, and matters connected with this question. Whether God can do whatever he could do. On God’s will, where it is first asked whether anything occurs against the sign of the divine will. Whether anything can occur against God’s will, which is God himself. On the terms “to be able by power,” “to be able by justice,” and “to be able by mercy”: whether they are mutually convertible in a proposition. On God’s knowledge. On God’s foreknowledge. On matters common to predestination and reprobation. Whether the name *reprobation* posits anything when said of God. Whether names such as “to be loved” and “to be feared” are said of God according to essence. On abstract terms, such as *deity* and *paternity*. On terms such as “to be from the Father,” “God from God,” and the like. On terms such as “Wisdom of the Father” and “unbegotten Wisdom.” What is signified by the verb “loves” when it is said, “The Father loves the Son.” The manifold distinction of persons in the Trinity. On the name *similar* and *equal*. On the name *distinct*. On terms signifying relations and naming but not conjoining, such as paternity and filiation. On terms signifying relations, conjoining, and standing for persons, such as Father and Son. On terms signifying relations and conjoining, but neither naming nor standing for persons, such as begetting, begotten, and proceeding. On matters pertaining to paternity and filiation. On unbegottenness. On the common notion of Father and Son, that is, spiration. On the eternal property of the Holy Spirit, that is, procession. On the name *Trinity*. On the plurality of the predicates Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; and whether this proposition too is singular: “God is.” On the name *Creator* and similar names: whether they predicate essence, relation, or neither. On the visible mission of the Holy Spirit. On the invisible mission of the Son and the Holy Spirit. Whether every person who is sent is sent by the Trinity. On the two final categories of terms.

# BOOK I

[Col. 0791]

## CHAPTER ONE. That God exists and is one

[Col. 0791A]

[Note: [Col. 0791A] Master, I, distinction 3.] “The invisible things of God are clearly seen from the creation of the world, being understood through the things that have been made” (Rom. 1). Man is called “the creation of the world” because of the excellence which he possesses in relation to creatures, and the likeness which he possesses with them. Through creatures he came to know God’s invisible things, as Ambrose says. [Note: [Col. 0792A] In his commentary on the first chapter of Romans.]

> “So that God, who was invisible by nature, might be known from the visible, he made a work which, by its own visibility, might reveal its Maker; so that by a certain proof he might be known, and that one might believe him to be the God of all, who made such a work as it was impossible for any creature to make.”

Therefore, seeing this structure of the world so vast and spacious, man understood that there must be something other than a creature which made so beautiful and spacious a work; and thus, guided most excellently by reason, he grasped God with the greatest certainty.

The same is also proved by another argument. Whatever exists in the totality of mutable things is either substance or accident. We commonly take *accident* broadly for everything that is not substance. But an accident cannot exist through itself; therefore neither can it exist from itself—that is, without a subject, or from itself and from no one. If it cannot do what is lesser, namely exist through itself, neither can it do what is greater, namely exist from itself.

Nor can substance exist through itself. For although substance is elsewhere called a thing existing through itself—that is, not existing in a subject—nevertheless it does not exist so through itself that it does not require other things to exist, in order that it may itself be under accidents, to which it serves as a subject. For substance is so called either from standing under (*substando*) or from subsisting (*subsistendo*). Bodily substance cannot exist without place and colour, nor spiritual substance without some affection which is not itself.

Therefore, the mind must conceive some being which exists through itself and from itself, that is, from no one, from whom all these things exist. That being is God, and, because an infinite regress would be impossible, there must also be but one such being. For if there were another from which that being existed, the process would continue to infinity.

Further, the same point is proved by another argument. Everything contained within the whole realm of mutable things is either a whole, or a part, or a quasi-whole, or a quasi-part, or a property of a whole or of a part. It is called a quasi-whole because not every whole is of the same kind or genus. For there is an integral whole and a universal whole. An integral whole is any body constituted of parts; an integral part of a whole. Any spirit is a quasi-integral whole in relation to the part of any body; while the parts of a quasi-integral whole are the powers themselves—not the gratuitous powers, I mean, but the potential ones, that is, the power of understanding and remembering. All these things must derive from one source. For no whole exists of itself. For nothing is temporally prior to that which exists of itself [Col. 0793C]. Again, the composition of a whole from its parts is not from any whole; and, since no part is prior to its own whole, no other whole can be God. For in that case something else would be prior to God. Similarly, no part is God, for every whole is worthier than any one of its parts, whereas nothing is worthier than God. That the properties of a whole and of a part are neither from themselves nor prior to it is proved by the reasoning by which it was shown above concerning accidents. Therefore, since none of these things, as has been shown, can exist from itself, there must be something else from which all of them are; that is God, one and alone.

Again, since the human mind cannot be ignorant of itself, it knows that it at some time began, nor can it be ignorant of this [Col. 0793D]; because, when it did not exist, it could not give itself an essence in order to exist, and thus it has its existence from another. But it is not established that the first Being began; for if it were from another, it would not be the first author of the existence of all things. Indeed, if it were from another, since that other could not give itself the principle of existence unless it had existed from eternity, one must ascend to something higher, from which it received its essence and which existed from eternity; and this is God, the cause of all things. Otherwise one would have to hold that some creature existed from eternity—although none does exist from eternity, since no creature can be conceived which did not receive its beginning from another. Thus this necessarily follows.

## CHAPTER II. That God must exist

[Col. 0794A]

Again, although some fools have denied that God exists—hence the Psalmist: “The fool said in his heart, There is no God” (Ps. 13)—nevertheless no one dares deny that, if there is any thing which is God, that thing is such as cannot fail to be. Hence it follows: if anything is God, it cannot fail to be; therefore something is God. The reasoning of this argument seems to rest on this: for the truth of the hypothetical proposition, “If anything is God, it cannot fail to be,” requires that God cannot fail to be. The contrary position would follow if, granted that something is God and cannot fail to be, it could instead fail to be. But the former follows necessarily; therefore it is impossible that God can fail to be [Col. 0794B], and consequently he must exist.

Again, it is evident that, if anything is God, no good can exist without him. Therefore, if any good exists, God exists. But some good exists; therefore God exists. It is as though one said: if anything is a human soul, a human being cannot exist without it; therefore, if some human being exists, a soul exists. But a human being exists; therefore a soul exists. Thus the matter is proved in many ways.

Once this has been granted, it is also proved that there is only one God. For if there were two principles, either both would be deficient, or one would be superfluous. For if one lacked something possessed by the other, it would not be supremely perfect. But if neither lacked anything which the other had, and each possessed everything, one would be superfluous.

## CHAPTER III. A distinction of names said of God and of the nine classes

[Col. 0794C]

[Note: [Col. 0793D] *Master*, I, distinction 22.] With these matters set forth, one must know that, among the terms said of God, some apply from eternity and others in time. Yet one must not understand that certain terms apply to God from eternity because the terms themselves exist from eternity, but because the signification of each of them applies to God from eternity.

Of the terms which apply from eternity, some apply to one person, such as “God” and the like; others are said of the three persons, in such a way that they are said of none of them individually—being, as it were, collective—such as the name “Trinity.” Of those which apply from eternity and are said of one person, some are said according to essence, such as “one God”; others according to [Col. 0794D] relation, such as “Father” and “Son,” and the like. Of those predicated essentially [Note: [Col. 0794D] Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book II], some, such as “divinity” and “essence,” are always taken essentially; others, such as “wisdom,” “goodness,” “power,” and “God,” are sometimes taken personally. Of those said relatively, some are relative in utterance only, such as “similar” and “equal,” according to some; others are relative both in utterance and in signification, such as “Father” and “Son,” and the like.

Of those which apply to God in time, some are metaphorical, such as “lion,” “lamb,” and “worm”; others are not metaphorical. Of the latter, some are said with reference [to something], such as “Creator” and “Lord”; others absolutely, such as “incarnate” and “made man.” Further, of those said in time with reference to a creature, some apply to the three [Col. 0795A] persons, such as “Creator” and “Lord”; others apply to some but not all, such as “sent,” and the like.

From distinctions of terms such as these are gathered the nine classes of words said of God. There are words which signify essence and are always taken essentially, such as “essence,” “divinity,” and the like. There are certain words which signify existence, yet are sometimes taken personally, such as “power,” “wisdom,” and “goodness.” There are also words said relatively from eternity, both in utterance and in signification, such as “Father” and “Son.” There are likewise quasi-collective words which are said of several persons but of none of them individually, such as “Trinity.” There are words said with reference to creatures and applying to all persons, such as “Creator” and “Lord.” There are also words which are similarly said in time with reference to creatures but do not apply to all persons, such as “sent.” There are words which apply in time without any reference, such as “incarnate” and “made man.” In the final class are terms said of God metaphorically and by likeness, such as “lamb,” “lion,” “imprint,” and the like. Each of these must be discussed in the order in which it has been stated.

## CHAPTER IV. Whether the name “person” follows the rule governing things predicated only essentially

[Note: [Col. 0795D] *Master*, I, distinction 22.] First, then, concerning things said essentially: Augustine lays down this rule [Note: [Col. 0795D] Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book V, ch. 8, near the end]: “Whatever is said of God with reference to himself is said likewise of each person and jointly of the Trinity itself; it is said not in the plural but in the singular, and it is so.” Whatever is said of God according to essence is said of each person and, when said of them collectively, is said in the singular rather than the plural: thus the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God; and these three are one God, not three gods [Col. 0795C; Note: *Master*, I, distinction 23].

Yet the name “person” is excepted from this rule. Although it is said according to essence and of the individual persons, it is not taken in the singular when said of all collectively, but in the plural. That this name is said according to essence is attested by Augustine [Note: [Col. 0796D] *On the Trinity*, VII.6]: “For God, to be is not one thing, and to be a person another; rather, it is altogether the same.” Many other authorities tend in the same direction; it would not be difficult to bring them forward, were it not that [Col. 0795D] writing out writings would seem the work of one idle and doing nothing.

Many objections are raised against this. The same thing is signified by the name “person” and by the name “essence”; therefore the Father and Son are one person, or they are not one essence. Again, for God to be God and to be a person are the same; therefore either God is not God by essence, or God is God by person. This seems contrary to Hilary’s statement: “God is not God by person, but by nature.” Again, the Father is not distinguished from the Son by a personal property in that he is a person, and the Father is the same as the Son in that he is a person; therefore [Col. 0796A] the Father is the same as the Son—that is, a person. Again, the Father is what the Son is, both in being a person and in being essence; therefore either he is not the same as the Son in essence, or he is the same in person. Again, for the Father to be a person and for the Son to be a person are the same. Therefore, the Father’s person is the Son’s person, or the person which is the Father’s is the person which is the Son’s. Again, the Father is Father by a property; therefore he is a hypostasis by a property; therefore he is some person by a property; therefore he is a person by a property. Thus the name “person” is not said of God according to essence.

Again, the Father is another person by a property, and by that property he is distinguished from the others; therefore being some person belongs to the Father alone. Again, for God to be God and to be person are the same; therefore he is person by that by which [Col. 0796B] he is God. But he is person by fatherhood; therefore he is God by fatherhood. For it is evident that he is person by fatherhood, because the person which he himself is is person by fatherhood; therefore he is person by fatherhood.

No solution to the foregoing is easy unless the equivocation of the name “person” is determined. The name “person” sometimes signifies essence, as when one says, “The Father is person, the Son is person, the Holy Spirit is person.” Sometimes it signifies what *hypostasis* signifies among the Greeks, as when one says, “The Father is one person, the Son another person.” Sometimes it is used to designate a personal property, as when one says, “The Son is one in person, the Father another.” Again, “the Son is personally another.” Sometimes it signifies only what this expression “this person” signifies. It is taken in this sense in a certain statement of Hilary: “The Father is person by a property,” that is, “this person.”

Since it has so many significations, the particular one intended is determined by different adjuncts. When it is used by itself in the nominative case, it refers to essence, as when one says, “The Father is person,” or “The Son is person.” But when it is used in the ablative, it refers to property; as when it is said, “The Father is other than the Son in person,” that is, in personal property. When it is joined with the indefinite term “some” in designating one of the three persons, it is taken determinately: “The Father is some person,” that is, this person—namely, the person of the Father, or the person of the Son, or the person [Col. 0796D] of the Holy Spirit. But when it is joined to a discriminating term such as “other,” “different,” or the like, it signifies hypostasis: thus, “The Father’s person is other than the Son’s.”

Jerome shows that the name “person” has these many significations when he says [Note: [Col. 0796D] In the explanation of the Creed addressed to Damasus; attributed not to Jerome but to Pelagius]: “We confess not merely names, but the properties of names—that is, of persons—or, as the Greeks express it, hypostases, that is, substances.” Here we find two significations of this name expressly stated. We confirmed by Augustine’s authority that it signifies essence. That it is also used determinately in designating some person [Col. 0797A], especially when coupled with the indefinite term “some,” is found in Hilary in the authority mentioned above: “The Father is person by a property.” It is manifest from this that the impediment in the foregoing arguments is the fallacy of equivocation.

An analogous objection to the first argument is this: the same thing is signified by “knowing” and by “foreknowing”; therefore God could fail to be knowing, or could not fail to be foreknowing. To the second: for God to be just and to be merciful are the same; therefore either God does not punish by justice, or he punishes by mercy. For in the ablative the name signifies a plural property. To the third: Socrates does not differ from Plato in being knowing, and Socrates agrees with Plato in being knowing; therefore [Col. 0797B] Socrates agrees with Plato in knowledge—even on the supposition that Socrates knows little and Plato is extremely learned. Whether it is suitable, however, to say, “The Father is the same as the Son in person,” where “same” is neuter, will be discussed later.

An analogous objection to the fourth proceeds thus: Socrates agrees with Plato both in being knowing and in being white. Therefore either he does not agree with Plato in whiteness, or he agrees with him in knowledge—even if he is not equally knowing, but is equally white. To the fifth: for Socrates to be human and for Plato to be human are the same; therefore the human being who is Socrates is Plato, or Socrates is Plato. The sixth and seventh may be answered in this manner. To the seventh: the Father is Father or Son by some property, and by it he is distinguished from the other persons. Therefore being Father or Son [Col. 0797C] belongs to the Father alone. Yet, because it has not yet been decided whether the Father is this person by fatherhood, or whether a kind of concurrence of the three properties which are in the Father is required—namely fatherhood, unbegottenness, and spiration—by whose concurrence, and by none of the others, he is said to be this person, just as Socrates is Socrates by the concurrence of his properties although none of them is Socrates—we postpone the solution until the following discussion, where the properties of the persons will be treated.

The question to ask rather is whether each of the persons is some person. This does not seem so, because, when joined with “some,” the name “person” is used to designate one person determinately, as seems to have been said above. But it is not true [Col. 0797D] that each of the three persons is this person. Therefore some say that the term alone is predicated there, and that it signifies nothing in itself. Yet it seems truer that it is used there to designate hypostasis, so that it is posited not determinately of any one but indefinitely. Therefore no person is each of the three persons, but each is some person, just as no human being is each of human beings, but each human being is some human being.

Again, the same predicate is asserted when I say, “The Son is some person,” and “The Son is the Son”; therefore, by that whereby he is some person, the Son is Son. But by that whereby he is Son he differs from the Father, and in the same respect agrees with the Father. Therefore he agrees with him in that in which he differs [Col. 0798A] from him. Again, by that whereby the Son is some person he differs from the Father. By interpretation, therefore, the statement that the same thing is predicated in “The Son is some person” and “The Son is the Son” must be resolved, because what is predicated is not the same when “The Son is some person” is said. The analogous objection to the second argument is: by that whereby God made the world, he is God, because his power is God.

Again, Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0797D] *On the Trinity*, book VII, ch. 6]: “When we speak of the person of the Father, we say nothing other than the substance of the Father; therefore, just as the Father himself is the substance of the Father—not by that whereby he is Father, but by that whereby he is—so also the person of the Father is nothing other than the Father himself.” Therefore, since the substance of the Father and the person of the Father are the same, just as the Father’s substance is common to the three persons, so too the person [Col. 0798B] of the Father is common to the three persons. Again, when I say, “The Father is person,” I predicate nothing other than when I say, “The Father is substance”; therefore the circumlocution “person of the Father” signifies nothing other than “substance of the Father.” This is false.

To this one must say that Augustine intends to show nothing other than that these two names, “substance” and “person,” when said of the Father, signify the same thing. Yet when joined with the adjunct “of the Father,” the name “person” signifies the hypostasis which is the Father, not essence. So too the names “essence” and “God” signify the same thing; yet when one says, “God is the essence of the three persons,” one does not say, “God is the God of the three persons.” For many names are either incongruously used with adjuncts [Col. 0798C] or transferred to other significations.

Again, the Father is other than the Son in person; to be essence and to be person are the same for the Father. Therefore the Father either is or is not other than the Son in essence. If it is said that he is other than the Son in essence, then the Father’s essence is other than the Son’s. If it is said that the Father is not other than the Son in essence, and the Father is the same as the Son in essence, then the Father is the same as the Son; therefore the Father is he who is the Son; therefore the Father is the Son.

Again, the Father is not other than the Son in essence. To be person and to be essence are the same for the Father; therefore the Father either is or is not other than the Son in person. But if the Father is not other than the Son in person, and the Father is the same as the Son, then the Father is the same as the Son in person; therefore the Father is [Col. 0798D] the same person as the Son.

To this and similar arguments it must be said that “The Father is other than the Son in person,” or “The Father is other than the Son in essence,” is spoken less grammatically. For although person and essence are the same, certain adjectives belong to person which do not belong to essence. The neuter *aliud* (“other thing”) and *idem* (“same thing”) are adjectives of essence; the masculine *alius* (“other”) and *idem* (“same”) are adjectives of person. Hence, by mixing the adjectives, one speaks less grammatically. Thus, although “proposition” and “sentence” are the same, it is proper to say, “This proposition is categorical or hypothetical,” but improper to say, “This sentence is categorical or hypothetical.” Likewise, it is proper to say, “This sentence is complete” [Col. 0799A], but improper to say, “This proposition is complete or incomplete.”

Apply an analogous objection to the foregoing arguments in this way: proposition and sentence are the same; this proposition is categorical; therefore this sentence either is or is not categorical. Yet this seems contrary to what Jerome says on the passage in Isaiah, “I am the Lord; this is my name; my glory I will not give to another” (Isa. 42) [Note: [Col. 0799D] At the place cited above]: namely, that the Son and the Holy Spirit are not another from the Father in deity. They have the same glory. It must therefore be understood that the essence is said not to be another, although the person is said to be another.

[Note: [Col. 0799D] *Master*, I, distinction 23, §8, etc.] It is customary to ask what the name “person” signifies when used in the plural, as when one says, “The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three persons.” [Col. 0799B] For if it makes us understand essence, we seem to confess several essences, because we acknowledge several persons, and therefore several gods. They wish to show by Augustine’s authority that essence is signified there. Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0799D] *On the Trinity*, VII, ch. 4, about the middle]: “Because the Father is person, the Son is person, and the Spirit is person, we say three persons.” And elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0800D] Ibid., shortly before]: “Therefore we say three persons, because that which is person is common to them.” Since, therefore, this is said on account of that, it seems that the name “person,” said personally, retains the signification of essence, just as when it is said in the singular of each person; and that the same thing is attributed by it when it is uttered in the plural as when in the singular.

Again, Augustine says [Col. 0799C; Note: [Col. 0800D] *On the Trinity*, book VII, ch. 4]: “Out of necessity we say ‘persons,’ so that we may have an answer to the question used by heretics, who ask, ‘what three?’ or ‘what things three?’” But by the word “what” one asks about essence. Therefore the name “person” also signifies essence. Otherwise the answer would not suit the question.

Accordingly some say that in the expression just mentioned the name “person” does not signify essence, but hypostasis or subsistence. Thus the sense of the authorities just cited is: because the Father is person and the Son person—that is, essence—they are called three persons, that is, three subsistences or three beings. For they would not be called three beings unless each of them were person or essence; but because that which is person, that is essence, is common to them, they are rightly called three [Col. 0799D] persons, that is, subsistences or subsistent beings. Thus, just as the essence common to them truly and properly exists, so these three are understood to be truly and properly beings.

Nor, when the heretics ask, “What three?” or “What things three?” does the word “what” signify essence. Rather, the sense is: “By what plural term are those three signified?” Thus the inquiry is more about the meaning of the word by which they may be designated than about essence—just as when one asks, “What is *anthrōpos* [human being]?” But these interpreters seem to struggle in explaining Augustine’s authorities quoted above. For how are they three persons, that is, three beings, because what is person, that is essence, is common to them? For if what is person, that is essence, were not common to them, they would not be called three beings; and thus, if they were three beings, they would not be called three beings.

Others wish to solve the matter differently, and quite reasonably, by saying that the name “person” signifies essence even when it is said in the plural: “The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three persons.” The sense is: because the Father is person, the Son person, and the Holy Spirit person, they are called three persons—that is, they are three who have in common what is person, namely essence. But by the same reasoning one could say, “They are three gods,” that is, they have in common that which is God [Col. 0800B]; and the same would hold for all substantial terms. But this is not so, because it contradicts Scripture, where it is said: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God” [Note: [Col. 0800D] Augustine, at the place cited above; *Master*, ibid., final §] (Deut. 6).

Although the name “thing” (*res*) might likewise be applied to him, one would not say, “They are three things,” because *res* is used both essentially and personally, though it is rarely used personally. Nor would saying “three things” settle anything, since the question would remain, “Which three things?” Although perhaps other terms might be found to resolve that question, none more fitting or more appropriate could be introduced than “person,” which, according to the etymology of the word, indicates not only the distinction of persons but also the identity of essence more fully when used in the plural. For *persona* is so called as though it meant *per se una*, “one through itself.”

Therefore, when it is said, “The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three persons,” it is the same as saying, “They are one and they are through themselves”—that is, they are one and distinct: “one” denotes unity of essence, while “through themselves” denotes distinction. Thus one commonly says, “This is one through itself,” that is, distinct from others.

But someone may say: if plurality is admitted because of the signification, why is singularity not admitted because of the principal signification? Thus, when it is said, “The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are persons,” that is, are one and distinct, why is it not said in the same sense, “They are person,” that is, they are one and distinct? Indeed, this seems more proper, since the principal signification—the unity of essence—ought more strongly to prevail over the co-signification of the word than the secondary signification should prevail over the principal in giving the right solution to this question. “For the Hebrews to be enriched, the Egyptians must be despoiled.”

Why do distributive terms lack vocatives? Because the vocative refers determinately to one particular person, whereas distribution has no place in one but in several. Hence, because the property of distribution conflicts with the signification of vocatives, distributives lack vocatives, as do “each of two” and “each.” Likewise, if this name is uttered in the singular and one says, “The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are person,” then, because the name is uttered in the singular [Col. 0801A], it belongs to one thing. But the distinction suggested by the implicit qualification *per se* has no place in one thing, but in several things to be distinguished. Therefore either the statement, “The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are person,” is false, or it is incongruous—which seems more likely if the foregoing is considered carefully.

For two things, it seems, prevent this expression from being fitting. First, because the name “person” is uttered in the singular and without an adjunct, it tends to refer to essence. Secondly, because a plural verb precedes three nominatives, the distinction implicit in that name seems to be suggested; but there is no distinction concerning one essence. Hence it seems incongruous, just as it would be to say, “O each-of-two friend of men.” Or, if it is spoken fittingly, it is spoken falsely.

But when it is said in the plural, “They are persons,” distinction among three beings is suggested, while unity of essence is signified by that term as though in the singular. Thus it is plural as regards co-signification, but singular as regards its principal signification. If someone argues, “They are three persons, and to be person and to be essence are the same; therefore they are three essences”—especially since, as stated above, it signifies essence there—the answer concerning “human being” and “sentence” has already been given: equivocation prevents the conclusion.

Again, since a person is an individual subsistence of a rational nature, the Father and Son are two persons; and since the definition converts with the thing defined, Boethius is charged with having offered that definition more as a philosopher than as a theologian [Col. 0801C].

## CHAPTER V. Whether verbs said of God fall under the aforesaid rule governing terms predicated only essentially

Verbs said of God which signify essence seem likewise to be excepted from the rule just stated. For although they are said of the individual persons, when said of them collectively they are taken not in the singular but in the plural. One does not say, “The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is,” but “are.” To this it must be said that, if the analogy of correct speech allowed one to say, “The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is,” it would be truer than saying “are.” For truth would underlie this expression if grammatical propriety were present. Augustine at one time thought that it ought to be said, “The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is,” but later retracted this [Note: [Col. 0801D] He retracts something similar in *Retractions*, book I, ch. 4].

For the expression must be uniform in subject and predicate, lest a horse’s neck be joined to a human head. Once the construction begins in such a way that the persons are treated as a plurality in the subject, the predicate must follow by attributing its signification to the things as plural; this cannot be done except by a word in the plural. Hence “are” is said.

But an objection is made: the verb “are,” when used properly and in the plural number, signifies essence; therefore it determines plurality with respect to essence; therefore several essences are attributed there to the Father, Son, and [Col. 0802A] Holy Spirit, and the expression signifies only what is true. Therefore the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are several essences.

The solution of the objection depends upon grammar. Verbs are called to be of a certain number for one reason, and nouns, pronouns, or participles for another. A noun, pronoun, or participle is said to be of a certain number because it signifies a thing under the property of a certain number—that is, as one or as several. But verbs are said to be of a certain number because they attribute their significates to things signified under the property of a certain number. The verb *curro* (“I run”) is not said to be singular because it signifies running under the property of the singular, but because it attributes running to a thing insofar as it is to be signified as one.

Therefore, when it is said, “The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are” (1 John 5), the verb “are” does not determine plurality concerning essence, just as other verbs do not do so concerning their significates. For then, since the statement is true, several essences would necessarily be attributed. Rather, it attributes essence to the persons insofar as they are signified as several; and it cannot do this except in a plural verbal form. Thus it is plural in utterance but singular in signification, because it couples not essences but essence—just as when one says, “Thebes are,” the verb “are” is plural in utterance but singular in signification [Col. 0802B].

Nor is it surprising if a plural verb follows expressions applying to three persons who are in one essence, since some accept the expression, “Marcus and Tullius are,” when the names refer to the same man, taking account of the words rather than the things. If “Marcus and Tullius are” is said in the plural merely because of plurality of names, and essences are not thereby coupled but essence, then much more, because of the distinction of persons—among whom enumeration is also fitting—the following verb is placed in the plural, though it attributes essence, not essences, in the singular.

But someone presses the point again, saying: “The Father and Son live; therefore they are living; therefore they are alive, and so they are just.” By the same reasoning, the Father and Son are omnipotent and are several omnipotent beings, even two omnipotent beings; but this is contrary to our faith. For Athanasius says: “Not three omnipotent beings, but one Almighty.” To this it must be said that [Col. 0802D] “The Father and Son are just” is not said truly; and there is a reason why. Two things make a term signifying essence be said in the plural, rather than singularly, of the three persons collectively: an implicit distinction, as has been shown in the name “person,” and the nature of the expression itself, which requires the predicate to conform to the subject for grammatical propriety and agreement of accidents. Therefore verbs following nominatives coupled by construction cannot be supplied except in the plural, as when one says, “The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are.”

Neither of these can be found in the name “just,” “powerful,” or any other [term], except in the name “person” [Col. 0803A]. For the nature of the expression does not require a noun in the plural in order to complete its grammatical propriety, since the supposition constituted by nominatives personally joined already has from the verb what it required, namely conformity in number. Hence it expects nothing further from any other word. Indeed, even if every verb were absent, the word “just,” or any other noun, pronoun, or participle, could not supply the place of a verb here so as to give the subject conformity of accidents and complete the expression; for without any other word a sentence is complete, but without a verb materially supplied no sentence is complete. Moreover, it belongs to the verb to predicate in an expression, since it is the sign of things said of another.

Nor is there found in any other word such an implicit distinction as is found in the name “person,” by the implication of which a noun uttered in the plural can designate essence in the singular. Since neither of the foregoing conditions is found in any essential term except verbs and the name “person,” none of these terms, uttered in the plural, designates essence in the singular; rather, it co-signifies plurality regarding essence. Hence one must not say: “The Father and Son are good, just, wise,” or anything else essential that one might add [Col. 0803B].

But someone will say: therefore, by the same reasoning, “The Father and Son are living” or “are able to do all things” must not be accepted, because neither condition is found in the participle; and, when said of God, this participle signifies not an act but essence, because a word which, when said of a creature, signifies an act, when said of God signifies essence. Hence, when I say, “The Father and Son are living,” I seem to add several essences, just as when I say, “They are alive.”

This is answered in two ways. Some say that a participle so placed signifies an act in the plural, not an act which is in God but one which is in creatures; and thus it proves nothing by plural inference. But it seems truer that it signifies essence, and that the expression consisting of a subject verb and a participle is used in place of one verb which, when said of God, predicates essence. Hence “The Father and Son are living” is accepted, that is, “they live”; but “they are alive” is not accepted in the same way, because a noun cannot be used with a verb in place of a verb as a participle can.

But he will press the point again, because in some places a participle [Col. 0803D] is used in the plural where it cannot be said to be placed with the substantive verb in place of a single verb. Thus it seems then to signify the essence plurally; for example, if I say: “The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are three beings.” For there the participle with the verb is indeed placed in place of a verb, while the expression *three* is used substantively. It is otherwise if I say, “they are three beings,” where the copula is the verb *are*, and the phrase *three beings* is used. Why then is it not similarly said, “they are three just ones,” or “three omnipotent ones”?

To this we say that there the name *three* is indeed used substantively, and the participle is predicated adjectivally and referred to the hypostases. But if it is said, “they are three omnipotent ones,” [Col. 0804A] the numeral *three* is used adjectivally, and the name *omnipotent* substantively. Therefore the logic of the expression does not allow the name *three* to be used substantively and the name *omnipotent* adjectivally. It would be true if it were thus said: “they are three omnipotent ones.”

Accordingly, against this argument, framed as follows: “The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are three living ones, and are three, each of whom is living; therefore they are three living beings,” one must press an analogous equivocation: “Socrates, Plato, and Cicero are three serving some man, and are three, each of whom is a servant of some man; therefore they are three servants of some master or man.” Again: “The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are three who can do all things; the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are three, each of whom is omnipotent; [Col. 0804B] therefore they are three omnipotent beings”—false. “Socrates, Plato, and Cicero are three making someone pontiff of one city, and are three, each of whom is pontiff of one city; therefore they are three pontiffs.”

Nor should it seem ridiculous to you to repel such quibbles—where they occur, where the more simply one proceeds, the more confidently one proceeds—by similar quibbles. For thus art is deceived by art; thus, as Isaiah III says, the crown of the daughters of Zion, who walk with neck outstretched, is made bald [Note: [Col. 0803D] “The Lord has made bald the crown of the daughters of Zion”]; thus the squared stones in the building of Samaria are thrown down (Micah I); thus, when enemies rise in an iron tumult, Rezin and his leaders are put to flight (Isaiah IX).

Again: “The Father and the Son are better than the angels; therefore they are good, or neither is good, or they are not good in that way; [Col. 0804C] therefore they are not better than the angels; therefore they do not surpass the angels in goodness”—which is plainly false. An easy counter-instance to this amplification is as follows: “The Pontic Sea is not sweet; therefore it is not sweeter than other seas”; or: “These pearls are not large; therefore they are not larger than these little stones”; or: “Ten thousand are not few; therefore they are not fewer than twenty thousand.”

It should nevertheless be noted, according to what has been said above: “The Father and the Son are better than the angels”; again, “The Father and the Son are equally powerful,” or “are coeternal; therefore they are eternal.” This is the fallacy: “These are fellow-brothers; therefore they are brothers.” Or: “This man is that man’s co-father; therefore he is that man’s father.” But, they say, the inference does not follow, because relation, not essence, is signified [Col. 0804D] by the terms *equally powerful* and *coeternal*. Therefore a name signifying essence—namely, *eternal* or *powerful*—cannot be inferred from them.

Nor should it be understood that these terms signify relation, but rather a certain comparison of the persons with one another. Yet if anyone looks more deeply, they seem rather to remove than to posit: “They are coeternal,” that is, neither is prior to the other. Again: “There is one single power by which Father and Son can do all things; therefore they are not more powerful, but are able to do all things.” A fallacy. “There is one essence of the three persons who are; therefore they are not three beings.” Or thus: “There is only one notion by which Father and Son breathe forth the Holy Spirit; [Col. 0805A] therefore they are not two persons breathing forth the Holy Spirit.”

There are, however, some who say: when these names are used thus—“The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are just,” or “powerful”—and are taken adjectivally, they are referred by their adjunct to the hypostases, not to the essence. But if a numeral is added, then, because they are used substantively, they are referred to the essence. Hence they accept the foregoing expressions: “The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are just; are powerful; are wise; are good”; yet they are not therefore gods, because that word cannot be taken except substantively.

## CHAPTER VI. Whether such names as *Someone*, *One*, and *Unbegotten*, when taken in the masculine, fall under the same rule

From the foregoing rule this name *someone* seems again to be excepted [Col. 0805B], because, although it seems to be said of God according to essence, it is nevertheless not said of the three persons collectively in the singular, but in the plural. For Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not “some persons.” For the Father is not he who is the Son, but that which the Son is. For masculine forms refer to person, neuter forms to essence.

Yet that Father and Son are “someone” seems capable of being shown thus: “Father and Son are one omnipotent being,” that is, to both Father and Son [understand: it belongs] to be omnipotent and to be one; therefore Father and Son are one, or they are not omnipotent. Again, ecclesiastical authority approves what is said in the hymn:

> Now, Holy Spirit,
>
> One with the Father and the Son for us.

[Col. 0805C] Therefore the Holy Spirit is one with the Father and the Son; therefore he is one with the Son on the same reasoning, and the Father is one with the Son; therefore Father and Son are one.

Again, the name *one*, said of God, either denotes essence or a relation that is not essence. Since then it is truly said, “Father and Son are one,” it denotes relation; and this name is said properly of the Father; therefore it posits a relation in him; therefore by it the Father is distinguished from the Son and the Holy Spirit; therefore the Father alone is one. Otherwise, indirectly: Father and Son are not one, and each is one; therefore Father and Son are two. Hence in the divine essence the Father is one thing and the Son another.

Again, if masculine forms [Col. 0805D] always refer to person and neuter forms to essence, it seems that one must not say, “The Son is from someone,” because he is not from the essence, since the essence does not beget. Hence it seems one must say, “The Son is from nothing.” Indeed, in whatever sense it is understood, there is the common expression: “The Father is God by one thing and Father by another.” For the first *by another* seems to refer to essence and to be put in the neuter gender; the second seems to refer to property and ought to be put in the masculine gender. Yet, since paternity is neither another masculine thing, nor another feminine thing, nor another neuter thing than God, it does not seem proper to say, “The Father is God by one thing and Father by another”; and thus the Father is Father in the same respect in which he is God.

Thus the Father is Father [Col. 0806A] or God by the same property or the same essence; but no one says that the Father is Father by a property and that that same property is God. Yet, conversely, since by paternity he is Father and not God, and by divinity he is God and not Father, he is Father by one thing and God by another. It seems that one must say: “He is Father by one thing and God by another.” Indeed, if anyone considers the matter more attentively, this seems improperly said. For the first *by another* is used for the hypostasis of the Father; the second is used for the essence. Therefore, if anyone substituted for the appellative the being of those things for which the repeated noun is used, the expression would be faulty; as if one said, “The Father is Father by one property and God by another.”

If, therefore, anyone accepts: “Father and Son are one; therefore they are not some persons; truly they are not two; therefore Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not three.” Indeed, if they are one, the Father is he who is the Son; [Col. 0806B] therefore he is the same person as the Son. It is manifest to all that one must not accept this: “Father and Son are one; they are someone.”

To resolve the foregoing points, some say that this name *someone*, said of God, signifies essence. “Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are some persons,” yet are not substances or essences. It was said above that this is permitted because of the poverty of Latin expression, in answer to the question posed by heretics, “Three who?” or “What three?”—lest no answer be given, and so that the answer might be “three persons,” though not therefore “three substances.” And a reason was indeed given why the name *person* [Note: [Col. 0805] Perhaps: “rather than another name,” or “with an understood or implicit qualification.”] is more suitably used than some other name in answer to such a question: because it contains in itself [Col. 0806C] an implicit distinction of this kind. This reason does not apply to the name *someone*, which likewise is said in the plural of the three persons. For, when used in the plural, it contains no implicit distinction such that it signifies the essence in the singular. Thus some reason must be assigned which applies to the name *person* together with the name *someone*—indeed, to all names which are said plurally of the three persons.

For understanding this matter, one must know that the name *substance* also involves an equivocation among the Latins, which is expressed among the Greeks by two terms, namely *hypostasis* and *ousia*. Yet among us it is partly explained by the origin of the word: for *substance* is said from “standing under” (*substando*), that is, [Col. 0806D] *substance* from “subsisting” (*subsistendo*).

“Substance” from “standing under” is the subject itself which underlies forms, whether it is a body or some other thing. “Substance” from “subsisting” is a form which, coming upon a subject, causes it to subsist—that is, to stand under itself and other forms, or makes it stand under itself and other things. Thus the impression of a seal causes wax, which is in a certain rough and fluid condition and is capable of receiving every form, through its imprint to stand firm, so that for the time being it cannot pass into another form.

But substantial form is twofold: either that which makes a “who,” and such is every individual property—that is, a property of an individual and denoted by a proper name—such as Platonity, by participation in which Plato is a “who”; or that which makes a “what,” whether specific or general—that is, [Col. 0807A] denoted by a specific or general name—such as humanity or animality, by participation in which Plato is a “what,” but not a “who.” Hence proper names answer the question “who?”, and specific and general names the question “what?”

For the property that makes a “who” is called personal or individual property, or, more properly in Latin, quality; in Greek, however, *hypostasis*. In Latin it can be called *substance* from “subsisting”; and likewise its subject, insofar as it is understood to participate in it, may be called a hypostasis. But the property that makes a “what” is called in Greek *ousia*, and in Latin *substance*; likewise, the thing subject to it, insofar as it participates through it, can be called *ousia*.

Therefore, if someone wishes to proceed by reduplication, that is, to express the force of the expression, he will say: “Plato is a hypostasis and is not an *ousia*,” because [Col. 0807B] Plato is a hypostasis not insofar as he is an *ousia*. Likewise, “A human being is *ousia* and not hypostasis,” because a human being is *ousia* insofar as he is human, not hypostasis insofar as he is human.

Now the name *person* is an appellative for things insofar as they participate in individual properties which make each a “who,” not a “what.” For a thing is a person insofar as it is Plato, not insofar as it is human. Likewise this name *someone*, and every name in the masculine gender which is said of God, if it is adjectival. Therefore the name *person* signifies substance, not *ousia* but hypostasis; likewise the name *someone* and the name *just*. Hence they accept: “Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are some persons, are persons, [Col. 0807C] are just”; likewise, “Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is someone, is just,” but they are not some determinate property signified by the name *person*.

And they press the foregoing arguments as follows. Against the first: “For both Father and Son, to be a person and to be a substance are the same; Father and Son are a substance which is person; therefore either they are not substance or they are person.” To the second objection they say that in the hymn one ought to say:

> Now, Holy Spirit,
>
> One thing with the Father and the Son;

or they say that this was spoken against Arius, who counted degrees in the Trinity, saying that the Father was great and the Son lesser, or that the Holy Spirit [Col. 0807D] was not the same as the Father. Others emend it by saying, “one of the Father with the Son,” that is, “one of Father and Son,” so that the preposition is put for a copulative conjunction. The solution to the third objection is clear on their view. Against the fourth they press: “Socrates is other than Plato in one face; therefore in face he is other than Plato”; or thus, “Socrates and Plato are of one face.” For just as this is said improperly, so too is this: “The Father is other than the Son in essence,” as was said above.

Others distinguish substance differently, saying that three things are signified by the name *substance*: hypostasis, [Col. 0808A] *ousia*, and *ousiosis*. They call hypostasis a thing insofar as it participates in an individual property. They call *ousiosis* every substantial form; but *ousia*, a thing insofar as it participates in a general or specific status, that is, a property making a “what.”

We, however, abandoning such ambiguities, say that nothing is posited by the name *someone* or *one* when it is said of God, just as neither is anything posited by other numeral names, as will be said below. Rather, one should inquire whether the word *something*, when used in the neuter, always belongs to essence, or sometimes to property. To this it must be said that it signifies essence. Hence one must not say, “The Son is from something,” because he is not from the essence; yet one must not therefore say, “The Son is from nothing,” because the negation removes more [Col. 0808B] than the affirmation posits. For it removes the essence together with the person. Nevertheless, it is true that the Son is not from something. Nor has it yet been fully investigated whether essence is from essence. For someone says that these names are sometimes taken personally, as will be explained in what follows.

But the final question—whether the Father is Father by one thing and God by another—we shall defer until the following discussion, where we shall deal with the properties of the persons.

## CHAPTER VII. On compound terms consisting of one word signifying substance and another signifying a notion, such as “able to beget”

[Note: [Col. 0807D] Master I, distinction 27, § 6.] There is another predicate believed of God [Col. 0808C] according to essence. It does not observe the rule of the categories, because not only is it not said collectively and in the singular of the three persons, but it does not even seem to be said of each person. For Augustine lays down this rule [Note: [Col. 0807D] Book VI, *On the Trinity*, chapter 2.]: “Of those things which are said of themselves, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not said one without another.” Such is the expression “able to beget” (*potens generare*).

That it is said according to essence seems evident from the name *able*, which, said of God, signifies essence; for God’s power and essence are the same. Yet, from the addition of the word *to beget*, it seems to vary its meaning. Therefore to be God and to be able to beget seem the same for the Father; thus, to be God and to be able to do something are the same for him. Yet it is not said of the Son that he can beget [Col. 0808D] a Son; for if this were so, the Son could be father of someone—therefore either of himself, or of the Father, or of the Holy Spirit, or of someone else. He could not be father of someone else, because no one else could have existed from eternity. Nor could he be father of the Father, because then the same person would be both Father and Son of the same person; nor of the Holy Spirit, nor of himself, because no thing begets itself. Indeed, if the Son could beget, and that Son another Son, since there is no greater reason in one case than in the others, the argument could be carried on even to infinity.

[Note: [Col. 0808D] Master I, distinction 7, § b.] Nevertheless, that the Son can beget is shown both by authority and by reason. Augustine says [Col. 0809A] [Note: [Col. 0809D] Augustine, book III, *Against Maximinus*, chapter 12, at the end]: “Far be it that the Father is more powerful than the Son because the Creator begot the Son, whereas the Son did not beget the Creator—not because he could not, but because it was not fitting.” Therefore the Son [14] could have begotten the Creator.

This is resolved thus: “Not because he could not,” that is, it was not owing to an impotence in the Son that the Son did not beget, but it did not belong to him; so the Son God is not Father God, yet this is not owing to the Son’s impotence. Or it may be understood only thus: “not because he could not, but because it was not fitting,” that is, not merely could he not, but it was also not fitting.

Many arguments are also brought forward to show this. “The Father has the power of begetting; the Son does not have the power of begetting; therefore the Father has a power which the Son does not have.” Thus indirectly; or directly: [Col. 0809B] “The Father has the power of begetting; the Son has the same; therefore the Son has the power of begetting.” Therefore the ancients resolved it by interpreting the statement, “The Father has the power of begetting, and the Son has the same.” For the term *power of begetting* denotes a notion, that is, paternity. For to say, “The Father has the power to beget,” is the same as saying, “The Father has generative paternity”; but the Son does not have the same, namely paternity.

Yet they seem to resolve the knot more conveniently thus: when it is said, “The Father is able to beget,” it is the same as if it were said, “The Father is able and is a begetter.” Thus two things are said of the Father: that he has power, and that he has generation—or rather, that he has it for begetting, that is, so that he begets. [Col. 0809C] But when it is added, “The Son has the same,” the pronoun, just as it does not refer to the gerund but to the action, so it refers only to the power, not to the property. The same power is in the Son, but not for begetting, that is, not so that he begets. For the gerund signifies both, namely action and passion.

But if someone asks why “the power of begetting is in the Father” is more readily granted because of the active meaning of the gerundive, while “the power of begetting is in the Son” is not granted in the sense that the gerundive signifies passion, this must be attributed to usage rather than reason. Therefore, when the whole term is resumed in place of the pronoun—which does not refer where active meanings are signified—and it is said, “The Son has the power of begetting,” it is false. Just as if it were said, “Socrates will see a white man, and [Col. 0809D] Plato will see him”: assuming that Plato will not see him while he is white, it is not permissible to resume, “Plato will see a white man,” because the pronoun did not refer to the meaning of the whole term but only to that of the subject noun, which can necessarily be resumed.

Hence you may press all such cases as follows: “This man’s son wishes to take a wife, and his father wishes the same; therefore the father wishes to take a wife.” Or: “Abraham had faith in the one who was to come, and you have the same; therefore you have faith in the one who was to come.” Or thus: “Peter had the power of sinning, and has the same; therefore Peter has the power of sinning.”

Again: [Col. 0810A] “The Father can beget; the Son cannot beget; therefore the Father can do something which the Son cannot do.” Or: “Whatever the Father can do, the Son can do; the Father can beget; therefore the Son can beget.” To this it must be said that to be able to beget a Son is not to be able to do something, because it is not something subject to divine power. For the generation of the Son is not an action among those subject to divine power, because it is not among creatures but is above all things. For he did not first have the power to beget and then beget.

Hence you may press thus: “The Father can be Father; the Son cannot be Father; therefore the Father cannot be something which the Son cannot be”—this is not true, because to be Father is not to be some thing. Or: “This man’s son wishes to take a wife, and the father does not wish to take a wife; [Col. 0810B] the father wishes something which the son does not wish.”

Another argument: “The power of begetting is in the Father; by it the Father can do something, because he can beget. Therefore that power can beget. Does the Son have the same power or not? If the same, then the Son can beget; if not the same, then the Father can do something which the Son cannot.” [Note: [Col. 0809D] The same argument is found in Pullus and Robert of Melun, as we have shown in our notes on Pullus (*Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXVI, [Col. 0810D]).]

To this it is said that “The Father can beget, and the Son has the same power or does not,” is not elegantly said, because to be able to beget is not to be able to do something—that is, it is not something subject to divine power. Therefore a relation extending to infinity is made improperly, just as if one said, “The Father is Father, and the Son is the same or not the same,” where the neuter gender is improperly used.

Again: “The power of begetting is in the Father, and the same is in [Col. 0810C] the Son; therefore the power of begetting is in the Father and the Son.” And it seems that no counter-instance can be drawn from accidental predicates; for if some pronoun refers to an action, then, once the pronoun is removed, the same truth of the statement remains when the two verbs are conjoined, if they can properly be conjoined [Note: [Col. 0810D] Master, same distinction, § 6 f and g.], as in, “He runs and the same man disputes; therefore Socrates runs and disputes.”

If it is granted, therefore, that the power of begetting is in Father and Son, then by the same reasoning the power of begetting is in Son and Father, and thus the power of begetting is in the Son. Therefore some think this statement true: “The power of begetting is in the Son,” because this expression does not indicate what is in relation to what in the Son, but only what is in the Son. Yet, in a qualified sense, it is denied that “the power of begetting is the power of begetting in the Son.”

If someone infers, “The power of begetting [Col. 0810D] is in the Son; therefore the Son can beget,” it is a fallacy. “Virginity will be in this person; therefore this person will be a virgin.” Or: “The power of sinning will be in this person, because he will now be confirmed; therefore he will be able to sin.” Or: “The ability to walk is in this person; therefore, though he lacks feet, he can walk.” For in all these cases it is not shown what is in relation to what in someone, but only what is there. Yet the former solution seems more common and more true.

Again: “The power of begetting which is in the Father is in the Son, and the power of begetting which is in the Son is in the Father; therefore the power of begetting is not in the Father or in the Son.” This is resolved by an interpretation [Col. 0811A] of one of the premises. Yet one may press thus: “The white man whom Socrates will see will be seen by Plato, and conversely; therefore either Socrates will not see a white man, or Plato will see a white man.” Just as: “The power of begetting is in Father or Son; the power of begetting is not in Father and Son”—a fallacy in the premises. “Socrates or Plato will see a white man; Socrates and Plato will not see a white man; therefore whatever Socrates sees, Plato will see.” Or one may draw the counter-instance from taking a wife.

Again: “The power of begetting or being born is in the Father; there is no power of begetting which is not a power of being born, and conversely; therefore the power of being born is in the Father, or the power of begetting is not in him”—a fallacy in the premises. “This man wishes to take a wife, and that man wishes nothing; [Col. 0811B] this man wishes what the other does not; therefore this man wishes to take a wife, or the other does not.”

Again: “This power of begetting is in the Son; therefore the power of begetting is in the Son.” This is resolved because of the interpretation.

For it has not yet been fully investigated whether a demonstrative reference can suitably be made to the divine essence, so that it may be said, “This power is essence.” Again: “Power is the power of Father and Son; therefore it is the power of the Son; therefore the power of begetting is in the Son”—a fallacy in the last inference. “The power of sinning will be this man’s power, because he will now be confirmed; therefore the power of sinning will be in this man.”

Again: “Some power is in the Son; therefore either the power of begetting or another power.” But it is proved that there is no other: “No power of begetting is in the Son which is not a power of begetting; therefore there is no power in the Son other than the power [Col. 0811C] of begetting; nor is there any power in the Son which is not the power of begetting”—a fallacy in the first argument. “The Father is Father by something; therefore by essence or by something else.” Or: “The Father is God by something; therefore by paternity or by something else.”

Again: “The Father can beget by the power of begetting; therefore it is possible for the Father to beget by power; therefore ‘possible’ can be posited. Let that be posited; therefore the Father begets by the power of begetting. But the power of begetting and God’s essence are the same; therefore the Father begets the Son by his essence”—a fallacy in the first inference. “Socrates can run by his power; therefore it is possible for Socrates to run by his power.”

And note that, since these are two words, “The Father can beget,” each may receive an ablative determination [Col. 0811D]. But the word *can*, because it is essential, receives an ablative essentially, which does not designate by relation. Conversely, because the word *beget* marks a notion, it receives an ablative of relation, not of essence. Hence it is suitably said: “The Father can, by his power, beget by generation.” But there is no interchange, as when it is said, “Socrates wills by his will to run with his feet,” or “Socrates exists today, about to die tomorrow.”

Again: “The power of begetting is in something; that thing is God; therefore something which is God can beget.” If he says that the power of begetting is in nothing, then: “The power of begetting is not anything able, and yet the Father is able by the power of begetting; therefore it is God [Col. 0812A]; therefore it is something.” Indeed, if this is said of God according to essence, then each person is something able to beget, and the three persons are one thing able to beget, as the rule stated above has already taught; and the divine essence can beget.

But if we remember the foregoing, the term *able to beget* marks not only essence but also relation. Hence, because of the relation, which is not said of the essence, one must not say, “The Father is something able to beget,” but “someone able to beget.” That power, however, is something able, because it is God and the divine essence; that power can do whatever God can do, yet not therefore beget, because this is not to be able to do something, as stated above.

Again: “To beget is one thing, to be begotten another; therefore to be able to beget is one thing, and to be able to be begotten another”—a fallacy. [Col. 0812B] “Good is one thing and evil another; therefore knowledge of good is different from knowledge of evil”—not so, because the same discipline concerns contraries. And note that the conclusion is false because its sense is: “The power by which the Father is able to beget is other than that by which the Son can be begotten,” which was denied above.

## CHAPTER VIII. The question why God is called omnipotent, and matters connected with this question
