[Note: [Col. 0811D] Master I, distinction 42.] It is commonly asked why God is called omnipotent: whether because he can do all things, or because he can do all that he wills. [Note: [Col. 0811D] In the Master, same place, § 1.] Augustine says that God can do all things: “God can do all things, but does only what accords with his will and justice.” Yet, since God cannot sin, cannot be deceived, and cannot become miserable [Col. 0812C], he does not seem omnipotent.

To this it must be said that to be able to do these things is not to be able to do some thing; indeed, it is natural impotence, not natural power. And if God could do these things, he would not then be called omnipotent, because there is no power by which we easily do something and suffer nothing easily, and do nothing easily. Hence to be able to sin is not a matter of natural power but of natural impotence, as Augustine teaches [Note: [Col. 0812D] See Augustine, book XV, *On the Trinity*, chapter 15]: “It is a great power of God not to be able to sin; nor should he therefore be thought less powerful because he cannot sin, since he is in no way omnipotent who cannot do this.”

Again, God cannot walk, eat, and the like; to be able to walk is to be able to do something; therefore there is something God cannot do.

[Col. 0812D] Again, it should be noted that all these things are subject to divine power, because the fact that someone walks, speaks, and the like is effected by God’s power as author. Yet God, in his own essence, cannot perform such actions, because he does not have the instruments by which, in his essence, he might exercise such actions. But when it is said, “God cannot walk, drink, or speak,” nothing is removed from God’s power [Note: [Col. 0812D] Master, same place, § b.], but only a mode pertaining to the defect and weakness of human beings, or of those to whom this belongs. For although he does not do this in himself, he does it in others; just as when it is said, “God is not in this man’s hood or purse.” It is not therefore less true that God is essentially in every place, [Col. 0813A] because only a mode of being there is removed—namely, that he is not enclosed in a place as a creature is.

They therefore say that God is called omnipotent not because he can do all things, but because he can do whatever he wills, as Augustine teaches [Note: [Col. 0813D] In the Master, same place, § f; and *Enchiridion*, 96]: “God is called omnipotent not because he can do all things, but because he can bring about whatever he wills, so that no one can resist his will, which he himself is.” To make this clearer, note that two things are considered in God’s power [17]: one is that he can do whatever he wills; the other, that he suffers absolutely nothing [Note: [Col. 0813D] This same teaching of the Master, § e.]. From these two a third follows: namely, that he can do those things which it is power to be able to do.

But the things which it is power to be able to do are those by which God’s majesty is not injured—this is said with reference to sins—nor his excellence [Col. 0813B] diminished—this is said with reference to defects. God is therefore called omnipotent because he can do all things which it belongs to power to be able to do. But for God in his essence to be able to speak, eat, and the like is not a matter of power, because God would seem to have defects if he required such acts and possessed the instruments by which to exercise them; in that respect his excellence would be diminished.

Therefore in the aforementioned authority of Augustine [Note: [Col. 0813D] The same Master, § 6.], the word *all* is taken so broadly that it includes defects and sins, where it is said that God can do whatever he wills, though he can also do what he does not will. But this was added because there were heretics who said that God wills something which he cannot do; or in order to show that God does nothing which he does not [Col. 0813C] will when he does it; or in order to establish a distinction between God’s will and human wills, since human beings will more things than they can do. God, however, can do more than he wills, and is not called omnipotent because he can do all things which he wills himself to do, or himself to be able to do, or himself to will. For on the same ground Peter would be called omnipotent, because he can do all things which he wills himself to do, or to be able to do, or to will; otherwise he would not be blessed. Rather, God can do all things which he wills to come about, which does not apply to Peter, who wills the predestined to be saved but cannot save them.

Yet it must not be passed over in silence that some [Note: [Col. 0813D] Among others, Abelard. For more on these matters, see our observations on Pullus; see Master I, distinction 43.] say that God can do nothing except what he does, restricting God’s power. They seek to establish this thus: “God can do nothing except what is good [Col. 0813D] for him to do; and nothing is good for him to do which he does not do; therefore God can do nothing except what he does.”

Again: “God’s justice requires him to do what he does, and not to do what he does not do; and God cannot do anything contrary to his justice; therefore God cannot do what he does not do, and thus can do nothing except what he does.” Again: “God cannot do what his justice requires him to do; but his justice requires nothing except what he does; therefore he can do nothing except what he does.” [Col. 0814A] That this statement is true—“His justice requires him to do only what he does”—is clear from its contradictory, which is false: “His justice requires him to do what he does not do.”

Again: “God cannot do except what he ought to do. But he ought to do nothing except what he does.” Again: “God either ought to omit, or ought not to omit, what he omits. If you say that he ought, then he ought not to do what he omits. But he cannot do what he ought not to do; therefore he cannot do what he omits.” The other alternative is plainly false, namely: “God ought not to omit what he omits.”

To all these points there is one nearly common reply, after first making this distinction: God is called good in one way, and a human being in another. A human being [Col. 0814B] is called good because of the good works which he performs, works informed by charity. But God is not called good because of good works. Rather, his works are called good because he, who is truly good, performs them. For if he did things which are evil, or things which would be evil if done by human beings, he would nevertheless not be said to do evil works. Rather, those things would be good works, and would then be called good because of their good author, namely God.

Therefore, when it is said, “God cannot do except what it is good for him to do,” if you understand it compositionally—“He cannot do anything except that which would be good if done by him”—it is true [Note: [Col. 0814D] Thus the Master answers, § c.]. But if it is understood divisively thus: “God cannot do except what is now good,” that is, “he can do nothing which [Col. 0814C] is not now good,” it is false. Rather, he can do what is now evil, and what would be evil if done by another; yet if he did it, he would perform a good work.

So also this statement must be qualified: “God cannot do except what his justice requires him to do.” Similarly, when it is said, “God cannot do except what he ought to do,” that is, except what would be fitting if he did it [Note: [Col. 0814D] Thus the Master, § d.]. You speak truly.

Note, however, that the word *ought* (*debet*) is improperly said of God, and is a poisonous word. [Note: [Col. 0814D] In the Master, ibid., as it seems to me, this word (*ought*) has poison in it. See the remainder, almost word for word.] For God is not our debtor, except perhaps by reason of a promise; whereas we are debtors by reason of what we have committed.

Likewise, there is in God an eternal reason, which is also God, by which God does what he does and leaves undone what he leaves undone. Therefore, while it remains, he cannot [Col. 0814D] do what he leaves undone, or leave undone what he does, without acting against that reason. He cannot act against it, because he would thereby act against himself. Therefore he cannot either do what he leaves undone or leave undone what he does. It is indeed true that, if that reason were temporal rather than eternal, he could leave undone what he does without acting against that reason. For, when formerly there was reason for something to be done, and now that which formerly had reason to be done were omitted, there would now not be reason for that thing or affair. Thus, when this man is predestined [Col. 0815A] and it is posited that he is to be damned—which is possible—then the one who was called predestined is not predestined, and never was; though it was true that he would be predestined. Since, then, that reason is eternal, it does not appear how, while it remains, God can do what he leaves undone.

To this it must be said that God, while that eternal cause remains, because he does everything that he does—that is, by himself—can do what he does not do, and conversely. Yet he cannot therefore act against that cause, [Note: [Col. 0815D] Lombard in the same place.] because that reason, although it is now the cause of some thing, can fail to be the cause of that same thing; it nevertheless cannot cease to be the cause of that which it is the cause of. This is apparent in predestination: from eternity God predestined Jacob, and he could have damned him. Yet he would not thereby have acted against predestination; for, if [Col. 0815B] he damned him, it would then truly be said: “He was never predestined.” For he could have not been predestined, just as he could have not been to be saved.

[Note: [Col. 0815D] Thus the Master, toward the end of the same section.] Likewise, indirectly, as follows: God can do something that he does not do, has not done, and will not do; therefore he can do something that was not. Therefore the one who will know can do something that he will not foreknow; therefore he can do something without foreknowledge. This is the fallacy of the final inference. For the premises are true, and there is a transition from division to composition. This man, who is still illiterate and would learn letters, can teach you letters which he does not know; therefore he can teach you letters without knowledge. Or thus: Some man can see who does not have eyes [Note: [Col. 0815D] Perhaps *which*, understood: “has,” in the Master, ibid., § e.]—for example, Antichrist; therefore someone can see without eyes.

Augustine says, [Note: [Col. 0816D] *Confessions*, Book VII, ch. 4.] addressing God: [Col. 0815C] “Nor are you compelled unwillingly to do anything, because your will is not greater than your power; it would indeed be greater if you yourself were greater than yourself.” From this it follows that not even God’s power is greater than his will, since will and power are identical. Hence the inference: Therefore God cannot do more things than he wills, or he wills to do more than he can do.

To this it must be said that by the name of power or will we sometimes understand the divine essence itself, according to which the foregoing statements are true; sometimes the things subject to will or power, according to which power is greater than will—that is, more things are subject to power than to will. Or: this man’s sight is not sharper than that man’s sight, nor conversely; therefore this man does not see more things than that man, [Col. 0815D] nor that man more than this man. Or thus: this house is not more capacious than that house, nor conversely; therefore this house does not contain more things than that one, nor does that one contain more than this.

Likewise Augustine says: [Note: [Col. 0816D] In the Master above, but I have not found it in the cited place, Book I, *On the Creed, to Catechumens*, ch. 1.] “Only what God does not will is something God cannot do.” Hence the inference: Therefore he can do nothing except what he wills. Or: “Only that is not an animal which is not a human being”; therefore no animal exists which is not a human being. That this proposition, “Only that is not an animal which is not a human being,” is true is clear: anything either is a human being or is not a human being; and it is not true that something is a human being and is not an animal. “That which is not a human being is not an animal”; therefore, “Only that is not an animal which is not a human being.” Likewise: “Only what God does not will is something God cannot do.”

Even if anyone doubts this, it is shown thus. With respect to anything whatever, God either wills it or does not will it; it is not true that God wills something and cannot do it; [Col. 0816A] therefore what God does not will he cannot do; therefore only what God does not will is something God cannot do. Likewise, God does not will only what he cannot do; whatever God cannot do, he does not will; therefore whatever God does not will, he cannot do. Likewise: only what God does not will is something God cannot do; God does not will only what he cannot do. God wills only what he can do; therefore only what God wills is something God can do.

Accordingly it should be noted, concerning these two statements:

“Only what God does not will is something God cannot do.”
“God does not will only what he cannot do.”

the first is true and the second false. For God does not will something that he can do. Therefore it is not the case that he does not will only what he cannot do. And in all the foregoing the word *do* must be understood. Otherwise it would not fittingly be said, “God can do this.” Nor should it trouble you that we say God cannot do something, since *something* is taken so broadly that it includes both deficiency and power.

Likewise: either it is possible for God to do whatever he can do, or impossible. If possible, then it can be true. Let it be posited: “Therefore it is true that God does whatever he can do”; therefore one says, “God does whatever he can do.” But if it is impossible for God to do whatever he can do, [Col. 0816C] then it is necessary that God not do whatever he can do; therefore necessarily God does not do whatever he can do; therefore God cannot do whatever he can do. And this last argumentative procedure seems to be the same as when one says: “It is necessary that God not sin; therefore necessarily God does not sin; therefore God cannot sin.”

Likewise, it is necessary that God not do whatever he can do; therefore it is necessary that God not do these things or other things. And their being able to be done is no more a reason concerning the others than concerning these; therefore it is necessary that God not do these things and that he can do them; and thus it is necessary that God not do these things which nevertheless he can do. Likewise, it is impossible [Col. 0816D] for God to be the author of every nature that he can make, since he can make infinitely many and numerous natures which he does not make; therefore it is necessary that God not be the author of some nature, and thus God is not the author of every nature.

It should therefore be noted that in all these cases there is the fallacy of equivocation arising from a changed reference of terms under different qualifications. Thus we grant this: “It is impossible for God to do whatever he can do,” because this statement can in no way be true. Yet it does not follow: “Therefore God cannot [Col. 0817A] do whatever he can do.” Just as it is impossible for white to be black; nevertheless white cannot be black. Likewise this is true: “It is necessary that God not do some things which he can do,” but not “these things or other things”—for it cannot be determined which things are proposed confusedly—since God cannot do other things by which he could not do more things. Thus perhaps it is necessary that Linus not know other things which Peter knows, but not these things or other things, because no item known by Peter can be pointed out which Linus could not know; since he knows that which cannot be known with greater difficulty, namely that God is three and one. Yet, as some have said, it is always necessary that Peter, who is more blessed, know other things which Linus, who is less blessed, does not know.

[Col. 0817B] Likewise, to this argument: “It is necessary that God not be the author of some nature of which he can be the author; therefore it is necessary that God not be the author of some nature and that he can be the author of that nature,” the objection is similarly made through the fallacy of division, as also here: “It is necessary that one of these contradictory propositions be a true proposition which has not been made.” [Note: [Col. 0817D] Master, I, dist. 44, § 1.] Therefore it is necessary that one of them be a true proposition, and that it has not been made.

Likewise someone says: [Note: [Col. 0817D] Augustine, *Eighty-Three Questions*, q. 50, throughout, with only a few words omitted.] “God the Father, because he could not beget one better than the one whom he begot—for nothing is greater than God—ought to beget an equal. For if he could and would not, he would be envious; if he willed and could not, he would be weak.” By analogy, as they say, if God [Col. 0817C] can make another creature better than it is and does not make it, he is envious; and if he wills to do so and cannot, he is weak. And so they wish to prove that God cannot make another thing better than it is, just as he cannot do otherwise than he does.

But that which is introduced as analogous is not analogous. For God the Father begot the Son of the same substance as himself, and therefore ought to beget one equal to himself, since a better one could not be begotten. But God creates a creature from nothing, which he can make better than he makes it. This is also shown indirectly: that God cannot make a thing better than it is either follows because every thing has in itself the perfection of every good, and thus all things are equally good—indeed, equal to the Creator in perfection—or because the thing itself cannot [Col. 0817D] be capable of that good which, if it had it, would make it better. If so, can God, who created from nothing that which is greater, make the thing capable of those goods, and thus better? Indeed, if he cannot, then there is already a defect in every creature.

[Note: [Col. 0817D] Master, I, dist. 44, § c.] In the same way they wish to prove that God cannot make a thing better in manner than he makes it. This is true, however, if *manner* is referred to God, because he cannot make a thing from better wisdom or from greater goodness. If it is referred to the creature, it is false. For God can grant to any creature whatever [Col. 0818A] a better state and more excellent gifts than it has. Hence Augustine says: [Note: [Col. 0818D] *On the Trinity*, Book XIII, ch. 10.] “Another manner of our deliverance was possible to God, but none more fitting for healing our misery.” Therefore, just as he could have delivered us in another manner, so he can make other things in another manner than he makes them, so that *manner* is referred to creatures, not to God’s mode.

Yet again it does not seem that God can do everything that is within the capacity of power, because he cannot restore a virgin after her fall, as Jerome says. [Note: [Col. 0818D] To Eustochium, *On the Guarding of Virginity*, ch. 2.] Some understand this as meaning that he cannot make the state of married persons, or of the continent, comparable to the state of virgins—that is, equally fit and ready for the service of God. He could indeed add certain preeminences to it so as to make it more excellent than the state of virgins; but in this respect, namely with respect to a certain fitness and suitability, he cannot make this state comparable to that one. But this does not seem to be precisely stated either; therefore Jerome’s word should not be adhered to. For he spoke hyperbolically in praise of virginity, speaking to Paula and Eustochium about virginity. Just as John also spoke hyperbolically at the end of his Gospel, and such a manner of speaking is frequently found in Holy Scripture.

Again, on that Gospel passage, “Such as a fuller cannot make on earth” (Mark IX), Bede says: “God cannot give his faithful on earth that brightness which he reserves for them in heaven.” But this must be understood as: “He cannot,” that is, “he does not will,” or “he cannot in justice.”

[Col. 0818C] Likewise, the same point may be demonstrated by arguments. By no work belonging to the class of goods can God’s majesty be injured or his excellence diminished; therefore God can perform every work belonging to the class of goods. But to repent is in the class of goods; therefore God can repent, especially since it is read of him: “I repent that I made man” (Genesis VI). Or thus: to repent is a good work, informed by charity, which belongs to the capacity of penitence. God cannot perform this work; therefore he cannot do whatever belongs to the capacity of penitence; therefore he is not omnipotent.

To this it must be said that repentance from charity is a good work and is God’s—that is, it is from God, because every good work is from him—and it is performed by a human being through ministry; but it is from God by authority. Thus, when Peter worked miracles, the work [Col. 0818D] was God’s by authority and Peter’s by ministry, and so it is the same work of God and of man, though in different ways. As in the book of *Retractions*: [Note: [Col. 0818D] See Augustine, *Retractions*, Book I, ch. 23.] “I thought that believing was the work of man alone; now, however, I know that it is the work of God and man.”

Likewise, God the Father cannot assume human nature in the unity of his person; and this is a work by which neither his majesty would be injured nor his excellence diminished, just as the Son’s majesty is not injured in any respect and his excellence is not diminished because he is man. Therefore there is some work within the capacity of power which God the Father cannot perform. [Col. 0819A] Why, then, is he called omnipotent?

That God the Father cannot assume human nature in the unity of person seems clear from this: if he could do so, he could surely be a man; and since he is a person other than the Son, he would have to be a man other than the Son, and thus the Father and Son would be two men; consequently, two substances. To this it must be said that the Father both could have been and can be a man, and one other than the Son; yet not therefore another substance, just as the Father is another person than the Son, yet not therefore another substance.

Likewise, the Son of God could not assume Peter’s flesh or Peter’s soul. But this was a work in which neither his majesty would be injured nor his excellence diminished; therefore there is some work which the Son could not do, [Col. 0819B] though it was not contrary to his majesty. Why, then, is it said that the Son of God could have assumed Peter’s flesh and soul? Therefore the Son of God could have been Peter. By the same reasoning he could have been Paul, and thus he could have been both natures of two human beings—two human beings.

To this it must be said that the Son of God could have assumed Peter’s body and soul, and that this alone could belong to him, but not that he would be Peter. For when this is said, it also signifies that Peter’s proper quality and singular status would be in him, which is impossible; just as, if that whereby Plato is Plato were to belong to Socrates. But while that belongs to him, it can belong to Socrates; and that whereby Plato is Plato can belong to Socrates, and Socrates can be that to which that whereby Plato is Plato belongs, [Col. 0819C] yet Socrates will not be Plato.

Therefore the Father and the Son of God could assume another soul and another body, so that he might have two or three souls and two or three bodies united to himself; yet he will not thereby be one man and another man. For if this were so, it would truly be said, “This man is that man,” because this is a humanized person and that is a humanized person. For this term, “this man,” signifies nothing other than “this humanized person.” And one person would exist in two human natures; and in God human nature is nothing other than body and soul. For, as Damascene testifies, [Note: [Col. 0819D] *On the Faith*, Book III, ch. 11.] a common species is not to be assumed concerning Christ the man, as will be taught later.

Likewise, if two opposed natures, such as an ass’s and a lion’s, are united singularly in one thing, neither [Col. 0819D] God’s majesty is thereby injured nor his excellence diminished. God cannot do this; therefore he cannot perform every work within the capacity of power; therefore he is not omnipotent.

That God cannot make the same thing both ass and lion seems established from this: if something is a human being, it is not an ass, and conversely. Yet God can make it the case that the same human being is a human being and is not a human being, and that the same thing is an ass and is not an ass, so that two contradictorily opposed things are simultaneously true. Indeed, by the same reasoning by which he can confuse specific statuses in the same person, so that the same thing is lion and ass, he can mingle two singular statuses, so that the same thing is Socrates and Plato. This is impossible, and impossible even for God, [Col. 0820A] because then two proper qualities would belong to the same thing, by each of which that thing would differ from every thing to which another proper quality belonged. Thus, since those qualities would be in one thing, some thing would differ numerically from itself, and so something would not be what it itself was; and God can by no means do this.

Hence, since two natures are in Christ, that by which the first proper characteristic exists according to the divine nature and another according to the human nature cannot belong to Christ. [Note: [Col. 0820D] That is, personhood or the principle of subsistence.] For each would signify a proper quality by which Christ would differ from the thing to which another proper quality belonged.

Yet conversely, that God could have made the same thing both human being and ass can be shown from the fact that he made the same thing human being and God. He also made the same woman both a virgin and a mother, both of which are as difficult as this. Likewise, he made the ass of such a nature that it should serve its Creator; it belonged to its nature that God could do with it as he pleased. Therefore, since God made it speak, he made it speak by nature. Likewise Moses’ rod was of such a nature that God might do with it whatever he willed; God willed it to become a serpent. Therefore it belonged to its nature that God should make it a serpent; therefore God made it a serpent by the rod’s nature. Therefore he did not do this contrary to the rod’s nature.

Likewise, because God swiftly unfolded the causes from primordial matter, could he not make it so that the causes which made one thing an ass should make another thing a human being, and those which made [Col. 0820C] another thing a human being should make another thing an ass—so that the effects of these causes should belong to those, and the effects of those to these—without acting against those causes? Thus someone who instituted that whereby *man* signifies a human being could, if he wished, institute it so that it signified a stone, and conversely. Therefore, if God now presides over those causes as formerly, the contrary claim is untenable: he can alter their effects without acting against them, so that the causes which make Socrates a human being, by God’s command make him an ass. Therefore, if he makes Socrates an ass, he does not act against nature; rather, there is a nature by means of which he does this, to which he gives this effect, so that it makes an ass what previously made a human being.

Likewise, pointing to the serpent into which Moses’ rod was changed: this substance was a rod and now [Col. 0820D] is a serpent; therefore it is a serpent contrary to nature, or it was a rod contrary to nature, since the natural statuses of rod and serpent are opposed. Likewise, this substance was made a serpent contrary to nature; therefore it is a serpent contrary to nature. Yet it is proved to be a serpent naturally: for there is some cause in this substance which makes it a serpent, namely serpentine nature, just as some cause makes that true serpent a serpent, naturally implanted by God in this kind of animals. Otherwise this substance would not be a true serpent. Therefore, if there is a cause making it a serpent, this substance is a serpent; and that cause is inferior; therefore this substance is [Col. 0821A] naturally a serpent—that is, by means of an inferior nature. Therefore, its being a serpent is not a miraculous work.

But if he says that, once the rod was changed into a serpent, the causes which were in the rod and made it a rod remained in the same substance and now make it a serpent, though the effect was changed, it will still no less follow that, by means of an inferior cause, this substance is a serpent, and thus is not contrary to nature.

Likewise, it is impossible for God to make Socrates an ass, but the conclusion is impossible; therefore so is the premise—or the premise is impossible; therefore so is the conclusion. Likewise, God’s making Socrates an ass is impossible either only according to the higher cause, or also according to the lower cause. If only according to [Col. 0821B] the higher cause, then it is simply impossible. But if according to the lower cause, then according to lower nature it can be true that God makes Socrates an ass; therefore it is possible for this to be true according to lower nature, that God makes Socrates an ass; therefore, if God does this, he does it according to lower nature.

Likewise, why should it be said that it is now possible that the Virgin gave birth, and not be said that it is possible for a creature to see because it will see, just as the Virgin gave birth? Augustine handed down this point in his work on Genesis, saying: [Note: [Col. 0821D] *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, Book IX, ch. 8, with a few omissions.] “The first condition of things did not contain the fact that a woman should be made from the rib of a man, but that she could be so made.” Therefore a woman could be made from a man’s rib, which is a miraculous work. By the same reasoning, therefore, a blind person can see.

[Col. 0821C] It must therefore be noted that there are three kinds of works which are from God. Some are performed by God’s authority through a seminal cause, such as trees flowering, bearing fruit, and other such things; these are called natural works. Some are so performed by human beings that they are nevertheless also from God, as are all artificial things—benches, temples, and the like. Some God performs by his own authority, with no intermediary, in order to show us his grace: for example, the Virgin’s giving birth, the rod’s being changed into a serpent, and the woman’s being turned into a pillar of salt; all these are miraculous works.

Therefore it belongs to the nature of each thing that God can make of it whatever he wills. [Note: [Col. 0821D] See Augustine, in the cited work *On Genesis*, ch. 17.] Yet it does not belong to its nature to make it, if he does make it, because he does not perform a miraculous work through nature as intermediary, but by his will alone. Hence the fact that this substance is a serpent is not through any inferior cause, but by God’s will alone; and it was nevertheless no less a true serpent. God can also make the same thing human being and ass, and make two contradictorily opposed statements true, if one is taken according to an inferior cause and the other according to a higher cause. Thus it is true according to higher nature that the Virgin gave birth; it is true according to inferior nature that the Virgin did not give birth.

But God could not make both [Col. 0822A] true according to higher nature, since in this his excellence would be diminished: he would be the author of contrariety and discord. Nor can God make both true according to lower nature, lest his excellence be diminished, as it would have to be because he would have posited contrary and mutually destructive causes in the same singular thing. Since the same thing is human being and God, human being and God are not opposed; so too, if the same thing were human being and ass, these predicates, human being and ass, would not be opposed.

But when it is said, “It is impossible for God to make a human being an ass without the human being being an ass,” this must be denied. Indeed, it is possible for this to be true: “God makes a human being an ass,” while this is true: “A human being is an ass.” For it will be false according to inferior [Col. 0822B] nature, although true according to higher nature. Whenever someone begins to speak of possibility or impossibility, therefore, one must consider in what respect he speaks: whether according to higher causes or lower causes. For some things are possible according to these causes which are impossible according to those.

Nor is it true that this substance was a rod; rather, from the rod this substance was made which is a serpent. Thus the substance of Christ’s body was by no means bread; rather, bread was changed into this substance. Nor was the substance itself made a serpent; rather, from the substance of the rod this substance of a serpent was made.

## CHAPTER IX. Whether God Can Do Whatever He Has Been Able to Do

[Col. 0822C]

[Note: [Col. 0821D] The Master, I, dist. 44, final section, contains the same material.] It is customary to ask whether God can do whatever he has been able to do. For if he has been able to do something which he cannot do, or conversely, it seems that his power increases or diminishes. Yet, if this is said, an incongruity seems to follow: “Whatever God has been able to do, he can do; God was able to become incarnate and die; therefore he can become incarnate and die.”

They therefore say: [Note: [Col. 0822D] By this solution he defends from error the opinion of his master here, which some maintain was placed far too rashly among the selected errors.] if it is understood thus, “Whatever God has been able to do, he can do,” that is, whatever power he had, he has, or he had and has the power concerning whatever thing, it is true. But if it is understood thus, “Whatever he has been able to do, he can do,” that is, whatever was subject to his power is now subject to his power; or, “Whatever he was able to do, he can do,” it is false. For when it is said, “God was able to become incarnate,” [Col. 0822D] the word *become incarnate* embraces all times in its signification, namely past, present, and future. But with the present-tense word *can*, it loses the signification of past time and pertains to the present and future. For what God did is not said to be something he does, but something he has done. Thus it is not truly said, “Whatever he was able to do, he can do,” but rather, “do,” “has done,” or “will do.”

This is a fallacy. “Every man whom you saw yesterday, you see today; yesterday you saw a man who was going to speak; therefore today you see a man who is going to speak.” Similarly [Col. 0823A] in the argument the premise encompasses more times—namely three—than the conclusion, which embraces only two, namely present and future, by reason of the present-tense verb *can*.

Yet some insist on proving that God can now become incarnate as follows: God could have been going to become incarnate now; he has had no power that he does not have, and conversely; therefore God can become incarnate. They argue that God could have become incarnate now as follows: God could have deferred his incarnation, according to his will, until the present time; for it was not necessary that he become incarnate at the time at which he became incarnate.

Likewise, let B be the time before C, at which God was incarnate. God could at B have become incarnate now; he had no power at B which he did not have at C, [Col. 0823B] and he had at B the power of no thing which he did not have at C; therefore God could at C have become incarnate now.

Likewise, if the Son of God was to be incarnated, he has not been incarnated. He is becoming incarnate or will become incarnate. It is possible that the Son of God was to be incarnated and was not incarnated; therefore it is possible that he becomes incarnate or is to become incarnate. That it is possible that the Son of God was incarnated is clear thus: everything that is impossible by nature or by chance is possible to God; but it is impossible that nothing was created; therefore this is possible to God; therefore it is possible that God created nothing, was not incarnated, and did nothing that he did. Thus it is possible that God will create this world, because it has already been created; and it is possible for God to die. Therefore it is possible for God [Col. 0823C] to die again, or to create the world from nothing twice.

But on the contrary, God in his flesh was glorified and made immortal—that is, unable to die; therefore it is impossible for him to die again.

This, however, is easy to resolve. Even if it is granted that it is possible for God to have created nothing, on account of the foregoing argument, and to be going to create whatever he was going to create, it is nevertheless not possible for God to create this world in these circumstances, because it was not necessary for God to have created the world and because God can have not created it. It is granted that God can be going to create it; and if he creates it, he has not already created it.

Likewise they say that he can become incarnate and die, because he can have neither been incarnated nor died. But it is also proved that he can become incarnate and die in such a way that he is incarnated [Col. 0823D] and has died, because the Son of God can now assume another soul and another body, assumed from a virgin other than Mary; in that flesh and soul he can die, although now, insofar as he is man, he is immortal.

But to this they say that in the flesh and soul which he has he cannot henceforth die, since that body is glorified and immortal and the soul impassible. Yet he can die in another flesh and another soul which he can assume, and this is not contrary to his power. In the same way the Father and the Holy Spirit can assume a body and soul.

Some, however, wish to object to this argument: “It is possible that nothing has been created by God; therefore it is possible that God created nothing,” identifying a fallacy of composition there, [Col. 0824A] and thus avoiding the foregoing incongruities—namely that God can be going to create this world.

It is also asked whether from eternity God could do whatever he could do at any time. If so, then from eternity he could create the world. For if he could do this in time and not from eternity, then he could do something in time which he could not do from eternity. Thus this cannot seem to be said of God according to his essence. But if from eternity he could create the world, then he could create a world coeternal with himself.

Likewise, God was never able to beget the Son without being able to create the world; he was able to beget a Son coeternal with himself; therefore he was also able to create a world coeternal with himself. Likewise, from eternity he had the power of creating the world, yet from eternity he could not create; therefore he could not use that power whenever he had it.

Accordingly, a distinction must here be made according to composition and division, or according to the amphiboly arising from the different syntactical construction of the phrase *from eternity*. If it is construed with the verb *could*, it is true that he could from eternity. But if it is construed with the following infinitive, so that one says, “From eternity he could create,” it is false; nor did this arise from his impotence, any more than his inability to sin does.

You can find the same fallacy in this similar statement: “Antichrist tomorrow will be about to be born.” For if the adverb determines the verb, it is true; if it determines the participle, it is false. Likewise, whatever God did, he could have not done; but he made it the case that all creatures could [Col. 0824C] exist from him; therefore he could have made it the case that no creatures could exist from him; therefore he could have made it the case that he was not omnipotent, and thus that he was not God.

Some therefore say that God did not make this in time, namely that creatures could be from him. For from eternity creatures could be from God. This is disproved as follows: no creature can exist except from God alone; therefore it is from God alone that creatures could be from him. But whatever is from God is from him either by generation, by procession, or by operation. This is from him neither by generation nor by procession; therefore it is from him by operation. Therefore God made it in time that every creature could be from him.

[Col. 0824D] Accordingly distinguish: “God made it in time that every creature could exist from him” is false. For that power is eternal. The power by which God could make a creature and that by which a creature could be made by him are the same power—namely, the eternal power which is God.

Likewise, when it is asked, “Is it from God that a human being is predestined?” if this is said of predestination, it is false. For predestination is God and is from eternity. If it is said of the truth, it is true, as some teach, saying: “Every truth is from God by operation.” I do not see how this is true, since every truth is from eternity, unless some other mode of being from God is meant. And it may be especially doubtful what is being discussed when it is said: “It is from God from eternity that this is future,” or “that this has been future from eternity”—if it is asked [Col. 0825A] whether it was from God from eternity that future things would be future, and how this was from him, whether by operation or in another way.

To suppress these objections, they say that one should answer thus: if one says, “It was from God that future things are future, or past,” and one is speaking of the truth, it may be granted, as they say, that this is from God by operation. I do not see how this can be true except in time and not from eternity. If you say, “It is from God that future things are future or foreknown”—that is, that the foreknowledge by which he foreknows them is from him—this is not true, because it is not from God but is God.

Yet it is objected: if God can be going to create whatever he was going to create, he can be going to make Peter and Judas, and can be not going to bestow grace upon Peter and be going to bestow it upon Judas; therefore he can be going to damn Peter and save Judas. If so, then he can either deprive Peter of his merits or save Judas contrary to Judas’s merits.

But, as they say, this does not hold, because God cannot damn Peter in such a way that Peter dies worthy of life. Others nevertheless try to prove this as follows: if God dealt strictly with everyone, he would save no one. Authority supports this, because if he dealt strictly with everyone, he would exact an account from each person for minor things and farthings. But if he pursued every particular, a human being could not render account for every particular, because throughout the whole time of his life Paul was bound to serve God and, during many instants, defrauded him of the service owed.

Although Peter through repentance [Col. 0825C] could humble himself so greatly that his humility equalled his preceding fault, he nevertheless could not humble himself as greatly as he was also and more bound to do—not by command, but by promise or by what he had committed. Therefore, if God damned Peter in such a way that Peter died worthy of life, he would not thereby act unjustly; rather, there would be a hidden justice in this.

They also show the same point thus: it is necessary that Peter died worthy of life. But it is possible that God will damn Peter; therefore it is possible that Peter died worthy of life and that God will damn him, because every necessary proposition is compatible with every possible proposition.
possible.

It nevertheless does not seem to us that God could damn Peter [Col. 0825D] without acting against justice, in such a way that Peter would die worthy of life. For the saying, “If He dealt strictly with each person, He would save no one,” is true in that we are all born children of wrath; and if He dealt strictly with us, He would not add the grace by which we might be saved. By the same reasoning by which it is granted that God can damn Peter and yet not act unjustly, it seems one must grant that God can commit adultery and thereby not sin; and, if He did it, He would do good, although adultery is evil. This is contrary to the saying: “If I say that I do not know him, I shall be a liar like you” (John 8).

## 26. CHAPTER X. On the will of God, in which it is first asked whether anything occurs contrary to a sign of the divine will.

[Col. 0826A]

[Note: [Col. 0825D] Lombard, I, distinction 45, *On the Will of God*.] Just as this predicable expression, “able to generate,” appears to be excepted from the foregoing rule, so too “willing to generate” appears to be excepted from it. Although it seems to be said according to the essence, it is said neither of the individual persons nor of all of them together: for neither the Son nor the Holy Spirit is willing to generate, nor are they together with the Father one willing to generate. The same objection is raised here as in the matters mentioned above. The Father wills to generate the Son; therefore the Father wills something which the Son does not will—namely, this man wishes to take a wife, that man does not wish to take a wife; therefore this man wills something which that man does not. [Col. 0826B] All the points raised when power was under discussion could be introduced regarding this question. But because the solution here is altogether the same, we shall omit matters common to both questions and dwell upon doubtful matters specifically bearing upon God’s will—first, however, showing in how many senses the term “will” is used, so that, when something is proposed in a statement, we may not be ignorant what is said, concerning what, and in what respect.

The term “will” is used in two ways. God’s will is called both his good pleasure and the sign of his good pleasure. His good pleasure is eternal and is God himself. But the signs of his will are diverse and temporal: command, prohibition, counsel, permission, and operation. All these are called, in the plural, God’s wills [Col. 0826C] [Note: [Col. 0825D] Lombard, ibid., § g.]. Hence: “Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all his wills” (Psalm 110 [Vulgate 111]), because they are signs of his will; just as the diverse effects of God’s justice are called, in the plural, “justices”: “The justices of the Lord are right, gladdening hearts” (Psalm 18 [Vulgate 19]). Likewise: “I shall sing for ever of the mercies of the Lord” (Psalm 88 [Vulgate 89]), because of the various effects of mercy. That God’s will is called his good pleasure is beyond doubt, according to the Apostle’s words: “Who has resisted his will?” (Romans 9). And David says: “He has done all things whatsoever he willed” (Psalm 113 [Vulgate 115]). That God’s will is called command, prohibition, and counsel, you read in the Lord’s Prayer: “Your will be done” (Matthew 6), that is, counsel and command; [Col. 0826D] for prohibition is included under command, since some commands are prohibitive and others affirmative.

[Note: [Col. 0826D] Lombard, above, § L, has these same points.] God’s permission and operation are also called God’s will. Hence Augustine [Note: [Col. 0826D] *Enchiridion*, ch. 95]: “Nothing happens unless the Almighty wills it to happen, either by permitting it to happen or by doing it himself.” When he says “wills,” he includes both good and evil things; but because he wills good things in one way and evil things in another, he then specifies, “by doing it himself,” with respect to good things, and “by permitting it,” with respect to evil things—which he permits without doing them. Since the term “will” is thus said both of God’s good pleasure [Col. 0827A] and of the sign of his good pleasure, good pleasure is properly called will. [Note: [Col. 0827D] Lombard, final § and § h, cited distinction.] A sign, however, is improperly so called, in the way that anger is said to be in God because he shows us signs of anger. For it is not permissible to understand in God such a movement either of anger or of joy. All names denoting a movement of the affections, when said of God, indicate not a movement of the affections—since there is none in God—but signs of affection.

In a human being, however, they can signify two things: both the inward affection and the outward expression of affection. When it is said, “This man loves that man,” I can understand this either of an inward affection or of an outward sign of love, because he displays a sign of love. But if it is said of God that God loves this person, you must refer it to an outward effect or sign, because, insofar as he is God, a manner of loving does not apply to him. Hence, because there are three notable signs of God’s love, three meanings are commonly assigned to the verb “I love” when it is said of God. He loves because he preserves things in their being, and thus he loves all things. He also loves because in time he bestows grace, and thus he loves righteous persons. He also loves because he predestines to life, and thus he loves only the predestined.

## 27.

[Note: [Col. 0827D] Lombard, same distinction, § b.] Therefore, when we say that God’s will and good pleasure are that which he himself is, the following objection is made: To will and to be are the same thing for God; but God wills this; therefore God is this. To know and to be are the same thing for God; God knows all true things; therefore God is all true things. Or, to be and to be able are the same thing for God; God can do all things; therefore God is all things. Note that this inference is false [Col. 0827C] because, when it is said, “God is willing,” the divine essence is posited simply. But when I add, “God is willing this,” the essence is posited with a certain relation to creatures, so that he alone is God, to whose will this is subject.

[Note: [Col. 0828D] Lombard, above, §§ i and k, and distinction 47, final §.] Events always accord with that will of God which he himself is; that is, nothing occurs contrary to the will which he himself is. But many things occur contrary to signs of the will—that is, contrary to commands, counsels, and so forth. For he commands many things which do not happen, and many things happen which he does not command; likewise, he prohibits many things which nevertheless happen. He commanded Abraham to sacrifice his son, yet it was not done. Why, then, did he command it? So that Abraham’s faith and love might become known to Abraham himself, not to God, whose [Col. 0827D] Spirit searches all things and to whom human hearts speak. Likewise, he forbade the man whose blindness had been cured to proclaim his fame, although he willed this to happen, and it therefore did happen. Why, then, did he forbid it? To set before us an example of avoiding human favour. But whether it is true that many things occur contrary to God’s command must first be examined; afterwards, whether anything can occur contrary to God’s will, which he himself is.

Let us therefore pursue the case proposed a little earlier concerning Abraham: namely, whether the man who did not sacrifice his son in obedience to God’s command acted contrary to the Lord’s command. They object in such cases: God commanded [Col. 0828A] Abraham to sacrifice his son; he did not sacrifice him; therefore he did not obey God. The same objection applies to the man whose blindness was cured. To this one must say that the blind man [Abraham] obeyed God—that is, he fulfilled God’s will—but did not obey the wording of the command. For the Lord first commanded him to sacrifice, and he did not obey that command because the same Lord later, through the angel, forbade it to be done.

The master of a household commands a servant to bring his vessels; the servant, knowing his master’s will, does not bring them. Therefore the servant does not obey his master—yet this is false, because by not bringing them he does his master’s will, although he does not do the command. Yet he did not disdain obedience—just as a household servant who does not obey the Lord by bringing the vessels does not therefore disdain obedience. Again, God commanded Abraham [Col. 0828B] to sacrifice his son, and God did not will this. Therefore God had one thing in his mouth and another in his heart; therefore he was twofold, since he spoke from his heart. To this one must say that, if you understand literally of God the statement “He had one thing in his heart and another in his mouth,” it is not well said. For God, insofar as he is God, has neither mouth nor heart. But if it is understood in this sense—“He had one thing in his mouth and another in his heart,” that is, he commanded something which he did not will—it is true. Yet he was not therefore twofold, as is clear from the foregoing example of the master of a household.

Again, Abraham wished to sacrifice his son, and God did not will this; therefore Abraham’s will was contrary to God’s will, and so Abraham did not merit by it. Yet this is proved as follows: His will was formed by charity, and charity was its end; and if he had willed the contrary [Col. 0828C]—that is, if he had not wished to sacrifice his son—he would have deserved punishment. Therefore Abraham merited by that will. That Abraham wished to sacrifice his son is evident from this: Abraham wished to obey God, but he knew that he could not obey God unless he fulfilled that command, which he could not fulfil unless he sacrificed his son. Therefore Abraham wished to sacrifice his son. It is also proved thus: there are two human wills, the will of reason and the will of sensuality. A person is said simply to will what he wills by the will of reason, provided it rules; and he is said not to will what he wills only by the will of sensuality. Abraham willed this by the will of reason; therefore he simply willed it.

[Col. 0828D] To this some say that Abraham did not wish to sacrifice his son; nevertheless, he wished to obey God, whom he knew he could not otherwise obey. If they are thus challenged: Abraham wished to obey God and knew that he could not obey him unless he sacrificed his son; therefore he wished to sacrifice his son—they reply that it does not follow that, if one thing is antecedent to another and someone wills or can do the antecedent, he therefore wills or can do the consequent. They seek to demonstrate this by both dialectical and theological examples. If God was going to be born tomorrow, God will be born tomorrow; and God could have been going to be born tomorrow, yet he could not be born tomorrow. If this soul was going to begin [Col. 0829A] to exist tomorrow, this soul will begin to exist tomorrow. This soul could have been going to begin tomorrow, yet it will not be able to exist tomorrow. Thus it does not follow: if Paul is with Christ, Paul is dissolved; Paul desires to be with Christ; therefore he desires to be dissolved. Nor does it follow: if this man is in Rome in some manner, he is in Rome; this man would wish to be in Rome in some manner, yet he would not wish to be in Rome. Thus it would not follow that, if he wishes to obey God, he wishes to sacrifice his son, even though he knows that the former can be true without the latter.

To us, however, it seems truer that Abraham did wish to sacrifice his son, and that this will was meritorious and not contrary to God’s will, although what God and Abraham respectively willed was contrary. For God willed that Abraham should will what God at that time did not will. The point must be pressed thus: This man makes a proposition; that man does not make it; [Col. 0829B] therefore the proposition advanced by the former is contrary to the proposition put forward by the latter. Or: this man’s father wills that his son should live; God does not will that; therefore his will is contrary to God’s will. This is false. For someone with a good will desires what God wills—for example, that his enemy be condemned. Someone with a good will desires what God does not will—for example, that his father should remain alive. Someone with an evil will desires what God does not will—for example, that his father should die. Someone with an evil will does not desire what God wills—for example, that his enemy be saved. Someone with a good will does not desire what God does not will—for example, that his father should remain alive.

Again, before the angel’s prohibition Abraham had a will formed by charity. Therefore, if he had carried it into action when he had the opportunity, [Col. 0829C] he would have merited more by will and deed than by will alone. Yet it is argued to the contrary that he would not merit, because, if he had sacrificed his son, he would have acted contrary to natural law, since he would have done to another what he would not have wished done to himself. Therefore he would have been a murderer and thus would have sinned mortally.

Again, God commanded Abraham something which, if it were done, would occur contrary to natural law; he commanded him something which, if it were done, would occur outside God’s will. Therefore he commanded him something which, if it were done, would occur contrary to God’s will. It was possible for that to be done; therefore it was possible for something to occur contrary to God’s will. To this one must say that Abraham then did not act, nor did he wish to act, contrary to natural law, but in accordance with natural law. For natural law is that a creature should obey its Creator, which Abraham intended to do. [Col. 0829D] Although he would have done to his son what he would not have wished done to himself, he would not have done so unjustly, and therefore he did not sin against natural law—just as Jacob did not sin when he surreptitiously obtained Esau’s blessing, because he did not do this unjustly.

Again, either God commanded Abraham what ought to have been commanded, or he did not. If he commanded what ought to have been commanded, then a father’s sacrificing his son ought to have been commanded; therefore it was good; therefore it could be done with a good intention. In that case every mortal sin—adultery, theft, and so on—could likewise be committed with a good intention. But if he commanded what ought not to have been commanded, then what was good was not good; therefore he did not rightly command it to be done. God did something which he ought not to have done when he assumed flesh; therefore he did not rightly do it. Or he can do something evil; therefore he does evil. [Col. 0830A] For that was not something that ought to have been commanded, yet it was something to be commanded by the Lord. Again, God commanded Abraham something which he did not will to be done; therefore it was not good. The solution depends upon what has already been said. Again, God commanded Abraham to sacrifice his son and afterwards forbade it; therefore there was some change in God.

## 29.

This kind of argument seems confirmed by what Bede says on Mark, chapter 10, concerning permission of a bill of divorce: “Is the Lord contrary to himself, so that he commanded something earlier and afterwards annulled the same thing by a new command?” To this one must say that there was no change in God, but in God’s command. For Bede’s statement that there would be contrariety in God if he commanded something earlier and later its contrary must be understood on the assumption that his will always adheres to the command. If he had first willed one thing and afterwards its contrary, there would indeed be contrariety in him, as you may see from a similar case.

The Lord announced through Isaiah to Hezekiah that he would die, yet he did not die. This does not mean that there was any change in the Holy Spirit through whose revelation Isaiah made this prediction; nor did the prophet lie when he said, “You shall die, and you shall not live” (Isaiah 38). Just as Jonah did not lie in saying, “Yet forty days and Nineveh shall be overthrown” (Jonah 3). Each spoke according to the lower cause, not the higher. It is as if someone says: “This blind man will not see.” He speaks truly, even if it subsequently happens by a miracle that the man sees. For whoever speaks thus speaks according to the natural course, not according to the higher cause.

Since [Col. 0830C] prophecy is “a divine inspiration, through words or deeds, announcing the events of things with unchangeable truth,” the truth of this prophecy was unchangeable if one considers the respect in which the prophet spoke—namely, according to the lower cause, that is, according to Hezekiah’s merits or his age. For the subsequent addition of twelve years was by the divine will, without a preceding natural cause; or, what is truer, the Lord had threatened, on account of his merits, to take fifteen years from the natural span of his life, but afterwards, when he had wept, restored them.

Someone will say that something must be understood beneath the surface of those words, “You shall die, and you shall not live.” For every prophecy made by threat, of which this is an example, has an implied qualification and may be changed. But that made through God’s providence without the cooperation of free choice cannot be changed; while that made through foreknowledge can be changed, although no hidden qualification is to be understood. All this is fully expounded in the commentary on Matthew.

Here one may ask whether Caiaphas prophesied when he said: “It is expedient that one should die for the people, lest the whole nation perish” (John 11). For the Evangelist seems to say that he prophesied, when he says: “But he did not say this of himself; rather, since he was high priest in that year” (ibid.). But if he prophesied, then what he prophesied was true or false. Since he did not have it from himself but from the Holy Spirit by reason of the dignity of the high priesthood, [Col. 0831A] he therefore prophesied truly; for he would not prophesy falsely through the Holy Spirit. Therefore he spoke truly. But by what proposition, except this: “It is expedient that one should die, lest the whole nation perish”? Therefore he spoke truth by that proposition. Yet it is proved that he spoke only falsehood. For he intended to say and persuade them to kill Christ, who was preaching the destruction of the legal observances, so that, once he had been killed, that worldly seed—which was held in reverence even by the Gentiles—would not perish, and thus their nation and place would not be taken away. And it was false that this was expedient for them, because what they planned, or what Caiaphas advised, did not come about, since they were afterwards destroyed by the Romans.

Therefore Caiaphas intended to say nothing but this falsehood. It is true that this sense could be elicited from that utterance: “It is expedient,” and so forth—namely, that it is beneficial for Christ to die, so that the human race may not perish in its sins but may be redeemed by his death. Yet Caiaphas did not have this sense in those words; it is nevertheless true, and so he uttered nothing but falsehood. Therefore he did not prophesy truly. Again, he prophesied truly; therefore, in prophesying, he stated a truth. Again, he uttered only falsehood, and he did not have it from himself but from the Holy Spirit; therefore by the authority of the Holy Spirit he uttered falsehood. Again, whatever he said, he said with an evil intention; therefore he sinned in the very act of prophesying, and thus his prophesying was a sin for him.

To this one must say that he prophesied only if this sense is received: [Col. 0831C] that he uttered an expression from which a prophetic and true sense could be drawn, while he himself said only what was false. Yet, by the prompting of the Holy Spirit, it came about that he uttered such an expression as would signify truth under a fitting interpretation. He himself, however, did not have that understanding there, so that he seems in a sense to have spoken truth unknowingly.

Jephthah may also be objected to here. His will did not please God, nor did the sacrifice; rather, it was the deliberation by which he anxiously considered what he should offer God. [Note: [Col. 0831D] This alludes to *Questions on the Old and New Testaments*, question 43, where that pseudo-Augustine inveighs at length against Jephthah; the genuine Augustine, however, excuses him in book VII of the *Questions on the Gospels*, question 49.] “Jephthah’s intention pleased God, but not the sacrifice” (Judges 11): “intention” is understood in that authority in this sense. For he made his vow foolishly: if a dog or something else had come out to meet him, would he have sacrificed it? And that his intention—that is, his will—in this matter did not please God can be proved: if the will were good, the work proceeding from that will would be good, because “a good tree cannot bear bad fruit” (Matthew 7). Again, that sacrifice did not please God. Therefore neither did the will by which he desired it. Yet an authority says the contrary: [Note: [Col. 0831D] Authority of Jerome on Jeremiah, chapter 7.] God willed Jephthah’s daughter to be sacrificed on account of her father’s foolish vow [Note: [Col. 0831D] In Augustine, cited above, in the Appendix to vol. IV, and in Jerome, cited above, and book I *Against Jovinianus*.]. Therefore, if God willed this, it was good. But this must be understood [Col. 0832A] of God’s will, that is, God’s permission: he permitted it, but did not will it by the will which he himself is. For the vow was foolish, therefore indiscreet, therefore not to be fulfilled. If “intention” is understood as deliberation, there is nothing that can be objected in reply.

“Intention” may also be understood as will. For often, while the will is good, the works that arise incidentally are evil—not works arising from an evil will. Thus Jephthah’s will was good, and the work which proceeded from it in the first instance was good—namely, to sacrifice whatever first came out to meet him—but the incidental work was evil, namely, to sacrifice his daughter. Conversely, Judas’s will was evil, yet the incidental work was good, namely, our salvation. Others say [Note: [Col. 0832D] This is founded on the teaching of the Master, I, distinction 45, § k, and distinction 47, final §.] that command is spoken of in three ways: in form and intention, as “Honour [Col. 0832B] your father and mother” (Exodus 20); in intention but not form, as “You shall not kill” (ibid.); in form but not intention, as “Go, tell no one” (Mark 1). Such was what the Lord commanded Abraham concerning the sacrifice of his son: it was not to be carried out, but intended to instruct.

## CHAPTER XI. Can anything occur contrary to the will of God which he himself is?

[Note: [Col. 0832D] Lombard, I, distinction 46.] From what has been said, it is clear that many things occur contrary to signs of God’s will—that is, contrary to commands, counsels, prohibitions, and so on. It remains to ask whether anything can occur contrary to the will of God which he himself is: that is, whether everything which God wills to occur does occur, and conversely. It seems not. For God “wills all [Col. 0832C] persons to be saved,” as the Apostle says (1 Timothy 2), yet not all are saved. Elsewhere he also says: “Jerusalem, how often I wished to gather your children under my wings, and you would not” (Matthew 21). This seems to mean that the Lord willed something which he was prevented from doing by Jerusalem’s contrary will, and thus willed something which did not happen.

But it is plain that God wills nothing to happen which he himself does not bring about, according to the words: “Who has resisted his will?” (Romans 9); and: “He has done all things whatsoever he willed” (Psalm 111 [Vulgate 113]). Therefore the first statement is explained as follows [Note: [Col. 0832D] You have all these points in Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapters 97 and 98. More is found in the notes on chapter 14 of the first part of Pullus’s *Sentences*.]: “He wills all persons to be saved,” that is, no one is saved unless God wills that person to be saved. Thus it is said: “God enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1), that is, no one is enlightened [Col. 0832D] except through him. The saying concerning Jerusalem is understood in the same way: “As often as I have gathered, by my ever-effective will, as many of your children as I have gathered, I did this while you were unwilling and resisting.” It is therefore established that God wills nothing to happen by the will which he himself is that does not happen.

[Note: [Col. 0832D] Lombard, above, § d and following.] It is also asked whether God wills whatever happens to happen. If so, since evil occurs, God wills evil to occur. Although this seems far from the truth, some try to prove it indirectly as follows. Evil things happen and God does not will evil things to happen; therefore evil things happen contrary to God’s will, or they do not happen outside his will—both false. This man is in this city, and the king does not will him to be in this city [Col. 0833A]; therefore he is in it contrary to the king’s will, or he is not in it apart from the king’s will. Again, evil things happen; therefore they happen either with God willing or with God not willing. If with God willing, then God wills evil things to happen; if with God not willing, then with God unwilling; therefore against his will.

We say in reply that evil things happen with God not willing, but not with God unwilling; for that would mean that they happen contrary to his will, which is false. Thus this man is in the city with the king not willing, but not with the king unwilling. And: “Socrates is an ass while the other of these two is not running”; yet it does not follow that Socrates is an ass while neither is running. Note that “God wills evil things to happen” is false; “God wills evil things not to happen” is also false; but “God does not will evil things to happen” is true.

Again: it is good that evil things happen. For Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0833D] *Enchiridion*, ch. 96]: “It is good not only that good things exist, but also that evil things exist; for, if it were not good for evil things to exist or happen, they would by no means be permitted by the omnipotently good One.” But God wills what is good to be; therefore God wills evil things to happen.

To this one must say that Augustine calls it good that evil things happen because God draws good things out of the evils which occur. It is not good in itself that evil things happen [Note: [Col. 0833D] The same matters occur in Lombard, cited distinction 46, § h.]. For something is called good when it is good in itself, for the person to whom it is done, and for the person by whom it is done—for example, giving alms from charity. Something may be good for the recipient and in itself, but not for the agent—for example, giving alms to a poor person for human favour. Something may be good for the agent and in itself, but not for the recipient—for example, preaching the faith to an unbeliever [Note: [Col. 0833D] Supply: “who does not obey the truth,” as in the Master.]. There is also something which is not good in itself nor for its agent, but is called good only for others: for example, the action of the Jews by which they crucified Christ. Yet it is called good because God drew good from it—he who draws good out of all evils. Hence [Note: [Col. 0833D] Augustine, *Enchiridion*, ch. 27, and frequently elsewhere.]: “God judged it better to make good things out of evils than to permit no evils at all.”

For when the wicked sin, the good advance in goodness: “When the pestilent person is scourged, the wise man becomes more prudent” (Proverbs 19). “While the wicked man is proud, the poor man is inflamed” (Psalm 10); and the sins of neighbours are a frying-pan for the righteous: “Let the wickedness of sinners be consumed, and you will direct the righteous” (Psalm 7). That God does not will evil things to happen is clear, for if he willed evil things to happen, he would be the author of sin. And although God’s will—that is, [Note: [Col. 0833D] “A sign” seems to be required.] a sign of God’s will—is not always fulfilled by human beings, it is always fulfilled concerning all, whether they are good or evil. Hence Gregory says [Note: [Col. 0833D] Also cited by the Master, I, distinction 47, § b, but [Col. 0834D] somewhat differently.]: “Many carry out God’s will by what they strive to change, and, while resisting his will, they serve it, since the divine dispensation is advanced by that which resists through human effort.” [Note: [Col. 0834D] Lombard, ibid., distinction 48, § b.] Such was the action of the Jews, which God did not will, though he did will the passion inflicted by them. Nevertheless, God did according to his own will concerning them when he punished those who had sinned. These matters, however, will be treated more fully here or in what follows when the Incarnation of the Lord is discussed.

## CHAPTER XII. On the terms “to be able by power,” “to be able by justice,” and “to be able by mercy”: whether they are convertible with one another in a proposition.

[Note: [Col. 0834D] Master, *Four Books of Sentences*, distinction 46.] Since “to be able” and “to will” are said of God according to essence, there is a question about such terms as “to be able by power,” “to be able by justice,” and “to be able by mercy”: whether they are said of God according to essence. [Col. 0834B] This seems so, because they are said of the individual persons and of all of them together. Hence it seems that whatever God can do by justice, he can do by mercy and by power, and conversely. But God can damn all by justice; therefore he can damn all by mercy as well, which seems false.

That he can damn all by justice is manifest, because all are born children of wrath, and all belong to the mass of iniquity lost and corrupted in Adam. If anyone is extracted from it through the addition of some grace, this is by God’s mercy. Therefore he could damn all by justice. Again, God can damn all by power; God can do nothing except justly; therefore God can damn all by justice. Conversely, if someone says [Col. 0834C] that God cannot do everything by mercy which he can do by justice, then God can do something justly and not mercifully. Therefore justice and mercy do not accompany each other in every one of his works—or justice; therefore some work of his can be without justice or without mercy.

Therefore some have said that in certain works of God there is an effect of mercy without an effect of justice: for example, in baptized infants, who are saved by God’s grace alone and without preceding merits. In other works there is an effect of justice without an effect of mercy: for example, in punishing Judas and Pilate, whom he cannot punish more than he punishes them. In still others there is an effect of justice together with an effect of mercy: for example, in those who are saved.

[Note: [Col. 0834D] In the Master here, from Augustine.] They seem to prove this in many ways by authority. For we read: “Mercy here, judgment in the future”; and elsewhere: “Judgment without mercy shall befall the one who has not shown mercy” (James 2). And again: “According to the measure of guilt will be the measure of punishment”; and similarly, on that verse of the Psalm [Note: [Col. 0834D] Psalm 71 [Vulgate 72], where Augustine reads: “More evil is found in punishments than was committed in sins.”]: “From usury and iniquity,” there is the statement: “More is exacted in punishments than was committed in sins.” They also seek to establish this by reasoning. God can deal strictly with Judas; therefore not mercifully. [Col. 0835A] Again, God can remit none of the punishment owed by Judas; but if he remits none of the punishment owed, he acts without mercy in punishing; therefore God can act without mercy toward Judas.

To this some reply that, even if God remitted none of the punishment owed by Judas, he would not act without mercy toward him, because he would preserve him in being, which is the greatest mercy; or because he would not permit devils to punish him more than he had deserved. There are infinitely many other hidden ways in which God could bestow an effect of mercy even if he remitted none of the owed punishment.

There are two effects of justice, manifest and hidden. The manifest effect is that God repays punishment, or a portion of punishment, for sin. Human ignorance does not presume to determine the hidden effect. For who [Col. 0835B] knows why God chose Jacob and rejected Esau? Similarly, there are two effects of mercy, manifest and hidden. God’s mercy is manifest in baptized infants, although hidden justice is also present there. Justice is manifest in the damned, although hidden mercy is present there. Therefore, in no work of God is there an effect of justice without an effect of mercy, whether hidden or manifest; nor conversely.

The saying, “Mercy here, judgment in the future,” thus refers to the manifestation of each. For here, in the wayfarer’s state, mercy is manifest, where the days of humanity and the year of jubilee are spoken of, although justice too is present here. Justice will be manifest in the future, when “these shall go into eternal life, but those into eternal punishment” [Col. 0835C] (Matthew 25). Likewise, when it is said, “According to the measure of guilt will be the measure of punishment,” this means: if guilt is great, punishment will be great—not, I say, equal in amount. For God will punish individual sins, and hence is said to judge strictly. But he remits some of the punishment owed for each, and in this lies God’s mercy.

When it is said, “Judgment without mercy shall occur,” and so on, supply: “without mercy,” that is, judgment which will appear to be without mercy because of the magnitude of the punishment. Likewise, the subsequent statement, “More is exacted in punishments,” and so forth, must be referred to duration, because punishments will be longer, since they are eternal, than offences, which were temporal. Or “more” means that a human being is punished in more respects than he sinned, [Col. 0835D] because he is punished in soul and body for a sin committed in the soul alone. Those who solve the matter thus solve it plausibly [Note: [Col. 0835] These points are founded on Augustine’s teaching on the cited Psalm 71 [Vulgate 72].].

Others hold differently. They say that God can remit none of the punishment owed by Judas, and that God can do this by power, but not by mercy or justice. For by power he can do many things which he cannot do by mercy, such as damning all persons. Whether this is so, however, will be determined after setting out certain people’s solutions.
