For some say that the proposition, “God can remit none of the punishment owed by Judas,” can be understood in two ways: in the composite sense and in the divided sense. If understood in the composite sense, it is false [Col. 0836A]: for it is impossible that Judas should have deserved so great a punishment and that God should remit none of it, since this would be contrary to God’s mercy. But if you understand it in the divided sense—Judas has deserved such a punishment; God can remit none of this punishment—it is true. Yet then it does not follow that God can act without mercy toward him, for if God remitted none of so great a punishment, Judas would have deserved a punishment greater than this.

That this composite sense is impossible is proved by another case: it is impossible that God should reward Peter with a lesser reward than he has deserved, if you understand it in the composite sense; for then God would deprive Peter of his merit. Yet, if you understand it separately, you speak truly. Similarly, it is impossible that God should afflict someone with a punishment more severe than he has deserved, if you understand it in the composite sense, because [Col. 0836B] he would then deal cruelly with that person. But if you speak in the divided sense, you speak truly.

Some, however, proceeding further, accept both the composite and divided senses, and—what is more—hold that God can damn Peter and save Judas. If he damned Peter, he would do well; and if he remitted none of the punishment owed by Judas, he would do well, and would not thereby act without mercy toward him, even if in no other respect he displayed toward him an effect of mercy. For there is no evil which, if he does it, he does not do well.

They show as follows that God can damn Peter. God can deal strictly with Peter; but if he deals strictly, he exacts an account of pennies and farthings. If he pursued every item, Peter could not render an account of everything, because throughout his life he was bound to service, and at many times did not render the service owed, which service he could not repay to God. Therefore, if God afterwards dealt strictly, he could justly damn him, since he could do so justly.

But someone will say that Peter humbled himself very profoundly, so that the humility shown in his repentance was greater than the transgression involved in his fault; and thus he made recompense for the due service by which he seemed to have defrauded God. Yet they still say that he could not humble himself so greatly that he was not bound to show God a greater humility, nor serve God so devoutly that he was not bound to serve him more devoutly—not by precept, I say, but by reason of the reward bestowed or to be bestowed: [Col. 0836D] “The sufferings of this present world are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us” (Rom. 8).

But they press the point again: Peter died deserving life, and Judas deserving death; therefore God could neither save the latter nor condemn the former, unless, both having been restored to their former state, Peter died deserving death and Judas deserving life. Otherwise he would condemn one worthy of life or save one unworthy; but it could not be that he should save those unworthy of life while they remained unworthy, or condemn those unworthy of death while they remained unworthy. For the one would be cruelty, the other injustice. Therefore God cannot [Col. 0837A] save Judas or condemn Peter unless each is restored to the state of life.

Again, God remitted to Peter the guilt of sin, and it is necessary that he have remitted it; nor afterward could or can Peter sin. Therefore God cannot impute to him guilt that has been remitted without acting unjustly. To this they reply: if God remitted the guilt of Peter’s sin, and Peter thus died, God will not condemn him. But it does not follow that, if he remitted it, he cannot impute it; just as, if someone is predestined, God will not condemn him; but it does not follow that, if he is predestined, God cannot condemn him. For by the same reasoning by which they admit, as they say, “God cannot condemn anyone who has died worthy of life,” because these two things cannot coexist—that he died worthy of life and that he is condemned—it seems, according to [Col. 0837B] them, that one must admit that God cannot condemn anyone who is predestined, because these two things cannot coexist: that someone is predestined and is afterward condemned. But this is invalid. One cannot fail to have died worthy of life when one has died thus; but someone can fail to be predestined although he has been predestined.

Indeed, I do not see how it can be certain that God can condemn someone who remains worthy of life and, if he does so, act not unjustly but justly—unless by the same reasoning it is said that God can commit homicide, adultery, or theft, and, if he does so, do so justly. Therefore we approve the first solution more, since it is more common and customary.

It is customary to ask whether the justice of God requires whatever [Col. 0837C] the mercy of God requires. For if God’s mercy requires that Judas be punished less than he deserved, God’s justice requires the same. Therefore it is just that Judas be punished less than he deserved. Again, whatever pleases supreme justice is just; supreme justice is pleased that Judas be punished less than he deserved. This does not follow, because in the first proposition “just” is taken to mean “pleasing to divine justice,” whereas in the conclusion it is referred to the demand of merits. The objection must therefore be put thus: Whatever pleased supreme justice was just; supreme justice was pleased that Christ should be crucified. Since this is referred to the demand of merits, it seems that it must be denied.

Some, however, distinguish the several senses of such expressions: “It is just that Judas be punished less,” that is, it is pleasing to the divine essence—this is true. “It is just,” that is, Judas’s merits require this—this is false. Likewise, one must simply deny that God’s justice requires Judas to be punished less than he deserved, because of the connotation of the term “justice.” For when it is said in this way, it principally signifies that God, who is just, requires this—that this pleases God as just. But it also suggests that he approves Judas’s merits, the demand of which would bring about a remission for him. Similarly, when it is said, “The mercy of God requires that Judas be punished less than he deserved,” it principally signifies that God, who is merciful, requires this; but it suggests that Judas’s merits would require him to be punished more severely. [Note: [Col. 0837D] The same material in the Master, IV, distinction 45, § c.]

For when one says, “God is [Col. 0838A] just,” or “God is justice,” the divine essence is predicated, and it is also intimated that he is the distributor and judge of merits. Similarly, when God is called good in essence, he is shown also to be Father and, in addition, the author of all good things. Hence some works are called works of mercy and others works of justice, although justice and mercy there are altogether the same thing. But certain works display him as distributor and equitable judge; these are called works of justice, as when he punishes a human being for sin. Others display him as one who has compassion and delivers; these are called works of mercy, as when he remits a punishment due to a human being. Thus in some works there is said to be an effect of justice, in others an effect of mercy—not because justice effects something other than mercy if you refer them to the [Col. 0838B] essence, but because from some effects he is understood as judge, and from others as compassionate.

Accordingly, one must grant that the mercy of God requires Judas to be punished less than he is punished, while God’s justice requires that he be punished according to his merits. From this it appeared that two contrary things please God as just and God as merciful: namely, that Judas be punished according to his merits, which pleases God’s justice, and that he be punished short of his merits, which pleases God’s mercy. Thus, since justice requires punishment according to merits, mercy punishment short of merits, and whatever mercy or justice requires pleases God, it follows that God is pleased that Judas be punished according to merits and short of merits—two contraries which cannot coexist.

But this does not follow, for [Col. 0838C] these two statements are not of the same kind. When it is said, “Mercy requires that Judas be punished short of his merits,” the meaning is: Judas is punished short of his merits, with God’s mercy requiring this; and this is properly said. But from this sense one does not say: “Justice requires that Judas be punished according to his merits.” For he is not punished as much as he deserved, with justice requiring it; rather, the indicative is used for the subjunctive, as though one said: God, being just, would require this if he considered all Judas’s merits. Thus one says: “It is just that a man who is for the time being worthy of death be condemned,” that is, it would be just if he died in that condition. And: “It is good for me to take medicine,” that is, it would be good if I took it.

Some, however, arguing to the contrary, admit [Col. 0838D] that God’s mercy requires whatever God’s justice requires him to do, and that God’s justice likewise requires whatever God’s mercy requires him to do. They seek to establish this as follows. God’s justice requires him to do whatever he does; and God punishes Judas through mercy, short of his merits. Therefore God’s justice requires that he punish Judas through mercy, short of his merits. Thus God does nothing to Judas except what strict justice requires to be done; therefore he spares him in no respect.

Again, God’s justice requires that he exercise mercy in all his works; therefore God’s justice requires that he deal mercifully with everyone. By the same reasoning, God’s mercy requires him to do what is just in everything that he does; he does nothing except justly. Therefore God’s mercy requires him to do what is just, and hence what justice requires. [Col. 0839A] Thus God’s mercy requires whatever God’s justice requires, and conversely.

To this it must be said that, if such names are taken without the connotation of effects, what is proposed is true. But if you refer them to their principal signification and additionally understand the difference of their effects, it is false. Therefore one should not grant: “Justice requires that he do through mercy whatever he does,” but only: “Justice requires that he do it.” But then the further inference, “God mercifully punishes Judas; therefore God’s justice requires that he mercifully punish Judas,” is false; for, when first the thing done is stated, afterward the manner is introduced, which is indicated by the adverb: this is a fallacy. “Whatever this man does, that man does; this man reads well; therefore that man reads well.”

Again, the effect of God’s justice is to punish [Col. 0839B] according to merits; the effect of mercy is to punish short of merits. He cannot observe both these effects simultaneously in punishing Judas. Therefore in this work he does not simultaneously exercise the effect of justice and the effect of mercy. But it does not follow that, if he cannot exercise simultaneously these two effects, which are opposed—namely, to punish Judas only to the full extent that he deserved to be punished, and to remit part of the punishment—he therefore cannot simultaneously exercise two other effects. For, as stated above, he can inflict the whole punishment due; in that case he will not preserve the effect of mercy by punishing less than Judas deserved. But he preserves it in other respects: for example, by preserving Judas in existence, by not allowing demons to rage against him more than he deserved, and in many other respects unknown to us which are hidden effects of mercy.

[Col. 0839C] Hence one must say that the effect of God’s justice should not here be stated as “to punish to the full extent that he deserved to be punished,” but “to punish to the extent that he deserved,” stated indefinitely. Then this effect of justice will not be opposed to the effect of mercy, and God can exercise both simultaneously in one work. For that he punishes will be from justice; that he punishes short of merits will be from mercy.

Again, for God to be merciful and to be just is the same thing; God is exceedingly merciful and exceedingly just. Therefore he is as merciful as he is just; and conversely, in all his works the effect of justice is simultaneous with the effect of mercy. Therefore, because he punishes Judas justly, he punishes him equally mercifully. But insofar as he punishes him justly, he inflicts so much of the punishment due; and insofar as he punishes him mercifully, he remits so much of the punishment. Therefore he remits to Judas as much of the punishment due as he inflicts; therefore he could justly punish twice as much.

It must therefore be noted that when it is said, “God is as just as he is merciful,” if this is referred to the essence, it means nothing, since comparison is not admitted in substantial matters. If it is referred to effects, it is true that in some works the effects of justice appear more strongly, and in others those of mercy more strongly. Yet both are present in all works, just as every human being knows grammar and music, though some know more grammar and others more music.

Again: the effect of justice is to punish only to the extent [Col. 0840A] that one deserved; therefore, if God inflicted the whole punishment, he would be most just. Or thus: the effect of mercy is to punish less than one deserved; therefore, if he wholly remitted the punishment, he would be most merciful. To this it must be said that, if you understand “he would be most just” as meaning that this effect of justice would be greatest, it is true.

Again, God provided from eternity how great a punishment he would inflict upon Judas; therefore he can remit none of it, or else his providence can change. This is false. God predestined from eternity those who are to be saved; therefore those to be saved cannot be damned, or else God’s predestination can change.

## Chapter XIII. On God’s Knowledge

[Note: [Col. 0839D] The Master, I, distinctions 38 and 39.]

Just as the names “just” and “merciful,” when said of God, have the same principal signification but connote different things, so also such names as “foreknowing,” “predestining,” and the like have the same principal signification—the divine essence which they predicate—but posit different effects in things. For the cause of the effects signified by them is the same; therefore, according to their differing suppositions, different attributions are made. Thus, although the terms “divine charity” and “essence” signify the same thing, a different thing is supposited when the supposition is made through the term “charity,” and another when it is made through the other term.

Hence it is truly said: “The divine essence is in a stone,” yet “God’s charity is not in a stone.” For in the latter statement it is principally signified that the divine essence is in the stone; yet the force of the term [Col. 0840C] additionally implies that God makes it a lover of God and neighbor. But when one says, “The divine essence is in something,” nothing is connoted or implied, because this term connotes or implies nothing.

Because of these significations, although in God essence and charity, knowledge and foreknowledge, predestination, and so on, are the same, nevertheless not everything that is truly said of essence is truly said of charity, nor everything said of mercy of justice, and similarly in other cases. In some cases their differing connotations are discerned from their origin or composition, as in “foreknowledge” and “predestination.” For the prefix *prae-* denotes priority, as though knowledge makes that thing known before it comes to pass. Thus, “God foreknew things,” that is, he knew them before they came to be; and “he predestined the elect,” that is, before they existed, he destined good things for them.

Hence when I say, “God predestines the good” and “God foreknows evils,” the same thing is predicated, but different things are implied. We must therefore treat such terms in order, and first knowledge.

God’s knowledge concerns goods and evils alike, things past, present, and future, and beings and non-beings, as some say; because “He calls those things which are not as though they were” (Rom. 4). Again, God had knowledge of things before they came to be, nor did things become known to him differently after they existed than before they existed. Therefore he knew things before they existed; therefore all things were subject to his knowledge before [Col. 0841A] they existed.

Again, I can beget a son; therefore a son can be begotten by me. God knows concerning him whatever he would know if he existed; nor would he have greater knowledge of him if he existed than he now has when he does not exist, nor would he know him differently as regards himself. Therefore my son is subject to divine knowledge. Thus it seems that God has knowledge of all non-beings and of everything; because, even if they do not exist, he would not now know more of them if they existed, nor know them differently, as regards himself, from how he knows them now when they do not exist.

But someone will object: “The son who can be begotten by me is the subject of divine knowledge; therefore he exists.” This inference is invalid, they say. Some also say that non-beings are subjects of God’s will because he wills that they be or not be, and wills many other things concerning them. [Col. 0841B] But in that way it would follow that no more things are subjects of power than of will, just as when one says, “This will be; therefore it is,” or, “It is past; therefore it is.”

But it is asked why non-beings are not called subjects of the divine essence and power. For just as God knows that which is not—that is, has knowledge concerning that which is not—so he can do that which is not—that is, he has power concerning that which is not, though it does not come to be. But only beings are subjects of his will, because he wills nothing except what exists; and therefore no non-beings are subjects of his will. For his power, or foreknowledge, is broader than his will; that is, more things are subjects of power and knowledge than of will.

Again, they object thus: More things are known by God than are beings; therefore the number of things known by God is greater [Col. 0841C] than the number of beings. This is false. More human beings will rise again than are alive; therefore the number of those who will rise is greater than that of the living.

37. It is also asked, since God knows non-beings—that is, has knowledge concerning them—whether he knows all non-beings, that is, has knowledge concerning all of them, or whether all are subjects of his knowledge. Some say that he has awareness of all things, but does not have knowledge of all things, nor does he know all things; just as I have awareness of astronomy, yet do not know astronomy, and astronomy is not the subject of my knowledge. For God knows only those things that were going to be. Therefore those possible things which can be true but were never going to be true, he does not know, nor has he knowledge concerning them. By the same reasoning, he does not know propositions that are merely matters of opinion and never were going to be true in reality.

Yet it can be proved to them that he knows also possible things which were never going to be true, just as it can be proved against those who say that only propositions are subjects of God’s knowledge. God also has knowledge of the son who can be begotten by me, though he is never begotten, if one proceeds in the manner stated above. Therefore others grant that God knows all possible and impossible things, because whatever things exist and can exist, and also many things that cannot exist but which God could nevertheless make, are subjects of God’s knowledge. For God knows concerning things that cannot exist—for example, that someone should be both a human being and an ass, or something of that sort—what kind and how great they would be if they existed, and how these things would have God bring them to completion; and he knows them in the same manner as though they existed. Likewise, concerning things that will be, he knows what kind and how great they will be, when they will be brought to completion by God, and when they will be. According to these thinkers, it follows that God can know nothing that he does not know.

But against this there is the objection: God knows whatever he can know; he does not do whatever he can do; therefore he can do more things than he can know—which is false according to the foregoing, since indeed he knows whatever he can do. The inference is false. Every pair of human beings is a pair of animals; not every pair of animals is a pair of human beings; therefore there are more pairs of animals than pairs of human beings.

Again, God can know each and every thing; he can make each and every thing; therefore he cannot make more things than he can know. Although the conclusion [Col. 0842B] of this argument is true, it may nevertheless be challenged thus: Whatever things exist can exist; therefore no more things can exist than exist. But, once the conclusion is granted, someone proceeds: God cannot make more things than he knows, nor conversely, and he does not make more things than he knows; therefore he does not know more things than he makes. This is false. No more human beings can exist than animals can exist, and conversely; no more human beings exist than animals exist; therefore no more animals exist than human beings.

Again, whatever God can make he can know; he can begin to make some things; therefore he can begin to know some things. This is false. Whatever you can read, you can be going to read; you can begin to read; therefore you can begin to be going to read.

Again, many things can exist which never will exist, concerning which some propositions can be true that are not true. God can know these truths, and does not now know them; if those truths were counted together with those truths now known by God, there would be more truths than those now known by God. Yet God is said to know all those truths without ceasing to know any of those which he now knows. Therefore he can know more truths than he now knows, and thus more things.

On the other hand: no more propositions can exist than are propositions; therefore no more truths can exist than are truths; nor can more falsehoods exist than are falsehoods; therefore no more things can be known by God than are known by God.

To this they reply that “God knows truths” is said in one way, [Col. 0842D] and other things in another. When one says, “God knows that Peter is an apostle,” the meaning is that this is understood to be so in the thing itself—in Peter—as it is, namely, that Peter is an apostle. This is the proper signification of the verb “to know,” according to which only truths are known and falsehoods are not known. Thus one says, “I know that I am a human being,” that is, I understand in my mind that it is so in reality as it is said to be: “Peter is a human being.” For it would not be so in reality that I was a human being unless I knew this—neither I nor anyone else. Hence, if one wishes to speak properly, no falsehood is known.

Yet falsehood, and anything else whatsoever, is also said to be known by God, that is, God has knowledge concerning every thing, anything whatever is a subject of his knowledge, and anything whatever becomes known to him. Even things which do not exist and cannot exist become known to him [Col. 0843A] and are subjects of his knowledge, because he knows something concerning all of them, namely, that they exist or that they do not exist.

In this sense some say that God cannot know things other than those he knows, and can do nothing that he does not know. But some understand this thus: that whatever he does not know is not a subject of his knowledge. This is false, because according to them what does not exist is not a subject of God’s knowledge, and God can make what does not exist. But if you understand “he can do nothing that he does not know” as “he can do nothing that he would not know if he did it,” it is true.

[Note: [Col. 0843D] The Master, I, distinction 39, §.]

These thinkers admit that God can begin to know something, that is, something can begin to be a subject of his knowledge; because everything that can begin would exist, and nothing is attributed to God when it is said, “God begins to know this.” For the change is in the thing subject to knowledge, not in knowledge. Either of these opinions is quite probable. But whatever is to be said about them, one must in no way say that God can know more truths than he knows. For if, concerning another thing which can exist but does not exist, he knew that it existed—which he does not now know, for it does not exist—he would no longer know of it the contradictorily opposite proposition, namely that it does not exist, which nevertheless he now knows. Therefore he cannot know more truths than he knows. Yet he can know other truths that he does not know, and fail to know other truths that he knows; and this is easy to show.

Something can be going to be true which will never be true; therefore it will never be known. By the same reasoning, it is neither known nor has been known; therefore something can be going to be true which [Col. 0843C] was in no way going to be known by God; therefore something can be true which is not known by God. Whatever can be true can be known by God; therefore something can be known by God which is not known by God.

By the same reasoning the contrary will be proved. Something known by God can fail to be known by God; for something that is true can fail to be going to be true. Therefore something known by God can fail to be going to be known by God. But when this is granted, someone less skilled may think he can conclude: “God can rightly fail to know something that exists; therefore he can forget something.” This must not be granted. For it would posit that God had first known some truth and afterward did not know it, which is impossible.

Accordingly, this argument must be challenged thus: God can know something which does not exist; therefore he can learn it. But because this is almost the same argument and of the same kind, elsewhere it is put thus: “These persons know this thing and did not previously know it; granting that only one of them knew it; therefore these persons learn it.”

Again, God can fail to know a truth which he knows; therefore his knowledge can diminish. Or he can know a truth which he does not know; therefore his knowledge can increase. This is false. This man sees something which he did not see; therefore his sight is keener than it was. Or he does not see what he saw; therefore his sight is keener.

Again, God can know another truth which he does not know; [Col. 0844A] therefore he can begin to know it. Or God can fail to know another truth which he knows; therefore he can cease to know it. This is false. Someone can be predestined who is not predestined; therefore he can begin to be predestined. Or someone who is predestined can fail to be predestined; therefore he can cease to be predestined. Or some soul can be to be saved which is not to be saved; therefore it can begin to be to be saved. In all these cases, one well trained in dialectical subtlety will identify the fallacy of composition and division.

Why it must not be granted that God can begin to know something is clear. For the meaning is: that which he had not previously known, he afterward knew; this cannot coexist with it, just as truth can be false and is not false, yet cannot begin to be false. For this would mean that it had first been true and afterward became false, which is impossible.

Nevertheless, according to those who say that truth and falsehood vary with respect to a proposition, I do not see how this can be true: “God will begin to know this truth” (which would occur because God would know that Antichrist exists, whereas now he does not know that Antichrist exists); therefore he will begin to know this, without there being a change in God’s knowledge. Unless it is said that the divine essence is not predicated when one says, “God knows this,” just as when one says, “God does this,” as some maintain.

[Note: [Col. 0843D] The Master, I, distinction 36, § A.]

Again, all things are in God’s knowledge, and knowledge is the same as essence or nature; therefore all things [Col. 0844C] are in God’s essence or nature. But to be in God’s knowledge is to be of the same essence. Therefore one must not grant that all things are in God’s essence, although they are in his knowledge. Augustine shows this thus: [Note: [Col. 0843D] Sermon II, *On the Words of the Apostle*.] “God had with himself all the elect, not in his nature or essence, but in knowledge or foreknowledge.”

This is a fallacy. God and essence are the same; God is God of all things. But God knows evils as well as goods, and conversely; therefore all things are in God through knowledge, and thus evils too. Therefore, if evils are in him through knowledge, they are from him and through him, because this is the same thing, as Ambrose says [Note: [Col. 0844D] Book II, *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 10.] concerning things that are good. Therefore good things are in God both through knowledge and through approval. Hence one says simply: “Good things are in God; evil things are not in God,” because evils are not in him through approval. [Col. 0844D] Therefore one says simply, “Good things are in God,” though through knowledge; but one does not simply say, “Evils are in God.”

## Chapter XIV. On God’s Foreknowledge

[Note: [Col. 0844D] The Master, I, distinction 35.]

Having settled the matters that seemed to require inquiry concerning knowledge, we must next discuss matters commonly investigated concerning foreknowledge. Foreknowledge concerns future evils as well as future goods.

The following objection is raised concerning foreknowledge: if there were no future things, there would be no foreknowledge in God. [Note: [Col. 0844D] The Master, § b.] To be foreknowledge is the same for God as to be knowledge. To be knowledge is the same for God as to be essence. Therefore, if there were no future things, there would be no essence in God; and thus, if there were no future things, there would be no divine essence.

Again, to be God is the same for God as to be foreknowing. It is possible for God not to foreknow certain things; therefore it is possible for God not to be God.

[Note: [Col. 0845D] The Master, § c.]

In resolving these arguments and similar ones, we say that in such composite names and similar expressions there is involved an understanding of the divine essence and of a temporal relation existing in creatures. For the simple noun signifies the divine essence, while the prefix signifies the temporal relation that exists in creatures. The divine essence is called foreknowledge with respect to creatures.

Therefore, if it is said, “If God were not going to do other things, there would be no divine essence which is foreknowledge,” this is false. But if it is said thus, “If God were not going to do other things, there would be no foreknowledge,” that is, God’s essence would not be called “foreknowledge,” a name it receives with respect to creatures—this is true. Similar statements must be resolved in the same way. It was possible for God not to foreknow certain things, and it was possible for nothing to be subject to the divine essence from which it would be called foreknowledge, or from which God would be called foreknowing; and the rest must be explained in this way.

Again, to be God and to be foreknowing are the same for God; God will always be God; therefore he will always be foreknowing; therefore there will always be future things. This seems contrary to Origen, who says that after the day of judgment there will be no future things—perhaps this should be understood of creatures, substances, or new kinds of things, since after the day of judgment the reprobate will pass from snowy waters into excessive heat, and this reciprocal passage will continue eternally. According to Cassiodorus also, future hope seems to be vocal praise.

Fallacy of the preceding argument.—To be essence and to be God are the same; God is God of all things; therefore he is the essence of all things. Or thus: essence and charity are the same; the essence of God is in this stone; therefore the charity of God is in this stone.

Again: God knows nothing that he cannot foreknow; therefore knowing and foreknowing are not the same for him. This is false. God knows nothing that he cannot will; therefore knowing and willing are not the same for him. For he knows sins. Or thus: he wills many things, and none of them can exist; therefore willing and existing are not the same for him.

Again, the foreknowledge of this thing was in God and was God, and God now does not foreknow this thing; therefore the foreknowledge of this thing is not now in God and is not God; and thus something was God which is not God. Therefore distinguish: “The foreknowledge of this thing was in God and was God; now it is neither in God nor God”—that is, the knowledge by which he foreknew this thing was in God and was God, but now neither—is false. But if it is understood thus: formerly it could truly be said, “God foreknew this thing,” and that foreknowledge is God; but now this cannot truly be said—this is true.

[Col. 0846A] Again, when this thing had not yet existed, and the knowledge God had concerning it was called foreknowledge, there was some reason why it was called foreknowledge whereas it is not so called now. If there was no reason, then it ought not then more to have been called foreknowledge than now; and therefore, just as God foreknew this thing then, so does he now. But if some reason is said to have existed why that knowledge was called foreknowledge, that reason either exists now or does not. If it exists, then by the same reasoning by which God’s knowledge was called foreknowledge of this thing, it is so called now as well. If it does not exist now but did then, it was either in the Creator or in the creature. It was not in the creature, because this creature did not then exist. If it was in the Creator and is not now in him, then something was in the Creator then which is not now; and thus there is change in God.

“Some have said that from the predication or removal of one relation or several relations concerning or from something, it does not follow that a thing or several things are posited in, or removed from, something. For they say that relations are nothing other than being referred to or being spoken of relatively. Hence they say that Aristotle declared that those things are relatives for which being itself consists somehow in standing in relation to something else. If the predication or removal of a relation entailed the predication or removal of a thing, it could at once be proved that upon the destruction of one smallest thing, as many things are destroyed as there are in the world, because there are that many relations, likenesses, or differences. Just as a coin is now the price of one thing and afterward will cease [Col. 0846C] to be the price of that same thing, yet there is no change in the coin, so likewise in God’s knowledge when it ceases to be foreknowledge.”

Again, when God foreknows future things, he wills to foreknow them as he foreknows them, and in the manner in which he foreknows them. But he wills nothing except good. Therefore that he foreknows future things, and foreknows them in the manner in which he does, is good. Therefore God’s foreknowledge is good in all future things; therefore it is good in foreknowing that this person will sin.

They therefore say that foreknowledge is good, and God wills that it be fulfilled; yet he does not will that person to sin, although it cannot otherwise be fulfilled. Nor does he will to foreknow sins; yet he foreknows them, just as he willed to be truthful in saying, “Peter, you will deny me three times” (Matt. 26:34). Yet he could not be truthful unless Peter denied him; nevertheless he did not will Peter to deny him. Similarly, when I confess a sin, I will to be truthful, but not that I have sinned.

Others say that although God’s foreknowledge is good in all things, it is not to be fulfilled in all things: permission was given concerning a writ of divorce, yet it was not to be done; and Abraham was commanded to sacrifice his son, yet it was not to be done. The same applies in the case of the blind man.

Others distinguish thus: God’s foreknowledge is good in all things, that is, it is good that everything which God foreknows, and in the manner in which he foreknows it, be accomplished in deed and brought into effect. But if “God’s foreknowledge is good in all things” is understood thus—namely, that it is good that whatever God foreknows, and as he foreknows it, should be known in its actual being when it comes to pass, and also beforehand—then it is true.

It is also customary to ask whether foreknowledge is the cause of future things, or conversely. They seek to show that divine foreknowledge is the cause of an event as follows. [Note: [Col. 0847D] The Master, I, distinction 37.] Either it is possible or impossible for things not to be going to happen when they are foreknown by God. But it is possible; therefore it is possible for God’s foreknowledge to be mistaken. But it is impossible; therefore, by the same reasoning, it is impossible for things to happen otherwise.

Again: it is possible for things to happen otherwise than they happen; but if they happen otherwise, they are foreknown otherwise; therefore [Col. 0847B] it is possible for things to happen otherwise than they are foreknown.

Again: it is impossible for things to happen otherwise than they are foreknown; things would not happen unless they were foreknown by God; therefore divine foreknowledge is the cause of things that happen. Augustine’s authority also supports this: [Note: [Col. 0847D] Book XV, *On the Trinity*, chapter 13.] “He knows all creatures, bodily as well as spiritual, not because they are, but they are because he knows them.”

But if divine foreknowledge is called the cause of things that happen, since foreknowledge concerns evils as well as goods, it will be the cause not only of goods but also of evils. Conversely, Origen seems to say that things are the cause of divine foreknowledge: [Note: [Col. 0848D] In the exposition of chapter 8 of the Epistle to the Romans.] “Something is not future because God knows it to be future; rather, because it is future, it is known by God before it comes to pass.” Yet if this is said, it seems false: the created is not the cause of the uncreated, the mutable of the immutable, nor the temporal of the eternal.

[Col. 0847C] But the foregoing arguments are easily resolved by identifying the fallacy of composition and division in the premises. For when it is said, “It is impossible for things to happen otherwise than as they are foreknown,” if this is understood compositionally—that is, it is impossible for these two things to be together, namely, that things happen thus and are foreknown otherwise—it is true. But if it is understood divisionally—“It is impossible for things to happen otherwise than as they are foreknown,” that is, things are foreknown thus, and it is impossible for them to happen otherwise—it is false. The authorities that seem contrary to this are readily reconciled by a brief exposition. In those passages that appear to maintain that foreknowledge is the cause of the occurrence of things, knowledge together with good pleasure must be fitted to the word “knows”:

[Col. 0847D] “He knows,”

for good pleasure is the cause of all good things, as in the authority, “All creatures,” etc. For in the statement “He knows,” knowledge and good pleasure are understood. Or “because” may indicate a cause without which something does not occur; or it may be an inferential, not a causal, conjunction. That is: if God knows certain things, they will be, have been, or will come to be. Thus, when it is said, “Because Socrates is a human being, Socrates is an animal,” “because” is inferential: it indicates that, if Socrates is a human being, we can infer that he is an animal. It is not causal there, since humanity is not the cause of animality, any more than animality is the cause of

[Col. 0848A] humanity; hence one says, “Because Socrates is an animal, Socrates is a human being.” In the contrary authorities, however, “because” indicates a cause without which something does not occur, as in “not therefore,” etc.; or *quia* is used in the sense of “that.”

Again: “God’s knowledge is God, nor is it any creature.” By this expression one truly speaks of something, but only of an essence or person; therefore it is truly said of it that it is not the cause of creatures. Fallacy. “An idol is not natural”: by this expression one speaks of the body which is an idol; it is truly said that it is not natural, and the expression signifies only truth; therefore it is truly said of the body which is an idol that it is not natural.

Again: God foreknows only future things, and all things; therefore he foreknows only things that do not exist. But God foreknows that he will judge the world; therefore that God

[Col. 0848B] will judge the world does not exist, and thus it is not true, nor anything else. We say that God foreknows only future things and things that do not exist; and we say that a statement designating what is said does not always signify a truth, but sometimes an event—an event of which one says that God foreknows it. But when that statement formed from the combination of different words is used to designate an event, and when it is used to designate something capable of being asserted, the prudent investigator of the force of language should discern this.

Fallacy. “I see you sitting; ‘you are sitting’ is true; therefore I see a truth.”

Again: if God foreknew something, it is necessary that it occur. God foreknew this; therefore it is necessary that this occur. This is resolved by interpretation. But the objection is again pressed thus: If God

[Col. 0848C] foreknew something, it will occur; it is necessary that God foreknew this; therefore it is necessary that this occur. And this is false, through an interpretation of the assumption. For it is not necessary that God foreknew this, although this is stated in the past tense, because its occurrence concerns the future. Hence it also seems that God foreknows whatever he has foreknown; and the solution is clear, because God does not always foreknow whatever he once foreknows: he foreknows only future things. For it is either incongruous or false to say that he foreknows past or present things. God foreknew the world as to be created; he does not now foreknow this, because it is already past. This does not happen because of a defect in God’s knowledge, but rather because of the priority in time expressed by the word “I foreknow,” and because of the occurrence of the thing that was future.

[Col. 0848D] Nevertheless, whatever God once knows he always knows; that is, whatever is once subject to his knowledge is always subject to his knowledge. For whether it exists or does not exist, it is subject to his knowledge, since he does not cease to know something about it because it itself ceases to exist—unless someone wishes to say that nothing is subject to his knowledge unless it is the divine essence.

But whatever may be the case in these matters, it is true that God always knows as true what he once knows. Yet this seems false, because he once knew that the world was to be created, and now does not know that, which is false; therefore he knew some truth that he does not know. To this

[Col. 0849A] objection I see no solution unless it is said that God never knew that the world was to be created—that is, never knew this assertible proposition—because the world had always been made; but he always knew that the world had been created, both when it was created and before, as he knows it now. [Note: [Col. 0849D] *Magister*, I, distinction 44, final section, and more explicitly distinction 41, section “and b.”] For times and words vary, but the faith and the meaning remain the same; and this proposition says one thing now, while the former said something else previously, because one and the same truth is expressed in different propositions by words uttered according to the diversity of times. Nor should anyone mock this solution before understanding it, lest he seem to despise what has been said from hatred and invective rather than from a judgment of mind.

## CHAPTER XV. On matters common to predestination and reprobation

[Col. 0849B]

[Note: [Col. 0849D] *Magister*, distinctions 40 and 41.] In the order already indicated, we must treat of predestination and reprobation, and of matters concerning them together, because in very many respects they demand a similar treatment. Concerning predestination, therefore, the first point to consider is that it has a twofold effect. The first is the bestowal of grace in time; the second, the final reward of eternal life. Thus there are three things: eternal election, or predestination, or eternal love; the temporal bestowal of grace; and the final reward of life. And, oppositely, there are three: eternal reprobation, the temporal withdrawal of grace, and the infliction of unending punishment. The first is properly designated by the name “reprobation”; the second

[Col. 0849C] is properly called “hardening.” Yet sometimes hardening is used for reprobation, and conversely. Likewise eternal election is designated by the name “predestination,” while the second is called justification. For authors sometimes use these terms indiscriminately, as in this example: [Note: [Col. 0850D] Augustine, *On the Words of the Apostle*, Sermon II.]

> “Those who do not yet exist are chosen; nor does he who chooses err, nor does he choose in vain. Yet he chooses and has as chosen those whom he is going to create in order to be chosen.”

Distinguish, when you hear “he has as chosen,” that is, predestined from eternity, those whom he is going to create to be chosen by temporal election—that is, by the bestowal of grace.

Although these three are opposed to those three, they proceed in equal step in some respects but not in others. For just as eternal predestination has no merit as its cause, neither does eternal reprobation; otherwise,

[Col. 0849D] what is temporal would be the cause of what is eternal. Again, just as eternal predestination is the cause of the bestowal of grace, so eternal reprobation is the cause of the withdrawal of grace. But the deprivation of grace is not the cause of final damnation in the way that the bestowal of grace is the cause of final recompense; nor is reprobation the cause of wickedness in the way that predestination is the cause of goodness. Again, just as predestination is the cause of final recompense, so eternal reprobation is the cause of final damnation.

Yet one should not affirm without distinction that eternal reprobation is the cause of the temporal withdrawal of grace. For deprivation or withdrawal may be understood positively or negatively.

[Col. 0850A] If understood negatively, the statement is true: eternal reprobation is the cause why grace is not bestowed, but it is not the cause why a bestowed grace is withdrawn. Indeed, the cause of this is human merit. But both eternal reprobation and human merit are causes of the other matter—that is, of the non-bestowal of grace. Perverse merits seem to be, as it were, indications and conjectural signs of both non-bestowal and eternal reprobation. A person therefore merits that grace not be bestowed upon him; for whenever it is not bestowed on someone, we must suppose that this happens to him because his merits demand it. If he is not baptized, it is not bestowed because of original sin; if he is baptized, by sinning mortally he merits that grace already bestowed be withdrawn. For grace alone distinguishes the redeemed from the lost,

[Col. 0850B] whom the common cause of perdition kept condemned in the apostate root, so that, if no one were delivered, no one could rightly blame God’s justice.

So that what we have said concerning eternal predestination and reprobation may become clearer, we must state what predestination and reprobation are. Predestination is the preparation of grace by which God from eternity prepared, without merits, good things for the man Christ and for those whom he foreknew would be made conformed to the image of his Son. Reprobation is foreknowledge of wickedness and the preparation of unending punishment. Predestination, therefore, is considered in two respects concerning one object: namely, foreknowledge and preparation concerning benefits. Reprobation is considered in two respects

[Col. 0850C] concerning two objects: namely, foreknowledge concerning sins and preparation concerning punishments. For God foreknew both sins and punishments; but he prepared punishments, not sins. Accordingly, the first of the two foregoing operations is to be assigned to each of the two following objects, while the other is assigned to one alone.

From this the preceding statements are clear: namely, that predestination is the cause both of the bestowal of grace in time and of final recompense. Yet this seems false. For since predestination consists of two things, as was said—foreknowledge and preparation—either preparation will not be the cause of the temporal bestowal, or foreknowledge will be the cause of the same. This is shown as follows: Because God predestined Peter, he grants him grace in time; because he foreknew that he would be good,

[Col. 0850D] and prepared good things for him, he grants him grace in time; therefore, he grants it either because he prepared good things for him or because he foreknew. This also seems demonstrable from Augustine’s authority. For he says: [Note: [Col. 0850D] The same is attributed to Ambrose in the Gloss on Romans, chapter IX.]

> “God, foreknowing their future evil will, did not count them among the good; just as by foreknowledge he judged Pharaoh worthy of condemnation, knowing that he would not correct himself. But he chose the Apostle Paul, foreknowing, indeed, that he would be faithful.”

Again, just as God withholds from many—that is, does not grant—temporal office, because he knows of each what he would be like were he placed in power, and thus does not grant him office because of the tyranny

[Col. 0851A] he would exercise if he were in power and because of the evils he would commit; so, conversely by a similar argument, it can be said that, because of the good things God foreknows that a person will do, he gives him grace. Thus, just as evil merits which would be present if he had this are the cause why God does not wish to give him this, so the good things which he will have or would have may be the cause why God gives him grace or even earthly office before those merits have altogether come to be.

On the contrary, however, if foreknowledge is the cause why grace is bestowed on someone in time, the same seems to be the cause of temporal hardening, since foreknowledge concerns goods and evils equally. Yet Augustine says that foreknowledge is not the cause why grace is bestowed in time: [Note: [Col. 0851] This too is attributed to Ambrose in the Gloss on Romans, chapter IX.]

> “God judges by justice, not

[Col. 0851B] by foreknowledge; for justice, not God’s foreknowledge, is the reason why someone is worthy before God of eternal life.”

We must therefore know that God’s predestination is not the cause of temporal justification in respect of foreknowledge, but in respect of preparation—unless the word “because” indicates a cause without which the effect does not occur. If God did not foreknow, he would not bestow grace in time; but he bestows it because he prepared—that is, determined to give it—provided that by the name “determination” we understand good pleasure together with foreknowledge, as was said above concerning the word “knows.” It can properly be granted that because he foreknew—that is, because it was in the good pleasure of the one foreknowing—he therefore bestowed grace in time. Or, better, in assigning the cause of justification,

[Col. 0851C] one should not take preparation alone or foreknowledge alone, but these two together, just as they themselves are understood in the word “he predestined”: namely, because he foreknew and prepared, that is, because it was in the good pleasure and preparation of the one foreknowing that he should grant grace in time to the elect, and afterwards eternal life. Therefore he grants it.

From this it is understood that by “preparation” divine disposition is meant. For for God to prepare is nothing other than to dispose; nor is to dispose anything other than to be. Thus to prepare is the same as to be. Hence it is clear that the divine essence is predicated when I say, “Predestination is the preparation of grace,” that is, the disposition by which God disposed himself to grant grace in time to the elect. Thus God is principally signified as God, and a certain temporal effect concerning the elect is additionally implied,

[Col. 0851D] just as the divine essence also seems to be predicated when it is said, “God predestined this person.”

But this is objected to in many ways. “Because God willed, he predestined this person,” that is, God’s will and predestination [are involved]; therefore the same thing is the cause of itself. God’s being God and his being one who predestines are the same; therefore he is God by that by which he is one who predestines; therefore he is God by that by which he predestines. But God is God by the divine essence; therefore God predestines by the divine essence. Therefore grace alone does not predestine.

Again: God is God by that by which he predestines, and conversely. But God predestines by his grace; therefore grace is God.

Accordingly, some resolve this by saying that when it is said, “God, by that by which he is

[Col. 0852A] God, is one who predestines,” the name “predestining” retains its principal signification; and it is the same as if it were said, “By that by which he is God, he is the one who predestines.” But when it is said, “God predestines,” the verb is reduced to a co-signification. Nothing is attributed to God; rather, something concerning the elect is signified, as if one said: “By God’s grace,” that is, by his goodness, it is gratuitous that the elect were from eternity going to receive eternal rewards. Therefore, although one must admit, “The divine essence is predestining,” that is, “is that which predestines,” one must not grant, “The divine essence predestines.” Rather, grace alone predestines. For the verb, having lost its principal signification, is reduced to co-signification.

But someone argues against this solution: Does the verb everywhere lose its principal meaning?

[Col. 0852B] If so, then it is everywhere used improperly in the expression. Again, if this verb, when always said of God, indicates a temporal effect concerning the elect and never retains its principal signification, then it is not truly said, “God predestined the good from eternity,” because no such temporal effect exists from eternity. Again, God predestines by grace alone; therefore by temporal or eternal grace. If he predestines by temporal grace, that temporal grace seems to exist in God; otherwise this expression does not seem admissible—just as one does not say, “God created the world by creation,” because no such creation exists in God. But if it is said that eternal grace predestines, then the word “predestines,” said of God, indicates something eternal.

Again,

[Col. 0852C] God freely chose Peter from eternity; therefore from eternity he freely predestined Peter; and thus the divine essence is proved when this is said. Otherwise “from eternity” would have no place there. Again, the word “predestines,” said of God, indicates only a temporal effect concerning creatures; therefore God does not predestine anyone by anything through which he is God. But God’s predestination is God; therefore God does not predestine by the predestination that he himself is. Again, God’s being and predestining, being God and being one who predestines, are the same; therefore he predestines by that by which he is God; or else he is not one who predestines by that by which he is God.

Those who follow the aforesaid solution do not find it objectionable to say that a principal word signifies something and yet never retains

[Col. 0852D] its principal signification when placed in an expression. Thus the word *uter* (“which of two”) when placed in an expression never follows the proper construction of adjectives, because it is not construed with a word of the same case and number. And although the verb *praedestino* signifies an effect concerning creatures, they nonetheless admit, “God predestined this person from eternity,” because the signification of this verb encompasses all times whenever it is uttered, owing to its indeterminate signification. Hence no effect is indicated as past, or as having existed from eternity, by such an expression; just as, if it is said, “God was going to create the world,” no effect is indicated as having been past,

[Col. 0853A] even though a verb in the past tense is used there. But when it is said, “God predestines by grace,” they do not admit any adjective, such as “God predestines by temporal or eternal grace,” because the noun “grace” is used there quasi-adverbially: “by grace,” that is, “gratuitously.”

They press the final argument as follows: God’s being able and understanding, being omnipotent and intelligent, are the same; therefore he is powerful by that by which he is intelligent. They say this is false, because power is powerful, not intelligent; indeed intelligence is intelligent. To me it seems absurd to admit such claims. But someone says that it ought not be denied merely because the expression is awkward, since there is no falsehood in it. For the inconsequence of the wording

[Col. 0853B] does not prejudice the truth of what is said. Therefore it seems that the proposition should be rejected not only because of the expression’s inconsequence, but because the term “intelligence” signifies or additionally implies something that the term “power” does not in certain cases, when no co-signification or imposed usage can be discerned. Yet one cannot consistently attribute to one what is attributed to the other, where it is difficult to give a reason for the inconsequence or a reason why one is admitted rather than the other.

[Note: [Col. 0853] What follows to the end of the chapter is not found in the manuscript of the Library of Saint-Victor; instead, certain other matters from the following chapter have been wrongly inserted.]

Others proceed somewhat further in resolving the foregoing objections, admitting: “God predestines by that by which he is God”; nevertheless, the divine essence does not predestine, although the divine essence itself is God. For in the first proposition the verb has its principal signification,

[Col. 0853C] while in the conclusion it loses it and returns to co-signification. Thus they press this argument: “God, by that by which he is Father, is God; he is Father by fatherhood; therefore he is God by fatherhood.” If anyone denies the first premise, they prove it thus: God is Father by something and God by something; therefore, either by the same thing or another thing—or rather, the very thing by which he is Father and the very thing by which he is God are identical; therefore he is Father and God by the same thing.

But they do not admit what was said above concerning will, which seems to be the cause of predestination. For in that case the same thing would be the cause of itself. Nor does the word “because” signify a cause there; rather, it is inferential, so that the sense is: “Because God willed, he predestined this person,” that is, if he willed to predestine, he predestined. Or “he predestined” is taken for the temporal bestowal

[Col. 0853D] of grace, of which God’s eternal will is indeed the cause, as was shown above.

Some hold that the verb “I predestine” signifies the divine essence when it is said, “God predestined this person,” or “God loved this person from eternity,” which they say is the same thing. For principally it is signified that God is God, and it is additionally implied that from eternity this person was subject to his will, so that God might bestow grace on him in time and finally grant eternal life. But if to predestine and to love from eternity are the same, it does not seem that God loved Judas from eternity, because he did not predestine him. Yet it seems that he did love him from eternity,

[Col. 0854A] because from his goodness he bestowed grace upon Judas in time, and from eternity willed to do this; therefore from eternity he loved Judas—or loving and willing are not the same for him.

Fallacy. God preserves every creature in its being out of his goodness, and from eternity willed to do this; therefore God loves every creature from eternity. This does not seem so, because when it is said, “He loves Judas” or “an irrational creature,” it is the same as saying, “He preserves it in its being”; and nothing is attributed to God, but to the creature. Likewise, when it is said, “God loved Judas,” it is the same as saying, “He bestowed grace upon him in time.” Nor is anything attributed to God by expressions of this sort.

Again: God loves Judas or an irrational creature; therefore he loves by temporal or eternal love. If by eternal love, then

[Col. 0854B] God loves Judas from eternity; if by temporal love, then temporal love exists in God—which is false.

This must be answered by saying that the verb “loves,” when said of God as God, has three meanings: it is taken for predestining, preserving in being, and bestowing grace. In the first sense he loves all and only those who will be saved. In the second sense he loves every creature. In the third sense he loves all and only those who are now just, whether they are to be saved or damned. Its proper meaning when said of God is the first. Therefore only in respect of those whom God loves in that sense do we admit, “God loves this person from eternity,” and “God loves this person by the love that he himself is”; and the divine essence is thereby proved. Moreover, a certain effect

[Col. 0854C] concerning the creature is implied. But in respect of those whom God preserves in being, or on whom he bestowed grace in time without predestining them, it is not admitted that he loved them from eternity; rather, that he hated them from eternity. Hence: “Jacob I loved from eternity, but Esau I hated” (Romans IX).

But he does not love the latter by any temporal or eternal love, because that expression attributes nothing to God but rather to the creature. Since it is a figurative expression, no valid argumentative procedure follows if one concludes, “God loves this person by temporal or eternal love.” Again: God loves an irrational creature; therefore, either as one uses it or as one enjoys it. Although this does not follow because of the impropriety of the preceding expression, it may nevertheless quite sufficiently be admitted: he loves it as one uses it.

Others hold that nothing is attributed to God whether one says, “God loved Peter from eternity,” or “God predestined Peter.”

[Col. 0854D] By such expressions nothing but the term itself is predicated. These proceed more cautiously, because it is difficult to judge concerning such predications, especially because of comparisons made either when something is compared with itself at different times—as when it is said, “God loves Peter more now than he would love him while Peter was on the way”—or between different persons—as when it is said, “God loves Peter more than Linus”; or when a new love seems attributed to God, as when it is said, “God begins to love the person who begins to be good.” For all these seem inconsistent with what was said about God’s love: that God loves human beings by the love which he himself is, or predestines by the predestination which he himself is, since God’s essence admits neither more nor less—unless one says that the comparison is transferred not to the principal signification but to the co-signification. For he loves more the one on whom he bestows greater grace

[Col. 0855A] and to whom he grants a greater crown; and he begins to love the one on whom he begins to bestow grace. Thus, according to them, nothing is attributed to God by any such expression. Hence, according to them, “God loves someone by some love” should not be admitted; nor should “He loves Judas by temporal love” be understood as “he bestows grace on him in time” or “preserves him in his being.”

Yet since it is difficult to state what that temporal love is or in what it exists, it is safer to deny the expression when the ablative is used there. Without the ablative, however, “He loves him” is truly said. Still, it must not be said that God loved Judas from eternity, although from eternity it pleased him to grant grace to Judas in time, because this type of expression—“to love from eternity”—is appropriated to predestination. Nor, because from eternity God loved Peter more than Linus, is it true that he predestined the former more than the latter, because this is not even said in Latin. For many things are mutually convertible when predicated personally, but it does not follow that one must enter into comparison when

[Col. 0855C] the other is compared.

According to what has been said, it is clear that God sometimes loves more one who is less worthy of love according to present justice. Perhaps Judas at some time had greater charity than Peter; nevertheless Judas was not loved more by God than Peter according to one of the three meanings of the word “I love” distinguished above. And when Saul did not love Christ but rather persecuted him, God loved Saul more than Linus, who was now enjoying eternal life. But how are you to understand “he loved Judas more,” when this word has three distinct meanings?

For elsewhere it is said, “God

[Col. 0855D] is equally said to be kind to all.” Hence the proposition “All are loved equally by God” seems to be understood thus: God freely gives human beings whatever he gives; or, as far as lies in himself, he loves no one more than another; or “equally kind,” that is, equally kind in kind, not in quantity.

[Note: [Col. 0855D] *Magister*, I, distinction 40, section b.] It is also customary to ask whether one who is predestined can fail to be predestined. This seems inferable as follows. Grace can be bestowed on someone on whom it was never going to be bestowed; if it is bestowed upon him, he can be predestined; if it was never going to be bestowed, he is not predestined. In the same way it is proved that someone who is predestined can fail to be predestined.

[Col. 0856A] Again: God can not have predestined this person; therefore this person can not be predestined by God; therefore this person can not be predestined. Again: this person can be damned; if he is damned, he is not predestined; therefore he can fail to be predestined. Again: this is necessary, namely, that this person be predestined; therefore anything necessary can be true together with it. Again, indirectly: “This person is predestined and is damned” is impossible; “this person is predestined” is necessary; therefore his being damned is impossible. Although this argument may be met thus: “For the soul of Antichrist to exist and for Antichrist not to exist or to have existed is impossible; the soul of Antichrist exists necessarily; therefore for Antichrist to exist or to have existed is impossible”—assuming that he now exists for the first time—nevertheless it must be granted without hesitation that it is possible for this predestined person who is on the way not to be predestined. Understand this divisionally: that is, this predestined person can fail to be predestined.

But it is objected: Many can be predestined who are not;

[Col. 0856B] therefore, without diminishing the number of those now predestined, but by adding to those who are predestined those who can be predestined and are not, more will be predestined than now are; therefore more can be predestined than are predestined; therefore the number of the predestined can be greater than it is; therefore it can increase. Augustine contradicts this, as is read in the Apocalypse: [Note: [Col. 0855D] Augustine, *On Rebuke and Grace*, I, chapter 13, near the beginning.]

> “Hold what you have, lest another receive your crown” (chapter III).

For if no one else will receive it unless you lose it, the number of the elect is fixed—that is, it cannot increase or decrease. But even the less learned can see that what Augustine says is true if understood conjunctively, false if understood divisionally.

Again: every truth concerning the past is necessary. “This person is predestined” concerns the past; therefore it is necessary. It must be said in response that it concerns the future and is therefore contingent, although it seems to concern the past. Again: what has been done cannot be undone; this person is predestined; therefore he cannot fail to be predestined. But now the point holds as well, because

[Col. 0856D] no past event is denoted when it is said, “This person is predestined,” just as when it is now said, “This person was going to read.” Hence, just as the latter is referred to all times, because of one who debates, has debated, and will debate, it is truly said that he “was going to debate”; so, concerning one on whom grace together with eternal life has been bestowed, is being bestowed, or will be bestowed, it is truly said, “This person is predestined.” And just as it is not necessary that someone was going to read unless he has already begun reading, so neither is it necessary that someone is predestined unless he has already obtained eternal life. Thus the forms distinguished by time in this verb do not signify actions, but those times to which they belong. Yet

[Col. 0857A] the present tense cannot always truly be used where the past tense is truly used. Hence one does not say, “God predestines Peter,” when he has predestined him. This is caused by the co-signification of the prefix *prae-* in this expression, which in composition denotes temporal priority; just as not everyone who was going to read is going to read.

## 48. CHAPTER XVI. Whether the name “reprobation,” when said of God, posits anything

[Note: [Col. 0857D] *Magister*, I, distinction 48, section d, and the following distinction.] The matters customarily investigated concerning predestination or reprobation are almost common to both; therefore, by an analogy of opposites, what has been said concerning one can be said concerning the other. Yet each also has special inquiries not shared with the other. Having determined the matters common to them, we must therefore

[Col. 0857B] treat specifically of reprobation.

Reprobation, as was said above, is foreknowledge of wickedness and preparation of unending punishment. But since God’s foreknowledge is the divine essence, reprobation by which God reprobates seems to be the divine essence, and thus to be God. Again: reprobation is foreknowledge of iniquity, etc.; therefore reprobation is the foreknowledge by which God foreknows; therefore reprobation is in God. But whatever is in God is God; therefore reprobation is God. Therefore reprobation is as great a good as predestination. Therefore one ought to love reprobation as much as predestination; therefore one ought to love being reprobated as much as being predestined.

Distinguish: “Reprobation is as great a good as predestination,” that is, God reprobating is as good as God predestining, is true; but if you refer it to the effect, it is false. Again: God prepares eternal fire for the wicked; therefore he wills that they suffer, because he ordains this, and whatever God wills, you ought to will—for you were created in such a way; therefore you ought to will your own damnation.

To this we say that you ought not to will everything that God wills. Again: God justly brings it about that this person receives eternal damnation; therefore he is the cause of this person’s damnation, and not this person’s sins alone. Accordingly, say that God and sin are causes of damnation in different ways. God is a cause because he is the author of punishment; sin is a cause because it draws one into eternal damnation.

Fallacy. God is the cause why we love; therefore love is not the cause why

[Col. 0857D] we love; or God is the cause of eternal life for us; therefore virtues alone are not [the cause].

Again: whatever occurs, occurs with God as its author; therefore, just as it is by God’s will that the good have eternal life, so it is by his will that the wicked have eternal punishment. Therefore the authority is false which says: “I do not will the death of the sinner, but rather that he be converted and live” (Ezekiel XXXIII). Likewise false is the saying: “We compel one unwilling to rage.”

To this say: just as God brings it about that the good have eternal life, so he also brings it about that the wicked have eternal punishment.

[Col. 0858A] Nevertheless, one must not say that just as it is by God’s will that the good have eternal life, so it is by God’s will that the wicked have eternal punishment. For he brings it about that the good have eternal life by producing in them the merit of life; but though he brings it about that the wicked have eternal punishment, he does not produce the merit of punishment. Therefore explain, “God does not will the death of the sinner,” as meaning: he does not bestow the merit of punishment.

Again: “We compel one unwilling to rage,” that is, by our merits we make him punish us, though unwilling to be the cause of our punishment. “Unwilling” must be understood conditionally: that is, he who would not wish to punish us if we did not sin.

Likewise, hardening is sin; but it is itself an effect of reprobation; therefore God produces sin. “Hardening” is spoken of in two ways: that by which a human being is hardened, namely the malice of the mind; and that by which God hardens, namely the withdrawal of grace, or its non-bestowal, which is an effect of reprobation. This is God’s work, not because it is some positive thing, but because, just as God is said to do something, so he is said to harden.

Again, original sin was the cause of Esau’s hardening; but he was hardened only in adulthood. Therefore, in adulthood original sin was in him the merit of hardening; therefore original sin had returned in him through some actual sin; therefore sin was or existed in him when he was hardened. But the authority says:

> [Note: [Col. 0857D] Augustine, Letter 105. For what did God love in Jacob before he was born and had done anything good, except the gratuitous gift of his mercy? And what did he hate in Esau before he had done anything evil, except original sin?]

Just as God found nothing in Jacob to love except the gift of his mercy, so Esau contracted a twofold liability from original sin before circumcision: he was liable for original sin both with respect to eternal damnation and with respect to hardening. With respect to eternal damnation it was wholly remitted to him; but with respect to hardening it was not remitted. Hence one may ask concerning that liability which remained after circumcision, by which he was still held with respect to hardening, whether there was in him beforehand a mortal or a venial sin. The objection is made thus: the liability which they say remains after baptism is venial sin, which is the merit of hardening; therefore through that venial sin one merits to be hardened in sin. To be hardened is nothing other than to lack gratuitous power; but for anyone to lack gratuitous power is mortal sin; therefore through venial sin someone possesses that by which he is worthy of eternal punishment; therefore venial sin is mortal.

It may be said that original sin was formerly the merit of hardening. This is not to be understood of the time of adulthood, but of the time when he deserved neither good nor evil, namely before external birth, when it was also said: “In Esau he found nothing to hate except original sin.” What, then, is the meaning of what is said:

> [Note: [Col. 0858D] Augustine, in the place cited above.]

“In Jacob he found nothing to love except the gift of his mercy”? It means that he loved Jacob himself out of mercy and predestined him to life. [Col. 0859A] For it may be said of Jacob, as of John the Baptist, that he was sanctified in the womb.

Again, God can bring it about that grace is not bestowed upon this person, so that he has no grace; but this is mortal sin for that person; therefore God can bring it about that this person sins. Distinguish: “To have no power” is mortal sin for him, that is, it is true that to disdain having it is mortal sin; but that the power itself, when not possessed, is mortal sin for him is false.

Again, reprobation is nothing other than foreknowledge of wickedness and preparation of punishment; therefore, because God foreknew Esau’s wickedness and prepared punishment for him, he reprobated him; and thus the justice by which he reprobated him does not seem hidden.

> [Note: [Col. 0859D] Master, Book I, distinction 41.]

Again, it is asked whether reprobation is the cause of hardening, just as it is the cause of recompense. [Col. 0859B] This is shown as follows. Because God reprobated this man, it was therefore his good pleasure not to bestow grace upon him in time, and he does not bestow it; therefore, because he reprobated him, he does not bestow grace.

Again, he does not bestow grace because,

> [Note: [Col. 0859D] This is Augustine in the Master, distinction 41, section “d.,” and the preceding distinction, final section.]

by a justice most hidden and utterly remote from human understanding, he decreed that it was not to be bestowed. Therefore, because from eternity he reprobated them, he does not bestow it. This seems to be resolved by an intention of this sort: because he reprobated them, it was therefore his good pleasure not to bestow grace. For if, because he reprobated them, it was his good pleasure not to bestow it, then because he reprobated them he willed not to bestow it; therefore, because he foreknew their iniquity and prepared punishment for them, he willed from eternity never to bestow grace on them or grant them life. Hence it seems objectionable in many ways that reprobation should be the cause of the non-bestowal of grace. [Col. 0859C]

Yet conversely it seems possible to show that it is not its cause, but rather that human merits alone are its cause, just as human merits alone appear to be the cause of the non-bestowal of grace. Augustine seems to assert this in his commentary on Malachi:

> [Note: [Col. 0859D] Book of Eighty-Three Questions, question 68, with some words altered.]
