> “God has mercy on whom he wills, and hardens whom he wills” (Rom. 9). “But this will of God cannot be unjust. For it arises from most hidden merits, because sinners themselves, although through the general sin they have made one mass, nevertheless have some diversity among them. For something precedes in sinners by which, although they are not yet justified, they are nevertheless found worthy [Note: [Col. 0860D] Alternatively, ‘are made worthy,’ as is also found below.] of justification; and likewise something precedes in other sinners by which they are worthy of dullness.”

See: here Augustine seems plainly to say that human merits appear to be the cause of the non-bestowal of grace, and therefore that God’s reprobation is not the cause of the same thing.

To this one must reply that the term “reprobation” posits nothing, but only removes and excludes. Augustine shows this as follows:

> [Note: [Col. 0860D] Book I, To Simplicianus, second question.]

Just as God’s reprobation is his unwillingness to have mercy, so hardening is his not having mercy. The former is eternal and is understood negatively; the latter is temporal. The former is the cause of the latter. For because from eternity [Col. 0860A] he did not will to have mercy, he therefore does not have mercy. But this—not having mercy—is not the cause why a human being is evil; for all are evil because they come from the corrupted mass. Hence he could rightly condemn them all; and when he has mercy by bestowing grace, it is mercy.

Conversely, however, it is otherwise where the whole expression is taken affirmatively. For because he predestines, he confers grace in time; and this temporal bestowal of grace is the cause why someone is good. Yet, conversely, the eternal unwillingness to have mercy is not the cause why someone is evil, nor is the reverse the case. For it is not because he is evil that God did not will from eternity to have mercy; but this is the cause of hardening: because he is evil, God does not have mercy on him temporally.

Therefore it must not be said: “Because he reprobated him, it was his good pleasure [Col. 0860B] not to bestow grace”; rather: “Because he reprobated him, it was not his good pleasure to bestow grace.” The negation must always be placed before the verb, not after it. For nothing is attributed to God when it is said, “God reprobated this man”; it means the same as if one said: “God did not will that grace should be bestowed upon this person in time, and life in the future.”

This also resolves at the same time the question whether God’s reprobation is the cause of temporal hardening; this may indeed be admitted without difficulty. For because he reprobated, he hardens; that is, because from eternity he did not will to have mercy, he does not have mercy in time.

Accordingly, the statement “Reprobation is foreknowledge of wickedness,” and so forth, is a kind of description, not a true definition; and it must be understood thus: all who are reprobated by God are reprobated while God foreknows their wickedness and prepares punishment. If anyone finds a more convenient way of resolving the matter, I do not begrudge it; and perhaps another path to a solution may be found, to which we may be led by what Ambrose says in his commentary on the Epistle to the Romans: one reprobation is eternal, another temporal. The temporal one is the same as hardening or falling away. The eternal one is that God foreknows someone as to be damned. For if reprobation is from eternity, how is it not God? And if it is God, who will say that nothing is attributed to God when I say, “God is Judas’s reprobation,” or “God reprobated Judas”?

Yet if anyone approves the earlier solution, he can easily adapt it to this author’s meaning [Col. 0860D] by saying that reprobation is said to be from eternity because God reprobated from eternity all whom he reprobated. What Augustine says concerning the prophet Malachi, some say, was retracted:

> [Note: [Col. 0860D] An allusion to chapter 23 of Book I of the *Retractions*, in which similar matters are retracted. Augustine’s passage from question 68 among the 83 Questions is explained.]

It may nevertheless be expounded concerning temporal election or justification as follows: “He has mercy on whom he wills, and hardens whom he wills,” that is, whom he wills he elects or reprobates temporally. And this will of God—that is, this effect of the divine will—cannot be unjust; for it arises from most hidden merits, that is, from hidden causes, [Col. 0861A] that is, from God’s hidden will, which he designates by the name “merit.” For just as recompense follows causally from merits, so temporal election—that is, the bestowal of grace—follows from God’s hidden will.

“Because sinners themselves, through the general sin, have made one mass”: from all persons, by reason of original sin, there has been made, as it were, one lost mass. “Nevertheless, there is some diversity among them”: for something precedes in sinners, namely God’s will anticipating those sinners, by which—that is, by that will—although they have not been justified, they are nevertheless made worthy of justification. By his will he justifies them as though there preceded in them something by which they were worthy of justification. And likewise: “Something precedes in sinners by which they are worthy of dullness.” This is plain. For original sin precedes indiscriminately in all, by which they are equally worthy of hardening:

> [Note: [Col. 0861D] See Augustine, Letter 105; *On Rebuke and Grace*, ch. 7; Book I, *To Simplicianus*, question 2; *Enchiridion*, 94; *On Predestination and Grace*, chs. 3, 6, and 7; *On the Predestination of the Saints*, ch. 8 and following.]

If God rescues some from that mass, it is mercy; if he leaves some in it, it is justice.

From what has been said it is clear that nothing is attributed to God when it is said, “God reprobated this man.” Still less does anything seem to be attributed when it is said, “God withdraws grace from this person,” or “God hardens this person,” which is the same thing, as is read concerning Pharaoh: “I hardened his heart” (Exod. 10).

Yet it seems that something is attributed to God by this expression, because to say “God withdraws grace from this person” is the same as saying that he causes him not to have it. But [Col. 0862A] since God’s causing is nothing other than willing, this seems the same as saying, “God wills that he should not have grace”; and thus by the term “wills” the divine essence seems to be predicated. But it should rather be understood negatively: “He does not will that he should have it.”

But someone will say: since, once grace has been withdrawn, a human being cannot avoid falling, judgment ought not to be imputed to the person, who can do nothing without grace, but to God who withdraws it. To this one must reply that it is to be imputed not to God but to the human being, because God always withdraws grace on account of human merit. Nevertheless, even if the human being did not deserve that grace be withdrawn from him, it would be imputed to him; for, since God bestowed it freely, he can in no respect be found unjust if, whenever he wills, he withdraws it. And it is from the person’s own defect that he immediately falls once grace is withdrawn.

This can be shown by an analogy. Suppose the wall of my house threatens to collapse. I have borrowed timber from my neighbour to support it. He lends it freely; he needs the timber, but reclaims it as he wishes; and the wall immediately collapses. The fault does not lie in the one who removes the timber, but rather in the wall’s own fault, because it collapses; nor does my neighbour wrong me in any respect.

So that the things said above concerning reprobation and predestination may more easily be conveyed to the understanding—which takes its beginning from sense—and committed to memory, the following diagram, placed before the eyes, explains what has been said.

[Col. 0861]

[Col. 0861C] **On Disposition**

Just as predestination concerns only persons to be saved, or goods to be conferred upon them in the present or the future, so disposition concerns only things to be done. For it is read in the Book of Wisdom: “The wisdom of God reaches from end to end” (Wis. 8), that is, immovably from eternity to eternity, “and orders all things sweetly.” Gregory says:

> [Note: [Col. 0862D] Cited by the Master, Book I, distinction 47, section b.]

> “Many carry out God’s will while striving to change it, and, in resisting his will, render service to it, since what resists through human effort serves the divine disposition.”

Therefore whatever is done by human beings serves the divine disposition; therefore God disposes all things. [Col. 0861D] If this is granted, the following absurdity seems to follow. God disposes all things, and he disposes only things to be done; therefore all things are to be done. Again, God disposes all things; therefore he disposes both good and evil; therefore he disposes evil; therefore he wills evil.

Again, God disposes all things and disposes nothing badly; therefore all things are disposed well by God. Nothing is disposed by God in one way and done in another; therefore all things are done well. Again, all things are done while God disposes them; God disposes nothing except well; therefore all things are done by a good disposer and one who disposes well.

Again, God disposes all things well; therefore all things serve God, as David also says: “All things serve you” (Ps. 118); therefore the devil too serves God. Isaiah also seems to say this: “The rod of my fury” (Isa. 10); and in the commentary on Daniel he is called “God’s dove”; likewise, in Isaiah, even “God’s ministers.” Yet if someone accepts this, the following objection seems to arise. The devil serves, or ministers to, God in all things in which God has disposed him to minister to himself, and in the manner in which God has disposed; therefore the devil serves God well; therefore he does so from charity.

Again, [Col. 0863A] the devil serves God; therefore some work of his pleases God. But, on the contrary, the devil performs no work in which God is not offended; therefore no work of the devil pleases God. Again, God either wills or does not will that the devil do what he commands. If he wills it, since God is offended in everything the devil does, God is offended by things which he wills to be done. If God does not will the devil to do what he commands him to do, why does he command him to do it? Again, the devil serves God; therefore he obeys him.

The foregoing must be answered in order. It must be said that God’s disposition is understood as providence, as when it is said: “God’s wisdom disposes all things and foresees all things before they occur.” Sometimes it is taken as providence together with good pleasure, according to which it is not to be accepted that God disposes all things except in this sense: he disposes concerning all things, because God draws forth his will from both good and evil, when he rewards the good and punishes the wicked. Thus, in this latter meaning, it is more frequently and more properly understood as providence and good pleasure. Hence one should not grant “God disposes all things” unless it is said in the aforesaid sense.

Nevertheless, it must not be denied that all things serve God. For all things serve him, that is, they furnish him material for praise; and the devil serves him, and God approves the works which the devil has wrought, not the works by which he wrought them: the works wrought, [Col. 0863C] as they are customarily called, not the working works. The latter are all evil, because none proceeds from charity.

> [Note: [Col. 0863D] From this infer that the designation *opus operatum* (“work wrought”) is not as modern as some suppose. It is also used below, in the final chapter of the book, where the sacraments are discussed.]

Just as God approved Christ’s passion inflicted by the Jews—and that was a work wrought by the Jews—yet he did not approve the working works of the Jews, nor the actions by which they performed that passion. For God is offended by the devil’s action, but not by the deed done; nor does God will that the devil do in the manner in which he does what the Lord commands him to do.

If, however, it is found written that the Lord commands the devil to do something—as perhaps in the Book of Kings, chapter 22, concerning Ahab’s deception, of which fuller treatment will be given later—it must not be understood that he commands as though he willed it, or, if he wills it, that the devil should do it as he does it. For although the devil does what the Lord wills, he does not do it as the Lord wills; therefore he always sins, and the devil’s serving is not reigning.

For this saying was made concerning that service which is from charity, [Col. 0863D] which is the cause of reigning. One who serves God from charity reigns, both over the flesh and over spiritual enemies. Nor is it surprising that the devil, a rational creature, should serve God, since the same is read even of an irrational creature: “The sea and the wind obey him” (Matt. 8), because he commands them as though they were animate, and speech is often addressed to them as though to animate beings. Hence Moses says: “Hear, O heavens, what I speak” (Deut. 32); Isaiah: “Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth” (Isa. 1).

They are therefore said to obey him because he brings about things from them at his will. Just as, in pharmacy, matter is called obedient to medicine because the medicine works from it and in it. Thus all things are said to serve God because God’s will is fulfilled from all things, and God draws certain things forth even from evils; therefore God’s good pleasure is fulfilled from all things, both good and evil. Yet disposition does not concern all things, but things to be done: namely, the rewards of the elect and the punishments of the reprobate.

Thus far, then, concerning the matters set out above: namely, foreknowledge and foresight, disposition and providence, wisdom and knowledge, predestination and reprobation.

> [Note: [Col. 0864D] Master, Book I, distinction 35, section 1.]

Foreknowledge, then, or foresight, which is the same thing, concerns both good and evil, and only future things. Providence concerns things to be governed; disposition concerns things to be done, and, if taken properly, only good things. Wisdom and knowledge concern both good and evil: present, [Col. 0864B] past, and future things; temporal and eternal things. Predestination concerns persons to be saved, as the Apostle says: “Those whom he predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son” (Rom. 8); and the goods with which they are enriched here in the present and crowned in the future. Thus Isaiah says: “No eye has seen, O God, apart from you, the things which you have prepared for those who love you” (Isa. 64). Reprobation concerns persons to be damned.

## CHAPTER XVII. Whether such names as “to be loved” and “to be feared” are said of God according to essence

It is customary to ask concerning such names as “to be loved” and “to be feared” whether they are said of God according to essence. [Col. 0864C] Since they belong to God from eternity, they are said either according to essence or according to relation. But it is certain that they are said according to an eternal relation; therefore they are said according to essence; therefore they are not said with “more” and “less,” because the divine essence admits neither increase nor decrease.

Again, because God is God, he is to be loved; because he is God, he is to be feared. Therefore he is not more to be loved than feared. Again, because he is merciful, he is to be loved; because he is just, he is to be feared. He is not more merciful than just, nor conversely; therefore he is not more to be loved than feared. Or thus: he is equally just and merciful; therefore he is equally to be loved and feared.

On the contrary, however, it is easy to show that he is more to be loved than feared. “His mercy exalts itself over judgment,” and “His mercies are over all his works” (Ps. 144). Therefore he is more merciful than just; therefore more to be loved than feared. Again, he is to be loved because he is God and to be loved because he is human; therefore he is more to be loved because he is God and human than because he is God. Again, in the Song of Songs, on the passage, “What is my beloved more than a beloved? A son from a father” (Song 5): on this account he ought more to be loved than feared.

It must therefore be understood that such names said of God predicate the divine essence and, moreover, indicate certain effects in creatures, as was said [Col. 0865A] concerning the names “just” and “merciful.” When it is said, “God is to be loved,” the dignity by which he is worthy to be loved is expressed, and that dignity is the divine essence. Moreover, a certain effect in creatures is implied, by which they are bound to love him. Likewise, when it is said, “God is to be feared,” the same dignity is expressed, and another effect is implied. Therefore, if “more” or “less” is added according to their primary signification, the expression is incongruous. But if the comparison is referred to the effects in creatures, it is true that for certain things we are bound to love him, and for others to fear him more, as was said regarding mercy and justice.

But when it is said, with an added ablative, “God is more to be loved by us than feared,” the divine essence is not expressed—just as it is not when I say, “God is creator”—but it is expressed that it is fitting for us to love God. Nor is it surprising if discourse is about God and, by implication, something is attributed not to God but to the creature; as when it is said, “God is creator,” that is, things, by God’s willing, come forth from non-being into being.

Therefore, if it is asked whether he is more to be loved by us than feared, we say that this is so. For the movement of love in us toward God ought to surpass all other movements; and for certain reasons he ought to be loved by us more than for others—for the works of re-creation more than for the works of creation. Thus perhaps we are bound to love him more because he suffered for us than because he is God; but we are not bound to love him more because he suffered for us than because [Col. 0865C] he is God; indeed, we are bound to love him more because he is God than because he suffered. For this movement ought to exceed all others. Thus it is clear that we are bound to love him more because he is God and human than because he is God, but not to love him more.

Some, however, maintain that we are bound to love him more because he is God than because he is human or because he suffered. This seems plausible because every benefit which he confers upon us in his humanity, he has conferred wholly from his divinity. Hence there is nothing for which we are bound to love him more than for his divinity.

But if it is asked whether he is more to be loved because he is God and human than because he is God: if the divine essence is expressed, the statement is incongruous; if you refer it to the effect, it is true that we are more bound because he is God and human [Col. 0865D] than because he is God, that is, than because he is re-creator; but we are not bound to love him more.

A fallacy: God is great because he is God, and he is great because he is human; therefore he is greater because he is God and human than because he is God. The solutions to other arguments are clear from what has been said. Again, since God is to be loved because he created the world, and since begetting the Son was incomparably far greater, he seems to be loved far more because he begot the Son; and *latria*—the worship due to God—seems due to him because he is Father, and likewise because he is God. Many other questions may be raised, but because they are unusual, they should be passed over in silence.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On abstract terms, such as “deity” and “fatherhood”

[Col. 0866A]

There are other terms concerning which there is doubt whether they are said of God according to essence: namely, all abstract terms such as “divinity,” “essence,” “fatherhood,” “sonship,” and similar properties. Concerning these we also leave under a special question whether they are said of the three persons according to essence or according to relation. For if these are said according to essence, then the Father, by his essence, is essence, and by deity is deity. Again, if the Father, by his essence, is fatherhood, then for him to be God and to be fatherhood are the same thing; therefore, since Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God, they are one fatherhood; and so [Col. 0866B] the Son and Holy Spirit too are fatherhood.

But if “fatherhood” is said according to relation, then by the name “fatherhood” the Father is related to the Son and the Holy Spirit; and so it may be said, “The Father is the fatherhood of the Son,” which seems an incongruous expression.

Therefore some say that these names must be excluded from the rule which states: “Everything said of God from eternity is said either according to essence or according to relation.” With respect to the names “fatherhood” and “sonship,” we have wished it to be certain that they do not predicate essence in God, as will soon be evident in the treatment of relatives; although we see no absurdity following if this is said of the names “essence” and “divinity.”

## CHAPTER XIX. On the terms “to be from the Father,” “God from God,” and the like

[Col. 0866C]

> [Note: [Col. 0865D] Master, *Sentences*, Book I, distinction 27.]

It is also asked concerning the terms “to be from the Father” and “God from God,” whether they predicate essence or relation. For “to be from the Father” seems to be said according to essence, since this could be said alike of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. But if so, the whole Trinity is from the Father, just as the whole Trinity is one God; therefore the whole Trinity is from something; therefore something is the principle of the Trinity.

Again, whatever the Son has, he has from the Father; the Son is from the Father; therefore he has from the Father the fact that he is from the Father. And whatever the Son has, he has from the Father; therefore the Son has from the Father to have his being from the Father. Thus the reasoning can proceed to infinity.

Again, if only the phrase “God from God” is said according to essence, then Father, Son, and [Col. 0866D] Holy Spirit are one God from God, according to the rule set out above: whatever is said of God according to essence is said severally of each person and, of them collectively, in the singular rather than the plural. And there is another rule: whatever in the Holy Trinity is said with reference to itself is said of each one without the others. Therefore not even the Son is “God from God” without the Father; yet it is said according to essence. Hence some say that these terms must be excepted from the same rules.

To others it seems that in such terms both the divine essence and relation are signified: “God” or “being” is said according to essence, whereas “from God” or “from the Father” is said according to relation, as was said above concerning the term “able to beget.” This opinion may be refuted on this point: on that account the divine essence would be said relatively, which is false. For the divine essence neither begets nor is begotten, as will later be taught more fully.

Others, then, may understand such terms to signify relations. For it is the same to say, “The Son is Son,” as to say, “The Son is God from God”; and similarly of the Holy Spirit. Yet this does not seem to be said by the term “to be from the Father.” For the same relation may be signified as by the name “Son,” so that to say “The Son is Son” is the same as saying “The Son is from the Father”; and “The Holy Spirit is Holy Spirit” is the same as “The Holy Spirit is from the Father or from the Son.” For in no way is he from the Father in which he is not also from the Son, and conversely. Thus “to be from the Father” is said equivocally of the Son and the Holy Spirit. But when it is said of the Father that he himself is from the Father, we posit nothing in God; indeed, we rather remove something. For it is the same as saying, “The Father is not from another than himself.”

Concerning the phrase “God from God,” it may be said that it predicates neither essence nor relation of God. For this rule was given concerning simple terms; and here the name “God” is taken personally for relative names, though not relatively. For it is the same as saying, “the Son from the Father.”

And note, as Augustine says:

> [Note: [Col. 0867D] Augustine, Book VI, *On the Trinity*, chapter 2, near the end.]

Only that is said of this which both are, and under that name an attribution of “this of this” may be made which belongs to both—or rather to all three. For it is not said of the Son because the Son alone is there. Nor is it surprising that in such a combination the name “God” is used personally. For it is also found used thus elsewhere, as when it is said, “God suffered, died, was buried,” and the like.

In other expressions also, names of essence are often brought down to personal significations: power is attributed to the Father, wisdom to the Son, goodness or love to the Holy Spirit, although each of these is said of God according to essence. Nor is this done without reason.

> [Note: [Col. 0867D] Master, Book I, distinction 34, section 7.]

When a human being heard in Sacred Scripture that God was called Father and God the Son, he perhaps supposed, or might suppose, that there was in God something like what there is in a human being, because he had not seen God the Father when he had seen a human father. For among human beings the father is prior to the son, and age brings defect with it; the son is subsequent to the father, and immaturity commonly brings imperfection of understanding. Lest anyone suppose something similar concerning God, Scripture comes to the fore by naming the Father powerful and the Son wise.

Likewise, the name “spirit” suggests puffing-up and pride. Therefore human consciousness might fear to approach God because of severity and cruelty; Scripture immediately comes to the fore by calling him kind and gentle. Thus Father as powerful, Son as wise, and Holy Spirit as kind or loving are understood.

> [Note: [Col. 0867D] Master, Book I, distinction 34, sections 6, 7, and 8.]

This is not because the Father alone is powerful there, or the Son alone wise there, or the Spirit alone loving there; but for the reasons stated above, such names are appropriated to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—an appropriation of the name, not of the thing. There are also other appropriations made both in name and in reality; we shall set these forth, comprehending them under a definite number, at the end of the following chapter, and demonstrate them visibly as we have gathered them from the authority of the Scriptures. Since we have discussed power sufficiently above, we shall say nothing about it at present; but we shall speak of wisdom and love, so that we may proceed in order with the matters we began above: namely, essential terms taken personally.

## CHAPTER XX. On the terms “the Father’s wisdom” and “unbegotten wisdom”

> [Note: [Col. 0868D] Master, Book I, distinction 32, section 3 and following; also the distinction cited above.]

First, for one wishing to treat of the Father’s wisdom, there arises for examination this statement of the Apostle: [Col. 0868B] “Christ is God’s power and wisdom” (1 Cor. 1). For if the Father is wise by the Father’s wisdom, and the Son is the Father’s wisdom, then the Father is wise by the Son. But for the Father to be wise is the same as for him to be; therefore the Father is by the Son. Thus the Son does not seem to be from the Father, but the Father from the Son.

That the Father is wise by the Father’s wisdom may easily be shown thus. The Father is wise by some wisdom; therefore by his own or another’s wisdom. But he is not wise by another’s wisdom; therefore the Father is wise by his own wisdom; therefore by the wisdom of himself. And so the Father is wise by the Father’s wisdom.

Again, the Father has only one wisdom, because he himself is wise, and this is the Father’s sole wisdom. Therefore there is no wisdom of the Father by which the Father is not wise; and the Father is wise by the Father’s wisdom which is the Son, and thus by the Son.

To this one must reply that the Father is indeed wise by the Father’s wisdom. But the phrase “the Father’s wisdom” is taken equivocally. It can be understood intransitively, between “known” and “begotten,” that is, as the wisdom which is the Father; in this sense it is true that the Father is wise by the Father’s wisdom, that is, by that wisdom which is the Father. For the whole Trinity is wise by that wisdom.

Again, “the Father’s wisdom” can be understood transitively, as that which proceeds from or is begotten by the Father. This is properly said of the Son, who is begotten wisdom; he is properly the Father’s wisdom because the Father begot him. But the divine essence, common to the Trinity, is called the Father’s wisdom because the Father is wise by it. Thus there is one rationale of the expression when the Father’s wisdom is said to be [Col. 0868D] the Son, and another when it is said to be the divine essence common to the Trinity; the prudent inquirer will recognize this from the difference of grammatical construction.

> [Note: [Col. 0868D] Master, cited above, section 6.]

But someone will say: according to this, the Father’s wisdom is not only one. He will also attempt to establish this by arguments. Thus the Son is the Father’s begotten wisdom, by which the Father is not wise; the Father is also the Father’s unbegotten wisdom, and by it the Father is wise. Therefore there is a wisdom of the Father by which the Father is wise, and it is not that wisdom of the Father by which the Father is not wise; therefore the Father’s wisdom is not only one.

Again, unbegotten wisdom is the Father’s wisdom, and [Col. 0869A] begotten wisdom is the Father’s wisdom. No begotten wisdom is unbegotten wisdom. Therefore the Father’s wisdom is not only one.

Again, the Son is the Father’s wisdom, but the Son is not his own wisdom or the Holy Spirit’s wisdom; therefore the Son is the wisdom of the Father alone; therefore the Son is not the wisdom of the three persons; therefore there is a wisdom of the Father which is not of the three persons, and a wisdom of the Father which is of the three persons; therefore the Father’s wisdom is not only one.

These and similar arguments are adduced by some who proceed more sophistically than truly, to show that the Father’s wisdom is not only one. For the contrary is clearly true: namely, that the Father’s wisdom is only one. Although in the Trinity there is wisdom common to the whole Trinity, which is the Trinity itself and by which each person in the Trinity is wise, and although there is also the Son, who is the Father’s wisdom, as the Apostle testifies (ibid.), by which wisdom the Father is not wise—and it is not the wisdom by which he begot, since it belongs to him not merely for being wise but also for being—yet there are not on that account two wisdoms. For the person of the Son, which is understood when “begotten wisdom” is said, is one and the same wisdom as the essence of God and is understood in the three persons.

For the Son, who is the Father’s wisdom by which the Father is not wise, is that wisdom by which the Father is wise—that is, the divine essence.

> [Note: [Col. 0869D] Thus the Master, cited above, section 7.]

You may see this from a parallel. In the Trinity there is love, which is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; yet the Holy Spirit is properly called the Father’s love, which is not the Father or the Son, just as the Holy Spirit is neither Father nor Son. Yet there are not for that reason two loves, because the Father’s love, which properly is the Holy Spirit, is also the love which is the whole Trinity. Just as the Holy Spirit is the essence which is the Trinity, yet is not the Trinity, so you may apply the same reasoning to wisdom.

Yet someone will again bark out: “The same wisdom is begotten wisdom and unbegotten wisdom; therefore the same wisdom is begotten and unbegotten”—a fallacy. “The same God is begotten God and unbegotten God; therefore the same God is begotten and unbegotten.” There is no need to repeat the solution to this argument, since it has already been given. Repetition of words produces, whether in teaching or in Scripture, more the disadvantage of prolixity and confusion of mind than it advances or exercises it.

Likewise: the Son is only that wisdom which is common to the three persons. That wisdom neither begets nor is begotten; therefore the Son is only that wisdom which neither begets nor is begotten; therefore the Son is only that wisdom which is not begotten (*non gignitur*), and thus which is not begotten (*non est genita*); and so the Son is wisdom which is not begotten. But the Son is one wisdom, and there is no wisdom which he is not—let that wisdom be so; therefore the Son is no wisdom that is begotten; therefore he is not wisdom that is begotten. Likewise, the Father and the Son are one wisdom alone which is not begotten; the Father is not wisdom which is begotten; therefore the Son is not wisdom which is begotten.

To this it must be said that, when the name *wisdom* is used by itself—that is, without a term causing it to be taken personally—it refers to the essence. But with *begotten*, *unbegotten*, and such additions, it is directed to the persons, so that “begotten wisdom” is said of the Son alone, and “unbegotten wisdom” of the Father alone—unless someone takes *unbegotten* so as rather to remove than to posit something. Then perhaps it signifies the essence, which is unbegotten, that is, not begotten. Thus also, when “wisdom from wisdom” is said, the very construction makes clear that one term is said of the Father and the other of the Son.

But when, through the insertion of a relative term, the foregoing names are joined to it—as when it is said, “The Son is wisdom which is begotten,” or, “He is wisdom which is not begotten”—it is less clear whether the expression is taken essentially or personally. If it is taken essentially, it is true that the Son is wisdom which is not begotten, that is, the divine essence which neither begets nor is begotten. But if it is taken personally, as the addition seems to require, it is not true that the Son is wisdom which is not begotten. Rather, the Son is the Son who is begotten, and consequently God who is begotten, or wisdom which is begotten.

Yet it is easy to reason thus: wisdom which is God is not begotten; the Son is that wisdom; therefore wisdom which is God and is not begotten is the Son. Likewise, the Father and Son are unbegotten wisdom; therefore the Son is wisdom which is not begotten. Likewise, the Son is wisdom which is begotten; therefore the Son is wisdom, and that wisdom is begotten—which appears true. But because the term *wisdom* is there placed by itself, without an addition, it seems to be referred to the essence, and the essence neither begets nor is begotten. Therefore the same term, without distinction, ought neither to be affirmed nor denied, lest a sophist, by forming a discordant syllogism, appear ridiculous.

“The Son is wisdom which is not unbegotten; therefore the Son is wisdom which is not unbegotten wisdom”; or thus: “Wisdom common to the three persons is not begotten; therefore it is not begotten wisdom”—there is a fallacy in either case. “The Son is God who is not begotten; therefore he is God who is not unbegotten God.” To the second: “The divine essence is not begotten; therefore it is not begotten God.” For all arguments which can be formed here with these terms, you will find a general counter-instance if you inspect carefully the relations and combinations of the arguments.

> [Note: Col. 0870D: *Magister*, §3.]

It is commonly asked whether the Father is wise by begotten wisdom or by unbegotten wisdom. That he is not wise by begotten wisdom is clear both from what has been said and also from this: since this expression, “The Father is wise by begotten wisdom,” can be resolved in only two ways—either “The Father is wise, that is, begotten wisdom,” or “The Father is wise through begotten wisdom”—both are plainly false. For the Father has nothing from the Son; rather, whatever the Son has, he has from the Father.

They also wish to show in this way that the Father is not wise by unbegotten wisdom: “The Father is wise only by that wisdom which is common to the three persons; therefore he is not wise by unbegotten wisdom.” This can be countered thus: “The Son exists only through divinity; therefore he does not exist through the Father; therefore the Father is wise by unbegotten wisdom, that is, by himself.” For he is wise from himself and is from himself. Yet when it is said that the Father is from no one, it must be understood, “from no other.” More properly, however, this is said negatively: the Father is from himself, that is, not from another, just as the Son is from another, that is, from the Father.

> [Note: Col. 0871D: X, *Liber Magistri*, §§4–5.]

The question is also asked concerning the Son: whether he is wise by begotten wisdom, or by unbegotten wisdom—that is, by wisdom unbegotten, namely the Father, from whom he also has that he is God—or whether he is wise through unbegotten wisdom, namely the Father, through whom he also exists.

Whether the Son is wise by begotten wisdom may be disputed here. For if the preposition *a* (“from”) is understood, so that one resolves it thus, “The Son is wise from begotten wisdom,” it is false, because he is not God from himself but from the Father. But if it is resolved thus, “The Son is wise by begotten wisdom, that is, by himself,” some grant nothing simply and without qualification to be through itself. For the Son is God through himself and exists through himself, but is not from himself or of himself. This is confirmed by the authority of Hilary:

> [Note: *On the Trinity*, after the middle.]

> “This is the unity of the nature which you oppose, heretic: that the Son acts through himself in such a way that he does not act from himself.”

Others distinguish when it is proposed, “The Son is wise by himself or through himself.” If he is understood to be wise by his own nature and essence, it is true; but if “from himself” or “of himself” is meant, it is false. What has been said of the Son is also to be understood of the Holy Spirit.

To put it briefly, then, there are four propositions, each of which may be understood in two ways. “The Father is wise by begotten wisdom,” in either explanation, is false. “The Father is wise by wisdom,” in either explanation, is true, whether through himself or through another. “The Son is wise by begotten wisdom”: if you resolve it by the preposition *a*, it is false; but if by the preposition *per* (“through”), you speak truly, as Hilary says. “The Son is wise by unbegotten wisdom” is true in either sense.

Some nevertheless say that neither the Father nor the Son should be called begotten wisdom or unbegotten wisdom, because neither Father nor Son is wisdom, and wisdom belongs to the three persons; it should be called neither begotten, nor unbegotten, nor proceeding, because that wisdom—that is, the divine essence—is undivided. Such terms as *begotten*, *unbegotten*, and *proceeding* signify properties. Yet if the name *unbegotten* removes rather than posits something, so that “unbegotten wisdom” means “wisdom not begotten,” it may be taken for the essence, as some hold. This term *unbegotten*, however, will be discussed more fully later.

## Chapter XXI. What is signified by the verb “loves” when it is said, “The Father loves the Son”?

> [Note: Col. 0871D: *Magister* I, distinction 32, §§1–2.]

Just as wisdom is appropriated to the Son by name, not in reality, so goodness or love is appropriated to the Holy Spirit. It must therefore be noted carefully that, for the same reason why it is said, “The Father is wise by the wisdom whom he begot”—for if he were said to be wise by that wisdom, it would be understood not that it is from him, but that he is from it—so likewise it should not be granted that the Father or Son loves by that love which is the Holy Spirit alone. For since to love there is the same as to be, if the Father or Son loves by it, the Holy Spirit would seem not to be from the Father and Son, but the Father and Holy Spirit—

> [Note: Col. 0871D: Perhaps, “but the Father and Son [would seem to be] from the Holy Spirit.”]

An objection is made thus: “To love and to be are the same both for the Father and for the Son. The Father and Son love by the Holy Spirit; therefore they are by the Holy Spirit.” Likewise: “The Father and Son are by that by which they love; but they love by the Holy Spirit; therefore they are by the Holy Spirit.”

Augustine says that the Father loves the Son by the Holy Spirit as follows:

> [Note: Col. 0871D: Augustine, book IV, *On the Trinity*, chapter 5, from the beginning.]

> “It is manifest that neither of the two is that by which both are joined together, by which the Begotten is loved by the Begetter and loves his Begetter; and they preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, not by participation but by their essence, nor by the gift of a superior nature, but by their own proper gift.”

> [Note: Col. 0872D: In Augustine, “of some nature” stands in place of “of a superior nature.”]

Here he seems plainly to say that the two who love one another are one thing, while that by which they love one another is a third, neither of those who love. More explicitly still, he adds that they love by their own proper gift, namely the Holy Spirit, who is the proper gift of Father and Son. Elsewhere Augustine also says:

> [Note: Col. 0872D: Book XV, *On the Trinity*, chapter 7; but somewhat differently in Augustine himself.]

> “In that Trinity, who would dare say that the Father and Son do not love except through the Holy Spirit?”

Some find it difficult to explain this question to the letter; nor have we dared to devise anything new, lest we set our mouth in heaven. Yet we set forth what we have heard from others in resolving it. Some say that the statement “The Father and Son love one another by the Holy Spirit” should not be admitted, meaning that they act unanimously and harmoniously by their goodness; this goodness is attributed to the Holy Spirit in Holy Scripture. On this account, nothing is attributed to the Father or Son when it is said that they love one another by the Holy Spirit, just as nothing is attributed when it is said, “The Father and Son create souls.” But according to this account, the Father and Son love one another by the Holy Spirit in time, not from eternity.

Others say better that the verb *to love* is not used there figuratively, but in its proper meaning, so that the sense is: “The Father and Son love one another by the Holy Spirit,” that is, by their own goodness, because goodness is attributed to the Spirit. Thus the divine essence is meant whether one says, “The Father loves the Son by the Holy Spirit,” “The Son loves the Father by the Holy Spirit,” “The Father and Son love one another by the Holy Spirit,” “The Holy Spirit loves the Father and Son by the Holy Spirit,” or makes the variation in any other way.

Therefore Augustine’s statement is apparently to be explained thus:

> [Note: Col. 0872D: As above.]

> “They preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace,”

that is, they love one another. This explanation is quite familiar in usage: persons bound by the bond of peace are said to preserve the unity of the Spirit—indeed, to be one Spirit. The sense, therefore, is: they preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, that is, they love one another not by participation—that is, not by a participated love, which is their essence—nor do they love one another by the gift of someone superior, that is, they do not have this love from any superior, since they have no superior. We, by contrast, receive from a superior that very thing by which we love. Rather, they love one another by their own proper gift, that is, by the essence which is their proper gift, namely the Holy Spirit; by their proper gift, that is, by their own goodness, which is appropriated to their gift and to the Holy Spirit. It signifies the goodness common to the three, but, put personally, predicates the notion—or rather, predicates it together with the notion.

Some, however, prefer another construction: “They preserve the unity of peace,” that is, “by the bond of the Spirit,” that is, through the bond of the Spirit, through the Holy Spirit who is the bond of the two. Thus Augustine seems to say more expressly that they love one another through the Holy Spirit. But if this is the explanation, it nonetheless accords with the preceding one: they preserve the unity of peace through the bond of the Spirit, that is, through the bond of goodness appropriated to the Holy Spirit. For the Spirit is called the ineffable bond of Father and Son only because goodness is appropriated to him, and that goodness is the ineffable bond. Thus the Father and Son are not understood to be united through the Holy Spirit personally, but through the goodness appropriated to the Spirit, which can be understood only as the divine essence.

Yet Augustine’s statement appears contrary to this:

> [Note: Book I, *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 5: “These three are one: all things because of the Father; all things equal because of the Son; all things connected because of the Holy Spirit.”]

> “Those three are one because of the Father, equal because of the Son, connected because of the Holy Spirit.”

If, however, the two preceding clauses are considered more carefully, nothing remains that can disturb what was first stated. For just as it is clearly false, on the surface of the words, that those three are one because of the Father and equal because of the Son—for they are not one because of the Father, but because of the unity attributed to the Father; nor are they equal because of the Son, but because of the equality attributed to the Son—so it will plainly appear to the more discerning reader that it is false for those three to be connected because of the Holy Spirit. Understand it thus: by the goodness attributed to the Holy Spirit. Why unity is attributed to the Father and equality to the Son, have we not discussed above in treating such appropriations? Thus, according to some, the foregoing statements are answered: wherever “The Father and Son love one another by the Holy Spirit” is found, goodness attributed to the Holy Spirit is to be understood under the name “Holy Spirit.”

But someone will say: if the Father is said to love by the Holy Spirit because he loves by love common to the three persons, which is sometimes appropriated to the Holy Spirit, then the Father should be said to be wise by the Son, because he is wise by wisdom common to the three persons which is attributed to the Son. To this it must be said that the consequence does not follow. For although what is common belongs to both, the Son does not signify commonality as the Holy Spirit does. For the Holy Spirit is referred to both, because he proceeds from both; the Son only to the Father.

Likewise Augustine says:

> [Note: Col. 0874D: These words occur in *Magister*, distinction 32, §3.]

“If the Father is wise by begotten wisdom, that wisdom is not from the Father, but the Father is from it.” Therefore, if the Father is wise by wisdom common to the three persons, the Father is from it; for it is not from the Father, although he is from it. Therefore, by generation or in some other way—

Thus we explain it: if the Father is wise by begotten wisdom, since it is from another person and another person is from it, the Father himself is from it, while it is not from the Father. This cannot be said of wisdom common to the three persons, since no person is from it.

Others say that the same notion is predicated when it is said, “The Father and Son love one another by the Holy Spirit,” and when it is said, “The Father and Son are the principle of the Holy Spirit.” Thus “The Father and Son love one another by the Holy Spirit” means: the Father and Son are united by breathing forth the Holy Spirit. Namely, “The Father loves the Son by the Holy Spirit,” that is, he breathes forth to the Son the Holy Spirit, who is the communion of both. Similarly, “The Son loves the Father by the Holy Spirit,” that is, he breathes forth the Holy Spirit, who is the communion of both. Or: “The Father loves the Son by the Holy Spirit,” that is, he breathes forth the Holy Spirit toward the Son, that is, he gives the Son that the Son breathes forth the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, when it is said, “To love and to be are the same for the Father; the Father loves the Son by the Holy Spirit; therefore he is by the Holy Spirit,” there is a fallacy of equivocation. For the verb *I love* first predicates the divine essence; afterward, when it is taken up again, it signifies relation. When it is said simply, “The Father loves by the Holy Spirit,” it is false, because essence is meant; but when an accusative is added, it is transferred to the signification of relation. Therefore they argue thus: “For God, to be and to be able are the same; God can do all things; therefore he is all things.”

But when it is said, “The Father and Son are by that by which they love the good,” they accept it, because the verb *they love* signifies essence if the question is in the neuter. But when it is assumed, “The Father and Son love one another by the Holy Spirit,” something other than what was proposed is assumed, since the middle term is taken differently. They therefore argue: “There is none but the Father through whom the Son exists; but the Son exists through himself; therefore the Son is the Father.”

But for those who say this, it is difficult to say what is predicated in such propositions as “The Holy Spirit loves the Father or the Son, or the Holy Spirit by the Holy Spirit,” or “The Father or Son loves the Holy Spirit by the Holy Spirit.” For relation cannot be predicated of these, since the Holy Spirit is not distinguished from the Holy Spirit by relation. They can be greatly pressed by propositions of this kind.

Therefore, since the verb *I love*, used by itself, signifies essence—and since, with an accusative, it does not signify relation, whence they accept “The Father loves the Son by the Holy Spirit”—it does not seem that one should grant: “The Father loves the Son by his essence,” just as the Father does not breathe forth the Holy Spirit by his essence. This appears contradicted by the authority cited above:

> [Note: Book XV, *On the Trinity*, chapter 7, in Augustine.]

> “In that Trinity, who would dare say that the Father loves neither himself nor the Son except through the Holy Spirit?”

This indicates not only that the Father loves the Son by the Holy Spirit, but also by his essence. Yet they think this was said because the Father does not have the authority to love from the Holy Spirit. Augustine therefore does not deny in that passage that the Father loves solely through the Holy Spirit, but denies that he has the authority to love from the Holy Spirit. Otherwise, for them, “The Father loves the Son by his essence” would not be the same as “by his gift.” For they find the former in the authority, understanding it thus: “The Father loves the Son by his essence,” that is, by the Holy Spirit, who is the Father’s own essence—just as, conversely, their opinion had interpreted “The Father loves the Son by the Holy Spirit” as “by his essence, which is the Holy Spirit.” Since that authority seems to say that the Father loves the Son both by the Holy Spirit and by his essence, it seems contrary to both opinions unless it is interpreted by both methods.

## Chapter XXII. The manifold distinction of the persons in the Trinity

> [Note: Col. 0876D: *Magister* I, distinction 34, §§6–8 and following; and distinction 31.]

It remains that we set forth briefly and clearly the distinctions of the persons, as we promised at the end of the preceding chapter, insofar as we have received them as determined by expositors of Sacred Scripture. The distinction of persons is twofold: it is made either by appropriation of names and realities, or by appropriation of names but not realities.

They are distinguished by appropriation of names and realities when it is said, “This one is Father, that one Son.” For the name *Father* and the thing—that is, the signification of the name—belong to the Father alone. The Son is not Father either in name or signification, for he is not begotten as the Son is.

The Son is distinguished by appropriation of name and reality. For the Father is not Son either in name or reality, since he is not begotten. Although the three persons are one Spirit and the same Spirit is holy, still by this conjunction of distinctions “Holy Spirit” is transferred to signify the third person in the Trinity and his personal property, by which that person is someone other than the Father and Son. To him, therefore, are appropriated both the name of the thing and the thing of the name. Neither the Father nor the Son, with the same signification retained, is the Holy Spirit, for neither is breathed forth.

When, therefore, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are said, the persons are distinguished by appropriation both of names to significations and of significations to names. Again, they are distinguished by appropriation of names. Although the three persons are the same undivided power, nevertheless the name *power*, not the reality signified by the name, is appropriated to the Father: either because that whereby the Father is powerful is from no one, whereas that whereby the Son or Holy Spirit is powerful is from another; therefore the Father is called power in a special sense—not that he alone is power, for the three persons are equally and alike the same power—or because, being Father, he is called powerful lest he be understood as powerless. Fathers are commonly decrepit and, through age, powerless. To remove from the name Father any suspicion of impotence, the Father is called—not, I say, uniquely—power in a special sense.

Likewise, although the three persons are the same wisdom, the name *wisdom*, not the reality of the name, is appropriated to the Son. This is drawn proportionally from natural things: wisdom or knowledge is from the mind, yet cannot exist without it; and whatever change occurs in the thing known, wisdom or knowledge of the thing nevertheless remains immovably with the mind. Therefore, since the Son is from the Father and is never without the Father, by whatever analogy from natural things, the name wisdom is appropriated to the Son, so that he alone may be designated wisdom who is not alone wisdom.

But you will say: on the same reasoning the Holy Spirit will be called wisdom. I reply: the name wisdom is appropriated more to the Son than to the Spirit because, where no words suffice, it is permissible to speak in whatever way we can. The first procession is that of the Son from the Father; from there comes the procession of the Spirit from both. I do not mean a succession in time, nor a priority in the power of nature, but only that the Son proceeds from the Father and not from the Spirit, while the Spirit proceeds from both.

Therefore the name wisdom is appropriated to the Son, because sons, as younger, are called indiscreet and foolish. Thus, lest the Son, when called Son, be believed foolish, he is called wisdom by an appropriated name, not by an appropriated reality. Likewise the three persons are the same goodness, yet the name goodness is appropriated to the Holy Spirit because the Spirit is the gift of Father and Son, and when that gift is given to us, an outpouring of graces is made to us.

For though the gift is one, in it every diversity of graces is given, just as—to speak by whatever analogy may be permitted—a horse is given to a man. Although there is one gift in it, many uses are given: whoever gives a man a horse gives him manifold use, to carry the man, transport wood, and so forth. Certainly the Holy Spirit has been given to us by the Father and Son as a gift, and in that gift manifold uses of graces have been given to us: for he was given to Solomon for wisdom, to David for gentleness, to Job for patience. “There are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit” (1 Cor. 12). Therefore, because the Spirit is the gift in which the outpouring of graces occurs, the name goodness is appropriated to him; for in natural things we are led especially to use the name goodness from generosity. Or the name *spirit* commonly suggests swelling or puffing up; therefore, lest the Spirit, when called Spirit, be believed swollen or inflated, the name goodness or kindness, but not the reality of the name, is appropriated to the Spirit. This, then, is said to occur by appropriation of names, not realities.

Again, although the three persons are one God acting—and we act through power—operation is appropriated to the Father, who is called power. Although the three persons are one God disposing—and we dispose through wisdom—disposition is appropriated to the Son, who is called wisdom. And although the three persons are one God preserving all things—because through goodness we preserve things unharmed—preservation is appropriated to the Spirit. Behold a third distinction of the persons: operation, disposition, preservation. It is made by appropriation of names, not realities. Thus the Father acts by power, the Son disposes by wisdom, and the Spirit preserves all things in their being by goodness.

Again, although the three persons are one author, the name authority, not the reality of the name, is appropriated to the Father. For by every rationale for speaking, it is said of the Father. The Father is author by generation, but the Son and Holy Spirit are not. He is author by spiration, as is the Son but not the Holy Spirit, for the Spirit proceeds from both. He is author by creation, as are the Son and Spirit, for the three persons create all things. He is author by the bestowal of graces, as are the Son and Holy Spirit, for the three persons bestow graces.

I do not understand this division as dividing the Father’s authorities; rather, it gives diverse reasons for calling him author, although the authority is one. Therefore, since the Father is called author for every reason by which he may be called author, the name author is appropriated to him, not the reality of the name; or because the Father is from no one, whereas the Son and Holy Spirit are authors from another, namely from the Father. Therefore the Father is called author by an appropriated name. Hence Hilary says:

> “In the Father is authority, in the Son nativity, in the Holy Spirit the communion of both.”

This might seem to mean: just as nativity belongs to the Son, not the Father or Holy Spirit, and communion to the Spirit, not the Father or Son, so authority belongs to the Father, not the Son or Spirit—which is far from the truth. Rather, when “nativity is in the Son” is said, the Father’s authority is understood to be in the Son, but through nativity: what belongs to the Father as from no one is understood to belong to the Son from the Father through generation. And when it is added, “in the Spirit is the communion of both,” the Spirit is thereby understood to possess the authority of Father and Son, but through common procession from both.

Behold again another distinction of the persons, made partly by appropriation of name and not reality, when nativity is said of the Son—for the Son alone is called born—or communion of the Spirit, for the Spirit alone proceeds commonly from both. Again, although the three persons are the one from whom are all things, the name unity, not the reality of the name, is appropriated to the Father by transference.

For just as unity is the principle of all things and every number is from unity, so likewise—though the analogy is not explicitly stated—the Father is the principle of all things: all things are from the Father; the Son through generation, the Spirit through procession, temporal things through the Creator. Or unity is said specially of the Father in order that otherness may be understood to be removed from him. For the Father, being principle without principle and author from no one, has no one after him in comparison with whom he might be called other; rather, he is the first one, in relation to whom the Son is called other and the Holy Spirit third.

Thus Hilary says that “unity is in the Father, but equality in the Son.” Yet since otherness is set alongside unity, rather than equality alongside unity, it would seem more fitting to add, “In the Son is otherness.” But lest the name otherness suggest some inferiority of the Son in relation to the Father—for one who is other than the king at court is inferior to the king—Hilary added, “In the Son is equality,” so that the name equality might remove suspicion of inferiority and suggest the meaning of otherness. For one equal to another is other than the one to whom he is equal.

Therefore, although the Father is equal to the Son and the Son equal to the Father, the Son is specially said—not, I say, uniquely—to be equal to the Father, rather than the Father equal to the Son.

> [Note: Col. 0877D: *Magister*, distinction 31, §4. Walter of Saint-Victor attacks this in his book *Against the Four Labyrinths of France*.]

For the Son is called the image of the Father, considering the relation of proportion: every image is derived from its exemplar. The exemplar is not compared to the image—as Achilles is not compared to his statue—but the image to the exemplar, as the statue to Achilles. Thus the Son is said to be equal to the Father, coeternal with him, and consubstantial with him, whereas the reverse is not said, though it may truly be said.

Again:

> [Note: Augustine, book VI, *On the Trinity*, chapter 10.]

Knowledge of the Father is received from the Son, as the Son himself shows when he says: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John 14). Therefore, because the image is compared to the exemplar, and not conversely, and the Son is the Father’s image, the name equality is appropriated to the Son as image.

> [Note: Col. 0878D: *Magister*, above, §11.]

In the Holy Spirit is the harmony of unity and equality. For the Spirit is called the harmony of Father and Son, who are called unity and equality, because he proceeds equally and harmoniously from both. The Father and Son are also harmonious in this: that they together breathe forth the Holy Spirit. Or he is called the harmony of unity and equality because, through the graces bestowed upon us in him, the Spirit reconciles us to unity, the Father, and equality, the Son.

Or it may be said that in the Holy Spirit is the harmony of equality and unity because unity and equality are assigned in him harmoniously. Since he proceeds from the Father, he thereby has that he is one with him who is one with the Son. Since he proceeds from the Son, he is equal to him by the Son’s equality, and therefore equal to the Father. Thus equality and unity are harmoniously in him. For since the name unity is appropriated to the Father in contrast with the Son, and the name equality to the Son in contrast with the Father, if we consider the reasons for these appropriations, unity and equality are in them discordantly. But since the Holy Spirit is called one with them and equal to them, and the term unity or equality is not appropriated to him in contrast with either, unity and equality are said of him harmoniously.

Behold another distinction of the persons, again partly by appropriation of names and not realities, when unity is said of the Father and equality of the Son; and partly by appropriation of name and reality, when harmony is said of the Spirit in the first and third senses. In the middle sense—when harmony is said because he reconciles us to God—the reality is not appropriated to him, for the three persons do not make themselves harmonious. Thus this distinction is unity, equality, harmony:

> “And yet these three are one because of the Father, equal because of the Son, connected because of the Holy Spirit.”

> [Note: Augustine, book I, *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 5.]

A trace of this Trinity appears in some manner in creation.

> [Note: Col. 0879D: All this is found in Augustine, book VI, *On the Trinity*, chapter 10 to the end.]

For all things made by divine art display in themselves a certain unity, form, and order. Whatever exists is one thing of some sort, whether bodies or spirits. Bodies are formed by shapes and qualities, and souls by arts; and they seek or maintain order: bodies by weights, so that what is less akin to earth is less heavy, and conversely; and by locations, so that the heavier things are pressed lower down and the lighter lifted higher up; souls by delights, for they delight in imitating the pattern of the heavenly order according to which they were created.

Of all these—unity, form, order—there are in the Trinity the highest origin, the most perfect beauty, and the most blessed love.

> [Note: Augustine, as above.]

This must, however, be understood distributively: unity is referred to origin, form to beauty, and order to love. Unity is called origin in the Trinity because, although there is unity in creatures, perfect unity, surpassing every unity, is in the Trinity. Yet it is appropriated to the Father in name, as has been said, not in reality. Thus, since in natural things unity is in some sense the origin of numbers, because by nature unity always precedes number, so that something may be other than it, unity is in the Father, who is the highest origin, because the Father is first one in such a way that he has no one after him from whom he may be other.

The most perfect beauty belongs to the whole Trinity; yet it is appropriated to the Son in name, not in reality, because he alone, as has been said, is called the image of the Father. Form belongs to an image, and beauty to form. Therefore, since there is beauty in creatures according to form, the perfection of all beauty is in him who is called the image of the Father.

The most blessed love likewise belongs to the whole Trinity, but is appropriated to the Spirit in name, not in reality, because in him every good is attributed to creatures, in which they delight. Order belongs to delight, for none have tranquil delight unless they preserve their due order.

The unity of creatures is referred to the Father as origin, who is origin without origin. For eternity is in the Father, and eternity is appropriated to him in name, not in reality. The form of creatures is referred to the Son, the most perfect beauty, for form is in the image. But their order is referred to the Holy Spirit, the most blessed love, for use is in the gift.

[Note: [Col. 0879D] Master I, distinction 31, §3, etc.] Here again he sets forth, following Hilary, distinctions of the persons by appropriation of names, not of things. [Note: [Col. 0880D] Supply: Augustine, *On the Trinity*, VI.10, from Hilary whom he cites.] Supreme origin, most perfect beauty, most blessed love; likewise eternity, form, use. Hence: eternity in the Father, form in the Image, use in the Gift. The Apostle also distinguishes the Trinity by such prepositions—“from,” “through,” and “in”—saying: “from whom,” [Col. 0880B] “through whom,” and “in whom are all things” (Romans 11). Although all things are from the three persons, [Note: [Col. 0880D] See Augustine above, and *On the Trinity*, I.6.] nevertheless, in saying “from whom,” he signified the Father particularly, to whom the name of authority or power, by which all things exist, is appropriated when spoken of as cause. But note that he said “from whom” more carefully than “of whom.” For although the prepositions *ex* (“from”) and *de* (“of, from”) are causal, they are used according to different kinds of cause. If I say, “A ring is of gold,” I signify matter; if I say, “That Son is from this Father,” I signify the cause of essence. Therefore, since we are not from God the Father as from matter, but are from him as an efficient cause, the Apostle says not “of him” but “from him are all things,” signifying him to be the author and efficient cause of all things.

Likewise, although all things are ordered through the three persons, [Col. 0880C] nevertheless, in saying “through whom,” he understood the Son. For we ordinarily arrange things through wisdom and at wisdom’s direction. To the Son, when spoken of as cause, the name wisdom is appropriated. Again, although all things are preserved in their being in the three persons and in the goodness of the three persons, nevertheless, because the name of goodness and harmony is appropriated, as was said, to the Holy Spirit, it is said particularly—understanding the Spirit—that all things are preserved “in him,” as in their bond and harmony. The Apostle therefore says: All things are from the Father creating; all things are through the Son ordering; all things, having been ordered, are preserved by the Spirit. But this distinction too is made by appropriation of names, not of things.

[Col. 0880D] Likewise, memory is attributed to the Father on account of eternity, [Note: [Col. 0880D] Augustine, *On the Trinity*, XV.17, applies these three to the Trinity.] lest you understand in him a defect arising from antiquity; understanding to the Son on account of wisdom; love to the Holy Spirit on account of goodness—so that the distinction is made by appropriation of the name, not of the thing. Observe therefore, whoever you are that read, when you encounter distinctions of the persons, whether they are made by names and things that are appropriated, or by neither, or partly by the one and partly by the other. The distinctions stated may be combined in this manner: From the powerful Father, one eternal author [Col. 0881A] by origin, created through the wise Son, born equal to the Father, ordering most perfect beauty, things are ordered in the kindly, harmonious, common Spirit; by the most blessed love, the use of gifts is preserved. Yet, though the persons are thus distinguished, the Apostle adds: “To him be glory”; and by saying “to him” in the singular he signifies the single essence of the persons as one. [Note: [Col. 0881D] Romans 11; Augustine, *On the Trinity*, I.6.]

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the terms “similar” and “equal”

[Note: [Col. 0881D] Master I, distinction 31, §12, etc.] First we have spoken of those names which are said of God according to essence; second, of those which, though said essentially, are sometimes taken personally. Third, we must speak of those which, though said relatively of God as to the [Col. 0881B] form of expression, nevertheless signify the divine essence. Such are the names “equal,” “similar,” and “coeternal.”

Some say that these signify the divine essence, since the equality or similarity of the three persons is their one essence; and this seems capable of support from Augustine’s authority. [Note: [Col. 0881D] *On the Trinity*, V.6, near the end.] For he says: “The Son is not equal to the Father according to that by which he is said in relation to the Father. It remains, then, that he is equal according to that which is said in relation to himself.” But whatever is said in relation to itself is said according to essence. Therefore it remains that the Son is equal to the Father according to substance.

But the following objection is made. The Father is similar to the Son and to the Holy Spirit; the Holy Spirit is similar to the Father and the Son. Since, then, these terms are said of individual persons [Col. 0881C] in the singular, they seem, according to the rules given above, to be said of them singly and not plurally in their totality. Therefore Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one similar or one equal—which, however, is said incongruously. Accordingly they say that terms of this kind must be excepted from the rule just stated.

Again, the similarity of the three persons is signified by the term “similar”; [65] that similarity is the divine essence; therefore the divine essence is signified by this word “similar.” Yet it is wholly relative, and is used wholly relatively when it signifies the divine essence. Therefore the divine essence is said relatively; therefore it is distinguished from something by a relation inhering in it.

To this one must say that “to be said relatively” is understood in two ways. For to be said relatively is to be predicated or signified by a relative term; and in this sense it is true that the divine essence is said relatively. But to be said relatively is also to be distinguished by the relation signified by the relative term; the divine essence is not said relatively in this way. Therefore, when from the premise “The divine essence is said relatively” it is concluded, “therefore the divine essence is distinguished from another by relation,” one must object that a conclusion is drawn from a proposition given in one meaning as though it had been given in another. This is the fallacy found in the statement: “I see myself; this verb *see*, with this accusative *myself*, is construed transitively; therefore there is a transition [Col. 0882A] between the thing denoted by this verb ‘see’ and that denoted by this active term ‘myself.’”

Again, nothing is signified by the name “similar” which is not signified by the name “equal,” and conversely. For similarity and equality are there the same thing. Therefore these propositions signify precisely the same thing: “The Father is similar to the Son”; “The Father is equal to the Son.” To this one must say that these names, when said of God, principally signify the same thing but connote different things. For when it is said, “The Father is similar to the Son,” it principally signifies that the Father is the same essence as the Son; further, that the Father is neither alien nor different from the Son. But when it is said, “The Father is equal to the Son,” it principally signifies that the Father is the same essence as the Son and is neither greater nor less than the Son. [Col. 0882B] They therefore signify the same thing principally, but connote different things.

It has seemed to others [Note: [Col. 0882D] Among them his teacher is especially noted—namely, the Master here, §b—from whom the disciple fortunately dissents in this matter.] that these words were introduced more to exclude than to posit, so that the sense is this: “They are similar,” that is, they are dissimilar in nothing, because the Father is neither alien nor different from the Son; likewise, “equal,” that is, unequal in nothing, because the Father is neither greater nor less than the Son. Nevertheless, it may be granted that the three terms are said according to essence. For “to be said according to essence” is understood in two ways. Something is said according to essence because essence is the cause of its being said; and in this sense it is true that “similar” is said of God according to essence. For the essence of the three persons is the cause why the Father is called similar to the Son. Something is also said [Col. 0882C] according to essence when it predicates or signifies essence. “Similar” is not said according to essence in this latter sense, because it neither signifies nor predicates essence, just as “similar” is said according to quality: quality is the cause why this is called similar to that. Something is also said according to quality when it predicates or signifies quality, as “white”; and in this sense “similar” is not said according to quality, because it neither predicates nor signifies quality.

Now the Son is equal to the Father according to essence, because the Son is coeternal with the Father according to essence, as is shown thus: the Father and Son are eternal; in God eternity and essence are the same; therefore Father and Son are coeternal according to essence. By the same reasoning they are equal or similar according to essence. [Col. 0882D] But if one concludes from this: “Therefore being equal or similar to the Father belongs to all three persons, because whatever is said of one according to essence belongs to all three”; or: “Being coeternal with the Father and Holy Spirit belongs to the Son alone; therefore this is not said of him according to essence”—neither conclusion follows. For when it is said that whatever is said of one of the three persons according to essence belongs to all three, or that nothing which belongs to only one of the three belongs to it according to essence, this must be understood of terms signifying the divine essence. [Col. 0883A] For there is no term signifying the divine essence which does not belong to all three, and conversely, as they themselves maintain.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the term “distinct”

[Note: [Col. 0883D] Master I, distinction 24.] There are two classes of terms said of God from eternity. [66] Some are said according to essence; others according to relation. Of those said according to essence, three classes were distinguished above. Some signify essence and are always taken essentially. Others signify essence and are sometimes taken personally, such as power, wisdom, and goodness. Others, while signifying essence, are said relatively as to the form of the word, such as “similar” and “equal”; [Col. 0883B] and all these have been discussed.

We must now deal with those which are said of God according to relation. The following must be understood as a rule concerning them: all that signify relations are said according to relation, but the converse does not hold. By “relation” here is understood any property, whether one person is referred to another by it, or is so distinguished that it is not referred to another. Thus the Father is distinguished from the Son by unbegottenness, without being referred to the Son by it. There is therefore another term which is said of God according to relation yet does not signify a relation: thus the term “distinct” is said according to relation, yet does not signify relation.

For “to be said according to relation” is used in many ways. Something is said according to relation because relation is the cause of its being said; and in this manner this term is said according to relation, because relation is the cause why the Father is called distinct from the Son and Holy Spirit—just as “to be said according to essence” is understood in two ways.

“But,” someone will say, “the term ‘distinct’ is said according to relation; therefore it signifies relation.” This is a fallacy. The term “similar” is said according to essence; therefore it signifies essence. Yet this is not true according to one of the opinions stated, just as “similar” is said according to quality. Again, the term “distinct” is an uncompounded term, belongs to God from eternity, does not signify the divine essence, and is said according to relation; [Col. 0883D] therefore it signifies relation. This too is invalid, because this term, along with others that have been excepted, must be excepted from the aforesaid rules.
