Again, wherever the term “distinct” is properly understood, it signifies distinction; and when said of the Father, it is properly understood with the propriety with which any term can properly be said of God. Therefore it either signifies distinction then or nowhere. The distinction, then, attributed to God and existing in God when it is said, “The Father is distinct from the Son,” is either the divine essence or a property of the divine essence. But if it is a property and is neither paternity, filiation, procession, unbegottenness, nor spiration, there is some property [Col. 0884A] in the Trinity besides one of those five—which it is impious to say.

To this it may also be answered that this term does not signify distinction. When said of one of the persons, it removes rather than posits, just as “similar” or “equal” posits nothing in God. Otherwise one could not avoid saying that equality or similarity is the divine essence, which has been denied according to one of the opinions stated above. Such terms are introduced more to exclude than to posit.

Others offer the merely probable solution that this term signifies distinction—that is, a distinct property—but neither paternity nor any of those five, nor something other than them. For it does not signify a property that is some determinate one; it signifies relation indeterminately, neither this nor that—just as the word “white,” even if there were only five whitenesses, would signify neither this whiteness nor that nor a third, but whiteness indeterminately.

“But,” someone will object, “when it is said, ‘The Father is distinct from the Son,’ this word ‘distinct’ signifies a distinct property and is predicated of the Father. There is no property in the Father by which he is not distinguished from the Son or from the Holy Spirit. Therefore ‘distinct’ is not said in the same signification of the Son and the Holy Spirit.” This is a fallacy. The term “Father,” “Son,” or “Holy Spirit” signifies a distinct property when it is said, “The Father is Father,” “the Son is Son,” [Col. 0884C] or “the Holy Spirit is Holy Spirit”; and it signifies no property that does not inhere in the Father. [67] Therefore, in the signification in which it is said of the Father, it is said of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

Again, the term “distinct” signifies a property when said of the Father; therefore it signifies a property by which the Father is distinguished, or by which he is not distinguished. If by one by which the Father is not distinguished from the Son or Holy Spirit, then there is some property in the Father by which he is distinguished neither from the Son nor from the Holy Spirit—which is false. But this term signifies a property by which the Father is distinguished from the Son or Holy Spirit; yet he is distinguished by no property except unbegottenness, paternity, or spiration. Therefore the term signifies one of these properties.

To this [Col. 0884D] one must say that no relation is to be admitted here. The term signifies a property which either is or is not—namely, none determinate. One must therefore press the earlier argument, in which there is a fallacy of figure of speech, when a “what sort of thing” is changed into a “this particular thing.” Fallacy: “The word ‘man’ signifies a man; therefore it signifies a man who is healthy or sick”; or “this image represents a lion which is in the forest or outside it.”

Again, the term “distinct from the Son” is said only of the Father and Holy Spirit, in the same signification of both, and signifies a distinct property. Therefore the Father and Holy Spirit are distinguished from the Son by that property. Therefore there is some property [Col. 0885A] common to the Father and Holy Spirit by which Father and Holy Spirit are distinguished from the Son—which is false. This is the fallacy of the first kind: the term “man” is said in the same signification of Socrates and Plato and signifies humanity; therefore some humanity is common to Socrates and Plato.

Many arguments may be constructed here, in all of which no necessity can be found because, as has been shown, the transition is from a “what sort of thing” to a “this particular thing.” Thus, if anyone argues: “The term ‘distinct’ is said of God according to relation; therefore it is said of one person and not of all,” this is a fallacy. The term “Father,” “Son,” or “Spirit” is said of God according to relation; therefore it is said of one of the three persons and not all. Or: the term “some [Col. 0885B] person” signifies a person; therefore it is said of one person and not all.

## CHAPTER XXV. On terms that signify and denote relations, but do not couple them, such as “paternity” and “filiation”

[Note: [Col. 0885D] Master, distinctions 27, etc., and 33, etc.] From what has been said it is clear that everything signifying relations is said according to relation; yet not everything said according to relation signifies relations, as was said regarding the term “distinct.” In treating those that signify relations, the first point in the teaching is that some signify persons together with notions, such as “Father,” “Son,” and the like; others signify relations alone. Of the latter, some signify and denote relations but do not couple them, such as paternity, filiation, [Col. 0885C] procession, and the like. Others signify relations and couple them, but do not denote them, such as “begetting,” “begotten,” and “proceeding.” We must deal with all these and with what they signify; and in this order, first refuting by authority and reason a false opinion of certain people concerning the properties, and answering their novel inventions which pertain generally to the properties of the Trinity. Then, comprehending the properties themselves under a definite number, we shall investigate by examination what may be specially asked concerning them.

Certain people, glorying in their own understanding, reduce what is read about the properties to modes of speaking. They do not wish to understand that the properties are something [Col. 0885D] or are things in the persons or in the divine essence, if authors speak in different modes concerning the persons, just as they establish that there are several persons in different modes. Therefore, when it is said, “Paternity is in the Father,” “unbegottenness is in the Father,” this is not referred to a plurality of properties, but to a plurality [68] of modes by which we speak about the Father. For they understand mere pluralities [Col. 0886A] of names, without a plurality of properties, just as Sabellius recognized only a trinity of names without a plurality of persons.

They are therefore not to be heard, because authority says: [Note: [Col. 0885D] In the preface to *On the Trinity*, attributed to Pope Pelagius.] “In the persons, property; in the essence, unity.” And Jerome says elsewhere: [Note: [Col. 0885D] Rather, this is the exposition of the Creed by the heresiarch Pelagius, writing to Innocent; see the notes on Robert Pullus, p. 291.] “Rejecting the heresy of Sabellius, we distinguish three persons expressly under property. For we confess not merely names but also the properties of the names—that is, persons; or, as the Greeks express it, *hypostases*, that is, subsistences.” John of Damascus also says: [Note: [Col. 0885D] *On the Orthodox Faith*, III.5; and not dissimilarly I.10: ‘For the three holy hypostases—that is, subsistences and persons—differ from one another only in these personal properties, being distinguished indivisibly not by substance but by the characteristic mark of their proper hypostasis.’ And in the following chapter: ‘We acknowledge one God; we understand difference only in the properties of fatherhood, sonship, and procession, according to cause and caused, and personal perfection, that is, difference of mode of existence.’] “We recognize the difference of the hypostases, that is, of the persons, by the paternal, filial, and processional property.”

For Augustine says: [Note: [Col. 0886D] *On Faith and the Creed*, ch. 9, near the end.] “In God’s substance there is nothing which is not substance, as though substance were one thing there and something else happened to substance. For whatever can be understood there is substance.” And elsewhere: [Note: [Col. 0886D] *On the Trinity*, XV.17.] “Such is the mode of being in the nature of each of the three that the one who has is what he has, except that a person has a person; yet he is not the one whom he has.” Countless authorities occur to us, which it would not burden us to bring forward, were it not that readers or hearers would be wearied.

This same point can also be shown by arguments. The Father is Father; therefore he is Father by something; therefore by paternity, or by something which is not paternity. If by something which is not paternity, and there is nothing by which the Father is Father that is not in him and is not the divine essence, then the Father is Father by divine essence. But if he is Father by paternity, then paternity is in the Father; therefore paternity itself is [Col. 0886C] Father, because nothing is in the Father which is not Father.

Again, the word “paternity” is a substantive noun: it belongs either to something or to nothing. If it belongs to something, then paternity is something. Nothing other than the Father can be found which is the Father’s paternity; for if the Father’s paternity is something else, since that thing is in the Father, something would now be in the Father which was not Father. If it is said that the term “paternity” belongs to nothing, then paternity is nothing; therefore Father is nothing, just as, if whiteness is nothing, nothing is white. Again, paternity either is something or is not something. If it is something, it is either Father or something else; it cannot be something else, for then it would not be in the Father; therefore it is Father. But if paternity is not something, how then is it a relation, or how is something said in relation to something according to it? [Col. 0886D] Many other arguments may be brought against them; but since they are not to be heard, neither are they worthy to be attacked further on this point.

Yet an answer must be made to their barking on this subject. For they say that nothing common to the three persons is proper to one of them; the divine essence [Col. 0887A] is common to the three persons; therefore it is not proper to one of them; therefore it is not proper to the Father. But paternity is proper to the Father; therefore the divine essence is not paternity. This is so frivolous as to be unworthy even of an answer. For they can infer in the same way: “The divine essence is not a *characteristicon*; therefore it is not a character.” The divine essence does not determine or distinguish, yet it is character. Likewise, the divine essence does not beget; yet it is a person who begets, a person who is begotten, and a person who proceeds.

Again, though it is said that the divine essence is paternity, there seems to follow what almost everyone denies: that the Father is Father by the same thing by which he is God. For all maintain that the Father is Father by one thing and God by another, and this is found in [Col. 0887B] authority. To this one need only answer: paternity and divinity are the same; the Father is Father by paternity and God by divinity; therefore the Father is Father by the same thing by which he is God. This is a fallacy. The divine essence is the same thing as the Son; the Son is begotten, the divine essence is not begotten; therefore the same thing is begotten and is not begotten. Again, the divine essence is that by which the Father is Father; therefore the Father is Father by the divine essence.

Note, therefore, that in the Trinity there is never a necessary inference from the name of a person or notion to any general name which, if used properly, signifies the essence. Fallacy: “The divine essence is the Father who begets.”

Again: “Paternity exists, and by it the Father is Father.” Does this [Col. 0887C] proposition speak of the divine essence or not? If it speaks of the divine essence, and nothing is said of it except that it exists and that by it the Father is Father, then the Father is Father by the divine essence. But if this proposition does not speak of the divine essence, and speaks of only one thing, then it speaks of nothing by reason of its being the divine essence; and thus it does not speak of paternity by reason of paternity’s being the divine essence.

To this one must say that the proposition “Paternity exists, and by it the Father is Father” does speak of the divine essence; it says of the essence that paternity exists and that by it the Father is Father. But “paternity exists and by it the Father is Father” is something other than this: it is another enunciable, just as the proposition “Charity is not in the devil” speaks of the divine essence and says of it that it is not in the devil—which is true—and is something other than the false proposition. This can also be made clear by a dialectical example: when it is said, “The Seine flows,” one speaks about something; yet one does not say of some thing that it flows—which would be false—but says that the Seine flows, which is true.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On terms which signify relations, couple them, and stand for persons, such as “Father” and “Son”

[Note: [Col. 0887D] Master I, distinctions 28 and 33.] There are other relative terms which signify relations and couple them, such as “Father” and “Son.” Since these belong to the same thing as enunciable terms, the question may arise whether they and those terms belong by the same thing: for example, whether the Father is Father by the same thing by which he is God, [Col. 0888A] or by another.

The objection is framed thus: The Father is Father by something; the Father is God by something; therefore the Father is Father by that by which he is God, or by something else. If by that same thing, since the Father is Father by one thing only and God by one thing only, then the Father is Father only by that same thing by which he is God. But the Father is Father by paternity and God by divinity; therefore the Father is Father by divinity, or God by paternity. If it is said that the Father is Father by one thing and God by another, yet the Father is Father by one thing only and God by one thing only, then the Father is Father only by another thing and God only by another thing. Therefore nothing by which the Father is Father is that by which he is God—which is false, because the paternity by which the Father is Father is the deity by which he is God.

Again, nothing is that by which the Father is Father which is not that by which he is God; [Col. 0888B] therefore the Father is not Father by another thing than that by which he is God. To this some say, quite plausibly, that one should not grant, “The Father is Father by one thing and God by another,” unless it is understood thus: that is, he is called Father in one manner, namely relatively, and God in another manner, namely simply and without reference; because names of the neuter gender refer to essence, masculine names to person. Thus one should not say, “The Father is Father by something,” taking “something” as neuter. For the Father is not Father by essence; and if this is found somewhere, it must be understood as was stated.

Again, the Father is paternity; therefore he is paternity by something or by nothing. If the Father is paternity by something, it is either by essence or by property. If by essence, then, since [Col. 0888C] Father and Son are one essence, they are one paternity, because in that respect it will be the same thing for the Father to be paternity and to be essence. If it is said that the Father is paternity by paternity, then it is the same thing for the Father to be paternity and to be Father. By the same reasoning it is the same thing for the Father to be Father and to be spiration, and to be unbegottenness. Hence one can infer that it is the same thing for the Father to be paternity, spiration, and unbegottenness.

Again, that which is paternity is unbegottenness or spiration; therefore paternity is unbegottenness or spiration. If it is the same thing for the Father to be Father and to be spiration, and the same thing for the Son to be Son and to be spiration, which is proved in the same manner, then it is the same thing for the Father to be Father and for the Son to be Son. Or thus: it is the same thing for the Father to be spiration and to be Father; [Col. 0888D] Father and Son are one spiration; therefore they are one Father.

Again, paternity, insofar as it is paternity, is not unbegottenness; therefore, insofar as it is paternity, it is distinguished from unbegottenness; therefore it is distinguished by some property or properties; therefore some property distinguishes paternity from unbegottenness which is in paternity and is not in unbegottenness; and so properties are distinguished from one another by properties, [70] just as persons are.

Again, paternity agrees with unbegottenness in this, that it itself is Father; paternity is Father by paternity; therefore unbegottenness is Father by the same or by another paternity; therefore unbegottenness is Father by the same or another paternity. [Col. 0889A] Again, spiration is Father by spiration; spiration is Son by spiration; therefore the spiration that is Father is the same as that which is Son; therefore being Father and being Son are the same, and thus something is the divine essence for which being Father and being Son are the same. Or, if one refuses to grant that spiration is Father by spiration, he will grant that the Father is Father by spiration. For why should one more readily grant that the Father is this person by paternity, by which he is, and not grant that the Father is the same person by unbegottenness or by spiration, since these are three properties in the Father? But if the Father is Father by spiration and the Son is Son by that same spiration, then it is the same thing for the Father to be Father and for the Son to be Son.

These and similar questions raised by some are [Col. 0889B] difficult and obscure. In all of them it may be said that, as in natural things one property is not distinguished from another property by a property, lest there be an infinite regress, since substance alone is capable of accidents, so also in the Trinity—if it is permissible to transfer an analogy from those things to these—one property is not distinguished from another by a property. Hence it must not be granted that the Father is paternity, spiration, or unbegottenness by something. Nor is paternity paternity by something, nor is paternity Father by something, if indeed it is true that paternity is Father. For this is doubtful, since the name “Father” may there predicate only the notion; but that does not seem to be granted, because paternity does not beget. Indeed, such expressions seem absurd. But this will be treated more clearly later.

The following could indeed be doubtful: “Paternity is the divine essence by something.” For it seems that paternity is God by divinity, and I see no inconvenience which can follow from granting this. Yet the converse does not hold: God is not paternity by divinity, nor is paternity paternity by relation. If someone argues: “The term ‘paternity’ is said of God according to relation; therefore the Father is paternity by relation,” this is invalid. For when it is said that it is said according to relation, the meaning is: it predicates relation. It has been said of God, but it does not couple; nor can mutual conversion of relatives be made according to it, so that one says “the paternity of filiation” or “the filiation of paternity,” nor conversely. For principal terms are not mutually referred, [Col. 0889D] but derived terms are, such as Father and Son. Thus it is established that spiration, though it is Father, is not Father by something; and therefore it is not Father by spiration.

What was said concerning whether the Father is Father by spiration is resolved by some as follows. They say that the Father is this person by paternity, but is not this person by spiration or unbegottenness. Likewise, the Son is the person of the Son by filiation, although spiration is in him. This is because paternity and filiation are personal properties, as is procession, which is in the Holy Spirit; but spiration and unbegottenness are not personal properties—that is, they do not constitute a person. There are only three personal properties, [Col. 0890A] that is, constitutive of persons: paternity, filiation, and procession. The remaining two are only distinctive and not personal: unbegottenness and spiration. [Note: [Col. 0889D] Namely, active spiration.] For a property to be personal, it must have two features: it must belong to one person alone—which spiration does not, since it belongs to two persons—and by it one person must be referred to another—which unbegottenness does not. Thus, although it belongs to one person alone, it is not personal. If anyone concludes, “One person is distinguished from another by this property,” this is a fallacy. Substance differs from substance by whiteness; therefore whiteness itself is a substantial property. Whether this solution is to be approved, however, will be explained more fully later, where unbegottenness is treated specifically.

[Col. 0890B] Again, paternity, filiation, spiration, unbegottenness, and procession are five properties distinct from one another, and each is the person in which it is; therefore they seem to be five persons, as there are five properties. Some answer that unbegottenness is understood in paternity, and therefore there are not five properties but three. Yet this will be made clearer later, when it is said that they are five distinct from one another, but nevertheless only three persons. If it is asked whether they are to be worshipped, since they are God, we say that usage does not admit this; therefore we attribute such expressions more to curiosity than to usefulness. “He who presses his nose hard draws blood.”

Again, paternity is Father and conversely filiation is [Col. 0890C] Son; contrariwise, Father is in the Son and Son in the Father; therefore paternity is in the Son, or filiation in the Father. But this is invalid, for it proceeds by accident. Hence an objection is taken even from the divine essence: the divine essence is the Father who begets; it is the same as the Son who is begotten; therefore the Father is begotten, or the Son begets. Again, the Son is distinguished from the Father by a property; the divine essence is the Son; therefore the divine essence is distinguished from the Father by a property. Fallacy: the Son is one person, not several; the divine essence is the Son; therefore it is one person and not several.

Again, just as generation confers existence upon the Son, so procession upon the Holy Spirit, as Augustine says; therefore the Son has essence from the Father by generation, but the divine essence is not from the Father; [Col. 0890D] therefore the Son has from the Father what is not from the Father. To this, although the following counterexample may be given: “A priest has a church from a bishop, and the church is not from the bishop; therefore he has from the bishop what is not from the bishop,” nevertheless the conclusion may be granted.

Again, the Son is from the Father by generation; being and being wise are the same for the Son; therefore the Son is wise from the Father by generation; therefore the Son is wise by generation. One must answer that the Son has from the Father, by generation—that is, through generation—that he is wise; nevertheless he is wise not by generation but by his essence.

Again, filiation is God; therefore it is from the Father or it is Father. To this, though the following objection may be made: [Col. 0891A] “The Trinity is God; therefore it is from the Father or it is Father,” nevertheless it must be granted that filiation is from the Father. Therefore it is from the Father either by generation, procession, or creation—which is false, because that division is to be understood of persons and creatures; it is an argument from an insufficient enumeration.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On terms which signify relations and couple them, but do not denote them or stand for persons, such as “begetting,” “begotten,” and “proceeding”

[Note: [Col. 0891D] Lombard, I, distinction 33, §§ 7–8, and distinctions 4–5.] It is customary to ask whether the properties, since they are in the divine essence, determine it, so that one may truly say, “the divine essence begets,” and the like; and thus to deal with those terms which signify and conjoin properties. Objections of this sort are commonly raised on this point: [Col. 0891B] the properties are both in the persons and in the essence; therefore either they do not determine the persons, or they determine the essence. But if so, then the divine essence begets, or is begotten, proceeds, or spirates; and this too seems capable of proof by authority. For Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0891D] Single book *On Faith and the Creed*, ch. 3. A similar statement occurs in Book III *Against Maximinus*, ch. 14, shortly after the beginning.]:

> “When God the Father begot the Word, he begot that which he himself is—not from nothing, nor from any matter already made and created, but from himself he begot that which he himself is.”

And elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0891D] Book VII *On the Trinity*, ch. 2.]:

> “Father and Son are together one wisdom, as they are one essence; and separately wisdom from wisdom, as essence from essence.”

Likewise [Note: [Col. 0891D] Fulgentius, *On the Faith to Peter*, ch. 2, shortly after the beginning.]:

> “God the Father, begotten of none, from his own nature once for all begot, without beginning, a Son equal to himself and coeternal in the same divinity by which he himself is God.”

[Col. 0891C] And elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0891D] Augustine, Book VII, ch. 2, as above, with a few words omitted at Col. 0892D.]:

> “When the Word is spoken of, let us understand it as though ‘wisdom born’ were said. In the former, namely ‘born,’ Word, image, and Son are understood; but in the latter, namely ‘wisdom,’ essence also is indicated.”

But if it is said of the divine essence that it begets essence, the objection is made thus: the Father begets the divine essence, and he himself is the divine essence; therefore, the Father is that which he begets. Nor, then, is that which the Father begets from the Father, and thus the begetter is not the cause of the begotten—or the begotten of the begetter—that it exists and is God. Augustine thus proves [Note: [Col. 0892D] Book VII, *On the Trinity*, and in Lombard, I, distinction 32, § 3.] that the Father is not wise by the wisdom which he begot, nor does he appear to be by it.

Therefore it must be said that, although the properties are in the essence, [Col. 0891D] they do not determine it—just as wine is in a cask, and the cask in a cellar: what is made damp? Not the cellar. And an individual quality is in the primary substance, while the secondary substance is in the things signified by its terms; the quality determines the primary substance, but not the secondary. That the essence is not determined by a property, John Damascene says [Note: [Col. 0892D] Book III, *On the Faith*, ch. 6, and Book I, chs. 10–11, as above.]: “The characteristic idioms”—that is, the determining properties—belong to the hypostasis, [Col. 0892A] not to the nature; for they determine the hypostasis, not the nature. For the essence to be determined by a property would mean that it received its designation from it, so as to be called “the divine essence begets” or “is begotten,” and that through it the essence were distinguished from another.

But we explain the authorities just cited, and all similar ones commonly introduced to prove this point, by referring what seems to be said of the essence to the persons who are of the same essence. For because the three persons are of one essence, the saints attribute to the proper essence what belongs to the persons. Thus when it is said, “When God the Father begot the Word, he begot that which he himself is,” this means: he begot the Son, who is of the same essence as the Father. The same applies elsewhere.

Yet, once it is denied that the divine essence begets, it seems one must deny [Col. 0892B] that God begets God, since “God” and “divine essence” mean the same thing. And, if this is granted, absurdities appear to follow. For God begets God—that is, either himself as God or another God. If another God, then another God is from God the Father. If himself as God, then the same one begets and is begotten. Again, God begets God; therefore he begets either God who is Father, or God who is not Father. If God who is Father, then the one begotten is the same one; and if he is Father, then the one who is Son is identical with the one who is Father. If God who is not Father, then there is a God who is not Father.

To this it must be said that the term “God” is sometimes taken personally. This is recognized from what is joined to it—not from the noun itself, but from a verb signifying [Col. 0892C] a notion; or when, with a preposition, it is referred to a person. Thus, when it is said, “God begot God,” or “God from God,” and the like, it is understood of persons. But when it is said absolutely, as “God is,” it pertains to the essence. Thus, in the argument, “God begets God who is not Father; therefore God who is not Father,” there is an equivocation. For the term “God,” which at first, with the verb “begot,” was referred to a person, is afterwards understood without that verb of the essence. This is a fallacy.

“A certain animal can exist and is not a human being; therefore a certain animal is not a human being,” on the assumption that every animal is a human being: this is the same fallacy. But when it is said, “God begets himself as God, or another God,” the statement has more than one meaning. For if you understand it by separation—“God begets another God,” that is, another who [Col. 0892D] is other, namely God (I do not say “another God”)—it is true: for the Son is a person other than the Father, yet is the same God. But if you understand “another God” as a combined, indivisible expression, it is false; for the Son is not another God than the Father.

You find this sort of expression in the Gospel: “Two other wicked men were crucified with him” [Note: [Col. 0892D] Luke XXIII: “And two other wicked men were led with him.”], that is, two others who were wicked. Accordingly, against the argument framed thus—“God begets God; therefore himself as God or another God”—one may object: “There is light from light; therefore from itself as light or from another light”; or, “The Word assumed a human being; therefore himself as a human being or another human being.”

Again, this proposition is made concerning God: “The Son is other than the Father,” and it is true of that concerning which the statement is made; therefore God is other than the Father. “This priest will be hanged tomorrow”: the statement is made concerning a human being, and it is true of that concerning which it is made; therefore this human being will be hanged tomorrow.

Again, paternity is in the divine essence; generation and paternity are the same; therefore generation is in the divine essence; therefore the divine essence generates. This is the fallacy of the first figure. The divine essence is in a stone; [Col. 0893B] the divine essence and the love of God are the same; therefore the love of God is in a stone—which is false. For the sense here is that the divine essence is in a stone and makes the stone a lover of God. Similarly, it is not true that generation is in the divine essence; for this would mean that it was in it in order to generate.

Again: the divine essence is he who generates; the generator is the divine essence; therefore the divine essence is a generator; therefore it generates. To this it must be said that if *generans* (“generator,” “begetting one”) is taken substantively in the masculine gender, it is true that the divine essence is a generator—that is, the one who generates. In this sense, to be a generator and to be Father are the same; yet it does not necessarily follow that the divine essence generates.

If someone argues thus: “The divine essence is a generator; the divine essence [Col. 0893C] is not begotten or proceeding; therefore the divine essence is a generator, or begotten, or proceeding,” it is not necessary that the word *generans*, which was first taken substantively, is used adjectivally in the conclusion because of the two adjectives placed with it. Analogous terms do not grammatically allow it to be used substantively. This is a fallacy. “This argument is necessary; it is not impossible; therefore this argument is necessary or impossible”: this is false, for “necessary” is there used substantively, whereas it was previously taken adjectivally.

Nevertheless, it seems better to those who say that the participle *generans* is used adjectivally when one says, “the divine essence is generating,” so that the phrase stands in place of a single [Col. 0893D] verb. Hence it must not be conceded. Yet one may concede, “the divine essence is begotten,” because there *genitus* is understood only substantively. Nor for that reason is the divine essence said to be feminine “begotten” or “is begotten.” If someone asks whether “the begetter” is the divine essence: if *gignens* is taken substantively in the masculine gender, it is true, because it is said of the person; but if it is understood in the neuter gender, it is improperly said, because the divine essence does not beget and is not something that begets.

[Note: [Col. 0893D] Lombard, I, distinction 27, §§ 3–4.] Again, the Father alone in the Trinity is Father; to be Father and to beget are the same for the Father; therefore to beget and to be Father are the same; therefore nothing is Father that does not beget. The divine essence is Father; therefore it begets. Again, [Col. 0894A] the divine essence is Father, and the divine essence is paternity. Therefore the divine essence is Father by paternity; therefore the divine essence begets, or else is determined by paternity.

To this it must be said that the term “Father” sometimes predicates only a notion, and sometimes a person together with a notion, if appositions are to be judged by their subjects; for subjects are such as the predicates permit. When it is said, “the divine essence is Father,” a person together with a notion is posited; but when it is said, “the Father is Father,” there the notion alone is predicated of the person. Hence, although from “the Father is Father” one may necessarily infer “therefore he begets,” one cannot make the same inference from “the divine essence is Father.”

For “the divine essence is Father” is an accidental predication, because it is the same as saying [Col. 0894B] “the divine essence is a generating person”: “person” is predicated of essence and “generating” of person. Thus, when it is said, “Marius is a good commander,” “commander” is predicated of Marius and “good” of commander; but this occurs more covertly in one term than in two. Therefore, if someone infers, “the divine essence is Father; therefore it begets,” this is a fallacy. “This man is a recruit; therefore he is new.” For just as the term “Father” makes two things understood, so to speak—person and notion—so the term *tiro* means the same as “new soldier.”

Again, given this, the objection is framed thus: the divine essence is Father of someone or of no one. If of no one, then something is Father which is Father of no one. If it is Father of someone, and of no one but the Son, then the divine essence is Father of a Son whom it did not itself beget. By the same reasoning, [Col. 0894C] the divine essence is Son of a Father who did not beget it. If anyone recoils from saying this, let him deny all expressions in which there is a relation, by which those persons are understood to be referred to the Father or the Son—or the divine essence is understood to be referred to them—in expressions of this kind. Yet I see no danger if they are simply admitted.

Some, however, do not judge the appositions made with the term “Father” from the diversity of their subjects. For, as they say, this term may always predicate a person together with a notion, and always the notion alone. Hence, when I say, “Father is Father,” it is understood in two ways, and is true in both; when I say, “the divine essence is Father,” it is true in one sense, [Col. 0894D] false in the other. To this one replies: “the divine essence is Father; Father is Father; in both cases the term ‘Father’ is taken in the same way; from one follows ‘begetting’ or ‘having begotten’; therefore it follows from the other.” Yet those who accept this must say that “begetting” or “having begotten” follows from neither.

There is, however, greater doubt whether it should be conceded that “the divine essence is Father by paternity.” They seek to prove this as though by a necessary argument: when I say, “Father is Father,” and “the divine essence is Father,” the same thing is predicated of these—namely, person together with notion. The Father is Father by paternity; therefore the divine essence is Father by paternity. But perhaps “Father is Father by paternity” is false if it is taken [Col. 0895A] subjectively; this will be discussed later.

Again: the divine essence is Father; therefore it is Father either by paternity or by itself. By the same reasoning, the divine essence is Son by filiation and Spirit by procession; thus the divine essence is distinguished by the properties, and so for it to be Father is one thing, to be Son another, and to be Holy Spirit another. To this it must be said that although the divine essence is Father, it is Father neither by itself nor by paternity, just as paternity is paternity neither by itself nor by a notion.

But someone will say: if this person is Father by paternity, why is not the divine essence likewise this person, namely Father, by paternity? [Note: [Col. 0895D] Lombard, I, distinction 33, §§ 6–7.] The solution is evident: since paternity is in the divine essence, it does not determine the essence as it determines the person of the Father. Hence the statement “the divine essence is Father [Col. 0895B] by paternity,” or “is the person of the Father by paternity,” is not admitted, because it is not the person of the Father by anything at all.

Again they press the point thus: paternity is the divine essence; therefore, according to it, nothing is said relative to something else. Again, the divine essence unites the Father with the Son, while paternity distinguishes them. Therefore the latter is not the former; or paternity is a relation, therefore it is not a substance, since these are opposites. What they seem able to confirm by Augustine’s authority, who says [Note: [Col. 0895D] *Expositions on Psalm* LXVIII, on verse 2: “and it is not substance.”]:

> “That by which, or in which, God is, is substance; and because the Son is of the same substance, without doubt the Son too is God. But that by which he is Father is not a matter of substance, but refers to the Son; thus we do not say that the Son is the Father as we say that he is God.”

This must be explained thus: that by which the Father is Father is not substance—that is, it is not the case that by that by which he is Father he is substance; for he is Father by the property of generation, whereas that property is not substance. Yet the property itself is substance. The argument that appears to proceed from opposites is invalid. For they are not opposites in God. God’s justice is such that God is just, whereas in a creature its justice is one thing and the creature itself another.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On Matters Pertaining to Paternity and Filiation

[Note: [Col. 0895D] Lombard, I, distinctions 27 and 28.] Having determined, as far as we could, those matters concerning the properties which seemed to require common investigation in the Trinity, let us consider those usually investigated in particular. There are, therefore, five: two proper to the Father, namely unbegottenness and paternity; one proper to the Son, namely filiation; one [Col. 0895D] proper to the Holy Spirit, namely procession; and one common to Father and Son, which our masters usually call *spiration*. This term, however, has no authority from the saints. Let us first speak of paternity and filiation, because these two have, as it were, a reciprocal reference to each other.

Note that the same property is signified by the names “Father” and “begetter”; and likewise by “Son,” “Word,” and “image.” Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0895D] Book V *On the Trinity*, ch. 13; rather, Fulgentius, ch. 1, *On the Faith to Peter*. The genuine Augustine has many similar statements in many places.]:

> “The Son is spoken of relatively, as are the Word and image; and in all these terms he is referred to the Father. Nor is any one of them said of the Father.”

Yet by “image” we sometimes understand the Trinity, as in: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. I). Hence Augustine: “The divinity of the Trinity is essentially one, and it is the image according to which man was made.”

It is first asked concerning such matters whether the Father is the person of the Father by something. For he is so either by his essence or by a notion. If the Father is the person of the Father by his essence, then, since the Father is his essence, he is the person of the Father; therefore to be the person of the Father and to be essence are the same for the Father. Therefore either Father and Son are not one essence of the Father, or they are one person of the Father. But if the Father is the person of the Father by a notion, and by none rather than paternity, then the Father is [Col. 0896B] the person of the Father by paternity, and likewise is generating. Therefore to be a person and to be generating are the same for the Father. By the same notion, to be Father, to be the person of the Father, and to be unbegotten or spirating are the same for the Father. Therefore to be unbegotten, begetting, and spirating are the same for the Father. Or, if to be the person of the Father is the same for the Father as to be generating, then to be a person together with a notion is the same as to be a notion.

If anyone approves the distinction stated above, that one property is personal and another is not, it is easy to say that the Father is the person of the Father by paternity, though not by spiration or unbegottenness. Or, as others teach, the Father is the person of the Father neither by essence nor by a property, [Col. 0896C] but, as it were, by the concurrence of the properties of unbegottenness, paternity, and spiration. Thus none of these is this person, just as Socrates is Socrates neither by his rationality, nor by his humanity, nor by another single property, but by the concurrence of all that is in him. From these is constituted the singular essence of Socrates, by which he is distinguished from every other thing.

Take care, however, not to understand “by the concurrence of some properties,” but “by whatever concurrence.” For one property is not something other than another; rather, they are the same thing, namely the divine essence; for analogies from natural things may be transferred to the Trinity. Therefore Hilary’s statement, “The Father is a hypostasis by paternity,” which seems contrary to this, must be understood as meaning: as it were, by the concurrence of these properties. Likewise, the Son is the person of the Son, as it were, by the concurrence [Col. 0896D] of two properties; whereas the Holy Spirit is the person of the Holy Spirit by procession, because no other property is in him.

[Note: [Col. 0896D] Lombard, I, distinction 9, § 10; Gregory, Book XXIX of the *Morals*, ch. 1.] It is customary to ask whether the Father begets the Son daily. Gregory seems to deny this, for he says:

> “The Lord Jesus Christ, inasmuch as he is power, because he is the wisdom of God born from the Father before time—or rather, because he did not begin to be born nor cease—let us say more truly that he is always born. But we cannot say that he is always being born, lest he seem imperfect.”

[Col. 0897A] He says this because the truth is not so clearly manifested when it is said, “the Son is always being born,” as when it is said, “the Son was born before time”; therefore one does not say, “the Son is always being born.” This is not because the latter is false, but because the truth is not as evident in the latter as in the former. For Origen elsewhere says [Note: [Col. 0897D] Homily 6 on Jeremiah.]:

> “Our Savior is the radiance of glory. But radiance is not born once and then ceases; rather, whenever the light from which radiance arises has arisen, the radiance of glory arises. Thus our Savior is always being born.”

Nor should this be understood as meaning that the generation is repeated, because it is continuous. My eating is not repeated while I eat continuously, nor does this lamp emit light twice while it continues to emit it.

Note that the name “Father” is sometimes said [Col. 0897B] determinately, but not in the sense in which it is said of the Father, because when it is said of God it posits nothing. Hence the Trinity can in no way be called Father, except by transference—perhaps on account of the adoption of children.

Again, the Father is the person of the Father by paternity, and is the person of the Father by himself; therefore to be the person of the Father and to be paternity are the same for the Father. Jerome says thus that the Father is the person of the Father by himself: “Persons are distinguished by persons and names.” To this it must be said that “person” there means a personal property. One may also say that the Father is the person of the Father by himself, just as God is God by himself. Thus there are three solutions to the matter mentioned above—whether the Father is the person of the Father by something: either one says that the Father is the person [Col. 0897C] of the Father by paternity, but not by spiration or unbegottenness; and the reason was given why; or one says that the Father is the person of the Father not by paternity but by the three properties, none of which, if taken alone, is that which is in him [Note: [Col. 0897D] It seems necessary to add: “the cause is thus in itself, if it is taken singly.”]; or one says that the Father is the person of the Father by himself, and not by essence or property.

Again, paternity is divinity; therefore to be Father is to be God. Fallacy. Blindness is insensibility; therefore to be blind is to be insensible.

Again: the Son has filiation from the Father; therefore filiation is from the Father; therefore, in that the Son is Son, the Father is his Father or principle. Some seek to show by Hilary’s authority that filiation is from the Father. Hilary says [Note: [Col. 0897D] In Book XII *On the Trinity*, about the middle of the book.]:

> “As birth is from authority, so eternal birth is from an eternal author.”

They explain it thus: birth is from an author, the Son is from the Father; and so eternal birth is from an eternal author—that is, the eternal one born is from the eternal author. An objection is made to the argument: “A priest has a church from a bishop; therefore the church is from the bishop.” Yet I do not see why the conclusion should be denied.

Again, whatever the Son has, he has it in the manner in which he received it. The Son received essence by birth; therefore he has [Col. 0898A] essence by birth. But for the Son to have essence is the same as to be God; therefore the Son is God by birth. Solution: “He has it as he received it” means that, just as he received it unchangeable and immutable, so he possesses it. But if it is said, “Just as he received it by birth, so he has it by birth,” it is false. Fallacy. The Son is God from God the Father by generation; and whatever is from the Father is so in the manner in which it is from the Father; therefore he is God by generation.

Again, the Father begot the Son; therefore he is prior to him. Fallacy. Radiance proceeds from fire; therefore fire is prior to heat or radiance.

Again, paternity is in the Father and not in the Holy Spirit; by paternity the Father is distinguished from something; therefore from the Holy Spirit; therefore by paternity the Father is referred to the Holy Spirit; therefore the Father is Father [Col. 0898B] of the Holy Spirit—which is false. Some reply that the Father is distinguished from the Holy Spirit by paternity, but is not thereby referred to him. For just as in natural things a subject in which every property is present is distinguished, by that property, from every subject in which it is not present, so the Father is distinguished from the Holy Spirit by every property that is in the Father and not in the Holy Spirit. Others, however, hold that the Father is not distinguished from the Holy Spirit by paternity, but only from the Son, to whom alone he is related by that property.

Again, the Son is Son of God by nature; therefore by essence; therefore by essence itself; therefore not by notion, or else by essence and notion together.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On Unbegottenness

[Col. 0898C]

[Note: [Col. 0897D] Lombard, I, distinction 28.] It remains to discuss unbegottenness, which is proper to the Father and concerning which there is much doubt. For this term seems to posit nothing, but only to exclude. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0897D] Book V *On the Trinity*, ch. 6, at the end; same book, ch. 7, at the beginning; Book V, ch. 7.]:

> “When ‘unbegotten’ is said, not what he is but what he is not is said.”

Again:

> “If, in place of ‘unbegotten,’ ‘not begotten’ is said, nothing different is said.”

And elsewhere:

> “Not begotten has exactly the same force as unbegotten.”

From these statements the term appears to posit nothing, and thus not to signify a notion. But understand [Note: [Col. 0898D] This solution is the Master’s in the same place, § 2, near the end.] that Augustine said this by alluding to the etymology of the name, not by assigning the rationale of its predication.

Again, elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0898D] It seems to be Augustine, Book XV *On the Trinity*, ch. 26, near the end.] he says: “The Father is called unbegotten because he is from no one.” [Col. 0898D] But if he is called unbegotten only because he is from no one, this term will seem to posit nothing. This could have force if Augustine had said, “He is called unbegotten only because he is from no one.” But when he says, “Unbegotten is said because he is from no one,” he did not say “for that reason alone”; for by excluding one thing it can posit something. Hence the same Augustine says elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0898D] Pseudo-Augustine, Book LXV, *Questions to Orosius*, question 2, at the beginning. See also Book XV *On the Trinity*, ch. 26, near the end.]:

> “Catholic faith declares the Holy Spirit neither begotten nor unbegotten. For if we call him unbegotten, we shall seem to affirm two Fathers; but if begotten, we shall be blamed for believing in two Sons.”

And elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0899D] Book XV *On the Trinity*, ch. 26, as above.]:

> “Since we do not call the Holy Spirit begotten, we do not dare call him unbegotten, lest in that term we seem to confess either two Fathers in the Trinity, or two who are from no one.”

It seems, therefore, that “unbegotten” signifies or connotes either both of these, or one of them: when it is said, “the Father is unbegotten,” either two things are said [Col. 0899A] of the Father—namely, that he is Father and that he is from no one—or only one of them. But if this expression signifies that the Father is Father and, in addition, is from no one, then the terms “unbegotten” and “Father” signify the same thing. This appears contrary to Augustine’s statement [Note: [Col. 0899D] Book V, ch. 5, near the end.]:

> “To say Father is not the same as to say unbegotten; for even if he had not begotten the Son, nothing would prevent him from being called unbegotten.”

Yet this seems false on the surface of the words. For if the Father had not begotten the Son, he would not be Father; if the Father were not Father, he would not be unbegotten; therefore, if the Father had not begotten the Son, the Father would not be unbegotten. Therefore it is false that, if he had not begotten the Son, nothing would prevent him from being called unbegotten.

It may therefore be resolved by an interpretation of this sort: if the Father had not begotten the Son, he would not be Father; it nevertheless follows that if the Father had not begotten the Son, he would not be Father. But it does not follow that if the Father were not Father, he would not be unbegotten, because even if he were not Father or had not begotten the Son, nothing would prevent his being called unbegotten—provided these two things existed together, namely, that he existed and [Col. 0899C] was not Father; though they could not in fact exist. Or it may simply be understood thus: if he had not begotten the Son, nothing would prevent him from being called unbegotten—that is, “unbegotten” is not said in relation to the Son.

Some therefore say that the Father is called unbegotten not merely because he is from no one, but because the others are from him. Hence it can be inferred that if the Son and Holy Spirit were not from him, he would not be called unbegotten, since he is called unbegotten because they are from him and he is from no one. Again, by unbegottenness, both he is from no one and the others are from him; therefore by unbegottenness the Son and Holy Spirit are from the Father; therefore by unbegottenness the Son is from the Father, and thus unbegottenness is in the Son. For the Son does not seem to be from the Father by a property which is not in him.

Again, [Col. 0899D] by unbegottenness the Holy Spirit is from the Father, and he is from him only by procession; therefore by unbegottenness the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father. But if [the text seems to require the addition: “the Holy Spirit does not proceed except by a property which is in him,”] namely procession, unbegottenness will seem to be procession, and to be more in the Holy Spirit than in the Father. Perhaps someone will say that by unbegottenness the Son and Holy Spirit are from the Father in such a way that neither is [perhaps: “the same”] from him. But this does not help either. If so, unbegottenness seems rather to be in the two than in the Father, since no notion is common to the Son and Holy Spirit. Therefore it does not seem admissible that by unbegottenness the Father is from no one and the others are from him.

To this they reply that by unbegottenness the Father has both that he is from no one and that the Son and Holy Spirit are from him; yet the Son and Holy Spirit are not from the Father by unbegottenness. Thus a master has the fact that these people are subject to him by his lordship, but they are subject or subordinate to him not by his lordship, but by their own servitude.

Again, by unbegottenness the Father has the fact that the Son and Holy Spirit are from him; therefore the Father is called unbegotten in relation to Son and Holy Spirit; therefore by unbegottenness the Father is referred to the Son and Holy Spirit. One may therefore say: “The Father is unbegotten of the Son and Holy Spirit.” Augustine too appears [Col. 0900B] to say that the Father is referred to the Son and Holy Spirit by unbegottenness. Thus:

> “When ‘unbegotten’ is said, nothing other is said than ‘not Son.’ But the negative particle *not* does not bring about this result: that what without it is spoken relatively becomes, when it is prefixed, spoken substantially; rather, it merely negates what was said without it.” [Note: [Col. 0899D] Book V *On the Trinity*, ch. 7.]

Again, just as “begotten” is not spoken absolutely but indicates that something is from a begetter, so “unbegotten” is not spoken absolutely but indicates that it is not from a begetter. Again, just as Son is spoken relatively to Father, and not Son to non-Father, so unbegotten must be referred to begetter, and not begotten to non-begetter. Hilary likewise says [Note: [Col. 0899D] Book IV *On the Trinity*, not far from the end.]:

> “There is one from one, begotten from unbegotten, by the property in each respectively of unbegottenness and origin.”

Therefore the Father appears to be called unbegotten in relation to the Son, in whom origin is found.

To this they reply that in the foregoing authorities Augustine takes the name “unbegotten” as positing nothing but removing, so that “unbegotten” is the same as “not begotten.” In this use it is spoken relatively; and by such an expression no property is attributed to the Father, but the property of the Son is removed from the Father—and removed relatively—just as, when I say “the Son is not the Father,” the Father’s property is removed from the Son.

That “unbegotten” posits in the Father both that he is from no one and that the others are from him, they seem to confirm by Augustine’s authority. He says [Note: [Col. 0900D] Book I *On Christian Doctrine*, ch. 5; Lombard, I, distinction 31, § 8.], “In the Father is unity.” He could have said, “In the Father is unbegottenness,” but he expressed it more clearly in this way, wishing to imply that those two things are understood under the name “unity”: as if to say, the other persons are from the Father, but the Father is from no one; just as every number is from unity, while unity is from no one.

For Augustine’s statement, “In the Father is unity,” and Hilary’s [Note: [Col. 0900D] Cited by Augustine, Book VI, ch. 10, *On the Trinity*.] “In the Father is eternity,” while some manuscripts read “In the Father is the authority of the principle,” and others “unbegottenness”—all convey the same sense. For unbegottenness in the Father is the same as the authority of the principle. But in the statement, “In the Father is unbegottenness,” one should properly understand both that the Father is from no one and that the others are from him. [Col. 0901A] For the authority of the principle would not properly be said to be in him if he were from no one and no one were from him, or if he were from someone and someone were from him. But because he is from no one and the others are from him—he from whom are all things—the authority of the principle is properly said to be in him; and unbegottenness, unity, and eternity are likewise said to be in him. All these terms belong to God on this account.

There are others who say that the name “unbegotten” signifies two things: namely, that the Father is from no one and that he is Father. Thus when I say, “the Father is unbegotten,” it is understood that the Father is Father; and in this it is also understood that the Son is from the Father, but not that the Holy Spirit is from the Father. Therefore unbegottenness does not make it understood that the others are from the Father, but that the other one, namely the Son, is; for it makes it understood [Col. 0901B] that the Father is Father, and therein it is understood that the Son is from him, and that the Father is from no one. Thus unbegottenness imports paternity, just as paternity and filiation import spiration. Therefore there are only three properties in the Trinity, since paternity is understood in unbegottenness. Hence it is not reckoned as another property, nor is it counted along with paternity. But rationality is understood in humanity in the way spiration is understood in paternity.

Against this the objection is made thus. Paternity is either a property different from unbegottenness or the same. If different, then there are five properties in the Trinity, which they deny. If the same, then the terms “Father” and “unbegotten” signify the same thing. Thus the propositions “Father is Father” and “Father is unbegotten” signify the same; and, just as the Father is referred to the Son by paternity, so also by unbegottenness, since this property is the same as that one.

This seems supported by Hilary’s authority cited above [Note: [Col. 0901D] Hilary, Book IV *On the Trinity*, as above.]:

> “There is one from one, begotten from unbegotten, by the property in each respectively of unbegottenness and origin.”

For he seems to say that unbegottenness and origin are properties which cause Father and Son to be related to one another, as are paternity, origin, and filiation—which is the same thing.

Again, Augustine seems to contradict this opinion in the authority already cited [Note: [Col. 0901D] Book V, ch. 5, *On the Trinity*.]:

> “To say Father is not the same as to say unbegotten; for even if he had not begotten the Son, nothing would prevent him from being called unbegotten.”

Therefore, if the Father had not begotten the Son, nothing would prevent the Father from possessing unbegottenness; but unbegottenness is some property, as is paternity; therefore the one is different from the other.

Again, if he had not begotten the Son, nothing would prevent the Father from being called unbegotten; but to say “Father unbegotten” is the same as to say that the Father is Father and is from no one. Therefore nothing prevents him from being Father even if he had not begotten the Son.

Again, if there is a Father, there is a Son, and conversely. Therefore, if there is no Son, there is no Father, and conversely. But if there is no Father, the Father is not unbegotten; and if the Son is not begotten by the Father, the Son does not exist, and conversely. Therefore, if the Son is not begotten by the Father, the Father is not unbegotten. Therefore Augustine’s statement is false: “If the Father had not begotten the Son, nothing would prevent the Father from being called unbegotten.” Thus, as has been shown from the foregoing, it does not appear [Col. 0902A] that, in the statement “the Father is unbegotten,” it is understood that the Father is Father or has a Son—which is the same thing.

Therefore some explain that authority thus: that is, if it were the case that the Father were something and did not have the Son (which is of course impossible), then nothing would prevent the Father from being called unbegotten, that is, not begotten; so that this term sets down nothing, but removes [something]. Others say thus: Nothing prevents the Father from being unbegotten and from not having a Son, because, if we judge of the Trinity in the same way as of created things, nothing prevents a father from being unbegotten and not having a son. Thus it happened in Adam: for he was unoriginate or unbegotten before he had a son, and he could have been unbegotten without having had a son. Others, however, think that this name *unbegotten* removes two things and posits one, because it posits being a person and excludes being begotten or proceeding; so that the sense here is: “The Father is unbegotten,” that is, since he is a person, he is neither begotten nor proceeds. Thus the Father, and not the Holy Spirit, is unbegotten, although neither is begotten; just as these two verbs, “it wearies” and “to read,” do not distinguish persons, and yet the former, and not the latter, is impersonal. For this impersonal name not only deprives, but posits: because, although it has the ending of impersonal expressions, it does not distinguish persons.

According to this, no notion is signified by the term *unoriginate*. But when it is said, “The Father is unbegotten, unoriginate,” the ablative does not indicate the predication of a notion, [Col. 0902C] but the ground of its suitability—that is, the reason why the name *unbegotten* is suited to the Father. For if a property were predicated, by the same reasoning one could say that in the Son there is a property through which it would be excluded from the Son that he is begetting or proceeding; and it would posit his being a person other than unorigination and the other four [properties]. Likewise, in the Holy Spirit there would be a property that would posit his being a person and exclude his not being Father or Son; and thus there would be more properties in the persons than the saints have determined.

Therefore, to gather briefly what has been said: in the first way, one is called unbegotten because [he is] from no one, and because others are from him; in the second way, because [he is] from no one and because he is Father; in the third way, because he is a person and is neither [Col. 0902D] begotten nor proceeds. Choose to whom you will say: “You alone please me.” [Note: [Col. 0902D] *Master*, I, distinction 13, §§ 6, 7, and 8.]

Yet Jerome appears to contradict each of these [accounts] when he says: [Note: [Col. 0902D] Jerome, ibid., cited by the Master.] “The Holy Spirit is not Father, but is unbegotten and unmade; he is not Father, but is of the Father and in the Father; he has procession from the Father, not birth.” Here he seems to say that the Holy Spirit is unbegotten, which has been shown to be false. To this it must be said that the name *unbegotten* is taken only negatively, not positively; so that *unbegotten* means the same as “not begotten.” This is clear from the division which he subsequently gives as follows: “Everything that exists is either unbegotten and unmade, as the Father and the Holy Spirit; or begotten and not made, [Col. 0903A] as the Son; or made and begotten, as a stone; or made, begotten, and reborn, as a human being; or made and begotten but not reborn, as a brute animal.”

## CHAPTER XXX. On the common notion of Father and Son, that is, spiration

[Note: [Col. 0903D] *Master*, I, distinction 29 throughout; likewise distinctions 11, 12, etc., of the same book.]

After this we must speak of the common notion of Father and Son, that is, of principle. It should therefore be known that the expression, “The Father and the Son are one principle of the Holy Spirit,” is figurative and admits a twofold understanding. For it may be understood either that the Father and Son breathe forth the Holy Spirit in one manner, or that they breathe forth the Holy Spirit by one notion, so that either identity of manner or identity of notion is indicated. That notion is called *spiration*, and this word is on the lips [Col. 0903B] of men, although it is not authoritative; indeed, it seems offensive in usage, since the word *spirans* is said of either one breathing a blast, and since, according to the analogies of grammarians who use this verb absolutely when they use it, it is properly used intransitively.

Nevertheless, let us say with others: when the Father and the Son breathe forth the Holy Spirit, although they have this in common, the Son nevertheless has from the Father the fact that he breathes forth the Holy Spirit. For whatever he has, he has from the Father. Therefore, although the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are each a principle, this is said of the Father in one way, of the Son in another, and of the Holy Spirit in another. The Father is called the principle of the Son by generation; hence from eternity he is the Son’s principle. The Father is also the principle of the Holy Spirit by spiration; hence from eternity [Col. 0903C] he is the Spirit’s principle. He is also the principle of creatures by creation, which is not in the Father but in creatures; and then it signifies a temporal relation which is in the creature, not in the Creator. In this respect, the Father began in time to be the principle of a creature.

But when this is said of the Son, it can signify only two things: either spiration, which is indicated when it is said, “The Son is the principle of the Holy Spirit”; or creation, which is signified when I say, “The Son is the principle of a creature,” and this relation is in the creature, not in the Creator. The Holy Spirit is called the principle of creatures in one way only: namely, temporally, not eternally. Thus it is said of the Father in three ways, of the Son in two ways, and of the Holy Spirit in one way only; and you may see this in the appended diagram. [Note: [Col. 0903D] It is not extant in our manuscript.]

[Col. 0903D] It may, however, be asked: since the Father and Son breathe forth the Holy Spirit by one spiration, are the Father and Son one principle of the Holy Spirit, or several? The objection is made as follows. This name *principle* is said of the Father and Son in the same signification: “The Father and Son are a principle of the Holy Spirit”; therefore the Father and Son are a principle, or principles, of the Holy Spirit. If the Father and Son are a principle of the Holy Spirit, since for each it is the same thing to be principle of the Holy Spirit and to be a person breathing forth the Holy Spirit, then the Father and Son are one person [Col. 0904A] breathing forth the Holy Spirit. Again, to be the principle of the Holy Spirit is the same as to be the author of the Holy Spirit. The Father and Son are the principle of the Holy Spirit; therefore they are one author of the Holy Spirit; therefore, one person.

Again, the Father and Son are one principle of the Holy Spirit; therefore they are one principle which is the Holy Spirit; therefore the Holy Spirit is the principle of the Holy Spirit. If they are one principle which is not the Holy Spirit, then the Father and Son are something that is principle of the Holy Spirit and is not the Holy Spirit; therefore they are something that is not the Holy Spirit.

But, to compress many objections into a few, the difficulty of this question cannot be resolved unless the different applications of this name *principle*, which it seems capable of making when placed as predicate, are made clear. This name therefore predicates either essence, or person together with a notion, or a pure notion. If it predicated essence, it would plainly be false that “The Father is principle of the Holy Spirit,” for the sense would be: “the essence that breathes forth the Holy Spirit,” whereas the essence neither begets nor is begotten, neither proceeds nor is breathed forth. What is found written [Note: [Col. 0904D] In Augustine, book IV, *On the Trinity*; *Master*, I, distinction 29, § 1.], “The Father is the principle of the whole Godhead” (whence someone might wish to conclude that the divine essence proceeds from the Father), must be understood thus: the Father is the principle of the Son and the Holy Spirit, in whom is the whole Godhead. It is therefore clear that essence is not predicated by this name.

But if person together [Col. 0904C] with a notion is predicated by it, it is indeed true that both Father and Son are principle of the Holy Spirit—that is, a person breathing forth the Holy Spirit. But since the Father is a different person breathing forth the Holy Spirit from the Son, the Father will be a different principle of the Holy Spirit from the Son; and thus Father and Son will be two principles of the Holy Spirit. Augustine denies this, saying: [Note: [Col. 0904D] Book V, *On the Trinity*, chapter 14, near the end.] “Just as the Father and Son are, in relation to creation, one Creator and one Lord, so in relation to the Holy Spirit they are one principle, just as [they are] one Creator and one Lord.”

It remains, then, that this name signifies a notion, since it predicates neither essence nor person together with a notion. But it can signify that notion in two ways: adjectivally, or concretely … or by coupling; or subjectively, mathematically, or without coupling. For example, the name *Father*, or *white*, or any such adjective, signifies such a property, couples it, and signifies it adjectivally. The name *whiteness* or *fatherhood* signifies mathematically, without coupling, and subjectively, since these are subjects. [Col. 0904D]

This name *principle*, therefore, since it signifies spiration, signifies it by coupling, like the expression *breathing forth*; and thus adjectivally. If this is so, it does not seem fitting to say, “The Father and Son are principle of the Holy Spirit,” since there is nothing upon which [Col. 0905A] the expression *principle*, used adjectivally, may rest. Just as it is improper to say, “The Father and Son are breathing forth the Holy Spirit,” or “Socrates and Plato are good.” Hence an exception could be made to the argument by which this was concluded.

Still less fitting does it seem to say, “The Father is some principle of the Holy Spirit,” or “one principle,” since the names *one* and *some* are improperly joined to expressions used adjectivally. For who says, “Socrates is some white man”? Much less can reference be made to this expression by *what* or *which*, since this word refers only to an expression used subjectively. Thus, in natural philosophy, according to some, when I say “A day is time,” the name *time*, although a substantive, is used adjectivally and does not admit the addition of the name *one* or reference by the name *which*, so that one might say, “A day is some time,” or “the time which is,” or “which is not.” Likewise, according to others, “A statue is a work of man”; one cannot say “some work of man,” or “a work which is,” or “which is not.” [Col. 0905B]

But if it is said that by this name a relation is signified in the manner in which it is signified by the name *spiration*, that is, mathematically, then it is indeed true that Father and Son are one principle of the Holy Spirit which is not the Holy Spirit—that is, one spiration of the Holy Spirit which is not the Holy Spirit. But according to this, since to be principle of the Holy Spirit is the same as to be the spiration of the Holy Spirit, just as it is not the same for the Father to be Father and to be fatherhood, it will not be the same for the Father to be principle [Col. 0905C] of the Holy Spirit and to breathe forth the Holy Spirit—unless it is said that the name *principle* equivocally signifies that property, both adjectivally and substantively. Yet it seems rather to signify it substantively, since it is a substantive.

To this some reply—departing in part, though not entirely, from the considerations of grammarians—that when I say, “The Father and Son are principle of the Holy Spirit,” this name signifies, couples, and predicates a relation, and not a person or essence. They do not accept “The divine essence is principle of the Holy Spirit,” just as “The divine essence is Father of the Son.” For although the name *Father* predicates a person together with a notion, the name *principle* predicates the notion alone. Yet the name *one* is fittingly placed with it, for greater explicitness, when it is said, “The Father and Son are one principle of the Holy Spirit,” in order to show that the Father breathes forth the Holy Spirit by the same spiration as the Son. Nevertheless, they do not admit the relative construction, “The Father is a principle of the Holy Spirit which is or is not the Holy Spirit,” just as these two differ in genus or species—though not in the genus of what is or is not. [Col. 0905D]

But someone will say: “The Father and Son are one principle of the Holy Spirit; there is no spiration by which the Father breathes forth the Holy Spirit and by which the Son does not breathe forth [Col. 0906A] the Holy Spirit; therefore the Father and Son are the same principle of the Holy Spirit; therefore the Father is a principle of the Holy Spirit which is the Son.” By the same reasoning, the Father is a principle of the Holy Spirit which is or is not the Holy Spirit. To this they reply that it does no harm if one admits that Father and Son are the same principle of the Holy Spirit—that is, that they breathe forth the Holy Spirit by the same spiration. But when “which is” is introduced there, it is not to be admitted, just as a human being is the same in genus as an ass, yet a human being is not the same in genus which is an ass or is not an ass.

My master, however, [Note: [Col. 0905] Peter Lombard, namely, I, distinction 29, near the end. If, however, he alludes to this passage and not to another which is now no longer extant.] wishing in no respect to detract from the truth of theology in order to preserve grammatical considerations, proceeds much further here. He says that “The Father is a principle of the Holy Spirit which is not the Holy Spirit,” freely admitting the relative construction; and that “The Father is a principle of the Holy Spirit which is the Son,” in the following sense: the Father is one breathing forth the Holy Spirit, and the Son, by the same notion, is one breathing forth; and in this place spiration is predicated by the name *principle*, is coupled, and this name is used adjectivally, while reference to it is made by the word *which*. In natural science it is never found that reference is made by the word *which* to a name used adjectivally.

Therefore, if someone argues: “The Father is some principle of the Holy Spirit which is not the Holy Spirit; therefore he is something that is principle of the Holy Spirit and is not the Holy Spirit,” this is a fallacy. “The Father is someone begetting who is not the Son; therefore he is something that is begetting [Col. 0906C] and is not the Son”—which is false, unless the neuter expression *something* is taken personally: “something,” that is, some person. Thus he would also admit: “The Father himself is something that is principle of the Holy Spirit and is not the Holy Spirit,” and, “some person is principle of the Holy Spirit and is not the Holy Spirit.” Yet, even granted this, if someone concludes, “Therefore the Father is something that is not the Holy Spirit,” an exception can be made in the same way: “The Father is something that begets and is not the Son; therefore he is something that is not the Son.”

Again, the objection is framed thus: for the Father, to be principle of the Holy Spirit and to breathe forth the Holy Spirit are the same; likewise for the Son. The Father and Son are one [Col. 0906D] principle of the Holy Spirit; therefore they are one [person] breathing forth the Holy Spirit. Or thus: for both Father and Son, to be principle of the Holy Spirit and to breathe forth the Holy Spirit are the same. The Father and Son are breathing forth the Holy Spirit; therefore they are principles of the Holy Spirit. But this is manifestly not to be accepted, for plurality would seem to be understood either with regard to the modes or with regard to the spirations.

Yet when the expression *breathing forth* is placed in the plural, it is plural not in signification but in sound, as was shown above concerning all verbs said of God according to essence, which, though uttered in the plural, are singular in signification. [Col. 0907A] Likewise, when I say “Athens are,” the verb is plural in sound but singular in signification. Nevertheless, in neither case should one admit, “The Father and Son are *spirantia* (‘breathing things’) of the Holy Spirit,” but [rather], “The Father and Son are *spirantes* (‘those breathing forth’) the Holy Spirit.”

Fallacy: for Father and Son, to be person and to be essence are the same; Father and Son are persons; therefore they are essences. Again, the Holy Spirit proceeds principally from the Father and not principally from the Son; therefore, in some manner he proceeds from the Father in which he does not proceed from the Son. This is false, because he proceeds from the one and the other by one and the same procession.
