Therefore it must be said that “to proceed principally” does not posit a mode of proceeding; rather, he is said to proceed principally from the Father because the Father gave the Son that the Spirit should proceed from the Son himself.

Fallacy: The Son is God from God the Father; the Father is not [Col. 0907B] God from God the Father; therefore the Son is God in some way in which the Father is not God. Again, the authority states [Note: [Col. 0907] In the Constantinopolitan Creed, from the addition of the Latins.] that the Holy Spirit proceeds from both; the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of both. Therefore, one who proceeds from both differs personally from both; therefore, because he proceeds from both, he is other than both. By a similar argument, because Father and Son are principle of the Holy Spirit, the Father and Son are something other, or others, than the Holy Spirit. Neither should be granted. Fallacy: because this one has been begotten by his father, he is another person from his father; therefore, because his father begot him, his father was another person from him. No: because he was a person before he begot him.

Again, if the Father had not begotten the Son and were principle of the Holy Spirit, by being [Col. 0907C] principle of the Holy Spirit he would be other than the Holy Spirit, and he would not be principle of the Spirit otherwise or in another mode. Therefore someone is now other than the Holy Spirit by being principle of the Holy Spirit; he himself is other than the Holy Spirit; therefore [he is] the Father or other than the Father. But [he is] other, therefore not the Father. But if [he is] Father, [he is] Father by the very fact that he is principle of the Holy Spirit; therefore conversely, insofar as he is Father, he is principle of the Holy Spirit. Thus the Father would now be Father of the Holy Spirit—which is absurd.

Fallacy of the first kind: if someone having two sons, one firstborn and the other born second, had not begotten [Col. 0907D] the one who is firstborn, but had begotten the other who was born second, that other would be firstborn, and yet he would not be his son in any other way than now. Therefore, just as then he would be firstborn, so now he is born earlier. Or thus: if someone who sees with the right eye and sees with the left saw only with the left, he would nevertheless not see with the left in another way than now, when he sees with right and left; therefore now he sees only with the left, just as then he would see only with the left.

We do not call that property by which the Father is principle of the Holy Spirit a personal property; rather, by a personal property we mean one by which a person differs from every other. But the objection is made: the property by which the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father is personal; therefore the property [Col. 0908A] by which the Father breathes forth the Holy Spirit is personal. Fallacy: the property by which the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father belongs to one person alone.

Again, it is one thing to be Father, another to be principle; therefore, just as the Father is other than the Holy Spirit insofar as he is Father, so insofar as he is principle he is other than him. Augustine confirms this argument as follows: “To beget is one thing, to be begotten another, to proceed another. Thus the Father is one, the Son another, the Holy Spirit another.” Yet this must be understood thus: to beget, to be begotten, and to proceed are different things—that is, generation is one personal property, birth another, procession another. But when it is said, “It is one thing to be Father, another to be principle,” this cannot mean that there is some personal property by which the Father is principle. Therefore the Father is not other insofar as he is [Col. 0908B] principle. For he would not be Father, since he could not be other; and thus he would be Father of the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, when it is said, “It is one thing to be Father, another to be principle,” understand it thus: the Father is shown to be of one property when he is called Father, and of another when he is called principle. Again, because the Holy Spirit proceeds, he is other than both from both; therefore, because the Father is principle of the Holy Spirit, he is other than the Holy Spirit. This does not follow, because the property by which the Holy Spirit proceeds from both is personal, whereas the property by which the Father is his principle is not personal.

Again, when it is said, “The principle of the Holy Spirit is Father and Son,” discourse is about something that is in the Trinity; therefore it is either about a person, essence, or [Col. 0908C] property. If about a person, then, since that of which discourse is made is said to be Father and Son, the person is Father and Son. If about substance, then the subject term signifies substance; therefore substance is principle of the Holy Spirit; therefore the Holy Spirit is divine substance; therefore he is not divine substance, because nothing is that from which it is. But if it is about a property, then the subject term signifies a property; therefore it is said of some property that it is principle of the Holy Spirit, and thus the Holy Spirit is from some property.

Some say that discourse is about nothing, but about two persons, namely, the Father and Son. Against this: “The principle of the Holy Spirit is Father and Son”; therefore, by conversion of a simple proposition, “Father and Son are the principle of the Holy Spirit.” Again, the same thing is signified by this term placed in subject and predicate; therefore, “Father and Son are principle of the Holy Spirit” means the same as “Father and Son are Father and Son.” But there is only one property by which they are principle; therefore there is one [property] by which they are Father and Son, and thus fatherhood and sonship are one property.

They therefore say that it is about neither one thing nor several things. But against this: by the true proposition, “The principle of the Holy Spirit is Father and Son,” something necessary is signified; it is true of some one thing or several things, and thus we have the preceding [Col. 0909A] objection. They therefore say that the name *principle* signifies a property—that is, it is a sign of a property—but does not designate, name, predicate, or stand as subject.

Again: “The Father and Son are principle of the Holy Spirit; therefore they are one or the same principle of the Holy Spirit, from which the Holy Spirit proceeds or does not proceed.” But they are a principle from which the Holy Spirit proceeds; therefore they are something from which the Holy Spirit proceeds; and thus the essence, [Col. 0909B] property, or person would be that from which the Holy Spirit proceeds. Therefore distinguish: “The Father and Son are one principle of the Holy Spirit,” that is, they are one [thing] from which the Holy Spirit proceeds—false; but they breathe forth the Holy Spirit by one and the same property.

Again, the Holy Spirit proceeds from the principle, Father and Son; therefore there is some principle of the Holy Spirit which is Father and Son; therefore either substance, property, or person is principle of the Holy Spirit which is Father and Son. This must be distinguished: “Some principle of the Holy Spirit which is Father is Son,” that is, “A principle of the Holy Spirit is something which is Father and Son”—false. But if [one says], “The Holy Spirit proceeds from Father and Son,” this is true.

It is customary to ask what this name *principle* stands for when the name is placed on the side of the subject and one says, “The principle of the Holy Spirit is Father and Son”; for it stands either for essence, person together with a notion, or a notion. But it does not stand for essence; for then the sense would be: “something—that is, some essence—which breathes forth the Holy [Col. 0909C] Spirit—is Father and Son,” and thus there would be a false affirmative expression, namely, that the divine essence breathes forth the Holy Spirit. This is false. If it stands for a person together with a notion, then “a person breathing forth the Holy Spirit is Father” says the same thing as “the principle of the Holy Spirit is Father.”

Since, then, the Father is one person breathing forth the Holy Spirit and the Son another, it will seem that the Father is one principle of the Holy Spirit and the Son another, since the same person breathing forth the Holy Spirit is not Father and Son. Again, this term, *principle of the Holy Spirit*, is said equally and indifferently of Father and Son. Therefore, when it is said of the Father, “The principle of the Holy Spirit is Father,” with supposition made for the Father, one may truly say, “The principle of the Holy Spirit is not [Col. 0909D] Son,” since Son and Father are opposed predicables, as it seems, because the Father neither is nor can be the Son.

Therefore this indefinite proposition, “The principle of the Holy Spirit is Father,” appears to be such that the name *principle* can be taken indifferently for Father and Son. But if it is said that the name *principle* cannot be taken except for the person of the Father because of the name *Father* placed in the predicate, according to the rule, “Subjects shall be such as predicates permit,” then one must grant: “The principle of the Holy Spirit is only Father.” Hence it follows: therefore the principle of the Holy Spirit is not Son; or, the same principle of the Holy Spirit is Father and Son.

Again: “The principle of the Holy Spirit is Father”; therefore, the principle of the Holy [Col. 0910A] Spirit is Father and Son, or is Father and not Son. If it is Father and not Son, then the principle of the Holy Spirit is not Son. If it is said that the principle of the Holy Spirit is Father and Son, since the name *principle* does not there stand for essence, as was said, because essence does not breathe forth; nor for person, because no person is Father and Son; it stands there for persons, and thus has the force of a collective noun, since it stands for Father and Son together. Therefore, since it is truly said, “Father and Son are not Father,” it will truly be said, in one sense in which this name is taken as a collective noun, “The principle of the Holy Spirit is neither Father nor Son”; and yet the principle of the Holy Spirit is Father, and the principle of the Holy Spirit is Son.

[Col. 0910B] But these propositions, “The principle of the Holy Spirit is Father and Son,” seem in no way true, whether *principle* stands for one person or two. This may, however, be proved thus: “The principle of the Holy Spirit is Father; the principle of the Holy Spirit is Son; the principle of the Holy Spirit is Father and Son; therefore the principle of the Holy Spirit is Father and Son.” Again, the predicate of this proposition, “The principle of the Holy Spirit is Father,” belongs to no one to whom the subject does not belong; the subject belongs to someone to whom the predicate does not belong, namely, to the Son; therefore in a true proposition its subject is excluded from the predicate; therefore there is no principle of the Holy Spirit.

Again, either some principle of the Holy Spirit is not Father, or none is. If one says that no principle of the Holy Spirit is not Father, and the Son [Col. 0910C] is principle of the Holy Spirit, and this is said in the same signification of Father and Son, then the Son is Father. Again, “No principle of the Holy Spirit is not Father; no principle of the Holy Spirit is not Son.” These two propositions are universal and true, in which these two predicables, Father and Son, are predicated of the same term taken in the same signification; therefore one of them is predicated of the other.

Again, the Father neither is nor can be the Son, and conversely; therefore these terms are opposed predicables. But this term, *principle of the Holy Spirit*, belongs to both in the same signification; therefore it is superior to those two; therefore each of the two can truly be particularly excluded from it. Again: “No principle of the Holy Spirit is not Father; no principle of the Holy Spirit is not Son; Father and Son are one principle of the Holy Spirit; therefore one principle of the Holy Spirit is Father and Son.”

Again, it is not true that the principle of the Holy Spirit is both Father and Son; the principle of the Holy Spirit is Father; the principle of the Holy Spirit is Son; therefore the principle of the Holy Spirit either is not Father or is not Son. Again, either some principle of the Holy Spirit which is Father is Son, or none is. If some, then a principle of the Holy Spirit which is Father is Son; therefore one principle of the Holy Spirit is Father and Son. If no principle of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0911A] which is Father is Son, and Father and Son are principle of the Holy Spirit, then Father and Son are not one principle of the Holy Spirit.

There are many other ways of showing that a person is not the suppositum of that term, unless one says that Father and Son are two principles of the Holy Spirit—which no one dares say because it contradicts the authority of Augustine quoted above.

But if it is said that the name *principle* there stands for a relation, it is certain that it could not then be used adjectivally; for the expression would then be improper. Just as “White is a human being” is improper if the adjective stands for [what is] used adjectivally. But if it is used substantively, “The principle of the Holy Spirit is Father” means the same as “The spiration [Col. 0911B] by which the Father breathes forth the Holy Spirit is Father.” Thus the relative construction will freely be admitted, as if the name *spiration* were placed there; and one will grant, “The principle of the Holy Spirit which is Father is Son,” that is, “The spiration which is Father is Son”; and, “The principle of the Holy Spirit which is Father is not the Holy Spirit,” that is, “The spiration which is Father is not the Holy Spirit.” Nor is that proposition indefinite, but singular.

And, granted this, I see no inconvenience except that the name *principle* varies its signification when placed as subject and predicate. For in the predicate it signifies the notion adjectivally; in the subject, substantively. Thus it varies its signification—or rather its mode [Col. 0911C] of signifying—since it signifies the same notion in both places, but in one way here and another way there.

Others think one must grant, “The Father is principle of the Holy Spirit,” because there *Father* is a notion alone; but not conversely. For if one said, “The principle of the Holy Spirit is Father,” essence together with a notion would stand [as subject], and the sense would be that the divine essence from which the Holy Spirit is is Father. Thus that expression would be a false affirmative, since the Holy Spirit is not from the divine essence. Therefore it is fitting to say, “The principle of the Holy Spirit is Father.”

Yet it is fitting to say, “The principle of creatures is Father,” that is, “The divine essence, from which a creature is, is Father,” because essence together with a temporal relation stands [as subject].

[Col. 0911D] It is customary to ask whether one should admit, “The Father is principle of the Son and the Holy Spirit.” This does not seem proper, because the Father is said to be principle of the Son on one ground, namely by generation, and of the Holy Spirit, of whom the Father is principle by spiration, on another ground. One should not grant, under one utterance, “The Father is principle of Son and Holy Spirit”; but under two [utterances], thus: “The Father is principle of the Son; the Father is principle of the Holy Spirit.”

Again, it is asked whether Father and Son are one author of the Holy Spirit or two. For if they are one [Col. 0912A] author of the Holy Spirit, then they are one person. But if they are two authors of the Holy Spirit, since to be principle of the Holy Spirit and to be author of the Holy Spirit are the same, they will seem to be two principles of the Holy Spirit. Or, if they are two authors of the Holy Spirit, they will seem to breathe forth the Holy Spirit by two notions. For this reason it was above denied that Father and Son are two principles of the Holy Spirit: lest they seem to breathe forth the Holy Spirit by a spiration or a mode other than the Son’s.

Again, if these two names, *human being* and *stone*, are called one part of speech because they have one and the same mode of signifying—because this is a figurative expression—then likewise it will seem that Father and Son are one author of the Holy Spirit, because the Father is called author [Col. 0912B] of the Holy Spirit on the same ground as the Son; especially since Father and Son are one principle of the Holy Spirit, and to be principle of the Holy Spirit is the same as to be author of the Holy Spirit.

To this one may say that it would do no harm to say that Father and Son are two authors of the Holy Spirit; nor is the plurality referred to modes or notions, but to the persons who breathe forth the Holy Spirit by the same notion. Yet one should not therefore grant that Father and Son are two principles of the Holy Spirit, because that contradicts authority. For one does not say that Father and Son are two authors of creatures, but one; nor two principles of the Holy Spirit, but one. Since they are one principle, and this is the same as that, the name *author* does not posit person or essence, but notion alone; and the same is true of the name *principle*. Nevertheless, whichever of these is accepted, the reason for the statement must always be considered. For, if the singular is granted, its singularity is to be referred to the mode and notion, not to person; but if the plural is granted, it is said on account of the plurality of persons, not of modes or notions.

[Note: [Col. 0911D] See our observations on chapter 6 of Pullus, [Col. 0912D] in Part I.] It is also customary to ask why the Son is called “principle from principle,” but not the Holy Spirit, and what is predicated of the Son by this expression. The answer is that, if the phrase “principle without principle” is taken with the force of a name, it is understood as equivalent to the name “unbegotten”; and thus the Father, by a certain notion—namely, unbegottenness—is principle without principle, just as by unbegottenness he is unbegotten. But if it has the force of a proposition, the nominative indicates the common principiality of the three persons, while the ablative suggests the mode by which principiality belongs from the Father—a mode in which principiality is not said of the other two persons.

Thus, to say “principle without principle” is the same as saying: “The Father is Creator,” or “the principle of creatures,” or “the divine essence from which all things are and which is from no one.” Likewise, when it is said, “The Son is principle from principle,” the phrase may have the force of a name, so that it is equivalent to saying, “The Son is Son”; and then the same notion is proved by the expression “principle from principle” and by the name “Son.” For this [Col. 0913A] circumlocution has been appropriated to the Son by the authors of sacred Scripture.

But if that circumlocution has the force of a proposition, it is equivalent to saying: “The Son is the principle of creatures,” or “is the divine essence,” and he is from the Father. Thus, through the nominative is indicated the common principiality of the three persons, which is the divine essence; through the ablative, the manner in which that principiality belongs from the Son and not from the Father—namely, that the Son is from the Father, one principle with him. Accordingly, some refuse to refer the statement that “the Father is the principle of the Son” merely to a diversity of modes of speaking, preferring it to be an equivocation in speaking rather than in being. Nor, according to them, when it is said, “The Father by fatherhood is the principle of the Son,” does the ablative indicate the predication of a notion; rather, a rationale is fitted [Col. 0913B] and a theological rationale—namely, principiality—is proved when one says “principle of the Son” or “principle of the Holy Spirit.”

If it is asked why the Son, rather than the Holy Spirit, is called “principle from principle,” the will of the authors who appropriate such expressions to the Son may suffice as an explanation. Yet some wish to offer an explanation of this. In their view, when “principle from principle” is said, the nominative does not signify the common 87 principiality of the three persons, but an eternal relation—namely, spiration—while the ablative signifies fatherhood. Thus, two essential relations are indicated when it is said: “The Son is principle from principle.”

But if one says, “Spiration is principle from principle,” the nominative [Col. 0913C] indicates a temporal relation, since the Holy Spirit is not principle eternally, while the ablative indicates an eternal relation. And since such a conjunction of relations of different kinds—one eternal, the other temporal—seems unfitting, and since the preposition *de* (“from”) does not permit such a conjunction, the Holy Spirit is not called “principle from principle.” Thus, according to them, the nominative here signifies an eternal relation, namely spiration.

Nevertheless, as we have from what was said above, it may be said that such names in the joined expressions “God from God,” “light from light,” “principle from principle,” and the like, are taken personally, not relatively but in place of relatives: the first occurrence is said for the person of the Son, the second for the person of the Father. This understanding is therefore necessary when, with such appellations placed in the subject, it is said, “The Son is principle from principle.” For there the name “principle” cannot stand for the essence or for a relation, since neither the divine essence nor spiration is from the Father as principle.

If the objection is made: “The Holy Spirit is principle and is not from principle; therefore he is principle without principle; therefore he is the Father,” it is resolved by denying the inference. For the Holy Spirit is principle from the Father. Hence, if one infers that the Holy Spirit is “principle from principle,” neither conclusion should be granted: neither that he is principle without principle nor that he is [Col. 0914A] principle from principle. For one of these expressions is appropriated to the Father and the other to the Son, because the Son proceeds from the Father in the first place—not first in time or in nature, but because he is from the Father in such a way as not to be from another. The Holy Spirit is from the Father in such a way that he is also from the Son. For this reason, we do not object if someone says that the Son alone is “principle from principle,” or “God from God,” or “light from light”; for he alone, as was said, is from the Father in the first place.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the Eternal Property of the Holy Spirit, That Is, Procession

[Note: [Col. 0913D] *Master*, Book I, distinction 13, etc.; likewise distinction 11, etc., Book I.] Having treated these matters, we must deal with the Holy Spirit’s proper property, according to which he is called [Col. 0914B] proceeding. Here it should be observed that the procession of the Holy Spirit is twofold: temporal and eternal. The eternal procession is ineffable: by it he proceeds eternally and without time from the Father and the Son. The temporal procession is that by which he proceeds from the Father and the Son in order to sanctify the creature.

We must first deal with the eternal procession, since this discussion has concerned only eternal relations; later the temporal properties will be treated separately. First, then, one may ask: since the Holy Spirit truly proceeds from the Father and is of the Father’s substance, why is he not called born or begotten? Augustine answers thus:

[Note: [Col. 0913D] Book XV, *On the Trinity*, chapter 27.] “If the Holy Spirit were called Son, he would surely be called the Son of both; and that is absurd, for no one is the son of two persons except of a father and a mother.”

[Note: [Col. 0913D] *Master*, cited above, §2.] It is also asked: since the Holy Spirit [Col. 0914C] is called not begotten but proceeding, why is the Son not called only begotten, but also proceeding, as he himself says of himself in the Gospel: “I proceeded from the Father and came into this world” (John VIII)? The answer is that, although the Son proceeds from the Father by the procession [of generation], and the Holy Spirit by eternal procession, “proceeding” is said of the Son in one way and of the Holy Spirit in another. For the Son proceeds by being born; the Holy Spirit does not.

But if one asks only why the Son proceeds from the Father by being born rather than the Holy Spirit, hear Augustine say:

[Note: [Col. 0914D] Book III *Against Maximinus*, chapter 14; the author has drawn upon this passage in many places.] “I do not know, I cannot, I am not able to distinguish between that generation and procession. Therefore, since both the one and the other are ineffable, just as the prophet, speaking [Col. 0914D] of the 88 Son, says, ‘Who shall declare his generation?’ (Isaiah LIII), so it may most truly be said of the Holy Spirit: ‘Who shall declare his procession?’”

It is enough for us, therefore, to know and believe that the Holy Spirit is from the Father and proceeds from him, and piously to remain ignorant of the mode, which is set above human capacity. Yet this is certain to us: by this property he is related to the Father and the Son. For he proceeds from both. The Apostle testifies that he proceeds from the Son: “He sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts” (Galatians IV).

[Note: [Col. 0914D] *Master*, Book I, distinction 11, §2, has the same.] Yet the Greeks deny that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son, because Truth, speaking in the Gospel about [Col. 0915A] the procession of the Holy Spirit, mentions the Father and not the Son, saying: “The Spirit who proceeds from the Father” (John XV); and because, in the principal councils held among them—in which the Creed was indeed formulated, and in which the Father alone is mentioned in these words:

[Note: [Col. 0915D] In the Creed of Constantinople I.] “And [we believe] in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and life-giving protector, proceeding from the Father, and to be worshipped and glorified together with the Son”—

it was decreed, with anathemas appended: “Whoever teaches otherwise or preaches otherwise, let him be anathema.” Therefore they call us anathematized because we say that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son. For what is said there according to us, “who proceeds from the Father and the Son,” has had one word added by the Latins, namely “and the Son.”

[Col. 0915B] [Note: [Col. 0915D] *Master*, cited above, §3; likewise on Galatians 1.] But we construe those words as meaning: “whoever preaches another—that is, a contrary—doctrine.” Thus in the Epistle to the Galatians, chapter I: “If anyone should preach another”—that is, a contrary—gospel, “let him be anathema.” He did not say, “if he should add”; for the Apostle himself wished to come to certain persons in order to supply what was lacking in their faith.

To the point which seems to be made in the Gospel—that the Holy Spirit proceeds not from the Son but from the Father, who alone is mentioned—we reply thus: although the Father is named, the Son is not thereby excluded, because it is not said, “from the Father alone.” But he mentioned the Father alone because what belongs to the Son is also customarily referred back to the Father, since the Son has it from him.

[Note: [Col. 0915D] The *Master* likewise has this, §4.] Yet the Greeks agree with us in meaning, because they accept that the Holy Spirit is the Son’s; and this is nothing other than that he [Col. 0915C] proceeds from the Son. Thus certain of their teachers, affirming one and the same meaning, testified that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son. Athanasius says:

[Note: [Col. 0915D] In the Creed.] “The Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son, not made, nor created, nor begotten, but proceeding.”

John Chrysostom likewise says in a homily:

[Note: [Col. 0915D] In the exposition of the Creed, as in the *Master*, cited above, §5.] “This is the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father and the Son, who distributes his own gifts as he wills.”

[Note: [Col. 0915D] *Master*, Book I, distinction 12.] It is also asked whether the Holy Spirit proceeded from the Father before he proceeded from the Son, or not. A certain heretic reasoned thus against Augustine: “The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father; therefore, either after the Son was born or before he was born. If after the Son was born, the Son’s birth preceded the Holy Spirit’s procession. [Col. 0915D] But if before the Son had yet been born, the Holy Spirit’s procession preceded the Son’s birth.” Augustine responds sufficiently to this rather childish question:

[Note: [Col. 0915D] Book XV, *On the Trinity*, chapter 26, at the beginning.] “In that supreme Trinity which is God, there are no intervals of time by which it can be shown—or even asked—whether the Son was first born of the Father and afterwards the Holy Spirit proceeded from them both.”

[Col. 0916A] [Note: [Col. 0915D] *Master*, cited above, §3.] It is also customary to ask whether the Holy Spirit proceeds more fully or more greatly from the Father than from the Son, or conversely. Augustine seems to say this:

[Note: [Col. 0916D] Book XV, *On the Trinity*, chapter 17, after the middle.] “Not without reason in this Trinity is only the Son called the Word of God, only the Holy Spirit the gift of God, and only God the Father principally that from whom the Word is begotten and from whom the Holy Spirit proceeds.”

Here he seems to say that the Holy Spirit proceeds more principally from the Father than from the Son. Augustine says this because, although the Holy Spirit also proceeds from the Son, the Son has this very fact from the Father; for whatever the Son has, he has from the Father, including his essence. Therefore all that belongs to the Son is referred to the Father.

It is asked, however, since the procession of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0916B] is the property by which he is distinguished from the Father and the Son, whether by it the Holy Spirit is related to the Father and the Son. If so, then the Father may be called the Father of the Holy Spirit, and the Son the Son of the Holy Spirit. Thus it will follow that the Holy Spirit has a Father and a Son. But if it is said that the term “Holy Spirit,” when said of God according to essence, is said of the Trinity, then the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were one Holy Spirit, just as they are one God.

The answer is that the phrase “Holy Spirit” is sometimes taken essentially, and then is said of the whole Trinity. Thus Augustine says:

[Note: [Col. 0916D] Book V, *On the Trinity*, chapter 11.] “The Trinity can in no way be called Son; yet it can be called Holy Spirit, according to what is written: ‘God is Spirit’ (John IV).”

Some nevertheless say that [Col. 0916C] the Father and the Son are Spirit, but not Holy Spirit—or not holy Spirit. The phrase “Holy Spirit” is also used to designate a relation. Hence:

[Note: [Col. 0916D] Augustine, ibid.] “The Holy Spirit, who is not the Trinity but is understood to be in the Trinity, insofar as he is properly called Holy Spirit, is spoken of relatively, since he is related both to the Father and to the Son. Yet the relation does not appear in this name, though it does appear when he is called Gift.”

[Note: [Col. 0916D] *Master*, Book I, distinction 18.] Note that “gift” and “given” are said for different reasons. For he is called “gift” eternally, but “given” in time. Augustine says:

[Note: [Col. 0916D] *On the Trinity*, chapter 15.] “The Holy Spirit always proceeds, and proceeds not in time but from eternity; and because he proceeded from eternity in order that he might be capable of being given, he was already a gift before there was anyone to whom [Col. 0916D] he could be given.”

And note that the Holy Spirit is properly called the gift of God; properly speaking, he is love, although this one term is said of the whole Trinity.

[Note: [Col. 0916D] *Master*, Book I, distinction 17, etc.] Hear Augustine say that the love itself by which we love God, or by which God loves us, is God:

[Note: [Col. 0916D] Book VIII, *On the Trinity*, chapter 8. The cited Master seriously stumbles against this rock.] “When in love we love a brother, we love a brother from God. And it cannot be that we do not especially love the love itself by which we love a brother, because God himself is love.”

And lest anyone suppose this to have been said causally, as when we say “God is our hope and refuge” because he is the cause of hope and refuge, hear what Augustine says elsewhere:

[Note: [Col. 0917D] Book XV, *On the Trinity*, chapter 17, with a few words omitted.] “The statement ‘You are my patience’ (Psalm LXX) is like ‘Lord, you are my hope’ (ibid.), and ‘My God is my mercy’ (Psalm LVIII). But it was not said in the same manner, ‘God is my love’; rather, it was said, ‘God is love’ (1 John IV), just as it was said, ‘God is Spirit.’”

[Note: [Col. 0917D] *Master*, cited above, §7.] If this is said, however, the question arises: since love is possessed more or less, increased and diminished, is the Holy Spirit increased and diminished, since love is the Holy Spirit? For thus he seems mutable. [Col. 0917B] The answer is that the Holy Spirit does not receive more or less in himself, nor is he himself exalted or magnified; rather, he is exalted in us who possess him and make progress in loving and knowing. Hence Augustine says:

[Note: [Col. 0917D] Tractate 74 on John.] “If the Holy Spirit were not possessed more by one person and less by another, holy Elisha would not have said to holy Elijah: ‘Let the Spirit which is in you be doubled in me’” (4 Kings II).

And elsewhere:

[Note: [Col. 0917D] Tractate 9 on the First Epistle of John, at the beginning.] “Let each person test how much love increases in him—or rather, how much he himself increases in love. For if God is love, he neither increases nor diminishes.”

[Note: [Col. 0917D] *Master*, here §9. See also what follows.] Again, someone possesses love who formerly did not possess it, and love is the Holy Spirit. Therefore someone [Col. 0917C] possesses the Holy Spirit who formerly did not possess him. Therefore the Holy Spirit is in someone in whom he previously was not, although that person previously existed. To this we say that not everyone in whom the Holy Spirit is possesses the Holy Spirit; otherwise irrational creatures would possess him. But only those possess him in whom he is through indwelling grace.

Again Augustine says:

[Note: [Col. 0917D] In *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 32, it reads thus: “Whence, then, comes that love, namely charity, through which faith works, except from him from whom faith itself obtained it?”] “Whence is faith, except from him from whom love is?”—that is, from the Holy Spirit. Therefore, just as faith which is from the Holy Spirit is not the Holy Spirit, so love which is from the Holy Spirit is not the Holy Spirit. To this we say that the Holy Spirit is indeed in us from himself; this must be supplied. For he gives himself to us; and thus both faith and the Holy Spirit are in us from him.

Again Augustine says:

[Col. 0917D] [Note: [Col. 0917D] Augustine, in the same place, near the end of the chapter.] “The love of God is said to be poured out into our hearts” (Romans V), “not that by which he himself loves us, but that by which he makes us his lovers.”

Here love by which we love God seems distinguished from that by which he loves us. Thus, since God loves us by the love which is the Holy Spirit, it seems that we do not love [Col. 0918A] him by the love by which he loves us; and so it seems that we love him not by the love which is the Holy Spirit, but by created love, which is a virtue of the mind. But we explain that authority thus:

[Note: [Col. 0918D] See the Master’s solution here, §11.] There is no distinction between the love by which he loves us and that by which we love him, both of which are the same Holy Spirit. Rather, “not that by which he himself loves us, but insofar as by it he makes us his lovers,” so that one and the same love is understood in both cases.

Again Augustine says:

[Note: [Col. 0918D] Book III, *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 10. *Master*, cited above, §§17 and 18.] “I call charity the movement of the mind toward enjoying God for his own sake, and oneself and one’s neighbor for God’s sake.”

But charity is said to be a movement of the mind in the way that God is called our hope—namely, causally. Thus Wisdom [Col. 0918B] in Holy Scripture is called “mobile, undefiled, sure”:

[Note: [Col. 0918D] Wisdom VII: “mobile, undefiled, sure.” — *Master*, §18.]

Yet Wisdom itself is not something mobile, except causally, insofar as it makes us move from virtue to virtue. But since charity produces in us acts of believing and hoping, just as it produces loving, why is it said that we love by charity, and not that we believe or hope by charity? The answer is clear: charity produces the manner of believing through the virtue of faith, and the manner of hoping through the Holy Spirit, but the manner of loving through no intervening virtue.

[Note: [Col. 0918D] Here is an error of the disciple as of the master.]

Therefore we believe and hope from charity, but not by charity; we love from charity and by charity.

Yet some—indeed almost all—on account of the Apostle’s words, [Col. 0918C] “Faith, hope, love: these three; but the greatest of these is love” (1 Corinthians XIII), say that this manner of speaking would create an incongruity of meaning unless charity were a virtue, like faith and hope. For comparison by a superlative, or communion, is not customarily made except between things of the same genus, especially not between Creator and creatures. They say that two things are signified by the name “charity”: a virtue of the mind, more intense in some persons than in others; and the Holy Spirit, who, according to some, is called charity only through charity itself and improperly, just as hope and mercy are so called.

[Note: [Col. 0918D] The remainder of this chapter is found in the Victorine manuscript, which elsewhere also lacks many passages in which our manuscript is fuller.] Besides these meanings, charity is also called the movement of that virtue which is in the soul. Therefore, when it is said that God loves us by charity, “charity” there is referred to [Col. 0918D] God according to all Catholics, since in God, as God, there is no virtue or quality of mind. When it is said that we love God by charity, this is not said of the Holy Spirit, but of a virtue of the mind or of the movement of that virtue.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On This Name, “Trinity”

[Col. 0919A]

[Note: [Col. 0919D] *Master*, Book I, distinction 24.] This name “Trinity,” which is somewhat collective, belongs to the fifth class of terms said of God; for to say “The Trinity is God” is equivalent to saying “The three persons are God.” Yet the name “Trinity” seems to be said of God according to essence, since it is “Trinity,” as though one said “the unity of three.”

[Note: [Col. 0920D] Isidore, *Origins*, Book I, chapter 4.]

But the unity of three is the essence of the three, and this is said of God according to essence, since it belongs to the individual persons and to them together in the singular, not the plural. Therefore “Trinity” too is said according to essence. Therefore each of the three persons is Trinity, since each is the unity of three.

The answer is that “Trinity” and “unity of three” are not identical. Rather, this is a certain allusion and a non-convertible etymology of words; “Trinity” is instead equivalent to the expression “three persons,” as has been said.

The objection is made thus: Whatever exists is either a person or not a person; the Trinity is something; therefore it is either a person or not a person. If the Trinity is a person, then the three persons are a person. If the Trinity is a non-person, and it is one thing only, then the Trinity is nothing that is a person. Some therefore say that this name is sometimes taken distributively, so that it is equivalent to saying: “Each of the three persons is a person.” Others think it is taken collectively except when the word “whole” is joined to it. Then it is also taken distributively. Hence they grant: “The whole Trinity is a person,” but not “The Trinity is a person.”

It is better, however, to say that by itself it is taken collectively, while, with the adjunct “whole,” it is taken both distributively and collectively, so that “the whole Trinity is a person” means: “the three persons are a person, and each of them is a person.” The first of these is false, just as it is not granted that “this whole people is a human being.” Accordingly, “The Trinity is a person” must not be granted.

But if one says, “The Trinity is a non-person,” some say that such implications of names are not found in sacred Scripture and therefore should not be introduced because of the profane novelty of words (1 Timothy VI). Augustine, however, as we said above, frequently uses them. Therefore, if anyone refuses to accept “The Trinity is not a person,” let him press the former argument thus:

Everything is either white or non-white; this people [Col. 0919D] [is something]. Therefore it is either white or non-white. Again, each of the three persons is a person; the whole Trinity is that which is a person. Therefore the whole Trinity is a person. This is a fallacy. This man will see each of the things belonging to the number of these troops; he will see the things which are those troops. Therefore he will see these troops—even if he will never see them assembled, but only separately.

Again: the whole Trinity is that which is a person; the Trinity is something; therefore it is either a person or a non-person. This is a fallacy. The Father and the Son are that which is Father; the Father and the Son are something; therefore they are either Father or not Father.

Again, nothing is the person of the Father which is not the person of the Son; the person of the Father is that which is the person of the Son, and the person of the Son is that which is the person of the Father. Therefore the person [Col. 0920A] of the Father is the person of the Son, and conversely. This is a fallacy. The name which is this word *album* [“white,” neuter] is this word *alba* [“white,” feminine]; and conversely, this word *albus* [“white,” masculine] is the name which is this word *alba*, and the name which is this word *alba* is this word *albus*. Therefore this word *album* is this word *alba*, or conversely.

Again, different things stand for the subjects in the propositions “a person is Father” and “a person is Son,” while the same things stand for the subjects in “God is Father” and “God is Son.” Therefore either the Father and Son are not distinct persons, or the Father and Son are distinct gods. This must be resolved by denying the inference, because when it is said, “God is Father,” “God is Son,” the divine essence stands as subject.

But since this is so, it is asked whether discourse can be made about the divine essence without discourse being made about a person—that is, [Col. 0920B] about the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit. If it can, then, since it is true of the divine essence that it is several persons, it is true of a person that it is three persons. Again, discourse cannot be made about the divine essence without discourse being made about some person; it is true of the divine essence that it neither begets, nor is begotten, nor proceeds. Therefore the same is true of one of the persons.

Again, discourse cannot be made about the divine essence without being made about one of the three persons; but the term “divine essence” does not determine of which person, since it belongs indifferently to each. Therefore, since the proposition “the divine essence is Father” is indefinite, just as “a person is Father,” it seems that one may truly say “the divine essence is not Father,” just as “a person is not Father,” in both cases understanding it as standing for the Son. But if one says that this term stands for the three persons such that it stands for none of them individually, then “the divine essence is Father” will be false, since the three persons are not the Father; and these two propositions will mean the same: “the Trinity is Father” and “the divine essence is Father.”

Thus the reasoning is indirectly brought to the conclusion that discourse can be made about the divine essence and not about the Father, Son, or Holy Spirit. This is done through the term “divine essence.” Yet in the proposition “the divine essence is Father,” discourse is made about the all-powerful one, not about the Father, Son, or Holy Spirit; therefore, it is made about that one who is co-omnipotent.

Again: “the divine essence is Father.” By this proposition discourse is made about God. There is no God who is not [Col. 0920D] Father, Son, or Holy Spirit. Therefore by this proposition discourse is made about God who is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Therefore by this proposition discourse is made about God the Father, God the Son, or God the Holy Spirit.

Again, these are two propositions, “the Father is Father” and “the divine essence is Father,” each of which makes a determinate statement about something. Therefore these two make statements about the same thing, or one about something of which the other does not make a statement. If one says only about the same thing, then both are about the Father, or neither is. If one says one is about something of which the other is not, then there is nothing about which one makes a statement that is not also that about which the other makes a statement. Therefore neither makes a statement about something of which the other does not.

For this reason, some say that one must not grant that one God is several persons, because [Col. 0921A] the name “God,” placed as subject, would have to stand, according to the purpose of the proposition, for one of the three persons; and on every such supposition the proposition would be false. Yet they do not deny that the three persons are one God, just as, in natural things, several utterances are one name, but one name is not several utterances. They seem to affirm this by Hilary’s authority:

[Note: [Col. 0921D] Book VIII, *On the Trinity*, before the middle.]

Addressing a heretic on the Apostle’s words, he says: “I ask now, in the Spirit of God, whether you understand nature or a thing of nature. For a thing of nature and nature are not the same; just as a man and that which belongs to man are not the same, and fire and that which belongs to fire are not the same, so God and that which belongs to God are not the same.”

Elsewhere it is also read: “Whoever does not distinguish person from nature falls either into the division of Arius or into the confusion [Col. 0921B] of Sabellius.” Since the Master sufficiently answers them in the *Book of Sentences*:

[Note: [Col. 0921D] Book I, distinction 34, §§1–2, etc.]

—and charges them, from the context of the passage, with being thieves of truth—we have not thought it necessary to answer them here.

But we want them to solve this: if the divine essence exists from eternity and is thus God, yet is not Father, Son, or Holy Spirit—because there is no reason why it should be one person more than another—then, if it is said to be Father, it will also follow that it is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Or, if it is Father and not Son, the divine essence is not Son. Therefore there is a God who is neither Father nor Son nor Holy Spirit; and thus there is a quaternity in the Trinity, not a Trinity.

If anyone wishes to adopt the foregoing solution—namely, the analogy of natural things—and to say, as is said, that whenever discourse is made about something by taking one of its appellations, discourse is also made about the same thing by taking any other appellation, as when one says, “The Seine is here and elsewhere,” a statement is made about the substance of which it is said that the Seine is here and elsewhere; and when it is said, “The Seine runs,” something is said about a thing, not because it itself runs, but because the Seine runs. Likewise, when a statement is made about a statue and one says, “This statue is artificial,” it is said of the work [or body; *corpore*] that the statue is artificial. If this consideration is applied in such cases, many absurdities follow.

First, when one says, “The divine essence is three persons,” about what is the statement made? For the name “person” belongs to no one to whom the term [Col. 0921D] “divine essence” does not belong; thus it is said of a person that the divine essence is three persons. And if the statement is about a person, then it is about the Father, Son, or Holy Spirit, since these three terms—“divine essence,” “person,” and “Father or Son or Holy Spirit”—belong in precisely the same way. Thus it is true of the Father, Son, or Holy Spirit that the divine essence is three persons.

Indeed, since the term “divine essence” belongs to no one to whom the term “Father” does not belong, and conversely, because each belongs only to the divine essence, when one says, “The divine essence is Son,” discourse is made about the Father, and it is said of the Father that [Col. 0922A] the divine essence is Son. Likewise, one may say that discourse is made about each of the three persons when “the divine essence is Son” is said.

Again, since the term “Father” belongs to no one to whom the name “Son” does not belong, whenever discourse is made about the Father, it is also made about the Son. Thus, when one says, “The Father is Father,” discourse is made about the Son, and it is said of the same that the Father is Father; and likewise of the Holy Spirit and each of the persons.

Likewise, since these three terms belong to one thing only—namely, “Father,” “divine essence,” and “Trinity”—because they belong only to the divine essence and to nothing that is not it, it will follow that by the proposition “the divine essence is Father,” discourse is made about the Trinity, and it is truly said of it that the divine essence is Father. Thus it is true of the three persons that the divine essence is Father.

[Col. 0922B] Again, the following three propositions make statements about one thing only: “the Father is Father,” “the divine essence is Father,” and “the Trinity is Father.” Therefore each makes a statement about the Trinity, or none does. If so, then, when one says “the Father is Father,” it is said of the Trinity that the Father is Father; and so it is true of the three persons that the Father is Father. Thus it is true of the same thing, because it is divine essence, both that it is Father and that it is Son.

Again, the following three propositions make statements about one thing only: “the Father exists,” “the divine essence exists,” and “the Trinity exists.” The first two make statements about the Father; therefore “the Trinity exists” does as well. If so, then we truly say of the Father that the Trinity exists, and so it is true of the Father that there are three persons; thus it is true of the Father that the Son and the Holy Spirit exist. [Col. 0922C]

Therefore the method of dialecticians does not seem transferable to such matters, because of the absurdities just stated. Rather, a distinction must be made between person and essence—not according to their mode of being, since person and essence are the same thing (as some denied, whom Augustine rebukes thus:

[Note: [Col. 0922D] Book VII, *On the Trinity*, chapter 6, around the middle; incorrectly in others, Book V.] “We say three persons of the same essence, or the same essence, but not from the same essence, lest essence be understood there as one thing and person as another”)—

but according to the manner of speaking, understanding, and signifying. For when the name “person” is placed as subject, one must say that the discourse concerns a person, not essence, although person and essence are the same thing. Thus, when one says “the Father is Father,” but places the term “divine essence” as subject, discourse concerns the divine [Col. 0922D] essence, not a person, although the divine essence is the same thing as person.

Just as, when one says, “This cup is worth ten marks, whose workmanship exceeds its material,” the statement concerns this cup, in which matter together with form is understood. But it does not concern this silver, although this silver is the same thing as this cup. And just as it does not follow from the other side that the discourse concerns that which is equally omnipotent, so here it does not concern that which is more precious, although this cup is more valuable than this silver. There is some analogy in natural things, though no exact one can be found. Thus, a distinction must be made between person and [Col. 0923A] nature according to the manner of speaking, signifying, and understanding, but not according to the manner of being.

Yet it may be doubted, and not without usefulness to inquire, whether by the proposition “the Trinity exists,” or “the three persons exist,” discourse is made about one thing or about several; and, if about one thing, whether it is about the same thing as that concerning which the proposition “the divine essence exists” is made.

Again, the divine essence is three persons, such that it is each of them. Therefore the divine essence is one of the persons, which is this one; therefore it is one person. Some do not accept this, because this name indicates distinction, and it would be equivalent to saying, “The divine essence is not several persons.”

Again, Boethius defines a person in the book *On the Trinity*:

[Note: [Col. 0923D] Book *On the Two Natures*.]

“A person is an individual essence of a rational nature.” But the Father and Son are two persons. Therefore [Col. 0923B] they are two individual essences of rational nature; and this is an argument from the definition. But most of our theologians do not regard that definition as authoritative, because Boethius was more a philosopher than a theologian and spoke more for probability than for truth.

Again, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are the divine essence; this is said concerning the particular persons. Therefore, when it is said, “The divine essence is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit,” discourse is made about several persons, and thus this term stands for the same thing as the name “Trinity.” This is a fallacy. When I say, “*albus, alba, album* [white, masculine, feminine, neuter] are one name,” this is said concerning several words; therefore, when one says, “this name is several words,” it does not follow.

It is commonly asked whether the divine essence can be introduced [Col. 0923C] as speaking or as receiving speech, so that it may be said: “I am the Father,” or “I am the Trinity.” If so, then that proposition speaks of a person; and thus some proposition which speaks of the divine essence speaks of a person. Again, if the divine essence is introduced as speaking, since it can truly say, “I neither beget, nor am begotten, nor proceed, nor breathe forth,” and since speech may also truly be addressed to it in the same terms—“You neither beget nor are begotten, neither breathe forth nor proceed”—then speech may be made of it in the same form, so that one says, “This neither begets, nor is begotten, nor proceeds, nor breathes forth.” Yet it is certain that here speech is made of a person.

To this one must say that the divine essence cannot be introduced in this way as speaking or [Col. 0923D] receiving speech, since this belongs to persons alone. Speech can, however, be made about it, though not about a person. Or, even if it were introduced as speaking, the pronoun *ego* (“I”) would have to be put in the neuter gender; likewise the pronoun *tu* (“you”). Hence in the third person as well one must say *istud* (“this [neuter]”), not *iste* (“this [masculine]”), so that the speech would concern the essence, not a person.

## 94. CHAPTER XXXIII. On the relation of these predicables—Father, Son, Holy Spirit—and whether the proposition “God is” is also singular.

[Note: [Col. 0923D] Master I, distinction 19, §8, 9 and following.]

There may also be doubt concerning the relation of these predicables—[Col. 0924A] Father, Son, Holy Spirit, divine essence, Trinity, and the like. That Father and Son, for example, are opposites seems easily shown as follows. The Father neither is nor can be the Son, and conversely. Therefore these predicables stand in some relation to one another. Therefore they are opposites; and the name “God” is predicated of them in the same meaning. Therefore they are contained under it, and all are predicated in answer to “what is it?” Therefore this predicable “God” is a genus or species, and they—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—are individuals.

John of Damascus seems to say this as follows:

> “The common is substance; the particular is hypostasis. The particular is so called not because it possesses a part of the nature, but by number. For hypostases are said to differ both in number and in nature.”

[Col. 0924B] Again, elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0924D] In the same book, chapter 4]:

> “Substance signifies the common and comprehensive species of *homoideōn* [ὁμοούσιον], that is, hypostases similar in species, that is, persons—for example, God, man. Hypostasis, however, indicates an individual, namely the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.”

Here he seems plainly to intend that God is a universal and that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are individuals. Augustine disproves this as follows [Note: [Col. 0924D] Book VII, *On the Trinity*, chapter 6]: for then the individuals would participate in their universal not singly but plurally, so that one would say, “The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are two gods or three,” not “one God”; just as one does not say, “Socrates and Plato are one man,” but “two men.”

From this it seems impossible to prove that Father and Son are coordinate predicables, since nothing belongs to one which does not belong to [Col. 0924C] the other, since both are the divine essence; and there is nothing which the Father is that the Son is not, and conversely. Therefore these predicables are coordinate. But if this is so, then Father and Son are [coordinate], or conversely.

To this one must say that predicables of this kind have no such relation to one another. For they are neither coordinate nor opposite, neither exceeding nor surpassed, nor part and whole—relations of the sort which you will find in abundance in natural philosophy, as “an animal which has existed” and “animal,” and many others.

Therefore what John of Damascus says must not be understood as though universals and individuals were being taken in the way they are in philosophical disciplines; rather, he spoke by analogy with them. For just as there a universal is called what is predicated of many, while an individual [Col. 0924D] is what is predicated of one alone, so the divine essence is called universal because it is predicated separately of all and each; and by the same analogy the Father is called singular or individual. [Note: [Col. 0924D] The Master cited, §14 at the end.] Augustine, however, perceiving a greater dissimilarity than similarity, excludes the foregoing terminology from the excellence of the Trinity.

If it is asked whether the predicable “God” is universal or individual, neither is to be admitted here. But John of Damascus’s statement that Father and Son differ in number should be understood soundly. For one thing is said to differ from another in number because it is neither that thing nor anything which is that thing or in that thing. The Father is not said [Col. 0925A] to differ from the Son in number in this manner, because the Father is that which the Son is and is in the Son. But he is said to differ from him in number because he is included in counting with him: one can say, “Father and Son and Holy Spirit are three”; or, “They are two.”

Yet the predicable “person” seems to be a universal under which Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are contained. For since this name is said of them in the same meaning, and is said plurally, not singly—“Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three persons”—they seem to be contained under it. This is the sole reason why Augustine denied that the predicable “God” is universal: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not three gods, but one God. If this is so, since the name “person” belongs to no one to whom [Col. 0925B] the term “divine essence” does not belong—and thus these are coordinate predicables—if Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are persons, they are essences.

Again, the name “person” belongs to no one to whom the term “divine essence” does not belong, and conversely. Therefore from whatever the term “person” is removed, that other term is also removed. But the term “person” is removed from the term “Trinity.” Therefore the term “divine essence” is removed from it as well.

Again, the name “person” belongs to no one to whom the term “divine essence” does not belong, and conversely. Therefore whatever is removed from this particular “person” is also removed from the term “divine essence.” But person is not the Father; therefore divine essence is not the Father. Thus the proposition “the divine essence is the Father” is indefinite.

[Col. 0925C] To this one must say that these personal [or particular] terms have no relation of this sort to one another. For one must not demand here the relation assigned by dialecticians. If there were no name except “white,” and the expressions were *albus*, *alba*, *album* (“white,” masculine, feminine, and neuter), this particular name would not be universal or individual.

But the argument, “Whatever belongs to one belongs to the other, and conversely; therefore whatever is removed from one is removed from the other,” is fallacious. The term “animal that has existed” belongs to whomever the term “animal” belongs; therefore whatever is removed from one is removed from the other.

Again: Father is one by unity; Son is one by the same unity; Father and Son are one. Therefore [Col. 0925D] they are one [person]: this, as we showed above, is false.

Again: Father and Son are two; Father is one by unity; Son is one by unity. Therefore the Father is one by a unity other than that by which the Son is one.

Again: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three. Therefore the number three is in them. Therefore something, or some things, are the subject of that number three. If something, then something is three; if some things, those things are Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Therefore they are three things. [Note: [Col. 0925D] Master I, distinction 24; but on this point he is charged with error.]

To this one must say that numerical names posit nothing in God but exclude. For when one says, “God is one,” the sense is: “There are not many gods.” Ambrose says this thus [Col. 0926A] [Note: [Col. 0925D] Book I, chapter 2, *On the Faith to Gratian*, and Book III, chapter 14, *On the Holy Spirit*]:

> “When we call God one, unity excludes a plurality of gods; it does not posit quantity in God, because neither number nor quantity is in God.”

But someone will say: then “Father and Son are two” and “Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three” are said in the same sense, since in both cases it is excluded that they are only one. To this one must say that “three” excludes more: it excludes their being only one, or only two. “Two” excludes less: it excludes their being only one and their being more than two. You must understand this also; otherwise Father, Son, and Holy Spirit would be two, since they are not only one.

[Col. 0926B] Again, when one says, “God is triune,” is speech made of a person or of the essence? If of a person, then it is true that a person is triune, and thus the Father is triune. If speech is made of the divine essence, then the divine essence is triune, and therefore threefold. Augustine denies this as follows [Note: [Col. 0926D] Book VI, *On the Trinity*, chapter 7]:

> “Because God is called triune or Trinity, he must not therefore be thought threefold.”

One may also ask what the name “triune” predicates: whether it is merely exclusive, like the name “one.” We leave this question to the judgment of the masters.

Again, three persons are in the divine essence. Therefore the Trinity is in the divine essence, and the divine essence is in the three persons. God’s essence is God’s unity, which is properly called “one,” as Boethius testifies in his *Arithmetic*. Therefore unity is in the persons; and thus [Col. 0926C] it will follow that Trinity is in the essence and unity in the persons; and conversely one says, “Trinity is in the persons; unity is in the essence.”

To this one must say that the expression “Trinity is in the persons; unity is in the essence” must be understood as meaning: there is one essence and there are three persons. Nor should it be granted that the Trinity is in the essence, for that would seem to say that there were three essences. Fallacy: charity is the divine essence, and the divine essence is in the devil; therefore charity is in the devil.

[Note: [Col. 0926D] Master I, distinction 21.] Again, it is asked whether one should grant: “The Father alone is God.” This is indeed true if it is not understood as excluding person or essence. Nor does “the Father alone” seem to exclude a person, because of the unity of essence which is between Father, Son, [Col. 0926D] and Holy Spirit. But if it excluded person, it would be false.

Again, it is asked whether it should be granted that “the Father is the only God.” Augustine seems to say that this belongs to the Trinity alone, because the Trinity alone is the only God—not the Father, not the Son, not the Holy Spirit. He seems to teach this thus [Note: [Col. 0926D] Book VI, *On the Trinity*, chapter 9]:

> “If someone asks whether the Father alone is God, how will the answer be that he is not, unless perhaps we say that the Father is indeed God, but that he is not the only God; whereas we say that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are the only God?”

Yet some wish to understand “alone” as belonging to the subject. [Col. 0927A] Elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0927D] Indeed, not elsewhere, but in the same chapter 9 of Book VI, *On the Trinity*.] he seems to say the contrary, where he says:

> “Since it has been shown how ‘the Father alone’ and ‘the Son alone’ are said, that statement must be considered in which it is said that not the Father alone is the only true God, but the Father and Son and Holy Spirit.”

For there he expressly says that the Father is the only God; for unless the Father were the only God, it would be incongruous to say, “Not the Father alone is the only God,” just as it would be incongruous to say, “Judas is not the only one who is evil,” unless Judas were evil.

After this it is asked whether, since God’s essence is the same as God, and one essence of the three persons is admitted, one should grant: “One God is God of the three persons.” We do not find this expression in Sacred Scripture, because the very construction of the phrase would seem [Col. 0927B] to subject the three persons to God, as when one says, “the God of Abraham.” Conversely, although God and essence are the same, one does not say, “One essence is the essence of Jews and Christians,” although one does say, “One God is the God of Jews and Christians.”

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the name “Creator” and similar names: whether they predicate essence, relation, or neither.

[Note: [Col. 0928D] Master I, distinctions 29 and 30.]

There are other names which are said of God in time, such as “Creator,” “Lord,” and “principle,” as in the passage, “The Principle, who also speaks to you” (John 8). They signify temporal relations which are in creatures, not in the Creator. Concerning them the first [Col. 0927C] question is what they predicate when one says, “God is Creator,” or “God is God of all.” Since they predicate something, it is either temporal or eternal. If temporal, then something temporal is in God. If eternal, then God is Creator from eternity; therefore from eternity there is some creature whose Author or Creator he is.

Again, if the name “Creator” predicates something eternal, it predicates either essence or a notion. But clearly it predicates none of the five notions which we distinguished above, nor any other, because no other is eternal. Therefore it predicates the divine essence. But God could have failed to be Creator. Therefore he could have failed to be God.

Some answer that names of this sort commonly signify divine power in relation to creatures, and predicate it. Thus God is Creator from eternity—that is, the divine essence whose will brought all things forth from non-being into being. They cite the text, “He who ascends above the setting, the Lord is his name” (Psalm 67), that is, the Almighty; and Ambrose: “God and Lord are names of power, not of nature.” [Col. 0927D] But if one argues, “God is Creator from eternity; therefore some creature exists from eternity,” they think they can properly answer by expounding the proposition thus: “God is from eternity he whose causality brought all things from non-being into being; therefore some creature exists from eternity.”

Others, however, say that the name “Lord,” insofar as it derives from *dominium* (“lordship”), signifies the divine essence; it is used in this sense here, and so God is Lord from eternity. It is also derived from *dominando* (“ruling”), and in this sense signifies a temporal relation which is in the creature and belongs to God in time. Yet if this name signified a temporal relation, it would not for that reason be less true that, according to Ambrose, it signifies—that is, indicates—God’s power. A term said of a human being also makes one understand power.

According to these thinkers, when I say “God is Lord,” nothing is predicated except the relative appellation [Col. 0928A] by which he is referred to creatures—or rather, by which the creature is referred to God. For that relation is in the creature, not in the Creator. On this account, God is not Creator, Lord, or Principle from eternity, but in time. Augustine says this thus [Col. 0928B] [Note: [Col. 0928D] Book V, *On the Trinity*, chapter 15]:

> “If he is called Lord only when he begins to have a servant, this appellation too is relative to God in time. For the creature of whom he is Lord is not everlasting. Therefore his being Lord is not everlasting, lest we be compelled to say that the creature is everlasting.”

But it is objected: when one says, “God is Creator,” speech is made concerning God, and the expression is wholly affirmative. Therefore something is attributed to God, either temporal or eternal. If eternal, then he is Creator from eternity; if temporal, and the proposition is wholly true, then something temporal is in God.

Again, when I say, “God is Creator,” nothing is attributed to the Creator but to the creature. Therefore speech is made of the creature, not of the Creator. It seems strange [Col. 0928C] that speech should be made of one thing and attribution made to another. Again, when one says “God, Creator,” it is said of something that it is Creator, or of nothing. If of God, then being Creator is truly attributed to God; therefore being Creator belongs to God. Hence one may ask whether this is temporal or eternal for him. It is not eternal, because he is not Creator from eternity. If temporal, then something temporal is in God.

Some answer that it is not strange for speech to be made concerning God while nothing is attributed to him by predication but rather to another, namely the creature. For when I say, “Caesar is praiseworthy,” or “worthy of praise,” I attribute nothing to Caesar, since nothing belongs to him now that he no longer exists; yet the expression is wholly affirmative, while it indicates that Caesar was [Col. 0928D] a vigorous emperor.

Others think it better that this name predicates the divine essence and signifies that there is a relation in the creature by which the creature is referred to the Creator. Yet God is not Creator from eternity but in time. For in such cases, with respect to the ground of predication, the principal signification—the divine essence—must be considered; but with respect to judging truth and falsity, attention must be given to the secondary signification. Hence he is not Creator from eternity, which I say on account of the relation that is in the creature. And although he could have failed to be Creator, he could not therefore [Col. 0929A] have failed to be God, since the divine essence is signified by this name, “foreknowing.”

Yet God seems to be Creator from eternity, because this truth—“God is from eternity and is from God, not by filiation as the Son is, nor by procession as the Holy Spirit is”—is true. Therefore it is by creation, because there is no other mode. Therefore this truth is from eternity a creature; therefore God is Creator from eternity. Thus the Holy Spirit is Principle from eternity, since Principle and Creator are the same.

They answer, therefore, that the enumeration is insufficient. And although this truth is from eternity, it is not eternal; for “to be from eternity” is never to have begun, whereas “to be eternal” is to be in such a way that nothing is past or future to it. This belongs to God alone, but all things are present to him.

[Col. 0929B] But someone will say: since every truth is from God, as Augustine also says, and this truth—“the Holy Spirit is the principle of this world”—is from eternity, the Holy Spirit is Principle from eternity; yet this was denied above. Therefore a subtler mode of solution must be sought, which cannot be found unless it is grasped by a definition of what truth is; certainty regarding this matter we have not yet heard.

Again, God’s willing and doing are the same; God’s willing is eternal; therefore his doing too is eternal; therefore God made something from eternity. Some therefore say that the foregoing expression is figurative and must be understood thus: God’s willing and doing are the same—that is, by his own will and without external assistance he does what he does. For he wills something [Col. 0929C] and it immediately comes to be.

Others say that this is said properly. For the same thing is predicated whether one says “God wills this” or “God does this,” namely the divine essence. When I say “God does this,” it means: God wills that this should come to be or exist in this manner.

Again, for a creature to be created by the Father is the same as for it to be from the Father; all things are created by the Father; therefore all things are from the Father. Thus: all things are from the Father, and all things are from the Son; therefore all things are through the Father and all things through the Son. All things are from the Father through the Son; therefore all things are from the Son through the Father. This is not granted, lest authority in relation to the Father seem to be in the Son. Fallacy: I hold this benefice both from the bishop and from the chaplain who invested me and interceded for me; and through [Col. 0929D] the chaplain I hold it from the bishop; therefore I hold it from the chaplain through the bishop. For the bishop himself does not seem to have interceded, since he himself gave it.

Again, it is asked what is predicated when I say “God is in every creature”: essence or relation? Not essence, because he is not in the creature from eternity. One may say: the divine essence is [predicated] together with a certain respect which is in the creature, just as was said concerning “God is Creator.”

Note that if anyone wishes to prove that God is Creator from eternity because the divine essence is posited when one says “God is Creator,” by the same reasoning it may be said [Col. 0930A] that God created the world from eternity, if the divine essence is predicated there by that verb. But if nothing is predicated by that proposition, one must return to the middle opinion, which says that only the appellation is predicated when one says “God is Lord.” Each of these propositions is sufficiently plausible and contrary to the faith in no respect, provided that the assumptions adopted in support of it are maintained consistently.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On the visible mission of the Holy Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0929D] Master I, distinction 51.]

Besides the foregoing terms said of God which signify relations, there are certain others which similarly belong to God in time and signify a temporal relation, such as “sent,” “given,” and the like. These differ from the foregoing because, whereas the former are said of the whole Trinity, such terms are said either of one person or of two, but not of all three. For the Father is not called sent, whereas this is said both of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

There is a twofold mission of the Son, apart from that eternal begetting by the Father through which the Son is begotten from him—if, indeed, it is called a mission: namely, visible and invisible. The visible mission is that by which the human nature became known to the world, concerning which the Apostle says: “God sent his Son” (Galatians 4), etc. The other is an invisible mission, by which, in time, the Son is perceived in someone’s mind. This mission is called invisible because he does not appear in any created nature.

The first mission occurred only once; the second occurs as often as someone happens through knowledge [Col. 0930C] and life to draw near to God. The first occurred into the world, because then he appeared visibly to the world; the second occurs in a human being. For the Son is not said to be sent into the world merely because, through grace, he comes to someone in order to enlighten that person. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0929D] Book IV, *On the Trinity*, chapter 20, before the middle]:

> “The Son is not called sent because he was born of the Father, but either because the Word made flesh appeared to the world, or because he is perceived in someone’s mind.”

Since this mission is the same as the Incarnation, it must be treated more fully later; only this point is determined here.

Is the Son sent by the Holy Spirit? This seems so, for otherwise the works of the Trinity would be divided. If the Son is sent by the Holy Spirit, the Son, insofar as he is sent by him, is less than the Holy Spirit. This is evidently true, since Isaiah says: “The Lord and his Spirit sent me” (Isaiah 48). Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0930D] Book I, *On the Trinity*, chapter 7. See also Book II, chapter 1, and Book I *Against Maximinus*.] that Christ, as man, is less than both the Father and the Holy Spirit, and less than himself as God. Hence, in the form of God, God’s only-begotten Son is equal to the Father; in the form of a servant, he is less than himself. Therefore [Note: [Col. 0930D] Augustine, Book II, *On the Trinity*, chapter 5, at the end] when Truth seems to say in the Gospel, “I did not come of myself” (John 8), it must be understood thus: “I did not bring about the Incarnation according to that human form which you see, but according to the divine nature.” This interpretation is indicated by the pronoun *ipso* [“myself”] used there.
