Nothing further need be determined here concerning the invisible mission [Col. 0931A] of the Son. But the visible mission must be discussed; and because it is common to the Son and the Holy Spirit—the Holy Spirit too was visibly sent, as was the Son—we shall set out the visible mission of the Holy Spirit, in order afterwards to speak of the invisible mission of each.

[Note: [Col. 0931D] Master I, distinction 16.]

It should therefore be noted that, besides that eternal mission by which the Holy Spirit proceeds from Father and Son, he has two temporal missions: one occurring visibly, the other invisibly. The Holy Spirit is visibly sent when, through the sign of some external thing, it is manifestly shown that he is poured into the hearts of the faithful [Note: [Col. 0931D] The same material is in Pullus, Part I, chapter 6.], as on the day of Pentecost through fiery tongues resting above the heads of the apostles [Col. 0931B] (Acts 2), and on the day of Epiphany through the dove descending upon the Lord, baptized by John in the Jordan (Matthew 3).

Here the first question is whether the Holy Spirit was in that dove, or otherwise related to it, more than he was to any other thing. For if he was in it in some way in which he was not in other things, and if the Holy Spirit can be in a thing only by essence, grace, or union, then—since he is in every thing by essence—he was there in some way other than by essence. If by grace, then that dove loved God; for to be present by grace is to make the one in whom he is a lover of God. If by union, then that dove was the Holy Spirit. But if he was in that dove in no way in which [Col. 0931C] he was not in every other thing, how is he said to have appeared in a dove or fire more than in another body?

To this one must say that he was in that dove in no way in which he was not in every thing, because he was there only by essence; but he was there for something for which he was not in other things, namely, to signify that the Holy Spirit is poured into the hearts of those over whom such signs occur.

Again, it is asked whether, according to that temporal mission, the Holy Spirit is less than Father and Son, just as we said above that the Son, insofar as he is visibly sent by the Father, is less than him. To this one must say that the Holy Spirit is not less than the Father because he is sent by him, although this is true of the Son. For the Son [Note: [Col. 0932D] See Augustine, Book II, *On the Trinity*, chapter 6, after the beginning.] so appeared in the flesh [Col. 0931D] that he was a human being, and he united flesh with a soul to himself in the unity of person. But although the Holy Spirit appeared in a created substance, as in a dove or fire, he united neither to himself in the unity of person. For the Holy Spirit did not become a dove or fire; he was not “made dove” or “made fire,” as the Son was made human or incarnate. Therefore, although the Son is less than the Father according to his human nature, the Holy Spirit is not less than Son or Father according to a fiery or dovelike nature, because he assumed neither. Nor is he less in his own nature than Father or Son, since he is of the same nature as each; [Col. 0932A] as Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0932D] Book II, chapter 6, as above]:

> “The creature in which the Holy Spirit appeared was not assumed in the same way as the flesh or human form assumed by the Son. For the Holy Spirit did not so bless that dove or fire, nor join it to himself in unity of person.”

Again, the Holy Spirit appeared in a dove, and the operations of the Trinity are undivided. Therefore the Father and Son also appeared in a dove. But this inference is plainly false, because the first proposition asserts one kind of thing and the second assumes another. When I say, “The Holy Spirit appeared in a dove,” two things are indicated: that the Holy Spirit was poured in, and that the dove was a sign of that mission. Both are true. But when one says, “The Son appeared in a dove,” two things are similarly indicated: that the Son was [Col. 0932B] sent, and that the dove was a sign of that mission. The latter is false. Fallacy: the Son was incarnate, and the works of the Trinity are undivided; therefore the Trinity was incarnate. Again, the whole Trinity effected the appearance of the Holy Spirit; the Holy Spirit appeared in a dove; therefore the whole Trinity appeared. Or: the whole Trinity effected the passion or generation of the Son; the Son suffered or was begotten; therefore the whole Trinity suffered or was begotten.

But someone will say: since one person cannot be poured in without the others, when the Holy Spirit was poured into the fiery tongues, was the Father or Son poured in with him, in accordance with the Word of Truth, which says: “I and the Father will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14)? In this [Col. 0932C] passage the Holy Spirit is understood, as the Gloss on that place states. If each person was poured into the hearts of the apostles in that appearance, then the whole Trinity was poured into the fiery tongues.

To this one must say that the preposition *in* may be understood temporally, so that “the whole Trinity was poured into the fiery tongues” means: while the fiery tongues descended upon them, the whole Trinity was poured in. This is true. But if it is understood as “the whole Trinity was in the fiery tongues,” that is, “the whole Trinity appeared in fiery tongues,” that is, “the fiery tongues were a sign of the mission of the whole Trinity,” it is false; for they were a sign only of the mission of the Holy Spirit. Hence we grant: “The Holy Spirit was poured into the fiery tongues and appeared in them.” But concerning the Trinity, one should grant that it was poured into the fiery tongues, but not that it appeared in fiery tongues. For “to appear” denotes two things: both infusion and a sign. Thus the whole Trinity will judge, yet the whole Trinity will not appear.

[Col. 0932D] But someone will ask: if the descending fiery tongues were a sign of the mission of the Holy Spirit, and the whole Trinity was then also poured in, since one person could not be poured in without the others, why was the descent of those tongues not a sign of the mission of the whole Trinity, so that the Father and Son might be said to have appeared in the dove and in fire, just as the Holy Spirit did?

I think the answer is that this was said because of likeness. The Holy Spirit is called, by antonomasia, charity and consuming fire (Deuteronomy 4; Hebrews 1), because, according to the words “Our God is a consuming fire,” he consumes vices and inflames our heart to love God. [Note: [Col. 0933D] See Augustine, Tractate 6 on John, etc.] Hence: “Our heart was burning within us on the way,” etc. (Luke 24). He appeared in tongues because speaking in tongues—the gift given to the apostles that day—is a gift of the Holy Spirit. Again, people are joined to one another through the use of language; and the Holy Spirit, who is the love of Father and Son, is the God of peace, not dissension. Through the charity given in him, people are joined to one another. Therefore he is said to have appeared more fittingly in the form of a tongue than in another form.

Likewise, among animals the dove is more simple, and simplicity, goodness, or humility is attributed in the Trinity to the Holy Spirit. Therefore [Col. 0933B] the dove is said more especially to have been a sign of the mission of the Holy Spirit than of the Father or Son.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the invisible mission of the Son and Holy Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0933D] Master I, distinction 17.]

Having determined, then, what occurs to our memory concerning the visible mission of the Holy Spirit, insofar as the Holy Spirit himself has supplied it to us in the reading of Sacred Scripture, we must speak of his invisible mission.

Therefore the Holy Spirit is invisibly sent when he is poured by grace into the human soul. In the same way the Father is poured in, and the Son too, because no person is poured in without another. Yet some distinguish between the temporal infusion of the Father, that of the Son, [Col. 0933C] and that of the Holy Spirit.

The Holy Spirit is properly said to be sent or poured in by a temporal and invisible mission when he is given to a human soul by grace in such a way as to make it love God, whether that soul has knowledge of God or not, and whether it possesses the power to persevere or not. The Son is said to be sent when he begins to be known in someone’s mind—as was said above in Augustine’s authority—whether the one who knows has God through indwelling grace or not, and whether that person perseveres or not. The Father is said to be poured in when he is given to a person in such a way that the person can persevere in good.

These three temporal missions or infusions seem to be derived from the fact that power is attributed to the Father, wisdom to the Son, and goodness to the Holy Spirit. Therefore the Father is properly said to be poured in [Col. 0933D] when a person is able to persevere in good; the Son, when a person has knowledge of God; and the Holy Spirit, when a person begins through grace to be good.

Yet the Father cannot be poured in by giving the power of perseverance without the Son and Holy Spirit also being poured in, since their power is one and the same; nor can the Son be poured in by giving knowledge without the Father and Holy Spirit, since their wisdom is one; nor can the Holy Spirit be poured in by giving the grace of virtues without the Father and Son, since their goodness is one.

Thus, according to this distinction, there seem to be three temporal invisible missions, one of each person: the Holy Spirit [Col. 0934A] is said to be poured in or given when a person is given the grace of loving, which is as though proper to the Holy Spirit; the Son, when a person mentally approaches knowledge of God, which is as though proper for the Son to give; and the Father, when a person is strengthened in perseverance in good works, the giving of which is as though proper to the Father. I do not call it proper because one person does nothing without the other.

Accordingly, it would follow that the Holy Spirit is given to one who has no virtue, who does not have charity, because knowledge of God is given to him; although no one is said to have the Holy Spirit unless he has him through indwelling grace, nor is the Holy Spirit given to anyone except one who loves God and has charity. Otherwise he would be said to be given to an unbeliever who has no knowledge of God. Therefore these foregoing distinctions do not appear acceptable; and although the whole Trinity is in every thing by essence, no one should be said to have the Holy Spirit, or the Father, or the Son, unless he has them through the grace of charity, whether he has them through knowledge or perseverance or not. Therefore what Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0933D] Book IV, *On the Trinity*, ch. 20], “Then the Son is sent when he is known in anyone’s mind,” must be understood of devotional knowledge. For although someone now has knowledge of the Son, and did not have it before, the Son is not therefore said to be sent to him unless he has charity. For on the same reasoning the Holy Spirit would be said to be sent, since no one has knowledge of one person without the others. Hence: “Philip, whoever sees me sees the Father also” [Col. 0934C] (John 14). And the whole Trinity is given, sent, and comes only to—and to all—those who have it through grace; and thus there is but one mission of the Holy Spirit, common to the Holy Spirit and the Son. Whether the Father is sent will be determined later.

But first an answer must be given to those who maintain that it is not the Holy Spirit who is given or sent, but his grace; and that the Holy Spirit is then said to be sent when his grace is given to a human being [Note: [Col. 0934D] *Master*, I, distinction 14, §§ 2 and 3], and that his temporal mission is nothing other than the infusion of grace and the bestowal of virtue. They wish to support this by the authority of Bede, who says in a certain homily [Note: [Col. 0934D] Book II of *Homilies*, homily 2]:

> “When the grace of the Holy Spirit is given to human beings, the Holy Spirit is said to be given. He is sent by the Father; he is sent by the Son; he proceeds from the [Col. 0934D] Father; he proceeds from the Son. For his mission is his procession.”

It is as though Bede said: the Holy Spirit is said to be given solely because his grace is given to human beings, not because his very person is sent to human beings. Further, the Holy Spirit is in the human soul before the grace of the Holy Spirit is infused; and nothing except the grace of the Holy Spirit. Therefore nothing other than this grace is now in this soul that was not previously in it. Therefore nothing other than this grace has been infused into this soul which had not previously been infused—which may perhaps be true, because the Holy Spirit, who is now infused through grace, was previously [Col. 0935A] infused through essence. Yet the following conclusion is drawn: therefore nothing other than this grace is now given to this soul which was not previously given to it. This too may be admitted, because, although the Holy Spirit is given to this soul though he was not previously given to it, his gift is not excluded by this excluding expression “other than the grace” which the Holy Spirit gives. Thus, when I say, “Nothing other than the priest’s voice is heard by me,” the priest whose voice it is is not excluded. But if one concludes: “Therefore nothing that is not this grace is now given to this soul which was not previously given to it,” or: “Nothing that is not this grace is possessed by this soul which was not previously possessed by it,” this is a fallacy. “Nothing other than the priest is heard by me; therefore nothing that is the priest’s voice.”

[Col. 0935B] Likewise: either something which is not grace is now in this soul which was not previously in it, or nothing is. If he affirms the former, 102 it can be said of nothing other than the Holy Spirit; and then the Holy Spirit was not previously in this soul—which is false, because he was in it by essence. If he says, “Nothing which is not grace is in this soul which was not previously in it,” then nothing which is not grace is given to this soul which was not previously given; or something is given to it which was previously in it. This is true. For the Holy Spirit is given to it, sent to it, comes to it, illumines it, remains in it; and yet he was previously in it by essence, and now by grace. For when the Son says, “I and the Father will come to him and make our dwelling with [Col. 0935C] him” (John 14), this is not said so as to deny that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were previously in him by essence. But he is said to come when he comes by grace; then he is given, then sent, then he illumines, then for the first time he remains, dwells, and is possessed.

Let that objection therefore cease which is commonly made in this way [Note: [Col. 0935D] See *Master*, I, distinction 37]: “The Son or Holy Spirit is sent; therefore he passes from place to place. Thus he ceases to be in the place from which he is sent, and begins to be in the place to which he is sent. Therefore he is not everywhere,” although he himself says: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jeremiah 23). This objection is plainly carnal, and made by carnal persons [Note: [Col. 0935D] See Augustine, II, *On the Trinity*, ch. 5], since God is not a corporeal thing occupying a place, nor is he bounded by place. For he is not in one place so as not to be in another, as a created spirit, soul, or angel is. Rather, he is in all places without spatial magnitude of his own, and nevertheless is said to be sent because of the foregoing likeness.

Likewise, since the Holy Spirit is given to this person, and the grace of the Holy Spirit is given to the same person; and since the Holy Spirit is not the grace which he gives, nor does that grace become the Holy Spirit: are two things given to this person? No, because one is said to be given through the other, just as two things are not heard by me when I hear both the priest’s voice and the priest; yet the Holy Spirit is given, and something which is not the Holy Spirit is given. Again, the Holy Spirit is in every thing by essence; therefore [Col. 0936A] he is also in the devil. Therefore the Holy Spirit is in the devil—something which does not seem admissible because of a certain implied meaning, since it seems to say that he makes the devil a lover of God, and because the term *devil* conflicts with the term *Holy Spirit*, since they are opposites: the one denotes wickedness, the other benevolence. Yet it must be granted that the Holy Spirit is in every thing: in the angel who is the devil, in the creature, because there is no such implied meaning there. The divine essence is in the devil, and the whole Trinity is in the devil. Yet the Holy Spirit is not, because of the foregoing implication. And in all such objections as may be raised here there is the fallacy of accident.

Likewise, it is asked whether one of the persons can be in something in one way without the other two [Col. 0936B] being in the same thing in the same way [Note: [Col. 0935D] See *Master*, III *Sentences*, distinction 1, § 4]. For if God is in no thing except by essence, grace, and union—and, by essence, no one person is in anything in which the other is not, since the whole Trinity is in every thing by essence; and in all who have God through charity the whole Trinity is present by grace—then, since the Son of God is in Christ the man by union, is the Father or Holy Spirit also in him by union? If so, Christ is the Father or the Holy Spirit. But if the Son is in him by union and the Father or Holy Spirit is not, then there is some thing in which one person is present by union and another is not in the same way. Let this therefore suffice as a solution: both the Father and the Holy Spirit are in Christ [Col. 0936C] by the union which they effect, not by the union through which they are united. But the Son is there by the union which he effects and by which he is united. Otherwise it would follow that the divine essence is in some thing in a manner in which the whole Trinity is not there in the same manner. Hence the divine essence would not appear to be the Trinity.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. Whether every person who is sent is sent by the Trinity

[Note: [Col. 0936D] *Master*, I, distinction 15.] Since, therefore, it is clear from the foregoing that the Holy Spirit is given, it is asked whether he is given by himself. For since 103 he is given by the Father and the Son, either he is given by himself, or the works of the Trinity are different. But if it is said that the Holy Spirit is given, and that for the Holy Spirit to be given is the same as to proceed temporally, then the Holy Spirit [Col. 0936D] proceeds temporally from himself, and thus the Holy Spirit proceeds from himself. To this it must be said that the Holy Spirit is sent by himself, is given by himself, and proceeds from himself in time. For his mission is the same as his gift and temporal procession, as we confirmed above by Bede’s authority. That the Holy Spirit is given by himself may also be proved by Augustine’s authority [Note: [Col. 0936D] Book XV, *On the Trinity*, ch. 19]. For he says: “The Holy Spirit is given as God’s gift, so that, as God, he gives himself.”

[Note: [Col. 0936D] *Master*, I, distinction 18, final §, and distinction 30, likewise final §.] Again: since what is given is related to the one who gives it, as the Holy Spirit is related to the Father and the Son, by both of whom he is given—and this is expressed when he is called [Col. 0937A] the Spirit of the Father and the Spirit of the Son—it is asked whether the Holy Spirit is related to himself, so that he may be called the Holy Spirit of the Holy Spirit. To this it must be said that he is not related to himself through the designation *Holy Spirit*, but through the designation *gift*, when it is said, “The Holy Spirit is the gift of the Holy Spirit.” Yet this is not properly called a relation, but a certain reference of the Holy Spirit, because he is given to himself by himself who gives. But someone will say: since the Holy Spirit is the gift of the Holy Spirit, and there are seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, none of which is the Holy Spirit, are there therefore eight gifts of the Holy Spirit? One must therefore say that when it is said, “The Holy Spirit is the gift of the Holy Spirit,” it is to be understood intransitively: that is, the Holy Spirit is the gift which is [Col. 0937B] the Holy Spirit. But when it is said of those gifts that they are gifts of the Holy Spirit, it is understood transitively: that is, gifts which are so from the Holy Spirit that they are not the Holy Spirit. Nevertheless, one reads in the exposition on the Epistle to the Corinthians: “The Holy Spirit is not properly called a gift except through the love by which the other things are held.” This is to be understood in this way: no term properly applies to God [Note: [Col. 0937D] See Book XV, *On the Trinity*, ch. 19]. Nor does even this term apply to him except because he makes us love him.

[Note: [Col. 0937D] *Master*, I, distinction 18, §§ 10 and 11.] Again, since what is given is customarily related to the one to whom it is given, it is asked whether the Holy Spirit can be related to all those in whom he is, so that he may be called the spirit of Peter, Paul, or Elijah. But not everything related to another is related through every one of its names. [Col. 0937C] Therefore the Holy Spirit is not related to Peter or Paul, in whom he is, through the designation *Holy Spirit*, but through *gift*, so that it may be said, “The Holy Spirit is Peter’s gift”; or through *spirit*, so that it may be said, “Peter’s spirit,” with *holy* understood—as when I say: “The Spirit breathes where he wills” (John 3). Likewise, although the Son is given to us according to Isaiah: “A child is born to us, and a son is given to us” (Isaiah 9), he is not nevertheless called our Son, but our bread, as it is written: “Give us this day our daily bread” (Matthew 6).

Again, since the Son proceeds from the Father as capable of being given, as does the Holy Spirit, why is the Son not called the Father’s gift, as the Holy Spirit is? And if he is, it is asked whether person or essence is predicated when it is said, “The Son is the Father’s gift.” [Col. 0937D] For if person is intended, then the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit will be three gifts of the Father, because there are three persons; and so the divine essence is three gifts. But if it is said that the divine essence is predicated, then the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit will be one gift of the Father; and no gift of the Father is Son or Holy Spirit which is not also Father; and the Son and Holy Spirit are one gift of the Father; nothing is a gift of the Father which is not also a gift of the Son and Holy Spirit; therefore the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one gift of the Holy Spirit, and thus the Father is given by the Holy Spirit, [Col. 0938A] and the divine essence is given by the Holy Spirit. The response offered is that the Holy Spirit is called the Father’s gift for two reasons: because he proceeds from the Father as capable of being given, and because he proceeds from him, he is called a gift. For *gift* denotes an eternal relation, whereas *given* or *bestowed* denotes a temporal one. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0938D] Book V, *On the Trinity*, ch. 15]:

> “The Holy Spirit, who is equal to the Father and the Son, is called ‘given’ or ‘bestowed’ in time; but he is eternally called ‘gift.’ Although the Son proceeds from the Father as capable of being given, he is not called gift because he proceeds from him, but begotten or born.”

Therefore the term *gift*, said of the Son, 104 denotes only a temporal relation and is understood as *given*. Said of the Holy Spirit, it denotes a temporal relation improperly and an eternal [Col. 0938B] relation properly.

But this does not make the question any less pressing: are the Son and Holy Spirit two gifts of the Holy Spirit or one? And what is predicated by the statement, “The Son or Holy Spirit is the gift of the Holy Spirit,” proceeding in the aforementioned way? Again, thus: the mission of the Father is nothing other than his infusion; the whole Trinity is infused into the human soul; therefore the whole Trinity is sent to it; therefore the Father is sent. This appears contrary to Augustine’s statement [Note: [Col. 0938D] Book IV, *On the Trinity*, ch. 21, at the end]:

> “The Father and the Spirit could appear through a subjected creature; nevertheless it would be most absurd for the Father to be called sent by the Son whom he begot, or by the Holy Spirit who proceeds from the same.”

Here Augustine seems to say that it would be absurd and false [Col. 0938C] to say that the Father is sent even if he had appeared visibly; much less now, when he is infused only invisibly. For he is never read to have appeared in a creature, unless perhaps some say that he himself visibly appeared to Abraham at the oak of Mamre (Genesis 18). But perhaps someone will cling to the wording, saying that Augustine did not simply say, “It would be absurd for him to be called sent,” but “by the Son or the Holy Spirit.” Thus, as they say, when he is now infused by himself, he is not absurdly said to be sent by himself; yet he would absurdly be said to be sent by the Son or the Holy Spirit. But in this there seems to be some derogation from the authority of principial origin that is in the Father; yet there is no derogation when it is said simply that he is sent, or that he is sent by himself.

But someone objects further: the Father is sent by [Col. 0938D] himself; therefore he is sent by the Son and Holy Spirit, or the works of the Trinity are different. Yet this inference is invalid—just as if one said: “The Son was incarnate; therefore the Father and Holy Spirit were incarnate, or the works of the Trinity are divided.” Again, the infusion of the person of the Father is a completed work of the Father; therefore it is a work of the Trinity; therefore the whole Trinity infuses the Father. Thus, since the incarnation is a work of the whole Trinity, the whole Trinity incarnated the Son. And since the mission of the Holy Spirit in tongues of fire or in the form of a dove was the work of the whole Trinity, the whole Trinity sent the Holy Spirit in tongues of fire. But although these examples seem to establish such an inference, there are many other [Col. 0939A] examples by which it may be refuted. For the whole Trinity brought about the utterance of that voice, “You are my beloved Son” (Luke 3), etc.; yet the Trinity did not utter it. The whole Trinity brought about the incarnation; yet the whole Trinity was not incarnate. And the whole Trinity brought about the appearance in tongues of fire; yet the whole Trinity did not so appear. But although the inference is not conclusive, it is nevertheless admissible to say, “The Holy Spirit infuses the Father”; for although to infuse the Father and to send him are the same, the Holy Spirit does not send the Father. Just as the essence of God is in this stone, and God’s essence is the same as charity, yet charity is not in this stone, because the term *charity* principally signifies that the divine essence is in this stone, but further implies that it makes the stone a lover of God; so the verb *to be sent* principally signifies that the Son infuses [Col. 0939B] the Father—which is true—and further implies that the Father is not a principle without a principle. For if the Father were said to be sent by the Son, it would seem to derogate from the Father’s authority of principial origin. Attending to that connotation or implication, Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0939D] As above], “most absurdly, however, by the Son whom he begot,” etc. It is as though he said: since the Father has the authority of a principle, it would be absurd to say that he is sent by the Son, even if he had appeared in a visible creature, because this very statement would seem to derogate from the authority of principial origin which is in the Father; much less is this so now when he is given. Yet the Father is said to be sent invisibly by the Son or Holy Spirit. Unless the foregoing implication is understood in Augustine’s wording, he seems to have said nothing at all if [Col. 0939C] he said, merely on this consideration, “It is absurd to say that the Father is sent by the Son because he is begotten by him, or by the Holy Spirit because he proceeds from him.”

But someone will say: if the Father is denied to be sent by the Son because of the implication that the Son is the Father’s principle, whereas the Father is rather the Son’s principle, then by the same reasoning it must be denied that the Son is sent by the Holy Spirit, because that implies that the Holy Spirit is the Son’s principle—which is false. To this it must be said that the statement “The Father is sent by the Son” principally signifies that the person of the Father is infused by the Son—which is true. Further, it derogates from the Father’s authority of principial origin: not in such a way as to posit the Son as the Father’s principle (which perhaps might seem to be implied because the Father is said to be sent by him), but [Col. 0939D] because it implies that the Father has a principle, on account of [Col. 0940A] the nature of this word, which is never said of anything in relation to another without indicating that it has a principle, whether from that other in relation to which it is said, or from another. But when it is said, “The Son is sent by the Holy Spirit,” it implies not that the Holy Spirit is the Son’s principle, since then it would be false to say this, but that the Son has a principle, whether the Holy Spirit or another—which is true, because the Father is his principle. This implication is produced by the nature of the verb *to be sent* mentioned above. Others, however, say that this expression implies that the Holy Spirit is the Son’s principle; accordingly they deny the statement, “The Son is sent by the Holy Spirit.” Thus, since it is allowed by some and denied by others—because the mind is carried differently because of different implied meanings—neither party is heretical [Note: [Col. 0939D] See *Master*, IV, distinction 13, final §], because, as Hilary says, “It is not the utterance but the meaning that makes a heretic.”

[Col. 0940B] [Note: [Col. 0939D] *Master*, I, distinction 14, §§ 4, 5, 6.] Finally, it is asked whether holy men can give the Holy Spirit. Augustine says that they cannot [Note: [Col. 0940D] Book XV, ch. 26, *On the Trinity*]: “No disciple of Christ gave the Holy Spirit; for they prayed that he might come upon those on whom they laid hands.” But the contrary seems to be shown by what prelates do when ordaining clerics: after laying hands on the heads of those being ordained, they say, “Receive the Holy Spirit,” etc. (John 20). And the Apostle, speaking of himself to the Galatians (ch. 3), says: “He who gives us the Holy Spirit.” But the Holy Spirit is said to be given by apostles or prelates because they exercise an office in which the Holy Spirit is given. For through the Apostle’s preaching [Note: [Col. 0940D] See Augustine on this passage, in his exposition of Galatians, ch. 3], many were converted to faith; and in [Col. 0940C] that conversion the Holy Spirit was given to them by the Lord. Just as a physician does not give health to a human being, but medicine, through whose operation health is brought about.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On the last two kinds of terms

There are other terms which, though said of God in time, do not appear to indicate a temporal relation. Nor do they belong to all the persons, such as *incarnate* and *made human*. There are other terms attributed to God by likeness and metaphor. Whenever these occur in Sacred Scripture, the devout and careful reader should understand them, in accordance with the author’s meaning, figuratively: such as *lion*, *lamb*, *imprint*, *splendor*, and the like. And let these remarks on the nine classes of terms which we distinguished at the beginning suffice for our small capacity.

## [BOOK TWO]

[Col. 0939]

106 THE DISTINCTIONS OF THE SECOND BOOK BEGIN.

When the angelic nature was made. Where it was made. What it was like when made. What it became afterward. On the excellence and orders of angels. On their offices and certain matters attached to their office. On the works of the six days insofar as their arrangement is concerned. [Col. 0941] What the first human being was like in body before sin. What he was like in soul before sin. What is the cause of sin. In what thing sin consists. Whether sin is something; and, if it is something, whether it is a nature or a defect of nature. On the difference between will, end, and intention. Whether the will is sin; and, if it is sin, whether it is the same sin as the action or another. Whether ignorance excuses a person from sin. Whether every action is evaluated by intention and end. And on sin against the Holy Spirit. Whether the ends of good wills are opposed, as those of evil wills are; where it is determined whether God ought to be served for temporal benefits. Whether Adam sinned more than Eve. What effect sin had upon Adam in body, where original sin is discussed. What effect sin had upon Adam in soul, where the powers of the soul are also discussed: first the natural powers, afterward the gratuitous. What the natural powers were like before sin and afterward; where sensuality, that is, first movements, is discussed. What free choice is, what it was like before sin, and what it was like afterward. Whether the power to sin is from God.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0941]

## CHAPTER ONE. When the angelic nature was made

[Col. 0941A]

[Note: [Col. 0941C] *Master*, II *Sentences*, distinction 2, etc.] If the order of treatment corresponds to the order of enumeration, after speaking of faith in the Trinity we should speak of the fall of humanity. But because the angelic nature fell before the human, and the latter fell through the former, we should first speak of the fall of the angelic nature, so that it may be evident why the latter was restored and not the former—that is, the human rather than the angelic nature—and how it was restored. This will be shown where we discuss the Incarnation and the sacraments. Therefore, in treating of angelic nature, we shall first show when it was made; second, where it was made; third, what it was like when made; fourth, what it was made like afterward; fifth, the excellence and orders of angels; sixth, their offices and certain [Col. 0941B] matters attached to their offices.

The angelic nature was made at the beginning of time. Hence the saying: “Wisdom was created before all things” (Ecclesiasticus 1), 107 that is, angelic nature. But this seems contrary to what the Prophet says: “In the beginning, Lord, you founded the earth” (Psalm 101). Likewise, what is read in Genesis: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Genesis 1). For if earth or heaven was created in the beginning, was angelic nature not created earlier? To this it must be said that he created them simultaneously, namely, in the beginning: spiritual nature, that is, angelic nature, and corporeal nature, that is, the nature of the four elements, namely in a confused condition and not as distinct as it was later made distinct in the works of the six days. [Col. 0941C] Hence: “He who lives forever created all things together” (Ecclesiasticus 18), that is, angelic and corporeal nature. For God now creates nothing whose nature or likeness he did not create in the beginning: matter in respect to bodies [Note: [Col. 0941C] Thus Pullus, part II, ch. 1], likeness in respect to incorporeal things, that is, souls.

[Col. 0942A] But this seems opposed by Jerome’s statement [Note: [Col. 0941C] On ch. 1 of the Epistle to Titus]: “Six thousand years of our time are being completed, and how many prior eternities, how many times, how many beginnings of ages must be thought to have existed, in which angels, thrones, and dominions served God and, at God’s command, subsisted without cycles and measures of time.” But it must be said that Jerome did not state this as an assertion; rather, he was refuting the opinion of certain persons who taught wrongly. Therefore, when it is said, “Wisdom was created before all things,” this must not be understood temporally, because corporeal nature, as said above, was created with it, but only in dignity.

## CHAPTER II. Where the angelic nature was made

[Col. 0942B]

[Note: [Col. 0942C] *Master*, above, § 6.] We must now say where angels were created. They were created in the empyrean heaven. Here *heaven* does not mean the firmament constructed from frozen waters, but the empyrean heaven, that is, fiery—not because of heat, but because of splendor—in which Christ according to his humanity, the angels, and the Blessed Virgin are present; and the structure of the elements extended up to that heaven before it was differentiated. But did heaven exist when the angels were created? It did indeed, because it was created in the beginning together with angelic and corporeal nature, and angelic nature was created in that heaven. Hence in the Gospel: “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10). But [Col. 0942C] what is meant by what is read in Isaiah concerning Lucifer: “I will ascend into heaven and be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14)? How is this to be understood, since he was in heaven [Note: [Col. 0942C] *Master*, § 8]? It must be said that *heaven* here stands for the sublimity of divinity, as if he said: “I will ascend to equality with God and be like him.”

## CHAPTER III. What the angelic nature was like when made

[Col. 0943A]

[Note: [Col. 0943D] *Master*, II, distinction 2.] We must now consider what angels were like when created. It should be noted that three things were bestowed on them in their creation: subtlety of essence, perspicacity of intelligence, and capacity for free choice. Yet they were not equal in that condition. Some were subtler than others, others more perceptive, others more capable. Just as among bodies some are heavier than others, some larger, some smaller.

But it is asked of those angels who fell whether they were created good or evil. For there is no doubt that the others were created good. Some say that those angels were created evil, and they adduce many authorities and fortify themselves with many arguments. For it is written: “That murderer was from the beginning and never stood in the truth” (John 8). Augustine too says concerning Genesis [Note: [Col. 0943D] Book II, *On Genesis*, chs. 19 and 20]: “It should not without reason be thought that the devil fell from the beginning of time or of his own creation, and never stood in the truth.” Job also says: “This was the beginning of God’s creation, which God made to be mocked by his angels” (Job 40, according to the Septuagint). The prophecy also says: “This dragon, whom you formed to mock him” (Psalm 70), that is, the devil. Besides these authorities, they adduce arguments. Those angels were created just or unjust; if unjust, then evil; 108 if just, then justice was in them. But justice is never idle; therefore [Col. 0943C] they had merits; therefore they merited. But merits do not exist without free choice, and so through free choice they merited to become such as they were made. But I prove this false. They could not bring it about that, in the moment in which they were created, they should be such as they were created; but through free choice they could bring it about that they would afterward be of some kind, for free choice concerns future things, not present or past things.

Again, those angels were created perfect or imperfect. If imperfect, then God created something imperfect; but if perfect, how could they fall? Or, if perfect, then they possessed perfection; therefore they did not fall. Again, those angels were created blessed or not blessed. If not blessed, then they were miserable either in fault or in punishment. If in punishment, then God was an avenger before anyone was a sinner. And if you say that they were miserable in fault, then they were evil. But if they were blessed, then they foresaw all things that would happen to them; but a fall was going to happen to them; therefore they foresaw their fall. They could either avoid it or could not: if they could and did not avoid it, then they were evil; but if they could not avoid the fall they foresaw, then they were not blessed, for blessed is he for whom all desired things succeed. Conversely, if God created an evil angel, then God was the author of evil, which must not be said.

Therefore the statement, “That murderer was from the beginning [Col. 0944A] and did not stand in the truth,” and Augustine’s statement, “It should not without reason be thought that he fell from the beginning of time,” etc., must be resolved thus: “from the beginning of time” means after the beginning. For the angel was not evil at the beginning, but immediately after the beginning. We find a similar explanation in many places, as in: “There is no predication from a primary substance,” meaning after the primary substance. Likewise in Persius (*Satires*, I):

> O Janus, whom no stork has painted from behind,

that is, behind the back.

As for what Job says, “This was the beginning of God’s creation,” etc., and what the prophecy says, “This dragon whom you formed to mock him,” they resolve it by saying that Job and the Prophet referred this to subsequent times, not to the time of the angels’ creation. For at that time the angel was not yet God’s creation in this sense, but became so afterward; and the devil is called a *creation* because he is the maker and inventor of evils. But when it is said, “Those angels were created good or evil,” they say that *good* is said in two ways: as participating in goodness, that is, virtue; or as being in a state of innocence. If you say, “The angels were created good and participating in goodness, namely virtue,” this is false. If they were good, that is, in a state of innocence, it is true. They possessed a certain innocence, and as yet there was no other goodness in them.

Again, when it is said, “The angels were created blessed or not blessed,” they say that they were neither blessed nor not blessed: that is, they did not possess the complete perfection of blessedness, nor any misery, but were in a certain state of innocence, as has been said [Col. 0944C]. Again, when it is said, “They were created either perfect or imperfect,” they say that *perfect* is understood in three ways: perfect according to time; perfect according to nature; and perfect simply. Perfect according to time is what has everything appropriate to its own time, as this boy who is born is called perfect because he has all that a boy ought to have at such a time, namely all his limbs. Similarly Noah is said to have been perfect and faithful according to time, because he believed what was required in his own time; and the angels had such perfection when they were created, namely perfection according to time. Perfect according to nature is that whose nature possesses perfect glorification. The angels did not have this, because their nature had not yet been glorified in them. Perfect universally is God himself, who has within himself the perfection of all goods.

## CHAPTER IV. What the angelic nature became afterward

[Note: [Col. 0944D] *Master*, II, distinction 5, § 4.] After this we must say what angels were made like afterward. Some were turned toward God; some were turned away from God. To be turned toward God was to love God; to be turned away from God, to hate God. But how is it said that they were turned toward God? Did they not love God before? Was anything bestowed on them in that turning? Yes: cooperating grace, [Col. 0945A] by which they could advance from good to greater good. For there is operative grace and cooperating grace. Operative grace is that which makes the impious devout, the evil good. Cooperating grace is that which cooperates and assists, which causes a person not to will in vain and to bring to completion what he has begun. Such grace was given to the good angels in their turning toward God, so that they could advance and love God more greatly.

[Note: [Col. 0945D] *Master*, above, §§ 5 and 6.] But someone will ask, and reasonably: since that grace was not bestowed by God on those angels who fell, and no fault had preceded in them by which they had merited not to have it conferred upon them, why was it imputed to them as fault that they fell? To this it must be said that, just as when grace was given to the good angels no merit preceded that grace—for then it would not be grace but would be from merits—but rather grace preceded merit (they had, however, a certain grace by which they merited nothing), so likewise, by a contrary analogy, in the evil angels fault preceded the withdrawal of grace, not in time but in cause. For no fault preceded in them in time, but only in cause. The cause of that fault is seen in this: before the withdrawal of grace they had a certain grace by which at least they could stand firm (although they could not advance through it) and could await until cooperating grace was given to them, by which they could advance. Because they did not await what they were able to await, they sinned by their own will; and God, who does not need another’s testimony in order to punish anyone, immediately punished them. This was an act of justice. For when he punishes immediately, it is justice; but when he postpones someone’s punishment, this is an act of his mercy.

[Note: [Col. 0945D] *Magister*, II, distinction 5, § g.] From these points it is clear that the good angels merited their confirmation and that blessedness through cooperating grace; but that grace did not precede in time, but in dignity. For grace, merit, and reward were given simultaneously. As soon as grace was given to them, they at once merited and received the reward—namely, blessedness and confirmation. There are others [Note: [Col. 0945D] Lombard himself among them, near the end of the same distinction.] who say that those angels did indeed merit blessedness through the grace bestowed upon them; but that this grace and the reward preceded merit in time. For in the bestowal of grace they received the reward, namely blessedness, but afterward merited it through their services, just as this hired laborer merits what he has already received by cultivating the vineyard. For the reward also precedes merit in time.

[Note: [Col. 0946D] *Magister*, II, distinction 11, § 4, or letter d and following.] Here, however, there arises a question which must not be passed over: whether angels daily merit, and advance in merit and reward. Some maintain that angels daily merit and will continue to merit until the day of judgment, and that they advance in merit and reward. They advance in merit when they provide for human needs [Col. 0946A] and labor for the progress of human beings. They advance in reward, as they maintain, in knowledge, because every day they learn and come to know many things which they did not previously know; and they endeavor to demonstrate this by authorities and arguments.

Isaiah, speaking in the person of angels seeing Christ ascending after the Passion, then marveling at the mystery of the Passion, says: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah?” (Isa. 63). The Psalmist likewise says in the person of angels: “Who is this King of glory?” (Ps. 23). The Apostle also says: “This is the dispensation of the mystery hidden from ages in God, so that the manifold wisdom of God may be made known through the Church to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places” (Eph. 3). On this passage Jerome says [page 110]: “The incarnation [Col. 0946B] and Passion of the Lord were not known to the angels until they were accomplished and spread abroad through the world by the apostles.” By these authorities they seek to prove their point.

Their arguments run as follows. Good angels merited blessedness; but it is certain that in that state of innocence which they first possessed, they did not merit, because they did not yet have cooperating grace by which they could make progress. Therefore, they merited after receiving it. If they merited in the first moment in which grace was given them, then by the same reasoning they merited in the second and third moments as well. Indeed, much more so, because the more grace abounded in them, the more they advanced and merited by it. By the same reasoning, they merit daily and will merit until the day of judgment.

There are others who say that angels now merit nothing [Col. 0946C] and make progress in no kind of knowledge; and in support of this they adduce authorities and arguments. Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0946D] Book V of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 19.]: “The mystery of the kingdom of God, revealed at the fitting time for our salvation, was not hidden from the angels.” Isidore also says [Note: [Col. 0946D] Book I, chapter 10, *On the Highest Good*.]: “Angels know all things in the Word of God before they come to pass.” Gregory likewise says [Note: [Col. 0946D] Book IV of the *Dialogues*, chapter 33.]: “What do angels not know, who know Him that knows all things?”

They also prove this by arguments. For if good angels do not know something and wish to know it, then they are not blessed; if they do not wish to know it and yet will know it, then likewise they are not fully blessed. Or thus: then there is change in them; therefore they do not possess the blessedness of eternity, because in eternity there is no change. Again, if human beings were bound [Col. 0946D] to believe in the Nativity and Passion, why did angels marvel, who saw God face to face? Again, if the least angel merits by a greater charity than any human being, however perfect, then the merits of any human being cannot attain to the merits of the least angel. Again, every angel has greater charity than any human being, and both human being and angel are worthy of reward because of their charity. Therefore every angel is worthy of a greater reward than any human being.

Again, every human being still on the way is lesser than every angel, [Col. 0947A] because “he who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than John” (Matt. 11). An angel merits with greater charity than a human being, and an angel never grows lukewarm in charity—a failing which human beings often suffer. Angels have merited from the beginning of the world and will merit daily until the day of judgment, because they are immortal; while a human being cannot live so long, nor merit on every day of life. Therefore the merits of even the most perfect human being will never attain to the merits of the least angel; and thus a human being cannot be equal to an angel in blessedness.

Nevertheless, Augustine says on the Psalmic passage, “Yet a little while, and the sinner shall not be” (Ps. 36): “You will not yet be where those are to whom it will be said, ‘Come, blessed of my Father’ (Matt. 25); but you will be in that repose where the rich man saw Lazarus covered with sores, and you will wait until the day of judgment, when, after receiving their bodies, the saints will be made equal to angels.” [Note: [Col. 0947D] Augustine, first exposition on Psalm 36, at that verse, though with certain words altered.]

They therefore say that the merit of any human being contributes more to blessedness than the merits of any angel, because of the grave labors and troubles endured by human beings, from which angels are free. Again, if angels now merit, then by the same reasoning the souls of saints now merit; and, by an analogy in the contrary direction, the souls of the wicked demerit—for example, the soul of Judas—and daily tend toward greater punishments. Hence: “The pride of those who hate you rises continually” (Ps. 73). But against this authority is another which says: “There is the place of receiving and not meriting; here is the place of meriting [Col. 0947C] and not receiving.” Again, what the angels themselves do, they do either in the state of the way or in the state of the homeland. If in the state of the way, then they can fall; therefore they are not blessed. If in the state of the homeland, then they do not merit.

Those who say that good angels advance in merit and reward say [Note: [Col. 0947D] Thus *Magister*, II, distinction 11, § f.] that some angels are of greater dignity and some of lesser. Those of greater rank, such as Gabriel, were not ignorant of the Incarnation; the lesser ones were ignorant of it. Thus it is true that the mystery of God’s kingdom was not hidden from angels—namely, from some of them. Isidore’s statement, “Angels know all things in the Word of God before they come to pass,” they resolve by saying: he did not say *all angels*; he did not speak [page 111] universally of all; nor did he say that what they know cannot be known more perfectly.

Gregory’s statement, “What [Col. 0947D] do angels not know, who know Him that knows all things?” they resolve thus: *not knowing* is used for *being ignorant*. Ignorance marks guilt and implies an obligation. But angels, even if perhaps they do not know many things, are ignorant of nothing. If, however, such an argument is made—“Angels do not know certain things; therefore they are ignorant of certain things”—it is fallacious. Adam, before he sinned, did not know many things; therefore he was ignorant. No: because ignorance is a punishment. Yet sometimes *to be ignorant* is used for *not to know*, and then it states nothing, but merely removes something. Having resolved the authorities, they also resolve the arguments.

As to the first statement, therefore: angels will know something which they do not know; they either wish to know it or do not wish to know it, and so forth. [Col. 0948A] They answer by saying that angels know some things which they do not wish to know, and will know some things which they do not know. Therefore there is some change in them. This is fallacious. God commanded Abraham to sacrifice his son and afterward prohibited it (Gen. 22); therefore there was then a change in Him. No. Or it may sufficiently be conceded that there has been some change in angels; for they do not yet possess the perfection of eternity.

As to the later statement, that if angels now merit, then by the same reasoning the souls of saints do as well; and, by analogy in the contrary direction, that the souls of the wicked daily merit greater punishments: they concede all this, and resolve the apparently contrary authority. “Here is the place of meriting, not receiving,” must be read comparatively: that is, here is more the place of meriting than of receiving; and there [Col. 0948B]—that is, in the other life—is more the place of receiving than of meriting. Or thus: here, that is, before the day of judgment, whether the state of the living or the state of the dead is meant, is the place of meriting; but there, that is, after the day of judgment, is the place of receiving and not meriting.

It is better, however, to say that a soul never merits once it departs from the body, and that the case of the souls of saints differs from that of angels. For the former are already in the homeland, while the latter are still on the way. As to the later statement, “The angels do what they do in the state of the way; therefore they can fall”: this is fallacious. The Blessed Virgin, after the Lord’s birth, did what she did in the state of the way; therefore she could then fall. No, because she had been so confirmed by God that she could not fall.

[Col. 0948C] It is the opinion of some [Note: [Col. 0948D] In *Magister*, above, § 7, or g.] that angels cannot advance in knowledge of the Godhead. They cannot know it more fully and perfectly than they know it and have known it since their confirmation; but they can and could advance in knowledge of external things, as occurred in the Incarnation. Nor can they therefore be more blessed, because such knowledge does not produce blessedness—only the knowledge of the Godhead does, and in this they cannot advance. Nor can they merit more than they have merited since their confirmation, or than they now merit. For they cannot have, nor could they have had, greater charity than they have; but they can merit through more acts. Their merit cannot increase in quantity, but only in number: that is, they can merit through more works [Col. 0948D] than they have merited.

Just as a person who was perfect for ten years, and is still perfect, did not merit a greater crown by the works done during those ten years than he merits by this meritorious work which he now performs, because he has never possessed greater charity than he possesses now; nevertheless, he has merited through more works.

[Note: [Col. 0948D] II, distinction 7, § b, etc.] It may next be asked whether angels can sin, or could have sinned, after they were confirmed. This seems capable of proof, because both good and evil angels have free choice. Therefore both the one and the other can be inclined in either direction. Therefore they can sin. Jerome also says [Note: [Col. 0948D] At the end of the tract *On the Prodigal Son*.]: [Col. 0949A] “God alone is one in whom sin cannot occur; all other beings, since they possess free choice, can be inclined in either direction.” Isidore likewise says [Note: [Col. 0949D] Book I, *On the Highest Good*, as above.]: “Angels are mutable by nature, immutable by grace.” If a thing is properly said to possess that which it has by nature, then angels are mutable; therefore they can sin.

The answer is that before confirmation angels possessed free choice in such a manner that they could be inclined in either direction. After confirmation, however, they were said to possess free choice, [page 112] but not in such a way that they could be inclined in either direction. Rather, they possess voluntary free choice, so that they can be inclined not to evil but only to good. Thus, free choice, insofar as it is said of angels, can be defined as follows: Free choice is the faculty by which angels can choose, not by necessity or compulsion but [Col. 0949B] by free will, what they have determined through reason to desire. This, however, is not a general definition of free choice.

As for Isidore’s statement, “Angels are mutable by nature, immutable by grace” [Note: [Col. 0949D] See *Magister* here, § d, etc.]: it is as if he said that it is incompatible with the grace by which they were confirmed—and not with their nature—that they should be able to change. Besides what has been said, many things might be investigated: namely, into what place angels were cast after their fall; whether angels are corporeal or incorporeal; and many matters of this kind. But these belong more to reading than to disputation, and are therefore to be passed over.

Before speaking, however, of the orders and offices of angels, we must say what evil angels became [Col. 0949C] after they turned away from God. In them natural goods are depraved and gratuitous goods removed—not because they had possessed these, but because they would have possessed them had they not sinned. Just as someone takes away from me a prebend, not one which I had, but one which I would have had had he not prevented it.

But an objection is raised: through sin no natural good was removed from the devil. Therefore not even the grace by which he naturally loved God was removed from him. Therefore he possesses it. Therefore he naturally loves God. Thus some movement of love is in him; and thus there is not only hatred in hell but also love. This is disproved as follows: the devil would wish God not to exist, and would wish himself not to exist. Therefore he loves neither himself nor God.

Again, the devil loves sin. Therefore he loves something. Therefore it pleases him that [Col. 0949D] he loves something, and so he takes delight in that love. Therefore there is some delight in him, and thus he does not have unceasing misery, since there is in him a remedy. Again, the devil rejoices in the punishments of the ungodly and in the wickedness of evil people; he also rejoices because he made a human being fall, and this joy is not taken away from him. Therefore it will continually remain in him, and thus he will always have a remedy for his punishment.

Again, Lucifer sinned more than Judas, and Judas has already been cast into hell. Therefore the devil ought to be thrust in more deeply. Again, the devil’s pride continually rises, according to the words: “The pride of those who hate you rises continually” (Ps. 73). Therefore [Col. 0950A] every day he sins more and more, and such sins are for him punishment as well as guilt. Therefore he is punished more and more every day. Therefore his misery always increases.

Again, the devil is a nature of some kind. Therefore there is some good in him, because not all goods in him have been corrupted through sin; and he sins more and more every day. Therefore the goods he possesses are more and more corrupted every day by the sins which he adds to the others; and the more they are corrupted, the more unlike God he becomes. Therefore every day he becomes more and more unlike God, and thus is punished more and more every day.

Again, the devil will always add sin to sin. Therefore some good that was in him will always be corrupted through the added sin. Or, if all the things he possesses are corrupted, he is corrupted more and more. Therefore [Col. 0950B] the devil will always be punished more and more. Therefore his punishment continually increases. Again, although he will always sin, no sin in him will be so grave, nor will the multitude of sins be so great, that the devil can be wholly corrupted in his nature and altogether cease to be, because he is a spirit.

Again, however evil the devil is, a person still on the way can be equally evil. This is proved thus. No one is so evil on the way that he cannot, while on the way, reach that summit of wickedness in which the devil is. This seems necessarily to follow, since both a human being and the devil can be evil without limit—the former while on the way, the latter in the homeland. Therefore, however evil the latter is, the former can be equally evil while on the way. For it is proved thus: as many things as are true, so many are existent, because truths are infinite and existent things are infinite.

But if someone grants this, it is disproved thus. No one is so evil on the way that he cannot be converted to God; but the devil is so evil that [page 113] he cannot be converted. Therefore no one can be as evil on the way as the devil is. Again, no one is so evil on the way that he does not naturally love God; but every devil hates God and would wish Him not to exist. Therefore no one can be as evil on the way as the devil is.

If someone were to grant this, then by an analogy in the contrary direction he would have to say that someone on the way can be as perfect in charity as someone in the homeland. Yet the truth of the Gospel says: “Among those born of women none greater than John the Baptist has arisen; and yet he who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he” (Matt. 11).

Again, Lucifer [Note: [Col. 0950D] Tome 2, distinction 6, § f; *Magister* IV, distinction 50, § b; see Augustine on Ps. 6, v. 7.]—who, as they say, has since the Passion of the Lord been cast into hell—is now wholly excluded from God’s light and suffers the outer darkness, that is, darkness separated from and external to the true light. For he does not see God in the vision of glory, as no one here does; he is far removed from Him by unlikeness, as many are here; and he would wish God not to exist, as no one here would. He experiences a certain malignity of hatred and a will toward forgetfulness of God, called outer darkness, because he is so afflicted by the pains of interior and exterior torments [Col. 0951A] that his mind can never be recalled from them to think anything about God.

No one here can be so wicked that he does not sometimes think of God and hope for pardon, and have hope and some little spark of reason which he directs toward God. Although one reads in the commentary on Isaiah, “It is a consolation for the wicked to have enemies as companions in punishment,” elsewhere the contrary is found: “And even if all souls at some time have rest, you never will.” From this it seems that the devil never experiences mitigation; and this is true. For his rejoicing over our adversities is not true consolation. Whether other souls experience remedies, however, is uncertain.

Yet in the commentary on Luke [Note: [Col. 0951D] In the *Gloss* on Luke, chapter 4.], where the Lord’s temptation is treated, it is said: “The Jews, pressing on in deed, were worse than Lucifer, who in tempting Him pressed on only in word, saying: ‘Cast yourself down.’” But it does not follow that, if they were worse in this respect, they were worse in every respect.

To the foregoing we answer by saying that the devil’s punishment continually increases, as does his guilt; and every day he merits eternal death, just as holy angels every day merit a greater crown. He will be punished more after the day of judgment, when his preeminence over sinners ceases, because then God will punish directly and not through ministers. Hence it will be said: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25). For then they will be thrust into hell, whereas now they are in the murky air; and [Col. 0951C] they suffer more now because the ungodly are not punished more than they rejoice that they are punished. Therefore that joy is not any remedy, although they always rejoice at having done it. For joy in evil is not properly called joy; just as, although they will live forever, they will not have eternal life.

Note also that no one on the way can be as evil as even the least evil person in hell, although the wickedness of one on the way can increase without limit, just as the heat of this fire can increase without limit when fuel is added; yet it cannot equal the heat of the sun, which is unchangeable.

Note also that the devil does not yet suffer outer darkness, because he does not yet completely forget God. That the devil does not yet endure his full punishment [Col. 0951D] may be proved from what is said in the Gospel: “What have we to do with you, Son of David? Why have you come before the time to torment us?” (Matt. 8).

## CHAPTER V. On the orders of angels

[Note: [Col. 0951D] *Magister*, II, distinction 9.] What follows concerns the orders of angels. We must therefore consider what an order is, insofar as the term is applied to angels; which and how many the orders of angels are; what causes their names; and whether they were so distinguished from the beginning of their creation.

An order is a multitude of heavenly spirits resembling one another in some office of grace, [Col. 0952A] just as they agree in their participation in natural gifts. There are nine orders of angels, divided into three triads. There are three higher, three [page 114] lower, and three middle orders. The three higher are seraphim, cherubim, and thrones. The three middle are dominions, principalities, and powers. The three lower are virtues, angels, and archangels.

The name *angel* is a general name for all orders, but sometimes a special name for one order; just as the name *confessor* and the term *person* are equivocal in relation to a proper name, since there are at most four species of person. And a term may sometimes belong specially to certain things, as the term *contingent* does in dialectic.

It should be noted that these orders received [Col. 0952B] these names not on their own account [Note: [Col. 0951D] *Magister*, § c.]—for in contemplating the divine majesty they make themselves known to themselves—but on ours, so that they may be made known to us by their titles. It should also be known that none of these orders received its name from a gift singularly bestowed upon it. For no gift is given to one that is not given to all; rather, each is named from the gift in which it is more vigorous and excels the others.

The first order is therefore called *seraphim*, that is, “burning ones,” because [Note: [Col. 0952D] The Master, § b.] those angels burn more in charity than the others; and it is called first because charity is prior and more worthy than the other virtues. The second order is called *cherubim*, that is, “knowing” [ones], because these angels excel in knowledge rather than in another gift bestowed on them by God. It is rightly placed after seraphim, because after charity knowledge is the greater [Col. 0952C] good. The third order is called *thrones*, as it were seats, because love of God shines so brightly in those angels that God is said to sit in them.

The fourth is called *dominions*, because those angels rule their subjects. The fifth is called *principalities*, because they arrange those subject to them and preside over them by fulfilling their offices. The sixth is called *powers*, because those angels have the power to expel demons, so that they cannot harm as much as they are able to tempt. The seventh is called *virtues*, because through them God works wonders. The eighth is called *archangels*, because they announce greater things. The ninth is *angels*, who announce lesser things.

It must not now be passed over that Gregory says [Note: [Col. 0952D] Homily 34 on the Gospels.]: “In that heavenly city, each order is designated by the name of the thing which it has received more fully as a gift.” But an objection is raised: the cherubim are designated by the name of knowledge; therefore they have received knowledge more fully as a gift than the seraphim. But whoever knows more loves more, as an authority says [Note: [Col. 0952D] In *Magister*, above, § d.]; therefore the cherubim love more than the seraphim. This is false, because the seraphim burn in charity.

That authority is therefore explained in different ways. “In that heavenly city each order,” and so forth, has received it more fully than the other lower orders—not excluding the higher order, that is, the seraphim. For the higher the order, the fuller its knowledge. Or otherwise: “which it has received more fully as a gift” means more fully than other things, that is, than other gifts, because, as we have said, they receive their names from the gift in which they are more vigorous. Or “has received it more fully as a gift” means in office: for although the seraphim have greater knowledge than the cherubim, the cherubim have a greater share in the office, because they are readier to inspire knowledge than are the seraphim.

It is asked whether the orders of angels were so distinguished from the beginning of their creation; some say [Note: [Col. 0953D] *Magister*, § c.] that they were. For it is read: “Angels fell from each of the orders,” Lucifer being from the seraphim according to some. *Lucifer*, however, is the name of a spirit and not of an order, as some say.

But it should be known that the orders of angels were not so distinguished from the beginning of their creation. For if this were so, then from the beginning [Col. 0953B] some angels would have been seraphim, and thus burning in charity; likewise, some would have been cherubim, that is, knowing ones; some thrones, that is, so full of love of God that God would be said to sit in them; and so of the others. If this were so, they would not fall. But it is certain that it was not so.

Moreover, it is certain that before confirmation they possessed no virtues; rather, these were bestowed on them by grace at confirmation. Therefore it is clear that before confirmation they were not so distinguished by participation in gratuitous gifts. But angels are said to have been distinguished from the beginning of their creation in two ways: either by participation in [page 115] universal gifts—for some were subtler than others in essence, others in intelligence, and others in similar respects—or by their capacity to receive not natural [Col. 0953C] gifts but gratuitous gifts, subsequently bestowed upon them by grace. For some were more capable than others of receiving those gifts, and others less so.

[Note: [Col. 0953D] *Magister*, above, § g and the two following sections; see Gregory, Homily 24 on Luke, chapter 15.] It is next asked how the statement is to be understood that a tenth order of angels fell; because of this, human beings are even now said to give tithes, so that they may be placed in that tenth order of fallen angels. It seems, then, that there was a tenth order of angels and thus ten angelic orders.

The answer is that this is not to be understood in this manner. There were never ten orders, but only nine. But a tenth order is said to have fallen because as many angels fell as could constitute a tenth order. Yet if they had remained and not fallen, a tenth order would not have been made from them; nor is a tenth order made from human beings ascending into heaven. For it is certain that as many human beings will ascend into heaven as angels fell. But whether more human beings will ascend than angels fell, or than angels remained in heaven, is uncertain; for more angels remained than fell.

Gregory maintains [Note: [Col. 0954D] Homily 34 on the Gospels.] that more human beings will ascend than angels fell, saying: “That heavenly city, our mother Jerusalem, consists of human beings and angels; and it is agreed that as much of the human race will ascend to it as we believe angels remained there. Hence: ‘He set the number of peoples according to the number of angels’” (Deut. 32, according to the Septuagint).

Again, since the fall of angels is repaired from the number of human beings, it is asked whether, since someone rises in the place of each fallen angel, John—who was greatest among those born of women (Luke 7)—could obtain the place which Lucifer would have had, had he not fallen. If so, then since Lucifer was the most excellent of angels, John will be above all angels and all human beings. It is also asked whether Christ, in this restoration, occupies the place of another angel who fell; and if so, he would seem more likely to occupy the place which Lucifer would have held had he remained, than the place of another. Yet no one doubts that the flesh of Christ [Col. 0954B] and his soul possess preeminence above every creature that God could make. It is also asked whether every human being restored in an angel’s place rises in as great a perfection as that from which evil angels fell, or as great as they would have possessed if they had remained; otherwise the restoration does not appear complete. Since none of these matters has yet been certainly determined by inquiry, we pass them over in silence.

## CHAPTER VI. On the offices of angels and certain matters connected with the office

[Note: [Col. 0954D] Master, II, distinction 10.] It remains for us to discuss the office of angels. This was the final topic of the preceding chapters. The office of angels is to be sent. It is therefore asked whether all angels are sent, or not. Some [Col. 0954C] say that not all angels are sent, and they seek support for this in the authority of Daniel, who says: “Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him” (Dan. 7), as if to say: they were not sent when they stood before him.

Others say that all angels are sent, and support themselves by authority. Isaiah says: “One of the seraphim flew to me” (Isa. 6); and if one of the seraphim was sent, who belong to the highest order, then those of the lower orders are also sent. The prophet says: “He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire” (Ps. 103). Moreover, if the Son of God, who is Lord of angels, was sent, on what grounds are angels said not to be sent because of their dignity?

They resolve Daniel’s authority, “Thousands of thousands,” and so forth, thus: angels are said indeed to stand before the divine majesty because they are sent rarely; yet even when they are sent, they stand before God, because they find God everywhere. For God is everywhere. And when they are sent, they are called angels, although, as has been said, the name *angel* is appropriated to others [page 116].

If it is asked why these lower orders are called angels rather than the higher, since the latter, like the former, are sent, the answer is that, as has already been said, the higher are sent more rarely than the lower, whose imposed office is to be sent; or because they did not possess some proper characteristic from which they could be named. They appropriated to themselves what is common, just as those are called confessors who have no preeminence from which to be named, unlike apostles and martyrs, although this name is common to all saints; and other books besides the Law and Prophets are called *Hagiographa*, although this is a common name for all those books.

[Note: [Col. 0955D] § d of the same distinction.] These same writers also say that names of this sort—Gabriel, Raphael, Michael—are not proper names of angels but appellative names, and that angels receive them according to the different purposes for which they are sent. Thus, when an angel is sent to accomplish or announce some mighty deed, he is called Gabriel, which is interpreted “strength of God”; when sent to bestow God’s healing upon someone, he is called Raphael, which is interpreted “medicine of God”; when [Col. 0955B] sent through mercy, he is called Michael, which is interpreted “Who is like God?” Likewise, evil angels have many appellative names, such as devil, Satan, Leviathan, Behemoth, and the like.

[Note: [Col. 0955D] *Magister*, II, distinction 11.] There is another office of angels besides being sent: namely, guarding a human being. For two angels are assigned to every human being, one good and one evil [Note: [Col. 0955D] Thus here with his master Lombard, § A, but less satisfactorily.]: the good one for protection, the evil one for suggesting evil. But an objection is raised: this angel is assigned to guard this person, yet does not guard him so that he never sins; therefore he does not fulfill the office imposed upon him. Therefore he sins.

The answer is that the angel fulfills the office imposed upon him insofar as lies in himself, not insofar as it lies in the human being. For someone is said to fulfill an office in two ways: insofar as it lies in himself, or insofar as it lies in another. You see, for example, that it is a bishop’s office to preach. A bishop preaches daily to the people, yet cannot wholly draw every person away from sin. Certainly, he fulfills his office insofar as lies in himself. Likewise, it is a physician’s office to cure a sick person; he applies the medicine and treatment which he ought to apply, yet the sick person is not cured because he is either irascible or violates the physician’s instructions. Yet the physician fulfills his office insofar as lies in himself. Likewise, even when an orator omits none of the available means, he sometimes fails to persuade; yet [Col. 0955D] he fulfills his office insofar as lies in himself. The same is true of the angel. For the fault must be attributed to human frailty and not to the angel.
