Again, the angel either wishes or does not wish this human being to be saved. If he wishes this person to be saved but the person will not be saved, then he wishes something that will not occur; therefore he is not blessed. For blessed is he to whom all desired things happen. If he does not wish this person to be saved, how then does he guard him from sin? And how can it be understood that he is assigned to guard him if he does not wish him to be saved? In no way.

[Col. 0956A] **SOLUTION.** The will of the good angel is always in accord with the will of God; and when God wills that this person not be saved, the angel wills this too, while nevertheless fulfilling the office imposed upon him. [Note: [Col. 0956D] See notes on chapter 12 of Pullus, Part I (*Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXVI, col. 1017).]

Again, the evil angel drives this person toward evil, and the good angel cannot draw him back from evil. Therefore the evil angel is more powerful than the good. No. The good angel’s inability to draw him back from evil does not arise from the angel’s weakness; for it is certain that the good is more powerful than the evil. Rather, it arises from the corruption of the human being. The argument is fallacious. This excellent physician does not cure this sick person, though the very best medicine has been given to him. Another physician, who knows almost nothing, cures him. Therefore the latter is more skilled than the former.

Moreover, it is asked whether a person existing in charity [Col. 0956B] merits more by those works which he performs of himself, without an angel’s admonition. For he seems to merit more in those things which he does of himself. To this it must be said that, in works done in charity, one must always consider the intention and the affection. For those works which are done from a better intention and a greater affection of charity are better, and by them one merits more. But that a person should do certain things without an angel’s admonition is certain; for God alone knows the counsels of hearts, nor can an angel know them except through outward signs, any more than can an evil angel.

Again, an angel rejoices over a person who repents for a time and afterwards becomes evil. Whatever goods the angel had previously in himself, he has now to the same extent, and in addition this joy; and he can be more blessed than he is. Therefore by that joy he becomes more blessed than before. [Col. 0956C] Likewise, he will become less blessed when that joy is taken from him, once the person begins to act evilly. Yet they say that this joy will be eternal, because even when that person sins, it will please the angel that he once acted well. Or, better, it should be said that in place of the joy which is removed he will have another joy in God’s justice—namely, because that man was blinded so as to sin. But it is asked whether Peter’s reward is similarly increased by human progress, because he has many joys over persons newly converted by his example which he did not previously have. Yet Peter does not merit as the angel does, because what is a reward to Peter is merit to the angel. [Note: [Col. 0956D] Here the author’s disposition must be excused, as in many other places.]

Again, it is asked whether it lies in a human being that an angel’s [Col. 0956D] reward should increase. This seems so, because the more good a person does, the more the angel rejoices; and that increase of joy is an increase of reward or merit in the angel. Therefore a person causes the angel to advance in reward and merit—which may be granted in the case of [lacuna].

Again, does an angel advance when those subject to him advance through his good, invisible admonition? This seems so, because the salvation of disciples assists holy teachers, just as one reads in the commentary on Isaiah that, conversely, as an evil angel deserves a greater punishment through wicked suggestion, so [Col. 0957A] the reward of the good angel and the punishment of the evil one increase daily. By the same reasoning Paul’s reward is increased, because many are converted to the faith through his teaching; and Arius’s punishment is increased, because many are deceived through his heresy. Yet it is said that after death there is no place for meriting; but, as was said above, the case is different for angels who are on the way and for holy souls who are in their homeland.

Again, an evil angel is assigned by God to this person in order to suggest evils to him; therefore God wills that he suggest evils to him; therefore that he make him sin, and thus that he sin. Again, in the Book of Kings the Lord is read to have said: “Who will deceive Ahab for me?” “I will deceive him,” says the evil angel, “who will be a liar in the mouth of his prophets.” And the Lord said: “Go forth and do so.” Therefore the Lord commands him [Col. 0957B] to deceive the king, and thus to make him sin. Again, he commanded him to do something—namely, to deceive or to do something else—not to do something else; therefore, to deceive. Again, he commanded him to do something, and the devil could do nothing in which he did not sin; and God knew this. Therefore he commanded him to sin. Again, the devil performed that deception either with God as author or with himself as author. If with God as author, then he did not sin; if with himself as author, then not by God’s command. Or God commanded him to perform it by his own authority—that is, the devil’s—and thus to sin.

Again, it does not seem that he did this with himself as author; for one reads on that passage of Isaiah: “Will the axe boast against him who cuts with it?” (Isa. 10). [Note: [Col. 0957D] In the Gloss.] “Just as these lifeless things are instruments which do nothing of themselves, [Col. 0957C] but act through the one who moves them, so Sennacherib acted not of himself but by God’s power. The work which Nebuchadnezzar did in overthrowing Tyre was rewarded, because Egypt was given to him, according to the saying: ‘Because you served me at Tyre, I will give you Egypt.’” Therefore he did not sin by doing that deed, because no sin is rewarded with a good, whether temporal or eternal. Unless perhaps someone says to the contrary that the Gospel states, “They have already received their reward” (Matt. 6), concerning those who pray in the streets—and they too sin. Likewise, a man gives to the needy what he acquired wickedly, and by that very fact sins because he gives another’s property; yet God rewards that deed temporally.

[Col. 0957D] To this it must be said that God commanded that deception insofar as it was punishment, not insofar as it was fault; or he commanded him to afflict Ahab, which he could have done so as to fulfill the Lord’s command. Yet he did not do it for that reason, but rather in order to rejoice in Ahab’s punishment; and so the Lord did not command him to sin, though he nevertheless sinned. “Go forth” was said ironically: “You shall do what will be to your own harm”; it was not a command. So the Lord says to Judas: “What you are doing, do quickly” (John 13). Note that God rewards no sin; but he is said to have rewarded Nebuchadnezzar because God permitted him to do this deed [Col. 0958A] and afterwards gave him those things. God was the author of the punishment which Ahab suffered when he was deceived; that punishment may be called a deception. But he was not the author of the deception by which the evil angel deceived him, for that was fault in the devil—unless one says that he was its author insofar as it was punishment.

[Note: [Col. 0957D] The Master above, § c.] Again, it is asked whether the same angel is assigned to different human beings. This seems to be so. There are more evil persons than good ones: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 20). But there are as many good persons as good angels. Understand that this universality includes all human beings who have been, will be, are, have ceased to be, or will begin to be. Therefore there are more evil persons than good angels; this is certain. Therefore there are more evil persons [Col. 0958B] than evil angels. Therefore not every evil person has an evil angel proper to himself, and thus an evil angel is assigned to several persons. This may be granted.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Works of the Six Days

[Note: [Col. 0958D] Master, II, dist. 12.] There are two rational creatures, namely the angelic and the human. The angelic has been discussed; now the human must be discussed: first, what man was like when made; then what he became through sin, where we shall also speak of sin and the kinds of sins. But since certain points concerning the distinction of the works of the six days seem doubtful and suited to discussion, let us touch on them in a brief treatment.

Scriptural authority has it that he who lives forever [Col. 0958C] “created all things at once” (Ecclus. 18). This is to be understood thus: he created the nature [matter] or likeness of all things in that confused structure of the elements—nature with respect to bodies, likeness with respect to souls. But an objection is raised: God did not create that structure from eternity; therefore he began to create it when he created it. Therefore there was change in God. To this it must be said that God is said to make something in one way, a human being in another. When a person makes something, he has a certain movement in willing and a passion in laboring. But God is said to make something when, according to his eternal will, something new appears to us; there is no movement in God, no passion, no labor. When God begins to make something, the beginning is not to be referred to God [Col. 0958D] but rather to the thing which begins to exist. Thus a ray of sunlight was as hot yesterday as it is today, yet today it warms this person more than yesterday; this is not due to the sunbeam, but to the recipient or to some other causes. For the sunbeam is always of the same heat. Likewise, a medicine cures someone which previously could not cure him, yet it is not now sharper or better than it had been before. Hence it is clear that this does not arise from the medicine but from the condition of the recipient.

Again, an objection is raised: before that cosmic structure was created, there was darkness; that darkness was something or some things. [Col. 0959A] Therefore something or some things existed before the creation of that structure. Again, God knew from eternity that he exists; from eternity it was true that God exists, and thus this was true from eternity, therefore before the creation of that structure. Therefore that structure was not the matter of that world, since this is not true of those things whose likeness God created, though not [their] matter. Such are souls, which he creates daily from nothing, though from the beginning he created them in likeness. Again, truth is from God. Therefore it is from God either by generation, as the Son is; by spiration, as the Holy Spirit is; or by creation, as creatures are. For whatever is from God is from God in one of these three ways. Again, that structure was created somewhere, namely in a certain void; that void was the place in which [Col. 0959B] that structure was created; therefore it existed before that structure.

[Note: [Col. 0959D] Master here, § d, or 4.] To the first point stated, we say that the term “darkness” sometimes posits something and sometimes does not. For it sometimes denotes the obscuring of air, and then the term posits something; at other times it denotes the absence of light, and then it does not posit something. It must therefore be said that before the creation of the structure there was darkness, that is, absence of light; and there was neither anything nor any things. As for their assertion, “Are truths from eternity, or eternal?” our teachers say that this belongs more to dialecticians than to theologians. They are from eternity, yet they are not eternal. For they distinguish between being from eternity and being eternal. That is from eternity which does not begin to be; eternal is that to which [Col. 0959C] all things are present. Hence God alone is eternal. We also say that that void was not a place, nor was it anything, just as darkness was not.

Again, God creates an existing thing; therefore, [it is] something that is, and it itself is not God; therefore he creates a thing that [variant: is not] created. If he creates a non-existing thing, then he is Creator of an existing thing; but “Creator” is said relatively to a creature; therefore a non-existing thing is God’s creature. Accordingly, some say that “to create” is not said relatively to a creature in the manner of “Creator,” and therefore, although he creates a non-existing thing, he is not thereby Creator of a non-existing thing. Just as someone generates a son who does not yet exist, yet he is not the father of one who does not yet exist.

But an objection is also raised against this. It is fitting for God to create some thing before he himself is [Col. 0959D] its Creator; therefore, since he was Creator at the first instant as soon as it existed, it was fitting for him to create the first instant before it existed; therefore he created time before all time; therefore he created time from eternity. Accordingly, it is truer to say that God creates only an existing thing, because to create is, by divine power, to make something begin newly to exist from nothing. Thus God creates a thing which is created, if the expression “created” is taken in force of a noun, without connotation of time; but if it is a participle and denotes past time, it is false.

## CHAPTER VIII. What the First Human Being Was Like in Body before Sin

[Col. 0960A]

[Note: [Col. 0959D] II, dist. 19.] Having dealt briefly with the distinction of the works of the six days, let us pursue the two points announced above: namely, what the first human being was like when made; secondly, what he became afterwards through sin. There sin and the kinds of sins will also be treated. But since a human being has two parts, body and soul, let us first show what he was like in body and then in soul.

One must know, therefore, that the first human being was made mortal and immortal—that is, able to die and able not to die. In the first state he could die and could not die. In the second, namely after sin, he could die and could not not die. In the third, that is, in the homeland, he will not be able to die and will be able not to die. For then his body will be glorified and spiritual, that is, not needing nourishment from food; but before sin his body was animal and needed food. Hence one reads in Genesis (ch. 2): “Man was made into a living soul,” that is, into a body which the spirit sustains through nourishment from food.

[Note: [Col. 0960D] Master, II, dist. 20, § g.] But an objection is raised: if Adam had never sinned, he would never have died; but if he had never eaten, he would never have died; therefore he could never eat and never die; therefore he could never eat and always live, and thus could always live without nourishment [Col. 0960C] from food. Again, if he had not sinned, he would have suffered no punishment; and if no punishment, no hunger. Therefore, if he had not sinned, he would have suffered no hunger. But without hunger it would have been superfluous to eat; therefore, if he had not sinned, he would always have lived; therefore he could always have lived and not eaten.

To the first, it must be said that the premise is false: if he had never eaten, he would never have sinned. Indeed, if he had not eaten, he would have sinned; nor could he fail to eat and fail to sin. [Note: [Col. 0960D] Master, II, dist. 19, § 2, or letter b.] For the Lord had given him two commands, one affirmative and one prohibitive: one by which he might know what he was to do, and one by which he might know from what he was to abstain. The Lord commanded him to eat from every tree in paradise—this is the affirmative command; [Col. 0960D] but he also commanded him not to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil—this is the prohibitive command. Therefore, since God had commanded him to eat from all the other trees, he would sin if he did not eat; and he would sin if he ate from the forbidden tree. Thus, by failing to observe either command, he would sin. The falsehood of this proposition is therefore clear: “If he had never eaten, he would never have sinned.”

We resolve the second argument similarly by examining this proposition: “Without hunger it would be superfluous to eat.” For he ought not to wait for hunger, provided only that he had the appetite for eating. [Col. 0961A] [Note: [Col. 0961D] Master, II, dist. 20, § g, as above.] Hunger is an immoderate appetite for eating; and such an appetite, if immoderate, is punishment; otherwise it is not punishment. For it could have been in Adam before sin, and Adam was not permitted to fast beyond the appointed time or to eat before it.

Again, it was Adam’s sin to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. But this would not have been a sin unless it had been forbidden. Therefore something was done whereby it was a sin for him. That thing, then, was done by God or by man—but not by man, for he had not then done anything that would be sin for him. Therefore it was done by God that it should be such for him. Thus God is the author or cause of sin. Again, after the prohibition it was unlawful for Adam to eat from the tree [Col. 0961B] of the knowledge of good and evil, yet it had not always been unlawful for him. Therefore someone made it unlawful. Therefore either God or man, but not man. Therefore God made it unlawful for him. Hence, since it was unlawful, a human being would sin if he ate. Therefore God made it such that a human being would sin if he ate; but the human being sinned because he ate. Therefore God made it such that the human being sinned because he ate; consequently, he is author and cause of sin. Again, it is good and pleasing to God that sin be unlawful; but for sin to be unlawful is for it to be sin. Therefore it is good and pleasing to God that sin be sin; consequently God is the cause of sin.

The response to the first argument is by denying and by disambiguating. It is denied thus: Before his fall, it was a sin for an angel to make himself equal to God; but this would not have been sin for him unless the angel himself or God existed. Therefore something was done whereby this would be sin for him. If “whereby” denotes an efficient or sufficient cause, this is false. But if it denotes a condition without which, or an occasion, it is true. The same is the solution in the second argument. The third is distinguished thus: God made it so that sin is unlawful, that is, not lawful—if you mean that he removes permission, this is true. But if you mean, “so that sin is unlawful,” that is, sin, it is false.

Again, it was Adam’s sin to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil as soon as it was forbidden. Therefore it was a sin through some author or through none. That sin cannot be without any author. Therefore it was sin for him with God as author or with man as author; but not with man as author; therefore with God as author. Accordingly distinguish the first statement [Col. 0961D] thus: “It was Adam’s sin to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil”—that is, it would be sin if he ate—is true. “It was sin”—that is, there was something which was then actually sin—is false. Thus, “It is good for me to take medicine” means that it would be good if I took it. But there is not something that is good, because I do not take it.

[Note: [Col. 0961D] 7. § II, dist. 19.] When it has been said that he was made mortal, that is, able to die, and immortal, that is, able not to die, it is asked whether he possessed this immortality by the endowment of nature or by the benefit of grace. It seems that he possessed it by the benefit of grace. For God gave him this grace: that he should eat from the tree of life and thus always be immortal, that is, able not to die. Augustine seems to mean this when he says: [Note: [Col. 0961D] Book VI, *On Genesis*, ch. 25.] “In a certain manner man was made immortal by the benefit of grace, [Col. 0962A] not by the endowment of nature.” He said “in a certain manner” to indicate that this was not true immortality, such as the immortality of God or of the soul by natural endowment; nor can it be said that he was immortal in that sense. For then he would naturally live forever; moreover, he would have had to lack an animal spirit. Therefore he was immortal—that is, able not to die—by grace, that is, because he was granted the eating of the tree of life.

The tree of life [Col. 0962B] [Note: [Col. 0961D] Augustine, book VIII *On Genesis*, ch. 5.] was a certain tree in God’s paradise, so called from its effect: if anyone ate its fruit, God would strengthen his limbs with perpetual soundness and stable health, so that neither an invading illness nor the weakness of age might bring him to decline or into a worse condition. But the tree of the knowledge of good and evil was not so named from its effect, as though it made one who tasted it know good and evil; rather, it was named from the event which followed afterwards. For through experience Adam learned how great a good he had lost and into how great an evil he had fallen.

[Note: [Col. 0962D] Master here, § 3, or letter c.] But supposing that God had not commanded him to eat from any tree, it is asked whether he could always live without eating from any tree. For if he could always live without eating from a tree, then his ability not to die [Col. 0962C] did not come to him from the tree. But if he could not always live without eating from a tree, then it came to him from the tree. There are two opinions on this point. Some say that he could not always live without eating from the tree, and that his ability not to die came to him from the tree. Thus he was called immortal because he could always eat from the tree, and by eating it would never die. Others say that two things brought about his immortality: the condition of nature and the benefit of grace, namely the eating of the tree. They explain Augustine’s authority cited above [Note: [Col. 0962D] Augustine is read above as follows: “The first human being was created immortal; this was granted to him from the tree of life, not from the constitution of nature.”]: “In a certain manner man was made immortal by the benefit of grace, not by the condition of nature,” by adding only the word “not.” But because many similar arguments are usually introduced here, let us set them out.

[Col. 0962D] Adam had the power of dying, by which he could both die and not die, because it lay within his choice what he should do. But he chose the worse course, namely not always to live, because he sinned. I ask, therefore: since he had that power from nature, from whom did he have it for this use, namely dying; and from whom did he have the use of not dying? For he could not have from nature a power for two contrary uses, just as it is impossible for me to be moved by the same movement of will toward running and toward not running at the same time. And if he had from nature the power for the use of always [Col. 0963A] living, then he would always live. Again, if he had from the same source the power for the use of never dying, then he would never die, because nothing natural was taken from him through sin, although something may be obscured. Again, if he had from nature the power for those two uses, what would the tree of life confer upon him, unless it conferred that he could not die, just as the tree of knowledge conferred that he could not not die—the former by the merit of fulfilling the command, the latter by transgressing the prohibited command?

But if he had this use—the use of always living [Note: [Col. 0963D] Understand: of always living.]—by observing the command, and the other use, that of not always living, by transgression, then, since he was commanded to eat from the tree of life and commanded not to eat from the tree of knowledge, just as transgression of the latter command entirely [Col. 0963B] destroyed in him the power for the use of not dying, because he could not not die and was necessarily consigned to death, so, if he had observed the command to eat from the tree of life, the power for the use of dying would have been absorbed and destroyed in him, because he could not die. Thus from that eating he would have acquired inability to die—especially since it had the efficacy of strengthening the limbs with perpetual soundness, so that after taking this tree a person could not decline into a worse state.

On this account he did not eat from that tree before sinning, because afterwards he could neither become corrupt nor sin, and thus could not eat from the tree of knowledge either. For if it is said that by taking the tree of life several times he would earn the necessity of not dying, rather than by taking it only once, why, conversely, did he not by eating several times from the tree of knowledge earn the necessity of dying, rather than becoming corrupt by taking it only once? Indeed, [Col. 0963C] one may ask how often he would have had to take from the tree of life in order to become unable to die. For there cannot be so large a number of occasions of taking it that, after those occasions, even if Adam had lived until today, he might not take from the tree of knowledge and thus become a transgressor.

Again, if it is said that by nature he had power for neither of those uses, but for one from the tree of life, if he ate it, and for the other from the tree of knowledge, if he ate it, then just as by taking from the tree of life once he would not become unable to die, since he could afterwards take [Col. 0963D] from the tree of knowledge, so by taking from the tree of knowledge once he ought not to have become unable not to die, but could take from the tree of life and become unable to die.

Again, if fulfilling this command, “Eat from the tree of life” (Gen. 2), preserved for him the power of not dying, so that so long as he ate he did not die, and did not eliminate the power of dying, then by analogy transgression of this command, “Do not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil” (*ibid.*), would not preserve his power of dying, yet would not destroy his power of not dying. Thus, after the forbidden eating, he could eat from the tree of life and become unable to die, just as after he had eaten from the tree of life [Col. 0964A] he could also eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil and thus transgress the command.

Again, since two commands were given him, affirmative and prohibitive, if he had observed the former with as much charity as he transgressed the latter with pride, as great a reward would have been owed him through observance of the former as the punishment through transgression of the latter—or else God is more ready to punish than to reward. But by transgressing the latter he earned the necessity of dying; therefore by observing the former he earned the necessity of not dying.

But if it is said that he had from the tree of life, and not from himself or his nature, the power for the use of not dying, while he had from himself the power for the use of dying, then he was not given natural endowments by which he could stand and fall equally. Indeed, he was more inclined to fall than to stand, because in himself he had that by which he would die, but not that by which he would not die.

To this it must be said that Adam had in himself and from himself the power for the use of dying; likewise, from himself he had the power for the use of not dying, though not for both uses together. Thus a man can marry this woman and also that other woman who is her sister, but cannot lawfully marry both women. And it is in my power to run throughout the whole of tomorrow, and to run during no part of tomorrow; yet I cannot do these two things at once.

Still, it may be said that Adam had power for either of these uses, dying or not dying, not merely for the use of dying nor merely for the use of not dying. And from neither of those [Col. 0964B] trees did he have power for the use of dying or not dying. But from the keeping of these commands—“You shall eat from the tree of life; you shall not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil”—he had the power for this use, namely never dying.

For two commands had been given him: “You shall eat from the tree of life.” He observed this, because he ate from it. Another command was given him: “You shall always abstain from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil”; and he had not yet completed the observance of this command. It is as if I were told, “Be good once”: if I have been good once, I have observed that command. But if I am commanded, “Be always good,” I have not observed it unless I am good throughout all the days of my life; nor can it ever truly be said of me [Col. 0964C] that I have observed that command until I have ended my life.

Thus, so long as he observed those two commands—although he had already observed one of them, because he had eaten from the tree of life—he would never die. Yet transgression of one of them was enough for him to die. For it is easier to destroy than to construct. Thus, to show that a definition is predicated of something, it is not enough to show that one of the elements set down in the definition is predicated of it; every one must be predicated of the same thing. But if we wish to show that the definition is not predicated of it, it suffices to show that one of the elements set down in the definition [Col. 0964D] is not predicated of it. Likewise, if we wish to show that a conjunction is true, it is not enough to show that one part of it is true; both must be true. But if we wish to show that it is false, it is enough to show that one part is false.

But someone will ask whether a limit was set to the observance of those commands, and when that limit was completed. For if he always had to guard against transgressing the command, and could therefore always transgress it, even if he always took from the tree of life, why would it be called the tree of life? For without taking it, if he remained in the divine commands, he could live forever. Thus he did not have from that tree the power of always living, nor was inability [Col. 0965B] ever to die conferred upon him by it. Why, then, was it called the tree of life? Just as this command, “Do not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil,” was not called a command of life, because neither could avail for this purpose without the other: even if he had taken from the tree of life innumerable times, he would never have been so strengthened that he could not afterwards take from the tree of knowledge of good and evil and thus sin.

To this it must be said that it is called the tree of life because by prolonged eating from it it brought about the result that a human being was confirmed in the power of not dying and afterwards could never die. For he would be transferred to such a state if he observed those two commands. Yet it is unknown to us how long he would have remained in that first state, and when he would have been transferred to that second state in which, once placed, he could not thereafter [Col. 0965C] take from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, and thus could not sin. He would have this from frequent eating of the tree of life, if he observed the other command not to take from the tree of knowledge.

Some say that a single taking of that tree was sufficient for this, namely that he should be confirmed so that he could not die; and consequently Adam never ate from the tree of life. For if he had eaten, he would have been so strengthened that he could not afterwards sin. They attempt to prove this because the Lord expelled him from paradise [Note: [Col. 0965D] Irenaeus, book II, *Against Heresies*: “[He expelled him from paradise and removed him far from the tree of life, not begrudging him the tree of life, but pitying him, lest he remain forever a transgressor and evil become immortal and without end for him.]” See Hilary, *Commentary on Psalm* 68; Gregory Nazianzen, *Oration* II, on Easter; Jerome [Col. 0966D] on Isaiah 65, etc.] lest he take from the tree of life after sinning. If he took from it, he would become unable to die; and God would then seem to act cruelly toward him, since he would live forever in misery. Therefore God acted mercifully toward him [Col. 0965D] when he prevented him from taking the tree of life, lest, living forever, he should remain forever in misery.

But Augustine says the contrary: [Note: [Col. 0966D] Book II, *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, ch. 21, at the beginning, though somewhat differently; likewise book XIII, *City of God*, ch. 20.] “Certainly the first parents are rightly understood to have abstained from the forbidden food before the evil persuasion, while using the trees permitted to them.” Yet this does not prove the point, because it was said indefinitely, whereas many other trees had been permitted. It is nevertheless asked whether the tree of life now has the effect which it had then; and if Adam had lived until now and ate from the tree of knowledge, whether persons born before then would be punished, as those who were to be born from him would be. We do not believe so.

It is also customary to ask whether Adam could then have been killed, and thus die, although no fault had preceded in him. This seems possible. For he could have been held shut up in prison, so that he had nothing to eat. We say that he would suffer no affliction unless he sinned, nor could anyone inflict anything upon him. [Note: [Col. 0966D] Master, II, dist. 20, §§ d, e, f. See Augustine, book I, *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, ch. 37.]

But since, by the condition of the maternal womb, it would have been necessary for the first parents to bear little children before sin, would their infants, immediately upon birth, have had perfection of bodily size, as young adults now have, and immediately exercise the functions of their limbs, such as feet and hands? Or would they not immediately have had full bodily size, but only the use of the limbs, as the young of certain brute animals now do, because they immediately run and see? Or would they have had neither bodily size nor use of limbs, but gradually arrive at a great age by growing, as happens now? This, I say, need not greatly concern us, since it is neither confirmed nor determined by the authority of the saints.

## CHAPTER IX. What He Was Like in Soul before Sin

[Note: [Col. 0966D] Master, II, dist. 16.] We must now say what the human being was like in soul. He was made in the image and likeness of God (Gen. 1): in the image [Col. 0966C] with respect to natural goods, namely reason, memory, and understanding; in the likeness with respect to gratuitous goods. But did he then possess gratuitous goods? Then he possessed virtues; therefore he could then merit. But this is disproved, because if he merits, he merits by free choice; but free choice pertains not to the present or the past, but only to the future.

Accordingly, it must now be said: “with respect to gratuitous goods,” that is, with respect to the capacity for receiving gratuitous goods—he was made fit to receive virtues, though he did not possess them immediately. Thus Josiah begot Jechoniah at the Babylonian deportation (Matt. 1), yet he did not immediately migrate; and the human being was placed in paradise (Gen. 2) to work and guard it, yet he did not work or guard it. Or it may be put thus: “with respect to gratuitous goods,” that is, with respect to that state of innocence in which he was made. Or otherwise: “in the image,” that is, in the knowledge of truth; “in the likeness,” that is, in the love of truth. Again, otherwise: “in the image,” with respect to form; “in the likeness,” with respect to essence, by which, just as God is simple and incorruptible, so is the soul—and this is with respect to essence. [Col. 0967A] [Note: [Col. 0967D] The Master is read here, § d, as follows: “Image pertains to form; likeness to nature.”] Likeness is with respect to form, because, just as God remembers, discerns, and loves, so these natural capacities are found in the soul; and these are called the soul’s form, because it is informed by such properties, and one soul more so than another.

[Note: [Col. 0967D] Master here, § 4, cited, and § e.] It should be noted that just as not only the painting which is on a panel is called the painting or image of something, but also the panel itself, so not only the soul is called the image of God, but also the human being. Again, one must know that the soul or human being both is the image of God and is made in the image of God. Christ, however, is the image of God the Father, but is not made in the image of God the Father. For the preposition indicates a certain inequality and inferiority of that which is an image in relation to that of which it is the image. Hence it is not customary to say that [Col. 0967B] the Son, although he is the image of God the Father, is made in the image of God the Father insofar as he is God. But the soul or human being both is the image of God and is made in the image of God. For it is certain that the human being is less than God.

But it is asked how a human being is like God through gratuitous gifts, when those gifts are not in God. Is a human being like God through that which is not in God? Again, a human being is like the Father through these things; therefore God the Father and the human being are alike in these things—or therefore the Father is like the human being in them. To this it must be said that a human being is said to be like God through gratuitous gifts, not because gratuitous gifts are in God insofar as he is God, but because the terms which, when predicated of a human being, signify gratuitous gifts are truly said of God and in him signify the essence, [Col. 0967C] as when God is called just, strong, powerful, and the like. For two things are called similar either because they partake in corresponding properties—which similarity is not found here—or because something occurs with respect to one which is like what occurs with respect to the other. In this way the kingdom of heaven is said to be like a mustard seed (Matt. XIII), or a ship to a city, as Boethius says. In this way the soul is said to be like God: not because it shares similar properties, but because, as God understands, remembers, and so forth, so too does the soul. And although the soul is like the Father through memory, the Son through understanding, and the Holy Spirit through love, it is not like the Father in one respect and the Son and Holy Spirit in another; for that appropriation is made by name, not by reality. Thus, although the Father is offended by the sin of weakness, the Son by the sin of [Col. 0967D] ignorance, and the Spirit by malice, nevertheless the Father is not offended otherwise than the Son or the Holy Spirit. For that appropriation is made by name and not by reality, as was said above.

Again, the term *image* there signifies the divine essence; therefore the divine essence is called the image of the Trinity. Again, if the term *image* signifies the divine essence when it is said, “Man was made in the image of God,” then God is the image of man, and therefore equal to him or inferior to him. Or thus: there it signifies the essence; therefore it is not there said relatively—which [Col. 0968A] seems to follow because it is placed with a genitive. For where it signifies the essence, it stands by itself. But if there it signifies a created thing, namely a property of the soul, then man was made in the image of the soul.

To this it must be said that there it signifies the divine essence, and the divine essence is the image according to which man was made. For *image* is said both of an exemplar and of a copy, though more properly of a copy; and the name *God* in that combination of words signifies the divine essence. The genitive must be resolved into a nominative: “in the image of God,” that is, “which is God,” so that it is an intransitive construction. And although the term *image* in one sense is said of the Son—namely, relatively—in which sense it is not said of the Father, it is not said that man was made in the image of the Son alone, insofar as *image* is taken there. [Col. 0968B] For there is an image of creation, namely natural goods; of re-creation, namely spiritual goods; and of likeness, namely the whole Trinity; and it is taken in this last sense in the authority cited above.

Again, Augustine says:

> “The soul is made like God because God made it immortal and indissoluble.”

[Note: [Col. 0968D] In *On the Greatness of the Soul*, book 2, ch. 2.]

But because it was made such by God, it is God’s creature; and because it is a creature, it is a substance other than God; and because it is another substance than God, it is unlike him. Therefore, because it was made immortal and indissoluble, it was made like God, and thus through the same thing it is both like and unlike. Therefore this statement must be distinguished: “Through the same thing it is like and unlike God.” If this means that through the same thing it is a thing which is similar in one respect and dissimilar in another, it is true; but if it means that being similar and being dissimilar to God are the same for it, it is false.

[Note: [Col. 0968D] Master, II, distinction 23, § C and following.]

It must again be known that the human soul had a threefold knowledge: it had knowledge of heavenly things, earthly things, and itself. It did not have complete knowledge of heavenly things or of itself; therefore it was imperfect in knowledge. Again, if Adam did not know something in that state, then ignorance was in him; therefore there was punishment, and therefore he was punished before he sinned. But those who thus object concerning ignorance seem not to know that ignorance denotes fault and implies an obligation. For one is said to be ignorant of that which one does not know although one ought to know it. But Adam then was not bound to know anything which he did not know, and therefore he was not ignorant.

[Note: [Col. 0968D] Master, above, § 7.]

But it is asked whether Adam foresaw his own fall. That he did is shown thus. Adam had faith; [Col. 0968D] therefore he believed that Christ would be born and die for the redemption of the human race; therefore he knew that the human race would fall. But it would fall through no human being other than himself; therefore he knew that the human race would fall through himself. But he knew that this could not happen unless he sinned; therefore he knew that he would sin, and therefore fall.

To this it must be said that he did not know that the human race would fall through himself, although he knew that it would fall; nor did he know through whom it would fall. But it is asked whether he could believe that the human race would fall in [Col. 0969A] another person, while nevertheless it would fall in him. If this were possible, then in that state he could believe to be true what was false, or conversely; and so he could have error—which is a punishment—before he sinned. But if he could not believe this concerning anyone except himself, and believed it concerning himself or another, then he believed it concerning himself. For if he believed it concerning another, he would have error.

To this it must be said that he could not know that it would fall in anyone other than himself or in one in whom it could fall; nevertheless, he did not believe that it would fall in himself. It is indeed true that he knew it would fall in himself or in another. And if he knew that it could not fall in another, it would necessarily follow that he knew it would fall in himself; but he did not know [Col. 0969B] that intermediate proposition. Just as someone knows that the stars are even or odd, and perhaps the stars cannot be odd, yet the person does not know this; it nevertheless does not follow that he knows the stars to be even. So Adam did not know that he could not believe the human race would fall in another. If he knew this, it would necessarily follow that he knew it would fall in himself.

Again, God could condemn him while he was such—that is, neither deserving of life nor deserving of death—as seems capable of proof from a passage contained in the commentary on the Epistles: “God could make one neither worthy of life nor worthy of death; if he condemned such a one, who would say, ‘Why do you do this?’” To this it must be said that he could condemn such a one, that is, not save him; but he could not condemn him, that is, lead or cast him into hell, [Col. 0969C] because he would act against mercy, since he is a ruler slow to punish and swift to grant rewards.

[Note: [Col. 0969D] Master, II, distinction 24, § C.]

Again, Adam was in such a state that he could stand; therefore one in which he could turn aside from evil, and thus resist temptation, and thus merit; therefore he had virtues. To this it must be said that to turn aside from evil is to refrain from doing evil. He who avoids guilt does not always merit the palm, according to the saying:

> “I did not commit theft; you will not feed ravens on the cross.”

Therefore Adam did not merit by turning aside from evil, because nothing impelled him toward evil: neither interior nor exterior temptation. But if someone had impelled him [Col. 0969D] toward evil, and he had not yielded but resisted out of charity, this would then have been meritorious for him.

For there were two states of man before sin. One was that in which he did not have grace by which he could make progress, but only stand; the other was that [in which] he had grace by which he could make progress, namely when he fell. Hence Augustine says:

> “Man had the ability by which he could will, but he did not have the will by which he could exercise that ability; if he had had it, he would not have sinned.”

[Note: [Col. 0969D] In *On Rebuke and Grace*, ch. 11, at the end. Thus [Col. 0970D] in Augustine: “He had received the ability if he willed, but he did not have the will by which he could exercise it; for if he had had it, he would have persevered.”]

But someone will say: at that time he had the intention that, if anyone impelled him to evil, he would not do it; therefore he merited by that good intention, just as one merits by fulfilling this commandment, “You shall not kill” [Col. 0970A] (Exod. XX), because one intends not to kill if impelled to do so. Again, Adam was then an adult, possessed discernment between good and evil, and used it rightly; therefore he was worthy of life or death, and thus had merited life or death. But it is evident that he could not merit life without virtues.

Again, only those things which merit life merit death also, and conversely. Adam was in a state in which he could merit death; therefore in that state he could merit life, and thus he had virtues. Again, no good goes unrewarded and no evil unpunished. That natural love by which Adam loved God was good, and he used it well; therefore its use was good, and thus, since no good goes unrewarded, that love merited something, whether temporal [Col. 0970B] or eternal. And there is no reason why it should merit temporal rather than eternal reward; thus he had virtues, since no one merits eternal things without virtues.

To this it must be said that the authority, “no good goes unrewarded and no evil unpunished,” must be referred to goods done on the way. But Adam then was neither on the way nor in the homeland. For what it would mean if he were on the way or in the homeland, you heard elsewhere. The other arguments just stated have a parallel case in the angels, who first possessed natural goods alone and afterwards gratuitous gifts.

Again, Adam then knew that God was to be established as the beginning and end of every action. For this knowledge did not afterward increase in him when charity was given to him. He also knew that he ought to establish God as the end and beginning of all his action, [Col. 0970C] and attribute to him all his goods; therefore he was bound to render him *latria*, worship; therefore he was bound to love him with charity.

Again, charity is love of God for his own sake and of one’s neighbor for God’s sake. Adam then loved God for God’s sake; therefore he then had charity. Again, Adam then loved God more than himself and himself as a neighbor; yet in such a way that God held first place, himself second, his neighbor third, and his own flesh fourth; and he did all this for God’s sake. For if he did it ultimately not for God’s sake but for another end, because he established as his end something [which] was not referred to the final end, then he sinned mortally by turning away from the due end. For he did not do this without establishing some end. But if he did all [Col. 0970D] this for God’s sake, then he had ordered charity.

Again, the least movement of charity surpasses any movement, however great, of natural love. But Adam, before the infusion of virtues, loved God by natural movement alone; after the virtues had been given, while not yet in the way, he loved God by the same natural love and in addition by a movement of charity; therefore he loved God far more strongly after the virtues had been given than before. Again, he then had far more gifts from God than before, both natural and gratuitous gifts, whereas previously he had natural gifts only; therefore God loved him more then than before, and thus Adam loved God more—or else he was a transgressor, for one who is loved more is [Col. 0971A] more bound to love.

To this it must be said that not every movement of charity exceeds every movement of natural love in quantity, but in dignity. For it can be that someone loves God less than another loves his own son by natural love alone. And it is true that Adam was more bound to love after gratuitous gifts were given—that is, to give love in return for more things. Nevertheless, *to love* is said equivocally of natural love and of charity. Thus the comparison does not hold. One may say that Adam was then bound to render *latria* to God, but not thereby to love with charity, just as is said also of the angels.

Again, after Adam’s sin the tinder of sin was inflicted upon him, which he did not have before. Therefore he was more bound to love God before sin than afterward. Again, at that time [Col. 0971B] he is said to have been present at the court of angels and to have prophesied concerning the Flood and many other matters, but not afterward. Therefore he was more bound.

The contrary seems to be the case: namely, that he was more bound after sin. For after what he had previously lost was restored to him, confession and punishment for sin were given him, both of which are goods. Therefore he possessed more goods after sin than before. Further, the work of re-creation is greater than that of creation. Therefore after re-creation he was more bound to love God than before creation.

Some say that he was more bound to love God before sin, because he possessed more goods before than afterward. For they were not restored to him in their entirety. If it is objected that repentance restores what has been taken away, this is true either in actuality or in hope. And perhaps before sin, [Col. 0971C] before gratuitous gifts were given, he was more bound to love God than Paul was afterward—if a comparison between natural love and charity is appropriate—because of the natural goods bestowed upon him, which were such as were afterward bestowed on no one. Paul, however, was bound to possess charity, whereas Adam was not in such a state.

But it is asked: since it could happen that Adam then died—perhaps this might have occurred if Eve killed him, though it is doubtful whether it could happen, because in that case there would have been punishment before guilt—would Adam have had eternal life? It seems that he would have neither outcome according to merits [Note: [Col. 0971D] That is, neither be saved nor damned.], unless it is said that God would by grace give him eternal life. But we more truly believe that at that time he could neither die nor suffer any affliction.

Again, it is impossible for anyone without mortal sin [Col. 0971D] before charity to be damned or saved. Therefore, if Adam had then died, he would neither have been damned nor saved, because he did not possess merit of life or death. But it may be said that he would have been saved by grace.

## CHAPTER X. What Is the Cause of Sin?

[Note: [Col. 0971D] Master, II, distinction 24, § D.]

It is asked what that grace was by which Adam could stand but could not make progress before sin. To this it must be said that this first grace was most acute free choice in man and a certain sensory faculty that was wholly upright and not crooked. Here it would be necessary to say [Col. 0972A] what free choice is, what the sensory faculty is, and also concerning gratuitous and natural goods, except that we shall later speak of how man fell, was stripped of gratuitous gifts, and wounded in natural gifts; in that place we shall discuss these matters. Therefore, lest we seem there to be doing over what has already been done, we shall reserve these matters until that point.

Here, then, we treat of Adam’s sin. [Note: [Col. 0971D] Master, II, distinction 34, § 1 and following.] And, in order to begin from a higher level, sin in general must be treated in the following manner: first, by investigating what is the cause of sin; second, in what thing sin exists; third, what sin is; fourth, the modes and distinctions of sins, so that we may thus proceed to Adam’s sin. But it would be superfluous to discuss the envy which the devil had toward man, how he suggested that he should sin, and similar matters, because these too are [Col. 0972B] commonly very well known.

It must therefore be known that there is a twofold cause of sin or evil: namely, a good, such as a human being or angel; and also an evil, that is, an evil will. That good is a cause and origin of evil is shown both by reason and authority. By reason, thus: evil was not from eternity; therefore it began to exist through some author. That which was the author of evil was either good or evil; but it was not evil—for here we speak of the first evil. Therefore that which was the author of evil was good. Therefore evil had its origin from good.

Again, indirectly: no evil had a beginning from good; every evil had a beginning; therefore none was the first of evils. But if it is said that not every evil had a beginning, then some evil had no [Col. 0972C] beginning; and thus there was some principle of darkness from eternity, as Manichaeus falsely taught. It must therefore be conceded that every evil had a beginning from good. Boethius also demonstrates this clearly and evidently in his *Arithmetic*, where he teaches how inequality is reduced to equality and takes its beginning from it.

Augustine also affirms this, saying:

> “I say that an evil will preceded evil; for it had its origin from good: first from an angel, and afterward from a human being. Evil is also a cause of evil, because an evil will is a cause of evil. In the first sin there was only one cause that was good, namely the angel; in all the following evils there was a twofold cause: the human being, which is good, and the evil will, which is evil.”

[Note: [Col. 0971D] See Augustine, book II, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, ch. 28, [Col. 0972D] and *Enchiridion*, ch. 14, near the end.]

Hence Augustine says:

> “The cause of evil things is the deficient will of a mutable good turning away from the immutable good: first that of an angel, and afterward that of a human being.”

[Note: [Col. 0972D] *Enchiridion to Laurentius*, ch. 23.]

## CHAPTER XI. In What Thing Sin Exists

[Note: [Col. 0972D] Master, above, § D.]

We must now say in what thing evil exists. It exists only in a good, as is shown thus: evil is nothing other than corruption of good; corruption of good exists only in nature; and nature is nothing but good. Therefore evil exists only in good. Again, evil exists only in that which is deprived of some good; but nothing is deprived of a good in which some good does not remain, [Col. 0973A] and there is no thing in which there is some good that is not good. Therefore evil exists only in good.

But if the proposition “nothing is deprived of a good in which some good does not remain” is denied, it may be proved thus: if something is deprived of some good in which being does not remain—for being is good—then something is deprived of every good. Therefore something is supremely evil, which is false. For Augustine says:

> “A thing, however evil it can become, cannot become supremely evil,”

that is, wholly lacking every good.

[Note: [Col. 0973D] *Enchiridion*, ch. 13.]

That evil exists only in good Augustine plainly states in these words:

> “Nothing is called evil unless something is good. For evil cannot exist where there is no good at all.”

[Note: [Col. 0973D] Ibid.]

Evil is in good; therefore good is evil; therefore contraries are predicated of the same thing. For the prophet says: “Woe to those who call good evil!” (Isa. V.) [Col. 0973B]

Therefore, to the first objection concerning contraries, Augustine says that “the rule of dialecticians is observed in all contraries except these.” [Note: [Col. 0973D] *Enchiridion*, ch. 14.] Or it may be said that the names *good* and *evil* denote substance in the neuter gender, but form in the masculine and feminine. Therefore, when both are put in the neuter, or both in the masculine or feminine, they cannot be predicated of one another. For a thing which is good is not evil, and one who is good is not bad. But when one is put in the neuter and the other in the feminine or masculine, one is predicated of the other, as: “A thing which is good is evil,” and conversely. Thus it is conceded that good is evil, with one term retained adjectivally.

[Note: [Col. 0973D] Master, above, § G.]

As for what the prophet says, “Woe to those who call good evil,” it must be said that he directs such great abhorrence against those who call the work of God—such as nature itself, or a human being, or any [Col. 0973C] creature, insofar as it is God’s work and thus good—evil; and against those who call vice, insofar as it is vice, good. For every work of God, insofar as it is God’s work, is good; and every vice, insofar as it is vice, is evil.

## CHAPTER XII. Whether Sin Is Something; and, If It Is Something, Whether It Is a Nature or a Vice of Nature

[Note: [Col. 0973D] Master, II, distinction 35.]

Having shown from where sin has its origin and in [Col. 0973D] what thing it exists, we must say what sin is. “Sin is every word, deed, or desire contrary to the law of God.” Again: “Sin is the will to retain or obtain what justice forbids.” These are the two definitions according to Augustine.

[Note: [Col. 0974D] Book I, book XXII *Against Faustus*, ch. 27; book III, *On the Two Souls*, ch. 11; and book I of the *Retractions*, 15, before the middle.]

Ambrose, however, defines sin thus:

> Sin is “a transgression of the divine law and disobedience to the heavenly commandments.”

[Note: [Col. 0974D] Ambrose, *On Paradise*, book IV, ch. 8.]

According to the first authority, sin is word, deed, or desire; according to another, sin [Col. 0974A] is a will; according to the third, sin is transgression of the law. Therefore there are differing opinions regarding the essence of sin.

[Note: [Col. 0974D] Master, § 2.]

Some say that sin is an act, and that act, insofar as it is an act, is good and comes from God; but it is sin on account of its depraved and distorted end. And insofar as it is sin, it is nothing and does not come from God, because the act is deformed through a depraved and distorted end. Some say that sin is only internal. Others say that both an interior movement and an exterior movement are sin, and that sin is something, because not everything insofar as it exists is good or comes from God, since something comes from the devil or from human beings. Let us first pursue the first opinion, proving it and afterward refuting it.

That sin is nothing is proved as follows. Whatever [Col. 0974B] exists is either a work of God or the work of a human being imitating God; for Augustine says this. If sin is not God’s work, then it is the work of a human being imitating God—which is false, because a work is called that of a human being imitating God when, by means of it, the human being does not depart from God; but through sin the human being departs from God. Therefore sin is not the work of a human being imitating God.

Again, evil is the corruption of good, but the corruption of good is nothing. Therefore evil is nothing. And although the corruption of good is sin, nevertheless not every corruption of a good is sin. For there is one highest good, by which all things are good, whose essence is its goodness. Therefore it cannot begin or cease to be, nor can it advance in good or fall away from [Col. 0974C] good. There is also another good, namely the creature. It does not possess within itself all goods, nor does every good come from it—for it would thereby be equal to the highest good—but it shares in some goods and lacks others, and can advance in good and fall away from good, because it can have what it does not have and can fail to have what it has.

Now creature is twofold, bodily and spiritual; and good likewise is twofold, one with respect to bodily creature and one with respect to spiritual creature. Again, the good of bodily creature is twofold: one is in it, the other outside it. In it is the proper functioning of the five senses; outside it is the ordering of natural things. For it is a great good for a human being that other things are so ordered—heaven and earth, brute animals, trees, [Col. 0974D] and the like. Likewise, the good of spiritual creature is twofold: knowledge of truth and love of truth.

Therefore the corruption of each of these goods is evil; but not the corruption of each of them is sin or guilt. For we distinguish three goods: one in the body, another in the soul, and a third outside body and soul. Corruption of the good in the soul is both guilt and punishment; corruption of the good in the body is punishment and not guilt, though it proceeds from guilt; corruption of the good that is [Col. 0975A] outside body and soul is neither guilt nor punishment, but is referred to punishment.

As was said, the good in the soul is twofold: knowledge of truth and love of it. Corruption of knowledge is ignorance; corruption of love is concupiscence. Therefore, the more these corruptions increase in the soul, the more the soul is corrupted—not because the soul itself is corrupted in its essence, for it is incorruptible, but because its goods are corrupted. Evil is also called punishment as well as guilt. Hence: “There is no evil in the city which God does not do,” that is, punishment (Amos III).

From the foregoing it is therefore clear that evil exists only in good and that sin, insofar as it is an act, is good. Augustine also testifies elsewhere [Col. 0975B] as follows:

> “God alone is the author of good; therefore he is not the author of evil. Yet he is the author of all things that are; and, insofar as they are, they are good.”

[Note: [Col. 0975D] *Eighty-Three Questions*, question 21.]

Thus, according to them, sin, since it exists, is good insofar as it exists. Again, there is no evil thing which is not good in some respect; but sin is an evil thing. Therefore it is good in some respect, and thus sin, insofar as it exists, is good.

The first proposition may be proved thus. There is no evil thing which is not evil by participation in evil; every thing that is evil by participation in evil is good in some respect. Therefore there is no evil thing which is not good in some respect. If anyone doubts the first premise, it can be proved indirectly. [Col. 0975C] For if some thing is evil, that thing is not something good, nor is there anything good in it. Therefore that thing is wholly evil. Therefore it possesses the fullness of all wickedness, just as the highest good possesses in itself the fullness of all goodness. Therefore it is the highest evil, and thus something can be made equal to the highest good, or analogous to it by contrariety—which cannot be.

[Note: [Col. 0975D] Master, above, § 2.]

Again, just as whatever is good is good by participation in the highest good, so whatever is evil is evil by participation in the highest evil. But adultery is evil; therefore adultery is evil by participation in the highest evil, and therefore is not wholly evil. Thus it has some good in itself, and is good in some respect. But if adultery is the highest evil, then by the same reasoning homicide is the highest evil, since homicide is something other than adultery. Therefore there are two highest evils. This is now disproved: since nothing belongs to the one which does not belong to the other, and this one participates in no evils in which the other does not participate, therefore this is that one.

Again, just as the highest good can admit no evil, so the highest evil can admit no good. But being and not-being are contraries, and being is good in the highest good; therefore, if being were in the highest evil, it would be evil there. Therefore not-being would be good in it. But the highest evil can admit no good; therefore it cannot admit not-being. [Col. 0976A] Therefore not-being cannot belong to it. Therefore it cannot cease to be. By the same reasoning it cannot begin to be. Therefore it always was. Therefore there were two principles: the highest evil and the highest good, the principle of light and the principle of darkness.

Again, nothing that belongs to the highest good belongs to the highest evil. But being belongs to the highest good; therefore being does not belong to the highest evil. Or thus: nothing that belongs to the highest good belongs to the highest evil; but being belongs to both the highest good and the highest evil. Therefore *being* is said in one sense of the highest evil and in another sense of the highest good.

Again, evil is something, and it was not always something. Therefore it began to be something. Therefore it was through some author: either God, human being, or devil. [Col. 0976B] But not through God, because God is not the author of evil. Therefore through a human being or devil. But this was either through creation or through making. Not through creation, because neither human being nor devil can create anything—that is, make it from nothing. Therefore it was through making. But if so, some matter preceded, from which evil was made. That matter was either good or evil. If it was good, then evil was good in some respect, at least in respect of matter. But if that matter was evil, then that evil came from some matter which was evil, and so on to infinity.

They show more subtly and clearly that sin is nothing insofar as it is evil in this way. There is a certain highest good above every [Col. 0976C] sense and every nature. It is the one and principal cause of all natures and all things, from which, by a descent through intermediate forms marking distinct and non-unified forms, all lower things proceed. For there are no lower things of which there is no unity. For example, from God, who is that highest good, all natures descend ineffably: human nature, asinine nature, and so on.

The philosophers called that highest good by the coined name *being* [Note: [Col. 0976D] Perhaps “essence” or the first BEING.], because that alone is truly and properly called being, and all things draw their essence from it. Hence *being* is said of every thing, because it bestows essence upon each thing. For the name *essence* denotes unity, not difference. All things agree in it and descend from it in a wonderful way, just as in an acorn [Col. 0976D] all the parts of a tree—branches and leaves—are present implicitly in an ineffable manner, and are ineffably unfolded through the working of the first nature. Thus all natures are in that highest good and descend from it. Yet the likeness is not complete, because they are in the acorn as in a material cause, but in God as in an efficient cause.

Nevertheless, this must not be overlooked: no term properly applies to God, for he is not properly called the cause of all things, or anything else that might seem more properly said. For he is not properly a thing, because he is above every thing. Yet he is frequently called [Col. 0977A] the efficient cause; his wisdom, the formal cause; and his goodness, the final cause. But I do not recall ever reading that he is called the material cause. Hence the preceding likeness is not complete.

Moses called that same good by this designation when he said: “He who is sent me to you,” that is, God (Exod. III). From that good some things descend in such a way that they are said to exist in themselves, as substances; others in such a way that they do not exist in themselves but in a subject, as accidents. Some of these are such as make a thing qualified, as qualities; others make it quantified, as quantities; and so on according to the tenfold distinction of the categories. Therefore, in this division that descends from the highest good according to the distinction of categories, [Col. 0977B] you can find all natures, and only natures; all are from God and are good. There you will find act in the category of action, and will in the category of quality. Therefore every act and every will is good.

Nor should it be overlooked that pride, lust, and the like are not names of qualities or natures, as are faith, hope, and charity, from which arise movements of believing, hoping, and loving. For evil movements do not have underlying qualities from which they arise, as good movements have the virtues underlying them. But if terms of this kind—pride, lust, and so forth—were names of qualities, what they signify would be natures, because they would be qualities. [Col. 0977C] But it is certain that pride and the like are not good; therefore they are not qualities.

Furthermore, in the catalogue of creatures [Note: [Col. 0977D] In the song of the three youths, Daniel III.] in which all natures are invited to praise God, pride, lust, and the like are not found. Hence it is clear that they are not natures. Again, if the highest evil is entirely distinct from the highest good, it has its own distinction and division, namely of the things that descend from it, just as the highest good has its own division of the things that descend from it. Therefore the things placed in the division of the highest good cannot be mixed with those placed in the division of the highest evil. For if things belonging to the division of the highest good are not mixed with one another—for substance is not equality or any of the others—then much [Col. 0977D] less could things placed in wholly distinct divisions be mixed with one another. But all acts are placed among the things that descend from the highest good. Therefore they are not placed among the things that descend from the highest evil. Therefore every act is good and not evil.

Again, if something descending from the highest evil is placed among those descending from the highest good, or conversely, something has its origin in the highest good which has its origin in the highest evil—which is impossible. Again, the highest evil is wholly distinct from the highest good. Therefore it signifies a form distinct from the highest good. Therefore the highest evil is fittingly designated by the negative of the name which [Col. 0978A] applies to the highest good. But the name *being* properly applies to the highest good alone. Therefore the name *non-being* applies to the highest evil. Therefore the highest evil is non-being. Therefore it is not.

Augustine also proves in another way that the highest evil is nothing. The highest evil has no measure, because its cause lacks measure; but every thing has measure. Therefore the highest evil is nothing. For it is contained under no species, and the whole name of evil is found to derive from privation of species.

From the foregoing the consequent absurdities are evident if anyone says that some thing is evil not by participation in evil, but is wholly evil. But if it is said that no thing is evil unless it is evil by participation in evil, it follows that sin is [Col. 0978B] good in some respect, at least insofar as it exists and insofar as it is a nature, as follows. No existing thing is evil unless it is evil by participation in evil; but no thing is evil by participation in evil unless it is evil through the corruption of some good which was in it. Therefore no existing thing is evil unless it is evil through the corruption of some good which was in it. Therefore no existing thing is evil insofar as it has been some good; but there was no good in any existing thing in which there is not some good. Therefore, since sin is an existing thing according to them, there is some good in it. Therefore it is good in some respect, and thus, insofar as it exists, it is good:

[Col. 0978C] [Note: [Col. 0978D] Master above, § II.] But those of us who admit this are met with the objection: “Homicide is an act; but every act is from God; therefore God is the author of homicide.” To this it must be said that terms of this kind are intended to be understood reduplicatively, as follows: adultery insofar as it is adultery, and likewise homicide insofar as it is homicide. Thus, when it is said, “Homicide is from God,” it is understood as “insofar as it is homicide”; and that is false. Similarly, when it is said, “An idol is a body, and every body is natural; therefore an idol is natural,” this does not follow, because “idol” is understood reduplicatively. The names of vices, however, signify two things: namely, an act and the deformity, or corruption, of an act which is good. But the corruption by which the act itself is deformed is vice, and it is not a thing.

[Col. 0978D] But an objection is raised: Every sin is an act. Therefore it is a nature. Therefore it is good. But not believing in God is a sin. Therefore it is an act. Therefore it is some good. Yet expressions of this kind—“not going to church,” “not believing”—seem rather to remove than to posit. Therefore some say that such expressions posit something: “not believing” posits contempt for believing, and that contempt is sin; likewise, “not going to church” posits contempt for going to church. Thus, turning away from evil—for example, not killing this man—is good, because “not killing this man” posits the good purpose of not killing him, even if one is provoked by him.

[Col. 0979A] [Note: [Col. 0979D] Master, § I, or 9.] Others, more correctly and more subtly, distinguish among sin (*peccatum*), vice (*vitium*), and offence or falling-away (*delictum*). Sin, or a committed sin, is an act, whether external or internal; and insofar as it is an act, it exists and is good. An offence makes us depart from true being, that is, from God. Hence it is called *delictum*, as though *derelictum* (“abandoned”), because an offence occurs when we abandon what we ought to do, and thus abandon and forsake God. Hence it is defined as: “The abandonment, through a perverse will, of a good which either was present or ought in future to have been present.” Vice also is the deformity and corruption of an act; it is nothing, but stains, corrupts, and deforms an act which is good in itself. Thus neither vice nor offence is anything.

Nevertheless, they differ. Vice makes us tend toward non-being; [Col. 0979B] therefore it does more than an offence. For the latter makes us depart from God; the former makes us not merely depart, but also tend toward non-being. Hence it is thus defined: [Note: [Col. 0979D] From Augustine, *Eighty-Three Questions*, q. 3; but the Master wrongly writes here, § F, “will.”] “Vice is of the will, by which a human being is made worse, and which is far removed from the will of God.” Here the difference between vice and sin is clearly suggested. For while the will itself—that is, the natural motion of a power—is sin, that motion is not properly called vice, but rather the corruption of that motion. Therefore Augustine did not say in the aforesaid definition, “Vice is will,” but “of the will,” because it deforms the will; and that vice is in no respect anything. Sin, on the other hand, is an act; but it is called sin according to its corruption (which is properly called vice). [Col. 0979C] For in that corruption an action which is good in itself deviates from God. Thus the evident difference among vice, sin, and offence is clear. Yet sometimes one term is used indifferently for another. Accordingly, expressions such as “not going to church” and “not praying” denote offences. Hence they only remove and posit nothing.

But an objection is raised against this: Contraries are things placed under the same genus which differ most from one another; but virtue and vice are contraries. Therefore, being placed under the same genus, they differ most from one another; therefore they are placed under the same genus. But they are under no genus except quality. Therefore they are under quality. Therefore vice is a quality, and thus the motions of vices are qualities . . . . . . from which they arise, just as are the motions of virtues—which we denied above. To this one may reply [Col. 0979D] that the motion of virtue and the motion of vice are contraries and fall under the same genus, namely action; and for this reason virtue and vice are said to be contraries. Or one may say that virtue and vice are opposed as contraries, yet are not contraries—just as these people love one another as friends, yet are not friends.

[Note: [Col. 0979D] Master here, § 10.] Again, sin is the corruption of a good, as was said above; but an act is sin. Therefore an act is the corruption of a good. Again, sin insofar as it is [Col. 0980A] sin is either the corruption of a good, or, insofar as it is sin, it is not the corruption of a good. If it is said that sin, insofar as it is sin, is the corruption of a good, then insofar as it is sin it is punishment. But every punishment is from God. Therefore sin, insofar as it is sin, is from God; and consequently, insofar as it is sin, it is good. But if it is said that sin, insofar as it is sin, is not the corruption of a good, then apart from being sin it is nothing that is not a nature. Therefore sin, insofar as it is a nature, is the corruption of a good; and thus, insofar as it is good, it corrupts good.

To this it must be said that the term “corruption” is taken both actively and passively, like other verbal nouns of this form. Taken passively, corruption [Col. 0980B] is a certain suffering of the soul which it undergoes because it is stripped of gratuitous gifts and wounded in its natural powers. Such corruption is a punishment inflicted by God, which a human being immediately endures as soon as he begins to sin. Its cause is sin committed by the human being, and that punishment is not guilt. “Corruption” is also said actively, in the sense in which sin is called corruption because it corrupts the goods of the soul insofar as it is sin, not insofar as it is a nature. Thus, since sin insofar as it is sin is nothing, and corrupts insofar as it is sin, it corrupts insofar as it is nothing.
