As Augustine teaches: [Note: [Col. 0979D] Thus in the Master, § L, from *On the Nature of the Good*. [Col. 0980D] “Abstaining from food is not a substance; yet the substance of the body, if food is wholly abstained from, languishes and is weakened.”] “To abstain from food is not anything; yet if one abstains from food, a human being’s substance perishes.” Concerning the first sin committed after baptism, it is easy to see [Col. 0980C] that it corrupts: for it strips a person of gratuitous gifts and wounds him in his natural powers. But this is less easy to see regarding subsequent sins. For what does a later sin find in a person to corrupt, when by the first sin the gratuitous gifts have been entirely removed and the natural powers corrupted? It may be said that those subsequent sins increasingly remove the capacity for receiving gratuitous gifts, because the natural goods are increasingly corrupted through habitual sinning. For the more a person sins, the farther he removes himself from the highest good, and thus the more difficult he is to heal. It is as if a person began to be ill with one disease and later another supervened: the second disease did not deprive him of health, since the first had already deprived him of it; nevertheless, [Col. 0980D] it is said to have deprived him of health, because the more diseases burden him, or the longer he is afflicted by some disease, the more his capacity for receiving health is destroyed and the farther he is removed from health.

[Note: [Col. 0980D] Master, II, dist. 36.] 134 Although corruption is active rather than passive, it is nonetheless asked whether sin is punishment. This is shown by many authorities. Gregory says: [Note: [Col. 0980D] Homily 11 on Ezekiel.] “Sin which is not washed away by repentance is either sin and the cause of sin, or sin and the punishment of sin, or at once [Col. 0981A] the cause and punishment of sin.” The Apostle also calls them—that is, sins—“passions”: “Therefore God gave them up to dishonourable passions,” etc. (Rom. 1). John says, “It is just that he who is filthy should become filthier still” (Rev. 22); Hosea says, “Blood has touched blood” (Hos. 4); and elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0981D] Augustine, book V *Against Julian*, ch. 3, according to the Master; but I do not find it in Augustine in my copy at that place.] it is said: “Crimes are judged by crimes.” That certain sins are punishments is clearly shown. For [Note: [Col. 0981D] Augustine, *Eighty-Three Questions*, q. 77, beginning.] “Every desire is a disturbance, and every disturbance is a passion; therefore every desire is a passion.”

Since both reasons and authorities establish that certain sins are punishments, one does not idly ask whether they are punishments insofar as they are sins. For desire, insofar as it is desire, is sin; the same desire, insofar as it is desire, is punishment. Therefore desire insofar as [Col. 0981B] it is sin is punishment, or conversely. They challenge this argument thus: Fire, insofar as it is fire, shines, and insofar as it is fire, burns. Therefore fire, insofar as it shines, burns, or conversely. Again: “Every desire, insofar as it is desire, is suffered by us (*ea patimur*), or suffered by us (*eam patimur*); every passion, insofar as we suffer it (*ea patimur*), or suffer it (*eam patimur*), is not sin,” because Augustine teaches this. [Note: [Col. 0981D] The same work, q. 77.] Therefore every desire, insofar as it is desire, is not sin. This is a fallacy. Fire, insofar as it is fire, burns; insofar as it burns, it does not illuminate. Therefore fire, insofar as it is fire, does not illuminate. Again, every desire, insofar as it is desire, is a passion; and every passion, insofar as we suffer it, is punishment. Therefore every desire insofar as [Col. 0981C] it is desire is punishment. Every punishment, insofar as it is punishment, is just and is called a penalty, as Augustine teaches: [Note: [Col. 0982D] Book III, *On Free Choice*, ch. 18: “Every punishment, if it is the punishment of sin, is just and is called a penalty.”] therefore every desire is just and is from God—which is plainly false.

Therefore you must carefully observe three meanings of the word *poena* (“punishment”). For if the force of names and words is unknown, it is necessary that nothing of what is investigated here be understood. Sin is called punishment because it is the cause of the punishment which is in the soul, namely, that it is not from God. In this respect sin, insofar as it is sin, is punishment—that is, the cause of punishment. But insofar as it is a nature or is from God, it is never punishment—that is, the cause of punishment—because by it a human being is punished. Hence Augustine, on the sixth psalm, says: [Note: [Col. 0982D] Rather, on the seventh, at the verse, “He made his arrows burning,” but with some words altered.] “God turns sins into punishment, [Col. 0981D] so that what had been delights to a person while committing them may become instruments for God while punishing.”

Just as the fire of Gehenna is called a punishment that is the instrument of punishment by which a human being is punished, and the cross is the punishment of a thief because the thief is punished by it, so sin is punishment—that is, an instrument by which a human being is punished—because unless sin existed, a person would never be punished by it in such a way that grace was withdrawn from him. Sin is also called punishment passively, that is, the punishment of a preceding sin. Every sin, therefore, which a human being commits after another sin [Col. 0982A] can in this sense essentially be called a punishment, which God inflicts in consequence of the preceding sin. Insofar as it is punishment, it is nothing but good and is from God; and it can be called a passion which we suffer, rather than one by which we suffer. Hence the Apostle calls such things “dishonourable passions” insofar as they are punishments inflicted by God.

Once these points have been settled, the solution of the foregoing objection is easy to see. Every desire, insofar as it is desire, is punishment—that is, a cause of punishment; or punishment—that is, an instrument by which a human being is punished. But insofar as it is desire, it is not punishment inflicted by God for sin. For then, insofar as it is desire, it would be from God—which nevertheless seems capable of proof as follows: Every desire, insofar as it is desire, [Col. 0982B] is a vicious motion of the soul. Therefore, insofar as it is desire, it is a motion of the soul. Therefore, insofar as it is desire, it is from God, because every motion of the soul, insofar as it is a motion of the soul, is from God and is good.

Accordingly, it must be known that to every nature that is sin there belong, as it were, three classes of terms. Some signify nothing but nature and imply no vice; some imply vice alone and no nature; and some imply both nature and vice. For example, the term “adultery” signifies a nature together with vice. For it is the same as saying “an act deformed by such a vice.” The term “action,” or the term “motion,” both of which apply to adultery, [Col. 0982C] conveys nothing but nature. The term “vice,” “vicious,” or the expression “to be from the devil” conveys nothing that is nature, but only vice.

When, therefore, it is said, “Homicide insofar as it is homicide is an act,” some hold that, through the reduplication which is in the subject, all terms of this kind signifying a composite of nature and vice retain, in the predicate, the signification of vice while laying aside the signification of nature. Thus it is the same as saying, “Homicide insofar as it is vice is an act,” which is plainly false. Yet it seems truer that the term “homicide” always retains both significations, of nature and of vice, so that “homicide” means the same as “an act deformed by such a vice.” Therefore, just as we accept, “Homicide insofar as it is a vicious act is an act,” so also, “Homicide insofar as it is homicide is an act”; and insofar as it is an act it is from God, yet homicide insofar as it is homicide is not from God, because being from God and being homicide are altogether incompatible.

Just as Socrates, by virtue of being a white man, is a man, and by virtue of being a man is something, yet not by virtue of being a white man is something, so it must be granted that homicide [Col. 0983A] insofar as it is homicide is from the devil, and insofar as it is from the devil is not an act; yet homicide insofar as it is homicide is not thereby not an act, as is evident in the foregoing examples, namely the burning and illumination of fire.

It should nevertheless be noted that in all the foregoing there is the fallacy called “making several questions into one”: concealed in one third term, and less concealed in two. When it is said, “Homicide, insofar as it is a vicious act, is from God or from the devil,” no simple answer seems appropriate, but a double answer because of the two questions: insofar as it is an act, it is from God; insofar as it is vicious, it is from a human being or from the devil. Likewise, when the question is proposed more covertly in the one third term, “homicide insofar as it is homicide.” For homicide signifies not merely *what* something is, nor merely *what sort* it is, but “a what-sort-of-thing,” like “a white man” and the like. [Col. 0983B]

Again, it is asked, since sin, as stated above, is called punishment, that is, the instrument by which a human being is punished, whether it is called the instrument by which we are punished insofar as it is sin or insofar as it is nature. For if God punishes a human being by homicide insofar as it is a nature, and withdraws spiritual goods from him, then it does not seem imputable to the person that God punishes him by withdrawing grace, using homicide as the instrument of punishment insofar as homicide is a nature and not insofar as it is vice. For a human being is not the author of homicide insofar as it is a nature, but insofar as it is vice.

Again, if a human being is thus punished by God for fornication through the first punishment—namely, the withdrawal of grace, which he feels immediately upon committing fornication—so that he falls into homicide, which is a graver sin, and because of that greater sin a greater penalty is due to him than for the first, because it is greater than the first: then the human being is punished more for sin than he deserved to be punished. Again, through the sin of fornication a person merits being punished by homicide; and through homicide he merits a greater punishment than that due for fornication. Therefore, through fornication he merits a greater punishment than is due for fornication.

Again, God punishes a human being by sin itself as an instrument, not insofar as it is sin, but insofar as it is nature. Therefore, [Col. 0983D] even if it were not sin, a person could be punished through that action which is sin by this punishment, if gratuitous goods were withdrawn from him—which is false. For although eternal fire is a penalty more grievous than a human being can endure, it is nevertheless not the cause of the withdrawal of gratuitous gifts, although God punishes us by this penalty as an instrument.

Some rightly say that sin, insofar as it is an instrument by which a human being is punished, is from the human being or devil, who is the author of sin insofar as it is sin; and that it is as an instrument that either the human being or the devil uses it to punish him by this penalty, namely, separation from God. Sin is not an instrument by which a human being is thus punished insofar as it is good, or from God, or nature, but insofar as it is sin—that is, it is nothing. For no nature, insofar as it is nature, [Col. 0984A] deprives anyone of a gratuitous good; consequently sin too, insofar as it is nature, is not the cause why a human being is deprived of a gratuitous good.

Therefore God is said to punish us by it as by an instrument because he permits us to be punished by it as by an instrument. Yet it is not an instrument for God, but for the human being, because sin itself is the reason why, as soon as we sin, God punishes us by withdrawing grace. Thus it is clear how sin is punishment, or the cause of punishment; and how in another way it is called punishment, namely, an instrument by which we punish ourselves or which the devil employs to punish us—that is, to bring about our separation from God. In neither of these senses is sin, insofar as it is punishment, said to be from God. Indeed, in both senses it is punishment insofar as it is sin; for unless it were sin, it would not be the cause of the withdrawal of grace [Col. 0984B] which God effects in us, nor would it be the instrument by which we could punish ourselves so as to be separated from God. For no nature, insofar as it is nature, separates us from God through unlikeness to him.

If, however, someone says that sin is an instrument of God punishing, not of a human being or devil, as we had above on Augustine’s authority, I see no inconsistency that follows.

Again, since homicide, apart from being sin, is nothing but an action, and since homicide in one respect is punishment inflicted by God insofar as punishment is said passively, but insofar as it is punishment it is a passion, therefore homicide insofar as it is an action is a passion. Again, homicide is a punishment inflicted by God; therefore someone can refrain from using it. To this it must be understood [Col. 0984C] that “passion” is said equivocally, both of that which I suffer and of that by which I suffer. Thus the action by which someone acts and the passion by which someone is acted upon are opposed genera. Yet the passion by which someone suffers is not contrary to the action by which he acts. For digging is an action by which this person acts, and yet it is a passion by which we suffer—just as fire was the passion by which Lawrence suffered. For the passion by which he suffered was a certain property in his soul.

Again, since every action which is sin is, insofar as it is sin, authored by the devil, and insofar as it is action authored by God; and since whatever belongs to that action insofar as it is authored by the devil belongs to it according to every other respect in which it is authored by the devil, it seems likewise that whatever belongs to that action as authored by God [Col. 0984D] belongs to it according to every respect in which it belongs to it as authored by God. Thus, since homicide insofar as it is sin is evil, and insofar as it is evil is authored by the devil, all predicates belonging to it as authored by the devil can be converted; similarly, it seems that all predicates belonging to homicide as authored by God can be converted. Thus homicide insofar as it is good is an action; insofar as it is an action it is punishment; and insofar as it is a passion inflicted by God, it is punishment and action. For all these belong to it as authored by God.

This, however, is not necessary. For sin, insofar as it is sin, is nothing; and consequently whatever belongs to it insofar as it is sin can be converted, because such properties do not differ through properties [Col. 0985A] making that action exist in different modes. For such [Note: [Col. 0985D] One or two words are missing.] . . . . . . is only from him from whom something exists, that is, from God. Thus, since sin, insofar as it is sin, is nothing and is thus authored by the devil, no diverse properties belong to it as authored by the devil whose diversity prevents that conversion of properties. Such conversion cannot occur in the action of sin insofar as it is action; for insofar as it is action, it is from God. Nothing prevents one thing from having from God several natural properties which, although they proceed from the same principle, are not mutually convertible in that action.

For homicide, insofar as it is an action, is not punishment, although neither of these belongs to it from God. Just as this man is grammarian and musician, and both belong to him from God: yet insofar as he is a grammarian he is not a musician, nor conversely. Although all those natures descend from one principle through diverse intermediaries, they all belong according to the intermediaries through which they descend from that principle. Thus homicide, insofar as it is action, is nature; insofar as it is nature, it is good; insofar as it is good, it is from God. Likewise homicide, insofar as it is punishment inflicted upon a human being for sin, is passion; insofar as it is passion, it is good; insofar as it is good, it is from God. Yet homicide insofar as it is action is not punishment inflicted by God, nor conversely. [Col. 0985B]

But someone will say: if homicide were not sin, committing homicide would not be punishment for a human being. [Col. 0985C] Therefore homicide does not seem to be punishment by reason of anything from God, or anything good, but rather by reason of its being sin, or of the devil’s authorship. For if homicide were punishment in a human being even though it were not sin, in what would a person suffer by committing homicide, if he did not offend God in it because it was not sin? Gratuitous goods would not then be withdrawn—which is the greatest present-life punishment for sin—nor would he be punished by any other punishment for it if it were not displeasing to God; and this would be true if it were not sin.

To this it must be understood that committing adultery would be punishment for a human being even if adultery were not sin, and even if the person were not deprived of a gratuitous gift through it. For there would be bodily defilement, and a desire full of anxiety because perhaps he could not obtain what he desired, [Col. 0985D] along with many other penalties.

Again, after the homicide which he first committed, this person commits fornication; and fornication makes him more prone to sin and worse than he was before. Therefore he sins more by committing fornication than he previously did by killing—which is false. Although he is now more prone to sin after committing fornication than he was previously after committing homicide alone, this is not because fornication is a greater sin than homicide, but because these two sins together are greater than one. Just as a person who is now burdened with a small load placed upon him in addition to [Col. 0986A] another large load is more burdened than before, not because of this load alone, but because of both together.

Again, an act corrupts insofar as it is sin; but it is sin insofar as it is corrupted. Therefore an act corrupts insofar as it is corrupted—which we grant. Just as medicine corrupts insofar as it is corrupted: for although medicine is itself good, if we corrupt it by adding poison, it corrupts the person to whom it is given, and thus corrupts insofar as it is corrupted.

Thus far we have pursued the first opinion concerning the essence of sin and confirmed it by its authorities and reasons. Let us now proceed to the second and third opinions. But because whatever can be objected to one can be objected to the other, let us treat those two under one discussion. The second opinion is that only the interior act is sin. The third opinion is that the exterior act is sin. Both groups, then, say that sin insofar as it is sin is something; likewise, insofar as it is an act it is something; but it is in no way good—indeed, it is evil only.

But an objection is raised from what is read in John: “Without him nothing was made” (John 1), that is, sin. Therefore sin is nothing. They reply that sin is called nothing because it makes us depart from true being and tend toward non-being. Again, since sin is nothing authored by God, but only by a human being or the devil, and sin is brought from non-being into being, therefore, through the authorship of a human being or devil, it comes forth from non-being [Col. 0986C] into being. But this is nothing else than being created. Therefore sin is created by a human being or devil; and thus the devil creates something and is the creator of some thing. They too resolve this by saying that to create is to bring something good from non-being into being, which God alone does, not the devil or a human being, because sin is not, nor has in itself, any good.

Yet the foregoing authorities of Augustine are raised against them: [Note: [Col. 0985D] *Enchiridion*, ch. 13.] “Every nature, insofar as it exists, is good.” Again: [Note: [Col. 0986D] Augustine, *Eighty-Three Questions*, q. 21.] “God is the author of all things which, insofar as they are, are good.” They reply that by “nature” Augustine understands substance, that is, a thing existing through itself, such as a soul or a human being. Concrete properties of a substance are called those which, together with the substance in which they inhere, [Col. 0986D] are created—for example, natural things that accompany the substance itself from birth, such as memory, aptitude, reason, understanding, and so forth in the soul; and rationality and the capacity for laughter in a human being. Thus neither a good nor an evil act is included under “nature.” They say Augustine seems to intend this. For, retracting something said elsewhere, he says: “This was said concerning substances and natures; for the discussion concerned these, not good actions and sins.” Behold, here he openly distinguishes acts from substances and natures. Again, elsewhere he says: [Note: [Col. 0986D] The author of the *Hypognosticon* attributed to Augustine, beginning of book IV.] “No evil is a nature, but an accidental act resulting from the defect of a good.”

[Col. 0987A] They also object as follows: Since sin, insofar as it is sin, is nothing, and God is not the author of sin insofar as it is sin, what is remarkable about that? How could he be the author of nothing? By the same reasoning, how is a human being the author of sin insofar as it is sin, when sin insofar as it is sin is nothing? Therefore they say this: when it is said, “God is the author of natures,” acts are not included under that universality. But when it is said, “God is the author of all goods,” good action is included.

## Chapter XIII. On the difference between will, end, and intention

[Note: [Col. 0987D] Master, dist. 2, 83, §§ F and G.] When we began to treat sin, we first set out the order upon [Col. 0987B] which the foundation of the whole teaching rests, lest our reading should toss like a shipwrecked vessel. First, we showed the source from which sin had its origin; second, the thing in which sin existed; third, what sin was. Now, following the order set out, we must discuss the differences among sins.

It must therefore be known that some say that every action, insofar as it exists, is good. They distinguish actions as follows. Some actions are good in kind, such as feeding the poor; some are evil in kind, such as killing people; while others are not simply good or evil, but are commended or deformed by their end, such as walking about the streets. If someone walks about the streets in order to feed the sick and poor, such an end commends that action; but if [Col. 0987C] he walks about the streets in order to look at women, the end makes the action deformed and blameworthy.

We shall discuss those actions which intention and end make blameworthy or commendable. But first we must establish the difference between end and intention. The order, then, will be this: first, we shall discuss the differences among these; second, whether the will is sin and, if it is sin, whether it is the same sin as the external action or not; third, whether an action is assessed by will and action; fourth, whether, just as evil wills have diverse and opposed ends, good wills also have diverse and opposed ends.

It must therefore be known that “will” is used in several senses. Sometimes will means a natural power; sometimes the natural motion of a power; sometimes it means what we will, which some call by the coined term *volitum* (“the willed object”); and sometimes that for the sake of which we will something. Intention, however, is composed of will and end; for example, my intention is to feed the poor so that I may have eternal life. Whether we sometimes will to have eternal life by the same will by which we will to feed the poor, or by another; and whether there are as many wills as there are willed objects—that is, things which we will—will be discussed below. [Col. 0987D]

## Chapter XIV. Whether the will and the action proceeding from it are the same sin or different sins

[Col. 0988A]

[Note: [Col. 0987D] Master, II, dist. 39.] With these matters established, since all agree that the will is sin, the question is whether the will is the same sin as the external action or not. Yet this question must first be resolved: since will is a natural power, why is it called sin rather than other natural powers, namely memory or aptitude? Why is a person who has an evil will called a sinner rather than one who has a sodden memory or a dull aptitude?

They reply that when will is said to be sin, “being sin” is to be understood of the motion of the will, [Col. 0988B] not of the natural power. But the same question still remains. For it is asked why the motion of the will is sin rather than a motion of memory or understanding, by which we are moved to remember evil things or to understand evil things. They reply that the motion of will belongs to another genus than the motions of understanding and memory: by it one is moved to desire something or to reject something. Hence wrongly willing evil things is sin; but remembering evil things or understanding evil things is not sin. Or perhaps, just as willing evil things is sin, so too remembering evil in order that we may do evil is sin.

[Note: [Col. 0988D] Master, II, dist. 42, §§ 1, 2, and 3.] The following objection is made against those who say that the will is the same sin as the external action. Suppose that this man willed to kill a man and has now killed him. He is held guilty of a mortal sin; but no sin has been committed in that action which was not previously in him. Therefore he is guilty of no sin for which he was not guilty before killing the man. Therefore he does not deserve more punishment by killing the man than he had previously deserved through will alone. Or thus: No sin is in him, after the man has been killed, which was not in him before the act. Therefore he commits no sin by killing the man. Again, to will to kill is not to kill. Therefore to will homicide is not homicide. [Col. 0988C]

The contrary is argued thus. The external action is the same sin as the interior action. The external action is homicide. Therefore the interior action is homicide, and thus willing to kill is homicide. Again, in one place the Apostle uses the plural, “homicides” (Gal. 5; Rom. 1), because there are two homicides: one of the will and the other of action. Again, the will to steal is prohibited by one commandment of the law—“You shall not covet your neighbour’s property” (Exod. 20)—and theft by another—“You shall not steal” (ibid.). Therefore the violation involved in the will to steal is a violation of a different commandment from theft. This is an argument from definition, for [Note: [Col. 0988D] Ambrose, ch. 8 of *On Paradise*.] sin “is a transgression of the divine law and disobedience to heavenly commands.”

Again, it is read [Col. 0989A] in the gloss on Exodus that one “adds iniquity to iniquity” who adds an evil deed to an evil will; but there is no addition unless there is another thing. Therefore an evil deed is an iniquity other than an evil will, and therefore another sin. If it is said that an evil will and an act are different sins, then a different satisfaction must be imposed for the will and another for the act. Again, a person is barred from holy orders because of an act; he is never barred because of will. Therefore an act is a greater sin than will. On the contrary, will is never without contempt, while an act can be without contempt. Therefore will is a greater sin than action. Again, all merit depends on the will, not on the act. Therefore an evil will is a greater sin than an evil act. Again, the will [Col. 0989B] is never without sin, while an act is sometimes without sin—for example, when someone, unknowingly, despite using the greatest diligence and having considered all circumstances, kills a human being. Therefore will is a greater sin than action. It is not greatly important whether will and action are said to be the same sin or different sins.

We therefore answer both the objections raised against the first position and those raised against the other. To the first argument: “This man is held guilty of mortal sin, but no sin,” and so forth, we say that after the action this man is guilty of no sin for which he was not guilty before; and yet he is guilty of something for which he was not guilty before, namely the act—not, however, of any sin for which he was not [Col. 0989C] guilty before. Thus we press the point as follows: suppose this man uttered the word “white,” and now utters the word “white.” He uttered no noun which he is not now uttering, nor was he going to utter anything except a noun. Therefore he uttered nothing which he is not now uttering.

In reply to the subsequent objection, “to will to kill is not to kill,” etc., it must be said that “to kill” pertains only to the act, whereas “homicide” pertains both to act and will; hence the conclusion does not follow. It is as if one were to argue, by a contrary analogy: “This grammarian is this musician; the same person is indicated. Therefore, to be this female grammarian is to be this female musician.” The Apostle, moreover, speaks in the plural of “homicides,” with reference to will and act, because they weigh as heavily as if they were two homicides. To the next assertion we say that the will is a transgression of a different commandment from the act; nevertheless, the will is not a transgression other than the act, for the same transgression belongs to each of the two commandments. This is a fallacy: “This man is today the servant of another person than he was yesterday; therefore, today he is another servant than he was yesterday.” The subsequent statement, “He adds iniquity to iniquity,” etc., is not said because the deed is a sin other than the will, but because the deed is one thing and the will another.

What is subsequently said against those who maintain that will and act are different sins, and that therefore one satisfaction ought to be imposed for the will and another for the act, may be answered by saying that two satisfactions ought not to be imposed for those two sins, [Col. 0990A] but a greater one for both than for either one alone. So likewise, for adultery and homicide, one satisfaction and then another is not imposed, but a greater satisfaction for those two than for one of them.

Whether the will is a greater sin than the act, or conversely, cannot be determined so simply. In some cases the will is the greater sin; in others, the act. For every circumstance must be considered: namely, by whom something is done—whether by a layman or a priest—and in what place, at what time, and the like. Or perhaps the comparison is unsuitable, as when it is said, “A tree is better than its fruit,” or conversely. But the assertion, “A man is barred from holy orders on account of the act and not on account of the will,” etc., has no force. For he is not [Col. 0990B] barred from holy orders because the act is a greater sin than the will, but because one who has shed blood ought not to approach the sacrament of the altar. If the act were for this reason called the greater sin, then by the same reasoning bigamy would be called a greater sin than the will, because a bigamist is barred from holy orders; yet bigamy is not a sin.

But against the statement that the will is a sin, an objection is raised. Suppose that a man has the will to kill someone after ten years, and not before: he wills to kill a man. Therefore, by his will he is a murderer; therefore, he is guilty of homicide. The first proposition may be proved indirectly. For if it is said that he does not will to kill the man—which seems plausible, because the meaning of the verb does not extend to so remote [Col. 0990C] a future, nor is one said to will what one intends to do after so long a time—then one is not said to will to go to Rome, though one will be going to Rome after ten years. Nor does this master wish to cease lecturing in Paris when he has not yet begun; rather, he has the will to cease lecturing ten years after he has begun. If, I say, this is asserted, why should anyone be said to will that which he will do in the immediate future rather than that which he will do in the remote future, when both are future? To this it must be said that he is guilty of the homicide of will, because he wills that he will kill a man. But whether he wills to kill 141 a man because he wills that he will kill a man after ten [Col. 0990D] years—on this point grammarians should be consulted. Yet for the theologian it is enough that, because he wills that he will kill a man after a long time, he is guilty of the will of homicide just as if he wished to kill him now.

Yet it may be said that it is not because he wills that he will kill a man after a long time that he therefore wills to kill a man. A grammatical reason may be given for this: just as the second person of the imperative shows its meaning with respect to the immediate future—for a command is not about the present—so the infinitive, when preceded by the verb *volo*, “I will,” extends its meaning to the immediate future and not to the remote: thus we are said to will to do what we are going to do in the immediate future, or what we then will ourselves to do.

[Col. 0991A] Again, since the will is said to be a sin, an objection is raised. Suppose that someone had the will to kill a man and [Note: [Col. 0991D] A negation *non* appears to be added.] did not kill him; but now he no longer has that will and repents, though not for God’s sake. There would have been no actual sin in him except the will, thus posited, to kill a man; but there was no will to kill a man in him which has not ceased to be in him. Therefore, there was no sin in him which has not ceased to be in him; nor did any sin afterward begin to exist in him. Therefore, no sin is in him. But conversely: a mortal sin was in him, and afterward he did not repent, nor does he repent for God’s sake; therefore, that sin is now in him. Indeed, it may even be proved that a greater sin is now in him than was formerly in him, [Col. 0991B] because, when previously will alone was in him, he added contempt for repentance to the will; and contempt is a mortal sin. Therefore, a greater sin is in him than was formerly in him.

To this it must be said that sin is said to be in someone in two ways: namely, in liability and in act. Sin is in someone in act while it is being perpetrated by him; it is said to be in someone in liability so long as his mind and conscience are stained and darkened by that sin, until he repents and is contrite concerning it. Liability, moreover, is spoken of in three ways: for guilt, for punishment, and for obligation to eternal or temporal punishment. Therefore, when the will to kill a man was in him yesterday, although the act is not now in him, [Col. 0991C] its liability is nevertheless in him. If it is asked whether liability and act, whether external or internal, are two sins or not, this is an unsuitable way of speaking. It is like asking whether this white thing and its whiteness are or are not, when a body is not counted together with its property. Although liability is not a property of the act, it is as it were a property, because it deforms the act and is the deformity of the act.

Whether contempt is a greater sin than will; whether the contempt by which a man commits sin is greater than the contempt by which he despises repentance; and whether a person sins more and becomes worse the longer he despises repentance—these would not be useless matters to investigate here. Yet for the present we set them aside; for we have undertaken not to provide a finished treatment, [Col. 0991D] but to open up a beginning and a path for the disputant. This, however, must not be passed over: contempt, liability, act, and will are reckoned as one sin, not as several; just as the noun [*unum*, “one”] signifies substance, quality, and understanding, yet does not signify several things, because these three are reckoned as one signification. But the act is more often called “sin,” because an act is evident to human senses. What we do, we see; contempt, liability, and will are not so evident. Likewise, the noun [perhaps *unum*] is said more principally to signify substance, because substance is more evident to sense than quality or understanding. [Col. 0992A] Again, it should be known that every sin arises from contempt, and if there were no contempt, there would be no sin. For if there were no contempt, there would be no transgression of commandments. And if there were no transgression of commandments, there would be no sin, either in will or in act. Therefore, if there were no 142 contempt, there would be no sin. Again, it seems that the will which was in this man is in him not only in liability but in act. For just as the same faith was in Cornelius by which he believed Christ to be about to be born, and afterward believed Christ to have been born, so it seems that the same will was in this man by which he willed that a man be killed by him, and afterward willed that the man had been killed by him.

Again, against the assertion that the will is a sin, [Col. 0992B] an objection is raised. Augustine says:

[Note: [Col. 0991D] Book I of the *Retractations*, ch. 13, and *On True Religion*, [Col. 0992D] ch. 14.]

> “Every sin is voluntary to such an extent that, if it were not voluntary, it would not be sin.”

But the will is sin. Therefore, that sin is voluntary to such an extent that, if it is not voluntary, it is not sin. Therefore, the sin which is will is voluntary; therefore it proceeds from a will. Again, that third will is sin and proceeds from a will, and so on to infinity. Again, this man either wills himself to will to sin or does not. If it is said that he wills himself to will to sin, he wills this by some will, and so on to infinity as before. If it is said that he does not will himself to will to sin, but wills to sin, then he wills something which he does not will himself to will; and this seems implausible. For just as [Col. 0992C] whatever is true to be true is true, whatever is necessary to be necessary is necessary, and whatever someone knows himself to know he knows, so it seems that whatever someone wills himself to will he wills, and whatever he wills, he wills himself to will. Yet this too seems implausible: for many persons would wish, and indeed do wish, to will to turn away from evil, and yet do not will to turn away from evil. Hence, if to desire eagerly (*concupiscere*) were the same as to desire (*desiderare*), why did the Prophet double these expressions in saying: “My soul longed to desire” (Psalm CXVIII)?

We are bound to answer the foregoing arguments in order. Therefore, Augustine’s statement, “Every sin is voluntary,” etc., must be understood of the external act which proceeds from the will. Whether it must be understood of every external act [Col. 0992D] is doubtful, because of acts which occur through ignorance and frailty. Or—and this is the stronger view—it must be understood both of internal and external act, because both proceed from a will: not an evil will, but only a good one. For the will is nothing but good, since it is a natural power of the soul; and nothing prevents evil from having its origin in good. To the subsequent point we say that whatever someone wills himself to will, he wills, and conversely, just as whatever someone knows himself to know, he knows, and conversely.

[Note: [Col. 0992D] Teaching of the Master, II, distinction 39, final section.]

But it should be noted that there are two movements in a human being: one is natural and is given to man by nature, by which he is naturally moved to love God and to hate [Col. 0993A] evil. No one is so wicked that he does not naturally love good and hate evil, because “even in Cain that spark of reason could not be extinguished.”

[Note: [Col. 0993D] This is Jerome, on Ezekiel, book I, on the words: “And the sparks, like the appearance of bronze,” etc.]

There is another movement in a human being, by which, abandoning the law of heaven, man has subjected himself to earthly things and takes delight in them. The first is called higher, and this latter lower. At times this one rules in a man, at times that one. But it should be known that a person is simply said to will that which he wills by the ruling movement. If the lower movement rules, what someone wills by it he simply [does not] will. The same is true of the other movement. Therefore, since in every evil the evil movement—that is, the lower movement—rules, the question arises: what does he simply will? He wills by the lower movement, and conversely. Hence it is clear that he does not will to turn away from evil, but nevertheless he would wish [Col. 0993B] to turn away from evil; for the one is different from the other. For this verb, namely *vellem*, “I would wish,” is either present optative or imperfect subjunctive. If it is optative, the adverb *utinam*, “would that,” is understood, so that the sense is: “Would that I wished to be good!”—that is, “Would that grace were present to me; so long as it is absent, I shall never truly be able to say, ‘I will to be good’ [and ‘I would wish to be king’].”

[Note: [Col. 0993D] The words in brackets are superfluous.]

Therefore, “I would wish to be good” differs from “I will to be good”; and this is clear from many examples, such as: “I would wish to go to Rome if perhaps some necessity or advantage should arise,” yet “I do not will to go to Rome.”

Again, since the will is said to be sin, an objection is raised: all merit lies in the will. And again: 143 “The will shall be reckoned as the deed.” Therefore, one merits only as much as one merits by will, neither more nor less. Therefore, a man ought to be punished as much for will alone as for act and will together. To this it must be said that when it is said, “All merit lies in the will,” *penes* here denotes authority, because the authority of all merit is referred to the will, including the merit of the act, because the will also precedes the act in authority. Thus all merit lies in the will, but not the quantity of merit; for a person merits more by will and act than by will alone. But the authority of meriting, as was said, is referred to will alone. When it is said, however, “All merit lies in charity,” *penes* here denotes cause: that is, charity is the cause of all merit. [Col. 0993D] Therefore, the statement, “The will shall be reckoned as the deed,” must be explained thus: just as a person will be punished for a deed, so also for a will. I do not say, “as much for this as for that,” but “for this as for that.” For the adverb “as” is not an adverb of quantity, but of likeness.

Again, every evil person can have a will more intensely directed toward evil than he in fact has. Suppose that there are two evil men and that one is worse than the other, as Cain and Judas; let Judas be worse. Cain can have a will toward evil as intense as Judas can have, and [Col. 0994A] all merit lies in the will. Therefore Cain can be as evil as Judas can be; but however evil Cain can be, it is possible for him to be that evil. Therefore it is possible for Cain to be as evil as Judas can be evil. Therefore this too can be true: Cain is as evil as Judas can be evil. Suppose, then, that Cain is as evil as Judas can be evil; and, as evil as Judas can be, Cain can be evil, and conversely. Therefore Cain is as evil as he himself can be evil. That Cain can have a will toward evil as intense as Judas can have is clear from this: no degree or limit of wickedness can be conceived to which [Col. 0994B] Cain’s will can extend and to which Judas’s will cannot extend or be intensified, and conversely. Therefore one can have a will toward evil as intense as the other can have. Again, either it is possible or impossible that Cain be as evil as Judas can be evil. If possible, the objection applies as before. If impossible—yet Judas can be evil to some degree—then Cain cannot be as evil. In the same way proceeds another objection concerning God’s power: namely, it is possible or impossible for God to do whatever good things he can do. If possible, then it can be true; let it be so. Therefore God does whatever good things he can do. If it is impossible for God to do whatever good things he can do, then it is necessary [Col. 0994C] that God not do some good things which he can do. Therefore it is necessary that God not do certain good things and be able to do them. Therefore God does not do certain good things. Therefore God does not do all good things: “The eyes of God saw my imperfection” (Psalm CXXXVIII). And so let it suffice to have supplied the principles of the disputation: let the vigorous investigator seek the solutions from his elders.

## CHAPTER XV. Whether ignorance excuses a person from sin

We must return again to Augustine’s authority:

[Note: [Col. 0994D] The Master, II, distinction 22, §§ 8, 9, and 10.]

> “Every sin is voluntary to such an extent,” etc.

We have explained this in one way, concerning both internal and external act; in another way, however, concerning external act.

[Note: [Col. 0994D] Augustine, *On True Religion*, ch. 14, as above.]

Whether it applies to every [Col. 0994D] external act, we left doubtful because of those acts which occur through ignorance, necessity, or natural frailty, concerning which we must speak. First, concerning things done through ignorance.

Sin occurs through ignorance in two ways. First, when someone commits a sin and does not think himself to be committing sin: for example, if someone kills a believer, thinking that this is not sin. In such a sin there is will of the deed, but not will of the sin: the person who does this wills to do it, but does not will to sin. In the other way, a person sins through ignorance when he intends to do one thing but, perhaps, unknowingly does something other [Col. 0995A] than that which he proposed to do, and his action accidentally turns to something else. For example, if someone, wishing to free his father from a lion, aims an arrow at the lion in order to kill it, and the arrow accidentally strikes his father and kills him. Here there is neither will of the deed nor will of the sin.

[Note: [Col. 0995D] Augustine, *On Nature and Grace against the Pelagians*, ch. 17; and *On Free Choice*, book III, ch. 22. See also *On Grace and Free Choice*, ch. 3.]

Either kind of sin is sometimes excused through ignorance. Ignorance is manifold. There is the ignorance of those who can know but do not wish to know; of these it will be said: “The ignorant person shall be ignored” (II Corinthians XIV). This is vincible ignorance, which can be overcome by learning and study; hence it can in no way excuse. There is another ignorance, that of those who wish to know but cannot; and such ignorance is not vincible, because those who have it cannot overcome it either by learning or by study, perhaps because their intellect is dull or their memory unreliable; and such ignorance may sometimes excuse. [Col. 0995B]

[Note: [Col. 0995D] See Augustine, *On Grace and Free Choice*, ch. 3.]

There is also another ignorance, that of those who neither refuse to know nor desire to know; and this is not excusable, because “the sluggard shall be stoned with bovine dung” (Ecclesiasticus XXII). The first ignorance is sin; the second is punishment, and perhaps was sin before baptism. Therefore, when someone commits a sin and does not think it a sin, he is excused through ignorance.

But when someone intends to do something good and accidentally does something evil, the question is whether that evil can be excused through ignorance, as in the case of the man who, aiming an arrow to free his father from a lion, accidentally killed [Col. 0995C] his father.

[Note: [Col. 0995D] See Abelard, book III of the *Exposition of the Epistle to the Romans*, [Col. 0996D] p. 625.]

In this matter, one must distinguish whether the man who shot the arrow acted in charity and from charity, and employed all the diligence he could employ. I say “from charity and in charity” because, if he was not in charity and was not acting from charity, he sinned mortally. I also say “employing all diligence.” Nor does it matter whether he shot the arrow in an indifferent action, namely while playing or walking about, as we often do when we throw stones and such things for bodily enjoyment. For if that was so, it was inexcusable. It also matters whether such an action was prohibited, as we read concerning Lamech, who hunted before the eating of meat, when men were not yet accustomed to hunting or eating meat; [Col. 0995D] he was also blind, and while hunting killed Cain. Hence this should be imputed to him as a lesser sin than it would be if that kind of activity were good. Therefore all such circumstances must be considered and brought to bear. If, then, this man shot the arrow from charity to free his father, and with every diligence he could employ, he is excused through ignorance, and it is not a mortal sin.

It should be noted, however, that a sin is not always so fully excused by vincible ignorance. [Col. 0996A] For there are four kinds of ignorance. There is ignorance from obstinacy, such as was in Pharaoh and in certain Jews who, from malice, wish to remain ignorant. There is also ignorance from negligence, when a man neglects to know because he is young and cannot bear punishment; and this is mortal sin. There is also ignorance from pride, as when a man disdains to listen to another because he scorns to learn from him. Any one of these is mortal sin and does not lessen sin. Thus, if there are two deacons here equally bound to know, the one who sins ignorantly in a certain kind of sin sins more gravely than one who knowingly commits the same kind of sin, because the former both despises being ignorant and commits contempt in the other sin. There is also pious ignorance, such as Paul had [Col. 0996B] when he persecuted Christ; and this lessens sin. Accordingly, he himself says:

[Note: [Col. 0996D] I Timothy I: “I was a blasphemer and persecutor and insolent man; but I obtained the mercy of God because I acted ignorantly in unbelief.”]

He obtained pardon more readily because he was ignorant in that way. Yet this ignorance was a venial sin, and Paul did not have a good conscience when he persecuted in that way; for although he did not act against conscience, his conscience was undiscerning, and thus evil. For although “whatever is not from faith is sin” (Romans XIV), not everything that is from faith—that is, from conscience—is good, if someone is ignorant. Therefore, vincible ignorance, as the authority says,

[Note: [Col. 0996D] Augustine, *On Grace and Free Choice*, ch. 3.]

does not fully excuse from sin: “For it does not prevent a man from burning, but makes him burn less.” Hence the Apostle says: “I obtained pardon more readily [Col. 0996C] because I persecuted ignorantly” (I Timothy I).

But against this an objection is raised. On this account, it seems that the man who killed his father—wishing to kill not his father but a beast—sins more gravely than the man who, wishing to kill the lion in order to free his father, accidentally killed his father. For the former sins venially, yet satisfaction is imposed on him as though for mortal sin, though he is not bound to it. Again, the action by which he killed the ass proceeds from some will: either from the will by which he wished to kill his father, or from another, indifferent will. If from the will by which he wished to kill his father, since that will is wholly evil, and every action whose will is evil is evil, therefore, in killing the ass by it he sins mortally. Again, the action by which this man kills his father, if it is a venial sin, cannot proceed [Col. 0996D] from the will by which he wishes to free his father with an arrow-shot, since that will is wholly good and formed by charity. Some do not consider it improper to say that the action by which he kills his father, though he wished to kill the lion, proceeded from no will. Others say that the will by which he wished to free his father was good and meritorious, being formed by charity; and that the work which was to proceed from it in the first instance—unless something else happened—was good, namely, freeing his father. But an evil work arose incidentally: namely, killing [Col. 0997A] his father, though it did proceed from that good will. Therefore the saying, “A good tree cannot bear evil fruit” (Matthew VII), must be understood in the first instance; and conversely. The will of one wishing to kill his father is evil; yet if it happens that, wishing to do this, he kills a lion which would already have devoured a man unless it had been killed, that work—which belongs to the class of good things—is not evil from the evil will from which it proceeded incidentally rather than in the first instance. In that work a person neither merits nor demerits, but does so in the perverse will.

[Col. 0997B] Again, suppose that this man aimed an arrow at another not to kill but to wound him. The latter is now bedridden with illness and will afterward die. Will the former become liable to greater guilt when the latter dies? Suppose also that he has already repented and performed satisfaction: when the other dies as a result of this wound, will the satisfaction he performed be rendered void because it was insufficient, since the other died, and so satisfaction should have been imposed upon him for homicide rather than wounding? And if he did not repent until the other died, would he be liable to greater satisfaction? It is also asked: when did he kill the man—when he aimed the arrow, or when the man died? If when he aimed the arrow, then he was killing him then; therefore the other also died then. But if afterward, when the other died, then he began to be a murderer then; therefore he was not a murderer immediately after the wounding, and so he was liable to greater guilt [Col. 0997C] when the other died than before. Therefore the will or the act of sin increased, which is false. Again, suppose that he wished to wound the man, not kill him. Immediately after the blow was struck, the assailant died, but the wounded man did not die immediately; rather, he died later. Did the assailant die as a murderer? It does not seem so, because when he died he had killed no man either in act or in will. Nor does it seem that he afterward began to be a murderer when the wounded man died, because at that time he no longer existed. To this it may be said that, from the moment he inflicted the wound which was the cause of death, he was a murderer, although this was not known until the other died.

[Col. 0997D] Again, the man who killed an ass is moved by a more intense will to kill his father than the man who both wishes to kill his father and kills him. Therefore the former sins more by will alone than the latter by will and act; or not every cause of meriting lies in the will. Conversely, the latter sins by will and act; therefore he sins more than the former, who sins by will alone. Again, a man kills two persons with one blow, though he wished to kill only one: therefore he does not sin in killing the other unknowingly, just as he does not merit if he saves two persons in temporal life, one through ignorance and the other by deliberate action; or God is readier to punish than to reward. Again, God rewards no work done through ignorance, and punishes many things done through ignorance; therefore God is readier to punish than to reward. Again, if Paul persecuted Christ knowingly, he would persecute less fiercely, because he would act against conscience, [Col. 0998A] than when he did so ignorantly; for then he believed himself to be rendering service to God. Therefore he sinned more by persecuting ignorantly than he would have if he had done so knowingly; for if he had done it knowingly, there would have been only one contempt, of ignorance and persecution. Therefore he sinned more in persecuting ignorantly than if he had done it knowingly. Again, Ambrose says on the passage, “Do you disregard the riches of God’s goodness?” (Romans II), etc.: “You sin grievously because you promise yourself impunity; more grievously because you despise; most grievously because you are ignorant.”

Again, Paul’s persecution was evil, but knowledge was good and ignorance evil; therefore evil could be diminished by one of them; therefore, more so by good than by evil. But this does not hold, because [Col. 0998B] Lot’s incest is diminished by drunkenness, which is evil, and our sins by infirmity; without infirmity, our sins would be greater than they are. For if we had the firmness which Adam had before sin, our sins would be greater than they are. Likewise, iron which is extremely hot becomes hotter when cold water is applied, provided it is brought near fire; it does not thereby become hot.

And note that the contempt involved in fornication, when knowledge accompanies it, is greater than the contempt involved in ignorance together with contempt for fornication. For although ignorance both benefits and harms, it benefits more by diminishing the sin which it accompanies than it harms by making the person ignorant. It is like a man who [Col. 0998C] interposes a stick while another wants to strike him with a sword: he benefits him more by freeing him from a greater punishment than he harms him by inflicting the slightest punishment with the stick-blow. Thus that objection, commonly framed as follows, fails. If no ignorance at all were present, the sin of fornication—or any similar sin which someone does not think to be mortal—would not in any respect be excused in him. Because ignorance is present, the sin of fornication is excused. Therefore, when greater ignorance is present, it is more excused. But ignorance itself of this matter is sin in itself. Therefore, to the extent that it would aggravate the sin of fornication in itself, if knowledge accompanied it, it aggravates the sin of fornication and ignorance together; for to the extent that there is remitted and diminished from the sin of fornication—which would be [Col. 0998D] sin in itself if it alone were present—so much is added to the sin of ignorance. Thus these two aggravate as much as the one sin by itself would aggravate, and ignorance seems in no respect to lessen sin.

But the statement made above in the authority, that the person who is ignorant sins most grievously, must not be understood with respect to the kind of sin. For it is not more grievous to be ignorant than to despise; rather, it is because it is more difficult to instruct one who thinks he knows what is good than one who simply does not know. For instructing one who does not know is a simple task; reforming one badly instructed is a double task.

Again, suppose that this man formerly committed fornication and did not know that this was sin, and therefore does not repent; but he would repent if he knew. He knows that fornication was [Col. 0999A] in him, and at that time he knew it to have been sin, but now he does not know it to be or to have been sin. Therefore fornication was a greater sin in him while knowledge was present than it is while ignorance is present; and thus the sin of fornication has been diminished without contrition and repentance, which seems impossible. For every sin, unless it is removed through repentance, increases and never decreases, because it always has contempt for repentance as its companion. Indeed, it can be proved 147 that he sins more now than before, because to contempt for fornication, which has not diminished in him, he has likewise added contempt for ignorance. Therefore he sins more than before, which we concede. For such ignorance cannot exist except as gross ignorance.

The question is also raised concerning a man who, approaching a maidservant, thought that he was sleeping with his wife. That ignorance seems then to excuse him from mortal sin; yet this does not seem so, because that intercourse was not lawful, and therefore was fornication, and thus mortal sin. Conversely, if it was venial, then, since the man now first knows that he approached the maidservant, it seems that it is now mortal; and so the liability for sin has increased in him, or a venial sin has become mortal. To this it must be said that if he employed every diligence he could employ, it was and is venial; yet if he scorns to repent of it, that contempt is mortal sin. Again, suppose that someone does not know fornication to be mortal sin, has many mortal sins, and begins to learn that it is mortal sin. Suppose that he has learned this: he no longer does not know that this is [Col. 0999C] sin, and so that ignorance—which was mortal sin in him—is no longer in him. Thus some mortal sin has been remitted to him without another mortal sin which was in him, and without contrition and repentance, which is impossible. To this it must be said that the ignorance is still in him with respect to liability. Again, this priest can repent of ignorance. Suppose it: he repents and is contrite concerning the ignorance which is in him as actual sin. Therefore it passes away in act and liability; or, if it passes away in liability but not in act, it is original sin. For this is the difference between original and actual sin: actual sins pass away in act but not in liability.

For this reason men of great authority not unreasonably said that ignorance is original sin. They established this as follows: there were two goods in the human soul, knowledge of truth and love of the same; one of these was impaired by concupiscence for evil, the other by ignorance of good. Why, then, is ignorance of good not called original sin, just as concupiscence for evil is? Thus it too is removed by baptism, as concupiscence is, with respect to liability but not with respect to act. Again, just as following concupiscence—without which a human being cannot exist—is mortal sin, so following [Col. 1000A] ignorance and failing to know what is necessary for salvation, when these things can nevertheless be fully known, is mortal sin. Those who do not hold this opinion say that this undiscerning priest can repent of ignorance, and it ceases to be in him with respect to liability; yet he does not thereby begin to know anything or cease to be ignorant of anything. Likewise, the learned man who is in mortal sin does not possess the gift of knowledge which is the Holy Spirit’s, because if he had it he would have charity; and when through contrition he begins to possess it, he will not begin to know anything. Whether, however, an undiscerning priest may remain in the exercise of his office after he has repented of ignorance, we do not assert, since Augustine says on the fortieth Psalm: “He does not rightly sing praise who does not understand what he sings.”

[Col. 1000B]

[Note: [Col. 0999D] See Augustine, *Retractations*, book I, ch. 13: “He who sins in ignorance does so, indeed, by will,” etc. And he who lusts against the spirit through the flesh does not do what he wills: he lusts unwillingly, and in this he does not do what he wills; but if he is overcome, he consents willingly to concupiscence, and in this he does nothing except what he wills.]

It is customary to ask whether the ignorance by which a man does not know that the stars are equal is the same as that by which he does not know the law of the Gospel. This does not seem to be so, because the latter is mortal sin and the former is not. But if they are different, then by the same reasoning there are as many ignorances as things unknown, as many knowledges as things known, and as many faiths as things believed. But to investigate these matters is more a matter of curiosity than usefulness. From the foregoing it is clear that acts done ignorantly are from the will; likewise, acts done from necessity, such as first movements, concerning which we shall speak later.

## CHAPTER XVI. But every action should be weighed according to intention and end
[Note: [Col. 1000D] The Master, II, dist. 40.] We must therefore proceed to the third of the topics set out above: whether every action [Col. 1000C] is weighed according to intention and end—that is, whether an action is called good or evil according to its intention and end. Some say that every act is naturally good, but that it should properly be called indifferent until it is judged good or evil from its end. For Ambrose says in his book *On Duties* [Note: [Col. 1000D] *On Duties*, I.30]: “Your disposition gives your work its name.” And Augustine [Note: [Col. 1000D] Augustine, Preface to Psalm XXXI]: “Intention makes a work good; faith directs intention. Do not attend too much to what a person does, but to what, in doing it, he intends to do, and toward what he directs the oars of his excellent steering.” Others say that some acts are good, others evil, and others indifferent. Acts which are admittedly good or evil are not judged good or evil from their end; only those which are neither simply good nor simply [Col. 1000D] evil, but indifferent, are weighed from their end. Evil acts cannot be done with a good end, nor good acts with an evil one. They adduce this authority [Note: [Col. 1000D] Thus in the Master here, from Augustine, Tractate 9 on the First Epistle of John; but that statement is not found in Augustine at that place.]: “Servile fear is not in charity; if something good is done in it, it is nevertheless not done well—that is, not with a good end.” Therefore, when Ambrose says, “Your disposition gives your work its name,” and Augustine, “Intention makes a work good,” and so forth, they apply these statements to indifferent acts; for it is disposition that gives such acts their name.

[Col. 1001A] [Note: [Col. 1001D] See *Against Lying*, chapter 7, etc.] Augustine, however, seems to hold otherwise. For he says that good and evil acts alike are judged according to will and end: for the end forms the will, and the will forms the action. He does not judge those actions which are admittedly evil to be good or evil from their end, because they are evil in themselves. Although they are sometimes judged to be done for a good end, nevertheless in them the will is not evil from the end, nor does the action become evil from the will; rather, the will becomes perverse from the action, because such an action can be done with no good will. Among such actions some place the act of the Jews, who, they say, set themselves a good end in crucifying Christ; yet it is certain that their action was perverse and their will evil. Hence he himself says [Note: [Col. 1001D] Chapter 7, *Against Lying*]: “Things which are admittedly sins are not to be done under any pretext of a good cause, under any supposedly good end, or under any seeming good intention”; and shortly afterwards: [Note: [Col. 1001D] Ibid., but with words both altered and omitted.] “If we once concede that, in evil acts, the question is to be asked not what is done but why it is done, so that whatever is done for good causes is not itself judged evil, then an evil deed may be said to be capable of being done rightly—not merely with impunity but even gloriously, so that punishment is not feared in it but reward is hoped for.”

But, according to Augustine, an exception is made concerning good and indifferent actions: the will is judged good or evil from its end, and the action from its will. Therefore, when it is said that a work receives its name from disposition in good and indifferent actions, the rule is true. In evil actions, however, those acts which are evil in themselves are excepted: they make the will [Col. 1001C] evil rather than become evil from the will.

[Note: [Col. 1001D] See the Master here, § c.] Take this, then, as a rule: all human works are judged evil or good according to their end and will, except those which cannot be done without transgression. Yet they say that Augustine does not except these because they ever have a good will or good end—for they are always done with an evil end and an evil will—but because they seem to have a good end. Someone who steals another’s goods in order to feed his father seems to act for a good end, namely, feeding his father. Yet that is not the end, for that is good. The end of this action is to feed his father from thefts; and that end is admittedly evil. Whoever offers God a sacrifice from plunder does the same as one who sacrifices a son in his father’s presence [Col. 1001D] [Note: [Col. 1001D] Ecclus. XXXIV: “He who offers sacrifice from the substance of the poor is like one who sacrifices a son in the presence of his father.”]. And Isaiah says: “I am the Lord, loving judgment and hating robbery in a burnt offering” (Isa. LXI). For the Lord did not accept the hire of a dog or of a prostitute, as the Law contains (Deut. XXIII). Thus they also say that Augustine spoke cautiously above when he said [Note: [Col. 1002D] The Master here, § d.], “a supposedly good end” or “a seeming good intention.” He did not simply say “a good end” or “a good intention,” but added “supposedly” and “seeming,” because such things are not done for a good end but for an end thought to be good, though it is not. From this it is now clear that one who distributes to the poor money wickedly acquired sins by that very act.

But the following objection is made. A man gives to the Church what he acquired wickedly and asks it to obtain for him the first grace. That Church is bound to pray for him, and by praying obtains the first grace. This man has merited from that Church that it should pray for him; [thus] that gift was meritorious for him. Therefore, there was no mortal sin in him. Again, from natural compassion, he sustains the starving body of a needy person from what he acquired wickedly; and that person was so needy that, unless he came to his aid, he would immediately perish. Therefore that work was good, or at least meritorious of some temporal good. Again, if he had not fed him [Col. 1002B] at the point of death, he would have sinned mortally. Therefore, because he fed him from money wickedly acquired, he did not sin. Again, suppose that a man has twenty shillings: ten acquired by usury and the other ten from lawful profit. It is certain that, while he remains in mortal sin, he can give alms from those he acquired lawfully. Although this does not merit eternal life for him, it nevertheless avails for obtaining a temporal good or mitigating the punishment of hell if he should then die. Yet from the other ten, which he acquired wickedly, he cannot perform any work meritorious of any good. Indeed, even if he gives them from natural compassion to another needy person, he sins mortally by that very fact, because he may lawfully give another’s property to no one. Even if he gives all that he has, he increases his sin and does not diminish his [Col. 1002C] guilt, as Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1002D] Sermon 15, in the Appendix, *On Various Matters*: “Even if he gives away everything that he has stolen, he adds to his sins rather than diminishes them.”]. The question, therefore, is whether he may lawfully give those twenty shillings, which he has mixed together and cannot separate, so that the gift may be meritorious for him of some temporal good and thus not involve mortal sin.

To this one must say that a little leaven corrupts the whole lump (1 Cor. V). He cannot merit any good by giving it; indeed, he sins by that very act because he gives another what is not his own. Thus, if I take your cloak in order to give it to someone who is cold, I sin. I cannot do this from natural compassion, because natural compassion itself opposes it when I take from this person in order to give to another. Nor do I deny that I sin if I retain it, for then I sin still more: “For it is worse to seize through covetousness than through pity” [Note: [Col. 1002D] Augustine, chapter 8, book I, *Against Lying*: “For he who steals through covetousness is worse than he who steals through pity.”]. Of these two things, one is not good merely because the other is worse, although one is lighter and the other graver. Nor is the Church which received money from him bound to pray for him, because it ought not receive it if it knows it was wickedly acquired. If it does not know how he acquired it, it is indeed bound to pray; but its prayer is hindered by his evil merits.

If an objection is raised concerning Phinehas, who pierced through the Israelite man and the Midianite woman [Col. 1003A], on the ground that this work belonged among those deeds which cannot be done without transgression, it may be said that this work was good, because he did it by divine inspiration and zeal for God’s justice. Therefore, not only did he not sin in that work, but he merited eternal life. No work is so evil in itself that, if a person does it by God’s command or by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, and as God commands him, it is not good; for God is above every law and every command. Hence, if in some case God’s command seems to differ from the law, one must obey the giver of the law rather than the law given.

But an objection is raised here concerning Mary Magdalene, who bought ointment from what she had wickedly acquired and anointed the Lord’s feet, although the Lord knew that the ointment had been [Col. 1003B] acquired by her wickedly. Therefore they distinguish among wickedly acquired goods. They say that what a woman acquires by exposing her own body is hers, although acquired in sin; and if she repents, she may give alms from it. But what is obtained through usury is plunder: it does not belong to the acquirer, who is bound to restore it to the person from whom he received it. Nor, even when he restores it out of charity—though he merits thereby—is he said to give alms. Yet we do not say this because it is certain that Mary bought that ointment from the profit of her own body, since she possessed an estate [Note: [Col. 1003D] And this must be believed with the fullest certainty concerning that pious woman.] from which she could have bought it.

If, therefore, someone calls the intention of an action its end, it is true that every action is judged good or evil from its end, and every action whose intention is good is good, and conversely. Likewise [Col. 1003C], every action whose intention is evil is evil, and conversely; for intention includes both will and end, as we have sufficiently clearly distinguished above between will, end, and intention. Yet not every action is judged from its end, but only one which is good in itself or indifferent. Therefore, if a poor person is fed for the sake of vainglory, that action is evil because its end is evil; and by that very fact a person sins and lies under a curse. As Jeremiah says: “Cursed is he who does the work of the Lord deceitfully” (Jer. XLVIII). Explaining this, Gregory says [Note: [Col. 1003D] Book IX, on Job XVII, chapter 9, about the middle, but with certain words altered.] that such deceit is committed either for the reward of a temporal thing, for a word of praise, or for the favor of human judgment. “For he alone commits no deceit in God’s work who, when he is intent upon the endeavors of good action, does not thirst after the rewards of bodily things, words of praise, or the favor of human judgment. For, as blessed Job testifies, our works must be regarded with fear, lest earthly desires, by thieving deceit, insinuate themselves into our actions.” Yet we do not say that everyone who loves temporal praise always sins mortally, nor everyone who chiefly aims at these things. For the Lord commands that the dust be shaken off one’s feet (Matt. X; Mark VI; Luke IX). But someone says: if feeding a poor person for the sake of vainglory [Col. 1004A] is a mortal sin, then it is not rewarded with a temporal reward. Yet the Lord seems to say the contrary concerning hypocrites: “Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matt. VI). But this was said ironically, because this was the reward they sought, and they have already received it.

Again an objection is raised. Suppose that a man studies sacred Scripture in order subsequently to attack it; later he comes to his senses and preaches as a Catholic. He will repent in charity of each of his sins. Therefore, concerning the exercise in study which he presently undertakes—because it is a mortal sin in him owing to his evil intention—he will wish that he had not learned it. Therefore, it will please him that he learned it; yet to learn it is a mortal sin. Therefore, it will please him that he sinned mortally. Again, suppose [Col. 1004B] he learns with a good end but later apostasizes: “It is better not to know the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn back” (2 Pet. II). He knows that knowledge of the truth is an accumulation of greater condemnation for him. Therefore he ought to grieve that he knew and learned the truth. To this one must say that he ought not grieve because he learned, but because he learned for such an end and because he apostasized—just as one who once had charity should grieve not because he possessed it but because he lost it.

[Note: [Col. 1003D] The Master, II, dist. 41.] Again, since it has been said that every good action is made good by a good end, the question is whether this is universally true. For if so, when one who is in mortal sin gives alms from lawfully acquired money with the intention of sustaining a needy person, and does so also for God’s sake, he seems [Col. 1004C] to perform a good work; thus one in mortal sin performs good works. Augustine confirms this as follows [Note: [Col. 1003D] See Psalm CXXVII, Sermon 13 *On the Words of the Lord*, chapter 41 on John, etc.]: “Servile fear is not in charity; if something good is done in it, it is nevertheless not done well.” And on that passage of the Psalm [Note: [Col. 1004D] Psalm LXXXIII; this is Augustine’s thought, though in different words.], “The sparrow has found herself a house, and the turtledove a nest where she may lay her young,” he says that unbelievers perform good works, but not in the nest of the Church—that is, in faith—and therefore their young are trampled underfoot. Yet this seems contradicted by the saying: “Whatever is not from faith is sin” (Rom. XIV); “the entire life of unbelievers is sin” [Note: [Col. 1004D] This is in Prosper’s *Book of Sentences*, no. 106.]; and David: “All his works [are] in faith” (Ps. XXXII); and James: “Whoever offends in one point is guilty of all” (Jas. II). Augustine also says [Note: [Col. 1004D] Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 121 and final chapter; see near the end of the Preface to Psalm XXXI]: “If something is done in such a way that it is not referred to charity, which is love of God and neighbor, it is not yet done as it ought to be done, even if it appears to be done.”

[Note: [Col. 1004D] The Master above, § c.] All these statements are easily harmonized if it is said that every work done under the guidance of compassion, by whomever it is done, is good.
