But “good” is said in many ways: for useful, rewardable, a sign of good, a hope of good, lawful, and perhaps in other ways. No work is good—that is, meritorious of eternal life—unless it is from charity; but it is not only such a work that is good. For if an unbeliever relieves the need of a poor person, he does a good thing, that is, a sign of good, and that work is rewarded with a temporal reward. Yet a work belonging to the class of good works, when it is performed from an evil end, is good in the sense that, if it were done in charity, it would be good; nevertheless it is evil from the disposition, and also belongs to the class of evil works—as when a poor person is fed for the sake of vainglory. Or, according to those who divide acts into three classes and say that good works cannot be done from an evil end, just as evil ones cannot from a good end, it may be said that these works are good—that is, of the class of good works—yet are called evil because those who perform them are evil and sin by that very fact.

## CHAPTER XVII. Whether the ends of good wills are diverse and opposed, as are those of evil wills; and whether God is to be served for temporal goods.

[Col. 1005B]

Of the four topics previously noted, we must pursue the fourth remaining one: namely, whether good wills have diverse and opposed ends. This seems to be so. For one person praises or loves God for temporal goods, while another praises God for God’s sake. Here the first person’s will is good, and these ends are diverse; therefore a good will has diverse ends. Yet that God ought not to be loved for temporal goods is shown indirectly as follows. A man loves God for temporal goods; therefore he does not love him freely. Again, in Job Satan is read to have said that Job does not love God freely, for he has temporal goods (Job I). Again: “He who [Col. 1005C] praises God for riches asks that riches should come to himself, not God.” Augustine says this [Note: [Col. 1005D] Augustine on Psalm LII: “He who calls upon God in order to become rich does not call upon God; for he calls upon that which he wants to come to himself.” See what follows.]. Again, the person who loves God for temporal goods does not love *dulia* [service or veneration] freely; therefore neither *latria* [the worship due to God] freely. Thus he loves God both freely and not freely. Solomon says: “Give me neither riches nor poverty, O God” (Prov. XXX). And Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1006D] See also what he has at the end of Psalm LIII and near the end of Psalms LV and CXLIV.]: “He truly calls upon God who calls upon him for his own sake, not for something else.” But one who calls upon him for riches calls upon him for something other than himself. Therefore, one who calls upon him for riches does not call upon him truly; thus he ought not be called upon for riches.

[Note: [Col. 1006D] See Augustine above.] But that God ought to be loved, prayed to, and praised for temporal goods is shown as follows. God ought to be praised for all his benefits; therefore, for temporal ones. Again, a person who does not give thanks to God for temporal things bestowed on him by God is ungrateful. Again, riches may lawfully be possessed; therefore they may lawfully be sought. Again, no one can continually and freely serve without bodily necessities, and no one can have bodily necessities without temporal goods. Therefore no one can serve God without temporal goods; therefore temporal goods ought to be sought, and thus God ought to be prayed to for temporal goods. Again, we read that Jeremiah sent letters to the Hebrews in captivity, directing them to pray for the peace of the ruler, because their deliverance depended upon his peace; thus one ought to pray for the removal of tribulation. Moreover, the Church daily prays for peace, crops, and temporal goods of this sort.

On this question, it seems to us that God ought to be praised, loved, and prayed to for temporal goods. But understand this proposition cautiously: it can denote either a final end or an end tending toward another. If it denotes a final end, it is false; if an end tending toward another, it is true. Thus, when it is said, “This man wants a physician for the sake of a draught,” if “for the sake of” denotes a final end, the statement is false: for ultimately he wants him for the sake of health. If it denotes an end tending toward another, it is true. Therefore God is to be loved for temporal goods, namely, so that through good temporal things we may acquire him—not for their own sake but [Col. 1006B] for God’s sake; so that we do not place our end in them, do not remain there, but, through them, love God, who is the final end.

Therefore, the first statement—that this person praises God for temporal things and hence not freely—involves a fallacy. “This person is saved for his merits; therefore not freely” is false, because merit does not exclude grace, nor vice versa. What is then said, namely that Satan said, “Job does not love God freely, for he has temporal goods” (Job I), is not true. Rather, Job then loved him freely, as was afterwards proved, when, after losing everything, his body was so ulcerated that worms even swarmed forth from it. The other arguments we have adduced are easily answered once the several meanings of this preposition *pro* (“for”) have been distinguished.

[Col. 1006C] Yet Augustine seems to oppose this solution when he says: “Do not set before yourselves two ends: that you seek the kingdom for its own sake, and temporal things for its sake; nor [seek] temporal reward alone, or even together with it.” Here he seems to show that temporal things are not to be desired for their own sake, nor even the kingdom for the sake of the kingdom. But we explain that authority thus: “Do not establish two ends for yourselves,” that is, opposed ends. Yet these ends—loving God for temporal things and loving him for his own sake—are not opposed, because the former is for the latter. Afterwards one must supply: “but one,” namely, that you seek the kingdom for its own sake and temporal things for its sake. For all things are to be sought for the kingdom’s sake; one who does this does not set before himself two [Col. 1006D] ends. What follows later—“we ought to do all things only for the kingdom’s sake; to contemplate a temporal thing neither alone nor together with God’s kingdom [lacuna] is not”—is incomplete. For we ought not set these two things before ourselves as two ends, but one for the sake of the other.

Since both eternal and temporal things are to be sought, but the latter for the former, one must know that temporal things are to be sought differently from eternal things. We ought to seek eternal things confidently and openly, because it is evident to all that we need them. But we ought not seek temporal things so openly; rather, with a certain condition, as when I say: “Almighty God, give me this and this, if you know that they are beneficial for me.” This is how we ought to ask, as shown by Christ’s example, when he said: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. XXVI; Mark XIV; Luke XX). He did not simply say, “Let it pass,” but, “If it is possible”; and he also added: “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will; let your will be done” (ibid.). Likewise, blessed Martin, when, for the benefit of his brothers who cried out, “Why, Father, are you leaving us? Or to whom do you leave us desolate?” he asked to live, did not ask so openly, but with this qualification: “If I am still necessary to your people, I do not refuse the labor; let your will be done.” Let us seek temporal things according to the example of Christ and Martin.

Some customarily form certain unsuitable comparisons regarding this question: whether God ought to be praised equally for temporal and eternal things, and prayed to equally for them. Whenever you hear this, criticize the incongruity of the expression—as if one said, “This man goes to Pavia as quickly as to Rome,” or “This man desires a physician and health equally,” or “wine and the taste of wine equally.”

Again, a will seems to have not merely diverse but even contrary ends, as when a person sins and wishes to sin because he delights in his sin and because he knows that God’s mercy is so great that it is sufficient for the blotting out of all sins. Here he proposes two ends, each evil: delighting in sin is evil, and so trusting in God’s mercy is also sin, namely, when excessive confidence makes us unafraid to sin. This is to sin against the Holy Spirit, and such a sin will never be forgiven [Note: [Col. 1007D] The Master, II, dist. 43.]. Hence: “Whoever sins against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come” (Luke XII). And John says: “There is a sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for it” (1 John V). And: “Cursed is everyone who sins in hope.” Therefore we must consider what sin against the Holy Spirit is, having first shown how many species of it there are. There are two: obstinacy and opposition to truth.

Obstinacy is the persistence of a mind hardened in wickedness, by which a person becomes unrepentant. There are two species of obstinacy: despair and presumption. Despair is that by which someone loses confidence in God’s mercy, judging the magnitude of sin to exceed the measure of divine goodness. Presumption is that by which someone abuses God’s mercy and, trusting his goodness beyond measure, attempts to render God’s justice void.

Both presumption and despair are called sin against the Holy Spirit, and not without reason. For in despair someone judges the greatness of sin to exceed the measure of God’s goodness, and thus, so far as he can, diminishes the measure of that goodness—as the one who said, “My iniquity is greater than that I may deserve forgiveness” (Gen. IV). But God’s goodness is properly and principally called [Col. 1008A] the Holy Spirit, just as the love of the Father and the Son is properly called the Holy Spirit. Likewise, in presumption there is, so far as a human being can do it, an abuse of God’s mercy and goodness, because someone trusts it too greatly and presumes that God will leave all sins unpunished, thus giving liberty as an occasion for the flesh and license to sin. Whoever does this attempts, so far as he can, to establish that God is not just.

It should nevertheless be noted [Note: [Col. 1007D] See Ambrose, *On the Holy Spirit*, I.3, at the end.] that one who sins thus sins against the Father and the Son just as against the Holy Spirit. The offense is common to the three Persons. One is said to sin against the Holy Spirit according to the appropriation of the name, not of the reality, because one sins against God’s goodness, whose name, not whose reality, is appropriated to the Holy Spirit; for Father, Son, and Holy Spirit [Col. 1008B] are one goodness.

The question is whether every despair or presumption is sin against the Holy Spirit. Some say so, and say that such sin is called unforgivable not because it cannot be forgiven, but because it is not easily forgiven; for it can be forgiven through repentance. Hence: “I will turn them into the depths of the sea” (Ps. LXVII); elsewhere: “He sends forth his crystal like morsels” (Ps. CXLVII); and elsewhere: “He brought out the bound in strength, likewise also those who provoke [him], who dwell in tombs” (Ps. LXVII). [Note: [Col. 1008D] See Augustine’s exposition on these passages, to which the author alludes.] Others say that not every presumption or despair is sin against the Holy Spirit, but only that which is accompanied by final impenitence—that is, one of which [Col. 1008C] a person will never repent. According to these, such a sin is called unforgivable because it is not forgiven. For no one will ever repent of it, since final impenitence will always accompany this sin. But they are asked: since, as they say, no one will repent of such impenitence, can he repent of it? If they say yes, the contrary follows: no one can repent of this impenitence. Therefore it can never be forgiven, since it is itself sin.

That no one can repent of final impenitence may be indirectly proved. Suppose that this person will repent of final impenitence. Then he will cease to have it. Therefore he will have it. Therefore he will be obstinate until the end of life. Therefore he will repent of no sin. Therefore he will not repent of final impenitence. Again, if he will repent of final impenitence [Col. 1008D], he will repent of no sin. He will have it until the end of life; and if he has it until the end of life, he will repent of no sin. Therefore, if he repents of impenitence, he repents of no sin. But the contrary is true: if he repents of impenitence, he repents of this sin. Therefore, if he repents of impenitence, he repents of some sin. Thus it seems possible to show that no one can repent of final impenitence.

Yet the contrary is argued thus. Someone can repent fully and perfectly of some sin; but he cannot repent perfectly of one without repenting of every sin. [Col. 1009A] Therefore he can repent of final impenitence. Again, no one is damned except because he does not repent. Therefore no one is damned except on account of final impenitence. Therefore no one is damned unless he sins against the Holy Spirit—which is false. If someone again says that a person can repent of final impenitence, the question is: when? Either after death, or in the last moment of life, or before the last moment. But it is certain that after death there is no place for repentance. If he repents at the last moment of his life, that impenitence is not final. If he repents before the last moment, it is even less final. Thus no one can ever repent of it.

Some say that no one can repent of [Col. 1009B] final impenitence. For this expression denotes two things: that the person had final impenitence and that he ceases to have it. But this is impossible, especially since he is still to live; for then it would not be final. It is like the expression “to begin,” when it is said: “God can begin to predestine this person.” It denotes that God predestines this person and did not previously predestine him—which is false, since he predestines no one whom he has not predestined from eternity. Thus they say that this person cannot repent of final impenitence: he can indeed act so that he does not incur it, but he cannot act so that he loses it.

But the objection is made: this person cannot repent of final impenitence; therefore it should not be imputed to him [Col. 1009C] as sin. They press the point in this manner: the devil cannot repent; therefore his sins should not be imputed to him. Yet anyone who looks more attentively will see that someone can repent of final impenitence in this sense: of impenitence which is final, not of impenitence which would be final if he repented. Thus it is said that blackness will be in what is white—that is, in that which will be white, not in something that is at once white and black.

Suppose that this person will live until A and then die, and after A there follow B and C, which are two instants. This person can be going to live at B, because, although he will die at A, his life could be prolonged until B and C. Thus, this person can be going to live at B, or can in this way be at B. Let us now coin such a participle: he can be going to repent at B of this impenitence which he will cease to have before B. Therefore he can be going to repent of final impenitence itself—that is, impenitence which is in him, or which will be final in him—not of final impenitence in the sense of that which would then be final if he repented.

Here they make the distinction between composition and division, as when it is said, “This person can see with closed eyes.” In the divided sense—that is, with eyes which are closed—it is true; in the composite sense—namely, that they are simultaneously closed and seeing—it is false. Yet when, on the part of the subject, it is said [Col. 1010A], “With closed eyes this person can see,” the sense of division is stronger, and the statement is true. Likewise, this person can repent of final impenitence; but if he repents, it will no longer be final. Therefore, if these things are placed in the predicate, the sense of composition is stronger, and the expression approaches falsehood.

Others, more plausibly and more truly in my view, maintain that “impenitence” is improperly said by itself, but is said in relation to a theft, homicide, or something of that sort. Such a construction can only remove [the qualification], so that the sense is: “a theft of which someone does not repent”; and then it is not sin against the Holy Spirit. It can also posit and remove [the qualification], so that the sense is: “impenitence concerning theft,” that is, theft of which someone [Note: [Col. 1009D] This negation seems to be deleted.] resolves not to repent; and such a resolution is [Col. 1010B] sin against the Holy Spirit, of which someone can repent, though with the greatest difficulty. They say the same about perseverance, as will later be explained in the *Treatise on the Virtues*.

[Note: [Col. 1009D] The Master here, § C.] Having therefore dealt with the first species of sin against the Holy Spirit, we must return to the other, called opposition to truth. Augustine says of it [Note: [Col. 1009D] Book I, *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, not far from the end.]: “Sin against the Holy Spirit occurs when, after knowledge of God through Christ’s grace, someone attacks brotherhood and is stirred by the torches of envy against the grace by which he has been reconciled to God.” This, however, is not to be understood unless impenitence accompanies it—that is, a resolve not to repent. [Note: [Col. 1010D] See Augustine, Sermon 11, *On the Words of the Lord*, after the middle.] Hence one must pray for every person on the way, for—unless it has miraculously been revealed to someone—while on the way [Col. 1010C] it cannot be known who sins against the Holy Spirit. Thus what John says, “There is a sin unto death,” etc. (1 John V), must be understood of those who have already died in unbelief, for whom the Church does not pray. Yet it prays for them while they live and can still merit, as for Jews and pagans. [Note: [Col. 1010D] He alludes to what Augustine says near the end of Book I, *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*.]

This sin consists in opposition to truth and envy of brotherhood. It is called unforgivable not because it cannot be forgiven, but because the stain of this sin is so great that it does not permit a person even to descend to the humility of repentance. Thus, when Judas recognized that he had sinned both by opposing truth and by envying the brotherhood and fellowship of Christ, and said, “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood” (Matt. XXVII), he ran more quickly to the noose than to repentance or the groan of contrition, more quickly to undergo punishment than to seek pardon.

But although it has been said that the sins previously mentioned are sins against the Holy Spirit if obstinacy is present—as with homicide and adultery [Note: [Col. 1010D] Something seems to be missing here.]—this is not true, because sin against the Holy Spirit is specifically that which is committed against God’s goodness. A person sins in three ways: through weakness, through ignorance, and through deliberate malice. One who sins through weakness [Col. 1011A] is said to sin against the Father, because power is attributed to the Father by name, although in reality it belongs to the three Persons. One who sins through ignorance is said to sin against the Son, because wisdom is attributed to the Son by name and not in reality. One who sins through deliberate malice is said to sin against the Holy Spirit, because goodness is customarily appropriated to the Holy Spirit, and one who sins deliberately does so from malice. It should nevertheless be understood that the offense against the three Persons is undivided; but on account of the foregoing consideration, such appropriations and species of sins are customarily made.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On Adam’s sin, where it is asked whether Adam sinned more grievously than Eve.

[Col. 1011B] [Note: [Col. 1011D] The Master, II, dist. 22.] Having carefully pursued the four topics noted above, insofar as the difficulty of the matter and the capacity of our intellect allowed—namely, from what actual sin has its origin, in what thing it exists, what it is, and how many kinds of actual sins there are—we must proceed to original sin. This should have been discussed earlier, had not another, weightier reason compelled us to alter this order. But because original sin is drawn from the corruption of the flesh, whose cause was Adam’s first actual sin, let us dispose of that sin, so that we may finally return to original sin.

[Note: [Col. 1011D] Book II, *On Genesis*, ch. 30.] The first question arising here is whether that sin had an origin, and whether, as Augustine would have it, a certain exaltation preceded it. For he says: [Note: [Col. 1011D] Same book, ch. 5.] “In the first human being, a certain exaltation needing to be checked preceded.” But on this account the preceding solution is advanced [Note: [Col. 1011D] The Master here, § B.], by which Lucifer’s sin is said to be irremediable and Adam’s sin remediable. For Lucifer’s sin was called irremediable because he sinned from his own innate malice—namely, from pride—with no preceding external temptation. Human sin, however, was called remediable because that sin had its origin in a preceding temptation. To this it must be said that temptation preceded exaltation, and exaltation preceded the deed; thus the deed had its origin in exaltation, but earlier still in temptation. For exaltation was present in both parents, but it was greater in Eve than in Adam. For when [Col. 1011D] the devil had said, “You shall be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. III), she thought that she could be equal to God. Adam, because he was most wise, never thought that he could be equal to God; and thus he was not deceived in the way in which the woman was. Therefore the Apostle says that he was not deceived (1 Tim. II). Yet he was deceived in this: he thought pardonable what was mortal; nevertheless, he was neither deceived first nor deceived in the same respect as the woman. Therefore not so great an exaltation preceded in him as in the woman. [Note: [Col. 1011D] Augustine has all this, and much else besides, here in Book II, [Col. 1012D] *On Genesis*, final chapter.] “Yet he sinned through a kind of friendly goodwill, by which God is often offended lest a friend be offended. For he did not wish to grieve his companion, whom he believed would perish without his consolation and waste away when estranged from him.”

Yet Adam appears to have sinned equally. For Augustine says: [Note: [Col. 1012D] Book II, *On Genesis*, ch. 35.] “They sinned with unequal sex, but equal arrogance.” Therefore, with equal pride; therefore, with equal contempt; therefore, equally. To this it must be said that this equality should be referred to their excuse, because they excused themselves alike. Or this equality should be referred to the eating of the forbidden tree, of which they both ate; for one sin is called equal to another either because it is of the same kind, or because it is equally enduring, or because it was committed arrogantly.

[Col. 1012B] Again, since it has been said that Adam never thought he could be equal to God, an objection is raised. For the Apostle says: “He did not consider equality with God a thing to be seized” (Phil. II). On this passage one reads: [Note: [Col. 1012D] See the Gloss there.] “Like the devil and the first human being.” Therefore it must be explained thus: “Like the first human being,” that is, like Eve, who was made from the first human being; just as “through the first human being death entered the world,” that is, through Eve, who was made from the first human being and sinned first. Or it may be said that although Adam did not believe that he could become equal to God, he nevertheless took delight in the promise. Eve, however, delighted in it because she believed it more fully. Thus a poor man takes delight when told, “You will be king or pope,” although he believes [Col. 1012C] that it can never happen. [Note: [Col. 1012D] I have supplied these points from Augustine, Book II, *On Genesis*, final chapter.]

Again, Adam sinned deliberately; Eve sinned ignorantly, because she was, as it were, [of limited understanding]. To sin deliberately is more serious than to sin through weakness, and more serious than through ignorance; therefore Adam sinned more than Eve. That Eve sinned ignorantly can be proved thus. Eve believed the devil; therefore she believed that she would become like God. She also believed that by eating that tree her good could not be lost, but rather increased. Therefore she believed that she was not sinning; since, then, she did sin, she sinned ignorantly. But against this: she knew that God had given her a command not to eat. Therefore she knew that it was a sin to act contrary to it. Therefore she sinned knowingly. Again, the woman had no excuse from ignorance, since she knew the command and did not fail to know that it was sin [Col. 1012D] to act otherwise.

They therefore say that the woman was so blinded by ambition at the promise, “You shall be like gods,” and so forth, that she did not even notice that it was God’s command, nor consider that acting against it was sin. Therefore she sinned ignorantly; therefore, through ignorance. This is not true: it is a fallacy. God punishes mercifully everyone whom he punishes eternally; therefore, he punishes eternally out of mercy. For although she sinned ignorantly, she did not therefore sin through ignorance, because ignorance was not the principal cause of that sin, but [Col. 1013A] a depraved will. Thus every good comes from free choice, yet the first good is not said to come from free choice but from grace alone, because grace is its principal cause.

[Note: [Col. 1013D] This excuse is removed from them when a command is given or knowledge of how not to sin is made manifest. So Augustine, *On Grace and Free Will*, ch. 2.] But Augustine’s statement that the excuse of ignorance is removed both where the command is known and where there is no doubt that acting contrary to it is sin may be understood to have been true before the suggestion. For then she knew the command and did not fail to know that opposing the command was sin. Or it may be said that she then knew both things and, by that sin, believed that she would be perfected in every good and diminished in none. Thus Antichrist will believe that through sin he will rise to immortality, as is found in the Psalm: “I shall not be moved from generation to generation [Col. 1013B] without evil” (Ps. IX), that is, “I shall move from this mortal generation to an immortal one, and this will not be without evil,” [Note: [Col. 1013D] So Augustine, in his exposition of this verse of the Psalm.] that is, without sin and wicked arts.

Some also ask here matters whose names we believe unknown, but whose knowledge we do not think necessary for attaining salvation: namely, if the woman had sinned and not the man, whether the human race would have been corrupted, or another woman formed for him; or if both had consented in will but not in deed, whether the corruption would have been only in the mind and not in the flesh; or if they had remained standing and their children had transgressed, whether the parents would be punished for their children’s sins, as would the children themselves. They further entertain questions about the old age [Col. 1013C] of the first parent and other such matters, in which more curiosity than usefulness is found.

This, however, seems much more relevant: did Lucifer believe that what he sought would come to pass? If so, then he believed that he could become equal to God; therefore he believed that his state could be made equal . . . [lacuna] and made lesser in no respect. But he knew that this could not occur if he sinned with that will; therefore he believed that he was not sinning by that will. Therefore he sinned ignorantly. Again, he knew that he was a creature and that God was the Creator. Therefore he knew that he could not be made equal to God, since no creature can be made equal to God. Again, Lucifer wished to be as God, but he knew that this could not be unless he were God. Therefore he wished to be God; but he knew that he could not [Col. 1013D] be the God who created him, nor another God, because he knew that there could be only one, as he knows this now, since this knowledge did not increase in him afterward.

Therefore some say that he wished to be like God not by imitation but by equality of knowledge. Yet it seems truer that he wished to be equal to God, although he knew that this could not be; and for that reason he sinned no less, indeed much more grievously. Yet, since such matters are not fully settled, to doubt [Col. 1014A] about them is not useless. This, however, must be known: we suffer every defect, both of soul and body, because of disobedience. Our sins too, which contracted their origin from them, are defects and passions of the soul—such as anger, sadness, pain, and excessive joy—and of the body, such as hunger, thirst, and cold. Yet every such passion is in the soul, though they are attributed to the body because the soul does not feel them except in the body and through the body’s instrument. And, as above we arranged this order—first to say what the human being made before sin was like in body and then what he was like in soul—so also we shall treat of his restoration: first we shall teach how his soul is restored, afterward how his body is restored, so that the same order observed in formation may be [Col. 1014B] maintained in deformation [restoration], and nearly the same order also followed in the final restoration.

## CHAPTER XIX. What the Human Being Is Like in Body; Here Original Sin Is Discussed

[Note: [Col. 1013D] Master, II, dist. 30 and following. For a proper understanding of the difficulties of [Col. 1014D] this chapter, see what I have written in my observations on ch. 28 of Pullus’s *Sentences*, Part II.] In respect of the body, therefore, a human being suffers hunger, thirst, sickness, and the like, and beyond these, “deadness,” so to speak. For although before sin the human being was mortal—that is, able to die and able not to die—after sin he did not possess such mortality, but rather deadness, because he is necessarily subject to death. Hence the Apostle says that after sin the human body was dead (Rom. V).

[Col. 1014C] Beyond these defects there is also another defect of human nature after sin: namely, a certain foulness, a certain stain arising from the ardent intercourse of the parents. This is the cause of original sin and, according to [Note: [Col. 1014D] Master, II, dist. 30, § E.] some, original sin itself: the liability to punishment, that is, the debt by which a human being is bound to temporal or eternal punishment for the sin of the first human being. This debt is neither punishment nor fault [Note: [Col. 1014D] He says this only as another’s opinion, as does the Master cited.], and thus is not sin, but is simply original sin. Like this statement: “A human being is dead,” yet “dead” is not a human being. And it is called original sin because through their parents’ sin human beings are bound to punishment, just as by civil judgment children are exiled for their parents’ crime.

Others say that [Col. 1014D] original sin is ignorance of good and desire for evil. Hence Augustine: “There are two comprehensive defects in a human being: ignorance and difficulty. From ignorance comes error, by which a person accepts the false for the true; from difficulty, distress, so that, when restrained by the carnal bond, a person cannot restrain himself from lust.” But how can desire for evil or ignorance of good be in this infant’s soul? He does not yet desire anything, nor is he ignorant of anything. For he is ignorant of nothing that at such an age he ought to know. Therefore it must be said that in him there is the beginning of desire, not the movement of desire. For the term *concupiscentia* is equivocal: it denotes movements of desire, a vice, and a natural faculty of the soul. Likewise, in this child’s soul ignorance is the vice of ignorance, just as in the eye of a blind person the defect is present during the night, although the difference between the seeing and the blind is not perceived until daylight comes. Thus in the child’s soul are the vice of desire and the vice of ignorance, but they are not discerned until the age of discretion arrives; for then he begins to desire evil and to be ignorant of good.

It is clear from this, therefore, that according to some original sin consists of two things: desire for evil and ignorance of good. Hence the Prophet says in the plural: [Col. 1015B] “In my sins my mother conceived me” (Ps. L), that is, in desire and ignorance. At times original sin is spoken of in the singular because ignorance depends [on] desire. For if desire had not preceded, ignorance would never follow. They wish to maintain that ignorance is original sin from Augustine’s statement on the Psalm verse, “The sins of my youth,” and so forth (Ps. XXIV).

Some, however—indeed almost all—sometimes say that original sin is nothing but concupiscibility, not reckoning ignorance as part of original sin. Following the public highway with them, let us say that concupiscibility, not ignorance, is original sin, which is in the soul, not in the body. [Col. 1015C] It is nevertheless said to dwell in the flesh because in the flesh there is a certain carnal corruption arising from the fact that it is transmitted through a defective generation from other flesh. This corruption is the cause of original sin, but is not original sin, because it is not sin. For if it were, then that little piece of flesh in which this carnal corruption exists would be punished for that sin if no soul were infused into it; which is not true. Since the soul is not infused into the body before forty-six days, if the woman died before then, that little piece of flesh would not be damned in itself. It is therefore clear that this corruption is not fault, for fault exists only in the spirit. Therefore that corruption is not original sin, which exists in the soul as its cause.

[Col. 1015D] But it appears that the soul ought not to be guilty of that sin immediately when it is infused, because this soul is infused by God into this body whether it wills it or not; and that union of body and soul does not displease God, nor has this soul deserved any punishment. Therefore original sin should not be imputed to it. Again, this soul never existed without being in a body, and it was never in a body without having sin. Therefore this soul never existed without sin. Therefore it never had the perfection by which it could stand. Therefore its failure to stand should not be imputed to it. For this is commonly given as the reason why the angels are charged with having fallen: they possessed the grace by which they could stand, and, if they did not have that by which they could advance, [Col. 1016A] they did at least have that by which they could stand. But if they had had no grace by which they could stand, their failure to stand would not have been imputed to them. Likewise, this soul never had grace by which it could stand: in being created it was infused, and in being infused it was created, and immediately it was unclean. Therefore it seems that sin should not be imputed to it.

Again, since the soul, when it is infused, has no stain of itself, why then is the stain of the flesh imputed to it as sin? This would be easy to solve if the soul, like the body, were derived by propagation. For one could say that, just as in Adam all bodies descending from him by seminal principle were corrupted, so in him—that is, in Adam—all souls were corrupted. But this cannot be said, because the soul is not derived by propagation as the body is; rather, [Col. 1016B] God daily creates new souls. Again, this soul, when created, was either clean or unclean. If clean, then at some time it was clean. But it never existed without being in a body; therefore it was clean in a body. If, however, it was created unclean, that uncleanness does not appear imputable to it as sin. Again, original sin is either voluntary or necessary. If necessary, then unavoidable; if unavoidable, then it cannot be avoided; therefore it should not be imputed to the soul. But it is not voluntary, because it did not proceed from free choice.

To this some say that the soul in some manner takes delight when it is infused into the body. In that infusion there is a certain social delight, and therefore the [Col. 1016C] soul itself is guilty of sin. But on this account that sin would be actual rather than original. Others, however, say better that in the first human being the soul was corrupted first and afterward the flesh. That corruption was not fault but punishment; and the corrupted soul made the flesh corrupted, not the reverse. In us the reverse occurs: the corrupted flesh corrupts the soul, and thus there is here, as it were, a certain retribution. For when in the first human being the soul, already corrupted through sin, corrupts the flesh still incorrupt, in us, as a kind of retribution [for] the first sin, the flesh corrupts the soul—and does so in all descendants—and therefore the soul is held guilty of sin.

We shall therefore answer the foregoing arguments in order. When, then, it is first said: “That [Col. 1016D] union of soul and body does not displease God, nor has the soul deserved any punishment; therefore it should not be imputed to it,” this is a fallacy. God is not displeased that Antichrist will come to be, nor has Antichrist deserved God’s rejection; therefore that rejection is not imputed to him. Again, the subsequent assertion that the soul never possessed the perfection by which it could stand is false, because it received nothing from God except good, in which, unless it had been corrupted by the admixture of flesh, it could have remained clean.

Here someone commonly frames the question: [Note: [Col. 1015D] Perhaps he means Pullus, who raises that question in ch. 28 of the second part.] if it could happen that some particle of flesh were transmitted from flesh without the defect of concupiscence, and a soul were infused into that flesh, would that soul be guilty of original sin, as perhaps was the case in [Col. 1017A] the resurrected Lazarus? Some answer that original sin comes partly from the defect of desiring and partly from corrupted flesh. [Note: [Col. 1017D] See Master, III, dist. 3.] Hence, for Christ to be free of original sin, it was necessary that the flesh he assumed be cleansed. For perhaps, if it had not been cleansed, although conceived without concupiscence, Christ would have had original sin.

When it is later asked whether the soul was clean or unclean, we say: clean, that is, by creation it possessed nothing but cleanness. But if you understand it thus—“it was created clean,” that is, existing in a clean condition—this is false. The argument was: “It was created clean; therefore it was clean at some time.” This is a fallacy. “This apple was given clean into your hands; therefore it was clean in your hands”—supposing that your hands become unclean [Col. 1017B] and that as soon as the apple was in them it became dirty.

Now that sin is called original because we have received flesh from our parents under a defective law, that is, according to carnal concupiscence. It is not called original because corrupt flesh is drawn from corrupt flesh. [Note: [Col. 1017D] In sense and wording this coheres with the Master, II, dist. 31, § h.] For in that case Christ would have had original sin, since his flesh was derived from the flesh of the Virgin, which was corrupted through original sin. But it is called original because that propagation occurs lustfully. Therefore the manner of transmission produces the sin, not transmission itself. Hence Augustine [Note: [Col. 1017D] Rather, Fulgentius, *On Faith to Peter*, ch. 2, [Col. 1018D] middle.] says: “It is not propagation but lust that pours the defect into children; not fertility but foulness.” But Christ’s conception was not performed through carnal concupiscence, but through the power of [Col. 1017C] the Holy Spirit; hence he was free from original sin. It is clear from this, therefore, that the third question was: how original sin was transmitted.

[Note: [Col. 1018D] Master, II, dist. 30, § m.] But an objection is made to the statement that we have all been transmitted from Adam and all sinned in Adam. For there were not as many atoms in Adam’s body as there are people descended from him. And if all were in Adam, it follows that Adam’s body exceeded the size of all bodies. To this it must be said that all human beings were in Adam’s body not essentially but by seminal principle. Yet some wish to prove that all were essentially in Adam as well. Whatever was part of Cain’s body was part of Adam’s body. This is a fallacy. Whatever was [Col. 1017D] part of the body of Cain’s son was part of Cain’s body; therefore whatever was part of the body of Cain’s son was part of Adam’s body. But whatever was part of Adam’s body was essentially in him. Therefore whatever was part of the body of Cain’s son was essentially in Adam, and thus Cain in his entirety was essentially in Adam. By the same reasoning, the son’s son, the great-grandson’s son, and so on to the last human being; and thus all human beings were essentially in Adam. Perhaps someone will deny the proposition and assumption of the preceding parallel argument; [Col. 1018A] for they are of the same kind. Either point may be asked; if denied, it will easily be proved.

But first let three states of the body be distinguished before a human being is born. The human body immediately after conception is a kind of fluid, which is gradually thickened a little each day. In the second state, within forty-six days, there is a formed body, that is, one possessing the shape and features of a human body. In the third state, after the forty-sixth day, the soul is infused into the body, and a human being comes to be from soul and body. Thus it may be said: whatever was part of Cain’s body while it existed as fluid was part of Adam’s body. For it is certain that that fluid flowed from Adam’s substance. Likewise, whatever was part of that body on the second or third day was previously part [Col. 1018B] of Adam’s body; and in this way progress may be made up to the time of the soul’s infusion. Thus whatever was part of that ensouled body was part of Adam’s body. By the same reasoning, it may likewise be said of every human being that whatever was part of his body was part of Adam’s body, and thus was essentially in him.

This reasoning appears probable. For where can the respondent stop in a state of the body, unless it be said that whatever was part of Cain’s body existing as fluid or as formed was part of Adam’s body, but that one must not proceed further? It seems more appropriate to stop at the time when the body is still fluid than at any other. But if someone says that whatever is part of Cain’s fluid body was part [Col. 1018C] of Adam’s body, but not everything that is part of his formed body or ensouled body was part of Adam’s body, by the same reasoning by which this is said, not everything will be said . . . [lacuna] and thus, since whatever was part of Cain’s fluid body was part of Adam’s body, but nothing that was part of the formed or even ensouled body [was part of Adam’s body], therefore nothing that was part of the fluid body was part of the formed body. Therefore this is different from that. Likewise, the ensouled is different from the formed—which is an unfitting thing to say.

There are, then, those who say that the semen which issued from Adam and from which Cain was formed was never in Adam, because it was never part of him; rather, it was transmitted from him through carnal intercourse, as a crop comes from grain through nature’s operation, although the crop was never [Col. 1018D] in the grain. Hence, even if an ensouled body were not made from it, it would not return at the resurrection to the body from which it was transmitted, but would perish, according to Augustine, who says: [Note: [Col. 1018D] *Enchiridion*, ch. 87.] “Who would not be more inclined to think that unformed offspring perish, like seeds not yet ensouled?”

The question is asked how children contract original sin from their parents, when their parents have been cleansed of original sin by the sacrament of baptism. For how do they contract original [Col. 1019A] sin from those in whom it does not exist? Yet Augustine shows that it is so by two comparisons: [Note: [Col. 1019D] Book III, ch. 8, *On the Baptism of Infants*, or *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*.] just as children are born with a foreskin from parents who do not have a foreskin, so children are born with original sin from parents who do not have original sin; likewise, just as wheat is cleansed by human diligence both of chaff and awns, yet wheat with chaff and awns is born from it, so, when parents have been cleansed of original sin, children with original sin are born from them.

Yet by these two comparisons Augustine shows that it is so, but does not show [quod, “that”; corrected to quomodo, “how”] it is so. Thus he does not appear to have settled the question plainly. Some therefore press the question more strongly. Let it be supposed that [Col. 1019B] an adult man and an adult woman are cleansed by the sacrament of baptism from original sin and also from every actual sin, and are immediately joined in lawful marriage. The man immediately has intercourse with his wife, also with the intention of having offspring. In that act he emits from himself a portion of his substance; that small portion is free from every liability to punishment. For the entire flesh of the human being is free from all liability to punishment. Hence if he died then, he would suffer no punishment, neither in soul nor body.

Although the human being’s passion is in the spirit, a certain passion is said to be in the body because it is present in the soul through the body; and flesh is said to be liable to punishment not because any liability exists in the body, or because the body suffers anything in itself without the soul, but because the soul is punished by certain passions according to the body, none of which it can suffer without the body, [Col. 1019C] even in hell. This is clear in the present life: the soul would never suffer hunger except through the body with which it is joined. Hence when separated from it, the soul does not suffer hunger for bodily food.

But when the forty-sixth day has arrived, a soul clean in itself is infused into it, and that union does not displease God. [Note: [Col. 1019D] Julian proposed similar points to Augustine, Book II, *On Marriage*, etc., ch. 28 and following.] Say, then, from what source does the child, consisting of these two most clean things, draw original sin? If someone says that the pleasure which the man had in intercourse was sin, and that the portion flowing from it drew sin from there, this is not true, for that pleasure is excused by the goods of marriage. [Col. 1019D] Even if that pleasure were sin, it would redound rather upon the parents who experienced that pleasure than upon that small piece of flesh which felt nothing.

Again, if someone says that that little piece of flesh into which no soul has yet been infused—for we are speaking of this—is liable to punishment, then, on the supposition that it will never be ensouled, one asks whether it will return at the resurrection to the man’s body from which it was emitted. This seems so, for whatever belongs to the truth of human nature will rise at judgment, since not even a hair from the head will perish [Col. 1020A] (Luke XXI). If this is so, then, since the man dies in this condition and is in charity, his body will be glorified at the resurrection. But if no soul were infused into it, this little piece of flesh would be part of that body in the resurrection; and since it is now liable to punishment, the soul would therefore be punished at the resurrection according to that part while the other parts of the body were unpunished—which cannot be. The solution to this objection is clear from what has been said above, because semen will not rise; or it may be said that even if it is to rise, since the flesh of the person who dies in charity will rise glorified, that part which returns to this body in the resurrection will be glorified and thus incorrupt.

[Note: [Col. 1019D] Master, II, dist. 33.] The question is also asked whether parents’ sins are transmitted to their children, as Adam’s sin is transmitted [Col. 1020B] to posterity. This appears to be so. For just as all human beings were in Adam by seminal principle, so children are in their parents and descend from them. Augustine also seems to mean this when he says: [Note: [Col. 1020D] *Enchiridion*, ch. 46.] “It is not irrationally said that children are bound to punishment for the sins of their parents—not only of the first parents, but also of their own parents from whom they are born.” Here he seems plainly to say that children are bound by their parents’ sins. And elsewhere: “Those sins of parents which parents commit after their children are already born do not pertain to the children.” As though to say: those sins pertain to them which are in the parents when they generate them. Moreover, one reads in Exodus: “I am a jealous God, visiting the sins of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation” (Exod. XX). If this is said, it follows that [Col. 1020C] a child who has had many parents and ancestors, and who is more remote from Adam in the sequence of generations, is all the more [obligaturus, “about to bind”; corrected to obligandus, “bound”] by sins. It also follows that an infant of one day is to be punished more than his father, since he is held guilty of his own original sin and of all the actual sins of his father, from whom he descends by seminal principle.

Therefore it must be said that parents’ sins are not transmitted to children except the sin of the first human being alone. That sin, rather than others, is asked about because all were materially in Adam, and he possessed the perfection of flesh by which he could stand. For before sin he had incorrupt flesh, whereas all who descend from him have corrupt flesh; and in no descendant of his were all present seminally as they were in Adam. Augustine afterward retracted and corrected [Col. 1020D] what he had said. [Note: [Col. 1020D] *Enchiridion*, ch. 93, Book I.] [Note: [Col. 1020D] *On the Merits of Sins*, ch. 15; Book V, *Against Julian*, ch. 11, etc.] Hence he himself said: “Certainly the mildest punishment will be for those who have not added sin to the original sin which they contracted.” They will have this punishment alone: they will not enjoy the vision of God, because of the stain of original sin.

Thus someone who is to be brought before a king is condemned by nothing else than that he does not see him because of a stain he contracted on the way, when he accidentally cast himself into mud. [Col. 1021A] Likewise, an infant is condemned by his own sin, just as wine placed in a corrupt vessel acquires in itself a corrupt taste, though it has contracted it from the cask.

Yet the statement that Adam’s entire posterity is made guilty because of his sin must be understood cautiously, so that the preposition *pro* (“for” or “because of”) signifies occasion, not cause. For is one person’s sin the cause why another is punished eternally? But it can be an occasion of punishment for another. Hence, when the Lord says that he visits the sins of parents upon their children, it must be understood of temporal, not eternal, punishment. Or he is said to visit the fathers’ sins upon the children because he punishes imitators of paternal wickedness for their fathers’ sins—that is, for their own sins in which they imitate their fathers. [Col. 1021B] [Note: [Col. 1021D] Master, II, dist. 33.] For they are heirs not only of their fathers’ inheritance but also of their fathers’ wickedness. Thus he says, “The sins of the fathers upon the children,” naming fathers and children, although the Lord likewise punishes imitators of strangers’ wickedness, because children are more accustomed to imitate their fathers. And he says, “to the third and fourth generation,” because fathers commonly live for so long a span of time that their children, seeing them, imitate them. For all are teachable and apt to imitate in the times [of their youth].

Yet it appears possible to show that Adam’s sin is the cause why a human being is eternally damned, because Adam’s sin is the cause why another person is eternally punished through every corruption that we suffer. Therefore it is also the cause of the corruption in the flesh. But [Col. 1021C] that corruption is the cause of the corruption in the soul, which is original sin. Therefore Adam’s sin is the cause why another human being is eternally punished. But if it is said that original sin in the soul is the cause of the corruption in the body—an interpretation Jerome seems to intend in his commentary on Jeremiah, when he says, “Whatever evil happens to us is from our own fault”—then the corruption of the soul naturally precedes the corruption of the body, although it is certain that the corruption in the body precedes in both time and nature that in the soul. To this it must be said that Adam’s sin is the cause of the corruption in the body, and the corruption of the body is the cause of the corruption of the soul—that is, of original sin or of the punishment due to that sin—just as God is the cause of free choice [Col. 1021D] in a human being, and free choice is the cause of sin, though God is not the cause of sin.

[Note: [Col. 1021D] Master, II, dist. 32.] It remains to investigate how original sin is remitted through baptism. For it appears not to be remitted through baptism: concupiscibility remains after baptism; therefore either concupiscibility is not original sin, or original sin remains after baptism. Likewise, ignorance remains after baptism. Therefore either it is not original sin or original sin remains after baptism. Therefore it is not destroyed in baptism.

To this some say that ignorance is not original [Col. 1022A] sin but actual sin. But this answer raises a more difficult question. It then appears that a person cannot repent of every actual sin, because he cannot repent of ignorance. For since ignorance is in a person, infinitely many things unknown to him are subject to his ignorance, and he cannot confess them. It also follows that an actual sin passes away in liability but not in actuality, though the opposite is the case. For this is commonly given as the difference between actual and original sin: original sin passes away in liability but not in actuality; actual sin, however, passes away in actuality but not in liability, until it is removed through confession and penitence.

Therefore, if ignorance is called actual sin, it follows that actual sin passes away in liability but not in actuality. For a person has ignorance, repents of that sin, confesses [Col. 1022B] that he is ignorant, has great contrition of heart, and performs penance. Behold, that sin is forgiven in liability, but still remains, since he still does not know everything that he previously did not know. But this question was above left undecided. For I do not see how ignorance is not original sin, just as concupiscibility is, since men of great authority said so; yet now almost all modern writers oppose them. Therefore, not daring to assert anything against the common opinion of all, I leave the matter undiscussed.

[Note: [Col. 1021D] From Augustine, Book I *On Marriage*, etc., ch. 25.] It should rather be said that original sin is said to be remitted through baptism in two ways. First, because carnal concupiscence is so diminished through baptism [Col. 1022C] that it remains slight and weak, unless someone gives weapons to the enemy and consents to concupiscence; for then it is actual sin. Again, it is said to be remitted through baptism because its guilt is wholly erased by baptism, and after baptism it is not mortal sin. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1022D] Augustine, cited above, ch. 26; but somewhat differently.]:

> “Carnal concupiscence is remitted through baptism, not in such a way that it does not exist, but that it is not imputed as sin. For this is to have no sin: not to be guilty of sin. Therefore, just as other sins pass away in act, not in guilt—as homicide does—so, conversely, concupiscence after baptism passes away in guilt and not in act.”

These are Augustine’s words.

[Note: [Col. 1022D] The Master, cited above, § c.] It is then asked whether, just as the soul is cleansed in baptism from original sin, so also [Col. 1022D] the flesh is cleansed there from the foulness and corruption of the flesh. Some say that, just as there are two things in baptism, namely water and Spirit, so two things are cleansed there: soul and flesh—the former from original sin, the latter from corruption of the flesh. Others say that only the soul, and not the flesh, is cleansed in baptism.

The following objection is made to them: the flesh of this infant now being baptized is not cleansed by baptism of its foulness. It contracts a certain foulness from the flesh of its father, which is corrupt; and because it descends from that flesh through carnal concupiscence, it contracts a certain foulness. Therefore the flesh of the offspring is more corrupt [Col. 1023A] than that of the parent; and thus, the more ancestors a person has preceding him in the line of generation, the more corrupt flesh he has. Accordingly, this person’s flesh is more corrupt than that person’s; and each corruption is a cause of the original sin which is in the soul. Therefore this person’s original sin is greater than that person’s.

Yet one reads in the Epistle to the Romans: “With regard to original sin all were equal, but mercy made distinctions among those whom it willed.” Nevertheless, it seems that every human being is worse the later he comes. For people used to live five hundred or four hundred years; now they do not live beyond eighty or a hundred years. They are now also duller in intellect, weaker in memory, and of smaller stature. For, as the poet says:

[Col. 1023B]

> The earth now produces evil men—and little ones.  
> (Juvenal, *Satires* 15.70.)

To this one must say that, although corruption in this flesh is greater than in that, original sin is nevertheless not greater in this person than in that, nor is the guilt for it greater—just as one who takes more food than another is not therefore more refreshed, though food is the cause of refreshment. Yet that flesh is more corrupt in one person than in another may be inferred because we often see that those not born of lawful marriage are more prone to works of the flesh: the greater the pleasure and the more unlawful the delight in which they are conceived, the more dissolute the children are found to be in conduct.

It is also asked whether a person is bound to confess original [Col. 1023C] sin. This seems capable of proof as follows. One mortal sin cannot be remitted to this person without another. This unbaptized person repents of homicide—and does so from charity. Therefore every mortal sin of which he is guilty is remitted to him, and consequently original sin also. Thus original sin is forgiven with the others through contrition. Therefore, through such contrition [perhaps: “that contrition”], it can be forgiven even if it exists without another sin; and thus an unbaptized adult, who has added no actual sin, can through contrition [with the desire for baptism], if he lacks baptismal water, erase original sin.

Likewise, he knows that he is guilty of mortal sin. Therefore he is bound to confess it. Therefore he is bound to confess that sin. Again, in one who has been baptized, sins return through apostasy; therefore original sin returns also. Yet he cannot [Col. 1023D] be baptized again; and so it cannot cease to be in him except by the benefit of contrition.

The contrary argument is this: this person did not commit this sin; therefore he is not bound to feel contrition for it, and therefore not to confess it. Accordingly, some say that, just as penance was instituted for actual sins, 164 although actual sins are sometimes erased through baptism, so conversely baptism was instituted for original sin, although original sin may nevertheless be erased through contrition.

[Note: [Col. 1023D] The Master, cited above, Distinction 33, § f.] It is then asked whether Adam’s first actual sin was greater than every other [Col. 1024A] actual sin. Augustine appears to maintain this when he says [Note: [Col. 1023D] Book XIV, *On the City of God*, ch. 12]: “Adam’s sin was committed with so much the greater injustice as it could have been avoided by an easier observance.” Again, it harmed more than any other sin. Therefore it was greater.

The first point is proved thus: Adam’s sin corrupted the whole human nature, which no other sin did. Therefore it harmed more. To this one must say that Adam’s sin was not greater than every other, because the sin against the Holy Spirit, the sin of Judas, and the sin of Cain were greater. Therefore the inference, “It harmed more; therefore it was greater,” does not follow and is false. Indeed Judas’s sin harmed Judas more than Adam’s harmed Adam. But it harmed more—that is, in more persons; thus “more” denotes not quantity but plurality.

That sin is said to have impaired and corrupted the whole [Col. 1024B] human nature because it corrupted Adam’s nature, from whom all humans descend by seminal propagation; but it is believed to have been subsequently erased. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1024D] Book II, *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, ch. 34]: “The first parents, by afterwards living rightly, are believed through the Lord’s blood to have been delivered from everlasting punishment.”

As for Augustine’s statement, “Adam’s sin was committed with so much greater injustice,” etc., this means “with injustice extending to more persons,” so that “greaterness” denotes plurality.

It is customary to ask whether the concupiscible faculty of the soul, which is original sin, is that power of the soul by which the soul is called concupiscible—a power which before baptism is sin and after baptism remains in act but is not imputed as sin. If this is said, it is asked [Col. 1024C] why that power is corrupted by the corruption of the flesh so as to be called sin, rather than the power by which the soul is called irascible, or that by which it is called rational. Again, if it itself is original sin and the corruption of the flesh, it is not the cause of that corruption. Therefore it is not the cause of original sin.

But if original sin is said to be a certain proneness to sin arising from the corruption of the flesh, since that proneness is a quality of the mind which, as Augustine testifies, remains even after baptism, it may be asked whether by it we desire only evil and never good. By the same reasoning, through natural concupiscence we desire only good and never evil. How, then, can we misuse those faculties unless we will evil by them, just as we sometimes misuse the irascible and rational faculties? We leave the solution [Col. 1024D] of these questions to those greater than ourselves, since we have received nothing concerning them here from our elders.

## CHAPTER XX. What Adam’s condition was after sin; also concerning the powers of the soul—first the natural powers, then the gratuitous.

[Note: [Col. 1024D] The Master, II, Distinction 24.] Having shown what man’s condition is after sin with respect to the body, it remains to inquire what his condition was through sin with respect to the soul. It must therefore be known that through sin he was wounded in his natural endowments and stripped of his gratuitous gifts; that is, his natural endowments were weakened by sin and his gratuitous gifts corrupted, [Col. 1025A] though not wholly destroyed and removed.

The order of our treatment, therefore, will be this. First, we shall say what natural goods and gratuitous goods are, so that the difference between the one and the other may be clear. Second, what the natural goods were like before sin and what they became after sin. Third, what the gratuitous goods were like before sin; for after sin they did not remain.

Natural goods are called those which a person has from birth, and hence are called natural: reason, intelligence, memory, and so forth. Gratuitous goods are those added to natural ones: virtues and branches of knowledge. They are therefore also called gratuitous, because they are bestowed upon a human being by God through grace. These goods are increased daily, diminished daily, withdrawn from some, 165 and given to others; and in this special sense of the word [Col. 1025B] “gratuitous,” natural and gratuitous goods are almost opposites. This word is also used in a broader sense, in which both a natural and a gratuitous good are called gratuitous, because both are given freely.

After this, we must see what natural goods were like before sin. But because the examination of two natural things—sensuality and free choice—seems especially pertinent to this inquiry, and because every sin, mortal as well as venial, is referred to these two, it is sufficient to treat of them; and first of sensuality.

It must be known, therefore, that although the soul is a simple thing lacking parts, it is nevertheless said by the saints to have parts, not essentially, [Col. 1025C] but because, on account of the diversity of its functions, it admits within itself what it itself is not. [Note: [Col. 1025D] See 28: Heloise’s problem to Abelard.]

Some distinguish the soul into three parts: mind (*mens*), spirit (*spiritus*), and that which is specifically called soul (*anima*), in accordance with the passage, “I will sing with the spirit; I will sing also with the mind” (1 Cor. 14). For just as the outer human being has three principal parts—the highest, namely the head, which contains two eyes; the middle, namely the belly; and the lowest, namely the two feet—so the inner human being has three principal parts: the highest, namely mind, which has the two eyes of love and knowledge; the middle, spirit, which is likewise divided into two, recognition and its effect; and the lowest, namely soul, which has, as it were, two feet, sensuality and sense.

Sensuality, therefore, is the power [Col. 1025D] of perceiving bodily things in themselves; it is not some body which we perceive by sight. Sense is the power of being affected naturally by things perceived through sensuality: as when, on seeing some body, I am affected by joy, sorrow, or similar feelings. Imagination is the power of perceiving bodily things through their images, as when images of things come before our mind in dreams. The effect of imagination is the power of being affected by things perceived in this way through imagination.

Mind also has two parts, or, as we said, eyes: one of knowledge and the other of love. Hence Augustine says:

[Col. 1026A]

> “Mind is, among all things that are in the soul, higher in dignity and more whole in loftiness; it is naturally capable of every affection and effect, possessing the image of God himself in its power of knowing, and his likeness in its power of loving.”

The two parts of the soul are also customarily distinguished in another way: reason and sensuality. Reason, again, is said to have two parts, the higher and the lower. The higher is that through which a human being gives attention to contemplating heavenly and divine things; the lower is that through which one is fitted to arrange these lower things and prudently deliberate concerning the outward affairs of temporal matters.

## CHAPTER XXI. What the natural endowments were like before sin, and what they were like afterwards; also concerning sensuality and first movements.

[Col. 1026B]

[Note: [Col. 1025D] The Master, II, Distinction 24, § f., etc.] Sensuality is a certain lower power of the soul, from which comes the movement directed toward bodily senses and those things necessary to the body. Sensuality has two parts, one lower and one higher. The lower part is the movement by which we desire unlawful things, such as being angry or committing adultery; and this movement is both punishment and fault. The higher part is the movement by which we desire lawful things necessary for the flesh, such as eating and drinking. This movement is sometimes moderate and sometimes immoderate. If moderate, it is neither fault nor punishment; but if immoderate, it is punishment but not fault, as in the immoderate appetite for eating or drinking. [Note: [Col. 1026D] The Master, cited above, § g., etc.]

If anyone [Col. 1026C] rightly and attentively considers these four movements or parts, he can readily perceive what mortal sin and venial sin are. Yet this must first be noted and understood: the same order of sinning which literally occurred in our first parents is present in the soul of every individual, according to the spiritual interpretation. For just as there was there a serpent suggesting to the woman, a woman who ate the forbidden fruit, and a man who consented to the woman, so in every human soul sensuality stands for the serpent, the lower part of reason for the woman, and the higher part of reason for the man.

And just as there was there a carnal marriage between man and woman, so there is a spiritual marriage in the soul between the higher and lower parts of reason. For the lower part ought to serve the higher, [Col. 1026D] which ought to correct it, just as the woman ought to serve and obey the man, who ought to correct her.

Thus the serpent is said to suggest without the consent of either man or woman when the movement of sensuality conceives an enticement to sin without any delight of thought; and such a movement is a most slight fault, because first movements are not within a person’s first control. They are erased by general confession, in saying *Confiteor*; by the Greeks it is called *propatheia* (προπάθεια), and by us *propassio*, “pre-passion.”

But the woman is said to eat, and not the man, when sin is retained in the soul with delight of thought, though it is not determined that it shall be carried out. Yet a distinction must be made, for sometimes the sin is retained only a little in the soul—that is, the will to sin together with delight in cognition—and sometimes for a long time. If that will to sin and that delight of thought are retained only a little in the soul, they are venial sin and can be erased by general confession. But if they are retained in the soul for a long time, such will and delight are mortal sin—namely, [Col. 1027A] because the man does not immediately correct the woman while she lingers in unlawful things or bursts forth into them. For whenever the woman breaks out into unlawful things, she must immediately be corrected by the man; that is, the lower part of reason by the higher.

But the man is said to eat when sin is retained in the soul with delight of thought, and is also determined to be done [Col. 1027B] and there is a will to do it, if there is opportunity. This is a mortal and most grave sin.

What was stated above—that a movement of sensuality is sin—does not seem true, since movements of this kind occur in brute animals as well as humans: for they desire as humans do. Yet humans, because they possess reason, sometimes resist. Why, then, is it imputed to us as sin rather than to them? To this it must be said that the very threshold of the question bears the trace of its solution. Because humans have reason through which they can suppress first movements, while brute animals do not, what is not imputed to the latter as sin is judged sin in the former.

Therefore, a movement of concupiscence, as long as it is held in sensuality, is venial sin; but when it is held in the lower part of reason, it is mortal sin if it is held for a long time, because delay brings danger with it. But a movement held in sensuality can be held in either the higher or lower part of reason. Therefore, what is venial can be mortal; and thus venial sin will be mortal.

Again, Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1027D] In Gratian, Distinction 25, chapter “unum,” before the middle. Related to this is what Augustine has in Tractate 12 on John, near the end: “Small sins, if neglected, kill.” See also his Sermon 4, *On the Souls of the Dead*, and Sermon 47, etc.] that no sin is so venial that, if it pleases, it is not mortal. But drinking too much is venial sin, and it pleases this righteous person. Therefore it is mortal sin; but charity is in this righteous person; therefore there is charity in someone in whom mortal sin exists. That this sin pleases the righteous person is proved thus: he does it willingly, not unwillingly. Therefore it pleases him.

[Col. 1027D] To this it must be said that, just as four grades or parts were assigned above in the soul, so four movements may be assigned there, and no other movement either is, will be, or can be: namely, two movements of sensuality and two movements of reason. A movement of sensuality cannot be a movement of reason, whether lower or higher; nor can a movement of reason be a movement of sensuality. Thus a movement of sensuality is said to become a movement of reason because, when a movement of reason supervenes, the movement of sensuality ceases to be and passes away in act, but not in guilt. For the guilt of venial sin remains together with mortal sin.

Similarly, venial sin is said [Col. 1028A] to be able to become mortal because, when mortal sin supervenes, that which was venial passes away in act but not in guilt, as you see in the ages of life. Childhood is said to pass 167 into youth and thereafter, because when youth comes childhood ceases to exist; nor can one age be another. Thus none of the aforementioned movements can be another.

For a fuller understanding of the subsequent statement—that no sin is so venial that, if it pleases, it is not mortal—a brief distinction must be made. Of sins committed in an outward act, one is mortal and another venial. Mortal, for example, are killing a human being and committing adultery; venial, for example, are drinking too much and eating too much.

It must therefore be known that if someone is moved toward mortal sin by a movement of the higher [Col. 1028B] reason, or even of the lower reason, and for a long time, that movement is mortal sin. But if one is moved toward mortal sin by a movement of sensuality, whether lower or higher, or even by a movement of lower reason if it is brief, that movement is venial sin. For if that movement is retained long in the lower part of reason, it is mortal sin, as we said above.

Again, if someone is moved toward venial sin by a movement of sensuality—whether of one kind or the other—or by a movement of reason—whether higher or lower—such a movement of concupiscence is venial sin, unless one is moved for a long time by the higher movement of reason, that is, habitually. For what is venial, if it turns into a habit, ceases to be venial and becomes mortal if it pleases; that is, approval of venial sin [Col. 1028C] and the habit itself are mortal sin. The venial sin itself cannot become mortal.

[Note: [Col. 1028D] See Augustine on this psalm, near the end.] That the first movement of concupiscence is sin is clear from the Prophet, who says: “Blessed is he who shall seize and dash your little ones against the rock” (Psalm 136 [137]). He calls first movements “little ones.” Therefore, if it is good to dash them against the rock, they are evil.

But an objection is again raised: before sin, Adam had neither punishment nor fault; but he had a first movement before sin. Therefore the first movement is neither punishment nor fault. Again, if the first movement in him was not mortal sin, why was it imputed to the Apostle as sin when he said, “What I do not will, that I do” (Rom. 7)? Again, the first movement is a stain on the soul. Therefore it is an offense against God. Through it, therefore, the soul becomes unlike God [Col. 1028D]; therefore it deforms the soul. Again, a human being is bound to be without offense. Therefore he is bound to be without a first movement, since the first movement is an offense against God. But one cannot be without a first movement. Therefore a human being is required to do what he cannot do: namely, to be without a first movement.

To this it must be said that before sin Adam had reason in both its parts, and sensuality in its higher part, since he had a moderate appetite for things necessary to the body. But he did not have a first movement—unless you call “first” that before which there was no other. For before sin he had neither the lower [Col. 1029A] part of sensuality nor corruption of the flesh. Hence he could not sin mortally. Nor is it true that a first movement is an offense against God: only mortal sin is called an offense against God. A human being is bound to be without offense against God, and is required to be without mortal sin.

It is asked whether it is better to abstain from venial than from mortal sin. For no one can abstain from venial sin without abstaining from mortal sin, while one can abstain from mortal sin even if one does not abstain from venial sin. But, conversely, it is proved that it is better to abstain from mortal than from venial sin, for mortal sin is more serious than venial sin. Therefore it is better to abstain from mortal than from venial sin.

We say in reply that, if mortal sin and venial sin were two things [Col. 1029B] each of which could exist without the other, it would be better to abstain from mortal than from venial sin. Similarly, it is asked whether it is better to abstain from an oath than from frequent swearing. Here likewise I say that it is better to abstain from an oath than from frequent swearing, because no one can abstain from an oath without abstaining from frequent swearing; but the converse does not hold. The same applies in other cases.

Or, because the very comparison implies a distinction between venial and mortal sin, the proposition “It is better to abstain from venial than from mortal sin” must be denied; and this argument must be pressed: one cannot abstain from venial sin without abstaining from mortal sin, and not conversely; therefore it is better to abstain from the former than from the latter. This is a fallacy. No one can have eyes without having a head, yet one can have a head even if one has no eyes. Therefore it is better to have eyes than a head.

By the same reasoning one can argue that it is more penal for a bishop to sin in conferring the subdiaconate than in conferring the priesthood. For if he knowingly admits an unworthy man to the order of subdeacon, he is punished thus: thereafter he cannot confer that same order; but, since he cannot confer the lesser order, neither can he confer the greater, and thus he cannot afterwards confer priesthood.
