But if he sins in conferring the priesthood, he is punished only in this: that he cannot afterwards confer priesthood, though he can confer every lesser order. Yet it is a greater sin to admit an unworthy person to priesthood than to the subdiaconate. [Col. 1029D] Nevertheless, one who sins in this lesser matter is punished more severely than the other who sins in that greater one.

This, however, is not because of the sin but because of the order, concerning which this rule is observed: one who does not confer the lesser may not confer the greater. Thus it is better to abstain from venial than from mortal sin, not because venial sin is greater than mortal sin, but because no one can abstain from the former without abstaining from the latter. From what has been said, it is clear that a movement of concupiscence, as long as it remains in sensuality, is venial sin; but if reason consents, it is mortal sin.

But according to this, it seems that such a movement is mortal. For reason never consents to evil; indeed, it always resists. Therefore reason consents to no perverse movement of concupiscence. Therefore no movement is mortal sin.

To this they say that reason is said [Col. 1030A] both to consent to the will and not to consent. It is said to consent because the will cannot of itself bring to effect what it desires without the assistance of reason; for it cannot of itself deliberate and investigate place, time, manner, and so forth—matters which the teachers call circumstances. Reason deliberates all these things, so that it may know when and how the deed can be done. It is said to consent when, without it, the will cannot bring what it desires into effect.

But reason is said not to consent because it always kicks back, always resists, judges that evil ought not to be done, advises the good, and dissuades from its contrary. No one is so evil that his reason does not prick his conscience, declaring this thing evil and that thing evil. This is that little spark of reason which cannot be extinguished even in Cain, and which the Greeks call *synderesis*. [Col. 1030B] Thus reason is said to consent to the will because the will cannot of itself tend toward what it desires without reason’s help; and it is said not to consent because it does this unwillingly.

Just as a boy who leads a blind man shows him two roads, one level and the other rough, and the blind man insists, despite the boy and against the boy’s will, on going by the rough road: the boy is said both to consent to the blind man and not to consent. He consents because the blind man cannot reach the intended place without his guidance; he does not consent because he leads him unwillingly and the blind man drags him along unwillingly. So the will drags reason along: though reason resists, it is overcome.

Again, it seems that sensuality has greater [Col. 1030C] efficacy in brute animals than in rational beings. For a brute animal is moved by sensuality, without free choice, to kill another animal. It does not have free choice; but a human being cannot be moved by sensuality, without free choice, to kill another human being. For if he could do this by sensuality alone, since its movement is not mortal sin, a human being could be moved to kill another human being without mortal sin. Therefore sensuality has greater efficacy in brute animals than in rational beings.

We reply that this is not true; indeed, it has as much efficacy in the latter as in the former. But it cannot do anything in rational beings without free choice because sensuality [Col. 1030D] and free choice exist together in a human being, as it were in the same subject; and sensuality cannot devise anything evil without free choice immediately perceiving it and consenting to it—unless it at once represses it. Nevertheless, it has as much efficacy in these as in those.

It is then asked whether the first movement in a human being has God or the devil as its author. One must say that the first movement, insofar as it is punishment, has God as its author; but insofar as it is fault, it does not have God as its author, because God is not the author of fault. Nor does it seem to have the devil as author, since first movements often arise without the devil’s suggestion; nor does it have a human being as author, since first movements arise against a person’s will, whether he wishes them or not.

To this one must say that temptation is twofold, outward and inward. Outward temptation occurs [Col. 1031A] when evil is suggested visibly from without by word or sign, so that the person to whom it is suggested may incline to consent to sin. Inward temptation occurs when evil is suggested invisibly from within by the perverse delight of the flesh. Sometimes the devil is the author of this temptation, because he sometimes suggests evil to a person; sometimes it is the frailty of human nature.

[Note: [Col. 1031D] See the Master, IV, Distinction 18, final section. See chapter 12 and the following part, where he teaches that sin is considered in two ways, namely in act and in guilt: in the first way while it is committed; [Col. 1032D] in the other after it has been committed. In both ways it is always sin.] It is also customary to ask whether the stain in someone’s soul which arises from mortal sin, and which remains even after the act of sin has passed away, is sin. This is argued as follows: through it a human being becomes unlike God; therefore it is sin. Again, it makes one deserving of eternal death; therefore it is sin. But on the contrary: it is sin; therefore it is either original or actual sin. Concerning [Col. 1031B] this, because we have received no definition from authors or teachers, we ourselves define nothing.

## CHAPTER XXII. What free choice is, and what it was like before sin and afterwards

[Note: [Col. 1032D] The Master, II, Distinction 25.] Besides the penal condition or punishment which we bear through the depression of sensuality by sin, we bear another from the depression of free choice by the same cause, namely sin. Therefore we must see what free choice is, what it was like before sin, and what condition it had after sin.

Free choice is defined by philosophers thus: “Free choice is free judgment concerning the will.” But theologians define it thus: “Free choice is the faculty of will and [Col. 1031C] reason by which good is chosen when grace assists, and evil when grace withdraws.”

Since this definition appears to contain some difficulty, let us explain its terms. Free choice consists in two things, namely will and reason. It is called “free” with respect to will: for will is free and cannot be compelled; hence it is free from necessity. It is called “choice” (*arbitrium*) with respect to reason, because choice is attributed to reason and distinguishes the things which the will seeks.

Will is mistress; reason is her attendant, showing her the straight way. But since will, as possessing dominion, draws reason along with it, if it inclines to good, reason gladly follows and consents to it; but if it inclines [Col. 1031D] to evil, reason resists, kicks back, urges the good, and dissuades from the contrary. Therefore, since free choice consists in two things, namely will and reason, it is clear that free choice exists only in those beings which possess will and reason. Accordingly, brute animals do not have free choice; they have appetite only.

Again, because authority to merit or demerit belongs to free choice—for no one merits eternal misery because of a weak memory or dull intelligence, nor eternal life because of a retentive memory or subtle intelligence—it is clear [Col. 1032A] that only that which has free choice can merit. Thus brute animals do not merit through appetite, for they cannot merit.

It must further be known that free choice concerns neither the present nor the past, but only the future; and not even every future thing, but only a contingent future. It does not concern the past, because deliberation whether to do or not to do has no place concerning the past or present. No deliberation can bring it about that what has been done has not been done; for what has been done cannot not have been done. Likewise, it cannot be changed so that what is now occurring does not occur now; but what will be can fail to be, and one can [Col. 1032B] deliberate whether it ought to be done.

But an objection is made. It is impossible for someone not to sin mortally by free choice without being now moved toward that sin, or without there previously having been a movement toward that sin, because deliberation precedes sin. But it is impossible for someone now to sin mortally and not first to be moved toward that sin, as we shall prove later. Therefore it is impossible for someone now to sin mortally by free choice without previously having been moved toward that sin; therefore it is impossible for someone now to have sinned mortally by free choice without having sinned mortally. For movement toward mortal sin by free choice is mortal sin. Therefore it is impossible for anyone [Col. 1032C] to begin to sin mortally.

The proposition which we undertook to prove is true. For it is impossible to sin mortally and now for the first time be moved toward that sin. For if someone now sins mortally, since every sin is preceded by deliberation, because every sin proceeds from free choice, it is impossible that someone now sins mortally without there having been a first movement toward that sin. Therefore it is impossible for him now for the first time to be moved toward that sin.

To this, I think one must say that when it is said that free choice concerns the future, and that every mortal sin is preceded by a movement of free choice, the true [variant: “bad”] meaning concerns outward acts which proceed from perverse movements of free choice. This is not true of inward movements: an inward movement to evil arising from free choice is not preceded by another movement, [Col. 1032D] lest there be an infinite regress and thus the beginning of sin never be found.

We must now see what free choice was like before sin and what condition it had after sin. Four states of free choice must therefore be distinguished. The first state was before sin; the second, after sin until reception of the sacraments—namely faith, circumcision, and baptism; the third, after restoration through the sacraments until the Day of Judgment; the fourth, after the Day of Judgment.

Before [Col. 1033A] sin, a human being could sin and could refrain from sin by free choice, because nothing impelled him to evil and nothing drove him from good. For he had no weakness of the flesh toward evil, but assistance toward good. In the second state, he could not avoid sinning mortally: for many things impelled a human being to evil, and nothing helped him toward good. He had weakness toward evil and no assistance toward good; then reason was pressed down and overcome.

In the third state, a human being cannot avoid sinning venially, but can avoid sinning mortally: something impels him to evil and something helps him toward good. He has weakness of the flesh toward evil and assistance toward good. In this state reason is pressed down but not overcome. In the fourth state, a human being will be unable to sin, for then [Col. 1033B] weakness will be wholly exhausted and grace increased; then reason will not be pressed down by the will or overcome.

But since it has been said that Adam in the first state was equally disposed toward sinning and not sinning, and that free choice concerns only future things, not present or past ones, this seems capable of being disproved in several ways. First, that free choice concerns present things as it does future things, thus: In the first moment in which Adam existed, he had a free will; therefore he could equally choose good and evil. Therefore, since at that time he was in the good given him by the Creator, and chose it, he was such as he then was by his will. But that good was then present to him; therefore his will had power regarding present things.

Likewise, [Col. 1033C] since at that time he chose to be in natural good (which is to love God by natural love), and since the will is equally free toward good and evil, therefore at that time he could will to love God by natural love; therefore he could will evil in the first moment in which he existed; therefore he could have never been good, and it is necessary that he was made by God; therefore he could be made by God and never be good in the same moment; therefore he could have been made evil by God.

Likewise, since his will in A, which was the first moment of his creation, could equally choose this good, namely loving God by natural love, and this evil, namely not loving him: if he was punishable for desiring evil, therefore he was rewardable because he desired to love; therefore he could be rewarded without virtue, since before he had virtues [Col. 1033D] he desired that good. Therefore he could merit without virtues. Thus, if it is said that by free choice he could not have it that there should be any … in A, since free choice concerns only the future and not the present: therefore, since in A he loved God, he did not have that momentary love from free choice, but rather from the other powers that he possessed uncorrupted; and thus he could not then fail to love.

Likewise, since he possessed virtues before sin, it seems provable that they were withdrawn from him before he sinned, as follows. Suppose that he possessed them in C, the third moment, and that in D he sinned in E. Given this: Adam had virtues in D; in E it was necessary that [Col. 1034A] Adam had had virtues in D. But it was impossible for Adam to have had virtues in D and then to choose to do evil in E. Therefore it was necessary in E that Adam had not deliberated to do evil in E. But it was impossible for Adam to do evil in E and not to have deliberated to do evil in E. Therefore it was impossible for Adam to do evil in E—which is false, because he then sinned.

The middle premise of this last argument is proved thus: In E it was not in the power of Adam’s free choice to do what he was doing in E, or not to do what he was doing in E, because free choice concerns not the present but the future; and it was impossible for Adam in E to perform an act meriting punishment that did not proceed from a movement of free choice. Therefore it was impossible for Adam to do evil [Col. 1034B] in E without having deliberated that he would do evil; and it was impossible for him to have deliberated that he would do evil without having lacked virtue for at least one moment. Therefore it was impossible for Adam to do evil without having lacked virtue, at least one moment beforehand. Therefore it was impossible that he had been evil without first having been evil; for whenever he lacked virtue, he was evil.

Likewise, Adam had will and reason in his soul. His reason then discerned what was necessary for his salvation; but loving God by charity and not loving God by charity were two alternatives, one necessary for salvation, the other deserving punishment. Therefore he discerned these by reason and had a will. Therefore he desired either this good [Col. 1034C] or that evil; but not evil, for then he was wholly good. Therefore he desired this good, namely loving by charity, and he did not have it. Therefore he was punished before sin.

Likewise, when it is said: “Free choice is a faculty of will and reason,” etc., is this said of that good which he had by creation, or of meritorious good? But it does not seem to be understood of the good which he had by creation, because for that he did not need grace. Therefore it is understood of meritorious good. If so, the objection is as follows: He could not choose that meritorious good without grace, while he could choose evil without anything added; therefore his free choice was more inclined toward evil than toward good; therefore, if he chose evil, he ought not to have been punished as much as he would have been rewarded had he chosen good. But I prove that it ought to have been more, because he could not choose good without grace, nor did he merit grace, whereas he could choose evil by himself. Therefore a greater punishment was due to him for choosing evil than a reward for choosing good.

Likewise, Adam was in good and knew it by experience; he did not undergo evil or know it by experience; and nothing impelled him toward evil, nor did anything attempt to remove him from good. Therefore it was easier for him to preserve the good [Col. 1034D] that he possessed than to admit the evil that he did not possess; therefore his free choice was freer toward good than toward evil.

I say that he had freer choice for incurring evil [Col. 1035A] than for acquiring the meritorious good which he then did not possess. For he could do the former without anything being added, but not the latter. Yet he had freer choice for remaining in that good of innocence than for falling; for he could do either without anything being added, and he was already in the one, namely the abiding in good.

The solutions to the other arguments can readily be drawn from what has been said above. For, if Adam sinned in E, it was not necessary that he had deliberated concerning that sin in D, which was the first moment before E; because in E there first arose from free choice a movement toward evil. Nor is it necessary that every evil movement of free choice be preceded by another movement, lest there be an infinite regress, as we said above. Yet an external action, whether good [Col. 1035B] or evil, is always preceded by a movement of free choice: a good action by a good movement, an evil one by an evil movement; and this naturally. Very often also—indeed perhaps always—temporally. Nor was Adam then bound to love God by charity, as we said above, where we distinguished the different meanings of this word “bound.”

Likewise, free choice has in its power only the future, and not the present or the past. Therefore, when Adam first existed in A, and then had free choice, he could not use free choice regarding what he did in A. Therefore he did not have it from free choice that he loved God in A. He had that love, which was coterminous with A, from another grace. But the love which he had in B he had from [Col. 1035C] free choice; for in A he deliberated that he would love God in B, and so with the remaining moments.

But if someone says that free choice concerns the present, I proceed thus. Adam in A had free will both to do what he did not do in A and not to do what he did in A. Therefore by will he could have it in A that he did not love God in A, just as by will he had it that he loved God in A; and thus by will he could have it that he was evil whenever he existed, and thus by will he could have it that he was made evil by God.

Likewise, Adam in A could misuse free choice. Therefore he could corrupt it in A. Therefore he could incline toward evil in A; and thus he could always incline free choice toward evil. Therefore he could always be evil. If one says that he could not misuse [Col. 1035D] free choice in A, and thus could not use it badly, then he had some grace which resisted this, since this did not come from nature. He either had that grace in C or D, when he could corrupt A [reading uncertain], or he did not have it. It seems that he did not have it; for if he had had it, he could not have been corrupted, just as neither could he in A. But if he did not have it, the question is why God withdrew it from him before he had yet sinned.

Likewise, if in A he could not corrupt free choice, then in A he could not sin in A. Thus, at some time he was in such a state that he could not sin. Likewise, in A he had free choice. Therefore in A he could sin [Col. 1036A] and not sin in A, since he was neither confirmed nor hardened.

Likewise, this man begins to be evil. Therefore he then begins to misuse free choice. Suppose that in D he begins to misuse free choice. From this follows: This man did nothing in D which he had not proposed to do before D. Therefore before D he had proposed to misuse free choice. Whenever he proposed to misuse free choice, he had an evil will; and whenever he had an evil will, he misused free choice. Thus it will be proved that he never began to misuse free choice.

These points are easily resolved if it is said that Adam could be created by God and never have been good, yet he could not for that reason be created or made evil by God. For it would seem that God had done something evil in him, which is false; because all his evil is from himself [Col. 1036B] or from the devil; all his good is from God, and nothing but good is from God. Thus this soul was created by God and was evil whenever it existed; nevertheless, it was not created evil by God.

It was likewise said above that in the second state—that is, after sin 173 and before restoration—man could not avoid mortal sin; indeed, he sinned mortally by necessity. But this is proved false. For Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1035D] *Enchiridion*, ch. 30]: “When man sinned by free choice, he destroyed both himself and free choice.” Therefore he then lost free choice and did not recover it afterwards. Therefore after sin he could not commit mortal sin, since mortal sin proceeds from free choice.

To this it must be said, [Col. 1036C] that freedom is spoken of in three ways. There is freedom from necessity, freedom from sin, and freedom from misery. Freedom from necessity belongs to man both before and after sin, because the will of no human being can be compelled; hence it is called free from necessity. Thus Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1035D] *On Grace and Free Choice*, ch. 15]: “The will is always free, but not always good.” Understand: free from necessity. For this is said of this freedom: the will cannot be compelled.

Freedom from sin is that by which a man is free from mortal sin. A man is not said to have freedom from sin because he is without venial sin, for this cannot be; rather, because he is without the dominion of sin, that is, without mortal sin. For mortal sin, but not venial sin, is said to have power over a man. Only the good possess this freedom [Col. 1036D]—that is, those who lack mortal sin, although they have venial sin. Of this freedom the Apostle says: “When you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness; but now, having been freed from sin and made servants of God, you have received fruit unto justification” (Rom. VI). Again: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (II Cor. III)—namely, from sin. And elsewhere: “If the Son has set you free, you shall truly be free” (John VIII).

Freedom from misery will exist only in the homeland. Only the righteous will possess it. Therefore, when Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1036D] Master, above, §§ h and s]: “Through sin man destroyed both himself and free choice,” this must be understood as freedom from sin, not freedom [Col. 1037A] from necessity—for he had this even after sin—and as freedom from misery. He never possessed the latter after he sinned; but he lost freedom from sin. For, since he had previously possessed it, that is, had been without sin, he lost it because he sinned mortally.

But what was that grace by whose assistance Adam chose good in the first moment? It was not virtue, since he did not yet possess virtues. Nor can it be said that he could choose good without grace, since free choice is that faculty of will and reason by which good is chosen with grace assisting, and evil with the same grace withdrawing. For free choice does not suffice to begin good, any more than to complete it. But this becomes clear once the equivocation [Col. 1037B] in this word “good” has been resolved.

Since every sin is from free choice, the question is according to which state this man ought to be judged: a man who from birth has free choice corrupted and who now kills a man. For one who had once been of sound mind was judged according to the state in which he was when he began to lose his mind. To this we say that we believe it impossible for a man thus to have his natural powers corrupted from birth; yet if this is so, let us leave it to God’s judgment.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Whether the power of sinning is from God

[Note: [Col. 1037D] Master, II, last distinction.] But it is asked whether the freedom which a man has to do good is free choice [Col. 1037C] [Note: [Col. 1037D] Book II, distinction 25]. If it is, then by the same reasoning the freedom which a man has to do evil is free choice. Some answer that the freedom which a man has to do good is not free choice, but a certain inclination of the mind toward good, arising from free choice and God’s grace.

But those who think more truly say [Note: [Col. 1037D] Thus the Master, II, distinction 25, § n]: The freedom which one has to do good and that which one has to do evil are the same freedom, and it is free choice; but according to different functions it receives different names. Sometimes it is free from sin, and then it is good; sometimes it is free from righteousness, and then it is evil. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1038D] *On Grace and Free Choice*, ch. 15]: “The human will is always free, but not [Col. 1037D] always good. 174 For sometimes it is free from righteousness and serves sin; sometimes it is free from sin and serves righteousness, and then it is good.”

But an inconvenient consequence seems to follow. For just as it is said that the freedom which a man has for good is the same as that which he has for evil, by the same reasoning it must be said that the power which a man has to do good is the same as that which he has to do evil. Therefore, since that which he has to do good is good, that which he has to do evil is also good; and so the power which a man has to sin is good.

[Col. 1038A] But it is objected: One can use every good well; but the power of sinning is good. Therefore one can use it well. Likewise, the power of sinning is good. Therefore it is either natural or gratuitous; but certainly it is not gratuitous; therefore it is natural. It was in Adam before sin, for then he could sin and not sin. But every natural good was corrupted in him through sin, and every gratuitous good was destroyed. Therefore the power of sinning was corrupted in him. Therefore after sin he was less able to sin.

But I prove that after sin he was more able to sin. For then he did not possess the aid of grace which he had previously possessed, and he also had corruption of the flesh; therefore then he could sin more readily. Likewise, before sin he could sin only mortally; but afterward [Col. 1038B] he could sin both mortally and venially. Therefore more after sin than before.

That the power of sinning is good is shown beyond doubt. It was in Adam before sin; therefore it is good, for nothing but good was in him before sin. Likewise, it is from God; therefore it is good. And that it is from God is evident. For it is said in the Gospel: “You would have no power unless it had been given you from above” (John XIX). Augustine also says [Note: [Col. 1038D] Sermon on Psalm XXXII, but somewhat differently]: “Human malice has from itself the desire to harm; but it does not have the power unless God gives it.”

Likewise, suppose that this confirmed man will shortly die. In him is the power of sinning, which is good; but every natural good now in him will be good after the resurrection. Therefore the power of sinning will be in this man after the resurrection. [Col. 1038C] Therefore he will then be able to sin.

To what has been said we answer that the power a person has for doing good is not other than that which he has for doing evil; it is free choice, and it is good. For the power of sinning is from God, because it is itself the same power of doing good. But the statement, “That good was corrupted in Adam through sin; therefore after sin Adam was less able to sin,” does not follow. Rather, he was less able—not, however, less able to sin, but more able.

What we said last can be conceded if someone considers it more subtly: namely, that the power of sinning will be in this confirmed man after the resurrection, but after the resurrection there will not be in him [Col. 1038D] a power of sinning. For this expression, “power of sinning,” is compounded of a nominative and a genitive, and is something accidental. Hence, if every human being ceased to be white and none would be white in the future, these propositions would not have the same meaning: “A white man will exist tomorrow” and “Tomorrow a man will be white.” Likewise, this is true: “The power of sinning will be in this confirmed man”—that is, the power which is now a power of sinning will be in him—yet a power of sinning will not be in him. For that would indicate that he would be capable of sinning.

But if someone says, “The power of sinning will be in him; therefore he will be able to sin,” the answer is by analogy: Insensibility is in this blind man, because blindness is; therefore this blind man is insensible. Or thus: Virginity will be in this person who will be continent or married; therefore he will be a virgin. Few or none, however, admit this statement: “The power of sinning will be in him after confirmation,” just as they do not admit: “The power of begetting is in the Son,” though either can rightly be conceded if properly understood. But if anyone gives a better solution, far be it from me not to be more ready to listen than to teach.

Yet this should not be omitted: “power of sinning” sometimes signifies the natural power which is free choice, and sometimes the capacity for sinning [Col. 1039A] that arises from it and has been increased by sin, just as “faculty” means both an art itself and the aptitude that we derive from it. Hence one speaks of a faculty arising from an art.

But against what was said above, that in the second state of free choice man could not avoid mortal sin, it is objected: Then he could not avoid mortal sin; therefore he was not free from necessity. But we said above that every human being is at all times free from necessity. Likewise, a man then could not avoid mortal sin, [Col. 1040A] therefore it ought not to be imputed to him.

It must be said that, although he could not avoid mortal sin, he was nevertheless free from necessity, and it was imputable to him, because through sin he had bound himself. It is like someone who is going to Rome and, while on the road, wraps and binds himself with his own hands so that he cannot move his feet: behold, he cannot go, and yet he is free from necessity. For if someone were to untie him, he could go; and his failure to proceed is imputable to him, because he himself bound himself. In the same way, in that state man could not avoid mortal sin, and yet he was free from necessity, and it was imputable to him, because he had bound himself and could not be loosed except by the working and cooperating grace of God.

The statement made above, “Man in [Col. 1040B] that state had free choice; therefore he was then equally disposed toward good and evil,” is not true. For God and angels also have free choice, yet they are not equally disposed toward evil and good—although free choice is said differently of God or angels and differently of human beings, as was said above.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 1039]

## The Distinctions of Book Three Begin

What is virtue? What is operative grace, and what cooperating grace? How many things concur in the justification of the ungodly, and do we merit first grace? Do we merit first grace? Here it is asked whether virtue is better than the work of virtue. Do we merit the movement that comes from grace and free choice, or do we merit by it? Is greater contrition required for the wiping away of mortal than of venial sin? Can someone be contrite from charity for one sin and not for another of which he is guilty? Are we bound to be more contrite for a greater sin than for a lesser? Does God punish a man to the full extent that he has deserved punishment for sin, and thus mercifully? Of two persons punished with an equal eternal penalty, and one of them additionally with a temporal penalty, is one punished more than the other? Does God punish venial sin eternally? Does contrition wipe away sin when a person is contrite—before or afterward? Do sins return through a single sin? 176 Is confession commanded, and of what thing is it a sacrament? Can one confess the same sins more than once? Must one confess a sin that one has not committed? What does God remit in confession, what the priest, and what a private person? Does one who has one virtue have all virtues? Is servile fear a virtue, and what of the matters connected with this question? Is initial fear a virtue? And of other matters pertaining to the same question. Do virtues fall away in the homeland? Concerning faith, hope, and charity, and first concerning their mode and order. On the equality and inequality of charity. On the perfection and imperfection of charity. Can charity, once possessed, be lost? Is virginity a virtue, and is it possessed by everyone who has one virtue? What objections can be made against those who say that one who has one virtue has all? Are virtues, wherever they are found, equal?

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 1039]

## CHAPTER I. What is virtue? What is operative grace, and what cooperating grace?

[Col. 1039C]

[Note: [Col. 1039D] Master, II, distinctions 26 and 27.] As we said above, from that state in which man cannot avoid mortal sin, man cannot rise by himself without operative grace, nor make progress without cooperating grace. Therefore the operative grace of God is necessary to raise him up, and cooperating grace to move his feet. We must therefore consider what operative and cooperating grace are. But because every grace treated here is virtue, we must begin with virtue, as with the higher matter.

The order of this chapter, then, will be as follows. First, we shall inquire what virtue is, what operative grace is, what cooperating grace is, whether operative and cooperating grace are the same grace, and, if they are the same, which virtue it is. Second, whether we merit virtues or merit in virtues. Third, whether one who has one virtue has all, and, if all, whether they are equally intense.

Virtue, then, is a quality of mind by which one lives rightly, by which no one uses badly, and which God works in a person without the person. For a fuller understanding of this definition, the following distinction must first be set forth [Note: [Col. 1041D] From Augustine, *Retractations*, I, ch. 9, middle; and *On Free Choice*, II, ch. 19]. Of goods, some are least, some intermediate, and some greatest. Least goods are those without which a person can live rightly and which one can use badly, such as bodily beauty. Intermediate goods are those without which a person cannot live rightly, but which one can use badly, such as free choice. For people misuse it when they incline toward evil. Greatest goods are those without which a person cannot live rightly and which one cannot use badly. Therefore this is a suitable definition: “Virtue is a quality of mind by which one lives rightly,” etc., because virtue belongs among the greatest goods.

That virtue is a quality of mind and not a movement, Augustine says concerning the verse of Psalm CXVIII, “I have done righteousness and judgment”: [Note: [Col. 1041D] Augustine on this verse of the Psalm.] “When the Prophet said, ‘I have done righteousness,’ he meant not virtue, which God works and not man, but its movement.” It is therefore clear that virtue is a certain quality and blessing [Col. 1041C] which God infuses into the soul. It is not a movement of the soul or of free choice, but it stirs free choice.

From that grace infused into the soul and free choice thus stirred, there is produced an interior movement, from which an exterior movement follows—that is, action—as appears in this very clear analogy [Note: [Col. 1041D] The Master says no differently, distinction 27, § 3]. Dew is poured into the earth; once poured in, it finds fertility in the earth and stirs it. From that stirred fertility and the dew a shoot is produced; from the shoot, fruit. The dew is divine grace; the earth’s fertility, or the earth itself, is free choice; the shoot is the interior movement; the fruit is exterior action. For grace is infused into this person’s mind. It immediately stirs free choice, and a movement of charity is produced—namely, loving. The person immediately loves, and that movement produces an external act [Col. 1041D] and manifests through works what is inwardly in the mind: he feeds the poor and clothes the naked.

That virtue is not a movement is clear, because it was said thus: Virtue is in a person without the person; but a movement of free choice is not in a person without the person, since it comes from free choice. Therefore virtue is not a movement of free choice.

Some nevertheless endeavor to prove that virtue is a movement of free choice. For Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1041D] On John]: “For what is faith except believing what you do not see?” But believing is a movement; therefore [Col. 1042A] faith is a movement. But faith is a virtue. Therefore virtue is a movement. Elsewhere he says [Note: [Col. 1042D] *On Christian Doctrine*, III, ch. 10]: “By charity I mean a movement of the soul.” Therefore charity is a movement. Therefore virtue is a movement. Likewise, “the good use of free choice is virtue.” All these authorities, therefore, must be explained and referred back to qualities of mind [Note: [Col. 1042D] See the Master, distinction 27, § 1]. Thus, when it is said, “What is faith except believing?” it must be understood thus: namely, except the quality from which that movement, believing, proceeds. Likewise, “By charity I mean a movement”: that is, the virtue from which the movement arises. Likewise, “good use,” etc.: that is, the quality from which good use proceeds.

Having shown what virtue is, we must consider what operative grace is. It is that which raises a person so that he may will. Cooperating grace is that which assists him so that he may will rightly, or [Col. 1042B] so that he may not will in vain. Operative and cooperating grace are the same grace, but on account of their different functions they receive different names. It is called operative because it raises a person so that he may will, because it justifies the ungodly, which is the same thing. It is called cooperating because it helps so that a person does not will in vain.

But after this explanation has been made, it seems that it is called operative and cooperating for the same reason. For, as was said, it is called operative because it raises one so that he may will; but it cannot do this without also helping him not to will in vain, for which reason it was called cooperating. Therefore it is called operative and cooperating for the same reason.

Hence some say that grace is called operative because it raises one so that he may will, but cooperating because it assists him to bring the work to completion and add the deed. Thus, according to them, [Col. 1042C] grace is first operative and afterwards cooperating, and it is called cooperating in relation to its own operation.

But it is proved that grace is operative and cooperating simultaneously. Grace is infused into this person; by being infused—that is, while it is being infused—it moves free choice to good or evil, but not to evil; therefore to good. Thus grace, while being infused, moves free choice toward good. Therefore it cooperates then. Therefore it operates and cooperates simultaneously.

Therefore we say that grace operates and cooperates in a person simultaneously in time, but not simultaneously in nature. For the infusion of grace naturally precedes, and cooperation follows, although they are simultaneous in time. For in its very infusion grace stirs free choice, which at the same moment consents and cooperates. More properly, free choice is said to consent to and cooperate with grace than grace with free choice [Note: [Col. 1042D] “With the will accompanying, not leading; following at the heel, not going before.” Augustine, Epistle 106 to Boniface]; just as a soldier is said to go with the king and a servant with his master, not the king with the soldier or the master with the servant.

Therefore from grace which is infused, and from free choice cooperating at the same time, two effects proceed at the same moment. The first is that grace, aiding free choice, frees the person from the evil in which he was; the second is that it helps him not to will in vain. The whole dignity of this deliverance must be ascribed to grace and not to free choice. [Col. 1043A] Grace itself moves and stirs free choice toward good, and it is called cooperating not in relation to free choice, nor even in relation to itself as operative, but in relation to the first two effects just mentioned: the second effect cooperates with the first, that is, operates with the first simultaneously in time.

[Note: [Col. 1043D] Master, II, distinction 26, § d.] The question is which virtue grace is—understand: first grace. It seems that it ought to be charity, since charity is the mother of all virtues. But we say that it is 178 faith [Note: [Col. 1043D] Understand: faith which works through love, as Augustine observes in several places], and that this rather than charity is first grace because faith is the foundation of all virtues and from it proceed the movements of all. For unless someone has faith, how will he have a movement of charity—that is, love? “Without faith it is impossible [Col. 1043B] to please God” (Heb. XI). This virtue naturally—not, I say, temporally—precedes all the others, and temporally precedes the movements of certain virtues, such as fortitude and temperance. For no one can endure adversities, which belongs to fortitude, or flee enticements, which belongs to temperance, unless faith has first preceded in him—that is, a movement of faith. When faith is said to precede the other virtues, however, this must be understood not of the virtue itself but of the movement, as will be shown more fully below.

But it is objected: First grace is a virtue which God works in a person without the person. God works every virtue in a person without the person. Therefore every virtue is first grace. To this it must be said that in the broad sense of the term “first grace,” it is true that every virtue is first grace; [Col. 1043C] if it is taken in a narrower sense, namely for faith, it is not true.

Likewise, since it has been said that grace, or faith, is infused into a person and that a good will proceeds from it, it is objected: For will precedes faith, since Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1043D] Augustine, Homily 26 on John]: “Faith belongs to one willing, not to one unwilling.” Therefore faith proceeds from will. To this it must be said that the statement must be explained thus: “Faith belongs to one willing, not to one unwilling”—that is, faith exists only in one who wills. “Although a person can do other things by willing, he cannot believe except by willing.”

But the Apostle clearly shows that the authority and capacity for acting well lie in faith, grace, and God’s mercy when he says: “It is not of one who wills nor of one who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. IX)—namely, the doing of good, which must be ascribed to divine mercy and the grace of God, not to the human will. For he did not say [Note: [Col. 1043D] Augustine, *Enchiridion*, ch. [uncertain]; and in the solution to Question 2 addressed to Simplician, near the middle], “It belongs to one who wills and not to one who shows mercy”; rather, conversely, “It belongs to one who shows mercy and not to one who wills.” Hence elsewhere: “By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace,” etc. (I Cor. XV). Isaiah likewise says: “You have wrought all our works for us, O Lord” (Isa. XXVI). Just as someone raises a person from mud and afterward, because he is weak, guides and supports him in order to complete his journey, so God’s grace raises a person from the mud of sins. [Col. 1044A] The same point is also expressed by: “To will lies near at hand for me, but I do not find the accomplishing of good” (Rom. I), because completion comes only from God’s grace, and so too the beginning of a will made effective.

## CHAPTER II. How many things concur in the justification of the ungodly, and do we merit first grace?

It should be understood that four things concur in the justification of the ungodly: the infusion of grace; the movement arising from grace and free choice; contrition; and the remission of sins. None of these is earlier than any of the others in time; yet the infusion of grace naturally precedes, and the other three follow in order—not temporally, but by nature. It should also be understood that each of these four is called “justification,” nor can [Col. 1044B] one of them exist in a person without the other three. To the first justification belongs what is read: “You have been justified freely” (Rom. III). Therefore first grace is given freely, not from merits; otherwise it would not be grace. To the same belongs what is read: “God effects justification in a human being without the human being,” which appears false. For as soon as grace is infused, free choice cooperates at that same instant; thus that infusion of grace is not without the human being. To this it must be said that the preposition *in* can signify two things: accompaniment in time and cause. If *in* denotes time, it is false that the infusion of grace occurs without the human being; indeed, when it is infused, the person cooperates by free choice. But if it denotes cause, it is true that the human being is not the cause why grace is infused into him. [Col. 1044C] To the second justification—that is, to the movement proceeding from free choice, with grace preceding it not in time but by nature—belongs the saying: “You have been justified by faith” (Rom. V), that is, because you believed. For believing is a movement arising from faith and free choice. To the same belongs this saying:

> [Note: [Col. 1044D] Augustine, *On the Words of the Apostle*, Sermon 15 (“Though God made us without us, he cannot justify us without us”).] “Although God made us without us, he cannot justify us without us.”

Likewise:

> [Note: [Col. 1044D] Augustine, Tractate 72 on John, after the middle, though somewhat differently: the sense is expressed, not the words.] “To justify the ungodly is greater than to create heaven and earth.”

This is also proved by reason as follows: God can of himself create heaven and earth, but he cannot of himself justify the ungodly unless free choice cooperates. Therefore to justify the ungodly is an act of [Col. 1044D] greater power than to create heaven and earth. Yet this authority seems to contradict it:

> [Note: [Col. 1044D] Augustine, same Tractate 72.] “Both are works of equal power, but one is of greater mercy”—namely, justifying the ungodly rather than creating heaven and earth.

Bede also says: “To heal the paralytic in body was not an act of lesser power than to heal him in mind.” Thus justifying the ungodly is not an act of lesser power than healing the sick.

Therefore, in order to make all these authorities agree, it should be understood that God’s power is sometimes referred [Col. 1045A] to God himself, and sometimes to effects, works, or creatures. If God’s power is referred to God, all God’s actions are equal with respect to him: for the same power can do the least things as well as the greatest, and conversely. But with respect to works and effects, justifying the ungodly is an act of greater power than creating heaven and earth.

Since, as has been said, God gives first grace not for merits but wholly freely, a distinction must be made among the four justifications mentioned above—a distinction to be retained not carelessly but deeply in the heart. Thus we neither merit the first justification nor merit anything by it; we do not merit the second, but by it we merit; we merit the third and by it we merit; we merit the fourth, but by it we do not merit. We do not merit the first because [Col. 1045B] it is given freely; nor do we merit anything by it, because we do not merit by virtue, but by an inward or outward act of virtue. We do not merit the second—that is, the movement—for no merits precede it; but by it we merit contrition and remission of sins. We merit the third—that is, contrition—through the movement which naturally, though not temporally, precedes it; and by contrition we merit the fourth, namely remission of sins. We merit the fourth through the movement and through contrition, but by it we do not merit. That we merit by the second—that is, by the movement—is evident from the Gospel: “Her many sins are forgiven her, because she loved much” (Luke III). Nor should it be understood, as has often been said, that love precedes the remission of sins in time, but only by nature.

[Col. 1045C] We are not unaware of the opinion of some who employ a transposition (*hypallage*) in this authority, saying: “Her sins are forgiven her,” etc., means that she herself loved much because her sins were forgiven her. Thus, according to them, remission of sins precedes love, and we are said to love God because of the remission of sins—although this is not usually said; rather, we are said to love him more. For when he forgives us our sins, we already love him; after remission we are not properly said to love him because of this, since we loved him beforehand, but we are said to love him more. They reverse that authority in this manner to avoid the inconvenience of saying that someone in mortal sin merits remission of sins—an inconvenience they could avoid [Col. 1045D] if they attended to the previously stated order of the four justifications. For Mary was no longer in mortal sin when remission of sins was given to her.

Others say that the word *because* (*quoniam*) there signifies a sign, so that the sense is: “Her sins are forgiven her,” etc., that is, forgiveness was a sign of love. Thus one says: “The king loves me greatly, because he gave me a horse,” that is, the giving of the horse was a sign that the king loved me, not its cause—indeed, rather the reverse. Therefore, since, as has been said, we cannot merit first grace, let us make friends for ourselves from the mammon of iniquity (Luke XVI): friends, that is, the poor or religious persons, so that they may pray for us, that God may deign to infuse his grace into us through their merits; from the mammon of iniquity, that is, from money not of fairness—that is, money which it is not fair, [Col. 1046A] that is, which is superfluous, for us to possess. “Having food and clothing, let us be content with these” (I Tim. VI). Or it is called mammon “of iniquity” because it can scarcely be acquired without iniquity, or is more often acquired with iniquity.

That another person’s merits can avail is shown in the Gospel, where it is read that the paralytic was healed through the faith and merits of those who carried him. Hence the Lord says to him: “Son, your sins are forgiven you” (Matt. IX; Luke V). Bede says on the same passage: “One’s own faith avails greatly where another’s faith avails so much.” Yet it should not be understood that sins are forgiven someone on account of another’s merits, except to children, as happens in baptism, or to adults who are mentally disabled or insane. For if a person is such, he is regarded as a child, especially if he did not deserve [Col. 1046B] to fall into such an illness by sinning. For all such persons, as they say, will be judged according to the state in which they were when they became incapable [perhaps *impotes*, “powerless”] in mind. Hence some say that the paralytic was mentally disabled; and thus sins are forgiven through others’ merits, but by means of the infusion of grace, because grace is infused through others’ merits, and, once infused, it remits sins.

But an objection is raised: grace is infused into this person for another’s merits. Therefore it is infused for merits—which is false. For the force of the expression would imply his own merits. This is a fallacy. “This bishop gives this man a prebend for the merits of his father; therefore he gives this man a prebend for merits”—not so, for it would seem to mean for his own merits. Again: this man merits first grace for that other person. Therefore he merits [Col. 1046C] eternal life for him. Therefore, by that other’s merits, this man has eternal life. Therefore this man is saved because of another’s merits. For where one’s own merits are lacking, another’s avail. To this it must be said that, although one person merits first grace for another, he does not thereby merit eternal life for him. No adult is saved solely by another’s merits, as is clear in this example. A king issued an edict that whoever entered into his presence and wished to obey him should receive a reward. Now the gatekeeper can cause this soldier to enter before the king, but cannot cause the soldier to receive the reward; for he cannot cause the soldier to obey the king unless the soldier himself wills it. Likewise, this righteous person can by his prayers and merits cause that person to have first grace, but not [Col. 1046D] that he have eternal life, unless he consents and acts by free choice.

Again: this person can merit charity for another. Therefore he can merit for him every lesser good than charity. But perseverance in charity is a lesser good. Therefore he can merit for that person that he persevere in charity. No one can have eternal life unless he perseveres in charity, and conversely. Therefore this person can merit eternal life for that other. It must not, therefore, be granted that one can merit perseverance for another, since free choice cooperates in it. Fallacy of the first kind. “This person can merit eternal life for himself; therefore he can merit every lesser good, and thus faith”—which is false.

Again, God requires from no one what that person cannot do; but he requires everyone to have faith with charity. [Col. 1047A] Therefore everyone can bring it about that he has faith with charity; therefore that he has faith; therefore that he has first grace. For if no one can bring it about that he has first grace, and no one can be saved without grace, then no one should be blamed if he is not saved. To this it must be said that the proposition “A person can bring it about that he has first grace” can be understood in two ways. If it is understood thus—“a person can bring it about that he has first grace,” that is, can make himself fit so that he can receive God’s grace if God wishes to bestow it—then it is true. But if it is understood thus—that a person can make God bestow grace upon him—it is false, as is clear in this example. This man owes his lord certain hospitality once a year. This man can bring it about [Col. 1047B] that he has his lord as a guest—that is, he can prepare and adorn himself and his house in such a way that, if his lord comes, he can receive him honourably. In this sense it is true. But he cannot bring it about that he has his lord as a guest—that is, that his lord comes to stay with him—unless the lord himself wishes it; for this lies within the lord’s discretion.

Again: this person can cause that hermit to merit first grace for him; for he can make friends from the mammon of iniquity. Therefore he can merit first grace—if not directly, at least through an intermediary. This is not true. For if this person asks his father to ask the bishop to give him a prebend, it does not follow that this person asks the bishop to give [Col. 1047C] him a prebend. For he does not know or see the bishop. Again: this person can merit first grace for another; he cannot do this for himself, for no one merits first grace for himself. Therefore he can benefit another more than himself. Fallacy. “This layman can acquire a prebend for his educated son, but not for himself; therefore he can benefit another more than himself.”

Again, by authority: “Penance restores everything that has been taken away.” But this man lost first grace through mortal sin. Therefore through penance he can recover it. Therefore through penance he can merit charity. Therefore someone can merit first grace through penance. To this it must be said that, when it is said “Penance restores everything that has been taken away,” this is understood of the merits of exterior actions performed in charity, not of virtues. [Col. 1047D] Therefore it does not concern first grace, since first grace is a virtue.

Again, it is asked whether a person is worthy of first grace when it is infused into him. If he is, then at that time he merits first grace. Fallacy. “The king’s son is worthy of the kingdom; therefore he has merited possessing the kingdom.” Again, before the infusion of grace this person either was or was not worthy of grace. If you say “worthy,” this is disproved: at that time he was in mortal sin; therefore he was not then worthy of grace. If it is said that he was not worthy, why then was it said to a human being: “Son, when you come to the service of God, prepare your soul” (Ecclus. II)? It is also said concerning the prophet Malachi:

> [Note: [Col. 1047D] In the Gloss on this passage of the prophet.] “Something precedes in hearts such that, although they have not yet been justified, [Col. 1048A] they are nevertheless found worthy of justifications.”

To this it must be said that before the infusion of grace a human being is not worthy of grace. Therefore the saying to a person, “Son, when you come,” etc., must be understood thus: make yourself fit to receive grace—which is done by understanding and reflection. For a person who wills to be fit to receive grace first understands how great God’s mercy is and how sweet his commandments are; then immediately he considers how he may fulfil them. These two things are the worthiness which the authority on Malachi says precedes in hearts, by which persons are found worthy of justifications—that is, of grace—although they are not yet justified. To such persons it is said: “Human being, come to the service of God.”

## CHAPTER III. Whether We Merit First Grace; Also Whether Virtue Is Better than the Act of Virtue

[Col. 1048B]

From these points it is clear that no one merits first grace for himself. To show that no one merits first grace, one argument will suffice. For this, we believe, is agreed by all: no one merits except in that in which he acts. But in the infusion of grace a human being does nothing—taking *in* causally, not temporally. Therefore in the infusion of grace no one merits anything. Therefore no one merits first grace.

On the contrary, virtues make us worthy of eternal life; therefore by virtues we merit eternal life. Fallacy. “This man is worthy of a prebend by learning; therefore by learning he merits a prebend.” Or: “This person is worthy [Col. 1048C] of a kingdom by nobility; therefore by nobility he merits a kingdom.” No.

Again, God imposes punishment for every sin, but he does not give a crown or reward for every good thing, since he gives it not for virtues but for acts of virtues. Therefore God is more inclined to punish than to reward. Fallacy. Before sin Adam could fall by himself but could not advance by himself; therefore he was more inclined to evil than to good.

Again, virtue and the act of virtue are two goods. By one of them we merit, by the other we do not merit. Therefore that by which we merit is better than that by which we do not merit. Therefore the act of virtue is better than virtue.

To this it must be said that a comparison of this kind is unsuitable, because the act proceeds from virtue. [Col. 1048D] Likewise are all such comparisons: “A tree is better than its fruit,” or “fruit is better than a tree”; “a field is better than its crop,” or conversely; “medicine is better than health,” and conversely; “eternal punishment is more to be avoided than sin,” or conversely. All comparisons of this sort are incongruous, because one thing exists for the sake of the other. For if you say that sin is more to be avoided than eternal punishment, I disprove it: sin can be removed by penance, whereas eternal punishment cannot be removed in any way. Therefore eternal punishment is more to be avoided than sin. Conversely, nothing is more to be avoided than offence against God; but sin [Col. 1049A] is offence against God; therefore it is more to be avoided than eternal punishment.

Again, being in hell is a loss which, once incurred, necessarily brings eternal punishment—a loss greater than which there is none. But someone can have mortal sin even though he is not to be punished with eternal punishment. Therefore being in hell is more to be avoided than committing mortal sin. Fallacy. Purgatorial fire is a punishment in which, if someone is, he will have eternal life; but it is not the case that, if someone has charity, he will have eternal life. Therefore being in purgatorial fire is more to be desired than having charity—which is false. For although purgatorial fire is a punishment such that, once it is undergone, eternal life—than which nothing is better—must be possessed, nevertheless, once charity is possessed, eternal life need not thereby be possessed. Yet [Col. 1049B] being in charity is more to be desired than being there.

So too there are two goods, one of which is more to be desired than those two goods together: for faith as a virtue is more to be desired than faith as a virtue together with imperfect charity. Likewise there are two things, one of which is as much to be desired as both together: for example, blessedness and justice. Thus all comparisons of this sort are to be rejected.

That virtue is more to be desired than the act of virtue seems to be shown thus. Without virtue an act cannot be meritorious. Therefore virtue is more to be desired than the act of virtue. Again, virtue is like a tree, an act like fruit; and fruit cannot be had without a tree. Therefore virtue is more to be desired than the act of virtue. Again, virtue justifies [Col. 1049C] without an act, but an act does not justify without virtue: for virtue justifies children and also certain adults. Therefore virtue is better than an act. The conclusions of all these arguments are incongruous, as has been said; yet these arguments can have solutions and counterexamples—the three arguments just stated.

Since virtues are to be loved, it is asked whether they are to be loved in one of the four ways usually assigned. For there are four things to be loved with charity: God, neighbour, flesh, and soul. We are bound to love God more than ourselves, but we do not love virtue in this way. We love our neighbour so that he may enjoy God, but not virtue in this way; the flesh so that it may be glorified, but neither virtue in this way; and the soul so that in it we may enjoy the vision of God. Yet apparently we do not love [Col. 1049D] virtue in this way. How, then, are virtues to be loved, since they are things to be loved? We say that love of virtues is included under love of the soul. For just as I love my flesh for glorification, so I love my head, which is a part of it, so that it may be glorified with it. Likewise, just as I love the soul, so too I love the virtues, which are goods of the soul, so that through them we may enjoy the vision of the Godhead in glory.

## CHAPTER IV. Whether We Merit the Movement That Is from Grace and Free Choice, or Merit by It

Having shown that we neither merit the first justification nor merit by it, we must proceed to the second justification, that is, the movement arising from grace and free choice. It is asked, therefore, whether we merit it itself. That we do not merit it is clear. For if we merited it, something would precede it in time or nature by which we merited it. But in time nothing precedes except sin; therefore, since we do not merit that movement by sin, nothing precedes it in time [Col. 1050A] by which we merit that movement. By nature nothing precedes except the infusion of grace. But by grace we merit nothing, as has already been shown. Therefore nothing precedes that movement, by nature or by time, by which we merit it. Therefore we do not merit it, which is true. Yet by that second justification we merit the third, that is, contrition; understand “third” not temporally but naturally.

But an objection is raised: by the movement arising from free choice and grace this person merits contrition; but contrition [Col. 1050B] is a punishment. Therefore by that movement he merits a punishment. But that movement is good. Therefore by a good movement he merits a punishment.

Again, it seems possible to prove that someone merits remission of sins by mortal sin. For the thief sinned mortally and merited some punishment. Therefore he merited either temporal or eternal punishment. But no eternal punishment was imposed upon him, because he was immediately in paradise; nor is it read that he endured any temporal punishment except contrition. Yet he merited some punishment; therefore he merited contrition. But through contrition remission of sins is obtained. Therefore the thief merited that through which remission of sins would be obtained; therefore that through which salvation would be obtained. Therefore by mortal sins he merited eternal salvation, and thus someone merits being saved by mortal sin.

Again, just as no good goes unrewarded, so no [Col. 1050C] evil goes unpunished. But the thief’s sin was not punished eternally; therefore it was punished temporally, but only by contrition. Therefore by mortal sin he merited contrition. And thus argue against the first point as stated.

We say that by a good movement he merits such a punishment, namely contrition, because it is a mild and medicinal punishment, since he has hope of future health—that is, of remission of sins. For it serves to mitigate, or even remove, a greater punishment. Thus a sick man with an ulcer willingly endures an incision made by a physician, because he hopes through it to be cured; and it serves to mitigate the greater illness which would follow unless [Col. 1050D] it were done, or wholly to remove the disease.

But when it is subsequently said that someone merits contrition or remission of sins by mortal sin, we do not grant this; rather, by mortal sin he merits only eternal punishment. Thus this argument is false: “This person merited some punishment by mortal sin, and no punishment was inflicted on him except contrition. Therefore he merited contrition.” Fallacy. “This murderer deserved hanging, and the king cut off his foot. Therefore he deserved only this punishment.” This is false, because the king dealt mercifully with him and changed the greater punishment owed into a lesser. Thus the heavenly King, by his mercy, changed the punishment owed for mortal sin—that is, eternal punishment—into a temporal punishment which the man did not merit.

What is subsequently said—“No evil goes unpunished”—is true [Col. 1051A] either eternally or temporally. But that sin of the holy thief was not punished eternally; it was punished temporally by contrition, because he was dealt with mercifully. Or one may say that no evil goes unpunished because God immediately withdraws grace. Or one may say that no evil goes unpunished, meaning that a human being is punished for every evil. Yet distinguish the equivocation of the proposition: a person is punished for evil either in order to remove it through contrition, by which sin is removed; or for sin—that is, by the desert of sin—and then eternally, if it is mortal.

> [Note: [Col. 1051D] See among others Augustine, *The City of God*, XXI, ch. 11, etc.; Gregory, *Dialogues*, book IV, ch. 44.]

It is asked, since God is merciful, why he punishes a human being eternally for sin, though sin is temporal. They give this reason: just as the person who refuses to repent and so dies [Col. 1051B] sins in his own eternity—and, if he were always to live, would always sin—so God punishes the human being

> [Note: [Col. 1051D] St Thomas, *Supplement*, q. 99, art. 1, in the body. [Another reason is that the human being sinned in his own eternity.]]

in his own eternity. Or, more reasonably, it may be said that God does not punish a person eternally for a temporal sin, but for an eternal sin. For mortal sin is eternal. Since it is in the soul and is not removed in the present life, it is certain that it will not be removed after death. For there will be no place there for removing sins; thus it will always be in the soul and will endure as long as the soul does. Therefore it is eternal; and so mortal sin, which here is not removed through contrition or confession, is eternal. Although, therefore, God punishes eternally for that sin, he nonetheless deals mercifully with the person, namely in this, that during this life [Col. 1051C] he does not punish him but waits, even until death, to see whether he will repent; for he does not will the death of the sinner but repentance (II Pet. III). If he has repentance, God changes that punishment into a temporal one.

## CHAPTER V. Whether Greater Contrition Is Required for Removing Mortal than Venial Sin

We must now proceed to the third justification, namely contrition. Since both venial and mortal sin are removed through contrition, it is asked whether greater contrition is necessary for removing mortal sin than for removing venial sin, or conversely. That greater contrition is necessary for the removal of grave sin than of venial sin is shown as follows. Both venial and mortal sin are removed by [Col. 1051D] contrition, but mortal sin is graver and greater than venial sin. Therefore greater contrition is necessary for removing mortal than venial sin.

Again, eternal punishment is owed for mortal sin, while only temporal punishment is owed for venial sin; and neither this nor that can be removed except through contrition. Therefore greater contrition is required for removing mortal than venial sin.

Again, according to an authority, a multitude of venial sins equals a mortal sin. Let this least mortal sin be indicated as equal to this multitude of venial sins. [Col. 1052A] Therefore the amount of contrition sufficient to remove this mortal sin is sufficient to remove that multitude; but whatever suffices to remove that multitude suffices to remove one sin from that multitude. Therefore, of that multitude, the amount sufficient to remove this mortal sin suffices to remove this venial sin. Or thus: the amount of contrition sufficient to remove mortal sin is sufficient to remove that multitude, and conversely; but greater contrition is required to remove that multitude than to remove any one sin of that multitude. Therefore greater contrition is required for removing this mortal sin than this venial sin.

Again, eternal punishment exceeds temporal punishment by more than any greatest contrition exceeds any smallest contrition, and more than any mortal sin exceeds any venial sin. But mortal sin is removed with respect to guilt by the greatest contrition. Therefore any venial sin whatsoever is removed by any contrition whatsoever, however small. Therefore greater contrition is owed for mortal than venial sin.

Again, venial sin is daily removed by the Lord’s Prayer, by however slight a contrition, by the beating of the breast, and such things; but mortal sin is removed only by the greatest contrition. Therefore greater contrition is required for mortal than for venial sin.

> [Note: [Col. 1052D] Augustine, book I, *Sermon on the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, before the middle. See notes on Pullus. *Master*, IV, distinction 16.]

Again, if greater contrition is owed for venial than for mortal sin, then venial sin is forgiven with greater difficulty than mortal sin. If so, that mystical sense found in the Gospel concerning the Lord’s raising of three dead persons is lost: one in the house (Matt. IX), another at the gate [Col. 1052C] (Luke VII), and the third in the tomb (John XI). By the first—because the Lord quickly raised him in the house and without a sign of labour—is understood sin existing in thought, which can be removed quickly and easily. By the second, whom he raised at the gate, but with a greater sign of labour than the first, is understood sin which had already reached the gate that is in a human being, namely the mouth, when a person speaks about the sin which he had conceived in his mind in order to bring it into action. This cannot be removed as easily as the first sin. By the third, whom he raised in the tomb with the greatest sorrow and groaning—hence he is said there to have wept—and already stinking because he had been dead four days, is understood mortal sin, which [Col. 1052D] is removed with the greatest contrition, groaning, and shedding of tears. Therefore greater contrition is required for removing mortal than venial sin.

> [Note: [Col. 1052D] See *Master* IV, distinction 21.]

Conversely, it seems possible to prove that greater contrition is required for removing venial than [p. 185] mortal sin as follows. A dying person is contrite for every sin and repents by name of every grave sin, and generally of every venial sin. What he has he carries with him: wood, hay, straw. Therefore he carries with him the guilt of venial sin. Therefore through that contrition venial sin has not been removed [Col. 1053A] with respect to guilt, whereas mortal sin has been removed by it both with respect to guilt and punishment. Therefore that contrition does not suffice to remove venial sin. Therefore some contrition suffices to remove mortal sin which does not suffice to remove venial sin; and so greater contrition is required to remove venial than mortal sin. For if the contrition by which mortal sin is removed suffices to remove venial sin, why, then, is venial sin not removed by that contrition as mortal sin is? What prevents it?

Again, it is possible for someone in charity to have venial sin. Therefore it is possible for someone to be contrite for every mortal sin and retain venial sin. Let it be so, then: this person repents by name of every mortal sin and generally of venial sin; he is contrite for every sin, [Col. 1053B] and venial sin remains while mortal sin is removed. Therefore that contrition does not suffice to remove venial sin.

Again, it is either possible or impossible for this person to repent of some sin without repenting of every sin. If one says that it is impossible for him to repent of some sin without repenting of every sin: but it is impossible for him to repent of every sin without abandoning everything. Therefore it is impossible for him to repent of some sin without abandoning everything. But this person repents of some sin. Therefore he abandons everything—which is false. For he does not abandon the intense affection which he has for his children, even though he repents of this.

But if one says that it is possible for him to repent of some sin and not of every sin: since he cannot repent of one mortal sin without repenting of every mortal sin, and conversely, and it is impossible for him to repent of every mortal sin—therefore it is possible for him to repent of every mortal sin and not of every venial sin. Therefore it is possible for him to be contrite for every mortal sin while venial sin remains, and thus it is possible for every mortal sin to be removed through some contrition while venial sin remains. Therefore the contrition which removes mortal sin does not suffice to remove venial sin.

Again, venial sin is forgiven to someone after death, but it is certain that nothing would be forgiven to anyone after death unless his mortal sins had been removed before his death. Therefore venial sin is forgiven after death to someone whose mortal sins were previously removed through contrition. Therefore through [Col. 1053D] some contrition mortal sins were removed but venial sins were not. Therefore that contrition suffices to remove mortal, but not venial, sin; and so greater contrition is required to remove venial than mortal sin. That venial sin is forgiven after death is derived from the Gospel saying: “Whoever sins against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven either in this age or in the age to come” (Matt. XII). This implies that some sin is forgiven after death. But if someone says that venial sin is said to be forgiven after death because it is remitted with respect to punishment, not guilt, then for the same reason mortal sin could be said [Col. 1054A] to be forgiven after death, since its punishment is remitted—yet this is not read in Holy Scripture.

To these arguments some introduce the following solution. They say that the contrition sufficient to remove mortal sin is not sufficient to remove venial sin, and they give an example. Thus it can happen that a medicine sufficient to remove a great illness is not sufficient to remove a very slight illness; and morning light suffices to remove the darkness of night, yet does not suffice to remove the smallest cloud which arises during the day.

Others think it better that whatever contrition suffices to remove mortal sin also suffices to remove venial sin; but not every contrition which removes mortal sin removes venial sin. For sometimes mortal sin is removed [Col. 1054B] while venial sin remains, as in one who dies with an intense affection for his children. But if that contrition suffices to remove venial sin, why does it not remove venial sin as it does mortal sin? Because he does not repent of it. He is sorry that he has it, but is not contrite for it; he does not abandon it, hindered by carnal affection. But it is asked whence it comes about that, when mortal sins have been removed, venial sin remains.

> [Note: [Col. 1053D] Augustine, *Enchiridion*, ch. 69; *The City of God*, book XXI, ch. 26; *Exposition on Psalm* 80, before the end; and Sermon 3 [Col. 1054D] on Psalm 103.]

This is because charity does not disdain to dwell with venial sin; yet it does disdain to dwell with mortal sin. Therefore, after mortal sin has been removed through contrition, someone can die with venial sin and carry with him wood, hay, straw—that is, venial sins. Some are compared with wood because they are graver and more difficult [Col. 1054C] to remove than the others, just as wood is harder to burn than hay or straw. Others are compared with hay because they are somewhat light and easy to remove; others with straw because they are very easy to remove, just as straw is easy to burn.

> [Note: [Col. 1054D] *Master*, IV, distinction 21, §3.]

It is asked whether building with wood, hay, and straw is the same as sinning venially. If it is, then building with gold, silver, and precious stones is likewise the same thing as loving God; and all who build with gold, silver, and precious stones—that is, who love God—sin venially, because no one in this life is without venial sin. Therefore all such persons build with wood, hay, and straw; therefore they will pass through purgatory, because all who build with wood, hay, and straw will pass through [Col. 1054D] purgatory.

To this it must be said that building with wood, hay, and straw is not the same as sinning venially. For to build with wood, hay, and straw is to have a carnal attachment to temporal things while preferring God. Therefore everyone who builds with wood, hay, and straw sins venially; but the converse does not follow, as will soon be clear. But to build with gold, silver, and precious stones is to love God perfectly and despise all earthly things. Therefore every such person loves God, but not everyone who loves God is such a person.
