Those who build with gold, silver, and precious stones sometimes sin venially, [Col. 1055A] but they do not build with wood or hay, because venial sin is immediately removed in them. So great is the fervour of charity which they have that venial sin is immediately extinguished in them, like a drop of water in a furnace.

## CHAPTER VI. Whether Someone Can Be Contrite from Charity for One Sin but Not for Another of Which He Is Guilty
[Note: [Col. 1055D] Lombard, Book IV, distinction 15.] But since it has been said that mortal sin can be removed while venial sin remains—not removed either as to guilt or as to punishment—an objection is raised. For Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1055D] *On True and False Penance*, ch. 6, not far from the end; [Col. 1056D]]: “It is impious unbelief to hope for a half-pardon from him who is supreme justice.” That is to say: whoever hopes that God remits to someone half of his sins and not all of them—that is, mortal sins but not venial ones—is unbelieving. Therefore mortal sins are remitted to no one without venial sins.

To this we say that this authority must be understood of grave sins. For no mortal sins are remitted to anyone unless all the mortal sins he has are remitted: mortal sins are not divided in half. Hence no one may divide his contrition or confession in half, grieving for some sins but not for all, or confessing some but not all, when he remembers them. Thus, if someone has two mortal sins and confesses one of them to a priest, grieving over it and resolving thereafter not to follow that sin, but conceals the other because he is unwilling [Col. 1055C] to confess it, and performs the satisfaction imposed upon him for the sin which he confessed: if, after a long time—for example, after two or three years—he confesses the other sin which he had kept silent, he must return to confess the sin which he had formerly confessed and again perform satisfaction for it. For the earlier confession was not a true confession but a fraudulent one; nor was the satisfaction a worthy satisfaction. Thus there will not be a double affliction, nor will God punish twice for the same thing (Nahum 1) [Note: [Col. 1056D] See Jerome on this passage.]; which indeed would occur if he had first repented and made satisfaction worthily, and were afterward compelled to make satisfaction again.

Yet some try to prove that the penitent who first confessed one mortal sin while concealing [Col. 1055D] the other truly repented: “Penance is to weep for sins committed and not to commit what ought to be wept for.” But he wept for that sin, resolved to abstain from it, and did abstain. Therefore he had true penance. This is false, because he was not weeping on account of God; he was not weeping with charity. For if he wept on account of God, he would keep silent about no sin that he remembered. I say this because, if he did not remember it, perhaps invincible ignorance would excuse him—unless he had fallen into that ignorance through the fault of sin. For when a person wishes to confess his sins, he ought beforehand to reflect diligently, lest, even after such prior examination, he omit some sin through ignorance. If he later recalls and confesses it, he is not bound to return to the earlier confession or satisfaction.

## Chapter VII. Whether we are bound to be more contrite for a greater sin than for a lesser one

It was said above that the greater the sin, the more a person is bound to be contrite. But an objection is raised: the more this man sins, the more he is bound to be contrite; but another man, who sins less, is more contrite. Therefore this man transgresses, or is insufficiently contrite. If he transgresses, therefore he sins mortally. Therefore he does not have charity.

To this it must be said that the more a person sins, the more he is bound *that he should be contrite*: the adverb “more” qualifies the verb “is bound”; yet he is not bound to be *more contrite*. However great [Col. 1056B] the sin may be, any contrition possessed with charity—whether great or small—suffices to remove it as to guilt, though I do not say as to punishment, provided only that it is possessed with charity. This is evident because, as soon as charity is present, mortal sin is removed; for the two cannot exist together. Therefore one who sins more is more bound to become contrite, but is not bound to become more contrite, since any degree of contrition, if it is possessed with charity, suffices to remove guilt. Yet he is bound to make greater satisfaction.

For satisfaction does not consist wholly in contrition, but also in prayer, the giving of alms, and the like. If it consisted wholly in contrition, then one who sinned more would be bound [Col. 1056C] to be more contrite, just as one who sins more is bound to make greater satisfaction. Therefore this argument is false: “The more one sins, the more one is bound to be contrite; but that other man is more contrite than this one; therefore this one transgresses.”

Observe, nevertheless, that the word *is bound* (*tenetur*) is equivocal in several ways. It is said with reference to a command, a reward, something entrusted, and perhaps in other ways. Thus no one is more bound than another by command, nor by reward; but one who has committed more, or to whom more has been entrusted, is more bound in respect of what has been committed, so that in both senses of this term *committed* what was said is true.

Again: contrition is a merit of eternal life, namely through the remission of sins. Therefore the more contrite a person is, the more he is bound to be good. [Col. 1056D] Therefore he is bound to be better. Therefore, if he is not better than one who has sinned less, he will be a transgressor. This is the fallacy of the first [figure].

Medicine produces health. Therefore, the greater the medicine this man receives, the healthier he becomes. Again, this man who sins more than that other is more contrite than the other. Therefore he has more intense charity than the other; for it does not seem that equal contritions can arise from charity of equally intense degree. But I prove that the other has more intense charity: for he is contrite, and contrition restores what was taken away. Therefore contrition restores what he lost. Therefore it restores him to a higher degree, assuming that he fell from that degree. [Col. 1057A] Therefore he is at a higher degree of charity. Therefore he has more intense charity than the one who is more contrite. We shall reserve examination of these matters until we treat charity.

If anyone considers what has been said, he can see that any contrition possessed with charity suffices to remove mortal sin as to guilt, though not as to punishment. God alone knows the latter, since he knows human thoughts and the hidden things of the heart. This is why our priests impose satisfaction to remove mortal sin as to punishment, although it has been removed as to guilt by contrition. Thus what is lacking in satisfaction through contrition they supply by external satisfaction: prayer, [Col. 1057B] the giving of alms, fasting, mortification of the flesh, and such things. For if the priest knew that the penitent’s contrition were so great that it sufficed to remove both guilt and punishment, it would not be necessary to impose another satisfaction upon him. But because he does not know—and even if he does know, it is good that he should impose it—it is better for us to do more than less. If satisfaction finds no punishment to remove, it contributes to a greater crown.

## Chapter VIII. Whether God punishes a person as much as he has deserved to be punished, and thus mercifully

It is asked whether contrition can be so great that it suffices to remove sin in both respects—[Col. 1057C] both as to guilt and as to punishment. We grant that it can, as happened in the thief. For we do not read that he suffered any punishment except contrition; similarly in blessed Mary Magdalene.

But an objection is raised. The contrition in this person is as great as the mortal sin formerly was in him. That contrition is a punishment inflicted by God. Therefore God punishes this man with as great a punishment as he deserved. Therefore God punishes him as much as he deserved. Therefore God does not deal mercifully with him.

Again: if contrition is as great as sin, can not some contrition be greater than sin and exceed it? But that contrition is punishment inflicted upon this man by God for sin. Therefore God punishes him with a greater punishment than he deserved. Therefore he punishes him more than he deserved. [Col. 1057D] Therefore God not only deals mercifully with him but cruelly as well.

That God punishes no one by temporal punishment as much as he deserves to be punished may be proved by one argument alone. Whoever sins mortally deserves to be punished with eternal punishment; but temporal punishment is nothing in comparison with eternal punishment. Therefore God punishes no one for mortal sin with temporal punishment greater than he deserved.

To this it must be said that God punishes no one as much as he deserved to be punished for sin. Understand “for” in two senses, as above: namely, neither for the removal of sin nor on account of the merit of sin. For if he punishes a person in order to remove sin, with temporal punishment, it is certain [Col. 1058A] that he does not punish him as much as he deserved, because he does not punish him with eternal punishment. Again, if God punishes a person for sin—that is, on account of the merit of sin—with eternal punishment, he does not punish him as much as he deserved, because God always spares and always remits something of the punishment due.

When it is said, “This man’s contrition is as great as his mortal sin was,” this can be understood in two ways. First note that sin is not called great by quantity, like a piece of wood or a stone, but by duration, contempt, or more frequently [perhaps: frequency]. For a great punishment is due to what is done out of contempt; hence one sin is called greater than another because a greater punishment is due to one than to the other.

Therefore, when it is said that this man’s contrition is as great as his sin was—that is, that [Col. 1058B] his contrition has as great an effect as his sin had—it is true. For as sin separated him from God, so contrition reconciles him to God. Likewise, the proposition “This medicine is as great as the abscess” can be understood in two ways. Taken in quantity, it is false; but that it has as great and such an effect is true. For as the abscess made this man ill, so this medicine makes him well.

[Note: [Col. 1057D] Lombard, Book IV, distinction 46.] Since, then, it is established that God punishes no one as much as he deserved, it is doubtful whether eternal punishment punishes someone as much as he deserved. Some say that it does, and distinguish as follows. Although God’s mercy and justice are essentially in all his works, his justice and mercy are not present in all his works in their effects; nor are the effects of his justice and mercy apparent in all his works. In some there is an effect of mercy and not justice, as in children who die immediately after baptism. In others there is an effect of justice and not mercy, as in the damned; in still others both effects, as in the saints. Hence they say that God punishes Judas as much as he can punish him justly. But since we treated this question above sufficiently clearly, unwilling to do what has already been done, let us pass to other matters appropriately arising here. For although it is settled that God punishes a person less than he deserves and never more, some attempt to argue the contrary.

## Chapter IX. Whether, of two people punished with equal eternal punishment, one is punished more than the other if he also undergoes temporal punishment

[Col. 1058D]

Let there be two equally wicked people, to be punished with equal eternal punishment. One is hanged, while the other dies a natural death. They deserved to be punished with equal eternal punishment, and will be so punished. Moreover, one is punished with temporal punishment and the other is not. Therefore this one is punished more than the other. But he did not deserve to be punished more than the other. Therefore he is punished more than he deserved.

Again, if each were to be punished only with temporal punishment—for example, if both deserved to be punished by hanging—and this one were compelled to suffer another temporal punishment besides the punishment he deserved, [Col. 1059A] would it not be said that he was punished more than he deserved? By the same reasoning, when he is punished with both temporal and eternal punishment, is he not punished more than he deserved, since he deserved to be punished only with eternal punishment?

Again, did this man deserve, or did he not deserve, the temporal punishment he suffers, namely hanging? If he did not deserve it but is punished by it, and nothing is remitted to him from the eternal punishment, which is equally due to him and the other man, then God punishes him beyond what he deserved. If you say that he deserved that punishment: the other man, equally wicked, is not punished by this punishment, nor does he withdraw himself from it. Therefore this punishment has been remitted to the other.

Again, this man deserved this punishment according to secular justice; but divine justice does not conflict with secular justice, nor the reverse. Indeed, the material sword was permitted [Col. 1059B] to the judge in order to punish people bodily. Therefore this man deserved this punishment according to divine justice. Therefore he deserved it.

Again, he deserved eternal punishment. But eternal punishment is a kind of successive whole: it has different punishments or parts, now fiery, now watery; and also, as Augustine says: “Among those particular punishments there is alternation and an interval during which bodies suffer nothing, so that afterward they may be tortured more grievously; for they pass from snowy waters to the heat of excessive fires” (Job 24). Therefore, since he deserved eternal punishment which has parts in this way, and deserved it whole, he deserved each of those parts. But each such particular punishment is temporal punishment, which begins and ceases to exist. Therefore he deserved temporal [Col. 1059C] punishment.

Therefore temporal punishment is inflicted upon a person by God [Note: [Col. 1059D] Lombard, Book I, distinction 46, §1; but especially Book IV, distinction 15, §1, to which Peter of Poitiers here alludes. See also [Col. 1060D] Augustine, Tractate 124 on John.] for five reasons: either to increase a person’s merits, as in Job; for the preservation of the good, as in Paul; for correction, as in Mary, Moses’ sister, who was struck with leprosy because she reproached her brother; as the beginning and sign of future punishment, as in Herod and Antiochus; or to make God’s glory manifest, as in the man born blind. But this temporal punishment was not inflicted on this man by God except as the beginning of future punishment, because it was not medicine to him but rather harm, since he did not endure it patiently—though it was the beginning of future punishment. Therefore it was a part of it; therefore he deserved it.

Different persons resolve this question in different ways. Some say that both these men deserved both eternal and temporal punishment. Although temporal punishment is inflicted upon this one and not upon the other, God does not therefore act unjustly toward him: he suffers nothing that he did not deserve. What is it to him if something of the punishment is remitted to the other and not to himself? “Is your eye evil because I am good?” (Matthew 20). This is like the case in which each of two thieves deserved to have both feet cut off, and the king removes both feet from one but only one from the other. He does not act unjustly toward the one who loses both, although he acts more mercifully toward the other.

Others think differently. They say that both [Col. 1060A] deserved eternal punishment and temporal punishment, agreeing with the others on that point; but neither will sustain a greater or lesser punishment than the other, because temporal punishment added to eternal punishment does not increase it, since it is nothing in comparison with eternal punishment, just as candlelight does not increase the brightness of day, nor a drop of water the sea. Thus the person who is hanged will be punished by more punishments, both temporal and eternal, but not by a greater punishment. For the magnitude of punishment is measured not by the plurality of punishments but by their severity, nor by duration. Therefore, although this man begins to be punished earlier through hanging, he is not punished more. The contrary is clear from eternal blessedness: although the thief who was [Col. 1060B] on the cross attained eternal blessedness before the Blessed Virgin, he did not therefore attain a greater blessedness.

Others again offer another solution. They say that God, who is a just judge and true weigher of merits, punishes these men equally. Although both deserved hanging in addition to eternal punishment, and one is hanged while the other is not, he nevertheless punishes them equally, because as much as he punishes this one with temporal punishment, so much he remits from his eternal punishment. It is like a king who gives equal pay to his soldiers: sometimes he gives one only gold, another silver and gold; yet he rewards them equally, so that what he gives one in silver he withholds from the other in gold.

Each of these solutions is plausible, but others seem to give a more subtle reason. They say that such a case cannot occur: namely, that two persons are equally wicked and one is punished by temporal death while the other is not. For that temporal punishment will either be medicine to him or the beginning of future damnation. If it is medicine, then it will be given to remove mortal sin, and he therefore no longer dies wicked but good. If it is given as the beginning of eternal damnation, it is certain that he is neither contrite nor repentant. Therefore he is contemptuous. Therefore he becomes obstinate; but obstinacy or contempt is mortal sin. Therefore he is worse than the other. If this is so, the question of why he is punished more no longer arises. That he becomes worse because he does not receive that punishment as medicine is clear; for it is a great mercy of God when he deigns [Col. 1060D] to heal us by temporal punishment. A father corrects his son because he loves him. Thus a person may hope more confidently for God’s love than if he were not scourged. For God allows the wicked to flourish because he reserves eternal punishment for them. Hence: “I will not punish your daughters when they commit fornication” (Hosea 4). As though he said: I shall not scourge them here, but punish them eternally.

The authors of this solution, therefore—and we with them—say that the man who is hanged did not deserve that punishment, and we answer the foregoing arguments as follows.

When it is first said: “This man did not deserve this [Col. 1061A] punishment, but God punishes him with it and remits none of the punishment due him. Therefore he punishes him beyond what he deserved,” this is a fallacy. This soldier, who deserves pay, does not deserve his daily food; yet the king provides for him daily and deducts nothing from his pay. Therefore the king rewards him beyond what he deserved.

As to what was subsequently said—“This man deserved this punishment according to secular justice, and divine justice does not conflict with secular justice; therefore he deserved it according to divine justice”—this too is a fallacy. According to the law concerning theft, a man deserves to be burned, or to lose a foot, or something of that kind; and the law concerning homicide does not conflict with the law concerning theft. Therefore, according to the law concerning homicide, he deserves to be burned. Secular law does not conflict with divine law. For the command, “You shall not kill” (Exodus [Col. 1061B] 20), should be understood as referring to killing from hatred of heart.

As to what was afterward said—“This man deserved eternal punishment, and it has particular parts, distinct from one another also by intervals; therefore he deserved it whole or not whole”—the inference does not follow, nor does the statement even seem fitting. It is like saying: “This man bought this house, which has parts; therefore he bought it whole or not whole.”

Observe carefully, however, that the human body will be punished by one kind of eternal punishment, the soul by another. The body will be punished by intolerable heat, immeasurable cold, and countless other punishments—not continuously by all these, but now by this one, now by that; at one time it will cease to undergo this, at another that. For it will pass [Col. 1061C] from snowy waters to the heat of fires (Job 14). Hence it must be granted that no body will be punished with eternal punishment, unless the noun is explained as an adverb: so that “it will be punished with eternal punishment” means “it will be punished eternally by some punishment,” but not by any one punishment eternally. Thus one says, “A person crosses a small bridge all day,” but no one crosses it for the entire day. For every punishment by which he is punished will cease, and another particular punishment will immediately succeed it, and another after that, and then another. Nor should it be said that he is to be punished by one punishment only, when he is to be punished by so many entirely different particular punishments—just as this man now suffers from fever, tomorrow from leprosy, afterward from lethargy, and so until the end of his life will suffer successively from different illnesses. Will it be said that he suffered from one illness only? No, but from many. Likewise, he is not to be punished by one punishment but by many; and none is eternal, nor indeed is any one undergone eternally, but some punishment is undergone eternally.

The soul, however, will be punished by eternal punishment eternally, incessantly, without variation of punishments. That punishment is called the eternal pain which will be in the soul because the body will suffer so many and such great punishments, and the soul through the body. This pain is denoted by the “outer darkness” (Matthew 22), described as follows [Note: [Col. 1061D] Lombard, Book IV, final distinction, §b.]. Outer darkness is the malice of hatred and will, which grows in the minds of the impious because their bodies will be subjected to so many and such great torments that their whole mind will be bent toward where pain is, so that no knowledge of theirs is directed toward God. They are rightly said to have outer darkness because they are separated from the light of the divine majesty.

To the final argument, let us say that this hanging is not inflicted on this man by God for correction, but as a sign of future punishment. It is therefore called the beginning of eternal punishment, not because it is a part of it, but because it lasts up to it—just as servile fear is called the beginning of initial fear because it endures up to it.

## Chapter X. Whether God punishes eternally for venial sin

God seems to punish someone more than he deserved not only for the reasons stated above, but for another reason: [Col. 1062B] he punishes eternally for venial sin. Suppose that someone dies in mortal sin and venial sin. He is guilty of both these sins and repents of neither, nor is he now punished for either. Therefore he will be punished for both. Therefore he will undergo some punishment for venial sin: either temporal or eternal; but not temporal, for he will be punished eternally. Therefore he will be punished with eternal punishment for venial sin. But venial sin did not deserve eternal punishment. Therefore he is punished more than he deserved.

Again, it is impossible for this person to be freed from venial sin without being freed from mortal sin. But he will not be freed from mortal sin. Therefore he will never be freed from venial sin. Therefore he will always be guilty of venial sin, [Col. 1062C] both as to fault and as to punishment; and so he will be punished eternally for venial sin. Therefore more than he deserved.

That no one can be freed from venial sin without being freed from mortal sin is clear, because no one can be freed from venial sin, whether before or after death, without having charity; and no one can have charity without lacking mortal sin. Thus no one can lack venial sin without lacking mortal sin.

But if someone says that this person is not punished with eternal punishment for venial sin, but is punished with temporal punishment, or quasi-temporal punishment, within eternal punishment—for there will be certain particular punishments in the body, now in fire and now in water—the following objection is raised. At some point it will be true that he has been freed [Col. 1062D] from venial sin, at least when that punishment has ended. For then every temporal punishment will cease to exist. It will be true that he has been freed both from fault and punishment. Therefore completely; therefore there will be some redemption in hell.

Again, at some point it will be true that he has been freed from this venial sin, and likewise from that one and another, and so on for the rest. Therefore at some point it will be true that he has been freed from this multitude of venial sins. But a multitude of venial sins is equivalent to one mortal sin. Therefore at some point it will be true that he has been freed from mortal sin.

Different persons offer different solutions. Some say that, in this case, the venial sin [Col. 1063A] in this person—when he has the will to commit it and does not repent of it—becomes mortal immediately upon his death. Thus he will be punished with eternal punishment only for mortal sin, because what was venial becomes mortal. But if he has venial sins which he does not remember and which he does not wish to commit further, they will not become mortal; rather, he will be punished for them in eternal punishment and thus by temporal punishment. It falls to them to resolve the last two arguments.

Others say that this person will be punished with eternal punishment, but neither solely for mortal sin nor solely for venial sin, but for them together—just as a king rewards a person neither solely for great services nor solely for small ones, but jointly for all of them.

Others say that he will be punished with eternal punishment solely for [Col. 1063B] mortal sin; for venial sin he will be punished neither eternally nor temporally, but there will be an increase in his eternal punishment on account of it. If you ask whether that increase is punishment or a part of punishment, it is not: it is a certain property. Nor is eternal punishment properly said to be increased, just as no day is properly said to grow. Rather, this is the meaning: his punishment will be increased, that is, he would suffer less if he had not sinned venially. It is like a king who, in rewarding someone with ten marks, remembers some small service which was very pleasing to him and increases the reward by giving twelve marks.

But an objection is raised: by venial sin he deserved temporal or eternal punishment; he will not be punished temporally; therefore eternally. This is a fallacy. This servant deserved from his lord ten shillings or a measure of grain; he will not receive ten shillings; therefore he will receive a measure of grain.

Others resolve the matter by saying that he will be punished eternally for venial sin, but because of its association with mortal sin—just as the just person is often punished because of association with the wicked [Note: [Col. 1063] What follows to the end of the chapter is not found in the Victorine manuscript.]. For because a person does not repent of venial sin in the present life, he is punished in the future by eternal punishment. Punishment is increased or diminished according to place and time. There God punishes differently, because by a much graver punishment; here differently, because by a much lesser one. Conversely, a person who has committed mortal sin, to which eternal punishment is due, is not punished eternally but temporally, and thus by a lesser punishment than is due to him.

[Col. 1063D] For although that venial sin is not deserving of eternal punishment, it is nevertheless its merit. For *meritorious* signifies aptitude, while *merit* signifies act. As you see, according to diversity of places, a different punishment is due for one theft and for the same theft elsewhere. Perhaps someone has merited having his foot cut off in Gaul for a certain sin; yet if he committed that same sin in Germany, he merits hanging for it. So one who deserves here to be punished only with temporal punishment for venial sin will be punished eternally because of the accompanying mortal sin, according to one life and another; for God judges more strictly there than here. It is like the Roman emperor, who rules the whole world: when he is in Gaul, he punishes adultery by a mild punishment according to the custom of that place; when he is in Rome, according to the custom of that place he punishes the same sin by a greater punishment.

But someone will say: if this sin is punished by a greater punishment, and this person will receive none because he will not be worthy of it, then he will be worthy of a greater punishment for this sin than he is now; and thus the guilt of this sin will increase because he dies in it—which perhaps can occur. Hence one may ask: if it increases so much that it becomes equal to the guilt of mortal sin, and thus venial sin becomes mortal, then as great a punishment is due to this man for mortal and venial sin together as to another for two mortal sins, since the guilt of this venial sin must be made equal to that mortal sin’s guilt. Indeed, however many venial sins there are in one who dies, there will be that many mortal sins in him, because all will become mortal.

Therefore they say that the guilt of a venial sin in which a person dies together with mortal sin will never be increased, although he will be punished by a greater punishment than he would have been punished here had he repented. Thus a person will be punished more severely in purgatory for this venial sin than he would be punished in the present life if he were punished for it.

Hence, if someone argues thus: “These two persons, one of whom is guilty of both mortal and venial sin, the other only of venial sin equal to the venial sin of which the first is guilty, will be punished by unequal punishments: the former eternally, the latter only in purgatory; and every purgatorial punishment will be less than every eternal punishment. Yet this man deserves no more to be punished for this venial sin than the other for that one. Therefore this man is treated unjustly”—this is a fallacy. Two persons guilty only of equal venial sin equally deserve to be punished for them; one will be punished for it in the present life, the other in purgatorial fire; and every temporal punishment is less than every punishment of purgatorial fire. Therefore he is treated unjustly.

## Chapter XI. Whether contrition removes sin when a person is contrite, before that, or afterward

Since it has been said above that sin is removed by contrition as to guilt, it is asked when contrition removes sin: when a person becomes contrite, before, or afterward. For one medicine does not immediately relieve the sick person, but one must wait a long time for its effect; another heals more quickly.

That contrition heals not only when a person is contrite [Col. 1064D] but even beforehand is proved thus. This man becomes contrite by contrition possessed with charity. Therefore contrition removes sin in him. Therefore it removes a sin which he has, or had, or will have. But it removes neither a sin which he has nor one which he will have, because he has none and will have none: for he has charity and will henceforth have charity. Therefore it removes a sin which he had and does not have. Therefore he has ceased to have it. Therefore it has been removed. Therefore it removes a sin which does not exist; or, if it removes a sin already removed, by what was that sin removed? Only by contrition? But there was no previous contrition in him. Therefore it was removed by contrition, and so this contrition [Col. 1065A] healed him before he became contrite.

Again, if it removes the mortal sin in this person, but he becomes contrite with charity, then mortal sin exists in him together with charity. Therefore he is worthy both of eternal death and of eternal life.

Again, every person has either mortal sin or charity, because there is no middle state. A sin is remitted to someone. Therefore it is remitted either to one who has charity or to one who has mortal sin. If to one who has charity, then it is remitted to one who is not guilty of mortal sin but was guilty of mortal sin; therefore it is remitted to one who has ceased to be guilty of mortal sin. Therefore it is remitted to one to whom it has already been remitted. Or thus: it is remitted to one who has charity; therefore to one who does not have mortal sin.

[Col. 1065B] But if you say that mortal sin is remitted to one who does not have mortal sin, yet mortal sin is never remitted to anyone except through contrition possessed with charity, then one who has mortal sin has contrition with charity; therefore he has charity and mortal sin at once.

By a contrary analogy regarding the withdrawal of grace: no one becomes worse by God’s action, but the withdrawal of grace is God’s action. Therefore no one becomes worse by the withdrawal of grace. Therefore no one becomes evil by it.

Again, this man has charity or grace, and will no longer have charity. Therefore he ceases to have it, and only by its withdrawal. Therefore charity is withdrawn from him. Therefore he is punished. Therefore he is punished for a sin which [Col. 1065C] is in him, was in him, or will be in him. But no mortal sin was or still is in him. Therefore he is punished for what will be in him. Therefore God is an avenger before anyone is an offender.

Again, grace or charity once possessed merits increase, but God withdraws charity from him. Therefore he is treated otherwise than he deserved.

Again, on the Book of Numbers: “The cloud withdraws before Mary is covered with leprosy,” because God first withdraws grace from a person before the person sins. Therefore the withdrawal of grace precedes sin. Therefore God punishes before a person deserves it.

Again, charity is withdrawn either from one who has it or from one who does not have it. If from one who has it, then it is withdrawn for some sin, and the argument proceeds as before. But if it is withdrawn from one who does not have it but had it, then it is withdrawn from one who has ceased to have charity. Therefore [Col. 1065D] it is withdrawn from one from whom it has already been withdrawn; and so it is withdrawn from no one from whom it has not already been withdrawn.

Again, to remit sin is not to impute it to a person for eternal punishment. Every day God does not impute sin to Paul; therefore every day he remits it to him. But it is certain that Paul does not sin; therefore sin is remitted to one who does not have it.

Concerning these questions dialecticians should be consulted rather than theologians. Nevertheless, lest the hearers depart empty, let it be said that grace is withdrawn from one who does not have grace, and when he does not have grace; because he ceases [Col. 1066A] to have it when he begins not to have it. And this argument is false: “Grace is withdrawn from this person when he ceases to have it; therefore when he has it.” Likewise this one: “He has it and will not have it; therefore he ceases to have it.” Yet anyone wishing to press these points will not thereby escape an obstinate opponent. For instead of the proposition “he ceases to have it,” he will put this: “He now has charity for the last time, and this is a punishment to him. Therefore he is punished for some sin,” and so on as above.

Perhaps one might reply that the proposition “he then has charity for the last time” does not signify that punishment is present in him, but that it will be present to him imminently. I see no other way of resolving the matter, unless it is said, as some say, that no time is simple. The example introduced by way of comparison—“Light drives away darkness”—has the same difficulty and is more apparent than a true example.

## Chapter XII. Whether sins return because the guilt which returns?

[Note: [Col. 1065D] Lombard, *Sentences*, IV, dist. 17, etc.] Since it has been said above that sin is wiped away through contrition, oral confession is nevertheless not therefore to be omitted. For there are many reasons why we ought to confess our sins after contrition. First, because we do not know whether the sins have been wholly forgiven; for if they had not been forgiven, an error worse than the former would follow. Moreover, we are bound to confess our sins when we have a place, a time, and a person to whom we may confess. For if, when we have such things, we have not confessed, we shall be contemptuous, and thus incur mortal sin; and then all sins wiped away through contrition will return [Col. 1066C]. Likewise, we ought to confess sins because confession is a part of satisfaction: for three things are considered in confession, namely contrition of heart, confession of the mouth, and performance in deed, just as sin is committed in three ways—[195] by thinking, speaking, and acting.

[Note: [Col. 1065D] Lombard, *Sentences*, IV, dist. 22.] But against what was said, that sins return if we have scorned to confess, this objection is raised: sins have been removed from this man, as regards guilt, through contrition; and through confession they are removed neither as regards guilt nor as regards punishment. Therefore this man confesses his sins superfluously. To this we say that the argument is invalid. For he ought to confess his sin in order to complete satisfaction, which consists in [Col. 1066D] three things: contrition of heart, confession of the mouth, and deed—that is, fasting, prayer, and almsgiving. Thus external satisfaction consists in these three things. Also, although confession does not contain the whole punishment, it is nevertheless part of the punishment.

[Note: [Col. 1065D] “Shame itself has a share in remission,” etc. “For he offered much satisfaction who, overcoming shame [Col. 1066D], withheld none of the things he had committed from God’s messenger.” *On True and False Penance*, ch. 10, attributed to Augustine.]

For the shame which we experience in confessing sin and accusing ourselves is part of the punishment. The fallacy of the foregoing argument is this: this man has been freed from illness by medicine; and the diet which follows does not remove the illness; therefore he ought not to keep the diet. On the contrary: if he did not observe it, he would fall ill again. Likewise, one freed from sins through contrition as through medicine ought to confess them lest he fall again [Col. 1067A].

[Note: [Col. 1067D] Augustine, bk. XXII, *Against Faustus*, ch. 27.] Again, against the assertion that sins return, this objection is raised: suppose that this man had three mortal sins which were removed as regards guilt through contrition, and now he commits fornication: “Every sin is something said, done, or desired.” But each of these three is in this man, because they have returned. Therefore homicide is in this man. Therefore homicide in this man is something said, done, or desired—which is false, because he neither does, desires, nor speaks of homicide now. To this it must be said that sin is in someone in two ways: namely, in act and in guilt. Thus homicide is in one who killed a man yesterday and has not afterwards been contrite; yet it is not something said [Col. 1067B], done, or desired, but guilt alone.

Again, this man commits fornication, as has been supposed; but suppose that another man commits incest. This man is afterwards guilty, through fornication, of four mortal sins, because of the three which returned and also of fornication. But the man who commits incest is guilty of only one mortal sin, for incest. Therefore this man is more guilty through fornication than the other through incest. Therefore fornication is a greater sin than incest. To this we say that the word *through* does not indicate a cause but an occasion, since fornication is not the cause why this man is guilty of four mortal sins, but only the occasion. Nor is this due to the force of fornication, but to habitual sinning and to the return of sins already forgiven. A man of weak [Col. 1067C] constitution is burdened more by this slight illness than a robust man by that severe one. Therefore this illness is greater than that one. No: for his being burdened more does not arise from the force of the illness but from the frailty of his constitution.

Again, of two persons mentioned, one has repented of homicide, completed the satisfaction imposed upon him, and perseveres; the other does not persevere, although he has performed the imposed satisfaction. This man repented with as much charity as that one, and conversely. The sin was forgiven to both. Therefore it was forgiven to both as regards guilt and punishment, or to neither. If it was forgiven to both as regards guilt and punishment, and is not again committed by this man in act or will, then he will no longer be [Col. 1067D] guilty of it. Therefore the guilt of it will not return through another sin. To this it must be said that he did not complete satisfaction, since he did not maintain perseverance.

Again, homicide is in this man because it returns. Therefore he is bound to be contrite for it, and therefore to confess it. Again, this man is guilty of four mortal sins; they cannot be removed except through contrition. Therefore he must be contrite and consequently confess; but he has already been contrite for those sins and confessed them. Therefore, if he confesses them, there will be a double affliction, and God will punish twice for the same thing.

[Note: [Col. 1067D] Lombard, above, §1, resolves it similarly.]

To this it must be said that he is bound to be contrite for those sins for which he has already been contrite [Col. 1068A], because they have returned; and he ought to confess them again. Yet there will not therefore be double affliction, nor will God punish twice for the same thing, [196] because the prior confession was not made worthily: what ought to have been observed was not observed, namely perseverance in good after confession and frequent recollection of sins in the heart—not for delight, but for erasing them. Hence: “My sin is ever before me” (Psalm 50); and again: “Every night I shall wash my bed with tears,” etc. (Psalm 6). Or it may be said, as others say, that he need not again be contrite for them or confess them, if he confesses this present sin: just as, through this act—that is, fornication—the sins formerly removed returned, so, when this is removed, those three are removed. But it is safer that he confess again.

Again, this man is guilty of four [Col. 1068B] mortal sins: of the three which returned, because he scorns to confess them, and of that contempt. But if he had not been contrite, he would be guilty of only the three prior sins, because he would not have this contempt which he now has. Therefore he is guilty of more sins than if he had not been contrite. Therefore he sins more than if he had not been contrite. But it is proved that he would sin more if he had not been contrite, because he would be worse. Therefore he would sin more. And that he would be worse is proved thus: he would have persevered longer in evil, and in evil as great as he now has, and continually. Therefore he would be worse.

Again, if he had never been contrite, he would have done no good works. But after and in contrition he did many good works, and did them also with charity; these were for him either for [delectation (deletion)] or for mitigation of punishment. Hence Jerome says:

[Note: [Col. 1068D] On Haggai 1, “You have sown much,” though somewhat differently.]

“When you see someone doing righteous works amid many sins, do not say that God is so unjust as to forget a few good things because of many evils. For he makes him reap and gather into barns what he himself has sown in good ground—that is, what he has done in charity.”

Therefore, according to Jerome, this man would sin more if he had never been contrite than he sins now. To this it must be said that he is less bad—that is, he will suffer a lesser punishment—than if he had not been contrite, because of these good works which he did in charity and which will mitigate his punishment. Or there is another reason: just as this man now has the sins which have returned [Col. 1068D], and also contempt for returning to them, so, if he had never been contrite, he would have them and also contempt—not merely, I say, of confessing, but also of being contrite—which is worse; and thus he would be worse if he had not been contrite.

Again, after what has been said, the question is asked: which of these sins more gravely? Let there be two men, one of whom has been sufficiently contrite for many mortal sins but now falls through fornication. They are alike, of the same profession, sin in the same kind of sin, at the same place and time, with all other circumstances removed. This man is guilty of many mortal sins [Col. 1069A]; the other is guilty only of fornication. Therefore this man sins more gravely than the other.

Again, more has been forgiven and granted to this man than to the other. Therefore he ought to love God more than the other, and he sins. Therefore he sins more gravely than the other, according to Simon’s judgment: when asked who would love more, he to whom little had been forgiven or he to whom more had been forgiven, Simon replied, “He to whom he forgave more”; and the Lord then said, “You have judged rightly” (Luke 7). Therefore this man ought to love more, because more has been forgiven him. Therefore, if he sins in any kind of sin, he sins more gravely than the other if the latter sins in the same kind. But it seems that the other sins more gravely, because he had greater grace and rejects it. Therefore he offends more gravely than this man, since we are said to offend friends more when we reject them than when some stranger rejects them.

[Col. 1069B] It is most difficult to determine which sins more gravely. For who can judge the contempt with which a man sins? Where contempt is greater, sin is greater. Therefore God alone, who weighs the burdens of faults and punishments in balance, knows which such person sins more gravely and which ought to love more. For if you say that the one to whom more is pardoned ought therefore to love more, then Mary Magdalene loves God more than Peter, because more was forgiven her. But perhaps you might say that the one to whom more has been granted or forgiven ought to love more, because, although more was forgiven Mary Magdalene than Peter, more was not granted to her; and thus in [197] this word, “he granted,” what is meant is “forgiven and given.”

Yet some say that one who has never sinned sins more gravely in simple fornication than [Col. 1069C] one who erased his sins through contrition; and yet the latter is more guilty than the former, because he bears the guilt of three mortal sins, while the other bears that of only one, although he sins more gravely. Others say that they sin equally in the fornication which they now commit—the one who has never sinned and the one to whom many sins have been forgiven—yet this man is more guilty than the other, because this man is guilty for all that he has done, whereas the other is guilty only for the act which he does.

It is like two men who eat beef with equal gluttony: one has recovered from a pain in his side, while the other has felt no illness, and yet it harms the former more than the latter. Or two men fall from an equal height: one is heavy, the other light, and yet the former is hurt more than the latter. Or two men are wounded equally: one [Col. 1069D] has previously been wounded many times, the other never; and yet the former is harmed more than the latter.

Again, in punishing God considers not only final works, but also past ones, because they return; but in rewarding he considers only final works, because, if someone has fallen from perfect charity and afterwards risen again, not all the good works which he performed return. Therefore God is more ready to punish than to reward. To this we say that in punishing he considers only final things, because no one can die in mortal sin without being guilty of all past evils [Col. 1070A], and thus all sins which he committed are final. That sins return is established from this authority of Augustine, who says:

[Note: [Col. 1069D] Or rather Gregory, *Dialogues*, bk. IV, ch. 60, in whom the phrase “by nature” is absent.]

“If we do not forgive from the heart what is committed against us, the very thing which we rejoiced had been forgiven us [by nature] through penitence is exacted from us.”

Rabanus also said:

[Note: [Col. 1069D] *On Penance*, dist. 4, ch. *If Judas*.]

“Not only the sins which a man commits after baptism will be imputed to him for punishment, but also those which by nature were forgiven him in baptism.”

[Note: [Col. 1069D] See Augustine, bk. I, *On Baptism against the Donatists*, ch. 12, [Col. 1070D] in reply to the second objection of the Gauls.]

Others, however, say that sins do not return in guilt, but are said to return because, just as God will punish someone eternally for past sins, so he punishes him eternally for that which he now does—not so much, however, as those say who maintain that the will is reckoned as the deed [Col. 1070B], that is, just as he would be punished eternally for the deed, so eternally for the will, but not to the same extent.

## CHAPTER XIII. On confession: whether it is commanded, and of what it is a sacrament

[Note: [Col. 1070D] Lombard, *Sentences*, IV, dist. 17, etc.] Therefore, since sins are erased through contrition as regards guilt, confession is necessary lest sins return through contempt. But an objection is raised: confession is necessary for salvation, but the command of confession is not found in the Gospel. Therefore not every command necessary for salvation is contained in the Gospel. Therefore the Gospel is insufficient.

Again, John baptized before the Gospel and taught men to confess their sins. Therefore confession was instituted before the Gospel, and [Col. 1070C] is not commanded in the Gospel. Therefore confession is not necessary for salvation, or the Gospel is insufficient.

Again, confession is a sacrament of the New Testament. Therefore it effects what it signifies; but it signifies cleansing from sins, therefore it effects that cleansing—which is false: rather, contrition does so. Again, confession is a sign of inward cleansing; therefore it precedes inward cleansing, and thus contrition—which is false. On the contrary, contrition precedes confession.

To this we say that the Gospel does not give an express command concerning confession, yet it is not insufficient, because elsewhere in the New Testament sufficient material is found, as in the Catholic Epistle: “Confess your sins to one another” (James 5). Yet we believe this to have been said [Col. 1070D] concerning the confession of venial sins, which is made twice daily and at Compline. We also say that confession was commanded there:

[Note: [Col. 1070D] Lombard, *Sentences*, IV, dist. 22, final §; in this matter he was a stumbling-block to his disciple, as appears at the end of the chapter.]

“Go, show yourselves to the priests” (Luke 17). It should be known that confession is a sacrament of the Old Testament and does not effect what it signifies, just as marriage does not. Others, however, say that confession is not a sacrament [198], but a sacramental, like holy water and blessed bread. Yet it seems truer that confession is a sacrament.

As for the objection that the thing precedes the sign—that is, contrition precedes confession—this is not surprising. For [Col. 1071A] sometimes, in many things, thing and sign are simultaneous, as a circle and a tavern. Sometimes the sign precedes the thing, as clouds precede darkness or rain. Sometimes the sign follows the thing, as footprints indicate that something has gone before.

[Note: [Col. 1071D] Lombard, IV, dist. 22, final §, contains all these points.]

Others also say that confession and contrition are one sacrament, just as bread and wine are not two sacraments but one; and they distinguish three things: inward cleansing, confession, and contrition. Cleansing is the thing alone. Confession is the sacrament alone. Contrition is both thing and sacrament. But whatever may be said, it seems truer that confession is a sacrament, that the thing precedes the sign, and that it is not a sacrament of the New Testament. This is also shown thus: confession is not God’s work but man’s [Col. 1071B], and has no efficacy except from charity; therefore confession is not a sacrament of the New Testament. It is therefore certain that remission of sin precedes confession.

[Note: [Col. 1071D] See Lombard, IV, dist. 17, §§a, or 1 and 2.]

Hence David says: “I will confess”; and: “You forgave” (Psalm 31); he does not say, “You will forgive.”

## CHAPTER XIV. Whether one may confess the same sins more than once

[Note: [Col. 1071D] Lombard, *Sentences*, IV, dist. 14.] Since it is clear from the foregoing that confession is a sacrament and necessary for the erasure of sins, three matters must be considered concerning confession: whether someone may confess the same sins more than once; next, whether someone ought to confess that he committed a sin which he did not commit; third, what the priest forgives in confession.

Several authorities seem to intend that no one can truly confess his sins more than once. For they say:

[Note: [Col. 1071D] Gratian, *On Penance*, dist. 3, ch. 1, cites this from an unpublished sermon of St Ambrose, or rather from Gregory, *Homilies on the Gospels*, homily 34, beginning “The summer season.”]

“Penance is to weep for sins committed and not to commit things to be wept for.” But someone may repent in such a way that he will commit things to be wept for—that is, sins. Therefore he does not truly repent. Therefore no one can truly repent who will commit things to be wept for. Therefore no one can repent unless he entirely ceases from sinning. Therefore, if anyone has truly repented, he was not going subsequently to commit sin. Therefore afterwards he could not confess sins, since he had none.

To this it must be said that when it is said, “Penance is to weep for past deeds and not to commit things to be wept for,” this must be understood as not committing them in will. [Col. 1071D] For if someone repents in such a way that, when he repents, he does not will that the sins be committed, whether he subsequently commits them or not, he truly repents. Hence Augustine defines repentance more clearly:

[Note: [Col. 1071D] Similar statements may be found in Ambrose and Gregory.]

“Penance is a grace by which, with a purpose of amendment, we weep for or hate past deeds and no longer wish to commit things to be wept for.”

Again, Isidore says against the same point [Col. 1072A]:

[Note: [Col. 1072D] *On the Supreme Good*, bk. II, ch. 16.]

“He is a mocker, not a penitent, who still does what he repents of.” But understand this thus: he does it in act or will. Augustine again says:

[Note: [Col. 1072D] *On Penance*, dist. 3, ch. *Vain*. It is not found in Augustine’s *Soliloquies*, but in Isidore’s *Synonyms*, before the chapter *On Chastity*. The cited Lombard has these solutions, and Gratian also draws some from them.]

“Penance is vain when subsequent fault stains it.” But understand “vain” thus: it is frustrated of its due end. The end of penance is the attainment of glory and avoidance of Gehenna; such repentance does not attain that end.

Again Ambrose says:

[Note: [Col. 1072D] *On Penance*, dist. 3, ch. *They Are Found*.]

“Some are found who think penance must be repeated often; if they considered rightly, they would not think that it should be repeated. For as there is one baptism, so there is one penance.” As though he said: just as baptism is not repeated, so neither is penance. But this must be understood of solemn penance and according to the custom of different Churches. For perhaps it is found in some [Col. 1072B] Churches but not in others.

## CHAPTER XV. Whether one ought to confess that one committed a sin which one did not commit

[Note: [Col. 1072D] Lombard, *Sentences*, IV, dist. 21, §f.] Secondly, the question is asked whether someone ought to confess a sin which he [199] did not commit, but thinks that he committed. Such a person has a seared conscience, and everything which conscience condemns is sin. Therefore he is bound to confess homicide, if he thinks himself guilty of it.

Again, he believes that he killed a man; therefore, if he does not confess, he is contemptuous. But contempt is a mortal sin. Therefore he is bound to confess that sin.

[Note: [Col. 1072D] *Extra*, *On Observance of Fasts*, ch. 2.]

Again, “It belongs to good minds to recognize fault where there is no fault.” Therefore he [Col. 1072C] ought to recognize this fault, especially since he thinks it exists. But because nearly everyone says this, arguments are made for the contrary. This man committed no homicide either in act or in will; therefore he is not bound to confess that he committed homicide.

Again, indirectly: this man confesses to a priest that he committed homicide, but he did not commit homicide. Therefore he says what is false. Therefore he lies. Therefore he is not bound to confess homicide, since, even if he were previously good, by saying what is false he would become bad.

Again, the priest imposes satisfaction on him and justly binds him; therefore he is bound to carry out that satisfaction.

To this it must be said that he is bound to confess homicide, since he thinks he committed it. The statement [Col. 1072D] that he committed no homicide either in act or will, and therefore is not bound to confess, is invalid; on the contrary, he is bound because he thinks that he did it. Just as he is bound to give alms to someone whom he thinks a beggar, although he is not a beggar. But the multiplicity of the term “is bound” must be determined; since we discussed it above, we do not address it here.

What is said next—that in confessing this sin the man says what is false—is true [Col. 1073A], but he does not lie; and by saying what is false he lies. What is said next concerning satisfaction is true: he is bound to perform that satisfaction as regards the Church, but not as regards God. Hence, if he died at once, he would suffer no punishment. But if he lives in this world, he is bound to perform it, because he is bound; and, if it does not lessen punishment, it increases his crown.

## CHAPTER XVI. What does God forgive in confession, what the priest, and what a private person?

[Note: [Col. 1073D] Lombard, *Sentences*, IV, dist. 18.] The third point which we proposed follows: namely, inquiry into what the priest forgives in confession. In order that this may be clearer, let us first see how God is said to loose and forgive sins, and how the priest does, and how a private person does. God is said [Col. 1073B] to forgive sins because he wholly cleanses the soul from sin, raises it when mortified, and entirely looses it from the guilt of sin. Hence: “I am he who alone blot out the sins and iniquities of the people” (Isaiah 43).

Again, God is said to forgive or loose sins as regards punishment, because he frees a person from eternal punishment; and thus he forgives and looses sins in two ways. Yet some say that this second manner of loosing sin must be attributed to priests. For they say that God looses sin as regards guilt, and afterwards the priest looses it as regards punishment in confession and frees the person from eternal punishment. We show this to be false by one argument:

[Note: [Col. 1073D] Thus Lombard here, §d.]

God looses this man from sin. Therefore he is in charity. Therefore he is worthy of eternal life [Col. 1073C]. Therefore he is not worthy of eternal punishment, though he was worthy of it. Therefore he has been loosed from that punishment—but by no one other than God. Therefore God looses him; not the priest.

The priest, however, does not loose sin either as regards punishment or as regards guilt; but he looses and forgives—that is, he shows it to have been loosed and forgiven by God as regards guilt.

[Note: [Col. 1073D] Consult the notes on Pullus.]

Because he does not know that it has been forgiven as regards punishment, he imposes a temporal punishment. Likewise, he binds—that is, he shows someone to be bound. Hence he absolves and excommunicates persons, as will be said more fully below. He looses and binds through two keys: through discernment, or knowledge of discernment, which is one key; and through the power of binding and loosing, which is the other [Col. 1073D] key and is attached to orders.

[200] [Note: [Col. 1073D] Lombard, *Sentences*, IV, dist. 19.] The question is then asked whether every priest, and only a priest, has the first key, namely the knowledge of discernment. It seems that not only a priest has it, because many others have this knowledge, and someone may possess it before becoming a priest. To this we say that only a priest has the key—that is, has this knowledge as a key. Although he possesses it before becoming a priest, nevertheless no other person has it as a key except a priest [Col. 1074A]. That not all possess this key is certain, because more persons are condemned by ignorance than are commended by knowledge.

Most, however, say: every priest has the discernment of binding and loosing which is a key attached to orders. For no priest, even an unlearned one, is without every degree of discernment. Nor should it be said that, if he studies after being ordained, he receives the key after ordination; this would have to be said if one maintained that not every priest has that key.

Whether, however, a priest who received orders while indiscreet may repent of having received them in such indiscretion and nevertheless remain in the exercise of his office is a very great question. What seems [perhaps: *conducit*, “is relevant”] to this point is what is read of David: that he repented of the adultery committed [Col. 1074B] with Bathsheba and yet retained her (3 Kings 1 and 2). On the other hand, concerning the Psalm passage:

[Note: [Col. 1073D] Psalm 46, in the Gloss.]

“Sing wisely,” one reads: “No one sings wisely what he does not understand.” On these matters I prefer to hear those greater than myself rather than rashly assert anything.

The question concerning the second key is whether every priest, and only a priest, possesses it. It is certain that only a priest does, but it does not seem that every priest does, owing to two classes of priests: those who are in mortal sin, and those who do not have care of a flock, such as monks and other contemplative men. Augustine seems to intend that the former do not possess it, for he says: “There will be a golden plate on the priest’s forehead” (Exodus 28), which signifies confidence arising from a good life.

[Col. 1074C] [Note: [Col. 1073D] A corrupt passage from Augustine, ch. 120 on Exodus, is to be restored thus [Col. 1074D]: “He who has [the priesthood] truly and perfectly, not in signification but in reality, alone can take away sins.”]

“He who has the priesthood truly and perfectly, not in signification but in reality, alone can forgive sins.” Again Gregory says:

[Note: [Col. 1074D] Gregory, *Homilies on the Gospels*, homily 26.]

“Those alone, placed in this flesh, have the power of binding and loosing, like the apostles, who hold their life together with their teaching.”

But, on the contrary, other authorities seem to maintain that the good and the bad alike can forgive and loose sins. Augustine says concerning this passage:

[Note: [Col. 1074D] Not Augustine: *Questions on the Old and New Testament*, question 2.]

“You shall place my name upon the children of Israel, and I the Lord will bless”: “Thus the transmission of grace through the hand of the ordainer may be poured into men, and the will of the priest may neither harm nor benefit, but rather the merits of the person seeking the blessing.”

Again [Col. 1074D] Gregory says:

[Note: [Col. 1074D] 1, question 1, ch. *Many*.]

“Some, while scrutinizing the priest’s life more than their own, fall into the pit of error, paying too little attention to the fact that the priest’s life would not harm them if they themselves submitted to his good admonitions.”

To this it must be said that sins are loosed equally through good and bad priests. Their wickedness harms only themselves, and a sacrament celebrated by a good priest has equal efficacy to one celebrated by a bad priest. They therefore resolve the first two authorities thus: it is true that only those who are truly good and maintain the apostles’ life can forgive sins worthily; and if the unworthy do it, they nevertheless do it, but what they do thus harms only themselves.

Concerning those who do not have care of a flock, we say that they possess the power of binding and loosing, for this is attached to orders and every priest has it. But they have that power only habitually and not actually, unless it is granted them by a bishop. Thus every priest, and only a priest, has this key.

[Note: [Col. 1075D] Lombard, *Sentences*, IV, dist. 19, §d.]

Therefore what is read in the prophet, “I will curse their blessings” (Malachi 2), must be understood of excommunicated priests. And what is read elsewhere, “Woe to those who slay the souls that live and make alive the souls that die!” (Ezekiel 13), must be understood of heretics or, as some wish, of those who unjustly excommunicate or absolve [Col. 1075B].

Thus, as has been said, God forgives sin in two ways: because he wholly removes guilt, and again because he removes eternal punishment. This latter manner, as we said, some falsely attribute to priests, confirming their error by the fact that the Lord [201] raised Lazarus but did not loose him, instead giving him to the disciples to be loosed.

But the priest is said to forgive or loose sin in three ways: first, because he shows the sin to have been loosed and forgiven by God; second, because he imposes satisfaction and remits some of the punishment due; third, because he excommunicates and anathematizes, absolves, and admits to communion [Col. 1075C] in the sacraments. As explained, only a priest has the first key, namely knowledge of discernment, though not every priest, according to some; but according to others, every priest has it. Only a priest, and every priest, possesses the second key—habitually, though not actually; I say this because contemplatives have wings that are bound.

[Note: [Col. 1075D] Lombard, *Sentences*, IV, dist. 18, §f.] Since, then, the priest is said to bind and loose temporally, is whatever he, being a man, binds on earth bound with God, and whatever he looses said to be loosed? For the Lord said to Peter and all his successors: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound,” etc., and “whatever you loose on earth,” etc. (Matthew 16). Yet, on the contrary, it seems that not everything which the priest binds or [Col. 1075D] looses is bound or loosed in heaven. Jerome says:

[Note: [Col. 1075D] On Matthew, ch. 16.]

“Many who do not understand this passage assume something of the arrogance of the Pharisees, when they think themselves able to condemn the innocent or loose the guilty, whereas it is not the sentence of priests but the life of the accused that is examined.”

Origen likewise says:

[Note: [Col. 1075D] Homily 14, on Leviticus, ch. 24; but it should be corrected thus: “Has someone departed from truth, faith, charity? By this he has departed from the camp of the Church, even though he is not cast out by the bishop’s voice; conversely, someone is expelled by an unsound judgment, but, if he has done nothing deserving expulsion, he suffers no harm.”]

“Has someone departed from faith and truth? He has already departed from the camp of the Church; conversely, if he is cast out by an unjust judgment, and has done nothing for which he should be cast out, he suffers no harm.” Thus it appears that not whatever [Col. 1076A] is bound or loosed here by a priest is bound or loosed with God.

Therefore this authority must be understood thus: “Whatever you bind on earth,” etc.—provided that the merits of the one bound or loosed require it. This occurs when both keys are employed, namely discernment and power. For although not every priest has the first key fully and perfectly, nevertheless each has it to some extent. For no one is entirely without some small degree of discernment; and if a priest binds or looses someone without discernment, the fault rightly rebounds upon him.

Although it has been said that a priest looses someone by imposing satisfaction or remitting something of punishment, it should nevertheless be understood that, if he does not impose upon the penitent satisfaction sufficient [Col. 1076B] to erase sin, that sin—as regards punishment, since it has already been forgiven by God as regards guilt—will be punished in purgatory, and what is done too little here will be supplied there. Therefore it is better for the penitent to do more than is required than to do too little. If a priest imposes three days’ penance on him for a mortal sin, should he therefore think the punishment wholly remitted? No.

Again, although a priest, whether bishop or not, can remove something from the punishment, it should be understood that, if a bishop or other prelate declares and makes public that at the dedication of a certain church he will remit a third or fourth part of penance, or forty days, or something of that sort, for all those who have contributed alms toward building that church, not everyone who brings his alms there has thereby obtained the promised remission. For if a rich man gives only a coin or a penny, like the poorest old woman, does he believe that as much has been remitted to him? Far from it! Do we not read that the widow gave as much, though she gave only two small coins (Luke 21), as Zacchaeus, who gave half his estate? (Luke 19). Each must give according to his means: one who has more should give more; one who has less, less. For God does not require from a person what he cannot do. He considers not how much is given, but out of how much—that is, from what disposition of will. For if a rich man has a good will, why does he not fulfill it, if it is good? Why does he not give according to his means? For this is what a good will requires; otherwise it is not good, nor is it even a will to give or to obtain remission [Col. 1076D].

Having shown in what way God, and in what way a priest, is said to forgive sin, it remains to show in what way a private individual is said to forgive sin. But how can he forgive sin? [p. 202] He is not God, priest, or judge; yet he can indeed do so. Otherwise he would not fittingly say in the Lord’s Prayer: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI). Therefore whoever says this [Col. 1077A] forgives, or ought to forgive.

We must therefore know that, when someone sins mortally against his neighbour, he offends three persons: God, the Church, and his neighbour. Before God he is bound by two bonds, guilt and punishment; before the Church by one, namely satisfaction; before his neighbour by a twofold temporal satisfaction, as will now be said. If, therefore, he wishes to make satisfaction to God, he must be deeply contrite and repent of that sin, so that he may be absolved both as to guilt and as to punishment, so far as concerns God. Then he must make satisfaction to the Church by confessing the sin and performing temporal penance. Finally, he must make satisfaction to the neighbour against whom he sinned. How? By humbling himself and begging him to forgive him—not the sin, which has already been forgiven him, [Col. 1077B] but those two things by which he is bound before God: rancour and hatred, and the signs of rancour and hatred.

Every person is obliged to forgive every other person rancour of mind and hatred, whether he is perfect or imperfect. For no one can be in charity and retain rancour or hatred against anyone; but he may retain signs of rancour or hatred—I say this if he is imperfect. [Note: [Col. 1077D] See Augustine, Homily 40 among the 50.] For if he meets him on the road, he is not obliged to say, “Greetings,” to him, nor to share a table with him, nor to receive the peace from him in church, and the like. He may indeed raise an outcry against him before an earthly ruler or before the Church, not in order to avenge himself, but in order that God’s justice may be carried out: so that the offender may be more humbled, and that both he himself and others may be corrected through him. But if the offender humbles himself [Col. 1077C] in the presence of the person against whom he sinned, begging him, bending his knees, and so forth, and has made satisfaction in proportion to the offence and according to the amicable judgment of the friends present, then that person ought to forgive him rancour, hatred, and every sign of rancour and hatred.

But if the person against whom he sins is more perfect than the other—for example, a deacon, priest, and so on, or a contemplative—he is bound to forgive everything; nor may he retain rancour, hatred, or even their signs, whether the offender humbles himself or not. Hence the Lord said concerning the perfect: “Vengeance is mine; I will repay” (Rom. XII).

Nevertheless, according to what has been said, it seems that someone who bears hatred toward another and says, “Forgive us our debts,” etc., sins mortally, because he prays that it may be done to him [Col. 1077D] as he does to another. But he forgives no one. Therefore he asks that he himself not be forgiven; and thus every prayer of one who is in mortal sin is sin to him, and consequently one who is in mortal sin ought never to pray. To this it must be said that one who bears hatred against another ought not to utter this clause while he persists in an intention of hatred; yet one who is in another mortal sin may utter it.

It is also customary to ask whether, when someone in mortal sin prays and says, “Judge me, O God, according to my righteousness,” etc. (Ps. VII), he lies and therefore sins because he calls himself righteous. But one must know that expressions of this kind are spoken in the person of the Church, not in the person of the speaker; as when it is said, “From the ends of the earth I cried to you” (Ps. LX). For there is not one man who is at the ends of the earth. Likewise, concerning Daniel, it is read that the youths spoke in the person of the Fathers when they said, “We have sinned” (Dan. III). Thus they also ask whether an unlearned priest prays on his own behalf when he says, “Have mercy on yourself, O God,” or whether he asserts falsely of God something which he does not know. All such questions belong more to overly curious than to useful inquiry.

Behold, in this final treatise we have distinguished seven things that justify a human being. They are: thought concerning God and his ways; the will or desire to act well; [Col. 1078B] the grace of God; the movement arising from grace and free will; contrition; remission of sins; and confession. The first two precede the remaining five both in time and in nature, [Note: [Col. 1077D] Yet in such a way that they too arise from prevenient grace, as the author has sufficiently indicated above.] and cannot justify by themselves. The four which follow precede one another in nature in the order in which they are listed, but none precedes another in time; none can be possessed without the other three; and these four [p. 203] can justify. Yet the seventh, namely confession, is necessary if there are time, place, and a person to whom one may confess one’s sins; if these cannot be had, one is not thereby less justified.

We may reduce this sevenfold division to six by putting satisfaction in place of contrition and confession. Satisfaction embraces not only those two but also a third thing in [Col. 1078C] the performance of the deed; and thus it embraces satisfaction of heart, mouth, and deed.

## CHAPTER XVII. Whether one who has one virtue has all virtues

[Note: [Col. 1077D] The Master treats this matter in part, as also what follows, in *Sentences*, III, distinction 36.]

To anyone considering the preceding treatise, it is evident that we have not departed even slightly from the order set out above. First, according to our capacity, we sufficiently showed what operative grace is and what co-operating grace is; how many and what kinds of justifications there are; and which things we merit, and by what means. We also inserted certain questions that seemed to contain some difficulty, and resolved them by reviewing the differing solutions of different persons, rather than inventing solutions of our own.

It remains, therefore, according to our order, to inquire whether whoever has one justification has them all [Col. 1078D]—that is, whether whoever has one virtue has all virtues; for by “justification” we mean nothing other than virtue. [Note: [Col. 1077D] The Master, III, distinction 33.]

We must therefore know that virtue is sometimes divided fourfold, when it is divided into the four cardinal virtues: justice, prudence, fortitude, and temperance. [Note: [Col. 1078D] Thus Augustine, *On the Trinity*, VI.4, at the beginning; *Tractates on John*, 83; Epistle 29 to Jerome, after the beginning; below, Jerome on Isaiah 56, Epistle to Gamachus, and to Fabiola, Station 38; Ambrose, Book V on Luke 1, on “Blessed are the poor” (Luke VI); Gregory, *Morals*, XXII.1; etc.] Whoever has one of these has every one of them. This is proved by an irrefutable argument.

Each of these virtues has [Col. 1079A] a mortal vice opposed to it; and whoever has one of these has charity. Therefore whoever has one of these lacks every mortal sin; and whoever has no mortal sin has every virtue opposed to a mortal vice. For it is necessary either to have a mortal vice or the virtue opposed to it, since there is no middle state. Therefore whoever has charity has every virtue opposed to some mortal vice; but every virtue is opposed to some vice. Therefore whoever has charity has every virtue. [Note: [Col. 1079D] From Augustine, *On the Trinity*, XIV.9.]

The effect of justice is to aid the wretched; of prudence, to guard against [Col. 1079B] snares; of fortitude, to endure hardships; and of temperance, to restrain enticements. These virtues will be possessed in the heavenly homeland, [Note: [Col. 1079D] Thus with the Master, literally, III, distinction 33; and both follow Augustine, cited above, and Bede on Exodus XXVI.] as here, but then they will have different effects.
