For the effect of justice will be to be subject to him to whom all things shall be subject; of prudence, to prefer nothing to God or make anything equal to him; of fortitude, to adhere firmly to God; and of temperance, to take delight in no harmful affection.

Virtue is sometimes divided threefold: into faith, hope, and charity.

At other times virtue is divided sevenfold, into the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, which are there numbered as the Spirit of wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear of the Lord (Isa. II). [Note: [Col. 1079D] These points are from Augustine, *On the Trinity*, XIV.1, in the middle.] Wisdom is, as the philosophers say, “knowledge of divine and human things.” [Col. 1079C] Augustine, however, distinguishes wisdom and knowledge as follows: wisdom is knowledge of divine things, whereas knowledge is only of human things. Yet it may be distinguished more clearly, in accordance with the authorities of the saints, so that wisdom is referred to and said to concern contemplation and delight in eternal truth. For wisdom in this sense is called knowledge seasoned by the savour of the virtues; it is said to derive from *sapor*, “taste,” not from *sapere*, “to know”—the wisdom of which it is said: “Wisdom shall not enter into a malevolent soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins” (Wis. I). Knowledge concerns the right ordering of earthly things and good conduct among evil persons; understanding, moreover, concerns contemplation of eternal majesty and invisible creatures. [Col. 1079D]

[Note: [Col. 1079D] The Master, above, § c.] It must be known that these—wisdom, knowledge, and understanding—are not the natural powers of the soul; rather, they are [p. 204] gratuitous gifts of the Holy Spirit. Yet through them the natural powers which are in the soul are restored and brought to life. It must also be known that, when the Holy Spirit infuses these gifts into someone, he does not therefore know more, understand more, or know more things; but perhaps he knows those things which he already knows [Col. 1080A] better and more fully. Thus one who repents of ignorance does not therefore know more or be less ignorant.

Piety is divine worship, called in Greek *theosebia*, that is, worship of God. Counsel belongs to ethics: namely, that a person may know how to take counsel and provide for himself and also for his neighbour. We have spoken before concerning fortitude. These virtues, moreover, will be possessed in the heavenly homeland, but perhaps then they will have other effects.

But this seems false because of fear, which will not exist in the heavenly homeland, as Augustine appears to hold. For he says: [Note: [Col. 1080D] In the middle of the exposition of Psalm V.] “Fear is a great safeguard for those journeying toward the homeland, but is cast out for those who have arrived.” Therefore fear will not exist in the homeland. We say that this is true of every sort of fear generally, except filial fear, which too will be cast out according to [Col. 1080B] one part or function of itself, [Note: [Col. 1080D] The Master, III, distinction 34, § k.] namely its function concerning separation.

That this may be clearer, four kinds of fear must be distinguished. [Note: [Col. 1080D] The Master, III, distinction 34, § d.] There is worldly or human fear; servile fear; initial fear; and filial, or chaste, or friendly fear. [Note: [Col. 1080D] Cassiodorus on Psalm CXXVII.] Worldly or human fear exists when we fear bodily dangers or the loss of earthly things and therefore sin. Hence the Lord says: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. X; Luke XII). [Note: [Col. 1080D] Augustine on Psalm CXXVII.]

Servile fear exists when someone refrains from sin solely through fear of hell, not through love of God. Initial fear exists when a person refrains from sin partly out of love of virtue and partly from dread of punishment. Filial fear exists when a person refrains from [Col. 1080C] sin solely from love of God. No one doubts that the first fear is evil. But there is doubt concerning servile fear; and where there is doubt, a disputation must be undertaken. Therefore we must deal with it.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On servile fear: whether it is a virtue, and on matters connected with this question

[Note: [Col. 1080D] The Master, III, distinction 34.]

Servile fear is good. Therefore it can coexist with charity. Or thus: servile fear cannot coexist with charity. Therefore servile fear is evil.

Again, the function of servile fear is to fear servilely; but this is evil, and no one can make good use of it. [Col. 1080D] Therefore servile fear is evil.

Again, servile fear makes one fear servilely. Therefore it makes one sin. Therefore it does not draw one back from sin. Therefore it does not introduce charity. Yet I prove that it does introduce charity, because it introduces initial fear, and initial fear cannot be possessed without charity. Therefore servile fear introduces charity. But I prove that it excludes charity: charity excludes servile fear, and servile fear cannot coexist with charity. Therefore servile fear excludes [Col. 1081A] charity. Therefore it does not introduce it.

Again, servile fear is a gift of God. Therefore it is either natural or gratuitous. But it is not natural; for if it were natural, it would not depart when charity arrived, any more than reason, memory, or intelligence does. Therefore it is a gratuitous gift. Therefore by it, or by its use, we merit eternal life.

Again, servile fear is the beginning of wisdom. Therefore it is a part of wisdom, or something belonging to wisdom.

Again, servile fear was given to a human being by God for some use, but for no use except fearing servilely. But to fear servilely is evil. Therefore it was given to him for an evil use. Therefore it should not be imputed to him if he fears servilely.

Again, servile fear makes a person refrain from sin through fear of hell. Therefore it makes a person refrain from sin. But whoever [Col. 1081B] has no mortal sin has charity. Therefore servile fear makes a person be in charity. Therefore it can coexist with charity.

Having set forth these arguments, let us answer them in order. To the first we say that “good” is used in many ways: meritorious good, useful good, and good [p. 205] in the class of goods. Servile fear is good—that is, useful—because it leads into charity; but it is not good, that is, meritorious. There is a fallacy in the first argument. The desire to possess charity not yet possessed is good. Therefore it can coexist with charity; or it cannot coexist with charity; therefore it is evil.

To the second argument, some say that to fear servilely is not a sin and that this use is good; yet everyone [Col. 1081C] who fears servilely sins, not because he fears servilely but because he does not have charity, since charity cannot coexist with servile fear. Just as desiring charity not yet possessed is not a sin, yet whoever desires charity not possessed sins—not because he desires it, but because he does not have charity.

If someone says: “Thus we are bound to have charity, but we cannot have charity and fear servilely. Therefore we are bound not to fear servilely”—this is a fallacy. We are bound to have charity, but we cannot have charity and desire charity not possessed. Therefore we are bound to desire charity not possessed. Or thus: we are bound to have faith; but we cannot have faith and give [Col. 1081D] alms without faith. Therefore we are bound not to give alms if we do not have faith.

To the third argument they say that servile fear makes one fear servilely, but not sin. There is a fallacy: “This desire makes this person desire charity not possessed; therefore it makes him sin.” We say, accordingly, that servile fear draws one back from sin and introduces charity. But when it is said that it excludes charity, this is true in the sense that it is not simultaneous with charity; if, however, you say “it excludes,” meaning that it does not prepare one for having charity, this is false.

To the fourth [Col. 1082A] we say that servile fear is a gratuitous gift; nevertheless, neither by it nor by its use do we merit eternal life. So too desiring charity not yet possessed is a gratuitous good, yet we do not thereby merit eternal life. [Note: [Col. 1081D] The Master, III, distinction 34, § 1.]

To the fifth we say that servile fear is called the beginning of wisdom in one way, and initial fear in another. Servile fear is the beginning of wisdom, that is, toward wisdom. Initial fear, however, is the beginning of wisdom, that is, within wisdom; it is, as it were, a part of wisdom, because it is possessed with charity. But servile fear is like a bristle [Note: [Col. 1081D] Augustine, *Tractate 9 on 1 John*: “Just as we see thread drawn through by a bristle when something is sewn, etc., [Col. 1082D] so fear first occupies the mind; but fear does not remain there, because it entered in order to introduce charity.”] which draws thread through the eye, because it precedes charity. There is a fallacy: “This stone is the boundary or landmark of this field; therefore it is part of this field, or something belonging to this field.”

To the sixth, some say that the use of servile fear [Col. 1082B] is good and was given by God. To the seventh we say that servile fear makes a person refrain from sin, but not from every sin. For although by servile fear one refrains from an evil deed, one does not refrain from an evil will, which is mortal sin. For he has the will to sin, but refrains solely on account of punishment.

Although it has been said that fearing servilely is good, it seems possible to prove that it is mortal sin. By fearing servilely, this person, in the act of fearing, turns aside from the due end, namely God, and refers himself to an undue end, namely punishment. Therefore in fearing servilely he sins; thus servile fear is not a gift of God. To this it must be said [Col. 1082C] that he is led to fear servilely not by free choice, but rather through the weakness of nature. Yet deliberation follows afterward, when he considers punishment; and therefore fear is not deprived of that due end, and consequently does not sin. Thus if someone deliberately fasts so that he may afterward grow hungry and then eat better, that hunger is a mortal sin; but if he does this accidentally, it is neither good nor evil in itself. Likewise someone is moved by free choice to commit fornication and therefore sins; but if not by free choice, it is not sin. Servile fear is good, that is, useful, because through it we avoid an evil, namely eternal punishment.

Again, to fear servilely is not in the class of evils. Therefore it can be done from charity. Or thus: it is not among [Col. 1082D] things evil in themselves, such as killing or committing adultery. Therefore it can proceed from charity. Thus some say that to fear [p. 206] servilely is evil, and that the function of servile fear is not to fear servilely. For the former is good and the latter evil; rather, its function is to fear punishment and to draw back from sin, both of which are good. Servile fear is a defect, not of fault but of punishment; yet it could not exist in Christ, for he did not assume all our defects, but only those which it was fitting to assume.

## CHAPTER XIX. Whether initial fear is a virtue, and other matters pertaining to this same question

[Col. 1083A]

[Note: [Col. 1083D] The Master, as above.] Against the assertion that whoever has one virtue has all virtues, an objection was made concerning servile fear. An objection is made in the same way concerning initial fear: whoever has one virtue has all virtues; therefore he has initial fear. But this is false, because perfect charity excludes initial [p. 207] fear, while imperfect charity accompanies it. To this they say that the statement was made about the kinds severally, not about every individual instance of the kinds. Whoever has one virtue has all virtues; and it is true that whoever has one virtue has fear, but not therefore this fear or that fear. There is a fallacy: “Whoever has one virtue has all virtues; therefore whoever has one virtue [Col. 1083B] has imperfect charity.”

Since many matters concerning initial fear are doubtful, let us settle them briefly. The question is whether initial fear can increase or not. It seems that it cannot increase. For it has two functions, namely love of righteousness and fear of hell; and the more love increases, the more fear decreases. Authority says this: [Note: [Col. 1083D] Augustine, *Tractate 9 on 1 John.*] therefore, as it increases on this side, it decreases on the other. But why should it be said to increase rather than decrease, or conversely? [Note: [Col. 1084D] Here a few points appear to be missing.] Nor can it increase and decrease at the same time.

Again, that it can neither increase nor decrease is proved by analogy. A natural day cannot increase or decrease, because as the artificial day increases, [Col. 1083C] the artificial night decreases, and conversely. But the natural day, consisting of artificial night and artificial day, remains unchanged. Similarly, it seems that initial fear remains unchangeable, although one of its functions increases and the other decreases.

To this some say that when it is said, “The more love increases, the more fear of hell decreases,” it should be understood thus: the more someone advances in love, the more he refrains from sin because of love of God and not because of punishment or fear of hell. Yet he fears punishment as much as any other person; but he does not refrain from sin through fear of punishment, but through love of God. On this account, however, the perfect person fears punishment as much as the imperfect person.

Against this, [Col. 1083D] initial fear looks partly toward heaven and partly toward hell; and the more it looks toward heaven, the more it looks toward hell. But to look toward heaven is to love God, and to look toward hell is to fear punishment. Therefore the more someone loves God, the less he fears punishment. Therefore the perfect person fears punishment less than the imperfect person.

To this some say that the less someone looks toward heaven, the more he looks toward hell on account of horror at punishment—not because he fears it on account of punishment, but because, when so terrible a punishment is considered, he loves God more intensely [Col. 1084A] and advances further in his love.

Again, this perfect person has no mortal sin, nor even any venial sin liable to purgatorial burning. Why then does he fear? To this they say that he fears because he abhors punishment, as someone standing on a very high tower knows that he cannot fall because he is securely bound, yet fears because he sees the ground far below like an abyss. Similarly, someone standing on a narrow bridge and seeing a torrent rushing below fears.

Again, it is proved that initial fear cannot increase. For either the definition of initial fear will be given thus: “Initial fear is that which partly loves and partly fears”; and then this definition will be false according to them, because a perfect person fears according to them, yet does not possess [Col. 1084B] initial fear, since perfect charity excludes it. Or the definition will be given thus: “Initial fear is that by which one refrains from sin partly from love of God and partly from fear of punishment.” For this is how the definition is usually given. But the movement of love can grow and increase, and the movement of fear can diminish. Therefore the movement of love can grow so much that the movement of fear is entirely destroyed. Therefore the movement of love can be increased by God so that it can truthfully be said that initial fear cannot increase.

Again, initial fear cannot be possessed without imperfect charity, and conversely. But imperfect charity cannot increase in this person without thereby becoming perfect. Let it be that this person is at the final point of imperfect charity. Therefore initial fear cannot increase in him, or it can cease to be initial.

Conversely, it is proved that it can increase as follows: charity can increase; therefore every virtue can increase; therefore initial fear can increase. Again, one who has initial fear can love more intensely and fear more intensely. Therefore initial fear can increase in him. Or thus: this person can love more intensely and fear less intensely. Therefore he can love more intensely and still fear; but this person’s love can advance so far that he becomes perfect. Therefore he can be perfect and fear.

Different persons resolve these points in different ways. Some say that initial fear ceases to be when filial fear arrives, as children’s instruction ceases [Col. 1084D] when the instruction of the advanced arrives. Likewise, it ceases when servile fear arrives—namely, when fear of punishment, or the function of fear, has been so increased by God that the function of love is entirely destroyed.

Others say better: initial fear can increase, but not while it remains initial. For when the function of love has been increased by God so that the function of fear is entirely destroyed, it does not cease to be but becomes filial. Likewise, when the other function increases and the first is eliminated, it becomes servile. Thus it is said to increase, not while remaining initial, but because it becomes filial when fear is eliminated, or becomes servile when love is eliminated. Thus that quality of mind [Col. 1085A] does not cease to be, but remains the same: what was servile fear is initial fear and will be filial fear. Likewise, in the reverse order, filial fear can become initial and servile.

But an objection is made to this, and it seems possible to prove that initial fear, while it is initial, can increase. For since that man has more intense initial fear than this man, let this be posited: since every virtue can increase, why can initial fear not increase in this man so as to be as intense in him as it is in that man?

Again, let there be two persons who fear servilely, one of whom fears hell less than the other. Let there be two persons who have initial fear, one of whom loves more than the other. The one who fears less servilely can, while that fear remains undiminished [Col. 1085B] and unrelaxed, advance so as to have as much love as the one who loves less among those two who have initial fear, and thus he fears initially. Therefore, by analogy, the one who fears servilely more can advance, while his fear remains undiminished, so as to have as much love as the one who loves more and has initial fear. Thus he can have initial fear more intense than that of the other who fears less, because he both fears more and can love more. Therefore initial fear can be more intense in him than in the other. Therefore initial fear can increase.

But conversely I prove that it cannot increase while remaining initial. Either there is no degree in initial fear [Col. 1085C] beyond which it cannot advance, or there is some degree beyond which this fear cannot advance without becoming filial or servile. If you say that there is no degree beyond which one fearing initially cannot advance, the same will be true in filial fear. Therefore no one can advance to any degree of filial fear so high that one cannot advance to an equally high degree of initial fear, since infinity exists on both sides. Therefore one who has initial [p. 208] fear can love as much as one who has filial fear. Therefore the imperfect can love as much as the perfect loves.

But if you say that there is some degree in initial fear beyond which progress cannot occur, let it be so. That degree is either the highest degree of love, the highest degree of fear, or a middle degree [Col. 1085D] in which fear and love are equal. But when progress is made to any of these degrees, initial fear does not increase. For if it reaches the highest degree of love, fear is already relaxed down to its lowest degree; and if it reaches the highest degree of fear, love is already relaxed down to its lowest degree. Just as on a balance, if this pan rises, the other is lowered, and conversely: what it gains on one side, it loses on the other. But if progress is made toward the middle degree by loving or fearing, it is necessary that one descend to the middle degree either from love or from fear. Therefore initial fear, while remaining initial, cannot increase in any way. And we grant this, because if it increases, it becomes either filial or servile.

To the two preceding arguments, therefore, we say that the positing which they make [Col. 1086A] is impossible. For it is impossible that one person have more intense initial fear than another. If he loves more, he fears more, and conversely. Likewise, it is impossible that someone who fears servilely should, while that fear remains undiminished, receive love in any degree whatsoever. For as soon as he begins to love, love immediately destroys either the whole fear or almost all of it. Likewise fear destroys love, if one who loves filially begins to fear.

Some nevertheless say that initial fear increases if its more worthy function, namely love, increases; but if its less worthy function, namely fear, increases, it is not therefore said to increase. Its increase or decrease must be judged according to its more worthy function. But if it is said, “This person has greater [Col. 1086B] initial fear than that person; therefore he fears more,” there is a fallacy: “This person has greater imperfect charity than that person; therefore he has greater imperfection.”

But an objection is again made: to fear hell is a function of initial fear; therefore it is a function of virtue; therefore it is meritorious. Again, these are the two functions of initial fear: to love God and to fear hell. Therefore those functions are opposed, or one is referred to the other.

To this we say that initial fear has not two functions but only one. Nor is loving God its function, but that of filial fear. What, then, is its function? To love God with fear of hell. This function is mixed from those two things; hence initial fear is called “love mixed with dread.”

Again, an objection is made concerning [Col. 1086C] filial fear: one who fears filially fears separation. Therefore he fears punishment, because separation from God is punishment; and thus one who has filial fear—that is, a perfect person—fears punishment. To this it must be said that a perfect person fears separation from God not because of punishment, but because it offends God. For although separation cannot occur without being punishment, the perfect person does not fear it because it would be punishment, but because it is an offence against God. For he has no regard whatever for punishment, but for the love of God.

Again, whatever can happen ought prudently to be feared, lest the perfect person fall and sin. Therefore he ought to fear falling; and he does what he ought to do. Therefore he fears falling. Therefore he fears punishment, because falling is punishment. To this we say that the perfect person fears falling, but not because of punishment; rather, because it offends God, since he looks only toward heaven.

Again, the Apostle says: “I am certain that neither death nor life can separate me from the charity of God” (Rom. VIII). But if he is certain that he will not be separated from the charity of God, then he does not fear separation from the charity of God; therefore someone who has filial fear does not fear separation. To this we say that it must be understood thus: “I am certain with the certainty which can be possessed on the way.” Yet no one is so perfect that he ought not to fear, because “Blessed is the man who is always fearful” (Prov. XXVIII).

There is a threefold fear: fear of awareness, experience, and caution. Fear from experience exists, for example, when someone who has been shipwrecked fears danger at sea. Another, whose ship has already broken up and is taking in water, has fear of awareness: [Col. 1087A] for he [p. 209] knows that he is in danger. Another, safe in a sound ship, has fear of caution, because every person fears at sea. Therefore one who has perfect charity, such as Paul, does not fear with fear of experience or awareness, but with fear of caution: “Let him who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Cor. X).

Thus, then, we have four kinds of fear. [Note: [Col. 1087D] The Master, above, § k.] There is worldly fear, which is evil and draws one away from charity. Servile fear is good, not meritorious but useful, because it introduces one to charity. Initial fear is possessed with imperfect charity. Filial fear is possessed with perfect charity; and it has two functions, reverence and separation. According to these two functions it is possessed on the way by the perfect. Yet Christ possessed it only according to the function of reverence, [Col. 1087B] and not according to that of separation, because he did not fear separation.

In the heavenly homeland it will be possessed only according to the function of reverence. For then we shall not fear separation, because: “In those days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell confidently” (Jer. XXIII); for then he will not fear separation. [Note: [Col. 1087D] The Master, above, § l.]

There is also a fifth fear, but a natural one, when a person naturally experiences dread. Hence: “Jesus began to be afraid and distressed” (Mark XIV).

## CHAPTER XX. Whether the virtues will pass away in the heavenly homeland?

[Note: [Col. 1088D] Lombard, III, distinction 31, §§ b, c.] As is clear from what has been said, virtue is sometimes divided into four, as into the four cardinal virtues; sometimes into seven, as into the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit [Col. 1087C]; and sometimes, especially among theologians, into three: namely faith, hope, and charity. The question therefore first arises whether these three virtues will exist in the heavenly homeland, or charity alone.

Now it seems that charity will exist in the homeland. For the Apostle says: “Charity never fails” (1 Cor. XIII); and thus it will exist in the homeland. But the contrary seems to be said: “When that which is perfect has come, that which is partial”—or imperfect—“will be done away” (ibid.). But charity on the way is imperfect and never wholly perfect; therefore, when perfection comes, which will truly be in the homeland, then charity, which on the way is only imperfect in comparison with the perfection to be in the homeland, will cease to be. Therefore charity will not exist in the homeland.

Again, knowledge is a companion of charity; but [Col. 1087D] knowledge will cease to be; therefore charity also. Therefore it will not exist in the homeland.

Again, indirectly: this person will have charity alone in the homeland, but on the way he has faith, hope, and charity; therefore he is better on the way than he will be in the homeland.

Again, on the way this person has charity that merits eternal life; in the homeland he will have charity that does not merit. Therefore charity in this person is better on the way than it will be in him in the homeland.

Again, the Lord says: “I know my sheep, and mine know me” (John X), and elsewhere: “This is eternal life, that they may know thee, and Jesus Christ our Lord whom thou hast sent” (John XVII). But on the way both the Father and the Son are known by the good. Therefore eternal life is present on the way.

Again, Christ says to the disciples: “All things whatsoever I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John XV). Therefore, while on the way, the disciples knew everything Christ heard from the Father. Therefore they knew everything that Christ himself knew. Therefore they had eternal life on the way.

Again, Peter in the homeland believes and has charity. Therefore he has faith formed by charity. Therefore he has faith as a virtue. Therefore faith exists in the homeland.

Again, Linus, who is in the homeland, has charity, and greater charity than Peter—let it be supposed that Peter is still on the way. Therefore he is worthy of a greater crown than Peter.

Again, the question is asked whether someone existing on the way can have as much charity as someone [Col. 1088B] existing in the homeland has; and this seems possible. For charity was given by measure to those who are in the homeland, but anyone existing on the way can advance in charity. Therefore he can so far perfect it as to attain the same fullness of charity as the one who is in the homeland has. Yet this is impossible, since he who is least in the homeland is greater even than John (Matt. XI).

Having set these matters forth beforehand, it must be known that neither faith nor hope will exist in the homeland, but charity alone. The foregoing objections must therefore be answered in order.

Accordingly, when it is said, “When that which is perfect has come, that which is imperfect will be done away” (1 Cor. III), this is to be understood as follows: when the perfection that will exist in the homeland comes, the imperfection [Col. 1088C] of charity will be done away, because charity will then be possessed perfectly alone; whereas here it is possessed only imperfectly. It is not to be understood that imperfect charity will cease to exist, since charity never fails, but rather that the imperfection of charity will cease.

To the second point, we say that the term *knowledge* is used in four ways. Sometimes knowledge means an art or the rules that are learned, such as grammar and the rules of the arts. Sometimes knowledge means a quality of the soul. Sometimes it means the movement arising from that quality by which one grasps those things from which a person is called knowledgeable—namely, the arts and their rules. Sometimes knowledge also means another movement arising from this first movement, and this grasps what is possessed through the rules and precepts of the arts, [Col. 1088D] that is, the fruit of the rules. In whichever of these senses knowledge is taken, it is true that knowledge will cease, except for the quality of the soul; for that will not fail.

[Note: [Col. 1088D] Lombard, above, § c.] Charity, however, never fails, nor does its movement—that is, loving God and loving one’s neighbor—nor its mode: loving God for his own sake and one’s neighbor for God’s sake. For some things are entirely destroyed, such as tongues and prophecies; others are changed, as faith into sight, and sight into reality; while some are perfected and increased, as charity.

To the third point we say that, although this person has had [Col. 1089A] faith, hope, and charity on the way, and charity alone in the homeland, he is nevertheless not better on the way than he will be in the homeland, because there he will have charity much more perfectly. It is as if someone now has gold, silver, and bronze, but tomorrow will have gold alone: he will not be poorer tomorrow, because he will have more gold than he now has of all metals together.

Similarly, to the fourth point we say that this person is not better on the way than he will be in the homeland, although here, and not there, he has charity that merits.

To the fifth point we say that there is enigmatic knowledge and comprehensive knowledge. We cannot know God on the way except by enigmatic knowledge, that is, as through a riddle, in a mirror; but in the homeland we shall know him by comprehensive knowledge, because then [Col. 1089B] we shall see him face to face (1 Cor. XIII). That knowledge will be eternal life, and it is of this that he speaks when he says: “This is eternal life, that they may know thee,” etc. (John XVII).

To the sixth point we say: “All things whatsoever I have heard from my Father” (John XV), etc.—namely, all things necessary for your salvation. It is true that everyone in the homeland will believe the articles of faith, namely that Christ was born and suffered; nevertheless, he will not have faith, [Note: [Col. 1089D] Lombard, III, distinction 26, § c.] just as Christ believed but did not have faith. And although Linus has greater charity and a greater crown because he is in the homeland than Peter the apostle, who is on the way, he is not thereby worthy of a greater crown; for he already has that crown as a reward and does not merit it. Just as a boxer who has won victory in a contest has greater praise and has already [Col. 1089C] been rewarded than another boxer who fights more bravely and against a stronger opponent than the first fought; nevertheless, the latter is not worthy of a greater reward than the former, if he is able to win, because he fights more bravely and against a stronger man.

What was said last is resolved if it is said that love on the way, however great it may be, cannot equal the love of the homeland; for “charity is a fire in Zion and a furnace in Jerusalem” (Isa. XXXI). Just as the number of souls can increase, because God can always create new souls, yet it cannot increase so much as to equal the number of existing things.

## CHAPTER XXI. On Faith

[Col. 1089D]

[Note: [Col. 1089D] Lombard, III, distinction 23.] The question is asked whether one who has one of these virtues has every one of them—that is, faith, hope, and charity. This does not seem to be so. For Augustine says:

[Note: [Col. 1089D] Book *On Faith and Works*, chapter 16, beginning.] “Faith which works through love is the foundation of virtues, not that faith of demons by which they believe and tremble” (James II).

See, he says openly that demons have faith, but it is certain [Col. 1090A] that they do not have hope and charity. Therefore someone has faith without the others, and thus not everyone who has one of these has them all.

To this it must be said that faith is sometimes called a quality of the soul by which a person grasps the things that ought to be believed. Charity sometimes accompanies that quality, and then the person has faith as a virtue, formed by charity. Sometimes charity does not accompany it; then that quality is unformed and is not faith as a virtue. Such faith is possessed by demons and wicked persons. But whether the same quality remains when it is unformed and when charity comes upon it, or whether it becomes another quality with charity while the prior quality ceases to exist, no one knows.

Sometimes that which we believe—that is, the collection of articles—is called faith. Hence: “This is the catholic faith.” The articles of our faith are the Incarnation, Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension, and so forth. But because certain people rise up against us, saying, “You believe the Lord’s Passion and Nativity, and so forth, but it is false that these articles are true; therefore you believe things which are false, and falsehood underlies your faith,” we can state the articles as propositional assertions: that Christ was born, that Christ suffered, and so forth. Abraham believed the same things, but in different words: that Christ would be born and that Christ would suffer.

When it is said that faith is the foundation of the other virtues, this must be understood of the movement of faith, because a foundation naturally, or in time, precedes [Col. 1090C] the things of which it is the foundation. The movement of faith is believing, that of hope hoping, and that of charity loving.

[Note: [Col. 1089D] Lombard, above, § i.] No one can hope or love unless he first believes by nature; but one can believe although one neither hopes nor loves. In whatever sense faith is spoken of—whether as a quality or as a collection of articles—it must be known that faith is one. For it is certain that the articles are the same among all believers. But if the quality is called faith, the faith of all believers is the same not in essence but [Note: [Col. 1089D] Faith is common to all believers, just as a face is said to be common to many persons, though each has his own. For faith is not numerically one, but one in kind: when it is in one person, it is also in others—not the very same faith, but a similar one; and because of this similarity we speak of one faith rather than many, just as a will is said to be one among those who will the same thing, although each has his own will, and as two very similar persons are said to have one face. Augustine, Book XIII *On the Trinity*, chapter 2.] in kind. For the quality of soul in different persons is not the same in essence, but it is the same in kind, just as one says that these persons have the same will or face because one is similar to the other.

[Note: [Col. 1090D] Lombard, above, § h.] Since many doubtful matters concern faith, [Col. 1090D] we must consider what faith is, concerning what things faith is held, and what difference there is between us and the ancients in faith. “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen” (Heb. XI), that is, that through which the things hoped for subsist in us; “proof,” that is, demonstration of things not seen. For through faith we demonstrate unseen things, saying: “The prophets foretold these things and believed them, and some of them have now been fulfilled. Therefore those that have not yet been fulfilled must be believed to be fulfilled in their own time, just as these have been fulfilled.” Thus it is the proof of unseen things.

But this definition seems defective in two respects: first, because it is not convertible with the thing defined, since hope likewise concerns only things hoped for, while faith too is the substance of things hoped for. Therefore faith is hope. It is also defective because it includes only future things, whereas faith concerns present, past, and future things alike. Therefore it must be said that this is not a definition, but a certain description.

[Note: [Col. 1091D] Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 1.] Or, more truly, it may be said that faith is one: faith concerning past, present, and future things, by which I believe that Christ was born, [Col. 1091B] that he will come for judgment, and that he is God. There are not three species of faith—faith concerning the present, another concerning the past, and a third concerning the future—but one and the same faith. Hence that definition, “the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen,” applies to faith generally. For the faith by which we believe that Christ was born is the substance of things hoped for, because by it we believe that Christ will come for judgment. Nor does this definition apply to hope, since nothing is truly and properly defined by its own term; faith can be defined thus:

[Note: [Col. 1091D] Thus in the terms of St Thomas, *Summa theologiae*, II–II, question 4, body of the article.] “Faith is voluntary certainty concerning absent things, situated below knowledge and above opinion.”

[Note: [Col. 1091D] Lombard, above, § g, and the following distinction.] It must be known that faith is not concerned with apparent things, but only with things not apparent. Hence [Col. 1091C] apparent things do not have faith, but recognition. For Augustine says:

[Note: [Col. 1091D] Rather Gregory, Book IV of the *Dialogues*, chapter 5, after the middle; and Homily 26 on the Gospels.] “That is truly said to be believed which cannot be seen. For what can be seen can no longer be believed. Thomas saw one thing and believed another: he saw a man and confessed God, saying, ‘My God and my Lord’” (John XX).

But that faith concerns only unseen things appears false; for the Gospel says: “And now I have told you before it comes to pass, so that, when it has come to pass, you may believe” (John XIV). Therefore the Lord wished the disciples to believe apparent things. Therefore faith concerns apparent things.

To this it must be said that, besides the meanings we have assigned to the term *faith*, there is another called credulity, according to which we say that we believe things we see and hear, and that we believe our own eyes. But we do not merit by this faith. For it is not meritorious, nor are we formed by it; rather, we are inwardly made certain by things that come to us from without.

There is again another faith, improperly called faith, but which should rather be called the thing of faith or the reward of faith. Of this the Apostle says: “Going from faith to faith”—from enigmatic faith to comprehensive faith. Augustine describes this faith thus:

[Note: [Col. 1091D] Book *Questions on the Gospels*, chapter 39.] “There is a faith of things, when belief is given not to the words themselves but to things present; this will be when the wisdom of God grants the saints contemplation of himself in sight.”

These words show that this faith should more properly be called certainty than faith. This will exist in the homeland; it is comprehensive, not enigmatic, faith.

[Note: [Col. 1092D] See Augustine, *Expositions on Psalm* CI, discourse 2.] Again, faith seems to concern apparent things, for Peter saw Christ’s Passion and believed it, as well as the other articles of faith. Therefore he believed what he saw. Therefore he did not merit. Again, Thomas would not believe until he saw the scars. Therefore human reason furnished experiential proof to his faith.

To this we say that both Peter and Thomas merited by believing. Peter saw a man suffer and die, but he believed him to be God, which he did not see, and in this he merited. [Col. 1092B] Thomas saw flesh, but believed God hidden beneath the flesh, and thus:

[Note: [Col. 1092D] Augustine, Tractate 79 on John.] he saw one thing and believed another.

What is said—

[Note: [Col. 1092D] Gregory, Homily 26 on the Gospels, on John XX.] “Faith has no merit where human reason furnishes experiential proof”—

must be understood thus: a person does not merit who is unwilling to believe unless the matter is proved to him by a human being.

Again, it is proved that faith concerns things known. For Augustine says:

[Note: [Col. 1092D] Book IX *On the Trinity*, chapter 1. “Certain faith begins both kinds of knowledge.”] “Nothing is more certain than faith.”

Therefore faith concerns certainties; but things that are certain are known. Therefore faith concerns things known.

Again, faith seems to concern things understood. Augustine says:

[Note: [Col. 1092D] On Psalm CXVIII, discourse 18.] “Some things are not understood unless they are believed, and some are not believed unless they are understood. For no one believes [Col. 1092C] in God unless he understands, since faith comes by hearing the preaching.”

See, he says openly that some things are not believed unless they are understood, and thus unless they are known. Therefore faith concerns things known.

Again, it is proved that faith concerns unknown things: no one is to be despaired of; this person hopes that another will be saved, but the other will not be saved. Let this be supposed. Therefore this person hopes something false. But whatever falls under hope falls under faith. Therefore he believes that the one who will not be saved will be saved. Therefore he believes something false.

To the first two arguments we say that there is enigmatic knowledge and comprehensive knowledge. It is true that faith concerns things known enigmatically, and that in the homeland they will be known comprehensively. Therefore, when he says, “Nothing is more certain than faith,” [Col. 1092D] this must be understood to mean that no certainty is to be preferred to the certainty of faith; that is, if one had to die for something, one should die for faith rather than for anything else. And although this certainty is so great, we are permitted to question the articles of faith, to inquire, and to dispute. I do not say that we may doubt whether the articles of faith are true; but we are permitted to question and dispute about the manner of the Nativity, the manner of the Passion, and the Resurrection. Hence Augustine: “Let us doubt with no unbelief concerning things to be believed, and affirm with no rashness concerning things to be understood.”

Similarly, when it is afterward said, “Some things are not believed unless they are understood,” that is, known, understand this enigmatically. Nor should one simply hope that this person, or any other, will be saved, except under such a qualification: if he perseveres in good until the end. Likewise, if a layman shows plain bread as Christ’s body, believing it to be Christ’s body and urging someone to believe it to be Christ’s body, that person ought not simply to believe that it is Christ’s body, except with this unstated qualification understood: namely, if the consecration was performed according to the ordinances of Christ and the Church.

[Note: [Col. 1093D] Lombard, III, distinction 25.] After the foregoing, the question is asked how we differ from the ancients in faith. There seems to be no [Col. 1093B] difference. For Augustine says:

[Note: [Col. 1093D] Book II *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, chapter 2; the sense is expressed, not the words.] “The same faith saves the little ones of old together with modern people. Yet they believed Christ would be born, while we believe him born and destined to suffer; they believed Christ would suffer, while we believe that he has suffered; they believed that he would rise, while we believe that he has risen; and both they and we believe that he will come for judgment.”

See, he says that their faith and that of modern people are the same. Scripture also says that those who went before and those who followed cried, “Hosanna” (Mark I; Luke XVIII); and thus the faith of ancients and moderns is the same.

But modern faith seems broader than ancient faith.

[Note: [Col. 1093D] Gregory, Homily 16 on Ezekiel.] For Moses, the teacher of the Law, knew more than Abraham, and David more than Moses. Hence David himself says: “I have understood more than the aged” (Ps. CXVIII). And [Col. 1093C] the Apostles knew more than the prophets. Thus the more recent men are, the more they have known of God; but one who knows more believes more.

[Note: [Col. 1093D] Gregory, above.] An authority states this; therefore modern people have a broader faith than the ancients.

[Note: [Col. 1093D] Lombard, III, distinction 25, § b.] Some reply that the ancients were bound to believe four things: namely, Christ’s Nativity, Passion, Resurrection, and coming for judgment.

[Note: [Col. 1093D] From Augustine, above.] They believed these distinctly as enumerated—as did Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Simpler persons, however, believed them under a veil, having veiled faith, as also happens today. For there are brutish people who do not know how to distinguish or even name the articles of faith, yet are saved in the faith of the greater members of the Church. Hence Job says: “The oxen were ploughing, [Col. 1093D] and the she-asses were feeding” (Job I). By the oxen are understood the greater persons;

[Note: [Col. 1093D] Gregory, Book II of the *Morals*, chapter 35.] by the she-asses, the simple.

Others say that the ancients believed only two articles: namely, the Nativity and the coming for judgment. They seek to establish this from John, who, while preaching, sent to the Lord and asked: “Art thou he that is to come, or do we look for another?”

[Note: [Col. 1094D] Gregory, Homily 6 on the Gospels, expressing the sense but not the words.] (Luke VII.) “Are you about to die and descend into hell?” [Col. 1094A] But if he had been bound to know this and did not know it, he would not have been perfect. Yet it is read that none was more perfect. Therefore no one was bound to believe those four things, but only two.

[Note: [Col. 1094D] Lombard, above, § c.] Those who hold the first opinion reply that John did not ask because he was ignorant, but out of compassion: for he had compassion on the Lord; or perhaps he doubted concerning the manner of the death and Resurrection.

[Note: [Col. 1094D] See St Thomas, *Summa theologiae*, II–II, question 2, article 7, reply to the second objection.] For he did not think that Christ would deign to suffer so ignominiously—to be struck, spat upon, and given gall to drink. Just as Peter, when he said, “Far be it from thee!” (Matt. XVI), etc., and the Lord said to him, “Get behind me, Satan” (Mark VIII), did not doubt the death, but the manner of the death. Nevertheless, both of the opinions stated are probable.

When it is said, “The more one knows, the more one believes,” this concerns [Col. 1094B] knowledge. For faith is called great through knowledge and great through devotion. The faith of the woman in the Gospel was great in devotion, not in knowledge; Peter’s faith, when he denied, was great in knowledge and not in devotion. Therefore modern people have a broader faith than ancients in knowledge, because the Gospel has been preached to them; and it ought also to be greater in devotion, because more abundant gratuitous gifts have been given to them than to the ancients.

Again, it is read in Leviticus that, if anyone is leprous, he should offer a sextary of oil; there it says: “If anything is lacking from the sextary, it is not a sextary” (Lev. XIV). So, if anything is lacking from faith, it is not faith; yet there is beginning, advancing, and perfect faith. Therefore beginning faith, [Col. 1094C] since something is lacking to it, is not faith.

It must be known that faith has a threefold perfection: perfection in comprehension, in understanding, and in fervor or steadfastness. Therefore, if anything necessary to be comprehended concerning the articles is lacking, faith is not full.

## CHAPTER XXII. On Hope

[Note: [Col. 1094D] Lombard, III, distinction 26.] Hope is the expectation of future blessedness arising from grace and preceding merits.

[Note: [Col. 1094D] Ibid., § 1.] But if merits precede hope, and merits do not exist without charity, then the movement of charity precedes the movement of hope. Yet it was said above that the movement of faith precedes the movement of hope and the movement of charity, and that the movement of hope precedes the movement of charity. Therefore it must be understood [Col. 1094D] that merits do not precede hope, but rather that which is hoped for; just as our merits precede not hope itself but what is hoped for, namely eternal life.

Not many matters worthy of investigation are found concerning hope.

[Note: [Col. 1094D] That is, investigation.] Yet this must not be omitted: no one is so perfect that he ought simply to hope that he will be saved, except thus: if he dies in charity. And no one is so obstinate [Col. 1095A] that he ought not to hope that he will be saved if he dies in charity. For no one is so perfect that he cannot fall, nor so wicked that he cannot rise, while he is on the way.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On Charity. First, on the Mode and Order of Charity, Where Many Doubtful Questions Are Treated

[Note: [Col. 1095D] Lombard, III, distinction 27.] Charity is to be discussed next. First, then, we must treat of the mode and order of charity; second, of equality and inequality; third, of perfection and imperfection; fourth, whether charity, once possessed, may be lost. All these matters will be clearer once it has been said what charity is.

[Note: [Col. 1095D] Ibid., § 2.] Charity, then, is love of God for his own sake and of one’s neighbor for God’s sake. The mode of charity is clearly discerned from this commandment: “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind” (Deut. VI).

[Note: [Col. 1095D] Augustine, Book I *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 22.] God must be loved with all the heart, that is, with the whole intellect; with all the soul, that is, with the whole will; with all the mind, that is, with the whole memory. But it is clear to anyone that this commandment cannot be fulfilled on the way. For a person cannot direct every movement toward God. Many movements arise from the concupiscence of the flesh, and many tend rather toward an evil than a good end. But this commandment can be fulfilled in the homeland, for there will be perfection.

[Note: [Col. 1095D] An allusion to Augustine, *On the Perfection of Righteousness against Caelestius*, before the middle.] Therefore it must be said that this commandment was given by God not according to the perfection of the homeland—for thus it could not be fulfilled on the way—but according to the perfection [Col. 1095C] of the way: namely, that it be fulfilled insofar as it can be fulfilled on the way. It must be explained and understood according to the perfection of the way thus: “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God,” etc., that is, you shall prefer the movement of charity to every other movement. For when many movements arise in the soul, the movement of charity must be preferred to all; and thus this commandment can be observed on the way.

Or thus: “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart,” that is, not falsely. Or thus: “Thou shalt love thy God,” etc., that is, in the present, nothing against God; in the future, nothing apart from God.

But according to the perfection of the homeland it must be explained differently: “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with,” etc., that is, with the intellect, without error; with the whole soul, that is, with the will, without opposition; with the whole [Col. 1095D] mind, that is, with the memory, without labor.

Again, otherwise: “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God,” etc., that is, all your movements will be spiritual in the homeland—for here both carnal and spiritual movements occur. Again thus: “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God,” etc., that is, all the movements of your soul will be from God and toward God, which is not so on the way. For some of our movements are from God but not toward God, as when we blaspheme. Some are toward God and not from God, as [Col. 1096A] when we have compassion on a neighbor. Some are neither toward God nor from God, as when we are moved toward adultery. Some are both from God and toward God, as when we love him perfectly; and this will be in the homeland. For there all our movements will be from God and toward God.

[Note: [Col. 1095D] Augustine, Book I *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 22.] The mode of loving one’s neighbor is this: we ought to love our neighbor as ourselves, because we must love ourselves for God’s sake and our neighbor for God’s sake, as well as the good that is in him and the good that is in us.

[Note: [Col. 1095D] Lombard, distinction 28, final §.] Since, however, *neighbor* is used in at least four senses—for someone is called a neighbor by the kinship of first birth, namely that of Adam and Eve; by the hope of conversion, as a Jew or pagan; by closeness of blood relationship, as a kinsman; and by the favor of a benefit conferred, as one who has bestowed many [Col. 1096B] benefits upon me—

[Note: [Col. 1096D] Book VIII *On the Trinity*, chapter 6.] here every human being is called a neighbor, because there is no human being to whom mercy ought not to be extended. By *neighbor* here we comprehend not only a human being, but also an angel,

[Note: [Col. 1096D] From the same Augustine, Book I *On Christian Doctrine*, chapters 23 and especially 30.] because he is rightly called our neighbor, and he guards and ministers to us. We also comprehend Christ here insofar as he is human, because, insofar as he is human, he is to be loved by us more than ourselves—that is, toward a greater good, and perhaps with a greater affection. But whether God is to be loved more, equally, or less than God and one’s neighbor together is doubtful; this seems incongruously stated, since one’s neighbor is not to be loved except for God’s sake.

[Note: [Col. 1096D] Lombard, distinction 28. The same, ibid.; Augustine.] The order, however, is this. First, God above us must be loved; second, we ought to love ourselves; third, that which is beside us, namely our neighbor; fourth, that which is beneath us, namely our flesh. We must love God with greater affection than ourselves, ourselves more than our neighbor, and our neighbor more than our flesh.

[Note: [Col. 1096D] The same, ibid., chapter 24.] But if anyone mortifies his flesh, he does not thereby hate his flesh, but its wantonness and pride.

It must also be known that loving God and loving one’s neighbor are sometimes called two commandments and sometimes one. They are two because of the different manner of loving: we ought to love God for his own sake, our neighbor for God’s sake, and God more than our neighbor. They are called one because of the identity of the charity by which we love both God and our neighbor.

[Col. 1096D] [Note: [Col. 1096D] Lombard, III, distinction 29.] The question is commonly asked whether we ought to love one neighbor more than another. Some are said to answer that we ought to love one more than another not with greater affection but with greater effect—for example, we are more bound to provide for those nearest to us by blood. They prove that all human beings ought to be loved with equal affection, that is, equal love, as follows: no one is to be loved except for God’s sake, nor is anything in a human being to be loved except for God’s sake. Therefore all human beings must be loved with equal affection. They show the same by Augustine’s authority, who says:

[Note: [Col. 1097D] In the exposition of Galatians VI, tome IV, V; also Book I *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 20.] “Eternal life must be desired for all with equal love, although the offices of love cannot be rendered to all.”

But Ambrose seems to oppose them, explaining the order of charity:

[Note: [Col. 1097D] On the words of Canticles II, “He ordered charity in me,” in the Gloss there.] “First God must be loved, then ourselves, then parents, then children; then members of the household, who, if they are good, are to be preferred to wicked children; finally an enemy, because you are not commanded to love him with all your strength as God, nor as yourself and your neighbor, but it is sufficient to love an enemy and not hate him.”

[Note: [Col. 1097D] Ibid., Ambrose, but with certain words omitted. It is not, however, found in Ambrose; indeed, all reject it as spurious.] See, Ambrose here says openly that we ought to love some persons with greater affection than others. Therefore some say that not all are to be loved with equal affection or equal effect, but some with greater and others with lesser affection and effect. They resolve Augustine’s authority thus: “Eternal life must be desired for all with equal love,” etc., that is, an equal reward and an equal crown must be desired for all. Thus they refer the equality not to affection or effect, but to reward. For we ought to desire as great a crown for this person as for that one, and conversely.

[Note: [Col. 1098D] Lombard, above, § e.] The question is asked whether what is set forth in Ambrose’s authority is true: namely, that good members of the household should be preferred to wicked children. It seems that they should be loved more, because no one ought to love anyone except for God’s sake or for the good that is in him; but there are many goods in this member of the household [Col. 1097C] and few in this man’s son. Therefore this man ought to love this member of the household more than his son.

Again, an authority says:

[Note: [Col. 1098D] Bede, on the words, “Who is my mother, and who are my brethren?” Matt. XII: “The bonds of minds are shown to be holier than those of bodies.”] “The bonds of minds are holier than those of bodies.”

But this man is joined to this member of his household by a bond of mind, and is joined by no such bond to his son; moreover, many gratuitous goods are to be loved in this member of the household, and none in his son. Therefore he ought to love this member of the household more than his son.

[Note: [Col. 1098D] Master of the Sentences, Book III, distinction 29, §§ d, e, etc.] My master, holding a spiritual view in this matter—which he himself practices and taught others not merely to teach but also to practice—asserts that good members of one’s household are to be loved with greater inward love than wicked children. For I ought to love the former with greater affection than the latter and to desire for them a greater reward because of the holiness of religion. Yet with outward love [Col. 1097D] I am more bound to provide for my children and other blood relatives, even if they are utterly wicked, than for good members of my household, if both they and the latter are in need. Nevertheless, I ought not to provide temporal goods to my blood relatives in superfluity, but only enough for bodily necessities; lest, if I give them excessive abundance whereby they become worse, I seem to encourage them in their error and thus become the author of their wickedness. But I ought to expend all that is mine for good persons.

Others think that, both as to effect and as to affection, I am more bound to love my wicked son than a stranger, even if the latter is excellent. If someone says that I am more bound to love the latter because of the many goods that are in him than my son, in whom there are no goods, then by the same reasoning I am more bound to love him than myself.

The question is then asked how the later statement in the authority is to be understood:

[Note: [Col. 1098D] From Ambrose above.] namely, “It is sufficient to love enemies and not hate them.” For above it was said that you must love your neighbor as yourself; but every human being is a neighbor; therefore I ought to love every human being as myself. Therefore I must love an enemy too as myself.

To this it must be said that you must love an enemy as yourself in such a way that *as* indicates similarity, [Col. 1098B] not quantity. For Ambrose, in order to indicate that an enemy is not to be loved as much as a neighbor, placed the love of enemies last.

Again, it is asked whether someone can, out of charity, love more what ought to be loved less, or love less what ought to be loved more. This seems provable as follows: a man loves his father as much as he ought; he also loves a stranger as much as he ought, and even more than he is bound to love him, because he loves him so greatly that the love he has for that stranger surpasses his love for his father; and he does this out of charity. Therefore, out of charity he loves more what ought to be loved less. For it is certain that a good father ought to be loved more than a stranger. [Col. 1098C]

But someone will say that the case proposed is impossible. Yet it can be proved as follows. Suppose that, out of charity, this man loves no one as much as his father. He is moved by one motion of charity to love his father, and by another to love this stranger; and this latter motion is less than the former. Can that lesser motion by which we are moved to love a stranger not increase, so that it becomes equal to the motion by which he is moved to love his father, or even exceeds it? If it can, it is now clear that out of charity he loves the stranger more than even his good father. But if one says that the lesser motion cannot increase without the greater, it is difficult to give a reason why. On the contrary, he loves more what ought to be loved less. [Col. 1098D] Therefore he has charity in a disordered form. Again, the order of charity is that a friend be loved in the first place and an enemy afterward. Therefore no one can love friend and enemy equally while preserving the order of charity.

Accordingly, some say that, since there are four motions of charity—the first toward God, the second toward oneself, the third toward a friend, and the fourth toward an enemy—a fifth may also be assigned toward one’s own flesh; [Col. 1099A] and among friends too a manifold distinction may be made. The motion of love toward an enemy, which is inferior, cannot increase without every superior motion increasing: that toward a friend, that toward oneself, and that toward God. For if this motion could increase while those did not increase, it could grow so great that it equaled the second; and thus the enemy would be loved as much as the friend. Indeed, it could exceed the second and equal the third, so that I loved my enemy as much as myself; indeed, even the fourth, so that I loved the enemy as much as God. This is plainly false, since the order of charity would thereby perish.

Others, however, think that a person can out of charity love an enemy more than a friend, and even more than a father; and thus he does not sin, but performs a work of supererogation in loving his enemy. So a poor woman loves God more than a bishop; yet the bishop does not sin, because he loves sufficiently, while the woman supererogates, though a much lesser love would suffice for her. Yet no one can love a neighbor more than God without sinning, because the motion of love for God exceeds all others and none is comparable to it. [Col. 1099B]

Again, one may ask whether the motion of love which a perfect person has toward his neighbor can be as great as the motion of love which an imperfect person has toward God. This seems possible. Many imperfect persons would not lay down their lives for Christ; rather, they would flee if danger arose. Conversely, many perfect persons love their neighbor so greatly that they would lay down their lives for him. Therefore the latter person’s motion toward his neighbor seems more intense than the former’s toward God. [Col. 1099C]

Conversely, this does not seem possible, because whoever loves God, whether perfect or imperfect, loves him more than himself; and no one is so perfect that he loves his neighbor more than himself. Therefore every imperfect person loves God more than any perfect person loves his neighbor.

Again, one may ask whether the natural motion by which someone naturally loves his friend can equal the motion by which someone loves his neighbor out of charity. Perhaps it can equal it in quantity, if not in dignity. It is also asked, since a man is moved to love a friend both because of benefits bestowed upon him and [Col. 1099D] because of God, whether he is moved by one motion or by different motions; and whether someone is moved, from the fact that he loves a creature with natural love because it pleases us, because it is God’s creature. We also do this for God’s sake, because we know it to be God’s creature; for thus we love the creature that is the devil. Since all these matters have not yet been fully worked out, we leave them under judgment for the present. It is more worth asking whether we love virtues with charity. If so, then we love them for the same end for which we love ourselves. This is true, not so that virtue itself may enjoy God, but so that those who possess the virtues may enjoy him through them.

[Col. 1100A] Again, Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1099D] *Enchiridion*, ch. 73.]: “There are not so many who love enemies as we believe to be heard in the Lord’s Prayer when saying, ‘Forgive us our debts’ (Matt. 6).” Therefore more people are heard in the Lord’s Prayer than love their enemies. Therefore someone who does not love enemies is heard in the Lord’s Prayer, and hence someone who does not love his neighbor. Therefore someone who does not fulfill this commandment, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Lev. 19; Matt. 5), is heard in the Lord’s Prayer.

To this we say that, when we say, “Many who do not love enemies are heard in the Lord’s Prayer” [Note: [Col. 1099D] Augustine, Homily 40 among the 50.], this is true with respect to outward effect and benefit: for not everyone who is heard in the Lord’s Prayer loves his neighbor by an outward act, but he must love him by inward [Col. 1100B] affection.

Again, it is asked whether every person is bound to love God as much as he can. If you say that no one is, then, since every person is bound to love God, everyone is bound to love him to a measure; therefore, if someone loves him more or less than a fixed limit requires, he is a transgressor. But if you say that some person is bound to love God as much as he can, then for the same reason everyone is. Therefore every person is bound to love God as much as he himself can; but no one loves as much as he himself can; therefore every person is a transgressor.

To this we say that no person is bound to love God as much as he can love him, because love of him can increase without limit. Therefore the argument, “Every person is bound to love God, and no one does so as much as he can; therefore he is bound to a measure,” is a fallacy. Every person wishes to know, and no one wishes to know so much that he cannot know more; therefore someone wishes to know to a measure. Again, every person is bound to love either perfectly or imperfectly. No one is bound to love imperfectly; therefore everyone is bound to love perfectly. A fallacy. [Col. 1100C] Each of these two knows this or that to be true: that the stars are even, or that the stars are odd. Neither knows this to be true, that the stars are even; therefore each knows the other to be true, that the stars are odd.

[Note: [Col. 1100D] Master, Book III, distinction 30.] It is also asked whether someone merits more by the motion through which he loves a friend than by that through which he loves an enemy, or conversely. But this question is perplexing. For if a comparison is made between the motion by which a man loves only a friend and that by which he loves both friend and enemy, there is no comparison. For the motion by which he loves only a friend is not good: no one ought to love only a friend. But let the question be put thus: does one merit more by loving a friend than an enemy, or conversely? Where the struggle is greater, there the crown is greater; but the struggle in loving an enemy is greater than in loving a friend; therefore the crown is greater. Therefore one merits more in loving an enemy than a friend. Yet this is proved false: for a man loves a friend [Col. 1101A] with greater charity than an enemy, and by a more intense motion; therefore he merits more by loving a friend than an enemy.

To this we say that where charity is more intensely directed, there merit is greater. Or it may plausibly be said that every person merits more by loving a friend than an enemy, because no one can love an enemy with a more intense motion than a friend. But the saying, “Where the struggle is greater, the crown is greater,” is not said universally.

Again, this person is bound to love every neighbor, and likewise every person. Therefore every person is bound to love every human being, known and unknown; therefore he is bound to love a person whom he has never seen and never known. To this it must be said that he is indeed bound to love every human being, known and unknown, with a general love. [Col. 1101B] For there is general love and special love, just as there is general confession and special confession.

Again, this man loves God with his whole heart and his neighbor with his whole heart; therefore he loves this one more than that one. A fallacy. Both Peter and Linus possess the highest good; therefore Peter does not possess more of it than Linus. Or: this man fights against that man and will fight with all his strength; therefore he will not fight more strongly than now. This is false, because then he will be stronger.

It is again asked whether someone ought to love his neighbor’s soul more than Christ’s flesh. They seek to prove this as follows: Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1101D] Book I, *On Christian Doctrine*, ch. 32. See ch. 16, Book X, *City of God*.], “Nothing is greater than enjoying the vision of God.” But a man loves his neighbor’s soul so that it may enjoy the vision of God; therefore he ought to love his neighbor’s soul more than [Col. 1101C] Christ’s flesh. But the contrary is argued: Christ’s flesh gives life to souls, and no one can have salvation except through Christ’s flesh; therefore Christ’s flesh ought to be loved more. Moreover, it is united to the Word of God, than whose gift there is nothing greater; therefore it ought to be loved more than a neighbor’s soul. Accordingly, some teach that Christ’s flesh ought to be loved more than a neighbor’s soul, with greater affection and for a greater end.

Again, it is asked whether someone ought to love his own flesh more than his neighbor’s soul. This seems so, because he is bound to love his own soul more than his neighbor’s soul, namely so that it may enjoy the vision of God; but he cannot love his own soul without loving his flesh, so that it may be glorified. For the soul cannot [Col. 1101D] enjoy eternal life [Note: [Col. 1101D] Understand this after the general resurrection of bodies.] unless it is to possess a glorified body. Therefore he is bound to love his own flesh more than his neighbor’s soul.

But the contrary seems true, because he ought to love his neighbor’s soul so that it may enjoy the vision of God, while his own flesh cannot enjoy the vision of God. Therefore he ought to love his neighbor’s soul more than his own flesh. To this we say that he ought to love his neighbor’s soul more, that is, for a greater end, because it is for enjoyment of the vision of God; or he ought to love his neighbor’s soul more than his own flesh because, if it comes to a crisis in which either his neighbor’s soul must be endangered in faith or his own flesh in suffering, [Col. 1102A] I ought rather to expose my own flesh to death than allow him to stumble in faith. For I ought to prefer the salvation of his soul to the temporal safety of my body. [Note: [Col. 1101D] It is not required by charity that a person expose his own body for his neighbor’s salvation, except in a case where he is bound to provide for that neighbor’s salvation. But voluntarily offering oneself for this belongs to the perfection of charity. Thomas Aquinas, *Summa Theologiae*, II–II, q. 26, art. 5.]

Yet this is true only of the perfect. It must be known that in another sense it is truly said that I ought to love my own flesh more than my neighbor’s soul, that is, with greater affection. For I ought to desire the glorification of my own flesh more than the blessedness of my neighbor’s soul, and I ought to work more for this end.

Again [Note: [Col. 1102D] Augustine, Book I, *On Free Choice of the Will*, ch. 10, replying to Evodius.]: “Below God, nothing is greater than the human mind.” Therefore, apart from God, nothing ought to be loved more than the human mind; therefore Christ’s flesh ought not to be loved more than [Col. 1102B] the human mind. This is untrue. Therefore that authority must be explained thus: “Below God,” etc., means that no use of any creature is greater or better than the use of the human mind; for its use is to contemplate God and direct thoughts to him. Or it may be explained thus: “Below God,” etc., means that below God nothing is greater than Christ’s mind, which is human.

Again, God’s will cannot be merit for this man unto eternal life; but his own will can be merit for him unto eternal life; therefore he ought to love his own will more than God’s will. A fallacy. This man’s soul cannot be merit of eternal life for him, but his works can be merit for him unto eternal life; therefore he ought to love [Col. 1102C] his works more than his soul.

Again, what is a greater good ought to be glorified more than what is a lesser good; but God’s power, which is God himself, is a greater good than Christ’s cross. Therefore God’s power ought to be glorified more than Christ’s cross; therefore the Apostle had disordered charity when he said, “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 6). To this it must be said that God’s power ought indeed to be glorified more than Christ’s cross. But the Apostle said this at the time when Christ’s cross was the greatest stumbling block to the Jews, and folly and derision to the Gentiles, so as to exalt the cross more and rebuke them more sharply. Or explain it thus: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord,” that is, except in the works which he performed for us by suffering on the cross. All this proceeded from mercy and goodness, which are the same as power.

Again, God ought to be loved because he is God, and he ought to be loved because he is man; therefore he ought to be loved more because he is God and man than because he is God. Again, in the *Song of Songs* you have, concerning the passage “What is thy beloved more than another beloved?” (Song 5): the Son from the Father. In this respect he ought to be loved more than feared. Again, “The mercies of God are over all his works” (Ps. 144). [Col. 1103A] Therefore he is more merciful than just; but he ought to be loved on account of mercy and feared on account of justice; therefore he ought to be loved more than feared.

But the contrary is argued thus. These names said of God signify the essence, and that essence is not compared, because it is neither increased nor diminished; therefore “more” and “less” are not said of it. Again, because he is God, he ought to be loved; because he is God, he ought to be feared; therefore he ought not to be loved more than feared. Again, because he is merciful, he ought to be loved; because he is just, he ought to be feared; he is not more merciful than just; therefore he ought not to be loved more than feared. Or thus: he is equally just and merciful; therefore he ought to be equally loved and feared.

It must therefore be known that these names said of God predicate the divine [Col. 1103B] essence and indicate certain effects in creatures, as was said concerning the names “just” and “merciful.” When it is said, “God ought to be loved,” the dignity by which God is worthy to be loved is established, namely the divine essence; moreover, certain effects in creatures are implied, namely that they are bound to love him. Similarly, when it is said, “God ought to be feared,” the same dignity is stated and another effect is implied. Therefore, if “more” or “less” is added to them according to their principal signification, the expression “God ought to be loved more than feared” is inappropriate. But if the comparison is referred to effects in creatures, it is true that for some reasons we are bound to love more, and for others to fear more, as was said concerning mercy and justice.

But when, with an added ablative, it is said, “God ought to be loved by us more than feared,” nothing is then asserted about God, just as nothing about God is asserted when I say, “God is Creator.” Rather, this is the sense: it is fitting that we should love God. Nor is it surprising if speech is made about God and, by implication, something is attributed not to God but to the creature; just as [Col. 1103C] when it is said, “God is Creator,” that is, by God’s willing, things came from non-being into being.

But if it is asked whether he ought to be loved by us more than feared, we say that this is so. For the motion of love in us toward God ought to surpass all other motions; and for some reasons he is to be loved by us more than for others. Thus, perhaps we are bound to love him more for works of re-creation than for works of creation; more because he suffered for us than because he is God. Yet we are not bound to love more; rather, we are bound to love more because he is God than because he suffered. For this motion ought to exceed all others. Thus it is clear that we are bound to love him more because he is God and man than because he is God, but not to love him more.

Therefore, if it is asked whether he ought to be loved more because he is God and man than because he is God: if the divine essence is predicated, the statement is inappropriate. If you refer it to effects, it is true, because we are bound to love him more because he is Mediator than because he is Creator; but we are not bound to love him more.
