A fallacy: God is great [Col. 1104A] because he is God, and he is great because he is man; therefore he is greater because he is God and man than because he is God. The solutions of the other arguments are clear from what has been said.

Again, since God ought to be loved because he created the world, and since generating the Son was incomparably far greater, it seems that he ought to be loved far more because he begot the Son; and *latria*—the worship due to God—seems to be owed to him because he is Father, and the same worship because he is God. Many other questions can be raised, but because they are unusual they should be passed over in silence. Yet this must not be omitted: the motion toward God surpasses even that which is toward him as man. For whatever good he bestowed upon us in his humanity, he did all of it from the goodness of his divinity, and all other motions are referred to the motion toward the divinity, from which every good comes.

[Col. 1104B] Just as it belongs to the order of love to inquire what ought to be loved in the first place and what in the second, so it seems to belong to the same order to inquire for what reason we are bound to love more or less. Therefore this question must be treated after the preceding one. Since, according to Augustine’s testimony, there are three kinds of goods [Note: [Col. 1103D] Book II, *On Free Choice of the Will*, ch. 19; and Book I, *Retractations*, ch. 9, middle.], greatest, intermediate, and least, it is asked whether God ought to be loved for all of them. This seems so, because, as was said above, God must be served for temporal things, which are least; therefore he ought to be loved for temporal things.

Again, before gratuitous gifts were conferred upon them, angels were bound to love God, and they had only natural endowments; therefore they were bound to love God with natural love for natural endowments. This is also known from the fact that gratuitous gifts were given to them according to [Col. 1104C] differences in the keenness of their natural endowments. Again [Note: [Col. 1104D] Thomas Aquinas, *Summa Theologiae*, II–II, q. 24, art. 2.], the Gospel says of a man going on a journey that he entrusted his goods to his servants, to each according to his own ability (Matt. 25), namely natural endowments; and thus according to differences in natural endowments each was bound to love more or less.

But the contrary is argued thus. This man is bound to love God for natural endowments, and only for God’s sake; therefore for natural endowments he is bound to love God in order to enjoy him. This also seems to follow from the authority: “Man was made in order that he might know God, love him once known, and enjoy him once loved.” Again, everyone is bound to love God for natural endowments; therefore, the better natural endowments he has, the more he is bound to love God. Therefore, if someone has better natural endowments than another and possesses equal charity, he sins more if he sins in any kind of sin than the other does if he sins in the same kind. Thus the more beautiful sins more than the less beautiful; the rich more than the poor; the person of keen intelligence more than the dull-witted. [Col. 1104D]

This is disproved, because when someone is poor, dull-witted, or suffers something of this kind, that is a punishment imposed upon him by God as medicine [Note: [Col. 1104D] Master, I, distinction 46, §1; from Augustine, *On the Trinity*. Also IV, distinction 15, §a. Pullus has similar material.], either for correction if he is a sinner, or for preserving virtues if he is good—as a thorn of Satan was given to Paul—or for a greater crown, as in Job. Therefore, unless one of these effects is produced in him, [Col. 1105A] he turns a medicine given to him for good into evil, and thus sins from greater contempt than one to whom no medicine has been applied—that is, a rich person or anyone else—according to the saying: “We treated Babylon, and she was not healed” (Jer. 52). And: “The furnace tests the vessels of the potter, and the trial of tribulation tests righteous men” (Ecclus. 27). Thus the poor person seems to sin more than the rich, the dull-witted person more than the intelligent.

For this reason, some distinguish between the foundation of love and its increase. The foundation is expressed where it says: “You shall love the Lord your God,” etc. (Matt. 5). The increase is indicated there: “To whom more is entrusted, more is required from him” (Luke 12). Therefore, with respect to the foundation of love, all are equally [Col. 1105B] bound to love, but by no means with respect to its increase.

Others say that one person is bound to love more than another; but as there is the worship of *dulia* and the worship of *latria*, so there is love of *dulia* and love of *latria*. By the love of *latria*, all are equally bound to love God; but by the love of *dulia*, some are bound more. Accordingly, one who has better natural endowments is bound to love more with the love of *dulia*. Those who solve it in this way do not solve it, but merely state it.

Therefore the rule to be maintained is that one who despises more sins more. But it is again asked who despises more, the rich person or the poor. A reason has been given on each side; and it seems truer that it is the rich person. For just as poverty is medicine through which a person ought to be removed from sin, so too are riches. Hence, if two persons, namely rich and poor, [Col. 1105C] sin in the same kind while having previously possessed equal charity, the rich person sins more, because the medicine of riches is sweeter than that of poverty.

It is like two people recovering from the same illness: one through a biting plaster, the other through a pleasant medicine. The one who recovered pleasantly is more indebted to his physician than the one who recovered through harsh medicine. For poverty, though it provides an occasion of greater merit to the person to whom the medicine is applied, as was said, nevertheless—even if it brings about none of the things mentioned—is not a cause of greater transgression.

As you see by a contrary analogy: this unbeliever sins if he does not love his children, yet he does not merit if he loves them. So too, the person who is not obligated to me but serves freely merits more from me by serving me [Col. 1105D] than one obligated to me; yet he does not transgress more, or offend more, if he does not serve. Likewise, this layman, who greatly supererogates by loving God more, merits more than this prelate who does not love so much; yet he does not transgress more if he sins.

But this too has its own doubt, which seems relevant here. Suppose this layman loves more than that prelate, while the prelate loves as he is bound to do and the layman supererogates. That increase of charity by which the layman surpasses the prelate in charity is greater and more excellent than all the gifts bestowed upon that bishop, [Col. 1106A] because nothing is comparable to charity. Therefore this man is endowed with a greater gift than that one; therefore more is required of him; therefore he is bound to love more.

Again, the authority says [Note: [Col. 1105] Augustine, Sermon 2 on Psalm 33. “For this is what is always paid and always owed.” He says precisely the same in Psalm 36.]: “The more fully the debt of charity is paid, the more fully it is owed.” This man pays more; therefore he ought to love more than the other. Again, he loves more than the other; therefore he is loved more; therefore he is bound to love more. Again, if he sinned, he would repel from himself a greater gift of the Holy Spirit than the other, because he has a greater gift; therefore he would inflict a greater injury upon the Holy Spirit; therefore, if he sinned, he would sin more in some kind of sin than the other in the same kind.

Again, “The more fully the debt of charity is paid, the more fully it is owed.” Therefore one who loves more is more bound to love; therefore the more he loves, the less he pays off the debt of charity; therefore the less he loves, the more he pays it off, and thus the less he loves, the less he is bound. Therefore, if he does not love, he is not bound to love. This is false, because there are many other things for which a person is bound to love besides love itself, namely intermediate and least goods. For if a person were not bound to love if he did not love, he would not transgress by failing to love. [Col. 1106B]

Conversely, the following objection is made. This prelate is bound to love perfectly; it suffices for this private person if he loves imperfectly. Therefore, not only is this man not bound to love more than the other, but the other is bound to love more. Again, if everyone possessing more intense charity is bound to love more than one possessing less intense charity, because [Col. 1106C] the least increase of charity surpasses all other gifts, then one who has the least charity is bound to love more than one who has none. Therefore he transgresses more if he sins than one who lacks charity. This is false, because “Sin which is not washed away by repentance immediately, by its own weight, draws one to another sin.”

To this they say that one is bound to love either by command, or by reason of reward, punishment, or a gift bestowed. All are equally bound to love by command; but one is bound more than another by reason of punishment, reward, or bestowed gifts, according as a reward or punishment is set before him, or lesser goods have been bestowed. But it is very difficult to balance punishments, rewards, gifts, or acts of contempt, because we believe these things are known only to God. [Col. 1106D] Here, then, it is certainly true that whoever despises more sins more; but regarding contempt we believe only God can readily judge.

Therefore it is true that no one is bound to love more than another in the sense that, if he did not love more, he would transgress. But one person is bound more than another, as was said, according to differences of reward, bestowed gift, or punishment.

Again, given two persons, one perfect and the other imperfect, each is bound to abstain from as great a wickedness as that possessed by a third person who is wicked; and the perfect person is bound more to abstain. Therefore, if each receives so great a wickedness, the perfect person sins more than the imperfect. [Col. 1107A] Thus he is worse; and they concede this. For they cannot sin in the same kind of sin, when one is less capable than the other.

But it is again objected: it may happen that this person receives some wickedness as great as that possessed by the other, neither greater nor less; and the imperfect person can receive as much, if not in the same kind of sin, at least in a different kind. Since they can receive equal wickedness in different kinds, they are either equally bound to abstain from it, or the perfect person is bound more. If he is not bound more to abstain from it, neither does he sin more by receiving it than one who has neither dignity nor perfection. Thus his fall seems to arise from wickedness alone, not from dignity.

But if he is bound more to abstain from it, and they receive equal [Col. 1107B] wickedness, then one sins more than the other. If he sins more, the perfect person is worse; therefore he receives greater wickedness and does not merely have so much. Indeed, even if the perfect person receives as much wickedness as the imperfect, since what is criminal for the imperfect is more criminal for the perfect, the perfect becomes worse from so great a wickedness than the imperfect from so great a wickedness.

Again, each receives as much wickedness as the other possesses, neither greater nor less; each becomes wicked. Therefore they become equally wicked. For if one denies the first proposition, he will say that it is impossible for the perfect and imperfect to take on equal wickedness; but if the person who was perfect becomes more wicked than the one who was imperfect, then he takes on greater wickedness.

[Col. 1107C] Some therefore say that all are equally bound to abstain from equal mortal [sins], and that whoever receives equal wickedness is equally wicked. Yet authority seems to say that the perfect person is more bound than the imperfect to abstain from equal sins. But they distinguish the phrase “is bound more”: that is, he is obligated by more things; this is true. If it is said, “He is bound more,” meaning that if he receives as great a sin as the other, he sins more gravely: this is false.

They also say that, if this perfect person sins equally with someone who was never perfect, he acts against more [goods] and becomes guilty of more things. Yet he does not sin more. Otherwise it could be proved that, whatever the least sin the perfect person committed, [Col. 1107D] he would sin more than someone never perfect who committed the greatest sin.

They also say that one who possesses dignity, if he sins, is guilty not only of the sin he commits but also because he acts against the honor of his dignity. Yet he does not sin more than one who commits the same sin, equally great, without dignity; though he is punished more by the Church, which considers not so much the will as the deed.

But there is no doubt that more is required of the perfect than the imperfect in abstaining from one and the same sin, and that by doing the same thing he sins more gravely, since what is venial for one is mortal for another. Therefore one must simply grant that a perfect person is sometimes bound to abstain from some sin which is less in its own quality than an imperfect person is bound to abstain from a sin greater in its own quality; and, by receiving it, he sins as much, even though it is not as great as that other sin in its own quality. Yet in this person it is greater; and this is because dignity is despised, so that he may truly be said to fall not only from the magnitude of sin but also from the height of dignity. [Col. 1108A]

From this it seems that, according to the greater or lesser degree of inward faculties—namely intelligence, memory, reason, and understanding—their possessors ought to direct themselves toward heavenly things. Yet we see many unlearned persons advance more in spiritual matters, while those who excel in natural abilities do not have as much grace in spiritual matters. Thus, to the extent that the former appear to supererogate, the latter appear to transgress. [Col. 1108B]

Again, we read of the master of a household who gave talents to each person, so that each might profit according to the talent entrusted to him. By these talents are signified both natural goods and outward actions entrusted to us, so that through them we may act well and thus deserve to hear: “Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25). Therefore each person, according to what he has received more abundantly, is bound to work more. Thus, if one who has received more does not work more than one who has received less, he transgresses.

Yet we see many educated persons work less than simple and dull people. Indeed, if everyone is bound to act according to his outward activity, then everyone is bound to distribute to the poor as much as he can, retaining for himself only what suffices for food [Col. 1108C] and clothing.

To this they say that God does not bestow gratuitous gifts according to those faculties, but according to the capacity of those faculties—a capacity known only to him who went on a journey. Each person ought to give as much as he can, but not all that he can, because he can reserve it for better uses. Thus, if I see someone in need, but not so badly that he cannot live without my assistance, I may reserve the money I have for repairing the fabric of a church rather than distribute it; or for supporting my father or mother, or for some good work.

Yet if he is in such need that he will die unless I give, I ought without delay to give, whether I am perfect or imperfect, and even if he is my enemy. [Col. 1108D]

Again, it is asked of someone who was formerly a Gentile and is now a Jew whether he is more bound to love or observe the commandments than before, or merits more by doing so. The answer is argued thus: what was afterward written on tablets of stone—“Honor your father and mother” (Exod. 20)—was written in human hearts. Formerly this man obeyed only the commandment of nature; now he obeys both the commandment of nature and the commandment of the Law. Therefore he merits more than before.

Again, he does not merit more than before; therefore it does not benefit him that he has become a Jew. The contrary is argued thus: he honors his father and mother with as much charity as before, not with greater or lesser charity; therefore he neither merits more nor less than before. The same objection concerns two persons, [Col. 1109A] one of whom observes chastity out of charity without a vow, while the other does so with a vow and with equal charity. The observance of the one who acts without a vow is less owed than that of the other; therefore it is worthy of a greater reward; therefore this man merits more than the other, according to the saying: “The less owed goods are, the more gracious they are.”

Conversely: this man merits from as much charity as the other, and in addition from his vow; and the vow itself is meritorious. Therefore this man merits more than the other.

Therefore, in the aforesaid case it must be said that those who have equal charity merit equally, although one who has now become a Jew merits through more things than when he formerly was a Gentile, or a monk than when he was formerly a layman; nevertheless, he does not merit a greater reward, because he does not do this out of more intense charity. Just as [Col. 1109B] one who has the will to give alms, but does not give because he lacks the means, merits as much as one who has the means and gives, as Zacchaeus and the widow did (Luke XI, XXI).

But posit this case concerning the Jew and the Gentile before Christ’s coming. For otherwise neither the one nor the other has charity; but then he could have had it. If, however, it is asked what benefit he gains from having become a Jew or a monk, it must be said that, because of his frailty, in order to be safer he bound himself by vow and religious profession. Thus it benefits him not toward a greater reward, but toward living more securely.

Again, Cain killed Abel (Gen. IV) before the commandment “You shall not kill” (Exod. XX) had been given; but when he killed, he transgressed this commandment; therefore he transgressed it before it had been given as a commandment. Again, Augustine says elsewhere:

> “We are not bound by the command because this was commanded us; rather, because we were bound by the command, it was given to us as a commandment.”

[Note: [Col. 1109D] See question 140, on Exodus, and the beginning of the exposition on Psalm LVII.]

Therefore we were bound by the command before the commandment was given; therefore, if we did not keep the commandment, we transgressed it before it had been given. This seems impossible. The answer is that there is a natural commandment and a written commandment; and Cain transgressed the natural commandment of the law before the written commandment was given. Therefore Augustine says, “Because we were bound by the command”—namely, that of nature—“it was given to us as a commandment”—namely, in writing. For the wicked were not restrained by the commandment of nature; [Col. 1109D] therefore, for fuller observance, the natural commandment was put into writing.

It is also asked whether God ought to be loved more in one place or at one time than in another. This seems to be the case [Note: [Col. 1110D] Leo, Sermon 5 on Lent], because it has been instituted that in the season of Lent and on feast days we should be more devout and serve God more than at other times; and God approves that institution. Therefore at that time God ought to be served more, and God ought to be loved more; and thus at one time we are more obliged to love than at another, and in one place more than in another.

On the contrary, God is always equally good, and he is to be loved only [Col. 1110A] on account of his goodness. Therefore he is not to be loved more at one time than at another. Again, indirectly, God is to be loved more at one time than at another; therefore [this must be] by the love of *dulia* or *latria*, and thus everyone is obliged to possess greater charity at one time than at another. Therefore, if one does not then possess greater charity, one transgresses. Thus no matter how great a charity one has, it is not enough for meriting God. Again, it seems beyond doubt that God ought to be loved more in the time of grace, when he is served out of love, than in the time of the law, when he was served out of fear. Therefore he is to be loved more at one time than at another.

A threefold service must therefore be distinguished. There is service owed, which is that of *latria*; pious service, which consists in works of mercy; and instituted service, which arises from [Col. 1110B] human institution. For it has been established that we should praise God in the canonical hours rather than at other times, and that in Lent we should be more devout and redeem the time. Therefore, by instituted service, I am obliged to serve God more at one time than at another, since at the time of Vespers I ought to say Vespers, which I am not obliged to do at another time.

But by service owed or pious service, no one is obliged to serve God more at one time than at another; for if he did not serve more at that time, he would transgress, though he might have served more at another time and performed works of supererogation. Likewise, no one is obliged to love God more than another person. So too, at one time no one is more obliged to love God and desire eternal life than at another, such that the adverb “more” qualifies the verb “is obliged,” [Col. 1110C] not the verb “to love” or “to serve.”

## Chapter XXIV. On the Equality and Inequality of Charity

That, after speaking of the manner and order of charity, we should speak of its equality and inequality is required by the order of the foregoing enumeration. For it is clear that all merit depends upon charity, according to the saying: “The fullness of the law is charity” (Rom. XIII). But if the fulfillment of all things depends upon it, how does not the fullness of all merits also depend upon it? And [Note: [Col. 1110D] See also Augustine, Tractate 5 on the First Epistle of John]:

> “What can be lacking to one who has charity?”

It is clear that equal charity entails equal merit, according to the saying concerning one “who gives a cup of cold water” (Matt. X) and one who gives an inheritance: their merit is equal because [Col. 1110D] their charity is equal. Yet the same is said of the will: equal merit depends upon equal will. This is shown where the Lord, speaking of the widow, says: “This poor woman put as much into the treasury as all these” (Mark XII). On this passage Bede says: “The means were unequal, but the will equal.” This may be illustrated by an example from the Old Testament. The Lord sent out a few of the children of Israel under the leadership of Phinehas; afterward he commanded that those who had been sent should have as large a share of the booty as those who had remained behind (Num. XXXI), because of the equal will which they had had. Likewise David, when he pursued the marauding [Col. 1111A] Amalekites and left the exhausted men behind this side of the river Besor, rewarded with an equal division of the spoil those with whom he pursued them (I Kings XXX).

But an objection is raised. Equal charity entails equal merit, and equal will entails equal merit; yet where charity is equal, will is unequal. Therefore either unequal merit exists in equal charity, or equal merit exists in unequal will. This necessarily follows if it is established that unequal will exists where charity is equal. It is shown thus. Suppose there are two persons having equal charity, who are moved to perform the same work of mercy for a poor man. Yet one is naturally moved more to it because the poor man is his brother. It is certain that the one in whom the natural movement is greater is [Col. 1111B] more inclined to show mercy, and thus has a greater will, although they have equal charity.

And who can deny this of Christ? For he did not will everything equally. He would not otherwise have said: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you” (Luke XXII), and, “I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how I am constrained until it is accomplished” (Luke XII), unless he had willed this with greater force [Note: [Col. 1111D] You have the same below, distinction 4, chapter 13.] than to speak with the Samaritan woman. Therefore it is certain that he willed some things unequally. Yet it is clear that he always possessed equal charity, since in it he could neither advance nor fail. Hence in all things he merited equally for himself. Unequal will may therefore exist in equal charity; and thus equal merit [Col. 1111C] in unequal will, if equal merit always accompanies equal charity. How, then, is the statement “equal will entails equal merit” resolved?

To this they say that wills are called equal either in quantity or in goodness. Thus wills can be unequally intense in equal charity, yet equally good. But it is asked whether, similarly, movements unequally intense arising from equal charity are equally good. This is otherwise, because the more intense is simply the better.

There is nevertheless doubt whether movements unequally intense can arise from equal charity. This is argued as follows. Suppose two persons in charity are moved to perform a work of mercy for a poor religious man, but one has been more intimately acquainted with his way of life. Thus it seems that, though their charity be equal, one is nevertheless moved by a greater movement of charity to assist him than the other; and so movements unequally meritorious proceed from equal charity. In what, then, is equality of charity to be considered? Surely in equality of movements? Indeed, it is. Charity [Note: [Col. 1111] This follows consistently indeed, but wrongly; see *Magister*, I, distinction 17, § h.] [Col. 1111D] is not increased or diminished in itself, but in its effect. Yet not everyone who is moved by a greater movement of charity toward something than another possesses greater charity toward that thing than the other, since the other may be moved by a greater movement of charity than he toward the same thing.

A comparison must be made of all [Col. 1112A] this person’s movements of charity together with all the movements of charity of that other person, so that, if they correspond equally, they may be said to have equal charity. The comparison must not be made of one movement with one movement. Just as, if I wish to show that two men are equal in riches, the comparison must be made of all this man’s riches together with the other’s riches, not of some riches with some others; so also in knowledge, the comparison is not of one item with one item, but of all with all, in order to show that one person is more learned than another.

It must nevertheless be understood that, although equal merit depends upon charity and likewise upon equal will, the reason for this saying is different in the one case and in the other. For in the first case, “depends upon” denotes an efficient cause; in the second, it denotes a certain authority of meriting attached to the will, which [Col. 1112B] is meritorious even without a work. A work, however, is never without will.

What has been said may cause difficulty if understood generally, namely: equal charity entails equal merit. Suppose there are two persons: one is a young man, whom the ardor of youth incites to lust and who resists with the greatest struggle; the other is an old man, possessing equal charity but feeling no disturbances of the flesh. These two have equal charity; therefore they are worthy of equal reward. This is disproved, because where the struggle is greater, there the crown is greater. But the young man sustains a greater struggle than the old man; therefore he merits more.

For this reason we say that, although in this respect the young man merits more than the old man, nevertheless [Col. 1112C] in another respect the old man merits more than the young man. For since they have equal charity, it is impossible that charity should be idle in him. The authority, “Where the struggle is greater, there the crown is greater,” is not, however, to be understood universally.

Again, this virgin and this married person have equal charity. To this virgin the hundredfold fruit is due; therefore it is also due to this married person, or unequal merit exists in equal charity. It must therefore be understood that when it is said that married persons receive the thirtyfold fruit, the continent the sixtyfold, and virgins the hundredfold, this does not show a difference in the quantity of reward according to a difference in the quantity of merits from which the rewards receive their names. For one who receives the hundredfold fruit is sometimes of less merit [Col. 1112D] than one who receives the thirtyfold. Rather, these numerical names are assigned because of their significations, as is explained elsewhere, not because of a difference in quantity; or perhaps in order to show that, by as much as those numbers surpass one another in quantity, these states also surpass one another in dignity. For by as much as one hundred exceeds sixty in quantity, the virginal state exceeds the state of continence in dignity. Yet someone in the state of virgins is of less merit than someone in the state of the continent.

Again, this prelate and this subject have equal charity; therefore they are worthy of equal reward. But against this: to this prelate both the *aurea* and the *aureola* are due; to this subject only the *aurea*. Therefore a greater reward is due to this prelate than to this subject.

Again, there are two persons possessing equal charity, one a martyr and the other a confessor. They have equal charity and an equal will for martyrdom, and no work is meritorious except through charity. Therefore they are worthy of equal reward on account of their equal will for martyrdom; therefore martyrdom is not a privileged work.

Again, there are two persons, one of whom, having less charity, ended his life by martyrdom; but the increase of merit that he receives from martyrdom corresponds equally to the increase of charity that the other receives through charity. These two are worthy of equal reward; therefore they are loved equally; therefore [Col. 1113B] they love God equally; therefore they have equal charity. Or thus: one of them loves more; therefore he is loved more; therefore he is worthy of greater reward; therefore he is rewarded more, or he is treated unjustly.

Again, suppose that the increase of merit which one receives from a privileged work exceeds the increase which the other receives from greater charity. Then the one who has greater charity is of lesser merit; therefore the one who loves God less is loved more by God. Again, this martyr merits a greater reward than that man, and has charity equal to his; therefore he merits from some source other than charity. This is false, because even martyrdom itself is not meritorious except through charity.

Again, that martyrdom adds nothing to merit where charity is equal seems to follow from what the Lord says in the Gospel to the two sons of Zebedee: “You shall drink my cup” (Matt. X). There he seems to make them equal in martyrdom as regards their will, because they had an equal will for martyrdom, although only one of them materially underwent martyrdom. Again, [Col. 1113C] the merit of endurance is not unequal for Peter, who suffered, and John, who did not suffer. [Note: [Col. 1113] Abelard, in Book III of his Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, p. 637, confirms his opinion by this authority drawn from Augustine.] Again, just as Stephen saw Christ in martyrdom, so Martin, while still a catechumen, saw Christ clothed in the cloak which he had given to a poor man.

Therefore some maintain that martyrs are privileged in this world because they do not pass through purgatory. Others say that the martyr or preacher receives more not by reason of merit but by reason of dignity or God’s mercy. In other works equal charity receives equal [Col. 1113D] reward; and if works are added by one person, merits are multiplied in number, not in meriting power, as in Christ.

Others say that if two people are equal in charity and one is a martyr, it should not be said that they love equally. Rather, the martyr loves more, if not in affection, at least in effect, and therefore has a greater reward. But this is worthless, because love exists only through affection, and God attends not to the effect but to the affection; not to what [one does], but from how much [love it is done]; not to the deed, but to the disposition.

Others more truly say that martyr and confessor merit equally where charity is equal, and an equal reward is given. But, beyond the reward which is given [Col. 1114A] for martyrdom, something is given to him which is, as it were, an addition and beyond merit, because he is a martyr or preacher: namely, an *aureola* and a certain joy. If he is a preacher, this joy arises because many have been converted to the faith by his preaching; if he is a martyr, because many have been strengthened in faith by his example. That joy is not part of the reward.

For example, if two persons love me equally, and one exposes himself to death for me, I reward them with equal reward. Yet, because of the outstanding deed, I give something beyond merit to the one who did it—not because he loves me more than the other, nor because he has merited more, since they had the same will to perform the deed, but because of the dignity of the deed performed by this one. Just as, if this man has as much sunlight as that man, and in addition has candlelight, he does not therefore have greater light. Likewise, [Col. 1114B] an *aureola* added to the *aurea* does not make the reward greater, because the *aurea* properly consists in the vision of God, which this man possesses as much as that one; and the *aureola* consists in joy at the conversion of brethren, which is not part of the reward but beyond the reward.

Again, suppose that, of two persons equal in charity, one receives the Eucharist and the other does not. Receiving the Eucharist increases the reward in the former. Therefore he merits a greater reward than the latter, yet they have equal charity; therefore unequal merit exists in equal charity. If “receiving the Eucharist” is understood intransitively—that is, the Eucharist having been received—the statement is true, because the Eucharist itself increases reward: it is God’s work, not man’s, and this does not belong to human merit [Col. 1114C] but to the power of the sacrament. If “receiving the Eucharist” is understood transitively—that is, as the action of one who receives the Eucharist—the statement is not true. For although he merits through this action, he does not thereby merit a greater reward than before. He therefore merits through more things, but not more greatly.

Nevertheless, it seems impossible that one of two equal in charity should receive the Eucharist while the other does not. This is shown as follows. Possessed charity merits to be increased; therefore charity equally possessed merits equally to be increased. It is possessed equally by these persons; therefore it is increased equally in them, because the sacrament of the Eucharist was instituted for the increase of virtues and as a remedy for daily weakness. Therefore it is impossible for anyone to receive the Eucharist worthily without charity being increased in him. But these two receive an increase through the merit of charity; [Col. 1114D] and beyond the equal increase which the one receives, he receives an increase through the power of the sacrament. Therefore charity is increased more in the recipient than in the non-recipient. Thus it is proved impossible that, of two equal in charity, one should receive the Eucharist without charity being increased more in him. Indeed, it seems to be increased more in the recipient through merit, for he merits the reception from which he receives an increase through the power of the sacrament, and thus merits the increase which he receives through sacramental power—hence, two increases.

But this is invalid. For one does not merit the consequent merely because one merits the antecedent. Thus this person merits the intercession of a poor man, from which the infusion of first grace follows; yet he does not merit the first infusion.

Therefore [Col. 1115A] it may be said that these persons merit an equal increase of charity from equal charity, and are equally increased through merits; but that one person has a greater increase through the power of the sacrament is due to grace, not merits. It is as if two persons laboring equally in a vineyard received equal reward, and one received more by grace. But on this account it might happen that two persons equally worthy of life would die, and one would receive a greater crown. We believe God can do this by grace, but that it never happens.

It should therefore be said that the equality of charity is not removed because one of two equal in charity receives the Eucharist while the other [Col. 1115B] does not. For to the non-recipient, beyond the increase received through the merit of charity, God graciously grants an increase equivalent to the increase which the other receives through the sacrament.

Again, this person has remained in charity, this other for two days, and they have equal charity. These persons are worthy of equal reward for works which they perform in equal charity; therefore the works done by the former are superfluous if he is not worthy of a greater reward on their account. To this it must be said that duration adds nothing to merit and does not increase reward where charity is equal. The number of merits is indeed increased, but not the right to merit, as in Christ. What, then, is the value of the foregoing works? [Col. 1115C] While he did them, he did not commit evils; and if he had then died, he would have been saved.

Again, this person persevered in charity longer than that one; therefore he merited more than the other. This is a fallacy. The thief was in Paradise before the Blessed Virgin; therefore he obtained a greater reward.

## Chapter XXV. On the Perfection and Imperfection of Charity

Just as the equality and inequality of charity, of which we have spoken, are considered according to inward dispositions, so the perfection and imperfection of charity are considered according to inward movements: charity is called perfect when it moves perfectly, imperfect when it moves imperfectly. Yet every perfection of this life is a kind of imperfection; for it will truly be perfected when every imperfection [Col. 1115D] has been done away with.

But because Scripture speaks of perfection in various ways, a distinction must be introduced to remove ambiguity. Scripture sometimes calls sufficiency perfection, as when it is said: “Perfect repentance is that which destroys the sins committed,” that is, sufficient repentance. There is also comparative perfection, of which it is said: “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V); and “Noah was perfect in his generations” (Gen. VI), namely by comparison with others. An example of imperfect charity may be found in either of these perfections: the sufficient and the comparative.

[Col. 1116A] Beyond these modes, four modes may be distinguished by their proper names and marks: the perfection of repose, of action, of order, and of certainty.

The perfection of repose is the disposition to leave all things for Christ, which is known by the act of leaving them. Hence: “If you wish to be perfect,” etc. (Matt. XIX). Cenobites are bound to this perfection.

The perfection of action is the will to lay down one’s life for the flock entrusted to one’s care; its mark is to show this very thing in deed. A priest having care of a flock is bound to it; concerning it it is said: “No one has greater charity than this,” etc. (John XV). [Note: [Col. 1115D] Augustine, Tractate 5 on I John.]

The perfection of order is complete continence, whose mark is to show this same thing in deed. [Note: [Col. 1116D] See the notes on Pullus, *On the Celibacy of the Subdeacon*.] Every priest, whether or not he has care of a flock, and every deacon, is bound to this. This perfection [Col. 1116B] is nothing other than a vow of continence, concerning which it is said: “He who can receive it, let him receive it” (Matt. XIX).

The perfection of certainty is perfection of conscience, when a person is conscious to himself of no venial or mortal sin; indeed, when he is, as it were, certain and steadfast that he is without every sin, and fears not punishment but separation. Of this it is said: “Be perfect as your Father [is perfect]” (Matt. V). Of this alone is it said: “Perfect charity casts out initial fear” (I John IV).

Nor is every perfect person bound to all kinds of perfection, but individuals to particular kinds. The first three kinds of perfection can exist with initial fear, but the fourth cannot. Anyone who has one of these perfections is called perfect, lest, if he were called imperfect, [Col. 1116C] all perfection should seem to be denied him—just as one who knows any of these sciences, grammar, music, rhetoric, or dialectic, is called learned, lest, if he were called unlearned, all knowledge should seem to be denied him.

This too deserves consideration: charity is called a virtue, and a work of charity a movement of virtue. One is said to possess more perfect charity than another either because one performs more works of perfect charity, or because one has a more fervent movement, or because charity is more deeply rooted in him, because he has a firmer purpose and constancy. This is true and more meritorious perfection.

That everyone is bound to the first perfection seems to be demonstrated thus: “Unless anyone renounces all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple” [Col. 1116D] (Luke XIV). Therefore everyone is bound to renounce all that he possesses, since everyone is bound to be Christ’s disciple. Therefore everyone is bound to have the disposition to leave all things for Christ, and thus everyone is bound to leave all things for Christ—not cenobites alone.

Therefore this saying, “Unless anyone renounces,” etc., is explained thus: unless one has subordinated love of earthly things to love of God, one cannot be my disciple; or, should necessity arise, unless one sets aside the love of temporal things for Christ, etc.

Again, whenever any prelate dies, he dies either perfect or imperfect. If he dies perfect, then he dies without venial and mortal sin; thus he bears no combustible matter, [Col. 1117A] and does not pass through purgatory. But if he dies imperfect, then he transgresses, since he is bound to be perfect; and thus he dies in mortal sin, and will go not to purgatory but to Gehenna. Thus it follows that no prelate passes through purgatory.

Again, every shepherd is either prepared to lay down his life, and so is a good shepherd, or is not prepared, and so is a hireling or a thief. Therefore everyone is either best or worst; thus no one is moderately good, and so no one can die with wood, hay, and stubble, which befit only the moderately good.

To this it must be said that not every perfect person is bound to every perfection, but each person is bound to some particular one: the cenobite to the first; the prelate who has care of a flock to the second. A prelate having care of a flock, or a monk, is not bound to that charity of which it is said, “Perfect charity casts out fear” (I John IV), whose mark is to endure life patiently and desire death. Such a person is conscious of nothing for which he fears punishment; from a kind of assurance of conscience, he desires to be dissolved and to be with Christ. The rest endure death patiently and desire life, because they are conscious of venial sins for which they wish to be punished here. Therefore a priest or monk is bound to the perfection attached to prelacy or vow, [Col. 1117B] not to the perfection of certainty. For someone may enter a monastery [Col. 1117C] from servile fear, and much more readily from initial fear. This would in no way be possible if he were bound to the perfection of certainty, since that cannot coexist with servile or initial fear.

Again, this person has ordered charity; therefore he loves God more than himself. Therefore, if a crisis arose, he would sooner lay down his own life than deny Christ. But “No one has greater charity than that a man lay down his life for,” etc. (John XV). Therefore this person does not have imperfect charity, and thus has perfect charity.

But against this, an objection is raised from this passage of the Apostle: “Just as you presented your members to uncleanness, so present them to righteousness” (Rom. VI). It is enough at least to love righteousness as much as we loved iniquity. But we loved [Col. 1117D] iniquity in such a way that we would not lay down our lives for it. Therefore it is enough to love righteousness in such a way that, although we love it, we do not lay down our lives for it.

Again, everyone is obliged to lay down his life for Christ, whether perfect or imperfect. How, then, has this been assigned as peculiar to prelates? Or, if all are bound to do this, then all are bound to this perfection, not prelates alone.

It must therefore be said that all are bound to this act if it comes to a crisis; nevertheless, not all possess this perfection. Indeed, if it came to a crisis, they would rather deny God; yet [Col. 1118A] they can be saved with this charity. Nor is there greater charity than to lay down one’s life for Christ—that is, there is no greater sign of charity than this. And if a prelate does not possess this perfection, he is a transgressor.

Therefore prelates have preeminence over others in this respect: prelates are bound to this more than others, although all are bound. Just as anyone at the point of death is bound to administer provisions to his enemy, but the more perfect person is bound more than another.

Again, no one is bound to lay hands on himself unless the chastity of faith is endangered; but then he is bound to lay hands on himself, that is, not to avoid the danger of death although he could escape it. Yet perfect persons are bound to expose themselves to death otherwise than imperfect persons. For the perfect ought to present themselves if they see the sheep weak and [Col. 1118B] endangered. If they then flee, they are hirelings, of whom it is said: “The hireling, when he sees the wolf, flees” (John X). But if they see the sheep strong and not endangered for that reason, they may flee. Hence it was said: “If they persecute you, flee from one city to another” (Matt. X).

An imperfect person, however, is not bound to present himself. But if he is asked whether he is a Christian, he must confess Christ, for otherwise he would sin mortally. Yet he may always lawfully flee, which is not permitted to the perfect except according to place and time, as has been said.

Again, suppose someone made a vow of continence and afterward marries. He is bound to render the marital debt to his wife; therefore he is bound to do contrary to what he vowed; [Col. 1118C] therefore he vowed imprudently. Therefore [he did not vow] from charity. Or thus: he is bound to render what he vowed. But he vowed continence; therefore he is bound to remain continent. Again, a priest has no care of a flock; therefore he is bound to remain continent, for this is the mark of that perfection.

The solution must be taken from the Decrees. [Note: [Col. 1117D] Gratian, Distinction 28, chapter “Presbyter.”] Some say that in such a case he is bound to render the marital debt but not to demand it. He ought also to render it weeping, grieving, and asking his wife not to request it; and he does not act contrary to the vow—that is, contrary to the devotion with which he vowed—though he acts with respect to the thing which he vowed. Thus one who wishes his father to live wills contrary to what God wills, but not contrary to the divine will.

Yet it is better to say that there is no marriage, because the persons joined are not lawful persons; and therefore the definition of married persons does not apply to them.

[Col. 1118D] There remain further questions concerning perfection: whether someone may descend from perfect charity to imperfect charity; whether, if he has fallen from perfection, he may rise again into imperfection; or whether, having fallen from imperfection, he may rise to perfection.

That no one can descend from perfect charity to imperfect charity is shown thus. The greater a good is, the greater is the loss from losing it. Perfection is a greater good than imperfection; therefore one suffers greater loss from losing perfection than from losing imperfection. But no greater loss from losing perfection can be [Col. 1119A] had than the loss of life, and this follows from it. Therefore the same loss follows from losing perfection; thus no one can lose perfection without losing eternal life, and hence without sinning mortally. But no one can simultaneously sin mortally and become imperfect; therefore no one can become imperfect from being perfect.

Again, no one can ascend to perfection except through merit worthy of eternal life; therefore no one can descend from perfection except through merit worthy of eternal death. Therefore no one can lose perfection except through mortal sin.

Again, one descends from perfection to imperfection either through venial or through mortal sin. Not through mortal sin, because mortal sin and imperfect charity cannot coexist. Therefore someone descends from perfect charity to imperfect [Col. 1119B] through venial sin. Therefore venial sin causes descent from perfect to imperfect charity, and so impedes ascent from imperfect charity to perfect. No one can be without venial sin in the present life; therefore no one can ascend from imperfect charity to perfect charity.

Again, someone can descend from perfect charity to imperfect through mortal or venial sin. Not through mortal sin, as has been proved; nor through venial sin. For Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1119D] Book *On Faith and Works*, chapter 16; if the Master is to be trusted, but not there]:

> “As a drop of water is in a furnace, so is venial sin in perfect charity.”

But a drop of water is consumed in fire because of its heat; therefore [Col. 1119C] venial sin is also consumed in perfect charity. Therefore venial sin never makes charity grow lukewarm.

Again, certain precepts are for all and only perfect persons; therefore all perfect persons are bound to them, and unless they fulfill them, they are transgressors. But they cannot be perfect without fulfilling them; therefore they cannot be imperfect without being transgressors, and thus cannot be imperfect except by sinning mortally.

Again, it will be proved that no one can descend from one degree of perfect charity to another, as follows. Possessed charity merits to be increased; therefore unless it is increased in the one who possesses it, he is defrauded of merit. Therefore no one can descend from one degree of charity to another, or he himself is defrauded of merit.

Again, [Col. 1119D] charity must have merited to be increased, and it is impossible for it to have merited to be increased without being increased. Therefore it must be increased in the one in whom it is; therefore it is impossible for it to be diminished, but [possible only] to be wholly removed. But charity either advances or declines in this person; it does not advance; therefore it declines in him. And one who acquires nothing loses something.

Again, charity is possessed equally by these two imperfect persons; therefore it merits equally in them to be increased or perfected. In one of them it is increased or perfected; therefore in the other also, or he is defrauded of merit—assuming that one of them becomes perfect.

Again, through venial sin someone can descend from one degree of perfect charity to another; therefore he can sin venially to such an extent [Col. 1120A] that he descends altogether from perfect charity to imperfect charity.

Again, through one sin someone can fall from perfect charity; therefore through a lesser sin one can descend from perfect charity to imperfect charity.

Again, a multitude of venial sins amounts to one mortal sin, and through mortal sin someone can fall from charity; therefore [he can fall] also through many venial sins equivalent to one mortal sin.

Again, through venial sin someone descends from one degree of perfect charity to another. Therefore venial sin makes charity grow lukewarm. Therefore, if someone is in the lowest degree of imperfect charity and commits venial sin, and charity cannot be diminished in him because it is already in the lowest degree of charity, he cannot sin venially in that degree without losing charity; [Col. 1120B] and thus charity is wholly taken away through venial sin.

[Note: [Col. 1120D] See Augustine, on the cited passage, *On Faith and Works*, ch. 16, and *Enchiridion*, ch. 68, etc.] Again, there are two kinds of venial sins. Some are lighter, from which no one, not even the perfect, can abstain; these are immediately absorbed, like a drop of water in a furnace. Others are more serious, called wood, hay, and stubble, which must be burned in the fire of purgatory. Now it has been said that imperfect charity grows cool through venial sin; but it cannot grow cool through the light venial sins that are immediately wiped away—indeed, they kindle charity, just as a drop of water feeds a fire. Therefore perfect charity grows cool through those sins that are wood, hay, and stubble; and thus a perfect person can die [Col. 1120C] with wood, hay, and stubble, and so pass through purgatory (1 Cor. XIII).

Therefore some say that charity grows cool of itself, just as certain hot things do of themselves when no cold thing is applied. They are answered as follows. Just as some hidden cause naturally precedes, and without cooling, the withdrawal of grace, so some cause naturally precedes, and without cooling, that cooling and defect of charity. But that cause is either good, evil, or indifferent. It is not good or indifferent, since it is the cause of an evil—for charity’s diminution is evil. Therefore it is evil, and thus either a venial or a mortal sin.

Moved by the foregoing arguments, some 232 say that no one descends from perfect charity to imperfect charity, but that one may descend through venial sin from one degree of perfect charity to [Col. 1120D] another. They are answered thus: this perfect person is not bound by a solemn or private vow; therefore he can descend from perfection to imperfection. Again, the lowest degree of perfect charity is no farther from the highest degree of imperfect charity than the next-to-last degree of perfect charity is from the last; but through some venial sin one may descend from one degree of perfect charity to another. Therefore through a graver venial sin someone may descend from perfection to imperfection.

In accordance with the assertion of the most eminent men, the solution to the foregoing objections must here be taken as principally concerned with [Col. 1121A] this point: that no descent from any degree of perfect charity to another takes place through venial sin. We believe this is true, because if such a venial sin is in a perfect person, it does not diminish charity in him, but rather kindles it, as a drop of water kindles a furnace. But if the venial sin that is wood, hay, and stubble in an imperfect person is present, it will be mortal in the imperfect person—as, for example, lying for someone’s safety—and thus there is a fall, not a descent.

We do not deny, however, that someone may descend from one degree of perfect charity to another. The cause of this descent is hidden in man, and it is neither fault nor punishment; or else it is not a punishment for charity to be diminished, but to be taken away; or, if it is a punishment, it is secretly inflicted by God. Just as the cause whereby He chose Jacob and rejected Esau is hidden. If one argues as above, [Col. 1121B] “This person’s charity merits to be increased; therefore it is increased, or he is deprived of his merit,” the inference is fallacious. This man has merited eternal life; therefore he will have it. For just as there is here an evident cause why he will not possess it, namely mortal sin, so there is there a hidden cause of time and of charity’s defect. The same answer must be made to similar arguments.

If someone asks whether, since venial sin is evil, it makes a person evil, and thus whether a perfect person who has venial sin is evil, we say this is untrue. Just as gold is not made worse by the mud with which it is soiled, so neither is a perfect person made worse by venial sins, although they displease God, just as mud on gold displeases me and I immediately wipe it away. It makes the gold duller and less bright, but [Col. 1121C] not worse. Yet no one can descend from perfect [Note: [Col. 1121D] It follows that charity cannot in any way be diminished, speaking directly. St Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* II–II, q. 24, art. 10, in the body of the article.] charity to imperfect charity, although one can ascend from the latter to the former. Someone may indeed fall from perfect charity through mortal sin and afterward rise again imperfect; but he can by no means descend from perfect to imperfect charity.

To the argument, therefore, “He is not bound by a solemn or private vow; therefore he can descend from perfect to imperfect charity,” the answer is: fallacy. “This man is obstinate, and can become less bad; therefore he can become less bad in obstinacy.” To the second argument we object as follows. The first level of this tower is no farther from the second than the second is from the third. One can ascend from the first to the second; therefore from the second to [Col. 1121D] the third. No: because after climbing the first he would be so exhausted that he could not climb the second.

This being granted, another question remains: can one who has fallen from perfect charity rise again imperfect? This is established as follows. We read [Note: [Col. 1122D] Exodus XXI, 18–19, in sense rather than words.]: “If anyone strikes another and he falls into a bed of sickness, the striker is bound to provide for the one struck until he can walk with a staff.” This is interpreted thus: “The person struck falls into a place of weakness: this is the person who falls from perfect charity through mortal sin. He goes with a staff when he rises weak and imperfect.” [Col. 1122A] Again: “The virgin Israel has fallen; shall she not rise again?” (Amos V). She will indeed rise, but not as a virgin. Again, one who falls from perfect charity, since he can rise again—which is agreed—must rise either perfect or imperfect, since there is no middle state. He cannot rise perfect, because no one suddenly becomes highest. And in a certain Gloss on Isaiah: “We do not immediately attain the strength of perfection.” Therefore no one can rise except imperfect, no matter whence he fell.

To this it must be said that one who fell from perfect charity can rise both perfect and imperfect. The authority is interpreted thus: “No one suddenly becomes highest,” that is, so confirmed that he cannot become better while on the way. But the following is objected: “Penance [Col. 1122B] restores all things taken away”; this is supported by authority. Therefore it also restores to this person the state of perfection that was taken from him, or else penance is not full and sufficient. Hence that statement must be understood of the works of virtues—which are merits taken away—not of the virtues themselves or of states; otherwise penance would be the cause of lost charity, which is false. Rather, the reverse is true.

Some nevertheless say that a distinction must be made. If someone is bound by a vow of perfection, he cannot rise imperfect. They prove it thus: he is bound by a vow of perfection; therefore, so long as he is not carrying out the vow, he is a transgressor. But if he is imperfect, he is not carrying out the vow; therefore he cannot rise imperfect. But if he is not bound by a vow of perfection—as lay people are—he can rise [Col. 1122C] imperfect. This distinction is invalid. For by the vow he is not bound to perfection of fervour, but to the works of perfect charity, which he can carry out equally in perfect and in imperfect charity. Yet if such works are revived by imperfect charity, though they were performed in perfect charity, they will be rewarded not according to perfect but according to imperfect charity, because they are formed and made alive by that charity which was previously dead.

That a priest bound by vow can rise imperfect, just as a layperson released from a vow can, is shown thus. These persons are equally guilty; in neither case is it up to the person that God should give him grace; therefore they can rise equally; therefore either both or neither can rise [Col. 1122D] imperfect. Again, these two perfect persons, one of whom is a priest and the other a layman, are equally good. Thus, assuming that each is as perfect as the other and all circumstances remain the same, they can equally commit a sin of the same kind; otherwise the layman’s condition is better than the priest’s. Indeed, a layman may commit a greater sin than a priest of the same kind, since place, time, and knowledge on the layman’s side may aggravate sin just as ordination does on the priest’s side. Therefore, if they can fall from equal charity, why can they not rise to an equal charity? Thus either both can rise imperfect or neither can.

[Col. 1123A] But the following is objected: the person who fell from perfect charity and thus rises in imperfect charity will be rewarded for his earlier works of charity; therefore, will he be rewarded according to the state of perfection in which they were performed, or according to the imperfection in which they revive? That they are rewarded according to the perfect state is shown thus. For those works done in perfect charity revive fully; otherwise God seems readier to punish than to show mercy, if through one sin all other things fully return as regards guilt, while through the merit of one work that revives other works do not revive. Therefore they make one worthy of equal reward. Therefore, if he dies imperfect, he will receive a crown of perfection, or he will be treated unjustly.

To this it must be said that those works revive, [Col. 1123B] but not immediately in their fullness. But one who rises in this manner will never die until that revival has been fully restored; and only then do they revive as before. But can he die immediately upon rising? Then perfection is immediately and fully restored to him—which is true. For even the thief, who had never been perfect, immediately became perfect. This is evident because he did not pass through purgatory; rather, on that same day he was with the Lord in paradise (Luke XXIII). Or it may be said that the periods in which the thief had initial fear and perfect charity were so continuous that they could scarcely be distinguished; hence he was immediately said to possess perfect charity, although he had previously possessed imperfect charity.

[Col. 1123C] And note that charity is so great that it cannot be reduced to the measure of faith or hope, however great faith or hope may be: for hope [perhaps “faith”] floats above like oil. Therefore the statement [Note: [Col. 1123D] Gregory, final homily on Ezekiel.], “As much as he believes, so much he hopes,” means: as capable as he is of believing, so capable is he also of hoping. It is therefore evident that however evil a person may have been, if he begins to have charity, the least movement of charity he can have is greater than any movement of love he has toward sin. Thus it is evident that no one can be as evil on the way as a person can be good on the way. Similarly, no one is so evil in the homeland that any good person is not then more good, as some say; yet this may still be doubtful. For by the same reasoning one could say that the least movement [Col. 1123D] of charity on the way surpasses every movement of hatred possessed by the devil, and thus the devil would not be more evil than some good person.

Again, if someone says that those works are rewarded according to perfect charity, the following is objected. These two persons, one of whom was perfect and the other always imperfect, are now imperfect and equally good; therefore they are worthy of equal reward. Either the former is a martyr or preacher, or else the imperfect person who was never perfect has less charity than the person who was perfect. Therefore the former imperfect person does not seem worthy of greater reward because of [Col. 1124A] works of perfect charity, or because of the perfection he once had but does not now have, but because of greater charity. For “where I find you, there I shall judge you” (Ecclus. XI); and “if a tree falls toward the south, there it will be; if toward the north, there it will be” (1 Kings II); and “the Lord shall judge the ends of the earth” (Ps. IX), and final works.

Again, this man will have an aureole; therefore he will die perfect. Again, he would have no reward if he returned to that perfect charity—so that he immediately died in it—which he does not now have in imperfect charity; therefore the former state is not more to be chosen than the latter. Again, someone who rises in imperfect charity is bound to works of perfect charity; therefore someone with imperfect charity can undergo martyrdom, for this [Col. 1124B] is a work of perfect charity. Therefore it is possible for someone to end life by martyrdom and yet be imperfect, and thus possible for one of the martyrs to pass through purgatory; for if he dies imperfect, he will pass through purgatory. But authority contradicts this: “Behold, I see the heavens opened” (Acts VII), because immediately after martyrdom they fly to heaven; and if they passed through purgatory, then prayer ought to be offered for them. But the authority says [Note: [Col. 1123D] Augustine, Sermon 17, *On the Words of the Apostle*, though in him it reads: “For it is an injury to pray for a martyr, to whose prayers we ought to commend ourselves.” See the same author, [Col. 1124D] *Tractates on John*, 84. Innocent III nevertheless cites it as authority, *Decretals*, “On the Celebration of Mass”: “He does an injury to a martyr who prays for a martyr.”]: “He does an injury who prays for him.”

Again, if he ended his life through martyrdom and yet passed through purgatory, something could be more reward-worthy than martyrdom. This is false, because “no one has greater charity than this,” etc. That someone can undergo martyrdom from imperfect charity is clear from the fact that one can do so from servile fear. Hence [Col. 1124C] the Apostle says: “If I give up my body to be burned but do not have charity, I am nothing” (1 Cor. XIII). Much more can one do this from initial fear, which is never without imperfect charity, nor vice versa.

To this some say that an imperfect person can die a martyr; and although he dies imperfect, he will not therefore pass through purgatory, because martyrdom is as it were equivalent to purgatorial fire. Others think that someone may begin to suffer martyrdom from imperfect charity, but in the suffering itself charity is perfected in him. Thus he cannot finish life through martyrdom without being perfect when he dies, even if he is imperfect when he first begins to suffer the punishment of martyrdom [Col. 1124D].

Again, some bishop is shut up in prison because he defends the rights of the Church or for Christ’s faith. It happens that, while he is asleep, he is killed by his torturer. While living, he had wood, hay, and stubble; for those venial sins he was neither contrite nor becomes contrite. Therefore he dies guilty of them, since he was guilty of them before; but he is a martyr; therefore a martyr passes on with wood, hay, and stubble. To this they say that it is impossible for him to perish so suddenly that he does not feel the blows; in that sensation, through enduring suffering, charity is perfected [Col. 1125A] in him, and thus he passes without sin.

From what has been said, therefore, it is clear that there is no descent from perfect charity to imperfect charity; but there can be a fall, and afterward one who fell from perfection can rise imperfect. It is also clear that certain works 235 of perfect charity can be performed in imperfect charity. But are all works performed in imperfect charity called works of imperfect charity, or are whatever works performed in perfect charity called works of perfect charity? Then greeting a person on the road, when done by a perfect person, will be a work of perfect charity—which no one says. Likewise, undergoing martyrdom in imperfect charity will be a work of imperfect charity. Therefore we say that those works are called works of perfect charity which are signs and indications of [Col. 1125B] perfect charity. For force must be given to the very connection of the expression; and thus not whatever things are done in perfect charity are works of perfect charity. Just as a work is called the work of a wise person when it is a sign and indication of wisdom in that person.

But if it is asked whether a perfect or imperfect person needs grace more, it must be said that there are arguments on both sides. A perfect person is bound to higher works, for which greater grace is required; therefore he needs grace more than an imperfect person. Conversely, many venial sins in the imperfect person must be wiped away, and greater charity is required to wipe these away than the few sins that are in a perfect person; therefore the imperfect person needs greater grace than the perfect person. To this it must be said that the word [Col. 1125C] “need” sometimes denotes necessity, as “a king needs food,” that is, food is necessary for the king to sustain life; sometimes it denotes lack, in which sense it is false that a king needs food. Therefore, if it is true that “need” denotes necessity, it is true that both the imperfect and the perfect person need grace; if it denotes lack, it is false. Thus the perfect person needs grace more in one respect, the imperfect person more in the other. Just as a rich man needs the king’s favour more to preserve riches than a poor man who has none; yet the poor man needs it more in order to receive provisions from him, of which the rich man has abundance.

And concerning perfection and imperfection as they are possessed on the way, we have brought forward for discussion the debatable points that we have learned under the teaching of the Holy Spirit; in these matters the diligent reader will find most doubtful and difficult questions resolved [Col. 1125D].

## CHAPTER XXVI. Can charity, once possessed, be lost?

[Note: [Col. 1125D] The Master, III, distinction 31.] The fourth chapter on charity remains: can charity, once possessed, be lost? It seems not. For the Apostle says: “Charity never fails” (1 Cor. XIII). And Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1125D] This wording is not found, though the author appears to be *On Friendship*, ch. 2, in the same author, and Jerome, Epistle 4 to Rufinus: “Friendship that can cease was never true.” Gratian nevertheless cites it, *On Penance*, in the manner in which the present author does, as does the Master of the Sentences above.]: “Charity [Col. 1126A] which can cease was never true.” And elsewhere [Note: [Col. 1126D] Augustine, Luke X.]: “Charity is the proper and singular fountain of good things, in which no stranger shares. For strangers are all who will hear: ‘I do not know you.’”

Yet conversely the Gospel says that many turned back whose names had been written in the book of life [Note: [Col. 1126D] Ambrose, on the Epistle to the Romans, at ch. IX, and Augustine, *Tractates on John*, 45], not according to predestination but according to present righteousness. And Ambrose says [Note: [Col. 1126D] Ambrose above, on the words: “For the greater shall serve the lesser.”]: “Often those who will later be good are first evil, and sometimes those who will later be and remain evil are first good, according as their names are said to be written in or erased from the book of life.” Therefore we incline to say that charity is often received and lost. Thus the Apostle’s statement, “Charity never fails,” must be referred to [Col. 1126B] its dignity as possessed in the homeland, when faith and hope are to be abolished. And Augustine’s statement, “It is not true charity,” etc., means that it does not make one truly blessed, because it is not possessed finally. Again, “Charity is the proper fountain in which no stranger shares” (Prov. V): understand, finally.

It should nevertheless be noted that some say charity, once possessed on the way, cannot be lost. Besides the foregoing authorities which they adduce, they seek to prove this by many arguments. First, thus: this man has charity; therefore he merits eternal life; therefore he will have it, or else God will act unjustly toward him. For they maintain that once someone has merited something, he cannot be deprived of the reward, whatever he may do afterward.

Again, indirectly: David, when he committed homicide, did not have charity, and in committing homicide sinned mortally; therefore at that time he deserved to be punished eternally, and this was just. Therefore God willed that it happen, because whatever is just God wills, and conversely. Therefore David was punished with eternal punishment. For God has willed nothing which has not happened or is not to happen. Again, God’s justice then required that he be eternally damned, because it required that he be repaid according to what he had merited; but what God’s justice required to be done, He willed to be done; therefore God willed David to be eternally punished. Again, David merited eternal [perhaps “death”] death in that work, and it was not given to him; therefore not everyone is repaid according to his works. Again, someone to be damned [Col. 1126D] has works of charity through which he merits eternal life, but afterward he will sin and be damned; therefore he will not be repaid according to what he merited through those good works. Again, God’s justice is to repay each according to his works; therefore David too, who was a sinner before he was justified, received according to his works; therefore he merited justification—which is false—and justification was given to him; therefore he was given what he had not merited.

[Col. 1127A] Therefore they do not wish it to be truly said of any reprobate that he “merited eternal life,” except of one who persevered in a good work until the end of life. For if a reprobate merited to possess eternal life, he merited to possess it either before death or after death. Therefore, if he possessed it neither before nor after death, God acted unjustly toward him—which is impossible.

This, however, is invalid. For one can demerit by acting badly what one previously merited by acting well. Nor does God repay according to individual works, but according to final works; indeed, He repays also according to all good works performed at whatever time, if the person does not afterward destroy the merits of those good works by living badly.

And note that “just” is sometimes said with reference to what is informed by divine justice, in which sense it is not true [Col. 1127B] that it is just for this elect person, who sins mortally once, to be damned; and it is sometimes said with reference to a man’s merit, in which sense it is true that it is just for this person to be damned according to his present merits. Yet God will not repay him according to these merits, because they are not final. Or one may say that God rewards all good works in the present life or in the future; for even if there were no other reward than that a person performed a good work, that is a great reward. For virtue does not seek a reward outside itself, and “in keeping them there is great reward” (Ps. XVIII).

But they object: if David had charity when he committed homicide, then he was then worthy of eternal life; therefore, if he had died then, he would have had eternal life. By the same reasoning, Judas, who according to them never had charity, had no time at which, if he had died, he would have had eternal life. Therefore they say that David, when he sinned, had charity which he previously had as a little stream; but then it dried up, suspended for a time, and later flowed again when contrition for the sin came. One may also ask whether David, when he sinned, had perfect or imperfect charity; but they grant neither, because just as fruits and leaves are said to be in a tree in winter, so charity was then in David.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Whether virginity is a virtue, and whether it is possessed by everyone who possesses one virtue

[Col. 1127D] Having divided the virtues into the four cardinal virtues and the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, and again into the three called faith, hope, and charity, it has been shown concerning each that whoever possesses one possesses all. Since theologians do not customarily make any other division of virtues than one of those stated above, it follows that everyone who has one virtue has all. But this is objected: whoever has one virtue has all; therefore he has virginity too, since virginity is one virtue. Therefore this married man, since he has charity, has virginity, and so is a virgin. Therefore he follows the Lamb wherever [Col. 1128A] 237 He goes, and thus with both feet, namely integrity of flesh and integrity of mind. Therefore he is bodily intact—which is false.

Again, this person has not ceased to have charity; therefore he has not ceased to have virginity, or virginity is not a virtue. And he had virginity; therefore he is still a virgin. Therefore the hundredfold fruit is owed to him; but he is married, and therefore the thirtyfold fruit is owed to him. Thus two fruits are owed to him. Again, every virtue or the mortal vice opposed to it must be in this person. No mortal sin has crept into the person who, having proposed to remain a virgin—not by vow—contracts marriage for some honourable reason. Therefore no virtue has ceased to be in him; therefore neither has virginity, since it was in him. Therefore he is now a virgin as before. Again, he has lost [Col. 1128B] only bodily integrity. Therefore he has lost no virtue, or bodily integrity is a virtue—which is false, since every virtue is in the soul or in an angel. Again, authority says [Note: [Col. 1127D] Jerome to Eustochium, *On the Keeping of Virginity*, ch. 2.] that “the elect will rise in every respect such as they were before sin, and even stronger.” But all were virgins before sin; therefore all will rise as virgins.
