The following authority seems to speak against this: “Although God can do all things, He cannot raise up a virgin after her fall.” Again, penance confers full remission of sins and perfect restoration of virtues; this is supported by authority. Mary Magdalene did sufficient penance (Luke VII); therefore every lost virtue was restored to her, and hence virginity, or else it is not a virtue. Again, married persons are owed [Col. 1128C] the thirtyfold fruit, widows the sixtyfold, prelates and virgins the hundredfold. No penance, however great, can bring it about that virginity be restored to one who has lost it; and no one can receive the hundredfold fruit unless he dies a virgin or a prelate. Therefore no one can be of as great merit after lost virginity as before.

For this reason some say that virginity is not a virtue, but something above every virtue. [Note: [Col. 1127D] Exodus XXVI. The ordinary Gloss there, said [Col. 1128D] to be Bede’s. St Thomas discusses these matters elegantly, *Summa Theologiae* I–II, q. 102, art. 4, reply to objection 8.] They seek to establish this from a certain Gloss on Exodus, where it says that martyrdom, the consummation of all virtues, is signified by the third covering of red skins, while virginity, which is above every virtue and which suggests an angelic manner of life, is signified by the fourth covering of hyacinth skins. For to live in the flesh above the flesh is angelic, not human. We believe that this was said in praise of virginity, as was Jerome’s statement: “Although God can do all things, He cannot raise up a virgin after her fall”; that is, He cannot make the state of married persons comparable with the state of virgins. For the saints sometimes speak hyperbolically to heighten the good or evil.

Others hold that chastity is a virtue whose lesser exercise belongs to married people, or marital modesty; whose greater exercise is widowed continence; and whose greatest exercise is virginal continence. Whoever has one virtue has chastity, either in this first and lesser exercise, or in the middle one, or in the last. For these are the three states of those to be saved, signified by Noah, [Col. 1129A] Daniel, and Job [Note: [Col. 1129D] As Augustine has it; see the notes on Robert Pullen.].

Others say that the name “virginity” signifies two things: bodily integrity, which is not a virtue, since many possess this integrity without having charity, as among Jews and unbelieving pagans. Hence in the Gospel the foolish virgins are called virgins (Matt. XXV), though they have bodily integrity; they would not be called foolish if such integrity were a virtue. The name “virginity” also signifies integrity of mind, or continence, which, being a virtue, arises from charity. Such continence has different names according to [Col. 1129B] the different states: among virgins it is called virginity, or, if you prefer, virginal continence; among married persons, marital modesty; among widows, widowed continence. Thus the virtue now called marital modesty in this married man, whose flesh is no longer intact, was formerly called virginity or virginal continence when he was bodily intact.

To the argument, therefore, “Whoever has one virtue has all; therefore whoever has one has virginity,” the response is made thus: “This person has every virtue; therefore he has initial fear,” or, “therefore he has imperfect charity.” For just as in the former case the conclusion ought simply to have been [Col. 1129C] “therefore he has fear,” or “therefore he has charity,” so that no descent might be made, so here it should be: “therefore he has continence.” For the word “all” there encompasses genera, not individual members or species of genera.

Again, the objection, “He did not lose virginity and he had it; therefore he still has virginity,” is a fallacy of accident through a change of category. Fallacy: “You have not ceased to see a white man,” assuming he has become black; or: “This person has not ceased to have imperfect charity and he had it; therefore he still has imperfect charity.” No, because what was imperfect is now perfect. Similar arguments in analogous cases must be answered in this way. Again, the saying, “The elect will rise in every respect such as they were before sin,” [Col. 1129D] includes in “every respect” only the robe of soul and body, both of which the elect will possess.

Again, note that one person’s fruit is less than some thirtyfold fruit, because these designations are not taken from the numbers according to the quantity of rewards, as was said above, but according to the meanings of the numbers. For a married person may have greater merit than some virgin, although the state of virgins is more dignified than that of married persons. Just as one bishop may be richer than some archbishop, although the state of archbishops is more dignified than that of bishops. [Col. 1130A] But everywhere in the foregoing arguments take the term “virginity” to designate integrity of mind. Otherwise you would wrongly take it to be a virtue.

But the following is again objected: this person who is now a virgin in mind and body will marry and sleep with his wife. Virginity is in him, and no virtue will cease to be in him; therefore virginity will be in him; therefore he will be a virgin. Fallacy of the consequent. Imperfect charity will be in him; therefore he will be imperfect—assuming that charity will now be perfected in him. Or: the power to sin will be in him because free choice will be in him; therefore he will be able to sin—assuming that he dies perfect.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Whether perseverance is a virtue, and whether it is possessed by everyone who possesses one virtue

[Col. 1130B]

Again, against those who say that one possessing one virtue possesses all, an objection is made concerning perseverance: this person has all virtues; therefore he possesses whatever is necessary for salvation. But final perseverance is necessary for salvation; therefore this person has final perseverance, even if he will lose charity at death. Again, this person has charity; therefore, if he died now, he would be saved, because the person who has charity lacks nothing for life. And [Note: [Col. 1130D] Augustine, *Tractates on John*, 83.]: “What can be lacking to one who has charity?” and “Have charity, and do whatever you wish.” Therefore, if this person died in this charity, he would be saved; but he has charity that is not persevering. Therefore this person can be saved in charity that does not persevere. Again, it is impossible for this person to be saved except in persevering charity. This person does not have persevering charity; therefore, if he died in the charity he has, he would not be saved.

But because there are certain doubtful matters concerning perseverance worthy of inquiry, let us confine them within three chapters: first, asking whether there is any perseverance that is not final; second, whether perseverance is commanded; third, whether perseverance is a virtue. Some seek to establish that there is perseverance even when it is not final from the Gospel passage, “He who perseveres unto the end shall be saved” (Matt. X). For, they say, “unto the end” would have been added for no reason unless there were [Col. 1130D] perseverance for a time, in distinction from which “unto the end” was said. They also seek to demonstrate this by arguing as follows: this person was 239 in charity for ten years, and did not fall from it, nor does he fall now; therefore he persevered in charity.

Others, however, think that just as in the words *perficio* (“I complete”) and *pervenio* (“I arrive”), the prefix *per-* denotes completion and perfection, so also in the verb *persevero* (“I persevere”); and that one cannot be said to persevere until that continuance has been completed by death. They say this was signified in Joseph’s long robe and in the tail of the sacrificial victim which was commanded to be offered.

[Col. 1131A] They seek to establish that perseverance is not commanded from this: if it is commanded, then everyone who lacks final perseverance is a transgressor. Therefore, one who has charity for a time and will not persevere finally is a transgressor, and thus in mortal sin. Again, many have been saved without perseverance, such as the thief; therefore perseverance is not among the things without which there is no salvation; therefore it is not commanded.

On the contrary, however, it seems to have been commanded in the same form as baptism. For just as it was said (Mark 16): “Whoever believes and is baptized shall be saved,” so it was said: “Whoever perseveres unto the end, he shall be saved” (Matt. 10). Again, whatever is necessary for salvation is commanded in evangelical teaching, either by Christ or by his [Col. 1131B] disciples; final perseverance is necessary for salvation; therefore it is commanded. Again, Augustine says:

[Note: [Col. 1131D] On Exodus 29 and Leviticus 3.]

> “Whatever was commanded to be offered figuratively in the old law is commanded to be offered truly in the time of new grace.”

In the old law it was commanded that the tail of the victim be offered with its head, and the truth signified by this figure is perseverance. Therefore perseverance is commanded in the new law. Again, perseverance is either under command or under counsel. If it is under counsel and not under command, and there is no salvation without perseverance, then there is no salvation without a certain counsel; therefore fulfillment of the commandments alone does not suffice for salvation. Those who say that there is no perseverance unless it is final may plausibly say that perseverance is commanded, not so that it may always be possessed, [Col. 1131C] but so that it may at some time be possessed.

Third, it is asked whether perseverance is a virtue. That it is so is shown thus: perseverance merits eternal life; therefore it is a virtue, or a work of virtue. Or thus: it is a gift of God and not natural; therefore it is a gratuitous gift. Therefore it is a virtue, or a work of virtue.

Against this: if it is a virtue, it is commanded. Again, if perseverance is a virtue, then whoever has one virtue has perseverance. This is false, for many possess virtues who will not persevere. They therefore say that perseverance is the simultaneous exercise of all the virtues. Others think that perseverance is something concomitant with virtue, which is not itself a virtue. Yet, upon closer [Col. 1131D] consideration, it seems truer that the name “perseverance” is spoken in relation to that in which we persevere. Hence, when placed without a genitive, it makes an improper expression. Just as it is improper to say, “Father is,” so when one says, “Perseverance is,” it is less fitting; rather one should say, “There is perseverance in charity,” or something of that sort. Nor is perseverance in charity anything other than the charity in which one perseveres. Thus perseverance in faith is a virtue, because it is the faith in which one perseveres; and perseverance in faith is commanded, because persevering in faith is commanded. Just as, you see, the continuation of reading is continued reading.

Having said this, it does no harm to say that [Col. 1132A] the prefix *per-* does not denote completion in the verb *persevero* (“I persevere”); rather, everyone is said to persevere in charity who has charity, or remains in it for the present, whether he will lose it or not. Or, if this prefix *per-* denotes completion, then one must not say that anyone has, or has had, perseverance in charity unless he dies in charity; for only then can it first be said, “This man persevered in charity.” For although it may truly be said of a man, “He will persevere in charity,” and this has been revealed to me, nevertheless it cannot yet be said, “He has perseverance in charity,” because the completion has not yet occurred. So too, although someone has begun to build a house and is building it now, and will thus finish it, one still cannot say that he completes the house, or has completed it, or that the completion of the house [Col. 1132B] exists; but this will first truly be said when the house has been finished.

Therefore, when it is said, “This man has everything necessary for salvation; final perseverance is necessary for salvation,” this may be understood in two ways: either that he has already persevered—and then it is false, for in that way no one would have salvation unless he had already persevered—or that he will persevere; and this is true, because it is necessary that he either has persevered or will persevere, otherwise he would not be saved. Yet he does not already have perseverance merely because he will persevere; nevertheless, he has everything necessary for salvation.

Therefore, once this solution has been given to the argument:

“This man has everything necessary for salvation; [Col. 1132C] perseverance is necessary for salvation; therefore this man has perseverance.”

(This would also be false if he were never going to lose charity.) One should take the following counter-instance: “This man has everything necessary for life; dying in charity is necessary for life; therefore the man who will live dies in charity.”

As for the second argument, which runs thus: “This man has charity in which, if he died, he would be saved; but he has charity without perseverance; therefore he can be saved without perseverance”—there is a fallacy in the premises. Or thus: “This man has eyes by which he can see, but he has his eyes closed; therefore he can see with his eyes closed.” Take a counter-instance in the same way for the third argument.

But against this opinion the following objection is made. “Persevering” [Col. 1132D] is denominated from some property; that property either is a virtue or is not. For if perseverance in faith is a virtue of faith from which “persevering” is denominatively derived, then “persevering” is denominatively derived from faith; by the same reasoning, from hope, and likewise from charity. Therefore, by sound reasoning, one must show something from which “persevering” is denominatively derived; and thus perseverance in faith is something other than faith—especially since every substantive can stand by itself, whereas what is said concerning the name “Father” is not analogous, because it is adjectival in meaning, though not in form.

[Note: [Col. 1132D] See Gregory, Homily 16 on Ezekiel.]

We leave this point to the exercise of those passing through it, not from ignorance:

[Col. 1133A]

> “Very many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied” (Dan. 12).

## Chapter XXIX. Objections that may be made against those who say that whoever has one virtue has them all

[Note: [Col. 1133D] Master, Book III, distinction 36.]

Having thus settled these matters, we believe that every objection to this universal proposition has now ceased:

[Note: [Col. 1133D] From Jerome, on Isaiah, chapter 56.]

> “Everyone who has one virtue has them all,”

because we have eliminated all apparent counter-instances. But what is read on Genesis (chapter 14) seems to object: “Abraham rushed upon his enemies with divers household servants.” On this passage there is the authoritative statement: “Abraham’s household servants are the virtues which succeed one another.” If, then, they succeed one another, they are not infused simultaneously.

Again, on Matthew it is said that [Col. 1133B] Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob signify faith, hope, and charity, and that faith begot both hope and charity. But these things must be referred to the acts or exercises of the virtues, one of which may exist without another. For whoever possesses one virtue need not immediately possess its exercise, even if he is an adult. In their primary infusion all are possessed habitually, but not in exercise or act. For they incline and dispose the soul toward the performance of their acts according to place and time.

But when virtues are in someone without their exercises, are they therefore idle? No. For even if they do not always have their own exercises, they always have their own effects, so that exercise may be distinguished from effect. Fortitude always makes one strong, temperance temperate, prudence prudent—that is, fit, disposed, and capable of [Col. 1133C] enduring hardships, restraining enticements, and guarding against snares—although he does not immediately endure, restrain, or guard against them.

Therefore, whoever has one virtue habitually or in its effect has all of them habitually or in their effect, whether child or adult. But not everyone who has one in act or exercise also has the rest in act or exercise. If any argument is made against this, it is false because it passes from habit to act. For example, if someone infers thus: “This child or adult has faith; therefore he believes,” or something of that sort—it is a fallacy. “This man, whose feet have been cut off, is able to walk; therefore he walks.”

And note that just as all virtues are infused at once, so all cooperate with one another in their acts. Thus, although loving is the work specifically appropriated to charity, faith nonetheless cooperates in it; and although believing is the work of faith, charity cooperates in that very act. Hence it seems possible to prove that the acts of the virtues are intermingled as follows: “Believing is an act meriting life; therefore it is an act of charity, since every merit belongs to charity.”

**Solution.** “An act of charity” is said in two ways: either an act informed by charity, or an act proceeding from charity and free choice, or denominated from charity—which is the same thing. In both senses it is true that loving [Col. 1134A] is an act of charity. Yet in the first sense it is true that believing is an act of charity. By the same argument one might prove that sparing is an act of justice, and condemning an act of mercy—something no one says except in the sense just stated.

## Chapter XXX. Whether the virtues are equal wherever they are present

[Note: [Col. 1133D] The Master, above, § B.]

It remains to inquire whether all virtues, wherever they are present, are equal. Modern doctors debate this with great uncertainty. Some say that they need not be called equal—that is, differing in no respect—so as to produce spiritual concord or harmony. Rather, some are possessed more and others less by a person, just as patience was eminent in Job, humility in David, and meekness in Moses. [Col. 1134B] They also grant that someone merits more through one virtue than through another if he possesses it more fully than the other; nevertheless, no one merits more through any virtue than through charity.

Others, however, think it truer that all virtues are equal wherever they are found: so that one who is equal to another in one is equal to him in all, and they are equally intense in every person who possesses them with respect to their inward habit,

[Note: [Col. 1133D] So the Master here, and in the same distinction, 15, § E.]

though not with respect to outward exercise. This is shown on Augustine’s authority:

[Note: [Col. 1134D] Book VI, *On the Trinity*, chapter 4, at the beginning.]

> “If you say that these persons are equal in fortitude, but that one excels in prudence, it follows that the fortitude of the former is less prudent; and therefore they are not equal even in fortitude, because the fortitude of the latter is more prudent.”

It is also read

[Note: [Col. 1134D] In Gregory, final homily on Ezekiel, well past the middle.]

that the sides of charity are equal: that is, [Col. 1134C] one works as much as one loves and as much as one believes. This must be referred to habit: one is as capable of believing as of loving.

Inequality in exercise is readily evident, because Job exercised patience more, Abraham faith, and David humility. This must be referred to outward exercises, or understood in comparison with other human beings. In accordance with this inequality of outward acts, Augustine says elsewhere that in a person one virtue is greater, another less, and one is present while another is not. Speaking to Jerome, he says:

[Note: [Col. 1134D] Augustine, Letter 29 to Jerome.]

> “If dispositions are like the members of a body—not because they are seen in places, but because they are felt in affections—and one is illuminated more, another less, while another wholly [Col. 1134D] lacks light: so, as each is illuminated according to the affection of charity, more in one act, less in another, and not at all in another, one may be said to have one virtue and not another, one more and another less.”

This surely concerns acts. It can also be explained by an apt comparison. A householder hires four servants and assigns to each his particular duties, on the condition that each be ready to perform every duty according to place and time. They are indeed ready in inward habit, but not in outward act. So, while the individual virtues have their privileged offices, [Col. 1135A] all are ready to perform their offices. For just as much as temperance directs the soul, in outward exercise, to restrain enticements in a time of prosperity, fortitude directs it, in inward habit, to endure hardships if a time of adversity arises. Yet in a time of prosperity it does not move the soul to this act, but disposes it, because there is no occasion for it.

[Note: [Col. 1135] For they do not lack the habit because they lack the exercise.]

For they do not possess the habit if they do not possess the exercise; yet they would possess it if the occasion arose.

But an objection is made: “A thing is done with as much prudence as justice; therefore, the more justly, the more prudently.” Fallacy. “With as much heat as the sun warms the Indians, it warms the Parthians; therefore it warms the Parthians as much as the Indians.” Or thus: “The more learned this man is than that one in grammar, the more learned [Col. 1135B] that one is in dialectic; therefore, the more expertly this man disputes grammar than that one, the more expertly that one disputes dialectic”—granting that the latter now disputes dialectic more subtly, although the former is more skilled in dialectic. For there is a transition from habit to act, as before.

Again: “The more justly someone does something, the more he avoids what ought not to be done and the less he omits what ought to be done; therefore, the more justly, the more prudently.” The conclusion can be twofold: either the comparison is between habit and habit, or between exercise and exercise. In the latter case it is false, and a counter-instance must be given as above.

Again: “A man is as prudent as he is just; therefore he acts as prudently as he acts justly.” This is true if the comparison is made between prudence itself and justice; [Col. 1135C] it is false if it is made between the exercise of the former and the exercise of the latter. Hence a counter-instance should be given by exposition: “This man is as good a dialectician as he is a grammarian; [Col. 1136A] therefore he disputes dialectic as well as he disputes grammar.”

Again, someone is naturally well disposed to perform works of justice, and naturally timid in enduring adversity. Are justice and fortitude equal in him? Yes, in habit but not in exercise.

Again: “The more just a person is, the more he renders to God what is God’s and to his neighbour what is his neighbour’s; therefore, the more just, the more prudent.” This is true if referred to habit; false if referred to exercise.

Again: “A person is bound to serve God with as much justice as prudence, and conversely; therefore, he acts as justly as prudently.” Fallacy. “With as much knowledge as you disputed with me yesterday, you dispute today; therefore, as knowledgeably yesterday, so knowledgeably today.”

Again: “The more justly something is done, [Col. 1136B] the more meritorious it is; and the more meritorious it is, the better it is; therefore, the more justly, the better. Thus a work equally just seems equally good as another work which is more prudent, because it has equal merit.” What advantage, then, is it that the latter is the more prudent work? The first premise is false.

Again: “Every justice is goodness; therefore what is more just is better.” Fallacy. “Every grammar is knowledge; therefore the more learned someone is in grammar, the more knowledgeable he is.”

Again, if all virtues are equal wherever they are present, how does the growth of virtues occur? It does not occur in essence; rather, it occurs in effect. Therefore justice has as much effect in this person as prudence, and thus he is as prudent as he is just [Col. 1136C]. This is indeed true if you understand it thus: he is as capable of discerning good from evil as he is capable of rendering to each what is his own.

# [Book Four]

**243. The distinctions of Book Four begin.**

Whether the saints who lived before Christ’s advent merited descent into hell. On the power of circumcision and its difference from baptism. On the ceremonial observances: whether they were a cause of eternal salvation for those who observed them. Where the ten commandments of the law are set forth, and it is asked whether it is permissible to do what is contrary to any of them. On lying and its kinds. On perjury, and the modes of oath-taking and perjury. On the Lord’s conception, and whether his flesh was tithed in Abraham. Whether the Son did anything that the Father or the Holy Spirit did not do, because he assumed flesh; and whether the Father could have been incarnate. Whether these propositions are true: “The divine nature assumed human nature”; “the divine person assumed human nature.” Whether nature assumed person, or person assumed person. Whether Christ, by created wisdom, knew everything that he knew by divine knowledge. Whether Christ had charity in the manner of the wayfarer or in the manner of the homeland, where matters pertaining to Christ’s charity are determined. Whether Christ merited equally by all his works. Whether it was given to anyone to become the Son of God, and whether Christ, in his human nature, merited to receive anything in the divine nature. On Christ’s will according to sensuality. On the will which he had according to reason: whether it agreed with the will of the Jews who desired his death. Whether Christ had ignorance, difficulty in doing good, or necessity of dying. Whether he had fear. [Col. 1137] What he bestowed on us by his Passion that he had not bestowed before, where it is asked whether he could have redeemed us in another way. Whether Christ was head of the Church according to his divine or according to his human nature. By what power Christ could lay down his soul, divine or human; and whether according to his human nature he was lower than the angels. In what subject Christ’s death existed, and of what union the dissolution was effected in his death.

# Book Four

**244. Prologue**

[Col. 1137A]

[Note: [Col. 1137C] Master, Book IV of the *Sentences*, distinction 1, § A.]

It has been shown in what precedes how the first man, descending from Jerusalem into Jericho and stripped of gratuitous gifts (Luke 10), was wounded in his natural endowments. Since it is written of him that he is “a spirit that goes and does not return” (Ps. 77), he could not rise from such misery by himself unless that Samaritan, to whom one cries out from Seir, “Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?” (Isa. 21), emptying himself into the form of a servant (Phil. 2), bowed the heavens and came down (Ps. 17), and, leaving the ninety-nine in the wilderness, carried on his own shoulders the hundredth sheep which had perished by wandering, back to the place from which it had fallen (Matt. 18; Luke 15). How this was done, with the assent of him who carried it back, we shall now [Col. 1137B] explain.

## Chapter I. Whether the saints who lived before Christ’s advent merited to descend into the lower world

The order of our restoration began from faith. For Abraham believed, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness (Rom. 4), before he was circumcised or received from God any law other than the natural law. And the prophet Habakkuk says: “The righteous lives by faith” (Hab. 2). Hence Abraham merited to be called the father of many nations, because he believed God’s promise: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22), as the Apostle testifies when speaking to the Romans (Rom. 4).

Even if Abraham had died before circumcision, [Col. 1137C] he would have been saved by the faith he possessed, as also were others before him who died uncircumcised: Abel, from whom the Church began, Noah, and others. But if the righteous died, why then did they descend into the lower world? Indeed, someone may reason as follows: “God renders to each according to his works; therefore also to Abraham. But Abraham had merited that after death he should enter eternal life; therefore immediately after the separation of soul and body he ought to have attained eternal life—or he was treated unjustly.”

**Solution.** It is true that he had merited to enter, but not immediately after death. So also one who passed through purgatory has merited to enjoy the vision of God, yet not immediately after dying; just as one who performs some distinguished deed merits a reward from a king, but not immediately after performing it.

[Col. 1138A]

Again: Abraham merited that he should pass immediately after death into life, if the victim had been given; he himself was no obstacle to its being given; therefore he merited to enter immediately after death. Fallacy. This most perfect person is of such perfection that, if he died, he would merit immediately to enjoy the vision of God. He himself is no obstacle to his dying, for he desires death; therefore he has now merited to enjoy the vision of God. Or take the foregoing example of the king and the valiant soldier.

Again, every saint of the New Testament, immediately upon dying, enjoys the vision of God. This has not been granted to any saint of the Old Testament; therefore every saint of the New Testament is of greater merit than anyone who died under the Old Testament. Fallacy. Every baptized infant who dies at once enters eternal rest, [Col. 1138B] whereas not every adult immediately enjoys the vision of God after dying in charity; indeed, he passes through purgatory. Therefore every baptized infant is of greater merit than an imperfect adult—which is false.

Again, a good obtained immediately after death is better than one delayed. Every saint of the New Testament immediately attains such a good; no saint of the Old Testament immediately enjoyed the vision of God. Therefore each of the former receives a greater crown than any of the latter. The solution is by interpreting the first premise: taken universally, it is false; if the argument is indefinite, it has no necessary force.

Again, Abraham was held in hell either justly or [Col. 1138C] unjustly. If justly, then because his sins demanded it; therefore he was not entirely freed from them by faith and circumcision—which is false. For Bede says:

[Note: [Col. 1137C] On the Gospel of Luke II: “Circumcision in the law supplied the same aid of saving healing against the wound of original sin as baptism,” etc.]

> “The same remedy of saving healing,” etc.

Again, Abraham lacked the vision of God; that lack was a punishment to him. For Gregory says in the *Moralia*: “The desire for a thing which is delayed is a punishment”; and Solomon says: “Hope deferred afflicts the soul” (Prov. 13). This punishment was not inflicted upon him unjustly. Therefore he endured it for sin, and thus his sins had not been fully remitted through faith and penitence.

To this they say that Abraham was held there justly because he had not been fully freed from sins with respect to every effect of the remission of sins. For although [Col. 1139A] his sins had been remitted with respect to guilt through circumcision, they had not been wholly remitted with respect to punishment, except in hope and expectation of the future truth, whose figures he venerated in shadow until the truth should come. Yet he was not justified by these figures.

For there are two effects of the remission of sin: being free from punishment and enjoying the vision of God. He was free from punishment, but he did not enjoy the vision of God. For that delay of enjoyment was not a natural punishment to him. For, in order that someone may have Gehenna, there must be a place of punishments, sensation, and lack of the vision of God. Abraham indeed was in a place, and lacked God’s vision—that is, he did not possess it, so that this verb *careo* (“I lack”) denotes mere privation and does not imply something due to him—but he felt no material punishment. Yet this seems false.

[Note: [Col. 1139D] Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 112; Sermon 14, *On the Words of the Apostle*; *Against Julian*, chapter 2; and Basil on Psalm 33, at “the fear of the Lord,” etc.]

For elsewhere [Col. 1139B] it is said that lacking the vision of God is the gravest of punishments, although elsewhere it is read that it is the mildest.

[Note: [Col. 1139D] Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 93.]

This is understood thus: it is the mildest with respect to sensation, because, if nothing else were present, no punishment is felt from this. Thus neither am I punished by not being a bishop. Yet it is the gravest with respect to loss; or “gravest” means general, because whoever is punished in hell lacks the vision of God. But this does not follow conversely, because neither the saints before Christ’s advent nor infants who now die unbaptized feel punishment, although they lack the vision of God.

Again, when Abraham died, it was necessary that he had died in faith in the Mediator, and it was impossible that his faith should become void; therefore it was necessary that Christ [Col. 1139C] would come, suffer, and die, and so forth. This seems contrary to the authority:

[Note: [Col. 1139D] Augustine, Book XIII, *On the Trinity*, chapter 10.]

> “Another mode was possible for God, but none more fitting for our misery.”

There is a similar objection concerning Christ, who said that Peter would deny him; it was impossible that he had spoken falsely. Therefore it was necessary that he had spoken truly; therefore it was necessary that this was true; and thus it was necessary that Peter deny Christ. Why, then, is it imputed to him unto death?

Again, it was possible that the human race would not be redeemed; if it were not redeemed, Abraham too would not be redeemed. Therefore it was possible that Abraham would not be redeemed; yet it was necessary that he had died in that faith. Therefore it was possible that that faith should become void, or that he should be deprived of his merits.

A twofold solution is customarily offered. Some say that it was not necessary that Abraham believed what he believed, nor was it necessary that Christ had spoken when he said to Peter, “You will deny me three times” (Luke 22). Others say—and this is what I received from my Master—

[Note: [Col. 1140D] See the same author, Book I, distinction 38; Augustine, Book V, *City of God*, chapters 9 and 10; *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 10; Tractate 53 on John, etc.]

that whatever was said by the prophets through the Holy Spirit was necessarily said, and that it was necessary for it to come to pass; and thus it was necessary that Peter would deny Christ, yet it was imputable to him, just as the devil necessarily sins and yet it is imputable to him. [Col. 1140A] On this account it is necessary that Antichrist will come, and impossible that Antichrist will be killed by his mother.

But against this solution it may be objected that, on the passage in Jeremiah where Jeremiah said to the false prophet Hananiah, “Amen” (Jer. 28), Jerome’s Gloss says:

> “He wishes what that man lies about to come to pass—for this is what ‘Amen’ signifies—and, for the sake of prosperity, prefers that he rather than himself should speak truly.”

It subsequently introduces the example of someone speaking through the Holy Spirit who said:

> “Would that I were not a man having the spirit, but rather spoke falsehood!” (Mic. 2.)

And shortly afterward:

> “Jonah is grieved because he has spoken falsely, and is reproved by the Lord: a falsehood is more advantageous than the ruin of so great a multitude.”

But [Col. 1140B] a substantial question seems to arise here. For if Jeremiah wished to be true what Hananiah falsely prophesied—which can be derived from the authorities just quoted—and knew that it could not be true unless Hananiah had lied, then Jeremiah wished himself to have spoken falsely, he who had promised adversity. Or, if he wished himself to have spoken truly—which cannot be denied, for he would not wish the Holy Spirit through whom he spoke to have spoken falsely—and he wished Hananiah to speak truly—which can be gathered from the preceding authorities—then he wished two contraries to occur simultaneously, since he and Hananiah predicted contrary things. For Hananiah promised prosperity, Jeremiah adversity.

To this one must say that the inference does not follow. If someone wishes [Col. 1140C] something and knows that it cannot be without another consequent, he does not thereby wish the consequent. For this person would wish henceforth to be in Rome; and he knows that this cannot be unless he is in Rome; therefore this person would wish to be in Rome. Thus Jeremiah wished for the outcome of the matter predicted by Hananiah, but did not therefore wish either Hananiah to speak truly or himself to have spoken falsely. He wished himself truly to have spoken, but did not wish what he himself had predicted to occur, or what the other had predicted not to occur. So one who repents of his sins wishes himself to speak truly, but does not wish what he says to have happened; for otherwise he would not repent from the heart. The meaning of these authorities must be directed back to this solution.

## Chapter II. On the power of circumcision and its difference from baptism

[Col. 1140D]

[Note: [Col. 1140D] Master, Book IV, distinction 1, § H, etc.]

Circumcision was commanded to Abraham, now justified by faith. Because we are hastening to other matters, it must be treated briefly: first, why it was instituted; second, of what it is a sacrament; third, why it was replaced by baptism.

It was instituted,

[Note: [Col. 1140D] See Augustine, *On Original Sin*, chapter 31.]

> “so that Abraham might please God through obedience to the command, he who had displeased him through Adam’s disobedience; and so that that people might be distinguished from other nations by a bodily sign,”

just as by the sign of the mind, [Col. 1141A] namely faith.

For that sacrament has two meanings. Circumcision, performed on the eighth day with a stone knife, signifies that through Christ the rock, in the general resurrection which will take place in the eighth age, every corruption will be cut away. It also signifies that through Christ’s resurrection the soul of each believer in him is washed from sin.

It was replaced by baptism because this sacrament is more universal and more perfect. It is more universal because circumcision concerned only one bodily member, in which concupiscence rules, through which we contract original sin. Circumcision was given as a remedy for this. Baptism, however, washes all the parts of the body. Again, circumcision benefited males only, whereas baptism benefits both sexes. This sacrament is also more perfect [Col. 1141B] because circumcision remitted original sin only; nor was assisting grace to do good conferred, nor were virtues increased—

[Note: [Col. 1141D] Thus in the Master’s terms, § K: “a stumbling stone to the disciple.”]

all of which takes place through baptism, besides the remission of original sin. Hence it conferred nothing inwardly on Abraham, since he was already righteous by faith, but was only a sign.

But an objection is raised: circumcision was instituted as a remedy for original sin; therefore either faith was insufficient to abolish original sin, or circumcision was superfluous. That faith was sufficient is established by authority. For it is said:

[Note: [Col. 1141D] Gregory, Book IV, *Moralia*, chapter 3.]

> “What baptismal water accomplishes among us, that among the ancients either faith alone accomplished for infants, or the strength of sacrifice alone for adults, or, for those who sprang from Abraham’s stock, [Col. 1141C] the mystery of circumcision.”

Fallacy. “This man made a vow of continence in order thereby to merit salvation; therefore either the works which he performed in charity before the vow were insufficient, or the vow was superfluous.”

Again, before circumcision original sins were remitted by faith alone; after circumcision had been instituted, they were not remitted by faith alone without circumcision. Therefore faith was more effective before circumcision than afterward. This is false. For the fact that faith alone could not abolish sin after circumcision was not because it had less effect, but because circumcision was commanded and anyone would have been disobedient unless he were circumcised.

Fallacy. “By those works alone which this man performs in [Col. 1141D] charity before a vow of continence, he could be saved; after making the vow, he could not be saved by those works alone unless he also fulfilled the vow. Therefore those works were of less merit afterward than before.”

Again, before circumcision faith alone sufficed to destroy original sin; once circumcision was instituted, both circumcision and faith were necessary. Therefore original sin was remitted more easily before circumcision than afterward. This is true in this sense: fewer things were required and sufficient for its remission; and with regard to sensible experience, no bodily pain was endured by one whose original sin was remitted through faith, as it [Col. 1142A] was remitted through circumcision. If it is inferred from this, “Therefore circumcision harmed more than it benefited,” it is a fallacy. “This man had an easier way of attaining life before his vow than afterward; therefore the vow harmed him more than it benefited him.”

Again, original sin was formerly remitted through faith without circumcision, while now it is by no means remitted without it; therefore faith then had greater power than it has now. Fallacy. “Peter’s soul, while in the way, merited through faith; now it does not merit through it; therefore faith then had greater efficacy than now.”

Again, [Col. 1142B] Abraham’s faith before circumcision had this power: by its merit Ishmael’s sin was remitted. It did not have this effect once Isaac was born, because circumcision was then commanded. Did Abraham merit to have that power taken from his faith?

Again, in circumcision original sin was remitted, and through charity virtues were given in it, though not by it; just as virtues were given in John’s baptism, though not by it.

Again, original sin was remitted to infants through the faith of parents: was this their own parents’ faith or that of others, or that of one parent only, if one was faithful and the other unfaithful? To this it must be said: it was remitted through the merit of those who had gone before, in whom faith had existed, and from whose family those infants came. Thus it is said:

[Note: [Col. 1142D] Augustine, Tractate 80 on John.]

> “The word is added to the element, and it becomes a sacrament—not because it is spoken, but because it is believed.”

This must not be understood to mean that it is now believed; for if everyone were unbelieving and it were spoken, remission would occur. Rather, it is because it was believed by our fathers.

[Col. 1142C] But someone will say: Why were sins remitted to some little children, and not to others, through Adam’s faith, if faith on the part of their own parents was not required? To this it must be said that many unbelieving families descended from Adam, and therefore remission was not granted to little children of such a family, but only to those belonging to the family that possessed faith—perhaps the family of Seth, and later, after the Flood, the family of Shem and Heber, from whom Abraham descended. But if it is asked whether original sin was remitted in the womb to little children through their parents’ faith, when the parents had as great a faith while the children were in the womb as when they were born and afterward, we say that before one is born one cannot be reborn except by a divine miracle, as is said of Jeremiah, [Col. 1142D] Jacob, John, and the Blessed Virgin. It must therefore be said that their sins were remitted through the faith of their parents, namely Adam and Noah, even if their own parents were unbelievers. But it has not been determined [Note: [Col. 1142D] Understand this concerning males before the law of circumcision was given.] on what day after birth this occurred, unless one says concerning females that remission was granted to them on the eightieth day, when an offering was made for them.

Likewise, then a person could become worthy of eternal life by another’s faith alone; now one cannot do so without baptism, because the parents’ faith does not make little children worthy of life unless baptism is excluded by necessity, not by contempt for religion. Therefore faith was of greater perfection [Col. 1143A] then than now. To this it must be said that parents’ faith, neither then nor now, makes anyone worthy of eternal life, although through the power of their faith sins were remitted to little children. Rather, charity—which God freely bestowed in the remission of sins—made them worthy of eternal life.

248 CHAPTER III. On ceremonial observances: whether they were a cause of eternal salvation for those who observed them.

[Note: [Col. 1143D] Master, Book III, last distinction.] After Abraham’s circumcision had been commanded, in the time of Moses and through Moses himself, God gave the Law to the Jewish people as they came out of Egypt, on Mount Sinai, on the fiftieth day after their departure, for two reasons: that through the Law given by God the natural law, which Adam and his [Col. 1143B] posterity had transgressed, might be restored; and that through legal observances that rough and unbelieving people might be instructed for the reception of the truth to come. He accomplished one of these purposes through the moral precepts, the other through the legal precepts. For apart from promises, there are two kinds of precepts in the Law: immovable and movable. The immovable are called moral precepts, whose observance was required at every time—before the Law, under the Law, and after the Law—as, “You shall love the Lord your God,” etc. They are called immovable because they are not displaced when truth comes; indeed, they are then observed all the more. Such are the moral precepts, which were given for every age. The movable precepts are those given temporarily for the sake of prefiguring, not justifying. They were held in reverence until [Col. 1143C] the truth came, of which they were given as signs; once it came, the shadow and figure of the ceremonial observances ceased. Such was the precept concerning the sacrifice of the Paschal lamb, which ended in Christ’s Passion, which it prefigured; likewise circumcision ended in baptism.

But an objection is raised: The Old Law retained its standing until the Gospel. Therefore it ought to have ceased when the Gospel arrived, according to the saying, “When the new things come, you shall cast away the old” (Leviticus 26). But Christ preached the Gospel before his Passion; therefore circumcision and the other things given in the Law for the purpose of prefiguring ought then to have ceased. But the contrary is argued thus: Baptism did not yet possess efficacy, because Christ, from whose Passion it derived its force, had not yet suffered. Nor had Christ yet given the form of baptism, which he gave after the Resurrection when he said, “Going into all the world, preach the Gospel to every creature, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” etc. (Matthew 28). Therefore some say that before the Passion Law and Gospel ran together while Christ preached, and each had efficacy in part. The Apostle’s statement, “If you are circumcised, it profits you nothing” (Galatians 5), must be referred to the state of the Gospel after the Resurrection.

[Col. 1144A] Likewise: “The Law and the Prophets were until John” (Luke 16). Therefore they ought not to have been observed in Christ’s time. SOLUTION: The Law prefigured, and prophecy foretold, what was fulfilled in John’s time. Hence then the Lord said, “It is finished” (John 17), what had been written concerning the Son of Man. Likewise, the Law was to be left behind for the Gospel; therefore it was to be despised for it; therefore it was not to be held in honor for its sake. To this it must be said that it was to be held in honor on account of the Gospel, which it contained through spiritual understanding; for it was like a wheel within a wheel. Hence on that passage of Isaiah [Note: [Col. 1143D] Isaiah 2, in the Gloss, there.], “From Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Matthew 12; Mark 2; Luke 6), the Gloss says: [Col. 1144B] “The Old Law spiritually understood, namely, the Gospel.”

Likewise, Christ began to destroy the Law when his disciples, going through grainfields, rubbed ears of grain on the Sabbath and ate them [Note: [Col. 1144D] Gratian, 25, question 1, chapter 16.]; therefore he abolished the Law. Thus the statement, “I have not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it” (Matthew 5), is false. To this it must be said that the Law is abolished in three ways: either when it is not understood spiritually, and thus the Jew abolishes it; or when, though rightly understood, it is not fulfilled, and thus the Christian abolishes it; or when some part of it is diminished. The Law consists in three things: promises, ceremonial observances, and moral precepts. The promises were fulfilled in Christ’s death. The ceremonial observances have been destroyed according to the letter, but their spiritual meanings are preserved, as are [Col. 1144C] the moral precepts. 249 Therefore Christ did not abolish the Law, because he understood and fulfilled it spiritually and diminished nothing of its spiritual understanding.

It is asked, moreover, since the ceremonial observances signify the same things as the letter of the Law, why, after those observances have been rejected, the letter is held in honor and read in the Church, when nothing there contained concerning ceremonial observances is observed according to the letter. We answer that there are signs which signify a present thing: for example, a circle hanging before a house signifies that wine is for sale in the house. Thus, if a circle hangs there and no wine is for sale, it is a false sign. Another sign signifies a past thing, as dampness of the earth signifies past rain. Another signifies a present and a future thing, such as blessed ashes, which on the Head of the Fast [Ash Wednesday] [Col. 1144D] are placed upon Christians’ heads: they signify their present humility and their future dissolution into dust. But the ceremonial observances were signs only of a future thing. Hence, if they were performed now, they would signify that those things were still future of which they are figures and signs. Since those things are not future, the signs would be false. For Christ has now suffered, which the Paschal sacrifice then signified. We now offer chastity and simplicity, which the offering of a turtledove and a dove prefigured. For that offering pleased God only on account of these things signified. But the letter of the Law is always to be venerated because, when it is read, [Col. 1145A] it confirms our faith by recalling to our memory those things that we believe were foretold by the holy prophets: “In this is the true saying, that one sows and another reaps” (John 4). It also instructs us by recounting what evils God brought upon the Jews when they were rebellious, and what goods when they were humble, so that we too may avoid pride lest something similar happen to us. It may also be said that the letter of the Law prefigured the letter of the Gospel: that is, what the Gospel openly taught ought to be done, the Law itself taught under figures [Note: [Col. 1145D] See St Thomas, I–II, question 102, articles 2 and 3, reply to objection 2.]. For the letter of the Law teaches chastity when it says, “You shall offer a turtledove”; simplicity, when it says, “You shall offer a dove” (Leviticus 5:14). The Gospel teaches the same thing more openly: “Be simple as doves” (Matthew 10).

[Col. 1145B] It is also asked whether ceremonial observances pleased God when they were performed in charity and from charity. That no one merited eternal life through them seems evident from many authorities. Isaiah says: “My soul has hated your sacrifices” (Isaiah 1). And Ezekiel [Note: [Col. 1145D] Jerome, there.]: “I gave them commands that were not good and ordinances by which they should not live” (Ezekiel 20). And the Apostle: “The Law leads no one to perfection” (Hebrews 7). Elsewhere: “The Law works wrath” (Romans 4). Again: “The Law entered in so that transgression might abound” (Romans 5). And in the Gospel: “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5). On the other hand, authorities to the contrary can be adduced. The Apostle says: “The Law indeed is holy, and the commandment good” (Romans 7). [Col. 1145C] And Bede: “The righteousness of the Law, observed in its own time, conferred not only temporal goods but also eternal life.” And Augustine: “He wished those sacrifices to be offered to him so that souls which had died in Egypt might be healed through them.” But all these may easily be reconciled if the multiple meanings of the term “law” are distinguished. For “law” sometimes means the whole sequence of the Old Testament; sometimes only the five books of Moses; sometimes the Decalogue written on tablets; sometimes only the ceremonial observances; and sometimes the letter together with its spiritual understanding. “Law” also means the observance of a single commandment. Thus one commonly says: “This is the law of leprosy,” “the law of jealousy,” “the law of Passover” (Leviticus 13; Numbers 5; etc.).

[Col. 1145D] Therefore all those authorities through which it seems possible to show that the Law does not justify must be referred to ceremonial observances, which were instituted for the sake of signifying, not justifying, even when [Note: [Col. 1146D] So also the Master, Book IV, distinction 1, § B; but here it is marked with an obelus.] performed from charity; and to moral precepts without grace. The remaining authorities we refer to moral precepts with grace and to spiritual understanding. Thus the statement, “The righteousness of the Law, observed in its own time, conferred not only temporal goods, etc.,” is to be understood of moral precepts possessed with grace, such as “You shall love the Lord your God,” etc., “You shall not kill,” and the like. Likewise, what Origen says, 250 that souls dead in Egypt [Col. 1146A] were healed through ceremonial observances, should be understood thus: “They were drawn back from idolatry, to which they had been accustomed in Egypt and through which they were dead.” For that healing was nothing else than the abandonment of idolatry.

That ceremonial observances did not confer salvation, though they were useful toward it, may be shown by a similar case. John’s baptism did not confer salvation because it did not bring remission of sins. It was in water, not in the Spirit; nevertheless, it was useful toward salvation and accustomed people to Christ’s baptism, which was the true cause of salvation. Yet the charity with which they approached John’s baptism conferred salvation. Similarly, an abbot commands his delicate monk, unable to endure the rigor of monastic life, to eat meat; the monk obeys. He therefore merits [Col. 1146B] through obedience, not through eating meat, because food and drink are not the kingdom of God—that is, not the cause of God’s kingdom (Romans 14). Yet that eating is useful toward life because it is the occasion of that merit. But if you ask why those works did not justify, hear what has been said: “Ceremonial observances were given to the hard as a scourge, to the foolish as a pedagogue, and to the just as a sign.” For there were just persons before the Law, and their righteousness received no increase through it, because “the law is not laid down for the just” (1 Timothy 1)—that is, it was given on account of the just—so that those who formerly said, “There is no lack of one who fulfills; there is only a lack of one who commands,” might recognize their weakness, in order that the truth and grace to come might be manifested; and, recognizing their own powerlessness and the insufficiency of ceremonial observances, might [Col. 1146C] run to Christ the physician and there possess salvation through faith, hope, and charity, by which they were justified, not by the Law.

Yet some say that the difference between the sacraments of the Old and New Testaments is not that these justify when performed in charity while those do not, since both justify if they are accompanied by charity. Rather, the difference is that the sacraments of the New Testament increase virtues, whereas the former do not. Baptism also has a greater effect now than in Christ’s time, because then it did not free one from the burden of the Law as it does now.

But again an objection is raised from Abel’s sacrifice, which pleased God, according to the text: “God looked upon Abel and his gifts” (Genesis 4); and in the canon of the Mass: [Col. 1146D] “May this sacrifice be pleasing to you, O God, as the sacrifice of Abel your servant was pleasing to you.” Therefore, if Abel merited through sacrifice in that time, why not Aaron also, who was commanded to sacrifice in the same manner? They therefore explain it: “As the devotion of your servant Abel pleased you when he sacrificed.” It should be noted that in themselves the Gospel’s commands are more difficult than those of the Law; but because these are kept from love and those from fear, these can be observed more easily than those. Thus the Lord says, “My yoke is sweet” (Matthew 11). It is easier to sit than to run through fields; yet it is easier for a hunter to run about through fields than for a monk [Col. 1147A] to sit in a cloister. For few observed those commands from love. An addition was made in counsels, not commandments; or an addition—that is, an explanation.

Likewise, observance of the Law was sufficient for life, because by it one could turn away from evil and do good, and in these two things righteousness is perfected. Therefore no addition needed to be made in the Gospel, or it was superfluous. Likewise [Note: [Col. 1147D] So in Master, Book III, last distinction, § A.]: “The Law restrained the hand, not the mind”; the Gospel restrains both hand and mind. Therefore the law of the Gospel is harsher than the law of Moses. Likewise, whatever moral precepts were observed in the time of the Law must be observed in the time of grace, and besides these, those added in the Gospel. Therefore a double burden of Law and Gospel rests upon us; hence it is more difficult to bear these two than [Col. 1147B] one alone. Since it was said of the burden of the Law, “This is a burden which neither we nor our fathers were able to bear” (Acts 15), this ought much more to be said of the burden of the Gospel. Likewise, the Law restrained the hand and not the mind, and someone could be saved through observing the Law. Therefore one who had the will to sin but did not sin in act could be saved; hence he could be saved without charity. But if someone says that the Law restrained both hand and mind, then the Gospel prohibits both; what addition, then, was made in the Gospel?

251 To this it must be said that the Law was called a restraint upon the hand, not the mind, because no penalty was imposed upon a person for willing to sin. Just as [Col. 1147C] today a priest imposes penance for the will to commit homicide, though not as great a penance as if the act had been added; nevertheless, such a person was [or: will be] not thereby acquitted before God. Likewise, one who wrote a bill of divorce was punished by no penalty according to Moses’ Law and yet [Note: [Col. 1147D] So with the Master and St Thomas, with many others, against certain recent writers.] sinned mortally. Hence the Church today does not permit this; and in this respect the Gospel is gentler, since it punishes temporally a will to sin so that one may not be punished eternally for the same thing, although the Hebrews say that only the act was prohibited there. Thus they explain it: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s thing” (Exodus 20), that is, you shall do nothing outwardly by which you appear to covet. Therefore, when it is said, “Observance of the Ten Commandments was sufficient for life; therefore an addition was superfluous,” see that you understand “observance” carefully. If [Col. 1147D] it was from love, it was sufficient; but if from fear, it is called observance as though “counter-observance” (*contra servantia*), because refraining from acts contrary to the commandments was not meritorious for life unless this was omitted from love, just as it is said, “The Jews were observing Jesus” (Luke 14), that is, they were watching against him, to see whether they might catch him in his speech. Fallacy: “The works this man performs suffice for his salvation; therefore the vow which he adds beyond them is superfluous.” One should know that an addition was made to the Law—that is, to its verbal command, which did not fully or plainly express its precepts or counsels, and which is properly called *lex* from *legendo*, “reading.” But no addition was made in the Gospel to the commandments, that is, the works [Col. 1148A] which Scripture commanded or advised one to “read,” because even the Gospel’s precepts were contained in the Law, either obscurely or manifestly. Rather, the Scripture of the Gospel was added to the Scripture of the Law, expressing more fully what lay hidden beneath the Law’s outer covering.

Likewise, it is said: “The Law commands us to love friends; the Gospel, friends and enemies; therefore the law of the Gospel is harsher than the law of Moses.” Or: “We are now bound to observe all moral precepts observed under the Law, and in addition those handed down in the Gospel; therefore a double burden rests upon us; hence the burden of the Law is harder than that of the Gospel.” This is invalid, because in the Gospel the greatest and overflowing grace is given. With its aid we could more easily fulfill twenty commandments than, in the time of the Law, one alone, since the Law gave no grace, having been given in the threat of punishment. Just as you see that this horse could more easily draw four large millstones on a two-wheeled cart than [Col. 1148B] one of them upon its back. So it is with the Gospel, which is a two-wheeled cart because of the two commandments of charity, love of God and love of neighbor.

Likewise, it is asked whether the Old Law is the New Law, which seems to be the case. An authority on Isaiah says [Note: [Col. 1148D] Isaiah 2, in the Gloss, on the words, “From Zion shall go forth the law.”]: “The Old Law spiritually understood is the New.” But as soon as the Old Law existed, it was spiritually understood; therefore the New Law existed as soon as it did, and thus before Christ’s coming. Conversely, it is proved that this is not that, because the one promises temporal benefits, the other eternal goods. [Col. 1148C] One should therefore know that the Old Law consisted in three things: promises, moral precepts, and ceremonial observances. The promises were meant to attract, such as a land flowing with milk and honey. The moral precepts instructed people to live well. The figurative observances taught them to understand greater things: manna prefigured the Eucharist, the red heifer Christ [Note: [Col. 1148D] See the Epistle of Saint Barnabas and the notes on it.]. Likewise, the New Law has the same moral precepts, but different promises, expressed in “Blessed are the poor in spirit,” etc.; it also has different significations, because the sacraments of the Old Law prefigured the sacraments of the New, which signify and effect the same things. Therefore, when it is said that the New Law is the Old or is contained in it, we use the manner of speaking by which things signified are said to be in the things signifying them: the sacraments of the New Law were signified by the sacraments of the Old Law. Or it is said to have lain hidden [Col. 1148D] in part, because certain moral precepts are contained both here and there. Yet this Scripture is different from that one, although in part the commandments are the same.

Likewise, every action of Christ was our lesson; therefore in every work that he did he instructed us and directed it toward our salvation. Therefore by every work that he did, 252 he merited; therefore he merited by ceremonial works, perhaps when he bowed before the mercy-seat or did something of that sort. Accordingly, even if we could say that, when mention is made of human merits, we must be silent concerning Christ, who is privileged and above every law, it may be said, as some teach, that he did not merit from every [Col. 1149A] work which he did in charity, but he merited from the charity which he possessed while working. So too this monk does not merit by sleeping or eating, though he directs these things to his salvation, so that he may rise more soberly for Matins and serve God. Likewise, if the argument is made: legal observances could be performed in charity; therefore they could justify, or someone could merit through them—it is a fallacy. A coin can be given in charity; therefore it can justify, or someone can merit through it. Or, according to the other opinion mentioned, it may more truly be said that people merited from legal observances if they were performed in charity. For there is no work from which a person does not merit if it is performed in charity. Yet there is this difference between those sacraments and these: those do not increase virtues, even when [Col. 1149B] performed in charity, as these do. For if two people are equal in charity, and one receives the Eucharist, charity is increased in that person.

Likewise, it is written in Deuteronomy: “Cursed is everyone who does not remain in all the things written in the book of the Law in order to do them” (Deuteronomy 27). Therefore everyone was bound to do everything before Christ’s coming, including those who understood the Law spiritually. For all were bound to understand the Law spiritually and to perform all ceremonial observances, as the aforementioned authority says. Therefore, if anyone omitted any ceremonial observance, that person was a transgressor, even if possessing faith. But it is stated on authority that they could not do everything; therefore all were transgressors. To this the authority in the Epistle to the Galatians (chapter [Col. 1149C] 3) says: All who were under the Law were cursed, because in all there was the guilt of transgression, from which those who trusted in grace were absolved. But how were they absolved? Were those who had faith in Christ not bound to observe legal observances? Then Moses would not sin if he ate pork. Rather, faith does not appear to have had as great a power before the Advent as it has now. For then no one could be saved through faith unless he observed ceremonial observances; now one can, because faith alone suffices. But if it is said that faith alone was sufficient before the Advent without observance of legal observances, then those who had faith were not bound to observe legal observances even then; yet all were bound to possess faith. Therefore all could then be saved without observing legal observances; hence [Col. 1149D] they were not transgressors if they did not observe them, and so were not under the Law’s curse. Whom, then, did it curse? Was it those who did not observe spiritually? If so, those same persons are cursed now. But if it was those who did not observe carnally, then everyone was bound to observe everything carnally. Therefore faith was not sufficient without legal observances for salvation even then.

CHAPTER IV. Where the Ten Commandments of the Law are set forth. And it is asked whether it is permissible to do the contrary of any of them.

[Note: [Col. 1149D] Master, distinction 37, etc. See Augustine, Treatise on the Ten Strings, chapter 5.] The Law’s precepts are ten. On the first tablet are three which concern the love of God. The first [Col. 1150A] is: “You shall have no strange gods. You shall not make for yourself a graven image, nor any likeness” (Exodus 20). A graven image, or idol, is called that which has no form resembling anything among created things. Hence [Note: [Col. 1150D] Origen, Homily 8 on Exodus, on chapter 20.] it is called an idol as a “nothing,” because it is not a form of any existing thing whose likeness it bears, but something fashioned by an inquisitive and idle mind. There are also other explanations, which, because they belong more to diversion than disputation, we omit for the present. A likeness is that which has something similar among created things. The second is: “You shall not take the name of your God in vain” (ibid.); seek its exposition in a lecture, not in a disputation. The third is: “Remember to keep holy the Sabbath day” (ibid.).

253 On the second tablet are seven precepts, [Col. 1150B] the first of which is: “Honor your father and mother, that you may be long-lived upon the earth” (Exodus 20). The second is: “You shall not kill” (ibid.). But it is asked whether all who do not kill fulfill this commandment. If so, then this person who does not love his father fulfills it; but he offends in one point, and therefore is guilty of all; hence he fulfills none. Therefore neither does he fulfill this one. How then does he do what is contrary to it? He kills, either in will or in act. Likewise, not killing is nothing, and this man merits by not killing; therefore he merits by what is nothing. We therefore say that no one fulfills this commandment unless he intends not to kill even if provoked; and no one can fulfill one commandment in intention or settled will without fulfilling all of them through charity. Yet one can fulfill one in fact without fulfilling all in fact. Hence what is said, [Col. 1150C] “Whoever offends in one point is guilty of all” (James 2), must be understood not because that person does the contrary of every commandment, but because he does not possess charity, and without it he is a transgressor of every commandment. To make the foregoing clear, someone is said to have observed the Decalogue in fact, in will or intention, or in pretense. Because one observed it in pretense, one did not possess charity. One who observed one commandment through charity could not observe one in will or intention without the others; nevertheless, one could observe one in fact and not another. For I am not said to observe in fact the commandment “You shall not kill” (Exodus 20) unless something impels me to kill and I restrain my hand.

[Col. 1150D] But it is asked whether it is permissible to kill. This seems to be so. When foreigners invaded Judah and his brothers on the Sabbath, it was established, by the Holy Spirit’s instruction, that they should not attack their enemies on the Sabbath but should resist attackers, because many Jews had fallen when they did not defend themselves that day (1 Maccabees 2). Likewise, [Note: [Col. 1150D] Cicero, *For Milo*.] it is permissible to repel force by force. Furthermore, soldiers who have crossed the sea would not kill pagans unless the Church permitted and consented [perhaps, “gave consent”]. Yet the contrary is found in the Gospel: “If anyone strikes you on one cheek, offer the other also” (Matthew 5; Luke 6). And the Apostle says: “Do not defend yourselves” (Romans 12). The Lord also rebuked Peter [Col. 1151A] because he had cut off the ear of the high priest’s servant (Luke 22), which he would not have done had this been permitted to him. To this it can be said that it is not permissible to kill from rancor of heart, but it is permissible from zeal for justice, or for the defense of truth, or lest faith be endangered. Hence Jerome, on Jeremiah: “To punish murderers, sacrilegious persons, and usurers is not the shedding of blood but the service of the law.” We also say, without prejudice, that what was said in the Gospel and by the Apostle was said for that time. For the divine Spirit, considering all things to their depths, foresaw that in the time of the primitive Church, while it was still little, it was useful to endure patiently. But now the number of the faithful has increased, and what was not permitted then is permitted.

Likewise, there is a man compelled either to single combat [*monomachia*] [Col. 1151B] or to hanging. In hanging only bodily death threatens; in single combat there is death of soul and death of body. And the more excellent the soul is than the body, the more harmful is death of the soul than death of the body. Therefore he ought rather to choose hanging than single combat. Conversely, in single combat he may prevail without harming the person with whom he fights, and he ought to flee temporal death as far as he can. Therefore it is better for him to fight than to be hanged. To this they say that, if he is perfect, he ought rather to choose hanging; but if he is imperfect, single combat. Likewise, the soul is more worthy than the body; therefore the person who kills a soul sins more than the person who kills a body; therefore one who draws a person into consenting to mortal [Col. 1151C] sin sins more than one who kills that person. To this it must be said that one who kills the body hates both soul and body, whereas one who kills a soul hates the soul alone. The argument from contraries is false: “The soul ought to be loved more than the body; therefore one who kills a soul sins more than one who kills a body.” It is like saying: “The soul is worth more than the body; therefore the person who feeds the soul is to be loved more than the person who feeds the body.”

254 The third commandment is: “You shall not commit adultery” (Exodus 20). Understand by this every unlawful use of the members for lust, taking the whole from a part. Here the act of adultery is forbidden according to the carnal sense; spiritually, however, the will to commit adultery is forbidden. Hence in the Gospel an addition was made to the letter of the Law: [Col. 1151D] “Whoever looks upon a woman in order to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5). The letter of the Gospel expresses the spiritual sense—that is, the sense according to which one lives spiritually. But they object: Under the words “You shall not commit adultery,” both adultery of the body and adultery of the heart are prohibited; and the perfection of this commandment consists in these two. If someone formerly abstained from bodily adultery but not adultery of the heart, that person was a transgressor. Therefore this commandment was as perfect then as it is now, and nothing was added to its perfection. One should know that those additions previously existed in the mind of the giver of the moral commandment, but did not exist in the mind of its interpreter, nor in practice—just as fruit is said both to exist in winter and not to exist on the tree: not to exist because it is not on the branches; to exist because it is in the root, in the tree’s nature.

[Col. 1152A] The fourth commandment is: “You shall not steal” (Exodus 20). Here every robbery, whether violent or secret, is forbidden. But regarding usury there are many doubtful matters, which we reserve for the disputation of canonists rather than theologians [Note: [Col. 1151D] Master, Book III, distinction 37, § C.]. It may be asked whether the children of Israel committed theft when, at the Lord’s command, they borrowed vessels from the Egyptians and did not later return them. After many disputes and indirect arguments attempting to prove or disprove this, we believe the resolution has this outcome [Note: [Col. 1151D] Augustine, *Questions on Exodus*, question 39; and Book XXII, *Against Faustus*, chapter 71.]: those who did this from zeal to fulfill the divine command, not from a desire to obtain property, should not be said to have sinned by this act; indeed, they even merited, just as Abraham did not sin when, in obedience to the divine command, he wished to sacrifice his son. Nor does the person sin who, by a king’s command, hangs a man in order to administer justice, not from rancor or hatred of heart. But those induced to do this by fear or desire for the goods they carried away were merely permitted to do it, and we believe that they sinned. For although they did what the Lord commanded, they did not do it as he commanded, or with that intention. Just as the devil did what the Lord willed or permitted in Job, and yet sinned. And the Jews, [Col. 1152C] by killing Christ, did what the Lord willed, and yet sinned. Nebuchadnezzar, by overthrowing Jerusalem, did what the Lord willed, and yet sinned. But it is objected: “Do not do to another what you do not wish done to yourself” (Tobit 4) is natural law. Those who carried away the vessels in order to fulfill the Lord’s command acted against this law; therefore they sinned. We therefore say that “unjustly” must be understood in that law: do not act unjustly. Otherwise a judge who pronounces judgment against someone would act unjustly against natural law.

CHAPTER V. On lying and its kinds.

[Note: [Col. 1151D] Master, Book III, distinction 38.] The fifth commandment is: “You shall not bear false witness” (Exodus 20), in which both the sin of lying and the sin of perjury are prohibited. Because questions are commonly raised about each, let us first discuss lying: first, considering what a lie is and what it is to lie; next, how many kinds of lies there are; third, whether every lie is a sin. [Note: [Col. 1152D] Augustine, *Against Lying*, chapter 12, at the end; *Enchiridion*, chapter 18.] “A lie is a false signification by speech with the intention of deceiving. To lie is to speak contrary to what one thinks in one’s mind.” It is therefore clear that everyone who utters a false statement lies, but not conversely: someone can lie while speaking truth, just as one can speak falsehood without lying. Accordingly, there is no doubt that [Note: [Col. 1152D] So the Master, above, § C.] a Jew lies when [Col. 1153A] he says that Christ is God and man, although he does not state a lie [Note: [Col. 1153D] Augustine on Psalm 5.]. There are three kinds of lies: one committed for someone’s salvation or advantage, such as the lie of the midwives; a second spoken in jest; and a third proceeding from malice and duplicity of mind, for the purpose of deceiving. Augustine, however, [Note: [Col. 1153D] *On Lying*, chapter 14.] elsewhere distinguishes eight kinds of lies. The first is committed under the teaching of religion. The second harms no one and benefits someone; it is divided into three, not because it has three species, but because there are three purposes for which such a lie is commonly told.
