First, if someone has money that is being unjustly taken away and says that he does not know where it is, though he does know. Second, if someone does not wish to betray to death a person being sought and lies by saying that he does not know where the person is, though he knows. Third, if someone by lying defends a man or woman from bodily defilement. Every kind of lie is a sin [Note: [Col. 1153D] From Augustine, chapter 22 of the *Enchiridion*.]. For speech was invented so that, as by a kind of vehicle, understanding might be carried from one person to another and our thought might come to another’s knowledge. If anyone abuses words in order to deceive, making another understand something other than what he thinks, that person abuses words, which are God’s gifts, and thus sins.

Whether a lie is a venial sin or a mortal one, and in what respect it is venial and in what mortal, must be distinguished according to the kinds of lies mentioned above. That third kind of lie which proceeds from duplicity of mind is a mortal sin both in the perfect and in the imperfect [Col. 1153C]. The first kind, which is made for someone’s safety, and the second, which is made in jest [Note: [Col. 1153D] Thus Augustine, on Psalm V, *Enchiridion*, chs. 22 and 18, *On Lying*, ch. 14 and final chapter, and *Against Lying*, ch. 8], are venial in the imperfect. Hence the midwives sinned venially when they lied to Pharaoh. This is proved by Augustine’s authority [Note: [Col. 1153D] Questions on Leviticus, question 68, on the same chapter]. For he says: “Perhaps, just as the midwives were rewarded not because they lied but because they saved the infants—on account of which mercy the sin was venial, though not nonexistent—so Rahab was delivered on account of the deliverance of the spies, for which her sin was venial.” Again, on Exodus [Note: [Col. 1153D] Gregory, *Morals*, book 18, ch. 4]: “If every fault is customarily purged by a subsequent pious deed, how much more easily is this one wiped away, when the piety that is the mother of a good work accompanies it.” Therefore the piety which is the mother of a good work [Col. 1153D], and hence charity, accompanied that sin. For this cannot be understood of natural affection, since natural affection is not the mother of a good work. Therefore that lie was a venial sin. Again Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1153D] Question 1 on Exodus]: “They used a lie for themselves, lest Pharaoh should harm them; this could pertain not to praise, but to pardon.” Therefore they sinned venially. Again [Col. 1154A], they preserved natural affection, which dictated to them that the children’s lives should be saved, and they had no other law; therefore either they did not sin, or they sinned venially.

Yet Gregory says to the contrary [Note: [Col. 1153D] Gregory, on book XVIII of the *Morals*, ch. 4—incorrectly ch. 2 in certain editions [Col. 1154D]]: “The reward which might have been repaid in eternal life was diverted into temporal recompense.” Behold, he says openly that, because of the fault of lying, the eternal reward was exchanged for a temporal one. Therefore that fault was mortal, since God does this only for a mortal sin. This should therefore be understood as though he said: if they had preserved the little ones out of charity, they would have been rewarded eternally. But here it appears that they acted not from charity but from natural affection, because they were rewarded temporally.

[Col. 1154B] Again, Augustine says that there are two kinds of lie which are venial [Note: [Col. 1154D] On Psalm V, etc.]: a lie in jest and a lie of kindly disposition. He calls a lie of kindly disposition one which harms no one and benefits someone. But the midwives’ lie was neither a jesting lie nor a lie of kindly disposition, because it benefited no one. For Pharaoh then commanded the Hebrew males to be drowned in the river; therefore it was not venial. To this it must be said that the lie benefited the other midwives in Egypt, over whom Shiphrah and Puah presided (Exod. I); and, insofar as it lay in their power, it benefited the Hebrews.

Again [Note: [Col. 1154D] Augustine, *Against Lying*, book 1, ch. 12, near the end]: “A lie is a false signification in speech with the intention of deceiving.” They intended to deceive by lying; therefore they sinned mortally. Again, a divided mind obtains nothing; they had one thing in their heart and another on their lips, and did this with intent to deceive; therefore they sinned mortally [Col. 1154C]. We say, then, that arguments of this kind have no necessity, because a lie is not always a mortal sin—just as the homicide committed by Phinehas is not, considered in itself, a mortal sin, nor is fornication. Why, then, is a lie more readily excused from mortal sin when done for another’s safety than fornication would be if someone lay with a woman pretending that she was already dying, unless he lay with her and knew her with this intention? It must be said that every kind of fornication, in every person, is a mortal sin; but not every kind of lie is. Therefore the question has no force [Note: [Col. 1154D] Thus the Master above]. But the perfect are not permitted to lie. [Col. 1154D] They may indeed keep the truth silent, but they are forbidden to tell a lie; otherwise they sin mortally.

But it is objected: no one is so perfect that he ought not to regard himself as imperfect. Yet, conversely [Note: [Col. 1154D] Gregory, *Morals*, book XXVI, ch. 2: “They are incautiously humble who…”]: “He humbles himself incautiously who entangles himself in the snare of lying.” And elsewhere [Note: [Col. 1154D] Augustine, *Sermons on the Words of the Apostle*, sermon 29: “When you lie for the sake of humility, if you were not a sinner before you lied, by lying you become what you had avoided”]: “By that very act, a person makes himself a sinner when he lies for humility’s sake” [Col. 1155A]. Therefore it must be said that no one ought to call himself imperfect if he knows himself to be perfect, unless he says this in comparison with the perfection that is in the homeland, to which no one on the way can attain; and we believe the foregoing authority should be understood in this sense.

Again: “When you have done all good things, say: We are unprofitable servants” (Luke XVII). Understand this thus: by living well we confer no benefit upon God, but God confers benefit upon us. Again Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1155D] Thus reported by Innocent III, *Extra*, “On the Observance of Fasting,” ch. 2; though it seems to have been taken from Gregory]: “It belongs to good minds to acknowledge fault where there is no fault.” Understand this thus: to fear or dread lest there be fault where there is no fault. Again, a man thinks that he has committed homicide when he has not committed it. He is bound to confess the sin of which he thinks himself guilty, though he is not guilty. He says that he did it, and this is false [Col. 1155B]. Therefore he sins. To this we say: he is bound to confess, and when he says “I did it” he speaks falsely; yet he does not lie, and merits by speaking falsely. But this question need not be pursued further here, since it has been treated more fully above.

[Note: [Col. 1156D] The Master above, final section, near the end.] It is customary to ask whether Jacob lied when he said that he was Esau, knowing that he was not Esau, in order to deceive his father (Gen. XXVII). Therefore he lied, and therefore sinned mortally, since he did this from malice of mind. They say that he did not call himself Esau except figuratively; for he meant: “I am the one who comes to receive Esau’s blessing.” Nor did he do this from malice of mind, but at the prompting of the Holy Spirit.

Again, Jacob would not have wished the blessing which Esau was taking from him to be taken from himself; therefore he acted against natural law, and hence committed a mortal sin. It must be said that he did not take it unjustly, for he did this at the prompting of the Holy Spirit. Moreover, Esau had sold his brother the right of primogeniture for a dish of lentils. Again, Jacob deceived his father; therefore he sinned. That he deceived his father is evident when Isaac says: “Your brother came deceitfully” (*ibid.*), that is, figuratively. For in that action it was signified that the lesser people would supplant the greater in the blessing; nor was Isaac deceived [Note: [Col. 1156D] The Master of the Sentences above, final section; yet it alludes rather to the teacher’s spoken than written statements]. My master, departing not far from this opinion, nevertheless seems to resolve the matter more fully and more straightforwardly. For he says that Jacob spoke falsely but did not lie, because he did not [Col. 1155D] go against his mind or conscience: both mind and conscience dictated that he must obey his superior, that is, the Holy Spirit, at whose prompting he said this. Nor did he intend to deceive his father, although he told him what he knew to be false and persuaded him of it—just as I persuade this man that another man is not in this house, although he is there, because I do not wish him to be killed by that man. He spoke contrary to what he knew, but not contrary to conscience.

You have a parallel in all things belonging to the class of evils which nevertheless, by the Lord’s command, are good and meritorious [Col. 1156A]: as in the taking of goods from the Egyptians, the command given to Abraham concerning the death of his son, and the killing by Phinehas. Although it was commanded: “You shall not speak falsely” (Exod. XX), if someone sets this command aside, to which he is subject, and submits himself to Him to whom this command also is subject, namely the Lord, he does not act against this command. Thus, if this priest sets aside the command of a bishop and submits himself to the pope’s command, he does not sin against the bishop. Jacob’s mind therefore dictated that Jacob should do what he did, under the Holy Spirit’s prompting.

257 Therefore, when it is said, “Your brother came deceitfully” (Gen. XXVII), this means “under the appearance of deceit”; for it appeared to be deceit but was not, nor was it a wrongful likeness. For one likeness is good, another evil, and another is used for signification, as was Jacob’s likeness, by which it was signified that the Christian people would be preferred to the Jewish people [Col. 1156B]. Another is used for protection, as in the likeness assumed by Tobit’s angel, who said that he was the son of the great Azariah. Another is used for understanding, as when the Lord pretended to be going farther while walking with the disciples to Emmaus, in order by this example to invite them to understanding of himself.

Again, Isaac invoked blessing for Esau or Jacob, and believed that the one for whom he invoked it was Esau; therefore he invoked it for Esau and not Jacob, and was not heard for the person for whom he invoked it; therefore his prayer was not heard. Or thus: Isaac intended to bless Esau and did not bless him; therefore his prayer was ineffectual. It must be said that Isaac invoked blessing for Jacob, although he believed that he invoked it for Esau. Yet he was no less heard on that account [Col. 1156C], just as when a bishop ordains someone while thinking that he is ordaining another, the person upon whom hands are laid is nonetheless ordained.

Again, Jacob spoke falsely by the prompting of the Holy Spirit; therefore the Holy Spirit was the author of falsehood. A distinction is necessary here. The Holy Spirit can be the author of falsehood, that is, of a false statement, a false utterance; but he was not the author of the falsity of the thing itself, which exists when someone departs from God through unbelief. Again, Jacob spoke falsely; therefore he sinned venially or mortally, and thus did not speak this by the Holy Spirit’s prompting. This is the fallacy of the first [figure]. Phinehas killed a man; therefore he committed either a venial or a mortal sin. Again, by the Son as author, someone could speak falsely; for if it was spoken by the Holy Spirit as author, then it was also spoken by the Son as author, since the operations of the Trinity are undivided. And the Son himself, according to his humanity, could utter a proposition that was significatively false because it was ambiguous; therefore [he could utter] falsehood.

To this it must be said that the argument has no force. A parallel may be adduced: the Father, by his own authority, is God, and the Son, being man, is God; yet the Son is not God by his own authority insofar as he is man [Col. 1156D]. If anyone resolves it otherwise, we do not begrudge him that. But we have set forth this solution because we received it thus from good teachers.

## CHAPTER VI. On perjury and the modes of oath and perjury

[Col. 1157A]

[Note: [Col. 1157D] Master, III, distinction 39.] Along with the foregoing commandment of the law, not only lying but also perjury is forbidden. Therefore, after discussing lying, we must add a discussion of perjury. In it we shall consider what it is to swear and what it is to commit perjury; in what modes an oath and likewise perjury are made; and whether it is lawful to alter an oath.

To swear is to call God as witness to some matter, or to pledge something to God. This definition, given by division, indicates that an oath is made in two ways. For sometimes a person swears by God, which is to call God as witness; for “by God” and “God is witness” mean the same thing [Note: [Col. 1157D] Augustine, sermon 28, *On the Words of the Apostle*]. Likewise, one who swears by a stone or another creature calls God, the Creator, as witness [Col. 1157B]. And one who, as Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1157D] *Ibid.*], swears falsely by a stone is perjured, because he calls as witness not the stone but God, Creator of the stone.

There is another kind of oath made by imprecation, as when someone says: “If I did that, may this happen to my children.” Thus one sometimes swears when saying, “By my children,” or “By my head”: for one binds to God that by which one swears, so that what proceeds from his mouth may happen to it—if it is true, truth; if false, falsehood.

Again, an oath is sometimes about lawful things and sometimes unlawful things. Whenever someone swears unlawful things, he commits perjury, that is, he swears improperly or badly, and sins mortally. An oath about lawful things is either uncertain, superfluous, or necessary. If what one swears is uncertain—for instance, if one swears without any condition that one will engage in disputation tomorrow, when this is uncertain for him—one sins mortally. Likewise, a superfluous oath is a mortal sin: for example, when someone swears from pleasure or habit. The Lord also prohibited this when he said, “Do not swear” (Matt. V), that is, do not make swearing a habit and pleasure, because such a habit is always a mortal sin.

But a necessary oath—that is, one made either to prove innocence, to confirm treaties of peace, or to persuade hearers of what is intended—is not evil and hence is not forbidden. Yet it is “from evil,” that is, from the weakness of one who refuses to believe unless an oath is sworn [Note: [Col. 1157D] See Augustine, *Sermon on the Mount*, book I, ch. 17, and *On Lying*, book I, ch. 15]. Therefore [Col. 1157D], when God had forbidden evil by saying, “Do not swear,” and had urged good by saying, “Let your speech be ‘Yes, yes; no, no’” (*ibid.*), he permitted what was necessary by saying that “what is more,” namely an oath, is from evil; he did not say, “It is evil.”

When someone makes a necessary oath, either he does not intend to do what he swears, and then he sins because he commits perjury; or he does intend it, and then he does not sin. But if afterward he changes his intention, when he changes it he commits perjury; and thus, by failing to fulfill it [Col. 1158A], he commits perjury—that is, he changes an oath rightly made—which is a mortal sin.

Perjury is a lie confirmed [by an oath]. Some hold that there is no perjury where there is no lie; for, just as something false may be spoken without lying, so, they say, there may be a false oath without perjury when a person swears to something false which he most certainly thinks true. Others think it better that an oath should have, according to Jerome, three companions [Note: [Col. 1157D] On Jeremiah IV: “It should be observed that an oath has these companions: truth, judgment, and justice. If these are lacking, it will by no means be an oath, but perjury”]: truth, justice, and judgment; and that where one is lacking there is perjury. Hence one commits perjury both who swears to what is false with an intention to deceive, who swears to what is false while thinking it true, and who swears to what is true while thinking it false. Thus perjury is either to speak falsely under oath with intent to deceive, to speak falsely under oath without intent to deceive, or to speak truth under oath with intent to deceive [Col. 1158B].

But it is objected: if everyone who swears falsely commits perjury, then the person who swears that he will do what he presently intends to do, but whose intention will nevertheless change, is now committing perjury. Therefore he sins mortally; therefore he does not have charity; therefore, if he died now, he would not be saved. This is false, because he intends to do what he swears, what he swears is lawful, and he does it to persuade others of what he means; therefore he swears well. Hence we say that he does not now commit perjury; rather, he will commit it when he changes his intention, as has been said. But on this account the foregoing definition is not convertible with the thing defined, namely perjury: for he will commit perjury when he does not speak [Col. 1158C], while now he commits perjury by swearing falsely. Therefore it must be said that speaking must be referred to the inward movement of the mind.

Again Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1158D] Sermon 28, *On the Words of the Apostle*]: “Only a guilty mind makes the tongue guilty.” The person who swears falsely what he believes true has no guilty mind; therefore neither has he a guilty tongue, and hence does not commit perjury. I say that he has a guilty mind insofar as he swears carelessly and asserts on oath what he has not grasped with complete certainty.

Again it is asked what perjury is. It occurs when someone swears that what is true is false. For the verbal signification itself is true. This indeed may readily be said, because thus to speak against one’s mind under the attestation of an oath is perjury. After this, to alter an oath is shown [to be perjury] as follows. Suppose that someone has sworn to kill a man. Behold here the testicles of Behemoth are in a dilemma (Job XL) [Note: [Col. 1158D] See Gregory, *Morals*, book XXXII, ch. 13]. For he must either commit perjury or perpetrate homicide; but of two evils the lesser must be chosen, and perjury is the lesser evil than homicide. Therefore he ought to choose perjury; therefore it is lawful for him to commit perjury.

Again, out of charity he can repent of the evil will of homicide which he had, and therefore also of the oath he made, which was a mortal sin [Col. 1159A], since no one can repent of one mortal sin without repenting of every other. Thus he is not in a dilemma, because it is not necessary to incur one of two evils. The same is also proved by authority. For it is read [Note: [Col. 1159D] 1 Kings XXV; 22, question 4, chapter *Quod David*; Bede, homily 43, otherwise 44, on the beheading of St John]: “David swore to kill Nabal, a foolish man; but at the first intercession of Abigail, a prudent woman, he withdrew his threats, sheathed his sword, and did not grieve that he had incurred any guilt through such perjury.” Again, the Church counsels him to change his oath; therefore one who commits perjury in this case does not sin mortally. For the Church would not give this as counsel if it were a sin. Conversely, however, the objection is made thus: every perjury is a mortal sin; this man commits perjury; therefore he sins mortally.

To this we say that *perjury* is used in the sense of an improperly, that is badly, sworn oath [Col. 1159B]; and every such perjury is a mortal sin. It is committed whenever one swears something lacking one of those three things: truth, judgment, or justice. Truth means fulfillment of the sworn matter and purity of conscience. Justice means that what is sworn is just, that is, lawful; and judgment means discretion. For if someone swore that he would give alms tomorrow for God’s love, and that this would indeed happen, there would be truth and justice, but not judgment, that is, discretion. Therefore it is perjury—that is, an oath badly made—because it is uncertain or superfluous.

Perjury is also used to mean a perverse or altered oath; and not every such perjury is a mortal sin. For when someone repents out of charity of a careless oath which he has made, he does not sin mortally, even though he changes the oath. Nor is there any dilemma in the foregoing case, since both things can be relinquished out of charity. For a dilemma exists when a person is so entangled in two evils that he must incur one of them. Perhaps such were the Jews whose conscience dictated that Christ was a destroyer of the law and therefore ought to be crucified. Their conscience likewise dictated that he was just and innocent and therefore ought to be released. Thus, whether they released or killed him, they would sin mortally [Col. 1159C]. Into this intention and dilemma they had fallen, their sins requiring it.

And note: where a dilemma arises, the Church does not advise that the lesser evil be done; but if it happens that either the lesser or the greater is done, it teaches that the greater should be avoided more carefully. Thus a doctor does not advise this sick man to eat ram’s flesh; but if it happens that he eats either ram’s or cow’s flesh, he prefers ram’s flesh, which is less harmful.

Some nevertheless say that, in truth, when the purity of conscience alone is considered, the subsequent outcome of the matter sworn is not required. For if someone has sworn that he will return a sword to its claimant, and the claimant asks for it while enraged, and he refuses to return it, he does not commit perjury, because he did not contemplate that the claimant would demand it in anger [Col. 1160A]. Likewise, when the Apostle promised that he would come to the Corinthians, had he sworn this, he would not have committed perjury even if he did not come, because he had it in his heart; thus there would be purity of conscience, though not fulfillment of the sworn matter. Yet one may rightly say that, on this supposition, he did not swear—this is false. For when he swore that he would return the sword, there was understood a hidden qualification: if he then knew that returning it would be beneficial to him.

Again, someone swore that he would not kill his father and does not so intend; therefore he commits perjury, and hence is not bound to do what he swears. But he swears that he will not kill his father; therefore he is not bound not to kill him. It must be said that he commits perjury, that is, he swears badly; yet he is bound to do what he swears badly, just as one who changes an oath commits perjury and is nevertheless bound to do what he changes. And the Jews lied when they said Christ was God, yet they were bound to say that he was king [Col. 1160B].

Again, it should be noted that if someone says, in an ordinary manner of speaking and without an intention to swear, “By God, I will do this,” he does not commit perjury if he does not do what he says, because he does not swear when he says it. But if he says this with the intention of swearing—the sign of which is either that he places his hand in another’s hand or that he touches holy things—then he intends to swear and commits perjury if he does not do what he swears. It may also happen that there is no sign at all, neither [“a great interpretation, nor a silent book” — uncertain text; Note: [Col. 1159D] Perhaps: “Neither the placing together of hands nor the touching of a book.”], but only the words “By God”; and nevertheless it is an oath, if it is made with the intention of swearing [Col. 1160C].

[Note: [Col. 1160D] The Master above, section d.] It is also asked whether it is lawful to swear by a creature, and whether an oath made by a creature is binding. We say that the Jews were forbidden to swear by a creature—because they were prone to idolatry and rendered to a creature the honour due to God—when it was said: “You shall render your oaths to God” (Matt. V). But it is lawful for the perfect, who venerate the Creator in the creature. Hence Joseph is read to have sworn by Pharaoh’s life (Gen. XLII).

If it is asked who is more bound by an oath: one who commits perjury by the Gospel, or one who does so by God? We say that the holier the thing named in the oath, the more punishable is the perjury, Chrysostom being witness, who says [Note: [Col. 1160D] In the Master, here, section E. Author of the *Imperfect Work* attributed to Chrysostom, homily 44]: “If some cause arises, the one who swears by God seems to do something slight; the one who swears by the Gospel, something greater.” To them one must say: fools, the sacred Scriptures are for God’s sake, not God for Scripture’s sake [Col. 1160D].

[Note: [Col. 1160D] The Master, section G. See Augustine, letter 154 to Publicola.] Again, it is asked whether someone who swore by idols is bound by the oath, or whether this was lawful for him. We say that he sinned in swearing by idols, because he rendered to an idol the honour due to God; and he commits perjury if he changes an oath made by idols, and thus sins mortally in this case. But it is asked [Col. 1161A] of what matter he invokes God as witness who swears by idols. Since God did not make the idol, he apparently does not invoke God as witness, because God is not author of the thing named in the oath. In contrast, when we say “by a stone,” as Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1161C] Sermon 28, *On the Words of the Apostles*], we invoke God, author of stones, as witness.

A distinction must therefore be made. If one swearing by an idol thinks that the idol is something composed of a body and a presiding spirit, he does not invoke God as witness; and therefore, in swearing, he sins, because he renders to the idol worship which he owes to God. If someone worships the Creator in that creature, he invokes as witness the Creator of that body; and therefore the oath is binding, if it concerns lawful things. But if it is asked whether someone who was compelled to swear is bound by the oath, Augustine says that he is bound; because, although he did not will what he swore [Col. 1161B], he nevertheless willed the reason why he did it, namely life. Likewise, if it is asked of someone who swore to do what he did not intend to do, but afterward did it, whether he was perjured: we say that he committed perjury and sinned mortally, because that oath lacked truth, namely purity of conscience.

[Note: [Col. 1161C] The Master, III, final distinction, section A.] The sixth commandment is: “You shall not covet your neighbour’s house”; the seventh is: “You shall not covet your neighbour’s wife, male servant, or female servant” (Exod. XX), etc. But these two commandments seem to be identical with, or included under, the third, “You shall not commit adultery,” and the fourth, “You shall not commit theft” (*ibid.*). Yet [Note: [Col. 1161C] Augustine, Questions on Exodus, question 71] in those two commandments [Col. 1162A] the actions themselves are identified and forbidden; in these final commandments, desire is forbidden.

By *concupiscence* one sometimes understands a certain quality of the mind which remains after baptism, not as guilt but as punishment, and the first movement which arises from that concupiscence. Neither of these is forbidden here, because if they were forbidden here, since no one can be without them, every person would be a transgressor. What is forbidden is the consent and delight proceeding from the first movement of concupiscence; this consent is understood here by the name *concupiscence*, and is forbidden because it is a mortal sin.

[Note: [Col. 1162C] The Master, section B.] But since here the will to sin is forbidden, it is asked how the usual distinction between law and Gospel can stand: that the law restrains the hand but not the mind. It must be said that this was said of the law with respect to ceremonial matters; or because under the law the will to sin was not punished as it is in the time of grace; or, as the Hebrews explain it: “You shall not covet,” that is, you shall not act outwardly in a way that makes you appear to covet inwardly, whether by sign, act, or word. The law is called the letter that kills because it forbids sin. Hence desire is increased by occasion and transgression is added, because what the law perceived could not be fulfilled without grace. This grace did not abound under the law but in the Gospel, and therefore the letter of the law is said to kill.

[Col. 1161] 261

# TREATISE ON THE INCARNATION

It has now been shown in part how the man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho; how the robbers, setting stumbling blocks beside the road, stripped him of the garments of piety, grace, immortality, and innocence; and how they wounded him and left him half dead. But neither the priest nor the Levite who passed by wished to bring aid to the wounded man (Luke X), because the wounds of the ailing world are cured neither through the priesthood of the Old Testament nor through the mystery—as has been shown—signified by the priest and Levite; the Samaritan alone is indicated.

Therefore he who, with the rod of vigils, keeps watch night and day over the care of his flock, at last stood beside the wounded man: “Made in the likeness of men and found in appearance as a man” (Phil. II). With his help, we shall discuss those matters suited to our inquiry concerning his sandal, by which he approached us with his feet veiled, and shall set them forth as the Holy Spirit grants us.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Lord’s conception, and whether Christ’s flesh was tithed in Abraham

[Col. 1161C]

[Note: [Col. 1162C] Master of the Sentences, book III.] For one who wishes to show the path which the giant of twofold substance ran rejoicing, this way of the Jordan seems, on proper reflection, to require the following order: first, to treat of the entrance upon this way; second, of the progress; third, of the departure. At the entrance were accomplished the first and initial works of our salvation; in the progress, the middle and advancing works; in the departure, the final and consummating works. The first and initial are conception and birth; the middle and advancing are the preaching of the Gospel and the working of miracles; the final and consummating are the Passion, death, and resurrection.

But since the Only-begotten Son of God assumed whole human nature—that is, body and soul, the two things which we understand by the name of nature or humanity—in order to heal it wholly, he assumed in it certain properties of the body, certain properties of the soul, and certain properties belonging to both. Hunger and thirst belong to the body, not because such affections are not in the soul—for every such affection is in the soul—but because they are in the soul only on account of the body. This is clear because without the body it neither hungers nor thirsts [Col. 1163A]. The soul’s properties are the natural and gratuitous goods which Christ assumed. To the composite of soul and body belong birth, death, speech, and similar things which belong only to beings composed of soul and body. Therefore what is said of God’s Only-begotten according to the soul, according to the body, and according to the composite of soul and body on this path must be considered attentively and not passed over without careful observation.

Conception, then, or first birth, is the first work cooperating in our salvation. I call it first birth because a human being has a twofold bodily birth. One is in the womb, when the soul is infused; hence: “That holy thing which is born in you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke I). The other is from the womb, when a human being is brought forth into the light; of this it is said: “A child is born to us” (Isa. IX), etc. Thus Christ’s conception occurred such that Christ’s flesh was conceived, united to the Word, and infused with a soul all at the same time. In other human beings this happens very differently: their bodies are first conceived, and after the body has been formed the soul is infused on the forty-sixth day.

That it was so, hear Augustine [Note: [Col. 1163D] Fulgentius, *On the Faith to Peter*, ch. 18]: “Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, that Christ’s flesh was not conceived in the Virgin’s womb without divinity before it was assumed by the Word; rather, the very Word God was conceived by assuming his flesh, and the flesh itself was conceived by the Word’s incarnation.” This seems, however, to be contradicted by what the same Augustine says on that Gospel passage [Note: [Col. 1163D] *On the Trinity*, book IV, ch. 5; *Eighty-Three Questions*, question 56; and tractate 10 on John]: “Forty-six years,” 262, etc. This number, I say, accords with the perfection of the Lord’s body, because, as physicians say, the form of the human body is completed in so many days. We believe Augustine said this [Note: [Col. 1163D] Solution: the Master, III, distinction 3, final section] because, at the very instant of conception and of the union of God and man, the differentiation of the Lord’s bodily members was so slight and small as scarcely to be subject to human sight. But in the days Augustine mentions it became complete and conspicuous.

The Son of God was united to flesh through the mediation of the soul. For John Chrysostom says [Note: [Col. 1163D] Thus in the Master, distinction 2, section 2, though without naming anyone]: “The divine essence is of such subtlety and simplicity that it was not fitting for it to be united to a body formed from the slime of earth except through a rational essence” [Col. 1163D]. But if someone objects—as seems objectionable—that at Christ’s death the soul was separated from the body, and therefore the Godhead ought to have been separated from the flesh because Godhead and flesh had been united through the soul, we defer this question to what follows, where we shall join its resolution with it.

[Col. 1164A] [Note: [Col. 1163D] The Master, III, distinction 3, section C.] Since the flesh which Christ derived from the Virgin was subject to sin in the Virgin [Note: [Col. 1163D] A free opinion before the definition of the dogma of the Immaculate Conception, but to be rejected today. EDITOR], and in all others in whom it was transmitted through carnal concupiscence, it is asked why Christ was not tithed in Abraham as Levi was (Heb. VII). The solution to this question is as follows. Levi’s flesh was in Abraham in one way in which Christ’s flesh was not. For Levi’s flesh descended from Abraham through carnal concupiscence; Christ’s flesh did not descend under that law, but through the operation of the Holy Spirit.

But it is objected: the authority says [Note: [Col. 1164D] Augustine, *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book X, ch. 20] that only what was healed was tithed in Abraham; but Christ’s flesh was not healed in him, for Levi was born with original sin. Therefore it was not tithed in him. Again, the authority says [Note: [Col. 1164D] Augustine, *ibid.*: “That same flesh had, not only in Abraham but also in the first earthly man himself, both the wound of transgression and the remedy of the wound, etc.”]: “In Abraham’s flesh there was [Col. 1164B] the wound of transgression and the remedy of the wound.” But where the remedy of the wound was, there was no need for a remedy. Therefore that which had the wound of transgression did not need a remedy. Therefore whatever had the wound of transgression there did not need the remedy of tithing, and thus nothing in it was tithed.

Again, Christ’s flesh and Levi’s flesh were materially in Adam; therefore they were there in the same manner. But Levi’s flesh was corrupt there, and all Abraham’s flesh was corrupt; therefore Christ’s flesh also was corrupt. But Levi’s flesh was healed there, and Christ’s was not; therefore Levi’s flesh was there in a better manner than Christ’s. Again, whatever corruption Levi’s flesh had in his forefathers, Christ’s flesh had the same. And afterward Christ’s flesh was in certain persons in whom Levi’s flesh was not corrupt; therefore Christ’s flesh was more corrupted than Levi’s. Yet, conversely, it is proved that Christ’s flesh was not in Abraham, because no part of it was in Abraham. For Abraham did not contain as many atoms as there were persons descending from him through concupiscence.

[Note: [Col. 1164D] The same is found in St Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, III, q. 3, a. 3, final reply.] To this it must be said that the Apostle, wishing to show that Christ’s priesthood is to be preferred to Levi’s priesthood, employs this manner of speaking: “Levi was tithed in Abraham.” Understand the meaning of this expression as follows: the one who receives tithes and blesses is greater than the one who gives and pays them. Therefore Abraham, who gave tithes to Melchizedek, is thereby shown to be inferior to him. In this was also signified that those who were to be born from Abraham—that is, the Levitical order—would be inferior to the future Melchizedek, and thus to Christ, who is understood through Melchizedek. In that first authority, then, “to be healed” is taken to mean “to be blessed,” because Levi was blessed by the Lord, as was signified in that blessing which Abraham received from Melchizedek. What is introduced secondly—“Where the wound of transgression was, there also was the medicine for the wound”—is to be understood thus: some descendants of Abraham [Col. 1165A] were to exist with the transgression of original sin, and Christ’s flesh, likewise deriving from him, was to be the remedy for every sin.

As to the later question, whether Levi’s flesh and Christ’s flesh were there in the same way: we say that neither was there except by seminal principle; and this is more truly not to have been there than to have been there. Thus a tree was not in the seed except seminally; nor was this man’s body in a man’s seed except by seminal principle; nor was the seed in the man, nor even the son’s flesh in the father. If this were so, since the whole flesh of the father was similarly in the third forefather, the whole flesh of the son was in . . . . . and thus it could be proved that all my flesh was in Adam.

If it is asked whether Christ’s flesh was subject to sin, this may be conceded in this sense: namely, flesh which is Christ’s. [Col. 1165B] But this is false when stated thus: “Flesh in Christ was corrupted.” So too “the justification of the righteous person will answer him” means “the righteousness in the righteous person.” [Note: [Col. 1165D] The Master above, § a.] Not only was Christ’s flesh cleansed at the conception, but also the remaining flesh of the Virgin, in whom the tinder of sin was wholly extinguished, so that afterward she could not sin.

But an objection is raised: the Son of God chose her clean; for she was clean when she was chosen. Otherwise her nativity would not be celebrated unless she had been sanctified in the womb. Hence we celebrate the nativity of no saint except the blessed Virgin Mary, blessed John, and Jesus Christ, because all others are born children of wrath. That second cleansing was therefore superfluous. To this we say that she was first so cleansed in the womb as to be without sin, yet capable of sinning; but at Christ’s conception, she was cleansed so that she could not sin at all.

By the angel’s words, and immediately when she said, “Behold the handmaid of the Lord” (Luke 1), she conceived, and not earlier. Hence also the angel’s words, “Blessed is the fruit of thy womb,” must be referred to the future, since she did not yet have the fruit; and the Virgin’s own words, “How shall this be?” and so forth, were spoken more in wonder than in doubt. Or she did not doubt that Christ would be born from her, but she doubted the manner of his birth. Therefore it should be punctuated distinctly, so that there are two words: “Thus, how?” Just as John himself, after the Incarnation, said, “I am not worthy to untie the straps of his sandal” (Mark 1), and so forth.

Again, before the conception the Son of God was in the Virgin only by essence and by indwelling grace; nor afterward was he there in any third way. Therefore he was not in her more excellently afterward than before. Again, in the womb he was only by essence, while in the mind he was both by essence and by indwelling grace; therefore he was there more excellently in the mind. We therefore say that he was in the Virgin more excellently after the conception than before, because he was in flesh taken from her. In that manner he could not be there without also being there by grace; but the converse does not hold.

Again, she alone was worthy for the Son of God to be born from her; therefore she alone merited this; therefore, if he had been born from another, an injury would have been done to her. [Col. 1166A] To this it must be said that, just as Christ’s soul, which was the most excellent of all creatures, could not attain by its merits to be united to the Word of God, much less could the blessed Virgin attain by her merits that the Son of God should be born from her. But when it is read that she “was worthy” or “merited,” this must be understood comparatively, because she was worthier than the rest. For no one existed of such great holiness.

Again, a certain small portion of flesh, by the ministry of the Holy Spirit, was separated from the remaining flesh of the blessed Virgin, and from that small portion the infant was formed. That part was animated by the blessed Virgin’s soul before the infant was formed from it; after the formation, it was animated by Christ’s soul. Therefore it was animated by two souls. Some do not regard this [Col. 1166B] as incongruous. My master, however, says [Note: [Col. 1165D] Book III, distinction 3, § c, as above; see Augustine, *On Genesis*, book X, ch. 20.] that Christ’s flesh was not a part of the Virgin’s flesh, nor was it in her except materially; it descended from her not through carnal concupiscence, and therefore it is not tithed. For two things concur for flesh to be tithed: that it descend by seminal principle and by carnal concupiscence. Christ’s flesh, although it was there materially, did not descend from there through carnal concupiscence. For if Christ’s flesh had been a part of the blessed Virgin, it would rise again in the Virgin, since every part of her will rise in her; and Christ’s flesh began to exist when Christ’s flesh began to exist.

## Chapter VIII. Whether the Son did anything that neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit did; and whether the Father could have become incarnate

[Col. 1166C]

[Note: [Col. 1166D] The Master, III, distinction 1.] Since the Son assumed flesh, but not the Father or the Holy Spirit, it is asked whether the Son did something which neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit did. The objection is made thus: the works of the Trinity are undivided; therefore whatever one of the three persons does, each does. The Son assumed flesh; therefore the Father also did so. [Note: [Col. 1166D] Fulgentius, *On Faith to Peter*, ch. 2, at the end.]

To this it must be said that the whole Trinity effected the incarnation of the Son, and whatever one of the three persons does, each does; nevertheless the Father did not assume flesh. For when it is said, “The Father assumed flesh,” not only what was done is indicated, but also to whom it was done. The meaning of the statement is that he received flesh into his own person, which is false. Therefore there is in the foregoing argument a fallacy of accident, or rather a fallacy of the qualified and unqualified, because first “what” is proposed, but afterward “what and to whom” is assumed. A fallacy: whatever one of these three does, either of the other two does; one dresses himself; therefore the other two do also—namely, suppose that one standing in the middle dresses himself and the other two assist him. Here there is the same fallacy and analogy.

It is further asked whether the Father could assume flesh, [Col. 1167A] because, if he could, and can now do nothing which he could not do, then he can now be a man. Thus the Father and Son can be two men, and thus two [persons] and two substances. Augustine shows that the Father could have become incarnate as follows: [Note: [Col. 1167D] *On the Trinity*, book IV, ch. 21.] “Although the Father could appear through a subjected creature, it would nevertheless be unfitting for him to be said to be sent by the Son whom he begot, or by the Holy Spirit who proceeds from him.” Therefore they say that the Father can be a man other than the Son, yet not another substance, just as the Father is another person than the Son, yet not another substance.

Again, the Son of God could have assumed Peter’s body and soul; therefore, Peter. Therefore he could have made himself to be Peter. A fallacy of the last term. “The name Plato can belong to Socrates; therefore Socrates will be Plato.” Yet, if you examine it closely, the reasoning is correct in the same way. For the Son of God could have assumed Peter’s entire nature and made the name “Peter” applicable to himself; but he could not have made himself to be Peter, because here “Peter” is used to designate the man whom it signifies.

It is also asked whether he could assume one human nature and another—that is, two bodies and two souls. For by “human nature” we understand nothing in Christ except soul and body; and therefore we properly say, “one human nature and another.” If so, therefore he could be one man and another man, and thus each of two men, and thus two men, and consequently several. For if he had assumed two bodies and two souls, would it truly be said, “This man is that man”? It seems so to me: this person is made human, [Col. 1167C] that person is made human; and so this man is that man. [Note: [Col. 1167D] See Epiphanius, heresy 6; Augustine, *City of God*, book XXI, ch. 17 ff.; Jerome, epistle against John of Jerusalem; Gregory, *Dialogues*, book IV, ch. 44, etc.] Thus, if the Son of God now assumed an angelic nature—as Origen testified in the book called *Periarchon*, for the redemption of the devil that was to occur after a thousand years—it would truly be said, “This man is that angel.” But if it were said that there were two, and thus two persons, there would now be two Sons in the Trinity, and hence four persons.

[Note: [Col. 1167D] The Master above, § B.] If it is asked why the Son rather than the Father was incarnate, the reason is ready: so that, just as God created the world in wisdom, according to the words, “Thou hast made all things in wisdom” (Psalm 103), so he might re-create it in the Son, who is the wisdom of the Father; or [Note: [Col. 1167D] Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Dogma*, ch. 2.] so that he who was Son in divinity might be the same Son in humanity. [Col. 1167D] For if the Father or the Holy Spirit were incarnate, there would then be two sons in the Trinity: one according to divinity, the other according to humanity.

## Chapter IX. Whether these propositions are true: “The divine nature assumed the human”; “the divine person assumed the human”

[Note: [Col. 1168D] The Master, III, distinction 5.] Since the Son assumed human nature, namely soul and body, it is asked whether one should concede: “The person assumed [Col. 1168A] nature.” This proposition indeed admits of no doubt, since it is unquestionably true. But did nature assume nature, or person assume person? The question is whether nature assumed person.

Augustine seems to show that nature assumed nature, saying: [Note: [Col. 1168D] Or Fulgentius, *On Faith to Peter*, ch. 2, before the middle.] “That nature which remains eternally begotten from the Father assumed our nature without sin in order to be born from the Virgin.” Here he seems even to say more: that the Father begot the divine nature.

Again, whatever belongs to one of the persons belongs either according to the divine nature or according to the human nature. It belongs to the Son to have been incarnate. Therefore he was incarnate according to the divine nature or according to the human nature. But to have been incarnate is the same as to have become man. Therefore [Col. 1168B] he became man according to the divine nature or according to the human nature. If according to the human, then human nature assumed human nature; if according to the divine, and the Son of God became nothing which he himself is not, then he is man according to the divine nature. But according to the divine nature he is God. Therefore he is man by that by which he is God.

Again, according to the divine nature he assumed human nature; “he was made a little lower than the angels” (Hebrews 2). Therefore according to the divine nature he is lower than the angels. Or: according to the divine nature he assumed human nature; he is also lower than himself. Therefore according to the divine nature he assumed the human. Whatever belongs to one of the three persons according to the divine nature belongs to each of them. Therefore [Col. 1168C] the Father was incarnate according to the divine nature.

To this it must be said that, if the word “according to” denotes the union of the person or its cause, it is true that the Son assumed human nature according to the divine nature—that is, in the divine nature. Or the divine nature was causal, because it is the cause of every good. But if it denotes a condition, it is false: for he did not assume human nature by virtue of the condition of the divine nature.

That the divine nature assumed the human is conceded by the saints and our doctors, because “the Godhead came to us shod.” Yet this seems contradicted by the authority: [Note: [Col. 1168D] Of the Holy Council of Toledo. See also Fulgentius above, ch. 2, etc.] “The whole Trinity effected the incarnation of the Son; nevertheless the Son alone assumed human nature into the unity of person.” Again, [Col. 1168D] the divine nature was incarnate; to be incarnate is the same as to become man. Therefore the divine nature became man. Again, the divine nature assumed the human, and not from eternity. Therefore it did so in time, and thus began to assume human nature: man began to be divine nature. Therefore divine nature began to be man; and thus it is man.

Again, divine nature was incarnate, and the Word, which is divine nature, was made flesh. Therefore divine nature was made flesh. Again, divine nature is identical with man. Therefore it is [Col. 1169A] man. Again, divine nature was incarnate in the Virgin. Therefore it is born, will be born, or was born from the Virgin. Again, divine nature is Christ, and man is divine nature. Therefore divine nature is man. Again, divine nature is this man, namely Christ. Therefore it is man. Again, divine nature is the man who is Christ. Therefore divine nature is some man. Therefore it is man. Again, whatever exists is either man or not-man; divine nature exists. Therefore it is man or not-man. If it is not-man and is one only, then divine nature is nothing that is man; therefore divine nature is not Christ, who is man. It remains, then, that divine nature is man. But if it is so, divine nature is either human nature or of human nature, both of which are false.

Again, [Col. 1169B] divine nature is man by humanity. Therefore humanity is in divine nature; whatever is in divine nature is divine nature. Therefore humanity is divine nature, and hence human nature is divine.

[Note: [Col. 1169D] Thus the Master above, § C.] Therefore they say that divine nature was incarnate and assumed the human; nevertheless divine nature did not become man, nor is it man, because, they say, such language would imply the convertibility of one nature into another, so that one composite nature might result from two. This was asserted by the Timothean heretics. Since both natures are complete in Christ, 266 it must be conceded that the Son became man, because the union of the two natures was made in one person. Thus “became” is accepted here, but by no means there.

[Col. 1169C] Note also that, when it is said, “Christ is man,” it is the same as saying, “Christ is of human nature,” as will appear from what follows; for in the predicate it predicates a possession. Hence, on this account, one must not say, “Divine nature is man,” because it is not human nature or of human nature. For it does not predicate the person simply, as most wish, but with an addition. Hence they accept, “Divine nature is the man who is Christ,” and “this man,” because then it signifies the person; and “man is divine nature,” because in the subject and with an addition, while without an addition it is most often referred to the person. Counterexamples to the foregoing arguments can easily be taken from analogous cases.

If it is asked whether the divine nature assumed two [Col. 1169D] natures, because it assumed the human nature which consists of two, namely the bodily and the spiritual—that is, soul—since the Son of God is united to both soul and body: for this reason we do not admit that he assumed two, because he is not united to either of them separately in the unity of person. For the Son of God is not called body, nor is he called soul, when he is called man.

But someone will press the point more sharply. Since God is in a thing in three ways—by essence, by grace, and by union—and in Christ alone was present by union (whence, as Damascene says, [Note: [Col. 1169D] *On the Orthodox Faith*, book III, ch. 4, in the Master.] “So great was the union of God with man and of man with God that God was called man, and [Col. 1170A] man God”)—why is it not admitted that God is soul, or that God is body, when he is in each by union? For no mode of God’s being in Christ the man can be conceived in which he is not likewise in Christ’s soul and body, since there are no modes other than those stated above. Perhaps it is because, as has been said, he is united simultaneously to soul and body in the unity of person, but in the three stated ways to neither separately. Therefore it is accepted that God is man and man God, but not similarly of soul and body. If anyone resolves it otherwise and better, I do not begrudge him.

Again it is asked: since the Son of God is in Christ the man by union, is the Father in him by union? If so, then just as the Son is man, so the Father is man, since each is [Col. 1170B] in human nature by essence, by indwelling grace, and by union. Thus there is in no way in which the Son is in human nature that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not also in it. Augustine, commenting on John, shows that the Father is in human nature by union: “Just as I, a man, live because of the Father, to whom I am united, so he who eats and is united to me lives because of me.” Otherwise one would have it that the Son is in some thing in some manner in which the Father or Holy Spirit is not, which I judge to be incongruous. Therefore it may be said that the Son of God is in human nature by the union through which that nature is united to him in the unity of person. But the Father is not in it by a union through which it is united to him, for he is not united to human nature [Col. 1170C] in the unity of person, but by the union which he effects, since the whole Trinity effected that union.

## Chapter X. Whether nature assumed person, or person assumed person

[Note: [Col. 1170D] The Master above, §§ D and E.] Much has been disputed concerning these two propositions: “The divine person assumed human nature,” and “the divine nature assumed human nature.” The former is undoubtedly true. That the latter also is true has been demonstrated by arguments and authorities. The order of enumeration therefore compels us to pass to the other two, namely: whether nature assumed person, or person assumed person. These are clearly false, although many arguments are customarily advanced to prove them.

For Christ’s soul was never present without being the part of some man; for it was created in being infused and infused in being created, as other souls are. Thus from Christ’s conception that soul was the part of some man. Likewise that body; and from these two a man is sufficiently 267 constituted. The Son of God assumed these two. Therefore the Son of God assumed some man, and thus a person.

To this they say that neither Christ’s soul nor his body is the part of any man. For neither of the two is or was a part; and as soon as that soul gave life to that body, the Godhead was united to both, body and soul. Nevertheless, [Col. 1171A] the union of flesh to soul was other than the union of the Godhead to those two.

Again, the Son of God assumed a soul, and a soul is a person because [Note: [Col. 1171D] Boethius, *On the Two Natures*, etc.] it is an individual substance of a rational nature; therefore the Son of God assumed a person. But they say [Note: [Col. 1171D] Thus among others the Master here, Hugh of St Victor, *Sentences*, book II, ch. 12; Abelard, etc. See the notes on Pullus.] that, so long as it gives life to a body, the soul is not a person—that is, it is not one by itself, in allusion to the origin of the word—because Christ’s soul was never separated from his body, except during the three days. Hence the Son of God is not said to have assumed a person, because he did not assume the soul separately.

Again, the Son of God assumed man; man was assumed by the Son of God. Therefore [he assumed] some person. That the first two propositions are true is proved by manifold authority. Augustine says: [Note: [Col. 1171D] Cited by the Master as from *On the Creed*, but it is found somewhat differently among Augustine’s sermons, Sermon 129, *On Time*, which is *On Right Faith*; this sermon is not of unquestioned authority and perhaps was not composed by a Catholic doctor.] “If anyone does not say and believe that the man Jesus Christ was assumed by the Son of God, let him be anathema.” Augustine likewise says in several places [Col. 1171B] [Note: [Col. 1171D] Tractate 28 on John; Sermon 8, *On the Words of the Lord*; *On Christ’s Contest*, chs. 11 and 12; *On Faith and the Creed*, 4, etc.] that man was assumed by the Son of God; and the Prophet, speaking of Christ the man, said: “Blessed is he whom thou hast chosen and assumed” (Psalm 64).

Therefore an expression of this kind—“Man was assumed by the Son of God”—whether it occurs in an authority or outside one, must be understood so that the word *man* refers to human nature, that is, to soul and body, and not to a person; although by the force of the expression it is used more for a person. Hence “Man was assumed by the Son of God” is not convertible [with its converse].

But someone will say: by what power could God cause himself to be united to flesh and soul at the conception? Could he not cause the flesh to be conceived first, [Col. 1171C] the soul then to be infused, and afterward the Son of God to be united to both? This would in no way diminish the divine power; nor would this require greater power than the former? Indeed, even if it did require greater power, since this would not derogate from divine majesty and nothing is impossible with God, why could he not do this as well as that? Indeed, could not the Son of God assume a soul alone without a body, or an angel for the redemption of angels?

If he had done so, who would doubt that the Son of God would then have assumed a person, and that the Son of God would have become something, and something would have become the Son of God? For then the angel would have become God and God an angel. If he could have done this, let it be posited that it happened. There is then no question that both person assumed person and nature assumed person.

Hence the objection: the Son of God is something which never existed without being the Son of God; and the Son of God is something which existed when it was not the Son of God, namely that which consists of soul and body, from which there was a man before God was united to it. [Col. 1172A] Therefore the Son of God is not one only, and thus there are two Sons of God, or one and another—contrary to the statement: [Note: [Col. 1171D] Athanasius, in the Creed.] “Yet he is not two but one Christ.”

Again, the Son of God is something; nothing which is not that thing is the Son of God; something has always been the Son of God. Therefore nothing is the Son of God which has not always been the Son of God. But this is false on this position, because that man is the Son of God who existed when he was not the Son of God. Yet it follows from this that something is the Son of God which is not the Father, and that some substance is the Son which is not the Father; thus the Son differs from the Father in substance, and the relation is not reciprocal.

To the foregoing question we know no answer except the one Augustine teaches: “Let us not seek what is not, lest we fail to find what is.” Therefore, since the Son assumed soul and flesh immediately upon their existence, let us not ask what would happen if flesh and soul existed before being assumed. Perhaps this could not have been done.

It is asked what the term *man* predicates when I say, “God became man,” or “God is man”: [Note: [Col. 1172D] The Master, III, distinction 6, § B.] does it predicate a person or an accident? If an accident, it follows that God, insofar as he is man, is not something but is of some kind, just as Socrates, insofar as he is white, is not something but is of some kind. But if it predicates person, it is true that God, insofar as he is man, is a person, a substance, something. Therefore different people understand this proposition differently.

[Col. 1172C] Some say that at Christ’s conception a certain composite substance was made from soul and flesh, which is a true man; and that it began to be God and God began to be it, though neither nature of that person—the divine nor the human—was a person. For it is sufficiently constituted from soul and flesh. To confirm this opinion, they adduce Augustine’s authority. He says: [Note: [Col. 1172D] *On the Predestination of the Saints*, ch. 15, and *Enchiridion*, ch. 36: “What did human nature in the man Christ merit, that it should be singularly assumed into the unity of the person of the only Son of God? What good will? What striving toward a good purpose? What good works preceded, by which that man deserved to become one person with God?” etc. See also *On the Trinity*, book XIII, ch. 17.] “What did that man merit, in order that, assumed by the Word coeternal with the Father into unity of person, he might become the only-begotten Son of God? What merit of his preceded, that he should attain this excellence?”

Others hold that the Son of God, who had previously been simply a person, while remaining at the Incarnation the same person as before, became composite by receiving soul and body as parts of himself. Though he became the person of a man, he nevertheless did not become simply a person. For he remains the same person as before, consisting of two natures, divine and human, whereas before he was a simple person. They likewise adduce Augustine’s authority: [Note: [Col. 1172D] Augustine, ibid.; the Master, III, distinction 7, § a. But what the prudent Master omitted there, this disciple here serves up to surfeit.] “Human nature could thus be [Col. 1173A] joined to the divine, so that one person might be made from two substances, and thus consist of three: namely God, flesh, and soul.”

Many objections are made against both positions. Some substance is Christ, and that substance has always been Christ; some substance is Christ, and it has not always been Christ. Therefore some substance is Christ, and some other substance is Christ; or the same substance has always been and has not always been Christ.

Again, some substance began to be the Son; no substance began, begins, or will begin to be the Father. Therefore some substance began to be the Son, and it is not the Father. Therefore no substance began to be the Son which is not the Son. Therefore some substance is the Son and is not the Father. Therefore the Son differs from the Father [Col. 1173B] in substance; and thus the Father differs from the Son.

Again, that substance which began to be Christ received all the properties of human nature that are not defects of fault or punishment. Therefore a substantial difference began to be in it, namely rationality, by which it differs from every thing of a nature other than man. Therefore that difference makes that substance something other than God, because God is of a different nature from man. Therefore that substance is other than the Father according to that difference. Therefore it is other than the Son and the Holy Spirit. And whatever is other than one of the three persons is other than each of them.

Again, Christ, insofar as he is God, is something; and insofar as he is man, is something. Therefore [Col. 1173C] he is the same or other. If not the same, then Christ insofar as he is God is something, and insofar as he is man is other. Christ is God and man. Therefore insofar as he is God and man, he is one and other. Therefore insofar as he is God and man, he is two.

Again, Christ insofar as he is man is other than God. Therefore insofar as he is man he is other than God. There is one God only, who is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Therefore insofar as he is man, he is other than the God who is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; and thus insofar as he is man he is not that God.

Again, Christ insofar as he is man is other than God. Therefore insofar as he is man he is other than God. Therefore insofar as he is man he is other than Christ, who is God. Therefore [Col. 1173D] insofar as he is man he is not Christ, who is God.

Again, Christ insofar as he is man is other than God. Therefore [he is] another substance or a non-substance; one will not say a non-substance. Therefore insofar as he is man, he is another substance than God; therefore, insofar as he is man, another substance than the divine.

Again, Christ insofar as he is man is other than God, and nothing is insofar as he is man which he himself is not. Therefore Christ is other than God, and Christ is God. Therefore Christ is God and other. Therefore he is one and other. Therefore he is two.

Again, some substance is Christ, and no substance which is not it is Christ. Some substance is Christ which is the Father; therefore no substance is Christ which is not the Father. Some substance is Christ which is composite. Therefore some composite substance, or a substance having parts, is the Father.

Again, one substance alone is both Father and Son; some substance is the Son which was born of the Virgin. Therefore some substance is the Father which was born of the Virgin. Therefore the substance of the Father was born of the Virgin. Thus the divine substance was born, begotten, and crucified.

Again, Christ is a substance which is not eternal. Christ is a substance which began to be. Therefore he is a substance which is not eternal. Nothing is God which is not eternal. Therefore Christ is a substance which is not God.

Again, John Damascene says: [Note: [Col. 1173D] *On the Orthodox Faith*, book III, ch. 3.] “One must not [Col. 1174B] take the common species, that is, *man*, from Christ, but one must take it from Peter.” Therefore “man” is said of Christ in a different sense than it is said of Peter. Therefore, although Christ is man and Peter is man, one must not grant under a single utterance, “Christ and Peter are man,” or “Christ and Peter are men,” just as one does not say, “This and that are dogs,” when the term *dog* belongs to them in different senses.

Again, Christ insofar as he is man is something, some thing, some rational or irrational substance, and thus insofar as he is man he is a rational substance, and thus insofar as he is man he is a person—either the third person in the Trinity or another. If insofar as he is man he is the third person in the Trinity, then insofar as he is man he is God; if another person, then there are more than three persons in the Trinity, since Christ is not any person who is not in the Trinity.

Again, Christ is a substance. Therefore he is simple or composite. If simple, then he lacks parts; therefore he does not have soul and body as parts. If he is a composite substance, then he is not a simple substance, or the same substance is simple and composite.

Again, something which is God began to be something; something began to be God. Therefore God began to be something.

Again, this soul, identified as Christ’s soul, and this body yesterday began to be something; yesterday they began to constitute some composite; and something sufficiently constituted from these two parts, sufficient parts of that composite, began yesterday to be constituted, while no part [Col. 1174D] existed before yesterday. Therefore that composite began yesterday to exist; and thus some composite substance began yesterday to exist. It is identical with the Son of God; therefore the identical thing with the Son of God began yesterday to exist. Therefore the Son of God began yesterday to exist.

Again, the Father is some substance which is man, and thus the Father is a composite substance whose parts are soul and body; thus the Father is a substance having a rational soul and flesh as parts. Therefore the Father is man, because this is what it is to be man.

Again, by some humanity which is in him Christ is something—man or other; not other. Therefore [Col. 1175A] man, and thus this man or another. If Christ is this man by this humanity, then by this humanity he is this person, and thus by this humanity he is God.

Again, Christ is one and not other, or he is both one and other. If one says, “He is one and not other, but he is God,” then he is God and not other; but he is man, therefore not—for if he is man, he is other than God. If one says, “He is one and other,” ask whether he is truly said to be one and other than that which Christ is; and thus one and another are God, and thus each of two is God, because *other* is said at least of two.

[Note: [Col. 1175D] The Master has this, III, distinction 6, § F, etc.] There are still others who think differently on the matters stated above. In the Incarnation of the Word they deny that a person composed of natures exists; indeed, they also deny that any man or any substance composed of soul and flesh as parts exists there. Rather, they say that those two, soul and flesh, are united to the person of the Word in such a way that by those two ultimate [realities] the Word of God was clothed as with a garment and appeared visible to mortal eyes, though formerly invisible. Therefore God is said to have become man for no other reason than that he received the reality of flesh and soul, which he joined to himself in the unity of person—not because those two, or any thing composed of them, is one person with the Word or is the Word.

According to them, when I say, “God became man,” the term *man* joins or predicates a possession. They confirm this by the Apostle’s authority: “And found in appearance as a man” (Philippians 2). For there are different kinds of possessions, as you find written [Col. 1175C] on that apostolic passage, “And found in appearance as a man,” by Augustine. [Note: [Col. 1175D] *Eighty-Three Questions*, q. 73.]

The term *man* may also be used to designate the person made human when it is said, “God became man,” that is, “God was made human,” so that it indicates, as it were, what kind of thing he is. Cassiodorus shows this when he says: [Note: [Col. 1175D] Also cited by the Master, distinction 8, § K.] “He became, so to speak, God made human; yet even in the assumption of flesh he did not cease to be God.” For although he became, or began to be, God made human, he nevertheless did not become, or begin to be, God—just as this man began yesterday to be a good man, yet did not begin to be a man.

Yet many authorities seem to oppose this opinion. For Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1175D] Book II against Felicianus, ch. 11]: “The Son of God is one thing, the Son of man another, but not another [person].” If, therefore, He is one thing and another, then He is both one and another: He is one insofar as He is God, and besides being God He is nothing except man. Therefore, insofar as He is man, He is another. And thus we shall fall into the objections stated above. Likewise [Note: [Col. 1175D] Augustine against Felicianus, ch. 12]: “The Son of God is one thing from the Father, another from the mother.” Likewise [Note: [Col. 1176D] Augustine, Book I, *On the Trinity*]: “Since the Son is both God and man, God is one substance, man another”; all these statements must be referred to nature, so that “God is one substance, man another” means that God is of one substance—that is, nature—and, insofar as He is man, of another. So too Augustine explains the following [Note: [Col. 1176D] Augustine, *On the Trinity*, I, ch. 7]: “Because the form of God received the form of a servant, each (*uterque*) is God, each (*uterque*) is man [both (*utrumque*) are God, both (*utrumque*) are man]; that is, in each nature the same one is God and man.” This cannot be referred to person, since there is no plurality of persons there. Nor should it be said that each nature is God. For God is of another nature, namely the divine; but, insofar as He is man, He is not of another [nature] but of another, namely the human.

I wish you to understand in the same way the saying [Note: [Col. 1176D] Augustine, *On the Gift of Perseverance*, final chapter]: “He who assumed, and that which He assumed, are one person in the Trinity.” The nature which assumed and the nature which was assumed neither divided nor altered the unity of person. Thus it came about that the person who was God in the divine nature was, in the assumed nature, the same unaltered person. The saying familiar on almost everyone’s lips, “Remaining what He was, He assumed what He was not,” must likewise be referred to nature, not person—and to nature in such a way that nature is not called a person, but the person is said to be in a nature.

It is also objected: Christ exists insofar as He is man. Therefore, insofar as He is man, He is something, or some things—not some things; therefore, something. And so He is God, or other than God—not other than God; therefore, insofar as He is man, He is God. Yet no one says this. The solution to the objection is easy once the several meanings of this preposition *secundum* (“according to,” “insofar as”) are distinguished. Sometimes it denotes the condition of a nature, as when I say, “Christ died insofar as He is man,” that is, by the condition of human nature [Col. 1176C]. Sometimes it denotes unity of person, as: “Christ, insofar as man, will judge,” or, “insofar as man, forgives sins,” that is, He Himself, being man, will judge or forgive sins. Sometimes it denotes a cause, as: “Christ rose insofar as He is God,” that is, because He is God, He rose; for that power came from divinity, not humanity [Note: [Col. 1176D] Here the prudent reader should note the foundation of this doctrine for what follows.].

If, therefore, unity of person is meant, it is true that Christ, insofar as He is man, is something—that is, He Himself, being man, is something. But if cause or condition is meant, it is false; for humanity does not make Him a “what,” unless, as some say, we impose by force upon the term *something* a meaning other than that of substance: “insofar as He is man, He is something” [Col. 1176D], that is, of some mode or of some nature.

Likewise: Christ, insofar as He is man, is another. Therefore, insofar as He is man, He is a substance; and thus, insofar as He is man, He is either the same substance as God or another. If the same, then Christ, insofar as He is man, is God; if another, then insofar as He is both God and man, He is both one and another substance.

271. Likewise, Christ is either a simple or a composite substance; both seem true. For He is the same substance as the Father [Col. 1177A]. Since, therefore, the Father is a simple substance, Christ seems to be a simple substance. Yet since Christ is a true man, and therefore has both body and soul like other human beings, He seems to be a corporeal substance and thus to have as parts of Himself soul and body. This is also shown in another way: Christ has as a part of Himself fleshly feet and hands. Otherwise, He would not have a true body, but a phantom body. Thus He is a substance composed of parts. Therefore, since He is man, He has two parts from which He sufficiently consists, namely soul and body. If this is so, the argument proceeds: that soul and that body began to exist and began sufficiently to constitute some composite thing without any extrinsic addition which would make a third part of that composite together with those two. Therefore, something began to exist from those two parts; and that thing began to exist when each of its parts began to exist. And that thing is now God. Therefore, something which is God began to exist.

To this they say that Christ, not insofar as He is man, is a substance; nor is He a composite substance, nor does He have soul and body as parts of Himself, although He assumed them in such a way that He who had previously been invisible appeared visible in them [Note: [Col. 1177D] Walter of St Victor touches upon these points in his book *Against the Four Labyrinths of France*.]. He indeed has a head, feet, and hands, not as parts of Himself, but as parts of the body which is His. For that body, being a composite thing, has parts; but Christ, since He is nothing but simple, has no parts.

[Col. 1177C] [Note: [Col. 1177D] Master, III, distinction 12.] Again it is asked whether that man began to exist, which seems to be proved by the authorities of the saints. Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1178D] Tractate 106 on John]: “At one time the Son of God had what the man Himself, the Son of God, did not yet have, because He was not yet man.” Likewise [Note: [Col. 1178D] The same, Tractate 105 on John]: “As we were elected, so He was glorified. For before the world existed, neither we nor He existed—the Mediator between God and men, Christ Jesus.” Likewise [Note: [Col. 1178D] The same, in the middle of his exposition of Psalm 82]: “Although Christ may be a recent man, nevertheless He is eternal God.” But the contrary is also found: “That child created the stars.” And He Himself says: “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” (John 8). It must therefore be noted here that names suitable to Christ according to His humanity, when placed as subjects, are chiefly used to designate the person. But in the predicate they are sometimes used to designate the person, sometimes to designate a habit or condition [Col. 1177D]. Therefore, just as that person always existed, so that man—that is, that person made human—always existed; but He was not always man. When, therefore, it is said, “That man began to exist,” understand this as said of nature: that is, according to human nature He began to exist. For His soul and body, which we understand under the name of nature, began to exist.
