Yet, as a safeguard against foolishness, one must never answer without qualification; whenever the question is proposed, one should not hesitate, against the importunity of sophists and for the satisfaction of those of lesser understanding, to distinguish whether the discussion concerns nature or person [Col. 1178A].

Likewise, Christ is either visible or invisible substance. If He is visible substance, then He is either visible divine or visible non-divine substance. If He is visible divine substance—since there is no such thing as divine substance that is visible non-divine substance, for then it would be non-divine substance—then divine substance is visible. Thus the divine substance is seen; and so the divine essence is seen, touched, injured, suffers, died, rose again, and was incarnate and born of the Virgin. Why, then, was it not born of the Father? For the name Son accomplishes nothing in humanity by God’s being God which the name Son does not also accomplish in deity; and thus the Father begot the divine essence—a claim refuted in many ways [Col. 1178B] in the *Treatise on the Trinity*. But if he says that Christ is invisible substance, and nothing exists which is not substance, then nothing can be seen which suffered for us on the cross and by whose death we were redeemed; nothing is Christ which the Jews crucified. All this appears absurd.

Likewise, a more difficult objection may be raised concerning those properties which belong neither to soul nor to body nor to divinity, but to the composite of soul and body, such as speaking. Something speaks with me; that thing knows how to speak; in it is knowledge of speaking; in that knowledge is created knowledge. Therefore, something speaks which knows by created knowledge; that thing is God. Therefore, something which is God knows by created knowledge; and so God is something which knows by created knowledge [Col. 1178C], and, by the same reasoning, something which is seen. Likewise, the authority says: “That holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1). Therefore, something was born of the Virgin; that thing is God. Therefore, God is something born of the Virgin.

For this reason some have said that names appropriate to Christ according to humanity, in the masculine gender, are referred to the hypostasis, and in the neuter to the essence of God. Hence they admit: “Christ is passible, mortal, temporal, visible”; but not: “He is a passible thing, a mortal thing, or a temporal thing.” Yet they do not admit: “There is nothing which is Christ that is visible,” because the word *nothing* removes before the word *something* posits. For *something* posits essence, not person; *nothing* [Col. 1178D] removes both person and essence. Hence they challenge this argument: “Christ is not something which is visible; therefore Christ is nothing which is visible.” For it is as though one concluded: “There is no essence or person which is visible.” This is false as regards the person. The fallacy is similar: “Christ is not something which is begotten by the Father; therefore Christ is neither essence nor person begotten by the Father.”

But they are also objected to thus: Christ both knows by created knowledge and knows by uncreated knowledge. Therefore either He is not something which knows by uncreated knowledge [Col. 1179A], or He is something which knows by created knowledge. Fallacy. [Note: [Col. 1179D] See St Thomas, III, question 16, article 7, reply to objection 4.] “This monk will be white, and this monk will be black; therefore either he will not be something that will be white, or he will be something that will be black”—assuming that there will be a white monk and a black monk, but that he will be affected only by whiteness. Likewise: Christ is not something which knows by created knowledge, and He knows by uncreated knowledge. Therefore, He knows only by uncreated knowledge; therefore He does not know by created knowledge. Fallacy of the first figure. “This monk will not be something which will be black; this monk will be a white monk; therefore he will be only a white monk.” Or thus: “This mountain is not something seen by those two, of whom one sees one half and the other the other half. This mountain is seen by these two. Therefore [Col. 1179B] it is seen only by these two”—which is false, indeed it is also seen by those others. Yet some say that the term *something* posits person as well as essence. Hence they admit: “Christ is something which is seen,” that is, some person; and something which is touched and something which dies.

[Note: [Col. 1179D] See Master, III, distinction 8, §B, and distinction 11, §§C and F.] Likewise, Christ insofar as He is man was predestined to be the Son of God, and He is that which He was predestined to be. Therefore Christ, insofar as He is man, is the Son of God. This does not follow, because He is not that which He was predestined to be according to that according to which He was predestined to be it. He is said to be predestined insofar as He is man because God predestined from eternity that He Himself, existing as man, should be the Son of God. Or it can be understood of the nature [Col. 1179C] as predestined, because it was foreseen by God that that nature would be united to the Word of God in unity of person.

[Note: [Col. 1179D] Master, III, distinction 11, §A.] Likewise, insofar as He is man, Christ is a creature which is God, or which is not God. If, insofar as He is man, He is a creature which is God, then insofar as He is man He is God. If, insofar as He is man, He is a creature which is not God, then insofar as He is man He is something which is not God. But nothing is, insofar as He is man, which He Himself is not simply. Therefore Christ is something which is not God.

[Note: [Col. 1179D] Here is sophistical sport, and a rich crop of material for Walter to speak against both Peters, Lombard [Col. 1180D] and of Poitiers.] To this it must be said that Christ, insofar as He is man, is a creature, but not a creature which is or which is not [Col. 1179D]; for after that expression no relative clause, whether nominal or pronominal, is to be admitted unless the phrase *insofar as* denotes unity of person. Likewise, by the word *what?* one asks concerning substance; and to a question put about Christ with the word *what?*, “man” is fittingly and truly answered: “What is Christ?” “Man.” This is answered by denial. For to “What is Christ?” I do not truly answer, “Man.”

[Col. 1180A] Likewise, Christ is God and man. It is asked whether the term in this statement predicates substance. This seems provable by grammatical reasoning: otherwise, unless both the term *God* and the term *man* were used substantively, they could not be joined to one another by a conjunction; or unless both were taken adjectivally. For an adjective in meaning is not suitably joined to its subject: no one says, “This man is grammatical,” but “a grammatical man.” By the same reasoning it seems one ought to say, “Christ is God-man,” that is, God made human, so that the word *man* is taken adjectivally; not, “Christ is God and man,” when one name is used substantively and the other, as it were, adjectivally. Or, if that is said properly, it is asked whether Christ was God and man, or whether Christ is God and man [Col. 1180B]. One appears to be said improperly, the other falsely. Therefore they say that both words are used, as it were, adjectivally, so that the sense is: Christ is God and man, that is, of divine and human nature.

Likewise, it is a rule of dialecticians that a name used equivocally of several things makes false a proposition in which it is said of them under one utterance—for example: “A barking animal and a sea-monster are dogs”; for a single utterance cannot retain two meanings. By the same reasoning, since *man* is said differently of Christ and Peter, it seems one should not grant, “Both Christ and Peter are man.” For of Peter it predicates a substance [Note: [Col. 1180D] Here “substance” is taken for a supposit, or for a nature ultimately complete and possessing its own subsistence.]; of Christ, a habit. Indeed, it seems one should grant, “Christ alone is man,” since the name *man* belongs to Him alone in the sense in which it is said of Him [Col. 1180C]. But theologians do not always observe this rule, because neither do dialecticians. Thus Aristotle says in the book of the *Categories*: “If someone should call them animals,” speaking of a real animal and a painted one, of which the term *animal* is used equivocally.

Likewise, the Son of God is only that which He alone was from eternity. From eternity He was only God, and the Son of God is God. Therefore He is only God. Therefore He is not God and man; or, therefore, He is not man. Fallacy of the first figure. “You are only that which you alone were yesterday: yesterday you were only a grammarian; now you are a grammarian; therefore you are only a grammarian.” No: indeed you are also a musician, assuming that you have only now become a musician. Likewise [Col. 1180D], assuming that the Son of God now first becomes man, the Son of God was a non-man who either was Himself and is, or was Himself and is not. He will not say, “who was and is not,” for it would then follow: “therefore He was a non-man who Himself ceased to exist,” and thus He was something which Himself ceased to exist. It remains, therefore, that the Son of God was a non-man who Himself was and is, and thus He was a non-man who Himself is. Hence the argument proceeds: “The Son of God was a non-man whom He Himself is; the Son of God is only that which the Father is, and the Father is non-man; therefore the Son of God is non-man.” Perhaps someone seeking evasions [Col. 1181A] will say that he is not bound to answer these quibbles, because theologians, like dialecticians, admit infinite names such as *non-man*, *non-God*, and the like. But let him hear Augustine [Note: [Col. 1181D] Book V, *On the Trinity*, chs. 6 and 7], who uses such names, saying “unbegotten” and, what is more, “not Son” and “not Father”; nor should he be surprised on hearing “non-man.” Fallacy concerning the preceding argument: “Yesterday you were a non-grammarian which you yourself are; you are only that which you were yesterday; yesterday you were a non-grammarian; therefore now you are a non-grammarian.” For just as *man* is quasi-accidental when said of God, so *grammarian* is when said of man.

Likewise, assuming that Christ is being born now, some man is being born. Therefore some man begins to live, and thus something begins to live [Col. 1181B]. Therefore that thing did not live; that thing is God. Therefore that which is God did not live. Therefore it was not living, and thus was not God. By the same reasoning, assuming we are at the moment when He died, some man dies. Therefore something dies. Therefore something ceases to live. Therefore [274] that thing lived and will not live; and thus that which is God will not live. Or: something ceases to live; therefore it is either God or not God. If it is not God, and only one thing ceases to live, then nothing which is God ceases to live; and thus no man who is God. It must therefore be said that Christ lives by the divine life which He Himself is, by which He always lived and always will live; and by the human life which is in Him while He has soul and body. And because the union which joins soul to body is now dissolved, He now dies—that is, He ceases to live the human life—yet He does not cease to live. Fallacy. “This man forgets some knowledge; therefore he ceases to know some knowledge.” The similarity is explicit: just as Christ is said to die with respect to the other life, namely the human life by which He ceased to live (whence it does not necessarily follow that He ceased to live, for that would mean that He ceased to live by both lives), so this man is said to forget some knowledge because he knows something which he will not know. Yet it does not follow that he now ceases to know some knowledge [Col. 1181C], which cannot be true unless he ceases to know everything which he knows.

Likewise, Mary has some property by which she is called mother in relation to her son; therefore the son has some property by which he is called son in relation to his mother. But what is that property except filiation? Therefore, by filiation, He is the son of the Virgin. But against this: that filiation is not in deity, because no temporal form can accrue to deity; nor is it in the soul, because a soul cannot be a son; nor is it in the flesh, because flesh is not a son; nor is there anything constituted there from soul and flesh in which it may be. Therefore He is not the son of the Virgin by filiation. To this it can be said that Christ is called the son of the Virgin, yet not by filiation. Just as the divine essence is Father, yet is not Father by paternity [Col. 1182A], and God is Creator, yet is not Creator by creation. Fallacy of the first figure. “In a creature there is some property by which it is called creature in relation to the Creator; therefore in the Creator there is some property by which He is called Creator in relation to the creature.” Or it may be said that filiation is in the flesh; yet that flesh is not called son by that filiation, but the Son of God is called son of the Virgin by that filiation, as appears from a parallel. Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1181D] Augustine has something similar in Book V, *On the Trinity*, ch. 16, etc. See Master, I, distinction 30, §§A and C]: “The accident by which He is called Creator is in the creature and not in the Creator; yet the creature is not called Creator according to that accident, but God is called Creator according to it. Likewise, the temporal sending by which the Spirit is sent to sanctify the creature is in the creature and not in the Holy Spirit; yet the creature is not said to be sent.”

[Col. 1182B] [Note: [Col. 1181D] Master, *Sentences*, III, distinction 8, §B. See Damascene, Book III, *On the Faith*, ch. 3, middle of chapter.] Likewise, Christ was born once from the Father and once from the mother, and not by the same birth. Therefore by two births, and thus He has two births, and thus was born twice. Therefore He is not born daily by eternal birth, or He was going to be born by it more than once. Therefore we say that He had two births and was born twice, though some have not improperly denied this last statement. For the adverb seems to indicate that both births are complete.

[Note: [Col. 1182D] Master, III, distinction 12, §§C and D.] Likewise, He could have failed to assume that soul and that body which He assumed. Those two could have constituted some man whom they did not constitute; that man could have been not God, and thus could have sinned. To this it must be said that, if the discussion concerns the person [Col. 1182C], it is certain that that man could not have sinned; but if it concerns nature, it is true that the nature itself, not united to the Word of God—which could have occurred—could have sinned. But that it should be united to God and sin could by no means have been possible.

[Note: [Col. 1182D] Master, III, distinction 10, §§D and E.] Likewise, Christ is son of the Virgin by human or by divine nature—not by divine nature; therefore by human nature; therefore by grace; therefore He is the adoptive son of the Virgin; therefore He was first a son and afterward adopted as a son—which is false. One must by no means say that the Son of God is an adoptive son, although He is son of the Virgin by grace. Fallacy. “God confers some grace upon this unbeliever; therefore he is the adoptive son of God.” The reason why He is not an adoptive son has been stated: from the beginning He possessed the fullness of all graces [Col. 1182D] (John 1), because “He was anointed with the oil of gladness above His companions” (Psalm 44), and “the Spirit of wisdom and understanding,” etc., rested upon Him (Isaiah 11).

[Note: [Col. 1182D] Master, III, distinction 14, §§C and D.] Likewise, whatever the Son of God has by nature insofar as He is God, the Son of man has by grace insofar as He is man. But insofar as He is God, He has omnipotence by nature. Therefore, insofar as He is man, He has omnipotence by grace. Thus, insofar as He is man, He has omnipotence—which is false. Therefore note [Col. 1183A] that “to have omnipotence by nature” denotes two things: what the man has, and how he has it. The cause of both is deity. Similarly, “to have omnipotence by grace” denotes two things; human nature is the cause of one of them, namely the mode of having it by grace, but is not the cause of the other, namely the thing possessed or its possession. For human nature is not the cause why He is omnipotent, but why it is by grace that He is united to God. Thus, if grammatical idiom allowed the sentence to be uttered without repeating the verb, it would be said: “Whatever the Son of God has insofar as He is God by nature, the Son of man insofar as He is man by grace,” so that the phrase *insofar as* would denote the cause of the mode, not of the thing possessed. Hence this argument must be challenged: “Christ, insofar as He is man, has omnipotence [Col. 1183B] by grace; therefore, insofar as He is man, He has omnipotence.” Fallacy. “Christ began to have omnipotence by grace; therefore He began to have omnipotence.” That the first premise is true is shown thus: Christ has omnipotence by grace; He has not had it by grace from eternity; therefore He began to have it by grace.

## Chapter XI. Whether Christ, by created wisdom, knew everything which He knew by divine wisdom

[Note: [Col. 1183D] Master, III, distinction 14, §B: “We say that Christ’s soul, by wisdom freely given to it in the Word of God to whom it is united—and therefore it understands perfectly—knows everything that God knows.”]

When Christ assumed soul and body, He assumed the defects of each which He ought to assume, and it was fitting that He should assume all the properties of each. Thus He had created wisdom—which properly belongs to the soul—by which He was wise; and by it He knew whatever He knows by uncreated wisdom [Col. 1183C], which is what He Himself is, because Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are wise from eternity. It is objected: Christ’s soul knows whatever God knows, and cannot know more perfectly than it knows. Therefore it is equal to God in knowledge. Therefore the Creator does not have greater sufficiency than the creature in every good. We say that the first argument is false because, although Christ’s soul knows whatever God knows, it does not know as penetratingly as God does; and the fact that it knows all things it itself has from God, and therefore is not equal to Him. Thus this man possesses as many and as precious things as that man, yet is not equal to him in riches because he possesses all these things from him.

[Note: [Col. 1184D] Master, III, distinction 13.] Likewise, it is asked whether Jesus advanced in human wisdom [Col. 1183D], and therefore was wiser at one time than another. This seems supported by the words of the Gospel: “Jesus advanced in age and wisdom” (Luke 2). Isaiah too, speaking of Christ, says: “Before the child knows how to name father or mother, he will receive the spoils of Samaria” (Isaiah 8). Here he seems to imply that Christ too was ignorant of something, which is far from the truth. But Jesus is said to have advanced in wisdom just as a bishop advances in his bishopric, because many persons advanced through his preaching and teaching; or because in human opinion [Col. 1184A] He seemed to advance, and behaved as though He did not know father and mother, though He possessed knowledge of all things, even beyond human wisdom. Hence Jeremiah says of Him: “The Lord will make a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man in the womb of her womb” (Jeremiah 31). For from the beginning of His birth He was a man, not in age, but in perfection of wisdom.

Likewise, before the Incarnation Christ was wise only by eternal wisdom; in the Incarnation He began to be wise by human wisdom and did not cease to be wise by divine wisdom. Therefore He was wiser after the Incarnation than before. Fallacy. God ought to have been loved before He was incarnate only because He was God; afterward He ought to have been loved because He was man, and did not cease to be loved because He was God. Therefore He ought to have been loved more after than before. Or [Col. 1184B]: this man was warmed yesterday by one heat alone, namely that of medicine; now he is warmed both by the heat of medicine and by that of the sun. Therefore he is warmer than before.

Likewise, whatever God knows, Christ’s soul knows. God knows how to create the world and Christ’s soul. Therefore Christ’s soul also knows how to create the world and itself. [Note: [Col. 1184D] Master, III, distinction 14, §B.] Likewise, God knows how to create the world, and Christ’s soul either knows or does not know the same thing. If it knows the same thing, then Christ’s soul knows how to create the world; but if it does not know the same thing, then God knows something which Christ’s soul does not know. To this it must be said that the verb *knows*, with infinitives of this kind, denotes a certain ability to perform the thing signified by the verb, belonging to the thing under discussion. Thus, “this man knows how to dispute,” that is, he has a certain ability by which he is qualified [Col. 1184C] to dispute. But it must not be granted that Christ’s soul knows how to sin, for it cannot sin. Nevertheless, it knows sin—that is, it has knowledge to which every sin is subject; and it knows how to create the world, that is, it has knowledge of the created world; and it knows how to create itself, that is, it knows how it was created. [Note: [Col. 1184D] Master, III, distinction 14, §C.] If it is asked why the soul was not given power without measure as it was given knowledge, the reason is that it is naturally capable of knowledge but not naturally capable of power; and therefore it was given without measure that of which it is naturally capable.

## Chapter XII. Whether Christ had charity in the mode of the wayfarer or in the mode of the homeland: in which matters concerning Christ’s charity are determined

[Col. 1184D]

[Note: [Col. 1184D] Master, III, distinction 23, and distinction 26, §C.] Just as Christ’s soul has knowledge without measure, which is a gratuitous gift, so it has the four cardinal virtues; it also has charity, than which none is more perfect. But it neither has nor had faith and hope, because it did not have charity in the mode of the wayfarer but in the mode of the homeland; and where there is perfect knowledge, there is no faith; likewise, where there is certainty of the thing, there is no hope. But it is objected: Christ believed and hoped. Hence: “In thee, O Lord, have I hoped” (Psalm 30), and “I believed, therefore I spoke” (Psalm 115). Therefore [Col. 1185A] He had faith and hope. Fallacy. “Peter, who is in the homeland, believes and hopes for the resurrection of bodies; therefore he has faith and hope.” Likewise, Christ had ordered charity. Therefore He loved God more than Himself, and His neighbor as Himself. But He Himself was God; therefore He loved Himself more than Himself, and His neighbor as God. Therefore He had disordered charity. Likewise, Christ was a true and supreme teacher. Therefore He possessed charity in the order in which He taught that it should be possessed, or else He did not possess it or teach it rightly. But He taught that it should be possessed in this order: first God should be loved, second one’s own soul. Therefore He had charity in this way. Therefore He loved Himself as God more than Himself as man. Likewise, Christ did what He taught, and conversely; and He taught or did nothing which He could not do or teach [Col. 1185B]. He taught that God ought to be loved more than one’s own person; therefore He loved God more than Himself. Likewise, Christ had perfect charity. Therefore He perfectly loved His neighbor. Therefore He loved his neighbor toward that end toward which He loved Himself. But He loved Himself for no other end or because of anything else except because He Himself was God. Therefore He loved His neighbor in order that he might be God; but it was impossible that the neighbor should be this. Therefore the neighbor was not to be loved in that way. Likewise, Christ had charity in the mode of the homeland, not in the mode of the wayfarer. Therefore He did not have it in order to merit, because the homeland is not a place of meriting but of receiving. Therefore Christ did not merit by the charity He had. Likewise, Christ had charity while on the way in order to merit; in the homeland He did not have it for this purpose, because then He could not merit. Therefore while on the way He had it for a different use than in the homeland [Col. 1185C].

For the solution of the preceding arguments, it must be said that Christ loved with charity no one whom He did not know to be predestined to life. He had ordered charity in that He loved Himself insofar as He was God more than He loved Himself insofar as He was man, and loved His neighbor as Himself—that is, toward that end toward which He loved Himself, though not toward every end, nor toward this end: that the neighbor should be united to the Word of the Father in unity of person. Christ was on the way, however, not in the way other human beings are. For to be on the way properly means to be on a journey of return to the homeland, whether through penitence or otherwise; and the expression was drawn from the children of Israel, leaving Egypt and coming to the land of promise, that is, Jerusalem. For we too, departing from Egypt—that is, from the affliction [Col. 1185D], sorrow, or darkness of this age—seek the future city, namely Jerusalem, the vision of peace, having no abiding dwelling-place (Hebrews 13). But Christ was not on the way in this sense, because he who did not depart did not return. Christ did not depart, because He had no sin, either actual or contracted. Yet He was on the way, that is, in the course of mortality and passibility, because “He rejoiced as a giant to run His course” (Psalm 18), and “He drank of the brook in the way” (Psalm 109). Those who lack charity are not on the way, because they do not find the way to the city of habitation; indeed, they are pathless. Nor is it surprising that Christ could merit from charity on the way what He could not merit [Col. 1186A] in the homeland. For the same is true even of other human beings.

Likewise, Christ always had equal charity. Therefore, all whom He loved, He loved with equal charity. Therefore He loved His mother and Peter with equal charity. Therefore He had disordered charity, because even among neighbors a distinction must be made, since parents ought to be loved more than others. Likewise, He loved Peter once with charity; therefore He always did so, including when Peter sinned mortally. But Peter then did not love God. Therefore he was then not worthy to be loved by God. Likewise, God loves every creature of His, who hates none of the things which He made. Therefore He loves Judas—either with temporal or eternal love. If with eternal love, then with charity, and thus unto life; if with temporal love, then temporal love [Col. 1186B] existed in Christ. Likewise, Christ loves this elect person who now lacks charity and is not presently worthy to be loved; and He does not love that reprobate person who nonetheless has charity and is worthy to be loved. Thus He loves one not worthy to be loved and does not love one worthy to be loved; therefore He loves disorderly. Likewise, He bestows greater charity on one for whom He prepared a lesser crown than on another for whom He prepared a greater crown; and the smallest increase of charity surpasses all gifts which can be conferred upon a human being in the present life. Therefore He loves the former more than the latter. Yet, on the contrary, from eternity He prepared a greater good for the latter than for the former. Therefore from eternity He loved the latter more; and whomever He loved from eternity He loves now. Therefore now He loves the former more than the latter. Likewise, this person loves God more [Col. 1186C] than that one, and whoever loves more ought to be loved more. Therefore this person is loved by God more than that one—which is false, because a greater good has been prepared for that other.

Likewise, from eternity God willed that grace should in time be bestowed upon this man; and for God to bestow grace upon him is to love him. Therefore God loved this man from eternity. Therefore He did not hate him from eternity—which is false. For He loved Jacob from eternity, but hated Esau. Yet this man is reprobate, although he is now good. Likewise, Peter was at one time better and at another time less good; and the authority says: “He who loves more is loved more.” Therefore, since when he was better he loved more, when he was less good he was loved less. And Christ never [Col. 1186D] loved Peter except with charity; therefore at one time He loved Peter with greater charity and at another with lesser. Therefore He did not always possess equal charity. Likewise, Christ at one time loved Judas with eternal love, and Judas then loved Him with charity. Therefore Judas was then worthy to be loved with eternal love. Therefore he was then worthy to be loved eternally by God. Therefore God too then loved him eternally.

It is difficult to derive a solution to the foregoing objections unless the multiple meanings of the word *to love*, as used of God, are distinguished. One must therefore know that this word *to love*, when said of a human being, can denote two things: either an inward affection, [p. 278] or an outward effect. Thus, when it is said, “This man loves that man,” it may be understood that he is moved, by a motion proceeding [Col. 1187A] from charity, to love him—which pertains to inward affection; or that he provides him with temporal benefits—which pertains to an outward effect. [Note: [Col. 1187D] See the Master, dist. 32.] When, therefore, this word *to love* is said of God according to the divine nature, it does not denote some motion existing in God, since nothing of that sort belongs to the divine essence; rather, it denotes the effect of God’s love—that is, of the love which is God. Hence, when it is said of God, this verb may be assigned as many meanings as there are effects of divine love. And because there are three notable signs of it—namely, preserving in its own being; bestowing grace in time; and predestining to life—when it is said, “He loves this man,” if love is taken according to the divine nature, one of these is meant: either that He preserves him [Col. 1187B] in his own being, and in this way loves every creature of His; or that He bestows grace, which He does only upon rational creatures, though not upon all, but upon both elect and reprobate; or that He has predestined him to life, which He does only for rational creatures. This last is the chief love, and it alone permits us to say that God always loved Jacob and Peter: from eternity, when Peter was in mortal sin, and before Peter existed in any way whatever. By such propositions the divine essence is affirmed, while a certain effect in creatures is implied. For “God loved Peter from eternity” is equivalent to saying: “God is God, whose will ordained that grace should be bestowed on Peter in time and a crown conferred upon him in the future.” And it is solely on account of this love that [Col. 1187C] God is said to love anything with charity, since He has never loved with charity anyone whom He has not always loved, and whom He has not loved unto eternal life.

Conversely, on account of the other two loves one must not say that God loved Judas, or an irrational creature, from eternity, or that He loved them with charity. Indeed, He loved them with no love, neither temporal nor eternal; for the ablative construction would appear to attribute something to God. But by such a proposition an attribution is made rather to the creature than to the Creator. Only the term is stated, as when I say, “God created all things.” Some, however, say that in such a proposition, as in the preceding one, the divine essence is principally predicated and an effect implied, so that the sense is: “God [Col. 1187D] loved Judas from eternity,” that is, “God is God, to whom it pleased from eternity that Judas should exist in time and that grace should be bestowed upon him.” Others say that neither this proposition nor the other proves anything except the term alone; they proceed more cautiously, though not quite so truly.

It is customary to ask whether that natural motion by which the Lord loved His mother was meritorious for Him. To this it should be said that, considered in itself, it was not meritorious; but if it was formed by charity, it was meritorious. It is also customary to ask whether the Lord loved Peter more than John. It seems that He loved John more, because John drank more fully from the fountain of the Lord’s breast [Col. 1188A]; and it is written of him: “He is a virgin chosen by the Lord and more beloved than the rest,” and he was His cousin. Hence, if Christ observed that order of charity which Ambrose teaches [Note: [Col. 1187D] On that passage of Song of Songs 2: “He has ordered charity in me.”], He was bound to love John more, by reason of kinship, than Peter, to whom He was not joined by a line of blood. For, although there were only twelve apostles in His fellowship, five of them were relatives of the Lord.

On the other hand, He seems to have loved Peter more, because He appointed him prince of the apostles and gave him the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Therefore almost everyone says that He loved John more familiarly, but Peter more—that is, with greater affection—as one by whom He was more loved. Yet Augustine says, on John [Note: [Col. 1187D] Augustine, final tractate on the Gospel of John, near the end [Col. 1188D].], that John signifies [Col. 1188B] the contemplative life and Peter the active life; and thus that He loved John more than Peter, because He loved the former life more than the latter. Yet, literally, He loved Peter more than John. [Note: [Col. 1188D] Master, III, dist. 31, § D.] For Christ was not bound by the order of charity observed on the way, since He possessed the charity proper to the homeland. [p. 279] Nor is John said to have drunk more fully than the others because he knew more. For then perhaps he would have loved more—for he who knows more loves more—but because at the supper he was physically nearer the Lord than Peter, who was somewhat farther away. Thus, when the Lord had said that one of them would betray Him, Peter, unable to ask the Lord privately who would betray Him because he was distant [Col. 1188C], signaled to John, who sat beside the Lord, that he should ask Him; and John did so, as though inclining toward the Lord’s ear. It was for no other reason that at supper he is said to have reclined upon the Lord’s breast. Indeed, even if he knew more, he did not therefore love more; for this is understood of those who are in the homeland, or it refers to aptitude: one more apt to know is more apt to love.

It is therefore evident from the foregoing that in God, insofar as He is God, there is no affection and no motion; and that He loves with charity no one except one predestined to life—just as neither those who are in the homeland, nor even someone still on the way to whom it has been revealed who are predestined and who are reprobate, if perhaps anyone on the way possesses this knowledge, loves with charity anyone else.

But it should be observed that the name *charity* signifies three things [Col. 1188D], which must here be distinguished: sometimes the Holy Spirit, or, according to others, a virtue of the soul; sometimes a motion of the soul proceeding from its cause; sometimes a work of charity, as when it is said: “No one has greater charity,” etc. (John 15). Therefore Christ always had the fullness of charity and could neither advance nor decline in it. Hence it is true that with the same charity—which could neither be intensified nor diminished—He loved all the elect, yet some more and some less according to the difference of rewards He was to bestow: just as the sun, with the same heat, which is neither intensified nor diminished, warms Indians and Britons [Col. 1189A], yet warms the latter more than the former, because, as there is no variation in the sun but in the regions according to their position, so there is no variation in God’s love but in those who love God. [Note: [Col. 1189D] See the Master, III, dist. 72.]

Yet it may be granted that Christ loved one person with greater charity than another—that is, that He was moved by a more intense motion of charity to love Peter than Linus. For there were unequal motions of charity in Christ, proceeding from the same charity while it remained unmoved. It is true that Christ at one time loved Peter when Peter was not worthy to be loved, and did not love Judas, who was worthy to be loved. Nevertheless, He did not possess disordered charity, for, as was said, *to love* is used equivocally.

If it is asked whether Christ was moved by an inward motion of charity [Col. 1189B] to love Peter when Peter was better, and this is granted because it is plausible, then the same objection is made concerning Peter, who is in the homeland: that he is now moved by a greater motion of charity to love this man than tomorrow, when that man will be less good. Thus, in those who are in the homeland, the motion of charity varies daily according to the changing merits of human beings. To this it should be said that Christ was moved by no motion arising from charity to love anyone according to present righteousness, except according to that righteousness in which he was to depart and according to which he was to be rewarded. For He knew concerning every person with what reward he would be rewarded. Thus the motions of charity in Him did not vary: although one was greater than another, none was greater at one time than at another. The same applies [Col. 1189C] to Peter.

## Chapter XIII. Whether Christ merited equally by all His works

[Note: [Col. 1189D] Master, III, dist. 18.] Since Christ merited by His charity, and was moved by a greater motion of charity to love His mother than Peter, therefore He merited more by that motion than by this, because greater motion brings greater merit. Likewise, Christ loved only the predestined; we are bound to love both reprobate and predestined persons. Therefore we are bound to possess a more ample charity than Christ had. This may [p. 280] have force also in the case of those who are in the homeland. Likewise, by more meritorious works Christ merited more in the Passion than before it, and performed more meritorious works. Therefore [Col. 1189D] He merited more. Likewise [Note: [Col. 1189D] In the chant *Exsultet*, Holy Saturday, in the blessing of the Paschal candle.]: “To have been born would have profited nothing, had redemption not taken place.” Therefore, by redeeming He merited more than by being born. Therefore He merited more by this work than by that.

That one motion of charity in Christ was more intense than another is clear because this was so in the motions of His will. For unless He had willed to be crucified by a greater motion of will [Note: [Col. 1189D] The same is found above, dist. 3, ch. 24.] than to speak with the Samaritan woman, He would not have said: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover” (Luke 22), etc. Likewise, Christ merited as much by one work [Col. 1190A] as by any other. Therefore He merited as much by speaking with the Samaritan woman at the well as by the work of His Passion; but by the work of His Passion He merited for us the opening of the gate and entrance into paradise; therefore also by the work of conversation.

That He merited by speaking with the woman is shown thus: every one of His actions was instruction for us; He directed every work He did to our salvation. Therefore He did everything He did from charity. Therefore He merited by every work He did. Likewise, Christ merited as much by one work as by any other. Therefore one work of His was as sufficient for our redemption as any other; or therefore one work of His was as necessary as another. Likewise: “Where the struggle is greater, there the crown is greater.” Christ struggled and labored more in the Passion [Col. 1190B] than in any other work. Therefore He merited more by that work than by any other. Augustine also shows this as follows [Note: [Col. 1189D] Augustine, Tractate 104 on John; Book II against Maximinus, ch. 5; and Book III, ch. 2.]: “The humility of the Passion was the merit of exaltation; exaltation, the reward of humility.”

On the other hand, it is proved that all Christ’s works were equally meritorious. Likewise, He merited a greater reward by one work than another, and none of His works was meritorious except by charity. Therefore one of His works proceeded from greater charity than another. Therefore at one time He had greater charity and at another lesser; and He advanced and grew lukewarm in charity.

To the foregoing it must be said that Christ merited for Himself and for His own; and whatever He merited for Himself, He merited from the first moment of His conception, in which He had such fullness of graces [Col. 1190C] that He could advance in nothing. Hence Gregory says [Note: [Col. 1190D] Homily 6 on Ezekiel. This, however, was said by the Master according to Gregory’s sense, not in Gregory’s actual words.]: “He did not merit more by the gibbet of the cross than previously, from His conception, by the grace of virtues.” For from that moment He merited for Himself the glorification of the body and the impassibility of the soul through charity, which He possessed so fully that He could not afterward possess it more fully. [Note: [Col. 1190D] Master, III, dist. 18, § A.]

But by the work of His Passion He merited for us the opening of the gate, the redemption of souls from the devil, from sin, and from punishment, and the unlocking of the kingdom: so that, when the fiery sword was removed, entrance might freely lie open, and when the bond written by the Father was cancelled—namely, that no one should present himself before His presence unless such humility of obedience should be found in some human being as the pride of disobedience found in Adam.

[Col. 1190D] But whether He also merited this for us before the Passion is asked here. For it is maintained on authority: “To have been born would have profited nothing, had redemption not taken place.” Thus, by the work of His birth or conception He merited nothing for us, but only by the Passion. On the other hand: whatever Christ did in human nature, He bent toward our salvation and did for us from the love He had toward us; and that love could neither fail nor increase. Therefore, with as great charity as [Col. 1191A] He deigned to be born of the Virgin for us, with that same charity He deigned to suffer on the cross for us. Therefore He merited as much for us by this work as by that, or He merited for us by neither of them. Likewise, from His conception He had as great obedience and as great a will to suffer for His members as when He came to endure death. Therefore He merited as much for His members from His conception as in the Passion. Therefore He merited as much by being born as by suffering. Likewise, He did no work from greater charity, either for Himself or for us, than another; and nothing is meritorious except through charity. Therefore He merited nothing, either for Himself or for us, by one work that He did not merit by every other work.

Yet, on the other hand, authority maintains that equal merit depends upon equal will. [Col. 1191B] Hence one may infer that unequal [p. 281] merit depends upon unequal wills; and so one may maintain that, because He willed to suffer with a more intense will than to speak with the Samaritan woman, He merited more by that work than by the other. But if He merited more by this than by that, those works did not proceed from an equal root of charity. Likewise, He willed to suffer more than to speak with the Samaritan woman, and He willed both from charity. Therefore He willed this more from charity than that. Therefore He willed this from greater charity than that. For one motion of will does not seem more intense than another, when both are performed in charity, unless the motion of charity from which the greater motion of will proceeds is also more intense than the motion of charity from which the lesser motion of will proceeds. If this is so, the work proceeding from a lesser motion of will [Col. 1191C] and a lesser motion of charity is less meritorious than the work proceeding from a greater motion of charity and a greater motion of will. For where motion is greater or more intense, whether of charity or of will, merit is greater.

But who will say that Christ willed whatever works He willed with equal motion of will and equal motion of charity, and thus say that by all works He merited equally for Himself? Who also will say that Christ willed one work with greater will, such as suffering, and another with lesser motion of will, such as speaking with the Samaritan woman, and yet loved those two works with equal motions of charity? A contradiction would follow. For because the motions of charity in those works would be equal, the merits would be equal; but because the motions of will would be unequal, the merits would be unequal. For, as authority holds that “equal merit depends upon equal charity,” so also it holds that unequal merit depends upon unequal will. If anyone here possesses a solution worthy of the question, God has revealed it to him. It is enough for me, therefore, to have set forth the starting-point of doubt, although it is not easy for me to impart the brightness of a solution, since I have heard it from no one.

But the assertion, “He merited through more works, therefore He merited more,” is invalid, because those merits which He had in the Passion were not more effective [Col. 1192A] than those which He possessed from His conception in meriting for Himself. So Zacchaeus merited through more acts than the widow, because he performed more good works, yet did not merit more. Again, the statement that Christ underwent struggle in the Passion is false: He approached martyrdom willingly, as He Himself said, “With desire I have desired” (Luke 22), etc. Even if this were true, it would not follow that He merited more, because it has been explained above how that authority is customarily expounded.

[Note: [Col. 1191D] The Master here, § C.] Likewise: Christ became obedient to the Father unto death, for which reason God exalted Him and gave Him the name above every name (Philippians 2). Augustine expounds this as follows [Note: [Col. 1191D] Book II *Against Maximinus*, etc., as above; it appears in the gloss there.]: God provided from eternity that He, being man in time, should have the name above every name—that is [Col. 1192B], should be God. It is asked whether Christ merited this in His human nature; for in the divine nature He merited nothing. The Apostle seems to intend that He did, when he said, “For which reason,” etc. Therefore Christ, according to His human nature, merited to be united to the Son of the Father—which is false. Human nature could never attain that excellence by merits, but only by grace. Therefore we say that Christ did not merit this; rather, He merited the manifestation of this reality, which took place after the Resurrection—not before, when He was thought to be a mere man. For a thing is said to exist or to come to be when it is said or made known that it comes to be.

## Chapter XIV. Whether it was granted to anyone to become the Son of God; and, if Christ merited in His human nature to receive this, whether He received it in the divine nature

[Col. 1192C]

[Note: [Col. 1191D] The Master above, § C.] Again it is asked: was it granted to anyone by grace that he should be the Son of God? If so, it was granted either to a nature or to a person: not to human nature, because human nature is not the Son of God; nor to divine nature, because divine nature receives nothing by grace. Therefore it was granted to a person that he should be the Son of God—not to a person other than the Son. Therefore the Son of God received by grace that He should be the Son of God. Therefore He is the Son [p. 282] of God from time and not from eternity.

To this it should be said that Augustine and Ambrose seem to contradict one another concerning this bestowal of the name. [Note: [Col. 1192D] As above.] For Augustine expressly says that Christ the man received by grace that He, existing as man or subsisting in human nature [Col. 1192D], both is and is called God. Yet He did not merit this, because human nature did not merit to be united to the Word of God. Nevertheless, by the obedience of the Passion which He endured in human nature, He merited that that man should evidently be exalted—that is, united to the divine nature. Although this was true before the Resurrection, it was unknown to human beings and demons.

Ambrose, however, says [Note: [Col. 1192D] The author of the Commentary on Philippians, ch. 2; and it appears in the gloss on the same chapter.] that this name was given to God, not to man. Yet he does not contradict Augustine [Note: [Col. 1192D] Thus the Master reconciles them above.], because Augustine speaks of the gratuitous bestowal, which is temporal and occurred in the man; Ambrose [Col. 1193A] speaks of the natural bestowal which the Son of God has from eternity, namely, that He is the Son of God by generation. Therefore, when someone obstinately asks whether it was granted to anyone in time that he should be the Son of God, one must never answer simply, lest someone ensnare one by pressing the question about person or nature. Rather, one must answer thus: it was granted to human nature that it should be united to the Son of God in time; I do not say, “that it should be so that He is the Son of God.” It was granted to Christ in time that He, being man, should be the Son of God; not that He should be the Son of God. For the latter is eternal, the former temporal; He has the latter by natural bestowal, the former by gratuitous bestowal; the latter is said by division, the former by composition; He has the latter in the divine nature, the former in the human.

Likewise, Christ in His human nature merited the manifestation [Col. 1193B] of His name insofar as He is God, as Ambrose says. [Note: [Col. 1193] Ambrose, Commentary on Philippians, ch. 2; and it appears in the gloss on the same chapter.] For although He was the Son of God from eternity, before the Passion it was not manifest, even insofar as He was the Son of God, that He was the Son of God; and this became manifest through the Passion. Therefore in His human nature He merited something that He received in His divine nature. For by the Passion He merited that it should become known not only concerning the human nature that it was united to God—which, although true, was unknown—but even that the Son of God was the Son of God the Father. Though this was true from eternity, it was unknown, since before Christ’s coming nothing was known about the Trinity.

To this it should be said that, although God became known to human beings through worship [Col. 1193C], nothing thereby accrued to Him. For if Christ were now worshiped by no one insofar as He is God, nothing would thereby accrue to Him, nor would He be less blessed. For He is God, who does not change, who does not need my goods, and who is not exalted in Himself; rather, His exaltation in you consists in your being exalted in Him. Therefore nothing accrued to the divine nature through Christ’s Passion, although the Trinity, previously wholly unknown to human beings, was manifested.

Likewise, it is asked whether Christ merited eternal life. This seems so, because He was a man placed on the way, an adult, and possessed charity by which He merited. Therefore He also merited eternal life. Likewise, Christ could not have been the man He was—namely, mortal and passible—unless He possessed virtues; and, being mortal and passible, He could not [Col. 1193D] possess those virtues idle, having fullness of virtues, without meriting—which indeed is not doubtful. Yet He did not thereby merit the eternal life which He possessed from the moment He became man, with respect to enjoyment of the vision of God; but He did not immediately possess the immortality which He merited afterward. Yet even then He merited that enjoyment of the vision of God which He had immediately. He possessed charity without measure, and His free choice immediately cooperated. Therefore, immediately a motion proceeded from charity and free choice toward God and neighbor. For He did not possess charity as little children do, in habit and not in use, since from the Conception He was a man, as was said above [Col. 1194A], not in perfection of age, but in the use and fullness of all natural and gratuitous gifts. In His body something accrued to Him; in His soul nothing, except impassibility, which He had either immediately when the soul was separated from the body, or at the Resurrection. Therefore Christ seems, by that motion of love toward God, to have merited the enjoyment of the vision of God which He possessed immediately, so that reward and merit [p. 283] existed together, as in the angels.

On the other hand, He seems to have possessed that enjoyment of the vision of God not from merits but gratuitously. Since He enjoyed the vision of God from the moment He existed, just as if from that moment He had possessed immortal and impassible flesh, and just as He immediately contemplated God most fully, who would say that Christ possessed [Col. 1194B] that immortality from merits? Yet even in this way it can be shown that He had immortality. For He so merited that immortality and glorification of the flesh through the Passion that He had also merited it by works of virtue from the Conception, even if the Passion had not followed; for the Passion itself was meritorious only through charity, and through the Passion nothing accrued to His merits with regard to the power of meriting, but with regard to the merits themselves. What, then, prevents Him from receiving that reward immediately—the glorification of the flesh—from the moment He became man? He possessed virtues by whose works He merited that glorification, so that reward and merit were simultaneous in time, although merit naturally preceded, as in the angels, in whom the merit of confirmation and its reward were simultaneous. Likewise, in every person sinning mortally, the merit of punishment—that is, guilt—and punishment—that is, deprivation of the highest good, which is part of the punishment due to mortal sin—are simultaneous. Thus it follows that Christ, through the fullness of graces which He possessed, free choice cooperating, could in the first instant in which He existed have possessed all that He had after the Resurrection: namely, a glorified body and an impassible soul. Then He would have had the whole from merits, not temporally preceding but naturally preceding.

But if it is impossible that He should have possessed all these from the Conception without possessing them by grace, then likewise, since He enjoyed the vision of God from the moment He existed, He possessed this from grace alone and not from merits—especially since His soul could not attain such knowledge of the divine majesty [Col. 1194D] unless it were united to the Word of God. Indeed, if that soul merited immediately to have that immeasurable knowledge of God, although it could not possess it without measure unless it were united to the Word of God—for if it were a mere creature, Christ the man could always advance in knowledge—then that soul merited immediately to be united to the Word of God, since to possess knowledge of God without measure and to be united to God are almost the same, and one cannot be possessed without the other. Likewise, Christ Himself was eternal life, living with the Father from eternity; how, then, was eternal life owed to Him by merits, unless it was owed to Him by merits that He should be united to God?

It would not be burdensome for me to write the solution to these matters [Col. 1195A], since I know that it is necessary both for myself and for others, were it not that I know a safer disposition: to seek truth than to take uncertain things as certain. “Let us seek as though we were to find; let us find as though we were to seek. In matters to be believed, let us doubt with no unbelief; in matters to be understood, let us affirm with no rashness.”

Let us rather ask whether Christ merited eternal life for us. If so, since He did not merit it for us more by suffering than otherwise, He merited eternal life for Peter when Peter was in mortal sin; for Peter had then denied Christ. Therefore Peter was worthy of eternal life because of Christ’s merits and unworthy because of his own. Therefore he was simultaneously worthy and unworthy. Likewise, Christ then merited eternal life for him; therefore Abraham had not already merited it for himself. [Col. 1195B] Likewise, Christ merited eternal life for this man who is now on the way; and this man possessed it; and it is impossible that Christ should be defrauded of His merits; and Christ must then have merited eternal life for this man. Therefore it is necessary that [Christ (this man, or he)] will have eternal life; therefore it is impossible for him to be damned. Likewise, Christ merited eternal life for all His members, and all His merits proceeded from equal charity. Therefore He merited an equal crown for all His members. Likewise, Christ’s merits made all good persons, whoever were to be good, good; and their own merits made them good. Therefore Christ’s merits made them good more than, less than, or equally with their own merits.

[Col. 1195C] To this it should be said that Christ merited eternal life for no one except [p. 284] in this sense: Christ’s merits were the efficient cause why each person’s merits should be sufficient for eternal life. For our merits would by no means suffice for us to obtain eternal life unless Christ’s merits had preceded or followed them; and observe how this is so. [Note: [Col. 1195D] Thus the Master, from St Ambrose, dist. 18, § e.] God decreed that no one should be admitted to behold the divine majesty unless He found in one man obedience as great as the disobedience He had found in the first man. But that consummation of righteousness was found in no one except Christ; for all had sinned in the first parent, were condemned, and had apostatized from the root. Therefore no one’s merits sufficed to cancel that decree, because no one had been found as humble as Adam was proud. Their merits nevertheless helped them in some degree—namely, to avoid Gehenna—but not to remove the fiery sword from the entrance to paradise and thereby admit themselves to the presence of the divine majesty.

But Christ the man was sufficient, a perfect sacrifice far more humble and obedient than Adam was proud and disobedient; and therefore He placed us in a higher station than that from which Adam expelled us through sin. Thus the question whether Christ’s merits make us good more than our own merits is not a proper comparison, because [Col. 1196A] our merits make us good by their own efficacy; as if one said: “God justifies me more than my righteousness does,” or, “The physician heals me more than the medicine does.”

If it is asked whether Christ merited eternal life for infants who have no merits, this may simply be granted. Yet He did not merit it for adults except in the sense stated above. Nevertheless, by His Passion He merited that, if anyone were baptized, no satisfaction should be imposed for past sins, because in His Passion He bore the sins of all His members in order to blot them out and make satisfaction for them, and the waters of baptism have been reddened by Christ’s blood. It is as if I had merited the mutilation of all my members for some sin, and my two ears were cut off for that multitude of punishments; and someone said: [Col. 1196B] “You must be punished in each individual member for the sin you committed.” I would answer that I need not, because I suffered in my head the punishment of all when my ears were cut off. So too Christ, our head, bore punishment for us all. Hence, if satisfaction for sins were imposed in baptism, the single death of Christ would not seem to have made satisfaction for our redemption, since baptism represents His death in many persons and derived its efficacy from it.

It is also asked whether Christ could have possessed these goods of soul and body without any merit. To this it should be said [Note: [Col. 1195D] Thus the Master here, § d.] that He could not be a mortal man without possessing virtues; He could not possess virtues without possessing them not idly; and He could not possess them not idly [Col. 1196C] without meriting. Therefore He could not be a mortal man without meriting. Yet He could have possessed what He possesses without merits, but then He would not have been the kind of man He was—namely, passible and mortal.

## Chapter XV. On the will Christ had according to sensuality

[Note: [Col. 1195D] Master, III, dist. 17.] Since it has been established what Christ merited according to the soul or according to the body, and by what means, before discussing what He merited for us and when, one must inquire whether Christ possessed in His soul natural goods like other human beings; for the order of discussion requires this. Since the preceding treatment taught that Christ assumed such properties of human nature as it befitted Him to assume, and since it has been shown that He possessed a fullness of gratuitous gifts, than which no more excellent gift could be conferred by God in this present life—whence they are called the greatest goods [Note: [Col. 1196D] By Augustine, *Retractations*, I.9, and *On Free Choice*, II.19]—we must descend to the intermediate goods, which hold the second place after these: natural ability, reason, memory, and understanding.

Thus Christ’s soul possessed reason and sensuality: reason according to [p. 285] both its higher and lower parts—not because the soul, which is a simple reality, has parts, but because for easier understanding we divide it, as it were, into parts. Christ also possessed sensuality according to its higher part [Col. 1197A], from which proceed motions of defects such as hunger, thirst, and the like; but He did not possess it according to its lower part, from which proceed motions of unlawful things—namely, pride, lust, and anger—from all of which the divine essence was free. For He did not assume any one state in its entirety, but something from each: [Note: [Col. 1197D] This doctrine is the Master’s, III, dist. 16, § b.] from the first, immunity from sin; from the second, penalties; from the third, fullness of virtues—not that He had all virtues, since He did not have faith or hope, as was said, nor contrition or repentance, but because He could possess none which He did have more fully; from the fourth, inability to sin and perfect contemplation of God.

Therefore Christ possessed two wills: one according to reason, the other according to sensuality, by which He willed [Col. 1197B] not to die when He said, “Father, if it be possible” (Matthew 26; Mark 14), etc.; but He subjected the latter to the former when He added, “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (ibid.).

But it is objected: Christ willed not to die; the Father willed Him to die; therefore Christ willed something discordant with the Father’s will. Likewise, Christ’s soul was confirmed like the angels. Therefore either the angels willed different things, or Christ did not will different things. Likewise, Christ willed not to die, and whatever He willed, He willed with God as author. Therefore God willed that He should not die.

To this it should be said that in Christ according to His human nature there were two wills, as in every other human being; but since, of these two wills, one always serves and the other rules, a person is simply said [Col. 1197C] to will what he wills by the ruling will, whether good or evil. What he wills by the other is not said simply to be willed, but only with a qualification. Therefore, since Christ subjected the will of sensuality to the will of reason, we say that He did not will not to die, although He did will not to die according to sensuality.

Likewise, the Father willed that Christ should will, but according to sensuality; therefore it was just for Christ to will this; therefore Christ justly willed this. Therefore He willed this according to reason, not according to sensuality.

[Col. 1197D] Note, therefore, that the proposition “he willed this by reason” has two meanings: “the movement by which he willed it was one of reason”—this is false; rather, it was one of sensuality. But if “by reason” means that reason brought it about that he should will this according to sensuality, then it is true. Again, Christ rendered the cup of salvation, and that rendering was good. Therefore whatever was contrary to it was evil; but Christ’s will by which he willed not to render it was contrary to it. Therefore it was evil. We say that no will is called simply “will” except that which belongs to reason.

Again, Christ asked for what ought to have been asked, or for what ought not to have been asked. If for what ought to have been asked, then he deserved to be heard. Therefore, if he was not heard, he was treated unjustly. If he asked for what ought not to have been asked, then he asked inordinately. Therefore he sinned. Again, no movement is meritorious unless it proceeds from reason and grace; that movement of sensuality by which he asked not to die did not proceed from [Col. 1198A] reason. Therefore it was not meritorious, because it was not informed by charity, which does not inform sensuality, but free choice, which consists in reason and will. Therefore by it he did not deserve to be heard. Again, by that movement Christ asked for what was contrary to our redemption, and therefore to our salvation, and what hindered the office for which he had been sent. Therefore in this he ought not to have been heard.

On the other hand, every action of Christ was a lesson for us; everything that he said, willed, and did, he directed to our salvation; therefore this also. Therefore he asked this from charity. Again, he himself said to the disciples: “Whatever you ask in my name, the Father will give you” (John 14); and he himself was far more blessed than they, and he asked this in Christ’s name. Therefore he ought to have been heard. If it is said that he asked this in Christ’s name, then not [Col. 1198B] through Christ. Therefore he asked inordinately, because every prayer not made through Christ is a sin to the one praying, like Judas’s prayer. Hence at the end of prayer it is always said, “through Christ,” who is mediator of God and human beings, and intercedes for their salvation.

To this it must be said that Christ asked for what ought to have been asked, and he was not treated unjustly, because it was a greater good for him to die than not to die. Therefore, in order that he might be granted the greater good, he was not heard in the lesser good. Thus the young man who asked the Lord to allow him to bury his father (Luke 9) was not heard, so that he might do the greater good—that is, follow Christ. And the Apostle who asked that Satan’s thorn be removed from him was not heard (2 Cor. 12), although he asked for a good thing, because it was better [Col. 1198C] that it not be removed. Therefore Christ merited nothing by that movement arising from sensuality. For no movement is meritorious except through grace and free choice; yet he merited by the movement of the will that comes from reason, by which he willed himself to will that thing.

Again, Christ willed that he himself should not die, and was not reproved; Peter willed that Christ should not die, and was reproved. Therefore a fuller perfection was required of Peter than of Christ. This is not true. For Peter willed this with the will of reason, whereas Christ willed it with the will of sensuality, which he subjected to the will of reason. Fallacy: this perfect man on a day of fasting wishes to eat and is not reproved; this imperfect man does not wish to eat and is reproved. Therefore a fuller [Col. 1198D] perfection is required of the imperfect than of the perfect.

Again, Christ willed not to die according to sensuality, and willed to die according to reason. Therefore in him the flesh lusted against the spirit; but whenever this happens there is some sin, as Augustine says. [Note: [Col. 1198D] Book X of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 12.] Therefore there was sin in Christ. It must therefore be said that the flesh is not said to lust against the spirit except when the soul feels, according to sensuality, a movement toward an unlawful thing which it contracts from the flesh; and this was not in Christ. Therefore in him the flesh did not lust against the spirit.

Again, the Father sent the Son to suffer for us; therefore that passion was a work of obedience. Therefore it was a work owed, [Col. 1199A] not one of will alone. To this we say that a work is called owed when a person is going to do it whether willing or unwilling; it is also called owed because he does it from will, and thus it was owed in Christ.

## CHAPTER XVI. Did Christ’s will according to reason agree with the will of the Jews who desired his death?

[Note: [Col. 1199D] The Master, Book III, distinction 20, and Book I, final distinction.]

Having spoken of Christ’s will according to sensuality, we must speak of Christ’s will according to reason. Thus, as by the former he willed not to die, so by the latter he willed to die. But an objection is raised: Christ willed to die, and the Jews willed him to die. Therefore the Jews’ will accorded with Christ’s will—which is false. For he did so from charity, [Col. 1199B] but they from hatred. Fallacy: Christ wills this man’s father to die, and his son wills the same thing, in order to succeed to his inheritance. Therefore this man’s will accords with God’s will—this is false. Or: God willed the destruction of Jerusalem, and Nebuchadnezzar willed the same. Therefore his will agreed with the divine will.

Again, it was good that Christ should be crucified by the Jews; and he could not be crucified by the Jews unless the Jews killed him. Therefore it was good for the Jews to kill Christ; therefore their action was good, and thus meritorious. Again, the Father willed Christ to be crucified by the Jews, and knew that he could not be crucified by them unless they killed him. Therefore the Father willed the Jews to kill Christ.

To this it must be said that the proposition, “The Father willed Christ to be crucified by the Jews,” [Col. 1199C] can be understood in two ways. If you understand it as, “He willed him to be crucified,” that is, to undergo that passion inflicted by the Jews, it is true. But if the will is referred to the manner of that passion or to the Jews’ action, it is false. Fallacy of the last inference: you would wish in some way to be at Rome, and you know that you cannot in some way be at Rome unless you are at Rome. Therefore you would wish to be at Rome. Or: this man wishes to repent of sins and knows that he cannot repent of sins unless he has sinned; therefore he wishes that he had sinned. Or thus: God wishes to give this spiritual thing to this simoniac, and knows that he cannot give it unless that man receives it. Therefore he wishes that simoniac to receive this spiritual thing.

[Col. 1199D] Again, whatever the Father wills by the will which he himself is, is just by the justice which he himself is; the Father willed Christ to die; therefore it was just that Christ should die; therefore he deserved to die—which is disproved, because he was innocent; therefore he had not deserved death. Therefore, when he was crucified, he was treated unjustly. It must therefore be said that when the term “just,” or the verb “deserved,” is joined to the verb “to be crucified,” such a combination of expression is suspect and must not be conceded, lest Christ seem to have deserved the death or passion which he underwent; one must insist on an exposition. Thus, then, he deserved to be crucified or to die.

[Col. 1200A] Again, the Father willed Christ to die; therefore he willed him to die with the sin of the Jews or without their sin. If with their sin, then he willed their sins; if without their sin—and he did not die without their sin—then he willed something that did not occur. Again, the Father willed Christ to die; therefore justly or unjustly. If he willed him to die justly, then he willed something that did not occur, because Christ did not die justly. If unjustly, then he willed their injustice.

Again, that the Father willed Christ to die with the sin of the Jews is shown because the Father asked, “if it be possible” (Matt. 26), etc., that is, if it be possible for the salvation of the Gentiles to occur without the blinding of the Jews, let it occur. “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (ibid.), that is, let it occur as I will by the will of reason—namely, that the salvation of the Gentiles occur [Col. 1200B] with the blinding of the Jews. Therefore the Father willed the blinding of the Jews, and therefore their sins.

To this it must be said that the Father did not will Christ to die with sin or without sin, because both are false. But this is true: “He did not will him to die with sin”; and this: “He did not will him to die without sin.” But if it is said, “He willed him to die with sin or without sin,” it is false. The same must be said concerning “justly or unjustly.” If, however, it is asked whether he willed the blinding of the Jews: if “blinding” is understood passively, it is true that he willed them to be punished in this way for a just and rational, though hidden, cause.

Again, God the Father willed Christ to die; therefore he could rationally have commanded it; therefore someone [Col. 1200C] could have fulfilled that command from charity. Therefore someone could have killed Christ from charity, and thus without mortal sin. If the contrary is said, the objection runs thus: God willed something which could not occur without mortal sin; therefore he willed mortal sin.

To this some say that, just as Abraham would have merited had he sacrificed Isaac at God’s command, so the Jews could have merited by killing Christ. If the Father had commanded this, and unless they fulfilled this command they would have done wrong. But if it is asked whether anyone could have merited a reward by killing Christ, in order to accomplish God the Father’s will, without a command, and without killing him from rancor of heart, we are unable to answer.

[Col. 1200D] Again, Christ willed the sayings of all the prophets to be true. They foretold that the Jews would crucify Christ; therefore Christ willed this. Therefore he willed their sins. To this they say that the term *dictum* (“saying”) sometimes signifies the events which the prophets foretold, which Christ never willed to occur if they were sins; sometimes *dictum* is equivalent to *dictio*, that is, the utterance by which those events were signified. He did will those utterances to be true; yet they could not be true unless those events occurred, which Christ nevertheless did not will. You have a similar case in what has been said above.

Again, we might ask here whether Christ willed himself to speak [Col. 1201A] truly when he said [Note: [Col. 1201D] Matt. 26; Jer. 28. See above, chapter 1 of this distinction, or part.], “Peter, you will deny me three times”; and whether Jeremiah wished that what the false prophet Hananiah foretold should be true, and thus that he himself had prophesied falsely; and whether it was possible for the human race not to be redeemed, and thus [whether] Abraham too, before Christ’s coming, would not [be redeemed], unless these matters had been determined above.

Again, the apostles were worthy to suffer for Christ’s name; therefore they were worthy to suffer. Therefore they deserved to suffer and die and the like. Why, then, did Christ not similarly deserve [to suffer]? For the apostles did not have mortal sins for which they deserved [understand: to suffer], just as Christ did not. That the apostles were worthy to suffer for Christ’s name is found in that authority: “The apostles went away rejoicing” (Acts 5), etc.

To this it must be said [Col. 1201B] that the term *dignum* (“worthy”) sometimes denotes dignity; in this sense it is true that the apostles were worthy to suffer for Christ’s name: for it was the highest dignity for those who were scourged for Christ. Sometimes the term denotes merits. In this sense it is not true that they were worthy to suffer, because they did not deserve to suffer, but rather to be honored. Therefore one must simply grant that they were worthy to suffer for Christ, yet they were not worthy to suffer—owing to the fallacy of equivocation and that of “in a respect” and “simply.” Fallacy: this man is white in respect of his teeth; therefore this man is white.

Again, Peter was punished more than he deserved; therefore he paid what he had not stolen. It is true that Christ [Col. 1201C] had neither contracted nor committed guilt, but only punishment, which is normally derived only from guilt; and thus he paid what he had not stolen, because he had the sack, but not the desert of the sack, and he alone did so. For when the apostles were punished, they paid what they had stolen, because no one was free from sin; even though they were punished more than they deserved, they did not pay what they had not stolen, because it is not paying what has not been stolen when that punishment increased their crown. That the apostles deserved punishment, though not so great a punishment, is found in the commentary on the passage of the Song of Songs, “My beloved is white and ruddy” (Song 5). Christ suffered through love alone; the others through merit.

Again, Christ suffered for sin; Peter suffered for Christ. Therefore the cause of Peter’s passion was worthier [Col. 1201D] than Christ’s; therefore Peter merited more than Christ. I say that *pro* (“for”) is understood differently: Peter suffered for Christ as one possessing him, not because Christ needed it; Christ suffered for Peter in order to free him, and also for himself, in order to be exalted. For you have in the commentary on Matthew that he paid the didrachma for himself and Peter (Matt. 17), but differently in the two cases, as is there distinguished.

Again, Christ’s death was the cause of our salvation; our salvation was to be desired; therefore everything that was its cause was also to be desired; therefore Christ’s death was to be desired. But conversely, Christ was innocent; therefore his death was not to be desired.

[Col. 1202A] Again, one ought to rejoice over Christ’s death; therefore, on the day on which he died, the whole Church ought to display every sign of joy. This is false, because on that day the bells and the angelic praise are silent, and a fast is observed in mourning and affliction.
