To this it must be said that Christ’s death was to be desired because of our salvation, not because of the anguish which the Jews themselves desired. Yet on the day of his death we show signs of sorrow in order to represent the mourning of the apostles, who were grieved at the killing of their Lord; and lest the Church be scandalized by unbelievers, should they reproach us for rejoicing on that day over the death, anguish, and passion which the Lord suffered for us. Because of the pain which he suffered on the cross, a fast is observed with one dish only, because on that day he incorporated only one person into the Church—namely, the thief—as he himself says: “I am alone until I pass over” (Ps. 140).

[Col. 1202B] But if it is asked whether one should likewise rejoice in the sufferings of martyrs, it must be said that the passion of no saint benefited us as much as Christ’s death; and therefore one should not rejoice so much over their death. Yet one should also rejoice, because through this the Church is made fruitful and its offspring multiplied. Hence: “As the richness of the earth was broken forth upon the earth” (ibid.). Therefore it is pious to rejoice over martyrdom, and pious to weep over martyrdom.

It is also customary to ask whether Christ was a martyr. This seems to be proved by that authority [Note: [Col. 1202D] Taken from the Song of Songs]: “Daughters of Jerusalem, come and see the martyr in the diadem with which his mother crowned him.” But if he was, since he suffered [Col. 1202C] before blessed Stephen, then blessed Stephen is not the protomartyr.

To this it must be said that the term *martyr*, besides the three senses in which one is called a martyr—by mortification of the flesh, compassion for one’s neighbor, and shedding of blood—also has other meanings. For martyrs are called those who died for truth, such as Isaiah, Jeremiah, and John; those who died for God’s law, such as the Maccabees; those who died in Christ’s place, such as the Innocents; those who died for human necessity; and those who died for testimony to Christ, testifying that he was true God and true man, such as Stephen. These are properly called martyrs, that is, witnesses, because no one can testify to Christ’s death more certainly than by exposing himself to death. For what greater thing can a human being do? Therefore Stephen was called [Col. 1202D] protomartyr because he was the first to die for this testimony.

Again, the Jews’ work was so great an evil, and Christ’s work was so great a good. Therefore either Christ’s passion was not the work of both Jews and Christ, or that work was good and evil. Again, the Jews were authors of Christ’s passion; therefore they were authors of a supreme good, and thus not God alone. Or, if the Jews were authors, and God too was author, then they are not to be judged guilty.

To this it must be said that God was the author of Christ’s passion and of every affliction inflicted upon his body; and that same passion was the work [Col. 1203A] of the Jews, but in another way—not as authors but as agents or ministers—because from their action came such a work, which is properly and principally God’s work. The Jews’ action was another action, and it was evil because of their evil intention; Christ’s action was another, good because of his good will. Yet one work proceeded from them: namely, the passion, which is the greatest good. Therefore, if you look at the act, Christ’s and the Jews’ acts are different; if at the thing done, the work of Christ and theirs was the same. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1203D] On Psalm 93, not far from the end]: “A different intention makes different deeds, although there is one thing arising from different deeds.”

Once these matters have been determined, there is no objection to raise, since you may also fortify yourself with a parallel: God was the author of the misery suffered by Job, the devil its minister; and the devil nevertheless incurred demerit by afflicting him thus, although God willed Job’s misery. Similarly, in the destruction of Jerusalem, which pleased God, Nebuchadnezzar’s action nevertheless displeased him, because it was evil, formed by an evil intention; and the same is true of those plundering the Egyptians.

[Col. 1203B] Again, the Jews crucified Christ out of zeal for the law, and thought they were rendering service to God; this was the end of their action; therefore their action was good, because that whose end is good is itself also good.

The solution to this objection must be taken from what was said above, where it was stated that all actions are to be judged good or evil by their end, except those which are evil in themselves, which no good end commends. [Col. 1203C] For although a man steals in order to feed his father, and thus proposes a good end, he is nevertheless not free from guilt. Such was the Jews’ action: although they had proposed a good end, it was nevertheless evil to kill a teacher and an innocent man, especially since they had heard that the Messiah had been promised in the law; and if they were ignorant, their ignorance was gross. For they could have learned this from Christ himself. Some, however, sinned more than others, namely those who did this from envy.

Again, the Apostle says: “If they had known, they would never [have crucified] the Lord of glory” (Rom. 1), etc. Therefore they could be excused through ignorance, since they did not know him to be the Messiah.

To this it must be said that if the demons had known him to be God or the Son of God, they would never have suggested that he be crucified. For what is elsewhere read as said [Col. 1203D] by the legion, “What have we to do with you, Son of David? Have you come before the time to torment us?” (Matt. 8), they said more by suspicion than by assertion. The leading men, even if they thought him God or God’s Son, would never have crucified him; but they thought him to be the Messiah whom they believed would be a mere human being—a belief which they still hold—and they crucified him from envy and because he seemed a destroyer of the law. The lesser people did not regard him as Messiah, God’s Son, or God; for if they had thought this, they would never have handed him over. They indeed had zeal for the law, but not according to [Col. 1204A] knowledge; and therefore, because they seemed in some measure excusable, Christ prayed for them: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23). And they were converted, as is read in Acts of the Apostles: four thousand on one day, five thousand on another (Acts 4).

Others say that the term *finis* (“end”) has two meanings: either final cause, and in that sense it is not true that everything whose final cause is good is itself good, as in the foregoing examples; or final intention, which comprises both the action itself and the final cause—for example, feeding one’s father by theft. In this sense it is true that everything whose final intention is good is good; but the Jews’ intention was not good in this sense, namely, rendering service to God by crucifying Christ, and therefore neither was their action good.

## CHAPTER XVII. Did Christ have ignorance, difficulty in doing good, or necessity of dying?

[Col. 1204B]

[Note: [Col. 1203D] The Master, Book III, distinction 15, etc.]

Christ assumed not only the goods of the soul, both gratuitous and natural, as has been said, but also defects not of fault but of punishment—not all defects of punishment, but those which it was necessary and fitting for him to assume. It was necessary and fitting for him to assume those defects which he assumed either to show human nature, such as hunger and thirst, or to fulfill the office for which he had been sent, such as mortality and passibility. Unless he possessed these two, he would neither have suffered nor died—the purpose for which he came.

Of the defects that are in the soul, some are according to the body, others according to the soul. Those are said to be [Col. 1204C] of the body which the soul suffers through the instrument of the body, such as hunger and thirst, because it does not hunger or thirst except when it is in a body. Those are said to be of the soul which it has even without a body, such as fear and anger, etc. Both kinds must be discussed. But first, certain matters must be settled concerning which there is doubt whether he assumed them or not.

There is one defect called ignorance, concerning things knowledge of which does not bring salvation and ignorance of which does not hinder it; this is punishment only, not fault. For if it concerned a matter that we are bound to know, it would be both punishment and fault. Christ did not have this ignorance, nor did he have difficulty in doing good, which is another penal defect; these are not defects of fault. For Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1203D] Book I of the *Retractions*, chapter 9; Book III of *On Free Choice*, chapters [Col. 1204D] 20 and 21; and *On the Good of Perseverance*, chapters 11 and 12] that ignorance and difficulty, even if they had been natural beginnings of humanity, would not make God blameworthy, but praiseworthy. But since these are also punishments, they do not seem able to have existed in humanity before sin without God’s acting unjustly toward humanity, since humanity would have been punished before deserving punishment. To this it must be said that they would not then have been punishments, just as not being able to advance before grace was bestowed upon humanity was not a punishment.

[Note: [Col. 1204D] The Master, Book III, distinction 16, §a.]

It is asked, moreover, whether Christ assumed that defect called the necessity of dying. Because of this the Apostle says that the human body after [Col. 1205A] sin is dead and necessarily subject to death, whereas before it was mortal (Rom. 8), that is, able to die, which would not have been a punishment or defect. But if this is so, Christ died of necessity and therefore not by will alone. Yet it is read: “He was offered because he willed it” (Isa. 53).

To this it must be said that there is a contracted necessity, which Christ did not have, since he neither committed nor contracted sin; and there is an assumed necessity, which Christ did have and from which he died. Yet this was no less by will alone. There is also an imposed necessity, from which he was free. For he was offered because he willed it. Fallacy: this monk who has taken a vow abstains from meat of necessity; therefore not by will alone. This is false, because he himself imposed that necessity upon himself.

We might ask here whether Christ could have passed beyond the bounds of human life, so as always to live while still mortal; whether Christ’s flesh in the tomb could have decayed and corrupted had he not risen on the third day; and similar questions. Since these exceed the powers of our intellect, or extend further than what we read, we leave them to be examined by greater minds. [Col. 1205B] This only we have on authority in the Epistle to the Hebrews [Note: [Col. 1205D] In chapter 9. See the Master above]: “Just as it is appointed to other human beings, by right and by necessity of nature, to die once, so Christ also by the same necessity and law of nature was offered once, not often.” Here it seems to imply that Christ could not pass beyond the limit set to the years of human life, although he could do even greater things than these, nor could this be a defect in him.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Did Christ have fear?

[Col. 1205C]

[Note: [Col. 1205D] The Master, Book III, distinction 15, §§d, e, f.]

There is another defect which the Son of God assumed for us: namely fear and sorrow. Hence: “Jesus began to be afraid” (Mark 14), etc.; “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. 26); and “My soul is filled with sorrows” (Ps. 87). Augustine, however, seems to maintain that Christ did not truly fear, saying [Note: [Col. 1205D] *Expositions on the Psalms*, on Psalm 93, after the middle]: “Christ, who was to rise on the third day, was not truly saddened, whereas Paul burned with desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ.” And Jerome says [Note: [Col. 1205D] On Matthew, chapter 26]: “Let those blush who say that Christ feared death and, from fear of death, said: ‘Let this cup pass from me’” (Matt. 26).

We understand this [lacuna] thus: lest we deny that fear and sorrow existed in Christ. Otherwise, since Scripture says that he was sad, if he was not, everything said of him is fictitious; and then neither could it be said that he truly slept or ate, but only that he had the appearance of one sleeping or eating, and that he did not have a true body but a phantom body—which is heretical. For fear was in Christ differently than in other human beings. In human beings fear existed both through *propassion* and through passion, and they also possessed the cause of fear, namely sin. In Christ [Col. 1206A] fear existed through propassion, not through passion; nor did he have the cause of fear, being free from sin.

For there are certain degrees in punishments, as there are in sins: namely passion and propassion. *Propassion* occurs when the mind is inwardly affected by fear while the intellect is nevertheless not moved away from God’s rectitude or contemplation. Thus Christ had pain and fear, but not through passion.

[Note: [Col. 1206D] See the Master here, §g.]

Certain chapters of Hilary must likewise be understood in this way; by them he seems to show the same thing, so that we may say that fear existed in Christ not through passion. Yet at no time did he have a countenance more troubled in respect of the disposition of his mind, or more severe, than at another. Jerome also teaches this [Col. 1206B] in commenting on that passage of Isaiah [Note: [Col. 1206D] On Isaiah, chapter 42]: “He will not be sad nor troubled until he establishes judgment on the earth.” There Jerome says of Christ that he always maintained an evenness of countenance, which philosophers falsely attribute to Socrates.

This must not, however, be understood of his outward facial appearance: for we read that he wept and sweated from sorrow; rather, it concerns the inner constancy and fortitude of his mind. For at no time was he inwardly more joyful than at another, or sadder, although signs of fear and joy often varied in his face—not on his own account, but on ours. “Countenance,” therefore, is understood as an inward quality, as in: “The light of your countenance, Lord, is marked upon us” (Ps. 4). For he was not lifted up by prosperity [Col. 1206C] nor cast down by adversity as other people are.

But an objection is raised: Christ feared what ought to be feared, or what ought not to be feared. If what ought not to be feared, then he was cowardly; if what ought to be feared, then he was fearful—though it served our common salvation and his own glorification. Again, he himself said to the apostles: “Do not fear those who kill the body” (Matt. 10), etc. If he feared death, therefore he acted contrary to what he had said.

To this it must be said that Christ prohibited worldly fear, not natural fear. Natural fear is the horror anyone experiences when seeing danger threatening; it is called natural not because it belongs to humanity’s original nature, but because it is present from birth through corruption by sin.

## CHAPTER XIX. What did he confer on us by his passion that he had not conferred earlier? Here it is asked: could he have redeemed us in another way?

[Col. 1206D]

[Note: [Col. 1206D] The Master, Book III, distinctions 18 and 19.]

Having now learned in part—for one who prophesies in part and understands in part cannot do so fully—with what weapons the author of our salvation armed himself in the first and initiating works of our salvation, we must proceed also through the intermediate and advancing stages to the final and consummate work. Thus it may be shown what God has conferred upon us through them, and the question may be resolved whose solution, by postponing it, we seemed to hold [Col. 1207A] suspended in the minds of our hearers.

If Christ from the beginning possessed the fullness of virtues by which he merited the glorification of his flesh and the passibility [read: impassibility] of his soul from his conception, why then did he will to suffer, die, and be crucified? To this it must be said that through these works he merited for us something which he had not merited for us through the preceding things: namely, entry into paradise, deliverance from punishment, sin, and the devil.

Entry into paradise: because, as Ambrose says, [Note: [Col. 1207D] In the Master, distinction 18, §e, but somewhat differently], “God had decreed, because of the first human being’s sin, that no one should enter into life unless in one man he found as great a humility as he had found pride in the first human being, so that, as that pride harmed all, so one person’s humility might benefit all. But none was found except [Col. 1207B] the lion from the tribe of Judah,” because scarcely could each person suffice to erase his own sins. Therefore, by bearing the sins of all upon the cross, he merited entry into paradise for all who would believe in him.

Through him we were also delivered from sin and the devil, because we have been justified in his blood; and insofar as we are justified, we are freed from sin; insofar as we are freed from sin, we are redeemed from the devil. That we were justified in his blood is certain because God’s charity is commended in us by the fact that he did not spare his own Son but, while we were still sinners, handed him over as a sacrifice for us. Hence we are more inflamed to love him; and the more we love him, the more we are freed from sin. “We have been justified in [Col. 1207C] his blood” (Rom. 5), because through faith in his passion we are freed from sins.

He also freed us from punishment, both temporal and eternal: from eternal punishment in actuality, from temporal punishment in hope. For we still await the redemption of the body, that this mortal may put on immortality and this corruptible incorruption (1 Cor. 15). Thus the Apostle says: “We await the Savior Jesus Christ, who will transform the body of our humility, made conformable to [his body]” (Phil. 3), etc.

Yet an objection is raised against what has been said. Christ destroyed death by his death, according to Hosea: “O death, I will be your death; O hell, I will be your bite” (Hos. 13). Therefore he destroyed either temporal or eternal death. He did not destroy temporal death, [Col. 1207D] because we die by it every day. He does not seem to have destroyed eternal death, since more are to be damned than saved.

To this it must be said that Christ destroyed temporal death in hope in all, and in actuality in some: in himself, who, rising from the dead, dies no more; “death shall have no more dominion over him” (Rom. 6); in the blessed Virgin, whom we believe to have ascended into heaven glorified in the flesh; and in the saints who slept and rose with him. He also destroyed eternal death in all sufficiently, not efficaciously; for his redemption was sufficient for all, and it is not through him that all are not saved. He also destroyed eternal death [Col. 1208A] by his descent into hell, to which all before Christ’s passion descended, both good and evil. Now, if they depart in charity, none descend into hell; hence they do not fear death, since they can say, “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1), which formerly both the perfect and imperfect feared.

Again, Christ came only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matt. 15), and did not save them, because blindness fell upon Israel so that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter. Therefore he did not accomplish the purpose for which he came. Again, he saved the elect from both peoples. Whomever he saved, he came [Col. 1208B] to save; therefore he came both to these and to those.

Again, Christ saved only those who were to be saved; therefore only those who did not need saving. Again, no more were saved through Christ’s death than before he died, nor did anyone receive a greater reward than he would have received; therefore Christ’s death benefited no one.

It must be said that Christ was sent only to the sheep of Israel in order to preach to them in bodily presence; yet he was sent to all Gentiles in order to save them. Nor is he read to have preached in his own person to anyone except Jews. He saved only those who were to be saved, yet they needed salvation. Just as this physician treats this man who is to be healed, while nevertheless treating one who needs health because he is now sick; nor were more saved through him than were previously to be saved, for no one would be saved unless he had come or another remedy of salvation had been applied.

Again, all the elect were reconciled through Christ’s death, and therefore Abraham too. Therefore he was not reconciled except in Christ’s death; thus not earlier. Therefore he had not previously died in charity or previously merited eternal life, of which he could not be deprived. Therefore he was reconciled to God.

This is true because he did not receive the full fruit of reconciliation except in Christ’s death, since then [Col. 1208C] the gate was first opened, because “the Lamb was slain from the foundation of the world” (Rev. 13). The meaning of this expression may be taken in two ways: either figuratively, with the preposition *ab* (“from”) used inclusively; or according to God’s predestination, with the preposition used exclusively, as in: “There is no predication from first substance.” Yet he had already received part of the fruit of reconciliation, because he was saved in hope and because he did not experience material punishment.

[Col. 1208D] Again, both the saints of the Old Testament and the saints of the New Testament were reconciled through Christ’s death. Those who are saints of the New Testament have life immediately upon departing in charity; the saints of the Old Testament did not have it immediately. Therefore Christ’s death is more efficacious for the latter than for the former.

This is true with respect to a more ready and easier entrance, not with respect to the magnitude of the reward. Nor does this arise from death itself, but from the saints who are in such a time, just as the sun heats Indians more than Britons; and this does not arise from a changeable heat of the sun, but from the position of places nearer [Col. 1209A] to the sun or farther removed from it.

[Note: [Col. 1209D] The Master, Book III, distinction 20.] Again, Christ could have liberated us in another way—either a less good, an equally good, or a better way. If in a less good way, then he could have forsaken a greater good for a lesser, which does not befit goodness. If in an equally good way, then in an equally rational way. But this is proved false: he could have liberated us in another way equally rational and good; yet he did not redeem us by that way, but rather by this one. Therefore, since he could do nothing without reason, there was a reason why he redeemed us rather in this way; and thus this way was more rational and, consequently, better. [Note: [Col. 1209D] Peter excellently argues these points against Peter Abelard, V, in the notes to the first part of Robert Pullen’s *Sentences*.] Hence it seems that he could not have liberated us in another way, because not in a better, a worse, or an equally good way.

To this it must be said that he could have liberated us in a less good way, and one less fitting and useful. Had he done so, he would not have forsaken a greater good for a lesser; rather, he would have forsaken it for his own sake, because whatever he does, he does for himself, as Solomon testifies: “God has made all things for himself” (Prov. 16). And he could have liberated us in an equally rational way—not a way which was equally rational, but one which would have been so if he had liberated us by it. For whatever cause there was why he liberated us in this way, the same cause would have existed for liberating us in another way, had he so willed: namely, his ordinance and rational will.

Again, if we had been redeemed so that we could not sin, we would have been redeemed better; he could have liberated us in this way. Therefore, he could have liberated us in a better way, by removing both guilt and punishment. Therefore that way [Col. 1209C] would have been more fitting. They say, then, that he could have liberated us in a more fitting way by taking away both guilt and punishment; but, while our weakness remained so that it might gradually recede, he could not have liberated us in a better way than through the passion of his Son, because he could not draw us more effectively to love of himself than by not sparing his own Son. Or it is explained thus: [Note: [Col. 1209D] Augustine, *On the Trinity*, XIII.10.] “Another method was possible to God, but none more fitting for the salvation of our misery”; that is, God the Father could not give a more fitting and better sacrifice for our liberation than his Son. Therefore his power was bounded in this respect. This is a fallacy: he could not beget a better Son; therefore his power was bounded in this respect.

[Col. 1209D] Again, God could not have liberated us without anyone’s guilt and without scandal by a word alone [Note: [Col. 1210D] Augustine, above, ch. 10.], because “another method was possible to God, but none more fitting for the salvation of our misery.” Therefore he could have liberated us in a more suitable way. Yet this is rejected, because he could not liberate us without remission of sins, since otherwise he would have acted against his justice; and thus he liberated us. Therefore he could not liberate us in another way.

To this they say that he could not have liberated us in a more suitable way with respect to us humans, because [Col. 1210A] he could do nothing that would move us more to love him than that he emptied and offered himself for us. Yet he could liberate us in a more suitable way with respect to himself, if he did not die. But the assertion that he could not liberate us because he could not liberate us without remission of sins, and thus liberated us, is invalid. For distinct modes are contained under that expression. This is a fallacy: “I cannot read except by speaking, and I speak; therefore I cannot read otherwise than as I am reading.”

Again, through Christ’s death the devil ceases from many evils from which he would not have ceased unless Christ had died. For his power was diminished in Christ’s passion; and if he did more evils than he does, he would be worse, and thus would sin more and be punished more. Therefore the devil’s punishment was mitigated [Col. 1210B] through Christ’s death. This is false. On the contrary, it was increased, because he does not harm persons who are better, and who have been redeemed at the inestimable price of blood, to so great an extent; and he has a greater will to harm if he had the capacity, and would rage more if he were permitted. Thus Christ’s death did not benefit the devil. [Note: [Col. 1210D] The manuscript of St Victor does not contain this material.]

[Note: [Col. 1210D] This should be read soberly, and with qualification in some respects.] Again, at the passion all who had been evil before the passion were evil, except the thief alone; and those who had been good beforehand were then evil and belonged to the devil’s kingdom. Therefore, at the passion the devil’s kingdom was greater than before; therefore it was not destroyed through Christ’s passion.

Again, the devil’s kingdom was destroyed through Christ’s passion. Here there is discourse concerning something, either good or evil. If concerning good, and concerning that of which it is truly said that it was destroyed, then some good [Col. 1210C] was destroyed through Christ’s passion. If the discourse concerns evil, then it is true of the devil’s evil that it was destroyed through the passion of Christ. Therefore the passion benefited not only us, but also the devil.

Again, it should be known that the devil’s kingdom—that is, his dominion—was destroyed by Christ’s death, not as to its essence but as to its exercise, because after Christ’s passion he cannot seduce us as much as before. We say, therefore, that in the passion his power was diminished as to its exercise by cause, because Christ’s passion was a sufficient cause of his weakening. Thus Christ said: “It is finished” (John 19): the mystery of our redemption was completed, although the passion had not yet been fulfilled, because [Col. 1210D] a sufficient cause of its completion had been given. Just as we say of one who, wounded in battle, dies at home, that he fell in war, because there he received the cause of death.

There was, therefore, in the devil a threefold power. The power to harm, given to him without any merit, was given at creation; the exercise of malice was given him through his own merit; and the effect or ability to harm was given him through our merits, as where it says: “He delivered the poor man from the mighty one” (Ps. 71 [72]). The first was not taken away through Christ’s death, nor the second, but the third. [Col. 1211A] You see, similarly, three things in an orator, corresponding well to these: knowledge of speaking, practice, and the end which he expects from us, namely, persuasion. Of the remaining two, he has one from God and the other from free choice.

Or the devil’s kingdom is sin, through which he ruled in us; this was destroyed in all who are reborn through faith, in whom sin may indeed exist, but not so that it reigns. Or because in the very hour of the passion [Note: [Col. 1211D] On this see the Master, Book II, distinction 6, § f.] Lucifer, the master of demons, who had tempted him and suggested that he be crucified, was cast down into hell, where he is bound.

But if it is asked what is being spoken of when it is said, “The devil’s kingdom is diminished,” one may say that it concerns evil, but that of which the discourse is made is truly said to be diminished. Therefore the devil’s evil is diminished. [Note: [Col. 1211D] Up to this point the Victorine manuscript fails.] This is a fallacy. [Col. 1211B] When I say, “This priest will be hanged tomorrow,” the discourse concerns a man, and it is truly said of that of which the discourse is made that he will be hanged tomorrow. Therefore this man will be hanged tomorrow.

Again, Christ redeemed us from someone who held us captive; no one held us captive except the devil; therefore he redeemed us from the devil. Therefore he paid him the price of redemption—or no one. But he himself was the price of redemption. Therefore he offered himself to the devil.

To this it must be said that Christ liberated us from the devil, who held us captive by the permission of God the Father, to whom he paid the price; just as an intermediary pays the price to the king by whose command captives are held by the magistrate.

Again, to redeem is nothing other than to liberate from sin. He liberates from sin every day; therefore he redeems every day. Therefore Christ was not a sufficient sacrifice once for sins. Paul similarly proves this from the rejection of carnal sacrifices, which could not cleanse sin and therefore had to be repeated (Heb. 9).

Again, [understand: Christ], insofar as he is God, alone liberates from sin; and to liberate is to redeem. Therefore, insofar as he is God, he alone redeems—not, then, insofar as he is man.

Observe, therefore, what “to redeem” contains: namely, to pay a price and to liberate from captivity. One who is released without a price being paid is not redeemed; if a price is paid but he is not released, he is not redeemed. Therefore, when it is said that, insofar as he is man, he redeemed—that is, gave the price and liberated from sin—it is false. Rather, insofar as he is God, he did both these things. But if it is said that, insofar as he is man, he redeemed—that is, he paid the price—it is true; but insofar as he is man, he did not liberate from sin.

Nevertheless, one should not hesitate to distinguish the meanings of the expression *secundum* (“according to,” “insofar as”), which sometimes denotes unity of person, sometimes cause, and sometimes condition. With this distinction applied, the foregoing is easily solved. For if it denotes cause or condition, he redeemed insofar as he is God; but if it denotes unity of person, then both insofar as he is God and insofar as he is man.

[Col. 1212A] [Note: [Col. 1211D] The Master, Book III, distinction 20, § b.] Again, the devil held us either justly or unjustly. If unjustly, it is proved that justly: because if we were held by the devil, the devil held us; we were justly held by the devil; therefore the devil held us justly. Therefore an injustice was done to him when we were snatched away.

Observe that the devil held us unjustly, though we were justly held by the devil—that is, because our merits required it. Thus “justly” refers to the human being, not to the devil, who had no right over the human being whom he had deceived and to whom he could not render what he had promised. [Note: [Col. 1211D] See these matters in the notes to Pullen.] Similarly, the human being wronged God, who had created him, and, by withdrawing himself from God, chose the devil as his lord.

Again, it is commonly asked whether Christ suffered for himself. [Col. 1212B] Authority frequently says, “He died for you, not for himself.” Yet, conversely, in the commentary on Matthew, where it is read how Christ paid the tax for himself and Peter, it is maintained that he suffered for himself and Peter (Matt. 17). Hence the question arises whether Christ’s death was more useful to Christ than to us. There it is shown [Note: [Col. 1212D] The author of the commentary ascribed to Ambrose on Philippians, ch. 2; also Augustine in his exposition on the same passage. See the Gloss there.] that “by enduring the passion he acquired for himself the name which is above every name.” No one could attain so great a reward through his death. Therefore his death was more useful to him than to us.

Conversely, he merited eternal life for us, which we could not possess without his death or another mode of redemption; he could possess eternal life without any merit, and did possess it, [Col. 1212C] because he was living. Therefore his death was more useful to us than to him.

Again, through his death he liberated us from punishment, guilt, and the devil, and opened the gate to us by his death. He liberated himself only from punishment, because he had no guilt and the devil exercised no dominion over him: “The ruler of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John 14). The gate was not shut to him. Therefore Christ’s death profited us more than it profited him.

To this it must be said that in one respect it benefited us more than him, because it liberated us from more things; in another it benefited him more, because he merited a greater reward. Yet from a statement made with a qualification one cannot simply infer what is asserted in a certain respect, any more than in other actions. Thus, when it is said, “He suffered for you, not [Col. 1212D] for himself,” understand: there were not as many persons for whom he suffered for himself as there were for whom he suffered for you.

Again, Christ says: “If I had not come, they would not have sin” (John 15). Understand this of the sin of unbelief *antonomastically*, that is, by pre-eminence. Therefore, because he came, they became unbelievers; therefore his coming was the cause of unbelief. Therefore his coming harmed more than it benefited.

To this we say that the term “unbeliever” sometimes merely negates, so that “unbeliever” is the same as “not a believer.” In that sense, it is not true that, if he had not come, they would not have been unbelievers. [Col. 1213A] For they were unbelievers—that is, not believers—before he came. Sometimes it includes contempt for faith; they would not have had this contempt unless Christ had preached to them. Thus Christ’s coming was an occasion of sin to them, not through any defect of its own, but through that of those for whom it ought to have been salvation, unless their enormity had prevented it.

So medicine is an occasion of illness for one who improperly observes a regimen, although it ought to be, and would be, a cause of health unless the person’s own perversity prevented it.

Again, all who heard Christ and despised him became worse because of the word of faith which they rejected; and he preached to many whom he knew would despise the word of the Gospel. Therefore he cast pearls before swine; therefore he acted against his own precept. [Col. 1213B] Again, Christ knew that they would despise him and would become worse through contempt; and is he not himself also the Father of mercies? Therefore, out of mercy, he ought to have withheld himself from those who would become worse through contempt of the word.

Bede raises a similar question on the Gospel passage: “Woe to you, Bethsaida! Woe to you, Chorazin! For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented” (Matt. 11; Luke 10). He therefore asks why Christ, being the Father of mercy who ought to provide for human salvation, preached to those who would not repent but would become worse, and not to those who would have repented and become better. For in this he seems to have acted against his mercy. But Bede resolves it briefly by saying: “He alone knows.” Yet it may be said in some fashion that, even if he preached in the presence of those whom he knew would not be converted, he did not preach *to* them.

Again, it is asked whether Christ’s first coming was more to be desired than his second, or conversely. That the second is more so is shown thus: in the first we were liberated from guilt and not from punishment; in the second we shall be liberated from both. Therefore the second is more to be desired than the first. Again, in the second we shall receive both robes, namely that of the soul and that of the body; in the first, only that of the other, that is, of the soul. Therefore, and so forth. Again, the first is desired only because of the second. Therefore the second is more to be desired [Col. 1213D] than the first.

Conversely, the ancient fathers desired the first more than the second. Therefore they had disordered desire. That they desired the first more than the second is attested by many authorities: “Do you think I shall see? Do you think I shall endure?” and, “Would that he would rend the heavens and come” (Isa. 64). Such desires are not found explicitly expressed concerning the second.

To this it must be said that the second is more to be desired than the first; but it is natural to human desire that, if it desires two things and knows that one cannot happen without the other preceding it, it desires more that which comes first. [Col. 1214A] I do not say that it desires it more, but that it wishes it to happen first. Hence, since the first coming was for warfare, in order that through it one might pass to the second, such desires are found expressed concerning it.

Thus a person desires the second course more than the first because it is more splendid; nevertheless, he wants the first course set before him first, because unless he were first satisfied by it, he would not be ready for the second, of which he does not have so great an abundance, whose flavor he enjoys more than he is satisfied by it.

Nevertheless, it seems possible to show that the second coming is not to be desired. For Amos says: “Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord! Why do they desire it?” (Amos 5). Therefore he would not pronounce “Woe” upon them if it were to be desired. Hence they say that he said this on account of certain persons who presumed upon their own righteousness and desired that day. [Col. 1214B] Yet it is to be desired by the good. Hence the Apostle says: “Longing toward that day,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 1213D] What follows to the end of the chapter is not found in the Victorine manuscript.] A similar objection is made concerning the Apostle, who had a desire “to depart and be with Christ” (Phil. 1). He likewise had a desire to remain in the flesh because of the need of the brethren (ibid.). He could not fulfil these two desires at one and the same time. Therefore, when it was necessary for one to occur before the other, and he desired both, he desired the thing which happened later; and thus he wished to depart, which he desired to occur last, so that, while still living in the flesh, he might first provide for the brethren.

Conversely, he knew that if he lived in the flesh he could always advance in charity and thus acquire reward. Therefore this was more to be desired than [Col. 1214C] that. [Note: [Col. 1214D] This should be read cautiously.] Conversely, while on the way he could fall. For although he himself had said, “I am certain that neither death nor life will separate me from the charity of Christ” (Rom. 8), he was certain only with the certainty belonging to the wayfarer, and he still groaned under the misery of the flesh. Hence he said: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7). Therefore he ought rather to have wished to depart than to remain in charity.

To this it must be said that the Apostle first wished what was expedient for many to happen in himself; nevertheless, he loved more what was better. But he wished first to happen in himself that which was less good for him, and loved it less. Yet he did not love the brethren more than himself, because he deferred that which was greater in love for them; and in that love [Col. 1214D] and postponement, the good which he loved more was increased.

Thus a hungry person loves the second course more than the first, but nevertheless wants the first set before him first, so that after it he may have what is better. For if he has this first, he does not thereby lose that, but postpones it so that he may have it later and be more satisfied. Thus the Apostle deferred the greater good in order first to have the lesser, yet in such a way that he did not lose the greater; and so he received the whole, in order afterward to become more glorious and more blessed. For the very delay was an increase of grace.

But an objection is raised from what the Apostle says elsewhere: that he wished himself to be anathema for his brethren [Col. 1215A] (Rom. 9). Therefore he desired to be separated from the unity of the Church so that others might become members of its unity. Therefore he loved the brethren more than himself, and thus had disordered charity.

To this it must be said that he did not wish to be wholly separated from the Church so that the brethren might be received into it forever; for this would not be charity. Rather, he wished to be separated for a time so that the brethren might be received there forever. But because he could not will this from charity—for if he had been separated for a time, he would not have possessed charity—it may better be said that he wished neither temporarily nor eternally to be separated from the Church so that the brethren might be received into it; but, if it could be, he would have wished this. And he knew definitely—perhaps by revelation of the Holy Spirit—that it was God’s will that he would never be separated.

## Chapter XX. Whether Christ, according to his human or according to his divine nature, was the head of the Church

[Col. 1215B]

[Note: [Col. 1215D] The Master, Book III, distinction 19, § f.] From what has been said another question arises, containing some uncertainty. Since Christ redeemed the Church by his death, and did so in his human nature, it is asked, since he is the head of the Church, whether he is head of the Church according to that nature in which he redeemed it—that is, according to his human nature—or according to his divine nature. Arguments are advanced for each side.

For if he is head of the Church according to his divine nature, then according to his divine nature he is conformed to it in the divinity of nature. Again, if he is head of the Church according to his divine nature, [Col. 1215C] then this is said of him either according to essence or according to personal property (*notio*). Whichever is said, it follows that Christ was head of the Church from eternity. Therefore he was head of the Church before the Church existed, and thus when there was no Church.

Again, if he is head of the Church according to a personal property, then by that property the Son is distinguished from the Father and the Holy Spirit; and thus neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit is head of the Church. Again, Christ is head of the Church according to his divine nature; therefore he is Mediator between God and human beings according to his divine nature.

But if it is said that he is head of the Church according to his human nature, and he began to be according to his human nature, then he began to be head of the Church according to his human nature. Thus: Christ [Col. 1215D] began to be head of the Church according to his human nature; before the incarnation he was not head of the Church according to his human nature; and the Church then existed. Therefore it existed without a head.

Again, before the incarnation Christ was not head of the Church, and there were then many members of the Church; thus the members of the Church preceded the head of the Church. Again, Abel before the incarnation was a human being and an adult. Therefore he was a member either of the devil or of Christ, because there is no middle position. If he was a member of Christ and Christ did not exist, then something was a member of Christ when Christ was nothing. Again, Christ was not yet mediator. Therefore he did not yet intercede for our salvation. [Col. 1216A] Therefore prayer was not yet made through Christ.

To this it must be said that the term “head of the Church” is applied to Christ figuratively, by this likeness: just as the head in a human being is more worthy than the other members, both in position, as surpassing the other members, and in governance, because the five senses flourish in it and it directs and rules the other members, and is of the same nature as the other members, being fleshly and bony; so Christ is the mountain of mountains, and ruler, from whose fullness all receive (John 1), because no one can possess the gifts of the Holy Spirit more fully; and he is of the same nature as the saints because he possesses human nature. For these two reasons he is called head of the Church: because he is ruler, and because he is of the same nature—both of which he has according to his human [Col. 1216B] nature. For according to his divine nature he is not of the same nature as the Church. Hence neither according to that nature is he head of the Church, unless the term “head” is taken in another meaning, namely, to denote authority rather than identity of nature. The Apostle seems to attest this when he says: “Christ is the head of man, and God is the head of Christ” (1 Cor. 11).

It is clear, therefore, that Christ was not head of the Church before the incarnation, unless you take that expression in this meaning. If they wish, they may press this argument: Christ is head of the Church according to his human nature; before the incarnation he was not head of the Church according to his human nature, and the Church existed; therefore it was without a head. This is a fallacy: “This man is strong according to his soul; yesterday he was not strong according to [Col. 1216C] his soul, and he existed; therefore he was not strong.”

And observe that Abel was then a member of Christ, though Christ was not yet Christ; and in Abel alone was the Church, because at that time he alone was faithful. If it is asked, assuming that no one had been faithful before him, though many had died and many more would come after him, whether the Church then existed when no one at that time was faithful: it is true, because the Church militant did not then exist, but the Church triumphant did, on account of those who had died.

Again, suppose that no human beings had faith, though later they would receive it and afterward lose it: would the Church militant have ceased to exist? No, because the people who were the Church did not cease to exist, but ceased to be the Church. Just as these people cease to be [Col. 1216D] a people; yet this people does not cease to exist.

Again, Christ was head of the Church according to his divine nature before the incarnation, and in the incarnation began to be head of the Church according to his human nature. Therefore, was the head of the Church which existed before the same head or another? If he began to be the same head of the Church, then that head did not exist before. If he began to be another head of the Church, and did not cease to be what he was before, then there were two heads of the Church.

To this it must be said that no relation is to be admitted—neither “same” nor “other.” Thus, this man today began to be strong according to his soul. But if it is asked whether he is the same strong person that he was yesterday, or another, the question is improperly asked [Col. 1217A] if yesterday he was strong in body.

Again, observe that although “head of the Church” belongs to Christ according to his divine nature, nevertheless he is not head of the Church from eternity. Just as the name “Creator” is said of God according to his divine nature, yet he is not Creator from eternity.

Again, Christ began to be head of the Church; therefore he began to be something. This is a fallacy: Christ began to be man; therefore he began to be something; or he began to be Creator; therefore he began to be something.

Observe that some not improperly say that Christ was head of the Church before the incarnation according to his human nature—that is, as foundation, which is nothing other than the faith in his humanity, or in his incarnation; this was the foundation of the Church. Hence it is said that, from the time he was ruler of the Church, he was [Col. 1217B] also head of the Church according to his human nature, namely, the foundation on which the Church relied with respect to faith in his humanity. For what we believe concerning his humanity as past, they before his advent believed as future.

Again, Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1217D] *On Faith and the Creed*, ch. 4. See also the exposition of certain propositions from Romans, ch. 56.]: “God, not insofar as he is the Only-Begotten, but insofar as he is the First-Begotten among the brethren who follow, did not disdain to have brethren; we who belong to the unity of the Church are his brethren.” Therefore this is either according to a common father, a common mother, or both. If it is said that it is according to a common mother, the Church, then he is a son of the Church; and thus the head or bridegroom of the Church is the Church’s son. But if it is according to a common father, since we cannot be sons by generation, it remains that we are sons by creation or by the bestowal of graces. But not by creation alone, for otherwise unbelievers would be Christ’s brethren, since they were created by God, as he was according to his humanity. But we are not children of God by these two means except adoptively. Therefore Christ too is an adoptive Son of God.

To this it must be said that the Only-Begotten has no brothers, because he is Son by generation; but insofar as he is First-Begotten, he has brothers. Hence: “I will declare your name to my brethren” (Ps. 21 [22]); “Go and tell my brethren” (John 20). And he is a son of the Church. Thus he himself said: “I am your servant and the son of your handmaid” (Ps. 115 [116]). And he is First-Begotten with respect to those who have been begotten [Col. 1217D] to God from the unity of the Church. Hence the Apostle says: “First-born from the dead” (Col. 1), that is, the first to rise to immortality. And from this it is said that he does not have brothers, because he has from God by creation and the bestowal of graces what we have; nevertheless, he is not an adoptive son as we are. Thus these two are brothers, and one has a father; therefore the other has the same father.

Again, the first to sin was Adam or Eve, and that person's sin corrupted the whole of human nature. Therefore that person too was the head of the church of the evil, or no one was; yet this is customarily attributed to Cain. By the same reasoning, the first to perform good and to have faith was Adam. [Col. 1218A] Therefore he was the head of the church of the good, or no one was; yet this is customarily attributed to Abel.

To this it must be said that Adam was neither wholly evil nor wholly good, and therefore the beginning of the church of the good or of the evil is not customarily attributed to him. But Abel is assigned as the beginning of the good, because he was wholly good; because he was a figure of Christ, the lamb slain from the foundation of the world; and because he was a virgin. Hence, according to one interpretation, he is called “nothing,” because he left no heir; and the Church is a virgin. He was also a martyr, and the Church was founded in the blood of martyrs.

Again, it is asked whether the devil was the beginning of the church of the wicked. If so, he was head of the church of the evil just as Christ is head of the church [Col. 1218B] of the good. Therefore either the fullness of all good was not in Christ, or the fullness of all evil was in the devil; and thus every evil comes from the devil. This is false, because evil thoughts do not come from the devil, since he does not know human hearts unless this has been revealed to him by good angels or through certain conjectures.

Hence, if authority is ever found saying that every sin comes from the devil, it must be referred to the kinds of individual things, not to the individual instances of the kinds. And it may be said that, although the devil was head of the church of the wicked, nevertheless the fullness of all evils was not in him in the way in which the fullness of all goods will be said to have been in Christ, since the devil is a good nature and many evils occur without his authorship. But he is said to have been head of the church of the evil because he sinned first and made the first human being sin: “Through the devil’s envy death entered into the world” (Wis. 2).

If it is asked whether Christ was the Church’s bridegroom before he was human, it is not properly said that he was bridegroom, because he was not of the same nature as she was; this is signified by marriage, which is customarily contracted between things of the same nature. Yet if he is found somewhere in the prophets to be called bridegroom of the Synagogue, as in Jeremiah—“I remembered you, pitying your youth and the love of your betrothal,” etc. (Jer. 2)—this is said by transference and metaphorically.

Again, Christ is king and priest. He is king [Col. 1218D] according to both natures; priest only according to his human nature, because in that nature he is Mediator between God and human beings, which is proper to a high priest. If it is asked whether his priesthood began at the supper, when he offered his body and blood to the apostles, or before conception, when he received the charisms of the Holy Spirit, it may reasonably be said that he became priest from the moment he was united in conception. But he exercised the office of priest when, at the supper, he gave his flesh and blood to the disciples, and when he gave himself as a sacrifice for our sins. [Note: [Col. 1218D] The Master, above, § f.]

Then too he was Mediator between God the Father [Col. 1219A] and the human beings whom he reconciled to him—not because God the Father had not loved beforehand those whom he loved from the beginning of the world, indeed from eternity, but because we, by sinning, practiced enmity against him, though he loved us. Therefore Christ reconciled us through his death, by blotting out the cloud of sins which prevented it from passing completely.

But an objection is made: Christ is Mediator insofar as he is human. Therefore he is Redeemer insofar as he is human. Therefore he redeemed us insofar as he is human. [Note: [Col. 1219D] The Master, § g.]

To this it must be said that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are our Redeemer by authority and exercise of power. Yet the Son is called Redeemer in another particular way: by the display of humility and obedience. For redemption is the possibility of freedom, granted to us when the power of the devil has been destroyed through the shedding of the blood of one who had no sin; and he fulfilled in himself, as human, the things by which we have been justified. For according to his humanity he received and fulfilled those sacraments which were made for our redemption. Observe that all of us were redeemed from the devil through Christ; nevertheless, the price was not given to the devil but to the Father, whose prisoners they were—both prison and jailer. [Col. 1219B] It is as if someone gave his slave into the hand of another who tormented him; the slave’s relatives come to the one who delivered the slave to another who torments him, and redeem him from the one who torments him; yet the latter does not receive the redemption, but rather the one by whom he had been handed over to him.

Again, God the Father could have put forward another as though a Son, who might suffer for us; that person would be head of the Church and Mediator between God and human beings. Therefore he would possess in himself the fullness of graces. It is true that he could put forward another who would be head of the Church through a certain pre-eminence over others, but not through fullness of virtues, which no one except Christ could possess. Thus the Lord Pope today is head of the Church; that other person too would be mediator, but not properly, because he would not share divinity with him. For if he were properly intermediate between both extremes, he would have to participate in both.

Again, it is the nature of an intermediate thing that it be neither extreme; Christ is Mediator between God and human beings. Therefore he is neither [Col. 1219D] God nor human. This is a fallacy. It is the nature of an intermediate thing that it be neither of the extremes: air is intermediate between hot and moist; therefore it is neither hot nor moist. This is false. Rather, it is not *that* hot thing and *that* moist thing between which it mediates, namely fire and water. Likewise, it should have said that Christ is neither God the Father nor those human beings whom he reconciles to him.

## Chapter XXI. By what power Christ could lay down his soul: divine or human; and whether, in his human nature, he was lower than the angels

[Note: [Col. 1219D] The Master, Book III, distinction 21.] It is asked by what power Christ could lay down [Col. 1220A] the soul which he had in his own power—something no human being can do, because no one can die when he wills unless he inflicts violence upon himself by killing himself. [Note: [Col. 1219D] See Augustine, *Tractates on John*, tractate 47, after the middle.] Hence in the Gospel of John: “I have power to lay down my soul, and I have power to take it up again. No one takes it from me” (John 10). And elsewhere: “The Son of Man goes as it is written of him” (Mark 14).

Therefore Christ could do this impossible thing by some power: either created or uncreated. If by uncreated power, then he could die insofar as he was God. If by created power, I ask likewise: did he not have a created power by which he could do every impossible thing, such that he could create heaven and earth by a created power insofar as he was human? Thus Christ would be omnipotent insofar as he was human, just as he was all-knowing according to his humanity.

Again, through the power of divinity he could become human. Therefore, through the power of divinity, he can undergo whatever is customarily present in a human being and is not a shameful defect: through the power of deity he could hunger, thirst, and be cold.

To this it must be said that created power was capable of laying down the soul whenever it willed, something impossible for any human being. Yet it does not follow from this that he had created power for doing every other thing; or, if he had it, he would not therefore be called omnipotent as man, since he had that power from the Godhead. Others say—and my master holds this opinion [Note: [Col. 1220D] The Master, above, § c. Walter of St Victor also mentions and censures this in Book IV *Against the Labyrinths of France*]—that uncreated power could lay down the soul whenever it willed, which no one else can do. Thus, when the centurion saw that he had yielded up his spirit, he said—marvelling at the work of the Godhead, that Christ had voluntarily yielded up his own spirit, which he could not have done had he been merely a man—“Truly this man was the Son of God” (Matt. 27). Yet uncreated power could not die: for death denotes a defect, whereas laying down the soul requires power. The power by which he could take up his soul again, that is, the power of the Godhead and no other, could also lay it down.

Again, Christ was made a little lower than the angels. Therefore this was either according to the divine or according to the human nature; but not according to the divine. If according to the human nature, it was either according to the soul or according to the body. It was not according to the soul, since neither could Christ’s soul have been made better by God, nor could any creature be equalled to it [Col. 1220D]. Therefore he is lower than them according to the flesh. This is rejected, because Christ’s flesh gives life to souls; this has been granted to no angel. Therefore Christ’s flesh is better than any angel.

On the other hand, angels can contemplate God, while flesh cannot at all. Therefore angels are better than Christ’s flesh. To this it must be said that Christ is not lower than angels either according to the divine or according to the human nature; indeed, according to the human nature he is greater than angels: “For his magnificence has been exalted above the heavens” (Ps. 2), that is, above angelic nature; and the Apostle says: “Having become so much superior to the angels, as he has inherited a name more excellent than theirs.” Yet according to the human nature he is in some respect lower than angels, namely in passibility and mortality, because he was mortal and passible, something found in none of the angels. Nevertheless, in some respects Christ’s flesh is better than angels, and in some respect angels are better than Christ’s flesh; yet neither is the flesh simply better than they, nor are they simply better than it, unless equivocation be introduced into the word “better.” For Christ’s soul is better, that is, purer and holier; angels, however, are better, that is, simpler. For it is certain that Christ’s soul is holier than every creature. Hence Ambrose says: “God alone is greater than the human mind” [Col. 1221B], because Christ’s soul could not be made better even in itself—a remarkable thing.

## CHAPTER XXII. In what subject Christ’s death existed, and what union was dissolved by his death

[Note: [Col. 1221D] The Master, III, distinction 21.]

Since Christ died according to his human nature, it is asked whether, at his death, the Godhead was separated from his flesh and soul. This seems to follow. For John Damascene says [Note: [Col. 1221D] Thus in the Master, III, distinction 2, § b. But in Damascene, Book III, chapter 6: “The Word of God was united to flesh through the mediation of mind.”]: “The divine nature is of such simplicity that it could not fittingly be united to a body formed from the mud of the earth except through the mediation of a rational creature.” Therefore, since the soul was then separated from the flesh, it seems that the Godhead was separated from the flesh, since it had been united to it through the soul; for, when the middle term is removed, the extremes are dissolved.

Again, if the soul has this office in the body—to give life and motion to the organs, make the tongue speak, the feet run, and the hands move—why could not the Godhead, while united to the body during those three days, do this as well, so that Christ’s body might move, live, and perform its other functions, and the Godhead might serve it in place of a soul? In the Gospel he also cries: “My God, why have you forsaken me?” (Ps. 21; Matt. 27). On this passage Ambrose says [Note: [Col. 1221D] Book X on Luke.]: “The man cries out, about to die through the separation of the Godhead; for since the Godhead is free from death, death could not occur unless life departed.” From all this it seems that the Godhead was separated from the flesh. Yet no one dares affirm this.

But the Godhead is said to have been united to the body through the mediation of the soul because it has a greater affinity with the soul, which is spiritual and simple, than with the flesh, which is bodily [Col. 1221D]. Once the reason for the statement has been considered, the objection disappears. It was not necessary for the divinity to be separated from the body, even though the soul, through whose mediation—as explained—it was united to the body, was separated from it [Note: [Col. 1222D] Thus Robert of Melun, as appears in the notes on Pullus.]. So too, through a man’s wife, her parents are related by affinity to him; yet when the wife is removed, the affinity is not removed.

As for the question whether the Godhead could have animated that body in the manner of a soul during those three days, who would deny that this could happen? Yet God does not do everything that he can do. Moreover, the line of the preceding argument has no force; for we often see a less valuable medicine effective where a more precious one has no effect: “what heals the heel does not heal the eye.” Therefore it is not surprising if the soul had animated that body, while it was not given life by the Godhead during those three days. Yet it must not be denied that God could have done this, had he willed.

The statement, “that man was forsaken by God,” is not to be understood as though the Godhead had been separated from flesh and soul, but because God left the human nature to be tortured and scourged by its tormentors. Since he could have protected it, he appeared to have been separated—not with respect to union, but with respect to protection [Col. 1222B].

[Note: [Col. 1222D] The Master, III, distinction 22.]

But someone will say: If the Godhead during those three days was united both to the soul and to the body, and if by “human nature” we understand nothing other than body and soul, then it was united to human nature at that time. God is called man for no other reason than that God assumed human nature into himself. Therefore Christ was a man at that time as well. This, however, is shown false by many arguments: Christ had ceased to live a human life; therefore during the three days he was not a man.

That he did not then live a human life is shown thus. That human life is an accident, and something was then alive. Therefore that life was then in a subject. Something, then, was its subject: either Christ’s soul or body—both of which are false—or the Son of God, which is equally false, because there are no accidents in the Son of God; or something composed of soul and flesh, which is likewise false [Note: [Col. 1222D] These words should be read cautiously, and one should see what the authors of the *Sentences* have written concerning such an opinion.]. For even when Christ was alive, there was not some thing composed from that soul and flesh; indeed, even if something had been composed from them, it ceased to exist at death, because that death was nothing other than the separation of the body from the soul.

Again, the temporal death which Christ endured was an accident in a subject. It existed in that in which human life had existed: either in Christ’s soul, or body, or in the person of the Word, or in a composite of flesh and soul. It was not temporal in the soul, since the soul cannot die; hence human life was not in the soul either. Nor was it in the body, because a body is not something that is moved. And since nothing but the body died, while Christ is not the body, he cannot be said to have died. That death was not in the person of the Word, because it is the subject of no accident. It follows, then, that it was in the composite of soul and flesh. Therefore, since that composite ceased to be something when the soul was separated from the body, something which is Christ then ceased to be something, because Christ was that composite.

Again, suppose that we are at the moment in which Christ is dead. Death is something; therefore, since it is an accident, it is in some subject. Therefore something dies, and that thing either is Christ or is not. If it is Christ, then something which is Christ dies; and this can be referred only to a nature. But the divine nature, which is Christ, does not die; nor does human nature die, because human nature is not Christ. If it is said that nothing which is Christ dies, it is difficult to say what dies.

Again, during those three days Christ either was wise with the wisdom that was in his soul, or he was not. No subject of the human wisdom by which Christ was wise can be found other than Christ’s soul; for it was not in the body nor in a composite of flesh and soul. Therefore, when the Son of God was then wise with human wisdom, there was wisdom which existed in something other than him, namely the soul, which is entirely distinct from the Son of God [Col. 1223B].

Again, Christ was then a man experiencing no infirmity that he had not previously assumed. Why, then, could he not previously die? Or else at that time he could die, speak, run, and do the other things human beings do. Again, he was then a man. Therefore he was either mortal or immortal. If mortal, then he could die; if immortal, then he could not die, and consequently he already had glorified flesh. Again, he was then a dead man, and a dead man is not a man; therefore he was not then a man. For if he was a dead man, he was a man not living a human life, and yet he was a living man; thus he was a man living by a life other than human life, and hence he lived by divine life.

Again, during those three days Christ was one man and Peter another man. Christ and Peter were then two men; therefore they then lived human life. Again, it is impossible for death to be in someone without life ceasing to be in him. Christ died a temporal death; therefore he then ceased to live a human life. Therefore during those three days he did not live a human life.

To remove quibbling, let what has been said be made clear: death cannot be in someone without life ceasing to be in him, because the predicates “death” and “life” are not opposites as privation and possession are—things which do not belong at a determinate time and in an irreversible order. For when a man ceases to live, death is then in him, and thus death and life are in the same thing; therefore they are not opposite predicates. Yet as soon as death is present, life must immediately depart, so that in the very next instant one can say: “This does not live.” Otherwise the statement “Death was in this person a little while ago” would be false.

This is to be understood of human death and human life. Therefore, since Christ died a human death, he ceased to live a human life, since this death destroys that life. I say this because spiritual death does not destroy human life, nor does spiritual life destroy temporal death. For Christ then lived a spiritual life, although he had died a temporal death [Col. 1223D].

Again, Christ was not then mortal; before, he had been mortal. That mortality was an accident, and therefore was in a subject [Col. 1224A]: either Christ’s soul or body; or a composite of soul and body; or the Son of God was its subject. Since the soul cannot die, it was not its subject; nor was the body, because just as a body does not live, so neither does it die; nor was it any composite of soul and body, because there was no composite of soul and body, as was said above [Note: [Col. 1223D] See the notes on Pullus.]; nor was it the Son of God, because in him there is no accident. Or, if he himself was mortal, this was not according to the divine nature. Therefore it was according to the human nature: according to either body, soul, or a composite of both. If according to the body, then that mortality was in the body as its subject; if according to a composite of the two, then something was composed of soul and body. For certainly he was not mortal according to the soul.

Again, if Christ had assumed only a soul or only a body, he would not be a true man. In hell he did not have both soul and body, but soul only. Therefore he was not a true man there. Likewise, he was not a true man in the tomb, where he was united only to the body; and thus nowhere was he a true man. Again, Christ was in hell; there he had only soul and not body; thus he was not wholly in hell, and so he was not wholly everywhere. Again, Christ was a man in the tomb. Every man fills a place; that place was filled by Christ. But this is rejected, because that place was filled by Christ’s body, and Christ’s body is not something that is Christ [Col. 1224C]. Therefore it was then filled by something other than Christ, or Christ was then there; therefore it was not filled by Christ. Again, it was filled by Christ and by Christ’s body, and these were two things; therefore two things simultaneously filled that place, which is impossible.

[Note: [Col. 1223D] The Master, above, § a.]

For the solution of the foregoing objections, one must know in what sense Christ is called man, and in what sense other human beings are called men; for there is a difference in the expression. Peter, or another person, is called a man for two reasons: because he has a soul and a body, and because he has them united. For if they were separated, one could not truly say, “Peter is a man.” But Christ is not called man for these two reasons, but for one only: because the Son is united to soul and body. It is not required that soul be united to body, for whether it is separated or united, the Son is called man no less, since he is united to human substance, that is, to soul and body.

Thus during those three days he was a man [Note: [Col. 1223D] Walter of St Victor attacks this also in the book *On the Four Labyrinths of France*.], just as before [Note: [Col. 1224D] Observe this also.] the union of flesh to soul was dissolved in Christ’s death. For that dissolution was called Christ’s death—whether the union of each with the other is the same union, which in the body might be called embodiment and in the soul animation; or whether there are two unions, one in the body and the other in the soul. The latter is more truly said, because no one property exists simultaneously in two subjects.

First, however, this must be held most firmly: the union of the Godhead to the soul and to the flesh was the same union, and it was not dissolved in Christ’s death [Col. 1225A]. Hence he was then called man because of that union, which was not dissolved. If it is asked of that union whether it was a property of the soul or of the body, it may be said that it belonged to both, since there is no reason why it should belong more to one than to the other—unless perhaps it is first said to have been in the soul, through whose mediation the Son of God was united to the body.

During those three days Christ was a dead man: man, on account of the union of body and soul with each other [or rather, with the Godhead]; dead, on account of each being separated from the other, namely flesh from soul and soul from flesh. Hence he was then neither mortal nor immortal.

The objection, “That mortality by which Christ was mortal was an accident; therefore it was in a subject,” and the inquiry in what subject it was, must be understood thus: mortality, human life, and human death were in the body, all of which had Christ’s body as their subject [Col. 1225B]. Ambrose clearly testifies to this:

> “Christ rose, and did not rise. He rose according to the flesh, which had died; and he did not rise according to the Word, which remained eternally with God.”

[Note: [Col. 1225D] Book III, *On the Holy Spirit*. See Book I, *On the Sacrament of the Incarnation of the Lord*, chapter 5.]

For the death of the body was nothing other than its separation from the soul. On account of that death Christ is said to have been dead, just as this mountain is said to be seen on account of the part of the mountain which is visible. In this way these matters can indeed be resolved.

But if an objection is raised concerning those properties which belong by reason of composition, such as speech and the capacity for laughter—among which temporal death, life, and mortality also seem to belong, though we have placed them in the body—it is most difficult to reply [Note: [Col. 1225D] Walter likewise attacks this and its author in the book mentioned above.]. Of the properties belonging to a human being, some belong according to the body: whiteness belongs to the body, and hence the person is called white. Others belong according to the soul, such as virtue, whose proper subject is the soul, and hence the person is called virtuous; likewise knowledge. Others belong according to the composition of soul and body, such as the capacity for laughter, whose subject is neither body nor soul but the composite of body and soul—as are speaking, running, and similar things, which belong neither to body nor soul but to their composite.

Concerning these properties which belong according to composition, it is difficult to see how they can be attributed to Christ [Col. 1225D]. When it is said, “Christ spoke,” is this said according to the soul or according to the body? Both are plainly false, because neither was the subject of Christ’s speech. Is it said according to a composite of soul and body, as in other men? No, because nothing was composed from that soul and body. Is it said according to the divine nature? No, because that was the subject of no accident. Therefore, since it is said of Christ neither according to the divine nor according to the human nature that he spoke, wept, and the like, how is it said of him?

For it is easy to see how one may understand that he was wise, namely according to the soul in which wisdom existed, or that he was coloured, according to his body in which colour existed [Note: [Col. 1225D] Peter’s confession is uncorrupted, and though slower in the trifles of the *Sophisms*, it is an old assault.]. But who will make me certain concerning these matters? I am not sufficient to explain such subtleties [Note: [Col. 1226D] From Ambrose, Book I, *On Faith*, chapter 5.]: “Remove arguments from sacred Scripture when faith is at issue.” Faith is not to be wise beyond what is fitting. Believe that it is so, and do not ask why he was a man although he did not live a human life, and was a man in hell though there he had soul only.

Just as this man is a father here, although he does not have his offspring here, so Christ was in hell having soul and body, but not having them there; that ablative “in hell” qualifies the verb, not the participle. So too, this man here is “having offspring,” where the qualification belongs to the verb and not to the participle: he is here, while having offspring elsewhere.
