Thus Christ was in hell, having his body in the tomb [Col. 1226B]. For—unless you are careful—the fallacy of qualified and unqualified assertion, or that of amphiboly, or of composition and division, may hinder you [Note: [Col. 1226D] The Master, above, § P.].

The question how he was a true man there when he had only a soul there—whereas, had he assumed a soul alone, he would not be called a true man—has now been answered. There he retained the union of the Godhead with soul and body; while that union remained, he could not truly be said not to be man. He was man there because he retained it there.

[Col. 1226C] When it is asked whether he was wholly in hell or wholly in the tomb [Note: [Col. 1226D] The Master, above, § C.], see what the saints say on this matter. According to his Godhead he was wholly everywhere, and thus wholly in hell and wholly in the tomb [Note: [Col. 1226D] Damascene, Book III, *On the Faith*, chapter 7, at the end.], because they refer this to the person; but not “the whole,” because this refers to nature, lest it appear to imply that both natures were entire in hell, which is false. Yet if we wish to speak properly, the term “whole” should not be admitted in reference to the divinity, because it involves composition into parts; whereas the Godhead is a simple reality and has no parts. Thus “whole God,” or anything similar, is said improperly.

As for the question whether Christ filled the place in the tomb which was filled by Christ’s body, so that two things filled that place: Christ was said to fill that place on account of the body which filled it [Col. 1226D]. Whatever that body possessed cannot be said not to have been possessed by the Son of God, because of the union of the one with the other. Therefore the Son of God and the body are not counted together, although that body was neither God nor a part of God, but united to him. Just as one does not say, “this body and its whiteness,” although whiteness is neither the body nor part of it, so whatever Christ’s soul suffered is said to have been suffered by God [Col. 1227A]. Thus God is said to have died, and man to have descended from heaven. And so Christ died, and did not die, according to one and the other nature [Note: [Col. 1227A] Thus with the Master, III, distinction 21, § D. But it must be interpreted favourably with Ambrose, *On the Incarnation of the Lord*, chapter 5.].

[Note: [Col. 1227A] Augustine, Book I, *On the Trinity*, chapter 13, at the beginning.]

> “But the devout and prudent reader should diligently inquire what is said, of whom, how, and in what respect.”

I am aware that I have heard some say that during those three days the Son of God was not a man, because he then did not possess the things which concur in the being of a man and for which other human beings are called men. For although he was united to soul and flesh, those were not united to each other. Thus, although in death he ceased to be man and in the resurrection began to be man, he was nevertheless not made man twice, because on the second occasion he was not made man.

For here it would be implied that in the resurrection he began again to unite body and soul and join those two together; the first of these claims is false [Col. 1228A]. Just as, in order that someone be a priest, he must be ordained and possess the power of performing the office: if someone is deposed and afterwards restored to his rank, he is not customarily said to begin to be a priest, because that would imply that he began to be ordained. Likewise it is not said that Christ then began to be a man.

Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1228A] This is not found in Sermon 129, *On Right Faith*, among the *Sermons for the Season*. In place of Augustine, restore Athanasius, Book VI, *On the Blessedness of the Son of God*, addressed to Theophilus.]:

> “Let anyone who says that the Son of God assumed man anew or twice be anathema.”

What Jerome says elsewhere, seemingly contrary—“Let anyone who says that the Son of God put off man be anathema”—must be understood thus: not that the Godhead was separated from flesh and soul, but that soul and flesh were divided from one another.

## [FIFTH BOOK]

## THE DISTINCTIONS OF THE FIFTH BOOK BEGIN

[Col. 1227]

What a sacrament is. What is the cause of the institution of the sacraments. What baptism is. What is the difference between the sacraments of the New Law and those of the Old. What is the form of baptism. What is the efficacy of baptism in infants, adults, hypocrites, and those who were pure before baptism. What is the difference between John’s baptism and Christ’s baptism. What force baptism has in those who are known with certainty to have been baptized and are baptized again. On confirmation. What is the sacrament of the Eucharist and what is the reality of the sacrament. What is the form of this sacrament. What is the mode of conversion. What is the mode of receiving. What is the sacrament of marriage and what is its reality. What is its institution. What is the efficient cause of marriage. What is its final cause; where it is said whether it is lawful to dismiss one’s wife. On the quality of resurrected bodies. On the spirit through whose mediation they say the soul is united to the body. On aids for the dead before the day of judgment. On the state of souls separated from bodies until the day of judgment: whether there is for them a place of merit. On the different dwelling-places of the blessed in the homeland.

## BOOK FIVE

[Col. 1227]

## CHAPTER I. What a sacrament is

[Col. 1227B]

[Note: [Col. 1227B] The Master, *Sentences*, Book IV, distinction 1.]

Among the works of our salvation which Christ undertook in human nature, the last were the resurrection and ascension into heaven. Accordingly, one ought immediately after the preceding matters to deal with them, were it not that we believe that the members will ascend where the head has gone before. Therefore, so that the upward way may be made clear, we must treat of the way by which we shall rise and ascend, namely participation in the sacraments, so that the work begun may finally be completed in the joy of the resurrection [Col. 1228B].

We must therefore consider what a sacrament is; what is the cause for the institution of sacraments; in what they consist; and what difference there is between the sacraments of the New Law and the sacraments of the Old Law. A sacrament is called either something sacred that has been signified, something sacred that signifies, or a secret [Note: [Col. 1228B] Augustine, Book II, *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 1.]. For a sacrament is a sign of a sacred thing. A sign is a thing which, besides the appearance (the text reads *spem*, with *rem* bracketed) that it presents to human senses, causes something else to come into cognition from itself [Col. 1229A].

Some signs are natural: rain is a natural sign of rainfall. Others are given: for example, a circle signifies wine for sale. Of given signs, some bring about what they signify, while others do not, such as the signs of the Old Law. For something properly to be called a sacrament, it must be such a sign of a thing that it both signifies and brings it about, and bears in itself an image of the thing figured. All of this can be seen in the water of baptism. Hence the sacraments of the Old Testament are improperly called sacraments, because they do not bring about what they signify. Therefore it is defined thus: A sacrament is a visible form of invisible grace conferred in it.

## CHAPTER II. What is the cause of the institution?

[Col. 1229B]

[Note: [Col. 1229D] The Master, §§ C and D.]

There is a threefold cause for the invention of sacraments: humiliation, instruction, and exercise. Of exercises, some serve the instruction of the soul, some the edification of the body, and some the destruction of both. We would not be reluctant to make all these matters clearer, were we not to regard writing writings as the work of an idle person doing nothing [Note: [Col. 1229D] Of Peter Lombard, his teacher.]. All these things, moreover, are treated more fully in Master Peter’s *Book of Sentences*; yet they had to be mentioned here, so that the transition to what follows might be easier.

## CHAPTER III. What difference is there between the sacraments of the New Law and those of the Old?

The difference between the sacraments of the Old and New Law is this: the former do not bring about what they signify, while the latter do bring about what they signify [Col. 1229C]. One of the former was called circumcision, in whose place baptism succeeded. Since this has been discussed above, nothing need be said of it here.

Among the sacraments of the New Law, some are necessary, or general; others are special, also called voluntary. Necessary sacraments are those without which salvation is scarcely attained: baptism, confirmation, Eucharist, penance, and extreme unction. Voluntary sacraments are those without which salvation can be attained: orders and marriage.

Again, some sacraments are for those entering, some for those advancing, some for those fighting, some for those returning, and some for those departing. Baptism is for those entering, because no one is said to belong to the Church before being baptized; then he enters, although beforehand he may belong to it by holiness of life [Col. 1229D]. For some belong to the Church by predestination, but not by holiness of life or participation in sacraments, as Paul when he was Saul; some by predestination and holiness of life, but not by participation in sacraments, as Cornelius before baptism; and some in every way, as Paul when he preached.

The Eucharist is for those advancing, and hence is called *viaticum*, provision for the journey. Confirmation, because it is given for strength, is for those fighting. Penance is for those returning from the region of unlikeness. Unction is for those departing from this life. Therefore we must first speak of baptism, considering what baptism is, what is its form [Col. 1230A], and what is its efficacy. There will also be said what difference there is between John’s baptism and Christ’s baptism; fourth, who may be baptized.

## CHAPTER IV. What baptism is

[Note: [Col. 1229D] The Master, Book IV, distinction 3.]

Baptism is an outward washing of the body performed under the prescribed form of words. Hence *baptism* is interpreted as “washing.” From this description it is evident that the sacrament of baptism consists of two things: water and the form of words. Thus Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1230D] Tractate 80 on John.]:

> “Take away the word, and what is water but water? Let the word be added to the element, and it becomes a sacrament.”

Thus the form of baptism cannot be preserved without either of these. They belong to the substance of the sacrament; the other things connected with the sacraments are accidental, introduced for beauty and solemnity—for example, the blessing of the water and the like [Col. 1230B]. Hence the sacrament exists without them.

But it is objected: if baptism is washing, and that washing is either the action of the washer or the passion of the one washed, and both are a human work, then baptism is a human work and therefore not a work of God. Again, since a triple immersion takes place in baptism and each immersion is baptism, the infant is baptized three times when immersed. For those three immersions do not appear to be one baptism. Again, that washing of the body is a sacrament of the New Testament; therefore it brings about what it signifies, and thus effects the inward cleansing of which it is a figure. Therefore a human work is the cause of the forgiveness of sins, and not God alone.

For this reason some say that baptism is something formed from the action of the washer and the passion of the one washed, which is from God and is a work of God rather than of man [Col. 1230C]. But if one comes to a strict inquiry about what this thing is—whether substance or accident—it is difficult to say what it is. Nor is there anything which has a more explicit likeness to that inward cleansing than the washing of the body. Therefore we call that washing the Church’s baptism. Nor is it surprising that it is a human work and is a cause of forgiveness of sins, just as Paul’s preaching, which was his own work, was the cause of many conversions.

Nor are three immersions three baptisms, but one baptism. Therefore, concerning what is found on the passage in John, “Unless someone be born again of water and the Holy Spirit” (John 3)—“water, understood as the visible sacrament, and Spirit, understood as the invisible”—we understand it so that we do not say that the water itself is the sacrament of baptism, but call it a sacrament as a thing sanctified by blessing [Col. 1230D].

## CHAPTER V. What is the form of baptism?

[Note: [Col. 1230D] The Master, above, § B.]

The form of baptism is that which the Lord teaches in the Gospel: “Go into all the world, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28). But it is asked whether the form of baptism is preserved if one says, “I baptize you in the name of Christ.” We say that it is preserved. For although this is the form of words under which baptism ought to be performed—“In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit”—yet by the name “Christ” are understood the one who anoints, namely the Father; the one who is anointed, namely the Son; and the one through whom the anointing is performed, namely the Holy Spirit [Col. 1231A]. Thus the apostles baptized in the primitive Church.

[Note: [Col. 1231D] The Master, § C.]

It is also customary here to ask whether the form of baptism is preserved when only one person is named. On this Ambrose says [Note: [Col. 1231D] Ambrose, *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 3.]:

> “Likewise, if in speech you comprehend one—whether the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit—yet in faith deny neither Father, Son, nor Holy Spirit, the sacrament of faith is complete. So too, even if you name Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, but diminish the power of the Father, Son, or Holy Spirit, the whole mystery is empty.”

Thus the Lord also says: “But you shall be baptized in the Holy Spirit” (Acts 1). Here it seems that the form of baptism is preserved although only the Holy Spirit is named. They say that the form of baptism is preserved when only one person is named, because when one is named, the others are understood [Col. 1231B].

[Note: [Col. 1231D] The Master’s solution, § E.]

The statement, “When all three are named, the mystery is empty if one is wrongly understood,” must be understood only of someone who neither intends nor believes that he baptizes, who lacks not only faith but also the intention of baptizing. But if one asks concerning a person who uses an inverted order, saying, “In the name of the Son, and of the Father, and of the Holy Spirit,” whether he preserves the form of baptism: it may be said that it is safer to name the three persons in the right order. Yet if this is done from ignorance and not in order to introduce heresy, it is indeed the form of baptism, just as when one person alone is named [Note: [Col. 1231D] He follows the Master in error. *On Consecration*, distinction 4, chapter *Retulerunt*.].

Likewise, if someone ignorant of Latin says, “In nomine Patrias et Filias et Spirituas sanctas,” he preserves the form, because he does this from ignorance and not in order to introduce heresy.

If, however, he pronounces the words in French or Romance, it is asked whether the form of baptism is preserved. This seems likely. For the Lord said to his disciples: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father,” etc. (Matt. 28). Since the languages of nations differ, the apostles had to baptize and preach to every nation in the language it knew; otherwise, they would not understand the preachers [Col. 1231D]. If this is so, then someone can celebrate Mass in the vernacular and consecrate the body. Therefore the sacrament will not be invalid if this is done. The same applies if someone does this in Hebrew or Greek.

They say, therefore, that unless necessity arises, it is not lawful to do this. For example, if someone placed among believing Hebrews knows no language except Hebrew, and the same is true of them, he may celebrate Mass in Hebrew [Col. 1232A], because the Lord pronounced these words in Hebrew: “This is my body,” etc. (Matt. 26). But where there is an abundance of persons who know Latin, there is no need.

Likewise, the question is raised concerning immersion: whether a single immersion suffices, or whether a triple immersion is necessary. [Note: [Col. 1231D] The Master, § 1.] In this matter, as the saints hand down, the practice of the Church is to be followed. Yet one who immerses once signifies the unity of the divine essence; triple immersion denotes the Trinity of persons or the three-day burial. It is nevertheless asked, if triple immersion is necessary, whether a child immersed once has been baptized if the priest dies after the first immersion; or, if he has not been baptized, whether another priest ought to begin where the first left off, provided he immerses him twice, or whether [Col. 1232B] he must begin the whole rite again from the outset. Likewise, concerning an interruption in the Eucharist, it is asked whether, if half of these words—“This is my body,” at the utterance of which transubstantiation takes place—has been spoken, another priest ought to begin where the first ended if the first dies after finishing half of them; or whether he should begin again from the outset. [Note: [Col. 1232D] These doubts of the author are to be excused in view of the time in which he lived.] The same question applies to one who, after immersing a child once, sees another person immediately about to die unless he leaves this one and assists the other with the remedy of baptism. [Note: [Col. 1232D] Thus Augustine answers in a similar matter; *On Consecration*, distinction 4.] In all these cases, one must implore the divine eye.

There are some who raise here a ridiculous question concerning a maimed priest and another who has hands but is mute: is the form of baptism preserved if the one with hands immerses, [Col. 1232C] and the handless man pronounces the words? For when he says, “I baptize you in the name of the Father and of the Son,” etc., he does not seem to speak truly, since the one who immerses is the one who baptizes. Likewise, it is asked whether, in necessity, someone may baptize himself, provided the form of baptism is observed; and concerning the form of the words uttered by John when baptizing Christ—of which form, however, nothing is found. [310] In all these matters I prefer to consult those more learned than myself rather than rashly assert anything. I judge it more suitable to proceed to the third chapter, where the efficacy of baptism must be discussed, than to labor over a council of cases that never occur, or to idle over their solutions.

## CHAPTER VI. What is the efficacy of baptism in infants, in adults, in the insincere, and in those who were clean before baptism?

[Col. 1232D]

[Note: [Col. 1232D] The Master, IV, distinction 4.] In infants baptism has this efficacy: it grants remission of original sins and bestows the gifts of the virtues, namely faith, hope, and charity. For if, as they say, infants do not then receive grace by which they can act well when they become adults, then the grace given them in baptism does not suffice, nor can they be good through it unless another grace is added. If [Col. 1233A] it is not added, this is not their fault, since they have been justified from sin. Therefore they teach that in baptism the grace of the virtues—namely faith, hope, and charity—is bestowed as a gift and habit, [Note: [Col. 1233D] This should be noted chronologically concerning the infusion of habits in infant baptism.] but not in use. For the infant neither believes, nor hopes, nor loves; nevertheless, he has faith, hope, and charity, just as he has rationality, though he does not reason, and the capacity for laughter, though he does not laugh.

Hence this argument has been made: “This infant has faith and does not believe; therefore that faith is dead”—which would mean that he is not good through that faith. This is a fallacy. “This person knows dialectic and yet cannot dispute, granted that he is mute; therefore he is not, according to that knowledge, a good dialectician”—which is false. He has it in habit, but not in use.

Again, since infants are cleansed in baptism [Col. 1233B] from all sins, it appears that, if they die immediately after baptism, they pass into glory, and thus we are certain of their condition. Why then does the Church pray for them? For it prays only for those who await purgatory. But such prayers are thanksgivings, [Note: [Col. 1234D] Thus Robert Pullus.] as will be said later.

In an adult baptism has this efficacy: if anyone approaches with a contrite heart, both original and actual sins are remitted to him. Furthermore, the virtues are bestowed. Nor is any penitential satisfaction imposed. But an objection is raised: “Before this person was baptized, he was contrite through charity; therefore his sins had already been forgiven. What then did baptism confer on him? It seems superfluous, since he already had charity.” Therefore [Col. 1233C] it must be said that baptism was not superfluous: for if he were not baptized when he had the place and opportunity, that contrition would not benefit him unless he received baptism; and because in baptism he was cleansed from sins more and more. Hence: “Wash me yet more from my iniquity,” etc. (Psalm 50). He was also freed from the penalty of satisfaction to which he would have been bound if he were not baptized, and his faith is increased through baptism. [Note: [Col. 1234D] Jerome, cited by the Master here, § E.] For “faith is nourished in the waters.”

Again: this adult who wishes to approach baptism is contrite through charity; therefore every mortal sin is remitted, and thus contrition removes original sin. Therefore baptism alone does not do so. They accordingly say that, just as by contrition concerning other sins a sin consigned to oblivion is removed, though one does not ordinarily say that it is removed by contrition, so too original sin is removed by contrition concerning other sins, though one does not simply assert: “Original sin is removed by contrition.” Yet I do not consider it a serious inconvenience to admit this.

Again, from Adam we contracted [the text is corrupt: “saccum et mentem succi”], that is, guilt and punishment; through Christ’s gift, that is, through baptism, we are not cleansed of punishment in the present life. Therefore Adam’s offense harmed more than Christ’s death benefits—which is false. For, although we are here freed from guilt, it is for our advantage that we are not freed from punishment, since by laboring in the struggle we thus obtain the crown. Hence Augustine says: “For the avoidance [Col. 1234A] of sin, weakness is retained, so that through this punishment which he feels, sick man may fear sinning more.” Just as you see that a physician treats one of the two wounds a man has, leaving the other so that through it the discharge may issue forth; and thus the man may eventually rise stronger. Therefore it is better that it not be healed now than that it be healed; for it will afterward be healed, and he will be made stronger.

Again, by sinning Adam earned eternal death for us all; no adult attains eternal life through Christ’s merits without his own merits. Therefore Adam was more effective in earning death than Christ in earning life. This is a fallacy. An eel, without a man’s consent, causes him to suffer a fever; medicine, without his consent, cannot produce health in him. Therefore the eel is more effective in harming than medicine in healing. This is not true.

Again, baptism accomplishes nothing unless contrition precedes it, accompanies it, or follows it. Therefore contrition produces baptism’s power. This is true conditionally, not causally. It is a fallacy: “This man cannot be a bishop unless he knows letters; therefore knowledge of letters is the cause of his episcopacy.”

Again, through baptism sin is removed both as to guilt and as to punishment; through contrition, however, only as to guilt. Therefore baptism is better than contrition. This is indeed true, because it has preeminence in more respects. Yet conversely: through contrition, without baptism, sins [Col. 1234C] can be removed in an adult; but not through baptism without contrition. Therefore contrition is better than baptism. This is a fallacy. “This man can be healed by medicine even without a physician, but not by a physician without medicine; therefore medicine is better than a physician.”

Again, through contrition someone may be cleansed from sins many times, but through baptism only once. Therefore contrition is better than baptism. This is a fallacy. “This man gave him something many times; that man only once; therefore the former gave more than the latter.”

Again, here are an adult and an infant: one is guilty of original sin, the other of original and actual sin. This adult is more seriously ill than that infant; both need a remedy. Therefore the adult needs baptism more than the infant. Conversely, the infant cannot be cleansed except through baptism, while the adult can be cleansed through contrition and baptism. Therefore the infant needs baptism more than the adult. [Col. 1234D] It is true that the adult needs a remedy more than the infant, but the infant needs the remedy of baptism more. This may be seen in two persons, one of whom is hungrier than the other: the less hungry cannot be satisfied except by one food, while the hungrier can be satisfied by several. The hungrier person needs food more, and yet the less hungry person needs this food more. It is likewise with two sick persons: one is sicker than the other; the one who is sicker can be cured by several [Col. 1235A] medicines, the less sick by one alone. The sicker man needs a remedy more; but the less sick man needs this remedy more.

It has been said what effect baptism has in infants and in contrite adults. Now it must be said what effect it has in adults who approach baptism insincerely. [Note: [Col. 1235D] The Master, § B and following.] That baptism has efficacy in them is proved in many ways, directly and indirectly.

Directly thus: this man is baptized with Christ’s baptism. Therefore baptism has full efficacy in him. Therefore it bestows full remission of sins on him. Again, he is baptized with baptism, and this baptism does not produce in him the remission of sins which it nevertheless signifies. Therefore it is not a sacrament of the New Testament, or the distinction [Col. 1235B] between the sacraments of the Old Testament and those of the New Testament has been inappropriately stated. Again, that washing does not produce that inner washing, nor will it produce it, nor has it produced it, on the supposition that he will always be insincere. Therefore it is not a true sacrament, since it produces nothing. Again, this man is baptized by the authority either of Christ or of the priest. If by the authority of the priest and not with Christ’s baptism, then the priest forgives his sins. But if by Christ’s authority, then his sins are forgiven.

Again, that person baptizes [lacuna]; his external washing is the work of someone, either of the baptizer or of the baptized. If it is the work of the baptizer and is done through charity, then the baptizer merits by that baptism. Likewise, he merits by baptizing, insofar as baptizing is called the action by which he baptizes—an act other than baptism, [Col. 1235C] because it is an *opus operans* [a working work], whereas baptism is an *opus operatum* [a work performed], if one may speak thus. Therefore the one who baptizes merits by two works. By the same reasoning, he merits by the alms he gives and by the house he builds—which is false. For no one merits except by the action through which he does something from charity, which is an *opus operans*. Therefore he does not merit by that baptism, because baptism is a property of the washed person, that is, a passion or undergoing.

But if it is said that baptism is the work of the baptized person, then it is either his good work or his evil work. It is not good for him, because it leads him to death. Therefore it is evil; and thus baptism is an evil work, and so is evil.

Again, if the man baptized in this way now merits eternal death by baptism, and afterward will merit eternal life by it [Col. 1235D] when his insincerity departs and baptism begins to have full efficacy, then a work is now done without charity which will later be vivified through charity. Why then is almsgiving given by someone in mortal sin not vivified when he begins to have charity, just as baptism is? Is it the same with the Eucharist?

Again, this person will merit eternal life by the work of baptism when his insincerity departs. Therefore he will then perform that work, because no one merits by a work except by performing it at the time at which he merits by it.

Again, given that this insincere person was baptized and that now his insincerity departs, he is bound to repent of every mortal sin that he has committed. Therefore he must also repent of that baptism which he received, since it was a mortal sin. For if it is a work meriting [Col. 1236A] in itself when done with a good intention, why can it not merit eternal death if done with an evil will? Therefore he is bound to repent because he was baptized. But he knows that that baptism benefits him toward salvation and that he is better through the efficacy of that baptism than he would have been had he never been baptized. Therefore he is not bound to repent of that baptism.

Again, baptism in this person has begun to have full efficacy. Therefore his sins are remitted both as to guilt and as to punishment. Therefore satisfaction ought not to be imposed on him, either for those sins he committed before baptism or for those he committed afterward.

Again, suppose that one man is baptized sincerely, while another was previously baptized insincerely and does not repent of his insincerity. To the former, sins are remitted as to guilt and punishment; to the latter, only as to guilt. Therefore baptism has a greater effect in the former than in the latter. This person who was baptized insincerely has the same will to sin as one who is never baptized. Therefore receiving baptism seems to aggravate sin in him. Therefore he is worse than the other, just as one who has an equal will to sin with another is worse than that other if he has greater knowledge. Therefore, since contrition with charity can in this person remove sin as to punishment and guilt without a subsequent baptism, that other person can, by equally great contrition without baptism, be cleansed as to guilt and punishment.

Again, baptism in this formerly insincere person who repents would have no efficacy unless contrition preceded it. Therefore contrition is more necessary than baptism. On the contrary, baptism has this effect in him: [Col. 1236C] no penalty is imposed upon him for sins committed before baptism; contrition does not have such force in him. Therefore baptism benefits him more than contrition.

The ancients said that sins are forgiven to one who approaches baptism insincerely while he is in the waters of baptism, but that as soon as he rises from the waters his sins return. Otherwise, they say, the crossing of the Red Sea would not fully retain its typological significance: there the Egyptians were drowned and the Israelites crossed over. Unless, therefore, sins are always forgiven and removed in baptism, the Egyptians were submerged together with the Israelites.

The moderns, however, say that baptism benefits one baptized insincerely in no way; indeed, it is an occasion of eternal death to him, and the good which he misuses is turned into evil for him. Yet afterward, when he repents and insincerity departs, baptism begins to have this force: no satisfaction is imposed upon him for sins that he committed before baptism; but satisfaction must be imposed for those that he committed after baptism; the gifts of the virtues are increased in him; and he need not be baptized again. For then he receives the reality of the sacrament.

Some receive both the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament, as infants do; others the sacrament but not the reality, as the insincere do; others the reality but not the sacrament, as those prevented by death who, while running to baptism out of charity, die before immersion. Therefore the claim that the distinction between sacraments of the Old and New Testaments has been inappropriately stated because baptism does not produce in this person [Col. 1237A] what it signifies has no force. For it would produce it unless his enormity prevented it. And although he is baptized by Christ’s authority, his sins are not thereby forgiven—just as Christ gave the Eucharist to Judas by his own authority, yet Judas’s sins were not forgiven.

[Note: [Col. 1237D] The Master, § F.] After this, it is asked what effect baptism has in others who are baptized while clean, as in John and Christ. Since John was sanctified from the womb and cleansed from original sin, baptism does not seem to have conferred anything upon him. Yet the contrary is proved in the Gospel: John said to the Lord, “I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?” (Matthew 3). And the Gloss on that passage says: “I indeed need to be baptized by you, while you do not need it from me.” If, therefore, John needed baptism, he had either actual or original sin.

We say that he did not need it [Col. 1237B] for the remission of sins, because they had all previously been forgiven through the operation of the Holy Spirit. John, Jeremiah the prophet, and the Blessed Virgin received a singular privilege. Yet he needed baptism for the bestowal of greater grace, for weakening the *fomes* of sin, or perhaps he was speaking in the person of the human race.

## CHAPTER VII. What is the difference between John’s baptism and Christ’s baptism?

[Note: [Col. 1237D] The Master, IV, distinction 2.] Henceforth the difference between Christ’s baptism and John’s baptism must be stated. It is manifest that sins were not remitted through John’s baptism as they were through Christ’s baptism. [Col. 1237C] Many objections are made to this.

John says: “I baptize in water, but one stands in your midst whom you do not know” (John 1). Therefore God, who was standing in their midst, forgave sins. Therefore that baptism was for the remission of sins. To this it must be said that sins were often forgiven by God through the contrition with charity possessed by those approaching John’s baptism, but not by the power of John’s baptism; rather, by the power of contrition accompanied by charity.

Again, John’s baptism was a baptism of repentance. Therefore it conferred repentance. Again, John’s baptism was for the remission of sins. It must be said that it was for remission, but not for the remission of sins, because remission of sins was not bestowed in that baptism. Rather, baptism had this value: it disposed people toward the remission of sins, because it accustomed them to Christ’s baptism, in which sins were remitted. Nor was it called a baptism of repentance because it conferred repentance, but because John baptized only the repentant, or those bearing a sign of repentance. This is a fallacy of the first argument: “A work performed from natural piety while in mortal sin avails for eternal life and confers something; therefore it confers eternal life.”

Again, John baptized in the name of the one to come. Therefore Christ was then still to come; hence he had not yet come. It should therefore be understood that although Christ had then come in the flesh, he was yet to come into the knowledge [Col. 1238A] of human beings, and was to come in order to suffer and die.

Again, Christ had not yet bestowed regenerative power upon the waters when John baptized, because Christ himself had not yet been baptized. Therefore Christ’s baptism was not yet for the remission of sins. Again, if Christ bestowed power upon the waters when he was baptized, then whoever afterward was baptized in the name of the Trinity received remission of sins. Thus, since John afterward baptized in the name of the Trinity, sins were remitted in that baptism. But if he did not then bestow power upon the waters, baptism was not instituted before the Passion, and thus Christ’s disciples did not baptize for the remission of sins before the Passion. [Note: [Col. 1238D] The Master, distinction 5, §§ F, G.]

To this some say that Christ’s baptism began to have [Col. 1238B] efficacy either immediately when he was baptized, or when he suffered, or when he said to the disciples, “Go, teach all nations” (Matthew 28), etc. But whichever of these ways is correct, no one was baptized with Christ’s baptism before Christ himself was baptized.

Again, John’s baptism was from God. Therefore it was God’s baptism, and thus remission of sins was conferred in it. One may say that it was from God, but was not called God’s baptism, because that designation was appropriated to Christ’s baptism.

Again, it is asked why remission of sins was not conferred in John’s baptism, as it was in the baptism of Christ’s disciples, although greater grace had been bestowed on John than on any of the disciples, he had been commanded to baptize just as the other disciples had, and that baptism was from God. It must be said that, although Christ is nowhere read to have baptized anyone in his own person except through his disciples, he granted to his disciples that they should baptize for the remission of sins because they baptized with his baptism. He did not grant this to John; for a king often grants to one of lower rank what he does not grant to one of higher rank.

But this is asked: if someone running to baptism is overtaken by death, are his sins removed through the contrition he has from charity, both as to guilt and punishment? This seems so. For contrition produces in him what baptism would produce; thus he does not pass through purgatory, and it follows that contrition removes sins both as to guilt and punishment. Yet in that other person [Col. 1238D] who has been baptized, equally great contrition would not suffice to remove so many sins; because this is unknown to us, we pass it over in silence.

Some, however, maintain that sin is never forgiven to anyone unless he is immersed in the waters of baptism. When someone is prevented by death, they say this happens through the person’s sin, and therefore a person who so dies does not die in charity. But this view is antiquated.

Again, Christ baptized John with the baptism performed in the Spirit; John baptized Christ with the baptism performed only in water; and baptism performed in the Spirit is much more worthy than baptism performed in water. Therefore John was baptized with a worthier baptism [Col. 1239A] than Christ. This is true if baptism is referred to the person baptizing, false if it is referred to the person baptized. Yet it is nowhere read that Christ baptized John, although this is a belief of the laity.

Again, John’s baptism was a sacrament either of the New or of the Old Testament. If it was a sacrament of the New Testament—for it does not seem to have been a sacrament of the Old Testament—then it produced remission of sins; therefore it was in the Spirit, and not merely in water. It is true that John’s baptism was a sacrament, just as the sacraments of the Old Law were called sacraments; yet they did not produce what they signified. Nor did John’s baptism do so. It may likewise be said that it was a sacrament of Christ’s baptism, and that it preached nothing except that it accustomed people to Christ’s baptism. Thus it was called John’s baptism because nothing was done there except what could be done by a human being: it did not produce forgiveness of sins, which God alone produces.

[Note: [Col. 1239D] The Master, distinction 2, § F: on this point he had earlier stumbled.] But if it is asked whether those baptized with John’s baptism needed to be baptized with Christ’s baptism, it is clear that they did if they did not have faith in the Trinity. If, however, they did have it, they did not need to be baptized again, because their sins had already been forgiven through the power of faith, not of John’s baptism. If they were subsequently baptized, nevertheless, the sacrament was not said to be repeated.

## CHAPTER VIII. What power does baptism have in those known to have been baptized who are baptized again?

[Col. 1239C]

It is also asked what power baptism has in persons already baptized but not known to be baptized. It must be said that their virtues are increased if they are good. But if they were not good, and were baptized from the heart, their sins were forgiven.

But an objection is raised: this priest knows that one of these two infants has been baptized, but does not know which; he baptizes them both. Therefore he baptizes one of them twice. Since this can be understood in two ways, it can be explained in two ways. “He knowingly baptizes one of them twice,” that is, he knows that he baptizes one who has been baptized: if this is understood compositionally, it is true; but if [Col. 1239D] it is understood determinately, so that the meaning is, “He knows this person whom he baptizes to have been baptized,” it is false. For in that way he would perform countless sacraments if he repeated the sacrament.

For one who baptizes twice seems to think that Christ’s single death does not suffice for human salvation, since baptism represents that death. This is false, because Christ, having died once for our sins, need not die again; nor does the one who has been baptized need to be baptized.

Note that concerning this issue many plausible arguments can be made, all belonging to the art of dialectic; thus they create a scrupulous dispute, and so we pass them by. [Col. 1240A]

[Note: [Col. 1239D] The Master, distinction 5, §§ A, B.] Again, Christ could confer upon someone the power that he possesses by which he forgives sins; but this is greater than creating heaven and earth. Therefore he could confer upon someone the power to create heaven and earth, and thus could create some omnipotent creature. Again, that power is God; he could confer it upon someone; therefore he could confer on someone that he should be God.

It must be said that baptismal power is threefold: the power of authority, the power of excellence, and the power of ministry. The power of authority is that by which God forgives sins; it is God, and he could confer it upon no one so that the person might forgive sins by his own authority. For this would derogate from his majesty. [Col. 1240B] [Note: [Col. 1239D] Augustine, *Tractates on the Gospel of John*, tractate 5.]

There is also a power of excellence which Christ has because he possesses preeminence over others in baptizing. He could have given it but did not will to do so. For if someone had it, people would not think themselves properly baptized unless baptized by him. Thus all are equal in baptism. No one says “my baptism,” although one says “my Gospel,” because one person surpasses another in preaching, whereas no one surpasses another in baptizing. [Note: [Col. 1240D] See the selected and rejected articles in the teaching of the Master.] God could nevertheless confer upon someone a created power by which he would forgive sins—not, however, by his own authority, but rather by Christ’s. He gave the power of ministry to all.

[Note: [Col. 1240D] The Master, distinction 6, § G.] It is also customary to ask in what sense a godfather says on behalf of the child, “I believe,” or “I ask for faith.” For he does not ask faith for a child who does not yet believe, nor can the priest give faith. Therefore “I ask for faith” should be understood as “I ask for the sacrament of faith,” that is, the sacrament of faith. But when the question is specified, “Do you believe in God the Father?” etc., and the godfather answers for the little child, “I believe,” you should understand this of the disposition of mind to which the child will be bound as soon as he becomes an adult, just as he will be bound to renounce the pomps of the devil.

But an objection is raised: when he is an adult, he sins venially, and venial sin is a work of the devil; therefore he does not renounce the works of the devil. Therefore he transgresses the promise he made. They answer that he can commit venial sins and at the same time renounce them, because he places love of them below love of God, just as someone may possess riches and at the same time renounce them, because he places love of them below love of God. [Col. 1240D]

[Note: [Col. 1240D] The Master, distinction 6.] Finally, it is asked by whom baptism may be conferred. Certainly by priests alone, unless necessity is imminent—by good priests as well as bad. But intention must be preserved just as the form must be; otherwise it would not be baptism. Therefore one who jokingly immerses another while uttering the words customarily spoken by baptizers does not baptize.

It is nevertheless related of Bishop Athanasius that he saw Jewish boys immersing one another and jokingly speaking these words. [Col. 1241A] When they came as adults for baptism, he refused to baptize them, lest baptism appear to be repeated in them, judging that the first baptism, performed as though in jest, had then acquired efficacy.

It should be noted that baptism is preceded by catechism, which means instruction, and exorcism, which means adjuration. These are sacramentals rather than sacraments, because they do nothing except diminish the devil’s power in us, and thus diminish our sins, which are the cause of the devil’s greater power; they are, as it were, preparatory to baptism, like a small medicine preceding the reception of a greater one.

## CHAPTER IX. On confirmation

[Col. 1241B]

[Note: [Col. 1241D] The Master, distinction 7.] Concerning confirmation I find nothing else doubtful except the question whether this sacrament is more worthy than baptism. That it is more worthy is shown thus: it is given in a better place, namely on the forehead; at a better time, namely after the recipient has already been cleansed; by more eminent persons, namely by a bishop, and in the time of the apostles by the apostles alone; and for a greater purpose, namely strengthening. Therefore the sacrament of confirmation is greater than the sacrament of baptism.

Again, in confirmation the Holy Spirit is given for strengthening, and confirmation is given to infants. Therefore they then receive an increase of the virtues. It must be said that baptism is better, that is, more useful, than confirmation. But confirmation is better, worthier, and more precious—just as water is more useful than wine, but wine is worthier and more excellent. [Col. 1241C]

## CHAPTER X. What is the sacrament of the Eucharist, and what is the reality of the sacrament?

[Note: [Col. 1242D] The Master, distinction 8.] After the two sacraments mentioned above, the sacrament of the Eucharist must be considered—and this with modesty, fear, and reverence, because here faith works more than human reason. Hence no one should presume, beyond knowledge, authorities, and testimonies, either to read or to write anything about these matters.

These things must be investigated: what this sacrament is and what the reality of this sacrament is; what its form is; what manner of conversion occurs; and the other questions pertaining to this final chapter. [Col. 1241D] This sacrament is called “the visible form of invisible grace,” namely the species of bread and wine.

For there are three things: sacrament and not reality; reality and sacrament; reality and not sacrament. The species of bread and wine which remain after the bread is changed into body and the wine into blood are the sacrament of the Lord’s body and the Lord’s blood. For just as among bodily foods none strengthens the human heart more than bread, nor does anything make it glad more than wine, so nothing refreshes and satisfies as do the body and blood of Christ.

The same species are also the sacrament of ecclesial unity; for just as that bread is made from many grains, and that wine flows from many [Col. 1242A] grapes, so ecclesial unity consists of many persons among the faithful. The flesh which Christ took from the Virgin is signified, not effected, by those species, and is a sacrament of ecclesial unity; for just as Christ’s body consists of many unstained members, so ecclesial unity consists of many faithful persons. Ecclesial unity itself is reality and not sacrament: it is signified and does not signify. Thus we have what this sacrament is and what is the reality of the sacrament.

But since that species of bread is a sacrament of the Lord’s body and is a sacrament of the New Testament, it produces what Christ’s body signifies; therefore it produces Christ’s body itself. For this is the difference between the sacraments of the New and Old Testaments. It must be said [Col. 1242B] that that species is properly called a sacrament; nor should it be called a sacrament of the New Testament. For then it would be what it signified, the thing it effected. This occurs only through one of the seven principal sacraments. But it is called a sacrament in the sense in which the sacraments of the Old Testament were called sacraments: as signifying, not effecting.

Again, since the species of bread is a sacrament of flesh, and the species of wine a sacrament of blood, and this species is different from that one, there are therefore two sacraments. This is a fallacy. The first immersion differs from the second, and each is baptism; therefore there are two baptisms—which is false: rather, there is one. So too the two species are one sacrament of Christ’s body and blood.

But then those two species are one sacrament either of some body, or of blood, or of both. If they are one sacrament of body, then the species of wine is a sacrament of body; if of blood, then the species of bread is a sacrament of blood. Again [perhaps: “therefore”], it must be said that the two are one sacrament of those two, in such a way that neither is the sacrament of the other: the species of bread is a sacrament of body, not blood; likewise, the species of wine is a sacrament of blood, not body. These two are of those two, in such a way that neither is of the other. [Col. 1242C]

Again, those species are one sacrament, but that sacrament is already there when the words “This is my body” have been uttered; and afterward, the same sacrament is celebrated when the words “This is my blood,” etc., are uttered. Therefore it is celebrated twice, and therefore repeated. This does not follow, because the blessing is not repeated over the same host: one blessing is over one offering of bread, the other over another offering of wine.

Again, Christ’s body is a sacrament of unity. Therefore it is the visible form of invisible grace. Yet Christ’s body lies hidden under the species of bread and is not seen; therefore it is not a visible form. It must be said that the body is not a visible form, because that definition is not universal. Christ’s body is not seen, just as a hand under a cloak is not seen. [Col. 1242D]

## CHAPTER XI. What is the form of this sacrament?

[Col. 1243A]

[Note: [Col. 1243D] Master, under § C.] After the foregoing, it must be considered what the form of this sacrament is. This is discerned in things and words: in things, namely bread and wine, which are transubstantiated into the flesh and blood of the Lord. The bread, however, must be wheat bread and not barley bread, because barley is food for beasts and irrational creatures, who are not in honour and do not understand. Hence the Prophet: “Man, though he was in honour, did not understand; he has been compared to senseless beasts” (Ps. XLVIII), etc. And the Lord compares himself to a grain of wheat, saying: “Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the ground, dies, it remains alone” (John X). [Col. 1243B] Wine also, and not another liquid, is used in this sacrament; because, as wine gladdens the heart of man, so the Lord’s blood refreshes and satisfies the soul, according to what is written: “And my inebriating cup—how splendid it is!” (Ps. XXII).

[Note: [Col. 1243D] From Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*, book IV, ch. 4.] The words at whose utterance bread is transubstantiated into flesh are these: “This is my body,” etc. But those at whose utterance wine is transubstantiated into blood are these: “This is my blood,” etc. Through all the rest that is said, praise is offered to God and prayer is made beforehand for the people and for kings, as the Apostle teaches (1 Tim. II). These, therefore—namely, the form of the words, bread, and wine—belong to the substance of the sacrament; for without them there is no sacrament.

But whether these suffice is not unreasonably asked.

[Col. 1243C] For if it is said that these do not suffice unless other things have first been said, the objection is made thus: These words, “This is my body,” etc., have no efficacy unless the invocation of the Trinity precedes; therefore, the words of invocation confer power upon them. Therefore they have greater power than these words. To this it must be said that invocation is twofold, external and internal. The internal invocation is faith in the Holy Trinity and intention, without which that transubstantiation does not occur. The external invocation consists in the preceding prayers, the Introit of the Mass with the Epistle reading, and the Gradual. All these give efficacy to those words by occasion, not by cause, because they are a necessary condition, not an efficient cause. Nor is Mass celebrated without these things; nevertheless, it was celebrated before these were devised, which were introduced as elements of solemnity.

[Col. 1243D] But the Holy Spirit gave this efficacy to these words, revealing this to the Church: that, clothed in such vestments, the priest should celebrate the divine mysteries by uttering them. For it is not by the power of the vestments that that celebration has efficacy, but rather by the Holy Spirit, who so instituted it.

If it is asked whether the form of bread that is there before transubstantiation is the sacrament of the body, some say that it is a sacrament as soon as it is placed upon the altar in order that Christ’s body may be made from it; and that it begins to be a sacrament upon the utterance of certain words.

[Note: [Col. 1244D] This must be understood favourably, and only analogically with reference to the consecrated host itself.]

[Col. 1244A] Again, the pronoun *hoc* [“this”] is used demonstratively in the sequence of these words: “This is my body,” etc. Therefore something is indicated there, either bread or the body. If bread is indicated, and the statement is about it, and it is truly said to be Christ’s body—for that utterance signifies nothing but what is true—then that bread is Christ’s body, which no one says. But if Christ’s body is indicated by the pronoun, then Christ’s body is already there before all the words have been uttered. Therefore transubstantiation does not occur through the utterance of those words, or it can occur without the words before the word *is* is uttered, once the pronoun *this* has been uttered; for Christ’s body can be indicated by it.

It should be observed here that this holds until all the words belonging to the form of the sacrament have been uttered.

[Col. 1244B] Thus it will be easy to solve this by saying that the priest does not utter *this* in order to signify something. Therefore nothing is indicated by that pronoun; rather, he is reciting Christ’s words addressed to the disciples at the Supper on the day before he suffered. Thus, when the priest says, “Jesus said to his disciples: ‘I am the light of the world’” (John VIII), he indicates nothing by the pronoun *I*, for he does not utter those words in order to signify. But although this is true, the objection concerning Christ remains, because he uttered those words at the Supper in order to signify. Therefore it must be said that nothing is indicated by this pronoun *this* until the utterance of the words constituting the form of the sacrament has been completed. This seems most true according to the disciplines of grammarians and dialecticians,

[Col. 1244C] without which it is not easy to resolve many questions that seem to fall under the fallacy of qualified and unqualified assertion. For example: “Every man of whom this Socrates speaks is a man; therefore Socrates, of whom no one speaks, is this man.” Others say that “This is my body” means: “This—that is, this bread—will now become my body,” that is, “this signifies my body”; and the form of bread is indicated. Others say that an intellectual demonstration is made toward Christ’s body, which will already exist through the conversion of the bread that is held into the body. Yet the first solution is more fitting.

But again it seems that bread is not changed into the body at the utterance of these words; indeed, this is argued from other considerations. For the Gospel reads in this order:

[Col. 1244D] “Jesus took bread and, blessing it, broke it and gave it to them, and said: ‘Take; this is my body’” (Matt. XXVI). According to this order of words, he seems first to have taken the bread, then to have blessed and given it to them, and finally to have said, “This is my body,” etc. But he said this afterward, as appears from the sequence of the Gospel’s words; and before he said this, transubstantiation had taken place, namely in the blessing already made. Therefore transubstantiation was not effected by the utterance of these words, lest it be effected twice. Or, if he had first uttered those words in the blessing before breaking or giving, and afterward uttered the same words again,

[Col. 1245A] then he uttered them twice. For we do not read that he uttered other words for blessing. Therefore transubstantiation was effected twice. Or else, in one of those utterances, nothing was transubstantiated, and thus it appears superfluous. Or, if the form of the words was uttered twice over the same host, an injury seems to have been done to the sacrament, because it was repeated.

To this it must be said that Christ uttered those words twice. For when he blessed, he uttered them, and thus transubstantiation was effected at their utterance. Afterwards he broke and gave it to them, and again said: “This is my body,” etc. But then he did not utter them in order to bless, and therefore the sacrament was not repeated. Some nevertheless say that at the consecration he uttered other words unknown to us, at whose utterance transubstantiation occurred;

[Col. 1245B] and thus he uttered one set of words in the blessing, while priests now utter other words.

A question similar to that raised above when baptism was under discussion is commonly asked: if half the words whose power effects transubstantiation have been uttered, would the sacrament be valid if the priest were perhaps compelled by necessity to stop there, or became mute, or were overtaken by death? And would another priest have to repeat the whole blessing over that host, or should he begin where the first had stopped? But we believe this has not been revealed to man; therefore one should not linger long here. Yet if, after these words, “This is my body,” etc., had been uttered in full, the priest were to pause, intending to complete nothing further,

[Col. 1245C] would the sacrament be complete, since the conversion of bread into the body had already taken place and the blood was there? It seems so, because flesh, blood, soul, and Deity are there. And if it is said that this does no harm, some nevertheless say that the sacrament is not complete until both sets of words have been uttered in their entirety, and that transubstantiation of bread into body has not taken place until these words have been uttered: “This is my blood,” etc.

Again, Christ’s body is never without blood, nor blood without body. At the completed utterance of these words, “This is my body,” etc., the transubstantiation of bread into body has occurred before these words, “This is my blood,” etc., are uttered. Then the body with blood is upon the altar; therefore the blood is there then.

[Col. 1245D] Therefore, either wine has been converted into blood or it has not. If wine has been converted into blood, just as the body comes about in the conversion of bread into flesh, then by the force of those words both bread has been converted into body and wine into blood. Therefore, at the utterance of what follows—namely, “This is my blood,” etc.—no conversion of bread or wine into body or blood occurs; therefore those words are uttered superfluously. Or, if at each utterance both conversions occur, then the words seem to have exactly the same power, and the sacrament is repeated, just as it would be if those words once uttered were repeated.

[Col. 1246A] Indeed, one may ask which bread or what wine is converted when the form “This is my blood,” etc., is spoken. For bread and wine do not remain upon the altar once the utterance of these words, “This is my body,” etc., is completed, because both have already been transubstantiated into both.

To this it must be said that by the utterance of these words, “This is my body,” etc., wine is not converted into blood, but bread into flesh; yet flesh is not without blood. For blood is there, but not by conversion—that is, something has not been converted there into blood until these words, “This is my blood,” etc., are uttered. By those words transubstantiation occurs of the wine that has been set forth into blood; it is not transubstantiated until these words,

[Col. 1246B] “This is my blood,” etc., are uttered. Likewise, the soul is in that body, yet not through a conversion into soul.

But this is objected: bread is changed into Christ’s body by the utterance of those words; therefore it is changed into a body with blood, or into a body without blood. If into a body with blood, then bread has been converted into blood. But if into a body without blood, then the body is without blood. Yet it is clear that one must grant that bread is converted into body, but neither with blood nor without blood, just as Christ willed to suffer, but neither with the Jews’ sin nor without their sin.

## CHAPTER XII. The mode of conversion, insofar as it can be explained

[Note: [Col. 1245D] Master, distinction 11. These three words were present in the Victorine manuscript, but not in ours.]

[Col. 1246C]

Having stated what the sacrament is, what the reality of the sacrament is, and what its form is, we must speak of the mode of conversion. There are three kinds of conversion.

There is one kind of conversion when one substance passes into another so as to become its matter, a variation of properties taking place around matter and what is constituted from matter. Hence an egg is said to be potentially an animal, because an operation of nature produces an animal from it; or a fern is joined together because it is made by the operation of an artisan. [The reading *filix unitur* is uncertain.]

The second is when a change of properties takes place, so that, while the same substance remains, there is variation of properties concerning the same thing. Thus, when softness is laid aside and hardness assumed by drying, bread is made; and thus Lot’s wife’s body was changed

[Col. 1246D] into a stone.

The third kind of change is found only here: namely, when the substance of bread passes into the substance of Christ’s body, while all the properties that were in the bread nevertheless remain. For after that conversion, whiteness, roundness, and markings appear in the host; yet the substance of bread has been changed into the substance of the Lord’s body.

[Note: [Col. 1246D] Master here, § B.] To this it is objected: Something passes daily into Christ’s body; therefore Christ’s body increases daily. For it is not surprising that so many substances should pass into Christ’s body without augmentation. To this

[Col. 1247A] it must be said that Christ’s body does not increase, because the substance of bread passes into that same body which he received from the Virgin; it is unchangeable, however many things pass into it, and it neither increases nor diminishes, because things that pass by conversion do not remain among the kinds of things. Thus, if it were possible for some piece of wood to begin to become my hand, my hand would not thereby increase, because that thing would not remain in the number of things.

Again, this bread will be changed into Christ’s body; therefore by that change it will be Christ’s body; therefore this bread will be Christ’s body, and so something that is not now Christ’s body will be Christ’s body; and thus what was not born of the Virgin will be Christ’s body. Therefore Christ’s body is not one only. Again, Christ’s body was this bread placed upon the altar by the priest, and it was that bread offered by him. Therefore it was both one bread and another,

[Col. 1247B] and thus it was one thing and another; and it is not now itself, and something not taken from the Virgin—

For this reason it must be said that it is truly said: “This bread will be changed into Christ’s body; it will pass over.” And whenever words pertaining to change are used there, they may be granted, especially when it is said: “This bread is transubstantiated into Christ’s body,” because no word is used here so properly as *to be transubstantiated*, since substance passes into substance while the same properties remain. But when it is said, “Bread will be transformed into Christ’s body,” this is not sufficiently exact, because form does not pass into form. Whatever may be said about these expressions, it must by no means be granted that “This bread is Christ’s body.” For it seems that, if a variation of properties had occurred, the identity of substance would remain according to the nature of the substantive word. Yet it may be granted that, through transubstantiation, bread will be Christ’s body.

The question is asked concerning the water mixed with wine: whether it passes into blood, or into the water that flowed from Christ’s side, or remains unconverted; and, if it is converted, at whose utterance of words? Is it by the force of “This is my blood,” etc., or of other words? For we do not read of other words at whose utterance transubstantiation occurs.

[Col. 1247C] Some maintain that its transubstantiation occurs, because if it is not converted, that which it signifies—namely, the Christian people—is not converted into Christ’s body, which is the Church. For “many waters [are] many peoples” (Apoc. XVII). Again, if the water is not changed, then pure water remains. Therefore after the celebration the priest is not fasting. Again, Jerome says on Mark: “Christ, forming his blood in the cup mixed with wine and water,

[Col. 1247D] so that by the one we may be cleansed from sins and by the other redeemed from punishments”—concerning this, because we have learned nothing certain from anyone else, we dare define nothing.

[Note: [Col. 1247D] Master, § II.] It is commonly asked whether the sacrament is invalid unless water is added.

[Note: [Col. 1247D] This answer is Hugh of St Victor’s, V, in the notes to Pullus.] And it is said that it is not thereby invalid.

[Col. 1248A] But if water is omitted through forgetfulness or negligence, the person who does not add it ought to be severely reproved. That water signifies the people of God, united to the Lord’s body—that is, to the Church—through charity, just as water is inseparably mingled with wine. It also signifies faith, just as wine signifies hope and bread charity, as is explained elsewhere.

[Note: [Col. 1247D] Master, distinction 12.] Again, those accidents that remain when the substance of bread has been changed are in some subject: either in the bread or in Christ’s body, because no other subject can be found. They are not in Christ’s body, because it does not have a round form, but a human one. They are not in the bread, because when transubstantiation of bread into body has occurred, bread does not remain there. In what subject, then, are they?

Again, when bread is converted into body, either it ceases to be

[Col. 1248B] or it does not. If it does not cease to be, then something will both be and not be except Christ’s body. Therefore this bread will be Christ’s body; for it will not be bread when it is now converted into Christ’s body. But if it now ceases to be, there is some destructive cause that makes it cease to be, just as old age makes a thing fail in itself, fire consumes it, and the dissolution of parts makes composite things cease to be. Thus this bench ceases to be when it is dissolved into parts. But none of these can be assigned here.

[Note: [Col. 1248D] Master, distinction 11, § D.] Therefore some say, on this reasoning,

[Note: [Col. 1248D] This is the error of the impanationists.] that bread is converted into body because, where bread is, body begins to be; so the latter comes to be together with the former, and those accidents are in that bread. Others say that bread is changed into body because where bread was formerly, body is now; and bread ceases to be there,

[Col. 1248C] being reduced to prime matter or consumed in itself. Others more truly say that, by the force of the words, bread essentially becomes Christ’s body, yet that bread will never be Christ’s body; and those accidents exist without a subject.

[Note: [Col. 1248D] Excellent, although this had not yet been settled in his time.] How this occurs belongs to him who can accomplish it. For they are not in Christ’s body, which does not have such a form but rather a human form, which is not seen there, although it is there in that form.

Again, Christ’s body is made from bread; therefore it does not consist only of the most pure blood of the Blessed Virgin. Fallacy. A statue consists only of bronze; therefore it does not consist of matter and form. For an equivocation intrudes itself, since the preposition *ex* [“from”] denotes conversion in the first proposition, but matter in the conclusion. As appears in the counterexample, where this preposition *ex*, used in the first proposition, signifies matter, but in the conclusion signifies a requirement. For bronze and form are required for something to be a statue, although neither is a part of it, nor are both its matter by nature.

[Col. 1248D] It is also commonly asked whether, if the Lord’s blood is mixed with a liquid, that liquid is changed into blood. For words at whose utterance such transubstantiation might occur cannot be found. Therefore they say that such transubstantiation does not occur after the blood has been consecrated.

[Col. 1249A] Hence, when a priest is about to celebrate Mass twice, he ought not at the first celebration to consume wine mixed with the blood, because he would not be fasting at the second celebration. If they are challenged concerning water that, when mixed with blessed water, itself becomes blessed, they answer that this is not authoritative, nor is anything ever found in authority to be sanctified in that way by touching some sacred thing, except what is read in the Old Testament: with respect to flesh offered by the ruler for sin, everything touched by it was sanctified in its own kind—flesh, flesh; fine flour, fine flour (Lev. VI and VII).

Again, on the day before he suffered Christ determined the form of words by whose power bread was to be transubstantiated into the true body of Christ, and he entrusted the ministry of this office to the apostles when he said: “Do this as often as you receive, in remembrance of me.”

[Col. 1249B] Therefore, on the second day after that command, Christ’s body could have been made from bread upon the utterance of those words. But Christ’s body was then separated from the soul by his true death. Therefore, if this were done, the body would then be inanimate; and whoever then received Christ’s body would receive it inanimate.

To this they say that on that day bread could not be consecrated into body, and this could not have been done by the apostles until after the resurrection. Hence the Church also instituted that Mass should not be celebrated on that day, for three reasons that present themselves: either because he is truly immolated on that day, while on other days these are mystical sacraments; or because on that day Christ himself, the high priest,

[Col. 1249C] descended in person into hell; or because, with the Temple destroyed and the altar removed, there is nowhere upon which the victim of Christ’s body and blood may be offered. This is also why blessed Ambrose instituted that Mass should never be celebrated on Friday at Milan.

Again, Christ’s body is held in the priest’s hands, eaten, ground by the teeth, and broken into three parts. These parts are something; none of them is a nonentity; each of them is Christ’s body. Thus, as many parts as there are of Christ’s body, so many bodies of Christ there are. Indeed, it is maintained that a part of Christ’s body is the body of which it is a part; this seems impossible.

[Note: [Col. 1249D] Thus Hilary: “Where there is a part of the body, there also is the whole”; and in Jerome, *On Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter *Singuli*. See, however, the glosses there.]

That Christ’s body is broken is clear not only from the preceding points but also from others. Where there is breaking,

[Col. 1249D] something is broken. It is not bread, because bread is not there; therefore Christ’s body is broken.

Yet what did the Lord Jesus answer the disciples who withdrew because of the saying that seemed harsh to them? They understood carnally what ought to have been understood spiritually. For they thought that Christ’s flesh, which they saw in the form they perceived, was to be torn and eaten with bites, ground by teeth. The Lord condemned that carnal understanding in them.

To this it must be said that Christ’s body is said to be seen because the form of bread under which it is veiled is seen.

[Col. 1250A] Therefore, when some word concerning Christ’s body is used that pertains either to human sense or implies some corruption, it must be referred not to Christ’s body essentially but to the form, which is said to be seen, touched, tasted, and broken. But the body itself is not seen essentially except in the sacrament—that is, in that external form of bread which presents itself to sight while veiling the mystery. Nor is the body itself broken essentially, since it remains incorruptible and whole, nor is it divided into parts.

Some nevertheless say that there is no breaking there, though it appears to occur. Ambrose speaks against them:

[Note: [Col. 1249D] Also cited by the Master here, § B.] “Nothing false should be thought to occur in the sacrifice of truth, as in the tricks of magicians, where the eyes are deceived by a certain illusion so that they see what does not exist.”

[Note: [Col. 1250D] Master, § D.]

Others say that there is breaking there, yet nothing is broken; for it occurs without a subject, and indeed miraculously. Berengar’s confession, however, was—and many hold this—that Christ’s body itself is essentially broken, ground by teeth, and yet remains whole and incorruptible.

Again, Augustine says:

[Note: [Col. 1250D] In Prosper’s *Book of Sentences*, and found in *On Consecration*, distinction 2, ch. *Hoc est*.] “The flesh is the sacrament of flesh, and the blood the sacrament of blood. By flesh and blood, both invisible, spiritual, and intelligible, Christ’s visible and tangible body, full of grace and divine majesty, is signified.”

And here he seems openly to say that Christ’s flesh is something seen, and likewise the blood.

[Note: [Col. 1250D] Thus the Master resolves it, distinction 10, § C.]

But he here employs a figure of speech by which a signifying thing is called by the name of the thing signified. Thus, since the species of bread signifies flesh, it is here called by the name of flesh; and the species of wine by the name

[Col. 1250C] of blood. Therefore both—the species of bread and the species of wine—are called invisible, spiritual, and intelligible, because Christ’s flesh is not seen as flesh under that form, nor is blood seen as blood under that form. By both, therefore, Christ’s body is signified: visible upon the altar, not to human beings but to the angels who stand by, to whom it appears there in its proper form, as in the empyrean heaven, “into which the holy angels themselves desire to look” (1 Pet. I); there too it is tangible.

Again, Christ’s body is local. Either it is in a place in such a way that it causes local extension, as every body does; or it is in a place by a definition of place, because it is so in one place as not to be in another, though it does not produce local extension there, as angels and souls do. But Christ’s body is not said to be local in either

[Col. 1250D] of these ways. For it does not fill a place by producing local extension; otherwise at one and the same time it would fill infinitely many places, which is impossible. Nor is it true that it is in a place by a definition of place—namely, that it is so in one place as not to be in another—since it is similarly in several places. Therefore it must be said that it is in a place such that it is contained by the definition of place: it is so in one place as not to be in every place, although it is similarly in several places.

Again, Christ’s soul is simultaneously in the empyrean heaven and upon the altar where Christ’s body is. Therefore it does not seem to be

[Col. 1251A] in a place by a definition of place, because it is so in one place as also to be in another; and so it seems to exceed the nature of other souls. For no spirit is simultaneously in several places—none except Christ’s soul. This is not surprising, for just as it had a unique state of blessedness, so it has a unique mode of locality.

Again, Christ’s soul is in heaven, and it is elsewhere: wherever Christ’s body is, Christ’s soul is, and conversely. Therefore Christ’s soul is in heaven and the body is elsewhere. Therefore the soul and body are separated from one another.

To this it must be said that, if an exclusion made by the word *than* is understood when it is said, “Christ’s soul is in heaven, and Christ’s body is elsewhere”—so that “elsewhere” is understood as “other than in heaven”—this is false, because the exclusion is general; the sense would be that Christ’s body is not in heaven.

[Col. 1251B] Thus no one accepts, “This man is more learned than any man,” when he surpasses one person in learning. But if an exclusion made by the ablative is understood, so that the meaning is, “Christ’s soul is in heaven, and the body is elsewhere,” that is, in a place other than heaven, this is true. For then its being in heaven is not excluded, just as you see that this man is wiser than some man.

Again, when Christ’s body is received into the mouth, is the mouth enlarged so that Christ’s body may be received into it, or is the quantity of the body contracted so that it may be contained in the mouth?
