To this it must be said that, by the same power by which he could walk upon the sea, with his body not lightened except by being raised and with the sea not made solid; and by which he brought forth his body from the maternal womb while virginity was preserved,

[Col. 1251C] or from the closed tomb; and by which power he caused his disciples to leave prison even though it remained shut: by that same power he makes his body, neither shortened nor diminished, to be received into the narrow confines of the mouth.

Again, after the consecration the canon of the Mass contains: “Command, O Lord, that this be carried to thy lofty altar, to be joined to thy body.” For the priest seems to request two things: first, that it be carried to the lofty altar—which request is pointless, because the Lord’s body is there already; second, that it be joined there to Christ’s body—which is useless, because the body upon the altar is the very same body that is in heaven. Therefore it is not joined to it; otherwise the same thing would be joined to itself. But there is no association except of different things. Nor can this be understood of pure bread,

[Col. 1251D] both because after consecration, when these words are uttered, there is no bread there, and because, even if it were there, it would not be carried into heaven.

Therefore what is said there must be understood thus. It is said to be carried because the priest prays that, just as Christ’s body has been carried into heaven, where Christ intercedes for us with the Father, so through that consecration and reception it may come about that he intercedes for us with the Father. For that association is nothing other than continual intercession for us.

Or thus: “Command, O Lord, that thy body be carried

[Col. 1252A] to thy lofty altar, to be associated with Christ’s body,” that is,

[Note: [Col. 1251D] This solution is found in the marginal gloss on chapter 72, *On Consecration*, distinction 2, canon *Utrum sub figura*.]

that the unity of the Church, which is signified and brought about by Christ’s body that is here, may be associated with Christ’s body—that is, the Church militant with the Church triumphant. This is a figure by which what belongs to the thing signified is attributed to the signifying thing.

Or thus: A certain disassociation appears in that Christ’s body is here seen under the form of bread and not in its proper form. Therefore it is requested that it cease to be seen here under the form of bread, and that it be seen by us in the empyrean heaven, where it is seen by angels in its proper form. Or it is said to be carried on high because after reception Christ’s body is no longer upon the altar. Yet concerning this it is doubted how

[Col. 1252B] Christ’s body is in the altar or in the one who receives it; and they say that Christ’s body remains there as long as the taste that remains after transubstantiation endures. But when neither taste is sensed nor the species of bread appears, Christ’s body is no longer there, because the sacrament under which it was veiled is no longer there.

Again, Christ’s body is either animate or inanimate. It is not inanimate; therefore it is animate, and bread is changed into Christ’s body. Therefore bread is changed into an animate body; therefore into a soul—which is false. Therefore those who have read much say that they have not found these words in authority, and for that reason do not admit verbal novelties in these matters. It seems to me that the truth cannot be expressed more truly than by saying that Christ’s body is animate—that is, enlivened by a soul;

[Col. 1252C] for it was never inanimate except during the three days of his death.

Again, Christ’s body is either simple or composite. It is not simple, since it was composite while it was mortal. Therefore it is in some way composite. Therefore it has parts. Therefore it can be divided into them, and thus is corruptible. Nor does it matter if it is said to be composite and to have parts; nevertheless it cannot be divided because it has been glorified and made incorruptible, just as the bodies of the saints after the day of judgment will be immortal and incorruptible, yet no less bodies on that account.

## CHAPTER XIII. The mode of reception

[Note: [Col. 1251D] Master, IV, distinction 9.]

Lastly, it remains to speak of the reception of the Lord’s body. The mode of receiving is twofold, sacramental

[Col. 1252D] and spiritual. The good and the evil receive sacramentally; for to receive sacramentally is to receive Christ’s true flesh itself, whether fruit is received from it—that is, ecclesiastical peace—or not. Only the good receive spiritually; to receive spiritually is to receive the fruit proceeding from the Lord’s flesh—that is, to belong to the unity of the Church—whether Christ’s body is received or not.

Augustine says of this reception:

[Note: [Col. 1252D] Commonly cited from the book *On the Remedy of Penance*, and in Alger, book II, *On Penance*. But this text seems to have been compiled from Augustine’s own Tractates 25 and 26 on John, as in Ivo.]

“Why prepare tooth and stomach? Believe, and you have eaten. For believing is eating.”

And note that ecclesiastical unity is called Christ’s spiritual flesh.

[Col. 1253A] Hence: “Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood,” etc. (John VI).

But it is objected: This reprobate person, who has charity at present, receives the Lord’s body; in him it effects what it signifies, since it is a true sacrament of the New Testament. Therefore he is elect, for an authority says:

[Note: [Col. 1253D] In a certain collect.]

“The sacraments effect what they signify only in the elect.”

Again, one who receives the Lord’s body receives Christ, than whom nothing is better. Therefore he receives that than which nothing is better; thus the priest speaks falsely when he prays

[Note: [Col. 1253D] In another collect; Master, distinction 9, § C.]

“that through the things which we receive we may receive better things,” since nothing is better than Christ.

Therefore that term, *better things*, must be resolved into an adverb, so that the sense is: “that we may receive in a better way,” namely, in a more excellent manner.

[Col. 1253B] For now he is received by us in such a way that eternal life is ours only through a cause; but then we shall enjoy the vision of his Deity, and with glorified eyes shall behold his glorified flesh; and thus we shall be united to him in a better manner than now—also by loving him, which happens here but more fully there, and by contemplating him face to face, which does not happen here. But there we shall not be able to be separated from him.

In the same way must be understood this statement:

[Note: [Col. 1253D] In another collect; Master, distinction 9, § C.]

“May thy sacraments accomplish in us what they contain, so that what we now bear in hope we may receive in the reality of things.” For now indeed we receive the reality of things, but hidden; then, however, manifest.

Or thus: that through those things which we receive here through this sacrament—namely faith, hope, and charity—we may receive better things, that is, eternal life, which is better than every virtue.

[Col. 1253C] Likewise, Christ gave his body to the disciples as mortal and passible; to us it is given immortal and impassible. Therefore it is given better to us than to them. This is true, not as regards its effect, but because the thing itself is better—that is, more glorious. Thus “better” is used in the Apostle: “having become so much better than the angels, as he hath inherited a more excellent name than they” [325] (Heb. I). For he cannot be said to have become better than the angels with respect to his divinity or soul, since nothing good accrued to these in the resurrection except impassibility; rather, it is with respect to the flesh, which was made glorious in the resurrection and surpassed angelic nature, whereas before it was subject to mortality and suffering.

Likewise, there is the authority: “The body of Christ effects in those who receive it what it has in itself.” When he gave it, it had mortality [Col. 1253D] and passibility in itself; therefore it effected mortality and passibility in those who received it. Hence they say that, although a mortal body was given to the disciples, it was nevertheless immortal—that is, able not to die—and effected immortality, that is, conferred this upon worthy recipients, that they might not be able to die. For the term to which a relation is made signifies one thing, while the term used in the utterance signifies another. So too when it is said: “My hands, which made you, were fastened with nails.”

Likewise, he then gave his disciples his mortal and passible body. [Col. 1254A] Therefore it was worn down by teeth, broken, and suffered. But this argument has no force, for it was said above that even now, when it is glorified, it is not worn down or broken except under the form; and so neither was it then. Yet from Berengar’s confession it is inferred that it is itself essentially broken and crushed, while nevertheless remaining incorruptible and whole. In whatever way this is to be understood has been determined elsewhere.

There were, however, some who said that Christ naturally possessed an immortal, impassible, and glorious body; but, in order that he might be seen and suffer, he had for a time made it mortal. At the supper he gave himself to his disciples such as he was by nature, because such a body can be in a small place. So too at the Transfiguration he appeared in flesh such as he naturally possessed. [Col. 1254B] But how he was simultaneously in the mouth of each individual at one and the same moment cannot be understood, unless this is said to occur miraculously—as indeed he is today simultaneously in many places, miraculously. For it is not a property of a glorified body to be in several places at once, any more than it is of an unglorified body. Yet it seems vain to me to labour over such matters and to follow nature in miracles.

It is also asked whether he sacramentally received his own body. This seems to be inferred from Augustine’s statement [Note: [Col. 1253D] Augustine on this verse of the Psalm: “He himself had received a sweet food when he ate the Passover with [Col. 1254D] his disciples; there he showed forth the sacrament of his body.”] on Psalm LXVIII: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.” “The Lord had already received food when he ate the Passover with his disciples.” [Col. 1254C] Yet this is proved impossible as follows: where the reality is, a sacrament is not necessary. But Christ, remaining the truth in himself, was there; nor would he be united to himself through reception, since he himself was the one to whom we ought to be united. Therefore he had no need of such reception, nor could he receive it.

We therefore say that he never received sacramentally; rather, he gave it sacramentally to the disciples’ hands for their reception. Thus he is said to have received sacramentally because it was in his hands in order to give, not in his mouth in order to eat.

[Note: [Col. 1254D] Cyprian has something similar in Epistle 63, On the sacrament of the Lord’s chalice.]

Likewise, there is the authority: “Let him be anathema who changes the order of Jesus Christ.” Christ, after the supper of the figurative lamb, gave his body to the disciples. Therefore we too ought, after supper, both to give and to receive. [Col. 1254D] Observe, then, that Christ gave his body after the supper of the paschal lamb in order to show that the legal observances had come to an end. Among these observances, after the sacrifice of the red heifer, the sacrifice of the paschal lamb was more worthy; and it was to be succeeded by the sacraments of the New Testament, of which the first and chief is the sacrament of the Eucharist. He did this also because we commit things said or done last more easily to memory. Therefore, being about to depart from his disciples in bodily presence and to pass to the invisible things of the Father’s majesty, he wished to impress this memorial upon the hearts of his disciples.

[Col. 1255A] [Note: [Col. 1255D] See Cyprian, cited above.] Therefore, after the immolation of the typical lamb, placing the thing represented after the representing thing, he gave his body to his disciples after they had eaten. Yet he willed that his successors should receive that same body fasting, out of reverence for so great a sacrament. Thus that order of Christ Jesus has not been changed, because Jesus Christ himself approves this order.

Likewise, Christ gave his body [326] to disciples whom he knew would shortly sin. Therefore he was not consulting their welfare. Therefore he was not their diligent teacher.

It is also asked whether a priest ought to give the body of the Lord to one whom he knows to be in mortal sin but cannot convict. Therefore he ought not to exclude him from the communion of the Church. Therefore, if he sins, he ought to give it to him. On the other hand, he is his teacher and is bound [Col. 1255B] to provide for his salvation. Therefore he ought not to give him that by which he becomes worse.

To this it must be said that, if the man asks, the priest ought to give it to him. Nevertheless, if he knows him to be in mortal sin, he ought to warn him not to receive, because “he who eats unworthily eats and drinks judgment to himself” (I Cor. XI). For Augustine says: [Note: [Col. 1255D] From this passage, De consecratione, distinction 2, chapter 67: “Let the steward not forbid the rich men of the earth to eat at the Lord’s table, but let him warn the tax-collector to fear.”] “Let the steward not forbid him to eat, but let him warn the tax-collector.” Yet anyone who openly persists in grave sin must be forbidden; one whose sin is hidden must be warned. The Lord Jesus often warned Judas not to receive, when he indicated that Judas would betray him, saying: “He that dippeth his hand with me in the dish, the same shall betray me” (Matt. XXVI). Yet he seems to have invited him when he said: “Take ye all of this” (Mark XIV). But this should be understood thus: [Col. 1255C] prepare yourselves so as to be able to receive worthily.

If anyone asks whether a priest acts better, when a man whom he knows to be in mortal sin asks for communion, by giving him plain bread rather than presenting the body of the Lord under the form of bread, it must be said that the priest sins when he offers plain bread; nor does the recipient sin any less, since he receives while thinking that he receives the body of the Lord. But when he receives the body, only the one who eats sins.

Likewise, it is commonly asked: when the Lord gave his body to the disciples, while it was not yet glorified, could it during those three days be seen by the disciples under its human form, not yet glorified—a form which nothing prevents mortal eyes from beholding without a veil? [Col. 1255D] And during those three days was it hidden under the form of bread and wine? And was it seen in its own form by those who received it? On this we have read or heard nothing settled.

Likewise, this man receives the whole Christ under the species of bread, and afterward the whole Christ under the species of wine. Therefore he receives twice. Thus there are two receptions, just as there are two species; or else he receives nothing under the species of wine that he had not previously received under the species of bread. Therefore the second [Col. 1256A] reception is superfluous.

[Note: [Col. 1255D] Master, distinction 11, § F.]

It must therefore be said that there is not a double reception, but only one. Thus neither does a man eat twice if he drinks and afterward eats again, nor is it superfluous that he receives the same thing under a twofold species. For bread refers to the flesh, wine to the blood, in which, according to the philosophers, is the seat of the soul. Therefore, in order to signify that he possessed both a true body and a true soul and redeemed both, he is received under a twofold species. For if he were received only under the species of bread, reception would seem to avail only for the change of the body; but if only under the species of wine, it would be indicated that reception occurs only for the healing of the soul.

If anyone asks whether there is a double reception if Christ’s body is received once under the species of bread and again under the species of bread, it must be said that it is not double in the [Col. 1256B] priest: for in one Mass he has sacrificed several hosts and, in that same Mass, receives the body under several species if the number of people does not suffice for eating. But if he has presented a layperson with it under a twofold species of bread, it may be said that the person has communicated twice.

Likewise, not all the blood flowed from Christ’s side: one part flowed, and another overflowed, and neither was the other. Yet if someone then received Christ’s blood, would he receive both that which flowed and that which overflowed? And if wine were converted into blood, would it be transubstantiated into both, or into one of them? I think that we should rather refrain from such quibbles than dwell upon them.

[Note: [Col. 1255D] Ambrose, above.] “Remove arguments where faith is required.”

One should rather inquire [Col. 1256C] whether it should be granted that he who receives the whole Christ receives Christ’s soul, or receives his divinity. But it is absurd to grant such things. For nothing is said here to be received except what is eaten. Therefore it should not be granted that this person eats Christ’s soul, because it does not belong to a soul to be eaten, although he receives the whole Christ. For *totus*, when it is masculine, refers to the person; but *totum*, when it is neuter, refers to the nature [327]. Thus one says: “The whole [*totus*] Christ was in the tomb, but not the whole [*totum*].”

[Note: [Col. 1256D] “Whole” [*totum*] represents nature, but “whole” [*totus*] hypostasis: Damascene, Book III, *On the Faith*, chapter 7, at the end.]

[Note: [Col. 1256D] Master, distinction 12, §§ G, H.]

Likewise, it is asked whether the immolation daily performed on the altar by the priest is a true immolation, and whether Christ is daily immolated and daily killed, so that Christ’s one death does not suffice. To this it must be said that [Col. 1256D] Christ is immolated in the sacrament. That immolation is called an immolation for no other reason than that it represents the true immolation which was once performed with his hands stretched out upon the cross. Just as a painting represents that of which it is an image, and just as an image is called by the name of the thing which it signifies—so that an image of Achilles is called Achilles—so that immolation is called by the name of the true immolation which was performed once.

[Note: [Col. 1256D] Incorrectly also Master, distinction 13, who was a stone of stumbling to the disciple.]

Nevertheless, although the other sacraments can be celebrated outside the unity of the Church, [Col. 1257A] those who have been excommunicated cannot make this sacrament, because they do not say “I offer,” but “we offer,” as though speaking in the person of the Church.

[Note: [Col. 1257D] Cited here in the Master.]

For, as Augustine says, the Mass is so called because the heavenly messenger is sent to consecrate the body; therefore, unless an angel comes, it cannot at all be called a Mass. But at the invocation of a heretic or an excommunicated person, the angel does not come.

## CHAPTER XIV. What the sacrament of marriage is, and what its reality is

[Note: [Col. 1257D] Master, Book IV, distinctions 26 and 27.]

There are seven sacraments. Of three of them we have spoken hitherto: baptism, confirmation, and the Eucharist. We should now treat of the fourth, namely penance, unless what concerned our purpose had already been said above when first grace [Col. 1257B] was discussed. Nothing should here be said of the fifth, namely orders, because the discussion of these belongs more to decretists than to theologians. The matters concerning the sixth, namely marriage, which theologians commonly investigate, must be dealt with briefly. For we do not intend to encompass everything that can be investigated concerning marriage, since most such matters serve the inquiry of decretists rather than theologians.

We must therefore consider what the sacrament of marriage is, what is the reality of the sacrament, what its institution is, what its efficient cause and final cause are, and what causes of divorce must be noted. These matters will become clearer once we first learn from the definition what marriage is.

[Col. 1257C] Marriage is the marital union of a man and a woman, between lawful persons, retaining an indivisible partnership of life. The sacrament here consists in the consent of minds and in carnal union. These are not two sacraments but one: the sacrament of Christ’s union with the Church, which occurs through charity, and of bodily union, which occurs through conformity of nature. Carnal union is the sign of this, just as consent of souls is the sign of spiritual union.

Thus you see that the species of bread and wine are not two sacraments but one. The species of bread signifies Christ’s body, not his blood; the species of wine signifies his blood, not his body. But an objection is raised. For authority says: [Note: [Col. 1257D] Augustine, as found here, distinction 26, § G.] “Marriage is not perfect without the mingling of the sexes.” Therefore there was not a perfect marriage between Mary and Joseph. [Col. 1257D] This must be understood thus: it was not perfect, that is, it did not fully express the union of Christ and the Church. It did not express the bodily union, but the spiritual union.

Likewise, marriage is a sacrament of the New Testament. Therefore it effects what it signifies; therefore it effects the unity of Christ and the Church. To this it must be said that this sacrament was celebrated in the Old Testament as in the New, and is older than all the sacraments. For it was instituted in Paradise, when the Lord said: “Increase and multiply” (Gen. II).

## CHAPTER XV. What its institution is

[Col. 1258A]

[Note: [Col. 1257D] Master, above.]

There is a twofold institution of this sacrament: one for an office in Paradise before sin. For just as a person now merits by some good work, so then he would have merited by the work of [328] marriage, and it would have been without the stimulus of lust. But after sin it was instituted as a remedy.

But an objection is raised: when the Lord said, “Increase and multiply,” he commanded marriage. Therefore those who did not marry were transgressors. But Abel did not marry. Therefore he was a transgressor, and consequently sinned mortally. But if this was said by way of indulgence, as the Apostle seems to say (I Cor. VII), and indulgence exists only where guilt precedes, [Col. 1258B] then there is guilt in every marriage.

To this it must be said that this command was given in Paradise and, after sin, before the multiplication of the human race. Likewise, after the flood, before the multiplication of humankind, this was stated as a command. But once the human race had multiplied, it was an indulgence—that is, a grant or permission. For this term *indulgentia* signifies both.

[Note: [Col. 1258D] Master, distinction 26, § D.]

A command concerns things without which there is no salvation; counsel concerns the greatest goods, such as continence; permission concerns lesser evils, such as sexual intercourse within marriage—which would be a mortal sin unless excused by the honourableness of marriage. A grant concerns lesser goods, such as marriage.

Likewise, marriage is a sacrament; therefore [Col. 1258C] a person can merit by the work of that sacrament. But intercourse is the work of marriage; therefore a person merits by it. But against this: at that time the whole human being is flesh. Therefore the Holy Spirit does not give his presence. Therefore it cannot occur without mortal sin. Likewise, Gregory says: [Note: [Col. 1258D] Gregory, response 10 to Augustine’s questions: “That pleasure itself cannot by any means be without guilt.”] “That pleasure cannot by any means exist without sin.” But intercourse cannot exist without pleasure. Therefore one cannot merit by that intercourse.

To this it must be said that a person merits by the work of marriage when he sleeps with his wife solely with the intention of receiving offspring from it. For that act is done from charity, and pleasure is present in it. This pleasure would indeed be a mortal sin unless excused by the goods of marriage, which are three: fidelity, offspring, and sacrament. [Col. 1258D] In fidelity it is considered that the husband should not approach another woman, nor the wife another man; in offspring, that they should unite for the purpose of begetting it, so that it may be brought up for God in religion; in sacrament, that while they live they should not separate spiritually, even if at times they separate bodily by the consent of both.

Therefore Gregory’s statement, “That pleasure is not without sin,” must be understood of the case when a man sleeps with his wife either because of incontinence or in order to satisfy lust. Then it is a venial sin.

## CHAPTER XVI. What is the efficient cause of marriage

[Col. 1259A]

[Note: [Col. 1259D] Master, above, § C, and distinction 28.]

The efficient cause of matrimony is consent of minds. But are these persons married if the man swears that he will take her, and she that she will marry him? No, unless consent is expressed through words in the present tense, as when the man says, “I take you as mine,” and the woman, “I take you as mine.”

But it is asked to what thing this consent relates: to carnal intercourse, or to cohabitation?

[Note: [Col. 1259D] See the book *On Holy Virginity*, chapter 5; the book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, as found in distinction 29, question 2, chapter *Sufficiat*.]

For if consent to cohabitation makes marriage, then a lawful marriage may exist between brother and sister, since they can live together without sin. But if consent to carnal intercourse is the cause of matrimony, then there was no true marriage between Mary and Joseph, since the Blessed Virgin never consented to carnal [Col. 1259B] intercourse. This is shown thus:

[Note: [Col. 1259D] Bede, on chapter 1 of Luke.]

She had resolved to remain a virgin. Therefore either she did not consent to carnal intercourse, or she broke her vow. Likewise, authority says: [Note: [Col. 1259D] Augustine, *On Holy Widowhood*, chapter 8.] “After a vow, not only marrying, but even wishing to marry, is a sin.” The Blessed Virgin had vowed virginity and afterward married. Therefore in this she sinned and so broke her vow.

Likewise, it is read that Christ recalled John when he wished to marry, if he wished to marry. Therefore he wished to be subject to the law of a wife. Therefore he wished not to have power over his own body, but for the woman to have it. Therefore he wished to render the marital debt to her if she demanded it. Likewise, John wished through charity to obey the law; the law wished everyone to take a wife—indeed, it cursed one who was barren and did not leave seed upon the earth (Deut. VII). [Col. 1259C] Therefore John wished to beget children and had vowed virginity. Therefore he acted against his vow.

[329] To this it must be said that consent to marital partnership, expressed in words of the present tense, makes matrimony; and such consent cannot lawfully be contracted between blood-relatives. Therefore it must be said: [Note: [Col. 1259D] From Augustine, Book XXIV *Against Faustus*, chapters 8 and 9.] the Blessed Virgin, like Joseph, had resolved to remain a virgin. Each knew this of the other through revelation of the Holy Spirit, yet neither had expressed a vow, which they did later. Therefore Mary did not consent to carnal intercourse, unless this qualification is added: if it pleased God, to whom she had entrusted her virginity. Yet she consented to marital partnership and consented to render the marital debt to her husband if [Col. 1259D] God should so ordain. The same must be said of John.

They also commonly ask whether the apostles could take wives, since the Apostle says: “Let every man have his own wife because of fornications” (I Cor. VII). But this must be understood as given by the Apostle not as a command, nor as counsel, but as permission. Apostles who had been confirmed could not afterward take wives without sin, because this belongs to the less perfect; for the Lord said to them: [Col. 1260A] “Let your loins be girded about, and your lamps burning” (Luke XII), and so forth.

It is also asked whether consent in words without consent of minds makes matrimony.

[Note: [Col. 1260D] Master, Book IV, distinction 27, § C. “But if they express in words what they nevertheless do not will in their heart—provided there is no compulsion or deceit—the obligation of those words by which they consent, saying, ‘I take you as husband,’ and ‘I take you as wife,’ makes marriage.”]

They say that marriage exists between persons consenting in this way, but those so joined sin mortally, because they speak with heart and heart. Yet the dignity of the sacrament itself does not thereby perish. Just as someone who approaches baptism deceitfully receives true baptism, although it does him no good until the deceit departs.

Likewise, these two are married. Therefore they will receive the thirtyfold fruit; but they also become continent and are not married. Therefore they will receive the sixtyfold fruit. But the others are only continent and not married. Therefore they will receive the sixtyfold fruit and not the thirtyfold. Therefore these married persons, who will receive a double fruit, will receive a greater [Col. 1260B] fruit than those who receive one—a false conclusion, since they possess charity equal to theirs.

To this it must be said, as stated above, that the fruits are not distinguished according to nature and quantity, so that rewards exceed one another in quantity as numbers exceed one another. For one who receives the thirtyfold fruit is sometimes more blessed than one who receives the sixtyfold. Rather, we assigned distinctions of rewards, according to the authorities of the saints, in accordance with the significations of the numbers that we distinguished above. Indeed, these married persons will not receive the fruit of the continent, because each is prepared to render the debt to the other if asked. But this is not so among the continent. Some, however, say that they are to be judged according to the more worthy state, so that they may be said to receive the fruit of continence and not that of married persons.

## CHAPTER XVII. What is the final cause of marriage, where it is said whether it is permitted for someone to dismiss a wife

[Note: [Col. 1260D] Master, Book IV, distinction 30, §§ D, E, and the following distinction.]

The final cause of marriage is manifold: some causes are honourable, some dishonourable. Honourable causes are the procreation of offspring and the restoration of peace. Dishonourable causes are the acquisition of wealth, a woman’s beauty, and the satiating of lust. Yet an evil end does not contaminate the sacrament, as in Jacob, who took Rachel on account of her beauty (Gen. XXIX). Nevertheless, we do not deny that one who takes a wife for the purpose of practising lust sins mortally. The marriage is nonetheless no less true. [Col. 1260D] Intercourse too is excused from mortal sin by the goods of marriage. Yet perhaps the action of one who takes a wife with the intention of satisfying lust is a mortal sin; but not if he does so because he cannot easily remain continent.

It is asked concerning two unbelieving blood-relatives who, being married, converted to the faith, whether they are now married. This is argued as follows. They were lawful [Col. 1261A] persons for contracting matrimony, and true marriage existed between them; both persons are alive; therefore they are true spouses.

This question, debated through many questions, is resolved by some in this way: they say that true marriage existed between these persons, but was neither ratified nor consummated [330]. For true marriage exists where there is only a spiritual bond, as in fully lawful persons and virgins. Ratified marriage [variant: “of neither”], however, is a spiritual bond of such a kind that it cannot be dissolved; where the persons are fully lawful but merely virgins, they may separate, although true marriage exists between them, because it is not ratified. Marriage is consummated where sexual union intervenes.

Yet it is more truly said that among blood-relatives, whatever their religious profession, there has never been [Col. 1261B] a true marriage since ceremonial observances began to cease. Hence, since all Jews are bound to be subject to Christ’s laws, and Christ’s law does not permit blood-relatives to be joined, persons in whom a bond of consanguinity is found are not lawful persons for contracting marriage. Therefore, if, while they were of the Jewish profession, they were not true spouses within the aforesaid degree of consanguinity because that Jewish rite of marrying blood-relatives began to cease with Christ’s coming, much less are they spouses while subject to Christ’s laws.

Likewise, suppose someone has taken his sister in marriage, not knowing her to be his sister, and now first realizes that she is his sister but cannot prove by witnesses that [Col. 1261C] she is his sister. This man’s wife demands the marital debt from him, and they are true spouses. Therefore he is bound to render it to her. On the other hand, they are blood-relatives. Therefore they are not true spouses. Therefore neither is bound to render the marital debt to the other.

Likewise, the Church joined these persons, observing the form of marriage, and applied a certain diligence in doing so. Therefore true marriage existed between them. Therefore God approves that marriage. Therefore the intercourse between these two does not displease God. Therefore it is not incest.

To this they say that, since he cannot prove by witnesses that she is his sister, he ought by every means possible to persuade the Church of this. But if the Church does not comply, he is bound to render the debt to his wife if she asks; yet he ought not to demand it. For the Church is mistaken in these matters. [Col. 1261D] Some nevertheless say that there is no marriage between them and that they ought not to live together as true spouses. Others say that they are spouses and that each is bound to render the debt to the other.

Likewise, it belongs to God alone to judge hidden matters, but to a human being to judge manifest matters. This man proves by witnesses that she is not his blood-relative, though she is; and each consents to the other. The Church judges that these persons are married. Therefore it judges hidden matters, because it is hidden from it whether they are married. Therefore it sins.

Likewise, he ought not to take her as his wife. Therefore it is manifest to no one that he ought to take her. Therefore it is not manifest to the Church either. Yet the Church [Col. 1262A] judges that he ought to take her. Therefore the Church judges hidden matters, and thus sins.

Likewise, whoever does what he ought not to do sins. The Church does what it ought not to do when it joins this woman to this man. Therefore it sins. That the Church does what it ought not to do is shown thus: it ought not to join blood-relatives, and it does join them, though it does not know them to be blood-relatives. Therefore it does what it ought not to do.

To this it must be said that the authority, “It belongs to God alone to judge hidden matters,” should be referred to good and indifferent actions, concerning which no one ought to judge maliciously, since they can be done with either a good or an evil intention. But a person may judge evil actions which cannot be performed with any good end, because these are manifestly evil. This may be applied both to actions and to all similar matters. In that case, [Col. 1262B] “manifest” is taken in a double sense. For that is called manifest which is certain; and thus that they ought to be joined, when it is not certain, is not manifest and is not true. But “manifest” is also used of what has been proved by witnesses, whether true or false. The Church may judge such manifest matters. Thus it will be called manifest that this man ought to take that woman as wife because it has been proved by witnesses—just as it is manifest that a man convicted of theft by witnesses ought to be hanged, although he is innocent.

[Note: [Col. 1261D] Master, distinction 33, § C.]

The Lord teaches in the Gospel that the cause of divorce between spouses is fornication, which must be understood of both spiritual and bodily fornication. Yet if they separate, neither may subsequently [331] marry. In the Old Testament, however, there were several causes, taught [Col. 1262C] by Moses in Deuteronomy, for which the Jews permitted wives to be dismissed after a bill of divorce had been given, containing one or several stated causes. The Jews observe this even to the present day, although the Gospel shows that those who dismissed their wives for any cause other than fornication sinned mortally.

Hence an objection is raised: Moses permitted them to dismiss wives, which was a mortal sin; he did this knowingly, and it belonged to him to rebuke them. Therefore he sinned mortally. Likewise, a mortal sin was permitted. Therefore the permission of the person permitting it was also sinful. Likewise, the institutions of Christ and Moses were contrary, because Moses permitted [Col. 1262D] dismissal of a wife for many causes, while Christ permitted it only for fornication. Therefore one or the other sinned in instituting this; but not Christ; therefore Moses. Likewise, before Moses assigned the causes for which it was lawful to dismiss a wife, dismissal was a mortal sin; and after the causes were assigned, it was likewise a mortal sin. Therefore that sin was in no respect removed from criminality by the permission.

Likewise, in the Old Testament a wife could not be dismissed for any cause without the husband’s sinning mortally; but now, if she is dismissed on account of fornication, it is not a mortal sin. Therefore the sacrament of marriage was stronger in the Old Testament than in the New.

To this it must be said that Moses [Col. 1263A] tolerated lesser evils in order to avoid greater ones. For he knew that the Jews were cruel, inclined to bloodshed, and would soon kill their wives if the women displeased them and they could not dismiss them. Therefore, after giving a bill of divorce containing specified grounds of divorce, he permitted wives to be dismissed—not because dismissing them was not a mortal sin, for it was, but lest they do something worse, namely kill them. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel that Moses gave this because of the hardness of their hearts (Matt. XIX).

Note that there are three kinds of permission. Sometimes something is permitted which, unless it were permitted, would be a mortal sin; but because it is excused, it is either not a mortal sin or no sin at all. Such permission may be called a grant, and such is marital intercourse, [Col. 1263B] which is permitted, that is, granted. Sometimes something is permitted because it cannot be avoided, and it is a venial sin; such are the first movements. Hence: “Be angry, and do not sin” (Ps. IV). Sometimes something is permitted lest a greater evil occur; not because it is not evil and a mortal sin, but because it is a lesser evil than another that would occur if this did not occur. Thus Moses permitted—that is, tolerated—the dismissal of wives, not because it was not a mortal sin, but because it was a lesser evil than killing them, which they would have done if forced to live with them. Yet Moses imposed no temporal punishment; God, however, punished it eternally.

You have an analogy to all these cases in a sick person who absolutely cannot refrain from eating either beef or mutton. The physician [Col. 1263C] dissuades him from both; but, because he sees him stubbornly resolved, he permits—that is, tolerates—that, if he is to eat one of them, he should eat mutton rather than beef, because it is less harmful.

But the sin was lightened by the permission in this respect: whereas Moses had previously imposed a punishment if a wife was dismissed, after permission had been given they were punished by no temporal penalty, though reserved for eternal punishment. Although Christ’s and Moses’ institutions were contrary, their acts of instituting were not thereby contrary—just as what God wills and what a human being wills are contrary, yet their wills are not contrary. But it seems better to me that in this passage “institution” means “that which has been instituted,” and that Moses’ institution was not [Col. 1263D] contrary to Christ’s institution. For Christ too wished Moses to permit—that is, tolerate—this; and Moses would not have approved if someone dismissed his wife for any reason other than fornication.

It is asked whether, if after dismissal the wife married another, that latter union would be a marriage. It does not seem so. For the former husband [332] and former wife were true spouses. Though bodily separated, they were not spiritually separated, and therefore the former marriage remained. Why, then, was the latter not a marriage?

[Col. 1264A] Therefore they say that there was no marriage between persons who contracted with one another after dismissing others. Yet intercourse was not thereby fornication, because at that time there were few believers and, however a man might unite with a woman, it was a lesser sin to beget a human being who would remain in the worship of the one God than it is now for someone even to take carnal pleasure in his own wife. Hence it was lawful then to have several wives, only one of whom was a wife in marriage.

[Note: [Col. 1263D] This is according to the thought of the Master, who says in distinction 33, § B: “From these things it appears that the holy Fathers before the Law had several wives or concubines without sin; for Scripture now calls them wives, now concubines.” See the Notes to Pullus, *On Extreme [Col. 1264D] Unction*.]

The remaining women were concubines for the purpose of increasing God’s people. We have briefly surveyed these among the many matters commonly investigated concerning marriage. We do not deny that many other matters concerning it are doubtful and worthy of inquiry, but most of them suit the disputation of those who handle the decrees rather than the sacred page. [Col. 1264B]

We ought lastly to treat of the last of the seven sacraments, namely extreme unction, unless we had heard almost no disputable questions concerning it; and, if there are any, they are contained sufficiently in writings elsewhere. Therefore, lest by writing we seem to perform the work of one who does nothing, we judge that these matters should be passed over.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the qualities of bodies that will rise again

[Note: [Col. 1264D] Master, Book IV, distinction 44.]

The final chapter of the work undertaken will conclude with that for which we humble ourselves through the foregoing sacraments and toward which the intention of our labour ought most earnestly to be directed: namely, resurrection and ascension.

[Note: [Col. 1264D] From Augustine, Book XXII, *The City of God*, chapter 14.]

Therefore all, both good [Col. 1264C] and evil, will rise again at the age at which Christ died, though of differing stature: each in the stature that was his when he was thirty-two years old, or which he would have attained had he lived to that age. The good, indeed, will rise without any deformity of their members.

For the individual parts will not return to those members of which they were parts, but either to those or to others. What was part of a hair need not become part of a hair in the resurrection, lest there be an unbecoming abundance of hair; rather, it will return either to the hair or to other parts. This is evident in an image: if it has been broken, not all of its parts will become the parts of which they were parts in its restoration; rather, they will pass either into those parts or into others.

But an objection is raised: pork, when eaten, passes [Col. 1264D] into human flesh, and the whole flesh of a human being will rise again. Therefore pork-flesh too will rise—not as pork, but as human flesh. The same may be said of a man devoured by a wolf: human flesh passes into the wolf’s flesh, and thus both the wolf’s flesh will rise and also the human flesh that had passed into it. But Truth resolves this objection by saying in the Gospel that everything entering the mouth goes out and is discharged into the privy (Matt. 15). [Note: [Col. 1264D] Likewise, a difficulty in the Master’s teaching here, § B.] Food nevertheless supplies nourishment to the body, [Col. 1265A] since it is sustained by it; it is multiplied and grows by an increase of parts. Yet food does not therefore pass into human flesh, as physicians testify; or, if it perhaps does pass into it, it does not pass into that flesh which belongs to the truth of human nature and which will rise at the future judgment.

Again, every person will rise with every part of himself; but the rib from which the woman was made was a part of Adam. Therefore it will itself rise in Adam, and thus there will be two souls in his body. Likewise, the flesh of every human being was in him, because the flesh of every human being was materially in him and belonged in him to the truth of human nature. Therefore we say that this must be understood of parts that were not animated; but that rib was animated.

Again, the semen which is formed for generation is of the truth of human nature. Therefore it will rise. Therefore [Col. 1265B] it will be a part of the body from which it is emitted, or of another body, since it will never rise by itself because it is never animated; but it will rise in the person from whom it is emitted, and it has corruption, by reason of which it is liable to punishment, because it was emitted in pleasure and has not been cleansed from that corruption [Note: [Col. 1265D] See the Notes on Pullus, chapter 28, part II.] by the remedy of any sacrament. Therefore the person will be punished in that part of the body to which the semen returns.

That matter itself has corruption is clear from this: if a soul were infused into it, it would contract corruption from it; and yet that person would be punished in body and soul unless he were cleansed by baptism or some sacrament. To this it must be said that seeds which are never conceived will never [Col. 1265C] rise again. Ambrose testifies to this as follows [Note: [Col. 1265D] Correct: “Augustine, *Enchiridion*, ch. 87.”]:

> “Who would not more readily judge unformed births to perish, like seeds which were never conceived?”

Again, the body of every saint after the resurrection will be spiritual and immortal, needing no nourishment from food; such was Christ’s body after the resurrection. Therefore it was not then subject to human senses—which is false. For Thomas touched him, placing his hands in the place of the nails (John 20). Afterwards he is also recorded to have eaten (Luke 24). It is further said that he preserves his scars until the day of judgment, in order to show them to his crucifiers, so that they may see whom they pierced (Isa. 16 according to the Septuagint, and Rev. 1). Therefore there is some corruption in his body, because a scar is a corruption.

To this it must be said that the bodies of the saints [Col. 1265D] after the resurrection will be spiritual and agile, since nothing will hinder them; for they will possess seven endowments in the body and seven in the soul, which they do not now possess. Such was Christ’s body after the resurrection. That he was seen, touched, and the like occurred miraculously. His eating was to show that he possessed a true body. Concerning the scars, however, some saints teach that he has them and preserves them until the day of judgment, and that they are for his glory, not his confusion—just as, after victory, scars are an ornament and glory to many, not a cause for shame. Thus there is no corruption in Christ’s body.

Others say that there are now no scars in his body, but that on the day of judgment he will miraculously display them in his glorified body, just as, conversely, on the day of the Transfiguration he miraculously displayed the glory of his brightness in corruptible and mortal flesh. And as that manifestation was temporary, so this one will be temporary. Yet some say that all flesh will see the salvation of God (Luke 3) at judgment in the corruptible form which he will then assume for a time—the form which he had on the cross; but after judgment he will appear to the good in glorified flesh. [Note: [Col. 1266D] See Augustine, *On the Trinity*, I, chs. 16–17; Isaiah 26:21; *On the Spirit and the Letter*, ch. 22.] They understand the words, “Let the wicked man be taken away, lest he see the glory of God,” not only of the glory of the Godhead but also of the glory of glorified humanity.

At this point one may ask whether, after the resurrection, the glorified body will possess the five senses—sight, [Col. 1266B] hearing, and the rest. For if taste will be there, and will serve the use which it now serves in the soul, then human nature will be able to desire food. Therefore the body will then be animal. Again, bodies will then occupy places, creating a distance of air from air; and if each person’s quantity is to be as great as it was at the age of thirty-two, then each will occupy as much empty space as it does now, and something will lie between one body and another. Thus not all will be able to be in the valley of Jehoshaphat.

Again, since sight is to be in the human soul, will a person see the entire body, externally and internally, in the manner of a lynx, so that nothing prevents him from seeing all parts of the world? Or will he see only the outer surface, as now? [Col. 1266C] Or will he sometimes close his eyes, so that he does not then see? For if he possesses lynx-like sight, he will not on that account see any less when his eyes are closed. Again, will he move from place to place by walking, employing the function of his feet? This seems unlikely, because the human body will be without all weight and sustained by itself.

Again, will touch be in it, so that something resists one who touches it? Will it hear something through an external sound, reported inwardly to its soul? Will each person know another’s heart and understanding without the vehicle of speech? Or what use will smell have there? Will the senses be in the soul in such a way that they will then have other functions, as the four cardinal virtues will have a function there different from their function here? Or will the soul be there altogether without sensibility and without the lower power of reason [Col. 1266D] by which it knows how to administer temporal matters?

334 However it may be, there seems destined to be in souls some action or passion of pleasurable joy which will have a beginning and an end; and thus it will be temporal. Thus not all things will be in eternity, but there will be a variety of time there as there is now. Since I have learned nothing certain concerning these matters, I leave them, readers, to the investigation of your inquiry. Yet we know with certainty that after the resurrection the Lord ate; but he did so miraculously as an indication of a true resurrection, and he was touched by a mortal body.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the spirit through which they maintain that the soul is united to the body

[Col. 1267A]

Concerning that spirit through which they say that the soul is united to the body—led by the authority of Daniel in the hymn of the three children, “In a contrite soul and a spirit of humility” (Dan. 3), and “Spirits and souls of the righteous, bless the Lord” (ibid.)—some ask whether it will rise again. The Apostle seems to say that it will (1 Cor. 15), yet this does not seem possible. For that spirit is either simple or composite. If it is simple and ceases to exist when the soul departs from the body, which is beyond doubt, and begins again when the soul returns to the body, and nothing is now made, then it will be created then and has already been created; thus it must have been created twice.

But if [Col. 1267B] it is composite and then ceases to exist when the soul departs from the body, it will be dissolved into parts. What will become of those parts? Will they be joined to one another again at the resurrection? Again, that spirit is, as it were, the bond of the soul to the body, which share contrary properties, because the body is visible and mortal. Conversely, the soul is invisible and immortal. But after the resurrection they will not be so contrary in their properties; indeed, the body will then be impassible, immortal, and spiritual. Therefore there will then be no need for a medium through which the soul is united to the body, as it is now.

Again, as physicians say, it is produced from the digestion of foods, since foods, digested in the stomach, are divided into four [Col. 1267C] kinds. But the body will then not be animal—that is, in need of nourishment—but spiritual. Therefore it seems that there will be no such thing in a human being. To this they say that this spirit is something simple and mortal, which dies in the body; and we possess this spirit in common with brute animals. Nor is it surprising if it had to be created twice: it will rise when the soul returns to the body, and will be glorified together with the soul and flesh.

But it seems to us that this opinion has been introduced from error rather than truth. For it is impossible that, alongside the Holy Spirit and the spirit of the soul, there should be another spirit in the human body.

## CHAPTER XX. On aid for the dead before the day of judgment

[Note: [Col. 1267D] The Master, IV, distinctions 45 and 49.] Once the universal judgment has been accomplished and completed after the common [Col. 1267D] resurrection, two cities will have their own citizens, one of the good and the other of the evil—each composed both of angels and human beings. The joy of the saints will be greater after the resurrection, and the punishments of the evil more severe. We must therefore first treat of the blessedness of the good and afterward of the punishments of the evil. Before this, however, something must be said concerning aid for the dead until the day of judgment. [Note: [Col. 1267D] From Augustine.]

> “For in the interval between the death of human beings and their common resurrection, souls are held in different receptacles, according as each is worthy of misery or rest, according to what it did while living in the body.”

Thus, among those [Col. 1268A] who have died, some are supremely good, such as Peter and Paul; some supremely evil, such as those who never possessed faith in the Lord; some moderately good; and some moderately evil. This is what is taught in another form of expression: some judge and are not judged; some neither judge nor are judged; some are judged and judge; some are judged and do not judge. Assign each category to its proper group. The prayers of the Church and alms given benefit the moderately good and the moderately evil, but in different ways. [Note: [Col. 1268D] We have explained all these matters in the notes on Pullus.] They benefit the good by a readier release from punishment, and the evil by mitigation. They do not benefit the supremely evil who never participated in the sacraments, because in this life they did not deserve that such things should benefit them. Nor, as the saints say, do they benefit anyone [Note: [Col. 1268D] Augustine, *Enchiridion*; Sermon 32, *On the Words of the Apostle*, etc.] unless he [Col. 1268B] lived in such a way that they could benefit him after death. Such are all who possessed charity and died in participation in the sacraments.

But an objection is raised in many ways. Just as place, time, rank, and knowledge aggravate sin, so the reception of a sacrament seems to aggravate it. Hence, if a believer and an unbeliever sin in the same kind of sin, with the same purpose and the same intention, all other circumstances being retained, the believer seems to sin and to show contempt more gravely than the unbeliever, and to inflict a greater injury upon the Holy Spirit, because he expels him from himself. But one who never possessed him does not expel him in this way. Therefore the Christian believer is worse in other respects than the unbeliever.

This is also proved by authority, because it is better [Col. 1268C] not to know the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn back (2 Pet. 2). Therefore, if the prayers of the Church benefit the worse evil person—that is, the believer—why do they not also benefit the less evil person—that is, the unbeliever? Thus the Church’s suffrages benefit the supremely evil. This can also be shown by an analogy. Let a layman and a priest be here, and let them sin in the same kind of sin, with the same purpose and intention: it is evident that the priest sins more gravely. Likewise, let a Christian and a pagan be here and sin in the same kind of sin: certainly the Christian sins more than the pagan if they sin with the same intention.

Therefore, on the passage in Jeremiah, “Behold, very bad figs” (Jer. 24), we understand the bad figs as bad Christians, who are even worse than unbelievers. For these are like cut-off branches fit for no use but prepared for fire; those are pieces of wood which, though they bear no fruit, are nevertheless suitable for the building of God’s house. These are enemies who are above all enemies, as is found in the Psalm passage: “I have become [Col. 1268D] above all my enemies,” etc. (Ps. 30).

Conversely, authority says: “It is beneficial to have believed, at least for a time.” It is also evident that the prayers of the Church benefit, for mitigation of punishment, those who at least once believed, and not the others. It is likewise evident that these will be judged, when it is said to them: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food” (Matt. 25). But the others will not be judged, because they have already been judged, since they did not believe.

[Col. 1269A] Again, the Church’s suffrages avail the moderately evil for the mitigation of punishment. That mitigation is a good which they possess eternally. Therefore they benefit them in possessing a good eternally. Therefore they benefit them with respect to an eternal good, and thus the evil enjoy an eternal good, because they will always possess mitigation of punishment. Again, all the good merits of the moderately evil which they possessed while they were in charity were wiped out by the mortal sins in which they died. Yet they merited then that, if they died in mortal sin, their punishment would be mitigated. Therefore those merits too have been erased, and they now possess mitigation of punishment. Therefore they do not possess it from merits, but gratuitously.

Again, the prayers of the Church benefit those held in hell who are moderately evil, by diminishing punishment. Therefore [Col. 1269B] their punishment is diminished every day. Therefore the Church can pray for them or give alms for them so extensively that their punishment will be entirely removed. Therefore some redemption can exist in hell.

To the foregoing arguments it must be answered that some Christians who died in the faith are worse than some pagans, while others are less evil. For there are degrees of excess and deficiency: some are worse than others according as they died in greater or lesser contempt. Yet in this respect they take precedence over those who did not so die, because they died in participation in the sacraments. For these will be judged; those too, if they are less evil, are worthy to be judged, because they have already been judged from the time when they contemned the faith [Col. 1269C] proposed to them.

As for the claim that suffrages avail toward possessing a good eternally because they mitigate punishment, it does not follow that they avail toward an eternal good, because no eternal good exists except eternal life. This is a fallacy: the devil has a life which he will possess eternally; therefore he has eternal life. As for the claim that the Church can pray so much for those in hell that punishment is entirely removed from them, it fails because the Church militant will not endure so long. After the day of judgment suffrages will benefit them no longer, because the Church will then not be militant, when kingdom comes to kingdom and works of charity cease. Indeed, even if the Church militant were to remain forever, their punishment would nevertheless never end; for it may [Col. 1269D] be alleviated [Note: [Col. 1269D] From Augustine’s *Enchiridion* and elsewhere. See the notes on Pullus.], but not entirely erased.

Again, when all good merits are said to be erased by mortal sin, this must be understood of those merits which could have been a cause of eternal life.

Again, authority says: “When our own merits fail us, the merits of others aid us.” Therefore someone can be made worthy of eternal life without his own merits. Therefore he can be called worthy of life without goodness; and thus someone can be saved by the merits of the Church without his own merits. Accordingly, understand the foregoing authority thus: God always gives more in the other life [Col. 1270A] than a person merited in this one. A person cannot attain that surplus without both his own merits and those of the Church. When his own merits are lacking, those of others assist, because through the prayers and merits of others God infuses into a person first grace; when free choice cooperates with this grace, good merits are produced.

Again, when we give alms, we ought to give them to those whose merits benefit us toward life; but the merits of evil persons do not benefit us, nor can they benefit us. Therefore we ought not to give alms to evil persons. For it is written: “Give to everyone who asks of you” (Luke 6). To this it must be said that the first proposition is false. For we give to many whose merits cannot benefit us.

Again, the Apostle says: “We shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what he did in the body” [Col. 1270B] (2 Cor. 5). Therefore both the saved person and the condemned person will be saved or condemned by his own merits. Therefore others’ merits neither harm nor benefit anyone’s salvation. Thus no one will be released from punishment more quickly on account of the merits of the Church, nor will punishment even be mitigated for him.

To this it must be said that one’s own merits alone avail toward salvation; nor does that “alone” exclude the merits of others, because [Note: [Col. 1269D] Augustine, Sermon 32, *On the Words of the Apostle*: “Thus new merits are not acquired for the dead when their good people [Col. 1270D] do something for them; rather, these subsequent things are rendered to them because of what preceded.”] the fact that others’ merits benefit someone itself derives from that person’s own merits.

One may also ask whether anyone in purgatory has greater charity than anyone who is still on the way. This seems so, because the former cannot lose charity, while the latter can lose it. Therefore whoever is in purgatory has greater charity than any person who is on the way. Conversely, many are on the way who, if they died, [Col. 1270C] would owe no punishment and would not be guilty of any sin. But whoever is in purgatory is guilty of some sin and deserves punishment to be inflicted upon him. Therefore someone on the way has greater charity than someone in purgatory.

In these questions I judge there to be more curiosity than edification; nevertheless, whatever is proposed here can be determined by distinguishing the several senses of this distinction: “greater” can designate either the strength of charity or the intensity of fervour.

Again, Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1270D] Augustine, Letter 80, to Hesychius.]:

> “Whatever state a person’s last day finds him in, in that state his last day will seize him; for as each dies on this day, so he will be judged on that day.”

But all imperfect persons, when they die, are worthy [Col. 1270D] of purgatorial punishments. Therefore on that final day they will be worthy of the same punishments. Therefore nothing in them will then have been purged. Accordingly, the saying must be explained thus: “As he is,” etc.—that is, whether prepared for death or for life.

[Note: [Col. 1270D] The Master, above, § D.] Again, two people died with equal venial sins; the Church prays for one and not for the other. They equally deserved that the Church should pray for them. The one for whom prayer is offered is released sooner, the other later. Therefore the latter is treated unjustly, because he is not repaid according to his merits. Thus some say that this delay is nothing in comparison with eternity. Others say that they are released equally [Col. 1271A] quickly, and that the general prayers of the Church benefit one as much as the special and general prayers together benefit the other.

But someone objects again. Those who die together and in an equal condition deserve an equal reward. Therefore one deserved to be released as soon as the other. Therefore, if one is held there longer than the other, he is treated unjustly. Again, the person released sooner deserved to be released as soon as he is released, because he experiences no remedy which he did not merit while alive; and this person merited nothing that the other did not merit, yet the latter is not released as soon. Therefore he is treated unjustly.

That this person did not merit the swift release is evident, because he obtains it through the Church’s merits, not his own. Therefore new merits are acquired for them after death. Again, if he merited to be released so soon, [Col. 1271B] then, if he were held there longer, he would be treated unjustly. This is proved as follows: he deserved to be held there as long as the other; the other is held there longer than he. Therefore, if he is held there for that same length of time, he will not be treated justly.

Again, this person dies equal to the other in charity; therefore he does not deserve to be absolved sooner than the other. Therefore, if he is absolved, it is by God’s grace or by another’s merits rather than his own. For he can do nothing by his own merits which the other cannot, since they died equally good. If the other merited so swift a release and this person does not have an equally swift one, it is bestowed upon the former in mercy. But if it is said that this person’s speedy release is from grace and not from merits, what benefit then do the prayers and benefits bestowed by the Church for him have? Indeed, if [Col. 1271C] he is released sooner not because of these benefits but because God mercifully releases him so soon, it seems that, if he would not have had the same release without them, why then is the person for whom no benefits are bestowed not released?

They also commonly ask whether it is possible for someone to die with wood, hay, and straw and not pass through purgatory. This seems possible: for just as they obtain a swifter release by the Church’s prayers, so also, if the prayers and benefits of the Church are multiplied, punishment may apparently be entirely erased in that person. Thus it is possible for someone dying liable to venial sin immediately to fly to life as if he were perfect.

No created mind can abound in power in any kind; for, [Col. 1271D] when it has found something among things found, it sees matters still to be sought; and when, by inquiry, it has reached these, it foresees still more. Thus wise Solomon says: “I shall become wise, but wisdom itself has gone far from me” (Eccl. 7). Warned by these words, I do not resolve the foregoing unusual questions, lest at the very threshold of a solution a more difficult knot of inquiry arise.

Again, one person gives one alms for his father; another gives one for his father and mother. An alms given for the father alone benefits as much as an alms given for those two; and conversely, one alms benefits as much as two given for two persons. Again, an alms cannot be given out of charity specifically for one person [Col. 1272A] without being given for all; nor can Mass be celebrated for one person without being celebrated for all. Therefore it cannot be celebrated specially for anyone. Therefore a Mass celebrated for one benefits no more than one celebrated for two together.

To this it must be said that whoever dies in the unity of the Church shares in all benefits performed for one dead person, according to the words: “I am a companion of all who fear you” (Ps. 118). For all those on the way merit to become participants in benefits performed for them. Yet special alms are offered for certain persons: they benefit all, indeed, but benefit those for whom they are offered by name more than others. But not every living person similarly shares in all benefits which living persons do for the living, because each has here a place for meriting and can perform goods which benefit himself and not another, since “they have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them” (Luke 16).

Again, it is asked whether a priest is bound to pray for a person who happens to become a martyr, although he does not know it. This seems not to be the case, since it is written [Note: [Col. 1271D] In Augustine, Sermon 17, *On the Words of the Apostle*.]: “He does an injury to a martyr who prays for him.” But this must be understood of one who knows him to be a martyr—that is, one who prays for him with the intention of expiation. For some prayers are expiations, others thanksgivings, and others consolations for the living. 338 Prayers for those held in purgatory are expiations; prayers for those already enjoying eternal life are thanksgivings; prayers for those in [Col. 1272C] hell, though it is uncertain whether they are there, are whatever kinds of consolation are available to the living.

Again, this priest imposes upon someone the penance which he deserves as satisfaction; but he will endure a greater punishment in purgatory because he will die before completing his penance. Therefore he will be treated unjustly, or else God does not approve this punishment, since he punishes him with a greater punishment. Again, he will endure in purgatory a greater punishment than he now suffers; but he will then endure no punishment of which he is not worthy. Therefore he will then be worthy of a greater punishment than now. Therefore he will be more guilty of sin than he is now.

To this it must be said that in the present state he is not worthy of a greater punishment. But in purgatory he will be worthy of a greater one, because different kinds of states have different kinds of punishments. Thus in the Law, [Col. 1272D] one who killed a person unwittingly fled to a city of refuge and remained there until the death of the high priest (Deut. 4). Therefore, while remaining in the city, he was worthy of that punishment and of a greater one; yet if he were found outside, he was killed and endured a greater punishment, not unjustly. So, while we are now in the city of refuge, we are worthy of temporal punishment. If we depart from it, after death the fire of purgatory will punish us more severely than any punishment now does; yet not unjustly.

The same can be shown by analogy. In Italy a punishment is due to a person for adultery, and in France a lesser punishment. If someone in France were punished for adultery with the punishment due in Italy, [Col. 1273A] he would be treated unjustly. For punishments vary according to places, and so according to times. Thus, as some teach, for venial sin in the present state only temporal punishment is due to a person. Yet if he dies at the same time with venial and mortal sin, he will be punished eternally for both, not unjustly.

Again, when this person is in purgatory he will be unable to sin, whereas now, while he is on the way, he can sin; and then he will have charity, as he has it now. Again, after he is released from the fire of purgatory, he will immediately enjoy the vision of God; while in purgatory he will not enjoy the vision of God. Therefore he will have greater charity afterwards than then. To this it may be said that in the fire he will have greater charity than he has now, and that he will receive a greater purification than [Col. 1273B] he will possess while being purified.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the state of souls separated from bodies until the day of judgment: whether they have a place for meriting

After souls have performed a more perfect repentance in those punishments and been purified, they immediately, without delay, enjoy the vision of God and will be made equal to the angels in blessedness. Yet this seems contradicted by what is written concerning the Psalm passage, “Yet a little while, and the sinner shall not be” (Ps. 36). There “a little while” is said to be the time remaining until the end of this life after the saints have been delivered. Then the address is made to the saint:

> “In this manner you will not yet be where those are to whom it will be said: ‘Come, blessed of my Father’ [Col. 1273C] (Matt. 25), etc. But you will be in that rest where the rich man saw Lazarus covered with sores, and you will wait until the day of judgment, when, having received their bodies, the saints will be made equal to the angels.”

From these words it seems to follow that the saints are not yet in blessedness and are not yet equal to the angels. But the first statement must be understood thus: “You will not yet be,” etc.—that is, you will not yet possess the double robe. The final statement, that they are to be made equal to angels, must be understood with respect to the body, because they are already equal with respect to the soul.

Again, it is asked whether the saints will merit until the day of judgment. If this is affirmed, many pressing objections arise. The saints will be judged according to the state which they possessed at the end of life, or according to that which they will then have—which seems more likely if they merit again. But if so, then the day of judgment will not be such for each person as the day on which he dies. Again, just as now, of two persons possessing [Col. 1273D] equal charity, one can surpass the other in charity so that they die unequal, what prevents two persons who die equal in charity, if they merit afterward, from one advancing beyond the other in the interval from the end of each one’s life to the day of judgment? If this is so, then, since they will be unequal in charity on the day of judgment, they will be unequal in glory, though they died equal in merits. This seems impossible, because neither has privileged merits.

Again, if saints are judged according to the state which will exist [Col. 1274A] on the day of judgment, and two persons die equal in charity, one having died a long time before the other, and the one who died first immediately receives charity equal to that which the person who died later was to receive, and the former merits anew by his charity until the time at which the latter dies—then the former has greater charity at the time when the latter dies than the latter then receives, because the latter receives it in the measure in which the former received it after death, though the former has meanwhile advanced. Therefore, since the latter cannot attain the former’s merits, and both will be judged according to the merits which they will possess on the day of judgment, the latter will be rewarded more than the former, although they died equal in charity.

But if they will be judged according to [Col. 1274B] the earlier state of the final merits of their life, while they themselves triumph in that state, the order seems perverse; or there will be no merits after death, or, if there are any, they are defrauded of those merits because they are not judged according to them.

If souls separated from their bodies merit, and each of them possesses greater charity than anyone who is on the way—because “he who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than John” (Matt. 11; Luke 7)—it seems that the souls of the blessed merit with more intense charity than anyone now does, and thus the merits of no one on the way can attain to the merits of one who is in the homeland. This is also clear concerning angels, if it is established concerning the souls [Col. 1274C] of the saints; for every person on the way is less than every angel. Therefore every angel merits with greater charity than any human being, and an angel never grows lukewarm in charity, which a human being often suffers. Moreover, angels merited from the beginning and will merit daily until the day of judgment because they are immortal, whereas a human being cannot merit so much, nor does he merit on every day of his life. Therefore the merits of any most perfect human being will never attain the merits of any least angel.

The contrary proposition—that both angels and souls merit—is shown thus. The soul of Judas would wish God not to exist; that will is evil and is sin; no sin goes unpunished. Therefore by that will the soul of Judas merits eternal punishment. Why, then, by analogy does the soul of Peter not now merit [Col. 1274D] eternal life? Again, Judas has no evil will which he does not now have, and he has some which he did not formerly have, because “the pride of those who hate you rises continually” (Ps. 73). Therefore Judas now sins more than he sinned before, and thus daily merits a greater punishment. By the same reasoning, the souls of saints daily merit a greater crown. This contradicts the authority [Note: [Col. 1273D] See Fulgentius, *On the Faith to Peter*, and Augustine, *Enchiridion*, ch. 3.]: “In the homeland there is a place for receiving, not for meriting.”

Again, if the souls of the damned, through the evil wills which they have, daily merit a greater punishment, the Church’s suffrages do not seem to benefit them by mitigating punishment; or, if they do benefit them, then insofar as these seem to help, their evil wills seem to harm. [Col. 1275A]

The solutions to the foregoing questions may be taken in two ways, according to different writers. Some say that the souls of saints merit until the day of judgment, just as angels now merit, as they say; but after the day of judgment there will be no merits. They explain the authority, “There is no place there for meriting but for receiving,” thus: it means that it is more a place for receiving than for meriting. Conversely, when it is said, “The present state is not a place for receiving but for meriting,” it means that this is more a place for meriting than for receiving. For we receive many things here according to merits, as we are taught in that Gospel passage: “Son, remember the good things in your life, and likewise [Col. 1275B] the bad” (Luke 16). On this passage the expositor says that it is credible that the man did some good things, for which he had received temporal things as reward.
