According to this opinion, the saints will be judged according to the state in which they died; after death, if they died equal, neither can advance in merits beyond the other. And the merits of anyone on the way contribute more to the blessedness of each person than do the merits of one in the homeland, even though the latter has greater charity; he nevertheless does not have greater merit. For the very difficulty, struggle, and interruption which exist on the way contribute to an increase of merit, and none of these exists in the homeland.

Others say that angels do not now merit, as was already said above, nor do souls separated from bodies; [Col. 1275C] for all merit belongs to the way. The evil will which they have is punishment only and not fault; or perhaps it is both punishment and fault, because by it they are made unlike God. The argument that no sin is unpunished should be referred rather to those who are in the state of meriting; or, rather, that will itself is fault, punishment, and the cause of punishment, and that sin is punished by itself.

As for the saying [Note: [Col. 1275D] From St Gregory, *Dialogues*, IV, ch. 44.], “The iniquity of those who hate you rises continually,” it is understood in our eternal—that is, in time. For just as a human being did not cease to sin in his own eternal, so God will not cease to punish in his own eternal; and just as, if the person were always to live, he would always become worse, so, because he will always exist, he will always endure punishment.

It seems possible again to show that God does not render to each person according to his final deeds, as follows. Lazarus died in charity, and it was necessary that he should have died thus; therefore it was necessary that he should be saved. He could not, then, afterwards be damned. This is disproved, because he was afterwards raised and could sin mortally and so die. Therefore he could afterwards be damned. Therefore he could first die in charity and afterwards be damned; which seems impossible. Again, as soon as anyone died, he was justly judged by the Lord; therefore that sentence ought not to have been changed. Again, he possessed glory, but only temporarily; therefore he did not possess eternal life. Again, Lazarus was recalled from the worthier [Col. 1276A] state which he had merited to a less worthy one. Worthier was that state in which he was certain of rest and could not sin, than that to which he was recalled, in which he could sin mortally and fall from charity. Therefore he was treated unjustly, since he did not deserve to be recalled from that state to this one. Again, in Lazarus the tinder of sin was extinguished; afterwards, in him recalled to life, that same tinder existed, whether contracted or committed. It was not contracted, since flesh was not afterwards created or generated in carnal pleasure; nor did he afterwards actually commit sin. Therefore, after he was raised, he ought to have been baptized, since he possessed the tinder of sin, as original sin. Again, Tabitha enjoyed blessedness after her first dissolution; therefore she too was treated unjustly. Again, [Col. 1276B] Lazarus died twice by temporal death: temporal death was first inflicted upon him for original sin, and a second time for the same sin. Therefore God judges twice concerning the same thing, or a double tribulation rises up from Him against it.

To all these objections some answer by saying that no objection should be made in this way from a miracle. Yet, lest they seem wholly to evade the issue, it is maintained that the first death was inflicted upon him in order to display the glory of God, as is commonly said concerning the man born blind. The second was inflicted as punishment for original sin; and a person is to be judged only according to the final merits of his last temporal death, which was properly due to him. For his first death occurred miraculously, as is evident from his raising, and not according to the course [Col. 1276C] of nature. It should nevertheless be known that one does not read of anyone having been raised of whom it is certain whether he had been assigned to eternal death or to eternal life.

## 341. CHAPTER XXII. On the diverse dwelling-places of the blessed in their heavenly country

[Note: [Col. 1275D] The Master, IV, distinction 49.]

Having treated these matters, it remains finally to inquire whether some souls of the saints are more blessed than others. This appears to be so. For just as, according to the diversity of merits, the souls of the wicked are punished differently in hell, so also the souls of the saints are glorified differently. Yet this seems capable of being disproved as follows. [Note: [Col. 1276D] Isaiah 31; thus Robert Rullus.] “As the Lord lives, whose fire is in Zion and whose furnace is in Jerusalem,” says Isaiah. By Zion the Church militant is understood; by Jerusalem, the Church triumphant; by fire, the charity [Col. 1276D] of the way; and by furnace, the charity of the heavenly country. For as much as a furnace surpasses fire, so much does the charity of the heavenly country surpass the charity of the way. Therefore, if someone were now to die in charity, he would have the most perfect charity. Therefore he would have such charity that none could be more perfect.

Again, Peter and Linus are blessed, and neither can be more blessed than he is. Therefore they are equally good. To this it must be said that, when the superlative is used for the adverb “very” together with its positive, it does not signify that the person to whom it applies surpasses all others in the quality denoted by the comparative. For if this person is “most perfect,” that is, very perfect, it does not follow that none is more perfect than he. [Col. 1277A] But when it is used with a plural genitive, it signifies that the person of whom it is said surpasses all those with whom the comparison is made in the quality denoted by it. Thus, if this man is “the most learned of all,” no one is more learned than he. Therefore the statement, “Linus is the most perfect of the saints,” is not to be accepted; rather, Linus is a perfect saint.

Again, the same penny will be given to the laborers in the vineyard (Matt. 21). Therefore all the elect will have the same reward. Therefore none will have more than another. Again, after the resurrection both good and evil persons will live, and none will be able to cease living; therefore all will live forever. Therefore all will have eternal life. To this it must be said that all will indeed possess the same penny, namely Christ, who is eternal life. But that penny will be golden for some, [Col. 1277B] silver for others, because there will be a difference among the saints in their manner of knowing. For some will know more clearly than others. This difference is called the diversity of dwelling-places, of which it is said: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling-places” (John 14). Nothing, then, prevents eternal life from being one and the same in kind for all, yet diverse in number, because each will have his own knowledge, greater or less than that of others.

But one should not say that the saints will have eternal life because their life is to be without end. For then the wicked too would have eternal life, since their life is not to end. Rather, they have the enjoyment of the graces attached to their life, inseparably joined to it; because of that enjoyment their life is called eternal life. [Col. 1277C] Among these graces there is one in which they take greater delight; hence, by antonomasia, eternal life is said—by transferring the name of the cause to the effect—to be the knowledge of God. Therefore eternal life is either unending life to which enjoyment of the graces is joined, or the knowledge of God itself, or Christ himself. But although the wicked will live forever, because the unavoidable necessity of punishment is joined to their life, their life is called eternal death: for it would be preferable for them to die rather than live thus. And among those punishments, the deprivation of the vision of God, which is more grievous, is sometimes called by the name of eternal death.

Again, all who will have eternal life will know that God is three and one; and nothing greater can be known of God. Therefore all will know whatever lesser things pertain to blessedness. Therefore [Col. 1277D] one will know nothing that another does not. In what, then, is the diversity of dwelling-places to be found? [Note: [Col. 1277D] Thus the Master here.] To this it must be said that the difference of dwelling-places lies in this: that some are more clear-sighted than others in divine knowledge, not in a diversity of things known, which are the same for all.

Again, Augustine says: [Note: [Col. 1278D] In the Master here, § D.] “In unequal charity there will be equal joy,” but blessedness consists only in the quantity of joy. Therefore all will be equally blessed because they will rejoice equally. It is said in reply that equality of joy would produce equality of blessedness if they were to have equal brightness; but because they will not have equal brightness, although there will be equal joy, there will not be equal blessedness. Or it may be better [Col. 1278A] said that this equality does not refer to equality in the intensity of those rejoicing, since they will rejoice unequally, but to equality in the persons over whom they will rejoice: for there will be as many persons over whom one rejoices as there will be persons over whom another rejoices.

Again, whatever displeases God displeases Peter. The sins Peter committed displease God; therefore they likewise displease Peter. Therefore Peter grieves over them. For an authority says: “For venial sins not to please one is to grieve over them.” Therefore Peter does not have full blessedness. Again, nothing displeases Peter except evil, and it displeases him that he sinned. Therefore sin exists; and this sin is found in no one except Peter. Again, Peter knows the sins that he committed, and God knows the same sins. Therefore they are not covered. [Col. 1278B] To this it may be said that the saints retain in memory the sins they committed, not so as to grieve, but so as to rejoice because they have been freed from them. This is how Isaiah’s saying is to be understood: “I create new heavens and a new earth, and the former things shall not be in memory, nor rise into the heart; and you shall rejoice forever” (Isa. 65): they shall not be in memory for grieving, but for rejoicing, just as a person rejoices in prosperity while remembering the adversity from which he has been delivered, according to that poetic line:

> Perhaps even these things it will one day help us to remember.  
> (VIRGIL, *Aeneid*, book I, verse 30.)

Nor are Peter’s sins called covered because they are not known, but because they are not known to him for punishment. [Col. 1278C] Hence they are called covered. But the statement, “For sins truly to displease one is to grieve over them,” must be referred to those who are on the way.

Again, Linus would love Peter’s greater good more if it were in himself than he loves his lesser good; but he loves his lesser good in himself more than he loves Peter’s greater good. Therefore Linus loves Peter’s greater good more in himself than in Peter. Therefore he would prefer it to be in himself rather than in Peter. Therefore Linus would wish Peter’s good to be in himself. Therefore he is not blessed, because not all that he desires comes to pass. Again, Linus knows that God loves Peter more than himself, and he disagrees with God’s will in nothing. Therefore Linus loves Peter more than himself. Therefore he does not have ordered charity. Again, whatever God wills, Linus wills; otherwise [Col. 1278D] God would not be all in all (1 Cor. 15). But God wills Peter’s good to be greater than Linus’s. Therefore Linus wills this too.

To this it must be said that whatever God wills, Linus wills. For the saints say that, just as a drop of water mixed with a measure of wine wholly takes on the flavor of the wine, so the wills of the saints pass wholly into the will of God. Nevertheless Linus loves himself more than Peter, because God wills this: that Linus should love Peter less than himself; and thus he disagrees with God’s will in nothing. So too, one who wishes his father to live, while God wishes him to die, differs in nothing from God’s will, because God wills him to will this.

Again, Peter loves his neighbor; the movement by which [Col. 1279A] he is moved to love his neighbor is not the same as that by which he is moved to love God. Therefore he does not love God with his whole heart. But from what has been said above it is sufficiently clear what it is to love God with one’s whole heart in the heavenly country: namely, so that every movement is spiritual and none carnal; or with the whole heart, that is, with a will without opposition, an understanding without error, and a memory without labor or difficulty; or with the whole heart, that is, so that every movement is in God and toward God. For there is a movement from God and toward God; a movement from God but not toward God; a movement toward God but not from God; and a movement neither from God nor toward God. Since all this is clear from what precedes, it would be superfluous to pursue it again.

It is rather to be inquired whether [343] the souls of the departed have knowledge of matters occurring among [Col. 1279B] the living. This seems established concerning the souls of the saints. [Note: [Col. 1279D] The Master, IV, distinction 45, §§ F–G.] For how would they offer to God the prayers and vows of suppliants unless they understood those praying and petitioning? Or how would prayer be directed to them when one says, “Saint Peter, pray for us,” unless they knew that we are praying? Augustine says as follows that both angels and holy souls offer our prayers to God: [Note: [Col. 1279D] In the book *On Praying to God*.] “Our petitions are made known to the angels who are with God, so that in some way they may offer them to God, consult Him concerning them, and report to us, either openly or secretly, what they have learned, at God’s command, must be fulfilled; whence the angel said to human beings: ‘When you were praying, he offered your prayer to God’” (Tobit 12).

Therefore the souls of the saints pray for us with the affection of compassion and assist us by their [Col. 1279C] merits. They do not speak in prayer, since they lack those instruments, but wish us salvation if they know it to be in God’s will; and when we humble ourselves before them, God hears us more readily through their merits assisting us. [Note: [Col. 1279D] Among others, Hugh of St Victor seems to hold this, question 228, in the *Explanation of Romans*, and book II of *On the Sacraments*, part XVI, final chapter.] Yet some say that speech is not directed to the saints, but rather to God—that He may hear us through the merits of the saints—when it is said, “Saint Peter, pray for us,” and “Saint Paul, pray for us”; and that they understand nothing of what is done here except insofar as they perceive it through God’s revelation. Augustine seems to agree with them, saying: [Note: [Col. 1279D] See *On Care to Be Taken for the Dead*, chapter 15, etc.] “Just as those who still live in the flesh do not know in what place the souls of the departed are situated, so the dead do not know how those living in the flesh are ordered in life; for as bodily and spiritual things differ in kind, so they are distinct in thought.”

But that authority is to be understood of the wicked who are punished in hell, because they do not know how those living in the flesh are ordered. Concerning the rich man placed in hell, who said, “Father Abraham, I have five brothers; send Lazarus” (Luke 16), and so forth, [Note: [Col. 1280D] Thus Augustine in the Master here, § C, in distinction 50, and in Psalm 108.] they say that he had no certain knowledge of what his brothers were doing; but because he did not see them with himself in the places [Col. 1280A] of torments, nor in the place of rest with Abraham, he supposed that they were living. [Note: [Col. 1280D] This is Gregory, Homily 40 on Luke.] For the good and the evil see one another until the Day of Judgment; but afterwards the good will see the evil, whereas the evil will by no means see the good, because “the wicked man shall be taken away lest he see the glory of God” (Isa. 26). Then the chasm will be fixed, so that those who wish to cross from here to them cannot, nor can they cross thence to here, [Note: [Col. 1280D] The Master, distinction 50, § F.] because justice will be established on this side and iniquity on that. Hence the good neither now nor then will have compassion on the wicked.

Yet they are said to wish to cross over to the wicked because, if God’s justice permitted it, the wicked’s deliverance would not be burdensome to them; or this may mean prayer, because, even if they wished it, they could not help them, since the wicked are placed in outer darkness and cannot have a will to act well or abandon their will [Col. 1280B] to sin. That will is for them both sin and punishment. But, according to some, that sin does not merit punishment, because that is a place of receiving, not of meriting. According to others, that evil will is not sin but punishment only: they would wish themselves not to exist, and God not to exist, if this were possible. For although they will then possess natural goods, just as demons still possess them, they will nevertheless be so benumbed and darkened in malice that they cannot direct any spark of love toward God, so as to love themselves, or God, even with merely natural love. [Note: [Col. 1280D] The Master, § B.]

Hence they will then properly be said to be in outer darkness. This darkness does not mean not seeing God by direct vision, which no one here possesses; nor not seeing through the dissimilarity produced by sin between [Col. 1280C] God and human beings, which many suffer here as well; but rather a certain malignancy of hatred and of the will, now growing in the minds of the reprobate, and a certain forgetfulness of God. For they are so afflicted by the pains of inner and outer torments that they can never draw their minds away from them to think anything about God: “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched; and they shall be a sight unto satiety for all the flesh of the elect” (Isa. 66).

But over the daughter of Zion God will rejoice as a bridegroom over a bride (Isa. 62); and He will bend over her like a river of peace, and like an overflowing torrent His glory, which we shall suck so as to be filled from the breast of His consolation, that we may draw milk and overflow with delights [Col. 1280D] from His all-encompassing glory; we shall rejoice and exult (Isa. 66), and no one shall take that joy from us (John 16). In order that we may enjoy this, charity above all things must be embraced by us here; it is the end of the commandment (1 Tim. 1), in which the whole law is fulfilled. Therefore, if it is not permitted to go over every individual writing, if it does not please one to read all the sayings of the prophets, possess charity, and do whatever you wish.” For there will be no end to making books. “Fear God and keep His commandments; this is the whole duty of man” (Eccl. 12).

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1208: GUIBERT, ABBOT OF GEMBLOUX

[Col. 1281]

## NOTICE

(OUDIN, *Commentary on Ecclesiastical Writers*, II, 1591)

Guibert Martin, abbot of Gembloux, was so surnamed because of a special devotion to Saint Martin, archbishop of Tours. He flourished from about the year 1180 and the years following. He wrote many works, preserved in manuscript in his monastery of Gembloux in Brabant, where he had formerly been abbot. John Mabillon saw these in three volumes, from which he reports a few items in summary in volume II of his *Analecta*, p. 544 and following; these we shall here reproduce word for word.

“It is useful to note certain matters concerning Wibert or Guibert, at whose instigation and request Hervard, archdeacon of Liège, wrote his letter to G., canon of Laon [Note: [Col. 1281] See below.], from the manuscript *Chronicle of Gembloux*, in which I read the following:

‘If anyone desires to know something concerning this Guibert, a man of great holiness, integrity, and learning, and what his merit was, he will be able to learn it abundantly from his writings. For he wrote letters to various persons, moral in character and full of excellent exhortations. Always holding Holy Scripture in hand and on his lips, he was, already burdened by old age, brought to the abbatial dignity. He lived in the priesthood for sixty-three years, as he relates more fully concerning himself in a certain letter recounting the early course of his life, which begins, “Blessed Augustine.” He was a great zealot for souls—especially his own, no less than those of others—as is evident in all his letters, which he sent to various persons, whether of exalted rank or of equal and companionable condition.

‘He lived in various monasteries. In particular, he went twice into France, to the monastery sacred to Saint Martin at Tours, where he was greatly loved both for the uprightness of his morals and for the *Life of Saint Martin* that he had composed in verse and presented to the people of Tours. Called back by them, he returned to Gembloux; and not long afterwards the monks of Saints John and Maurus, martyrs, at Florennes requested him as abbot. He presided over them commendably for five years and eight months. In the meantime John, abbot of Gembloux, died. The said abbot of Florennes was summoned by the monks of Gembloux to celebrate his funeral rites. When he wished to return to Florennes, the brethren of Gembloux chose him as their abbot, about the year of the Lord 1194, and he presided for ten years.’

And after much else:

‘Let us return to our abbot Guibert, who lived at different times in various places and monasteries. He first professed the monastic life in this monastery of Gembloux; afterwards, having gone into France, he lived at Tours, whence, departing, he returned to Gembloux. In the meantime the people of Florennes chose and requested him as their abbot, and, after the abbot of Gembloux had died, he was made abbot there. But after ten completed years in the government of Gembloux, and fifteen years and eight months in that of Florennes, he resigned both abbeys and lived among the people of Florennes. From there he came to Villers Abbey; after leaving it, he again went into France and lived at Tours. Taking leave of them, he turned aside to a certain virgin named Hildegard, wishing her much happiness; then, returning to Gembloux, his former and proper nest, he died there, old and full of days and rich in many good works. He lived in the priesthood, as stated above, for sixty-three years and more. He entered upon the way of all flesh on the twenty-second day of February. These few details are selected from his many worthy deeds.’”

“These matters concerning Guibert, who, I think, has hitherto been little known to learned men, I considered worth noting. But in order that a more accurate knowledge of his works may be had, I have thought it worthwhile to state what I myself observed concerning them on my Belgian journey. I found Guibert’s literary works in three parchment codices, especially his letters, of which it is useful to sample some here.

“He wrote several letters to Arnulf the Schoolmaster: namely, on friendship, on the Easter solemnity, on the departure from Egypt—that is, this world—on patiently enduring tribulation, on voluntary poverty and the treasures of wisdom, on Saint Vincent the martyr, and on patience, and so forth. In two letters addressed ‘To John, most dear brother,’ he exhorts John, brother of Arnulf the schoolmaster, to conversion and spiritual warfare. He sympathizes with his most sweet brother Rainer in illness and exhorts him to conversion. To the same man he writes on priestly dignity, and then another letter on the Easter solemnity, in which he calls Rainer ‘Schoolmaster.’ He directs three letters to his nephew Lambert, who was more occupied than was proper in secular affairs, exhorting him to the pursuit of virtues. These I found in the first codex; those which follow, in the second.

“First occurs the work *On the Life and Miracles of Saint Martin*, written rhythmically in four books. Its prose prologue indicates that this work was presented at Boppard to Philip, archbishop of Cologne, while Philip was being held in the count’s custody. Many letters addressed by Guibert to the same Philip follow; throughout them he calls him the vicar of the Supreme Shepherd and of Christ. The first is on the mysteries of creation and restoration. The second is apologetic, because, in writing about pastors, he seemed to have touched him. The third, in Philip’s name, is addressed to the abbot of Marmoutier and to the primicerius of the Church of Châteauneuf; in it he asks them concerning the custom of closing the monastery gates on the night of the feast of the ordination or translation of Saint Martin, [Col. 1283] and concerning the report then current that Saint Martin celebrated Mass on that night.

“The fourth is the reply to Philip from Hervé the abbot and the brethren of the chapter of Marmoutier; they satisfy his inquiries and praise Guibert. The fifth and sixth are written to Philip by Philip the dean, Rainald the treasurer, and the whole chapter of Saint Martin of Tours. In the former of these letters they give thanks for the *Life of Saint Martin* sent to them; in both they relate certain miracles of Saint Martin. The seventh is Guibert’s letter to Philip, giving thanks for benefits. The eighth, by the same author to the same recipient, concerns the praiseworthy conduct of the brethren of Marmoutier. The ninth concerns the nobility and magnificence of the church of Châteauneuf. In the tenth Guibert exhorts Philip to the cultivation of his office and to the task of restoring peace at the assembly of Liège. The eleventh congratulates him on peace restored.

“He gives thanks to Hervé, abbot of Marmoutier, and his sacred community, for the hospitality given him and because he obtained from them permission to copy the books *On the Miracles of Saint James*, *On the Wars Waged in Spain by Charlemagne*, and *On the Martyrdom of Duke Roland*. He declares that copies of these books were eagerly snatched from him for transcription. Indeed, at that time false wares of this kind had begun to be peddled; this is the subject of the twelfth letter. In the thirteenth, addressed to the brethren of Marmoutier, he praises their religious life and notes certain matters needing correction. The fourteenth is directed to Abbot John and the brethren of the same monastery. Guibert thanks them, requests from them books of Paulinus, and writes that, after previously being set over two abbeys, he then presided over the single abbey of Florennes.

“After these, in the same codex, follows Guibert’s letter to Philip, archbishop of Cologne, in which he says that he is obeying Philip’s command to write the *Life of Saint Hildegard*. Then follow various letters of the same Guibert to Lady Hildegard, mistress of the monastery of Saint Robert at Bingen. The first concerns the excellence of Saint Martin the bishop; the second concerns Hildegard’s visions, concerning which he asks: whether, as rumor had it, after writing her visions she forgot them; then whether she herself wrote them in Latin; and finally whether she had learned the Latin language. At the end of the letter: ‘Your beloved friends, known to you by sight, greet you: Siger of Waha, and Nicholas, the young knight of Niel, whom you saw when you visited him in Lent. Brother Franco the Recluse, a worthy son in Christ of your church, greets you; and Brother Robert, weak in body but strong in mind, lying on the mountain called Saint Guibert’s. Lord Emmo, priest of the parish of our church, greets you,’ etc.

“Furthermore, there are eight other letters of this same Guibert to Hildegard, and then various replies of Hildegard to him; various letters of the same Guibert to the sisters of the church of Blessed Mary and Saint Robert at Bingen, and replies of those same sisters to Guibert; and other letters written to other persons: namely, Joseph, a schoolmaster of outstanding integrity, who, being about to go to Jerusalem with the archbishop of Canterbury, offered Guibert a prose composition on Saint Martin for examination; Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz, on the virtues of Saint Martin; Conrad, bishop of that same church, on the various fortunes of the Church of Cologne; and finally Godfrey, abbot of the monastery of Saint Eucharius and Saint Willibrord, concerning the *Life of Saint Hildegard*, which Guibert himself committed to writing.

“Moreover, Bartholomew Fisen, in the *Flowers of the Church of Liège*, where he treats of the abbots of Gembloux, attests that Guibert also wrote certain things to Blessed Lutgard, then living in the nearby convent of Aywières; and that in 1208, that is, two years after resigning his office, he passed to the saints above.”

Guibert Martin therefore became abbot of Florennes in 1188 and abbot of Gembloux in 1194. Having resigned these offices in 1206, he is recorded to have died at last in 1208, on 22 February, at approximately eighty-eight years of age and after sixty-three years in the priesthood. I think that nothing by this writer has been published except [his letters and] the account of the destruction—or rather the burning—of the monastery of Gembloux, which took place in 1137. Guibert, after becoming abbot both of that monastery and of Florennes, committed this account to writing. It is in book II, chapter 8, p. 904, of the *Commentaries on the Imperial Library at Vienna*, where he also mentions his books that had been carried off in this destruction.

Hervard, archdeacon of Liège, mentions Guibert Martin and his writings in his letter to G., canon of Laon; so too does the anonymous author of the *Chronicle of Gembloux*, in volume II of Mabillon’s *Analecta*, p. 544; Valerius Andreas, in the *Belgian Library*, p. 303 of the 1643 quarto edition, Louvain, where he lists various manuscript codices of Guibert’s works in Belgian libraries; and Peter Lambecius, book II, chapter 8, p. 904, of the *Commentaries on the Imperial Library at Vienna*, where he speaks of manuscript codex 296, brought from the Ambrosian fortress at Datten into the Imperial Library.

[Col. 1283]

## LETTER OF HERVARD, ARCHDEACON OF LIÈGE, TO G., CANON OF LAON, CONCERNING GUIBERT, ABBOT OF GEMBLOUX, AND THE WRITING OF A LIFE OF ST MARTIN

(D. MABILLON, *Analecta*, new edition, p. 480.)

[Col. 1283A] To the reverend father and lord G., canon of Blessed Mary, Mother of God, at Laon: Hervard, archdeacon of Liège, wishes that he may manfully run the course of this present life by living justly, and happily obtain the prize of eternal blessedness.

It is an established custom, approved by the long agreement of good people, for friends to grant one another’s requests of every kind, and especially those that are easy and honorable, [Col. 1284A] so that through a cheerful and ready performance of an outward work, the desirable fruit of hidden affection may come forth into light and public view. Therefore, I devoutly entreat and earnestly [Col. 1285A] beseech your fatherhood—whose generosity, lavish and available to me from my cradle whenever need required, I have read and reread in the book of experience—that when the favorable, wholly worthy, and readily to be received request of Lord Guibert, surnamed Martin, comes or is sent to you, you may receive it affectionately and gratefully without rejection, and carry it out effectively.

For its accomplishment will gladden and edify many; it will also bring you great praise and glory, even if you do not wish it (although you ought neither to wish nor seek this); and it will inspire in Lord Guibert himself a more ready disposition to intercede with God on your behalf. This is that Guibert who formerly exercised the office of abbot, first in the monastery of Florennes and afterwards in that of Gembloux, but did not die while holding either office. For, having sought out and secured a useful opportunity, he preferred honorably to withdraw rather than fall beneath a burden which he bore alone and sorrowfully, without a faithful fellow-bearer, and by his fall become an object of mockery to foolish scoffers.

For what purpose would he uselessly wear himself out in a furnace of scandals and tribulations, burning with flames, [Col. 1285B] especially when he could neither extinguish those flames by himself nor endure them long without the great harm of injury—when, that is, within that same furnace, no gentle whisper of breeze blew for him, and no aid of pious consolation cooled his fiercest heat? Therefore, making prudent use of counsel, he chose rather to be saved in a low place than to be endangered in a high one, and rather to imitate, so that he might be saved, the footsteps of the humble and poor Christ than to walk in things great and wonderful above himself, and someday be punished with those things for the arrogance of pride.

This same man is Guibert Martin, devotee and in some measure imitator of the glorious bishop Martin, and a diligent celebrant in speech and writing of Martin’s works and virtues. Accordingly, because of the constancy of his long-standing and affectionate devotion toward him, the personal name of that most eminent bishop was turned into this man’s surname; so that he is now called Guibert Martin everywhere he is known, not only by his own proper name, Guibert, but also because of the conspicuous service of the aforesaid devotion [Col. 1285C] which he diligently renders to Martin.

But let us now set forth the matter for which we have prefaced these things and toward which we are tending. This same Guibert Martin, whom we warmly commend to you because of his merits dear to us, having heard and read certain of your little works—namely those in which, using heroic verse, you have set forth in a distinguished work either the life of Servatius, the eminent confessor of Christ, or the worship and manner of life that clerics who wish to live devoutly in Christ ought to observe—is attracted and delighted beyond expression by the elegance and beauty of those writings.

Therefore, because, being less known to you, he distrusts your assent concerning his proposal—and this is no wonder—he came to me, bound to me by the bond of mutual acquaintance and affection, and, hoping that you would refuse me nothing that I might justly ask, repeatedly besought me most humbly and insistently to obtain through my intercession with you that [Col. 1285D] you also might adopt as your patron Blessed Martin, whom, because of the benefits that he experiences from him daily, Guibert venerates and exalts with all the devotion he can; and that, just as all who serve Martin with pure affection are supported by the aid of his intercessions in times of need, you too may be supported by them. He asks that you show Martin some honor with diligent and eager purpose.

Nor should you be troubled in the least about complying with the request of this same Lord Guibert Martin, for he will not ask you to spend in Saint Martin’s service either gold, silver, or anything whatever by which your purse or pantry might be emptied. What then? Does he ask you to build a church for him? [Col. 1286A] Not even this, for no saint is found richer than he in possession of churches, except the Mother of Christ and the Key-bearer of heaven. If none of these things, then what does he have to ask? Surely, what you can provide most easily.

What is it? Words, of course. What flies more lightly than winged words? Thus both he and I with him ask—and ask with the most earnest intention we can—that, after most diligent investigation and consideration of the almost incomparable eminence of so great a bishop, by which he is deservedly equated, both in works of virtue and in the greatness of his name, with the highest princes of the heavenly court, that is, the prophets and apostles, you apply all the strength and sharpness of your most subtle intellect. You who have surpassed certain others in your writings should, by surpassing yourself in this matter, write in elegiac verse, to the praise of God and for the profit and delight of readers, some memorable things in honor of that blessed Martin, from material which will be conveyed to you by letter.

[Col. 1286B] Nor will you labor vainly in this little work, because the labor itself, besides driving away from us harmful idleness by usefully exercising you, will produce a twofold benefit of reward: while living and after death, you will be exalted in the proclamation of praise even against your will; and you will be protected by the patronage of your Martin in all the dangers and tribulations of this life, and in that necessity than which none is harsher, namely at the point of death.

Therefore, you who have long grown dull in sleepy idleness, at last awaken, at least when summoned; and, like a cock which makes itself more wakeful for singing by striking itself with clapping wings, polish and sharpen as though by filing the powers of your intellect, overgrown with the rust of long disuse, so that they may shine. Receive gladly and energetically the exercise of praiseworthy labor—that is, a work pleasing to God and useful to posterity—which God Himself offers you, lest, if you delay sluggishly, another secretly put forth his hand and snatch it from you, and thus, through the lukewarmness of your delay, you be deprived of both rewards: temporal praise and eternal [Col. 1286C] recompense.

Therefore undertake it without delay, and complete it swiftly, before the mind’s edge has been blunted by old age and too-late repentance makes you begin to wish—when, God avert it!, you have become deficient in memory and judged unequal to the task—and when you are ashamed of idleness only when you can no longer amend it. Free yourselves, then, I beg you, as far as possible from every hindrance of other business; devote yourselves with watchful attention to this work, which God lays upon you to accomplish through such a man; and, with his aid, bring it to an end with all the speed you can, without injury to the work itself. Beware, moreover, I ask, lest, if you wait any longer, time—which flies past more swiftly than any arrow or bird—will not wait for you; lest, when the day of life is closed, the darkness of death, in which no one can work, overtake you; and, what is most to be feared, lest you offend God himself, who knocks at you through his servant, [Col. 1286D] and incur the punishment of the slothful and useless servant who refused to gain profit from the talent entrusted to him. And now, that this excessively long letter may at last be brought to a close, with filial affection I beg your fatherhood that charity may prevail with you to grant what charity asks with sincere and devout affection: lest, if you refuse to heed charity, he who is supreme Charity may likewise not heed you at all in your prayers, which may that same Charity—that is, God—in his loving-kindness grant by turning away from you, through the prayers of blessed Martin: namely, that all your affairs may be fulfilled in that very charity.

[Col. 1287]

# LETTERS OF GUIBERT, ABBOT OF GEMBLOUX

(D. Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. I, col. 916.)

## LETTER I. TO PHILIP, ARCHBISHOP OF COLOGNE  
He describes the conduct of corrupt shepherds, whom he urges him to avoid.

[Col. 1287A]

To the venerable and most beloved father PHILIP, vicar of the supreme Shepherd in the Church of Cologne: Brother G., his own in affection, wishes him an abiding remembrance, borne in the breastplate of his heart, of God’s chosen bishops, and through their examples happily to enter, with the manifold increase of the holy flock, the pastures of Paradise ever green.

It has always belonged to the goodness and mercy of God, reverend Father, to provide for fallen humankind and to supply fitting means of instruction. Humankind found the way of restoration for this reason also: it had exceeded the bounds of obedience laid upon it, not through its own wickedness but through deception by another’s malice. And because we are those upon whom the ends of the ages have come (1 Cor. 10), through many experiences we perceive fulfilled the words of the Apostle: “In the last days,” he says, “perilous times will come, and people will be lovers of themselves, covetous, gluttonous, arrogant, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, wicked, without affection, without peace, slanderers, incontinent, fierce, without kindness, traitors, insolent, puffed up, lovers of pleasures rather than of God” (2 Tim. 3). Certainly our monstrous age has produced all these kinds of beasts in the fullness of human form; but through excessive familiarity we are not horrified by what is horrible. Therefore “my eyes shed streams of water” (Lam. 3), because “the sun has been darkened at its rising, and the moon does not shine in its fullness” (Isa. 13). The blind people do not lack guides, but their guides are blind; for, as their sins demand, according to the prophet, the Lord sends them kings in his wrath (Hos. 13), and raises up shepherds in the land who do not visit what is held back, seek what is scattered, or heal what is broken, but eat the flesh of the fat ones and clothe themselves in the wool of the flocks (Ezek. 34).

Thus sons are born in the bosom of the Church in place of fathers, but they are degenerate sons; they are established in her land, but forgetful of the Lord’s name and his commands. For most of them enter not through the door, but climb up another way (John 10): they enter by ambition and money, not by grace; by the gift of princes, not by the election of the clergy. And they enter [Col. 1288A] not to feed, but to be fed; not to minister, but to be ministered to; not to sow, but to gather; not to labor, but to rest; not to guard the sheep from wolves, but themselves, more savage than wolves, to plunder the sheep. They also wish to replenish by plunder what had been emptied in acquiring office, and to clothe themselves not merely in soft but even in costly garments. Because they exercise authority over many, they desire to be called benefactors (Luke 22), not by giving to the poor but to their dependents, friends, and superfluous retainers. Accordingly, that they may abound in such things, they love gifts and pursue rewards (Isa. 1), and with various motives seek occasions for extortion; hence they often pervert judgment for this purpose (1 Sam. 8).

Though, in imitation of the fathers whose sons they are, they ought—not by pursuing their fathers’ life, but by holding only their outward office and place—to despise earthly things, long for eternal things, and draw others to the love of God, they greedily desire earthly things with most wretched ambition, and give little thought either to correcting themselves or governing those subject to them. Alas! “How the gold has grown dim; how the finest color has changed; how the stones of the sanctuary have been scattered at the head of every street!” (Lam. 4). O stupor of utter madness: to seek earthly and passing things with the whole compass of one’s heart and neglect heavenly and eternal things; to scatter one’s own goods among wealthy strangers and forget the children of the poor. And to whom should this evil be attributed, if not to the idleness of prelates? For almost every evil found among subjects either grows through the carelessness [Col. 1288C] of negligent prelates or is strengthened by their corrupt examples. Therefore the Lord threatens them through Jeremiah: “Woe to the shepherds who scatter and tear apart the sheep of my pasture! Behold, I shall feed them with wormwood and give them gall to drink” (Jer. 23). I do not see in what hope of future things they may console themselves, when the Lord promises blessedness only to the poor, the meek, those who mourn, those who hunger and thirst, and those who suffer persecution (Matt. 5); whereas these men, on the contrary, are clothed in purple and fine linen and feast splendidly, and whatever trifles and follies the world possesses and practices, they either themselves perform or permit their own people about them to perform.

In all these matters, reverend Father, if anything seems applicable to your person, receive it with a kindly ear as an incitement to your advancement, and reckon it neither folly in me nor an injury to yourself. [Col. 1289A] Whatever is here plainly said about others, understand it as said to you in proverbial fashion. May God, the gracious ruler and guardian of all, preserve your holiness unharmed and make you, in the care entrusted to you, a vigorous imitator of himself.

## LETTER II. TO THE SAME  
He confirms what he had said in the preceding letter.

To the great priest PHILIP, by God’s grace Archbishop of Cologne: Brother GUIBERT, the least of his servants, wishes him, through the aid of the eternal King and Priest, worthily to exercise the priesthood in the present life and to govern the care of his flesh with discipline, so that in the future he may deserve to attain the most blessed fellowship of priests and kings of this kind.

[Col. 1289B] When a scruple arose in me concerning the letter sent to you through me, and I anxiously considered whether it would be better to alter or erase certain things placed there, or to send it to you, I fled to the protection of prayer, asking that, if the speech had proceeded from the Lord and he had placed it in my mouth, it might stand and might remove from me my own hesitation concerning it. I prayed, and satisfaction was given me. For I saw and understood, not only through the guidance of reason but also through the prompting of truth, that the best method of admonition is one in which the admonisher proceeds faithfully and cautiously, neither deceiving the person admonished by flattery, nor provoking him by harshness, nor scorching him by open denunciation; but, having considered the character of the person, diligently endeavors, as he sees expedient, to incite him to what is useful and healthful—either sparing his shame [Col. 1289C] or showing deference to his honor. For I saw and proved that nothing more right, fitting, or sound can ever be proposed to one who stands in God’s place over souls to be led back to salvation than, first, the kindness of the providence of that merciful God himself, who cares for all and disposes us with reverence, always to be considered and imitated; then also the evil examples of the wicked and the good examples of the good, together with the punishments of the former and the rewards of the latter, so that, terrified by those and drawn by these, he may be instructed in all things and concerning all things. This, therefore, is an effective mode of admonition and worthy of every acceptance.

### CONCLUSION

[Col. 1289D] May almighty God, who stands in the assembly of gods and judges them in their midst (Ps. 81), rebuking those who judge unjustly, and so forth—“How long will you judge unjustly and show partiality to sinners?” (ibid.)—bring forth your justice as light and your judgment as the noonday (Ps. 36), lest, walking in ignorance, you walk in darkness and incur a greater judgment. May he inspire your heart to judge the needy and the orphan justly, and to vindicate the lowly and the poor (Ps. 81), and to perform the remaining works of justice and mercy, so that both with the merciful you may possess the earth (Matt. 5), and with the righteous judges of the age you may hold the judicial throne of dignity when the Lord comes to judgment with the elders of his people. Amen.

## LETTER III. TO THE SAME  
He gives thanks for benefits received from him.

[Col. 1290A]

To his most beloved father and reverend lord PHILIP, by God’s grace Archbishop of Cologne: Brother GUIBERT, the least of all who serve God, gives himself in Christ in the affection and effect of most vigorous love.

To render thanks, venerable Father, for what the abundance of your kindness has bestowed upon my insignificance, even if every movement of my body were changed into tongues and my voice were of bronze, I would not suffice. Therefore, because I fail in this respect, turning to those resources which, however slight, are available through God’s bounteous grace: whatever a prayer either of sluggish devotion or of a sinner can accomplish, I expend entirely and daily for your aid, and am prepared to expend it continually as long as I live, etc.

## LETTER IV. TO THE SAME  
He excuses himself for not having come to him.

To the venerable lord and father, by God’s grace Archbishop of Cologne: Brother G., his own in affection, wishes him to have praise not in the vanity of the world but in the name of the Lord, and to be magnified by him who exalts the meek unto salvation (Ps. 149).

That I have not yet come to you is due neither to sloth nor negligence, but to the affairs by which I know you are occupied. Since I neither wish nor am able to travel abroad often, [Col. 1290C] I have sent three letters to your excellency. May the supreme Priest acknowledge you in his blessings; and because of the mercy preserved by you in the present life and enduring without end, may God, the Father of mercies, preserve mercy for you in the future. Amen.

## LETTER V. TO HERVEUS, ABBOT, AND THE BRETHREN OF MARMOUTIER  
He declares that he undertook a pilgrimage to Saint Martin’s tomb not from a desire for wandering but from devotion, and that monastic enclosures are corrupted by the bad conduct of secular persons.

To his most beloved father HERVEU[S], and to the sacred community of Marmoutier, worthy of every reverence and most orderly engaged in God’s service under his [Col. 1290D] care: Brother GUIBERT, servant of their holiness, wishes that, from him with whom supreme order is found in the heavenly palace, they may be ranked among the righteous at the time of recompense.

Although some persons, who “speak with a double heart” (Ps. 11) and do not keep watch over their ways so as not to sin with their tongue (Ps. 38), have criticized my pilgrimage to the tomb of blessed Martin and ascribed it more to wandering than devotion, I know that it greatly pleases you; and I glory and rejoice in it. Yet in this ground of glory—by which I desire, through Christ’s gift, to be a peaceful and healthy member in Christ’s body—I do not act against him who is the head of the body (Col. 1), nor do I raise myself above his head, remembering what is written: “He who says that he abides in Christ ought himself also to walk as he walked” (1 John 2). Indeed, if I wished to glory according to the flesh, it would rightly be reckoned madness in me, for he himself said: “I do not seek my own glory” (John 8). If, then, forgetful of that saying, “Let him who glories glory in the Lord” (1 Cor. 8), I desired human favor and empty glory, I would be eager to conform myself to this age, to love which is to commit fornication against God (Hos. 9) and to become his enemy (Jas. 4), so much so that the Apostle James says: “Adulterers, do you not know that friendship with this world is enmity with God?” (ibid.). Would not my conscience convicting me condemn my mouth? Would not the Apostle immediately confront me, saying: “If it is necessary to boast, indeed it is not expedient” (2 Cor. 12)?

[Col. 1291B] Yet how dangerous it is to wish to commend oneself by boasting is evident also from the words of the Psalmist, where he says: “For God has scattered the bones of those who please men” (Ps. 52). But whoever, not understanding how serious the vice of ingratitude is, thinks that he ought to be angry with me because I recognize a heavenly gift and humbly glory in it with thanksgiving, will surely deservedly be judged foolish. Yet I, comparing and measuring myself by myself, “not thinking lofty things, but consenting to the lowly” (Rom. 12), shall glory not beyond measure but somewhat, and according to the measure which God has measured out to me. For, as someone says, it is fitting for anyone to measure himself and to be aided by his own praises.

And whence, I ask, my lords, do such great evils boil up in cloisters? Whence, do you suppose, are cloisters corrupted? Unless from the introduction of worldliness, which enters by no other route than through the sloth, ignorance, carelessness, and laxity of foolish prelates, who, corrupt themselves, are corruptly appointed by corrupt men. Some, moreover, are appointed by entering another way after the door has been abandoned; or, burrowing underneath it, they are intruded—through money, to which all things obey, or through the violence of powerful relatives—against every divine and human law. And what should such men do—hirelings rather than shepherds, made fruitful by no reasoning of the Spirit and rooted in no charity—what, I say, should such men, whom the Lord in the Gospel calls thieves and robbers (John 10), do except seek their own interests (Phil. 2), neglect God’s interests, and thus, to conclude innumerable matters briefly, bear fruit for death rather than life, and destroy themselves and their blind followers, to whom they themselves, being blind, offer guidance (Matt. 15)?

## LETTER VI. TO THE BRETHREN OF MARMOUTIER  
He explains why hospitality and the discipline of the Rule are less observed in the dependent cells.

To my sweetest lords and friends, brethren of Marmoutier, to be embraced forever in Christ’s love and humble devotion: Brother G., servant of their holiness, wishes them whatever may most fittingly be desired for the salvation of the inner and outer person.

I, venerable Fathers, a little man—or rather “a worm and no man”—seeing nothing more grievous in the course of things and enduring nothing more bitter than that the monastic order, once exalted and splendid and venerable even to the sons or tyrants of this world, should in our day—shame upon us!—be rendered contemptible by an infamous life by those whose disciplined conduct ought to have commended it: not only stripped of the glory of its beauty, but deprived of almost every sound element of its condition, cannot at all conceal my heart’s grief concerning this. Hence, whenever an occasion is afforded, in speech and writing, I attack and oppose the wrongdoers with all the strength I can; and for the order’s injuries, when I am granted no power to do more, I at least cry out.

For this reason, in your monastery—than which nothing can be found more abundant in riches, more splendid in religious observance, cleaner in purity, more guarded against vices, or more circumspect in preserving the renown of good repute for God’s praise—I saw certain matters relating not precisely to the head but to some of the members. If I dared, without forfeiting your favor, I would humbly advise the vigilance of your holiness, not reproving in rashness but suggesting in charity, to investigate the truth of the matter carefully and correct whatever needs correction. There appear, however, in some of your members certain corruptions, though very small and not difficult to correct. But why should I state everything, when it is written not merely, “Admonish,” but, in words that sound harsher, “Rebuke a wise man, and he will love you” (Prov. 9)? Therefore do not wait with ears pricked in fear, as though I were going to say something great and shameful; but fear the heavenly Inspector who “searches Jerusalem with lamps” (Zeph. 1), [Col. 1292C] who will judge strictly not only open matters but hidden and slight ones as well. Strive that your whole body, from the head to the sole of the foot, may be found sound and unstained in his sight.

But, to come now to the matter, I shall put first what I have experienced. When I was once travelling toward you, I turned aside to one of your dependent cells for lodging; but I could not obtain admission, although I promised to purchase what I needed at the market. What was done to me could certainly have been done to others, and I know—as I later learned from many—that it was done neither to me alone nor for the first time. Likewise, while I was staying with you, I learned from some persons, and from more especially when I was returning home, that certain priors [Col. 1292D] of your cells sometimes indulge improperly in feasts and drinking and are not free from the vices generated by satiety—that is, with their loins loosened and their lamps extinguished, they perform works of the night. And so that unlawful things may be freely permitted to them there, and that they may not themselves appear alone blameworthy, they do not forbid such practices to those subject to them. For how could they restrain others from matters in which they themselves are found guilty? For that Gospel saying would be brought against them: “Physician, heal yourself” (Luke 4).

I urge this so earnestly because, God is my witness, after the Church which nourished and reared me at her own breasts and, with Christ’s help, brought me to this stage of life, I venerate and love your Church alone; and just as I rejoice with lively exultation in her renowned glory and splendor, so also, if [Col. 1293A] I happen to hear or learn anything of unfavorable report about matters established in her administration, I grieve from the marrow of my being. Since members ought to be concerned for one another, and especially the head for the members (1 Cor. 12), strive, I beg you, that in your cells which have resources sufficient for this purpose, the humane duty of hospitality may not be performed more negligently than is right through the greed or carelessness of the priors. Take care also that the purity of chastity may be preserved in every place under your authority as singularly preeminent among virtues, continuously surrounded for its protection, on one side by frugality against luxury, on the other by humility against pride, lest it be attacked in any degree. Furthermore, give the most earnest attention to diligently investigating everything done in your cells, especially the remote ones, and what sort of life and conduct those whom you have assigned to govern them lead.

For I say—though I am ashamed, yet truth compels me to say it—that sacred religion suffers no greater prejudice to its dignity and no greater loss to its honor than from the cells. Though in very many abbeys the beauty of monastic glory has already been darkened by wicked sons and almost reduced to nothing, nevertheless the greater part of its ruin and injuries has arisen from cells or priories—that is, from those who dwell in the cells or priories—and every disgrace emerges from those mockers of the order. What has been done by them is shameful to say, so much so that in our land the order itself, once held in the highest reverence, [Col. 1293C] has now widely become an object of reproach and a byword, mockery and derision, blasphemy and hissing throughout the surrounding region. Stand firm, then, most reverend Fathers, in the Lord; and as you have done until now, hold fast until the end the traditions of the order which you once received from antiquity. And lest “dead flies spoil the ointment of good repute” (Eccl. 10) in you also, now especially, when everything is in decline, withdraw yourselves from the example of every Church that walks disorderly.

Therefore, attributing absolutely nothing to yourselves as though it came from yourselves, but giving it to him from whom all good things proceed (Jas. 1), and offering thanks from a simple heart, all come together in one judgment: be of one mind, say the same thing with one mouth: “Blessed is God in his gifts, and holy [Col. 1293D] in all his works, through whose gift it comes to pass that he is served worthily and laudably.” To him be praise and glory, honor and dominion for ever. Amen.

## LETTER VII. TO J., ABBOT, AND THE BRETHREN OF MARMOUTIER  
He praises their religious observance and requests their prayers after his death.

To the most reverend lord and father J. [Note: [Col. 1293D] Joffrey or Geoffrey, who was appointed in 1187 to succeed the most devout retiring Abbot Herveus.], by God’s grace abbot, and to the most beloved brethren serving God and blessed Martin at Marmoutier under his rule: Brother GUIBERT, least and always and everywhere servant of their holiness, wishes them salvation in the true Savior, and gives himself wholly from his whole heart.

[Col. 1294A] I give inexhaustible thanks to the mercy of almighty God, who deigned to inspire me to seek acquaintance with your holy excellence, and by his goodness brought it about that I found it. Truly, I both perceive and confess that through dwelling with you I have profited greatly, both from your examples and your teachings; and I confidently presume that after death I shall receive still more abundant profit from your prayers. And because, as “one generation passes and another comes” (Eccl. 1), so in your monastery brethren must often be replaced, both because of departure from life and because of the burden of the order and service, I suppose that there is no one among you who knows or remembers me. If you ask who I am who write to you, I am Brother N., etc. If you carefully inquire in the Rule into the character of the fellowship granted me by the aforesaid abbot and chapter, you will find it written there. For God’s sake, I beg you, acknowledge it for me while I live; and when my death, which I believe is near, has been announced to you, faithfully discharge it for me after death. May the Creator and Redeemer of all the faithful preserve your holiness forever from every evil, as it prays unceasingly for all the faithful and for me, the last among them; and may he by his merciful grace bring us together with them to the joys of eternal blessedness. Amen.

## LETTER VIII. TO RODULF, MONK OF VILLERS  
He gives the reason why he abandoned pastoral care.

[Col. 1294C]

To the servant of God RADULF, monk of Villers [Note: [Col. 1293D] The monastery of Villers, a notable house of the Cistercian order, lies [Col. 1294D] three or four hours’ journey from Gembloux; we published its history in vol. III of the *Anecdota*.], our brother always to be received in the embrace of love: F. G., a monk only in habit and name, wishes him to seize the citadel of the heavenly kingdom with the weapons of virtues.

Pressed by frequent letters both from you and from others, and reproached also by the words of certain persons coming from those regions to these parts on business, concerning my departure, I judge it shameful any longer to disregard either the dutiful remonstrance of friends or the insolent criticism of detractors. For I fear that, unless I respond, I shall both expose myself to infamy and give my detractors an occasion to sin while they speak evil freely. Yet, if it had been possible, I would rather have imitated Bishop Martin in these matters than blessed Jerome the priest. We know that the former assumed such patience toward every injury that, though he was a high priest, he could be harmed with impunity even by the lowest clerics. Of the latter, we read that he was carried against his critics by so great an onrush of words that, as though the rein of patience had broken, he seems to be driven headlong, directing powerful and sharp arrows with desolating coals against deceitful tongues (Ps. 109), and destroying by disputation every invention of heretical perversity.

But although I lie beyond all estimation beneath the feet of such great men, walking between them I shall, if I can, govern both my pen and my mind so that I may neither lose inwardly the tranquility of patience [Col. 1295A] nor outwardly rush, by accusing anyone by name in intolerable words, to the destruction of fraternal peace and charity. Let my talkative friends know that I have hitherto kept silent not as though guilty or checked by conscience, but because I wished wholly to extinguish by my silence every fuel of discord, which contention increases rather than quells. Since, as I judge, this cannot be done, I think it right, if I am able, briefly both to show my innocence and to stop the mouth of iniquity, lest it open wider against me (Ps. 106).

For I know, as I have experienced, that while I was still among you many spoke against me with a deceitful tongue (Ps. 108): openly as though favoring me, but secretly in truth detracting from me, like scorpions. Hence the Lord says to Ezekiel: “Son of man, subversions are with you and you dwell with scorpions” (Ezek. 2). For how do flatterers overthrow and deceive their hearers? By taking away from them their own judgment and self-understanding, lest they assess themselves by what they are, but rather by the qualities falsely proclaimed of them by such flatterers. Such people are altogether worse than those who curse to one’s face and assail their enemies with open insults. Why is this so? Because the latter sometimes occurs through impetuosity; the former never except through deliberation. By the attack of abuse, the hearer is often confounded and corrected; but by the birdlime of flattery he is held fast in his error. Against such persons the Psalmist says: “Lord, deliver my soul from wicked lips and from a deceitful tongue” (Ps. 119).

[Col. 1295C] But what shall I say of those who, drenched either in the poison of envy or kindled by the torches of anger, restrained by no shame, rush into open blasphemies, “surrounded me with words of hatred” (Ps. 108), and wounded me with the spears of their words, not sparing even to spit in my face? What, I say, shall I say of these, or what shall I judge them like, except irrational beasts or most savage wild animals? David also laments concerning them in the Psalm: “Many dogs surrounded me” (Ps. 21), and elsewhere, “They opened their mouth against me,” etc. (ibid.). Why, then, did I endure the mockeries, assaults, attacks, and reproaches of such persons? Certainly for no other reason than because I turned away from their paths; because at their revelries and drinking-parties I avoided their companionship; [Col. 1295D] because I would neither cast lots with them nor share their purse. Because I reproved in them transgression of the order and of God’s commandments; because I strove not only to restrain carnal impulses in myself, but also to call them back from the crookedness of depravity to the straightness of equity and justice. And what did they do in return? Surely they “set evil against me for good and attacked me without cause” (Ps. 119).

What was I, a frail little man surrounded by such great evils, to do? Set among them, what could I do but turn to divine protection? I found in my own case that the teeth of these beasts were nothing less than weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword (Ps. 56). I cried out with the Prophet: “Deliver from the sword,” etc. (Ps. [Col. 1296A] 21). This was for myself; but for them, what did I do? Following the example of the protomartyr, I said: “Lord, do not lay this sin to their charge” (Acts 7). And behold, I give thanks to God because through the power of prayer and patience some of them were converted to the good of peace; and, without my seeking or demanding it, but with God taking vengeance, this offense was punished in some of those who persisted in evil.

But what good does this do? Sons, both good and bad, are always born in place of fathers; and alas, a greater number of the wicked rises up than of the devout. Like a water-vessel, when one shoot is cut off, it sends forth a more numerous sprouting of useless growth. Therefore, because the perverse are hard to correct and multiply beyond number, and no one can correct what God has rejected, I leave these men—subverters of the holy order, transgressors of the divine law, and lovers of their pleasures rather than of God (2 Tim. 3)—to his judgment, for I am unequal to correcting them. When I was present, because I dared to rebuke them for these matters, they poured out foul calumnies and gnashed their teeth at me; and even now, though I am absent, they pursue me with wicked reproaches. Leaving them, I judge it right—indeed necessary—to disclose the truth of my departure for the satisfaction of those who do not know my case and therefore err, not through malice but ignorance, lest they be further scandalized concerning me and I furnish them an occasion for sin.

For I did not abandon my place through caprice or instability. Away with envy and devouring jealousy; away with zeal and rivalry “hard as hell” (Song 8)! Let them gnaw and ulcerate themselves—or rather those whom they assail and hold captive. But for me “it is good to cling to God and to place my hope in the Lord” (Ps. 72). Under his protection some enemies are in my hands; by his aid I pursue the rest and shall overtake them, “and shall not turn back until they fail” (Ps. 17), according to that saying of the Apostle Paul: “The Lord will crush Satan under your feet speedily” (Rom. 16). Know that I consider it truly good for me to cleave to him, and most healthful for me to place my hope in him. Farewell.

## LETTER IX. TO JONAH, PRIEST OF SAINT MARTIN’S AT PÉTRÉ-LE-VAU  
That, in accordance with the interpretation of his name, he should express dove-like simplicity in his actions.

[Col. 1296D]

To JONAH, priest of the church of blessed Martin at Pétré-le-Vau, a friend dear to my heart and always to be honored by me with sincere affection: G., his own, wishes him to despise the passing world and ardently seek the enduring joy of the heavenly kingdom.

I exhort and admonish you, dearest brother, carefully to consider the interpretation of your name and to rejoice in being called Jonah, that is, “dove,” not to your shame but to your praise and honor. You will fittingly fulfill this if, emulating dove-like simplicity, you maintain an upright and innocent conduct before God and people, and are found free from the gall of bitterness [Col. 1297A] and the rancor of envy. But what are you doing amid the rivers of Babylon, in the midst of a city full of iniquity and strife, destined on account of its sins to be overthrown in a moment? Open your eyes and see: day and night iniquity surrounds it upon its walls, etc. Why do you not take up wings like a dove and flee, etc., lest you too perish with it? Why do you take upon yourself what belongs to another, at your own peril, when you are unequal to bearing your own sins? Do you not know that an account will be required not only of your own affairs but also of that entrusted to you? Why, like a hireling, do you count the possessions of your wage and number the days of your servitude in another’s house, when you could freely order your own house as its master, eating not another’s bread but your own?

I beg you, unburden yourself of all these loads, and imitate your patron, whose praises you pursue day and night: he followed Christ even against his parents’ wishes and attained apostolic glory throughout the Christian world. And because it is written, “Let him who hears say, ‘Come’” (Rev. 22), receive this counsel for salvation and strive both to bring others with you to God and, especially at a fitting time, those who can yield God abundant fruit in the gain of souls. Greet our common friend, admonishing him both to preserve the faith he owes to his beloved and to keep the deposit intact.

## LETTER X. TO A CERTAIN BROTHER  
He rejoices at his conversion, though he is somewhat apprehensive concerning it; he exhorts him to fulfill his vows and transfer himself to a cloister governed by the Rule.

[Col. 1297C]

To his dearest brother: G., his beloved, wishes him steadfastness in pursuing his purpose and confidence concerning the reward of his labor.

Having read your brief letter, I rejoiced exceedingly, learning from its report that the work of life had already been accomplished in you which I had never hoped for from you. For who, knowing your former manner of life—or rather, I should say, your dissipation—would readily have believed that your frivolity would be gathered into the maturity or moderation of that sacred religious life which you used to mock, and that your proud and stiff neck would at last be placed beneath Christ’s humble yoke? Yet this is the gracious and customary work of our kind [Col. 1297D] Savior: unexpectedly calling and changing those whom He foreknew and predestined to be made conformable to the image of His Son (Rom. VIII), He teaches them to despise earthly things and love heavenly ones, and brings lawless persons into conformity with the rule of the law of life and discipline.

But, to disclose to you my own thought concerning this very conversion of yours, and to strengthen you thereby: I rejoice indeed most heartily at its beginning, yet not without anxiety, since its end is uncertain; and this especially because it seems sudden and forced—not the fervor of the spirit or a deliberate resolve of mind summoning you to this course, but the extreme danger of death urgently pressing you. And although I am certain that the merciful Lord is able both to complete and to establish what He has begun in you (I Pet. V), this too increases my inward fear: that [Col. 1298A] you have gone to a place exposed to very many dangers, where not only may the feet of the inexperienced and newly planted be moved and their steps slip, but even the standing of the strong may be shaken unless they attend to themselves with the greatest circumspection. I do not say this to advise you either to leave the place or to change your purpose—far be it!—but to make known my concern for you, born of brotherly love, and to make you more watchful against the snares of the crafty tempter. Since, if you wish to live not lukewarmly but under discipline, you will read of these dangers more fully than is expedient in the book of experience while I am absent, I refrain from writing of them.

For the rest, I exhort and [Col. 1298B] entreat my lords and brethren, who have received you into their fellowship as one called or compelled by God, to teach you to render to the Lord the vows uttered by your lips (Ps. LXV), to kindle you by holy words and examples, and to assist you by their prayers. But you, whom I embrace with all my strength and with all my heart, I beg—and desire that my plea may be granted—that, since now is the time when very many do not endure sound doctrine but turn aside to fables, etc. (II Tim. IV), you may be vigilant against the unjust tales of flatterers and detractors. And, according to the Apostle: “Whatever things are true, whatever things are just, whatever things are holy, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report, if there be any virtue, if there be any praise of discipline, think always on these things” (Phil. IV); and the God of peace will be with you and will render you the reward of your labors. Nor need you complain of the rarity or scarcity of persons whom you may rightly follow; for [Col. 1298C] although the poverty of good people precedes the coming of Antichrist, and the wicked multiply beyond number, nevertheless, by God’s favor, even among the trees of the woods an apple-tree is found, and among thorns a lily (Cant. II); and, to speak more plainly, there is scarcely anyone so perverse that you will not find something in him worthy of imitation.

Therefore, since you have been called to a most valiant kind of warfare, but stand in a place poorly fortified against enemies, your inward diligence must provide what outward protection does not afford you. As a wise man, use the evil of the time for the exercise of virtue; and let your zeal be clothed in a double armor for vengeance upon the enemies. For since those who live according to the flesh shall die (Rom. VIII), fight bravely [Col. 1298D] against flesh and blood, not only by abstaining from fleshly desires which wage war against the soul (I Pet. II), but also by fleeing the company of fleshly people. And, in the Apostle’s words: “Take up the armor of God, that you may be able to withstand in the evil day and stand perfect in all things,” and what follows (Eph. VI). Stand, therefore, with your loins girded in truth, clothed with the breastplate of righteousness, etc. (ibid.).

Yet, if I were able to advise and you to act accordingly, I would think that nothing better could be advised for you than to enter some cloister where religious discipline flourishes—not to remain there permanently, but to learn the monastic order. Thus, when well instructed and armed, you returned from an ordered battle-line to your own people, you would thereafter both fight securely against spiritual wickedness and know how, and be able, [Col. 1299A] to summon others to the fight. But know this: according to the Lord’s words in the Apocalypse, it would be more pardonable to remain cold in the world than to sit lukewarm and slack in a cloister (Apoc. III). For, stirred by fear and repentance, you could more readily be converted from the great coldness of sins to the paths of innocence than be warmed again from the lukewarmness of security to the fervor of pursuing righteousness.

## LETTER XI. THE BRETHREN OF GEMBLOUX TO THEIR GUIBERT. They grieve at his absence.

To their most beloved brother and lord GUIBERT, the brethren of Gembloux and all their friends together, both outwardly and inwardly: whatever may be wished more joyfully, whatever may be enjoyed more happily.

[Col. 1299B] As greatly, O most longed-for of friends, as your presence was formerly pleasing, useful, and welcome to us, so greatly—and far more—does your absence, sweet and dear to you in the meantime but become to us beyond measure hateful and bitter, make us sorrowful day by day. For after your departure from us had taken place, many mouths were opened to reproach us with disparagement, namely, because those who were jealous of your good manner of life had known the reason for your departure. Therefore your loving mother requires of you steadfastness in perseverance, etc.

## LETTER XII. TO THE BRETHREN OF GEMBLOUX. He excuses himself from resuming the abbatial dignity of the monastery of Gembloux.

[Col. 1299C] To the lords, sons, and brethren of his venerable mother, the Church of Gembloux, GUIBERT, their least one: to remember mercy in wrath.

I rejoice and give thanks that you deign to remember me; because you attempt to recall me, I redouble my thanks, but I do not rejoice for that reason. I would rejoice more if you permitted me to live with you in peace, as useful and welcome as I was ever able to be, in those things in which God by His grace makes me welcome and useful. But since some among you urge the abbot to summon me back, I would rather that they urged him to give relief and to restore the walls and morals of the house that have fallen, and that they pressed him to place in religious houses those whom, I know well, have as yet little sense of order among you, [Col. 1299D] arranging them accordingly.

Indeed, if through me any good could be done or restored among you, I would rejoice and return; and I would rather be humbled, rejected, and afflicted with you than divide spoils among the proud (Prov. XVI). But since among you, where there are many wise persons, I am not worthy to possess this grace and authority, or wisdom, I beg you to allow those fools who exult over me and boast that they profit through me to regard me as a fool without calumny. Why are letters multiplied to recall me?
