As soon as I hear of a change or correction in the house, setting aside every excuse and every delay, I will gladly return and willingly undertake whatever labor you command for its restoration. For what could my insignificance accomplish there now? Once I tried to help, [Col. 1300A] and suffered what my spirit shrank from undertaking, and achieved nothing. Therefore I am now greatly afraid to return, lest perhaps, after the tranquility of peace which I have enjoyed for nearly three years, I fall back into a pit of my miseries [reading uncertain], and my return prove burdensome to me and onerous to you. May the God of peace and love be with you all (II Cor. XIII), that you may all think the same thing, and unanimously glorify God, through our Lord Jesus Christ (I Pet. IV). Amen.

## LETTER XIII. TO THE VIRGIN GERTRUDE. On the plundering of his monastery by the Count of Namur.

To GERTRUDE, bride of Christ and virgin, G., servant of God [Col. 1300B] and of her: himself, not as a secular man gives himself to secular persons, but in the Holy Spirit.

I received in charity, not in pleasure, the letters of your mistress and your own, together with the small gift you sent. For what pleasure can there be where bitterness wholly occupies the heart? O dearest sister, the affliction of remembrance which lately surrounded me, and the sight of the destruction of our church, in which I was almost endangered unto death, have stunned all my bodily senses and swallowed up all the strength of my soul. I will relate this briefly, if grief allows me strength to relate it.

Our town is known to lie on the border of the duchy of Louvain and the county of Namur. A quarrel having lately arisen between the duke and the count, the count unexpectedly surrounded it with [Col. 1300C] his army. Setting fire to the lesser structures—that is, those outside, adjoining the rampart and wall—he utterly burned and plundered them. Since nothing of the kind had been feared, and since very violent winds carried the fire onward, blazing sparks were scattered throughout the whole interior of the town. Thus both town and monastery were consumed together in an exceedingly fierce blaze, so completely that in the town no house remained except two very humble ones newly covered with earth, and in the cloister not a single building remained unburned.

During that conflagration, while I was singing the morning Mass at the lesser altar, unwilling to leave anything unfinished, I withdrew to safety rather later than I ought. Having removed my sacred vestments, I could not escape outdoors because the fires were already ravaging everything widely [Col. 1300D] around. I entered the nearest open sacristy and found there four of my brethren grieving and anxious. In that place, while flames surrounded us on every side beyond hope, we were so scorched and suffocated by smoke and heat that two of them were grievously injured, while I and the other two, certainly breathless through distress and like dead men, lay there until evening. Yet I survived by God’s help; the two companions of my martyrdom died a few days later.

But, as it is written in the prophets, “that report might come upon report, destruction upon destruction, and terror upon terror” (Jer. IV), on the ninth day after the burning the aforesaid Count of Namur summoned his nephew by his sister, the Count of Hainaut, [Col. 1301A] and again surrounded the town with a great multitude. Having demolished the walls in certain places, both armies entered; moving freely everywhere—for they had found everyone unprepared and fearing none of this—they plundered everything that had survived the fire. In this plundering nothing was left either to us, to the townspeople, or to the people of the countryside who had brought their possessions there. Livestock and domestic fowl were either burned to ashes or carried off by the enemy. No reverence was shown to sacred things or altars. Indeed, before the principal altar in the middle of the presbytery, and throughout the spaces of both churches, our men and the enemy engaged in fighting on foot and horseback; many were killed, and the monks and priests themselves were beaten and stripped. Not one of the brethren escaped wholly unharmed. One, pierced through the side by a deadly weapon, died; another was carried away naked, as nature had brought him from his mother’s womb into the light.

After they had stripped the abbot himself of his remaining clothing and even [Col. 1301B] his shoes, he scarcely escaped from a man known to him and fled naked and alone through the darkness of the dreadful night. And rightly enough, indeed: since while his spiritual father and lord was still alive, he had by intrigue and simony deprived him of his own office, he should learn by such dishonor what he must await at his end. For such an entrance—indeed, not an entrance, since it was not through the door, but an invasion and a headlong climbing in by another way—will nowhere be concluded with a blessed end.

[Col. 1301C] But, to return to my subject, in the aforesaid plundering no reverence at all was shown even to the female sex; women themselves were left naked, and no mercy whatever was shown to those in distress. Mothers were stripped of their clothing, and children were torn from their mothers’ breasts; contrary to the laws of nature, they were carried into captivity with a great part of the townspeople. In the greater church, being profaned by murders, neither reading nor singing takes place; but in a certain crypt we perform the divine office as best we can. Hence come groans, sighs, and sobs, because the crown has fallen from our head; and our riches—not only outward riches, but also, what cannot be related without great contrition of heart, [Col. 1301D] inward riches—have passed to strangers, while we sit amid the confusion of a common life, without the adornment of God’s service and without the safeguards of order and religious life.

Forgive me, I beseech you, dearest sister, for pouring such things out to you and urging you to grief with me. For a sad heart can never utter cheerful things; a bitter mouth cannot spit out honey; and, by some instinct of nature, even to speak with a friend concerning one’s own miseries seems to be a kind of remedy. Since, then, our house has been destroyed and in my lifetime there is no hope at all that religious life may be restored in it, I must change my place. I have decided to return to the cloister of Marmoutier, from which I returned nearly five years ago, because it has pleased my soul.

## LETTER XIV. JOHN WILLIAM TO GUIBERT, ABBOT OF GEMBLOUX. He declares that he deservedly suffers much from an unjust abbot, since he himself had been the author of evil for others.

[Col. 1302A]

To his most desired lord and venerable brother G., JOHN, called William’s, greeting and every good thing.

Because it is written, “Blessed is he who speaks wisely in the ears [of the wise],” therefore, my lord, I direct my speech to you as to a resting-place for the wretched. Yet if unrestrained talkativeness exceeds due measure in speaking, necessity itself, full of grief, will have grounds for a just excuse. I, however, though once abusive, now, with the situation reversed, would—if it were [Col. 1302B] possible—faithfully and sincerely serve you. With great contrition of heart I make known to your love the calamity and misery which, deserved by my sins, I have long endured. For the man of perdition, daily renewing his cruelty beyond measure, intensifies against me the manifold and intolerable madness of his wicked rage and persecution. Since he never ceases, wearied by nothing, to kindle against me into renewed flames the ashes of anger or hatred, even when they have slept for a little while, I would, if possible, make known to the hearts and ears of all discerning religious persons the cause of so harmful a quarrel. For it is usually no small consolation to one suffering injury if he entrusts the cause of his innocence for discernment—or rather settlement—to the judgment of good people. [Col. 1302C]

But if I, long ago repentant of my deed, wished from the secrecy of an audacious conscience to invent grounds of false innocence, I would not say with the Prophet, “Judge me, O Lord, according to my righteousness,” etc. (Ps. XXXIV). Surely my own mouth would condemn me. Nor is it surprising if I, who by my own evil devised every snare and trap to entangle and ensnare innocent persons, have been wrapped in the same nets of confusion. Indeed, as I did, so have I received. If I opened for others a snare of ruin, I myself prepared for myself a fall into destruction. Knowing and seeing this, I cast fire into straw; nor did I consider that the fire once kindled scattered sparks of mighty heat in others, but, turning the reins of its devastation back upon me as the instigator of all the evil, burned more savagely and with cruel voracity. Behold: the very affliction of long calamity gives understanding, although late, of how execrable and hateful to God was the execution of our evil scheme. [Col. 1302D]

Indeed, we were many in number who were authors and accomplices of this deed. Some we corrupted by pleasant flatteries and other empty favors; more by an oath that we would raise them to various high offices or administrations; others by lavish gifts. But what happened? Having obtained the seat of simoniacal eminence, he put aside the counsel of nearly all those who had supported him, whether they wished it or not. He began to appear great and wise in his own eyes, and to please himself by doing whatever evils he could, and threatening what he could not do. Though formerly, as you know, he had been considered of no importance—for he was endowed with neither inward nor [Col. 1303A] outward learning—he now presumed beyond his powers in both; empty of every good but swollen with the mere arrogance of pride, he began to exercise an intolerable tyranny of power. Thus, not to mention the peasants for the moment, he bound certain monks and knights in iron chains, as you yourselves saw when you were still with us, and thrust them into prison.

To continue the rest: only the powerful men, namely those whose authority had brought this about, were, by agreement, richly enriched from the property of the church. The rest—that is, the middling and the lowly—were deservedly disappointed in their vain hopes. But for me, a sufficient reward for my labor was to see my friend and lord, as I thought him, attain the object of his desire. Yet the fitting recompense for my labors came not long afterward, and otherwise than I had supposed. For, as a gift from the one from whom I expected good things, he prepared for me, insofar as he could, a contrary gift, unlike favors: a gallows and a noose.

If, as the common saying goes, “There ought to be moderation even in beating dogs,” how much more in exasperating and torturing human beings? He, an adherent of the simoniacal heresy, an invader and betrayer of his father’s office, appears, in relation to me, more wicked than that Haman in the Old Law (Esther V), and more cruel than Dacian and Nero, those inventors of every evil through their disorderly conduct. Truly, I am ashamed, yet I must confess that I was in every respect privy to his detestable bargain. Already the mouths of many, and even the very stones, cry out that his promotion was wrought by the devil for evil; so much so that it has become a proverb that, in place of a ruler, there has been set up “an idol of jealousy to provoke emulation.” [Col. 1303C]

The evil danger of this falls upon us chiefly, since we, knowing authors of this pestilential contrivance, gave this clear proof of our faithlessness: rejecting a man of good simplicity, we created for ourselves at our pleasure a ridiculous abbot, who had no learning at all and more than enough wickedness. Hence it is that, as though insane and without brains, he often publicly professes that he would rather encounter the devil than me. So much is this the case that, when recently I, as priest of the week, visited his house according to custom with holy water and the sign of the Lord’s Passion, [Col. 1303D] he fled in terror and paid no honor whatever to the divine sacraments.

But why say more? Many abbots and monks, knights and clerics, and Lord Archdeacon Amalric himself, have labored very often to put an end to this hatred; but they have been unable to accomplish anything worthy of concord. Since there is now within me despair of these great evils, which will never end, removal to another place for the sake of peace pleases me. Therefore I beg you to procure for me, now wandering and a fugitive, a place of certain refuge among you, that you may be a harbor of desired rest to me, and that on this account you may have before God a place of eternal [Col. 1304A] reward. Farewell, and write back through the bearer of this letter whatever seems good to you.

## LETTER XV. TO A CERTAIN NUN. He excuses himself for not visiting them more frequently, because his profession does not permit it.

To his beloved sister in Christ, handmaid and bride of that same Christ, Brother G. sends greeting, prayers, service, and himself in the Lord.

Whenever I recall in my mind the kindness and benefits you have bestowed upon me, I grieve that I lack you, do not see you, and do not enjoy your goodwill and religious services. So much so that, if opportunity were granted and the obligation of my profession allowed it, I would often visit your place out of regard for you and your other companions, who, when I was present, honored me with such devotion. But since this is neither permitted nor fitting, and perhaps not expedient, I do what is permitted, fitting, and expedient: with whatever affection of piety I can, I embrace you and commend you to God in my prayers. For I say at once and altogether that the little which I am, and whatever I do in Christ’s service, is as much yours as mine. I send you no small gifts, because I have none. For you know that I have never taken care to gather possessions of this kind, since this is not at all the way of monks. Yet I still have the small gifts which I brought away with me when I left you, and I cherish them above gold and topaz. Farewell in Christ, and pray for me.

## LETTER XVI. TO THE ABBOT OF ST. EUCHARIUS. He asks him, after his death, for participation in prayers.

[Col. 1304C]

To his most beloved lord and father, G., by God’s grace abbot of St. Eucharius—[Note: [Col. 1303] St. Eucharius: the celebrated monastery in the suburb of the city of Trier, commonly known by the name of St. Matthias.]—whatever a faithful friend can wish for a friend that is sweeter and more salutary.

Since I consider it useless to occupy your ears, already occupied with hearing many words that are as if flattering or superfluous, our beloved W., custodian of our church and bearer of this letter, will tell you, should you wish to know, what is being done or has been done concerning me. Through him you too may communicate to us what concerns you. But there is one thing which, because I cannot speak face to face, I earnestly ask by letter: that you may deign to remember me in your holy prayers [Col. 1304D] and mercifully renew for me both the communion in the benefits performed among you and the fellowship which your predecessor as abbot kindly granted me. Thus, if perhaps you hear of my end, since I am now placed in my last age, you may do for me what you would do for a brother.

I ask still more earnestly that what you would wish to be justly bestowed upon yourselves, if you had the matter in your own power, you may bestow upon the abbot of Florennes, in that which is within your power—which, thanks be to God, is considerable—namely, that in the court of the archbishop and of your brother the archdeacon, you may defend the just rights of the Church, [Col. 1305A] and not permit the assaults of its persecutors to prevail. But may almighty God, venerable Father, preserve you long in soundness of soul and body, always fearing and guarding against the strict examination of judgment in which you will stand to render an account for yourself and for those entrusted to your care: to His own honor, to the benefit of yourself and of the Churches you govern, and as an example to good persons who may wish to imitate you. Amen.

## LETTER XVII. G., ABBOT OF ST. EUCHARIUS, TO GUIBERT, ABBOT OF GEMBLOUX. He promises him the suffrages due to one of his own brethren.

To the most reverend friend in Christ, the venerable man GUIBERT, G.—[Note: [Col. 1305D] Godfrey, who is said to have governed the monastery of St. Matthias from 1181 to 1210.]—called by God’s grace abbot of St. Eucharius, [Col. 1305B] greeting in Him who is the salvation of all who wait for Him in truth.

We wish your brotherhood to know and firmly hold that we have always had a most ready and earnest will for your service and honor. Although your bodily presence is absent from our eyes, the memory of your love nevertheless always clings to the eye of the heart. Therefore we renew for you the association and brotherhood which you received in our Church in the time of our predecessor, Abbot L. of blessed memory—[Note: [Col. 1306D] Louis, who administered the same monastery under Hillin, Archbishop of Trier.]—and we grant you full participation in all good things done among us, as to one of our brethren. Farewell.

## LETTER XVIII. MASTER JOSEPH TO GUTBERT, ABBOT OF FLORENNES. He excuses himself for not coming to him; he is distressed that Guibert called him “master”; he exhorts him to make the monastery of Florennes, to which he had been elected, flourish.

[Col. 1305C]

To his father and lord, beloved to him above all others with singular affection, G., by God’s grace abbot of Florennes: JOSEPH, whatever he is, and, if he has any power, wholly yours, greeting which he desires for himself in the true Savior.

I give thanks to God, dispenser of all things, because in His gracious providence He has provided this consolation among men: that absent persons may declare through the exchange of letters what they cannot declare by living speech. Delighted by this benefit, I apply myself diligently to my pen, that the letter of my devotion may go where, absent in body, I am always present in heart. [Col. 1305D] Certainly, impelled by the highest desire, I would have hastened in every way to the sincerity of your love; but detained and hindered by domestic affairs, I cannot do what I desire. I shall come when opportunity permits—or rather, when it pleases the command of your sincerity.

I received your letter with the joy I owed and could offer. In it, what I bear most painfully is that you call me “master” and “lord”; you speak wrongly, for I do not deserve to be called even the servant, much less the disciple, of your holiness. Besides, since there is one Master and Lord of all, Jesus Christ (Matt. XXIII), you, who have borne His yoke from your youth (Lam. III), should endeavor by the holy and effectual persistence of your prayers to gain me for the Lord, so that we may be fellow servants, serving Him for whom to serve is to reign. I call God to witness that, trusting in the holiness of your prayers, I have conceived no small hope for my salvation. [Col. 1306A]

I thirst to hear something certain concerning your condition. Yet I have heard from some that the brethren of the monastery of Florennes, by a devout and unanimous election, have resolved to have you as abbot. Therefore, considering not honor but burden, not the softness of riches but the weight of office, provide for the Church of Florennes in such a way that, if it flourished under other shepherds, it may rejoice that under the care of your governance it has found not only a flower but also abundant fruit. I delay with my oars, as is customary, etc.

## LETTER XIX. BY THE SAME AUTHOR TO THE SAME RECIPIENT. He asks for his continual prayers to God for himself.

To his dearest lord, greatly beloved in Christ, GUIBERT, JOSEPH, his with all the devotion he can offer, sends sincere affection together with the greeting of one who offers greeting.

May your holiness know that I am always and everywhere continually stirred by longing for you and for your presence. Since distance of place grudges me this, I have done what I could, [Col. 1306C] pursuing by writing your presence which I cannot attain in body. My spirit does not merely lodge with you, but dwells with you; it can no longer return to us in exchange, because it never departs. Perhaps you do not return the favor, though a greater necessity presses upon me that you should keep continual remembrance of me, especially there where the Son is offered to the Father.

Indeed, since from the great confidence of sincere love I speak with you as with myself, I am not ashamed to uncover my wounds, especially to a friend and physician. I am distracted, wandering and defiled by thoughts; I too eagerly embrace wanton speech; I perform deeds displeasing to God; I continually incline toward worse things, so that death now strikes me everywhere: death in the house, death outside the house, death in the tomb. Alas for me! [Col. 1306D] What shall I do? What defenses shall I seek? What counsels shall I use? Thus I ask from your holiness a singular protection: that you may be willing to implore God for me, you who have power to obtain what you ask. For I know that the continual prayer of a righteous person avails much (James V). See, then, that the prayer which I ask to be poured out for me is continual. Either you have the reputation of righteousness and not its reality, or I shall perceive that the prayers of your holiness benefit me. Therefore you, in whose holiness I place great confidence, attend to my petitions with all care and diligence, because it will doubtless be gain to you to gain your neighbor.

## LETTER XX. MASTER JOSEPH TO GUIBERT, ABBOT OF FLORENNES. About to depart for Jerusalem with the Archbishop of Canterbury, he commends himself to Guibert’s prayers.

[Col. 1307A]

To his reverend lord and friend, singularly beloved to him in Christ, G., by God’s providence abbot of Florennes: JOSEPH, always yours, yours everywhere, wholly yours, greeting and his whole self altogether.

I speak to your holiness with wallet and staff, about to set out for Jerusalem with my lord, the Archbishop of Canterbury, God’s grace calling me and—would that it may accompany me! But you, whom I sincerely and singularly love in the Lord, let your love travel as a pilgrim with me while I depart, so that [Col. 1307B] we who are separated in body may be joined together. The chief point of my petition is that you may surely pursue me as your own by the holy persistence of your prayers, and pray to God, the commander and guide of our journey, for me more assiduously than frequently. For I know that the continual prayer of a righteous person avails much (James V).

Would that I might see you once, my lord, my most beloved one, before I die. But since I do not know whether I shall see you again in the body, I ask that when you find any of my writings among yours, the memory of your Joseph may in some measure be renewed in you. For if, according to that poetic saying,

> Love grows drowsy if it is not fed by the sight of a friend,  
> [Col. 1307C] and does not often enjoy conversation with him,

what will become of the remembrance of you, my lord, when, after I have departed to such a distant region, no hope remains thereafter of mutual sight or conversation? Because of this fear, according to the words of blessed Peter, I think it right, while I remain in this tabernacle—not knowing whether the laying aside of this tabernacle, that is, of my body, will be swift or delayed—to stir you up by reminding you of what is of great utility and benefit to us both.

Yet I ask that you not receive me as foolish, as though I wished to teach you, whom, as I hope, the teaching anointing of God instructs (I John II) concerning all necessary things to the extent it judges expedient. But bear [Col. 1307D] with this foolishness of mine: I presume at least to remind one sufficiently watchful, for the love of Christ compels me to this (II Cor. V). Therefore, love obtaining pardon and giving confidence, I act as a friend ought; indeed, concerned for one who is concerned, I exhort and beg you to conduct yourself in all things reverently and diligently, circumspectly and carefully, according to matter, place, time, and persons, since the salvation of so many rests in your hand. For you will render an account to God, the strict Judge, not only for yourself but also for those whose care you have undertaken. Among these things, keep no slight remembrance of me as well, whether I still remain in the body or after my death.

I beseech you now to receive what, I think, is the final farewell of your beloved Joseph, which I cannot utter without tears; and from my [Col. 1308A] small gifts, so long as it pleases you to retain them, recall by faithful observance the steadfastness of my devotion toward you.

## LETTER XXI. GUIBERT TO JOSEPH THE SCHOOLMASTER. On their mutual friendship.

G., by God’s permission—and would that it were by His will—abbot of Gembloux, to JOSEPH, schoolmaster of outstanding virtue, whom he embraces with singular affection now because of his merits: whatever a father wishes to a son.

Long ago, dearest friend, when I knew you to be living in the town of Geldern, I considered the dignity and beauty of your countenance, the grace of your mouth, the elegance of your speech, the cheerfulness of your brow, the restraint of your eyes, and [Col. 1308B] the moderation of the movements of your whole body. I was delighted and amazed beyond belief to find in a young man such a model of integrity; receiving you with all the affections of love, my spirit found rest in you. The practice and boldness of familiarity thereafter increased our acquaintance; and the better known you became, the dearer and sweeter you began to be to me. I experienced in you what blessed Gregory says: that a friend is called, as it were, the guardian of the soul, because love itself is knowledge.

I saw, considered, and loved the face of your inward person, radiant with the great beauty of virtues; and my soul clung after you (Ps. LXII), melted by the fire of love and, so to speak, ran into yours. By some hidden instinct of nature, it sometimes happens that many persons, merely through mutual [Col. 1308C] sight or conversation, are bound together in the bonds of indissoluble friendship, drawn and affected by the abundance of inward beauty, by which even the outward person is sometimes formed according to the inward one, as it is written: “The wisdom of a person shines in his face” (Prov. XVII).

Thus you, sweetest brother, as you observe and imitate disciplined behavior in religious men and those who conduct themselves devoutly, show yourself wonderful and worthy of imitation. Turning the eyes of those who look upon you, you make them fly toward you; you render your voice pleasing to those to whom you deign to speak, your conversation sweet, and your face—adorned with the marks of many virtues—desirable. Drawn by these incentives, I desire [Col. 1308D] and am moved to see you, embrace you, and speak with you; but I neither obtain nor attain what I desire. Uncertain and divided, placed between faith and affection, hope and fear, I do not know what to choose or determine. Faith, which according to Chrysostom preserves friendships and joins holy fellowships, makes me certain of the indissoluble brotherhood of your love. Affection, when it is denied the opportunity of enjoying you, grieves that it is deferred from the grace of dwelling with you and, what it finds more grievous, fears that it will be perpetually deprived. It is distressed, sighs, and groans. But amid these things, sweetest brother, what will you do? Will you wholly disregard us? Will you despise us as we long for you, seek you, and sigh for you, etc.?

## LETTER XXII. TO PHILIP, ARCHBISHOP OF COLOGNE. He offers him a small work composed by himself.

[Col. 1309A]

To his lord and father, PHILIP, bishop of Cologne, distinguished by outstanding devotion of soul and praiseworthy excellence and uprightness of character, and exalted by Christ’s grace among the foremost members of Christ: Brother G., the humble servant of his holiness, wishes that nothing more wholesome may be desired for his head than to conform in all things through imitation of him and of the saints.

I have completed, as best I could with God’s help, the work dedicated to Your Reverence; and I rejoice and exult that I have not laboured in vain upon a work accepted not only by you but by all. Yet I humbly beseech your holiness, venerable Father, that you receive my little gift [Col. 1309B] with the affection in which it is offered by me, and do not refuse to commend it, according to the saying:

> When a poor friend gives you a small gift,  
> Receive it graciously, and remember plainly to praise it.

And what gift is more useful than that of good counsel? As it is written: “A good word is better than the best gift” (Prov. 15). Therefore I also exhort you at the end: gathering your mind from the scattering of souls, devote yourselves to that best part of Mary (Luke 10), and cleave to that one highest Good, so that you may deserve to be one of those of whom the Apostle says: “He who is joined to God is one spirit with him” (1 Cor. 6).

## LETTER XXIII. TO THE USURPER OF MAINZ

[Note: [Col. 1309] Christian of Buche, as we believe, chancellor of the Emperor Frederick, who, while Conrad, the legitimate pontiff, was still alive, occupied the see of Mainz.]

[Col. 1309C] To the imitator of the zeal of Him “whose winnowing-fan is in his hand, to cleanse his threshing-floor” (Matt. 3), and from whose mouth proceeds a two-edged sword (Rev. 19), for executing vengeance upon transgressors of the Law and contemners of grace; to the angel and officials of the Church of Mainz: recompense according to their deserts.

“If not to know how to pity,” etc., as in the first volume of the *Anecdota*, p. 323.

## LETTER XXIV. TO SIFRED, ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ

At his command he undertakes to write a certain small work.

To the father ever to be honoured with the purest affection of pious love [Col. 1309D], SIFRED, archbishop of the holy and illustrious city of Mainz: Brother GUIBERT, by his own reckoning the least of the servants of God, wishes him always in all things to cleave to the teachings and examples of Jesus Christ, the supreme and eternal Priest.

Since the exalted rank of your fatherhood has deigned to command my humility to write something for instruction or for the ordering of the mind, and since I shrink from being further pressed beneath the great weight of your command, choosing rather to be criticized by some for ignorance than reproved by you for disobedience, I have at last resolved, after a long time, to obey. Indeed much could be said [Col. 1310A]; but, as experience teaches, we sometimes find in reading what commonly happens at banquets: just as a multiplicity of dishes, producing satiety, is dangerous, so also the uninterrupted prolixity of reading is burdensome to readers. May the most good God preserve the crown of your head, most holy Father, sound for a long time, as a defence and an honour to his Church; and when the end of life, which cannot be escaped, [shall come], may he receive you, resting in a blessed end and full of good days and good works, into the fellowship of the holy bishops. Amen.

## LETTER XXV. TO THE SAME

He congratulates him because, having rejected the schismatics, he adheres to Pope Alexander, the legitimate pope.

[Col. 1310B] To the venerable Father to be received with every reverence, S., by God’s grace archbishop of the noble and illustrious city of Mainz: Brother GUIBERT, formerly the humble abbot of the monastery of Gembloux, now a simple monk in the course of this present life and amid the miseries of this age, wishes him so to run that he may deserve to receive in the homeland of future blessedness the prize—that is, the reward of worthy recompense—from God, the beholder of those who strive.

We see and rejoice that there has been fulfilled in you what the Lord says: “He who walks by day does not stumble” (John 11); and, “He who follows me does not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life” (John 8). Nor have you negligently heard the word of the Lord saying: “I am [Col. 1310C] the door: whoever does not enter through me, but climbs up by another way, is a thief and a robber” (John 10). You left darkness and passed into the light when, rejecting the most obstinate defenders of the wicked schism, you came over to the rightful side of Alexander, the Catholic pontiff; and, after the example of Moses looking to the Rewarder, you chose rather to be afflicted with the people of God than to abound in the pleasures of Egypt under Pharaoh (Heb. 11). Indeed, after the example of him who, according to the Apostle, “though he was rich, became poor for our sake” (2 Cor. 8), despairing in no respect over the loss of your bishopric, you preferred voluntary exile from your country, etc. May almighty God keep you and all who prepare themselves to perform good works by continual protection from every evil; free you from all obstacles by which they might be impeded from their holy purpose [Col. 1310D]; defend your departure from the body, sending to your aid an army of holy angels, from the assaults of malignant spirits; and bring your souls unharmed into that glorious and peaceful heavenly city, Jerusalem. Amen.

## LETTER XXVI. TO SIGIFRID, ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ, AND PHILIP, ARCHBISHOP OF SALZBURG

He exhorts them courageously to endure exile for God’s sake.

To the holy fathers, apostolic priests, and most beloved lords, SIGIFRID, by God’s grace archbishop of Mainz [Col. 1311A], and PHILIP, bishop of Salzburg: Brother G., the least of the servants of God, offers every service which one least person can render to the greatest, and the undivided and equal office of sincere affection toward both.

I rejoice, reverend rulers, and take very great pride that, as I believe through God’s ordering, the smallness of my insignificance has reached the knowledge of your high estate, confidently supposing that this itself will be for me an occasion of great advancement. For if you are what you ought to be—that is, fruitful olive trees, shining lampstands, stars or angels of the Churches, priests of God, shepherds of sheep, mediators between Christ and the peoples—why should I not hope from olive trees for the oil of consolation; from lamps for the brightness of counsel and the ardour of salutary example [Col. 1311B]; from stars, lest I stray as though in the night of this perilous life, for a showing of the way; from angels for the safeguard of defence against evil spirits; from priests or mediators for the offices of sanctification or reconciliation; and from shepherds for the care of spiritual oversight and the food of inward refreshment? Therefore I have said—and rightly said—that I rejoice not a little at obtaining your holy and pleasing friendship; for by your patronage I hope and expect to be helped in the many things which I have mentioned, indeed in more than I have mentioned. For who is so foolish that he would not rejoice greatly to acquire the acquaintance of such persons, through whose counsels and benefits he can, if he wishes, make no small progress in body and soul? Yet because one of you is greater in rank and more abundantly supplied with wealth and resources [Col. 1311C], let him not suppose me so inept that, on account of the unequal abundance of external things, I embrace him with an unequal affection of love, since I believe myself to be loved again with equal affection by each of you. Now then, reverend Fathers, since you prefer exile in order to preserve innocence, do not lose [Col. 1312A] your confidence, which will have, through God’s granting, a great reward. Stand manfully in faith, be strengthened in hope, be enlarged in charity—so greatly that you do not exclude even your persecutors from the embrace of your compassion and prayer. For if you are held fast to the supreme Trinity by the cord of these three virtues, be assured: you shall not fall. For just as there is no good which can fail those so firmly fixed, so there is no evil which can harm you.

But as blessed Peter says: “If you suffer anything for righteousness, you are altogether blessed” (1 Pet. 3). For according to the Lord’s sentence: “In your patience you shall possess your souls” (Luke 21); and according to Prudentius:

> A virtue is feeble which patience does not strengthen.

Therefore patience is very necessary for you, lest [Col. 1312B] your souls be endangered and the condition of your virtues weakened. Thus, judging that you are being instructed and advanced, not rejected, by the correction of the wisest Father and Provider, trust more in his mercy amid adversity than amid prosperity. For after the purgation which—not prosperity, which sometimes makes men negligent and destroys fools, but adversity, which trains the wise and adorns those proved with virtues—brings about, the Lord will by no means leave “the rod of sinners over the lot of the righteous” (Ps. 124). Rather, when his anger has flamed forth briefly in chastisement, blessed are all who are reproved and corrected, who shall trust in him for recompense (Ps. 2). May God, the protector of all who hope in him (Ps. 17), receive you, reverend Fathers, into the defence of his protection [Col. 1312C]; and, protected from every evil and made perfect in every good, may he transfer you from labour to rest, from mourning to joy, from death to everlasting life, and, filled with joy at his countenance (Acts 2), make you blessed without end in the land of the living. Amen.

[Col. 1311]

## A
Accidents of the Eucharist exist without a subject, 321. Whether an action is judged good or bad from its end or intention, 147. All human acts are judged evil according to their end and will, except those which cannot be performed without transgression, 148. Whether Adam could always have lived without eating of the tree of life, 121. Whether he was expelled from paradise lest he take from the tree of life and not die, 123. Adam is said to have been present at the court of the angels and to have prophesied concerning the Flood, etc., 127. Why his son Abel, and not Adam himself, is the head of the Church of the good, 299. In Adam pride was less than in Eve, 155. Adultery was formerly punished more severely at Rome than in Gaul, 193. What it means to build wood, hay, stubble, gold, silver, and precious stones, 186. The terms “equal,” “similar,” and “coeternal” do not merely exclude, but are also affirmatively said of God, 65. Why equality is said to be in the Son, 62. How “to be eternal” differs from “to be from eternity,” 119. Angels are said to have been created first, not with respect to time but to dignity, 107. What they were like when created, ibid. The angel was evil “from the beginning,” that is, immediately after the beginning, 108. See more there. How angels merited blessedness, 107. Whether they daily advance in merit and reward, 109. According to the author’s view, angels are still on the way, 111. All are sent without distinction, 115. The author holds that a good angel and another, evil angel are assigned to each human being, 116. The soul by itself is a person, 267. The apostles, confirmed in grace, could not take wives, 329. Whether water in the chalice is converted into blood, 320. It signifies faith, just as wine signifies hope and bread charity, ibid. What the golden crown and the aureole are, 227.

## STEPHEN, ABBOT OF SAINTE-GENEVIÈVE AT PARIS, LATER BISHOP OF TOURNAI

Historical notice, 295. Preface by R. P. du Molinet, 303. Notice by M. J. J. Brial, 305.

### THE LETTERS OF STEPHEN OF TOURNAI

#### PART ONE (1163–1177)

Letter I.—Lament of the Church of Orléans over the murder of John, dean, which he set forth at Sens in a council of bishops and clergy of the province, 309.  
Letter II.—To William, bishop-elect of Chartres.—He asks him to reconcile to him the favor of the king, who had taken adversely a letter written concerning the death of John, dean of Orléans, 311.

[Col. 1328]

Letter III.—From Pons, bishop of Clermont, to Maurice, bishop of Paris, and Stephen, abbot of Saint-Euverte.—He asks them whether the baptism of one of his diocesan flock had been valid, 312.  
Letter IV.—From Maurice, bishop of Paris, to Pons, bishop of Clermont.—He answers the questions and sets out his opinion concerning the validity of this baptism, 313.  
Letter V.—From Stephen to Pons, bishop of Clermont.—He states his own view concerning the same baptism, 314.  
Letter VI.—To Aldebert, bishop of Mende.—He clears himself concerning certain statements falsely reported to him, 317.  
Letter VII.—To Godfrey, abbot of Saint-Satyrus.—He asks him to retain with himself one of Stephen’s canons, 317.  
Letter VIII.—To the dean of Saint-Martin at Tours.—He seeks alms for the repair of the church of Saint-Euverte, 318.  
Letter IX.—He writes to his friend concerning the restoration of that church, 318.  
Letter X.—To the abbot of Cluny.—He urges him to remove the prior of the monastery of Pont-des-Moines, who was squandering the property of Stephen’s church, 319.  
Letter XI.—To William, archbishop of Sens.—He commends the church of Saint-Samson at Orléans, 320.  
Letter XII.—To Pope Alexander III.—He asks him to show favor to John, a cleric of Orléans, 321.  
Letter XIII.—To William, archbishop of Sens.—He asks on behalf of a clerical student that his property be preserved for him, 321.  
Letter XIV.—To Alberic, jurist of Bologna.—He petitions on behalf of Hugh, a cleric of Orléans, that Alberic may assist him, 322.  
Letter XV.—To William of Bologna.—He commends the same cleric of Orléans, 322.  
Letter XVI.—To a certain prior of Naples.—He commends one of his canons residing at Naples, 322.  
Letter XVII.—To Roger, abbot of Saint-Euverte.—He writes that he will return to the monastery, as the abbot had commanded, 323.  
Letter XVIII.—To William, archbishop of Sens.—He gives an account of a certain matter entrusted to him, 324.  
Letter XIX.—To the bishop of Le Puy.—He asks him to keep and fulfill his promise, 324.  
Letter XX.—To B., canon of Le Puy.—He asks him to show himself kindly disposed toward Stephen’s people, 325.  
Letter XXI.—To Hugh, abbot of Saint-Bartholomew at Noyon.—He asks him to receive a certain fugitive canon, 325.  
Letter XXII.—To Jothon, archbishop of Tours.—He seeks his favor on behalf of the bishop-elect of Comminges, 326.  
Letter XXIII.—To William, archbishop of Sens.—He asks him to protect the cantor and archdeacon, lest their enemy prevail against them, 326.  
Letter XXIV.—To the lord pope.—He addresses prayers to the supreme pontiff on behalf of the same cantor and archdeacon, 327.  
Letter XXV.—To John A. S., legate.—He congratulates him on his fortunate return, 328.  
Letter XXVI.—To the prior and brothers of the convent of La Charité.—He petitions for a certain fugitive monk who had been his teacher, 328.  
Letter XXVII.—To the subprior of La Charité.—He asks, concerning the same fugitive, that he be received again, 329.  
Letter XXVIII.—He solicits his friend’s favor on behalf of the same monk, 330.

#### PART TWO (1177–1192)

EPISTLE XXIX.—To the abbot of St Bartholomew.—He relates what is taking place among the canons of Naples. 331  
EPISTLE XXX.—He makes entreaties to him on behalf of a friend of his who needed his assistance. 332  
[Col. 1329] EPISTLE XXXI.—To the archbishop of Rheims, on behalf of the abbot of St Bartholomew of Noyon.—He asks him to show himself kindly disposed toward this abbot. 332  
EPISTLE XXXII.—To the king’s almoner.—He asks him to enable a Jew converted to the faith to benefit from the king’s alms. 333  
EPISTLE XXXIII.—To the abbot of St Bartholomew.—He gives a devout discourse on contempt for temporal things. 334  
EPISTLE XXXIV.—To the king of Hungary.—He testifies that a certain young Hungarian, now dead, lived piously at Paris. 334  
EPISTLE XXXV.—To L. and his wife.—He consoles parents distressed by the death of their son. 335  
EPISTLE XXXVI.—To the bishop of Porto.—He asks him to receive and see fulfilled the petitions of the dean and precentor of Chartres. 337  
EPISTLE XXXVII.—To the bishop of Palestrina.—He entrusts to his care the cause of the dean and precentor of Chartres. 337  
EPISTLE XXXVIII.—To Cardinal Gratian.—He asks that he not be compelled to receive a certain canon who had been expelled five times. 338  
EPISTLE XXXIX.—To William, archbishop of Rheims.—He deals with the celebrated dispute between the archbishop of Tours and the bishop of Dol, because the bishop of Dol presumed to enjoy the title and right of archbishop and metropolitan. 339  
EPISTLE XL.—To the supreme pontiff.—He asks that Bartholomew, archbishop of Tours, be excused because he was unable to go to Rome. 341  
EPISTLE XLI.—To Bartholomew, archbishop of Tours.—He excuses himself, on account of illness, from delivering sermons. 342  
EPISTLE XLII.—To the supreme pontiff.—He asks him to support the cause of the abbot of St Victor and to receive him graciously. 342  
EPISTLE XLIII.—To Peter, bishop of Tusculum.—He requests that he take the abbot of St Bartholomew of Noyon under his protection. 343  
EPISTLE XLIV.—To the archbishop of Toledo.—He deals with a certain man ordained simoniacally. 344  
EPISTLE XLV.—To the abbot of St Satyre.—He asks him to release a certain one of his canons who is bedridden. 344  
EPISTLE XLVI.—To Peter, cardinal-priest of St Chrysogonus.—He congratulates him on his promotion to the cardinalate. 345  
EPISTLE XLVII.—To Arald, abbot of St Benedict.—He commends to him a certain widow and her son. 346  
EPISTLE XLVIII.—To Pope Alexander III.—He informs him that he has carried out his command concerning a pension for a certain cleric. 346  
EPISTLE XLIX.—To the chancellor of the Roman Church.—He asks that his case be entrusted to impartial judges, with the clause “appeal removed” inserted. 347  
EPISTLE L.—To Albert, chancellor of the lord pope.—He assures him that, out of regard for him, he has paid a pension to a certain cleric. 347  
EPISTLE LI.—To Brother John of St Satyre.—He demands back money which he had lent him. 348  
EPISTLE LII.—To Godfrey, abbot of St Satyre.—He excuses himself for being unable to visit him. 348  
EPISTLE LIII.—To the same.—He gives thanks for benefits conferred on one of his canons. 349  
EPISTLE LIV.—To the lord pope.—He implores his protection for the church of Corbie. 349  
EPISTLE LV.—To the bishop of Senlis.—He supplies testimonial and dimissory letters for the ordination of one of his canons as priest. 350  
EPISTLE LVI.—To William, archbishop of Rheims.—He complains of the monks of Longpont, who were troublesome and hostile to him. 350  
EPISTLE LVII.—To Hugh, abbot of St Bartholomew of Noyon.—He excuses himself, because of his various occupations in administering justice, for not coming to him. 351  
EPISTLE LVIII.—To the lord pope, on behalf of the abbot of St Bartholomew of Noyon.—He testifies that the church of St Evurtius at Orléans is free from the bishop’s procuration. 351  
EPISTLE LIX.—To the same.—He bears the same witness for the same church of St Evurtius. 352  
EPISTLE LX.—To the archbishop of Rheims.—He commends the cause of a certain Simon, which was being heard in his court. 353  
EPISTLE LXI.—To the lord pope.—He complains of the rebellion of the canons of St John of Soissons who lived in parishes and refused obedience to Abbot Hugh. 354  
[Col. 1330] EPISTLE LXII.—To Lord Vivian, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church.—He pledges his service to him. 354  
EPISTLE LXIII.—To Heraclius, bishop of Caesarea.—He commends his kinsman, who was departing for Palestine. 355  
EPISTLE LXIV.—To the bishop of Lydda.—He likewise commends his kinsman, who was hastening to the Holy Sepulchre. 356  
EPISTLE LXV.—To John, notary of the pope.—He asks him to bring his petitions to effect. 356  
EPISTLE LXVI.—To Pope Alexander III.—He begs him to protect the canons of St Mary of Blois. 357  
EPISTLE LXVII.—To the same.—He again asks him to protect the rights of the regular canons of Blois, which secular canons were usurping. 358  
EPISTLE LXVIII.—To John, bishop of Poitiers.—He exhorts him to steadfastness in adversity. 359  
EPISTLE LXIX.—From Peter, apostolic legate, to R., dean of Rouen.—He warns that a priest should be removed from the nuns of St Cyricus because he conducted himself insufficiently chastely. 359  
EPISTLE LXX.—To William, archbishop of Sens.—He censures the same priest’s decidedly immodest life. 360  
EPISTLE LXXI.—To Robert, monk of Pontigny.—He raises and resolves the question whether novices of the Order of Grandmont may receive the Cistercian habit. 361  
EPISTLE LXXII.—To Peter, apostolic legate.—He deals with the same novices of Grandmont. 370  
EPISTLE LXXIII.—To Raymond, prior of St Geneviève.—He recounts various dangers that he underwent. 371  
EPISTLE LXXIV.—To the bishop and dean of Bayeux.—He deals with a certain affair of the archbishop of Tours with the bishop of Dol, mentioned above. 373  
EPISTLE LXXV.—To John, apostolic legate.—He congratulates him on his translation to the church of Narbonne. 373  
EPISTLE LXXVI.—To Godfrey, abbot of St Satyre.—He asks him to assist his friend. 374  
EPISTLE LXXVII.—To the brethren of St Evurtius at Orléans.—He demands the annual pension granted to him. 374  
EPISTLE LXXVIII.—To the abbot of Charroux.—He asks him for rams for his flock. 375  
EPISTLE LXXIX.—To A., archbishop of London.—He assures him that his nephew Peter has made canonical profession at St Geneviève. 376  
EPISTLE LXXX.—To the same.—He judges that his sick nephew Peter should be sent back to his native land, that he may recover better. 376  
EPISTLE LXXXI.—To a certain archbishop.—He pleads for a priest unjustly oppressed. 377  
EPISTLE LXXXII.—To Pope Lucius III.—He commends the chancellor of France against the objections of canons who alleged against him the defect of illegitimate birth. 378  
EPISTLE LXXXIII.—To the archbishop of Rheims.—He pleads for a priest from whom the bishop of Soissons had withheld part of a benefice. 379  
EPISTLE LXXXIV.—To Henry, king of the English.—He asks him to confirm and enforce the will of the supreme pontiff’s nephew, who was his cleric. 380  
EPISTLE LXXXV.—To William and Robert, notaries of the pope.—He deals with advancing his affairs in the Roman curia. 380  
EPISTLE LXXXVI.—To Pope Lucius III.—He asks him to preserve the ancient rights of the chaplain of St Benedict at Paris. 381  
EPISTLE LXXXVII.—To the abbot of St Bartholomew of Noyon.—He asks him to receive graciously a certain fugitive canon and to show him mercy. 382  
EPISTLE LXXXVIII.—To the prior and brethren of Charity.—He makes entreaties for a certain fugitive monk. 382  
EPISTLE LXXXIX.—To the lord pope.—He pleads for an acolyte ordained by a schismatic bishop. 383  
EPISTLE XC.—To Pope Lucius.—He asks that the cleric Hervé be enabled to enjoy a benefice. 384  
EPISTLE XCI.—To Henry, bishop of Senlis.—He declares himself ready to comply with his commands. 384  
EPISTLE XCII.—To William of Orléans, scribe of the lord pope.—He gives an account of what he did at Meung concerning the benefice conferred upon him by the pope. 385  
EPISTLE XCIII.—To the lord pope.—He asks him graciously to receive the messenger of the canons of Salicosa. 386  
EPISTLE XCIV.—To Henry, bishop of Senlis.—He pleads for his chaplain Hubert, asking that he deign to forgive his offence. 387  
EPISTLE XCV.—To the lord pope.—He asks him to suppress the disobedience of the canons of St John of Soissons living in parishes. 387  
[Col. 1331] EPISTLE XCVI.—To the lord pope.—He commends the abbot of St Satyre, extolling his life and virtues with praise. 388  
EPISTLE XCVII.—To the lord pope.—He commends the monks of Compiègne and asks him to protect them against their assailants. 389  
EPISTLE XCVIII.—To Godfrey, abbot of St Satyre.—He asks him graciously to receive a certain canon of St Geneviève who wished to live at St Satyre. 390  
EPISTLE XCIX.—To the master, archdeacon of Cambrai.—He reports that he has set out on a journey to meet his lord. 390  
EPISTLE C.—To Manasses, bishop of Orléans.—He exhorts him not to delay payment of a certain debt. 391  
EPISTLE CI.—From Philip, king of the French, to the supreme pontiff.—He asks him to place full trust in Stephen, whom he is sending to Rome on affairs which he has instructed him to conduct. 391  
EPISTLE CII.—From Stephen to Cardinal Octavian.—He recounts how the men of Apulia cleared themselves against the Roman scholars. 393  
EPISTLE CIII.—To Cardinal Albert, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church.—He reports how he reconciled certain people who were quarrelling with one another. 393  
EPISTLE CIV.—To Prior Raymond.—He informs him of the state of his health. 394  
EPISTLE CV.—To the archbishop of Rheims.—He asks on behalf of Master Hugh that he may obtain a benefice. 394  
EPISTLE CVI.—To Lord Albinus, cardinal-priest.—He sends him a new surplice and a long garment. 394  
EPISTLE CVII.—From Philip, king of the French, to Pope Lucius III.—He asks him to protect the cause of the archbishop of Tours against the bishop of Dol, who claimed the title of archbishop for himself. 395  
EPISTLE CVIII.—To the same, on behalf of King Philip.—He commends the same cause of the archbishop of Tours. 397  
EPISTLE CIX.—To Lord Octavian, on behalf of King Philip.—He complains that the Roman curia is insufficiently favourably disposed toward him. 398  
EPISTLE CX.—To Cardinal Master Melior, on behalf of the lord of Rheims.—He commends the same affair of the archbishop of Tours. 399  
EPISTLE CXI.—To the archbishop of London.—He sends him a flask of theriac. 400  
EPISTLE CXII.—To Raymond, prior of St Geneviève.—He asks him to excuse him before his fellow abbots because he cannot be present at the chapter. 401  
EPISTLE CXIII.—To L., cardinal of the Holy Roman Church.—He asks that a dispensation for receiving orders be granted to a certain judge of the count of Flanders. 402  
EPISTLE CXIV.—To the dean and chapter of Holy Cross at Orléans.—He exhorts them to show goodwill toward a certain cleric, on whose behalf the pope had written to them. 403  
EPISTLE CXV.—To Fulk, master of the schools of Holy Cross at Orléans.—He asks him to allow a certain cleric to lecture publicly in the school at Orléans. 404  
EPISTLE CXVI.—To William, archbishop of Rheims.—He implores his help for a certain peasant unjustly oppressed by the king’s officers. 404  
EPISTLE CXVII.—To the same.—He writes on behalf of a certain guest of St Geneviève, asking that he be freed from the exaction of the provost of Pontoise. 405  
EPISTLE CXVIII.—To R., bishop-elect of Chartres.—He commends to him his church and canons of Soisy, asking that they not be unjustly burdened by officials. 406  
EPISTLE CXIX.—To William, archbishop of Rheims.—He requests the transfer of a certain monk to another monastery. 407  
EPISTLE CXX.—To Hugh, abbot of St Vincent at Senlis.—He requests that he grant pardon to a certain canon returning to his monastery. 408  
EPISTLE CXXI.—To Urban, supreme pontiff.—He asks that he deign to receive and fulfil the petitions he makes on behalf of his church of St Geneviève. 409  
EPISTLE CXXII.—To Master Reginald, archpriest of the church of Orléans.—He asks him to see that an injury inflicted upon his brother is remedied by fitting satisfaction. 410  
EPISTLE CXXIII.—To Master Berter, archdeacon of Cambrai.—He asks him to petition his lord concerning a certain affair. 410  
EPISTLE CXXIV.—To Henry, bishop of Orléans, on behalf of the abbot of St Evurtius at Orléans.—He complains of a royal tax-collector by whom he was oppressed. 411  
[Col. 1332] EPISTLE CXXV.—To G., abbot of St Ambrose of Bourges.—He commends a certain canon residing with him at Paris. 411  
EPISTLE CXXVI.—To Roland of Dinan.—He exhorts him to complete the work he has begun. 412  
EPISTLE CXXVII.—To William, archbishop of Rheims.—He reports that the king has excused him from the journey to Rome. 413  
EPISTLE CXXVIII.—To Nivelon, bishop of Soissons.—He exhorts him to complete what he had begun in the church of St John. 413  
EPISTLE CXXIX.—To William, archbishop of Rheims.—He complains of the bishop of Senlis, who had struck his mayor of Borret with an anathema. 414  
EPISTLE CXXX.—To Nicholas, prior of St Bartholomew of Noyon.—He commends to him his nephew Peter. 414  
EPISTLE CXXXI.—To W.—He gives thanks for an elegant horse sent to him from Denmark. 415  
EPISTLE CXXXII.—To Albert, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church.—He commends to him the affairs of a noble cleric, being conducted in the Roman curia. 416  
EPISTLE CXXXIII.—To the abbot of St Denis.—He grants permission to a certain canon of St Geneviève to receive the habit of St Benedict. 416  
EPISTLE CXXXIV.—To the abbots of Cîteaux and Clairvaux.—He deals with the lay brothers of Grandmont rising up against the clerics. 417  
EPISTLE CXXXV.—To A., chancellor of the Holy Roman Church.—He asks him to show favour to the clerics of Grandmont against the lay brothers. 417  
EPISTLE CXXXVI.—To the archbishop of Lund.—He commends his nephew Peter, a canon of St Geneviève, asking him to ensure that he enjoys a benefice. 418  
EPISTLE CXXXVII.—To G., abbot of St Satyre.—He pleads for a certain fugitive, asking that he forgive him his fault. 419  
EPISTLE CXXXVIII.—To the abbot of Cîteaux, on behalf of the clerics of Grandmont.—They give thanks for benefits bestowed upon them. 419  
EPISTLE CXXXIX.—To Peter of Dacia.—He exhorts him to embrace ever more fully the higher things. 420  
EPISTLE CXL.—To the lord pope, on behalf of the queen of the French.—He asks him to postpone judgment in the affair of the archbishop of Tours and the bishop of Dol until the king’s return. 421  
EPISTLE CXLI.—To R., dean of Rheims.—He exhorts him not to allow the rule of common life, which had until then endured in the church of Rheims, to be driven out of it. 423  
EPISTLE CXLII.—To Godfrey, abbot of St Satyre.—He commends one of his canons. 427  
EPISTLE CXLIII.—From the abbots of St Denis, St Germain, St Victor, and St Geneviève to the pope.—They give an account of what they did and determined in the affair of the Grandmontines. 427  
EPISTLE CXLIV.—To the lord pope, on behalf of the clerics of Grandmont.—They complain of the attacks of their lay brothers. 430  
EPISTLE CXLV.—To Peter of Dacia.—He informs him of the goodwill of the brethren. 431  
EPISTLE CXLVI.—To the archbishop of Lund.—He congratulates himself on the promotion of his canon Peter to the episcopate. 432  
EPISTLE CXLVII.—To Valdemar, bishop of Schleswig.—He asks for lead for the repair and adornment of the church of St Geneviève. 434  
EPISTLE CXLVIII.—To William, abbot of the Paraclete.—He requests lead from him also. 435  
EPISTLE CXLIX.—To Omer, bishop of Ribe.—He commends his canon G., whom he sends to Denmark. 436  
EPISTLE CL.—To the archbishop of Lund.—Under the name of Solomon, he commends Peter, his nephew. 437  
EPISTLE CLI.—To a certain canon.—He grants one of his canons permission to enter another order and remain in it. 437  
EPISTLE CLII.—To Canute, king of Denmark.—He deals with a noble Danish youth who died and was buried at St Geneviève. 437  
EPISTLE CLIII.—To the same.—He also asks him for lead to roof the church of St Geneviève. 438  
EPISTLE CLIV.—To Nivelon, bishop of Soissons.—He pleads for his canons of La Ferté-Milon, asking that he arrange for them to be relieved of a certain burden. 440  
EPISTLE CLV.—To the pope.—He asks, on behalf of the church of St Victor, that he preserve for it the annual revenues of the church of Paris which had been granted to it. 441  
EPISTLE CLVI.—To the lord of Arras.—He commends and praises the abbot of Les Cernés, who had been rashly accused. 443  
EPISTLE CLVII.—To the archbishop of Lund.—He excuses himself for not having handed over money entrusted to him. 444  
EPISTLE CLVIII.—To the chapter of Laon.—He asks the canons willingly to release their dean Michael, elected dean of Paris. 444  
EPISTLE CLIX.—To W. of Bieria.—He neither advises nor dissuades the eremitical life which he had embraced, but gives certain counsels for living it rightly. 445  
EPISTLE CLX.—To the lord pope.—He pleads for a cleric unjustly accused. 449  
EPISTLE CLXI.—To a certain prelate.—He gives thanks for gold and gems bestowed to adorn the tomb or shrine of Blessed Geneviève. 450  
EPISTLE CLXII.—To the pope.—He deals with the canons of St John of Soissons living in parishes, who refused obedience to the abbot. 451  
EPISTLE CLXIII.—To the abbot of Ourscamp.—He asks him to confirm in his resolution the treasurer of Noyon, who had embraced the monastic life. 452  
EPISTLE CLXIV.—To the abbot of Clairvaux.—He clears himself of the stain of simony, a charge of which detractors had rashly accused him before the abbot. 453  
EPISTLE CLXV.—To the abbot of Cîteaux.—He commends the abbot of Les Cernés and asks that he not compel him to make restitution. 454  
EPISTLE CLXVI.—To William, archbishop of Rheims.—He asks him graciously to receive and protect the abbot of St Vincent at Senlis. 454  
EPISTLE CLXVII.—To Cardinal Sofredus.—He asks him to show his goodwill toward the archbishop of Rheims, of whose friendship he assures him. 455  
EPISTLE CLXVIII.—To William, archbishop of Rheims.—He asks him to protect the abbot of St Germain-des-Prés, unjustly oppressed. 456  
EPISTLE CLXIX.—To the same.—He complains of the count of Dammartin, hostile to him. 457  
EPISTLE CLXX.—To certain judges.—He deals with a case pending between the archbishop of Sens and the church of St Germain-des-Prés. 458  
EPISTLE CLXXI.—To the abbot of St Bartholomew.—He advises him to resign his administration. 459  
EPISTLE CLXXII.—To D., archbishop of Rheims.—He asks the same thing. 460  
EPISTLE CLXXIII.—To the convent of St Bartholomew of Noyon.—He admonishes them to show honour to the abbot even if he has resigned the abbey. 460  
EPISTLE CLXXIV.—To William, archbishop of Rheims.—He deals with the resignation of the abbot of St Bartholomew of Noyon. 461  
EPISTLE CLXXV.—To the same.—He writes on behalf of Peter, cantor of Paris, elected bishop of Tournai, asking him to support his election as lawful and canonical. 462  

## PART THREE (1192–1203)

EPISTLE CLXXVI.—To the abbot of Hautvillers.—He informs him that his nephew John has been elected abbot of St Geneviève. 463  
EPISTLE CLXXVII.—To the archbishop of Tours.—He informs him that he has been promoted to the bishopric of Tournai. 465  
EPISTLE CLXXVIII.—To the same.—He gives thanks for gifts sent to him. 466  
EPISTLE CLXXIX.—To Celestine, supreme pontiff.—He deals with his promotion to the church of Tournai, which the supreme pontiff had not welcomed. 466  
EPISTLE CLXXX.—To the archbishop of Rheims.—He inveighs against certain preachers who adulterate the word of God and lead lives infected by vices. 467  
EPISTLE CLXXXI.—To Lambin of Bruges.—He asks him to prepare lodging for him at Amiens on the day of the queen’s coronation. 467  
EPISTLE CLXXXII.—To the pope.—He writes on behalf of Hugh Clement, elected dean of Paris. 468  
EPISTLE CLXXXIII.—To the bishops of Arras and Amiens.—He asks them to support the case between himself and the abbot of St Bertin. 469  
EPISTLE CLXXXIV.—To Lambin, bishop of Thérouanne.—He complains of the monks of St Bertin. 470  
EPISTLE CLXXXV.—To Octavius, bishop of Ostia.—He excuses the abbot of St Germain-des-Prés from the killing of a certain scholar. 471  
EPISTLE CLXXXVI.—To Fulk, abbot of St Germain-des-Prés.—He gives thanks for a benefice bestowed upon his brother. [Col. 1334]  
EPISTLE CLXXXVII.—To the same.—He asks him to allow his brother peaceably to enjoy the benefice conferred upon him. 472  
EPISTLE CLXXXVIII.—To the bishop of Soissons.—He requests permission to administer the sacrament of confirmation at Marizy. 473  
EPISTLE CLXXXIX.—From N., bishop of Soissons, to the bishop of Tournai.—He most willingly grants the requested permission. 473  
EPISTLE CXC.—To Master Berter, archdeacon of Cambrai.—He complains of the burden he was unjustly suffering because of debts. 474  
EPISTLE CXCI.—To the abbot of St Evurtius at Orléans.—He commends his nephew William, asking him to show him kindness. 475  
EPISTLE CXCII.—To the same.—He writes again on behalf of the same William. 475  
EPISTLE CXCIII.—To the same.—For the third time he asks him graciously to receive his nephew William. 476  
EPISTLE CXCIV.—To the pope.—He asks him to restrict the apostolic mandate concerning all ordained persons to specified orders. 476  
EPISTLE CXCV.—To the lord of Rheims.—He asks that, by his authority, a canon of St Geneviève be received by the chapter of Tournai to administer a benefice. 478  
EPISTLE CXCVI.—To William, archbishop of Rheims.—He gives thanks for letters written to the chapter of Tournai. 479  
EPISTLE CXCVII.—To the pope.—He deals with a fugitive monk of St Martin of Tournai. 479  
EPISTLE CXCVIII.—To the pope.—He writes concerning the same fugitive monk, asking that he not allow himself to be deceived by him. 480  
EPISTLE CXCIX.—To the abbot and convent of St Geneviève at Paris.—He instructs them what must be done in the matter between them and the archdeacon of Paris concerning the chaplain of the parish of St Geneviève in the city. 481  
EPISTLE CC.—To the archbishop of Rheims.—He asks that the church of Bredenai be restored to the monks, so that they may perform the divine office there. 482  
EPISTLE CCI.—To the same.—He writes that, by his command, he will confer a prebend in the church of Tournai upon a certain cleric. 482  
EPISTLE CCII.—To a certain abbot.—He answers a question concerning the marriage of a certain novice who, having abandoned the habit, contracted it; he judges it valid. 483  
EPISTLE CCIII.—To Pope Celestine.—He commends G., elected abbot of Corbie, and extols his prudence and piety. 483  
EPISTLE CCIV.—To Berter, abbot of St Evurtius at Orléans.—He consoles him, burdened by illness. 484  
EPISTLE CCV.—To John, abbot, and the chapter of St Geneviève at Paris.—He exhorts the canons of St Geneviève to show themselves perfect in all things. 484  
EPISTLE CCVI.—To the abbot of St Bertin.—He asks him for a horse suitable for his use. 485  
EPISTLE CCVII.—To the archbishop of Rheims.—He deals with disputes between the monks of St Amand and their abbot, whom he commends. 485  
EPISTLE CCVIII.—To Master Berter, archdeacon of Cambrai.—He rebukes him for rashly injuring his reputation and recounts the course of his life. 486  
EPISTLE CCIX.—To Hugh, dean, and Peter, cantor, of Paris.—He asks them to defend the cause of his friend. 487  
EPISTLE CCX.—To the lord of Rheims.—He seeks his favour for the dean of Tournai. 488  
EPISTLE CCXI.—To John, abbot of St Geneviève.—He invites him to be present at the dedication of the chapel he had built. 488  
EPISTLE CCXII.—To the bishop of Thérouanne.—He likewise invites him to deign to attend the dedication of his chapel. 489  
EPISTLE CCXIII.—To John, abbot of St Geneviève.—He excuses himself for being unable, because of business, to attend the solemnity of this dedication. 490  
EPISTLE CCXIV.—To William, archbishop of Rheims.—He gives an account of certain forgers who were falsifying bulls. 490  
EPISTLE CCXV.—To the abbot of Laude.—He asks him to show kindness to a certain Brother William who had sinned. 491  
EPISTLE CCXVI.—To the bishop of Lisieux.—He exhorts his friend to provide for his own salvation and that of his subjects. 491  
EPISTLE CCXVII.—To the abbot and chapter of Cîteaux.—He deals with a certain cleric, whom he clears of the charge of usury. 492  
[Col. 1335] EPISTLE CCXVIII.—To Odo, bishop of Paris.—On behalf of Th., archdeacon of Tournai. 492  
EPISTLE CCXIX.—To Everard, abbot, and the convent of St Bavo.—He commends a certain craftsman whose son was seeking the monastic habit. 493  
EPISTLE CCXX.—To Peter, bishop of Orléans.—He complains of the monks of St Bertin, who had chosen him as arbitrator. 494  
EPISTLE CCXXI.—To Arnulf, dean of Bruges.—He asks him to arrange for herring to be prepared for him. 494  
EPISTLE CCXXII.—To the same.—He asks that fish and certain ecclesiastical offices be sent. 495  
EPISTLE CCXXIII.—To Hugh, abbot of St Denis.—He asks him not to delay paying a pension to his brother. 495  
EPISTLE CCXXIV.—How Lord Stephen, bishop of Tournai, having with him the abbots of St Amand and St Callixtus, came in the presence of Lord Peter, bishop of Arras, to the church of St Martin of Tournai, in order to reform for the better the peace and condition of that monastery, and to rebuke and correct the abbot of the monastery concerning his offences. Also, how the same abbot swore that he would observe the matters set before him by the bishop. 495  
EPISTLE CCXXV.—To the archbishop of Rheims.—He complains of the improper administration of that same abbot. 498  
EPISTLE CCXXVI.—He complains again of the same abbot. 498  
EPISTLE CCXXVII.—To Louis, son of King Philip Augustus.—He exhorts him to devote himself seriously to his early studies and promises to send the horse that he had requested. 499  
EPISTLE CCXXVIII.—To Lambin, apparently bishop of Thérouanne.—Concerning a certain Hugh who was said to have risen from the dead. 499  
EPISTLE CCXXIX.—To a certain prelate of the Roman Church.—He petitions for the renewal of a certain privilege. 500  
EPISTLE CCXXX.—To a certain friend.—He sends small gifts, which he explains in a moral sense. 500  
EPISTLE CCXXXI.—To the lord of Rheims.—He deals with the interdict imposed in the territory of the count of Flanders. 501  
EPISTLE CCXXXII.—He treats the same interdict. 502  
EPISTLE CCXXXIII.—To William, archbishop of Rheims.—He writes of the same interdict and implores his assistance. 502  
EPISTLE CCXXXIV.—He deals with the fortification of the city of Tournai and with the truce or armistice granted. 503  
EPISTLE CCXXXV.—He laments the miserable effects of the same interdict. 504  
EPISTLE CCXXXVI.—Letter of John, bishop of Cambrai, addressed to the lord of Tournai in response to the preceding letters sent by that bishop of Tournai to the lord of Rheims. 504  
EPISTLE CCXXXVII.—Reply of the lord bishop of Tournai to the preceding letters sent to him above by Lord John, bishop of Cambrai. 505  
EPISTLE CCXXXVIII.—To the dean and canons of Bruges.—He deals with a doubled rent and explains in what sense it should be understood. 508  
EPISTLE CCXXXIX.—To the lord archbishop of Rheims.—He complains that the king is summoning him to arms. 508  
EPISTLE CCXL.—He answers an obscure and intricate question put to him, in which various matters pertaining to law are explained. 509  
EPISTLE CCXLI.—To Master Berter, archdeacon of Cambrai.—He praises a young man whom he commends to him. 511  
EPISTLE CCXLII.—To the pope.—He asks him not to protect his adversary, who is attacking his rights. 511  
EPISTLE CCXLIII.—To the archbishop of Rheims.—He implores his assistance against the citizens of Tournai, hostile to him. 512  
EPISTLE CCXLIV.—He deals with the same controversy involving the citizens of Tournai. 512  
EPISTLE CCXLV.—He writes concerning the same affair and dispute. 513  
EPISTLE CCXLVI.—He describes the hostile attitude of the citizens of Tournai toward him. 513  
EPISTLE CCXLVII.—He gives thanks concerning the dean of Tournai, to whom service had been rendered. 514  
EPISTLE CCXLVIII.—To the abbot of St Amand.—He rebukes him because he had had monks promoted to sacred orders by another bishop. 514  
EPISTLE CCXLIX.—To the bishop of Arras.—He complains that he had conferred sacred orders upon the monks of St Amand without his permission. 515  
[Col. 1336] EPISTLE CCL.—To the abbot of St Geneviève at Paris.—He instructs him concerning what he must do to obtain peace. 516  
EPISTLE CCLI.—To the pope.—He censures the excessive multitude of decretals and the professors who abused them. 516  
EPISTLE CCLII.—To a certain prelate.—He asks him to obtain from the king a dispensation so that he may not be compelled to attend court. 518  
EPISTLE CCLIII.—To a certain dean.—He asks him to grant pardon to his nephew Peter. 518  
EPISTLE CCLIV.—He makes entreaties for the same nephew. 519  
EPISTLE CCLV.—He judges that subjects who appeal improperly, in order to escape the correction of regular prelates, ought not to be heard. 519  
EPISTLE CCLVI.—To the bishop of Cambrai.—He consoles him in illness. 520  
EPISTLE CCLVII.—To a certain prelate of the Roman Church.—He asks him to prevent a certain cleric from obtaining a prebend in his church. 521  
EPISTLE CCLVIII.—To the dean of Kortrijk.—He complains of a certain person who had disregarded his command. 521  
EPISTLE CCLIX.—To the bishop of Arras.—He deals with his own condition and that of the city. 522  
EPISTLE CCLX.—To Robert, abbot of St Victor at Paris.—He sends the epitaph of Maurice, bishop of Paris, which he had composed at the request of those who asked for it. 522  
EPISTLE CCLXI.—To Hugh, canon of St Geneviève at Paris.—He attempts to lighten the grief caused by the death of his nephew. 523  
EPISTLE CCLXII.—To William, archbishop of Rheims.—He writes on behalf of Queen Ingeborg, for whose benefit he implores his help and assistance. 523  
EPISTLE CCLXIII.—To the same, on behalf of the same queen.—He asks that he not permit the dissolution of her marriage, nor compel her to enter another marriage or to fall into another’s hands. 525  
EPISTLE CCLXIV.—To Lord Sofredus, cardinal of the Holy Roman See. 526  
EPISTLE CCLXIV (bis).—To John, son of the chancellor of the noble city. 526  
EPISTLE CCLXV.—To a certain regular prelate.—He warns him diligently to examine and correct faults discovered during the course of his visitation. 526  
EPISTLE CCLXVI.—To his friend.—He warns him to beware lest he suffer any loss from his nephews. 527  
EPISTLE CCLXVII.—To the bishop-elect of Orléans.—He congratulates him on his election. 527

EPISTLE CCLXXIII.—To the same.—He writes concerning a lawsuit between two canons of Seclin. 531

EPISTLE CCLXXX.—To Hugh, bishop, and the chapter of Orléans.—He asks them to correct certain abuses which had arisen in the church of St Evurtius. 537

EPISTLE CCLXXXII.—To Hugh, bishop of Orléans.—He testifies that the church of St Evurtius is not bound to furnish procuration to the bishop of Orléans. 539  
EPISTLE CCLXXXIII.—To Pope Clement III.—He gives the supreme pontiff an account of what he did against the bishop of Troyes, by authority of the apostolic mandate entrusted to him, Dean Berner, and Peter the cantor of Paris. 540  
EPISTLE CCLXXXIV.—He pleads for a certain cleric who had committed a serious offence. 541

## Letters of Guibert

Letter I.—To Philip, archbishop of Cologne.—He describes the conduct of wicked pastors, whom he exhorts Philip to avoid. 1288

Letter IV.—To the same.—He excuses himself for not having come to him. 1290
